title: Chemostratigraphy and U-Pb geochronology of the Late Cretaceous on James Ross Island, Antarctica
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: Biebesheimer, Ellie [1], Suarez, Marina B. [2], Möller, Andreas [3], Atkinson, Brian [4], Smith, Selena Y. [5], Roberts, Eric [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(3) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(4) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, ; KU Biodiversity Institute and Natural History Museum, Lawrence, KS,
(5) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI,
(6) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
abstract:
James Ross Island (Antarctic Peninsula) is an important high-latitude location for understanding climatic and ecologic changes through the Late Cretaceous as it has one of the most continuous sequences of Cretaceous strata in the Southern Hemisphere. Global temperatures declined in the Late Cretaceous, while angiosperms (flowering plants) evolved and diversified to become dominant components of terrestrial ecosystems. The Santa Marta (SMF) and Snow Hill Island (SIF) Formations contain abundant mixed terrestrial and marine fossils that document these changes in the Southern Hemisphere, an area traditionally lacking in data. NSF-sponsored paleontological expedition (G-074-E) recovered a wealth of fossils including many new species of plants, which will illuminate the diversity and ecology of these ancient polar forests. To put these findings into a global context, we aim to better constrain the strata from three field localities (Sitio Feliz, Ugly Creek, and 14S) using integrated U-Pb geochronology of carbonates and C-isotope chemostratigraphy.

The three sections are currently assigned to the Campanian Stage based on bio- and magnetostratigraphy. Stratigraphically, the lower-most section is Sitio Feliz (Beta Member of the SMF), followed by Ugly Creek, and 14S (Gamma Member (SIF). To more precisely constrain each section, 198 samples were analyzed for d 13 C org (‰ VPDB). Carbon isotope values range from -28.85‰ to -24.78‰, and average -26.10‰. These represent some of the first chemostratigraphic data from James Ross Island. A positive excursion in the Sitio Feliz profile is tentatively correlated to the Mid-Campanian Event, while a pronounced negative isotope excursion in the Ugly Creek section is preliminarily correlated to the Late Campanian Event. A minimum depositional age of 72.2 +/- 2.7Ma was obtained from U-Pb analyses of calcite infill (diagenetic) in vertebrate bone material from the Sitio Feliz section and is consistent with these interpretations. Additional U-Pb analysis of calcite cements from Ugly Creek and 14S along with zircon geochronology and Sr chemostratigraphy will test these interpretations.

title: An Approach To Mantle Heterogeneity Through Multiple Machine Learning Methods
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Burges, Jarrod M. [1], Goltz, Andrea [2], Codillo, Emmanuel [3], Morrison, Shaunna M. [4], Prabhu, Anirudh [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, New Jersey, USA

abstract: Mid-ocean ridge basalts and ocean island basalts record the isotopic variability present in the mantle. Machine learning (ML) algorithms provide new opportunities to analyze geochemical data through similarity algorithms. We report a multi-method machine learning study that employed three dimension reduction. The dimension reduction algorithms employed are: Principal component analysis (PCA), t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). Through these three dimension reduction algorithms we provide a well-rounded approach to dimensionality reduction that does not bias a single method or approach. As each method is a singular “view” of the multidimensional (5D) Sr-Nd-Pb isotope mantle tetrahedron, we show that careful analysis of ML dimension reduced latent representations creates geologically significant and interpretable results. These results enable a holistic comparative analysis of global mantle heterogeneity observed in MORBs and OIBs. We finally compare recent studies applying machine learning methods to mantle heterogeneity. We demonstrate that varied input data (Sr-Nd-Pb±Hf±TE±MORB) and methods (PCA, PCA+t-SNE, T-SNE, UMAP) have little impact on resulting latent space representations, which allows the comparison of data structures across studies. We note that these data structures span individual hot spots to global similarities. For example, the Mauna Kea and Loa trends, extreme HIMU-like samples, depleted mantle variation, DUPAL flavored Indian MORB samples and OIBs (e.g., Caroline Islands), and single OIB heterogeneity (e.g., Cape Verde Islands, Azores, Galapagos, Iceland) are common across studies. This analysis and similarity across studies opens opportunities for greater comparative analysis of individual samples, while comparing against observed global variability with greater ease.

title: Urban Geochemistry and Health Risks of Potentially Toxic Elements in Sediments from the Lower Passaic River Superfund Site, New York–New Jersey Harbor
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: ISLAM, Md Shahnul [1], ASEPERI, John [2], FENG, Huan [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Studies, Montclair State University, Montclair, NJ, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Studies, Montclair State University, Montclair, NJ, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Studies, Montclair State University, Montclair, NJ, USA
abstract: The Lower Passaic River (LPR), a highly urbanized and industrialized tributary within the New York–New Jersey Harbor estuary, has experienced decades of contamination from municipal, industrial, and transportation-related activities. This study evaluates the distribution, source apportionment, and ecological and human health risks of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in sediments collected from the lower 8.3 miles of the LPR Superfund site. Sediment analyses revealed elevated concentrations of As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Mn, Pb, and Zn, with spatial trends indicating downstream enrichment associated with urban-industrial influences. Contamination indices, including contamination factor ( CF ), geoaccumulation index ( I geo ), enrichment factor ( EF ), pollution load index ( PLI) , and potential ecological risk index ( PERI ), classified the sediments as heavily to severely contaminated, with Cd and Pb contributing most strongly to ecological risk. The mean PERI value of 2270 substantially exceeded the threshold for serious ecological risk. Sediment quality guideline metrics ( mERMQ , TRI , and mHQ ) further indicated a moderate to high potential for toxicity to benthic ecosystems. Probabilistic human health risk assessment for dredging workers showed negligible non-carcinogenic risks ( HI < 1), whereas the mean total carcinogenic risk (1.81 × 10⁻⁶) remained within acceptable regulatory limits, with Cr representing the dominant carcinogenic contributor. Monte Carlo simulation and sensitivity analysis identified exposure frequency ( ExF ), exposure duration ( ED ), adherence factor ( AF ), skin surface area ( SA ), and sediment contaminant concentration ( C s ) as the principal positive drivers of carcinogenic risk, while body weight ( BW ) and averaging time ( AT ) exerted inverse effects. Principal component analysis (PCA) resolved three major source-related components corresponding to geogenic background inputs, legacy industrial contamination, and localized urban traffic-related emissions. The results highlight the strong influence of urbanization and industrial history on sediment geochemistry in the LPR and underscore the importance of continued remediation and sediment management efforts to reduce ecological degradation and protect human health in urban estuarine environments.

title: Caracterización de la mineralización en el área de Santa María - Proyecto Arenizo, Ayacucho - Perú
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part I)
authors: FLORES, LEONID ESPINAL [1]
affiliations: (1) GEOLOGIA, UNIVERSIDAD NACIONAL DE INGENIERIA, Lima, San Juan de Lurigancho, Peru
abstract: El área de Santa María del Proyecto Arenizo se encuentra entre el distrito de Pullo, Provincia de Parinacochas, Región Ayacucho y en el Distrito de Quicacha, Provincia de Caraveli, Región Arequipa, en el flanco occidental del sinclinorio de Parinacochas a 3600 msnm en el cuadrángulo de Coracora, hoja 31-O de la Carta Nacional del Perú. Litológicamente está conformado por cuaternario de depósitos aluviales, los volcánicos del Huaylillas del Terciario Superior constituido de tobas de cristales y de lapilli, la Formación Huanca constituida por depósitos molásicos de color rojo, la Formación Arcurquina del Cretácico Superior constituida por el miembro Aguas Verdes de calizas carbonosas y el miembro Arenizo de calizas blanquecinas. Las rocas ígneas plutónicas son del Batolito de la Costa del Cretácico Superior-Inferior, la Superunidad del Tiabaya con tonalita-granodiorita y diorita no diferenciada. Hay eventos magmáticos jóvenes del paleógeno que no pertenecen al Batolito de la Costa formados por diorita horbléndica y pórfido dacítico. Hay fallas regionales de rumbo E-W, NW y NE, la falla regional Arenizo es la que más afecta a los eventos de actividad magmática de las rocas intrusivas. A nivel local la falla Arenizo tiene rumbo promedio N15°W y presenta fallas transversales a la mineralización en el área del proyecto. Las alteraciones hidrotermales presentes son alteración fílica (cuarzo-sericita-pirita), alteración argílica (arcillas), alteración propilítica (clorita-epidota-calcita) y la silicifación (SiO2). En el metamorfismo de contacto se tiene presencia de skarn y mármol. La mineralización económica importante se observa en los afloramientos de las Vetas Anita, María y en las venillas tipo stock work. Se ha identificado óxidos de hierro, sulfatos (jarosita, baritina), hospedados en el pórfido dacítico y la diorita horbléndica. La mineralización del yacimiento es epigenética, la dispersión de los elementos es primaria, se reportan anomalías geoquímicas significativas de importancia económica en Au, Ag y Cu.

title: U–Pb Zircon and Apatite Constraints on Silurian–Devonian Arc Magmatism in the Ekibastuz Region, Central Asian Orogenic Belt, Kazakhstan
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics
authors: Regmi, Kamal Raj [1], Teklay, Mengist [2], Cottle, John M [3], Imayama, Takeshi [4]
affiliations: (1) Nazarbayev University Research Administration Private Institution, Nura District, 53 Kabanbay Batyr Ave., Astana, Kazakhstan, BIN: 101240004319, Nazarbayev University Research Administration Private Institution, Nura District, 53 Kabanbay Batyr Ave. BIN: 101240004319, Astana (Nur-Sultan), Akmolinskaya obl., Kazakhstan
(2) Life and Earth Science Department, Perimeter College, Georgia State University, Decatur, GA 30034, Atlanta, USA, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
(3) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106, USA., Santa Barbara, California, USA
(4) Research Institute of Frontier Science and Technology, Okayama University of Sciences, Okayama, Japan, Okayama, Japan
abstract:
The Ekibastuz region of northeastern Kazakhstan forms part of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB) and is dominated by volcanic rocks with subordinate sedimentary and intrusive units belonging to the Precambrian–Devonian Bozshakol–Chingiz arc system. This study presents the first U–Pb geochronological constraints and in situ trace‑element data for zircon and apatite from two rhyolite samples (EK074/25 and EK084/25) and one diorite sample from the region.

Zircons from the rhyolites yield concordant U–Pb crystallization ages of 405 Ma (EK074/25) and 424 Ma (EK084/25), whereas apatite from the diorite defines a U–Pb discordia lower‑intercept age of ~420 Ma, interpreted as a cooling age following magma emplacement. Together, these ages document Silurian–Early Devonian arc magmatism in the Ekibastuz region. A subset of zircon analyses from EK084/25 yields older ages of 500–512 Ma, interpreted as inherited zircons derived from Cambrian basement rocks of the CAOB or assimilated country rocks.

Zircons from EK084/25 are characterized by lower total rare earth element (REE) contents compared to those from EK074/25, likely reflecting co‑crystallization with REE‑bearing accessory minerals such as apatite, monazite, and titanite. Titanium‑in‑zircon and Ce‑based oxybarometry indicate contrasting redox conditions during zircon crystallization: EK074/25 records strongly oxidized conditions (average ΔFMQ ≈ +2.5), consistent with subduction‑related arc magmatism, whereas EK084/25 records conditions close to the fayalite–magnetite–quartz buffer (average ΔFMQ ≈ +0.9). In both rhyolites, ΔFMQ estimates show an inverse relationship with zircon Ce anomalies, suggesting decoupling of Ce behavior from redox conditions due to evolving melt composition and competition with other REE‑hosting phases.

Apatite from the diorite exhibits relatively flat chondrite‑normalized LREE patterns ((Ce/Sm)ₙ ≈ 1.1–1.6), moderate negative Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu* ≈ 0.6–1.1), and depleted HREE ((Eu/Yb)ₙ ≈ 0.6–2.4), consistent with crystallization from an evolved, fractionated melt under plagioclase‑stable conditions. These new zircon and apatite data provide robust constraints on the timing, redox state, and magmatic evolution of Paleozoic arc magmatism in the Ekibastuz region and contribute to improved understanding of crustal growth processes within the CAOB.

Keywords:

Geology of Ekibastuz (NE Kazakhstan); U-Pb zircon and apatite ages; Ti-in zircon thermometry; Redox arc CAOB magmatism

title: Deformation Kinematics of Peak-Ring Formation: Unique Evidence from Brittle Fault Analysis of the Chicxulub IODP-ICDP Expedition 364 Drill Core
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Bahr, Louisa [1], Riller, Ulrich [2], IOPD-ICDP 364 Scientists, [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth System Sciences, University of Hamburg, Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany
(2) Department of Earth System Sciences, University of Hamburg, Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany
abstract: The formation of peak rings in large meteorite impact craters is not well understood. The IODP-ICDP Expedition 364 drill core revealed that shocked target rock of the peak ring of the Chicxulub impact crater is pervasively affected by decimeter-scale brittle shear faults, apparently formed toward the end of peak ring formation. Shear faults lend themselves excellently to infer the deformation kinematics under which they formed. Hence, the orientations and slip senses of 602 shear faults extracted from the drill core were kinematically analyzed to better understand peak ring formation, a novel approach in impact cratering studies. Specifically, the inversion of the fault slip data allowed us to determine the orientations of principal kinematic axes and their variation with depth. The results revealed that overall, the peak ring formed by horizontal shortening and vertical extension. However, horizontal concentric extension prevails at greater depths within the drill core. Collectively, the deformation kinematics are consistent with rock flow during peak ring formation characterized by simultaneous rollback of the crater margin and outward displacement of collapsed central peak material. Not only do these results refine current numerical models of peak ring crater formation, they also support gravity-controlled cratering of the dynamic collapse model.

title: The unbearable lightness of northward shifting of monsoonal precipitation in North Africa during the early-middle Holocene: A new perspective on the “Green Sahara” hypothesis
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Enzel, Yehouda [1], Armon, Moshe [2], Ben Dor, Yoav [3], Dente, Elad [4], Adam, Ori [5], Zerboni, Andrea [6], Quade, Jay [7]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Earth Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel

abstract: Lacustrine, marsh, spring, fluvial, archeological, and botanical evidence have been interpreted to indicate a substantial northward early-to-middle Holocene (11-5 ka) ITCZ and associated rain-belt shift into the heart of the Sahara and even farther north. This shift is attributed to increased boreal summer insolation shifting north the thermal equator and pushing African summer monsoon northward. This substantial shift is not predicted by GCMs for that interval; GCMs indicate only minimal rain-belt northward shift, of <<5 o (<<500 km) reaching at most ~21 o N. A shift of monsoonal precipitation that is able to cover the entire Sahara results only from models initialized (i.e., prescribed/enforced) with presumed conditions favoring a-priori increased rainfall, including: pre-allocation of substantial lake areas (facilitating northward moisture recycling), vegetation and soil moisture (reducing albedo), and reduced dust sources (impacting rainfall). The difficulty of producing large shifts with insolation-based energy indicates major data–modeling discrepancy may reflect over-interpretation of geological evidence, rather than a modeling mismatch. Therefore, re-examinations of data collected from multiple sites, underlying this comparison, is warranted. We reassess evidence to test whether indicators of increased precipitation are independently supported and rooted in space and time, or whether local observations have been interpreted circularly based on prior claims of a wetter Sahara in the literature. Indeed, we concluded that field data do support North African monsoonal rain belt shift, but only slightly and to ~20-21 o N, in agreement with GCMs. Farther north, the data are insufficiently robust and/or guided by prevailing assumptions. These assumptions are based on a limited availability of ages, weak stratigraphy, lack of lake shorelines features/deposits, distant pollen transported further, and weak correlations with previous studies (exceptions are at the westernmost Sahara, with an additional 1 o –2 o shift). Thus, we suggest that GCMs analyses for this region provide plausible representations for the extent and magnitude of climatic change of the wetter Holocene interval in the Sahara, particularly outside the influence of major high mountain acting as rain towers, hydrologically affecting their respective nearby areas, generating proxy-records that were expanded for the entire Sahara.

title: Strain rate variation or transitions in slip systems? Contextualizing flow stress and fabric variability across the Cordillera Blanca Shear Zone

abstract: Paleopiezometry provides a rare avenue to quantify flow stresses in the middle crust. Contextualizing the results of recrystallized grain size piezometry in temperature-differential stress space is challenging and requires assumptions surrounding pore fluid pressures, strain rate, water fugacity, and fault dip. Existing interpretations of deformation conditions within the footwall shear zone of the Miocene-modern Cordillera Blanca Detachment evoke variability in strain rate during deformation of an immediately sub-solidus batholith. However, recent work on deformation of wet quartz indicates that there is a transition from prism <a> to basal <a>-dominate slip that is facilitated by dislocation-accommodated grain boundary sliding. The transition from prism <a> to basal <a> slip is accompanied by a transition in stress exponent from n = 4 to n =2.7. High-resolution electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) mapping, contextualized by detailed microstructural observations, constraints on deformation temperature, and d 2 H values of micas from 28 samples of quartzofeldspathic mylonites from 9 vertical transects through the Cordillera Blanca Detachment support a transition from prism <a> to basal <a>-dominate slip in quartz that correlates with temperature, flow stress, and deformation in the presence of meteoric water. Based on these relationships, it is probable that the strength of this structure is controlled by transitions in quartz slip systems and a variable stress exponent, however, strain rate variability cannot be fully excluded as a rheologic control on the exhuming shear zone.

title: The Totschunda-Denali intersection of Alaska: A low-angle (<25◦) strike-slip fault intersection since at least ~25 Ma
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Benowitz, Jeffrey [1], Rosenthal, Jacob [2], Fitzgerald, Paul G. [3], Perez Consuegra, Nicolas [4], O'Sullivan, Dr. Paul [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado Boulder, BOULDER, Colorado, USA
(2) Trilogy, Ambler, Alaska, USA
(3) Syracuse University, Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY, USA
(4) Weber State University, Weber State University, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
(5) GeoSep Services, Moscow, Idaho, USA
abstract: Fault intersections are ubiquitous to strike-slip fault systems and can enable significant displacement when slip is transferred between splays over time during earthquake events. If and how these strike-slip fault intersections endure and evolve is an ongoing question in tectonics. The Cretaceous-aged and dextrally active subvertically dipping Totschunda and Denali faults of Alaska currently intersect at a low angle ( < 25◦) and communicate slip as these faults transfer strain inboard from Alaska’s southern convergent margin. However, when the Totschunda-Denali low-angle fault intersection formed, and how this junction has responded to far-field stress changes, is unconstrained. We apply geochronology (zircon U–Pb) and low-temperature thermochronology (zircon and apatite [U–Th]/He and apatite fission-track) with inverse thermal modeling to constrain the spatial-temporal cooling history of palinspastic restored crustal blocks proximal to the Totschunda-Denali fault intersection through time. The block bounded within the apex of the Totschunda and Denali fault intersection (DENT block) began to rapidly cool ( > 30 ◦C/Ma) by ~25 Ma. The DENT block’s late Oligocene-early Miocene cooling rate surpasses magnitudes in the palinspasticly restored surrounding blocks ( > 10 ◦C/Ma vs ≤ ~2 ◦C/Ma). We link the onset of ~25 Ma DENT block rapid cooling with the probable existence of the fault intersection by this time, as both strands of the fault intersection had to be active and connected to accommodate vertical block extrusion and exhumation. Subsequently, late Miocene-Quaternary rapid cooling ( > 6 ◦C/Ma) along the Totschunda fault occurs when this fault becomes the principal slip strand, which is linked to a change in the Pacific-Yakutat plate vector. The vertical extrusion of the DENT block and the switch to increased slip along the Totschunda fault post ~6 Ma has enabled long-lived (≥25 Ma) geometric stability of this intersection, even during changes in relative convergence, by limiting fault system reorganization. Globally, low-angle ( < 25◦) strike-slip fault intersections are mechanically efficient and may endure for tens of millions of years.

abstract: This communication presents an approach integrating environmental and hydrologic isotope tracers (δ 18 O H2O , δ 2 H H2O , δ 15 N NO3 , δ 18 O NO3 , and δ 11 B) with emerging organic compounds (EOCs) to acquire an enhanced understanding of the anthropogenic impact on groundwater quality. This multi-tracer approach is applied to a Mediterranean aquifer underlying a strategic agricultural area affected by various anthropogenic stressors and random urban development. In this study, the measured nitrate concentrations in water samples revealed high concentrations of up to 180 mg/L indicating an anthropogenic-based contamination. By combining the results of the analyzed isotope tracers δ 15 N NO3 and δ 11 B, nitrate is found to be mainly sourced from manure that is used on agricultural fields. There was no isotope evidence that nitrate was sourced from inorganic fertilizers or human wastes. However, some EOCs of human origin were detected in groundwater and surface water samples with concentrations >10 ng/L, suggesting contamination spread via possible groundwater-surface water interaction, which was supported by observation from δ 18 O H2O and δ 2 H H2O values. In this study, bisphenol A was detected in all water samples with high concentrations of up to 123,000 ng/L in groundwater. This indicates the impact of plastic-derived contamination, which is suspected to originate from discharged urban wastewater, from contaminated leachate derived from a neighbouring landfill, or derived from plastic pipes used during irrigation activities. This study highlights the integration of common environmental isotope tracers with EOCs as an effective method for investigating the anthropogenic impact on groundwater quality.

title: Micron-Scale Uranium Speciation Across Varying Marine Redox Environments
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales (Posters)
authors: Meyer, Frances M. [1], Chappaz, Anthony [2], Riedinger, Natascha [3], Figueroa, Maria C. [4], Mizell, Kira [5], Gregory, Daniel David [6], Lau, Kimberly V. [7]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(2) STARLAB - Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI,
(3) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, Santa Cruz, CA,
(5) USGS, Santa Cruz, CA,
(6) University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada
(7) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
abstract:
Reconstructing the changes in oxygenation of the oceans throughout Earth’s history is important for understanding the evolution of seawater, the geochemical response to shifts in climate and tectonic regimes, and the role of oxygen change during evolutionary events. Redox-sensitive trace metals such as U are therefore central to paleoenvironmental reconstructions. In marine sediments, U reduction enhances burial of U and associated isotope fractionation of 238 U/ 235 U ratios; consequently, U systematics are widely used to reconstruct oxygenation (e.g., [ 1 ]). In low-oxygen marine conditions, U is thought to accumulate through multiple pathways (including association and incorporation into organic matter, pyrite, carbonate, and apatite), predominantly as U(IV) with a minor contribution of U(VI) (e.g., [ 2 ]). Complicating this framework, the nominally metastable oxidation state U(V) has recently been observed as stable in some sedimentary systems [ 3,4 ]. Yet the pathways controlling U reduction and the resulting oxidation-state distributions remain unresolved in modern marine sediments.

To investigate U burial controls and speciation in organic-rich, reducing marine sediments, we collected micron-scale X-ray Fluorescence (XRF) maps and high energy resolution fluorescence detection X-ray absorption near edge structure (HERFD-XANES) spectra at the U L3-edge in sediments deposited across a range of reducing environments. Samples were selected from the Namibia continental coast margin, the Saanich Inlet on Vancouver Island, BC, and the Gulf of California, capturing distinct depositional redox regimes. Sediments from all three sites show heterogeneous U distributions and multiple oxidation states. These results constrain U burial in modern marine sediments and the role of depositional conditions on U oxidation state distribution, strengthening interpretations of marine U cycling and the use of U systematics as a redox proxy.

[ 1 ]Weyer, S., et al. (2008) Natural fractionation of 238U/235U Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 72, 345–359.

abstract: Rapid Arctic warming is deepening the seasonally thawed active layer and prolonging unfrozen conditions in permafrost landscapes, increasing the exposure of soil organic matter (SOM) to microbial metabolism. Leaching of SOM supplies the dissolved organic carbon (DOC) for microbial and abiotic reactions that produce CO 2 and CH 4 , strengthening the permafrost-carbon feedback. Groundwater also transports DOC, reaction products, and heat through the active layer, towards surface waters. Coupling and feedbacks between physical and biogeochemical processes make it difficult to predict how warming will alter carbon transformation and export. In particular, it is important to know how longer unfrozen periods sustain subsurface carbon processing, what forms of carbon are consumed and produced, and how and what other elements, such as iron, affect the biogeochemical reactions. Here, we examine how warming alters the seasonal coupling among freeze-thaw dynamics, groundwater flow, and carbon transformations across an Arctic hillslope-riparian-stream continuum. We coupled Advanced Terrestrial Simulator (ATS) and PFLOTRAN to simulate thermal hydrology and biogeochemistry along a representative hillslope-riparian transect in the Imnavait Creek watershed on Alaska’s North Slope. The high-resolution framework resolves variably saturated surface and subsurface flow, energy transport, freeze-thaw dynamics, DOC production and transport, and key reactions involving carbon such biotic and abiotic respiration, methanogenesis, and iron redox reactions producing CO 2 and CH 4 . Simulations indicate that warmer winters extend the zero-curtain period and expand the volume of unfrozen soil sustaining groundwater flow and carbon reactions beyond the traditional thaw season. This increases the time available for DOC mobilization and transformation. Persistent unfrozen zones strengthen the hydrologic connectivity along the hillslope-riparian corridor to the stream. Our results suggest that winter processes, often neglected in assessments of the permafrost-carbon feedbacks, may become important as the Arctic warms. Supra-permafrost aquifers can potentially shift from seasonally active systems toward year-round carbon sources.

title: Did the Taconic and Salinic Orogenies Affect Oklahoma?
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Watkins, Chase Sterling [1]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma State University, Norman, OK,
abstract:
While we have known that some Late Ordovician formations in Oklahoma appear to have been affected by tectonic activity that coincided with a pulse of the Taconic Orogeny, some workers believe that this is a coincidence. Recent work has improved our understanding and detection of previously hidden signatures of tectonic activity in younger formations in central Oklahoma. Comparing known and speculated pulses of pre-Pennsylvanian tectonic activity in Oklahoma against orogenic events on the eastern margin of Laurentia indicates that multiple pulses of tectonic activity in Oklahoma may have been caused by orogenic events around 1,500 miles away.

Furthermore, it appears that these tectonic events in Oklahoma may have caused repeated inversions of fault blocks. This has implications for interpreting sea level curves if they were generated on a fault block that was repeatedly raised and lowered. Additionally, this behavior of repeatedly changing the elevation of a fault block may lead to erroneous interpretations of 2-D seismic lines if the fault block is reset to its original elevation, or nearly so. Some of the formations in Oklahoma that have been affected by this phenomenon are the Bromide, Viola, Hunton, and Woodford, which are all oil- and gas-producing horizons.

abstract:
Abstract

This study examines the postcranial morphology and morphometrics of

proboscideans (true elephants of the genera Elephas, Loxodonta, Mammuthus,

and Palaeoloxodon), with a particular focus on the nearly complete Elephas recki

atavus skeleton from Area 123 of Koobi Fora, Kenya. This skeleton, still in situ,

represents a key specimen for understanding the postcranial adaptations of

Early Pleistocene elephants and their ecological implications. The skull and molar

morphology of the Area 123 specimen confirm its classification as Elephas r.

atavus, distinct from later Pleistocene Palaeoloxodon. Morphometric analyses

indicate that the skull of E. atavus shares greater similarity with extant Elephas

maximus than with Loxodonta or Palaeoloxodon, particularly in having a taller

skull, elongated neurocranium, shorter face, and narrower rostrum. Forelimb

proportions of the Area 123 individual closely resemble those of E. maximus,

though it possesses a relatively longer ulna, possibly reflecting an adaptation for

more efficient movement in open landscapes. Comparisons across

proboscideans reveal that taxa adapted to forested environments, such as

Mammut americanum, have proportionally shorter distal limb elements,

particularly in the manus, whereas species adapted for traversing open

landscapes, like Loxodonta africana, exhibit an elongated manus. Notably,

Deinotherium proavum possesses an exceptionally long manus, potentially

facilitating efficient locomotion in open savannas or enhancing canopy-level

browsing. The findings from Area 123 contribute to broader research on

proboscidean postcranial adaptations and their role in reconstructing past

environments. This study underscores the utility of limb morphometrics in

distinguishing locomotory strategies and ecological adaptations among extinct

proboscideans.

Keywords: Proboscidean, Postcranial, Morphometrics, Ecomorphology,

Environments

title: Improving Prediction, Response and Safety through Real-Time Surface Monitoring
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies
authors: Leshchinsky, Ben [1], Fulmer, Erik [2]
affiliations: (1) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(2) School of Civil and Construction Engineering, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA
abstract: Across the state of Oregon, USA, landslides regularly diminish the reliability of transportation systems and pose risks to nearby communities and infrastructure. Understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics of these active hazards is critical for predicting and mitigating risk to person and property. In 2019, our team began instrumenting landslides across the State with RTK-GNSS arrays that provide the 3D position of strategically placed rovers installed on the landslide surface with centimeter-level accuracy. These systems telemeter data to cloud storage every 30-minutes, providing the opportunity for real-time monitoring and analysis. Here, we evaluate the displacement timeseries of several instrumented landslides across the State, and investigate responses to precipitation both spatially and temporally. We focus on case studies of active landslides, both during, and after surge events. With the expanded network of systems installed in diverse geologic and climatic regimes, we explore the sensitivity of several slow-moving landslides to hydrometeorological forcing, as well as the evolving kinematics of landslide complexes evaluated over the monitoring period. These data offer insights into the spectrum of slow-moving landslide behaviors, providing a deeper understanding of both landslide sensitivity to various forcings and their associated kinematics. The findings demonstrate the utility of integrating high-resolution displacement monitoring with rainfall data in investigating the temporal and spatial evolution of landslides.

title: Evolution of Monitoring Approaches and Consequent Understanding of Landsliding Mechanisms at the Slumgullion Landslide, Colorado, USA
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies
authors: Schulz, William [1]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Geologic Hazards, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Landslides present significant hazards and are incompletely understood. Monitoring landslides and related conditions has enabled improved understanding of landsliding dynamics and mechanisms. The Slumgullion landslide, a continuously moving ~20x10 6 m 3 translational debris slide, was monitored by U.S. Geological Survey scientists and colleagues since 1958 using a variety of evolving approaches, evolving our understanding of landsliding mechanisms. This talk describes some of those studies.

Surface displacement was monitored using stake lines, tide gauges, time-lapse photography, leveling, aerial photographs, cable extensometers, Global Positioning System (GPS), manual and robotic total stations, lidar, unoccupied aerial systems, and terrestrial, aerial, and satellite interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) providing line-of-sight to inverted three-dimensional displacements. Subsurface displacement was monitored using a borehole inclinometer array. Subsurface hydrology was monitored using electronic piezometers and tensiometers, and surface hydrological features were monitored using GPS. Seismometer arrays monitored landslide seismicity. Most in situ sensor measurements were nearly continuously recorded by solar- and battery-powered dataloggers.

Earliest monitoring found that slide movement was block-like along narrow bounding shear zones, whose shear mode and location were later found to temporally vary using GPS, resulting in periods of dilative shear. Lidar and InSAR reinforced block-like movement and were utilized to infer landslide basal geometry; GPS monitoring revealed tens-of-m-scale undulations along the landslide base that modify sliding stresses. Photogrammetric and GPS-based kinematic element mapping was advanced by InSAR. Initially believed steady movement thought to result from steady hydrological conditions was later found to vary nearly continuously. GPS and extensometers revealed variable speed ranges along the slide’s length and ~10x speed variation on daily-seasonal scales. GPS revealed that the slide head preferentially slowed, apparently in response to drying conditions. Terrestrial InSAR revealed mm-scale displacement propagation along the slide length on hourly bases. Extensometers showed acceleration during low atmospheric tides when landslide seismicity was greatest. Earliest groundwater monitoring revealed response to snowmelt and rainfall within a few weeks. Later, deeper monitoring showed responses within hours and that pore-pressure drop along a bounding shear zone accompanied acceleration; this and observations of shear-zone dilation suggested that dilative strengthening restrained landslide motion, possibly resulting in its ~300 y movement absent catastrophic failure. As monitoring approaches continue to evolve, I expect additional evolution of the understanding of mechanisms controlling Slumgullion and other landslides.

title: EPMA INACCURACY AND THERMOBAROMETRIC UNCERTAINTY

authors: Donovan, John [1], Ducharme, Andrew [2], Allaz, Julien Marius [3], Nachlas, William O. [4], Wieser, Penny Elaine [5], von der Handt, Anette [6]

abstract:
Electron Probe Micro-Analysis (EPMA) is a widely used technique for high accuracy determination of major (> 10 wt%), minor (<1 wt%), and many trace elements (<0.1 wt%) at the micrometer-scale. Many geothermobarometers in the Earth (and Planetary) Sciences rely on accurate and precise determination of element concentrations in minerals and, in some cases, coexisting melts or glasses.

Recent work by Wieser et al. (2023) documents that inter-laboratory accuracy offsets of ~5% or more relative resulting from differences in EPMA protocols can introduce significant and systematic bias in geological interpretations. For instance in clinopyroxene-based thermobarometric calculations, where crystallization pressures for identical clinopyroxene-couples differ by as much as ~0.6 GPa among laboratories. This equates to ~20 km of crust which is nearly the thickness of the lithosphere, which makes these efforts pointless unless we obtain better consensus between EPMA laboratories.

Such discrepancies likely arise from multiple sources, inadvertently introduced through misunderstandings of the statistical and physical basis of EPMA measurements. A key problem is the use of poorly characterized natural reference materials that may exhibit unconstrained compositions or internal heterogeneity (Fournelle and Scott, 2017). Even the venerable Smithsonian mineral standards can exhibit significant grain to grain compositional variability, the use of which contributes to these systematic biases between laboratories (Fournelle, 2009).

Additional improvements in data accuracy can be achieved by utilizing modern dead-time correction expressions which are accurate at count rates up to 200 to 300 kcps, using integral-mode PHA baseline tuning (Donovan et al., 2023), and assessing beam-sensitivity effects during major- and minor-element analyses (Allaz, in preparation). Because many geo-thermobarometers depend on minor and trace elements, particular attention must also be paid to spectral interferences (Donovan et al., 1993) and secondary fluorescence from nearby phases (Borisova et al., 2018), all of which can be quantitatively corrected for in modern software.

Efforts are now underway to improve interlaboratory reproducibility and reduce systematic bias by developing a globally accessible suite of high-purity, homogeneous reference materials for key geological elements, suitable for routine EPMA use worldwide (Allaz et al., 2025). Given that modern standard-based matrix corrections routinely attain ~2% relative accuracy, and continue to improve, proper calibration of the electron microprobe, when performed rigorously, can significantly reduce uncertainty in thermobarometric interpretations.

title: Three-Dimensional Stromatolites and Depositional Environments of the Honeycut Formation (Lower Ordovician), Central Texas.
session_title: PALEONTOLOGY, BRYOZOANS, DINOSAURS, REEFS, STRATIGRAPHY, AND MILITARY GEOLOGY: IN HONOR OF ROGER CUFFEY AND HIS ECCLECTIC CAREER
authors: Cuffey, Clifford A [1], Walker, Amber D [2]
affiliations: (1) Cliff's GeoTours LLC, 2502 Gulf Ave, Midland, Texas, USA
(2) 605 County Road 157, Bangs, Texas, USA
abstract:
The middle part of the Honeycut Formation exposed in Colorado Bend State Park (Llano Uplift) contains four main lithofacies (and interpreted depositional environments): 1) burrowed carbonate (shallow subtidal); 2) fossiliferous (gastropods, sponges) carbonate (shallow subtidal); 3) stromatolite-rich carbonate (very shallow subtidal to intertidal); and 4) thinly laminated carbonate (intertidal to supratidal). These four lithofacies are arranged in repetitive shallowing-up parasequences, each approximately 1.0 to 1.5 meters thick, deposited on a carbonate platform or ramp similar to parts of the Bahama Bank or the Trucial Coast of the Persian Gulf.

One area exposes approximately 12 square meters of a single bedding plane. 85 stromatolites are preserved in three dimensions on this bedding plane. The stromatolites are hemispherical to slightly conical, and circular to somewhat oval in outline; they range from 6cm to 32cm in diameter. Where observable, they are faintly and thickly laminated internally. Some of the stromatolites occur as “isolated individuals,” whereas others occur as rows of adjacent individuals, in some cases partially grown together. Given their stratigraphic position within the parasequences, we infer that the stromatolites primarily lived on intertidal flats and in adjacent very shallow subtidal environments.

These stromatolites are broadly comparable to stromatolites found in other carbonate rocks deposited in shallow-water, restricted environments. Analogous stromatolites are found in other Lower Ordovician carbonates in the USA (New York, Pennsylvania, Missouri, and Oklahoma), as well as in the Permian Seven Rivers Formation of the Guadalupe Mountains. The modern stromatolites of Hamelin Pool (Shark Bay, Western Australia) provide a good modern analog.

abstract: Over the past five decades, our understanding of Caribbean subduction and arc evolution has undergone a profound transformation. Early studies, driven by the plate tectonics revolution, established the Lesser Antilles as a classic oceanic subduction zone where Atlantic lithosphere descends beneath the Caribbean Plate, providing a first-order framework for arc volcanism and seismicity. Subsequent advances in geochemistry demonstrated that magma generation reflects not only mantle melting but also the recycling of sediments, fluids, and volatiles from the subducting slab, revealing significant along-strike variations in mantle source composition and slab inputs. More recently, high-resolution geophysical imaging, geodesy, marine geoscience, and petrology have shown that the Caribbean subduction system is inherently three-dimensional and highly heterogeneous, with variations in slab geometry, mantle flow, crustal structure, magma storage, and tectonic deformation all contributing to the diversity of volcanic behavior observed along the arc. These developments have shifted the field from a largely descriptive, plate-scale perspective to an integrated Earth-system approach that links deep mantle processes, crustal evolution, surface dynamics, and natural hazards. Today, Caribbean subduction is recognized as one of the world's premier natural laboratories for investigating the complex interactions among tectonics, magmatism, volatile cycling, and geohazards, illustrating how interdisciplinary research is essential for understanding the evolution of convergent margins. By integrating structural geology, marine geophysics, stratigraphy, geochronology, and plate kinematic reconstructions across both the Greater and Lesser Antilles recent work has significantly advanced our understanding of Caribbean subduction revealing that the evolution of the Caribbean plate boundary reflects a succession of tectonic reorganizations driven by changing convergence rates, plate motions, and interactions with inherited lithospheric structures. These reconstructions provide a unified framework linking arc migration, deformation, basin development, and variations in magmatic activity through time. By connecting upper-plate deformation with deep geodynamic processes, this work highlights the Caribbean as a dynamic, evolving convergent margin whose present-day architecture records a complex history of plate interactions spanning tens of millions of years.

abstract:
Precipitation in arid and semi-arid regions shows considerable spatial and temporal variability, creating challenges for effective water resource management, particularly in areas with limited monitoring infrastructure. This study evaluates four satellite-based precipitation products over the Draa Oued Noun basin in southern Morocco, using data from eleven ground stations during the period 2000–2015. Accuracy was assessed at daily, monthly, annual, and seasonal time scales. Results show that all products perform poorly at daily resolution but improve significantly with temporal aggregation.

The spring season yielded the most reliable estimates. Among the products tested, TRMM and IMERG consistently showed the best performance across most indices and conditions, including high altitudes and varying rainfall intensities. These two products achieved the lowest error metrics and the highest correlation coefficients, particularly at monthly and seasonal scales. In contrast, CHIRPS and PERSIANN were less reliable, with CHIRPS tending to overestimate precipitation during wet months without capturing peak events observed by ground stations. The findings suggest that TRMM and IMERG are suitable for seasonal monitoring and water resource planning in data scarce and topographically complex regions, supporting their integration into hydrological and climate-related applications in semi-arid mountainous environments.

abstract: Future hydroclimate projections for the Southwestern US remain contentious. While most models forecast increased aridity under greenhouse warming, paleoclimate archives often reveal a significantly wetter state during past warm periods. To resolve this ‘warm-wet’ paradox, we investigate the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO, ~17–15 Ma) in the Española Basin, New Mexico. We present triple oxygen isotope (δ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O) data from authigenic smectite minerals in paleosols. Our results reveal a statistically significant correlation between terrestrial soil water δ 18 O and North Pacific sea surface temperatures (SSTs). Specifically, high-latitude warming appears to suppress cool-season moisture transport via a teleconnection resembling the modern Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO). However, our findings suggest this regional drying mechanism was effectively overridden during transient peaks of global warmth (e.g., at 15.6 Ma), where a broader, greenhouse-driven wetter state prevailed. These results underscore the importance of oceanic controls, and suggest that the ‘warm-wet’ state of the US Southwest is a non-linear response to global and regional SST gradients.

title: From seafloor spreading to subduction: Tectonomagmatic evolution of Neo-Tethyan Ophiolites in the Muslim Bagh-Khanozai and Naweoba regions, Western Pakistan
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: Khan, Akram Ullah [1], Dong, Yunpeng [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Northwest University, State Key Laboratory of Continental Evolution and Early Life, Xi'an, Shaanxi, China

abstract: The Western Pakistan Suture Zone (Ophiolitic Mélange Belt) extends approximately north-south. Its northern end passes through the Kohistan Ladakh-Island Arc connecting the Eastern Neo-Tethys Ocean, while its southern end passes through the Makran Subduction Zone connecting the Western Neo-Tethys Ocean. This suture zone formed through the Cenozoic collision of Indian and Eurasian plates and play a key role in determining the lithospheric oceanic crust of Neo-Tethys Ocean. Both Muslim Bagh-Khanozai and Naweoba ophiolites formed along this critical suture zone. However, due to specific regional, political, and economic issues, poorly research has been constrained. We present new petrography, whole-rock geochemistry, and zircon U-Pb geochronology from the Muslim Bagh-Khanozai and the Naweoba ophiolites in NW Pakistan. Field excursion documents classical ophiolitic lithologies: harzburgitic to dunite peridotites, layered gabbros, basalt, pillow andesites, and dolerite intrusions at Muslim Bagh-Khanozai; and gabbro, plagiogranite, basalt and boninite at Naweoba. Zircon U-Pb analyses yield crystallization ages of ~200 Ma for Muslim Bagh-Khanozai and ~92 Ma for Naweoba. Whole-rock major and trace element geochemistry shows MORB-type tectonic setting for Muslim Bagh-Khanozai’s gabbros and associated dolerites with arc related tectonic setting for basaltic components, whereas Naweoba’s gabbro and plagiogranite shows MORB with OIB basalts and boninite lava characteristics which are the first ever known boninite in this whole region of Western Mélange Belt. Our research data from Muslim Bagh-Khanozai supports the idea of Early Jurassic sea floor spreading (MORB) and arc related subduction during the Late Cretaceous. In contrast, Naweoba records a distinct Late Cretaceous ridge-plume (MORB-OIB) magmatism and followed by subduction initiation marked by boninite formation during Neo-Tethys tectonic evolution. These results provide the first U-Pb ages for the Naweoba mélange, revise the timing of magmatism at Muslim Bagh-Khanozai, and demonstrate that Western Pakistan preserves temporally discrete oceanic domains and magmatic events along a key transitional segment of the Neo-Tethys Ocean. Our integrated results refine regional plate-reconstruction models and highlights the need for focused sampling to resolve spatial variations in mantle source, spreading dynamics, and tectonic emplacement across the suture.

title: 'Unraveling the Potential of Reduced Intrusion-Related Gold System (RIRGS) Mineralization in Antaña, Southern Peru'
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics
authors: Puma , Mirian [1]
affiliations: (1) Puno, Peru
abstract: Reduced Intrusion-Related Gold Systems (RIRGS) represent an important source of low-grade, high-tonnage gold mineralization worldwide. Major examples occur in the Tintina Gold Province (Yukon–Alaska), and in South America within the Bolivian Polymetallic Belt, including the Kori Kollo (~2 Moz Au) and Tasna deposits. These deposits provide a valuable reference framework for evaluating similar systems in the Central Andes. The study area is located within the Sn–Cu–W metallogenic belt of southern Peru, associated with Oligocene–Miocene intrusions and Ag–Pb–Zn (±Au) epithermal systems. Santiago de Pupuja lies approximately 1,200 km northwest of the Bolivian Polymetallic Belt and is structurally controlled by the NW–SE–trending Urcos– Sicuani–Ayaviri regional fault system. The area exposes Silurian to Paleogene sedimentary sequences intruded by reduced magmatic bodies. Petrographic analysis indicates that mineralization is hosted within the Chagrapi Formation (slates and dark phyllites), occurring as fissure and microfault fillings. The mineral assemblage is dominated by galena, pyrite, and chalcopyrite, with minor alteration minerals including talc, muscovite, and chlorite. These characteristics suggest structurally controlled, intrusion-related mineralization. The geologic, structural, and mineralogical evidence supports an Au–Ag–Pb–Sb– rich base metal system consistent with a distal RIRGS model. This study expands the metallogenic framework of southern Peru and demonstrates the applicability of internationally recognized RIRGS exploration models to the Andean orogenic context. abstract: The oxidation-hydration weathering products of the primary ore mineral of uranium, uraninite (UO 2+x ) display extraordinary structural, chemical, and, as a result, optical vibrational spectroscopic diversity that is related to the geologic conditions in which they are formed. Analogously, structure-property-observable relationships developed for U minerals are transferable to describing features of U materials found in the nuclear fuel cycle and observations made for mineral phases can provide insight into the process history, and resulting chemical and structural identity of technogenic materials resulting from fuel cycle processes. Recently, we have developed a Compendium of Uranium Raman and Infrared Experimental Spectra (CURIES) to fully exploit the diversity of U minerals for identification and interpretation of inorganic U phases relevant to the nuclear fuel cycle and found that, when grouped by secondary oxyanion chemistry, average spectra of U mineral phases possessed common Raman spectroscopic features that are identifiable and interpretable using a machine learning (ML) based approach. Here, we examine the translatability of this ML approach for identification of complex, mixed-secondary oxyanion mineral species. Raman spectral features of ammoniomathesiusite, coconinoite, horákite, ježekite, mathesiusite, schröckingerite, szilagyiite, uramarsite, and an unnamed mineral related to szilagyiite were analyzed and interpreted relative to their structural origins, and ML models were applied for potential identification of secondary chemistry for these complex phases.

abstract: The Tiddiline Formation of the Bou Azzer–El Graara inlier (Central Anti-Atlas, Morocco) records the final sedimentary stage of the Pan-African orogenic cycle along the northwestern margin of the West African Craton. Field observations reveal a ~350 m-thick siliciclastic succession resting unconformably on Cryogenian arc–ophiolitic complexes and overlain by volcanic rocks of the Ouarzazate Supergroup. The sequence comprises arkosic to feldspathic sandstones, siltstones, and mudstones, locally interbedded with conglomerates and minor diamictites, deposited in alluvial to lacustrine environments within a tectonically active continental basin. U–Pb analyses of detrital zircons from a representative sandstone using the SHRIMP IIe/mc instrument yield two main age populations: a dominant Paleoproterozoic component (2188 Ma and 2075 Ma) derived from the West African Craton, and a younger Neoproterozoic cluster (weighted-mean ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U = 611 ± 11.5 Ma, MSWD = 2.72) that constrains the maximum depositional age. This age places the Tiddiline Formation within the latest Ediacaran, synchronous with the terminal Pan-African deformation (B2 phase, 620–600 Ma) and preceding Ouarzazate magmatism (574–548 Ma). Structural and sedimentological evidence indicate deposition in a transtensive pull-apart basin formed during orogenic relaxation, contemporaneous with dextral–sinistral strike-slip reactivation along the Pan-African suture. The Tiddiline Basin and its equivalents thus represent the transition from compressional to extensional tectonism in the Anti-Atlas and record the last phase of crustal reworking before the onset of widespread late Ediacaran volcanism.

title: Statistic and Geologic Analysis of Volcanic Field boundaries on the Transmexican Volcanic Belt, Mexico
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Aguilar-Tomasini, Joel [1], Cañón-Tapia, Edgardo [2]

abstract: Volcanic Fields (V.F.) are groups of volcanic structures within a given area. Their definition, border and method of selection remains debated. Several V.F. borders are often influenced by economic or non-geologic factors. Sometimes statistical methods are used to define V.F., but there is no concensus about which method to choose and how to apply it. The lack of well-defined borders is important since the extension of the area and structure density are fundamental to define a V.F.. Border definition also may influence predictive models for risk management. To address this issue, volcanism within the Cinturón Volcánico Trans-Mexicano (CVTM) was examined applying several statistical methods (KDE, HDBSCAN,K-means, OPTICS). Known aspects about geochemistry, geophysiscs and structural geology of the CVTM were compared with the obtained statistical groups and the (many) proposed borders for each field. The methods KDE and HDBSCAN yield results that roughly match some previously proposed V.F borders. Nevertheless, the division does not have an evident geologic justification of the entire CVTM on volcanic fields, due to the lack of distinctive features for individual fields. In practice, although seemingly arbitrary, the division in various V.F. has the main advantage of facilitating the study of the entire area.

title: Will Tunguska’s Evil Twin Return on Halloween 2026? Science and Skepticism in a Clickbait World
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Boslough, Mark [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
Did the Tunguska object have an unseen companion that missed the Earth in 1908? Is this hidden cosmic nightmare on its way back to finish the job? As we celebrate this Halloween behind our masks and in our costumes, will it unleash the ultimate trick-or-treat from hell?

For nearly a century, the mainstream narrative has been this: If the Tunguska space rock had arrived 4 hours and 47 minutes later, it would have destroyed St. Petersburg. New orbital calculations have revealed the stunning truth. If it had been mere minutes late, it could have destroyed a city in the US or Canada. A couple minutes after that it would have missed Earth altogether, only to return and menace our planet in the future. That time could be now. Other parts of a broken space rock could also come back, like the formation-flying fragments of Shoemaker-Levy 9 did when they all struck Jupiter in 1994.

The Tunguska trajectory suggests it was from the Taurid meteor stream, which crosses Earth’s path twice a year. “Halloween fireballs” come from this stream during its autumn crossing. Published models suggest the existence of a Taurid swarm in an approximate 61-year resonance with earth. Two 61-year periods after the 1908 Taurid crossing will be 2030. The fall crossing would be 4 years earlier, within a few weeks of October 31, 2026.

The previous paragraphs of this abstract are written in clickbait style. The idea of a dark Tunguska companion is pure speculation. The Taurid resonant swarm model does, however, predict close approaches of a hypothetical swarm in 2032 and 2036. There is no evidence for a concentration of large objects, but there is no reason not to search for them in 2032 as a precaution. The Tunguska object’s Earth encounter was six years before the hypothetical swarm, and there is no theoretical basis for it to have the same resonant period.

This idea is simply a speculative “what if?” (much like the St. Petersburg counterfactual was a playful, but incorrect, idea first published by astronomer I.S. Astapowitsch in a 1934 version of modern-day clickbait).

This poster will present arguments, pro and con, about whether we should try to exploit the clickbait industry to provide accurate scientific and skeptical information to the public.

title: Beyond Binary Mixing: Quantitative Provenance Unmixing Reveals Cryptic Sediment Sources in a Tropical Foreland Basin, NW Borneo
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools
authors: Adepehin, Ekundayo Joseph [1], Fong, Yi Ning [2], Arifin, Hariri Mohd [3], Garzanti, Eduardo [4]
affiliations: (1) Josephus Institute of Earth Sciences, Redeemer’s University,, Ede, Osun State, Nigeria
(2) Applied Geology, Curtin University Malaysia, Miri, Sarawak, Malaysia

(4) Department of Environmental and Earth Sciences, University of Milan-Bicocca, Milan, Italy
abstract: Conventional provenance models for foreland basins commonly predict dominant sediment supply from adjacent orogenic belts, yet these assumptions remain largely untested in many tropical systems. This study presents the first statistical quantification of multi-source sediment provenance for the Oligocene–Miocene Nyalau Formation of the Sarawak Basin, northwest Borneo, integrating sandstone petrography, XRD mineralogy, SEM imaging, whole-rock geochemistry, heavy-mineral data, and detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology. Detrital zircon age populations were evaluated using constrained non-negative least-squares statistical unmixing, demonstrating that conventional two-source mixing models are insufficient to explain the observed provenance signatures. The optimal solution identifies three distinct sediment contributors: the Malay–Thai Peninsula (58%), the Rajang fold-thrust belt (31%), and a previously unrecognized cryptic source (11%) characterized by syn-depositional Oligocene–Miocene volcanic zircons mixed with recycled Precambrian populations. Results reveal that long-distance axial drainage transported quartz-rich sediment more than 500 km from Sundaland-derived continental sources and volumetrically exceeded sediment input from the adjacent Rajang orogen. This pattern challenges proximity-based expectations for sediment dispersal in foreland basins and suggests that drainage integration, zircon fertility, and sustained monsoonal discharge can outweigh source proximity in controlling sediment budgets within tropical convergent-margin settings. Petrographic and geochemical variations further record coupled tectonic-climatic controls on basin filling. Quartz-rich intervals with elevated ZTR indices reflect extensive recycling and prolonged tropical weathering, whereas lithic-rich intervals indicate increased transverse sediment supply from the Rajang fold-thrust belt during episodes of enhanced local erosion and discharge variability. These results demonstrate that quantitative provenance unmixing can identify cryptic sediment contributors overlooked by binary provenance models and provide new constraints on sediment routing, paleogeography, and basin evolution during Oligocene–Miocene tectonic reorganization in Southeast Asia.

title: Microbial community composition and development under experimental leaching conditions for critical mineral recovery from legacy wastes
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources (Posters)
authors: Best, Mackenzie B. [1], Gresham, Mary Li [2], Davis, Ryan Wesley [3], Xu, Guangping [4]
affiliations: (1) Geomechanics and Geochemistry, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA

abstract:
Mining and industrial wastes including waste rock, tailings, coal refuse, and fly ash from coal-powered power plants have been identified as non-traditional resources for critical minerals including base metals and rare earth elements (REEs). However, the path to extraction from these wastes is not yet economically viable, with challenges related to waste mineralogy, dilute element concentration, and elemental distribution within a given waste pile, among others. Additional complications arise from concerns about water consumption and power inputs for relatively small returns. Microorganisms are powerful catalysts for metal release through their production of inorganic and organic acids and other chelators that can enhance mineral weathering and metal solubilization, and may represent a lower-cost method to enhance recovery from wastes. Previous work has shown that critical mineral-bearing hard rock mine wastes from New Mexico host diverse communities dominated by organoheterotrophic microorganisms as well as many novel populations, particularly in tailings samples, that may contribute to mineral weathering and metal cycling. We will report new DNA- and RNA-based analyses of microbial communities endemic to hard rock mine tailings, coal refuse, and coal fly ash under different experimental conditions designed to maximize critical mineral dissolution to better understand the effect of microbial community consortia on mineral weathering and aqueous metal speciation. We will also report the differences in microbial community composition and development over time in different experimental treatments, and discuss how communities correlate with geochemistry and mineralogy across the different waste types and conditions, and implications for high density cultivation of bioleaching consortia. This work has implications for future initiatives aimed at harnessing microbially-mediated metal release for critical mineral recovery from mine and industrial wastes, including in situ leaching and recovery or heap leaching.

title: Constraining Ice and Life in the Neoproterozoic: Application of Multi-Method Geochronology to the Lower Huqf Supergroup of Oman

abstract: The Neoproterozoic is typified by dramatic climate fluctuations, major shifts in the carbon cycle, and the proliferation of complex life. Our understanding of the links between the Earth’s ancient environments and the expansion of multicellular eukaryotes is underpinned by the sedimentary rock record of this time. The Huqf Supergroup of Oman comprises a near-continuous stratigraphic record from the Cryogenian period to the onset of the Cambrian. Thus, studies of the Huqf Supergroup have been crucial for reconstructing the Neoproterozoic world, including global scale ‘Snowball Earth’ glaciations, the largest single carbon isotope excursion (CIE) ever recorded (the Shuram negative CIE), the oxygenation of shallow marine environments, and the radiation of complex multicellular life. However, the validity of such assertions is limited by the paucity of precise age constraints on the Precambrian sedimentary successions of Oman. The current chronostratigraphic framework for the lower Huqf Supergroup relies primarily upon correlations to well-dated globally equivalent strata and detrital zircon ages, which are limited in their capacity to constrain the exact time of deposition for these sedimentary rocks. Therefore, the present study aims to address the temporal uncertainty within the Cryogenian and lower Ediacaran Huqf Supergroup of Oman using a range of novel and traditional dating techniques coupled with carbon isotope stratigraphy. We compare multiple chronometers – including Re–Os, U–Pb carbonate, and Rb–Sr shale ages – to explore the strengths and limitations of each. Consequently, these new ages from Oman have implications for the timing and extent of the Snowball Earth glaciations, the subsequent post-glacial aftermath, and the eventual rise of complex life in the Neoproterozoic.

title: Cataclasite Formation in the Chicxulub Impact Crater Gleaned from 2D Image Analysis of the IODP-ICDP Expedition 364 Drill Core
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: Bahr, Louisa [1], Grolms, Nele [2], Riller, Ulrich [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth System Sciences, University of Hamburg, Hamburg, Hamburg, Germany

abstract: The IODP-ICDP Expedition 364 drill core is characterized by the pervasive presence of cataclasite zones in shocked target rocks underlying the peak ring of the Chicxulub crater. The formation of these zones is attributed to the transition from acoustic fluidization to localized shear faulting during cratering. Hence, the question arises to what extent cataclasis is the result of acoustic pressure fluctuations, possibly leading to pure crushing target rock, and comminution of rock caused by zone-parallel shearing. We applied a novel semi-automated workflow for the 2D image analysis of thin section microphotographs to characterize shapes and orientations of fragments in cataclasite zones to better comprehend the possible change in the deformation mechanisms. Pure crushing is expected to produce random orientations of fragments with diverse shapes, while shearing may result in shape-preferred orientations of elongate fragments. The analyses indicate that the fragment ellipticity can vary significantly within any cataclasite zone, while a preferred orientation of elliptical fragments is evident. Furthermore, cataclasite zones from different depths of the core appear to mostly exhibit shape-preferred orientations. These observations suggest that shearing may have played a significant role in cataclasite formation. This implies that zone-parallel shearing may have indeed triggered a reorientation of elliptical fragments formed by initial crushing. Therefore, acoustic fluidization may have ceased at an earlier stage than previously thought.

abstract: The mineralogy of altered volcanic rocks represents a record of low-temperature hydrothermal and meteoric processes. They may also host economically important deposits, including bentonite and zeolite-rich rocks. Bentonite forms through the devitrification and chemical alteration of volcanic ash and is composed predominantly of smectite-group minerals, mainly montmorillonite and often beidellite. In volcanic setting, bentonite formation is commonly associated with hydrothermal fluid circulation followed by meteoric overprinting, resulting in mineralogical heterogeneity over a range of spatial scales. Despite the economic and scientific relevance of these systems, conventional mineralogical approaches including X-ray diffraction, petrography, and bulk geochemistry, rely on discrete sampling and therefore provide only limited insight into continuous mineralogical variations and fine-scale alteration gradients. This highlights a methodological gap between the needed for high-resolution mineral mapping and the spatially discontinuous nature of traditional analytical methods. Hyperspectral core imaging in the VNIR-SWIR spectral ranges has emerged as a non-destructive approach for rapid and continuous mineral identification in drill cores. This technique enables the identification of textural relationships and associated mineral assemblages and offers significant potential for screening variation in alteration degree within the volcanic deposits. In this study, we applied hyperspectral core imaging to (1) bentonite deposits from northern Morocco and (2) low-temperature altered basaltic tuffs from Surtsey Island, to evaluate its effectiveness in mapping mineralogical variability and distinguishing hydrothermal from meteoric alteration pathways. By comparing these two volcanic-volcaniclastic systems, we assess the robustness of hyperspectral methods for characterizing low-temperature clay-rich environments and explore their potential integration into mineral exploration and geoenvironmental workflows.

title: Hydrogeochemical Evolution and Groundwater Quality Assessment in a Fractured Basement Aquifer System, Southeastern Rwanda
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part I)
authors: Ngendahayo, Emmanuel [1], Nilsson, Erik [2], Larson, Magnus [3], Wali, Umaru Garba [4], Nsabimana, Antoine [5], Persson, Kenneth M. [6]
affiliations: (1) Lund University, Lund, Sweden
(2) Water Resources Engineering, Lund University, Lund, Sweden

(5) Biology, University of Rwanda, Kigali, Rwanda

abstract: Groundwater from fractured Precambrian crystalline basement aquifers is the primary source of drinking and irrigation water in drought‑prone southeastern Rwanda. However, despite increasing supply risks, the hydrogeochemical processes governing groundwater quality in these aquifers remain poorly understood, limiting effective monitoring and management. This study aims to identify the processes controlling the chemical evolution of groundwater and the spatial distribution of water quality risks. Groundwater samples were collected from 167 boreholes between 2022 and 2024 across an area of 7,843 km². A multi‑technique approach combining hydrochemical analysis, multivariate statistics, bivariate relationships, graphical methods, geochemical modelling, and an Integrated Weighted Water Quality Index (IWQI) based on entropy and Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) objective weighting was applied. The results show that groundwater is circumneutral (mean pH = 6.34), generally fresh and low mineralized (mean EC of 411.89 µS cm⁻¹ and TDS of 192.99 mg L⁻¹), and dominated by Ca-HCO₃ facies, controlled mainly by carbonate and silicate weathering, with a spatial transition toward mixed and Na‑enriched (Na-Cl) facies in northeastern catchments. Four principal components account for 83% of the total variance, reflecting mineral dissolution and progressive mineralization, carbonate buffering, redox‑controlled reactions, and localized nitrogen inputs. Gibbs diagrams indicate water-rock interaction as the primary control on groundwater chemistry, while negative chloro‑alkaline indices and Na⁺ enrichment relative to Cl⁻ suggest reverse cation exchange as a secondary process. Although 67% of boreholes fall into the best water quality category (IWQI < 26), spatial clustering of elevated IWQI and EC values reveals localized water quality constraints. Sodium hazard for irrigation is negligible (SAR < 10 in all samples), whereas salinity poses localized limitations (EC > 750 µS/cm in 13% of samples). These results establish a process-based framework linking groundwater chemical evolution to spatial water quality risks. The identified water quality hotspots support targeted monitoring, drinking water risk screening, and evidence-based borehole siting, with a preference for Ca-HCO₃-dominated locations. The integrated methodological workflow is transferable to other drought-stressed fractured basement aquifers and supports groundwater quality management under increasing climatic and anthropogenic pressure.

title: Airborne Geophysical Surveying of the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Connell, Dylan M [1], Amaral, Chelsea M. [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract:
The U.S. Geological Survey's (USGS) Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) represents a strategic, multi-phase effort to modernize the available data to study the Nation's geologic framework in support of domestic critical mineral resource assessments. Here we discuss a high-resolution airborne geophysical data collection campaign that was started in 2019 as part of this effort and is now well underway, covering areas identified as containing or with potential to contain critical minerals. The USGS list of critical minerals includes rare earth elements, lithium, cobalt, nickel, and other commodities essential to modern technology and national security supply chains.

Airborne geophysical data collection under Earth MRI currently utilizes three primary methodologies: (1) high-resolution aeromagnetic surveys, which can delineate subsurface lithologic and structural controls on mineralization; (2) airborne gamma-ray spectrometry, which provides near-surface radioelement distributions (Potassium, Uranium, and Thorium) useful for surficial geologic mapping and identification of lithologies associated with critical mineral deposits; and (3) airborne electromagnetic surveys, which characterize the electrical conductivity structure of the upper few hundred meters and map surficial cover thickness, lithologies, structure, hydrologic features, and in some cases conductive ore-bearing horizons such as those associated with graphite. Surveys are designed in coordination with state geological surveys and prioritized using a data-gap analysis overlain with critical mineral deposit-type models.

To date, Earth MRI airborne geophysical data collection covers over 75,000 square miles across geologically diverse mineral systems of the United States. All acquired data are processed to modern standards, rigorously quality-controlled, and released publicly through ScienceBase (www.sciencebase.gov), ensuring broad accessibility for governmental, academic, and industry users. Integration of Earth MRI airborne data with geologic mapping, geochemical sampling, hyperspectral, and topographic lidar products provides a powerful, multi-layer framework for understanding critical mineral systems at various scales. The large volume of newly acquired geophysical data also presents an opportunity for the USGS to potentially create and refine regional and national-scale compilations. Earth MRI's airborne geophysics component exemplifies the role of foundational public-sector geoscience underpinning prospectivity studies, informing land-use and resource management decisions, and strengthening domestic mineral supply chains for a 21st-century economy. Beyond furthering the understanding of the Nation’s mineral resources, these data are valuable for understanding energy and water resources; hazards (e.g., landslides, earthquakes); mine waste; abandoned wells; and other natural and anthropogenic features.
