title: Decelerated Latitudinal Drift of the North China Craton During Rodinia Assembly Revealed by Paleomagnetism and Cyclostratigraphy
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Zhao, Hanqing [1]
affiliations: (1) State Key Laboratory of Geomicrobiology and Environmental Changes, and School of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing, China
abstract:
The Mesoproterozoic–Neoproterozoic transition was a critical interval in Earth history, marked by the breakup of the Nuna/Columbia supercontinent and the assembly of Rodinia. Paleomagnetic data indicate that several major cratons underwent large-scale paleogeographic changes between ca. 1.2 and 0.9 Ga. In particular, paleomagnetic records from the North China and Laurentian cratons suggest substantial latitudinal motion from polar to equatorial regions during ca. 1.1–1.0 Ga, potentially driven by plate motion, rapid oscillatory true polar wander, or a combination of both. Integrating paleomagnetism with cyclostratigraphy provides a means to quantify plate-motion rates and trajectories at higher temporal resolution.

Here we report new paleomagnetic, rock magnetic, and cyclostratigraphic results from carbonate successions of the Zhaowei and Niyuan formations of the Huaibei Group, northern Anhui–Jiangsu region, North China craton. The paleomagnetic directions pass a reversal baked-contact test, supporting a primary or early-acquired magnetization. The Zhaowei and Niyuan formations yield broadly similar declinations but markedly different inclinations, indicating a paleolatitudinal shift of ~20° between their depositional intervals. High-resolution cyclostratigraphic analysis of mass magnetic susceptibility, rock color reflectance, and elemental proxy records from thin-bedded limestones of the Zhaowei Formation suggests an average sedimentation rate of ~21 m/Myr. Assuming relatively constant sedimentation across the continuously deposited Zhaowei–Niyuan succession, which has a total thickness of ~580 m, we estimate a latitudinal drift rate of ~8 cm/yr for the North China craton during this interval.

This rate is substantially lower than the >15 cm/yr latitudinal drift inferred for the underlying Xinxing/Nanfen formations. Together with published paleomagnetic constraints from the Huaibei Group and related late Mesoproterozoic–early Neoproterozoic successions, these results suggest that the North China craton experienced significant deceleration in latitudinal motion during Rodinia assembly. This deceleration may reflect a transition from rapid plate motion and/or true polar wander toward plate interactions associated with Grenvillian-age convergence and collision.

title: Modeling a Moving Target: A Chemical Conceptual Model for Groundwater Plumes Under Changing Pumping Conditions
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part I)
authors: Yu, Lily [1], Stefani, Aline Ansara [2], Araujo, Carlos Henrique [3], Carvalho, Ligia [4], Henderson, James King [5], Silva, Ruy [6], Ribeiro, Lucas Andreata [7]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA; Corteva Agriscience, USA
(2) Civil and Mineral Engineering, University of Toronto, Canada; Worley, Brazil
(3) Protel Consultoria Empresarial, Brazil
(4) Corteva Agriscience, Brazil
(5) Corteva Agriscience, USA

abstract: At a former pesticide manufacturing facility in Brazil, groundwater and contaminant models must account for frequent changes in nearby pumping from multiple aquifers and depths as a growing population increases demand. Since start-up in the 1970s, municipal and industrial supply wells were added in waves (1980s–1990s, ~2004, and 2017–2024), shifting hydraulic gradients, flow directions, and groundwater velocities. Models set up for current conditions can therefore misrepresent earlier plume movement and require repeated recalibration as new wells are installed. This presentation shows how a Chemical Conceptual Model (CCM) improves modeling by anchoring interpretation in time-stable information: production history, primary source areas, release mechanisms, and the chemistry of site 'mixtures of interest', mainly non-aqueous phase products (NAPPs). Mixtures are sampled and analyzed to build simple one-dimensional diagrams of vertical transport that reflect phase changes and likely transformations over time. Accelerated column experiments mimic key attenuation processes under representative layering while compressing field timescales into manageable laboratory timeframes. The CCM provides a consistent foundation for variable-rich modeling, improving confidence in plume interpretation and focusing sampling on zones where contaminants are most likely to accumulate and persist.

title: Hutton's Error: Fact and Fallacy on the Road to Deep Time
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Lester, Alan [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, Colorado,
abstract:
Science is all too commonly viewed as an engine driving implacably toward truth or as a metaphorical Excalibur cutting through ignorance and misconception. In fact, history shows that science is nothing of the sort; it progresses in fits and starts, and it is heavily influenced by prevailing culture and societal attitudes. The connection between science and the social and intellectual climate in which it operates is often best exemplified by the errors and misconceptions of pivotal figures as opposed to a celebration of their triumphs.

James Hutton, appropriately revered as a key progenitor of modern geology and the concept of Deep Time, espoused a number of false assumptions and his legacy is fraught with misrepresentations. For example:

Hutton was hardly the first serious intellectual to recognize earth’s great antiquity. Many serious thinkers were starting to consider earth’s age as a legitimate realm of investigation; perhaps encouraged by a dramatic increase in the ability to quantify and measure time at virtually all scales.

Hutton (and his supporters like Playfair and Lyell) championed an unwarranted and excessive emphasis on cyclical, i.e. “uniformitarian,” process. The aversion to accepting unique or “catastrophic” events was construed by many, at the time, as a winner-take-all battle.

From 19 th century geologists like Archibald Geikie to many of our modern textbooks, Hutton has been lauded as a quintessential field observer and an inductive reasoner, when in reality he went looking for exactly what he hoped to find—namely, evidence for recurring cycles of erosion and uplift, driven by earth’s internal heat.

Hutton was mired in a pre-Victorian worldview of constancy and continuity, effectively standing astride a watershed-like divide between an old monarchical world of static patterns and a new age marked by emergent change and revolution. As scientists internalized the new cultural dynamic in the early 19 th century, they quickly began to elucidate evolutionary processes within stars, life, and even the physical earth.

Finally, we view Hutton’s mistakes and misconceptions, with two centuries of hindsight, not for ridicule but as reminder that science of the past, present, and future is deeply affected by its social, political, and cultural environment.

title: Hyperspectral core scanning at the Iron Creek Cu-Co Deposit, Idaho Cobalt Belt: Development of New Exploration Vectors
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Archer, Will [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Abts, Miranda [3], Koerting, Friederike [4], Santaguida, Frank [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Idaho Cobalt Belt hosts several important cobalt-copper deposits, but only limited research has been conducted on these deposits over the past decades. While the market for cobalt is currently dominated by the Democratic Republic of Congo and riddled with ethical and geopolitical concerns, development of domestic resources is a high priority to supply the metals needed to support the green energy transition.

This project aims to determine whether the Iron Creek Co-Cu deposit is associated with a hydrothermal alteration halo that can be identified hyperspectrally. Various models for metal enrichment have been proposed for the deposit, ranging from syngenetic metal deposition in the sedimentary rocks to models that suggest deposit formation occurred during or after metamorphism. Shortwave infrared hyperspectral core scanning of exploration diamond drill core enabled identification of spectrally active minerals within the alteration halo and unraveled mineralogical gradients around the ore zones. The data resulted in a better understanding of the deposit geology and assisted in drill target generation.

To understand deposit-scale mineral gradients, ~10 km of exploration drill core was scanned in Salmon, Idaho. A HySpex SWIR-384 core scanning solution with a pixel resolution of ~1.75 mm/pixel was used for data acquisition. The Breeze GEO software was utilized for data acquisition and post-processing, including depth registration of core and mineral classification using USGS MICA. The software outputs included hyperspectral mineral maps of the core, which were stored in the software IMAGO. The hyperspectral mineral maps were used to identify textural relationships that cannot be identified with the unaided eye. In addition, hyperspectral core scanning allowed the generation of mineral abundance data, which were plotted in three dimensions using Leapfrog GEO. Visualization of mineral abundance data unraveled the geometry of the alteration halo and the mineralogical gradients within it.

title: Carbonate Clumped Isotopes Indicate Kilometer-Scale Uplift of Northern New Mexico Since the Neogene
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic
authors: Bernstein, Rachel [1], Koning, Daniel J. [2], Maloney, Ashley [3], Spaur, Siânin D. [4], Lee, Olivia [5], Sanchez Ortiz, Gabriela [6], Ibarra, Daniel Enrique [7], Acosta, R. Paul [8], Snell, Kathryn E. [9], Rugenstein, Jeremy Kesner Caves [10]

abstract: The uplift history of the southern Rocky Mountains is both well-studied and perpetually contested. The Colorado Front Range displays topographically young features which have been hypothesized to have developed after its initial uplift during the Laramide Orogeny ca. 40-80 Ma, but the drivers behind this topographic rejuvenation remain similarly contested. Eastward tilting of the Colorado Front Range and Great Plains suggests a tectonic mechanism, though increases in erosional efficiency via continued late Cenozoic cooling, Quaternary glacial-interglacial oscillations, and the hypothesized strengthening of the North American Monsoon ca. 6 Ma provide alternate climatic drivers of incision. New temperature estimates from clumped isotope analyses of authigenic carbonates from the well-dated Santa Fe Group of the central Rio Grande Rift document a long-term cooling of 18.3 ± 10.3°C between the mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO) and the Pleistocene. This Neogene cooling trend in New Mexico tightly tracks the global benthic d 18 O record and Pacific sea-surface temperature records over the same period, suggesting that paleotemperature change throughout the record is controlled by global climate. However, climate models are unable to match the degree of continental MCO warmth in New Mexico indicated in our data even at atmospheric CO 2 concentrations 8x higher than pre-industrial levels. While the total cooling suggested by this record is greater due to relatively cool temperature estimates in the Pleistocene, clumped isotope temperatures at the MCO are ~10°C warmer than modern mean annual temperatures in New Mexico. Meanwhile, high-CO 2 (560 ppm) Miocene and modern simulations can only simulate 3.6°C and 3.2°C of warming respectively. The disagreement between the magnitude of MCO warmth indicated by our clumped isotope record and that resulting from models can be explained by other factors that modify local temperature, such as changes in elevation associated with ongoing rifting along the Rio Grande rift and/or epeirogenic uplift. We suggest that our record not only demonstrates that global drivers pace long-term temperature change in the U.S. Southwest but also provides evidence for about a kilometer of intracontinental uplift in northern New Mexico since the early Miocene.

title: New constraints on Neoproterozoic Extension and Breakup of Rodinia in Southern Mexico: Geochemistry and Geochronology of the Lachirioag Suite
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Quintana Delgado, Andres [1], Weber, Bodo [2], Monreal Roque, Eduardo [3], Inguaggiato, Claudio [4], Frei, Dirk [5], Martens, Uwe C. [6]
affiliations: (1) Ciencias de la tierra, CICESE, Ensenada, Baja California, Mexico
(2) CICESE, Geology Department, Ensenada, Baja California,
(3) CICESE, Ensenada, México,
(4) Centro de Investigación Científica y de Educación Superior de Ensenada, Baja California (CICESE), Ensenada, Baja California,
(5) UWC, Stellenbosch, Western Cape,
(6) UNAM Instituto de Geociencias, Juriquilla, Queretaro, QRO,
abstract:
The Cuicateco Belt of southern Mexico (Oaxaca state) is a fault-bounded terrane mainly constituted of Paleozoic metasedimentary rocks. We discovered Precambrian basement inliers that occur as deformed, lower crustal slices composed of igneous protoliths, here defined as the “Lachirioag Suite”. The rocks are characterized by gabbroic to tonalitic igneous protoliths that were mylonitized and overprinted by greenschist-facies metamorphism (M2). Locally, an earlier medium- to high-grade metamorphic event (M1) is represented in metagabbroic protoliths by relics of brittlely fractured garnet in elongated chlorite porphyroclasts, rutile in ilmenite, and clinopyroxene.

The U-Pb zircon geochronology by LA-ICPMS revealed prominent age groups at ca. 850 Ma, which we interpret as the time of igneous crystallization or an ultra-high temperature event, as supported by Ti-in-zircon temperatures > 900 ºC. Some zircons contain inherited cores with ages between ~1.2 and ~1.0 Ga, indicating recycling of Oaxaquia-type crust. The timing of M1 is constrained by garnet-whole-rock Sm-Nd geochronology (ID-TIMS) at 696±4 Ma. Geochemically, these define a tholeiitic affinity, ranging from basaltic to dacitic compositions. Chondrite-normalized REE patterns define two trends: (1) metagabbros display smooth LREE-enriched patterns, negative Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu* = 0.57–0.93), flat HREE patterns, La N /Yb N ratios of 0.76–5.23 and ∑REE = 70–223; and (2) metatonalites show weakly enriched LREE patterns, positive Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu* = 1.27–2.35), and flat to slightly depleted HREE patterns, with La N /Yb N ratios of 1.1–1.7, and ∑REE = 13–34. In tectonic discrimination diagrams, most rocks plot within N-MORB fields.

Weakly deformed, hornblende-rich mafic dikes intrude the older Tonian, sequence. These dykes also belong to the tholeiitic series, ranging in composition from basalt to basaltic andesite. In tectonic discrimination diagrams they plot in the E-MORB or OIB fields. The REE show flat subparallelenriched patterns and minimal Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu* =1.06–0.85), La N /Yb N of 4.19–0.50; and ∑REE = 43–121. Zircons from one mafic dyke yielded an Ediacaran crystallization age of 606 ± 7 Ma.

Whereas the Ediacaran dykes are consistent in age and composition with those from other localities in Mexico that have been related to the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province during Rodinia breakup.In contrast, the Tonian-Cryogenian event(s) remain not fully understood, but they may reflect the consequence of a first plume-head impact beneath Rodinia followed by the onset of crustal extension

title: InSAR Data-Driven Building Damage Risk Assessment for Coastal South Asian Cities using BRASE Framework
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Isiaka, Ibrahim Opeyemi [1], Sadhasivam, Nitheshnirmal Opeyemi [2], Khorrami, Mohammad polytechnic institute and state [3], Wise, Clayton Opeyemi [4], Shirzaei, Manoochehr Opeyemi [5]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences Department, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA

abstract: Land subsidence represents a persistent yet undercharacterized hazard across part of South Asian coastal cities, where rapid urbanization, groundwater extraction, and sedimentary geology collectively drive land sinking. This study presents a multi-city assessment of vertical land motion (VLM) and building-scale subsidence risk across 14 South Asian coastal cities using Sentinel-1. InSAR-derived deformation estimates integrated within BRASE, a novel open-source building risk framework synthesizing hazard, vulnerability, and exposure across approximately 6.3 million building footprints. Mean subsidence rates range from -1.4 mm/yr in Visakhapatnam to -10.6 mm/yr in Chittagong, with temporally accelerating deformation identified in Chittagong, Karachi, Mumbai, Kochi, Visakhapatnam, and Thiruvananthapuram. Mean distortion angle thresholds indicative of building failure have in most areas within each city yet to exceed the 1/500 threshold. However, population exposure analysis reveals that tens of thousands of residents across Karachi, Chittagong, Mumbai, and Chennai occupy high- or very high-risk buildings, with risk burdens possibly falling disproportionately on economically vulnerable populations and smaller urban centers. Non-residential buildings exhibit systematically disproportionate fractional risk exposure, highlighting threats to economic stability. These findings provide an evidence base for integrating subsidence risk into disaster risk reduction, groundwater governance, and urban planning across South Asia.

title: Tracing Ediacaran to Earliest Cambrian Biodiversity: Global Patterns in the Trace Fossil Record
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Uttinger, Lara [1], Liu, Alex [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom
abstract:
The late Ediacaran to earliest Cambrian is a key interval in Earth’s history, when the first representatives of nearly all major metazoan phyla appear in the fossil record. Despite its importance, body fossil data from this interval remain sparse and unevenly distributed across palaeogeographic regions, limiting our ability to evaluate early macroevolutionary and biogeographic patterns. One such pattern is the presence of a latitudinal biodiversity gradient (LBG), which has been proposed to originate early in animal evolution but for which direct evidence is limited using the body fossil record alone.

Trace fossils provide an alternative and complementary archive of early animal activity, capturing behavioural diversification even where body fossils are rare or absent. Here we compile a comprehensive dataset of trace fossil occurrences spanning the Ediacaran–Terreneuvian interval from key palaeogeographic regions (including Avalonia, Laurentia and Baltica) to investigate large-scale patterns in the early diversification and distribution of animal behaviour. This dataset allows us to test whether latitudinal changes are detectable in the trace fossil record and to evaluate potential shifts from more provincial behavioural assemblages to increasingly cosmopolitan distributions during the earliest stages of the Cambrian Explosion.

In addition, this dataset facilitates comparisons between regional patterns and global diversity trends while accounting for uncertainty in Early Cambrian geography through the use of multiple palaeogeographic reconstructions. This approach allows us to evaluate how different reconstructions may influence interpretations of early biodiversity patterns.

By combining a global ichnological dataset with multiple palaeogeographic models, this research assesses the role of palaeogeography in shaping early animal ecosystems, and provides new constraints on macroevolutionary patterns during a critical interval in the history of life when body fossil evidence alone remains limited.

title: Evaluating Accessibility in Geoscience Programs at New England Universities for Students with Physical Disabilities
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: Cupples, Marin [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Maine at Farmington, Department of Earth & Environmental Science, Farmingto, ME, USA
abstract: This study evaluates accessibility in geoscience programs across New England for students with physical disabilities, with particular attention to fieldwork requirements, accommodation practices, institutional supports, and perceived barriers. Prior research has shown that disability inclusion in geoscience is shaped by professional perceptions, instructional design, and field-based norms (Atchison & Libarkin, 2016; Fairfax & Brown, 2019; Stokes et al., 2019). However, much of this work has focused on professional perceptions, single-institution contexts, or workshop-style interventions rather than cross-program comparison. Survey responses in this study indicate that most respondents believe firmly that accessible and inclusive instructional practices strongly influence student success, yet many report limited confidence in their department’s ability to accommodate students with mobility-related disabilities in field settings. Responses also reveal substantial uncertainty about whether departments provide formal training, dedicated funding, or wheelchair-accessible field opportunities. Together, these findings suggest that support for accessibility often exists in principle, but implementation remains uneven, under-resourced, and fragmented across institutional roles. This project extends prior literature by moving beyond studies centered on perception and single-site intervention toward a regional, comparative analysis of geoscience program practices, perceived barriers, and role-dependent knowledge. In doing so, it builds on previous calls for broader structural, instructional, and cultural change in geoscience accessibility (Atchison & Libarkin, 2016; Fairfax & Brown, 2019; Stokes et al., 2019). The findings can help inform more equitable field-course design and support the development of wheelchair-accessible geoscience field curricula.

title: Engaging Learners: Introducing Secondary School Students to Geoscience Through a Variety of Diverse, Innovative, and Inquiry-Driven Lessons and Curriculum Methods
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Smith, Janet E. [1]
affiliations: (1) Bixby High School, Bixby, OK, USA; Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract:
Today’s secondary school students tend to perceive geoscience as an abstract subject, often feeling it is disconnected from their lived experiences or less visible than other sciences offered in traditional curricula. Creative instructional design is essential to build meaningful entry points that encourage curiosity, foster scientific literacy, and promote broader participation. Throughout the school year, several classroom-based instructional approaches were implemented in a high school geoscience course, utilizing inquiry-driven, interdisciplinary pedagogy to make Earth science concepts personally meaningful.

One such approach was a forensic-style investigation centered on the anorthosite sample collected by the Apollo 15 astronauts. Tasked with constructing a scientific argument using the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework, students synthesized concepts of plate tectonics, mineral formation, and igneous petrology to solve the mystery of lunar crust formation. To bridge abstract theory with physical processes, students also engaged in hands-on modeling. They simulated mineral precipitation using eggshells and salts to create synthetic geodes, investigated isostasy using wooden blocks alongside raw granite and basalt samples, and evaluated structural integrity against seismic hazards by testing student-built designs on a custom shake table. Finally, a comparative regional case study challenged students to examine oolitic sand from the Bahamas alongside local Oklahoma soil samples, exploring how differing geologic settings dictate distinct environmental issues, climate impacts, resource management, and sustainability challenges.

Together, these strategies emphasize multiple entry points into Earth science through narrative engagement, localized relevance, interdisciplinary problem-solving, and authentic scientific argumentation. Preliminary classroom outcomes demonstrate that these methods significantly enhanced students' systems thinking capabilities and elevated general engagement. These scalable, adaptable frameworks offer secondary educators practical strategies for revitalizing geoscience curricula and broadening student interest in the Earth sciences.

title: The Subsurface Time Machine: Modeling Compaction Dynamics
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Davis Hughes, Joseph D [1], Ellis, John H. [2], White, Jeremy [3], Saberi, Laila [4]
affiliations: (1) INTERA Incorporated, Chicago, IL,
(2) Intera Inc, Houston, TX, USA
(3) INTERA Incorporated, Fort Collins, Coloradp, USA

abstract: Time, not just depth, is a governing dimension of subsidence. This presentation uses one-dimensional MODFLOW CSUB models to explore how interbed representation controls lag behavior, critical head evolution, and long-term compaction trajectories. The first part of the presentation contrasts delay versus no-delay interbeds, showing how models that omit delay artificially shorten system memory, accelerate preconsolidation head ratcheting, and distort future subsidence predictions under recovery or stabilization scenarios. The second part examines how many delay interbeds are needed to realistically capture subsurface behavior, progressing from single equivalent interbeds to multi-interbed configurations, and demonstrating the diminishing returns of excessive discretization. Sensitivity tests highlight the dominant role of interbed thickness and vertical hydraulic conductivity in setting characteristic response times. The presentation illustrates how simplified vertical models can clarify subsidence mechanics while avoiding unnecessary complexity.

abstract: This presentation discusses the Mile High Flood District's evolving approach to nature-based urban waterway design – an approach they’ve been experimenting with for over 10 years. The presentation emphasizes a shift from solely focusing on flood protection through hydrology and hydraulics to more holistic, nature-based designs that incorporate geomorphology, vegetation, and multiple community values. The urban context presents special challenges related to geomorphology and hydrology that require a balance of systems thinking, community input, and judgment to improve waterways corridors in a way that will optimally balance flood mitigation, ecology, and community. Example projects will be shared to illustrate the dynamics, considerations, and long-term outcomes including how some of our projects fared during the 2013 Colorado floods.

title: Volcanic Massive Sulfide Metals (VMS) at Detachment Faults in Arizona: Evidence for Overriding of the East Pacific Rise by the North American Plate
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits.
authors: Brooks, William E [1]
affiliations: (1) Colbrook Expl, Reston, VA, USA
abstract: Volcanic massive sulfide metals (Cu-Mn-Ba-Pb-Zn-Ag-Au) are present in the upper-plate volcanic rocks at pathway detachment faults in Arizona: 1) the Harcuvar Mountains [1400 ppm Cu, 5300 ppm Mn, 2300 ppm Ba, 180 ppm Pb, 1000 ppm Zn, 3-6 ppm Ag] and, 2) Picacho Peak [120 ppm Cu, 2700 ppm Mn, 2469 ppm Ba, 470 ppm Pb, 1100 ppm Zn, 2-3 ppm Ag]. Gold is present in upper plate rocks at four detachments. Overriding of a part of the 13,000 km long, 2,000-4,000 km wide East Pacific Rise (EPR) mantle convection cell (~500 km thick) by the North American plate provides a regional tectonic mechanism to explain VMS mineralization burned into the overriding crust by hydraulic fracturing along the pathway detachments—this mineralization has previously and consistently been described as hydrothermal. Other regional effects that are consistent with, and fingerprint, overriding of the EPR mantle convection cell by the North American plate include: 1) widespread K2O metasomatism and Na depletion (~12 wt% K2O; ~1.0 wt% Na2O), typical of VMS alteration halos, in upper-plate volcanic rocks at numerous detachments; 2) discordant K-Ar (whole-rock, biotite) and fission-track ages resulting from low temperature (250°-300°C) hydrothermal alteration at ~17-18 Ma in upper-plate volcanic rocks that time detachment; 3) shallow seismicity known since the 1960s; 4) thinned continental crust, extension, and regional detachment faulting in Arizona; and 5) heat flow of ~1.5-3.0 HFU in southwest Arizona comparable to EPR heat flow of 3 HFU. Regionally, these EPR-sourced metals are present at Lucifer-Boleo [Cu-Mn-Zn], Baja California, MX; Artillery Mtn. [1600 ppm Cu, 230,000 ppm Mn, 44,000 ppm Ba, 2300 ppm Zn, 5900 ppm Pb, Au, Ag], AZ; and the Olympic Peninsula [pillow basalts, Cu-Mn-Ba-Zn-Hg-Ag-Au], WA.

title: Carbon and Sulfur Isotope Constraints on Marine Redox Change During the End-Sunwaptan Extinction
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part I)
authors: Hermosillo, Natalie Grace [1], Gill, Benjamin Charles [2], Hagen, Amy [3], Pruss, Sara B. [4], Tarhan, Lidya [5]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(2) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(3) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(4) Smith College, Northampton, MA,
(5) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
abstract:
Multiple episodes of marine biodiversity loss occurred in the Early Paleozoic between the Cambrian Explosion and the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. Among these events, the end-Sunwaptan extinction (~490 million years ago) remains one of the least understood despite its impact on trilobites and other marine groups. The extinction has been interpreted as occurring in two principal pulses of faunal turnover: an extinction of the majority of a diverse shelf fauna followed by a second extinction of the survivors of the first pulse and their replacement by a low-diversity assemblage of trilobites. Several of the late Cambrian and early Ordovician extinction events, including the end-Marjuman and Stairsian extinctions, are also associated with pronounced positive carbon isotope excursions and evidence of marine deoxygenation.

To investigate the environmental conditions associated with end-Sunwaptan extinction, we analyzed carbonate carbon (δ¹³C carb ) and carbonate-associated sulfate sulfur (δ 34 S CAS ) isotope records from sedimentary successions at Lawson Cove, Utah; Lange Ranch, Texas; and Radford Dam, Virginia. These proxies provide insight into changes in the global carbon and sulfur cycles and marine redox conditions during this portion of the later Cambrian.

Our δ 13 C carb record at Lawson Cove captures the previously documented Hellnmaria Red Tops Boundary (HERB) negative carbon isotope excursion (−2‰) below the end-Sunwaptan extinction but shows no significant carbon isotope excursion across the interval with the extinctions. The δ 13 C carb data from Lange Ranch similarly do not record a pronounced positive carbon isotope excursion within the sampled interval. In contrast, δ 34 S CAS values from Lawson Cove increase before and through the extinction interval, consistent with enhanced pyrite burial, reducing marine conditions, and thus a perturbed marine sulfur cycle. Unlike the end-Marjuman and Stairsian extinctions, this event appears to lack a comparable perturbation to the carbon cycle despite evidence in the sulfur cycle for redox changes and similar extinction events. These results suggest that the driving mechanism(s) behind the end-Sunwaptan extinction may have differed from other later Cambrian and Early Ordovician extinction events.

abstract: Climate extremes such as floods, droughts, and heatwaves are becoming more frequent across South Asia. However, high-resolution vulnerability assessments are still limited in regions with scarce data. This study introduces an integrated remote sensing and machine learning framework to map climate vulnerability in Pakistan by leveraging multi-source geospatial and socioeconomic data. Satellite-derived datasets, such as land surface temperature, NDVI, precipitation anomalies, and soil moisture, are processed to capture environmental variability and long-term climate stress. These environmental variables are combined with population density, land-use patterns, and infrastructure accessibility to construct a multidimensional vulnerability dataset that represents exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Supervised machine learning models, such as Random Forest and XGBoost, are utilized to classify and predict spatial vulnerability patterns. Interpretability is improved using SHAP analysis, which reveals key environmental and socioeconomic drivers of risk. Temporal trend analysis assesses changes in vulnerability hotspots over time. The results reveal significant spatial clustering of high-vulnerability zones within floodplain regions and rapidly urbanizing areas, where environmental stress aligns with high population exposure and insufficient adaptive infrastructure. The findings demonstrate that nonlinear machine learning models surpass traditional index-based approaches in capturing complex interactions between climatic and socioeconomic factors. This research highlights the value of integrating Earth observation data with interpretable AI techniques for scalable climate risk assessment. The proposed framework supports disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation planning in data-limited regions of the Global South.

title: Scaling AI-Driven Salinity Advisory and Collaborative Water Governance for Climate-Resilient Agriculture in Coastal Bangladesh
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part II)
authors: Habib, Dr. Md Ahasan [1], Chakraborty, Shreya [2], Haque, Md. Rashedul [3], Bhattacharya, Prosun [4], Matheswaran, Karthikeyan [5], Jampani, Mahesh [6]
affiliations: (1) Research, NGO Forum for Public Health, Dhaka, BANGLADESH, Bangladesh; KTH-International Groundwater Arsenic Research Group, Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
(2) International Water Management Institute, Sri Lanka
(3) NGO Forum for Public Health, Dhaka, Bangladesh; University of Central Florida, Orlando, Florida, USA
(4) KTH ROYAL INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, Department of Sustainable Development,, Stockholm,
(5) International Water Management Institute, Sri Lanka
(6) International Water Management Institute, Sri Lanka
abstract:
Geogenic salinity intrusion driven by tidal dynamics, reductive dissolution of iron oxyhydroxides, and reduced upstream freshwater discharge constitutes one of the most severe co-mobilization hazards in the coastal aquifer systems of southwestern Bangladesh. In the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta, hydrogeochemical processes governing sodium, chloride, and co-mobilized trace constituent enrichment including elevated arsenic under reducing conditions interact directly with anthropogenic irrigation and sluice gate management, amplifying exposure pathways for approximately 35 million people across 19 coastal districts. Salinity-affected land has expanded 27% over three decades, with climate projections forecasting a 26–39% median increase in soil and surface water salinity by 2050. Despite this escalating geogenic risk, predictive management tools and institutional frameworks remain critically underdeveloped.

This study integrates hydrogeochemical field assessment with participatory governance analysis across four polders (22, 30, 31, 34/2P) in the Khulna region. A mixed-methods design combined household surveys (n = 384), Key Informant Interviews (n = 25), Focus Group Discussions (n = 10), and continuous electrical conductivity (ECw) monitoring at sluice gate entry points. A key methodological finding was that instrument-based salinity measurement detected moderate contamination (0.75–3 ppm) in 30% of water samples, versus only 8% identified through traditional taste-based methods a critical perceptual gap undermining risk-informed irrigation decisions. Field data revealed that 54% of households experienced salinity-induced crop losses, with water scarcity and unregulated gate operation exacerbating geogenic contaminant exposure during critical dry-season windows (January–May).

To operationalize predictive risk management, the study proposes an AI-driven hybrid LSTM–GRU forecasting framework delivering 30-day-ahead ECw predictions from hydro-climatic time-series data. This system is coupled with threshold-based irrigation advisories (safe threshold: ≤4 dS/m) and a phased governance roadmap encompassing Water Management Group reactivation, designated gate operator appointment, and BWDB–DAE coordination protocols aligned with the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 and Water Act 2013. Stakeholder surveys confirmed near-universal demand for forecast-based advisory services (98%). This study demonstrates that coupling hydrogeochemical forecasting with adaptive governance reform provides a scalable, evidence-based model for geogenic contaminant risk management in climate-vulnerable deltaic aquifer systems.

title: Modeling Fracture Networks and Fluid Flow in the Þeistareykir geothermal area, NE Iceland
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
abstract:
Structures such as fractures and faults play an important role as fluid flow pathways in geothermal reservoirs located in active tectonic regions. Fracture networks can act as either conduits or barriers to the movement of fluids and regulate the permeability, heat flow and associated geothermal activity in the subsurface. The Þeistareykir geothermal field, located within the Northern Volcanic Zone (NVZ) of Iceland, represents a structurally complex geothermal system governed by the interaction of both rift-related extension and transform-zone tectonics. Geothermal drilling results reveal substantial variations in temperature and permeability across the field, indicating strong structural controls on reservoir behaviour.

Fracture analysis based on borehole televiewer interpretation highlights the structural character of the permeable feed zones, ranging from high-density fracture clusters, damage zones, very large aperture fractures, lithological boundaries and localized silicic intrusions. Moreover, fracture orientations also vary widely, implying that fluid flow is accommodated by multiple intersecting fracture sets rather than a single dominant structural trend. These results strongly indicate that geothermal fluid movement in Þeistareykir is constrained by the fault and fracture networks. To better understand these structural controls, we integrate a range of geological, geophysical, petrophysical, and drilling datasets from the Þeistareykir geothermal field into building 3D discrete fracture network (DFN) models across all major lithological units. Fluid flow simulations are performed through the DFNs to quantify permeability and its anisotropy. Such integrated structural characterization and modelling approach provides new insights into the fracture network geometry and connectivity at reservoir scale and how it governs bulk permeability and preferential fluid pathways in this tectonically complex environment. This study will lead to a better prediction of the reservoir behaviour and defining geothermal reservoir boundaries, ensuring the sustainable management and long-term utilization of geothermal resources in the region.

title: Geochemical evolution, health risk and source apportionment of high arsenic and fluoride groundwater in semiarid Gilgit, Pakistan
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part I)
authors: Javed, Asif [1], Rashid, Abdur [2], Ayub, Muhammad [3], Bibi, Sara [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciencies, Hazara University, Mansehra, Pakistan
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciencies, Hazara University, Mansehra, Pakistan
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciencies, Hazara University, Mansehra, Pakistan
(4) National Centre of Excellence in Geology, University of Peshawar, Peshawar, Pakistan
abstract: Worldwide, more than 200 million people are affected by high arsenic (As), and fluoride (F-) groundwater causing arsenicosis and fluorosis health concerns in people. This study was therefore carried out to investigate the co-occurrence and geochemical hazards of high As and F- groundwater in semiarid Gilgit, Pakistan. Groundwater samples (n=48) were evaluated for As, and F- contamination using δ18O, δ2H and δ34S isotopes to trace the origin of groundwater pollution. The As, and F- concentration in groundwater ranged from 0.50-42.2 µg/L, and 0.4-6.5 mg/L, respectively. The abundance of higher As and F- groundwater were 30.2 %, and 28.0%, respectively. The significant positive correlation between As and F- were observed with pH, TDS, EC, Na+, HCO3-, and negated with Ca+2, Mg+2, and NO3- in poor aquifers. The F/Cl ratio, δ2H, and δ18O and As with SO4 revealed that evaporation favored As and F- enrichment in aquifers. The groundwater facies showed that NaHCO3 and NaCl contributed 42.7%, and CaHCO3 43%, reflecting the alteration of CaHCO3 to NaHCO3 type. The saturation indices (SI) values of fluorite, in groundwater, increased from -2.60 to -0.56, and F- from 0.2 to 6.6 mg/L. The higher δ2H and δ18O values indicate intense evaporation, whereas the depleted values indicate precipitation mechanisms. However, δ2H and δ18O isotopes conclude that all water significantly deviates from the local meteoric water line (LMWL), showing a common origin of water from granitic rock, water-rock interaction, mineral dissolution, aquifer sediment, and evaporation processes. The photomicrographs of granite and granodiorite rocks investigated under a polarized microscope determined the dominance of fluorite, quartz, calcite, biotite, muscovite, hornblende, plagioclase, and epidote minerals. The health risk and community arsenicosis indexing (CAI), and community fluorosis indexing (CFI) reveal that children are more susceptible to As and F- toxicity in the region. The CAI, and CFI values recorded (CAI) >1.0×10-4 and >0.6 reflecting moderate to severe As and F- contamination in the entire region. The geochemical data help minimize the As, and F- contamination in the groundwater. Therefore, the local government and NGOs are recommended to install water de-arsenication and de-fluorination plants to reduce health risks from As, and F-

title: Palynological analysis of the Upper Strawn Group on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin, Katz Field, Stonewall County, Texas
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Adejoh, Christian [1], Zobaa, Mohamed [2], Flaig, Peter [3]
affiliations: (1) Texas Commission on Environmental Commission, Midland, Texas, USA; Geosciences, The University of Texas Permian Basin, Odessa, Texas, USA
(2) Geosciences, The University of Texas Permian Basin, Odessa, Texas, USA
(3) Bureau of Economic Geology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract: The Pennsylvanian Strawn Group on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin is a regionally important mixed siliciclastic–carbonate succession that hosts diverse hydrocarbon reservoirs. However, the evolution of its depositional systems and internal stratigraphic architectures are only recently becoming better understood. Despite the Strawn’s considerable economic value and the importance of accurate stratigraphic correlations across the Eastern Shelf, palynological studies of the Strawn Group remain limited. In fact, the economically significant Upper Strawn interval has not previously been analyzed using dedicated palynological or palynofacies methods. To partially address this, we sampled the Phillips CB Long C-16 core from the Katz Field in Stonewall County, Texas that contains deposits of the Upper Strawn. Twenty-three core samples were examined for palynology, revealing a low-diversity assemblage of 12 sporomorph taxa. The presence of Camptotriletes certus likely limits the stratigraphic age to Desmoinesian, aligning with established chronostratigraphic frameworks for the Eastern Shelf. Quantitative palynofacies analysis, based on 200 palynomorph counts per sample, indicates a systematic upward transition through the section from a lower interval dominated by amorphous organic matter (AMOM), reflecting offshore-to-distal delta-front depositional environments, to an upper interval rich in phytoclasts, consistent with progradation into a higher-energy delta-front-to-shoreface or tidal shelf system. These findings offer new biostratigraphic and paleoenvironmental insights into the regional stratigraphic framework of the Upper Strawn Formation on the Eastern Shelf.

title: Using a Modified Water Table Fluctuation Method to Constrain the Groundwater Recharge Patterns of a Coral Atoll
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Dimicco, Abby [1]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach, CA, USA
abstract: Atolls are biodiversity hotspots where coral reefs surround sandy "motu" (Polynesian for islets) to create a central lagoon. Due to their low-lying nature, atolls are highly susceptible to climate change, making an understanding of freshwater resources crucial for water supply management. Atolls function as interconnected land-ocean systems where groundwater serves as the primary conduit for nutrient flow, but our current understanding of nutrient cycling is limited by a lack of data on recharge gradients (Steibl, 2024). The goal of this study is to reveal groundwater recharge gradients of the Tetiaroa Atoll in French Polynesia using CTD data collected from piezometers on four motu: Honuea, Onetahi, Iti, and Rahi. Each motu is characterized by differences in hydrogeology (low vs high hydraulic conductivity aquifers), ecology (presence of seabirds and/or rats, high vs low biomass density, and native vs nonnative vegetation), and climate (wet vs dry season). The evaluation of recharge on each motu will establish new hydrogeologic datasets to better understand the impacts of hydrogeology, ecological restoration, and climate on atoll groundwater and create a baseline for future researchers to estimate nutrient fluxes within the groundwater system. I will calculate groundwater recharge on each motu over a three-year period using a modified Water Table Fluctuation (mWTF) Method, which defines recharge as specific yield times change in height over change in time for each recharge episode. I will first filter out tidal oscillations from water table depth data using the Butterworth low-pass filter to better constrain recharge by meteoric waters. I will process pump test data in AQTESOLV from tests conducted at each motu in January 2026 to estimate specific yield. I will use the Episodic Master Recession (EMR) method, which focuses on hydrologic episodes instead of fixed time intervals, to calculate changes in water table depth at each given episode divided by change in time. Then I will make calculations using the mWTF to establish a dataset of groundwater recharge rates from each motu. I predict Onetahi to have the lowest recharge rates and Iti or Rahi to have the highest recharge rates due to differences in ecology and hydrogeology. These findings will advance our understanding of atoll groundwater systems, providing critical insight into the resilience of island freshwater resources in an era of rising seas.

title: Terrestrial analogue analysis of Oasis Crater, Libya and regional tectonic fabrics supports a hybrid model for Polygonal Impact Crater formation
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Binkley, Amanda Paige [1], Crane, Kelsey [2], Potter-McIntyre, Sally [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, Carbondale, IL,
(2) Geology, Seres Engineering & Services LLC, Charleston, South Carolina,
(3) Geology, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, Carbondale, IL,
abstract: The geometries of Polygonal Impact Craters (PICs), impact craters with straight rim segments, are important tools for investigating subtle or hidden tectonic patterns on planetary bodies. Insights into PIC formation have increased in recent years, with studies demonstrating associations between tectonic features and PIC rim orientations (e.g., Aittola et al., 2010; Beddingfield and Cartwright, 2020; Yazici et al., 2024; Beddingfield et al., 2024). Despite these studies, terrestrial comparisons of complex PICs and surrounding tectonic structures are lacking. For example, Meteor Crater in Arizona remains the most well-known and -studied PIC on Earth, yet being a simple, square crater, it does not represent the norm for planetary PIC observations. We used a GIS and R statistical code to map and analyze multi-scale tectonic features and preserved crater geology for a prominent PIC in Libya, Oasis Crater, and found that the crater morphology demonstrates a strong geometric correlation to surrounding tectonic structures and fabrics. Through analyzing these geometric relationships, we found that the central uplift utilized deeper, older tectonic fabrics than the outer rings and that a combination of excavation along more surficial fracture sets and slumping along crater walls during modification influenced the rings and central peak formation. Our observations motivate a hybrid PIC formation model that relies on both excavation and modification stages, and our results suggest that different geologic units of complex PICs can be utilized as mapping tools on other rocky bodies to investigate different types, ages, and depths of various tectonic structures.

title: Petrogenetic and Mineralization Age of the Gaositai Chromium-bearing Ultramafic Complex in the Northern Margin of the North China Craton and Constraints on Supercontinent Breakup
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: Li, Fanglan [1], Wang, Lu [2]
affiliations: (1) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, China University of Geosciences (Wuhan), Wuhan, Hubei, China
(2) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, China University of Geosciences (Wuhan), Wuhan, Hubei, China
abstract: The petrogenetic and mineralization age, material sources, and tectonic setting of the chromium-bearing ultramafic-mafic complex in Gaositai, Hebei, remain highly controversial. A comprehensive study was conducted through field structural mapping, combined with petrography, whole-rock geochemistry, and LA-ICP-MS U-Pb dating of zircon and apatite. Zircon U-Pb geochronology of the host rocks (including granite porphyry, gneiss, felsic mylonite, and syenite) associated with the comagmatic origin of the Gaositai chromite deposit indicates that the formation age of the deposit is ca. 1.71 Ga (Mesoproterozoic), consistent with the timing of the Columbia supercontinent breakup. In contrast, apatite in the granite porphyry and gneiss largely preserves magmatic signatures but has been altered by hydrothermal fluids; their U-Pb ages (ca. 400 Ma) record a later magmatic-metamorphic event. This age corresponds to a regional thermal event triggered by lithospheric extension following the early Paleozoic collision between the Bainaimiao island arc and the northern margin of the North China Craton, which superimposed and reworked the pre-existing deposit. During the Mesoproterozoic, mantle-derived ultramafic magmas intruded in an extensional setting. Repeated magma replenishment, fractional crystallization, and injection of Fe-rich melts in shallow magma chambers promoted chromite saturation and crystallization, accompanied by partial melting of the lower crust that generated A-type felsic magmas. The protoliths of comagmatic granite porphyry and granitic gneiss are A 2 -type granites, enriched in alkalis and low in CaO and MgO contents, reflecting crust-mantle interaction in a rift environment. In summary, this study provides new geochronological and geochemical constraints for elucidating the metallogenic mechanisms of Mesoproterozoic stratiform chromite deposit along the northern margin of the North China Craton and the regional tectonic evolution.

title: Architecture and Evolution of Transcrustal Magmatic Systems: Multi-Level Reservoir Processes in the Early Jurassic Tongshi Syenite, Luxi Terrane, Eastern North China Craton
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: Xu, Qi-lai [1], Yu, Hao-cheng [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing, (None), China
(2) School of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing,
abstract:
Crustal magmatic systems facilitate transcrustal transit of mantle materials, wherein transport, storage and differentiation at multiple crustal levels govern the physicochemical evolution of alkaline magma. The Early Jurassic Tongshi syenite, Luxi Terrane, eastern North China Craton, represents a unique intraplate alkaline intrusion exhibiting diverse lithologies (clinopyroxene-bearing and garnet-bearing porphyritic syenite, mafic microgranular porphyritic syenite enclaves (MME), and aplite) and complex phenocryst assemblages, recording transcrustal magmatic differentiation. This study integrates petrography, mineralogy, bulk rock geochemistry, and Sr-Nd-Pb-Ba isotope geochemistry to reconstruct plumbing system and understand petrogenesis of the Tongshi syenite.

Based on paragenetic relationship, mineral texture, and composition, phenocrysts from all syenite lithologies are classified into two distinct groups. Group1 comprises clinopyroxene displaying either equilibrium crystallization cores or inherited mantle cores with peritectic reaction rims, high-Mg# amphibole (Mg# = Mg 2+ /(Mg 2+ + Fe 2+ )), and high-Ca plagioclase. Empirical geothermobarometry indicates crystallization depths of ~35-13 km at ~1165-842°C, representing a primitive, deep magma reservoir at the crust-mantle boundary that preserve substantial mantle signatures. Group2 consists of low-Mg# amphibole, andradite, low-Ca plagioclase, and sanidine exhibiting well-developed equilibrium crystallization textures, estimated at ~12-7 km depth and ~785-715°C, representing an evolved, shallow reservoir at the upper and lower crust boundary. Similar but slightly enriched Sr-Nd isotopic signatures of phenocrysts from deep to shallow reservoirs indicate their cogenetic relationship. This multi-level reservoir plumbing architecture is consistent with recent magnetotelluric observation.

Equilibrium melts compositions estimated from the deep reservoir phenocrysts consistent with ~50% amphibole + clinopyroxene and ~10-15% plagioclase fractionation trends, suggesting the development of a gabbroic crystal mush within the deep reservoir. While melts estimated from low-Mg# amphibole, together with MME matrix and aplite compositions indicate shallow-level evolution was dominated by ~50% amphibole, ~15% andradite, and ~20% plagioclase fractionation, comprising a garnet-bearing dioritic crystal mush.

Depleted Sr-Nd-Pb isotope ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr i = 0.7057±27, ε Nd (t) = 1.30±1.06, 206 Pb/ 204 Pb i = 18.061±0.007) and weakly fractionated DMM-like Ba isotope (δ 137 Ba = 0.0383 ± 0.029) signatures of all syenite samples indicate a depleted subcontinental lithospheric mantle (SCLM) source. Inherited clinopyroxene with low Hf/Sm and high CaO/Al 2 O 3 further attests to carbonatite metasomatism of the SCLM source. Estimated deep reservoir melt also align with 6-10% batch melting of garnet lherzolite, implying magma was originated from the bottom of SCLM triggered by asthenospheric upwelling.

title: World-class pegmatite uranium deposit at Husab, Namibia: Enrichment mechanisms and insights
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: Li, Shanshan [1], Deng, Jun [2]
affiliations: (1) China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing 100083, China, State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, Frontiers Science Center for Deep-time Digital Earth, Beijing, China

(2) China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing 100083, China, State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, Frontiers Science Center for Deep-time Digital Earth, Beijing, China
abstract: Pegmatite-type uranium deposits constitute a major global source of uranium. Enrichment of uranium in magmatic-hydrothermal system is associated with three processes, namely partial melting of the source, magmatic fractional crystallization, and hydrothermal fluid activity. However, the relative efficiency of each process has remained poorly quantified. In this study, we performed thermodynamic phase equilibrium modeling and Li‑Ba‑Sr isotope analyses on the Husab deposit in Namibia. Our modeling results indicate that under low water content and low degrees (<20%) of partial melting, uranium can be concentrated up to ~120 ppm in the melt. During fractional crystallization to 90%, the crystallization of biotite, plagioclase, K‑feldspar and quartz enriches uranium in the residual melt to ~180 ppm. Extensive alteration features including silicification, fluoritization, sericitization, pyritization and chloritization point to strong fluid‑rock interaction, which is further supported by isotopic data. Specifically, the pegmatite displays high δ⁷Li values from –2.39 to +24.33 together with low δ ¹³⁸/¹³⁴ Ba values from –1.29 to +1.20 and low δ⁸⁸/⁸⁴Sr values from –0.19 to 0.43, demonstrating that fluid‑rock interaction promotes additional uranium mobilization and enrichment. Collectively, our data suggest that fluid‑rock interaction, rather than partial melting or fractional crystallization alone, is the primary driver for efficient uranium hyper‑enrichment in granitic pegmatite systems. These results provide new quantitative constraints on the ore-forming process of the Husab deposit and underscore the critical role of water‑rock interaction in generating giant pegmatite-type uranium deposits.

authors: PALEI, RINA RANI [1], Gupta, Anil [2], Vleeschouwer, David De [3], Samant , Rohit [4], Gaudio, Arianna V. Del [5], Sanyal , Prasanta [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, India, Kharagpur Technology, West Bengal, India
(2) Geology and Geophysics Department, Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, India, Kharagpur Technology, West Bengal, India
(3) Institute of Geology and Palaeontology,, University of Münster, Münster, Münster, India

abstract: The Indonesian Gateway (IG) underwent significant tectonic restriction of deep-water circulation during the early Miocene, and subsequent tectonic adjustments have modulated both regional surface hydrography and global thermohaline circulation since the Late Miocene. Nevertheless, the surface ocean dynamics in the Southeastern Indian Ocean (SEIO) and Southwestern Pacific Ocean (SWPO) were coupled through this tectonic and climate forcing, which remains poorly constrained. Progressive restriction in the Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) likely reduced poleward heat transport, driving a weakening of the Leeuwin Current (LC) in the SEIO while simultaneously intensifying the East Australian Current (EAC) in the SWPO, which needs to be investigated. To address this, we used planktic foraminiferal assemblage data and stable isotope ratios from Site 763 (20°35.20′S, 112°12.50′E; 1367 m water depth) in the SEIO and Site 1195 (20°24.28′S, 152°40.24′E; 420 m water depth) in the SWPO. At Site 763A, planktic foraminiferal records document a regional extinction of Globoquadrina dehiscence in the SEIO at ~9 Ma, approximately 3 Ma earlier than its global extinction at ~5.6 Ma. We interpreted this as evidence for the restriction of Pacific intermediate water to the Indian Ocean and the establishment of the modern LC behaviour from the elevated mixed layer assemblage. A coeval rise in siliciclastic input from ~9.2 Ma points to enhanced terrigenous influx driven by the onset of semi-arid conditions across NW Australia, likely reflecting the initiation of the Australian monsoon system as the Australian plate drifted into the tropical latitudes. At Site 1195, proxy records indicate surface cooling and elevated primary productivity during the Late Miocene (~7.5–6.5 Ma), accompanied by elevated relative abundances of the surface-dwelling taxa Globigerina bulloides and Globigerina glutinata. Between ~5.4 and 3.3 Ma, EAC strengthening is linked to the expansion of the West Pacific Warm Pool (WPWP). Thereafter, intensified Southern Ocean cooling coupled with progressive ITF reduction drove a weakening of the EAC, promoting the progressive replacement of warm, oligotrophic WPWP waters by cooler, more productive subantarctic-influenced water masses from ~3.3 Ma to the Holocene.

title: The Curious Case of the Ultra-high Peaks in the Western United States: Products of Neogene/Quaternary Tectonism
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: MATTHEWS, VINCENT [1], Cumella, Stephen P. [2]
affiliations: (1) N/A, Eleva, WI, USA
(2) N/A, Ouray, Colorado, USA
abstract:
More than 1,000 ultra-high peaks decorate the landscape of seven of the eleven western states. Their lofty eminences rise to heights between 13,000 (3962m) and 14,505 feet (4421m) above mean sea level─ the “13ers” and “14ers.” These ultra-high peaks cluster into three tectonic provenances of coeval, but differing origins. The peaks in all three areas reached their heights during the Neogene and Quaternary Periods (Ng/Q).

Contractional tectonism (orogeny) built only two of the peaks, which are volcanic edifices of the Cascades Range. Yellowstone’s dynamic hotspot created another thirty-six of the ultra-high peaks by doming and footwall uplift of the fractured crust. However, GPS and thermochronological data combine with geologic relations to show that a cohesive system of Ng/Q regional extension (taphrogeny) created most of the peaks. Thermochronological data is invaluable in understanding the timing and amount of uplift but can also be misleading (e.g., the Front Range of Colorado).

Regional, extensional tectonism thinned about 350,000 square miles (906,495 sq km) of the crust during the Ng/Q. The thinned crust partially melted the underlying mantle causing varying degrees of buoyancy and magmatism. A cohesive Ng/Q extensional tectonic event uplifted the footwalls of normal faults in the Southern Rocky Mountains, Uinta Mountains, Southern Sierra Nevada, and Basin & Range. Collectively, these footwalls in the four regions elevated the remaining 96.5% of the ultra-high peaks. The tectonically active areas of crustal extension were/are driven by interactions between the Pacific and North American plates.

This extensional tectonism is as much as 1,000 kilometers across. The uplift of ultra-high peaks is anchored on the west by Mount Whitney (14,505’ AMSL) and on the east by Mount Elbert (14,438’ AMSL), the first and second highest peaks in the conterminous United States. Our tectonic model for Ng/Q tectonism in the western United States is built by applying 21 st century datasets and tools to concepts reported in the 1973 topical session of the GSA Rocky Mountain Section meeting. The inference that ultra-high peaks in the Western United States are ‘leftovers’ from the Laramide orogeny, or are the result of epeirogeny, is not supportable by the data.

title: Codisposal of acid generating tailings and waste rock: A Case Study for the Alacrán Copper-Gold-Silver Mine Project, Cordoba, Colombia.
session_title: New approaches and emerging technologies for the prevention, control, and remediation of acidic rock drainage and legacy mine waste
authors: Williamson, Patrick Thomas [1], Muir, Wilson [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental and Mining, INTERA, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Knight Piesold, Thunder Bay, ontario, Canada
abstract:
Disposal of potentially acid generating tailings and waste rock frequently poses significant long-term challenges for mining projects. While the geochemistry of the tailings and waste rock at a project may be very similar, their acid drainage potential can differ significantly due to differences in grain size, storage methods, and physical controls affecting the availability of atmospheric oxygen (diffusion rate) and hydraulic conductivity. These in turn control sulfide oxidation rates and mobilization of the oxidation products, respectively.

Fine-grained tailings, especially when partially or completely saturated, have limited oxygen diffusion rates and low hydraulic conductivity. These factors vary across the spectrum of tailings deposition methods, from traditional spigotted disposal to thickened, paste, or “dry stack” disposal. Waste rock is frequently exposed to the atmosphere and can have a much higher infiltration rate and hydraulic conductivity to drain oxidation products. An emerging technology that makes use of the physical limitations on pyrite oxidation in tailings to limit acid drainage from waste rock is co-disposal or co-mingling, where reactive rock is mixed with tailings.

The Alacrán Cu-Au-Ag Mine Project in northwestern Colombia will produce potentially acid generating waste rock during mining. Disposal sites are limited due to the steep and rolling terrain. Water management is also challenging, as the site receives approximately 3 m of rain annually.

Based on an evaluation of site conditions, waste characteristics, and the mine plan, co-disposal was selected as the preferred waste management strategy for this project. Thickened tailings will be deposited across the entire waste management basin. Waste rock will be placed and spread across the basin by a dozer, away from the perimeter embankments. The tailings will partially penetrate the waste rock voids, increasing the available tailings storage volume by approximately 20–30%. Waste rock will be buried in lifts and separated by subsequent tailings deposition to encapsulate the waste rock, minimize infiltration and oxygen diffusion, and prevent acid generation and metal leaching. This waste management strategy will develop a low permeability waste deposit, reduce foundation seepage, and store all wastes from mining and ore processing in one location. Post-closure monitoring requirements will also be reduced by creating a landform that will blend into the local topography and shed runoff to the environment.

title: Geological Resources Beyond Extraction: A Perspective on Provisioning Geosystem Services and Geoheritage Values
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Garcia, Maria da Glória [1]
affiliations: (1) University of São Paulo, Institute of Geosciences, São Paulo, SP, Brazil
abstract:
Resource extraction and geoheritage conservation are commonly approached as conflicting perspectives, particularly in contexts involving mining, quarrying, fossil extraction, energy production and other activities that transform geological landscapes. However, extractive activities have historically played a central role not only in economic and social development, but also in exposing geological features, advancing geoscientific knowledge and revealing sites of geoheritage significance. Recent discussions in geoconservation and geodiversity studies have increasingly highlighted the complex relationships between extraction, geosystem services, geoheritage values and sustainable territorial management.

This contribution presents a perspective on geological resources as provisioning geosystem services, arguing that mineral, water and energy resources are frequently approached and managed as benefits provided by geodiversity, even when this relationship is not explicitly recognised. Rather than viewing geological resources only as commodities, the geosystem services approach broadens discussions on their scientific, cultural, social, economic and ethical dimensions, recognising that nature involves different forms of value relevant to governance and public decision-making. In this context, geoheritage values are understood not only through conservation and scientific relevance, but also through their contribution to societies, territorial identities and long-term sustainability. This perspective also contributes to broader discussions on the role of geodiversity as an essential component of nature and as part of the abiotic foundation of socioecological systems.

Examples from Brazil demonstrate both opportunities and challenges associated with geological resource use. In regions such as the Seridó UNESCO Global Geopark and the Carajás National Forest, extractive landscapes coexist with sites of high geological, hydrological, speleological and cultural significance, illustrating how these areas may simultaneously support resource provision, environmental regulation, cultural meanings and knowledge generation. At the same time, extractive activities may generate irreversible losses, environmental degradation and governance conflicts, reinforcing the need for integrated management strategies capable of balancing resource use, conservation and intergenerational responsibility, especially in contexts of increasing demand for geological resources and growing environmental pressures.

title: What the Clay? Using GPR and Vibracores to Investigate the Origin and Extent of a Unique Sediment Layer Found in a Prograding Salt Marsh in Greenbackville, VA.
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Stutz, Rhianna I [1], Oakley, Adrienne J [2], Cornell, Sean [3], Sherrod, Laura [4], Friehauf, Kurt [5]
affiliations: (1) Kutztown University, Prescott, WI, USA
(2) Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
(3) Shippensburg University, Shippensburg, PA, USA
(4) Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
(5) Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
abstract:
The Greenbackville salt marsh is located on a promontory point along the western edge of Chincoteague Bay (CB), Eastern Shore, Virginia. Previous work at this site has documented an unusual bay-ward progradation of the saltmarsh over the Holocene. Here we present an analysis of an anomalous clay layer sitting directly below the disconformity interpreted as the Late Pleistocene– Early Holocene transition.

The blue-grey clay layer is sampled in 7 vibracores extracted from the modern salt marsh beginning at depths of 125-150 cm and thickening toward CB. The clay caps an organic carbon-rich sandy silt layer likely deposited in a lacustrine environment circa (46-28 ka cal bp, Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3)). The disconformity separates the clay from Late-Holocene to ~1800 y cal bp bedded and massive fining-upward quartz sands deposited in a high energy coastal plain environment.

XRD analysis indicated that the clay layer consists of predominately kaolinite, montmorillonite, illite, detrital plagioclase and muscovite, and diagenetic pyrite. SEM imaging revealed the clay layer contains fecal pellets, pine pollen, marshmallow pollen, and diatom fragments, including Cyclotella distinguenda, a centric diatom found in freshwater lakes and rivers. The lack of oxidized iron, the presence of freshwater diatoms, pollen, and fecal pellets indicate that the clay layer was likely deposited in a deep pond/lake.

Taken together, the sediments in the vibracores reveal Pleistocene environmental change in the region, i.e. from a fluvial system to a sand-dominated coastal plain to a muddy marine bay, and the overall bay-ward movement of the salt marsh to its current location.

GPR radargrams show primarily horizonal reflections correlating with modern marsh facies and sand layers in the cores. More detailed GPR interpretations and correlation with new sediment cores will allow us to map the extent and lateral variations of the clay layer in the subsurface. Further analysis of microfossils and other mineralogical indicators of the depositional environment’s pH and oxidation state will help more tightly constrain the type of vegetation, climate, and water-level conditions present during the time of environmental transition when the clay was deposited. This transitional clay layer will provide clues to the puzzling bay-ward growth of the Greenbackville salt marsh and add to our record of post-MIS 3 coastal evolution and relative sea level history of the Delmarva.

title: Hydrogen Generation Potential from Glauconitic Sand During Water-Rock Reactions: Insights from Hydrothermal Experiments
session_title: Advances in Understanding and Predicting the Geochemical and Microbiological Conversion and Transport of Hydrogen in Deep Geological Repositories
authors: Darwish, Shahad [1], Salisu, Anas [2], Mohammed, Isah [3], Al-Ramadan, Khalid A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, College of Petroleum Eng. and Geosciences, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
(2) Geoscience, College of Petroleum Eng. and Geosciences, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
(3) Petroleum Engineering, College of Petroleum Eng. and Geosciences, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
(4) Geoscience, College of Petroleum Eng. and Geosciences, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
abstract: Natural hydrogen exploration has focused largely on ultramafic systems, yet Fe-bearing sedimentary minerals may also generate H 2 during water-rock interaction if reactive iron is available. Herein, the evaluation of the hydrogen-generation potential of glauconitic sand from the Arnager Greensand Formation, using batch experiments that vary temperature and solid-liquid ratio, was conducted. Across the investigated conditions, the generated gas is commonly H 2 -dominant, with impurities such as H 2 S and CO gases whose proportions vary with temperature and solid-liquid ratio. Post-reaction XRD and XRF data indicate that quartz remains the dominant framework phase, whereas glauconite abundance and bulk Fe decrease relative to the starting material. These changes are consistent with selective alteration of the Fe-bearing fraction during H 2 -generating reactions. These results suggest that glauconitic sands may represent an underexplored sedimentary host for geologic hydrogen generation, while also highlighting the importance of sulfur control, carbon speciation, and fluid-rock ratio in determining gas quality.

title: Marine to Non-Marine Correlation of the Norian Alaunian-Sevatian Substage Boundary: Chronostratigraphic Implications
session_title: ‘GTS2030’ – Toward an Open Science Geologic Time Scale
authors: Tanner, Lawrence [1]
affiliations: (1) Biological & Environmental Cciences, Le Moyne College, Syracuse, NY, USA
abstract:
Correlation of stage and substage boundaries between the marine and terrestrial realms and establishing chronometric ages for these boundaries continues to be problematic. One illustrative example from the Late Triassic is the boundary between the Alaunian and Sevatian substages of the Norian stage. This boundary, originally defined in the marine realm by ammonoid biostratigraphy, is now widely defined by conodont biostratigraphy, specifically the first occurrence of Mockina bidentata , particularly in the Tethyan realm. Although the taxon used is cosmopolitan, the zone base appears to be slightly diachronous between Tethys and Panthalassa. The biostratigraphically anchored composite magnetostratigraphy for the marine Late Triassic places the base of the Mo. bidentata Zone at the base of the UT21n or high in the UT20r magnetochron as currently defined in the Geomagnetic Polarity Time Scale (GPTS-B) [1]. When correlated to the magnetostratigraphy of the terrestrial Newark Basin, the base of the Mo. bidentata Zone appears equivalent to the base of the E15n or upper E14r magnetochron. The current version of the Newark Astronomic Polarity Time Scale, based on fitting the lithologic cyclicity of Newark Basin strata to the 405 kyr long eccentricity (McGlaughlin) cycle places the Alaunian-Sevatian substage boundary at an age of ca. 213.4 to 213.8 Ma (allowing for diachroneity of the Mo. bidentata Zone base) [2]. The Manicouagan impact event in eastern Canada is well-dated to 215.5 Ma [3] and an ejecta layer in Japan linked to the Manacouagan structure occurs very near the base of the Mo. bidentata Zone [4]. If the age of the Manicouagan impact is reasonably accurate, the Newark time scale is inaccurate by ca. 1.7 to 2.1 Myr. Detrital zircon ages from the lower Sonsela Member of the Chinle Group core PFNP-1A suggest that the date of the Manicouagan impact occurs within the upper PF5n or lowermost PF4r magnetochrons, or potentially within an unconformity within this interval [5].
