title: Evaluating Cross-Well Generalization for Subsurface Pore Pressure Prediction Using Explainable Machine Learning
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: , Ramyashree [1], Amjad, Muhammad Raiees [2], Amjad, Tehmina [3]
affiliations: (1) Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, San Jose, California, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Bahria University, Islamabad, Pakistan
(3) Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, San Jose, CA, USA
abstract:
Accurate pore pressure prediction is critical for safe drilling operations, well planning, and the prevention of hazardous events such as blowouts and formation damage. However, machine learning models trained on a specific set of wells often perform poorly when applied to well log data from different geological regions. While this limitation is widely recognized in the petroleum and geoscience industries, less is understood about why certain features and model architectures generalize more effectively across wells than others. Understanding this behavior is particularly important for building robust AI systems that can operate reliably in data-scarce subsurface environments.

To investigate this problem, the study evaluated five machine learning architectures, including Random Forest, XGBoost, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTM), and a deep feedforward neural network, using data from 21 wells in the Potwar Basin, Pakistan. The models were tested under a strict leave-one-well-out protocol in which each well was completely excluded during training and used only for blind evaluation. This setup was designed to simulate realistic cross-well deployment conditions rather than conventional random train-test splitting.

In their standard form, all models failed to generalize across wells and even performed worse than a naïve baseline that simply predicted the mean pore pressure. These findings demonstrate how conventional random cross-validation can conceal severe generalization failures and emphasize that evaluation design is as important as model selection itself. To overcome this limitation, the study incorporated targeted domain adaptation, which substantially improved performance. The ensemble framework achieved the best results, reaching an R2R^2R2 value of 0.938 on the blind test well.

Beyond predictive accuracy, the study also investigated why certain models performed better than others. SHAP-based explainability analysis revealed that the Eaton ratio was the most influential physics-informed feature in both tree-based models, contributing up to 29% of prediction influence in XGBoost. In contrast, deep resistivity contributed negligibly despite being included in training. The analysis further showed that shallow intervals were better handled by tree-based models, whereas deeper zones favored neural networks, reflecting changes in subsurface pressure mechanisms with depth. Overall, the findings demonstrate that physics-informed features contribute meaningfully to prediction performance and that explainability analysis provides a practical way to verify when models genuinely utilize physically relevant information.

title: A Multi-Basin Open-Source Benchmark Comparing Physics-Informed and Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network Synthetic Well Log Generators under Bayesian Optimization
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Monteiro, Tiago [1], Carneiro, Tomás [2], Amjad, Muhammad Raiees [3], Yoon, Ilmi [4], Amjad, Tehmina [5]
affiliations: (1) Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, San Jose, CA, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Department of Geology, University of Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Bahria University, Islamabad, Pakistan
(4) Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, San Jose, CA, USA
(5) Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, San Jose, CA, USA
abstract:
Pore pressure prediction is critical for safe well planning, yet machine learning models designed to automate it remain constrained by the scarcity of labeled training data. Synthetic well log generation has emerged as a promising alternative, with two dominant paradigms: physics-informed generators that encode petrophysical knowledge, and data-driven models such as Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Networks (CTGAN) that learn directly from empirical well distributions. In this work, we introduce the Physics-Informed Synthetic Well Generator (PISWG), a modular forward-modeling framework that chains classical petrophysical relationships into a unified synthetic data generator. PISWG is calibrated using Tree-structured Parzen Estimation (TPE) with a softmax-weighted multi-objective fidelity loss. We benchmark PISWG against an identically tuned CTGAN baseline across five geologically distinct regions. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has systematically compared these approaches on a multi-basin benchmark under a controlled hyperparameter budget while incorporating both distributional and downstream evaluations.

Our results reveal a consistent but incomplete picture. CTGAN achieves substantially better distributional fidelity across all tested regions, attaining lower Jensen–Shannon divergence (0.197 vs. 0.372 mean JSD) and higher downstream Train-Synthetic-Test-Real (TSTR) performance across six regression baselines. In contrast, PISWG provides approximately three times higher Distance-to-Closest-Record (DCR) protection, calibrates nearly an order of magnitude faster (31 vs. 339 minutes average wall time), and exposes interpretable physical parameters that can be inspected by domain experts.

However, neither approach achieves reliable generalization under a strict leave-one-well-out protocol on the Eastern Potwar Basin. Even with up to 20% real-data augmentation, both synthetic-data approaches and real-only baselines yield predominantly negative R 2 values on several held-out wells. These findings expose a fidelity–utility gap: strong distributional similarity does not necessarily translate into robust downstream predictive performance in low-data scientific machine learning settings.

title: Petrogenesis and mineralization potential of Neoproterozoic granitoids from the Gabal El-Bakriya Ring Complex, Egypt: new insights from remote sensing, mineralogy and geochemistry
session_title: Granite-related mineral systems: Advances in understanding their genesis, distribution, and exploration implications (Posters)
authors: Abanumay, Faris A [1], Azer, Mokhles K [2], Ali, Shehata [3], Farahat, Essam S [4], Bartoli, Omar [5], Shebl, Ali [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
(2) Geological Sciences, National Research Centre, Cairo, Egypt, Arab Rep.
(3) Geology, Minia University, El-Minia, Egypt, Arab Rep.
(4) Geology, Minia University, El-Minia, Egypt, Arab Rep.
(5) Geoscience, University of Padova, Padova, Italy
(6) Department of Geology, Tanta University, Tanta, Egypt, Arab Rep.; Department of Mineralogy and Geology, University of Debrecen, Debrecen, Hungary
abstract: Late Neoproterozoic post-collisional granites exposed at Gabal El-Bakriya area include calc-alkaline granite (monzogranite) and A-type granites (syenogranite and alkali feldspar granite). The post-collisional A-type granites form a ring complex that consists of an inner core of alkali feldspar granite and outer syenogranite with gradational contacts between them. The outer parts of the alkali feldspar granites are highly tectonized with the development of alteration zones of sericitization and silicification. Most of mineralization in the El-Bakriya area is concentrated in alteration zones, where many fluorite and barite veins or stocks are found to be closely associated. PRISMA hyperspectral data were implemented to distinguish among these post-collisional granitoid types, including monzogranite, syenogranite, and alkali feldspar granite utilizing various image processing techniques. Remote sensing analysis further highlights that the transitions between the granitic plutons are predominantly affected by hydrothermal alteration. A-type granites contains diverse of accessory minerals including silicate minerals (garnet, zinnwaldite, muscovite, zircon, allanite, thorite, topaz, titanite, chlorite and epidote) and non-silicate minerals (columbite, pyrochlore, bastnaesite, monazite, apatite, fluorite and Fe-Ti oxides). Monzogranite has geochemical characteristics of post-collisional calc-alkaline granite, whilesyenogranite and alkali feldspar granite show characteristics of anorogenic granite. Compositional gaps and sharp intrusive contacts between the two phases suggest distinct magma sources.The post-collisional calc-alkaline monzogranite was evolved from a primary magma that was generated during delamination process. This process induces extensive partial melting, generating mafic magmas that eventually evolved into monzogranite. The overall chemical characteristics of the A-type granites are consistent with evolution from a single parental magma that was generated by partial melting of a juvenile crust, followed by extensive fractional crystallization and overprinting by late magmatic fluids. The post-collisional calc-alkaline monzogranite is crystalized at higher temperatures (601-750 oC, av. 677 oC) than the A-type granites (609–623 oC, av. 609 oC in syenogranite and 620-651 oC, av. 620 oC in alkali feldspar granite).The alkali feldspar granite was formed at shallower depth (5.50−9.31 km; av. 7.32 km) than syenogranite (6.30−9.98 km; av. 8.38 km). Gabal El-Bakriya intrusions have mineralized zones associated with the apical and marginal parts of the alkali feldspar granite, where the hydrothermal solutions and the volatiles are concentrated in the upper part of the magma chamber before complete crystallization of granitic melts.

title: Ferrocarbonatite Complex at Cerro Manomó: Possible Geological Evolution and Potential for Rare Earth Elements, Bolivia
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Quispe Chata, Rocio Maryori [1], Jimenez, Nestor [2], Uzquiano, German [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Engineering, Universidad Mayor de San Andres, La Paz, La Paz, Bolivia; Geology, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Instituto de Investigaciones Geológicas y del Medio Ambiente (IGEMA), Universidad Mayor de San Andres, La Paz, La Paz, Bolivia
(3) Colegio de Geologos de Bolivia, La Paz, La Paz, Bolivia
abstract:
Cerro Manomó is interpreted as a silicified ferrocarbonatite complex with a highly complex geological history that involved many geological processes that significantly modified the original rocks. Since the initial studies in the 1980s, its geological interpretation has been the subject of debate due to the extensive replacement of the original lithologies by metasomatic, hydrothermal, and supergene processes. Even though this is complicated, Cerro Manomó is crucial for science and strategy because it has strange amounts of rare earth elements (REE), positioning it as a relevant target within Bolivia’s growing interest in this field.

By addressing uncertainties regarding lithological origins, structural controls, and the processes responsible for the observed geochemical enrichment, this study sought to define the geology of the northeastern region of Cerro Manomó and improve understanding of its potential genetic evolution. In order to provide a preliminary evolutionary model for the complex, the work's scope concentrated on combining field, laboratory, and remote sensing data.

A multidisciplinary approach that included photogeology, satellite image analysis, thorough geological field mapping, petrographic and mineragraphic mineragraphic studies, X-ray fluorescence (XRF) geochemical analyses, and fluid inclusion investigations was used to achieve this. Important structural characteristics, such as the existence of potential annular carbonatite dikes and areas of severe hydrothermal alteration, were identified thanks to this technique.

The findings show that at temperatures near 400 °C, hydrothermal alteration and widespread silicification dominated the development, with secondary mineral assemblages consisting of quartz, hematite, kaolinite, limonite, barite, and bastnaesite. Significant concentration in REE, Nb, Th, and U is shown by geochemical data; this is equivalent to other regional alkaline–carbonatite complexes and compatible with carbonatitic affinities. Overall, this study demonstrates that Cerro Manomó is a highly developed ferrocarbonatite complex rich in rare earth elements (REE), whose exploitation potential may be structurally regulated by annular features. Drilling, geophysical surveys, and a thorough assessment of the potential for rare earth elements are suggested methods for more investigation

title: The Spatial Distribution of Iron Oxides and Secondary Minerals in a Weathered Campo Del Cielo Meteorite Fragment: SEM Analysis
session_title: Big Science from Small Worlds
authors: Ormsbee, Mariah Kay [1], Kackstaetter, Uwe Richard [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
abstract: The Campo Del Cielo meteorite is an iron-nickel meteorite containing mainly kamacite (Fe-Ni alloy, Ni<7.5%) and taenite (Ni-Fe alloy, Ni>25%) which are rare minerals found only in meteorites (Tilley and Bevan, 2013). Kamacite forms iron-nickel alloy crystallization bands through slow cooling over millions of years within the parent body and taenite is the byproduct of excess nickel. Bandwidths are used to establish cooling rates in iron and stony-iron meteorites. The kamacite in the Campo Del Cielo meteorite has an octahedrite structure and the bandwidths of 3mm classifying the meteorite as a coarse octahedrite. The band pattern within kamacite can be made visible on a polished meteorite surface through acid etching and is known as a Widmanstatten pattern. The Campo Del Cielo meteorite is classified as a type IAB meteorite which contains inclusions of mafic silicates, such as plagioclase and various sulfides, oxides and phosphates (Rubin, 1997). The Campo Del Cielo meteorite impact site, 800 kilometers northwest of Buenos Aires, Argentina, is estimated to be 5,800 years old based on carbon-14 dating of samples beneath the crater ejecta. Crustal oxidation of meteorite fragments in Argentina’s temperate humid climate can be minimal because of the relatively recent impact. However, studies showing the spatial distribution of iron oxides in the weathered crust of an iron-nickel Campo Del Cielo meteorite fragment are rare and inconclusive. Such spatial distribution of various secondary minerals created in the oxidized meteorite crust using a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) with pinpoint x-ray fluorescence chemical analysis (EDX) capabilities. The anticipated results should give better insight on how Earth’s climate can affect and deteriorate meteorites over time.

title: Episodic Magmatic Activities with Changing Tectonic Settings in an Evolving Craton – Evidence from Major, Trace and Platinum-Group Element Geochemistry of the Singhbhum Dykes, India
session_title: Using mafic and ultramafic deposits to decipher volcanic and magmatic processes (Posters)
authors: ROY, Sagnik [1], MONDAL, Sisir K [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Jadavpur University, Kolkata, WB, India
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Jadavpur University, Kolkata, WB, India
abstract: This study focuses on dyke samples from the Singhbhum Craton, India, collected from the ~2.8 Ga Keshargaria (trending N27°) and Keonjhar (trending N17°) dykes, the ~2.3 Ga Kaptipada dyke (trending N26°), and the ~1.8 Ga Mohuldih (trending N118°) and Satkosia (trending N143°) dykes. Based on modal mineralogy, the ~2.8 Ga and ~2.3 Ga dykes are gabbro-noritic, the Satkosia dyke is doleritic, and the Mohuldih dyke is more felsic. Magnetite and ilmenite are the main accessory minerals in the Mohuldih and Satkosia dykes. The Mohuldih and Keshargaria dykes host base-metal sulfide mineralization. All dykes are hydrothermally altered, with alteration assemblages comprising sericite, amphibole, chlorite, biotite, quartz, and feldspar. Compositionally, the Keshargaria and Keonjhar dykes are high-Mg, siliceous basaltic, whereas the Kaptipada dyke is boninitic, the Mohuldih dyke is andesitic, and the Satkosia dyke is basaltic. The ~2.8 Ga Keshargaria–Keonjhar dykes contain 6.76–16.64 wt% MgO and 51.66–54.24 wt% SiO 2 and display LREE enrichment (20–100× chondrite), with flat to slightly declining HREE patterns. In contrast, the ~2.3 Ga Kaptipada dyke exhibits a U-shaped chondrite-normalized REE pattern, indicating boninitic affinity. The Satkosia dyke shows a comparatively flat REE pattern, whereas the Mohuldih dyke is characterized by LREE enrichment and relative HREE depletion compared with Satkosia. The Keonjhar, Kaptipada, and Satkosia dykes show negative Ir and Pt anomalies in normalized PGE plots. Except for Mohuldih, all dykes show a PGE-fractionated character, with Pd/Ir ratios ranging from 7 to 132. Low PGE concentrations in the Mohuldih dyke suggest derivation of parental magma from a PGE-depleted source. Positive correlations of MgO with Ru and Pt in the Keonjhar and Kaptipada dykes indicate that PGE fractionation was controlled by early-segregated oxide or Fe–Mg silicate phases. Trace-element geochemistry suggests the incorporation of variable amounts of continental crustal material into the parental magmas of all dykes except the Kaptipada dyke. The studied dykes record changes in geotectonic setting through time, including an active continental-margin setting for the ~2.8 Ga Keshargaria and ~1.8 Ga Mohuldih dykes; within-plate magmatism, probably in a back-arc rift setting, for the ~2.8 Ga Keonjhar and Satkosia dykes; and an oceanic-arc setting for the Kaptipada dyke. The episodic emplacement of these dykes can be correlated with global supercontinent cycles and associated ultramafic–mafic magmatism and ore mineralization.

title: Mining Insights: The Role of the Extractive Sector in Advancing Geoheritage Science and Protection
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Monge-Ganuzas, Manu R. [1], dos Santos Costa, Silas Samuel [2]
affiliations: (1) ProGEO, Gernika-Lumo, Spain
(2) Institute of Earth Sciences, University of Minho, Braga, Portugal, Portugal
abstract:
The extractive sector has traditionally been perceived as a driver of landscape transformation and geodiversity loss; however, it also represents a largely underexplored source of scientific knowledge and opportunities for geoheritage identification, characterization, and protection. This contribution examines how mining and quarrying activities can actively support geoheritage science, providing exceptional exposures, subsurface data, and access to otherwise inaccessible geological features.

Drawing on a set of international and illustrative case studies, the communication highlights three key contributions of the extractive industry to geoheritage. First, active and abandoned mining sites often expose unique stratigraphic, mineralogical, structural, and paleontological features of high scientific value, contributing to the identification of new geoheritage sites. Second, collaboration between industry, researchers, and public administrations facilitates the documentation, monitoring, and interpretation of geosites, improving their scientific robustness and management. Third, post-extraction landscapes offer opportunities for innovative geoconservation strategies, including site rehabilitation, public outreach, and integration into geoparks and protected area networks.

The paper also addresses the growing need to reconcile resource extraction with geoheritage protection through adaptive governance frameworks. Particular attention is given to regulatory instruments, environmental impact assessment processes, and corporate sustainability practices that incorporate geodiversity and geoheritage values. The role of local communities and Indigenous knowledge systems is discussed as a critical component in ensuring inclusive and socially responsible geoconservation strategies.

Ultimately, this contribution argues that the extractive sector can transition from being viewed solely as a threat to becoming a strategic partner in geoheritage science and protection. Recognizing and operationalizing this dual role is essential for advancing geoconservation in a world increasingly shaped by resource demand and land-use pressures.

title: Educational Interventions and Blanket testing:An effective Mitigation Strategy for arsenic
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part II)
authors: Farooqi, abida [1], Bibi, Ayesha [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Sciences, Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad, Pakistan
(2) Environmental Sciences, Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad, Pakistan
abstract:
Groundwater arsenic contamination is a significant public health challenge, particularly in South Asia, where millions depend on groundwater for drinking. This study investigates the spatiotemporal variations in arsenic levels and behavioral responses to contamination across five villages in southwest Lahore over a decade (2014–2024). In 2014, blanket testing of 1,559 wells revealed that 49% of wells had arsenic concentrations exceeding the WHO limit of 10 µg/L, while 27 % had levels above 50 µg/L, posing severe health risks. In a follow-up assessment in 2016, 647 wells were retested. These retested wells showed a decline in arsenic exposure due to educational outreach and well-switching behaviors, with 63% of affected households initially switching to safer wells. The testing was done in the same 5 villages in 2024, and 575 wells, which were tested, showed a resurgence of arsenic contamination in some areas, with maximum levels reaching 500 µg/L. This increase was attributed to the absence of sustained monitoring and intervention programs.

Despite this, a positive behavioral shift was observed in 2024, where highly contaminated wells were no longer in use, indicating that educational interventions and blanket testing had a lasting impact on community decision-making. While, well-switching remained an effective mitigation strategy, socioeconomic constraints, lack of alternative safe water sources, and limited access to arsenic testing hindered its widespread adoption. Additionally, no consistent correlation between well depth and arsenic concentration was found, reinforcing the importance of localized hydrogeochemical factors in arsenic mobilization. The study concludes that regular testing, community engagement, and policy-driven interventions are critical to ensuring long-term water safety.

title: Geological heritage and indigenous sacred territoriality: resource exploitation challenges in the brazilian amazon
session_title: Webinar 2: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives
authors: Basilio, Cisnea Menezes [1]
affiliations: (1) Secretaria de Estado de Desenvolvimento Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação do Amazonas, Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil
abstract:
The Brazilian Amazon is home to one of the world's richest geodiversities, encompassing mountain ranges, caves, rivers, waterfalls, and rocky outcrops that sustain ecosystems and Indigenous territories. Geodiversity comprises the variety of nature's abiotic elements and constitutes the physical foundation of biodiversity and sociocultural relationships (Gray, 2013; Brilha, 2016). For Indigenous peoples, these elements hold cosmological and spiritual significance, intrinsically linked to origin narratives, sacred places, and collective memory (Kopenawa & Albert, 2015). Territory is understood as an extension of the body and as a space of life, belonging, and cosmopolitical relationships. The earth/life (Dita kahtiro) is also known as 'Mother Earth' for its fertility, fecundity, and generosity, as it generates all beings and their natural resources, providing nutrition and protection for life (Barreto, 2021). In this context, geoconservation should integrate the protection of both geological and geocultural heritage by recognizing the scientific, cultural, and symbolic values of geodiversity (Brilha, 2005).

The growing exploitation of resources in the Amazon intensifies conflicts between economic interests and indigenous territorial rights. Infrastructure projects such as mining, hydroelectric dams, and highways alter the landscape and impact sacred sites (Acselrad, 2018). As in the case of the Belo Monte Hydroelectric Power Plant, which altered the hydrological regime of the Volta Grande do Xingu, impacting the Juruna, Arara, and Xikrin Indigenous peoples (Fearnside, 2017). Illegal gold mining in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory causes mercury contamination (Ferrante et al., 2023; Vale et al., 2023). Similarly, the Autazes Potash Project has sparked socio environmental conflicts involving the Mura indigenous people, specifically concerning their right to free, prior, and informed consultation as mandated by International Labour Organization Convention No. 169 (Zhouri & Oliveira, 2023). In the Brazilian Amazon, development and licensing processes ignore Indigenous peoples' deep territorial connections. By neglecting their cosmologies, social organizations, and traditional practices, State and market actors fail to recognize these forms of knowledge as critical paths for addressing resource exploitation impacts. In this context, geological heritage serves as a vital geoconservation tool, strengthening public policies that reconcile geodiversity conservation, the protection of sacred Indigenous territories, and the promotion of the Amazon's geobiocultural diversity.

title: Predictive Modeling of Water Distribution Practices and Farmer Satisfaction for Sustainable Agriculture in Swabi Pakistan
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: Ahmad, Shakeel [1], Khan, Sikandar [2], Khan, Khurram Shams [3], Ahmad, Javed [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Sociology, Hazara University, Mansehra, KP, Pakistan

(3) World Bank, Pakistan, World Bank, Islamabad, ICT, Pakistan

abstract: The present study was carried out to investigate the level of satisfaction of the farmers on distribution of water and associated practices of the farmers in Swabi-Pakistan using predictive modeling approach. The Study objectives were therefore designed to evaluate farmers’ opinions of the management, equity and sufficiency of water distribution system and to pinpoint the major variables effecting their level of satisfaction. A multistage sampling technique was used to collect primary data from farmers (n=384) with a structured questionnaire. The data was analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression model, which were used to determine the association between water distribution practices and the satisfaction levels of farmers. There was a positive and significant relation between farmers' satisfaction and timely availability of water, good operation and maintenance of canals, transparency of water allocation, equal distribution of irrigation water and supervisions of irrigation authorities (p<0.05). In contrast, the variables of water theft, political interference, poor canal infrastructure and canal maintenance delays were not significantly related to satisfaction. The binary logistic regression analysis revealed that the farmers belonging to joint family system were seven times more likely to be satisfied with water distribution than the farmers belonging to nuclear family system. Likewise, farmers with high family income were three times more likely to be satisfied than the low family income farmers. The overall satisfaction index showed that farmers' satisfaction was moderate, suggesting significant gaps in the current irrigation management system. The study findings suggest that significant improvement of the farmers' satisfaction can be achieved through improvement of canal infrastructure, institutional monitoring, promoting participatory water management, and transparency in water allocation. It is recommended that farmer groups in irrigation water management and implement water governance strategies are highly beneficial in irrigation water practices and farmers satisfaction.

title: Dissolved organic matter as electron shuttling for arsenic enrichment in groundwater
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part I)
authors: Guo, Huaming [1], Feng, Xiaojun [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Water Resources and Environment, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing, Beijing, China
(2) School of Water Resources and Environment, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Bejing, Bejing, China
abstract: Little is known about electron shuttle ability of dissolved organic matter (DOM) and its effects on arsenic (As) mobilization and the molecular transformation of DOM during the repeated electron shuttling and its impact on reduction of Fe oxides-adsorbed As, which makes the underlying mechanism of groundwater As enrichment elusive. In this study, both the electrochemical properties and molecular compositions of DOM in high As groundwater were quantified in the Hetao Basin, China. We found that, along the flow path, the electron-transferring capacity (ETC) of DOM, including the capacities of electron-accepting and -donating, continuously increased from 2.85 to 3.59 mmol e- /gC along with As concentrations. The increasing ETC reflected an increase in electron shuttle ability of DOM. Furthermore, the increasing electron shuttle ability was mainly attributed to the recalcitrant compounds in DOM, especially CHOS and CHONS formulas in highly unsaturated structures with high oxygen (HUSHO) and CHO and CHON formulas in aromatic structures (AS). The significantly positive correlation between As concentration and ETC indicated that recalcitrant DOM promoted groundwater As enrichment through electron shuttling for inducing the reductive dissolution of As-containing Fe(III) oxide minerals, which was further supported by our culture experiments showing that goethite was more reduced (133 µM Fe(II)) in the presence of DOM with higher ETC (3.35 mmol e- /gC) as electron shuttling than that (65.2 µM Fe(II)) with relatively lower ETC (2.41 mmol e- /gC). We also found that higher electron transfer capacity (ETC) of high-As groundwater DOM resulted from the higher aromaticity and more functional moieties (i.e., total phenols and quinones) than that in low-As groundwater DOM, and irreversible loss of aromaticity and the functional moieties during the repeated electron shuttling lowered the ETC. This decreasing ETC of DOM reflected the decrease in its electron shuttle ability to reduce As(V)-bearing goethite. The positive correlation between total dissolved As (mainly as As(V)) and total Fe(II) concentration illustrated that electrons shuttled by the DOM preferentially reduced goethite, thus releasing the adsorbed As(V) into water. Our study highlights that recalcitrant DOM compounds with unsaturated and aromatic structures have high electron shuttle ability, promoting As enrichment in groundwater.

title: Sulfide Excavation and Informatics (SEI) : An Organics-Based Classification Model for Carbonaceous Chondrites
session_title: Planetary Exploration and Education: How We Learn About Our Solar System and Beyond

affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Science, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USA
(2) Planetary Science Division, Southwest Research Institute, San Antonio, TX, USA; Physics and Astronomy, University of Texas At San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USA
abstract: Carbonaceous chondrites are a rare class of meteorite defined by a high carbon content and the presence of small inclusions of melted silicates called chondrules. These meteorites record the early solar system’s aqueous alteration history through their mineralogy and organic inventories. Our study investigates the transformations outlined by Li et al. (2023) involving the amino acids glutamate, alanine, and aspartate, catalyzed by iron and nickel sulfides. Using NASA’s AstroMat database, the Ni content of pentlandite and pyrrhotite samples from Hayabusa2 and CI, CM, and CR meteorite classes was compared to assess these transformations at a large scale. The results demonstrate a split in synthetic pathways as alteration progresses, which implies that two asteroids of the same class may record distinct parent body alteration histories. These results will enable us to refine our current classification schemes using organic-based proxies and allow us to better contextualize future sample return missions.

title: Micropaleontology at the Florida Museum of Natural History, University of Florida
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: BRYAN, Jonathan R [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Northwest Florida State College, Niceville, FL, USA
abstract:
The Micropaleontology Collection (MC) at the Florida Museum of Natural History (FLMNH) is a part of the larger Division of Invertebrate Paleontology. It has extensive holdings in Cenozoic foraminifera from Florida and the Gulf of Mexico Basin, as well as ostracods. Larger benthic foraminifera are especially well represented. Included are historic collections from Esther Applin, Louise Jordan, Storrs Cole, Joseph Cushman, CW Drooger, Wayne Moore, Lyman Toulmin, Alan Cheetham, Robert Vernon, Harbans Puri, James Miller (USGS), and Paul Huddlestun. Many specimen lots are up to 100 years old and in excellent condition. Recent acquisitions from the Florida Geological Survey and independent researchers have rapidly increased the size and scope of the collection. It is expected that the continued assimilation of historic and private microfossil collections will further increase the value and research potential of this important resource. Microfossils not only represent the most complete archive of past biodiversity but remain the primary means of stratal correlation and have proven utility in hydrogeologic, geoengineering, and environmental subsurface applications.

There are several noteworthy and instructive aspects of this collection. First, the MC is primarily biostratigraphic in nature and largely organized with reference to early research on deep wells from which the stratigraphy of Florida was first established. More than 500 wells are represented, including 120 early oil and gas test wells, some reaching into the Lower Cretaceous. Second, the emphasis on larger foraminifera is uniquely important for the geology of the Florida Carbonate Platform and the establishment of American Shallow Benthic Zones. First developed in Tethyan regions, SBZ use larger foraminifera to develop high resolution biozones in shallow water facies which usually lack planktonic foraminifera. The development of American SBZ will strengthen the chronostratigraphic resolution of Gulf Coastal Plain lithostratigraphic units and the MC will necessarily be foundational in this effort.

Third, under the direction of Collection Director RW Portell, the commitment of the FLMNH to properly curate and archive the MC is a lesson on the enduring value of historic collections, the increasing need to salvage “orphaned” collections, and the inescapable “authority of the specimen”—the unchanging “hardcopy” and point of reference for all past, present, and future research—in an AI-assisted virtual age.

title: Rivers of Change: How Rivers Demonstrate Change over Multiple Time Scales
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Dodge, Rebecca Lee [1]
affiliations: (1) Kimbell School of Geosciences, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA
abstract: Earth Science standards for K-12 education contain key words and phrases common among multiple state-based standards and the Next Generation Science Standards, across multiple grade levels ranging from Elementary through Middle and High School. “Earth’s systems continuously change over a range of time scales” is an example of such a key phrase. Change is targeted specifically with reference to Earth’s surface features caused by erosion and deposition, the formation of deltas, changes to rivers caused by natural hazards such as flooding, and changes caused by humans though engineering and climate change. The application of satellite imagery to interpret such changes is also indicated in multiple standards. With the more than fifty-year-old archive of Earth Observation imagery now available NASA documents global change though its World of Change collection, including change detection animations focused on rivers. An animation along the Wabash River reveals the rapid (approximately one month) development of a new meander cutoff that took place during a flood event. Numerous meander scars demonstrate repeated cutoff events over hundreds of years. An animation showing seasonal water level and floodplain conditions change over a one-year span along the Indus River highlights short-term changes from month to month, and from one year to the next. An animation of the human-induced impacts on the Yellow River Delta over a 30-year time span demonstration both erosional and depositional changes caused by engineering interventions in the river channel. An animation showing the growth of deltas into Atchafalaya Bay documents the 45-year long emergence of new land along the Gulf Coast of Florida. Two deltas have emerged, one from Atchafalaya River deposition and one from the engineered Wax Lake diversion channel. Human intervention has also reduced the flow of two rivers in Central Asia into what was formerly the world’s fourth largest lake. The Aral Sea has virtually disappeared. An animation using MODIS satellite data shows the death spiral, which began in the 1960s, over the period from 2000 to 2018. Finally, with reference to the “river of Ice” known as the Columbia Glacier, we see dramatic climate change induced changes in the glacier over a nearly forty-year period. Each animation informs both multiple time scales and geologic concepts.

title: Did the Shatsky Conjugate Drag the Yellowstone Hot Spot?
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: Lehman, Gordon Bayard [1]
affiliations: (1) Santa Rosa, CA, USA
abstract: The ascent of the low velocity plume imaged by Nelson and Grand in 2018 from the Core/Mantle boundary in northern Baja California to the surface near Yellowstone closely matches the purported path of the Shatsky Rise Conjugate and affiliated plateaux beneath North America. The Yellowstone plume is unique among imaged plumes in its exceptional tilt. It travels 1500 km laterally in its 2900 km ascent. Steinberger et al in 2019 found that although they could not replicate the progression of calderas up the eastern Snake River Plain, the best chance that the plume was generally involved in Miocene regional volcanism is if it were at least ninety million years old. This puts it in the time frame of conjugate passage. The possibilities for a connection are explored including entrainment of the plume head and the plume drafting in the wake of the multiple conjugate passage. It is concluded that while the uncertainty is large, the correlation between two unusual phenomena in both time and space is difficult to ignore. The wake hypothesis is favored as conjugate removal of mantle lithosphere must have created disturbance to considerable depth.

title: Going Beyond NAGPRA: Building Geoheritage Through Geoethics

abstract: In geological collections, geoethical work to fulfill the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) requires an in-depth understanding of the collection's history and provenance to properly identify and return ancestors and belongings to Native American Tribal Nations. The resulting archive of information provides meaningful details on institutional and collection-based geoheritage, which can then be used in myriad ways, particularly as a preservation strategy that encourages geoethical understanding. The knowledge gathered can foster institutional memory, intellectual reflection, and strategies to guide continual and innovative curation of geological collections. This presentation will outline the ongoing process at the Rutgers University Geology Museum, including the early inventory and cataloging work, the development and management of the archival database, NAGPRA compliance efforts, and how that work has provided a pathway to go beyond NAGPRA. The collections and institutional knowledge that were developed provided opportunities for student experiential learning through exhibit redevelopment and through standalone projects, including collaborations with outside universities and scholars, an art exhibit, the study of historical scientific networks based on collections exchange, and a children’s book on the museum mastodon. The acknowledgement and repair of past harms and the archival history built through NAGPRA fulfillment can have profound effects on the museum's collections, research and engagement with students and the community.

title: Global spatial prediction modeling of groundwater manganese
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes

affiliations: (1) Eawag, Duebendorf, Switzerland

abstract: Although manganese (Mn) is necessary for human health, high levels of Mn consumption may be toxic. In addition to food, drinking water coming from groundwater can provide a substantial amount of Mn to the diet. Several years ago, the World Health Organization (WHO) reduced its Mn drinking water guideline from 400 µg/L to 80 µg/L due to greater adverse health effects than previously known, particularly for infants. To assess how this large decrease in the Mn drinking water guideline affects the areas and people at risk, we have created global prediction maps of Mn in groundwater using machine learning. The first step was to compile a large dataset of Mn concentrations along with spatially continuous environmental variables relating to climate, hydrogeology, soil and topography. Once the best model was determined, this was applied to the predictor variables to produce global hazard and health risk maps. Based on these, we estimate that over 200 million people are potentially exposed to Mn concentrations in drinking water >80 µg/L, as opposed to 39 million people potentially exposed to the previous WHO guideline of 400 µg/L. This number of people at risk is comparable to that associated with the other geogenic groundwater contaminants of arsenic and fluoride, though Mn generally receives much less attention. Therefore, the new prediction maps produced in this study are important for raising awareness of the hazard posed by Mn in groundwater and in helping identify safe groundwater sources.

title: A Century Written in the Valley Floor: 100 years of Subsidence in California's Central Valley
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Ellis, John [1], Saberi, Leila [2]
affiliations: (1) INTERA, Houston, TX, USA
(2) INTERA, Chicago, IL, USA
abstract:
Land subsidence in California's Central Valley is both an old and a new problem. Historical leveling surveys documented widespread subsidence exceeding 30 ft by the late twentieth century and established the Central Valley as one of the world's most extensively studied examples of aquifer-system compaction. However, most discussions of subsidence focus on historical groundwater overdraft and provide a limited perspective on how subsidence patterns have evolved over the past century.

This study integrates historical leveling data, extensometer records, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) measurements, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) observations, and groundwater-level records to reconstruct and evaluate 100 years of subsidence across California's Central Valley. A previously published map of cumulative subsidence from 1926–1970 is combined with newly developed reconstructions for 1970–2026 and 1926–2026, providing the first consistent century-scale assessment of regional subsidence patterns. The results show that while the locations of maximum subsidence have shifted substantially through time, significant subsidence persisted well beyond the period commonly associated with historical overdraft. Some areas that experienced severe historical subsidence have stabilized, while new centers of subsidence have emerged in response to changing groundwater-use patterns, prolonged droughts, and continued reliance on groundwater pumping.

To investigate the causes of these changes, long-term groundwater-level and subsidence records from 50 representative locations throughout the Central Valley were analyzed using one-dimensional aquifer-system compaction models. Estimated critical heads and site-specific subsidographs demonstrate that modern subsidence behavior is strongly influenced by historical groundwater stresses, preconsolidation conditions, and aquifer-system properties. Sites with similar contemporary groundwater levels can exhibit markedly different subsidence responses because of differences in stress history and aquifer-system memory accumulated over decades of groundwater development.

Together, the mapping and modeling results reveal how the magnitude, distribution, and controls on land subsidence have changed over the past century. The findings provide a long-term perspective on subsidence evolution in California and demonstrate how historical groundwater stresses continue to influence present-day subsidence risk and groundwater-management decisions.

title: Evolution of Volcanic Eruption Styles recorded in Valles Marineris, Mars: Observations of Effusive vs Explosive Deposits
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: MATIELLA NOVAK, Alexandra [1], WHELLEY, Patrick [2], PETERS, Sean Isaac [3], XANTHOUDAKIS, Aris [4], MEYER, Heather [5], RICHARDSON, Jacob A. [6], BUCZKOWSKI, Debra [7]
affiliations: (1) Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD, USA
(2) University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA
(3) Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT, USA
(4) Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT, USA
(5) Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD, USA
(6) NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, MD, USA
(7) JHU Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD, USA
abstract:
The walls of Valles Marineris expose approximately 7 km of stratigraphy, presumably recording billions of years of surface evolution on Mars. Previous studies have investigated the origins of layered deposits observed in the walls, with many interpreting a volcanic origin for some of these layers. Our work aims to understand the relative abundances of effusive versus explosive deposits over time within Valles Marineris, which provides constraints on the early volcanic history of Mars and the expected range of resulting compositions. The stratigraphic distribution of these deposits provides a relative timescale for when different styles of eruptions were more likely to have occurred. Linking effusive and explosive volcanic deposits on Mars to general source regions, and the compositional evolution of those source regions, remains a key goal of expanding our knowledge of Martian volcanology.

In order to determine the relative contribution of effusive and explosive volcanic products, we utilized CTX and HiRISE images and DEMs, along with CRISM mineralogy data, to identify and characterize exposed layering of deposits suspected to be of volcanic origin. We mapped and assessed the inferred origin of these layers based on morphology, mineralogy, bed thickness, and vertical and lateral distribution. For effusive deposits, which are limited by cooling or the volume of erupted material, sources are likely to have been relatively nearby (e.g., fissure vents), although such sources could have been 100s of kilometers away, as seems typical for flows in the Tharsis region. Explosive deposits, on the other hand, can reach 1000s of kilometers away from their source regions due to lofting of fine-grained material in the atmosphere and subsequent wind dispersion and transport of those materials.

High-resolution CRISM data (~20m/pixel) have provided adequate observations of layering within many chasmata of Valles Marineris. We also utilized the Geologic Map of Valles Marineris (Witbeck et al., 1991) to identify areas that were mapped as volcanic lava flow and ash fall/pyroclastic units. So far, we have identified several sites throughout Valles Marineris that satisfy our requirements. These sites include layered deposits within Ophir Chasma, Melas Chasma, Candor Chasma, and Tithonium Chasma. Combining CTX DEMs with high-resolution CRISM imagery has enabled us to make some determinations about the stratigraphic ordering of explosive versus effusive deposits in Valles Marineris.

title: Published is Better Than Perfect: How Legacy Data Liberation Drove A Survey Paradigm Shift
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n)
authors: Filippelli, Hailey [1], Oest, Christopher [2]

(2) Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Pennsylvania Geological Survey, Middletown, PA, USA
abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing emphasis on increasing access to legacy data from geological surveys. The Pennsylvania Geological Survey (PaGS) maintains extensive holdings of legacy data in varying states of completeness, including uninterpreted borehole records, field notebooks, hand-drawn maps, and nearly finished projects that were never formally published. These materials often present significant challenges due to issues such as poor legibility, incomplete information, and inconsistent or nonexistent data standards. Recognizing the long-term value of these resources, the PaGS has undertaken efforts to “liberate” these data from map drawers and external hard drives that are inaccessible to the public. Staffing changes within the survey provided an opportunity to reevaluate how legacy data is managed and published. As a result, the PaGS has developed a tiered approach for handling legacy datasets through three primary methods: publication “as is,” digitization of analog data, and incorporation with larger, compilation mapping efforts. This flexible strategy enables the survey to release valuable data to the public while continuing to provide high-quality mapping products. It also better aligns with the survey’s mission statement, which explicitly calls for data availability to the public. In addition, the shift in workflow has led to a broader range of publication products and a more flexible strategy for releasing legacy data based on data quality, completeness, and project constraints.

title: QGG J. Hoover Mackin Award: Spatiotemporal Trends in Slip Rate and Earthquake Recurrence on the Sierra Madre-Cucamonga Fault Zone, Southern California
session_title: Recurrence of what?
authors: Weigandt, Caje K. [1], Dolan, James F. [2], Rodrigues, Kathleen [3], Jordan, Frank [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA,
(3) Desert Research Institute, Reno, Nevada, USA
(4) San Bernardino County, Fontana, CA, USA
abstract: The north-dipping Sierra Madre-Cucamonga reverse fault system (SMdF-CF) in southern California extends for ~100 km east-west along the southern base of the ~1.5- to 3-km-tall San Gabriel Mountains. Joint rupture of both the SMdF and CF portions would result in a M w ≥7.5 earthquake adjacent to the major population centers of the Los Angeles metropolitan region. Despite such a major looming seismic threat, the slip rate and paleoseismic histories of these faults remain under-constrained. Previous studies using geomorphic analyses of mountain front sinuosity and low-temperature thermochronology have demonstrated relatively fast long-term uplift rates on the eastern (CF) portion of the San Gabriel mountain front compared to the central and western (SMdF) portions. However, review of the current literature on Quaternary fault slip rates obtained along the SMdF-CF provides an ambiguous result as to whether or not this gradient in uplift along the San Gabriel mountain front persists today. We present newly determined luminescence ages of alluvial fans and, combined with vertical separation measurements extracted from high-resolution lidar data, calculate the slip rate of the CF over two distinct time intervals within the Holocene. Our results suggest that the CF is indeed slipping significantly faster than the SMdF. Additionally, we present three previously unpublished paleoseismic trenches, one on the eastern SMdF and two on the CF, excavated over the past 30 years in order to assess the potential record of previous throughgoing rupture along the entire fault system. We find that ruptures at the eastern and western ends of the SMdF-CF system, such as the 1971 M w 6.7 San Fernando-Sylmar earthquake, occur more frequently than ruptures within the central part of the system. Large displacements observed in the MRE of several central SMdF trenches suggest occurrence of a large magnitude event, likely involving rupture of the entire SMdF-CF system. Recurrence of such an event, albeit rare, could have devastating consequences for the Los Angeles metropolitan region.

title: Assessing Carbon Pool Stability in Coastal Prairie Soils Using Thermal Analysis
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Nguyen, Pauline Van [1], Bouton, Nicolas [2], Radovic, Jagos [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmosphereic Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, Texas, USA
(2) Geochemistry Department, Vinci Technologies, Nanterre, France
(3) Department of Earth and Atmosphereic Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, TX,
abstract:
Quantifying where terrestrial carbon resides and how durably it is held is central to constraining carbon–climate feedbacks and to designing land-management practices that bolster soil carbon sequestration. Coastal prairies are an under-examined component of this picture, despite their potential to act as concentrated carbon reservoirs within regional inventories.

Here, we compare soil carbon stocks in remnant coastal prairie (never plowed, native vegetation intact) with adjacent restored prairie (managed after the removal of invasive species) to determine how these soils respond to past disturbance and subsequent recovery efforts. Thirty-five soil samples, collected from both surface and subsurface horizons, were sampled at the University of Houston Coastal Center and characterized by programmed pyrolysis on a Rock-Eval 6 (RE-6) instrument, which separates and quantifies organic carbon pools according to their thermal stability.

Total organic carbon (TOC) varied from 0.16% to 4.05% across the sampling network, pointing to pronounced spatial variability in carbon storage. The S1 signal, reflecting the most thermally labile organic matter, fell within a narrow range (0.02–0.13 mg/g), while S2 yields, released at higher pyrolysis temperatures and indicative of more recalcitrant carbon, spanned a much wider interval (0.17–6.63 mg/g). Compared with restored plots, remnant prairie soils consistently held more TOC and a larger share of S2-type carbon, indicating that management history exerts a strong influence on the persistence of soil carbon.

Beyond the conventional RE-6 outputs (TOC, S1, S2), we apply two recently published machine-learning approaches that build on pyrolysis data: a correction routine that mitigates systematic bias in RE-6 estimates of soil organic and inorganic carbon (SOC and SIC) [1], and the PARTYSOC framework, which separates SOC into a centennially stable pool and a more dynamic, active pool using RE-6 thermograms [2]. For example, preliminary PARTYSOC results suggest a range of 47% to 84% for centennially stable carbon.

Collectively, the results help to delineate terrestrial carbon hotspots, sharpen estimates of soil carbon permanence, and gauge the wider applicability of emerging RE-6–based analytics for regional and global carbon accounting.

[2] Cécillon et al., 2021, Geosci. Model Dev. , 14, 3879–3898.

title: Untangling Taxonomy at the Turn: Morphological Diversity in Estonian Blue Clays
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology (Posters)
authors: Vantoorenburg, Haley [1], Bykova, Natalia [2], Vinn, Olev [3], Toom, Ursula [4], Isakar, Mare [5], Selly, Tara [6], Schiffbauer, James D. [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(3) University of Tartu, Tartu, Estonia
(4) Tallinn University of Technology, Tallinn, Estonia
(5) Natural History Museum, University of Tartu, Tartu, Estonia
(6) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(7) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract:
Recent reassessment of fossils from the early Cambrian (Terreneuvian Series) blue clays of Estonia revealed exceptional diversity in both morphology and taphonomy. Through the use of multiple advanced imaging techniques, fourteen distinct morphotypes were identified. Our study aims to resolve longstanding taxonomic and taphonomic uncertainties regarding the Baltic Basin in this critical transitionary period in evolutionary history.

Among these Estonian fossils are specimens identified as cloudinomorphs, tube-building organisms that have long been thought to have gone extinct at the Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary. These fossils, along with similar reports of cloudinomorphs on either side of the E-C boundary from South China, Russia, and Spain, contribute to a growing body of global evidence challenging long-held assumptions about the extent of biotic replacement within the evolutionary transition across the E-C boundary (~539 Ma). The persistence of cloudinomorphs and other tubular forms already suggests a much more complicated ecological transition than previously recognized; the diversity present within the Estonian samples adds another layer of complexity. To refine our understanding of this pivotal transition period, we have examined the structure, preservation, and ecology of these blue clay cloudinomorph fossils. These findings provide evidence of resilience within communities at a time of dramatic ecological change and new insight into the Ediacaran extinction.

Through the use of advanced imaging techniques, including high-resolution X-ray tomographic microscopy (µCT) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), we have begun to unravel the taxonomic and taphonomic details of these fossils. Three distinct preservation modes have been identified, with both three-dimensional and compressed forms. We have, through µCT, discovered a high morphological diversity that exceeds expectations and discovered previously undetected fibrous structures that vary in density throughout the samples. Through µCT and plan view analysis of specimens, ten overarching morphotypic groups were identified, with a total of fourteen distinct morphotypes described. Understanding the taxonomic diversity of these samples is a critical step to understand the controls on persistence across the E-C boundary.

title: Shifting Coastal Hazards and Rocky Coast Evolution Along the Cascadia Margin Across the Earthquake Cycle
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Masteller, Claire [1], Lopez, Cesar Gavrie [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington Univerity in St. Louis, Saint Louis, MO, USA
abstract:
Rocky coast evolution along the Cascadia margin reflects interactions among gradual interseismic deformation, abrupt coseismic subsidence, and wave driven erosion. Yet how these processes interact across individual earthquakes and multiple seismic cycles to shape coastal erosion remains poorly quantified. Observations of shoreline retreat, shore-platform morphology, tectonic uplift, wave climate, and tidal range across the U.S. West Coast reveal a timescale dependent tectonic influence on shoreline retreat. Over decades, faster uplift is associated with slower shoreline retreat and narrower shore platforms, indicating that uplift temporarily buffers erosion by continually shifting the locus of wave attack offshore. Over millennia, however, higher uplift rates correspond to wider shore platforms, implying greater cumulative retreat. We hypothesize that this apparent reversal reflects repeated seismic cycles in which long periods of uplift-driven tectonic buffering is overprinted by enhanced coastal erosion following coseismic subsidence.

We evaluate this mechanism by modeling the effects of coseismic subsidence during a future Cascadia megathrust earthquake at 32 rocky coast sites with diverse near-shore morphology across a range of subsidence magnitudes, earthquake timings, and sea level rise trajectories. Across all modeled sites and scenarios, coseismic subsidence instantaneously increases shoreline wave power by shifting wave action landward and reducing nearshore energy dissipation, despite an overall reduction in wave breaking. Wave power amplification is negligible along steep rocky coasts but can reach eight orders of magnitude on low gradient platforms. Sea level rise controls both the timing and persistence of this earthquake driven wave power amplification. Under a high emissions scenario, accelerated sea level rise shifts the window of maximum amplification earlier in the century and promotes subsequent recovery toward pre-earthquake wave conditions. These observations and modeling reveal a Cascadia coast alternately buffered and exposed by the seismic cycle, with episodic subsidence creating transient but potentially long-lived periods of enhanced wave exposure that may disproportionately shape long-term coastal retreat and the evolution of rocky coast landscapes.

title: Do Beavers Pee in the Woods? Fostering a Shame-Free Bathroom Field Culture in Undergraduate Geosciences Courses
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: McCarville, Katherine [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Science-Geosciences, Minot State University, Minot, ND, USA; Iowa Lakeside Laboratory, Milford, IA, USA
abstract:
Recently, several authors have called for implementation of a more broadly inclusive bathroom culture across the field sciences. A host of different challenges arise under conditions of group travel, camping, fieldwork, and other situations that are often encountered in scientific fieldwork settings. Even a brief "walking" trip to a nearby outcrop or interesting landscape stone can present challenges to an undergraduate student. Addressing these issues forthrightly, providing appropriate supplies and equipment, and sharing communication methods can promote students’ feelings of acceptance and safety, and could ultimately result in more students pursuing geoscience education and careers.

Lessons learned through many years of family travels, field study trips, and outdoor work—including Grand Canyon/Colorado River raft trips where elimination locations and techniques are specified and controlled—provide the basis for suggested strategies for de-stigmatizing and normalizing bathroom and privacy-related concerns in undergraduate courses. Raising awareness among colleagues, building kits with supplies and equipment, and introducing students to new terminology and behaviors are all necessary steps in changing the cultural norms around this most universal of human activities.

title: Uruguay's amethyst deposits as a georesource: geological and mining heritage
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Faraone, Mauricio [1]
affiliations: (1) National Directorate of Mining and Geology, Montevideo,
abstract:
Although Uruguay is a small country in the South American context, is territory presents a remarkable geodiversity that is reflected in its geological and mining heritage. In recent years, work on geological heritage in Uruguay has been consolidated at an academic level, reflecting a growing awareness among the national geoscientific community of the importance of this type of natural heritage, with a focus on its scientific value. However, there is still no systematic knowledge of mining heritage at a national level. Nevertheless, some mining districts have been well studied by academia and the geological survey.

A prime example of this work is the amethyst deposits of the Los Catalanes Gemological District, defined by DINAMIGE (Techera et al., 2007), in the department of Artigas (northern Uruguay). Currently, several mining companies are extracting world-class amethysts there, employing hundreds of workers and enabling some abandoned mines to support a local geotourism venture as part of the Botucatú Mining Geopark project. Since 2016, the company that operates the municipal hotel “San Eugenio del Cuareim” (in the city of Artigas) has offered a tourism package that includes a tour of an inactive mine belonging to “Oliveira Minerals,” located 70 kilometers southeast of the departmental capital, near the town of La Bolsa. The “Mining Safari” excursion includes transportation, safety equipment, and a guided 1,000-meter tour through galleries designed to showcase geodes containing agate and amethyst mineralizations (Fig. 3). The visit concludes at the raw stone processing workshops, where tourists can view and purchase ornamental pieces and jewelry while learning about the deposit's origin, exploitation, and environmental stewardship. This is an example of a geological resource with economic and heritage value, recognized for its international scientific relevance by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) in 2022 (Goso and Faraone, 2022), with potential for educational and tourism use, thus providing another alternative for the local socio-economic development of a mining district.

title: Geophysical Evaluation of Terminalia Mantaly Tree Root System and its Implications for a Nearby Structure

authors: Ogundeji, Victoria Seun [1], Eluwole, Akinola Bolaji [2], Olaseeni, Olayiwola Grace [3], Adekoya-Iromini, Modinat Adejoke [4], Aroyehun, Morufu Tope [5], Olasupo, Temitope Emmanuel [6], Idowu, Idowu Olatunji [7], Olorunleke, Ayobami Jeremiah [8]

(2) Department of Geophysics, Federal University Oye-Ekiti, Oye-Ekiti, Ekiti, USA
(3) Department of Geophysics, Federal University Oye-Ekiti, Oye-Ekiti, Ekiti, USA

(8) Department of Geophysics, Federal University Oye-Ekiti, Oye-Ekiti, Ekiti, USA
abstract:
Tree roots are known to pose serious threats to building foundations if not properly checked. It became necessary to study the root zone geometry of a Terminalia Mantaly Tree close (6.5 m) to the Theatre and Media Arts (TMA) Building at the Federal University Oye-Ekiti (FUOYE) Nigeria. The electrical resistivity method of geophysical prospecting was adopted for the study. The 2D Electrical Resistivity Imaging (ERI) technique was used, with the dipole-dipole array as the preferred array. The electrode spacing (a) was 0.5 m and the expansion factor (n) varied from 1 – 5. Measurements were taken along eleven (11) E – W traverses which had 0.5 m separation. The data were converted into 2D subsurface Electrical Resistivity Images (ERIs) with the aid of the Dipro for Windows software. The 2D data were migrated into quasi 3D electrical resistivity depth slices. On the 2D images the root zone manifested as near-surface low resistivity media while the observed oval shaped high resistivity closures on the traverses with the closest proximity to the tree were suspected to be the mirror images of the tree’s tap root. Similarly, on the 3D depth slices, the root zone was characterized by central low to moderate resistivity ( 500 ohm-m) encircled by a near-elliptical high resistivity (> 500 ohm-m) ring around the tree position. The root zone orientation, radius and area were estimated from the dimension of the ellipse. A predominant NN – SE orientation was estimated for the fibrous/horizontal roots with major and minor radii to the tree stem estimated at 2.05 m and 1.75 m respectively. The taproot was suspected to manifest adjacent opposing resistivity characteristics directly beside the tree stem. The area covered by the fibrous/horizontal roots could not be identified beyond 0.61 m depth. The study identified that although the horizontal roots are prone to rapid growth in the NW – SE direction, their moderate growth in the western and eastern directions still calls for concern as they pose future threats to the foundation of the TMA Building.

Keywords:Tree roots, Electrical Resistivity Imaging (ERI), Root zone geometry, Building foundations, Terminalia Mantaly Tree

title: Geology-Groundwater Digital Twin for Groundwater-Energy Studies in the U.S. Gulf Coastal Plain
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Tsai, Frank [1], Elkharakany, Mohammed [2], Khadem, Sharfaraj [3], Kuo, Eric [4], Song, Yuqi [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA,
(2) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(3) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(4) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(5) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
abstract: The massive Cenozoic sediments in the U.S. Gulf Coastal Plain (GCP) offer great potential for carbon geological storage and groundwater resources to support energy industries. However, concerns have been raised regarding potential drinking groundwater contamination from CO 2 injections as well as groundwater depletion from excessive pumping for mega data centers. To support a sustainable energy transition and resilient data center operations, this study develops a geology-groundwater digital twin through geological and groundwater models for informed decision-making. We construct a detailed geological model for the Lower Mississippi-Gulf (LMG) region that comprises the Mississippi Embayment aquifer system (MEAS), the Coastal Lowlands aquifer system (CLAS), and the Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer (MRVA). Using more than 164,000 well logs, we apply a horizon-assisted lithologic modeling (HALM) method to integrate horizon surfaces and borehole lithology on USGS National Hydrogeological Grid (NHG) of 1-km resolution. The LMG geological model is then further developed into a MODFLOW 6 groundwater model using an unstructured-grid discretization. Moreover, the existing USGS GULF model and the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) GMA 11, 12, 13, 15 and 16 groundwater models, which cover the CLAS and the Coastal Uplands aquifer system in Texas are converted to MODFLOW 6 unstructured-grid configurations. These models are seamlessly coupled into a GCP regional groundwater model via Groundwater Flow to Groundwater Flow exchange (EXG-GWFGWF) packages and executed with parallel computing to reduce simulation time. The resulting regional-scale GCP geology-groundwater digital twin provides a platform to evaluate groundwater availability for current and future energy development scenarios.

title: An Integrated Methodology for Rockfall Risk Assessment Across the U.S. National Park Service
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies
authors: Reagan, Briana G. [1], Wood, John R. “Jack” [2], Capps, Denny [3], Farny, Nicholas [4]
affiliations: (1) Conservation Legacy, Durango, CO, USA; US National Park Service, Geologic Resources Division, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) US National Park Service, Geologic Resources Division, Lakewood, CO, USA
(3) US National Park Service, Geologic Resources Division, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(4) Federal Highway Administration, Western Federal Lands Highway Division, Vancouver, WA, USA
abstract:
A multi-agency team of geologists developed an integrated methodology to assess rockfall risk, improve visitor and staff safety, and strengthen infrastructure resilience across the National Park Service (NPS) system. Rockfall is one expression of the geologic processes that create and shape many park resources and values, but these same processes can also threaten preservation, access, and use. This tension is central to NPS geohazard management: protecting people and infrastructure while preserving the dynamic landscapes and resources that parks were established to conserve.

The methodology combines geotechnical asset-management frameworks, field instrumentation, remote-sensing data, rockfall modeling, statistical analysis, and management-oriented reporting. It integrates established tools such as the Unstable Slope Management Program for Federal Land Management Agencies (USMP) with data from LiDAR, GNSS, photogrammetry, uncrewed aerial systems (UAS), and telemetered tensiometers. After acquisition, these datasets are processed using standard geospatial, statistical, and rockfall modeling software to evaluate modeled rockfall trajectories, potential impact zones, associated hazards, and potential risks to infrastructure, visitors, and staff.

We developed and tested the methodology in problematic areas across multiple national park units so that it could be generalized to other areas. These examples allowed us to evaluate how different site conditions, data sources, and model parameters influence rockfall trajectory modeling and risk interpretation. One site provided a rare opportunity to compare model behavior with the real-time observation of an approximately 11 m³ rockfall. The naturally initiated event occurred on a vertical rock ledge and propelled meter-sized boulders downslope, with many large blocks stopping in a swale adjacent to the park unit’s sole road. Photogrammetry data generated through UAS flights provided the needed rockfall runout geometry for modeling. Incorporating these observations into model attributes allowed us to better mimic the observed rockfall and improve comparative analysis of model parameters, strengthening the utility of probabilistic rockfall models in other settings.

We present repeatable asset-management analytical methods to be linked with site-specific observations, high-resolution geospatial data, probabilistic modeling, and quantitative analysis. In turn, these tools provide a transferable decision-support framework for rockfall risk assessment across the NPS. Broader application can help managers prioritize risk-reduction actions, improve visitor and staff safety, strengthen infrastructure resilience, and protect the resources and values that define many park landscapes.

title: Making Science Fun: Developing Educational STEM Games for the Classroom to Explore Water Resource Management
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part II)
authors: Siomades, Sunday Honor [1], Schneider, Blair [2], Seybold, Erin [3], Zipper, Sam [4]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, ; University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA; University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA

abstract: Groundwater contained by aquifers is an essential domestic and economic resource in western Kansas. Trans-generational understanding of how to sustainably manage limited Kansas groundwater reserves––a topic encapsulated in Earth science/geoscience courses––begins in Kansas classrooms. Earth science is poorly represented in secondary education, despite Kansas state science standards providing a basis for including the discipline in curricula. The Kansas Geological Survey (KGS) developed a groundwater-focused educational package including the original aquifer game, OGALLALA , as a supplement to Kansan secondary school curricula to foster enhanced water resource literacy. The KGS partnered with secondary educators across Kansas to introduce and evaluate the effectiveness of the game in classroom learning during the 2025-26 academic year. Statistical and qualitative analysis demonstrated significant increases in student knowledge of groundwater systems, as well as enhanced engagement in classroom learning. Evaluating OGALLALA and its accompanying educational package (a) expands on how geoscience can be better communicated, (b) provides insight into game learning as an educational mechanism, and (c) equips educators with accessible geoscience education resources.
