title: Landslide Risk Assessment Strategies in the Himalayas
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment
authors: Henke, Bryson [1], Sanchez, Veronica [2]
affiliations: (1) Physics & Geosciences, Texas A&M University - Kingsville, Kingsville, TX, USA
(2) Physics & Geosciences, Texas A&M University, Kingsville, TX, USA
abstract: Many factors affect slope stability and landslide risk, including slope, relief, seismic activity, rock or soil types, rainfall, and human development. Seismic gaps, long periods without earthquakes, in active seismic areas may reflect an unseen addition to the severity of risk. The study area includes the region of central Nepal, and extends along the Himalayas. This area on the southern side of the Himalayas experiences frequent seismic events, with some notable gaps, and possesses several other contributing risk factors against slope stability, such as monsoonal rains and weak soil or rock. This project investigates the effects of local factors on a high-risk area, as well as how seismic gaps influence slope risk. Seismic data for the selected area was compiled, analyzed, and mapped against landslide reports and other geologic and terrain data to better understand and plan around the seismic effect on slope stability. Satellite imagery and landslide inventories were compared to locate, confirm, and categorize the type of landslides involved, as that provides insight into which factors contributed to the event. Preliminary analysis shows a correlation between landslide report density and slope hazards, rainfall, and seismicity. While preliminary results show a majority of landslides in the study area are influenced by rainfall, 10% are directly related to seismicity and 20% of local reports had unknown causes. This could be due to poor imagery or difficulty with accessing affected regions. The continuing investigation plans to work with seismic and landslide databases in order to connect and map the two categories to identify potential buffer zones and define local (10-100’s km scale) seismic gaps. The goal of the project is to define the extent to which local hazards correlate to their respective landslides and potentially produce a hazard probability map.

title: Enhancing Miocene Turkana Basin Fossil Interpretations with Site-Specific Biomarker Paleoecological Reconstructions
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic
authors: Tweedy, Ruth Rosegrant [1], Saslaw, Mae [2], Henkes, Gregory A. [3], Stinchcomb, Gary [4], Lukens, William E. [5], Green, Daniel [6], de los Rios, Natalia [7], Uno, Kevin [8]
affiliations: (1) Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Georgetown University,
(3) Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY,
(4) University of Memphis, Memphis, Tennessee, USA
(5) James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA,
(6) Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
(7) Harvard College, Cambridge, MA, USA
(8) Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract:
The Turkana Basin is an ideal setting for investigating the effects of tectonics and climate on the mammalian fossil record. As part of the East African Rift System, the basin has evolved substantially throughout the Neogene, with rifting, basin segmentation, and related and independent climatic shifts. Turkana preserves one of the most complete records of Late Cenozoic mammalian evolution in Africa, making it an exceptional natural laboratory for reconstructing how these pressures shaped mammal evolution over time. Though regional biomarker records are well established from marine cores, terrestrial records tied explicitly to fossil-bearing localities remain sparse, particularly through the Miocene.

This study applies isotopic and chain-length-based n -alkane proxies to reconstruct paleohydrology and vegetation at ten sites across the basin, spanning the late Oligocene (Topernawi, ~29 Ma) to early Pliocene (Lothagam, ~5 Ma). A total of 170 sediment samples (primarily paleosols) were screened for plant-derived n -alkane lipids and analyzed for chain-length distribution and, where sample yield allowed, compound-specific and δD. n -Alkane δ 13 C values from seven sites indicate C3-dominated ecosystems, while chain-length-derived Fraction Woody Cover (FWC) estimates reveal that some sites (e.g., Buluk, ~16.2 Ma) supported open C3 ecosystems, perhaps reflecting locally abundant C3 grasses. These signals are corroborated by published tooth mesowear studies and δ 13 C values from herbivore tooth enamel. Recent work within the basin and in broader Eastern Africa suggest local C4 vegetation signals from the early Miocene, however, this signal is not evident within our dataset. Analyses for some sites remain ongoing.

The eleven δD measurements from these sites represent the oldest terrestrial application of plant wax δD in Africa. Although the Turkana Basin is among the driest places in eastern Africa today, mean δD values are over 15‰ depleted relative to modern precipitation, suggesting wetter Miocene conditions supported by paleosol geochemistry, sedimentary geology, and fossil communities. These Miocene δD reconstructions span a ~40‰ range, which likely reflects a combination of long-term variability in δD (modern values span ~50‰) and error associated with measurements.

Ongoing work will integrate these results with tectonic and ecosystem-web analyses to more fully resolve the paired influences of tectonics and ecology on mammal evolution.

title: From Field to Phone: Mobile Device Workflows for 3D Digitization of Paleontological Specimens and Sites
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research
authors: Avrahami, Haviv [1]
affiliations: (1) Paleontology, Museum of the Rockies, Bozeman, MT, USA
abstract:
Three-dimensional (3D) surface digitization has become an increasingly important component of paleontological research, museum curation, education, and scientific visualization. Historically, the generation of high-fidelity 3D surface data required either traditional DSLR-based photogrammetry workflows or expensive commercial scanners, both of which often involve extensive equipment, steep learning curves, computationally intensive processing, and limited portability. Recent advances in mobile-device hardware and computational photography have rapidly transformed this landscape.

In this presentation, I provide an overview of mobile-device workflows for the rapid 3D digitization of paleontological specimens, field localities, and museum collections focusing primarily on the application Polycam. These workflows leverage modern smartphone capabilities including LiDAR sensors, depth mapping, multi-lens imaging systems, and rapid cloud based, AI-assisted, reconstruction algorithms to generate high-fidelity textured meshes directly from handheld devices. Comparative evaluations between mobile-device workflows and commercial scanners demonstrate that modern smartphones can now rival or exceed traditional approaches in several key areas, including texture fidelity, portability, workflow speed, ease of use, and the reconstruction of small or geometrically complex specimens. Using macro-lens enabled workflows and inexpensive supplemental lighting, submillimeter-scale surface detail can be captured in objects ranging from microvertebrate fossils to large mounted skeletons and in situ field sites.

These workflows have enabled the rapid generation of research-quality 3D datasets in both laboratory and remote field settings, while substantially reducing equipment costs and technical barriers for students, researchers, museums, and community-science initiatives. Full 360° watertight models can often be generated in minutes using only consumer-grade devices, allowing for scalable digitization of large collections and temporary collection visits. Applications extend beyond paleontology into archaeology, historical artifact conservation, geoscience specimen documentation, forensic science, education, digital outreach, and 3D printing.

As mobile-device hardware and computational imaging continue to improve, accessible photogrammetric workflows are increasingly democratizing the creation, sharing, and long-term preservation of high-quality 3D scientific data.

title: Fluid Distribution And Water Saturation Variability In A Heterogeneous Gas-Condensate Reservoir: A Petrophysical Study Of The Kapuni Field, New Zealand
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment (Posters)
authors: Elbarouni, Rodwan A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
abstract: Accurate characterization of fluid distribution and water saturation variability is critical for reliable estimation of gas-in-place volumes and production forecasting in heterogeneous gas-condensate reservoirs. This study investigates the controls on water saturation distribution and free water level (FWL) variability across three wells — TK-01, TK-02, and TK-03 — penetrating the Mangahewa Formation of the Kapuni Field, Taranaki Basin, New Zealand. An integrated petrophysical approach combining Archie water saturation estimation, bulk volume water (BVW) analysis, and depth-saturation cross-plot evaluation was applied to identify capillary transition zones, irreducible water saturation regimes, and free water level positions across the field. Results demonstrate that water saturation varies systematically between wells and is strongly influenced by structural elevation. TK-03, positioned at the anticlinal crest, exhibits the lowest mean water saturation values in productive Bearing intervals (Sw = 28.7–32.4%) and the longest estimated hydrocarbon column heights, consistent with a predominantly irreducible saturation regime. In contrast, TK-02 shows elevated mean water saturation values in the Bearing zones (Sw = 53.8–58.9%), variable BVW distributions, and limited hydrocarbon column development, indicating active capillary transition zone effects at this structurally lower position. TK-01 exhibits intermediate saturation characteristics consistent with a mixed irreducible and transition zone regime. The estimated free water level deepens from TK-02 toward TK-03, suggesting possible reservoir compartmentalization or tilted fluid contacts associated with the structural complexity of the Kapuni anticline. These findings demonstrate that structural position is the primary control on fluid distribution within the Mangahewa reservoir and that capillary transition zone effects significantly reduce effective hydrocarbon saturation in structurally lower well locations, with important implications for reserves estimation and production strategy.

abstract: The La Tesorera granite, is located in the northern part of Mesa Central of Mexico, intrudes Lower Cretaceous volcanosedimentary and sedimentary sequences, forming skarn zones and polymetallic mineralization of Pb-Zn-Cu-Ag. Field and laboratory analyses, including petrography, X-ray diffraction, and whole-rock geochemistry, indicates that La Tesorera is a Type-I, calc-alkaline, magnesian, metaluminous granite, slightly oxidized and moderately evolved, belonging to the magnetite series. Primary mineral assemblages include albite + quartz + orthoclase + actinolite + biotite, with alteration minerals such as montmorillonite and clinochlore, reflecting sericite and chlorite alteration. Geochemical signatures, as Y/Nb ratios and negative Eu anomalies, suggest emplacement in a volcanic arc environment. Elevated large-ion lithophile elements (LILE) relative to high-field-strength elements (HFSE), together with mafic enclaves and feldspar fractionation, point to partial melting associated with thinning of the upper continental crust during post-Laramide extensional relaxation. Hydrothermal alteration is evidenced by high K/Rb ratios, indicating early fluid interaction rather than late-stage postmagmatic processes. Its metalliferous potential and petrogenetic significance lie in the behavior of oxidation ratios (Fe₂O₃/FeO vs. FeOT) that range from 0.26–0.34 in fresh samples, increasing to 0.40–0.85 in altered granite, indicating a transition from ferric to ferrous states and association with the magnetite series (magnetite > ilmenite). Low Rb fractionation suggests limited magmatic differentiation, consistent with Type-I granites linked to Cu–Au metalliferous deposits. Contact with Lower Cretaceous limestones produced polymetallic skarn mineralization (Pb–Zn–Cu), with emplacement age (~73 Ma) correlating to mineralization timing. According to petrogenetic analysis it is identified a crystallization system with minimal fluorine (0–1%), with samples containing Li (0.01%) and F (0.03%). Variations in albite– orthoclase relations suggest crystallization under fluorine-rich conditions, with hydrothermal alteration driving fluorine loss to vapor phases. Lithium concentrations (17–100 ppm) remain below highly fractionated granite systems, indicating limited enrichment compared to riebeckite-bearing granites where Li is introduced during post-magmatic processes. The La Tesorera granite represents a moderately oxidized, Type-I system with metallogenic associations to Cu–Au and Pb–Zn–Cu skarns, while its petrogenetic traits reveal minimal fluorine and lithium enrichment, underscoring its role in regional magmatism and mineralization processes.

title: A new orodromine (Dinosauria: Ornithischia) from the Upper Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Northcentral Montana.

abstract:
Orodromine dinosaurs are a frequent constituent of the Campanian Two Medicine Formation fauna, especially in the Flag Butte Member. Since the erection of Orodromeus makelai in 1988, all orodromine skeletal material from the Two Medicine Formation subsequently fell under the purview of this monospecific genus. However, these skeletal occurrences span approximately five million years and morphological variation previously observed in this sample warrants a comprehensive reexamination.

Here we report the first new orodromine taxon to emerge from the Two Medicine assemblage, informally referred to as the “Landslide Butte Orodromine”. This taxon represents the stratigraphically youngest orodromine known in the Two Medicine-Judith River-Belly River clastic wedge. The “Landslide Butte Orodromine” exhibits a jugal horn morphology distinct from other Early and Late Cretaceous orodromines and illuminates important aspects of the orodromine body plan that have remained poorly understood, particularly the manus and tail.

Furthermore, the “Landslide Butte Orodromine” raises important questions about the disappearance of the clade from Laramidia after the Campanian, and how orodromines were able to coexist with other small-bodied ornithischians. Lastly, referred “Landslide Butte Orodromine” specimens from Alberta suggest previously unrecognized faunal connectivity between the upper Two Medicine and Dinosaur Park Formations among small-bodied dinosaur taxa.

abstract: Earth sciences affect human life in countless ways and represent one of the most essential branches of knowledge for understanding our planet. Geosciences are the foundation of the resources we rely on daily to sustain a functional society, nevertheless are frequently misrepresented in public communication. To address this challenge, the Earth Sciences department of the Faculty of Engineering create a science communication group, which is conformed by leaders representing each academic program, in this case we share information of the Geology Engineering and Metallurgy and Materials Engineering programs. We have developed a wide variety of didactic activities, most of them are inspire by Mexican traditional games, modified to present geological, materials and metallurgical process with concepts in a clear, engaging, and accessible way, tailored to the age, needs, interests, and preferences of younger and older generations. The goal is to promote accurate and appealing knowledge while fostering curiosity and participation. With these activities, participants can gradually develop critical and analytical skills that will enable them to question, interpret, and understand the geological heritage around them through education.

abstract:
Lithium-rich evaporite basins of the Central Andes are strategic resources for the global energy transition, yet groundwater systems hosted within these basins may accumulate arsenic (As), boron (B), lithium (Li), and associated trace elements (TEs). This study characterizes the hydrogeochemical signature of As, B, Li and associated TEs, in groundwater of the Coipasa Salt Flat Basin, Bolivia. The hydrogeochemical processes that control groundwater quality in these systems remain poorly understood. Groundwater wells and springs, influenced by hydrothermal water and volcanic mineral units were sampled[MO1] to evaluate hydrogeochemical characteristics and identify the main geogenic sources responsible for the co-occurrence of TEs.

Based on hydrogeochemical, geological and geostatistical data, three aquifer types were identified. (i) Shallow, oxidizing alluvial aquifers with naturally elevated concentrations of As, B and Li at levels hazardous to human health; (ii) Confined aquifers, with low levels of As, B and Li, where natural attenuation occurs through redox and adsorption/desorption processes; and (iii) saline semiconfined aquifers with low As concentrations but elevated Li and B contents. Groundwater[MO2] used for human consumption shows concentrations of up to 595 µg/L of As (73% exceeding the WHO guideline of 10 µg/L), up to 8441 µg/L of B (17% exceeding the WHO guideline of 2400 µg/L) and up to 1964 µg/L of Li (100% exceeding the US EPA guideline of 10 µg/L)

Hydrothermal waters were classified as reducing Na–Cl-rich waters enriched in As, B, Li, and other TEs (Rb, Sr, and Ba), sharing the basin hydrogeochemical signature and linked to volcanic mineral units. XRF analyses further demonstrate that these mineral units contain trace concentrations of Rb, Sr, Ba, As, S, and Sb, confirming that hydrothermal fluids transport and incorporate these elements during silica precipitation The coexistence of silica and TEs phases in the sinter matrix indicates that these deposits act as mineralogical archives of deep geothermal fluid signatures.

Hydrothermal water/rock interaction, redox, mineralogical and evaporation inputs define the basin’s hydrogeochemical signature from the Andean Volcanic Belt towards Coipasa Salt Flat and confirm the predominantly geogenic origin of these elements in the basin. These findings are crucial for distinguishing natural contamination from potential anthropogenic impacts on groundwater resource security in Li-rich regions.

title: Testing Tectonic Controls of Rock Exhumation and Topographic Evolution in the Western Bhutan Himalaya: Insights from Thermokinematic and Landscape-Evolution Modeling
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse (Posters)
authors: Fan, Suoya [1], McQuarrie, Nadine [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, PITTSBURGH, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA,
abstract:
The geometry of the megathrust in the eastern Himalaya is strongly debated. Previous studies also suggest a marked decrease in exhumation and/or shortening during the late Miocene across this region, potentially related to the Shillong Plateau uplift. In the western Bhutan Himalaya, isolated high-elevation, low-relief surfaces south of the main High Himalaya plateau are deeply incised by major transverse rivers. These features make this region an ideal area for investigating interactions among tectonics, climate, and surface processes.

We construct balanced cross sections incorporating flexural isostasy and erosion constrained by a surface similar to modern Himalayan topography and test representative kinematic models using thermokinematic modeling in the western Bhutan Himalaya. Although different reconstructions may reproduce the surface geology comparably well, they imply contrasting subsurface structures and kinematics. The thermochronologic data are best reproduced by a model with a hinterland-dipping duplex beneath the Paro window, a long megathrust flat, and a crustal-scale ramp ~160 km north of the frontal thrust. In the preferred model, the Paro duplex and frontal imbricate thrusts developed broadly synchronously during ca. 9–6 Ma and were subsequently translated to their current locations above the upper megathrust flat. Farther north, rocks including a hinterland duplex exposing the Great Himalayan Sequence that formed at ca. 12–11 Ma, were translated from a lower megathrust flat across the crustal ramp, producing renewed hinterland rock uplift and exhumation. This kinematic history reproduces both the broadly flat spatial pattern of low-temperature cooling ages (mostly 4-8 Ma) across the frontal part and young ages (mostly 3-6 Ma) above the hinterland duplex, replicating measured data. In contrast, a model with a foreland-dipping Paro duplex, a modern ramp ~90 km from the frontal thrust, and a long hinterland flat generates pronounced cooling-age variations of >10 Myr for all chronometers over distances of only 10-20 km above and to the south of the Paro duplex and insufficient late-stage hinterland exhumation.

These results suggest that the isolated high-elevation, low-relief surfaces are likely relict topography that has been translated southward rather than products of recent ramp-induced uplift. Small-magnitude out-of-sequence thrusting may have transiently reorganized uplift and facilitated river incision, allowing transverse rivers to dissect the topography and isolate the high surfaces. Landscape-evolution modeling incorporating reconstructed kinematics is in progress to test these structural models.

abstract:
Advancements in inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) instrumentation equipped with a collision/reaction cell technology have enabled in situ Rb-Sr isotopic analyses without the isobaric interference of 87 Rb on 87 Sr through fluorination of Sr using SF 6 . In this study, we used a Thermo Fisher Scientific Neoma MC-ICP-MS/MS coupled with an ESL NWR 193 nm nanosecond excimer laser system to establish methods for in situ Rb-Sr geochronology and applied the methods to lunar samples and achondrites. 87 Rb/ 86 Sr and 87 Sr/ 86 Sr ratios for feldspar were normalized to the NIST SRM 610 glass and the AMNH 107160 labradorite standard, respectively.

Analyses of plagioclase and K-feldspar from the Dartmoor and Shap granites define isochrons ages of 285.9 ± 1.2 Ma and 409.6 ± 3.7 Ma, respectively, using a slope correction factor of 0.77. These ages are identical to published data acquired by TIMS. Analyses of the ungrouped achondrite Erg Chech 002 require a correction factor of 0.84; applying this factor to the achondrite NWA 6704 produces a feldspar age of 4509 ± 88 Ma and ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) i of 0.69807 ± 0.03360 (2 s.e.), consistent with a previously reported TIMS Rb-Sr data [1]. Plagioclase from the lunar meteorite NWA 6950 defines a Rb-Sr isochron age of 3268 ± 111 Ma (2 s.e.), which is consistent with the Rb-Sr internal isochron age of 3.29 ± 0.11 Ga for the paired meteorite NWA 2977 [2]. Analyses of Apollo impact melt rock 60635 yield an isochron age of 3881 ± 79 Ma with ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) i of 0.699201 ± 0.000051 (2 s.e.) consistent with previously reported reference age: 3831 ± 10 Ma [3] and ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) i = 0.699234 ± 36 [4]. These results demonstrate that LA-MC-ICP-MS/MS enables in situ Rb-Sr geochronology for both terrestrial and extraterrestrial materials when appropriate matrix-matched calibration strategies based on feldspar composition are employed.

title: Tracing West to East Himalayan Sediment Transport: Detrital Zircon U-Pb Geochronology from the Kosi, Kali Gandaki and Manas Rivers
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)

abstract: The Kali Gandaki, Kosi and Manas Rivers are three major tributaries of the Ganges-Brahmaputra River System. Kali Gandaki River drains the northwestern Himalaya while Kosi River drains the central Himalaya, and they merge with the Ganges River downstream. On the other hand, Manas River drains the northeastern Himalaya and merges with the Brahmaputra River downstream. These tributaries are the first order sediment signal carriers towards the Himalaya to Ganges-Brahmaputra (GB) source-to-sink (S2S) sediment dispersal system. Large scale sediment provenance of the GB System highlights the presence and changes of different source signatures. However, they are unable to identify the origin of these different source terranes; where and how each of these signatures amplify and shred down. Hence, we propose to study the major tributaries of the GB River System: Kali Gandaki, Kosi and Manas Rivers based on detrital zircon (DZ) U-Pb geochronology. We aim to systematically collect 27 samples from the tributaries from upstream to downstream before their confluence with the GB system. We will also include results from the downstream Ganges and Brahmaputra Rivers. The results from this study will distinguish the first order source terrane signatures from the source region, spatial differences moving from west to eastern Himalaya and finally reveal what signal is being carried towards the main trunk river. On regional scale, this study aims to provide insights into S2S sedimentary provenance for modern systems which will be used as a framework for other modern systems.

abstract:
The Cerralvo Basin, located in the southern Gulf of California, represents a key geological setting for investigating tectonomagmatic processes associated with the transition from subduction to lithospheric extension. This study presents a petrographic, geochemical, and geochronological characterization of volcanic, volcaniclastic, and sedimentary rocks recovered from submarine escarpments within the basin, with the goal of reconstructing its magmatic and tectonic evolution.

Samples were collected during the FK210922 cruise of the Schmidt Ocean Institute using the ROV SuBastian (dives S0-461 and S0-469) at water depths ranging from 245 to 996 m. The analyzed lithologies include andesitic lava flows, volcanic breccias, tuffs, and fossil-bearing sedimentary deposits, recording a complex depositional and volcanic history. Petrographic observations and whole-rock geochemical data indicate predominantly calc-alkaline affinities consistent with arc-related magmatism, along with evidence for post-emplacement hydrothermal alteration.

Four main evolutionary stages are recognized: (1) explosive volcanism, (2) transgressive terrigenous sedimentation with fossiliferous deposits, (3) renewed explosive volcanic activity, and (4) a final phase of effusive andesitic volcanism. K–Ar geochronology of the volcanic groundmass constrains the effusive andesitic stage to ca. 20–16 Ma, These results provide new petrographic and geochemical constraints on the evolution of the western Gulf of California margin and establish a comparative framework for understanding magmatic and sedimentary processes in similar tectonically active basins.

title: Flow-Induced Redistribution of Biochar Alters Hydraulic Conductivity in Sandy Porous Media
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science
authors: Howell, Amanda Marie [1], Lowe, Jude [2], Dugan, Brandon [3]
affiliations: (1) Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA

abstract:
Biochar amendments can substantially alter soil hydraulic behavior, yet the mechanisms controlling these responses remain poorly constrained because biochar particles are physically mobile under saturated flow conditions. This study investigates how imposed hydraulic gradients influence biochar redistribution and the resulting hydraulic conductivity of saturated sand-biochar systems. Homogeneous mixtures of silica sand and ground hardwood biochar (0.5 wt%) were packed into laboratory columns and subjected to three contrasting saturation regimes: strong upward saturation, gradual capillary rise, and strong downward infiltration. Visual observations and repeated constant-head hydraulic conductivity testing were used to evaluate redistribution behavior and flow evolution over time.

Distinct redistribution architectures developed under each hydraulic regime despite identical initial packing conditions. Rapid upward saturation mobilized fine biochar particles toward the column surface, producing the highest hydraulic conductivity values relative to pure sand controls. Gradual upward saturation generated localized internal aggregation with hydraulic conductivity values similar to unamended sand. Forced downward infiltration produced stratified structures and localized pore clogging near the lower column, resulting in the lowest hydraulic conductivity. Results indicate that hydraulic gradient magnitude and direction strongly govern the spatial organization of biochar within porous media and can produce fundamentally different hydraulic outcomes from the same starting material.

These findings demonstrate that saturation history and transient flow conditions represent first-order controls on biochar mobility and effective hydraulic conductivity. The results have implications for laboratory testing procedures, engineered filtration systems, irrigation practices, and predictive models of fines migration in granular porous media.

abstract: As approaches for applying supervised machine learning to create geothermal resource maps and similar products (for example, play fairway analyses) mature, opportunities to improve model predictions become increasingly concentrated in the choice of more informative independent input datasets (that is, input features). Recognizing that topography in the Great Basin of the western United States reflects subsurface structures that contribute to permeability (for example, faults), recent work by DeAngelo and others isolated local topography from regional trends in elevation change to deconvolute signals that may help to locate hydrothermal systems. Herein, we evaluate the impact of replacing raw elevation with separated features for regional elevation trend and detrended elevation as input features on favorability maps by assessing model performance through the ability to predict known power‑producing hydrothermal systems not used in the training data and through visual inspection of the favorability maps. In doing so, we find that deconvoluting elevation signals enhances the predictive skill of the model for known power‑producing systems not used in the training data and transforms predicted high-favorability areas from cutting across basins and ranges to following range fronts within basins, providing a more accurate and geologically defensible favorability map.

abstract: After the East Troublesome Fire in 2020, Willow Creek Reservoir in Colorado has experienced regular algal blooms. Previous studies of wildfire impacts on water quality have identified phosphorus and other nutrients as major contaminants linked to severe burns. Ammonium phosphate-based fire retardants are often used to control major wildfires but may also serve as a high concentration source of phosphorus to the environment. In this study we measure soil concentrations of phosphorus to identify the location of a retardant deployment upslope of Willow Creek Reservoir and use lake sediment chemistry and remote sensing maps of algal bloom concentrations to distinguish between the phosphorus contributions from retardant and the burned watershed upstream. Using these soil chemistries, bloom behaviors, and water chemistry, we evaluate the long-term fate of phosphorus in Willow Creek Reservoir. We show that the burned watershed, not the retardant, is the major contributor of phosphorus flux into lake sediments and that algal blooms are likewise dependent on nutrient contributions from the burned watershed rather than the retardant deployment. We also show that phosphorus concentrations are not accumulating in the sediment and that concentrations in the water column and algal bloom intensities are returning to pre-fire baseline conditions. These results contribute to the understanding of water quality impacts of fire and post-fire biogeochemical cycling of phosphorus in other fire-impacted lakes, especially those that lack the pre- and post-fire water quality monitoring present at Willow Creek Reservoir.

title: Stream-Riparian Connectivity in the Permafrost Landscape of the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Collins, Jared Michael [1], Gooseff, Michael N. [2]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: Riparian zones define the area of connectivity between streams and the surrounding landscape and are areas of high ecological import. In the McMurdo Dry Valleys (MDVs), Antarctica, glacial melt during the austral summer provides water to stream channels and their surrounding riparian zones, reactivating microbial communities and contributing to geochemical weathering in and adjacent to the streams. Riparian connectivity in the MDVs is dependent on several factors, including discharge, local morphology, and active layer thaw dynamics. Here, we present data on seasonal riparian connectivity in two streams with varied flow patterns and morphologies. Our analyses utilize over ten years of subsurface temperature and water content at multiple depths and locations on a continuum from thalweg to the stream banks. The two streams, Von Guerard Stream and Green Creek, differ greatly in channel morphology, stream length, discharge patterns, and microbial abundance. By combining this subsurface data with surface discharge and water quality metrics collected by stream gages, we determine metrics of riparian connectivity, including active layer thaw and refreeze patterns, riparian wetting timing and magnitude, and drivers in the differences between the two streams. We find that the exchange between stream water and the riparian sediments serves as an important thermal conductor, contributing to active layer thaw and stabilizing sediment temperatures when compared to dry soils. In addition, comparing the two streams reveals that the highly channelized and intermittent Von Guereard Stream has a smaller riparian area that exhibits more fluctuations in subsurface temperature and soil moisture compared to the wider and steadier streamflow of Green Creek. Overall, these findings highlight physical processes in the riparian zones of MDV streams that have strong implications on local biogeochemical processes.

abstract: Raman spectroscopy and laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) are complementary laser-based vibrational spectroscopy techniques that together can provide a comprehensive characterization of geologic environments. Raman spectroscopy is a mostly non-destructive surface technique that provides structural and chemical information to identify a wide variety of materials including organic compounds and mineral polymorphs. In natural systems, factors such as grain size/orientation, crystallinity, sample heterogeneity, and weathering can create challenges in obtaining meaningful Raman spectra. Techniques like LIBS help to clarify the chemical composition by measuring the atomic composition. We use a new approach that utilizes laser-induced plasma emissions in mid-IR (2 to 12 µm, 833 – 5000 cm -1 ), which enables LIBS to reveal the molecular structure of the sample components. This capability increases the confidence for mineral identification as well as how the minerals are chemically related to spatially associated organic species. Here we present data from host basalts and secondary mineral deposits from geographically distinct lava tubes. Lava tubes are subsurface environments that provide dynamic hydrogeological niches where microbial and mineral processes are intertwined. The host basalts and abiotically-precipitated secondary mineral deposits are habitable environments that provide cation- and nutrient- rich substrates, and a wide variety of microbial metabolisms contribute to bioalteration processes in these environments. Our ultimate goal is to understand the relationships between abiotically and biotically induced mineral phases, microbial metabolisms, and the host rocks in lava tube environments. In the process, this work is helping to improve the use of Raman spectroscopy and LIBS for biogeochemical studies in natural settings as well as for life detection and disseminating environmental processes on worlds beyond Earth.

title: Revealing the Reef: Satellite Remote Sensing of Navassa Island's Benthic Geomorphology
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Yates, Jacob [1]
affiliations: (1) Mariner Space Institute, San Diego, CA, ; San Diego Miramar College, San Diego, CA, USA
abstract: An observational study utilized the blue spectral band (445-516 nm) of satellite data to examine the spatial distribution of submerged reef complexes around Navassa Island. The island itself is 3.5 km long and 2 km wide, characterized by a raised plateau and steep-sided cliffs that descend to a submarine terrace at depths of approximately 23-30 meters. The reefs extend from the near-shore environment to approximately 1 km offshore. While the windward east coast is exposed to significant wave energy, resulting in extensive rubble fields and minimal coral reef development, the more protected southwest coast exhibits the largest coral cover. The blue spectral band was found to depict intricate submerged reef patterns where wave dynamics were minimal, but showed subdued complexes in areas with high wave action. This study suggests that using satellite imagery in the blue spectral band could be an essential diagnostic tool for monitoring changes in the spatial distribution of similar oceanic island reef complexes.

abstract: The hypervelocity impact experiments on Lunar Highland Simulant-1 (LHS-1) offer a compelling geological analogy for the formation of breccias on the Moon. Projectiles were launched at speeds at or near the Moon's escape velocity of 2.38 km/s, mimicking the high-energy impacts of meteorite ejecta. The kinetic energy (KE) of these projectiles, ranging from 240 J to 1680 J, was sufficient not only to halt their progress but also to induce significant changes in the target material. These impacts yielded friable lithic fragments measuring between 3 and 20 mm and a dense, 1.4-cm-diameter lithic plug. The fragments and plugs were easily comminuted and disintegrated into their constituent grains, providing physical evidence that intense pressure from hypervelocity impacts can compact loose regolith particles and "weld" them together to form new composite rock structures. This process is analogous to the shock metamorphism that occurs during natural meteorite impacts, where shock pressure waves travel through the regolith, causing varying levels of metamorphic change from melting to fracturing and brecciation. The presence of these impact-generated structures in the tests supports the theory that meteorite bombardment is a key process in the formation of lunar breccias, a dominant rock type found across the lunar highlands, and offers valuable insights into the ongoing geological activity on the Moon.

title: Fracture-Controlled Alteration in Igneous Terrains: Implications for Microbial Habitability on Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars (Posters)
authors: LaRocca, Veronica Tyler [1], PETRONIS, MICHAEL S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Natural Resource Management, New Mexico Highlands University, Geology, Santa Fe, NM, USA
(2) Natural Resource Management, NMHU, SANTA FE, NM, USA
abstract:
Volcanic and intrusive igneous systems create fractures that act as pathways for heat and mineral-rich fluids, producing alteration zones that can support microbial life. On Earth, these environments develop dike margins, intrusive contacts, and hydrothermal systems where fluid-rock interactions alter mineralogy and generate chemically favorable conditions for microbial communities. These similar volcanic and tectonic processes occurred throughout Martian history and may have produced environments capable of supporting life while preserving evidence of past biological activity. Understanding how these systems develop can be detected remotely is important for identifying future astrobiological exploration locations.

This study investigates fracture-controlled alteration systems in connection with igneous intrusions in the southwestern United States as terrestrial analogs for Mars. Field sites include well-exposed dike swarms, volcanic vents, contact alteration, and evidence of fluid migration. An integrated approach combining multispectral remote sensing, uncrewed aerial system photogrammetry, geologic mapping, and ground-based magnetometry is used to characterize alteration patterns and identify potential microbial habitats. These datasets are supplemented by rock magnetic, mineralogical, and microbial analyses to look at relationships between fracture systems, fluid pathways, mineral alteration, and biologically influenced environments.

Magnetic anomalies associated with iron oxides and alteration minerals are examined alongside visible and near-infrared spectral signatures to determine whether remote sensing techniques can reliably identify environments favorable for microbial colonization. A Raman spectrometer is used to characterize mineralogical compositions and identify potential biosignature-bearing phases within alteration zones, providing complementary information to remote sensing observations. Attention is given to intrusion-host rock contacts and alteration locations where mineral precipitation, fluid circulation, and geochemical gradients may enhance habitability and biosignature preservation. These environments provide opportunities to evaluate how biological and geological processes interact to produce detectable signatures in volcanic terrains. Similar fracture associated alteration zones have become important for planetary exploration because they may preserve evidence of past habitable conditions and serve as targets for future missions.

By comparing terrestrial fracture-controlled alteration systems with volcanic and tectonic features observed on Mars, this research is used to improve interpretation of Martian alteration zones and developing strategies for identifying future exploration targets. Results can contribute to ongoing efforts in planetary geology, geomicrobiology, andastrobiology by increasing our understanding of how volcanic systems may create and preserve habitable environments on rocky planets.

title: Scaffolded Sketching of Plate Tectonic Processes in an Asynchronous Online Introductory Geology Lecture
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Seegers Szablewski, Gina [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI, USA
abstract:
The benefits of using concept sketches in introductory geology classes are clear and have been demonstrated repeatedly in classrooms of varying sizes, with different student populations, and at schools ranging from 2-year colleges to immense research institutions. Teaching intro geology online also is not new to many of us, but we find ourselves continually faced with the challenge of encouraging deep learning while sparking interest in a topic that is new to many students. Having been an early adapter of concept sketches as a learning tool in my face-to-face lectures, I have found a way to use them successfully in an online class with over 100 students.

Using short, live, weekly recorded lectures that demonstrate how to create concept sketches is an uncomplicated way to take a learning tool with proven efficacy and apply it to an online class. Beginning with two sets of practice sketches based on geology basics, students then complete scaffolded sketches for two plate tectonic settings: an oceanic-continental subduction zone and a mid-ocean ridge. The first week concentrates on the basics of each setting and is then followed by adding details regarding igneous processes, metamorphism and deformation, and earthquakes in the following three weeks. All sketches are graded individually using a simple, structured rubric and constructive comments. The plate tectonic sketching progression culminates with a student-centered mid-term reflection of their learning process using the concept sketches.

In addition to the primary goal of helping students understand plate tectonics, the live recorded lectures and scaffolded sketches attain other educational objectives: graded interaction with faculty, significant investment and effort over time, critical analysis of presented scientific data, structured integration of learning, and application of creativity.

title: Compound Multi-Hazard Assessment Under CMIP6 Climate Scenarios: Tracking Seasonal Flood-Landslide and Drought-Fire Interactions Across Nepal
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Shrestha, Kripa [1], Reddy Duddukunta, Karthik [2], Lal, Pankaj [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Studies, Montclair State University, Montclair, New Jersey, USA
(2) Center for Computing and Informational Science, Montclair State University, Montclair, NJ, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Studies, Montclair State University, Montclair, NJ, USA
abstract:
Climate-induced hazards in mountain systems rarely occur in isolation, instead they interact through cascading and compounding pathways that single-hazard assessments fail to capture. In Nepal, extreme monsoon rainfall can trigger landslides that dam rivers and generate secondary flooding, while prolonged dry spells create drought, desiccate vegetation fuels, and elevate fire risk. Yet, most regional studies map hazards independently, providing limited insight into how compound zones emerge under climate change. We develop a seasonal multi-hazard framework that model drought, forest fire, flood, and landslide susceptibility for historical baseline (1991-2020) and future (2021-2100). Three machine learning algorithms (Explainable Boosting Machine, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting) were trained and evaluated under an identical protocol in which RF performed best for flood, landslide, and fire, while XGBoost performed best for drought. Drivers were interpreted with Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP). Future susceptibility was projected using a 13-model, bias-corrected, downscaled Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) ensemble under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5) for near, mid, and far future. Beyond mapping, we organize the results into two hydroclimatic regimes, water-excess (flood + landslide) and water-deficit (drought + fire) and tracked seasonal compound co-occurrence within each regime. Results under SSP5-8.5 shows flood-landslide compound zones expand most during monsoon and post-monsoon, while the deficit regime reconfigures, with stronger pre-monsoon drought and increased winter fire dominance. Compounding hazard zones across multiple seasons represent persistent multi-hazard hotspots concentrated along major population and infrastructure corridors, indicating that climate change disproportionately amplifies multi-hazard risk where human systems are most concentrated.

Compound Multi-hazard Risk; Disaster Risk Reduction; Machine Learning; Seasonal hazard assessment; SHAP interpretability

title: Collecting the Earth: Reinterpreting German Mineralogical Collections in a Transatlantic Context
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Cassia, Antonella [1]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Florida, North Miami, FL, USA; Modern languages, University Miami, Miami, FL, USA
abstract:
This paper examines German mineralogical collections as sites where geology, cultural history, and systems of knowledge intersect. Drawing on research conducted through the Jednak Fellowship, the project investigates how mineral specimens and mining collections in German-speaking regions, from early modern Wunderkammern to contemporary Naturkunde museums, have been classified, displayed, and interpreted across changing scientific and political contexts.

Focusing on collections associated with major mining regions such as Saxony and Idar-Oberstein, as well as museum collections in Berlin, the study explores how minerals functioned not only as scientific objects but also as symbols of extraction, industrial modernity, national identity, and humanity’s relationship with the Earth. Particular attention is given to the development of classificatory systems and museum practices that helped shape broader European and transatlantic traditions of geology, mineral collecting, and natural history display.

By reexamining historical collections through contemporary interdisciplinary perspectives, this paper argues that mineralogical collections can reveal overlooked narratives about labor, mining economies, environmental imagination, and the cultural construction of geological knowledge. The project additionally considers how reinterpretation of older collections resonates with ongoing conversations in American museums and geoscience institutions regarding geoheritage, provenance, public science communication, and the social histories embedded within scientific collections.

Combining approaches from German Studies, geoheritage studies, museum history, and mineralogy, this paper demonstrates how historical geological collections continue to generate new scientific, cultural, and ethical questions relevant to both European and North American contexts.

title: Preliminary evidence from submerged sites in the Taiwan Strait: A new perspective on the origins of the Austronesian
session_title: Geoarchaeology of the Land–Sea Interface: Processes, Preservation, and Palaeolandscape Reconstruction
authors: Zhang, Ke [1], Zhang, Suixin [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, Guangdong, China
(2) SPPM, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
abstract: The Austronesian people, strongly connected to the ocean, are widely believed to have originated from Taiwan and the southeastern Chinese coast. However, how their ancestors reached Taiwan and later spread across the Pacific remains unclear. Neolithic sites on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, such as the Dabenkeng culture (Taiwan) and the Keqiutou culture (Fujian), share common features like stamped pottery, net sinkers, and shell middens, but also show differences in decoration. Most of these sites date no earlier than 7.4 kaBP, coinciding with the post-glacial sea-level rise to near-present levels. This suggests that sea-level changes played a key role. We propose that the Austronesian ancestors emerged during the early Holocene (11.7–7.4 kaBP) in the nearshore areas of the Taiwan Strait and the Taiwan Shoal, developing a “proto-Austronesian culture” there. As sea levels rose, their low-lying habitat was progressively submerged, forcing them to retreat to the highlands on both sides of the strait. The well-known cultures like Dabenkeng and Keqiutou are actually later offshoots of these submerged ancestors, inheriting their marine characteristics. The scarcity of Neolithic remains older than 7.4 kaBP in the region is likely due to “survivor bias” – most early coastal sites are now underwater. Based on archaeological and molecular evidence, three prehistoric human lineages existed in the Taiwan Strait area. The first was a late Paleolithic local group that went extinct without leaving inheritable traces. The second lineage comprised the proto-Austronesian people (exemplified by Liangdao Man I), who developed early pottery and maritime skills in the early Holocene or late Pleistocene. Their descendants include the Dabenkeng and Keqiutou cultures, which retained marine traditions. The third lineage was an immigrant community from the Yangtze River middle-lower reaches, bringing rice farming. They merged with the second lineage around 4 kaBP, forming a middle Neolithic culture that advanced voyaging capabilities and enabled Austronesian expansion into the open ocean. We conclude that the submerged nearshore areas of the Taiwan Strait and the Taiwan Shoal were the cradle of Austronesian culture. During an NSFC-supported voyage, bottom trawls recovered pottery shards, rotten wood (Salicaceae), and mammal bone fragments from these submerged areas. Further investigation is needed to confirm this hypothesis.

title: Tracing Hydraulic Connectivity Between the Okefenokee Swamp and the Upper Floridan Aquifer
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers (Posters)
authors: Werley, Audra Alise [1], Evaristo, Jaivime [2]
affiliations: (1) Warnell School of Forestry & Natural Resources, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
(2) Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
abstract: The Okefenokee Swamp is commonly assumed to be hydraulically isolated from the Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA) by the Hawthorne Formation, a regional confining unit. Recent isotopic and hydraulic evidence challenges this assumption: an estimated 27%-95% of groundwater sampled beneath the swamp may be swamp-derived, and water level signals appear to propagate across the confining unit with a lag of approximately 30 days. The extent, spatial variability, and pathways of this exchange remain uncertain, particularly whether leakage is diffuse or focused through preferential pathways. We address these uncertainties using an expanded suite of environmental tracers in surface water, groundwater, and municipal-supply wells along three regional flowpaths defined from the predevelopment potentiometric surface. Stable water isotopes (δ 2 H, δ 18 O), tritium, SF 6 , noble gases, major ions, and 222 Rn constrain recharge sources, groundwater age, mixing, and hydraulic connectivity. We interpret these tracers using lumped-parameter age models and two-end-member mixing models. Preliminary results indicate spatially variable mixing between young, locally recharged water and older regional groundwater, consistent with nonuniform leakage across the confining unit. Integrating the full tracer suite will quantify the magnitude and spatial controls of swamp-aquifer exchange, refine the conceptual model of UFA recharge in southeastern Georgia, and provide a field-based basis for evaluating the swamp’s vulnerability to nearby groundwater withdrawals.

title: Geochemical and Petrographic Evidence of Monogenetic Magma Evolution in the Guatemalan Back-Arc
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Neidlinger, Allison Marie [1], Graettinger, Alison H [2], Custis, Andrew [3], Wroblewski, Angelina [4], Rodriguez, Dulce [5], Gordillo, Carla [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology, University of Missouri-Kansas City, Independence, Missouri, USA

abstract: Determining the geochemical and petrologic patterns of the understudied Holocene-Pleistocene Guatemalan back-arc reveals compositionally and texturally distinct magmatic signatures compared to the volcanic arc, demonstrating the need for better understanding of the processes that drive back-arc magmagenesis in Guatemala. Samples of lava and blocks from pyroclastic deposits were collected from nine monogenetic volcanoes within the southeastern Guatemalan back-arc region in the Jalapa and Ipala grabens 30-60 km east of the main volcanic arc. The nine samples were analyzed using whole-rock major and trace element analysis using X-ray Fluorescence and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectroscopy, Petrographic Analysis, and Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS). Whole-rock geochemistry classifies the lavas as basalt to basaltic andesite in composition and transitional calc-alkaline to tholeiitic magma series. Samples present a broad range of MgO contents (3.5-9 wt %) and inverse relationship with K₂O. Petrography and EDS backscattered electron imaging and point spectra show different relative abundances of olivine, clinopyroxene, and rare orthopyroxene crystals and abundant glomerocrysts across the sample suite. The variability in chemistry and mineralogy point to heterogeneous melt evolutions across the back-arc. Primitive mantle-normalized trace element diagrams display a slight enrichment in LREE typical of back-arc magmatism. The overall trend in REEs is similar to 2021 lavas from Pacaya, an arc volcano, but back-arc samples are uniformly less enriched than Pacaya lavas. These geochemical and petrographic signatures indicate diverse magmatic histories for small volume monogenetic eruptions across the back-arc. The enrichment of Guatemalan back-arc lavas relative to mid-ocean ridge basalts reflects a complex melt evolution that likely involves combinations of fractional crystallization, crustal assimilation, and diverse mantle wedge inputs. Studying these back-arc volcanoes is important for determining the mechanisms of melt generation in an understudied Holocene to Pleistocene volcanic field to help determine if there is future volcanic risk and more fully understand the tectonic setting.

abstract: Early Pleistocene burial ages of the ‘Ubeidiya Formation sediments in the Jordan Valley, Dead Sea Rift, are presented. Simple cosmogenic burial ages (one long exposure period followed by one period of burial) calculated from 26 Al/ 10 Be ratios and 10 Be concentrations indicate ages of ~3 Ma, contradicting geological, paleontological, paleomagnetic, and archeological constraints as the ‘Ubeidiya site contains human remains. By combining numerical modeling of cosmogenic nuclide build up during repeated burial-exposure cycles, paleomagnetic analysis and a minimum age of 1.1 Ma set by U-Pb dating of Melanopsis shells, two most probable time slots (1.19-1.77 and 1.93- 2.14 Ma) for the age of the ‘Ubeidiya Formation are given. The skewed distribution of cosmogenic isotope burial ages, with a median age of 2.05 Ma, indicates a higher probability of the older ages, ≥1.9 Ma. The exposure-burial history that emerges from the model and the unique position of the isotopic results on the burial plot imply that Ubeidiya sediments are sourced from recycling of sediments previously deposited and buried in the rift valley, between 4.5-3.2 Ma, subsequently exhumed, eroded, transported and redeposited along the ‘Ubeidiya paleolake shoreline, rather than from early Pleistocene erosion of bedrock along the shoulders of the rift.

title: Where are all the Chondrichthyans? Exploring the fossil record gap of Post P-TR extinction Utah
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Reed, Austin Mackenzie [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
abstract: During the end Permian mass extinction, approximately 80-90% of all marine species were lost. Recovery from this event likely gave rise to a new fauna of Early Triassic chondrichthyans. Early Triassic sharks are exceedingly rare in the first 1.2 million years after the mass extinction. A few fossils have been reported in Idaho, Nevada, and Arizona, but Utah lacks any record of Early Triassic sharks. This project aims to determine whether the apparent Early Triassic chondrichthyan gap in Utah reflects true biological absence or results from poor preservation, stratigraphic incompleteness, or inadequate sampling. Surface samples were collected from the Dinwoody Formation, Woodside Shale, Sinbad Limestone, and Black Dragon Member of the Moenkopi Formation. Two localities were examined for each formation, and approximately 20lbs of carbonate rich matrix were collected per formation. No chondricthyan material was discovered in the surface material. Acid dissolution is being employed to isolate microvertebrate remains, including denticles and teeth, from the matrix. Establishing the nature of Utah's chondrichthyan gap will contribute to broader models of post-extinction marine recovery.

title: Effects of Strongly Directional Mach Pulses Induced by Supershear Ruptures on the Seismic Hazard to Near-Fault Long Tunnels
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Lu, Lidong [1], Chen, Zhiyi [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geotechnical Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China
(2) Department of Geotechnical Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China
abstract:
Supershear rupture is an important geological process that can strongly affect near-fault seismic hazard. Once the rupture speed exceeds the shear-wave velocity of the medium, directional shear Mach waves may develop and concentrate high-amplitude, short-duration ground motions within narrow wave beams. This mechanism can locally amplify seismic demand and threaten engineering infrastructure crossing active fault zones or located in near-fault regions.

In this study, an analytical model is developed for the dynamic response of long tunnels subjected to Mach waves induced by supershear rupture. Based on the Mach angle relationship, the geometric conditions of a finite rupture segment and the criterion for the critical source points, the spatial mapping relationship between the Mach wave beam and the tunnel axis is derived, and the effective action interval of the highly directional ground motion along the tunnel is determined. On this basis, the tunnel-surrounding rock system is idealized as a beam on an elastic foundation, and analytical expressions are obtained for the tunnel displacement, bending moment, and shear force responses. The controlling effects of rupture velocity, Mach angle, rupture segment location, tunnel orientation, and surrounding rock constraints on hazardous response zones along the tunnel are analyzed. The results indicate that the Mach wave effect induced by supershear rupture can transform strongly directional seismic energy generated during fault rupture into a highly localized moving pulse load along the tunnel axis. This mechanism may lead to stronger spatial concentration and asymmetry in the tunnel response. As a result, the maximum bending moment, shear force, and displacement may not necessarily occur at the location closest to the fault, but may instead be jointly controlled by the Mach wave incidence angle, rupture propagation direction, and tunnel orientation. The study further suggests that the geometric relationship between the tunnel and the direction of supershear rupture may be one of the key factors for identifying hazardous zones in near-fault underground structures. The results provide useful insights for seismic hazard analysis of long tunnels located near active fault zones.

title: An Exceptional Trace Fossil Locality from the Permian Coconino Sandstone in the Grand Canyon
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Robinson, Cierra [1], Bartlett, Rickey [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, Michigan, USA
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, Michigan, USA
abstract:
A newly documented trace-fossil locality in Grand Canyon National Park preserves the richest known concentration of vertebrate and arthropod traces yet recognized within the Permian Coconino Sandstone. The locality contains abundant tetrapod footprints, arthropod trackways, insect burrows, and associated sedimentary structures preserved on numerous rockfall blocks derived from the Coconino Sandstone. Although the collapse of the outcrop precludes precise stratigraphic control, the widespread occurrence of trace fossils across the assemblage suggests that biologically active surfaces persisted throughout a substantial portion of the formation's stratigraphic thickness.

Exceptional preservation of delicate traces provides new evidence regarding substrate conditions within the Coconino erg. Several surfaces exhibit intense bioturbation, unusually abundant clay-rich horizons, raindrop marks, and desiccation cracking — indicating repeated colonization of the substrate and environmental conditions that periodically differed from those expected in a hyper-arid dune field. These features may reflect episodic availability of near-surface moisture and, potentially, intermittent surface water.

Preliminary observations suggest that such moisture played an important role in both ecosystem sustainability and trace-fossil preservation by increasing substrate cohesion and promoting the formation and preservation of tracks, burrows, and other structures. The combination of exceptional ichnodiversity, extensive biogenic modification of sedimentary surfaces, and evidence for periodic wetting substantially expands current understanding of the Coconino paleoecosystem. This locality provides an important new dataset for reconstructing the paleoecology, hydrology, and preservational mechanisms operating within one of the largest Permian desert systems in western Pangea.

abstract: The Mississippi Alluvial Plain (MAP) contains one of the most intensively pumped agricultural aquifers in the United States, where the Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer (MRVA) continues to experience long-term groundwater depletion. Assessing MRVA’s sustainability under changing future climate conditions requires hydrologic models capable of integrating climate forcing, anthropogenic drivers, groundwater flow dynamics, and geological heterogeneity at regional scales. Here we present a climatic assessment framework based on a Hydrogeological Digital Twin of the MAP developed using MODFLOW 6 with an unstructured quadtree discretization. The model integrates hydrostratigraphic characterization, groundwater pumping records, climate-driven recharge simulations, and existing statewide Louisiana and Mississippi Embayment studies to evaluate the alluvial aquifer sustainability under future climate conditions. Climate-driven groundwater recharge was simulated using a modified U.S. Geological Survey Soil-Water-Balance (SWB) model driven by historical observations from the Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) and downscaled Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) NEX-GDDP climate projections extending through 2100. Simulation results indicate that increasing precipitation generally leads to elevated evapotranspiration and recharge across much of the alluvial plain. However, enhanced recharge does not uniformly alleviate groundwater stress because agricultural pumping and hydrogeologic variability produce persistent regional hotspots of depletion. Pronounced cones of depression remain evident in the Mississippi Delta, Grand Prairie, and northeastern Louisiana regions under multiple climate scenarios, indicating continued vulnerability of heavily irrigated areas. Results demonstrate that wetter climate conditions do not necessarily translate into groundwater recovery, highlighting the nonlinear relationship among precipitation, evapotranspiration, recharge, and groundwater storage. The modeling framework provides a scalable decision-support tool for evaluating long-term aquifer sustainability and identifying regions where groundwater management strategies may be required to mitigate future depletion under changing climatic conditions.

abstract: Atmospheric particulate matter as light-absorbing particles (LAPs) deposited to snow cover can result in early onset and rapid snow melting, challenging management of downstream water resources. We identified LAPs in 38 snow samples (water years 2013-16) from the mountainous Upper Colorado River basin by comparing laboratory-measured spectral reflectance, chemical, physical, and magnetic properties. Dust sample reflectance, averaged over the wavelength range of 0.35-2.50 µm, varied by a factor of 1.9 (range, 0.2300-0.4444) and was suppressed mainly by three components: (1) carbonaceous matter measured as total organic carbon (1.6-22.5 wt. %) including carbon-based synthetic black road-tire-wear particles, inferred black carbon, and natural organic matter, (2) dark rock and mineral particles, indicated by amounts of magnetite (0.11-0.37 wt. %) as their proxy, and (3) ferric oxide minerals identified by reflectance spectroscopy and magnetic properties. Fundamental compositional differences were associated with different iron oxide groups defined by dominant hematite, goethite, or magnetite. These differences in iron oxide mineralogy are attributed to temporally varying dryland source-area contributions implying strong interannual changes in regional dust-source behavior, dust-storm frequency, and (or) dust-transport tracks. Observations of dust-storm activity in the western U.S. and particle-size averages for all samples (median, 25 µm) indicated that regional dust from deserts dominated mineral-dust masses. Fugitive contaminants, nonetheless, contributed important amounts of LAPs from many types of anthropogenic sources.

abstract: Our nation's future energy, minerals and resource management relies on future generations' knowledge of, appreciation for, and skills in the earth sciences. Developing both a future workforce and a knowledgeable public that supports essential earth science begins with igniting the curiosity and excitement of our youth. To achieve this, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Geology, Energy, and Minerals Mission Area (GEMMA) outreach project is developing a suite of educational materials and resources to make science accessible and engaging for K-12 students with a focus on real-world application of energy, minerals, and geologic data. Our educational products include activity sheets such as critical mineral coloring sheets and word puzzles, as well as informative graphics to engage K-12 students. Additionally, we are developing lesson plans and activities that introduce critical minerals and incorporate actual USGS data, providing hands-on learning experiences. Our efforts are centralized through the USGS GEMMA education website, which serves as a hub for mineral resource learning materials with multiple entry points stemming from the USGS Youth and Education in Science (YES) program resources page, science center pages, and through QR codes included on educational handouts to increase discoverability. While our initial focus was on mineral resources, we are now broadening our scope to cover energy resources and geology, reflecting the full scope of GEMMA’s mission in leading the Nation’s geologic mapping and providing impartial scientific information on geologic resources and their supply chains. Through USGS-run teacher workshops, we have been able to test our draft products with our intended end-users, helping USGS become an authoritative resource for educations materials related to our field(s) of study. We have found that these efforts are strengthening relationships between educators and the USGS and raising the visibility of USGS science to the public.

title: Cambrian Paleosols and Paleoenvironments of Ireland
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science
authors: Retallack, Gregory J [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oregon, USA
abstract: Early Cambrian rocks of Ireland have been recognized by the fossil Oldhamia antiqua , which has been considered a deep-sea trace fossil of the graphoglyptid type. Early Cambrian age has been confirmed by other trace fossils ( Manykodes pedum , Arenicolites didymus , A. sparsus , Histioderma hibernicum ) and by acritarch palynology ( Skiagia orbicularis ) near Bray, County Wicklow. Oldhamia has now been found in paleosols at its type locality near Bray, along with microbial traces of “old elephant skin” ( Rivularites repertus ) and drab-haloed filament traces ( Prasinema gracile ). These red paleosols have distinctive gypsum desert roses forming a subsurface (By) horizon, as evidence of hyperarid precipitation (MAP 130-152 mm), comparable with paleosols associated with vendobiont fossils in Ediacaran rocks of South Australia and Nevada. Cambrian land surfaces were not barren wastes, but supported microbial earth communities with animal burrows, fed in part by aerobic photosynthetic organisms, revealed by organic δ 13 C of -18.2 to -25.4 ‰. Measured rates of chemical weathering in molar depletion per year and per mm of precipitation of 0.3-0.6 μmol/yr/mm cationic bases and of 0.07-0.2 μmol/yr/mm phosphorus, were comparable with Ediacaran paleosols, and with Phanerozoic soils and paleosols. Ediacaran-Early Cambrian biotic enhancement of weathering on land was a prelude to provision of nutrients for the spectacular Cambrian evolutionary explosion of life in the sea.

title: The Rheological Visco-Elasto-Plastic Regime of Magma Mingling
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Hayman, Nicholas W [1], Allen, Benjamin [2]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma Geological Survey, University of Oklahoma, NORMAN, OK, USA
(2) Oklahoma Geological Survey, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
abstract: Magma mingling, broadly part of magma-mixing processes, occurs when the physical interactions between mafic and felsic melts do not proceed to total mixtures. Such incomplete mixtures leave well-described heterogeneous structures in outcrop including enclaves, interfingering of different magmas, magma-fille fractures, and dikes; many of these features are thought to drive explosive eruptions. Magma-mingling studies often use physical (a.k.a. analog) modeling as a visualization and parameter-scaling tool. Such experiments typically mix fluids of contrasting viscosity to produce lobate plumes and viscous fingers. Yet, it is well known that otherwise viscous flows also undergo brittle deformation. Approaches to modeling ‘brittle-ductile’ transitions include a high-enough Deborah number – the ratio of relaxation to flow – that the magma will behave as a true brittle solid, and/or spring-and-dashpot models that haved both elastic and viscous components. Here, we present the results of experiments wherein we inject low-viscosity fluid into a visco-elastic-plastic carbomer (trademarked Carbopol) gel in a quasi-2D Hele-Shaw cell, essentially two plexiglass plates. The injection experiments produce a wide range of mesoscopic structures, ranging from pooling lenses, to branching patterns with tipped-out fluid-filled fractures, to interfingering of the fluid and gels. These experiments bracket the “finger-fracture transition”, and also illustrate widely varying ranges of recovery/elasticity/memory. The well-characterized controls on the experimental system’s rheology allow us to define a broader rheological phase space that encompasses a range of elastic, plastic, and viscous forces. Applying this approach to the magma mingling problem shows that the commonly observed outcrop structures all formed as the ratio of these forces approached unity. Therefore, the conspicuous mesoscale magma-mingling structures should be viewed as having formed in a rather specific rheological regime for an instability, rather than in widely disparate regimes of different instabilities.

title: Integrated Carbon-Isotope and Molecular Biomarkers Chemostratigraphy of the Valanginian Weissert Event at DSDP Site 535, Southeastern Gulf of Mexico

authors: Orihuela, Johanset [1], Liu, Xiao-Lei [2], Fu, Junpeng [3], Maurrasse, Florentin J-M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environment, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA

abstract:
DSDP Site 535 in the southeastern Gulf of Mexico preserves one of the few biostratigraphically constrained Valanginian records of the Proto-Caribbean, where a positive carbon-isotope excursion was recognized and subsequently associated with the Weissert Event. The Initial Reports documented an organic-rich, deep-marine carbonate succession, nonetheless the molecular composition of the organic matter (OM), including lipid biomarkers and metalloporphyrins, remains uncharacterized.

Here we integrate twenty GC–MS lipid biomarker and LC–qTOF–MS metalloporphyrin characterization, n -alkane, tocopherol derivatives with new high-resolution δ¹³C org from 215 Valanginian core samples to evaluate Weissert carbon cycling, OM provenance, and water-column redox evolution. The δ¹³C org record defines a positive shift from a pre-excursion baseline near −28‰ to a sustained Late Valanginian plateau of −27‰ to −26‰ within the Diadorhombus rectus interval of CNC3, reaching a peak of −25.31‰ and yielding a net positive excursion (CIE) of ~+2.7‰. GC–MS analyses of lipid extracts spanning the CIE onset, plateau, and recovery show C₁₀–C₁₉ n -alkane dominance and TAR values <1, indicating predominantly marine phytoplanktonic OM, with subordinate gymnosperm-derived sesquiterpenes, including di-epi-α-cedrene, reflecting episodic terrigenous input. The application of LC–qTOF–MS detected vanadyl, nickel, and iron porphyrins. Their co-occurrence supports fluctuating redox conditions across a shallow chemocline, with intervals ranging from suboxic to euxinic during the main carbon-isotope plateau.

Methyltrimethyltridecylchroman, α-tocopherol quinone, and trimethylphytylbenzoquinone isomers co-occur with metalloporphyrins, consistent with preservation of phototrophic lipids under a stratified, reducing water column in which the redoxcline periodically shoaled into the photic zone. Recurrent dimethylbenzothiophenes, elemental sulfur near the CIE peak, isorenieratane degradation products across the isotope plateau and at the onset of recovery further support progressive sulfurization and episodic photic zone euxinia (PZE) persisting beyond the excursion peak.

Together, these data confirm that Site 535 accumulated OM in an open-marine, carbonate-dominated basin setting in the SE Gulf of Mexico–western Proto-Caribbean seaway. Marine OM preservation was likely favored by basin restriction, water-column stratification, a fluctuating chemocline, and episodic PZE. These conditions reaffirm Site 535 as an important regional organic-carbon sink during the Valanginian Weissert Event and demonstrate that the paleo-Caribbean record preserves both the carbon-isotope signal and a complex molecular-biomarker response to this Early Cretaceous carbon-cycle perturbation.
