title: Record of subduction accretion of a passive margin in western Mexico: Taray/Chilar/Arteaga Accretionary Complex
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Centeno-Garcia, Elena [1]
affiliations: (1) Instituto de Geología, UNAM, Mexico, Mexico, Mexico
abstract:
Exposures of a subduction complex in central and western Mexico have been described as the Taray Formation, the Chilar, and the Arteaga Complexes. They all, along with other small outcrops, share the same composition and age and are considered to have formed during the same subduction process in Late Triassic-Early Jurassic Time, dispersed by Late Jurassic-Cretaceous supra-subduction rifting.

The accretionary complex consists of tectonic mélanges with a sedimentary matrix that makes up to 80 to 60% of the complex. It contains blocks and slabs of WPB and MORB pillowed and massive basalts, banded and massive gabbro, serpentinized mafic rocks, mafic tuff, radiolarian chert (some chert blocks with MORB micro-gabbro dikes), and scarce limestone blocks. These range in size from approximately 1 km to a few cm.

The matrix is interpreted to have formed as a passive margin that was deformed in a west-dipping subduction zone that approached the continental margin.

Evidence of involvement of a passive margin is:

1) The matrix is composed exclusively of submarine-fan silicic terrigenous sediments with a few chert strata. Sandstone in all the studied localities is predominantly fine- to medium-grained, and channel-fill fine-grained conglomerate is rarely found. Sandstone is composed almost totally of quartz grains (mean Qt=89, F=2, L=9). With variable amounts of polycrystalline quartz vs monocrystalline quartz vs. microcrystalline (chert) grains. Argillaceous and feldspathic fragments are less abundant, as well as igneous grains (mostly granite and felsic in composition). Metamorphic clasts are rare, and have schistose texture. Sandstones with similar composition have been considered as derived from a source analogous to an uplifted fold-thrust belt or collision suture belt that might have mixed with some continental cratonic material.

2) Detrital zircon provenance yielded ages clustering around 300 Ma, 600 Ma, and 1 Ga. The youngest zircon ages (260 Ma) are up to 30 Ma older than paleontological ages from radiolarians, ammonites, and bivalves, found in the matrix and in blocks, indicating no contemporaneous input from a volcanic arc.

3) There is no evidence of soft sediment deformation; most of the mélange structures suggest brittle deformation, although locally green-shist facies occur.

title: A Geoarchaeological Approach to Early Neolithic Coastal Wetlands and Land Use: An Example from The Netherlands
session_title: Geoarchaeology of the Land–Sea Interface: Processes, Preservation, and Palaeolandscape Reconstruction
authors: Familetto, Elena [1], Smuk, Ana [2], Cohen, Kim [3], Schepers, Mans [4], Huisman, Hans [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical Geography, Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands
(2) Groningen Institute of Archaeology, University of Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands
(3) Department of Physical Geography, Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands
(4) Groningen Institute of Archaeology, University of Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands
(5) Groningen Institute of Archaeology, University of Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands; Section Archaeology, Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands, Amersfoort, Netherlands
abstract:
Marginal coastal wetlands can preserve exceptionally rich archaeological and paleoenvironmental records, yet their dynamic geomorphic evolution makes reconstructing past landscapes challenging. In the central Netherlands (beneath present-day Lake IJssel), Early Neolithic farming communities lived within a dynamic lagoonal-fringe landscape shaped by rising sea level and meandering river systems.

We investigate this buried and submerged landscape using an integrated geoarchaeological approach that combines multiple scales of analysis, from regional to microscopic, including large-scale paleogeographic mapping, local geophysical survey, sedimentary geology, targeted coring, archaeological soil micromorphology, Bayesian age-depth modeling, and multiproxy archaeobotany. Together, these datasets reconstruct the evolution of a lagoonal-fringe landscape composed of paleochannels, natural levees, and floodbasins and identify mature levees as key landscape features for land use, particularly crop cultivation.

Despite their marginal coastal position, mature levees remained above daily high-water levels, thereby reducing flooding and promoting surface drying, soil development, and ecological stability for up to 900 years. Multiproxy archaeobotanical analyses document vegetation change associated with increasingly stable, better-drained conditions, while archaeological soil micromorphology reveals repeated anthropogenic burning, ceramic fragments, and evidence of repeated tillage, indicating a more sustained engagement with this fringe landscape than previously recognized.

Rather than viewing the coastal wetland as environmentally uniform, our results show that small-scale variations in geomorphology and hydrology created locally favorable landscape niches that shaped human activity and land use. Beyond the Dutch wetlands, this study demonstrates how an integrated geoarchaeological approach can link landscape evolution, archaeological preservation, and human land-use choices in dynamic wetland, fluvial, deltaic, and coastal environments, where subtle topographic variation creates persistent opportunities for human activity.

abstract:
The New England Appalachians record a complex history of Paleozoic peri-Laurentian and peri-Gondwanan terrane accretion onto eastern Laurentia, culminating in Alleghanian continent-continent collision. In central New England, the traditional interpretation of these orogenies attributes the majority of regional metamorphism to the Ordovician Taconic and Devonian Acadian orogenies, with a limited overprint from the Quabogian (i.e., Neo-Acadian) and/or Alleghanian orogenies. Although Alleghanian-aged metamorphism has been recognized in southern New England, the nature of the Alleghanian metamorphism and deformation in central New England is not well constrained.

Here, we present preliminary results from garnet petrochronology, phase equilibria modeling, and quartz-in-garnet Raman inclusion barometry from two samples of the Littleton and Mt Mineral formations in central MA that show that the extent and grade of Alleghanian metamorphism in central New England is more extensive than previously thought. A sample of garnet-staurolite schist from the Littleton Formation immediately east of Pelham Dome yields a ca. 300 Ma Upper Pennsylvanian garnet Sm-Nd age with peak metamorphic conditions of ~5-8 kbar and 550-650. Structurally beneath this sample, a garnet-kyanite±staurolite schist from the Mt Mineral Formation also yields a garnet Sm-Nd age of ca. 300 Ma with peak metamorphic conditions of 8 kbar and ~700. Garnet growth in both samples appears pre-kinematic, and there is no textural evidence of polymetamorphism. Furthermore, the preservation of major and trace element zoning in garnet from both samples suggests limited time spent at peak metamorphic conditions and supports the interpretation that these are garnet growth ages. Thus, our results suggest that the bulk of high-grade metamorphism and deformation recorded in these rocks are a result of Alleghanian orogenesis, which is inconsistent with tectonic models of protracted Devonian–Mississippian (Acadian or Quabogian) metamorphism in the region. Instead, these conditions require relatively rapid perturbations to the crustal geotherm and suggest that the peak metamorphism experienced by the rocks in this area was an Alleghanian event.

title: A Technique in Its Own Right: Advances, Opportunities, and Unique Applications in Laser-Ablation (U-Th)/He Chronology
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications
authors: Kortyna, Cullen David [1], Metcalf, James R. [2], McDowell, Paige Riley [3], Ross, Catherine Haggard [4], Courtney-Davies, Liam [5], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA

abstract:
Laser-ablation (LA)-(U-Th)/He chronology is frequently presented in contrast to its conventional (U-Th)/He counterpart, often with a list of pros and cons comparing grain selection limitations, alpha-ejection corrections, uncertainty levels, and analytical throughput, resulting in LA-(U-Th)/He being couched as a low-resolution, high throughput complement to the conventional method. Whereas LA-(U-Th)/He chronology certainly can supplement the conventional method, its microanalytical subgrain sampling capability has opened a diverse range of analytical opportunities that never were within the purview of the whole-grain conventional method. Furthermore, the LA-(U-Th)/He technique is undergoing continued methodological development and refinement to increase accuracy and precision. The analytical breadth of the LA-(U-Th)/He technique has grown to the point where it should now be thought of as an analytical technique in its own right with its own range of applications and capabilities, rather than as an addition to or a replacement of conventional (U-Th)/He dating.

We present an overview of unique geochronology and thermochronology research opportunities that have emerged with LA-(U-Th)/He chronology from research performed at the Thermochronology Research and Instrumentation Lab at the University of Colorado Boulder. First, LA-(U-Th)/He microanalysis allows for in situ dating of texturally complex minerals such as hematite, where the closure temperature is related to the crystallite size. Preserving the textural information is a critical component of (U-Th)/He date interpretation. The in situ nature of the method presents a range of opportunities for performing (U-Th)/He dating within the textural context of the host rock. Second, certain oxide minerals, such as rutile, may undergo U loss during diode-laser-induced heating. LA-(U-Th)/He is a minimal-collateral-heating solution by virtue of excimer-laser ablation, thereby expanding the roster of chronometers to thermochronologists. Third, microanalytical sampling allows for the measurement of He-distribution maps of individual grains at a ~10x10 µm resolution. The ability to create He-distribution maps has a wide range of applications from closely examining how crystal deformation, defects, and radiation damage affects He retentivity to spatially mapping He-diffusion profiles. LA-(U-Th)/He chronology is no longer a niche technique with a narrow set of applications compared to conventional (U-Th)/He dating, but is becoming a stand-alone technique with its own breadth of unique applications and use cases.

title: The Fossil Record of Cretaceous North American Western Interior Terrestrial Arthropods: Insights from Body Fossils
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part II)
authors: Easterwood, Jesse E [1], Slattery, Joshua S [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
(2) Cheyenne, WY, USA
abstract:
North American Cretaceous terrestrial deposits preserve diverse assemblages of fossil plants, mollusks, and vertebrates. However, insect and arachnid body fossils remain comparatively rare despite the importance of these groups in both ancient and modern terrestrial ecosystems. This disparity largely reflects preservational bias, as delicate arthropod exoskeletons are rarely preserved except under exceptional conditions. Here, we synthesize published records and occurrences from the Paleobiology Database to evaluate the diversity, taphonomy, and spatiotemporal distribution of Cretaceous terrestrial arthropod body fossils across North America. Our dataset comprises more than 585 fossil occurrences representing 21 orders and 190 described genera.

Cretaceous insect and arachnid body fossils are concentrated primarily in Konservat-Lagerstätten, particularly amber deposits and fine-grained shales preserving compression fossils. Most occurrences are documented from western Canada and New Jersey, whereas comparatively fewer records are known from the U.S. Western Interior and Mexico. This geographic pattern reflects strong preservational and sampling biases, with amber inclusions disproportionately represented in Cretaceous deposits from western Canada and New Jersey. These amber deposits formed from resin produced by abundant high-latitude conifer forests, creating exceptional conditions for preserving terrestrial arthropod communities. In contrast, compression fossils are mainly associated with fine-grained lacustrine and floodplain deposits of the U.S. Western Interior and Mexico, where low-energy depositional environments occasionally facilitated the preservation of arthropod remains.

Body fossils provide critical insights into Cretaceous terrestrial arthropod diversity, morphological disparity, and evolutionary history. Compression fossils are often fragmentary but document a broad range of arthropod lineages and provide important evidence of taxonomic diversity during the Cretaceous. In contrast, amber inclusions preserve a diverse array of taxa, often revealing patterns of morphological disparity, functional adaptations, and ecological interactions.

When integrated with insect trace fossils, body fossils provide a more comprehensive view of Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystems. Together, these records reveal patterns of arthropod diversification, ecological interactions, and evolutionary responses during a period of major ecological transformation, including the rise of angiosperm-dominated ecosystems, restructuring of terrestrial plant communities, and significant ocean–climate changes preceding the Cretaceous–Paleogene (K/Pg) mass extinction.

title: A Pilot Monitoring Program to Improve Understanding of the Inland Migration of Saltwater Through Coastal Canals in Miami-Dade County, Florida
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Root, Tara [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Caribbean-Florida Water Science Center, Davie, FL, USA
abstract: Surface-water drainage and groundwater withdrawals in southeast Florida have lowered the inland water table and led to gradual saltwater intrusion along the base of the Biscayne aquifer. The US Geological Survey (USGS), in cooperation with Miami-Dade County, operates an extensive monitoring well network to track the inland migration of saltwater near the base of the Biscayne aquifer, an EPA designated sole source aquifer. As early as 1942, researchers recognized that leakage of saline water from coastal canals likely also contributes to saltwater contamination in the Biscayne aquifer. Salinity control structures are operated to maintain inland freshwater stages above sea level and provide a barrier to prevent saltwater from flowing inland through canals. Saltwater can flow inland when the gates at the structures are opened to allow seaward discharge or if the gates are leaky. Saltwater can also circumvent these structures by flowing through the adjacent highly porous aquifer. Existing canal salinity data for southeast Florida are sparse, but in 2024, the USGS began a pilot monitoring program to characterize the inland migration of saltwater through coastal canals in Miami-Dade County. This includes continuous specific conductance monitoring in canals at the headwater side of the control structure and an upstream location. Additionally, when saltwater reaches the upstream site, measurements are taken by the USGS to obtain cross-sectional profiles of specific conductance. Data from the Biscayne Canal show that specific conductance greater than 40,0000 uS/cm can persist for long periods (over a month) on the headwater side of the structure when the gates are closed. During these periods, specific conductance at the upstream site (approximately 1.5 miles upstream from the structure) increases to as high as 10,000 uS/cm. The cross-sectional profiles of specific conductance show the canal is not well mixed vertically or horizontally. These observations indicate saltwater is getting trapped upstream of the structure when the gates are closed and is likely migrating upstream through the deepest portion of the canal. Specific conductance changes rapidly, at times fluctuating nearly two orders of magnitude in less than half an hour. This, combined with large spatial variability due to poor mixing, make continued monitoring at high temporal and spatial resolution important for further characterization of the inland migration of saltwater through southeast Florida’s canals.

title: Revisiting the Fort Hays Limestone and Smoky Hill Chalk members of the Niobrara Chalk, Western Kansas, USA: Updates to Hattin’s (1982) High-resolution Stratigraphy and Biostratigraphy
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part I)
authors: Elder, William [1], Sawyer, David [2]
affiliations: (1) Consultant, Lafayette, California, USA
(2) University of Colorado, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Coniacian–Santonian Niobrara Chalk of western Kansas, comprising the Fort Hays Limestone and Smoky Hill Chalk members, records deposition in the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) from approximately 89.5 to 81.5 Ma during a period of widespread anoxia or dysoxia that coincided with Oceanic Anoxic Event 3 (OAE3) and the preservation of abundant marine vertebrate remains. Donald E. Hattin’s (1982) landmark monograph, Kansas Geological Survey Bulletin 225, established a high-resolution stratigraphic framework for these units, using 23 numbered marker units defined by distinctive bentonite beds, limonite stringers, and prominent calcareous horizons to enable centimeter-scale correlation across tens of miles of poorly exposed outcrop. As part of a Kansas Geological Survey mapping project in Logan County and vicinity, the authors revisited Hattin’s measured sections in Logan, Gove, and Trego Counties to integrate his work into a modern context of taxonomy, biostratigraphy, geochronology, and subsurface log data.

Field work focused on relocating Hattin’s sections, photographing outcrops, remeasuring beds, and tying them to his marker units, and attempting to reestablish his correlations. Although access to several key localities was limited—including the only section that Hattin measured in the Fort Hays Limestone—an alternate vertical exposure at Cedar Bluff State Park matched Hattin’s section bed-for-bed, confirming both his measurement precision and the lateral continuity of the chalk beds. We also examined Hattin’s invertebrate collections at the University of Kansas, University of Indiana, and the Fort Hays State University Sternberg Museum, reviewed his unpublished field notes, maps, and additional sections. Macroinvertebrates—dominated by inoceramid bivalves ( Cremnoceramus , Platyceramus , Volviceramus , Cladoceramus , Magadiceramus , Cordiceramus , and Cataceramus ), Pseudoperna oysters, and rare aberrant ammonites—were rephotographed at high quality and identified using updated taxonomy.

We present photo-based cross sections with marker units identified at the relocated section sites, an updated invertebrate biostratigraphy (including inoceramid species not previously identified in the Niobrara of Kansas), and refined correlations to coeval sections elsewhere in the WIS and to European reference sections. We also establish ties between the invertebrate and vertebrate biostratigraphies. Finally, we document salt-tectonic structural complications affecting Hattin’s correlation of marker beds from reference sections, and tie Hattin’s sections to the extensive subsurface record in Kansas to provide a field-ready bridge between Hattin’s classical framework and a modern Niobrara stratigraphy.

abstract: A method is described for assessing Ambient Low-Temperature (<90 °C) Geothermal Resources of Groundwater (AmbLT) and Aquifer and Reservoir Thermal Energy Storage (ATES and RTES, respectively). It is demonstrated that these resources are end-members of a single resource that grade continuously into each other with geologic position or technologies applied. The method can be used to create maps of regionally distributed resource potential in terms of annualized thermal energy density (joules per square meter) or annual heating and cooling supply density (watts-thermal per square meter). The method is demonstrated for the RTES resource potential for the Columbia River Basalts underlying the Columbia Plateau, USA, providing a map of estimated total resource for seasonal heating and cooling energy assuming a maximum allowable thermal departure of 10 °C. The extended implication is that there are potentially terra-watts of seasonal heating and cooling that could be supplied for the USA. Resource development projects nationwide may use the simplified estimation methodology described herein as an approximation of local resource potential, but site-scale characterization is necessary to handle the more complex reality.

abstract: Quaternary sciences rely on an extensive accumulation of data, inclusive of physical collections and digital archives, to reconstruct past environments and human-ecosystem interactions. However, a stark discrepancy has emerged between the data stewardship principles our disciplines value in theory and how we handle older datasets and physical collections in practice. While modern funding mandates and professional standards emphasize ethical workflows, these frameworks overwhelmingly center on active, new data collection, bypassing previously collected ‘legacy’ data and collections. Consequently, a massive volume of legacy data remains unaddressed, a symptom of the centering on newly collected data and the broader curation crises our disciplines face. Working as a subgroup of the Ethical Open Science for Past Global Change RCN, we evaluate the state of Quaternary legacy data across the data lifecycle and argue that current standards are often inadequate for historical records. By re-examining current disciplinary standards (or lack thereof) regarding legacy data, which result from intersecting scientific and cultural histories, we demonstrate how old data and collections can be reclaimed, repurposed, and redressed within ethical modern archaeological and paleontological practices. These assets are not only scientifically indispensable for modern large data science and synthesis, but also serve as critical tools for rewriting historical narratives and contributing directly to discussions of social justice. Because many legacy datasets originated from settler-colonial expansion and extractive practices, bringing them into compliance with both FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and CARE (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics) principles provides a pathway to mitigate ongoing historical harms and actualize Indigenous data sovereignty. Truly ethical open science of global change data cannot be achieved by focusing solely on future field seasons; we must dedicate expert time and funding to mobilizing, contextualizing, and repairing legacy data inherited from outdated practices and historical and ongoing injustices.

title: Cretaceous Two-Steppin’: New Ichnological Evidence for Smaller Theropod Activity within the Upper Glen Rose Formation, Hamilton County, Central Texas, USA
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments
authors: Cerna, Evan P. [1], Peppe, Daniel J. [2], Yann, Lindsey T. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee, University of Tennessee Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Baylor University, Baylor University Department of Geosciences, Waco, TX, USA
(3) National Park Service, Waco Mammoth National Monument, Waco, TX, USA; Baylor University, Baylor University Department of Geosciences, Waco, TX, USA
abstract: The Lower Cretaceous (Aptian-Albian) Glen Rose Formation and other similarly aged stratigraphic formations exposed across much of Central Texas are world-renowned for yielding thousands of fossilized tracks of theropod, sauropod, and ornithopod dinosaurs. The sedimentary context of the Glen Rose reflects the initial transgression of a transgressive-regressive (T-R) sequence within the Lower Cretaceous Trinity Group (Aptian–Albian), highlighting sea level fluctuations throughout Early Cretaceous North America. Typically, Glen Rose track sites are found on shallow marine carbonate deposits that formed at sequence boundaries. The JCIC Tracksite assemblage, located in Hamilton County in Central Texas, represents a short-lived single event along a shoreline during a marginal-marine sequence boundary within the Upper Glen Rose Formation (Albian). Thalssinoides ( Cruziana ichnofacies) burrows and other sedimentary structures consistent with marginal-marine conditions are found alongside the theropod tracks of the JCIC Tracksite assemblage. The majority of tracks present at the JCIC Tracksite are interpreted to belong to large theropod dinosaurs, attributed to Acrocanthosaurus atokensis based on size and shape, many of which have undergone some form of soft-sediment deformation due to the super-saturated rheology of the track-bearing layer. However, one of the tracks (JCIC-28) is considerably smaller than other Glen Rose theropod tracks (Total length = 12 cm). JCIC-28 is a right footprint that clearly preserves digit III (DIII) and digit IV (DIV), while digit II (DII) appears unimpressed. This track is smaller than any other published theropod track identified within the Glen Rose Formation (Total lengths > 20 cm). It has long been believed that substrate controls/taphonomic biases prevented the preservation of smaller tracks on the carbonate tidal flat settings of the Glen Rose Formation, with JCIC-28 likely being preserved due to the extremely muddy rheology preserved at the JCIC Tracksite. While the possibility that this smaller track is attributed to a juvenile Acrocanthosaurus cannot be entirely excluded, the morphological characteristics of JCIC-28, including the lack of an impressed DII, suggest that this is not the case. Instead, the track appears to be comparable to tracks attributed to smaller theropods (Total length = 10-20 cm) belonging to the ichnogeneras Grallator or Dromaeosauripus . Taken together, the size, morphology, and occurrence of this unique track suggest that smaller, gracile coelurosaurs co-occurred with Acrocanthosaurus atokensis on the tidal flats of the Glen Rose Formation.

title: Chronostratigraphic Revision of the Cerro del Pueblo Formation (Campanian, Upper Cretaceous), Coahuila, Mexico Suggests Dinosaur Fauna Is ~1.5–2 Ma Older Than Previously Thought, With Biogeographic and Evolutionary Implications
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Barrera Guevara, Daniela [1], Freedman Fowler, Elizabeth [2], Fowler, Denver [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, Alaska, USA; Badlands Dinosaur Museum, Dickinson Museum Center, Dickinson, North Dakota, USA
(2) School of Applied Sciences, Dickinson State University, Dickinson, North Dakota, USA; Badlands Dinosaur Museum, Dickinson Museum Center, Dickinson, North Dakota, USA
(3) Badlands Dinosaur Museum, Dickinson Museum Center, Dickinson, North Dakota, USA
abstract: Since the late 2000s there has been a surge in Mexican dinosaur research, predominantly based on partial to relatively complete remains from the Late Cretaceous Cerro del Pueblo Formation (CdP) of northeastern Mexico. As the southernmost unit in Laramidia with abundant dinosaur remains, the CdP has potential for testing latitudinal biogeographic hypotheses, which depend on accurate chronostratigraphic correlation. Although no radiometric dates have been recovered from the CdP, historical work using other methods suggest a latest Campanian age (72.3–71.3 ± 0.5 Ma, biostratigraphy; 72.5 Ma, magnetostratigraphy; 73 ± 1 Ma, strontium isotope analysis). However, these prior methods were indirectly based on Ar/Ar dates calibrated to previous standards, resulting in ages ~0.5–1 Ma younger than would be produced by current standards. The morphology of dinosaurs within the CdP has been noted to be unexpected given the purported age of the unit, resembling older taxa from the southern United States. Various hypotheses have been proposed to explain this, such as higher origination rates and lower extinction rates in the south, where primitive taxa survive and go extinct later in the south compared to that of northern dinosaur assemblages. Revised invertebrate biostratigraphy and sedimentological geometry indicates that the CdP represents the lower part of a west–east clastic wedge. Significantly, hitherto overlooked ostreid biostratigraphy indicates west–east diachroneity, with the older Exogyra ponderosa only occurring in the lower section of the western CdP, being overlain by E. costata , whereas only E. costata occurs at the central and eastern sections. This is particularly significant as the boundary between E. ponderosa and E. costata correlates with the base of the Western Interior Baculites compressus ammonite zone (~74.21 Ma/~73.79 ± 0.38 Ma), ~1.5–2 Ma older than the previously suggested age of the CdP. This stratigraphic reassessment is important as most dinosaurs from the CdP have been recovered from the western section of this unit, suggesting that these taxa may be ~1.5–2 Ma older than previously regarded, perhaps equivalent to the Fruitland or Kirtland Formations of New Mexico or the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah. The revised chronostratigraphy presented here introduces an alternative to the biogeographic refugium hypotheses, as various taxa from the CdP closely resemble and might be synonymous with that of other of Campanian units of the southern United States.

title: The Question Behind the Paper: What Drives Public Engagement with Geoscience Research?
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation
authors: Pineda-Munoz, Silvia [1]
affiliations: (1) Communications, Climate Ages, Alexandria, Virginia, USA
abstract:
Public understanding of science plays an important role in building trust in scientific evidence and reducing vulnerability to misinformation. Consequently, many geoscientists now communicate their research through social media, newsletters, podcasts, and video platforms. Understanding how audiences engage with geoscience research may help scientists communicate evidence more effectively and foster lasting engagement with science.

To explore patterns of audience engagement, I analyzed 113 paleontology and Earth history stories published on Climate Ages, an independent science communication platform that reaches more than 21,000 readers across Medium, Substack, and LinkedIn between 2024 and 2026. Stories were categorized according to topic, narrative framing, and the extent to which they focused on a specific publication versus a broader scientific question. Audience metrics included presentations, views, reads, read-through rates, newsletter open rates, engagement rates, and subscriber growth.

Topic and framing influenced audience discovery on Medium. Deep-time stories converted presentations into views at significantly higher rates than non-deep-time stories (16.0% versus 8.9%; Mann-Whitney U test, p < 0.05), and several title-framing variables also showed significant effects on story discovery. In contrast, newsletter open rates on Substack varied little across topics and narrative frames. Together, these patterns suggest that topic and title framing play a larger role in attracting new audiences than in maintaining engagement among established subscribers.

A qualitative review of the highest-performing stories revealed a recurring pattern: the stories were rarely about the paper itself. Instead, research papers were used as evidence to explore broader questions about evolution, extinction, climate change, adaptation, and Earth history. Conventional distinctions such as mystery versus explanatory framing produced comparatively modest differences in audience engagement.

These observations suggest that audiences engage most strongly when individual studies are presented as evidence contributing to larger scientific questions rather than as isolated discoveries. Effective geoscience communication may therefore depend less on simplifying research findings and more on helping audiences understand how scientific evidence contributes to our understanding of Earth and its history, fostering trust not only in scientific conclusions but also in the scientific process itself.

title: Reimagining the Glacial History of Arena Valley, Antarctica, Using Detrital Zircon and Geochemical Provenance Proxies
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools (Posters)
authors: Lamson, Lauren [1], Chen, Ming [2], Morgan, Daniel Jones [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, Tennessee, USA
(2) Geography Department, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, USA

abstract: Glacial landforms in the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica, have been interpreted as evidence of a major northeast-flowing East Antarctic Ice Sheet expansion through the Transantarctic Mountains during the mid-Miocene, when the ice sheet took the robust form we know today. However, this hypothesis has not been reexamined since wind erosion measurements in the western uplands of the MDV showed that glacial deposits have been deflated by as much as 54 cm, altering their appearance. Arena Valley contains glacial tills associated with the mid-Miocene EAIS overriding event and subsequent south-flowing glacial intrusions from Taylor Glacier, making it an ideal setting to test for a distinct EAIS till geochemical fingerprint. This project uses immobile geochemical provenance proxies in Arena Valley to test for two glacial sources, examining detrital zircon U-Pb ages and Zr/Ba for fingerprints of the East Antarctic shield and local Taylor Glacier material. Using PDP cross-correlation coefficients, we find statistically similar zircon age populations in tills associated with EAIS overriding and Taylor Glacier. Further, Zr/Ba ratios suggest that overriding tills do not contain a relatively greater portion of rocks from inner East Antarctica. We propose four explanations for similar geochemical fingerprints in tills of supposedly different sources: 1) the overriding event was cold-based and did not transport material long distances from inner East Antarctica, 2) the overriding ice took a flow path through the TAM rather than through inner East Antarctica, picking up Beacon Supergroup and Ferrar dolerite similar to the parent rock in Arena Valley, 3) erosive overriding occurred, and the cold-based Taylor Glacier is reworking that material today, or 4) tills identified as overriding were actually deposited by a local alpine glacier. We believe it is most likely that the EAIS did not expand into the McMurdo Dry Valleys during the mid-Miocene and that an alpine glacier deposited tills and shaped landforms in Arena Valley. This changes our understanding of ice flow dynamics in the McMurdo Dry Valleys and demands further investigation to understand the complementary roles of alpine and continental glaciers as geomorphic agents in the region.

title: Breathing Snowball Earth: Syn-glacial Weathering and its Implications for the Global Carbon Cycle
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records
authors: Kadoya, Shintaro [1], Melwani Daswani, Mohit [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth-Life Science Institute, Institute of Science Tokyo, Meguro, Tokyo, Japan
(2) Earth-Life Science Institute, Institute of Science Tokyo, Meguro, Tokyo, Japan
abstract: Global glaciation, or a “snowball Earth” event, is traditionally thought to preclude continental water-rock reactions, including silicate weathering, due to the absence of liquid water. Because continental silicate weathering is a major sink for atmospheric CO 2 , its shutdown is believed to cause atmospheric CO 2 accumulation, thereby enhancing the greenhouse effect and eventually triggering deglaciation. Therefore, the absence of continental weathering has been considered key to understanding snowball Earth events and determining their duration. However, a recent discovery of syn-glacial dolomite precipitation during the Sturtian glaciation suggests that weathering may persist during the global glaciation, though its impact on the global carbon cycle and snowball duration remains uncertain. Here, we investigate water-rock reactions in the subglacial environment using a numerical model to elucidate their controls and impacts on the global carbon cycle. Our model demonstrates that the steady state of subglacial chemical weathering depends on the flux ratio of meltwater to fresh-rock particles (the water-to-rock flux ratio, or WRF ratio). While the hydrologic cycle governs the meltwater supply, glacial erosion controls the fresh-rock supply. Accordingly, these results imply a tight connection and feedback loop between subglacial weathering and climate. Under optimal conditions comparable to modern Antarctica, the calculated CO 2 consumption is equivalent to the modern volcanic CO 2 supply rate. Consequently, subglacial weathering has the potential to significantly delay the accumulation of atmospheric CO 2 . These findings underscore the importance of syn-glacial continental weathering—a mechanism long discarded—for a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of snowball Earth climate.

abstract: The first arrival of isotopically distinct continental material in the source regions of arc magmas provides a robust geochemical tracer for the onset of continental collision. Here, we present molybdenum (Mo) isotope data from the Gangdese Batholith in southern Tibet, constrained by zircon, apatite, and titanite U-Pb geochronology. Our data reveal a pronounced magmatic pulse between 53 and 50 Ma characterized by anomalously light Mo isotopic compositions (δ 98/95 Mo = -0.96‰ to -1.32‰). This isotopic shift is accompanied by systematic variations in geochemical proxies (Ba/Th, Th/Y) and radiogenic isotope systems, indicating a fundamental change in the metasomatic agent fluxing the mantle wedge — from melts of dehydrated Neo-Tethyan mafic oceanic crust at ~53 Ma to those derived from the Indian mafic lower crust by ~50 Ma. This transition requires that Indian lower crustal materials were subducted to subarc depths and incorporated into the Gangdese magma source by ~50 Ma. Numerical simulations integrating lithospheric thickness and plate convergence rates constrain the timing of initial India-Asia collision to before ~55 Ma to account for the observed shifts in Mo and other isotopic tracers. Our findings establish a direct petrogenetic link between arc magma chemistry and collisional tectonics, demonstrating that coupled isotope systematics can precisely define the timing of initial continental collision.

title: Geologic Mapping on the Brink of a Renaissance
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Allmendinger, Richard W. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell University, Warner, NH, USA
abstract:
Geological field mapping has suffered decades of decline due to increasing expense and decreasing financial support for mapping, retirement of older faculty with qualifications to teach mapping, and a student body less inclined to be attracted to mapping. However, several developments, primarily technological, over the last two decades have set the stage for a renaissance. These advancements include base map imagery from LiDAR and satellite with 1 m resolution, new ways of processing those data, smartphones and tablets, powerful field data collection apps on mobile devices, and mapping-specific online databases such as StraboSpot. Texture shading of LiDAR digital terrain models (DTMs) can provide bed-scale resolution, even beneath tree cover, and taking the DTM, itself, into the field enables the mapper to calculate orientations, thickness, and fault slip, predict contacts by having the app draw them for verification, and upload and download data to StraboSpot while still in the field using apps such as GMDE Lite. I illustrate the use of these technologies by revisiting virtually the Newfoundland Mountains in NW Utah, a place that I mapped 40 years ago for the USGS with very traditional methods. The improvements in the Newfoundlands, as well as reevaluation of mapping by other geologists elsewhere, demonstrate that virtually every geologic map made in the pre-digital age can be improved, commonly significantly, by remapping using digital methods.

For the renaissance to happen, we need to change, in some cases drastically, the methods taught in field schools and trips. Map scale is irrelevant in the age of multi-scale tiled maps, and resolution is paramount. Geologists must learn to make their own base maps and how to put DTMs on their devices as well as teach the capabilities and limitations of their devices. Students need to learn that the sensors in their devices are identical to sensors in geophysical instruments and understand that data redundancy and signal-to-noise ratio can complement and improve their own qualitative filtering of field data. Accurate description and evaluation of uncertainty is essential. Incorporation of digital technology can demonstrate to students that field geology is a modern science and not an arcane art form. Ironically, even the rise of artificial intelligence plays a role as students look to acquire skills that AI cannot easily duplicate and replace.

title: Identification and Quantification of Atmospheric Microplastics at Several Locations in Nacogdoches, Texas
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Alade, Motunrayo Peace [1], Jerez, Sheryll [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental and Geospatial Sciences, Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
(2) Environmental and Geospatial Sciences, Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
abstract:
Atmospheric microplastics (MPs) are emerging contaminants smaller than 5 mm, they pose potential risks to the ecosystem, environmental and human health through atmospheric transport, deposition, and inhalation. While extensive research has been done on aquatic and terrestrial environments, limited baseline data and the lack of standardized analytical protocols have constrained the understanding of their distribution, particularly in East Texas. This study aims to identify, characterize, and quantify atmospheric microplastics at five strategically selected locations in Nacogdoches, Texas, representing high-traffic corridors, industrial facilities, and landfill sites.

Passive atmospheric deposition samplers equipped with Whatman GF/C glass microfiber filters (1.2 µm pore size, 90 mm diameter) housed in custom stainless-steel mesh collectors will be deployed concurrently at each site to collect dry and wet deposition samples. Laboratory processing includes sonication, oxidative digestion (using 30% H₂O₂), density separation using ZnCl₂ 1.63g/cm 3 , and vacuum filtration in a flow hood under strict contamination-control protocols. Identification and characterization will be performed using a high-resolution digital stereomicroscope (VHX 7000) and Scanning Electron microscopy coupled with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) to determine particle abundance, morphology, size, and elemental composition. Statistical analyses, including ANOVA and regression analysis, will be used to evaluate spatial variations in microplastic abundance and potential relationships with meteorological conditions.

This research will provide baseline assessment of atmospheric microplastic deposition in Nacogdoches, contributing to a better understanding of airborne plastic pollution in East Texas. This study will also contribute to the development of standardized methodologies for airborne microplastic monitoring. Findings will enhance understanding of atmospheric microplastic pollution and support future environmental management and public health risk assessment efforts.

title: Introducing NGDRedux: New Data Source-Agnostic 40Ar/39Ar (and Noble Gas) Data Reduction Software
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data
authors: Mercer, Cameron Mark [1], Calvert, Andrew T. [2], Stelten, Mark Evan [3], McAleer, Ryan Joseph [4], Morgan, Leah [5]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, California Volcano Observatory, Moffett Field, CA, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(5) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, based on the decay of 40 K to 40 Ar*, provides important constraints on the timing and duration of geologic processes throughout geologic time. Many 40 Ar/ 39 Ar labs use community-sourced software applications for both data acquisition and reduction, such as Mass Spec by Al Deino or Pychron by Jake Ross. Other labs use software provided by instrument manufacturers for data acquisition and either software like ArArCALC by Anthony Koppers or custom-built solutions for data reduction. Still others have used in-house software for both data acquisition and reduction. Here, we introduce new Java-based software dedicated to noble gas data reduction called NGDRedux for use in 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology and noble gas geochemistry.

We designed NGDRedux to be data source-agnostic, allowing data to be imported from any source—provided an import plugin is developed for each unique source. Plugins will be provided “in-the-box” for both Mass Spec and Pychron , and template code will be made available for developing custom import plugins. Raw data and supporting metadata (e.g., information about instruments, samples, irradiation packages, monitor ages, etc.) are imported into an NGDRedux workspace for local storage and data reduction, which can be performed without an active network connection.

Data reduction is performed in batches, which include all necessary analyses of blanks, airs (or cocktails), fluence monitors, and unknowns. Reduction operations are fully customized by the user, from the overall order of operations to the detailed settings of an operator for an individual analysis. Reduction operators are linked in a network, permitting robust uncertainty propagation that includes handling of covariances that naturally arise during reduction. A change in configuration anywhere in the network triggers updates to all downstream operators, allowing live updates for the analyst to quickly evaluate reduction choices following community best-practices. Outputs include configurable graphics for data visualization (data regression, age spectra, ideograms, isochrons, etc.) and tabulated data files for visualization, data release, and publication.

Following validation testing and peer review, we will release NGDRedux as a cross-platform desktop application. The Java source code will be made freely available on the U.S. Geological Survey public GitLab at https://code.usgs.gov. Community feedback and contributions are welcome.

title: Stochastic Pore Network Modeling for Absolute Permeability Predictions in Dolomites
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Senevirathna, Shaluka [1], Vilcaez, Javier [2]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
(2) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
abstract: Predicting fluid flow behavior in carbonate rocks such as dolomites remains challenging due to their strong heterogeneity. In this study, we introduce a hybrid framework that integrates high-resolution micro-CT imaging of dolomite core plugs with stochastic construction of 3D pore-networks and OpenPNM pore-network modeling. Hundreds of 3D pore-networks of equal probability of occurrence are stochastically constructed from pore-size distribution and porosity extracted from micro-CT images. Absolute permeability simulations, conducted within the OpenPNM framework, on hundreds of 3D pore-networks are used to statistically determine the most probable absolute permeability of the core plug. As such, this approach explicitly addresses carbonate heterogeneity by accounting for the stochastic connectivity of pore-bodies through pore-throats, while preserving key rock physics characteristics, namely pore size distribution and overall porosity. Core flooding experiments were conducted to validate the numerical results, and multiple spatially distinct sub-volumes were analyzed within the same core plug to assess intra-sample heterogeneity. The stochastic simulations produced mean permeability values that are within the same order of magnitude as experimental measurements. However, variability across different sub-volumes within the same rock sample was found to be greater than the variability introduced by stochastic realizations, highlighting that natural spatial heterogeneity dominates permeability uncertainty at the core scale. The results demonstrate that the proposed stochastic pore-network workflow is both physically consistent and robust in predicting permeability in complex carbonate systems. The ability to reproduce permeability behavior across multiple representative sub-volumes using statistically constrained pore-size information suggests strong potential for upscaling, which provides a practical pathway for bridging pore-scale physics with core- and reservoir-scale permeability estimations.

title: Volatile-rich magma, a critical carrier for gold transfer from mantle to crust in the giant Jiaodong gold metallogenic province, North China Craton: Evidence from zircon mineralogy and geochemistry
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: SUN, Huashan [1], Koua, Kadio Aka D. [2], Li, Zhanke [3], Song, Fanyue [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Resources, China University of Geosciences(Wuhan), Wuhan, Hubei Province, China

abstract: The process by which the substantial gold was transferred from the deep mantle to the shallow crust in the Jiaodong gold metallogenic province (GMP) in the North China craton is still under debate. In this study, zircon grains from the granite hosts and their mafic microgranular enclaves (MMEs) related to pre- and syn-large-scale gold mineralization (pre-large-scale gold mineralization/syn-large-scale gold mineralization) were examined as proxies. A range of analytical methods, including transmitted light microscopy, cathodoluminescence imaging, backscatter electron, energy dispersive spectrometer, laser Raman spectrometry, in-situ LA-ICPMS U-Pb dating and trace elements, and zircon mapping, were employed to gain insights into the volatile contents of magma during the pre-large-scale gold mineralization and syn-large-scale gold mineralization events. Five distinct types of zircon grains, each exhibiting diagnostic characteristics, were identified. Interestingly, zircon crystals from the syn-large-scale gold mineralization granite hosts and their MMEs show extensive hydrothermal alteration, while zircon grains associated with pre-large-scale gold mineralization events exhibit little hydrothermal effect. This observation suggests that the magma associated with syn-large-scale gold mineralization contains significantly higher amount of volatile compared to that of pre-large-scale gold mineralization. Furthermore, the syn-large-scale gold mineralization magma also shows enrichment in alkali and ore-related sulfides, indicating that the massive volatile and ore-forming metals may have been primarily transported from the source to the upper crust by the syn-large-scale gold mineralization magma rather than through alternative mechanisms, such as the translithospheric Tan-Lu fault. Our results and previous works further suggest that the extensively outcropped Weideshan monzogranite, which is the predominant intrusions of syn-large-scale gold mineralization and experienced mixing/mingling between mantle- and crust-derived magma, likely played a critical role in facilitating the transfer of abundant volatile and ore-forming metals from the deep mantle to shallow crustal faults, where gold finally precipitated. Our finding underscores the significance of the Weideshan granite and warrants further attention in future research on gold metallogenic processes.

title: What Have We Learned from 50+ Years of Hydrologic Research in the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica?
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Gooseff, Michael N [1], Doran, Peter T [2], Dugan, Hilary [3], McKnight, Diane [4]
affiliations: (1) INSTAAR, Department of Civil, Environmental, & Architectural Engineering, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA

abstract:
The McMurdo Dry Valleys is one of the coldest and driest locations on earth, yet its hydrologic cycle is defined by snowfall, glacier melt, streamflow, and ablation. Glacers in the valleys melt during the austral summer to generate streamflow for 8-10 weeks per year, and most streams terminate in closed-basin, ice-covered lakes, whose levels fluctuate with the annual swings in streamflow and lake ice sublimation. In the late 1960s, the New Zealand Antarctic Research Programme established two stream gages on the Onyx River (Wright Valley), which remain in operation today. Since 1993, the McMurdo Dry Valleys LTER project established 17 more stream gages across several valleys and lake basins along with a network of meteorological stations. Lake levels are now carefully monitired with automatic sensor deployments and annual manual measurements.

These monitoring data have been useful in quantifying the hydrologic cycle of this polar desert region, especially in the context of extremes, which vary from 'no-flow' years for some streams, and a 'flood year' in 2022. These data also contextualize extensive research in hyporheic exchange in these streams and habitat conditions for extensive algal mats on streambeds and the collections of diatoms in each stream. History of closed basin lake levels, going back to 1909, provide an excellent record of the net changes in water storage and movement across this landscape.

abstract: Two research projects supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science are currently investigating landslides in Japan, Romania, and Italy. Through close collaboration among researchers from these three countries, the projects seek to clarify landslide characteristics by conducting comparative analyses across contrasting environmental settings. One major objective is to identify efficient and economical techniques for acquiring topographic data in areas where direct access is difficult, particularly on the steep slopes of active landslides. To achieve this, three survey methods are evaluated: uncrewed aerial system-based structure-from-motion photogrammetry (UAS-SfM), pole-camera structure-from-motion photogrammetry (PC-SfM), and terrestrial laser scanning (TLS). UAS-SfM allows rapid mapping of relatively large areas (approximately 1 km²) at a spatial resolution of about 10 cm without requiring field access, since all observations are collected from aerial platforms. Field data acquisition typically takes around one hour. For smaller sites (approximately 0.1 km²), PC-SfM can produce higher-resolution topographic models and orthorectified imagery. Still, it requires extensive fieldwork, as the operator must walk across the survey area, which can take several hours of data collection. Low-cost TLS represents another alternative, generating point clouds and digital elevation models at a moderate resolution (approximately 40 cm) from safe observation points without entering unstable slopes. Although TLS does not provide RGB imagery, it generally requires less field time than PC-SfM. The most suitable survey strategy therefore depends on site accessibility, the required spatial resolution, and data characteristics; combinations of these methods can be selected to satisfy different landslide investigation needs. A second objective is to improve landslide detection and susceptibility assessment using advanced machine-learning and deep-learning techniques. The analyses integrate optical satellite imagery, InSAR observations, DEM-derived terrain variables, geological information, and other environmental datasets. The modeling framework incorporates deep-learning algorithms. The combination of state-of-the-art field surveying technologies and data-driven analytical methods has substantially improved the accuracy and efficiency of landslide investigations. Furthermore, the projects examine landslides triggered by different mechanisms, particularly intense rainfall and earthquakes. By comparing regions with contrasting environmental conditions and varying triggering and predisposing factors in Japan, Romania, and Italy, the research aims to establish broadly applicable knowledge of landslide processes that extends beyond individual study areas.

abstract: Lithium (Li)-rich metasedimentary rocks are critical sources for pegmatite-hosted lithium deposits, yet controls on Li pre-enrichment and subsequent melting remain unresolved. Data from the Songpan-Ganze Belt, eastern Tibet, show that Li pre-enrichment originates from older collision-related felsic rocks in the source orogens, and that long-lived, hot I-type crustal magma reservoirs provide the thermal engine and volatiles for anatexis of Li-enriched metasedimentary rocks to generate S-type magmas. We propose that Li enrichment in flysch-dominated orogens evolves through four linked stages: Li-enriched felsic rocks form via crustal melting in early collision-related orogenic cycles; weathering and erosion transfer this detritus to flysch basins, where authigenic clay enrichment and metamorphic recrystallization concentrate Li in mica-rich pelites; long-lived, hot I-type reservoirs then melt the Li-enriched sediments to generate S-type magmas; and moderate fractional crystallization of these pre-enriched melts forms Li pegmatites. This framework yields three testable criteria: collision-related felsic provenance, thick Li-enriched flysch basins, and long-lived, hot I-type crustal magma reservoirs, for evaluating Li potential in flysch-dominated ancient orogens.

title: Timing the Silurian Yangtze Uplift and Early Gnathostome Radiation: New High-Precision U-Pb Geochronology From South China

abstract: Evaluating the precise timeline of Paleozoic tectonic movements and biotic revolutions requires robust radioisotopic constraints. In South China, Silurian successions preserve critical records of the regional Yangtze uplift and the earliest diversification of jawed vertebrates (gnathostomes). However, because these shallow-marine clastic facies rely primarily on complex biostratigraphic correlations, the exact timing of these fundamental events has remained debated. To address this chronological uncertainty, we present high-precision zircon U-Pb ages obtained via chemical abrasion-isotope dilution-thermal ionization mass spectrometry (CA-ID-TIMS) from three distinct volcanic tuff beds within the Xiushan Formation in the Upper Yangtze region. Our geochronological data yield tight ages of 433.93 ± 0.52 Ma, 432.92 ± 0.54 Ma, and 430.68 ± 0.62 Ma. Integrated with Bayesian age-stratigraphic modeling, these results securely position the fossiliferous upper portion of the Xiushan Formation within the Telychian-Sheinwoodian boundary interval, refining previous older biostratigraphic estimates. This newly established chronological framework significantly alters our understanding of early vertebrate evolution. It places the exceptional Chongqing Lagerstätte and its diverse gnathostome fauna into the Wenlock epoch, thereby resolving the long-standing “anachronism” regarding the sudden appearance of complex jawed fish characters. Our findings confirm that a major radiation of early vertebrates was already well advanced by the Wenlock. Furthermore, the presence of a prominent regional unconformity directly above the youngest 430.68 Ma tuff demonstrates that marine sedimentation preceding the massive regression lasted until the late Sheinwoodian within the platform interior. This chronological recalibration delays the recognized onset of the Yangtze uplift by approximately 4 million years, offering crucial new insights into the dynamics of intraplate orogenesis in East Asia.

title: A Geochemical and Petrographic Characterization of the Barranquitas Porphyry in Puerto Rico
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics
authors: Locker, Caroline [1], Bilenker, Laura [2], Hudgins, Thomas [3], Gottardi, Raphael [4]

abstract:
Porphyry systems are recognized for hosting large amounts of low-grade mineralization and are responsible for ~70% of the world’s current Cu resources and production [1]. The demand for Cu resources continues to skyrocket along with predicted consumption and remaining resources worldwide due to rapid expansion of infrastructure and global electrification. The addition of Cu to the 2025 Critical Minerals List brings additional attention to Cu-bearing deposits and how best to find and utilize these resources [2]. The Barranquitas porphyry Cu±Au±Mo deposit in central Puerto Rico contains both Au and Cu mineralization associated with the Barranquitas stock, a middle Eocene dioritic intrusion [3]. Previous work Barranquitas was limited to macro-scale observations and bulk rock geochemical assays of three drill cores. As a result, questions about the formation and composition of Barranquitas are outstanding.

This study will elucidate the formation of the Barranquitas porphyry deposit and differences between the geochemical signatures of unaccreted and accreted Cu and Au-bearing porphyry deposits. Bulk rock geochemical analyses on drill core and surface samples show Cu concentrations decreasing with depth, mirroring elevated concentrations in saprolitic surface pluton samples. Preliminary laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging on pyrite grains revealed trace element signatures suggesting multiple overprinted metasomatic events that led to the formation of pyrite and other associated sulfides (e.g., chalcopyrite, sphalerite, bornite). Zonation within pyrites shows minor enrichment of As in cores and Ti in rims. Au and Ti nanoparticles are observed as inclusions in pyrite as well. Lastly, multi-phase Bi-Te-Ag assemblages are observed with adjacent micron-scale Ag droplets within calcite veining of the diorite.

Additional geochemical analyses will help determine the conditions and geochemistry of the fluids involved in the formation of Barranquitas, and full characterization of the observed mineral assemblages. These new data will provide context for producing a refined genetic model for Barranquitas, and findings would be compared to similar Au- and Cu-bearing porphyry deposits across the world. In addition, these results will expand our knowledge of Puerto Rico’s natural resources as many of its ore deposits have not previously been well characterized.

abstract: Oxygen fugacity ( f O 2 ) governs iron speciation in silicate minerals, yet its quantitative impact on crustal melt productivity has been largely overlooked. Using thermodynamic modeling and representative crustal lithologies, we demonstrate that the effect of f O 2 on melt fraction reverses with pressure. Above ~10 kbar, reduced conditions suppress ferric iron incorporation into amphibole, clinopyroxene, and garnet. This causes contraction of stability fields of these minerals and shifts iron into the melt, lowering its viscosity and increasing the absolute melt fraction by up to 13 wt.%. Below ~10 kbar, this relationship inverts: reduction stabilizes biotite, retaining water in the residue and suppressing melting. We apply these findings to the 60–40 Ma magmatic flare-up in the Gangdese belt (Tibet), where the input of reducing Tethyan sediments amplified deep-crustal fertility. This sediment-driven reduction provides a mechanism to boost magmatic output during the magmatic flare-up related to continental collision without requiring additional heat.

title: Hydrochemical Evolution and Cation Cycling Along a Regional Groundwater Flow System: Insights from Sr-Li-Mg Isotopes
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: Jiang, Xiao-Wei [1], Geng, Xiao-Hong [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Water Resources and Environment, China University of Geosciences, Beijing, Beijing, China
(2) School of Water Resources and Environment, China University of Geosciences, Beijing, Beijing, China
abstract:
Water-rock interactions accompanying regional groundwater flow are critical for hydrochemistry and water quality. However, it is usually difficult to constrain the processes of water-rock interactions based on ion concentrations alone. With recent development in multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (MC-ICP-MS), stable metal isotopes can provide key constraints on elemental cycling. In a subbasin of the North China Plain, we find divalent cations like Ca, Mg and Sr gradually increase with flow distance in the upstream alluvial aquifer, but decrease with flow distance in the downstream. To investigate the mechanisms controlling cation evolution, we combine Sr, Li and Mg isotopes to identify and quantify the main processes.

In the upstream aquifer, the increase in 87 Sr/ 86 Sr ratios along the flow path indicates that silicate dissolution dominates the release of dissolved cations, whereas the δ 7 Li values being higher than the silicate endmember indicates occurrence of clay formation which removes cations. The cations released by silicate dissolution exceed that removed by clay formation, resulting in the observed increase in concentrations of cations along the flow path. In the downstream aquifer, CO 2 becomes progressively depleted and clay formation does not occur. The trend of increasing δ 7 Li accompanying decreasing Li, with a fractionation factor equaling 0.9985, indicates occurrence of cation removal by chemisorption, whereas the trend of decreasing [Mg+Ca] accompanying increasing [Na*] indicates occurrence of cation exchange. The combined effects of chemisorption and cation exchange result in the decreasing concentrations of Li, Mg, Ca and increasing concentrations of Na along the flow path.

Based on the main processes identified based on Li and Sr isotopes in the upstream, the trend of δ 26 Mg versus Na*/Mg is also explained by silicate dissolution and clay formation. we find groundwater in the upstream is a mixture of groundwater from the mountain-block and infiltrated water from the vadose-zone of the alluvial aquifer. Moreover, up to 77.3% of total released Mg has been removed in the upstream. In the donstream, a two-step calculation reveals that the mean ratios of Mg removed by clay formation, chemisorption and cation exchange are 77.3%, 18.6% and 1.6%, respectively.

This study enhances our understanding of regional groundwater flow paths and cation cycling in large scale aquifers where groundwater is closed with respect to CO 2 .

title: Carolina Bays and Drainage Courses as Sand Sediment Sinks in the Pleistocene Erg of the Atlantic Coastal Plain; Evidence Provided by Lidar Mapping of Eolian Landforms in South-Central North Carolina
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Watkins, Douglas [1]
affiliations: (1) Wagram, NC, USA
abstract:
Abstract

Mapping gridded lidar elevation data in Scotland County and adjacent areas, North Carolina, provides evidence that Carolina Bays, drainage courses and other topographic depressions were sandy sediment sinks during Pleistocene desert episodes. Pervasive remnant barchan, parabolic and longitudinal dunes suggest that the study area was an inland erg featuring mobile sand landforms atop the Late Cretaceous Middendorf Formation sandstone bedrock. In a regional context, mapped eolian landforms suggest two phases of paleo-wind direction. An earlier wind field created barchan dunes and their consequent leeward elliptical depressions (Carolina Bays), the orientation of which indicates a wind field from the southeast. Parabolic dunes that are present along the eastern margins of the Bays, rivers and creeks suggest a subsequent wind field from the southwest. The sediment source for these parabolic dunes, based on mapping and spatial relationships, is interpreted to be a) eolian sands within the sediment sinks, i.e. infilled Carolina Bays and drainage courses and b) widespread regional Pleistocene erg sheet sands. The sediment sinks have been partially exhumed by southwesterly winds, resulting in classic chevron shaped parabolic dunes along their eastern margins. Mapping shows that Carolina Bay subsidence (caused by differential compaction of Bay sediments) can post-date parabolic dune formation. Similarly, mapping suggests that eolian sands in rivers and creeks were remobilized by southwest winds and deposited as dunes along the east side of the drainage courses prior to fluvial erosional action. Mapping examples of these eolian landforms will be presented, as well as interpreted shallow subsurface stratigraphy as shown in structural profiles.

session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas

abstract: Coastal groundwater systems are increasingly stressed by sea-level rise, groundwater extraction, climate-driven shifts in recharge, and extreme hydrologic events. Predicting the vulnerability of these systems remains challenging because subsurface heterogeneity strongly controls seawater intrusion dynamics yet is often poorly constrained in numerical models. We present an integrated hydrogeophysical modeling framework that combines groundwater-level and salinity observations, electrical resistivity imaging (ERI), and three-dimensional variable-density groundwater flow simulations to evaluate coastal aquifer vulnerability in southern Rhode Island. ERI-derived subsurface information was used to constrain the spatial distribution of hydrostratigraphic properties, while field observations were incorporated to reduce uncertainty in geophysical inversion and model calibration. The resulting framework improves representation of subsurface heterogeneity across scales and enables assessment of groundwater response to sea-level rise, drought, pumping, and changing recharge conditions. Results demonstrate the value of integrating hydrogeophysical observations with process-based modeling to reduce uncertainty in coastal aquifer vulnerability assessments and improve management of freshwater resources in coastal environments.

abstract:
The Silurian Ireviken extinction event (IEE) at the Llandovery-Wenlock boundary (~433 Ma) was an extinction of many marine clades such as graptolites, conodonts, trilobites, corals, brachiopods, and acritarchs. The IEE is coincident with a large positive carbon isotope excursion (+5‰) known as the early Sheinwoodian carbon isotope excursion (ESCIE). The expansion of marine reducing conditions has been proposed as a driver of the IEE, with evidence from carbonate-associated sulfur isotopes suggesting an increase in global pyrite burial and the expansion of euxinic water column conditions (characterized by anoxia and the presence of free hydrogen sulfide) in the early Wenlock. However, studies of local redox conditions using Fe speciation systematics from multiple ocean basins in Laurentia and Baltica suggest persistently anoxic conditions locally prior to the onset of the ESCIE and IEE. The enrichments of redox sensitive trace metals from these sites are oftentimes lower than expected from continuous anoxic depositional conditions.

Because anoxic and especially euxinic environments bury redox sensitive trace metals (i.e., V and Mo) more efficiently compared to well oxygenated environments, and previous work has shown an expansion of reducing conditions in the Telychian, we hypothesize a depletion of the marine trace metal inventory prior to the ESCIE and IEE. Here, we present concentrations of V and Mo from the Twilight Creek section of Laurentia and the Priekule-20 core of Baltica, alongside previously published data spanning from the Aeronian through the Sheinwoodian stages. The V and Mo concentration data is paired with a geochemical mass balance model that links trace metal accumulation with the proportion of the total anoxic (not euxinic) seafloor area. Model results suggest V and Mo accumulations similar to or lower than crustal abundances throughout the entire Telychian stage (~5.7 Myr) correspond to ~6% anoxic seafloor coverage, suggesting that large expansions of anoxia alone may draw down V and Mo during this interval, without invoking an increase in euxinic conditions. The low V and Mo concentrations throughout the Telychian correspond to stable sulfur isotope records suggesting that there was limited pyrite burial. Following the onset of the ESCIE and IEE, a greater proportion of this pre-existing anoxic seafloor area then became euxinic, reflected in the carbonate-associated and pyrite sulfur isotope records, while the total anoxic seafloor area remained relatively constant.

abstract: The management of mine discharge water presents a challenge to regulators and stakeholders worldwide due to potential impacts of high metal loads on surface and groundwater resources. While active treatment of mine water can be very costly and difficult to implement in remote locations, management through passive infiltration basins presents a compelling alternative in such instances. Here, we present details of a site investigation, impoundment design, attenuation evaluation, and construction of infiltration basins as part of a multi-disciplinary team at an abandoned mine in Idaho. Discharge water from this mine seasonally contains elevated concentrations of arsenic, iron, manganese, and uranium. Groundwater and surface water quality data, results from selective sequential extraction of metals from soils, mineralogical information, surge pond microbial community analysis, and geophysical data allowed for the development of a robust conceptual site model and supported key geochemical modeling. Geochemical modeling, using MIN3P, PHREEQC, and PHAST, supported by a MODFLOW-USG groundwater model was used to determine if infiltration ponds could safely manage mine discharge. MIN3P modeling indicated 60 to 100% vadose zone saturation based on a range of design infiltration rates, with decreasing near-surface porosity from iron (hydr)oxide precipitation in the bottom of the infiltration ponds. Modeling using PHAST demonstrated that arsenic and uranium attenuate in the vadose zone and no offsite exceedances are expected even at higher design infiltration rates due to iron (hydr)oxide formation and attenuation through sorption. However, results indicate that manganese concentrations may exceed compliance limits offsite in approximately 20 years as iron-based sorption capacity in the vadose zone is exceeded. Overall, the multi-discipline approach described demonstrates the complexity required to thoroughly evaluate the feasibility of passive mine water infiltration and the need to evaluate pretreatment options as part of the design phase to ensure groundwater and surface water is not impaired.

title: "Hot-Diggity-Dog!": How John Garver Inspired My Hunt For Arsenic
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Thurston, Olivia G [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, Norwich University, Northfield, VT, USA
abstract:
As an undergraduate I worked with John I. Garver, PhD tracking uranium-enrichment in the Lucerne Pluton in Maine. This project left me with a lasting curiosity about how heavy metals stored in seemingly innocuous rocks can naturally become released into the environment and pose serious health risks to the public. The research and teaching methodologies that John Garver passed down to me through years of mentorship has directly informed my research campaign tracking possible arsenic enrichment though northeastern Vermont bedrock.

Focusing on the Northeast Kingdom Batholith (granites) and Waits River country rock (phyllite) located in the northeastern corner of Vermont, USA, 16 whole rock geochemical samples and 11 groundwater samples were collected and processed using an Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometer (ICP-OES) to measure overall arsenic concentrations in the environment. The bedrock samples showed no distinct difference in arsenic concentration between the granitic intrusives and phyllite and have an average arsenic concentration of 0.0562 ppm. The groundwater, collected from both public and private wells, has an average arsenic concentration of 0.0072mg/L, which exceeds the EPA action limit for arsenic of 0.005 mg/L. Scanning electron microscopy energy-dispersive x-ray spectrometry maps of the bedrock samples show that arsenic in the bedrock occurs in anhedral, rare-element rich blebs along existing grain boundaries, indicating that arsenic is hosted primarily in secondary minerals formed during a later alteration event. The presence of arsenic in secondary minerals along grain boundaries makes the arsenic more likely to interact with infiltrating groundwater, thereby entering the public groundwater drinking supply in the Northeast Kingdom. There is no safe exposure level of arsenic for humans and the presence of elevated arsenic levels in both bedrock and groundwater in the Northeast Kingdom of Vermont poses a serious and lasting health risk to the local population that has been hereto unrecognized and thereby has received little to no mitigation efforts.
