title: Early–middle Mesozoic Tectonic Evolution of the Amdo Area, Central Tibet
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse
authors: Wang, Ping [1], Li, Lin [2], Duan, Liang [3], Kong, Kai [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, State Key Laboratory of Continental Evolution and Early Life, Northwest University, Xian, Shaanxi, China; Department of Earth, Environmental and Geographical Sciences, University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Charlotte, North Carolina, USA

abstract: The Mesozoic closure of the Bangong–Nujiang Meso-Tethys Ocean and the successive amalgamation of the Lhasa, Amdo, and Qiangtang terranes established the initial conditions for the growth of the Tibetan Plateau and influenced its subsequent development. Constraining the tectonic evolution of these events is critical for quantifying shortening and informing models of crustal deformation and convergence accommodation that shaped the current Tibetan Plateau, yet the timing and mechanisms of these processes remain poorly constrained. Here, we integrate petrographic observations with zircon U–Pb geochronology from the Triassic Tumengela Formation in the South Qiangtang terrane and the Jurassic Amdo Formation in the Amdo terrane to provide some new constraints. Detrital zircon age spectra show that the Tumengela Formation was sourced from the Qiangtang terrane to the north. In contrast, the Amdo Formation is dominated by Jurassic populations (peak at ~172 Ma), consistent with a Jurassic arc source to the south. This is further supported by petrographic observations of abundant volcanic lithic fragments (> 70%), suggesting a dominant arc source with negligible input from the Qiangtang terrane to the north. Zircon U-Pb ages of pyroclastic rocks constrain the depositional age of the Amdo Formation to 178–162 Ma. These data indicate that the final Amdo–Qiangtang collision did not occur prior to ~162 Ma, suggesting that final accretion was at least ~13 Myr later than previously proposed (182–175 Ma). Combined with regional geological constraints, our results support a revised two-stage Amdo–Qiangtang collision model and provide new constraints on the timing of terrane amalgamation in central Tibet.

title: Studying Dispersion in Karst Aquifers by Living and Dyeing
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Jones, Sid [1]
affiliations: (1) Clarkrange, Tennessee, USA
abstract:
Most groundwater traces in karst settings have not been designed for the purpose of gathering information on solute transport parameters such as dispersion coefficients or Peclet numbers. Experience has shown that transport characteristics of karst aquifers depend so much on both the scale of the test and the hydrologic conditions that the data from any individual test has limited value for predictive purposes. However, a better understanding of dispersive processes in karst drainage systems can inform the design of tracer tests with regard to the mass of tracer to be used and the duration and frequency of sampling.

A review of published data from tracer studies done through explored cave streams or other major conduits for flow in karst aquifers revealed that Peclet numbers range from tens to hundreds, verifying intuition that advective movement of solute is the dominant transport mechanism in these tests. Analysis of tracer recovery curves in surface and subsurface streams with variable cross-sections and velocity profiles, such as pool and riffle sequences, indicates that apparent dispersion increases due to partitioning of some fraction of tracer into stagnant regions of the field of flow.

Empirical relationships from dye recovery data generated by sinking stream-to-spring tests suggest dispersion along more complex flow paths is often significantly greater than dispersion that occurs in water table cave streams and major phreatic conduits. This may be the result of hold-up and dispersion of tracer mass prior to migration through the more permeable pathways in the aquifer. In tests initiated above the water table, transport through vadose pathways may control the shape of the tracer residence time distribution and significantly increase the measured dispersion coefficient.

Groundwater tracing in karst settings has occasionally resulted in objectionably high dye concentrations in springs or wells. To the extent possible, tracer test design should consider the means by which dye is introduced to the aquifer, especially where migration to springs or wells that serve as drinking water supplies is possible.

title: Fluorescence of Titan tholins depends on provenance
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Bober, Katherine Mae Maxine [1], Mackenzie, Shannon [2], Hörst, Sarah [3], Pesciotta, Cara [4], Hodyss, Rob [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Space Exploration Sector, Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, Baltimore, MD, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA
(4) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA
(5) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
abstract:
The Dragonfly mission to Titan will use multiple observations to inform decisions about sampling with the DraMS mass spectrometer, including images from the DragonCam camera suite. In particular, LED-illuminated images of the surface will provide the first hint of organics through UV-stimulated fluorescence. Interpreting these images requires laboratory constraints on potential provenances of Titan’s surface organics: pristine organics, organics that interacted with liquid water in impact melts, and organics that interacted with cryovolcanic deposits. To obtain these constraints, we used tholins, laboratory analogs of the complex mixture of organics expected to form in Titan’s atmosphere. Tholins were produced from 90% N 2 / 10% CH 4 (90:10), 95% N 2 / 5% CH4 (95:5), 99% N2 / 1% CH 4 (99:1), and 90% N 2 / 5% CH 4 / 5% CO (90:5:5) gas mixtures under Titan-like low temperature (~90 K) and low pressure (a few mbar). Fluorescence spectra were measured for the pristine tholins and for tholins mixed with pure water as well as aqueous solutions of 1/5/15% NH 4 OH, 1% MgSO 4 , and 1% Na 2 SO 4 using an excitation light at 375 nm. The tholins were tested at room temperature (297.15 K) as well as Titan’s temperature (94 K) using a modified cryogenic stage. PAHs were also examined for their fluorescence in the same conditions.

Tholins alone did not emit any fluorescence, but once immersed in any solution, fluorescence was observed. In frozen water and frozen 1% Na 2 SO 4 , the tholins’ spectra were closer to coronene in wavelength emission range as well as spectral structure or shape, except for the 90:10 tholin. In frozen 15% NH 4 OH and frozen 1% MgSO 4 , the tholins’ spectra were closer to anthracene with regard to spectral structure and wavelength emission range. The spectral peaks for the tholins immersed in 1% MgSO 4 solution were noticeably better defined than in the 15% NH 4 OH solution. When compared against the PAH spectra, the 90:10 tholin tended to differ more frequently from the other tholins (specifically within 1% NH 4 OH at room temp, 5% NH 4 OH frozen, 15% NH 4 OH at room temp, and 1% Na 2 SO 4 frozen). These results suggest that UV-stimulated observed fluorescence with DragonCam may not only reveal whether Titan’s organics have interacted with liquid water, but may also help distinguish among different aqueous and cryogenic alteration histories.

title: Subglacial Erosional Features in the Dry Valleys from the East Antarctic Ice Sheet
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations (Posters)
authors: Norstad, Abigail [1], Hall, Brenda [2], Denton, George [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Climate Sciences and the Climate Change Institute, University of Maine, Orono, Maine, USA
(2) School of Earth and Climate Sciences and the Climate Change Institute, University of Maine, Orono, Maine, USA
(3) School of Earth and Climate Sciences and the Climate Change Institute, University of Maine, Orono, Maine, USA
abstract: Improved understanding of future East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) behavior in a warmer-than-present climate can come from determining how the ice sheet reacted to past warming. A widespread erosional landscape in the Dry Valleys region of the Transantarctic Mountains (TAMS), with potholes, channels, ribbed bedforms, escarpments, and remnant drift patches, is suggestive of large amounts of subglacial meltwater produced by growth of an extensive ice sheet that covered most of the TAMS in this sector. This erosional landscape previously has been attributed to the mid-Miocene (or earlier) based on dates of volcanic ash preserved in frost cracks on adjacent till and colluvium patches. It has been assumed that this ash is too delicate to have survived an overriding ice sheet, and therefore its dates serve as minimum-limiting ages for the landscape. However, new understanding of subglacial erosion and heterogenous basal thermal regimes from areas formerly covered by Northern Hemisphere ice sheets requires re-evaluation of this assumption. Here, we present new mapping showing the extent of the erosional surface and the types, sizes, and orientations of the associated landforms. To constrain the timing of this event and the massive ice-sheet expansion it represents, we are examining relative, cross-cutting relationships between the erosional surface and depositional features of known age in order to place the event into a stratigraphic framework. We also have reinterpreted previously published 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates of volcanic ash and cosmogenic exposure ages through the lens of subglacial meltwater corridors, which occurred beneath Northern Hemisphere ice sheets during the last glaciation. Our preliminary estimates suggest that parts of the erosional surface may date to the Pliocene and/or early Quaternary, rather than the mid-Miocene. This work provides information on the extent and timing of one of the largest known EAIS expansions. Additionally, if our time constraints are correct, this expansion likely occurred under conditions warmer than present, as much as 2-3°C warmer (globally) from the mid-Pliocene to early Pleistocene period. This suggests that portions of the EAIS may thicken greatly under conditions moderately warmer than present.

title: Critical-Zone Hyporheic Exchange Characterization Integrating Deep Learning and Physics-Informed Time-Lapse Self-Potential Tomography
session_title: From Deep Earth to Digital Twins: Artificial Intelligence in Earth System Science and Predictive Subsurface Systems
authors: Carroll, Kenneth C. [1], Yin, Huichao Cooper [2], Ikard, Scott J. [3], Rucker, Dale F. [4], Brooks, Scott C. [5], Dai, Zhenxue [6]
affiliations: (1) Plant and Environmental Science Department, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA
(2) Plant and Environmental Science Department, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA

(4) hydroGEOPHYSICS, Inc., Certerra-Subsurface, Tucson, AZ, USA
(5) Environmental Sciences Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN, USA
(6) College of Construction Engineering, Jilin University, Changchun, China
abstract: Electrical geophysical methods, including self-potential (SP), are increasingly used to characterize subsurface flow because of their sensitivity to hydrogeological and geochemical processes. Within critical zone science—the study of interactions from the vegetation canopy through soils and groundwater to bedrock—SP provides a noninvasive means to observe coupled water–rock–biogeochemical dynamics that govern hyporheic exchange and solute transport. However, SP inversion is ill-posed, limited by sparse data coverage, and susceptible to transient noise. We developed a hybrid framework to image hyporheic exchange using time-lapse SP data from Oak Ridge, Tennessee. Physics-informed numerical inversion first generates dipole moment tomography grids, which are used to train a Vision Transformer (ViT) that maps surface SP sequences to 2D source distributions. The numerical solution is responsive to transient signals, whereas the ViT captures persistent spatial structures. Joint spatiotemporal analysis of both outputs isolates dynamic hyporheic exchange zones and separates transient from steady-state subsurface flow features, improving interpretability and temporal awareness. We further develop an autoencoder (AE)-based framework for spatiotemporal localization of subsurface fluid movement from time-lapse SP tomography. Temporal segments derived from long-term monitoring at a floodplain with active hyporheic exchange are used to train AE models based on ViT, ConvLSTM, CNN, and TCN architectures. Reconstruction error provides an anomaly score to detect periods of active SP variation, while spatial error patterns delineate zones of anomalous subsurface flow. ConvLSTM- and ViT-AE achieve the most robust localization, yielding consistent anomaly patterns. Applications to SP arrays, oriented both parallel and perpendicular to the stream, identify coherent anomaly zones near subsurface fault or karst features, demonstrating robustness and generalization. These approaches highlight a scalable, interpretable framework for resolving spatiotemporal subsurface flow dynamics, illustrate the benefits of nondestructive, noninvasive geophysical methods, and improve data assimilation and the interpretation of SP-based observations of critical zone processes in complex hydrogeological systems.

title: It’s the Faults’ Fault: Kilometer-Scale Folds and Internal Deformation in the Chuckanut Formation, NW Washington State, USA
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Anderson, Josephine B. [1], Crider, Juliet G. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
abstract: When tectonic stresses exceed elastic limits at low temperatures and pressures, rocks fail by brittle deformation, leading to faulting and jointing. So how do folds form in the upper crust? The Chuckanut Formation is a brittlely deformed Eocene fluvial sedimentary formation in northwest Washington composed of sandstone, siltstone, shale, and coal. The formation underwent significant SW-NE contraction due to the accretion of the Siletzia terrane about 50 Ma, which created gently plunging, upright, tight-to-close, concentric, kilometer-scale folds, with no apparent grain-scale deformation. Details of the internal deformation are obscured in the field due to heavy forest cover, but are beautifully exposed in LiDAR imagery. For this investigation, we used Geologic Map Data Extractor (GMDE) to trace bedding formlines, extract bedding attitudes, and identify previously unmapped faults within the formation on a 250 square kilometer texture shade LiDAR image of the southwestern Chuckanut Formation. We found evidence of abundant brittle faulting, including splay faults branching from the basal unconformity with the underlying Easton Metamorphic Suite, which we interpret to be a detachment fault. The intensity of faulting increases in the cores of folds, where there are also secondary folds, some of which are themselves internally faulted. Stereonet analysis of bedding attitudes suggests that the formation likely underwent two phases of cylindrical folding: folding first around an axis with an average trend of 325° and plunge of approximately 15° to create the dominant fold pattern, which was later warped around a sub-vertical fold axis trending approximately 160°. The minimum shortening of the formation, estimated from the line-length change of the primary kilometer-scale syncline-anticline pair, is about 30% from SW to NE, but including internal deformation, the total contraction is much larger. The many alternating layers of stronger sandstones and siltstones with weaker shale and coal likely permit flexural slip that facilitated fault-related folding.

abstract: Dr. John Garver’s extraordinary career traverses the heights of Alaskan mountains and down to the riverbeds in New York State. Dr. Garver cemented his legacy in the field of tectonics, with research spanning zircon geochronology, sedimentology, and field geology, but his impact moves beyond these disciplines. Equally important is his dedication to applying geoscience to societal challenges, including natural disasters, flooding and ice jams, and especially the Mohawk Watershed. Further, Dr. John Garver’s unparalleled mentorship is embodied in the spirit of all the students who were lucky enough to work alongside him. As a former student, it’s my honor to share a window into the incredible adventure and everlasting teachings from Dr. Garver that shaped my life beyond my wildest imagination. At the heart of my scientific pursuits sits Dr. John Garver and his infectious worldview on discovery, the scientific method, and unraveling the never-before-seen to the human eye. This presentation celebrates a career defined not only by discovery, but also by generosity, curiosity, and the lasting success of his students.

title: La falla de Papalutla: la crónica de una estructura crónica
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part I)
authors: Fitz Díaz, Elisa [1], Ruiz-Arriaga, Daniel [2], Vásquez Serrano, Alberto [3], Stockli, Daniel [4]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Geology, UNAM, CDMX, DF, Mexico
(2) Harquail Earth Sciences, Laurentian University, Sadbury, Ontario, Canada
(3) Instituto de Geología, UNAM, CDMX, DF, Mexico
(4) Jackson School of Earth Sciences, UT, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
La falla de Papalutla (FP) es una estructura prominente en la tectónica del sur de México. En su localidad tipo pone en contacto a la cubierta sedimentaria cretácica con rocas metasedimentarias de bajo grado del Ensamble San Jerónimo, el cual colinda al oriente con el Complejo Acatlán a lo largo de la zona de cizalla La Encinera. En esta zona conviven cizalla dúctil, cataclasitas y espejos de falla, evidencia de deformación en distintos niveles corticales. Datos termocronológicos (U-Th-He en circones) revelan que el bloque de techo sufrió una exhumación rápida entre 100–90 Ma y un posible enfriamiento a los 40 Ma. No obstante, la FP corta estructuras de piel delgada de la Plataforma Morelos-Guerrero que afectan a rocas maastrichtianas, lo cual indica que su actividad inversa ocurrió en múltiples estadios y modificó sustancialmente su traza.

Con una expresión topográfica de ~250 km desde Quechultenango hasta La Malinche, la FP muestra variaciones en su inclinación y nivel estratigráfico. Su registro regional revela una prolongada historia de reactivación: aprovechó foliaciones del Carbonífero de la zona de cizalla La Encinera como estructura extensional en el Jurásico, acomodó contracción en el Cretácico-Paleógeno, fallamiento dextral en el Oligoceno (cuencas pull-apart en Izúcar de Matamoros) y fallamiento normal-dextral en el Mioceno preservado en depósitos volcánicos en el estado de Tlaxcala.

Actualmente, el emplazamiento de conos cineríticos al norte y un relieve rejuvenecido al sur sugieren que la FP continúa activa, o como mínimo continúa localizando el emplazamiento de magma. Su monitoreo es crítico debido al peligro geológico por deslizamientos en el sur y potencial actividad volcánica en el norte, en una zona altamente poblada entre los estados de Puebla y Tlaxcala, en el centro de México.

title: The Use of Stable Isotopes to Unravel Primary Productivity in Fenestrate Microbialites from the 2.52 Ga Gamohaan Formation, South Africa
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology
authors: Alatorre-Acevedo, Eduardo [1], Sumner, Dawn Y. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA
abstract:
In modern microbial mats, autotrophic and heterotrophic microbial communities each influence the local Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC) pool as they metabolize carbon and cycle nutrients. Local changes in DIC can be preserved in the stable carbon isotope ratio of calcite (δ 13 C cal ). The δ 13 C cal can preserve evidence of metabolisms that were active through time and space within a microbial mat. Modern microbialites growing in lakes of the Antarctic McMurdo Dry Valleys are analogous to fenestrate microbialites from the 2.52 billion year old Gamohaan Formation, South Africa. These modern analogs are a guide for targeted δ 13 C measurements of different structures within ancient fenestrate microbialites.

Samples from 4 stratigraphic locations in the Gamohaan Formation were microdrilled to collect carbonate powder from three textures within the microbialites: microspar, herringbone, and bladed/blocky calcite. The microspar calcite is associated with organic inclusions that define vertically oriented planar structures called microbial supports by prior researchers. Herringbone calcite is interpreted as a marine cement that directly precipitated on the seafloor, including on microbial communities. Bladed/blocky calcite precipitated on herringbone calcite and is interpreted as a burial void-filling cement. The microspar calcite has a δ 13 C range of -1.12‰ to 0.80‰ and an average δ 13 C of 0.09‰ vs bladed/blocky calcite, which had a range of -0.60‰ to -0.06‰ and an average of -0.35‰. The herringbone calcite has a δ 13 C range of -0.69‰ to 0.46‰ and an average δ 13 C of -0.10‰. All δ 13 C cal values are reported in standard delta notation relative to VPDB. ANOVA and Tukey's HSD tests show that there is a statistically significant difference between δ 13 C of the microspar calcite and the bladed/blocky calcite with a P-value of 0.00.

In combination with other published geochemical and sedimentological data, we interpret the δ 13 C enrichment found in the microspar calcite of the microbial supports as a signature for an autotrophic metabolism, likely oxygenic photosynthesis. This interpretation implies that an oxygen oasis was present within the deep subtidal facies of the 2.52 billion old Gamohaan Formation, approximately 100 million years before the oxygenation of the Earth’s atmosphere.

title: THE EVOLUTION OF NORTH AMERICAN CAMELS: IMPLICATIONS FOR PALEONTOLOGICAL DATABASES
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Prothero, Donald [1], Welsh, Ed [2], Watmore, Kristin [3], Balassa, Daniella [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, California Polytechnic State University, Pomona, CA, USA; Vertebrate Paleontology, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Badlands National Park, Interior, South Dakota, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA; Dinosaur Institute, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(4) Geological Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, CA, USA
abstract: Camels were one of the most common and diverse endemic mammals in the Oligocene through Neogene of North America. Yet their systematics have been a shambles for over a century, due to the lack of any comprehensive revision of the overall group—even though there are huge unstudied collections, such as the 20,000 specimens in the Frick Collection in the American Museum of Natural History in New York, that have been available for study since the 1970s. We have just published a complete systematic review of the entire group, and an updated cladogram and temporal and geographic range information of all the valid genera and species of North American camels. The old literature had over 60 named genera and over 200 named species. By contrast, we recognize only 40 valid genera of North American camels, with 79 valid species. Only one rare genus occurred in the late Uintan (late middle Eocene), then camels were completely unknown in the Duchesnean (latest middle Eocene), and relatively rare and low in diversity in the late Eocene (Chadronian). Only a handful of genera are known from the early Oligocene (Orellan to Whitneyan). By the late Oligocene (early Arikareean), camels began to diversify with Miotylopus , the gazelle-like Stenomylinae, plus primitive nothokemadines. In the early Miocene (latest Arikareean-Hemingfordian), camels underwent substantial diversification, with Oxydactylus , several genera of floridatragulines, miolabines, protolabines, and primitive aepycamelines, resulting in 15 genera in the late Hemingfordian, and 19 genera of camels in the late Barstovian-Clarendonian (middle Miocene), before reducing in diversity in the late Clarendonian-Hemphillian (late Miocene) and Pliocene. Only three genera remained in North America by the end of the Pleistocene, all of which vanished during the end-Pleistocene megafaunal extinction. Despite this absence of valid taxonomy, numerous studies have tried to draw paleoecological conclusions about Miocene land mammal communities with camels, one of the most important groups missing or inaccurately represented. The diversity curves drawn from outdated taxonomic sources are completely different from the true diversity curve, based on our current research. Many online databases, such as the Paleobiology DataBase (PBDB) or MIOMAP are grossly outdated their information about camels, with many invalid taxa. As long as research is based on these inaccurate taxonomic sources, the results are “garbage in, garbage out.”

title: Trends in Megafaunal Fruit Evolution Following the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction Event
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination (Posters)
authors: Clifton, Wolf Gordon [1]
affiliations: (1) Theology and Science, Graduate Theological Union (current affiliation), Berkeley, California, USA; Earth & Environmental Geosciences, Ohio University (where research was conducted as a M.S. student), Athens, Ohio, USA
abstract: Clear adaptations for endozoochory, in which disseminules are consumed and passed through an animal’s gut, appear in fossil angiosperms or flowering plants from the Early Cretaceous (132 to 112 Ma) onward. “Megafaunal dispersal syndrome,” which targets large herbivores that can facilitate long-distance seed dispersal, is a common strategy seen across various plant families. Many living species are adapted for primary dispersal by animals that became extinct during the Late Quaternary Extinctions (50,000 to 10,000 Ka), now depending on secondary dispersal mechanisms associated with decreased germination, range contractions, reduced gene flow, and other adverse consequences. Prior to the Late Quaternary Extinctions, the last major extinction event to wipe out large herbivores on a global scale was the Cretaceous-Paleogene (KPg) extinction event ~66 Ma. Characterizing how plants adapted for endozoochorous seed dispersal were affected by the KPg extinction event, before the evolution of megafaunal mammal dispersers ~50 Ma, could improve our ability to assess the ecological impacts of recent and ongoing megafaunal extinctions. This study uses several existing data sets to test the hypothesis that megafaunal fruits were adversely impacted by the KPg extinction event: phylogenetic data which reconstructs the timing of transitions in fruit size within the palm family (Arecaceae) and custard apple family (Annonaceae), and fossil data revealing trends in fruit size and other aspects of angiosperm seed dispersal from the Cretaceous through the Cenozoic. Contrary to expectations, megafaunal fruits appear to have diversified within extant lineages of the Arecaceae during the Paleocene (66-56 Ma), while fruit size increased both within extant lineages of the Annonaceae and across angiosperms in general. These findings suggest that plants adapted for megafaunal dispersal can survive and even diversify long-term in the absence of large herbivore dispersers, likely via recourse to secondary short-distance dispersal mechanisms within isolated refugia. Nonetheless, further study is needed to substantiate or refute the observed trends, fossil data being especially important to calibrate phylogenetic trees and account for the extinction of taxonomic groups with no living members. Moreover, the apparent diversification of disconnected populations of plants in the wake of mass extinction does not negate the adverse impacts of decreased overall abundance and restricted dispersal upon ecosystems, nor does it lessen the importance of conserving megafaunal fruit species amid the present biodiversity crisis.

title: Bryozoa as model organisms for detangling paleoenvironments and microevolution: A case study of P=G+E with Electra pilosa
session_title: PALEONTOLOGY, BRYOZOANS, DINOSAURS, REEFS, STRATIGRAPHY, AND MILITARY GEOLOGY: IN HONOR OF ROGER CUFFEY AND HIS ECCLECTIC CAREER
authors: Hageman, Steven J [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Appalachian State University, Boone, NC, USA
abstract:
The fossil record provides empirical evidence of morphological change in lineages in contexts that extend beyond ecological time scales. Such data contain information about the evolution of heritable traits preserved in the skeletal phenotype. This information can be used to interpret patterns and rates of microevolution and test hypotheses of processes that lead to the origin of species. However, the contribution of environmental sources of variation in shaping the phenotype of every individual organism confounds the direct interpretation of relevant genetic evolution from the fossil record.

Because bryozoan colonies are a clone of modules with a shared genotype, with careful experimental design, the environmental and genetic sources of variation can be partitioned from the overall phenotypic variation in biological populations or fossil assemblages (P = G + E). In this study, morphological variation of the skeletal phenotype of the modern bryozoan Electra pilosa was documented in multiple colonies pre- and post- growth for clones transplanted to different macroenvironments, within a sea loch in western Scotland. Because within-colony genetic variation is zero, barring somatic mutation, the magnitude of environmental (ecophenotypic) variation within and among sea lochs is quantifiable.

An environmental gradient (wave energy) of three sample stations through one sea loch accounted for 0.0% of morphological variance of five zooecial characters (5 replicates); variance among four genotypes nested within environmental stations accounted for 46.9% of the total variance; and within-colony variance associated with ultra-microenvironmental and differential life histories of colonies accounted for 53.1% of the total variance. These values are consistent with results from related studies by the author and from other studies that have employed common garden methods. A separate study attempting to characterize environmental variation among six Scottish sea lochs was compromised by small and unbalanced sample sizes resulting from loss of colonies during the experiment.

Results from this and similar studies can be extrapolated to fossil bryozoans, allowing for an improved understanding of genotypic evolution within and among species at ecological and geologic time scales. This work builds on foundational studies of morphologic variation in fossil bryozoans conducted by Roger Cuffey throughout his career.

title: Key hydrologic, lithologic, and geomorphic indicators of channel pattern: McGee Creek, eastern Sierra Nevada, California
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Sanchez, Bryan [1]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Northridge, Northridge, California, USA
abstract:
Lower McGee Creek (eastern Sierra Nevada) has been impacted by loss of native riparian vegetation, bank erosion owing to grazing, and variable flow from water diversions and periods of below average rainfall and snowpack. The creek is fed by seasonal snowmelt, spring fed groundwater, and additional small tributaries prior to its debouchment into Convict Creek.

Previous field studies suggest changes in lithology and sediment size found in pools and riffles in a downstream direction. This may reflect a shift from the glacial and fluvial provenance of Upper McGee Creek to the boundary where volcanic sediments derived from the Long Valley Caldera begin to dominate channel pattern with fewer high angle meanders, diminishment of pool - riffle sequences, and increased vertical incision in the lower reaches of the channel.

In order to evaluate these geomorphic changes, channel and bank sediments were sampled at pools and riffles at 6 sites along Lower McGee Creek. Coarse sediments were evaluated for size, sorting, and lithology. Fine sediments were collected through grab samples and cores and subsequently analyzed for lithologic sequence, grain size composition and the presence of organics. All sites were surveyed for channel geometry (cross-sections) and discharge. Additionally, an Unmanned Aerial System collected imagery to support identification of the location of channel pattern changes.

title: The Perils of Radiocarbon Dating and Chronological Modeling in Cosmic Impact Claims
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Breslawski, Ryan [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Anthropology, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, Texas, USA; AR Consultants, Inc., Richardson, Texas, USA
abstract: Recent claims for late Quaternary impact events frequently rely on radiocarbon dating to establish synchronous deposits of potential impact proxies between geographically separated sites. On its face, radiocarbon dating appears to be a principled method for establishing that potential impact proxies were indeed deposited at the same time between different locations, or, conversely, disproving synchronous deposition. However, 14 C measurement errors, statistical uncertainty in the radiocarbon calibration curve, redeposited materials, and “old wood” effects complicate this approach. Over the last three decades, statistical modeling tools have been developed to reduce these uncertainties and refine chronologies, which proponents of some recent claims have employed to demonstrate the plausibility of inter-site synchroneity within varying levels of statistical uncertainty. Using the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis as an example, this talk demonstrates that applications of these models often violate statistical assumptions or rely on inadequate radiocarbon datasets, effectively extending the methods beyond their intended use. In addition to methodological problems with these applications, results are often misrepresented as supporting confirmation rather than plausibility.

title: The role of crustal thickness in governing heat-producing element distribution and cratonization
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)

affiliations: (1) Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA

abstract: As much as sixty percent of today's continental crust consists of cratons that have remained stable at Earth's surface for over 2.5 billion years. The long-term stability of these cratons cannot be maintained without a cold lithospheric thermal state, which is governed not only by the total heat production within the crust but also by the vertical distribution of heat-producing elements (HPEs). Through analysis of a global geochemical database of arc magmatism, we show that crustal thickness exerts a first-order control on HPE concentrations in these building blocks of the modern continental crust and thus the vertical HPE distribution within the continental crust. Thicker crust, which drives more extensive magmatic differentiation, preferentially concentrates K, Th, and U in the upper crust and depletes the lower crust. The extent of enrichment can be related to crustal thickness as: , where A is the surface heat production and represents the heat production expected for an undifferentiated, primitive composition. Thermal modeling demonstrates that this vertical stratification reduces lower crustal temperatures by hundreds of degrees compared to an undifferentiated crust of equivalent thickness. Extrapolating back to the Archean, higher heat production and orogenic thickening generated basal temperatures high enough for widespread lower crustal melting. The upward migration of these crustal melts, together with initial magma differentiation, concentrates HPEs in the upper crustal layers, which are subsequently eroded away owing to the high topography resulting from isostatic adjustment to crustal thickening. Through this preferential differentiation and denudation, the thickened lithosphere starved itself of heat production, progressively cooled and strengthened into the cold, rigid cratons seen today. These results indicate that crustal thickening may be a necessary step in the formation of long-term stable cratons.

title: Assessing the Environmental Impacts of Historical Iron Smelting in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Sheridan, Kylie Bree [1], Hinkle, Margaret Anne G [2], Uffelman, Erich S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, Virginia, USA; Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Missouri - Kansas City, Kansas City, Missouri, USA

abstract: Centuries of iron smelting in Virginia have left a persistent environmental legacy in the form of widespread slag deposits. This study characterizes the geochemical composition of these slags and assesses the environmental risk they may pose to surrounding ecosystems at three study sites in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, with differing proximity to nearby communities: Glenwood Furnace, Roaring Run Furnace, and Grace Furnace. At each site, samples of slag, ash, iron ore, soil, and stream water (where applicable) were collected and analyzed. Additionally, to study the mobility of metals from the slag into the surrounding systems, a leaching experiment was conducted reacting select slag with synthetic rainwater at initial pH of 4.2 and 5.3 to mimic pre- and post-1994 Eastern United States rainwater, respectively. The principal results show that the surrounding topsoils are particularly elevated in Mn, Ti, and Pb when compared to national reference soils, with Roaring Run, Grace, and Glenwood furnaces containing on average 500 ± 200, 400 ± 200, and 120 ± 40 ppm Pb, respectively. Slag are compositionally dominated by Ca, Fe, and Mn, with lesser concentrations of Ti, K, Pb, and Sr, and trace concentrations of Ni and Cu. Surface water analyses revealed the main contaminants of interest (Pb, Cr, Ti, and Mn) are well below safe drinking water levels. The leaching experiments similarly revealed potential contaminants of interest remain low in solution after reacting slag for 18 hours, with the exception of Mn. Substantial Ca, K, and Si leach from the slag into solution, and the pH of the synthetic rainwater increases substantially from initial values of 4.2 and 5.3 to over 10. Thus, these results suggest the elevated contaminant concentrations in slag-impacted soils may be due to leaching from the slag followed by rapid reprecipitation due to increased pH, or via the retention of fine grain (10-50 μm) slag particles within topsoil and limited leaching of contaminants. In both cases, soil contamination is increased while surface water contamination is limited. Based on the metal concentrations in the soils and within the slags themselves, these results also indicate that Glenwood Furnace, the site that is nearest to a community, poses the lowest environmental risk.

title: Defining the Triple O-Isotope Fractionation Between Serpentine and Water Using Natural Samples
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade (Posters)
authors: Boyer, Isabelle R. [1], Zakharov, David O. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA

abstract: Serpentine is one of the most abundant minerals on our planet that forms during interaction between water and ultramafic rocks from 0 to ~650°C. Despite its importance in planetary systems, the temperature of serpentinization remains challenging to constrain. While previous work has provided multiple calibrations for 18 O/ 16 O fractionation between serpentine and water, the traditional challenge of needing to assume the equilibrium fluid remains. Hence, here we explore the potential of the triple oxygen isotope fractionation. This novel method allows for single-phase thermometry without needing to assume the equilibrium water. Here, we present the results of a new serpentine-water fractionation curve based on measurements of natural serpentines from the ocean floor. We compare our results to an ab initio calibration, and previous 18 O/ 16 O calibrations. Oceanic serpentines were collected by ODP/IODP seafloor basement drilling expeditions across the Atlantic Ocean, reflecting a range of serpentinization from ~75 to 400°C. The δ′ 18 O-Δ′ 17 O values in serpentine separates were measured using laser-fluorination mass spectrometry. The high-temperature samples range from +1.9 to +3.0‰ in δ′¹⁸O and with an average Δ′ 17 O value of –0.01‰. The low-temperature serpentines have δ′ 18 O ranging +7.2 to +9.1‰ and a Δ′ 17 O of −0.03‰. These values define the serpentine-water triple O-isotope calibration curve - reflecting temperatures between 200°C and 75°C, respectively. Preliminary data aligns well with the ab initio theoretical fractionation curve. Suggesting that triple oxygen isotopes are a promising proxy of serpentinization temperatures. Ultimately, these data demonstrate that triple oxygen isotopes are a robust proxy for serpentinization, a critical process that regulates geochemical budgets and shapes the environment on Earth and other planets.

title: A step change in Earth’s thermal history driven by the onset of plate tectonics.
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics
authors: Mou, Jia-Le [1], Lee, Cin-Ty [2]
affiliations: (1) Rice University, Houston, TX, USA
(2) Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
abstract: Earth is the only planet that currently has plate tectonics, but it is widely thought that Earth initially operated in a stagnant lid regime, akin to present day Venus. Exactly when the transition to plate tectonics happened is debated. Because these different tectonic regimes reflect different efficiencies of convective heat loss, reconstructing the thermal history of Earth’s interior may provide valuable insight into the timing of the transition. Here, we use the composition of mantle residual peridotites as a direct constraint on the temperature of the Earth’s interior. Residual peridotites, through their olivine forsterite compositions, provide records of melting degree and mantle temperature. Our results reveal a rapid change in olivine forsterite composition from 92.0 to 90.9 between ~2.7-2.3 Ga, corresponding to a change in mantle potential temperature from ~1630 to ~1450 °C. Parameterized thermal evolution modeling shows that this shift requires a fundamental change in the efficiency of heat loss from the mantle. We interpret this change as the onset of a new geodynamic regime, from a stagnant or sluggish lid regime with slow cooling to a mobile-lid regime that efficiently dissipates heat. These results provide direct petrologic evidence that modern-style plate tectonics may have begun around 2.5 Ga.

abstract: The late Silurian to Early Devonian was a time of significant perturbations in the Earth system, including the radiation of vascular land plants, a likely rise in atmospheric oxygen, and substantial changes in both the marine and terrestrial biospheres. Here we report superheavy pyrite sulfur isotopes (i.e., pyrite sulfur isotopes heavier than coeval sulfate sulfur isotopes) up to +55‰ spanning the Wenlock to Pragian. These data were generated from multiple open margin, marine stratigraphic sections on the northern margin of Laurentia, including from the Road River Group of Yukon, Canada, and the Cape Philips and Bathurst Island formations of Nunavut, Canada. Although superheavy pyrite isotopes have been previously documented from immediately after the Sturtian Snowball Earth event and from the late Ediacaran, our dataset provides the first example of Phanerozoic sustained superheavy sulfur isotope values of which we are aware. The presence of these enriched isotopic values in multiple successions across the northern margin of Laurentia suggests they are primary marine or early diagenetic features. This is corroborated by NanoSIMS analyses, which confirm that the enriched isotopic values are recorded in individual pyrite crystals, including well-preserved framboids. Standard hypothesized mechanisms for the formation of superheavy pyrite provide imperfect explanations for these Paleozoic occurrences, as 1) the interpreted depositional environments were too low-energy for pervasive sulfide oxidation through substantial sediment reworking; 2) the stratigraphic columns record low sedimentation rates; 3) the basins were not highly restricted; and 4) we observe no evidence for local post depositional hydrothermal activity. Nonetheless, all the current hypotheses for superheavy pyrite formation invoke the presence of low (single digit millimolar to micromolar) marine sulfate concentrations. This suggests that, at least regionally along the northern Laurentian margin, marine sulfate concentrations in the late Silurian to Early Devonian may have been as low as during critical intervals of the Neoproterozoic or that other aspects of the sulfur cycle were more similar to the Neoproterozoic than the modern.

title: Manganese is Mobilized by Microbes and Retained by Sediments During Managed Aquifer Recharge in the Potomac Aquifer System, Virginia
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Kirr, Delaney Aine [1], Schreiber, Madeline E. [2], Akob, Denise M. [3], Mason, Allison R. [4], Edwards, Keely [5]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA

abstract:
Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) can benefit communities by increasing groundwater yields, preventing land subsidence, and reducing saltwater intrusion in coastal areas. However, introducing chemically distinct water into native groundwater may unintentionally release naturally occurring contaminants, including manganese (Mn). In 2018, the Hampton Roads Sanitation District in Virginia introduced the Sustainable Water Initiative for Tomorrow (SWIFT), a MAR project. SWIFT addresses the overuse of groundwater in the deep, confined Potomac Aquifer system and aims to reduce nutrient load to the eutrophic Chesapeake Bay by injecting oxygenated, highly treated wastewater into the sub-oxic to anoxic aquifer. This research investigates whether the resulting shift in redox conditions has the potential to stimulate biogeochemical transformations of Mn.

We conducted microcosm experiments using Potomac Aquifer sediments, groundwater, and SWIFT recharge water to test the capacity of the native microbial community to reduce and oxidize Mn under different redox conditions. Aerobic microcosms were supplemented with Mn(II) and aseptically vented to allow for air exchange, while anaerobic microcosms were supplemented with synthetic δ-MnO 2 and incubated anoxically. Aerobic and anaerobic microcosms were tested in triplicate for the following treatments: amended with dissolved organic carbon, unamended, and abiotic control (sodium azide). Microcosms were incubated for 21 days and sampled over time for dissolved Mn(II) and Fe(II) concentrations, as well as microbial community characterization. Sediments from the microcosms were analyzed with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive spectroscopy.

Anaerobic microcosms demonstrated that microbial Mn reduction can occur in the Potomac Aquifer before and after SWIFT recharge in the absence of oxygen, even in initially aerobic environments. Aerobic microcosms demonstrated that Mn(II) is removed from the water of the Potomac Aquifer likely by adsorption, with possible oxidation. Aerobic and anaerobic conditions selected for two distinct types of microbial communities, with water type (native groundwater vs. SWIFT recharge water) having a stronger influence on microbial community composition than the initial redox condition. These results indicate that SWIFT recharge can result in alterations of the microbial community in the Potomac Aquifer linked to Mn cycling. These experiments provide insight into Mn removal and mobilization mechanisms in a large-scale MAR operation and will inform operational conditions to minimize the release of naturally occurring contaminants during the SWIFT and other MAR efforts worldwide.

abstract:
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) has become a means for addressing broad paleobiological questions on an expanding list of taxa. We apply and assess GIS as a methodological tool for collecting morphometric data using fenestrate bryozoans as our study taxon. We further employ the built-in analytical tools of the GIS to process the character dataset to assess the morphological meaning of earlier efforts to partition fenestrate zoaria into theoretical morphospaces.

Our project involves only exterior zoarial surfaces. For the available characters, the data collected with the GIS are statistically reproducible among worker pairs involved on the project and comparable with morphometric data collected previously using a traditional microscope + data collection software setup. Moreover, the GIS-compiled dataset plots favorably among conspecific populations from the Wreford Megacyclothem (Sakmarian/Wolfcampian), from which all specimens were collected.

Using the built-in spatial analytical tools of the GIS we “re-characterized” earlier efforts by Starcher and McGhee (2000) to apportion fenestrate zoaria into zooidal domains (ZDs), areas controlled by individual zooids (i.e., areas occupied by juxtaposed lophophores). We asked: how do their “derived” efforts to characterize zooidal morphology compare to results using actually-measured characters that demarcate interapertural spaces? In doing so we believe we have found an alternative model for partitioning zoarial surfaces into zooidally-controlled spaces. Spatially-referenced data (i.e., linked to specific zooids and/or regions across zoarial surfaces) have potential for studies of intrazoarial variation at fine-scales, such as colonial hydrodynamics, ambient currents, feeding currents, and more. Gradients based upon zoarial regions and age should be mappable.

abstract:
The last integral studies in the Aconcagua fold-thrust belt (AFTB) presented 30 years ago proposed it was constructed entirely within the Miocene, constituting a key component of the flat-slab subduction paradigm in the Southern Central Andes. However, this paradigm has been put to the test over the last decade, leading to a complete revision of the AFTB at 33°S, which revealed an overlooked tectonic stage prior to slab flattening. Ignored for more than a century, evidence for Late Cretaceous contraction continues to pile up, and new geochronological data have revealed the presence of previously mismapped Paleogene deposits. After intensive field work performed in the highest Andes, we report key field observations supported both by new U-Pb detrital zircon ages and several stratigraphic profiles that have been captured in a detailed geological map of the AFTB between 32°45’ and 33°15’S.

Upper Cretaceous red beds rest unconformably over Lower Cretaceous marine deposits, bracketing a 30 Myr long hiatus developed over a karst-weathered carbonate substrate. The presence of contractional growth strata in these beds composed of coarse-grained deposits with a mixed clastic provenance both from the eastern cratonic area and underlying sedimentary units suggests structural activity during sedimentation. The latest Cretaceous in this area is registered in a series of basaltic rocks interbedded with fine-grained shale deposits, which exhibit extensional growth strata developed within a lacustrine to brackish environment.

The transition to the Paleogene is marked by the accumulation of another red nonmarine unit capped by green shales and limestones, which present a marked shift in provenance towards the contemporary magmatic arc located to the west. However, this sequence is absent in the higher peaks, where a truncation by volcanic rocks of presumable upper Eocene to Oligocene age generated a pronounced angular unconformity, evidence of a newly recognized contractional event affecting the area.

The combination of stratigraphic and structural observations in the Upper Cretaceous to Paleogene deposits is interpreted as the result of tectonic regime switching over this interval, which was followed by an important Neogene exhumation event already documented in the AFTB. This complex arrangement likely reflects the rise of the Late Cretaceous orogen in the Southern Central Andes, followed by its demise due to the passage of a mid-ocean ridge along the Pacific margin.

abstract: The onset of Cenozoic Basin and Range extension in NE Nevada is commonly regarded as initiating during the middle Miocene at ca. 17–16 Ma with the development of widespread synextensional basins filled with the Humboldt Formation. However, there is growing evidence of an earlier phase of Eocene–Oligocene extension between ca. 38 Ma and 17 Ma based on recent work documenting synextensional sedimentary deposits underlying the Humboldt Formation. Published reconnaissance mapping in the southern part of Knoll basin between the Snake Mountains and Knoll Mountain suggested that some of the Cenozoic strata in this area are Eocene. Our new mapping in this area indicates that these strata lie between the 16 Ma to ca. 5 Ma Humboldt Formation and Eocene volcanic rocks. We informally refer to these strata as the Red Point formation. It is exposed over a 50 km 2 area, is ~1,200 meters thick, consists of clast-supported conglomerate, volcaniclastic sandstone, and shale, and is interpreted to have been deposited in a fluvial environment. The lithology of conglomerate clasts indicates that they were derived from local Eocene volcanic and Paleozoic sedimentary rocks. The formation has a wedge-shaped geometry and pinches out to the northwest. Two new detrital zircon U-Pb maximum depositional ages from sandstone samples in the middle part of the formation yield YC2 ages of 25.1 ± 0.1 [0.5] Ma (average of 84 overlapping ages, no younger grains ignored) and 26.8 ± 0.4 [0.7] Ma (average of 5 overlapping ages, 2 younger grains ignored). In both samples, grains of 25–30 Ma make up the majority, and the youngest suite of ages, and are sourced from distal ash-fall eruptions. We interpret the formation to be deposited in a structurally isolated synextensional basin. This newly recognized basin lies between the two areas with documented Oligocene synextensional basins in NE Nevada, the Ruby metamorphic core complex domain ~38 km to the south, and the Copper Mountains area ~65 km to the northwest. The sedimentary characteristics and Oligocene age of the Red Point formation suggest that Oligocene extension in NE Nevada is more extensive than previously recognized.

abstract:
What is the basal state of the scleractinian skeleton, and how long did it persist in the fossil record? Retention of traits linked to basal morphologies may indicate long-term evolutionary resilience to major global environmental shifts. The main architects of modern reefs, corals from order Scleractinia, evolved during the Middle Ordovician according to molecular data, persisted in mostly soft-bodied forms through shifting climates of the Paleozoic, and retained skeletonized forms from the Middle Triassic to the present day. Modern scleractinian corals face numerous pressures from a warming climate, including rising sea surface temperatures and acidifying oceans. This work utilizes Mesozoic and Cenozoic fossil records of order Scleractinia along with a comprehensive record of Paleozoic scleractiniamorphs and members of subclass Rugosa to reveal skeletal traits basal to all anthozoans. Additionally, the fossil record of scleractinians is examined with extant corals to determine traits basal to order Scleractinia, and their persistence from deep evolutionary time to modern oceans.

Skeletal macromorphologies were compiled for 31 fossil and 19 extant solitary scleractinian families, 3 fossil scleractiniamorph families, and 74 fossil rugosan families. Occurrences of 69 skeletal traits were quantified for each epoch independent of taxonomy. Results indicate that epitheca, tabulae, dissepiments, synapticulae, axial structure, and septal lobes are basal to all anthozoans. To identify the basal scleractinian state and link it to modern corals, parsimony-based trait node analysis was performed using trait data for extant scleractinian families combined with a published molecular phylogeny. Results indicate the basal scleractinian state possesses a trochoid or discoid shape, laminar septa, septal teeth, ornamented lateral flanks, axial structure and costae. These findings identify specific traits basal to all anthozoans which were lost early or repeatedly within the scleractinian lineage. Pertinent to modern conservation practices are the basal scleractinian traits retained today by extant, solitary, ahermatypic scleractinian corals that inhabit deep water environments, such as Rhombopsammia (Micrabaciidae) and Deltocyathus (Deltocyathidae). The persistence of these basal morphologies through the stratigraphic record guides conservation, biodiversity, and climate research agendas toward the cryptic solitary and deep-water corals, which are often overlooked. Solitary corals inhabiting deep waters, while still at substantial risk, may hold secrets to modern reef resilience.

title: Multi-Objective Optimization with Groundwater Models: Framing Complex Results for Resource Management Decisions
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Corson-Dosch, Nicholas T [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Upper Midwest Water Science Center, Madison, WI, USA
abstract: Groundwater management decisions require balancing competing objectives under uncertainty. Managers must weigh tradeoffs between sustaining water supply, protecting ecosystems, or addressing contamination within systems that are imperfectly understood. Numerical groundwater models can be effective tools for evaluating these systems, yet their complexity can make it difficult to translate simulation results into clear, actionable guidance for decision-makers. Multi-objective optimization offers a framework for systematically exploring tradeoffs and presenting model outcomes in terms that are relevant and understandable to resource managers and stakeholders. This talk presents applications of multi-objective optimization to groundwater remediation design, drawing on two projects involving pump-and-treat systems. In both cases, optimization was used to evaluate tradeoffs among competing remediation objectives, producing sets of solutions that reveal the structure of the decision space. Through these examples, the talk explores the opportunities and challenges of using optimization to move beyond single "best" answers toward a broader characterization of what outcomes are achievable and at what cost, reframing complex model outputs into information that more readily supports decision-making. However, challenges remain. One is distilling large sets of optimal solutions into decision‑relevant advice without overstating model certainty. Another is computational demand: multi‑objective analyses often require thousands of model runs, limiting accessibility for many practitioners. Model emulators - surrogate representations trained on subsets of full model runs - offer a promising way to reduce this burden by enabling efficient exploration of the decision space once essential decision variables and forecasts are identified. The talk will highlight lessons from applied optimization studies, strategies for effectively communicating tradeoffs, and opportunities to make these methods more computationally efficient and broadly useful in groundwater management.

title: The Role of Bedrock Erodibility in the Origins of the Blue Ridge Mountain Highlands, USA
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Chilton, Kristin [1], Curtiss, Elizabeth Rose [2], Stephens, Angelina [3], Richards, Amelia [4], Hughes, Katie [5], Spotila, James A. [6]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, BLACKSBURG, VA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(3) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(4) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(5) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(6) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
abstract:
The Southern Blue Ridge Mountains (SBR) retain impressively rugged topography more than 200 m.y. after the cessation of mountain building. The origins of this relief have yet to be fully explained, though it has been cited as evidence for late Cenozoic uplift and subsequent topographic rejuvenation of the South-Central Appalachians. However, the influence of bedrock erodibility on topography in the SBR remains unknown, partly because spatially complex bedrock properties remain insufficiently characterized throughout the region. Therefore, we collect data on the material properties of bedrock at a range of elevations in the most rugged regions within the SBR in North Carolina (Great Smoky Mtns., Roan Mtn., Mt. Mitchell, and Elk Knob) to inform our understanding of the role of bedrock erodibility on topographic patterns in the SBR.

We find that bedrock found at high elevations is consistently stronger than bedrock found at low elevations. Within each region, the average point load index of high-elevation rocks is 1.2-1.7x higher than that of surrounding low-elevation rocks, even though high-elevation samples are consistently more weathered than those from low-elevations. The magnitude of the difference in rock strength between high and low elevations scales with relief, implying a causal relationship between rock strength and topography. We also observe location-specific relationships between mineral content and topography, suggesting a different suite of rock properties may produce resistant bedrock within each highland region. These results suggest that spatial patterns of lithologic properties play an important role in shaping and sustaining topography in the SBR. Therefore, efforts to extract baselevel histories from topography in this multifactorial landscape face the challenge of disentangling geomorphic signatures of uplift from the effects of lithologic complexity.

title: BEDROCK AND SURFICIAL GEOLOGIC MAP OF THE NORTHERN HALF OF THE MOUNT LOGAN 7.5’ QUADRANGLE: INVESTIGATING COLORADO’S PROTEROZOIC OROGENIES
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Ransom, Hunter Stephen [1], Kuiper, Yvette D. [2], Ruleman, Cal [3], Pream, Ayden [4], Olson, Eric [5]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Evergreen, CO, USA
(4) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(5) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
A preliminary 1:24,000 bedrock and surficial geological map of the northern half of the Mount Logan quadrangle, around Grant, CO, was produced for a USGS EDMAP project to investigate deformation of Proterozoic bedrock in relation to the Paleoproterozoic Yavapai and Mazatzal and Mesoproterozoic Picuris orogenies. The mapping area lies adjacent to the Continental Divide at 2740-3925 meters asl. The primary lithologies are granodioritic gneiss, quartzofeldspathic gneiss, and biotite-quartz-feldspar gneiss. Granodioritic gneiss locally includes xenoliths of biotite gneiss, amphibolite, and hornblende gneiss. Foliations in these units dip moderately towards the northwest and locally towards the northeast. To the south of these gneiss units is a pluton of moderately foliated biotite and muscovite-bearing monzogranite with K-feldspar phenocrysts resembling the ~1.42 Ga Silver Plume granite, with foliations dipping gently to the north and northwest. Migmatitic biotite-quartz-feldspar gneiss and interlayered hornblende gneiss, calc-silicate gneiss, and quartzite in the center of the mapping area show northwest- and northeast-dipping foliations and are intruded by irregularly shaped dikes and sills of monzonite and granodiorite with northerly-dipping foliations. Granitic dikes and sills in migmatitic zones are commonly pegmatitic. Migmatitic zones are also locally crosscut by discontinuous pegmatite veins and dikes, which typically contain the same foliation as the granite sills. Quartzite appears in ~0.5-1.0 meter-thick layers within the calc-silicate gneiss. This unit resembles, and may be related to, a previously discovered ~1.4 Ga quartzite in the Mount Blue Sky quadrangle, immediately north of the Mount Logan quadrangle.

Within the granodioritic gneiss, quartzofeldspathic gneiss, biotite-quartz-feldspar gneiss, hornblende gneiss, and calc-silicate gneiss, isoclinal folds typically plunge moderately to the north-northwest, and tight and open folds typically plunge shallowly to the northeast. Locally, fold hinges and some mineral stretching lineations plunge shallowly to the southwest. Generally, foliation orientations change from northwest-dipping in the northern part of the mapping area to north-dipping in the southern part. Bedrock units are offset by moderately-dipping west-northwest striking and west-southwest striking fractures showing minor reverse or normal offset, locally with a right-lateral component. The Pleistocene geomorphic setting is characterized as glacial, glaciofluvial, and periglacial, with late-middle Pleistocene deposits of the Bull Lake glaciation and late Pleistocene glacial till and outwash of the Pinedale glaciation. Pleistocene erosional fluvial channels are back-filled by Holocene alluvium and alluvial-colluvial deposits.

title: Organic Preservation of Vase-Shaped Microfossils from Shales of the Togari Group, Tasmania
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age (Posters)
authors: Mchale, Caroline L. [1], Porter, Susannah M. [2], Riedman, Leigh Anne [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Goleta, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
abstract: Vase-shaped microfossils (VSMs), thought to be the remains of testate amoebae, occur in late Tonian deposits around the world. VSMs are most commonly preserved as casts made of silica, pyrite, carbonate, or iron oxide. This, in addition to the rare preservation of organic VSMs, suggests that in life, VSMs had a test composed of labile organic material. Organic VSMs recently reported from shales of the Chuar Group were hypothesized to be preserved via sulfurization, based on X-ray absorption spectroscopy of a single sample showing the presence of reduced organic sulfur species in the test walls and surrounding matrix. Here, we report organically-preserved VSMs from shales of the ~725 Ma lower Black River Dolomite, Togari Group, Tasmania, as determined by scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and electron probe microanalysis. Silicified and clay-mineralized VSMs also occur in shales from this unit, including in samples that contain organic specimens. In contrast, cherts (silicified shales) from the same unit preserve silicified or clay-mineralized specimens but do not contain completely organic VSMs. Clay-mineralized specimens across all lithologies contain degraded organic material and are associated with sulfur or iron. We find that the organic VSMs are not associated with sulfur, suggesting that sulfurization may not have been important to their preservation. We also find no evidence for preservation by clay mineral coatings, as has been hypothesized for other deposits of organically preserved Proterozoic microfossils in mudrocks. Instead, organically preserved specimens have internal and external siliceous rinds, suggesting that early diagenetic silica coatings might have played a key role in their preservation. We propose that fully silicified specimens in chert represent the completion of this process, with the preservation of labile organic material in mudrocks being confined to a narrow window in the early stages of silicification. Early post-mortem silicification may also explain why organic VSMs are preserved three-dimensionally in shales, while more recalcitrant organic-walled microfossils are flattened.

title: Latitudinal Manganese Gradient Dynamics Associated With Earth’s Major Ice Ages
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Wang, Xubin [1], Pohl, Alexandre [2], Rickaby, Rosalind E. M. [3], Lu, Zunli [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY, USA
(2) Université Bourgogne Europe, Dijon, France
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom
(4) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY, USA
abstract: Distinct sedimentary deposits of manganese are known to be associated with extreme and severe glaciations in Earth's deep time. The redox-sensitive nature of manganese has attracted scientists for decades - especially theories about how oxygen and climate collaborated to cause major perturbations in the global geochemical cycle of this important metal. Temporal analyses of a large database focusing on sedimentary geochemistry demonstrated high manganese concentrations in marine sediments were commonly linked to oxygenation events and glaciations in deep time. Here we show spatial analyses of those crucial intervals that reveal a recurring pattern of relative enrichment of manganese in sediments at high latitudes during the six greatest glaciations of Earth's history. The manganese concentrations were generally lower in tropical sediments, which was most likely driven by ocean dissolved oxygen gradients. This latitudinal manganese gradient increasingly flattened as the oxygen level rose in the atmosphere and ocean over the geological time scale. Our analyses suggest that anoxia frequently occurred during icehouse conditions, challenging the conventional wisdom of warming-driven ocean deoxygenation.

title: Classroom to Core Shack – Building a Resilient and Skilled Geoscience Mining Workforce
session_title: Mineral Resources and Society
authors: Thompson, Anne J.B. [1]
affiliations: (1) PetraScience Consultants Inc., Vancouver, BC, Canada; Past President, Society of Economic Geologists, Littleton, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The challenges society faces in securing the mineral resources needed for the energy transition and global economic development are well known. We need to find more minerals, extract and process them more sustainably, and use them more effectively. Solutions typically require a robust workforce and greater innovation in exploration and mining.

Workforce demand projections point to massive retirements that together with apparent declining university enrolments, are a major worry for the future. The analyses do not typically detail geoscience needs and do not account for the growing use of data science and AI in exploration and mining projects. We cannot predict how many geologists will be needed in the future. However, we do know we need new skills, new approaches, and what geologists have always shown – a passion for discovery.

Early education and improved public awareness are typically cited as solutions to long-term workforce needs. But success requires multiple approaches. Changes led by universities, industry, and professional societies are already yielding positive, near-term results.

Examples include redesigned undergraduate geoscience curricula that focus on process and the dynamic Earth rather than traditionally structured frameworks. Exposure to data science and modern mapping tools plays an important role in these programs.

Innovative, industry-supported programs designed in collaboration with professional societies are proving successful. An exciting new effort is MiEX – the mining industry experience program, a two-week immersive program for first-year undergraduate students in science and engineering. A Canadian course (S-IMEW) just celebrated 20 years of providing students with two weeks of hands-on experience with relevant skills and opportunities.

The Society of Economic Geologists is building a Discovery Skills Program that directly addresses key skills needed by early-career geoscientists entering exploration and mining careers, including modern drill core logging and mapping. Training incorporates new digital core data viewing platforms, tools, and techniques. Support from mining professionals and companies is foundational to success.

Technical work in mining will always be grounded in fundamental geoscience, but the tools and approaches are changing quickly. Collectively, these programs will help build a workforce that is both resilient and talented, and ready to help fulfill the future needs of human society.

title: Morphological and Diversity Analysis of Fossil Leaves of the John Day Formation, UW Oshkosh Collection
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Fennessy, Abbigale [1], Peterson, Joseph [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, University of Wisconsin Oshkosh, Oshkosh, Wisconsin, USA

abstract: Fossil leaves are a glimpse into ancient forests and the way our environment once was. The John Day Formation in north-central Oregon is known for its preservation of mammal and plant fossils from the Eocene to Miocene Epochs, ranging from 39 to 16 million years ago, within the Cenozoic Era. While the tuffaceous matrix preserves flora well, it can also make the specimens very fragile and difficult to handle. This study looks at a sample group that was donated to the University of Wisconsin Oshkosh Geology Department, collected by Dr. Muldoon at the Hancock Field Station, that contains 35 intact specimens. Each sample was identified at the genus level and scanned into a digital 3-D model to avoid further damage from handling. Measurements were taken to capture the scope of the leaf’s size, including midvein length and lamina size classes. Together, the data sets display the dominant genera in our sample size, along with the shape and size of individuals that make up the group. This sample group displays 18 different genera, including an abundance of Alnus, Metasequoia, and Sequoia , but the rest make up a small percentage of the samples. The largest midvein present in the sample group was an Alnus , spanning 93.8 mm. Lamina size only accounts for angiosperms, which ranged from microphyll, notophhyll, and mesophyll, with only one specimen in the mesophyll category. This specimen was the only Platanaceae , and as a lobed leaf it is expected to align with the larger lamina class.

session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape (Posters)
authors: Salgado, Federico Ezequiel [1], Acevedo, Eliana [2], Álvarez, Orlando [3], Rocher, Sebastián [4], Pallares, Carlos [5], Hauser, Natalia [6], Folguera, Andrés [7]

abstract:
It is widely accepted that the Neogene evolution of the Southern Central Andes flat-slab segment (29°S) is characterized by the eastward migration of the deformation front, leaving the High Andes (Frontal Cordillera), located to the west, tectonically quiescent since the late Miocene. However, recent evidence of accelerated Plio-Quaternary exhumation suggests that strain continued to be accommodated in the hinterland, implying that active deformation and associated seismic hazards may be underestimated. Here, we evaluate the neotectonic activity and deformation mechanisms of the High Andes hinterland at 29°S through an integrated study of the previously unassessed Colangüil Fault along the Plieguesitos Stream valley.

We combined structural and geomorphological mapping, river-profile analysis, paleoseismological investigation of soft-sediment deformation structures (SSDS), landslide-volume reconstructions, remote sensing, and gravity data to assess fault activity and its geodynamic controls.

Field observations document a growth-strata anticline developed within Quaternary fluvial-lacustrine deposits that onlap the toe of a landslide emplaced above the Colangüil Fault, indicating syn-sedimentary uplift. These paleolake deposits also contain high-energy seismites indicative of minimum earthquake magnitudes of Mw 6–7, consistent with those inferred from landslide-volume reconstructions. We propose that repeated paleoseismic activity triggered a 23-km-long linear cluster of landslides parallel to the fault, damming the Plieguesitos Stream and generating cycles of aggradation, dam breaching, and terrace incision. River-profile analysis allows the identification of knickpoints spatially coincident with the fault trace and a linear topographic bulge developed on the landslide surface. In addition, remote sensing highlights hydrothermal alteration along the fault zone, whereas vertical gravity-gradient data reveal a deep lithospheric structure spatially associated with the active segment. Together, these observations provide strong evidence for Quaternary activity along the Colangüil Fault.

We propose that this out-of-sequence deformation is driven by a subcritical orogenic wedge influenced by: (1) reduction in orogenic taper caused by focused hinterland denudation; (2) reduced internal friction facilitated by a NW-striking translithospheric structure channeling high-pressure hydrothermal fluids; (3) localized increase in basal friction along the décollement due to fluid depletion; and (4) the Paleozoic Colangüil Batholith acting as a crustal buttress that promotes localized uplift. Our findings indicate that the High Andes hinterland at 29°S actively accommodates strain, challenging conventional models of deformation in flat-slab subduction systems and revealing a previously unrecognized source of regional seismic hazard.
