title: Evaluating the Ecological, Developmental, and Biogeographic Dimensions of a Post-Extinction Radiation in Flexible Crinoids using Phylogenetic Comparative Methods
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology
authors: Crowley, Kiera D. [1], Wright, David F. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA; Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA; Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA
abstract:
Crinoids of Superorder Flexibilia originated during the late Middle Ordovician and, following the Late Ordovician mass extinction (LOME), radiated to comprise one of the major constituents in Paleozoic crinoid communities. However, the mechanistic underpinnings of this radiation and the role of the LOME in shaping post-extinction diversification trajectories remain unclear. Previous uncertainties regarding the time and place of origination for members of the clade have hindered our ability to characterize the ways in which flexible crinoids were impacted by (and responded to) the Late Ordovician mass extinction (LOME). But the recent construction of a species-level phylogeny for early flexibles provides the most robust framework yet for modeling the likely divergence times and biogeographic affinities for flexible species. From this spatiotemporal foundation, analyzing the species-level response of this group during its post-LOME radiation provides a nuanced case study for interpreting the processes shaping macroevolutionary dynamics during an interval of significant environmental and biotic change. Specifically, the use of tip-dated fossil phylogenies along with paleontologically-motivated phylogenetic comparative methods (PCMs) permits novel modeling approaches for investigating the tempo and mode of diversification in multiple, quasi-independent macroevolutionary currencies: taxonomic diversity, morphologic disparity, and functional ecology.

Here, we present the results of a study aimed at clarifying the biogeographic and ecomorphological dynamics of Late Ordovician to middle Silurian flexible crinoids using PCMs. We use a discrete-state Markov model to estimate the most probable geographic origin and evolution for Flexibilia, and assess the differing biogeographic patterns among flexible subclades in light of their differential success during the LOME. Then, we use our phylogenetic framework for 103 flexible species to fit multiple process-based macroevolutionary models of trait diversification across three morphologic characters directly related to crinoid feeding and development: body size, relative filtration fan area, and calyx complexity. Five alternative hypotheses of trait diversification are tested, including time-homogenous Brownian Motion and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models as well as time-heterogenous combinations of the two involving shifts in tempo and/or mode of trait diversification across the LOME. Models involving an evolutionary regime shift across the LOME are supported for body size and calyx complexity, although relative filtration fan area is largely constrained across the event. However, differing ecomorphological dynamics among flexible subclades suggests the possibility of extinction selectivity shaping subclade evolutionary trajectories during the LOME.

title: Late Oligocene-Late Miocene Fossil Camels from the John Day Basin, North-Central and Eastern Oregon
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic (Posters)
authors: Parod, Scarlet O. A. [1], Prothero, Donald R. [2], Famoso, Nicholas A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State Polytechnic University, Pomona, Los Angeles, California, USA; Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, California, USA
(3) John Day Fossil Beds National Monument, U.S. National Park Service, Kimberly, Oregon, USA; Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oregon, USA
abstract: The camels from the John Day Basin in central Oregon have long been confused and misidentified, both because they are rare and highly fragmentary, and because North American camelid systematics has been chaotic for over a century. With the new revision of North American camels, it is now possible to correctly identify the higher-quality specimens. Contrary to the internet and all the literature for over a century, there are no fossils referable to the Orellan-Whitneyan High Plains camel Paratylopus anywhere in the late Oligocene-early Miocene John Day Formation. In the Arikareean (Turtle Cove and Kimberly members of the John Day Formation), the most common camel is the nothokemadine Gentilicamelus sternbergi , which has been placed in several invalid genera over the past 150 years. From the latest Arikareean Haystack Valley Member and higher members, we describe a new genus and species of long-snouted floridatraguline. This is the first published occurrence of the floridatragulines outside the Gulf Coast region, previously known only from Florida to Texas to Mexico to Panama. The enigmatic camel from the John Day Formation that was long misidentified as “ Paratylopus” cameloides is actually a primitive protolabine, now assigned to Michenia cameloides . It is rare but found in the late Arikareean to Hemingfordian parts of the section. The John Day camels are all unusual, with almost none of the Arikareean and Hemingfordian camels found in the High Plains, such as the stenomylines, miotylopines, miolabines, oxydactylines, or other taxa found across most of North America. Instead, it is dominated by two unusual and rare groups, the floridatragulines and the nothokemadines, which were previously only known from the Gulf Coast of Florida, Texas, and Central America. The literature and the Paleobiology DataBase (PBDB) and MIOMAP are grossly outdated concerning John Day camels, and must not be relied upon for information concerning their taxonomy or distribution.

title: Refining Fossil Lizard Identification for late Quaternary Great Basin Paleoecology
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Katuin, Abby [1], Cole , Kasey [2], Irmis, Randall B. [3], Faith , J. Tyler [4]
affiliations: (1) Biomedical Informatics, Eccles School of Medicine, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA; Natural History Museum of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(2) Sociology and Anthropology, Weber State University, Ogden, Utah, USA
(3) Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA; Natural History Museum of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(4) Anthropology, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA; Natural History Museum of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
abstract: Species-level identification of fossils is critical for accurate paleoenvironmental reconstruction, as many organisms occupy distinct ecological niches and habitat preferences. Lizards are useful paleoecological indicators because many species occupy distinct microhabitats and exhibit narrow ecological tolerances. In the Great Basin, however, there are few fossil squamate (lizard) studies, and diagnostic osteological characters remain poorly documented compared to those of mammals. Consequently, fossil lizard remains are often identified only at high taxonomic levels (i.e., above species), limiting their paleoecological utility. Here we document the fossil lizard assemblage (excluding snakes) preserved within Quaternary cave deposits of western Utah’s House Range, and evaluate how increased taxonomic resolution improves paleoecological interpretation. These fossils were recovered from surface collections and excavations within chambers of three caves between 6400-6800 ft elevation. 91 lizard cranial specimens were analyzed; 34 of which were identifiable to genus and 33 to species. Osteological collections and published literature were used to identify diagnostic cranial characters and facilitate species-level attributions where possible. This assemblage was compared with published nearby cave assemblages from the late Pleistocene-Holocene transition, and with modern georeferenced museum records from VertNet. After accounting for differences in sampling intensity using rarefaction analyses, fossil and modern assemblages retained similar levels of species richness. However, substantial shifts in relative abundance and species composition may indicate long-term restructuring of lizard communities through the Holocene. In particular, Uta stansburiana was more abundant in modern records than in the paleo-assemblage (30.59% vs 8.89%), whereas Aspidoscelis tigris was absent from the paleo-assemblage despite occurring in both nearby fossil assemblages and modern VertNet records. The House Range assemblage preserved three species of horned lizards (Phrynosoma douglasii, P. platyrhinos, and P. hernandesi), taxa that differ in modern habitats and elevation associations. Notably, P. douglasii was recovered from burnt deposits radiocarbon dated to 14,322-14,745 years Cal BP, indicating a latest Pleistocene age. Today, however, P. douglasii is absent from the House Range and restricted to the northern Great Basin. The coexistence of these three ecologically distinct species suggests environmental conditions and habitat distributions differed from those of the modern eastern Great Basin. These ecological patterns were only detectable through species-level identifications and detailed osteological assessment, highlighting the value of improved diagnostic descriptions for fossil lizards.

session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part I)
authors: Chambi , Maria Isabel [1], Quino, Israel [2], Ormachea, Mauricio [3], Ramos, Oswaldo [4], Bhattacharya, Prosun [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering (SEED), KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden; Instituto de Investigaciones Quimicas (IIQ), Universidad Mayor de San Andres, La Paz, Bolivia
(2) Instituto de Investigaciones Químicas (IIQ), Universidad Mayor de San Andres, La Paz, Bolivia
(3) Instituto de Investigaciones Quimica (IIQ), Universidad Mayor de San Andres, La Paz, Bolivia
(4) Instituto de Investigaciones Química (IIQ), Universidad Mayor de San Andres, La Paz, Bolivia
(5) Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering (SEED), KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockhol, Sweden
abstract:
Sajama National Park (SNP), located in the Bolivian Altiplano at elevations of 3860–4184 m above sea level, represents a high-altitude volcanic hydrogeochemical system where evaporative processes, geothermal inputs, and water–rock interaction converge to control groundwater chemistry. The volcanic complex is composed of dacitic–andesitic rocks, pyroclastic deposits, and Quaternary lava flows (~0.6 Ma), providing a reactive lithological framework for trace element mobilization. This study investigates how salinity evolution and redox conditions jointly regulate the distribution and speciation of arsenic (As), boron (B), and lithium (Li) in groundwater and surface water.

A total of 64 water samples from rivers, wells, springs, and thermal springs were analyzed. Field parameters show wide variability, including temperature (12.1–41.4 °C), pH (5.9–9.3), electrical conductivity (54–3322 µS/cm), and oxidation–reduction potential, reflecting strong hydrogeochemical gradients. Water types are dominated by Mg–Ca–Na–HCO3–SO4 and Mg–Ca–Na–HCO3 facies. Dissolved concentrations exhibit pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with As ranging from 0.5 to 2094 µg/L, B from 57 to 12,079 µg/L, Li from 0.1 to 2394 µg/L, and F from 0.2 to 1.4 mg/L. Elevated concentrations exceeding Bolivian NB512 and WHO guideline values are concentrated in the northern and western sectors, where porous alluvial deposits, evaporative concentration, and geothermal influence enhance solute accumulation.

Hydrochemical evolution, interpreted through Gibbs diagrams, indicates dominant control by water–rock interaction within volcanic lithologies, with superimposed evaporative enrichment driving increased salinity. Speciation modeling shows that As occurs primarily as H2AsO4 ⁻ and HAsO4 2- under oxidizing conditions, with mobility influenced by interactions with Fe(III) mineral phases, whereas B and Li occur mainly as H3BO3 and Li + and are largely governed by salinity-driven concentration and water–rock interaction processes.

Overall, the results demonstrate that the coupled effects of evaporative salinization and redox dynamics act as key controls on trace element mobilization in high-altitude volcanic aquifers, leading to the persistence of geogenic contaminants at concentrations of concern. These findings provide new insights into the hydrogeochemical functioning of Andean volcanic systems and highlight critical implications for water quality and resource sustainability in arid high-mountain environments.

title: Geogenic Molybdenum in Carbonate Aquifers - Implications for Drinking Water and Aquifer Management
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Pichler, Thomas [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Bremen, Bremen, Germany; Earth Science, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
abstract:
While point-source contamination scenarios with molybdenum (Mo) are more commonly studied, geogenic (natural) Mo release from aquifer matrices is an underrecognized drinking water hazard, particularly in poor urban and rural settings where supply is decentralized and rarely tested. Carbonate aquifers are especially prone to this risk, as Mo is known to accumulate in marine sediments.

Integrating detailed characterization of aquifer matrix mineralogy, sequential chemical extractions, groundwater geochemistry, ³H/³He age dating, and reactive transport modeling, more than 10 years of work on the Floridan Aquifer System (USA) demonstrates that Mo is hosted not in pyrite or other sulfide minerals — despite Mo's chalcophile character — but in sulfurized organic matter within the aquifer matrix. Alteration of hydrologic flow paths due to faulty well installation, pumping-induced water table decline, and managed aquifer recharge (MAR) injection of oxic water drives a rapid shift from high-pH reducing to low-pH oxidizing conditions, releasing Mo to groundwater at concentrations up to 5,050 µg/L — far exceeding the EPA health advisory of 40 µg/L. This contamination occurs at scales too fine to be captured by regional or national groundwater monitoring networks, leaving affected wells undetected for years.

These findings have direct implications for drinking water safety, well siting, and aquifer management, leading to three recommendations: (1) reconnaissance-scale Mo monitoring targeted at organic-carbon-rich zones within carbonate aquifers, (2) mandatory testing of suspected aquifers before new well installation, and (3) explicit inclusion of Mo in risk assessments for managed aquifer recharge projects, where injected oxic water can trigger the same redox-driven release mechanism.

title: U-Pb Zircon Geochronology and Igneous Geochemistry of the Ediacaran Hamill Group Volcanics, Selkirk Mountains, British Columbia, Canada
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Warburton, London C. [1], Crowley, James L. [2], Miller, Keegan A. [3], Kellogg, William B. [4], Ootes, Luke [5], McClelland, William C. [6], Strauss, Justin V. [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA

(6) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(7) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
abstract: Ediacaran rocks of the southern Canadian Cordillera have great potential to aid in our understanding of the Ediacaran Earth system due to their extensive exposure, interlayered volcanic sequences, varied depositional settings, and proven fossil occurrences. Despite this, local and global stratigraphic correlations have been hindered by a dearth of radiometric age constraints. One such constraint, a ca. 570 Ma date from greenschist- to amphibolite-grade metavolcanic rocks in the Hamill Group of the northern Selkirk Mountains, British Columbia (Colpron et al., 2002, CJES), has been widely cited as both a regional stratigraphic marker and evidence for rift-related volcanism. Here, we refine this geochronological constraint using high-precision U-Pb zircon chemical abrasion-thermal ionization mass spectrometry (CA-TIMS) and expand published geochemical data through additional field sampling and modern geochemical and isotopic datasets. In addition, we present new U-Pb detrital zircon geochronological data from the surrounding Hamill Group metasedimentary succession. Our results agree with the previously reported ca. 570 Ma age for regional volcanism but decrease the uncertainty approximately 50-fold, to within ±0.1 Ma. The new geochemical and geochronological data not only support other evidence for protracted Ediacaran extension along the western Laurentian margin but also help elucidate the regional depositional context of the Windermere Supergroup in the southern Canadian Cordillera.

title: Constructivism and its Implications, or Why Presenting Settled Science does not Provide the Royal Road to Learning:
session_title: Making Sense of Methodologies and Theoretical Frameworks in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Dolphin, Glenn [1], Khan, Samia [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
(2) Department of Curriculum and Pedagogy, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
abstract: Humanity faces growing concerns from the natural world, including clean air and water supplies, mineral and energy resource extraction and consumption, natural hazards and increased climate change-related risks. To mitigate such concerns, we need a population that is geoscience literate. Engagement and learning within the geosciences are highly dependent on the nature of teaching and how responsive instruction is to how students learn. Recent research documenting the order of topics taught in undergraduate introductory geoscience course as well as a survey of several commercially available introductory geoscience textbooks shows that the first topics students experience in introductory courses deal with the origin of the universe, the solar system and earth, as well as the theory of plate tectonics (the macrocosm), before then addressing chemistry – atoms, bonding, and molecules (the microcosm). These concepts are well outside the students’ experiential frameworks (the mesocosm) in both scales of time and space. Presenting settled science does not provide the royal road to learning: What we know from how people learn, philosophically, theoretically and empirically, is that students require concrete experiences as building blocks for developing abstract ideas. Learning must begin within the scale of the students’ everyday concrete experiences before moving to the abstract. It is most common to present students with the (abstract) explanatory models first, followed by the (concrete) evidentiary support, when students really require the concrete to precede the abstract. This presentation elaborates on this argument and then puts forth implications for instruction to be effective, including understanding the origin of common misconceptions, breaking down large explanatory concepts (like theories) into hierarchies of supporting elements that are more concrete, and providing students with concrete experiences they can leverage effectively to develop more reliable (i.e. scientific consensus) concepts.

title: Buried Soils, Holocene Alluvium, and a Life Changed by Rolfe Mandel: Reflections from His First Graduate Student
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Dillon, Jeremy S. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Earth Science, University of Nebraska at Kearney, Kearney, Nebraska, USA
abstract: In this presentation I will share stories of Rolfe Mandel as an advisor, a mentor, and a friend; a story shared by many students across the country. I met Rolfe in 1989 when he was applying for his first academic position. Rolfe introduced me to buried soils, Holocene alluvium, landscape evolution, and geoarchaeology. He changed the way I view the landscapes of today, and helped me to visualize landscapes of the past. This will be a light-hearted, yet heart-felt tribute to Rolfe, from the perspective of his first graduate student.

title: Domestically Sourced Lithium Precursor Validation in Battery Cathodes​
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Coyle, Jaclyn [1], Adhikari, Pashupati [2], Harrison, Katharine [3]
affiliations: (1) National Laboratory of the Rockies, Materials, Chemical and Computational Science, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) National Laboratory of the Rockies, Materials, Chemical and Computational Science, Lakewood, CO, USA
(3) National Laboratory of the Rockies, Materials, Chemical and Computational Science, Lakewood, CO,
abstract:
The growing demand for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in energy storage systems requires a robust, diversified supply chain for critical raw materials. Lithium carbonate (Li 2 CO 3 ), a key precursor for LFP production, faces price volatility and concentrated global supply. Validation of domestically sourced lithium precursors, including those derived from brines, is essential to reduce supply chain risks and support domestic lithium-ion battery manufacturing. Li 2 CO 3 quality can strongly influence LFP synthesis and thus electrochemical performance. Critical metrics for Li 2 CO 3 include purity, particle size, morphology, and crystal structure. Li 2 CO 3 sources that are considered “Battery-grade” typically require purities above 99.5%, with premium grades exceeding 99.9%. The targeted outcome of this work is to determine the impact of physical and chemical properties of domestically sourced Li 2 CO 3 on scalable LFP synthesis and electrochemical performance.

In this study, five commercially available Li 2 CO 3 materials were evaluated, including a NIST standard, various purities of Sigma Aldrich reagents, a battery-grade commercial material with flake morphology, and Li 2 CO 3 produced domestically from brine. Prior to LFP synthesis, all samples were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), particle size analysis (PSA), inductively coupled plasma spectroscopy (ICP), and thermogravimetric analysis–evolved gas analysis (TGA-EGA), with selected analyses performed before and after drying. Elevated sulfur concentrations were identified in both the battery-grade flake material and the domestically sourced brine-derived Li 2 CO 3 relative to Sigma Aldrich reagents and the NIST standard. Significant differences in particle size and morphology were also observed across the sample set. SEM and PSA revealed distinct spherulitic and flake-like morphologies that, together with measured purity variations, enabled direct evaluation of how precursor characteristics influenced scalable LFP synthesis and electrochemical performance. This work will help demonstrate the importance of these parameters for the performance of cathode materials synthesized from domestic lithium precursors to both lithium brine extraction and battery material manufacturing industries.

title: Formation of the Boxwork Unit in Gale Crater, Mars
session_title: Boxwork and Fracture Halos: Changes in mineralogy and erosion resistance around fracture features on Earth, Mars, and across the Solar System
authors: Siebach, Kirsten Leigh [1], Seeger, Christina [2], Mondro, Claire A. [3], Hausrath, Elisabeth [4], O'Connell-Cooper, Catherine [5], Dietrich, William Eric [6], Schwenzer, Susanne [7], Gasda, Patrick [8], Thompson, Lucy Margaret [9], Scuderi, Louis [10]
affiliations: (1) Rice University, Houston, TX,
(2) Rice University, Houston, TX, USA
(3) Planetary Science Institute, Knoxville, TN, USA
(4) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(5) University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, NB, Canada
(6) University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
(7) The Open University, Milton Keynes, UK, United Kingdom
(8) Los Alamos National Lab, Los Alamos, NM, USA
(9) University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, NB, Canada
(10) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
The Mars Science Laboratory rover Curiosity explored the orbitally-described “boxwork unit” on Mt Sharp in Gale crater between May 2025 and March 2026 (mission Sols 4534-4844). This stratigraphic interval, ~14 km across and ~10s-100 meters thick, is distinguished by the presence of rectilinear intersecting erosion-resistant ridges ~5 meters across that create a network of polygons ~10-20 meters across with ~1-2 meter-deep hollows. Based on orbital observations, the ridges were interpreted as fractures and fracture-adjacent rocks that were strengthened relative to hollows by groundwater cementation, with relatively recent erosion highlighting the contrasting rock strengths. We will discuss how Curiosity’s observations inform our current interpretation of the formation of the boxwork unit, following a temporal sequence of steps:

(1) Deposition and Lithification: On the ground, the rocks that host the orbitally-mapped boxwork are dark-toned, friable, fine-grained, and planar laminated, making them sufficiently distinct from the surrounding light-toned, sandy, cross-stratified Chenapau member rocks to define a new Altadena member of the Mirador formation. The Altadena member is interpreted to have formed in lakes that were likely contemporaneous with surrounding sand sheets (Seeger et al, this meeting). Based on mineralogy in a hollow floor, the lakebeds include detrital igneous silicates cemented by siderite, with some amorphous materials.

(2) Fracturing: After deposition, lithification, and some degree of burial, rectilinear fractures formed within the Altadena member lake beds, with fractures occasionally crossing into adjacent sandy rocks (Mondro et al, this meeting).

(3) Ridge-Strengthening: After fracturing, while the Altadena member was still buried, groundwater fluids migrated through the fracture system. The fluids had the strongest influence on rock within ~2 meters of the fracture conduits, creating more massive textures with occasional large nodules, and diminishing influence further away from the fractures, with small nodules or flaky textures. The fluids did not dramatically change the chemical composition of the bedrock as measured by APXS and ChemCam, but did dissolve some of the detrital silicates and siderite cement to generate phyllosilicates and iron oxides.

(4) Erosion: The “boxwork” pattern is visible today due to eolian erosion that preferentially erodes more friable or poorly lithified materials. Turbulent eddies exploit heterogeneities to make incipient hollows that grow deeper and wider into 1-2 meter deep hollows. North-south winds create elongated hollows along Curiosity’s traverse.

title: Increased Rainfall Under Warm Surface Temperatures, Likely Linked to Southern Storm Trajectories, in the Southern Negev During the Middle Pleistocene
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Kuzmenko, Alyona [1], Quade, Jay [2], Wang, Zhennan [3], Kapp, Paul [4], Matmon, Ari [5]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Earth Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(5) Institute of Earth Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
abstract: Paleoclimatic interpretation of the stable isotope composition of CaCO 3 deposits in the alluvial channels of the hyper-arid southern Negev has been held back by uncertain formation temperatures. Here, we measured δ 13 C, δ 18 O, and clumped isotope composition (∆ 638 ) in laminated carbonate cementing Middle Pleistocene (>500 ka) alluvial terrace sediment in the Shehoret catchment. Clumped isotope derived cementation temperatures (23.6±4.9 °C to 31.0±5.5 °C) fall within the range of modern temperatures at the carbonate formation depths, and were used to calculate, for the first time in this hyper arid region, the precipitating water δ 18 O. Stable isotopic values in the CaCO 3 deposits ( δ 13 C = -3.4‰ to -2.1‰ and δ 18 O = -10.5‰ to -8.1‰) are the most depleted values observed in the southern Negev and suggest enhanced soil respiration relative to modern conditions. Calculated precipitating water δ 18 O ranges from -7.4‰ to -5.5‰, more depleted than modern southern Negev precipitation, pointing to a greater contribution of southern origin storm trajectories. Internal cement stratigraphy further records at least two cycles of moisture conditions during the alluvial phase. These results indicate decreased aridity in the Middle Pleistocene southern Negev, during which increased rainfall supported higher biogenic activity in alluvial channels at warm surface temperatures.

title: REE Patterns and XRD Analysis of Possible Bentonite Layers in the Jurassic Wanakah Formation in Western Colorado, USA
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Fenton, Cassandra R. [1], Chamberlain, Benjamin [2], Jones, Lawrence S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(2) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(3) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
abstract:
Thin layers (1-10 cm) of sandy mudrock with variable color, waxy luster, and a slick, greasy, and soapy texture when wetted are common in the Bilk Creek (middle) and Crooked Tree (upper) members of the Wanakah Formation at Escalante Canyon (ESC) and Rabbit Valley (RV) in western Colorado. These layers have been interpreted as bentonites. XRD analysis of these layers indicates the presence of smectite, illite, and in places kaolinite at Escalante Canyon, and illite and less commonly kaolinite at Rabbit Valley.

Analysis of rare earth element (REE) concentrations in ESC and RV bentonites might provide insight into volcanic ash chemistry and subsequent interactions with changing water chemistry during and after deposition. Chondrite-normalized REE analysis of whole-rock samples gave La/Sm and Gd/Lu values from 2.25 to 5.27 and 0.78 to 1.00, respectively, for ESC Bilk Creek samples and from 1.92 to 3.53 and 0.72 to 1.90, respectively, for ESC Crooked Tree samples. RV Crooked Tree samples have La/Sm and Gd/Lu values that range from 3.06-4.59 and 1.27-1.57, respectively. Generally, ESC and RV samples exhibit REE patterns that are typical of volcanic ash. However, one ESC Bilk Creek sample (ESCBCA-02) has La/Sm and Gd/Lu values of 1.73 and 0.41, respectively, and a pronounced positive Ce anomaly. Furthermore, three (possible) Bilk Creek samples (RVA-01, -1.5, and -02) at RV have La/Sm and Gd/Lu values, which range from 1.55 to 1.87 and 0.51 to 0.57, respectively, similar to those of ESCBCA-02. These three RV samples also exhibit a slight positive Ce anomaly. Overall, Negative Ce anomalies are more common than positive anomalies among ESC and RV samples.

ESCBCA-02 and RVA-01, -1.5, and -02 REE patterns exhibit HREE enrichment relative to LREE values. These REE patterns do not resemble typical volcanic ash REE signatures and may instead reflect the adsorption of elements in saline pore waters (marine or lacustrine) onto clays produced through alteration of volcanic ash within these layers. The observed positive and negative Ce anomalies in ESC and RV samples may also indicate shifts between oxidizing and reducing depositional conditions, respectively, in the Bilk Creek and Crooked Tree Members.

title: Divalent Metals Drive Changes in Fungal Manganese Oxide Formation and Metal Speciation
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Xu, Tingying [1], Ren, Wei [2], Staggs, Jacob [3]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(3) Environmental Sciences, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: Manganese (Mn) oxides are widespread in terrestrial and aquatic environments and strongly influence trace metal mobility and speciation. In nature, Mn oxide formation is largely driven by microbial Mn(II) oxidation, producing highly reactive phyllomanganates structurally similar to birnessite. Although many environments contain multiple coexisting metals, their effects on fungal Mn oxide formation, structure, and reactivity remain poorly understood. This study examined the influence of divalent metals on Mn oxidation by two fungal strains with distinct Mn(II) oxidation responses: Curvularia lunata TC1, isolated from wastewater at the Tar Creek Superfund site (Oklahoma), and Paraconiothyrium sporulosum AP3s5JAC2a, isolated from Mn-oxide-rich pebbles in Ashumet Pond (Massachusetts). Fungal Mn oxidation experiments were conducted in AY medium containing 200 µM MnCl₂ and varying concentrations of Zn, Pb, Co, and Cd. Dissolved metal concentrations were measured by ICP-OES to quantify Mn and other trace metal removal. Synchrotron-based micro-X-ray fluorescence (µXRF) mapping and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (Mn, Zn, and Co K-edge XANES/EXAFS) were used to characterize metal distributions, oxidation states, and Mn oxide phases. Our results show, at low Zn concentration, both strains removed Zn concurrently with Mn oxidation. However, high Zn concentration strongly inhibited Mn oxide formation by C. lunata without affecting fungal growth, whereas P. sporulosum exhibited only partial inhibition. µXRF mapping showed Zn co-localized with fungal Mn oxides in C. lunata , indicating that Zn removal was primarily associated with Mn oxide formation rather than fungal uptake. XANES/EXAFS analyses will further reveal that how divalent metals will affect average Mn oxidation state and Mn oxide phase composition. These findings demonstrate that coexisting metals can regulate fungal Mn oxidation and modify Mn oxide properties, with important implications for trace metal speciation and mobility in contaminated environments.

title: Geoheritage Values of Flakeable Stone: Lithic Resource Extraction, Mobility, and Territorial Landscapes on the Southern Plains
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Hurst, Stance [1], Speer, Charles [2], Johnson, Eileen [3]
affiliations: (1) Heritage and Museum Sciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Anthropology, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(3) Heritage and Museum Sciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA
abstract:
Flakeable stone — chert, jasper, agatized dolomite, and related siliceous toolstones — constitutes one of the most geographically diagnostic categories of geoheritage on the Southern Plains. Unlike most geological resources, these materials have been actively selected, transported, and transformed by prehistoric peoples over millennia. These actions have encoded, within archaeological assemblages, a direct behavioral record of how human groups perceived, valued, and moved across geologically diverse landscapes. Lithic raw material systems represent a distinctive form of geoheritage: one in which the scientific significance of geological formations is inseparable from the cultural significance of the stone they produced. The Southern Plains present an ideal context for this argument. The region's chert-bearing formations — including Edwards Group cherts, Alibates Agatized Dolomite, Tecovas Jasper, and Ogallala Formation gravels — are unevenly distributed across a broad landscape. This distribution creates structured patterns of scarcity and abundance that shaped prehistoric mobility, territorial organization, and exchange. Pilot research has established the Lubbock Lake Landmark–Idaho State University North American Lithic Source (NALS) Collection. pXRF geochemical data come from an initial sample of specimens collected from key source localities in Texas, Oklahoma, and adjacent regions and is supplemented by LA-ICP-QQQ-MS trace-element analyses of selected samples. These combined data demonstrate promising geochemical differentiation among visually similar sources, including complete separation of Tecovas Jasper from Alibates Agatized Dolomite and strong discrimination of West Texas from Central Texas Edwards Group cherts.

These results carry direct geoheritage implications. Geochemical fingerprinting of individual formations enables the reconstruction of prehistoric procurement territories, the identification of long-distance transport corridors, and the definition of the spatial boundaries of toolstone exchange networks. Quarry localities such as Alibates — a designated National Monument — represent geoheritage sites of exceptional cultural depth, where geological formation processes and human technological traditions intersect across thousands of years. The NALS Collection, housed at the Lubbock Lake Landmark and the Idaho Museum of Natural History, further advances geoheritage stewardship by creating an open-access, loanable reference archive that connects geological provenance to archaeological interpretation. Taken together, these results demonstrate that lithic sourcing research and geoheritage frameworks are mutually reinforcing, each enriching the other's capacity to communicate the deep human relationship with the geologic landscape of the Southern Plains.

title: The Lucy Flyby of (52246) Donaldjohanson: A Bilobed Asteroid With Tumbling Rotation
session_title: Big Science from Small Worlds
authors: Marchi, Simone [1], Levison, Harold [2], Noll, Keith [3], Simon, Amy [4], Spencer, John [5]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA
(4) NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA
(5) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
The Lucy spacecraft flew past the inner main belt asteroid (52246) Donaldjohanson (hereafter DJ) on 2025 April 20. This flyby included a sequence of observations using the spacecraft’s closed-loop terminal tracking system, which autonomously points the instruments at the target during the flyby. Lucy’s closest approach to DJ was 961.4 km at 17:51:16 Universal Time (UT), when the relative speed was 13.4 km s-1. DJ was only observed on the inbound leg of the flyby—observations were terminated 31 seconds before closest approach, to avoid pointing the instruments at the Sun.

DJ is a likely fragment of a larger Erigone parent asteroid that was destroyed in a collision about 155 Myr ago. Thanks to Lucy data, we find that DJ is composed of two heavily cratered lobes, connected by a smoother neck, with overall dimensions 8.8×4.4×3.1 km. The crater density is consistent with the Erigone family’s age, except for craters <0.4 km, which have been preferentially erased. DJ rotates slowly in a tumbling state, likely due to spin down by radiative forces. Surface spectra show iron-bearing phyllosilicates, indicating moderate aqueous evolution on the parent body.

title: The Case of the “Curious Vertebra”: New Insights into F.V. Hayden’s Mysterious 1869 Discovery of the First Allosaurus Fossil and Colorado’s First Dinosaur Fossil
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Deibert, Jack E. [1], Breithaupt, Brent H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Austin Peay State University, Clarksville, TN, USA
(2) Wyoming State Office, Bureau of Land Management, Cheyenne, Wyoming, USA
abstract:
During his 1869 survey of Colorado, F.V. Hayden obtained a “curious vertebra” fossil. The partial vertebra was identified by Joseph Leidy as belonging to the dinosaur Poicilopleuron but ultimately would be regarded as from the famous Jurassic theropod Allosaurus . This vertebra is the first discovery known of Allosaurus and was the first dinosaur fossil discovered in Colorado. Although attributed to Hayden, he got the fossil from someone else. Despite its importance, exactly where and how the specimen was collected still remains a mystery.

Leidy presented on the fossil at an 1870 Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia meeting. Published meeting minutes state Hayden “thinks” it was derived from a Cretaceous formation in Middle Park and locals called it “a petrified horse hoof.” However, when Hayden shipped the fossil during his survey, he asserted it was from South Park and the original meeting minutes also indicated it was from South Park. Thus, indicating the fossil was not found in Middle Park by locals and given to Hayden during his exploration there as long suspected by historians. More likely Hayden obtained the specimen from a mineral cabinet in a bank in Georgetown during a visit as the bank had recently acquired “a pair of petrified pony hoofs.” These “hoofs” were publicized in the local newspaper and were found by a prospector “somewhere west of the range.”

Without explanation, after the 1870 meeting, the stated location of the fossil changed from South Park to Middle Park in the final published minutes. We argue the location was changed because Hayden did not know specifically where the specimen was collected; and after it was determined to be a dinosaur, he ascribed a Cretaceous age to it. During his survey Hayden determined that South Park was principally composed of Triassic strata, whereas Middle Park had significantly more Cretaceous units, and thus, the fossil was more likely from Middle Park.

However, if indeed the Allosaurus vertebra was collected by a prospector, a probable location for the fossil would have been where active gold/silver mining and exploration, and outcrops of the Jurassic Morrison Formation were in proximity to each other. In this scenario, the fossil was not likely from Middle or South park, but from Morrison Formation outcrops near the Breckenridge-Silverthorne area.

abstract:
NASA’s Lucy mission will study the Jupiter Trojan asteroids, which are early Solar System relics yet to be explored by a spacecraft (Levison+2021). Prior to the first Trojan encounter, Lucy flew by two never-before-visited main-belt asteroids: asteroid (152830) Dinkinesh in 2023 (Levison+2024) and asteroid (52246) Donaldjohanson in 2025 (Marchi+2026).

Here we present the first geologic map of the observed portion of Donaldjohanson, which is ~8 km long and appears to be an elongated contact binary composed of two lobes (the bigger named Olduvai Lobus and the smaller Afar Lobus) joined by a narrower neck (named Windover Collum). We base our geologic map on images from the L’LORRI camera (instrument details in Weaver+2023) and the derived shape model (Mottola+2026). Due to Donaldjohanson’s highly irregular shape, we used the Small Body Mapping Tool to create our geologic map (Barnouin+2018). We define two geologic units: the cratered terrain dominates the two lobes while the smooth material is concentrated on Windover Collum. The contact between the two types of units sometimes takes the form of a lobate scarp, which we interpret are the flow fronts of areas where mass wasting occurred. We infer that mass wasting flowed from Olduvai Lobus to Windover Collum and from Windover Collum to Afar Lobus. We define linear features: chains of depressions and grooves, ridges and raised crater rims. Based on our observations that the chains of depressions and grooves have a preferred orientation and potential en echelon patterns, we interpret them as pit chains (see also Nichols-Fleming+2026). We map 166 discrete high-standing features, some of which can be grouped into clusters and others that are isolated. We interpret these features as boulders and use them to estimate the thickness of the outer layer of looser material to be between ~17 m to ~33 m deep. We map areas of brighter and darker material based on their appearance in low phase images, some of which correlate with identifiable morphological features (see also Spencer+2025). We also discuss how these geomorphological observations correlate with modeling of the spin period and surface acceleration of Donaldjohanson.

The Lucy mission is funded through the NASA Discovery program (contract NNM16AA08C) and part of this work is funded by ROSES grant 24-LUCYL4PSP-0031.

title: Facies-Specific Dual-Clumped Isotope Disequilibrium in Eocene Terrestrial Carbonates
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Loveall, Zachary C [1], Olsen, Ellen K [2], Ingalls, Miquela [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA

abstract: Terrestrial carbonates preserve valuable paleoclimate records in their isotopic compositions. However, the kinetics of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) cycling, including CO 2 degassing, absorption, and water mixing, can shift isotopic systems out of equilibrium. Because isotopic equilibration in the DIC–H 2 O system occurs over hours to days, rapidly forming carbonates may preserve transient states of disequilibrium. Dual-clumped isotopes (Δ 47 -Δ 48 ) provide a powerful framework for identifying disequilibrium effects during carbonate formation. To investigate these disequilibrium effects, we analyzed terrestrial carbonates from different facies and lake stages of the Green River Formation, which records lacustrine, wetland, and shoreline environments during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. Petrographic screening and mineralogical analyses were conducted on samples to assess diagenetic overprinting prior to isotopic analysis. We interpret δ 13 C, δ 18 O, and Δ 47 –Δ 48 isotope measurements to characterize departures from thermodynamic equilibrium. Our results indicate facies-specific variability in dual-clumped signatures, with placements on and below (-Δ 47 /+Δ 48 ; CO 2 degassing) the thermodynamic equilibrium line within a single lake system. Deviations from equilibrium were identified in biogenic and microbially-influenced samples, with preserved partial disequilibrium present in some diagenetically altered samples. While these results complicate the interpretation of clumped isotope paleotemperature records, they also provide new opportunities to reconstruct carbonate formation pathways and microbial influences in deep time.

title: The Importance of Implementing Explicit Teamwork Skills Pedagogy in Undergraduate Classrooms
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Yager, Stacy L [1], Kenderes, Elizabeth [2], Nyarko, Samuel Cornelius [3]

abstract: Teamwork is a vital part of not only higher education curriculum and pedagogical strategies but also in the workforce, with 56% for geologist positions and 50% for environmental scientist positions listing teamwork or working in teams as part of the job description. Yet, teamwork is commonly taught through implicit pedagogical approaches, which may not adequately equip students with the skills needed for effective collaboration. Currently, few studies have directly compared the development of teamwork skills through implicit versus explicit pedagogical approaches. This research investigates the effects of explicitly (EXP) and implicitly (IMP) taught teamwork process skills on students' teamwork efficacy. To achieve our goal, we used a quasi-experimental design to evaluate two pedagogical strategies in different semesters of a single course that seeks to achieve common teamwork skills learning outcomes. In addition to both the EXP (N=18) and IMP (N=18) groups reading articles on teamwork, the EXP group further engaged in an explicit, active, lecture-based workshop style instruction. We measured the efficacy of the two pedagogical strategies using self-reflections, pre-and post-survey, observations, and interviews. While EXP (M=3.98, SD=.45) and IMP (M=3.98, SD=.45) achieved the same mean scores in pre-test, the post-mean score from EXP was calculated as 4.31. Surveys from the IMP sample are in the process of being completed. Qualitative data suggests that students from the EXP group reported increased confidence in teamwork and have become more considerate with their team members. Students from the IMP group described lower awareness of how to function as a team member, and they could not articulate the skills involved in teamwork processes. Both EXP and IMP state that course instructor and course design influenced their teams. By comparing these two pedagogical approaches for workforce development, students’ confidence around these essential, non-technical skills are strengthened, fostering increased competences. Additionally, explicitly discussing these skills improves not only the “buy-in” within a course, but also the ability for students to communicate on resumes/interviews.

title: What Indigenous Disability Studies Can Teach Us About Creating Inclusive Programs in Geoscience Education
session_title: Impactful Indigenous Geoscience: STEM, data science, and education
authors: Marshall, Anita M. Stone [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
abstract:
Indigenous students and scholars are underrepresented in all STEM fields, with the underrepresentation in the geosciences especially acute. There are numerous compounding factors that lead to the lack of Indigenous representation in the geosciences – one of those factors being the disconnect from - and devaluing of - Indigenous ways of understanding the natural world. People with disabilities make up more than 30% of the indigenous population face the additional challenge of moving between cultural settings with dramatically different views of human difference when moving into academic spaces. The majority of educational spaces are squarely rooted in the medical view of disability as a deficit or even an excluding characteristic and this can be especially prevalent in experiential learning settings such as field work. In contrast, many Indigenous languages don’t have a word or concept to akin to “disability”, because difference is understood to simply be part of the human condition, with an understood value and natural place in the social fabric of a community. For these students, the disconnect from their cultural community carries with an additional negative categorization and othering that is rarely considered in efforts to recruit and retain Indigenous students in academic spaces.

An emerging field within Indigenous scholarship is Indigenous Disability studies. Drawing from traditional ways of understanding human difference, this body of literature seeks to reconceptualize how disability is understood and engaged with. In the geosciences, where residential experiential learning creates countless unique social microcosms, what lessons can we learn from Indigenous Disability studies that we can apply our efforts to broaden participation in the geosciences? In this talk, we will explore this question and consider the possibilities for applying these concepts to building more inclusive educational spaces for everyone.

abstract:
To best predict the future contributions of polar ice-sheet retreat to sea-level rise, we require a rigorous understanding of the timing, rates, and mechanisms of past ice retreat. Over the last few decades, the grounding zones of ice streams draining the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) into the Amundsen Sea Embayment (ASE) have rapidly retreated. To contextualize the observed ice-sheet loss, we reconstruct the retreat histories of major ASE paleo-ice stream systems since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM; ~19-23 calibrated kyr before present), with specific focus on the Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers—that together drain one third of the WAIS.

To revise existing retreat trajectories, we compiled more than 400 published and new radiocarbon ( 14 C) dates obtained from calcareous microfossils and organic matter (OM) in marine sediment cores recovered from the ASE, spanning the outer to inner shelf. A well-known dilemma when calibrating 14 C-dates from Antarctic sediments is the choice of the marine reservoir effect, due to the lack of Antarctic calcareous remains from the 20 th Century constraining the regional “pre-atom bomb” reservoir effect in these basins. We address this by extracting minimum deglacial 14 C-dates from the compilation and correcting these using pre-bomb and post-bomb reservoir effects before the calibration. Furthermore, we apply an additional correction to the OM-derived 14 C dates to compensate for the reworked, fossil OM mixed with young in situ OM at the time of deposition. We compare pre-bomb and post-bomb reservoirs and determine a systematic framework for deglacial trajectories. To identify chronological outliers, we consider the geomorphological setting of each core together with the sedimentological context of the sampled interval that provides the minimum deglacial age.

Our results show that while different correction methods can introduce a variability of up to 500 years, most of the calibrated 14 C-ages fall within statistical error (±2σ). By integrating our newly obtained 14 C-dates with previously published retreat trajectories, we observe various retreat styles across the ASE. Our extended dataset improves the temporal resolution of the Holocene retreat of Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers, yet remains in agreement with the 5 kyr time slices of post-LGM retreat previously published by the RAISED consortium, suggesting that rapid retreat rates in recent decades are unprecedented since the LGM.

title: Eolian Interdune Surfaces vs. Deposits and Pedogenesis: Criteria to Distinguish Hydroclimate and Life in the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone Erg
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Parrish, Judith Totman [1], Hasiotis, Stephen T. [2], Chan, Marjorie A. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Idaho, Viola, ID,
(2) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,
abstract:
Interdunes contain most of the evidence for life and hydroclimatic conditions in ancient sand sea deserts, but they have been confusingly addressed in the literature. The term ‘interdune’ has been used as (1) the space between dunes and the first-order bounding surface formed by the propagation of that surface as the dunes migrated ( sensu Brookfield 1977 and Kocurek 1981, 1991) and (2) deposits that accumulated between the dunes under certain circumstances. The bounding surface resulting from the propagation of the space between dunes has sometimes been referred to as a ‘dry interdune’, possibly because steadily marching dunes do not leave much time for deposits to accumulate in the space between dunes, particularly when the climate is dry. Thus, under these migrating conditions and with good sand supply, the interdune migration surface has no alteration by pedogenesis.

Interdune deposits include windblown (eolian), water-lain (lotic; fluvial), standing-water (lentic; pond), or a combination (windblown, water-lain, and/or standing-water or playa) of deposits. Pedogenesis can modify these deposits, as well as the adjacent and underlying dune sands. The types of interdune deposits and the duration of pedogenesis and preservation potential are related to eolian depositional processes and accommodation, as well as hydroclimate.

In the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone of southern Utah, well-developed paleosols occur along complex surfaces. Well-developed simple paleosols are sometimes observed on the dune sand. The adjacent interdune deposits, bounded by the same complex surface, generally have well-developed cumulative or composite paleosols. Together, these indicate stabilization of the dune field. Complex bounding surfaces and the associated paleosols have implications for the role of water and understanding of pedogenesis, life, and hydroclimate in ancient deserts. Individual bounding surfaces may hold records of ecosystems that required significant time to develop. We recommend (1) dropping the term ‘interdune’ to describe first-order bounding surfaces and use the descriptive term ‘simple surface’ ( sensu Hasiotis et al. 2021) to delineate the surface produced by dune migration across the erg landscape, and (2) restrict the term ‘interdune’ to deposits between dunes. These important records of complex surfaces and paleosols have valuable implications for reconstructing climate conditions in ancient dune fields.

title: A New Compilation of Extreme Hydroclimate Events in Eastern North America
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Saslaw, Mae [1], Fastovich, David [2], Degroot, Dagomar [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Commons, Georgetown University, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Department of Geography, University of Georgia,
(3) Department of History, Georgetown University,
abstract: Droughts, floods, and major storms have significant impacts on ecosystems and societies, but they can be difficult to identify and characterize in terrestrial proxy records. Today, hydroclimate extremes are a growing concern along the Atlantic seaboard— forward modeling projects an increase in frequency and severity of storms, and understanding the spatiotemporal characteristics of these extremes is hampered by a short instrumental record and model uncertainties. This project synthesizes archives from eastern North America that record hydroclimate variability at annual, decadal, and multi-decadal scales to identify extreme events in the Common Era. We examine the spatiotemporal characteristics of extreme events using empirical orthogonal functions and find distinct modes of variability across the region. Our analysis is coupled with perspectives from environmental history and archaeology; using historical documents and archaeological evidence of social responses to extreme events, we consider the effects on a human scale. A goal of this project is to establish contemporaneity between extreme events in paleoclimate records and changes in technology, settlement patterns, and language, which historians, archaeologists, anthropologists, and human geographers can use to explore correlation and causality. For example, historians have argued that heavy winter precipitation in New England at the end of the 17th century influenced relations between the Wabanaki and the English, but firsthand accounts of extreme events are limited to the past few centuries. Our approach has the potential to illuminate environmental factors contributing to cultural change when written and oral histories are unreliable or not available. This compilation is an important contribution because it is among the first data syntheses to analyze extreme events using the paleoclimate record within the context of environmental history.

abstract: Fossil sites at Nakwai (~21 to >24 Ma) in the southwestern Turkana Basin in northern Kenya are an important location for the study of the continental-scale Afro-Arabian Oligocene-Miocene faunal transition. Sedimentary sequences at Nakwai include paleosols, mudstones, and sandstones, and fossils have been found in many strata. We use stable isotope measurements of paleosol carbonate nodules and bulk paleosol geochemistry to reconstruct temperature, annual precipitation, and vegetation type. In order to account for incorporation of diagenetic calcite that produces high (> 50 °C) clumped isotope temperatures (T(Δ 47 )), we determine the fractions of primary micritic calcite and secondary, more crystalline calcite in each measured sub-sample using pixel classification, then apply an inverted, two-end-member linear mixing equation to calculate primary (paleoenvironmental) and secondary (diagenetic) end-member stable isotope ratios. This method produces reliable results for most of the samples collected and illustrates the need for careful pairing of carbonate petrography with isotope data, particularly when they are very old and are known to have been exposed to elevated temperatures due to volcanism and rift basin burial. Elevated carbonate δ 13 C values from the Turkana Basin have been interpreted as evidence for early emergence of C 4 plants, however, we show that samples for which δ 13 C > -5‰ VPDB are associated with high T(Δ 47 ) and δ 18 O values, suggesting that some pedogenic carbonate δ 13 C values at Nakwai are influenced by secondary overprinting. End-member δ 13 C range -9.4 – -7.9‰ VPDB (indicating wooded biomes) for samples with T(Δ 47 ) consistent with terrestrial, tropical environments, and the median primary T(Δ 47 ) = 23 °C. Bulk paleosol samples were analyzed for abundance of ten elemental oxides, which were then input as variables for a random forest model of mean annual precipitation (RF-MAP 2.0). Results for seven profiles indicate that they formed under aridic soil moisture regimes, which is consistent with reconstructed carbonate δ 18 O ~ -3‰ VPDB. Today, mean annual air temperature in Turkana is approximately 30 °C, MAP ranges 200–300 mm, and xeric grassland and shrubland cover the terrain. Our data show that Nakwai in the Early Miocene was cooler and > 50% wetter than today, and the vegetation was characterized by woodland/bushland/shrubland.

authors: Magi, Fredrick Fiyeboju [1], Petcovic, Heather L. [2], Yildirim, Aylin [3], Honer, Justin A [4], Teal, Alexander [5]
affiliations: (1) Mallinson Institute for Science Education (MISE), Western Michigan University Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, Kalamazoo, MI,

abstract:
Students in introductory geoscience courses often struggle to translate 2D topographic maps into coherent 3D mental models of terrain. In large-enrollment introductory courses, limited access to authentic field experiences and continued reliance on 2D maps and lecture-based instruction may hinder spatial reasoning, reduce engagement, and limit opportunities to build scientific literacy among non-majors. In this mixed-method study, we examined how a scaffolded, immersive virtual reality (IVR) lab exercise supported conceptual understanding of topographic map interpretation and triggered situational interest in geosciences among non-major students enrolled in two introductory geoscience courses.

In one 1.5-hour course laboratory session, students progressed through a layered instructional sequence consisting of an introductory presentation, 2D map and physical 3D model matching activity, and immersive navigation of the Mt. Etna 1809 crater using the open-source GEAVR platform through head-mounted displays. In the VR, students used placement, line, and topographic profile tools to mark locations, measure 2D/3D distances, and predict, then compare, slope profiles.

Data included pre- and post-VR usability surveys measuring students’ dispositions toward IVR in learning, pre- and post-Adapted Topographic Map Assessment (ATMA) measuring students' ability to interpret contour lines, elevation, slope, inter-visibility, and stream flow direction, and semi-structured student interviews on students' affective experience of learning topographic maps.

The ATMA demonstrated acceptable internal consistency, with a pretest KR-20 (Cronbach's α) of .717. Preliminary results from 38 students across three course sections (Fall 2025 and Spring 2026) show that students performed comparably at pretest and posttest, with p-values, p = .600 and p = .627, respectively, in the Kruskal-Wallis test, supporting a pooled sample. Students' whole-class ATMA performance improved from 63% to 69%, with the largest gains on items requiring students to explain their reasoning. Students scored lower on a few line-of-sight items, a pattern being examined through the qualitative data. Students also rated the VR experience positively on the usability survey, with effectiveness (Mean = 3.91/5) and interest/enjoyment (Mean = 4.07/5) among the highest-rated subscales.

This study aims to provide empirically grounded evidence on the use of IVR as a 3D visualization tool for teaching topographic maps to non-geoscience majors as well as geoscience majors, and to offer instructional design insights for geoscience instructors on integrating immersive virtual field experiences into their classrooms.

title: Picking Apart the Picuris Orogeny: Campaign-Style Petrochronology Reveals a Heterogeneous and Diachronous Mesoproterozoic Orogen
session_title: One orogeny is not like the other: changes in orogenic styles through the Proterozoic
authors: Hillenbrand, Ian [1], Williams, Michael L. [2], Karlstrom, Karl E. [3], Gilmer, Amy K. [4], Jercinovic, Michael J [5]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA

abstract:
Tectonic processes during the Mesoproterozoic are poorly understood, with proposed models ranging from nonuniformitarian single-lid regimes to high-temperature, thin-crust styles to plate tectonic processes similar to today. The ca. 1470–1350 Ma Picuris orogeny is a regionally significant Mesoproterozoic orogenic system across southwestern Laurentia. Does the broad spatial and temporal range of the Picuris orogeny represent a single protracted event, or a long-lived system with spatial and temporal variability? We conducted a campaign-style monazite–xenotime petrochronology study to constrain high-resolution pressure–temperature–time–deformation paths from more than 20 gneiss and quartzite samples across Colorado and New Mexico.

Our results reveal resolvable regional variations in tectono-metamorphic style. Samples from central and northern Colorado record isobaric P-T paths and short (1–5 Myr) metamorphic peaks at ca. 1460–1440 Ma. Peak temperatures were synchronous with ferroan granitic magmatism and spatially associated with plutons. In contrast, southern Colorado and northern New Mexico samples record peak metamorphic conditions at ca. 1420–1400 Ma, more protracted durations of garnet stability (≥10 Myr), and clockwise P–T paths.

These P–T–t–D data are consistent with paleo-crustal thickness estimates from chemical mohometry, indicating ~10 km of thickening in Colorado, dominated by magmatic underplating, versus ~20 km of thickening in northern New Mexico. We suggest that shortening was localized in areas of previously thinner crust, such as northern New Mexico. This area may have acted as an intraplate "crumple zone,” against the previously thicker, colder, and rheologically stronger Colorado buttress. Basaltic underplating and advective heat from ferroan granitoids led to elevated mid-crustal temperatures, reduced crustal strength and development of an orogenic plateau. These findings refine suggest the Picuris orogeny was a long-lived, spatially heterogeneous mountain building system. Present evidence suggests that the Picuris orogenic plateau developed inboard of the active plate margin through the interaction of far-field contraction, inherited lithospheric heterogeneities, mafic underplating, and syntectonic ferroan granitic magmatism, similar to processes observed in more recent collisional orogens.

abstract: Hydrogen (H 2 ) is an energy resource with the potential to supplement or replace hydrocarbons in a variety of applications. H 2 is attractive as an alternative fuel because it can utilize existing infrastructure (e.g., pipelines) for transport and does not produce carbon dioxide when burned. One area limiting the adoption of H 2 as a fuel is the ability to store sufficient volumes of H 2 gas in proximity to power plants. While depleted petroleum reservoirs have been proposed for H 2 storage, there are knowledge gaps regarding reservoir capacity and the suitability of geologic seals for containing injected gas. With regard to reservoir storage capacity, densification effects (i.e., internal pressure exceeding external pressure) have been observed for H 2 in small pores within polyfurfuryl alcohol-derived activated carbon used in fuel cells. However, the occurrence of such phenomena has not been demonstrated for H 2 in porous geologic materials. To evaluate the extent to which H 2 densification occurs in unconventional petroleum reservoir mesopores (pores with diameters 50 to 2 nm) and micropores (pores with diameters <2 nm), we applied total neutron scattering to measure D 2 (deuterated isotope of H 2 ) behavior in two samples from the Marcellus Shale at reservoir-relevant temperature (90ºC) and pressures (up to 30 MPa). The samples represent the clay-rich facies of the Marcellus Shale, one at high thermal maturity (R o ~2.2%) and one at a lower maturity (R o ~1%). Our data show that D 2 can readily access pores within both samples, including clay interlayers for the lower thermal maturity sample. Additionally, there appears to be minor densification of D 2 in both samples at high (>25 MPa) pressures, although not to the density levels observed previously for carbon-based fuel cell materials. Furthermore, organic matter in both samples swelled following exposure to D 2 , and these changes persisted following removal of D 2 pressure. This swelling was markedly enhanced for the low thermal maturity sample and most likely altered the sample’s organic matter pore architecture. These neutron-scattering data provide rare direct experimental evidence of hydrogen behavior under confinement in geologic meso- and micropores and contribute to an understanding of the capacity of depleted shale petroleum reservoirs for storing injected hydrogen resources.

title: Carbon Sequestration Dynamics in Beaver and Beaver Dam Analog Wetlands
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Dicianna, Kelsey [1], Havranek, Rachel [2], McKeon, Quinn [3]
affiliations: (1) College of Science, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(2) College of Science, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(3) College of Science, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
abstract:
The North American beaver (Castor canadensis) is a keystone species that provides many ecosystem services through ecosystem engineering. In particular, dam construction significantly slows surface water, promotes the connection between channel and floodplain, and expands wetlands. Similarly, beaver dam analogs (BDAs) mimic the function of beaver dams and provide many of the same ecosystem services. In both beaver- and BDA- influenced watersheds, the slowing of water leads to enhanced sedimentation in the riparian zone and promotes the accumulation of organic carbon. Previous work has demonstrated that the amount of organic carbon stored in beaver ponds can be highly variable, and very little work has been done to quantify organic carbon accumulation in BDA riparian zones. The natural variability of carbon storage makes predicting the impacts of dam construction or removal on carbon stocks challenging.

In this project, we investigate what sediment characteristics, such as grain size and mineralogy, are associated with greater organic carbon accumulation. We hypothesize that there will be greater organic carbon sequestration associated with a greater proportion of charged clay particles. We compare four beaver-impacted and two BDA environments in northern Utah and Colorado. Of these sites, two are underlain by granite, three are underlain by sandstone-conglomerate, and one is underlain by the glacial till of sandstones. As expected, in both beaver- and BDA- environments, the greatest accumulation of clay and silt particles occurs adjacent to the channel in the floodplain. Initial x-ray diffraction results demonstrate sediments are dominated by quartz and feldspars, and that the clay component is dominantly composed of 2:1 clays. The highest levels of organic carbon occur adjacent to the main channel and ponds. This indicates that for conservation efforts and management projects that aim to promote carbon storage, an emphasis on lateral landscape and floodplains protection is critical.

abstract: Epithermal deposits are a major source of gold, currently supplying ~10% of the global production of this precious metal. In many epithermal deposits, ores occur as high-grade veins, with the ore zones having a vertical extent of up to several hundred meters. Ore minerals in high-grade veins are commonly located in distinct bands that are separated by barren bands of gangue minerals. The ore minerals can form delicate dendrites that resemble fractal trees, consisting of a trunk and branches that recursively split into smaller branches, each scaled down and rotated relative to the previous segment. The ore minerals are hosted by quartz formed through maturation of a noncrystalline silica precursor that originally was comprised of microspheres. Textural relationships suggest that the microspherical silica provided the structural framework for the delicate ore mineral aggregates to grow. Subsequent to initial deposition, the morphology of the ore mineral dendrites and their textural relationships with the silica host were modified. In many deposits, recrystallization of the ore minerals resulted in textural reequilibration through grain coarsening and grain boundary migration. In addition, exsolution of initially homogeneous ore minerals may have occurred, as evidenced by the presence of symplectic intergrowth between ore minerals. In most epithermal deposits, the thermodynamically unstable noncrystalline silica has completely converted to quartz. Common quartz textures formed through silica maturation include fine-grained mosaic quartz characterized by interpenetrating grain boundaries, polygonal quartz, flamboyant quartz characterized by radiating arrays of abundant inclusions arranged into radial patterns, feathery quartz showing splintery domains in cross-polarized light, and large prismatic quartz grains hosting pseudoprimary inclusions defining recrystallization fronts. The microtextural characteristics suggest that deposition of noncrystalline silica along the vein walls and growth of the ore mineral dendrites within the silica occurred rapidly at far-from-equilibrium conditions, requiring supersaturation of solutes in the hydrothermal liquid. It is proposed that these conditions were reached during short-lived events of violent flash vaporization.

title: Regional assessment of susceptibility to debris-flow inundation across southern Appalachia, North Carolina, USA

authors: Mirus, Benjamin B. [1], Leb, Isaac Henry [2], Korte, David [3], Reid, Mark E. [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Golden, CO, USA

abstract: Models of landslide and debris flow susceptibility used at regional scales emphasize initiation potential, but they generally do not consider mobility or runout behavior. Such models correctly predicted the initiation locations of the many thousands of landslides triggered during Hurricane Helene in 2024, but inundation from the most damaging and deadly debris flows was not represented. To address this gap, we present a method for estimating susceptibility to debris-flow inundation over regional extents. We employ a simple Monte-Carlo application of the new U.S. Geological Survey software, Grfin Tools, which features low computational expense and minimal input data. In this Monte-Carlo approach, we used a subset of the observed debris flows from Hurricane Helene within three HUC-12 watersheds (~320 km 2 ) to calibrate the range of empirical parameters for the Grifin Tools runout model. We validate the parameter range with quantitative model performance evaluation for two contrasting debris-flow complexes that drain into Hickory Nut Gorge, North Carolina. One highly mobile complex in Fairview was captured only by the more extreme parameter values controlling debris flow growth, whereas the less mobile one in Chimney Rock, is captured by even the lower growth parameterizations. We use the same parameter range and modeling approach to extrapolate susceptibility to debris-flow inundation across all 16 HUC-12 watersheds over western North Carolina (>25,000 km 2 ), which we evaluate using both post-Helene and historical mapping of flow-type landslides. Preliminary results provide an improvement in capturing runout extent relative to previously available models in southern Appalachia. Based on these results, we demonstrate the feasibility of our approach for regional-scale application of Grfin Tools, which warrants further testing of the Monte-Carlo approach across other debris-flow prone settings.
