title: Controls on Exfoliation Fracture Geometry in Granitic Domes, Yosemite National Park, USA: New Constraints on Structural Inheritance and Near-Surface Stress Drivers
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Reynolds, Aislin N. [1], Collins, Brian D. [2], Stock, Greg M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Rock Structure and Mechanics, Czech Academy of Sciences, Prague, Czech Republic
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA, USA
(3) Yosemite National Park, Yosemite National Park, CA, USA
abstract:
Exfoliation fractures are a defining structural feature of Yosemite’s granitic domes, yet the combined influence of lithology, inherited joint fabrics, surface curvature, and near-surface stresses in controlling fracture geometry within a broader tectonic and geomorphic stress regime remains incompletely understood. Mechanical models predict that convex dome surfaces amplify tensile stresses, whereas pre-existing damage may localize or limit fracture propagation. Large diurnal and seasonal temperature fluctuations have also been implicated in cyclic subcritical fracture growth and linked to rockfall activity. This study evaluates whether observed exfoliation geometries are consistent with these proposed stress modifiers using systematic field methods. We conducted measurements of exfoliation sheet thickness, spacing, and orientation across multiple domes spanning glaciated and non-glaciated settings and distinct granitic lithologies in Yosemite National Park, California. Measurements were integrated with GPS transects and lidar-derived topography to assess dome-scale spatial variability and scaling relationships.

Preliminary analyses indicate that sheet thickness and spacing vary among domes and lithologic units, with glaciated domes commonly exhibiting broader thickness distributions. Length-thickness scaling relationships show substantial scatter, with frequent termination of exfoliation sheets against pre-existing vertical joint sets suggesting such inherited structural fabrics locally influence lateral fracture persistence. Spatial variations in sheet geometry are evaluated relative to dome-scale curvature and predictions from topographic stress models. Together, these data support a framework in which exfoliation geometry reflects the combined influence of lithologic properties, inherited structures, curvature-modified stresses, unloading and tectonic stresses, and modern thermal forcing, with implications for progressive damage accumulation, landscape evolution, and rockfall hazards in granitic terrains.

title: Jay Quade and Testing Scientific Theories
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Cerling, Thure E. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract: “It is easy to obtain confirmations, or verifications, for nearly every theory — if we look for confirmations” wrote Karl Popper in 1963. Jay Quade was a field geologist who tested geochemical theory with field evidence; he was also a geochemist who tested field observations with precise and demanding geochemical measurements. Geological, geochemical, and mathematical models make predictions; a true test of these models is to examine the “risky” predictions with observations or experiments that could plausibly fail. Even then the model is not proven, but the continued testing of a surviving model earns the model an increasingly higher degree of confidence in its validity. Jay’s work cut both ways – theories required careful field observations and measurements; excellent measurements required revisions of models and field observations to test revised models. In this talk I will discuss how Jay tested models related to using soil carbonates as indicators of past chemical weathering, climate, diagenesis, ecology, elevation, and temperature.

authors: Acosta, Marisa D. [1], Nayda, Tanya [2], Hofmann, Florian [3], Talbot, Indie H. [4], Larimer, David [5], Van Treek, Christopher [6]
affiliations: (1) Geophysical Institute & Dept. of Geosciences, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, Alaska, USA

abstract:
Alaska comprises accreted terranes, each with a unique tectonic history. The ore deposits in any given terrane may have formed before, during, or after it was accreted. Overprinting episodes of metamorphism, magmatism, and related hydrothermal activity are common. Long-lived structures can be repeatedly reactivated, focusing different generations of fluids so that weakly mineralized zones can be upgraded into rich ore bodies over time. Deciphering these deposits requires integrating lithospheric-to-microscopic structural observations with robust petrography, geochemistry, and geochronology.

The Pogo Au deposit is hosted in amphibolite-facies para- and orthogneiss of the parautochthonous Lake George assemblage, structurally beneath the allochthonous Yukon-Tanana terrane. Regional 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates record Early Cretaceous metamorphic cooling ages. Petrographic and field observations at Pogo record an early phase of syndeformational gold mineralization in shear quartz veins. Rapid mid-Cretaceous extension caused uplift and exhumation, with attendant magma formation, ascent, and emplacement resulting in suites of locally derived migmatites and externally derived intrusions of a broadly intermediate composition (52 – 69 wt.% SiO 2 ). These melts locally reworked earlier wall rock Au mineralization and some, but not all, of the veins as indicated by melt infiltration textures in contact metamorphic zones adjacent to intrusions, and likely coexisted with immiscible, Bi-rich polymetallic melts. As these melts crystallized, hydrothermal fluids were variably focused along existing structures and lithologic contacts, imposing a final hydrothermal alteration event on the system.

Like Pogo, the Manh Choh Cu-Au skarn deposit is hosted in the Lake George assemblage, but the similarities largely end there. Manh Choh differs from typical magmatic-hydrothermal skarn deposits in that it is not a massive metasomatized marble but rather lenses of carbonate-rich domains in a mixed pelitic schist and calc-schist unit. At Manh Choh, Au-rich mineralization post-dates base metal massive sulfide mineralization, which is variably overprinted by the latter. The pre-existing fabrics and folds formed a highly anisotropic host rock that forced mineralizing fluids to exploit complex structural/lithological pathways rather than forming a single massive body. The highly variable skarn geometry highlights a core challenge of Alaskan metallogeny: deciphering how inherited crustal architecture and complexly overprinting metamorphic/magmatic/hydrothermal histories influence the genesis, geometry, and grade of ore systems.

title: Early fossil eukaryotes were benthic aerobes
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age
authors: Riedman, Leigh Anne [1], Lechte, Maxwell [2], Porter, Susannah [3], Halverson, Galen [4], Whelan, Margaret [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Earth Research Institute, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA

abstract: All complex life on Earth is descended from a single-celled eukaryotic ancestor that lived more than a billion years ago. Although the timing and environmental context of eukaryogenesis, the prolonged origin and evolution of the eukaryotic cell, are poorly constrained, the geological record offers considerable insight. Through integrated paleontological, sedimentological, and geochemical analyses we reconstruct the habitats of the oldest known (ca. 1.75–1.4 billion-year-old; Ga) fossil eukaryotes. These data show that although eukaryote microfossils are found in samples deposited in a range of marine environments from coastal to offshore, they are almost entirely restricted to settings with oxygenated bottom waters. This distribution suggests that these organisms were aerobic and, given their size and morphological complexity, likely possessed mitochondria by this time. Further, the absence of eukaryotes from otherwise fossiliferous samples that record bottom water anoxia suggests a benthic habit, since planktonic eukaryotes would be expected to have been deposited in those settings. These data in context of recent biomarker and diversity studies suggest that eukaryotes were largely restricted to oxic, benthic habitats for much of the Proterozoic and expanded into planktonic habitats later, likely during the Neoproterozoic Era (ca. 1–0.54 Ga). This late ecological expansion could help reconcile the “sterane gap”, the billion-year mismatch between the appearance of eukaryotic body fossils and molecular biomarkers, and may also help explain the sharp increase in eukaryote diversity apparent in the Neoproterozoic Era.

title: North America’s Table Top: Deciphering Eolian Input to the Southern High Plains with Grain-Size End-Member Analysis

authors: Sweet, Dustin E. [1], Stine, Jonathan M.G. [2], Feinberg, Joshua M [3]
affiliations: (1) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
(2) Institute for Rock Magnetism, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

abstract:
The Southern High Plains (SHP) average ~1000 m in elevation standing above surrounding topography as a broad, southeast-dipping plateau. Despite lacking basin-forming conditions or fluvial inputs, the SHP functions as a sediment sink because the Quaternary Blackwater Draw Formation (BDF) accumulated across its surface. Although the BDF is widely interpreted as an eolian deposit, grain-size distributions are multi-modal and very poorly sorted (2–3 σ₁) compared to typical unimodal eolian sand and silt deposits (<2 σ₁), suggesting contributions from several inputs.

To assess these inputs, we applied end-member modeling to two stratigraphic sections, the southern Type Section and the northern Bushland Core, with dense (5-10 cm) sampling intervals. Results indicate that 3 to 5 end members explain 76–83% of the variance, with additional end members providing little improvement. The coarsest end members (~3.5 ϕ) contribute most in the lower part of the BDF. Coarse silt-sized populations explain the largest proportion of variance (35–40%) and dominates the upper part of the BDF, particularly in the Bushland Core. A fine silt- to clay-sized end member ranges from 0–80% abundance occurring as spikes stratigraphically.

We interpret the sand fraction as locally derived from reworking of BDF deposits and/or underlying Ogallala Formation. The coarse silt population is inconsistent with coeval eolian sand transport and thus is attributed to periods when suspended eolian dust accumulated on the SHP. The clay-rich component likely reflects episodic pedogenesis, which also homogenized the unit through illuviation into the observed grain-size distributions. Preliminary magnetic polarity data from the Bushland Core suggests that in addition to the Brunhes-Matuyama Chron boundary the Jaramillo, Cobb Mountain, and Olduvai Subchrons may be present, which would extend duration of deposition beyond the oldest previous age control (Guaje Ash; ~1.4 Ma) and through most of the Quaternary. Variations in the coarse silt component across the Mid-Pleistocene Transition further suggest a possible linkage to North American loess deposition where more suspended silt deposition occurs in the syn- and post Mid-Pleistocene Transition part of the stratigraphy.

abstract: Effective conservation requires a thorough understanding of how non-native species impact ecosystem structure and functioning. However, the long-term effects of invasive species remain difficult to quantify as neontological baseline data before invasions are rare. Ancient invasions preserved in the fossil record provide a means to evaluate the impacts of biological invasions on evolutionary time scales and document changes through time from the arrival of invaders to their integration into the community. The well-defined stratigraphy of the Cincinnati Arch in Ohio, Indiana, and Kentucky (USA) preserves the Richmondian Invasion during the Late Ordovician (Katian), where a large influx of invasive species in the Cincinnati Basin is believed to have resulted in significant changes to ecosystem structure. Here, we use fossil food web reconstructions for six 3 rd order stratigraphic sequences (C2 through C7) to directly assess potential changes in ecosystem structure and functioning during the Richmondian Invasion over approximately seven million years. Species level food webs (SLNs) for each of the six sequences were stochastically modeled (500 SLNs per sequence) to evaluate network trophic position (NTP), maximum chain length (MCL), and connectance. Structural changes to food web dynamics demonstrate altered relationships between top predators and basal-level producers, as well as changes to the flow of energy through the ecosystem. A Generalized Linear Model showed that mean guild NTP, mean guild MCL, and mean connectance significantly differed between all pairwise comparisons of the six sequences. Mean NTP and MCL decreased in post-invasion communities while connectance increased, likely from the arrival of a greater number of generalist and omnivorous species, resulting in an increase in the number of interactions. These changes to food web structure during the time of the Richmondian Invasion demonstrate a significant shortening of trophic chains and an increase in ecological interactions. Integrating non-native species into shallow marine communities can have lasting impacts, and a better understanding of how food web structure changes over the long-term will better inform the conservation of modern marine ecosystems.

abstract: In marine sediments, spatial variations in oxygen create variations in the distribution of redox-sensitive ions, including many transition metals and Rare Earth Elements and Yttrium (REE-Y). These variations can be significant over fine (submillimeter) spatial scales and may provide insight into the conditions for sedimentary processes such as phosphate mineralization (phosphogenesis). However, redox conditions continue to evolve after deposition, altering the trace element chemistries of phosphatic sediments and cements. Ca-phosphate minerals precipitating from fluids readily incorporate redox-sensitive metals and REE-Y as they form, but it is unclear to what extent primary and earliest diagenetic processes control the distribution and textural associations of those elements compared to later diagenetic processes. Here we report detailed petrography and REE-Y compositions of early Cambrian fossiliferous phosphorites from the Bayangol and Salaagol formations of southwestern Mongolia. Petrographic observations strongly indicate organic matter-associated authigenic and early diagenetic phosphogenesis within fossil skeletons and restricted pore spaces rather than wholesale diagenetic replacement of a non-phosphatic primary phase. Spatial distributions of apatite and carbonate cements are highly variable across and within bioclasts, suggesting unique parageneses and non-uniform phosphatization. REE-Y compositions of texturally diverse apatite cements were measured using laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, revealing broad preservation of depositional and early diagenetic signals. La N /Yb N ratios in most samples are above seawater values, indicating adsorption as the primary mechanism of diagenetic REE-Y uptake, and La N /Sm N ratios are consistently greater than values associated with late diagenetic uptake. Strong middle REE (MREE) enrichment can therefore be explained by uptake from MREE-enriched porewaters during early diagenesis rather than preferential substitution of MREEs into apatite during recrystallization. While MREE enrichment in porewaters results from dissolution of Fe-Mn oxyhydroxides in reducing conditions, true negative Ce anomalies in almost all samples suggest prolonged interaction with seawater, suggesting phosphogenesis occurred near the sediment water interface and, likely, across a relatively shallow redoxcline. Y/Ho values decrease with increasing Sm N /Yb N , indicating the progressive release of particulate-bound Ho and MREEs in anoxic porewaters. Further, REE-Y patterns are strongly controlled by locality and only weakly controlled by sample type. Localities in close spatial proximity to each other (meter-scale) show high variability, suggesting differences in local depositional or early diagenetic conditions produced the observed variability in coeval sediments rather than late diagenetic processes.

title: Lyell in Chicago: An Historic Collection Illustrates a Missing Chapter in Nineteenth Century Geology
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Plotnick, Roy E. [1], Krick, Rachel [2], McIntyre, Pamela [3]

abstract: From June 17–24, 1841, Charles Lyell followed the footsteps of Roderick Murchison in visiting “Silurian” localities in Wales and the Welsh Borderland. While there, he collected paleontological and lithologic specimens representative of the units described in The Silurian System (Murchison 1839). This collection travelled with Lyell during his first visit to America that began in July of that year. His goal was to share these materials with the geologists of the New York State Natural History Survey, particularly James Hall, who were developing their own New York System as an alternative to the European stratigraphic divisions of the Paleozoic. The collection was originally intended for the Lowell Institute in Boston. At some point, it ended up in Hall’s possession and then eventually at the Field Museum in Chicago. Although Lyell’s travels in America have been extensively discussed, his trip to collect these specimens has never been documented. In addition, the collection has only received passing mention, none of which describe its contents or its current status. Using Lyell’s notebooks, with the assistance of experts, we have reconstructed his collecting journey. Contemporary letters shed light on the interactions between Hall and Lyell concerning the specimens. As far as possible, again with expert advice, we have identified the specimens in the collection, determined their localities, and placed them within the current stratigraphy for the Ordovician and Silurian. This collection, and the interactions between Charles Lyell and James Hall, were key to the nascent efforts to produce a global correlation for those time periods.

abstract: In sedimentary provenance studies, detrital garnet chemistry has traditionally been applied to distinguish broadly between mafic and felsic source rocks or basic metamorphic and igneous lithologies. However, matching detrital garnet compositions to those in hinterland bedrock sources provides access to associated metadata (tectonic and unit affiliations, metamorphic or magmatic conditions, structural and geographic locations, relationships to drainage pathways and geomorphological features), enabling the use of sedimentary archives to test models of exhumation and sediment routing. The Himalayan Siwalik Group foreland basin deposits contain a wealth of information regarding Himalayan tectonics, erosion, paleoclimate, and paleontological changes. A core problem is whether its provenance records a simple, regionally progressive unroofing sequence or a more complex system in which sediment supply varied with local catchments, drainage reorganizations, thrust activation, and differential exhumation/erosion of specific units. Here, detrital garnet compositions from the Siwalik Group (n = 2,515; Surai, Tinau, Muksar Khola, and Karnali River, Nepal) and the Pre-Siwalik (n = 14; Kasauli Fm., NW India) were compared with those in the Himalayan Garnet Analysis Database (n = 12,434; HGAD v1.0, tinyurl.com/HimalayanGarnetDB). The maximum depositional ages range from 27.7 to 2.8 Ma. Almandine, Grossular, Pyrope, and Spessartine end-members were compared using Aitchison distance and dominance thresholds were applied if non-unique unit matches occurred. Siwalik Group garnets are similar to those from the Himalayan core [Greater Himalayan Crystallines (GHC), Lesser Himalaya Sequence (LHS), Tethyan Himalaya Sequence (THS), and Main Central Thrust]. Suture-zone and magmatic garnets first appear at ~15.1 Ma, with Gangdese Batholith-affiliated garnets increasing in the Middle–Upper Siwalik Group. Siwalik Group matches ≤ 300 km apart occur at faults, klippen, tectonic windows, gneiss domes, or contact-metamorphic settings, clustering at amphibolite facies. Siwalik Group garnets match those from the Himalayan core, but Muksar Khola samples are similar to those from the Indian Shield (interpreted as upper LHS or skarn sources), gneiss domes, and High Himalayan leucogranites. abstract:
Endemic brachiopods are a defining component of the Ethiopian Faunal Province (EFP), a paleobiogeographic realm extending from India through East Africa and Madagascar to southern Israel, the Sinai and Arabian Peninsulas, parts of North Africa, and possibly as far as South America and New Caledonia. These taxa are distinguished from their ancestral populations by unique morphological features (apomorphies) and are restricted to specific environmental and geographic settings, particularly along the southern margin of the Tethys Sea. New material from Gebel El Minshera (Callovian, northern Sinai) includes two new species, Bihenithyris marianae and Somalithyris briani , and a rare genus, Goliathyris lewyi . These taxa may represent a previously unrecognized endemic subregion within the EFP, expanding the known distribution of endemic faunas in this realm. Endemism within the EFP is not limited to brachiopods; among associated faunas, trigoniacean and crassatellacean bivalves also display endemic patterns that contribute to defining the province. The faunal assemblages of northern Sinai, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel mark the northernmost extent of the Indo/African faunal realm and provide key constraints for delineating paleobiogeographic boundaries.

Ongoing analysis of brachiopod distributions within the EFP supports models of progressive rifting along the southern Tethyan Platform. This tectonic evolution ultimately led to the isolation of the EFP from northern boreal regions following the establishment of the Tethyan/North Atlantic Ocean barrier.

title: Determining Groundwater Flow Patterns in a Glacially-Influenced Midwestern Wetland
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)

affiliations: (1) Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI, USA

abstract:
Wetlands provide critical ecological functions including groundwater storage and recharge, nutrient cycling, and biodiversity support. The Fish Lake Environmental Education Center is a 240-acre glacially-influenced site near Lapeer, Michigan, that includes a bog, kettles with vernal pools, and interconnected surface water features. Previous research at Fish Lake has investigated groundwater recharge, groundwater/surface water interactions, wetland chemistry, and the influence of precipitation on groundwater flow and water quality.These studies demonstrated that precipitation strongly influences groundwater levels and chemistry within the wetland system. However, groundwater flow relationships between the bog, kettles, and surface water features have not been evaluated in detail.

This study characterized subsurface flow patterns within the Fish Lake wetland system to evaluate how wet and dry years influence groundwater-surface water interactions and recharge/discharge dynamics. Groundwater elevation data were obtained using pressure transducers, manual water-level measurements, and high-resolution survey data, which were used to develop groundwater flow maps. Long-term monitoring data including precipitation, groundwater elevations, electrical conductivity, pH, temperature, and nutrient concentrations were also evaluated to compare hydrologic conditions during wet and dry periods. Groundwater flow direction within the bog alternated flow directions between wet and dry years. This reversal suggests that precipitation-driven changes in hydraulic gradients influences groundwater/surface water interactions and recharge/discharge processes within the wetland system. This research contributes to long-term hydrogeologic monitoring efforts at Fish Lake and supports broader applications in wetland management, watershed protection, and climate resilience planning for similar upper Midwestern wetland environments.

title: Geophysical Investigations and Numerical Modeling Reveal Complex Saltwater-freshwater Transition Zones in a Peninsula Aquifer and Adjoining Coastal Embayment
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Di Iulio, Martina [1], Kurylyk, Barret [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
(2) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
abstract:
Groundwater provides a major source of drinking water in coastal communities worldwide, yet many rural communities lack the adaptive capacity and technical and financial resources to protect these critical water resources. In coastal aquifers, the classic Ghyben-Herzberg model predicts a terrestrial wedge of saline groundwater separated by overlying fresh groundwater through an interface (or transition zone) maintained by density differences and meteorological and oceanic forcing on the aquifer. The thickness and seaward extent of the freshwater zone are influenced by the groundwater flux and head distribution, and accordingly, are dependent on processes including changing sea level, recharge, and pumping. Recently, fresh groundwater resources have been identified in offshore and nearshore marine environments, and there is ongoing research on onshore-offshore aquifer connectivity.

We focus on a rural coastal community (Stanhope) in Prince Edward Island, Canada that is situated on a peninsula and surrounded by an embayment on one side and the Gulf of St. Lawrence on the other. Stanhope relies entirely on groundwater for drinking water but has continuously experienced elevated salinity levels in private wells in recent decades. Our ultimate project goal is to investigate the present geometry and dynamics of the freshwater zone in the peninsular aquifer and to use numerical modeling to explore potential impacts of future climate conditions and anthropogenic activities. Field investigations were conducted in Stanhope and the adjacent national park. Piezometers were installed and instrumented with conductivity-temperature-depth loggers, and onshore and offshore (above ice) electromagnetic geophysical surveys were conducted. A 3D groundwater flow and transport model has been developed for the peninsula community using MODFLOW6, with calibration primarily based on transition zone locations inferred from resistivity distributions from the geophysical investigations. Results from offshore geophysical surveys over the saline embayment indicate the presence of freshwater at depth and a possible continuity between terrestrial and sub-bay fresh groundwater resources. These groundwater salinity distributions are further supported through the numerical model results, which indicate a complex transition zone around the aquifer with the potential to impact future drinking water quality for Stanhope residents. Findings from this study will help inform coastal protection guidelines for rural communities relying on island and peninsular aquifers worldwide.

title: Geological Evolution and Correlation of the Togiak Terrane, Southwestern Alaska
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Waldien, Trevor Scott [1], Regan, Sean P. [2], Patton, Alex [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) Geosciences Department, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, AK, USA; Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, AK, USA

abstract:
The geology of southwestern Alaska provides a critical link between disparate terranes that evolved in the Panthalassan and Arctic realms. Here, we overview recent advances in the understanding of the bedrock geology of southwestern Alaska and test regional correlations.

The bedrock geology of the Ahklun-Wood River Mountains consists of Jurassic-Cretaceous arc rocks (Togiak arc) and near arc marine basin strata (Greywacke of Kulukak bay), which collectively make up the Togiak terrane. New igneous and detrital zircon U-Pb-εHf(t) data from Togiak arc rocks indicate that juvenile arc magmatism lasted from ca. 215-145 Ma. Inherited Paleozoic and Precambrian zircon in the Togiak arc rocks correlate with detrital zircon U-Pb-εHf(t) data from quartzose metasediments in the structurally underlying Tikchik complex to the east of the arc, which suggests that the Tikchik complex is basement to the Togiak arc. Southeast of the Togiak arc and Tikchik complex, the Greywacke of Kulukak Bay consists of turbidite strata with dominantly juvenile 215-140 Ma detrital zircons and maximum depositional ages ranging from ca. 169-147 Ma. Zircon U-Pb-εHf(t) data from the Togiak arc rocks and Greywacke of Kulukak Bay are both highly juvenile and overlap in age, suggesting that the turbidite strata were derived mainly from the arc. Localized exposures of blueschist facies metamorphic rocks to the northwest of the Togiak arc suggest that the turbiditic strata to the east formed in a backarc basin during southeast-dipping subduction (modern coordinates).

Comparing the Togiak terrane U-Pb-εHf(t) data to equivalent data from other Jurassic arc terranes in the cordillera indicates the highest level of overlap with components of the Insular superterrane. We propose a tectonic model that involves evolution of the Togiak terrane as part of the Insular Superterrane until ca. 170 Ma, after which the Insular superterrane was separated from the Togiak terrane by oblique left lateral opening of the Kulukak-Kahiltna-Gravina marine seaway.

abstract: Arkansas ranks third in the nation for irrigated land, with irrigation water being primarily sourced from the Mississippi River Valley alluvial (MRVA) aquifer. Extensive irrigation along with the region’s geology have led to the designation of critical groundwater areas due to declining groundwater levels. Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) refers to a suite of methods used to intentionally replenish groundwater systems, with a focus on increasing groundwater availability while sustaining or improving water quality. This study evaluates the operation of two infiltration galleries (IG) in the Cache River Critical Groundwater Area of northeast Arkansas. IG are gravel-filled trenches excavated to the permeable sand layer of the upper MRVA, with subsurface plumbing connected to a recharge source. Recharge water was sourced from a nearby on-farm storage reservoir. Recharge period is restricted to the six-month period of November 1 to April 30. Therefore, findings will be reported for the partial period of 2021/2022 and complete period of 2022/2023, 2023/2024, and 2024/2025. Construction and design will be briefly described and followed by reports of water pumped and infiltration rates through the system. Spectral analysis of groundwater level response to the recharge activity will also be presented. Water quality monitoring occurred throughout the entire flow path of recharge water and will be described. Findings from site suitability evaluation for dry well installation in the region will also be presented. This study aims to provide insight on current and future MAR research in Midsouth with a distinct focus on water resources for agricultural use now and into the future.

abstract: Wildfire ash is highly mobile and represents an acute water quality risk when it enters water bodies. Ash can introduce nutrients and toxic elements while increasing turbidity, degrading aquatic biodiversity, raising water treatment costs, and, in severe cases, rendering water unsafe for human consumption. Ash color, ranging from black semi-recognizable organic material to white mineral ash, is an easily observable characteristic that we hypothesized would serve as a proxy for physical properties. Through a standardized ash color characterization, we also predicted it would exhibit distinct spectral signatures. Establishing robust relationships between ash color, physical properties, and unique spectral signatures would enable use of Earth Observation (EO) data to map ash characteristics at the landscape scale, providing rapid post-fire ash impact assessments. We collected 507 samples across 20 wildfires in the Western United States between 2017 and 2024, measuring ash volume within a 20x20 cm metal frame, water repellency, spectral reflectance, and ash color. Ash color was assessed using the Ash Spectrum and Height rulER (ASHER) tool, developed by the United States Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station. High soil burn severity was associated with white ash, consistent with complete combustion. Red ash was associated with Douglas-Fir stands under conditions of high fire intensity potential and with Spodosols, rich in iron, which may contribute to its reddish coloration. The standardized ash color classes exhibited statistically significant distinct spectral signature across visible, near infrared, and short-wave infrared regions, with pink and white ash showing the highest reflectance values. Results showed that ash color significantly predicts generated ash volume and water repellency (p-value < 0.005), though the latter was additionally influenced by pre-fire vegetation type and moisture conditions. Black ash was characterized by low volume (200 cm 3 ) and strong water repellency (0.33 mL s -1 ), while white ash showed high volume (628 cm 3 ) and weak water repellency (1.4 mL s -1 ), representing the two ends of the ash color gradient. Overall, differences were significant between light and dark colors, confirming that ash physical properties are detectable through spectral signatures, supporting the potential to use EO data for ash characterization and risk contamination mapping.

abstract:
Ongoing and future sea-level rise poses a major threat to coastal ecosystems, communities, and infrastructure worldwide. A major uncertainty in future sea-level projections is the response of the Antarctic and Greenland Ice Sheets to ongoing warming. Ice-sheet models rely on geologic records of sea level from past warm periods to provide constraints on the sensitivity of ice sheets to warming. The Last Interglacial (LIG) period (Marine Isotope Stage 5e, ~129,000 to 116,000 years ago) is an especially valuable interval because global mean temperature was slightly higher than pre-industrial and comparable with many low-end 21st century warming scenarios. Fossil corals are among the most reliable indicators of past sea level and can be precisely dated using the U-Th method, but many regions still lack well-dated in situ coral records, leaving important gaps in regional and global sea-level compilations.

Here we present 15 new high-precision (<±1 ka) U-Th ages, together with stratigraphic observations and elevation measurements from emergent in-situ fossil corals collected in 2023 from the Archipelago of San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina in the western Caribbean. The dated samples are dominated by Siderastrea siderea and Pseudodiploria strigose, while the in-situ assemblage also includes Orbicella nancyi , Siderastrea siderea , Orbicella annularis , and Colpophyllia natans . The absence of shelf-edge and shallow water species such as Acropora palmata and Acropora cervicornis along with the observed coral reef assemblage suggest formation of a shallow leeward fore-reef environment at an estimated water depth of ~10 m. Because post-depositional alteration and open-system behavior can bias U-series ages, we apply screening criteria based on coral mineralogy, uranium concentration, initial 234 U/ 238 U activity ratios, and detrital thorium content to identify the most reliable samples. These provide the first robust, well-screened sea-level constraints from this archipelago and indicate that corals were growing at this depth by ~130 ka, in the very early LIG. The record fills an important geographic gap in Caribbean sea-level data and strengthens regional and global reconstructions of LIG sea level.

abstract: The northern hemisphere between late Miocene to late Pliocene (~7 Ma to 2.6 Ma) was characterized by expanded icesheets over the continents and sea ice in the oceans. However, the paleoenvironmental conditions during this period of glacial expansion are poorly constrained. Sediments from Björn Drift site hold critical information on ocean circulation, bottom water formation, sediment provenance and sea-level change. In this study, we analyze major and trace element geochemistry to constrain weathering intensity, sediment provenance, paleosalinity, and redox conditions recorded from Björn Drift sediments recovered during IODP Expedition 395 at Site U1562C within the subarctic North Atlantic. The interval of interest spans ~6.72 Myr (from ~9.3 Ma to 2.58 Ma) and comprises 199.13 m of sediment, recording a late Miocene increase in sediment accumulation followed by a decline, and then a sharp late Pliocene rise to rates 3x higher than late Miocene values, coincident with expanded glaciation. According to geochemical analysis, the silty clay sediments are graywacke. The sediments of Björn Drift Site U1562C originated from moderately weak weathered to unweathered mafic (basaltic) to intermediate (andesitic) igneous rocks under largely oxic to minor suboxic paleoredox conditions and were deposited in a deep marine environment. The minimal weathering intensity may be linked to ice-sheet dynamics of the time intervals characterized by cooling sea surface temperature. The source rocks show active continental margin and oceanic island arc (OIA) affinities, illustrating tectonic activities in the North Atlantic region between late Miocene through late Pliocene. Two distinct paleosalinity phases identified across late Miocene to late Pliocene with largely dominating marine conditions and pulses of brackish conditions in late Miocene.

abstract: Fault seal is the effect of a fault zone on capillary trapping and migration of a nonwetting phase such as oil or CO 2 . Fault seal analysis is uncertain because of field data limitations and gaps in our mechanistic understanding and resolution of fault architecture development, motivating a probabilistic framework. We calibrate and validate PREDICT (Saló-Salgado et al., Geology, 2023), a process-based, stochastic model of sand and clay smearing, for fault seal analysis in normally-consolidated siliciclastic sequences. The study field, located in offshore Nigeria, hosts dual phase hydrocarbon accumulations in Miocene-aged shallow water marine and deltaic reservoirs. Buoyancy pressures in seven fault-controlled hydrocarbon pools were estimated based on structural relief and fluid pressures observed in wells. These fault traps are vertically stacked along the same fault and have a common charge mechanism; yet buoyancy pressures against the fault differ by more than an order of magnitude and have no correlation with SGR values. For each model realization, our method populates fault-core materials in a three-dimensional throw window, estimates each material’s fine-scale entry pressure, and computes the minimum capillary pressure required to cross the finite-thickness fault (breakthrough capillary pressure, P cb ) via invasion-percolation. We optimize so that 10% of modeled P cb realizations exceed the field buoyancy pressure (a best estimate of the field P cb ), equivalent to matching the 90 th percentile of the P cb distribution. Five of seven windows were used in the optimization; the remaining two were withheld for validation. A calibration using structurally restored faulting depths, a permeability shift, and a critical shale-smear factor reproduces field-derived breakthrough pressures within a factor of 1.4 across the seven throw windows, resolving the order-of-magnitude spread that SGR cannot distinguish. This work shows that three-dimensional, process-based, probabilistic fault modeling improves fault seal estimates for CO 2 containment assessment, where the 90 th percentile target is conservative against overpredicting seal capacity.

title: Land as a Mnemonic: Interrogating Geology’s Relationship With Place, Land, and Resources to Inspire Sustainable Futures

authors: Chavez Reed, Cameron [1]

abstract:
Cultivating relationships between landscapes and communities through place-based education is fundamental to addressing many of the wicked problems that we face today. Geologists play an important role in communities as educators, professionals, and experts in a variety of roles. Historically, geologists have been trained in scientific field that values objectivity and neutralizing lenses of land-based science. However, without critically examining the ways that deep geologic time informs historical and modern events that shape landscapes, places, economies, and politics, we will fail to effect change to build sustainable futures. To address these complex anthropogenic issues in the 21st century, geologists will need to consider the historic roots of these regime shifts. This means exploring more than the objective and sometime neutralizing lenses of Earth systems taught in most Earth science programs. Geology’s connection to unjust systems and hierarchies cannot be ignored.

The places in which we study and teach our students are constructed from complex histories of that land which fundamentally transform the interactions between people and place in that locality. I draw from studies and practices in critical placemaking and Indigenous scholarship among the storied landscapes of the Southwestern US to encourage budding geoscientists to examine the ways geology is connected to complex and painful histories in the lands we study. Global communities continue to experience risks to sustainable place making due to unjust and unsustainable practices with deep historical roots primarily as a result of ongoing colonial projects. Geologists also must take up the responsibility of recontextualizing their studies of land through multiple ways of seeing. Here, we present methods of expanding geoscience education past the geologic landscape into human and more-than-human relations that weave the inseparable connections between communities and landscapes in the Southwestern US.

abstract: Aiaktalik Island, located in the southern portion of the Kodiak Archipelago, was once home to the largest Alutiiq settlement at the time of Russian contact. Russian accounts assert that over 400 people lived on Aiaktalik at this time. In June of 2026 a team of archaeologists surveyed Aiaktalik Island and conducted soil probing and test pit excavations to identify archaeological sites, ascertain the likelihood of archaeological preservation and facilitate landscape reconstruction. These observations, in conjunction with the interpretation of exposed cliff face profiles, have allowed for broad strokes characterization of the geomorphology. Geomorphological interpretation is applied to identify desirable areas for ancestral Alutiiq settlement and describe archaeological preservation potential. We consider suitability for house pit construction, proximity to subsistence resources, and accessibility for kayaks as influential factors for ancestral Alutiiq settlement location choice. Coastal erosion and estuarine/marine sedimentation are used to identify areas with poor archaeological preservation. Our findings show that a majority of the eastern and southern coasts of Aiaktalik Island are exposed to wave action, resulting in poor preservation. Archaeological deposits and house pits were instead found clustered in the western and northern promontories of Aiaktalik which feature gently sloped, prograding shorelines. The presence or absence of volcanic ash deposits in stratigraphic profiles is used to describe the general chronology of the region’s geomorphology. Although the earthquake-driven subsidence that affects the Kodiak Archipelago is complicated and highly variable, pedestrian survey and subsurface testing allows us to describe how Aiaktalik Island looked in the past and how ancestral Alutiiq people may have interacted with this dynamic landscape/seascape.

Dams are increasingly being removed as they age into obsolescence. Dam removal typically initiates geomorphic and ecological recovery in affected river reaches, enabling the erosion of previously impounded sediment, the resumption of water and sediment delivery from upstream to downstream, and the transition of the former impoundment from a lentic to a lotic environment. Most dam removals, including those where river responses have been monitored, have occurred in water-rich regions like the Pacific Northwest, the Upper Midwest, and New England. In water-scarce, semi-arid regions like the U.S. Mountain West, aging dams are common but dam removals are not. Monitoring dam removals in semi-arid environments can provide insight into the applicability of conceptual models developed in water-rich regions, and reveal potential management considerations unique to semi-arid landscapes. Here we present a Before-After Control-Impact study examining geomorphic and ecological response to the first intensively monitored dam removal in Colorado, USA.

We measured channel cross-section form, bed grain size, and benthic macroinvertebrate community composition in three reaches—in the former impoundment, immediately below the former dam, and at a distant upstream control site—for one year before, and three years following, removal of an ~8 m tall dam. We found that geomorphic adjustment was rapid: average channel-margin elevation changes were only significant during the first year after removal. The only consistent grain size changes occurred in the former impoundment, with bed sediment coarsening due to transport of previously impounded fines. Benthic macroinvertebrate community composition in the dam-affected reaches was more similar to the control reaches after removal than before, indicating return of the community towards reference conditions. We also observe overall, though not monotonic, improvements over time in common community health metrics. The formerly impounded reach showed more complete recovery, as defined by similarity to the control reach, than the reach downstream of the dam did. We hypothesize that streamflow and sediment management decisions set the timescale of river response to dam removal, and that geomorphic context influences the relative recovery trajectories of the upstream and downstream reaches.

title: Predicting Groundwater Salinity in Louisiana using a Random Forest Approach
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: Elsheikh, Ahmed A [1], Knierim, Katherine J. [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi-Gulf Water Science Center, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi-Gulf Water Science Center, Little Rock, AR, USA
abstract:
Fresh groundwater resources in Louisiana are threatened by, and susceptible to, increasing salinity. Several aquifers which serve as sources of water for irrigation have experienced groundwater declines which are attributable to groundwater pumping. These conditions have allowed saline water to migrate into freshwater zones, potentially affecting water availability for agricultural uses and underscoring the need for enhanced groundwater monitoring and management strategies.

Recent national‑scale salinity mapping efforts provide an assessment of freshwater status across the United States. However, these models often fail to resolve localized salinity anomalies because they rely on coarse datasets and they lack high‑resolution geophysical data required to characterize site‑specific variability. Louisiana currently lacks regional‑scale salinity‑prediction models capable of describing subsurface salinity conditions within the state.

Recent advancements in computational power and machine learning now offer new opportunities to improve salinity mapping efforts. Specific conductance (SC), a reliable proxy for salinity due to its strong correlation with dissolved ion concentrations, provides a measurable basis for these models.

This study applies a Random Forest classification approach to predict groundwater SC using a water quality dataset spanning 1908–2023. Predictor variables include soil characteristics, topographic attributes, groundwater levels, water‑use patterns, and well depth information. Model performance is evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy metrics to assess predictive capability.

Preliminary results show that groundwater salinity increases with depth and toward the Gulf Coast, consistent with known regional hydrogeologic patterns. Ultimately, this research will contribute to the growing body of literature aimed at understanding and mitigating the effects of salinity on freshwater systems within Louisiana, promoting informed decision making for future resource management.

title: Developing an interpretive framework for triple oxygen isotope analyses of planktic foraminifera through sampling in the Sargasso Sea
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Gadson, Olivia Marie [1], Hull, Pincelli M. [2], Weber, J.C. [3], Pedrosa-Pàmies, Rut [4], Wostbrock, Jordan [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences Department, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences Department, Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(3) The Ecosystems Center, Marine Biological Laboratory, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(4) The Ecosystems Center, Marine Biological Laboratory, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(5) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
abstract:
Triple oxygen isotope measurements are paired δ 17 O-δ 18 O (hereafter referred to as: Δ′ 17 O) values that can identify whether a mineral precipitated in equilibrium with a given seawater δ 18 O value at a specific temperature. We can leverage the deviation of δ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O values away from expected calcite-water equilibrium values to quantify hydrological conditions (e.g., evaporation and humidity), calcification mechanisms, and diagenesis–all of which are difficult to identify using traditional δ 18 O measurements alone. This study aims to understand modern, multispecies variability in foraminiferal δ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O values and establish a framework that distinguishes the effects of early diagenesis from vital effects at the organism or species level. Our framework can then be applied to better understand the triple oxygen isotope values of fossil foraminifera specimens.

In this study, we present δ 13 C, δ 18 O, and Δ′ 17 O values of 14 species of modern planktic foraminifera from the northern Sargasso Sea, near the Oceanic Flux Program (OFP) and Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (BATS) sites. We collected foraminifera from plankton tow nets, OFP sediment traps (500 m, 1500 m, and 3200 m water depth with ≈biweekly collection), and sediment core samples from two cruises in October 2024 and April 2025. This vertical sample scheme allows us to trace post-mortem isotopic change that occurs as tests descend through the water column (sediment traps) and from shallow burial (core-top sediments). We classify foraminifera obtained from plankton tows as the least altered specimens, compared to those from the deeper sediment traps and sediment core samples. We also collected water samples with concurrent CTD measurements to capture the vertical variation of seawater δ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O values within the Sargasso Sea and calculate in-situ, δ 18 O-Δ′ 17 O calcite-water equilibrium values.

Our preliminary results show differences between plankton tow, sediment trap, and core-top sample d 13 C, d 18 O, and Δ′ 17 O values, potentially reflecting the addition of gametogenic features formed deeper relative to the rest of the shell or from partial post-mortem re-equilibration/diagenesis. We also find systematic offsets from equilibrium δ​​​​​​ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O values between Globigerinoides and Globorotalia taxa. Our study is the first to explore multi-species variability of foraminifera δ 18 O-Δ′ 17 O values and assess these values through paired water and foraminiferal shell analyses. This study lays the foundation for using foraminiferal δ 18 O-Δ′ 17 O measurements to conduct more accurate and dynamic paleoclimate reconstructions.

title: Yet Another Supply Chain: Developing Stable Mineral Supplies Through a Thriving Human Capital Supply Chain
session_title: Mineral Resources and Society
authors: Keane, Christopher Matthews [1], Gonzales, Leila [2]
affiliations: (1) American Geosciences Institute (AGI), Alexandria, VA,
(2) American Geosciences Institute, Alexandria, VA, USA
abstract: Meeting society’s increasing demand for minerals requires skilled individuals at every stage of the mineral supply chain. Talent development is often framed around a few “key roles,” such as exploration geologists or metallurgists, but the larger challenge is ensuring that the right combination of geoscience talent (including geoscience professionals, skilled trades, and geoscience-adjacent occupations) is available throughout the system. Without this breadth and depth of talent, existing mineral supply chains will falter, or if not already established, will fail to develop successfully within a country. We will examine the evolving talent landscape that is needed to support a stable supply of minerals for society’s needs, including geoscience enrollment trends and the growing gap between mineral development demand and the pace at which new workers are entering the field. We will also explore factors such as artificial intelligence, demographic and political pressures, shifting career expectations, and changes in the types of employers hiring geoscientists—especially in Western societies—that are intensifying competition for the people needed to meet future mineral needs. Understanding and addressing the human capital system as a whole will be central to achieving success in managing a stable mineral supply to meet society’s demands.

title: Free Flowing: Benefits and Costs of Dam Removal In Idaho
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Brighten, Grace Elizabeth [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Mount Holyoke College, South Hadley, MA, USA
abstract: The subject of dam removal in Idaho is a multifaceted issue with economic, environmental, social, and structural factors. Dam removal has become a topic of contentious debate in the last several years in Idaho, as both serious benefits and costs exist due to river damming. Analyses of the advantages of dam removal exist for the Northwest as a region, but none have been performed specifically for Idaho, which necessitates this analysis. This paper, through a synthesis of existing research, federal documents, and grey literature, constructs a thorough examination of the benefits and costs of dam removal in Idaho. A focus on highlighting the effects on native biodiversity and ecosystems, Indigenous perspectives, potential consequences for energy production, and impacts on agriculture and navigation aims to create as holistic a view of dam removal as possible. Allowing fish stocks, sediments and water to travel freely up and down undammed rivers would improve the health of riparian ecosystems, and would honor treaties between the federal government and Indigenous groups in Idaho. Conversely, the disadvantages of dam removal include the costs of upgrading energy infrastructure and the power grid to accommodate solar, wind and geothermal energies, as well as the necessary testing and remediation of possible sediment contamination. This analysis indicates that the burdens imposed upon Indigenous groups and ecosystems by the damming of rivers cannot be completely alleviated by any amount of money or other remedial efforts, but only by dam removal. In contrast, the costs associated with dam removal can be eased by monetary supplementation, as well as changes and upgrades to transportation and irrigation infrastructure. Ultimately, the choice between whether or not to breach dams in Idaho comes down to a decision between protecting economic interest in the present and near future, versus protecting ecosystems, the environment, and the lives of indigenous Idahoans for years to come.

authors: Powers, Ella [1], Whipple, Kathryn [2], Ahlefeld, Greta [3], Li, Hannuo (Bridget) [4], Winkler, Stefan [5], Pedley, Katherine [6]

abstract: Cirques are armchair-shaped erosional features that form in high alpine settings by cirque-type glaciers abrading the base-rock and carrying away material. These features are useful for understanding the extent of previously glaciated environments. Cirques are characterized by a steep headwall, an overdeepened bowl-shaped basin that often has a tarn, and a lip that marks the bottom extent of the cirque. There is minimal data on cirques in New Zealand, especially in the Southern Alps, and this study seeks to fill this gap. Here we create a dataset identifying 255 cirques across ten sections in the Southern Alps region of New Zealand and complete six morphometric measurements on each cirque. These measurements, conducted using GIS, included aspect, minimum elevation, depth, width, length, and area. Comparisons were drawn between cirques located closer to the Main Divide – the principal mountain ridge of the Southern Alps – and cirques located further from the Main Divide. Cirques closer to the Main Divide form at higher elevations, show a wide array of aspects, and are seemingly less developed than cirques further away from the Main Divide. We observed that cirques further away from the Main Divide exhibited strong directionality and were often larger in size. We anticipate that our data could be of use to future researchers studying cirques in the Southern Alps. Our observed trends can be used to interpret geological and climatic conditions under which cirques formed, and to understand the post-glacial processes which may have altered the morphology into present-day cirques. Additionally, our data can provide a basis for further research of cirque morphology, tectonic uplift, climate patterns, or further comparison of the Southern Alps area cirques with those from other regions worldwide.

title: Cosmogenic 10Be Dating of Pinedale and Bull Lake Glacial Maxima Along the Northeastern Range Front of the Beartooth Mountains, U.S.A.
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations (Posters)
authors: Licciardi, Joseph [1], Pierce, Kenneth L. [2], Licciardi, Avriel D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of New Hampshire, Durham, NH, USA
(2) US Geological Survey, Northern Rocky Mtn Science Center, Bozeman, MT, USA
(3) John Wiley & Sons, Hoboken, NJ, USA
abstract:
The Beartooth Mountains of Montana and Wyoming, USA, served as one of several major high-elevation ice source regions that coalesced to form the Greater Yellowstone Glacial System (GYGS) during successive Pleistocene glaciations. Previously published cosmogenic 10 Be exposure ages of terminal moraines around the periphery of the GYGS exhibit a pattern of asynchronous glacial maxima during the last (Pinedale) glaciation, reflecting temporal shifts in the dynamics of various glacial source areas. The oldest dated Pinedale terminal moraines (19.8 ± 0.9 ka) are near the mouth of Clarks Fork (of the Yellowstone) Canyon, which hosted a glacier flowing down from the Beartooth highlands in the northeastern sector of the GYGS, whereas Pinedale maxima are up to several millennia younger in the southwestern portions of the Yellowstone ice complex. These regional differences in Pinedale terminal moraine ages suggest that the earliest phase of GYGS ice buildup occurred in the Beartooth Mountains, but evidence for this interpretation is limited to a single drainage and pertains only to Pinedale-aged deposits. Given the early Pinedale culmination of the Clarks Fork glacier, we predict that terminal moraines marking glacial advances in other drainages emanating from the Beartooth highlands likely also date to the early Pinedale, and that these valleys presumably also experienced early ice advances during the penultimate (Bull Lake) glaciation.

Here, we present emerging results from cosmogenic 10 Be dating of terminal moraines preserved at the mouths of several major valleys along the northeastern range front of the Beartooth Mountains. Boulders were sampled on prominent lateral and terminal moraine ridges in the East Rosebud Creek, West Rosebud Creek, and Stillwater River drainages that have been previously mapped and assigned Pinedale and Bull Lake ages in earlier studies based on relative weathering criteria and geomorphic expression. To our knowledge, our ongoing 10 Be dating efforts provide the first numerical age constraints on the terminal moraine complexes in these drainages, thus allowing us to test our hypothesis that the development of the GYGS initiated as early ice buildup and glacier culminations in the Beartooth Mountains during the last two glaciations. These new 10 Be ages also lead to an improved understanding of the overall timing and regional pattern of GYGS evolution during Pleistocene glacial periods.

title: Laser-ablation He analysis avoids heating-induced U loss in (U-Th)/He dating of oxide minerals
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications (Posters)
authors: McDowell, Paige Riley [1], Kortyna, Cullen David [2], Metcalf, James R. [3], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
(4) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Over the past 25+ years, conventional whole-crystal (U-Th)/He thermochronology has become a widely applied tool for determining the thermal histories of rocks. Zircon and apatite are the two minerals most dated by (U-Th)/He, but developing other minerals as (U-Th)/He thermochronometers can broaden the range of problems that can be explored with the technique. Oxide minerals such as rutile, hematite, and baddeleyite have been dated with (U-Th)/He, but some samples of these phases are difficult to date using conventional whole-crystal diode-laser heating methods owing to U loss induced by laser heating. Laser-ablation (LA) (U-Th)/He has the potential to circumvent these analytical challenges by ablating rather than heating the crystal to release the He, thus leaving the U abundances unaffected.

This work explores whether rutile, a Ti oxide, can be successfully dated using LA-(U-Th)/He methods. We examine rutile from three samples: a Proterozoic felsic granulite from the Snowbird tectonic zone in SK, CAN; a Proterozoic amphibolite-facies albitite from the Madison Range in MT, USA; and an Ordovician eclogite from the Appalachians in NC, USA. Each sample has been previously dated by U-Pb and conventional (U-Th)/He dating (Robinson et al. 2018). Rutile from the two Proterozoic samples are highly He retentive, difficult to fully degas for He, and yielded unreasonably old (U-Th)/He dates due to U loss during He degassing. In contrast, rutile from the Ordovician sample are less retentive, easily degassed, and yielded sensible(U-Th)/He dates. Our approach is to assess if LA-(U-Th)/He can generate reliable dates for all three of these samples. We utilized an 80 μm spot and experimented with laser fluence, lasing duration, and repetition rate for the release of He by laser ablation. The results yield rutile (U-Th)/He dates for the Proterozoic samples that are compatible with other independent geochronologic and thermochronologic data and replicate the conventional rutile (U-Th)/He dates for the Ordovician sample, demonstrating that LA-(U-Th)/He can avoid U loss issues associated with conventional (U-Th)/He dating of rutile. We expect that this method can bypass similar challenges associated with dating other oxide minerals such as hematite and baddeleyite, expanding the range of rock types and temperature conditions accessible with (U-Th)/He thermochronology.

title: Groundwater to the Human Gut: Arsenic Exposure and H. pylori Infection Prevalence
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Obi, Christabel Ifechukwu [1], McIntosh, Jennifer C [2], Brown, Heidi E [3]
affiliations: (1) Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(3) Mel & Enid Zuckerman College of Public Health, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract:
Geogenic arsenic (As), an IARC Group 1 carcinogen, is a widespread contaminant of surface water and groundwater, mobilized from documented sources such as volcanoclastic sediments, geothermal fluids, felsic rocks, and basin-fill deposits. Although the U.S. drinking water maximum contaminant level (MCL) for arsenic is 10 ppb, some epidemiological studies suggest that chronic exposure to the far more widespread low-range concentrations (1-5 ppb) may still lead to adverse health outcomes. In the arid southwestern U.S., arsenic is a particular concern for private well owners whose water is not federally regulated and may often exceed drinking water limits. Northern Arizona illustrates the severity: aquifers there show documented arsenic exceedances with reported groundwater concentrations up to 190 ppb.

Helicobacter pylori, another IARC Group 1 carcinogen, is one of the most common bacterial infections worldwide and is a known risk factor for chronic gastritis (stomach inflammation), peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer. Some research works hypothesize an association between arsenic exposure from well water and susceptibility to H. pylori infection heightens gastric cancer development risk; because both arsenic and H. pylori damage the stomach lining cells, thus, their co-occurrence may accelerate progression from chronic gastritis to malignancy.

This study integrates hydrogeochemical and epidemiological datasets to map the geographic distribution of arsenic exposure in groundwater and H. pylori infection nationwide and to evaluate them as co-located risk factors for gastric cancer. Preliminary results from an ongoing systematic scoping review of published H. pylori seroprevalence (past exposure to the pathogen) and demographic data reveal geographic and demographic heterogeneity: U.S. seroprevalence ranges from 30 – 36% nationally (our work has found 30.7% in southern Arizona to 56.4% in northern Arizona), with American Indian/Alaska Native, Black, and Hispanic populations bearing the highest infection burden. As H. pylori and arsenic mapping proceeds, overlaying these datasets will help pinpoint where geologic and infectious cancer risks converge, guiding targeted screening and future well water testing.

title: Same Course, New Rules: Embedding Professional Practice in a (Mostly) Undergraduate GIS Class
session_title: Learning to be a Geoscientist: Professional Exposure, Agency, and Transferable Skills in Undergraduate Education.
authors: Barquero Molina, Miriam [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX,
abstract:
What do employers want from geoscience graduates that our courses don't explicitly teach? Reliability, time management, independent troubleshooting, and clear documentation come up again and again in conversations about workforce readiness, yet these habits are rarely named, much less assessed, in technical coursework. And as AI reshapes technical work in ways we cannot yet predict, these durable professional habits, along with the judgment to know why a workflow works, may prove more valuable than proficiency with any particular tool.

With this in mind, I redesigned my upper-division GIS course (30-35 students, mixed undergraduate and graduate) to work a little more like a workplace. The technical content did not change; what changed was how the course asks students to work. I had long assumed that upper-division students would meet deadlines out of internal motivation. A difficult semester proved me wrong, so rather than simply bolting on a late policy, I made professional practice an explicit, graded part of the course: deadlines treated as deliverables under a clear, published late policy; built-in flexibility replacing case-by-case negotiation; class time treated as structured work time; and three short reflections asking students to examine their own workflows, troubleshooting, and readiness for professional work.

The first iteration was promising but preliminary. Late submissions fell by roughly a third, and the reflections drew genuine engagement: students measured their own habits against workplace standards, described how organization and planning practices transfer to research and other coursework, and identified the gaps now driving a revised iteration, underway this fall. This talk shares what I did, what worked, what didn't, and what I'm trying next.

title: New Crinoids from the Upper Ordovician (Katian) of Anticosti Island, Québec, Canada: Implications for early Paleozoic Faunal Turnover
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination (Posters)
authors: Zazubec, Alysha [1], Crowley, Kiera D. [2], Hopkins, Melanie Jane [3], Koniecki, Joseph M. [4], Wright, David F. [5], Cole, Selina R. [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(2) University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA

(4) Milford, MI,
(5) Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA
(6) Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK,
abstract:
The transition from the Ordovician to the Silurian represents one of the most significant intervals of ecological and evolutionary restructuring in Paleozoic marine ecosystems. Widespread faunal turnover during this interval has long been linked to environmental perturbations associated with the Late Ordovician mass extinction (LOME), the first of the "Big Five" mass extinction events in Earth's history. However, the timing, magnitude, and underlying mechanisms of taxonomic and ecological change remain insufficiently understood, in part because relatively few fossiliferous successions preserve a continuous record spanning the extinction interval and the Ordovician–Silurian boundary. Among marine invertebrates, crinoids experienced a particularly pronounced macroevolutionary transition, characterized by substantial changes in taxonomic composition, ecological structure, and patterns of clade dominance that ultimately shaped middle Paleozoic crinoid communities. Determining whether these changes were driven directly by the extinction, or began prior to the LOME, is essential for understanding the evolutionary dynamics of this critical interval in crinoid evolutionary history.

Anticosti Island (Québec, Canada) preserves one of the most complete and fossiliferous sedimentary successions spanning the Late Ordovician through the Early Silurian, providing an exceptional natural laboratory for investigating biotic responses before, during, and after the LOME. Continued study of the island's exceptionally preserved fossil crinoid fauna has already improved our understanding of both pre-extinction diversity and post-extinction recovery, and continues offering new opportunities to evaluate the rise of middle Paleozoic crinoid assemblages.

Here we describe a new genus of monobathrid camerate and a new genus of flexible cladid from the Katian-aged Vauréal Formation of Anticosti Island. These taxa belong to clades that underwent major evolutionary radiations following the LOME, subsequently becoming important components of Silurian faunas and, more broadly, the middle Paleozoic crinoid evolutionary fauna. Their occurrence in pre-extinction Katian strata demonstrates that these lineages originated before the onset of the primary extinction pulse and were already diversifying within Late Ordovician ecosystems. Taken along with other recent discoveries, this suggests that the macroevolutionary transition traditionally attributed to post-extinction recovery may instead reflect evolutionary processes initiated prior to the LOME, with the extinction event acting to enhance, rather than solely generate, the composition and ecological dominance of subsequent crinoid communities.

abstract:
Spring-fed, freshwater ecosystems across Florida are increasingly threatened by human impacts and environmental changes. Shifting conditions are recorded in the shells of live, dead, and fossil aquatic gastropods. This study compared isotopic values from live (living individuals, n=145), dead (loose shell accumulations, n=28), and fossil ( in situ Pleistocene-Holocene riverbank sediments, n=32) specimens of two gastropod species, the freshwater Elimia floridensis and the euryhaline Vitta usnea from 11 sites along the Wakulla River in Florida to assess the accuracy of using freshwater gastropods to isotopically reconstruct water paleotemperature. Powdered shell samples (150 E. floridensis from live, dead, and fossil and 55 V. usnea from live only) were processed and analysed to obtain δ18O and δ13C isotopic values.

Results show lower δ18O and δ13C isotopic values among the live specimens and higher values among fossil specimens. Death assemblage specimens display the greatest range of values, with some specimens similar to live specimens and others to fossil specimens. Paleotemperatures were calculated using the isotopic values of 111 water samples (average -3.1‰) collected from the same sites along the Wakulla between 2022-2026. Temperatures reconstructed from live specimens averaged 21.0 °C, comparable to the average measured water temperature of 21.0 °C as measured by a USGS monitoring station at the headspring. Live V. usnea reconstructed temperatures (average 21.4 °C) are warmer than live E. floridensis (average 20.7 °C). Further work is needed to determine if this trend reflects differences in shell formation or geographic trends in temperature along the modern Wakulla River as live E. floridensis are present in the headspring and uppermost 5 km of the river but absent in the lower river where V. usnea are present and abundant. Reconstructed paleotemperatures from the fossil specimens averaged 17.5 °C, suggesting water temperatures have warmed by almost 4 °C from the Late Pleistocene to today. Assessing the use of freshwater gastropod shell isotopes in reconstructing a more complete paleotemperature history of the Wakulla River allows for more informed analysis of historical and ecological trends within the river in the context of shifting environmental conditions. This will allow us to better address future ecosystem impacts as water temperatures continue to rise.

abstract: The stability of carbon isotope values of sedimentary carbonates (δ 13 C carb ) is a defining factor of the mid-Proterozoic (ca. 1.8 to 0.8 Ga) and has been interpreted to reflect a relatively stable global carbon cycle during this interval. However, the emergence and diversification of early eukaryotes during this interval represents a major evolutionary milestone. Similar evolutionary milestones (e.g., radiation of eumetazoans during the Ediacaran period) have been linked to perturbations to the δ 13 C carb record. If primary, this stable δ 13 C carb record might indicate a prolonged interval of environmental stability providing a permissive setting for early diversification of eukaryotes. Alternatively, the apparent invariance of δ 13 C carb values may partially reflect resetting of the primary signal of the carbon cycle by post-depositional processes. Distinguishing these possibilities requires careful evaluation of diagenesis based on geochemical and petrographic evidence. We present δ 13 C carb and δ 18 O carb chemostratigraphy for the Waterton and Altyn formations, the oldest preserved sediments of the lower Belt-Purcell Supergroup (ca. 1.47 to 1.38 Ga) in Waterton Lakes National Park, Alberta, Canada. These strata comprise alternating limestones and dolostones deposited across carbonate ramp and platform environments. We combine isotopic measurements with carbonate trace element concentrations and petrographic observations to evaluate how diagenetic and local basin signals have shaped the geochemical record of these rocks. New δ 13 C carb data across different depositional environments from a previously unstudied mid-Proterozoic basin add to the still growing δ 13 C carb record of this interval. This study provides new insights into mid-Proterozoic carbon cycling, crucial to improving our understanding of the co-evolution of the Earth system and early eukaryotic life.
