title: Determining the Triple Oxygen Isotope Compositions of Potential Iron and Manganese Oxide-Rich Standard Reference Materials
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Havel, Riley [1], Nigro, Emily R. [2], Chen, Jiquan [3], Piccione, Gavin [4], Hodgin, Eben Blake [5], Ibarra, Daniel Enrique [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA
(2) Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA
(3) China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing, China
(4) Brown University, Providence, RI,
(5) Brown University, Providence, RI,
(6) Brown University, Providence, RI,
abstract:
Iron and manganese oxides are abundant in marine environments, low temperature continental environments, and ore deposits on Earth as well as across the surface of Mars. With empirical, experimental, and computational constraints on mineral-water oxygen isotope fractionation behavior, oxygen isotope compositions of iron oxides can be used to infer mineral formation conditions like temperature, pH, or formation and alteration fluid compositions. Oxygen isotope fractionation behavior for manganese oxide-water pairs, however, remains unconstrained. Furthermore, triple oxygen isotope measurements are increasingly being used to analyze a diversity of geologic and planetary materials with variable mineralogies.

Isotopic compositions of well-characterized standard reference materials (SRMs) are measured alongside samples. Measured SRM compositions are used to accurately determine sample compositions across laboratories and to assess systematic differences between analytical techniques. However, the mineralogies of triple oxygen isotope SRMs have historically been limited to primarily non-oxide phases, which may fail to reflect mineralogy-specific processing differences. In this work, we measure triple oxygen isotope compositions of five iron and manganese oxide-rich potential SRMs (KTS, Harvard 92649, FeMn-1, NOD-A-1, and YSBC28756-2008) using laser fluorination isotope ratio mass spectrometry (LF-IRMS). Additionally, we compile iron and manganese oxide-rich geologic samples’ δ′ 18 O (x=440) and δ′ 18 O-Δ′ 17 O (x=96) compositions from the literature and assess how triple oxygen isotope measurements can be used to reinterpret conclusions made based on δ′18O only. The range of isotopic compositions of the SRMs (δ′ 18 O = ~-3.13 to 10.85‰, Δ′ 17 O = ~-0.26 to -0.04‰) is representative of the range of most environmental iron and manganese oxide-rich samples. Therefore, these SRMs can be used to assess systematic differences across analytical methods and laboratories and to reliably determine the compositions of mineralogically similar geologic samples.

title: Investigating the Effects of Sulfur Abundance and Speciation on Triple Oxygen Isotope Measurements of Planetary Materials
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials
authors: Havel, Riley [1], Fischer, Emily [2], Salinas, Exiquio [3], Parman, Stephen W. [4], Ibarra, Daniel Enrique [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA; Institute at Brown for Environment and Society, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA
(2) Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
(3) Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA
(4) Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA
(5) Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
abstract:
Fluorination reactions are used to extract oxygen from rock-forming minerals for isotope measurements using gas-source isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS). In planetary science, triple oxygen isotope compositions reflect the origin and evolutionary history of planetary materials. High abundances of S in planetary materials like enstatite chondrites (ECs) (~4 wt%) and the Mercurian crust (up to ~4 wt%) can affect the stoichiometry of traditional fluorination reactions. Sulfur is highly reactive with fluorinating agents and can scavenge significant amounts of fluorine, such that oxygen is not able to be quantitatively extracted and converted to O 2 . Furthermore, oxygen may be incorporated into S-O-F reaction products, which are not measurable for triple oxygen isotope compositions using the conventional IRMS methods. Consequently, the overall impacts on oxygen yields induce isotope fractionation.

In ECs, sulfur primarily occurs in exotic, highly reduced sulfides such as CaS and MgS. Sulfur speciation is assumed to be similar on Mercury due to its inferred low oxygen fugacity. To better understand how sulfur abundance and speciation may influence triple oxygen isotope compositions of reduced, sulfur-rich planetary materials, we measured a suite of mixtures consisting of an andesite rock standard (JA-2), with chemistry similar to the surface of Mercury, and S or FeS, as well as synthesized glasses with Mercury-like compositions (0-4 wt% S) from high pressure, low oxygen fugacity experiments. To complement our experimental results, we also model potential reaction products formed during these fluorination reactions.

Here, we show how the triple oxygen isotope compositions of Mercury-like materials containing abundances of sulfur comparable to those found in ECs and on the surface of Mercury are influenced by the presence and speciation of sulfur. Our results indicate that measured triple oxygen isotope compositions may vary as much as ~3‰ in δ′ 18 O and ~0.1‰ in Δ′ 17 O, where more significant changes in composition generally correlate with higher S/O and F/O ratios. The shifts caused by the presence of sulfur have the potential to influence EC meteorite classifications made based only on triple oxygen isotopes, as well as interpretations that could be made if a sample of Mercury’s surface were to ever be measured. Finally, we provide general recommendations for data correction schemes based on sulfur abundance and speciation.

title: OneEarth: Earth Systems Analysis as a Fundamental Prerequisite for Next Generation AI Models
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Chuchla, Richard [1], Xiao, Yitian [2], Bouquet, Grant [3], Ye, Jieping [4], Chen, Hongyang [5]
affiliations: (1) GeoGPT Governance Committee, Hangzhou, China
(2) Deep-time Digital Earth Research Center of Excellence, Hangzhou, China
(3) Zhejiang Lab, Hangzhou, China
(4) Zhejiang Lab, Hangzhou, China
(5) Zhejiang Lab, Hangzhou, China
abstract:
To truly understand our planet and confront the immense challenges facing society, we need a way of thinking that is both holistic and integrative. Earth system science demands that we consider the interplay of all domains: the lithosphere, asthenosphere, mantle, and core; the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere, while recognizing that Earth itself is part of a larger cosmic system (solar system and the universe). Yet despite decades of progress, our ability to weave these threads into a coherent fabric of Earth remains limited.

Paradoxically, the challenge grows as our data grows. Nearly 750 Earth‑observing satellites now generate between 100 and 150 terabytes of data every day. This torrent of information is immensely valuable, but without a unifying framework, it risks overwhelming rather than enlightening us.

Our models remain siloed and limited to only a small part of the very highly dimensional nature of earth science. Earth is not a set of compartments. Likewise, A 4D Digital Earth platform is not a climate model, a basin model, a geodynamic model or an AI chatbot with maps. It is a unified, evolving, data‑assimilating representation of the earth system across space and time, built on a first principles understanding of physics, chemistry and biology. It has spatial intelligence and is orchestrated and driven by AI. It is a single, coupled, multi-scaled dynamic system. This is the scientific frontier and this is the goal of OneEarth.

OneEarth adopts an AI-native architecture in which artificial intelligence functions as a core orchestration, integration, and reasoning layer throughout the platform. AI is intended to not only process data, but to also connect observations, simulations, scientific literature, expert knowledge, and evolving earth system models within a continuously interacting scientific platform. Among the grand challenges that we can tackle in ways we could not before include climate change and strategies for climate resilience, resourcing future generations, water scarcity and soil erosion.

OneEarth will be open sourced to encourage equitable access to data and tools and to foster co-creation and improvement through iterative user feedback. Important building blocks like the 021 Large Science Model will be released as they are developed.

title: From Sediment Sink to Sediment Source: The Emptied Space Between Aeolis Mons and the Walls of Gale Crater, Mars
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Edgett, Kenneth S. [1]
affiliations: (1) Retired, Magnolia, TX, USA
abstract:
During descent and landing in 2012, the Curiosity rover passed through a volume of atmosphere previously occupied by kilometers-thick rock. Those rocks were coeval with mudstones and sandstones recording the lacustrine, shore, fluvial, and eolian facies composing Aeolis Mons, the 5-km-high stratified mountain inside the 154-km-diameter Gale crater.

The missing rocks indicate a profound environmental change. Before it, Gale was a net sediment sink. Water contributed to sediment retention and cementation. Afterward, Gale became a net source.

A second profound change, the ultimate drying of Mars, is indicated by the cessation of water erosion, debris flows, and the loss of pore fluids from Aeolis Mons’ rocks.

Most of the rock that occurred between the crater walls and present-day Aeolis Mons broke down and left Gale during the interval between these changes.

Clasts can exit Gale as distal impact ejecta or via wind. Wind dominates. Rocks are/were broken-down to sand-, silt-, and clay- sizes and removed in eolian suspension, if not also sand ramps and climbing dunes.

The stratified portion of Aeolis Mons is a remnant, not an “exhumed” landform. Its shape is related to its rock physical properties (the product of its depositional and diagenetic facies); and to rock breakdown and erosion via running water, mass movement, wind, impact cratering, and rock fracturing and displacement. These processes acted throughout the time Aeolis Mons was forming. Water dominated. Breakdown and erosion slowed, considerably, after water stopped flowing across the landscape.

Just as rivers supply most eolian sand (dunes) and silt (loess) on Earth, intracrater fluvial systems likely supplied most of the clasts transported by wind from Gale. Gediz Vallis—one of the preserved valleys on Aeolis Mons—illustrates. Gediz would have terminated in a sediment fan, but these materials were not retained (Bryk et al., 2026, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2026.117051). Ultimately, its clasts (derived from mudstone and sandstone) were removed by wind.

A tiny fraction of clasts liberated/produced from the missing rocks did not exit Gale. For example, the eolian Stimson sandstone, deposited unconformably on the lower north slope of proto-Aeolis Mons, pre-dates Gediz Vallis and may include recycled sands. Other unconformably-deposited rocks and sediments on Aeolis Mons, and between the mountain and crater walls, might also incorporate recycled clasts that never left Gale.

title: Differences in Physiological Tolerance to Global Warming Caused the Permian-Triassic Transition Between the Paleozoic and Modern Faunas
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Marquez, Jose Andres [1], Penn, Justin [2], Stockey, Richard G. [3], Boag, Thomas H. [4], Duncan, Murray Ian [5], McClure, Kyra N. [6], Matsumoto, Kendall [7], Ashing-Giwa, Kemi Folasade [8], Noll, Christopher P. [9], Deutsch, Curtis Anthony [10], Payne, Jonathan L. [11], Sperling, Erik A. [12]

abstract: The rapid global climate change at the end of the Permian Period (~251.9 million years ago) coincided with the greatest macroevolutionary faunal turnover event in Earth’s history. As the oceans warmed, lost dissolved oxygen, and became more acidic, the dominant animal groups in the Paleozoic fauna (including brachiopods and crinoids) suffered differentially high rates of extinction, allowing the Modern fauna (including bivalves and gastropods) to rise to ecological dominance. The end-Permian kill mechanism(s) are not fully understood, but differences in extinction intensity among Linnaean classes suggest an important physiological component. Here we use a trait-based model of species’ metabolic O 2 balance to demonstrate that temperature-dependent hypoxia can explain the taxonomic selectivity of the end-Permian mass extinction. Direct respirometry experiments and physiological trait estimates derived from biogeographic data reveal that species belonging to the Paleozoic fauna have a higher temperature dependence of hypoxia than those belonging to the Modern fauna. In simulations of the climate transition, this trait difference leads to a greater loss of aerobic habitat for Paleozoic fauna, consistent with their observed greater extinction intensity. These results demonstrate that differences in average physiological tolerances to environmental change across biogeography, taxonomy, and functional ecology drove end-Permian extinction patterns and could eventually characterize the modern biodiversity crisis. Temperature-dependent hypoxia is the only kill mechanism that has been shown to explain the magnitude, biogeography, and now taxonomic selectivity of the end-Permian mass extinction, ultimately underlying the permanent shift in marine ecosystems across this transition.

title: Pedogenesis in Modern and Ancient Erg Systems: The Balance Between Sediment Supply, Wind Power, Accommodation, Hydroclimate, and other factors, with examples from the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone, Utah
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science
authors: Hasiotis, Stephen T. [1], Parrish, Judith Totman [2], Chan, Marjorie A. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(2) University of Idaho, Viola, ID,
(3) University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,
abstract:
A surprising lack of integration exists between the literature on soil formation (i.e., pedogenesis) and modern ergs with the geological literature. Pedogenesis in ancient erg systems has been overlooked because the focus is typically on dune formation and wind modification of crossbeds, crossbed sets, and bounding surfaces. Here we review the bio-physicochemical factors that control soil formation in both modern and ancient erg systems, including examples from the Lower Jurassic Navajo Sandstone (Ss) of southern Utah.

Soil formation is a function of climate (Cl), organisms (O), relief (i.e., topography; R), parent material (P), and time (T). Of these, Cl and O are active factors, whereas R, P, and T are passive. Other contributing factors include the magnitude and frequency of depositional events, sedimentation rate and accumulation, distance from sediment source, duration of T between sedimentation events, and the hydrology and groundwater profile.

In modern and ancient erg settings, Cl is the most important factor because the amount of effective precipitation (EP) is controlled by the potential evapotranspiration, seasonality and amount of annual precipitation, and temperature. The abundance and diversity of O and the green and brown food webs are also controlled by Cl. Although dunes move, accumulate, degrade, and erode at different rates based on sediment supply, wind power, and accommodation, most occur in areas with < 150 mm of precipitation and some with < 100 mm or less. When effective precipitation exceeds these amounts for some T interval and pedogenesis outpaces sedimentation, soils of varying of maturity will develop.

The balance between sedimentation and pedogenesis in the Navajo Ss determined the types of soils that formed in the stratigraphic succession when EP was great enough to establish vegetation and support animals. When pedogenesis outpaced sedimentation for some extended period, a simple soil developed––immature to mature in features––which was subsequently buried by sedimentation. When sedimentation was nonsteady, compound, or composite soil successions resulted, reflecting increasing periods of pedogenesis vs. sedimentation and EP. When sedimentation was steady but outpaced by pedogenesis, a cumulative soil developed. This record of pedogenesis occurs mostly in interdune deposits and those bounded by complex surfaces.

More studies integrating paleosol processes in modern and ancient ergs has strong potential to help better understand the hydroclimate conditions in these complex continental systems in deep time.

title: Bedrock geology impacts dissolved inorganic carbon availability to snow algae blooms across the Western US
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Hamilton, Trinity L. [1]
affiliations: (1) Plant and Microbial Biology, University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN, USA
abstract: Snow algae are globally distributed photosynthetic microorganisms that contribute to snowmelt by lowering albedo. As photoautotrophs, snow algae require inorganic carbon, which is typically limited in snow. Here, we examined the role of carbonate bedrock in supplying inorganic carbon to snow algae by comparing biomass and snow from sites in the Rocky Mountains in the US with and without carbonate bedrock to sites in the Cascade Range where silicic rocks are devoid of carbonates. Snow algae were more abundant in sites with carbonates where dissolved inorganic carbon concentrations were higher due to carbonate dissolution and biomass degradation (heterotrophy). Both internal carbon cycling and allochthonous inputs, including carbonate bedrock, were important for snow algae abundance. Increasing atmospheric CO 2 is a positive feedback on snow algae bloom abundance and thus their impact on albedo, but additional sources of CO 2 can lead to bigger blooms that could impact melt and water resources.

abstract: I received an unidentified skull eight years ago from an unknown provenance. I have taken it upon myself to identify the specimen. I completed comparative morphological analysis on fossils, diagrams, scientific papers and casts. I have also completed comparative measurement on the skull using fossils, casts, and diagrams. I report a new genus and species of an Entelodontidae, Novaculatherum mccaehie gen. et sp. Nov. New taxa is represented by a nearly complete upper half of the skull. Among 12 points of study, the two most significant distinctions between N. mccaehie and other entelodonts are its unusually small and sharp incisors and its unusually large orbit size. I do not find that this is simply a juvenile Entelodon, because of the tooth wear patterns. The provenance is unknown. However, I suspect N. mccaehie to be from the White River formation, based on the matrix. This means N. mccaehie would have been in the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene.

title: Mechanical Characterization of the Mississippian Boone Formation: Experimental Constraints on Deformation and Damage Evolution in the Seneca Fault Zone
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems (Posters)
authors: Cotton, Steven Tyler [1], Chen, Xiaofeng [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
(2) Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
abstract: The Senaca Fault in northeastern Oklahoma exposes the Mississippian aged Boone Formation – limestone and chert as interbeds/nodules within a structurally complex dextral strike-slip graben system. While field mapping has documented fracture localization and lithology-controlled damage patterns, the mechanical controls on fracture initiation and propagation in these carbonates remain poorly constrained. This research will investigate and quantify the strength, failure behavior, frictional properties, and fracture-mechanical properties of the Boone Formation through a combination of triaxial compression experiments, triaxial shear, and fracture mechanics experiments. Laboratory-generated fracture geometries and attributes will be compared with field mapped natural fracture patterns to evaluate the role of existing fractures and mechanical stratigraphy in controlling damage-zone architecture. Intact limestone and chert cores, as well as compositely layered limestone-chert-limestone samples will be tested under varying confining pressures to quantify strength, failure behavior, frictional properties, fracture toughness, and subcritical cracking. The resulting deformed samples will be integrated with porosity and permeability measurements, micro-imaging such as XRD, SEM, and thin-section petrography analysis to characterize microcrack development, grain scale fracture mechanisms, and fracture tip processes. Laboratory-generated fracture geometries will be compared with field-mapped natural fracture patterns to evaluate the role of existing fractures and mechanical stratigraphy in controlling damage-zone architecture.

title: Snowball Earth and giant ore deposits: bastnäsite U-Th-Pb geochronology records Cryogenian overprinting of Mesoproterozoic Cu-U-Au-Ag-(REE) mineralization
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records
authors: Campo Rodriguez, Yuri Tatiana [1], Cook, Nigel J [2], Ciobanu, Cristiana L [3], Gilbert, Sarah [4], Ehrig, Kathy [5], Nasreen, Anwesha [6]
affiliations: (1) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(2) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(3) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(4) Adelaide Microscopy, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(5) Cooper S.A., BHP, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(6) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
abstract:
Bastnäsite is an important host of rare earth elements in many hydrothermal ore systems and commonly contains low, yet measurable concentrations of U, Th, and Pb. Despite this, its application as a geochronometer for dating rare earth element mineralization and hydrothermal events remains limited because of its variable Th/U ratios, compositional complexity, and low closure temperatures. When anchored by complementary mineral geochronometers targeting coexisting minerals and backed up by detailed petrographic and geochemical data, bastnäsite can nevertheless provide reliable ages for both primary mineralization and for a later remobilization event.

Oak Dam West is a uranium-bearing Mesoproterozoic iron oxide-copper-gold system in South Australia, which locally hosts significant concentrations of rare earths. Texturally and compositionally distinct generations of bastnäsite record two events separated by ca. 900 million years. Fine-grained, low-Th bastnäsite associated with skeletal hematite from deep levels in the low-sulfide central ‘core’ of the deposit yield U–Pb ages of ca. 1590 Ma, coincident with the U-Pb ages of coexisting hematite. In contrast, coarse rosette-textured, high-Th bastnäsite, characterized by strong positive Ce anomalies, yields Th–Pb ages of ca. 718–681 Ma. This younger generation of bastnäsite is restricted to relatively shallow levels of the orebody immediately beneath an unconformity. Coexisting hematite preserves the same 1590 Ma U-Pb age of its deeper analogues, emphasizing the robustness of hematite geochronology. The 718–681 Ma bastnäsite generation is associated with U-, Pb-, Cu-, and Te-bearing minerals, which all display evidence of alteration under oxidizing conditions.

These features support remobilization and reprecipitation of rare earths and other ore components by oxidized, CO₂-bearing fluids that infiltrated the upper parts of the orebody during the Sturtian glaciation. Deep penetration of subglacial meltwaters through 1 km of the superjacent Pandurra Formation and into bedrock was likely facilitated by reactivation of deep faults. Likewise, heat supplied by U decay in the ores and basement rocks may have promoted local convection and subsequent fluid–rock interaction. These results demonstrate that bastnäsite can preserve primary ore-forming events but also reveal younger low-temperature remobilization histories. More broadly, the new data suggest that Cryogenian glacial systems, like those that covered South Australia, likely promoted extensive oxidative fluid circulation and metal redistribution in Precambrian basement environments, significantly impacting on the distribution of elements in the ore.

title: Land use and natural resources exploitation in the Bisya and Salūt oasis (Sultanate of Oman) since the Bronze Age
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part II)
authors: Zerboni, Andrea [1], Pietrogrande, Sofia [2]
affiliations: (1) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra “A. Desio”, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Italy
(2) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra “A. Desio”, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Italy
abstract: We present the geomorphological and geoarchaeological survey of the Bisya and Salūt oasis in northern Oman, developed to investigate the long-term relationships between landscape evolution, water management, and land use in an arid environment. The survey integrates detailed field investigations, high-resolution drone photogrammetry, and multi-temporal satellite imagery. It reconstructs the geomorphological framework of the Wadi Sayfham system, including alluvial fans, pediments, and the Khabra silty deposits that provided suitable soils for agriculture, together with anthropogenic features such as the aflaj irrigation systems. A detailed analysis of the central sector of the historical oasis illustrates the spatial organisation of agricultural plots, terraces, field subdivisions, sunken fields, and irrigation structures associated with the long-lived settlement of Salūt. The survey documents the evolution of agricultural practices from the Bronze Age, when early water-harvesting systems and terracing were established, through the Iron Age introduction of the aflaj system, to subsequent phases of agricultural expansion and landscape modification. Multi-temporal remote sensing further reveals substantial changes in the extent and configuration of cultivated land over recent decades, largely driven by deep groundwater exploitation. By integrating geomorphological mapping with archaeological and remote sensing evidence, this contribution provides a comprehensive framework for understanding long-term human adaptation to environmental change and the co-evolution of landscapes and water management systems in oasis environments.

title: U-series isochron dating of last interglacial evaporites from the Dead Sea Deep Drilling Core: a two-component initial thorium model
session_title: U-series Disequilibrium Geochronology: Advances, Applications, and Emerging Frontiers
authors: Kiro, Yael [1], Goldstein, Steven L [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rehovot, Israel
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA
abstract:
Dating evaporite minerals by U-series methods remains challenging because halite and gypsum precipitate from hypersaline brines and typically incorporate both dissolved (initial) Th from the ambient brine and detrital Th. When both components are present in variable proportions, standard isochron approaches, which assume a single, uniform initial ²³⁰Th/²³²Th ratio, can yield inaccurate ages. This problem is particularly prevalent in lacustrine evaporites from hydrologically restricted and hypersaline lakes like the Dead Sea, where detrital input and dissolved Th concentrations in the brine are both significant.

We present a new U-series isochron framework developed for evaporitic sediments recovered from the Dead Sea Deep Drilling Project (DSDDP) core, targeting Last Interglacial (MIS 5e) intervals. Rather than relying on ²³²Th alone as a proxy for the detrital component, we incorporate measured niobium (Nb) concentrations as an independent geochemical tracer of the silicate detrital fraction. Nb is nearly immobile in aqueous systems, making it a robust proxy for detrital input. This allows us to explicitly partition total measured Th into (1) a detrital Th component tracked by Nb, and (2) an initial dissolved Th component derived from the Dead Sea brine at the time of mineral precipitation.

We derive modified isochron equations that account for both components simultaneously and apply them to a suite of evaporite samples spanning a range of detrital loadings. The resulting ages are consistent with the DSDDP age model, though uncertainties are high. The initial ²³⁰Th/²³²Th ratios recovered by the two-component model differ from the glacial initial ratios, indicating changes in source composition, Th solubility, and the residence time of uranium. This method offers a broadly applicable framework for U-series dating of evaporitic and other impure archives where both dissolved initial Th and detrital Th must be resolved.

title: Submarine groundwater discharge as a driver of ocean chemical budgets and glacial-interglacial climate feedbacks: implications for future sea-level rise
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Kiro, Yael [1], Sternberg, Ohad Shalom [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, Israel
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rehovot, Israel
abstract:
Understanding the sources and sinks of major elements to the ocean is fundamental to constraining climate, atmospheric CO₂, and biogeochemical feedback mechanisms across geological and anthropogenic timescales. Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD), the flow of water through coastal aquifers into the sea, represents a globally significant but historically underappreciated pathway of chemical exchange. By compiling a large dataset of coastal aquifer geochemistry, we quantify the long-term contribution of SGD to the ocean’s major-element budget. We demonstrate that long-term SGD acts as a net source in the Ca and Sr budgets, and as a net sink in the K and Na budgets, with flux magnitudes sufficient to influence ocean alkalinity and carbonate chemistry over geological timescales.

Because coastal aquifer fluxes are tightly coupled to sea-level change, SGD constitutes a geochemical feedback mechanism during glacial-interglacial cycles. Sea-level lowstands enhance outflux from coastal aquifers, acting as a source with a higher Ca/(K+Na) ratio and promoting CO 2 release, a negative feedback that slows glacial cooling. Conversely, sea-level highstands suppress SGD, reducing Ca input and facilitating CO 2 drawdown. Geometric estimates of aquifer-driven flux indicate potential increases or decreases by ~10% (given ~100 meters of sea level change in 5000 years, typical beach slope and hydrological gradient) in water and solute flux during sea-level changes. Using an ocean box model with end-member geochemistry, we calculate the effect on atmospheric CO 2 as a function of these flux changes, quantifying the magnitude of this negative feedback.

Looking forward, ongoing and projected sea-level rise is already suppressing coastal SGD globally. Using the same carbon-cycle ocean box model, we explore the transient consequences of declining SGD for ocean alkalinity and atmospheric CO 2 under sea-level rise. Our results suggest that, even on shorter time scales, given ocean mixing timescales, suppressed SGD acts to reduce atmospheric CO 2 . These findings position coastal aquifers as dynamic participants in the global carbon cycle and highlight the need to incorporate SGD variability into projections of future ocean chemistry.

abstract: Abrupt millennial-scale climate variability during MIS 5d–5a is well documented in Greenland ice cores, North Atlantic marine records, and speleothem records from Europe and East Asia, but comparable terrestrial records from North America remain scarce. Here we present a new multi-proxy stalagmite record from Crevice Cave, Missouri, spanning ~112.3 to ~75 ka. This record integrates carbonate δ 18 O with TEX 86 and dual clumped isotopes (Δ 47 –Δ 48 ) thermometry to assess how the early Wisconsin glaciation was expressed in the North American midcontinent. Temperature changes are recorded during Dansgaard–Oeschger events 24–21, Heinrich events 10–7b, cool surface ocean events 22 and 24, and precursor events 23 and 24. Temperature reconstructions exhibit amplitudes that approximate those observed in Greenland, with the largest variability occurring during late MIS 5d (~10°C). This record demonstrates that abrupt climate oscillations similar in magnitude to events in Greenland affected the continental interior of North America.

title: Holocene cave sediments reveal early human impacts on the Earth's Critical Zone
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution
authors: Zerboni, Andrea [1], Forti, Luca [2]
affiliations: (1) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra “A. Desio”, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Italy
(2) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra “A. Desio”, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Italy
abstract: Underground karst systems are highly sensitive components of the Earth's Critical Zone (ECZ), preserving sedimentary archives that record interactions among climate, hydrology, geomorphic processes, and human land use. In the Apennines (Italy), Holocene cave sediments provide evidence of both natural environmental variability and increasing anthropogenic influence on Critical Zone dynamics. Alternating phases of clastic sedimentation, sedimentary hiatuses, and speleothem growth reflect changes in karst hydrology driven by Holocene climatic fluctuations. From the mid-Holocene onward, however, cave deposits record a marked increase in charcoal fragments and heated soil aggregates, indicating enhanced soil erosion linked to human activities. These deposits coincide with the archaeological evidence for the expansion of farming and pastoral practices during later prehistory, when forest clearance and slash-and-burn land management accelerated hillslope erosion and sediment transfer from the surface into the karst system. The resulting cave stratigraphy demonstrates how early land use modified sediment fluxes and altered the functioning of the Critical Zone well before the industrial era. This study highlights the value of cave sedimentary archives for reconstructing long-term interactions among climate, geomorphic processes, vegetation change, and human activities, providing new insights into the role of prehistoric societies in shaping Critical Zone evolution across Mediterranean mountain landscapes.

title: Arsenic as a Pathfinder for Critical Mineral Resources in Groundwater Systems: A Hydrogeochemical Case Study from the Atacama Region of Chile
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part I)
authors: Alam, Mohammad Ayaz [1], Bhattacharya, Prosun [2]
affiliations: (1) Departamento de Ingeniería Geoespacial y Ambiental, Universidad de Santiago de Chile, Santiago, Región Metropolitana de Santiago, Chile

abstract:
Arsenic mobilized in groundwater is typically framed as a health contaminant, yet its geochemical behavior also encodes information about buried or weathering mineralization. In arid, mineralized terranes such as northern Chile's Atacama Region (III Region), arsenic released through sulfide oxidation, volcanic-hydrothermal alteration, and evaporative concentration in closed basins co-mobilizes with critical and strategic elements, including boron, lithium, molybdenum, selenium, antimony, and rare earth elements. This makes arsenic distribution a practical pathfinder for identifying zones of enhanced critical-mineral potential alongside associated groundwater risk.

This study integrates regional hydrogeochemical data from groundwater and surface-water systems of the Copiapo and Salado basins with mineralogical context from adjacent porphyry copper and epithermal districts. We evaluate covariation between dissolved arsenic and co-occurring trace elements across redox and salinity gradients, applying multivariate statistics and geochemical modeling to distinguish sulfide-oxidation, geothermal, and evaporitic sources. Preliminary results show arsenic anomalies correlating spatially with elevated boron and lithium near basin margins influenced by hydrothermal input, while sulfide-hosted zones display tighter As-Sb-Mo associations tied to weathering of mineralized bedrock.

We propose a framework combining pathfinder-element hydrogeochemistry with predictive spatial modeling to simultaneously delineate groundwater arsenic risk for water-resource management in a water-scarce region and prioritize areas of critical-mineral exploration interest. This dual-use approach offers a transferable template for other arid, mineralized basins where water security and mineral resource development intersect.

title: Microplastic Degradation and Interactions with Iron Redox in a Simulated Martian Agriculture Environment
session_title: Planetary Potpourri (Posters)
authors: Zager, Madelyn Rose [1], Clements, Jacob William [2], McKinney, Michael [3], Schaeffer, Sean [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA

(3) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA

abstract:
Human-manned missions to Mars are planned by agencies such as NASA and CNSA for the 2030s. A human presence is already detectable on Mars, with microplastics (MPs) left behind from high-durability plastics comprising various parts of the six successfully landed rovers. The effects of MP presence in Mars regolith are unknown and may alter the Fe speciation in regolith potentially used for agriculture in Mars colonies. We aim to quantify the changes to Mars regolith simulant (MGS-1) in the presence of Rover-derived plastics and agriculturally relevant MPs. To our knowledge, this is among the first experimental studies to test how anthropogenic polymer materials alter acid-extractable iron speciation, and thus agricultural properties in MGS-1.

We simulated Martian conditions by degrading six relevant MPs with Martian-intensity UVC light: polypropylene, Kapton, Teflon, Nylon, Kevlar, and PBAT. These were incubated for three weeks in MGS-1 and 0.1M MgSO 4 brine. We included compost-amended replicates, introducing a microbial community likely present in future Martian agriculture. We injected pure CO 2 into the incubation vessels to simulate the CO 2 -rich atmosphere of Mars. To simulate the temperature extremes of Mars, we incubated replicates at -80°C and 20°C. Every three weeks for nine weeks, we quantified Fe using a ferrozine colorimetric method, pH with a pH probe, and DOC using a Mn(III) pyrophosphate colorimetric method.

Preliminary three-week results reveal an increase in the average extractable Fe(III) concentrations in every MP treatment excluding Teflon, with pH increasing for MP treatments excluding PBAT and Nylon, indicating a shift towards Fe(II) oxidation. Teflon treatment showed a decrease in the average extractable Fe(III) compared to the control. The pH of Nylon and PBAT treatments was acidified relative to the control, with Nylon showing the greatest increase in average Fe(II) concentration, indicating a reduction in total extractable Fe. Among the six treatments, there was no significant variance in the average extracted DOC when compared to the control. Therefore, DOC release and contamination fail to explain the shifts in the Fe speciation, with the possibility of Fe(III) forming complexes with DOC. Importantly, our preliminary results suggest Rover-derived and agriculturally-relevant MPs are shifting the extractable Fe redox ratios and pH of MGS-1 regolith, indicating possible soil acidification in simulated Martian environments.

title: Reconciling metamorphic pressures in Sevier hinterland metamorphic core complexes by extensional reactivation of a major Sevier thrust ramp: An example from the Raft River-Albion-Grouse Creek metamorphic core complex, western United States
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Jacobs, Cole B. [1], Wells, Michael L. [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
abstract:
The Raft River-Albion-Grouse Creek (RAG) metamorphic core complex (MCC) is one of over 25 recognized MCCs in the Cordilleran orogenic belt. Passive-margin strata within these MCCs record mid- to deep-crustal burial depths in their metamorphic pressures (6–10 kbar) and temperature conditions, which equate to approximately two- to three times that of stratigraphic thickness, requiring significant tectonic burial. However, contractional structures with sufficient stratigraphic throw to account for the recorded metamorphic pressures are in some cases not recognized, leading to the proposal that tectonic overpressure contributed to produce the elevated metamorphic pressures. We present field relationships from the Albion Mountains that instead support later extensional reactivation of originally large-displacement Mesozoic thrusts, which can help to explain these pressure discrepancies.

The central and northern Albion Mountains in the RAG MCC of southern Idaho and northern Utah preserve a major Sevier hinterland thrust: the Basin-Elba fault (BEF). The BEF emplaced allochthonous Neoproterozoic to Cambrian quartzite packages to the east over Cambrian to Ordovician passive-margin strata beginning in the earliest Cretaceous (138–132 Ma), followed by a period of reactivation at 85 Ma, as indicated by Lu-Hf garnet isochron ages. Tracing the southern continuation of the BEF is complicated by the abundance of amphibolite-facies quartzites and marbles lacking distinctive characteristics, making correlations with regional stratigraphic units by traditional mapping methods difficult. Consequently, its relationship to the structurally higher, top-west, polyphase (Eocene to Miocene) extensional Middle Mountain shear zone (MMSZ) and associated Middle detachment has remained unclear. We combined 1:10,000 scale geologic mapping with U-Pb detrital zircon geochronology in a critical ~85 km 2 area in the central Albion Mountains that has both the BEF and MMSZ. Our mapping results (1) identify previously unrecognized Cambrian stratigraphy, which supports its removal via low-angle normal faulting in the southern RAG MCC, and (2) delineates the eastern mylonitic front of the top-west-northwest fabrics associated with the MMSZ. These results indicate that the base of the MMSZ is localized in the BEF footwall and that extensional reactivation of the BEF can reconcile observed metamorphic pressures. More broadly, major Sevier hinterland crustal ramps and their associated thrust loads may be similarly masked by extensional reactivation in other metamorphic core complexes where metamorphic pressures appear anomalously high relative to preserved contractional structures.

title: Build like a Beaver: Comparing Hydraulic Parameters between Beaver Dams and Beaver Dam Analogs (BDAs) to Improve Restoration Effectiveness
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Bojdak-Yates, Itai S [1], Rathburn, Sara [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: Beavers instinctively dam low-order streams, altering the hydrology, geomorphology, water chemistry, and ecology of streams and valley bottoms. The resulting positive effects on water and sediment attenuation, flood and fire mitigation, and biodiversity are driving broad implementation of beaver-based stream restoration and construction of beaver dam analogs (BDAs). However, key hydraulic parameters of both BDAs and natural beaver dams remain ill-constrained, limiting practitioners’ ability to effectively design and implement restoration projects. Our research quantifies and constrains values of permeability, hydraulic roughness, and water residence time for natural beaver dams and BDAs. We collected data from 12 BDAs and 5 beaver dams across five stream reaches in the northern Front Range, Colorado, USA. Field data consisted of discharge measurements, depth transects, surveys of pond area and dam dimensions, and salt slug tracer tests. Preliminary results indicate that beaver dams have Manning’s n roughness values between 1.2 and 12.4, while BDAs have roughness values between 0.6 and 2.4 (compared to values of 0.03-0.08 for undammed mountain streams). Residence times vary from 2-11 minutes for BDA ponds (n=5) and from 4-38 minutes for beaver ponds (n=5). In short, BDAs tend to have lower roughness values, shorter residence times, and greater permeability compared to natural beaver dams, but increased stream roughness and transit time compared with undammed channels. BDA and beaver dam roughness, permeability, and transit time vary widely with stream discharge and structure design. These differences have important implications for BDA-based restoration efforts and suggest that BDA construction, while often effective, could be improved at many sites to better mimic beaver dams.

title: Suspended Sediment Transport Regimes in Urban Streams are Governed by Natural and Human-Modified Sediment Supply
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Jefferson, Anne J. [1], Safdar, Suffiyan [2], Underwood, Kristen [3]
affiliations: (1) Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
(2) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA

abstract: Urbanization reshapes stream channels and sediment supply, and this transformation often degrades ecosystems and threatens infrastructure. To reduce these environmental and economic costs, understanding suspended sediment supply and transport is essential. We combined geospatial analysis of 117 US urban watersheds with a combined 50,000 storm events for which turbidity and discharge data were available. We found that the longitudinal distribution of geomorphometry, soil texture, and riparian impervious cover, which we called the erosion and sediment supply potential (ESSP) index, is associated with four distinct suspended sediment transport regimes, characterized by their hysteresis behavior. The ESSP index was validated with field mapping in three Ohio urban streams, where bedrock outcrops and hardened reaches modulated sediment dynamics. The national analysis also revealed that suspended sediment response (turbidity-discharge slope) is suppressed in watersheds with >40% imperviousness, likely due to extensive channel hardening. This result was validated in a Vermont urban watershed, where stream burial reduced suspended sediment loads in a >40% impervious tributary, relative to the mainstem where mostly natural banks were present. Stormwater management also modulated suspended sediment response across a range of storm sizes. Combined, our results show that infrastructure- and geologically-mediated bank sediment supply governs suspended sediment transport regimes in urban streams, pointing the way to strategies for proactive management that protects communities and the environment.

title: XTL CIF-AR: Teaching Crystallography with Augmented Reality
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Lee, Trey Olen [1], Thompson, Elizabeth Colette [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
(2) Department of Earth & Environmental Systems, The University of the South, Sewanee, TN, USA
abstract:
Among the general population, the capacity for retaining and manipulating visual information is highly variable, and approximately one in 25 people has aphantasia, i.e., the inability to internally visualize (Dance et al. 2022). Introductory geology and mineralogy courses typically teach crystallographic structures using a limited number of physical ball-and-stick models, supplemented by desktop programs such as VESTA. Unfortunately, neurodiverse students may struggle to analyze and describe structures they cannot physically interact with. Virtual Reality (VR) has been used to visualize molecular structures, but these applications are typically optimized for molecular engineering professionals rather than the classroom and are not compatible with Crystallographic Information Files or CIFs —the standard format of the International Union of Crystallography.

We built a Unity application named XTL CIF-AR for visualizing crystal structures in augmented reality (AR). XTL CIF-AR allows students to manually manipulate and measure crystal structures, bridging the gap between the observational skills developed in introductory physical geology courses and the abstract visualization required for mineralogy and crystallography. It parses the CIF format and renders the atomic structure in 3D. Users can interact with the structure by orbiting, panning, zooming, and measuring interatomic distances. Crystal metadata, such as the space group, crystal system, and cell dimensions, are displayed as an in-scene overlay. Additional features visualize lattice planes to enable teaching Miller indices and the ability to see unit volume change as a function of pressure. We will use this presentation to demo the program (a free beta is available), share example companion lesson plans, and discuss the potential impact of AR applications for enhancing learning outcomes in classrooms.

C.J. Dance, A. Ipser, and Simner J. The prevalence of aphantasia (imagery weakness) in the general population. Consciousness and Cognition, 97:103243, January 2022. doi:10.1016/j.concog.2021.103243.

abstract: Future changes in high latitude shrubification are expected to amplify warming. However, the elevational range and climate sensitivity of shrubification is poorly constrained, which hinders our ability to tune predictive Earth system models. To constrain these variables, we leverage multiple lake sediment records that span low to high elevations in Iceland (151 to 422 m asl), birch ( Betula ) ancient DNA, and mean summer air temperature (MST) reconstructed from bacterial lipids. Our data show that Holocene Thermal Maximum MSTs were up to 2.3 o C warmer than present. At this time, birch woodlands quickly spread into low elevation area and were even present in highland lake catchments (>420 m asl), significantly higher than their current regional limit (250 to 350 m asl). During the Middle and Late Holocene, birch generally persisted around the lakes until its disappearance in the last millennium due to Little Ice Age summer cooling. Our findings demonstrate that climate, rather than human impact, has been the dominant Holocene control on Icelandic woodland cover and are therefore ideal constraints for Earth system models. Using Holocene Thermal Maximum warmth as a partial analog for future climate change, model ensemble climate projections suggest that the re-expansion of birch to higher elevations is likely by 2100 CE.

title: Wildfire and River Restoration: Assessing Potential Impacts and Risks to Projects
session_title: Understanding and Facilitating River Corridor Resilience to Wildfire
authors: Windoloski, Sara [1], Sudman, Zach [2], Johnston, Gardner [3], Iskin, Emily [4]
affiliations: (1) Inter-Fluve, Hood River, OR, USA
(2) Rio Applied Science & Engineering, Boise, Idaho, USA
(3) Inter-Fluve, Hood River, OR, USA

abstract: River restoration activities are growing in number, size, and complexity at the same time as wildfires are growing in number, size, and intensity. Fire and river restoration are not inherently at odds, however. When collocated, fire can directly burn project elements (wood and vegetation) and indirectly enhance or detract from projects via increased runoff, debris flows, sediment loading, and wood loading. Functioning river corridors can act as fire breaks, provide refuge, and attenuate runoff, sediment, and wood, but context such as river corridor width, pre-fire fuel loading, and fire intensity can influence local outcomes. It is important to consider the potential direct and indirect impacts of wildfire and the risk of the impacts occurring during the early stages of restoration planning in (recently) unburned watersheds. With support and leadership from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, we developed a GIS-based methodology using existing wildfire hazard and other national datasets that characterize the susceptibility of a site to increased debris flows, wood loading, sediment loading, and altered runoff conditions. Our goal is to help practitioners assess potential risks to a project if wildfire was to occur at the site or in its contributing basin. We applied the methodology to three case study sites in Oregon and Washington: Phipps Meadow, Lookingglass Creek, and the Chiwawa River. Phipps Meadow has a low overall risk of potential wildfire-related response. Both Lookingglass Creek and the Chiwawa River have varied risks of potential wildfire-related responses, ranging from low to high. These results and feedback compiled from project partners indicate that the methodology provides quality planning-level data prior to a wildfire occurring in a watershed. The methodology does not, however, consider site-specific routing of fire-related impacts, and therefore watershed-specific knowledge must be employed to interpret the results. The outputs should not be used to prioritize site selection and should instead be used for planning once a site has been chosen. Since the methodology makes use of publicly-available national datasets, we encourage practitioners to use it to assess the potential impacts of wildfire in watersheds slated for restoration anywhere in the United States. Future work will compare the outputs of the methodology with the actual observed effects of the 2026 wildfire season on restoration projects in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Helium Isotope Evidence for Mantle Fluid Contribution to Au-Ag Ores, from Crushing and Stepwise Heating of Gangue Minerals in The Low Sulfidation Epithermal Deposits of The Northern Great Basin (NGB).

abstract: Recent studies within the Northern Great Basin (NGB) confirm a likely genetic association between the Au-Ag epithermal deposits and early Yellowstone hotspot activity. The earliest manifestation of the Yellowstone plume magmatism is interpreted to be recorded by mafic magmatism of the Steens Mountain Basalt at 16.58 ± 0.18 Ma (Brueseke et al., 2007). Pb isotope compositions of trace Pb alloyed with gold, together with 40 Ar/ 39 Ar adularia ages, further correspond to signatures of the earliest Yellowstone plume basalts (Kamenov et al., 2007). Combined crushing and two-step heating experiments on quartz and adularia from mineralized veins in the Silver City District, Idaho, and Fire Creek in Nevada reveal 3 He/ 4 He ratios normalized to the atmospheric ratio (Ra) that suggest a substantial contribution of mafic magmatic volatiles to the ore forming fluids. Crushing analyses of five samples (two quartz separates and three adularia separates) from the two deposits yield 3 He/ 4 He (R/Ra) ratios ranging from ~2.4 – 11 Ra, well above typical crustal values (~0.02 Ra). This therefore suggests a significant input of mantle derived volatiles (≥8 Ra) in the gold bearing fluids. The quartz samples recorded the lowest ratios (5.64 Ra and 2.4 Ra for Trade dollar and Fire Creek veins, respectively), while all the adularia samples show R/Ra values consistent within uncertainty, with magmatic-mantle volatile sources. Two heating steps at 600°C and 900°C applied to the crushed residue produce greatly elevated R/Ra values accompanied by reduced 4 He concentrations relative to the crushing measurements. These high 3 He/ 4 He ratios arise from a combination of minor primary fluid inclusions and high 3 He in interstitial or lattice sites not accessed during the crushing step. The elevated ratios may therefore reflect a possible mixture of magmatic 3 He and nucleogenic 3 He produced by thermal neutron capture on 6 Li. These initial findings provide new important constraints on the origin of Au-Ag rich fluids in these low sulfidation epithermal systems and help quantify the contribution of deep mantle derived magmatic volatiles, their role in the transport of ore metals and epithermal deposit formation.

abstract: River corridors are essential to life, but have been subjected to centuries of alteration, disconnection, and simplification. Process-based river restoration has increased in recent years, with the goals of reversing degradation and reestablishing natural processes. Our objectives are twofold: (a) qualify the historic, ecologic, and geomorphic contexts of eight U.S. projects with information gathering, and (b) quantify the causal impact of treatments on remotely-sensed floodplain vegetation with counterfactual analysis. The most frequent goals were to increase connectivity and support beaver, and the most frequent degradation drivers were grazing/agriculture and beaver removal. There is a >99% probability that treatment increased the floodplain area of vegetation in Oregon at Bridge Creek by an average of 20%, at Whychus Creek by 21%, and at Lost Creek by 29%; and in Idaho at the Yankee Fork by 8%. There is no evidence that treatments affected vegetation area in Idaho at Baugh Creek (>90% probability); or in Colorado at either the South Fork South Platte River (>70% probability) or Fourmile Creek (>70% probability). There is a >90% probability that treatment decreased vegetation area in Idaho at Tincup Creek by 12%. Additional study is needed to determine how key characteristics, such as ecoregion and land use intensity, influence outcomes. We recommend that restoration monitoring pair remote sensing with local knowledge and field data collection to fully measure treatment effects. As ongoing restoration projects mature, our study can serve as a roadmap for further investigation into the long-term outcomes of river restoration.

abstract: Carbon on Enceladus is theorized to exchange between three reservoirs: mineral phases, seawater, and hydrothermally generated gases. Understanding how carbon moves between these reservoirs is essential for interpreting the carbon cycle of Enceladus's subsurface ocean, as well as its implications for habitability. This study measures dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentration in a synthetic Enceladus-analog seawater reacted separately under anoxic conditions with forsterite and a carbonaceous chondrite simulant. A set of incubations were also inoculated with Shewanella oneidensis to test microbial impact on Enceladus carbon cycling. The seawater and headspace carry their own initial carbon load: the seawater is prepared as a compositional analog to Enceladus ocean water and contains DIC, while the anoxic headspace contains CO₂ equilibrated with analog seawater. To test carbon exchange between these reservoirs, we combined each mineral with seawater and monitored DIC concentration and headspace CO₂ concentrations over a 5-day incubation. DIC concentrations were quantified by acidifying analog-seawater samples on a Schlenk line and measuring the resulting CO₂ pressure via transducer. Similarly, a fixed volume of headspace gas was withdrawn at each time point to quantify headspace CO₂ using the same approach. Preliminary results show that both headspace CO₂ and seawater DIC concentration changed significantly over the course of incubation in forsterite and chondrite treatments, with the largest change in DIC concentration evident in Shewanella- inoculated incubations. This indicates that carbon actively exchanges among the mineral, brine, microbe, and headspace reservoirs. The magnitude of DIC and headspace CO 2 change varies by treatment and appears to depend on a combination of factors, including mineral identity and the presence of microbes in the system. These results indicate that carbon cycling in this system is more complex than a simple mineral-dissolution model predicts, and additional experiments are underway to isolate the specific processes responsible for the observed carbon exchange.

title: Testing Mohometry Calibrations using Trace Elements in Plutonic Clinopyroxene, Cascades Crystalline Core, WA
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Posters)
authors: Brodie, Emily [1], Ardill, Katie Erin [2], Ratschbacher, Barbara [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(2) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(3) German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR), Hannover, Germany
abstract:
The crustal thickness of ancient magmatic arcs is an important parameter influencing economic deposits, volcanic hazards, and sediment pathways. Trace element proxies, or “mohometers”, like Sr/Y and La/Yb are used to estimate paleo-crustal thickness and are hypothesized to indicate the presence or absence of garnet in the lower crust. However, Sr/Y and La/Yb signatures can be modified by magmatic processes such as fractionation and crystal accumulation. Mineral analysis of clinopyroxene (CPX) from plutonic rocks is an alternative approach to exploring petrologic-mohometric relationships; its utility relies on the CPX preserving a geochemical snapshot of lower crustal melt chemistry prior to modification by magmatic processes.

Three Late Cretaceous plutons in the Northern Cascades, WA, emplaced between 3–30 km, were studied to determine if Sr/Y and La/Yb ratios from CPX and their equilibrium melt compositions represent reliable paleo-crustal thickness proxies. Geologic evidence, including magmatic epidote, metamorphic rocks, and estimates of crustal shortening, indicate that the crust reached ~55 km in the Late Cretaceous (e.g. Miller et al. 2001), consistent with garnet-presence. Bulk rock Rare Earth Element patterns display HREE depletion (<10x chondrites) consistent with removal of a garnet-bearing magma.

The Mount Stuart and Black Peak plutons contain clinopyroxene with diverse textures, including relict CPX cores in hornblende, euhedral and anhedral CPX reacting with hornblende, and granular CPX in plagioclase. CPX equilibrium melt compositions were calculated using the Higgins et al. (2022) model. The clinopyroxenes formed at temperatures between 935-1070 ºC from basaltic to dacitic melts. Some CPX grew in melts similar to their bulk rock equivalent, while others grew in a more felsic melt. Petrographically, CPX samples that are out of equilibrium with their bulk rock are anhedral, embayed, and/or display reaction rims of hornblende. Disequilibrium indicates that crystal accumulation and melt loss did affect some of the bulk rock compositions. Thus, the bulk rock proxies may not reflect the true crustal thickness. Trace element melt compositions from CPX will be examined for signs of garnet presence and therefore whether a record of lower crustal melt chemistry is preserved. The study of melt compositions calculated from minerals such as CPX offers new insight into the early magmatic history contained within plutonic samples and how individual minerals can be utilized in mohometric calculations.

title: Investigating the response of Glycymeris septentrionalis (Bivalvia) and Terebratalia transversa (Brachiopoda) to euxinia: Implications for mass extinctions
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Ashing-Giwa, Kemi Folasade [1], Payne, Jonathan L. [2], Sperling, Erik A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
(2) Earth & Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
(3) Earth & Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
abstract: In the wake of the end-Permian mass extinction, bivalves replaced articulate brachiopods as the dominant benthic marine filter-feeders, despite morphological and ecological similarities. Several factors have been suggested as drivers of the extinction's selectivity, including competition, ocean acidity, CO 2 poisoning, and differing reproductive potential. The spread of sulfidic water (euxinia) has been proposed as a general kill mechanism, but its physiological selectivity has not been investigated. Survival studies of the co-occurring bivalve Glycymeris septentrionalis and articulate brachiopod Terebratalia transversa from San Juan Island, Washington, USA, were carried out in anoxic and euxinic environments at 13.7, 16, and 22°C. In colder anoxic conditions without sulfide, the brachiopod exhibited greater survival than the bivalve, but at higher temperatures, the bivalve generally outlasted the brachiopod, and by a greater margin in euxinia. The alignment between physiological tolerance in experimental settings and survival patterns in the paleontological record indicates that euxinia may have played a role in end-Permian extinction severity and selectivity, serving as an additional stressor in already warm, oxygen-depleted oceans.

title: Metagenomic Characterization of Microbial Diversity in Drinking Groundwater in Lusaka, Zambia
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: Nchimunya, Muzila [1], Mutiti, Samuel [2]
affiliations: (1) Biological and Environmental Sciences, Georgia Colleges & State University, Milledgeville, Georgia, USA; Geology and Environmental Earth Sciences, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) Biological and Environmental Sciences, Georgia College & State University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Groundwater is a critical source of drinking water and national water security. However, in many developing countries, its exploitation and management remain poorly managed and regulated, increasing vulnerability to contamination. In rapidly urbanizing cities, drinking water boreholes within different geological formations may be particularly susceptible to contamination from inadequate sanitation infrastructure and the transport of microbial pollutants through groundwater systems. This study characterized groundwater bacterial communities using a metagenomic approach based on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing (V3–V4 region) on the Oxford Nanopore Technologies platform. Water samples collected from drinking water boreholes in planned and unplanned settlements underlain by carbonate and schist formations were analyzed to profile microbial communities and assess relative microbial risk using a Relative Microbial Risk Index (RMRI). Microbial community composition varied according to geological setting, while groundwater from unplanned settlements exhibited higher pathogen abundance and elevated RMRI values. Across all samples, the phylum Pseudomonadota dominated, primarily represented by the classes Gammaproteobacteria and Betaproteobacteria. Other abundant phyla included Actinomycetota and Bacillota. Species-level analysis identified opportunistic pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii , Klebsiella pneumoniae , and Salmonella enterica , along with environmentally persistent taxa including Dechloromonas sp. A34, Acinetobacter lwoffii , Acinetobacter nosocomialis , and Klebsiella variicola . Fecal indicator bacteria, including Escherichia coli , Shigella flexneri , and Enterococcus faecalis , were also detected, suggesting potential fecal contamination of groundwater sources. Multivariate analyses revealed that geological setting was strongly associated with microbial community structure, while groundwater from unplanned settlements relying on pit latrines exhibited microbial profiles distinct from those of planned settlements served by septic systems. These findings highlight significant public health risks associated with untreated groundwater use and underscore the need for improved groundwater policies, community education, sanitation infrastructure, routine monitoring, and hydrogeologically informed water safety management strategies.

title: Applications and Workflows of LA-ICP-ToFMS for High-Speed Petrochronology
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications
authors: Adamson, Morgan [1], Cottle, John [2], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [3], Seward, Gareth [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(3) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(4) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
abstract: Matching trace-element concentrations with isotope-ratio dates is invaluable for deciphering the complex growth and thermal histories of minerals and mineral populations. These petrochronologic interpretations are greatly aided by detailed knowledge of the spatial context but are currently limited to either low-spatial-resolution spot data or maps that are time-consuming and expensive to produce. The advancement of laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometers (LA-ICP-ToFMS) has enabled rapid, quasi-simultaneous multi-mass acquisition for element and isotope-ratio quantification, sampling at <5 µm pixel resolution and 1000 Hz. Here, we benchmark ToFMS as a quantitative approach for petrochronologic investigations. We first develop a theoretical sampling model to optimize laser and mass spectrometer parameters and examine the interplay between sampling parameters, spatial resolution, and elemental concentration across a range of realistic measurement conditions. Guided by these theoretical constraints, we use a suite of reference glasses and minerals to assess the accuracy, precision, and reproducibility of elemental concentrations and isotopic dates. The utility of this high-throughput ToFMS workflow for rapidly interrogating trace-element and isotope-ratio zoning and mineral-phase classification is demonstrated by analysis of natural garnet, zircon, and REE-mineralized domains. These results show that LA-ICP-ToFMS complements EPMA and QMS analyses by providing a rapid, full-mass-range, spatially correlated geochemical context for an array of materials with geologically useful accuracy and precision. Finally, we developed a user-friendly software package that enables the application of a suite of spatial statistics to interrogate the large datasets of minerals and mineral populations generated by the ToFMS method.

title: From Rock to Print: Identifying key morphological features in Peltosauria with the use of 3D printing techniques and CT scan data.
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research (Posters)
authors: Dewitt, Dylan M [1], Peters, Nathaniel [2], Saulsbury, Pat [3]
affiliations: (1) High Plains Paleontology, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, USA; Dinosaur Ridge, Morrison, Colorado, USA
(2) High Plains Paleontology, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, USA
(3) High Plains Paleontology, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, USA
abstract:
3D printing technology is at the forefront of various paleontological methods and purposes, including educational outreach, non-invasive analysis, reconstruction, preservation, and specimen accessibility, to name a few.

For this study, we used Computer-Aided Design (CAD) files from a Peltasaur skull put under a CT scanner, and with the use of 3D printing through fused deposition modeling, we were able to successfully produce a high-resolution model that was able to be identified as said species by directly observing unique morphological traits present. Utilizing this technology has allowed the possibility of analyzing and identifying specimens normally under hard matrix by the use of standard commercial 3D printers.

The potential use of this technique could open the door for other specimens that previously were too small and under hard matrix, to be more easily identified and accessible through means previously thought not possible. Compared to traditional casts, 3D printing is much more affordable for smaller institutions, and the freedom it offers allows multiple copies to be made without the significant cuts to funding and logistics that typical resin casts entail. The ability to take a direct scan and create a 3D physical copy for viewing and research offers the potential to examine previously unknown specimens encased in difficult-to-prepare rock with the same resolution and clarity as any other prepared specimens. The overall findings highlight the untapped potential for new research insights to be gained through specimens once thought too difficult to view/prepare.

title: Scientific Highlights of the MAHLI Investigation After 15 Years on Mars
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Yingst, R Aileen [1], Minitti, Michelle E [2], Malin, Michael [3], Bennett, Kristen [4], Herkenhoff, Kenneth [5], Kah, Linda C [6], Rowland, Scott [7], Schieber, Jurgen [8], Weitz, Catherine [9], Cowart, Aster [10], Fey, Deirdra [11], Henderson, Marie [12], Imbeah, Samara [13], Kennedy, Megan [14]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) Framework, Silver Spring, MD, USA
(3) Malin Space Science Systems, San Diego, CA, USA
(4) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(6) University of Tennessee-Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(7) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Manoa, HI, USA
(8) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(9) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA

(12) Goddard Spaceflight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA
(13) Malin Space Science Systems, San Diego, CA, USA
(14) Malin Space Science Systems, San Diego, CA, USA
abstract:
The Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) is a 2-megapixel, color camera with resolution as high as 13.9 µm/pixel, designed to acquire handlens-scale images of the martian surface. For 15 years, MAHLI has supported the mission objectives of the Curiosity rover and the Mars Science Laboratory mission: to assess the possibility of past habitability on Mars. MAHLI is the brainchild of Ken Edgett, who led the design, development, testing, and first years of operations. Building on the tremendous science return of the Microscopic Imagers on Spirit and Opportunity, MAHLI has been crucial in documenting the succession of sedimentary rock types along traverse, returning roughly 85,000 high-resolution images over the mission thus far.

Though it supports a wide range of science endeavors, MAHLI uniquely excels in (1) discriminating grains ~60 µm diameter or more; (2) determining whether grains smaller than very fine sand-size are present; (3) resolving lateral structures ~0.5-1 mm in size and discerning lateral heterogeneity and continuity at ~100 µm/pxl; and (4) providing science-enabling activities. Key science highlights made possible or facilitated by MAHLI include:

1. MAHLI is Curiosity’s primary tool in determining grain size, grain orientation and sorting. For example, the contact between the Bradbury Group (sandstone) and Murray formation (fine grained laminated mudstone) was observed over a scale of 50-100 m. The juxtaposition of fine- and coarse-grained sediments, varying in elevation along traverse, with the lower-lying Murray occasionally overlapping the Bradbury Group, suggested a fluviolacustrine setting.

2. MAHLI is designed with a best resolution (~15 µm/pixel) such that very fine sand grains can be resolved but smaller grains cannot. Determining the grain size of the Sheepbed member as smaller than very find sand was pivotal in interpreting it as a mudstone – the first ever clearly identified on another planet.

3. The combination of MAHLI’s high resolution and its arm mounting allows MAHLI to image lateral structures over many centimeters. These “dog’s eye” mosaics document structures horizontally and vertically, informing stratigraphic interpretations. Arm motion also enables stereo pairs and highly-resolved photogrammetric 3D models.

4. Science-enabling activities include products such as range maps, observations supporting rover safety and health, such as images documenting the state of the wheels, and observations supporting other science investigations, such as imaging the APXS footprints and ChemCam laser spots.
