title: Refining the Detrital Zircon Record of the Catalina Schist: New Catchment-Scale Zircon U-Pb Constraints from Catalina Island Modern Sands
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Toto, Starla [1], Grove, Marty [2], Seymour, Nikki [3], Bebout, Gray [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA, USA
(3) Occidental College, Los Angeles, CA,
(4) Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA,
abstract:
The Catalina Schist records the history of the Mesozoic subduction complex of southern California. Previous U-Pb geochronology and 40Ar/39Ar thermochronology record mid-Cretaceous assembly of the Catalina subduction complex prior to 90 Ma. Here we use zircon U-Pb to compare outcrop samples and modern drainages of the Catalina Schist to test whether outcrop sampling of detrital zircon from metasediments missed geologically important U-Pb age signals. The outcrop samples represent the stacked metamorphic sequence of fault-bounded map units that increase structurally upward in metamorphic grade from lawsonite blueschist to amphibolite facies. These samples yielded Cretaceous (> 90 Ma), Jurassic, and older Mesozoic, Paleozoic, and Proterozoic ages. Significant evidence for metamorphic recrystallization (122-105 Ma) of detrital zircon was observed in the higher-grade units. In a recent related study, younger (105-70 Ma) metamorphic growth was determined to affect zircon from lawsonite blueschist facies mafic metaconglomerate cobbles of the Catalina Schist.

Preliminary results from four catchment-scale samples of modern sands from arroyos that drain areas underlain by epidote amphibolite, epidote blueschist, and lawsonite blueschist units yield a subset of U-Pb ages consistent with previous outcrop sampling. However, all four modern sand samples also yield an unexpected young Late Cretaceous age population (85-65 Ma). The composition of the Miocene San Onofre Breccia represents unroofing of the Catalina Schist during rifting of the southern California borderland, and the sand matrix also contains this Late Cretaceous age population. We are evaluating two working hypotheses for the 85-65 Ma detrital zircon ages: (1) Were the young zircons present in the modern sands contributed by erosion of Late Cretaceous-Cenozoic forearc basin sediments that resided in the upper plate before Miocene rifting?; or (2) Do the 85-65 Ma zircon ages reflect post-peak metamorphic zircon crystallization within the Catalina Schist? More detailed intragrain and depth profiling zircon U-Pb age and trace element analyses are ongoing to select between these possibilities. If anomalously young zircon ages revealed by modern sand sampling are a result of metamorphic recrystallization, this would be consistent with recent work from the lawsonite blueschist metaconglomerate of the Catalina Schist. This would indicate that the southern California accretionary complex continued to be affected by subduction-related processes, including devolatilization and fluid flow throughout the Late Cretaceous.

title: From Waves to Grains: Linking Wave Characteristics to Sediment Sorting Across the Drakes–Limantour Littoral Cell
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Jacob, Toby [1], Sumner, Dawn Y. [2], Largier, John [3]
affiliations: (1) UC Davis Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, California, USA
(2) UC Davis Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, CA,
(3) UC Davis Bodega Marine Laboratory, University of California, Bodega Bay, California, USA
abstract:
Understanding how waves transport sediment is critical for predicting shoreline stability and erosion, especially in environmentally sensitive zones such as Drakes Beach and Limantour Beach at the southern tip of the Point Reyes peninsula in Northern California. These two beaches occupy a semi-sheltered littoral sub-cell bounded by coastal headlands that limit sediment exchange with adjacent cells. Given this limited exchange, we suspected that wave-driven processes within this embayment could be creating spatial gradients in sediment characteristics due to isolation from other sediment transport systems. Specifically, we hypothesized that grain size decreases and sediment sorting improves in the direction of net longshore transport due to selective sorting and cumulative abrasion.

Sediment grain-size distribution was quantified and paired with nearshore wave data to evaluate how wave climate influences sediment transport and beach morphology within the Limantour–Drakes littoral sub-cell. Spatial variability in grain size was compared with modeled wave energy and wave approach angle to assess patterns of longshore transport and sorting across the study area.

Results support the hypothesis at Limantour Beach, where wave direction was the strongest predictor of median grain size (D50; R² = 0.420, p < 0.001), indicating that wave-driven longshore transport exerts a primary control on sediment distribution and produces predictable coarse-to-fine sorting associated with prevailing northwest swell and shoreline orientation. In contrast, no wave parameter at Drakes Beach correlated significantly with sediment characteristics, suggesting that local sediment inputs from adjacent bluffs and Drakes Estero overprint the broader regional wave-driven transport signal.

These findings demonstrate that beach dynamics within the same littoral system can vary depending on the balance between wave forcing and localized sediment supply, improving understanding of how sediment is redistributed along high-energy coastlines. Because grain-size distributions influence beach slope, sediment movement, and erosion susceptibility, identifying where wave climate dominates sediment transport versus where local sediment sources control beach morphology provides a useful framework for predicting shoreline response and long-term coastal vulnerability under changing wave climates, increasing storm intensity, and sea-level rise.

title: No Loess? No Problem! Grain Size End-Member Modeling Reveals Eolian Processes and Stratigraphy in Mixed Deposits
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Staley, Spencer E. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Ecosystem Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
abstract:
Loess deposits are almost entirely composed of eolian dust and are therefore prime targets of eolian process research. However, loess records are limited in space and time to areas near major dust sources and to periods of major emissions. Limited observations outside of major loess belts contribute to climate model uncertainties in both the magnitude and direction of climate forcing by atmospheric dust. Furthermore, in dusty regions without loess deposits, like the southwestern US, modeled paleoclimatic trends do not appear to match direct observations. Populating the terrestrial dust archive in space and time requires developing records in deposits where dust is intermixed with sediment from other sources but can still be adequately characterized and quantified.

Young volcanic basalt fields offer an ideal setting to study dust in mixed deposits. Craters, flow-top pressure troughs, and collapse features form small, enclosed basins high on the landscape—natural dust traps. Sediment accumulating here is limited to two sources: windblown material and products of basalt weathering. Quantitative unmixing of these two types of sediment is possible due to their distinct mineralogy, geochemistry, and grain size.

In this study, I perform particle size distribution end-member modeling on sediment samples from lava flow-top basins across Nevada, Arizona, and New Mexico. The source and/or process responsible for each sedimentary end member is interpreted within the context of the local landscape’s sedimentary geomorphology, mineralogy, and geochemistry. Depositional chronology and calculations of dust accumulation rate and local denudation are underpinned by IRSL dating.

XRD analysis indicates dust (quartz and mica) is present in all lava flow-top sediment samples from across the region. Particle size end-member modeling of flow-top basins and surrounding geomorphic features like hillslopes, axial channels, small playas, sand sheets, climbing dunes, and V horizons illuminate sedimentary connectivity across the landscape and processes of erosion, dust deposition, sand saltation, and soil formation.

At one site, in a small playa catchment basin within the Lunar Crater volcanic field, NV, sediments are 92% eolian dust, 7% alluvium, and 1% eolian sand. Since 8 ka, the catchment’s dust mass accumulation rate is 0.22–0.33 g/cm 2 /kyr with a denudation rate of 0.006–0.009 cm/kyr. Surrounding surface sediments contain varying amounts of eolian sand, dust, and weathered basalt depending on geomorphic position and proximity to source.

title: Longevity and Reactivation of Intracontinental Walled Basins: Thermochronologic Evidence from Western Mongolia
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools
authors: VanDyke, Eli Jordan [1], Stevens Goddard, Andrea Lynn [2], Leary, Ryan [3], Batsukh, Gombodorj [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, USA
(4) Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract: The Altai Mountains of western Mongolia have been interpreted as either reactivated relict Mesozoic relief or Neogene uplift of a Jurassic peneplain. Today, relief along the Altai creates structurally confined depocenters – including the Dzerega and Dariv basins – that trap sediment, but if the modern range represents long-lived Mesozoic topography, relief persistence sustained through episodic range exhumation may also explain how these basins maintained accommodation space and retained sediment for more than 150 Myr. We present detrital apatite fission-track (AFT) and apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He (AHe) thermochronology with inverse thermal modeling and stratigraphic constraints from Jurassic – Oligocene sandstone samples from the Dzereg and Dariv basins to reconstruct the coupled evolution of sedimentation, intrabasinal deformation, and range exhumation. Thermally reset samples constrain the timing and magnitude of post-depositional burial, reheating, and basin inversion, whereas statistical unmixing of unreset AFT age populations records progressive unroofing of source terranes. Together, these complementary approaches reconstruct multiple tectonic episodes, including Jurassic source-terrane exhumation related to Mongol-Okhotsk closure, mid-Cretaceous basin inversion and bounding-range exhumation potentially driven by far-field effects of the Lhasa terrane collision, and an Oligocene-Miocene phase of renewed basin burial and intrabasinal exhumation likely associated with the India-Eurasia collision. These results support a model in which long-lived Mesozoic topography, repeatedly reactivated and exhumed, maintained structural ponding and sediment accommodation for more than 150 Myr.

title: Disentangling Natural and Anthropogenic Drivers of Hydro-Geomorphic Hazards: Implications for Multi-Hazard Risk Reduction in the Western Himalayas
session_title: Contemporary research in geomorphological hazards
authors: Ansari, Intejar [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi, India, India
abstract: Mountainous regions are increasingly experiencing multiple hydro-geomorphic hazards due to the combined influence of natural processes and accelerating human-induced landscape modifications. Although floods, landslides, and soil erosion have been extensively investigated individually but little attention has been given to understanding what is the relative influence of natural and anthropogenic driver multiple hazards within the same river basin? Therefore, in this study explainable machine learning has been applied to systematically investigate and compare the dominant drivers of flood, landslide, and soil erosion susceptibility in the Beas River Sub-Basin (BRSB) of Western Himalayas. The results indicate that 16.4% (2,061 km 2 ) of the sub-basin is highly susceptible to flash floods, 24.6% (3,086.47 km 2 ) to landslides, and 57.7% (7,141 km 2 ) to soil erosion, indicating that soil erosion is the most spatially extensive hydro-geomorphic hazard within the BRSB. Such widespread susceptibility poses significant challenges to agricultural productivity, watershed sustainability, and the long-term livelihood security of communities that rely heavily on agriculture and other land-based resources. Further, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis shows distinct controlling mechanisms, with hydrological factors dominating flash floods, topographic factors governing landslides, and land-use changes exerting the strongest influence on soil erosion. Sensitivity analysis is done to corroborated the SHAP findings, demonstrating that flash floods and landslides are predominantly controlled by natural hydro-geomorphic conditions, whereas, soil erosion exhibits substantially greater sensitivity to human-induced land-use changes. The proposed framework provides new insights into hazard-specific controlling mechanisms and improves our understanding of the relative influence of natural and anthropogenic drivers on hydro-geomorphic hazards in mountainous environments. The findings are expected to support integrated multi-hazard risk reduction, sustainable land-use planning, and evidence-based river basin management in the Himalayan region.

title: Pathways of carbon and water through proglacial lake sediments during the Last Termination
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Edwards, Graham Harper [1], Piccione, Gavin [2], Melara, Julio Cesar [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(3) Earth & Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
In the context of modern climate warming and deglaciation, proglacial wetland and lake systems are rapidly evolving, emergent environments. These dynamic systems are sensitive to cryosphere change and have recently received increased attention for their potential roles in mobilization/sequestration of organic carbon. Glacial Lake Hitchcock (GLH) was a transient proglacial lake that occupied the modern Connecticut River Valley from 18.2–12.5 ka as the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated during the Last Termination. The varved sediments of GLH have been well-studied, establishing a robust geomorphic and depositional history of the proglacial lacustrine environment.

Post-depositional, authigenic carbonate concretions are distributed heterogeneously through GLH sediments and reflect the oxidation and mobilization of buried organic carbon within the proglacial sedimentary environment. We report stable and radiogenic isotopic geochemistry of concretions for two sedimentary sections (deposited 16–14.8 ka) to reconstruct pathways of water and carbon cycling through the GLH sedimentary environment. Carbonate concretion δ 13 C values indicate buried organic matter as the source of dissolved inorganic carbon in the sedimentary environment. Carbonate concretion δ 18 O compositions correspond to water compositions ranging from -6 to -11 ‰ (VSMOW, assuming 5 ºC water temperature), several per mille heavier heavier than estimated LIS meltwater compositions (17–20 ‰). These compositions indicate influence(s) from meteoritic water and/or lake water evaporation. Both interpretations support formation in littoral settings (supported by sample sites) or a post-GLH environment.

Preliminary U-series data for concretions from ~14 ka GLH sediments are consistent with sedimentary carbon oxidation and concretion growth in the Late Pleistocene-Early Holocene. Ratios of 234 U/ 238 U near secular equilibrium reflect either short-lived water-sediment interaction or chemical weathering of fine-grained glacial sediment. In either case, the near-unity activity ratios contradict supply of groundwater with extended subsurface residence.

Collectively, these data indicate oxidation of buried organic carbon in proglacial GLH sediments shortly after sediment deposition or after lowering of the local water table. We will present refined U-series geochronology as well as radiogenic Sr isotopes to more fully reconstruct pathways of oxidizing waters into and through the GLH sedimentary system.

title: Assessing controls on the aqueous geochemistry of a crystalline hosted terrestrial subsurface ecosystem from the Sanford Underground Research Facility
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science
authors: Beeler, Scott Randall [1], Keenan, Sarah Wheeler [2]
affiliations: (1) Engineering and Mining Experiment Station, South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD,
abstract: Subsurface environments host the largest terrestrial reservoir of liquid water on Earth and contain diverse and abundant microbial ecosystems. Likewise, because they offer protection from the inhospitable conditions found on the surface of other planets, subsurface environments have emerged as key targets in astrobiological investigations. Accordingly, understanding biogeochemical cycling within these systems has key implications for our understanding of global elemental cycles on Earth and as an analog for assessing the processes governing the habitability of extraterrestrial systems. The Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota, USA provides access to the continental subsurface and the ability to directly sample groundwater hosted in the metasedimentary lithologies comprising the facility. We performed monthly sampling of waters from natural fracture-hosted drips over a six-month period at six locations across three levels (800, 1700, and 2000 ft. below surface) at SURF to assess the spatiotemporal variability in groundwater geochemistry. We found that geochemistry was highly variable between sites with conductivity varying from 0.72 – 4.77 mS/cm and the concentration of individual elements varying up to four orders of magnitude between sites. Geochemistry was also variable temporally with conductivity varying up to two times and individual elements varying up to ten times within individual sampling sites over the six-month sampling period. Pairwise correlation analysis between major ions found a strong positive correlation (r > 0.8) between Mg 2+ , Ca 2+ , Fe 3+ , Mn 2+ , SO 4 2- , and conductivity. The cations reflect the geochemistry of the dominant lithologies (i.e. phyllite and schist) and mineralogies (i.e. sericite, biotite, ankerite, calcite, pyrrhotite, pyrite, hornblende, graphite and quartz) within SURF. In contrast, sulfate bearing minerals occur only rarely at SURF indicating that sulfate is primarily sourced from the oxidation of iron sulfide minerals that are abundant in the system. This interpretation is consistent with previous work identifying the oxidation of sulfide minerals as an energetically favorable microbial metabolism and a potentially important control on fluid geochemistry. Additionally, we interpret the correlation of sulfate with major cations and conductivity to occur because of enhanced mineral dissolution by the acidity generated from sulfide mineral oxidation. These results further demonstrate the key role of sulfide mineral oxidation on overall fluid geochemistry at SURF and highlight how the interplay of biology and geology combine to drive geochemistry in subsurface systems.

title: Spatial distribution of Holocene-Pleistocene Back-Arc Volcanism of SE Guatemala in the Jalapa and Ipala Grabens
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Wroblewski, Lina [1], Graettinger, Alison H. [2], Neidlinger, Allison [3], Custis, Andrew [4], Rodríguez, Dulce [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, California State University, Chico, Chico, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Missouri-Kansas City, Kansas City, KS, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Missouri-Kansas City, Kansas City, KS, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Missouri-Kansas City, Kansas City, KS, USA
(5) Centro Universitario del Norte, Cobán, Cobán, Alta Verapaz, Guatemala
abstract: This study mapped the distribution of Holocene to Pleistocene volcanoes in relation to extensional faults within the back-arc of SE Guatemala. It is important to study the distribution and eruption style of these abundant volcanoes to understand potential future eruption risk. Research was conducted within the departments of Jalapa, Chiquimula, and Juitiapa in south- eastern Guatemala, focused on the Jalapa and Ipala grabens. Field work was conducted to identify volcano locations and eruption style. Additional volcanoes were recognized using a Copernicus 30 m Digital Elevation Model (DEM) based on morphology, the Smithsonian Global Volcano database (GVP), and published literature. Published faults and geomorphic lineaments were used to identify faults in the grabens. Volcano locations were used to map the density of features and measure nearest neighbor distance. This study recognized 76 volcanoes including six polygenetic features and 70 monogenetic features. Previously published dates and morphology indicate the eruptions occurred across the Holocene and Pleistocene. Of the monogenetic features 58 were scoria cones and 12 maars, meaning 17% of eruptions were phreatomagmatic. Both Jalapa and Ipala grabens are dominated by N/S extensional faults, but less than 50% of volcanoes sit on a mapped fault (35/76). Two thirds of the volcanoes were located within the grabens, the remaining occurred on the footwalls of graben bounding normal faults. Additional buried faults may be present in the grabens as indicated by occasional N/S alignment of volcanoes especially in Ipala graben. The average nearest neighbor distance between volcanoes was 2 km with the largest distance being 7.5 km. The SE portion of the Ipala graben exhibited the highest density of monogenetic features (39 maars and scoria cones). Based on the distribution of volcanoes and types the most likely future eruption would be a scoria cone. Based on nearest neighbor distance of 2 km, a future vent could appear in the SE Ipala graben. Additional monogenetic features occur outside this study area, but at lower densities. Future hazard assessments should include a larger area but could leverage the methods presented here. However, this study demonstrated there are more phreatomagmatic features than previously recognized and topographic data highlighted a complex relationship with extensional structures.

title: Silicate Weathering Across Cryogenian Icehouse-greenhouse Transitions in Death Valley, California
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Zhang, Ziyue [1], Herx, Elim [2], Balestra, Rizzieri [3], Ramezani, Jahandar [4], Crockford, Peter W. [5], Nelson, Lyle L. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA

abstract: Two global glaciations, the Sturtian and Marinoan, are interpreted during the Cryogenian, reflecting major perturbations to Earth’s climate and carbon cycle. The onset of these glaciations has been linked to enhanced silicate weathering during the fragmentation of the supercontinent Rodinia, whereas post-glacial super greenhouse climates were likely moderated by renewed silicate weathering and CO2 drawdown. Nonetheless, direct records of how continental weathering changed across these climate transitions remain limited. Cryogenian strata in Death Valley, CA preserve deposits spanning both glaciations and their post-glacial aftermaths, providing an opportunity to test hypotheses regarding changes in continental weathering through geochemical analyses of carbonate and mudrock units. Major-element compositions of shale were used to calculate the Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) as a proxy for local chemical weathering intensity. Leached carbonate samples were analyzed for strontium and carbon isotope ratios to constrain global weathering, establish chemostratigraphic correlations, and evaluate carbon cycle perturbations. Together, these datasets help to constrain secular changes in continental silicate weathering during the Neoproterozoic, a key control on the global carbon cycle and climate regulation.

title: Iron oxide-copper-gold deposits: A one-size-fits all genetic model does not work
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Simon, Adam Charles [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI,
abstract: There are enough similarities among iron oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) deposits globally that they would seem to fit a single genetic model. However, genetic models in the literature often take twists and turns to invoke processes for which there may or may not be evidence in the rocks. IOCG deposits are iron and copper rich, sulfur poor, and most contain gold but some do not. IOCG deposits in many districts are spatially and temporally associated with igneous rocks, but not always. IOCG deposits are sometimes hosted in igneous rocks, but not always. IOCG deposits formed in orogenic and post-orogenic settings and back-arc extension seems to have been particularly important for some districts. Drill core reveal that IOCG mineralization in some deposits transitions with depth to iron-rich, sulfur-copper-gold-poor mineralization. Stable copper, hydrogen, iron, oxygen and sulfur isotopes fingerprint a magmatic source for the ore fluids in some deposits, but seawater derived brines in others. Regional sodic-calcic alteration is observed in some districts, but not all. Petrographic observations of drill core indicate that some IOCG deposits but not all, record multiple episodes of fluid infiltration with hematite followed by magnetite followed by copper-iron-sulfide in some deposits. Some deposits contain mushketovite, which is best explained by the reduction of primary specular hematite and requires at least two generations of fluid. The trace element composition magnetite, which modally dominates IOCG deposits, sometimes vary systematically with depth and petrographic observations of magnetite textures reveal multiple episodes of hydrothermal dissolution and reprecipitation. In this presentation I will review the characteristics of IOCG deposits from different districts and tectonic settings and try to frame a genetic model that can be adapted to explain their formation globally.

title: Unusual Silica-rich Spinel in Metacumulate Granulite Xenoliths from the Geronimo Volcanic Field, SE Arizona
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Roppe, Benjamin James [1], Kempton, Pamela [2], Hindall, Andrew G. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
(2) Geology, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Ks, USA
(3) Geology, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Ks, USA
abstract: Spinel is a common accessory mineral in lower crustal granulites. It is an oxide with the general mineral formula AB 2 O 4 , where the A site typically hosts Mg 2+ , Fe 2+ , and Mn 2+ , while the B site hosts Al 3+ , Cr 3+ , and Fe 3+ . Incorporation of Si in the crystal structure is uncommon and when present, and is generally limited to concentrations below 1 wt%. Spinels containing higher concentrations are known but are usually associated with the high pressure and temperature conditions of the mantle rather than the crust. However, preliminary petrography and scanning electron microscopy - energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) analyses of an unusual mineral in a two-pyroxene + plagioclase metacumulate granulite xenolith from the Geronimo Volcanic Field, SE Arizona, suggest it may be a silica-rich spinel. The mineral has a distinct dark honey-gold color and is crosscut by reddish black discontinuous bands or striations that intersect at an angle of ca. 60-70 o . Superficially, it resembles rutile in thin section and is petrographically and compositionally distinct from the oxide phases typical of other GVF metacumulates, which tend to be anhedral, black to olive green (hercynite) spinels ± magnetite ± ilmenite. SEM-EDS analyses show conclusively that the mineral is not rutile and, instead, suggest it is a Si-bearing spinel with magnetite (?) exsolution. However, the currently available analyses were determined by relatively low precision (standardless) SEM-EDS methods. Consequently, high precision electron microprobe analyses (EMPA) of the spinels are planned for the near future, providing the opportunity to confirm or refute the validity of the originally obtained Si-rich compositions of the spinels. If confirmed, the presence of high-Si spinels in the lowermost crust beneath SE Arizona would be indicative of unusually high temperature conditions, potentially associated with influx of hot asthenospheric mantle during Oligocene rollback of the Farallon slab.

title: “Top down” insight into hypothesized flat-slab subduction and underthrusting processes
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Zuza, Andrew Vincent [1], Vlaha, Dominik Richard [2], Lee, Terry [3], Cao, Wenrong [4]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Peking University, China
(3) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(4) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada Reno, REno, NV, USA
abstract: The Late Cretaceous–Paleogene North American Laramide is a classic zone of intra-plate deformation, with localized deformation occurring >1000 km from the paleo-plate boundary. This orogen has traditionally been interpreted to result from flat east-dipping subduction of the Farallon slab that exerts basal tractions on the upper plate, but alternative models argue for plate-margin end-loading or continental indentation to drive intra-plate deformation. Similar arguments have been made for the Mesozoic SE China (Yanshanian) orogen associated with the west-dipping Paleo-Pacific (Izanagi) plate. Numerous bottom-up geophysical surveys and numerical simulations have been conducted to probe these geodynamic scenarios, but in the theme of this session, here we take the top-down approach of examining upper-plate geologic records in the hinterland regions to investigate these processes. Our goals are not to definitively arrive at a particular solution but instead discuss important observations that any viable model should explain. Both orogens involved inboard and outboard sweeps of magmatism that are interpreted to track shallowing and steepening of the subducting slab, although alternative explanations invoke slab foundering or breakoff. Notably, both orogens involved wide expanses of crust between the plate boundary and intraplate orogen that did not experience strong contractional deformation during the phase of postulated flat-slab subduction or indentation. Nevada was a quiescent highland with limited Cretaceous shortening and local extension, that became dominated by Eocene lake systems. The SE China hinterland experienced shallow marine sedimentation that has been attributed to downward flat-slab pull. These hinterland regions both experienced peak temperature conditions and widespread porphyry copper mineralization during this time, which reflects the heat and fluids transported into the upper plate. In particular, the hot, weak, and negligibly deforming hinterland regions between the plate boundary and intra-plate orogens appear inconsistent with simple plate-boundary-driven models (end loading or indentation), which would be expected to also deform this intervening weak crust. A strong lithospheric mantle or elevated gravitational potential energy could explain the hinterland quiescence for such plate-boundary-type models. Consideration of these geological observables and comparisons to analogous orogens can help resolve some of these open questions. In summary, the geologic record is inherently noisy and incomplete, which can lead to real preservation and confirmation biases, but bottom-up approaches that do not fully engage with geologic observations are no more than wishful thinking.

title: Experimental and Stratigraphic Constraints on Paleozoic Seawater Silicon Cycling

authors: Tarhan, Lidya G. [1], Slagter, Silvina [2], Wang, Jiuyuan [3], Syverson, Drew D. [4], Asael, Dan [5], Planavsky, Noah J. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) Instituto de Ciencias de la Ingeniería, Universidad de O'Higgins, Rancagua, Chile

abstract: The modern marine silicon cycle is strongly regulated by the uptake of dissolved silicon (DSi) by silicon-biomineralizing organisms such as diatoms, radiolarians and silicifying sponges. However, the extent to which marine silicon cycling and seawater DSi levels were similarly regulated by early silica-biomineralizers—particularly prior to the emergence of diatoms—remains poorly constrained. Sedimentological, geochemical and paleontological data have previously been leveraged in support of varying interpretations of Paleozoic seawater DSi levels, ranging from elevated (Precambrian-style) to low (modern-style) concentrations. Silicon isotopes (δ 30 Si) have emerged as a potentially powerful tool to reconstruct past marine silicon cycling and recent work has proposed that coupled measurements of fossilized radiolarian tests and sponge spicules may provide a means to reconstruct Paleozoic DSi levels and the scale and environmental distribution of biosilica production. However, the susceptibility of biosilica δ 30 Si signatures to early diagenetic overprinting has not been extensively scrutinized. We present the results of long-term incubation experiments of sponge spicules and diatom frustules, conducted using 29 Si as a tracer to reconstruct extents of biosilica dissolution and isotopic exchange. We find that, under certain environmental conditions, substantial isotope exchange can occur on early diagenetic time scales. We therefore urge that caution should be exercised in utilizing biosilica δ 30 Si signatures to reconstruct past seawater DSi levels. We also discuss the role of key environmental and evolutionary factors that may have influenced biosilica δ 30 Si fidelity across the Neoproterozoic–Paleozoic transition and during the radiation of early silica-biomineralizers.

title: Pit Crater Dimensions Across the Solar System: A Comparative Planetology Perspective
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Hansen, Hiu Ching Jupiter [1]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
abstract:
Pit crater chains are linear arrays of collapse depressions formed above subsurface extensional fractures and are observed across the Solar System, from meter-scale pits in Iceland to kilometer-scale chains on Mars, Vesta, and Ceres. Despite extensive mapping efforts across individual bodies, pit crater dimensions have yet to be systematically compared across the full extent of available planetary bodies and datasets in a unified comparative planetology framework. This work presents an exploratory comparative planetology analysis of pit crater diameter and depth datasets compiled from ten planetary bodies, supplemented by new mapping on Ceres and Vesta. Multiple statistical approaches are used to address three fundamental questions: (1) how pit dimensions vary among planetary bodies, (2) how they are correlated to planetary physical properties, and (3) how pit depth scales with diameter. Addressing these questions test various hypotheses on whether planetary-scale parameters and geological factors control pit dimensions.

Pit dimensions differ significantly among most planetary bodies, with a general trend of increasing from the large terrestrial planets to Vesta before decreasing toward the smallest bodies. Pit depth shows the strongest and most consistent correlations with body size, mass, and thus surface gravity, consistent with gravity governing the depth of the jointing-to-faulting transition, together with the thickness of the brittle lithosphere, set an upper bound on subsurface structural openings and therefore pit dimensions. Pit diameter and depths are significantly correlated and display moderate to strong sublinear scaling across most individual datasets and the overall compiled data. Such scaling relationship is consistent with the geometry of the underlying fracture systems. Local geological factors including volatile interactions, magma withdrawal, and post-formation erosion produce departures from this general trend, and datasets combining pits from diverse geological settings show consistently weaker scaling than localized datasets. Regolith thickness alone cannot account for these planetary-scale trends and depth-diameter scaling, complicating the use of pit depth as a proxy for regolith thickness on planetary surface.

These analyses remain exploratory and should be interpreted cautiously, given the limited number of large terrestrial bodies in the solar system and the availability of spacecraft observations at sufficient resolution. Nonetheless, these results provide a comparative framework for evaluating pit crater dimensions and testable predictions for future planetary missions.

title: GUrdion Knot: Deconvolving the Competing Effects of Weathering, Diagenesis, and Radiation Damage on Zircon Geochemistry from Sub-Great Unconformity (GU) Samples in the Wyoming Craton
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems (Posters)
authors: Ellia, Zachary [1], Murray, Kendra E. [2], Pearson, Dave [3], Ibanez-Mejia, Mauricio [4]
affiliations: (1) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(2) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(3) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(4) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract: Across the Wyoming Craton, the Great Unconformity (GU) surface is a >2 Gyr gap in the rock record. We hypothesize that in-situ chemical weathering of zircon grains in plutonic rocks directly below the GU preserves geochemical information about the nature and timing of surface exposure, providing novel information about the region’s history. We collected samples from meter-scale vertical profiles (two in the Teton Range, one in the Owl Creek Range) of Neoarchean granitoids below GU surfaces to compare relatively unaltered samples (deep) to samples exposed to ancient weathering conditions (shallow). Each sample was analyzed for whole-rock major and trace element composition. Zircon grains were CL/BSE-imaged and mapped using Raman spectroscopy to provide radiation damage context for split-stream U/Pb and TEA LA-ICP-MS spots. Whole-rock data confirm that shallow samples exhibit significant K-enrichment, evidence of post-burial K-metasomatism. Shallow zircon grains have higher concentrations of non-formula elements relative to deep grains, including >10x concentrations of P, Y, and HREEs. U, Th, and effective U ([eU]), a proxy for radiation damage, are relatively higher in shallow samples. Alpha doses calculated from zircon Raman spectra are similar for both sample types (1x10^18 to 3.5x10^18 α/g), but shallow samples have more metamict grains/spots that cannot accurately fit Raman bands. In all samples, alpha dose and [eU] are strongly correlated with non-formula element concentration: alpha doses <1x10^18 α/g have low non-formula element concentrations while alpha doses >2x10^18 α/g are non-formula element enriched (especially LREEs). These results suggest radiation damage, and thus time at relatively cold conditions (<330 ˚C), are key controls on how zircon grains archive weathering processes. We argue that zircon chemical complexity reflects ≤2 Gyr shared history of radiation damage accumulation followed by shallow sample alteration via surficial weathering and/or metasomatism. Undamaged deep grains (≤1x10^18 α/g) were least altered and likely resemble primary zircon geochemistry, whereas damaged deep grains (≥2x10^18 α/g) were susceptible to non-formula element uptake at subsurface conditions. Undamaged shallow grains were largely unaltered despite being exposed to surface conditions, whilst damaged shallow grains experienced extreme non-formula element uptake during surficial alteration. Our findings update current understandings of how weathering, diagenesis, and radiation damage affect zircon geochemistry and demonstrate that zircon grains may contain information that can bridge “missing” time at unconformities.

title: Fractionation of Alkali Feldspar: On Making High Ga/Al Granite
session_title: Granite-related mineral systems: Advances in understanding their genesis, distribution, and exploration implications (Posters)
authors: Zhang, Jingnan [1], Lee, Cin-Ty [2], Keller, Duncan [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, TX, USA
(3) Geosciences Department, Skidmore Colleges, Saratoga Springs, NY, USA
abstract: The classification of granites is marked by inconsistencies. For example, the widespread classification of granites into A-type was initially based on associations with extension-related tectonic environments while the I- and S-type classifications were based on inferred source rocks using major-element chemistry and mineralogy. Here, we revisit the significance of one geochemical signature that has been widely used to classify granites. Specifically, elevated Ga/Al has long been used as an empirical signature of A-type granites, but the petrogenetic processes responsible for Ga/Al enrichment in granitic melts remain poorly quantified. Because the term “A-type” originally combines compositional, tectonic and petrogenetic implications, whether Ga/Al systematics reflect tectonic environment or reflect petrogenetic processes requires an understanding of the processes that control Ga/Al fractionation. Here, we present a comprehensive evaluation of Ga/Al exchange coefficients among major rock-forming minerals from experimental and natural mineral-melt pairs. We find that segregation of alkali feldspar is the primary driver for high Ga/Al ratios in granitic melts. We demonstrate that significant increases in Ga/Al ratios occur predominantly when alkali feldspar segregates efficiently from the melt. Elevated Ga/Al ratios are not unique to specific tectonic settings or source rocks; rather, they reflect a distinct petrogenetic history of alkali feldspar saturation and subsequent segregation. Thus, Ga/Al ratios should be utilised as a tool to understand magmatic differentiation processes (specifically, the efficiency of alkali feldspar segregation) rather than as an indicator of tectonic environment.

title: Proposed Design for the NOVA: Nodal Observation of Volcanic Activity Project
session_title: Imaging, measuring, and characterizing the Earth’s changing surface through remote sensing
authors: Wilfong, Collette [1]
affiliations: (1) Colorado Space Grant Consortium, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
The NOVA: Nodal Observation of Volcanic Activity project is designed to collect data near active volcanic sites. Data is collected by deploying a network of sensor suites, called GeoSats, on the earth's surface. This project will specifically work on Kilauea in Hawai’i, as there are previous and current studies being done by the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (HVO) and NASA. HVO provides research about past eruptions, lava flow patterns, geochemistry, imaging, and NASA provides satellite topography data, lava flow maps, and gas emission data. For this work, each GeoSat includes a GPS unit, a single axis and tri-axis accelerometer, thermometer, and magnetometer. The purpose of NOVA is to document the dynamic properties and volcano seismicity of magmatic systems to understand and forecast the evolution and eruption of magmatic chambers through targeted measurements beyond traditional geophones.

NOVA will use a network of small sensor packages, called GeoSats, to collect data continuously. GeoSats will collect seismic, temperature, GPS, and magnetic data. This data will then be pre-processed to filter noise and integrated to determine velocity and displacement. Data will also be used to create a preliminary map of the internal magmatic structure. Pre and post imagery from NASA satellites, along with field observations, will be used to estimate the amount of magma from a given eruption and be compared to the pre-cursory seismic activity to see if there is a relationship. NOVA will also explore rates of magma flux into the chamber (using accelerometer and magnetometer data), understanding surface temperature over time before an eruption (thermometer data), and potentially finding magnetic anomalies associated with magma flow and eruption events (magnetometer data).

This presentation focuses on data collection methods and the integration of undergraduate engineering students applying their skills to answer scientific questions.

title: An Integrated Approach to Establishing Volcanic–Plutonic Links in the Miocene Searchlight Magmatic System, Southern Nevada, U.S.A.
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Dodge, Michele C. [1], Miller, Jonathan S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) Geology, San José State University, San Jose, CA, USA
abstract:
The Miocene Searchlight magmatic system of southern Nevada preserves an exceptional volcanic–plutonic record, providing a rare opportunity to reconstruct the evolution of an intermediate-to-silicic magmatic system from shallow crustal intrusions to erupted volcanic products.

Previous work has shown that high-silica rhyolites of the Highland Range are products of fractional crystallization within a silicic mush that solidified to granite within the middle part of Searchlight Pluton (Middle Granite) in its terminal stages. However, the relationship between older intermediate lavas and intrusive units comprising the upper and lower portions of Searchlight has been largely unexamined.

Overlapping U-Pb zircon ages, equivalent mineral assemblages, and similar plagioclase CSDs indicate that trachydacite roof porphyry and erupted trachydacite lavas are equivalent and shared similar crystallization histories involving magma recharge and mixing. Whole-rock major and trace element data demonstrate extensive compositional overlap between the intermediate volcanic rocks (trachyandesite/trachydacite) and quartz monzonite in lower Upper Searchlight and upper Lower Searchlight. Hierarchical cluster analysis of trace element data independently groups many intrusive and extrusive samples together. Sr-Nd isotopic compositions further support derivation from a common magma system. Additionally, some geochemical characteristics inferred to be indicative of felsic cumulates (e.g. high, Ba, Sr, Zr) are common to both erupted and plutonic intermediate rocks and complicates the general interpretation of Lower Searchlight pluton as predominantly cumulate.

Between ~17.5 and 16.3 Ma, the system generated intermediate magmas that erupted as trachyandesite and trachydacite lavas and domes, intruded as hypabyssal trachydacite porphyry near the roof of the pluton, and crystallized at deeper levels as quartz monzonite. At ~16.3 Ma, the system underwent a pronounced transition to silicic magmatism with establishment of a granite magma body that evolved through fractional crystallization to produce high-silica rhyolite. These evolved magmas erupted as rhyolitic lavas and tuffs, while compositionally equivalent intrusive counterparts were emplaced as dikes, leucogranite sills, and pods.

title: Following the Fluids: Reconstructing Fluid Pathways in Fossil Subduction Interfaces
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Flores, Kennet E. [1], Tsujimori, Tatsuki [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC,
(2) Department of Earth Science, Tohoku University, Sendai,
abstract:
Subduction complexes preserve one of the few direct records of processes operating along the slab–mantle interface. Through decades of meticulous field investigations, John Wakabayashi demonstrated how the structural architecture of subduction-related mélanges and associated high-pressure–low-temperature (HP–LT) metamorphic rocks provides the framework for reconstructing the evolution of fossil subduction zones. His pioneering studies of the Franciscan Complex fundamentally changed how geologists interpret these tectonic assemblages and continue to guide investigations of subduction complexes worldwide.

Building upon this field-based framework, petrology and geochemistry provide a complementary record of the fluids that once circulated through these complex systems. If subduction-related mélanges preserve the architecture of fossil subduction interfaces, metasomatic rocks preserve the chemistry of the fluids that once flowed through them. Although commonly preserved only as veins, pods, and dismembered blocks, these rocks record fluid-mediated element transfer, metasomatism, and chemical exchange that cannot be reconstructed from structural relationships alone.

Viewed collectively, high-pressure vein-related rocks from subduction-related mélanges worldwide reveal a coherent geochemical framework rather than a collection of isolated lithologies. Whole-rock geochemical data indicate that rocks traditionally classified as jadeitites, omphacitites, albitites, and phengite-rich rocks are better interpreted as products of two recurring fluid end members: (1) a sodic to sodic-calcic fluid responsible for Na-rich metasomatism, and (2) a potassic fluid responsible for K-rich metasomatism. Intermediate compositions record the evolving chemical nature of subduction-zone fluids through fluid-rock interaction and local mixing between these end members. The recurrence of these fluid systems in the Franciscan Complex, Japanese serpentinite mélanges, the Guatemala Suture Zone, and other well-characterized subduction complexes, despite major differences in tectonic age, metamorphic evolution, and convergent-margin setting, suggests that they reflect fundamental controls on fluid production, migration, and fluid-rock interaction within fossil subduction interfaces rather than locality-specific processes.

Rather than representing isolated geological curiosities, high-pressure vein-related rocks provide one of the few direct geochemical records of fluid evolution preserved in exhumed subduction complexes. Interpreting these rocks within the structural framework established through decades of field investigations provides a new perspective for reconstructing fluid production, migration pathways, and chemical exchange between the subducting slab and the mantle wedge. By integrating structural geology, petrology, and geochemistry, this approach extends the field-based legacy of John Wakabayashi from the Franciscan Complex to subduction complexes worldwide.

title: Holocene Ecosystem Response to Seawater Incursions in Lake Izabal
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling (Posters)
authors: Kettleborough, Bethany R. [1], Berke, Melissa A. [2], Williams, Ross [3], Spanbauer, Trisha L. [4], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [5], Stone, Jeffery R. [6], McMahan, Caleb D. [7]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, USA
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, USA
(3) Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA

abstract: Eastern Guatemala’s Lakes Izabal and El Golfete form a single connected freshwater system with a complicated tectonic history shaped by coastal forces. Both Lakes Izabal and El Golfete have lake floors below sea level. This elevation gradient makes the system highly sensitive to sea level shifts, which can result in the lakes becoming inundated with seawater during intervals of high sea level or weakened hydraulic head from arid conditions on land. It is unclear how the lacustrine ecosystem responds to this marine inundation, how rapidly the system might recover, and how the response may vary spatially across the lakes. We use sedimentary organic geochemical biomarkers from a newly recovered transect of cores from 4 sites in the lakes (between 15.75°N, 88.86°W and 15.50°N, 89.15°W) to investigate aquatic community disturbances and recovery of the lake ecosystem, in addition to hydroclimate changes in the region. Preliminary results using terrestrial leaf wax compound abundances and compound specific δ 2 H values suggest Holocene climate shifts coincide with lacustrine disturbances in the Izabal system, with important implications for future marine inundations.

title: Caught in the Carbonates: Exploring Phosphorus Dynamics Beyond EPC in Marl Lakes
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Westover, Maddie [1], Bickmore, Barry R. [2], Sorensen, Mary A. [3], LeMonte, Joshua J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
(3) Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
(4) Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
abstract:
Excess phosphorus (P) negatively impacts surface water globally, particularly those near population centers where it often feeds harmful algae blooms that can disrupt local ecosystems and economies. The equilibrium phosphorus concentration (EPC) framework is commonly used for predicting whether lakebed sediment will act as a source or a sink of P and to improve water quality models. However, when applied to carbonate-rich, alkaline marl lakes with sediments containing more than 50% calcite, the EPC framework may not adequately represent phosphorus dynamics because it assumes sorption processes dominate P mobility and does not account for calcite co-precipitation within the system.

To investigate P dynamics in marl lake systems, sediment and water samples were collected from seven sites across Utah Lake, a shallow, hypereutrophic marl lake located in northern Utah at the eastern edge of the Basin and Range province. The EPC for each site was determined using sorption isotherm experiments conducted at pH values of 7.5, 8.0, 8.5, and 9.0 with total P additions ranging from 0–762 mg/L. The samples were analyzed using ion chromatography and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry and the resulting data were modeled using a modified Langmuir approach (Zhou et al, 2005).

The EPC values across all sites and pH levels were found to be substantially higher (EPC avg = 0.53 mg/L) than the average lake P concentration (P = 0.03 mg/L), suggesting that the sediment should act as a P source. However, an estimated 90% of the P that enters the lake remains within the system (Merrit and Miller, 2016). This suggests that phosphorus mobility within the lake is not dominated by sorption processes, but rather by another mechanism that leads to P retention. This mechanism is likely to be calcite co-precipitation. Using the Danen-Louwerse model, calcite co-precipitation was estimated to account for 159–434 mT P/yr, significantly exceeding the sorption-based estimate of 6–18 mT P/yr.

These findings demonstrate that calcite co-precipitation can be underrepresented when modeling P dynamics in marl lakes, and that accurate models and predictions require the use of a framework that includes both sorption and co-precipitation processes. Improved representation of these processes is necessary for understanding P cycling and developing management strategies for marl lakes, especially those near populated areas that are particularly vulnerable to eutrophication.

title: Compost vs. Biochar: Optimizing Amendment Strategies to Immobilize Metals in Mine Tailings
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Juarez, Lynette [1]
affiliations: (1) BYU, Geological, Provo, UT, USA
abstract:
Global mine tailings reclamation is of paramount importance within environmental research to elucidate how toxic elements impact surrounding ecosystems and to ensure safe living environments. To evaluate targeted mitigation strategies, batch sorption extractions were conducted by combining unique tailings samples, chemical amendments, and synthetic rainwater. Throughout the mixing phase, pH, electrical conductivity (EC), and oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) were continuously monitored prior to a 24-hour equilibrium period involving shaking, centrifugation, filtration, and subsequent inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis.

While biochar has historically been widely adopted as the benchmark paradigm for heavy metal immobilization due to its high porosity and carbon-sink capacity, its efficacy in complex, multi-element systems remains highly constrained. The investigations revealed highly divergent, pH-dependent geochemical behaviours for the primary target elements, copper (Cu) and molybdenum (Mo). Crucially, our sequential extraction data challenged conventional geochemical assumptions; while Cu typically exhibits high mobility under neutral conditions, our results demonstrate that it maintains exceptionally high mobility under acidic conditions as well. To address this persistent mobility across varying pH levels, the application of compost and fertilizer mixtures successfully stabilized the mine tailings, effectively immobilizing Cu through organic complexation and restricting Mo migration. Conversely, biochar failed to provide a comparable stabilizing effect. Furthermore, a distinct pH reversal was observed when the metals were structurally combined. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that strategic combinations of chemical amendments decisively alter the transport pathways of highly toxic elements. By unveiling how these metals behave under unique environmental conditions, this method provides a practical model for environmentalists to select targeted soil amendments and guarantee the long-term success of regional reclamation efforts.

title: Towards Spatially Explicit Flood Risk Assessment: Integrating Machine Learning-Based Hazard Mapping with Multi-Dimensional Exposure Assessment in the Western Himalayas
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Rahman, Atiqur [1], Ansari, Intejar [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi, India, India
(2) Department of Geography, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi, India, India
abstract: Floods are among the most destructive hydrometeorological hazards, accounting for 35-40% of all weather-related disasters globally. Between 1990-2022, floods affected more than 3.2 billion people, 218,000 fatalities, and resulted in US$ 1.3 trillion losses globally. Despite these impacts, studies continue to emphasize susceptibility mapping, while the risk assessment of socio-economic assets remains comparatively limited, particularly in Himalayan basins. Therefore, this study uses a four-dimensional multivariate flood exposure framework to quantify the flood risk across 35 administrative blocks of the Beas River Sub-Basin (BRSB) in Western Himalaya. The hazard component developed through sequentially optimized XGBoost model, whereas the flood exposure index was developed using the CRiteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) method. The robustness of the derived exposure index was further evaluated using the joint cumulative distribution function and Entropy Weight Method. Subsequently, the normalized flood hazard and exposure indices were integrated to develop a composite Flood Risk Index (FRI). The study shows that 2061 km 2 (16.5%) area of BRSB is highly prone to floods, and approx. 1.20 million people, 75.9 km 2 of built-up area, 553.5 km 2 of agricultural land, and 2,921 km of road network are exposed to flood within the BRSB. The FRI identified Panchrukhi, Nagrota Bagwan, Nurpur, Dharamshala, Mandi Sadar, and Kangra blocks is highly prone to flood and should be prioritized for flood mitigation, emergency preparedness, and resilient infrastructure planning. The proposed framework provides a systematic approach for integrating flood hazard and exposure information, thereby, supporting evidence-based flood risk management and spatial planning in mountainous river basins of the Himalayas.

title: Paleosol Development and Landscape Response to the Eocene–Oligocene Transition (White River Group, Colorado)
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science
authors: Huwaldt, Jacob Emil [1], Hembree, Daniel I [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, The University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA
abstract:
This study aims to quantify variations in paleosol development and landscape processes across the Eocene-Oligocene transition in northeastern Colorado. Progressive cooling and drying in the North American midcontinent during this transition has been linked to a shift from relatively mature soils (Alfisols, Ultisols) to less developed (Entisols, Inceptisols) in South Dakota and Nebraska, reflecting increased environmental stress and reduced pedogenic development. Studies of coeval strata in Colorado have suggested a less uniform transition. This study focused on exposures of the White River Group (WRG) in the Pawnee National Grassland (PNG) of northeastern Colorado. The objectives of this study are to (1) characterize pedogenic features and pedotypes through the WRG; (2) reconstruct environmental gradients such as water-table depth, soil moisture, and pedogenic development; and (3) relate these patterns to autogenic processes or allogenic climate change. These objectives provide a framework for testing how continental soil systems in this region responded to prolonged climatic stress.

Paleosols of the WRG were investigated at three localities across approximately 10 km (east to west) of the PNG near Pawnee Buttes. Paleosol development was analyzed both vertically through the White River section across six different stratigraphic levels and laterally between localities and within study sites using closely spaced sections. Paleosol successions were identified at each level and described in the field by thickness, color, structure, horizonation, nodules, redox features, rhizoliths, and bioturbation. Samples were collected from each profile every 20-50 cm to characterize micromorphology, bulk geochemistry, and clay mineralogy.

The White River section showed frequent shifts between fluvial and eolian depositional processes, with increased eolian influence higher in the section. Paleosols within these deposits generally display a low level of development throughout the section, dominated by Inceptisols and Entisols. However, higher levels of development, characterized by larger, deeper rhizoliths, stronger soil structure, and higher clay content, were present in paleosol successions both near the base and top of the three sections.

These exposures preserve a stratigraphic succession across the late Eocene-Oligocene transition, providing an ideal setting for studying the effects of changing climate and shifting environments on soil development and landscape stability. Initial results obtained from this study area suggest that the landscape response to the Eocene-Oligocene transition was spatially and temporally complex and characterized by long-term instability.

title: Tracking Temporal Changes in Arc Magma Sources During a Flare-up: North Cascades Arc, Washington and British Columbia
session_title: Continental magmatic-volcanic flare-ups: multidisciplinary investigations on their causes and consequences
authors: Bakshi, Sarnav [1], Gordon, Stacia M. [2], Hoinville, Alex [3], Shea, Erin K. [4], Wegener, Jeffrey Philip [5], Miller, Robert B. [6], Karmakar, Sourav [7], Eddy, Michael Patterson [8]

abstract: Continental magmatic arcs are characterized by flare-up magmatism which play a large role in the growth and compositional evolution of arc crust. The North Cascades continental magmatic arc, Washington and southern British Columbia, experienced three flare-ups between ca. 45–90 Ma, with the middle flare-up occurring between ca. 60–79 Ma. New U-Pb zircon analyses from 25 orthogneiss samples, together with geochemical and isotopic data, were used to investigate temporal changes in magma sources during this flare-up. The older ca. 70–79 Ma orthogneisses are hornblende bearing, metaluminous tonalites that lack inherited zircon and display trace element and εNd i values (+3.5 to +4.1) similar to coeval plutons, interpreted to be mantle-derived magmas with some crustal component. Conversely, the younger ca. 60–66 Ma orthogneisses are hornblende free and more silicic. More specifically, the ca. 64–66 Ma orthogneisses are peraluminous trondjhemites with εNd i values (+3.3 to +4.8) similar to older orthogneisses and plutons, but they contain ca. 70 and ca. 90 Ma inherited zircon grains. The inheritance is coeval with adjacent orthogneisses and plutons indicating that magma was generated through partial melting of older igneous arc rocks. In comparison, the youngest (ca. 60 Ma) orthogneiss have no coeval plutons, are peraluminous trondjhemitic to granitic leucogneisses, and they contain inherited zircon grains derived from plutons/orthogneisses (ca. 63–90 Ma) as well as metasedimentary rocks (ca. 100–500 Ma and Proterozoic ages). They also have the lowest εNd i values (+1.3 to +3.2) and most depleted trace-element compositions, indicating the magma formed from partial melts of both crustal igneous and metasedimentary rocks. Whole-rock Rb/Sr values of <4 indicate partial melting of the crust occurred under fluid-fluxed conditions at temperatures of ~710–740 °C based on zircon-saturation temperatures. The ca. 60–79 Ma flare-up event in the North Cascades arc therefore records changing magma sources through time and likely reflects progressive pinching out of the mantle wedge through likely slab flattening. This was followed by magma generation through fluid-fluxed partial melting of arc crust. This transition in magma source is only recorded by the orthogneisses in this continental arc system, whereas plutons mainly show a mantle source.

title: Fluvial Reworking and Provenance Heterogeneity of Late Paleogene Loess in the Western USA
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Baul, Shankhadeep [1], Fan, Majie [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Texas, Arlington, TX, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Texas, Arlington, TX, USA
abstract: The late Paleogene loess in the western USA is an extensive dust record for surface processes and paleoclimate studies, yet the sediment sources and silt generation mechanism remain poorly understood. In this study, we study detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology on late Eocene to early Oligocene fluvial deposits and their overlying loess at the Wagon Bed Spring (western Wyoming) and Pawnee Buttes (northeastern Colorado) sections to constrain loess provenance and evaluate the role of fluvial systems in supplying silts. Our data reveal that the loess at both sites has Proterozoic and Neoproterozoic-Paleozoic age populations common to Phanerozoic sedimentary cover, along with distinct signatures characteristic of local Laramide uplifts. The fluvial samples from western Wyoming show temporal variability and contain Archean and middle Eocene zircons sourced from nearby Granite Mountains. The Wyoming loess samples resemble the associated fluvial deposits characterized by Archean and middle Eocene zircon populations derived from the Granite Mountains, indicating that the loess was recycled from local fluvial sediment. The Colorado loess contains fewer Archean grains and has abundant Proterozoic Yavapai-Mazatzal and midcontinental granite-rhyolite populations. This signature is similar to the underlying Cretaceous Laramie Formation, suggesting that the loess was derived from the eolian reworking of local Cretaceous sedimentary cover, with fluvial erosion serving as a necessary intermediate process. When combined with published zircon data from four other late Paleogene loess sites, our results show that each site preserves a common signature of recycled Phanerozoic sedimentary cover with a distinct, locally-sourced zircon signature. This spatial variation follows the regional drainage pattern, specifically the transition from internally drained Laramide basins in central and western Wyoming to eastward-flowing regional river systems in eastern Wyoming and Colorado. These findings identify fluvial erosion as a primary mechanism for the production of silt-sized sediments for late Paleogene loess in the western USA. This model parallels documented loess provenance heterogeneity in both the Chinese Loess Plateau and the South American Pampean loess, highlighting the fundamental role of fluvial processes in facilitating loess formation during periods of limited or absent continental glaciation.

title: Detrital Rutile Geochronology and Trace Element Analysis in the Ouachita and Arkoma Basins
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Bolin, Mikaila [1], Sharman, Glenn R [2], Smith, Tyson [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Geosciences and Environmental Change Science Center, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract: Provenance studies of Carboniferous sedimentary rocks in the Arkoma and Ouachita basins incorporate petrographic analyses and detrital zircon geochronology where distinctive Laurentian and peri-Gondwanan sandstone compositions and zircon age-modes have been identified. However, there is uncertainty about the specific sediment-routing pathways to these basins. While detrital zircon has been widely accepted as an ideal mineral for U-Pb geochronology because of its high closure temperature, pervasiveness in various geologic settings, and tendency to incorporate uranium while excluding lead during crystallization, it does not readily record cooling histories or metamorphic deformation which are key components of source terrane characterization. This study uses detrital rutile U-Pb geochronology and trace element geochemistry alongside an existing detrital zircon U-Pb dataset to better understand source terranes and constrain sediment-routing pathways during the Carboniferous. In two samples, preliminary data show both peri-Gondwanan and Laurentian age peaks are younger in detrital rutile than their detrital zircon counterparts, suggesting that rutile records either the age of metamorphism or post-metamorphic cooling. Sample 20AR-02 is from the Bluejacket Sandstone, a Desmoinesian quartzose recycled sandstone, and has a prominent peri-Gondwanan and Laurentian detrital zircon source signal. In this sample, the Neoproterozoic Peri-Gondwanan peak age shifts from 569 Ma in the zircon to a 538 Ma rutile age peak, and the Neoproterozoic Laurentian age peak shifts from 417 Ma to 363 Ma. Sample OD-10A represents a Middle Atoka quartz arenite and displays a more Laurentian dominated source signal in the detrital zircon U-Pb age plots. In sample OD-10A, a prominent Laurentian zircon 428 Ma age peak shifts to a 363 Ma peak for rutile. For both samples, zircon-in-rutile thermometry indicates temperatures between 500°C and 750°C in the eclogite-amphibolite facies though many grains also plot in the granulite facies with calculated temperatures up to 1000°C. Cr/Nb ratios are non-differentiating between both samples as most grains plot in the metapelitic range. These data provide detailed information on lithology, geochemistry, and temperature histories of Laurentian and peri-Gondwanan source rocks, which allows us to better characterize these source terranes exposed during the Carboniferous.

title: Geaorchaeological and Stratigraphic Considerations about Abu Hureyra "Meltglass" & the Site’s Purported Decimation by Cosmic Impact
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Nicoll, Kathleen [1], Boslough, Mark [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Environment, Society & Sustainability, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
“Meltglass” is presented as evidence for a cosmic airburst ~12.8 ka during the Younger Dryas that decimated Abu Hureyra, an important large (~11.5 hectares) archaeological site in modern Syria that is now entirely under water due to construction of the Tabqa Dam along the Euphrates River. Records at Abu Hureyra are highly significant for understanding the earliest development of agriculture during the Epipaleolithic-Neolithic, when people transitioned from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle towards animal pastoralism and farming in the Levantine Fertile Crescent. A multi-authored 2020 paper published in Scientific Reports suggests that Abu Hureyra was impacted by a fragmented comet that exploded in the atmosphere, instantaneously vaporizing thatched huts in the settlement and splashing “meltglass” onto local sediment grains and animal bones – an event that has been suggested as a major forcing factor for impact survivors to invent and adopt agriculture.

To better understand this hypothesis, we (1) review the original fieldwork and findings from the 1972-3 field excavations of Abu Hureya that are documented in the complete site report published in 2000; (2) assess the original field data in context of the later stratigraphic reinterpretations and data presented in more recent publications; and (3) discuss the putative evidence of the cosmic impact in context of site taphonomy, records, available samples, and airburst physics.

title: POTENTIAL, ADVANCEMENTS, AND TECHNOLOGY ASSOCIATED WITH GREEN ENERGY, WITH A FOCUS ON ENERGY EFFICIENCY PROJECT APPROVALS, PERMITS, AND REGULATORY COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies
authors: Kavana, Ezra Kaombwe [1]
affiliations: (1) Paveway Africa Limited, Paveway Africa Limited, Dar es Salaam, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania
abstract:
The potential of green energy is vast, encompassing solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, and biomass sources. These renewable resources provide considerable benefits, such as reduced greenhouse gas emissions, energy security, and long-term sustainability. Taking use of this potential necessitates a thorough understanding of the many technologies involved.

Green energy technology development has accelerated in recent years. Solar photovoltaic (PV) systems have become more efficient and cost-effective, making them a popular alternative for household and commercial applications. Wind turbines, both onshore and offshore, have also evolved in size and production capacity, providing a competitive alternative to traditional fossil fuel-based power generation.

Hydroelectric power is a prominent force in the green energy sector, with large-scale projects producing steady and reliable electricity. Furthermore, geothermal energy uses the heat of the Earth to generate power, providing consistent energy production in geologically active areas. Biomass technologies, which use organic materials such as agricultural waste and forest residues, also contribute to green energy generation.

Despite their enormous potential and technological developments, green energy project development is subject to a variety of approvals, permits and regulatory compliance requirements. These restrictions are intended to safeguard the environment, promote public safety, and assure compliance with energy standards. Assessing the environmental impact of projects, holding community consultations, and adhering to regulations regarding zoning and land-use restrictions are all part of the permitting process.

Furthermore, compliance with regulations is critical for the successful execution of green energy projects. Local, regional, and national authorities impose emissions regulations, renewable portfolio targets, and other legal obligations on developers. Compliance with these regulations promotes a responsible and long-term strategy for green energy deployment.

Finally, green energy promises a promising path toward a more sustainable and environmentally responsible future. Exploiting the potential of renewable sources and utilizing innovative technologies will propel the green energy sector forward. However, getting authorizations and complying with regulatory frameworks, supporting responsible growth, and guaranteeing a cleaner and greener energy landscape are all critical to attaining successful project outcomes.
