title: Refining Model Hydrogeology Using Geophysical Data Can Reduce Model Forecast Uncertainty
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling (Posters)
authors: Richins, John G. [1], Duncan, Leslie L. [2], Fienen, Michael N. [3], Befus, Kevin M. [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi-Gulf Water Science Center, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi-Gulf Water Science Center, Nashville, TN, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Upper Midwest Water Science Center, Madison, WI, USA
(4) University of Arkansas, Department of Geosciences, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract: Airborne electromagnetic (AEM) and other geophysical data have been used to refine the hydrogeologic structure in groundwater models. Geophysical products can guide modelers in creating a more realistic representation of subsurface heterogeneity for groundwater flow models compared to models based on more traditional subsurface data collected from well logs. However, it is unclear if the geophysically based representations can quantitatively improve model forecasts. To determine this, we quantitatively assessed the usefulness of geophysical data in constraining model hydrogeology to forecast hydrologic responses by systematically testing how model parameters reduce forecast uncertainty for two MODFLOW 6 models created for the Shellmound, Mississippi groundwater transfer and injection pilot project: one that used AEM data to highly parameterize and discretize the alluvial aquifer model layers, and another that did not use AEM data to highly parameterize and discretize the alluvial aquifer model layers . Using tools built into the PyEmu Python library, we calculated the percent variance reduction contribution of model parameters to groundwater head and flow path forecasts. For the model that used geophysical data to highly parameterize and discretize the alluvial aquifer, parameters highly influenced by geophysical data were the most important for reducing model forecast uncertainty. This finding allowed us to conclude that when geophysical data is used for refining model hydrogeology, the parameters informed by geophysical data become more important for reducing model forecast uncertainty.

abstract:
Biodegradable plastic mulches (BDMs) offer the agronomic advantages of polyethylene (PE) films while, in principle, reducing end-of-season plastic waste. Yet current test methods (e.g., ASTM D5988) quantify only relative CO2 evolution, leaving unknown how much BDM-derived carbon enters non-respired soil pools, or which microbes truly drive degradation. Here, we quantify the fate of BDM-derived carbon in soil and identify its microbial degraders using separately labeled 14 C- and 13 C-labeled poly-L-lactic acid (PLA).

We synthesized 14 C- and 13 C-enriched PLA via azeotropic polycondensation and amended triplicate 100 g agricultural soil microcosms (0.1% w/w PLA), incubated at 25 °C for one year. Continuous NaOH trapping is capturing cumulative 14 CO 2 , and at day 365 we will destructively harvest microcosms to partition 14 C among microbial biomass, dissolved organic carbon, particulate organic matter, mineral-associated soil organic matter (MAOM), and residual polymer, yielding a closed 14 C mass balance. In parallel, a set of 13 C-PLA microcosms was destructively sampled weekly for eight weeks to capture peak mineralization, and heavy DNA was separated via CsCl density gradients. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of heavy versus light DNA identified bacterial taxa actively assimilating PLA-derived carbon.

14 CO 2 data indicate that approximately 5.94% of added PLA-C was respired within the first 18 weeks. 13 C-qSIP results show enrichment of PLA-C in heavy DNA from Actinobacteria , Proteobacteria , and Firmicutes, implicating a specific decomposer guild in both mineralization and stabilization of BDM-derived carbon. This study provides one of the first full soil carbon budgets for BDM-amended soil and explicitly links polymer fate to definite microbial degraders, advancing both sustainability assessment and the mechanistic understanding of polymer–microbe interactions in agricultural soils.

title: Preliminary Geologic Map of the Brush West 7.5-minute Quadrangle, Morgan County, Colorado
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee (Posters)
authors: Marr, Alexander Edwin [1]
affiliations: (1) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
The Brush West 7.5-minute quadrangle is currently being mapped by the Colorado Geological Survey (CGS) through the U.S. Geological Survey’s STATEMAP program. The map area is located in the Colorado Piedmont near the center of the Denver-Julesburg Basin. The quadrangle preserves a record of Pleistocene and Holocene alluvial and eolian deposition that reflects drainage evolution along the South Platte River corridor. This study includes a 1:24,000-scale geologic map of the quadrangle, three geologic cross sections, new optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) and radiocarbon ages, assessments of groundwater, geologic hazards, and mineral resources.

Quaternary surficial deposits cover nearly the entire map area and overlie Upper Cretaceous Pierre Shale. The surficial deposits record repeated cycles of fluvial incision and aggradation driven by glacial-interglacial climate shifts in the adjacent Rocky Mountains. Mapping distinguishes coarse, inverted-topography gravel of probable middle Pleistocene (Verdos Alluvium-equivalent; age is ~600 ka), based on its elevation above the active channel, and at least four younger generations of South Platte River and tributary alluvium. These include paleovalley incision and fill tentatively correlated with Bull Lake glaciation (~190–120 ka), extensive fluvial deposition tentatively associated with Pinedale glaciation (~30–12 ka), and Holocene aggradation and incision. Eolian loess, dunes, and sand sheets sourced from reworked alluvium and local bedrock mantle the uplands and record predominantly northeasterly winds since the Pinedale glaciation.

New OSL and radiocarbon ages provide preliminary chronological constraints on eolian and alluvial deposition in this area. Preliminary results indicate that eolian deposits in the northern part of the quadrangle are as young as 3 ka for loess and approximately 100 years for dune deposits. Additional samples collected during fieldwork await laboratory results.

Mineral resources in the quadrangle include (1) oil and gas and (2) sand and gravel. The principal oil and gas reservoirs in the area are the J (Muddy) and D Sandstones of the Dakota Group. Most of the sand and gravel extraction has occurred within the Holocene and middle Pleistocene alluvial units. The Bull Lake and Pinedale-associated alluvial units also form the principal shallow groundwater aquifer in the area. The two principal geologic hazards are expansive soils developed in clay-rich sediments and bedrock and flooding along the South Platte River and its tributaries.

title: Reshaping the Rio Grande at Eagle Pass, Texas: Laws, Landscapes, and Border Lives
session_title: International Collaborations in the Geosciences: Celebrating Science Without Borders
authors: Martinez, Adriana [1]
affiliations: (1) Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL, USA
abstract: Within the last two decades, the Rio Grande on the U.S.-Mexico border has undergone several significant phases of border militarization with the most recent and controversial addition being the in-channel buoys placed at Eagle Pass, Texas and elsewhere. The buoys are the latest in a series of other types of infrastructure including bollard style fencing, concertina razor wire, and train car containers. Each layer is an effort to deter undocumented immigration in an area that does not experience many immigrant crossings. Originally 1,000 feet long, the buoys placed in July of 2023 in Eagle Pass were later expanded to double that length in January of 2025. Along with buoy placement, the State of Texas took over the city owned Shelby Park and leveled and cleared multiple islands and riverbanks. Each of these actions caused Eagle Pass to be thrust into the national news and multiple lawsuits were filed regarding immigration enforcement, local’s access to the river, and the negative environmental impact on the river. To monitor river changes over time, I have conducted field work including sediment sampling for size distribution analysis, drone imagery for channel change monitoring, and water samples for microplastic and pollutant quantification. Each layer of fence, including the buoys, has caused river channel changes, altered water quality, disrupted habitat, altered immigrant pathways, and has the potential to increase injuries and casualties. Monitoring construction and river alterations of this nature is particularly important given the two international treaties that prevent river changes and ongoing new construction along the river.

abstract: The Guatemala Geohazard program is an innovative international collaboration that provides university students an internship opportunity that features individual mentoring of students by US and Guatemalan professors from Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala in Guatemala City and Cobán. Each year of this three-year program, a group of eight US and three Guatemalan undergraduate students, graduate students, and mentors conducted field research for three and a half weeks in January in Guatemala and two weeks of data analysis, synthesis, and poster presentation in May at UMKC. The goal of the Guatemala Geohazards program is for student participants to increase their scientific inquiry and research skills, to learn integrative field and lab research approaches to investigate exciting and cutting-edge geologic questions, and to practice international cooperation by collaborating side-by-side with Guatemalan students, professors, and professionals. The plate boundary setting of Guatemala exposes the country to numerous natural hazards, including earthquakes from four source areas, volcanic eruptions along the active volcanic arc and backarc setting, and landslides and floods that have intensified by more frequent tropical storms and hurricanes in a warming Earth. The broad aim of our research is to characterize the Quaternary record of geologic hazards associated with motion of the Motagua Fault, which last ruptured in the devastating M7.5 earthquake of 1976, and the region surrounding this left-lateral transform fault. Students and faculty were grouped into thematic research teams including volcanology, paleoseismology, and surface processes/landslides. Each team used digital mobile phone apps, Apple iPads equipped with GIS mapping software, real-time kinematic GNSS, UAS, and LiDAR aerial imagery in our field research component, and integrated these with lab analyses of geospatial, petrographic, geochemical, mineralogical, and sedimentological data. By participating in this program, in addition to research, students had the opportunity to collaborate internationally with peer students, interact with engineering and mining geologists, develop a first-hand view of a range of geoscience careers, and participate in professional development training and research that helped prepare them for the global workforce and the pursuit of degrees in higher education. Furthermore, the program provided an unparalleled avenue for cultural enrichment.

title: Global Terrestrial Primary Productivity Collapse at the K–Pg Boundary Supported by New Evidence for a Fungal Spore Spike from West Bijou (Colorado, USA)

abstract:
The Cretaceous–Paleogene (K–Pg) mass extinction (66.0 million years ago) is marked by a catastrophic disruption to Earth’s biosphere, coincident with the Chicxulub asteroid impact. Geophysical modelling has suggested that impact-generated dust and combustion-derived soot severely reduced incoming solar radiation, suppressing photosynthesis on a planetary scale. In addition to the immediate mass devastation to terrestrial plant ecosystems caused by the blast of the impact, wildfire ignited by the release of thermal energy, and acid rains from sulfate aerosols, the post K–Pg “impact winter” is hypothesized to have led to a collapse of primary productivity lasting several years. This hypothesis is supported by a unique occurrence of a fungal spike at the Moody Creek Mine K–Pg section in New Zealand.

We report the second discovery of a fungal spike at the Bowring Pit K–Pg section in West Bijou Creek, east of Denver, USA. From relative abundance counts of pollen and spores in 40 samples spanning ±30 cm across the K–Pg boundary, a spike of 31.9% fungal spores is observed within the topmost 3 cm of the boundary clay layer. The West Bijou spike is remarkable as it shows, for the first time, a germinating succession unfolding in two distinctive phases. This particular succession represents a completed asexual reproductive cycle of hyphal growth to mass sporulation, which has a duration of days to weeks in modern Ascomycetes. The fungal spike is immediately followed by a 20–40% Cyathidites spp. fern spore spike, indicating the recovery of devastated landscapes by pioneer plant recolonizers as photosynthesis resumed after post-impact darkness. This new evidence of a fungal spike from Colorado underscores devastation of forests at the K–Pg boundary which provided a dramatic increase in available substrates for saprophytic organisms and that this response occurred at a global scale. The collapse of primary productivity during the years of post-impact darkness would have greatly affected higher trophic levels relying on disappearing resources, while food webs based on detritus and decomposing communities would have been more resilient to the K–Pg mass extinction event.

title: Timing and kinematics of sackungen at Welcome Pass, North Cascades, Washington: establishing a GNSS and structure-from-motion baseline for detecting modern deep-seated slope deformation
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies (Posters)
authors: Brennan, Aidan [1], Clark, Douglas H. [2], Grant, Alex [3], Amos, Colin [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(3) Earthquake Science Center, USGS, Seattle, Washinton, USA
(4) Department of Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
abstract:
Sackungen, a class of deep-seated gravitational slope deformations (DSGSD), are widely recognized in the recently deglaciated ranges of the Pacific Northwest, yet the timing and kinematics of deformation are poorly understood. Better constraints on past and present deformation rates may illuminate the relationship between sackungen and postglacial unloading, inherited bedrock structure, hydrologic forcing, and seismic shaking. The importance of these drivers could help inform whether extant sackungen develop into rapid bedrock landslides.

Here we analyze a suite of DSGSD landforms near Welcome Pass, in the Nooksack River drainage of northwest Washington State, where several large Holocene rock avalanches have initiated on nearby slopes with similar sackung morphology. We use high-resolution lidar to identify uphill-facing scarps, ridge-top troughs and grabens, double-crested ridges, and water-filled sag ponds. Through geochronology, structural mapping, and kinematic analysis, we investigate when deformation initiated, whether it has proceeded as steady creep or in discrete episodes, and how the geometry is controlled by bedrock structure. Three datasets will address these questions.

Sag ponds formed between sackung ridges provide datable sediment archives; radiocarbon ages on terrestrial macrofossils and tephra identification in these sediments will bracket the onset of trough subsidence and test for episodic versus steady accumulation. Lidar-based geomorphic and structural mapping, paired with field foliation measurements, will test the hypothesis that scarp orientation is controlled by a northeast-southwest foliation that runs subparallel to a nearby Holocene fault. Preliminary lidar mapping has delineated 23 antislope scarps, 2 ridgetop troughs and grabens, and about 32 benches along ~1 km of ridge crest. Repeat GNSS and drone structure-from-motion (SfM) surveys will constrain modern deformation. Thirteen survey monuments installed in September 2025 were surveyed to establish a baseline set of positions along a transect through a potentially active portion of the Welcome Pass sackungen. Because reported DSGSD rates are low (~0.1 to 5 mm/yr) relative to our positional uncertainty (3-5 cm), annual survey intervals are not expected to resolve displacement yet. Rather, the network quantifies the detection threshold and anchors a repeat-occupation series over which motion may eventually become resolvable. Surveys in July and September 2026 will extend the series over three epochs. We will present the results of our structural mapping, preliminary deformation analyses, and hypotheses on the triggering mechanisms for the Welcome Pass sackungen.

title: Coastal Erosion, Legacy Oil Wells, and Drone-Based Methane Detection: Investigating Hydrocarbon Migration in California's Historic Summerland Oil Field
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Rathmann, Tim [1]
affiliations: (1) SCS Engineers, Long Beach, CA, USA; Earth Science, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, California, USA
abstract:
The Summerland Oil Field of Santa Barbara County, California, represents one of the world's earliest examples of coastal and offshore petroleum development. During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, hundreds of wells were drilled along the shoreline and from wooden piers extending into the Pacific Ocean. Many of these wells predate modern drilling, documentation, and abandonment standards, leaving behind poorly characterized infrastructure within a highly dynamic coastal setting. Recent storm events and shoreline erosion have exposed previously buried well casings, pipelines, and abandoned well remnants within the intertidal zone, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the interaction between coastal geomorphic processes, legacy petroleum infrastructure, and hydrocarbon migration.

This study documents exposed well casings, corroded wellheads, seep-affected infrastructure, and active hydrocarbon accumulations observed along Summerland Beach. Field investigations integrate historical oil-field records, coastal geomorphologic observations, geological interpretation, and abandoned-well assessment methodologies to evaluate potential fluid and gas migration pathways associated with legacy wells. Observations indicate that ongoing shoreline erosion can expose century-old infrastructure and create pathways linking historic wellbores to the modern coastal environment. These conditions present ongoing environmental, engineering, and resource-management challenges for coastal communities and regulatory agencies.

A key component of the investigation is the application of drone-based methane detection technology utilizing Tunable Diode Laser Absorption Spectroscopy (TDLAS). Unmanned aerial surveys provide a rapid, non-intrusive approach for identifying methane anomalies associated with leaking wells and hydrocarbon seepage in difficult-to-access coastal environments. Integration of aerial methane measurements with geologic mapping, coastal-process observations, and visual seep indicators creates a multidisciplinary framework for identifying potential leakage sources and prioritizing further investigation. The approach demonstrates how emerging remote-sensing technologies can complement traditional geological and environmental assessments of legacy oil infrastructure.

Results highlight the value of combining coastal geomorphology, petroleum geology, historical infrastructure reconstruction, and advanced drone-based monitoring to better understand the long-term environmental impacts of historic oil development. This work provides a transferable methodology for identifying, evaluating, and managing legacy wells exposed by coastal change and offers new insights into the geologic and environmental legacy of California's earliest offshore oil field.

title: The Effects of Anoxia on Panthalassan Food Web Stability during the Late Triassic
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part II)
authors: Bingham, Joseph D. [1], Ramirez-Guasp, Fiorella S. [2], Lacherez, Lena Jude [3], Tackett, Lydia S. [4], Dineen, Ashley A. [5], Banker, Roxanne M.W. [6], Roopnarine, Peter D. [7], Tyler, Carrie L. [8]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA

(7) Department of Zoology and Geology, California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA, USA

abstract:
Anoxia ranks among the most widespread deleterious anthropogenic effects on modern marine ecosystems, and ancient analogues are critical for forecasting their resilience. The geological record provides crucial context for understanding the long-term effects of recurring anoxia on food web stability. The Late Triassic was an interval of prolonged extinction characterized by a series of stepwise biotic turnovers that culminated in the end-Triassic mass extinction (ETME). These biotic crises are heavily associated with anoxia, prompted by massive volcanic eruptions from the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, which may have significantly destabilized marine communities. Here, we examine marine food webs from the Norian and Rhaetian stages to determine how anoxia may have impacted food web stability prior to the ETME. To quantify these impacts on ecosystem stability, we analyzed the network structure of these food webs, specifically focusing on modules and modularity. In food webs, modules act as structural compartments of heavily interacting species. High modularity increases ecosystem resilience because these compartments act as buffers, preventing local secondary extinctions from cascading across the entire network. We assessed the number of modules and modularity in food webs reconstructed from fossil assemblages found in the Gabbs Formation in the Muller and New York Canyons (west-central Nevada, USA).

Food web links were assigned based on the potential for consumer-resource interactions for 154 taxa in the Norian and 67 taxa in the Rhaetian. The Norian food web has a higher modularity of 0.382 and consists of four modules: (1) a detritivore module, (2) a grazer module, (3) a bacteriovore module, and (4) a carnivore module. During the Rhaetian, this structure collapsed to a lower modularity of 0.098 and two modules: (1) a detritivore module and (2) a bacteriovore module. This decrease is likely due to extinctions driven by anoxia, which also resulted in the loss of associated interactions among taxa—producing a sparser, less connected food web. These structural changes suggest that anoxia significantly destabilized marine food webs across the Norian–Rhaetian boundary. If modules are an important feature of stable marine ecosystems that can be disrupted by anoxia, this study would provide critical insights for modern conservation by using the breakdown of specific modules as an early warning indicator for ecosystems currently facing severe oxygen depletion.

title: A Synthesis Center for Paleoenvironmental Records of Extreme Events: A National Academies Report
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250

abstract:
Extreme environmental events such as floods, droughts, wildfires, earthquakes, and tsunamis pose growing risks to ecosystems, infrastructure, economies, and human life. Yet modern instrumental records are often too short to characterize the full range of rare, high-magnitude events that shape long-term societal risk. Paleoenvironmental records from sediments, tree rings, ice cores, corals, speleothems, and other natural archives can extend observations across centuries to millennia, revealing events outside the range of modern experience and informing planning for future extremes.

This presentation will discuss findings from the 2026 National Academies consensus report A Synthesis Center for Paleoenvironmental Records of Extreme Events. The report finds that the United States has a rich but fragmented information ecosystem for paleoenvironmental data, spanning collection, characterization, interpretation, integration, and translation. Existing repositories, databases, and scientific efforts provide essential foundations, but inconsistent metadata, uneven discoverability, weak linkages between physical samples and interpreted event histories, and limited long-term synthesis capacity constrain broader societal use.

The report concludes that while many aspects of the information ecosystem could be improved, the most urgent unmet need is sustained capacity for synthesis and translation: the work of transforming dispersed records into usable knowledge for planners, engineers, resource managers, emergency managers, businesses, and communities. Drawing on models from successful synthesis centers, the report recommends creation of a physically based synthesis and translation center with sustained support, dedicated staff, competitive working groups, stakeholder engagement, and capacity to produce mission-oriented products that improve resilience, risk evaluation, infrastructure planning, and emergency preparedness. This center would help connect deep-time geologic records with forward-looking decisions about hazards, management, and society.

abstract:
Apatite, a hexagonal phosphate with ideal endmember formula Ca 5 (PO 4 ) 3 (OH,F,Cl), can host rare earth elements (REEs) through coupled substitutions such as [REE 3+ +Si 4+ ]↔[Ca 2+ +P 5+ ]. Although the REEs are typically in minor concentrations, in some occurrences, the modal abundance of apatite is high enough that their economic recovery can be considered. Here we report the progress of a study investigating preferential pathways to decompose REE-bearing apatite with the objective of simplifying the mineral processing stage and minimizing reagent consumption.

The starting material was an 1.87 Ga iron oxide–apatite (IOA) assemblage from the Great Bear magmatic zone, NWT, Canada. Apatite, with a modal abundance up to 16 wt%, is coarse with each grain displaying two distinct compositional domains, one with total REE oxide concentrations reaching 4 wt% associated with significant actinide content (e.g. ThO 2 ≈ 400 ppm), the other closer to the ideal endmember with < 0.2 wt% REE 2 O 3 . Rock samples were fragmented along grain boundaries by high-voltage electrical pulses using a Selfrag Lab system. The liberated material was sieved and magnetite was then removed by magnetic separation. A single-phase apatite feed was also produced by individually picking grains ranging in size from 300 to 750 µm.

Leaching experiments on the monomineralic apatite material reveal high reactivity with a faster decomposition rate for the domains enriched in REEs than for the REE-depleted sectors. Characterization by Raman spectroscopy shows a broadening of the 𝜈 1 [PO 4 ] band in the REE-rich regions, indicative of a lower degree of crystallinity potentially inherited by radiation damage considering their higher actinide content and the great age of the IOA mineralization.

To evaluate if the observed high reactivity can be used as a strategy to selectively decompose apatite directly from the original mineralogical assemblage, diluted hydrochloric acid treatments were performed on the fragmented +45/-300 µm fraction consisting mainly of apatite (72 wt%) and actinolite (23 wt%), in its pristine form, as well as doped with 20 wt% of the recovered magnetite. Complete apatite decomposition was achieved at room temperature while leaving the associated minerals intact through a control of the concentration of HCl relative to the stoichiometric apatite requirement and the extent of water dilution to adjust the acid strength, hence minimizing energy and reagent consumption without the need to produce a concentrate.

abstract: The continental-scale Colorado River system developed from 8 to 4.8 Ma from precursor paleoriver segments that became integrated north to south. This is traced by an assemblage of 60–40 Ma detrital sanidine (DS) sand grains ultimately derived from ignimbrite eruptions in Idaho. They sequentially appeared in the 25-8 Ma Browns Park Formation, 7-6 Ma upper Bidahochi Formation, and 4.8 Ma Bouse Formation of the lower Colorado River and proto-Gulf of California. Molecular clock estimates of divergence times among fish lineages mimic this southward progression. A several-million-year-timeframe of integration is most compatible with mantle geodynamics as driver, with integration responding to epeirogenic uplifts along the Yellowstone hotspot track, western Rocky Mountains, and Jemez lineament that tilted the Colorado Plateau region toward the southwest, synchronous with fluvial baselevel fall at the opening Gulf of California. Shorter wavelength lithospheric drips may also have created, then uplifted, sedimentary/volcanic basins along the path. This hypothesis is compatible with the heterogeneous upper mantle velocity structure and Cenozoic magmatic record. Shorter-lived, perhaps catastrophic, geomorphic events such as river piracy and lake spillover may have contributed, as is documented from 5.4 to 4.8 Ma in the Lower Colorado River corridor. Data gaps for the 8-7 integration from Browns Park into Bidahochi basin and the 6-5 Ma integration through Grand Canyon need to be filled-in to help resolve the interaction of tectonic and geomorphic processes during Colorado River integration and formation of Grand Canyon. Surface magmatism suggests: 1) multistage delamination beneath the San Juans (38-23 Ma and 10-0 Ma); 2) lithospheric sagging beneath eastern Browns Park basin (23-8 Ma) followed by ~8 Ma drip detachment and uplift; 3) Hopi Buttes magmatism recording sagging (16-6 Ma) leading to 7-6 Ma upper Bidahochi Formation deposition and 6-5 Ma drip detachment and uplift; and 4) uplift of the San Francisco Peaks area ~2.5-0 Ma involving crust removal and melt reservoirs. Ongoing sinking lithosphere with asthenospheric return flow around the Escalante anomaly drip is proposed to be driving ongoing uplift of the Lees Ferry knickpoint and Lake Powell area. The latter uplifts may be driving accelerated incision in the past 2 Ma in the Virgin River headwaters, Grand Canyon, and Glen Canyon regions based on the strath-to-strath terrace record of differential incision.

title: Height-Diameter Relationships of Fossil Agathoxylon, Black Forest Unit, Chinle Formation, Petrified Forest National Park.
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Farr, Kathleen R. [1], Wagner, Victoria N. [2], Fairley, Jerry P. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Idaho, Moscow, ID,
(2) University of Idaho, Moscow, ID,
(3) University of Idaho, Moscow, ID,
abstract: During the spring of 2026, we measured the orientation, length, and diameter of 111 permineralized logs in the Late Triassic Black Forest bed of the Chinle Formation in Petrified Forest National Park (PEFO). The measured fossil logs, which primarily belong to the species Agathoxylon, ranged in height from 0.3 m to 21 m, with diameters between 0.15 to 1.6 m. We examined preserved trunk lengths as a function of diameter to determine what, if any, relationship existed between the two factors. We also compared our data to multiple models from the literature in which investigators inferred the heights of living Araucaria trees. The best-fit line for our measured diameter/height relationship significantly underpredicts tree height in comparison to all existing models; this result was expected, due to the inevitable truncation of the fossil logs in the Black Forest bed. However, predictions from the published models also differ significantly from one another; therefore, in this study we examine the published height-diameter relationships for fossil and living trees, with particular emphasis on identifying the influence of factors such as wood structure, trunk taper, stand size, and branch structure on predicted tree heights.

title: When Facies Reflect Faunas: Integrating Sequence Stratigraphy and Paleontology Across the Norian–Rhaetian Boundary
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Tackett, Lydia [1], Clement, Annaka M. [2], Golding, Martyn [3], Rigo, Manuel [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
(2) University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, Chattanooga, TN, USA
(3) Geological Survey of Canada, Vancouver, BC, Canada
(4) University of Padova, Padova, Italy
abstract:
The Norian–Rhaetian boundary (NRB) has been proposed to record the only oceanic anoxic event (OAE) of the Late Triassic, providing an opportunity to evaluate how oxygen stress influenced carbonate environments and faunal change. On carbonate ramps and platforms, however, ecological turnover can alter biosediment composition, making it difficult to distinguish depositional change from paleoecological transition. We integrate high-resolution facies analysis, sequence stratigraphy, chemostratigraphy, and macro/micropaleontology from multiple sections of the Gabbs Formation (west-central Nevada, USA) to test whether faunal turnover across the NRB reflects changing depositional environments. New strontium isotope data, combined with carbon isotope stratigraphy, improve correlations between sections and constrain the position of the boundary despite local differences in isotope excursions.

The Gabbs Formation records an overall shallowing-upward forced regression from outer- to inner-ramp environments, but no significant facies shift occurs across the chemostratigraphically defined NRB (the inferred anoxic interval). Bed thickness, sedimentary structures, and other non-biogenic sedimentological features remain consistent across the boundary. In contrast, fossil and biosedimentary assemblages change markedly: shelly macrofossils decline, carbonate-producing skeletal grains decline, micrite becomes more abundant relative to other grains, siliceous sponge spicules increase, and several benthic groups decrease substantially in abundance while overall invertebrate diversity changes comparatively little.

These results demonstrate that carbonate microfacies may record ecological reorganization as much as changes in depositional environment. Facies interpretations based primarily on bioclastic abundance can conflate environmental gradients with changes in carbonate biosediment-producing assemblages during intervals of environmental stress. Integrating sequence stratigraphy with paleontological and chemostratigraphic data provides a more robust framework for distinguishing depositional change from ecosystem response during anoxia.

title: Legal Reforms for Advancing Managed Aquifer Recharge
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Owen, Dave [1]
affiliations: (1) UC Law San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA
abstract: Managed aquifer recharge is a promising and increasingly popular way to meet water-supply challenges. But managed aquifer recharge also can fit awkwardly with existing legal frameworks. That awkward fit can arise from a variety of reasons. Applicable laws may have been crafted with other types of projects in mind and have unclear implications for MAR; states may lack permitting programs and oversight systems tailored to MAR projects; and general gaps and weaknesses in state systems of water law can create uncertainties for MAR projects. This presentation will explain these and other legal challenges for MAR, and it will identify ways in which legal reforms could help MAR better fulfill its promise.

title: Trait shifts in plant fossils predict survival in a heating Earth: simulated vegetation-climate interactions across the Triassic-Jurassic Boundary
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Matthaeus, William J. [1], White, Joseph Daniel [2], Lunt, Daniel J. [3], Jones, Wray [4], Dimitropolis, Kyra [5], Wilson, Jonathan P. [6], McElwain, Jennifer C [7]
affiliations: (1) Discipline of Botany, Trinity College Dublin, Glen Mills, PA,
(2) Baylor University, Biolgy, Waco, TX,
(3) School of Geographical Sciences, University of Bristol, United Kingdom
(4) Department of Geology, Baylor University, USA; National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institutions,
(5) Department of Geology, Baylor University, USA
(6) Haverford College, Haverford, PA,
(7) Discipline of Botany, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland
abstract: Heating episodes in Earth’s past have likely acted as ecological filters for plant traits. Volcanism at the Triassic-Jurassic (T-J) boundary in the middle Mesozoic elevated atmospheric CO2 (>2000 ppm) and induced heating (GMST >24°C). Biogeographic limitation and macrofloral turnover have produced hypotheses regarding the ecology and traits of survivor taxa. For example, leaf temperature may be reduced in narrow leaves capable of transpiring in hot, dry conditions. Here, we parameterize a process-based model of ecosystem processes (i.e., paleo -BGC) using paleo-traits (functional traits measured in fossils) to test the impact of leaf width, maximum stomatal conductance (g max ), and xylem vulnerability to cavitation-induced embolism (Ψ C ). Using Paleo -BGC, trait combinations are tested in the climate space of the T-J, based on global climate model simulations (HadCM-3B). We test whether water-use trait coordination (1) limits forest cover and (2) corresponds with the pattern of community turnover observed at classic T-J sites. We compare the maximum temperatures of T-J leaves at several CO 2 levels with the thermal tolerance of forest trees from neo-botany. Process-based simulations parameterized using fossils show where, how, and why plants survived or went extinct during deep-time heating episodes, and allow hypothesis testing against the fossil record—enabling better vegetation projections under different anthropogenic CO 2 emissions scenarios.

title: Quantifying Treptichnid Behavior: is Treptichnus pedum a Reliable Marker for the Cambrian?
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Cover, Zachary J.R. [1], Darroch, SIMON A.F. [2], Mitchell, Emily G.H. [3], Gutiérrez, Carolina [4]
affiliations: (1) Paleozoology, Senckenberg Gesellschaft für Naturforschung, Frankfurt am Main, Germany; Goethe-Universität Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Germany
(2) Paleozoology, Senckenberg Gesellschaft für Naturforschung, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
(3) Department of Zoology and University Museum of Zoology, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom
(4) Instituto de Estudios Andinos Don Pablo Groeber (IDEAN, CONICET), Capital Federal, Buenos Aires, Argentina
abstract:
Trace fossils belonging to the ichnogenus Treptichnus (informally referred to as ‘treptichnids’) were among the first 3-dimensional burrow systems to emerge over the Ediacaran-Cambrian transition, and helped drive early phases of the ‘Agronomic revolution’. Treptichnids display a wide range of morphologies, likely reflecting not only taphonomic differences but also behavioral variation, which allows different ichnospecies to be distinguished. In some cases, however, identification at the ichnospecies level remains uncertain, and the morphological differences both among and within ichnospecies have not yet been quantitatively characterized. This is a problem given that Treptichnus pedum is currently used as a criterion for recognizing the Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary. This raises the question: can we reliably and accurately identify treptichnid ichnotaxa, and – specifically – T. pedum ? This issue is especially relevant, given the increasing number of treptichnids being described from late Ediacaran strata. Here, we address this question using a combination of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), trained on a large dataset of identified specimens from published literature and museum collections.

The results of our PCA suggest that T. pedum is morphologically distinct from T. pollardi, T. coronatum, and Bicavichnites (a putative treptichnid), but indistinguishable from T. lublinensis, T. bifurcus , T. vagans, T. apsorum, T. rectangularis, and T. triplex . Cross-validation of the LDA showed that Treptichnus ichnospecies could be accurately classified with varying degrees of confidence but also showed that T. pedum is the most readily identifiable (~90% accuracy).

Finally, we apply the results of our LDA to predict the identity of unidentified Ediacaran-aged specimens from several Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary sections. Our model identifies multiple specimens from unequivocally Ediacaran-aged sediments as being behaviorally most-similar to T. pedum , including some of the oldest known treptichnids. These findings illustrate: 1) that treptichnid behavior rapidly diversified into more complex forms during the last ~5-10 million years of the Ediacaran; and 2) that T. pedum in isolation may be an unreliable marker for Cambrian-aged strata.

title: No Boots Required: Developing Geologic Mapping Skills using Immersive Virtual Reality
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research
authors: Bursztyn, Natalie [1], D'Antonio, Ashley [2], Masters, Barton [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Environmental Science, James Madison University, Dayton, VA, USA
(2) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(3) Center for Immersive Experiences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract:
The geosciences have long been considered an inaccessible field, with field camp being a limiting factor to many. Further, evidence suggests the spatial skills essential for reasoning in geosciences can be improved through field-based training. The development and testing of ways, including virtual immersive technologies, to train spatial reasoning through mapping problem solving skills without the physical, cultural, and economic barriers of travel, hiking, and camping will improve accessibility and inclusion in the geosciences. Strike & Dip (S&D) is an immersive Virtual Reality (iVR) program that scaffolds geologic problems via increasingly challenging geospatial relationships delivered through a flexible, discovery-based, student-centered, approach within the safety of the classroom with a professor nearby.

The main components of S&D are the compass and field stops. Users explore one of five virtual field mapping environments to field stops where they take strike and dip measurements and identify lithologic units. Once the user is near the surface they need to measure, they grab the compass (with their hand and VR controller) and adjust its orientation to take their measurements, just like a real field compass. Unlike a real compass, users can opt to use a feature that checks their measurements against the true values – instantly informing them of a measurement error.

We embraced iVR to implement sound pedagogical practice into developing S&D by utilizing a scaffolded inquiry-based structure that enables students to develop the skills to visualize the Earth’s subsurface and interpret strike and dip measurements. This iVR program was piloted in spring of 2024 with a group of geology majors with limited field mapping experience and very limited VR gaming experience. Performance on the mapping problems was excellent, and all were comfortable navigating S&D in iVR by the second mapping exercise. Students reported improved confidence and resonated well with the ease and opportunity to revisit sites, compass orientation practice and having their measurements checked instantly, as well as having the safety net of the proximity of peers and professor. Students also noted it felt like a steppingstone to develop skills and/or provide experience to others they knew could not access traditional mapping areas.

Having options like S&D for virtual field-based mapping investigations can broaden the reach and accessibility for all students to develop essential geologic spatial reasoning skills.

title: Testing the Utility of LLM-Based Approaches for Determining Depositional Environment in Large Paleontological and Geochemical Database Studies
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Leibovitz, Sarah Cameron [1], Sperling, Erik A. [2], Dobbs, Stephen Cole [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, Stanford, CA, USA
(2) Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
(3) Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
abstract: Large database-scale studies are essential for understanding patterns in paleontological and geochemical records across Earth history, but are limited by the geologic context data available. For instance, taxonomic records in the Paleobiology Database (PBDB) and national geologic survey data included in the Sedimentary Geochemistry and Paleoenvironments Project (SGP) frequently have little to no paleoenvironmental metadata associated with them. Studies aiming to use such data with paleoenvironmental control thus require extensive filtering, significantly limiting the amount of usable data, or manual paleoenvironmental coding, which becomes time prohibitive at large scale. Recent advancements in publicly accessible large language models (LLMs) provide an appealing, readily-available, and low-cost tool to fill in metadata gaps. LLMs have the potential to excel at paleoenvironmental classification because they are able to find, synthesize, and interpret information using natural language processing (NLP). However, drawbacks include lack of reproducibility, lack of access to paywalled scientific literature, and a propensity to hallucinate. This study develops and evaluates a methodology to test the ability of publicly-available LLM models to find and interpret geologic literature to determine the depositional environment of marine strata. Specifically, for each given formation and location, the LLM (1) performs an Internet search to find published sedimentological descriptions, (2) interprets those descriptions using formalized sedimentological criteria, and (3) outputs classifications, sources, and reasoning. To determine whether an LLM-based approach is appropriate for interpreting depositional environment in large datasets, results are evaluated against (1) human classifications for a PBDB test set and (2) a test set drawn from the SGP database and largely coded by researchers working on those samples. To effectively apply this methodology to determine paleoenvironmental setting, AI-generated classifications must agree sufficiently well with human-generated classifications and, in cases of disagreement, must not show a significant directional bias. Preliminary results using Claude Sonnet 4.6 have fairly low (~55%) agreement with SGP paleoenvironmental classifications and tend to classify outer shelf environments as slope/basinal. Further work aims to improve accuracy, reduce bias, and compare against other AI models.

title: Impact Cratering on Early Earth: A Kaleidoscope of Effects
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Marchi, Simone [1]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
abstract:
Recent advances have improved our understanding of the nature and rate of collisions between the early Earth and leftover planetesimals from planetary accretion. A combination of geophysical observations, geochemical data, and dynamical models have been used to constrain the oldest (>3.8-3.9 Ga) terrestrial collisional history (e.g., Marchi et al. 2014; Morbidelli et al. 2018; Nesvorny et al. 2022). These models primarily rely on observational constraints, such as lunar cratering rates inferred from crater counts and sample radiometric ages, as well as concentrations of highly siderophile elements in lunar and terrestrial rocks. The subsequent ~3.5-2.5 Ga impact flux has been constrained thanks to preserved records of terrestrial collisions in impact-generated spherule layers (Glass & Simonson 2013; Marchi et al. 2021; Drabon et al. 2024).

These impact models show that the Hadean Earth (4.5-4.0 Ga) was pummeled by hundreds of impactors larger than 100 km in diameter, and countless smaller ones. It is hard to overstate the profound effects these collisions had on the environment. Processes such as widespread crustal melting, excavation, and hydrothermal circulation fundamentally reshaped Hadean surface environments. In this talk, I will review current knowledge of the early Earth impact flux and discuss its key environmental consequences.

title: Methane Sustained the Cretaceous-Paleogene Hothouse Climate
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Herring, John [1], Goldblatt, Colin [2], Garduño Ruíz, Daniel [3], Johnson, Benjamin W. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere and Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA, USA
(2) School of Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of Victoria, Victoria, BC, Canada
(3) School of Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of Victoria, Victoria, BC, Canada
(4) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere and Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA, USA
abstract:
Anomalously warm “hothouse” periods, such as the late Cretaceous and early Paleogene, provide crucial context for major transitions in past ecosystem evolution (e.g., the Angiosperm Terrestrial Revolution) while serving as potential analogues for future anthropogenic climates. However, the high temperatures of these periods are often poorly correlated with proxied carbon dioxide levels (pCO 2 ). This suggests that other warming mechanisms must have sustained these hothouse climates despite insufficient pCO 2 , but no quantitative solution to this problem has been demonstrated thus far.

To explain this standing problem in paleoclimatology, we propose that emissions of methane (CH 4 ) from ancient wetlands were strongly intensified in response to higher temperatures, potentially driving a greenhouse-warming positive feedback in Earth’s past. We revise an existing model approach and incorporate an updated surface temperature history to reconstruct CH 4 emissions since the late Devonian. In particular, we rescale natural wetland CH 4 emissions with a robust temperature sensitivity and a lithologically based proxy for relative coal-forming wetland area over the past 375 Ma. After running our emission history through a 1-D photochemical model, we resolve steady-state pCH 4 over deep time. We ultimately validate our modeling approach against the pCH 4 record from late Pleistocene ice cores.

Our results suggest that methane emissions from coal-forming wetlands were strongly amplified under past greenhouse climates, sustaining >50 ppm CH 4 during the Cretaceous and Paleogene hothouse periods. Such high pCH 4 could have supported >5 W/m 2 of radiative forcing, helping to explain anomalously high surface temperatures during these intervals despite relatively modest pCO 2 . We thus suggest that accounting for terrestrial CH 4 emissions could substantially improve our understanding of extreme climate warming in Earth’s Phanerozoic past, with implications for prediction of future climate evolution.

title: Disentangling Tectonics, Lithology, and Climate: Bayesian Inversion of River-Incised Landscapes for Long-Term Rock Uplift
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Oryan, Bar [1], Gailleton, Boris [2], Olive, Jean-Arthur [3], Malatesta, Luca C. [4], Jolivet, Romain [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Géosciences Rennes, Univ. Rennes, Rennes, France
(3) Laboratoire de Géologie, École normale supérieure, Paris, France
(4) Earth Surface Process Modelling, GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, Potsdam, Germany
(5) Laboratoire de Géologie, École normale supérieure, Paris, France; Institut Universitaire de France, Paris, France
abstract:
Earth's topography records the combined forcing of tectonics, lithology, and climate, and separating these contributions is essential for using landscapes as quantitative archives of crustal deformation. Here we present a new Bayesian inversion framework that recovers spatially variable fields of long-term rock uplift and rock erodibility directly from fluvially incised landscapes. Because rivers incise at rates set by local slope and drainage area, the shape of their profiles encodes the spatial pattern of rock uplift. We build on this property by extending the χ coordinate system, which integrates drainage area changes along river networks assuming a steady-state landscape and account for spatial variability in rock uplift, erodibility, and precipitation (χ UKQ ). We then develop a quasi-Newton Bayesian inversion scheme that solves for the uplift and erodibility fields that best linearize river profiles in χ UKQ -space.

After validating the method with synthetic landscapes, we apply it to a 200-km-wide region of the central Himalaya and to landscapes shaped by normal faulting. Our inversion resolves the imprint of lithology and precipitation while recovering uplift patterns consistent with independent estimates from geomorphic markers and with expected patterns of upper crustal deformation. By isolating tectonic signals from climatic and lithologic effects, this approach turns river networks into quantitative recorders of long-term rock uplift, paving the way to deciphering tectonic fingerprints in landscapes where patterns of deformation remain unknown.

title: Geochemical Controls on Euendolithic Microboring by Green Alga, Phaeophila dendroides
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Lincoln, Tyler [1], Trower, Lizzy [2], Brininger, Christian [3], Cameron, Jeffery [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(3) Department of Biochemistry, University of Wisconsin –Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(4) Department of Biochemistry, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA
abstract: Euendolithic microorganisms actively dissolve carbonate substrates, producing microborings that they inhabit. These organisms are commonly found in shallow, marine, CaCO₃-supersaturated seawater, yet they dissolve CaCO₃, working against the thermodynamic tendency toward precipitation. The persistence of euendolithic boring under these conditions implies there must be ecological or physiological benefits to this lifestyle, but these benefits remain poorly constrained. We tested whether euendoliths benefit from this behavior through protection from excess light, availability of carbonate-derived inorganic carbon, and access to substrate-hosted micronutrients, namely Fe, Mn, and Zn. Additionally, we predicted windows during the diel cycle in which carbonate chemistry is more favorable for dissolution. We use the green alga Phaeophila dendroides , enriched from ooid sand collected from the Turks and Caicos Islands. By measuring pH, alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentration, δ¹³C DIC values, and major ion concentrations, we constrained the carbonate system across a light-availability gradient, a gradient of CaCO₃ saturation state (Ω), a suite of aragonite and calcite substrates containing variable concentrations of trace micronutrients, and sampled at time points across the diel cycle. All full-light treatments consumed DIC and alkalinity to low concentrations, consistent with net photosynthetic carbon uptake coupled with carbonate mineral formation. This pattern occurred across both the Ω arag gradient and the suite of CaCO₃ substrates, whereas treatments under opaque conditions showed evidence of net dissolution, evident in increases in alkalinity, DIC concentration, and δ¹³C DIC values. The diel time series provided context for this observation: pH, Ca²⁺ concentration, δ¹³C DIC values, DIC concentration, alkalinity, and Ω arag values trace a hysteresis across the light–dark cycle. Nighttime increases in alkalinity and δ¹³C DIC values were consistent with carbonate dissolution, but this signal was partly overprinted by the much larger effects of daytime photosynthesis and carbonate mineral precipitation. Daytime increases in Ca 2+ concentrations may reflect delayed release of intracellular Ca 2+ pools resulting from nighttime dissolution. These results provide preliminary evidence of temporal separation of CaCO 3 dissolution from photosynthetic activity in an euendolithic alga.

title: Following Rolfe Mandel into the Eastern Mediterranean: Insights into the Origin of the Late Pleistocene Sinai and Negev Dunes, Egypt and Israel, from New Trace Element Geochemistry
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Muhs, Daniel R. [1], Roskin, Joel [2]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(2) Department of Environment, Planning & Sustainability, Bar Ilan Univ, Israel, Ramat-Gan, Israel
abstract: Rolfe Mandel is well known for his studies of the geomorphology, geoarchaeology, and Quaternary geology of the North American Great Plains, but he has also made tremendous contributions to these fields in the eastern Mediterranean region (Egypt, Cyprus, and Jordan). Here, we follow him into this region and present new thoughts concerning the origin of minority minerals in eolian sands of the Sinai and Negev dune fields of Egypt and Israel that likely date to the late Pleistocene. In a previous study (Muhs, Roskin et al., 2013, QSR 69, 28-48), we concluded that these quartz-dominated dune fields owe their origin primarily to quartz-rich Nile River delta sediments and secondarily to Sinai wadi sediments (Wadi El Arish and its tributaries). New trace element geochemistry provides additional information on the minority minerals of these dunes. K/Rb and K/Cs values (proxies for K-feldspar) show that both Nile River delta and central Wadi El Arish sediments were likely contributors to dunes in both Sinai and the western Negev. Ca/Mg and Ca/Sr values show that calcite in both dune fields is derived dominantly from Wadi El Arish sediments. Heavy minerals are proxied by Zr/Hf (zircon), Ti/Nb (ilmenite, rutile, sphene), magnetite (Fe/V), and chromite (Fe/Cr). These data show that both Wadi El Arish and the Nile Delta could have been contributors to the dune fields. Present winds capable of transporting sand are dominantly from the northwest in spring-summer months (favoring a Nile source), and from the southwest in winter (favoring a Wadi El Arish source). If such winds prevailed during the times of dune formation, the Sinai and Negev eolian sands provide an example of how seasonal shifts in winds can provide more than a simple, single source of sand to build dune fields.

title: Coupling Cloud: An Open Cyberinfrastructure for Global Subduction-Zone Coupling Models
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era (Posters)
authors: Oryan, Bar [1], Gabriel, Alice-Agnes [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
abstract:
The largest earthquakes on Earth occur along subduction zones, where one dense tectonic plate sinks beneath another. The interface between these plates, known as the megathrust, contains asperities, regions that remain ``locked’’ for decades to centuries during the interseismic period before rupturing in powerful earthquakes. The interseismic accumulation of elastic strain generates slow surface displacements that geodesists routinely measure and invert to estimate the distribution of slip deficit along the megathrust. These “coupling models”, are key tools for identifying locked portions of the megathrust, thereby highlighting regions potentially prone to future seismic rupture. This information is critical for assessing seismic hazard along subduction zones.

Despite their critical importance, coupling models derived from geodetic observations face several methodological challenges. Differences in assumptions about fault geometry, density and quality of geodetic observations, and imposed smoothing constraints in coupling inversions can affect the resulting coupling maps. Furthermore, coupling maps have traditionally lacked a unified format and are typically scattered across publications in forms that are difficult to extract, evaluate, or systematically compare.

To address these challenges, we have developed the Coupling Cloud (CC), an open-access online platform that aggregates more than twenty-five published coupling models from fifteen subduction zones globally. CC offers a consistent, intuitive interface to explore, visualize, download, and quantitatively compare coupling maps across different subduction zones. By centralizing these critical datasets, the CC facilitates more rigorous, reproducible, and efficient scientific analyses, ultimately enhancing community accessibility to key earthquake science resource.

title: New Record of a Motile Grazer from the Latest Neoproterozoic of Southern Nevada
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Jamison, Paul G. [1]
affiliations: (1) Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
abstract:
The late Ediacaran biota of the lower Wood Canyon Formation includes a number of enigmatic, flattened ovoid forms of varying sizes and morphologies. These ovoids have been previously noted and variously described as load casts, fluidization structures, rounded pebbles, and erniettamorphs. Based on a new collection of several dozen specimens from the Tom Rich Site in Nye County, this author proposes that at least some of these flattened ovoids are motile grazing animals similar to Kimberella , and are likely responsible for the many Kimberichnus -like grazing traces found in the same beds.

Evidence for this includes ovoids with "teeth" at one pole, sometimes associated with scratch marks, here interpreted as grazing traces. Some ovoids show a radially divided fringe similar to Kimberella . Rare serial grazing traces suggest backward movement during feeding.

One specimen appears to record forward locomotion, showing an animal that left behind a "footprint", revealing details of a complex, three-part ventral surface. Evidence suggests that movement was accomplished through the use of a hydrostatic skeleton, transferring fluid within the body through muscular contraction, allowing it to grip the sediment to propel itself forward.

Taken collectively, the evidence suggests that at least some of the flattened ovoids of the lower Wood Canyon Formation are bilaterally symmetrical, motile grazing animals similar to Kimberella . They may have moved through the use of a hydrostatic skeleton, and they are likely responsible for the Kimberichnus -type grazing traces found in relative abundance at the site.

title: The Future of STEM education, AI and GSA
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Chaddock, Lisa Bridenstine [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, San Diego City College, San Diego, California, USA
abstract: At the Future of Scientific Education and AI Summit held in San Francisco on May 15, 2026, participants discussed how organizations such as the Geological Society of America (GSA) can help shape policies for the responsible integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in science education. A central conclusion was that AI should be used to enhance, rather than replace, the development of core scientific competencies, including critical thinking, evidence evaluation, communication, collaboration, and ethical reasoning. Attendees emphasized that classroom policies should promote transparency in AI use, require students to critically assess AI-generated content, and prioritize authentic demonstrations of learning over traditional assessments that can be easily automated. Suggested guidelines included using AI as a tool for inquiry, data analysis, scientific communication, and source verification while maintaining student accountability for interpretation and conclusions. Participants also highlighted the need for professional development that equips educators to incorporate AI effectively, evaluate its limitations and biases, critically examine sustainability issues and foster scientific literacy in an environment increasingly shaped by automated information systems. For professional societies such as GSA, the summit underscored an opportunity to develop best-practice frameworks that encourage ethical, equitable, sustainable and pedagogically sound AI adoption while preserving the human-centered skills essential for future geoscientists and scientific leaders.

title: Shedding New Light on Old Collections: Spectral Characterization of Mineral Specimens from the Idaho Museum of Natural History
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Allen, Jean [1], Williams, Thomas [2], Zinzer, Bailee [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
(2) Earth & Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
(3) Earth & Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
abstract: Spectro radiometry techniques in geology and mineralogy use optical reflectance and radiance spectra to provide a fast and reliable way to identify and analyze mineral compositions in a field and laboratory-based environment. The goal of this study was to develop a simple laboratory protocol for the characterization of rock and mineral specimens utilizing a portable spectroradiometer as a benchtop instrument. Variables considered included light source, working distance, background surface, FOV or spot size, reference scans, and sample variability (e.g. grain size, surface roughness, etc.). The spectroradiometer used in our study was Spectra Vista Corporation HR-1024i with a wavelength range from 350 nanometers to 2500 nanometers. Illumination source for all scans was a tungsten-halogen standard photography lamp. We selected a set of mineral specimens to characterize utilizing the protocol. Housed on the University of Idaho campus, the Moscow Branch of the Idaho Museum of Natural History curates an extensive mineral collection ideally suited the purpose. We selected 50 (mostly) ore mineral specimens and collected spectra in the uv-visible to near infrared spectral range. The mining industry uses field spectroradiometers to distinguish rock types and to identify potential ore mineralization. The laboratory characterization of bulk mixed mineral specimens, such as those in our study, will aid in a better understanding of field and remote sensing-based optical spectrometry. The authors wish to thank the Idaho Museum of Natural History for access to the minerals specimens used in this study.

title: Exploring Macropredator Dynamics in Miocene-Pliocene Oceans Using Stable Calcium Isotopes
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Holzmann, Tessa Anneke Beate [1], Valenzuela-Toro, Ana [2], Gili, Stefania [3], Higgins, John [4], Koch, Paul L. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA,
(2) Corporation for the Research and Advancement of Paleontology and Natural History of (CIAHN) Atacama Park, Chile
(3) Department of Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(5) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA,
abstract:
In the Miocene, high ocean productivity supported a diversity of large marine carnivores, and potentially the longest food chains in Earth history. In the Pliocene, declining ocean productivity associated with climate cooling led to widespread extinctions and ecological restructuring. Miocene-Pliocene marine species are famous (e.g., Otodus megalodon and Livyatan melvillei ) and well-studied in taphonomy and distribution, but almost no geochemical work has been done to assess trophic level (position on the food chain), niche breadth, or habitat partitioning. Many modern marine mammal lineages diversified during the Miocene (Delphinidae, Ziphiidae, Physeteridae, Otariidae, Phocidae, and Odobenidae), making this interval important for understanding the origin and evolution of modern marine mammal foraging ecology.

Stable calcium and carbon isotope ratios of fossil tooth enamel provide complementary information about ecology: calcium isotopes reflect trophic level, whereas carbon isotopes indicate foraging habitat. Here, we reconstruct the foraging ecology of Miocene and Pliocene fishes, sharks, and marine mammals using stable calcium and carbon isotope ratios. Our dataset includes 235 fossil specimens from four marine formations spanning the eastern Pacific and western Atlantic coasts of the United States: the Monterey (CA; Middle Miocene, n = 61), Temblor (CA; Late Miocene, n = 59), Calvert (MD; Middle Miocene, n = 46), and Yorktown (NC; Early Pliocene, n = 69) formations. Calcium isotope results are consistent with oceanic food chains up to one trophic step longer than modern oceans, with the lowest δ 44/42 Ca values from the tooth enamel of apex predators such as Otodus auriculatus (Calvert Formation, n=8, δ 44/42 Ca = -0.86‰ ± 0.11) and raptorial sperm whales (Yorktown Formation, n=9, δ 44/42 Ca = -1.30‰ ± 0.16); these macrocarnivores likely occupied higher trophic positions than any modern marine animal. In contrast, calcium and carbon isotope data suggest that most Miocene and Pliocene marine mammals occupied trophic positions and habitats broadly comparable to those of their modern analogues. These results demonstrate the potential of calcium isotopes to reconstruct ancient marine food webs, providing a framework for interpreting the evolution of ecosystem structure and trophic complexity through time.

abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Landslide Hazards Program supports landslide risk reduction by providing competitive grants to state, local, Tribal, and territorial governments through the Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Grant Program. Since its launch under the 2021 National Landslide Preparedness Act, the program has awarded $3.1 million across three grant cycles to 37 recipients, funding work in landslide hazard mapping, assessment, planning, coordination, and public outreach. authors: Jang, Hyungjoo [1], Kowalewski, Michal J. [2], Torres, Luis [3], Liyanagedara, Pamod Heshan [4], Portell, Roger W. [5], Bostic, Lexie [6], Harder, Sophie [7]

abstract: Seagrass cover in Tampa Bay had declined significantly from the 1950s to 1982 because of extensive dredging operations and high total nitrogen loads due to insufficient wastewater treatment. Tightened policies on nutrient discharge and seagrass restoration efforts have proven successful, with seagrass cover more than doubling between 1982 - 2016. With different parts of Tampa Bay having varied histories of seagrass disruption and recovery, we aimed to explore how these histories affected local mollusk assemblages. Using a Conservation Paleobiology approach, we sampled nine sites along the north-northeastern coast of Tampa Bay with differing histories of seagrass coverage: (1) Bahia Beach (recovery since 1990s); (2) Pelican Cove (persistent); (3) Davis Island (never established); (4) Courtney Campbell Causeway Trail (established between the 1930s - 1980s); (5) north of Port Redwing (recovery since the late 1980s); (6) Archie Creek (recovery since the mid-1990s); (7) Bayshore Boulevard (recovery/Loss since the early 2000s); (8) Picnic Island Park (persistent); (9) north of Picnic Island (persistent) in order to evaluate whether these short-term changes in seagrass cover are captured in the live and dead mollusk assemblages. Surface (0-10 cm benthic depth) and subsurface (15-25 cm benthic depth) sediments were sampled and sieved through a 1 mm mesh. All mollusks were identified to the lowest taxonomic level possible. Three sample sets (live surface, dead surface, dead subsurface) were compared using non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) to evaluate differences in spatial composition between each of the sites using Bray-Curtis distances. Results show that live mollusk samples, regardless of collection site, cluster together in the ordination space. Dead samples, which likely pre-date major anthropogenic impacts, differ in faunal composition from live samples and are more heterogeneous in terms of faunal composition, suggesting notable changes in mollusk communities over the period of anthropogenic change. These changes include spatial faunal homogenization and a shift in faunal composition toward assemblages dominated by more opportunistic taxa. Historical archives provided by molluscan assemblages represent a useful baseline that can guide conservation assessment, habitat management and seagrass restoration in the northern Tampa Bay area.

title: Toward a range-wide, unified exhumation history: new (U-Th)/He dates fill an important gap in the northern Sierra Nevada
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Allard, John [1], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [2], Borders, Nick [3], Cassel, Elizabeth J. [4], Cecil, Robinson [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Earth and Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, ID, USA
(4) University of Idaho, MOSCOW, ID, USA
(5) California State University, Northridge, CA,
abstract:
Though fundamental to understanding the tectonic evolution of the U.S. Cordillera, the uplift and exhumation history of the Sierra Nevada remains disputed. Despite its common treatment as a single orogenic and topographic feature, the northern and southern Sierra Nevada differ sharply in geologic, geochronologic, and geomorphic character. North of 37.5°N, subdued relief and a patchwork of Jurassic-Cretaceous intrusions contrast with the deep canyons and voluminous, dominantly Cretaceous plutons of the southern Sierra. The north preserves Eocene-Oligocene (E-O) fluvial and volcanic deposits, which are mostly absent in the south. Consequently, paleoaltimetry and detrital zircon studies have focused on the north, whereas nearly all published apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe) data (>98% of dated grains) are from the south. These datasets underpin competing “old” (Cretaceous-Paleogene) and “young” (Neogene) uplift models, but the spatial dichotomy of the data hinders development of a unified uplift history for the range.

We address this problem by applying AHe thermochronology to the northern Sierra Nevada for comparison with the extensive southern dataset. We sampled from regions with high vertical relief, targeting modern river channels, bedrock at the E-O unconformity, and topographic highs to test for date-elevation gradients within and across the range. Preliminary AHe dates range from 85.3 ± 2.1 Ma (2σ) to 65.6 ± 1.0 Ma, broadly becoming younger from west to east. This pattern agrees with that documented by Cecil et al. (2006), but with older dates in the west that overlap with published zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe) dates. For the existing dataset, the youngest AHe dates in the northern Sierra are much older than those in the south (which are as young as <40 Ma). The Late Cretaceous AHe dates in the north suggest rapid post-magmatic unroofing rather than substantial exhumation from a high-magnitude uplift pulse in the late Cenozoic. Thermal history modeling will resolve additional exhumation details. This dataset will be expanded with AHe and ZHe analyses from the Feather, American, and Mokelumne drainages to further test whether (U-Th)/He patterns are similar or different between the northern and southern Sierra, implying shared or separate uplift histories.

title: Tracking the First Americans: LGM-age human tracks at White Sands, New Mexico
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Holliday, Vance T [1], Windingstad, Jason D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences & Anthropology, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(2) Statistical Research, Inc, Tucson, Arizona, USA
abstract: Our research mirrors some of that conducted by Rolfe Mandel, both supported by endowments to better understand the timing and character of the initial peopling of the Americas. Discovery of human footprints at archaeological site WHSA Locality 2 in deposits dated to the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) at White Sands National Park in the Tularosa Basin of southern New Mexico, was a notable step in understanding the initial peopling of the Americas. It is one of the oldest archaeological sites in the Americas with the oldest documented human footprints. Eight track horizons date from ~23 to ~21 ka based on 29 AMS radiocarbon dates. The site is in lake-margin alluvium of paleo-lake Otero. We conducted an independent study of the chronology of a previously unrecognized stratigraphic record of the paleo-lake that is directly traceable into the track-bearing alluvium. The stratigraphic data along with 26 additional AMS radiocarbon dates on palustrine mud determined by two labs independent of the original investigations document an aggrading lake/wetland/stream record dated >23.6ka to ~17.0ka, providing further evidence supporting the validity of an LGM age for the tracks. Of archaeological significance, the alluvium was delivered into the lake basin via a stream heading in the Sacramento Mountains and was therefore a freshwater source along the margins of an otherwise brackish lake. The paleo-drainage also provided access to a broad array of alluvial, lacustrine, and palustrine resources in addition to a diverse Late Pleistocene fauna documented for the basin.
