title: Cryogenian temperature reconstruction from South Australian giant ooids
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Millikin, Alexie E.G. [1], Gerasimov, Stacey H. [2], Wallace, Malcolm [3], Ryuba, Mana [4], Simpson, Carl [5], Trower, Lizzy [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Victoria, USA
(4) University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Victoria, USA

abstract:
Although geochemical proxies have enabled geoscientists to constrain seawater temperatures going back ~500 million years, these tools are ineffective further back in time due to increased chemical alteration in older rocks. The recent development of a proxy based on ooid grain size is a promising tool for reconstructing temperature further back in time, especially in the Neoproterozoic Era (1000–539 Ma), where giant ooids are more ubiquitous than at any other interval in the stratigraphic record. Here we present analyses from the Cryogenian Period (720–635 Ma) in South Australia (Umberatana Group), which preserves ooid grainstones in the Angepena Formation, Weetootla Member, and Trezona Formation. Stable isotope chemostratigraphic data (δ 13 C and δ 18 O) allow us to align this record with global compilations and demonstrate that the Trezona Formation records the youngest carbonates in the Cryogenian non-glacial interval globally, thus temperature reconstruction will constrain climatic trajectory leading into Marinoan glaciation (640–635 Ma), the second of two Snowball Earth glaciations during the Neoproterozoic. Ooid grain size measured via Segmenteverygrain 1 , petrographically determined original mineralogy, carbonate associated phosphate measurements, and literature-based estimates of Neoproterozoic seawater parameters will be used to constrain Cryogenian dissolved inorganic phosphorous concentration and temperature through a physiochemical sedimentation model ( Oomega Toolbox 2 ) and carbonate system model ( PHREEQC 3 ). Temperature constraints generated herein have important implications for determining the cause(s) of Marinoan glaciation, representing one of the most drastic climate change events in all of Earth history.

title: Can Faults Sustain Geothermal Fluid Circulation in a Non-Volcanic Rift? Insights from Magnetotelluric Imaging at the Ihimbo Geothermal Prospect, Uganda
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: DUAH-BOAKYE, DANIEL [1], Katumwehe, Andrew B. [2], Halihan, Todd [3], Vilcaez, Javier [4], Mickus, Kevin Lee [5], Matende, Kitso [6], Emishaw, Luel [7]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
(2) Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(3) Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(4) Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(5) Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
(6) Geology, University of Botwswana, Gaborone, Botswana
(7) Geoscience, Midwestern State University, Wichita, Texas, USA
abstract:
In the Western Branch of the East African Rift System (EARS), which developed along the ancient Congo and Tanzania cratons, thick lithospheric keels limit extension, resulting in largely magma-poor rifting. Geothermal fluid circulation in the Western Branch is therefore thought to be controlled primarily by deep-penetrating fault systems rather than shallow magmatic heat sources. This study investigates the geothermal potential of Ihimbo, located within the southern Lake Edward Rift segment of the Western Branch, using magnetotelluric (MT) methods to image the subsurface resistivity structure and evaluate how fault-controlled permeability sustains geothermal fluid circulation in an amagmatic rift setting.

Our results from 49 of the 74 broadband MT stations over a frequency range of 0.0079–320 Hz indicate: (1) Periods >100 s sample depths of ~40 km based on combined Transverse Electric (TE) and Transverse Magnetic (TM) mode responses. (2) Phase tensor analysis reveals predominantly three-dimensional subsurface conditions (phase tensor skew, β > 3°), suggesting significant structural complexity across the study area. (3) Geoelectric strike analysis shows a non-uniform strike distribution at short periods (<0.001 s), alignment with the regional NE–SW rift architecture between periods 0.001s and 1s, and a gradual rotation from N–S to NNW–SSE and NW–SE orientations at depth. This steady change suggests that shallow- to mid-crustal fluid circulation is primarily controlled by rift-related fault systems, whereas deeper fluid pathways are influenced by inherited Precambrian basement fabrics. (4) Occam 1D inversions reveal shallow conductive zones overlying resistive basement rocks at most stations whereas other stations exhibit moderately resistive near-surface units underlain by increasing conductivity at depth, consistent with localized fault-controlled fluid circulation. (5) Apparent resistivity maps between 100 and 5,000 m below sea level show detailed resistivity contrasts and linear conductive-resistive boundaries interpreted as major fault-controlled permeability zones. (6) Preliminary 2D inversion models show conductive zones at ~8 km depth, overlain by moderately resistive zones at ~2 km depth. Further 2D and 3D MT inversions will be used to constrain the geometry and continuity of these structures, evaluate their influence on geothermal fluid flow, and identify prospective geothermal reservoirs and their controlling fault architecture beneath the Ihimbo prospect.

title: K-means clustering of Jeju Island beach sands: Provenance and mineralogy
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Woo, Juhwan [1], Lee, Seungyeol [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chungbuk National University, Cheongju, (None), Korea (The Republic of)
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chungbuk National University, Cheongju, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract:
Jeju Island, located on the continental shelf of the Yellow Sea off the southern coast of the Korean Peninsula, represents a unique geological setting. The island’s volcanic edifice, dominated by Mt. Halla (1,950 m), was constructed through multiple stages of eruption spanning approximately 1.8 million years. The volcanic activity produced a diverse suite of lavas ranging from alkali basalt to trachyte, creating a distinctive mineral assemblage in the coastal sedimentary systems.

Integration of XRF and XRD data, combined with PCA and k-means clustering (k = 3), reveals three geochemically and mineralogically distinct facies in Jeju Island beach sands. Facies A represents carbonate-dominated sediment derived mainly from biogenic material, with calcite and aragonite as the dominant mineral phases. Facies B reflects strongly weathered basalt-derived detritus supplied to the coast via fluvial and erosional processes, characterized by elevated Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃, and TiO₂ contents. Facies C represents a transitional composition in which carbonate minerals coexist with primary basaltic silicates, indicating mixing between biogenic carbonate and volcanogenic detritus under moderate weathering conditions.

The spatial distribution of the three facies, carbonate-dominated beaches on the northern coast, silicate-dominated beaches along the remaining coasts, and transitional compositions on the southwestern and eastern coasts demonstrates that sediment provenance on Jeju Island is characterized by the proximity to weathered basaltic source terrains and the local availability of biogenic carbonate. To quantitatively assess geochemical maturation, the Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) was integrated with TiO₂ immobility systematics. CIA values reflect the mixed-provenance nature of the sediments, whereas the TiO₂ gradient provides a carbonate-insensitive proxy for weathering advancement, peaking in the residual volcanic assemblages of Facies B (2.30 ± 0.81 wt%). SEM-EDS analysis confirmed that Fe-Ti oxide phases serve as the primary mineralogical carriers of this elevated TiO 2 . These results demonstrate that Jeju’s coastal sediments are a cumulative record of the island's transition from an active emergent stage to a currently quiescent, erosion and biogenic carbonate dominated terminal state. This study highlights the utility of unsupervised machine learning in decoding the complex provenance of high-energy volcanic coastal systems.

authors: Miao, Shipeng [1], Shen, Tianyi [2], van der Beek, Peter [3], Wang, Guocan [4], Wang, An [5], Cao, Kai [6], Li, Tianyang [7]

abstract:
The ongoing collision between the India and Eurasian plates has driven the sustained uplift of the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayan, shaping the complex geomorphic pattern and drainage network of the plateau and its surrounding areas. As the largest river system, the Yarlung-Tsangpo River (YTR) and its evolution with Brahmaputra River have exerted a profound influence on regional drainage reorganization and erosion intensity. In addition to headwater erosion, fluvial incision may also be modulated by localized tectonic activity. Since the Miocene, active extension along north-south oriented normal faults within the Tibetan Plateau has caused differential uplift along the YTR, influencing local relief and erosion. However, the timing and mechanisms of incision along the YTR remain debated, particularly the relative role of regional base-level changes and localized tectonic processes. Therefore, distinguishing whether fluvial incision in the middle YTR was primarily driven by headward erosion related to drainage reorganization or by local fault activity is thus crucial for understanding its geomorphic evolution.

Here, we examine various landforms in the middle YTR, present channel profile analysis, and calculate the response time of knickpoint. Combing with low-temperature thermochronological data, we reconstruct the late-Miocene exhumation history of the middle YTR. Channel profile analysis and knickpoint response time indicate two main phases of incision. Cooling ages and thermal-history modeling also reveal two phases of rapid cooling and exhumation. The first phase (12-8 Ma) was regionally distributed along the middle YTR and associated with exhumation rates of ~0.5 km/Myr. And the second phase (8-6 Ma), during which exhumation rates exceeded 0.6 km/Myr, was restricted to deeply incised gorge segments, along with a section of the river that appears rejuvenated. These results indicate that Miocene incision along the middle YTR occurred in two stages: an earlier regionally extensive phase related to a major base-level perturbation and a later localized phase of intensified gorge incision. The earlier phase may reflect drainage integration downstream, whereas the later phase likely involves local tectonic deformation and river reorganization.

Our results highlight the combined influence of regional base-level changes and localized tectonic processes on the evolution of the YTR valley system. It provides new insights into the coupling between surface processes and tectonics along the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau.

title: Epicontinental C[h]aOs: Using Calcium, Osmium, and Stratigraphic Analysis of Western Interior Seaway and Saxony Basin Cores to Evaluate Spatial and Temporal Variability in Late Cretaceous Volcanism and Ocean Acidification

authors: Carlson, Rose L. [1], Selby, David [2], Jacobson, Andrew D. [3], Flaum, Jason A. [4], Wan, Chuyan [5], French, Katherine L. [6], Birdwell, Justin E. [7], Sageman, Bradley B. [8]

abstract:
The global chemostratigraphic record of Late Cretaceous Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2) features a pronounced shift to unradiogenic 187 Os/ 188 Os (Os i ) values followed closely by a well-defined positive carbon isotope (δ 13 C org ) excursion at its onset. These patterns are interpreted to reflect an episode of globally-enhanced organic carbon burial and marine anoxia caused by increased submarine volcanism.

Despite the relative global homogeneity of the OAE2 δ 13 C org excursion, geochemical expressions of the event vary within and between epicontinental basins. Proposed explanations for differences in the shape and degree of the OAE2 unradiogenic shift in Os i across these sites include differences in basin connectivity and circulation, water depth, and proximity to shoreline weathering inputs.

Another proxy of interest in epicontinental settings is δ 44/40 Ca. Ocean acidification likely occurred as ana consequence of increased volcanic inputs to the Earth system during OAE2, and documented changes in carbonate δ 44/40 Ca interpertedinterpreted to reflect decreases in precipitation rates have been identified. Moreover, published δ 44/40 Ca records for several OAE2 sites display positive excursions consistent with acidification, but global variations in the signal and the role of diagenetic alteration in certain facies have not been extensively constrained.

We present Os i and δ 44/40 Ca records for epicontinental sites at the southern opening of the Western Interior Seaway (the USGS GC-3 core) and the Lower Saxony Basin (the Wunstorf core) that feature volcanically-driven Os i signals as well as shifts in δ 44/40 Ca. We demonstrate that diagenetically-induced δ 44/40 Ca shifts in OAE2 sediments can be constrained and isolated from acidification signals using facies analysis and δ 13 C carb measurements. We also argue that similarities between the shape of published Os i records for IODP site 1260B (Demerara rise) and new Os i data for the GC-3 core constitute further evidence for at least partial connectivity with the open ocean during this dynamic period in Earth’s history.

abstract:
Predicting the evolution of contractional fault-propagation folds has implications for the movement and storage of fluids in the subsurface, including hydrocarbon resources, ore mineralization, and for implementation of carbon capture and storage. Past studies have successfully used trishear kinematic numerical modeling to replicate the generation of fold geometries established in the field, demonstrating how underlying fault networks control the deformation of layers in front of the fault system.

We investigated two localities within the steepest east-dipping section of the Laramide-age San Rafael monocline in central Utah. There, canyons have dissected the fold, providing excellent exposure across the entire system, permitting us to document axis-perpendicular changes in dip at high-resolution. Previous researchers hypothesized that the fold formed in front of a propagating, steeply west dipping basement fault system, but those studies did not include detailed field-based structural data to constrain finite fold geometries. In this study, we used imagery from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and field-based structural measurements to document changes in fold geometry and dip through the two canyons. The UAV imagery was used to construct 3D virtual outcrop models of rock exposures based on structure-from-motion algorithms. We then used these models and field data to constrain cross-section construction.

Although cross sections for both canyons display similarly steep eastward dips in the forelimb of the fold, their cross sections display notable geometric differences, especially in the transition from the forelimb of the monocline to sub-horizontal bedding to the east. We used trishear forward modeling (FoldFault7) to replicate the real-world fold system and explain geometric differences. To do so, we tested variations in fault geometry, fault slip, propagation-to-slip ratio, number of faults, and trishear angle. Our initial results suggest that complexity in the underlying fault system has generated different curvatures in the forelimb transition, with a secondary fault splay a possible driving mechanism for geometric differences.

These kinematic forward models can be used to explain fold-axis-parallel changes in monocline dip to the north and south, where dip decreases to low (<20 degree) angles, likely related to lower displacement(s) on the underlying fault system. Our future research will focus on developing testable, high-resolution, field-based cross-sections along the fold, providing us a richer data set for constraining fold evolution.

abstract: The elevational controls on isotopic composition of snowmelt, stream water, and groundwater were examined using isotopic data collected from 1998 to 2017 to understand surface water and groundwater interactions and spatial variability of hydrologic connectivity across the Green Lakes Valley in Colorado Front Range, Rocky Mountains, USA. The study focused on headwater catchments of Boulder Creek above the Albion Lake outlet, with an area approximately 7 km 2 and elevation range of 3,250-4,000 m. The results indicate that an average lapse rate for the Green Lakes Valley catchment from Arikaree Glacier outflow to Albion Lake was -0.36‰ per 100 m for δ 18 O (R 2 = 0.59, p = 0.016), -2.06‰ per 100 m for δ 2 H (R 2 = 0.67, p = 0.025), and 0.60‰ per 100 m for deuterium excess (R 2 = 0.72, p = 0.032). Snowmelt, stream water, and groundwater in the Martinelli catchment, the Green Lake 5 Rock Glacier outflow, and Green Lake 1 outflow did not fit this elevation gradient. The isotopic elevational gradient was a reversed pattern in the Martinelli catchment and vicinity, with more depleted isotopic signature at lower elevations (2.73‰ per 100 m for δ 18 O, R 2 = 0.33, p = 0.012; 20.66‰ per 100 m for δ 2 H, R 2 = 0.32, p = 0.014; -1.42‰ per 100 m for deuterium excess, R 2 = 0.14, p = 0.122), as snow accumulation was deeper in the lower elevations than in the higher elevations due to snow redistribution. The Green Lake 5 Rock Glacier outflow experienced freeze-thaw cycles, resulting in deuterium excess enrichment during the fall months with more enriched δ 2 H relative to δ 18 O. Green Lake 1 is a seepage lake in contrast to the other lakes in the watershed and is mainly groundwater fed, with isotopic values strongly affected by evaporation. These results help understand the sources of stream water and heterogeneous streamflow generation processes within a relatively small, alpine, seasonally snow-covered area.

title: Strain Accommodation within the San Rafael Monocline, Utah: Reconnaissance Investigation of Deformation within the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone During Contractional Fault-propagation Folding

authors: Larson, Daniel Quinn [1], Nordquist, Sienna [2], Rueda, Isabella [3], Surpless, Benjamin E. [4]

abstract:
By documenting deformation mechanisms associated with contractional fault-propagation folds, researchers can better predict fluid flow in subsurface systems. As a fold forms in front of a propagating fault, deformation bands, shear fractures, pressure solution features, and minor faults initiate, propagate, and interact within sedimentary layers, affecting potential flow paths.

In this study, we investigate the steepest dipping (>60 degrees) forelimb exposure of the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone within the San Rafael monocline. The Laramide-age monocline, the result of folding of sedimentary strata in front of a steeply west dipping basement fault system, is arguably the best exposed fault-propagation fold in the world. Previous researchers used trishear kinematic modeling to explain 2D cross-sectional fold evolution and strain accommodation within the fold; we situate our investigation in the context of their results but expand our analysis to 3D, parallel to the fold axis.

To gather data, we used imagery from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), field-based structural measurements, and thin-section analysis from canyon exposures to document changes in the type, orientation, and distribution of deformation through the monocline. The UAV imagery was used to construct 3D virtual outcrop models of rock exposures. We used these models and field data to map the monocline and create a conceptual model that explains how porous sandstone deforms in response to the evolving stresses associated with fault-propagation folding.

We suggest that deformation bands, low (<1 m) displacement faults, and conjugate faulting dominate the accommodation of strain within the steepest (~60 degree dip) exposures of strata within the forelimb. Structural data indicate that faults form parallel to cross-bed set contacts and at boundaries between individual cross-beds. In addition, at several excellent exposures of low-displacement faults and deformation band networks, we document conjugate fault sets with kinematics and orientations consistent with a sub-horizontal sigma-1 oriented WNW-ESE, approximately perpendicular to the NE-trending monocline axis. Low-angle (<30 degree) deformation band networks commonly bound high-angle (>50 degree) ladder bands, which abut these low-angle structures, consistent with published research results.

We suggest that a diverse set of mechanisms accommodate fault-propagation folding in porous sandstone, with most structures likely reducing porosity and therefore fluid-flow potential. Future research will focus on providing better three-dimensional spatial constraints on how these mechanisms interact and could affect fluid flow within folded strata.

title: The Metalliferous Pennsylvanian Mecca Quarry Shale of the Illinois Basin: Deposition, Early Diagenesis, and U-Mo-V-Zn Enrichment

authors: Liu, Bei [1], Mastalerz, Maria [2], Ames, Philip [3]
affiliations: (1) Indiana Geological and Water Survey, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Indiana Geological and Water Survey, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
(3) Indiana Geological and Water Survey, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract:
The Pennsylvanian black shales of the U.S. Midwest, such as the Mecca Quarry Shale (MQS) and Excello Shale, are rich in organic matter and various trace metals including uranium (U), molybdenum (Mo), vanadium (V), and zinc (Zn). The metalliferous MQS in the eastern (Indiana) part of the Illinois Basin was studied based on core description, trace element geochemical characteristics, X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy, and organic petrography. Thirteen drill cores were studied, and 63 black shale samples were collected for mineralogical, geochemical, and petrographic analyses. The average total organic carbon (TOC) and total sulfur content is 14.38 wt % (maximum 45.35 wt %) and 2.64 wt % (maximum 5.29 wt %), respectively. U, Mo, V, and Zn contents of the MQS are all highly enriched compared to the concentrations in the Upper Continental Crust and range from 10.42 to 235 ppm (average 84.68 ppm), < 2 to 1,620 ppm (average 619.45 ppm), 233 to 2,770 ppm (average 1,241.65 ppm), and 58 to 5,480 ppm (average 1,412.58 ppm), respectively. Organic matter in the MQS includes alginite, bituminite, liptodetrinite, sporinite, vitrinite, inertinite, and solid bitumen, with bituminite being the dominant maceral. XRD analysis shows that the MQS is composed of illite (average 41.0%), quartz (average 24.1%), kaolinite (average 10.2%), plagioclase (average 6.3%), pyrite (average 4.5%), dolomite (average 3.3%), calcite (average 2.7%), K-feldspar (average 2.7%), chlorite (average 1.3%), and minor amounts of fluorapatite, ankerite, sphalerite, and siderite. From a geochemical proxy perspective, the U/Th, Ni/Co, and V/Cr ratios suggest deposition of the MQS under anoxic conditions, whereas stratigraphic context (directly above a coal bed), sedimentary texture (lenticular fabric), trace fossils, and maceral attributes (micrinized bituminite) collectively support deposition by oxygenated bottom currents in a shallow-water environment (probably several meters deep). This discrepancy between geochemical and sedimentological attributes clearly shows that redox-sensitive trace element ratios need to be combined with sedimentological and petrographic observations to arrive at more complete interpretations of black shale successions.

Based on multiple sources of evidence, we suggest that U-Mo-V-Zn enrichment in the metalliferous MQS was primarily controlled by deposition and early diagenesis. During early diagenesis, mineralization mainly occurred in the sulfate reduction zone where H 2 S was present. Although contribution by hydrothermal fluids cannot be excluded, it lacks direct evidence.

title: Practical Civics and Applied Geoscience: Drafting an Ordinance Protecting Groundwater and Controversial CO2 Sequestration
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Stohr, Christopher J. [1], Hall, John [2]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State Geological Survey [retired], University of Illinois, Urbana, IL, ; Recent Past Chair, Champaign County Carbon Sequestration Activities Task Force, Mahomet Aquifer Council, USA
(2) Director and Zoning Administrator, Department of Planning and Zoning, Champaign County IL, Urbana, IL, USA
abstract:
County land use ordinances regulate activities which might conflict with established land use zoning. In Illinois, the ordinances must align with surrounding land uses and adhere to LaSalle and Sinclair Criteria to withstand legal challenges and also require approval by multiple units of government.

Advocates and opponents of Carbon Capture and Storage [CCS] also called Carbon Dioxide [CO2] Sequestration are reasonably concerned about elevated atmospheric CO2 and its impact on climate change as well as the security of indefinite subsurface storage of the fluid. Typically, such matters are considered by state legislatures because of cross-country jurisdictional concerns. However, local county governments regulate surface facilities and activities beyond municipal jurisdiction by means of zoning regulations.

CCS is controversial in East Central Illinois because of a 2016 subsurface natural gas storage leak that contaminated drinking water wells; two CO2 injection well leaks; a pipeline leak in another state; and public safety concerns for the Mahomet sole-source Aquifer and surrounding lesser aquifers. However, East Central Illinois is located in the Illinois Basin which has ideal geology for CCS for climate and economic opportunities but also requires protection for the local water resources.

What is the role of Professional Geologists to intervene in controversial issues that sometimes include politically-charged dialogue when scientific information is a critical element?

The authors were members of a local government appointed task force composed of representatives of farming, water supply engineers, and nonprofit organizations tasked with drafting a zoning ordinance amendment to protect groundwater, promote economic development by allowing for the possibility of CO2 Sequestation, and preserve public safety.

Only those who are elected or appointed to offices and boards have voting authority to determine the legal requirements for a restricted activity. It has been the author’s experience that the intrinsic authority of a technical expert i.e., scientist or engineer serving as a voting member of a board can profoundly influence the outcome of a complex and controversial matter - IF the scientist can exercise diplomacy, courtesy, and patient [repeated] teaching through communications i.e., leadership.

Importantly, partnership with other experts particularly planners, committee members representing vested interests, and working with departmental staff ahead of meetings is key to successful outcomes.

authors: Calvert, Emma G [1], Beethe, Sarah [2], Scarberry, Kaleb Christian [3], Balbas, Andrea [4], Konrad, Kevin [5]

abstract:
The Yellowstone hotspot track provides a unique opportunity to study physical and chemical relationships between mantle plumes and the overriding continental lithosphere. We propose that the Yellowstone hotspot was active in southeastern Oregon during the Oligocene — predating eruptions of CRBs and extensional tectonics. Here, we present preliminary 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, detailed core logging, and surface reconnaissance mapping that provides new insight into the longevity of the Yellowstone hotspot and its relationship to Cenozoic tectonics in the northwestern Basin and Range.

Large igneous provinces are constructed primarily from flood basalt volcanism. These volcanic provinces are generally considered to represent the arrival of a plume head that later transitions into an age-progressive hotspot track. However, in continental settings, this model can be complicated by plume volcanism being suppressed by tectonic processes including subduction or lithosphere interaction. Camp & Wells (2021) suggest an active Yellowstone hotspot has underlaid western North America and the proximal Farallon plate since at least 56 Ma. Siletzia, an obducted large igneous province, is hypothesized to be the first preserved expression of the Yellowstone hotspot. Siletzia accreted onto the western North America margin during the Eocene. Afterwards, there is a lack of Yellowstone hotspot volcanism or preserved volcanic products on the North American continent until the Miocene eruptions of the Columbia River Flood Basalts (CRB). After CRB emplacement, the Yellowstone hotspot produced an age-progressive track through the Snake River Plain and is currently sourcing volcanism at Yellowstone. However, pre-CRB stratigraphy is rarely exposed on the surface in southeastern Oregon.

Two drill holes at Crump Geyser, originally drilled to study geothermal resources on the northwestern boundary of the Basin and Range, contain approximately 6,000ft (~1829m) of volcanic stratigraphy. Preliminary core logging indicates at least 3,000ft (~914m) of basement cover and ~1,500ft (~457m) of stratigraphy that predates Steens Flood Basalt. Stratigraphic relationships indicate relative ages of at least 22 Ma. Additional evidence suggests at least one hole crossed the range bounding normal fault and transitioned from the hanging wall to the foot wall on the northern edge of the Warner Mountains, potentially preserving older stratigraphy. In-situ subsurface stratigraphy preserved in these drill holes is essential for assessing Yellowstone’s influence on the Western North America margin.

abstract: Constraining the timing of explosive Pleistocene volcanism is fundamental to volcanic hazard assessment, evaluating volcano–climate and volcano–tectonic interaction, and reconstructing the evolution of large silicic magmatic systems. Developing robust eruption chronologies, remains challenging because Quaternary deposits commonly approach the limits of individual geochronologic methods and petrologically controlled mineral assemblages restrict the availability of suitable dating materials. Consequently, no single chronometer can resolve the complete eruptive and magmatic history of a long-lived volcanic system. Integrating multiple chronometers requires careful consideration of both the material being dated and the geological process each chronometer records. Here we present an integrated geochronologic framework for historical (<726 CE) to middle Pleistocene (c. 0.8 Ma) eruptions from Santorini, Greece, during IODP Expedition 398, using 14 C dating of entrained organic material, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar age determinations of glass and mineral phases, and U–Pb zircon geochronology. Radiocarbon analyses (n = 10) of plant remains prepared at the Oregon State University Radiocarbon Laboratory and measured at the Australian National University constrain the age of the 726 CE eruption. Fifty single-crystal total-fusion and incremental-heating 40 Ar/ 39 Ar analyses of glass, plagioclase, amphibole, and mica yield eruption ages ranging from 32.6 ± 5.3 ka (2σ; MSWD = 0.97; n = 28/54) to 764.1 ± 3.3 ka (MSWD = 1.85; n = 174/294). U–Pb zircon analyses from the same deposits, filtered for >90% radiogenic 206 Pb, define minimum crystallization ages of 775 ± 18 ka, a central age of 810 ± 19 ka (MSWD = 3.1; n = 49), and a minor xenocrystic population between 2.1 and 8.6 Ma (n = 5). These complementary datasets demonstrate that each chronometer records a distinct stage of Santorini's magmatic evolution: radiocarbon constrains eruption and deposition of the youngest deposits, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar records eruption ages across the Quaternary, and U–Pb zircon geochronology reveals earlier episodes of magma crystallization, recycling, and recharge. Rather than viewing these methods as competing chronometers, we show that their combined application provides a more robust framework for reconstructing the evolution of multi-cyclic, repeatedly recharged island arc magmatic systems and for developing internally consistent eruption chronologies across a broad range of geologic timescales.

title: Precipitation Uncertainty Influences the Interpretation of Post-Wildfire Flood Hazards
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Partridge, Trevor Fuess [1], Ebel, Brian [2], Murphy, Sheila [3], Cho, Se Jong [4], Johnson, Zach [5]

abstract: Wildland fire can substantially alter hydrologic processes and result in post-fire hydrologic hazards — such as flash floods, debris flows, sediment-laden flows, and impaired water quality — that challenge water resources management. Because these hazards are driven by precipitation, spatially distributed Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPEs) at appropriate scales are critical for interpreting flow dynamics, modeling runoff generation, and forecasting hazard potential. Yet QPEs in post-fire settings are often poorly constrained, especially in remote forested headwater catchments prone to wildfire. This study compares several widely used QPE datasets against documented post-wildfire peak flow events across fire-affected catchments in the western United States. For each dataset, we compare gridded precipitation estimates against available rain gage observations to evaluate spatial and temporal biases, and assess uncertainty in the timing, intensity, duration, and magnitude of precipitation associated with post-fire peak flows. We quantify how post-wildfire hydrologic amplification varies between QPE products by evaluating the precipitation and flood return intervals associated with each event. We find that the choice of QPE dataset can alter the apparent degree of hydrologic amplification attributable to wildfire, particularly for the high-intensity, sub-daily metrics that govern infiltration-excess runoff. QPE products tend to agree on multi-day storm totals but diverge on the timing, location, and magnitude of peak intensities, such that the same flood may be interpreted as more or less fire-amplified depending on the precipitation product used. These results carry direct implications for precipitation intensity-duration thresholds used in hazard prediction and provide a foundation for assessing how changing precipitation regimes may alter post-fire flood recurrence.

abstract: Legacy marine sediment records of deglaciation are critical for constraining ice-ocean interactions, ocean circulation, and offshore transport patterns before the satellite observational record. The sedimentological records preserved in the northeastern Pacific Ocean provide a means to assess ice-ocean interactions of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet (CIS) during the most recent deglacial period. Sediment records from this region provide a critical analogue for modern Greenland-ocean interactions in a rapidly warming modern climate. Whereas the southernmost and northernmost reaches of the CIS have been well constrained, our understanding of how the central CIS, from the coast of British Columbia along the Queen Charlotte Sound, contributed to sea level change is poorly bracketed. In order to elucidate source and process of sediment transport from the central CIS and disentangle ice-ocean interactions through the Pleistocene, we use 44 meters of legacy glaciomarine sediment records collected 140 km off the coast of San Josef Bay on Vancouver Island during the Deep Sea Drilling Program (DSDP) expedition 18. We then compare the high-resolution sedimentological, geochronological, and trace element data from DSDP-18 to a sediment core collected directly along the coast of Vancouver Island to find records of southern glacial input in the form of ice rafted debris (IRD) and calcium present offshore in the final deglacial period. However, evidence of northern glacial input dominates older deposits, indicating there may have been a switch from northern to southern ocean influence on central CIS margins throughout the Pleistocene. We observe a transition between marine deposition and glacially-transported material within the core as evidenced by an increase in grain size to above 45 microns and a decrease in foraminifera abundance. This novel dataset demonstrates the utility of legacy core samples in addressing key questions related to the role of central CIS sediment contributions to the Pacific Ocean and offshore glacial sediment transport during the critical period of ice sheet retreat in the Pleistocene.

title: Through the Student Lens: A Mixed Methods Study of Geoscience Identity and Perspectives on Recruitment and Retention
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Wright, Carrie [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Teacher Education, University of Southern Indiana, Evansville, IN,
abstract: Geoscience degree programs across the country struggling to maintain enrollments face multiple headwinds in recruitment and retention, including the relative invisibility of geoscience that masks its importance in maintaining modern society through managing resources and mitigating natural hazards. Science identity (Carlone & Johnson, 2007), or the recognition by oneself and others as a science person in a science context, has been used for almost two decades to examine recruitment and retention issues in STEM. This explanatory sequential mixed methods study began with a quantitative measure of the geoscience identity of current geoscience students and geoscience degree program graduates ( N = 55) at a medium-sized Midwestern public university experiencing declines in majors and course enrollment. The Measure of Geoscience Identity (MoGI) instrument was modified from the Measure of Chemistry Identity (Hosbein & Barbera, 2020), includes scales to measure geoscience self-efficacy, recognition, and interest, and was tested for validity and reliability in this study. Mean participant responses were 85.9% for total self-efficacy, 94.5% for total interest, 75.9% for total recognition, and 87.8% for total geoscience identity. Descriptive and non-parametric inferential statistics reveal differences in MoGI responses and total scale scores for recognition and interest based on student status, employment in the geosciences, and gender. Phase two involved semi-structured interviews ( N = 10 ) and questionnaires ( N = 15 ) to explore student and graduate perspectives on the impact of their geoscience degree program on their geoscience identity and their ideas for retention and recruitment efforts. Quantitative and qualitative findings converged, indicating participant geoscience identities are mostly based on moderate to high self-efficacy and interest, moderate self-recognition, and relatively low recognition by others. Participants credited geoscience degree programs with improving primarily their self-efficacy while revealing the social construction of their geoscience identities in a small department. Suggestions for recruitment and retention focused on outreach involving geoscience career education, increasing field experiences for current students, and increasing opportunities for social interaction within the department. Barriers to geoscience identity development include lack of career and field knowledge, social isolation, and delays in degree program progress. Recommendations include a recruitment and retention plan maximizing geoscience visibility through field and career education while mitigating low enrollment via degree program restructuring, increasing strategic outreach, increasing support from university administrators, and continued geoscience identity research.

abstract: Fieldwork in polar sciences can be either an exciting opportunity or a terrifying ordeal. Discrimination, stereotypes and harassment are all well documented perils of fieldwork. For many, acquiring the right equipment or knowing what to pack can be a barrier to engaging in fieldwork, especially for early career scholars. This need for resources and gear sharing, packing lists, and access to local used gear shops was reiterated by early career scholars at the 2023 West Antarctic Ice Sheet Workshop. To address this need, the NSF-funded Virtual Ice Community Engagement squad developers, with support from the Polar Science Early Career Community Office (PSECCO), developed a webpage through CryoCommunity to directly connect individuals seeking to borrow gear to those willing to lend gear. In addition to providing a platform for these connections, this shared community space includes packing lists for region-specific field work, locations of affordable used or repaired gear in cities across the United States, and lists of gear discounts relevant to field-going polar scientists. This initiative has become self-sustaining by creating connections across geographically isolated and siloed glaciology departments in lieu of developing and maintaining a localized “gear repository”. In 2024, a survey was shared with the wider glaciology community to determine direction of efforts (n=25). Among other results, the majority of respondents indicated the gear they would lend is new, slightly, or well used (94.7%). To address respondent concerns regarding quality assurance, timeliness of gear receiving/return, transparency of use, sanitation, and responsibility of cost, we have developed a gear lending agreement template that users can adapt for their own purposes. In the summer 2025 field season, three early career field scientists were supported by connections from the CryoCommunity Gear Sharing page. Overall, the development of this shared resource addresses a gap in field accessibility within the polar sciences and increased opportunity and access to the field for all polar scientists.

title: Radon, the Invisible Geologic Hazard: Measuring Soil Levels in Kentucky
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Robinson, Donna [1]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
abstract: Radon gas is a geogenic Class A human carcinogen produced from the radioactive decay of naturally occurring uranium and thorium in the ground. Radon is known to be the second leading cause of lung cancer in the United States and the number one cause among nonsmokers. The National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences is funding a collaboration between the Kentucky Geological Survey and the University of Kentucky College of Nursing to investigate the phenomenon known as the limestone paradox, where higher indoor radon levels are statistically linked to geologic map units in Kentucky with lower uranium potential. Isolating the geologic and atmospheric variables that lead to spikes in soil radon and resulting indoor radon levels is a major focus in the advancing field of geology and health, or geohealth, with the aim of reducing lung cancer deaths and better understanding geologic pathways for this deadly natural hazard. In 2025, the Kentucky Geological Survey deployed state-of-the-art Durridge radon monitoring equipment to measure soil radon gas levels at several locations across the Bluegrass region of Kentucky using optimized soil gas testing methods developed after rigorous field testing. A soil sample was also collected from each site, and total uranium content was quantified using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry at the University of Kentucky. The preliminary data showed a weak positive correlation between in-situ soil radon and total uranium in the soil (R 2 = 0.15) and a slightly higher positive correlation between expected surficial uranium concentrations and total measured uranium in the soil (R 2 = 0.18). It was also found that measured soil radon values were not always consistent within the same localized testing areas. The early results of this multiyear study suggest that there are complex processes involved in the spatial distribution of soil radon, more than previously hypothesized. More data points are needed to bolster the statistical significance of these relationships and to fine-tune the sample collection methodology to account for elevated soil heterogeneity during future soil gas testing.

title: Deformed Shorelines Record a Sequence of Oceans on Early Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Citron, Robert [1], Marchi, Simone [2], Manga, Michael [3], Hemingway, Douglas [4]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA
(4) University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract: The existence of ancient oceans on Mars remains debated. Geological contacts encircling the northern lowlands, interpreted as paleo-shorelines, provide the most direct evidence for past oceans but are controversial because their present-day elevations vary by several kilometers, inconsistent with the equipotential surface a coastline should follow. Prior work showed that loading from the Tharsis volcanic province can account for much of this variation, but significant misfits remain near the circum-Tharsis trough and the Isidis basin, and the Isidis shoreline tilts opposite to the predicted deformation. Here we construct surface-loading models that resolve the Tharsis load into its individual volcanic centers, and add flexure from post-shoreline Isidis basin loading and the relaxation of dynamic topographic support from a Syrtis mantle plume. The corrected elevations are consistent with paleo-equipotential surfaces, supporting their interpretation as past ocean margins containing 317, 105, and 86 m global equivalent layer thickness of water for the Arabia, Deuteronilus, and Isidis shorelines, respectively. The corrected long-wavelength topography of the Arabia shoreline is shared by independent coastal markers, including valley-network termini, open-basin deltas, and outflow-channel knickpoints. These oceans formed in two episodes – an earlier, larger ocean coincident with widespread valley network activity and a smaller, later ocean accompanying the circum-Chryse outflow channels – each tied to a phase of volcanic activity, suggesting that Mars' early oceans were episodic and co-evolved with the volcanism that both deformed the shorelines and could have transiently warmed the climate. The restored ocean levels also provide context for landing sites: Zhurong's coastal deposits lie below the Deuteronilus level, Jezero crater sits above the Arabia level once Isidis loading is included, partial flooding of Gale crater may explain its degraded northern rim, and Rosalind Franklin will land near the Arabia margin at Oxia Planum, offering an in-situ test of the shoreline hypothesis. More broadly, long-wavelength deformation from volcanic and basin loading is a first-order control on reconstructing ancient Martian landscapes, and the load-corrected topography provides a framework for evaluating paleo-lake levels, drainage patterns, and coastal landforms across the northern plains.

title: From 1960 to the Present: Tracking Year-by-Year Changes to the International Commission on Stratigraphy's Geologic Timescale
session_title: ‘GTS2030’ – Toward an Open Science Geologic Time Scale
authors: Britt, Benjamin [1], Walker, Doug [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
(2) Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
abstract: The historical development of the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) Geologic Timescale has been covered by numerous authors, but a detailed review, especially of the nomenclature, has not yet been compiled. This has led to inconsistent information between publications that increases confusion about the timescale’s developmental history. We report here on the historical development of the entire ICS timescale’s radiometric dates, nomenclature, and GSSPs, from the period starting in 1960 and ending on December 31st, 2025. Sources from official ICS timescale compilations/documents (annual reports, Episodes papers, etc) were incorporated first. Where these references presented gaps in knowledge, information was then taken from widely accepted, non-ICS-affiliated timescale publications. A set of animations is also presented, based on the data collected above, that shows timescale changes on a yearly resolution over the last 65 years. This animation illustrates the complex changes that have occurred throughout the timescale’s history and addresses several common misconceptions. A more complete understanding of timescale historiography can encourage more transparency and better historical note-keeping, and inform future timescale development efforts.

title: The Sodom Airburst Retraction and the Clickbait Index
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Boslough, Mark [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
On Sept. 20, 2021, the paper, “A Tunguska sized airburst destroyed Tall el‑Hammam a Middle Bronze Age city in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea,” was published by Bunch et al. and the Comet Research Group (CRG). I was notified that day by a colleague who wrote, “I suspect you've seen the recent Nature paper about the airburst in the Jordan Valley.”

It was actually published by Nature Scientific Reports , which is not Nature . Many others were also misled by the “nature.com” domain, and this confusion was exploited by one of the paper’s coauthors. The group’s “Cosmic Tusk” blogger and cofounder of the CRG that cosponsored the work tweeted, “This week's Monday night post is on today's Nature pub on our discovery of Sodom.”

He left ambiguous which “Nature pub” he was referencing but didn’t keep his followers guessing about the subject matter. His coauthors put out multiple press releases, blogs, and social media posts the day it was published. All played up the Sodom connection. The Cosmic Tusk announcement didn’t talk about the science other than to say that the paper had “extraordinary implications for science and faith” and that “the data also support significant portions of the Book of Genesis itself.”

The intense focus by the authors on Sodom and the biblical implications turned out to be a winning formula for boosting clicks and maximizing their paper’s Altmetric score (a published measure of online engagement). The CRG press release was titled, “Fire from the Sky destroyed Ancient City, possible source of the Biblical Story of Sodom,” and stated, “The flash of heat and devastation described in the new publication supports the story of the destruction of Sodom in Genesis 19:24-29.”

This presentation will describe the damage that this type of clickbait-oriented science-by-press-release can do to the credibility of a field. It introduces the concept of a Clickbait Index (CBI) that is based on the ratio of Altimetric score to citation count and appears to be inversely correlated with a paper’s scientific legitimacy. Of the top five CBI papers of 2020, as of 2022, one had been retracted and one had been withdrawn. The now-retracted Sodom airburst paper by Bunch et al (2021) had a similarly high CBI.

abstract: RISE-Guadeloupe is an interdisciplinary research and innovation project dedicated to improving the understanding, assessment, and management of natural hazards in island environments. Located in the Lesser Antilles, Guadeloupe is exposed to multiple interacting hazards, including earthquakes, tsunamis, extreme rainfall, coastal erosion, landslides, and the impacts of climate change. These threats affect both natural ecosystems and human societies, requiring integrated approaches that combine Earth sciences, environmental studies, and social sciences. The project aims to generate new scientific knowledge on the origin, dynamics, and impacts of natural hazards while producing operational tools that support risk reduction and territorial resilience. A major objective is to enhance the characterization of tectonic and tsunami hazards through the development of an integrated database of active faults, the reconstruction of past seismic and tsunami events using sedimentary archives, historical records, and field observations, and the improvement of numerical models of tsunami generation, propagation, and coastal impacts. In parallel, RISE-Guadeloupe investigates erosion processes and sediment transfers under extreme conditions by combining field measurements, monitoring systems, and modeling approaches. These studies will improve understanding of the interactions between watersheds, coastal environments, and marine ecosystems, as well as their influence on shoreline evolution. The project also examines the ecological consequences of natural hazards on terrestrial and marine ecosystems, assessing their vulnerability, recovery capacity, and long-term resilience. A complementary social science component explores risk perception, adaptation practices, historical memory, and societal vulnerabilities, providing valuable insights into the development of locally adapted prevention and adaptation strategies. Beyond its scientific contributions, RISE-Guadeloupe places strong emphasis on operational outcomes and knowledge transfer. The project will deliver integrated data management platforms and, most importantly, a suite of decision-support products, including hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and risk maps specifically designed for public authorities, emergency managers, and crisis-response stakeholders. These cartographic products will facilitate preparedness planning, emergency response, land-use management, and long-term resilience strategies. By combining cutting-edge research with practical decision-making tools,RISE-Guadeloupe will establish a transferable framework for multi-hazard risk assessment and management in island territories, contributing to both regional resilience and international scientific advancement.

title: Spatial Evolution of Elastic Wave Properties during Confined and Full-Fault Ruptures on a 3-m Laboratory Fault
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Poku_Agyemang, Kwabena [1], Van Linn, Joseph [2], McLaskey, Gregory C [3], Shreedharan, Srisharan [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(2) School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, USA
(3) School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, USA
(4) Department of Geoscience, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
abstract: Monitoring of stress state along faults remains central to earthquake hazard assessment. Elastic wave properties are sensitive to both stress and rock damage; hence, they may serve as a key proxy for fault stress monitoring. Variations in elastic properties of faults over the seismic cycle have been documented in numerous laboratory experiments and a limited number of field studies. However, it remains unclear how these elastic wave properties evolve during rupture nucleation and termination, partly because fault lengths in conventional stick-slip experiments are too short to produce confined ruptures with clear nucleation and termination signatures. Here, we perform experiments on a 3-m granite block under normal stresses of 5 MPa and 10 MPa, which produce a range of slip and stress drop behaviors including fully- and partially-confined ruptures as well as full-fault ruptures. We monitor variations in the amplitudes of P and S waves and velocity variations (dv/v and Vp/Vs) across two sets of wave paths: 8 fault-piercing paths that cross the fault plane and 8 non-piercing wave paths that are equivalently long but sample only the intact block without crossing the fault plane. For piercing wave paths, we observe a decrease in dv/v within the rupture zone only for the partial ruptures, while dv/v decreases along the entire fault for full ruptures across normal stresses. For non-piercing wave paths, an increase in dv/v is observed during partial ruptures within the ruptured area. At a normal stress of 10 MPa, higher coseismic dv/v changes are observed, corresponding to more slip and a greater stress drop than at 5 MPa. While amplitude varies over the seismic cycle, these variations are less robust and less consistently interpretable than dv/v. These results suggest that dv/v can spatially resolve rupture nucleation and extent, act as a near-fault strainmeter, distinguish partial from full ruptures, and potentially scale with the magnitude of stress drop.

title: Preparing the Next Generation of Geoscientists: A Multi-Year Assessment of Skill Development and Personal Growth from a Traditional Geology Field Camp
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Tully, Lancen S [1], Ryker, Katherine [2], Barbeau, David L [3], Leier, Andrew [4], Rademacher, Laura K [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Ocean and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA

(5) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, University of the Pacific, Stockton, CA, USA
abstract:
Traditional geology field camps serve as intensive capstone experiences that integrate hands-on data collection, outcrop observation, and geologic mapping in authentic outdoor settings. Although field-based courses are widely regarded by the geoscience community as essential for the development of workforce-ready geoscientists, systematic multi-year assessments of their impacts on both technical skills and personal growth remain limited. This evidence gap is especially salient amid the declining availability of traditional field camps, a trend driven by financial, logistical, and accessibility challenges, even as employers continue to prioritize field-related competencies.

This presentation highlights key findings from a four-year (2021-2024) mixed-methods study of the University of South Carolina’s geology field camp program. The study was framed by the National Association of Geoscience Teachers’ Learning Outcomes for Capstone Field Experiences (LOCFEs). Pre- and post-field camp Likert-scale surveys (65 paired responses) document significant perceived gains in core technical competencies (mean normalized change 45%, Cohen’s d = 1.8) aligned with LOCFEs, such as designing field strategies to answer geologic questions and interpreting Earth systems using spatially distributed evidence. Despite some ceiling effects, the surveys also revealed substantial growth in affective domains (mean normalized change 35%, Cohen’s d = 1.1), notably a strengthened science identity, an enhanced sense of belonging in the scientific community, and the development of grit. Survey control items on non-emphasized topics (e.g., earthquakes) confirmed that the reported gains were specific to the field camp experience.

Post-field camp reflections (n = 68) prompted students to consider newly acquired competencies, their relevance to careers, and the broader impact of the field camp experience on everyday life. Students frequently noted how field camp strengthened the practical value of geoscience skills for professional pathways and improved career awareness. They also described enhanced self-awareness of their own capabilities fostered by a supportive peer and instructor community. Some students identified opportunities to strengthen field camps through greater incorporation of modern technologies.

Collectively, these findings underscore the substantial benefits of traditional field camps for developing workforce-ready geoscientists. They provide robust evidence for prioritizing and sustaining these signature geoscience experiences despite challenges. Attendees will leave with concrete strategies for assessing their own field-based courses using the community-validated LOCFE framework.

title: 3D Photogrammetric Analysis of a Segmented Normal Fault System, Southern Utah: Damage Zone Evolution and Implications for Geothermal Energy Potential
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Rueda, Isabella [1], Surpless, Benjamin E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, Texas, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
A fault damage zone, the fractured rock surrounding a fault plane, forms by fault propagation, accumulated displacement, and seismic energy dissipation. A damage zone increases rock permeability and affects hydrothermal fluid upwelling within a fault system, which is necessary for geothermal energy production. However, damage zone deformation is below the resolution of subsurface geophysics, underscoring the need for high-resolution, field-based analysis and exploration.

We performed an outcrop-based study to investigate how the damage zone develops near the tip of a low displacement (<5 m) normal fault within the segmented, NNE-striking, steeply WNW-dipping Sevier fault zone of southern Utah. The low displacement Spencer Bench fault segment is in right-stepping en echelon geometry with the high displacement (~800 m) Mt. Carmel segment and represents a structural discontinuity within the broader Sevier system.

We used field mapping, virtual outcrop model (VOM) analysis, and fracture network topology to constrain cross-sectional characteristics of the fault damage zone. Using drone-based imagery, we built the georeferenced VOM using Agisoft Metashape Professional . From the VOM, we created cross-sectional orthomosaics for scanline, cumulative frequency, and network topologic analysis. We collected data for scanline and cumulative frequency analysis in Agisoft Metashape Professional, and we performed topologic analysis using the NetworkGT toolbox in QGIS.

Our results show that damage zones formed by fault tip and wall processes, when affected by linking stress and strain fields associated with nearby fault segments, can widen rapidly early in a fault’s displacement history. Cumulative frequency analysis reveals fracture network characteristics inconsistent with generation by a single, isolated fault; cumulative frequency graphs display the influence of the nearby Mt. Carmel segment. Topologic analysis of the fracture network indicates far greater fracture intensity and connectivity in the hanging-wall damage zone than in the footwall, and connectivity in the hanging wall decreases with increasing distance from the fault plane but remains significantly higher than intact rock even >100 m from the fault.

We suggest that a structurally similar subsurface system could host an unexpectedly wide zone of elevated hydrothermal upwelling. The growth potential of geothermal energy depends on the discovery and development of blind geothermal systems, and our fine-scale geologic analysis provides evidence that geothermal energy potential for structurally similar low-displacement faults may be higher than previously documented.

title: Monitoring Process Cycles to Understand Riverscape Resilience to Wildfire
session_title: Understanding and Facilitating River Corridor Resilience to Wildfire
authors: Scott, Daniel [1], Shahverdian, Scott [2]
affiliations: (1) Riverscape Science and Stewardship, Longmont, Colorado, USA; Colorado State University Department of Geosciences, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(2) Riverscape Science and Stewardship, Longmont, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Wildfires alter both watershed-scale fluvial regimes of water, sediment, and wood, and local valley bottom ecogeomorphic context (i.e., biota, material properties, etc.). This can test a system’s resilience, or ability to sustain a substantial change in form without losing its fundamental character in response to disturbance. Despite our general desire for healthy, resilient riverscapes, resilience can be difficult to discern from empirical observations collected over short timescales, and the processes that generate resilience can exhibit equifinality. Here, we present paired restoration monitoring and historical analysis from multiple post-fire riverscapes across the western United States to illustrate both the complexity of evaluating resilience and the nature of the processes that generate it. Specifically, we focus on the resilience of water, sediment, and wood retentiveness driven by channel-floodplain lateral connectivity, in-channel obstructions, and partial avulsion.

We analyze riverscapes using a process cycle framework in which we hypothesize the processes that must repeat over varying timescales to create and maintain retentiveness. We determine historical range of variability through our examination of historical aerial imagery. This historical range of variability interpreted through the lens of process cycles establishes an empirical and mechanistic basis for evaluating whether riverscape change constitutes evolution along a trajectory (i.e., a lack of resilience) or simply variability in form despite maintenance of character (i.e., resilience). We evaluate modern monitoring observations in the context of this historical variability to determine whether, why, and for how long these sites can be said to be resilient to wildfire in terms of their retentiveness.

From monitoring results, we show that resilience derives from the presence of a fully functional process cycle in which key riverine constituents are replenished by both local and non-local processes as they are depleted. We show how systems can evolve towards greater resilience through both fire-driven change (e.g., simultaneously increasing influxes of water and wood) and interventions by biota (e.g., humans, beavers). The mechanistic and temporally explicit conceptualization of post-fire resilience provided by a process cycle framework helps illustrate that continued resilience in many watersheds will very likely require restoration, or, rather, stewardship, of watershed-scale regimes over decades to centuries.

abstract:
Wideband magnetotelluric (MT) surveys are used to map heterogeneous electrical resistivity structures and are essential to understanding the geologic frameworks of complex tectonic domains. In 2025, the U.S. Geological Survey began collecting wideband MT data at 35-km spacing across the eastern United States (Georgia to Maine, from the Atlantic coast to west of the Appalachian Mountains), refining the spatial resolution of the long period US MTArray (70-km spacing) through higher-density data collection. Wideband MT data, sensitive to upper-crustal structure, is non-existent across the eastern U.S. save for two legacy profiles. While the survey’s primary aim is to estimate geoelectric hazards due to geomagnetic storms—which can cause damage to or collapse the electric power grid—high resolution 3D resistivity models derived from new MT data will further advance our understanding of Appalachian tectonics and provide context for critical mineral assessments. In a region overlapping more than three dozen known mineral deposits (e.g. tin, tungsten, and zinc) and hundreds of kilometers of Earth MRI focus areas (e.g. marine chemoclines and basin brine paths), these improved models may help identify new crustal or lithospheric discontinuities that act as pathways for deposit-forming fluids.

To date, we have collected data at 189 out of ~600 planned MT soundings. Collected data spans the entirety of Delaware, Maryland, Viginia, and West Virginia and parts of Ohio, New Jersey, Kentucky, and Pennsylvania. Challenges specific to working in semi-urban environments include poor data quality from pervasive cultural noise (pipelines, powerlines, electrified railroads, etc.) and permitting in areas where public lands are limited. Additionally, highly resistive lithosphere underlies much of the survey area, resulting in noise contamination at sites far removed from infrastructure. With innovative data processing methods to combat infrastructure noise, we have successfully produced preliminary 3D resistivity models, which will be used to better forecast the impact of space weather events, refine our understanding of Appalachian tectonics, and improve our ability to map subsurface mineral systems and fluid pathways.

title: Machine Learning-Based Gap Filling of Soil Moisture Data from Agricultural Fields: A Hybrid XGBoost Approach
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Senevirathna, Shaluka Rajantha [1], Bhatta, Anjan [2], Zipper, Samuel C. [3]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, ; Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
Continuous soil moisture monitoring at high temporal resolution is essential for understanding vadose zone dynamics under agricultural management, yet sensor failures and removal during field operation frequently interrupt continuous field measurements, creating data gaps. Gap filling in multi-plot, multi-depth experiments is further complicated when field heterogeneity and treatment differences constrain where sensors can reliably serve as predictors for one another, which is a challenge largely unaddressed in existing literature. Machine learning can provide a framework to address such constraints while preserving experimental integrity.

This study developed a hybrid gap-filling framework that combines linear interpolation and XGBoost to fill gaps for a 15-minute soil moisture timeseries dataset (July 2025– May 2026), collected at an agricultural research site in Ames, Iowa, comprising of 12 plots, where multi-depth moisture sensors installed (15,30,45,60,75 and 90 cm depths), yielding 72 plot-depth combinations. The sensors were installed in plots growing continuous corn with enhanced nitrogen applications, where treatments were designed in a 2 X 2 factorial design with and without cover crops and tillage.

Predictor selection was restricted to same-treatment plots to preserve treatment-level independence, combining vertical moisture coupling, same-treatment spatial coupling, a temperature profile, multi-scale rainfall, and seasonal indices. Short gaps (≤ 6 hours) were filled using linear interpolation, and long gaps were filled using XGBoost with 3-fold time-series cross-validation. For combinations in which spatial predictors failed (R² < 0.20), primarily due to cross-block heterogeneity, only within-plot prediction features were used. To improve predictions during extended gaps, measurements from a co-located Iowa Mesonet station (AKCI4, 0.89 km) were incorporated into the gap-filling model but excluded from cross-validation to prevent the external station's different land management from biasing model selection against treatment-sensitive combinations.

Results showed that out of 72 combinations, 32 met the usability threshold (R² ≥ 0.20). Combinations failing the threshold were mostly concentrated at deeper depths (75–90 cm), where slowly varying soil moisture dynamics decouple across time series cross-validation folds. These results demonstrate that treatment-constrained gap filling is viable in agricultural field experiments, and that external reference data can improve long-gap prediction quality without compromising model selection integrity. However, further exploration is necessary to improve model performance for sensor combinations with high field-level variability.

title: Plugging the Past, Mapping the Future: Leveraging Geospatial Tools for Post-Oil Urban Revitalization
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Hernandez, Julia [1]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Services Group, EKI Environment & Water, Inc., Irvine, CA, USA
abstract:
As Los Angeles County transitions away from oil production, well sites across unincorporated communities require closure, remediation, and purposeful reuse planning. Many of these sites are concentrated in communities bearing disproportionate environmental and public health burdens, creating an urgent need for equitable reinvestment. This study examines how oil well sites can be systematically evaluated and repositioned for community-serving reuse through an integrated, Geographic Information System (GIS)-based evaluation.

GIS-based spatial analysis served as the methodological backbone of this research. By mapping oil well sites, community data, and nearby off-site contamination sources, GIS enabled comprehensive database reviews that characterized sources of uncertainty, community needs, and brownfields redevelopment opportunity alike, influencing both remediation costs and regulatory pathways. Critically, GIS tools support the development of conceptual site models (CSMs) by visualizing multiple layers of data, including spatial relationships between well sites and sensitive receptors, lateral and vertical contamination extents, petroleum impacts, and land reuse feasibility.

GIS-enabled insights directly shaped the study's core findings, revealing widespread ownership complexity, mixed operational statuses among wells, and proximity constraints that necessitate consideration of coordinated remediation approaches. These findings point to a central conclusion: oil well site transition is a multi-year, multi-agency process that demands careful sequencing of technical activities, coordinated regulatory alignment, and site scoring to improve success rates. Building on this conclusion, the research produced a six-phase process framework and decision-tree model that identifies key feasibility thresholds, including site control, regulatory clarity, technical and financial feasibility, and land use compatibility.

The findings demonstrate that GIS tools are not merely supplementary but essential to transforming how counties can identify, prioritize, and plan for site reuse for areas of greater need. The County is currently prioritizing reuse opportunities for parks, affordable housing, community facilities, and clean energy infrastructure. This study establishes a replicable, spatially-informed foundation for safely closing oil well sites while equitably reinvesting in historically overburdened communities.

title: Time-Aware Hazard Monitoring: Post-Wildfire Debris Flows along Mediterranean and Aegean Coastal Areas of Türkiye
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies (Posters)
authors: Mert, Ertan [1], Cakir, Recep [2]
affiliations: (1) Kocaeli University, Kocaeli, Türkiye, Turkey
(2) IZTECH Izmir Institute of Technology, Izmir, Turkey
abstract:
The Mediterranean and Aegean coastlines of Türkiye, where the steep Toros and coastal ranges meet fire-prone Mediterranean-climate vegetation, are increasingly exposed to cascading post-wildfire geomorphological hazards, such as debris flows triggered by short-duration autumn storms on recently burned slopes. This study searched for and analyzed evidence of post-wildfire soil evolution, rapid loss of infiltration capacity through hydrophobicity and ash sealing, followed one to two years later by macropore-driven infiltration increase and collapse of root-derived cohesion, to characterize the temporal hazard trajectory documented after fires such as Antalya-Manavgat (2021), Muğla-Marmaris (2021), and Çanakkale-Kayadere (2023), where post-fire runoff rates reached two to three times the unburned levels. For these coastal catchments, relying solely on static single-snapshot hazard assessments is inadequate. This is because the threshold for triggering debris flows decreases as soil cohesion weakens during the initial one–three years following a fire. This period coincides with peak exposure of populations and infrastructure along the Aegean-Mediterranean coast.

To address this, we propose an integrated, time-aware monitoring framework combining multi-sensor satellite remote sensing, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery for burn-severity mapping via normalized burn ratio indices, InSAR for tracking vertical land motion and surface displacement, and machine-learning classifiers such as random forest models trained on burn severity, slope, rainfall intensity-duration, and antecedent soil moisture data to forecast debris-flow likelihood and volume at the catchment scale. Coupling these AI-driven susceptibility models with a geographic information system enables dynamic, updatable Debris-Flow Hazard Assessment maps that evolve alongside measured soil recovery.

Finally, we recommend an early warning architecture for the Turkish coastal watersheds: 1) rainfall intensity-duration thresholds, recalibrated periodically using satellite-derived soil and vegetation recovery metrics, and 2) automated alerts, issued when radar-estimated rainfall exceeds these evolving thresholds. Emergency managers working along the fire-prone coastlines of Türkiye may use this adaptable model, which integrates satellite and AI technology, as a scalable tool to predict flood and landslide risks in the crucial years after a wildfire.
