abstract:
In Rockbridge County, Virginia, about 80% of the residents obtain their drinking water from private water wells and springs. Located primarily within the Valley and Ridge Province, Rockbridge County is underlain predominantly by carbonate bedrock that hosts an extensive karst aquifer system, with interbedded shale and fewer occurrences of siliciclastic units, that form the bounding ridges along the county margins. Its extreme eastern edge lies within the Blue Ridge Province. Systematic data on the county’s groundwater system remains limited, while the karst setting complicates the characterization of hydrogeochemical patterns, groundwater flow paths, and contaminant transport. This study aims to characterize the hydrogeochemical signatures in the groundwater system across the county. A total of 106 groundwater samples were collected from unfiltered sources, comprising 88 wells and 18 springs across the county.

Preliminary results indicate that the groundwater is predominantly of the Ca-Mg-HCO₃ type, reflecting carbonate bedrock control, with a few samples displaying mixed types marked by elevated Na and/or K. This is consistent with the elevated total dissolved solids (TDS; mean = 375 mg/L), near-neutral to basic pH (mean = 7.29), and relatively high alkalinity (mean = 257 mg/L as CaCO₃) across the groundwater system. The strong positive relationship between TDS and alkalinity (R² = 0.824) further establishes that carbonate mineral dissolution, and the resulting increase in dissolved bicarbonate, is a primary control on both parameters. pH and alkalinity exhibited a moderate inverse relationship (R² = 0.381), potentially reflecting consistency with CO₂-driven dissolution of carbonate bedrock. Well depth showed little to no relationship with either DO or TDS, suggesting that rapid conduit flow and groundwater mixing may obscure depth-dependent hydrochemical patterns within the karst system. Ongoing analyses of groundwater-age tracers and isotopic compositions will help to further constrain recharge sources, residence times, and flow paths.

title: Paleoecology of the Jurassic-Cretaceous Transition within the Great Valley Sequence of Northern California
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Little, Samuel A. [1], Bottjer, David J. [2], Reyes, Melonie D. [3], Brophy, Shannon K. [4], Shapiro, Russell [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA

(5) Department of Earth and Environmental Science, California State University Chico, Chico, CA, USA
abstract: The Jurassic-Cretaceous transition is an important yet relatively understudied interval within the Phanerozoic. While there is evidence for significant turnover and extinction, lack of correlation between index fossils as well as a general rarity of stratigraphic sections have made detailed study challenging. In northern California, the Jurassic-Cretaceous aged Stony Creek Formation (Great Valley Sequence) is expressed in uniquely continuous and fossiliferous outcrops which can be used to identify and quantify change across this enigmatic time interval. These outcrops are primarily comprised of shales with cyclic cemented siltstone, sandstone, and conglomerate beds which were deposited as sediment flows in a deep marine forearc basin. Species of the bivalve Buchia as well as rare ammonites have been used to constrain the biostratigraphy. Evidence for further faunal and environmental change is present but subtle. High resolution stratigraphic measurements and serial samples were taken to identify the abundance, distribution, and diversity of marine invertebrate communities both within shales and cemented beds. Benthic communities were almost exclusively comprised of Buchia species, which remain remarkably uniform within each biozone. Species moving up section appear to become both more robust and abundant, especially in the uppermost Valanginian (early Cretaceous) exposures. Nektonic taxa, such as ammonites and belemnites were also present, but rare in samples. Faunas within shales are generally the same as those within cemented beds. An increased frequency of cemented beds moving up section may indicate changing environmental conditions in the basin. There is also evidence for variation in oxygen levels. Common carbonized plant material and a lack of bioturbation outside of a few heavily bioturbated horizons suggests generally low oxygen conditions with brief oxygenated intervals related to debris flow activity. Future work aims to constrain time within the section and confirm interpretations of environmental conditions using geochemical techniques. Interpreting these conditions will further our understanding of the paleoecology of these faunas in addition to the degree and timing of changes across the Jurassic-Cretaceous transition.

title: Pysochron 2: A standalone software package for calculating 26Al/10Be isochron burial ages
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data (Posters)
authors: Odom, William E. [1]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
abstract:
Isochron burial dating with cosmogenic 26 Al/ 10 Be is a powerful tool for constraining the ages of Pliocene and Pleistocene deposits, but special care is needed to properly model the production and decay of cosmogenic nuclides throughout the exhumation and burial history of a sample. Pysochron was designed to facilitate isochron burial dating calculations by providing an open-source Python script with a graphical user interface that allowed users to easily adjust burial parameters and account for analytical and external uncertainties using a Monte Carlo framework. This approach was validated against 40 independently published isochrons from buried deposits around the world.

Pysochron 2 (https://code.usgs.gov/recon/pysochron2) improves on this framework by providing isochron modeling software in both standalone .exe and .py file types. The introduction of an .exe version is intended to facilitate use on machines running Windows. This update introduces the ability to automatically calculate site-specific surficial and postburial production rate ratios following established methods, run calculations until convergence rather than a set number of Monte Carlo simulations, process batches of isochrons, and generate advanced statistical and graphical outputs of burial datasets. As with the original Pysochron, this software has been tested against 40 independently published isochrons and found to produce consistent results. Users are encouraged to explore the capabilities of Pysochron 2 and provide feedback to be incorporated into future updates of the software.

title: Assessing Health Risk of Groundwater from Microbial and Geochemical Contamination in the Karst Aquifer of Rockbridge County, Virginia
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Robbins, Wynn Katherine [1], Watson, Alexandra Ruth [2], Cao, Vi [3], Chakraborty, Madhumita [4]
affiliations: (1) Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
(2) Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
(3) Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, Virginia, USA
abstract:
In Rockbridge County, Virginia, about 80% of residents rely on private wells and springs for their drinking water, underscoring the need for routine water-quality testing to protect public health. Rockbridge County is underlain by a carbonate-dominated karst aquifer system, making groundwater highly vulnerable to surficial contamination. This community-focused study assesses groundwater quality and suitability for drinking by characterizing microbial, nutrient, and trace metal contamination in the groundwater system. A total of 106 groundwater samples were collected from unfiltered sources (88 wells and 18 springs) at 91 residences across Rockbridge County during the summers of 2025 and 2026.

Microbial contamination was more prevalent in spring samples; coliform bacteria were detected in all springs and E. coli in 66.7%, compared with 46.6% and 3.4%, respectively, in wells. Of the E. coli-positive samples, 81.8% were from springs or wells less than 7 m deep, and all but two samples with coliform counts exceeding 5 CFU per 5 ml sample originated from groundwater sources within 70 m of the ground surface. Of the samples, 13% of Total Dissolved Solids measurements exceeded the EPA secondary maximum contaminant level (SMCL) of 500 mg/L. In 2025 and 2026, samples collected from shallow groundwater sources (0–50 m deep) had the highest median nitrate concentration (1.27 mg/L), with 59.09% exceeding 1 mg/L. Median nitrate concentrations decreased with source depth, from 0.85 mg/L at 50-100 m to 0.51 mg/L at 100-150 m and 0.21 mg/L at 150-250 mg/L. These depth-related patterns are consistent with the microbial data, suggesting that shallow groundwater sources are more vulnerable to surficial contamination from agricultural runoff, septic systems, and other near-surface inputs.

In 2025, 31% of samples had lithium concentrations exceeding the USGS health-based screening level of 0.01 mg/L, potentially reflecting the natural occurrence of lithium-bearing geologic materials in the Appalachian region. Two samples exceeded the SMCL for iron (0.3 mg/L), and two exceeded the SMCL for manganese (0.05 mg/L); however, the two metals were not significantly correlated to the dataset. Collectively, these findings highlight the vulnerability of Rockbridge County’s karst aquifer to contamination and demonstrate the need for continued monitoring of private water sources to protect public health.

authors: Karlstrom, Karl E. [1], Crossey, Laura J. [2], Polyak, Victor James [3], Asmerom, Yemane [4], Dehler, Carol M. [5], Schmitz, Mark D. [6], Xiao, Shuhai [7], Love, Gordon Davidson [8], Porter, Susannah [9], WorkingGroup, BOCP [10]

abstract: The fundamental transition from a prokaryote- to eukaryote- dominated marine ecosystem took place in the Tonian Period (1000-720 Ma) but the timing, contributing mechanisms, and environmental settings for this shift are not resolved. The 1.6-km-thick unmetamorphosed Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon provides a globally important test section. Its 770-729 Ma age is synchronous with breakup of Rodinia and predates the 717 Ma Sturtian Snowball Earth event. It preserves diverse microeukaryotes, early predation, possible biomineralization, and sterane/hopane ratios indicative of substantial eukaryote abundance. Chuar shales have 2-10% TOC suggesting a productive setting and >10 per mil organic carbon isotope excursions record large perturbations in the carbon system. The extent to which the setting was marine, restricted marine, or non-marine is important for assessing the roles of local environmental drivers of biosystem change, versus global secular changes, for the rise of eukaryotes. As one proxy for its depositional setting, we analyzed 87 Sr/ 86 Sr from dolostone interbeds throughout the shale-dominated section. Thirty-six dolostone samples were first analyzed for their elemental concentrations to evaluate relative degree of diagenetic alteration. The nineteen least-altered samples were then analyzed for 87 Sr/ 86 Sr and formed three groups. 1) Samples from the upper Chuar Group (Walcott Member) have near-primary marine 87 Sr/ 86 Sr Neoproterozoic values of 0.70695-0.70697 and are interpreted to be marine. 2) Some samples of the Walcott and the Awatubi members have more radiogenic values of 0.70700-0.70848 compatible with their elemental values that show evidence of significant diagenetic alteration; these are interpreted to be altered carbonates of probable marine and restricted marine origin. 3) Samples from the lower Chuar Group (Galeros Formation) have near primary elemental values but high radiogenic 87 Sr/ 86 Sr values of 0.70707-0.70991 and are interpreted to be non-marine or intermittently marine. These data suggest that the eukaryote abundance and diversification seen in the upper Chuar Group at 740-730 Ma may record global marine and biosystem changes 10-20 million years before the Snowball Earth.

abstract: Late Triassic marine communities experienced deoxygenation and acidification associated with volcanism, resulting in the depletion and extinction of taxa. This event could be used to forecast how ecosystems today may respond to similar disturbances. Functional diversity—the number and types of functions—influences ecological processes, is crucial for ecosystem stability and resilience, and has become a focus for conservation. To better assess how the productivity of shallow-marine ecosystems has fluctuated due to anoxia and ocean acidification in the past, here we quantify changes in functional diversity throughout the Norian and Rhaetian stages of the Late Triassic in New York Canyon, Nevada (USA). Four traits (tiering, feeding, motility, and mineralogy) were assigned to 170 genera from the Gabbs Formation to assess changes in functional diversity. 154 Norian and 67 Rhaetian taxa correspond to 31 and 22 unique functional entities (FEs) respectively. Functional redundancy (average taxa per FE; 4.97 to 3.05), over-redundancy (proportion of taxa filling FEs above the average; 0.46 to 0.32), and vulnerability (FEs containing one taxon; 0.42 to 0.32) were all lower in the Rhaetian, suggesting reduced ecosystem functioning before the end-Triassic mass extinction. Multivariate measures show decreased functional richness (volume of functional space), but increased divergence (how much abundance is at the edges of functional space) and evenness (distribution of traits among functional space). Despite substantial diversity loss, the distribution of genera among functions does not differ (Spearman’s ρ = 0.79, p < 0.001). In the Rhaetian, ten functions disappeared, with rare functions preferentially lost, and one new function emerged. In addition, the most abundant functional group (low-tiering, sessile attached, filter-feeding, mixed aragonitic and calcitic taxa) declined by 53.1%—consistent with reduced carbonate production indicative of acidification. Overall, functional space contracted in the Rhaetian but traits were more evenly distributed among functions. Despite most FEs persisting, declines within FEs could have changed the rates at which functions were performed, lowering productivity. These results suggest that disturbances preceding the end-Triassic mass extinction may have weakened functional capacity, thereby disrupting the ecosystem's natural functioning. This work is relevant to modern marine research, where the preservation of functionally important taxa should be prioritized over taxon richness in the face of anthropogenically-altered ecosystems.

title: Lithology, Petrology, and Geochemistry of a Lithified, Basalt-Derived Paleosol Horizon from Moku’auia Island, O’ahu, Hawai’i, USA

authors: Sharp, Nadia [1], Dennis, Logan [2], Jordan, Benjamin R. [3]

abstract: Moku’auia Island, locally known as “Goat” Island, is a small island off the northeastern coast of O’ahu, Hawai’i. It lies between the communities of Kahuku and Laʻie. It is one of several, sea‑stack islets along this shoreline. This group of islets are collectively tied to traditional Hawaiian mythologies and legends. Mokuʻauia/Goat Island is distinct from the neighboring islets in that it is both the largest and exhibits the lowest overall profile and elevation. This study is an amendment to a previous study, in 2023, that there were young basalts from an undocumented lava flow forming part of Goat Island. Research using satellite imagery, drone surveys, field mapping, and thin sections of samples obtained from Goat Island, determined that the previous study was incorrect and that there are no primary basalts on the island. Instead, the outcrop in question is composed of basalt-derived, lithified soils. This new interpretation supports previous work by Stearns (1979). Most of the island is composed of uplifted reef limestone; cross-bedded, lithified, sand dunes; and modern aeolian deposits. The paleosol consists mainly of oxisols and mollisols, matching compositions of other soils along the eastern shore of O’ahu. The paleosols are composed of weathered silicates, iron oxides and carbonates, including abundant, weathered shell fragments. Whole-rock analysis of two samples, GOAT 4 and GOAT 5, have typical, normalized values for SiO 2 (GOAT 4: 25.78 wt%, GOAT 5: 16.40 wt%), Al 2 O 2 (GOAT 4: 25.07 wt%, GOAT 5: 22.22 wt%), and FeO* (GOAT 4: 17.20 wt%, GOAT 5: 14.84 wt%), compared to other Hawaiian, basalt-derived soils analyzed by Hough and Gile (1941). However, the samples are enriched in TiO 2 (GOAT 4: 3.09 wt%, GOAT 5: 2.76 wt%), and CaO (GOAT 4: 14.31 wt%, GOAT 5: 21.89 wt%). This may be due to the incorporation of significant amounts of coral and shell material, either during soil formation or by post formation contamination. These soils are associated with other Pleistocene shoreline deposits that ring the island of O’ahu. Goat Island was likely isolated by recent sea-level change as the coral base and lithified soil outcrops were exposed by isostatic uplift and subsequent erosion. Age dating of the underlying corals indicates that the paleosol layer is younger than approximately 75,800 years old (U-Th) and 26,300 years old (C 14 ).

title: An Evaluation of Flight Origin Using Phylogenetic Mapping in Oviraptorosaurian Families
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Lowe, Viridian [1], McNett, Gabe [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Biology and Environmental Science, Westminster College, Fulton, MO, USA

abstract: Oviraptorosaurians, a group of theropod dinosaurs, are understood to be secondarily flightless, meaning they evolved from ancestors capable of flight and are widely regarded as extremely bird-like. Our goal was to assess the distribution and variation of flight-related traits to better understand the evolution of flight. We constructed a character matrix of traits known to be important for avian flight and mapped them onto a published phylogenetic tree representing the current understanding of Oviraptorosaurian relationships. Using ten representative taxa across three families (Oviraptoridae, Caudipteridae, and Caenagnathidae) and two outgroups ( Archaeopteryx sp . And Velociraptor sp .). We learned that these traits showed considerable variation. Some traits, such as quill knobs, appear to have been lost once in an Oviraptorosaurian ancestor. Other traits, including the pygostyle and furcula, show significant variation, suggesting they are very labile traits. The ability of some traits to change easily suggests they may have other, non-avian functions. Although we were unable to determine whether the distribution of traits supported one flight origin hypothesis over another, there is support for current ideas that suggest avian flight may have evolved multiple times in the ancestors of birds and their flighted theropod relatives.

title: Hydrographic Characteristics of AI Data Center Siting in the Contiguous United States
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Olaseinde, Adeyinka [1], Frame , Jonathan [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA
abstract:
AI data centers require reliable water supplies for cooling and are expanding rapidly across the contiguous United States (CONUS), raising concerns about their implications for freshwater resources. This study evaluates the hydrographic and hydrologic settings of AI data centers (n = 1,383), including hyperscale facilities under construction, relative to other water-dependent industries. Comparisons were made with thermoelectric power plants (n = 15,569) and Toxic Release Inventory (TRI) facilities (n = 21,130), representing major water-dependent industrial sectors across CONUS. Using national hydrographic, streamflow, water-use, and water-stress datasets, we examined proximity to surface-water resources, watershed hydrologic regimes, water-supply pathways, and basin-scale water stress.

Water-supply pathway classification showed that AI facilities are primarily associated with surface-water-related settings, whereas groundwater-leaning pathways represent a smaller proportion of locations. Hydrographic analysis showed that AI facilities were located closer to major rivers than thermoelectric power plants and TRI facilities, with median river distances of 10.90 km, 19.30 km, and 15.63 km, respectively. Lake proximity showed smaller differences among sectors, with median distances of 5.57 km for AI facilities, 5.72 km for thermoelectric power plants, and 5.15 km for TRI facilities, while coastline proximity showed limited differences relative to basin-matched random locations across all sectors. AI-associated watersheds exhibited lower discharge variability and weaker streamflow seasonality than those containing thermoelectric power plants and TRI facilities.

AI facilities also occurred slightly more frequently in high water-stress basins than thermoelectric power plants and TRI facilities, with 60.2% of locations classified as high stress compared with 57.2% and 56.2%, respectively. Overall, AI data centers were associated with shorter distances to major river networks, watershed conditions characterized by lower discharge variability and weaker streamflow seasonality, and slightly greater occurrence in high water-stress basins relative to other water-dependent infrastructure sectors. This analysis quantifies the hydrographic and hydrologic conditions associated with AI infrastructure locations across the contiguous United States.

abstract: Spatial reconstruction of historic flood disasters provides opportunities to examine relationships among earth processes, landscape change, infrastructure failure, and community impact. To commemorate the 50th anniversary of the June 5, 1976, Teton Dam failure, BYU–Idaho students, faculty, museum collaborators, and library personnel developed a GIS-based virtual field trip to reconstruct and communicate the flood’s historical, spatial, and geologic significance as a place-based earth science case study for public geoscience communication. The project integrates archival records, post-flood aerial imagery, flood-extent data, historical photographs, newspaper accounts, and firsthand narratives within an interactive web map and story map. Methods included georeferencing post-flood aerial imagery, mapping the flood extent, and linking archival materials to specific locations using 1976 aerial imagery and modern GIS tools. These spatially referenced materials document the flood’s physical damage, economic impacts, and effects across the Teton Dam flood inundation zone. The resulting virtual field trip allows users to visualize how floodwaters moved through the Teton River system, affected the floodplain, and shaped community experience. This project demonstrates the value of integrating geospatial analysis and historical archives to communicate flood hazards, landscape change, and infrastructure failure while engaging students and the public in earth science, spatial thinking, and hazard awareness.

abstract: An unresolved question about the Middle to Late Jurassic development of the Western Sierran Foothills (WSF) of California is the polarity of subduction along the continental margin. We examined conglomerates and sandstones of the Colfax Formation, a Middle-Late Jurassic sedimentary unit within the Central Foothills belt of the WSF. We conducted ten conglomerate clast counts (100 clasts per outcrop) from the Colfax Formation to characterize compositions of proximal sediment sources. Colfax conglomerates are typically clast-supported and contain abundant volcanic lithic clasts, chert, and vein quartz. Volcanic lithic clasts comprise 6-45% of each counted conglomerate, which is more than previous analyses documented. Volcanic clasts are predominantly felsic but include felsic to mafic compositions, characteristic of a continental arc source. Chert clasts were primarily black and make up 19-78% of each sample. Chert occurs within the Calaveras Complex, a subduction complex east of the Colfax Formation that developed above east-dipping subduction in Triassic-Early Jurassic time, and in the chert-rich Clipper Gap Formation, a Middle Jurassic subduction complex stratigraphically below the Colfax Formation. Vein quartz quantities are variable, up to 41% across eight samples, and are interpreted as authigenic metamorphic fracture fill developed within the Calaveras Complex. Although not present in all counts, six counts showed carbonate clasts that comprised up to 36% of clasts and are predominantly marble with lesser limestone; both lithologies occur within the Calaveras Complex. Sixteen thin section point counts (300 points counted per thin section) of fine- to medium-grain sandstone also contain abundant volcanic lithic grains, chert, and quartz grains. Volcanic lithic grains include identifiable andesitic grains with plagioclase laths. A few chert pebbles contain radiolarian ghosts, suggesting a deep marine origin for the chert. Colfax Formation sandstone samples cluster in undissected arc and recycled orogen provenance fields in a quartz-feldspar-lithics ternary diagram, and in transitional or lithic recycled orogen fields in a monocrystalline quartz-feldspar-total lithics ternary diagram. Together, these conglomerate and sandstone provenance data suggest that the proximal sediment sources of the Colfax Formation include a continental volcanic arc and older subduction complexes along the continental margin. Our findings support east-dipping subduction beneath North America throughout the Middle to Late Jurassic deposition of the Colfax Formation.

abstract: NASA’s Psyche mission is a Discovery-class robotic planetary mission designed to travel to and orbit Main Belt asteroid (16) Psyche, the largest M-type (presumably metal-rich) asteroid in the Solar System. Launched on October 13, 2023, the spacecraft conducted a flyby of the planet Mars for a gravity assist in May 2026. Although the main purpose of the Mars flyby was a momentum boost and a plane change to put the spacecraft on final course to asteroid Psyche, it served a secondary purpose as a calibration and characterization opportunity for the science instruments, particularly the Psyche Multispectral Imagers (“Imagers”). As the Mars flyby was the only planetary object flyby for the spacecraft prior to arrival at our target asteroid, it was the only opportunity to calibrate and characterize the Imagers while observing a well-studied planetary surface up close. The Mars flyby imaging campaign included both unique opportunities and practice testing of some of the observations planned to be conducted at asteroid Psyche, including checking and adjusting the radiometric and geometric performance of the cameras. Beginning with a rare high phase angle set of timelapse and infield stray light observations approaching Mars from its dark side with a thin (~4%) illuminated crescent, the Imagers obtained a high-resolution (~230-530 m/pixel) 9-color series of continuous nadir-pointed observations spanning Utopia Planitia to Isidis Planitia to southern Syrtis Major Planum, followed by several off-nadir-pointed observations to image the south polar cap and surrounding terrains. Satellite search observations, including several mosaics covering a large fraction of the planet’s inner Hill Sphere of gravitational influence, were also acquired before and after Mars closest approach, to practice and refine similar observations planned to be made on approach to (16) Psyche. In this presentation we will show examples of these observations and discuss the performance of the Imagers. The spacecraft will arrive at asteroid Psyche in August 2029.

title: Detrital Zircon Analysis of the Colfax Formation to Assess Models of Jurassic Subduction in the Western Sierran Foothills

authors: Aldrich, Alissa Sara [1], Ingrum, Joy [2], Sikes, William Wiley [3], Surpless, Kathleen DeGraaff [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA

abstract: The Middle to Late Jurassic evolution of the Sierra Nevada is debated, with several competing models to explain this time of transition in relative plate motion. These models predict different frameworks for understanding the overall development of the central North American Cordillera during Jurassic time. The Colfax Formation was deposited along the continental margin during the Middle to Late Jurassic and understanding its provenance will provide insight into Jurassic subduction dynamics and help evaluate proposed models. We present data from six detrital zircon samples, increasing the total detrital zircon dataset from N=6 (n=621) to N=12 (n=2,085). Our six samples contain 21-35% Mesozoic grains and 65-79% pre-Mesozoic grains. Mesozoic age spectra contain prominent Middle-to-Late Jurassic age modes with smaller Triassic and Early Jurassic modes. Calculated maximum likelihood ages (MLAs) range from ~174 to ~165 Ma for the six new samples. Combined with prior data, the complete dataset provides robust MLAs that indicate basin deposition began as early as 174 Ma and continued until at least 156 Ma, spanning up to 18 million years of deposition. Previous εHf data from Mesozoic zircon grains revealed mostly juvenile grains but included several evolved grains, indicating incorporation of continental crust in arc magma. Additional εHf and detrital zircon trace element data from Jurassic grains further characterize this continental arc. The abundant pre-Mesozoic grains include prominent age modes of ~2600 Ma and ~2000-1800 Ma, and more variable modes of ~1400, ~1200, and ~400 Ma. These ages are characteristic of the North American detrital zircon signature and indicate recycling of strata from the western United States. The abundance of pre-Mesozoic age modes typical of North America combined with Jurassic zircon with evolved εHf values support preliminary conclusions that the Colfax Formation was deposited on the continental margin. Our expanded detrital zircon dataset establishes that Colfax Formation deposition occurred along the continental margin during Middle to Late Jurassic eastward subduction underneath North America.

abstract:
Lithium brine systems are critical resources for the energy transition, yet the structural controls governing lithium mobilization, transport, and enrichment remain poorly constrained. Although faults are widely recognized as fundamental components of lithium-bearing basins, direct evidence linking individual fault and fracture systems to lithium-bearing fluid flow through time is rare. Here, we combine structural geology with calcite U–Pb geochronology, clumped-isotope thermometry, stable isotope geochemistry, and lithium analyses of calcite-mineralized faults, opening-mode fractures, and paleo-spring deposits from Clayton Valley, Nevada, to directly constrain the timing and character of lithium-bearing fluid circulation.

Calcite U–Pb ages associated with Basin and Range extension span 15.4 ± 6.4 Ma to 4.2 ± 2.3 Ma, recording repeated episodes of structurally focused fluid flow during basin evolution. Clumped-isotope temperatures range from 24.6 ± 4.1 °C to 139.2 ± 12.6 °C, indicating fluid circulation over a wide range of depths. Bulk lithium concentrations in calcite span <2 to 460 ppm, with the highest concentrations occurring in basin-fill-hosted veins and paleo-spring deposits and generally lower concentrations in basement-hosted and basin-bounding fault veins. Several lithium-bearing veins yield ages older than the ~6 Ma Rhyolite Ridge Tuff, the principal volcanic lithium source unit in the region, indicating that structurally focused lithium-bearing fluid circulation locally predated emplacement of this unit. The highest lithium concentrations, however, are associated with younger veins that formed contemporaneously with, or after, late Miocene silicic volcanism.

Stable isotope compositions and reconstructed fluid δ¹⁸O values indicate that most mineralizing fluids were dominantly meteoric, with elevated temperatures reflecting circulation to depth and fluid-rock interaction rather than requiring direct magmatic fluid input. One sample records a heavier reconstructed fluid composition, suggesting localized involvement of more evolved basin fluids.

These results demonstrate that fault and fracture networks acted as long-lived, repeatedly reactivated pathways for lithium-bearing fluids throughout >10 Myr of Basin and Range extension. Rather than serving solely as passive features within lithium basins, brittle structural networks likely enhanced hydraulic connectivity, promoted water-rock interaction, and facilitated repeated redistribution of lithium during basin evolution. This study provides one of the first direct geochronologic constraints on fault-controlled lithium transport in an active continental lithium brine system and highlights the importance of integrating structural geology with geochronology and geochemistry to understand critical mineral systems.

title: Finding molecular biosignatures using machine learning: The next frontier
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Prabhu, Anirudh [1], Hazen, Robert M. [2], Wong, Michael L. [3], Scharf, Caleb [4], Team, DeLIMIT [5]
affiliations: (1) Carnegie Institution for Science, Earth and Planets Laboratory, Washington, DC,
(2) Carnegie Institution for Science, Earth and Planets Laboratory, Washington, DC,
(3) Carnegie Institution for Science, Washington, DC,
(4) NASA, NASA Ames Research Center,
(5) Various Organizations, USA
abstract:
The search for biosignatures—unambiguous markers of past or present life—has long been a central goal of scientists all over the world. Astrobiology uses many different forms of analysis to capture data about the information in living systems in the world: whether in molecular fossils, active metabolisms, or physical structures. These data can contain biological and non-biological features that exhibit extremely complicated, correlative, informational properties that are challenging to interpret and exploit. ML approaches show enormous potential for decoding such features and enhancing our ability to detect and characterize living systems.

Encouraged by our successes at extracting molecular biosignatures from individual instrument data, we are now developing a multi-messenger ML framework for biosignature detection that combines laboratory measurements from pyrolysis–gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (py-GC-MS), Raman spectroscopy, and isotope-ratio mass spectrometry.

Major milestones in this effort include (i) the creation of a systematic dataset of more than 1,000 samples spanning modern biological materials, taphonomically altered remains of ancient life, abiotic extraterrestrial materials, and synthetic products of geochemical organosynthesis, (ii) integration of historical laboratory and planetary datasets and develop standardized representations that account for differences in sample preparation, analytical conditions, instrument sensitivity, and data quality, (iii) development of supervised, unsupervised, and anomaly-detection approaches to identify biosignatures and integrate evidence across measurement modalities, and (iv) model interpretation to determine which molecular and spectroscopic features drive predictions and to identify patterns that may provide new insights into the informational signatures of life.

Additionally, we plan to use the models we develop to evaluate strategies for combining measurements and optimizing flight-ready instrument suites, with an emphasis on reducing false positives and improving confidence in life-detection measurements. This work will establish a data-driven framework for molecular biosignature detection that connects laboratory experimentation, machine learning, and planetary exploration, providing a path toward more robust and interpretable searches for extant or extinct life in the Solar System.

title: Ironing Out OAE1a: Reconstructing Water-Column Redox Conditions in the Vocontian Basin
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Posters)
authors: Tretina, Veronika C. [1], Herlinger, Jillian F. [2], Sageman, Bradley B. [3], Hurtgen, Matthew T. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL,
(3) Departmental of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA
abstract:
Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a (OAE1a; ~120.5 Ma) represents a major perturbation to the Early Cretaceous carbon cycle, characterized by enhanced organic carbon burial, widespread black shale deposition, and global marine deoxygenation. Although OAE1a has traditionally been interpreted as an interval of widespread euxinic (anoxic and sulfidic) conditions, recent geochemical evidence suggests that ferruginous (anoxic and iron-rich) conditions may have been more extensive than previously recognized. Distinguishing between these redox states is important because ferruginous and euxinic environments exert fundamentally different controls on nutrient availability and marine biogeochemical cycling. However, the distribution and evolution of these redox states during OAE1a remain poorly constrained, limiting our understanding of their roles in Earth-system biogeochemical feedbacks.

Here, we present iron-speciation data from the Les Sauzeries core (Vocontian Basin) to reconstruct local bottom-water redox conditions across OAE1a. As a semi-restricted basin with terrigenous input and limited ventilation, the Vocontian Basin provides a setting where bottom-water redox conditions may be more closely linked to changes in weathering-derived iron fluxes than more open, abyssal environments. Sequential iron extractions quantify highly reactive iron phases, including carbonate-associated iron, ferric oxides, magnetite, and pyrite iron and are integrated with phosphorus-speciation data and existing carbon isotope data to evaluate changes in redox conditions and nutrient cycling. These results provide new constraints on the temporal evolution of ferruginous and euxinic conditions in the western Tethyan and clarify how redox heterogeneity influenced biogeochemical cycling during OAE1a.

title: The Many Side of Historic Mining in the Sierra Nevada, California
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Lee, Jacob [1]
affiliations: (1) California Geological Survey, Redding, CA, USA
abstract:
As part of the Sierra Nevada Earth Science Atlas, the California Geological Survey (CGS) is highlighting a variety of geoheritage sites across the Sierra Nevada, include historic mining sites. Historically, the CGS was primarily focused on documenting California’s mining mineral resource development. Today, the CGS is approaching this history with a more holistic view—reflecting on how State history is intertwined with Sierra Nevada Gold Rush.

In the western foothills, Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park marks the site where the discovery of placer gold concentrated in river gravels sparked global migration and laid the foundation for California’s Gold Rush–era cultural transformation. In contrast, the nearby Empire Mine represents the deep hard‑rock mining legacy of the Northern Sierra Metamorphic Belt, where gold‑bearing quartz veins formed along ancient fault systems and were pursued through hundreds of miles of underground workings.

North of these districts, Malakoff Diggins demonstrates the scale and environmental cost of hydraulic mining. Entire hillsides of gold-bearing "auriferous" gravels were washed away, delivering enormous sediment loads downstream and ultimately leading to the first major environmental ruling in California history. Downstream from these hydraulic operations, the Yuba Goldfields preserve some of the most dramatic anthropogenic landforms in the Sierra Nevada. Here, vast deposits of hydraulic mining debris were later reworked by bucket‑line dredges that excavated deep pits and left behind extensive linear tailings piles, creating one of the largest human‑made geomorphic landscapes in the world. The Yuba River continues to reshape these tailings, making the Goldfields a natural laboratory for studying fluvial systems.

In the eastern Sierra, Bodie State Historic Park preserves an epithermal gold‑silver district formed by volcanic and hydrothermal processes. The intact mining town sits directly atop the mineralized volcanic rocks that created its wealth, illustrating the tight link between geologic processes, mining activity, and settlement patterns.

Finally, the State Mining and Mineral Museum provides geologic context through collections that showcase the mineral‑forming processes—igneous, metamorphic, and hydrothermal—that underpin the Sierra Nevada’s mining history.

Together, these sites reveal how a diversity of rock types, ore‑forming environments, and mining technologies shaped distinct mining landscapes across the Sierra Nevada, each leaving enduring cultural and environmental legacies central to California’s geoheritage.

title: CARE Project for Marginal Wells: Plug or Improve?
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Zimmerle, Daniel [1]

abstract:
Colorado State University will lead a $300M project to improve operations and reduce emissions from marginal conventional wells (MCWs) – low-producing oil and gas (O&G) wells, many of which are decades old. The project will distribute funds to small operators who own and operate these wells to keep ‘product in the pipe’, improve safety, and reduce emissions. MCWs generally have less infrastructure, are more dispersed, and less economically attractive than newer unconventional (horizontal drill) wells. The project will focus on adapting repair and operation solutions, many of which have been developed for more recent wells, to MCWs.

CARE will include both solution incubation and technical assessment. Teams will help solution and service developers adapt their product offerings to MCW and do field trials of equipment. Solutions may include improved sensing, fixes to physical plant equipment, and SCADA systems. A separate team will perform pre- and post-improvement assessments. Data will be published throughout the project. Participation is open to all MCW operators who are below the program’s financial cap, and to any interested solution developers.

title: Exploring the Potential for Radiolytic Ecosystems on Mars
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Calvin, Wendy M. [1], Moser, Duane P. [2], Hedlund, Brian P. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Division of Hydrological Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(3) School of Life Sciences, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
abstract:
The subsurface of planets and moons is the most likely location for life given the general inhospitality of their surfaces. The radiolytic hypothesis posits that natural radioactive decay in rocks splits water, producing oxidants and reductants that support subterranean chemotrophic food webs. We are studying radiolytic ecosystems on Earth and the potential for radiolysis to contribute to habitats in the Martian subsurface. Radioactive elements are concentrated by a variety of mechanisms, but mobilization of metals in fluid is a necessary step. Past hydrothermal activity on Mars that could have concentrated radionuclides is known from the mineralogic, geologic and geomorphic signatures associated with impact craters and volcanism. Additionally, amagmatic hydrothermal systems associated with radiogenic heat have been proposed (Ojha et al. Nature Comm, 2021, 12:1754).

Data from the Mars Odyssey gamma-ray spectrometer (GRS) reveals three regions where high concentrations of K and Th co-occur on Mars (Isidis, Acidalia, Terra Cimmeria-Sirenum). We examine these locations and their association with alteration minerals identified by CRISM and OMEGA. K and Th are proxies for U and other radiogenic elements and alteration suggests the potential for hydrothermal systems that might concentrate radiogenic material, whether magmatic, impact related, or radiogenic.

The first location is northeast of Isidis Planitia on the margin with Utopia Planitia. Although there are numerous alteration exposures to the northwest and south of Isidis, none overlap with the strongest K and Th signatures. The second location in Acidalia Planitia abuts the strong alteration observed near Mawrth Vallis, but the strongest K and Th signatures are farther north. Only three alteration locations are within the highest radiogenic concentrations, Kunowsky crater and two spots in Acidalia Colles. The third location bridges Terra Cimmeria and Terra Sirenum and spans the Eridania basins. Alteration in this region is abundant and has been previously interpreted as basin floor or hydrothermal seafloor deposits (Adeli et al. 2015, JGR, 120, 1774; Michalski et al. Nature Comm, 2016, 8:15978). This is also the location proposed to have amagmatic radiogenic hydrothermal systems noted above. However, outcrops at the eastern edge (Gorgonum Chaos) and outside the basins have received less attention. The presentation will review these regions and their associations with characteristic alteration types and their potential to host hydrothermal systems that would concentrate radiogenic elements.

title: GROUNDWATER CONTRIBUTION TO NUTRIENT FLUXES IN THE SURFICIAL AQUIFER ALONG THE PENNSYLVANIA COASTLINE OF LAKE ERIE
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Abdulsalam, Aminat Tosin [1], Housego, Rachel [2], Foyle, Anthony M. [3], Keirn, Alison [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA

abstract: Shallow groundwater discharge through coastal bluffs represents a direct but poorly constrained pathway for agricultural nutrient delivery to Lake Erie, where eutrophication and harmful algal blooms remain persistent water-quality concerns. To quantify groundwater-driven nutrient loading, groundwater levels and nutrient concentrations were monitored at the Lake Erie Regional Grape Research and Extension Center, Pennsylvania, within an agricultural catchment extending nearly 1 km inland and representative of poorly surface-drained catchments along the Pennsylvania coast. Six wells (10–12 m deep) were installed in 2024 and instrumented to record groundwater level, conductivity, and temperature at 15-minute intervals. Water samples from monitoring wells, bluff piezometers, and springs were collected seasonally for nitrate (NO₃–N) and phosphate, with higher-frequency sampling around fertilizer application and rainfall events. Wells were also sampled for major ions. Hydraulic heads were higher inland and decreased toward the bluff, indicating persistent north-northeast groundwater flow toward the coastal discharge zone. Mean hydraulic gradients ranged from 0.015 to 0.017. Phosphate concentrations were below detection. Nitrate concentrations varied significantly among wells, ranging from 0.04 mg/L in Wells 2 and 5 to 10.6 mg/L in Well 4 (Kruskal–Wallis H = 35.83, p = 0.0003). This variability appears partly controlled by stratigraphic heterogeneity: Wells 2 and 5, where a clay lens was encountered, had the lowest nitrate concentrations and hydraulic conductivities (0.136 and 0.212 m/day), compared with a mean of 3.863 m/day across the remaining wells. Major-ion chemistry indicates that sediment lithology alone may not fully explain spatial variability in groundwater chemistry. Most wells plot within a calcium–magnesium–bicarbonate facies, consistent with fresh groundwater dominated by carbonate weathering, whereas Well 6 and bluff springs exhibit sulfate and chloride enrichment, suggesting localized mixing, anthropogenic inputs, or interaction with a geochemically distinct groundwater source. Darcy-based nitrate flux through the saturated aquifer thickness, normalized per meter of bluff shoreline, ranged from 2.38–3.80 g NO₃–N day⁻¹ m⁻¹ in spring and 3.36–5.37 g NO₃–N day⁻¹ m⁻¹ in summer. Higher summer estimates reflect increased nitrate concentrations following spring fertilizer application despite lower hydraulic gradients; ranges reflect variability in measured hydraulic conductivity. These findings suggest that groundwater is a non-negligible pathway for nitrate delivery to the Lake Erie nearshore zone, with permeable sediments facilitating transport through coastal agricultural catchments.

title: InSAR ground deformation observations in predictive modeling: treasure trove or hidden dragons?
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Markovich, Katie [1], Lindsey, Eric [2], White, Jeremy [3], Davis Hughes, Joseph [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(3) INTERA Incorporated, Fort Collins, CO, USA

abstract:
Groundwater systems are under-constrained by observations, and the distribution of these observations are highly non-uniform across the globe. Over the past two decades, the promise of remote sensing and geophysical data for filling in spatial and temporal gaps in groundwater monitoring has grown. Yet progress towards that promise has largely remained in the realm of academic research and routine assimilation into applied groundwater modeling remains rare. A major barrier is insufficient characterization and methodological approaches for coping with the complex noise structures and uncertainties in these datasets for predictive modeling applications.

InSAR-derived ground deformation illustrates this gap. Since 2014, the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-1 satellites have provided weekly, near-global geodetic imagery which can be processed to detect millimeter-scale ground deformation at high spatial resolution. These measurements capture subsidence from compaction of aquifer sediments due to pumping and elastic rebound from recharge. Hence, InSAR data holds immense promise for informing and constraining elusive parameters such as pumping rates, storage properties, and recharge. However, InSAR ground deformation measurements contain complex, correlated noise and parameterizing poroelastic properties in groundwater models is more akin to a dark art than a reasoned, data-driven process. In other words, including these observations in history matching could degrade predictive skill due to model error.

We present a proof-of-concept exploration of using InSAR data in predictive groundwater modeling. Using a synthetic “truth” model and real-world noise from a non-deforming region, we quantify the value of InSAR data in improving accuracy and reducing bias/uncertainty in model forecasts relative to traditional calibration targets.

title: Don’t Call Me Grenvillian: Orogenic Diversity during the Assembly of Rodinia
session_title: One orogeny is not like the other: changes in orogenic styles through the Proterozoic
authors: Spencer, Chris [1]
affiliations: (1) Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada
abstract:
Rodinia has long been viewed through the lens of a few dominant orogenic events, with the Grenville Orogeny often treated as the defining feature of its assembly. This perspective has contributed to the widespread adoption of a simplified, monolithic model, in which diverse tectonic histories are subsumed within a single framework largely centred on Laurentian geology. Such an approach has led to broad assumptions regarding Mesoproterozoic geodynamics, including the extent of orogenic quiescence, the prevalence of stagnant-lid tectonics, and the continuity of Nuna and Rodinia as a singular supercontinent cycle. However, emerging evidence challenges these interpretations, revealing a far more complex and heterogeneous tectonic landscape.

In this study, we employ a multi-proxy approach to reassess Mesoproterozoic orogenesis and the assembly of Rodinia, integrating geochronological, geochemical, and isotopic data from a variety of orogenic systems. Our findings demonstrate that these systems exhibit distinct geochemical and metamorphic signatures, reflecting significant variations in heat flow, crustal reworking, and tectonic style. While the Grenville Orogeny represents a key component of Rodinian assembly, it was neither a singular nor globally representative event. Instead, orogenic belts such as the Albany-Fraser, Sveconorwegian, and Kibaran provide critical evidence for concurrent but regionally distinct tectonic activity.

Recognizing the diversity of Rodinian orogenies allows for a more refined view of Mesoproterozoic tectonics that is not biased by a single orogenic system and does not hide regional orogenic idiosyncracies with a global average. This orogenic perspective requires an interpretation of a more dynamic, evolving geodynamic system rather than a prolonged phase of tectonic stagnation. These results highlight the need to reassess traditional models of Rodinia’s assembly and advocate for a more nuanced approach that acknowledges regional variability and multiple orogenic drivers in the formation of supercontinents.

title: Oceanic arcs with continental memories
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Spencer, Chris [1]
affiliations: (1) Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada
abstract:
Subduction zones play a central role in shaping Earth’s crust, yet the origin of inherited zircon in oceanic arc magmas remains unresolved. Oceanic arcs are commonly assumed to form on entirely oceanic lithosphere, which implies that ancient zircon found in arc lavas must be introduced by sediment subduction. However, the physical feasibility of zircon surviving transport through the hydrous mantle wedge, from which arc magmas are derived, has yet to be demonstrated. In this study, we report new and compiled zircon U-Pb geochronology from the Luzon, Solomon, Vanuatu, Izu, Bonin, and Lesser Antilles arcs to reassess how inherited zircon becomes incorporated into oceanic arc systems. We also perform diffusion-limited dissolution modelling that indicates typical detrital zircon grains dissolve rapidly (conservatively hours to days) in primitive arc magmas, suggesting that survival of subducted zircon is unlikely.

Instead, we find that the distribution of inherited zircon ages aligns closely with documented histories of slab rollback and arc migration. Several of the arcs examined here overlie thinned continental fragments or earlier arc lithosphere that predate the present magmatic systems. As rollback drives trench retreat and arc migration, magmatism can shift across heterogeneous upper plate lithosphere, locally entraining zircon from older crustal components. Even arcs commonly regarded as strictly intra-oceanic preserve evidence for earlier continental or arc substrates that may serve as sources of inherited zircon. These theoretical and empirical observations support a model in which inherited zircon in oceanic arcs reflects interaction with subarc continental crust, rather than deep survival of zircon transported through the mantle wedge. Oceanic arcs may therefore be less juvenile than they appear, with arc mobility and lithospheric inheritance playing a substantial role in their formation and evolution.

title: Why “Cosmic Processes (C)” Is Not Merited as an Addition to the ClORPT Soil Forming Framework
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: McFadden, Leslie D. [1], Boslough, Mark [2]
affiliations: (1) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
(2) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, ; Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
A recently published paper proposed that the hypothesized Younger Dryas impact caused a “global conflagration” that altered or obliterated many major properties of soils. These changes and their global scale are claimed to be sufficiently profound to justify adding the letter “C” (“cosmic processes”) to the set of “ClORPT” factors that most strongly influence processes of soil formation as proposed by Hans Jenny (1941), Climate (Cl), Organisms (O), Relief (R), Parent materials (P) and Time (T). “ClORPT” provides the conceptual framework for a large body of published research in the disciplines of Soil and Earth science.

Key arguments for justifying the addition of C principally included: (1) Features in Quaternary soils interpreted to provide evidence of dramatic changes in soils with depth that can only be explained by thermal and shock impacts produced by a cosmic airburst comparable to a nuclear blast (one million degrees C ); and (2) A global conflagration would have impacted soils across all continents, as an initially large comet would have been shattered into thousands of fragments that would in turn produce Tunguska-scale or larger surface impacts globally.

There are fatal flaws with both (1) and (2).

(1) The energy density of a meteoritic airburst is many orders of magnitude lower than a nuclear explosion, so the associated temperatures are also orders of magnitude lower. Low altitude meteoritic airbursts can only melt surface materials in cases for which the hot meteoritic vapor makes direct, but brief contact with a localized surface at thousands of degrees (called a “contact” or “type 2” airburst).

(2) In addition to a very large number of impacts required to alter soils globally, the frequency of such impacts during the Quaternary required to alter and spatially dominate soil landscapes would require a population of near Earth objects many orders of magnitude higher than what has been established by astronomers. Pedogenic evidence to support this in extant soil landscapes has not been reported in relevant publications.

Nevertheless, the fact this study was proposed by a well-respected scientist in a field unrelated to planetary science and was subsequently published shows that at least some researchers in diverse science disciplines are accepting the YDIH as a hypothesis worthy of their consideration, a phenomenon that should elicit concern amongst many Earth scientists.

title: A Siluro-Devonian dismembered ophiolite in northernmost New Hampshire?
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part II)
authors: Converse, David Rhys [1], Bothner, Wallace A. [2], Jahrling, Christian E. [3], Koch, Philip S. [4], Summa, Lori L. [5], Awwiller, David Neel [6]
affiliations: (2) University of New Hampshire, Durham, NH,
(4) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(5) Rice University, Lancaster, NH,
(6) University of New Hampshire, Lancaster, NH,
abstract:
Recent geologic mapping and geochemical analyses yield new insights into the Siluro-Devonian tectonic history and the Salinic Orogeny in northernmost New Hampshire. Updated mapping of the East Inlet Intrusive Complex (EIIC) and Clinton River meta-igneous units, plus nearby ultramafic bodies, suggests that these units may be pieces of a dismembered Siluro-Devonian ophiolite. The updated maps confirm the presence of anorthosites, anorthositic gabbros, tonalites and mafic pegmatites, and ultramafic rocks, gabbros, basalts, diorites and granites as well as sheeted basaltic dikes and tonalites that may be plagiogranites. Anorthosite and mafic pegmatites are known to be associated with ophiolite bodies (e.g., Cyprus and Oman ).

Our interpretation of U-Pb isotopes indicates age dates of ~ 419 Ma for anorthosite and tonalite samples, and ~ 423 Ma for the youngest age population found in the mafic pegmatite. The age determinations are quite similar, given the uncertainties of 4-7 Ma. Interpretation of Hf-Lu isotopes is ongoing.

While the ultramafic rocks appear to be present only as small bodies in New Hampshire, mapping in Maine (Green, 1968, Moench et al, 1995, Harwood, 1973) indicates larger ultramafic bodies extending along strike to the northeast. Differentiation of mafic basalts and gabbros from ultramafic rocks without fibrous veins can be difficult in the field due to the pervasive greenschist metamorphism and limited outcrops but are easily distinguished via geochemical analysis. The ages of the ultramafic rocks are undetermined but based on the ages of the surrounding units, a Siluro-Devonian age is likely. Note these ultramafic rocks don’t appear to be part of the Boil Mountain ultramafics which have been dated as Ordovician (Gerbi et al., 2006). The Marble Mountain gabbro-diorite complex is located in Maine and Quebec, less than 5 km along trend to the northeast of the EIIC (Cousineau,1995, Cheve,1978). The Marble Mountain rocks have not been dated but appear similar to the Siluro-Devonain EIIC (based on SiGeom geochemical analyses).

Of similar age (419 ± 1Ma – Rankin et al., 2007)) is the Comerford Intrusive Suite Complex, located along the eastern flank of the Connecticut Valley-Gaspe Trough and within the Bronson Hill arch ~ 80 miles to the south which has a well-developed sheeted dike zone as well as mafic pegmatites.

title: Origin of Devonian-Mississippian Critical Mineral-Enriched Metalliferous Black Shales in the U.S. Midcontinent: Intersection of Acadian Far-Field Tectonics and Global Biogeochemical Events
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: McLaughlin, Patrick I. [1], Paton, Timothy [2], Zambito, James Joseph [3], Day, James E. [4], Malone, David H. [5], Emsbo, Poul [6]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State Geological Survey, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL, USA
(2) Illinois State Geological Survey, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL, USA
(3) Department of Geology, Beloit College, Beloit, WI, USA
(4) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(5) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(6) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
The successful application of the marine chemocline mineral system model for identifying potential critical minerals resources in the U.S. midcontinent is highly dependent on the accuracy of regional basin reconstructions. Several competing models were previously proposed for genesis of Devonian-Mississippian metalliferous black shales in this region. However, few incorporate robust regional chronostratigraphic and paleogeographic constraints. New findings challenge traditional midcontinent paleogeographic reconstructions and pinpoint the timing of regional basin restructuring via far-field Acadian tectonism and the variable manifestation of global biogeochemical events in adjacent basins.

Devonian core and outcrop samples collected across the midcontinent (Iowa to Ohio, Oklahoma to Tennessee) were analyzed to map facies changes, unconformities, critical minerals anomalies, and sediment provenance. Sections were logged; whole-rock elemental profiles were generated using EDXRF, WDXRF, and ICP-MS; carbon isotope samples were analyzed from associated carbonates; weakly cemented shales and carbonates and were disaggregated and dissolved for conodont biostratigraphy; and zircon separates from sandstones were analyzed via LA-ICP-MS. The resulting chronocorrelation framework shows significant regional thickness changes reflecting truncation and onlap patterns that document areas of uplift and provide minimum displacement estimates. Detrital zircon results reinforce these finding through evidence for reworking older lower Paleozoic strata and unroofing of crystalline basement.

The midcontinent basin was tectonically partitioned during the later Givetian Age into northern and southern components, adjacent to the Acadian foreland basin. Facies analysis reveals the asynchronous timing of black shale deposition across these basins. The newly partitioned northern midcontinent basin (IA, IL, WI, MI) hosted initial carbonate-evaporite deposition that abruptly shifted into long-lived black shale deposition with the upper Kellwasser Event. Black shale deposition persisted through much of the Famennian Stage and ended with onset of the Hangenberg Event. By contrast, the southern midcontinent basin (IL, IN, KY, TN) initiated with black shales deposited on karst remnants of Devonian carbonate platform strata. Black shale deposition was interrupted by widespread phosphorite deposition associated with the Kellwasser Event(s) and critical mineral-enriched metalliferous black shales proliferated during the Hangenberg Event. These findings emphasize the ability of regional basin conditions to modulate global biogeochemical events and provide important considerations in the application of marine chemocline mineral systems models.

title: Partial Edifice Collapse and a Major Explosive Eruption at Volcán Ticsani, Southern Peru: Stratigraphic and Geochronologic Constraints
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Gillen, Abby Marie [1], de Silva, Shanaka L. [2], Danisik, Martin [3], Ramos, Frank C. [4]
affiliations: (1) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(2) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(3) Curtin University, Bentley, WA, Australia
(4) New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM, USA
abstract: Volcán Ticsani (16°45′S, 70°36′W) is an active Central Andean volcanic complex that is designated as high-risk by the Instituto Geofísico del Perú. Ticsani’s history is defined by two primary phases of activity comprising an older andesitic composite volcano and a younger dacitic dome complex. Associated with the dome complex is a major (VEI 4–5) eruption of suspected late Pleistocene to Holocene age. Stratigraphic relations raise the possibility that partial edifice collapse triggered the explosive eruption and subsequent extrusion of the youngest dome. However, existing radiometric ages do not adequately resolve Ticsani’s most recent eruptive activity. Here we refine the eruptive chronology of Ticsani using zircon double-dating (ZDD: combined 238 U- 230 Th disequilibrium and (U-Th)/He dating approach), together with 14 C dating. These geochronological data are integrated with petrologic constraints to test the hypothesis that the major explosive eruption and emplacement of the youngest dome were part of a single eruptive sequence. New ZDD eruption ages of 11.6 ± 1.1 ka and 10.1 ± 2.2 ka for the tephra and dome, respectively, overlap within uncertainty (2σ errors for all reported ages). The tephra and youngest dome also share a mineral assemblage of plagioclase+amphibole+biotite, notably lacking quartz and titanite which are found in older dome lavas. Three new 14 C ages were determined from a peat sequence underlying ~1.5 m of tephra from the explosive eruption, approximately 12.5 km southeast of Ticsani. Cyperaceae seeds and leaves collected at the contact yield 14 C ages of 12,350 ± 70 BP and 12,400 ± 75 BP, respectively. Leaves sampled approximately 24 cm below the contact yield an age of 12,700 ± 75 BP, confirming a stratigraphically consistent chronology. Although additional fieldwork is needed to further test the link between partial edifice collapse and the major eruption sequence, our radiometric ages reveal the tephra and dome to be coeval, a relationship not previously recognized. Additionally, the age for the dome that we report here is significantly older than the previously inferred age of <400 years. A well-resolved eruption chronology for Ticsani is crucial for understanding post-collapse eruptive behavior and for informing volcanic hazard assessments in Peru.

title: Ground Penetrating Radar Comparison of Late Pleistocene Rodent Burrows and Modern Burrow Systems of Prairie Dogs
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Smart, Sierra [1], Keim, Elizabeth [2], Sherrod, Laura [3], Simpson, Edward [4], Lucas, Spencer [5], Fiorillo, Anthony [6]
affiliations: (1) Kutztown University, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Kutztown University, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) Kutztown University, Department of Physical Sciences, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
(4) Kutztown University, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
(5) New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(6) New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
Prairie dogs, genus Cynomys , inhabit a large portion of the western central United States and have been extant for approximately 2 million years, first appearing in the late Pliocene. These burrowing ground squirrels are known for their complex social structures, sophisticated methods of communications, and keystone position in the ecosystem. This work presents a comparison of the ground penetrating radar (GPR) results of surveys of three modern burrow systems of Cynomys gunnisoni near Taos, New Mexico and a Late Pleistocene rodent burrow system west of Bernalillo, New Mexico in the Ojito Wilderness within the Jurassic Todilto Formation.

The modern burrow systems are in two zones of distinct geology. Alluvial fan deposits comprise the first zone within the town of Taos, while the second zone is east of Taos at Valle Escondido Golf Course, with one burrow system adjacent to a fairway and another directly beneath a fairway. Each of these modern burrow systems are active, with prairie dogs visibly maintaining the entrances. The Pleistocene burrow system is in Todilto Formation gypsum with burrows infilled by fine-grained siliciclastic sediments of Pleistocene age. The current surface exposure clearly shows one level of burrows radiating in multiple directions, with evidence of mammoth tracks crosscutting the burrows.

GPR results from both the modern and the ancient burrow systems show complex networks, with tunnels in multiple directions and inclines. While the geophysical results with the alluvial fan deposits are very noisy due to the poorly sorted clastic sediments and several anthropogenic disturbances, the sediments at the golf course are much more conducive to GPR surveying, producing a greater signal to noise ratio. Burrow entrances are clearly imaged with the upper level of the burrow system distinctly shown in the modern systems. Results show inclined and branching tunnels, multiple connections between entrances, and possible chambers. Deeper levels are challenging to identify in the GPR data from the modern burrow systems, with only faint traces visible. The ancient burrow system shows at least one level of burrows below the surface expression of the burrow system.

Although limited by the depth of penetration of the equipment used, results demonstrate similarities shared by both ancient Pleistocene age rodent systems and modern prairie dog burrows, suggesting complex social behavior of the Pleistocene burrow makers.

title: An EPMA Study of Garnet-Bearing Pelites and Psammites from the Altnaharra Psammite, Port Vasgo, Northern Sutherland, Scotland
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Wood, Johanna [1]
affiliations: (1) School of the Earth, Ocean, and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA; Department of Geology, Cedarville University, Cedarville, OH, USA
abstract:
Garnet zoning can act as a chemical archive of changes in temperature, fluid composition, protolith makeup, and pressure conditions during mineral growth. While previous research has captured garnet zoning patterns across Scotland’s Northern Highland Terrane, limited electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) data exists for garnets hosted at Northern Sutherland’s Port Vasgo locality. To address this gap, we sampled loose pelite and psammite from three outcrops of the Altnaharra Psammite. After the rocks were prepared as standard polished thin sections, we used a JEOL JXA-8530FPlus EPMA to generate WDS elemental maps and core-rim transects for thirteen mm- to cm-scale garnets. Targeted elements included Fe, Mg, Mn, Ca, Cr, Ti, Sr, and Y. Finally, MinPlotX was used to convert raw oxide data into end-member mole fractions.

Initial study revealed size-dependent zoning and growth patterns. Large garnets displayed distinct core-rim structures with noticeable diffusion of Mn, Mg, and Ca. Medium garnets preserved abundant oscillatory Ca zoning and localized Cr zoning. Small garnets, primarily hosted in nutrient-limited psammitic lithologies, were often severely retrogressed and displayed significant cation diffusion with an occasional sharp Mn ring near the edge. These small garnets hosted 10–20% higher grossular content than larger pelitic variants, though almandine dominated all samples. Special patterns included a “snowball” garnet and a garnet hosting a jagged core that resembled a lightning bolt in shape. These textures provide evidence for Ca’s low diffusion rate and Port Vasgo’s extreme deformation, while highlighting the potential influence of fluids and protolith heterogeneity on zoning. Future Lu-Hf geochronology is required to constrain the exact timing of these growth events and the likelihood of several distinct garnet populations.

title: From terrestrial systems to planetary bodies: Silician magnetite as a nanoscale record of fluid–rock interactions
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials (Posters)
authors: Campo Rodriguez, Yuri Tatiana [1], Ciobanu, Cristiana L [2], Cook, Nigel J [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(2) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(3) School of Chemical Engineering, Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
abstract:
Magnetite is a common and highly refractory mineral that preserves evidence of formation and alteration conditions that may otherwise be overprinted or obliterated in complex geological systems. Silician magnetite is especially valuable in this regard, as it records mineral reactions and fluid-rock interaction in which silicon is incorporated into magnetite as lattice-bound Si, Si-rich defects, or nanoscale silicate inclusions.

Magnetite is also widespread in planetary materials, including Martian meteorites, lunar regolith, interplanetary dust particles, and returned asteroid samples. Magnetite inclusions in zircon from a Martian meteorite provide critical evidence for early hydrothermal activity on Mars, while returned samples from asteroid Ryugu contain a variety of magnetite textures, including framboidal, plaquette, and spherical, that are closely associated with phyllosilicates. Some spherulitic grains contain abundant Si-Mg-rich domains and pores with unresolved Fe-Si interactions during aqueous alteration. These occurrences indicate that extraterrestrial magnetite may retain mineral-scale records comparable to those already recognised in terrestrial hydrothermal systems. However, interpreting these records requires a process-based framework grounded in the detailed characterisation of comparable analogues.

Terrestrial studies provide this process-based foundation. In banded iron formations, skarns, and iron oxide-copper-gold systems, integrated micron- to atomic-scale investigations have shown that Si-rich defects in magnetite can act as nucleation sites for silicate minerals, while inclusions, replacement textures, and crystallographic relationships record successive stages of overprinting. Silician magnetite can therefore fingerprint multistage processes, including protolith inheritance, metasomatism, deformation, redox evolution, and silicate growth. In magmatic–hydrothermal systems, for example, the transition from inherited trellis textures to silicate-mottled domains with amphibole and non-classical pyribole inclusions in magnetite preserve distinct stages of fluid-rock interaction and overprinting.

Building on these results, we present a proof-of-concept for transfer of magnetite-characterisation approaches to planetary materials. This framework integrates micro- to atomic-scale mineral textures, inclusions, crystallographic relationships and chemistry to determine whether extraterrestrial magnetite preserves process signatures analogous to those recognised on Earth. Identifying comparable silician defects, nanoinclusions, and reaction textures could help distinguish primary mineral formation from later overprinting and constrain the roles of aqueous fluids, thermal evolution, and changing redox conditions in asteroid parent bodies and other primitive Solar System objects. More broadly, this approach establishes the potential of magnetite as a process-sensitive archive for fingerprinting aqueous alteration and geological evolution in planetary materials.
