title: Pore Architecture, Mineralogy, and CO2 Storage Potential of the Sembar Formation, Lower Indus Basin, Pakistan
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies
authors: Ahmed, Adeeb [1], Khan, Tahseenullah [2], Mustapha, Khairul Azlan [3], Jahandad, Samina [4], Khan, Muhammad Asif [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Bahria University, Islamabad, 44000, Pakistan
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Bahria University, Islamabad, 44000, Pakistan
(3) Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Universiti Malaya (UM), Kuala Lumpur, 50603, Malaysia
(4) Hydrocarbon Development Institute of Pakistan (HDIP), Islamabad, 44000, Pakistan
(5) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Bahria University, Islamabad, 44000, Pakistan
abstract: CO 2 storage in organic-rich shales requires favorable pore architecture, mineralogy, and organic matter chemistry to enable adsorption, structural trapping, and containment. Pakistan's Lower Indus Basin remains underexplored for CO 2 storage despite hosting extensive organic-rich shales. This study characterizes the pore architecture, mineralogy, and CO 2 storage potential of the Lower Cretaceous Sembar Formation through integrated organic geochemistry, core analysis, thin-section petrography, X-ray computed tomography (CT), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Prior organic geochemistry and basin modeling indicate total organic carbon (TOC) of 0.53-4.76 wt%, vitrinite reflectance of 1.16-1.64%, and kerogen transformation of 80-98%, conditions favorable for the development of organic matter-hosted nanopores. CT analysis reveals tight matrix porosity of 0.97-1.06% across an upper sealing interval, contrasted with a high-porosity zone of 5.09% in a lower, fractured, quartz-veined interval. The porosity contrast coincides with a threefold decrease in mean sulfur content, from 2.99 wt% in the upper zone to 1.01 wt% in the lower zone. SEM and petrographic analyses directly image organic matter-hosted nanopores (70-150 nm), interparticle pores in kaolinite booklets, intercrystalline pores within pyrite framboids, euhedral microquartz, and multi-scale microfracture networks providing CO 2 migration pathways. XRD identifies quartz and kaolinite as the dominant phases, with illite, montmorillonite, glauconite, pyrite, and magnetite as additional phases. FTIR confirms aromatic-rich, mature kerogen chemistry supporting CO 2 adsorption. Brittleness indices range from 0.55 in the storage interval to 0.82 in other sampled intervals, all within the mechanically favorable range. Fractured, quartz-rich, less-pyritic intervals are identified as primary CO 2 storage targets, with the overlying pyrite-rich shale providing a potential intraformational seal. Hence, the Sembar Formation represents a significant CO 2 storage prospect within an unconventional shale reservoir in Pakistan. This study presents a replicable, integrated, multi-scale screening framework for organic-rich shales that can be applied regionally. To advance this prospect toward a quantified storage assessment, future work should prioritize direct CO 2 sorption isotherms, capillary sealing measurements, geomechanical characterization, and clay-CO 2 interaction studies to rigorously constrain storage capacity and containment security.

title: Minerals, Mountains, and Metals: An Orogenic Journey from Himalayan Tectonics to Copper Deposits in the Andes and Tibet
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Cooper, Frances J [1], Adams, Byron A [2], Yang, Chao [3], Wang, Tingting [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University College London, London, United Kingdom
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University College London, London, United Kingdom
(3) College of Earth Sciences, Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu, China
(4) College of Earth Sciences, Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu, China
abstract:
The history of a mountain belt is preserved in features spanning individual minerals, regional structures, and entire landscapes. Minerals record heating, deformation, and cooling, while faults, folds, rock fabrics, and landscapes reveal how orogens are constructed and eroded. A defining strength of Kip Hodges’ research has been to connect records of pressure, temperature, deformation, and time to disentangle the evolution of complex orogenic systems. This way of thinking shaped my work with Kip in Bhutan, where we combined field geology, petrology, geochronology, and remote sensing to investigate extension in the eastern Himalaya. When my research shifted from Himalayan tectonics to porphyry copper deposits in the Central Andes, the focus changed but the underlying approach did not.

Porphyry copper deposits are magmatic-hydrothermal systems formed above subduction zones when metal-bearing fluids are released from shallow magmas. Explaining why they form, become enriched, and survive requires a systems-level approach that treats individual deposits as integral parts of evolving orogens. Tectonics influences magmatism and exhumation, while climate and erosion shape groundwater circulation and near-surface enrichment. Together, these processes help determine copper grade and whether an orebody is preserved or eroded away.

Research in northern Chile shows that exhumation rate and timing are critical to porphyry copper formation. Rapid early exhumation advects heat toward the surface, helping magmas and fluids reach the shallow crust, while later slowing permits groundwater-driven copper enrichment. Thermokinematic models incorporating magmatic heating, constrained by emplacement depths and cooling histories, show ore formation coinciding with the fastest exhumation before slowing prior to exposure. Constraining how exhumation varies through time and along an orogenic belt may help identify where conditions favored high-grade, well-preserved copper deposits.

This approach is now being extended along the western segment of the Bangong–Nujiang suture in Tibet, where Early Cretaceous northward subduction was accompanied by widespread magmatism, including the ore-forming intrusions of the supergiant Duolong porphyry copper–gold district. We are integrating preliminary apatite (U–Th)/He ages with crystallization ages and emplacement depths from intrusions sampled across the belt. Duolong preserves copper mineralization, weathering, volcanic burial, and renewed erosion, allowing tests of how exhumation influenced ore formation, enrichment, exposure, and preservation. This work brings us back to the Himalayan–Tibetan orogen where my collaboration with Kip began, but now asking how mountain building shapes mineral resources.

title: Mineralogical Evolution of Disordered Dolomite and Trace Metal Incorporation in the Presence of Arsenic, Cobalt, and Manganese.
session_title: Early career investigators in mineralogy and crystallography
authors: Hill, Cheyenne Rose [1], Xu, Tingying [2]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State Univ, Stillwater, OK,
(2) Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,
abstract: Understanding how trace metals interact with disordered dolomite is essential for determining the controls of carbonate mineral transformation, metal sequestration, and geochemical evolution in natural systems. Dolomite is a carbonate mineral composed of calcium, magnesium, carbon, and oxygen, with the chemical formula CaMg(CO₃)₂. It can exist in two cation ordering states within its crystal lattice: ordered and disordered. In disordered dolomite, calcium and magnesium atoms are distributed more randomly throughout the crystal structure. This less ordered structure makes the mineral more chemically reactive, less stable, and better able to incorporate or trap trace metals such as arsenic (As), cobalt (Co), and manganese (Mn). This study investigates how the crystal structure and mineralogy of disordered dolomite are affected by the incorporation of As, Co, and Mn. To evaluate these effects, disordered dolomite will be synthesized in the presence of 1, 2, 5, and 10 mM of arsenate chloride, cobalt chloride, and manganese chloride, respectively. The synthesized samples will be analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) following acid digestion. These analytical techniques will be used to determine how the crystal structure and morphology of dolomite change in the presence of these metals. Preliminary ICP-OES results of acid-digested samples, together with XRD results, indicate that samples synthesized with 10 mM Mn can form kutnohorite through extensive substitution of Mn into the dolomite crystal lattice. SEM analyses are still underway to characterize the mineral morphology of these samples. In addition, disordered dolomite containing As and Co has yet to be synthesized and analyzed using ICP-OES, SEM, and XRD. This study illuminates the mechanisms of Mn, As, and Co incorporation into disordered dolomite and their influence on carbonate mineral chemistry and phase evolution. These findings enhance our understanding of trace metal sequestration, mobility, and mineral transformation, providing new insights into the geochemical evolution of carbonate-rich systems

title: New Arrivals in the TennesSEA: The Clarksville Phase of the Richmondian Invasion in the Nashville Dome
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Forsythe, Ian James [1], Brett, Carlton E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
abstract: The Late Ordovician (Katian, Richmondian) “Richmondian Invasion” is among the best studied biotic immigration events in the Phanerozoic fossil record. However, due to the temporal limitations of the stratigraphic framework, the vast majority of this work has treated the invasion as a single event, despite long standing recognition that it was comprised of multiple discrete pulses of faunal influx. The first and largest pulse of the "Richmondian Invasion", known as the Clarksville Phase, introduced a suite of novel, mainly warmer water, taxa into the shallow epicontinental seas, which covered eastern Laurentia. Study of this individual pulse of the Richmondian Invasion has progressed as the stratigraphic framework for this region has been refined and various ecological impacts have been documented. These studies have documented changes in ecospace utilization, paleocommunity composition, and biodiversity. However, work on the Clarksville Phase has thus far been restricted to the Jessamine Dome of Ohio, Kentucky, and Indiana despite recognition that it impacted the Nashville Dome of central Tennessee as well. We analyzed the Clarksville Phase in the Nashville Dome from a synecological perspective, revealing both similarities with, and differences from the better studied ecological impacts documented in Jessamine Dome to the north. We employed a suite of methods including Breakaway, Rarefaction, and Simpson's Index of Diversity to assess changes in biodiversity and Q and R mode cluster analysis paired with detrended correspondence analysis to assess changes in paleocommunity composition. Finally, we conducted a guild analysis to assess changes in ecospace utilization. Preliminary results suggest that similar to the Jessamine Dome, richness increased, evenness decreased, novel invader dominated paleocommunities formed, and there was an increase in the dominance of the low-tier unattached epifaunal passive suspension feeding guild. Despite these similarities, notable differences from the Jessamine Dome were also documented including the persistence of the incumbent Orthid Vinlandostrophia ponderosa into the invasion interval, and the presence of the invading Rhynchonellid Rhynchotrema dentata and the Orthid Retrosirostra carleyi in the post-Clarksville assemblage. Aside from these differences, the taxonomic compositions of the Nashville Dome incumbent and invader assemblages are very similar to those observed in the Jessamine Dome.

title: Digital elevation models of stellate monticules on the Ordovician cystoporate bryozoan Constellaria florida and implications for extrazooidal feeding currents
session_title: PALEONTOLOGY, BRYOZOANS, DINOSAURS, REEFS, STRATIGRAPHY, AND MILITARY GEOLOGY: IN HONOR OF ROGER CUFFEY AND HIS ECCLECTIC CAREER
authors: Key, Marcus M. [1], Wyse Jackson, Patrick N. [2], Edwards, Benjamin R. [3], Håkansson, Eckart [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Dickinson College, Carlisle, PA, USA
(2) Geology, Trinity College, Dublin, Ireland
(3) Geosciences, Dickinson College, Carlisle, PA, USA

abstract: Excurrent chimneys centered on monticules are a common tools for bryozoans to improve extrazooidal feeding efficiency. We used the iconic stellate monticules of the Ordovician cystoporate bryozoan Constellaria florida Ulrich, 1882 to quantify the effect of monticule topography on extrazooidal feeding currents. Colonies came from the Kope and Fairview Formations in the Cincinnati, OH tristate area. Stratigraphically these colonies were deposited 451–450 Ma in the Upper Ordovician series (Katian global stage, Cincinnatian regional series, Edenian-Maysvillian regional stages). Paleogeographically, they were deposited in the Cincinnati Basin at ~22ºS paleolatitude. Topography was quantified using the Structure-from-Motion method to build digital elevation models of monticules. Topographic maps and profiles were made with QGIS. Fascicle crests were spaced on average 0.82 mm apart and elevated 0.33 mm above the adjacent cystopore-covered valleys. Topographic profiles were made along the axis of a valley between adjacent fascicles, up across the monticule’s central excurrent chimney, and down the opposing side of the monticule’s valley. The topographic profiles ranged in length from 2.44 mm to 3.14 mm. The centers of the monticular excurrent chimneys were on average 0.64 mm above the surrounding non-fascicle colony surface. The area of the monticular subcolonies was dominated 10:1 by feeding autozooids compared to non-feeding cystopores. This should roughly correlate with the ratio of excurrent chimney velocity in the center of the monticules to the incurrent velocities generated by the autozooids. The elevated fascicles create a distinctive asterisk-shaped monticule with a central excurrent chimney. Such stellate monticules are indicative of centripetal fluid flow found in other biotic and abiotic systems.

title: Isotopes and statistics for pollution source tracing: Tips for forward-thinking research
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Dietrich, Matthew [1]
affiliations: (1) MineraLogic LLC, Cincinnati, OH, USA
abstract: Tracing pollutant sources in the environment has regulatory relevance, human and ecological health relevance, and importance in the broader realm of understanding contaminant fate and transport across different environmental domains. Over the years, advancements in analytical instrumentation and computer programming have enabled increasingly sophisticated geochemical and statistical techniques for differentiating pollution sources in the environment. However, these advanced applications are not always properly utilized for pollutant source tracing, nor fully taken advantage of to their full capabilities. Case studies showcasing the utility of metal stable isotope data used in conjunction with Bayesian statistics to differentiate sources and quantity relative contributions of these sources will be provided. Examples will include examination of lake sediment cores, road sediment, house dust, soils, lichens, human blood, and groundwater samples to differentiate between pollution sources such as leaded gasoline, lead paint, coal combustion residuals, and steel plant particulate matter through statistics and isotopes of lead, boron, and/or strontium. Advantages and disadvantages of these techniques will be presented, with an eye towards advancing the field of environmental geochemistry and environmental health to appropriately utilize Bayesian statistical techniques, stable isotope systems, and supplemental analytical techniques such as microscopy. The ultimate goal is to provide a helpful roadmap for researchers and practitioners to better utilize and understand the utility of geochemistry and statistics to address important questions on contaminant sourcing. This in turn can help improve the efficiency of pollution remediation and source reduction to help better protect human health and the environment.

abstract:
Brownfields represent one of Europe’s greatest challenges for sustainable land management. Thousands of contaminated and degraded sites hinder urban regeneration, reduce ecosystem services, and pose risks to environmental and human health. Despite decades of remediation efforts, inconsistent monitoring methods and fragmented datasets continue to limit evidence-based decision-making and large-scale soil restoration.

The Horizon Europe Soil Mission project REGENSOILL addresses these challenges through an integrated Living Lab (LL) approach that combines scientific research, stakeholder co-creation, and policy-oriented innovation. The project establishes five interconnected LLs across Europe: Birmingham (United Kingdom), Budapest (Hungary), the Silesian Metropolis (Poland), the European Metropolis of Lille (France), and the Baltic cluster (Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia). Together, these encompass approximately 75 experimental brownfield sites representing diverse environmental, climatic, and governance conditions. The Baltic LL includes 20 urban, industrial, and former military brownfield sites across the three Baltic States.

REGENSOILL combines harmonized soil health monitoring with stakeholder engagement to ensure restoration strategies support future land-use needs and transform degraded sites into socially and ecologically valuable landscapes. Standardized monitoring protocols, aligned with the forthcoming EU Soil Monitoring and Resilience framework, assess inorganic and organic contaminants, soil physicochemical properties, biodiversity, microbial communities using environmental DNA, vegetation, and plant health. Nature-based remediation measures, including phytoremediation, microbial enhancement, biochar, compost amendments, and tailored vegetation systems, they are implemented through a common remediation toolkit while allowing site-specific adaptation. FAIR data principles, Before–After–Control–Impact (BACI) monitoring, digital twins, and decision-support tools provide transparent, interoperable, and policy-ready evidence for planners, landowners, and public authorities. Citizen science and soil literacy activities further engage local communities in monitoring selected soil parameters, increasing public awareness, social acceptance, and long-term stewardship.

Beyond technical innovation, REGENSOILL brings together researchers, public authorities, landowners, industry, and citizens within a structured Living Lab framework that supports policy implementation and investment decisions. High-performing demonstration sites will serve as transferable "lighthouse" examples for sustainable brownfield regeneration. By integrating standardized monitoring, ecological restoration, digital innovation, and stakeholder collaboration, REGENSOILL aims to transform contaminated brownfields into resilient, soil-safe assets while contributing to the objectives of the EU Soil Mission and providing a scalable model for urban soil restoration. The research was supported by the Horizon Europe Soil Mission project REGENSOILL, Geo IT Ltd., and TEN4.

title: Sourcing and Monitoring of Heavy Metals using Nontraditional Isotopes in the Hyperaccumulator Brassica juncea
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Gibbs, Barrett Paul [1], Rader, Shelby True [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
abstract:
Given rising national and global demands for metals, developing cost-effective methods for identifying new deposits and passively monitoring metal mobility throughout the natural environment are of high priority for societal advancement. Some metal isotope systems have shown great promise in helping to identify the provenance of either valuable metal resources or environmental contaminants, even within plant biomass. Thallium (Tl), which is a highly toxic heavy metal and an emerging environmental pollutant, is one such element that has been shown to accumulate or even hyperaccumulate in a number of plant species, including Brassica juncea ( B. juncea – brown mustard). Thallium in B. juncea has shown evidence of reflecting inherited geogenic signatures from the underlying soil, providing a non-invasive means of understanding metal provenance and changes in sourcing or availability over time. However, to ensure that geogenic signatures within biomass can serve as a tool for differentiating background soil metals from anthropogenic metals arising from industrial processes such as smelting and coal combustion, consistent and persistent reproducibility of original metal signatures within plant material must be established.

To determine how well distinct soil-based Tl isotopic compositions and variable metal concentrations are reflected in plant signatures, four greenhouse trials of B. juncea grown in distinct Tl-bearing soils along with a control were grown in triplicate in the IU Botany Greenhouse. For each trial, the soil was spiked with either USGS Nod-P-1 or USGS Nod-A-1 at 2 mg/kg Tl or 10 mg/kg Tl. Plants were harvested and separated into individual parts (i.e., roots, stem, leaves, etc.), dried, ground, and digested in preparation for metal concentration and Tl isotopic analysis via Q-ICPMS and MC-ICPMS. As expected, higher soil metal concentrations resulted in higher plant metal concentrations and, regardless of soil composition, metal distribution trends within tissues were consistent: the majority of Tl (and several other metals) was sequestered within the leaves, accounting for ~35-45% of all plant-based Tl. This translocation of Tl and other metals can be both beneficial, for phytoremediation, or detrimental, as B. juncea leaves are commonly consumed globally. Ongoing Tl isotopic analysis aims to further refine the applicability of Tl biogeochemical signatures as a tool to assess and monitor metal remediation and fingerprint Tl sources.

title: Bedrock Fluorapatite Dissolution Rates and Phosphorus Fluxes from the Granitic Periglacial Headwater Loch Vale Watershed, Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado, USA in a Warming Climate
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers
authors: Price, Jason R. [1], Bricker, Suzanne [2], Andelt, Emerson [3]
affiliations: (1) Physical Sciences and Mathematics, Wayne State College, Wayne, NE, USA
(2) National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Retired), National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science, Cooperative Oxford Laboratory, Oxford, Maryland, USA

abstract: The global phosphorus and carbon cycles are intimately linked through marine photosynthetic productivity with bedrock chemical weathering being the sole source of phosphorus to natural waters and ecosystems. Solute-based watershed mass-balance modeling is one of the most accurate means for quantifying mineral weathering rates and elemental transfers, including phosphorus, at the Earth’s surface. Such methods have been utilized for the 1984-2008 measurement period to calculate the fluorapatite dissolution rate, and associated phosphorus flux, for the 680 ± 2 hectare granitic headwater periglacial experimental Loch Vale watershed (LVW) in Colorado, USA. Because phosphorus primarily leaves the LVW adsorbed to sediment, the fluorapatite dissolution rate was determined from the calcium, bicarbonate, and fluoride stream fluxes. Two standard deviation uncertainty on all hydrogeochemical kinetic calculations were determined using bootstrapping statistical methods. It was impossible to achieve a watershed mass-balance after 2008, likely a result of escalating loss of the permanent cryosphere disrupting the watershed-scale geochemical weathering stoichiometry. Despite the LVW bulk bedrock containing only ~0.07 weight % P 2 O 5 and ~0.1 % modal primary fluorapatite, the 1984-2008 fluorapatite dissolution rate for the LVW was 16 ± 1 mol ha -1 yr -1 with an associated phosphorus flux of 48 ± 2 mol ha -1 yr -1 . This area-normalized watershed-scale phosphorus flux for the LVW is almost double that of any other location reported in the literature to date. However, because fluorapatite dissolution in the LVW is controlled by winter frost-cracking, climatic warming will likely reduce future phosphorus fluxes which may adversely impact downstream natural terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, agriculture, and aquaculture.

title: Towards More Rigorous and Transparent Interpretation of Thermochronologic Data
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data
authors: Murray, Kendra E. [1], Abbey, Alyssa L. [2], Stevens Goddard, Andrea Lynn [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(2) Earth Science, California State University Long Beach, Long Beach, CA, USA
(3) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract: The geochronology community is successfullying investing in making data production, reduction, and sharing more accessible and interoperable. However, for thermochronologic data, ages are rarely the end product. Instead, they are commonly inputs to numerical thermal history (time-temperature, tT) models that transform cooling ages into dates and rates. If we improve access to data generation and sharing without also supporting rigorous, transparent data interpretation, we will have addressed only half of the data life-cycle. The distinctive power of thermochronometers to fill gaps in geologic knowledge lies in their time-integrated sensitivity to a rock's temperature history. However, this same sensitivity means that cooling ages alone are non-unique. Thermal history models can resolve this non-uniqueness by combining chronometer kinetics with independent knowledge of a sample's geologic history to find histories that fit a dataset. Consequently, interpreting thermochronologic data requires making choices and assumptions that can have a profound impact on the knowledge thermochronology produces. Our community currently lacks general guidance on what makes a tT model result robust, and this gap can produce conflicting conclusions and distracting controversies. Here, we offer some suggestions. First, we argue that the fundamental feature of a robust model result, regardless of modeling software or statistical philosophy, is that the one can clearly articulate “The Why”: the specific reason(s) a particular history is required, i.e., a geologic constraint, an assumption of complexity, a kinetics choice, and/or a specific part of the dataset. We highlight two concrete practices for finding this "why": (1) building thermochronologic intuition by modeling synthetic data before interpreting real data, and (2) using sensitivity testing to develop a working relationship with your dataset. Board adoption of these and other practices could extend the community's growing emphasis on transparency and reproducibility to the interpretive side of thermochronology. More broadly, we call for the geochronology community to treat interpretation as integral to data infrastructure; we should invest in ongoing conversations about community standards and accessible modeling training alongside efforts in data production and sharing.

abstract: The Mingus Shale is a Pennsylvanian deposit on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin, exposed in Palo Pinto and Parker Counties, Texas. The Mingus is composed of gray shale with included sands, silts, paleosols, and occasional carbonaceous intervals. Two localities along the northern portion of the outcrop belt (MS180, MST) and two localities along the southern portion of the outcrop belt (MSPP, WMTN) have been investigated. Shales were collected at various intervals for analysis. Geochemical analysis was completed using spectral gamma ray (SGR), magnetic susceptibility (MS), portable x-ray fluorescence (pXRF), and total organic carbon (TOC). Petrological analysis includes grain-size and lithological descriptions. Paleontological collections from the shale include microfossils, palynomorphs, and fossil plants. The two northern sections (MS180, MST) can be effectively correlated using total gamma ray, magnetic susceptibility, and grain-size distribution signatures. Few, heavily-fragmented, plant fossils have been recovered from the northern localities. The two southern sections (MSPP, WMTN) can be divided into discrete units with distinctive SGR-based elemental concentrations. The total gamma ray signature is not as useful for correlation in the southern sections as it is in the northern sections. The strongest correlation between the two southern sections is a distinctive, well-developed, purple sandy paleosol. At MSPP, the paleosol is overlain by one meter of dark gray shale with marine fossils (bivalves and gastropods). A similar interval has not been found at the WMTN site. Abundant plant fossils including lycopsids, Cordaites, Calamites, Sphenophyllum and several species of ferns were recovered from the southern localities. The northern sections are interpreted to be closer to deltaic input due to previous paleomapping, higher sand-size fractions in the shale, and fewer and more fragmented plant fossils. The southern localities are interpreted to be further from deltaic input and in a more swampy coastal setting, supported by increased mud concentrations, higher gamma ray response, and a more diverse and complete flora. Strong correlation is less clear between the northern and southern sections. Different depositional settings can account for the challenges in correlating existing geochemical data. Mingus outcrops in the northern portion of the study are limited to the upper portion of the Mingus Shale, while sections in the southern portion are more complete in nature.

abstract:
Understanding young volcanic terrains provide essential insights into the volcanic, magmatic, and thermal evolution of the planet. The youngest volcanic plains on Mars—such as in Elysium and Amazonis Planitia—show evidence of complex interactions with aqueous processes, including the formation of large outflow channels and rootless cones. Identifying near-surface ice is critical for reconstructing Mars’s water history, locating sites of potential astrobiological interest, and supporting future human exploration.

To date, the origin and relative timing of the material composing the plains is still debated. Current hypotheses include various sedimentary and volcanic processes with some of the youngest aqueously derived deposits and lava flows. Both Planitiae show indications of past groundwater or ground ice presence, e.g., a recent impactor exposed subsurface ice in Amazonis Planitia and lava-volatile interaction as evidenced by countless rootless cones.

Combining orbital and aerial observations is essential for characterizing these terrains because the respective instruments provide complementary constraints across a wide range of spatial scales and, for radar sounders, subsurface depths. The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) Shallow Radar (SHARAD) and Context Camera (CTX) observations of Elysium and Amazonis Planitia can delineate the regional extent and stratigraphic relationships of volcanic, sedimentary, and volatile-bearing materials, including water ice. These regional-scale constraints can then guide target selection for higher-resolution, localized investigations by future unoccupied aircraft systems (UAS).

Multiple projects are currently dedicated to developing concepts for aerial exploration in analog settings in the Icelandic Highland. The 2014–2015 Holuhraun eruption site and the Askja Volcano are especially well-suited, offering access to young volcanic materials that have interacted with water and ground ice.

Several recent efforts aim at maturing the technology of potential payloads for future UAS missions, including the Rover–Aerial Vehicle Exploration Network (RAVEN). Likewise, the Passive Autonomy, Navigation, Topography, and Habitability Exploration Radar (PANTHER) is a passive radar package to detect and map subsurface volatiles in young volcanic analog terrains. Rather than transmitting its own radar signal, PANTHER uses naturally occurring radio emissions from the Sun and Jupiter, reducing instrument mass, power consumption, and data requirements. While also validating the findings with an active GPR. Integrating radar sounders on mobile aerial platforms could enable localized detection of shallow subsurface structures and volatile-bearing deposits at spatial scales below the resolution of current orbital radar systems.

authors: Dossa, Sam [1], Ely, Lisa L. [2], Gazis, Carey [3], Squeochs, Danielle [4]

abstract: The Toppenish Fan Shallow Aquifer Recharge Project (TFSARP) is a managed aquifer recharge (MAR) project in central Washington State conducted by the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation. The project diverts excess flow from Toppenish Creek into existing unlined irrigation canals and paleochannels during winter and early spring. Water is used to recharge the alluvial fan aquifer before the start of the irrigation season. The TFSARP has shown success in raising local groundwater levels and supporting spring-fed streams that are important to riparian habitat and cultural values of the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation. The goal of this project is to quantify the hydrochemistry, stratigraphy, and hydrogeology of the Toppenish alluvial fan to assess the extent, location, and seasonality of recharge; mixing of surface water with groundwater; groundwater travel times and flow directions; and physical characteristics of the Toppenish Fan aquifers. The hydrochemistry and stratigraphy are used to assess the sources of water that contribute to groundwater wells and springs on the Toppenish Fan and what proportion of that water is from the Toppenish Fan Shallow Aquifer Recharge Project. Specifically, this project examines existing well logs, water-level readings, major ion analysis, and repeated oxygen and hydrogen stable isotope samples before, during, and after the recharge season. Results show a strong connection between recharge water and critical spring discharge. Isotopic differences in groundwater response are present depending on monitoring well depth, location, and time from the start of recharge events. This variability in response indicates potentially different groundwater flow paths. This is shown by wells that are geographically close but have different depths and isotopic signatures. This research can help inform the use of MAR during the non-irrigation months on other parts of the Toppenish Basin or other alluvial fans in the Yakima Basin. The project is being conducted in collaboration with the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation.

title: Paleoclimate in Exposed Layers of Pedestal Craters On Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars (Posters)
authors: Checketts, Brianne [1], Sori, Michael [2], Byrne, Shane [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric, and, Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana, USA

abstract:
Pedestal craters on Mars are impact craters surrounded by a plateau-like ejecta blanket which have tens of meters of topographic relief [1]. These features are thought to form when impact ejecta protects underlying material from subsequent erosion. Previous research has shown that these features are most likely icy due to characteristics like external layering, low dielectric constant [2], and sublimation pits along the margins [3]. Pedestal craters are significant because they could preserve evidence of past surface conditions and climate-driven processes, particularly in mid-latitude regions where ice-rich deposits are inferred to have been widespread during the Amazonian period [4, 2]. Here, we conduct preliminary analysis of HiRISE images of a pedestal crater in the southern hemisphere revealing 17 distinct, well-preserved layers exposed in the pedestal walls. These layers likely represent episodic deposition of icy material over different climates from Mars’ changing orbital conditions. We also performed preliminary SHARAD analysis near the external layers in the HiRISE images. We were able to identify multiple subsurface reflectors and there appears to be about 7 resolvable internal layers. Additionally, using SHARAD we found a dielectric constant of this pedestal to be approximately 5.3. This value would indicate that the pedestal is rich in water-ice and sediments. Our future work plans to examine more pedestal craters across Mars including performing HiRISE-scale topographic analysis to reveal what their external and internal layers reveal about the past climate.

title: Silica Scaling at the Coso Geothermal Field near Ridgecrest, California: Textural Characteristics of Banded Opal-AG Deposits and Implications for the Formation of Veins in Epithermal Precious Metal Deposits

authors: Terry, Lauren R [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Buck, Cliff [3], Kasprowicz, Filip [4]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Department of Geology & Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA

abstract:
The Coso geothermal power plant in California produces two-phase fluids from a reservoir with temperatures up to 340°C. Production fluids undergo a double-flash process to extract steam for power generation, progressively concentrating dissolved silica in the residual liquid and producing fluids highly supersaturated with respect to noncrystalline silica. Geochemical data demonstrate that silica remains supersaturated throughout the production and reinjection, indicating that silica deposition is controlled primarily by polymerization kinetics rather than thermodynamic equilibrium.

Silica scales recovered from reinjection well 56-16 consist of opal-AG microspheres arranged in crustiform bands with complex three-dimensional microstructures. Individual bands vary in porosity and the degree of microsphere fusion, preserving sedimentary textures produced by colloidal particle growth, aggregation, and deposition from highly supersaturated fluids. The resulting scales provide a rare opportunity to directly observe silica precipitation processes.

Comparison of these silica scales with crustiform quartz veins from low-sulfidation epithermal deposits reveals striking similarities in banding, depositional fabrics, and microtextures. These observations suggest that many epithermal veins originally formed through deposition of noncrystalline silica composed of microspheres before recrystallization to quartz during silica maturation. The results indicate that the kinetics of silica polymerization, aggregation, and deposition exert a fundamental control on vein development and may also influence the localization of bonanza-grade precious metal mineralization. By linking observations from an active geothermal system with fossil hydrothermal systems, this study provides new insights into silica deposition processes and the formation of precious metal-bearing epithermal veins.

abstract:
Decoding Mixed Tidal Cycles and Sedimentary Structure Dynamics in the Neoproterozoic Siliciclastic Aaron Formation, North Carolina, USA

A stratigraphic section of the Neoproterozoic (Ediacaran; 580-575 Ma) Aaron Formation, located along the South Fork Little River (North Carolina, USA) was studied. The rock succession displays sedimentary structure (microbial mats) alternating with background deposits. In the millimeter- to centimeter-scale stratigraphy, a tidal signal was detected. Petrographic analyses by light microscope and electron probe micro-analysis were conducted on thin sections. These derived from subsamples taken along an 8.75-cm transect crossing a rock sample taken from an outcrop. The analyses reveal alternating Si-rich and Fe-rich mm-cm-scale laminae that are relatable to a grayscale scan taken along the slab. A 4.4-cm-long section of the scan exhibits two co-occurring lamination frequencies interpreted as semidiurnal (M2) and diurnal (K1, O1) tidal constituents. Tuning the scan to the interpreted M2 constituent yields a 46-day-long depositional time series and reveals a weak ~14-day spring-neap modulation. Microbial-mat horizons align closely to neap-phase minima, indicating episodic neap-tide colonization. Comparison of the M2-tuned Aaron Formation grayscale time series with a modern mixed-tide record from Port Angeles, Washington (USA) shows close agreement between their power spectra, with evidence in both for M2, K1 and O1 tidal constituents. The M2-tuned Aaron grayscale time series frequencies are K1=0.996 cycles/day and O1 =0.9109 cycles/day, compared to the modern Port Angeles values of K1=1.002 cycles/day and O1 = 0.93102 cycles/day. The M2:K1 ratio of 1.95:1 of the Ediacaran Aaron record is close to the 1.93:1 ratio of the modern Port Angeles record. The frequency difference K1-O1 yields the fortnightly cycle frequency; the Port Angeles record indicates the expected K1-O1=1/(14.088 days), but the Aaron Formation record indicates K1-O1=1/(11.75 days), suggesting that the M2-tuning procedure was imprecise, or that some of the tidal laminations are missing (i.e., not recorded or measured), or both. Despite this shortfall, the results provide strong evidence for the preservation of a mixed-tide regime in the Ediacaran Aaron Formation locality. Microbial stabilization of the deposits leads to the retention of a well-resolved tidalite.

Keywords: Tidal rhythmites, Sedimentary Structure, Stratigraphy, Semidiurnal-diurnal tides, Microbial mats, Spectral analysis, Siliciclastic tidal flats, Neoproterozoic.

title: Ascocerid Hydrostatics: Digitally Reconstructing Locomotion and Ecology of Cephalopods with Deciduous Shells
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Coppess, Caleb [1], Peterman, David Joseph [2]
affiliations: (1) Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Miami University, Oxford, OH,
abstract: Ascocerids are an extinct, enigmatic group of cephalopods that were ecologically successful in shallow seas of the Ordovician and Silurian periods. Ascocerids are unique among cephalopods because they periodically shed apical shell portions throughout their life cycles. No quantitative approaches have assessed swimming constraints such as orientation, maneuverability, or stability for ascocerids at any life stage. Currently, hydromechanical changes are only inferred by these drastic ontological events, which abruptly alter shell morphology. To address these knowledge gaps, three distinct computer reconstructions (representing adult, juvenile, and composite life stages) of ascocerids have been created based on morphometrics from available fossil remains. Modeling was completed using a combination of Blender, Netfabb, and Meshmixer. Morphometrics were calculated using Meshlab and converted to dimensionless index values for comparisons at multiple levels, ranging from individual ontogenetic stages, different morphogroups, and among the broader class. Results for the juvenile model with its whole shell intact yielded a high stability index of 0.29, roughly six times the value previously calculated for the chambered nautilus. The composite model with no shell shedding was extremely positively buoyant (weighing only 70% of the water it displaces). The juvenile model with its whole shell was also positively buoyant, to a lesser degree (80% weight difference). These results strongly support the deciduous nature of ascocerids’ shells. Both the juvenile and composite models resulted in an expected near vertical static orientation. The adult model yielded a stability index of 0.043, very similar to the stability of modern chambered nautilus. Additionally, adult ascocerids had a larger lever arm (~2.5x higher than nautilus when nondimensionalized), implying a distinct increase in maneuverability throughout the maturation process. Interestingly, the orientation of the adult model’s long axis is 53 degrees from vertical, significantly different from the hypothesized near-horizontal orientation. Although initially thought to have shared swimming positions with analogous cephalopods such as cuttlefish, adult ascocerid hydrostatics may tell a different story. With future modeling efforts, we will explore more detailed hydromechanical scenarios, involving: 1) shell shedding within the juvenile stage, 2) the degree to which soft body retraction influences static posture, and 3) the relationships between hydrostatics and active locomotion.

title: Did Convergently Similar Trilobites Evolve in Similar Paleohabitats?: The Paleoecological and Paleobiogeographic Affinities of Harpetida and Trinucleioidea
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Beech, James D. [1], Bottjer, David J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Anthem Preparatory Academy, Great Hearts Academies, Glendale, AZ, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract: During the Ordovician, trilobites of the order Harpetida and the superfamily Trinucleioidea independently evolved an unusual morphology with reduced eyes, marginal facial sutures, and—in the most derived taxa—a broad, flattened and pitted cephalic brim, quite unlike any structure known in modern arthropods. Why this ‘harpiform’ morphology should have evolved twice in two distantly related groups of trilobites is currently unknown. One possibility is that these trilobites were living in similar habitats or responding to similar ecological pressures. This study seeks to test this hypothesis while also improving scientific understanding of harpiform trilobites by exploring their paleobiogeography and paleoecology. Stratigraphic age and locality data from the PBDB were combined and plotted using the PaleoData Plotter Program to reconstruct the paleobiogeographic distributions of harpiform trilobites through time, revealing widespread geographic overlap between harpetid and trinucleid trilobites during the Ordovician period. In addition, latitudinal and paleocontinental associations were tracked across a recent phylogenetic tree of harpiform trilobites. Finally, a three-dimensional habitat affinity space for harpiform trilobites was created by recording and plotting each genus’ bias towards three important paleohabitat variables: paleolatitude (low versus high-mid), water depth (shallow versus deep), and sedimentary lithology (carbonate versus siliciclastic). This approach revealed that although some harpetid and trinucleid trilobites do overlap in terms of their habitat affinities, trinucleids as a group appear to have been less restricted in terms of lithology, while harpetids appear to have been less restricted in terms of water depth. These findings may help to explain why the end-Ordovician mass extinction was more destructive for trinucleids than for harpetids, as previous studies have shown that the extinction event preferentially eliminated genera restricted to deeper waters.

title: Quantifying Groundwater Response and Uncertainty in Beaver-Influenced Mountainous Floodplains Using Machine Learning-Based Model Calibration
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Wang, Lijing [1], Babey, Tristan [2], Perzan, Zach [3], Pierce, Sam [4], Briggs, Martin [5], Boye, Kristin [6], Maher, Kate [7]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs Mansfield, CT, USA

abstract: Beavers alter river corridor hydrology by creating ponds and inundating floodplains, and thereby improving surface water storage. However, the impact of inundation on groundwater, particularly in mountainous alluvial floodplains with permeable gravel/cobble layers overlain by a soil layer, remains uncertain. Numerical modeling across various floodplain structures considers topographic and sediment complexity and multidirectional flow, linking inundation to groundwater response. This study develops a model-data integration workflow to address uncertainty in groundwater response to beaver-induced inundations in a mountainous alluvial floodplain in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Uncertain factors include seasonal hydrologic dynamics, hydraulic conductivities, floodplain structures, and meteorological forcings. We employed an ensemble of groundwater models, based on geophysical and hydrologic data, with machine learning-based calibration using a neural density estimator. This allowed us to quantify the vertical flux from the soil layer to the permeable gravel bed, the down-valley underflow within the gravel bed, and their ratios. Results show a significant increase in the vertical flux relative to down-valley underflow, from 2% during dry pond periods to 20% during wet periods, serving as an analogy for conditions without and with beaver ponds. The study highlights the influence of floodplain structure on groundwater storage, water balance, and water quality impacted by beaver ponds. A thick gravel bed layer, with a large down-valley underflow, minimizes the effect of beaver-induced inundation on water quality. We emphasize the need for field-scale measurements of floodplain structure and improved characterization of evapotranspiration changes to reduce uncertainty in groundwater response.

title: The Petrogenesis of Magnet Cove Alkaline Rocks: Constraints from Trace Element Concentrations and Radiogenic Isotope Data
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Bickham, David Arthur [1], Potra, Adriana [2], Samuelsen, John R. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(3) Arkansas Archeological Survey, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract:
The Magnet Cove Igneous Complex is a ~100 Ma old pluton that is a part of the wider Arkansas Alkaline Province. Magnet Cove has been described as a ring dike complex that is composed of various rare and exotic alkaline igneous rocks, including nepheline syenite, ijolite, jacupirangite, and carbonatite. These rocks, collectively known as alkaline igneous rocks, are characterized by their alkaline rich and silica poor compositions. They are rare types of igneous rocks, especially carbonatites which have only just over 600 known occurrences globally. This rarity is a result of highly specific processes required for the generation of an alkaline rich, silica poor magma that these rocks will crystallize from. These processes are currently understood to require low-degree partial melting of a carbonated mantle source, particularly for carbonatites. These processes also lead to enrichment of REEs within alkaline igneous rocks, shown to be true for Magnet Cove as well in previous studies.

Although Magnet Cove has drawn a lot of attention due to the uniqueness of its rocks, these very rocks result in the nature of its magmatic origin and evolution being subject to considerable debate. One of the earliest hypotheses suggested that the magma was generated by the Bermuda hotspot as the North American plate travelled over it. Others have rejected this and proposed other hypotheses such as decompression melting caused by the reactivation of the Mississippi graben or melting induced by deep subduction and fragmentation of the Farallon plate.

This study aims to evaluate these hypotheses and determine which one most accurately fits Magnet Cove characteristics. This will be achieved through a comprehensive geochemical and petrological characterization of the complex, including trace element concentrations, radiogenic isotope (Pb, Sr, Nd) ratios, and mineralogical analysis of various rocks within the complex. The rocks used in this study have been chosen based on a combination of accessibility and sufficient variety in order to properly represent the entirety of the complex. The current and previously published geochemical data will be plotted on various isotopic and REEs graphs along with geochemical characteristics of different magma reservoirs. While this study is still in progress, these graphical comparisons are a major part of determining the magmatic origin and evolution of Magnet Cove.

abstract: Mountainous headwater streams are sustained by both snowmelt-driven streamflow and groundwater discharge in the Upper Colorado River Basin. However, predicting headwater stream discharge magnitude and peak flow timing is challenging in mountainous terrains, where snowmelt rates vary with vegetation type and elevation, and heterogeneous subsurface physical properties influence groundwater storage and its release. We used a model-data integration approach to investigate the roles of snowmelt and subsurface structure in stream discharge and groundwater level. We ran an ensemble of 100 integrated surface-subsurface hydrologic models for a mountainous headwater catchment near Crested Butte, Colorado, USA. We also evaluated and calibrated these models against observed datasets, including snow depth measurements using distributed temperature probes, stream discharge, and groundwater level. Calibration with multiple data sources using neural density estimators has further constrained uncertainty in subsurface properties and snowmelt rates. Results indicated that observed slower snowmelt rates in evergreen forests delayed the peak flow and baseflow onset. In upstream areas with lower subsurface permeability, water was stored within the subsurface but was not released as interflow or shallow groundwater flow, and thereby not contributing to downstream streamflow during recession limb periods. Double peaks in groundwater occurred in areas with spatial subsurface heterogeneity, in our case due to the contrast between granodiorite and Mancos shale. These process-based insights into groundwater and snowmelt dynamics in mountainous headwaters will help improve predictions of headwater hydrology.

title: Notes from the Field (Anticosti Island, Quebéc): New Echinoderm Taxa and Occurrences Illuminate the Causes and Consequences of the Late Ordovician Mass Extinction
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Cole, Selina R. [1], Wright, David F. [2], Crowley, Kiera D. [3], Zazubec, Alysha [4], Hopkins, Melanie J. [5]
affiliations: (1) Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA; School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA

abstract:
The Late Ordovician mass extinction (LOME) was the first of the “big five” extinction events and the second most severe, resulting in the extinction of around 85% of marine species. Although most higher taxa survived the LOME, the event resulted in substantial faunal turnover, morphologic evolution, changes in relative abundance and dominance of clades, and restructuring of Silurian communities. However, the LOME coincided with glacially-induced eustatic sea level fall that resulted in a major unconformity in much of the global rock record, which has made it challenging to investigate the precise timing and nature of the extinction event and its impacts on invertebrate faunas.

Anticosti Island (Quebéc, Canada) preserves a fossiliferous, shallow-water rock record that spans the LOME and early Silurian recovery (Katian–Telychian) and has long been recognized as one of the premier localities worldwide for studying this critical interval. Renewed efforts to sample the strata of Anticosti Island across seven recent field seasons have produced extensive, new collections of fossil echinoderms that illuminate outstanding questions surrounding the LOME. These collections include numerous new crinoid species and genera as well new occurrences that extend known stratigraphic and/or biogeographic ranges during the LOME interval. At least six additional cyclocystoid, edrioasteroid, and asterozoan species have also been recovered that reflect new occurrences, some of which may also constitute undescribed species. Combined, these new field collections clarify how echinoderms responded to and recovered from the LOME and provide additional data that inform the timing of extinction and recovery, extinction selectivity, patterns of morphological evolution, and origins of lineages that radiated in the aftermath of the extinction.

title: SYSTEMATIC REVISION OF SPECIES CONCEPTS IN PLATYCYSTITINAE (PARACRINOIDEA: ECHINODERMATA): A MORPHOMETRIC AND COMPARATIVE APPROACH
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Higdon, Colby Ray [1], Cole, Selina R. [2]
affiliations: (1) Sam Noble Museum, Norman, OK, USA; School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(2) Sam Noble Museum, Norman, OK, ; School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
abstract:
Echinoderms are an extremely diverse phylum with a fossil record dating back to the Early Cambrian. Like most groups, echinoderms have long been the focus of taxonomic scrutiny, and taxonomic revisions are commonplace. Morphometric analyses combined with comparative approaches can inform these revisions, giving us a clearer picture of the true species/genus-level diversity in this group.

The Subfamily Platycystitinae (Class Paracrinoidea) has a long history of systematic revision at the species and genus levels, although some of these changes have been called into question due to lack of formal analysis and/or clear reasoning for revisions. Here, we reevaluate all species of Platycystitinae with particular focus on Platycystites fimbriatus, which was previously synonymized and is not currently recognized as a valid species, and Platycystites ovalis, which has a poorly defined species concept. Within this subfamily, we investigate traits that are diagnostic at the species level, reevaluate the validity of species and genus concepts, and provide justifications for previous taxonomic revisions that have not been explained in depth.

We measured 12 morphological characters and calculated an additional 3 traits across 108 specimens belonging to nine nominal species spanning three genera. These measurements were made from specimens located in museum collections. These taxa include Platycystites cristatus, P. levatus, P. faberi, P. ovalis, P. fimbriatus, P. sp. (Frest et al, 1979), Globulocystites infundus, G. rotundatus, and Arbucklecystis pyriformis. Measurements of morphological features include the number of thecal plates, the number of intercalated plates, thecal height, thecal width, thecal depth, periproct height, periproct width, length of right and left ridge (from mouth to facet), length of right and left ambulacral arm, and recumbent ambulacral width. Calculated traits include the number of total callus plates, the average callus plate width, and the average callus plate height. These traits were analyzed using multivariate statistical methods to capture morphological similarities and differences between taxa. We then examined the morphospace occupation of each taxon to inform systematic revisions in addition to comparative study of specimens. Preliminary results suggest that P. fimbriatus should be reinstated as a valid species and that Globulocystites and Platycystites constitute a single genus. However, additional data needs to be collected to inform the validity of P. ovalis.

title: Towards a mechanistic understanding of clay templating in fossilisation through modelling, experiments, and de novo protein design

abstract: Exceptionally preserved fossils preserve not only hard shells and skeletons, but decay-prone soft tissues and are a vital archive of ancient life on Earth. Notably, in the famous Cambrian Burgess Shale, fossil soft tissues are associated with the clay mineral kaolinite, which has also been documented in association with exceptionally preserved organic-walled microfossils from the Proterozoic. Experimental studies suggest clays, including kaolinite, may aid the preservation of soft tissues by: (i) promoting the polymerisation of such tissues, (ii) providing a physical barrier to oxidants, or (iii) being antibacterial. However, the precise mechanisms by which clays template organic material in the first place remains poorly understood. Through geochemical modelling and controlled precipitation experiments in shale pore-fluid analogue solutions, we show that the postmortem release of organic acids (dominantly lactic, acetic and formic acid) followed by release of ammonia creates a conducive chemistry for kaolinite precipitation. Lactic and acetic acid complex strongly with aluminium and raise Al³⁺ activity into the kaolinite supersaturation window at pH 5.0–5.5. However, only experiments with lactic acid yield detectable Al-silicate, possibly revealing a biochemical specificity to kaolinite formation and, thus, soft tissue preservation. We trial tailoring computational de novo protein design to the kaolinite crystal structure to reveal which proteins are most conducive to its formation. This new approach, combining geochemical modelling, experiments, and computational de novo protein design, provides a pathway to determine the role of biochemistry in mineral-organic interactions and ultimately soft tissue fossilisation, unveiling biological biases that may underpin the early fossil record.

title: Corridor of Cataclysm--Mapping the Perilous Geologic Journey of the Owyhee River, SE Oregon
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: House, Peter Kyle [1], O'Connor, Jim [2], Ely, Lisa [3], Safran, Elizabeth B. [4], Grant, Gordon E. [5]
affiliations: (1) Arizona Geological Survey, University of Arizona, FLAGSTAFF, AZ, USA; U.S. Geological Survey (Emeritus), Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Portland, OR, USA
(3) Central Washington University, USA
(4) Lewis & Clark College, Environmental Studies Program, MSC 55, Seattle, WA, USA
(5) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
abstract:
Over the last 2 My, the Owyhee River, aided by diverse geologic events, has carved a spectacular landscape into the high desert of SE Oregon. River-corridor-focused geologic mapping reveals a repeating ‘triad of catastrophe’: lava dams that fossilize valleys, regrade canyons, and fail incrementally in association with outburst floods; landslides that block channels, reorganize drainage, and generate dam-breach outburst floods; and pluvial lake barrier-breach outburst floods from remote source(s) that sweep through the corridor. Yet through each episode, the river reasserts itself and resumes incision until the next cataclysm. This catastrophic cycle is regenerative. A late Miocene, pre-river framework of volcanic and lacustrine deposits is susceptible to slope instability. As the river incises, it exposes additional unstable strata, while lava damming redirects channels into vulnerable slopes and reloads the canyon with basalt flows and lacustrine deposits. In this way, lava damming reconstitutes the failure-prone stratigraphy.

When lava enters the corridor, momentum drives lobes upstream, where explosive contact with the river builds a prograding delta composed of a weak assemblage of subaerial lava, pillow lava, and hyaloclastite. As the dam and lake grow, the canyon downstream becomes a conduit for lava that repaves and regrades the dry channel with tens of meters of basalt in the form of a steeply sloping wedge. The battle upstream produces the dam’s internal vulnerability; the downstream flows produce its mass. Together they construct a blockage that self-destructs. Water fills reservoirs faster than sediment. The first phase of dam degradation is hydraulic. The dam consumes itself via plucking and transporting coarse monolithologic gravel we term cannibal gravels. Lowering of the crest accelerates delta advance. Once the delta reaches the declining outlet, its sediment load accelerates incision, while the poorly consolidated lava-delta margins serve as landslide food, rebuilding slope instability along the canyon walls. The river then resumes incision into an even narrower canyon where the triad looms.

Drawing on two decades of field mapping, this presentation traces and maps the Owyhee’s course through repeated impoundment, catastrophic release, and drainage reconstruction. Moreover, this remarkable record reveals how rivers persist and landscapes evolve in the face of multiple origins of channel blockage and outburst flooding.

title: Mountain Streams, Glaciers, and Wetlands: A Multi-Proxy, Mandelian Story of Late-Quaternary Geomorphology and Environmental Change in the San Juans of Colorado, USA
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Beeton, Jared Maxwell [1]
affiliations: (1) Environment & Sustainability, Fort Lewis College, Durango, CO, USA
abstract: Geomorphology and soils research in the San Juan Mountains and adjacent high-elevation San Luis Valley of Southern Colorado has been ongoing for over a decade and reflects the wide-ranging influence of Dr. Rolfe Mandel. We use multi-proxy evidence collected from wetlands, forests, alpine areas, river systems, and soils to unravel how landscapes and environments have changed from the late Pleistocene through modern times. The geomorphology and sedimentology of three wetlands (Mitchell Lakes) and their moraines shed light on glacial fluctuations in the Animas River Valley of the San Juan Mountains. A radiocarbon- and optically stimulated luminescence-controlled study of two paleo wetlands in the Monte Vista National Wildlife Refuge shows pollen species and groundwater levels fluctuating between cooler, wetter environments and warmer, drier conditions through the late Quaternary with a modern warm and dry signal; these peat and alluvial fan deposits also house Pleistocene megafaunal remains. Temporally controlled data from upper Rio Grande moraines, kames, glacial outwash deposits, and fluvial terrace sediments also suggest a cooler and wetter Younger Dryas and a fluctuating Holocene climate with mountain river systems entrenched in glacial cobbles for the past 9,000 years. Temporally controlled alluvial soil and sediments combined with pollen data near Chimney Rock suggest basin-scale paleo forest fires at intervals of 200 to 300 years from 860BP until present. A synthesis of these studies suggests that a multi-proxy approach to paleoenvironmental research can help draw connections between paleo and modern climate change. Specifically, our research on late Quaternary glacial and wetland systems connects through our studies of late-Pleistocene and Holocene streams and into a modern story of forest change in the San Juan Mountains.

title: Geology of the eastern Silurian Hills, CA
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Eden, Ryan [1], Gans, Phillip B. [2], Cottle, John [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) UCSB, Goleta, CA,
(3) University of California, Santa Barbara, CA,
abstract: The eastern Silurian Hills, located ~20 miles north of Baker, CA, at the physiographic confluence of the Sevier Fold and Thrust Belt and the coeval magmatic arc, preserve structural and geometric relationships between a cogenetic suite of Mesozoic plutonic rocks and Pahrump Group, Ediacaran and Eocambrian metasediments. The south-dipping Riggs Shear Zone has previously been interpreted as a back thrust (Riggs Thrust) that separates a Mesozoic plutonic complex and highly strained marbles in the hanging wall from domed greenschist- to amphibolite-grade metasediments in the footwall. New detailed (1:5,000) geologic mapping indicates that the Riggs Shear Zone broadly parallels the margin of a heterogeneously strained dioritic pluton of the Teutonia Batholith, which has a U-Pb zircon date of ~100 Ma. The shear zone fabric and batholith are cut by undeformed ~98 Ma aplite dikes, providing a minimum timing of shear zone movement. Our mapping suggests that the hanging wall marbles are stratigraphically continuous with the underlying Neoproterozoic to Cambrian rocks in multiple places, encouraging their correlation with the Cambrian Bonanza King Formation and eliminating the need for a thrust contact. Pervasive grain boundary migration in mylonitic quartzites and abundant syn-kinematic sill + bt ± st in metapelites within the shear zone footwall suggest that deformation and metamorphism took place at temperatures exceeding 500°C. Due to the doming of stratigraphy in the footwall, units can be traced outside of the shear zone where they host greenschist grade assemblages, preserve original detrital textures, and are largely unstrained, necessitating the involvement of an external heat source in deformation and metamorphism. Taken together, these data suggest that the Riggs Shear Zone represents one margin of the metamorphic and deformational aureole of a Teutonia Batholith pluton rather than a back thrust in the Sevier hinterland, demonstrating the caution that must be used when interpreting structures in intra-arc settings.

abstract: The Jiangnan W Metallogenic Belt and the Middle–Lower Yangtze River Metallogenic Belt developed nearly coevally along the northeastern margin of the Yangtze Craton during the Late Mesozoic, producing extensive W and Cu mineralization, respectively. These belts intersect a contemporaneous nearly north-trending arc magmatic belt along the eastern continental margin of South China, a spatial configuration difficult to reconcile with classical subduction-related metallogenic models. Focusing on the Taqian–Fuchun Belt in the central segment of the Jiangnan W Metallogenic Belt, this study examines the spatiotemporal coupling among Middle–Late Jurassic deformation, magmatism, and mineralization to constrain the regional geodynamic framework. Structural analysis combined with zircon U–Pb geochronology reveals a transition from a compressional to an extensional regime in northeastern Jiangxi. NW–SE-directed compression (D 1 ) produced a regional thrust–nappe system and persisted until after ~160 Ma, as indicated by the youngest age of 159.8 ± 1.2 Ma from thrust-deformed granites. These granites are metaluminous to weakly peraluminous intermediate–silicic I-type rocks with adakitic affinities and are associated with Cu–Mo mineralization. In contrast, NW-directed normal faults developed during the extensional phase (D 2 ), providing pathways for magma emplacement and hydrothermal circulation. Undeformed granites from this stage yield zircon U–Pb ages of 150.6–152.7 Ma and are predominantly weakly to strongly peraluminous S-type felsic rocks linked to W mineralization. Geochemical and isotopic data indicate that the early I-type magmas originated from mixing between hybrid mantle materials and lower crustal melts, whereas late S-type magmas were mainly derived from partial melting of Neoproterozoic crustal rocks of the Shuangqiaoshan Group. The compressional–extensional transition in northeastern Jiangxi predates that in the Middle–Lower Yangtze River region and shows progressive northeastward propagation. Integrated geological, geophysical, and zircon Hf isotopic evidence supports localized asthenospheric upwelling related to slab window opening beneath central northern Jiangxi, implying progressive tearing of the Paleo-Pacific Plate.

title: Uncovering the Provenance of Sediment Entering Lake Tanganyika: A Geochemical and Mineralogical Study of Sediment in the Luiche River, Tanzania
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Hein, Aspen [1], Soreghan, Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
abstract:
Extensive changes in land use near growing urban centers harm adjacent freshwater ecosystems by increasing sediment pollution. In Tanzania, the Luiche River enters the eastern side of Lake Tanganyika, carrying sediment from its expansive watershed to the east. Lake Tanganyika, located in the East African Rift Valley, is one of the longest and deepest freshwater lakes in the world and holds impeccable ecological and economic value for its biodiversity, freshwater, and protein resources. Recent land use changes have threatened these resources by increasing sedimentation into Lake Tanganyika.

This source-to-sink study focuses on observing the properties of sediment entering the Luiche River to identify the provenance of the sediment entering Lake Tanganyika. We examined 18 samples collected from tributaries entering the Luiche River and used grain size analysis, mineralogical analysis, and whole-rock geochemical characterization to map the sediment characteristics within four major tributary watersheds. The findings show a comparable grain size across the Luiche watershed, but distinct differences in trace element geochemistry among the different tributary watersheds. The sediment from near the mouth of the Luiche River has a geochemical signature similar to that of the southern tributary sediments, suggesting that the majority of sediment entering Lake Tanganyika originates from the southern Luiche watershed. This appears to correspond with differences in land cover and geomorphology among the different tributaries. We are presently analyzing a sediment core offshore of the Luiche River to examine how anthropogenic and climate changes may have impacted the provenance of sediment entering Lake Tanganyika in the recent past.

This study is significant for its geological findings and the mitigation of human impacts on lake and river ecosystems. Understanding the pathways that result in sedimentation in depositional settings allows us to deepen our understanding of sedimentation rates in active rift systems. Additionally, each tributary in the Luiche watershed is being affected by different land use changes. Understanding the provenance of sediment improves our perspective on the ways that land use change impacts sedimentation. These findings have the potential to assist local conservatories to monitor land use and positively impact the Lake Tanganyika ecosystem.

title: Beyond Quartz – Revisiting Whole-Rock In Situ Cosmogenic 14C
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Lifton, Nathaniel [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
I n situ cosmogenic 14 C ( in situ 14 C) in quartz has emerged as a key addition to the cosmogenic toolbox, since its 5.7 ky half-life renders it dominantly sensitive to late Pleistocene and Holocene exposure histories and processes not available using long-lived nuclides. Yet while common at Earth's surface, quartz is not ubiquitous. Early in situ 14 C extraction efforts focused on whole-rock samples but ultimately proved problematic, leading to quartz as the preferred target mineral for in situ 14 C. However, recent advances in laboratory techniques, paired with software to adjust quartz-calibrated production rates to other compositions, suggested reassessing in situ 14 C extraction from whole-rock samples would be worthwhile. Development of robust extraction methods for such targets paired with broader understanding of in situ 14 C production systematics in silicates would permit wider application of in situ 14 C to geomorphic and Quaternary geologic questions globally.

Preliminary whole-rock in situ 14 C extraction experiments were conducted on archived CRONUS-Earth calibration samples in-hand from the Tabernacle Hill basalt flow, Utah, and from glacially scoured gabbro and granite sites from the Isle of Skye, Scotland. Both sites are associated with in situ 14 C analyses on quartz from CRONUS-Earth (Promontory Point, Utah, and western Scottish Highlands). Deeply shielded mafic and felsic samples were also analyzed as a procedural check. Experiments generally followed Lifton et al. (2023, Geochron. 5, 361–375) protocols but used pre-fused ultra-pure 50% Li-tetraborate/50% Li-metaborate (LiT/LiM) flux to dissolve a broader silicate compositional range than the 100% Li-metaborate (LiM) flux typically used for quartz. Mafic samples interacted with the O 2 process atmosphere quite differently during extraction than quartz and felsic samples, likely due to Fe and Mg reactions, but otherwise all samples processed normally. Resulting concentrations in surficial samples were input into MATLAB production rate calibration code (Balco et al., 2008, Quat. Geochron. 3, 174–195) modified to account for compositionally dependent in situ 14 C production (Koester and Lifton, 2023, Geochron. 5, 21–33). Calibrated compositionally dependent in situ 14 C sea-level high-latitude (SLHL) production rates (LSDn scaling) for two mafic and one felsic bedrock whole-rock samples were within 1% of corresponding quartz production rates – an extremely promising initial result. However, a granitic glacial boulder exhibited significant excess 14 C, warranting further technique development to identify and mitigate 14 C contaminant sources.
