title: Progressive Downstream Modification of Quartz Sand Along the Chitina River, Alaska, Using Automated Grain Shape Analysis
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Madduma Bandarage, Omalka Kaumadi Chandrasiri [1], Sweet, Dustin E. [2], Campaña, Isidoro [3], Bowen, Rocco [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
(2) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(3) Department of Geodynamics, Stratigraphy and Paleontology, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
(4) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Missouri City, TX, USA
abstract:
Rivers shape landscapes through erosion and transport of sediment, with grain morphology a partial record of that history. Abrasion during fluvial transport alters grain morphology of gravel, sand grain shape remains less understood because morphological changes are subtle and require large datasets for reliable analysis. This study investigates the progressive shape modification of glacially derived quartz sand along the 188 km Chitina River, Alaska, using automated image analysis. Grain shape trends are compared with the Salmon River and Spain's Arlanzón River to evaluate the consistency of fluvial abrasion patterns across contrasting river systems.

Ten samples were analyzed from the Chitina River. Organic matter and magnetic minerals were removed, and quartz grains from two sand-size fractions (1.0–0.5 mm and 0.5–0.25 mm) were isolated using heavy-liquid separation. Across all samples, approximately 8,000 quartz grains were analyzed with a Malvern Morphologi G3 system to measure HS Circularity, Convexity, Solidity, and Aspect Ratio. Regression analysis identified which of these grain shape parameters were most sensitive to fluvial abrasion. The 1.0–0.5 mm fraction showed systematic downstream modification, with HS Circularity (R2 = 0.95), Convexity (R2 = 0.88), and Solidity (R2 = 0.80) increasing with transport distance, while Aspect Ratio remained unchanged. In contrast, the finer 0.5–0.25 mm fraction exhibited greater scatter and weaker relationships with transport distance potentially suggested more suspension transport of this grain size fraction. Consequently, the coarse fraction preserves the downstream abrasion signal more clearly than the fine-grained quartz population.

The proglacial Salmon River of British Columbia and Alaska shows rapid grain rounding, whereas the Chitina River exhibits gradual downstream changes potentially because of continuous glacial sediment replenishment. The Arlanzón River displays the highest overall Circularity, Convexity, and Solidity values, potentially reflecting the non-glacial character of this river. Across all three rivers, Aspect Ratio remains nearly constant with distance, suggesting grain elongation is largely source-controlled. Overall, Circularity, Convexity, and Solidity are more sensitive indicators of transport induced abrasion than Aspect Ratio.

title: VERTEBRATE TRACKS IN SANDY MEDIA: NAVIGATING THE PRESERVATION-IDENTIFICATION RAPIDS
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments
authors: BUYNEVICH, ILYA [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, Temple University, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract: Vertebrate tracks offer a rich archive of tracemaker behavior and interaction with a wide range of substrates (media), with sand-dominated matrix posing unique challenges due to its geo-mechanical properties. Ichnological research focuses on one or more aspects of registering, accentuating, preserving, identifying, and studying (RAPIDS) a particular ichnite, with each phase requiring a satisfactory completion of the previous one. Preservation can be improved by temporary freezing of moist tracks, followed by rapid burial (e.g., aeolian settings). Accentuation by heavy-mineral concentrations (HMCs) in otherwise light (e.g., quartz-dominated) matrix, improves visual detection. These anomalies can be also detected by geophysical methods, such as low-field magnetic susceptibility (MS) and ground-penetrating radar (GPR). In the upper 1-2 m of the subsurface, high-frequency GPR (500-2300 MHz) allows detection and resolution of decimeter-to-centimeter scale features such as individual large tracks and trampled surfaces. In carbonate and evaporite sand, preservation may be enhanced by partial lithification, which also improves detection in the absence of HMCs. A distinct challenge is presented by mafic volcaniclastic substrates, although these are relatively uncommon as ichnological research subjects. Experimental neoichnology of bison hoofprints, as examples of a tracemaker with the highest edge loading, focus on quantifying moisture content, effects of substrate freezing, varying modes of HMC occurrence characterized by MS, and detection of non-accentuated tracks and undertracks in a dry substrate using GPR imaging. To illustrate the various phases of vertebrate ichnite RAPIDS, examples from Quaternary siliciclastic and evaporite sandy media demonstrate a wide spectrum of textural, moisture, and footprint density patterns that affect the taphonomic aspects and identification of vertebrate tracks.

title: Holocene Paleofire and Fuel-type Characterization from a Coastal Lake in the US Gulf Coast
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Solomon, Joshua Avong [1], Shepherd, Stephanie L. [2], Waters, Mathew N. [3], Vachula, Richard [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(3) Department of Crop, Soil & Environmental Sciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
abstract: Fire affects coastal ecosystems, but few records exist along the US Gulf Coast that quantify these extreme events over the Holocene (~8000 cal yr BP). This research provides a high-resolution, long-term Holocene ( radiocarbon ( 14 C) and 210 Pb dates) record of fire and fuel types based on sedimentary charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR) from Little Lake. CONISS analysis was used to identify key CHAR and morphometric stratigraphic intervals, and peak analysis was used to reconstruct local fire episodes. We find two distinct intervals of elevated fire activity and fire episodes in the Early and Late Holocene, which showed statistically positive correlations with particle aspect ratio (L:W) and Feret diameter. During the Early Holocene pollen data show the vegetation was typified by a high percentage of Pinus (30-70%) and Quercus (15-20%), and fire episodes corresponded with charcoal morphotypes (C, D & F) characteristic of conifer needles, leaves, grasses, and herbaceous roots. During the cool Late Holocene (~2200 to 0 cal yr BP), pollen records show a transition to mixed conifer forests ( Picea , Pinus, and Abies ) in the region, which corresponded to increases of L:W and Feret diameter. Simultaneously, there was sudden increase in morphotypes S/B, M, and P, associated with agricultural practices including of wood clearance and the burning of fuels and leaves. The Late Holocene, was identified to experience increased fire episodes, high signal-to-noise index (SNI), and more diverse fuel types. As such, our data support the mechanism of forest floor fuel accumulation as the driver of increased fire in the last two millennia.

title: Drilling for a Killing: What does whole-body stable isotope analysis reveal about the diet of Urosalpinx cinerea?
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Buchholz, Simon M. [1], Casey, Michelle M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physics, Astronomy, & Geosciences, Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
(2) Department of Physics, Astronomy, & Geosciences, Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
abstract: Predatory drilling snails have long been utilized by paleoecologists to study predator-prey interactions in the fossil record. Accurate interpretation of evolutionary and ecological trends in predatory drill holes requires an in-depth understanding of the feeding habits of modern drilling snails. Previous isotopic diet studies of predatory drilling snails found unexpectedly low δ15N values for Urosalpinx cinerea, calling their predatory diet into question. These unusual δ15N values could be the result of an anomalous N fractionation factor in this species or reflect an omnivorous diet including primary producers and molluscan prey. To evaluate these possibilities, we conducted a laboratory feeding experiment in which U. cinerea were exclusively fed Crassostrea virginica for nine months. Experimental U. cinerea yielded a median N fractionation factor of 0.86‰, far less than the multi-taxon average of 3.4‰ and previously studied drillers. The carbon signatures of the experimental snails were intermediate between their wild and experimental food sources, indicating that the experiment was not run long enough for snail tissues to fully equilibrate. To combat tissue turnover issues, we calculated the “isotopic equilibration completeness” to determine how much of the expected isotopic turnover had been completed over the duration of the experiment. By assuming that the C signature of the experimental drills would have eventually equaled those of their oyster prey (given an average C fractionation factor of 0-1‰ and sufficient time), we determined that experimental U. cinerea completed 34% of the expected C shift. We then compared this value to the “isotopic equilibration completeness” value for N calculated two ways: 1) based on the experimentally derived average N fractionation factor for all animals (experimental food N signature + 3.4‰) = 22%, and 2) based on the apparent N fractionation factor for wild U. cinerea (experimental food N signature + 1.67‰) = 76%. While the duration of the experiment precludes refutation of the anomalous fractionation factor hypothesis, the N isotopic equilibration completeness values are more consistent with an average fractionation factor, supporting an omnivorous diet in the field. Understanding the prevalence of omnivory among drilling gastropods is important as the effects of omnivory on predator-prey dynamics are still being evaluated by modern ecologists.

title: Multi-millennial, Multi-Proxy Reconstruction of Pacific Coast Extreme Events and Paleoenvironmental Change: A Sedimentological Investigation from Estero Chorro, Jalisco, Mexico

authors: Bianchette, Thomas A. [1], Das, Meenu Sandhya [2], de Alba Martínez, Hugo [3], Aragón-Moreno, Alejandro A. [4], Vargas-del-Río, David [5], Rizo-Decelis, L. David [6], Sahagún, Luis A.T. [7]

(2) Department of Chemistry, Oakland University, Rochester, MI, USA
(3) Departamento de Procesos Tecnológicos e Industriales, ITESO, San Pedro Tlaquepaque, Jalisco, Mexico
(4) Departamento de Conservación de la Biodiversidad, ECOSUR, Chetumal, Quintana Roo, Mexico
(5) Departamento de Hábitat y Desarrollo Urbano, ITESO, San Pedro Tlaquepaque, Jalisco, Mexico

(7) Uella Environmental Research and Consulting S.A. de C.V., Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, Mexico
abstract:
The Eastern North Pacific (ENP) is considered one of the most active basins, globally, for cyclogenesis. Despite this, proper regional assessments of coastal risks are unsatisfactory, especially since reliable instrumental records extend back only several decades for ENP hurricanes. While the spatial coverage of paleotempestological reconstructions has improved for Western Mexico over the last decade, vast coastlines are untouched in part due to the complex geomorphological and geological settings of regional estuaries and lagoons. We will display preliminary sedimentological results from Estero Chorro, located along Jalisco’s central coast and ~85 km south of Puerto Vallarta. This region has been devastated by numerous hurricanes in recent times, namely Lidia (2023) and Patricia (2015), both category 4 events at landfall. Results will be shared with local governmental officials to assist with coastal management, while determining periods of hyperactivity and the responsible climatological mechanisms for frequent storminess will lend crucial information to policymakers, risk modelers, and other stakeholders.

Estero Chorro was visited in October 2025 for fieldwork; in a shore perpendicular transect, five sediment cores (~12 total m, longest core ~471 cm) were extracted with a vibracorer and collected in 3-inch diameter aluminum tubes. To help determine sediment provenance, ten surface samples were extracted from the site. Samples were transported to the Coastal Hazard and Environmental Reconstruction Laboratory at Oakland University and stored in refrigerators to await analysis. To date, each core has been analyzed via loss-on-ignition (LOI), x-ray fluorescence (XRF), and magnetic susceptibility analysis at 1-cm resolution.

The five cores are dominated by gray shelly clay; sedimentological units of interest consist of severely broken shell hash layers and sand layers, commonly with sharp lower contacts. Notably, core 3 (~272 cm long) contains at least two distinct sand layers and two shell hash layers. These units are each being investigated as potential extreme event deposits, presumably from hurricane overwash or tsunami runup. Additionally, other units of interest due to their geological and/or geochemical distinction require additional probing. Elemental concentration spikes of Ti are being investigated as potential slopewash signals from heavy rainfall events, while sudden Cl and S increases may indicate periods of extreme event-induced marine inundation. Future analysis to determine the origin of these events will include microfossils (i.e., pollen, dinoflagellates), x-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy.

title: From Points to Patterns: Unlocking Lunar Geology through Distributed Surface Sensing
session_title: Planetary Potpourri (Posters)
authors: Herzog, Emma Rose [1], Jackson, Ferrah [2], Ferraro, Madison [3], Sobhani, Barbra [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado Space Grant Consortium, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(2) Colorado State University, Colorado Space Grant Consortium, Ft. Collins, Colorado, USA
(3) University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado Space Grant Consortium, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(4) University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado Space Grant Consortium, Boulder, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Understanding the Moon requires more than isolated measurements; it requires observations that resolve how geological processes vary across both space and time. The great Lunar Expedition for Everyone (GLEE) explores a new approach to planetary field science by deploying a distributed network of LunaSats that function as a coordinated surface observatory. Rather than relying on a single lander or stationary instrument package, GLEE investigates how synchronized measurements from dozens of spatially separated sensors can reveal patterns in the lunar environment that would otherwise remain undetected.

Each LunaSat carries a complementary suite of accelerometers, a magnetometer, temperature sensor, and capacitive sensor, enabling simultaneous measurements of seismic activity, micrometeoroid impacts, magnetic anomalies, thermal cycling, and regolith dielectric properties. Together, these observations address fundamental questions about lunar surface evolution, including the frequency and spatial distribution of impact events, the persistence and variability of crustal magnetic anomalies, environmental changes over the lunar day, and variations in regolith physical properties relevant to future exploration. Timestamped measurements from a distributed array also provide new opportunities to investigate the propagation of shallow moonquakes and other transient surface phenomena.

A central objective of GLEE is determining how network architecture, including deployment geometry, sensor density, synchronization accuracy, and spatial coverage, affects the scientific interpretation of these datasets, Rather than viewing deployment as solely an engineering constraint, GLEE treats network design as an integral component of the scientific method, recognizing that the ability to localize events, resolve environmental gradients, and construct geological maps depends directly on the spatial distribution of measurements. Current analyses evaluate deployment strategies that maximize scientific return while maintaining robust distributed observations across the lunar surface.

GLEE demonstrates how distributed sensing can transform planetary field investigations by shifting from isolated observations to spatially resolved datasets, providing a scalable framework for future lunar science and in situ geological exploration.

title: Preliminary Hypothesis of Geophysical, Geochemical and Structural Correlation of Hydrothermal Activity in Humming Bird Mine, Unaweep Canyon to the La Sal – Uncompahgre Region in Western Colorado
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling (Posters)
authors: Johnson, Verner C. [1], Scheve, Kyle P. [2], Patterson, Christopher Grant [3]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
(2) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
(3) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Unaweep Canyon is geomorphologically unique, featuring two mouths with East and West Creek flowing in opposite directions from a central drainage divide. Previous aerial magnetic surveys suggested high-magnetic anomalies near Nancy Hanks Gulch, potentially indicating a mafic source associated with rare earth elements. This study integrates ground-based magnetic surveying, structural mapping, and geochemical analysis to characterize these anomalies, estimate source depths, and test whether structural and weathering controls, rather than magnetic intensity alone, better explain mineral distribution across the survey area.

Magnetic data was collected with a GPS-integrated magnetometer and interpolated using an improved method, refining depth-to-source estimates beyond the standard Peter Half-Slope approach. This refined interpolation allows for more precise resolution of anomaly boundaries and source geometry than earlier aerial surveys provided. Structural data, supplemented by drone LiDAR, characterized fracture and fault geometry across the survey area. Multispectral drone analysis was done on areas with known silicification and mineralization, which was shown to correlate with regional structure. Geochemical and mineralogical analysis of hydrothermal vein material bearing quartz, green fluorite, and barite hosting copper mineralization was used to test a hypothesis for the magnetic source's composition. Hydrothermal activity seen in the area, supplemented by regional tectonic history, suggests an argument for mantle plumes in the region correlated between the La Sal – Uncompahgre. Enriched supergene layering, reflecting leaching and oxidation, was also identified and evaluated as a control on near-surface mineral concentration, distinct from any signature tied to the underlying magnetic source.

Results show magnetic anomalies are less pronounced than aerial data suggested, and mineralization is concentrated in low-magnetic zones rather than high-magnetic ones. Structural trends correlate with vein orientation, supporting structural control on fluid pathways as a stronger predictor of mineralization than magnetic intensity. Regional comparison with analogous mineralized systems in the La Sal Mountains suggests these patterns reflect broader Colorado Plateau tectonic and hydrothermal processes rather than a phenomenon unique to Unaweep Canyon. Together, these results indicate that structural architecture and near-surface weathering processes play a larger role than magnetic source strength in governing where mineralization occurs, refining the current understanding of the relationship between geophysical signature, structural setting, and epithermal mineralization in Unaweep Canyon.

title: Redox Reorganization of Sedimentary Phosphorus Cycling from the Archean to the Mesoproterozoic
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry
authors: Gutoski, James Richard [1], Wing, Boswell A. [2], Lepland, Aivo [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(3) Geological Survey of Norway, Trondheim, Norway
abstract:
Few elements connect the biochemistry of life to planetary surface evolution as directly as phosphorus. Over geologic timescales, phosphorus is regarded as an ultimate limiting nutrient, linking organic carbon fixation and burial to ocean-atmosphere redox coevolution. Because geological processes govern its supply, the sedimentary record archives past phosphorus cycling. Yet phosphorus is effectively monoisotopic, so its sources, sinks, and transformations must be reconstructed from elemental concentrations, mineral hosts, and proxy relationships.

Precambrian phosphorus records appear contradictory. Low phosphorus concentrations in shales and low phosphorus-to-iron ratios in iron formations suggest persistent phosphate scarcity. In contrast, elevated carbonate-associated phosphate indicates appreciable incorporation during carbonate precipitation, while the near-synchronous global appearance of phosphorites after the Great Oxidation Event documents phosphorus concentration and burial in a new sedimentary host. This paradox partly reflects comparisons among archives that record different processes. Resolving it requires distinguishing changes in sedimentary phosphorus inventory from shifts in its delivery, recycling, retention, remobilization, burial, and preservation across depositional environments.

We compiled approximately 16,000 sedimentary geochemical analyses spanning 4.0–1.0 Ga from the Sedimentary Geochemistry and Paleoenvironments Project and published datasets. Bulk phosphorus in shales, fine-grained siliciclastics, carbonates, and chemical sediments varies by orders of magnitude and shows a gradual, nonmonotonic increase through time. Era-level distributions are statistically distinct, but the uneven pattern indicates dynamic evolution rather than a single GOE-associated rise. Phosphorus-to-iron ratios show a stepwise shift, suggesting that phosphorus relationships with iron-bearing phases changed more strongly than bulk concentrations alone. Phosphorus-to-sulfur ratios follow a contrasting trajectory, rising nearly 2000% from the Archean into the GOE, declining sharply afterward, and rebounding in the Mesoproterozoic.

These patterns suggest that oxygenation reorganized phosphorus cycling through competing redox-sensitive pathways rather than initiating a simple positive feedback in bioavailability. Across the GOE, oxidative weathering likely increased phosphate and sulfate delivery, while Fe(III) oxyhydroxides scavenged phosphate and promoted burial. Concurrent sulfate reduction generated sulfide, drove reactive iron sulfidization and pyrite formation, weakened iron-associated phosphorus retention, and enhanced phosphate remobilization. Paleoproterozoic phosphogenesis may therefore have developed where increased nutrient delivery coincided with sulfur cycling, iron sulfidization, Ca-rich pore waters, and limited clastic dilution. However, the rarity of Mesoproterozoic phosphorites despite higher bulk phosphorus and renewed phosphorus-to-sulfur enrichment indicates that phosphorus abundance alone was insufficient to drive widespread phosphogenesis.

title: Quantifying Patterns of Skeletal Completeness in the Crinoid Fossil Record: a Preliminary Investigation of Paleozoic Taxa
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology and Geomicrobiology (Posters)
authors: Pringle, Camden [1], Wright, David F [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(2) Invertebrate Paleontology, Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA; School of Geosciences, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK,
abstract:
Quantifying the fidelity of the fossil record is essential for establishing whether paleontological data are adequate for addressing key questions in macroevolutionary theory and documenting general patterns in the history of life. Paleontologists have developed numerous methods for assessing the completeness of the fossil record (e.g., the proportion of taxa that left a fossil record), with the majority of approaches utilizing either taphonomic controls or sampling theory to evaluate preservation biases that impact our perceptions about how taxonomic diversity has changed both spatially and temporally.

Setting aside how taxonomically complete the fossil record is, relatively few approaches assess variation in the quality of fossil record we do have. For example, studies documenting patterns of morphological disparity and/or inferring phylogenies of fossil taxa utilize matrices of morphologic characters, which often include missing entries as a result of incomplete fossil preservation. For groups like vertebrates, with multi-element skeletons that disarticulate after death, the Skeletal Completeness Metric (SCM) was developed to quantify the relative completeness of anatomical characters preserved among fossil taxa. To our knowledge, the SCM has not previously been applied to fossil invertebrate taxa like echinoderms. Although they differ with respect to numerous taphonomic processes, clades within the Echinodermata also have complex, multi-element endoskeletons that can be quantified using the SCM approach.

In this study, we develop a new SCM system for the Crinoidea (Echinodermata) and present a preliminary analysis of skeletal completeness in Paleozoic taxa. Over 900 specimens were examined for skeletal completeness, with a majority of specimens analyzed from the Invertebrate Paleontology collections of the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. Each specimen was scored according to features preserved across three anatomical regions: calyx, arms, and stem. A score was assigned to each skeletal module and the SCM for each specimen was calculated as the total proportional completeness. Patterns of SCM values were visualized to detect variation in SCM values through time and across major crinoid subclades (e.g., Camerata, Flexibilia, Disparida, Eucladida, etc.). Results from this pilot study illuminate our understanding of skeletal completeness in Paleozoic crinoids and serves as a reminder that incomplete fossil preservation may impact our understanding of morphologic evolution and diversification

title: Quantifying Zircon Fertility of Sediment and Sediment Sources: A Comparison of Geochemical and Volumetric Methods
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools (Posters)
authors: St.Peter, Jack D. [1], Malkowski, Matthew A. [2], Ketcham, Richard A. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX,
(2) University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX,
(3) University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX,
abstract:
Provenance studies commonly use detrital zircon mixture modeling to determine the relative contributions of sediment sources to a given sink or basin. Because zircon fertility varies by lithology, different bedrock sources, even if exposed to similar erosion rates, can contribute different amounts of zircon to a basin. The relative zircon fertility of each source region must be considered in order to accurately infer relative sediment fluxes and to quantify changes in those sediment fluxes through time. This project tests the efficacy of using whole-rock wavelength dispersive x-ray fluorescence (WD-XRF) spectrometry for estimating the zircon fertility of sediment, sedimentary rocks, and igneous rocks and to provide easily obtainable and widely accessible zircon abundance data.

We present results from a suite of 20 samples, which capture a range of lithologies and crystallization environments. This suite includes sediment and bedrock samples of mafic, intermediate, and felsic composition, as well as samples from plutonic, volcanic, and recycled orogenic settings. In some cases, bedrock samples are paired with river sediment samples whose drainages include only that bedrock unit, in order to compare the relative zircon fertilities of bedrock sources and their associated sediments. Aliquots of each sediment sample and of milled bedrock samples were split for two analyses. (1) Micro-Computed Tomography (CT) scans were conducted on zircon separates of one aliquot to provide the true number and volume of zircon grains in each separate. We assume this to be the most accurate measurement of the zircon yield from a sample. (2) Bulk sediment was powdered, pressed into a disc, and melted into a glass bead for WD-XRF whole-rock geochemistry to determine the Zirconium mass concentration in each sample. Results show that zircon fertility as measured by CT can vary by orders of magnitude between different lithologies. Additionally, in all cases, the zircon fertility of a given sample as predicted by XRF is consistently significantly higher than the actual zircon yield measured by CT analysis. The degree of overestimation, however, appears to decrease with increasing zircon fertility such that the disparity is most profound in sediment and bedrock with low zircon fertility. Ongoing and future work aims to use energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy data from select samples aimed at identifying other potential reservoirs for Zr that may account for this disparity.

title: High-Accuracy Forest Type Mapping Using Remote Sensing Foundation Models
session_title: Imaging, measuring, and characterizing the Earth’s changing surface through remote sensing
authors: Liu, Chang [1], Lu, Ying [2]
affiliations: (1) Arthur Temple College of Forestry and Agriculture (ATCOFA), Stephen F Austin State Univ, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
(2) Arthur Temple College of Forestry and Agriculture (ATCOFA), Stephen F Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
abstract: Forests play a critical role in biodiversity conservation and climate regulation and are central to global sustainability goals and carbon neutrality targets. Although natural forests, plantation forests, timberlands, and orchards have distinct ecological and economic roles, they are often spectrally similar, making them difficult to distinguish using conventional remote sensing methods. Conventional forest maps generally identify forest cover but do not distinguish forests with different ecological and economic functions, which limits the interpretation of forest composition, function, and dynamics. Our objective is to develop an improved forest type classification framework using remote sensing foundation models. Texas was selected for initial model development and evaluation. Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery were used to fine-tune Prithvi EO 2.0, with reference labels generated through manual image interpretation. Prithvi EO 2.0 was selected because it is a remote sensing foundation model pretrained on multi-temporal satellite imagery, enabling the extraction of spatiotemporal patterns associated with land surface dynamics, including forest management-related changes and disturbance processes. Preliminary results achieved an overall accuracy of 0.78, with an mIoU of 0.66 and a macro F1-score of 0.75. Natural forest, timberland, and orchard classes achieved relatively high classification accuracy, whereas the plantation forests remained the most challenging class due to its spectral and structural similarity with other managed forest types and their limited representation in the training dataset. These preliminary results demonstrate the potential of foundation models for forest type mapping while highlighting remaining challenges in distinguishing plantation forests. Future work will further evaluate alternative model architectures and optimization strategies to improve classification performance. The developed framework provides a foundation for scalable forest type mapping across broader geographic regions and supports forest management, conservation planning, and long-term monitoring.

authors: Gaytan, Federico DS [1], Nearpass, Catherine N [2], Salanitri, Nicholas J [3], Goldsmith, Steven T [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography and the Environment, Villanova University, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA

abstract: Rivers are an important delivery system for microplastics (MPs; < 5mm in diameter) to coastal areas. However, some MPs can be left behind during transport in riverbed sediments. Once deposited in sediments, these MPs can chemically degrade and leach harmful chemicals into the environment, including metals, phthalates, and bisphenols. These contaminants can then be incorporated into ecosystems and our water supply. Despite these environmental health risks, few studies have examined watershed-scale controls on the delivery and storage of MPs in riverbed sediments. This investigation analyzes the relationship between impervious surface cover (ISC) and MP concentration and character in riverbed sediments in a watershed that traverses a rural to urban gradient. In Summer 2026, 18 samples of riverbed samples were collected from the Darby-Cobbs Creek Watershed in the greater Philadelphia area. Samples were collected from the watershed. Samples were pre-treated with 10% H 2 O 2 and followed by three sequential density separations in a 0.35 g mL -1 NaCl solution. The resulting supernatant was filtered through 0.45µm polycarbonate filter and analyzed using a stereomicroscope. MP concentrations and character were compared to the relative ISC in the upstream area using GIS analysis. Additionally, the study results were placed in the context of the existing literature for MPs in streambed sediments as well as the results of a previously collected sediment core from the mouth of the watershed. The study results provide insights into the source and distribution of MPs in freshwater systems.

abstract: Escumasia roryi , called the Y-animal for its characteristic shape, is an enigmatic extinct animal found only at the Middle Pennsylvanian Mazon Creek fossil site in Illinois. In the original and as-yet only description from 1978, the Y-animal was described as a bilaterally symmetrical, soft-bodied, sessile animal with two arms and a mouth between them, a trunk without complex internal organs but containing a complete gut, and a stalk that ends in a bulbous holdfast. Although the authors did not place E. roryi within a specific phylum, they suggested its preserved morphology was most consistent with the coelenterates, a now defunct phylum that encompassed Cnidaria and Ctenophora. In this study, we analyzed 58 specimens of E. roryi to re-examine its morphology, ecology, and taxonomic affinities. A small subset of these specimens was analyzed with scanning electron microscopy to assess their preservation and micromorphology. Although our morphological interpretation generally agrees with the original description, we reinterpret the ‘anal opening’ to instead represent internal organs, suggesting the Y-animal may not have had a complete gut, and that it likely did have complex internal organs. In addition, we re-interpret the holdfast to be a wide, flat, snowshoe-type holdfast appropriate for sticking to soft sediment. Finally, we determined that some specimens retain small regions with preserved cartilage. Although we also cannot place the Y-animal within a phylum, the newly morphological interpretations, and particularly all specimens having exactly two arms, is most consistent with a deuterostome affinity.

abstract:
In the February 6, 2023 event the first earthquake ruptured a 350-km-long segment of the East Anatolian Fault Zone between Çelikhan (Malatya) and Kırıkhan (Hatay). Situated immediately south of this surface rupture is the Antakya Fault Zone (AFZ), which underlies the city center of Antakya (Antioch). This 43-km-long, NE–SW-trending zone is positioned at the intersection of the East Anatolian Fault Zone, the Dead Sea Fault Zone, and the Cyprus Arc, comprising the Narlıca, Dağdüzü, and Meydan segments.

To evaluate the long-term seismicity and surface-rupture history of the AFZ, three paleoseismic trenches were excavated. Twelve radiocarbon determinations were calibrated (95.4% probability), providing a robust chronological framework for the stratigraphic successions. In the first trench, nine samples from successive levels yielded ages spanning 400 cal BCE to cal CE 382. Within this sequence, samples from the lower stratigraphic part fall primarily within the fourth to second centuries BCE, while samples from the overlying levels are concentrated in the second to fourth centuries CE. In a second trench location, deeper stratigraphic levels were dated to 1612–1316 cal BCE and 791–546 cal BCE, whereas the uppermost units date the deposition to the late seventh to mid-tenth centuries CE.

When integrated with the sample positions relative to faulted units and event horizons, these ages establish the depositional sequence and provide critical maximum and minimum limiting ages for successive surface-rupturing events. Ongoing OSL analyses of quartz-bearing horizons will be integrated with this radiocarbon chronology to refine event-age brackets and evaluate age-depth consistency in units lacking organic material.

This combined dataset documents recurrent Late Holocene surface faulting along the AFZ and provides essential constraints for regional seismic-hazard assessments. This study is supported by TÜBİTAK-KAMAG 1007 Project No. 123G009, with the research fellowship funded through the 2025-year TÜBİTAK 2214-A Doctoral Research Fellowship Program.

title: Rarus, Indeed: Resolving Taxonomic Uncertainty Surrounding Prionocheilus rarus (Cooper & Kindle 1936), and Describing a New Species of Prionocheilus from the Ellis Bay Formation (Hirnantian, Ordovician) of Anticosti Island, Québec, Canada

authors: Cavanaugh, Emily Macy [1], Wright, David F. [2], Cole, Selina R. [3], Hopkins, Melanie Jane [4]
affiliations: (1) Division of Paleontology (Invertebrates), American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA

abstract:
Faunal composition and diversity at the Ordovician-Silurian boundary (upper Hirnantian) is poorly understood, due to a near-global unconformity caused by a eustatic fall in sea level. This coincides with the Late Ordovician Mass Extinction (LOME), the earliest mass extinction event in Earth history. Anticosti Island (Québec, Canada) is one of the only localities worldwide that preserves fossils from this interval, allowing for a greater understanding of faunal assemblages and turnover during and after the LOME. Here we describe a new species of Prionocheilus Rouault 1847 [= Pharostoma Hawle and Corda, 1847] from the Ellis Bay Formation of Anticosti Island. This species is the youngest known member of the genus with a stratigraphic range extending locally to within meters of the Ordovician-Silurian boundary.

Despite occurring throughout Baltica, Gondwana, peri-Gondwana, and portions of Laurentia, occurrences of the genus Prionocheilus are very rare in continental North America. Prior to this study, a single Prionocheilus specimen had been documented in North America from the Katian of Perce (Gaspe Peninsula, Québec, Canada). This specimen served as the sole representative of the species Prionocheilus rarus (Cooper & Kindle 1936). The validity of the species, whose concept was based on a single juvenile specimen, has been a subject of debate for ninety years, but a lack of additional material made revision impossible. We have identified material from stratigraphic collections housed at the National Museum of Natural History (NMNH; USNM) that makes it possible to differentiate the Prionocheilus species found on Anticosti Island from Prionocheilus rarus ; additionally, the new material provides enough information to synonymize Prionocheilus rarus with Prionocheilus obtusus (M’Coy 1845). We also provide an updated paleobiogeographic distribution of the genus gathered from a review of available literature. The discovery of a new Prionocheilus species from Anticosti Island and the revision of Prionocheilus obtusus provides insight into the global distribution of Prionocheilus during the LOME, contributing to a greater understanding of trilobite diversity and faunal turnover at a significant mass extinction event.

abstract:
Mesozoic plant communities gave rise to modern floral ecosystems. One prominent extinct clade, the bennettitaleans, were key components of paleoecosystems during this period and remained dominant until the rapid diversification of angiosperms in the Cretaceous. While the anatomy and morphology of the reproductive structures of these enigmatic taxa have been extensively studied, very little is understood about their vegetative structure functions, or their ecophysiology, throughout the Mesozoic.

Permineralized wood is common in the fossil record, preserving large quantities of plant vascular tissue. Analysis of fossilized secondary xylem characteristics provides insight into how plants interacted with their environments and indicates survival through climatic perturbation. Xylem hydraulic characteristics such as pit density, tracheid diameter, and pit area are used to quantify wall-specific conductivity (K SP ) and mean cavitation pressure (Ψ P50 ). These parameters, when coupled, create a hydraulic ecospace in which plants occupy specific zones relative to their water use efficiency and stress resistance. This study focuses on bennettitalean wood permineralizations in the Wieland Type Collection housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and the Smithsonian Type Collection. We considered four bennettitalean species ( Cycadeoidea dartoni , Cycadeoidea wielandii, Cycadeoidea dacotensis, and Cycadeoidea paynei ), all from the Valanginian-Barremian aged Lakota Formation in southwestern South Dakota. We analyzed thin sections of permineralized trunk material which still preserve measurable vascular tissue that were originally prepared in the early 20 th century. Preliminary results from these specimens reveal that all four Bennettitales species cluster together in hydraulic ecospace (i.e., K SP vs. Ψ P50 ), in which they show low conductance and relatively moderate water stress vulnerability. This region of ecospace occupied by these bennettitalean taxa is distinct from extant plants with similar morphological features (e.g., cycads) and other Mesozoic taxa that lived with similar environments (e.g., conifers). These results suggest that bennettitalean hydraulic capabilities may have been the possible cause of their extinction. Further, this investigation into bennettitalean ecophysiology is a step toward understanding their unique role throughout deep time. Quantification of the hydraulic capabilities of this once-dominant clade provides important constraints ecosystem dynamics, including water and carbon cycling, in Mesozoic terrestrial environments.

abstract: Tapirs were found across North, Central, and South America during the Pleistocene. However, behavioral and morphological adaptations to Quaternary conditions of northern tapirs during this time are not well understood. Tapirus veroensis from Hollidaysburg Fissure, Pennsylvania (originally excavated by Roger Cuffey and Shirley Fonda) is one of the northernmost occurrences of Pleistocene tapirs. This study describes the morphology and taphonomic context of fossil materials and explores the palaeoecological implications of this specimen. Identification was performed through comparisons of dental measurements to published Tapirus datasets through bivariate plots and z-score analyses. These results indicate the specimen is a juvenile individual (1-1.5 years old) of the smaller Rancholabrean species, Tapirus veroensis . Such a northern occurrence of this species in association with other cold-adapted mammals may suggest that they were more tolerant of cooler climates than other tapir species, similar to the modern mountain tapir, Tapirus pinchaque .

abstract: Large-bodied herbivore communities have changed drastically since the Pleistocene but quantifying these changes and their impact on ecosystems remains a challenge. We currently cannot quantify functional shifts in herbivore community composition at the same temporal resolution as climate and vegetation records. Fecal steroids, which include sterols, stanols, and bile acids, have been proposed as a potential proxy for tracking herbivore community composition via soils and sediments. However, calibration studies that measure these compounds in dung have focused on livestock species, which are not appropriate analogs for wild herbivore communities in the past. To overcome this limitation, we analyzed fecal steroids and dietary DNA in 124 wild herbivore dung samples from 14 functionally diverse species to test the relative influence of body size, fermentation type, phylogeny, and diet on fecal steroid distributions. We found that, while fermentation type, body, size and diet were predictors of sterols and stanols distributions, these patterns could not be tied to herbivore-specific compounds. In contrast, we found that phylogeny and fermentation type, but not diet, strongly impacted bile acid distributions and that functional groups were related to distinct compounds. Based on our observations, we propose three bile acid ratios that characterize different functional dimensions of the ungulate community—differentiating between perissodactyls, non-ruminant artiodactyls, and ruminant artiodactyls. The application of these ratios to mixed sedimentary records has the potential to track shifts in large-bodied ungulate communities alongside climate changes at high-resolution.

title: Redox-Driven Mobilization of Geogenic Contaminants During Managed Aquifer Recharge: Field-Scale Evidence and Cross-System Synthesis
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Dahlke, Helen E [1], Waldman, Kira J.Z. [2], Morales, Veronica L [3], Fakhreddine, Sarah [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Land, Air and Water Resources, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA

abstract:
Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is expanding rapidly to counter groundwater overdraft, yet infiltration-driven biogeochemical shifts can mobilize naturally occurring geogenic contaminants. We present field-scale evidence from a Flood-MAR experiment in a fallowed almond orchard on the Tuolumne River alluvial fan (Central Valley, California), where continuous vadose-zone monitoring, porewater sampling, and groundwater analysis tracked six redox-sensitive elements (As, Cr, Mn, Mo, V, U) across three 28-day flooding trials. Flooding with surface water rapidly depleted oxygen (20–21% to <1%) and drove oxidation-reduction potential from +501 mV to −145 mV at 20 cm depth, converting the shallow vadose zone into an active biogeochemical reactor. Reducing conditions mobilized manganese and iron first, followed by arsenic, which rose 64% in porewater relative to pre-flood levels and briefly approached the WHO 10 µg/L benchmark in groundwater. Uranium and chromium responded inversely, declining 84% and 64%, respectively, after a brief increase, while vanadium and molybdenum showed intermediate, less redox-coupled behavior. Principal component analysis confirmed that vadose-zone contaminant chemistry was organized primarily along a redox axis (O 2 , ORP, Fe, Mn, As, DOC) accounting for 31% of variance, whereas groundwater chemistry was structured instead by nitrate, alkalinity, and uranium–chromium coupling, indicating that porewater mobilization did not translate directly into sustained groundwater impairment. Recharge source water had low contaminant concentrations, confirming that enrichment developed in situ within the vadose zone rather than through the applied surface water.

These field observations align with a broader synthesis of laboratory, field, and recharge-system studies showing that increasing hydrologic variability, from climate-driven precipitation extremes to engineered practices such as irrigation and MAR, intensifies wetting-drying cycling and redox oscillation in the vadose zone. Across systems, three recurring response patterns emerge: Fe-coupled co-mobilization of trace elements at reductive thresholds, asynchronous redox windows that decouple element-specific mobilization timing, and progressive weakening of geochemical buffering capacity under repeated cycling. Together, the field and synthesis results demonstrate that contaminant mobilization during recharge is element-specific, spatially heterogeneous, and governed by reactive mineral phases rather than bulk sediment inventories. As recharge is implemented at scales ranging from large managed basins to distributed, small-footprint systems, water-quality assessment and monitoring design should adopt a multi-contaminant, redox-informed framework, spanning both vadose-zone and groundwater compartments, rather than relying on arsenic alone as a proxy for geogenic contaminant risk.

abstract:
Comparing the ratios of stable oxygen and hydrogen isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H) in meteoric water has been an effective method for tracing water flux through the hydrologic cycle. Variability in the d-excess values between meteoric waters can be explained by multiple factors, including season, elevation, and moisture source, all of which are connected to temperature changes. In this context, we explored the controls on δ 18 O and δ 2 H values in precipitation at four sites in the Upper Colorado River Basin from 2020 to 2024. Four hundred ninety-eight (498) precipitation samples were collected across sample sites in Grand Mesa (elev. 10,800 ft), Cedaredge (elev. 6350 ft), and Grand Junction-Fruita, CO (elev. 4500 ft). Supplemental data from Moab, UT (elev. 4000 ft) was collected from the literature. Baker et al. (2022) reported a preliminary local meteoric water line (LWML) of δ 2 H=7.27(δ 18 O) +2.91 based on data from 2020-2021 in Grand Junction, CO. In our study, we calculated average, annual LMWL slopes of 7.09 for Grand Mesa, 7.31 for Cedaredge, 7.38 for Fruita-Grand Junction, and 7.58 for Moab. The largest variability in calculated d-excess values occurs seasonally. For Grand Mesa, Cedaredge, Fruita-Grand Junction, and Moab, d-excess values ranged from 3.90 to 18.30, -16.57 to 25.44, -27.27 to 30.00, and-26.18 to 20.75, respectively. Average d-excess values for Grand Mesa, Cedaredge, Fruita-Grand Junction, and Moab, d-excess values are 10.51, 8.39, 6.14, and 2.76, respectively. We found that the primary control on the d-excess values in meteoric waters at our sites was elevation. We calculated an isotopic lapse rate of -0.30 ‰/100m for this region of the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, we hypothesize that sub-cloud evaporation plays a significant role on isotopic signatures, especially during summer months. This research provides a better understanding of regional atmospheric water flow and hydrologic processes in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, this research provides groundwork for detecting the effects of long-term climate change on those processes, particularly on long term increases in surface air temperature and sub-cloud evaporation of raindrops in summer.

abstract: The Chicxulub impact on the Yucatán Peninsula triggered the end-Cretaceous mass extinction ca. 66 million years ago, but ejecta generation and transportation remain complicated to parameterize correctly in models. To better constrain these processes, we analyzed detrital zircon U-Pb ages and zircon shock microstructures from four K-Pg boundary sites—Ramonal, El Guayal, Bochil, and Brazos River—located ~300–1300 km from the crater. Our study identifies diagnostic zircon age modes (~66 Ma, ~334 Ma, ~420 Ma, ~550 Ma, and 1–1.3 Ga) that match the age groups of the Chicxulub target lithologies and impact age, and documents a range of shock microstructures including fractures, planar deformation features, twins, and granular textures. While previous studies correlate the younging of ages to increased shock pressures and textures, our results suggest no strong correlation between intensity of shock deformation and age resetting. These observations suggest complex mixing of variably shocked material in the ejecta curtain, sourced from a variety of structural levels within the impact structure, with shock pressures estimated from 0 to >30 GPa. Our results reveal spatial variability in ejecta composition and shock intensity, influenced by impact trajectory and depositional environment. By integrating geochronology with shock metamorphic textures, this study provides new constraints on the excavation, P-T history, transport, and deposition of ejecta, offering a refined framework for interpreting the K-Pg boundary and the environmental consequences of large impacts.

abstract:
The rapid rise in energy demand is leading to transformational growth in energy storage to reduce costs and increase reliability for energy. Demand for energy storage is growing rapidly both in the United States and across the globe, with battery chemistries competing for market share. Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries are becoming favored for major end uses such as EVs and stationary storage applications due to reduced cost and increased performance compared to alternative technologies. A portion of these reduced costs are related to reduced demand for critical materials in the LFP cathode production.

While LFP requires less critical materials, significant challenges exist in procuring these non-critical precursors at sufficient volume and purity to meet performance standards. Current LFP production is concentrated in China, where the dominant manufacturing process relies on a cheap and widely available waste product, FeSO4. FeSO4 supply is expected to decline in the coming decades due to shifting industrial practices, further this waste product is not available in other countries seeking to grow LFP production capability. Thus, an alternative precursor for Iron must be identified and supply chains sufficient for battery production must also be established for the other prominent precursor, phosphoric acid.

Widely available, low-cost iron precursors include products of the iron and steel industry. Caution must be taken when considering potential offtake locations, as added alloying elements for steelmaking may represent undesirable impurities. The volume of demand for batteries compared to steel is very small, but the demand for high purity is atypical for the target iron industries. Additionally, it is unknown which elements must be removed to create a battery grade product.

Phosphoric acid is widely available as a precursor to fertilizers, however the demand for phosphoric acid for batteries compared to fertilizers could be disruptive, at 4-22% of the current market. In addition, it is also unknown what impurities must be removed to create a high-functioning battery. It is unknown if origin deposit type or production method plays a role in battery grade products, which is critical to understand to minimize cost and protect US industry.

Impurity testing both of commodity precursors and their impact on battery products are critical to inform industries and successfully grow energy and electronic manufacturing in the US.

abstract:
Tanganyika rift, a mid to late Miocene non-magmatic rift segment of the Western Branch of the East African Rift System provides an ideal place for investigating active deformation and how faults grow and interact during rift propagation. In Tanganyika, several studies have documented the style and evolution of faulting based on seismic stratigraphy of the basin, but the nature and impacts of active tectonics within the watershed of the rift remains a question. In this study, five geomorphic indices including hypsometric integral (HI), drainage basin shape (BS), asymmetric factor (AF), normalized steepness index (Ksn), as well as the valley floor width-to-height ratio (VF) were computed on 584 drainage basins from ALOS World 3D 30m resolution digital elevation model to investigate the relative active tectonics of the rift and how these tectonic processes have greatly influenced the drainage system and geomorphic expressions of the region.

Geomorphological and structural investigation indicates that tectonic activity across the Tanganyika rift varies along strike, being high along border faults. These regions are characterized by elongated drainage basins and steep V-shaped stream channels that have been influenced by strong tectonic uplifts and differential tilting. As a result of normal fault growth and propagation that raise rift flanks, trunk streams seem to flow axially before draining water into the lake that significantly impact sediment supply and deposition within the rift. Additionally, steep slopes and high lineament densities are localized along rift flanks; this affirms that the watershed geomorphology is predominantly shaped by active deformation of the rift that in turn corresponds to higher rates of erosion. In these regions of abundant lineaments, steep geomorphology and increased erosion, earthquakes from further faulting and rift propagation can increase chance of future mass flows and ground failures.

title: Evidence From Past Mass Extinctions: Managing the Current Extinction Crisis
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Bottjer, David J. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA; Wrigley Institute for Environment and Sustainability, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract: Extinction requires knowing about the past. Understanding the concept of extinction was through discovery of fossil mosasaurs, mammoths, and mastodons. We are currently in what has been called the sixth mass extinction, caused by human activities. The sixth mass extinction has progressed through several stages, with the earlier stages largely involving hunting and the last stage involving global warming due to burning of fossil fuels. Two of the Big 5 mass extinctions known from the fossil record were primarily due to geological warming caused by unusual volcanic outpourings. What can we learn from them to help understand and manage the global warming phase of the current mass extinction, particularly for marine environments which cover ~70% of the modern Earth? For example, the Siberian traps are one of these extensive episodes of volcanism and they led to the largest of the Big 5, the end-Permian mass extinction, ~252 million years ago. Among many effects this end-Permian warming caused much of life to migrate towards the poles, so that equatorial regions are considered to have been "dead zones". Another big effect of this mass extinction was to greatly diminish reefs in the oceans. Effects of this extinction also caused the sizes of many organisms to decrease and for several small shelly invertebrates to proliferate in shallow marine systems, so-called "disaster taxa". Therefore, the record of the end-Permian mass extinction and its Early Triassic recovery is about more than increased extinction and includes detailed evidence on variability of the extinction and recovery from a variety of viewpoints. This provides the opportunity to produce useful information for us to understand and manage the effects of the current mass extinction in modern oceans. These studies tell us that we need to prepare for a world with not only increased extinction but also including oceans that have dead zones, disaster taxa, significant size reduction of animals, and loss of reefs produced by animals like corals. The pace of environmental change seems to be going faster that we had thought it would. Therefore, it seems imperative that studying our biggest ancient mass extinction and associated recovery in a detailed fashion, in the context of helping to manage the current mass extinction, is an increasingly compelling course of action.

title: Incorporation of heavy metals in dolomite
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales (Posters)
authors: Custis, Andrew [1], Murowchick, James B. [2], Fang, Yihang [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Division of Natural and Built Environment, University of Missouri - Kansas City, Kansas City, Missouri, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Division of Natural and Built Environment, Univ Missouri - Kansas City, Kansas City, MO,
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Division of Natural and Built Environment, University of Missouri - Kansas City, Kansas City, MO, USA
abstract:
Dolomite (CaMg(CO 3 ) 2 ) is one of the most abundant carbonate minerals in the geologic record and serves as an important archive of paleoenvironmental conditions, fluid evolution, and biogeochemical cycling. In particular, manganese (Mn), cobalt (Co), and arsenic (As) are redox-sensitive elements whose distributions in sedimentary carbonates have been widely used to infer depositional environments, diagenetic alteration, hydrothermal fluid interactions, and metal enrichment processes. However, interpretation of these geochemical signatures is hindered by the long-standing lack of experimentally synthesized dolomite formed under environmentally relevant temperatures and by limited understanding of how trace elements are incorporated during dolomite nucleation and growth.

This project reports the first-ever room temperature synthesis of Mn-, Co-, and As-bearing dolomite under near-surface environments. The resulting product was analyzed with X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to understand the mineralogy, chemical composition, and morphology of the precipitates. We found that Mn preferentially incorporated itself into the carbonate structure over Mg to such an extent that kutnohorite (CaMn(CO 3 ) 2 ) forms instead of dolomite even when the concentration of dissolved Mn is far lower than that of dissolved Mg. Under similar conditions, As and Co were found in the carbonate precipitates but not outcompeting the Mg as Mn did.

These findings have important implications for understanding the role of dolomite as a sink for environmentally significant trace elements in modern and ancient sedimentary systems. This experimentally derived partitioning behavior provides a mechanistic framework for interpreting trace-element signatures preserved in dolostones throughout the geologic record. By demonstrating room-temperature formation of trace-element-bearing dolomite, this work advances efforts to resolve the long-standing "dolomite problem" while providing new insights into carbonate mineral controls on metal immobilization, contaminant sequestration, and paleoenvironmental reconstruction.

abstract:
The Finca la Concepcion Tuff (FCT) is a previously undescribed biotite, clinopyroxene (cpx) dacite crystal tuff found in 600-m-thick valley fill deposit. The FCT deposit is a part of the larger Quaternary-Neogene Volcanics group, which blankets western Guatemala. Although younger ignimbrites like Los Chocoyos (LCY) have been well studied, Neogene eruptive deposits like FCT are less well known despite playing an important role in landscape evolution and recording the eruptive history of the volcanic arc. The FCT was also used as a building material in the first phase of construction at the Mixco Viejo Archaeological site, a Postclassic Maya settlement. The deposit was described using field observations, valley-fill modeling, petrography, whole rock major and trace element geochemistry, and energy dispersive spectroscopy. The FCT fills valleys made of metamorphic basement rock and was subsequently cut and filled by the ca. 80 ka LCY. The Mixco Viejo site sits on a terrace of LCY cut into the FCT and this study focused on outcrops of FCT north and west of the archeological site. The Finca la Concepcion crystal tuff shares some characteristics with the regionally extensive LCY and T Tuff (119 ka), as a massive lithic-poor biotite crystal tuff. However, FCT is more indurated, geomorphologically marked by spheroidal boulder weathering, and contains large cpx crystals not seen in other units.

The FCT has not been linked to an eruptive source but valley-fill modelling indicates that such a source could be the Pleistocene Atitlan or Neogene Xela caldera to the west of the Motagua Valley. Although Mixco Viejo is located on LCY Tuff, blocks of LCY pumice are rarely seen as building material. FCT is an abundant block material in the older phases of construction, especially buildings in Group B. Handheld Xray Fluorescence Spectra from the FCT are not distinct from the T and LCY ignimbrites despite differences in laboratory whole rock trace element analyses. Characterizing the Finca la Concepcion Tuff helps deepen our understanding of the history of volcanic eruptions in western Guatemala as well as providing an insight into the building materials available during the first phase of construction at Mixco Viejo.

title: Chloride Contamination and Urban Water-Quality Degradation in a Second-Order Urban Stream: Evidence of Urban Stream Syndrome and Freshwater Salinization Syndrome
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Miller, Ava C [1], Peterson, Eric W. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA

abstract: Urbanization alters hydrologic and biogeochemical processes in streams, producing characteristic degradation known as Urban Stream Syndrome (USS). In cold-climate regions, these effects are often accompanied by Freshwater Salinization Syndrome (FSS), which is characterized by increasing concentrations of dissolved ions (salts) from anthropogenic sources. This study investigated a second-order tributary of Sugar Creek in Normal, Illinois, to evaluate symptoms of USS and FSS, assess the severity of impairment, and identify likely contaminant sources. Weekly water samples were collected from upstream and downstream locations between fall 2023 and spring 2025 with any gaps in data resulting from brief pauses in research activities. Samples were analyzed for major anions, with emphasis on chloride (Cl⁻) and nitrate-nitrogen (NO₃⁻-N). Chloride concentrations were evaluated against U.S. Environmental Protection Agency aquatic-life criteria and compared with local weather conditions. Results revealed chronic chloride contamination throughout the study period at both sampling locations. Nearly all samples exceeded the EPA chronic threshold (230 mg L⁻¹), and several winter samples exceeded the acute threshold (860 mg L⁻¹). Chloride concentrations peaked during freezing conditions and snowmelt events meaning there is a probable connection between chloride concentration and winter road-salting events. While NO₃⁻-N concentrations remained below the EPA drinking-water standard, they closely tracked chloride patterns, indicating shared hydrologic pathways. Nitrate–chloride relationships suggest a mixture of urban contaminants, including road salt, septic leakage, pet waste, and other anthropogenic inputs. Road salt was identified as the dominant source of chloride and the primary driver of seasonal salinization. These findings demonstrate that even moderately urbanized Midwestern watersheds can experience severe winter salinization, chronic chloride impairment, and multiple symptoms of USS and FSS. The study highlights the disproportionate impact of urban land use on small streams and emphasizes the need for improved winter road-salt and stormwater management to protect downstream aquatic ecosystems.

title: Teaching Key Geologic Concepts With "Facies: The Stratigraphy Game"
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part II)
authors: Evans, Kevin Ray [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, Missouri, USA
abstract:
Gamification is widely accepted as an effective educational approach for learners of all ages. Multi-player card games especially can help students by providing for subject matter engagement within a social learning framework. Facies , The Stratigraphy Game (aka, Facies) , is a new card game designed for two to eight students with the goal of teaching the concepts of lithofacies, facies relationships, facies models, associated interpretive depositional settings, various unconformities, and application of Walther's law.

The game consists of a deck of 90 cards that include lithology, resource, and feature cards, such as basement, angular unconformities, disconformities, paraconformities, and one nonconformity card. Resource cards include petroleum accumulations, coal, evaporite, and ore mineral cards. Lithology cards include: conglomerate, sandstone, siltstone, black, gray, and red shales, greywacke, marl, limestone, boundstone, k-bentonite, and impact breccia.

Facies is a points-based competitive card game, comparable to a combination of dominoes and rummy; cards are assigned values that correspond with general economic value. A few cards also trigger some actions in the play sequence. Generally, cards are played in predictable patterns in turn-based play to construct vertical stratigraphic successions. Unconformity cards can be played to remove portions of the successions. Two charts govern the order of play in the successions: an idealized facies model and a game-play sequence chart, which provides a Markov-chain-like diagram of valid plays. During a player's turn, melds of three cards can be played for points, a valid discard play is added to the succession, and a card is drawn from the deck until the deck is exhausted or a player discards the last card in their hand. Students employ various strategies to shift the trajectory of deposition from either terrestrial or distal depositional settings, to overcome challenges presented and achieve goals that are conducive to an accumulation of points and going out.

The fall semester of 2026 marks a seventh year of playtesting this game with Missouri State University geology students. Students have contributed to the overall play and organization of the current game. They consider it to be fun and endorse the idea that it is a useful tool for learning key concepts about stratigraphic successions.

title: Exceptional Soft-Tissue Lagerstätte Preservation: Multi-Species Bivalve Hinge Ligaments From the Early Pleistocene, Lower Waccamaw Formation (~2Ma), Register Quarry, North Carolina
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: McCall, Linda J. [1]
affiliations: (1) NCFC, Reidsville, NC, USA; University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
The preservation of unmineralized invertebrate soft tissues, such as conchiolin protein hinge ligaments, is extremely rare. Normally these organic structures are subject to rapid decay. This study documents a unique taphonomic pocket in the Early Pleistocene, Lower Waccamaw Formation (~2Ma) of North Carolina at Register Quarry, revealing an exceptional lagerstätte-level concentration of diverse marine bivalves retaining their original organic hinge material.

A comprehensive study of this high-density shell bed identified 24 distinct bivalve species displaying intact, unmineralized ligament material. Species identifications were made with the assistance of David and Timothy Campbell. Five species show hyper-abundance, with hundreds of individuals retaining ligaments: Glycymeris americana , Arcinella cornuta , Diplodonta acclinis , Stewartia anodonta , and Lirophora varicose athleta . Four species are moderately common: Mercenaria mercenaria , Chama macerophylla , Corbicula densata , and Anadara lienosa . The remaining thirteen species represent rarer occurrences of ligament preservation, consisting of one to several specimens: Anadara aequicostata, Chionopsis cribraria , Kalophus gibbesii , Macrocallista greeni , Astarte concentrica , Dallocardium muricata , Semele sp. cf. S. rosea , Trachicardium emmonsi , Callucina keenae , Caloosarca rustica , Dosinia elegans , Leporimetis magnoliana, Argopecten sp ., Carolinapecten sp . and Cyclocardia granulata .

The preserved organic ligaments range from a distinct dark brown ( G. americana ) to silvery-grey (e.g., D. acclinis , L. varicose athleta ) and display highly sensitive moisture dynamics. Upon initial extraction from the damp matrix, the unmineralized ligaments remained pliable and stable under gentle rinsing. However, post-collection drying (dehydration) induces irreversible denaturation, causing the conchiolin to harden into a brittle state. Subsequent re-hydration triggers an immediate phase change into an amorphous gel, confirming the survival of original, hydrophilic glycoprotein chain networks that have bypassed standard mineral replacement or total carbonization pathways.

Because this multi-species assemblage provides a high-volume, statistically significant sample size of pristine Quaternary biomaterial, it offers an unparalleled baseline for molecular taphonomy. This presentation serves as an open invitation for collaborative geochemical analysis. The pristine nature of the unmineralized conchiolin presents a prime target for micro-FTIR spectroscopy to analyze protein degradation pathways, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructural mapping, and Amino Acid Racemization (AAR) to test regional Pleistocene chronostratigraphic models. Specimens will be deposited in the permanent collections of the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences. Additional material is being processed.

abstract: Biopolymer mulches are emerging as a biodegradable alternative to conventional polyethylene mulches in agriculture, yet their effects on soil water dynamics are still not well understood. This study examines how biopolymer mulch influences key hydrological processes including surface runoff, evaporation, root zone water retention, infiltration, and deep percolation. HYDRUS-2D with the Dual-Porosity package was used to simulate water movement and solute transport in the vadose zone under different mulch treatments. Model parameters were derived from field, laboratory, literature and refined through HYDRUS's inverse modeling functions, then calibrated and validated against these combined data sources. By comparing simulated outcomes across biopolymer-mulched, bare soil, and control conditions, this study quantified the mulch's impact on soil hydraulic behavior. Results show that biopolymer mulch reduces evaporative losses and enhances water retention in the root zone, improving overall soil moisture conservation. These findings offer new insight into the hydrological performance of biodegradable mulches and their potential to boost water-use efficiency. More broadly, this work supports the development of climate-resilient, sustainable agricultural practices and offers a modeling framework for assessing biodegradable mulch technologies across varied soil types and climates.

abstract: The Jurassic Emigrant Gap ultramafic to granodioritic composite pluton in the northern Sierra Nevada batholith, California, records tholeiitic crystallization-differentiation of H 2 O-poor near-primary arc basalts followed by open-system hybridization and crustal assimilation that generated calc-alkaline diorite to granodiorite. We integrate field relationships, petrography, mineral chemistry, and zircon U-Pb-O-Hf isotopic data to understand the details of assimilation and magma mixing that produced seemingly contrasting rock suites in a single intrusive complex. Zircon oxygen isotope ratios were measured by secondary ion mass spectrometry, followed by U-Pb geochronology and Hf isotope analysis via laser ablation multi-collector mass spectrometry within the same core and rim domains as SIMS spots in zircon from gabbronorite, two-pyroxene diorite, and granodiorite. The tholeiitic gabbronorite crystallized at 165.8±3.3 Ma and contains zircon with depleted mantle-like d 18 O VSMOW = 4.7 to 5.8‰ and eHf t = +11.1 to +15.2. This mantle-derived mafic intrusion, which crystallized from a basaltic andesitic magma, then hybridized with a separately derived granodioritic magma, producing heterogeneous two-pyroxene diorite. Mixing models suggest approximately equal proportions of granodioritic and gabbronoritic endmembers to produce the hybrid diorite. During hybridization, orthopyroxene from the gabbronorite reacted to form framboidal orthopyroxene clusters surrounded by reaction coronas. The granodiorite contains metasedimentary xenoliths and zircon populations consistent with significant crustal source materials. Jurassic autocrystic zircon from the granodiorite yield ages of 164.3 to 168 Ma with d 18 O VSMOW values of 5.4 to 9.1 and eHf t values of –36.8 to +16.9. The granodiorite also hosts inherited zircon with concordant older Jurassic (~180–200 Ma), Devonian (~365 Ma), and Proterozoic (~1200–1895 Ma) ages. Locally derived xenoliths indicate some incorporation of metasedimentary rocks at the emplacement level, as prominently exposed along the margins of the granodiorite. However, additional assimilation could have occurred at greater depths—further study is required to clarify the relative importance of shallow contamination versus partial melting of deep crustal sources. Together, these observations show how crystallization-differentiation combined with magma mixing and assimilation created Emigrant Gap’s seemingly conflicting evidence for tholeiitic versus calc-alkaline magmatic lineages.
