abstract: The early Paleozoic evolution of the proto-Andean margin of southwest Gondwana was characterized by the successive accretion of numerous Laurentian derived terranes following the breakup of the supercontinent Rodinia. Accretion of the composite Cuyania/Precordillera terrane to Gondwana represents the second and final phase of Famatinian orogenesis although the timing, extent, and bounds of this event remain debated. Punctuated Famatinian deformation is estimated to have occurred in the mid-late Ordovician (~470-450 Ma) with evidence for later deformation attributed to subsequent accretion of the Chilenia terrane during the mid-late Devonian Chanic Orogeny (~405-360 Ma). We integrate field mapping, microstructural analysis, and zircon and apatite U-Pb geochronology to constrain the timing and evolution of early Paleozoic deformation across the western Sierras Pampeanas. Field relationships and structural observations of metasedimentary units at basement island exposures correlate along strike with Sierra Pie de Palo displaying consistent top-west kinematics across a broad ductile thrust belt. The detrital zircon U-Pb record for the western metasedimentary cover sequence (Caucete Group) and metamorphosed basement units (Pie de Palo Complex and Central Complex) reflect a shared Grenville/Sunsas provenance while the eastern metasedimentary units (Difunta Correa Metasedimentary Sequence) include a strong eastern Brasiliano signal. Apatite U-Pb data from across Sierra Pie de Palo and along-strike basement island exposures yield ages that span the Silurian to Early-Devonian (~430-360 Ma). Microstructural observations and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis of quartz shows evidence of dynamic recrystallization through dominant dislocation creep mechanisms consistent with deformation at mid-crustal temperatures. Apatite grains show a strong LPO with their c-axes aligned with stretching lineations supporting synkinematic metamorphic growth. Paired with microstructural analyses, apatite U-Pb ages record the timing of deformation and metamorphism across exposures at Sierra Pie de Palo and basement islands resulting from protracted Famatinian orogenesis. Consistent apatite U-Pb ages for deformation across the Cuyania/Precordillera terrane presented here are concordant with published geochronology data recording Ordovician-Devonian deformation in the western Sierras Pampeanas and reveals a broad ~500 km long eastern boundary basement-involved thrust belt that kinetically links along the Sierra de Valle Fértil Lineament transform shear zone to the north.

title: Linking Geosymbols and Geosites: Integrating Comcaac Cultural Values into Geoheritage Conservation in Northwestern Mexico
session_title: Webinar 1: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives
authors: MIROS-GOMEZ, JORGE ALBERTO [1]
affiliations: (1) Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Estación Regional del Noroeste - Instituto de Geología, Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico
abstract: Geoconservation commonly relies on the inventory, characterization, quantitative assessment, and management of sites of geological relevance, typically guided by expert knowledge and scientific data. However, these approaches often overlook the cultural meanings and values that communities attribute to landscapes and landforms. This issue is especially important in Indigenous territories, where places frequently hold material and symbolic significance central to collective identity. This study develops an integrative geoconservation framework in the territory of the Comcaac (Seri) people, located along the central coast of Sonora and the eastern Midriff Islands region of the Gulf of California, northwestern Mexico. The framework combines conventional geoheritage assessment with the identification and characterization of geosymbols, allowing Indigenous cultural values to be incorporated into geoheritage evaluation. Geosites were inventoried and quantitatively assessed using adapted international methodologies, whereas geosymbols —places recognized by the community for their symbolic, historical, or practical importance in the construction of collective identity— were documented through ethnographic and participatory approaches, including semi-structured interviews, community mapping, participant observation, and field validation. A total of 24 geosites and 137 geosymbols were identified, allowing for an analysis of the spatial overlap and relative prominence of geological and cultural importance across sites, revealing a spectrum of relationships between both dimensions. Further classification of geosymbols by their dominant form of cultural appropriation and geological interest demonstrated relationships between specific geomorphological contexts and different Indigenous landscape uses or interactions. For example, springs and coastal lagoons were associated with resource procurement and settlement patterns, whereas rock shelters and pareidolic rocks were linked to sacred places and geomythological narratives. Together, these findings demonstrate that geosymbols provide a practical framework for incorporating Indigenous cultural values into geoheritage assessments and geoconservation strategies. Geosymbols expand the portfolio of places considered relevant for local management, offering a robust mechanism to integrate Indigenous cultural dimensions into conservation practice.

title: Quantitative Constraints on LIP Basalt Weathering Required to Sustain Sequential Snowball Earth Events
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records (Posters)
authors: Kadoya, Shintaro [1], Fujii, Masakazu [2], Kodama, Takanori [3]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Science Tokyo, Earth-Life Science Institute, Meguro-ku, Tokyo, Japan
(2) National Institute of Polar Research, Tachikawa, Tokyo, Japan
(3) Institute of Science Tokyo, Earth-Life Science Institute, Meguro, Tokyo, Japan
abstract: Neoproterozoic Earth experienced two sequential global glaciations, known as the Sturtian glaciation (717 Ma to 651 Ma) and the Marinoan glaciation (650–639 Ma to 635 Ma). Despite their temporal proximity, the event durations are thought to differ by a factor of 4 to 15, raising questions about the mechanisms driving these distinct snowball Earth events. A recent study (Minsky et al., 2026) suggested that the Sturtian glaciation was a sequence of multiple short glaciations, rather than a single long glaciation, resulting from the supply of fresh basalt (especially Ca) via the eruption of the Franklin Large Igneous Province (FLIP; ~720 Ma). To complement the previous study, this study investigates the minimum Ca supply required for sequential snowball events of >56 Myr, using Monte Carlo simulations with a one-dimensional energy-balance climate model coupled with a carbon cycle model. The simulations show that the required Ca amount is obtained as the product of the Ca consumption per snowball event and the number of snowball events within the specified duration (56 Myr). The minimum consumption of LIP-derived Ca per snowball glaciation increases with the steady-state amount of inorganic carbon (IC) in the atmosphere-ocean reservoir, asymptotically reaching the IC level at deglaciation from a snowball state. Also, since the snowball duration is much longer than the interlude warm period, the number of snowball cycles can be approximated by the ratio of the total event period (~56 Myr) to the duration of a single snowball event. Because both the steady-state IC level and a single snowball's duration depend on the CO 2 degassing rate, the rate also determines the minimum cation supply required for sequential snowball events; for example, given the modern CO 2 degassing rate (8 Tmol CO 2 /yr), the minimum estimate required to explain 56 Myr of sequential glaciations is 3 x 10 8 Tmol Ca, corresponding to the weathering of a ~100-m-thick layer of the FLIP area. This quantitative constraint provides a plausible physical threshold for basalt weathering during Neoproterozoic glaciations and supports the multi-cycle Sturtian scenario.

title: Differentiation of Asteroid Vesta: New Insights into Protoplanetary Evolution
session_title: Big Science from Small Worlds
authors: McSween, Harry Y. [1], Raymond, Carol A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
abstract: Vesta, one of only a few intact asteroids, has long been considered a textbook example of differentiation via a magma ocean. Emerging evidence suggests otherwise. Thermal models that consider the complexities of heating by 26 Al decay and magma segregation indicate a magma ocean (>50% melting) is possible only if Vesta accreted <1.15 Myr after CAIs; later accretion allows formation of a shallow magma sill or serial magmatism. Radiometric ages indicate Vesta accreted and differentiated at 1-2 Myr, but tighter time constraints are challenging because of overprinting thermal metamorphism, and accretion was not instantaneous. Robust U-Pb ages from zircons indicate peak eucrite magmatism occurred at ~15 Myr and continued episodically for another 30 Myr, considerably longer than magma ocean solidification models (2-3 Myr). Petrogenetic interpretation of the most Mg-rich basaltic eucrites is consistent with early partial melts of a primitive chondritic source rather than fractional crystallization products of a magma ocean. Crystallization ages of cumulate eucrites are several Myr younger than basaltic eucrites, ruling out models where these are cumulates and residual liquids, respectively, from a magma ocean. Varying trace element ratios in diogenites preclude their crystallization from a homogeneous magma ocean. Vesta’s structure does not accord with the layering – a basaltic eucrite upper crust grading downward into cumulate eucrite, overlying a diogenite mantle – expected from classic magma ocean solidification models. Gravity anomalies on Vesta mapped by the Dawn spacecraft are interpreted as crustal diogenite plutons rather than a global diogenite layer, and independent estimates of the relative proportions of diogenite to eucrite in the crust are too high for magma ocean models. FeNi metal grains in eucrites imply inefficient core formation, and a new determination of Vesta’s moment of inertia from reanalysis of its rotational state is within 6.6% of a homogeneous body, challenging the idea of complete magmatic differentiation. In summary, Vesta’s differentiation is best accounted for by protracted magmatic models that invoke shallow, unconnected magma sills, or serial magmatism. The complex magmatic history of this unused planetary building block may have important implications for understanding other differentiated protoplanetary bodies – the accretionary feedstock for the terrestrial planets.

title: AN UPPER EOCENE IMPACT HORIZON ALONG THE SAVANNAH RIVER. EAST-CENTRAL GEORGIA, U.S.A.
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Jaret, Steven J. [1], Harris, Robert Scott [2], Albin, Edward [3]
affiliations: (1) Kingsborough Community College (CUNY), Brooklyn, NY,
(2) University of Georgia, Loganville, GA,
(3) American Public University System, Space Studies, Charles Town, WV,
abstract:
The Eocene-Oligocene boundary is a known period of increased impact activity with multiple impact events spread out between 39 Ma and 34 Ma. This includes the Chesapeake Bay and Popigai Impact Structures. Additionally, the sedimentary record near this boundary exhibits elevated extraterrestrial 3 He suggesting a potential 3 rd impact event yet to be identified (1).

In the coastal plain of east-central Georgia this record is most prominently indicated by the presence of Georgiaite tektites, a small subfield of the North American Tektite strewnfield associated with the Chesapeake Bay Impact Structure. These tektites have an age of 35.2 Ma and are geochemically matched with target lithologies from the Chesapeake Bay Impact Structure. These macro-scale tektites occur was reworked material and have not been found in-place within Eocene sediment. Shocked quartz, zircons, and tektite fragments however, has been found in situ from this is at many mines from the Hardie mine in Wilkison, Georgia to kaolin mines in Aiken, South Carolina.

Here we report observations of a new outcrop along the Savannah River along a riverbank where a 31.5 g Georgiaite was previously recovered (2). Here we identified an approximately 1-cm thick black clay layer below the Dry Branch Fm (Twiggs Clay member) and within the “Clinchfield Sand” Fm. This clay has an unusual platinum group element (PGE) signature with elevated Ir (1.5 ppb) and extremely high Ru concentrations (11 ppb). Preliminarily petrographic work has identified at least one 100-mm teardrop-shaped microtektite within the clay. These suggest an extraterrestrial origin, although not entirely consistent with PGE analysis of either Popigai or Chesapeake Bay ejecta, particularly the relatively low Pt and exceptionally high Ru. Ongoing petrographic work aims to link this layer to broader regional contexts but it likely is related to a 3 rd Eocene impact layer that has been previously reported [3] because this layer is several inches below the Twiggs Clay fully within the Clinchfield Sand.

title: New Life for an Old Quarry: History and Development of the Little Bear Creek Diversion Recharge Enhancement Site, Hays County, Texas

authors: McKinney, Samuel Tyson [1], Sydow, Lindsey [2], Markowski, Michael [3], Thomas, Dana [4], Slocombe, Meghan [5]
affiliations: (1) Watershed Protection, Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Watershed Protection, Austin, Austin, TX, USA

abstract: The Little Bear Recharge Enhancement Site was completed by Austin Watershed Protection (WPD) in 2025 in northern Hays County, Texas. The recharge enhancement site consists of a 60-foot-wide excavated diversion channel that will siphon a portion of stormwater from the adjacent ephemeral stream, Little Bear Creek, into an abandoned limestone quarry within the recharge zone of the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer (BSEA). The project is the culmination of over 20 years of collaborative work across multiple governmental agencies, involving land acquisition, scientific investigations, permit negotiations, design, construction, and monitoring. To date, no diversion events have occurred, so this talk will focus on the decades of work that went into making the project a reality and the current status of monitoring. The site is located on a parcel of land purchased by the City of Austin (COA) in 2002 using Open Space Bond Funds. In 2004, the Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District (BSEACD) performed a hydrogeologic investigation and concluded that the pond in the lower pit of the quarry represents the water table of the BSEA. In 2017, WPD performed a dye trace and confirmed a hydrologic connection between the quarry and the Barton Springs complex. In 2011, the COA established an Interlocal Agreement (ILA) with the BSEACD and the Lower Colorado River Authority (LCRA) and in 2022, obtained a Water Use Permit from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) that, together, allowed the COA to construct the Little Bear Creek diversion channel to enhance recharge to the BSEA. Engineering site plan review occurred from 2022-2024, and construction of the diversion channel was completed in April 2025. The TCEQ Water Use Permit requires that the COA record and report flow in the diversion channel and in the creek within 300 feet of the diversion point. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) has installed flow stations in the diversion channel and creek to satisfy the permit requirements. Additionally, WPD has established monitoring sites in the quarry pond, diversion channel, creek, and two nearby groundwater monitoring wells to analyze water quality and groundwater levels before, during, and after diversion events. The Little Bear Recharge Enhancement site demonstrates the logistical and bureaucratic hurdles that can exist when designing and implementing and recharge enhancement project.

authors: Accotto, Cristina [1], LaFlamme, Crystal [2], Therriault, Isabelle [3], Guilmette, Carl [4], Tournier, Simon [5], Jouhari, Mehdi [6], Larson, Kyle [7]
affiliations: (1) Departamento de Ingeniería, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú, Lima, Peru; Department de Géologie et Génie Géologique, Université Laval, Quebec City, Quebec, Canada

abstract: The Ungava Orogen in Nunavik, Quebec, represents a segment of the Paleoproterozoic Trans-Hudson Orogen. The Southern Domain (SD), part of the foreland of the Ungava Orogen, was deposited along the rifted margin of the Superior Craton. It comprises the Povungnituk Group — a volcano-sedimentary sequence deposited ca. 2.10–1.96 Ga — and the Chukotat Group, which consists of a kilometre-thick basaltic sequence related to the Circum-Superior Large Igneous Province (ca. 1.88 Ga). The entire SD was deformed during the Ungava/Trans-Hudson Orogeny and the assembly of the Nuna supercontinent, producing NW- and E-trending folds and cleavages, as well as NW- and NE-trending brittle structures. Several tectonic models have been proposed to describe the evolution of the SD during the Ungava orogeny; however, key questions remain unresolved: (1) what accounts for the ca. 90 Myr gap between the Povungnituk and Chukotat groups? and (2) why are structures attributed to a late deformational phase (i.e., NW-trending folds) concentrated exclusively within the older Povungnituk Group? The field structural data and aeromagnetic interpretations presented here reveal at least two phases of deformation in the SD. A first compressional event (D1) produced NW-trending folds and faults, followed by a south-vergent shortening phase (D2) associated with the juxtaposition of the Northern Domain and the construction of the Ungava Orogen. D1 affected only the Povungnituk Group, generating structures that likely served as conduits for magma emplacement into the upper sequence. The ca. 90 Myr gap between the two groups suggests that this first deformational event occurred between ca. 1.96 and 1.88 Ga, predating the Ungava Orogeny. The subsequent D2 phase transposed pre-existing structures and deformed the entire SD sequence, corresponding to the main orogenic stage. These updated structural models and the revised tectonic interpretation presented here improve our understanding of the evolution of this region, including tectonic events that may have occurred shortly before the onset of the Trans-Hudson Orogeny.

title: Linking Mantle Source Changes to Tectonic Reorganization: Evidence from Eocene to Oligo-Miocene Basalts of the Dillon Volcanic Field, Southwest Montana (U.S.A.)

authors: Brueseke, Matthew E. [1], Everhart, Wyatt [2], Kempton, Pamela D. [3], Miggins, Daniel Paul [4], Vervoort, Jeff David [5], Haley, J Christopher [6], Endrich, Alyssa [7]

abstract: Eocene to Oligo-Miocene basalts of the Dillon volcanic field, Montana (U.S.A) crop out as lavas and intrusives across southwestern Montana but are concentrated in the Gravelly Range. Prior work suggested lower Dillon volcanism-initiated ca. ~54-39 Ma, which occurred adjacent to ~51-43 Ma central Idaho Challis and ~54-44 Ma Absaroka volcanism, thought to mark Farallon plate subduction cessation, and the onset of the mid-Tertiary ignimbrite flare-up and coincident slab rollback. Multiple tectonic models have been proposed to explain the ~33-16 Ma middle and upper Dillon volcanism (e.g., continued Farallon slab rollback, slab tearing or foundering, lithospheric drip). This younger, second, phase of Dillon basalt eruptions occurred during a period of regional extension and basin sedimentation. Dillon mafic rocks are mainly high-K and subalkaline but include eruptions of alkali basalts. Lower Dillon rocks range from basaltic trachyandesite to basaltic andesite. Middle/upper Dillon rocks range from basanite to basaltic trachyandesite. Trace element and Sr-Nd isotope ratios of lower Dillon volcanics display arc-like signatures, which reflects earlier Farallon slab subduction coupled with crustal interaction (e.g., Ta/Th <0.2, 87 Sr/ 86 Sr i 0.7072 - 0.7078; 143 Nd/ 144 Nd i 0.51206 - 51231). Most middle and upper Dillon rocks have intermediate Ta/Th (0.2-0.6) coupled with Sr-Nd isotope ratios ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr i 0.7048 - 0.7078; 143 Nd/ 144 Nd i 0.51214 - 0.51238) indicative of mixed asthenospheric and lithospheric mantle sources. Some middle/upper Dillon rocks have high Ta/Th (>0.6) with lower 87 Sr/ 86 Sr i ratios (0.7043-0.7057), consistent with an asthenospheric source, but they also have lower 143 Nd/ 144 Nd i ratios (0.51206-0.51232) unlike any other documented regional Cenozoic volcanics. Isotope mixing models indicate that these magmas were primarily sourced from asthenosphere, coupled with crustal interaction. Dillon basalts record magmatic source evolution through time associated with the regional tectonomagmatic change from subduction and massive flare-up style magmatism to extensional tectonics and much smaller volume eruptions, following slab rollback/foundering of the Farallon plate into the Oligocene and Miocene. Accordingly, Dillon basalts provide a record of this significant tectonic change that aligns with other well-studied regional upper plate features (e.g., sedimentary basin development, core complex exhumation, etc.) across the central North American Cordillera.

title: Geoscience in Service: Turning Expertise into Community Action
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Shores, Amanda Rose [1]
affiliations: (1) American Geophysical Union, Thriving Earth Exchange, Washington, DC, USA
abstract:
Science has long advanced society—from early observations that improved agriculture and navigation to modern discoveries that have extended life expectancy and strengthened resilience to environmental change. Yet despite these contributions, many people experience science only indirectly, and opportunities for meaningful collaboration between scientists and communities remain limited.

While scientists are motivated by discovery, innovation, education, and public benefit, academic systems continue to reward publications and grant funding more than community-engaged applications. As a result, scientific expertise is often disconnected from the communities that could most benefit from it. At the same time, scientists typically receive little formal training in building equitable, ethical partnerships with communities.

Many of today's environmental and societal challenges do not require entirely new scientific breakthroughs. Instead, they require applying existing knowledge in ways that reflect local priorities, values, and lived experience. Communities possess critical expertise about their own environments, histories, and needs that complement scientific knowledge and lead to more effective and durable solutions. However, traditional research models have too often treated communities as sources of data rather than equal partners, creating extractive relationships in which community members contribute significant time and expertise without receiving commensurate benefits. Centering community priorities from the outset is essential to creating more equitable and impactful collaborations.

As the world's largest association of Earth and space scientists, the American Geophysical Union (AGU) has worked to bridge this gap through its Thriving Earth Exchange program. Since 2013, the program has supported more than 400 community science projects that connect communities with volunteer scientists and project managers to co-develop solutions to locally identified environmental challenges. Over more than a decade of practice, the program has identified approaches that foster trust, strengthen partnerships, and improve community outcomes.

This presentation will highlight lessons learned from these collaborations and offer practical strategies for scientists seeking to engage more effectively with communities. It will also explore how institutions can better recognize and reward community-engaged science, helping create incentives that value societal impact alongside traditional academic achievements.

title: Contamination of the Mid-Hawthorn Aquifer with saltwater at the City of Cape Coral, Florida: Conflicting water policy over domestic well abandonment

affiliations: (1) Department of Bioengineering, Civil Engineering and Environmental Engineering, U. A. Whitaker of Engineering, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, Florida, USA

abstract: The City of Cape Coral, Florida, has thousands of unused or abandoned wells constructed into the Mid-Hawthorn Aquifer. As potable water, irrigation water, and wastewater collection service lines have been extended throughout much of the city, domestic wells used for drinking and irrigation water supply in the past are no longer needed. The city has requested a regulatory agency to require that these wells be properly abandoned by filling them from bottom to top with cement. This request was denied because domestic wells receive special protection under the Florida Water Resources Act of 1972 (Chapter 373 of Florida Statues). However, the wellheads decay over time because of exposure to the sun (e.g., UV deterioration of PVC pipe), and outdoor conditions. The failure of the wellhead seals at land surface creates a condition that allows potential contamination of up to 20,000 wells. On September 28, 2022, Hurricane Ian swept over the City of Cape Coral with a surge of over 3.05 m (10 ft), covering thousands of these improperly abandoned wells. Any wells having defective or damaged seals that were submerged caused contamination of the Mid-Hawthorn Aquifer with during the hurricane surge.The submergence of wellheads during tropical storm surge events will become a global problem in the futre as sea level rises and the frequency and intensity of tropical storms increase. This is becoming a primary issue in seawater contamination of confined aquifer wells occurring in the coastal zone

title: Intersectionality of climate change and gender identity risk factors when transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people consider relocating
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Feig, Anthony D. [1], Kosciesza, Aiden [2], Mamun, Md Mahmudul Hasan [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography & Environmental Studies Central Michigan University, Mt Pleasant, MI, USA
(2) School of Communication, Journalism, & Media Central Michigan University, Mt Pleasant, MI, USA
(3) Statistical Consulting Center, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI, USA
abstract:
Transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people are a socially vulnerable population that will likely be disproportionally harmed by climate change yet have not been included in climate impacts studies.

We surveyed 122 TGD people to document how concerned they are about specific climate harms (heat, drought, wildfires, sea levels, flooding, severe weather, dust), and their sense of social/political safety. We also asked about their interest in relocating. Each participant was placed in a Legal Risk category using Reed’s (2025) Legislative Risk Maps, and their Koppen climate zone was recorded. We calculated indices for Climate Perceived Vulnerability (CPV), Political Perceived Vulnerability (PPV), and Desire to Move (DMI) for each participant. We hypothesized positive correlations between PPV-DMI, and CPV-DMI. We further hypothesized a relationship would exist between CPV-PPV.

We analyzed data using proportional odds models and Spearman’s rank correlations. Results show that neither PPV nor CPV showed a significant association with DMI (p=0.5959 and 0.7539, respectively). Koppen climate zone showed a significant association with PPV (p=0.0002); however, climate zone was not significantly associated with CPV (p=0.9281). Legal risk showed no significant association with CPV (p = 0.4842). However, a significant correlation exists between legal risk and PPV (p = 0.001). Legal risk showed no significant association with CPV (p = 0.4842). The desires of U.S.-based TGD people to relocate were not strongly determined by either their CPV or PPV, suggesting that decisions to relocate are complex and not primarily driven by either concerns about climate risk, or concerns about social risks associated with being TGD.

Takeaways from our pilot study are: 1) Connections to place are complex (e.g., employment, education), which were not captured by our survey. 2) Respondents reported less concern or awareness about climate dangers than about the political/legal dangers they face as TGD people. 3) Interactions between social phenomena (e.g., gender identity) and physical processes are complex and require further interdisciplinary research to apply an appropriate intersectionality framework.

title: A Novel 3-D Visual-spatial Model for Assessment of an Undergraduate Sustainability, Environment, & Society Major
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Feig, Anthony D. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geography & Environmental Studies Central Michigan University, Mt Pleasant, MI, USA
abstract:
Degree programs in sustainability studies focus on human-environment interactions, where science, policy, and society intersect. Such programs have increased in number in the US over the last 5-10 years. In new programs design and curriculum are usually given the most attention, but assessment is a key component, especially for continued institutional support.

Because of their integrated and multidisciplinary nature, sustainability, environment, & society (SES) programs present greater complexity in assessment, but also greater opportunity to deepen understanding of how a program’s curriculum, purpose, and student achievement interrelate. Ideally, an SES curriculum would evenly distribute courses in sustainability (resilience, land-use, etc.), environment (science), and society (law, policy, behavior). Student achievement in each realm should be documented and at the same time, the assessment strategy should be innovative and showcase the integrated nature of such programs.

A spatial-visual model was constructed for the SES major at Central Michigan University. This model maps the curriculum on a ternary diagram with the sustainability, environment, and society components at the vertices. Each required course’s position on the diagram is determined by an analysis of its student learning outcomes (SLOs), i.e., what the students do in the course, as codified in the master course syllabus (MCS). Visual inspection of the diagram allowed faculty to identify areas of the curriculum that are redundant or need reinforcement. Results show that as a group, the program’s 12 required in-house courses are evenly distributed among the three SES components. However, the courses themselves and their SLOs are not equal blends of components. Courses with more internally balanced SLOs are at the 300-level.

Student achievement data can be added to this diagram in a third dimension, analogous to how a sandstone’s matrix content is displayed on a QFL diagram. For each course, whether 80% of students demonstrated 80% proficiency in the SLOs was plotted on the third axis to form a 3D snapshot of student achievement. Visual inspection of the plot shows where students are meeting benchmarks and/or opportunities for improvement. 3-D printing technology potentially allows for a tactile deliverable: an assessment report as a physical object.

This model would allow for immediate feedback on proposed curricular changes, as opposed to the more common “let’s add a class and see what happens” strategy.

abstract:
The Cretaceous Mancos Shale is a natural source of sediment, salinity, and selenium in western Colorado, and anthropogenic disturbances on Mancos Shale landscapes can expose and mobilize those constituents, leading to increased concentrations in surface water. Stinking Water Creek is an arroyo and a tributary to the White River near Rangely, Colorado. The basin, which overlies Mancos Shale, experienced land-use change in the 1800s and 1900s with the introduction of grazing and oil and gas development. Continued development of oil and gas resources has the potential to increase landscape disturbances and alter water quality. Understanding the effects of past land-use change could help resource managers to prepare for increased landscape disturbance that might occur in the future.

The U.S. Geological Survey used optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) and radiometric dating techniques to characterize the ages of sediment on Stinking Water Creek and provide information about the timing of arroyo cutting relative to periods of land-use change. In general, the ages of OSL samples from Stinking Water Creek fall into five broad categories: 8.5-8 thousand years ago (ka), 4.7-4.5 ka, 3.8-3.1 ka, 2.0-1.6 ka, 1.2-0.91 ka, and 0.73- 0.68 ka. One date that reflects a younger deposit (160 ± 10 years) was obtained in a previous study of headwater subbasins of Stinking Water Creek. Although no other modern deposits were identified, the results of this study help to characterize the geomorphic history of Stinking Water Creek. The OSL results provide evidence of multiple cycles of cutting and filling, similar to other arroyos in the Southwestern United States. Given the existing OSL dataset and the lack of data on past streamflow and loads, it is not possible to attribute portions of erosion in the Stinking Water Creek basin to time periods with intense grazing and energy development. However, this study nonetheless provides an important keystone site for future arroyo studies.

title: Validating a Numerical Model of Large Wood Transport in Forested River Corridors
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Welsh, Josie Taylor [1], Lininger, Katherine [2], Ruiz-Villanueva, Virginia [3]
affiliations: (1) Geography, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Geography, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Geography, University of Bern, Bern, Bern, Switzerland
abstract:
Large wood (LW; >10 cm in diameter and >1 m in length) in river corridors (channels and adjacent floodplains) shapes hydraulic conditions, sediment dynamics, nutrient cycling, and habitat availability for diverse species. Thus, to fully understand how a river system functions, and how it will change through time, we must be able to predict why, when, and how LW is stored and transported.

We assessed the ability of IberWood, an existing 2D numerical model which couples hydraulics, sediment, and LW transport, to reproduce LW transport behavior in forested river corridors. We compared numerical simulations with results from physical experiments conducted in a 1:20 scale fixed bed flume with a sinuous channel inset into a planar floodplain. The flume contained vertically fixed dowels in a grid pattern to represent floodplain trees, and we varied the grid spacing across experiments to explore the role of forest stand density (FSD) on LW depositional patterns. We applied the IberWood model to reproduce the physical experiments, representing floodplain trees as holes in the computational mesh. We used flow depth and velocity measurements from the physical experiments to calibrate the modelled surface roughness parameters, then ran the model for multiple FSD scenarios to replicate the flume experiments. The simulated hydraulic conditions were compared with the experimental results to validate model performance. For each scenario, we compared curves for LW volume vs distance downstream and metrics such as the fraction of LW retained in the model overall and the fraction of LW retained on the floodplain only. Preliminary results show that LW accumulates against floodplain trees, consistent with flume experiments and previous field observations that identify trees as key retention sites for transported LW. However, IberWood generally underestimated LW retention for all FSD scenarios tested, aligning with previous studies, which observed IberWood underestimating LW deposition in other riverine environments. Still, the model is able to reproduce observed depositional patterns.

This work represents a step forward in understanding LW transport in complex forested environments and demonstrates the potential of IberWood as a powerful tool for exploring scenarios beyond those that can be readily tested in physical experiments. Future numerical simulations will leverage this capability to investigate how channel sinuosity, planform complexity, and forest structure influence LW transport and deposition dynamics.

title: Hydrogeologic parameters for the Tensleep aquifer in Wyoming
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes (Posters)

affiliations: (1) Wyoming State Geological Survey, Laramie, WY, USA
(2) Wyoming State Geological Survey, Laramie, WY, USA
abstract:
Comprehensive characterization of the Tensleep aquifer's hydrogeologic properties and water quality is essential for sustainable water resource management and for understanding regional, basin-scale groundwater flow systems in Wyoming. This study synthesizes hydrogeologic data for the Tensleep aquifer and related rock units throughout the state.

Long-term average recharge estimates, based on baseflow studies, are highest in the central-western Bighorn Mountains, central Wyoming Range, northwestern Gros Ventre Range, and southeastern Bighorn Mountains. Analysis of water-drive oil fields, using data from Wyoming Geological Association field symposium volumes, indicates groundwater flow within the Tensleep aquifer basinward from Tensleep outcrops and beyond springs associated with suspected rejected recharge.

Water-quality mapping, using U.S. Geological Survey and Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission databases, shows that salinity generally increases from mountain flanks toward deeper parts of the basins. The northeastern Powder River Basin exhibits exceptionally high salinity, including peak chloride and sodium concentrations. Statewide, many parts of the Tensleep have high sodium-adsorption ratios, which limit the aquifer’s suitability as a source of irrigation water.

Borehole and water-sample temperatures generally increase with depth; however, an anomalous zone of cooler water coincides with the highly saline region in the northeastern Powder River Basin. The cause of this localized thermal and chemical anomaly remains unknown.

abstract: Nutrient availability plays a fundamental role in regulating biological productivity, ecosystem structure, and biogeochemical cycling in freshwater environments. Nitrogen and phosphorus are key nutrients that influence ecosystem productivity and can exhibit unique behavior in glacier-influenced landscapes. Recent research suggests that glacial ice, meltwater, and newly formed proglacial lakes can serve as important sources and reservoirs of phosphorus, influencing downstream nutrient availability. This study investigates phosphorus concentrations in glacial ice, proglacial lakes, and rivers across Iceland. Water samples collected from sites representing different stages of the hydrologic continuum were analyzed in the field for phosphate concentrations. Spatial patterns in phosphorus availability were evaluated to assess how nutrient concentrations vary from glacial sources to downstream aquatic environments. Findings from this work will improve our understanding of nutrient cycling and phosphorus dynamics in glacier-influenced regions and provide insight into the potential effects of continued glacier retreat on freshwater ecosystems in Iceland.

title: Building a Geological Field Team on the Moon: The GLEE Distributed Exploration System
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation
authors: Herzog, Emma Rose [1], Sobhani, Barbra [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado Space Grant Consortium, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(2) University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado Space Grant Consortium, Boulder, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Traditional planetary missions are fundamentally limited by their ability to investigate only a single location on the surface. While orbiters provide regional context and landers deliver local measurements, connected observations across multiple spatial scales remains a persistent challenge in planetary geology. The Great Lunar Expedition for Everyone (GLEE) introduces a distributed exploration architecture that bridges this gap by transforming a single landed mission into a coordinated network of autonomous surface instruments capable of investigating geological processes over a broad area.

GLEE consists of a Housing and Deployment Module (HDM) that delivers and deploys more than one hundred solar-powered LunaSats following lunar landing. Each LunaSat operates as an independent scientific station equipped with accelerometers, a magnetometer, temperature sensor, capacitive sensor, and wireless communications. Together, these nodes function as a synchronized surface observatory, allowing simultaneous measurements of seismic activity, magnetic variability, thermal evolution, and regolith properties while preserving the spatial relationships necessary to interpret geological processes. The architecture combines distributed sensing, autonomous operations, communication through a mesh network, and synchronized timing into a scalable platform designed to extend the scientific reach of a single landed mission.

Rather than emphasizing individual technologies, GLEE demonstrates how systems-level integration enables a fundamentally different approach to planetary field investigations. Distributed networks are a well-practiced Earth method of studying seismic activity that has not yet been applied in planetary explorations. Additionally, deployment strategies, networking, communication architecture, and mission operations are designed as interconnected components that maximize spatial coverage while maintaining coordinated scientific observations. This systems perspective allows geological investigation to move beyond isolated measurements, toward regional datasets capable of resolving environmental gradients, transient events, and heterogenous surface properties.

GLEE represents a scalable framework for future distributed planetary missions, illustrating how coordinated networks of compact surface instruments can complement traditional orbiters and landers while expanding the scientific capabilities available for lunar and planetary exploration.

title: Whispers from the dead: Fossil-informed diversification trajectories and their impact on phylogenetic inference
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Mongiardino Koch, Nicolás [1], Wang, Shelley L [2], Simões, Tiago R [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Biology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA; Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(2) Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(3) Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
abstract:
The introduction of the fossilized birth-death (FBD) process as a means of proposing phylogenetic histories during inference has revolutionized phylogenetic paleobiology. Underlying its success is the mechanistic realism that it provides: trees are built using the same processes that dictate the diversification (speciation, extinction) and recovery (fossilization, sampling) of lineages within a clade, providing a framework that naturally accommodates lineages that are sampled across geologic timescales. FBD processes can also directly leverage stratigraphic information, often allowing for a greater paleontological input than alternative methods of phylogenetic reconstruction. This can be done in two major ways: 1) using tip dates, which force extinct lineages to occur at a given temporal window; and 2) incorporating estimates of speciation and extinction rates obtained from large collections of fossil occurrences. In recent years, new methods and protocols have been developed in an attempt to combine both approaches. One example is the implementation of tip-dated inference under time-variable diversification regimes (known as a skyline FBD process). While this represents a promising avenue that simultaneously maximizes both paleontological input and modelling realism, studies have been ambiguous regarding whether it significantly enhances phylogenetic accuracy.

Recent efforts have produced a phylogenetic framework for living and extinct sea urchins (Echinoidea) that simultaneously leverages their exceptional genomic, morphological, and stratigraphic information. We extend these efforts by exploring the topological and temporal effects introduced through the use of fossil-informed skyline FBD processes. To do so, we characterize the temporal signal of diversification for crown-group Echinoidea using the software PyRate on a curated list of fossil occurrences drawn from the Paleobiology Database. We then explore the phylogenetic effects of incorporating these diversification estimates as tree priors on total-evidence dating. Results are compared against those obtained using various simpler priors, as well as against first fossil occurrences of major clades. Our efforts provide an empirical benchmark that informs the extent to which paleontological estimates of past diversification contribute to phylogenetic estimation.

title: XRD and Major Element Analysis of the Wedington Sandstone Member, Arkansas, as a Terrestrial Analog to the Shenandoah Formation, Western Fan, Jezero Crater, Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars (Posters)
authors: Lafevers, Michael B [1], Testa, Maurice [2]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, University of Arkansas Fort Smith, Van Buren, AR, USA
(2) Geoscience, University of Arkansas, Fort Smith, AR, USA
abstract:
Terrestrial analogs guide how we read Martian sedimentary structures, but morphological similarity does not guarantee compositional or process similarity. Previous work on the Mississippian Wedington Sandstone Member (WSM) in northwest Arkansas shows it is a topographically inverted river-delta deposit with coastal backwater signatures, setting it apart from megafan analogs commonly used for Martian fans. The Shenandoah Formation, the lower 25 m of Jezero crater's western-fan eastern scarp, is a sand-dominated succession found on Mars that records a shift from distal alluvial-fan deposits through a saline lake to river-delta progradation. We test whether bulk chemistry supports using the WSM as more than a morphological proxy for that succession.

Using Perseverance traverse and sol data in GIS, compared against published Shenandoah member boundaries and Planetary Data System images, the Rockytop member stood out as the strongest visual analog to the WSM, based on shared soft-sediment deformation and honeycomb weathering.

XRD and major element analysis were conducted on samples from an exposed WSM outcrop near Bayyari Park. We sampled at 6-inch vertical intervals, pulverized powders in a ball mill, and screened them by X-ray diffraction (XRD). Samples spanning a range of mineral signatures were analyzed for major elements by X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) and compared with published Perseverance geochemistry from Rockytop/Shenandoah intervals.

authors: VanHook, Matthew [1], Galarza, Mason A [2], Bieker, Ross [3], Kelly, Tucker [4], Testa, Maurice [5], Larson, Erik [6]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fort Smith, AR, USA

abstract:
Polycam® is a low-cost application installed on mobile devices such as phones and tablets and utilizes a combination of the low power LiDAR and camera technologies of the device to create 3D models; however, the limitations and functionality of Polycam® have not yet been fully tested for accuracy in a scientific setting. Previous research investigated the best methodology for submeter accuracy using a LiDAR equipped mobile device and Polycam®. For this project, a LiDAR camera equipped Apple iPhone®16 Pro was used.

First, this project assesses low-light capabilities within a littoral cave in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. Because Polycam® integrates photogrammetry with LiDAR, ambient or artificial light is required. By attaching an artificial light source to the iPhone, this test evaluated how variations in light intensity and color temperature (3000–5000 Kelvin) impact in-app measurement accuracy and the resolution of the resulting photogrammetry layer.

Second, the project investigated large-scale data acquisition by scanning a 40-meter ancient knoll reef, expanding beyond previously tested 8-meter outcrop limits in previous work. The area scanned also had natural challenges from varying ambient light and shadows from tree coverage. The reef was mapped using two distinct methods: a gridded approach (sixteen 10-meter grids processed individually on-site and then merged using Polycam® stitching and extended scan function) and a single, continuous large-scale scan. Both scans were measured using Polycam® in-app measurement and were compared to manual measurements.

Ultimately, this work establishes clear methodological guidelines and defines the practical constraints of mobile LiDAR applications for field researchers.

abstract: In this contribution, our team shares perspectives on a partnership built initially by Mario Assine (São Paulo State University - Campus Rio Claro) and Andy Cohen (University of Arizona) in 2004, which subsequently has grown through several cohorts of dedicated graduate students that continues the research and training program through the present day. The focus of partnership is the fluvial geomorphology and limnogeology of the Pantanal, one of the world’s great topical wetlands, situated in the headwaters of the Paraguay River (South America). Research by international teams in the Pantanal face a daunting set of challenges, including: (i) the Pantanal spans three international borders (Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay) with various federal agencies holding responsibility for regulation, governance, and permitting, (ii) the Pantanal is a vast, wild, and remote riverine environment with limited infrastructure and shifting patterns of seasonal flooding, making navigation and fieldwork very difficult, (iii) bi-directional language and cultural differences in research and training processes, (iv) limited access to private property and protected areas and (v) few opportunities for building trust and networking with local pantaneiros . The partnership has thrived, despite numerous hurdles, owing to the mutual respect and friendship among the team members, a strong commitment to progressive student mentoring, and an unwavering interest in advancing geoscientific knowledge on the form, function, and history of the Pantanal. abstract:
We are producing a standardized USGS Scientific Investigation Map (SIM) series geologic map of Mars Transverse Mercator (MTM) quadrangles 05022, 05017, -00022, and -00017 that encompasses the initial and medial portions of the Ares Vallis channel from the chaotic terrain at Aram Chaos, Iani Chaos, and Hydaspis Chaos (-2.5 to 7.5°N latitude, 335 to 345°E longitude). All mapping is being done at 1:1,000,000 (1:1M) in ArcPro using a CTX mosaic as the basemap, supplemented with THEMIS Daytime and Nighttime IR mosaics, HRSC-MOLA DEM topography, HiRISE images, and CRISM spectral parameters. We have defined 32 geologic units in our map and have divided them into 6 groups: Chaos Units, Highland Units, Crater Units, Channel Units, Landslide Unit, Sedimentary Units. Surface features include secondary crater chains and linear features include depression margins, wrinkle ridges, troughs, grabens, crater rims, and channels.

All surface flow can be mapped back to chaos terrain in the south, supporting the idea that formation of the chaos terrain resulted in the release of surface water that modified and eroded much of the map region. Sedimentary deposits composed of smooth fill occur throughout much of the highlands, indicating periods of both erosion and deposition as the flow changed in velocity and strength. The ferric hydroxysulfate found within Aram Chaos can only form by heating hydrated ferrous sulfates above 100°C and it is associated with upturned and tilted chaos blocks, implying a heating event within the subsurface relatively recently in martian history (<3 billion years ago). Potential geothermal heating could have arisen from intrusion of magma near the surface that would have melted and released large quantities of water stored in the subsurface, leading to formation of the chaos and surface water flow. A summarized geologic history includes: (1) Formation of the impact basin which now encompasses Aram Chaos; (2) Collection of water in the subsurface from the Uzboi-Morava-Ladon outflow channel system; (3) Magmatic heating in the subsurface that released water across a broad area and formed the chaos; (4) Confinement of water into major channels (Ares and Jhelum Vallis); (5) Deposition of sulfates within Aram and Iani chaos; (6) Continued heating in the subsurface to alter some monohydrated sulfates to ferric hydroxysulfate, and also uplift and tilting of pre-existing chaos blocks within Aram.

abstract:
Dye tracing is a well-established method for mapping groundwater flow in karst aquifers; however, it has only recently been applied within the Eastern Unit of the Hiawatha National Forest in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. The area's underlying geology consists of early Silurian dolostones characterized by prominent epikarst features, including grikes, alvar, sinkholes, and springs. No solutional caves have been identified in the Forest, however there are numerous littoral caves formed by prior high lake levels in proximity to the forest.

Previous research involved qualitative dye traces conducted within the forest to lay the groundwork for future tracing initiatives. A trace was conducted at Biscuit Sink, a sinking stream that flows directly into joints in a rock face near the Mackinac–Chippewa county line, approximately 400 meters away. Dye was detected after the charcoal packets were collected two weeks after dye injection.

This project continues the previous work with a quantitative approach. Two pounds of fluorescein dye were released in Biscuit Sink. An autosampler was used at Biscuit Spring, located approximately 400 meters away and collected 500 mL of water from the spring every 15 minutes for 10 hours. This analysis was used to determine discharge rates and determine the shape of the breakthrough curve. Peak fluorescence was observed approximately 3 hours after dye injection at 415 ppb. The breakthrough curve was a typical shape with a steep rising limb, and a gentler falling limb that becomes shallow. This suggests that flow is conduit based with some mixed and diffuse flow

title: Detrital Versus Neoblastic Metamorphic Minerals: Textural Criteria and the Challenge of High-Grade Metaclastic Rocks
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Wakabayashi, John [1]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Fresno, CA, USA
abstract: Detrital metamorphic minerals are easy to petrographically identify when present in clastic sedimentary rocks of lower grade than their formation. For example, glaucophane is clearly detrital in rocks of prehnite-pumpellyite facies or lower, as is biotite in sub-greenschist facies rocks. Metamorphic minerals of the same metamorphic grade as the host metaclastic rock require detailed textural examination to differentiate neoblastic from detrital origin. The textural relationships in little-metamorphosed and lightly-deformed rocks prove useful in distinguishing detrital versus neoblastic minerals in more strongly metamorphosed and deformed rocks. The key grain boundaries are those oriented at high angles to the foliation. For detrital minerals, such boundaries abruptly truncate (no drag features) internal mineral structure such as cleavage or exsolution lamellae. Such apparent detrital grain boundaries may show primary detrital rounding that has been physically removed from foliation-parallel surfaces. This textural relationship can be viewed in clasts in conglomerates. The detrital nature of blueschist clasts in blueschist facies conglomerates is shown by abrupt truncation of internal mineral growth along the clast boundaries. Neoblastic minerals grow across apparent detrital grain boundaries and commonly exhibit sharp mineral terminations in such cases, in contrast with the expectation for a detrital metamorphic mineral (rounded/subrounded). Metamorphic mineral growth entirely within a detrital grain (and not reaching its boundaries) cannot be distinguished as neoblastic or detrital if such minerals are compatible with unambiguous neoblastic mineral assemblages in the same rock. Commonly, neoblastic overgrowths form fringes on detrital metamorphic minerals, such as fine glaucophane needles on the margin of a larger detrital glaucophane grain. Owing to their platy habit, distinguishing neoblastic from detrital micas is difficult, because mica plates tend to be parallel/subparallel to foliation whether detrital or neoblastic. In some blueschist facies metaclastic rocks, apparent detrital phengite is significantly coarser than the probable neoblastic phengite. At higher metamorphic grades post-depositional recrystallization makes recognition of detrital minerals difficult. An alleged detrital eclogite clast in an eclogite is defined by abrupt truncation of omphacite and phengite across a boundary at high angle to the foliation. Finer phengite and omphacite locally overgrow such boundaries. Apparent detrital garnets are coarser, subhedral to anhedral, with more complex zoning than apparent neoblastic euhedral ones. Chemical compositions of metamorphic minerals may test detrital versus neoblastic interpretations based on petrography.

title: Lead Contamination in Soils at a Former Trapshooting Site in Cheney, Washington, USA
session_title: Mineralogical Insights from Modern Spectroscopic Techniques (Posters)

abstract: Characterizing the distribution of lead (Pb) at trapshooting sites provides a clearer understanding of environmental impacts and informs the development of potential remediation strategies. The goal of this study was to investigate the factors that determine the mobility, availability and vertical distribution of Pb in the soil at a trapshooting range. The study area is a trapshooting range on a 120-acre parcel owned by Eastern Washington University in Cheney, Washington. The land was used for wheat farming from the 1950s to the early 2020s and is currently being restored to native prairie landscape. Trapshooting occurred for several decades as part of university-sanctioned activities. Soils were sampled at 20-m intervals along a transect (perpendicular to the firing line) from the presumed location of the trap house to 140 m downrange. Soils were collected at depths of 0-5, 5-10, and 10-15 cm, and were gently crushed and sieved with 0.5-mm mesh to separate shot pellets from soil particles. The pellets were examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The <0.5 mm fraction was leached in 1 M nitric acid and analyzed using inductively coupled plasma – optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). The soil Pb concentration at 20 m was 26 ± 2 mg/kg soil, comparable to the background concentrations in soils surrounding the trapshooting range. Along the transect, Pb values peaked at 664 ± 20 mg/kg soil at 80 m then decreased to 82 ± 57 mg/kg soil at 140 m. The spatial distribution of Pb in soils mirrored that found in plants analyzed in a previous study. Elevated soil Pb concentrations were detected throughout the sampled soil profile at distances of 40 m to 140 m, likely reflecting physical mixing associated with tillage. Shot pellets (~2-mm diameter) were recovered from several samples at various depth intervals. SEM imaging of pellets revealed surface weathering, and EDS analysis confirmed that the pellets were composed dominantly of Pb.

title: Wildfires as Drivers of Differential Headwater Stream Geometry in the Colorado Front Range, USA
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society (Posters)
authors: Larkin, Katherine E. [1], Wohl, Ellen E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA

abstract: Headwater channels function as primary controls on downstream resources, including sediment, water, and organic matter. We define headwaters as Strahler first- and second-order streams as determined in the field, where first-order channel heads are the farthest upstream zones of channelized flow with fluvial features, and second-order channels are created at the intersection of two first-order channels. Headwater channels are highly sensitive to fluctuations in sediment and water supplies and thus can be transient features following disturbances. We hypothesize that headwater channel networks respond dynamically to post-wildfire changes in surface and subsurface conditions that alter rainfall-runoff relationships and influence the magnitude and timing of surface flow, resulting in diverging widths, depths, and lengths between recently burned and unburned areas. Our primary objective is to evaluate differences in headwater channel geometry and flow sources (groundwater, runoff) between sites that have recently burned and sites that have not recently burned. We delineated headwater channel networks and measured bankfull widths, depths, and approximate lengths for 160 first-order channels and 26 second-order channels in seven northern Colorado catchments, and evaluated i) pairwise relationships within the dataset and ii) statistical distributions characterizing the range of flow geometries observed in recently and non-recently burned first- and second-order channels. Preliminary findings indicate that geometries and dominant flow sources of recently and non-recently burned channels vary significantly, but statistical distributions characterizing channel geometry remain similar regardless of disturbance history.

abstract: Soil inorganic carbon (SIC) plays a critical role in carbon storage, particularly in semi-arid environments where it often constitutes a significant portion of the total soil carbon pool. This study investigates how land use and soil thickness influence SIC accumulation in soils across a semi-arid landscape of the Snake River Plain, near Kimberly, in south-central Idaho. Twenty-two soil profiles were sampled from native and agricultural soils to determine the SIC storage. Our results show that the depth-normalized mean SIC density for one meter is 33.6 ± 4.8 (kg/m 3 ) for native soils and 38.9 ± 5.4 (kg/m 3 ) for irrigated soils. The mean SIC stocks for the entire soil profile is 91.2 ± 12.8 kg/m 2 for native soils for an average thickness of 2.54 m and 102.2 ± 14.3 kg/m 2 for irrigated soils that are 2.79 m thick on average. Results reveal a moderate, but statistically significant positive correlation (R² = 0.63) between soil thickness and SIC stocks, suggesting that soil thickness is an important factor influencing SIC storage. As soil thickness increases, the capacity for SIC accumulation also increases. Both extrapolated SIC and soil depth maps produced larger estimates of SIC stocks (kg/m 2 ) and soil depth, respectively, compared to previous studies in our study area. These higher estimates resulted from incorporating measured data points of both soil depth and SIC stocks for reliable depth estimation and SIC quantification/storage. Our results show that SIC stocks in irrigated soils are apparently higher, however, the ANOVA results for three paired native and irrigated soil profiles show broadly similar SIC distributions between land uses, with depth exerting a significant effect, while land use and its interaction with depth were not significant. This suggests that land use has no statistically detectable effect on SIC storage after ~120 years of cultivation.

abstract: A paleoseismic trench was excavated across the western end of the 1976 earthquake rupture of the Motagua Fault at the Finca de Concepción site near San Martín Jilotepeque, Guatemala, to identify evidence of earthquakes that predate the 1976 event. To support this objective and constrain the depositional environment, this study characterizes the exposed sedimentary units using X-ray diffraction (XRD), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) coupled with scanning electron microscopy (SEM), grain identification, and grain-size analysis. Radiocarbon dating of carbon samples, together with the identification of Maya pottery sherds and modern debris, provided chronological constraints on the sedimentary units. The trench exposed nine sedimentary units. The lower sequence (Units 6–9) consists primarily of silty clays and the sandy Unit 7 channel, whereas the upper sequence (Units 1–5) is composed mainly of poorly sorted sandy-clayey silts overlying the sandy Unit 5 channel. Both channel deposits are filled with quartz grains and biotite-rich crystal tuff sand derived from the local bedrock. Plagioclase, hornblende, and quartz occur throughout many of the units. The clay in the upper sequence contains smectite, vermiculite, and zeolites compared to the kaolinite and smectite-rich lower sequence. Multiple clay-filled fractures along shears are present throughout the lower sequence, with some extending into the upper units. The fracture-fill mineralogy differs from that of the surrounding sediments, consisting only of quartz and clays and lacking hornblende and plagioclase. Units 6–9 were deposited between approximately 8.5 and 4.5 ka and are interpreted as overbank floodplain deposits. The sand fraction of the fine-grained Unit 7 contains roots but no identifiable microfossils, indicating there was no standing water. Radiocarbon age modeling indicates that Unit 6 is separated from the overlying Units 1–5 by a ~4,000-year hiatus, likely due to erosion. The upper sequence is therefore interpreted as younger fine-grained overbank deposits that were subsequently modified by pedogenic processes and agricultural activity. Collectively, these data suggest that the small Finca de Concepción basin within the Motagua Fault zone has been shaped primarily by tectonic subsidence, likely associated with multiple fault strands. However, the erosional hiatus in the stratigraphic record leaves an incomplete archive of paleoearthquakes, limiting reconstruction of the site's earthquake history.

abstract: Soils and paleoenvironmental research in the San Juan Mountains of Durango, Colorado reveal spatial and temporal patterns of Holocene forest change on a geomorphic template dominated by glacial end moraines and 150m-high glaciofluvial terraces. The treeless landscapes depicted in late 19th century photographs stand in stark contrast to the city’s rich, modern canopy. We use a multi-proxy approach that combines soil stratigraphy, pollen analysis, radiocarbon dating, historical research, and repeat photography to ask the following question: Do early photographs accurately reveal a semi-arid and treeless late-Holocene Durango, or was the Durango area naturally forested, clear-cut by 19th century settlers, and later reforested? Wetland cores from within city limits produced early Holocene ages of ~9570 to 8700 14C years BP with dominant herbaceous pollen species such as Artemisia, Asteraceae, and Amaranthaceae and limited forest pollen. These results suggest early-Holocene Durango was likely semi-arid and open, as opposed to forest. A buried paleowetland at the base of an Animas River terrace, also within city limits, produced ages of ~920 14C years BP with pollen showing 63% pine and spruce suggesting dominant conifer forest cover in the late Holocene. Soil and sediment profiles from Animas River cutbanks show multiple stacked AC profiles and two continuous charcoal lenses providing evidence of general instability and basin-wide forest fires in the late Holocene. Durango's 2024 tree inventory shows the modern canopy includes many introduced and ornamental species. These lines of evidence suggest that Durango's tree canopy is not simply a remnant of a lost forest, but rather a living archive shaped by Holocene climate change, disturbance, settlement, planting, and urban management. Further data are being collected to fill in the gaps, specifically between ~150 and 900 years BP. This novel study opens a new window into Durango's paleoenviroment and offers useful context for future urban forest planning in a changing climate.

abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) has acquired high-resolution airborne geophysical surveys over the Idaho-Montana porphyry belt to investigate mineral systems and their underlying geologic framework. Approximately 80,000 line-kilometers of magnetic and radiometric data now characterize historic mining areas associated with Late Cretaceous igneous rocks of the Boulder batholith region of southwestern Montana and sedimentary rocks that comprise large structural culminations of the Sevier fold-thrust belt and Laramide intraforeland uplifts. As a corollary to use in identifying, mapping, and assessing mineral systems, we demonstrate that geophysical datasets are sufficiently detailed for intermediate-scale (i.e., 1:100,000-scale) geologic mapping and thus may be used predictively in frontier field areas. We compare new radiometric datasets to existing 1:100,000-scale geologic map data across the Devil’s Fence Anticline, which lies immediately east of the Boulder batholith. The structure exposes approximately 4 km of Mesoproterozoic through Lower Cretaceous siliciclastic and carbonate strata, as well as various Late Cretaceous intrusions and volcanic rocks. Our comparison clearly shows stratigraphically controlled radiometric responses that highlight four distinct rock packages corresponding to the Mesoproterozoic Belt Supergroup, Paleozoic miogeoclinal strata, Mesozoic foreland basin strata, and Late Cretaceous through Cenozoic igneous rocks. By grid-sampling radiometric data using 1:100,000-scale geologic map polygons, we quantify K, Th, and U signatures of individual stratal units to simulate, on a coarse scale, traditional gamma ray logs from cores. Mesoproterozoic strata and Jurassic-Cretaceous strata are characterized by relatively high K and Th, whereas K and Th in Paleozoic strata are relatively low. U is uniformly low across all stratigraphic levels. The observed trends, verified with handheld gamma ray spectrometer measurements, closely follow lithologic and compositional variation through the section, wherein high K and Th in siliciclastic Mesoproterozoic strata correlate to quartzofeldspathic compositions; low K and Th in Paleozoic strata correlate to quartzose sandstone compositions and thick carbonate intervals; and higher K and Th in siliciclastic Mesozoic strata correlate to abundant lithic detritus. The integration of these data can, therefore, aid in mapping and understanding sedimentary environments in frontier areas with uncertain geologic histories.

abstract:
The tectonic evolution of the southern North American Cordillera reflects multiple episodes of Cretaceous–Paleogene contraction, magmatism, and extension, complicating links between deformation structures and their geodynamic drivers. In the Old Woman Mountains (OWM), southeastern California, penetrative ductile fabrics have been interpreted to record either synmagmatic partial melting and deformation during the emplacement of the Late Cretaceous Old Woman Mountains pluton or to a separate shearing event in the OWM Western Shear Zone (WSZ). To evaluate the relationship between magmatism and deformation, we integrate apatite U-Pb petrochronology, zircon U-Pb geochronology, field and structural observations, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) from Proterozoic basement and Late Cretaceous plutonic rocks.

Overlapping zircon and apatite U-Pb ages constrain the emplacement of the Old Woman Mountains pluton to ca. 72 Ma within the Proterozoic crystalline basement (zircon ages of ca. 1350–1750 Ma). Apatite U-Pb ages from WSZ biotite schists and foliated dikes surrounding the pluton (ca. 70–73 Ma) are consistent with deformation-related apatite recrystallization or growth synchronous with pluton emplacement. The dominant WNW–ESE magnetic lineations in the pluton (AMS) and ductile deformation fabrics in the host biotite schists (EBSD) indicate development of a coherent, pluton-scale ductile domal geometry during emplacement. Biotite schists outside the WSZ also yield Late Cretaceous apatite U-Pb ages (ca. 67–72 Ma), demonstrating that deformation associated with pluton emplacement extended beyond the mapped WSZ in the OWM. Collectively, these datasets indicate deformation was synchronous and spatially linked with Late Cretaceous pluton emplacement, supporting a synmagmatic origin for the penetrative ductile fabrics in the OWM.

Unlike nearby ranges of the Colorado River Extensional Corridor, where Paleocene–Eocene and Miocene deformation events extensively overprint the Late Cretaceous record, the OWM preserve a predominantly Late Cretaceous record of magmatism and deformation. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that hinterland architecture was constructed diachronously across the southern Cordillera, with individual mountain ranges recording distinct magmatic and tectonic processes. Furthermore, these results demonstrate that integrating petrochronology with microstructural and magnetic fabric analysis provides a robust framework for reconstructing the relative contributions of magmatic versus tectonic events to the fabric development in plutonic terranes elsewhere in the Cordillera and other orogenic systems.

abstract:
The Rutgers University Geology Museum (RUGM) seeks to inspire curiosity about Earth’s history by connecting scientific discovery with public education. My Friend Manny, a children's book about Manny, the museum’s mastodon fossil, demonstrates how storytelling and visual art can expand public engagement with geological and historical concepts.

Through Manny’s story, readers explore Ice Age ecosystems, mastodon biology and extinction, and the geologic processes that shaped their world. The narrative also highlights the historical development of the Rutgers University Geology Museum and the individuals whose efforts helped preserve and interpret New Jersey’s natural heritage. Artwork and character design enhance accessibility and engagement, demonstrating the role of visual communication in interpreting scientific and historical information. By integrating art, science, and history, My Friend Manny demonstrates how museum collections can serve as powerful tools for informal geoscience education, connect audiences to Earth's deep past, and foster appreciation for scientific and cultural heritage.

abstract: Iceland's volcanic landscape provides a unique natural laboratory for investigating how basaltic lava compositions vary across space and time. This study examines geochemical differences among basaltic lava flows of varying ages across Iceland to evaluate patterns of geochemical variability and magmatic evolution. Representative lava flow samples spanning approximately 10,000 years were analyzed in the field using portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) to determine major and trace element abundances. Elemental concentrations and selected geochemical ratios are being compared to identify spatial and temporal trends in basalt composition. The results will contribute to a better understanding of the factors influencing geochemical variability in Iceland's volcanic systems and provide insights into the evolution of one of the world's most active volcanic landscapes.

abstract:
The pre-Illinoian Kansan glaciation dammed the ancestral Kansas River valley in northeastern Kansas, forming proglacial Kaw Lake and depositing a thick succession of glaciolacustrine sediments preserved within a buried valley system. A 20 m (65 ft) sediment core recovered in 2008 from the buried valley on the Kansas State University campus documented the sedimentary sequence, but the age of Kaw Lake remains uncertain. Existing age estimates are based primarily on stratigraphic and paleomagnetic evidence rather than direct numerical dating. Preliminary paleomagnetic data indicate that the lake sediments have normal magnetic polarity and are likely younger than 780 ka. The objective of this project is to establish the direct chronology for Kaw Lake sediments using luminescence dating techniques and to evaluate the hypothesis that lake formation occurred during the late Kansan glaciation (~600-700 ka).

Future field investigations will include recovery of a second sediment core from the buried valley northwest of Manhattan, Kansas, followed by luminescence dating of the recovered sediments to further test and refine the chronology. Preliminary K-feldspar IRSL analyses of samples from the 2008 Kaw Lake core suggest depositional ages of several hundred thousand years. To establish a more robust chronology, elevated-temperature K-feldspar infrared stimulated luminescence (IRSL) methods, including post-IR IRSL (pIRIR) and post-isothermal IRSL (pIt-IR) protocols, will be applied. Several dating protocols have been proposed related to IRSL signals, with successful applications demonstrating their capability to date Middle Pleistocene deposits. These protocols will be applied to both the newly recovered core and the remaining samples from the 2008 core, archived in the Luminescence Dating Laboratory at Kansas State University. Quartz optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating will also be applied to younger deposits, where appropriate, to provide comparative age data to IRSL in the upper loess units.

Comparison of results from the two cores will refine the depositional chronology of Kaw Lake and better constrain the timing of glacial advance. The resulting age framework will improve correlations between regional glacial deposits and marine isotope stages and contribute to a better understanding of Middle Pleistocene ice-sheet dynamics.
