abstract: Colorado’s Tavakaiv (Tava) sandstone preserves a rare terrestrial record of sedimentary injectites formed during low paleolatitude Sturtian glaciation (690-660 Ma) during the Cryogenian Period. The injectites consist of mostly structureless quartzose sandstone that preserves textures characteristic of fluidization, and sufficient pressure to force sand into fractured granite. Lesser known are elongate ridges of Tava sandstone that are kilometers long, and tens to hundreds of meters wide. Here, we focus on a km-scale Tava ridge and injectite complex in Buffalo Creek, CO (BC). Mapping the contacts at the site creates a baseline for comparison with other Tava sites and modern analogues. Imaging the surface textures of BC Tava quartz grains using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) determines the mechanisms of transport for Tava sediment. We take advantage of minimal structural overprinting at BC to investigate the processes of sedimentation for the Tava sand ridge via microstructural classification of thin sections, drawing upon recent frameworks for modern subglacial tills (Menzies et al., 10.1139/cjes-2022-0048). Mapping identified a ~2.8 km-long sandstone ridge and injectite complex. This ridge is one of five known Tava sand ridges associated with a network of injectites in the adjacent bedrock. SEM analysis of quartz textures in the Tava yielded mature grains, with polygonal cracking, solution pits, and silica pellicles. The diverse textures indicate multiple transport mechanisms, suggestive of a multi-cycle transport history, consistent with the provenance of Tava detrital zircons from Grenville and local sources. Some thin sections display plasmic fabrics, with rotational structures, grain stacking, and impingement. In others, we observe grain crushing, necking structures, and strain shadows associated with shear planes. The contrasts suggest cyclic textural development due to variations in pore-water presence. The samples may reflect conditions in different parts of a mass of mobilized sediment. Modern bedforms of similar dimensions to the BC sand ridge (km x m) are known to exist under the Rutford Ice Stream in West Antarctica. Radar surveys of the ice stream’s bed identify sediment property variations within streaming bedforms, consistent with the textural differences observed between BC samples. Together, these results represent the first application of micromorphological classification to a Cryogenian terrestrial subglacial deposit, strengthening the case for Tava’s subglacial origin and opening a new avenue for characterizing ancient glacial systems.

abstract:
U.S. led scientific ocean drilling (US SciOD) has revolutionized the geosciences using the dedicated riserless drilling vessels, the Glomar Challenger (1968-1983) and the JOIDES Resolution (1985-2024) to access the subseafloor record, collecting ~97% of the current scientific ocean drilling archive. With the retirement of the Resolution in 2024, US SciOD is transitioning into a new phase using a mission specific platform (MSP) model (i.e., vessels of opportunity). To coordinate MSP activities the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is funding the Scientific Ocean Drilling Coordination Office (SODCO), a partnership between Texas A&M University (TAMU) and Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory at Columbia University (LDEO). SODCO is responsible for assisting principal investigators (PI) with developing operational plans for drilling proposals, coordinating community expedition staffing, and planning and implementing expeditions, including contracting drilling platforms. In addition, SODCO is charged with providing support for community planning via workshops, training and workforce development opportunities, innovation and pre-drilling activity grants, the Schlanger Ocean Drilling graduate fellowship, and program communication and outreach. The award also supports a site survey data bank for site characterization data at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the downhole logging database, LogDB, at LDEO. Drilling proposals can now be submitted to NSF’s Sub-Seafloor Sampling Program (S3P). PIs need to work with SODCO prior to submission to develop the drilling plan and other required documentation.

SODCO will continue to capture the core, fluid, and borehole measurements that compose the robust legacy of SciOD data through offshore operations and onshore laboratory analyses. Critical and ephemeral measurements will be conducted offshore in customized laboratory and support containers by a subset of the expedition science team. Seven containers (physical properties, chemistry, microbiology, curation, IT/database, and two offices) have been designed, acquired, and are being customized by a vendor with expected delivery at the end of the year. Following the shipboard phase, expedition cores will be shipped to the TAMU Gulf Coast Repository (GCR) for the onshore phase of the expedition where the cores will be split, analyzed, and described by the expedition science team in the extensive GCR laboratories.

abstract: Uranium-thorium (U-Th) dating of coastal sedimentary archives has provided valuable insights into the timing and evolution of late Pleistocene sea-level cycles, as well as the underlying climatic mechanisms that drive sea-level change on these timescales. Here, we present a 450,000-year relative sea-level (RSL) reconstruction from the Bahamas derived from U-Th dated cave deposits (speleothems). These caverns, known as “blue holes,” are presently submerged at ~20-50 m below present sea level but developed during past ice ages, when global mean sea level (GMSL) was lower and the caverns were subaerially exposed. In addition to providing an upper bound on sea-surface position during periods of active speleothem growth, many of the growth hiatuses in these speleothems contain iron oxide framboids, which form below the freshwater-saltwater interface in modern cave environments and indicate that the hiatuses were cause by marine inundation. The speleothems used in this study were recovered by experienced cave divers in the late 1980s/early 1990s and played a seminal role in constraining maximum sea levels during the last glacial period. Thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS) measurements have long indicated that the Bahamas cave record extends back to at least Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 12 but generating robust U-Th age controls for growth phases that formed prior to the last glacial cycle have been complicated by slow growth rates, anomalous initial thorium isotopic ratios, and the analytical limitations of early mass spectrometry techniques. Our study targeted these older growth phases to extend the RSL record back to MIS 12 using modern multicollector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (MC-ICP-MS) measurements. The combined Bahamas RSL dataset constrains the timing of sea-level rise in response to the Termination I-IV deglaciations and confirms the presence of active speleothem deposition (and, hence, subaerial exposure) during MIS 12. Isochron measurements reaffirm that an initial [ 230 Th/ 232 Th] ACT ratio of ~7-8 is an adequate first-order approximation for The Bahamas, but we caution that this ratio can meaningfully vary from speleothem to speleothem – even within the same cave system. Taken together, our new reconstruction represents the culmination of more than 30 years of effort to unravel the sea-level story told by these older growth phases.

abstract: Heavy mineral sands (HMS) are of high economic interest owing to their enrichment in “critical minerals” (i.e., those essential to economic function but at risk of supply chain disruption). Unconsolidated HMS have been mined for decades in the eastern USA along the Atlantic Coastal Plain, where recent U.S. Geological Survey (Earth MRI) airborne magnetic and radiometric surveys have revealed strong lateral heterogeneity in heavy mineral concentrations linked to depositional environment, with the highest concentrations consistently observed in beach-shoreface deposits. Similarly, fossil HMS of Upper Cretaceous age have been known for over 100 years across much of the Western Interior region, outcropping in areas extending from Montana and Wyoming southward to Arizona and New Mexico. Although their ages and spatial occurrences vary, they are ubiquitously associated with progradational beach-shoreface deposits. We studied one HMS-bearing section of the Upper Cretaceous Trinidad Sandstone of the Raton Basin (New Mexico) to investigate detailed relationships between depositional environment, sandstone composition, heavy mineral concentration, and critical element occurrence. The Trinidad Sandstone (~20 m-thick at the study location) clearly records an upward-shoaling beach-shoreface succession characterized by key intervals of hummocky cross-stratification near its base and beach lamination near its top. The section is dominated by quartzofeldspathic sandstone. Thin-sections reveal the presence of heavy minerals (e.g., zircon, monazite, apatite, ilmenite, titanite) at all stratigraphic levels, with the highest modal abundances (e.g., up to 90% of grains) corresponding to highest-energy environments (e.g., beach deposits). Whole-rock geochemistry data paired to the thin sections mirror those trends, with highest abundances of critical elements (such as Ti, Zr, and total REE content) corresponding to the highest proportions of heavy minerals. In those intervals, total REE concentrations range from ~300-700 ppm, two- to four-times greater than average crustal values. Importantly, the relative proportions of individual REEs are remarkably consistent across all samples, supporting that the observed up-section changes in REE concentrations are unlikely related to temporal changes in provenance, and rather, illustrate the efficacy of density sorting in beach-shoreface environments.

title: A Possible Late Source of Water to Margaritifer, Iani, Aram Chaos and Ares Vallis
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Grant, John A. [1], Weitz, Catherine [2], Wilson Purdy, Sharon A. [3], Irwin, Rossman Philip [4], Manogaran, Roodra [5]
affiliations: (1) NASM Center for Earth and Planetary Studies, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA

(3) Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC,

abstract:
Prior studies have concluded that multiple periods of discharge along the northward-draining Uzboi-Ladon-Morava (ULM) meso-scale outflow channels and the Samara-Himera and Parana-Loire valley networks. This discharge occurred into the area that includes Margaritifer, Iani, and Aram Chaos and the headward reaches of Ares Vallis. Any direct connection between this discharge, however, and the cause and timing of chaos formation, and incision of Ares Vallis remains incompletely defined. These prior studies suggest that the collapse of the chaos and drainage in Ares Vallis likely began in the late Noachian and occurred into the Hesperian and perhaps the Early Amazonian. While discharge through the larger ULM system may have dominated delivery of water to the chaos regions and beyond, it may have been augmented by later discharge from the Samara-Himera system.

Relatively pristine valley segments along medial-to-distal Samara Valles in Margaritifer Terra stand in contrast to more degraded and southerly valley segments and they originate within the continuous ejecta surrounding the Late-Hesperian Jones impact crater. Valley expression varies from well-incised to diffuse, some segments appear anastomosing or truncate one another, are more than a kilometer across and 100s of meters deep, and display interior terraces and depositional forms. More pristine segments continue north where they are typically less confined and are associated with finely layered, alternating relatively darker- and lighter-toned deposits partially filling a large crater well beyond the Jones ejecta deposit. The fate of the water that formed the relatively pristine valleys is unclear, but it likely reached Margaritifer basin and the regions of chaos to the north.

We interpret the formation of the relatively pristine Samara Valles segments to be the result of drainage of impact-melted ice caused by Late-Hesperian formation of the Jones crater and emplacement of associated ejecta. Regional topography caused most drainage to flow westward where it accumulated in one or more local basins that eventually overflowed and released water to the north at rates as high as 10 4 m 3 s -1 . Although late drainage along Samara only persisted for a period of months or years, it may have reached the chaos regions to the north, helped to trigger late chaos collapse, and late discharge along Ares Vallis.

title: Libanka Mining District (Eastern Slovakia): From the World's Oldest Precious Opal Mines to Identification of Geoheritage Values and Geotourism Development
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Štrba, Ľubomír [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geo and Mining Tourism; Faculty of Mining, Ecology, Process Control and Geotechnologies, Technical University of Košice, Košice, Slovak Republic
abstract:
The Libanka Mining District in eastern Slovakia represents the largest and most important mining area within the Dubník Opal Mines, one of the world's most significant historical precious opal mining landscapes and the world's oldest known precious opal mining locality. For centuries, this area was the principal source of precious opal worldwide and played a significant role in the history of the gemstone trade before the discovery and development of major Australian opal deposits. The exceptional geological setting of this area, characterized by precious opal mineralization associated with Neogene volcanic rocks, together with a remarkable mining legacy, has created a unique geological and cultural landscape of outstanding scientific significance.

The Libanka Mining District is an exceptional example of the interaction between geological processes, mineral resources, and human activity. It presents the geological framework of precious opal formation related to low-temperature hydrothermal fluids, the characteristics of opal mineralization, and the historical development of mining, including the surviving underground workings and mining features that document centuries of exploration and extraction.

Currently, visitor interpretation is primarily focused on mining history, while the geological and geoheritage values of the area remain only partly reflected in its presentation. Beyond its importance as a historical mining site, the area possesses significant geodiversity and geoheritage values and provides important opportunities for geoeducation and sustainable geotourism. The Libanka Mining District demonstrates how geological and mining heritage, preserved in the long-neglected remnants of a globally significant resource exploitation history, can be further reinterpreted and utilized as a foundation for education, scientific communication, heritage interpretation, and regional development.

The Libanka Mining District provides an outstanding case study of how the world's oldest precious opal mining area can serve as a bridge between Earth's geological history, mineral resources, cultural heritage, and sustainable geotourism development.

title: Benthic habitats of an Ordovician shelf: Environmental controls and depositional setting of the Postolonnec Formation of NW France using trace fossils and sedimentologic analyses

authors: Roos, Anika [1], Paz, Maximiliano [2], Gougeon, Romain [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Oberlin College, Oberlin, Ohio, USA

abstract: The Darriwilian–Sandbian (Ordovician) Postolonnec Formation, located in the Crozon Peninsula of NW France, records marine deposition during renewed continental subsidence in Northern Gondwana. This study analyzes trace fossils and sedimentary facies of the unit to reconstruct environmental conditions and stressors affecting benthic communities throughout deposition. The succession is characterized by thick mudstone intervals, mudstone interbedded with 5–50 cm-thick sandstone layers, and a sandstone-rich interval in the middle of the unit with hummocky cross-stratification and minor mudstone intercalations. Syneresis cracks and normally graded beds occur in the heterolithic intervals. The sedimentary characteristics of the unit indicate deposition in a storm-dominated shelf-to-offshore setting, with episodic salinity fluctuations and shifts in depositional regimes consistent with intermittent deltaic influence. The trace fossil content is dominated by Asterosoma, Cylindrichnus, Gyrolithes, Palaeophycus, Phycosiphon, Planolites, Rosselia, Skolithos, Spirophyton, Teichichnus, Trichichnus, and Trichophycus, which are mainly characteristic of the Cruziana Ichnofacies and reflect deposit- and detritus-feeding behaviors during periods of relatively high food availability within the seafloor. In contrast, low-diversity intervals dominated by Teichichnus and Trichophycus, or by Palaeophycus, likely reflect stressed conditions associated with freshwater input from a delta. The mudstone deposits exhibit massive or mottled bioturbation fabrics due to intense biomixing on a normal-marine seafloor with high food availability, thereby precluding preservation of discrete trace fossils. Overall, the Postolonnec Formation reflects a dynamic system with alternating deltaic processes affecting a storm-dominated shoreline that evidences some evolutionary innovations related to the Ordovician radiation. Notably, the succession may contain the oldest known occurrence of Phycosiphon incertum, providing insight into the early evolution of such deposit-feeding behaviors in worm-like organisms. Moreover, massive fabrics indicate that fully mixed seafloors were common in the Ordovician, further supporting the idea that thick sediment mixed layers were widespread during the early Paleozoic.

affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, Nj, USA

abstract: Why do most hyperuricemic patients never develop gout? Their blood can remain supersaturated with urate for years, yet most never suffer from pathogenic crystals. Stranger yet, blood urate is sometimes even BELOW the saturation threshold during acute gout flares. Supersaturation therefore cannot be the whole story; the decisive step must occur earlier. We argue that it is set by ions, which govern precursor self-assembly, attachment kinetics, and polymorph selection during crystallization by particle attachment. Guanine and uric acid are parallel, low-solubility purines that we propose crystallize through a shared mechanism. Metabolism decides which purine accumulates, chemistry sets the phase, and natural selection acts on the result: guanine's optical advantages drove its repeated selection as a functional biomineral, whereas urate was recruited only rarely. Their trajectories diverge with the degree of biological control. Under biological control, both crystallize as anhydrous phases, though only guanine assembles into the stacked platelet arrays that optical function requires: reflectors in teleosts, tunable color in chameleons, whereas urate crystallizes in medaka leucophores as spherulites. Without it, both shift toward hydrated forms: guanine monohydrate in bacterial colonies, monosodium urate monohydrate in gout, and uric acid monohydrate in snake waste. Yet although pH, precipitation rate, and composition are recognized polymorph controls, the ionic environment is not. Our halophilic cultures exposed this gap: guanine monohydrate formed at pH 9, far from the acidic pH range of 0 to 3 reported for abiotic solution growth, implicating cations, including ammonium generated by deamination, as drivers of nonclassical polymorph selection. Our follow up abiotic dynamic light scattering data showed Na⁺, K⁺, Cs⁺, and NH₄⁺ drive guanine into discrete precursor populations and onward into mesocrystals, whith similarly sized precursors in uric acid, indicating a shared assembly pathway across both purines. Across brines, biological reflectors, and gout, one control dominates: ions steer a purine’s fate before bulk saturation is even reached.

title: Winter Hydrologic, Thermal, and Biogeochemical Dynamics in a Salt Marsh on Prince Edward Island, Canada
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Argiro, Adam [1], Kurylyk, Barret [2], Somers, Lauren [3]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Resource Engineering, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada
(2) Civil and Resource Engineering, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada

abstract:
Salt marshes provide many critical ecosystem services including carbon sequestration, wave attenuation, and coastal storm protection. Salt marsh hydrology research has primarily focused on salt marshes in warmer climates or during the summer. Furthermore, research regarding climate change impacts on salt marshes has focused on changes in water level and less on the effect on sediment thermal regimes. Very little is known about winter salt marsh dynamics in colder regions, where snow and ground ice can influence marsh hydrology, sediment thermal regimes, and biogeochemistry. These dynamics are critical for the Canadian province of Prince Edward Island (PEI) where salt marshes promote coastal resilience, including during winter nor’easter storms.

The purpose of this study is to investigate present and future hydrologic, thermal, and biogeochemical dynamics in a salt marsh along the north shore of PEI, focusing on the influence of snow and ice on the integrated salt marsh-bay system. A multi-methods approach was used to assess winter hydrologic, thermal, and biogeochemical dynamics. A piezometer transect revealed shallow groundwater level and electrical conductivity dynamics from mid-November 2025 to present, including water table decline during winter freezing and subsequent rise during spring snowmelt and rain. During February 2026, greenhouse gas measurements were taken which indicated far lower winter emissions of methane and carbon dioxide compared to summer months. Frequency domain electromagnetic surveys were conducted during July 2026 and suggested that salt pannes on the marsh surface during summer act as preferential pathways for the infiltration of saline water into the subsurface. Data from sediment temperature probes indicated that the maximum marsh frost (temperature < 0°C) depth was ~ 0.25 meters for the high marsh and increased to ~0.9 meters for the low marsh. These data are being used to develop a better understanding of present-day winter salt marsh dynamics to inform the development of process-based models to investigate how these systems may respond to atmospheric and oceanic climate change.

title: Detrital Zircon Geochronology as a Tool for Student Engagement in Understudied Communities
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part II)
authors: Cohen-Garcia, Abraham Visher [1], Jaret, Steven J. [2]
affiliations: (1) New York City Department of Education, Jackson Heights, NY,
(2) Kingsborough Community College (CUNY), Brooklyn, NY,
abstract:
Students who are older than typical grade-level and behind on credits from New York City report a lack of connection to their natural environment, particularly their local geology. One approach to re-engaging underserved high school students is through participatory research in place-based geology. In the South Bronx, one open question is the provenance of local metasedimentary rocks and whether these rocks originated prior to the assembly of Pangea. A related open question is the location of a major terrane boundary, often called Cameron's Line, which separates Laurentian rocks from those of a Gondwanan affinity.

Over the course of three years, students from Bronx Arena High School have collaborated with local organizations, including Kingsborough Community College and the American Museum of Natural History, to investigate these open scientific questions. Students used the lens of detrital zircon geochronology to sample, process, and date zircon crystals from the Bronx River to better understand their community's Proterozoic origins and contribute to ongoing research, presented their work to their peers and later at New York's Long Island Geology Conference at Stony Brook University, and led educator professional development on the Bronx River. Preliminary U-Pb ages from the Bronx River zircons indicate a Laurentian source and offer a new constraint on the position of Cameron's Line in the South Bronx. According to the NYC Student Perception survey, students engaged in the project reported an overall 20% increase in classroom engagement, including greater excitement in participation and understanding of how these ideas applied to their daily life.

Place-based, inquiry-driven geology offers a unique opportunity for under-represented students to contribute to the study of their communities and develop connections to their local geology and geography. Furthermore, the study of detrital zircon can meaningfully re-engage students who have struggled in traditional high school environments. Finally, participatory science offers a meaningful avenue for geologists and researchers to expand their impact, and accelerate scientific discoveries.

abstract: Rivers play a critical role in transporting anthropogenic litter (AL), including macroplastics (> 5mm in diameter), from land-based sources to the ocean. However, recent studies have suggested that most of this material introduced to watersheds is retained and broken down into microplastics, which can be easily ingested by aquatic organisms or enter the water supply. For example, macroplastics and other forms of AL are typically transported in streams during high-flow (e.g., storm) events and can be entangled in riparian vegetation. While some studies have used video cameras to determine the amount of AL transported in a river system during a storm event, this approach does not capture the material sequestered or dislodged from riparian zones. The Wissahickon watershed (164.92 km 2 ) in Philadelphia, PA, experiences a disproportionately high amount of AL pollution. However, it’s currently unknown how much AL pollution is transported from the watershed during storm events. This study used a combined approach of GoPro™ cameras deployed during storm events and mass-balance sampling within the adjacent floodplains before and after to provide one of the most accurate delineations of AL transport in river systems to date. All visible debris items within each river segment, and observed during each storm event, were counted and categorized via the NOAA Marine Debris Checklist to determine the relative influence of AL sources. The results of this experiment help to inform litter intervention strategies in upstream areas and cleanup events associated with riparian areas.

title: Large-Scale Prediction of Post-Wildfire Stream Water Temperature
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Philippus, Daniel [1], Corona, Claudia R [2], Hogue, Terri S [3]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA

abstract:
Stream water temperature (SWT) is a key control on lotic species lifecycles and survival, drinking water treatment, and reservoir water quality. Because of its influence on ecology, fisheries, and infrastructure, disturbances to SWT are a major concern across management applications. One increasingly major disturbance is wildfire, which can alter evapotranspiration, shading, and runoff dynamics, resulting in SWT disturbances. For example, summer SWT tends to increase after wildfires, particularly for streams within the burned area. Unfortunately, few sites with pre- and post-fire SWT observations in the contiguous United States (CONUS) exist, limiting analyses. Studies of post-fire SWT have mostly focused on specific regions (e.g., the northern Rocky Mountains of Idaho and Montana) or used relatively small samples (e.g., 31 sites) over larger domains. The available datasets have been sufficient to broadly characterize post-fire SWT response, but do not provide the means to identify specific post-fire SWT shifts outside of the few streams with sufficient monitoring.

The spatial coverage of post-fire SWT analyses could be expanded through prediction at unmonitored sites, which would allow for identification of SWT shifts at remote sites. In this study, we test the performance of an existing SWT model for unmonitored sites, TempEst 2, when predicting pre- to post-fire SWT shifts. We then use TempEst 2 predictions to identify spatiotemporal trends in post-fire SWT over an expanded scale of 1,177 watersheds burned from 2006-2023. Across 40 sites throughout the mountainous western CONUS with suitable pre- and post-fire SWT observations, TempEst 2 captured 37% of the variance between sites in post-fire summer SWT shift, matching specialized post-fire models within a widely-applicable framework. Application of TempEst 2 to 1,177 unmonitored, burned watersheds revealed that SWT primarily increased in the first two years after a fire. Most SWT increases were small (≤0.3 °C), but hundreds of burned headwaters exhibited August SWT increases of ≥1 °C. For example, in 2022, a cluster of streams impacted by Oregon’s 2021 Bootleg fire had August SWT 1.5-2 °C above average, outpacing other severely fire-impacted regions like Colorado’s 2020 Cameron Peak and East Troublesome fires (+1-1.5 °C). The application of unspecialized SWT models to post-fire SWT at unmonitored locations has the potential to inform large-scale identification of post-fire SWT effects and enhance water management activities.

abstract: Our research examines several taxa of benthic foraminifera, dominated by Trochammina inflata , Siphotrochammina lobata , and Miliammina spp., from six surface sediment samples collected in January 2026 from Carpinteria Salt Marsh in Carpinteria, California. Water quality parameters, including temperature, dissolved oxygen, specific conductivity, salinity, pH, and turbidity, were measured at each sampling location at the time of collection. In addition, the proximity of each site to a potential source of anthropogenic impact (e.g., the railroad tracks adjacent to the marsh) was recorded as a possible influence on water quality and foraminiferal distribution. Results show a general increase in foraminiferal abundance (#Forams/ml) with increasing salinity across the sampling sites as we move away from the railroad tracks. The exception to this relationship is Site 1 (closest to the railroad tracks) which has the lowest salinity but the highest foraminiferal abundance (11.6/ml). This suggests that salinity influences foraminiferal assemblage distribution but is not the only controlling factor. Foraminiferal abundance also demonstrates a positive relationship with turbidity, which may indicate that higher turbidity is associated with environmental conditions favorable for our identified taxa. Across all sites, the 150–250 µm size fraction contained the highest percentage (68.4%-82.3%) of recovered individuals, whereas specimens larger than 425 µm represented only a small proportion (0.3%-2.5%) of the total assemblage. By examining benthic foraminiferal assemblages in relation to water quality parameters and potential sources of anthropogenic influence, this study provides a better understanding of the environmental factors affecting the distribution of foraminifera in Carpinteria Salt Marsh and establishes a baseline for future monitoring of environmental changes.

abstract:
Cone-in-cone (CIC) structures are enigmatic sedimentary features composed of nested, concentrically stacked cones of authigenic carbonates. Despite more than a century of discovery, the mechanisms responsible for CIC formation remain poorly understood due to the scarcity of modern analogues and limited geochemical investigation. Exceptionally well-developed CIC structures occur in the Cretaceous Kiowa Formation of Kansas, reaching lengths of up to 10 cm, representing some of the largest CIC examples reported globally. These structures were first described by H. J. Harnly in 1896, yet they have never been investigated using modern geochemical approaches.

Here we present an integrated sedimentological, mineralogical, and geochemical study of CIC structures within the Kiowa shales. Petrography and micro-XRF mapping reveal individual cones separated by thin clay films interpreted as resulting from early diagenesis. Carbonate carbon isotope compositions from 40 micro-drilled spots across 8 CIC samples show an average value of −26.75‰ (VPDB), with the lowest down to −33.21‰. Organic carbon isotope compositions of the Kiowa shale show consistent values of ~−25‰. These data indicate strong influence of anaerobic oxidation of methane during CIC precipitation. Strontium isotopic ratios (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr ≈ 0.7073) match Cretaceous seawater signals, supporting early diagenetic formation. Trace element patterns show weak negative Ce anomalies (Ce/Ce* = 0.7), no Eu anomaly, and Y/Ho ratios ~31.8, consistent with porewater signals with partial seawater influence. The presence of Mn oxide (e.g., birnessite) within CICs and elevated Mn concentrations suggest Mn oxides may have acted as electron acceptors facilitating methane oxidation.

δ³⁴S values measured from sulfide crystals and thin gypsum layers closely associated with the CICs show distinct ranges. Sulfide δ³⁴S values of +12.9 to +16.4‰ (mean = +14.1‰, n = 12) approach or even slightly exceed those of coeval marine sulfate (~+15‰), indicating minimal fractionation and elevated rate of microbial sulfate reduction under relatively closed-system conditions. Thin gypsum layers yield broader δ³⁴S values from −1.7 to +10.5‰ (mean = +5.3‰, n = 17), suggesting mixing with sulfur derived from pyrite oxidation under shallow diagenetic or evaporative conditions.

Our results suggest that coupled methane oxidation with sulfate reduction and likely Mn 4+ reduction during early diagenesis played a key role in CIC formation, revealing previously unrecognized links between carbonate growth and methane cycling in organic- and sulfate-rich marine environments during Cretaceous greenhouse conditions.

title: Microtextural Controls on the Dissolution of Monazite and Zircon during Biotite-Dehydration Melting
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Kelsall, Laura [1], Smye, Andrew [2]

abstract:
Differentiation of the continental crust into an upper layer enriched in heat-producing elements (U, Th, K) and a complementary lower crust depleted in these elements is key for continental stability. Recent analysis indicates that ultrahigh temperatures (>900°C) may be required to effectively redistribute U and Th from the lower to upper crust, however the exact mechanism that accounts for this observation is uncertain.

Here we test the hypothesis that mineral armouring modulates the dissolution of monazite and zircon—key Th and U carrier phases, respectively—in silicate melt produced during biotite-dehydration melting. Using image analysis of automated SEM maps we present microtextural observations from a suite of aluminous metasedimentary rocks (Ivrea-Verbano Zone) that preserve a record of partial melting under peak temperatures spanning the biotite-dehydration melting interval (700-900°C). A strong positive correlation between biotite and monazite modal abundances was found. In the amphibolite-facies samples 15-80% of monazite is included within biotite grains whereas in granulite-facies and ultrahigh temperature samples that decreases to 0-28% and 0% respectively. The amount of monazite included in garnet increases from 3-25% in amphibolite to 100% in ultrahigh temperature samples. Zircon abundance is poorly correlated to biotite but still shows a similar trend of decreasing inclusion with biotite (9-40% to 0%) and increasing association with garnet (3-10% to 19%) from amphibolite to ultrahigh temperature samples.

We additionally present a forward model describing the evolution of monazite and zircon dissolution during crustal melting. This model allows for incorporation of zircon and monazite into a reservoir within biotite that does not interact with melt until released when biotite-dehydration occurs. Initial results show that monazite that would otherwise dissolve in melt may be sequestered within biotite from 720-850°C. Zircon breakdown is instead primarily controlled by its solubility in melt over the same temperature range. Work is ongoing to incorporate apatite dissolution into the model and to model an open system where melt loss can occur.

These findings suggest that the textural availability of accessory phases imposes an important control on the flux of U and Th into silicate melt produced during anatexis. Prior to the consumption of biotite, included carrier phases may be shielded from interacting with melt; peritectic growth of garnet serves to sequester carrier phases in the residuum.

title: Differentiating Spatial Visualization and Algebraic Reasoning in Teaching Crystallographic Planes: A Teaching-as-Research Study
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Afra, Mahsa [1]
affiliations: (1) The Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (EPS), The University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USA
abstract: Crystallographic calculations such as determining Miller indices remain challenging for many introductory mineralogy students, even after repeated exposure to worked examples. Faculty observations suggest that student difficulties stem from at least two distinct cognitive barriers: (1) spatial visualization of three-dimensional unit cells and plane intercepts and (2) procedural mathematical skills required to convert intercepts into Miller indices. This teaching-as-research project investigates the extent to which targeted instruction addressing these separate skill domains influences student performance in determining crystallographic planes. The study will be conducted in an undergraduate mineralogy course over one to two instructional sessions. Students will participate in learning activities designed to emphasize either spatial visualization skills (e.g., mentally deconstructing unit cells, identifying and sketching plane intercepts along crystallographic axes) or algebraic/procedural skills (e.g., organizing fractional intercept values, calculating reciprocals, and clearing denominators to obtain integer indices). Student learning outcomes include the ability to accurately interpret three-dimensional crystallographic geometry and correctly perform the mathematical procedures necessary for expressing crystallographic planes. A mixed-methods approach will be used to assess learning gains and identify persistent misconceptions. Quantitative data will include pre/post assessments, targeted Miller index problem sets and survey responses. Qualitative evidence will be gathered through student interviews and open-ended reflections conducted during and after instruction. Comparisons of learning gains across skill domains will be used to determine whether difficulties are primarily spatial, procedural, or a combination of both. The project aims to provide evidence-based guidance for mineralogy instructors seeking to improve student understanding of crystallographic concepts. Findings will contribute to geoscience education research by clarifying the relative importance of spatial reasoning and mathematical fluency in crystallographic problem solving and by identifying instructional strategies that may improve student success in foundational mineralogy coursework.

title: From supercomputer to desktop: training and deploying open-source deep learning software for mapping piles at mines and quarries
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Odom, William E. [1], Doctor, Daniel H. [2], Gray, Alexander A. [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Herndon, VA,
abstract:
High-resolution lidar data are available for nearly the entire continental United States. These datasets are useful for mapping surficial geology, geomorphology, hydrology, and anthropogenic features, especially in areas covered by dense foliage. Manually outlining features in lidar has been conventionally done for mapping limited areas; however, it does not upscale to the regional extents for which lidar data are now available. Through the Appalachian Manganese Oxide Research Effort (AMORE), we developed deep learning models that were trained on mine site polygons and lidar data, and that produce high-resolution maps of surficial features over large extents. Producing maps from trained models is straightforward on office workstations; however, training models is a resource-intensive process and may take several days per model on these machines.

We overcame this computational barrier by using large-language-model-assisted coding to translate our training workflows into open-source Python scripts that run on the USGS Tallgrass Supercomputer. These scripts more efficiently use computer resources, perform grid searches across training parameters for up to 100 models per session, and enable remote training on Tallgrass. These advances improved model tuning and performance, while reducing training time by over an order of magnitude and freeing up office workstation resources.

Here, we present a model trained on Tallgrass to map piles at quarries and mines. It was trained on 274 manually drawn piles in the Winchester, Virginia 30- x 60-minute quadrangle. Piles had a median area of 1507 m 2 and documented commodity types included iron, manganese, crushed stone, limestone, and sand & gravel. Because the model is trained on lidar data, it maps all piles regardless of commodity. We ran the model on the Sunbury, Pennsylvania 30- x 60-minute quadrangle, which features numerous coal mines, and the Big Levels, Virginia 7.5-minute quadrangle, which features several manganese mines. The model correctly identified numerous piles yet suffered from false positives in areas with different physiographies from the original training zone. Subsequent retraining included the false positive areas as background imagery, which improved performance as the mapping footprint expanded. This iterative approach of mapping beyond a model's training area, identifying false positives, retraining with a larger footprint, and rerunning models highlights the benefit of high-performance computing in the deep learning mapping space.

abstract:
This study examines lavas erupted at the 17°20′S segment of the South East Pacific Rise (SEPR) to evaluate the petrologic processes controlling geochemical variability at a superfast-spreading mid-ocean ridge. During the 2024 AT50-31 expedition aboard the R/V Atlantis , we investigated this ridge. A total of 127 lava samples were collected over 7 km of the ridge using the HOV Alvin submersible (55 lavas from four dives) and rock coring (72 lavas). Sampling included both on- and off-axis locations recorded through shipboard bathymetry and AUV Sentry, allowing spatial comparisons of lava compositions along and across the ridge axis.

Major and trace element concentrations of all 127 glassy lavas were measured by EPMA and LA-ICP-MS at Boise State University. The samples comprise 97 D-MORB and 30 N-MORB following the characterization scheme of Gale et al. (2010). MgO concentrations range from 5.9 to 8.9 wt%, K₂O/TiO₂ values from 0.04 to 0.13, La/Sm N ratios from 0.45 to 0.81, and La/Yb N ratios from 0.54 to 1.14, reflecting variability in both magmatic differentiation and mantle source composition. Major and trace element variability is greater across the ridge axis than along it, with the greatest variability preserved in older off-axis D-MORB lavas.

Petrologic modeling indicates that the full observed compositional range is best explained by 3–8% dynamic melting of a heterogeneous mantle source involving depleted and enriched DMM, followed by 20–30% fractional crystallization, with some samples recording up to 60% crystallization. Modeled crystallization pressures range from 1–5 kbar. These results demonstrate that mantle source composition and variations in melt fraction are the primary controls on geochemical variability, whereas shallow crustal differentiation plays an important secondary role. Comparison with the fast-spreading 9°50′N East Pacific Rise and slow-spreading 14°N Mid-Atlantic Ridge shows that all settings preserve heterogeneity in mantle source and differences in the degree of partial melting, and that spreading rate is not a first order control on magma homogenization at mid-ocean ridges.

session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Narbonne, Guy M. [1], Fitzgerald, Danielle M. [2], Xiao, Shuhai [3], Dalrymple, Robert W. [4], Spencer, Christopher J. [5], Schmitz, Mark D. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences and Geological Engineering, Queen’s University, Kingston, Ontraio, Canada

abstract: The Ediacara biota records the appearance and diversification of Earth’s first large, soft-bodied eukaryotes, including interpreted early animals, yet their evolutionary origins remain unresolved. Previously, the oldest-known large (centimeter- to meter-scale) Ediacara-type macrofossils known anywhere were <571 Ma leaf-shaped fronds from the upper Drook Formation at Mistaken Point in the Avalon Peninsula of Newfoundland. The Drook fossils are large, diverse, and architecturally complex, implying that they may have had macroscopic precursors, a view consistent with molecular clock estimates of a Tonian or Cryogenian origin of animals. Here we describe macrofossil remains from deep-water strata of the Mall Bay Formation at two sites on the Colinet Islands offshore of the Avalon Peninsula of Newfoundland. These remains, radioisotopically dated at 580 Ma, occur in the cold-water prelude to the overlying Gaskiers diamictite. Both new fossil sites are more than a kilometer stratigraphically lower and probably 8-10 million years older than the oldest previously described Ediacara-type macrofossils from Mistaken Point or anywhere else worldwide. The Colinet Islands structures include simple cm-scale discoidal remains similar to the Ediacaran form-genus Aspidella , and the newly named bipartite fossil Colinetia which comprises a centimeter-scale disc attached to an unbranched, clay-lined, decimeter- to meter-long, cylindrical tube that is preserved horizontally at the top of the bed. The tube contains an inner tube (tube-in-tube morphology) and maintains a consistent diameter along its length and among all specimens in the assemblage. Colinetia specimens exhibit features consistent with a biological reconstruction as open cylindrical tubes that were at least partly infaunal, with post-mortem fill by sediment injection guided by the horizontally oriented tubes. They range up to 2 m in length and thus represent the first abundant occurrence of large lifeforms in Ediacaran evolution. Morphologically, they strongly resemble the basal parts of younger Ediacaran fronds and tubular organisms, suggesting a possible evolutionary affinity, but they lacked the morphologic complexity of many younger Ediacaran taxa. Discovery of two mid-Ediacaran fossil sites in a deep-water glaciomarine environment near the beginning of large size and biological complexity supports the hypothesis that the Ediacara biota first emerged under cold conditions, and adds weight to the hypothesis that increased oceanic ventilation during glacial onset ~580 Ma may have played a role in the origin of the Ediacara biota.

abstract:
This project utilizing Ground Penetrating Radar was developed from a request by a Salt Lake City based investigative reporter seeking help to locate the remains of a victim of Ted Bundy, an American serial killer. The study used the NOGGIN® GPR cart to collect data in grid surveys at a suspected clandestine gravesite located in Sevier County, Utah.

One major goal of the project was to help provide a form of finality for family members of the victim. Additionally, it provided undergraduate students with valuable experience in planning and executing a real-world GPR survey. Two undergraduate students participated in the planning, surveying, and analysis of the GPR data, with mentoring by faculty/staff from the University of South Florida and Weber State University. They had the opportunity to work with the investigative reporter and better appreciate the significance of geoscience research to the community.

The Sevier County GPR surveys were conducted over four sites in primarily dry, sandy-silty soils using the NOGGIN® GPR system with a 250 MHz antenna unit. This antenna was chosen because of its ability to produce adequate signal to depths associated with the clandestine burial location, balancing less resolution with greater depth. Initial processing and analysis of radargram line profiles and grids were completed using Reflexw GPR and seismic processing software. Several possible targets were identified as notable diffraction patterns (hyperbolas). One promising shallow target (70-80 cm depth) at Site 4 was later excavated, but turned out to be a large tree root system.

Data from Sites 1, 2, and 3 were then examined for subtle hyperbolas representing potential targets using newly learned processing workflows in the Sensors & Software EKKO Project V6 R 2.1 Software, recently used in an EarthScope Consortium Instructor Workshop on near-surface geophysics methods. Three isolated targets at depths ranging from 25 cm to 55 cm were identified in several radargram profiles accessed from the software grid view of Site 2. They require further investigation. A cluster of targets was also identified in one line profile (45 - 65 cm depth) which we interpret to be tree roots. No notable targets were identified in the GPR data for either Sites 1 or 3.

abstract: Every year, watersheds across the western United States face increased risk from postfire flooding and debris flow. Some communities continue to address the effects of wildfires from previous years. Others face the immediate challenges posed by new wildfires, especially as seasonal rains approach. This presentation will provide an overview of collaborative efforts by the U.S. Geological Survey and partners to respond to 2026 wildfires and postfire flow events. We will highlight new capabilities used to help assess postfire hazards and discuss areas where further improvements are needed. These include new capabilities for estimating zones of debris-flow inundation and the need for complementary mapping of longer runout flood inundation. We will also review some of the major flow events of the year and discuss how data from these events can be used to test and subsequently improve models for postfire hazard assessment. Events include debris flows in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park following the 2025 South Rim Fire in Colorado and flooding and debris flow following the 2026 Cottonwood Fire in Utah.

abstract: Zircon is a common, highly refractory accessory mineral found in sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic rocks that forms through various processes (e.g., magmatic, hydrothermal, metamorphic growth, recrystallization). Trace element compositions of detrital zircon have been widely applied to understanding tectonic processes and continental reconstruction. Previous studies have shown that no single compositional parameter (i.e., REE pattern, Th/U) can distinguish zircon petrogenesis. Here, we employ novel machine learning methods to differentiate between “metamorphic-like” and “igneous-like” zircon, independent of researcher-labeled lithologies and categorized by their dominant REE signatures. With advancements and the adoption of machine learning algorithms by the geochemical community, we holistically analyze n-dimensional geochemical data (14 dimensions for the full REE suite) to ascertain or confirm complex geological processes. We utilize a dataset of previously identified zircon with varying proposed origins (i.e., metamorphic, igneous, S-type granites, early Earth detrital) and unsupervised machine learning algorithms (i.e., UMAP, Mclust), which reveal two distinct clusters that we interpret as the dominant magmatic-like and metamorphic-like REE signatures. The two REE signature clusters are used to define a comprehensive REE equation that matches an unknown zircon into the most similar interpreted cluster (magmatic-like or metamorphic-like) through probabilistic bimodal logistic regression. The logistic regression equation was derived exclusively from REE signatures independent of previous classification. Model validation was achieved using confusion matrices and yielded a mean accuracy of 0.91 (balanced accuracy = 0.88), with average precision = 0.90, recall = 0.80, F1 = 0.85, and AUC = 0.96, indicating robust discriminative performance. Unsupervised machine learning demonstrates that two distinct REE signatures emerge, which vary in their HREE enrichment and LREE depletion. We demonstrate that machine learning can decipher complex multi-elemental relationships in zircon REE data and can be used to classify zircon.

abstract: In the United States, rural and Indigenous communities face elevated health risks from arsenic and uranium in drinking water. In some cases, both arsenic and uranium are present in the water. Water treatment for uranium is challenging, and is often insufficient for arsenic. We have been developing water treatment technologies that overcome these limitations through active microbial iron cycling. Bioreactors containing cultures with iron oxidizing and reducing microorganisms continuously generate adsorption media and can reduce uranium to insoluble forms. In this study, we examine the efficacy of iron-containing bioreactors installed on private wells impacted by arsenic and uranium (>10 ppb) to establish if such systems work effectively under real-world conditions. Synchrotron-based spectroscopy indicates that the iron minerals formed are ferrihydrite and lepidocrosite, both of which have strong affinity for metal adsorption. The composition of untreated groundwater and treated water samples were collected daily, with measured flow rates and composition, determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, to evaluate bioreactor performance. Field data indicates that reactors achieved up to 80% removal of arsenic, with removal rates increasing as flow rates decreased. Measured rate constants (~0.02 min -1 ) are consistent with residence times of about 1 hour to achieve 2 ppb target effluent levels. Uranium removal was minimal under experimental conditions. As such, our data demonstrate sufficient arsenic removal for water treatment, but suggest reactors need to maintain Fe(II) levels to improve uranium removal. Understanding specific conditions under which the system treats water effectively will inform future steps in optimizing the system, ultimately improving critical, sustainable access to clean water in rural areas.

abstract: Trace metals are naturally present in soils, but agricultural practices can alter their distribution and accumulation. In Wisconsin dairy systems, feed concentrates and mineral supplements often contain elevated concentrations of Cu and Zn, along with trace amounts of Cr, As, and Cd. These elements can enter manure streams and accumulate in agricultural soils through repeated manure application. Despite Wisconsin's prominence as a dairy-producing state, relatively little research has evaluated long-term trace metal accumulation in manure-managed soils. This study establishes a baseline assessment of trace metal concentrations in western Wisconsin. Soil samples were collected from long-term manure-amended fields, non-manured agricultural fields, and non-agricultural undisturbed reference sites. Corn plant samples were collected from agricultural treatments, while manure and groundwater samples were obtained to evaluate trace metal distribution throughout the agroecosystem. Samples were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) to quantify trace metal concentrations. This baseline dataset provides critical insight into trace metal occurrence and accumulation patterns within Wisconsin dairy production systems. The findings will support future monitoring efforts, inform nutrient management decisions, and improve understanding of trace metal cycling in agricultural landscapes.

title: Diachronous Provincial Biozones Along the Northeast Pacific Margin: New Geochronologic Constraints on the Refugian and Zemorrian Stages in Oregon and Washington

authors: Darin, Michael H. [1], Armentrout, John M. [2], Goedert, James L. [3], Tsai, Cheng-Hsiu [4]

abstract: Provincial benthic foraminiferal stages have long anchored Paleogene chronostratigraphy along the northeast Pacific margin, yet their synchrony with the global timescale has rarely been tested with absolute age control. We present detrital zircon (DZ) U–Pb and strontium isotope data from the lower Lincoln Creek Formation in western Washington — the foundation of a widely used regional chronostratigraphic framework — that constrain local upper Refugian Stage assemblages to ~30–26 Ma, firmly mid-Oligocene and substantially younger than the Refugian type section in southern California (~35.3–33.8 Ma). These results require reassignment of the Refugian interval of the Canyon River magnetostratigraphic reference section from subchrons C15r–C12r to C11r–C8r, placing the Refugian-Zemorrian boundary in western Washington at ~26 Ma. New DZ data from the Alsea Formation in Oregon extend this pattern southward with a maximum depositional age (MDA) of 25.9 ± 0.2 Ma just below the Refugian-Zemorrian boundary. DZ ages are dominated entirely (98%) by 40–26-Ma zircon diagnostic of the Ancestral Cascades Arc, indicating direct sourcing from the active arc and suggesting the MDA closely approximates the true depositional age. This age is indistinguishable from the Refugian-Zemorrian boundary in the Lincoln Creek Formation, suggesting termination of the Refugian ecological niche across Oregon and Washington at ~26 Ma. Combined with evidence that the basal Refugian in Oregon is ~36–35.5 Ma, the Oregon-Washington Refugian spans ~36–26 Ma — roughly five times longer than in southern California. These results demonstrate that the Oregon-Washington Refugian and Zemorrian stages are diachronous eco-stratigraphic units that reflect persistent regional oceanographic and bathymetric conditions rather than a synchronous time interval. Although long recognized by regional biostratigraphers, this ~7–8 million year difference in the age of the Refugian-Zemorrian boundary between the Pacific Northwest and California type sections is here quantified for the first time. The temporal framework underpinning current interpretations of Pacific margin marine vertebrate evolution — including early cetaceans and plotopterids — is built on chronostratigraphy that has not been systematically tested throughout the region. Inferred patterns of faunal origination, diversification, and extinction near the Eocene-Oligocene transition may therefore be displaced in time by millions of years. Resolving these uncertainties will require systematic DZ U-Pb dating of strata bearing each key biozone boundary along the northeast Pacific margin.

title: Cobalt Mining in Zambia: Geology, Production Trends, and Environmental Challenges
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: McClelland, Lilly [1], Nchimunya, Muzila [2], Krekeler, Mark P. S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA

abstract:
The African Copperbelt occupies the Lufilian Arc, a significant geologic structure that is host to high‑grade copper‑cobalt stratiform deposits. Cobalt mineralization is hosted within the Katanga Supergroup, where stratiform copper-cobalt ores contain chalcopyrite, bornite, and the cobalt‑bearing sulfide carrollite within the regionally extensive Ore Shale. Northern Zambia is situated within the African Copperbelt, as is its neighbor, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which produces over 75% of the world’s cobalt supply. Since the 1920s, these deposits have shaped the development of the Copperbelt, driving settlement, infrastructure growth, and national economic policy through colonial expansion, post‑independence nationalization, and re‑privatization.

Recent production trends indicate a structural shift in Zambia’s cobalt sector. Between 2019 and 2022, cobalt output remained low at about 250-400 tonnes per year, reflecting limited recovery capacity and constrained copper production. In 2023, output rose sharply to 1,506 tonnes as several copper mines recommissioned cobalt recovery circuits, enabling greater extraction from existing ores. Production remained high in 2024 at about 1,409 tonnes, suggesting that Zambia has entered a new growth phase driven by expanded copper operations, improved processing infrastructure, and policy supportive of critical mineral mining. The recent designation of cobalt as a critical mineral due to its use in high-technology products also suggests a continued and growing importance to global economies. Because cobalt is produced as a by‑product of copper, future output will depend on copper expansion, energy reliability, global cobalt prices, and continued investment in recovery circuits and domestic refining.

Increased demand for cobalt mining in Zambia aids economic development but also exposes local communities to mine pollution without effective mitigation measures. For example, in February 2025, a tailings dam collapsed into the Kafue River, which serves as a critical water source for approximately 40% of Zambia’s population. This event underscored the urgent need for improved tailings characterization and management. As mining expansion continues, comprehensive characterization of mine waste is needed to design effective environmental protection and sustainable waste management plans. By synthesizing current knowledge on Zambia's copper-cobalt industry, this review establishes the scientific foundation for future investigations of mine tailings characterization and their role in supporting cobalt resource development.

abstract:
Context is everything. Context is a frame that provides meaning to everything. Just as there is very little meaning in a single word, there is much less meaning in a single mineral than in the mineral assemblage that constitutes the rock than in the rock that constitutes a deformed lithology. Context determines interpretation and it determines causality. As you digest the increasing dimensionality of the geology you are mapping, you build an increasingly credible story. Maps provide you with spatial context, temporal context, physical context, causal context and uncertainty context. Because maps are such high dimensional representations of geology, they are irreplaceable in geologic analysis.

There are at least three areas in which the value of geologic maps is being significantly enhanced:

1) Improved technology to gather information. These include exceptionally high-resolution drone, airplane and satellite-based platforms. Their ability to gather high resolution data is complemented by their vast spatial perspective.

2) Improved processing of the enormous data sets being generated by airborne, satellite and ground sensors.

3) Ability to use AI to convolve maps with the massive geologic knowledge resident in multimodal Large Language Models. This gives the interpreter instant information regarding virtually any feature in the maps. GeoGPT's mapping tools do this, integrating LLMs with geospatial analytic capabilities to enable intuitive, AI-assisted mapping for geoscientists. These tools allow users to process and visualize complex geological datasets such as satellite imagery, LiDAR, seismic profiles, and field observations through natural language commands or automated workflows. Key functionalities include automated feature extraction (e.g., identifying faults or lithological boundaries), dynamic map generation with customizable layers, cross-disciplinary data fusion (e.g., merging geochemical and structural data), and predictive modeling for resource exploration or hazard assessment. By leveraging open-access global datasets they provide contextual insights through embedded geoscientific knowledge.

Perhaps counterintuitively, the need for the geoscientist (“mapper in the loop”) to critically verify all of the data and AI analysis is more important than ever. While new technologies provide focus for the more laborious field mapping, they do not in any way obviate it.

abstract: Complementary histological analyses may help resolve decades of conflicting geochemical signals from shark teeth. While enameloid microstructures of shark teeth preserve morphology during diagenesis, the geochemical properties remain more complicated. Despite the multi-layered enameloid and its intricate entanglement of enameloid tissues with dentin, the shark tooth enameloid has traditionally been considered geochemically uniform. We demonstrate, with high-resolution geochemical mapping, geochemical zoning within the enameloid, in alignment with the distinctive enameloid layers: the single crystallite enameloid and the parallel-, tangled-, and radial bundled enameloid layers. This geochemical mapping allows us to identify geochemically pristine zones in the enameloid, as well as altered geochemistry. The tangled bundled enameloid shows how dentinal intermingling may have been the culprit behind the mixed geochemical signals historically observed in shark tooth enameloid. For geochemical analyses, this section must therefore be avoided to sample pristine geochemistry, as the dentinal tissue is known to be more prone to recrystallization and diagenetic alteration. We examine the enameloid of numerous taxa of cartilaginous fish through geological time to better understand the geochemical properties of the different enameloid layers and the extent of dentinal intrusion and interconnection with the enameloid. We conduct a detailed study using multiple sections throughout the whole crown to capture a full three-dimensional perspective. This geochemical screening is essential for attributing pristine geochemistry and for recognizing compromised enameloid and zones with diagenetic alterations. Identifying and distinguishing between compromised and altered tissues highlights the potential for analyzing trace-element geochemistry and radiogenic isotopes in shark teeth as paleoenvironmental proxies and exposes probable pitfalls in a historical context.

title: Impact of Land Use/Land Cover Practices and Configuration on Freshwater Salinization Syndrome Solute and Nutrient Export in Two Suburban Headwater Streams

authors: Salanitri, Nicholas J [1], Weston, Nathaniel B [2], Kremer, Peleg [3], Goldsmith, Steven T [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and the Environment, Villanova University, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Department of Geography and the Environment, Villanova University, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA

abstract: In winter 2024-2025, Pennsylvania applied over 600,000 tons of road salt to state roads alone. Upon application, road salt is transported to nearby freshwater systems through surface runoff and groundwater via baseflow. Excess sodium in road salt-impacted runoff can lead to reverse cation exchange in nearby soils, causing increased cation and trace metal exports to waterways through a process known as the Freshwater Salinization Syndrome (FSS). Additionally, excess sodium can degrade soils, thereby enhancing the mobilization of organic matter and nitrogen into waterways, where they can affect downstream ecosystems and water supplies. While the FSS has many recognized negative impacts, little is known about how land use/land cover practices and configuration can affect the timing and delivery of FSS ions and nutrients (ex. dissolved organic carbon [DOC] and nitrate [NO 3 - ]) to suburban watersheds. We hypothesized that (1) FSS-related solutes will decrease as % forest cover increases longitudinally in the downstream direction reflecting dilution, and increase as % impervious surface cover (ISC) remains stable longitudinally reflecting a cumulative effect; (2) there will be a temporal lag between Cl - and NO 3 - /DOC pulses, and the relative time differences will differ as a function of sub-watershed area with larger watersheds experiencing greater lag times; and (3) DOC and NO 3 - pulses will be the highest following a winter storm event. To address these research questions, we performed weekly synoptic sampling over the 2026 water year for nine subwatersheds in the greater Philadelphia, Pennsylvania area that comprise the two larger watersheds of the Mill Creek and East Branch of the Indian Creek, which vary in ISC in their upstream area. Samples were analyzed for major cations (Na + , K + , Mg 2+ , Ca 2+ ), anions (Cl - , Br - , NO 3 - , PO 4 3- , SO 4 2- ), and DOC. GIS analysis was conducted to determine relative ISC and forest cover in each subwatershed. A spatial analysis of FSS solute concentrations was also performed to assess responses to the relative amount of ISC and forest cover in the upstream area. Likewise, a temporal analysis of Cl - and DOC/NO 3 - was performed at a subwatershed scale to determine the relative lag time of solutes following a winter storm event. The study results contribute to the understanding of FSS solute and nutrient transport in suburban watersheds, particularly those in road salt-affected regions.

title: Evidence of Magma Mingling and Mixing in a Mafic Magmatic Enclave in the Tuolumne Intrusive Complex, California, USA
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Harris, Morgan Ann [1], Gualda, Guilherme A. R. [2], Miller, Calvin F. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
abstract:
Magmatic enclaves are interpreted to reflect processes such as magma mingling and mixing, and as such can provide insight into pluton construction and open-system processes that influence evolution of magmatic systems. We are studying in detail a single large (~0.5 m), heterogenous, relatively mafic magmatic enclave (MME) from the equigranular Half Dome unit (eHD) of the Tuolumne Intrusive Complex (TIC), California. This enclave comprises three distinct lithologies: (1) dark grey enclave interior; (2) medium grey discontinuous rind on (1); (3) white discontinuous rind on (2). The enclave is enclosed within typical eHD granodiorite. Contact between (1) and host eHD is sharp; contact between (1) and (2) is diffuse; contact between (2) and (3) is sharp; and contact between (3) and host eHD is diffuse.

We characterize rock textures and plagioclase and amphibole major and trace-element compositions in this MME using SEM (BSE imaging and EDS quantitative analysis) and LA-ICP-MS. (1) and (2) contain both macrocrysts (~ 1 - 5 mm) and microcrysts (~ 0.05 – 0.60 mm) and (3) contains macrocrysts of plagioclase, amphibole, biotite, and alkali feldspar. Plagioclase macrocrysts display three textural patterns: 1) concentric zoning with some inclusions; 2) no visible (in BSE) zoning with few inclusions; 3) an anorthite-rich, ring-like zone and many inclusions. All plagioclase macrocrysts, regardless of overall pattern, have ~An 35 cores and ~An 25 rims. The anorthite-rich, ring-like zone and cores of plagioclase microcrysts in (1) are distinctly rich in Ca (~An 55 ). Rims of microcrysts in (1) are ~An 25 . These zoning patterns and compositional changes suggest that macrocrysts with the An-rich ring were entrained first, followed by the macrocrysts with concentric zoning, and finally the macrocrysts with no visible zoning. This suggests at least 3 stages of mingling during the formation of this enclave.

We estimate crystallization pressures using an amphibole geobarometer from Médard and Le Pennec (2022) using a different amphibole formula calculation from Gualda and Vlach (2005). Resulting pressures are: (1): 300 – 400 MPa; (2): 300 – 450 MPa; (3): 350 – 450 MPa; host eHD: 200 – 300 MPa. This variation in estimated crystallization pressures imply a multi-stage history of the enclave over a depth range on the order of 5 km, possibly involving several magmas and mingling events prior to emplacement of the eHD.

title: Multi-phase petro- and thermochronology resolves a progressive kinematic transition during emplacement of the northern Coast Mountains batholith

authors: Regan, Sean P. [1], Hofmann, Florian [2], Schmitz, Mark D. [3], Gillis, Robert [4], Waldien, Trevor Scott [5], Johnson, Sophia [6], Condit, Cailey Brown [7], Muller, Veleda Paiva [8]

(2) University of Alaska, Fairbanks, AK,

(4) Alaska Division of Geological & Geophysical Surveys, Fairbanks, AK,
(5) South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD,

abstract:
Cordillera-type arc batholiths are characteristically associated with transpressional deformation, and work along multiple active margins has demonstrated that magmatic periodicity modulates upper plate deformation. However, batholiths form over millions of years and exhibit punctuated addition rates, which make assessing progressive shifts in boundary conditions and resulting strains difficult without deconvolving detailed emplacement, deformation, and thermal histories. To address this issue, we performed high-precision CA ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon, in-situ titanite U-Pb petrochronology, and multiphase 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology from the northern Coast Mountains batholith (CMB) to constrain a time-resolved history of the axial portion of the CMB and the development of the Coast Shear zone. The northern CMB is an ideal location for this analysis as it trends directly into the >2000 km long Denali fault with a well-constrained <52 Ma slip budget.

The western margin of the axial portion of the CMB is composed of tonalitic protoliths exhibiting a strain gradient ranging from protomylonitic to completely undeformed within 15 km of its western contact. Stretching lineations are consistently down-dip independent of grain-size, apparent macroscopic strain, or age, and exhibit reverse-sense kinematic indicators. Paired zircon and titanite geochronology suggests that attenuation during reverse-sense, west-vergent deformation accompanied incremental emplacement from ca. 70-58 Ma. The remainder of the batholith was predominantly emplaced at or after 58 Ma and preserves shallowly plunging NW-SE lineations, including aligned enclave swarms consistent with tracking instantaneous strain during emplacement. We analyzed 18 biotite, feldspar, and hornblende samples for 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology, which document an inward cooling trend to 52 Ma, when the entire batholith cooled below biotite Ar closure temperatures. Cessation of arc magmatism corresponds to rapid integration of the Denali fault. Collectively, these data suggest a steady transition from pure-shear-dominated transpression resulting in contractional deformation, wrench-dominated transpression accompanying emplacement of the axial portion of the CMB, and integration of the Denali strike-slip fault during batholith cooling and strain hardening. While lower plate dynamics are increasingly recognized as primary contributors to high-flux magmatic events, perhaps rotating upper-plate kinematic boundary conditions contribute to the generation of high-flux events preserved in large Cordilleran-style arc batholiths.

title: Chemical Mohometry Gone Astray: Critical Appraisal and Recommendations for Improvement
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Kohn, Matthew J [1], Glazner, Allen F [2], Yakymchuk, Chris [3], Lopez, Armando [4], Roman, Gloria [5]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, Idaho, USA
(2) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, USA

abstract: Calculation of crustal thickness based on the geochemistry of arc magmas (chemical “mohometry”) relies on empirical correlations between seismically determined thickness and either elemental concentrations or elemental ratios in modern arcs. Such calculations ignore effects on magma chemistry of other intensive parameters, including oxygen fugacity (f O2 ), water fugacity (f H2O ), and temperature, as well as crystallization history. Here, we review the global arc database to show that data scatter is intrinsic to arc segment and volcano compositions. Minimum uncertainties are uniform and large, ranging from ±17-19 km (2s) for arc segments to ±21-23 km for volcanic complexes. Systematic compositional differences among volcanoes and arc segments, and strong correlations among proposed mohometers, prevent reduction of this uncertainty through either increased number of analyses or application of multiple proxies. Other factors besides crustal thickness – especially f O2 , f H2O , temperature, and crystallization history of major and accessory minerals – strongly affect trace-element chemistry of magmas and increase uncertainties. Large uncertainties and correlation of arc chemistry with both temperature and f O2 render many past estimates of crustal thickness and trends through time unreliable. Quantitative mohometry is currently no better than ~±20 km, irrespective of number and quality of analyses, and may be much worse depending on effects of intensive parameters – an uncertainty that is similar to or perhaps even greater than random variation in modern arc thickness (±25 km). Mohometry may be improved through analysis of detrital zircon, simultaneous characterization of f O2 and T, development of a geochemical proxy for f H2O , and further modeling.
