title: Microscope Mastery Levels: Applying Mastery Grading to Microscope Skills
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Taylor, Jennifer [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Biology, Geology, and Environmental Science, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, Chattanooga, TN, USA
abstract: Mastery grading is a strategy for providing students with flexible options for demonstrating mastery of learning objectives, and it is particularly useful for assessing skills that are used repeatedly and built gradually. This presentation describes a novel mastery grading scheme designed for assessing petrographic microscope skills across a 1-semester petrology class, but could be adapted for assessing any set of related skills practiced across multiple classroom or lab activities. In this example, students learn the fundamentals of microscope operation, identification of common minerals and rock textures, and optical properties used to identify minerals at the beginning of the semester, then practice and apply those skills during lab activities throughout the rest of the semester. This approach allows students to practice their microscope skills with the goal of achieving mastery by the end of the class. Students are supplied with a checklist of skills they have the opportunity to master, and are asked to self-assess which skills they have mastered after each lab activity. As students progress, they track their competency via Mastery Levels, which correlate to the number of skills they have mastered. The novel mastery grading scheme implemented here replaces lab practical exams with short oral exams wherein students choose the skills on which they will be tested, and the instructor chooses a random subset of the chosen skills to assess. Students who assess themselves at a higher mastery level have a larger pool of skills on which they could be tested. The purpose of the oral exam is for the instructor to assess the accuracy of the student’s self-reported Mastery Level, and the instructor can adjust the student’s level based on their performance. Mastery Levels are directly correlated to a Microscope Mastery Grade, with higher levels associated with higher grades. A student’s Mastery Level at the end of the semester determines this portion of their overall grade. Student feedback indicates this mastery grading scheme reduces stress associated with lab assessment (compared to a traditional lab practical exam), improves transparency surrounding learning expectations, and provides students with agency over their own learning. This grading scheme also provides instructors with a consistent means to track students’ progress throughout the semester and facilitates consistent and constructive feedback for students.

title: Delineation of a Mylonitized and Metamorphosed Pseudotachylyte System in the Homestake Shear Zone, Colorado
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Griffith, Gabriella Marie [1], Lowman, Charles J [2], Madajewicz, Maya Jasmin [3], Allen, Joseph L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Concord University, Athens, WV, USA
(2) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Concord University, Athens, WV, USA

abstract:
The nature of earthquakes in the mid-crust has been subject to extensive debate. We use mylonitic and metamorphosed pseudotachylyte (mpt) to characterize the nature of mid-crustal earthquakes along an 80-m-long outcrop in the Homestake shear zone (HSZ) as part of an NSF REU study. Mpt’s are notably difficult to identify and trace in the field; we use injection veins, branching veins, and a distinctive internal foliation and light-gray color to identify mpt. To aid in identification on the outcrop, we utilize handheld XRF and note a distinctive mpt chemistry reflected by the ratio (FeO+MgO+CaO+TiO 2 )/SiO 2 which averages 0.27 ± 0.01 for mpt, versus 0.16 ± 0.01 for host rock and 0.15 ± 0.08 for nearby pristine pseudotachylyte (pst).

Mpt zones are traceable for tens of meters, striking 060° parallel to the host-rock composite foliation. Mpt is composed of finely foliated biotite with s-c fabrics and elongated quartz porphyroclasts. Decimeter-scale sinistral offsets with an oblique reverse component are observed along 060° mpt zones. A Riedel-like fracture system striking 015° and 290° crosscuts the 060° mpt. The 015˚ set was reactivated and offsets the 060˚ mpt with a synthetic, sinistral shear sense by as much as 105 cm. Some 015˚ sets are lined with a second generation of mpt.

Field observations suggest an early and previously unrecognized, midcrustal polydeformation sequence in the HSZ pst system. Pristine pst was generated along the 060˚ foliation, and subsequently mylonitized and metamorphosed, followed by development of 015˚ and 290˚ brittle tensile fractures. The 015˚ fracture set was subsequently reactivated and locally generated mpt with a 3-5-m-length scale. Contrasting 015˚ and 060˚ orientations accommodating sinistral shear suggest the stress field rotated from ~N-S to ~NW-SE. The limited length scale of 015˚ mpt suggests ruptures originated in the mid-crust as opposed to downdip propagation from the upper crust.

title: Meteor (Barringer) Crater Chronicles: A Geophysical Investigation and Educational Field Campaign Using Drones, GPR, Seismic, Magnetic, Radiation. and Seismic Surveys
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Stewart, Robert R. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Houston, HOUSTON, TX, USA
abstract: Meteor (Barringer) Crater is one of the world’s most remarkable geologic sites and best preserved impact craters. It has been extensively studied. However, it remains somewhat enigmatic in shape (squarish) and still has much to teach us, for example, about ejecta distributions and the type and extent of subsurface deformations. We thus convened part of our 2026 University of Houston Environmental Geophysics Field Camp at Meteor Crater to undertake research into these questions as well as provide instruction about a range of geophysical instruments and surveys. We performed detailed airborne drone surveys, including flying into the crater itself, which have provided excellent topographic maps of the crater and surrounding area. We used Geiger counters in radial transects to find that there appears to be a correlation of rock and ejecta type and radioactivity with distance from the crater (this finding might be useful for planetary remote sensing). In addition, we conducted magnetometer surveys around the crater floor and in radial lines. GPR line and grid surveys, with a 250 MHz system, show good penetration to about 2 m and some details of the eject blanket. A series of seismic lines using a 48-channel recording system (both with planted geophones and a towed land streamer) using accelerated weight drop sources (500 kg and 40 kg) gave deeper penetration to several hundred meters. We are currently processing and integrating the data sets to refine estimates of the crater’s ejecta thicknesses, characterize near-surface structure, and investigate radial and circumferential fault systems associated with crater formation and the pre-existing geologic fabric.

authors: Madajewicz, Maya Jasmin [1], Kolawole, Folarin [2], Colet, Meritxell [3], Allen, Joseph L. [4], Kuehn, Stephen C. [5]

abstract: Pseudotachylytes serve as unique markers of ancient and modern rheology. While historically thought to have primarily mafic matrix composition, we propose pseudotachylytes cross-cutting quartzo-feldspathic granitic host rock, especially when forming in fluid-rich environments, can exhibit primarily felsic matrices. We used EPMA to conduct EDS and BSE imaging on four samples of suspect pseudotachylyte collected along exhumed fault rocks in the Kgomodikae Shear Zone in Kaapvaal Craton, Botswana, and the Kilosa border fault in Tanzania. The host rocks along these fault zones lack common mafic minerals such as biotite and amphibole, which melt at significantly lower temperatures than quartz and feldspars and typically contribute to the composition of pseudotachylyte matrices. The Tanzania suspect pseudotachylyte matrix is composed primarily of quartz with streaked albite and oxides containing iron, titanium, and magnesium. The pseudotachylytes cut hydrothermal veins of kaolinites and rocks containing chloritized biotite. Younger iron oxide veins cut the pseudotachylytes. The Botswana suspect pseudotachylytes have a similar matrix of quartz and muscovite with Ti-silicates. The pseudotachylytes exploit the boundaries of and cut through quartz veins. Survivor clasts in both pseudotachylytes are composed primarily of 50-150 µm quartz and feldspars with embayments and semi-rounded edges. The pseudotachylyte matrices are likely recrystallized from a finer-grained precursor. The unusual felsic matrix suggests extremely high temperatures of shearing: up to 900C hotter than necessary to begin melting mafic biotites and amphiboles. Hydrothermal veins and hydrothermally altered minerals throughout the host rocks suggest that there may have been fluid present at the time of melt, lowering mineral melting points and mediating the necessary temperature increase to melt the host rock. Ongoing work examines titanium in quartz to obtain a better understanding of the temperature of formation of the host rocks.

authors: Beirl, Aaron Michael [1], Hummer, Daniel Robert [2], Henson, Harvey [3], Devera, Joe [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, Carbondale, Illinois, USA

abstract: Hicks Dome is a crypto-volcanic feature found in the southeastern corner of Hardin County, Illinois. Forming around 270 Ma (late Permian), as part of the Permian Wauboukigou Igneous Province (PWIP), through a series of explosive igneous intrusions that caused uplift and clear structural deformation to the area.The overall geochemistry of these intrusions have high amounts of iron (Fe) and calcium (Ca), with relatively low amounts of silicon (Si), forming amalgamations of alkaline, carbonatitic, and ultramafic gabbros. A previous characterization of the Grant Intrusive revealed the potential for economic concentrations of barium (Ba), titanium (Ti), and thorium (Th), as well has Heavy Rare Earth Elements (HREEs) including scandium (Sc) and yttrium (Y).The Grant Intrusive has been cited in several studies including Bradbury and Baxter, (1992); Reynolds et. al. (1997); and Trela et. al. (2024). However, the Vaughn Intrusive has not been previously studied or cited in any publications or papers until now. The composition and mineralogy of the Vaughn Intrusive has been unknown, but it still leaves the question of whether or not this intrusion is possibly connected to the Grant Intrusive, due to its close vicinity, or were these intrusions formed from different magmatic episodes? Initial samples for the Grant Intrusive were provided by the Illinois State Geological Survey (ISGS), and additional samples for the Grant Intrusive and initial samples for the Vaughn Intrusive were collected during a field expedition on October 19th 2024. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD), Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM-EDS), and an optical petrographic analysis were all utilized to analyze potential ore and gangue minerals. X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) was used to determine bulk geochemistry and make inferences on element partitioning and economic viability, Electron Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) was used in conjunction to confirm the presence of critical elements such as palladium and niobium. A magnetic anomaly model of the intrusion was also constructed using a dual sensor cesium vapor magnetometer, and Surfer Pro Modeling Software. Results show extensive emplacement of ultramafic material throughout the Hicks Dome region, and strong potential for economic HREE ores in breccias proximal to Grant Intrusive. Geochemical and mineralogical data also show many differences between the Grant Intrusive and Vaughn Intrusive magmas, indicating that multiple magma sources or episodes of magmatic differentiation have taken place.

title: Groundwater Contributions Dominate for Export of Most Solutes in Urban Streams near Baltimore, MD
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Moore, Joel [1], Marsh, Melinda [2], Duncan, Jonathan [3], Navarre-Sitchler, Alexis K. [4]
affiliations: (1) Towson University, Towson, MD,
(2) Penn State University, State College, PA, USA
(3) Penn State University, State College, PA, USA
(4) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Decades of research have documented increased stream discharge in urban watersheds due to runoff from impervious surfaces with accompanying increases in erosion. Additionally, solute concentrations are commonly found to be elevated in urban streams over nearby forested streams. However, much less is known about patterns of solute export from urban streams, including how export is partitioned between quick flow (e.g., overland flow) and slow flow (predominantly groundwater). We investigated solute concentrations and export in four small watersheds (<7 sq km) in the Mid-Atlantic of the United States near Baltimore, Maryland. In a mostly forested (>70%) watershed with ~1% impervious surface cover (ISC) and two urban watersheds with ~25% ISC, we collected biweekly water samples, stormwater samples, and high-frequency data with specific conductance (SpC) probes. In a fourth watershed that was forested with no ISC, we collected biweekly samples. Discharge data came from US Geological Survey gaging stations. High-frequency concentrations were calculated using relationships with SpC or discharge (depending on the solute) and then were used to calculate export. We used a digital recursive filter to separate quick and slow flow contributions.

The two urban watersheds had much higher flashiness than the (mostly) forested watershed with solutes typically exhibiting strong dilution as discharge increased (except for dissolved organic carbon). Baseflow export of water was 85% of total discharge in the forested watersheds and ~45–55% in the urban watersheds. In the mostly forested watershed, solute export at baseflow was ~85%, matching baseflow water export. By contrast, in the urban watersheds, baseflow solute export was much higher than baseflow water export as a percentage of total export, e.g., ~70% for chloride and dissolved silica and ~65% for alkalinity. Higher concentrations of most solutes in the urban watersheds resulted in larger export from these watersheds than the forested watersheds. The urban watersheds also had a much higher percentage of total chloride export (~70%) during winter months (Dec–Mar) than water export (~38%); export of other solutes was more similar to water export though with some variability. Our results indicate that groundwater was the predominant contributor to export of most solutes in small urban watersheds even though only ~50% of water in these watersheds was exported at baseflow.

(2) Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(3) Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
abstract:
Surface water–groundwater interactions in low-gradient streams draining glaciated terrain remain poorly constrained, particularly where low-permeability diamicton limits groundwater flux while evapotranspiration strongly influences watershed water balance. Previous investigations of a third-order stream in central Illinois documented persistent upward hydraulic gradients from the surficial aquifer to the stream, indicating groundwater discharge. However, streamflow decreases along the study reach, suggesting apparent losing-stream behavior despite gaining hydraulic conditions. Resolving this contradiction is critical for characterizing groundwater flow systems and associated solute transport.

This study uses diel air–water temperature signals to independently evaluate groundwater influence on the stream. Continuous temperature and hydraulic head data were collected at 15-minute intervals from the stream and streambed wells at upstream and downstream locations. Temperature records were reduced to daily maximum air and water temperatures and analyzed using paired air–water signal metrics, including amplitude ratios, to quantify thermal coupling and evaluate spatial and temporal variations in groundwater influence.

Results indicate that groundwater influences stream temperature year-round, although the magnitude of influence varies between locations and through time. Groundwater control on stream temperature increased from late May through early August and decreased during storm events, reflecting shifts in streamflow generation mechanisms. The thermal analysis confirms groundwater upwelling throughout the study reach. Consequently, the observed downstream reduction in discharge is more consistent with evapotranspiration-driven water loss than with seepage from the stream to the aquifer. These findings demonstrate the value of integrating thermal methods with conventional hydraulic measurements to resolve apparent inconsistencies in stream classification and improve understanding of groundwater–surface water exchange in low-gradient glacial landscapes.

title: Cordilleran exhumation patterns during Mesozoic accretion and extension of the Yukon-Tanana upland (eastern Alaska) and Cenozoic strike-slip along the Tintina fault: New insights from detrital and bedrock thermochronology
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Lease, Richard Oliver [1], Bender, Adrian M. [2], Jones, James V. [3], Gooley, Jared T. [4], Stockli, Daniel F. [5], O'Sullivan, Paul B. [6]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK,
(4) United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK,
(5) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(6) GeoSep Services, Moscow, ID,
abstract:
Assembly of the North American Cordillera occurred through accretion and translation along terrane boundaries that drove intracontinental deformation, however regional space-time and local fault-controlled exhumation patterns in the Northern Cordillera are poorly constrained. We use detrital thermochronology of modern rivers to illuminate regional Mesozoic–Cenozoic exhumation patterns across the entire Yukon-Tanana upland of east-central Alaska, and bedrock thermochronology to ascertain local Paleocene–Eocene exhumation adjacent to the Tintina fault.

Detrital apatite U-Pb (dAUPb) ages show a spatial contrast in middle crustal cooling between terranes. The Yukon-Tanana Terrane exhibits Triassic–Jurassic dAUPb ages that reflect exhumation during collisional orogenesis, whereas parautochthonous North America displays Cretaceous dAUPb and detrital apatite fission-track (dAFT) ages that reflect rapid cooling during subsequent extensional collapse. In contrast, Cretaceous and Cenozoic dAFT ages are ubiquitous across both terranes and suggest a shared upper crustal cooling history. Cretaceous dAFT ages suggest exhumation of both the upper and lower extensional plates to shallow crustal levels, and regionally widespread Paleocene–Eocene dAFT ages overlap documented strike-slip along the Tintina and other regional faults.

We further constrain Paleocene–Eocene exhumation with four vertical transects through Cretaceous-Cenozoic plutons along 270 km of the Tintina fault. Bedrock (U-Th)/He ages from apatite (AHe) and zircon (ZHe) indicate that the onset of exhumation youngs from ~65 Ma to ~45 Ma to the northwest, mirroring regional dAFT age patterns. Inverse modeling of vertical transect data suggests a pulse of >2–4 km of Paleocene-Eocene exhumation occurred sequentially along strike of the Tintina fault and may record fault linkage and propagation, coeval with the fault’s inferred ~430–490 km of dextral offset. North of the Tintina fault, a 5-km-thick Paleogene stratigraphic succession accumulated in the Yukon Flats basin, whereas the plate margin to the south was characterized by terminal Wrangellia terrane accretion, rapid convergence, and spreading ridge subduction. The Tintina fault thus localized Paleocene–Eocene exhumation and sedimentation in interior Alaska while facilitating large-magnitude coast-parallel dextral translation during formation of the southern Alaska orocline. Subsequently, <1 km of Oligocene–recent exhumation is indicated by AHe-ZHe data, consistent with a plate reorganization that led to exhumation and strike-slip waning in the Yukon-Tanana upland and shifting southward to the Alaska Range and St. Elias Range, where they were later intensified by Yakutat flat-slab subduction.

title: Thermal Structure Beneath the Atlas Mountains of Algeria Revealed by a Two-Stage Bayesian Framework of Aeromagnetic Data with Uncertainty Quantification
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Salawu, Banji [1], Kusumoto, Shigekazu [2], Mickus, Kevin Lee [3], Oussou, Ahmed [4]
affiliations: (1) BS Geophysical and Consultancy Ltd. Nigeria, Lagos, Nigeria
(2) Institute for Geothermal Sciences, University of Kyoto, Kyoto, Japan
(3) Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
(4) Université Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah, Fez, Morocco
abstract: Understanding the lithospheric thermal structure is essential for deciphering tectonic evolution and evaluating geothermal resources. However, the thermal regime of the Algerian Atlas remains poorly constrained owing to the limited availability of direct heat-flow measurements. This study presents a two-stage Bayesian inversion framework for estimating the Curie point depth and associated uncertainty from aeromagnetic data, providing a probabilistic characterization of the regional thermal structure. The Bayesian approach integrates radial power spectrum analysis with posterior probability estimation, allowing robust quantification of model uncertainty. Estimated Curie depths range from approximately 11 to 29 km, revealing pronounced lateral thermal heterogeneity across the Algerian Atlas. Shallow Curie depths are concentrated beneath the Tell Atlas and parts of the High Plateaus, whereas deeper magnetic boundaries occur mainly within the Saharan Atlas, reflecting variations in lithospheric architecture and tectonic deformation. The uncertainty analysis indicates generally low posterior uncertainties across most of the study area, with localized increases restricted to regions of weak magnetic signal or complex subsurface structure. Integration of the Curie depth model with radiogenic heat production and thermal conductivity yields geothermal gradients of approximately 20–55 °C km⁻¹ and geothermal heat flow values of 50–110 mW m⁻². Elevated geothermal gradients and heat flow consistently coincide with shallow Curie depths, indicating anomalously warm crust and enhanced geothermal potential beneath the Tell Atlas and adjacent tectonically active regions. These results demonstrate a strong coupling between Curie depth, lithospheric thermal structure, and regional tectonics. The proposed two-stage Bayesian framework provides a robust and reproducible methodology for regional thermal modelling, uncertainty quantification, and geothermal assessment in tectonically complex regions.

title: Gravity analysis of Biscuit Basin, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources (Posters)
authors: Mickus, Kevin Lee [1]
affiliations: (1) Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
abstract: Yellowstone National Park contains the largest concentration of geothermal features in the world. The majority of the larger springs and geysers are in the western portion of the park along the Firehole River and include the world famous Old Faithful Geyser. However, there are several smaller and interesting geothermal basins near Old Faithful including the Black Sand and Biscuit Geyser basins. Biscuit Basin has recently become of great interest despite only having a few smaller geyser and hot springs because of a large steam explosion that occurred on July 23, 2024 of the previously inactive Black Diamond Pool. Since this eruption, Black Diamond has continued to explode at irregular intervals and with no precursor events and in May-July of 2026, other explosions have occurred to the north of Black Diamond Pool. To better understand the subsurface structure of the region, geophysical surveys including 35 seismic sensors, electrical resistivity and time-domain EM surveys, thermal and magnetic drone surveys by the Univ. of Utah and the USGS have been conducted. To compliment these surveys, a gravity survey was conducted where initially 55 stations were recorded surrounding the pool in 2025 and in 2026, 82 additional stations have been recorded within the entire basin. The initial complete Bouguer gravity anomaly patterns indicate low density regions to the west (extending to Jewel Geyser) and to the north, however the new data indicates that these regions still have lower values than the surrounding regions, the amplitude of these anomalies are considerably less. Residual and derivative maps confirm these locations and a 3D inverse model indicates that the low density sources are between 20 to 50 meters of the surface.

title: Igneous Activity within the Western and Central Offshore Libya, Part of the North African Passive Margin
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Reeh, Guima [1], Gharbi, Mohamed [2], Mickus, Kevin Lee [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom
(2) Water research and Technologies Center, Soliman, Tunisia, Tunisia
(3) Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
abstract: The western and central offshore Libya occupies a strategic position within the Pelagian Domain of the central Mediterranean, where the interaction between lithospheric extension, inherited basement structures, and magmatism has played a fundamental role in passive-margin evolution. Although numerous studies have documented volcanic activity across the Mediterranean region, the origin, spatial distribution, and tectonic significance of igneous bodies beneath the offshore Libyan margin remain insufficiently constrained. This study presents a regional synthesis based on tectonic reconstruction, structural interpretation, bathymetric analysis, exploration well data, magnetic and gravity map analyzes, and two-dimensional gravity–magnetic forward modelling. The integrated interpretation demonstrates that magmatism within the study area is polyphase, with major igneous episodes occurring during the Mesozoic, and Neogene–Quaternary tectonic phases. Several exploration wells penetrate volcanic rocks, with the thickest volcanic interval being encountered in the Jarrafa-1 well, where 409 m of volcanic rocks were penetrated. Petrographic investigation of basaltic material from well B1-NC-35A indicates that these volcanic rocks are altered and fragmented, with hydrothermal alteration resulting in densities lower than those of fresh basalt. Consequently, the shallow volcanic successions alone cannot explain the high amplitude magnetic anomalies observed in the area. These anomalies exhibit predominantly WNW and north-south orientations that closely follow inherited basement structures established during Hercynian and Pan-African tectonic events. Map enhancement methods demonstrate that these anomalies are structurally controlled and associated with major crustal discontinuities. A power spectrum analysis identifies three magnetic sources. Shallow sources correspond to volcanic rocks whereas intermediate and deep magnetic sources indicate extensive basement-controlled bodies extending several km beneath the sedimentary succession. Two-dimensional modelling confirm that shallow volcanic rocks alone cannot reproduce the observed anomaly amplitudes. Instead, satisfactory models require the presence of deeper, high-density and high-susceptibility intrusive bodies emplaced within the basement or lower crust. These observations support a two-level magmatic system consisting of shallow volcanic and volcaniclastic sequences overlying deep intrusive complexes. The deep intrusions are interpreted to have been emplaced along basement fault systems r reactivated during successive tectonic episodes. The study therefore suggests that structural inheritance exerted first-order control on magma ascent and emplacement throughout the evolution of the Pelagian Domain.

title: Element mobility and alteration styles recorded by PIXL in the Jezero Crater Margin unit on Mars
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Li, An Y. [1], Ramo, Kirtee [2], Kizovski, Tanya [3], Hurowitz, Joel A. [4], Treiman, Allan H. [5], Schmitz, Nicole [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(2) Stony Brook University, USA
(3) Brock University, Canada
(4) Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY, USA
(5) Lunar & Planetary Institute, Houston, TX, USA
(6) German Aerospace Center (DLR), Germany
abstract: Characterized by high carbonate and silica content, the Margin unit in Jezero crater has an enigmatic origin with hypotheses ranging from in-situ alteration of an igneous cumulate to serpentinization of a clastic, olivine-rich rock. Using the Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry on the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, we apply elemental ratios to bulk sums and distinct mineral phases at fine scale (~120 μm spot size) to understand differences between the compositions of the Eastern and Western Margin. We find that altered olivine––defined as 0.6<(Fe+Mg)/Si<1.0, SiO2 wt%<50, and Ca/(Mg+Fe)<0.05––exhibits progressively higher Mg# than coexisting pristine olivine from the Eastern to the Western Margin, and this trend persists even after accounting for differences in the pristine olivine Mg#. This increase in altered-olivine Mg# coincides with progressively higher bulk CO₂ wt% concentrations toward the Western Margin and increasing elevation. Together, these observations are consistent with progressively greater Fe partitioning during alteration, suggesting that the Western Margin records a more advanced stage of serpentinization to carbonation pathway. The Si-rich (>70 wt%) interstitial phases Eastern and Western Margin also record distinct alteration histories. The Eastern Margin Si-rich phase is enriched in SiO₂, TiO₂, Al₂O₃, FeT, CaT, Na₂O, K₂O, and Cl relative to the Western Margin. This geochemical signature is consistent with diagenetic cementation of a porous clastic framework that incorporates external silica cement and mobile element concentration from pore fluid interaction. The co-enrichment of Na₂O, K₂O, and Cl in particular is difficult to explain by in-situ serpentinization of an olivine-dominated protolith, which provides no local source for these elements. In contrast, the Western Margin Si-rich phase is enriched in MgT. This enhanced MgT in both the altered olivine and Si-rich phase is consistent with more closed-system alteration of a less porous in-situ protolith with limited external fluid access. Whether the Western Margin represents an in-situ altered igneous cumulate or a less reworked clastic end-member (in which open-system Mg loss was limited) cannot be fully resolved with the current dataset and represents a priority for returned sample analysis. The differences in altered-olivine Mg#, CO₂ abundance, and Si-rich interstitial phase composition indicate that the Western and Eastern Margin record distinct alteration histories rather than representing a single, compositionally uniform alteration process.

title: Magma hydration and oxidation in porphyry Cu-forming magmas: Insights from whole-rock hygrometry and zircon geochemistry
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits.
authors: Rezeau, Hervé [1], Bo, Hongze [2], Jagoutz, Oliver [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA
abstract:
Porphyry copper deposits are the world's primary source of copper and also provide substantial amounts of gold, molybdenum, and several critical metals essential for the global energy transition. Despite their economic importance, the discovery rate of new porphyry copper deposits has declined over the past decade, widening the gap between projected copper demand and future supply. Magmatic water content is widely recognized as a first-order control on the fertility of arc magmas and the formation of giant porphyry copper systems, yet robust and broadly applicable methods for estimating melt H₂O remain limited.

Here, we combine a newly developed whole-rock hygrometer with zircon trace element geochemistry to establish practical geochemical proxies for assessing magma fertility. Application of the hygrometer to magmatic suites associated with porphyry copper provinces globally demonstrates that fertile magmatism is consistently associated with melt H₂O contents of approximately 4–6 wt.%, providing quantitative constraints on the hydrous conditions favorable for ore formation. Further application to four major porphyry copper districts from the North and South American Cordilleras and the Central Tethyan belt further reveals that intrusions predating mineralization are on average less hydrous than those presumably associated with ore formation.

These whole-rock estimates provide an independent framework for assessing zircon trace element chemistry as indicators of melt hydration. Zircon Hf-Ti systematics closely mirror whole-rock hygrometer estimates, with zircons crystallized from relatively dry magmas exhibiting higher Ti concentrations than zircons crystallized from more hydrous melts at comparable zircon Hf contents. Moreover, positive correlations between zircon Hf-Ti systematics and Ce-Eu anomalies indicate that increasing melt H₂O and oxygen fugacity evolved together during the generation of fertile magmatic systems. This relationship may reflect the combined effects of progressive magma cooling and sulfur degassing.

Because magmatic rocks in porphyry copper districts are commonly overprinted by extensive hydrothermal alteration, obtaining representative fresh whole-rock samples is often challenging. By calibrating zircon trace element chemistry against whole-rock hygrometer estimates, this integrated approach provides complementary, inexpensive, and widely applicable tools for assessing magma fertility and prioritizing exploration targets in porphyry copper districts.

title: South American and West African Records of Gondwana Assembly
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Caxito, Fabricio [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte, MG, Brazil
abstract: The Neoproterozoic to Cambrian assembly of western Gondwana was a prolonged and diachronous process developed through successive episodes of subduction, accretion, ocean closure, collision, and lateral escape of crustal blocks. These processes are recorded within the network of Brasiliano/Pan-African orogenic belts formed through the convergence of paleocontinents and magmatic arcs, with fragments of oceanic lithosphere squeezed in-between, due to closure of the external Goiás-Pharusian and Adamastor oceans and other minor internal seaways. The latter formed through early Tonian rifting of a former Central African Block (1000-900 Ma), that comprised what would later become the São Francisco-Congo cratonic core and reworked basement tracts found within the Brasiliano/Pan-African provinces. This process led to decratonization of the hyperextended blocks, generating ribbon continents that separated newly formed V-shaped oceans. Despite regional diachronism in the thousands-of-km long orogenic systems, magmatic arcs developed broadly in two main pulses, in the Tonian (ca. 900-717 Ma, mostly in the external oceanic realms) and late Cryogenian/Ediacaran (ca. 650-560 Ma, in both internal and external oceans), with flare-ups related to changes in subduction dynamics. Both arc systems are comprised of expanded calc-alkaline, magnesian, metaluminous gabbro-tonalite-granodiorite-granite/basalt-dacite-andesite-rhyolite rock series. The Tonian arc systems are mostly juvenile, with mantle-like isotope signatures, interpreted as representing oceanic island arc systems. The Ediacaran arcs, on the other hand, show mixed mantle-crustal isotope signatures, and are interpreted as developed in continental (Andean-like) arc settings. Regional records of continental collision and widespread Himalayan-like anatexis occurred in distinct pulses: ca. 630-600 Ma (collision of the southwestern São Francisco margin and the Paranapanema paleocontinent, collision of the southernmost blocks), ca. 570-560 Ma (closure of the Araçuaí-West Congo gulf) and finally, ca. 540-520 Ma, with collision of the Rodinia-derived Amazonian paleocontinent to the amassed central African blocks. Due to the deformable nature of the intervening decratonized ribbon continents, enduring convergence after the main collisional stages led to the development of large tracts dominated by transcurrent tectonics, generating thousands-of-km long strike-slip shear zones in large-scale keirogens. The rifting, accretion and collisional processes involved in Gondwana amalgamation coincide with major shifts in Earth’s biosphere, atmosphere, plate tectonics and climate, and might have influenced these processes in both positive and negative feedback loops. This work is supported by Instituto GeoAtlantico, Brazil (CNPq 405653/2022-0).

title: New Insights into the Onset of the PETM from the Hanna Basin in Wyoming
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Howard, Luke [1], Dechesne, Marieke [2], Currano, Ellen [3], Foreman, Brady Zangs [4], Dunn, Regan Elizabeth [5], McLane, Korion [6], Terrell, Hannah [7], Diefendorf, Aaron [8]
affiliations: (1) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
(4) Western Washington University-Geology Department, Bellingham, WA, USA
(5) Natural History Museum of Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(6) Vassar College, Poughkeepsie, NY, USA
(7) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
(8) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
abstract:
The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) was one of the hottest and most rapid warming events triggered by a large carbon release in the geologic past. The PETM is well recognized from numerous marine and terrestrial sites across the globe. Terrestrial settings especially provide critical information about the structure and timing of carbon cycle perturbation. In the western USA, most records of the PETM have poor organic matter preservation, which complicates reconstructing the PETM using organic geochemistry proxies. The Hanna Basin, in southeast Wyoming, preserves abundant organic matter due to the prevalence of carbonaceous shales and coals. To better understand the carbon release during the PETM, we are analyzing the carbon isotope excursion (CIE) in the Hanna Basin at high resolution.

The Hanna Basin late Paleocene and early Eocene stratigraphy is characterized by repeating layers of coal, shale, and sandstone. Preliminary identification of the PETM was established by stratigraphic relationships to previously studied outcrops. To produce a high-resolution isotopic record of the PETM, we sampled every 2.5 feet of core drilled through the PETM section, along with every 10 feet of core above and below the PETM. This was done to measure carbon isotope values of the CIE and the pre- and post-recovery sections for a total of 455 samples across 1,300 feet of core. Many samples contain siderite, which complicates analyzing the carbon isotopic composition (δ 13 C) of the total organic carbon (TOC). Because of this, samples were decarbonated to remove siderite. This was done by acidifying the samples with 6M HCl for 3 days at 50ºC. On average, the mass loss from the acidification process was 9.47%. Samples are currently being analyzed for δ 13 C and %TOC.

Initial results indicate that we can likely constrain the onset, body, and recovery of the CIE in high resolution, which will provide unique insights into the structure of the early CIE and carbon release at the onset of the PETM.

title: Chondrule Mesostasis in the Allan Hills 81189 Enstatite Chondrite
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials (Posters)
authors: Bhandari, Maya [1], Weisberg, Michael [2], Ebel, Denton [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Occidental College, Los Angeles, California, USA; Earth and Planetary Sciences, American Museum of Natural History, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, American Museum of Natural History, New York City, California, USA; City University of New York, New York City, New York, USA
(3) Earth and Planetary Sciences, American Museum of Natural History, New York City, New York, USA
abstract:
Chondrites are among the oldest materials in our solar systemand thought to be the “leftover building blocks” of the terrestrial planets. Enstatite Chondrites (ECs) are the most reduced primitive materials in the solar system, and isotopically closest to the Earth and Moon. Allan Hills (ALH) 81189 is one of the most primitive ECs, so its analysis can offer a clearer glimpse into the early solar system environment in which they formed. Many chondrules– submillimeter, semi-round melt droplets which formed in the protoplanetary disk– contain a glassy quenched silicate melt between olivine and pyroxene grains. This material is called mesostasis and is interpreted to be residual melt which was unable to completely crystallize. The compositions and textures of chondrules and their mesostasis constrain their formation conditions, including their thermal histories and volatile behavior.

We analyzed chondrules and mesostasis in a thin section of ALH 81189 using optical microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and Electron Probe Microanalysis (EPMA) to examine textures and chemical compositions across 15 chondrules. A Time-Dependent Intensity (TDI) correction was used to compensate for alkali ion migration under the beam, which may contribute to higher sodium values. EPMA analysis reveals that the mesostasis in this EC is especially sodium-rich (up to 12.3 wt%), an interesting result given sodium’s moderately volatile nature and the subsequent expectation of significant depletion during chondrule formation. We further identified the pyroxene mineral pigeonite in two chondrules thus far, which constrains those chondrules’ thermal histories. The pigeonite is Mg-rich, which brings its crystallization temperature up to ~991 ℃, and its preservation indicates a cooling rate of >100℃/hr. This is consistent with the barred olivine (BO) texture seen in one of these chondrules.

These findings indicate volatile retention despite high crystallization temperatures, which may be due to a high dust to gas ratio and/or high sodium fugacity in the formation environment. The abundance of chondrule mesostasis, and the presence of pigeonite and BO texture indicate very rapid cooling, which may have further contributed to the retention of volatiles, including sodium. The texture of the mesostasis remains glassy throughout, without development of secondary feldspars. This, along with the sharply defined chondrules and their heterogeneous chemical compositions, confirms the very primitive nature of ALH 81189.

title: A New Angle: Reinterpreting the Faulting in the Alexander Hills, Southeastern California.
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Sorber, Thomas M. [1], Lutz, Brandon M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Appalachian State University, Boone, NC, USA
(2) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Appalachian State University, Boone, NC, USA
abstract:
The Alexander Hills are relatively low-relief hills that lie near the southern terminus of the Nopah Range in southeastern California. The area exposes a folded and faulted Mesoproterozoic-early Cambrian stratigraphic sequence. Previous 1:24,000 scale mapping shows both strike-slip and normal faulting, consistent with regional transtension. However, our detailed 1:10,000 scale mapping documents predominantly strike-slip and contraction, consistent with transpression. The main, previously unmapped E-W trending strike-slip fault displays a left-lateral slip gradient with ~270 m of separation near the fault center and tips out into a fault-propagation fold within the upper Noonday Dolomite and Johnnie Formation. The fold axis is steeply inclined to subvertical.

Lithology controls both deformation style and the location of small, abandoned talc mines in the field area. Strain is localized within weak rock units, while more competent dolostones show distributed brecciation. The eastern segment of the fault jogs to the south, forming a restraining bend where it cuts across the most competent Noonday Dolomite. This bend produces localized contraction which formed a small anticline and thrust fault. Hydrothermal fluids within the Noonday dolostones were likely trapped by the overlying shale-rich Johnnie Formation, leading to intense brecciation and mineralization along the fault tip. We use detailed 3D subsurface modeling and 2D forward kinematic modeling to explore the local kinematics and geomechanical controls on faulting and fluid flow. In January 2027, we plan to resume fieldwork in the Alexander Hills, expand the map to the south, and collect additional structural data to better understand the local controls on deformation.

title: An Approach to Engineering Geological Characterization for Research, Development, and Hazard Mitigation
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Schulz, William [1]
affiliations: (1) Landslide Hazards Program, US Geological Survey, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Geodynamics operating from millions of years ago to the present determine the properties and distribution of earth materials from sub-millimeter to regional scales, while also contributing to future processes that may affect those materials and Earth’s inhabitants. For humans to best interact with the natural environment, effective engineering geological characterization is needed that accounts for these dimensions of time and space. In 1951, the Geological Society of America defined the Professional Engineering Geologist as someone “…qualified…for…assuring that the geologic elements affecting…projects are adequately treated...” Seventy-five years later, that definition still rings true whether those “geologic elements” relate to contaminated water supplies, expansive soil destroying infrastructure, landslides sweeping through communities, or myriad others. Today, “projects” extend beyond those related to site construction and hazard mitigation to include research studies that rely upon understanding variables determinable from current knowledge. Since the 1928 St. Francis Dam disaster killed hundreds and essentially marked the beginning of engineering geology as a discipline in the United States, its importance has waxed and waned with hazard recognition. Recent decades present a frustrating paradox, with fewer educational opportunities in engineering geology despite seemingly escalating disasters. Geological disasters are often preventable following the systematic approaches to engineering geological characterization developed by Terzaghi, Bjerrum, Legget, Johnson, and others. This presentation briefly describes such an approach with hopes of improving the outcomes of “projects” addressed by our field.

Although the underlying premise of the engineering geological characterization approach is simple, achieving a solution requires rigorous geological discipline. The approach relies on creating a dynamic engineering geological model beginning with the present-day regional scale, which is then systematically tested and refined through iterative, spatiotemporally focused studies. Following such an approach helps to ensure accounting for the grand scale of geological materials and processes. The final output is a robust, four-dimensional model of project materials and processes that invariably extend far beyond project boundaries.

abstract: The Tyee Ridge Complex Fire in the Oregon Coast Range burned 32 km 2 from 24 August 2023 to 28 September 2023. The site has a history of logging, including salvage logging that occured immediately after the fire. In March 2025, back-to-back atmospheric river storms (12-14 March 2025 and 14-17 March 2025) affected the site, leading to widespread debris-flow activity throughout. Eyewitnesses reported that debris flows initiated on 16 March 2025 (from 8:00-11:00 am local time). In this study, we developed an inventory of >200 landslide-generated debris flows using orthoimagery and topographic data from an uncrewed aerial vehicle. The study site was categorized into three vegetation cover types: prefire logged, postfire salvage logged, and not recently logged. Landslide-initiated debris flows were observed in all three cover types, but most of the mass movements were observed in the salvage logged areas (61%). We also observed more debris flows in after the fire compared to pre-fire debris-flow activity recorded in historic widespread non-fire related events in 1996-97, indicating wildfire may result in more debris-flows events. Additionally, we found that rainfall thresholds established for runoff-generated postfire debris flows did not match the observed rainfall triggering characteristics (e.g., the timing and intensity of the measured rainfall). However, existing regional rainfall thresholds in western Oregon for 24-hr cumulative rainfall totals matched the timing of observed landslide initiation well. This study indicates that longer duration rainfall thresholds may be a better metric for estimating the timing of postfire landslide-generated postfire debris flows in the Oregon Coast Range, and logging activities increased the density of landsliding compared with burned-unlogged areas.

title: Double-Dipping: It Happens More Than You Think (An In Situ Geochemical Perspective of Subduction Cycling from Franciscan Garnets)
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Page, F. Zeb [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Oberlin College, Oberlin, OH, USA
abstract:
In the Franciscan Formation of California, USA, detailed outcrop and thin section analysis of serpentinite mélange has provided a record of as many as three distinct subduction - exhumation - erosion - deposition cycles (Wakabayashi, 2012, Tectonophysics; 2015, Int Geo Rev). Garnet-bearing high-pressure rocks (hornblende, eclogite, blueschist) that are found within these mélange deposits are the oldest materials in the Franciscan (~147-169Ma), and, thus, had the most time available for multiple excursions within the subduction zone. However, field evidence of these cycles is limited to events later than ~130Ma due to the age of the preserved mélanges.

Almost 60 years of petrological studies of high-grade blocks have identified polymetamorphism (e.g., Essene, 1967, Contrib Mineral Petrol) and complicated chemical zoning in minerals (e.g., Dudley, 1969, Am Min), that could be (but generally have not been) attributed to multiple subduction cycles. More recent work on inclusions, oxygen isotope and trace element zoning in garnets have shed light on multiple processes that affect these records (including metamorphic reactions, rates of diffusion, transient porosity, and fluid metasomatism) beyond changing pressures and temperatures. There is also a growing body of geochronological and petrological studies that show subduction cycling took place within the Catalina Schist, as well.

In this contribution I will review the considerable amount of data from Franciscan garnets and suggest an alternative interpretation to existing P-T records through the lens of subduction cycling. If “double-dipping” is a fundamental part of forearc processes, the canonical anti-clockwise P-T path of Franciscan high-grade blocks may be in need of an update. The paths could be more parsimoniously viewed as multiple clockwise hairpin subduction “dips” in an aging and cooling subduction zone. Although the percentage of petrological and geochemical publications on high-grade blocks from the Franciscan greatly exceeds their volumetric contribution to the Formation (<<1%), those studies focus on a comparatively small number of actual samples, which show a high degree of variability in terms of garnet zoning. New results from Franciscan and Catalina garnets suggest an even greater variety of prograde paths than previously reported. Given the complex and chaotic nature of sedimentary subduction cycling, this degree of variability among samples seems a likely result.

title: Declining Groundwater Contributions to Western U.S. Headwater Streams: 75 Years of Base-Flow Trends and Future Projections
session_title: The State of Headwaters
authors: Mroczek, Caelum [1], Springer, Abraham E [2], Lucas, Benjamin [3]
affiliations: (1) Arizona Institute for Resilience, University of Arizona, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(2) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(3) Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
abstract:
Headwater streams make up nearly 88% of the western U.S. river network and supply most of the region's surface water, leaving them especially vulnerable to warming, snowpack loss, and drought. As surface water declines, groundwater increasingly sustains streamflow, making trends in base flow — and their climatic drivers — critical to understand.

We analyzed 75 years of streamflow records (1950–2024) from 115 headwater basins across the western U.S. Statistical analyses were combined with cluster-specific LSTM models trained on downscaled climate data to characterize historical base-flow behavior and project future trajectories under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5.

Historically, we find widespread base-flow declines concentrated in early summer, driven by warming, reduced snowmelt, and declining antecedent moisture. Antecedent moisture was the strongest driver overall, correlating with with higher base flow when present, while snow and temperature effects varied by hydroclimatic regime. Looking ahead, projections point to continued declines of 45–65% by late century, with earlier seasonal peaks and reduced summer flows. Snowmelt-dominated and arid basins see the largest relative losses, while mixed-regime basins drive the greatest volumetric losses. We extend this framework to Arizona headwater systems, where groundwater pumping compounds climate-driven base-flow declines, sharpening the tradeoffs between water supply, ecosystem health, and wildfire resilience across the region. Collectively, these results underscore the vulnerability of groundwater-supported streamflow to climate change and the value of coupling statistical and machine-learning approaches for regional hydrologic assessment and management.

abstract: Multiple lines of evidence, including molecular clock estimates and putative eukaryotic-grade macro- and microfossils, suggest that eukaryotes diverged from their archaeal ancestors during the Paleoproterozoic (2.5–1.6 Ga), if not earlier. However, the oldest widely accepted fossil evidence for total- or stem-group eukaryotes does not appear until the Paleoproterozoic–Mesoproterozoic transition (~1.78–1.63 Ga), where they are represented by large organic-walled microfossils with diagnostic features such as complex wall ornamentation and excystment structures (e.g., pylomes and medial splits). The 1.88 Ga Rove Formation of the Animikie Group (Ontario, Canada) is a mudstone-dominated siliciclastic succession that directly overlies the renowned 1.9 Ga Gunflint Formation, which preserves one of the most diverse Paleoproterozoic microfossil assemblages, including cyanobacteria and enigmatic unicellular fossils that have been proposed as early eukaryotes. Given the debated affinities of the Gunflint fossils, the Rove Formation provides an important opportunity to investigate near-contemporaneous organic-walled microfossils preserved in fine-grained siliciclastic sediments. Here, we describe a new assemblage of organic-walled microfossils from the lower Rove Formation preserved in drill core. The microfossil assemblage comprises diverse sphaeromorphs as well as filamentous taxa, many of which exhibit variable wall textures revealed by scanning electron microscopy. Differential preservation of microfossils within the same mudstone layers suggests key compositional differences between taxa. In this light, we describe and assign several new microfossil taxa and discuss their biological affinities, evaluating their potential as eukaryotic candidates. In addition, we integrate this micropalaeontological data with high-resolution palaeoredox proxies (Fe, Mo, V, Re and U) and detailed sedimentological analyses, building on the well-characterized redox history of the Animikie Basin, to evaluate the environmental conditions that supported this assemblage during a critical interval in early eukaryotic evolution.

title: What Do Continuous Measurements Reveal About Leaking Orphan Wells?

authors: Gianoutsos, Nicholas Joseph [1], Haase, Karl B [2], Birdwell, Justin E [3], Hofmann, Michael H [4], Shuck, Curtis E [5]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA

abstract:
Over 4,000 hours of continuous emission measurements from 15 high emitting open-hole orphan wells on the Kevin-Sunburst dome in Toole County, Montana were analyzed by the U.S. Geological Survey and the Well Done Foundation. The wells were drilled in the 1920s and 1930s in the same producing formation and share similar drilling and production histories. Some wells are physically located in close proximity to each other but have significantly different mean emission rates. The producing formation for the wells is the Mississippian Madison Group consisting of the Ellis Group and Madison Group combined carrier zone, which primarily produced oil in the northern part of the dome where the wells are located. Time-weighted mean methane emission rates ranged from non-detectable levels up to 2.7 kg/h in their as-discovered conditions, with leaking wells averaging 211 g/h. Measurement intervals ranged from 12 hours to 2 weeks for each well, and revealed leak rates can fluctuate by an order of magnitude within hours.

Emission rates were influenced by surface winds and diurnal temperature swings, based on continuous monitoring data where some wells showed correlating spikes in emissions and others demonstrated independent flow. Additionally, fluctuations in emission rates often synchronized between wells with overlapping measurement intervals, suggesting weather conditions, such as temperature and wind, affect emission rates up to a factor of 4 with the most relevant being the effect of wind on wells with open holes. These findings indicate that weather-driven processes can significantly influence orphan well leak rates but remain an understudied source of variability in orphan well emissions.

title: A cosmogenic perspective of Laurentide Ice Sheet retreat from the Sturgis Moraine, southern Michigan
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations
authors: Portenga, Eric W. [1], Caffee, Marc William [2], Lifton, Nathaniel A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geography & Geology Department, Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI, USA; Environmental Science & Society Program, Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI, USA
(2) Department of Physics & Astronomy, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA; Department of Earth, Atmospheric, & Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

abstract: The Sturgis Moraine in south central Michigan was produced during retreat of the Saginaw Lobe of the Laurentide Ice Sheet shortly after the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). How shortly after the LGM remains an open question because existing chronological constraints on the timing of ice retreat from the moraine using optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) and radiocarbon geochronometers provide a broad envelope in time from ~30 ka to ~16 ka. In this study, we measured the cosmogenic isotopes, 10 Be and 14 C – both produced in situ in quartz – from granitic glacial erratic boulders ( n = 6) positioned across the crest of the Sturgis Moraine. In situ 14 C concentrations for two boulders at the highest elevation of the moraine had reached saturation, and the inferred 10 Be exposure ages from these samples are similar (~20.9 and ~21.9 ka). Three boulders were scattered around the margins of an ice-walled lake plain (IWLP); of these, one boulder’s 10 Be age was similar to the high-elevation boulders (~23.9 ka) whereas the other two were younger (~18.8 ka, ~19.3 ka). The in situ 14 C ages of the three boulders around the IWLP were younger than 10 Be ages (~18.1 ka, ~16.2 ka, and ~14.8 ka, respectively) but similar within 1σ analytical uncertainties. 10 Be and in situ 14 C ages for the sixth boulder, which was geographically isolated from the other five, were early- to mid-Holocene, respectively. From these new cosmogenic exposure ages, we infer that the Saginaw Lobe of the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated from the Sturgis Moraine ~21 ka (based on the older-aged boulders and some prior OSL and radiocarbon ages) but in doing so thinned, leaving behind stagnant and buried ice, which later melted by ~16 ka (based on the younger-aged boulders and prior radiocarbon ages). Through this study, we learn that a complete history of ice retreat and subsequent stabilization of the Sturgis Moraine is not reflected by any one geochronological dataset alone. We also demonstrate that small datasets of paired cosmogenic isotopes can be as useful in exposing the glacial history of continental moraines in continental interiors as larger single-isotope datasets.

title: Flake Tectonics: An Explanation for the World-Class Jiaodong Gold Endowment
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: Goldfarb, Richard [1]
affiliations: (1) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, School of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences, Beijing, China; Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Jiaodong Peninsula is China’s largest gold province, producing at least 2% of the world’s gold annually and with a pre-mining resource >5000 t Au mainly hosted in the North China block (NCB). It represents a geological anomaly with Phanerozoic gold hosted in Precambrian rocks. Nevertheless, deposit characteristics resemble those of most orogenic gold deposits. A typical crustal metamorphic model for deposit genesis has been considered unlikely because the Neoarchean NCB was metamorphosed to high grades long before the ca. 120 Ma gold event. Other genetic models for this unique gold province are also inconsistent with geological processes. Fluid and metal release from the top of the underplated paleo-Pacific slab is unreasonable because this would have occurred 40-50 myr prior to the gold episode. An Early Cretaceous magmatic-hydrothermal model is impossible because of spatial-temporal considerations, as well as due to gold deposition at depths of 6-10 km. A mantle model for a water-dominant ore-forming fluid streaming upward along trans-lithospheric shear zones is impossible because such water would melt the mantle and enter hydrous magma.

We present an alternative model that best explains Jiaodong gold genesis. Triassic continent-continent collision between NCB and South China block (SCB) buoyant continental masses led to large parts of SCB being flaked off and thrust onto and into NCB. Some nappes are represented by exposures of the Neoproterozoic Penglai Group sediments obducted onto the NCB. Seismic images indicate additional sheets of metasedimentary rock from the leading edge of the SCB were thrust across the length of the Jiaodong Peninsula at depths of 15-20 km within the high-grade NCB basement. Furthermore, a large roof pendant of Neoproterozoic-Paleozoic SCB rocks is hosted by the 160 Ma Linglong batholith 100 km landward of the suture between blocks. The 2.5- to 3.5-km thick detached layer(s) comprise prospective sources for the gold deposits during heating and devolatilization. Rapid lithospheric erosion at the base of the NCB at 130-120 Ma caused upwelling of asthenosphere and such heating at the base of the block. At 122-118 Ma, clockwise rotation of the paleo-Pacific slab led to translational motion and dilations along the normal faults bordering the uplifting core complexes on the Jiaodong Peninsula causing auriferous metamorphic fluids to be focused into these regional conduits in a relatively brief time.

title: Shifting Gears in the North America Cordillera: Rapid Tectonic Mode Changes Recorded by Detrital Zircon Lu-Hf from Jurassic-Cretaceous Strata in California
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Surpless, Kathleen DeGraaff [1], Orme, Devon A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
abstract: Long-lived, oblique-convergent continental margins may undergo rapid transitions between upper-plate transpression and transtension related to changes in relative plate convergence rate and direction. Detrital zircon U-Pb and Lu-Hf data from the Mariposa Formation and Great Valley Group (GVG) provide an integrated record of Jurassic-Cretaceous arc magmatism during eastward subduction of the Farallon plate beneath North America. The Mariposa Formation was deposited ca. 159-148 Ma in the western Foothills belt of the Sierra Nevada, prior to and during latest Jurassic contractional deformation that produced a well-developed cleavage in Mariposa slates and sub-greenschist grade metamorphism. GVG strata were deposited unconformably on ophiolitic basement rocks within half-graben systems in the forearc region west of the Foothills beginning ca. 148 Ma. Both basins contain abundant pre-Mesozoic detrital zircon that link them to North America. The Middle to Late Jurassic magmatic flare-up in the Sierra Nevada is well-represented in the detrital zircon record; ca. 170-150 Ma zircon from the Mariposa Formation and GVG span > 30 Ԑ Hf units, indicating that source magmas incorporated evolved continental material. In contrast, the magmatic lull from ca. 148-135 Ma is characterized by juvenile Ɛ Hf values in detrital zircon from the lower GVG, suggesting minimal crustal involvement. Abundant pre-Mesozoic detrital zircon and a pull-up in Ԑ Hf values for 148-135 Ma detrital zircon in lower GVG strata likely reflect the combined effects of a westward shift in magmatism with trench retreat and transtension following Late Jurassic contraction as the North America plate direction shifted northward and the subducting plate steepened. Mid-Cretaceous GVG samples have reduced pre-Mesozoic detrital zircon and Cretaceous detrital zircon trend toward evolved Ԑ Hf values with time, reflecting the growth of topography and crustal thickness with a return to nearly orthogonal convergence during the Cretaceous magmatic flare-up. These results highlight the utility and power of the detrital record in tracking upper plate conditions within long-lived subduction systems and suggest that oblique convergent margins may experience both transtensional and transpressional tectonics simultaneously in different parts of the convergent system.

abstract: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) landslide scientists and engineers have long worked with partner agencies following consequential landslide events. USGS activities have included characterization of failure mechanisms, spatial distribution, triggering conditions, and downstream hazard propagation. In 2023, the USGS formalized its event-response capacity through the establishment of the Landslide Assessments, Situational Awareness, and Event Response Research (LASER) team. LASER integrates field-based, remote, and modeling investigations within a structured response framework, enabling rapid distribution of scientifically grounded products across a range of landslide-triggering scenarios. Since its formation, LASER has assisted with 31 events including 12 full event responses, spanning rainfall-induced regional failures, seismically triggered slope instabilities, and large tsunami-generating landslides. Response products have included event-specific landslide hazard assessments developed in coordination with partner agencies, collaborative multi-institution mapping efforts, aerial and satellite reconnaissance, and rapid geomorphic characterization of failure types and runout behavior. For example, the 2024 Hurricane Helene response, which documented over 2,200 landslides across the southern Appalachians through a live-updating public platform, illustrated a scientific and logistical scale these responses can reach. Ongoing LASER research and development targets improvements in capabilities, models, and workflows applicable during active response windows. This presentation summarizes the LASER framework, highlights methodologies, and presents case examples from recent responses to illustrate current capabilities and research.

authors: Miller, Rachel [1], Eddy, Michael Patterson [2], Pamukcu, Ayla [3], Hammond, Keiji [4]

abstract:
Silicic arc volcanic eruptions are typically sourced from the upper crust, indicating that these magmas record some degree of pre-eruption residence and evolution at that crustal level. The voluminous granitoid plutons exposed within most exhumed volcanic arcs offer an ideal location to study these potential magma staging areas. Over the past few decades our understanding of these features has changed as structural, petrologic, geochemical, and geochronologic data support incremental growth of most upper-crustal granitoid plutons. This construction style means that the rate of magma emplacement into the upper crust is a fundamental variable in understanding the evolution of silicic magma bodies. Low rates indicate that any eruptible magma body would have been ephemeral and volumetrically limited to the size of an individual magmatic increment. High rates may indicate the development of a magma reservoir with eruptible magma volumes larger than any individual increment.

The exhumed, upper-crustal Oligocene Spirit Lake pluton is a 120 km 2 granitoid intrusion within the Cascadia arc, just north of the modern Mt. St. Helens volcano. Previous geologic mapping has identified three major intrusive phases of the pluton based on compositional differences and intrusive field relationships. We present new high-precision U-Pb zircon geochronology from this pluton to better assess its magma emplacement rate. Initial results suggest that all three intrusive episodes occurred over a relatively short time period of 500 kyr. We discuss these initial results in terms of the rate and style of deformation required to accommodate magma emplacement, as well as the expected melt residence time within the pluton.

abstract:
Unplugged abandoned oil and gas wells are a significant and understudied source of atmospheric methane (CH₄), yet characterizing emissions at a regional scale requires surveying hundreds of wells — a task that strains closed-chamber methods, particularly in difficult terrains, extreme heat, and dense vegetation, or at sites with large well structures that impede equipment deployment. We present the first systematic comparison of high-flow sampler (HFS) and closed-chamber methane emission measurements at 116 unplugged abandoned wells in the Shreveport (oil-producing, n=83) and Monroe (gas-producing, n=33) districts of Northern Louisiana. We developed the HFS-GC method: exhaust-port gas samples were analyzed by gas chromatography and applied in the HFS flow equation to provide a more more robust estimate, especially for wells with low methane emission rates

Across 116 valid paired measurements, the two methods show strong agreement: linear r = 0.926, log–log r = 0.833 (R² = 0.694, p < 10⁻³⁴), and a median HFS-GC/Chamber ratio of 1.11. The HFS-GC regional mean of 53.2 g hr⁻¹ agrees with the companion closed-chamber mean of 57.4 g hr⁻¹ to within 7% — approximately 93% agreement at the regional scale. Agreement is consistent across both the oil-dominated Shreveport (r = 0.828) and gas-dominated Monroe (r = 0.823) districts. Both methods yield emission rates approximately 5.3× the EPA's Gulf Coast factor of 10.02 g hr⁻¹, independently corroborating substantial national inventory underestimation. Scaling to Louisiana's 28,975 unplugged abandoned wells implies approximately 13,500 metric tons CH₄ yr⁻¹ — more than five times the EPA projection.

HFS-GC achieves roughly three times the field throughput of closed chambers (12–15 vs. 4–5 wells per team per day) and requires no hermetic wellhead seal, making it well-suited for Louisiana's challenging wetland and swamp environments. These results establish HFS-GC as a validated, scalable alternative to closed chambers for regional abandoned-well surveys, with chamber follow-up reserved for high-emitters identified by initial HFS screening.

abstract:
The Upper Mississippi River Region (UMRR) is experiencing substantial climate change due to natural variability with superimposed anthropogenic forcing. Long-term records are required to contextualize past millennium environmental change, yet instrumental records are short, local, and often discontinuous. Our aim is to use varved lake sediments to produce an annual record of hydroclimate variability in the UMRR that spans the past millennium. There are established methods that use tree ring records calibrated by instrumental records, and varved sediments may be used as a complimentary archive in locations where tree ring chronologies are spatiotemporally limited. This calibration can be applied to achieve a continuous reconstruction that extends well beyond the temporal limitations of instrumental data.

Freeze cores preserving an undisturbed sediment water interface and varve structure were collected from Steel Lake, LaSalle Lake, and Elk Lake, MN over the past two years. While excellent for preserving high-resolution stratigraphy, freeze cores are challenging to analyze, particularly in the case of scanning that requires core exposure to standard lab temperatures (well above freezing). To address this, Steel Lake sediments were used to develop a method for high-resolution (200µm) X-ray fluorescence (XRF) core scanning. The sediment remains frozen throughout scanning when segmented and placed in a custom-made cold box. Measurement drift was observed during core scans, which we attribute to surface water content changes and variable lab room conditions. To account for drift, we developed a bilinear piecewise mathematical correction that approximates the drift in time and depth space for individual scans using multiple quality control points as anchors.

High-resolution XRF-derived geochemical data enables analysis of rhythmic sedimentation, characterization of seasonal deposition and its variability, and offers a framework for geochemically assisted semi-automated varve counting. Preliminary results suggest that iron deposition associated with lake mixing exhibits greater interannual variability in both seasonal expression and magnitude than previously recognized. Varves containing four visually distinct laminae have been identified, suggesting greater variability in seasonal depositional patterns than was previously resolved. To further constrain depositional regimes, smear slide microscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses of individual varves and seasonally deployed sediment traps are being used to identify seasonal mineral assemblages and inform future carbonate isotope analyses. These seasonal signatures will improve interpretation of climatic variability, stratification regimes, productivity, and other paleoenvironmental processes.

title: Developing a Hydrogeologic Framework for Numerical Groundwater Flow Modeling in the Biscayne Aquifer, Florida
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling (Posters)
authors: Mohammedridha, Shahd [1], Holt, Robert M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Univ Mississippi, Dept Geology and Geological Engineering, University, MS, USA
(2) Univ Mississippi, Dept Geology & Geological Engineering, University, MS, USA
abstract:
The Biscayne Aquifer is a highly transmissive carbonate aquifer that serves as the primary source of drinking water for southeastern Florida. Its high hydraulic conductivity and heterogeneous hydrostratigraphy complicate the characterization of groundwater flow and contaminant migration, making comprehensive hydrogeologic frameworks essential for numerical groundwater modeling. This study focuses on a chlorinated solvent-impacted site in Miami Gardens, Florida, where multiple site investigations conducted over several decades have generated an extensive hydrogeologic dataset.

Available lithologic logs, hydrostratigraphic interpretations, groundwater elevation measurements, hydraulic conductivity estimates from slug testing, and historical site investigation reports are being compiled and evaluated to develop a comprehensive conceptual hydrogeologic model of the study area. These datasets are being integrated to define the hydrostratigraphic framework, characterize groundwater flow conditions, and establish the spatial extent and boundary conditions of a future numerical groundwater flow model. Emphasis is placed on synthesizing data collected during different phases of site characterization into a consistent hydrogeologic interpretation suitable for numerical modeling.

The resulting hydrogeologic framework will provide the foundation for constructing and calibrating a three-dimensional MODFLOW groundwater flow model. This work establishes a reproducible workflow for integrating diverse hydrogeologic datasets into numerical model development and will support future investigations of groundwater flow, contaminant migration, and groundwater management within the Biscayne Aquifer.
