title: Cretaceous to Pleistocene deformation along the Porcupine Fault System of Yukon and Alaska
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Odlum, Margo [1], Rasbury, Emma Troy [2], Strauss, Justin V. [3], Donaghy, Erin Elizabeth [4], McClelland, William C. [5], Faehnrich, Karol [6], Hatton, Kevin M. [7], Kirk, Jason [8]

abstract: The Porcupine Fault System (PFS) of northern Yukon and Alaska initially evolved as part of a major craton-bounding fault zone that accommodated Paleozoic terrane translation of Arctic Alaska along the northern margin of Laurentia. The Mesozoic-recent history of the PFS remains poorly understood but is critical for kinematic and paleogeographic models for the circum-Arctic and northern Cordillera. We integrate regional low-temperature thermochronology, Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material (RSCM), and fault rock geo-thermochronology to understand faulting and exhumation patterns along the PFS. RSCM analyses show similar peak temperatures of ~325 °C across the various structural blocks in the PFS, supporting lateral juxtaposition of para-autochthonous and allochthonous rocks against autochthonous rocks of the Laurentian margin. Zircon (U-Th)/He (He) dates across the PFS are ~115-75 Ma, and apatite He dates are dominantly between ~80-50 Ma. Inverse thermal history models indicate major periods of cooling in the Cretaceous and Paleocene. Faults at various scales within the PFS exhibit normal, thrust, and strike-slip kinematics and are commonly coated by hematite and/or calcite cements and slickenlines, which are amenable to (U-Th)/He and U-Pb geo-thermochronology. Field and microstructural observations support synkinematic growth and deformation of these minerals, allowing us to target them to date deformation. Calcite U-Pb ages record Early Cretaceous, Late Cretaceous, and Paleogene faulting, consistent with the timing of exhumation from thermochronology. Fault rock hematite He dates range from ~8.5-0.7 Ma, and microstructural observations support that dates record hematite precipitation and deformation along brittle faults in the shallow crust. Field observations and structural data integrated with regional and fault rock geo- and thermochronology support reactivation of the PFS during the Cretaceous and Paleogene with deformation as young as Pleistocene, suggesting the PFS played a role in the opening of the Arctic Ocean and widespread Cenozoic strike-slip faulting in the northern Cordillera. These new chronometric constraints on deformation along the PFS highlight the need for reevaluation of the kinematic evolution and relationships between Arctic and northern Cordilleran fault systems.

title: Something Old, Something New: The Power of Combining Fossil Specimen Data with Evolutionary Modeling to Explore Cretaceous Ammonoid Paleobiology
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Yacobucci, Margaret M. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Society, Bowling Green State University, Bowling Green, OH, USA
abstract: Traditionally, paleontologists studying ammonoid cephalopods have focused on producing detailed descriptions of fossil specimens and their stratigraphic occurrences for the purpose of defining biostratigraphic frameworks. Over the last fifty years, however, more and more workers have studied the paleobiology of these fascinating creatures, using new analytical tools to explore questions about their growth, function, ecology, and evolution. In this presentation, I will review the novel approaches our research team has employed to better understand the evolution and extinction of ammonoids through the Cenomanian–Turonian interval of the early Late Cretaceous, a time of extreme greenhouse warming leading to Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2) and a second-tier extinction event. Our work has focused on three disparate Cretaceous ammonoid groups, including the planispiral desmoceratoids and acanthoceratids, and heteromorphic baculitids. We have compiled new anatomical character datasets based on direct observation of museum specimens along with species-level stratigraphic occurrence data. These datasets were then used to conduct the first ever Bayesian phylogenetic analyses of these groups, which allowed us to document evolutionary patterns and estimate rates of character evolution, compute speciation and extinction rates, and track how these rates changed before, during, and after OAE2 and the Cenomanian/Turonian extinction. These analyses have revealed a much richer and more complex story than we initially hypothesized, demonstrating that drivers of ammonoid evolution and extinction varied significantly between groups. While some predictions, like preferential extinction of larger and more metabolically active ammonoids during OAE2, were supported, the notion that all ammonoid groups would respond similarly to this type of environmental perturbation was falsified, as rates of speciation and extinction showed clearly different temporal patterns across clades. Analytical results also provided surprising new insights into ammonoid evolution, from significant differences between clades in the rates of budding vs. bifurcating speciation or anagenesis, to variations in rates of character evolution, demonstrating that different ammonoid groups experienced different selective pressures and morphogenetic constraints. Our results highlight both the importance of continuing to work directly with fossil specimens and the benefits of integrating these data with cutting-edge quantitative modeling approaches to explore ammonoid paleobiology.

title: Elongate Wanderers, Subquadrate Endemics: Outline Shape and Diversification Patterns in Gomphocythere (Ostracoda) Across the Afro-Syrian Rift
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches (Posters)
authors: Bradshaw, Julia [1], Park Boush, Lisa E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut, USA
(2) Earth Science, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT,
abstract:
The Afro-Syrian Rift is an extensive (35°N to 20°S) system of interconnected divergent plate boundaries between the Nubian, Arabian, and Somalian tectonic plates, forming the Great Rift Valley. The region is characterized by numerous lakes of different origins, including deep rift lakes (e.g. Lakes Tanganyika and Malawi), expansive lakes in inter-rift depressions (e.g. Lake Victoria), and shallow pools within the boundaries of the Great Rift Valley (e.g. Tavas pool). These aquatic systems are subject to distinct climatic, stratification, and ecological regimes driven by their broad latitudinal extent and variability in origin and depth.

From Turkey to South Africa– the ostracod genus Gomphocythere is widely distributed across the Afro-Syrian Rift system and has been reported from Australasia. Gomphocythere species are morphologically diverse with a range of ornamentation, with nodose ( G. coheni , G. woutersi ), alate ( G. downingi , G. alata ), and unornamented species ( G. besni , G. curta ). However, genus-wide trends in bauplan are not yet well understood. A morphometric analysis was conducted using published images (e.g. SEM and line drawings) of all available species of Gomphocythere , sourced from descriptions, published studies, and taxonomic keys. Although body size and ornamentation can be environmentally influenced, valve shape, quantified here using outline geometry and length-to-width (L/W) ratios, is generally consistent within a species. Shape, excluding ornamental structures, was measured by projecting 128 equidistant points around the valve perimeter. Due to pronounced sexual dimorphism in Gomphocythere and variations between right and left valves, images of right female, left female, right male, and left male valves were analyzed separately.

Analyses indicate two primary morphological groupings,irrespective of sex or valve type: elongate forms characteristic of Levantine and broadly distributed taxa, and wider, subquadrate forms typical of endemic species. Morphological diversity is greater in endemic species within certain individual lakes than in the species found across the rift system. Endemic assemblages from Lakes Tanganyika and Malawi exhibit particularly high variability in both L/W ratios and outline shape, suggesting that lake age, depth, and hydrological variability are dominant controls on diversification.

title: Grain shape trends of quartz sand from the Salmon River, British Columbia and Alaska
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Bowen, Rocco J [1], Sweet, Dustin E. [2], Campaña, Isidoro [3], Madduma Bandarage, Omalka Kaumadi Chandrasiri [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
(3) Department of Geodynamics, Stratigraphy, and Paleontology, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
(4) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
abstract:
The Salmon River is a short (26.7 km) pro-glacial stream located along the Alaska–British Columbia border that experiences seasonal jökulhlaups capable of generating abrupt increases in discharge. These high-magnitude flow events may accelerate grain rounding and surface chipping over relatively short transport distances compared to sustained moderate-flow conditions. Although downstream changes in gravel roundness have been extensively documented, comparable studies of quartz sand are limited because it is generally thought that water viscosity limits grain-to-grain contact, reducing abrasion making quantitative research challenging. Automated grain-shape analysis provide an opportunity to quantify these morphological changes with greater precision.

To investigate downstream evolution of sand-grain morphology, quartz sand samples were collected along the length of the Salmon River and analyzed using the Malvern Morphologi G3 automated imaging system. Using 0.5-1mm and 0.25-0.5mm sized grains, hundreds of grains from each sample were measured to quantify circularity, convexity, aspect ratio, and solidity. Trends of these parameters indicate that the greatest increase in grain shape change occurs within the first several kilometers of transport, after which the rate of morphological change decreases substantially.

The observed downstream trends suggest that the largest grain shape modifications occur rapidly following entrainment from glacial sources, with progressively smaller changes occurring as transport continues. This stretch of river is also the steepest, which is likely to increase turbulence and thus grain abrasion. These results are consistent with other investigations of quartz grain modification in fluvial systems, including rivers in central Spain, indicating that similar controls on sand grain rounding may operate despite substantial differences in fluvial geomorphic setting. Together, these findings demonstrate that automated grain shape metrics provide a useful quantitative proxy for sediment transport history while highlighting the need for additional studies across a wider range of fluvial environmental settings.

title: Staying Power: How Proterozoic Tava Sandstone in the Colorado Rockies withstood 660 m.y. of Tectonism/Erosion and 135 Years of Geologists’ Inquiry
session_title: From outcrop to orogen—field-based perspectives on stratigraphy, structural geology, and mineral resources in the Rocky Mountain region—a session in honor of David A. Lindsey
authors: Siddoway, Christine [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Spgs, CO, USA
abstract:
The Colorado Rocky Mountains are home to Tava sandstone, an unusual Proterozoic siliciclastic formation sparsely preserved over >18,000km^2. Tava eluded understanding for more than a century, owing to its occurrence as quartz-sand injectites (sedimentary dikes) within granite and gneiss. Naturalists of the 1890s explored the paradoxical relationship of clastic rock within plutonic, finding clear sedimentologic evidence for fluidization and forceful injection. Field geologists in the 2000’s discerned that the sandstone is pebbly diamictite, having non-touching clasts within a nonsorted sand matrix, indicating rapid emplacement. Mapping revealed the presence of sand ridges up to 850m long/120m wide, specifically near Pikes Peak (Tavá Kaa-vi, of the Nuuchiu/Ute), as well as evidence of Tava sandstone clasts in Pennsylvanian and Pleistocene alluvial fans.

Tava research since 2011 entailed interdisciplinary, collaborative work of the sort exemplified by USGS geologist David A. Lindsey, whose approach involved long, deep examination of field problems from multiple angles, enlisting colleagues who contributed expertise or pioneering methods. Methods employed to determine sediment provenance, paleoenvironment, and age of Tava sandstone include: Detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology, brittle kinematic analysis, magnetic properties, (U-Th)/He thermochronology, process microsedimentology, computation of topography using drone photogrammetry, REE geochemistry, and U-Pb hematite geochronology using LA-ICPMS.

Key findings are: Detrital zircon age spectra show that Tava derived from Proterozoic sources in local basement rocks and distant Grenville Orogen. Consistent dike margin geometries reflect ENE-WSW to NE-SW-oriented subhorizontal regional tensile stress. Hematite-quartz veins associated with Tava injectites offer evidence of hydrothermal fluids alongside meteoric waters. In-situ hematite U-Pb dates are ~690 to 660 Ma for veinlets that crosscut and are cut by Tava dikes, constraining injection events to the time of Sturtian glaciation when Colorado was situated at low latitude within supercontinent Rodinia. Thin sections display microtextures (grain-stacks, rotational structures, crushed grains, microshears) resembling those in modern subglacial sediments that underwent porewater pulses, hydro-fracture, and fluidization. The findings support a conceptual model for formation of Tava beneath a Snowball Earth ice sheet where overpressured subglacial meltwater injected sand into fissured, faulted bedrock. Ridges developed as streaming bedforms localized within troughs in a continental subglacial setting, where faults channeled Fe-rich fluids and geothermal heat into the upper crust. Tava sandstone stands as one of the only known terrestrial records of the Sturtian glaciation.

title: Building a Workforce-Driven Mining Technician Program at a Two-Year Institution: Year One Results from the College of Western Idaho (CWI)
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Sundell, Ander J [1]
affiliations: (1) Physical Sciences, College of Western Idaho, Boise, ID, USA
abstract:
Mining in the western United States faces a growing workforce shortage driven both by looming retirements and a lack of technically trained entry-level professionals. The College of Western Idaho (CWI) has developed and deployed a Mining Technician Associate of Science degree focused on applied geoscience, workforce readiness, and industry engagement.

The Mining Technician program grew out of a small, field-focused geology curriculum with strong regional relevance but limited workforce alignment. Early program development was guided by collaboration with Idaho-based mining companies, locally active professional societies, four-year transfer partners, and state advocacy groups. Support from NSF-ATE later strengthened our curriculum development, instructional infrastructure, and assessment while preserving the program's workforce-driven origins.

The curriculum emphasizes hands-on learning and professional practice through coursework in core logging, drilling operations, geologic mapping, hydrology, GIS, environmental compliance, and mining operations, complemented by MSHA certification. Instructional strategies include embedded field laboratories, industry site visits, project-based assessments, a robust internship program, and mentorship from practicing professionals.

Early indicators of success include increased enrollment, strong student engagement, internships and job placements with regional mining operations, and increased statewide recognition of CWI as a workforce pipeline. This case study presents a potentially replicable model and encourages two-year institutions, professional societies, and industry partners to collaborate in developing regionally relevant, workforce-aligned geoscience programs.

title: Molecular mechanism of capturing Li+ from aqueous solution using gibbsite.
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Ho, Tuan A. [1], Thomas, Elisabeth R [2]
affiliations: (1) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
Lithium–aluminum layered double hydroxides (Li–Al LDHs) are promising materials for selective lithium recovery from brines because of their high affinity for Li⁺. Their formation proceeds through a phase transition from gibbsite, yet the atomic-scale mechanism governing lithium uptake and the gradual decline in uptake with time remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with experiments on gibbsite–polymer composites to elucidate the lithium incorporation mechanism and evaluate their adsorption performance.

MD simulations reveal that the hydration state of the gibbsite interlayer controls lithium transport. In strongly confined bihydrated interlayers (2W), Li⁺ experiences an unfavorable free-energy landscape for entering the pore from bulk solution. Expansion to trihydrated interlayers (3W) substantially reduces confinement effects, facilitating lithium entry into the interlayer. Once inside, migration of Li⁺ into vacant octahedral sites within the gibbsite lattice becomes thermodynamically favorable, producing a deep free-energy minimum associated with lattice incorporation. The free-energy profile further identifies a kinetic barrier separating inner-sphere adsorption from lattice incorporation; however, this barrier is readily overcome at elevated temperatures. In contrast, competing ions, including Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, remain in hydrated or adsorbed states and do not complete the incorporation pathway, highlighting the intrinsic selectivity of the gibbsite-to-Li–Al LDH transformation.

Guided by these molecular insights, we fabricated gibbsite–polymer composites for lithium capture via adsorption from aqueous solutions. We accomplish this by using the moiety groups on the polymers as attachment locations for the gibbsite synthesis process. This gives us greater access to active sites where Li + can easily incorporate into the structure. Batch adsorption experiments demonstrate significant lithium uptake over multiple adsorption cycles, with substantial Li + release during washing steps, confirming the potential of the composite material for repeated lithium recovery. These combined computational and experimental results provide new mechanistic understanding of the gibbsite-to-Li–Al LDH phase transition and offer design principles for developing efficient and selective sorbents for sustainable lithium extraction from aqueous resources.

title: Tracking the Geochemical Effects of Subaerial Weathering on Mule Deer Antlers from the Big Bend National Park Region of Southern Texas

authors: Shea, Adam T. [1], Booth, Skylor L. [2], Ash, Richard D. [3], Laker, Rachel M. [4], Miller, Joshua H. [5], Ullmann, Paul V. [6]
affiliations: (1) Harold Hamm School of Geology and Geological Engineering, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND, USA
(2) Harold Hamm School of Geology and Geological Engineering, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND, USA

abstract: Immediate burial after death is not guaranteed; rather, skeletal remains are often exposed on ground surfaces for months-to-years before burial. While exposed, bones are subject to processes such as weathering, microbial attack, and elemental uptake and exchange. However, few studies have explored the spatial distribution of physicochemical alterations throughout the cortex of bone across a timeseries progressive subaerial weathering. To explore how bone geochemistry is impacted by weathering before burial, we used laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS) to examine the distribution of trace elements in ten antlers of Mule Deer (Odocoileus hemionus) collected from Big Bend National Park and surrounding areas. Antlers exhibited varying weathering stages from fresh (WS0) to highly weathered (WS5; n = two of each weathering stage). This constituted the first use of LA-ICPMS to examine geochemical effects of pre-burial weathering. Diagenetic trace element uptake was observed in every antler, regardless of weathering stage. However, nearly all trace element uptake was confined to the outer 100 µm of the external cortex, with heavy rare earth elements (HREEs) displaying the greatest variation in relative enrichment. Specimens in higher weathering stages exhibited higher concentrations of most trace elements examined, especially of iron (Fe), lanthanum (La), scandium (Sc), and yttrium (Y); these elements thus served as the most informative indicators of pre-burial diagenesis. Among REEs, this trend was most dramatic for concentrations of La, which, at the cortical margin, increased by nearly an order of magnitude (from 2–3 ppm to 10–20 ppm) between antlers in weathering stages 0 and 4. Rates of elemental uptake also increased with weathering. For example, uptake of Fe increased from 148 ppm/yr to 365 ppm/yr (a 146% increase) and La from 0.44 ppm/yr to 0.62 ppm/yr (a 41% increase). Finally, all weathered antlers exhibited negative (traditional) cerium anomalies and elevated Sc concentrations in the external 250 µm of the cortex, reflective of exposure to oxidizing conditions during weathering. Cumulatively, our findings demonstrate how trace elements can viably be used to track and characterize the incipient diagenesis of skeletal remains prior to burial. To reveal how these geochemical alterations correlate with protein decay, we are currently evaluating the relationships between bone weathering and both loss of collagen I and the decay of peptide sequences in these specimens.

title: Beyond Zircon: Integrated Multi-Mineral U-Pb Geochronology and Trace-Element Provenance Analysis of Sedimentary Archives for Reconstructing Source-Region Evolution
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools
authors: Wang, Lijun [1], Lin, Shoufa [2], van Staal, Cees R. [3], Chew, David [4], Hanchar, John [5], McFarlane, Chris R.M. [6], Peverelli, Veronica [7]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada
(3) Geological Survey of Canada, Vancouver, BC, Canada
(4) Department of Geology, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland
(5) Department of Earth Sciences, Memorial University of Newfoundland, St. John's, NL, Canada
(6) Department of Earth Sciences, University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, NB, Canada
(7) Department of Geology, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland
abstract:
Integrated U-Pb geochronology and trace-element geochemistry of multiple detrital minerals, including zircon, rutile, apatite, monazite, and titanite, provide a more comprehensive record of sediment provenance and source-region evolution than zircon alone. By combining minerals with different closure temperatures and distinct petrological and petrogenetic affinities, a multi-mineral approach advances provenance analysis beyond simple correlations between detrital age spectra and regional magmatic events. Instead, individual mineral populations can be interpreted as recording specific aspects of source-region evolution, including magmatism, metamorphism, exhumation, and crustal recycling.

In the Appalachian orogen of western Newfoundland, application of this multi-mineral approach to three Middle Ordovician to Devonian foreland-basin successions reveals distinct tectonic shifts that are not recorded by detrital zircon, which is overwhelmingly Grenvillian (~1000 Ma) in age. The Middle Ordovician Goose Tickle Group contains pronounced ~480 Ma apatite and monazite age peaks with mafic- and S-type magmatic as well as high-grade metamorphic signatures derived from an early Taconic arc. The Upper Ordovician Long Point Group features dominant 475-465 Ma monazite, apatite, and titanite age peaks, together with predominantly metamorphic apatite signatures, reflecting unroofing of the Taconic hinterland. The Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian Clam Bank Formation yields ~455 and ~425 Ma monazite age peaks that track exhumation of a polyorogenic hinterland influenced by both Taconic and Salinic tectonic events.

In South China, this approach refines the depositional history and tectonic setting of Ediacaran-Cambrian strata in the West Cathaysia terrane, suggesting deposition in overlapping synorogenic basins during the assembly of eastern Gondwana. Ediacaran units were likely sourced from Australia's Paterson-Petermann Orogen (PPO) and contain dominant 650-600 Ma rutile and apatite populations that record an Ediacaran high-pressure metamorphic event. In contrast, Cambrian strata contain Cambrian and Tonian rutile and apatite populations derived from the Kuunga-Pinjarra Orogen. These data place West Cathaysia adjacent to both orogens and support a collisional origin for the PPO.

Additionally, multi-mineral analysis of Marinoan glacial diamictites from the Yangtze Block of South China reveals the 970-720 Ma evolution of the Panxi-Hannan orogenic belt. Detrital rutile thermometry and trace-element geochemistry identify a distinct Tonian (ca. 870-820 Ma) cold-subduction signature. This low-geothermal-gradient signature, captured through glacial unroofing of otherwise unexposed basement crust, provides crucial evidence for a long-lived accretionary system and contributes to the growing global record of Tonian cold subduction.

abstract: As friends of Brad Sageman who are not listed as a coauthors on any publication, we wish to point out his influence in steering the research directions of other colleagues involved in Cretaceous paleoclimatic records. A specific example is the year 2000 Sageman Miniconference at Northwestern University where Brad’s feedback on group presentations catalyzed a new focus on Cretaceous stable isotopic records from the tropics (Suarez et al. 2009, doi: 10.1130/B26453.1; Suarez et al., 2010, doi: 10.2110/jsr.2010.048; and Suarez et al., 2011, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.palaeo.2011.05.027). Moreover, colleague interactions at the Sageman Miniconference with the late Mark Pagani led to investigations of integrated oxygen & hydrogen isotopic records from the Cretaceous Arctic (Ross et al, 2020, https://doi.org/10.1144/SP498-2018-134; Ludvigson et al, 2022, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3263/12/4/143; and Andrzejewski et al., 2023, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3263/13/9/273). Brad Sageman’s career-long leadership investigating the global-change record of the Cretaceous OAE 2 inspired an effort at the Kansas Geological Survey to carry out carbon isotope chemostratigraphic studies of Albian-Turonian strata in long-line cores in northern Kansas recently culminating in the report of Andrzejewski et al., 2025 (https://doi.org/10.5724/gcs.38.001). That work focused attention on the local expression of the Albian-Cenomanian OAE 1d and the Mid-Cenomanian Event along the cratonic margin of the Cretaceous Western Interior Basin. Continuing studies of these global-change events in newly pulled cores in Nebraska and Kansas are leading to a deeper understanding of that record. One particular outcome involves diagenetic studies of cone-in-cone calcite structures associated with the Mid-Cenomanian Event that indicate formation as offshore fresh-water seeps.

title: Fidelity of trace element modeling applied to zircon petrochronology
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Yakymchuk, Chris [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON,
abstract: Zircon is the most used petrochronometer. Several intensive variables influence the rare earth element signatures of zircon. The interplay between these variables—notably pressure, temperature and bulk composition with a particular emphasis on the H 2 O content and Fe 3+ vs Fe 2+ —can lead to similar geochemical signatures in zircon that formed in diverse crustal settings. Here, a ferric-iron rich sapphirine–quartz gneiss is modelled to assess the controlling intensive variables on zircon composition and the consistency between measured values and the prediction of equilibrium models. An equilibrium model reproduces heavy rare earth element ratios and cerium anomalies of zircon. Heavy rare earth element ratios are a function of garnet proportion, but are also influenced by the proportion of melt in the system. Cerium anomalies in zircon are primary controlled by f O 2 . In general, the widely held assumption that HREE-ratios in zircon are tied to garnet proportion seems appropriate for most metamorphic rocks and the link between cerium anomalies and source redox appears robust. The interplay between feldspar behaviour (e.g., fractional crystallization) and redox complicates interpretations of europium anomalies in zircon. However, even in the Fe 3+ -rich systems investigated here where >90% of europium in silicate melt from which zircon crystallizes is expected to be trivalent, there is expected to be a substantial control of feldspar on zircon europium anomalies in anatectic systems.

title: Something Calcareous this Way Comes: Role of Mineralogy and Diagenesis in the Silurian-Devonian Klonk δ13C Event
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: Saltzman, Matthew R. [1], Griffith, Elizabeth M. [2], Phillips, Kayleigh [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(2) School of Earth Sciences, OSU, Columbus, OH,
(3) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State Univ, Earth Sciences, Columbus, OH, USA
abstract: The Silurian-Devonian transition (419.2 Ma) coincides with an up to 5‰ positive carbon isotope (δ 13 C) change in carbonates around the world, known as the Klonk Event. Though the Klonk Event is recorded globally, peak δ 13 C values vary by location up to 2.5‰, suggesting influence of water mass variations, differences in primary minerology, or post-depositional alteration. These local processes could decouple the recorded δ 13 C signal in carbonate sections from the global carbon cycle. Small differences in δ 13 C values aimed at calculating global organic carbon burial fluxes result in large changes in CO 2 or O 2 in isotope mass balance models. We utilize calcium isotope (δ 44/40 Ca) and minor-element geochemistry (Sr/Ca) paired with δ 13 C measurements in the Appalachian Basin of West Virginia (WV) and the Arbuckle Mountains of Oklahoma (OK) to investigate the impact of local variation in carbonate mineralogy and diagenesis on the records. The WV section contains open marine to peritidal carbonate facies overlain by sandstone in a rapidly subsiding foreland basin, while the OK section contains open marine to shallow subtidal limestone and shale in an aulacogen with lower sedimentation rates. The WV section’s peak δ 13 C is 1.85‰ higher. The OK section has stable δ 44/40 Ca (-1.03 to -0.88‰, n = 4), while the WV section demonstrates significant variation in δ 44/40 Ca (-1.57 to -1.00‰, n = 14). Since WV stratigraphic δ 44/40 Ca variation is too large to attribute to seawater changes on the timescale of the Klonk Event, diagenesis regimes (fluid- vs sediment-buffered), precipitation rate, or mineralogy are likely drivers. In contrast, lack of variation in δ 44/40 Ca in OK suggests little mineralogic or diagenetic changes in this section. Local process shifts may explain the higher δ 13 C peak in WV, which may have contained a greater percentage of original aragonitic skeletal grains (higher δ 13 C and lower δ 44/40 Ca) or more sediment-buffered diagenesis. Alternatively, lower δ 13 C peak value in OK could be a result of increased seawater-buffered diagenesis suggested by higher δ 44/40 Ca and low Sr/Ca. The Silurian-Devonian δ 44/40 Ca suggest that Klonk Event records are locally influenced by carbonate mineralogy and diagenesis, but still partially represent a primary signal of global organic carbon burial which coincides with the rapid spread and diversification of early land plants and a rise of atmospheric oxygen levels.

title: High-resolution chemical stratigraphy of saline lakes of the Southern High Plains
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Strang, Ian [1], Rodriguez, Erin Anais [2], Piccione, Gavin [3], Edwards, Graham Harper [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(3) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
The saline lakes of the Southern High Plains of Texas and New Mexico are sensitive to regional climate shifts. The shallow, transient state of the lakes today reflects the modern interpluvial climate, while Late Pleistocene records of expanded lake depth and extent reflect corresponding pluvial conditions. Prior studies of basin morphology, palynology, and stratigraphy document the millennial-scale drying of the saline lakes during the Late Pleistocene and Holocene. We present a higher-resolution stratigraphy of sedimentation and evaporite formation to interpret smaller-scale changes and variability in the region's climate over the late Quaternary.

We collected two sediment cores (both ~4 meters in length) and float samples of carbonate strata (thicknesses range 1–4 cm) from White Lake and Salt Lake, near Muleshoe, TX, and Arch, NM, respectively. We measured downcore geochemistry with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer and sub-millimeter-scale geochemical variability in carbonate strata with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX).

We report preliminary data from a 129 cm core section of White Lake (389–261 cm depth) and two 2-cm carbonate strata from Salt Lake. Downcore chemical proxies record changes in evaporite formation, lake salinity, and relative detrital content, all of which reflect trends of wetting and drying. In the lowermost 43 cm, these proxies indicate initially wet conditions, followed by drying that culminated in precipitation of an evaporitic carbonate layer, and then increased moisture and lake expansion. The remaining 86 cm reflect prolonged drought conditions. Salt Lake carbonates evidence a monotonically warming and/or drying climate across the 2 cm of precipitation. Both littoral and basinal samples record increasing carbonate growth and salinity in rising Mg/Ca ratios. While the more littoral sample exhibits continuously decreasing detrital content (inferred from falling Si/Ca), the more basinal sample records episodic increases in detrital input, implying that shoreline retreat and rearrangement changed and redirected detrital inputs to the system.

We will report additional XRF bulk chemistry for the remaining 3 m of core from White Lake and a 4 m core from Salt Lake. We will also report additional carbonate EDX geochemistry for float samples from White Lake and for in-place carbonate strata from White Lake and Salt Lake.

title: Archives and Agents of Ecological Change: Evidence for Taphonomic Feedback in Modern Offshore Shell-Gravel Seabeds
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Kokesh, Broc S. [1], Finnegan, Seth [2]
affiliations: (1) University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA; Morningside University, Sioux City, IA, USA
(2) University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA,
abstract:
A notable mechanism by which biological communities modify their environment is the accumulation of skeletal debris (shells, bones, sclerites, etc.). Although paleontologists have long recognized these “death assemblages” as time-averaged records of past biodiversity and proxies for fossilization, they also alter physical conditions that may influence living communities. These “taphonomic feedback” dynamics have been proposed as a mechanism for the formation of dense shell beds in the fossil record, but they have not been explicitly tested in modern marine systems where living communities and their associated death assemblages can be sampled simultaneously.

Here, we characterize living and dead benthic shellfish (mollusks and brachiopods) from the San Juan Islands, Washington, where a regional benthic fauna occupies highly variable seabed depths and substrates offshore from continental sedimentation. This setting thus provides an ideal natural laboratory for evaluating live-dead fidelity and taphonomic feedback. We analyzed 13 dredge samples spanning mud-, cobble-, and shell-dominated seabeds and assessed patterns in relation to water depth and sediment shell volume.

Death assemblages had consistently higher abundances and richness compared to living assemblages while maintaining similar evenness but lower proportional abundances of epifaunal taxa. Abundance, richness, and evenness showed no relationship with either water depth or shell volume. In contrast, epifaunal proportions in both living and death assemblages were strongly and positively correlated with shell volume as previously demonstrated in Miocene fossil deposits.

These results indicate two concurrent dynamics in offshore shell-gravel seabeds. First, a modest but consistent taphonomic bias reduces the representation of epifaunal taxa in death assemblages relative to shallow infaunal taxa. Second, sediment shell density strongly predicts the abundance of epifaunal taxa, providing evidence consistent with taphonomic feedback as a mechanism linking skeletal accumulations community composition. These findings suggest that shell beds may function as both archives and agents of ecological change.

title: Unearthing the Bedrock of Geoscience Academic and Career Choice: Exploring Cognitive and Affective Layers
session_title: Learning to be a Geoscientist: Professional Exposure, Agency, and Transferable Skills in Undergraduate Education.
authors: Manzanares, Amanda [1], Pugh, Kevin [2], Pugh, McKayah [3]
affiliations: (1) CO, USA
(2) University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO, USA
abstract:
Recruitment and retention challenges are prevalent as universities struggle to attract and retain geoscience majors resulting in fewer geoscience majors, minors, and professionals. Social cognitive career theory and prior geoscience research have established the importance of certain affective factors in predicting academic and career choice. These factors include domain interest, identity, and self-efficacy. Cognitive factors, such as domain knowledge, may also play a role. However, research is lacking in the relation between domain knowledge and academic and career choice. Transformative experience is a cognitive and affective factor characterized by experiences in which students use in-school learning to see and experience the world in meaningful new ways in their everyday lives. Such experiences likely interact with other cognitive and affective factors and may help explain academic and career choice. Accordingly, we proposed and tested a model of relations between geoscience interest/identity, geoscience self-efficacy, geoscience knowledge, transformative experience, and geoscience academic and career choice. We also tested the model for gender differences as gender differences have been found in prior research.

A total of 407 students from five universities were included in the final analysis (214 female students, 193 male students). At the beginning and end of the semester, participants completed pre- and post-surveys of geoscience interest/identity, geoscience self-efficacy, and transformative experience along with the geoscience concept inventory. Path analysis was used to test our proposed model.

In line with prior research, we found that students’ inclination to pursue a geoscience degree and career was strongly associated with their interest in and identification with geoscience. Self-efficacy was predictive of geoscience interest/identity and initial geoscience knowledge. Further, we found that, instead of being a direct predictor of geoscience academic and career choice, transformative experience helped explain change in geoscience interest/identity over the course of a semester. That is, initial geoscience interest/identity predicted transformative experience and transformative experience in turn predicted higher end-of-semester geoscience interest/identity. We also found that transformative experiences predicted end-of-semester geoscience knowledge. However, geoscience knowledge was unrelated to students’ inclination to pursue a geoscience degree and career. We found no significant gender differences.

Our findings highlight the importance of creating curriculums and learning environments that encourage students’ geoscience interest and identity, self-efficacy, and transformative experiences.

title: Plant-insect interactions across secondary succession in temperate deciduous forest (North Carolina, USA): Implications for recognizing disturbance in the fossil record
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Bugos, Beatrice V. [1], Lowe, Alexander [2], Currano, Ellen D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
(2) University of California Museum of Paleontology, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA
(3) Botany, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
abstract: The fossil record of plant-insect interactions has been studied temporally and spatially on large scales and provides critical information about environmental controls on ecosystem interactions, like disturbance. However, interpretations of disturbance-related drivers of leaf herbivory patterns in the past relies on a comprehensive understanding of them today. Methods used in modern ecosystems rarely capture insect herbivory at the landscape level and are fundamentally different from methods used in fossil studies. Therefore, we used fossil methods on a modern successional gradient to study plant-insect interaction patterns across forest succession. We collected leaf litter, a modern analog to plant macrofossils, from early, mid, and late successional stages (21, 44, 94, and >200 year old stands) in a temperate deciduous forest. Leaves were identified to species and scored for insect damage using the damage type system. Plant traits were compiled for each species, and damage was analyzed at the bulk-assemblage and individual-species levels. We hypothesized that insect herbivory would be highest in the late successional stage, where previous work had shown plant diversity to peak. Instead, we observed a peak in insect herbivory and plant diversity within the litter of the mid-successional stage (44 years old). The litter reflected a bias towards tree species and excluded some understory species. The insect herbivory patterns showed no correlation with leaf traits known in other contexts to be important influences, including carbon and nitrogen ratios and leaf mass per area. Although, there is little variation in these traits among the deciduous species present, and thus they may not be important factors when considering deciduous dominated forests. Our study highlights that high tree diversity supported elevated insect herbivory. The litter’s bias towards trees made specialist feeders on understory plants underrepresented in the herbivory metrics. However, trees can still reflect stand level herbivory because they contribute significantly to forest biomass and have a larger impact on their environment than understory plants. A critical understanding of deciduous dominated forests is important when interpreting patterns in the fossil record, such as those existing in the Pacific Northwest during the Mid Miocene Climatic Optimum (~16.9-14.7 Ma), a future climate proxy to 2100 if carbon emissions go unabated.

title: Effects of Storm Events on Suspended Solids and Phosphorus under Varying Levels of Groundwater Influence
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Mathews, Madeleine [1], Schneider, Grace [2], Holmes, Tucker [3]
affiliations: (1) Gonzaga University, Spokane, WA, USA
(2) Gonzaga University, Spokane, WA, USA
(3) Gonzaga University, Spokane, WA, USA
abstract: The extent of groundwater-surface water connection in a watershed can dictate nutrient transport during periods of elevated discharge. Nutrients, such as phosphorus, are mobilized due to factors including biogeochemical influences, hydrogeologic connections, and land use, subsequently increasing the risk of eutrophication downstream. Generally, phosphorus tends to be retained within a river system, either via sorption to sediment or through biological uptake. However, storm events introduce periods of elevated discharge, often amplifying the total suspended solids (TSS) load moving downstream and potentially transporting phosphorus as well. This effect depends on watershed connectivity to subsurface flowpaths as well as the accessibility of TSS mobilized by over-land flow. Here, we examine phosphorus and TSS transport over a range of discharge levels in two tributaries to the Spokane River, USA. The Hangman Creek (HC) watershed is a flashy, event-dominated system with commonly elevated TSS levels during high flow; conversely, the Little Spokane River (LSR) watershed is deeply dominated by the regional aquifer system, the Spokane Valley-Rathdrum Prairie aquifer. In particular, we assess the concentration-discharge (C-Q) behavior of TSS, total phosphorus (TP), and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP) from high frequency samples collected over the course of four storm events in 2026. We also investigate the impact of varying discharge levels on a long-term monthly dataset, using piecewise regression to quantify significant Q thresholds exporting phosphorus and TSS to the Spokane River. We find that TSS was not significantly exported in LSR during the sampled storm events, although it was significantly exported at HC during elevated spring discharge. Similarly, at low levels of discharge, the respective aquifer systems are likely the major contributors of phosphorus to both watersheds. At elevated flow, a significant difference between TP and TDP at both sites demonstrates the importance of particulate phosphorus transport. While the nature of TSS and phosphorus watershed export remains complex and multi-faceted, C-Q relationships quantified at both the event and long-term scales provide insight into how groundwater-surface water connectivity influences the integration of event input and subsequent nutrient transport at varied Q levels.

title: Chicxulub Impact - Effects and Deposits in Northern Louisiana, USA
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Kinsland, Gary L [1], Shellhouse, Kody [2], Muchiri, Eric G [3], Frederick, Forrest E. [4], Snedden, John [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, Louisiana, 70503, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, LA, USA
(3) School of Geosciences, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, Louisiana, USA
(4) School of Geosciences, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, Louisiana, 70503, USA
(5) Institute for Geophysics, The University of Texas at Austin,, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
Impact of the 10 km asteroid which struck in the water of the shelf at what is now Chicxulub, Yucatan, Mexico 66 MYA radiated seismic energy, a tsunami and ejected debris across the Gulf of Mexico (America) to the northern shelf of the Gulf. Rayleigh waves/earthquake waves arrived in northern Louisiana in about 5 minutes and fluidized carbonate muds (marls) which flowed downslope as mass transport deposits (MTD)…the first phase of the K/Pg boundary deposit. About 80 minutes later the tsunami arrived and formed, within/upon the fluidized thixotropic muds of the MTD, megaripples with wavelengths about 600 m and amplitudes about 15 m (compacted in today’s strata). Next, materials within the impact plume settled through the Gulf waters for up to years, draping over the megaripples, completing the K/Pg boundary deposit. 200 m of the Paleogene Midway Shale were deposited above.

Justiss Petroleum Co., seeking to conventionally core their IPNH #2 well at the top of the Cretaceous on the LaSalle Arch, set their core barrel at a depth based on the tops of the marl in two adjacent wells. After coring about 9 m of shale the marl of the K/Pg boundary deposit was encountered…they had drilled in a trough of the megaripples. The coring continued for about 27 m bottoming in Cretaceous marly chalks.

We have access to the core, which we believe is a unique complete core of the K/Pg boundary deposit in the northern Gulf. We present results and interpretations from the core: 1) inch (cm) scale visual description, 2) visual descriptions of 35 thin-sections, 3) XRF of the core, 4) acid dissolution of 35 samples, 5) XRF, XRD and visual analyses of the insoluble material, and 6) minimal SEM of some samples and thin-sections.

Our present interpretation is that the MTD flowed over a hardground at the top of Cretaceous carbonates on the LaSalle Arch. This contact, being the first stratigraphic evidence of the impact, is the K/Pg boundary. 12 m of MTD over lie the K/Pg. At the top of the MTD a hardground is developed containing air fall debris from the impact. Above this is the Midway Shale.

We seek help/collaboration to continue analyses of the core (SEM, paleo, micropaleo, nanos, palynology).

title: Constraining Quaternary Deformation within the south-central Basin and Range through Fault Mapping, Relative Dating, and Analysis of Cosmogenic Nuclides
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Berry, Nicholas M. [1], Abbey, Alyssa L. [2], Bierman, Paul R. [3], Corbett, Lee B. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, California, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, California State University, Long Beach, CA, USA
(3) Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources, University of Vermont, Burlington, Vermont, USA
(4) Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
abstract:
Nevada’s Basin and Range province is a diffuse continental rift zone with different strain rates across the region. The western and eastern margins of the province display high cumulative strain rates compared to the central Basin and Range (CBR), which is less tectonically active. However, many of the faults in the CBR display evidence of recent activity, including those in the Hot Creek Valley (HCV), south-central NV, which contains numerous intra-basin faults for which the Quaternary rate of deformation is not yet quantified. A better understanding of the relatively recent rate of deformation will shed light on how the HCV fits within the CBR’s status of tectonic quiescence.

Here, we combine new fault mapping with relative and numerical dating techniques to understand better Quaternary deformation of the HCV. Our mapping reveals groups of fault arrays and previously unmapped faults, which predominantly strike northeast. Relative dating of faulted alluvial fans using geomorphic characteristics allows us to assign fan surface ages ranging from young (Holocene-Late Pleistocene), intermediate (Late-Mid Pleistocene), and old (Early Pleistocene). Most fans in the HCV are young to intermediate-aged, with the surface area of individual fan deposits decreasing as relative age increases.

Measurements of cosmogenic 10 Be and 26 Al, in quartz-bearing sediment collected from the Keystone Canyon Alluvial Fan (KCAF, ~1880 m asl), provide chronological data. 10 Be concentrations of the 9 surface clasts analyzed so far range from 1.1 to 4.7 x 10 6 atoms/gram (mean = 3.3 x 10 6 ), the equivalent of several hundred thousand years of surface exposure. 26 Al concentrations in the same clasts are between 6.3 and 32 x 10 6 atoms/gram. 26 Al/ 10 Be ratios range from 5.8 to 7.0 (mean 6.3), consistent with surface or near-surface exposure and no extended burial. Based on our field observations, fault orientation throughout HCV correlates with the generally west-northwest directed extension in the CBR. The presence of faulted Quaternary-age fan deposits indicates that the HCV has undergone Pleistocene tectonic deformation.

title: Ecological Niche of Modern Nautilus: Utilization of a Three-Dimensional Ecological Niche Modeling Approach to Marine Conservation
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Hernández Gómez, Noel Jose [1], Myers, Corinne [2], Machado-Stredel, Fernando [3], Owens, Hannah L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(3) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(4) University of Copenhagen, Frederiksberg C, Hovedstaten, Denmark
abstract: Extant taxa in the family Nautilidae are heavily restricted to the shores of Indo-Pacific islands and their surrounding seas. Nautilids are the most ancient class of cephalopods and were once globally distributed among a large proportion of marine ecosystems and experienced a myriad of environmental changes of varying magnitude, duration, and frequency. However, since the Oligocene, nautilid diversity has dropped precipitously, resulting in only two modern genera encompassing a handful of species (Bonacum et al., 2011). Teasing apart contributing factors to this change has been difficult, in part because of data scarcity, but also due to the unique ecology of nautiloids, which are known for their daily water column migration over 500 m. Consequently, models are generally limited to single-depth range tests of environmental niche occupation and ignore the impacts of spatiotemporal changes to size and connectivity of 3-Dimensional habitat (Dzik and Gaździcki, 2001; Lai et al., 2025). To tackle this challenge, we apply newly developed 3D ecological niche models to a high-resolution and well-vetted dataset of modern nautiloid species. Specifically, we test for changes in abiotic niche occupation across time, space, and depth, including potential niche contractions or evolution over this period. Model results are compared to traditional 2 dimensional niche models that are also applied to future oceanographic conditions in a conservation paleobiological context. Gaining a better understanding of the controls on nautiloid distributions will inform future conservation strategies and prevent the loss of a clade that has flourished in the oceans for over 400 million years.

title: Uncovering the Cretaceous Mojave shortening story: Bracketing deformation and metamorphism on the Scanlon thrust and Meteor fault, eastern Mojave Desert
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Jacobs, Cole [1], Wells, Michael L. [2], Lamont, Thomas N. [3], Schatz, Henry P. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(3) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(4) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
abstract:
The Kilbeck Hills–Old Woman Mountains–Little Piute Mountains (KOWL) area lies in the eastern Mojave Desert and hosts the Scanlon thrust and Meteor fault, which are major northeast-trending thrust- and normal-sense ductile shear zones extending for ~45 kilometers. Despite many studies since the 1980s, timing of deformation has remained poorly bracketed. The KOWL is situated in a corridor of both proposed low-angle subduction and terrane collision during the Cretaceous, making it a critical locality to document the style and timing of deformation to test competing tectonic models. Despite various records indicating >60-km-thick crust and high paleoelevations in the Mojave during Late Cretaceous time, contractional structures of this age are sparsely documented while many extensional shear zones are recorded.

Exposures of the Scanlon thrust, Meteor fault, and associated nappes terminate to the southwest in the Kilbeck Hills and at their type localities to the northeast in the Little Piute Mountains (LPMs). In the LPMs, ~600 meters of metamorphosed Paleozoic cratonal strata form a southeast-verging syncline and are juxtaposed between mylonitic basement orthogneisses above and below via the oppositely verging Scanlon and Meteor shear zones, respectively. Stretching lineations in the Meteor nappe are parallel to fold hingelines, shifting from gently WSW-plunging to more steeply NW-plunging towards the southwest, possibly suggesting a sheath fold geometry.

In the Kilbeck Hills, undated metasedimentary strata lie in the footwall of the Scanlon thrust. U-Pb analyses of 600 detrital zircon grains from this unit yields a maximum depositional age of 96.0±0.74 Ma from eight zircons, providing a new maximum age of deformation. Metamorphic conditions were determined for both footwall and hanging-wall garnet-bearing metasedimentary strata using THERMOCALC Average P-T and Theriak-Domino petrological modelling. Garnets preserve prograde Mn zoning profiles, with garnet inner rims recording peak metamorphic conditions of ~650–700°C and ~6.5 kbar. U-Th-Pb monazite petrochronology provides age controls on garnet growth and resorption, and thus peak metamorphic conditions. The youngest monazite age populations (<73 Ma) are depleted in HREEs, in addition to those with the highest Dy/Yb values indicating monazite growth in the presence of garnet at ca. 76 Ma. Considering that later ~73 Ma plutons are emplaced at 4.0–4.5 kbar and cross-cut shear fabrics, we suggest that peak metamorphic conditions occur at ca. 76 Ma due to thrust burial.

title: Investigating the Presence of a Cryptic Horse Genus in the American Falls Formation of the Snake River Plain, Idaho, USA
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic (Posters)
authors: Fridel, Miriam Catherine [1], Peecook, Brandon R [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(2) Department of Biological Sciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA; Idaho Museum of Natural History, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
abstract:
The phylogenetic relationships and distribution of Pleistocene North American stilt-legged horses have been a subject of paleontological debate. Ancient DNA analyses showed that this group diverged from stout-legged horses ( Equus ) in the Pliocene, with specimens assigned to Hargintonhippus francisci . Since its discovery, H. francisci has been found across the interior of western North America, from the Yukon, Canada to Chiapas, México. All localities where H. francisci has been found have also contained Equus . Currently, this genus has not been recognized in Idaho, despite the abundance of Plio-Pleistocene horse fossils and the fact that H. francisci is well represented at nearby Natural Trap Cave, WY (NTC). Due to its history of being synonymized with Equus , it is likely that unidentified H. francisci specimens exist in Idaho museum collections.

This study aims to refine the knowledge of the range of H. francisci and Equus . Here, we use linear morphometric methods to quantify subtle differences in equid metacarpal and metatarsal shape (N= 65) in the American Falls Formation collection at the Idaho Museum of Natural History (IMNH). Principal component analysis and linear discriminant analysis were performed, incorporating a priori data from published records.

All measured IMNH specimens are grouped in Equus morphospace. The linear discriminant analysis assigned “ Equus ” to all tested IMNH specimens. None of the metapodials can be confidently assigned to H. francisci . Of the thousands of horse specimens from NTC, ~17 individuals have been IDed to either H. francisci or Equus based on molecular data, at a ratio of 3.5 to 1. Given this current ratio, the apparent absence of H. francisci from Idaho is striking. The next phase of this research will use cheek teeth to test the hypothesis that H. francisci is indeed missing from American Falls with the benefit of a larger sample size (est. N = 171).

The morphological similarity of these clades reflects the similar evolutionary pressures acting on these populations. If Idaho has evidence for only Equus , this would make it a unique region in western North America where H. francisci is not sympatric with Equus . Notably, significant topography lies to the east of American Falls and may have prevented H. francisci from moving into Idaho. This difference in distribution points to how two morphologically similar populations still respond to their environment in different ways.

title: Temporal resolution of marine fossil assemblages scales predictably with sediment accumulation rates
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Kowalewski, Michal J. [1], Tomasovych, Adam [2], Nawrot, Rafal [3], Scarponi, Daniele [4], Zuschin, Martin [5], Kosnik, Matthew [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Florida, Gainesville, FL,
(2) Earth Science Institute of Slovak Academy Sciences, Bratislava, Slovak Republic
(3) University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria
(4) University of Bologna, Bologna (BO), Italy
(5) University of Vienna, Vienna, Italy
(6) Macquarie University, Sydney, Australia
abstract: Age mixing of non-contemporaneous skeletal remains results in time-averaged fossil assemblages. Time averaging limits the resolution of paleontological data and determines which biological and geological processes can be investigated in the fossil record. We quantified time averaging for 384 samples of marine calcifying organisms derived from late Quaternary cores and surficial death assemblages. Using amino acid and radiocarbon methods, we dated 7,593 specimens, which were dominated by bivalve mollusks but also included gastropods, scaphopods, echinoids, brachiopods, and foraminifera. The resulting sample-level estimates of time averaging, measured as two standard deviations of individual specimen ages, varied from decades to millennia. The estimated time averaging scaled inversely with sediment accumulation rates, which was the overriding driver controlling the scale of temporal mixing (r 2 = 0.78). Numerical simulations suggest that the observed estimates of time averaging show best fit to a three-parameter model that includes sediment accumulation, vertical mixing, and skeletal disintegration. Whereas time averaging appears to be primarily driven by sediment accumulation time, vertical sediment mixing inflates time averaging as sediment accumulation rate increases and disintegration suppresses time averaging as sediment accumulation rate decreases. The results indicate that sediment accumulation rate is the primary determinant of the temporal resolution of fossil assemblages, irrespective of other potential factors that may influence temporal resolution. These results provide a numerical baseline for assessing the temporal adequacy of the fossil record and quantitatively confirm an important and long-anticipated principle: the temporal resolution of marine fossil assemblages scales predictably with sediment accumulation rate.

title: Complex association of morphological change with dispersal in triarthrine trilobites during the late Cambrian through Ordovician
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology
authors: Hopkins, Melanie Jane [1], Monti, Daniela S [2], Wright, David F [3], Smith, Patrick M. [4], Bicknell, Russell D. C. [5]
affiliations: (1) Division of Paleontology (Invertebrates), American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY,
(2) Instituto de Ecología, Genética y Evolución de Buenos Aires (IEGEBA, UBA-CONICET), Universidad de Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires, Argentina
(3) Sam Noble Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA; School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(4) Geological Survey of New South Wales, Londonderry, New South Wales, Australia; School of Natural Sciences, Macquarie University, North Ryde, New South Wales, Australia
(5) Division of Paleontology (Invertebrates), American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA; College of Science and Engineering, Flinders University, Bedford Park, South Australia, Australia
abstract:
The Ordovician is characterized by long-term trends in global cooling and sea level changes, dramatic diversification of animal clades, and the restructuring of marine ecosystems. The restructuring of ecosystems occurred at different spatial scales. For trilobites, there is evidence for latitudinal and bathymetric controls on distribution and dispersal, long-term shifts in relative abundance within basins along bathymetric gradients, as well as complex biogeographic patterns dominated by trends towards increasingly asymmetric dispersal and decreasing endemicity between paleocontinents. Earlier biogeographic studies were based solely on occurrence data, but recent studies have considered these changes within a phylogenetic framework.

Here, we expand this effort to include a comparison of rates of dispersal with rates of morphological character change. To do this we sampled 84 discrete, meristic, and continuous characters for 71 species of olenid trilobite, focusing particularly on the subfamily Triarthrinae, which is the only subclade whose stratigraphic range extends from the latest Cambrian to the end of the Ordovician. We ran a tip-dated Bayesian analysis using the fossilized birth-death model and allowing for sampling ancestors. We explored paleogeographic patterns using DEC models which allow for sympatry, subset sympatry, and narrow vicariance at cladogenesis. Using the best-fit model, we reconstructed ancestral ranges and quantified biogeographic events within each of four time intervals (Furongian, Early Ordovician, Middle Ordovician, Late Ordovician) through stochastic mapping. To assess rates of character evolution, we applied stochastic character mapping using a Markov hidden rates model and then tallied the number of discrete character transitions estimated along each branch and for the same intervals.

Preliminary results show that a model which allows dispersal rates to vary among time intervals is best supported, and that the clade originated in East and peri-East Gondwana. Dispersal continued through west Gondwana and then Laurentia, via either Baltica or Avalonia, depending on the genus. Rates of dispersal and rates of character change show different patterns with a possible decoupling of peak values, suggesting that geographic expansion may have established the ecological and evolutionary opportunities that subsequently fuelled morphological innovation.

title: Adsorption of Non-spherical Microplastics in Saturated Porous Media
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Posters)
authors: Efobo, Oghenevwede [1], Brown, Megan R.M. [2], Lenczewski, Melissa [3], Oo, Chit Wityi [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, Illinois, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, Illinois, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, lllinois, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb,, lllinois, USA
abstract:
Microplastics (MPs) are tiny plastic particles smaller than 5 mm. MPs have gained considerable attention worldwide in recent years because of their widespread occurrence in the environment. MPs have been found in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial environments. Their interaction with soil and sediments is important for understanding their fate and transport. Many previous laboratory studies on MPs in porous media have used polyethylene (PE) or polystyrene (PS) microspheres and, in some cases, a single type of porous medium. Thus, there is limited information on other polymer types and microplastic shapes and different types of porous media. Available evidence suggests that fragments are among the most frequently detected microplastic shapes in groundwater. However, their adsorption behavior remains poorly understood.

In this study, we conducted batch isotherm experiments in glass sample vials, using quartz sand classified into three grain-size ranges: fine (0.2-0.3 mm), medium (0.45-0.55 mm), and coarse (0.7-0.8 mm) as the porous media. PE and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fragment microplastics, with size ranges of 20-50 μm and 50-100 μm were utilized to analyze the effect of the action time and initial microplastic concentration on adsorption of fragment microplastics in saturated porous media. PE and PET were selected because they are among the most frequently detected polymers in environmental samples. Data from the batch experiment were fitted using the adsorption kinetic models (pseudo-first-order and pseudo-second-order kinetic equations) for action time and the adsorption isotherm models (Langmuir and Freundlich) for initial concentration. Findings from this study will improve our understanding of the behavior of fragment-shaped microplastics in saturated porous media.

abstract: Growing recreational use in National Parks and other popular recreation areas has led to concerns regarding impacts to ecosystems. Human waste introduced to watersheds in popular wilderness areas has emerged as a significant non-point source pollutant, posing harmful impacts on critical sources of water while potentially adding significant quantities of exotic nutrients to ecosystems. Our goal was to identify any presence of human waste in the Yosemite Wilderness Area and to determine how soil in areas of high recreation may differ in anthropogenically sourced nitrogen and exotic materials. We hypothesize that with higher amounts of recreational use along trails, the %N and d 15 N in soils adjacent to the trail will increase, and the human sterol biomarker coprostanol will be observed in levels indicative of human activity. Soil cores (n = 291) were collected using line transects originating in predefined campgrounds in the Dorothy Lake watershed (n = 152) along the popular Pacific Crest Trail and control plots in a rarely visited adjacent watershed (n = 139). Both watersheds are similar in terms of timing of deglaciation, elevation and aspect, vegetation, poorly developed soils, and management under Yosemite National Park, with the biggest difference between the sites being significant recreational use at Dorothy Lake and minor visitation at the adjacent watershed. Nitrogen isotopic data and human sterol biomarkers were quantified using an Elemental Analyzer Mass Spectrometer and an LC-MS/MS respectively. Preliminary data shows the detection of coprostanol in soil cores from the Dorothy Lake Watershed.

title: Contrasting Tectonic Histories of the Sveconorwegian and Grenville Orogens Challenge Traditional Rodinia Models
session_title: One orogeny is not like the other: changes in orogenic styles through the Proterozoic
authors: Slagstad, Trond [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geophysics, Geological Survey of Norway, Trondheim, Norway
abstract: The Sveconorwegian and Grenville orogens have traditionally been viewed either as parts of a continuous, ca. 1.1 Ga collisional orogenic belt or opposite sides of such a belt. Together with the Sunsas Orogen, these orogenic belts are typically used to reconstruct SW Baltica, SE Laurentia and W Amazonia in an interior position in the Rodinia supercontinent, marking the termination of crustal growth along these margins. Late Paleoproterozoic crustal growth along the SE Laurentian and W Baltican margins is both temporally and tectonically similar and often viewed as one, extensive active margin referred to as the Great Proterozoic Accretionary Orogen. Isotopic and geochemical data suggest that the active margin was established on an Archean substrate before moving to more distal positions, apparently associated with a series of trench-retreat events. Although the traditional view is that this evolution continued until the onset of Sveconorwegian–Grenvillian orogeny, recent isotopic, geochemical, metamorphic, and paleomagnetic data suggest significant contrasts in tectonic evolution that appear incompatible with this view. In the Grenville Province, <1.4 Ga juvenile arcs and back-arc assemblages were thrust onto the Laurentian margin during collision at 1.1 Ga, marked by rapid change towards more evolved isotopic compositions. Similar juvenile assemblages may have existed outboard of Baltica, but they were never thrust onto Baltica in a final collisional event. Instead, the Sveconorwegian Orogen records continuous crustal recycling, with or without juvenile mantle additions, starting at 1.3 Ga and lasting until 0.9 Ga. The hot crust in the orogenic hinterland did not undergo significant crustal thickening, as indicated by geochemical and metamorphic data. Unlike the Grenville, the Sveconorwegian displays no evidence for a significant change in overall tectonic setting between 1.3 and 0.9 Ga, and the 1.1–1.0 Ga compressional phase is best explained by reamalgamation of a fragmented western Baltican margin. Paleomagnetic data from the Sveconorwegian Province argues against correlation with the Grenville Province and an increasing body of data suggests a still-active post-Sveconorwegian margin west of Baltica. Finally, recent paleomagnetic work questions the link between the ca. 615 Ma Egersund and Long Range mafic dykes, often cited as evidence for opening of the Iapetus Ocean and final break-up of Rodinia. Significant modifications to Rodinia reconstructions are likely as we gain a better understanding of the continental margins involved.

title: Brachiopod Perspectives on the Permian-Triassic Transition: Resilience, Rebound, or Both?
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Carlson, Sandra J. [1], Sclafani, Judith A. [2], Fitzgerald, Paul C. [3], Dievert, Rylan K. V. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, CA, USA
(2) Geological and Environmental Sciences, University of the Pacific, Stockton, CA, USA
(3) Biology, Northern Virginia Community College, Annandale, Virginia, USA
(4) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, CA, USA
abstract:
The “Great Dying” looked like the end for brachiopods; 96% of genera became extinct. And yet, both rhynchonellide and terebratulide brachiopods survived, albeit at lower diversities, occurring today in patchy distributions of extremely high abundance in certain cold, deep, temperate to polar habitats. These post-Paleozoic brachiopods are distinct from their Paleozoic forebears; they are generally more globose, attaching to hard substrates with a pedicle, with curved hinge lines and interlocking dentition. When so many lineages became extinct, why, and how, could these brachiopods persist?

The most diverse and abundant brachiopods today are the “long-looped” Terebratellidina; determining their origin is critical to our understanding of long-term brachiopod survivorship. Some long-looped terebratulidines first occur in the Devonian, but other evidence suggests that Recent, long-looped brachiopods are a clade with post-extinction Triassic origins (Dagys, 1972; Guo et al., 2026). Are the long-looped Paleozoic brachiopods closely related to those living today, or is the modern Terebratellidina a clade originating in the Triassic, after the end-Permian extinction?

To test the Triassic origin hypothesis, we assembled a data matrix of 30 Permian terebratulidine (“short-looped”) genera, added seven Triassic terebratulidines, and then five Triassic terebratellidines, using five Paleozoic cryptonelloid terebratulidine outgroups, including some with long mineralized loops. We analyzed these three matrices in succession, with Mk and FBD models of evolution, and compared MCC (maximum clade credibility) consensus trees.

The phylogenetic patterns that result are consistent with a peramorphic ontogenetic pattern of loop development, from crura to acuminate to deltiform to teloform loops. Our results support a Triassic origin for the long-looped terebratellidine clade, with Devonian long-loops evolving convergently. These Paleozoic long-looped taxa lack a septal pillar, which is instrumental in the development and greater mineralized lophophore support of extant long-looped terebratellidines. Angustothyridides, the short-looped terebratulidines from which the long-looped terebratellidines are thought by some to have originated, appear to be polyphyletic and are unlikely to indicate direct ancestry.

At the end-Permian, a spike in seawater temperature led brachiopods down one of two paths: to extinction for many with smaller three-dimensional mantle cavity volumes, living on soft substrates, or to deeper and colder-water habitats for more globose forms generating lateral inhalant mantle cavity water currents, able to adapt to lower oxygen conditions (Marquez et al., 2026), such as the long-looped terebratellidines.
