title: “Hot Tub Time Machine”? Extreme Lacustrine Environments in Cretaceous Sevier Foreland Inferred from Dual-Clumped Isotopes
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Lonsdorf, Tara Kelsey [1], Niemi, Nathan A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, ; Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI,
abstract: Stable isotopic measurements of carbonate materials deposited in uplifting orogens have been widely used to infer paleoelevations and paleoclimates — but in these regions, high potential for geothermally-heated waters may have resulted in disequilibrium precipitation of carbonates, complicating these reconstructions. This study provides a framework for assessing such uncertainties by investigating formation temperatures of the McKnight Canyon limestone unit of the Beaverhead Formation in southwestern Montana. The McKnight Canyon limestone unit was precipitated in the foreland of the Sevier thrust belt at the onset of Laramide uplift. We present the first isotopic measurements of the McKnight Canyon limestone unit, including δ13C, δ18O, and dual-clumped isotope (Δ47, Δ48) temperature proxies, which we contextualize with U Pb dating and geochemical methods (SEM, Raman spectroscopy) to confirm carbonate authigenesis. Most notably, we observe a larger degree of Δ47/Δ48 disequilibrium than ever previously published, which we attribute to sulfate-reducing microbial metabolism in a warm spring environment. Though Δ47 temperatures from the McKnight Canyon limestone agree largely with previous published records of Cretaceous terrestrial temperatures, Δ47/Δ48 disequilibrium suggests that “true” precipitation temperatures were likely higher, though still plausibly in the range of “acceptable” hothouse climate conditions proposed for the Cretaceous. Overall, isotopic measurements from the McKnight Canyon limestone unit (travertine) and similar deposits may be appealing as materials from which to derive high-elevation isotope records — but the identification of the limestone as associated with geothermal activity suggests that such isotopic measurements may not be suitable for drawing conclusions about paleoclimate or paleotopography.

title: From Museum Dark Data to Open Access: Building Digital Infrastructure for Sharing Historically Significant Mineral and Petrology Collections at South Dakota Mines’ Museum of Geology

abstract:
The Museum of Geology at South Dakota Mines is completing a major digital infrastructure initiative to improve the preservation, management, and open accessibility of its mineralogy and petrology collections. This project addresses long-standing stewardship challenges within one of the museum's least digitally curated collections. The project targets approximately 30,000 specimens representing previously cataloged specimens and uncurated Black Hills specimens primarily from historical ore deposits.

A comprehensive digital infrastructure was established first with PastPerfect collections software and transferred to a geology schema in Specify 7, creating standardized digital records that integrate specimen data with associated archival metadata, including images and available geochemical information. These records were further prepared for open-access through the System for Earth Sample Registration (SESAR), transforming previously inaccessible "museum dark data" into discoverable research resources for a broader geoscience community.

The resulting digital catalog substantially expands access to one of North America's most significant collections documenting mineral diversity in the Black Hills, including ores of critical minerals and strategic elements as well as specimens from historic mines that are now exhausted, inaccessible, or reclaimed. These collections preserve irreplaceable geological records representing historically important pegmatite and carbonatite deposits, including materials relevant to studies of rare earth elements (REE) such as Li, Ta, Nb and other strategic minerals.

By integrating archival preservation with digital access, the project aligns these collections with modern museum standards and significantly expands their value for education, research, and public engagement. Beyond improvements in collections stewardship, the project strengthens institutional capacity by developing standardized curation workflows and providing intensive museum training for undergraduate and graduate students. Students gain practical experience in specimen handling, cataloging, digitization, archival rehousing, and collections management, in addition to exhibit design, all of which build skills directly applicable to museum and geoinformatics careers.

title: Sedimentological and Geochronological Evidence for Cenozoic Strike-Slip Displacement on the Porcupine Fault System, Northeastern Alaska
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Donaghy, Erin E. [1], Strauss, Justin V. [2], Odlum, Margo L. [3], McClelland, William C. [4], Rasbury, E. Troy [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(3) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California, San Diego, CA, USA
(4) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(5) Department of Geosciences, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY, USA
abstract:
The Porcupine Fault System (PFS) in northern Alaska and Yukon has been identified as a significant Paleozoic craton-bounding fault zone. It is a critical part of the Canadian Arctic Transform System (CATS), where offset along the PFS and correlative faults are responsible for large-scale transport of circum-Arctic terranes across the northern margin of Laurentia. The PFS has undergone multiple periods of reactivation in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic; however, the kinematic history of these later faulting events remains poorly constrained.

We integrate new sedimentologic and geochronologic data from Cenozoic terrestrial strata exposed along the PFS to better understand the depositional and structural history of regional basin formation. These strata are exposed in isolated regions along the central portion of the PFS, where they are unconformably overlying Paleozoic to Proterozoic basement rocks and cross-cut by numerous sub-vertical faults. Overall, the Cenozoic strata are characterized by matrix- to clast-supported cobble conglomerate, trough cross-stratified sandstone, and organic-rich mudstone interbedded with peat horizons and mafic-andesitic volcanic flows and tuffs. High-precision U–Pb zircon geochronology (CA-ID-TIMS) on tuffs and palynology from mudrocks yield abundant Paleocene and Late Miocene ages. U–Pb detrital zircon geochronology (CA-LA-ICP-MS) from Paleocene volcaniclastic sandstones primarily yield Paleocene (55–65 Ma) and Mesoproterozoic (1000–1600 Ma) ages, whereas Miocene strata are dominated by Mesoproterozoic and lesser Paleoproterozoic (1600–2000 Ma) ages. Whole-rock and trace rare earth element geochemistry from the Miocene basalts indicate they are alkaline in composition and were derived from an enriched mantle source. The Paleocene–Miocene sedimentary and volcanic succession is capped by latest Miocene–Pliocene ancestral Porcupine River gravels.

Our data suggests Cenozoic reactivation of the PFS resulted in the formation of isolated, fault-bounded pull-apart basins. Sediments were derived primarily from exhumed Proterozoic–Paleozoic basement rocks along basin-bounding faults in basin-margin alluvial-fluvial and basin-axis lacustrine depositional systems. Continued transtension and lithospheric thinning through the Miocene resulted in the eruption of primitive alkaline basalts along the PFS axis. Cenozoic strike-slip displacement along the PFS was synchronous with regional dextral strike-slip faulting in the northern Cordillera, particularly along the adjacent Tintina fault. Therefore, future tectonic models for the northern Cordillera must address the Cenozoic evolution of the PFS in order to create more realistic paleogeographic reconstructions.

abstract:
Preparing students for careers in conservation paleobiology (CPB) requires competencies and skills that extend beyond those typically fostered by geology and paleontology courses and programs. Students, educators, and mentors therefore need accessible resources that support career exploration and education. To address this need, the Conservation Paleobiology Network’s “Pathways to Careers in Conservation Paleobiology” Working Group (henceforth “Pathways”), with support from a Paleontological Society Education and Outreach grant, is developing a new website intended to serve as a community-built hub for career exploration, educational resources, and community collaboration.

This presentation introduces the website, demonstrates its key features, and invites the CPB community to help shape its future development. Designed for students (primarily undergraduate and graduate), educators, and mentors, the website illustrates possible career pathways through interactive career story maps that follow individual conservation paleobiologists from their education journey to entry-level positions to current roles. Along the way, the story maps highlight job responsibilities, the skills needed to succeed, and how and why specific education and career moves were made.

Beyond career exploration, the website also features Pathways products such as open access publications regarding core competencies and skills needed in CPB, pedagogical approaches to fostering them, best practices in mentoring CPB students, and a variety of pedagogical resources (model curricula, syllabi, reading lists, lab and field exercises, case studies, projects, service-learning activities, assessment vehicles, etc.). An interactive map connects students with educators and training programs in CPB, and community members are encouraged to contribute educational resources, share career stories, and expand the collection of training opportunities. By enabling ongoing community contributions, the website is intended to evolve alongside the field, strengthening CPB education and lowering barriers to careers in conservation paleobiology. Learn more, explore the website, and contribute at: www.conpaleopathways.org.

abstract: Water quality is a global crisis needing infrastructure and professional talent development. Global Water Consortium (GWC) is an Ohio non-profit that has over 20 international projects installing clean water bottling plants. In February 2026, a collaborative effort was initiated between the Miami University (MU) Student Chapter of the American Institute of Professional Geologists (AIPG), MU faculty and students, and GWC staff to develop environmental site assessments for GWC projects. Around 20 undergraduates and 4 graduate students were granted unpaid internships from GWC. Students formed site-specific working groups during the first three weeks. Target goals included identifying the sites to be prioritized, the information available for each site, and the general structure of the chapters. A hybrid distributed work model was adopted, where the group would meet biweekly, and students worked on the project independently between meetings. Students presented initial work at an MU student forum and at a local professional meeting to obtain feedback and benchmark progress. Common issues were gaps in available data, differences in skill backgrounds, and scheduling challenges. To address these issues, recent MU alumni were engaged to assist remotely. MU’s Center for Career Exploration and Success provided nearly $10,000 in financial support for students to attend this GSA Connects meeting and awarded several students competitive internship funding grants totaling around an additional $8,000. Support was also provided by faculty research funds. The students have refined several skills: literary analysis, writing and figure preparation, ion chromatography, high-resolution inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, and scanning electron microscopy from samples collected by GWC in Honduras. A compendium of the first few site assessments is expected soon. This effort provides a foundation for continuing internships for MU students and a basis for new GWC facilities.

authors: Krekeler, Mark P. S. [1], Gugino, Jack P. [2], Lytle, Marion [3], Belak, Ethan [4], Zimmerer, Maddy [5], Wudke, Hannah [6]
affiliations: (1) Miami University, Oxford, OH,
(2) Miami University, Oxford, OH,
(3) Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(4) Miami University, Oxford, OH,
(5) Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(6) Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA
abstract: Talc is a widely used mineral in numerous applications globally, including cosmetic, industrial, and pharmaceutical uses. However, the association of asbestos and talc is recognized and is a major concern. Moreover, talc was indicated to be a Type 2A carcinogen by IARC in 2024. One additional area of concern is the occurrence of trace and minor metals that may be naturally occurring. We analyzed 43 samples of Johnson's talc-based baby powder (JBP) that was sourced from China to assess the nature of trace metal content. Metals which occurred in all samples include V (8.55 - 12.58 mg/kg), Cr (2.25 - 31.01 mg/kg), Ni (1.34 - 4.64 mg/kg), Zn (2.09 - 884.21 mg/kg), Pb (1.41 - 5.55 mg/kg), Th (0.33 - 1.08 mg/kg) and U (0.53 - 1.44 mg/kg). Ba was below detection in 8 of the 44 samples and otherwise varied from 0.63 - 87.31 mg/kg. Hg was analyzed in 29 samples and was detected only in 4 samples, varying from 0.19 - 0.39. Cd was analyzed in all samples and was below detection limit. Compared to a population of industrial talc crayons, JBP has higher average concentrations for V, Cr, Ni, Zn, Ba, Pb, Th, and U. Results contradict the notion that marketing-defined cosmetic talc is always “cleaner” than marketing-defined industrial talc materials, at least in this case, comparing similar source regions. Compositions observed are distinct from other JBP samples interpreted to be from Vermont, which have distinctive and greatly elevated Cr, Ni, and Co concentrations compared to JBP sourced from China. Results provide some context in interpreting other cosmetic data for forensic purposes. JBP data may be useful for medical professionals in assessing exposure to metals in those who have used JBP and more broadly talc. The presence of Pb in all samples of JBP may be significant in the context of understanding infant, mother, and health professional exposure. This investigation points to the need for more study to understand trace and minor element chemistry in talc products.

title: Investigating Eocene Forearc Basin Development Following Oceanic Plateau Accretion: Stratigraphic and Geochronological Constraints on the Raging River Formation and Puget Group, Western Washington
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins (Posters)
authors: Raymond, Tay'Lor [1], Lozano, Isabel [2], Donaghy, Erin [3]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, Nevada, USA
(3) Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, Nevada, USA
abstract:
The Eocene collision of the Siletzia oceanic plateau significantly modified the continental margin of the Pacific Northwest. Following accretion, renewed subduction outboard of Siletzia resulted in deposition of a thick succession of Cenozoic strata in the forearc region, extending from the Olympic Peninsula to the Cascade foothills. However, it is unclear how strata in the outer forearc correlate to inner forearc strata exposed in the Puget Lowlands. Marginal marine and fluvial-deltaic Eocene forearc basin strata in the Puget Lowlands are known as the Raging River Formation and Puget Group. At Tiger Mountain, the Puget Group overlies the Raging River Formation and is subdivided into the Tiger Mountain, Tukwila, and Renton Formations, whereas ~30 km to the south, Eocene strata are mapped as undifferentiated.

New U–Pb detrital zircon geochronology from the Raging River Formation (N=2; n=586) and Puget Group (N=3; n=846) are integrated with lithofacies mapping to determine sediment provenance and routing systems during early development of the Cascade forearc basin. Raging River Formation age spectra are characterized primarily by Late Jurassic (145–160 Ma) and Cretaceous (110–120 Ma) peak age groups and yield a maximum depositional age (MDA) of ~44 Ma. The Tiger Mountain Formation is dominated by Late Cretaceous (85–95 Ma) and Latest Jurassic–Early Cretaceous (140-150 Ma) peak ages, yielding an MDA of ~46 Ma. In contrast, the Tukwila Formation contains primarily Paleoproterozoic (1.6–1.8 Ga) and Late Cretaceous (90-100 Ma) peak ages, with minor <45 Ma ages that yield an MDA of ~33 Ma. Moreover, undifferentiated Puget Group age spectra are characterized by an increase in Eocene (45–50 Ma) ages and similar Paleoproterozoic ages, but lack distinct Cretaceous peak ages observed at Tiger Mountain.

Our new geochronologic data indicate that the Eocene–Oligocene transition occurs within the Puget Group and that portions of the succession are younger than previously recognized. Differences in detrital zircon age spectra between the Raging River Formation and Puget Group record spatial and temporal changes in sediment provenance during early forearc basin development. Additionally, comparisons with previously published detrital zircon datasets from the outer forearc on the Olympic Peninsula provide new constraints on the depositional history of the early Cascade forearc region and are critical for paleogeographic reconstructions of western Washington during the Eocene.

title: The Role of seamount subduction in the Eocene tectonic development of the Olympic subduction complex, western Washington
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: Montano, Hali [1], Donaghy, Erin [2], Mulcahy, Sean [3]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, University of Nevada Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) Geoscience, University of Nevada Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(3) Geoscience, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
abstract:
Eocene collision of the Siletzia oceanic plateau in the Pacific Northwest resulted in tectonic plate reconfiguration and development of the early Cascade forearc region. Additionally, recent work suggests a previously undocumented and subsequent episode of seamount collision, distinct from the accretion of Siletzia, significantly impacted the continental margin and played a key role in the early construction of the Olympic subduction complex (OSC) in western Washington. This period of seamount collision is evidenced by volcanic and sedimentary assemblages within the Eocene Blue Mountain Unit (BMU), which is structurally juxtaposed between Siletzia basalts (Crescent Fm.) and the oldest strata of the OSC (Needles-Gray Wolf lithic assemblage—NGW). However, the duration and structural style of this event of seamount accretion, and whether its record is also preserved in strata of the NGW, remains poorly constrained.

We integrate new U–Pb detrital zircon geochronology with thin section petrography, sedimentary and volcanic lithofacies characterization, and structural mapping to determine the timing and accretion style of the oldest units of the OSC: (1) the NGW, and (2) the Grand Valley lithic assemblage (GV). Lithofacies mapping indicates a transition from abundant volcanic sequences in Eocene units (BMU and NGW) to primarily sedimentary strata in Oligocene units (GV) of the OSC. Additionally, structural mapping and thin section petrography show strata of the NGW and GV are heavily faulted and have undergone greenschist facies metamorphism. Detrital zircon age spectra from the NGW (N=1; n=281) and GV (N=2; n=558) are nearly identical and are dominated by Paleoproterozoic (1.9–1.6 Ga), Mesoproterozoic (1.5–1.4 Ga), and Late Cretaceous (80–100 Ma) peak age populations, with subordinate Eocene (40–55 Ma) peak ages. Additionally, the youngest zircon in the NGW and GV yield maximum depositional ages of ~36 Ma and ~33 Ma, respectively.

Our results indicate deposition of the NGW and GV spanned the Eocene–Oligocene transition and both units were supplied by common sediment sources. Major sediment sources include the Western Mélange Belt and southern Coast Mountains batholith, whereas minor Eocene populations record contributions from Siletzia-related and early Cascade Arc volcanism. Overall, our new data provides valuable insight into the transition from Eocene underplating and accretion of seamount stratigraphy to a sediment rich accretionary margin in the Oligocene during development of the early Cascade forearc region.

title: Paleoenvironmental reconstructions within the Neoproterozoic Tsagaan-Olom Group, western Mongolia
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Gerasimov, Stacey H. [1], Millikin, Alexie E. [2], Lonsdale, Mary Catherine [3], Fitzgerald, Danielle Mary [4], Sandagdorj, Uyangaa [5], Stratton, Ashlee N. [6], Gonchigdorj, Sersmaa [7], Simpson, Carl [8], Trower, Elizabeth J. [9]

abstract: The Neoproterozoic Era (1000–539 Ma) was a critical interval in Earth’s history that encompassed two global glaciations known as “Snowball Earth” events, in addition to the proliferation of complex multicellularity. Conventional wisdom suggests that these Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth events would have created an inhospitable environment for life. However, recent work suggests that multicellularity may provide an evolutionary advantage in subfreezing oceans. Testing the idea that Snowball Earth events acted as an evolutionary driver for complex multicellularity necessitates a better understanding of seawater temperatures during the Neoproterozoic. Applying traditional geochemical paleotemperature proxies to the Neoproterozoic has historically been hindered by a loss of primary geochemical signals due to factors such as fluid alteration and tectonism. To overcome this problem, we leverage a novel ooid paleotemperature proxy to reconstruct ancient seawater temperatures during the Neoproterozoic. This study focuses on the Neoproterozoic Tsagaan-Olom Group within the Zavkhan Terraine in western Mongolia, where giant ooids occur in two discrete intervals. The first giant ooid interval occurs within the Taishir Formation and is constrained to the Cryogenian Snowball Earth interglacial (ca. 661–639 Ma) while the second giant ooid interval occurs within the Ediacaran (ca. 635–539 Ma) Shuurgat Formation. We used high resolution mapping and stratigraphic sections across multiple fault blocks to provide spatial and temporal context for the giant ooid occurrences. Grounded in this sedimentological and stratigraphic context, we present ooid size data, insights into primary minerology via thin section petrography, and analyses of carbonate associated phosphate (CAP), which together can contribute to a better understanding of Neoproterozoic climate. This work will allow us to test the idea that temperature was a key factor driving the evolution of complex multicellular life.

title: Gravity and magnetic analysis of the crustal structure of Iceland
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources (Posters)
authors: Jones, Elizabeth [1], Mickus, Kevin [2]
affiliations: (1) missouri state university, springfield, missouri, USA
(2) Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
abstract: Iceland is located on the northern Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is a large accumulation of mafic igneous material created by the combination of eruptions from the Mid-Atlantic spreading center and its interaction with Iceland mantle plume. This interaction has created a larger than normal crustal thicknesses for spreading ridges and reaches a little of 40 km based on seismic receiver functions and seismic refraction modeling in the southeastern part of the island. Within the rest of the island, the thicknesses ranges between 18 and 30 km with the thinnest crust being in the north-northeast part of the island. The active spreading within Iceland occurs within three rift zones composed of central volcanoes within rifts and fissure zones. Southern Iceland contains two subparallel rift zones (western rift zone (WVZ) and eastern rift zone (EVZ) separated by a transform fault. The northern rift zone (NVZ) extends to the north of EVZ to the northern coast. In order to investigate the crustal structure of Iceland and specifically the rift zones, a gravity and magnetic analysis was conducted. We used available data and made a number of transformed maps including residual gravity, reduced to the pole magnetic, tilt derivative gravity and magnetic and decompensative gravity anomaly maps. The decompensative gravity anomaly maps which emphasizes upper crustal density sources indicate that the WVZ and EVZ are associated with gravity minima and a SE-trending gravity minima connecting the WVZ with the southern portions of the NVZ. The gravity field of the NVZ is more complex the gravity a series of isolated gravity maxima along its western edge and small amplitude gravity minima under the center of the zone. The RTP magnetic map indicates that the all the zones are associated magnetic maxima in the center of the zones with minima along the edges which may be related to remnant magnetization. Future analysis will be the creation of 2 and 3-D dimensional gravity and magnetic models.

title: Machine Learning of gravity, magnetic and geochemical data to aid in locating ore deposits in northwestern Minnesota
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies (Posters)
authors: Waterman, Michell [1], York, Carl [2], Mickus, Kevin [3]
affiliations: (1) Doe Run Company, St. Louis, Missouri, USA
(2) Missouri State University, Springfield, Misssouri, USA
(3) Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
abstract: The Precambrian lithologies within Minnesota are known for their world-class ore deposits including banded-iron formations, volcanogenic massive sulfides and granitoid-hosted gold and copper. The majority of these deposits occur within the Archean Superior Province in Minnesota, which is dominated by granitic and granitoid intrusions, with smaller amounts of metamorphic rocks formed through orogenic events between 2.8 and 2.6 Ga. In northwestern Minnesota, minor Cretaceous clastic sediments and glacial deposits overlie the Archean lithologies, complicating direct identification of lithologies. Thus the ore deposit potential remains largely unknown and additionally there are only scattered drillholes encountering Archean lithologies and there have been few detailed geophysical surveys. Thus, a high-resolution aeromagnetic and radiometric survey was conducted under the USGS Critical Mineral Program and these data were integrated with the gravity data were into a geophysical analysis to produce residual and derivative anomaly maps, along with two-dimensional gravity and magnetic models correlated with geochemical data. Then Machine Learning methods were applied to the above data sets to determine the best areas for future exploration of gold and copper deposits. The gravity and magnetic data indicate minima aligning with Archean granites, while maxima correspond to banded-iron formations and basaltic dikes. Larger amplitude anomalies trend SW-NE, while smaller-scale anomalies linked to iron formations and dikes trend SE-NW. Tilt derivatives and CET lineament analyses validate these patterns and refine source body locations. Forward modeling identified dikes with high densities and magnetic susceptibilities, including localized zones of even greater values, suggesting potential mineralized or lithologically distinct bodies. The models also reveal boundaries between the sedimentary Quetico subprovince and the adjoining Wabigoon and Wawa subprovinces. The machine‑learning workflow used a hybrid approach that begins with target‑aware MICE imputation using a random‑forest subset to address missing data in the limited geoscience dataset. Iterative data augmentation supported sequential Random Forest and XGBoost models, each refined using probability rasters generated from earlier iterations. These rasters provided spatial feedback that improved classification stability and mineralization‑signal coherence. Final model outputs were combined with gravity and magnetic lineaments to incorporate regional structural information. A final filtering step using empirical Bayesian kriging Au‑ppm rasters ensured that predicted targets aligned with geochemical patterns derived from core geophysical inputs. Our results indicate potential gold mineralization within a few regions of known magnetic anomalies.

title: The Value of Environmental Tracers in Constraining the Ever-Elusive Depth of Mountain Groundwater Circulation
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: Manning, Andrew [1], Ball, Lyndsay [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract: The depth of active groundwater circulation (below which flow is a negligible component of the watershed hydrologic budget) is a key feature of mountain bedrock aquifers, governing stream response to climate variability and the amount of subsurface flow to lower elevations. The latter is particularly important for regional groundwater flow in mountainous terrain, providing mountain-block recharge to adjacent alluvial basins. However, characterizing permeability-depth relationships that control active circulation depth remains a fundamental challenge in mountain hydrology and examples of robust constraints are rare. Circulation depths assigned in numerical models of mountain groundwater flow are thus typically highly uncertain, limiting the reliability of model results. We have developed an approach to address this knowledge gap utilizing discrete-depth hydrologic, geophysical, and environmental tracer data, coupled with numerical flow modeling, to constrain groundwater flow rates at different depths in a mountain hillslope. The method requires at least one mid-slope borehole that enables discrete-interval aquifer testing and the collection of borehole nuclear magnetic resonance data (for porosity estimates), hydraulic head and temperature monitoring, and 3 H/ 3 He groundwater age data from nested wells. The method was applied at Gamble Gulch in the northern Colorado Front Range, underlain by crystalline metamorphic rock. Results indicate active groundwater circulation to a depth of approximately 50-60 m, with limited flow at greater depths. The active zone can be coarsely divided into a shallow, high-permeability weathered layer extending to a depth of ~20 m and a deeper, less permeable unweathered layer. The deeper layer accommodates roughly 25-40% of the bedrock groundwater flow and ~60% of the drainable bedrock storage. While these results underscore the importance of extending watershed hydrologic models to depths below the weathered zone (such models often extend to only 10-20 m), a circulation depth of 50-60 m is substantially less than the 100-200 m range often invoked for crystalline rock. This study demonstrates the value of environmental tracer data for constraining the active circulation depth and highlights the need for more such studies in different representative bedrock lithologies.

title: A Scalable Geospatial Workflow for Quantifying Urban Canopy Architecture and Above-Ground Biomass via Multi-Seasonal LiDAR Integration
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Ahmed, Md Sabbir [1], Mahmud, Kashif [2], Elkins, Elizabeth [3], King, Zantia [4], Lowe, Thomas [5], Devereux, Tim [6]
affiliations: (1) Kimbell School of Geoscience, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA

abstract: Urban forests provide essential ecological services, yet accurately quantifying their structural characteristics and biomass remains a significant challenge because traditional field inventories are time-consuming, costly, and difficult to scale. This study evaluates the applicability of the RayCloudTools framework for automated urban forest inventory and biomass estimation using terrestrial Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) at Midwestern State University campus. Unlike previous studies conducted in relatively homogeneous natural forests, this research focuses on structurally complex urban landscapes where buildings, infrastructure, and diverse tree species create additional challenges for automated tree reconstruction. A multi-season analysis compares summer (leaf-on) and winter (leaf-off) LiDAR acquisitions to investigate the influence of canopy conditions on the extraction of Diameter at Breast Height (DBH), tree height, stem geometry, and wood volume. The workflow includes point-cloud preprocessing, scan alignment, vegetation filtering, terrain surface generation, automated tree segmentation, and three-dimensional structural reconstruction to generate urban tree inventories. Model performance is evaluated using field measurements collected across the study area. Preliminary results indicate that the default RayCloudTools configuration achieved a DBH estimation with coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.38, highlighting the need for parameter optimization under heterogeneous urban tree ecosystems. The resulting workflow demonstrates the potential of scalable three-dimensional geospatial methods for urban ecosystem assessment, supporting carbon estimation, environmental monitoring, and long-term management of urban green infrastructure.

title: Investigating Drivers of Increased Maximum Size in Planktonic Foraminifera From the Pliocene to the Recent
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Vizcaíno, Maoli N. [1], Brombacher, Anieke [2], Dowsett, Harry J. [3], Hull, Pincelli M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) National Oceanography Centre Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom
(3) US Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(4) Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
abstract:
Since the Miocene Epoch (23–5.3 Ma), planktic foraminifera assemblages have generally increased in size with the size of the largest individuals in assemblages nearly doubling in low to mid-latitudes. At the same time, planktic foraminifera species underwent a global turnover in the dominant species, with total species richness peaking in the Pliocene before declining by nearly a third over the last ~2.5 million years. In this study, we seek to understand why test size increased in low to mid-latitude assemblages over the last 23 million years and assess whether these changes are due to replacement of smaller taxa by larger taxa over prolonged extinction, or if certain species are driving size trends? Is there a consistent relationship between species size and species abundance, reflecting the suitability of habitats, as has been hypothesized? Previous work has been limited to assessing the size distribution of the entire assemblage of planktic foraminifera, or by looking at focal species or lineages, across study sites. This study measures and examines changes in the size distribution within and across all species present in samples across latitudes and ocean basins for the first time, with expanded spatial coverage.

We collected morphometric data to investigate size changes in planktic foraminifera species from two well sampled intervals: the late Pliocene (Piacenzian stage, 3.6–2.58 Ma) and the Recent, using the extensively sampled PRISM and CLIMAP slides. Morphometric patterns were assessed globally, both at the assemblage level and with a focus on five common species at 13-paired (Pliocene and modern) sites. We find that taxa have variable intraspecific size changes and no strong relationship between change in abundance and change in size. These results differ from patterns described in previous studies and highlight the value in revisiting old fossil collections with new approaches.

title: Origin of Holocene Aeolian Sand in the Sonoyta Dune Field, Northwestern Sonora, México
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Muhs, Daniel R. [1]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract: The Sonoyta dune field is a 250,000 hectare tract of mostly stabilized aeolian sand in northwestern Sonora, Mexico. Linear, parabolic, and coppice dunes and sand sheets are found. Geomorphology indicates that the main dune-forming winds were from the south or southwest (summer, monsoon-derived). Hypothesized dune sources include bioclastic beach sands of the upper Gulf of California, alluvial sands of the Colorado and Sonoyta rivers, Pinacate volcanic sediments, and Gran Desierto dune sands. Both coastal and inland dunes contain quartz, plagioclase, and K-feldspar (Q, P, K). Coastal dunes also contain aragonite and calcite and have Q-P-K abundances similar to Sonoyta River sands, indicating derivation from beach and alluvial sources. Most of the extensive inland dunes lack calcite and have Q-P-K abundances intermediate between those of Sonoyta River sands and Colorado River sands, mirrored by major element compositions. Inland dunes may owe their composition in part to southerly inputs from feldspar-rich Sonoyta River and beach sources in the upper Gulf of California (summer-monsoonal winds) as well as westerly inputs (winter, Pacific-frontal winds) from quartz-rich dunes of the Gran Desierto, in turn derived primarily from quartz-rich Colorado River sands. Although eolian sand of the Sonoyta dune field is undated, it appears to be relatively youthful, likely of Holocene age. Based on packrat midden data, increased summer monsoonal flow with stronger southerly winds may have characterized northwestern Sonora during the middle Holocene. If so, then dune geomorphology, sources of sand from the south, and the present stabilizing vegetation for the Sonoyta dune field are explained. Thus, the Sonoyta dune field may provide an example of a counterintuitive situation where dune field formation is enhanced during a relatively humid period.

title: Using UAS Photogrammetry to Monitor Underground Coal Fire-Induced Surface Deformation in Western Colorado
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Hiatt, Jessica [1], Zhou, Wendy Wei [2], Wood, Lesli J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Underground coal fires (UCFs) can burn for decades, producing persistent geologic hazards including ground deformation, subsidence, fracturing, and slope instability. Monitoring these changes is challenging because active coal fires commonly occur in steep, unstable terrain where direct field observations can be hazardous and provide limited spatial coverage. Unmanned aerial system (UAS) based photogrammetry provides a means to remotely collect repeat, high-resolution observations of these dynamic landscapes.

This study evaluates multi-temporal UAS photogrammetry for monitoring surface deformation at the Axial underground coal mine fire in northwestern Colorado, which has been active for more than 70 years, and has produced recurrent surface impacts, including wildfire ignition and slope instability adjacent to Colorado Highway 13. UAS surveys conducted between 2018 and 2025 were processed using structure-from-motion photogrammetry to generate high-resolution orthomosaics and three-dimensional point clouds. Orthomosaics were used to identify and track geomorphic indicators of coal fire activity, including fractures, vents, subsidence features, trenches, and slope failures. Point clouds from 2018, 2023, and 2025 were co-registered using stable terrain and compared using Multiscale Model-to-Model Cloud Comparison (M3C2) to quantify surface displacement through time.

Multi-temporal observations document progressive development of a prominent fracture and trench system, localized subsidence, and continued deformation of steep slopes associated with the active coal fire. Point-cloud comparisons identify spatially coherent displacement concentrated within areas of mapped surface disturbance and provide a quantitative measure of changes that are difficult to characterize through field observations alone.

The results demonstrate that repeat UAS photogrammetry can effectively identify, map, and quantify surface deformation associated with underground coal fires. Integrating orthomosaic interpretation with three-dimensional change detection provides a repeatable approach for monitoring hazardous and inaccessible terrain and can support field investigations, hazard assessment, reclamation planning, and long-term management of underground coal fires.

title: Tracing Toxic Lead in Spices: Pb Isotope Systematics as a Provenance Tool
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part I)
authors: Marcantonio, Franco [1], Kim, Yerim [2], Morton, Peter [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Oceanography, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(3) Oceanography, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
abstract:
Lead isotope ratios, particularly 206 Pb/ 207 Pb and 208 Pb/ 206 Pb, are established geochemical tools for distinguishing environmental lead sources. Because these ratios reflect the time-integrated evolution of uranium-thorium-lead systematics in source rocks, they yield distinct isotopic signatures tied directly to a deposit’s crustal age and geologic history. We apply this isotopic provenance framework to an urgent public health concern: toxic lead contamination in culinary spices, specifically turmeric and cinnamon, where lead chromate (PbCrO 4 ) is a known synthetic adulterant added for color enhancement. Such contamination has been linked to elevated blood lead levels in children and represents a persistent, difficult-to-regulate exposure pathway that isotopic fingerprinting can help address.

To evaluate potential source materials, we characterized the isotopic signatures of two commercial PbCrO 4 reagents using multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, which affords the high-precision measurements required to resolve subtle isotopic differences between sources. The two reagents were clearly resolvable ( 206 Pb/ 207 Pb = 1.1219 vs. 1.1486), demonstrating that commercial lead chromate stocks do not represent a uniform, single-isotopic endmember. This observed heterogeneity reflects either distinct primary ore provenance or a blended signature inherited from recycled lead processing.

We subsequently analyzed three adulterated spice samples of concern: two severely adulterated cinnamon samples from Ecuador and one 25-ppm-lead turmeric sample packaged in the US (Brooklyn, NY). The first adulterated cinnamon sample contained 0.25% Pb with an isotopic ratio ( 206 Pb/ 207 Pb = 1.1489) indistinguishable from one of our commercial reagents. The second adulterated cinnamon sample contained 0.55% Pb and yielded a higher, unmatched ratio ( 206 Pb/ 207 Pb = 1.1695) plotting well outside the field defined by the reference materials, confirming a distinct lead origin. The turmeric sample ( 206 Pb/ 207 Pb = 1.1282) plotted close to, but significantly offset from, one reagent endmember, consistent with a related ore source or a two-component binary mixture.

This study establishes a robust analytical framework for identifying toxic lead additives in food products, with direct application to consumer protection, regulatory testing, and forensic tracing of contamination events back to specific manufacturing sources. An expanded suite of commercial reagents and culinary cinnamon and turmeric samples—complemented by trace-element signatures to help disentangle primary ore origins from recycled or blended lead sources—will be presented.

session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session

affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Rare Earth Elements (REEs) have become increasingly sought-after as key components in modern electronics, green energy infrastructure, and industrial catalysts. With growing geopolitical tensions and our dependence on REE imports, there has been renewed interest in developing more domestic REE resources to close the gap in domestic supply and demand. One potential type of source of REEs in the United States is well-illustrated by the Capitan Pluton, a large (35 x 8 km), zoned, and evolved granitic pluton located in Capitan, New Mexico, USA. In this study, we aim to fully characterize the mineralogy and geochemistry of the pluton’s three zones and their associated REE hydrothermal veins.

We collected samples from 13 locations within the pluton, including all three granite zones (porphyry, aplite, granophyre) and their respective REE vein assemblages. All 13 samples were processed into polished thin sections for analysis by petrographic microscope, scanning electron microscope – energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), and laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS). Bulk-rock geochemistry of the samples agrees with previous results, showing a trend of increasing magma evolution from the porphyritic core to the granophyric carapace of the pluton, with intermediate compositions in the aplitic transition zone. Using SEM-EDS and EPMA, quantitative analysis of the thin sections revealed previously unidentified minerals in all pluton zones, including multiple REE-bearing phases.

EPMA analysis indicates that the dominant REE-bearing mineral in the porphyry unit is perrierite-(Ce), with subdominant REE-enriched titanite. Conversely, titanite in the aplite unit is REE-poor, with cerium concentrated in manganese oxides. The granophyre unit, which lacks titanite, hosts REEs in sparse accessory grains, including a REE fluorocarbonate, although additional EPMA analyses are needed to confirm the species. Porphyry-hosted hydrothermal veins contain abundant REE-enriched titanite and allanite-(Ce) as the REE-bearing phases. Hydrothermal veins in the aplite are instead dominated by REE-enriched thorite. Finally, granophyre-hosted veins contain REE-enriched thorite and a REE silicate mineral, which is tentatively identified as allanite-(Ce).

From our analyses, it is evident that the magmatic-hydrothermal evolution of the Capitan Pluton had a significant effect on the nature and extent of REE mineralogy within the groundmass and hydrothermal veins of each granite unit, which will better inform future REE exploration efforts in the Capitan Pluton and similar granite systems elsewhere.

title: Hydrochemical Evolution of Glacier-Fed Watersheds in the Cordillera Blanca, Peru
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Loeffler, Claire [1], Mark, Bryan [2]
affiliations: (1) The School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA; Glacial Environmental Change Group, Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center, Columbus, OH, USA
(2) Department of Geography, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA; Glacial Environmental Change Group, Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center, Columbus, OH, USA
abstract: Accelerated glacial retreat in the Cordillera Blanca of Peru is altering watershed hydrochemistry by exposing sulfide-rich bedrock to weathering (1). This study investigates the impact of acid rock drainage on water quality in the glacier-fed Quilcay River valley and compares these waters to synoptic samples collected throughout the larger Santa River watershed. Field measurements and laboratory analyses using ICP-MS and ICP-OES reveal highly acidic waters within the valley (pH ~1.5–5.5), driving elevated concentrations of Fe, Mn, Al, and trace metals including Co, Ni, Zn, and Cu. Rare earth elements (REE), including Dy, Er, Eu, Gd, La, Nd, and Sm, systematically increase with decreasing pH and display coherent fractionation patterns consistent with acid-driven mineral dissolution. Strong correlations between these elements and decreasing pH indicate sulfide oxidation as the dominant geochemical control. Despite elevated Ca and Mg concentrations, carbonate buffering is kinetically overwhelmed by proton production, resulting in a reaction-rate controlled system. Comparison with data from filtered samples collected previously (2008-2013) demonstrates persistent elevation-controlled trends but suggests a downstream shift in peak trace metal mobilization (1, 2). Quilcay valley waters are chemically more aggressive than the Santa River synoptic samples, reflecting strong glacial influence and limited dilution. These results indicate the presence of distinct hydrochemical regimes and highlight the long-term implications of glacial retreat for downstream water quality and ecosystem health.

title: Decoupled behavior of zircon and monazite in the recording of Paleoproterozoic anatexis and Permian–Triassic reworking in the Gaya Anorthosite Complex, Yeongnam Massif, Korea
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Lee, Yuyoung [1], Cho, Moonsup [2]
affiliations: (1) Center of Earth and Planetary Materials Analysis, Korea Basic Science Institute, Cheongju, Chungcheongbuk-do, Korea (The Republic of)
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract: The timing and mechanisms of reactivation in ancient continental crust are often difficult to constrain, because zircon and monazite respond differently to magmatism, metamorphism, and deformation. To evaluate how these accessory minerals record polyphase crustal reworking, we investigated Paleoproterozoic migmatitic gneisses and Permian granitic rocks exposed along a ductile shear zone in the Gaya Anorthosite Complex, Yeongnam Massif, Korea. This complex consists primarily of ca. 1.86 Ga anorthosite and migmatitic gneisses, which are intruded by Permian granitoids. Following the emplacement of the latter, all of the lithologies were affected by ductile deformation, yielding a mylonitic-to-ultramylonitic shear zone. Phase equilibrium modeling indicates that the migmatitic gneiss underwent partial melting at ~670–760 °C and 3–5 kbar via muscovite dehydration melting. Sensitive high-resolution ion microprobe (SHRIMP) U(–Th)–Pb analyses of zircon and monazite permitted us to identify three distinct tectonometamorphic episodes. Zircons in migmatitic gneiss commonly preserve the sedimentary protolith ages of > 2.0 Ga but lack metamorphic overgrowth rims. In contrast, monazite grains in this paragneiss not only record Paleoproterozoic anatexis at ~1.86 Ga, but also Triassic metamorphism at 229 ± 2 Ma. On the other hand, zircon and monazite grains from granitic and mylonitic rocks yielded Late Permian to Early Triassic ages of ca. 263–246 Ma, which are interpreted as dating the emplacement of granite and the associated contact metamorphic overprint. This is in marked contrast to monazite grains, which only record Late Triassic ages of ca. 231–227 Ma, interpreted as corresponding to the time of ductile shearing. These petrochronological records suggest that the behavior of zircon and monazite is decoupled during repeated crustal reworking associated with the transition from continental collision to arc settings at the margin of the Sino-Korean craton. Zircon largely preserves inherited sedimentary and magmatic ages, whereas monazite records multiple episodes of recrystallization in association with metamorphism and deformation. In addition, our preliminary study indicates that δ 18 O values of monazite increased from 7.27 ‰ to 9.29 ‰ during the Triassic shearing event. This suggests that mylonitic recrystallization was facilitated by externally derived fluids. Our results demonstrate that integrated zircon–monazite petrochronology provides a robust framework for determining the timing and mechanisms of the successive reactivation of Paleoproterozoic continental crust, and highlights the contrasting but complementary behavior of these accessory minerals in polymetamorphic terranes.

title: Integrating Remote Sensing, Hydrologic, and Water Budget Analyses Reveals Surface Water–Groundwater Connectivity Through a Karst Watershed: Snake Creek, Great Basin National Park

authors: Burns, Olivia N. [1], Sorenson, Mary A. [2], Travers, Marea [3], Carling, Gregory T. [4], LeMonte, Joshua J. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA

abstract: Both surface water and groundwater are economically and ecologically indispensable to agriculture, forests, industry, and residential communities. The location of water within a system is important; while agriculture depends on surface flow to fill water diversions, forest ecosystems and residential communities depend on groundwater storage. Because of the intricate paths of sub- and over-surface flow and the diverse water needs of anthropogenic and natural systems, devising successful water resource management plans is difficult. This difficulty is heightened in Great Basin National Park (GRBA), where limestone and dolomite streambeds increase karstic drainage, numerous fault zones abruptly alter flow paths, and aridity causes streams to be ephemeral. Snake Creek is one such stream in GRBA, and it was diverted in 1961 by a three-mile pipeline that bypasses a losing reach of the stream and delivers water to downstream users. The pipeline over Snake Creek has exceeded its life expectancy and is degrading, and future management of Snake Creek requires a more complete understanding of groundwater–surface water connectivity and its impact on riparian zones and downstream users. Although it was previously thought that infiltration from the losing reach of Snake Creek was lost to deep aquifers, analyses combining satellite-derived measures of riparian vegetation condition, streamflow measurements, and regional water budgets show that Snake Creek infiltration recharges both shallow and deep aquifers. This finding, along with an improved understanding of water behavior in the region, will prepare National Park Service water managers to make an informed decision regarding updates to the pipeline. The decision to restore or remove the pipeline will not only affect local water availability but will also influence water security on a broader scale, as excessive groundwater depletion in Snake Valley could reduce groundwater recharge in neighboring aquifers. This research advances the management of a critical natural resource by integrating larger datasets and more comprehensive analytical methods. The resulting synthesis of Snake Creek's hydrologic and ecological function equips stakeholders throughout the region to better steward the river's health and share its water in a fair and organized manner. Water planners across the greater Great Basin region should consider taking similar steps to fully understand the water systems on which they depend.

title: The Forearc Record for a Continental Margin Modified by Eocene Oceanic Plateau and Seamount Collision in Western Washington

authors: Donaghy, Erin E. [1], Eddy, Michael P. [2], Ridgway, Kenneth D. [3], Regier, Nicholas [4], Montano, Hali [5], Raymond, Tay'Lor [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA

abstract:
The Eocene collision of the Siletzia oceanic plateau at ~50 Ma fundamentally modified the continental margin of the Pacific Northwest and set the stage for development of the early Cascade Arc and broader forearc system. During and following accretion, a thick section of Cenozoic sedimentary strata accumulated on top of Siletzia basalts (Crescent Formation) in the outer forearc region on the Olympic Peninsula (e.g., peripheral rock sequence, Blakely Formation) and east of the Siletzia boundary in the Puget Lowlands in the inner forearc (e.g., Raging River Formation and Puget Group). Furthermore, new research on volcanic and sedimentary strata of the Eocene Blue Mountain Unit (BMU) in the Olympic Mountains suggests it is an ocean plate stratigraphy mélange characterized by seamount stratigraphy, deep-marine pelagic strata, and continentally-derived trench turbidite sequences. The BMU is structurally juxtaposed against Siletzia basalts and suggests a previously unrecognized event of seamount collision immediately followed Siletzia’s accretion and was synchronous with early forearc basin and accretionary prism development.

We integrate new and previous U–Pb detrital zircon geochronology from Eocene–Oligocene forearc basin (N=17; n=4320) and accretionary prism (N=4; n=1115) strata with structural and lithofacies mapping to better understand how early forearc basin geometry and sediment routing systems were impacted by the accretion of Siletzia and subsequent seamount(s). Our results show there are distinct differences in detrital zircon peak age groups of the deep-marine peripheral rock sequence compared to age-equivalent fluvial-deltaic strata of the Puget Lowlands. We also note a lack of Eocene-aged trench turbidite sequences in the Olympic subduction complex relative to the thick metasedimentary packages in the latest Eocene–Oligocene Needles-Gray Wolf and Grand Valley lithic assemblages.

The collision of numerous buoyant oceanic features to the continental margin of the Pacific Northwest during the middle to late Eocene resulted in partitioning of the greater forearc region by structural highs, creating isolated subbasins. Continued subsidence through the Oligocene resulted in a regionally integrated forearc system and an influx of sediments to the trench and a transition to an accretionary margin. Overall, our study provides new insight into depositional and tectonic processes associated with how forearc sedimentary systems and accretionary prisms evolve following the accretion of a large igneous province to the continental margin.

title: Multiple atmospheric-oceanic oxidation events before the Great Oxidation Event: 1-D photochemical model for S-MIF and geochemical data compilation
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Mihori, Ryota [1], Komiya, Tsuyoshi [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science and Astronomy, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
(2) Department of Earth Science and Astronomy, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
abstract:
Recent geochemical evidence suggests that oxidation events occurred before the Great Oxidation Event (GOE). However, most proxies reflect ocenic, not atmospheric, redox conditions, so it is still unclear whether these events represent global atmospheric-oceanic oxidation episodes or local oceanic oxygenation. Mass-independent fractionation of sulfur isotopes (S-MIF, Δ 33 S and Δ 36 S) is widely recognized as a tracer of atmospheric chemistry. Its presence has been regarded as evidence for an anoxic atmosphere and variation of Δ 36 S-Δ 33 S slope has been thought to reflect changes in atmospheric composition. Nevertheless, photochemical experiments and atmospheric models have never reproduced the Δ 36 S-Δ 33 S slope observed in the geological record (~-0.9); therefore the specific mechanism responsible remains unresolved. In this study, we compiled sulfur isotope compositions together with various redox-sensitive elemental data from the drill cores and performed S-MIF calculations using a one-dimensional photochemical model to constrain atmospheric variations before the GOE.

The data compilation reveals that both the Δ 36 S/Δ 33 S and the Δ 33 S/δ 34 S slopes decrease at several intervals before the GOE. These systematic variations in quadruple sulfur isotope compositions strongly suggest that the signals reflect atmospheric changes rather than fractionation during deposition or diagenesis. Furthermore, coeval changes in δ 34 S, iron speciation, Mo isotopes, and Tl isotopes indicate that local or global ocean oxidation occurred during these intervals. The temporal coincidence between systematic shifts in quadruple sulfur isotope compositions and ocean oxidation signals suggests that multiple short-lived atmospheric–oceanic oxidation events occurred before the GOE.

The simultaneous decreases in Δ 36 S/Δ 33 S and Δ 33 S/δ 34 S slopes can be qualitatively explained by the reduced contribution of SO 2 photoexcitation relative to SO 2 photolysis. Because the preservation of S-MIF generated via SO 2 photoexcitation requires reactions with reducing gases such as CO and CH 4 , a decrease in these gases would lower the effective contribution of the photoexcitation pathway. To further evaluate this hypothesis, we performed calculations using the one-dimensional photochemical model ‘Atmos’. The results suggest that an increase in O 2 level might lead to decreases in both the Δ 36 S-Δ 33 S and the Δ 33 S-δ 34 S slopes. Taken together, the compiled data and model calculations suggest that multiple atmospheric-oceanic oxidation events occurred before the GOE, and that transient decreases in reducing gases such as CO and CH 4 led to the decrease in the Δ 36 S-Δ 33 S slope.

title: Terrestrial Groundwater Shapes a Changing Coastal Critical Zone
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Pratt, Dannielle [1], Guimond, Julia A. [2], Michael, Holly A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Delaware Environmental Institute, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA
(2) Applied Ocean Physics and Engineering, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, Massachusetts,
(3) Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA; Geological Sciences, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA
abstract: The Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia (Delmarva) Peninsula is a hotspot for sea level rise and marsh migration, due to its low elevation, ongoing isostatic depression, and extensive fringing salt marshes. Sea level rise and intensifying coastal storms are widely cited as the primary drivers of coastal salinization and subsequent marsh migration, but observational data tell a more complex story. Using high-resolution, multi-zone, and multi-depth time series data from six well-instrumented sites along the mid-Atlantic coast, we unravel hydrological stressors across a range of temporal and spatial scales. We find that even mild declines in the upland water table drive substantial salinization of terrestrial groundwater near the coast, even more so than sea level rise or storm surges. Pairing field observations with a numerical model, we further show that storm surges only salinize shallow soils when the terrestrial water table isn’t high enough to buffer saltwater infiltration. This finding highlights that terrestrial processes and their timing relative to surge events are a major control on coastal salinization. Finally, time series analysis reveals that groundwater levels on the Peninsula are rising faster than sea level rise itself, suggesting that terrestrial processes, not seaside forcing alone, contribute to driving flooding and salinization that push upland vegetation to transition to marshes at rapid rates.

title: Fire and Ice (and Rock): Laboratory Experiments on Lava-Ice-Sediment Interactions Reveal Insights on Glaciovolcanism and Meltwater Production
session_title: Volcano-climate interactions
authors: Ryan, Catheryn Helena [1], Kolzenburg, Stephan [2], Gregg, Tracy K.P. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, State University of New York, Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, State University of New York, Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, State University of New York, Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
abstract: Glaciovolcanism and lava-ice interactions are plentiful through time and space on Earth and likely on Mars as well, leading to flooding and lahars. Although lava interactions with sediment-free ice have been observed and reproduced experimentally, the effect of sediment contained within ice (as in rock glaciers, permafrost, or massive ground ice) on heat transfer and meltwater production are poorly constrained. We investigated the effects on meltwater production of sediment-ice-lava interactions through laboratory experiments using basaltic melts (~111-426 g) poured over or placed under blocks of ice with sediment:ice ratios of 0 wt% sediment, 20 wt.% sediment, or 50 wt% sediment. Meltwater discharge and heat flux peaked within 30 seconds of lava-ice contact, with maximum heat flux values of 76 to 326 kW m -2 and meltwater discharge rates as high as 2 to 7.1 g s -1 depending on experimental conditions. There is a positive correlation between lava mass and final meltwater mass, but no apparent correlation between lava surface area and meltwater mass. These results highlight the challenges in accurately assessing heat flux at the dynamic lava-water-ice interface. We observed two consistent patterns: markers of efficient heat transfer (lava cooling rate, meltwater mass and discharge, heat flux) were higher in ice-over-lava configurations than in lava-over-ice configurations; and these same markers decrease with increasing relative sediment volume, regardless of lava position. This reduction in heat transfer efficiency when sediments are introduced suggests meltwater production may be inhibited when lava encounters subsurface ice or permafrost.

title: Systematic evaluation of grain size variation and loess input on hydrogen and oxygen stable isotope composition of pedogenic minerals in modern soils from Kansas
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Butzlaff, Claire [1], Andrzejewski, Kate [2], Layzell, Anthony [3], Ibarra, Daniel [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
abstract:
Due to the relative abundance of pedogenic phyllosilicates preserved in both modern soils and paleosols, paleoclimate proxies have been developed and employed to estimate mean annual soil temperature using the stable isotopic composition in combination with temperature dependent mineral-water fractionation factors. Despite the prevalent use of this proxy system, few studies systematically evaluate the effect of analyzing various clay sized grain size fractions and/or the influence of detrital loess input to soil and paleosols systems. Here we present data systematically testing the stable isotopic composition of various clay size fractions in addition to analyses of loess units that contribute to the soils in northeast Kansas. The stable oxygen and hydrogen isotope climate proxy system is then evaluated using the NSF NEON soil database which provides ten years of continuous monitoring of soil parameters, including soil temperature.

Three cores were collected from the Kansas Biological Field Station in Lawrence, KS using a hydraulic Giddings rig. Drilling was conducted in close proximity to the NSF NEON observation tower. Samples were collected at each B-horizon and from loess dominated horizons. Samples were crushed and pretreated to remove carbonate and organic compounds. Three splits from each sample where then prepared to analyze clay size fraction at the < 2µm, <0.5µm, and <0.2µm. Each sample split was prepared as oriented aggregate mounts and analyzed on a Rigaku Miniflex benchtop XRD to determine mineralogical composition. Samples were then analyzed to determine stable hydrogen and oxygen isotopic composition. Oxygen isotopic composition of samples ranged from 17.1‰ to 19.3‰ VSMOW with an average value of 18.3‰ VSMOW and hydrogen isotopic composition of samples ranged from -43‰ to -104‰ VSMOW with an average value of -84‰ VSMOW. Estimated MAT produced from hydrogen and oxygen isotopes of pedogenic phyllosilicates of the B-horizon fine fractions (<0.5µm and <0.2µm) matched measured mean annual soil temperature values despite potential input from loess deposits, confirming loess did not influence the overall isotopic composition of the samples collected from B-horizons. Conversely, MAT estimates from larger clay fraction (<2µm) and loess deposits were 4-7℃ higher than measured soil values. This confirms previous recommendations that only fine fraction phyllosilicate minerals (<0.5 or <0.2 µm) should be used for this paleoclimate proxy.

title: Phylogenetic Informed Predictions of Climate from Leaf Size and Shape: Model Development and Application to Fossil Record
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Royer, Dana L. [1], Boyko, James D. [2], Peppe, Daniel J. [3], Butrim, Matthew J. [4], Hagen, Eric R. [5], Lowe, Alexander J. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Wesleyan University, Middletown, CT, USA
(2) Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA

abstract: Paleobotanists use leaf size and shape (physiognomy) to reconstruct mean annual temperature (MAT) and precipitation (MAP), correlating a site-mean average of fossil leaf physiognomy to climate based on extant calibrations. For example, among woody non-monocot angiosperms, the percentage of species lacking toothed margins scales with MAT and leaf size scales with MAP. Current implementations of leaf-climate methods ignore taxonomic information, despite it being long known that phylogenetic signal is present in leaf-climate relationships. Here we propose a workflow for incorporating phylogenetic information into leaf-climate methods using phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS). We apply our workflow to Digital Leaf Physiognomy (DiLP)—a multivariate leaf-climate method based on traits that can be measured on fragmentary fossil leaves. PhyloDiLP has greater skill than standard DiLP at predicting climate at 92 globally distributed extant sites: the root mean square error for MAT is 3.4 vs 3.7 °C and for MAP is ln(0.52) vs ln(0.59) cm. We apply phyloDiLP to ten fossil sites and, promisingly, find that many of the climate predictions are more in line with independent assessments. For example, phyloDiLP predicts a warmer (16.8 vs. 10.9 °C MAT) and wetter (170 vs. 127 cm MAP) climate for the warm, everwet early Eocene Laguna del Hunco site in Argentina.

title: Expanding the Geographic Reach of Postfire Debris-Flow Change Detection Using Interagency Elevation Archives
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Guido, Lauren Elizabeth [1], Santi, Paul M. [2], Rengers, Francis Kevin [3]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Golden, CO,
abstract: United States Geological Survey (USGS) postfire debris-flow hazard assessments are computed using empirical models developed with measured debris-flow volumes; these assessments perform best in areas where volume data are most abundant. Recent and ongoing efforts to incorporate volume data from fires across diverse geomorphic and climatic settings aim to improve the transferability of these models. Moreover, the widespread availability of high-resolution elevation data has also expanded opportunities to estimate debris-flow volume and investigate broader postfire geomorphic processes. However, locating temporally appropriate pre- and postfire elevation data across open-source archives, evaluating their spatial coverage, and preparing them for analysis has remained a time-intensive barrier to broader application. Here we present a new search algorithm that pairs USGS postfire debris-flow assessment records with interagency elevation archives, evaluating spatial overlap and temporal relationships between available data acquisitions and each fire and assessment date. This algorithm provides a streamlined path from dataset identification to co-registered terrain products ready for analysis. The resulting database includes 151 fires with high-confidence elevation dataset pairs, where pre- and post-event acquisitions fall on either side of the timeframe of a wildfire, and an additional 58 fires with viable coverage under broader time windows, where acquisitions may partially overlap the start or end of fire activity, or span the fire's full duration. A subset of these fires has multiple post-event acquisitions, offering further opportunities to examine postfire recovery and sediment connectivity over time. We are currently using the database to analyze debris-flow volumes and postfire landscape recovery at 14 fires spanning diverse geomorphic and climatic settings in the western United States. This work demonstrates the algorithm's utility for postfire debris-flow research specifically, and highlights the database's broader value as a resource for the postfire hazard and geomorphology community.

title: From Ultramafic Ore Host Rocks to Carbon Sinks: Mineralogical Control on CO2 Sequestration Potential at the Nikolai Ni-Cu-PGE Project, Alaska
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies
authors: Titizano Ortega, Maria Rosa [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Kasprowicz, Filip Antoni [3]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE deposits are commonly evaluated for their metal endowment, but their ultramafic host rocks are not typically considered to be a reactive substrate that could be used for CO 2 sequestration. At the Nikolai Project in the Wrangellia large igneous province of Alaska, dunite and wehrlite host variable assemblages of olivine and secondary alteration phases such as serpentine-group minerals. The Nikolai Project provides a natural laboratory to examine how primary mineralogy and serpentinization influence the capacity of ultramafic rocks to act as carbon sinks through mineral carbonation.

This study evaluates the mineralogical controls on ex-situ CO 2 sequestration potential using an integrated workflow that combines automated mineralogy, SEM-EDS observations, and whole-rock geochemistry. Polished epoxy mounts prepared from coarse reject material were analyzed to quantify modal mineral abundances and document the textural relationships, including olivine and serpentine-group minerals. These observations were used to guide normative mineral calculations from whole-rock geochemical data, allowing reactive Mg-bearing mineral abundances to be estimated for assay intervals.

The results provide a basis for evaluating theoretical CO 2 uptake as a function of mineralogy, alteration intensity, and whole-rock composition. Intervals with higher proportions of reactive Mg-bearing igneous phases have a high carbonation potential, with strongly serpentinized intervals recording previous fluid-rock interaction that affects mineral reactivity. This work shows that exploration datasets from ultramafic-hosted magmatic ore deposits can be used not only to evaluate metal resources, but also to identify lithologies with potential value for future carbon management strategies in mining.

title: Geospatial Reconnaissance of the Intersection of Wildfire and Legacy Mine Waste in the Western U.S.: Potential Implications for Water Supply
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Ebel, Brian A. [1], Murphy, Sheila [2], Blake, Johanna M. [3], Tomaszewski, Elizabeth [4]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Burlington, VT, USA
(2) USGS, Boulder, CO,
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Albuquerque, NM,
