abstract:
Wildfire and legacy mine waste can threaten water supplies through increases in availability and transport efficiency of sediment and metals. The intersection of wildfire and legacy mine waste can lead to synergistic shifts in mobilization that may enhance the magnitude, extent, and duration of metals transport into receiving waters. The western United States of America is a known nexus of legacy mine features and growing wildfire hazard, yet regional assessments of the combined hazard are lacking. In response to this assessment gap, we conducted a geospatial reconnaissance of the convergence of legacy mine features with (1) areas already burned by wildfires from 1984 through 2024, and (2) areas of present moderate-to-very-high wildfire hazard. Our analysis of past and future wildfire intersection with legacy mine features incorporates established post-wildfire thresholds of local slope and rainfall rate to assess exposure of legacy mine waste to floods and debris flows.

Multiple important findings emerged from our analysis. Small-scale mining features, such as prospects and adits, most frequently intersected with past wildfires and are most vulnerable to future wildfires. The compact size and distributed nature of small-scale legacy mine features present unique challenges for both hazard characterization and remediation. Numerous legacy mining features are present in moderate to very-high wildfire hazard areas and floodplains. Together with projected increases in wildfire prevalence, this portends substantial potential for future wildfire effects on water quality. Regions are identified for forensic investigations of the severity and extent of mobilization of metals following past wildfire events in historically mined watersheds. Our analysis further pinpoints sites with legacy mining and high wildfire hazard as targets for pre-wildfire measurements to separate the degree of amplification of metals mobilization when wildfire and mining align, compared to legacy mining presence alone.

We identify opportunities for advancing understanding and assessment of the wildfire/mining/water nexus that include: unified and improved mine waste databases, evaluation of metals transport downstream of burned areas, robust regional estimates of flood and debris flow risks in burned and mined areas, and building new modeling approaches for metals fate and transport that incorporate important pyrologic and landscape attributes.

abstract:
The Black Hills of South Dakota preserve an extensive record of mammals from the climatically dynamic Pleistocene and Holocene epochs. Yet, few quantitative assessments of Quaternary community structure and paleoenvironments have been conducted in this region of the Great Plains. Three fossil sites within Wind Cave National Park (WICA)—Salamander Cave, Graveyard Cave, and Beaver Creek Rock Shelter—preserve seven mammal communities spanning ~250,000 years to present. We assessed the genus-level functional traits of Glires within each community by quantifying the distributions of hypsodonty, diet, foraging stratum, and body mass and compared them to WICA's extant community using chi-square goodness-of-fit tests. Next, we used a community-level ecometric approach to estimate paleoprecipitation based on the inverse relationship between hypsodonty and annual precipitation (AP), where communities with greater mean hypsodonty occur in lower-precipitation environments. We sampled extant herbivorous mammal range maps (Glires and ungulates) across North America to generate community assemblages with associated hypsodonty and AP values. An ecometric model was constructed from the mean and standard deviation of community hypsodonty, and maximum likelihood was used to estimate precipitation for each trait bin before applying the model to fossil communities.

No significant differences were detected between fossil and extant community trait distributions (p > 0.05). However, Pleistocene through mid-Holocene communities were primarily hypsodont taxa (>50%) and transitioned to primarily brachydont taxa during the late Holocene. Arboreal and scansorial taxa increased from absent in the sole Pleistocene-aged community to ~20% of late Holocene communities. No trends were noted for diet or body mass. Paleoprecipitation estimates ranged from 251-698mm/yr, with the wettest estimates occurring during the late Holocene. No estimate could be generated for the Pleistocene community because it represented a no-analog assemblage outside the range of modern community trait values. The predominance of hypsodont taxa from the Pleistocene through mid-Holocene suggests drier, more open environments. In contrast, increased arboreal, scansorial, and brachydont taxa and wetter precipitation estimates during the late Holocene indicate a shift towards moister environments with greater woody vegetation. These patterns are consistent with previous paleoenvironmental studies from the surrounding Great Plains and demonstrate that herbivorous mammal traits from WICA can provide insight into regional climate and vegetation change through time and establish a paleoecological baseline for managing WICA mammal communities under future climate change.

affiliations: (1) New Mexico Institute of Mining & Technology, Socorro, NM, USA

abstract:
Alternative sources of critical minerals include unconventional ore deposits as well as other sources such as legacy mine waste. New Mexico has an extensive mining history resulting in a variety of historic mine wastes that have been preserved in the arid climate. The wastes that were sampled at inactive mine sites consist of unprocessed bulk waste rock and processed tailings, both of which have different geochemical compositions and characteristics. For this project, we are investigating the microbial communities in these deposits by combining cell counting, metagenomics, and rRNA gene and transcript sequencing with whole-rock geochemistry to evaluate the microbial community composition, activity, and metabolic potential of different waste types. Previous work from Best et al. (2025) on five sites in three historic mine districts in New Mexico showed that microbial communities varied by waste type and composition, and that the majority of the population was composed of uncultured or undescribed taxa. We have expanded Best et al.’s work to five new mine sites to include more deposit types representing different geological and geochemical conditions. Results from rRNA gene sequencing shows similar correlations between tailings and bulk waste rock with abundant Actinobacteria, Gamma- and Alphaproteobacteria, and ammonia-oxidizing archaea such as “Candidatus Nitrososphaera”. Statistical analyses also show variation in community composition with depth in a tailing depth profile, and among deposits of varying ages. Metagenomic results indicate the presence of genes for carbon fixation, and lithotrophic metabolisms like ammonia and sulfide oxidation. Analysis of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) is currently ongoing, but so far has shown that some of the abundant uncultivated groups identified by Best et al. (2025) are lilkely organotrophic populations, and that high-quality MAGs with pathways for autotrophy and, in some cases, lithotrophy, include unclassified members of the Thermoleophilaceae, Pseudonocardiaceae, and Acidimicrobiales. These communities represent a potential resource for future mineral extraction or waste management using biomining or bioremediation approaches.

Best MB, Kazemi Motlagh Z, McLemore VT, Jones DS. 2025. Historic mine waste contains diverse microbial communities that reflect waste type and geochemistry. Appl Environ Microbiol 91:e00434-25. https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.00434-25

abstract: The National Landslide Hazard Risk Reduction (NLHRR) Working Group is a coalition of professionals including emergency managers, geoscientists, planners, engineers, resource managers, academics, and others, who collaborate to reduce landslide hazards. Members span multiple jurisdictions (federal, state, Tribal, territorial, and local) whose work includes landslide hazard risk reduction, primarily at the regional-to-local levels. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) Landslide Hazards Program launched the NLHRR in November 2024. Aligned with the goals of the National Landslide Preparedness Act (Public Law 116-323) of 2021, this initiative follows a strategic action articulated in the National Strategy for Landslide Loss Reduction to enhance coordination of landslide risk reduction activities across the country. The NLHRR meets virtually each month to a) share announcements, b) plan for or report out on relevant conferences or workshops, and c) host presentations and discussions on topics such as regional landslide risk reduction activities, new tools/methods, cooperative activities across state agencies, and findings from grant recipients funded through the USGS Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Program. The USGS Landslide Hazard Program Office staff supports the organization and management of the NLHRR, and group members have assumed leadership roles to chair eight Interest Groups: 1) Mapping and Modeling, 2) Forecasting and Warning, 3) Education and Outreach, 4) Response and Recovery, 5) Mitigation and Preparedness, 6) Landslide Loss, 7) Eastern Region, and 8) Intermountain West Region. These topically or regionally themed subgroups meet in addition to the monthly NLHRR virtual meetings to engage in focused discussion and realize annual work plans. This presentation will describe the history, structure, and activities of the NLHRR since initiation and aim to inspire discussion about potential future activities of the working group to facilitate regional and local coordination of landslide risk reduction across the nation.

title: Across Oceans: Patterns of Shell Morphology Across Pacific and Atlantic–Gulf Coast Glycymerid Bivalves

affiliations: (1) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, Texas, USA
(2) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, Texas, USA
abstract: Glycymerid bivalves have an extensive fossil record spanning the Upper Cretaceous to recent, yet their predominantly isometric shell growth has limited quantitative investigations of morphological evolution. We applied geometric morphometric analyses to the external and internal shell morphology of fossil specimens to evaluate species-level variation and test long-standing taxonomic and evolutionary hypotheses for Pacific and Atlantic–Gulf Coast Glycymerids. Among the Pacific coast taxa, quadrate shell outline historically used to distinguish between Glycymerita and Glycymeris is not consistently supported by geometric morphometric analysis. In addition, the morphological variation between species is not strongly associated with differences in postero- and antero-dorsal shell slopes as suggested by other authors. The most distinctive representatives of each genus on Pacific coast, Glycymerita veatchi and Glycymeris pacifica, exhibit overlap in shell shape. This overlap is likely related to the broad range of shell outlines observed in G.veatchi , suggesting that shell outline alone is insufficient for genus-level distinction. In contrast, internal shell shape analysis of Atlantic and Gulf Coast species supports the two evolutionary lineages proposed by Thomas (1970): the Glycymeris americana lineage and the Glycymeris subovata lineage. These lineages, which currently include seven species, were established based on overall shell outline (pear-shaped versus apple-shaped), umbo angularity, and ligamental area length. Morphometric data collected here supports this hypothesis and pairwise permutation tests on Mahalanobis distances demonstrate that all seven species possess significantly distinct shell shapes. Analyses of species represented by large sample sizes also indicate measurable morphological change across their stratigraphic ranges. Thus, intraspecific temporal morphological variation should be considered when reconstructing evolutionary relationships. Together, these results highlight contrasting patterns of morphological diversification depicted by Pacific and Atlantic–Gulf Coast Glycymerid bivalves.

title: HYDRODYNAMIC CONNECTIVITY IN TELOGENETIC KARST AQUIFERS IN SE BRAZIL: THE ROLE OF SOIL COVER, EPIKARST, AND DEGREE OF KARSTIFICATION
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: TANIKAWA, WENDY [1], Galvão, Paulo [2], Padoan, Lucas [3], LOURENÇO, GABRIEL [4]
affiliations: (1) LEHID, UFMG, Ouro Preto, Brazil
(2) Federal University of Minas Gerais, Brazil
(3) Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais,

abstract: Karst aquifers are natural groundwater reservoirs developed in soluble rocks, characterized by high heterogeneity and hydrodynamic anisotropy resulting from triple porosity and complex conduit networks. The role of the epikarst and soil cover in modulating recharge and discharge is well documented in temperate karst settings but remains underrepresented in tropical karst, where thick residual soils and higher rainfall volumes condition recharge dynamics. Moreover, most studies rely on single methods, which may limit the interpretation of processes operating at different timescales. This study adopted an integrated approach combining high-resolution time series (15-min intervals over 18 months) of discharge, electrical conductivity, and water temperature; autocorrelation and cross-correlation analyses; baseflow separation; recession-curve analysis and degree of karstification; and hydrochemistry, applied to six hydraulically connected systems in the São Miguel River watershed (Pains, MG), Bambuí Group Karst Province, southeastern Brazil. The resulting model proposes that soil-mantled systems display predominantly diffuse recharge and attenuated responses, with more stable electrical conductivity and stronger memory effects; thinly covered, highly karstified systems exhibit rapid, flashy responses, short recessions, and direct point recharge through conduits and dolines; and mixed porous–karst systems show the lowest chemical regulation capacity, associated with water mixing promoted by lithological contacts, lateral flow, water-table oscillations, and temporary hydraulic connections capable of expanding contribution areas and integrating different hydrogeological basins. Two flow components were identified: a slow component derived from allogenic recharge and a fast component associated with conduit circulation. Conduit sinuosity influences water residence time, generating lagged discharge pulses that sustain baseflow during the dry season.

abstract: Both the quantity and quality of water have become an increasingly pressing issue worldwide, and resources to build drinking water facilities are limited in remote or underdeveloped regions. Global Water Consortium Projects (GWC) is a non-profit organization with the aim of constructing self-sufficient and community-led water treatment centers. Areas across 4 countries, including India, Nepal, Kenya, and Honduras, have been highlighted for such sites. Development and understanding of underlying geology and environmental conditions is crucial in assisting the use of water resources in these areas. Florida, in the department of Copan, Honduras, is a GWC Projects site and lies approximately twelve miles from the Guatemalan border. It is underlain by Rendzina soil, denoting humic-rich soil derived from calcitic parent material. Despite having an abundance of water, with approximately 84% of its days experiencing rain, many parts of Honduras face limited access to clean drinking water due to poor sanitation infrastructure. Copan, specifically, is known to have an abundance of E. coli in its water and likely has high sulphur concentrations owing to naturally occurring sulphur deposits. High sulphur concentrations are likely derived from the surficial volcanic rock of the Padre Miguel Group (Garza), consisting of fine-grained tuffs and pyroclastic flow deposits with some andesite lava flows. Many of the surface rocks are strongly silicified and highly fractured, especially near faults, making them brittle and allowing them to circulate hot fluids. E. coli and other biological hazards, such as intestinal parasites, are believed to be largely sourced from livestock fecal matter in runoff. The area is susceptible to droughts, landslides, wildfires, and floods, making infrastructure development difficult. This area is currently understudied, meaning the compilation of any data is important for informing water purification needs and geohealth risks associated with this area. Results of this preliminary study provide new information for GWC Projects to better understand the environmental challenges of proposed water treatment and bottling facilities for Florida, Copan, and surrounding regions.

abstract: The Mars 2020 Perseverance Rover mission has been exploring the ancient (3-4-billion-year-old) terrains of Jezero crater since landing in February of 2021. The mineralogy of rocks and aqueously altered sediments discovered during Perseverance’s traverse inside of Jezero crater have revealed new information about the nature of habitable climates and the potential for ancient life to have once existed inside Jezero crater. This work summarizes the mineralogical and chemical properties of three notable discoveries by Perseverance. These first include the Fe/Mg sulfate-cemented sandstones and mudstones of the Jezero sedimentary fan front (Hogwallow Flats) that point towards a habitable lacustrine or floodplain environment with high biosignature preservation potential. Nearby, the rover also encountered light-toned, cobble-to boulder aluminum-rich float rocks that contain kaolinite or halloysite, marking the first time that a kaolin-group mineral has been encountered by a landed mission to Mars. On Earth, these aluminum-rich minerals are typically associated on Earth with deep rainfall-driven weathering at the surface, or alternatively, hot hydrothermal alteration in the subsurface. More recently in August-September of 2024, Perseverance explored the ancient river channel of Neretva Vallis and discovered mm-scale Fe-phosphate- Fe/Ni-sulfide nodules and reaction fronts residing in fine-grained, organic-matter-bearing mudstones lining the river channel. These features strongly resemble terrestrial “reduction spots” that form from microbial activity in buried soils and sediments, marking their occurrence as a potential biosignature on Mars. This talk will highlight these discoveries, the implications on our understanding of Mars’ mineralogic evolution, and the potential for Martian minerals to preserve evidence of abiotic-prebiotic chemistry or ancient microbial activity.

authors: Ma, Chong [1], Mako, Calvin Andrew [2], Kwiatkowski, Chad Joseph [3]
affiliations: (1) Arizona Geological Survey, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(2) Arizona Geological Survey, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA

abstract: The Picuris orogeny was established from southwestern Laurentia in the Mazatzal and Yavapai Provinces. This study reports new field, geochemical, isotopic, and geochronological evidence from Arizona for Picuris-related geologic processes further north than previously recognized. Detrital igneous zircons [(U/Ce)/Th < 1] from biotite psammites yielded 1) a unimodal age spectrum (n=158/175) with a major peak around 1.74 Ga from the Peacock Mountains and 2) a multimodal age spectrum (n=246/252) with major peaks around 1.72 Ga, 1.64 Ga, and 1.57 Ga from the Hualapai Mountains. The multimodal age sample that yielded a maximum depositional age of 1474 ± 17 Ma (n=27) has intense mylonitic foliations and is crosscut by non-foliated megacrystic potassium-feldspar granite. Three samples of this granite yielded crystallization ages of 1425.8 ± 8.8, 1424.3 ± 9.5, and 1423 ± 15 Ma (zircon ƐHf (i) = -4 to +4). Therefore, the biotite psammite protolith was deposited and deformed between 1474 ± 17 and 1426 ± 9 Ma, consistent with typical Picuris metasedimentary rocks in central Arizona and northern New Mexico. Metamorphism/partial melting broadly coeval with the granitic magmatism is documented by a 1427.0 ± 8.6 Ma metagabbro (zircon ƐHf (i) = -4 to +2), a 1418.0 ± 8.2 Ma biotite gneiss (zircon ƐHf (i) = -3 to 0), and a 1412.7 ± 8.8 Ma migmatite (zircon ƐHf (i) = -4 to +3). U-Pb monazite geochronology from a garnet-cordierite gneiss yielded an age of 1396.5 ± 9.4 Ma (Y-poor). Mesoproterozoic tectonism concluded with 1395.4 ± 9.6 Ma potassium-feldspar pegmatite (zircon ƐHf (i) = -6 to +2) dikes that crosscut all previous rocks. The biotite gneiss and 1.42 Ga potassic granitic rocks (K 2 O/Na 2 O >1.5) are REE-rich (>1000 ppm) and the latter are mostly magnesian, metaluminous, and alkalic to alkali-calcic. Whole-rock geochemistry of felsic-mafic samples show strong mantle affinities (Mg# > 45, Ni+Cr > 100 ppm), and both the felsic and mafic igneous rocks have prominent negative Nb, Ta, and Ti anomalies. These geochemical and Hf data indicate the original magmas, including the 1.42 Ga potassic magmas, were generated or affected by subduction. This study documents clear examples of Mesoproterozoic deformation, metamorphism and magmatism at a local scale, and suggests that subduction processes of the Picuris orogeny affected areas further inboard into the Mojave Province.

title: From Mine Symbols to Data: A National Compilation of Mine Features from USGS Topographic Maps
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: San Juan, Carma A. [1], Horton, John D. [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO, USA
abstract:
The rich history of mining and mineral exploration across the United States landscape is preserved symbolically on U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) topographic maps and is a deep reminder of our country’s mining heritage. Thousands of mine symbols depicting prospect pits, mines, adits, dumps, tailings, and more reflect a long history of resource extraction that supported evolving national needs. The remains of that legacy persist as abandoned mine or exploration-related features. Modern efforts to restore mined areas, evaluate environmental impacts or pursue new exploration relies on an understanding of where and when historic mining occurred.

The USGS Mineral Resources Program supported work that compiled data from USGS topographic maps published between 1886 to 2006 from the Historical Topographic Map Collection (HTMC). The decade long effort produced 725,690 point and polygon features digitized from 106,350 multi-scale maps across 50 states, Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia (Horton and San Juan, 2016). Fifty-three symbol types were captured and nearly half include information about the extracted material (e.g. “gravel” pit). In areas where multiple map versions exist, the dataset preserves changes through time, such as expanding open pit mines.

A recently released second version of the dataset reduces duplication. For example, overlapping mine pit outlines that reflect pit expansion through time were merged into a single perimeter. Where features were represented as a point on an older map and a polygon on a newer map, the point feature was removed. These refinements reduced the number of features by 18% for a total of 597,612 points and polygons. Prospect pits make up nearly 35% of the total, followed by sand and gravel features at 23%, and adits and shafts at 20%.

Because modern USGS topographic maps no longer include mine symbols due to safety and liability considerations, this dataset serves as the most comprehensive national geospatial archive of historical mining activity in the United States. The content, temporal context, and nation-wide extent make this a valuable resource for projects and land managers addressing many of our environmental, land management, and mineral resource challenges.

Horton, J.D., and San Juan, C.A., 2016, Prospect- and mine-related features from U.S. Geological Survey 7.5- and 15-minute topographic quadrangle maps of the United States (ver. 10.0, May 2023): USGS data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/F78W3CHG

title: Rethinking the Shuram-Wonoka Carbon Isotope Excursion: Evidence for Sedimentological and Sea-Level Controls
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology (Posters)
authors: Halstead, Grace [1], Gong, Zheng [2], Rowley, Brayden [3], Cui, Huan [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
(2) School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China
(3) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
(4) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
abstract:
The Shuram–Wonoka carbon isotope excursion (SWCIE), the largest negative carbonate carbon isotope (δ¹³C) excursion in Earth history, has commonly been interpreted as recording a major perturbation of the Ediacaran global carbon cycle. Here, we present integrated petrographic and chemostratigraphic investigations for the Ediacaran Wonoka Formation (South Australia) that reveal an important sedimentological control on the stratigraphic expression of this excursion. Petrographic observations reveal a systematic upsection transition from siliciclastic-rich lithofacies, including coarse siltstone and fine sandstone-bearing intervals, in the lower part of the formation to increasingly carbonate-rich lithofacies upward. This lithofacies transition is coupled with a progressive increase in carbonate δ¹³C values, from typical SWCIE values (~–10‰) in the lower part of the formation toward normal marine values (~0‰) in the upper part. Carbonate abundance increases while siliciclastic content decreases upward, consistent with progressive depositional shoaling. Furthermore, carbonate δ¹³C values show an overall negative correlation with quartz abundance and a positive correlation with carbonate abundance, indicating a potential relationship between isotopic composition and lithofacies evolution.

Furthermore, a remarkably similar lithologic and isotopic relationship is also observed in the Ediacaran Shuram Formation of Oman, where the most negative δ¹³C values (~–10‰) also occur in siliciclastic-dominated facies and become progressively less negative upward in shallower, more carbonate-rich facies. The reproducibility of these patterns in two geographically distant basins suggests that relative sea-level change may have exerted a first-order control on the stratigraphic expression of the SWCIE.

We propose two testable, non-mutually exclusive hypotheses. First, the SWCIE may represent the stratigraphic expression of a large water-column δ¹³C gradient associated with relative sea-level change, rather than a synchronous perturbation of the global carbon cycle within an isotopically homogeneous ocean. Second, variations in the abundance of isotopically depleted authigenic carbonates, which commonly form within siliciclastic sediments, may have substantially influenced bulk δ¹³C values. Under this framework, stratigraphic variations in the magnitude of the SWCIE among different sections may reflect differences in depositional environments, water-column δ¹³C gradients, and the relative contribution of authigenic carbonate phases. If correct, these conceptual models suggest that some Ediacaran negative δ¹³C excursions may primarily reflect facies evolution and depositional processes rather than global biogeochemical perturbations. Our results highlight the importance of integrating sedimentology and chemostratigraphy when interpreting δ¹³C excursions.

title: 150 Years after the Discovery of Septarian Concretions in Kansas: Windows into Authigenesis and Greenhouse Carbon Cycling
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Rowley, Brayden [1], Suarez, Marina B. [2], El-Shenawy, Mohammed I. [3], Liu, Xiao-Ming [4], Cheng, Yanan [5], Kaufman, Alan Jay [6], Goderis, Steven [7], Smith, Rachel [8], Fang, Yihang [9], Sumrall, Jonathan B. [10], Lacroix, Brice [11], Spencer, Joel Quintus Godfrey [12], Cui, Huan [13]

abstract:
Septarian concretions are authigenic carbonates characterized by complex crack networks filled with multiple generations of cements, yet the mechanisms governing their formation and paleoenvironmental significance remain poorly understood. Although first described 150 years ago by Benjamin Franklin Mudge, the first State Geologist of Kansas, septarian concretions from Kansas have rarely been investigated using modern petrographic and geochemical approaches.

Here we present integrated sedimentological, petrographic, and geochemical analyses of well-preserved septarian concretions (up to ~1 m in diameter) from the Blue Hill Shale Member of the Carlile Formation (~90 Ma) in western Kansas. These concretions formed within sediments from the Western Interior Seaway during the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, one of the warmest greenhouse intervals of the Phanerozoic. Petrographic observations show that the concretion matrix contains densely packed calcite spherulites (up to ~1.2 mm in diameter), suggesting rapid carbonate precipitation under supersaturated pore-water conditions during early diagenesis. Septarian cracks are filled with fibrous calcite cements that grew inward from both crack walls. Fabric-specific trace element and micro-XRF analyses reveal distinct negative Ce anomalies (Ce/Ce* = ~0.5, n=7) only in crack-filling cements and enrichment of Fe, Mn, Al, Rb, and Nd in the matrix relative to the crack cements. These geochemical pattens indicate greater incorporation of clay-derived components during matrix growth and more oxidizing redox conditions during precipitation of the crack-filling cements.

Carbonate carbon (δ¹³C) and oxygen (δ¹⁸O) isotope analyses from 47 microdrilled spots across 9 concretions reveal highly heterogeneous compositions, with δ¹³C values as low as −22.80‰ (VPDB), indicating variable contributions from organic matter degradation during concretion growth. An overall negative correlation (R² = 0.6) between δ¹³C and δ¹⁸O is consistent with methane-influenced diagenesis. Strontium isotope ratios (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr = 0.7068–0.7072, n = 7), the absence of positive Eu anomalies, and Y/Ho ratios of ~30 support an early diagenetic origin with partial input from Cretaceous seawater through diffusion.

These results indicate that the septarian concretions formed through rapid early diagenetic carbonate precipitation followed by cryptic cracking and cementation under evolving redox conditions. They provide a previously underexplored archive for reconstructing carbon cycling, pore-water evolution, and diagenetic processes in epicontinental seas during extreme greenhouse climates.

title: Stratigraphic Trends in Preservation in the Terrestrial Fossil Record: Insights and Updates from the Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) Two Medicine and Judith River Formations, Montana
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Rogers, Raymond R. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Macalester College, Saint Paul, MN, USA
abstract:
The Two Medicine (TMF) - Judith River (JRF) clastic wedge accumulated in the Western Interior foreland basin during the Claggett regression and subsequent Bearpaw transgression. Both formations are largely terrestrial in nature, and both are richly fossiliferous, preserving abundant vertebrates (most notably dinosaurs), invertebrates (mostly mollusks), and plants in proximal (TMF) and distal (JRF) settings characterized by different facies (semi-arid alluvial vs. coastal paralic) and distinct accommodation regimes. Decades of research integrating sedimentology, stratigraphy, geochronology, and taphonomy have yielded important insights into patterns of fossil preservation in these terrestrial records. Initial work in the study interval identified a proximal to distal gradient in the quality of the vertebrate fossil record. The distal JRF record is characterized by an abundance of vertebrate microfossil assemblages (microfossil bonebeds), that, under current models of formation, reflect attritional accumulation and relatively high levels of time-averaging. In contrast, although fossil occurrences in the more proximal TMF are also abundant, they are generally more “snapshot” in nature, reflecting rapid burial over relatively short time intervals. Placing the TMF-JRF interval in a sequence stratigraphic framework, with its emphasis on key surfaces in the terrestrial record, revealed associations between skeletal concentrations and discontinuity surfaces of various origins and durations. Importantly, concentrations of fossils (vertebrate and invertebrate) associated with surfaces in the terrestrial record tend to be patchy and localized regardless of the durations of erosional and omissional hiatuses. Further, they tend to track the abundance of fossil material in underlying and laterally-disposed facies, reflecting the significant role of reworking in generating skeletal concentrations.

Ongoing investigations in the TMF-JRF study interval are now informed by high-resolution U-Pb ages and Bayesian age modeling. Eleven new ages bracket key fossiliferous intervals and align with stratigraphically significant surfaces, including the throughgoing expansion surface that delineates the boundary between the low accommodation (LAST) and high accommodation (HAST) systems tracts across the clastic wedge. In the proximal TMF accommodation is much greater overall and the fossil record exhibits little discernable change from LAST to HAST. In the distal JRF relatively low rock accumulation rates more than triple across the expansion surface, and this pulse of accommodation coincides with marked shifts in alluvial architecture and fossil preservation, including a pronounced increase in the abundance and quality of bonebeds within the HAST.

title: Evaporite-Based Chemostratigraphy of Permian Wellington Formation, Central Kansas: Implications for Depositional Environments and Biogeochemical Cycles
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)

abstract:
The Permian Period was characterized by elevated atmospheric oxygen concentrations, widespread exposure of the supercontinent Pangea, and arid climates that favored evaporite deposition. Thick successions of gypsum/anhydrite and halite accumulated throughout the North American midcontinent, providing an exceptional archive for late Paleozoic sulfur cycling. Previous studies have proposed that these Permian evaporites formed within an extremely acidic lacustrine system. However, geochemical constraints on their origin, age, and sulfur cycling, particularly from Kansas, remain limited.

Here, we present new sulfur isotope (δ³⁴S) chemostratigraphy based on gypsum/anhydrite and halite-associated sulfate (HAS) from well-preserved drill cores of the Permian Wellington Formation of the Sumner Group near Hutchinson, Kansas. Sulfate extracted from gypsum/anhydrite and halite exhibits a remarkably narrow δ³⁴S range of approximately +14‰ to +16‰. The nearly identical δ³⁴S mean values of gypsum/anhydrite (+15.0 ± 1.1‰, 1 SD, n = 13) and HAS (+14.8 ± 1.1‰, 1 SD, n = 29) suggest that HAS retains its primary sulfur isotopic signature. These results demonstrate that HAS is a robust proxy for δ³⁴S chemostratigraphy where gypsum or anhydrite is absent.

The δ³⁴S data of Kansas Permian evaporites show substantially lower values than those from most other Phanerozoic intervals, further confirming that the Permian Period witnessed the global minimum in sulfate δ³⁴S during the Phanerozoic. However, the precise depositional age of the Kansas evaporites remains uncertain, although previous studies have suggested an age of approximately 275 Ma. Assuming this proposed age, our measured δ³⁴S values are slightly higher than those predicted for contemporaneous seawater sulfate by the published sulfur isotope composite curve of Claypool et al. If the Wellington evaporites faithfully preserve contemporaneous seawater sulfate compositions, their slightly elevated δ³⁴S values imply that deposition may have occurred older than previously proposed. Alternatively, if these evaporites formed in an isolated, extremely acidic lacustrine basin, the elevated δ³⁴S values may reflect localized sulfur cycling with enhanced pyrite burial, resulting in sulfate isotopic compositions that diverged from the global marine sulfate reservoir.

Our δ³⁴S data provide new insights into the age, depositional environment, and regional sulfur biogeochemical cycling of Permian evaporites in the North American midcontinent. More broadly, these results demonstrate that sulfur isotope chemostratigraphy is a useful tool for reconstructing the timing and depositional history of ancient evaporite systems.

Erratum: Errors were made in the pre-issue publication version of this paper, first published online on 21 August 2026. The formation was referred to as the Nippewalla Group instead of the Wellington Formation. The correct title and text now appear in the final published version of the abstract to which this erratum is appended.

title: Mapping in Technicolor – A Multiphysics View of the Alabama Graphite Belt Through Two Earth MRI Airborne Geophysical Surveys
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: MacQueen, Patricia Grace [1], Bollen, Elizabeth [2], Whitmore, John Paul [3], VanDervoort, Dane Scott [4], Shah, Anjana K. [5], Bedrosian, Paul A. [6]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Morrison, CO, USA
(2) Geological Survey of Alabama, Northport, AL,
(3) Gegological Survey of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL,
(4) Geological Survey of Alabama, Geologic Investigations Program, Tuscaloosa, AL,
(5) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(6) United States Geological Survey1 Denver Federal Center, Denver, CO,
abstract:
Demand for flake graphite has risen sharply in recent years as a critical component of modern high-capacity batteries and other industrial and military uses, but the US is currently 100% reliant on imported graphite. To help evaluate potential domestic sources of graphite, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) conducted two airborne geophysical surveys over the Alabama graphite belt - a historically mined region of graphitic schists in the southern Appalachian Mountains - as part of the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI).

The first survey, flown in 2023, collected electromagnetic data primarily over the graphite belt and surrounding areas. A subsequent 2024-2025 survey collected magnetic and radiometric data over a 450 km long region from the graphite belt to the Florida coast. Electromagnetic methods are particularly effective at mapping graphite bearing rocks due to their ultra-low electrical resistivity, whereas magnetic and radiometric methods provide complementary information on crustal structures (kilometers deep) and near-surface (tens of centimeters) materials, respectively, with tighter line spacing and more continuous coverage. Together, these data provide valuable subsurface structural and lithologic insights in an area where traditional geologic mapping is hindered by thick vegetation and soil cover.

Combining datasets has refined the extent of graphitic units and illuminated previously unresolved tectonic features within the Alabama graphite belt, traditionally defined by the graphitic members of the Higgins Ferry and Poe Bridge Mountain groups. Integrated data analysis shows that extensive graphitic rocks likely also occur outside the traditionally defined graphite belt. Magnetic and electromagnetic data suggest that low resistivity, moderately magnetic graphite-bearing rocks extend beneath Coastal Plain sediments, possibly as far as 25 km to the southwest. Resistivity modeling shows low resistivities extending continuously beyond the northeastern Poe Bridge Mountain Group into the Wedowee Group to the southeast. Previous mapping divides the Poe Bridge Mountain and Wedowee Groups in this area by a single fault, however, radiometric and magnetic data show no expression of the mapped fault in this area. The combined datasets suggest a more complex boundary.

Together, these new Earth MRI datasets provide a detailed, multiphysics view of the Alabama graphite belt and offer critical insights into its geologic framework, supporting future resource assessments in this strategically significant region.

title: Regional Tectonism, Not Global Events, Controlled the Devonian–Carboniferous Boundary in North America
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: HEDHLI, Makram [1], Dewing , Keith [2], Grasby, Stephen E [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
(2) Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, AB, Canada
(3) Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
abstract:
Studies of critical geological boundaries and associated Earth system shifts often overlook regional geological contexts, favouring correlations with purported global events over investigations of local geodynamic controls. The Devonian–Carboniferous Boundary (DCB) interval of western North America (Laurentia) is an example. The margin underwent major depositional and environmental changes, including widespread unconformities, collapse of warm-water carbonate platforms, clastic influx, anoxia, localized shallow-water extinctions, and warm- to cool-water carbonate turnover.

Stratigraphic analyses of 10 DCB outcrops spanning 700 km across western Canada and the western United States, combined with new geochemical data and a review of published sedimentological and geochronological datasets, demonstrate that these events were largely controlled by tectonism along a convergent margin related to the Antler Orogeny. This contrasts with previous interpretations that linked these changes to purported global events, including the Hangenberg Crisis in Europe (∼359 Ma), while assuming western North America remained a passive margin.

We propose a model whereby Antler-related geodynamic inversion transformed western Laurentia from a passive to a convergent margin, causing lithospheric loading, foreland basin development, restricted marine circulation, and diachronous uplift, leading to the collapse of warm-water carbonate platforms, shallow-water anoxia, clastic influx, and unconformity development. An Early Carboniferous episode of subsidence and deepening promoted the return of cool-water carbonate production across western Laurentia. We conclude that Earth system changes during the DCB in western Laurentia were primarily driven by regional tectonism rather than global mechanisms.

title: Geologic mapping of the southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains with emphasis on ARM tectonics and Taos trough basin evolution
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Sapkota, Gyanendra R. [1], Johnstone, Charlie B. [2], Sweet, Dustin E. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract:
The southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains of northern New Mexico expose late Paleozoic strata deposited within the southern Taos trough during the Ancestral Rocky Mountains (ARM) orogeny. These rocks presently occupy the hanging wall of a Laramide-aged thrust, and much of the deformation has been attributed to Laramide shortening despite the well-documented Pennsylvanian-aged deformation in the region.

Here, we present a new geologic map, cross section, and balanced cross section through the southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains to reconstruct the structural and depositional evolution of the southern Taos trough. The study encompasses the San Jose, North San Ysidro, Sena, Villanueva, and Tecolote 7.5-minute quadrangles. Only the North San Ysidro quadrangle has previously been mapped at 1:24,000 scale; the remaining four quadrangles represent new geologic mapping and synthesis of previous geologic mapping.

The map area consists predominantly of Pennsylvanian and Permian strata. Structural relationships indicate that deformation began during the Early Pennsylvanian with the development of northwest–southeast trending, high-angle reverse faults that exhume Precambrian basement and influenced sediment transport pathways. Lower–Middle Pennsylvanian strata record approximately north–south trending folds kinematically consistent with the reverse faults. In the western map area, Pennsylvanian strata form east–west trending folds, a structural style that continues into the quadrangle immediately to the north. These folds are inconsistent with east-west shortening observed in the eastern map area, but consistent with timing and kinematics of dextral slip along the Picuris–Pecos fault along the Taos trough western margin. Permian strata in the northeastern part of the map area preserve folding produced by Laramide reactivation of Pennsylvanian structures. Restoration of a cross section to the base of the Glorieta Sandstone demonstrates that the Early–Middle Pennsylvanian structures remain after removing the effects of Laramide deformation.

These results indicate that many classical Laramide-aged structures in the region contain a late Paleozoic history highlighting the complexity when multiple orogenies overlap. The results also show new structures of Pennsylvanian age that help to refine our understanding of Taos trough basin evolution.

title: No Melt? No Problem: A Discordance Approach to Dating Smaller Impact Craters.
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Millin, Madison [1], Schoonover, Erik Jeffery [2], Beckman, Renan [3], Jakovac, Evan [4], Feineman, Maureen D. [5], White, Emily [6], Reimink, Jesse [7]
affiliations: (1) Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
(2) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(3) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(4) Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania,
(5) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(6) Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA,
(7) Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania,
abstract:
Impact cratering events are notoriously difficult to precisely place within our geologic record. Large craters, like Sudbury and Vredefort, produced new melt and dateable phases during impact, however smaller, non-melt producing craters are more difficult to precisely date. However, all craters produce shock features in rocks and minerals within and around the impact site. Zircon is a refractory mineral with high utility of dating deformation, via U-Pb discordance. Discordance in shocked zircon provides a precise alternative to dating small craters, broadening our range of novel techniques available. Here, we will expand upon our previous zircon discordance U-Pb age of the Middlesboro impact crater using new data from shocked zircons.

The Middlesboro impact crater (ca. 5.5 km diameter) lies in southeastern Kentucky, along the Appalachian Range, superimposed upon the Pine Mountain Thrust Sheet. Previous work focused on the classification of Middlesboro as a confirmed impact crater and relatively dated the crater to be <300 Ma, postdating local orogenic movement. Understanding the precise age of the crater’s formation could provide meaningful context within the orogenic system, helping to constrain the timing of the Pine Mountain Thrust Fault reactivation and the conclusion of Alleghenian deformation, furthering our understanding of this complex mountain range.

We estimate the age of the crater to be 273 ± 37 Ma based on the U-Pb discordance dates of two possible neoblastic grains found within a local shatter cone. We interpreted these grains as presenting similar textures to systematically oriented granular zircons. Notably, these zircons have a propensity for Pb loss and are found only within impact environments, making them ideal candidates for dating impact events. Here we present more data from newly collected samples to further investigate the age of the crater. We employ backscatter electron imaging to examine zircon textures and Raman analysis to evaluate if reidite, a high-pressure polymorph of zircon found in impact settings, is present. Potentially shocked zircons are then analyzed by laser ablation split-stream inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry for chemistry and U-Pb geochronology. These results supplement our previous findings by providing integrated texture, geochronology, and geochemistry for each grain. Utilizing this new data, we interpret the impact event in the context of the nearby orogenic system to demonstrate the usefulness of U-Pb discordance dating for smaller impact craters.

title: Imaging Intrusions and Mineralization in the Colorado Mineral Belt Through Magnetic and Radiometric Data: Overview and Preliminary Results from Recently Completed Earth MRI Airborne Geophysical Surveys
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: MacQueen, Patricia Grace [1], Grauch, V.J.S. [2], Magnin, Benjamin [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Morrison, CO,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Evergreen, CO,
(3) Bureau de Recherches Géologiques et Minières (BRGM), France
abstract:
The Colorado Mineral Belt is an enigmatic northeast trending, broad swath of historic metallic mining districts, many with the potential to host critical minerals. As part of the Earth Mineral Resources Mapping Initiative (Earth MRI) program, the USGS conducted three airborne magnetic and radiometric surveys over the Colorado Mineral Belt from Fall 2023 to Fall 2024. The surveys were flown at a nominal terrain clearance of 100 m, along lines spaced 200 m apart, and covered 17,560 km 2 in total

Across the survey areas, magnetic data reveal buried intrusions and map the subsurface extent of poorly exposed geologic units. While radiometric data typically reveal shallower structures, the chemical information inherent in these data can help reveal mineralization related to critical mineral deposits.

The Neoproterozoic Powderhorn alkaline-carbonatite complex is well known for high concentrations of thorium, which is clearly visible in airborne radiometric data collected in this survey. The mafic alkaline rocks produce a magnetic high that extends outside their current exposure, suggesting the intrusion is larger at depth. Crosscutting Cambrian diabase dikes also produce linear magnetic highs that appear more extensive and continuous than previously mapped. Tertiary age granodiorite laccoliths in the Elk Mountains are imaged as sharp edged, positive anomalies ringed with a negative anomaly, suggesting a thin, shallow magnetic source in line with geologically inferred structure. In contrast, buried intrusions of likely Proterozoic age to the east present as smooth, laterally extensive positive anomalies, with small wavelength structures where intrusive units outcrop at the surface.

In the Front Range northwest of Boulder, CO, a pronounced magnetic high images the fluorspar bearing, Tertiary age Jamestown stock, while the Proterozoic age, felsic St. Vrain pluton to the north is associated with an area of subdued magnetic signatures . A northwest trending, linear Th high is present northwest of the Jamestown stock in the St. Vrain pluton. The northern part of this anomaly follows a mapped zone of brittle deformation. Although the southern part of the anomaly continues along the same trend, no mapped geologic structures coincide with the southeastern part of the anomaly.

These preliminary findings show the potential for this survey data to illuminate the structural underpinnings of the Colorado Mineral Belt and pinpoint areas of interest for future critical mineral exploration.

title: An Integrated Critical Zone Perspective on Groundwater Dynamics and Hydrogeochemical Evolution in Guwahati City, India
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes
authors: Nath, Bibhash [1], Choudhury, Runti [2], Rahman, Mohammad Mahmudur [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Environmental Science, Hunter College of the City University of New York, New York, NY, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Gauhati University, Guwahati, Assam, India
(3) Global Centre for Environmental Remediation (GCER), College of Engineering, Science and Environment, The University of Newcastle, Callaghan, NSW, Australia
abstract: Groundwater dynamics and hydrogeochemical processes within the Critical Zone govern the availability, quality, and sustainability of freshwater resources. This study integrates hydrogeological and hydrogeochemical investigations of the shallow aquifer system in Guwahati City, Assam, India, to evaluate groundwater dynamics and the processes controlling groundwater quality within the Critical Zone. Hydrogeological characterization based on borehole lithology and groundwater-level monitoring revealed heterogeneous aquifer conditions dominated by clay, sand, and granular deposits. Spatial variations in water-table depth and groundwater flow reflect the combined influence of topography, aquifer heterogeneity, and localized groundwater abstraction, with regional flow toward the Brahmaputra River. Trend analyses using the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope identified both declining and rising groundwater levels, while the absence of significant long-term rainfall trends suggests that local hydrogeological conditions and anthropogenic activities primarily govern groundwater dynamics. Hydrogeochemical analyses indicate that groundwater evolution is controlled by rock–water interactions, including silicate weathering, carbonate dissolution, and cation exchange, producing predominantly Ca–HCO₃-type waters. Elevated concentrations of As, Al, Ba, Cu, F⁻, Fe, Mn, and Pb exceeding World Health Organization and Bureau of Indian Standards guideline values, together with Water Quality Index and Heavy Metal Pollution Index assessments, reveal widespread groundwater quality deterioration and the need for targeted interventions. Integrating groundwater flow with hydrogeochemical evolution provides new insights into the hydrological and geochemical processes regulating contaminant distribution in shallow urban aquifers and offers a scientific basis for sustainable groundwater resource management in rapidly urbanizing regions.

title: Geological and Hydrologic Controls on Groundwater Flow to a Fen: Insights from a Passive-Seismic HVSR Investigation
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Thomas, Renie [1], Levy, Jonathan [2], Norris, Tyler Alan [3], Currie, Brian S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Oxford, OH, USA
(3) Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR), Ohio Geological Survey, Columbus, OH, USA
(4) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Fens are groundwater-dependent wetlands whose ecohydrological functions are closely tied to the quantity and consistency of subsurface groundwater inputs. The source aquifer supplying groundwater to a fen is often poorly characterized in glaciated terrains such as west-central Ohio. The discharge may originate in surficial outwash sand and gravel aquifers, in the underlying fractured or jointed carbonate bedrock, or in combination of both. In order to distinguish between these source aquifers requires knowledge of the bedrock depth and unconsolidated sediment thickness, which is difficult to obtain because the ecological sensitivity of the wetland restricts direct subsurface investigation. This study investigated the viability of using passive seismic Horizontal-to-Vertical Spectral Ratio (HVSR) analyses for identifying subsurface controls on groundwater flow to a fen in the Mud Run watershed, Clark County, Ohio. Using a TROMINO BLU portable seismometer, 50 HVSR measurements were collected across the fen and its catchment. The depth to bedrock at each station was estimated using a power-law calibration curve against known well-log bedrock depth from the fen catchment. The resulting depths were interpolated by kriging to a high-resolution bedrock-surface map, integrated with seasonal groundwater elevation maps derived from two years of monitoring (August 2024 - August 2026) at 13 piezometers installed within and around the fen. The results reveal a bedrock high on the northern side of the fen, with bedrock at ~11 to 13 m bgl compared with ~18 to 20 m bgl beneath the fen, where shallow bedrock likely provides a preferential upward discharge pathway for groundwater to discharge to the wetland as springs. This zone spatially coincides with elevated, seasonally stable groundwater levels and sustained groundwater discharge. The results show that HVSR peak frequencies, calibrated against well-log bedrock depths and combined with groundwater elevation data, can decipher the subsurface bedrock morphology controlling source aquifer geometry and groundwater flow to fens.

title: U.S. Geological Survey’s Nationwide Products for Landslide Hazard Assessment and Risk Reduction
session_title: The National Landslide Hazard Reduction Program (NLHRP): Advancing Landslide Hazard Reduction in the U.S. through Working Groups and Landslide Risk Reduction Grants
authors: Mirus, Benjamin B. [1], Woodard, Jacob [2], Luna, Lisa V [3], Palermo, Lauren [4], Belair, Gina [5], Baxstrom, Kelli W. [6], Dunlap, Ramon [7]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Golden, CO,

abstract: Understanding past landslides is essential for anticipating future hazards, and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is advancing this effort through several nationwide products. In response to the 2021National Landslides Preparedness Act, the USGS Landslide Hazards Program has published a national strategy for landslide loss reduction, and has subsequently developed several nation-scale products and research efforts. This includes assembling foundational datasets such as (1) a compilation of landslide inventories that were mapped largely by state and local partners, (2) digitized records of previously unmapped landslide events from other sources, and (3) a framework for systematically reporting landslide damages and losses. Drawing on the national inventory and digital elevation data, the USGS has produced a national landslide susceptibility map that shows, in general, where landslides are more or less likely across the United States. We have since used the susceptibility model and updated information on landslide timing to estimate annual landslide frequency at the county level, to quantify landslide seasonality for National Weather Service Forecasting Offices, and to explore universal hydrologic metrics for landslide forecasting. This presentation will provide an overview of these national-scale products and related research efforts.

title: Body Size and Taphonomy of Bivalves and Gastropods across the mid-Piacenzian Warm Period of the Yorktown Formation
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: Khurana, Sage Arjun [1], Lockwood, Rowan [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(2) Department of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
abstract:
In a rapidly-changing world governed by anthropogenic perturbations, predicting physiological shifts in marine taxa will be critical to ameliorating the effects of future climate change. Body size in marine ectotherms scales with several traits, including fecundity, lifespan, and metabolic rate. Under changing environmental regimes, shifts in these traits have implications for aquaculture productivity and ecosystem integrity, particularly with respect to mollusks. Previous literature has suggested that body size is linked to extinction risk in fossil mollusks; however, there is mixed evidence for significant relationships existing between body size and temperature, acidification, oxygen availability, water depth, and productivity. Taphonomic overprinting additionally complicates the study of body size in the fossil record, often augmenting the size distributions that are sampled from the record.

The Pliocene Yorktown Formation of Virginia and North Carolina records the mid-Piacenzian Warm Period (mPWP), in which sea surface temperatures rose ~2-3 °C and atmospheric CO 2 concentrations reached a maximum of ~425 ppm. This system presents a useful analogue to modern conditions for studying biotic responses to environmental change. Previous research in this system has focused on evaluating macroecological shifts of mollusks; however, data on body size and taphonomic overprinting have not been assessed. Across this warming interval, I predict that 1) the preservation state of molluscan lineages will decline with warming as the abundance of epibionts increases (shown in previous works) and 2) body size will decrease with warming as mollusks experience physiological tradeoffs with declining shell thickness in an acidic, warmer world.

A total of 1,080 specimens, comprising 9 bivalve and gastropod taxa, were randomly subsampled from before and during the warming interval from field samples and museum collections. Museum samples were borrowed from the Virginia Museum of Natural History and the Florida Museum of Natural History. Specimens were assigned a taphonomic score based on potential volume loss from different taphonomic modifications and were then microCT-scanned at Virginia Tech (Nikon VOXLS 40 C 450). These data were processed in MeshLab and were used to calculate geometric mean size, shell volume, and shell thickness. Preliminary results show that only epifaunal non-stationary taxa ( Chesapecten , Bostrycapulus ) exhibit significant differences in taphonomic score before and during the mPWP, indicating that body size changes must be differentiated from taphonomic differences.

title: GEOLOGIC MAPPING AND FIELD WORK FORCES “THE WHY” OF IT ALL TO THE SURFACE
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Davis, George H. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, The University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
abstract:
An apocryphal truth attributed to Yogi Berra is this: “ If you don’t know where you’re going, you’ll end up somewhere else .” Applied to geological mapping, “ you may think you know where you’re going, but you’ll surely end up somewhere else .” Mapping takes in everything, leading to unanticipated realizations and new methodologies. This has been my experience at the Sanctuary of Zeus, Mt. Lykaion (Greece), where a Zeus-devoted history was sustained from 1600+ BC to ~100 BC. My goal from the start was interconnecting the geology and archaeology through mapping and field work. Observations followed. Built structures follow the curved trace of a low-angle thrust fault. Springs emerge from the base of a tectonic klippe. Baths are fed from a sink hole. The hippodrome and stadium space is provided by a broad syncline. The unlikely building stone of choice is heavily stylolitized limestone of the Pindos Group. Over time new approaches emerged from new revelations. Cross-section construction demanded state-of-the-art 3D modeling. Limestone-block scree swaths at the mountaintop altar appeared to be fault-scarp collapse, yet trenching into the scree (1:24-scale mapping) uncovered the source to be a 7 th century BC collapsed retaining wall for bone ash. Shockingly, the unlikely stylolitized limestone proved also to be the stone of choice at the Temple of Apollo Epicurius Bassae and at the Arcadian Gate at Messene.

Serendipity led our Lykaion team to connect with two experts who could carry out Greece-wide mapping of lightning and thunder. This work established Mt. Lykaion as the best place to hear thunder in the Peloponnese, and Dodoni, yet another Zeus site, the best in all of Greece. The mapped association of Zeus and thunder thus added another specific factor in answering “ the why” of it all: What was it about Mt. Lykaion that sustained Zeus-cult activity for 1500 years?” The atmo-dynamics at Lykaion are viscerally felt. The same is true at Dodoni, 280 km away in NW Greece. There, lightning shelters protect visitors, few of whom would have noted that the walls of Dodoni’s Sacred House of Zeus is composed of stylolitic limestone possibly sourced from the Pindos Group at its type locality, the nearby Pindos Mountains. This tale is just one example of following where mapping and field work lead.

title: Basin Restriction or Global Anoxia? Millimeter-Scale Trace Element Evidence Favors a Global Trigger for the Upper Kellwasser Event
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology
authors: Blood, David R. [1]
affiliations: (1) DRB Geological Consulting LLC, New Brighton, PA, USA; DRB Mudstone Research Laboratory, New Brighton, PA, USA
abstract:
In the Appalachian Basin, the Upper Kellwasser Event is recorded by the Point Gratiot Bed (PGB), a black shale characterized by an upward increase in most anoxia indicators. Molybdenum, however, behaves differently: at every locality studied, Mo rises from the base of the bed to a maximum in the lower third to half, then declines to background or below detection toward the top. This pattern is consistent with two competing models — basin restriction, in which a stratified water column progressively draws down a limited local Mo reservoir, or an ocean anoxic event (OAE), in which Mo depletion reflects drawdown of the global seawater reservoir. Distinguishing between them requires resolving whether Mo tracks local redox conditions or is decoupled from them.

I present millimeter-scale geochemical and sedimentological analysis of the PGB from Eighteenmile Creek, Eden, New York, designed as a direct test of this question. A vertical core was cut from an outcrop sample, and energy-dispersive XRF was run on the sanded core surface, repeated every millimeter after resanding, for a total of 186 analyses. Each layer was classified by lithology (gray mudstone, black mudstone, siltstone) and bedding fabric (massive, mottled, burrowed). Profiles of Al, Si, Zr, and Ti define four distinct clastic regimes (CR1–CR4), while Mo/Al declines by roughly 80% from base to top.

Critically, the bed's most heavily bioturbated intervals — representing episodes of bottom-water oxygenation and renewed sediment-water exchange — occur in the lower, high-Mo half of the section, not the upper, Mo-depleted half. If basin restriction controlled Mo delivery, these oxygenation events should have allowed the local reservoir to recharge, producing a rebound in Mo concentration. No such recovery is observed at any bioturbated horizon, nor is there any consistent relationship between clastic regime and Mo profile. Mo depletion instead proceeds independently of local redox oscillations recorded in the sediment.

This decoupling of Mo behavior from local oxygenation history indicates that Mo drawdown in the Appalachian Basin was likely governed by depletion of the global seawater reservoir rather than basin-scale restriction, supporting an OAE as the primary driver of the Upper Kellwasser Event's trace metal signature.

authors: Binetti, Liliana Juliet [1], Mackaman-Lofland, Chelsea A. [2], Capaldi, Tomas N. [3], Odlum, Margo [4], Weeks, Chloe [5], Ortiz, Gustavo [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,

(3) University of California, La Jolla, CA,
(4) University of California, San Diego, CA,
(5) University of California, La Jolla, California, USA
(6) Universidad Nacional de San Juan, San Juan, Argentina
abstract: The Argentina-Chile (Pampean) flat-slab segment at 32°S poses ideal opportunities to examine the effects of subducted slab flattening on middle- to upper-crustal deformation and related structural interactions in the overriding plate. Connections between deeply rooted, seismogenic faults underlying the Sierra Pie de Palo basement-cored uplift and upper-crustal faults involving sedimentary cover rocks in the Eastern Precordillera remain poorly understood. We integrate thermochronology data, inverse thermal history models, and preliminary flexural kinematic modeling to constrain the timing and magnitude of deformation and investigate potential geometric and kinematic linkages between sedimentary cover- and basement-involved tectonic domains. New apatite (N=9) and zircon (N=4) (U-Th)/He analyses of Paleozoic bedrock within the thin-skinned Precordillera fold-thrust belt, interpreted using inverse thermal history models, reveal sample cooling to <30°C by ~20–40 Ma, followed by protracted residence at near-Earth surface conditions until present day. In contrast, thermal histories from overlying Neogene foreland basin deposits require up to ~60°C of post-depositional burial reheating, followed by structural exhumation and eastward (foreland)-younging cooling from ~18 to 2 Ma. We compare the range of thermal histories permitted by the thermochronology data with thermal pathways predicted by forward flexural thermokinematic models to examine the influence of end-member interpretations on patterns of uplift, exhumation, and subsidence. Preliminary models testing published structural interpretations and in-sequence kinematics failed to replicate the modern topography and bedrock exposure within the Precordillera. However, revisions to incorporate out-of-sequence faulting—including synchronous activity along most Precordillera faults—yielded significantly improved fits to the regional geology and topography while highlighting the sensitivity of model results to deformation kinematics. In addition, our models demonstrate that interpretations of west-directed structural linkages between Sierra Pie de Palo and the Eastern Precordillera would generate ~4 km of Neogene rock uplift and exhumation in Sierra Pie de Palo, conflicting with thermal histories indicated by thermochronology data. Conversely a preliminary east-directed kinematic model that incorporates preferred (out-of-sequence) deformation kinematics successfully replicates modern topography, produces <1 km of basement exhumation in the Sierra Pie de Palo, and yields partially to unreset predicted AHe, AFT, and ZHe ages consistent with thermochronology results. Ongoing flexural thermokinematic models will further validate and refine patterns of structural deformation, exhumation, and heating/cooling based on comparison with geological datasets.

title: Shell-ective Hearing: The Middle Ear as a Proxy for Predicting Fossil Ecology in Turtles
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Ortega, Joseph [1], Jenkins, Kelsey M. [2]
affiliations: (1) College of Letters and Sciences, University of California−Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, California, USA; Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC, USA
abstract: The morphology of reptilian auditory systems varies immensely across species, often reflecting the acoustic landscape in which an animal lives. Because of this, the inner ear commonly is used as an ecological proxy, though at times it possesses a greater phylogenetic signal. Furthermore, inner ear anatomy is not always preserved in fossils, hampering its utility as an ecological proxy. Recent work shows that the main bone of the reptile middle ear, the stapes, could be a good ecological proxy in squamates (lizards and snakes). However, it is unknown if this applies to other clades of reptiles. Herein, we investigate morphological variation in the stapes of turtles to determine its utility as an ecological proxy. Through openly sourced CT data, 83 extant and 11 fossil turtle stapes were segmented and measured for: length, circumference of the footplate, midshaft, and distal tip, and the anterior and dorsal angles it holds within the skull. With these measurements, we conducted two linear discriminant analyses (LDA) of extant turtle stapes and found a distinction between marine turtles and turtles of all other ecologies, and found a weaker distinction for fossorial turtles. The two analyses differentiated in scaling properties but yielded comparable results. Marine turtles typically had stapes with a dorsal angle greater than 90° and a thicker midshaft, and wide distal tip measurements correlated to fossorial habits. Our models, however, failed to distinguish between terrestrial and freshwater species. We used the same measurements from fossil stapes to predict species ecology in our models. Our models correctly predicted ecology for marine fossils, while other fossil ecology predictions remained ambiguous. Additional data will refine predictions and hopefully reduce ambiguity which will aid in fossil interpretation.

title: How Inherited Deformation and Mineralogy Affect the Frictional Strength of Wasatch Fault Damage Zone Rocks
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Bensing, Kaiya Noelle [1], Broderick, Lindsey [2], Ault, Alexis Katherine [3], Shreedharan, Srisharan [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH,
(2) Department of Geology, Utah State University, Logan, UT,
(3) Department of Geology, Utah State University, Logan, UT,
(4) Department of Geology, Utah State University, Logan, UT,
abstract: The Wasatch fault zone (WFZ), extending along the eastern side of the state of Utah, is one of the largest and most researched active normal faults in the world. Living along this fault is around 80% of Utah’s population. This poses severe geohazard risk as the WFZ is capable of M W 7 earthquakes. In 2020, a M W 5.7 earthquake occurred along the WFZ at a depth of 9 km, which suggested the WF may be listric, or dipping at low angles (< 30°) at depth, which could result in greater ground motion. This is contrary to what is predicted to happen during normal faulting as Andersonian theory requires a failure angle of around 60°. One explanation is that inherited deformation can cause frictional weakness at seismogenic depths that allows slip at a shallow angle. Inherited deformation includes microfractures and grain size reduction during both ductile and brittle fabric development. Preliminary work on the WFZ demonstrated that material from the fault damage zone is weaker than material from the less deformed fault footwall. To evaluate how inherited fabric affects frictional strength, samples within a kilometer-long transect perpendicular to the fault were directly compared. The four samples are granodioritic gneiss from the Farmington Canyon Complex along the Brigham City segment of the WFZ and each display different combinations of brittle and ductile deformation. Friction experiments were conducted in a direct shear apparatus at 45 MPa effective normal stress on wafers and powders of these samples. All samples were weaker than “Byerlee” friction (< 0.6) and sample powders are likely stronger than the wafers because they lack existing weak planes. This observed lower friction (relative to Byerlee) is notable, given the lack of weak phyllosilicates, which are prominent along several other low angle normal faults. This study contributes fault-specific mechanical and frictional information to advance earthquake rupture models and simulations and make quantifying hazards for communities more effective.

abstract: The Global Water Consortium (GWC), a nonprofit installing local drinking water facilities in water-stressed areas abroad, has identified ~20 sites for small-scale bottled water production. Environmental assessments are needed to understand water resources and direct future efforts. Jaggirajupetta village (T.Narasapuram block, Eluru district) sits within an intensively cultivated agro-landscape of mixed agriculture, where marginalized communities rely mainly on Krishna-Godavari canal water for drinking and domestic use, with ponds and tanks used during shortages. These surface-water systems are vulnerable to contamination from agricultural runoff, sewage disposal, and inadequate storage. Existing GWC borewell reports (2018, 2021) indicate persistent hard, alkaline, and mineralized Mg-Ca-HCO3 groundwater, with elevated total dissolved solids, alkalinity, hardness, conductivity, and localized microbial contamination, limiting groundwater suitability for drinking and reinforcing dependence on surface water. Nearby oil and gas drilling infrastructure introduces a potential but understudied source of hydrocarbon contaminants, including VOCs via runoff, leakage and subsurface infiltration. Literature on Eluru district, largely published since 2017 and expanding after the 2020 neurological outbreak, reports legacy organochlorine and organophosphorus pesticide residues in drinking water, suggesting links between agricultural contamination and acute health impacts. Regional studies from the basin document pesticide occurrence in irrigation and surface water, indicating plausible contaminant loading from intensive agriculture and aquaculture. However, no peer-reviewed studies have investigated pesticide or VOC occurrence in Jaggirajupetta, highlighting the need for integrated investigation into contaminant sources and transport pathways. This analysis ensures GWC interventions are technically sound and locally relevant, while delivering safe drinking water to the community.
