title: Go with the Flow: Novel Quantitative Methods for Estimating Transport Potential of Bones in Fluid Flow
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Chiappone, Michael [1], Guala, Michele [2], Paola, Chris [3], Rogers, Raymond [4], Makovicky, Peter [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) Department of Civil Engineering, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA; St. Anthony Falls Laboratory, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
(3) St. Anthony Falls Laboratory, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(4) Geology Department, Macalester College, St. Paul, Minnesota, USA
(5) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
abstract:
Understanding taphonomic processes that shape the fossil record is integral to interpreting the composition and functioning of extinct ecosystems. Bones preserved in fluvial environments make up a major part of the terrestrial vertebrate fossil record, and the preferential transport and sorting of bones can bias fossil data. Experimental work going back over 50 years has resulted in the creation of methods for interpreting bone transport and sorting in the fossil record, with Voorhies Groups being the most widely used of these. Voorhies Groups attempt to describe the relative transport potentials of bones, acting as a qualitative equivalent to critical mobility conditions (flow conditions required to move an object) in sediment transport. Application of Voorhies groups in the literature outstrips the limited scope of the initial experiments used to define them, and some researchers have raised concerns that bones of varying sizes and shapes could exhibit different mobility patterns than implied by their Voorhies Group classification. New quantitative methods for predicting the transport potentials of bones in fluvial environments would be highly beneficial for interpreting taphonomic histories of field sites. We conducted a series of flume experiments at Saint Anthony Falls Laboratory to characterize the transport potentials of bones across a wide variety of bone sizes and shapes in a range of flow conditions.

Measured transport potentials were correlated with a combination of bone size and density. However, transport potentials of most bones did not organize into the traditional Voorhies Groups or other similar transport categories. We therefore used our experimental data to develop a non-dimensional mathematical model that predicts critical mobility conditions of bones in flow based on similar models for predicting sediment motion. Estimated transport potentials can serve as null hypotheses for bones that can be compared to flow indicators in their sedimentological context (e.g. grain sizes and bedforms) to test whether distributions of bones can be explained by fluid transport. Our model facilitates comparisons of sorting across not just individual skeletons, but whole multitaxic fossil sites, allowing researchers to take advantage of broader sets of taphonomic data. Quantitative methods like ours will help produce more precise interpretations of biostratinomy at fossil quarries, aid in clarifying potential biases in the fluvial fossil record, and may even be applicable to other complexly shaped objects in flow.

abstract: Owing to their ubiquitous nature in the environment and negative impacts on ecological health, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have become an important focus of water-quality research across the United States. Many well-known PFAS sources are associated with urban activities such as firefighting foams, industrial discharges, and consumer products. However, PFAS contamination has also been found in rural areas, with potential sources including wastewater, pesticides, land-applied biosolids, and other agricultural practices. This study examined PFAS concentrations in 120 small streams from pasture, cropland, mixed agriculture, and urban watersheds across the Chesapeake Bay region. PFAS were found in 68% of sites, with detections in all four land-use types. Perfluorobutanesulfonic acid (PFBS), perflurorooctanoic acid (PFOA), and perfluoropentanoic acid (PFPeA) were the most detected across all sites, with detection frequencies over 40%. Although the urban streams had the highest PFAS concentrations (378 ng/L maximum urban total PFAS versus 123 ng/L maximum agricultural total PFAS), the cropland and mixed agricultural streams showed diverse chemical profiles with detections of multiple PFAS compounds. Multivariate analyses were used to determine likely sources and potential proxies between levels of PFAS and each area’s land-use characteristics, highlighting distinct differences between pasture, crop, and urban lands.

title: Modeling an April 2025 Flooding Event to Understand Central Kentucky Tributary Flooding
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Swallom, Meredith Leigh [1], McGarvey, Kendall Morgan [2]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA; Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
abstract:
River flooding represents a substantial hazard in Kentucky, with multiple events occurring across the Commonwealth in the last five years. Kentucky River communities such as Beattyville experienced flooding in March 2021, and summer floods occurred in eastern Kentucky (2022) and western Kentucky (2023). In February and April 2025, statewide flooding was observed, and central Kentucky has experienced notable flash flooding twice in the summer of 2026. While high-order streams and large rivers are well studied, their tributaries are not often monitored. This study applied a modeling workflow using ArcGIS Pro and TUFLOW to replicate observed April 2025 flooding along Elk Lick Creek, a 5 th order tributary of the Kentucky River.

A default model was assembled using a digital elevation model and vegetation layer generated from 2014 statewide 5 ft lidar point cloud data. Slope angle and vegetation height thresholds were used to create a materials raster of the watershed, and the surface hydrology of each material class was characterized. Manning’s n values were assigned based on field observations, and single ring soil infiltration rates were directly measured where possible. TUFLOW’s global rainfall method was used to apply five-minute precipitation data from an on-site weather station to the study area. For comparison to the default model, two end-member models were run using no infiltration and estimated infiltration rates based on scaled relationships between material classes.

Model results indicate that soil infiltration rates can substantially impact possible downstream flood heights. The flood height predicted by the model with the highest infiltration values was nearly 6 m below the elevation of a mud line deposited during the April 2025 flood, and even in a scenario with no infiltration, the predicted flood height was ~3 m less than the observed flood. These results suggest that the observed mud deposits within the tributary were likely only possible due to substantial back flooding of the Kentucky River and offer new insights into the contribution of higher-order streams to flooding in upstream (often ungaged) watersheds.

title: Landslide Differencing Using Lidar in Floracliff Nature Sanctuary

authors: Bales, Jillian [1], Bibbins, Evelyn [2], Koch, Hudson [3], Johnson, Sarah [4]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA; Department of Geological Sciences, Ohio University, Athens, OH, USA

abstract:
Floracliff Nature Sanctuary, located in central Kentucky, is in an area with steep slopes and narrow valleys that are conducive to rainfall-triggered landslides. A recent slide impacted a trail upslope of Elk Lick Creek, causing concern for visitor safety and environmental impact. To support the sanctuary managers’ evaluation of trail safety and maintenance planning, we characterized the landslide morphology and evaluated its activity using multitemporal lidar differencing. We acquired unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) lidar data through two flights completed three months apart to examine possible topographical change over short time scales. Laser point clouds from these two flights, as well as data from statewide point clouds, were compared using CloudCompare software and the multiscale model-to-model cloud comparison (M3C2) tool. The resulting difference output was then rasterized and analyzed in ArcGIS Pro over a multidirectional hillshade, and a polygon was added to the map to indicate the landslide's extent.

Additionally, we explored precipitation data for recent years from two adjacent weather stations to find anomalous rain events that may have contributed to the landslide initiation. Based on an anomaly recorded by the weather stations and corroborated by sanctuary staff reports, the landslide most likely occurred between April 3 and April 7, 2025. While flight data quality due to leaf-on conditions prevented quantification of short-term changes using lidar differencing, this research supported extent mapping and characterization of this landslide and its impacts on Floracliff Nature Sanctuary while also contributing to a broader understanding of the environmental conditions that trigger landslides. Detailed landslide analyses like these may ultimately improve the identification of areas susceptible to future slope failures.

title: Heat-Pulse Distributed Fiber-Optic Sensing of Groundwater Flow in a Fine-Grained Alluvial Aquifer System, Long Beach California
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Ross, Jasmine [1]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Long Beach, Long Beach, California, USA
abstract: Groundwater flow in stratified alluvial aquifers is difficult to characterize because hydraulic conductivity can vary sharply over short vertical distances, concentrating flow within thin sand-rich intervals while adjacent clay-rich units restrict movement. Conventional aquifer tests typically provide bulk hydraulic properties and may not resolve discrete inflow zones along long-screened wells. This study evaluates heat-pulse active distributed temperature sensing (A-DTS) as a high-resolution method for characterizing groundwater flow in a fine-grained alluvial aquifer at California State University Long Beach, California. Two deep long-screened monitoring wells were installed and equipped with composite fiber-optic cable that supports distributed temperature measurement and controlled electrical heating. Temperature profiles will be collected with a Silixa XT-DTS system at 25-cm spatial resolution and 0.01 °C precision. Heat-pulse experiments will be conducted under ambient, pumping, and step-drawdown conditions. Groundwater inflow is expected to remove heat from the cable, responses will be analyzed to distinguish conduction-dominated behavior from advective heat transport and to estimate thermal conductivity and apparent groundwater flux. Packer testing, geophysical logs, and conventional flow-meter measurements will provide independent comparison where available. Results will evaluate A-DTS for resolving stratigraphic controls on groundwater flow and supporting well-performance assessment for groundwater management, including managed aquifer recharge applications.

session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon

abstract: Floracliff Nature Sanctuary is a topographically diverse natural area in central Kentucky, containing narrow ravines, steep slopes, bedrock cliffs, and waterfalls. The sanctuary’s guided hikes are a popular attraction; however, in April 2025, a landslide occurred, destroying part of a trail. Concern about the potential for future landslides highlighted a need to better understand how the landscape evolves in this area. Geomorphic landform maps can provide insight into the geologic and hydrologic processes that shaped the current landscape. Using statewide 5 ft lidar data and its derivatives, as well as existing landform workflows and glossaries, we mapped 16 distinct landform types in Floracliff and sections of the surrounding Elk Lick Creek watershed. We updated the landforms glossary to be specific to this area with newly identified landforms, as well as tested an automated GIS workflow to map the remaining watershed and compared it to the manually mapped landforms. We made a number of observations from the manually generated landforms map: a connection between landslide activity and specific landforms, a new subtype of an existing landform morphometry with strong correlation to bedrock, potential relict landforms, and a notable lack of depositional landforms. These observations simplify a more complex record of regional landscape evolution and indicate that Floracliff Nature Sanctuary is an erosion-limited landscape likely conditioned by the reorganization of the Ohio River affecting the Kentucky River. Further research for this area could include investigating correlations between landform types and other natural characteristics (e.g., soil infiltration) and undertaking additional automation efforts to attempt to improve matches to manually mapped landforms as preliminary tests had a weak match. Strengthening the automatic mapping process would allow for mapping and interpretations at larger scales.

title: Gaining Insight into Long-term Vegetation Changes Through Modern Day Insects
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials
authors: Velin, Denyce Santana Ella [1], Entrekin, Sally Santana Ella [2], Kennedy, Lisa Santana Ella [3], Reid, Rachel E B [4]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(2) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA

abstract: Previous research has shown that insect carbon isotope (d13C) values in arid and tropical Australia reflect the relative abundance of forest (C3) versus grassland (C4) vegetation at a regional scale. Isotopes serve as reliable proxies of insect diets consisting of either vegetation or the diets of their prey. Plants photosynthetic pathways, i.e., C3 or C4, have distinct δ13C values (averaging -27 ‰ vs. -12 ‰, respectively). Using these known isotopic differences, plant type can be identified and tracked up the food chain. Not yet known, however, is whether insects from temperate, largely C3 environments will be sufficiently sensitive recorders of relatively small amounts of C4 vegetation on the landscape. To assess whether carbon isotope values in insects from temperate southwest Virginia reflect the proportion of C4 plants (warm-season grasses) on the landscape, we measured the isotopic values of terrestrial and aquatic insects collected across a variety of vegetation types at three field sites in the Virginia valley between May 2024 and September 2025. We targeted d C3-dominated landscapes, such as forests and croplands with wheat and soy, and C4-dominated landscapes, including corn fields and native and non-native grasses. We took a remote sensing approach to estimate the proportion of C4 plants at any given site. By comparing truly aquatic insect orders to truly terrestrial ones, we determined that there is no significant difference in δ13C values between them, suggesting that aquatic-emerging insects do not alter the relationship between site-level insect d13C values and terrestrial vegetation type. Taking insects from all three sites and from multiple different locations within those sites we were able to determine that insects in C3 and C4 environments, even when the vegetation is in close proximity (crops that are planted next to each other) show distinct δ13C levels. These results allow for the calibration of a model we can use for predicting landscape-level vegetation structure. Ultimately, we will use the results of this study to interpret carbon isotope values measured in insectivorous bat guano accumulations and estimate the proportion of native grassland habitats (C4) on Virginia's pre-European Valley and Ridge landscapes.

title: The “Petrified Waterfall” at Floracliff Nature Sanctuary: New Insights on Tufa Development in Central Kentucky.
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Pollard, Breana [1], McGlue, Michael M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, Cincinnati, OH, USA

abstract: Floracliff Nature Sanctuary (FNS) was founded in 1987 to protect an iconic landscape along the Kentucky River and provide community space for environmental education in the Inner Bluegrass region of central Kentucky. One of the most important geological features of FNS is an 18 m high tufa deposit on Elk Lick Creek, a tributary of the Kentucky River fed by two springs whose chemistries are dominated by Ca2+, HCO3−, and SO4−. Tufas are generally classified as terrestrial carbonates that form from cold spring waters and interactions with plant life. In the 1950s, several Kentucky geologists noted the tufa on their maps and reported a “petrified waterfall” of freshwater carbonate. Apart from these observations, little is known about the geo-environmental processes that influence the development of this tufa or the timeline of its formation. We studied the tufa on Elk Lick Creek in 2026 to address these unknowns, using an approach that combined field observations and direct sampling. At Elk Lick Creek, turbulent spring waters flowing down a series of waterfalls drive CO2 degassing and increase pH, allowing carbonate to precipitate. Curtains of bryophyte mosses act as nucleation sites for carbonate encrustations, which progressively grow downward, coalesce, and lithify. This set of processes occurs at different stages at the study site, such that we observe the coexistence of young and weakly calcified bryophyte curtains along with much older and thicker tufa at the base of Elk Lick Falls with surficial plant growth. A core extracted from the base of the falls was analyzed using X-ray computed tomography, X-ray fluorescence, X-ray diffraction, and conventional petrography. The data revealed a highly porous internal structure dominated by calcite, with trace amounts of accessory minerals such as quartz and illite. Tufa calcite exhibits a microcrystalline texture with clotted micrite fabric in thin section, and large pores are filled by bladed calcite cement; microscopic features suggest multiple cycles of calcite crystallization and dissolution probably characterized the formation of the tufa. Our results indicate that this tufa is a composite feature that has developed over several stages, with the oldest material potentially at the base of the waterfall near the bedrock contact. Ongoing research aims to resolve the age of this tufa and build an inventory of central Kentucky tufas for geoheritage.

title: Tracking Iceberg Delivery Pathways and Circulation Shifts Across the Mid-Pleistocene Transition at IODP Site U1564 (Gardar Drift): An Integrated Geochemical and Petrographic Provenance Approach
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change (Posters)
authors: Salami, Ifeoluwa Mistura [1], Paterson, Molly [2], Ibrahim, Halima [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, Binghamton University, Binghamton, New York, USA
(2) Earth Science, Binghamton University, Binghamton, New York, USA

abstract:
The Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT ~1.25–0.7 Ma) marks a fundamental climate reorganization from 41-kyr to 100-kyr cycles. While ice-rafted debris (IRD) records track Northern Hemisphere ice-sheet calving, understanding the spatial routing and shifting currents that steered these icebergs remains a challenge. We investigate variations in iceberg delivery routes and surface current pathways across the MPT by integrating high-resolution X-ray fluorescence (XRF) core-scanning data with manual lithic grain petrography at IODP Site U1564 (Gardar Drift, 2208 m water depth).

Preliminary Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of bulk elemental data reveals distinct geochemical clusters reflecting sediment source regions. PC1 (64%) isolates heavy basaltic (Icelandic) and detrital carbonate IRD from Laurentide sources, alongside coarse crystalline basement IRD. PC2 (24%) captures a detrital silicate/basaltic mineral continuum depleted in biogenic fractions, while PC3 (6%) and PC4 (3%) isolate pure biogenic carbonate and Laurentide-derived detrital carbonate, respectively. Downcore variations in key elemental ratios—specifically K/Ti (felsic vs. basaltic provenance), Ca/Sr (detrital carbonate tracking Laurentide discharge), and Ti/Al (Icelandic inputs)—demonstrate pronounced orbital pacing.

Preliminary results suggest that during critical MPT intervals, including super-interglacial MIS 31 (~1.07 Ma), systematic provenance shifts occurred between distal continental and proximal Icelandic inputs. These fingerprints record major front migrations relative to the "Nordic Heat Pump," providing crucial empirical benchmarks for ice-sheet models and North Atlantic legacy reconstructions.

title: Geologic Map of the Southern Portion of the Mount Harrison and Connor Ridge Quadrangles, Cassia County, Idaho
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Vega, Daniel Arteaga [1], Anderson, Ryan [2], Pearson, Dave [3], Smart, Tyler [4]
affiliations: (1) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(2) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(3) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,

abstract:
The northern Albion Mountains of southern Idaho, within the Mount Harrison and Connor Ridge 7.5-minute quadrangles, form part of the Albion-Raft River-Grouse Creek metamorphic core complex. New geologic mapping at 1:12,000-scale supplemented with U-Pb detrital zircon geochronology documents the distribution and kinematics of mylonitic fabrics in the footwalls of low-angle faults near Mount Harrison and refines the structural-stratigraphic framework of the Albion Mountains. This map builds on unpublished 1:48,000-scale mapping of the Oakley 15’ quadrangle by Armstrong (1980) and 1:24,000-scale mapping of the Mount Harrison and Connor Ridge 7.5’ quadrangles by Miller (1979) and resolves stratigraphic correlations between the fault-bounded Raft River Mountains sequence (RRM), Mount Harrison sequence (MHS), sequence of Robinson Creek (SRC), and Paleozoic strata.

Mapping and sedimentary structures confirm the MHS is overturned, whereas the underlying RRM and overlying SRC are stratigraphically upright. U-Pb detrital zircon data record an up-section loss of Stenian (1.0–1.3 Ga) grains within the MHS and a strong Statherian (1.8–2.0 Ga) peak at the top of the section, like the unimodal peak at the top of the RRM. The SRC displays prominent Stenian ages. Multidimensional scaling comparisons of detrital zircon age spectra with data across the northern Rocky Mountains indicate that the MHS and SRC are not allochthonous but represent parts of the Neoproterozoic to Cambrian rift-to-passive margin succession. Lithostratigraphic observations and new U-Pb zircon data permit correlation of rocks across structural boundaries between the RRM, MHS, and SRC. Notably, the MHS may represent regional stratigraphy missing from the RRM. Lithostratigraphic correlations and a new MDA of 475–483 Ma from rocks between the MHS and RRM is reinterpreted as overturned Cambrian–Ordovician strata. This reinterpretation removes the age contrast previously used to infer thrust sense on the regional Basin-Elba thrust. Furthermore, kinematic indicators across the Basin-Elba fault zone show a top-to-the NW, normal sense of shear. Collectively, these results refine the regional tectonostratigraphic framework and support a tectonic model where a Cretaceous fault-propagation-style recumbent fold overturned the SRC, MHS, and overlying Cambrian–Ordovician rocks. A thrust fault developed subparallel to, but structurally below, the fold hinge carrying the fold to higher structural levels. However, Eocene low-angle normal faulting during metamorphic core complex formation reactivated the thrust and dismembered the recumbent fold into its current configuration.

title: Creating a Chemostratigraphic Framework for Archival Great Salt Lake Sediment Cores
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections
authors: Parks, Brayden Matthew [1], Trower, Lizzy [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA

abstract: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, a series of sediment cores up to 6.5 m in length were collected from the South Arm of Great Salt Lake, Utah by a collaborative team. Their analyses of these cores included a variety of approaches for stratigraphic correlation and lake elevation interpretation, such as acoustic stratigraphy, sedimentology, mineralogy, geochemistry (major element; C, O, and S isotopes; and organics), paleontology, and palynology. The findings of this previous work point to three major steps of lake level rise, starting ~32,000 years BP and reaching a maximum at ~17,000 years BP, followed by a rapid decrease in elevation, resulting in levels akin to present-day levels. The study also showed that carbonate mineralogy shifted between calcite- and aragonite-dominated sediments as lake conditions changed, demonstrating that mineralogical changes provide an important record of past lake environments. We now have these cores at the University of Colorado Boulder. This project aims to refine the record of lake history from these cores, expanding on and refining interpretations of lake level changes by looking for smaller changes that were not recorded in the original findings. Although the original study measured stable isotopes on select samples, it did not produce a high-resolution carbonate δ 18 O and δ 13 C record of the core. We are initially focusing on core D, which captures a relatively complete record of lake history based on previous work. Using X-ray diffraction, we determined the abundance of carbonate minerals (i.e., calcite, aragonite, and dolomite) in the core at 5 cm intervals. For depths with sufficient carbonate content in the samples, we then used Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry (IRMS) with a gas bench device to determine the δ 18 O and δ 13 C values of our samples, since these values can help determine whether a rise or fall in lake water levels has occurred. We will identify any events of lake water level rise and fall over the range of time represented in core D by looking for periods when both δ 18 O and δ 13 C values increase (lake level fall) or decrease (lake level rise). Our data will add depth and improved clarity to previously determined trends of lake level over time.

title: Along-Strike Structural, Magmatic, and Thermal Variations Reveal Polyphase Evolution of the Ruby Mountains-East Humboldt Range Metamorphic Core Complex, Northeast Nevada

authors: Lee, Terry [1], Zuza, Andrew Vincent [2], Vlaha, Dominik Richard [3], Odlum, Margo [4]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(3) School of Earth and Space Sciences, Peking University, Beijing, China
(4) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California, San Diego, San Diego, CA, USA
abstract: Metamorphic core complexes (MCCs) are characteristic features of Cordillera-type orogenic belts, exposing pervasively deformed, metamorphosed, and intruded lower-plate rocks beneath unmetamorphosed upper-plate rocks. While MCC structural architecture has been extensively evaluated along the tectonic transport direction and through structural depth, the along-strike variations orthogonal to shear remain insufficiently constrained. The Ruby Mountains-East Humboldt Range (REHR) MCC, northeast Nevada, exhibits an along-strike transition from the penetratively deformed migmatitic core in the northern REHR to unmetamorphosed, undeformed rocks in the southern Ruby Mountains. We integrate geologic mapping, field observations, Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material thermometry, zircon U-Pb geochronology, and whole-rock geochemistry to characterize the structural, magmatic, and thermal architecture of this transition. Results indicate that the migmatitic core, characterized by a mylonitic shear zone, penetrative coaxial flow, kilometer-scale recumbent folds, and a Late Cretaceous-Paleogene dike-and-sill complex, terminates sharply at the northern margin of the Jurassic pluton in the central Ruby Mountains. This transition is marked by the King Peak nappe, the southernmost of a series of kilometer-scale recumbent folds, which records a southward transposition from recumbent to upright geometry and formed during the Late Eocene. South of this nappe, the Jurassic and Eocene plutons and adjacent Neoproterozoic-Paleozoic stratigraphy lack internal deformation, preserving primary sedimentary structures and relict Jurassic folds indicative of low Cenozoic finite strain. Peak temperature thermometry results suggest that the lower plate remained hot (>600 °C) and near-isothermal from the East Humboldt Range to the southern contact aureole of the Eocene pluton. In contrast, geochronological and thermochronological records indicate that the central Ruby Mountains are unaffected by Cenozoic magmatism and heating, defining a Cenozoic magmatic-thermal gap. The localized termination of the migmatitic core is incompatible with models invoking pronounced along-strike differential extension by detachment faulting. Instead, localized heating and magmatism driven by Eocene–Oligocene slab foundering likely promoted thermal instabilities and mid-crustal diapirism in the northern REHR, producing the observed along-strike architecture that were later exhumed by middle Miocene detachment faulting. We therefore suggest that slab foundering was a primary geodynamic driver of MCC formation in Cordillera-type orogens globally. Ongoing detrital zircon U-Pb and Hf isotopic analyses across the REHR will further resolve the complete along-strike Mesozoic-Cenozoic magmatic evolution and constrain the role and timescale of magmatism and crustal melting during MCC formation.

title: Mostly Gasless: The Impact of Volatile Exsolution and Outgassing on the Depth and Height of Lateral Dikes Beneath a Volcanic Edifice
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Aksit, Gui Guenther [1], Townsend, Meredith [2], Scholz, Kate [3], Harp, Andrew [4]
affiliations: (1) Whitman College, Walla Walla, Washington, USA
(2) Lehigh University, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, New Jersey, USA
(4) California State University, Chico, Chico, California, USA
abstract: Lateral dike propagation has been observed or interpreted at many modern and ancient stratovolcano systems. External factors, such as edifice load or tectonic stresses, have been extensively studied to explain this horizontal emplacement. However, dynamic, internal processes during magma ascent and intrusion, such as volatile exsolution and outgassing, may impact both the density and pressure conditions driving crack opening and lateral growth, and remains largely understudied in dike modeling. Here, we investigate the impact of including volatile exsolution in magma on vertically stable dikes geometries and conditions of intrusion within a stratovolcano edifice. This work reconciles field data collected from 15 large silicic dikes observed at the eroded, Oligocene-aged Summer Coon volcano in Colorado that show dominantly lateral intrusion pathways, and average preserved porosities between 8-11%, with a new coupled mechanical and thermodynamic model of dike propagation. Dikes are modeled as a two-dimensional, vertical, elastic crack in an external stress field derived from a finite-element model of an idealized Summer Coon edifice. Stability conditions are limited to those promoting lateral propagation, where the top and bottom of the crack are not growing. We test stability of the two main magmatic compositions observed in the silicic dikes at Summer Coon (trachytic and rhyolitic) and for three porosity and overpressure scenarios (0%, 50% and 15% porosity; 2, 4, and 6 MPa). From our modeled scenarios for all compositions, volatile exsolution encourages dike propagation higher into the edifice even at the lowest overpressures, and results in dikes that are considerably shorter, and lower volume, than the non-porous scenario. The 15% porosity scenario best captures the conditions interpreted for Summer Coon, with low porosities regulated by a combination of a lower percolation threshold in a crystal-rich magma combined with higher shear during intrusion. While the low stress gradients from the edifice are the greatest factor promoting lateral propagation, volatile exsolution promotes dike intrusion within the edifice to shallower depths and at greater radial distances from the volcanic center. This work demonstrates the importance of considering dynamic density variations and a coupled gas-melt phase when modeling silicic dikes at stratovolcanoes.

abstract: Se identificó un extenso apilamiento de depósitos de transporte en masa (MTD, por sus siglas en inglés) en la Cuenca de Guaymas mediante la interpretación de diecisiete perfiles de sísmica de reflexión de alta resolución y núcleos de sedimento. La Cuenca de Guaymas es una cuenca marginal joven en el Golfo de California que se caracteriza por la expansión activa del fondo oceánico, altas tazas de sedimentación, una cubierta sedimentaria de hasta 5 km de espesor, y múltiples sills basálticos que intrusionan a los sedimentos marinos. El apilamiento está constituido por cinco unidades de MTD de espesores, áreas y volúmenes variables, caracterizadas por una facies sísmica transparente, con reflectores lateralmente discontinuos, y superficies superiores irregulares e inferiores erosivas. A partir del análisis de núcleos de sedimento del Sitio U1551A de la Expedición 385 del International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP), definimos las litofacies de los MTD y utilizamos la procedencia de las arenas para inferir que el apilamiento se originó en el delta del río Yaqui, en el margen de Sonora, desde donde el material fue transportado hacia el suroeste. Proponemos que la combinación de altas tasas de sedimentación y tectónica activa favoreció la ocurrencia de estos eventos de transporte en masa. Las estructuras en flor identificadas en perfiles sísmicos indican que el apilamiento de MTD sepultó una porción de la falla transformante que separa la cuenca de Guaymas del margen continental de Sonora. Asimismo, la interpretación sísmica sugiere que parte del apilamiento rellenó el graben sur, modificando localmente el campo de esfuerzos y promoviendo una reorganización de la expresión superficial de la expansión del fondo oceánico. Como respuesta al emplazamiento de los MTD y al relleno del graben sur, se desarrolló un graben adicional en el sector norte de la Cuenca de Guaymas. Nuestros resultados contribuyen a comprender las interacciones entre las altas tasas de sedimentación, la estabilidad del talud continental y la tectónica activa, así como su influencia en la evolución de la expansión de placas en la Cuenca de Guaymas

authors: Uhlenbrock, Geneva [1], Belak, Ethan [2], Gray, Morgan [3], Krekeler, Mark P. S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA

abstract: Agricultural runoff and nutrient pollution are a growing issue, with roughly 5 million tons of phosphorus used in the United States annually. This runoff leads to eutrophication and water quality issues. This has led to pressure on both landowners to use less fertilizer and other agencies to find ways to mitigate the effects of nutrient pollution. Phosphorus is generally the limiting nutrient in freshwater systems and has lower mobility compared to other nutrients like nitrogen. Phosphorus readily binds to many minerals, most notably goethite, with this interaction being studied extensively. In previous studies, synthetic hydrotalcite and thermally modified sepiolite have been used to adsorb phosphorus and reduce bioavailable levels, presenting an opportunity for a mitigation strategy. However, the effectiveness of phosphorus fixation and stabilization in joint conditions has not been investigated. A pure sample of both hydrotalcite and sepiolite, along with 20:80, 80:20, and 50:50 mixtures, is being initially investigated by using varying phosphorus solutions and anion concentrations. Pre- and post-adsorption water compositions are measured via ion chromatography. Phosphorus solutions were generated via the addition of potassium dihydrogen phosphate to concentrations of between 0 and 10 mM; calcium chloride was also added for a constant background electrolyte concentration. Mineralogy of both hydrotalcite and sepiolite materials was confirmed via X-ray diffraction and limited study via electron microscopy. While this is still in a preliminary stage, it is expected that hydrotalcite will have higher phosphorus adsorption on its own compared to sepiolite. But the mixture will likely have a higher overall adsorption over time in flow conditions due to the sepiolite providing more surface area and reducing hydrotalcite loss. This has potential implications for developing phosphate remediation and the reduction in nutrient runoff capabilities.

title: The digital seafloor: shaping Earth science discovery using machine learning and global data analysis
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Dutkiewicz, Adriana [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, The University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia
abstract:
Deep-sea sediments cover most of the ocean floor. Their composition and distribution underpin our understanding of climate, ocean circulation, biological productivity, and the occurrence of metal deposits. Over the last 50 years, hundreds of research cruises have collected >200,000 seafloor samples in addition to more than 4,000 scientific ocean drill holes. Yet for decades, this vast archive of sedimentological data has remained underutilized in in global studies. We show how the integration of open geoscience archives, global environmental grids and computational methods has transformed scattered seabed observations into a global framework for geological discovery.

We classified nearly 14,500 sediment samples into 13 lithology classes based on data in the Index to Marine and Lacustrine Geological Samples and historical cruise reports. Using a support vector machine we produced the first data-driven global map of seafloor lithologies, revealing distributions substantially more complex than those depicted in earlier hand-drawn maps. The digital representation of seafloor sediments enabled the relationship of seafloor lithologies with surface oceanographic parameters, and bathymetry to be quantified. A probabilistic Gaussian process classifier showed that the occurrence of major lithologies can be predicted largely from sea-surface temperature, salinity and bathymetry, providing a new approach for constraining paleosurface ocean environments from the geological record of deep-sea sediments.

Our application of machine learning methods to seafloor sediments was further extended to understanding the environmental predictors of polymetallic nodule occurrence in the global ocean. We integrated more than 10,000 seabed observations with global geospatial layers describing seafloor lithology, bathymetry, sedimentation, ocean productivity, bottom-water oxygen, organic carbon, ocean circulation, and benthic biomass. Using a Bayesian logistic regression framework, we ranked the environmental controls on nodule formation and generated the first global probability map of nodule occurrence, identifying both known deposits and previously unrecognized prospective regions. The analysis also challenged a long-standing geological hypothesis by showing that bottom currents are generally too weak to keep nodules exposed, instead pointing to benthic megafauna as the most likely mechanism maintaining nodule growth at the sediment surface.

Together, these case studies demonstrate how integrating legacy geoscience data with machine learning is transforming the seafloor into a quantitative, predictive Earth-system archive. As global geoscience datasets continue to grow, geoinformatics will play an increasingly important role in accelerating Earth science discovery.

title: Origin of Large Pyrite Concretions in Cretaceous Dakota Formation of Kansas: Evidence from Sedimentology and Sulfur Isotopes

authors: Weiss, Evangeline Adelle [1], Rowley, Brayden [2], Kaufman, Alan Jay [3], Wollney, Jenna [4], Fang, Yihang [5], Cui, Huan [6]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS, USA

(3) Department of Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA; Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA

abstract:
Iron oxide concretions are common on Mars and are widely interpreted as evidence of past water-rock interaction. On Earth, analogous iron oxide concretions are well documented, including those within sandstones of the Cretaceous Dakota Formation. In contrast, reduced iron (sulfide) concretions are comparatively rare. Here we document large pyrite concretions (up to 10 cm in diameter) from the Dakota sandstones in Kansas, and investigate their origin using integrated sedimentological, petrographic, and sulfur isotope analyses.

The pyrite concretions occur locally within fine to medium-grained sandstones deposited in deltaic environments. They are spherical to ellipsoidal and commonly surrounded by an iron oxide-rich rim within the host sandstone. Petrographic and XRD analyses show that pyrite forms pore-filling cement between quartz grains, indicating rapid mineralization during early diagenesis, prior to sediment lithification. Fossil fragments and carbonaceous organic matter are preserved within the concretions, suggesting that organic matter fueled microbial sulfate reduction and pyrite precipitation.

Pyrite sulfur isotope (δ³⁴S) compositions were determined from 92 microdrilled spots collected along 18 transects spanning the full diameters of nine concretions. The δ³⁴S values exhibit a distinct bimodal distribution, with two dominant populations centered at –35.7 ± 1.8‰ (1 SD, n = 21) and

+11.5 ± 1.4‰ (1 SD, n = 67). Individual concretions are either isotopically homogeneous and dominated by one population or contain both. In the latter case, the cores consistently exhibit more negative δ³⁴S values, whereas the outer portions are characterized by more positive values.

Assuming a coeval marine sulfate δ³⁴S value of ~+15‰ inferred from the barite record, the isotope data indicate two distinct episodes of pyrite precipitation. The strongly depleted population (~–35.7‰) is consistent with microbial sulfate reduction under relatively open-system conditions, where sustained sulfate diffusion permitted large sulfur isotope fractionation. In contrast, the positive population (~+11.5‰) reflects substantially reduced fractionation, likely resulting from elevated microbial sulfate reduction rates and/or more closed-system conditions that limited sulfate replenishment.

These results indicate that the pyrite concretions formed during early diagenesis through dynamic interactions among microbial sulfate reduction, iron reduction, and organic matter degradation. We further propose that these sulfide concretions may represent precursors to some iron oxide concretions in the Dakota Formation, providing a potential terrestrial analog for iron concretion formation on Mars.

title: Temporal constraints on ancient volcanic arcs in the Central Belt of the northern Sierra Nevada foothills, California.
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California (Posters)
authors: Hayes, Cole [1], Roeske, Sarah M. [2], Rack, Sierra [3]
affiliations: (1) University of California, Davis, USA
(2) University of California, Davis, CA, USA
(3) University of California, Davis, USA
abstract:
The northern Sierra Nevada foothills preserve a record of Mesozoic tectonic evolution along the margin of the North American continent, but the tectonic and temporal relationships of igneous rocks in the Western and Central belts remain poorly understood. Previous interpretations suggested that Triassic and Jurassic volcanic assemblages formed as separate arcs that were tectonically juxtaposed after deposition. To better constrain the timing of volcanism and the contact between the volcanic rocks and the basement, this study conducted detailed field mapping and acquired U-Pb zircon dates from volcanic rocks and volcanic lithic-bearing epiclastic sandstones in the Central and Western belts.

A Jurassic volcanic sample in the Central belt yielded a maximum depositional age (MDA) of ~163 Ma, and adjacent epiclastic sandstones yielded Mid-Jurassic MDAs of 162-164 Ma, whereas a nearby Triassic volcanic sample yielded a crystallization age of ~207 Ma. Field relations show that the Jurassic volcanic breccia and epiclastic units were deposited directly on top of the serpentinite and chert-mudstone basement assemblage, while the relationship between the ~207 Ma Triassic volcanic unit and the basement remain uncertain. Excluding the Triassic volcanic sample, the samples have an abundance of Precambrian and Paleozoic zircon grains, indicating a proximal old continental source during Jurassic magmatism and sedimentation, consistent with recent detrital zircon studies from nearby in the Central and Western belts. An epiclastic sample from the Western belt yielded an MDA of 162 and shares similar zircon age distributions with the Central belt Jurassic samples, suggesting that both localities were part of the same regional sedimentation system despite residing in different belts across the Bear Mountain/Wolf Creek fault system.

The coexistence of ~207 Ma Triassic volcanics adjacent to ~163 Ma Jurassic volcanics, together with Jurassic sedimentary rocks containing locally derived ~198 Ma zircons, suggests that the Triassic volcanic rocks were exposed near the Jurassic arc during development and sedimentation. These data and field observations refute interpretations of separate arc systems tectonically juxtaposed and are instead consistent with prolonged or episodic arc construction. The depositional contact between the volcanic and basement units, combined with abundant Precambrian zircon populations in both the Central and Western belts, supports volcanism proximal to a continental source during east-directed subduction and does not support a bi-directional subduction model.

title: Does Body Size Correlate with Ecological Innovation?
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Novack-Gottshall, Philip M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Biological Sciences, Benedictine University, Lisle, IL, USA
abstract: An organism's mass is widely recognized as a convenient measure for representing a wide range of physiological, ecological, and evolutionary concepts. However, it remains unclear to what extent a clade's body size distribution correlates with its ability to perform novel ecological functions. Here, we test this hypothesis using a new data set of body sizes for more than 20,000 Phanerozoic marine animal genera merged from original and previously published datasets, each also coded according to their life habit. We test whether clades with broader body size distributions have greater ecological disparity, whether the largest members of a clade have greater ecological (functional) disparity, and whether the largest and smallest genera in a clade inhabit more extreme regions of ecospace. Results are surprising, demonstrating that body size and ecological disparity are broadly uncorrelated. The largest genera in animal clades share nearly identical levels of ecological disparity as do smaller genera. However, the smallest and largest animals exhibit more extreme life habits. These patterns reiterate that body size is an integral if complicated factor in how clades evolve ecological novelty. Whether body size is a driver or a passenger of such innovation remains unclear. This research has been supported by NSF grant #2322080.

title: Unraveling the Drivers and Coastal Flood Implications of Spatially Decoupled Land Subsidence at San Francisco International Airport
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Dasho, Oluwaseyi Adeola [1], Shirzaei, Manoochehr [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA; Institute for Water, Environment and Health, United Nations University, Richmond Hill, Ontario, Canada
(2) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA; Institute for Water, Environment and Health, United Nations University, Richmond Hill, Ontario, Canada
abstract:
Land subsidence at coastal airports compounds sea-level rise (SLR) to increase flood exposure, yet the subsurface processes governing spatially variable subsidence at these sites remain poorly resolved. San Francisco International Airport (SFO), built on hydraulically placed fill overlying thick, compressible Young Bay Mud (YBM), provides a representative setting to examine these processes. We use Sentinel-1 InSAR observations from 2017–2024 to resolve spatially dense vertical land motion (VLM) across SFO's runway system at 15×15 m resolution, revealing rates locally exceeding −10.0 ± 0.1 mm/yr, with the most pronounced deformation along Runway 10R/28L (−7.8 ± 0.1 mm/yr near its 10R end).

A key process-level finding, resolved along a 3.2 km geotechnical transect, is that the location of peak subsidence does not coincide with the greatest YBM thickness, indicating that additional factors beyond compressible-layer geometry shape the deformation pattern. A Geographical Detector analysis quantifies these controls: along the transect, YBM thickness (47.8%), paleoenvironmental setting (35.9%), and construction year (8.2%) jointly explain 91.9% of VLM variance, with strong nonlinear interaction between thickness and depositional environment. At the runway scale, where thickness data are unavailable, construction year emerges as the dominant proxy (18.6%). A Gibson-Lo secondary consolidation model calibrated at eleven cone penetration test sites, reproduces observed rates closely (R² = 0.98, RMSE = 0.26 mm/yr), showing that calibrated creep-rate parameters decrease systematically with fill-induced effective stress (r = −0.97), linking present-day deformation to construction-era loading history.

Comparison with 2007–2010 InSAR rates reveals a broad deceleration in subsidence, with 82% of collocated pixels slowing (median rate ratio = 0.62), consistent with ongoing secondary consolidation approaching its asymptotic limit at most sites. Despite this deceleration, projected cumulative subsidence could lower airfield surface elevations by up to 0.60 m by 2100, exceeding the projected regional SLR of 0.19 m (SSP2-4.5), substantially amplifying effective relative sea-level rise at the airfield. These results demonstrate that mechanistic consolidation modeling combined with dense InSAR monitoring is essential for disentangling the drivers of heterogeneous coastal subsidence and anticipating its long-term compounding effect on coastal flood risk at reclaimed infrastructure worldwide.

title: A Methods-Based Framework for Assessing Riparian Vegetation Health in Human-Impacted and Natural Streams Using UAS Imagery
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Apostolides, Victoria [1], Sama, Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Appalachian State University, Benson, North Carolina, USA
(2) Department of Biosystems and Agricultural Engineering, University of Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA
abstract:
Riparian vegetation is important for river health because it reduces erosion, controls runoff, regulates water temperature, and stabilizes streams. However, the southwestern United States has lost an estimated 80–95% of its riparian vegetation due to human activities such as land-use change, mining, and deforestation. Monitoring remaining vegetation is important for understanding how streams respond to disturbance, but traditional field methods can be time-consuming and limited in area. Unmanned aerial systems (UAS) provide high-resolution imagery over larger areas in less time. This study develops and evaluates a UAS-based machine-learning approach for mapping riparian land cover at a human-impacted stream and a natural reference stream in central Kentucky.

RGB imagery was collected at Camden Creek, a human-impacted stream, and Cane Run, a natural reference stream, and processed into high-resolution orthomosaics. Trees, grass, riparian grass, algae, water, sediment, shadows, and human-made features were manually outlined to create training data. Random Forest Classification (RFC) was used to classify land cover at the pixel level, with training data refined to improve classification. Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) was used to identify feature boundaries from image tiles using reference polygons and point prompts. SAM2 performance was measured using Intersection over Union (IoU), which compares predicted and manually outlined features. The Visible Atmospherically Resistant Index (VARI) was also used to compare vegetation greenness.

Results show that refining training data improved RFC class separation, while SAM2 successfully identified feature boundaries. Trees had the highest SAM2 performance (mean IoU = 0.917), followed by algae (0.855) and riparian grass (0.841). Visually similar features were more difficult to separate, likely due to similar colors, changing light conditions, and shadows. Combining SAM2 with RFC reduced pixel-level noise and produced cleaner feature boundaries, changing 14.7% of classified pixels. Similar performance between RFC and the combined classification suggests that SAM2 improved feature boundaries more than land-cover identification. VARI also showed differences in vegetation greenness, with riparian grass having the highest values.

These results show that combining UAS imagery with two machine-learning approaches can improve riparian land-cover mapping. However, RGB imagery alone may not be enough to separate vegetation types with similar colors and appearances. This approach provides a framework for future monitoring of riparian vegetation and changes associated with human disturbance, erosion, flooding, and channel change.

authors: Miller, Reese [1], Velasco, Julia Karina [2], Martinez-Melo, Alejandra [3]
affiliations: (1) Invertebrate Paleontology, Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA, USA

abstract:
The Academy of Natural Sciences (ANSP) houses a paleontology collection belonging to R.H Palmer. Through the years 1930 to 1935, he collected various echinoderms across the island country of Cuba. The geology and formation of Cuba were caused by the subduction of the north and south of Pangea in the Jurassic, forming what is now North and South America. The Caribbean plate, left above the North and South American plates, then collided with the Greater Antilles Arc, causing the west end of the plate to uplift in the late Cretaceous. Echinoderms arrived very early in the geologic timeline during the Cambrian explosion, but because Cuba formed late, most of its echinoderms date to the Eocene and onward.

The goal for the project is to make the information on the collection readily available for anyone looking for data. To inventory and rehouse them, a revision of the taxonomy had to be done because the majority of previous records were out of date. Once it’s all reorganized, the localities of each specimen need to be georeferenced and mapped, and data can be standardized for ease of use.

With numerous taxonomic changes within the collection, the number of taxa increased, along with many more orders added. Of these, multiple were completely undescribed species. Palmer visited multiple new localities across the island in its provinces and geologic formations.

title: Geological mapping and airborne geophysics in the Alabama graphite belt
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Bollen, Elizabeth [1], MacQueen, Patricia Grace [2], Whitmore, John Paul [3], VanDervoort, Dane Scott [4], Shah, Anjana K. [5], Bedrosian, Paul A. [6]
affiliations: (1) Geological Survey of Alabama, Northport, AL,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Morrison, CO,
(3) Gegological Survey of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL,
(4) Geological Survey of Alabama, Geologic Investigations Program, Tuscaloosa, AL,
(5) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(6) United States Geological Survey1 Denver Federal Center, Denver, CO,
abstract:
The Alabama graphite belt, located in east-central Alabama, potentially hosts the most geographically extensive high-grade flake graphite deposits in the conterminous Unites States. The belt is lithologically and structurally complex, containing numerous faults and folds, each of which can control graphite concentration and quality. Graphite in the belt occurs as disseminated flakes in schist, gneiss, and quartzite. However, the extent of these graphitic lithologies in the belt is poorly constrained due to a paucity of detailed geologic mapping in the region.

The Geological Survey of Alabama (GSA), in partnership with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI), has conducted two mapping projects in the Alabama graphite belt. The GSA has completed detailed geologic maps in an area that hosts past producing graphite mines (Flag Mountain and Mitchell Dam 7.5-minute quadrangles) and is completing maps in an area that is underexplored for graphite (Micaville, Newell, and Wedowee 7.5-minute quadrangles). Mapping results confirm the belt experienced prograde upper-amphibolite facies metamorphism and deformation followed by retrograde greenschist facies and concomitant deformation. Newly identified kilometer-scale isoclinal folds contain discontinuous layers of partially melted graphitic schist and gneiss that pinch and swell along strike. Detailed 1:24,000-scale mapping revealed textural evidence that suggests graphite may be concentrated in areas of anatexis and deformation.

Recent high-quality airborne geophysical surveys (electromagnetic, magnetic, and radiometric) have been flown over the Alabama graphite belt in conjunction with Earth MRI projects. Graphite-bearing units are more electromagnetically conductive and have radiometric and magnetic signatures that differ from surrounding lithologies. These data greatly assist with mapping in the region by highlighting graphitic lithologies and identifying cryptic structures that are otherwise difficult to trace due to dense vegetation cover and poor exposure. For example, several new foliation-parallel faults and late brittle faults that cross the foliation and lithologies have been identified by studying all three geophysical datasets. Additionally, these data provide important information on the locations and, in some cases, existence of major faults and other structures in the area, such as the Goodwater-Enitachopco and Alexander City faults. These maps and geophysical data will serve as valuable precompetitive data to industry and academia and will be key in deciphering the assembly of the southern Appalachian orogen.

title: Antibiotic-Resistant Fecal Bacteria in Urban Floodwaters of Charleston, SC
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Murray, Griffin [1], Vulava, Vijay M [2], Fullerton, Heather [3]
affiliations: (1) Environmental and Sustainability Studies, College of Charleston, Charleston, South Carolina, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Geosciences, College of Charleston, Charleston, South Carolina, USA
(3) Biology, College of Charleston, Charleston, South Carolina, USA
abstract: Rapid urbanization in coastal areas, combined with intense precipitation events and climate-change-driven coastal flooding, poses an existential challenge for many coastal communities. Floodwater in coastal urban areas contains nonpoint-source pollutants, but antibiotic-resistant fecal coliforms pose an additional threat to human health. In this study, floodwater samples from tidal and rainfall events were collected at multiple locations on the Charleston peninsula: some sites were affected by both tidal and rainfall flooding, and another site was affected only by tidal flooding. All sites are highly urbanized, but a green buffer surrounds the tidal flooding site. All water samples were analyzed for nutrient and trace metal contaminants, turbidity, coliforms, and E. coli . Coliforms and E. coli were also tested for antibiotic resistance to amoxicillin, ampicillin, and augmentin. Antibiotics are commonly prescribed for bacterial illnesses in humans and animals; this study aims to analyze antibiotic resistance patterns in coliforms as correlated to flood sources, land-use patterns, and chemical contaminants. Floodwater from all areas contained elevated concentrations of chemical contaminants and high counts of coliforms and E. coli . Antibiotic-resistant coliforms and E. coli were also found in all water samples. The most densely urbanized sites had the highest contamination levels, while the lone site with a green buffer had lower contamination. Coliform and E. coli concentrations correlated with rainfall, suggesting rain runoff is a primary vector for pathogen transport. Among the antibiotics tested, coliforms and E. coli were the least resistant to augmentin. Augmentin, which includes amoxicillin and clavulanic acid (a beta-lactamase inhibitor), was expected to inhibit bacterial defense mechanisms, and the data supported it. A positive correlation was observed between the percent coverage of impervious surfaces and coliform counts at all sites. Overall, the results suggest that land-use patterns increase the prevalence of antibiotic-resistant coliforms and increase the likelihood of human exposure to these potential pathogens. Climate change is expected to increase the prevalence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in floodwater generated by rainfall and tidal flooding in coastal cities like Charleston.

abstract: Sediment samples collected from small agricultural and recreational ponds surrounding a coal-fired power plant in Mississippi, USA, were evaluated to determine trace-element concentrations and contamination status. Sediments were collected from two depth intervals (2–5 and 8–12 cm) to assess vertical variations in trace-element accumulation. Following acid digestion, As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Pb, Hg, and Zn concentrations were determined by ICP-MS and evaluated using background concentrations, sediment quality guidelines, contamination factor (CF), pollution load index (PLI), geoaccumulation index (Igeo), and the Hakanson ecological risk index (RI). Samples collected north (downwind) of the facility exhibited the highest average trace-element concentrations, consistent with a potential influence of prevailing wind direction on contaminant distribution. Pollution and ecological risk indices likewise indicated substantially greater contamination at downwind locations (CF = 0.82–76.33, PLI = 0.58–9.05, Igeo = 6.5–11.5, average RI = 1,519) than at other sampling sites (CF = 0.79–18.21, PLI = 0.60–4.53, Igeo = 6.6–9.5, average RI = 164). Although additional anthropogenic and natural sources may contribute to the observed contamination patterns, the results identify localized hotspots of trace-element enrichment and ecological risk surrounding the facility. By focusing on small, privately owned agricultural and recreational ponds, an environmental setting that has received comparatively little attention, this study provides new baseline data for the southeastern United States and improves understanding of localized contaminant accumulation and potential exposure pathways in rural landscapes.

title: Petrogenetic Reconstruction of the Quad Creek Metanorite in the Eastern Beartooth Mountains, MT, USA as a Tool for Examining the Archean Evolution of the Northern Wyoming Province
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Tuttle , Larry [1], Henry, Darrell J [2], Mogk, David W [3], Mueller, Paul A [4]
affiliations: (1) Division of Natural Sciences, University of Maine at Farmington, Farmington, Maine, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, Montana State University, Bozeman, Montana, USA

abstract: The Quad Creek Metanorite (QCMN) provides a critical temporal and petrogenetic reference point for resolving the late Archean geologic history of the eastern Beartooth Mountains, northern Wyoming Province. This investigation integrates field relations, petrography, mineral chemistry, whole-rock geochemistry, and U-Pb zircon geochronology to constrain petrogenetic processes and tectonic environment responsible for the formation of QCMN. The QCMN is an undeformed km-scale plutonic body that intrudes the adjacent, volumetrically dominant gneissic granitic rocks of the 2.79-2.83 Ga Long Lake Magmatic Complex (LLMC) and exhibits sharply cross-cutting contacts and a meter-scale chilled margin. The QCMN preserves a cumulate texture and an original igneous mineral assemblage consisting of chadacrystic orthopyroxene (X Mg =0.70-0.84), oikocrystic plagioclase (An 55-65 ), biotite (X Mg =0.70-0.85) and magnetite. Quartz as well as a portion of the clino-amphibole present may represent late magmatic phases. The metamorphic overprint involves local hydration and is expressed by development of clino-amphibole (magnesio-ferri-hornblende, X Mg =0.78-0.97) along orthopyroxene-plagioclase interfaces and by partial modification of magmatic plagioclase to more sodic compositions (An 33-52 ). The highly magnesian (16-22 wt% MgO), low Ti (0.2-0.7 wt% TiO 2 ) whole-rock geochemistry of QCMN samples is consistent with the volcanic equivalent of boninites. Based on magma geothermobarometry, the QCMN parent melt separated from the mantle at conditions of ~1250-1400°C and 1.1-1.2 GPa. Multiple mineral chemical thermobarometers yield (sub)solidus (re)crystallization conditions of ~750-800°C and 0.7 GPa, conditions that are the similar to analogous thermobarometry in surrounding rocks of the LLMC. Separated zircon grains display oscillatory zoning patterns and lack discrete rim overgrowths indicating a magmatic origin. 207 Pb/ 206 Pb ages calculated for these zircons display a range of ~2.78-2.81 Ga with a weighted average age of 2.79 Ga. Field and geochronologic constraints demonstrate that the QCMN crystallized ~2.79 Ga, late in the magmatic cycle that produced the LLMC, followed by metamorphic overprinting. The boninitic whole-rock chemical affinity as well as the calc-alkaline chemical trends of the adjacent LLMC suggest that the QCMN was emplaced and metamorphosed in a setting similar to modern subduction zones, a tectonic setting previously invoked for the waning stages of the Archean in the study area.

title: Another Piece of the Laurentian Puzzle Exposed in the Grand Canyon: Subduction-Accretion of the 1.84 Ga Elves Chasm Gneiss from 1.75 to 1.73 Ga
session_title: Proterozoic Tectonics of Western Laurentia: New Perspectives on Crustal Growth, Orogenesis, Mineralization, and Intracontinental Reworking (Posters)
authors: Boryszewski, Jason R. [1], Karlstrom, Karl E. [2], Cruz, Danilo J.N. [3], Williams, Michael L. [4], Hillenbrand, Ian W. [5], Foster, David A. [6], Mako, Calvin Andrew [7]
affiliations: (1) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey, Madison, Wisconsin, USA; Department of Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(2) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,

abstract: The Middle Granite Gorge of the Grand Canyon exposes Paleoproterozoic basement tectonites that record lithospheric assembly in southwestern Laurentia. We provide new geologic mapping, structural analyses, monazite petrochronology and whole rock geochemical data for Middle Granite Gorge basement rocks, including the 1.84 Ga Elves Chasm Gneiss (the oldest rock in the Southwest) and younger ~1.75 Ga supracrustal rocks of the Granite Gorge Metamorphic Suite. We interpret the contact zone between these units as a ~ 100-m-wide shear zone of D1 generation, older than D2 shear zones recognized elsewhere in the Grand Canyon. The zone contains interleaved gneisses that are mapped in five discontinuous outcrops and includes lenses of different lithologies, asymmetric shear sense indicators and garnet/cordierite + felsic leucosome partial melting structures. The shear zone records underthrusting of the Elves Chasm tectonic block beneath rocks of the Granite Gorge Metamorphic Suite. Structurally overlying the contact zone we identify reclined F1 folds of metamorphosed turbidites which contain deformed lenses of mafic and ultramafic rocks with geochemistry similar to arc-cumulates from elsewhere in the Grand Canyon. D1 shear sense is top-to-the-south with P-T of ≥0.6 GPa and ~650°C based on metamorphic assemblages. M1 monazite, which show fabric alignment and/or record growth in strain shadows, ranges in age from 1.75 to 1.73 Ga suggesting D1 was a progressive event. The D1 Elves Chasm shear zone was folded into NE-plunging F2 regional folds during the 1.70 to 1.68 Ga Yavapai orogeny (D2). Garnet/cordierite + leucosome partial-melting structures are interpreted as the result of fluid-flux partial melting. Negative Eu anomalies and enrichment of HREEs of interleaved felsic gneisses in the shear zone also support partial melting. The new 1:24,000 digital geologic map and down-plunge projection of the Middle Granite Gorge accompany the analytical data to provide map pattern insights and support data synthesis. We interpret the D1 Elves Chasm shear zone to have originated in a forearc accretionary prism and evolved to be a major tectonic suture involving the accretion of the Elves Chasm tectonic block (an allochthonous microplate) during assembly of Proterozoic lithosphere. These interpretations support accretionary tectonic models for the Proterozoic of Southwest Laurentia that explain basement of widely varying petrogenetic origin and age across the American Southwest.

title: Land is Mostly Diffusive: What Earth Teaches Us About Planetary-Scale Landscape Evolution
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Martin, Harrison K. [1], Lamb, Michael P. [2]
affiliations: (1) Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, CA,
(2) Division of Geologic and Planetary Sciences, Caltech, Pasadena, CA,
abstract: Planetary landscapes - from mountains to river deltas - are shaped by sediment erosion, transport, and deposition. On Earth, these geomorphic processes redistribute solid mass across our planetary surface from highlands to oceans. However, there are multiple fundamentally different modes of surface transport, and the relative abundance of these different geomorphic processes - on Earth or other planets - remained unquantified. To address this question, we mapped the abundance and distribution of eight major geomorphic process domains across Earth’s surface, finding that ~75% of Earth’s land area consists of soil-mantled hillslopes and flatlands dominated by diffusive soil creep, while 0.5% is a bedrock river corridor. While other process domains (glaciers, lakes, alluvial river corridors, aeolian deserts, and bedrock hillslopes) make up only ~24% of Earth’s land area, they transport most of the sediment from continents to oceans. Process domains align with different topographic, climatic, and tectonic conditions, indicating a pathway to improve coupled global landscape, climate, and tectonic evolution models. Overall, our results reveal the distribution of the eight major geomorphic process domains across Earth's surface and highlight the spatial dominance of diffusive topography. Finally, we consider these results through the stratigraphic lens to inform comparisons with other planetary surfaces and to distinguish maps of formative historical processes from those of modern sediment transport processes.

title: The Relationship between Geographic Range, Stratigraphic Longevity, and Niche Breadth of North American Brachiopod Genera through the Late Paleozoic Ice Age
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space (Posters)
authors: Rizza, William [1], Petsios, Elizabeth [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Baylor University, Waco, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
abstract:
The Late Paleozoic Ice Age (LPIA; 362-256 Ma) is the longest and penultimate icehouse condition of the Phanerozoic Eon, characterized by global climatic shifts related to repeated glacial-interglacial cycling. In these conditions, generalist eurytopic taxa are expected to thrive, as they are tolerant of a wide variety of environmental conditions. Here, we investigate the relationships between several measures of ecological and evolutionary “success” of eurytopic taxa during the LPIA. Taxon stratigraphic longevity can be understood as one aspect of a taxon’s resistance to extinction, which is influenced by several environmental factors such as substrate composition, water depth, grain size, and thermal affinities. These characteristics together can be used to parameterize a taxon’s breadth of environmental tolerances, though their relative influence in conjunction with geographic range has yet to be fully understood. To investigate the relationship between longevity, niche environmental characteristics, and geographic range across the LPIA, we use a dataset of North American brachiopod occurrences from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB). This dataset holds over 19,000 generic-level occurrences from 408 genera. Macrostrat integration within the PBDB provided additional lithologic context of fossil occurrences.

Preliminary results show a strong correlation between genus longevity and maximum latitudinal range across the LPIA, suggesting that breadth of thermal tolerance is protective against extinction during cyclic glacial-interglacial climate change. Additionally, genera without strong substrate affinity express a longer duration on average than genera with either strict carbonate or siliciclastic affinity. Genera without a strong bathymetric affinity express a longer duration on average than genera with either shallow or deep affinity. Interestingly, genera with a fine-grain sediment affinity express a longer duration on average than genera without any affinity or a coarse-grain affinity. Ultimately, we aim to identify the strongest predictor of genus longevity, which has further implications for macroevolutionary mechanisms among brachiopods across the LPIA. Further clarification into the mechanisms that control niche behavior will subsequently create a better understanding of the mechanisms that govern macroevolution.

title: Seismic-Velocity Models and Converted Time-To-Depth Seismic Reflection Sections Provide Insights into the Eastern Arm of the North American Midcontinent Rift, Eastern Lake Superior
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Grauch, V.J.S. [1], Heller, Samuel J [2]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Evergreen, CO, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract: The ca. 1.1 Ga North American Midcontinent Rift System (MRS) is recognized as two arms of a series of elongated volcanic and sedimentary troughs with related intrusions. The western arm stretches northeastward from Kansas to central Lake Superior where it joins the eastern arm, which extends southeastward through eastern Lake Superior into southern Michigan. The MRS initiated with voluminous magmatism followed by an extensive period of clastic sedimentation and was eventually arrested by ongoing compressional events. Based on interpretations of 1980s seismic-reflection data acquired from Lake Superior and outcrops around the western lake, both arms have been interpreted as a series of superposed volcanic/sedimentary basins bounded by thrust faults that placed basalts over the youngest of the Mesoproterozoic sedimentary rocks. To better interpret seismic data for the poorly exposed eastern arm, we used legacy seismic-refraction studies to develop velocity models for converting reflection sections in two-way travel time to depth. The velocity models and resulting reflection depth sections improve the definitions of the lithology, thickness, and depth of MRS geologic units. Along the western margin of the eastern arm, upturned wedges of NE-dipping, subparallel seismic reflections flatten and collectively thicken from about 5 to 15 km to the NE. They were inferred to be the hinges of half-grabens or edges of subsiding basins composed of layered basalts that were later faulted to place older basalts over younger sedimentary rocks. Five-km-wide zones of vertically stacked, concave-down reflections near the upturned edges were interpreted as fault rollovers. Contrary to this view, however, our models indicate that the rock units under the wedges must have a different lithology and/or age than expected and that the zones of concave patterns penetrate the layered reflections rather than connect to them as rollovers would. Several alternate hypotheses are proposed: (1) intrusions or buried volcanic structures are located at the edges of basalt-filled basins with only minor thrust faulting; (2) reverse faulting here occurred much earlier than what is recorded in outcrops in the western lake; or (3) the subparallel reflections represent multiple conformable sills that intruded a pre-existing sedimentary basin. There are arguments against all these hypotheses, but the problems suggest that the tectonic history of the eastern arm is dissimilar from the western arm and warrants further study.
