title: A Geologic Nomenclature Mystery: Deciphering the Upper Devonian to Lower Mississippian Marine to Continental Transition in Northern Clearfield County, Pennsylvania
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n)
authors: Thacker, Hayden A [1], Spatz, Andrew A [2], Oest, Christopher [3]
affiliations: (1) Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Bureau of Geological Survey, Middletown, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Bureau of Geological Survey, Middletown, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Bureau of Geological Survey, Middletown, PA,
abstract:
A marine to continental transition occurs in Upper Devonian and Lower Mississippian rocks in Pennsylvania, represented by multiple rock-stratigraphic units that vary both genetically and spatially. These units include the Huntley Mountain, Rockwell, and Spechty Kopf Formations in north central, south central, and the anthracite region, respectively. Within the Allegheny Plateau, this interval is split amongst several marine shale and sandstone units.

In compiling Map 1, Berg and others (1980) note that the transition between the Huntley Mountain Formation and its marine equivalent units occurs within the Huntley 7.5-minute quadrangle, but do not provide a rock-stratigraphic term to account for this interval. New mapping by the Pennsylvania Geological Survey (PAGS) in the Huntley, The Knobs, and Devils Elbow 7.5-minute quadrangles in north central Pennsylvania aims to resolve this stratigraphic interval.

Reference sections for the Huntley Mountain Formation, Rockwell Formation, and the latest Devonian through early Mississippian marine clastics were examined to compare to the northern Clearfield County stratigraphy with “end member” examples. While elements of each end member are present in the study area, the characteristics of the stratigraphy in Clearfield County does not neatly fit within the definition of any of these lithostratigraphic units. The Clearfield County section is a basal interval of interbedded siltstone, shale, and sandstone that is commonly rippled, thin bedded, with sparse marine fossils in lags. Above this is an interval of fine-grained, olive-gray, flaggy sandstone. The lower interval is characteristic of the Oswayo Formation, however the sandier portions vary from the original Oswayo definition.

Additionally, the Oswayo Formation is often bioturbated, but little evidence of bioturbation has been observed in outcrops from Clearfield County. Further, thin grayish red mudstones bearing pedogenic features are present within the upper sandy facies. These mudstones likely represent tongues of the dominantly continental Huntley Mountain Formation. However, applying the name “Huntley Mountain” to this interval is problematic given the relative abundance of marine signatures within this section compared to “standard” sections of Huntley Mountain, which are dominantly fluvial. Potential solutions to this mapping problem include formally modifying the definition of existing stratigraphic nomenclature or utilizing MapUnitOverlayPolys (a Geologic Map Schema feature class) to delineate the extent of the transitional interval. Additional outcrop examination and borehole drilling are planned to test these potential solutions.

title: Assessing Critical Mineral Enrichment in Coal Waste Piles in Southeast Kansas
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Rosekrans, Jax [1], Gilbert, Myka [2], Oliva, Olivia [3], Schneider, Blair Benson [4]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
(3) Kansas Department of Health and Environment, Topeka, Kansas, USA
(4) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
abstract:
Between 1869 and 2016, Kansas produced 300 million tons of coal in Southeastern Kansas through underground and surface strip mining. Today, critical mineral mining is resurging in importance to facilitate the transition to renewable energy technologies and combat geopolitical competition. Developing domestic mining practices allows the United States to have a secure supply chain, reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, and avoid production bottlenecks. Recently, there has been renewed interest in the potential for mining in our region. A recent Department of Energy grant awarded to the Kansas Geological Survey (KGS) in 2022 focused on identifying areas of critical mineral enrichment within the remaining coal seams that stretch across multiple states. The second phase of this research at the KGS is to assess critical mineral enrichment in the gob piles that remain in the region. Gob piles are piles of accumulated waste - in this case, they are the accumulations of coal waste that were left behind.

A total of three trenches and three augers were collected at two gob piles within the Mined Land Wildlife Areas in southeastern Kansas. Our research is utilizing a portable XRF (X-ray fluorescence) to measure the geochemical composition of gob pile samples. XRF is an analytical technique used to determine the elemental composition of materials. X-ray energy causes electrons to transfer in and out of inner shell levels, which creates a response X-ray with a corresponding intensity peak. These intensity peaks are shown in a spectrum, which is a graphical representation of X-ray intensity peaks as a function of energy peaks. The peak energy identifies the element, and the peak height/intensity is generally indicative of its concentration.

This poster will present preliminary results of our geochemical analysis of coal waste collected within the Mined Land Wildlife Areas in southeastern Kansas. Preliminary geochemical analysis reveals potential enrichment in several critical minerals, including silica, lead, uranium, tungsten, zinc, and arsenic. The accuracy of the results collected with the pXRF will also be compared to the results of XRF collected with a new microXRF desktop analyzer that was acquired by the Kansas Geological Survey in the summer.

title: Cenozoic Growth of the Tibetan Plateau: Insights from Multi-system Thermochronometry
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Kirby, Eric [1], Furlong, Kevin P. [2], Shi, Xuhua [3], Danisik, Martin [4], Hodges, Kip [5], Kamp, Petrus J.J. [6]
affiliations: (1) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(2) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(3) Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
(4) Curtin University, Australia
(5) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
(6) University of Waikato, New Zealand
abstract:
Over the past decades, the advent and application of low temperature thermochronologic systems have led to widespread advances in our understanding of the coordinated influence of tectonic and surface processes inorogenic systems. Such studies, however, commonly rely on a single thermochronologic system and are limited to a relatively narrow range of temperature/crustal depths. Here, we show how the application of multiple thermochronometers to densely sampled age-elevation transects can provide insight into histories of mountain building.

Along the eastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, a long-standing debate exists over whether topographicmassifs that are substantially elevated above the plateau interior developed largely along upper-crustal faults or, alternatively, were built by flow and thickening in the lower crust. Conflicting interpretations of the exhumation histories of these massifs argue that that mountain building initiated in either Oligocene orMiocene time. To help resolve these questions, we collected samples from the Xuelongbao massif (5527 m elevation) along an age-elevation transect with nearly 4000 m of relief and analyzed a suite of thermochronometers spanning closure temperatures from ~60° to ~400°C. Modeling these data with a 1D finite-difference approach that considers both conductive and advective heat transport (TQTec) reveals that 1) rapid exhumation initiated in the Late Oligocene, consistent with nearby basement massifs (Wang et al., 2012) but that 2) exhumation has been sustained at rates in excess of ~500 m/Myr for nearly ~30 Ma. Sustained, rapid exhumation coincident with high relief along the plateau margin requires a sustained influx of crustal mass at depth, and we suggest that uplift reflects thickening in the deep crust beneath eastern Tibet.

title: 2026 Kirk Bryan Award: Tectonic Geomorphology and Subduction Zone Geodynamics: Insights from the Calabrian Forearc, Italy.
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Gallen, Sean F. [1], Perez Hincapie, Ana Maria [2], Ghamedi, Omar Mohammed [3], Seymour, Nikki [4], Glotzbach, Christoph [5], Stockli, Daniel F. [6], O'Sullivan, Paul [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(4) Geology, Occidental College, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(5) Geologie, Universität Tübingen, Tübingen, Germany
(6) Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(7) GeoSep Services,
abstract: Geomorphology provides an integrated record of deep Earth processes across spatial scales from individual landforms to entire plate boundaries and timescales spanning decades to millions of years. Subduction forearcs provide powerful natural laboratories because they record interactions among plate motions, mantle flow, and surface processes over millions of years. In this study, we integrate field investigation, analytical data, digital topographic analysis, and state-of-the-art modeling to explore the geodynamics of the Calabrian subduction forearc from ~30 Ma to the present. The Calabrian subduction zone is a classical retreating subduction system, with contemporary slow subduction rates of ~5 mm/yr, yet rates have been variable throughout Calabria’s retreat history across the central Mediterranean from the Oligocene to the present. A reconstruction of 30 Myr rock uplift histories from three catchments that span this narrow, ~250 km-wide plate boundary reveals that rock uplift is positively correlated with subduction velocity from 30 Ma to ~10 Ma, as the subducting slab descended through the upper mantle and draped atop the 660 km discontinuity. After ~10 Ma, this relationship is reversed; rock uplift rates and subduction velocity became inversely correlated, with uplift remaining modest during rapid rollback but accelerating dramatically after ~1.5 Ma, coincident with an order-of-magnitude decrease in subduction rate and development of slab tears along the plate margins. These results indicate that the Neogene to present forearc uplift history is primarily controlled by slab-mantle dynamics, rather than crustal processes. Analysis of fluvial topography across the forearc further resolves the spatial and temporal pattern of the ~1.5 Ma acceleration in rock uplift, revealing diachronous forearc uplift. Marine terraces along the east coast of Calabria, which are largely unaffected by surface-breaking faults, provide a detailed record of rock uplift over the past ~250 kyr. Marine terraces reveal broad anticlinal forearc uplift, with maximum rates above the northern and southern slab tears and substantially lower rates above the central slab. Flexural isostatic modeling indicates this uplift pattern primarily reflects mantle-driven geodynamic processes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that slab tearing and slab-mantle interactions have governed the long-term evolution and uplift of the Calabrian forearc, illustrating how tectonic geomorphology can illuminate geodynamic processes operating deep within subduction systems.

title: Modeling transient shallow groundwater temperature dynamics near mountain-front streams: Implications for noble gas thermometry
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: Markovich, Katie [1]
affiliations: (1) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract: Dissolved concentrations of atmospheric noble gases in groundwater are powerful environmental tracers for estimating temperature or elevation of recharge. In situations where both temperature and elevation are unknown, as is the case for mountain-front recharge, it is common to develop or assume a constant recharge temperature lapse, to break the correlation of these two variables and estimate both temperature and elevation uniquely. Markovich et al. (2022) found noble gas recharge temperatures for wells with primarily modern groundwater in the Tucson basin-fill aquifer system, which, when assuming a constant recharge temperature lapse rate from air temperature, indicated that recharge to the well was occurring 1500 m upgradient in elevation from the basin floor. They hypothesized from numerical experiments of flow and heat transport, that focused infiltration of cold snowmelt in a nearby wash could suppress recharge temperatures, producing a nonlinear recharge temperature lapse rate. However, the modeling assumed steady-state conditions, potentially over-emphasizing the temperature suppression effect of seasonal snowmelt recharge. Here, we revisit the nonlinear lapse rate concept using transient numerical experiments for a hypothetical well located near a losing stream with a pronounced snowmelt period to test whether transient and heterogeneous recharge dynamics alter the steady-state interpretation of noble gas temperatures and the elevations they imply.

title: Deflation-Deposition or Deposition-Pedogenesis Cycles Preserved within High Plains Playa-Lunette Systems
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Bowen, Mark W. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth Systems Laboratory, Minnesota State University, Mankato, Mankato, MN,
abstract:
Playa-lunette systems (PLSs), ephemeral depressional wetlands with isolated dunes along downwind margins, represent important paleoenvironmental archives for arid and semi-arid landscapes, including the High Plains of the central United States. While PLS formation is likely time and space transgressive, they have been a part of the High Plains landscape for tens of thousands of years, with some forming as long as 250,000 years ago. Previous stratigraphic investigations of PLSs throughout western Kansas identified a series of alternating light-dark bands, sometimes extending for several meters, within lunettes, while playas consist of thick clay-rich and organic-matter-rich deposits. It is hypothesized that light-dark bands in lunettes represent either incipient soil-sediment couplets or sequences of redeposited sediment deflated from playas interbedded with loess deposits. Further, banding may be related to site-specific changes in playa hydrology or may be linked to broader regional to global climate events.

To interpret stratigraphic sequences and drivers of their formation, soil-sediment cores were collected from PLSs in western Kansas. Cores were collected near playa centers and lunette windward slopes using a hydraulic coring machine. Cores were described in detail (i.e., color, structure, horizonation) and analyzed for volumetric magnetic susceptibility (MS) in 1 cm intervals, particle size distribution in 2-10 cm intervals, and stable carbon isotopes (δ13C) in 4-10 cm intervals. Age control is provided by radiocarbon analysis.

Preliminary results indicate that for two lunettes with the best-preserved light-dark bands, dark bands correspond to decreases in sand and increases in clay and carbon content while light bands are coarser with lower carbon content. Light-dark bands at either site do not closely correlate with δ13C or MS trends. At both sites there is a distinct decrease in sand in Holocene-aged deposits compared to Pleistocene-aged deposits. Light-dark bands appear to primarily correlate with the late Pleistocene, a period characterized by increased regional landscape instability, but lack of precise age control prevents confirmation that all banding does. Given the shifts in particle size and carbon content, banding is interpreted to represent shifts in sediment source to lunettes rather than deposition-pedogenesis cycles. Light bands are interpreted to represent regional loess inputs, while dark bands are interpreted as reworked deposits deflated from playa floors during dry periods. Further analysis is required to confirm these interpretations.

title: Constraining Seismic Hazard through Quaternary Geologic Mapping at Bare Mountain, Nevada
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Gross, Maya [1], Koehler, Richard D [2]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, Nevada, USA
(2) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, Nevada, USA
abstract: Bare Mountain is a seismically active mountain range bounded on its eastern flank by a normal fault system which lies within the transition zone between the Walker Lane and Basin and Range geomorphic provinces. The Bare Mountain Fault (BMF) is approximately 15-km west of the proposed nuclear waste repository at Yucca Mountain, Nevada and may present a seismic hazard to the proposed facilities. Previous studies conducted along the BMF to constrain slip rates and evaluate its potential associated hazards and risks have produced slip rate results that vary by several orders of magnitude, in some cases, which has led to remaining uncertainty in the seismic potential of the BMF. This work will reassess the depositional and slip history along the BMF with tools not previously available during previous studies (e.g. 1-m lidar and geoprocessing tools) to better characterize the fault. Presented here are new (and ongoing) Quaternary geologic mapping of Bare Mountain with emphasis on historical paleo-seismic trench site locations along the BMF. New mapping shows that preserved fault scarps are primarily observed in bedrock or pediment surfaces; only few alluvial scarps exist. A soil described in a faulted alluvial surface suggests that the surface is at least middle Pleistocene or older. These observations corroborate some previous studies that describe very slow, if any, Quaternary activity along the BMF. These new data and maps are intended to clarify both the depositional history of Quaternary surfaces and the relative seismic history of the BMF, both important for better understanding the seismic hazard and risk at the nearby proposed Yucca Mountain facility. The results will also contribute to improving regional seismic hazard models such as the USGS National Seismic Hazard Model.

title: Investigation of Welding Intensity and Deformation in the Wineglass Welded Tuff (Mazama, OR, USA) Using X-ray Computed Tomography
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: O'Donnell, Sean B. [1], Beachy, Micah [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Science and Mathematics, Cedarville University, Cedarville, OH, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Ohio University, Athens, OH, USA
abstract: Welding refers to the collective processes by which some unsolidified volcanic ash and pyroclastic deposits become compacted and solidified. During welding, pore space between pyroclasts decreases, pumice are flattened into fiamme, and ash particles sinter. Welded volcanic deposits are found worldwide, occurring in deposits spanning the full range of magma compositions. The Wineglass Welded Tuff (WWT) is one such deposit that formed during the caldera-forming eruption of Mazama (OR, USA), dated at ~7700 YBP. Rhyodacite (~71% SiO 2 ) ash, pumice, and other pyroclasts were deposited during the initial, single-vent stage of the eruption and welded together before the subsequent, caldera-forming, ring-vent stage. In order to better understand the welding and deformation processes that formed the WWT, 2D and 3D X-ray computed tomography (XCT) and field measurements were used to analyze and compare unwelded pumice and WWT fiamme. Along the caldera rim, the WWT has eutaxitic texture and is qualitatively highly welded. In deposits further downslope, the eutaxitic texture disappears and the WWT is qualitatively poorly welded. 3D XCT analysis shows decreasing clast volume, increasing clast surface area, increasing clast surface area/volume ratio, and decreasing sphericity going from unwelded pumice to caldera rim fiamme. 3D oblateness values, where a value closer to 1 indicates that the longest axis of a clast is much longer than its shortest axis, increases from an average of 0.42±0.13 to 0.69±0.16 going from unwelded pumice to caldera rim fiamme. 2D XCT analysis was performed to compare fiamme oblateness in scanned WWT samples to oblateness calculated from in situ field measurements of long and short fiamme axes from several exposed WWT deposits of varying welding intensity along the flanks of Mazama. 2D fiamme oblateness measured from scanned caldera rim WWT is nearly identical to the fiamme oblateness from in situ caldera rim WWT, which have oblateness values of 0.51±0.21 and 0.52±0.23, respectively. Fiamme oblateness from in situ WWT downslope is nearly identical to scanned unwelded pumice oblateness, both of which have much lower oblateness values of 0.35±0.21 and 0.35±0.15, respectively. XCT not only provides similar fiamme oblateness as field measurements, it also provides 3D shape and volume data that help better understand welding processes, intensity, and deformation within the WWT.

title: Geological Setting, Fluid Characteristics, and Timing of Detachment-Related IOCG Mineralization near Wickenburg, Arizona
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Riley, Matthew Kyle [1], Frieman, Ben M. [2], Monecke, Thomas [3], Reynolds, James T. [4], Courtney-Davies, Liam [5]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(4) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA; FLUID INC., Denver, Colorado, USA
(5) San Diego State University, San Diego, CA, USA; University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA
abstract:
A widely accepted definition for iron oxide copper-gold (IOCG) deposits remains enigmatic as they are principally classified by their mineralogical associations, rather than a distinct set of processes. Most well-studied IOCG deposits are located in Precambrian intracratonic settings or Mesozoic magmatic arcs. However, deposits with similar characteristics also occur in Cenozoic extensional settings, possibly representing a distinct subtype of IOCG deposits. Characterizing these occurrences is important for evaluating their relationship with other IOCG deposits, determining genetic processes, and developing predictive exploration strategies that can be applied in extensional tectonic settings regardless of age.

This study reports on the geological characteristics of detachment-related IOCG deposits near Wickenburg in west-central Arizona, integrating field mapping, sample petrography, field-emission scanning electron microscopy, fluid inclusion petrography and microthermometry, and U-Pb isotopic dating. The study area is situated along the eastern edge of the Colorado River Extensional Corridor, at the boundary between the Basin and Range and the Colorado Plateau physiographic provinces. This region experienced significant Miocene extension accommodated by large regional-scale development of detachment fault systems. Field relationships reveal strongly localized high-grade ore zones within high-angle normal faults. Fault zones contain massive accumulations of specular hematite associated with quartz veins and breccias, with locally abundant chrysocolla and malachite. These structures are laterally extensive, forming map-scale lineaments ≥3 km in strike length. The Wickenburg occurrences closely resemble other detachment-related deposits in the Colorado River Extensional Corridor but are predominantly hosted by Paleoproterozoic basement host rocks. Homogenization temperatures of fluid inclusions hosted by quartz range up to 300°C, with salinities of 9.5-21.5 wt.% NaCl equivalent. The entrapped fluids are compositionally complex brines that are distinct from ore-forming fluids in Laramide porphyry deposits and Miocene epithermal deposits in Arizona. Hematite U-Pb dating yielded mid-Miocene ages (~15-10 Ma). This suggests that mineralization was synchronous with or slightly post-dated peak extension in the Basin and Range-Colorado Plateau transition zone in central Arizona. This indicates that extensional structures along the plateau margin may be prospective for undiscovered Miocene-aged IOCG deposits. Furthermore, these results establish that a distinct subtype of IOCG deposits, formed by high-salinity basinal fluids localized along extensional faults, may be a characteristic of this environment.

title: Evolution and Interpretation of the Geomorphic Record of Earthquakes
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape
authors: Zuckerman, Malinda Grace [1], Rodriguez Padilla, Alba Mar [2], Scott, Chelsea [3], Arrowsmith, Ramon [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA
(2) Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(3) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(4) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract:
Surface-rupturing earthquakes leave a geomorphic record that serves as the foundation for fault mapping and probabilistic fault displacement hazard analyses. Over time, the record degrades as surface processes modify fault-related landforms. Both the progressive degradation of fault-related landforms and uncertainty in interpreting the remaining tectonic evidence limit our ability to reconstruct past coseismic ruptures from the modern landscape.

Landscape evolution models based on post-earthquake lidar digital elevation models from the 2019 M6.4 and M7.1 Ridgecrest earthquake sequence and 2010 M7.2 El Mayor-Cucapah ruptures suggest that fault zone morphology changes rapidly during the first century after rupture and progressively simplifies over millennial timescales, with only 20–80% of the original fault trace remaining after 10 kyr and apparent fault zone width decreasing from ~30 m to ~2 m. Older ruptures are represented in the geomorphic record by narrower fault zones and fewer preserved fault traces. We conducted a complementary regional mapping experiment that quantifies interpretation uncertainty, showing that even when fault-related landforms are well preserved, independent mappers place faults a median of 34 m from geomorphic indicators of rupture and commonly miss subtle indicators of future rupture. Together, these findings show that the geomorphic record becomes progressively less complete as time since rupture increases. Consequently, reconstructions of older surface ruptures based on human interpretation underestimate the original width, distribution of fault strands, and extent of surface faulting, with important implications for fault characterization and probabilistic fault displacement hazard analyses.

title: Salt or Fault? Preliminary Evaluation of Potential Cenozoic Deformation Along the Northern Grand Hogback Monocline, West-Central Colorado
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding (Posters)
authors: Lamont, Ellen A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
The Grand Hogback Monocline (GHM) lies at the interface between the Colorado Plateau and the Southern Rocky Mountain province in west-central Colorado. Both the Colorado Plateau and the Southern Rocky Mountains have long been assumed to be mostly tectonically quiescent, with the majority of the regional deformation having occurred during the Cretaceous Laramide orogeny. Yet, active extension associated with the northward migrating Rio Grande Rift to the east and Basin and Range extension to the west has reactivated and/or overprinted many of the local Laramide structures. Understanding more recent deformation observed at this interface is complicated, however, due to salt tectonism associated with the extrusion of Pennsylvanian age evaporite deposits at depth. Seismogenic faults, those created by tectonic stresses and reaching seismogenic depths, differ markedly from non-seismogenic faults (such as those generated by halokinesis – gravitational processes) in both their respective expected magnitude (potentially large vs. moderate-low magnitudes) and maximum potential slip rate. Tectonic- versus salt-driven deformation is frequently difficult to differentiate in practice, but their distinction is critical to assessment of seismic hazard.

In this study, we conducted a preliminary evaluation of the GHM fault north of the I-70 corridor and Colorado River near Glenwood Springs. Previous studies of the southern segment of the GHM fault, adjacent to the Carbondale evaporite collapse center, revealed evidence of numerous late Quaternary displacements >1 m that have been attributed to halokinesis. Because the evaporite deposits are suspected to thin northward, however, it is unclear if recent deformation has occurred along the northern GHM and if it is associated with the same processes. Therefore, we conducted an extensive literature review of local evaporite distribution, an assessment of regional seismicity, subsurface, and stress-state data, completed lidar mapping and field reconnaissance, and conducted morphometric analyses of drainages along the GHM. Our preliminary assessment suggests that the evaporites, though significantly thinned, likely extend the length of the northern GHM and contribute to moderate deformation observed along the hogback and adjacent pediment surfaces.

session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Simoneau, Victoria [1], Sonnenberg, Stephen [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Inherited basement structures exert a first-order control on deformation, fracture development, and fluid migration in many Rocky Mountain basins. The Spring Creek Fault system of the North Park Basin, Colorado, is a basement-rooted structure associated with structural compartmentalization, elevated fluid pressures, and significant hydrocarbon production, making it an ideal natural laboratory for evaluating the influence of inherited basement fabrics on younger brittle deformation.

This study combines detailed field-based structural mapping with planned geochronologic, seismic, and subsurface analyses to evaluate the relationship between basement deformation and fault evolution. Preliminary field investigations from basement exposures at Sheep Mountain and Delaney Butte have identified discrete structural domains characterized by dominant NW–SE-trending foliations, interpreted to represent the primary ductile basement fabric. These fabrics are locally overprinted by predominantly E–W-trending joint and fracture sets, with minor crenulation cleavage, indicating a later phase of deformation. The orientation and overprinting relationships suggest that these younger brittle structures developed during reactivation of the basement-rooted Spring Creek Fault system.

These preliminary observations suggest that inherited basement fabrics suggest that inherited basement fabrics strongly influence the localization and geometry of subsequent brittle deformation and fracture development. Ongoing work will further define structural domain boundaries, constrain the timing of deformation using U–Pb geochronology, and integrate 3D seismic interpretation with well logs, pressure data, and production data to evaluate how basement inheritance influences fracture connectivity and hydrocarbon migration pathways. Establishing these relationships will improve understanding of fault evolution, fracture network development, and reservoir compartmentalization in basement-involved Rocky Mountain basins while providing a transferable framework for predicting structurally controlled fluid migration in analogous settings.

title: Archean continental exposure captured by low-δ¹⁸O hydrothermal systems
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Zakharov, David [1], Foley, Michelle [3], Boyer, Isabelle [4], Chiaradia, Massimo [5], Bouvier, Anne-Sophie [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(2) Kola Science Center,
(3) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(4) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI,
(5) University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland
(6) ISTE, University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
abstract: Traditional reconstructions of Archean continental exposure heavily rely on indirect proxies such as zircon δ¹⁸O. Yet, because zircon δ¹⁸O values originate through the multi-stage incorporation of meteoric water into magma, they provide a far-removed record of the original surface interactions. This fundamentally limits accurate reconstruction of surface exposure due to strong geographic gradients in meteoric δ¹⁸O, and the inability to eliminate recycling of low-δ¹⁸O materials produced in absence of meteoric waters (e.g., oceanic crust). Here, we circumvent these limitations by utilizing a novel triple oxygen-isotope (Δ¹⁷O) dataset to unravel direct interaction with pristine meteoric waters. Applying this approach to the Neoarchean 2.7 Ga Keivy complex (Kola craton), we reconstruct a resilient, direct meteoric imprint with a δ¹⁸O of −18±4 ‰ across a ~2500 km 2 domain, establishing Keivy complex as the oldest documented magmatic-hydrothermal system on Earth. We couple the Δ¹⁷O values with new lithological constraints, in-situ zircon and quartz measurements to reconstruct the mechanism of the meteoric water imprint, serving as an analogue for the environments, where low-δ¹⁸O zircons are generated world-wide. The anomalously low-δ¹⁸O magmas (down to −1 ‰) were generated at 2.67 Ga, while the meteoric water-rock interaction is recorded in the slightly older cogenetic hydrothermally altered lithologies (down to −8 ‰). The extreme isotope depletion is unique for the Archean time, necessitating cold climate at high latitudes, calling for steep global thermal gradients at 2.7 Ga. Supported by a global zircon compilation, paleomagnetic constraints, and glacial records, we demonstrate that Archean continental emergence might have been extensive but remains invisible to traditional proxies unless exposure occurred at cold, high latitudes.

title: Stream Classification and Drivers of Thermal Variability Across Alaska
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Kammerdiener, Carly [1], Jenckes, Jordan [2], Hare, Danielle Kristina [3], Russo, Aeon [4], Munk, Lee Ann [5], Boutt, David [6], Gabriel, Aiden [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Alaska Anchorage, Anchorage, AK, USA
(2) University of Alaska Anchorage, Anchorage, AK, USA
(3) University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA,
(4) University of Alaska Anchorage, Anchorage, AK, USA
(5) University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Anchorage, AK, USA
(6) University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
(7) University of Alaska Anchorage, Anchorage, AK, USA
abstract: Hydrologic behavior in the arctic is being largely driven by rapid reworking in water storage as temperatures increase, leading to changes such as increased snowmelt and glacier melt, changing seasonality, formation of proglacial lakes, and loss of wetland cover. Alteration of these factors leads to changes in thermal regimes of streams and can cause decreased thermal resilience, leaving important cold-water species, such as Pacific Salmon, at risk for widespread loss of habitat. Currently, information on stream thermal regimes in Alaska has been limited due to low data coverage and quality, exacerbated by streams freezing over during winter months. To investigate spatial and temporal trends in stream thermal regimes in Alaska, filtered stream temperatures from the AKTEMP stream gauge database were paired with air temperatures from NOAA sites across Alaska. We performed yearly and long-term sinusoidal regressions for site data to show long- and short-term trends. These results were then compared against stream and watershed characteristics using a mixed-effects modeling framework. Model results identified the dominant watershed controls on stream thermal regimes and thermal sensitivity, highlighting the extensive, cascading impacts of climate change on Alaska's hydrology. Finally, a new classification scheme is proposed for stream flows in Alaska incorporating thermal regimes, watershed characteristics, and previously defined discharge regimes for Alaska. This multi-perspective approach to stream classification provides a more accurate assessment on stream variability throughout Alaska, which will be crucial in handling changes in these systems.

title: Discovering a Hidden Orogenic System: The Role of Interdisciplinary Investigations at the Mendocino Triple Junction
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Furlong, Kevin P. [1], McKenzie, Kirsty [2], Herman, Matthew William [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, CSU Bakersfield, Bakersfield, CA, USA
abstract: The Mendocino Triple Junction (MTJ) region, where the Pacific, North America, and Juan de Fuca (Gorda) plates meet is one of the most tectonically active regions on Earth, hosting more earthquakes than virtually any other location in North America. Although its importance as a region of active tectonics is well recognized, what is less well appreciated is that the region hosts one of the most active orogenic systems, involving a 'hidden' rapidly uplifting and exhuming 'mountain'. Our preliminary analyses indicate this region is uplifting (and exhuming) at rates exceeding 5 mm/yr. However, in contrast to most relatively stationary orogenic systems, the MTJ orogen migrates northward along North America with the triple junction. This results in a topographically subdued, but substantially exhumed ~50-km wide tectonic corridor that is the remnant of this orogenic process along the coast of Northern California, formed in the wake of the migrating MTJ. The evidence for this relic orogen comes from interdisciplinary studies that combine observations and modeling of thermal processes (heat flow, low-T thermochronology), lithospheric structure (seismic tomography, active/passive source seismology), active faulting, and petrology. Combining this wide range of geological and geophysical systems allows us to determine that associated with the MTJ is a migrating orogenic system comprising initial rapid burial in advance of the MTJ (Eel River Basin), a short (~ 5 million years) hiatus, and finally very rapid uplift and exhumation at rates of ~ 5+ mm/yr, driven by 8-10 km of uplift. The result is a unique orogenic system that is short-lived at any location, but over the past 15 million years has reshaped the coastal belt of Northern California. It is only through a broadly interdisciplinary study that this enigmatic orogen can be discovered and delineated.

title: Slowing the Flow: Drivers of Sediment Movement in Burned, Steep Catchments
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Lewis, Sarah [1], Robichaud, Peter [2], Sheppard, B. Scott [3], Kean, Jason W. [4], Orland, Elijah [5]
affiliations: (1) USDA Forest Service R&D, Moscow, ID, USA
(2) USDA Forest Service R&D, Moscow, ID, USA
(3) USDA Forest Service R&D, Moscow, ID, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(5) University of Maryland, Baltimore, MD, USA
abstract:
The 2022 Hermit’s Peak–Calf Canyon Fire burned approximately 140,000 ha of steep, forested terrain east of Santa Fe, New Mexico. In response, we initiated a collaborative study to evaluate the effectiveness of post‑fire mulch and seeding treatments in reducing runoff and erosion at the sub‑catchment scale (4–120 ha). These catchments drain into the Gallinas River, which is the primary drinking water source for the city of Las Vegas, New Mexico.

Starting after the fire in June 2022, three treated and four untreated control catchments were monitored for three years using a network of flow-monitoring stations and repeat measurements of ground cover, rainfall, and LiDAR. Monsoonal rainfall produced high‑intensity storms each summer. A storm in early August 2022 with 34 mm of cumulative rainfall and a peak 10-minute rainfall intensity of 110 mm hr -1 (2-yr return interval storm) triggered a large debris flow in one watershed and substantial channel erosion in several others. Sediment erosion responses decreased during the study period, even though intense, monsoon-driven rainstorms continued to occur in subsequent summers. LiDAR differencing analyses documented sediment transport primarily through alternating scour and deposition. Key factors influencing sediment mobility included catchment size, channel length and steepness, geology, rainfall amount and intensity, and time since fire.

Watershed treatments included: agricultural straw, wood shred mulch, and a native seed mix. These treatments were applied aerially across the target catchments in mid-to-late August 2022. The timing of these treatments was critical, as they were all applied after ten storms had already occurred since the fire, including the debris-flow event. Field observations and Sentinel‑2 ground cover estimates indicated greater mulch retention at higher elevations and minimal mulch deposition at lower elevations within monitored channels. Across the treated catchments, an estimated 30–35% of the area received mulch cover, whereas a target mulch coverage is closer to 60–80%. Mulch persisted in some locations at low cover levels throughout the study, and both mulch and seed treatments may have contributed to increasing vegetation cover over time, though further study would be needed to quantify the effect. However, statistical analyses showed no significant effect of mulch or vegetation cover on reducing sediment movement, likely due to the late timing and overall low coverage of the mulch treatments.

title: Structural Data Compilation of the Avalon Terrane
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Posters)
authors: Shallenberger, Zachary F [1], Pipkin, Jonese C [2], De La Calle, Reuben [3], Borsook, Ariel J [4], Arolkar, Nikhil [5], Severson, Allison R [6], Kuiper, Yvette D [7]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(4) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(5) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(6) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(7) Geology and Geologic Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
The Avalon terrane in southeastern New England is comprised of Proterozoic metamorphic and igneous rocks, Cambrian metasedimentary and volcanic rocks, Silurian–Permian granites, and Devonian-Pennsylvanian sedimentary rocks, primarily deformed during the Pennsylvanian–Permian Alleghenian Orogeny. We compiled foliation orientations from 56 USGS 1:24,000- and 1:31,680-scale geologic maps and our own data, available in StraboSpot, to define 26 structural domains and examine the deformation history of the terrane. The domains were grouped into North, Central, Southeast, and Southwest regions. In the North region, foliations in Proterozoic and Paleozoic igneous and metamorphic rocks generally dip steeply NW. In the Central region, foliations in Proterozoic metamorphic rocks dip moderately to shallowly N to NE, with prominent folds such as the Milford Antiform around Milford, MA, clearly defined. The North and Central regions are separated by a 3-km wide E-trending zone of moderately N-dipping foliation, at the latitude of Boston and north Framingham, MA. It coincides with a lineament in gravity and magnetic anomaly data, south of which Ar-Ar hornblende ages have been reset by the Alleghanian orogeny. We name this the Boston Lineament, previously interpreted as the 'Alleghanian Front’. Foliations in the Southeast region generally dip E to N in Proterozoic igneous and metamorphic rock and Cambrian to Pennsylvanian sedimentary units, with locally W- to NW-dipping regions in the Mississippian Scituate Granite. A lineament defined by NE-dipping foliations extends from Fall River to Slatersville, RI, crossing Pennsylvanian, Mississipian, and Proterozoic units and aligning with metamorphic isograds. In the Southwest region, structures in Proterozoic metamorphic rock and Permian granites are generally moderately N-dipping, alternated with tens-of-kilometer-scale fold systems such as the Lyme Dome and Mystic Basin of southeastern CT. Structures here affect Proterozoic to Permian units.

A major structural transition occurs across the Boston Lineament. North region foliations dip steeply with local strike variations, and show greater variations in orientations than foliations in domains to the south. Central, Southeast, and Southwest region foliations dip shallowly, and exhibit clear, kilometer-scale fold patterns. The changes in structures across the Boston Lineament, and cross-cutting relationships in Pennsylvanian and Permian rocks south of the lineament suggest that much of the deformation south of the lineament was a result of the Alleghanian orogeny.

title: Lacustrine Carbonate Paleoenvironmental Reconstructions: Evaluating Cleaning Methods for Dual-Clumped Isotope Analysis
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Ruby, Jillian Marie [1], Germeau, Hailey [2], Schauer, Andrew J. [3], Huntington, Katharine W. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Science, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(2) Earth and Space Science, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(3) Earth and Space Science, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(4) Earth and Space Science, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
abstract: Lacustrine carbonates facies preserve isotopic records of mineral formation temperatures, influenced by local climate, tectonics, and hydrologic conditions that can be reconstructed using δ¹³C, δ¹⁸O, and clumped isotope (Δ 47 ) thermometry. However, recent isotopic studies have shown that biological activity in lakes can produce carbonate isotopic signatures that do not reflect equilibrium water chemistry or carbonate formation temperature. Dual-clumped isotope analysis, paired Δ 47 -Δ 48 , enables tracing of these physicochemical and biologically-mediated processes driving isotopic disequilibrium in carbonate archives, making it important for paleoclimate reconstructions. Despite this potential, applying Δ 47 -Δ 48 analyses to lacustrine carbonates remains challenging because these samples commonly contain organic matter and sulfur-bearing contaminants that generate isobaric interferences at m/z 47 and m/z 48. These contaminants bias Δ 47 -Δ 48 measurements unless they are effectively removed prior to analysis. An ideal cleaning protocol removes contaminants without altering the carbonate; however, commonly used oxidative methods (e.g., H₂O₂, NaOCl, and low temperature roasting) can induce partial recrystallization or secondary carbonate formation, compromising isotopic measurements. Here we test the efficacy of oxidative cleaning methods for Δ 47 –Δ 48 analysis in carbonates, considering none have systematically studied Δ 48 . Acidic and alkaline H 2 O 2 solution treatments were performed on two carbonate standards (Merck and IAEA-C1) with known Δ 47 –Δ 48 values, distinct isotope compositions, and contain no known organic material. Thus, any change in Δ 47 –Δ 48 will be due to the applied cleaning methods. It is predicted there will be larger offsets in Δ48 than in Δ47, sourced from secondary carbonate formation (NaOCl and alkaline H 2 O 2 treatments) or carbonate dissolution and recrystallization (acidic H 2 O 2 ). Ongoing work will test for secondary carbonate formation during high pH methods stabilized with NaOH, such as alkaline H 2 O 2 and NaOCl, and compare to those treated in an N 2 atmosphere. Cleaning experiments will be replicated on lacustrine sediments from a modern lake core that contains abundant organic material. The results of this study will inform future carbonate cleaning methods for stable and clumped isotope analyses. Directly tracing physicochemical and biologically-mediated processes with dual-clumped isotope analysis will contribute to more precise and accurate measurements for paleoclimate reconstructions in lacustrine-carbonate facies.

title: 3D Printing for Field-Based Geoscience Education
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research
authors: Christie, Max [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science & Environmental Change, The University of Illinois, Urbana, Illinois, USA
abstract:
Fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printers are widely available, inexpensive, and simple to operate, making them well suited to field education.

The Lightning Strike and Dip Frisbee target a persistent problem in field mapping instruction, getting students to build maps and structural hypotheses while still in the field. The Lightning Strike plots strike and dip symbols through a stencil on a rotating window over a fixed 0-360° bezel; students set it directly from their compass measurement and trace the symbol onto their map, without a ruler or mental math for strikes over 180°. The Dip Frisbee, a 3D-printed version of a device described in Pettijohn and Potter's Paleocurrents and Basin Analysis , is a flat disk with a bubble level marking the line of strike and a shelf that rests a Brunton compass parallel to that line. This splits the strike measurement into aligning the compass on the shelf, then tilting it level, removing the twisting motion students often struggle to learn. A perpendicular line on the disk then guides the dip measurement to exactly 90° from strike, correcting a common error made when resetting the compass after reading strike. This procedure lowers the barrier to data collection and, anecdotally, students plot data throughout the day instead of at its end.

FDM printing also turns reference and research data into physical teaching objects. DEMs, freely available from national and international databases, can be processed in QGIS and printed with filament-color changes marking contour intervals, giving students a 3D model of a field area that matches their map's contours and helps them learn to read the landscape while mapping. On the research side, we used photogrammetry to capture flute casts, a sole mark formed when turbulent flow erodes a mud bed that is then capped by sand. As the mud erodes, the negative image of these features is exposed on the base of the sand bed, but the positive image is rarely seen. Extruding the 3D model lets us print that reciprocal surface, an erosional form most students would otherwise never see.

Low-cost FDM printing, paired with free or education-licensed software, lets instructors design, iterate, and widely share custom 3D tools and models that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive to develop.

title: Cyclic Microstructures in Veins Exhumed from the Seismogenic Zone: Allocyclicity of Autocyclicity?
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Fisher, Donald [1], Okamoto, Atsushi [2], Akishiba, Manato [3], Smye, Andrew [4], Hooker, John [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Department of Environmental Studies for Advanced Society, Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan
(3) Department of Environmental Studies for Advanced Society, Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan
(4) Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(5) University of the Incarnate Word, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract: Quartz vein microstructures in rocks exhumed from the seismogenic zone of subduction plate boundaries record cyclic behavior related to fluctuations in fluid pressure. These microstructures include evidence for crack seal, crack collapse, and oscillatory zoning within quartz crystals. For antitaxial crack seal veins, repeated fracturing and sealing incorporates bands and trails of phyllosilicates that seed off grains in the wall rock and become embedded in the vein when the fracture is closed by precipitation of quartz. Quartz crystals increase in grain size and develop a preferred orientation due to anistropic growth and competition within the open fluid filled fracture. Partial sealing of fractures leads to discontinuous bands, restricted to faster-growing quartz grains that form bridges that are repeatedly reestablished. Syntaxial crack seal veins are found within sandstone blocks in tectonic mélange. Fracturing occurs in the vein interior and growth of quartz from both sides traps a band of fluid inclusions. The vein consists of quartz in optical continuity with many bands of fluid inclusions perpendicular to the mélange block. Collapse is depicted by jagged films of insoluble residue that occur in veins where escape of fluid from an open fracture results in collapse and penetration of the vein relief into wall rock. Finally, oscillatory zoning, best observed in SEM-CL, occurs in quartz crystals that grow into an open fluid-filled fracture. EPMA maps depict cyclic variations in Al concentration, with high-Al zones coincident with a high density of inclusions in bands that follow the contours of euhedral faces. Experiments indicate that such variations can reflect fluctuations in fluid pressure. The fluid pressure variations near the subduction interface have been attributed to allocyclicity, where rupture of the plate interface leads to fault-valve behavior; precipitation reflects advection of an external fluid to lower pressure/temperature, or down a chemical potential gradient. Alternatively, these variations could reflect autocyclicity, where frequency of cracking events reflects the fracture toughness and the rate of restoration of fluid pressures after fracturing by quartz precipitation and fluid production. Given the ubiquity of microstructures that demonstrate cyclic variations in fluid pressure, the cause- allocyclicity vs. autocyclicity—is fundamental to our understanding of the evolution of the subduction interface at depths of seismogenesis. This presentation explores evidence for these end member explanations.

title: Exploring endocerid cephalopod stability: Did endosiphuncular deposits function as counterweights?
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Anderson, Tasha Jane [1], Peterman, David Joseph [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Orthocone cephalopods (distant relatives of squid with conical shells) were key components of Paleozoic marine ecosystems. While many orthocones had outwardly similar shell shapes, their internal features differed considerably. Endocerids were a highly successful group of orthocones, often regarded as apex predators. They were characterized by having syn vivo mineral deposits within their siphuncles (the organ responsible for regulating buoyancy). These deposits are traditionally interpreted as counterweights that offset soft-body mass, enabling horizontal swimming. However, the function of these features remains uncertain because key body proportions are rarely preserved in the fossil record, limiting the accuracy of existing reconstructions. This project works to bridge that gap by building computer reconstructions that span the full possible range of endocerid mineral deposit and soft body proportions. Our objective is to determine if any scenario can produce conditions that differ from the stable, vertical orientation of orthocones lacking deposits. To capture a wide range of morphologies, we digitally modeled shells that varied in shell expansion (taper angle), as well as siphuncle size and position. For each scenario, we computed body chamber proportions required to achieve neutral buoyancy with deposits infilling 0%, 50% and 100% of the available siphuncular volume. This procedure produced 12 models that span nearly the full range of stability, maneuverability, and tilt experienced by endocerids. Increasing apical angle, siphuncle size, and the volume of deposits produces conditions with lower stability because more mass is distributed in the apical direction. However, the most extreme scenario (a large, ventrally displaced siphuncle with 100% infill) only slightly reduces stability and tilts the shell ~10 degrees from vertical. We use the ratio of the swimming lever arm to restoring lever arm to explore whether stability was reduced enough to allow horizontal orientations with active swimming. In all cases, this lever arm ratio is lower than the modern chambered nautilus, which cannot considerably alter its orientation. These results demonstrate that endosiphuncular deposits could not have functioned as counterweights, pointing towards alternate functional or physiological explanations. We also explore these hydrostatic constraints in a hydrodynamic setting using 3D-printed, self-propelling robots. Matching mass distributions between the robots and their virtual counterparts enables the evaluation of lifelike swimming maneuvers for a broad variety of orthocones.

title: Post-Fire Debris Flows in a Changing Climate: A Case Study from the Southern Wasatch Mountains, Utah, USA
session_title: Imaging, measuring, and characterizing the Earth’s changing surface through remote sensing (Posters)
authors: Pollock, Nicholas M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA
abstract: Debris flows are hazardous natural processes that occur more frequently in wildfire-affected landscapes. With continued expansion of the wildland-urban interface, and with climate change altering both fire regimes and extreme precipitation events, the hazards associated with post-fire debris flows are expected to evolve over time. This study examines a prominent debris flow fan in the Southern Wasatch Mountains of Central Utah, USA. Pervasive charcoal throughout the debris flow deposits indicates that wildfire has played a major role in triggering debris flows throughout the recent past. The site most recently burned in September 2020 during the 6,000-acre William Fire, and we began an initial field survey in Spring 2021. After a heavy rainstorm on July 30, 2021, we revisited the site and documented a new debris flow event. Using UAV imagery collected before and after the debris flow, we constructed digital terrain models (DTMs) to characterize patterns of erosion and deposition associated with the flow. Rainfall records from nearby weather stations were used to establish an intensity-duration threshold for debris flow initiation, which we then compared against historical rainfall data and future climate projections to assess how frequently this threshold has been, and will be, exceeded. This analysis serves as a foundation for understanding how post-fire debris flow risk may change going forward. Finally, the population of nearby communities is projected to grow 300% by 2050, with much of that development pushing into the wildfire-prone foothills; we must therefore work to more fully characterize future debris flow hazards in light of a changing climate.

title: Literature vs. Museum Records: Congruence and Confidence in the Application of Species Names in Paleontology, with Examples from the Plio-Pleistocene of the Southeastern United States
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: Hendricks, Jonathan R. [1], Portell, Roger W. [2]
affiliations: (1) Milwaukee Public Museum, Milwaukee, WI, USA
(2) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, FL, USA
abstract: The diverse fossil record of Plio-Pleistocene mollusks from the southeastern United States has been systematically studied for over 200 years. The profusion of material available for examination, together with taxonomic complexity that for some species extends to the Recent, has served to defy synthesis to date, with most effort focused on describing new species or monographing individual localities, subregions, or clades. Collecting activity has greatly outpaced published taxonomic effort in this system, with many specimens in museum collections identified from stratigraphic units or places not previously reported in the literature. We explore the significance of such mismatches by evaluating literature vs. Florida Museum of Natural History (FLMNH) occurrence records for species reported by Angelo Heilprin in 1886-1887 from the banks of Florida’s Caloosahatchee River. Heilprin’s monograph has significance as first published work on Plio-Pleistocene mollusks from Florida. The species therein are ideal targets for this study because they presumably represent relatively common taxa that have had nearly 140 years available for collection and review. For each species described by Heilprin, we attained all known published taxonomic treatments and built new, full synonymies and literature-based lists of stratigraphic occurrences. We then used the digitized collections records of the FLMNH to determine the specimen-based stratigraphic occurrences of each species to evaluate if its range is largely congruent or not with literature results. Identification of stratigraphic mismatches is important for highlighting specimens that might be misidentified or alternatively significant as vouchers that document new stratigraphic occurrences. We suggest some potential best practices for confidently documenting such new occurrences in the future but also highlight that some of the fundamental tools and resources that paleontologists need for making primary identifications or recognizing misidentifications in collections remain underdeveloped and require broad community attention. This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation under grant number 2525946.

title: Two Degrees, One Discipline: Assessing the Differences Between BA and BS Geology Degrees Offered in the United States
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Klyce, Annie [1], Arney, Claire [2]
affiliations: (1) Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
abstract:
Geoscientists are essential to our evolving society and culture and, as such, understanding the training they receive is vital to addressing growing needs to meet workforce and economic demand (Mosher et al., 2021, Moss et al., 2025). While several studies are working towards understanding student interest in the geosciences and how to increase recruitment, one underlying thread is student interest in the discipline as a whole. An important factor students likely consider is the title of their degree and if their degree will be a Bachelor of the Arts or a Bachelor of Science.

We see the relevance of the distinction between Bachelor of the Arts (BA) and a Bachelor of Science (BS) degrees show up in job advertisements, graduate school applications, discussions around accreditation, and work within departments around course planning. However, with no standardized difference between a BA and a BS degree, we wondered how these degrees are distinguished from one another currently, and what pathways forward best support student recruitment, learning and success.

Here we present findings from a systematic review of Geology degrees represented by 67 programs with BA degrees and 191 programs with BS degrees within the United States. Methods from Klyce and Ryker (2023) were used to reliably categorize and quantify the courses required across different institutions. Our findings show that the “core” geology curriculum remains the same between these two degree types, including high frequency of Introductory, Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Historical Geology, and Structure courses being required. BA degrees tend to represent more room for individualized variability, and have a greater emphasis on environmental topics and process-skills (e.g. communication, presentations, grant writing). BS degrees, on the other hand, require more field work as well as cognate courses such as physics, chemistry, and calculus, which may influence graduate school admittance and preparedness. Future work by this team continues to assess the differences in degree types (BA v. BS) and degree titles (Geology v. Earth Science) and their relationship to student interest in the discipline and pursuit of a college degree.

title: Geo/Thermochronologic Records of Late Stage Mountain Building, Basin Accumulation, Magmatism, and Foreland Exhumation in The Crazy Mountains, Montana
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling (Posters)
authors: Starkey, Ainsley Lynn [1], Mackaman-Lofland, Chelsea [2], Binetti, Liliana Juliet [3], Constenius , Kurt [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Spring Hill, Tennessee, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville TN, Tennessee, USA
(3) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(4) University of Arizona, Tuscon, Arizona, USA
abstract: Paleogene sedimentary and igneous rocks preserved within the Crazy Mountains of Montana provide a unique record of the final stages of Cordilleran Mountain building, foreland basin deposition, magmatism, and subsequent landscape evolution. These preserved foreland basin deposits, comprised of both marine and nonmarine strata, are currently exposed at elevations of ~1.5–3 km and are the youngest in the North American Cordillera. Their preservation is owed to contact metamorphism associated with emplacement of the Eocene Big Timber Stock. Constraining the timing and rates of sedimentation, basin exhumation, and topographic development is essential for (1) reconstructing the transition from active orogenesis to orogenic collapse and (2) understanding the processes driving topographic evolution. This work aims to clarify the regional history of sedimentary burial, magmatic heating, and post-intrusion exhumation with low temperature thermochronology and inverse thermal history modeling. We present apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe) and apatite fission-track (AFT) thermochronology from 13 sedimentary and igneous foreland samples. Comparing ages from multiple thermochronometer systems helps to distinguish short-lived thermal perturbations associated with Big Timber Stock emplacement from longer-term heating and cooling driven by sedimentary burial, regional uplift, and exhumation. AFT ages from Paleocene (~66-56 Ma) Fort Union Formation sedimentary rocks that are generally younger than depositional ages, whereas AFT ages from the Big Timber Stock overlap its ~49–51 Ma emplacement age within analytical uncertainty. In contrast, AHe ages from the stock are younger than corresponding AFT ages and exhibit spatial patterns consistent with erosion-driven exhumation following cessation of magmatism. Thermal history models of the Fort Union Formation AFT data indicate peak post-depositional temperatures below 120°C, consistent with limited heating from sedimentary burial and/or emplacement of the Big Timber Stock. Models incorporating AFT and AHe data from the stock suggest emplacement at depths shallower than the AFT closure temperature, followed by relatively rapid cooling from ~51 to 42 Ma and slower cooling to present-day conditions. These preliminary results constrain the extent and duration of magmatic heating, provide a framework for quantifying burial and exhumation, and highlight the need to jointly evaluate magmatic and erosional processes when interpreting low-temperature thermochronology data.

title: Quantifying Geomorphic Change in Dryland Non-Perennial River Corridors
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Blakey, Bethany [1], Scamardo, Juli [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(2) Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
abstract: Non-perennial rivers in southwestern U.S. drylands face changing disturbance regimes due to development, diversions, and shifting flash flood frequency and intensity, but little is known about how these rivers adjust over time. Geomorphic heterogeneity, or variability of landforms, helps describe the form and functions of these rivers and their floodplains. It is generally understood that morphologic, anthropogenic, hydrologic, and biotic drivers contribute to geomorphic heterogeneity as they create, alter, and destroy landforms. While research has been conducted on the geomorphic heterogeneity of non-perennial dryland rivers, few have explored how geomorphic heterogeneity changes over time in response to static and dynamic drivers. We aim to answer questions regarding rates and characteristics of change in geomorphic heterogeneity across non-perennial river corridors. Geomorphic units were mapped using field-based transects and aerial imagery across 20 river corridor reaches from 2007 to 2023 in southern Utah and Arizona. To quantify changes to geomorphic heterogeneity, heterogeneity metrics adapted from landscape ecology—Shannon’s Diversity Index, Shannon’s Evenness Index, and Interspersion and Juxtaposition Index—were calculated for each reach over time. Reaches were then classified as sensitive, resistant, and resilient based on their heterogeneity trends. Potential drivers of geomorphic change, including drainage area, stream slope, grain size, and precipitation, were quantified and linear regression models were used to determine the relative importance of each potential driver for describing changes in geomorphic heterogeneity. Preliminary results show that most reaches experience no notable change in heterogeneity over time, with only a few reflecting sensitivity. We expect that the magnitude of change in geomorphic heterogeneity will correlate with valley morphology, land use practices, and vegetation characteristics more than precipitation. By quantifying geomorphic change at each reach and the relative importance of drivers, this work will develop general rules for how and why dryland non-perennial rivers adjust to disturbance, inform hazards in sensitive reaches, and identify rivers suitable for restoration projects.

title: Deep Lithospheric Structure of Ancient and Recent Continental Collision Zones: Possible Large-scale Continental Underthrusting based on Vote-Maps of Multiple Seismic Tomography Models from North Africa and Tibet
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Chan, Lung [1], Alvarez, Walter [2], Wolf, Jonathan [3]
affiliations: (1) Dept of Earth & Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA; Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
(2) Earth & Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA
(3) Earth and Marine Science, University of California, Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA, USA
abstract:
Continental collision accommodates crustal shortening through a combination of lithospheric underthrusting, crustal thickening, lateral extrusion, and lower-crustal flow, yet the relative importance of these mechanisms remains debated. We compare the deep lithospheric structure of two collisional systems—the Neoproterozoic Trans-Saharan Orogen of North Africa and the active India–Asia collision—using ‘vote maps’ that identify robust velocity anomalies consistently resolved among multiple independent seismic tomographic models.

In this study, vote maps were constructed along varying latitudes across North Africa and along several transects extending from the Indian Craton to North China. The vote maps reveal a similar lithospheric geometry in both regions despite their markedly different tectonic ages. Both regions show a high-velocity structure that can be traced from the subducting craton, dipping at approximately 45° before flattening at a depth of about 400 km. For North Africa this high-velocity body, extending eastward laterally for more than 1,500 km beneath the Trans-Saharan Belt and Saharan Metacraton, is tentatively interpreted as a preserved continental lithospheric slab emplaced during the Pan-African collision. In contrast, the underthrust slab beneath Tibet extends only about 500 km beyond the Himalayan front. While both collision zones exhibit significant lateral extrusion of tectonic slices, the dimensions of the preserved deep slabs suggest that continental underthrusting may accommodate a substantially greater proportion of crustal shortening than tectonic extrusion.

In North Africa, emplacement of the underthrust slab beneath the East Saharan Craton may have contributed to the long-term decratonization of the latter, producing the Saharan Metacraton. On the other hand, destruction of the North China Craton is generally attributed to prolonged subduction of the Pacific Plate rather than continental underthrusting, because the underthrust Indian slab beneath Tibet is comparatively limited in extent. Both decratonized regions are characterized by widespread alkaline magmatism. We hypothesize that prolonged presence of an underthrust continental slab can modify the thermal and chemical state of the overlying mantle. Radiogenic heat generated within its granitic crust can enhance mantle metasomatism and localized partial melting, leading in turn to alkaline volcanism. These observations suggest that continental underthrusting plays a fundamental role in the long-term evolution of continental collisional zones and the subsequent modification of cratonic lithosphere. The study highlights the role seismic tomography vote-maps can play in understanding continental evolution.

title: Puzzling Out Hydrograph Separation in Urban Streams
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Toran, Laura [1], Nyquist, Jonathan E. [2], Frederiks, Ryan S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA,
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, USA
abstract: Groundwater contributions to urban streams are poorly understood, particularly where impervious surfaces and storm sewer pathways can be activated differently depending on the storm event. In addition, urban streams can have a wastewater treatment component that is typically lumped in with “pre-event” or baseflow water. Thus, hydrograph separation into stormwater runoff and baseflow (groundwater plus wastewater if present) components using end member mixing is challenging in urban watersheds. We developed a method that improves hydrograph separation for urban streams because it does not require return to pre-storm conditions. We used the method to compare groundwater contributions to stormwater hydrographs in three urban streams and a nearby rural stream (130 to 165 km 2 area). Two of the urban streams had wastewater treatment plant contributions and one did not. As expected, the rural stream showed more groundwater contributions than urban streams. When the percent new fraction is plotted against peak flow (an indicator of storm size), the original method showed poor fits to logarithmic curves (R 2 0.5 to 0.7). The improved method of picking a storm endpoint showed R 2 of 0.8 or better. The urban stream with the lowest groundwater contributions was heavily channelized (hardened to prevent erosion and thus prevent interaction with the surrounding groundwater). The streams with wastewater treatment plant contributions behaved similarly to the stream without, indicating that wastewater influx did not vary during storms. Applying hydrograph separation to tributaries (10 km 2 area or less) produced poor fits (R 2 of 0.1 to 0.5) in the urban stream, indicating greater sensitivity to changes in stormwater flow paths due to anthropogenic influences. The rural stream tributaries had better fits (R 2 of 0.8 or better). This study showed that hydrograph separation can be conducted on large urban watersheds even with wastewater contributions. The resulting data could be used to calibrate groundwater models in urban watersheds and better understand groundwater road salt contributions to stream salinization.

title: Multiple origins of Pleistocene detrital carbonate beds on the northwest Greenland margin

authors: Frank, Tracy D. [1], Utterback, Elias [2], Hohensee, Josef [3], Cargill, Samantha K. [4], Jennings, Anne [5]
