abstract: In Baffin Bay, between Greenland and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago (CAA), conspicuous detrital carbonate mud-, sand-, and gravel-rich beds occur in Pleistocene strata recovered by multiple drilling projects. Widespread beds in latest Pleistocene piston cores have commonly been interpreted as basin-wide records of glacial variability. Sites U1603 and U1604 on the northwest Greenland slope, recovered during IODP Expedition 400, contain a longer record extending back to the Early Pleistocene, allowing investigation of the sedimentological processes responsible for detrital carbonate deposition through time. At these sites, deposits are predominantly mud-rich with variable sand and gravel contents and occur as isolated beds, laminae, or compound sequences with sharp or gradational contacts, ranging from massive to laminated or cross-stratified. Petrography of the coarse fraction reveals carbonate clasts with textures, Paleozoic fossils, and dolomitization styles most consistent with source regions in northern Baffin Island, Canada. Comparisons among closely spaced holes suggest that some beds have limited lateral extent. The inferred provenance implies transport of carbonate debris from the CAA to the NW Greenland margin, where it was deposited in ~1800 m water depth. Mud-only deposits could have been derived from subglacial plumes or debris-flow suspension clouds in source areas and transported across Baffin Bay, potentially producing regionally extensive deposits. In contrast, beds containing carbonate sand and gravel are more consistent with ice rafting coupled with processes capable of depositing mud-sand-gravel mixtures on the deep seafloor, including rapid settling of dense sediment aggregates or buoyancy-controlled melt-out of sediment-rich icebergs. Although internal stratification indicates that some deposits were reworked by downslope transport or bottom currents, the apparently limited lateral extent of some beds suggests that depositional processes and source-to-sink configuration may influence the stratigraphic significance of detrital carbonate deposits. Ice rafting and plume-related transport can produce deposits with different spatial distributions, potentially affecting their utility as regional stratigraphic markers.

abstract: Atmospheric warming is reducing snowpack, with uncertain effects on mountainous streamflow, a crucial water resource. Despite limited historical observations of groundwater–streamflow interactions above 2,500 m, new measurements in the Upper Colorado River headwaters indicate declining groundwater storage that is dated decades to millennia old. Here we use integrated hydrologic modelling spanning water years 2015–2021 to determine whether the loss of old-age groundwater buffers streamflow during low-snow years and whether that loss is exacerbated with warming. Results show that old-groundwater contributions to streams remain relatively steady through time, unlike the more variable contributions from young groundwater. Numerical experiments of increased surface air temperatures (+2.5 °C and +4 °C) increase rain–snow fractions and evapotranspiration and decrease runoff ratio by 2–3% per degree Celsius increase. As streamflow declines with warming, the age of groundwater supporting it gets older, in part owing to intermediate-aged (1–3 year) groundwater declining twice as fast. Simulations show that water table depths at higher elevations (>3,700 m) decline disproportionately and fail to recover even during wet years. These findings suggest altered groundwater–streamflow interactions with warming and snow loss, with implications for water resources.

title: Stable or Mobile? Sediment Effects on Divide Migration Along Strike-Slip Faults
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens (Posters)
authors: Aránguiz-Rago, Tamara [1], Duvall, Alison R [2], Morgan, Paul [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(2) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(3) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
abstract: Divides are topographic highs on hillslopes that serve as natural boundaries between neighboring drainage networks and exert a primary control on erosional, depositional, and ecological systems. Divides have been increasingly recognized as dynamic features that migrate in response to asymmetric uplift and contrasts in erosion rates across adjacent catchments. While both tectonically inactive and active landscapes document divide migration, some of the most dynamic divides occur in strike-slip fault landscapes. In these settings, lateral fault motion progressively offsets fault-crossing rivers, forcing channel lengthening until it is interrupted by river capture and subsequent river shortening. This process juxtaposes two channel segments, generating a knickpoint that propagates upstream and can induce ridgeline mobility. Because this lengthening-shortening cycle repeats as slip continues, strike-slip systems provide a natural setting for examining the conditions under which disequilibrium propagates from channels to hillslopes and ultimately to drainage divides. Here, we test whether sediment transport and deposition alter divide migration by simulating synthetic strike-slip fault landscapes expected to trigger ridge mobility. To account for the effects of sediment while maintaining comparable hillslope diffusion and bedrock erodibility, we explore a parameter space altering transport capacity. To span a range of divide mobility, from highly mobile to stable, we use fault slip rates from 0.1 to 20 mm/yr. Our results indicate that sediment cover alters topographic relief asymmetry measured on profiles parallel to the fault, and hillslope curvature along divides perpendicular to the fault. However, qualitative time-series observations do not indicate a clear sediment control over the intensity of ridge mobility across experiments. Instead, models that simulate coarse-grained sediment conditions develop long, fault-parallel rivers that prevent capture, suppressing divide migration. Together, these results indicate that sediment supply can alter how strike-slip disequilibrium is expressed in channels and hillslope relief, and that sediment grain size can control whether divides remain mobile or stable in strike-slip landscapes.

abstract:
We conducted a study investigating the morphology and structure of impactites from Barringer Crater (also known as Meteor Crater). For the study, we used optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, electron backscatter diffraction, and synchrotron microdiffraction to test samples selected from the USGS’s Meteor Crater Sample Collection. These aggregates were produced by impact-induced melting of Permian–Triassic carbonate and terrigenous sedimentary rocks and precipitated from a high-temperature cloud during the meteorite impact that formed Barringer Crater ~50,000 years ago. The particles consist of two types of glass (pristine glass and banded glass), metallic phases (taenite and troilite), skeletal olivine and dendritic pyroxene crystals, polycrystalline spherules, aggregates (detrital and partially melted lithic fragments), glassy spherules, and secondary precipitates (calcite and barite).

The results demonstrate that mafic minerals can crystallize from melts derived predominantly from sedimentary target rocks and that rapid quenching preserves disequilibrium phase assemblages. The preservation of taenite, together with skeletal olivine and dendritic pyroxene, is consistent with rapid cooling under extreme nonequilibrium conditions. Detailed examination of these components suggests that the particles largely solidified during ballistic flight, as neither the particles nor the glassy spherules show evidence of ductile deformation associated with landing. Some particles were probably ejected by impact jetting, causing their bulk compositions to be strongly influenced by millimeter-scale heterogeneity in the target bedrock. A synthesis of estimated jetting velocities and flight-path lengths suggest that complete solidification occurred very rapidly.

This study provides new insights into the phase evolution and crystallization history of impact-generated melts during ejection, flight under extreme thermal conditions, and pressure–temperature conditions associated with hypervelocity impacts on Earth and other planetary bodies.

title: Reliability of fire-wide debris-flow runout hazard assessments
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Barnhart, Katherine R. [1], Kean, Jason W. [2], Lindsay, Donald N [3], Bilderback, Eric L. [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Geologic Hazards Science Center, Denver, CO, USA

abstract: Postfire debris flows pose a hazard to human life, property, and infrastructure when they travel from steep source areas to urbanized alluvial fans or other developed areas. Existing methods for rapid (<1 week) postfire debris‐flow hazard assessment document the increase in the likelihood and size of debris flows as the magnitude of high‐intensity rain necessary to initiate debris flows increases but do not indicate the extent of downstream debris‐flow runout. Although many models for the simulation of debris‐flow motion are available, there is no established approach for using these models to delineate locations susceptible to postfire debris‐flow runout that (a) is feasible to use at the spatial scale of an entire fire; (b) is appropriate for runout onto unconfined areas; (c) reproduces observed relations between runout and rainfall intensity; and (d) characterizes inherent uncertainty in runout, even without spatiotemporally variable rainfall. We propose and evaluate a method for generating postfire debris‐flow runout hazard maps that has all the above qualities. Selection of case studies prioritized events triggered by a range of rainfall intensities, locations within and outside of southern California, and observed runout onto unconfined topography. Qualitative and quantitative assessment of performance for four events indicate that simulation results broadly match observations albeit with some discrepancies at a scale larger than structure or land parcel level (approximately 20‐m by 20‐m). The method may be used to identify potentially hazardous areas immediately following a fire and to provide approximate runout forecasts when a storm is imminent.

title: James Hutton’s (1726–1797) Theory of the Earth: Did the Messenger (Almost) Kill the Message?
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Clary, Renee M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS, USA
abstract: The year 2026 marks the tercentenary of James Hutton’s birth and a celebration of the ‘birth of modern geology’ that is attributed to Hutton’s proposals for the molten origin of granite, uniform Earth processes, and Deep Time. Hutton presented his theory in a 1788 paper and expanded it with the publication of two of four intended volumes of Theory of the Earth with Proofs and Illustrations. Scholarly response to the theory was not positive; Hutton’s friends cited his prolix writing as a reason for the negative reception. When Hutton died, his unpublished manuscript for the remaining volumes passed to his good friend, John Playfair (1758–1819). In 1802, Playfair published his own elucidation of Huttonian theory. On his death, Hutton’s manuscript passed to Lord Web Seymour and shortly afterwards to Leonard Horner, who reposited it in the Geological Society of London in 1856. The manuscript languished until it came to Archibald Geikie’s (1835–1924) attention. Geikie noted that, problematically, Hutton’s intended illustrations had not accompanied his manuscript and at least 138 pages were missing. In 1899, Geikie published Hutton’s volume III with substituted illustrations. He declared that if the manuscript had been published in Hutton’s lifetime, it would have established him as a field geologist because of his geological interpretation of the Island of Arran. In 1968, a folio with John Clerk of Eldin’s (1728–1812) drawings surfaced, containing some illustrations intended for Hutton’s manuscript. Comparison of Clerk’s drawings with Geikie’s substitutions revealed Clerk excelled at visual communication and would have furthered Huttonian theory. However, analysis of Playfair’s 1802 book, Charles Lyell’s (1797–1875) contributions, and Geikie’s 1899 edited volume demonstrate that all three men more successfully promoted Huttonian theory; without their efforts, the theory may not have readily succeeded on its original merit as presented through Hutton’s writings.

abstract:
Cretaceous to Quaternary intracontinental magmatism in the far inboard portions of the Western U.S. Cordillera formed several margin-perpendicular, northeast-trending, ~300-800 km-long belts from Montana to Texas associated with a variety of magmatic-hydrothermal mineral systems. Previous workers focusing on individual inboard magmatic belts have generally interpreted them to reflect localization of magmatism and mineralization along major crustal-scale structures associated with Proterozoic assembly of southern Laurentia and(or) Farallon slab-mantle-upper plate interactions. Here, we bring together existing datasets to present an alternative perspective that treats these inboard magmatic belts as a coherent group rather than individual features.

A new synthesis derived from geologic mapping, geochronology, geophysics, geochemistry, and summarized geologic relationships reveals the spatiotemporal patterns of magmatism within and across these inboard belts. Northeast-trending magmatic belts include the: Idaho-Montana Porphyry Belt (ca. 85-45 Ma), Yellowstone hotspot (15 Ma-present), Wyoming Mineral Belt (60-45 Ma), Colorado Mineral Belt (80-40 Ma), Jemez Lineament (40 Ma-recent), Arizona-New Mexico Laramide Porphyry Belt (75-55 Ma), and Balcones Igneous Province (85-75 Ma). Spatiotemporal patterns demonstrate that: (a) The extent of Cordilleran magmatism widened considerably into the foreland beginning in the Late Cretaceous. (b) Individual magmatic belts vary widely in timing and duration, with no clear relationship to geodynamics or location. (c) Aside from the Yellowstone hotspot, which is distinct from these other belts, no belts show coherent internal migration of magmatism on 1-10 myr timescales. (d) Although broadly associated with major structures and lithospheric boundaries, spatiotemporal correlations between mapped structures and intrusions or vents are generally weak or poorly documented.

The persistence of northeast-trending magmatic belts before and after the end-Laramide geodynamic transition is inconsistent with hypothesized preferential channeling along favorably oriented, pre-existing lithospheric structures. The lack of clear time-transgressive migration or focusing within individual belts or across the entire western U.S. is inconsistent with control by Farallon slab geometry or its interactions with the upper-plate. Instead, we hypothesize that these inboard magmatic belts reflected margin-perpendicular trends of magma generation in the deep lithosphere or upper aesthenospheric mantle, which may have been controlled by either (1) variations in melt fertility of the deep lithosphere persistent since the Proterozoic or imparted during long-lived Cordilleran subduction or (2) interactions between mantle convection and steps in the lithosphere-aesthenosphere boundary.

abstract:
Groundwater levels in the unconfined Ogallala Aquifer continue to decline in response to over-exploitation for agricultural, industrial, and domestic uses. In Texas the Ogallala is commonly referred to as the Southern High Plains Aquifer. Since 1940, the water table has declined more than 13 m in places and is found between 34 m and 130 m below the land surface today. This decline is driven by irrigation pumping to grow corn, cotton, sorghum, wheat and peanuts. This aquifer dewatering underlying the semi-arid agricultural region has caused rising salinity from evaporation and transpiration, concentrating dissolved elements toxic to humans and crops, including arsenic (As) and fluoride (F). Furthermore, As-bearing pesticides and herbicides have been used throughout southern US, representing a possible source that may have contributed to As concentrations that exceed the US EPA maximum contaminant limit (MCL) of 10 µg/L. Identifying the sources and processes concentrating As is vital to predicting the present and future quality of the remaining groundwater. My research question is: what is the contribution of irrigation return flow to As enrichment in the Ogallala aquifer? I hypothesize that As concentrations are driven by enrichment from evaporation and transpiration of groundwater in irrigation return flow. To test this hypothesis, I analyzed water chemistry and isotopic composition using bivariate plots, multivariate statistics, and stochiometric forward modeling. Preliminary analysis of 334 recently collected groundwater samples reported by the Texas Water Development Board shows toxic As concentrations in the southern part of the aquifer exceeding 50 µg/L. Mapping and principal component analysis revealed that high As concentrations correspond with near-neutral pH (7.0 - 7.3) and higher concentrations of chloride, fluoride, dissolved silica, sulfate, nitrate, and total dissolved solids. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model was utilized to explore parameters that contribute to As concentrations. The MLR suggested that evaporative enrichment from irrigation return flow (Cl, SO 4 , Na; R 2 = 0.48) contributes the most to As concentrations, followed by silicate weathering (SiO 2 , Ca, Mg; R 2 = 0.26). The co-occurrence of As with high chloride and TDS suggests enrichment of As from evaporated or transpired irrigation water.

Well sampling for water isotopes in August, 2026 will be utilized to apportion the enrichment to evaporation or transpiration with implications for irrigation practices that minimize unnecessary evaporative loss of the scarce water.

abstract:
Caves found in karst landscapes are a unique, highly oligotrophic environment. All life is limited by both nutrients and energy. As such, cave microbes are difficult to study in that the low nutrient conditions favor microbes that often resist cultivation. However, the survival strategies, novel compounds, carbon fixation, and energy-generating metabolic capabilities of these microbes are fascinating. Here we investigated the microbial communities from 3 cave systems in the Philippines. Drip and pool water samples from the Puerto Princesa Underground River, Maningning Cave, and Bangalau Cave in the Philippines were collected every 1-2 months (between 2022-2026) and analyzed for physical and chemical parameters. Water samples and drip site swabs have been collected over the past 2 years. To assess the microbial diversity and whether it is influenced by environmental parameters (e.g. temperature, pH, changes in bedrock), cave water samples were analyzed using both cultivation (on low-nutrient R2A agar) and culture-independent methods (16S rRNA barcoding). At each of the 20 sites, trace elements and other biologically relevant compounds were also analyzed, including sulfate, nitrate, Fe, Cu, and other metals.

Using principal component analysis, we found significant differences in the trace element concentrations not only between the 3 different cave systems, but also between fast- and slow-dripping sites in proximity within 2 of the caves. Thus far, we’ve been able to cultivate bacteria from 4 phyla, 16 different families, and ~20 genera, many of which are known from literature to be well-adapted cave-dwellers and were major constituents of the community based on barcoding. Preliminary molecular barcoding suggests that surfaces sampled via swab were dominated by nitrogen-cycling bacteria (Nitrospira) and archaea (Nitrosotenius), while water microbial communities were much more diverse (ex. Acinetobacter and various Burkholderiales), to name a few, and appeared to be influenced by drip rate. Additional analysis of microbial diversity with respect to trace element concentrations will be performed using the data from further microbial barcoding to investigate the exact impact of certain trace elements (e.g., Fe, Mn, Cu, etc) and physical parameters on the makeup of microbial communities. These results will allow us to deepen our understanding of how the different chemical and physical parameters in each cave drive microbial diversity.

session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: McLemore, Virginia T. [1], The Exploration Geochemistry Class of Fall 2023, [2]

abstract: Re-examination of the Zuni Mountains for critical minerals is important because of the diverse geology in the area as well as the need for critical minerals. Stream sediments, mineralized zones, mine wastes, and host rocks were sampled in the Zuni Mountains as part of the U.S. Geological Survey’s Earth MRI program. The purpose of this study is to assess the critical minerals potential of this area, as well as to train the next generation of geologists and engineers in geochemical exploration techniques. Samples were collected by a graduate-level exploration geochemistry class, taught during the fall semester of 2023. Seventeen students with varying field experience learned how to plan and execute a geochemical sampling program. The students were split into five groups to sample different areas. The class learned valuable lessons in teamwork, field safety, and the importance of good communication. Most of the exposed rocks in the Zuni Mountains consist of Proterozoic granites, pegmatites, and metavolcanic rocks, Permian sedimentary rocks, and Quaternary basalt flows. Mineral deposits in the Zuni Mountains include 1) veins and replacements in Proterozoic rocks, 2) stratabound, sedimentary-copper deposits, 3) fluorite veins, 4) episyenites (REE-Th-U metasomatic bodies), 5) high-calcium limestone, 6) volcanic cinders (scoria), 7) mica, and 8) iron deposits. Proterozoic ultramafic rocks may host nickel and platinum group elements. Total production from the district amounts to 30,000 pounds copper, 260 ounces silver, 2 ounces gold, and 416,657 short tons of fluorite from 1923 to 1965. Results indicate that areas near the stratabound, sedimentary-copper deposits have elevated copper, heavy rare earth elements (REE), vanadium, cobalt, and arsenic. Several elements correlate positively with one another and may indicate a common host deposit style, such as copper-veins (As, Bi, Cu, Sb anomalies) or mafic and ultramafic rocks (Co, Cr, Ni, V anomalies). The northern Zuni Mountains also appear to have elevated REE, probably associated with the granitic rocks and pegmatites. Quartz Hill and Copper Hill areas in central Zuni Mountains have elevated arsenic anomalies surrounding areas of known Cu-Ag veins and stratabound, sedimentary-copper deposits. While the tonnage of mineral deposits in the district may be too small to be of current economic interest, the possibility of co-producing critical minerals associated with these deposits may affect the economic viability of future exploration and production.

title: Mammoth Cave Postcards: An Archive of Social Injustice
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Clary, Renee M. [1], Owen Nagel, Athena [2], Kambesis, Patricia N. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Mississippi State University, Starkville, MS,
(3) Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, KY, USA
abstract: Once the Post Office Department permitted privately printed "Post Cards" in 1901, tourists could readily share their travels with friends and family. In 1907, the divided back, a personalized message on the left, the recipient's address on the right, ushered in the "Golden Age of Postcards," and photographic postcards emerged alongside it. The earliest known Mammoth Cave postcard dates to 1 April 1901, and Mammoth Cave postcards were designed, produced, and mailed throughout the twentieth century. Many of these cards document cave features that no longer exist, reference tour routes made impossible by changing landscapes, and illuminate the disenfranchisement of Black Americans during the Jim Crow era. Black history at Mammoth Cave long predates the postcard era. Enslaved people worked in saltpeter production in the early nineteenth century, peaking during the War of 1812. As tourism displaced mining as the cave's principal economic use, enslaved people supported that industry as cooks and hotel domestic workers; they also explored the cave, established tour routes, and guided visitors. After the Civil War, Black men continued to guide at Mammoth, the Bransford family alone producing four generations of guides. Once postcards became available, Black guides sold individual portrait cards to tourists, and postcards likewise advertise Matt Bransford's hotel for Black travelers. When Mammoth Cave was established as a National Park on 1 July 1941, Black guides were not retained, and their portrait cards abruptly disappear from the postcard record. Twentieth-century postcards thus constitute a significant sociological archive bearing directly on questions of social justice. They document that Black Americans built durable professional identities at Mammoth Cave within a Jim Crow society, and that the National Park Service extinguished those roles upon assuming stewardship of the cave.

title: Looking toward the Future: Leveraging Multiple Perspectives in Support of Geoheritage Values
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Clary, Renee M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS, USA
abstract: Societal needs drive the identification, extraction, and development of geological resources; “If we don’t grow it, we mine it.” These resources contribute to our geoheritage, along with landscapes’ scientific value, place cultural significance, and opportunities for geoeducation and geotourism that can accompany the sustainable management of our geodiversity. Founded in 2016 at the International Geological Congress in Cape Town, the International Commission on Geoheritage (ICG) determines global standards for conservation and management of geological heritage sites, building stones, and collections of scientific significance. Prior to the ICG, the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) worked with geoparks, and established the Global Geoparks Network (GGN) in 2004 to protect geological heritage while empowering local communities to develop sustainable geotourism and resource extraction. UNESCO Global Geoparks were officially recognized beginning in 2015. While these international organizations function within a global audience, numerous national and local organizations operate on smaller scales to protect and promote their local geoheritage. Geoheritage definitions vary; nations and municipalities also personalize and implement sustainable development plans tailored for their communities. After a decade of the ICG, multiple opportunities now exist to leverage local, national, and international organizations along with their expertise, skillsets, and experience. As we further define and develop the concept of geoheritage and its standards for conservation, our goals should include leveraging these multiple perspectives to create communities of geoheritage stakeholders at local, national, and international levels.

title: Preliminary assessment of new structural kinematic and thermochronologic results from the Chatham Strait fault and northern Coast Mountains Batholith: Implications for Paleogene strain transfer from the plate margin into the continental interior

authors: Gillis, Robert [1], Regan, Sean P. [2], Hofmann, Florian [3], O'Sullivan, Paul [4], Schmitz, Mark D. [5]
affiliations: (1) Division of Geological & Geophysical Surveys, Department of Natural Resources, State of Alaska, Fairbanks, AK, USA

abstract: The dextral ≥350-km-long Chatham Strait fault (CSF) in Southeast Alaska links the Queen Charlotte transform plate boundary to the eastern limit of the dextral intra-continental Denali fault system (DFS) to the north. Along its northern segment, the CSF serves as a terrane-bounding structure, placing the Intermontane terrane’s Coast Mountains Batholith (CMB) against Insular terrane rocks at a ~30° restraining bend. However, little is known about the CSF evolution, as it is nearly entirely concealed beneath the Chatham Strait and Lynn Canal, leaving important questions about its role in transferring plate boundary stress into the continental interior, terrane translation, and northern CMB exhumation unanswered. To better resolve its slip history, we collected structural kinematic and multi-method thermochronologic data at the restraining bend where the CSF exits the canal system. Fault surfaces measured in rocks adjacent to CSF strands record principally dip-slip reverse motion, implying a component of strain partitioning. Preliminary evaluation of zircon U-Pb, hornblende, biotite, and potassium feldspar 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, and apatite fission-track results from an ~1.5 km vertical transect in the upthrown CMB’s Tonalite Sill (TS) suggests nearly 700 °C of cooling from ca. 59–56 Ma of the youngest samples following incremental TS emplacement from ca. 70–59 Ma. Rapid cooling was coeval with extensional exhumation of the central and southern CMB roots linked to a change in Pacific Plate motion. We provisionally interpret a second phase of rapid cooling at ~30 Ma to record inception of CSF slip and rejuvenated CMB exhumation at the restraining bend. Thermal models suggest northern CMB exhumation persisted until about 25 Ma—a period characterized by slow cooling rates in the central and southern CMB. Inferred mid-Oligocene CSF slip corresponds with northwestward translation of the Yakutat terrane along the plate boundary to the south. We suggest that strain was transferred through the CSF onto the eastern DFS as the oceanic plateau subducted beneath the curved margin, driving of a sliver of the Insular terrane northward as much as 150 km based on previously established map relations. These results imply that CSF activity post-dated earliest DFS slip and accounts for only a fraction of its ~480 km post-middle Eocene slip budget, requiring another mechanism for concentrating strain inboard of the plate margin in the early Paleogene.

title: New Body Mass Estimates in Mammals of the Morrison Formation (Late Jurassic, North America) using Extant Analogues and Phylogenetic Comparative Methods
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology
authors: Watmore, Kristin Isabelle [1], Smith, Nathan [2], Bottjer, David J. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, ; Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Los Angeles County Natural History Museum, Los Angeles, 90008, USA
(3) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract: Estimating body mass in many Mesozoic mammal species is complicated by the, often, limited fossil material available to make estimations from. In the case of many North American, Late Jurassic mammals, the most commonly preserved elements are dentaries and teeth. As such, body mass estimates for these species must be derived from various dimensions of the dentary and dentition. Previous studies presented such estimates using linear regression models based upon datasets of extant analogues, including small-bodied metatherians and eulipotyphlans. Recent approaches to estimate unknown metrics (like body mass) of an extinct taxon have included the use of phylogenetic comparative methods, which is a significant consideration because many traits observed in a single taxon are not completely independent of their evolutionary relationships. In this case, small body size in a mammal, from a clade of small-bodied mammals, is likely not independent. Rather, it is evolutionarily influenced. Here we use phylogenetic comparative methods to 1) test the strength of the relationship between molar row length, dentary length, and dentary depth with body mass using an expanded extant dataset and 2) present updated body mass estimates for several Morrison Formation mammals, now phylogenetically informed. Previous sample size and taxon breadth of the extant dataset were increased through measurements in the LACM Mammalogy Collection. We use phylogenetic subsets for relationships of the extant dataset and time calibrated trees from the literature that include relevant Mesozoic species to attach fossil taxa. Through phylogenetic independent contrasts, we find that dentary length and dentary depth (R 2 = 0.69 and R 2 = 0.84, respectively) have a stronger relationship with body mass in our extant dataset than molar row length (R 2 = 0.61). Our phylogenetically informed body mass estimates for Morrison Formation mammals are larger than previous, non-phylogenetic estimates though are still consistent with previous findings of mass distribution within the assemblage. That is, there appear to be two mass groupings in Morrison Formation mammals, one with taxa under approximately 50 - 75 g and the other above approximately 100 g (with some variation between dimensions used for estimation). Ultimately, we highlight the influence that phylogeny has on the estimation of body mass for these taxa and the importance of accounting for phylogeny in estimates where the original body mass is unknown.

abstract: The Lower East Rift Zone (LERZ) eruption of 2018 at Kīlauea volcano was one of the most destructive on Hawaiʻi Island in recent memory. Lava flows destroyed nearly 2000 structures, isolated 9.3 square miles (24 square kilometers) of land by cutting off road access, and displaced over 5,500 people temporarily or permanently. At the end of the eruption, flows came within 230 feet (70.1 meters) of Pohoiki Boat Ramp, a critical piece of infrastructure for the lower Puna District. Sediment from eruptive fragmentation at the ocean entry and erosion of the new coastline filled the bay that housed the boat ramp, cutting off its access to the Pacific Ocean within a few days. Sediment transport modeling was conducted by the US Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC) Coastal and Hydraulics Laboratory (CHL). Modeling indicated that maintaining a navigable channel would require an initial dredge of approximately 42,000 cubic yards (32,000 cubic meters), followed by maintenance dredging of at least 5,500 cubic yards (4,200 cubic meters) three times per year. In July 2023, five years after the eruption ended, a plan to dredge the sediment and reopen the boat ramp was approved. Dredging began in July 2025 and finished that October. Three days after dredging was completed, sediment began rapidly refilling the dredged channel, once again cutting off access to the boat ramp. The University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo's Departments of Geology and Aeronautical Sciences performed several geodetic surveys using uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) and kinematic GPS (kGPS) before dredging began and after refilling occurred. Structure-from-Motion (SfM) photogrammetry was used to create high-resolution digital elevation models (DEMs) from these surveys. This study quantifies how much sediment refilled the channel and how the dredge scar has evolved over time. These results can be used to validate and inform models for future dredging projects, or help guide discussions on building a boat ramp in a new location less prone to dramatic sediment transport.

abstract: Groundwater supplies drinking water, supports agriculture and ecosystems, and is an essential freshwater resource worldwide. When we consider karst aquifers, groundwater recharge is particularly complex because of water moving through highly heterogeneous networks of fractures, conduits, and epikarst storage. Although prior research has examined cave drip responses and groundwater recharge, the combined effects of antecedent wetness, epikarst storage, and drainage behavior on subsurface flow remain underexamined. Understanding how these processes interact is crucial for improving predictions of groundwater recharge in karst aquifers. This study investigates these processes using data from Natural Bridge Caverns (NBC), a limestone karst system located in Comal County, Texas, within the contributing zone of the Trinity Aquifer and the recharge zone of the Edwards Aquifer. Using two years of daily rainfall, soil moisture, and cave drip observations, we examine how rainfall is transformed into subsurface flow and cave drip responses through the epikarst. Seasonality was examined using a data‑driven identification of wet and dry periods based on rainfall and soil‑moisture patterns. Antecedent Precipitation Index (API) was used to estimate antecedent wetness and seasonal controls on storage development. Recession analysis was used to quantify drainage behavior. Finally, an Auto-Regressive model with Exogenous inputs (ARX) was proposed to evaluate rainfall-storage-drip relationships and classify drip behaviors into distinct hydrological response types. The result indicates that incorporating soil moisture into the API better explains cave drip behavior than a rainfall-only API. The recession analysis identified three dominant drip responses, with most monitoring sites exhibiting slow drainage, suggesting substantial epikarst storage. Overall, the subsurface flow appears to be predominantly storage-driven rather than event-driven, indicating that previously stored water has a greater influence on cave drip responses than individual rainfall events. By integrating these complementary analytical approaches, this study provides a more comprehensive characterization of epikarst functioning and subsurface flow dynamics. The findings improve our understanding of groundwater recharge processes and support more effective management of vulnerable karst aquifers under changing climatic conditions.

title: Identifying robust tectonic features by mapping agreement among seismic tomography models: Quantile area maps as a tool for research on lithospheric and upper-mantle tectonics
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling (Posters)
authors: Wolf, Jonathan [1], Álvarez, Walter [2], Chain, Lung S [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Planetary Sciences, UC Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, California, USA
(2) Earth & Planetary Science, UC Berkeley,
(3) Earth & Planetary Science, UC Berkeley,
abstract:
Seismic tomography reveals velocity patterns in the lithosphere and upper mantle. However, different tomographic models commonly give incompatible images. Seismologists use a vote-map procedure to identify where deep-mantle models agree. Here we adapt it to the lithosphere and upper mantle, where tectonic questions live. Our procedure shows which features, either high-velocity or low-velocity, are seen by most or all models and can thus be used to develop a robust interpretation.

Existing vote-map procedures usually flag a fraction of cells that varies from model to model. Our procedure instead uses a tunable fixed-fraction percentile, flagging the same fraction of cells in every model at every depth; we call the result a Quantile Area Map (QAM). We sample each model, either globally or for some geographic area, down to some chosen depth. That volume is divided into cells, whose size sets the resolution of the QAM. If we are interested in high-velocity bodies, like subducted slabs, then for each depth level, we flag all the cells where the model velocity is among the highest x% (typically 30%) of all the cells at that depth, or conversely, for low-velocity bodies like hot-spot plumes, the lowest x%.

We present a map of model agreement: the value for each cell is not a shear-wave velocity but the vote, the number of models for which the velocity is either among the highest x%, or alternatively is among the lowest x%. For example, if high-velocity bodies are being studied and 5 existing shear-wave models are being considered, a vote of 0 or 1 means none of the models, or just one, place this cell among the x% fastest, a vote of 2 or 3 means the voting is about even, while a vote of 4 or 5 indicates that this cell is reliably high-velocity. Structures agreed upon in this way are robustly supported by seismic tomography, and are therefore suitable for interpretation. The QAM can then be displayed as horizontal slices at various depths, or as cross sections.

Vote maps have rarely been employed by geologists. Our QAM approach should be applicable to many tectonic studies, for example, testing the hypothesis that the West African Craton was partially emplaced beneath the Saharan Metacraton during the Neoproterozoic Panafrican Orogeny.

title: Geochemical Evolution and Mobility of Geogenic Contaminants in a Hydrothermally Mineralised Crystalline Aquifer
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Ganveer, Swati [1], Pruseth, Kamal Lochan [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, IIT Kharagpur, Kharagpur, WestBengal, India
(2) Geology and Geophysics, IIT Kharagpur, Kharagpur, WestBengal, India
abstract:
Hydrothermally mineralised crystalline aquifers are important sources of naturally occurring groundwater contamination, yet the geochemical processes governing the behaviour of multiple geogenic contaminants remain poorly understood. This study investigates the sources, release mechanisms, and transport of arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), and fluoride (F⁻) in the fractured crystalline aquifer of the Dongargarh–Kotri region, central India. Groundwater is enriched in arsenic, cadmium, and lead, whereas fluoride generally remains within drinking-water guideline limits. Petrographic and SEM–EDS analyses identify a hydrothermal assemblage of sulfide- and fluoride-bearing minerals as the primary geogenic source of these contaminants. Hydrogeochemical modelling indicates that these minerals remain thermodynamically unstable under present groundwater conditions, favouring continued contaminant release through sulfide weathering and mineral dissolution. Although the contaminants originate from a common hydrothermal source, they exhibit distinct geochemical behaviours. Arsenic transport is controlled primarily by redox reactions and limited attenuation by iron oxyhydroxides; cadmium remains highly mobile because of weak adsorption; lead mobility is moderated by carbonate complexation and secondary mineral equilibrium, whereas fluoride is governed by fluorite dissolution and calcium availability. Health risk assessment identifies arsenic as the dominant carcinogenic contaminant and, together with cadmium, as the principal non-carcinogenic hazard, particularly for children. These findings establish a source–pathway–mobility framework for understanding multi-contaminant groundwater systems and provide insights for improved groundwater quality assessment and management in hydrothermally mineralised crystalline aquifers.

Keywords: Geogenic contamination; Hydrothermal mineralisation; Crystalline aquifer; Hydrogeochemistry; Groundwater mobility

title: Beyond Wetter or Drier: Reconstructing Precipitation Regimes from River Deposits
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Plink-Bjorklund, Piret [1], Slawson, Jake [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Space and Planets, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA; School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Warming is pushing Earthʼs system towards unfamiliar climate conditions, complicating predictions of future change. Consequently, deciphering climate signals from the sedimentary record is increasingly important not only for reconstructing past environments, but also for testing climate models under extreme forcing. Future precipitation changes remain especially uncertain. In sedimentary systems, precipitation influences river discharge and sediment transport, producing deposits that may preserve information about rainfall. Here, we evaluate how fluvial deposits and trace fossils preserve changes in precipitation regimes and apply these proxies to investigate hydroclimatic responses to extreme warmth during early Paleogene global warming events (66–47.8 Ma), a period considered a possible analogue for worst-case future climates.

We compiled global terrestrial paleoclimate data and developed a multi-proxy approach integrating sedimentary proxies from river and floodplain deposits with trace fossil, paleosol, plant fossil and geochemical proxies. River sedimentary structures constrain flood intensity and discharge variability, whereas trace-fossils provide information about water-table variability. Together, these proxies constrain precipitation intermittency (seasonal and interannual variability) and intensity (rainfall rate) that are not adequately captured by proxies emphasizing mean annual conditions.

The compilation reveals a significant hydroclimate shift 3 million years before and persisted 7 million years after the Palaeocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum—the warmest period of the Cenozoic Era, suggesting that extreme warmth induces nonlinearities in the hydrological cycle’s sensitivity to temperature increase. Polar humidity and mid-latitude aridity further indicate a departure from the expected wet-gets-wetter and dry-gets-drier response. Shifts towards aridity were decoupled from mean annual precipitation and driven by seasonal and interannual precipitation distribution, such as shorter wet-season lengths and longer interannual rainfall recurrence intervals.

This work highlights the importance of considering precipitation intermittency and intensity and the potential of fluvial deposits to reveal these dimensions of past hydroclimate.

title: From a heritage of tin to a future with Lithium: Geoheritage and Community in the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscapes World Heritage site, SW Britain
session_title: Webinar 2: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives
authors: Page, Kevin Neil [1]
affiliations: (1) ProGEO, SANDFORD, CREDITON, Devon, United Kingdom; Camborne School of Mines, University of Exeter, Penrhyn, Cornwall, United Kingdom
abstract: The ancient realm of ‘Cornubia’ in SW England, including the counties of Devon and Cornwall, is dominated by an Upper Palaeozoic geology paying testament to the Variscan Orogeny, from its initiation in the Devonian through its climax in the Early Permian and to later intense post-orogenic erosion. Throughout this evolution, a variety of mineralization processes created a range of deposits, most famously hydrothermal veins with tin and copper ores. The former, in particular, have been worked for over 4,000 years, culminating in the intense mining of the late 18 th and 19 th centuries. By the beginning of the 20th Century, however, with the opening up of large deposits on other continents, Cornubian tin-mining was in catastrophic decline and by the later 20th century, only one mine was in - intermittent – production. Driving the 18 th to 19 th century mining boom was the development of industrialization, leading to increasing sophistication of mining techniques and machinery and major cultural changes. This included the creation of an expertise amongst Cornish miners, who, as the local mines closed, migrated globally to wherever their skills were needed, taking their cultural traditions with them. Not surprisingly, the pivotal role of the region in the history of mining was celebrated in 2006 with listing as the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscapes World Heritage Site. In the virtual absence of the former mining industry – excepting ongoing China Clay working - the economy of the region is now dominated by tourism. However, with the change to more sustainable industries, mining is making a comeback, especially as both hydrothermal systems and the minerals associated with the China Clay may contain lithium. And with this renewed interest in mining a wide range of mining related jobs, including technical and geological are now once more available across the region. This renewed interest is also beginning to reflect on the much-neglected geological heritage of the region, and a number of community and industry linked projects to recover aspects of this heritage are beginning to develop. Crucially, these new projects provide a link between a culturally still very significant historical, mining legacy and a future in which once more mining is fundamental, but a clean and sustainable way, without the historical disbenefits of pollution and contamination.

title: North American Plants and Mammals Tracked Climate With High Fidelity, but Mammals Fell Behind Under Anthropogenic Pressure
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Gibert, Corentin [1], McGuire, Jenny L. [2], Shipley, Benjamin R. [3], Schap, Julia A. [4], Wang, Yue [5], Pineda-Munoz, Silvia [6]
affiliations: (1) Evo-Eco-Paleo, University of Lille, Lille, France; School of Biological Sciences, Georgia Tech, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
(2) Schools of Biological Sciences and Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Tech, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) School of Biological Sciences, Monash University, Melbourne, Australia; School of Biological Sciences, Georgia Tech, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
(4) School of Biological Sciences, Georgia Tech, Atlanta, GA, USA; Department of Integrative Biology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(5) School of Ecology, Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen, China
(6) Amazon Conservation Association, Washington, DC, USA
abstract: The relationship between climate and species distributions is often described as complex, partly because many species do not appear to track climate in directions predicted by niche and distribution models. However, large-scale climate tracking is a long-term process that may be obscured at ecological timescales and increasingly constrained by human land use. Here, we reconstruct the realized climatic niches of 16 plant taxa and 45 mammal species across North America from the end of the last deglaciation (11,700 years BP) to the present, introducing climate fidelity as a metric of the temporal stability of climatic niches across changing climates and human land-use regimes. Across all timescales, plants exhibit higher climate fidelity than mammals, despite their limited dispersal ability. During the early Holocene, when climate change was rapid but anthropogenic pressure was minimal, mammalian climate fidelity was 11% lower than that of plants, with 42% of mammal species having lower climate fidelity. Nonetheless, at this time, some large mammals tracked climate as effectively as plants, whereas small mammals already exhibited lower climate fidelity. As human land use intensified after European arrival, mammalian climatic niches shifted dramatically, experiencing a 17% loss of climate fidelity, decoupling from climatic gradients, and instead aligning with patterns of land-use intensity. Large mammals were preferentially extirpated from warm, humid climates now dominated by cities and croplands and displaced toward colder, drier, and montane regions, while many small mammals expanded into anthropogenic landscapes. In contrast, plant climatic niches remained largely structured by latitude and climate throughout the Holocene, with comparatively weak responses to land-use change. At the community scale, these processes erased long-standing latitudinal gradients of mammalian climate fidelity, replacing them with spatial patterns driven by human modification of the landscape. By integrating deep-time fossil records with modern occurrences, climate fidelity provides a framework for identifying taxa and communities most vulnerable to ongoing climate change, particularly species that historically tracked climate well but are now constrained by anthropogenic barriers. This approach highlights how human land use has fundamentally altered the capacity of mammals, more than plants, to respond to a rapidly changing climate.

title: Underground Thermal Energy Storage in Mines - Results from an in-situ Field Scale Test
session_title: Hydrogeology of Geothermal Resources: From Shallow Systems to Deep Reservoirs
authors: Scheytt, Traugott J. [1], Arab, Alireza [2], Grab, Thomas [3]
affiliations: (1) Chair of Hydrogeology and Hydrochemistry, TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Freiberg, Germany; Freiberg Center for Water Research, TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Freiberg, Germany

(3) Lehrstuhl für Technische Thermodynamik, TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Freiberg, Germany; Freiberg Center for Water Research, TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Freiberg, Germany
abstract:
Flooded and partially flooded mine galleries represent a largely untapped class of underground thermal energy storage (Mine Thermal Energy Storage - MTES) reservoirs. This study presents a long-term field demonstration of a fully equipped MTES test-reservoir at the Reiche Zeche underground Research and Teaching mine of TU Bergakademie Freiberg in Germany / Europe. Three controlled heating–cooling cycles with a combined duration of 504 days were carried out and monitored through dense thermometry, tracer testing, and hydrochemical and materials analyses. A total of 38.0 MWh of heat was supplied.

Approximately 90 % of the stored energy resided in the surrounding gneiss, confirming that the rock mass functioned as the principal store while the basin water acted as a rapid carrier and exchanger interface. The rock warmed by 10.1 K at 1.8 m depth after the hottest cycle, consistent with a conduction-dominated regime. Tracer dilution determined a throughflow of 79 L h⁻¹ with a residence time of about 10.5 days, corresponding to an advective heat-loss coefficient of 0.092 kW K⁻¹. Warm phases triggered Fe(II) oxidation and precipitation of Fe-oxyhydroxides that dominated exchanger fouling, while hydrophobic coatings limited conductance losses to roughly 18 %. Integrated field, laboratory, and numerical analyses showed that hydraulic isolation and oxygen control were the main levers for improving efficiency. The results demonstrate reproducible MTES operation under mine conditions and show that advective loss and exchanger fouling govern recoverability. The derived metrics provide a robust basis for MTES design in similar underground settings and highlight the potential of post-mining infrastructure to contribute to the energy storage.

title: Taking the Long View: Geomorphic Effects of Instream Wood 38 Years After the Great Yellowstone Fire
session_title: Understanding and Facilitating River Corridor Resilience to Wildfire
authors: Wohl, Ellen [1], Marshall, Anna [2], Triantafillou, Shayla [3], Larkin, Katie [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geography and Sustainability, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: Wildfire can strongly influence the recruitment, mobility, and geomorphic function of large wood in mountain streams, yet long-term responses of instream wood following fire remain poorly constrained. Wildfires in the Yellowstone region during 1988 collectively formed the largest fire recorded in the history of the national park and changed the trajectory of fire management strategies. Jones and Crow Creek are two parallel catchments on the eastern boundary of the park with comparable catchment morphology and flow regimes. Jones Creek burned in the 1988 fires and Crow Creek did not. Michael Young measured large wood in both creeks during 1990. In 1999, Zelt and Wohl resampled large wood and channel morphology in these creeks. The unburned catchment had smaller channel width and more closely spaced, small accumulations of wood, suggesting greater wood mobility in the burned catchment. We repeated these surveys in summer 2026 to evaluate nearly four decades of post-fire recovery. We found minimal changes in bankfull channel width in the unburned catchment since 1999 and a slight increase in the burned catchment. Wood load in the unburned catchment increased slightly from 1990 to 1999 and then returned to 1990 values in 2026. Wood load in the burned catchment was consistently lower than the unburned catchment in all sample years, rising slightly in 1999 and then declining to half by 2026. Wood pieces in the burned catchment also create fewer geomorphic effects: about 15% of all pieces surveyed in both catchments had rootwads, but 38% of pieces in the unburned catchment had associated erosional or depositional features whereas only 17% of pieces in the burned catchment created geomorphic effects. Similarly, 11.6% of the wood pieces in the unburned catchment had associated fine sediment deposits in 1999, whereas only 7.5% of pieces in the burned catchment had deposits. Very slow forest regrowth in the burned catchment indicates minimal potential wood recruitment to the stream corridor for the next few decades, suggesting that recovery of instream wood loads and geomorphic effects will require more than a century.

abstract:
Zircons contain geochemical signals that are distinctive of their origin in igneous (I) and sedimentary (S) protoliths, in the latter case potentially revealing records of ancient surface environments. Trace elements in detrital zircons as old as ~4.4 Ga have been investigated by increasingly sophisticated methods, from correlation diagrams to machine learning (ML) discrimination methods. The latter studies broadly agree that >4 Ga Jack Hills (JH) zircons contain roughly equal proportions of I and S sources. Using a domain-adversarial neural network approach that recognizes shifts in trace element availability over geologic time, we found a similar distribution in a database of 215 JH zircon analyses. To assess the veracity of this approach, we examined the primary inclusion mineralogy (i.e., those isolated from both cracks and diffuse regions indicative of fluid interactions) of 85 of those grains (43 S- and 42 I-types as designated by ML) using SEM/EDAX and CL methods for identification of minerals and their proximity to alteration features.

Most (77 to 91%) polished surfaces examined did not contain primary minerals diagnostic of magmatic origin (i.e., lacked key phases such as muscovite in S-type and hornblende in I-type ML designated zircons). For those that did, we found Archean (<4 Ga) grains predicted by ML as I-type to contain 33% I- and 67% S-type inclusions whereas Hadean (>4 Ga) I-type predicted grains contain 67% I- and 33% S-type inclusions. Archean zircons predicted as S-type contain 100% S- and 0% I-type inclusions whereas Hadean S-types contain 50% of both types. By type, there is an overall 50% and 80% agreement for I- and S-types, respectively. This comparison of ML magma type classification with observed inclusion assemblages in Hadean grains suggests both similar abundances of I- and S-type protoliths as previously reported and a path for improved ML performance by examining the algorithmic basis of incorrect designations. We can increase the fraction of grains that yield identified inclusions by exposing deeper surfaces for SEM/EDAX analysis or utilizing Raman confocal imaging. Overall, these observations support the view that primary continental crust formation and sediment-recycling/assimilation was occurring on Earth in the presence of water as early as ca. 4.3 Ga.

title: Impacts of Biochar on Metal Uptake and Tl–Pb Stable Isotope Fractionation in Brassica juncea (Brown Mustard)

authors: Humbarger, Mel [1], Rader, Shelby True [2], Mastalerz, Maria [3], Sauer, Peter E. [4], Liu, Bei [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, Indiana, USA

abstract:
Remediating metal-contaminated soils is often disruptive and resource-intensive. However, application of biochar, an adsorbent derived from organic waste, and phytoremediation, which uses plants to stabilize and/or extract metals via accumulation in their tissues, are low-impact strategies that have been shown to maximize metal removal from soils, particularly when combined. Metal isotopic signatures within plant tissue have also shown promise to serve as a provenance tool, allowing for identification of natural or anthropogenic metal sources through passive and more cost-effective plant extraction. However, outcomes vary among types of biochar, soils, and metals. Thus, optimizing this metal remediation strategy requires better constraints on how biochar properties like reactivity, surface area, porosity, and composition affect metal behavior in the critical zone.

To test the effects of biochar properties on soil metal mobility and plant uptake, Brassica juncea (brown mustard) was grown using different biochar amendments (hardwood 1 (HW1), hardwood 2 (HW2), rice hull (RH), and almond shell (AS) in two trials with biochar added at ~1.5 and ~3 wt.%, respectively. Prior to seeding, amended soils were spiked with a 100 mg/kg mixture of 29 metal(loid)s. Once mature, plants were harvested, separated by organ (e.g., roots, stems, leaves, etc.), dried, and digested in preparation for metal concentrations and thallium (Tl) and lead (Pb) isotopic characterization. Biochar characterization revealed varying degrees of carbonization (reflectance ranged from 1.49% in AS (most reactive) to 5.06% in HW1 (least reactive), surface area (from <2 m²/g (HW2, AS) to >3.5 2 m²/g (HW1)), oxygenated functional group content (only measurable FTIR signals for HW1 and HW2), and trace metal content (e.g., arsenic (As) concentrations ranged from 60 mg/kg (HW2) to 3,500 mg/kg (HW2)) among other physical characteristics, all of which could impact metal bioavailability, translocation potential, and isotopic signatures. Ongoing concentration and lead (Pb) and thallium (Tl) isotopic analysis aims to evaluate the relationship between biochar properties and plant-based signatures and whether property-specific patterns depend on biochar application rate. These results will inform more strategic implementation of biochar-enhanced phytoremediation to minimize metal entry into food chains and potentially determine metal sources at the same time.

abstract: Impact craters provide the foundation for crater-based planetary surface chronology across planetary bodies. While proximal secondary craters commonly display elongated and asymmetric morphologies, distal secondaries can resemble primary craters, increasing the risk of their misclassification and introducing further uncertainty into surface age estimates derived from crater populations. Here, we use S-band (12.6 cm wavelength) radar observations acquired by the Miniature Radio Frequency (Mini-RF) instrument aboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) to identify and investigate distal secondary craters associated with Tycho. Previous studies (Wells et al., 2010, Rivera-Valentín et al., 2024) noted that some small craters near the lunar south pole exhibit radar-bright, asymmetric ejecta deposits that extend in the downrange direction from Tycho. We investigate the origin of these distinctive radar signatures and their implications for ejecta emplacement processes. S-band radar data is sensitive to cm-to-dm-scale scatterers within the upper ~meter of the lunar regolith, enabling measurements of surface and shallow subsurface roughness as well as dielectric contrasts. The returned polarization measurements are used to derive the Stokes parameters which describe the total backscatter power (S1), linear polarizations (S2 and S3) and circular polarization (S4). These parameters also permit calculation of m-χ decomposition products that elucidate different scattering behaviors at the radar wavelength into a three components product. Using these observations, we identified 663 secondary craters along Tycho’s rays that meet the criteria of having radar bright, asymmetric ejecta deposits that align with the downrange direction from Tycho. We also evaluated complementary morphometric evidence and find that although many of these craters appear in linear chains or clustered groups, others are isolated and would otherwise be difficult to recognize as secondaries based on morphology and morphometry alone. The radar-bright asymmetric ejecta generally aligns with ray orientations, although ~10% of craters show ejecta patterns likely influenced by local topography. Radar backscatter from the ejecta is enhanced in depolarized and even-bounce scattering, indicative of rough terrains. Inspection of NAC and ShadowCam images, though, indicate little to no contribution by meter-scale surface boulders. As such, these results suggest that the radar scattering behavior of the ejecta may be dominated by subsurface structure or small-scale roughness below the image resolution.

title: Development of the Regional Carboniferous Unconformity, Paganzo Basin, Argentina: Insights from Multichronometer Thermal History Modeling
session_title: Pre–Neogene Tectonic evolution of South America
authors: Biddle, Julian [1], Fosdick, Julie [2], Sinoplu, Ozan [3], Milanesio, Delfina [4], Otamendi, Juan [5], Armas, Paula [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Connecticut, CT, USA

abstract:
Basement unconformity surfaces beneath younger sedimentary strata are major geologic features that represent erosion driven by diverse tectonic, geodynamic, and/or climatic processes. Thermochronology methods, which can measure the timing and magnitude of crustal exhumation, are useful to evaluate the effect of differing processes on erosion and unconformity development. In northwest Argentina, a regional Carboniferous unconformity separates the Carboniferous–Permian Paganzo Group sedimentary units from diverse Proterozoic to Late Paleozoic crystalline and sedimentary rocks. Previous low-temperature thermochronology work in individual localities has associated this unconformity development to exhumation produced by tectonic uplift and the <2 km glacial erosion observed in the Paganzo Group during the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. However, there is limited spatial coverage of thermochronologic methods sensitive to >120 °C (e.g., zircon (U-Th)/He and zircon fission-track thermochronology) across the region, and the timing of formation and processes responsible for the Paganzo unconformity across the entire basin remain unclear.

To resolve the timing and formation of the Carboniferous unconformity, we present novel monazite (U-Th)/He ages along with conventional zircon fission-track, and zircon and apatite (U-Th)/He datasets, representing a temperature sensitivity range of ~60–270 °C in the upper crust. Sample localities targeted crystalline basement rocks underlying Carboniferous deposits at 13 locations across the Paganzo Basin, including plutonic rocks from the Ordovician Famatinian arc, Precambrian metamorphic rocks of the Cuyania terrane, and metamorphosed Cambrian Gondwana margin rocks. Monazite (U-Th)/He dates from range from 426–333 Ma, whereas ZFT ages yielded a narrower range from 332–298 Ma. Zircon (U-Th)/He dates range from 378–245 Ma. Apatite (U-Th)/He results yield a broad spread of dates ca. 209–9 Ma, with the majority younger than 100 Ma due to later tectonic activity.

Inverse thermal history modeling with the thermochronology datasets, using constraints from the timing of incipient Paganzo sedimentation in the early Carboniferous, points to rapid rock cooling from above 300 °C between 380–320 Ma across the Paganzo Basin. Modeled time-temperature results indicate rapid cooling rates of ~2.5–18.5 °C/Myr and substantial basement exhumation of ~4.9–12.6 km across the study region. The magnitude of exhumation is incompatible with purely glacial erosion, and is best explained by tectonically driven rock uplift and erosion enhanced by local denudation following the waning of the regional Ordovician–Devonian Famatinian orogeny.

abstract:
Social media platforms are a primary venue for sharing new scientific findings, not only with other scientists, but also with policy makers, practitioners, and the general public. These platforms allow scientists to expand the reach and impact of their work, engage in discourse regarding new discoveries, and build a network of peers. But where do you begin? As the social media landscape continues to evolve, it can be confusing to know where to post and how to create engaging content.

Using real examples, this presentation will give an overview of best practices for using social media to promote your research. The session will report on the overall benefits and impact of social media promotion, provide tips for identifying and avoiding scientific jargon, and demonstrate how to create an engaging post about your work across a variety of platforms.

title: Seasonal and Event-Based Groundwater Dynamics of a Sandy Beach Barrier in Atlantic Canada
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Hill, Audrey Marie Rivera [1], Hall, Sarah [2], Mulligan, Ryan [3], Kurylyk, Barret L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering and Centre for Water Resources Studies, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
(2) Department of Civil Engineering, Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada
(3) Department of Civil Engineering, Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada

abstract:
Coastal groundwater environments are dynamic systems with hydraulic and salinity regimes that are strongly influenced by both terrestrial and oceanic processes. Beaches are important coastal landforms of cultural, ecological, and recreational significance. Beach groundwater systems help to sustain beach ecosystems but can be salinized by overextraction, coastal storms, and sea-level rise. The overall goal of this study is to characterize beach groundwater response to atmospheric and oceanic forcing through paired field investigations and numerical modelling of a beach groundwater observatory in a high-energy environment.

Martinique Beach is a 3.5-km long, sandy beach barrier along the eastern coast of Nova Scotia, Canada with high-energy waves in the foreshore and calm, estuarine waters in the backshore estuary. In August 2025, we launched an ongoing field campaign at Martinique Beach to understand storm-driven, tidal, and seasonal dynamics of the beach groundwater system. Four piezometers were installed in a cross-shore transect from the intertidal zone to the backshore estuary and instrumented with conductivity-temperature-depth loggers to record pressure, temperature, and electrical conductivity at 5-minute intervals. Pressure readings show tidal signal propagation into the beach aquifer and water level rise from rainfall events, confirmed by simultaneous freshening. We also installed pressure, temperature and electrical conductivity loggers in the foreshore ocean and backshore estuary to investigate their mutual influence on the observed freshwater lens dynamics. Periodic multi-frequency electromagnetic surveys were performed to measure the freshwater lens and upper saline plume geometry. Surveys indicate a thin (< 3 m), dynamic freshwater lens, with seasonal, tidal, and event influences. Data from the piezometers and geophysical surveys combined with results from our repeated topographic surveys with drone-based LiDAR and manual differential GPS surveys revealed that 2025 coastal storms (Hurricane Erin and Hurricane Melissa) drove vertical beach erosion (up to 60 cm) and lens salinization. These field data are being used to develop a numerical model of variable-density flow and solute transport to better understand the response of small freshwater lenses to atmospheric and oceanic forcing.

abstract:
The Escalante River drainage is well-studied for the presence of iron-oxide/manganese-oxide cemented structures, including boxwork structures (boxworks). Rapid incision of the Colorado River over the past few million years exposed evidence of past fluid-flow and fluid-rock reaction in a paleo-aquifer system. Groundwater moved downgradient from the Aquarius Plateau in a SSE direction toward the Colorado River (a 2.3 km vertical drop). Ongoing reactive transport modeling indicates that the groundwater, interacting with CH 4 and CO 2 from gas reservoir in the Escalante Anticline, reduced hematite grain coatings in the sandstone and transported Fe 2+ downgradient. Fe 2+ -enriched fluids migrated along the vertical joint, mixing with oxygenated groundwater, to reprecipitate Fe oxide cements.

As part of a larger effort to understand the subsurface microbe-rock-fluid systems, we have mapped out boxworks, streamers, and pipes in the Jurassic Navajo sandstone. Boxworks are elongate structures with multiple joints within them, that range in length from m to 10s of m, with a width and high occurring on the m scale. Boxworks are typically horizontal elongated. We characterize boxworks as non-strataform or strataform. Strataform boxwork structures occur along major stratigraphic bounding surfaces in the aeolian sandstone; non-strataform boxwork structures cut across bedding planes. Interior cores of boxwork structures commonly contain calcite cement, low concentrations of transition metals, and concave-up REE patterns. In contrast, exterior rinds are densely Fe-oxide cemented, display concave-up REE patterns, and have higher concentrations of REEs, U, V, and As. The complexly patterned mantle regions of boxwork have intermediate compositions, but relatively high Cu. One model for the origin of these features involves Fe-precipitation around large carbonate concretions, perhaps caused by migration of low-pH and/or -Eh water. Streamers are zones of yellow staining, which are associated with boxworks and pipes, but also exist independently of these features. In specific locations, the streamers are constrained to be tunnel-shaped, with m-scale length and width dimensions and 10 m-scale length dimensions. Critically, boxworks appear to form within streamers, such that streamers are observed both up-gradient (to the NNW) and down-gradient (to the SSE) of boxwork structures. Our tentative conclusion is that the streamers appear to be channelized paleo-fluid flow that exerted a primary control on the formation of the boxworks.

title: Myriad Mini-Sinkholes Years After Forest Clearing: Groundwater and Old Stumps
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)

abstract: More than 100 small sinkholes, 12 to 50 cm wide and 10 to 80 cm deep, developed rapidly in sandy-clay soils in two adjacent fields in south-central Mississippi, USA, following installation and operation of a nearby high-capacity water well. The local area is not known for karst features, evaporite dissolution cavities, underground mining, soil erosion around manmade structures, or desiccation fractures of shallow clays. When studied several years after first appearing, the sinkholes had nearly vertical walls, with some cavities widening with depth. Some had tree stumps visible in the center. Further investigation found remnants of stumps or roots in and radiating outward from most of the sinkholes. Installation of piezometers along a transect revealed a continuous hydraulic gradient under the effected property toward the production well and evidence of reduced overall water levels. The most plausible cause of rapid sinkhole formation is (1) initial partial preservation of tree stumps in saturated soils created by a high water-table and capillary action, (2) lowering of the water table and aeration of surface sediments, and (3) accelerated decomposition of stumps faster than soil could creep into the cavities.

abstract:
The Pliocene–Pleistocene marine molluscan faunas of Florida and the southeastern US Atlantic Coastal Plain (USACP) have been the subject of paleontological investigations for over 200 years. A significant faunal turnover event took place between the late Pliocene and today, with substantial extinction of Pliocene forms followed by a substantial recovery in species richness by the modern. The fauna is extremely diverse, with over 2,500 Plio–Pleistocene and 1,600 modern bivalve and gastropod species reported from the region. However, the timing and pulsed nature of this extinction has been disputed in analyses which are now over 30 years old. Here we reevaluate the extinction event at the species level across the entire southeastern USACP using specimen data derived from the fossil mollusk collections of the Florida Museum of Natural History in conjunction with modern OBIS data.

Fossiliferous deposits were binned into four time intervals, with the modern representing an additional interval. Prior analyses indicated that extinction would be highest at the end of our bin 1 (late Pliocene) or occur in pulses at the terminations of both bins 1 and 2 (early Pleistocene). Our revised dataset, however, indicates that the greatest extinction rate occurred between bin 3 (middle Pleistocene) and 4 (late Pleistocene), with ~70% of species in bin 3 becoming extinct by the transition. Origination rate was also lowest in bin 4 (0.07, compared with 0.16 and 0.12 in bins 2 and 3, respectively). Both prior research and our dataset agree that bin 4 was the lowest molluscan diversity interval. Ecologically, bin 4 showed an increase in the abundance of infaunal siphonate taxa and away from epifaunal predators.

Shareholder quorum subsampling (SQS) was used to assess diversity changes in a robust sample-sized standardized framework. SQS also finds the greatest decline in diversity [RL1] occurred between bins 3 and 4, finding an approximately 60% decline in quorum diversity (at a quorum level of 0.9) from the prior interval (in comparison, diversity declined by ~20% from bin 1 to bin 2 and ~13% from bin 2 to bin 3).

Comparing SQS diversity estimates from the latest Pleistocene to the Recent indicates modern diversity represents an approximately 8-fold increase from the lowest diversity interval, and a return to nearly 90% of latest Pliocene richness.
