abstract: Arctic coasts are increasingly exposed to sea-level rise, sea-ice melt, wave-driven flooding, and rising ocean temperatures. In temperate zones these factors are known drivers of lateral and vertical seawater intrusion into coastal aquifers. In permafrost regions, however, coastal aquifer salinization has not been widely investigated even though the potential impacts on subsurface thermal regimes, permafrost distribution, coastal infrastructure stability, and groundwater processes have been recognized. We integrate frequency-domain and time-domain electromagnetic geophysical surveys, in situ porewater salinity and ground temperature measurements, and analytical modeling to investigate how coastal morphology, stratigraphy, and oceanic forcing govern distributions of subsurface salinized zones and frozen ground along an Arctic shoreline. Fieldwork occurred during the summers of 2023 to 2025 at contrasting coastal sites near Cambridge Bay (Nunavut, Canada): one narrow beach backed by an eroding coastal bluff, one wide, prograding linear beach, and another wide beach shaped to a point by converging waves. Subsurface electrical conductivity distributions reveal groundwater flow paths and salinity patterns influenced by stratigraphy and beach morphology, which regulates overland, wave-driven flooding. Sites with wider swash zones appear to have an upper saline plume, unlike the narrower bluff-backed site. High porewater salinity and resultant freezing point depression also allow for a larger zone of unfrozen porewater than would occur for the same sub-zero temperatures if the porewater were fresh. Resistivity results inferred from time-domain electromagnetic surveys suggest a wedge of deep unfrozen material along the bluff-backed beach, with potential influences of saltwater intrusion or thermal conduction from the ocean. Unfrozen ground can enable groundwater flow and transport and, potentially, unfrozen sediment mobilization, which are critical considerations when assessing the vulnerability of Arctic coasts to climate-change-driven hazards.

abstract:
The La Colorada deposit in Zacatecas, Mexico, features intermediate sulfidation epithermal (IS), carbonate replacement (CRD), skarn, and porphyry mineralization. Volcanic-hosted IS veins transition to CRD veins in underlying carbonates, with total (measured, indicated, inferred) resources of 18.3 Mt containing 161.3 Moz Ag, 0.1 Moz Au, 0.3 Mt Pb, and 0.5 Mt Zn, separate of total reserves (proven, probable) of 9.5 Mt containing 90.7 Moz Ag, 0.06 Moz Au, 0.1 Mt Pb, and 0.2 Mt Zn (6/30/2025). To depth, CRD veins transition to massive CRD, then to skarn and minor porphyry mineralization. The skarn was first drilled in 2018 by Pan American Silver and contains 327.1 Mt of total (indicated, inferred) resources hosting 367.3 Moz Ag, 4.2 Mt Pb, and 9.1 Mt Zn (6/30/2025).

Skarn surrounds eastern and western concealed intrusive centers. Stage 2 (prograde) skarn minerals are spatially zoned. From proximal to distal, garnet color lightens from red to brown to yellow-green; pyroxene color changes from green to brown with minor distal rhodonite, and the garnet:pyroxene ratio decreases. This study investigates zoning in the composition of Stage 4 (late retrograde) carbonate minerals that occur together with quartz, sulfides, sulfosalts, and less commonly chlorite, K-feldspar, and biotite, through EPMA and LA-ICP-MS analyses. Siderite and some dolomite are slightly earlier than calcite and contain up to 6.9 and 6.7 wt% Mn, respectively. In the eastern center, Mn in calcite increases from 2.2 (red garnet skarn) to 4.2 wt% (brown pyroxene skarn) with local rhodochrosite, then decreases to 3.6 wt% ~130 m beyond the skarn (CRD), ~740 m from the ~600 m-wide main syn-skarn stock. In the western center, Mn in calcite decreases from 2.8 (brown garnet skarn) to 0.1 wt% (green pyroxene > yellow garnet skarn), ~515 m from a ~20 m wide syn-skarn RDP dike. Mn in calcite sampled along this dike increases vertically upwards from 1.1 to 7.0 wt % over ~550 m. REEs + Y, Sc; Mo, Fe, and Th in calcite decrease away from both centers. Zn, Sb, and Rb in calcite increase to ~740 m from the eastern center where sampling ends, but from the western center they increase to ~320 m before decreasing, suggesting with Mn that the western center is relatively more distal.

title: Developing a Standardized Porosity Workflow for Multi-Resource Assessments in the Delaware Basin, West Texas and New Mexico
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: LaGesse, Jenny [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, USGS Central Energy Resources Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Subsurface porosity characterization provides foundational reservoir data for evaluating resource potential, storage capacity, and geologic suitability across a wide range of energy resources, including hydrocarbons, geothermal systems, mineral brines, hydrogen, and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS). Reliable porosity estimates are therefore essential for informed decision-making by federal agencies, academia, industry, and the public.

Accurately characterizing porosity remains challenging where core and wireline data are sparse and reservoir lithologies are heterogeneous. In these settings, reproducible workflows that integrate petrophysical interpretation with available geologic data are needed to generate consistent, defensible porosity estimates while explicitly acknowledging data limitations and uncertainty.

Here we present a case study in the Delaware Basin focusing on selected petroleum-bearing, CCUS, and enhanced oil recovery (EOR) formations. Two deterministic total porosity estimation methods, density-log porosity and the standard root-mean-square neutron-density, are evaluated using a limited suite of commonly available wireline logs (gamma ray, density, and neutron) and calibrated against available core data. Gamma ray logs are normalized and used for clay-volume assessment and core-to-log depth alignment. The methods are compared to determine which provides the most reliable and reproducible porosity estimates from a limited wireline log suite, with the goal of developing a standardized workflow for regional resource assessments across multiple lithologies and energy-resource applications.

This work contributes a transparent, reproducible workflow for porosity estimation that establishes a consistent foundation for subsurface characterization across multiple energy resource applications. Preliminary results highlight the importance of rigorous data quality control and accurate matrix-density estimation as key factors influencing porosity calculations from limited wireline log suites. Initial comparisons also suggest that deterministic method performance varies with lithology, emphasizing the need for workflow flexibility rather than a single universally applicable approach. By documenting assumptions, applying standardized methods, and addressing uncertainty, the workflow reduces the potential for inconsistent interpretations, supports efficient future resource assessments, and provides a defensible framework for determining when additional characterization is warranted.

abstract: Plastics are a diverse material, manufactured for a range of purposes and applications. Plastics are ultimately a petroleum product, often have mineralogical components, and occur in a wide range of depositional and hydrologic environments, thus making these materials geologically relevant and environmentally significant. They generally have a half-life of several hundred years and continuously break down into small particles under ultraviolet light, heat, and other degradation processes. Plastic pollution and consumption have negative impacts environmentally and biologically. Approximately 40% of plastics are single-use; humans interact with and dispose of plastics frequently. A prime example is plastic disposable consumer-marketed water bottles. Identifying the quantity as well as textures of microplastics in consumer-marketed water bottles and breakdown mechanics is imperative to understanding exposure risk for humans and assessing transport and filtration strategies. This study characterizes and quantifies microplastics in a major brand’s water bottles via vacuum filtration through a black polycarbonate filter paper and subsequent staining using Nile Red. Additionally, plastic surface morphology was observed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using a centrifugal concentration technique. Initial results indicate results that match the literature, with plastic concentrations between 6 and 20 particles greater than 25 micrometers per liter. Greater than 25 micrometers is an important distinction, as smaller size detection limits can increase values 5 to 10 fold, given a decrease to a minimum of 6.5 micrometers, and even in the tens of thousands for smaller values. Overall morphological data support that plastics have a low-level of surface degradation, indicating recent generation, likely from the bottling process itself, and that over 99% of particles are fragments. Plastics are generally very small, with over 90% of plastics larger than 25 micrometers being smaller than 80 micrometers. Results set a baseline reference for degradation, transport, and filtration experimentation to better understand how different conditions affect concentrations and morphology of this critical pollutant type.

abstract: The United States Geological Survey (USGS) uses a suite of empirical models to rapidly assess hazards from debris flows after wildfire in the western United States. One of these models (the “M1” model) is a logistic regression equation that uses topographic, burn severity, and soil information to predict debris-flow likelihood and identify quantitative rainfall thresholds that can be used as guidance for warning and decision support. The M1 model was calibrated to a debris-flow inventory from southern California (USA) and has been applied throughout the western United States. But, limited spatial coverage in the calibration dataset motivates evaluation of M1 model accuracy when applied outside of the calibration region (e.g., the Sierra Nevada or the eastern Cascade Range, USA). Previous test cases showed that M1 overpredicts debris-flow likelihood and underpredicts rainfall thresholds for some locations (e.g., Arizona, Colorado, USA). We sought to improve the regional applicability of a debris-flow likelihood model by expanding the debris-flow inventory used for calibration, testing multiple versions of M1-like models, and generating a revised model. The new inventory includes debris-flow data from more locations paired with a rainfall metric that normalizes recorded rainfall intensity for each debris-flow observation by the relevant 1-year recurrence interval storm to account for regional variability in the rainfall intensities associated with debris-flow triggering. The revised model predicts debris-flow likelihood and estimates rainfall thresholds with better performance than the original M1 model, based on comparisons of model predictions to observed rainfall and debris-flow activity. These predictions result in reduced false positives relative to M1 and rainfall thresholds that are better aligned with relative differences in regional climatology and debris-flow activity.

abstract:
Human exposure to toxic arsenic (As) concentrations in shallow groundwater continues to drive a wide range of diseases and premature deaths in South and Southeast Asia. In Bangladesh alone, over 38 million people consume groundwater with As exceeding the WHO guidelines. The dissolved As in shallow aquifers is derived from fluvially deposited sediments physically and chemically weathered from the Himalayas and associated uplifts. Sediment provenance has been suggested to be associated with As release from primary geologic formations. The evolution of As mineral hosts during fluvial transport owing to chemical weathering and hydrodynamic sorting must also play a role in explaining the spatial distribution of dissolved As in low-lying shallow aquifers.

This study investigates the sources and transformation of As-bearing phases along the Brahmaputra River in Assam, India. The study focuses on suspended and bedload sediments derived from three broadly different geologic provenances during the monsoon season. We hypothesize that (1) sulfide-rich and granitic source uplifts contribute larger As loads, (2) hydrodynamic sorting concentrates primary As-bearing minerals in the bedload near source regions followed by weathering and subsequent transfer to clay fractions during downstream transport, and (3) Fe-oxides represent an important final host phase for As in suspended sediments, alongside clays and silicates.

Suspended and bedload sediments were collected from the Brahmaputra main channel and three major tributaries: the Kopili, Dhansiri, and Subansiri Rivers. These rivers drain the Shillong Plateau, Naga Hills, and Himalayas, respectively. Suspended sediments were sampled at 25% and 50% depths using a Van Dorn sampler, and riverbed sediments were collected using a weighted bucket. To analyze Fe-oxide–associated metals, sediments were separated into clay, silt, and sand fractions and measured for As and trace metals using sequential extraction with hydroxylamine hydrochloride, followed by total digestion for clays and silicates. A handheld XRF was used to scan bedload sand samples for bulk element composition.

Iron oxide bound As is primarily concentrated in silt grain sizes. Silt grains with As bound to Fe-oxide coatings are concentrated at the top of the water column, which implies Fe-oxide coatings primarily occur on phyllosilicate minerals that are concentrated to the top of the water column via hydraulic sorting.

authors: Veroeven, Andrew Robert [1], Heidinger, Gwenyth Patricia [2], Bhattacharyya, Prajukti [3]

abstract: Maghemite is a weathering product that forms as magnetite transitions to other iron oxide minerals. Although maghemite has been observed on Earth as well as on Mars through rover exploration and remote sensing, how maghemite forms naturally is not yet clearly understood. Since it has been observed on Mars, the conditions of maghemite formation can be used to make inferences about Martian surface processes. In this research, we use controlled experiments to study maghemite formation from magnetite in order to better understand how it may occur on Mars. In our studies, we wanted to simulate an oxidizing environment that might facilitate maghemite formation. We conducted experiments at room temperature by mixing two grams of powdered magnetite into four separate 25ml solutions: A.) 99% acetic acid, B.) 1:2.5 mix of hydrochloric and sulfuric acid, C.) 35% hydrogen peroxide, and D.) deionized water. The sealed solutions were stored in a low-light environment. After 3 months, the solid residue was dried and analyzed using Powdered X-Ray Diffraction (PXRD) to identify chemical changes that may have occurred. Preliminary results from the reaction between magnetite and solution B under these conditions showed the strongest evidence of maghemite formation. Continued experimentation includes other solutions to react with magnetite: E.) sodium hydroxide solution with a pH of ~8.5, F.) 29.4ppt sodium chloride solution to simulate seawater, and G.) a 1:1 mix of solutions E and F. One vial each of solutions C, E, F, and G were placed in a water bath at 50C for 3 weeks before PXRD analysis. Preliminary results are inconclusive regarding the impacts of temperature and alkalinity on maghemite formation from magnetite. The preliminary experimental results using both acidic and alkaline solutions show that more analysis is needed to identify the relative effects of pH level, temperature, and time on magnetite to maghemite transformation. Future work will include placing all of the solutions under both high and low temperature conditions and extending the duration of the experiment. Additionally, we will conduct similar experiments on iron-rich basalts from the Reykjanes Peninsula in Iceland as a proxy for Martian bedrock material.

abstract:
Coral reefs are productive and diverse ecosystems, fostering approximately a quarter of marine biodiversity. Over the last century, reefs have undergone dramatic changes due to anthropogenic disturbances (e.g., warming, pollution, overfishing, acidification) and natural perturbations (e.g., hurricanes, disease). One enduring challenge in reef management is determining the effect of local environmental stressors, such as nutrient loading and elevated temperatures, especially in regions with submarine groundwater discharge (SGD). Studies have noted positive and negative effects of SGD on reefs. Groundwater discharge can cool coastal waters during hot intervals, providing a local refuge for thermally-sensitive organisms (i.e., reducing coral bleaching); however, SGD may instead deliver waters with lower pH and salinity or excessive nutrients, resulting in damage to oligotrophic reef communities. Discovery Bay, Jamaica, has numerous well-documented SGD sites across the bay and fringing reef, with foundational research demonstrating these sites as diffuse and point sources of nutrients to the coast.

Many early studies of reef ecology and morphology documented coral reefs across the Discovery Bay region, but since the 1980s, hurricanes and other disturbances have caused major degradation. Following the devastating landfall of Hurricane Melissa (Category 5, October 2025), our study examined the impact of SGD on reefs in Discovery Bay. The team monitored temperature (every 15 minutes) and nutrient concentrations–nitrate(+nitrite), phosphate, total dissolved nitrogen, and phosphorus (monthly)–at several sites around Discovery Bay starting November 2025, as well as pH (every 45 minutes) at an SGD site (starting March 2026). When compared to sites without documented SGD, sites with SGD have higher concentrations of nitrate (2-5 times higher) but similar concentrations of phosphate. Even so, these do not exceed nutrient excess thresholds known to induce coral stress responses. Temperatures are broadly comparable across sites (<0.2°C difference on average). The pH data captures high-resolution temporal variability, with clear diel cycling that likely represents metabolic influences (i.e., fluxes in photosynthesis and respiration) on calcification and dissolution. There are also intervals with suppressed cyclicity, which may be due to tidal cycles and SGD flushing or recharge. Data collection will continue throughout Summer 2026, which is predicted to be another heat-induced bleaching year. These data provide critical insights into the influence of SGD on coral reef health in the Caribbean.

abstract: Exfiltration storm sewer systems are a low impact development stormwater control designed to reduce stormwater runoff volumes by promoting infiltration. These systems are integrated into conventional storm conveyance systems and consist of a perforated pipe embedded in a gravel trench beneath the main storm sewer. While effective for runoff attenuation, exfiltration systems may increase the risk of groundwater contamination, including from winter de-icing salts in the study region. This study evaluates the runoff reduction performance of an exfiltration system installed in low-permeability soils, its effect on groundwater levels and quality, and the influence of urban karst preferential pathways associated with subsurface infrastructure. A 75 m section of an exfiltration system installed in low permeability soils beneath a road in London, Ontario, was monitored over 13 months, with monitoring within the sewer system and surrounding groundwater. Despite low-permeability soils and a shallow (potentially perched) groundwater table, the system achieved high runoff volume reductions (>83%). Storm-sewer chloride loads were reduced by ~99.8% via infiltration-driven volume losses, transferring chloride to the subsurface. Limited groundwater level and quality responses observed in piezometers installed in native soils, contrasted with significant groundwater level and water quality fluctuations in a downgradient piezometer installed in high permeability backfill material (i.e. urban karst zone). Data indicate that the high hydrologic performance of the exfiltration system may be due to urban karst features, which may also control the subsurface fate of infiltrated contaminants. Study findings provide insights into the effectiveness of exfiltration system for stormwater management and interactions between enhanced-infiltration stormwater controls and anthropogenic urban karst features.

title: The afterlife of glaciers: how residual ice patches shapes early paraglacial adjustment
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Azzoni, Roberto Sergio [1], Valzasina, Stefano [2], Zerboni, Andrea [3]
affiliations: (1) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra "A.Desio", Università degli Studi di Milano, Milan, Italy
(2) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra "A. Desio", Università degli Studi di Milano, Milan, Italy

abstract:
When a glacier tongue becomes dynamically disconnected from its upper reaches, large patches of debris-covered ice may persist for years or decades. This residual ice patches are part of the paraglacial system, but its influence on landform evolution, drainage, and sediment transfer is still not well constrained. We examine how stagnant or slowly moving debris-covered ice affects the early evolution of glacier forefields, and whether similar patterns emerge across different topographic and lithological settings.

The study compares selected glacier systems in the Central and Western Italian Alps. Their recent evolution is reconstructed from multitemporal aerial photographs and orthophotos, detailed field geomorphological mapping, UAV surveys and DEM differencing. The sites differ in glacier size, valley geometry, lithology, debris supply, and degree of dynamic disconnection.

The lower tongues do not simply retreat and disappear. Their decay is dominated by uneven downwasting, fragmentation, and local collapse. Thick debris can preserve residual ice, while nearby sectors undergo rapid lowering or ice-cliff retreat. As the surface loses coherence, drainage lines shift, temporary ponds form or drain, and local areas of sediment storage are repeatedly created and removed. At the same time, incision and erosion of lateral and frontal moraines feed the developing proglacial plains and modify connections between slopes, residual ice, channels, and downstream reaches. The balance between storage, remobilization, and transfer differs from site to site and appears to depend on lithology, sediment availability and the persistence of buried ice.

These examples indicate that dynamic disconnection does not mark a simple shift from glacial to paraglacial conditions. Paraglacial adjustment is already underway, but stagnant and buried ice continues to control local relief, drainage organization, and the timing and location of sediment release. The “afterlife” of glaciers therefore represents a phase in which residual glacial controls and paraglacial processes operate simultaneously, producing rapid and spatially uneven changes in landforms and sedimentary connectivity.

title: Morphometric, Stratigraphic, Sedimentological, and Taphonomic Analysis of Eocene Bee Brood Cell from the Wind River Basin, Wyoming
session_title: Paleontology, Biogeography/Biostratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Easterwood, Jesse E. [1], Rubin, David [2], Currano, Ellen [3], Vietti, Laura [4], Clementz, Mark T. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
(2) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA

abstract:
The Eocene strata of the Wind River Basin, Wyoming, preserve abundant plant, vertebrate, invertebrate, and trace fossils that document how terrestrial ecosystems responded to warming temperatures during the Paleogene greenhouse. Among these fossils is the recently described bee brood cell ichnospecies Celliforma rozeni Knecht and Buchmann, 2026. Here, we present the first comprehensive morphometric, stratigraphic, sedimentologic, and taphonomic analysis of C. rozeni and its type locality, one of the world’s largest known fossil bee nesting sites. The locality was characterized through field mapping, high-resolution stratigraphy, and analyses of brood cell density, orientation, preservation, and morphometric variation.

Field mapping and stratigraphic analysis at this locality show that the brood cell-bearing interval extends approximately 2.7 m stratigraphically and more than 700 m laterally. The assemblage is preserved within carbonate-cemented sandstone and is associated with rare turtle shell and mammal bone fragments. Analysis of successive 45 × 45 cm quadrats indicates that brood cell density was greatest in the western part of the study area. Two preservation modes were recognized: fine-grained, sediment-filled cells lacking caps and calcite-filled cells with intact caps. Calcite-filled burrows account for slightly more than 2% of cells at most outcrops but comprise approximately 20% of the assemblage at one locality. Burrows are consistently oriented vertically to subvertically. Additional small burrows resembling Celliforma are also present and were probably produced by other trace-making organisms.

Sedimentologic evidence indicates that the nesting horizon formed adjacent to a water body subject to periodic flooding. The vertical thickness and lateral continuity of the brood cell-bearing interval suggest repeated occupation by successive generations of ground-nesting bees, a pattern consistent with the nest-site fidelity of many modern solitary bees. Sediment-filled cells probably formed when floodwaters introduced fine-grained sediment into abandoned burrows. In contrast, calcite-filled cells with intact caps were protected from sediment infiltration and later filled during early diagenesis. Repeated nesting, episodic flooding, and favorable diagenetic conditions produced one of the largest and best-preserved fossil bee brood cell assemblages known. This locality provides new insight into Paleogene solitary bee ecology and the preservation of insect nesting behavior in the fossil record.

title: Stochastic Fault Zone Analysis: Modelling Variable Throw patterns using Nested Parabolas
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
authors: Grant, Neil T [1]
affiliations: (1) ConocoPhillips Inc., ConocoPhillips UK Holdings Ltd, Aberdeen, United Kingdom
abstract: Interpreting faults in seismic data is largely a deterministic exercise: it leads to one interpretation of the fault plane and its throw profile. The result can be qualitatively controlled using 3D mapping tools combined with an understanding of fault geometry and expected displacement patterns. Due to the spatial limitations of seismic imaging however, uncertainties remain in the both the fault architecture and mapped fault throw patterns that relate to sub-seismic fault zone complexity. Lower absolute throw may occur relative to the seismically mapped throw due to displacement partitioning within the fault zone, resulting from any combination of relay zone development, fault lenses, internal layer rotation, normal drag, and the presence of multiple slip planes. Seismically imaged throw tends to be a maximum possible throw (in the absence of horizon miscorrelations). The presence of throw partitioning potentially impacts fault seal calculations by changing juxtapositions, affecting for example, both the calculated SGR and modelled shale smear patterns. By inference, this impacts how fluids are modelled to move around and across a fault. This uncertainty can be partly addressed by using a newly developed nested parabolic throw model. The technique fits a series of conjoined (or nested) parabolas to the measured throw profile for a horizon. Each parabola effectively represents a component fault segment that has linked together during fault growth. Fault branch lines are easily accommodated if they are parallel to displacement. The use of mathematically prescribed parabolas enables a throw adjustment to be made that can be distributed coherently along the fault. The adjustment is based on an empirical fractional throw model that tries to capture the uncertainty in throw distribution caused by the sub-seismic structure as a function of throw magnitude and is based on published field studies. This is applied stochastically allowing the uncertainty in fault throw to be better represented in a Monte Carlo model. The uncertainty in fault throw can be used to assess its impact on fault seal calculations and potential fault behaviour in reservoir models.

title: Optimizing InSAR Processing for Regional-Scale Landslide Monitoring in Challenging Environments
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment
authors: Eiden, Elizabeth [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Geologic Hazards Science Center, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Accurately identifying and characterizing landslides, including patterns of deformation, is critical for reducing hazards to both communities and infrastructure. Deep-seated landslides can accelerate downslope before rapid failure, but the movement is often only measured retrospectively. Regional-scale monitoring of slow-moving landslides is key to understanding the physical processes that precede such events and to better understand landslide hazard characterization. A top priority outlined in the U.S. Geological Survey’s National Strategy for Landslide Loss Reduction is to improve landslide detection and monitoring by leveraging available satellite imagery. Remote sensing methods can provide more spatial coverage to identify, assess, and monitor landslides and inform where to direct field resources.

The near-global availability of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery enables regional scale studies, but there are several challenges to address with interferometric SAR (InSAR)-based landslide monitoring before it can be scaled up. Surface deformation studies often require customized InSAR processing, with factors such as snow cover, rapid ground displacement, vegetation, soil moisture, steep topography, and landslide speed influencing the interpretability of data. This research evaluates the accuracy of different InSAR processing choices in reliably measuring landslide displacement across a variety of challenging environments, including the vegetated Hooskanaden earthflow in Oregon, the fast-moving (for InSAR time series) Slumgullion landslide in Colorado, and the snowy Barry Arm landslide in Alaska. We compare the results from varying spatial resolution and network connectivity in InSAR processing with in-situ data to evaluate accuracy and optimize workflows for broader application. The analysis includes both C- and L-band InSAR data from the Sentinel-1 and NISAR satellites, as well as ground-based data from GNSS stations, extensometers, and ground-based radar. We evaluate measurement reliability, quantify error margins, and identify the best tools and workflows that support improved landslide inventories and monitoring. Defining how different InSAR processing choices affect the reliability of surface deformation measurements in difficult landslide monitoring environments can help practitioners interpret and more confidently apply this data for landslide risk reduction applications.

title: A New Multipurpose Grass Waterway that Uses the Natural Landscape for Nitrate Reduction
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes
authors: Schilling, Keith E. [1], Streeter, Matthew T. [2], Anderson, Elliot S. [3], Doyle, Thomas [4]
affiliations: (1) Iowa Geological Survey, University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA

abstract: In the rolling glacial till plains of the U.S. Midwest beyond the extent of Wisconsin glaciation, tile drainage often occurs in grass waterways and there is potential to utilize organic-rich waterway sediments for nitrate reduction. In this project funded by the Iowa Nutrient Research Center, we developed and tested a new “multipurpose grass waterway” (MGW) practice that leaves surface conditions unchanged while redirecting subsurface tile flow into shallow waterway sediments for nitrate remediation. Using standard control boxes and a series of tile valve structures, the MGW allows tile water to seep into subsurface sediments and hydrate waterway sediments from the bottom up. Geologic characterization indicated that the waterway was filled with fine-textured and organic-rich alluvial soils derived from erosion and deposition of upland loess and till. Using continuous flow monitoring data, approximately 51,500 m 3 of tile water seeped into the waterway sediments over a two-year period. The water table was raised in a stepped fashion upgradient in the waterway but it remained >0.5 m below ground surface and allowed the producer to drive across the waterway with heavy farm machinery. Based on hydraulic heads and nitrate concentration reductions measured in 16 monitoring wells, the MGW removed 27 kg of nitrate mass from tile water. Given the ubiquity of grass waterways in rolling hills of the Corn Belt, there is great potential for MGWs to reduce tile nitrate loss to surface water across the region.

abstract: Jamaica is home to numerous vital and complex ecosystems, including forests, mangroves, coral reefs, and seagrass beds. Historically, the stability and dynamics of these ecosystems have not been actively monitored, and conservation solutions are seldom tailored to the needs of local communities. In response to this history, the need for collaborative conservation strategies, and the desire to broaden recruitment and participation in the geosciences, we created ‘GEOPAths GO Jamaica’. In this third year (2026), the team includes partners from The University of Texas at Austin, The University of the West Indies (UWI), Mona, Georgia Institute of Technology, The UWI Discovery Bay Marine Lab, and the Forestry Department (Jamaica). During our program, which culminated in a three week immersive field experience in Jamaica, we introduced a team of students (undergraduate and graduate) from American and Caribbean institutions to (a) the different, interconnected elements of Earth sciences on land, at the coast, and in the ocean; (b) the communities and people that collaborate to promote conservation; and (c) the broad community of scholars uniting to preserve the natural world and communities affected by modern climate threats. Undergraduate and graduate student participants learned fundamental skills in geoscience research practices in marine and terrestrial biomes through experiences that included sampling and chemical analyses of marine and river water; assessment of numerous biophysical factors governing mangrove community health; basic quantitative surveys of Jamaica's reef ecology (Pleistocene and present); and how data from local geoscience research help inform the conservation of environmental, cultural, and historical sites of significance. Here, we showcase findings and lessons learned from our third and final year, as well as the three-year program overall.

abstract:
Investment in the economic development along the north-south State Highway 15 corridor in North Mississippi (MS), near the southern border with Tennessee, has funded a large highway expansion project; this has created the opportunity for an update to the resolution of publicly available geological data in the region.

The only currently available geologic map for this region is the 1:500,000 scale state geologic map published by Bicker and the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) Office of Geology in 1969. The highway 15 corridor area of interest borders with a series of 7.5’ geologic maps published more recently by MDEQ, on its easternmost border. The highway 15 corridor area consists of a group of geologic quadrangles immediately east through Union and Tippah counties, MS. Accordingly, this project is to produce two 7.5’ quadrangles for the Northwest Pontotoc, and New Albany West quadrangles. The humid subtropical climate of north Mississippi and highly erosive, dissect, sedimentary strata, and thickly vegetated ground, make this area challenging to map. In areas such as this, large construction projects like those currently underway, are a boon to geological field work. Initial fieldwork has included visitation to multiple temporary exposures created during the highway construction efforts. Specifically, to map the Cretaceous Ripley Formation, Cretaceous Owl Creek Formation, Paleocene Clayton Formation, and Paleocene Porters Creek Formation. Strata represent a sedimentary fill of the Mississippi Embayment (MSE) and, following the regional trend, they strike approximately north-south with a shallow, westward dip.

Outside highway 15 construction sites, aerial imagery has been used to identify exposures and areas of interest to further investigate through field work. Additionally, traditional methods of mapping will include, on-foot field mapping, augering, and drilling to ground truth geologic units. Methods such as XRD, and hand sample analysis will be used to confirm units based on sampling. Each geologic map will be constructed with the corresponding US Geological Survey 7.5′ topographic map as its base.

abstract:
Landslides are a ubiquitous hazard in mountainous regions. A sudden triggering event like an earthquake can destabilize slopes, cause mass wasting over tens of kilometers, and pose immediate and cascading risks to people and infrastructure. Rapid identification of hillslope failures supports emergency responses, and thorough inventories inform empirically based predictive models of landslide distribution in future earthquakes. Mapping widespread events quickly is challenging, but satellite remote sensing data present a solution. Specifically, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites operate on the microwave spectrum, allowing observations even in nighttime and cloudy conditions. SAR backscatter can detect changes in surface properties, such as those caused by mass wasting events, but the physical interpretation of the surface changes can be difficult.

On December 6, 2025, a M7.0 earthquake occurred ~10 km below the Hubbard Glacier in the Saint Elias Mountains of southwest Yukon, Canada. This remote region is heavily glaciated, hosts extreme topographic relief, and was covered by a significant seasonal snowpack at the time of the event. Within one week, there were multiple acquisitions of multi-frequency SAR data, as well as an aerial reconnaissance flight over the region. These observations revealed hundreds of earthquake-induced rock, ice, and snow avalanches, along with damage to glacial ice. We use these data to better understand how different mass wasting processes are represented in SAR imagery. We use amplitude data from the C-band Sentinel-1 and L-band NASA-Indian Space Research Organization SAR (NISAR) satellites to map regions of surface change and subsequently verify the physical cause of change with oblique aerial photos. We compare co- and cross-polarized data from both wavelengths to better understand the relationship between deposit characteristics and polarization. We find the longer wavelength (L-band) data are less sensitive to thin and snow-dominant deposits. In both datasets, cross-polarized data were more sensitive to snow-dominant surface change, likely due to increased volume scattering. Snow-dominant deposits are less autocorrelated than large rock-and-ice-dominant deposits, which means self-similar pixels are less clustered in snow-dominant deposits. Our results highlight the importance of combining multi-frequency and dual-polarization SAR datasets to improve detection, interpretation, and classification of mass‑wasting events following major earthquakes in remote, snow‑ and ice‑covered terrain. This work strengthens the foundation for building reliable, scalable landslide‑inventory workflows that can operate rapidly after large triggering events.

abstract: Mountainous areas recently affected by wildfire are susceptible to increased runoff and erosion during intense rainfall due to fire-induced changes to the soil and vegetation. This often leads to widespread flooding and debris flows within the burned area. The 2020 Cameron Peak Fire started in Northern Colorado and burned an area encompassing the upper Poudre Canyon, located west of Fort Collins, Colorado. Debris flows initiating in the burned area were observed via field and remote sensing observations during subsequent years. The Williams Gulch watershed, located north of the Cache la Poudre River in Larimer County, produced debris flows during the summer of 2021, 2022, and 2023. We used this site as a natural experiment to test techniques for mapping the debris-flow channels (e.g. length and width) as well as debris-flow deposits. Using an uncrewed aerial system (UAS) we collected imagery from both a standard camera (red, green, and blue bands) as well as a multispectral sensor (red, green, blue, rededge, near infrared, and panchromatic bands). Following data collection, we generated 1-meter orthophotos using Structure-from-Motion image processing. The multispectral and true-color orthophotos were classified using image analysis tools in ArcGIS Pro to separate debris-flow channels and deposits from the rest of the watershed. For both the multispectral and true-color orthophotos the area was segmented in order to group regions of like-pixels together, then each segment was classified as debris flow channel, debris flow deposit, or hillslope using a supervised classification. We found that nearly 25% more of the debris-flow deposits were correctly classified using multispectral imagery than using true-color images alone. Moreover, debris-flow channel identification was slightly more successful using multispectral versus true-color images. Ultimately, the utility of the multispectral orthophotos proved beneficial in automated generation of maps of debris-flow channels and deposits as well as identifying important geomorphic features (channel and deposit initiation, length, and width).

abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Candy Lane 1 core was drilled in Montrose County, Colorado in 2005, recovering ~540 ft of Upper Cretaceous mudstones of the Mancos Shale. Since its collection, a variety of characterization studies have been conducted to better understand the source rock potential of organic-rich units, as well as the depositional setting in the central Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway. Detailed biostratigraphy of the core provides age control based primarily on fossils of molluscan species. New high-resolution (approx. two-foot sampling intervals) bulk organic and elemental geochemistry datasets, along with mineralogy, have been collected, providing additional insights into the variable hydrocarbon-generating potential and fluctuating paleoenvironmental conditions between and within mudstone units in this part of the Seaway. Programmed temperature pyrolysis parameters (Tmax, production index) and preliminary organic petrography indicate that the organic matter throughout the core is thermally immature for hydrocarbon generation. Organic richness is greatest in the Juana Lopez Member, with total organic carbon (TOC) content ranging from 3 to 4 wt. %. The remaining units show lower TOC values (< 2 wt. %), though samples in the Fairport Member have TOC values up to 4 wt. %. Based on hydrogen index values, the Juana Lopez and Fairport Members have nearly double the hydrocarbon-generating potential of mudstones in other parts of the core. The available data are somewhat ambiguous as to the origin of the organic matter in much of the core, and it is unclear if terrigenous organic input varied or if variable organic matter preservation conditions, as interpretation of redox-sensitive trace element concentrations indicate, explain the observed bulk organic geochemical results. Sulfur-to-iron ratios and molybdenum enrichment factors imply periods of anoxia during deposition of the Juana Lopez Member but more oxic conditions during deposition of the other units. Subtle shifts in detrital sources across the late Cenomanian to early Coniacian at this location are inferred, based on Si/Al, Si/Ti, and light-to-heavy rare earth element ratios. Mineralogy and major element data show that the units below the Montezuma Valley Member are dominated by clay minerals and quartz whereas shallower intervals contain more carbonate. The geochemical features observed in the core are generally consistent with previous regional scale paleoenvironmental reconstructions.

title: Paleomagnetism of the Northwest Pilbara Terrane: An Investigation of Archean Tectonics

abstract: The theory of plate tectonics is the central paradigm of modern geology, as it provides a framework for understanding the history and morphology of continental and oceanic crust, as well as the distribution of volcanoes and seismic zones on the modern Earth. While there is evidence that some form of plate motion has occurred since ~3.5 Ga, there is little consensus about whether plates were driven by similar forces as during the present day. Determining the drivers of plate tectonics holds implications for the existence and duration of subduction zones and the flux of light elements into and out of the surface environment. This study attempts to investigate whether ancient tectonics occurred at modern-like rates and geometries through paleomagnetic analysis of ~3.1 Ga volcanic rocks from the Whundo Group in the Sholl Terrane, collected from the Northwest Pilbara Craton in Australia. Due to the potential for comparison with existing paleomagnetic data from the East Pilbara Terrane, this study location provides an opportunity to probe the relative rates of motion between ancient continents, the size of ancient ocean basins, and the petrogenesis of potential subduction-related volcanic rocks. The orientation of the ancient magnetic field was determined by measuring the magnetic moment of 114 oriented rock samples from 11 field sites, using a 2G Enterprises DC-SQuID Rock Magnetometer. Through progressive thermal demagnetization past the blocking temperatures of the dominant ferromagnetic mineral phases, the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) component was isolated. We find that our isolated ChRM component fails a fold test across the ~2904 Ga Bradley Syncline, remaining clustered in geographic coordinates and diverging upon tilt correction. Therefore, our samples were magnetized after ~2940 Ga and likely carry a ~750 Ma overprint. Further investigation to define paleomagnetic poles for the Northwest Pilbara Craton may focus on alternative field areas such as the Karratha Terrane.

abstract: Rapid increases of CO­ 2 in our modern atmosphere necessitate understanding carbon removal mechanisms. Soils are one of many potential carbon sinks. In dryland environments, a large part of soil carbon is stored in soil carbonates. However, there are uncertainties surrounding whether these carbonates are a source or sink of carbon. This research looks to analyze the responses of soil gases in experimental soil pits to rain events of varying sizes to improve our understanding of the effects of soil carbonate dissolution and precipitation on the soil carbon cycle. These pits in central Texas contain soils with (treatment) and without (control) calcium carbonate and are equipped to measure daily automatic, high precision soil CO 2 and O 2 concentrations. Rain events are grouped into small, medium, and large events based on daily rain totals and the response of soil gases. During almost all (95%) small to medium (0-60 mm) rain events, soil CO 2 concentration of both control and treatment pits increases while soil O 2 concentration decreases, most likely due to an increase in soil respiration rates. The size of the spike in soil CO 2­ ranges from 500 to 4000 ppm, depending on the amount of rain and the temperature of the soil. Soil CO 2 in the carbonate pits increases by a smaller amount than the control pits due to dissolution of soil carbonates into pore water, resulting in a larger transfer of CO 2 from gas to water as dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) than in the control pits. In contrast, after large rain events (60+ mm), the soil CO 2 concentration of treatment pits temporarily decreases before increasing while control pits increase. The soil O 2 concentration of the control and treatment pits decreases by similar amounts, indicating that the presence of carbonate does not influence the response of respiration rates to rainfall. We hypothesize that this decrease in CO 2 concentration in the treatment pits is due to very rapid dissolution of soil carbonate causing rapid transfer of CO 2 into DIC. Modeling will be used to quantify the rates of CO 2 removal from soil gas to 1) quantify the response differences of the control and treatment pits to variable rain events and 2) determine if soil carbonates are acting as a source or sink of carbon during these large rain events.

title: Airborne Electromagnetic Inversion Results Validate Analog Model Predictions of Strike-Slip Fault Reactivation and Potential for Hydrogeologic Compartmentalization
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms. (Posters)
authors: Karki, Kapil [1], Larsen, Daniel [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Center for Applied Earth Sciences and Engineering Research (CAESER), The University of Memphis, Memphis, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Memphis, Memphis, TN, USA
abstract: The New Madrid seismic zone overlies the Reelfoot Rift (RR), an intracontinental extensional structure reactivated as a strike-slip system during Phanerozoic. Complex fault interactions in this region including the 1811–1812 New Madrid earthquake sequence and modern seismicity reflect incomplete understanding of fault geometry and strain partitioning across the region. Traditional borehole-based subsurface mapping and seismic reflection reveal broad structural trends, but subsurface fault-zone architecture and precise fault orientations remain poorly constrained. Many scaled analog models predict development of Riedel shear arrays and secondary structures during strike-slip reactivation; however, systematic validation of these predictions using high-resolution geophysical data has not been applied yet. We apply airborne electromagnetics (AEM) to image subsurface fault geometry and electrical conductivity anomalies in Eocene-Quaternary sediments deformed along the southeastern margin of the New Madrid seismic zone. We compare AEM-derived fault orientations, kinematic indicators, and structural geometries with previous analog model predictions for progressive strike-slip reactivation. Specifically, we test whether the RR system exhibits the characteristics of Riedel shear components predicted in analog models. AEM data reveal (1) the continuity of the previously identified faults while also delineating several previously unidentified faults, (2) the geometry and orientation of newly identified and previously mapped faults, providing the basis for constructing a new regional cross section that more accurately represents the structural framework than earlier interpretations, (3) characteristics of en echelon fault spacing and segmentation patterns matching analog model predictions, and (4) distributed shear zones with widths correlating to model-predicted stress partition between primary and secondary faults. This study validates analog model predictions for strike-slip fault evolution within the RR system and establishes a quantitative framework for interpreting fault-zone complexity in this seismically active region. These findings also clarify the distribution and structural style of fault zones that may provide lateral compartmentalization of the Memphis aquifer, a regionally important and vulnerable water resource.

title: Who Moved My Soil: Microbial Ecology and Soil Geochemistry Across Landslide and Reference Settings at Floracliff Nature Sanctuary, Kentucky
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: , Mamie Clark [1], Backus, Jason [2], Connor, Andrea [3], Washburn, Rachel L. [4]

abstract:
Who Moved My Soil: Microbial Ecology and Soil Geochemistry Across Landslide and Reference Settings at Floracliff Nature Sanctuary, Kentucky

Mamie Clark 1 , Jason Backus 1 , Andrea Connor 1 , and Rachel L. Washburn 2

1 Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA

2 Kentucky Geological Survey and College of Pharmacy, University of Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA

Landslides are among the most common and damaging geologic hazards in Kentucky (USA), causing millions of dollars in infrastructure and property damage each year. Soil microbial communities can influence erosion, water infiltration, and soil aggregation through processes including biocrust formation and the production of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS). Although slope stability is generally evaluated using geologic, hydrologic, and geotechnical factors, the potential contribution of soil microbial communities remains poorly understood. We hypothesized that landslide-associated soils contain distinct microbial communities and geochemical characteristics relative to non-landslide reference soils. Surface soils were collected using sterile field techniques from four geomorphic settings at Floracliff Nature Sanctuary (Lexington, Kentucky, USA) approximately 11 months after an April 2025 landslide: the landslide deposit, landslide scarp (1 meter from landslide), reference hillslope (7 meters from landslide), and reference floodplain (900 meters from landslide). Soil mineralogy and elemental composition were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities were characterized using 16S and 18S rRNA gene sequencing, respectively. Alpha- and beta-diversity analyses were used to evaluate diversity within each setting and differences in community composition among settings. Preliminary results indicate that microbial community composition and soil geochemistry differ between landslide-associated and reference soils, and each geomorphic setting exhibited distinct microbial and geochemical characteristics despite the close spatial proximity of all four settings. Ongoing metabolomic analyses and molecular networking will evaluate secondary metabolites with potential roles in soil aggregation and stabilization. These results demonstrate associations among geomorphic setting, microbial community composition, and soil geochemistry. Future work will apply this approach across multiple landslides and reference sites to determine whether the observed microbial and geochemical patterns are consistent across landscapes and associated with measurable differences in soil stability. This work provides a foundation for testing whether biological processes contribute to slope stability and could eventually inform soil stabilization strategies.

abstract: Global Water Consortium (GWC) is an Ohio-based nonprofit organization working internationally for over 10 years to install local drinking water facilities in water-stressed areas. There is a need for environmental site assessment for these sites to better understand water resources and utilize funds generated from future operations for humanitarian use. Water accessibility, security, and infrastructure is a major concern within the municipality of San Pedro Zacapa, Santa Bárbara, Honduras. Small towns within the region lack infrastructure to transport, treat, and maintain a clean water supply to the population in general. This lack of infrastructure causes increased risk of exposure of pollutants and pathogens to local citizens which can cause serious adverse health effects. An initial review of GWC supplied information was undertaken. Suspended solids are present at drinking water sites in San Pedro Zacapa, being an initial indicator that the quality of drinking water is subpar. In order to support GWC site development, an initial environmental site assessment was conducted, assessing nine factors through a literature review deemed necessary for a successful installment. Factors analyzed were, hydrogeology, soils, climate, disease, social issues, water quality, surficial geology, infrastructure, and environmental health. Significant findings from the literature review indicate a lack of sanitation expertise in the local community, potential locations of source pollution, geologic data influencing the flow and quality of the groundwater, and research gaps in the region. Information and data gaps identified during the literature review process were communicated to GWC personnel for the purpose of guiding sampling and more detailed field investigations for future development efforts. The initial environmental geoscience background research for the Zacapa region allows GWC to better understand how to install treatment facilities and distribute clean water for Hondurans suffering from deteriorated drinking water.

abstract: The Motagua Fault is a left-lateral, strike-slip fault along the North American-Caribbean plate boundary in Guatemala. It last slipped in the devastating 1976 Mw 7.5 earthquake with a 230 km-long surface rupture. Field surveys documented 142 cm of left-lateral displacement at the western end of the rupture at Finca La Concepción, near San Martín Jilotepeque. To investigate the earthquake history of this fault section, a paleoseismic trench was excavated across the 1976 rupture. Nine stratigraphic units were identified within the trench, separated by a major erosional unconformity between a lower sequence of floodplain and channel sediments (Units 6–9) and an upper sequence of channel, overbank, and soil deposits (Units 1–5). Unit ages were constrained by Bayesian modeling of 14 C charcoal ages in OxCal, supplemented by Maya pottery sherds and modern cultural debris. Fault-related deformation is expressed by distributed, clay-lined fractures that deform the lower sequence, with several fractures extending upward into the upper deposits. Three paleoearthquake horizons were recognized based on upward-terminating fractures, displaced strata, and fissure fills. The oldest earthquake (Event 3) is broadly constrained to date to ~3 ka. The penultimate earthquake (Event 2) produced fractures and faults at the base of Unit 4 and dates to between 1678 and 1904 CE. Historical earthquakes that fall within this interval include those of 1717, 1751, and 1773. Historical macroseismic data suggest that the one of the major (~Mw 7.5) earthquakes that destroyed Antigua in 1773 is the most likely candidate for Event 2. The youngest earthquake (Event 1) occurred between 1682 and 2018 CE. Because fractures extend to the base of the modern soil, this event is interpreted as the 1976 earthquake. A nearly 4,000-year hiatus between the lower and upper sedimentary sequences indicates that a substantial portion of the earthquake record is absent at this site. The lack of significant lateral displacement preserved on fractures suggests that strain is distributed across multiple faults or a broader shear zone within the basin. These results indicate that the location of past surface ruptures at this site remains uncertain and raise new questions regarding westward rupture propagation and the long-term behavior of the Motagua Fault.

title: Karst-related flooding and domestic water-supply concerns linked to artificial recharge effects from leaky aqueduct tunnels in the Rondout Valley, New York
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: DeMott, Laura Michelle [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, New York Water Science Center, Cortland, New York, USA
abstract:
The Catskill-Delaware Aqueduct system supplies drinking water to New York City through tunnels that pass beneath the Rondout Valley. Leakage from these tunnels has contributed to increased groundwater levels in the valley, resulting in flooding and other effects on domestic water supply wells. The tunnels are bored into tilted and faulted Silurian-Devonian sedimentary rocks, including several karst-prone limestone units such as the Onondaga Limestone, Helderberg Group, and Rondout Formation. Numerous karst features, including sinkholes, springs, and small caves, have been documented in the area.

To better understand the scope of aqueduct leakage and the hydrogeologic factors related to groundwater flooding, water levels have been continuously monitored in domestic, production, and observation wells since 2008 using pressure transducers. During planned tunnel closures, some wells exhibited rapid declines in water level, characteristic of well responses in karst aquifers. A statistical cluster analysis of time-series data encompassing tunnel closures shows that wells can be clearly separated into those that respond strongly to closures and those that do not. The most responsive wells were predominantly completed in bedrock, with the majority of these in limestone units. These results indicate that karstic flow within the bedrock aquifers may be a primary factor controlling the zones of flooding and observed water-level changes.

Continued monitoring, combined with improved mapping of karst boundaries and regional karst features, will improve understanding of the groundwater conditions in the Rondout Valley and inform mitigation efforts.

title: New Constraints on Glacial Erosion Processes from Tracer Thermochronology in the Southern Alps of Aotearoa New Zealand
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond (Posters)

abstract: The role of glaciation in moderating the flux of sediment and solute from mountain landscapes remains debated, and the expansion of alpine glaciers has been argued to accelerate bedrock erosion and increase the amount of terrestrial sediment produced in mountain landscapes. However, the mechanisms by which glaciation augments sediment production are complex, and there are few observational constraints on the patterns of erosion during a glacial period. Here, we present a novel approach to compare models of glacial erosion using new fission-track and U-Pb multi-dating of detrital zircons from Otiran (45–11.7 ka) outwash and moraine deposits in the Southern Alps of Aotearoa New Zealand. The Southern Alps acts as a model landscape with well-constrained lithology and a predictable pattern of zircon fission-track (ZFT) cooling ages with distance from the Alpine Fault. This tracer approach exploits the systematic relationship between ZFT cooling ages and distance eastward into the Alpine Fault hanging wall. Our results show that relative to modern sediment, Otiran samples exhibit an older ZFT age population, consistent with greater headwater erosion during glacial-maximum conditions. We also find that moraine sediment records the clearest headwater-sourced signal, while outwash sediment is decoupled from both moraine and modern populations, and instead records a distinct older age signature. Using zircons from moraine deposits we test a model of subglacial abrasion where the probability of sediment contribution is scaled by basal shear stress derived from an Otiran ice reconstruction. We compare this to an alternative model in which a portion of sediment is also contributed from supraglacial deposition. From these results we establish two primary conclusions: 1. Glacial outwash deposits may reflect broader sourcing than simple moraine sediment recycling, and 2. The best model of glacial erosion combines subglacial abrasion with supraglacial deposition. These findings are novel because they show that facies-specific decomposition, rather than a single glacial-versus-fluvial signal, is essential for interpreting glacial-period detrital records, and because they suggest that the muted glacial erosion signature observed in modern Southern Alps rivers reflects a transient postglacial state rather than a fundamental limit on glacial erosional efficiency, further advancing our understanding of how glaciers reshape mountain landscapes.

title: Geochemical Sampling Error and Paths Toward Better Sampling Processes
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Reimink, Jesse [1], Pearson, D. Graham [2], Chacko, Thomas [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) University of Alberta, Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Edmonton, AB,
(3) Univ Alberta, Dept Earth & Atmospheric Science, Edmonton, AB,
abstract:
Whole-rock geochemical data underpin resource estimation, deposit characterization, and processing decisions, yet the relationship between sample mass, mineral grain size, and analytical precision is difficult to explicitly quantify. This issue depends critically on our understanding of geochemical sampling error — the compositional difference between a collected sample and the rock body it represents. Sampling error is a fundamental but underappreciated source of uncertainty in modern geochemistry, as most workers focus on analytical precision and accuracy while ignoring the difficult-to-determine sampling error. There is a long and rich history of geochemical sampling error estimation, with both theoretical and empirical solutions offered to the exploration community. We build on this work by presenting an empirically calibrated sampling error estimation model with substantial improvements over previous approaches.

We draw on previously published theoretical frameworks and an empirical test using a coarse-grained K-feldspar megacrystic granite and mantle peridotite samples. Inconsistencies between previous models and our empirical data led us to introduce a modified theoretical approach incorporating the closure effect — the mathematical requirement that mineral modal proportions and elemental concentrations sum to 100%. This modified approach produces sampling error estimates that better match observations. Sampling errors for abundant elements like Si and Al are dampened relative to theoretical predictions, while errors for elements hosted in accessory or minor phases are amplified. These patterns have direct implications for how geochemists and exploration geologists interpret variability in drill core and outcrop suites, ultimately affecting resource estimation.

Practical guidance on minimum sample masses for common ore deposit types is discussed, with emphasis on how inadequate sampling can bias datasets in ways that are difficult to detect after the fact. We discuss potential avenues for integration of geochemical sampling uncertainty estimates within existing sample documentation and exploration workflows, as well as how such integrations can benefit end user decision-making.

title: Triple O-isotope ratios in diagenetic silica from carbonate-hosted formations

abstract: Diagenetic silica present as chert nodules and silicified carbonates is ubiquitous in the geological record. Without a doubt they formed in a subsurface diagenetic environment, probably within several Ma after the deposition. These cherty aggregates are useful to understand what diagenetic fluids were present and at what temperatures they circulated through the host rock. Moreover, due to susceptibility of carbonates to isotope resetting at low temperature, diagenetic silica itself is a useful proxy for near-surface conditions. Here, we summarize the results of δ¹⁸O-Δ′ 17 O investigation based on silicified carbonates and cherts from several case studies ranging from Paleocene to Proterozoic, where diagenetic conditions are constrained a priori . Silica δ¹⁸O values in our collection range from +15 to +30 ‰. The Δ′ 17 O range between −0.05 to −0.16 ‰, which indicates low-Δ′ 17 O fluids, such as strongly evaporated groundwater. In a well-studied case of Silurian dolomites from Wisconsin, fluid inclusions indicate brine at 40-90 °C. The δ¹⁸O and Δ′ 17 O values conform to highly evaporated marine water that induced silicification at 60-80 °C, likely representing the latest silica phase transition, preceding dolomitization of the host. Extending our approach to a more distant past, the Proterozoic (2.2 Ga) Kona Dolomite from the Upper Peninsula (Michigan) hosts ubiquitous silicified aggregates within the stromatolitic formation. The triple O-isotope values are consistent with high-temperature silicification and low-δ¹⁸O meteoric fluids (silica values δ¹⁸O=+15 ‰ and Δ′ 17 O = −0.05 ‰), although the history of recrystallization is complex. In general, our findings inform the early diagenetic history of sedimentary basins that might represent the best available proxy for the near-surface fluids in absence of other reliable archives.

title: Seeing the Unseen With LIFE’s Ray: Uses for Fluorescent Fossil Imaging
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research (Posters)
authors: Bier, Jeremy [1], Chrpa, Michelle E. [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Delaware, Newark, DE,

abstract:
Laser Stimulated Fluorescence (LSF) is a useful tool for revealing normally invisible aspects of fossils. This project builds and utilizes a modular LIFE’s Ray (Laser Induced Fluorescence Equipment) to identify soft tissue preservation, repairs and added material; and aid in determining possible localities for specimens missing their origin data.

The LIFE’s Ray consists of a modular mount for a visible wavelength laser and Powell lens on a rotating base. A DSLR camera fitted with a longpass filter selected to block the chosen laser’s wavelength is used to obtain a final image that includes only fluorescence from the fossil. As the LIFE’s Ray is rotated over a given duration, the laser line formed by passing through the Powell lens stimulates the fossil to fluoresce, revealing previously unseen aspects of the specimen. The relative ease of construction and access to components can make LSF via the modular design of the LIFE’s Ray a valuable educational resource for demonstrating the benefits of multispectral imaging in paleontology when compared with similar methods such as X-ray Fluorescence (XRF).

Understanding the degree of soft tissue preservation in fossils is important to form a more complete picture of a given organism’s ecology, life appearance, and taphonomic conditions. The use of LSF allows for the visualization of such structures that would otherwise be obscured or entirely invisible with visible light alone. In addition to highlighting aspects or features of a specimen that may not be visible to the naked eye alone, LSF can be used to differentiate original fossil material from repairs or added materials. LSF can also narrow potential provenance for data deficient specimens based on unique fluorescent responses associated with particular formations.

The University of Delaware Fossil Teaching and Systematic collections have thousands of specimens in varying conditions and from several phyla. Using LIFE’s Ray, we explore and test the suitability and limits of LSF in identifying soft tissue preservation within several fossils and preservation styles. Use of the LIFE’s Ray will be integrated in future undergraduate paleobiology classes as a lab exercise in soft tissue preservation and identifying histories of preparation where such data is limited.

title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Explore Disaster Scenarios, Environmental Decision-Making, and Resilience Development in Undergraduate Geoscience Education
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Bhattacharyya, Prajukti [1], Barnum, Linda [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology, Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin, Whitewater, WI, USA
(2) Department of Human Relations, University of Oklahoma, Tulsa, OK, USA
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into geoscience research and education, yet little is known about its effectiveness in helping students critically evaluate catastrophic environmental scenarios while fostering resilience rather than ecological distress. This study examined the educational use of ChatGPT.edu and Google Gemini in two undergraduate discussion-based geoscience courses at the University of Wisconsin–Whitewater: Environmental Geology (GEOLGY 301) and Volcanoes (GEOLGY 203). Students developed their own AI prompts to investigate the hypothetical impacts of a Yellowstone VEI-8 super eruption on communities surrounding Janesville, Wisconsin, a small town in Southern Wisconsin near Whitewater campus. Students compared AI-generated analyses of short-term (0–1 year) and long-term (1–10 years) impacts on human systems (food and water security, health, infrastructure, transportation, energy, and economy) and ecological systems before evaluating the accuracy of the responses using their own geological knowledge. A follow-up assignment required students to use AI to identify feasible mitigation and adaptation strategies while reflecting on their psychological responses, including stress, climate anxiety, hope, and resilience. An anonymous IRB-approved pre- and post-survey accompanied the project besides open-ended graded questions constituting both assignments. Preliminary findings indicate that students were able to identify strengths and limitations of both AI platforms and compare AI-generated information with disciplinary knowledge. Student reflections also suggested that moving from catastrophe-focused analyses toward solution-oriented problem solving encouraged greater feelings of efficacy and resilience when confronting large-scale environmental disasters. This project demonstrates that AI can serve as an effective pedagogical tool for enhancing critical thinking, disaster preparedness, and systems-level reasoning in undergraduate geoscience education. Future work could investigate differences between attitudes and responses of environmental science majors and non-majors and evaluate whether structured AI-assisted scenario planning can reduce environmental stress while strengthening climate resilience and informed decision-making in student populations.

title: The middle ear as a proxy for determining the ecology of long-extinct, earless species
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Jenkins, Kelsey M. [1], Jenkins, Xavier A. [2], Mann, Arjan [3], de Queiroz, Kevin [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Paleobiology, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC,
(2) American Museum of Natural History, New York City, New York, USA
(3) Negaunee Integrative Research Center, National Museum of Natural History, Chicago, Illinois, USA

abstract: Hearing is one of the most ubiquitous senses across tetrapods, allowing them to detect crucial information about their surroundings. Despite their utility, external ears have been secondarily lost numerous times, particularly in limbless and limb-reduced reptiles (e.g., snakes, amphisbaenians, several clades of skinks). Although this loss results in reduced hearing capacity, the primary bone of the reptilian ear, the stapes, exhibits remarkable morphological variation across “earless” reptiles. This raises the question: What, if anything, drives variation in middle ear morphology when the outer ear does not exist? Using linear discriminant analyses, we demonstrate across a wide range of limbless and limb-reduced reptiles and amphibians (n=617 specimens, 526 unique species) that convergent stapedial morphologies are present in taxa that inhabit similar environments. Fossorial taxa inhabiting dry or moist soils typically have stapes with enlarged footplates and reduced columellae and oftentimes are oriented anteriorly. Furthermore, those morphologies are distinct from those seen in terrestrial, arboreal, and aquatic forms. This trend may be associated with the acoustical properties of the media in which sound waves travel, with denser environments (e.g., compact soil or water) propagating lower frequencies more effectively than less dense environments (e.g., air). Because distinct stapedial morphologies are associated with particular environments, we hypothesize that the stapes could be used to predict ecology within Recumbirostra, a Carboniferous and Permian clade of stem amniotes which were among the first tetrapods to experience limb reduction. Machine learning algorithms classify sampled recumbirostrans as fossorial and associated with moist soils, consistent with what has been formerly inferred based on gross morphological observation of the skull. Our models suggest that the middle ear may be an indicator of ecology in many circumstances. As such, the middle ear represents a previously underexplored source of ecological information for extinct tetrapods and complements traditional approaches based on gross morphology and inner ear anatomy.
