title: Reservoir Sedimentation and Upstream Sediment Sources in Kansas
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part II)
authors: Layzell, Anthony [1], Lloyd, Cayen [2], Harris, Ted [3], Ketterer, Michael [4], Husic, Admin [5]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(2) Department of Civil, Environmental & Architectural Engineering, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(3) Kansas Biological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(4) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ,
(5) Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
abstract:
Reservoir sedimentation poses a critical threat to water storage capacity globally and particularly in the Midwestern U.S. where storage loss has continually declined over the past several decades. In Kansas, six federal reservoirs have lost over a third of their original water storage capacity, with two of those reservoirs having capacity losses of over 50%. Regional management often prioritizes streambank stabilization based on the assumption that streambanks are the dominant contributor to reservoir sedimentation. However, decades of considerable investment in bank stabilization upstream of priority reservoirs has failed to remediate sedimentation issues. Rolfe Mandel, with his expertise in alluvial stratigraphy and geomorphology, sowed the seeds and inspired over a decade of research on streambank erosion, the effectiveness of bank stabilization projects, and reservoir sediment sourcing in Kansas.

Here, we present results from a study designed to answer a simple question: are streambanks the main source of sediment to Kansas reservoirs? We employed a sediment fingerprinting approach to apportion streambank, cropland, and grassland contributions to lakebed sediment for 14 federal reservoirs. We also investigate systematic drivers, such as flow regime, land use, and geology that control sources of reservoir sedimentation.

Mixing model posterior distributions show that the dominant source contributions to reservoir sediment varies across study watersheds. Streambanks were the dominant contributor to only 5 of the 14 reservoirs with bank contributions varying from 48–69%. Cropland sediment was the dominant contributor for 7 other reservoirs with cropland contributions between 35% and 52%. However, for all but 3 of those reservoirs, cropland contributions were only marginally greater (between 1–3%) than bank sources. Grassland was the dominant sediment source for only 2 reservoirs.

Reservoirs with bank-dominated sources have contributing streams with flow regimes that are confined within the channel, reflecting a dominance of bank erosion processes. In contrast, the 3 reservoirs with the lowest bank contributions (cropland dominated) had contributing streams that experienced more frequent out-of-bank flood events. During out-of-bank flows, hydrologic connectivity expands beyond the channel to the cultivated floodplain, mobilizing vast quantities of surficial cropland soil and delivering it to downstream reservoirs. Our findings allow for the development of mitigation strategies that are tailored to the unique drivers and sources of sediment for each reservoir thereby maximizing the return on investment.

title: Do the Cordillera, Punta Algarrobo, and Mayagüez Faults connect? Implications for Seismic Hazards in Western Puerto Rico

authors: Laó-Dávila, Daniel A. [1], Bastoen, Chloe [2], Katumwehe, Andrew B. [3]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,

abstract: The Cretaceous-Paleogene arc of the northern Caribbean is currently undergoing extension in western Puerto Rico as part of the broader deformation occurring in the Mona Passage. The Punta Algarrobo and Mayagüez faults are two offshore structures striking NW-SE toward the city of Mayagüez. Previous work suggests these faults may connect to the longer onshore Cordillera Fault based on spatial proximity and orientations. Confirming structural linkage between these offshore and onshore systems is critical for regional seismic hazard assessment, as total rupture length directly controls maximum earthquake potential. This study evaluates whether the Cordillera, Punta Algarrobo, and Mayagüez faults form a continuous fault system. We mapped the westernmost extent of the Cordillera Fault using a 1-m digital elevation Model (DEM), derived from lidar, to identify geomorphic indicators such as offset drainage channels and fault scarps that would suggest active faulting. The DEM was analyzed in QGIS using terrain analysis tools such as multidirectional hillshade, slope, aspect, and roughness. In addition, we mapped the subsurface using aeromagnetic data. The aeromagnetic data were processed using Geosoft software. Multiple mathematical filters were applied to the reduction-to-the-pole (RTP) total magnetic intensity (TMI) grid to enhance magnetic anomalies associated with variations in rock types and subsurface structures. Preliminary results show limited geomorphic indicators east and north of Cerro Las Mesas. These include triangular facets, bedrock scarps, over-steepened range front, and deflected streams. However, a continuation of the Cordillera Fault system is not conspicuous at the surface. In contrast, the resulting magnetic derivative maps delineated zones of high and low magnetic gradients, which were interpreted as regional and local lithologic boundaries, lineaments, and structural features that define the basement fabric. Preliminary trend analysis reveals a northwest-trending, left-stepping en-echelon low-magnetic fabric consistent with the structural grain and orientation of the Mayagüez, Punta Algarrobo, and Cordillera fault systems.

title: Costs of Cooperation? Testing Competitive Advantages of Division of Labor in Bryozoans
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Posters)
authors: Dayton, Parker [1], Leventhal, Sarah [2], Edie, Stewart [3]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Allegheny College, Meadville, PA, USA
(2) Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
(3) Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
abstract:
Competition is often invoked as a powerful evolutionary driver, influencing how organisms survive and reproduce. Identifying traits associated with competitive outcomes offers one way to evaluate how individual ecological interactions scale to evolutionary change. In bryozoans, division of labor among polymorphic zooids is associated with greater taxonomic diversity, with improved colony performance during direct overgrowth competition as a proposed mechanism. Here, we tested whether colonies involved in overgrowth interactions differed in zooid types and morphologies from colonies without visible interactions and whether, among interacting colonies, these traits were associated with winning or losing. We quantified colony-level polymorphism and morphology of 100 shallow-water, modern bryozoan colonies collected from coastal reefs in Curaçao and Panama. We used logistic mixed-effects models to test whether a colony’s interaction status or its competitive outcome was associated with colony size, zooid size, and the number of distinct polymorphs and their relative frequencies, accounting for genus identity as a random effect.

Across genera, none of the measured traits were significantly associated with whether a colony was interacting or not, and among interacting colonies, whether it won or lost. Within Stylopoma, however, zooid size was larger in interacting colonies, but this factor did not predict competition outcomes. Larger zooids might help colonies persist during interactions long enough to reproduce before being overgrown; alternatively, zooid size might be tied to higher growth rates, which would be an important factor to consider in future models of competition. Thus, these results do not support a simple link between the colony traits measured here and competitive interaction and its outcomes, leaving the ecological basis of the association between polymorphism and diversity unresolved. Future studies incorporating growth rate and energetic efficiency may improve our understanding of how competition shapes trait evolution in bryozoans.

title: Analysis of Landslide Occurrences using SBAS InSAR, Harrison County, Southeastern Ohio
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment (Posters)
authors: Alfiero, Sarah [1], Pollock, Nicholas M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, Ohio, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA
abstract: Landslides are a prominent natural hazard that affect society and infrastructure, damaging buildings, roads, and property. These have high costs of repair and maintenance, which motivates the monitoring of active landslides and the assessment of future landslide susceptibility. Multiple factors influence slope stability and landslide susceptibility including slope angle, pore pressure, lithology, vegetation, and seismic activity. Southeast Ohio, particularly Harrison County, has significantly rugged topography with steep slopes comprised of lithologies like shale, clay, and sandstone that are susceptible to landslides. The south and eastern regions of Ohio also receive relatively high precipitation, which leads to elevated pore pressure and increases landslide risk. Additionally, hydraulic fracturing and drilling are common in Harrison County due to the underlying oil and gas resources. Fracking involves the injection of fluid into the substrate at high pressures, potentially inducing seismic activity. Here we investigate whether the observed increase in hydrofracking-induced seismicity in Southeast Ohio leads to increased rates of ground motion and landslides. To address this question, we use remote sensing techniques to visualize and analyze the relationships between seismic activity and landslide occurrences. We analyze Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data using Sentinel Application Platform (SNAP), MintPy, and ArcGIS Pro to identify where ground motion occurred during the time period between 2015-2025. We conduct interferometric SAR (InSAR) analyses on SAR images every two weeks during the study period using the Small Baseline Subset (SBAS) technique. SAR images throughout 2015 to 2025 are compared on a bi-weekly, monthly, and yearly basis. The changes in landslide occurrence are interpreted as they relate to local seismic activity and precipitation rates. Early results suggest that landslides in Harrison County increase with seismicity and precipitation. The conclusions from this study support further monitoring and management of landslide hazards to mitigate the effects on society and infrastructure.

title: Size matters: Investigating mechanisms behind body size trends in three species of Glycymerid bivalves from the Atlantic Coastal Plain
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Posters)
authors: Carnes, Ciara Lilyan [1], McMinn, Marissa [2], Moss, David Kelton [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, HUNTSVILLE, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, HUNTSVILLE, Texas, USA
(3) Department of Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, HUNTSVILLE, Texas, USA; Natural History Collection, Sam Houston State University, HUNTSVILLE, Texas, USA
abstract: A major pattern over the Phanerozoic is that of increasing body sizes in marine organisms. Larger body sizes could be driven by faster growth or longer lifespan, but so far little work has been done to investigate changes in life history strategy. Furthermore, such patterns could be the result of heterochronic processes, but understanding the nuanced patterns requires organisms which record age-at-size in their skeletal structures. Fortunately, bivalves offer an avenue to do just that. Here we present preliminary data using three species of Glycymerid bivalves: Glycymeris anteparilis (Oligocene) , G. parilis (Miocene) , and G. americana (Pliocene and Pleistocene). These species allow us to examine trends between an ancestor-descendant pair ( G. anteparilis and G. parilis ) and within a species over time ( G. americana ). To do this, we first measured the heights (anterior to posterior) of specimens from museum collections using a digital caliper to confirm reported body size increases. Next, we made polished thick sections to count and measure internal annual growth increments on selected individuals. Finally, we fit a von Bertalanffy growth equation to these data to compare the parameters k (a proxy for growth rate) and H∞ (body size), and to compare the ages of taxa at 50% of H∞, which is a proxy for reproductive maturity. Our results confirm increasing body size trends in these three species: G . anteparilis (n = 29, max = 56.75 mm, mean = 35.30 mm) is smaller than its descendant G . parilis (n = 53, max = 93.18 mm, mean = 40.66 mm), whereas Pliocene G. americana (n = 17, max = 73.96 mm, mean = 66.63) are smaller than Pleistocene individuals (n =40, max = 113.78 mm, mean = 75.72 mm). In both pairs, descendant populations grew slower and lived longer than ancestral populations ( G. anteparilis, k=0.25, max lifespan = 23; G. parilis, k=0.08, max lifespan = 87; Pliocene G. americana, k= 0.08, max lifespan = 78; Pleistocene G. americana, k=0.03, max lifespan =93). In addition, the age at 50% of H∞, is reached at a later age in descendants. In the taxa studied here, larger body sizes are attained in descendant species through hypermorphosis whereby, descendants maintain juvenile growth rates longer, reach maturity later, and live longer than their ancestors.

title: Effects of Vegetation Colonization on Shoreline Retreat Following a Channel Avulsion in the Caraulun River Delta, Timor-Leste
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Max, Ronin [1], Lyster, Sinéad [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA
(2) Earth Science, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA
abstract: River channels deliver sediment to delta shorelines, where deposition promotes land building and shoreline advance. However, channel avulsion can redirect sediment delivery to different parts of the shoreline, leaving the abandoned shoreline vulnerable to inundation and erosion. Vegetation colonization may stabilize abandoned shorelines by trapping and reinforcing sediment, but the influence of vegetation colonization on post-avulsion shoreline retreat remains poorly constrained. To address this gap, we investigated the relationship between vegetation colonization and shoreline change in the Caraulun River Delta, located in southern Timor-Leste, following a channel avulsion that occurred in the mid-to-late 2000s. We obtained Landsat imagery for a 30 year period spanning pre-, syn-, and post-avulsion conditions and generated seasonal composite imagery for each year of the study period. We used these composites to identify shoreline positions throughout the observational record and calculate shoreline retreat rates for the pre-, syn-, and post-avulsion phases. We then used post-avulsion composite images to calculate the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) within the abandoned shoreline region and assessed the relationship between vegetation colonization and shoreline retreat during the post-avulsion period. Preliminary results indicate that shoreline retreat rates decrease as vegetation cover increases, but further analyses are required to determine the strength and significance of this apparent relationship. This study will improve understanding of the role of vegetation in regulating delta shoreline response following channel avulsion.

title: Design, construction, calibration, and automation of a custom He analysis line for laser-ablation (U-Th)/He chronology
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications (Posters)
authors: Metcalf, James R. [1], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
(2) Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
abstract:
Laser-ablation (U-Th)/He chronology (LA-He) is a developing technique with significant potential to expand the application of (U-Th)/He chronology to understand different materials and geologic processes. Whereas traditional (U-Th)/He chronology involves degassing and then dissolving whole crystals, LA-He can sample He, U, and Th in situ with an excimer laser and retain important spatial information lost during conventional analyses. Additionally, LA-He can efficiently measure He, U, and Th on phases that have proven difficult to thermally degas (e.g. rutile) or dissolve (e.g. zircon).

The refinement of LA-He analytical protocols requires advances in the laboratory equipment used for the different analysis steps. Here, we describe the design, construction, automation, and metrological calibration of a custom 4 He extraction and analysis line as part of establishing LA-He methods in the University of Colorado Thermochronology Research and Instrumentation Lab (CU TRaIL). While commercial He analytical lines are available, He analysis lines that are custom-built in-house can be modified, customized, and optimized for specific lab needs and allow for continued maintenance, repair, and upgrades. Despite being both less expensive and more flexible than commercial machines, there is little information in the published literature about the methods and approaches for building a custom He line. The new custom line, called the Jimbochron, is designed to precisely measure very small (~fmol) amounts of 4 He while being fully automated and easily modifiable in the future. These goals are achieved by minimizing the line volume, adopting a unique double-hexagonal manifold configuration, installing a high-sensitivity quadrupole mass spectrometer, and developing editable LabView code for instrument communication and automation that is straightforward to update. We also explain the steps used to calibrate the Jimbochron metrologically from first principles with a new in-house calibration volume to ensure high-accuracy He measurements. The Jimbochron accurately and precisely measures small gas amounts (<0.1 fmol) and now routinely generates accurate and precise He data for laser-ablation (U-Th)/He applications.

title: Felsic Rocks in the Eastern Bushveld Complex: Indicators of Early Underplating of the Kaapvaal Basement?
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Hetherington, Callum J. [1], Lever, Megan [2], Roberts, Richard James [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
(2) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA

abstract:
The Bushveld Complex, best known for the mafic-ultramafic Rustenburg Layered Suite, contains many examples of granitic rocks commonly attributed to the Lebowa Granite Suite. In the eastern Steelpoort region, such units are found at Magnet Heights, Tigershoek, and Steelpoort Park, and are attributed to the Nebo Granite, the most voluminous sub-unit of the Lebowa Granite Suite. Models for their petrogenesis include fractional crystallization, assimilation, and crustal melting, but geologic and petrologic connection between the granites and the underlying Rustenburg Suite remain uncertain. Samples from Magnet Heights, Tigershoek, and Steelpoort Park localities were petrographically and geochemically characterized and selected samples were dated using LA-ICPMS U-Pb methods.

The three felsic units are geochemically and lithologically similar to the Bushveld Nebo Granite and likely share a common history. But no direct connection between the individual units was established. In addition, the Magnet Heights samples have evidence for magma contributions from a non-Bushveld magmatic system. Inherited xenocrystic cores in zircon from Magnet Heights and Steelpoort Park suggest mass contributions to these granites from (meta)-sedimentary host-rocks. The U-Pb ages of the Steelpoort Park and Magnet Heights samples are 2060 to 2055 Ma, and skew older than 2056 Ma Bushveld magmatism. Their ages conflict with their lithological and geochemical affinity to the Bushveld Nebo Granite, but may be reconciled by a model that involves widespread underplating of the Kaapvaal basement producing early, low-volume partial melts prior to the main phase of mafic Bushveld magmatism.

affiliations: (1) University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,

abstract:
Salinity is an important environmental control that is difficult to reconstruct in the geologic past. Sedimentary trace metal ratios such as Sr/Ba, S/TOC, and B/Ga are gaining popularity in the paleoenvironmental research community and being applied across a wide range of geologic timeframes. These trace metal ratios are qualitative indicators of salinity and capable of distinguishing between fresh, brackish, and marine conditions. A reliable quantitative paleosalinity tool remains elusive. Preliminary data described in this presentation suggest a potential use for sedimentary thallium (Tl) isotope ratios as a quantitative paleosalinity tool.

Thallium isotope ratios within the waters of modern semi-enclosed basins are set by the relative contributions of freshwater and seawater to the system. Freshwaters have an average ε 205 Tl value of -2.0‱, whereas the globally homogenous open ocean ε 205 Tl value is -6.0‱. Natural brackish waters typically possess intermediate ε 205 Tl values between -2.0‱ and -6.0‱, dependent on their relative Tl contributions from freshwater and seawater. These water column Tl isotope ratios can be transferred to the underlying sediments, so long as the local redox conditions are not conducive to the precipitation of manganese oxide minerals.

Sedimentary Tl isotope data from multiple modern to Holocene sites with known or estimated salinities plot along a binary freshwater-seawater salinity mixing line. These sites include Deming Lake in Minnesota, the East Gotland Basin in the Baltic Sea, Siders Pond on Cape Cod, and the Cariaco Basin. Younger sediments from the Black Sea and East Gotland Basin, both of which could have been impacted by strong anthropogenic Tl sources, plot well above the mixing line. The case for anthropogenic forcing is stronger in the East Gotland Basin.To continue testing the proxy, we will evaluate and obtain more Tl isotope ratio data from Holocene sediment cores from Siders Pond, Landsort Deep in the Baltic Sea, the Old Currituck Inlet in North Carolina, and the Gulf of Mexico.

title: Exhumation of the Canadian Rocky Mountain fold-thrust belt revealed through detrital zircon fission-track thermochronology from the Alberta foreland basin
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond (Posters)
authors: Basnet, Deepak [1], Jepson, Gilby [2], George, Sarah W. M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, The University of North Carolina, Chapel HIll, North Carolina, USA; Department of Mines and Geology, Government of Nepal, Lainchour, Kathmandu, Nepal
(2) Department of Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, The University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, The University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA
abstract:
The Canadian Cordillera is an archetypal thin-skinned fold-thrust belt whose evolution is used to understand the kinematics of fold thrust-belts globally. Despite its prominence, the timing of Mesozoic shortening in the Canadian Cordillera remains poorly resolved due to significant post-orogenic unroofing in the late Cenozoic. The Late Jurassic to Paleocene Alberta foreland basin preserves a continuous record of sediment derived from Canadian Cordillera, which provides an archive for reconstructing mountain-building processes.

To quantify exhumation rates and sediment transfer from the Canadian Cordillera to the Alberta foreland basin we apply detrital zircon fission-track (ZFT) thermochronology, lag-time analysis to nine sandstone samples from Jurassic through Paleogene stratigraphic units. Zircon fission-track thermochronology and its cooling ages will record cooling through deep structural levels (~210–270 °C; ~8 – 12 km), likely associated with the Mesozoic unroofing of the presently exposed thrust sheets. New zircon U-Pb ages are integrated with published detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology and biostratigraphy to establish depositional age constraints. Together, these datasets will be enabling for calculation of lag times, the difference between depositional age and cooling age, which will be used to evaluate temporal variations in erosion rates and unroofing.

We hypothesize that intervals with increased shortening within the Canadian Cordillera will be associated with shorter lag times, reflecting exhumation caused by fold-thrust belt development. Conversely, longer lag times and broader cooling-age distributions may indicate increased sediment recycling and/or periods of tectonic quiescence.

authors: Hups, Kent Michael [1], Kortyna, Cullen David [2], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [3]

abstract:
Abstract

Partnerships between universities and high schools are uncommon and often limited to speakers and field trips. However when the partnership extends authentic research into the high school classroom where the students are actively assisting university researchers, the partnership takes on an entirely different scope. A university-high school problem-based learning (PBL) approach benefits the high school students by introducing them to the construction and execution of current scientific research, including forming testable hypotheses, choosing appropriate methodologies, and performing data analysis and interpretation. This approach also has important benefits for university staff and researchers, including improving their understanding of high-school curricula and making suggestions on vertical alignment ideas that will better prepare students for college.

In the spring of 2025 and 2026, the Thermochronology Research and Instrumentation Lab (TRaIL) at the University of Colorado Boulder (CU) and the 11/12th grade geology classes at Northglenn High School collaborated in a PBL partnership SNODASE (Students of NOrthglenn Date Ancient Snowball Earth). This outreach collaboration engaged the students in real geochronology research performed in the CU TRaIL, and the content of the research was worked into a PBL curriculum for the 11/12th grade geology classes. SNODASE is centered on performing detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology of the Tava sandstone, a Snowball Earth-era sandstone, to determine the Tava sandstone’s provenance and timing of deposition.

Students actively participated in rock sampling, preparation, acquisition of U-Pb dates by LA-ICP-MS, and U-Pb data analysis and interpretation of detrital zircon provenance data, culminating in a student-led poster symposium judged by CU researchers. This partnership exposed ~160 students to key research processes such as reading scientific journals, maintaining analytical rigor, working with highly sensitive instruments, visualizing and interpreting data, appropriate use of AI for scientific purposes, and showcasing results and findings. Authentic collaborations between universities and high schools can have lasting impacts on scientific training, and provide early exposure for students to research opportunities at the undergraduate level.

title: Mixing of River Water and Groundwater in Aquifers near Dam-Controlled Rivers
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions
authors: Neupauer, Roseanna M [1], Greer, Anderson [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil, Environmental and Architectural Engineering, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Environmental Engineering Program, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: In the shallow subsurface in the vicinity of a losing river, river water and groundwater mix, promoting biogeochemical reactions as the waters with distinct chemical compositions interact. The position and extent of the zone of mixing and reaction is controlled by the flow dynamics in the river and aquifer. In a dam-controlled river, the river experiences periodic fluctuations in water level due to hydropeaking as water is released from the dam, leading to periodic fluctuations of the water flux between a dam-controlled river and the adjacent aquifer. These fluctuations ultimately produce spatio-temporally-varying velocity fields within a heterogeneous aquifer, which are marked by pathways for coalescence of river water and groundwater that create hot spots of reaction. This work investigates the spatio-temporal evolution of the mixing zone and identifies reaction hot spots within the mixing zone. We use numerical simulations of groundwater flow and river/aquifer exchange to calculate the spatio-temporally-varying flow fields for several combinations of hydropeaking parameters (period and amplitude of river stage fluctuation), river geometry (straight or meandering), and aquifer hydraulic conductivity (mean, variance, and correlation length of smoothly varying random fields). We use advective particle tracking to delineate the extent of the mixing zone, and we use Lagrangian coherent structures (LCS) to identify regions of high and low mixing to reveal locations of reaction hot spots. Lagrangian coherent structures identify the skeleton of complex flow fields and can act as dynamical attractors of fluid trajectories, promoting mixing if two fluids of distinct chemical composition coalesce. By comparing the evolution of both the mixing zone and the LCSs, we identify hot spots of reaction and determine whether their locations change in time. These hot spots of reaction are vital for river purification and nutrient cycling, so understanding the relationship between human-controlled flow conditions, like hydropeaking, and the locations of reaction hot spots is critical for maintaining river water quality.

abstract: The middle Cambrian to Lower Ordovician Los Cabos Group from Asturias, Spain, constitutes shallow-marine deposits that have been previously interpreted as originated in tide- and wave-dominated coastal subenvironments (e.g. tidal flats, lagoon, beach, shoreface). However, investigations in the area have found evidence of deposition in storm-flood deltas. The goal of this study is to perform a facies analysis of the Los Cabos Group to construct a depositional model based on current advances in deltaic sedimentology. About 5700 m of strata were logged between the towns of Luarca and Cadavedo (Spain), describing sedimentary facies and facies associations. This group consists of mudstone, sandstone, muddy sandstone, and sandy mudstone deposited on shelf, tide- and wave-dominated coasts, tide-dominated, fluvial-influenced coasts, and storm-flood-dominated delta environments. Evidence of storm-flood deltas is extensive and includes: (1) cm- to m-thick, mudstone, sandy mudstone, and muddy sandstone structureless or with normal gradation, banding, load casts and convolute bedding, associated with hummocky cross-stratified sandstone, interpreted as storm-influenced hyperpycnal flows; (2) heterolithic bedding containing low-angle, current-ripple (regular and climbing), wave-ripple (regular and aggrading), and micro-hummocky cross-stratified, muddy sandstone, constituting prodelta deposits, (3) hummocky and swaley cross-stratified muddy sandstone and sandstone and low-angle cross-bedded to parallel-laminated sandstone, characterizing delta-front deposits; and (4) cross-bedded sandstone, heterolithic bedding with low-angle and current-ripple cross-laminated sandstone, and structureless sandy mudstone, representing distributary channels. Characterizing the depositional model of the Los Cabos Group will improve our understanding of the stacking patterns and stratigraphy architecture of storm-flood deltas. Interestingly, the storm-influenced hyperpycnal flows may be analogous to slurry flows reported from the Cretaceous of the North Sea, a rare type of sediment-gravity flows transitional between turbidity and debris flows. Moreover, the fact that these deltas were active in the Cambrian and Ordovician presents the opportunity to analyze storm-flood processes in deltas fed by braided-sheet fluvial systems, before the colonization of land plants.

abstract: Dry coniferous forests in the Southern Rocky Mountains are experiencing widespread increases in tree mortality and high-severity wildfires. Understanding the societal implications of these changes requires a long-term context for interactions among climate, vegetation, wildfire, and humans. However, high-resolution sedimentary archives are rare from elevations that are most sensitive to change. Whereas most sedimentary records from the Southern Rocky Mountains are from high-elevation lakes, dramatic changes, including high-intensity wildfire and drought-related tree mortality are centered in warmer, lower-elevation forests and woodlands. We addressed this limitation with a multiproxy record from Santa Fe Lake, NM, a small subalpine lake. We combined pollen analysis to document local to regional vegetation, with macroscopic charcoal to reconstruct local wildfire history, and microscopic charcoal and molecular markers to infer regional biomass burning. Santa Fe Lake formed as alpine glaciers receded in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains after 14,000 cal yr BP. Pollen data indicate that ponderosa pine forests, the dominant lower-elevation, forest type, expanded after 12,200 cal yr BP. Subalpine forests reached Santa Fe Lake by 10,300 cal yr BP. The influx of both macroscopic charcoal and levoglucosan increase after 10,000 cal yr BP and remain high until about 5500 cal yr BP. However, microscopic charcoal influx, an indicator of regional burning, is generally low during this period. This result may mean that during the warmest period of the Holocene, most biomass burning occurred in subalpine forests. Macroscopic charcoal and levoglucosan influx decline from about 5500-2000 cal yr BP as microscopic charcoal influx remains low. Influx of microscopic charcoal and levoglucosan, but not macroscopic charcoal, more than double after 2000 cal yr BP, indicating an increase in regional, but not local, burning. This late Holocene increase in regional burning coincides with the expansion of maize agriculture by ancient Puebloans and probably resulted from the use of fire to open lower-elevation forests for cultivation. Maize pollen, an unambiguous but rare cultural indicator, is consistently present in sediments from 800-350 cal yr BP (1150-1600 cal yr CE), which demonstrates the intensity of agriculture at lower elevations near Santa Fe Lake. Our data record millennial-scale interactions among climate, vegetation, and wildfire but also demonstrate that the largest changes in regional burning during the Holocene resulted from human impacts.

title: Geologic Salinity Sources in the South Platte River Basin within Colorado
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: Sebol, Lesley [1], Buch Leviatan, Orna [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Potential groundwater salinity contributions in the South Platte River sourced from sedimentary bedrock were studied from the Colorado Front Range to the Nebraska state line. Eleven geologic bedrock formations or groups located at or near the ground surface spanning the Pennsylvanian-Permian-Triassic (P-T) to Neogene were sampled for salinity constituents.

Sixty weathered rock outcrop samples were collected, and ten unweathered core samples were obtained from the USGS Core Research Center in Lakewood, Colorado. All 70 rock samples were submitted for laboratory leachability via water extraction for soluble metals (arsenic, barium, boron, calcium, iron, magnesium, manganese, potassium, selenium, sodium, & uranium), bromide, chloride, fluoride, nitrate as N, nitrite as N, nitrate/nitrite as N, sulfate, Alkalinity as CaCO 3 , hardness, electrical conductivity (EC), sodium adsorption ratio (SAR by wet extraction), pH (wet extraction), and total dissolved solids (TDS by filterable residue).

Unweathered rock concentrations higher than the weathered rock occurred for all except for the youngest bedrock (Paleogene White River Group and Neogene Ogallala Formation). Where unweathered rock leachate concentrations exceeded the weathered rock range, possible loss/dissolution due to the weathering process was inferred.

The Pierre Shale and White River Group had the most salinity constituents with maximum and median concentrations, respectively. The Pierre Shale included TDS, sodium, calcium, magnesium, chloride, and sulfate. The White River Group included potassium, magnesium, and bicarbonate as HCO 3 . One weathered Pierre Shale sample had gypsum crystals and white salt-like precipitants. Although avoided during sampling, it contained the highest TDS and sulfate concentrations (10,800 and 6,490 mg/L, respectively).

When graphing TDS versus the various rock salinity constituents in both milligrams/Liter and milliequivalents/Liter, sulfate was the largest contributor. The highest rock leachate sulfate concentrations were measured in the weathered Pierre Shale, P-T Lyons Formation, and Laramie Formation. Using our compiled bedrock geologic map, the Pierre Shale accounts for 26.2 % of the South Platte River Basin area. Together, these three formations account for 43.5 % of the urban/ag basin.

title: Detailed Analysis of a Central Wisconsin Pegmatite and Implications for Critical Element Exploration
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Roys, Kybie D. [1], Stoner, Ghost [2], Buchholz, Thomas [3], Bhattacharyya, Prajukti [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology, and Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin - Whitewater, Whitewater, WI, USA
(2) Geography, Geology, and Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin - Whitewater, Whitewater, WI, USA
(3) Stevens Point, Wisconsin, USA
(4) Geography, Geology, and Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin - Whitewater, Whitewater, WI, USA
abstract:
Critical elements, such as Rare Earth Elements (REEs) and High Field Strength Elements (HFSEs), have high societal and economic importance for technological advancement. The conditions concentrating these elements into economic deposits need detailed study. Pegmatites are common igneous formations often enriched with REE and HFSE bearing fluids leading to unusual mineral formations. This research focuses on a pegmatite from the Stettin Complex in Central Wisconsin to understand how REEs may have been concentrated in different minerals. The Stettin Complex is the oldest (1565 Ma) and most alkaline of the four intrusions of the Wausau Syenite Complex (WSC). Previous work on the WSC and associated pegmatites have shown presence of REE-bearing minerals, such as Euxenite-Y and Monazite-Ce. We hypothesize that our studied pegmatite can provide important information about REE mobilization. Five samples were collected from different parts of the pegmatite: sample A from the contact area between the pegmatite and surrounding rocks, sample D from the core of the pegmatite, and samples B, C, and E from areas between the core and the contact zone. Hand sample analysis of mineral size shows significant heterogeneity, with crystals of arfvedsonite and aegirine up to several centimeters in size next to millimeter scale albite crystals. Sample A displays zones of coloration and textural change that may imply fluid flow. Additionally, all samples show distinct red fluorescence under 254nm ultraviolet light which may be due to the presence of trace elements as well as REEs.

In order to conduct detailed chemical and mineralogical analysis, a rotary tool was used for precise extraction of materials to be analyzed by Powder X-Ray Diffraction (PXRD). Preliminary mineralogical data from PXRD aligns with previous work. These data will be complemented by future chemical analysis to identify any economically viable critical elements. In this poster we present our findings and implications for future research.

title: Depositional Gradients Shape Early Triassic Carbonate Geochemistry: Insights From a 500 km Transect of the Virgin Limestone (USA)
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)
authors: Todes, Jordan P. [1], Bryant, Roger N. [2], Pruss, Sara B. [3], Gill, Benjamin C. [4], Blättler, Clara L. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA; The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
(2) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(3) Smith College, Northampton, MA,
(4) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(5) University of Chicago, Chicago, IL,
abstract:
The Early Triassic reflects the prolonged scars of the end-Permian mass extinction, as recorded in depauperate marine communities and marked geochemical instability. Geochemical records have long been employed to explore the drivers of this crisis, and have been used to frame hypotheses about the extinction and subsequent delayed environmental recovery, typically centered around global-scale environmental processes such as expanded shallow-marine anoxia, extreme hothouse conditions, and widespread ocean acidification. As an alternative, a growing body of evidence suggests that facies-dependent and post-depositional factors may exert a dominant influence on Early Triassic geochemical signals, particularly given the widespread occurrence of ‘anachronistic’ carbonate facies during this interval. As such, distinguishing the impact of local and diagenetic vs. global signatures would be useful for understanding the timing and drivers of Early Triassic paleoenvironmental recovery.

The Lower Triassic Virgin Limestone Member of the Moenkopi Formation and the Union Wash Formation (collectively, the Moenkopi Platform) span a transect from shoreline to deep basin. Collectively, they contain both a variety of anachronistic carbonate facies – including microbial bioherms, seafloor carbonate fans, subtidal laminated micrites, and flat-pebbled conglomerates – and evidence for biotic recovery, including the oldest Triassic metazoan bioherms. The Moenkopi Platform therefore provides an ideal venue to explore how depositional gradients and facies-level environmental variability shape Early Triassic geochemical records.

Here, we leverage a multi-proxy carbonate geochemical framework (δ 13 C, δ 18 O, δ 44/40 Ca, δ 26 Mg, trace-metals) to help distinguish the relative importance of global paleoceanographic change, local environment variability, and diagenetic processes on Moenkopi Platform carbonate geochemistry. Preliminary results suggest that there are strong depositional gradients in both primary geochemical signals and the extent of diagenetic resetting. Nearshore sections are generally typified by fossiliferous facies, and ‘altered’, seawater-buffered geochemical signatures. In contrast, deeper shelf, slope, and basin sections preserve a diverse assortment of facies and generally capture ‘primary’, sediment-buffered geochemical signatures. These patterns coexist with an asymmetric δ 13 C gradient, in which δ 13 C values tend to be heaviest in nearshore and slope settings, and significantly lighter on the shelf. Collectively, these results suggest that depositional gradients may have a profound influence on preserved sedimentary geochemistry. Put another way, the massive environmental variability recorded in the Moenkopi Platform may be partially facies- and depth-dependent, suggesting Early Triassic records must be interpreted through this lens.

title: Exhumation and Extensional History of the Priest River Metamorphic Core Complex: Apatite Low-Temperature Thermochronology Constraints on the Collapse of the North American Cordillera
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Saha, Rajib Kumar [1], Jess, Scott [2]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
(2) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
abstract:
The North American Cordillera (NAC) underwent widespread Cenozoic crustal extension and orogenic collapse, expressed most clearly through the formation and exhumation of metamorphic core complexes along low-angle detachment faults. Positioned at the critical juncture between the northern and central segments of the orogen, the Priest River Metamorphic Core Complex (PRMCC) is bounded to the east by the east-dipping Purcell Trench Fault and to the west by the west-dipping Newport Fault. Together, these structures exhume mid-crustal metamorphic rocks from beneath a brittle upper plate; yet the timing, magnitude, and style of extension remained incompletely resolved.

To address this gap, low-temperature thermochronologic (apatite fission track [AFT] and (U-Th-Sm)/He [AHe]), apatite U-Pb, and whole-rock geochemical data have been collected from bedrock. Average AHe ages of 103.1±6.2 Ma reflect prolonged residence time in the helium partial retention zone, further modified by radiation damage effects. AFT ages from seven samples range from 26.1 ± 3.1 Ma to 55.0 ± 3.9 Ma, with mean track lengths of 10.2-13.5 μm indicating spatially variable exhumation histories. Thermal history models, constrained by U-Pb ages and previously published K-Ar dates, reveal two distinct cooling episodes. Samples east of the Purcell Trench fault record an earlier moderate phase of cooling of ~14-16 °C/Myr between ~80 and 60 Ma. Samples within the core complex display a later major phase of Eocene cooling (~55-35 Ma) at rates of ~21°C/Myr, with little evidence of any subsequent reheating or cooling. Additionally, whole-rock geochemistry infers a continental arc setting derived from partial melting of a metasomatized mantle wedge with variable crustal assimilation; when combined with U-Pb geochronology, these results imply that the granite occupying the core of the PRMCC likely resided at ~40-50 Myr before rapid rising through the crust.

Thermal-history models based on AFT and AHe data demonstrate that the PRMCC experienced multi-phase Eocene exhumation, representing one of the earliest extensional events in the central NAC. While multi-phase exhumation has also been documented in the Canadian Cordillera, it is not confined to the Eocene there. In contrast, the PRMCC preserves a significantly earlier multi-stage exhumation history that appears unique within the central NAC, providing new constraints on the age, rates, driving mechanisms, and spatial variability of Cordilleran collapse.

title: Cross-sets as a Paleohydrologic Proxy: Insights from the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum of the Bighorn Basin, Wyoming
session_title: Morphodynamics and preservation of bedforms across scales and environments
authors: Novak, Filip [1], Howes, Bolton John [2], Foreman, Brady Zangs [3], Mehra, Akshay [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA; Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA
(2) Wheaton College, Wheaton, Illinois, USA
(3) Western Washington University-Geology Department, Bellingham, WA,
(4) University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
abstract: Sedimentary structures such as cross-sets encode paleohydrologic information about the environments they formed in. For example, researchers have proposed that the variance in thickness of fluvial cross-sets can reveal whether beds formed in equilibrium (i.e., steady-state) or disequilibrium (i.e., flashy flood) conditions: A greater coefficient of variation (CV) indicates thorough reworking under a steady flow, while lower CVs are indicative of rapid changes in flow velocity. Therefore, cross-sets may facilitate understanding of flood behavior in the sedimentary record. Leveraging this fact, analyses of cross-sets from analogous climatic events in Earth’s past could provide insights into modern fluvial responses, a utility that is especially valuable given the fact that climate change-driven flooding represents a major risk to millions of people that live near rivers today. The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM), which witnessed a drastic rise in temperatures (6-8 °C) likely coupled with increased precipitation variability, is one such analogous event. Here, we analyze over 200 cross-set thicknesses from strata before, during, and after the PETM in the Willwood Formation of Wyoming, determining CVs for each. Despite paleosol, paleofloral, and trace fossil evidence for increased rainfall variability during the PETM, we observe no significant change in bedform dynamics across the event, with cross-sets recording disequilibrium conditions throughout the Willwood Formation. The lack of an observed signal, combined with a dominance of disequilibrium dynamics in the stratigraphic record, raises questions about the utility of cross-sets as a paleohydrologic proxy. We propose that cross-sets may not be sufficiently sensitive to climate-forced changes at an intraformational scale. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of further investigation into how rivers preserve hydrologic signals, with implications for the broader interpretation of depositional environments.

title: Detrital Zircon U-Pb & Hf Isotopic Analysis of the Gravina-Nutzotin Basin, Southeast Alaska: Insights into timing of Insular and Intermontane Interaction

abstract: The Gravina-Nutzotin basin (GNB) formed within a subduction-related setting along the northwestern Laurentia margin between ca. 156 and 110 Ma. In Southeast Alaska, the GNB consists of two facies based on their inferred depositional basement; a western facies depositionally overlying the Alexander and Wrangellia terranes (Insular Superterrane) and an eastern facies interpreted to overlie the Yukon-Tanana, Taku, and Stikine terranes (Intermontane Superterrane). The GNB is dominated by marine turbiditic sequences of argillite, phyllite, greywacke, and minor pebble conglomerate. Many aspects of the basin, such as its width, provenance characteristics, and deformation history, are poorly known. To improve our understanding of basin formation and provenance, we analyzed four detrital zircon samples from the western facies in the Petersburg area for U-Pb (n = 1,119) and Lu-Hf (n = 340) isotopes by LA-ICPMS. Detrital zircon age and ƐHf(t) values yield major Mesozoic age peaks of ca. 200, 150 and 120 Ma which are highly juvenile, subordinate Paleozoic age peaks at ca. 430 and 350 Ma that range from juvenile to evolved, and minor Proterozoic and Late Archean grains ranging from 2700-560 Ma which are mostly juvenile. Juvenile (+15 to +5) Paleozoic grains are compatible with juvenile sources in the Alexander and Yukon-Tanana terranes. The 600-360 Ma grains of the intermediate to evolved (+5 to -15) population are consistent with the Alexander terrane Banks/Saint Elias Mtns assemblage, whereas the 360-320 Ma grains are more compatible with evolved Intermontane Superterrane sources. The juvenile (+11 to +4) 240-220 Ma group is most similar to the juvenile Triassic arc of the Intermontane terrane. The juvenile (+14 to +5) ca. 200-170 Ma group is compatible with the Jurassic Insular arc source. Juvenile (+16 to +5) Jurassic and Cretaceous grains are inferred to be derived from the active arc associated with the GNB, providing maximum depositional ages that approximate true depositional ages. Previous studies suggest western facies deposits are completely Insular derived; however, one new sample (25ZP06) contains evolved Carboniferous grains that indicate input from Intermontane sources. These results suggest mixing of both eastern and western sources into a relatively narrow GNB formed inboard of the active magmatic arc built on juvenile crust of the Alexander terrane.

title: Temporal Reconstruction of Pedogenic Carbonate Formation Using Clumped Isotope Analysis and Seasonal Soil Moisture from Shinfa River Fluvial Terrace Soils, Northwestern Lowlands of Ethiopia
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Diriirsa, Meklit Yadeta [1], Tabor, Neil J. [2], Kappelman, John W [3], Rosenau, Nicholas A [4], Khormali, Farhad [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Southern Methodist Univ, CUL Fond, Dallas, TX, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Southern Methodist University, Earth Sciences, Dallas, TX,
(3) Department of Anthropology, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(4) Environmental Protection Specialist at US Environmental Protection Agency, Manassas, Virginia, USA

abstract:
The seasonality of precipitation strongly influences the timing and temperature of pedogenic carbonate formation. The Shinfa River valley fluvial terrace landscape in the northwestern lowlands of Ethiopia includes carbonate-bearing clay and silty clay soils that were examined to understand the conditions of carbonate formation in this semi-arid tropical climate. Twenty-one years of meteorological records and geochemical data from nine fluvial terrace soil profiles were integrated with clumped-isotope thermometry and carbonate δ 18 O values to estimate the temperature and soil-water δ 18 O values during carbonate crystallization and to quantify the seasonal soil-moisture balance of these terrace soils.

Pedogenic carbonate δ 18 O values range from −7.7 to 2.0‰ VPDB (mean = −1.7‰; n = 38) and Δ 47 -derived crystallization temperatures range from 16 to 28°C (mean = 20 ± 5°C; n = 19), corresponding to reconstructed soil water δ 18 O values of −5.3 to 3.8‰ VSMOW (mean = – 0.5‰; n = 19).

Neither pedogenic carbonate δ 18 O values nor Δ 47 temperatures show systematic variation with depth or terrace-related trends. However, the estimated Δ 47 soil carbonate crystallization temperature is lower than any contemporary mean monthly soil and air temperature. A monthly soil water balance model shows that precipitation exceeds potential evapotranspiration during July–September, resulting in seasonal soil moisture recharge, whereas evapotranspiration dominates from October through June, producing prolonged soil moisture deficits. The modeled maximum soil water storage (25.6 cm) closely agrees with texture-based water-holding capacity estimates (27.1 cm), indicating near-saturation of the soil profile during peak rainfall and limited surplus water available for leaching during exceptionally wet years. Comparison of clumped isotope-derived carbonate formation temperatures with modeled seasonal soil temperatures indicates that pedogenic carbonate precipitation occurred primarily during November, coinciding with declining soil moisture following the rainy season. Reconstructed soil water δ 18 O values closely overlap with those of wet-season Shinfa River water δ 18 O (~ – 2‰, n = 95) values, suggesting that carbonate formation occurred before substantial evaporative oxygen isotope enrichment of soil water.

This modern study provides an environmental framework for comparison with the Shinfa Metema1 (74 ka) human occupation site on the ancestral Shinfa River by comparing stable isotopes of these modern soils with fossil river mollusks, ostrich eggshells, and vertebrate teeth.

abstract: Quantifying sulfate sources in tributaries is key to quantifying the efficiency of carbon dioxide export as dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and identifying geologic formations which source pyrite-derived arsenic that contaminates low-lying floodplains. The objective of this study is to track sulfate sources in Brahmaputra River tributaries which originate in the Eastern Himalayas, the Belt of Schuppen, and the Shillong Plateau. We measured pH, alkalinity, major ion and trace element chemistry, sulfate δ 34 S, and DIC δ 13 C at 28 locations along tributaries and the mainstem river on all sides of the Brahmaputra Basin in the wet (August) and dry seasons (February). Nine sites were re-sampled during both seasons. We examined the data spatially (n = 56), temporally (n = 18) and performed geochemical forward modeling. In the wet season the nine re-sampled rivers contained higher DIC (median 69 mg/L) than in the dry season (46 mg/L). Calcium concentrations in the wet season (18 mg/L) were higher than in the dry season (14 mg/L). In contrast, sulfate concentrations in the wet season (18 mg/L) were lower than the dry season (34 mg/L). pH was lower in the wet season (7.7) than in the dry season (8.1). Dry season rivers (n = 28) exhibit the 1:1 Ca:SO 4 molar relationship predicted by: 1) calcite dissolution by sulfuric acid from pyrite oxidation, and/or 2) gypsum dissolution. Water type transformed from Ca-HCO 3 to Mg-Ca-SO 4 from the wet to dry seasons. Sulfate concentrations were generally high in the Siang Valley with three tributaries having δ 34 S values ranging between +19 and +27‰ compared to the median +4‰ across all seasons and sites, indicating sulfate sourced from marine gypsum. Gypsum dissolution helps explain why half of all samples were supersaturated with respect to calcite, contributing to CO 2 sequestration. DIC δ 13 C was higher in the dry season (-8‰) than in the wet season (-12‰), indicating a greater proportion of marine calcite-sourced DIC in the dry season but more carbon from respiration of plant organic matter in the wet season. The relatively high δ 34 S values in rivers with the highest sulfate concentrations suggests that only minor amounts of sulfate are derived from pyrite oxidation. Therefore, pyrite oxidation has a limited role in titrating alkalinity and producing arsenic in the Brahmaputra Basin.

title: Dust activity in East Asia in the 21st century: Beyond declining
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Li, Junran Jimmy [1], Pan, Qidi [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
(2) Geography, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
abstract: With combined dryland of nearly 7.0 million km 2 in China and Mongolia, East Asia is a significant source of dust in the global dust cycle. Multiple lines of evidence showed that dust activities in the region, have declined since the 1970s. Despite intense debate on the contributing factors and their relative importance, most studies agree that improved vegetation cover, the weakening of surface wind, and increased soil moisture are the primary contributors. These studies and those reporting a decline in dust activity in East Asia, however, focused predominantly on records and observations in China, with little known about the role of Mongolia-sourced dust in the dynamics of dust in East Asia. The relative contributions of Mongolia and China to both total and decreasing dust emissions in this area remain unclear. In this study, we used a well-established model to quantify dust emissions during 2001–2023 in East Asia. The results show that China dominated the reduction in East Asian dust activities, contributing 70% to the regional downward trend (−13 Tg yr⁻¹) over the study period. Reductions were driven primarily by increased vegetation cover and soil moisture in China, with more variable contributions from vegetation and wind speed in Mongolia, highlighting distinct regional responses to climatic and land use changes. Precise quantification of these disproportionate contributions from China and Mongolia is critical for developing targeted land management strategies to mitigate transboundary dust impacts across East Asia.

title: Mineral Weathering Reflects Changing Hydrology in Southwest Greenland
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Salinas Reyes, Jenifer Tatiana [1], Martin, Ellen E. [2], Martin, Jonathan B. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(3) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
abstract: Arctic amplification of global warming is reshaping the hydrology of Greenland through glacier retreat, increased rainfall, and permafrost thaw. The intensified hydrological cycle and exposure of glacially comminuted fine-grained sediments in deglaciating landscapes enhance mineral weathering, which regulates stream water composition and greenhouse gas cycling. Consequently, temporal variations in stream water geochemistry provide a means to identify changes in mineral weathering and track evolving hydrological processes in deglaciating landscapes. Here, we analyze the elemental and radiogenic isotope geochemistry of water samples collected during the relatively dry 2022 and relatively wet 2023 melt seasons from one proglacial and two deglaciated watersheds in southwest Greenland that have similar underlying granitoid bedrock but contrasting exposure ages (~0, ~7, and ~10 kyr). We also analyze mineral separates from stream bedload to identify the mineral sources controlling solute chemistry. Variations in mineral weathering across seasonal, annual, and millennial timescales reflect changes in subglacial drainage and active layer/permafrost dynamics. Relatively high concentrations of REE in the proglacial stream (0 kyr), Mg, Ca, and Fe in the most recently deglaciated stream (7 kyr), and Na and K in the older deglaciated stream (10 kyr) indicate preferential weathering of REE-bearing accessory minerals, such as allanite and apatite, during early exposure, followed by greater influence of mafic rock-forming minerals, including hornblende and biotite, and ultimately feldspars with increasing weathering extent. Superimposed on this millennial-scale evolution, intra- and inter-seasonal hydrological changes modify weathering reactions. Higher REE concentrations during the wetter 2023 melt season, particularly in the youngest deglaciated watershed, suggest enhanced weathering of recently thawed fresh sediments likely due to rainfall-driven deepening of the active layer. In the proglacial stream, dilution of elemental concentrations around mid-June reflects the transition from distributed to channelized subglacial drainage, while episodic enrichments in redox-sensitive elements are consistent with subglacial lake outbursts. Preferential weathering of accessory silicates during early deglaciation and permafrost thaw would strengthen the negative feedback of silicate weathering on climate warming as they consume more CO 2 on a per-mole basis than more abundant and weathering-resistant minerals such as feldspars. Our results demonstrate that mineral-specific chemical weathering signatures serve as tracers of hydrological changes over a range of timescales in deglaciating Arctic landscapes.

title: Investigating Antarctic Ice Sheet Growth During the Middle Miocene
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence (Posters)
authors: Doiron, Oliff G. [1], Kraus, Emily [2], Acosta, Renee Paul [3], Browne, Imogen [4], Halberstadt, Anna Ruth [5], Lam, Adriane R. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY,
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(3) J. Shukla Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
(4) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
(5) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(6) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
abstract: During the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO; 16.9–14.7 Ma), Earth’s climate was warmer and wetter than the modern (global mean surface temperature was 8–10°C higher). Although Antarctic ice sheets were generally smaller during the MCO, deep-sea geochemical records and Antarctic margin drill core data reveal large-scale ice sheet growth events during the MCO, when ice-proximal surface temperatures were warm. These observations suggest that local ocean warmth as well as poleward transport of heat and moisture could have been a dominant mechanism driving Antarctic ice sheet growth during a past warm climate. In current models, projected ocean temperatures warm rapidly under a high emissions scenario reaching MCO levels in the Southern Ocean by ~2125. Similarly, orbital parameters will approach a configuration that is hypothesized to be conducive to ice sheet growth (ie. low eccentricity / obliquity node configuration) this coming millennium. Therefore, the MCO represents a target interval for investigating orbitally modulated changes in moisture availability and the importance of polar precipitation on driving Antarctic ice mass changes during a past warm climate. To better understand the processes driving ice sheet growth during the MCO, we compile geochemical records of sea surface temperature (SST), bottom water temperatures (BWTs), ice sheet volume, and sea level. Understanding the evolution of SSTs and BWTs will provide insight into latitudinal temperature gradients and behavior of thermohaline circulation, both of which influence atmospheric moisture transport. Data compilation across this key climate interval is one of the first steps in identifying where there are spatial and temporal gaps in the MCO geochemical records. With identification of these research gaps, additional deep-sea sites will be targeted for further geochemical analyses. This data will be used to broaden our understanding of Antarctic ice and the role that moisture transport plays in ice accumulation and growth under warmer than preindustrial climate conditions.

title: Niches and neighbors: examining factors that promote niche evolution versus stability across biotic invasions
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Stigall, Alycia L. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental & Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract: Ecological niche stability is often assumed to accompany morphological stasis, but the environmental and biotic controls governing when niches remain stable versus expand, contract, or shift require direct testing against fossil data across multiple temporal and spatial scales. This body of work uses paleo-ecological niche modeling (PaleoENM) of marine invertebrate faunas from the Late Ordovician epicontinental seas of eastern Laurentia to identify the conditions that promote niche evolution versus stability. Over the longer Sandbian through Katian interval, brachiopod genera exhibited substantial niche expansion and limited stability during the Sandbian to early Katian, driven by a feedback loop linking tectonics, sea level, and climate to basin connectivity, dispersal, and speciation; intermittent isolation of depositional basins fostered diversification, manifesting as niche expansion. During the late Katian, increased basin connectivity facilitated widespread dispersal, including the Richmondian Invasion, a regional biotic immigration event; reduced isolation suppressed speciation and shifted the dominant niche response toward conservatism. Zooming into this invasion interval specifically, community-wide analyses across nine time slices spanning roughly three million years in the Cincinnati Basin showed that taxa—including brachiopods and a broader community of crinoids, trilobites, molluscs, bryozoans, and corals—maintained niche stability during gradual, abiotic sea-level change, but shifted toward niche evolution during and after the invasion pulse, contracting their realized niches into a subset of prior parameter space rather than colonizing new ecospace. This response was most pronounced among generalist taxa and congruent across clades, feeding modes, and taxonomic levels. Comparison with a contemporaneous fauna in the Nashville Basin, subject to the same invasion, revealed a markedly different outcome: sustained niche stability throughout the invasion interval, implicating basin-specific tectonic setting, sedimentary regime, pre-invasion community structure, and invasion timing as controls on ecological response to a shared biotic perturbation. Together, these studies demonstrate that niche evolution is governed by an interacting set of factors—dispersal, isolation, competition, and generalist versus specialist ecology—operating across geographic and temporal scales. Biotic invasion emerges as a particularly potent, though not universal, driver of niche contraction relative to gradual abiotic change, with outcomes ultimately contingent on the broader ecological and geographic context in which invasion unfolds.

title: Abiotic Drivers of Paleozoic Echinoderm Diversification: Continental Fragmentation Fuels Origination, Temperature Triggers Extinction
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Lam, Adriane R. [1], Bauer, Jennifer E. [2], Jouault, Corentin [3], King, Gretl [4], Swain, Anshuman [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
(2) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan,
(3) University of Oxford, Oxford, England, United Kingdom
(4) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
(5) Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
abstract:
The echinoderm fossil record spans the entire Phanerozoic. Major echinoderm classes were established in the Cambrian, and order-level diversity expanded during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event; many of the clades were short-lived, morphologically experimental, and regionally restricted, making the group a sensitive recorder of Paleozoic environmental change. Identifying what drove this diversification is representative of a broader, foundational question in paleobiology: do origination and extinction respond to the same or different abiotic forces throughout deep time?

We extracted 29,943 Paleozoic Echinodermata fossil occurrences from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, assigned to 1,011 genera, and dated using formation-level ages from Macrostrat. Genus-level evolutionary rates were estimated using two complementary Bayesian birth-death approaches implemented in PyRate: a birth-death model with constrained rate shifts and a reversible-jump MCMC model, both of which infer the number, timing, and magnitude of rate shifts. A Multivariate Birth-Death (MBD) model was used to test six candidate abiotic drivers: continental fragmentation, global temperature, sea level, atmospheric carbon dioxide, ice volume, and volcanism, plus within-clade diversity dependence, against origination and extinction.

Diversity increased from ~0 at the base of the Cambrian (~552 Ma) to a sustained plateau of ~150–175 genera through the Ordovician to Devonian (~470–360 Ma). Maximum diversity was reached during the early Carboniferous (~340–320 Ma) before declining to ~0 at the end- Permian mass extinction. Origination and extinction rates are variable throughout the dataset, with the largest uncertainties in the Cambrian. The Late Ordovician Mass Extinction exhibits elevated extinction rates and stable origination rates, whereas the end-Devonian extinctions exhibit stable extinction rates but depressed origination rates, providing additional support that this extinction event was a biodiversity crisis. Rates at the end-Permian mass extinction exhibit highly elevated extinction relative to stable origination, but with greater error than in prior time periods.

Results of the MBD model indicate speciation of Paleozoic echinoderms was driven by continental fragmentation. This follows similar studies which have identified founder-event speciation, or jump dispersal, and dispersal over vicariance as important processes to echinoderm diversification. Extinction of echinoderms was driven by temperature, a finding also in line with prior studies of marine invertebrates. Although resilient, echinoderms are sensitive to changes in ocean temperature and warrant careful consideration under future warming scenarios.

title: A High-Resolution Multi-Core Reconstruction of the Kuroshio Current Extension across an Analogue Warm Period using Planktic Foraminiferal Stable Isotopic Analyses
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Lam, Adriane R. [1], Kwarteng, Helena [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY,
(2) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
abstract:
The Kuroshio Current and its Extension (KCE) is one of the world’s largest subtropical western boundary currents with a volume transport of ~65 Sverdrup of water from the low- to mid-latitudes of the northwest Pacific Ocean. This current is critically important to sustaining high biodiversity in the region and providing a rich fishing industry to nearby countries. Venting of heat and moisture to the troposphere affect regional to Northern Hemisphere weather patterns, and changes in the KCE flow path and/or strength affect storm paths and intensity. As western boundary currents have decadal modifications, deciphering their longer-term behavior in response to climate shifts is difficult, but critical due to their societal, biological, and meteorological importance.

As such, we can utilize the sedimentological and micropaleontological records to reconstruct the behavior of the KCE across analogue climate states. In this study, we used stable isotopes of the planktic foraminifera, Globoconella inflata (a thermocline-dwelling species) to reconstruct the temperature and nutrients at three Ocean Drilling Program sites that were drilled across the modern-day position of the KCE across the mid-Piacenzian Warm Period (mPWP; 3.3–3.0 Ma) at a ~3 kyr resolution. Sediment trap data indicate Gc. inflata reaches its maximum abundance in the winter months; as such, our reconstructed temperatures and nutrient gradients reflect a very seasonal signal across this climate interval.

These new data highlight the spatial and temporal variability of the KCE across the mPWP. Several key findings indicate the KCE is extremely sensitive to elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide levels and global temperature changes. For example, we have quantified the degree of warming and cooling across 5° latitude within which our sites lie and can calculate the rates of change with respect to temperature and nutrient distribution. Our data provide the first detailed, high-resolution look into the behavior of a subtropical western boundary current across key glacial and interglacial events, allowing for a deeper understanding of how these complex systems will continue responding to anthropogenic warming scenarios of the future.

title: Climate Science Literacy and Sense of Civic Responsibility: A Community College-University Collaborative Classroom Experience Involving Interviews with StoryCorps.
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Kobilka, David William [1], Urban, Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) Central Lakes CollegeGeoscience, Brainerd, MN, USA
(2) Bemidji State University, Bemidji, MN, USA
abstract:
In an age where unscientific misinformation is just as easily accessible via technology as empirical facts, the general citizenry of the world is charged with advocating informed knowledge over opinion. Essential workforce skills include clearly and articulately presenting information and completely and accurately listening. The latter, often called active listening, can be taught in college courses at undergraduate and graduate levels. Essential knowledge for everyone is that of climate science. To make that more personally meaningful to learners, to dispel climate misunderstanding, to promote climate action, and encourage an attitude of global citizenship, learning to listen carefully in conversations about the climate crisis can have a positive impact. Conducting interviews is an effective tool for practicing active listening. Recording frees an interviewer to listen carefully, and to concentrate more deeply on what is being said. The StoryCorps mobile app is a tool specially designed for these purposes (StoryCorps, 2025).

A research study and curricular lesson were developed to examine the effect of blending a curriculum of climate science literacy with active listening on student attitudes toward their own knowledge of climate, and their sense of personal and collective agency toward a warming world. The project involved students gathering the perspectives of others through audio-recorded interviews to enhance their own climate literacy and to understand the climate attitudes in their community.

Students from two institutions, a community college introductory geoscience survey class and a university level methods course for future science teachers, collaborated to develop interview questions and discuss findings to increase their awareness and understanding of the climate change issue. To identify prior knowledge, assess science learning and changes in attitude, the researchers developed a Likert-style survey using a pre- and post-test self-reporting methodology. The survey instrument measured five dimensions in each of three areas: (a) attitudes toward civic engagement, (b) general climate science knowledge, and (c) application of climate science knowledge. No statistically significant results were obtained, but the sample size was small (N=8). Qualitative student comments were also collected and revealed interesting insight into what students learned and took away from the lesson.

title: The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary in the Bighorn Basin (northwest Wyoming, USA)
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation
authors: Weaver, Luke [1], Tobin, Thomas S. [2], Sweedler, Rory Elizabeth [3], Fulghum, Henry Z. [4], Cheong, Hee Jun [5], Sprain, Courtney Jean [6], Korasidis, Vera A. [7], Dansted, Hanne [8], Neilson, Oliver [9], Fendley, Isabel M. [10], Wing, Scott L. [11], Carvalho, Mónica R. [12]
