abstract:
The Bighorn Basin (BHB) of northwestern Wyoming, USA, is renowned for its record of terrestrial ecosystems spanning the Paleocene-Eocene boundary; however, the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary (KPB) has received comparatively little attention. As in other continental sections, the KPB in the BHB occurs at a previously recognized lithological change, in this case between the Cretaceous Lance Formation and the Paleogene Fort Union Formation. We describe four conformable KPB sections—two in the northcentral basin (Little Polecat Dome, Elk Basin) and two in the southcentral basin (Kirby Ditch, Sand Draw). All are characterized by positive iridium anomalies (0.1–1.5 ppb) that occur in reddish-pink mudstones at the contact between the Lance and Fort Union formations. Preliminary palynological work has identified (i) the Wodehouseia spinata Zone in the uppermost Lance Formation at Little Polecat Dome, (ii) an absence of Aquilapollenites spp. in the lowermost Fort Union Formation, and (iii) a fern spike (94.2% Laevigatosporites spp.) coincident with the iridium anomaly at Elk Basin. The strata immediately below the iridium anomaly at Little Polecat Dome have reversed polarity (i.e., C29r)—additional geochronological and chemostratigraphic data are pending.

We also recognize and describe several sites in the BHB where the KPB is unconformable. In the western BHB, the Eocene Willwood Formation fills deep scours into the Lance and underlying Meeteetse formations, and its base is sometimes represented by a thick, quartzite-cobble conglomerate. In the eastern and southeastern BHB, the Fort Union Formation is usually present, but much thinner than elsewhere in the BHB. Below the Fort Union Formation, we describe a lithologically-distinct unit, informally referred to here as the K-Pg unconformity beds (KPUB), that may warrant formal definition as a member of the Fort Union or Lance formation. The KPUB predominantly consist of white channel sandstones and red-purple paleosols that fill scoured topography on the Lance or Meeteetse formations. They in turn are scoured and filled by typical Fort Union Formation strata. The KPB may exist at the base, within, or at the top of KPUB; at present, we lack definitive data to place it more precisely. Together these observations suggest that, during the latest Cretaceous and early Paleogene, the flanks of the BHB experienced low sediment accumulation rates or active erosion, even as sediment accumulated rapidly along its axis.

title: Evidence of Miocene Exhumation along Rift-Flank Uplifts of the Magma-Poor Lake Tanganyika Rift System, Tanzania
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Konguthaithip, Natthakorn [1], Jepson, Gilby [2], George, Sarah W.M. [3], Soreghan, Michael [4], Miller, Elisha J. [5], Mtegeki, Fred Bahati [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, USA

abstract: The East African Rift (EAR) system is an archetypal example of early-stage continental break-up. Despite extensive work on the structure and magmatic history, the timing of rifting in the magma-poor western branch of the EAR remains debated. Presently, the proposed timing of rift initiation in the western branch ranges from Oligocene to Miocene. At Lake Tanganyika, a Miocene onset of rifting is supported by sedimentation rate calculated from syn-extensional strata. The Oligocene onset of rifting is inferred from geochronology of syn-depositional sediment in the adjacent Rukwa rift. To resolve the timing and magnitude of rift exhumation, we applied apatite fission track (AFT) low-temperature thermochronology to bedrock samples from the high-relief (~1700–800 m) footwalls that bound Lake Tanganyika in western Tanzania. We present six samples collected from the Mwomgongo area in the northern rift basin and Mahale National Park in central Lake Tanganyika on a horst block separating two major sub-basins. Our results show a spread of AFT dates ranging from 6 Ma to 1559 Ma. All six samples show Jurassic to Miocene groups, indicating a polyphase exhumation history across the Lake Tanganyika rift. Samples from the northern Mahale and Mwomgongo yield Jurassic AFT central ages (174-160 Ma). We interpret these ages to reflect exhumation associated with the early stage of Gondwana supercontinent break-up, which was widespread across eastern Africa. A second set of samples from central Lake Tanganyika yields two discrete populations comprising Late Cretaceous (86 Ma) and mid-Miocene (10 Ma) AFT ages. The mid-Miocene population is consistent with the proposed ~12 Ma onset of rifting along Lake Tanganyika. These results suggest that Lake Tanganyika has experienced multiple phases of exhumation in multistage rifting during the Gondwana break-up in the Jurassic-Cretaceous and the most recent Miocene East African rifting. Based on AFT thermochronology from exposed footwalls along Lake Tanganyika, we suggest a mid-Miocene onset of rifting along the western branch of the EAR in Tanzania.

title: Assessing CO2 Absorption and Clumped Isotope Disequilibrium in Experimental Direct Air Capture Products
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies (Posters)
authors: Hayhow, Claire [1], Bergmann, Kristin [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Earth Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract:
Avoiding the most deleterious effects of climate change necessitates reducing emissions and developing geoengineering solutions to reduce atmospheric CO 2 concentrations. A wide range of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies have emerged to meet this need; however, most carbon mineralization technologies rely on modeling CO 2 fluxes or using stoichiometric calculations to estimate CO 2 absorption. Additionally, environmental conditions that promote rapid and efficient CO 2 absorption into carbonate minerals are poorly constrained, as are their isotopic consequences. Clumped isotopes, particularly Δ 47 -Δ 48 dual clumped isotope measurements of carbon mineralization products, can constrain the mechanisms of kinetic isotope effects and precipitation rates. We aim to test the utility of dual clumped isotopes as a standardized method for verifying sequestered CO 2 , which remains a critical gap in the CCS field.

We have begun to test this with a series of precipitation experiments, largely modeled after direct air capture (DAC) technologies. To estimate CO 2 fluxes, we monitored changes in mineral phase, mass, and δ 13 C, δ 18 O, Δ 47 , and Δ 48 . In these experimental carbonates, we observe significant kinetic fractionation associated with CO 2 absorption, characterized by enriched Δ 47 and depleted Δ 48 relative to equilibrium with the largest KIEs (ΔΔ 47 = 0.277, ΔΔ 48 = -0.695) in samples simulating DAC. We compare these experimental carbonates with other known CO 2 -absorbing systems, including: travertines associated with basalt weathering, archeological concrete, and modern concretes engineered to absorb CO 2 .

We compare these results from experimental and natural samples with modeled kinetic isotope effects associated with exchange reactions in the DIC-H 2 O system and crystal growth reactions in the CaCO 3 -DIC system using the COAD model. Through this work, we aim to assess the feasibility of using dual clumped isotopes as an independent method to quantify carbon sequestration rates across CCS technologies. If a dual clumped approach shows promise, it could serve as a useful geochemical tool to rigorously quantify carbon sequestration across a suite of mineralization techniques.

title: A Multi-Method Approach to Bedrock Mapping for an Improved Understanding of Aquifer Behavior
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: Fehling, Anna [1], Stewart, Eric [2], Stephens, Nat P. [3], Stewart, Esther K. [4]
affiliations: (1) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey, Madison, WI, USA
(2) Wisconsin Geological Survey, Madison, WI,
(3) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey Honorary Associate, ; ExxonMobil Corp, retired, Houston, TX,
(4) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
abstract:
Geologic mapping is foundational for understanding and managing groundwater systems. Ongoing bedrock mapping in Dunn County in northwest Wisconsin, funded by the STATEMAP program, was driven by the need to map and understand the properties of Cambrian units to inform groundwater use decisions. In the study area, the Cambrian Eau Claire Formation and the upper Mount Simon Formation have the potential to behave as aquitards. However, while the Eau Claire Formation is a well-documented aquitard in south-central Wisconsin, regional changes in lithology and hydraulic properties are poorly understood. Additionally, modern 1:100,000 mapping would greatly improve upon previous 1:250,000-scale mapping currently used by resource managers.

The novelty of this study is combining regional-scale bedrock mapping and studies of regional stratigraphic changes with local hydrogeologic investigation. Bedrock mapping at the county scale illustrates contacts and informs lithological changes in the units. Regional sequence stratigraphic and depositional models developed by Stephens et al. (2026) provide the framework for understanding basal Cambrian hydrostratigraphy in the Upper Mississippi Valley. An ongoing field study of the vertical hydraulic conductivity of the bedrock will inform the potential for Cambrian units to serve as aquitards. Initial results of geophysical logging and water-level measurements in a new well suggest the presence of shaly layers in both the Eau Claire and Mount Simon Formations and a strong downward hydraulic gradient. The novel approach of integrating regional mapping with local hydrogeologic investigation improves the understanding of Cambrian hydrostratigraphy and provides direction for future groundwater management.

title: Mineralogy in 3D: Digital and Fabricated Models for Visualizing Symmetry
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research
authors: Cobb, Sarah C. [1], Price, Jonathan D. [2], Cobb, Andrew [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Mathematics, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX,
(2) Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX,
(3) Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract:
Familiarity with crystal symmetry and indexing is a valuable tool for understanding properties of minerals: habit, cleavage, and optics are all closely tied to symmetry. Unfortunately, many students find groups, forms, and classes to be among the most challenging topics encountered in mineralogy. Models of various kinds have always been a key tool for teaching these concepts. Novel technology provides new methods to create models, both digital and physical, that encourage learners to interact with three-dimensional shapes and their symmetry groups.

Desmos is a free, online graphing calculator; since 2024, it has included 3D graphing capabilities. In addition to static graphs, it can incorporate dynamic and easily controlled changes in variables, including as animations. It uses a simple, straightforward scripting language. These features support the creation of interactive models illustrating expressions of the forms in a crystal of a particular tracht, as well as animations showing the nature of various symmetry elements.

Advances in computer-controlled fabrication have also introduced new ways to create precise physical models with minimal investment of time, money, and specialized training. A computerized cutting machine (e.g. Cricut) can be used to create foldable paper models of specific minerals or forms. Paper allows for large, inexpensive models that permit informational marking. Students may assemble, annotate, and keep their own models. Custom models reflecting specific mineral samples create a bridge from the abstraction of groups to the natural world.

Digital and physical models have been successfully incorporated into the mineralogy class at our institution. Using zircon as an entry point, students interacted with models of crystal morphology, families of lattice planes, and intersecting forms, as well as with actual zircon samples. Zircon’s symmetry group is sufficiently large to introduce important symmetry elements and concepts, but avoids the complications of the isometric system. Multiple representations of this pattern promoted exploration of the connections between lattice structure and external morphology. Students exhibited an increased comprehension of symmetry, habit, and indexing.

title: Unlocking Legacy Well Log Databases Using AI: A Case Study from El Paso County, Colorado
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Buch Leviatan, Orna [1], Sebol, Lesley [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
(2) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
As part of the Colorado Geological Survey (CGS) El Paso County groundwater resources study, roughly 25,000 active water wells are being assigned to specific hydrogeologic units. Assigning these wells relies on critical geological data within each well record, including lithology within the screened interval, depth to bedrock, and coal occurrence. These data are stored as scanned PDF well reports on the Colorado Division of Water Resources (DWR) website, many of which include handwritten entries that standard Optical Character Recognition (OCR) cannot reliably interpret.

To unlock these legacy records for large-scale analysis, we developed two in-house Python scripts utilizing Claude AI (Anthropic). The first script automates the bulk download of well log PDF files directly from the DWR website. The second uses AI vision and large language model (LLM) extraction, guided by a structured geologic prompt, to read and interpret each PDF, including handwritten geology logs, and output structured data into a standardized format.

For each well, the AI pipeline extracts lithology within the screened interval, depth to bedrock, and coal occurrence and depth range, writing the output to a Quality Control (QC) ready table for geologist review. The system handles multiple log formats, applies geologic abbreviation standards, identifies and corrects in-log typos, and generates specific QC flags to highlight uncertain, ambiguous, or incomplete entries requiring manual verification.

This approach has proven cost-effective relative to manual digitization, enabling efficient processing of large well populations across multiple formation types with geologist review running in parallel. The project illustrates the potential of AI-assisted workflows to transform large collections of unstructured legacy documents into queryable, analysis-ready datasets, a methodology applicable to geologic databases well beyond Colorado.

abstract: International Ocean Discovery Program Expedition 383 drilled a sequence of sites in the southeastern sector of the Southern Ocean. The sites’ lithologies contain assemblages of both calcareous and siliceous microfossils, with recovered magnetic reversals through the Late Neogene. This provides a fantastic opportunity to re-calibrate calcareous plankton datums, specifically for planktic foraminifera, and quantify diachroneity of key datums used in the mid- to high-latitudes. Site U1541 (54°12.756′S, 125°25.540′W) was drilled on the eastern flank of the East Pacific Rise just north of the modern-day position of the Subantarctic Front. Shipboard biostratigraphic investigations indicate several Late Neogene planktic foraminiferal first and last occurrences. Paleomagnetic interpretations provide the backbone for which to re-calibrate these datums and compare these datum events to other sites both in the Southern and Northern Hemispheres. Participants of the 2026 CORE School re-sampled Hole U1541B to double the resolution of seven key datum events of six species and re-interpreted magnetic reversal boundaries using revised diatom biostratigraphic constraints, including improved placement of F. weaveri and F. interfrigidaria, and published geochemical records. Newly calibrated planktic foraminiferal datums at Hole U1541B were compared to other first and last occurrence dates from deep-sea sediment cores in the Pacific Ocean and to the global tropical-subtropical biozonation scheme’s datum dates if available. Results of the study indicate that on average for all seven datums, diachroneity ranges from 2.85–5.78 Myr across the Pacific Ocean and 0.24–1.39 Myr between Hole U1541B and the dates from the global biozonation scheme. Paleobiogeographic patterns of the three species’ first occurrences indicate that species first evolved in the South Pacific 36–40°S. The four last occurrences indicate that species went extinct in the tropical South Pacific to Northwest Pacific, 21°S–37°N. Range constrictions from the Southern to Northern Hemisphere have been found for other species, and likely related to changing water mass conditions that occurred first in the Southern Hemisphere due to increased Antarctic ice and later in the Northern Hemisphere with increased global cooling and equator-to-pole temperature gradients. These data add to a growing body of evidence that indicates regionally-calibrated planktic foraminiferal datums and biozonation schemes are needed and necessary to provide the first-order means to determine age in deep-sea and land-based sections.

title: An Improved Model for Predicting Postfire Debris-Flow Volume in the Western United States
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Gorr, Alexander Nicholas [1], Rengers, Francis Kevin [2], Barnhart, Katherine R. [3], Thomas, Matthew A. [4], Kean, Jason W. [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Golden, CO, USA

abstract: Methods for predicting debris-flow volume are important for estimating postfire debris-flow hazards across the western United States. However, most postfire debris-flow volume models are trained to predict volume in a specific region (e.g., southern California) and are less accurate when applied beyond the region of their calibration dataset. This limits model applicability in postfire hazard assessment frameworks intended for widespread use and underscores the need for a broadly applicable postfire debris-flow volume model. In this study, we introduce a new empirical model designed to better predict regional variability in postfire debris-flow volumes. Specifically, we developed a multiple linear regression model that predicts postfire debris-flow volume as a function of rainfall, watershed terrain, and burn severity and calibrated the model using a dataset of 227 volumes collected from 34 burn areas across six states. This model improves on existing volume models, as it (1) uses a rainfall ratio metric to normalize regional differences in rainfall characteristics and (2) was developed using a more geographically diverse training dataset. As a result, the new model can accurately predict postfire debris-flow volume in multiple geographic regions using a single regression equation. Results show that it more accurately predicted postfire debris-flow volume than three existing regional models. For example, it outperformed existing models against the entire volume database and matched or exceeded their performance in the regions for which they were developed, including southern California, the Intermountain West, and the interior Southwest. The new model also performed well in data-limited regions that lack the volume data needed to develop region-specific models, such as the Sierra Nevada, the Middle Rocky Mountains, and the Pacific Northwest. The broad applicability and consistent performance of the new debris-flow volume model make it a promising tool for improving postfire hazard assessment in the western United States.

authors: Kmetz, Andrew J [1], Crowley, Brooke E [2], Canterbury, Ronald A [3], Bataille, Clément P [4], Diefendorf, Aaron F [5]

abstract: Researchers typically use chemicals to clean and remove lipids from feathers, but common methods involve hazardous chemicals and may differ in their efficacy. We compared lipid removal and carbon (δ 13 C) and nitrogen (δ 15 N) isotopes for 10 published methods: untreated feathers; three single chemical treatments (ultrapure water, methanol, and petroleum ether); and combinations of chemicals (2:1 chloroform/methanol, 4:1 and 9:1 ethyl acetate/methanol, 9:1 hexanes/ethyl acetate, and detergent followed by 2:1 chloroform/methanol or 4:1 ethyl acetate/methanol). We used body feathers from an adult mourning dove ( Zenaida macroura ) that died hitting a window in Cincinnati. Groups of 10 feathers were sonicated 5x in a chemical and 3x in ultrapure water. Liquid was refreshed for each round, and all chemical rinses plus the first water rinse were retained for lipid analysis. Based on untargeted lipid extractions (identifying and quantifying any acid, alcohol, ketone, or hydrocarbons present), we estimate the dove’s feathers contained 3–5% lipid by mass. 2:1 chloroform/methanol removed the most lipid, closely followed by 4:1 ethyl acetate/methanol, and both removed nearly all extractable lipids in the first rinse. We analyzed isotope values for individual feathers, in which we found unexpected clustering of feather isotope data. For δ 13 C, we identified four clusters, with means (± 1 s ) differing by >12‰: (1) -23.5 ± 0.6‰; (2) -15.6 ± 1.3‰; (3) -15.2 ± 0.5‰; and (4) -11.7 ± 0.7‰. For δ 15 N, differences among clusters were less pronounced (< 3‰): (1) 6.5 ± 0.6‰; (2) 6.2 ± 0.2‰; (3) 9.0 ± 0.2‰; and (4) 7.6 ± 0.6‰. We suspect these clusters reflect seasonal difference in reliance on bird seed versus local vegetation. Doves do not migrate, but they molt throughout the year. K‑means clustering and mean‑centering of the data allowed us to isolate the effects of chemical treatment for statistical analyses. Using these corrected isotope values, all methods, including no treatment, had statistically indistinguishable variances and median values. Chloroform/methanol has been the standard feather cleaning method for many years, but ethyl acetate/methanol may be a safer and more eco-friendly alternative. We will also analyze hydrogen and sulfur isotopes to determine if results are similarly uniform among methods.

abstract: Rapid growth in battery energy storage is creating interest in exploration for new geologic sources of Ni. Conventional Ni-sulfide and Ni-laterite mining and refining techniques have often produced significant surface environmental impacts, which incur remediation costs and can spur public opposition to new projects. CO 2 -enhanced metal recovery (CO 2 -EMR), a process where CO 2 is reacted with olivine- and serpentine-rich rocks—either in the subsurface or with surface mine tailings—offers a potential alternative process to recover critical minerals such as Ni, Co, Cr, and Mg. CO 2 -EMR has the potential to reduce CO 2 emissions and surface impacts compared to conventional production, as well as increase metal yields from Ni-sulfide mine waste. We present a new whole-rock geochemical and mineralogical dataset for representative mafic and ultramafic rock units across the United States and construct an exploration vector for coupled Ni and CO 2 mineralization resource potential. Using fuzzy logic, we integrate geochemistry and mineralogy data streams for CO 2 -EMR prospectivity scoring. We also apply regularized regression to predict primary olivine (olivine plus serpentine) abundances, which extends the scoring method to more common datasets without mineralogy data, such as the legacy and updated National Geochemical Databases. This national-scale reconnaissance of CO 2 -EMR prospectivity highlights sites and regions that might support development of lower-grade, unconventional Ni resources with the potential for reduced environmental impacts and carbon sequestration.

abstract: The Proterozoic fossil record of early eukaryotes is a crucial archive for major events in the evolution of life, yet it is composed almost entirely of non-biomineralized organisms which required special environmental conditions to be preserved. Emerging work has shown that clay minerals can enhance preservation, with fossils of early eukaryotes documented in close associated with these minerals. Thus, understanding the role of clay minerals in organic preservation directly affects our interpretation of the early eukaryotic fossil record. Here, we perform taphonomic experiments using green algae and clay mineral substrates to investigate how clay minerals ‘template’ protist-grade organisms and enhance their preservation potential. We show that clay mineral templating occurs on geologically instantaneous timescales (days to-weeks)—while organisms are still alive—via interactions with extracellular polymeric substances. Furthermore, we show that the extent of templating is affected by both light and mineralogy. These results illustrate a plausible pathway by which eukaryotic algae - and more broadly, organic matter - might readily become fossilized, illuminating potential environmental and/or mineralogical biases that likely affect the Proterozoic fossil record.

title: Mapping Reservoir-Backwater Geomorphic Transitions in Tropical Mountain Rivers: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Ohr, Sewon [1], Ramos-Scharrón, Carlos [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and the Environment, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Department of Geography and the Environment, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
Dams alter sediment transport and channel morphology both downstream and upstream, yet the geomorphic footprint of reservoir backwater in steep tropical rivers remains poorly constrained. We quantify multidecadal topographic change upstream of two Puerto Rican mountain reservoirs, Lago Caonillas and Lago Lucchetti, and develop an uncertainty-aware framework for delineating the riverine–lacustrine transition zone (RLTZ). We differenced a 1946 map-derived digital elevation model (DEM) from a 2016 LiDAR DEM to map net elevation change after approximately 65–70 years of impoundment. Longitudinal DEM-of-Difference profiles were segmented using Pruned Exact Linear Time (PELT) change-point detection, and candidate transitions were evaluated using cross-sectional evidence for downstream-to-upstream weakening of depositional valley-floor expression. Spatially variable interpolation error, slope-dependent horizontal-to-vertical error leakage, and potential datum bias were propagated through 500 Monte Carlo realizations per site.

At Lago Caonillas, strong reservoir-proximal aggradation attenuates gradually across a broad, spatially ambiguous corridor. Of three proximal PELT candidates, only the 1.3 km candidate was supported by cross-sectional reorganization; the representative mapped transition is located 1.53 km upstream of minimum pool level within a 0.40–4.01 km geomorphic ambiguity zone. Within this zone, pre-dam valley width is positively associated with net elevation change. At Lago Lucchetti, an abrupt transition occurs 0.40 km upstream, but renewed aggradation farther upstream produces competing candidate locations and a bimodal Monte Carlo boundary distribution. Synthetic tests further show that closely spaced longitudinal features can cause incorrect automated boundary selection.

These results demonstrate that statistically detected breaks are candidate transitions rather than definitive boundaries. Representing the RLTZ as an uncertainty-explicit geomorphic band, supported by cross-sectional validation, provides a more defensible basis for assessing reservoir sediment storage and upstream channel adjustment in steep tropical landscapes. This framework also distinguishes the concentrated depositional corridor from the broader hydraulic influence of the reservoir, avoiding interpretation of a mapped boundary as the upstream limit of impoundment effects. This distinction is important for estimating sediment accommodation, reservoir capacity loss, and spatially targeted sediment management interventions in mountain watersheds worldwide.

title: Patterns of biogeography in Paleozoic marine invertebrate organisms
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology (Posters)

abstract:
Biogeographic patterns of Paleozoic invertebrates were likely heavily influenced by large climatic cycles and tectonics. One way to explore how organisms responded to these changes is through using phylogenetic frameworks. We investigated the diversification and biogeographic patterns of arthropods, molluscs, brachiopods, and echinoderms from the Cambrian to the Permian (~538.8 – 251.9 Myr). We used the phylogenetic matrices from nine published genus and species-level trees. We then collected stratigraphic data (i.e. formation, age) for each taxon and assigned defined basins based on each taxon’s collected geographic and stratigraphic location data.

We re-inferred all of these phylogenetic matrices in RevBayes to produce fully resolved tree topologies, which are required for biogeographic modeling. We used the R package ‘BioGeoBEARS’, which contains six models, to explore the phylogenetic biogeographic patterns for each of the datasets. We performed statistical analyses to determine which model fit each dataset best by using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) scores. Finally, we used biogeographic stochastic mapping to estimate the number, type, and direction of dispersal events in each phylogeny.

The examined trees herein spanned hundreds of millions of years of evolution, and therefore, taxa occupied different basins. Thus, direct comparisons between all datasets cannot be made. We consider the similarities between time periods, basins, and within and among groups of taxa. We also explore how dispersal patterns varied across larger climatic and tectonic events, such as the Late Ordovician glaciation and changing continental configurations throughout Paleozoic, in order to better understand how abiotic those climatic events have affected biodiversity. Results indicate that jump dispersal was the dominant mode of speciation among most datasets, supporting other Paleozoic paleobiogeographic studies. Across all phylogenies, there is a reduction in speciation and diversity as time progresses, which is most apparent in the Devonian. Among brachiopods and echinoderms, there was a strong migration to the Upper Mississippi Valley and Western Midcontinent basins in Laurentia. Additionally, across three echinoderm clades, there were repeated migrations back to Gondwana, from which their ancestors likely originated. Further investigations of these paleobiological patterns can inform us of how Earth systems processes have impacted the evolutionary outcomes of Paleozoic marine invertebrates.

abstract: The Ediacara biota is the morphologically diverse product of early experiments with complex, large, multicellular eukaryotic lifeforms across a wide range of paleoenvironments over tens of millions of years. The oldest dated Ediacara biota in the fossil record are preserved in deep-water deposits in Newfoundland, Canada. However, the Ediacaran fossil record in Newfoundland shows a 1,000-meter stratigraphic and evolutionary gap between the pre-Gaskiers 580 Ma decimeter-to-meter-scale macrofossil Colinetia (i.e., a disc with an attached tube-in-tube structure) found in the Mall Bay Formation, and the post-Gaskiers <571 Ma more complex, centimeter- to meter-scale leaf-shaped fronds and other soft-bodied taxa preserved in the upper Drook Formation. The Mall Bay Formation fossils are large relative to the preceding record, but their simple morphology hinders interpretation of the evolutionary relationship (or lack thereof) between Colinetia and frondose fossils from the upper Drook Formation of the Avalon biota or tubular fossils from the Ediacaran White Sea biota. Thus, this gap in the fossil record poses questions about how biological complexity arose in the Ediacara biota. Our team recently discovered a surface containing more than 250 in situ specimens of a newly identified taxon that fills a stratigraphic, temporal, and morphological gap between Colinetia and Ediacaran fronds. Most specimens of the new taxon are centimeter-scale discs with eight lobes surrounding a central lobe. Several specimens display the same lobate disc attached to a conical extension composed of parallel unbranched tubular elements that are reconstructed as twisting clockwise into a cone. The tubular elements have millimeter-scale orthogonal architecture similar to the branching architecture of younger Ediacaran fronds. Each tube extends from a lobe in a communal discoidal holdfast. The twisting tubes may have helped the conical structure to maintain an upright position on the seafloor. The new taxon might be a colonial descendant of Colinetia, with its modules, orthogonal structure, and distribution in double-Thomas clusters potentially hinting at Ediacaran frond construction, architecture, and ecology. New U-Pb dates place the new taxon between 580 Ma and 571 Ma, supporting its intermediate position between Colinetia and later Ediacaran fronds. We interpret the new fossil taxon as representing the beginnings of biological complexity in the Newfoundland rock record and worldwide.

title: Southeast Alaska’s Western redcedar exhibit an enigmatic cold-season climate response
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Knowles, Anika [1], Wentz, Cheyenne [2], Wiesenberg, Nicholas [3], Pakula, Dexter [4], Wiles, Gregory [5]

abstract:
The Western redcedar ( Thuja plicata) is under researched in dendroclimatology despite the species’ ecological and cultural importance in North America’s Pacific Northwest. No previous studies have explicitly examined the climate response of the Western redcedar of Southeast Alaska (SEAK). A new 750-year ring-width chronology based on 80 redcedar cores from Ketchikan was compared with monthly climate records of the region. The Ketchikan chronology was also combined with the previously collected records from Kake and Klawock to build a composite SEAK Western redcedar chronology (150 series) to obtain a regional tree response.

In all chronologies, particularly in the Ketchikan record, there is a clear upward trend in ring width since the 1870s, especially in the last 60 years, likely a response to recent rising temperatures in SEAK. The positive correlations with cold-season NE Gulf of Alaska (GOA) sea surface temperatures (r = 0.52, p < 0.0001) show that Alaska redcedar are sensitive to decadal modes of climate variability in addition to warming. A significant low growth marker in 1876 CE is notably the same start year as the most recent super El Niño that contributed to massive famine in parts of Asia, Brazil, and Africa. El Niño years bring warmer than usual conditions to Southeast Alaska, and the extreme El Niño in 1876 may have raised temperatures beyond T. plicata ’s range of tolerance, inhibiting tree ring growth. With climate scientists predicting a 2026 super El Niño, there could be a similar impact on these trees in the coming years. In addition, the SEAK redcedar records exhibit a winter/spring signal, the first tree species growing along the GOA to show a strong winter response. While the climate driving mechanism is not known for certain, increasing temperatures in SEAK, especially in the past 200 years, could continue to be favorable for tree growth as winters slightly warm and T. plicata tolerates the warming. This enigmatic winter signal could be partially explained by further investigating the response to the 1876 event. Ongoing research is framed in the context of the upcoming possible super El Niño, particularly examining the regional redcedar latitude/altitude range to better construct historical environmental conditions and tree response.

title: Abundant Rangeomorph Specimens in the Lowermost Ediacara Member, South Australia
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology (Posters)
authors: McCandless, Heather K. [1], Hughes, Ian V. [2], Hughes, Emmy B. [3], Droser, Mary L. [4]

abstract: Fossils of the soft-bodied Ediacara biota are commonly divided into three assemblages – the Avalon, White Sea, and Nama –that have traditionally been interpreted to be largely temporally successive. However, recent evidence suggests that the degree of temporal distinction between these assemblages may be more nuanced. Previous research on the Ediacara Member (Rawnsley Quartzite), South Australia, anecdotally reported fossils characteristic of the oldest Avalon Assemblage within the same facies as taxa characteristic of the youngest Nama Assemblage at Nilpena Ediacara National Park (NENP). Here we expand upon this report following the exploration of a locally dense occurrence of over 80 specimens of rangeomorphs found within a single bed from the Flat Laminated Sandstone facies at NENP. These fractal fossils are most similar to Bradgatia as they are bush-like, inflate their size distally (in the direction of growth), and preserve no visible stalk or holdfast. Petals exhibit radiating rather than parallel secondary branching, possess no visible growth axis, and commonly exhibit tertiary fractal branches. Specimens are preserved three dimensionally within the bed, commonly present on multiple fractured layers. The medium-grained bed lies within the lowermost Ediacara Member just above the Chace Member unconformity, so these fractal forms represent the oldest fossils known from NENP. Although dominant within this bed, this fractal form is rare elsewhere, found in one other locality at NENP within sandstones interpreted to represent canyon fill. In alignment with initial reports from NENP, Pteridinium , a classic member of the Nama Assemblage, is also found within this locality in close stratigraphic position to fractal specimens. Notably, both this fractal form and Pteridinium are absent from the Oscillation Rippled Sandstone (ORS) facies despite the excavation of over 400m 2 of fossil surface and thousands of specimens representative of the White Sea Assemblage. The segregation of the rangeomorph taxon and Pteridinium from taxa common in the ORS facies supports the notion that environment, rather than time, may exert a stronger role over the distribution of the Ediacara Biota in select cases.

title: Preliminary Constraints on the Timing and Tempo of Anatexis of the Hartland Schist at Orchard Beach, New York City

abstract:
Crustal anatexis during regional metamorphism acts as a control of lower crustal rheology, strain partitioning, the composition and generation of continental crust, and exhumation of deep orogenic crust. The relationship between anatexis, deformation, and exhumation is underexplored in the Central Appalachians. The Hartland Formation in Pelham Bay, The Bronx, New York is a natural lab for exploring the relationship between anatexis and deformation, and how melt segregation accommodates strain. Here, we apply structural analysis in the field, petrological observations, and thermodynamic modeling to constrain the pressure-temperature (P–T) evolution of the Hartland Formation. The Hartland Formation is a unit of metasedimentary rocks underlying the Manhattan Prong thought to record metamorphism and deformation (d) associated with the Devonian Acadian orogeny. Constraining the P–T–d history of these rocks will thus provide key insights into the dynamics of Acadian orogeny and post-Acadian exhumation.

The Hartland Formation at Orchard Beach is exposed as a ~320 m-long discontinuous outcrop consisting of complexly deformed metasedimentary migmatite and minor amphibolite. Diatexite preserves m-scale similar folds with cm-scale parasitic folds (F1). Metatexite preserves extensional shear bands with ponded leucosome at a low angle to foliation. Both structures suggest suprasolidus deformation. Discontinuous high strain zones through diatexite and ptygmatic folding (F2) suggest subsequent subsolidus deformation. Diatextite preserves the assemblage kyanite-plagioclase-muscovite-biotite-garnet-rutile-ilmenite-quartz. Preliminary phase equilibria modeling in the MnNCKFMASHTi system constrains peak P–T conditions to ~10 kbar and 800 °C, consistent with the petrographically determined peak assemblage kyanite-plagioclase-muscovite-biotite- garnet-rutile-melt. Sillimanite pseudomorphs after kyanite require subsequent (near)isothermal decompression to 8 kbar. These results are consistent with an overall clockwise P–T path, rapid (melt facilitated?) exhumation, and syn- to post-peak P-T strain accumulation in a transpressional regime. These results will be supplemented by in situ U-Th-Pb monazite dating and bulk garnet Sm-Nd geochronology to better constrain the P-T-t-d evolution of the Hartland Formation.

title: Multi-phase exhumation of Mongolian Altai along terrane boundaries recorded by apatite thermochronology
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse
authors: Stevens Goddard, Andrea Lynn [1], Batsukh, Gombodorj [2], Leary, Ryan J [3], VanDyke, Eli Jordan [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN,

abstract: The Mongolian Altai is part of one of the largest intracontinental orogenic systems on Earth, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB), located over 2,000 km from a modern plate boundary. Although there is modern seismicity in the Mongolian Altai, including some of the largest continental earthquakes that have ever been recorded, competing hypotheses predict different timing and timescales of deformation and orogenic growth including primary orogenesis during Mesozoic, middle Cenozoic, and late Cenozoic times. We present new apatite fission track and (U-Th-Sm)/He data and thermal history modeling from 15 new samples in the Mongolian Altai that were collected from 5 different ranges on the Lake, Zavkhan, and Hovd terranes. Our results identify three major phases of exhumation including a period of Triassic/Jurassic cooling interpreted as a record of Mongol-Okhotsk ocean closure and terrane assembly, Middle Cretaceous cooling observed across the CAOB and commonly interpreted as accommodation of Lhasa-Eurasian collision, and Oliogocene-Miocene cooling interpreted as tectonic reactivation in response to India-Asia collision. Most samples preserve a record of 2-3 episodes of these cooling events demonstrating the importance of structural inheritance for subsequent reactivation even over periods spanning 100+ million years. Importantly, the spatial pattern of exhumation and cooling events appears to depend on the terrane. For example, the Hovd terrane was clearly reactivated during the Cretaceous exhumation event, but does not have a thermochronologic record of Cenozoic cooling. By contrast, samples from the Zavkhan terrane record Jurassic cooling and Oligocene- Miocene cooling, but do not have evidence of Cretaceous cooling. These geographic patterns suggest that stresses from different sources are not transferred equally to structures on different terranes. The result is that the presence and magnitude of a particular exhumation event may be consistently recorded locally in samples from one mountain range, but be absent in a mountain range located on a different terrane only ~ 30 km away.

abstract: The Harris-Galveston Subsidence District (HGSD) provides groundwater regulation to prevent further land subsidence in Harris and Galveston counties, southeast Texas, USA. HGSD has worked with academic institutions, local- state- and federal agencies, and private consulting firms to research subsidence mechanisms, monitor changes in the aquifer system and the land surface, as well as predict subsidence impacts of projected population growth along with associated increased water demand. Over the past fifty years, HGSD has utilized a variety of datasets to inform decision-makers on groundwater management strategies from advancements in data acquisition, to application of remote sensing technologies, to enhancements on groundwater flow and subsidence models. With the continued collaboration with water providers and regional water authorities, alternative water supplies, primarily surface water, have contributed to the successful mitigation of subsidence along the coastal areas, which measured over nine feet of subsidence in the 1900s to no subsidence since 2000. HGSD has built a framework that incorporates annual well pumpage from permittees, annual measurements of the aquifer system and continuous land surface monitoring presented in a publicly available report in addition to decadal regulatory reviews that model the impact of future water demand on the aquifer system and potential land subsidence. Results from these efforts drive policy decisions and provide insights into future research opportunities to minimize subsidence risk in evolving conditions.

abstract: The Gore Range fault stretches ~70 km north-northwest within the Southern Rocky Mountains Province. Mapped as a Quaternary normal fault for decades, the activity and true surface trace of this fault was obscured in thick vegetation, steep topography, and complex glacial geomorphology. Lidar data allowed for closer inspection of the fault and revealed apparent fault scarps through Last Glacial Maximum deposits indicating at least latest Pleistocene activity. The observed fault scarps are primarily east-facing with down-to-the-east displacements. To determine the timing of the most recent ground-rupturing earthquake on the Gore Range fault, we excavated a single fault-perpendicular trench across the south-central portion of the fault near Rainbow Lake (Frisco, CO). The trench site is located east of Ten Mile Canyon and at the mouth of Miner’s Creek drainages. Locally, the site is low gradient and the trench was excavated within low-gradient water lain sediments impinged between ~ENE-trending moraine crests associated with the Ten Mile Creek lobe. Scarps at the site are broad, about 1-2 m tall, and crosscut the moraines with a ~NNW-trend. We exposed sequences of silt, sand, and lenticular packages of pebble to cobble-sized gravels, as well as a localized deformation zone. The deformation zone included a west-dipping thrust fault on both trench walls with fault propagation folding outboard of the fault. Although this is a peculiar observation in an assumed extensional environment, fault propagation folding above normal faults is indicative of possible rupture through saturated, heterogeneous sediments (i.e., a glaciofluvial depositional environment), and has been documented globally in similar settings. We find evidence of at least one post-glacial earthquake occurring during dry loess deposition. We sampled the trench for traditional optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) samples and densely sampled (n=100) with portable OSL within the pre- and post-event loess. Our investigation points to on-going extension accommodated in (likely) infrequent surface rupturing earthquakes through the Southern Rocky Mountains, well north of the main Rio Grande Rift.

abstract:
New geochronologic results improve our understanding about the timing and processes of lower Colorado River integration. Detrital mineral geochronology can confirm the provenance of ancestral Colorado River deposits and direct dating and tephrochonology of interbedded ashes can determine depositional ages and rates of river system development. Results from the Bidahochi Formation, east of Grand Canyon, indicate that the basin there was fed by the Colorado River from about 6.6 to at least 6.0 Ma. West of Grand Canyon, in the Lake Mead area, newly mapped deposits with Colorado River provenance correlated to the Bouse Formation are 4.8 Ma or less, based on dating of an underlying ash. These are the oldest known Colorado River deposits in the area and suggest the establishment of a Colorado River through Grand Canyon more recently than previously thought. Lake spillover or overflow is the simplest mechanism to transition from filling of the Bidahochi basin to establishment of the river course through the Grand Cayon region, but other processes could have been involved and paleocanyons were almost certainly utilized.

Downstream from Lake Mead in the Blythe basin, 4.8 Ma zircons dated in a clay layer at the base of the Colorado-River-derived Bouse Formation give the maximum age of that unit, which is less than paleontological estimates. Farther downstream the first Colorado River sands in the proto-Gulf of California are about 4.8 Ma but could be as young as 4.6 Ma based on detrital sanidine dating coupled with magnetostratigraphy. Together these results suggest very rapid downward integration of the Colorado River through a series of previously closed basins downstream from Grand Canyon at about 4.8 Ma, potentially in 100,000 years or less. In contrast, filling of the Bidahochi basin upstream could have been prolonged for almost 2 million years, likely due to lower sediment loads during the late Miocene. Integration was followed by the deposition of the Bullhead Alluvium, a >250 m thick aggregational package, from 4.5 until 3.6 Ma. This episode is likely related to the initial deepening of Grand Canyon and the erosion of deposits that previously filled basins along the course of the river. Together these results suggest downward integration driven by climatic changes, fluvial processes and tectonics.

title: Large Recurring Earthquakes in the Mexico Subduction Zone: Evidence for Adjoining Pattern of Interplate Asperities
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part II)
authors: Mendoza, C [1]
affiliations: (1) Instituto de Geociencias UNAM, Queretaro, Queretaro, Mexico
abstract: Large magnitude (M) earthquakes resulting from underthrusting of the Rivera and Cocos plates beneath North America occur relatively often in Mexico, affecting coastal regions and inland areas susceptible to amplified ground motions. The seismic record of the last 120 years indicates that the Mexico subduction zone produces, on average, one M > 7 thrust earthquake every three years. Some events, with repeat times of about 30-40 years, have occurred in the same general location and have similar aftershock areas, suggesting that the earthquakes may have ruptured the same portion of the plate boundary. Large earthquakes occurring in the last 50 years have been recorded by modern digital instruments, producing high-quality, broadband seismograms used to derive images of the co-seismic fault slip. Areas of large slip observed in these images are interpreted to be regions of high relative strength, or asperities , that are surrounded by weaker zones of low slip. Despite the similarity in aftershock extent, distributions of fault slip for recurring M > 7 events show little overlap. Also, the zones of high co-seismic slip for sequential events are located adjacent to or away from each other. This adjoining pattern of asperity distribution is consistent with a model of earthquake occurrence where the principal slip in large events is located in plate-boundary areas unoccupied by asperities of previous large earthquakes, identifying possible future locations of primary slip for expected earthquakes along the Mexico subduction zone. This observation has important implications for the evaluation of the seismic potential in the region and the assessment of seismic hazard.

title: Co-Evolution of Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayan Orogenic Wedge
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Hodges, Kip [1], Whipple, Kelin X. [2], Kirby, Eric [3], Arrowsmith, Ramon [4], Shirzaei, Manoochehr [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA

abstract: Many large, hot orogenic systems feature both orogenic wedges and adjacent, high-elevation, low-relief orogenic plateaus. This duality has important geodynamic consequences because lateral expansion of plateau crust under the influence of gravity may strongly affect wedge evolution. In the Himalayan-Tibetan orogenic system, the southern Tibetan Plateau margin is a long-lived – not transient – feature, represented by deformation zones with complex kinematic histories that record plateau-wedge interactions through time. The modern boundary that separates the Tibetan Plateau and the central Himalayan orogenic wedge appears not to have migrated significantly since middle Miocene time a significant fraction of the entire evolutionary history of the orogenic wedge. It is marked by multiple generations of oblique-slip faults striking subparallel to the Himalayan arc. In the past, these structures accommodated both normal and dextral strike-slip displacement, reconciling contemporaneous arc-parallel displacement of the extending Tibetan crust and arc-normal shortening within the Himalaya. Several lines of geomorphic, structural, and geochronologic evidence combine to indicate ongoing structural activity along this boundary in the central Himalaya west of 88° East longitude. However, surface evidence for similar deformation at the plateau-wedge boundary is lacking farther east along strike. This change coincides spatially with a zone of predominantly dextral transcurrent faulting – the Dhubri-Chungthang fault zone of Diehl et al. (2017) – separating the orogenic wedge into distinctive central and eastern domains. Seismicity in this zone reflects active strike-slip deformation in the sub-wedge Indian basement, in contrast to the thrust-related seismicity characteristic of the basal decollement of the central Himalayan wedge. We suggest that this change in the nature of the orogenic wedge as well as the plateau-wedge transition zone is not only related to changes in the subjacent Indian lithosphere but also to focused, south-southeastward flow of Tibetan Plateau crust. In our model, this flow may have played an important role in broadening of the Himalayan orogenic wedge to include the enigmatic Shillong Plateau region of NE India and a substantial (up to ca. 6 mm/yr) increase in the rate of net shortening across the wedge. Reference: Diehl et al., 2017, Earth and Planetary Science Letters , 471, 54-64.

title: Geomechanical Controls on Fault-Zone Mixing and Implications for Fluid Flow in Sedimentary Rocks
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
authors: Runyon, Brook [1], Shaw, John H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract:
Energy applications involving subsurface fluid production, storage, and injection face significant uncertainties arising from the interactions of fluids and fault zones. Accurately predicting fluid migration and trapping associated with fault zones, which can act as both barriers and conduits to fluid flow, is often critical to energy exploration, production, and subsurface storage operations. Traditional methods for assessing fault transmissibility rely primarily on estimating the clay or shale content entrained along fault surfaces. Although these approaches have an empirical basis, their predictive capability is limited by basin-specific datasets and simplified representations of the deformation processes that control fault-zone architecture, composition, and textures.

To address these limitations, we apply a physics-based Distinct Element Method (DEM) to model fault development in sedimentary rocks, with particular focus on the geomechanical controls governing shale entrainment and fault-zone mixing. These models are calibrated to reproduce laboratory-based sand-clay-sand box experiments while capturing structural complexities observed in natural fault systems. This approach enables systematic investigation of the mechanisms controlling fault-zone architecture and the distribution of entrained shale within deforming fault zones.

Our results indicate that variations in the mechanical strength of the deforming granular material strongly influence the extent of mixing, fault-zone width, and the localization of secondary fracturing. These structural variations have important implications for the spatial distribution of shale within fault zones and, consequently, for fault-zone permeability and fluid-flow behavior. The DEM framework provides a robust approach for linking deformation processes to fault-zone architecture and fluid-flow properties across a range of geologic settings, improving predictive models used in petroleum systems, geothermal development, subsurface energy storage, and carbon capture and storage applications.

abstract:
Over the last ~3.5 billion years, life has increasingly modified our planet with successive waves of evolutionary innovation, leading to stronger controls over the distribution and flow of resources and influencing the character and distribution of ecological niches. The recognition that some taxa have oversized effects on other species and the environment led to the concept of ‘ecosystem engineers’ (EE). Extending this concept into a deep-time and evolutionary context poses conceptual challenges. To accommodate uncertainty and unknowns in the fossil record, we focus on the resultant processes rather than on specific taxa as ecosystem engineers. We also propose a new concept – ‘Earth system engineering’ (ESE) – to describe biologic processes whose influence is particularly extensive, altering the structure and function of planetary spheres and impacting the habitability of the planet as a whole. Using this framework, we quantify the richness and functional diversity of ecosystem and Earth system engineering processes over the last 4 billion years encompassing six broad organismal groups (microbes, fungi, vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, and humans). We find that ecosystem and Earth system engineering processes appear as soon as life evolves, and once they appear they rarely go extinct. Ecosystem engineering processes are much more common than Earth system engineering processes, but the diversity of both increases with the evolution of multicellular life. The functional diversity of ecosystem and Earth system engineering processes reached their maximums by the Devonian and remained at that level until humans began engineering ecosystems and the planet. Humans, a single species, perform almost as many ecosystem or Earth system engineering processes as entire divisions of the tree of life. Moreover, human bioengineering increases the overall functional diversity of ecosystem and particularly Earth system engineering processes, suggesting that at least some of their engineering processes are unique in the history of life on the planet.

title: Developing Low-Cost Digital Imaging Methods for Improved Surface Water Microplastic Concentration Estimates
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Posters)
authors: Elliott, Jack [1], Thompson, Ellen [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA; Department of Integrated Engineering, Minnesota State University, Mankato, Virginia, MN, USA

abstract: Since the recognition of microplastics as a contaminant in 2004, concerns have grown regarding their potential for environmental harm and human health impacts. Targeting mitigation and remediation of these contaminants requires accurate estimates of their distribution in the environment. Environmental cycling tends to accumulate microplastics in surface waters, where they can act as carriers of toxic chemicals when ingested by aquatic animals. Thus, developing and deploying accurate and accessible methods for estimating microplastic distributions in aquatic environments is a particular area of concern. Surface water filtration is a common sampling method that collects buoyant microplastic particles by trawling a fine mesh through the surface water of interest. The captured particles are then analyzed for characterization and concentration estimates. This strategy provides a method for rapidly estimating microplastic distributions in a large water surface area. However, existing methods to estimate the volume of filtered water include potential sources of systematic error, which propagate into the final concentration uncertainties. Specifically, most measurements assume that the net remains completely submerged during sampling, which can systematically underestimate the volume of sampled water. In addition, most methods assume a uniform velocity across the net entrance plane, neglecting potential for velocity gradients parallel to the sampling device inlet. Our group is targeting the first issue by actively developing low-cost, deployable methods to continuously estimate the wetted net area using a digital action camera. These methods are a work in progress, currently at the conclusion of the laboratory testing phase. This presentation will focus on the initial laboratory methods and results, including the single-pose camera calibration, free surface detection, and total uncertainty of the wetted area measurement. This presentation will also discuss the anticipated next steps to deploy these methods in situ and validate their use in context for comparison with state-of-the-art results.

title: Major and Trace Element Mapping of Garnets in Hornblendite from Catalina Island to Search for Different Prograde Paths
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems (Posters)
authors: Gordon, Grace [1], Page, Zeb [2]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Oberlin College and Conservatory, OBERLIN, Ohio, USA

abstract:
Tectonic blocks of garnet hornblendite in the Catalina Schist subduction complex are the result of partial melting in a particularly hot subduction environment. However, some blocks contain relict evidence of a previous colder subduction environment, but it is unclear if the pattern is consistent across the island.

Variability in major and Rare Earth Elements (REE) in metamorphic garnet is an important source of information of geochemical and geodynamic processes at depth. Advances in high-resolution and high-speed mapping by Laser Ablation - Inductively-Coupled Plasma - Mass Spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) combined with major element mapping by X-ray have the possibility to record multiple such events in single garnets, and potentially tie them to the P-T path of the sample.

The largest (~3mm) garnets from a garnet-hornblende-epidote-rutile tectonic block were analyzed for select trace elements using a 20x20µm laser spot. Garnets show complex growth, resorption, and inclusion patterns. Garnet cores (Alm55 Pyr10 Grs30 Sps5) contain numerous Gd- and Sm-rich titinite (sphene) inclusions. Yttrium and Heavy Rare Earth Elements (HREE: Dy, Er, Yb) decrease with Sps from the center to the edge of the core zone, which is truncated in an irregular resorption boundary. A sharp (~50µm thick) annulus of HREE decorates the outside of the resorption boundary. Garnet rims (Alm60 Pyr13 Grs21 Sps6) are ~500µm thick, with lower grossular and spessartine concentrations and increased Sm concentrations. Garnet rims contain rutile (not titinite) inclusions. Rims also contain faint oscillatory zoning in Y and HREE. Garnet grain boundaries are irregular, truncating oscillations, and are slightly enriched in Mn, suggesting a final period of resorption.

Taken together, the inclusions and major and trace element zoning suggest a colder prograde path interrupted by resorption and partial melting at higher temperatures (and perhaps pressures). Other blocks of similar lithology contain ilmenite inclusions in garnet cores, suggesting a hotter prograde path. Ongoing work includes additional garnet mapping and thermodynamic modelling to tie events recorded in garnet trace elements to P-T conditions.

abstract:
Geoscience is paramount in many job sectors and aspects of life. However, exposure to geoscience is limited in primary and secondary institutions and is not a required course in Pennsylvania K-12 schools. In college, geoscience is still a primarily a “found” science major. Pennsylvania features diverse geology, which makes the state a valuable outdoor classroom for geoscience education. There are 125 State Parks and 2.2 million acres of State Forestland in Pennsylvania, all free to the public thereby reducing the financial barriers to access. Many important and unique geologic features are located on these lands.

The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) employs approximately 134 environmental educators (EE) across the Bureau of State Parks and Bureau of Forestry. In 2025, DCNR State Parks surveyed their EEs to learn in which content areas they would prefer additional training. Geology was the 2 nd most requested topic for instruction. The Bureau of Geological Survey (also known as the Pennsylvania Geological Survey or PaGS) has taken several steps to leverage the unique geologic features of Pennsylvania in our State Parks and Forests for more public exposure and geoscience education. These efforts include webinars for EEs on Pennsylvania geology, field excursions to geologic features in State Parks, collaboration directly with the EEs to develop programs, and PaGS-led programs at State Parks. PaGS has started to produce simplified geologic maps and other materials for geoscience education by request for State Parks, and we continue to publish guides for outstanding geologic features in the state.

Based on these efforts and that the PaGS is comprised of less than 30 geoscientists with limited availability, it has become clear that State Park EEs would benefit from a more in-depth training workshop. Future steps include hosting a workshop that will provide information on the basics of Pennsylvania geology and the opportunity to work directly with PaGS geoscientists to research the geology of EE’s specific state parks. State Park EEs will then build a geology program for their park that will be reviewed by a PaGS geoscientist and deployed independently by the State Park EEs.

abstract: The Wausau Syenite Complex (WSC) in north-central Wisconsin is a series of igneous intrusions. It consists of four plutons ranging in age from 1565-1506 Ma: from oldest to youngest, these are the Stettin complex, the Wausau pluton, the Rib Mountain pluton, and the Nine Mile pluton. The mineralogy and chemistry varies within and between each pluton, and the relative alkalinity and silica content of each intrusion can be correlated with their age: the most alkaline is the Stettin complex, and the Nine Mile pluton is the most silicic. Though this relationship is clearly observable, its cause is unknown. The goal of this project is to expand upon prior research on the mineralogical and chemical heterogeneity of the WSC's plutons and to explore the implications this has for the formation of these intrusive bodies. Research on the WSC is extensive and ongoing, and through this project we intend to make meaningful contributions toward understanding its tectonic history. Preliminary analyses have been performed through Powdered X-Ray Diffraction (PXRD) and petrographic thin sections of collected samples from the WSC. Quartz, albite, and orthoclase are commonly seen in all analyzed samples. The samples collected from Stettin bore moonstone, a semi-precious gemstone formed of alternating layers of albite and orthoclase. Results from thin section analysis showed variable cooling rates in all analyzed samples reflected by variations in grain size, which aligns with published research. Wausau pluton samples showed consistently small crystals, while samples from the Nine Mile pluton possessed generally larger grains. Smaller, currently unidentified minerals appeared in cavities in a sample from one location in the Nine Mile pluton, which could indicate miarolitic texture. Future work will involve detailed chemical analysis with a handheld X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) analyzer to identify chemical characteristics of each sample. This will complement previous data from PXRD and thin section analysis, and provide further information about the chemical heterogeneity of the intrusions. In this poster, we present our findings and implications for future research.

abstract:
The predicted shortage of geoscientists in the workforce is becoming reality each year as the number of jobs outpace the number of geoscientists entering the field. Unfortunately, colleges and universities that prepare for the geoscience field are also facing challenges with enrollment in geology programs. This has led to department closures or complete restructuring of programs that sometimes remove critical geoscience curricula. To help combat the resulting gap in professional geoscience preparedness that some undergraduates face, the Pennsylvania Geological Survey (also known as the Bureau of Geological Survey or BGS) is working to revamp the way we approach our summer internship program.

Pennsylvania Geological Survey internships have provided valuable work experience and field work opportunities for decades. However, each section of BGS handled their interns differently and there was no cohesive strategy in place for the internship program. Over the last three years, focused efforts to improve the value of the internship program and to emphasize workforce development have included an orientation event called “BGS Intern Days” that gathers all the interns from both BGS offices (Middletown & Pittsburgh) for a complete introduction to the work of BGS as well as an all-intern field trip, a learning series titled “BGS Snack n’ Learn,” and an end-of-internship feedback survey. Planning for the internship season starts shortly after the previous internship season has ended and involves a coordinated effort led by the Outreach Coordinator between section supervisors. The goal of this planning period is to plot out the summer internship season by setting dates for the BGS Intern Days, the Snack n’ Learn series, and recording planned summer field work for all the sections of BGS. This information makes field experience opportunities more accessible to the intern cohort at large rather than keeping the work silo-ed to each section’s interns. title: Critical Behavior in Aquifer Response to Sea Level Rise Rates
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Sukop, Michael C [1]
affiliations: (1) Florida International University, Institute of Environment, Miami, FL, USA
abstract:
New models capable of simulating global groundwater flow systems are appearing and are being used to estimate the effects of long-term sea level rise. A major benefit of such models is that inland boundary conditions that may force groundwater systems into certain behaviors are not required. In practice, inland boundary conditions may not be strongly rooted in flow system physics but are instead set to accommodate model size limitations. The end-member flux-limited and head-limited boundaries that characterize coastal flow systems demonstrate the importance of the inland boundaries in the coastal context.

Coastal boundaries are usually less problematic and are frequently treated as fixed position time-variable constant head boundaries, though more elaborate schemes are appropriate if the land surface becomes inundated over time. Models that operate at continental, peninsular, or island scales can be surrounded exclusively by such boundaries.

One of the key targets of coastal groundwater models is often estimating the impact of sea level rise (SLR) on aquifer water levels. Low-lying coastal areas are dominated by shallow groundwater and SLR-induced water table rise can create and/or exacerbate flooding problems.

A fundamental question that does not seem to have been previously addressed is the relationship between SLR, recharge ( R ), and aquifer storage properties. Specifically, is there a relationship between these parameters that will indicate if the SLR might outpace a groundwater system’s ability to adjust to SLR? The implications of this seem ominous in that sea level rise is expected to continue for at least 1,000 years and landward gradients would effectively drive the sea into coastal aquifers.

Here we consider the 1-dimensional confined aquifer flow governing equation that describes the 1-D ‘continental’ scale groundwater flow system with time varying constant head boundaries. The conclusion is that the dimensionless storage coefficient S reaches a critical value given by the value of the dimensionless ratio R / SLR . At S < S crit , recharge dominates and flow is toward the ocean. When S > S crit , SLR outpaces the groundwater system’s ability to adjust and flow moves inland.

title: The Stability of Wastewater-Derived Phosphorus in a Florida Keys, USA Karstic Aquifer Under Rising Sea Levels
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Lundy, Christian [1], Spielman-Sun, Eleanor [2], Kump, Lee [3], Ingalls, Miquela [4], Housego, Rachel [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA

abstract:
Submarine groundwater discharge is an often-overlooked source of nutrient loading in coastal ecosystems. Large phosphorus (P) inputs into ocean surface waters can cause eutrophication, leading to algal blooms and deoxygenation. The City of Marathon (Florida, USA) injects up to 700,000 liters of high-P treated wastewater daily approximately 20 meters into the Key Largo Limestone (KLL) aquifer for disposal. However, P concentrations are greatly decreased due to dilution, adsorption of P to the calcite lattice, and precipitation of P minerals. The KLL aquifer is karstic, and groundwater residence time and therefore P mineral precipitation is strongly impacted by preferential karstic pathways. This P sink is under threat as rising sea levels cause saline intrusion into previously fresh aquifer regions, mobilizing P by desorption and mineral dissolution. This study aims to characterize P minerals precipitated from shallow wastewater injection to assess the KLL P sink stability under future saline intrusion scenarios. We hypothesize that more stable P minerals will be present in aquifer regions with lower salinity and less secondary porosity, and that higher P concentrations will be present in KLL calcium carbonate closer to the injection well and in fresher aquifer regions.

Carbonate cores were collected at three locations along a cross-island transect through the Marathon wastewater plume in September 2025. Adjacent monitoring wells were instrumented with conductivity-temperature-depth sensors to determine core salinity zones, and water samples were collected for wastewater plume geochemical characterization. Core intervals representing different salinity regimes and a range of secondary porosities were selected for thin section preparation and geochemical characterization. These samples were analyzed using µ-X-Ray Absorbance Near Edge Structures (µ-XANES) and µ-X-Ray Fluorescence (µ-XRF) at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) to determine P mineral speciation. Additionally, carbonate-associated phosphate (CAP) concentration was measured every 5 centimeters of core length. Preliminary XANES results show presence of hydroxyapatite, amorphous calcium phosphate, and polyphosphates within the cores. CAP concentrations are variable across sites and cores. Ongoing work seeks to characterize core CAP trends and to correlate mineral speciation with geochemical data using PCA analysis to better understand the geochemical controls on mineral stability in the aquifer. This project holds significant implications for P loading under future saline intrusion scenarios and can provide important constraints for shallow wastewater injection reactive transport modeling.

abstract: The Invertebrate Paleontology Collection at the Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University (ANSP) holds a personal collection that has gone uncatalogued. This being Axel A. Olsson’s fossils from South America. Olsson was a geologist and invertebrate paleontologist who conducted research on Cenozoic Mollusca. The main goal of Olsson’s expeditions in South American during the early to mid-20th century was to track the ancient mollusks in areas such as Panama, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, and among many other South American locations. This collection holds important scientific evidence for the diversity of the Mesozoic and Cenozoic molluscan fauna in those regions. For that reason, our department's main objective for this project is to catalog and publish this historically important collection to allow easier accessibility for future researchers. To accomplish this goal, the specimens were classified, cataloged, and rehoused as required. So far, there are 1,289 total records with 1,247 of them being mollusks. On top of the large number of fossils, Olsson’s research signifies a geological change in the isthmian straits around Panama during the end of the Pliocene and the Pleistocene. This goes to show that there is plenty of important scientific evidence contained in Olsson’s collection. Meaning that it will be beneficial to researchers wanting to learn more about the prehistoric mollusks of South America. With that being said, there is more of Olsson’s collection split up amongst other institutions such as the Paleontological Institute in Ithaca (PRI) and the Smithsonian Institute of Natural History which will hopefully be brought to light.
