abstract: Community-based participatory research (CBPR) deepens scientific understanding while addressing local environmental challenges, both increasing the relevance and the reach of the scientific research. In undergraduate classrooms, integrating community knowledge, place-based learning and collaborative research into curriculum can motivate students to not only pursue STEM careers, but to embody a high standard of community and environmental stewardship. Drawing from instructional strategies utilized in the Collaborative Community-Aligned Research Experience (CoCARE) course taught at Michigan State University this Spring, this presentation provides an overview of lessons learned from planning a community-based environmental science course, including practical considerations for building relationships with community partners, navigating ethical responsibilities, and facilitating and assessing student learning. By centering lived experience alongside disciplinary expertise, CBPR methods in the CoCARE course enhanced the relevance, inclusivity, and real-world applications of the research students complete in the course.

authors: Mills, Christopher T [1], Morrison, Jean M [2], Walton-Day, Katie [3], Kane, Tyler J [4], Campbell, Kate M [5], Chapin, Thomas P [6], Croteau, Marie-Noële [7]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, DENVER, CO,

abstract:
Legacy mining impacts often include metal-bearing mine waste dispersed in fluvial sediments downstream of historical mining and milling sites, which can persist long after point-source remediation and affect ecosystem recovery. Understanding the extent, mineral hosts, and mobility of dispersed metals is needed to assess lingering impacts.

We investigated Pb, Zn, and Cd concentrations, mineralogy, and mobility in mining impacted fluvial sediments along an approximately 4 km reach of Tomichi Creek downstream of the Akron Mine (Colorado, USA). The mine and mill were active from the 1880s to1950s (primary commodities Pb, Ag, Zn, Cu, and Au) and were remediated in 2016. We compared automated mineralogy (AM), a high-throughput scanning electron microscopy-based technique that characterizes sample mineralogy, with sequential extraction (SE) which assesses element mobility by targeting increasingly recalcitrant phases. Sample types included bed sediments, suspended sediments, and floodplain alluvium.

Pb, Zn, and Cd concentrations were consistently highest in the fine-grained fraction (<0.64 um) of both bed and suspended sediments. Fine-grained Cd and Zn concentrations were highly correlated (Cd/Zn=0.005±0.001) and increased twofold from immediately below the mine to downstream sites, where they ranged from 14-26 and 2500-4000 mg/kg, respectively. Sediments contained 0.05-0.9 weight % sphalerite (ZnS) contributing an estimated 18 to >100% of total Zn. Sequential extraction results showed that sulfide plus residual fractions contained 51±5% of total Zn. Both methods indicate substantial Zn and Cd hosted in phases more labile than sphalerite.

Fine-grained Pb concentrations were 1000-3500 mg/kg. Cerussite (PbCO 3 ) was more abundant (0.00-0.42 weight %) than galena (PbS; 0.00-0.12 weight %) and accounted for 4 to >100% of total Pb, though it did not correlate well with Pb released in the carbonate SE fraction. However, a phase of Pb associated with Fe was also identified by AM and its abundance correlated well with Pb released in the Fe/Mn oxide SE fraction. A weathering profile of mill concentrates in floodplain alluvium exhibited major variations in Pb, Zn, and Cd mineralogy and mobility with depth and may represent a continuing stream sediment source. The profile provided further opportunity to compare AM and SE methods and results will be presented. Our findings highlight the complementary strengths of AM and SE for evaluating dispersed mine-waste mineralogy and metal mobility in mining-impacted watersheds.

title: Columbine Lake Varve Chronology Reveals Indigenous Landscape Stability and Colonial Disruption
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Telles, Franklyn [1], McKay, Nicholas [2], Davis, Kaitlyn [3], Arcusa, Stephanie [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth & Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA; Institute for Tribal Environmental Professionals, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(2) School of Earth & Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(3) Department of Anthropology, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(4) School of Complex Adaptive Systems, Arizona State University, Phoenix, AZ, USA; Thunderbird School of Global Management, Arizona State University, Phoenix, AZ, USA
abstract:
Columbine Lake in the San Juan Mountains preserves a geoheritage record of two starkly different land-use philosophies: centuries of active Indigenous stewardship followed by a sharp colonial disruption. Drawing on a 3,400-year dust accumulation record, we focus on the last 2,000 years, when two major shifts mark this transition. Dust declined around 900 CE and remained low throughout the expansion of Ancestral Puebloan society, even as agricultural intensification and population growth expanded across the broader Four Corners region. This pattern suggests that actively maintained Indigenous landscape practices, including soil-armoring and moisture-conserving strategies, suppressed regional dust mobilization rather than allowing widespread erosion.

A second transition began in the mid-17th century, with the most probable onset of increased dust accumulation centered on 1667 CE. This rise marks a sharp departure from the actively engineered stability of the preceding era. It aligns with Spanish colonial settlement, livestock introduction, and other extractive land uses that altered vegetation cover and reduced soil resilience. The resulting dust regime shift indicates that colonial transformation, not later 19th-century American expansion, fundamentally changed how the landscape functioned.

Together, these two shifts show that the Columbine Lake record is both a paleoclimate archive and a geoheritage record of Indigenous stewardship and Spanish colonial disruption. It offers a clear example of a landscape record showing that Spanish colonization, not 19th-century American expansion, was the true turning point in the region's environmental history.

title: Long-term trends in discharge of high-latitude rivers
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Harms, Tamara K. [1], Jorgenson, Karen L. [2]
affiliations: (1) University of California Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
(2) University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK, USA
abstract: Flow regimes of high-latitude rivers influence food and energy provisioning, productivity of coastal ecosystems, global carbon budgets, sea ice formation, and circulation of the Arctic Ocean. Rapid warming is changing the amount and timing of flows in high-latitude rivers. However, circumpolar heterogeneity in the mechanisms of flow generation and climate variability have contributed to uncertainty in estimated discharge trends across river basins and time periods. We characterized discharge regimes of Alaska and northern Canada and estimated time-varying trends in monthly discharge and high-flow events. Distinct ecoregion-level flow regimes were characterized by contrasts in relative contributions of seasonal compared to stochastic variation and were distinguished by climate and presence of glaciers in the watershed. Discharge increased (median increase 8.3% per decade) at decadal or longer timescales in 30/72 of rivers over 1967-2024. Increasing discharge was more common at higher latitudes and in non-glacial rivers. Discharge increases were strongest and most widespread during winter and spring, whereas flows have declined in summer, particularly during the last 20 years. High flows associated with snowmelt in spring have shifted earlier in the year whereas the magnitude of high flows during summer have declined and shifted later in the year. Trends in river discharge were concurrent with increasing temperature and rainfall and decreasing snowpack. However, the effect of snowmelt on discharge has weakened over the last several decades while the effects of temperature increased through time in some regions. Accelerating climate change at high-latitudes is likely to amplify time-varying and non-linear trends in river discharge, resulting in less predictable river flow regimes.

title: How bad could it be? Comparing U-Th analysis of pedogenic minerals with other Quaternary geochronometers as a landscape dating tool
session_title: U-series Disequilibrium Geochronology: Advances, Applications, and Emerging Frontiers
authors: Hudson, Adam M. [1], Gray, Harrison James [2], Ruleman, Cal [3], House, Peter Kyle [4], Crow, Ryan [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO,
(2) US Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO,

abstract: Pedogenic minerals (carbonate and silica) are common in soils of arid and semi-arid regions, forming cumulatively over time from native mineral substrate, soil respiration, and dust in response to repeated wetting and drying. Because of this cumulative growth and their widespread occurrence, carbonate development is commonly used as a relative-age indicator in Quaternary geologic mapping and landscape evolution studies. U-Th series disequilibrium dating of these minerals offers a radiometric age constraint for deposits, but it is not commonly applied due to unfavorable U/Th ratios and susceptibility to open-system weathering. When successful, however, this method can provide close minimum-limiting age constraints for deposits recording fault offset, river incision, or paleoenvironmental change. Building on previous studies, we present a framework for developing and interpreting U-Th ages in soils of coarse alluvial deposits using examples from a range of middle and late Pleistocene soils in the San Luis Valley (CO/NM) and lower Colorado River Valley (AZ/CA). In both regions, minimum depositional ages derived from the oldest observed U-Th dates within a correlative soil profile are consistent within uncertainty with either cosmogenic surface exposure or luminescence dates from the same or correlative deposits. However, in all study sites, repeated analyses targeting stratigraphically-early mineralization in a single soil profile display a span of dates increasing from 20-30 kyrs in late Pleistocene deposits to >100 kyrs in middle Pleistocene deposits of ~200 ka age. This meets the expectation for cumulative buildup of carbonate through time, but highlights the importance of producing representative sample sizes to derive a reliable minimum depositional age. Other factors, such as open-system uranium loss or reworking of clasts from older deposits, also introduce erroneous dates that must often be evaluated or rejected based on isotopic systematics and other geomorphic/stratigraphic constraints on deposit age. Despite these issues, our minimum depositional age estimates show good constraint on incision of the inner gorge of the Rio Grande River in the San Luis Valley after ~200 ka, and track the incision rate of the Lower Colorado River from ~90 ka to 30 ka following ca. ~100 ka deposition of the Chemehuevi Formation. This demonstrates the utility of U-Th dating of pedogenic minerals in desert geologic mapping and landscape studies where other opportunities for geochronology can be sparse.

title: Empowering Indigenous-Serving Educators through Place-Based Geoscience: Innovative Lesson Design and STEM Identity Outcomes
session_title: Geoscience Education (Posters)
authors: Telles, Franklyn [1], McKay, Nicholas [2], Semken, Steven [3], Nelson, Mansel [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth & Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA; Institute for Tribal Environmental Professionals, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(2) School of Earth & Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(3) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(4) Institute for Tribal Environmental Professionals, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
abstract:
The U.S. Southwest's historic megadrought creates an urgent need for innovative geoscience lesson plans that resonate with today's classrooms, particularly for Indigenous students disproportionately affected by climate change. We present a one-day, place-based professional development workshop and curriculum built around dust as an anchoring phenomenon: a locally observable, culturally resonant environmental challenge shaping Diné and Hopi community memory. Twelve K-12 teachers in Flagstaff, Arizona, engaged in hands-on lessons structured around Bybee's 5E instructional model and Cajete's "Igniting the Sparkle" framework for Indigenous science education. Hands-on activities drew on Paleoclimate Reconstruction Storehouse (PReSto) map visualizations and integrated Navajo (Diné) and Hopi Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) with Western geoscience content, including physical lakebed coring to model sediment sampling, tree-ring ("tree cookie") analysis linked to the North American Drought Atlas, and tactile dust-transport simulations such as "Dust in a Box" and a modified cloud-in-a-bottle demonstration. We designed each lesson so teachers would experience it first as learners, model implementation for their own students, and demonstrate how a single locally grounded phenomenon can anchor standards-aligned instruction across grade bands (K-12) and disciplines.

Matched pre- and post-workshop surveys assessed geoscience knowledge, teaching confidence, pedagogical practice, and values and beliefs. Teachers reported large gains in content knowledge, confidence, and place-based teaching practices, with the two dust-focused activities rated most valuable by 83% of participants combined (50% and 33%, respectively). Thematic analysis of open-ended responses showed a marked shift in STEM identity, from pre-workshop expressions of inadequacy toward post-workshop statements of professional confidence and concrete plans for adapting activities to participants' own communities. These results demonstrate a replicable, transferable model: hands-on lessons built around a locally salient phenomenon and grounded in Indigenous ways of knowing can be adapted by educators in other regions to connect place, culture, and geoscience content. This model offers a practical toolkit of activities and pedagogical strategies for classrooms serving diverse student populations.

abstract:
Have you ever wanted to find data from a planetary mission but couldn’t? Or tried to find data products for a specific rock mentioned in a paper? Or found a data product appropriate for your work, but didn’t know how to access or analyze it, or what caveats might come with it? If you’re interested in Spirit and Opportunity data, the Mars Exploration Rovers Portal to Observations, Resources, and Tools to Advance Legacy Science (MER PORTAL) is designed for you.

MER PORTAL’s goal is to enable anyone, anywhere, to find MER data — from “pretty pictures” to spectra on a desired target — in an intuitive way, accompanied by user-focused instrument descriptions and data analysis guides. Our team includes dozens of members of the MER mission team, whose roles included science analysis, mission operations, and engineering; high school, college, university, and informal educators; science communicators and journalists; and professional Mars and Earth scientists who have not (yet!) used MER data. We conduct internal peer review of our products to ensure accuracy, accessibility, and usability.

Products currently available on the MER PORTAL include:

* Guides to the MER vehicle and instruments

* A glossary

* Links to tools such as the MER Analyst’s Notebook, the ASU Spectral Library, and the Pancam Instrument Site

* Educational activities for grades 2-10 that align with Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS)

* Lesson plans appropriate for introductory college and advanced high school classes, developed by a community college instructor in conjunction with MER PORTAL team members, and piloted on multiple classes at the Central New Mexico Community College and the Southwestern Indian Polytechnic Institute

We are in the midst of interviewing the MER team members on our project team to record their institutional mission knowledge. Our Technical Writer, who worked on the mission for nearly two decades, will synthesize that knowledge and write Data Analysis User Guides for each instrument.

Our future plans include creating an intuitive, science-base search of MER data, with the capability of downloading data products from the PDS; incorporating the Mars Target Encyclopedia; and developing tools requested by the user community.

We invite you to explore the MER PORTAL! If you’re interested in creating a PORTAL for your spacecraft mission, please contact us — we love collaborating.

title: The Colfax Pritchard Limestone Quarry and Holmes Lime Kiln—A Local Geosite Important to California’s Late 19th Century Building Boom
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Wood, James L [1], Higgins, Chris [2]
affiliations: (1) Colfax, CA, USA
(2) California Geological Survey (retired), Davis, California, USA
abstract:
California is rich in metallic and other mineral resources that were mined to support the state’s burgeoning economy after the Gold Rush of 1848. Several of these extractive mineral localities are preserved as State Parks to interpret this geologic heritage, such as Bodie ghost town (gold), Malakoff Diggins (hydraulic mining-gold), and Empire Mine (underground gold). Many other local non-metallic mining geosites throughout California also have great potential to convey the state’s rich geoheritage to the general public. These have contributed to the state and local economies, fostered cultural development of communities, or have significant scientific and educational value.

One such geosite is the historic Pritchard limestone quarry and Holmes lime kiln in the Sierra Nevada foothills northeast of Sacramento in Placer County. This limestone was quarried for dimension stone in the 1870’s and for lime manufacturing in the early 1900’s. Fractures in the rock were filled with calcite, which created a massive stone riddled with marble-like features. Fossils are abundant and have aided understanding of Sierran geology. Its attractive texture made it one of the first stones to be quarried in California to supply dimension stone for the manufacture of architectural ornaments such as floor tile, fireplace mantels, and building facades for many significant public buildings in San Francisco and other large cities in the 1870’s. Floor tile of this stone is still in place in the c.1872 US Mint Building in San Francisco.

In 1903, the Holmes Company built a double-stack continuous lime kiln to the latest designs at the Pritchard Quarry to supply lime to growing markets in Oregon and Nevada. The manufacture of Portland cement in California beginning in 1906 largely displaced lime for use in construction and building applications in that state. Abandonment of the Holmes lime plant in 1910 and its remote location left a rich archaeological legacy for modern industrial archaeologists to better understand the culture of the lime industry in Northern California.

The Pritchard-Holmes site is now listed on the Placer County Register of Cultural and Historic Resources. When a formal geoheritage program is adopted by the California Geological Survey, the Pritchard Quarry and Holmes lime kiln are among many other historic mineral-extraction sites that will be suitable candidates to interpret California’s rich geoheritage and mineral wealth.

title: Neogene Tectonomagmatic Capture and Pleistocene Glaciofluvial Integration of Southern Rocky Mountain River Systems
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: Ruleman, Cal [1], Hudson, Adam M. [2], Odom, William E. [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Evergreen, CO, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
abstract:
The southern Rocky Mountains and intermountain western North America feature Neogene tectonomagmatic landscapes modified by cold, wet Pleistocene glacial, glaciofluvial, and periglacial processes, a theme originally introduced by Wallace Atwood in 1938. This concept generally provides an explanation for the high plateaus and broad surfaces within mountain ranges above ~ 2200 m asl , juxtaposed with 1-3 km depth structural basins brimming with Neogene to Quaternary sediment and volcanics, all of which are presently incised ~ 200-300 m . Herein, we present a conceptual model coupling neotectonic and chronologic relationships for the southern Rocky Mountain region. This model attempts to incorporate all historic and contemporary structural/tectonic, geophysical, stratigraphic, paleoclimate, geomorphic, paleoseismic, and chronologic data.

Tectonic data show that Neogene deformation has occurred on NW-, NE-, and N-S-trending faults and fault zones from the Great Plains to the Colorado Plateau in different styles and temporospatial rates, ranging from ~ 0.01 to 0.3 mm/yr . Chronologic and geomorphic data demonstrates the onset of major glacial-periglacial processes began at ~1.5-1.0 Ma , followed by a profound 0.3 to 0.5 Myr hiatus in widespread glacial geomorphology and identified deposits. Major incision and topographic development in western North America on the order of ~ 200-300 m occurred after the Middle Pleistocene Transition (MPT), following the last major eruption from Yellowstone at ~630 ka . A major globally recognized erosional/incision interval occurred across North America during marine oxygen isotope stages (MIS) MIS 12-11 (~478-374 ka) , the strongest glacial-interglacial signal in the Cenozoic MIS record. MIS 9-7 (~337-191 ka) is primarily an erosional interval, with very weak glacial and strong interglacial frequencies, inducing further canyon-incision and arroyo cutting. The following MIS 6-2 (~200-12 ka) interval shows a reintroduction of strong glacial-interglacial frequencies producing abundant glacial and glaciofluvial deposits at much lower base levels, or inset within canyons. All of these geomorphic and chronologic relationships emanate from transient Ice Age-generated source regions for metlwater runoff above ~2200 m asl, explaining the cause of most underfit drainages . Additionally, major landslides sourced above 2200 m asl most likely formed from Pleistocene permafrost and permanent snow meltout along margins of mesas and within mountainous regions. Coupled together, this conceptual model provides a foundation for understanding the Neogene-to-present climate and tectonic histories forming southern Rocky Mountain landscapes.

abstract: Version 1.0 of the Cooperative National Geologic Map (CNGM) was released in 2025 as a new map synthesis of the conterminous 48 U.S. States. Version 2.0 expands the CNGM to include Alaska, Hawaii, and some island Territories. The state of Wisconsin is also updated based on a new statewide Quaternary map recently published by the Wisconsin Geological Survey. Addition of these components creates a first-ever map synthesis of all U.S. states and Territories at this scale. The CNGM is assembled from published geologic maps of states or large regions produced by State Geological Surveys and the USGS, ranging from more detailed than 1:24,000 for some small island territories to 1:1,000,000 for some regional maps, but mostly in the 1:500,000 scale range. Source maps are formatted in the Geologic Map Schema (GeMS), the USGS standard for digital geologic maps. Formatted maps are brought together in a single integrated database by an automated routine that preserves the original map data unmodified. Additional standardization is applied in the integrated database, such as matching source map unit ages to terms from the International Geologic Time Scale. From the integrated database, whole maps and/or pieces of maps are procedurally assembled to create synthesis maps showing different aspects of the Nation’s geology, leaving “mismatches” visible in some places along source map boundaries. Different regions of the United States map geology differently, most prominently the contrast between separate Quaternary and bedrock maps in the glaciated regions of the central and northeastern U.S., vs. single-layer maps of the “earth’s surface” elsewhere. To consistently portray geology nationwide, we create four synthesis maps, a Quaternary map, an “Earth’s Surface” map, a Pre-Quaternary “bedrock” map, and a Precambrian map (not all layers cover all 50 States). The version 2.0 update highlights the strength of this map synthesis strategy, whereby individual state “tiles” are added or updated quickly and with relative ease compared to traditional compilation strategies. The CNGM is available as both downloadable data files and via a user-friendly interactive web application hosted by the National Geologic Map Database (https://ngmdb.usgs.gov/nationalgeology), which allows users to visualize the geology based on different attributes and execute basic queries.

abstract:
Phylogenetic paleoecology grants us insight into the potential environmental drivers of evolution by incorporating paleoecological data into a phylogenetic framework. This intersection of fields allows for a nuanced understanding of how environments influence an organisms’ evolutionary history. Echinoderms, especially during the Ordovician Period, are exemplary candidates for phylogenetic paleoecological study due to their sensitivity to environmental sensitivities, abundance, and diversity in the fossil record. Many stemmed echinoderms, such as crinoids and diploporitans, first appeared during the Early Ordovician and diversified throughout the period. By exploring the evolutionary trends of these early stemmed echinoderms, we are better able to quantify how and when different paleoecological modes evolved. Here, we present the results of a phylogenetic biogeography and paleoecology study on a group of Ordovician stemmed echinoderms. The framework for our study was based on a previously published phylogenetic tree composed of both crinoids and blastozoans. We then conducted a literature review to identify occurrences of the genera selected for this study. We collected age and formation-level data, along with seven categories of paleoenvironmental data for each formation interpreted from lithological descriptions (e.g., substrate composition, bathymetry, and energy of deposition). Locality data were converted into basins adapted from previously published analyses. We inferred Bayesian phylogenetic hypotheses using RevBayes to produce a fully resolved tree structure, upon which we could explore further evolutionary patterns.

To explore these biogeographic patterns, we subjected the phylogenetic hypotheses to statistical analyses in the R package BioGeoBEARS. We used the paleoenvironmental data to explore phylogenetic signals across ecological niche concentrations using the R package "phytools".

Preliminary results from the analysis of the biogeographical analysis shows that the studied organisms likely employed a mix of dispersal and vicariance, without jump dispersal being a main contributor, a finding that differs from other Paleozoic invertebrate biogeographic studies. We also find differing levels of phylogenetic paleoecological signal and niche conservation across the environmental variables. We used these results to explore the relationship between phylogeny, biogeography, and paleoecology to understand the broader picture of how early stemmed echinoderms evolved.

title: Cerium Adsorption and Speciation on Clay Minerals: Implications for Secondary Rare Earth Element Resources Formation
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: YANG, YANYI [1], Xu, Tingying [2]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, STILLWATER, OK, USA
(2) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,
abstract: A reliable supply of Rare Earth Elements (REEs) is essential to the global transition toward a sustainable energy infrastructure. The secondary ion-adsorption clays (IACs) represent technically viable and prospective sources of REEs. IACs form under intense weathering of REE-enriched host rocks, after which mobilized REEs are adsorbed onto and scavenged by secondary minerals like clay minerals. Understanding geochemical mechanisms controlling the distribution and formation of IACs and similar adsorptive deposits is fundamental to future exploration and optimizing subsequent REE extraction. This study systematically investigated macroscopic adsorption behavior and molecular-scale speciation of cerium (Ce) as an REE representative during its interaction with typical clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, montmorillonite, and nontronite). Ce adsorption isotherms quantified the capability of studied clay minerals to substantially adsorb Ce(III) from aqueous solutions. Synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy was employed to determine if mineral sorption induced Ce redox transformation in terms of potential oxidation state change. XANES spectral analysis confirmed sorbed Ce remained trivalent oxidation state across all tested clay minerals, including Fe(III)-rich nontronite as a viable oxidative scavenger, ensuring Ce remains chemically analogous to other trivalent REEs despite its unique redox-sensitive property. Confirming the non-redox retention of Ce on these ubiquitous clays provides a crucial mechanistic framework for predicting REE distribution and optimizing extraction efficiency in weathered regolith deposits.

abstract: Geochemical data obtained from sedimentary records are used to make interpretations about Earth’s past surface conditions. However, most geochemical datasets used in paleoenvironmental reconstructions are generated from outcrop samples, which are known to be subjected to surficial weathering processes. There is therefore a risk that weathering may alter geochemical signals preserved in sedimentary rocks. To investigate the robustness of geochemical archives to surficial alteration, we conducted a multiproxy (δ 13 C carb , δ 18 O carb , δ 34 S CAS , δ 34 S py , δ 13 C org , TOC), core-outcrop comparative study of fine grained siliciclastic and carbonate samples from the late Ediacaran (~550-538 Ma) Nama Group (Namibia, Republic of South Africa), leveraging recently drilled geologic core (International Continental Drilling Program–Geologic Research through Integrated Neoproterozoic Drilling–Ediacaran Cambrian Transition; ICDP-GRIND-ECT). Our results demonstrate that 1) lithology is a dominant control on the robustness of geochemical archives to surficial weathering, and 2) different geochemical records are variably susceptible to surficial alteration.

title: Mapping lithology in Wolfcampian–Leonardian strata in the Delaware Basin, and how it informs tectonic history and petroleum resources of the region
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment

abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey has digitized general lithology data from over 700 stratigraphic logs of subsurface borehole cuttings and published measured sections on key outcrop belts flanking the Delaware Basin in West Texas and southeastern New Mexico. The dataset highlights regional trends in the proportion of carbonate (dolostone and limestone) and siliciclastic (sandstone and mudstone) strata that span the Wolfcampian–Leonardian interval. In particular, the distribution of sandstone is critical for reconstructing tectonic history, mapping sediment fairways, and assessing energy resources in the basin. Mapping of lower Wolfcampian strata show that sandstone is concentrated in the southern part of the basin, directly adjacent to the Marathon thrust front, and along the Grisham trough, a prominent geological feature in the west-central part of the basin. These trends suggest that both the Ouachita–Marathon–Sonora orogen and the basement-cored uplifts flanking the eastern and western margins of the basin, primarily the Diablo Platform in the west, played a significant role in the deposition of sand during the early Wolfcampian. In contrast, mapping of upper Wolfcampian and Leonardian strata show that sandstone is concentrated in the northern part of the basin, specifically in New Mexico, where much of the recent oil and gas drilling is focused. This spatial and temporal shift in the sandstone distribution likely indicates a transition from a tectonically active basin to a more stable intracratonic basin, where subsidence and sediment accumulation were primarily driven by the compaction of underlying sediment and eustatic sea-level fluctuations.

title: New insights into shifting winter atmospheric teleconnections to the North Pacific from Alaskan lake sediment oxygen and carbon isotope records
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Anderson, Lesleigh [1], Finney, Bruce [2], Baxter, W. Brad [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences and Environmental Change Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA; Institute of Arctic Antarctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA

(3) Department of Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
abstract:
Documenting the geographic extent of major global climate reorganizations during the last deglacial period is essential for improving our conceptual models of atmospheric teleconnections and their impacts on regional climate systems. Key uncertainties persist about the nature and timing of deglacial climate oscillations in the North Pacific Arctic sector and Beringia - the area spanning Alaska, eastern Siberia and the once exposed landmass submerged beneath the Bering Sea. A persistent challenge has been that most environmental proxies in this region are primarily sensitive to summer conditions and provide conflicting records. Winter proxy records are comparatively scarce and hypothesized to provide the key to identifying relationships with the North Atlantic.

We developed precisely dated records of oxygen and carbon isotopes from thick authigenic organic and carbonate sediment packages (marl) within groundwater-fed lakes in Upper Cook Inlet, southern Alaska. Detailed hydrogeologic studies establish that regional groundwater is sourced by snowmelt originating as winter precipitation. Furthermore, we selected lakes that reflect contrasting seasonal controls on lake water oxygen isotopes to generate records more sensitive to winter or summer conditions.

The robust deglacial oxygen isotope chronologies confidently correlate Younger-Dryas atmospheric adjustments in Alaska with Greenland ice core records and their seasonal sensitivity are consistent with cooling during winter. During the early Holocene, as rising sea levels flooded the Bering Land Bridge, a brief early Holocene warm-dry period was likely, followed by a regional increase in precipitation. Results clarify shifting winter atmospheric teleconnections known to play an important role in regional vegetation patterns, thermokarst, and hydrologic connectivity and underscore the unsettled nature of North Pacific atmospheric patterns that continue to challenge climate models, past and present.

title: Disconnected by Design? Modeling Hydrodynamic Effects of Navigation Spoil Mounds in the Lower Apalachicola River Floodplain, Florida, USA
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Davidson, Malia B [1], Stokes, Maya F [2]
affiliations: (1) Florida State University, Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science, Tallahassee, FL, USA
(2) Florida State University, Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science, Tallahassee, FL, USA
abstract:
Dredging – or sand mining – is a common occurrence globally to make large alluvial rivers navigable for barges. Despite it being a common occurrence, the effects of the system are still relatively unknown. From the early 1900s to 2005, the Apalachicola River in Florida, USA, was regularly dredged to allow for navigation of commercial barges. The excess material from the river channel was subsequently placed in mounds on the adjacent floodplain, potentially reducing floodplain connectivity to the main channel.

To test the impact these spoil mounds may have on floodplain connectivity, we employed a two-dimensional, surface-water hydrodynamic model using Hydrologic Engineering Center’s River Analysis System (HEC-RAS). The model utilized LiDAR-derived elevation data along a 3.1-km reach of the floodplain and mainstem below Wewahitchka, Florida, where spoil mounds are abundant. As a comparison, the LiDAR elevation data was smoothed to approximate a floodplain without anthropogenic spoil mounds while retaining natural levees. The hydrodynamic model was calibrated using landcover-specific roughness values (Manning’s n ) and stage-discharge data from the U.S. Geological Survey stream gauge near Wewahitchka, FL.

Preliminary model results indicate that spoil mounds inhibit floodplain inundation relative to the smoothed floodplain, whereas natural levees alone do not produce the same degree of connectivity loss. These results indicate that navigational spoil mounds alter the timing and extent of floodplain inundation, of particular importance in a river system with a highly regulated flow regime. Modelling experiments will test the hypothesis that the reduction of connectivity is most pronounced at intermediate river stages, when water can overtop natural levees but remains impounded by spoil mounds, delaying or preventing flow into adjacent floodplain channels and subsequent return to the mainstem. Although preliminary, these findings suggest that the placement of dredged material on the floodplain has the potential to reduce floodplain connectivity and alter the hydrologic processes that support habitat connectivity, nutrient transport and storage, and overall floodplain ecosystem function. Additionally, our findings can inform on best practices for spoil mound placement in systems with ongoing dredging.

abstract:
Climate during the late Ediacaran is poorly constrained. Geochemical data including δ 18 O values have been used to suggest the global climate state was warm, but sedimentological records paired with paleomagnetic interpretations have been used to suggest that it was cold. Specifically, <45 glacial deposits—many of which are interpreted to be from mid-low latitudes—have been reported globally. Many of these purported late Ediacaran glacial deposits are limited by uncertainties on their age, paleolatitude, and/or sedimentology, calling into question whether these deposits truly reflect major late Ediacaran glaciation. Additionally, the interpreted mid-low paleolatitude of some purported glacial deposits render these ‘glacial events’ inconsistent with Budyko-Sellers climate models, which predict that runaway albedo feedbacks will drive climate into a ‘snowball’ state if low altitude ice reaches mid-low latitudes. Here, we interrogate the evidence for one of these purported late Ediacaran glacial deposits on the Kalahari Craton.

The c. 545 Ma Vingerbreek Member of the late Ediacaran Nama Group hosts purported low altitude glacial deposits thought to be deposited at mid-low latitudes (c. 30­–40 ⁰), close to this tipping point in Budyko-Sellers climate models. We present results demonstrating that these deposits can instead be explained by a combination of 1) misidentified Permian-Carboniferous glacial deposits of the Dwyka Formation and 2) non-glacial Ediacaran-age mass wasting deposits. These results show that there is no robust evidence for Ediacaran glaciation on the Kalahari Craton and demonstrate the importance of re-evaluating other purported late Ediacaran glacial deposits.

abstract: The Poleta Formation, located in the White Inyo Mountains in eastern California and in Esmeralda County in western Nevada, is constrained to Series 2 of the lower Cambrian based on the presence of the trilobite index fossil, Nevadella . This formation captures lower Cambrian paleoecology and biodiversification as well as key examples of Cambrian animal reef-building. The Poleta Formation is divided into three informal members: the lower, middle, and upper Poleta. While most research has focused on the famous lower Poleta archaocyathan reefs and small shelly fossils preserved in the middle Poleta, the less fossiliferous upper Poleta has received comparatively less attention. Here, we present the results of a deeper investigation into the upper Poleta in which we initially point counted and analyzed thin sections of carbonates that were collected every 2 meters stratigraphically through the unit. The results showed that (1) confirming previous observations, the abundance of animals is the lowest of all members of the Poleta Formation, and yet despite this, (2) there are a few calcareous organisms in the uppermost fossiliferous part of the member that have not been previously reported. Subsequent sampling focused on collecting higher-resolution samples from the upper 10 m of the unit, which yielded specimens of the problematic fossil Archaeotrypa , putative bryozoans, and other chambered organisms. These problematic fossils were photographed, measured, and tentatively grouped into categories based on their morphological similarities. One of the most significant findings was the presence of multiple fossils that may represent putative bryozoans, which, if confirmed, would be the earliest occurrence of the organism in the western United States (lower versus mid-Stage 4 Cambrian). Further investigation of the calcareous organisms preserved in the upper Poleta and nearby units will provide a deeper understanding of early calcifiers, and the environments that hosted them, during the early Cambrian.

title: Extinction and Recovery of Brachiopods during the Frasnian-Famennian (Late Devonian) Mass Extinction in the Appalachian Basin: Updated Results
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Gallagher, Brett [1], Bush, Andrew M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA; Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
abstract:
The Late Devonian Mass Extinction was one of the most severe biodiversity crises of the Phanerozoic. It featured two major extinction pulses, the Lower and Upper Kellwasser events, both of which are associated with taxonomic turnover and positive carbon isotope excursions at sites around the world.

Shallow-marine Upper Devonian rocks of the Appalachian Basin of south-central New York and north-central Pennsylvania span the Frasnian-Famennian boundary interval, preserving both Kellwasser events. However, an understanding of these events has been hindered by difficulties correlating these strata with their deeper-water, distal expressions in western New York. Based on new evidence from conodont biostratigraphy (Over 2025, doi: 10.1130/abs/2025NE-407407), we discuss the correlation of the Frasnian-Famennian boundary interval, including the West Falls, Java, and Canadaway groups. In particular, a dark shale unit previously correlated with either the Lower Kellwasser Event or the lower Famennian Dunkirk Formation appears to be correlative with the Upper Kellwasser Event (uppermost Frasnian).

Within this stratigraphic context, brachiopod collections from the upper Frasnian and lower Famennian preliminarily suggest that about a third of species were lost during the Lower Kellwasser, and nearly half in the Upper Kellwasser. Species richness recovered completely after the Lower Kellwasser and partially after the Upper Kellwasser.

Additionally, our stratigraphic revisions suggest the presence of a third, more minor event in the early Famennian. It is associated with a gray siltstone bed in the Canaseraga Formation, as well as with a positive isotope excursion. The last atrypid species in the basin disappears at this event, leading previously to the suggestion that it might correspond with the Upper Kellwasser Event. It is unknown whether this was a local event, or whether it can be correlated with geochemical or faunal changes in other basins. Brachiopod faunas display a spatial reorganization along the onshore-offshore paleoenvironmental gradient across this horizon despite minimal taxonomic turnover. This “Canaseraga Event” may indicate continued biotic upheaval between the Frasnian-Famennian and Devonian-Carboniferous crises in the Appalachian Basin.

title: Water Use Niche Space of North America’s Late Quaternary Megafauna from Enamel Triple Oxygen Isotopes

abstract: An animal’s water requirements shape both its biotic and abiotic interactions. To investigate these interactions, terrestrial taxa are often grouped by their primary habitat (e.g., aquatic, semi-aquatic, terrestrial) using skeletal metrics or depositional setting, and these designations are useful for first-order trait analysis and establishing ecological network interactions. However, although surface water availability varies among different habitats, we cannot assume that primary habitat classification is synonymous with a taxon’s water requirements; doing so could result in loss of information about an animal’s behaviors and its ecological interactions. To investigate the water use niche space of extinct taxa, we use a new isotopic tool: the triple oxygen (Δ′ 17 O) isotope composition of tooth enamel carbonate. In herbivorous mammals, enamel Δ′ 17 O values are highest among taxa which require substantial drinking water and are lower for taxa which require minimal drinking water and obtain water primarily from their diet. We analyzed enamel Δ′ 17 O values from 9 genera of Late Quaternary megafauna from Texas to investigate whether hydroclimate change may have contributed to widespread megafaunal extinctions from 15,600–11,500 years ago. Our data indicate that Castor (beaver), Mammut (mastodon), and Mammuthus (mammoth) required regular access to drinking water, while Odocoileus (deer), Camelops and Paleolama (camelids), and Antilocapra (pronghorn) were less dependent on regular access to drinking water. Bison (bison) and Equus (horses) represent intermediate water use ecologies. Interestingly, we observe that extinct taxa (e.g., mastodon, mammoth, camelids, horses) span a range of water use ecologies. Furthermore, some highly water dependent taxa (e.g., beaver) persisted until the present day. Taken together, the Δ′ 17 O data do not support the hypothesis that aridification and dwindling water availability were major factors in the Late Quaternary extinctions in Texas. From an ecological perspective, our data suggest that the loss of megafaunal ecosystem engineers (especially proboscideans and equids) likely had consequences not only for terrestrial environments, but also aquatic and riparian environments. Consequently, the megafaunal extinctions may have had cascading effects on ecological functions which have not yet been explored through the lens of water use. Building a more complete picture of the water use ecology of extinct taxa using enamel Δ′ 17 O values represents an untapped opportunity to generate new insights into the habitat requirements, physiological, and behavioral traits of extinct species and to improve ecological network models.

abstract: The M6.4 and M7.1 2019 Ridgecrest Earthquake Sequence caused an extensive surface rupture through a variety of desert landscapes that include playa, alluvial, and bedrock surfaces. Since then, eolian, fluvial, and mass wasting processes have affected the landscape. The availability of airborne lidar collected in the weeks following the earthquake, and another survey completed in 2024, affords an opportunity to document the initial post-seismic landscape response to a major earthquake by generating a 0.5-meter-resolution map of elevation change. We completed remote mapping of landscape change from the repeat lidar and are in the process of incorporating field assessments of these changes. While many of the observed changes are expected—scarp erosion, fluvial modification of surface ruptures, and eolian erosion and deposition—we can now quantify those changes and observe the details of fault zone modification in a manner that may be useful to paleoseismologists that study past earthquakes using the subtle record of sedimentation and erosion preserved in fault zones. We also observed unanticipated landscape changes such as modification of extant ground fissures that have been present since at least the 1980s, and development of new ground fissures that have appeared since the 2019 lidar was collected. These fissures manifest as elongated narrow zones of material collapse and subsidence with no relative motion across them and are not aligned with earthquake surface ruptures or apparently connected to fluvial channel networks. The temporal lag in fissure development may indicate long-term response to the earthquake on adjacent fault zones that did not appear to change in the coseismic and immediate post-seismic period, or may be a result of non-tectonic processes. This integrated field and remote sensing study will document 5.5–6.5 years of landscape change following a significant surface rupturing earthquake and provide a snapshot in time for future observations of landscape change.

title: Experimental Assessment of the Capacity of Red Bed Facies in Sandstone to Enrich Sedimentary Brines with Pb, Zn, and Cu: Implications for the Origin of Mississippi Valley-type Ore Deposits in the Southeast Missouri District
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Posters)
authors: Plambeck, Kacey C. [1], Appold, Martin S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract:
The Mississippi Valley-type (MVT) deposits of the Southeast Missouri district represent the largest known concentration of lead in the Earth’s crust and additionally contain major concentrations of zinc and copper. The Southeast Missouri MVT deposits are known to have precipitated from sedimentary brines that may have been quite metal-rich. Lead isotope data suggest that lead, and by analogy possibly other metals, were derived mainly from the Cambrian-age Lamotte Sandstone, which is widely distributed across the central U.S. Ore-forming sedimentary brines are hypothesized to have flowed northward through the Lamotte Sandstone from the Arkoma basin in Arkansas to Southeast Missouri during the Pennsylvanian-Permian in response to the Alleghanian-Ouachita orogeny. As the brines traveled northward, they may have dissolved diagenetic iron oxide cement in the Lamotte, releasing adsorbed Pb, Zn, and Cu into the brines. Iron oxide cement is now largely absent from the Lamotte Sandstone from central Missouri southward. However, it is abundant in northern Missouri in red bed facies that the ore-forming brines may not have reached. The purpose of the present study was to test how effectively red bed facies in the Lamotte Sandstone could have released Pb, Zn, and Cu into a potential MVT ore-forming sedimentary brine.

Representative samples of Lamotte red bed facies were collected from three drill cores in central-northeastern Missouri, archived by the Missouri Department of Natural Resources. Whole rock compositional analysis was performed on digested samples using ICP-MS and showed them to contain between 1 to 10 ppm Pb, 1 to 3 ppm Zn, and 0.5 to 2 ppm Cu. Two grams of red bed sandstone were placed in two mL of synthetic sedimentary brine and sealed in a Parr reaction vessel. The samples were then placed in an oven at 200° C and allowed to react for 1-4 weeks. The resultant composition of the brines was then analyzed using ICP-MS. The results so far showed the brines to reach Pb and Zn concentrations of 0.1 to 3.3 and 0.5 to 1.75 ppm, indicating that much of the available Pb and Zn was released into solution within the duration of the experiments. This suggests that red bed facies in the Lamotte Sandstone would have been very effective sources of base metals for potential MVT ore-forming sedimentary brines.

abstract: Examining fire activity in response to natural climate changes of the past is key to better understanding future fire dynamics. Sedimentary charcoal records can be used to pinpoint past fire events within a watershed and document long term regional trends in fire activity. In this study, we present a c. 13,000-year paleofire record from Ossipee Lake in central New Hampshire. Charcoal particles (>125 µm) were isolated, counted, and charcoal morphologies were quantified by using image analysis software integrated with a transmitted light microscope. Trends in the morphometry of the particles including: aspect ratio, area:perimeter ratio, roundness, and circumference were analyzed to infer changes in the source of charcoal and intensity of fire events. Additionally, select charcoal samples were imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Charcoal accumulation rates show elevated fire activity from c. 10,100-5600 cal yr BP and two peaks, c. 10,100 cal yr BP and c. 8,300 cal kyr BP. Generally lower charcoal accumulation rates define the last c. 5,600 cal yr BP, although elevated values are observed from c. 1000-700 cal yr BP. Greater fire activity in the early Holocene was likely in response to warmer and drier climate conditions and is supported by other regional records, but few exist in close proximity to our site. The largest paleofire events are also characterized by distinct charcoal morphometries likely related to burn temperature and intensity, as well as transport distance. This study contributes to our understanding of the northeastern United States fire history. Ongoing work will examine the connections between fire activity, changing climate, human activity, and vegetation throughout the region to better understand the drivers of these trends.

authors: Marshall, Adrienne [1], Cowherd, Marianne [2], Rahimi, Stefan [3], Ye, Yuhong [4], Corrigan, Rachel [5]

abstract: Extreme event attribution methods have advanced rapidly in recent years, but have generally not been applied to the phenomenon of snow drought. Yet snow drought has many of the characteristics best suited to extreme event attribution: it is well represented by (downscaled) climate models, covers large spatial extents, and is highly impactful to society from a water resource perspective. Over the winter of 2025-2026, an unusually widespread and severe snow drought developed that substantially affected winter recreation and water supplies. Here, we apply probabilistic extreme event attribution to ask: to what extent was this snow drought attributable to the climate change that has occurred since the pre-industrial period? To do so, we sum March 15 snow water equivalent (SWE) data from the ERA5-Land product across the major river basins of the western U.S. We assess the probability of SWE volumes at least as low as those observed on March 15, 2026 with respect to a 21-year factual period centered on 2026 in the SSP3-7.0 scenario, and a 50-year counterfactual period spanning 1850-1900. Factual and counterfactual data originate from a dynamically-downscaled set of 10 members of the CESM2-large ensemble. We find that a snow drought this severe across the western U.S. was approximately 4.4 [95% CI: 2.6, 9.4] times more likely in the current factual period than in the pre-industrial counterfactual. In the Upper Colorado River Basin, the snow drought was approximately 14 times more likely [0.09, 4300]. In the western U.S., the annual probability of a snow drought this severe would be expected to triple by the 2050s and become more common than not by the 2090s. We also evaluate the evolution of snow drought attributability over the winter season, quantify the relative contributions of temperature and precipitation anomalies, and assess snow drought attributability as a function of severity. The results ground projections of changing snow in the lived experience of a particularly low snow year, and could be used to inform adaptation and motivate mitigation. They should also spur additional scientific inquiry into the attributability of snow drought and its impacts.

title: On Thin Ice: Investigating Subglacial Volcanic Systems in a Warming Climate
session_title: Volcano-climate interactions
authors: Banik, Tenley J. [1], Carley, Tamara L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Geosciences, Lafayette College, Easton, PA, USA
abstract:
Volcano-ice interactions result from processes acting simultaneously from below (lithosphere/aesthenosphere) and above (atmosphere/hydrosphere/cryosphere). Magma flux and eruptions respond to deglaciation and decompression; ice volumes are influenced by changing climate and precipitation patterns; magmatic heat and meltwater create unique hazards like jökulhlaups and phreatomagmatic eruptions. Understanding the dynamic interactions between magmatic systems and glaciers often requires in situ fieldwork. However, access to partially or completely ice-covered volcanoes is rapidly changing along with global climate. These changes may be simultaneously beneficial (e.g., new outcrops revealed) and detrimental (e.g., safety) to scientific exploration of subglacial volcanoes. Travel on glaciers, while always risky, is now more dangerous in scope and scale. Crevasse fields grow where the forces on the ice can no longer be mitigated by thickness; meltwater pools degrade snow and ice quality and endanger transit; always-dangerous icefalls are even more unpredictable; and many more threats lurk under thinning ice.

We detail some of the impacts of deglaciation on science and society observed in Iceland while investigating emerging subglacial volcanoes and their environments. We especially focus on an area in southwestern Iceland including Vatnajökull, Europe’s largest temperate glacier; Esjufjöll, a largely ice-covered volcano and the outlet glacier Breiðamerkurjökull that surrounds it; and Jökulsárlón, the famous iceberg-filled lake at the foot of the glacier. A reduction in Breiðamerkurjökull’s ice volume has made the few nunataks of Esjufjöll more exposed and visible. Expeditions several decades ago report being able to ski and hike around Esjufjöll with relative ease; this is no longer practical because the area is surrounded by extensive and dynamic crevasse fields. As glacial ice melts, Jökulsárlón grows; its surface area increases ~0.5 km 2 /yr and is trapped in positive feedback loop, with melting ice increasing lagoon volume, which incites more melting and calving at the toe of Breiðamerkurjökull. The resulting icebergs now draw >300k tourists to Jökulsárlón annually. But even on shore, hazards exist. In July 2025, Jökulsárlón was closed for 2 days due to a jökulhlaup (outburst flood) emanating from an ice-dammed lake amongst the Esjufjöll nunataks. Incidents like these underscore not only the importance of close scientific study of this increasingly dynamic and unpredictable region, but also effective communication and public outreach to educate the public as melting ice reveals what lies beneath.

abstract: Very few lab studies have investigated the appearance and behavior of sediment-rich flows and eruptions at relevant Mars surface conditions. Studying the physical processes that occur during these events has been challenging from remote sensing and terrestrial field work, because the temperature and pressure conditions at the surface of Mars are very different from those in which Earth analogs form. Here we present a variety of laboratory experimental campaigns that were performed in a Mars environment chamber over the course of several years, and led by several co-investigators. While these experiments are unable to recreate the lower gravity on Mars, they do recreate many other aspects of the surface conditions (e.g., atmospheric pressure and temperature) and sediment composition (testing multiple regolith simulants) to build a robust set of laboratory analog results. In this talk we will show results representing sediment flows in different time periods (Noachian through Amazonian) and spanning different compositions and amounts of water. We will also present an update on the quest to create the first Mars mud volcano in a laboratory setting. Our findings indicate that lab experiments, even at small scales, can give insights into how sediment flows in extreme conditions behave differently than those on Earth. This could have a great impact on how we choose to analyze and target future images of the surface of Mars to better constrain the record of paleoclimate and habitability.

abstract: There has been a lot of discussion in the past decade about the use of digital tools in teaching and studying structural geology and in the collection of spatial data. These tools now have a strong presence in field studies. However, there has been less investigation into whether or not learning is impacted by the use of these digital tools. Our work is guided by this broad research question: do students learn equally from both analog and digital methods when learning new spatial and structural concepts? Here we present preliminary results from a survey of structural geology and field methods instructors as part of our nascent project investigating the impact of digital versus analog tools on learning of spatial concepts, both in the classroom and in the field. Examples of these differing tools include using a Brunton compass versus a compass clinometer built into a tablet, plotting paper stereonets by hand versus plotting on a computer, navigation using a paper topo map versus using a GPS and/or tablet, and many others. We are not trying to determine the accuracy of the digital techniques, but rather whether the students comprehend what they are measuring as effectively as when taught with analog techniques, or perhaps more effectively. We surveyed instructors of structural geology, field methods, and related courses to build a basis for the project. We collected demographic information about how long they have taught and with what type(s) of institution they have experience teaching. We also polled what tools they use in both the classroom and the field, and their personal, qualitative, perception of the effectiveness of different tools. We present the results of this preliminary survey and discuss the next steps in our project as informed by the outcomes of the survey.

abstract: The complete evolutionary history of a clade, encompassing both the origination and extinction of subclades, presents significant analytical challenges due to the sheer number of evolutionary events, environmental changes, and other extrinsic influences impacting the clade. The Order Proetida, which persisted from the Ordovician to the Permian, is an example of a clade with a complex evolutionary history that is poorly understood. Recent work has elucidated part of the Late Paleozoic history of this clade, but little has been done to examine the early evolutionary history of this clade in a phylogenetic context. Here, we examine diversification patterns of Order Proetida from its beginnings in the Ordovician (~485 Mya), through its radiation during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, and persistence across the Late Ordovician Mass Extinctions into the Silurian Period. We character-coded 110 trilobite specimens representing 110 species within Order Proetida using 116 discrete characters arranged across the full trilobite dorsal exoskeleton. We sampled species from many diverse families, including Aulacopleuridae, Bathyuridae, Brachymetopidae, Otarionidae, Proetidae, and Telephinidae. We used a fossilized birth-death (FBD) phylogenetic approach in a Bayesian framework to hypothesize clade-level relationships and evolutionary rates of proetids through these important intervals in the Ordovician. We trace the shift in dominant clades over time. This study adds to the limited number of Bayesian phylogenetic analyses performed on trilobites, and the results provide clarity about the diversification dynamics of the earliest proetids.

abstract: We report a revised stratigraphy and chronology for the late Quaternary sequence at Red Dog Table based on new fossil ages. These data also provide a basis for a new estimate of stream incision and landscape-deflation rates. Red Dog Table is the type locality for the Red Dog Loess, a term that applies to the last glacial loess found in North and South Dakota. The Quaternary stratigraphy at Red Dog Table includes a basal fluvial terrace (10 m) overlain by a loess-paleosol sequence approximately 24 m thick. Paleosols developed at the top of the fluvial terrace, at the base of the loess section, and at the top of the loess section below the aeolian cliff-top deposit. The entire Quaternary section rests on a strath terrace formed in the Oligocene-age upper Brule Formation. We interpret the sequence to have begun with the aggradation of local streams on the strath terrace. As local streams switched from aggradation to incision, protected upland areas formed that allowed loess to accumulate. Using OSL and radiocarbon dating of loess paleosols and fossil snails, we determined absolute ages of 5 ka to present for the uppermost loess (0-6 m), 13 ka for the upper paleosol (7 m), and ~25–22 ka for the lower loess section (8-22 meters). However, the age of the loess and fluvial paleosols (22-24 m) remained unknown due to ambiguous OSL results and absence of fossil gastropods. We also could not determine the time of the switch from aggradation to incision. Here we present a revised chronology based on 14 C results from gastropods ( Succineidae ). Because the dated Succineidae fossils were collected from the base of the fluvial section, we their ages predate terrace abandonment, indicating the switch from aggradation to incision occurred no earlier than 43 ka. The new age constraint on terrace abandonment permits the first quantitative estimate of long-term stream incision and landscape lowering in the western section of the White River Badlands. By constraining the maximum age of the basal fluvial section, we were able to estimate a minimum stream incision/landscape deflation rate. Assuming deposition by an ancestral White River, whose modern channel is now 56 m below the terrace surface, we calculated a minimum incision/deflation rate of 1.30 mm yr -1 since 43 ka.

title: Controls on Normalized Undrained Shear Strength Across Active and Passive Margins: A Linear Mixed-Effects Model
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections (Posters)
authors: Korsah, Isaac Attah [1], Reece, Julia S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA
abstract:
Studies have shown that active continental margins possess normalized undrained shear strengths (Sᵤ/σ′ᵥ) that are two to three times greater than those on passive margins within the upper 100 meters below the seafloor (mbsf). This disparity is frequently attributed to seismic strengthening. However, this hypothesis has not been thoroughly investigated at the field scale against alternative explanations, including inherent sediment properties, such as void ratio and clay mineralogy, as well as depositional controls, such as sedimentation rate and depositional setting. Thus, the relative contributions of seismic strengthening and these other factors to the contrast in undrained shear strength remain unquantified.

Here, we use a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) at eight Integrated Ocean Drilling Program (IODP)/Ocean Drilling Program (ODP) sites, comprising four active- and four passive-margin locations. The model evaluates the impact of intrinsic and depositional covariates on normalized undrained shear strength, incorporating site as a random intercept to account for baseline variability. The analysis focuses predominantly on fine-grained siliciclastic sediments within 100 mbsf. Predictor variables for the model are obtained from core-based measurements. These include undrained shear strength, predominantly from shipboard automated vane shear (AVS) measurements with handheld Torvane data used where AVS coverage is limited, and void ratio from the moisture and density (MAD) dataset. We estimate vertical effective stress assuming hydrostatic conditions. This assumption is validated at each site with Gibson’s (1958) time factor using continuous 1D consolidation indicating negligible excess pore pressures[IK1] . Bulk and clay mineralogy are assessed using full-pattern Rietveld refinement (Profex–BGMN) of bulk X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses including total clay, the illite–smectite (I/S) group, kaolinite, chlorite, and framework minerals such as quartz and feldspar, expressed as isometric log-ratio (ilr) balances, with published oriented <2 µm analyses serving as a cross-check.

This study elucidates the extent to which sediment properties and depositional processes account for the strength contrast between active and passive margins. Additionally, it investigates whether a residual margin effect remains significant beyond these factors, thereby offering a field-scale framework for evaluating the susceptibility of submarine slope failures across margins.

title: Xenolith constraints on lower-crustal temperatures and total crustal heat production

affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA

abstract: Temperatures of the lower crust and Moho, coupled with surface heat flow data, constrain models of heat transfer and bulk composition of the continental crust. Unlike granulite terranes that undergo retrogression during exhumation, xenoliths entrained and launched to the surface by magmatism directly sample the lower crust and can provide a window to lower crustal thermal conditions at the time of host eruption. However, extracting ambient temperatures from granulite xenoliths is not straightforward. Traditional thermobarometry of lower-crustal xenoliths yields temperatures that are generally at odds with pressure-temperature data for mantle-derived xenoliths from the same volcanic hosts, owing to the refectory and anhydrous character of granulites which ihibits their equilibration to ambient conditions. Another avenue is U-Pb thermochronology, which utilizes the temperature-dependent diffusivity of Pb in different accessory minerals; in lower-crustal xenoliths, rutile (Pb closure 600–500 °C) and apatite (Pb closure 450–350 °C) are particularly relevant. Rutile and apatite from various xenolith suites from stable continental regions produce U-Pb isotopic arrays that extend from the timing of regional metamorphism to host eruption age and are interpreted as (1) protracted cooling through the partial retention zone of rutile and/or apatite or (2) re-heating of cool lower crust. High spatial resolution multi-element studies of rutile show evidence for transient depth-dependent heating of the deep crust before eruption, implying that long-term lower crustal temperatures are cool (<400°C). A salient conclusion drawn from such data is that P-T data from peridotite xenoliths from the same areas capture the thermal state of the lithosphere prior to eruption. From this, it can be inferred that the lower crust has exceedingly low heat production (<0.5 μW/m 3 ) for stable continent crust, which in turn implies a bulk mafic lower crust composition and/or extensive depletion of heat-producing elements from felsic lower crust during high-temperature metamorphism and melt extraction. The latter scenario would require removal of a complementary, enriched upper crustal layer to produce the low surface heat flow observed in ancient and stable continents today.

abstract: Trace elements in zircon are physiochemically robust records of both magma chemistry and crystallization age, making them important proxies for studying the Earth’s surface and subsurface evolution in deep time. Proposed application of zircon trace and rare earth elements (T/REE) to identify crustal thickening events and secular tectonic styles rely on empirical relationships between zircon T/REE and depth of melting, attributed to the effects of pressure dependent co-crystallization of plagioclase (Eu/Eu*) and MREE- or HREE-concentrating minerals (garnet; Gd/Yb) with zircon. However, recent work has challenged the validity of zircon T/REE crustal thickness estimators, emphasizing the importance of magma redox conditions and water fugacity on co-crystallizing phases and partitioning of T/REE in zircon. This study uses zircon U-Pb geochronology and T/REE from 23 arc-derived ash deposits within measured stratigraphy spanning 70 Myr to track the Jurassic-Cretaceous evolution of the Southern Patagonian magmatic arc from slab roll-back induced back-arc extension and seafloor spreading to compression, basin closure, and arc-continent collision (150-80 Ma). Zircon Eu/Eu* based calibrations predict >20km of crustal thickening during basin extension (150-120 Ma), inconsistent with independently supported crustal attenuation. Ce/Nd values and oxygen fugacity relative to the fayallite-magnetite-quartz buffer (𝚫FMQ) were co-elevated with Eu/Eu*, suggesting increasing melt oxidation state during slab rollback exerted a dominant influence on zircon T/REE. Between the initiation of compression and ophiolite obduction (120-80 Ma), conditions remain oxidizing with stable high Eu/Eu* and Ce/Nd. Low Gd/Yb during fold-and-thrust belt development is contrary to expectations during thickening by garnet-dependent proxies, instead indicating increasing crystallization of lower pressure medium REE-sequestering minerals (e.g. amphibole ± titanite). We propose that slab steepening and trenchward arc migration promoted the flux of slab-derived oxidizing fluids and thus more oxidized arc magmas. Stable T/REE values throughout the inversion in stress regime and back-arc closure suggest that zircon T/REE track phases of slab-moderated redox conditions instead of crustal thickening events for the Southern Patagonian Andes. Our results highlight the importance of melt oxidation state on the partitioning of T/REE into zircon and demonstrate the potential of zircon T/REE as a temporal proxy for changing slab dynamics at subduction zones.

title: Could plate tectonic reconstruction be used to identify mineral systems? An orogen-scale test in eastern Australia
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: Rosenbaum, Gideon [1]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia
abstract: The transition to clean energy demands new approaches to mineral exploration. Large mineral systems, such as copper porphyry belts, are empirically linked to identifiable plate tectonic processes, including crustal thickening and contractional deformation, ridge subduction, slab flattening, and terminations of arc magmatic cycles. Can these patterns be used to target exploration in fossil arc systems? I address this question through an orogen-scale synthesis of mineral deposits in the New England Orogen of eastern Australia. This orogen represents a long-lived continental arc that hosts numerous relatively small mineral deposits but lacks world-class porphyry systems. By integrating deposit geochronology and styles with plate tectonic reconstructions, I identify three distinct metallogenic belts controlled by changing plate configurations: (1) a ~290 Ma epithermal Au-Ag belt formed during trench retreat in an extensional backarc setting; (2) two ~250 Ma belts, porphyry Cu-Mo and intrusion-related Sn-W, whose formation coincided with contractional deformation and the end of a magmatic cycle; importantly, the porphyry belt is restricted to an arc segment that was underlain by a relatively shallowly dipping slab; and (3) 235–230 Ma Au-Cu porphyry and intrusion-related deposits that developed within the arc during the final phase of contractional deformation. The New England Orogen thus experienced favorable conditions for mineralisation, including slab shallowing, cyclic arc magmatism, and structural focusing by pulses of contractional deformation. Nevertheless, repeated periods of trench retreat that prevented crustal thickening may have undermined the mechanism for metal enrichment, thus explaining the absence of major, economically significant, mineral systems. These findings demonstrate that plate tectonic reconstructions can effectively identify tracts of enhanced fertility but also reveal why some tectonic settings remain poorly mineralised.

authors: Kuiper, Yvette D. [1], Arolkar, Nikhil [2], Severson, Allison R. [3], Buchanan, J. Wesley [4], Hepburn, J. Christopher [5], Link, Frederik [6], Long, Maureen D. [7]
