abstract:
Detailed structural mapping, and U-Pb zircon analyses on migmatitic gneiss and felsic plutonic rock samples suggest that the Nashoba terrane of eastern Massachusetts reflects a ductile extrusion zone similar to that proposed for the Himalayas. Extrusion occurred as a result of northwestward subduction and accretion of the New England Avalon terrane to the southeast during the latest Silurian to Devonian Acadian orogeny.

The Nashoba terrane is a NW-dipping, shear zone-bounded early Paleozoic arc/back-arc complex on the trailing edge of Gondwana-derived Ganderia. It is characterized by NW-dipping isoclinal folds, overprinted by NW-side-down asymmetric folds in the northwestern part of the terrane and symmetric folds in the southeastern part. The isoclinal folds formed during a ~430-410 Ma period of initial partial melting and extensive plutonism in the Nashoba terrane. High-grade metamorphic conditions in the Nashoba terrane prevailed between ~410 Ma and ~370 Ma, while plutonic rocks intruded mainly in the overlying Merrimack belt. At ~370-360 Ma, NW-side-down folding and subsequent localized shearing occurred in the northwestern Nashoba terrane, while it started cooling, based on new ages of fine-grained dikes and previous 40 Ar/ 39 Ar hornblende ages. Partial melting occurred as late as ~364 Ma in the south-central part. These characteristics are consistent with a model of ductile extrusion, although the lower part of the flow zone, where NW-side-up folds would be expected, is not exposed. Previously recognized ~330-320 Ma partial melting in the southern tip of the Nashoba terrane may have resulted from the onset of the Alleghanian orogeny, related to the formation of Pangea.

Rocks of the Avalon terrane, as well as the Merrimack belt to the northwest, generally reached lower peak metamorphic conditions than the Nashoba terrane. Structures and metamorphic conditions in a ~4x10 km wide zone of the Avalon terrane adjacent to the Nashoba terrane do resemble those of the Nashoba terrane, but zircon ages from three migmatitic gneiss samples are ~602-590 Ma, and no partial melting occurred during the Acadian orogeny.

The data are interpreted in a model of channel flow and ductile extrusion similar to the Himalaya–Tibetan Plateau system. The ductile extrusion zone may have been cut off by the brittle Bloody Bluff Fault and/or an eastward-dipping converter visible in receiver function data from the GENESIS array of broadband seismometers.

authors: Rosenbaum, Gideon [1], Barrett, Alana [2], Toledo Rodrigues, Raiza [3], Allen, Charlotte M. [4], Weinberg, Roberto F [5]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia

abstract: Granitic dome-and-basin patterns, documented in Archean terranes, are typically attributed to vertical, pre-plate tectonic, tectonism. What could be the origin of similar structures in younger (Phanerozoic) rocks? We show an example of tabular granitic bodies, intruded into a Carboniferous sedimentary succession in northeastern Australia. Together with the country rocks, the granitic plutons form macroscopic dome-and-basin fold interference patterns. Field relations indicate syn-kinematic emplacement of the granitic intrusions, which occur as folded sill-like microgranitic bodies, mildly deformed stocks at structural domes, and undeformed granite that cuts across the folded sedimentary sequence. U-Pb zircon ages from the various intrusions yielded an age range of 335–320 Ma, thus constraining the timing of folding. The deformed zone is restricted to a ~30 km wide corridor bounded by two crustal-scale shear zones. Kinematic indicators show that folding was generated by dextral transpression, giving rise to the dominant orientation of folds. The domes and basins are generally concentrated in the proximity of the granitic intrusions, indicating that their development was likely controlled by the syn-kinematic emplacement of these plutons. To explain our field observations, we propose a model whereby the added volume of granite to the exposed section have altered the local strain regime. In response to the forced syn-kinematic intrusions, the strain in the confined transpressional zone of our study area (dominated by flattening strain) was locally altered to constrictional strain. The fold interference pattern in the proximity of the granite intrusions was not necessarily generated by two distinct phases of folding but may have resulted from a local constrictional strain regime involving two orthogonal orientations of shortening.

title: PLATINUM GROUP ELEMENTS DO NOT SUPPORT A METEORITE IMPACT AT THE YOUNGER DRYAS.
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Claeys, Philippe [1], Goderis, Steven [2]
affiliations: (1) Archaeology, Environmental Changes & Geo-Chemistry,, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Brussels, Belgium; Pacific Centre for Isotope and Geochemical Research, Dept. of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada

abstract: The onset of the Younger Dryas (YD) at approximately 12.9 ka has been associated with elevated concentrations of platinum-group elements (PGEs), including platinum (Pt), iridium (Ir), palladium (Pd), osmium (Os), and ruthenium (Ru), in a range of terrestrial and ice-core archives primarily in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. These elevated anomalies constitute one of the most central lines of evidence for the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH), which proposes that an extraterrestrial impact or airburst contributed to abrupt climatic cooling, megafaunal extinctions, and cultural changes near the Pleistocene–Holocene transition. However, several laboratories have failed to reproduce the Ir positive anomalies, using samples from various Yuounger Dryas sites, including the very same sections (Blackwater Draw, NM, Topper SC, and Lommel, Belgium) where elevated Ir was originally reported. Indeed, most YD boundary sections analyzed exhibit no Ir or PGE enrichment. Furthermore, the initially reported Younger Dryas positive Ir anomalies correlate negatively with nickel (Ni) concentrations, which seems highly unusual for two siderophile elements, both abundant in meteorites that normally share the same geochemical behaviour. This is also contradictory to analyses reported at other stratigraphic levels marked by a major meteorite impact such as the K-Pg boundary, or within the impactite, enriched in meteoritic component from several craters, such as Popigai, Morokweng, or Lapparjärvi, where Ni and Ir are clearly positively correlated. Elevated Pt concentrations have been reported from the Greenland Ice Sheet Project 2 (GISP2) that seem to slightly post-date the Younger Dryas. However, this Pt peak is not coupled with an enrichment in any of the other PGEs. This decoupling renders a mantle or meteoritic source for the Pt highly unlikely. Terrestrial and marine Osmium isotopic data have generally not provided unequivocal evidence for a dominant extraterrestrial source, either. This presentation examines the current status of the distribution and origin of highly siderophile elements within the Younger Dryas sequence, argues that there is limited support for a meteorite impact occurring approximately 12,9 ka ago, and discusses different explanations to account for the observed geochemical signatures.

abstract:
Proterozoic rocks of the central Front Range, Colorado, have been deformed during the Paleoproterozoic Yavapai (~1.75-1.68 Ga) and Mazatzal (~1.65-1.60 Ga) orogenies, and the ~1.4 Ga Picuris orogeny. The Picuris orogeny is part of the larger ~1.50-1.35 Ga Pinware-Baraboo-Picuris orogen that extends across North America into Quebec and Labrador, Canada. Initially, ~1.4 Ga deformation in Colorado was thought to be restricted to tectonic foliations in ~1.4 Ga granitoids and ~1.4 Ga reactivation of Paleoproterozoic shear zones, while widespread folding had only been recognized in the Wet Mountains in southern Colorado. Past and ongoing mapping, structural analysis, petrography and geochronology in the central Colorado Front Range has yielded increasing evidence for the effects of the Picuris orogeny.

U-Pb detrital zircon LA-ICPMS analysis of a quartzite provided the first evidence for <1.43 Ga sediment deposition in Colorado, about ten km south of Mount Blue Sky. To date, no other Mesoproterozoic metasedimentary rocks have been found in Colorado. Isoclinal F 1 folds in Paleoproterozoic rocks are overprinted by predominately NE-, N- and NW-trending F 2 folds, folded by shallowly to moderately west-, and locally east-plunging and generally NNW-dipping F 3 folds. Foliation patterns in the ~1.42 Ga Silver Plume granite and the ~1.44 Ga Mount Blue Sky batholith indicate NNW-directed shortening at or after ~1.42 Ga, and suggest that NE-plunging F 2 folds are younger than ~1.42 Ga. Localized, shallowly north-dipping top-to-the-south shear/fault zones with a ten meter-scale spacing indicate south-directed transport. U-Pb LA-ICP-MS zircon data of a syn-tectonic pegmatite indicate that this transport occurred at ~1.4 Ga. Structural, petrographic and U-Pb LA-ICP-MS monazite data show evidence for pervasive ~1.43-1.42 Ga folding (F 3 , and possibly F 2 ) in parts of the central Colorado Front Range and metamorphism as young as 1.39-1.33 Ga.

The <1.43 Ga quartzite is younger than quartzites in New Mexico and Arizona that were deposited prior to or early during the Picuris orogeny, and the relationships between them is not clear. The 1.39-1.33 Ga monazite dates suggest that the quartzite was buried and metamorphosed late during the Picuris orogeny. While the architecture and evolution of the Picuris orogen is still under investigation, our data show that its effects in the central Colorado Front Range were pervasive and widespread.

abstract:
Restoring watersheds affected by legacy mining requires consideration of mine waste dispersed in streambed and alluvial sediments. The Akron Mine in the Tomichi Creek Mining District, Colorado (USA), operated from the 1880s to the 1950s, producing Pb, Ag, Zn, Cu, and Au. Reclamation of the mine and mill sites (2015-2016) improved water quality in Tomichi Creek immediately downstream. However, a September 2021 baseflow synoptic study of an approximately 4 km reach of this circumneutral stream showed downstream increases in concentrations (0.45-µm filtered) of Pb (from <1 to 3 µg/L), Cd (from 0.1 to 0.4 µg/L), and Zn (from 10 to 70 µg/L). Much of the increased metal loading occurred just below two separate beaver ponds. The loading increases occurred with negligible increase in discharge suggesting inputs were due to seepage with relatively high metal concentrations and/or stream water interaction with mine wastes dispersed in bed sediments and alluvium.

Follow-up investigations (2023-2025) evaluated stream-water chemistry under different discharge conditions (spring runoff to baseflow) and interactions between stream water and dispersed mine waste in sediments and alluvium. Stream-water concentrations (0.45-µm filtered) of Cd, Zn, and Pb again increased downstream of the mine-mill site but were less than those observed in 2021, including in Oct. 2024 when stream conductivity and major ion concentrations were similar to those observed in 2021 suggesting variability in metal transport. Metal loads were greatest during spring runoff. Filtration through 0.2- and 0.1-µm pore sizes and ultrafiltration showed Pb associated with Fe-rich colloids whereas Cd and Zn were predominantly dissolved.

Fine-grained streambed sediments (<64 µm) contained elevated Pb (2,100-3,600 ppm), Zn (1,700-3,800 ppm), and Cd (7-21 ppm) throughout the reach, although Cd and Zn were substantially lower near the Akron mine-mill site. Substantially higher metal concentrations were observed in alluvial material previously submerged by beaver ponds during the 2021 study, where metal loads increased. Concentrations of Pb, Zn, and Cd in associated seep and surface waters exceeded stream water concentration by an order of magnitude or more and represent a persistent source of downstream metal loading. Elevated Pb, Zn, and Cd measured in aquatic invertebrates indicate a pathway for ecological exposure and may contribute to impaired trout populations observed at some locations in the stream.

title: Hidden redox heterogeneity regulates trace-metal motion across soils and sediments
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales
authors: Noel, Vincent [1], Paulus, Elizabeth [2], Boye, Kristin [3], Fendorf, Scott [4], Kumar, Naresh [5], Hamann Duncan, Aria [6], Engel, Maya [7], Babey, Tristan [8], Webb, Samuel [9]

abstract:
Trace-metal mobility is commonly interpreted from bulk geochemical conditions, despite soils and sediments exhibiting pronounced physicochemical heterogeneity across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Among these heterogeneities, localized reducing environments embedded within otherwise oxic systems generate steep redox gradients that fundamentally alter trace-metal retention, release, and speciation. Because these anoxic microsites remain difficult to detect and quantify under natural conditions, their influence on trace-metal motion remains largely overlooked, despite increasing evidence that microscale redox heterogeneity could exert first-order controls on trace-metal redistribution across soils and sediments.

To investigate these processes, our Laboratory for Observing Anoxic Microsites in Soils (LOAMS) combines multi-energy synchrotron X-ray fluorescence imaging of intact soil and sediment cores with laboratory-controlled experiments to characterize natural redox heterogeneity and evaluate its influence on trace-metal motion.

Laboratory studies demonstrate that anoxic microsites function as dynamic biogeochemical reactors whose geochemical function depends on both their physicochemical environment and the intrinsic redox properties of individual trace metals. As trace-metal sinks, sulfidic microsites sequester dissolved Ni, Zn, and U through reduction and sulfide precipitation. Their long-term stability depends on resistance to oxidant diffusion, whereas subsequent remobilization depends on the oxidative reactivity of each element. In contrast, anoxic microsites may also directly generate trace-metal sources. For example, particulate organic matter exported from reducing microsites creates proximal reduction zones that mobilize sediment-inherited arsenic. Beyond controlling trace-metal mobilization, anoxic microsites may also preserve the imprint of environmental conditions. For example, contrasting hydrological regimes, such as continuous flooding and alternating wetting–drying, generate distinct populations of redox microsites that produce different arsenic redistributions, illustrating how trace-metal distributions can record environmental history through microsite evolution. To extend these mechanistic observations to natural systems, LOAMS enables direct observation of these hidden reactors in natural systems. Using multiple redox-sensitive elements (e.g., Fe and Mn) as functional proxies, the approach detects and characterizes microsites exhibiting different redox functionalities. Across a mountainous watershed, Fe(II)-rich microsites reveal strong seasonal and topographic variability, providing the field-scale constraints needed to incorporate microsite abundance, distribution, and functionality into predictive models of trace-metal motion.

Together, these observations demonstrate that anoxic microsites represent a missing control on trace-metal motion. Recognizing their prevalence, diversity, and dynamics provides a new mechanistic framework for interpreting trace-metal cycling, past environments, fluid transport, and critical zone evolution across heterogeneous Earth systems.

title: Investigation of Plutonic Igneous Rocks in the Soda Mountains For A-Type Granites in a Non-Arc environment
session_title: Geochronology of Ore Deposits Containing Critical Minerals: Analytical Advances and Applications (Posters)

abstract:
Widespread intermediate-to-felsic intrusive rocks in the Mojave Desert are generally considered to be a product of arc magmatism, mostly produced in higher-flux periods during the mid to late Jurassic and the mid to late Cretaceous. New field and petrographic study suggest the ~ 200 km 2 dark-weathering granitoid of the Soda Mountains, in the central Mojave, does not fit this pattern. Investigation of the study area was accomplished by reconnaissance sampling and more detailed mapping of the area north of I-15 before the Zzyzx Road exit. Samples were processed for petrographic, geochemical (XRF + ICP-MS), and zircon U-Pb analysis.

In hand samples, these granitoids are fine to medium grained, with ca. 1 cm purplish feldspar phenocrysts, as well as miarolitic cavities in some areas. Petrographic analysis shows that these rocks are mostly perthitic one-feldspar syenogranites with micrographic textures. Mafic and accessory minerals include clinopyroxene, rutile, magnetite, and pyrite. The presence of accessory pyrite may account for the dark patina acquired by these rocks upon weathering. Geochemical analysis shows that these granitoids are alkali-rich and ferroan but iron poor. SHRIMP U-Pb zircon ages are Late Jurassic (ca. 153-149 Ma), matching petrographically similar rocks in surrounding areas that are Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous. The perthitic feldspars and accessory pyrite suggest that these rocks were formed in an anhydrous, reduced melting environment not associated with arc magmatism. Rather, these A-type granites could be a symptom of back-arc extensional tectonics or mantle delamination at this time.

abstract: Cratonic lithospheric mantle has survived for billions of years and records the complex evolution of the Earth. However, its compositional evolution and refertilization mechanisms remain controversial due to the relatively scarcity of direct samples from the craton root. Here we present Mg isotopic data of whole rocks and mineral separates (phlogopite, clinopyroxene, K-richterite, orthopyroxene, olivine, and garnet) for a set of mantle-derived mica–amphibole–rutile–ilmenite–diopside (MARID), phlogopite–ilmenite–clinopyroxene (PIC) and associated peridotite xenoliths from the Kaapvaal Craton, southern Africa to study the vertical heterogeneity and evolution of the lithospheric mantle. Systematic Mg isotopic differences are observed among these xenoliths, with peridotites exhibiting near mantle δ 26 Mg values (−0.31‰ to −0.20‰), the mid-depth MARID rocks having low δ 26 Mg values (−1.02‰ to −0.14‰), and deep PIC rocks displaying high δ 26 Mg values (−0.19‰ to −0.07‰). Their mineralogical, geochemical and isotopic stratification reflect the changes caused by metasomatic agents at different depths, which transitioned from predominantly silicate melts/fluids in the deeper mantle to increasingly carbonatite-rich and sediment-derived melts at shallower levels. Such depth-dependent metasomatism promoted craton lithospheric mantle refertilization and compositional layering, which weakens and rejuvenates the lithosphere. Our results further identify MARID rocks as an important long-lived low-δ 26 Mg silicate reservoir that may contribute isotopically light signatures to mantle-derived magmas such as continental basalts.

abstract:
High-level radioactive waste (HLW) generated from nuclear energy production requires long-term isolation due to its high radiotoxicity. Accordingly, deep geological disposal has been internationally recommended, with safety assessments conducted to evaluate repository performance using advanced numerical modeling. While process-based simulations enable high-fidelity modeling of coupled Thermal–Hydraulic–Mechanical–Chemical (THMC) processes, the substantial computational cost limits their application in field-scale simulations. Therefore, system-based simulations have been widely adopted to evaluate integrated radionuclide transport across the near-field, far-field, and biosphere over long timescales. However, previous system-based modeling studies have simplified radionuclide transport in the host rock by assuming conventional single-, dual-, or triple-fracture models, thereby potentially overestimating radionuclide migration.

To address these limitations, a Discrete Fracture Network (DFN) algorithm applicable to system-based models was developed based on a sequential multi-layer concept extending from the repository (source layer) to the ground surface (sink layer). Multiple nodes were assigned to each layer and stochastically connected to nodes in the adjacent layer to capture heterogeneous fracture distributions in the far-field. This framework enables systematic evaluation of the impact of network characteristics (fracture number and length) and repository depth on radionuclide transport and radioactivity. For application to realistic repository conditions, the near-field, far-field, and biosphere domains were integrated into a system-based model implemented in GoldSim. The DFN parameters were subsequently varied to evaluate their effects on ingestion dose through four biosphere exposure pathways–groundwater, crop, meat, and marine fish.

The total ingestion dose predicted by the DFN model was 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than that of conventional fracture models. Notably, multi-peak dose behavior was observed only in the DFN model, suggesting that this feature originated from structural differences in the far-field. The first peak was driven by radionuclides with low distribution coefficients (K d ), which migrated rapidly through the fracture network. In contrast, the second peak was governed by daughter radionuclides exhibiting relatively high sorption (high K d ). This behavior reflects the coupled effects of parent radionuclide retardation and continuous daughter radionuclide ingrowth along the complex fracture network. Across additional sensitivity scenarios, repository depth exerted the dominant influence on the ingestion dose, followed by fracture number and length. These results emphasize the importance of incorporating DFN-based modeling and complete radionuclide decay chains into system-based long-term performance and safety assessment of a HLW repository.

title: From Lake to Raised Bog: Multi–Proxy Reconstruction of Holocene Environmental Change in the Juodymas Peatland
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Ūsaitė, Augustė [1], Gedminienė, Laura [2], Skuratovič, Žana [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Mineralogy, Vilnius University, Vilnius, Lithuania
(2) Department of Geology and Mineralogy, Vilnius University, Vilnius, Lithuania; Quaternary Research Laboratory, Nature Research Centre, Vilnius, Lithuania
(3) Laboratory of Nuclear Geophysics and Radioecology, Nature Research Centre, Vilnius, Lithuania
abstract:
Peatlands are sensitive recorders of past environmental and hydrological change, yet their developmental trajectories remain understudied in many regions of Eastern Europe. This study presents a multi–proxy reconstruction of Holocene environmental change based on a 6.9 meter sediment core from the Juodymas peatland (NE Lithuania). Our aim was to reconstruct the development of the peatland from a postglacial lake through minerotrophic fen and transitional mire stages to an ombrotrophic raised bog, integrating lithological, geochemical, and decomposition–based indicators.

We combined sediment lithology, loss-on-ignition (LOI), granulometry, pH, magnetic susceptibility (MS), energy-dispersive X–ray (EDX) elemental composition, and peat decomposition degree with AMS radiocarbon dating. The obtained age–depth model shows that sedimentation began ca. 10,000–12,000 calibrated years BP in a shallow lacustrine environment, characterized by low organic content, fine mineral matter, and low decomposition. Around 8,500 cal BP, the basin transitioned into a fen as organic accumulation increased and mineral influx declined. Decomposition values exceeded 50%, indicating sustained minerotrophic, waterlogged, and reducing conditions. Between 5,500 and 4,500 cal BP, the peatland underwent a transitional mire stage distinguished by declining peat decomposition values, which fell below 50%, reflecting improved preservation of organic matter and a gradual reduction in groundwater influence. By approximately 4,500 cal BP, proxies collectively record the onset of ombrotrophication: pH decreased, MS stabilized at very low values, and elemental profiles (especially Ca, Na, Mg vs. S, Fe) shifted, reflecting the establishment of predominantly rain–fed conditions. The uppermost sediments show slight mineral enrichment, suggesting possible recent changes in the hydrological regime or external environmental influence, without evidence of major drainage.

Together, these proxies reveal a coherent environmental sequence from lake to fen, transitional mire, and raised bog, consistent with regional postglacial hydrological and climatic trends. The study demonstrates the value of integrating peat decomposition degree with geochemical and lithological indicators for reconstructing long–term peatland dynamics. Juodymas peatland represents a largely intact raised bog, highlighting its importance as an archive of Holocene environmental history and its relevance for peatland conservation.

title: Misfit ferromanganese: characteristics of nodules from the Blake Plateau and updated comparison with pelagic occurrences
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Mizell, Kira [1]
affiliations: (1) Pacific Coastal and Marine Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Santa Cruz, CA, USA
abstract: Seabed ferromanganese crusts and nodules are large reservoirs for manganese (Mn), cobalt (Co), and nickel (Ni) that are being considered as potential resources to supplement metal supply needs for current battery technologies. Nodules are of particular interest due to decades of international research in the Clarion Clipperton Zone and the perceived feasibility of their recovery as loose rocks at the surface of seafloor sediments. Most sampled marine nodule occurrences with high Mn contents paired with high Co and/or high Ni and copper (Cu) contents are found in pelagic abyssal plain regions of the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans at water depths of more than 4,000 meters. The Blake Plateau is an exception to this, where ferromanganese nodules occur along the continental margin of the southeastern United States at depths of 500-1,000 meters. As interest in offshore mineral resource potential has recently resurged, updated and expanded analysis of previously sampled Blake Plateau ferromanganese nodules has been completed. New mineralogical and geochemical data for recharacterized archive samples are presented and compared with data from abyssal regions. For example, Blake Plateau nodules contain approximately 10 times less Cu and less lithium (Li) than the compiled average for Clarion Clipperton Zone nodules. An important and unique property of Blake Plateau nodules compared with pelagic occurrences is the presence of many fractures and veins of aragonite, calcite, and sometimes carbonate fluorapatite that dilute ferromanganese oxides in the bulk material. Despite this, Mn and Co concentrations are comparable to abyssal nodules, and concentrations of the U.S. Geological Survey-defined critical minerals tellurium (Te) and platinum (Pt) are enriched. The discussion of these and other properties of Blake Plateau nodules and their setting will help differentiate this mineral occurrence within the broader context of abyssal ferromanganese nodule resource potential.

title: Late Quaternary source-to-sink palaeohydrology, erosion and aeolian dynamics recorded in a small, dune-dammed, arid dunefield margin playa
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Roskin, Joel [1], Golovaty, Nitay [2], Vainer, Shlomy [3], Faershtein, Galina (Gala) [4], Bookman, Revital [5]
affiliations: (1) Bar-Ilan University, RAMAT GAN, Israel
(2) Bar-Ilan University, RAMAT GAN, Israel
(3) Ben-Gurion University in the Negev, Israel
(4) Geological Survey of Israel, Jerusalem, Israel
(5) University of Haifa, Haifa, Israel
abstract:
The extent of the Holocene climate fluctuations and their palaeoenvironmental responses in the northern Negev desert, situated along a climatic gradient, are crucial for interpreting remarkable regional cultural transitions and for referencing current climate changes. Cored sediment archives from a terminal playa of a ~2 km² dune-dammed basin along the southern margin of the northwestern Negev desert dunefield reveals evidence of Late Quaternary to current, source-to-sink palaeo-hydrologies and environments, aeolian dynamics, sediment accumulation and erosion rates of basinal aeolian deposits. Six main stratigraphic units determined by texture, geochemistry port-OSL and OSL ages, reflect four distinct paleoenvironments. A sharply truncated basal unit records fluvial reworking and accumulation of loess-dominated fines in the MIS-3, in an open fluvial system. An overlaying sand unit marks an abrupt transition to a windy Younger Dryas climate driving windblown sand to dune-dam the basin. Fluvial reworking of dune sand and contemporaneous deposition of the sand and secondary sandy to silty loess until the early Holocene followed. The subsequent three early-late Holocene units document stabilized dunefield conditions and sustained, slow fluvial playa infilling, dominated by upbasin, loess-derived sediment. Renewed aeolian sand input during Roman-Byzantine times corresponds to anthropogenic dune destabilization. The last ~500 years have been characterized by sedimentation of fine-silt loam, reflecting dune stabilization and loess diminishment.

Evidence of ten, distinct, high-magnitude flood events by a sharp sand content decrease in the core sediments, imply sporadic, ~millennial-scale recurrence along the Holocene and not climate-controlled environmental change. The upper four units dating since the middle Holocene lack sedimentological and geochemical evidence of significant climatic change. Upbasin loess erosion fluctuating along the Holocene between ~0.003–0.007 mm yr⁻¹ may reflect slight changes in climate-controlled paleohydrology but also declining loess availability and erodibility. These proxies demonstrate that the northern Negev has undergone altogether a moderate, arid Holocene climate. Runoff calculations based on modern high-resolution rainfall data, supported by field-based observations and calculations indicate playa water-depths of ~4 cm per average-sized flood, usually with single occurrence per annum. The water infiltrates in several days, demonstrating short-term seasonality of current and probably past small, dune-dammed waterbodies along the Negev dunefield fringe.

title: 1st-order basin Terminal Pleistocene to Modern Pedosediment Accretion Rates Reflect Late Holocene Anthropogenic Impact Overriding Late Quaternary Climate Change on Pedosediment Cover in the Judean Highlands, Central Israel
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Roskin, Joel [1], Faershtein, Galina (Gala) [2], Tiano, Jamie [3], Sivan Mizrahi, Ahuva [4], Salomons, Noa [5], Klimova, Tatiana [6]
affiliations: (1) Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel
(2) Geological Survey of Israel, Jerusalem, Israel
(3) Israel Antiquities Authority, Jerusalem, Israel
(4) IAA, Jerusalem, Israel
(5) Bar-Ilan University, Jerusalem, Israel
(6) BIU, Israel
abstract:
The highlands of Israel and Transjordan within a Mediterranean climate have undergone intensive culture changes since prehistory. These changes, apparently peaking with dry agriculture terracing, have impacted the landscape, alongside longer timescales of deposition-pedogeneis-erosion cycles of aeolian-sourced red-brown mountain (Terra Rosa/Lithic Rohodoxeralf) soils. Together the natural processes and human engagements have led to the depletion of long-term sedimentary and pedogenic archives. Here we present as part of archaeological surveys and excavations, a rare, well-preserved quasi-continuous type-section of pedosediment accumulation in a local depression of a small (0.2 km 2 ) 1 st -order basin in the hard carbonate terrain of the Judean Highlands (Israel). The depression pedosediments host a double-stage Chalcolithic settlement and an ancient thick dam-like wall within the pedosediment.

The 2.5 m thick type-section contrasts with thin and young soil cover on the adjacent slopes. The section possesses uniform silt texture and geochemistry that reliably support portable optically stimulated luminescence (port-OSL) profiling. Coupling port-OSL measurements with six full OSL ages yields a (R 2 =0.96) port-OSL – OSL linear regression that can enable calculation of pedosediment accretion patterns and rates and roughly estimate ages of nearby ancient agriculture installations, sediments and soils. The accretion rates reflect upbasin sediment erosion rates that help interpret the post-LGM pedosedimentary processes, that in turn assist in interpreting the cyclic pedosediment mantling of the Levant highlands.

Low pedosediments accretion rates from the middle Epipalaeolithic period at the section base to the Middle Bronze Age suggest that along these ~10 kyrs of Pleistocene-Holocene transition of regional climate fluctuations, only subtle geomorphic change occurred, probably due to dense maquis cover and limited human involvement. Whilst the region began to undergo fluctuations in agricultural-oriented village occupations since Chalcolithic times, only by the Middle Bronze Age did accretion rates significantly increase until pre-modern times. We therefore associate sediment accretion increase with erosion due to progressive anthropogenic maquis decimation for fuel, construction, grazing and agricultural clearing along with speculated growing fire recurrence. During Roman times, accretion rates rocketed but already relaxed since Byzantine times. The enhanced soil erosion rates may have been eventually observed by locals, motivating sustainable solutions like dry agriculture terracing that regionally peaked only in the 2 nd Millenium. The finds suggest that ancient human activities generated larger geomorphic impacts than late Quaternary climate changes.

title: Milankovitch Cyclicity and the Pacing of Middle Miocene Planktic Foraminiferal Plasticity
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: King, Gretl [1], Swain, Anshuman [2], Lam, Adriane R. [3]
affiliations: (1) Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY,
(2) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI,
(3) Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY,
abstract:
The global shift, 14.7 million years ago, from the warm Miocene Climate Optimum (MCO) to the cooling Middle Miocene Climate Transition (MMCT) provides an opportunity to investigate how biotic and abiotic Earth systems processes respond to increased CO 2 scenarios. These processes are recorded in ocean sediments, with mid-latitude deep-sea sites serving as archives for investigating the interaction of atmospheric, oceanic, and organism response to climate shifts. This study uses sediments from IODP Expedition 371, Site U1510, which contains carbonate ooze with fantastic planktic foraminiferal preservation and a complete Middle Miocene section.

Fossilized planktic foraminifera provide a unique dataset that contains ecological data in the form of isotopic signatures and ecosystem data in the form of assemblage counts and assemblage-level test size changes. Using computational methods, we will compare test size data and thermocline and surface isotope data at a ~3 kyr resolution from 14 to 15.25 million years ago. The datasets will be analyzed for orbital signatures and lead-lag offsets.

Foraminiferal sizes in this record change in sync with Hadley Cell expansion and contraction, suggesting that species plasticity at the site is driven in part by Milankovitch cycles. Breakpoint analyses on the test size data also indicate three clear intervals: 1) the MCO where test sizes become smaller with warming and are paced by eccentricity; 2) the transition from the MCO to MMCT where sizes remain ~stable across the interval, but shorter-term size changes are paced by obliquity and precession; and 3) the MMCT where again sizes decreases across climate cooling. Foraminiferal test size changes are likely responding to surface water temperatures, as indicated by lower-resolution stable isotopic analyses, in response to shifting water masses with Hadley Cell contraction and expansion.

With climate cooling, thermoclines cooled and saw increased particulate organic matter flux to deeper waters, which opened a new niche space for thermocline-dwelling planktic foraminifera. We hypothesize that during the transition from the MCO to MMCT, the thermocline species’ test sizes are driven by Antarctic sea ice sensitivity to obliquity forcing, whereas mixed-layer dwelling species’ test sizes were driven by changing surface ocean water masses over Site U1510. More analyses are underway to connect micro- and macroevolutionary processes in the planktic foraminifera to orbital drivers.

abstract:
Lead (Pb) exposure remains a well established cause of impaired neurological development and an increasingly recognized risk factor for premature death worldwide, with both burdens falling disproportionately on marginalized communities. In agricultural settings, legacy Pb contamination in soil continues to pose risks decades after major emission sources have been eliminated, particularly in urban and peri-urban soils used for food production. This presentation synthesizes two complementary chapters in the 92nd volume of Reviews in Mineralogy and Geochemistry focused on Lead: the geochemical characterization and mitigation of agricultural soil Pb, and the participatory science frameworks needed to leverage this science towards equitable, community-driven action.

The first chapter traces the natural and anthropogenic origins of Pb in agricultural soils, its environmental fate and transformation, and the risks to human health, with emphasis on urban farms and community gardens. We review existing guidance values and best management practices for reducing exposure and present a decision-support framework for determining appropriate growing strategies when elevated soil Pb is identified. Case studies demonstrate that covering contaminated soil with clean soil, compost, or other amendments can be a highly effective, lower-cost alternative to full remediation—provided that covers are maintained and future land users remain informed of underlying contamination.

The second chapter addresses how this science is generated and applied. Drawing on lessons from collaborations with impacted communities, we outline principles for participatory and community science that avoid extractive "parachute" research and instead center community priorities in setting research agendas, interpreting data, and determining outcomes. We draw from published literature on participatory science in general, research projects focused on lead, and lessons from case studies in which the authors have participated. We also provide responses to frequently asked questions to guide new researchers and highlight non-traditional products of this work—including co-developed public-facing materials, construction of new soils, youth mentoring programs, and policy advocacy tools—products that carry as much value to communities as peer-reviewed publications.

Together, these perspectives argue that addressing legacy soil Pb contamination requires the integration of rigorous science and sustained, trust-based partnerships with the communities most affected—an approach with broad relevance to other environmental contaminants and settings.

title: Groundwater Vulnerability Assessment in an Area Under Agricultural and Urban Influence.Case Study: The Xochimilco Lacustrine Zone, Mexico City
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: Torres Rojas, Susana Rocio [1], Archundia Peralta, Denisse [2], Olea-Olea, Selene [3]
affiliations: (1) Instituto de Geologia, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Geologia, Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico

(2) Instituto de Geologia, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico; Secretaría de Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación (SECIHTI), Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico
(3) Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Geologia, Ciudad Universitaria, Mexico, Mexico
abstract:
The Xochimilco lacustrine zone is one of the last remaining wetlands in Mexico City and has been recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site because of its traditional chinampa agricultural system. This area is currently subjected to significant anthropogenic pressure from both agricultural and urban activities. Agricultural practices, particularly the application of fertilizers and livestock manure, represent important sources of nutrient inputs that may affect environmental quality, groundwater resources, and human health (He et al., 2018). At the same time, rapid urban expansion surrounding the canal network, together with inadequate wastewater management infrastructure, has increased nutrient loading from domestic sources. These combined pressures pose a growing threat to the Xochimilco aquifer, which represents an important groundwater resource for Mexico City's water supply.

This study evaluated aquifer vulnerability under these urban agricultural pressures using the DRASTIC index proposed by Aller et al. (1985). The index was developed using field measurements of groundwater depth from monitoring wells, modeled net recharge, aquifer lithology interpreted from well logs, laboratory determined soil characteristics, topography, vadose zone lithology, and hydraulic conductivity obtained from pumping test data. The resulting DRASTIC index ranged from 63 to 110, indicating low to moderate vulnerability across the study area. The highest vulnerability values were identified in the ejidos of San Gregorio Atlapulco, Santa Cruz Acalpixca, San Luis Tlaxialtemalco, and Ciénega Grande, where intensive chinampa agriculture coexists with irregular urban settlements. These conditions increase the potential risk of groundwater contamination and may also affect the quality of canal irrigated crops, with possible implications for the health of local producers and consumers.

Historical hydrogeochemical records from 2007, 2018, and 2025 revealed increasing concentrations of nitrate, nitrite, and phosphate, together with a hydrochemical evolution from calcium magnesium bicarbonate facies to mixed sodium chloride bicarbonate facies. Comparison of these data with the vulnerability map indicates that nutrient enrichment occurs in several moderately vulnerable areas, suggesting a partial spatial correspondence between intrinsic aquifer susceptibility and observed anthropogenic impacts. These findings also indicate that additional factors, including land use and localized nutrient sources, influence groundwater vulnerability. A modified DRASTIC index is currently being developed by incorporating land use, geological faulting, and nutrient concentrations to produce a more representative vulnerability assessment and provide scientific support for groundwater protection and sustainable management strategies.

title: Implications of Newly-Discovered Pliocene Trace Fossils for Understanding of the Formation of Death Valley, California
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics
authors: Norton, Ian O. [1], Venn, Matthew [2]
affiliations: (1) Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Fredonia, NY, USA
abstract: The Sierra Nevada forms the western boundary of the East California Shear Zone (ECSZ), with the Owens Valley Fault being the westernmost major fault within the zone. Death Valley is within the shear zone, and was formed as a pull-apart basin bounded to the north and south by dextral strike-slip faults offset by about 20 km across the valley. The basin is asymmetric, bounded on the east side by the Black Mountains fault system with as much as 7 km throw and relatively minor documented faulting on the west side. The pull-apart basin is thought to have initiated at 6 Ma, the same time as the San Andreas Fault. Within the Black Mountains there are several sedimentary basins that attest to a complex tectono-sedimentary history. One of these basins is represented by the Copper Canyon Formation, a fluvio-lacustrine unit deposited between about 5 and 3.1 Ma. It is notable for the preserved tracks of many Pliocene birds and mammals, including camels. It is now situated about 500 meters above the floor of Death Valley. Similar-age sediments have not previously been identified on the west side of Death Valley. In this paper we report the discovery of camel tracks very similar to ones found in Copper Canyon, at a site on the west side of the valley. The samples are at a slightly higher elevation relative to those at Copper Canyon and are found in outcrops that were previously mapped as simply ‘Tertiary Volcanics’. Dips are about 20 degrees to the east. These new data shed important light on the paleogeography of Death Valley over the last 3.1 million years.

title: Random Forest Modeling of Informal Settlement Runoff Treatment in a Constructed Wetland (Franschhoek, South Africa)

affiliations: (1) Computer Science, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA

abstract: Inadequate wastewater services in rapidly growing informal settlements in South Africa cause raw human waste to enter river systems during rainfall events, resulting in high concentrations of Escherichia coli (E. coli), ammonia nitrogen (NH₃-N), and orthophosphate (PO₄³–), which compromise aquatic ecosystems and human health. To remediate pollutants, a multi-stage constructed wetland was built along the Stiebeuel River downstream of an informal settlement in Franschhoek. The Water Hub, a research center affiliated with the University of Cape Town’s Future Water Institute, developed the wetland to provide decentralized, nature-based water treatment. This study developed a machine learning model based on the Random Forest algorithm using hyperparameter tuning, variable importance rankings, robust evaluation metrics, and leave-one-out cross-validation to estimate concentrations of E. coli, NH₃-N, and PO₄³– throughout the wetland, based on location data and physicochemical properties, including dissolved oxygen, electrical conductivity, pH, and turbidity. Historical water quality data were obtained in-situ from the Water Hub. Location within the wetland was the strongest predictor for E. coli, NH₃-N, and PO₄³–, accounting for 82.9%, 44.6%, and 45.2% of relative variable importance, followed by electrical conductivity and turbidity. The models for NH₃-N and PO₄³– consistently recovered spatial treatment patterns, while the model for E. coli could not differentiate between low-concentration stages. Model errors were skewed towards high-concentration sample locations, with each model reproducing only 40%-52% of the observed concentration range across sampling locations. These findings suggest that location data within the constructed wetland is a crucial water quality metric for Random Forest regression. However, additional climatological and seasonal parameters are needed to reliably predict peak pollutant concentrations. Incorporating these parameters can provide a tool to help researchers predict pollutant concentrations throughout a constructed wetland under temporal pollution contributions from an informal settlement.

abstract:
The catastrophic flood of 29–30 October 2024 in the Valencia region (eastern Spain) caused 231 fatalities and $11–18 billion in losses, ranking among the deadliest European floods in over five decades. Triggered by a cut-off low (up to 621 mm of rainfall in six hours), it reached 2282 m³/s in the Rambla del Poyo (384 km²) before the gauging station collapsed. This was nearly five times the previous instrumental maximum of 527 m³/s, which was recorded in 2000. Widely portrayed as "unprecedented", the event is here tested by placing its magnitude within a multi-century framework from paleoflood and documentary evidence (written reports, flood marks, and photos). Slackwater deposits were investigated and dated using ¹⁴C and OSL methods along five reaches of the Rambla del Poyo catchment, including the main stem and four major tributaries. The 2024 high-water marks were surveyed, and modern and paleoflood discharges estimated by 1D–2D hydraulic modeling (HEC-RAS v6).

Documentary records at Chiva (stream headwaters) list 18 major floods since 1731. The event in 1776 event reached a slightly higher stage (3.6 m) than in 2024 (2–2.95 m), indicating that the 2024 flood was no unprecedented in the headwaters. In the middle Poyo (downstream Cheste), the oldest of five units (277±18 yr, likely 1731 CE) yields a minimum discharge of 1620 m³/s and the most recent (post-1865 CE) 2080 m³/s, versus 2820 m³/s in 2024 based on HWMs. The Barranc del Gallego (40 km²) records 24 floods since the 17 th century; its largest (likely 1776) reached 650–950 m³/s, unmatched until 2024 (1100 m³/s). In the Barranc de la Horteta (91 km²), three benches hold >30 paleoflood units; five younger than 690±90 yr (likely post-1427 CE) exceeded 940–1140 m³/s, and the highest bench is capped by 2024 sand (1630 m³/s) overlying a likely historical paleoflood unit. Flood frequency analysis places 2024 at the highest rank of recorded paleofloods, with shorter recurrence in headwater streams (T: 250 yr) than in mid-lower tributaries (T: 400–500 yr). These paleoflood discharges provide new information for updating the hazard maps for the Valencia district and for developing adaptation strategies.

title: STRUCTURAL EVIDENCE FOR LEFT-LATERAL STRIKE-SLIP DEFORMATION IN THE SOUTHERN OZARKS: A LIDAR AND FIELD-BASED STUDY
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: Meservey, Warren [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Enviroment, and Sustainibility, Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
abstract: The tectonic mechanism and timing of the Ozark Uplift remain subjects of regional debate. While recent models hypothesize that midcontinent deformation was driven by late Paleozoic oblique collision and governed by a network of regional strike-slip faults, field-based kinematics validating lateral displacement have historically been sparse. This study integrates high-resolution 1-meter LiDAR data (3DEP) and targeted field mapping within the southern Ava District of the Mark Twain National Forest (Taney and Ozark Counties, Missouri) to evaluate a prominent, sub-parallel lineament cluster adjacent to the WSW-ENE-trending Foil Fault. Geospatial analysis of approximately 360 digitized lineaments reveals systematic, systematic spacing averaging 169 meters, with individual lengths reaching up to 1,500 meters. The lineaments are preferentially hosted within the Lower Ordovician Cotter Dolomite and exhibit a geometric orientation acute to the Foil Fault. This acute angular relationship structurally aligns with established mechanical criteria for synthetic primary Riedel shears () operating under a left-lateral strike-slip regime. Stratigraphic ground-truthing and drone imagery confirm that these lineaments intensely fracture the Ordovician strata but do not occur in Mississippian Pierson Limestone. Stratigraphic offsets of the Bachelor Sandstone indicate a subsequent post-Mississippian dip-slip reactivation along the Foil Fault, resulting in 11 to 12 meters of north-side-up vertical displacement. These findings provide direct structural evidence supporting strike-slip fault models. The episodic timing of midcontinent brittle deformation, offer critical geometric constraints for managing fractured-bedrock groundwater aquifer pathways.

title: Understanding the Lived Experiences of Neurodivergent Geoscience Faculty and the Impact on Their Education and Career
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Potter, Erin M [1], Sheffield, Sarah L. [2], Cook, Meghan Lindsey [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, New York, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
(3) Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA, USA
abstract:
Neurodivergent faculty are underrepresented in higher education; evidence suggests that they experience barriers such as stigma, disclosure challenges, inaccessible workplace practices, and limited institutional support, which can lead to higher rates of attrition. Within the geosciences these barriers may be amplified by discipline-specific norms, such as field-based instruction, and more ubiquitous academic barriers, like traditional academic expectations, and a historical lack of accessible practices. While previous researchers have explored accessibility and inclusion for geoscience students, there are few studies on how neurodivergent geoscience faculty experiences influence teaching, research, mentoring, and career progression.

We study the lived experiences of neurodivergent geoscience faculty in the United States to explore how institutional environments shape disability experiences. Specifically, we investigate the (1) barriers neurodivergent geoscience faculty encounter in their professional roles, (2) strategies and resources they use to navigate these challenges, and (3) personal experiences that might inform their approaches to teaching practices and research.

We collected responses to an anonymous Qualtrics survey distributed nationally via professional geoscience organizations, listservs, and social media platforms. Respondents represent a range of identities, but are geoscience faculty at higher education institutions in the United States that identify as neurodivergent. We used open response and Likert scale questions to gather participant responses to questions about their experience as a neurodivergent faculty member in a higher education institution, including questions about perceived barriers and supports. To make meaning of the data, we performed inductive thematic coding. Themes are guided by our theoretical frameworks of Critical Disability Theory and Self-Concept Theory. We present the themes we produced to better define the specific barriers that neurodivergent faculty members faced or continue to face. We also use the themes from participant responses to present recommendations for better institutional support of neurodivergent faculty. Initial results support systemic changes to inclusive pedagogical approaches that are necessary to not only enhance the experiences of faculty in academia, but for student experiences as well.

By documenting the experiences of neurodivergent geoscience faculty, our research seeks to inform evidence-based practices that promote accessibility and inclusion across geoscience education. Our findings contribute to ongoing efforts to improve faculty support and strengthen inclusive teaching practices benefiting the higher education learning environment as a whole.

title: Revisiting evidence for Triassic-Early Jurassic divergent double subduction in the northern Sierra Nevada
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Shimabukuro, David H. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, California State University, Sacramento, CA, USA
abstract:
Two broad tectonic models are commonly applied to the Triassic-Jurassic evolution of the northern Sierra Nevada metamorphic belt. In the first, the belt was assembled largely above a continuously east-dipping subduction zone, with episodes of arc rifting, translation, and back-arc basin collapse. In the second, an arc constructed over a west-dipping subduction zone collided with the continental margin. This west-dipping subduction zone is often depicted as part of a Molucca Sea-style divergent double-subduction system that consumed an intervening oceanic basin. Recent detrital zircon and geophysical studies have called this second model into question. Here, we evaluate whether a west-dipping subduction zone is still required to explain the Triassic-Jurassic evolution of the northern Sierra Nevada.

Two Triassic-Jurassic subduction zones are preserved in the northern Sierra Nevada. The eastern subduction zone is represented by the Feather River ultramafic belt, its metamorphic sole, and the underlying blueschist-bearing Red Ant Schist. Recent ca. 255 Ma high-temperature U-Pb ages from the sole link this system to the inboard Permo-Triassic Cordilleran arc, indicating that it was likely east dipping. The western subduction zone is exposed in the Foothills Belt and is evidenced by eclogite and high-pressure amphibolite preserved in metamorphic soles underlying ophiolites. Although this subduction zone is associated with the Triassic-Jurassic Slate Creek-Lake Combie-Peñon Blanco oceanic arc, its polarity remains uncertain.

Arguments for west-dipping subduction have largely relied on interpretations of east-vergent thrust systems and regional tectonic relationships. However, the early structure has been overprinted by late west-vergent thrusts, making their original geometry unclear, and no single across-strike transect preserves the complete arc-forearc-subduction complex architecture. Several recent detrital-zircon studies in Jurassic clastic overlap sequences have identified continentally derived zircons, which seem to indicate that the arc formed near the continental margin above an east-dipping subduction zone. However, the Jurassic clastics are underlain by Triassic cherts, suggesting that the arc initially developed in a distal oceanic setting. This transition from deep basin to clastic sedimentation could be explained through closure of an intervening oceanic basin.

Two approaches may help resolve this problem. First, tectonic vergence should be determined within high-pressure rocks of the subduction complexes. Second, additional work is needed to understand the tectonic setting of the Triassic-Early Jurassic cherts that underlie the clastic overlap sequences.

title: Digging into Diversity Dynamics: Vertebrate Faunas from Holocene Painted Rock Shelters Near the Pecos River in Arid Western Texas
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination (Posters)
authors: Sheridan, Ella J. [1], Quiros, Natalia [2], Stidham, Thomas A. [3], Boulanger, Matthew [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Biology, Austin College, Sherman, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Biology, Austin College, Sherman, Texas, USA
(3) Department of Biology, Austin College, Sherman, Texas, USA
(4) Department of Anthropology, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, Texas, USA
abstract: Excavation of two small painted rock shelters on the western part of the Edwards Plateau by SMU produced archeological and faunal remains that have been largely unstudied. Artifacts (arrowheads and dart points) and the Pecos River style paintings in the Sotol (41CX9) and Meadows (41CX3) sites point to a range of dates for the shelter deposits extending across the middle to late Holocene (500-6,000 years BP for Sotol and 500 years BP for Meadows). That time interval in the Pecos River area experienced variation in aridity interrupted by more mesic conditions. We investigated these vertebrate fossils and the paleoecology of the sites across this background of changing climate, as well as compared these sites to each other and other sites in the Pecos River area to better understand potential changes to arid land faunal composition and dynamics. Our study and identification of >2,000 bone fragments from the sites reveal a diverse fauna comprised of ~30 species of fish, amphibians, snakes, turtles, birds, and mammals ranging from a few grams to 1,000 kg. The fauna is dominated by mammals including rabbits ( Lepus , Sylvilagus ) and rodents ( Cratogeomys , Neotoma , Sigmodon , Peromyscus ). Other abundant groups are carnivores ( Vulpes , Urocyon , Canis ) and ungulates ( Odocoileus , Bison , Antilocapra ). The shelter faunal assemblages are representative of habitats in the area, including the river valleys (cotton rat, pocket gopher, quail), river/streams (muskrat, soft shell turtle, catfish), rock shelters (woodrat, coyote, raptorial bird), and dry mesas (jackrabbit, roadrunner). Among that diversity, the only species not present in the area today is bison, pointing to a broad stability of the faunal diversity over thousands of years. The rock shelter faunas appear isotaphonomic (and thus comparable) with a shared combination of human impacts (cut marks, burned bones, fractured bones), small skeletal fragment sizes, and natural accumulation via carnivore (mammal, reptile, and avian) action, along with that of woodrats. Faunal comparisons of Sotol, Meadows, and other sites demonstrate similar faunal lists, and little stratigraphic variation in fish (Sotol) also points to no obvious impact of Holocene climate change. However, the rabbit relative abundance decreased in the top portion of the Sotol sequence (coincident with Meadows), and in-depth statistical treatments may uncover more subtle climate related variation in these and other area faunal assemblages.

title: Beyond Burial: Heat Flow and Exhumation of the Central Appalachian Basin, USA
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Ellis Curry, Magdalena [1], Symanski, Kris [2], Lutz, Brandon M. [3], Hackley, Paul C. [4], O'Sullivan, Paul [5], Wageley, Holly [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA
(2) North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA
(3) Appalachian State University, Boone, NC, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(5) GeoSep Services, USA

abstract: The Appalachian Basin is an archetypal foreland basin system. However, the timing, rates and magnitudes of orogenic loading, fold-thrust belt exhumation, and foredeep burial and exhumation are not well constrained. Here, we present a new suite of low-temperature (~60°-300°C) thermochronometric and vitrinite reflectance (%R o ) data from a ~350 km transect through the Valley and Ridge and Appalachian Plateau of Virginia and West Virginia. The dataset includes new zircon fission track (ZFT, n=7), zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe, n=8), and apatite fission track (AFT, n=8) ages from Devonian, Mississippian, Pennsylvanian, and Permian strata. ZFT analyses yield a wide-range of single-grain ages spanning 1,850-275 Ma, consistent with partial resetting of the ZFT system. ZHe and AFT grain ages are unimodal with post-depositional (Permian through Cretaceous) ages, suggesting burial and heating fully reset these systems. These data are consistent with published and new (n=6) %Ro data. Inverse thermal history modeling (time-temperature and time-depth) of the new data coupled with structural restoration suggest that the fold-thrust belt was exhuming prior to significant Pennsylvanian-Permian sedimentation. Based on the modeling results, we infer burial depths ranging from 3.6 km in the western foredeep to 11 km in the fold-thrust belt. Results indicate that samples from the western foredeep experienced elevated temperatures beyond what would be predicted by burial. Time-depth models support a pulse of elevated heat flow in the western foredeep in the Mesozoic, which is consistent with other studies. The heat flow may have been driven by crustal thinning and mantle-derived rock emplacement along the Rome Trough. The new thermal data and analyses presented here help constrain the thermo-tectonic conditions of the Appalachian foreland basin system during late Paleozoic orogenesis, late-stage relaxation of the orogenic wedge, and Mesozoic rifting.

title: Beyond the Faunal List: Stability and Change of Holocene (Small) Mammal Assemblages in Arid Lower Pecos River Rock Shelters
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Quiros, Natalia [1], Sheridan, Ella J [2], Stidham, Thomas A [3], Boulanger, Matthew [4]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Austin College, Sherman, Texas, USA
(2) Biology, Austin College, Sherman, Texas, USA
(3) Biology, Austin College, Sherman, Texas, USA
(4) Department of Anthropology, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, Texas,
abstract: Broadening our understanding of the dynamics of long-term ecosystem diversity, structure, and function is key to advancing biological conservation practices, particularly for projected future aridification and community change. The fossil record preserves essential environmental and biological change datasets that allow us to study community responses to past climate change. Excavations of two rock shelters in the Pecos River area on the western part of the Edwards Plateau recovered faunal remains that provide key data. Pecos River style pictographs and artifacts from the Sotol and Meadows Shelters help date the deposits to the middle to late Holocene (~500-6,000 years BP for Sotol; ~500 years BP for Meadows). The lower Pecos River area has experienced changes in aridity during that time interval, potentially influencing ecosystems and recorded as alterations in vertebrate assemblages. Our study aims to better understand the drivers of biodiversity change observed in an arid, low elevation setting documented in the abundances of small mammals. We identified a high diversity vertebrate fauna of ~ 30 vertebrate species from >2,000 bone fragments, consistent with other records from the area. Mammalian taxa include rabbits ( Lepus , Sylvilagus ), rodents ( Spermophilus, Cratogeomys , Neotoma , Peromyscus , Sigmodon ), carnivores ( Vulpes , Urocyon , Canis ), and ungulates ( Odocoileus , Bison , Antilocapra ). All recovered vertebrate taxa remain present in the area with the exception of Bison, pointing to a broad stability in alpha diversity over thousands of years that has been recorded at similar sites across the region. While species diversity was not greatly altered over time, other biological and ecological changes might have occurred in the landscape. We applied a variety of statistical analyses based on species richness, numbers of specimens, and relative abundances over time and space to explore this idea. Similar assessments at other sites across the west uncovered more subtle climatic responses, but analyses in the Pecos River area and Edwards Plateau have not been fully explored. Overall, the Sotol small mammal assemblage exhibits relatively low evenness across all stratigraphic levels, and has a high abundance of rabbits. However, Shannon’s diversity index increased through time related to a relative decrease in rabbit abundance in the youngest levels of Sotol, paralleling the similarly young Meadows assemblage. That fluctuation may link to climate change, but requires analysis with a greater temporal resolution from radiocarbon dates.

title: What Climate Conditions Control Water Track Dynamics in Thawing Permafrost?
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Gaylor, Samantha [1], Del Vecchio, Joanmarie [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, College of William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia, USA
(2) Department of Geology, College of William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia, USA
abstract:
Water tracks are unchannelized subsurface soil moisture lineations concentrating water to downslope channels in permafrost landscapes. Water tracks are a fundamental feature of Arctic channel networks, as they transport water and nutrients from hillslopes to channels. Water tracks form on hillslopes where channels should exist, but the impermeability of permafrost inhibits drainage network development. Water track subsurface flow is confined to the thawed active layer, which is variable across permafrost regions. We hypothesize that, across the Arctic, water track presence in watersheds is correlated with a greater active layer depth compared to watersheds with no water tracks. Additionally, top-down and bottom-up climate and geological factors such as mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation and slope may affect water track occurrence.

The study area of this project is composed of permafrost regions in the Northern Hemisphere, including parts of Alaska, Canada, Russia, and Greenland. We paired satellite imagery of watersheds (n=39) with active layer thickness data from the CALM (Circumpolar Active Layer Monitoring) dataset, in which field depth measurements have been taken annually across more than 200 locations since 1990. Preliminary results suggest that there is no correlation between average active layer thickness (cm) and water track presence in watersheds (%). Similarly, there does not appear to be a correlation between active layer thawing over time (cm/yr) and water track presence in watersheds. We are currently exploring decadal trends in temperature and precipitation, as well as topographic attributes like slope, to determine if there exists a correlation with water track occurrence.

As temperatures rise in the Arctic, permafrost melts, disrupting surface and subsurface flowpaths, affecting entire watersheds. Additionally, water tracks incise into hillslopes, releasing carbon held in permafrost. Determining the conditions behind water track formation, and whether their presence and dynamics are linked to changes in the depth of the active layer, can help to inform future studies on Arctic hydrology and geomorphology, as well as how Arctic watersheds may respond to future warming.

title: Following the Carbonate: Spatial Variability in Pleistocene Detrital Carbonate Beds from Baffin Bay to the Labrador Sea
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change (Posters)
authors: Hohensee, Josef L. [1], Frank, Tracy D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs Mansfield, CT, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
abstract: Prominent, detrital carbonate-rich beds are widespread in latest Pleistocene piston cores in Baffin Bay and have been interpreted as recording basin-wide glacial variability; however, some uncertainty remains regarding their stratigraphic continuity, provenance, and depositional mechanisms. Here we characterize dozens of detrital carbonate beds recovered at ODP Sites 645, 646, and 647 in Baffin Bay and the Labrador Sea, extending the record into the Early Pleistocene to investigate their provenance and depositional history. This study integrates observations from high-resolution core photographs, granulometry, petrography, and stable isotope geochemistry to document spatiotemporal changes in composition and sedimentology. At these sites, the deposits are dominated by mud, with sand and gravel contents increasing toward Site 645, which is proximal to a potential carbonate source in the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, and decreasing toward the more distal Labrador Sea sites. Bulk carbonate δ 18 O and δ 13 C values differ between Baffin Bay and Labrador Sea sites. Site 645 beds are characterized by lower and more uniform values than those of beds from Sites 646 and 647. Spatial variability in the composition and sedimentology of detrital carbonate beds may reflect differences in source region, sediment sorting during transport, and/or depositional pathways. These findings provide new constraints on the provenance and depositional history of detrital carbonate beds and suggest that their composition and sedimentology should be considered when interpreting these deposits as regional records of Pleistocene ice-sheet variability.

title: Analyzing Stream Morphology, Sedimentation, and Erosion Patterns Using LiDAR and Multispectral Imagery
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Atienza, Bennett [1], Wijesinghe, Dhanuska [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
abstract: Understanding changes in stream morphology is essential for effective water resource management and ecosystem health. Stream morphology evolves constantly due to natural factors such as flow and sediment, and human activities can exacerbate these changes. Monitoring alterations in cross-sectional area provides valuable insight into a stream’s morphological evolution. Traditional surveying methods for measuring cross-sectional area are often time-consuming and less accurate. The integration of drone-based and terrestrial LiDAR technology enables high-resolution tracking of morphological changes via point clouds. This study examines the channel morphology of two streams with riparian buffer strips in Shenandoah Valley, Virginia, utilizing aerial and terrestrial LiDAR alongside multispectral imagery. The incorporation of multispectral imagery enables tracking of vegetation changes, which can then be correlated with LiDAR data to explore the relationship between vegetation characteristics and channel morphology. Data will be collected following major storm events and through initial and final surveys using GPS-acquired cross-sections. Initial stream cross-sections were completed in June 2026 using a Topcon HyPer VR GPS system. For these surveys, GPS points were collected along multiple cross-sections within each stream segment, extending up to 50 meters from the bank (the 100-year floodplain) to capture horizontal migration. Drone data will be initially processed in DJI Terra, followed by the creation of high-resolution digital elevation models (DEMs) in ArcGIS Pro. All data will be georeferenced for accuracy using a base station. In post-processing, software such as CloudCompare will assess whether channel changes represent net deposition or net erosion. Cross sections of point clouds at regular intervals will be used to estimate volume changes over time, highlighting areas of increased activity after storm events. Ultimately, this integrated approach will clarify the dynamic relationships among vegetation, land use, and stream morphology, supporting the development of effective management and restoration strategies.

abstract:
La teledetección es fundamental para investigar la geología de cuerpos planetarios donde no es posible realizar mediciones in situ . El radar de apertura sintética (SAR) resulta especialmente valioso porque la retrodispersión es sensible a la rugosidad y los contrastes dieléctricos a la escala de la longitud de onda, proporcionando información tanto sobre las propiedades de la superficie como del subsuelo. Por ello, las observaciones de radar son ideales para estudiar procesos geológicos que modifican las superficies planetarias.

En este estudio, utilizamos observaciones de radar en banda S (longitud de onda de 12.6 cm) obtenidas con el instrumento Miniature Radio Frequency (Mini-RF) a bordo de la sonda Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) de la NASA para caracterizar los deslizamientos lunares y los cráteres secundarios formado por el eyecta del cráter Tycho. Mini-RF es un SAR de polarimetría híbrida que transmite una señal con polarización circular y recibe componentes lineales tanto horizontales como verticales. Los datos de radar en banda S son sensibles a elementos dispersores a escala de centímetros a decímetros presentes en el metro superior del regolito lunar, lo que permite caracterizar las propriedades tanto en la superficie como en el subsuelo y nos permiten entender la morfología de lugares rugosos. A partir de los datos de polarización calculamos los parámetros de Stokes (S1–S4) y productos de descomposición m-χ, los cuales representan tres comportamientos de dispersión distintos: rebote par, polarización despolarizada y rebote impar.

Observamos que los depósitos de deslizamientos en la Luna presentan una elevada retrodispersión despolarizada, característica de superficies rugosas. Esto permite identificarlos fácilmente en los productos de la descomposición m-χ, incluso cuando imágenes ópticas no están disponibles o las condiciones de iluminación son desfavorables, como en las regiones polares.

Asimismo, utilizamos observaciones de Mini-RF para identificar cráteres secundarios asociados a Tycho. Estudios previos (Wells et al., 2010; Rivera-Valentín et al., 2024) observaron que algunos cráteres pequeños en el polo sur lunar presentan depósitos con una geometría asimétrica, elongados en dirección radial respeto de Tycho, y brillantes en radar. Nuestro análisis investiga el origen de estas estructuras visibles en radar y sus implicaciones para los procesos de formación de cráteres secundarios en la luna.
