title: Evolution of the Pea Ridge Iron Oxide - Apatite - REE deposit in SE Missouri: 30 million years of carbonate-sulfate-silicate melts and aqueous fluids interaction
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Sahdarani, Dyah [1], Lamadrid, Hector M [2], Hunt, Will [3], Appold, Martin [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA
(4) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA
abstract: The demand for critical minerals to sustain the green energy transition and the expansion of the technology sector has increased scientific interest beyond conventional REE-rich deposits to other deposits that host discrete REE-enrichment, such as iron oxide-apatite (IOA) deposits. The Pea Ridge deposit, hosted in Mesoproterozoic felsic ignimbrites from the St. Francois Mountains of SE Missouri, is the best-documented IOA system of the region. The reported U-Pb zircon ages of the mineralization suggest the system was thermally reactivated for over 30 My from the emplacement of the main Fe body to the REE mineralization (up to 12 wt. % in REE-oxides). However, the genesis of Pea Ridge and IOAs at large remains unclear, and different contrasting models have been proposed, from purely magmatic immiscibility to purely hydrothermal (and everything in between). Regardless of the genetic model, carbonate-sulfate melt inclusions have increasingly been reported from IOA deposits worldwide, suggesting interactions between silicate melts and sedimentary rocks. Although Pea Ridge is the best studied in the district, only a few studies have used fluid inclusions to constrain chemical and thermal evolution, and molten salt inclusions have not yet been documented. In this study, we present results of a systematic petrological and geochemical characterization of fluid and melt inclusion assemblages from the different stages of the mineralization to constrain potential mechanisms of emplacement of the Fe-P mineralization, the different episodes of alteration, and subsequent REE transport and precipitation. Our results show a complex geochemical and thermal evolution of the mineralizing fluids and the ubiquitous presence of carbonate, sulfate, and calc-silicate melt inclusions, as well as consistently high concentrations of dissolved carbonate and sulfate species in fluid inclusions across all the mineralization. Moreover, careful microthermometric measurements of the fluid and melt inclusion assemblages show a systematic variation in homogenization temperatures from magmatic temperatures ~1200 ºC during the emplacement of the Fe-P mineralization, to ~150ºC in the late REE-rich hydrothermal breccias. The thermal variability is a response to the complex compositions of the mineralizing fluids (that cannot be approximated by the H 2 O-NaCl system) and the reactivation of the magmatic-hydrothermal system for over 30 My.

title: Metamorphic Sulfur Release During Large Igneous Province Emplacement
session_title: Volcano-climate interactions
authors: Allman, Lindsi Jane [1], Stewart, Emily M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
(2) Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL,
abstract:
Large igneous province (LIP) emplacement causes catastrophic changes to Earth’s climate and extreme biotic crises. U-Pb geochronology links LIPs to at least three of the big five mass extinctions. As LIPs are emplaced, they release volatiles into the atmosphere through igneous degassing, but also metamorphic processes as volatile rich sediment is heated by hot magma releasing sequestered carbon and sulfur. These sediment-derived volatiles include both greenhouse gases that warm the planet and sulfur species that cool the planet. While metamorphic LIP-derived greenhouse gasses have been given consideration for their impact on warming, few studies have considered the impact metamorphic sulfur. Recent work has presented results of sediment metamorphism modeling combined with simple planetary carbon cycle and energy balance models to conclude that emissions from contact metamorphism could be sustained long enough to impose centennial scale sulfate aerosol cooling spikes of several kelvin on top of millennial scale warming from greenhouse gas emission (Stewart et al. 2026). However, this modeling result relies on many simplifications and untested assumptions. We therefore aim to test this result with direction observation of the rock record.

Here we present geochemical results from a field test of metamorphic sulfur emissions to verify modeled results using an observational approach. We selected samples from the Sugar Grove dike, a late Jurassic intrusion into Devonian black shales. This location provides an accessible proxy for diabase LIP intrusion into sulfur rich sediment. We find both sulfur isotopic shifts and changing sulfur species approaching the intrusion that indicate sulfur mobilization along with isotopic evidence of carbon dioxide movement. We find evidence of decreasing pyrite and increasing pyrrhotite concentration in shale samples approaching the sill along with a ~10‰ negative shift in sulfur isotopes. Carbonate carbon and oxygen isotopes show up to 50% carbonate carbon mobilization based on Rayleigh fractionation. Further, we will present petrographic and thermodynamic modeling data to determine the magnitude and fate of volatile mobilization. Combined, these results will help resolve if contact metamorphic sulfur release during LIP emplacement is a viable mechanism for sustained cooling.

title: Puzzles in the Miocene Evolution of Italy’s Apennine Mountains

affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, California, USA
abstract:
The NE-vergent Apennine Mountains of Italy began to form at their NW end in the Oligocene. Initiation of deformation proceeded SE-ward and continues today. In the 1990s it was suggested that this behavior is caused by the progressive tearing off and sinking of a slab that is rolling back toward the NE, and this suggestion was supported by the SE-ward progression of the foredeep basin, matching the moving tear point. The attribution of the Apennines to slab rollback has been favorably received, but how this fits into the broader context of Mediterranean tectonics remains an interesting question. The present abstract points out two possible connections.

(1) In 1974 it was suggested that counterclockwise rotation of the Corsica-Sardinia-Calabria continental microplate away from the south margin of France was followed by rifting away of the Calabria portion, which then moved SE toward its present position forming the toe of the Italian boot. A seismically active slab beneath the SE Tyrrhenian confirms that this motion continues, and ODP Leg 107 showed that during the Messinian (the last Miocene stage) Calabria was about 400 km farther back, because Messinian evaporites are present in the NW Tyrrhenian Sea, but not in the SE, where Pliocene rests on volcanic basement. It thus appears that Calabria was travelling SE-ward, matching at least roughly the slab tear-off point. Calabria was approximately SW of the intensely thrusted Central Apennines during the Messinian, when those thrusts were active, and may have caused the thrusting. The suggestion that the motion of Calabria initiated the Apennine deformation appears to be new.

(2) A second interesting connection to explore is that the Apennine fold-thrust belt was active during the Messinian Salinity Crisis (MSC), when Mediterranean sea level fell by about 3 km and suddenly recovered in the Zanclean Flood that defines the beginning of the Pliocene at 5.33 Ma. This would have caused formerly deep-marine foreland turbidite basins to become river valleys and would have changed the balance of overburden pressure between exposed and deep regions, possibly affecting thrust development. A series of spectacular landslides moved down the Marcchia Valley during the Messinian, and may possibly be related to the MSC, and it is interesting that a mid-Messinian tectonic phase is recognized in the Northern Apennines.

title: Additional Tiger Stripe Structures on Enceladus? Morphometric Constraints from Tiger Stripes in the South Polar Terrain
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Perez-Cortes, Santa Lucia [1], Martin, Emily S. [2], Nichols-Fleming, Fiona [3], Patthoff, Alex [4], Bramson, Ali M. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, INJ, USA
(2) Center for Earth and Planetary Studies, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, DC, USA
(3) Center for Earth and Planetary Studies, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, Washington, DC, USA
(4) Planetary Science Institute, La Habra Heights, CA,
(5) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
abstract:
Enceladus, an icy moon of Saturn, hosts a tectonically active south polar terrain characterized by a system of subparallel fractures known as the tiger stripes. These fractures exhibit a distinctive double ridge morphology and are associated with plume activity observed by the Cassini mission. Historically, plume activity has been linked to four primary tiger stripes: Alexandria, Cairo, Baghdad and Damascus. Some studies have also recognized an apparently inactive fracture informally referred as Zone E. However, the extent of tectonic activity beyond the canonical tiger stripes, the geometry of the erupted material, and the processes controlling fracture morphology remain subjects of ongoing debate.

Here we investigate whether additional fractures within the south polar terrain share morphometric characteristics with the canonical tiger stripes. We show that both candidate and canonical fractures exhibit similar double ridge morphology and comparable morphometric characteristics, suggesting that the tiger stripe system is more extensive than previously recognized.

Our results also indicate that the fracture geometry is controlled by both local and basin-scale processes. Ridge elevations and symmetry vary systematically with basin-scale topography, implying that the broader geometry of the south polar basin influences fracture morphology and extent. Meanwhile, their geometries do not show a systematic relationship with the present-day observed plume activity, indicating that plume activity does not play a primary role in the double ridge morphology. These findings imply that the morphometry preserves information about the tectonic evolution of the south polar terrain and the subsurface processes controlling plume transport and eruption style. They also raise the possibility that the candidate fractures experience intermittent activity or represent older, now inactive, tiger stripes fractures.

title: Application of Drone-Based Imagery (Thermal and NIR) to Enhance Recreational Fishing in the Shenandoah Region of Virginia

authors: Walsh, Coyt [1], Meaney, Luke [2], Wijesinghe, Dhanuska [3], Leslie, Stephen A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA

abstract: Temperature variations in streams influence aquatic ecosystems, as cooler water holds higher dissolved oxygen (DO), which supports aquatic life. The primary goal of this study was to determine whether high-resolution thermal sensors can detect localized temperature deviations associated with groundwater inputs or variations in geologic materials. This study utilized high-resolution aerial imagery collected by unmanned aerial systems (UAS) equipped with an H2OT thermal sensor, a Zenmuse L2 LiDAR sensor, and a DJI M3M drone with multispectral and RGB cameras. Surveys were conducted on the North River near the JMU Farm and on the South Fork of the Shenandoah River near Stanley, VA, to measure water temperature, vegetation, and channel morphology. Multispectral and RGB data were processed in Metashape to create orthomosaics, and both multispectral and LiDAR data were analyzed in DJI Terra and ArcGIS Pro to generate DEMs and vegetation indices. Initially, thermal images were converted to .tiff format using a Python script to extract temperature data and then processed in Metashape to generate an orthomosaic. Geology maps of the Harrisonburg and Stanley quadrangles were digitized using ArcGIS Pro to extract surface geology information. Once all layers were developed, we overlaid the geology layer on the DEM to detect changes in surface elevation and inspected areas where we observed thermal anomalies to determine whether variations in surface geology were causing them. Of the two locations, the site near Stanley exhibited a notable temperature difference according to results from the initial scan conducted in early April 2026. When we inspected the DEM and geology layers in the area where we observed the thermal anomaly, we noticed signs of fracturing and faulting. To verify the thermal anomaly detected during the initial scan, we conducted a follow-up scan in late July 2026. However, no thermal anomaly was observed at Stanley during the second scan. No temperature variation was detected near the JMU Farm during the initial scan, possibly due to extremely cold conditions that may have frozen the surface layer. The next phase involves ground-truthing the thermal data at both sites. Following this, we plan to conduct additional scans at the Stanley location to determine whether a genuine thermal anomaly exists, which could help identify localized temperature deviations linked to groundwater inputs or variations in geologic materials.

title: Metamorphism of mixed-carbonate silicate rocks during the Proterozoic Grenville Orogeny: implications for orogenic CO2 degassing in deep time.
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Sengupta, Kanwa [1], Stewart, Emily M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
(2) Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL,
abstract:
Lithospheric carbon fluxes play a fundamental role in regulating Earth's long-term carbon cycle. Quantifying CO₂ released from the metamorphic decarbonation of calc-silicate rocks during mountain-building events is therefore critical for evaluating the contribution of metamorphic processes to the global carbon cycle and their influence on Earth's long-term climate and habitability. Modeling studies indicate that metamorphic CO₂ fluxes may have been elevated during the Proterozoic as a result of the abundance of mixed silicate-carbonate rocks and higher geothermal temperature-pressure (T/P) gradients. We therefore report preliminary results of a field-based test of this hypothesis.

Here we explore the P-T-XCO 2 evolution of carbonate bearing rocks with a focus on understanding carbon loss during regional metamorphism in the Proterozoic Grenville province. We focus in particular on (1) the Fernleigh Formation, consisting of laminated calcareous pelites to schists, as a representative mixed calcareous-siliciclastic unit and (2) Grenville supergroup marbles as a more carbonate-dominated metasediment.

Metamorphic grade ranges from greenschist to upper amphibolite-facies conditions. Calc-silicate rocks are characterized by a dominant dolomite-ankerite + biotite assemblage at lower grades, with the appearance of titanite, epidote, scapolite, amphibole, and clinopyroxene as metamorphic grade increases. Preliminary thermodynamic modelling suggests two distinct fluid evolution pathways during metamorphism. Titanite and epidote-bearing assemblages are predicted to have equilibrated in the presence of relatively H 2 O-rich fluids (Xco 2 = 0.05- 0.5), consistent with externally derived fluid infiltration and open-system behavior. In contrast, titanite and epidote-absent assemblages evidently equilibrated with relatively CO2-rich fluids (Xco 2 >0.5), consistent with internally buffered, closed-system metamorphic evolution.

The rocks of the Fernleigh formation record substantial decarbonation (~80–90%) even at lower amphibolite-facies conditions. In contrast, carbonate-dominated lithologies of the Grenville Supergroup exhibit limited decarbonation due to the limited availability of reactive silicate phases. Even under upper amphibolite-facies conditions, clinopyroxene-bearing assemblages record only ~20% decarbonation at temperatures of ~700 °C. These preliminary results are consistent with enhanced decarbonation efficiency relative to, e.g., Acadian metamorphism.

title: From Holes to Piles: Geoheritage, Hazards, and Hidden Resources
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Karl, Nick A [1], Murzyn, John A [2], San Juan, Carma A. [3], Taylor, Ryan D. [4]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Mining in the United States has left a considerable mark on the landscape. From mining-related features such as adits and shafts—from which valuable materials were extracted—to mine waste features such as tailings piles and waste dumps representing the residual materials of mining, the landscape provides a tangible record of our geoheritage. These features document where resources have been explored, developed, and produced while also leaving physical and environmental hazards, along with remnant mine waste.

The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is developing two complementary national inventories to better characterize this mining legacy. The first, the National Mine Waste Inventory, is being developed through the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) in collaboration with State Geological Surveys to provide publicly available data on the locations and general characteristics of mine waste features. These data improve our understanding of potential sources of critical minerals that may remain within mine waste. The second, the National Abandoned Mine Land Inventory, is being developed for the Department of the Interior's Office of Environmental Policy and Compliance (OEPC) by integrating Federal, State, and Tribal datasets of abandoned mine land features. This inventory identifies physical and environmental hazards, records past mitigation efforts, and supports informed decisions for public safety, particularly aiding the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation (AHMR) Program.

Together, these inventories reveal the geographic legacy of mining in the United States, documenting features that represent both the Nation's mining geoheritage and its enduring environmental and physical hazards. They also identify mine waste features that may provide opportunities for critical mineral recovery while informing future environmental remediation and land management.

title: Rain, Rain, Go Away: An Analysis of the Effect of Atmospheric Conditions on the Decomposition of Sus domesticus through Electrical Resistivity Surveys
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Steinauer, Kaitlin Marie [1], McDaniel, Alleh [2], Schneider, Blair Benson [3]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
Once an organism perishes, the five stages of taphonomy begin immediately. These stages—characterized as fresh, inflation, decay, advanced decay, and skeletonization—produce varying volumes of fluids, with the highest volume produced during the decay stage. The rate at which an organism progresses through these stages can be affected by conditions such as climate, geologic setting, and burial style. Methods such as electrical resistivity have been used to locate a buried decaying organism and have been sought out to aid in forensic investigations due to their relatively fast data collection. To research this method, domestic pigs ( Sus domesticus ) have commonly been used as proxies for humans due to similar physiology and chemical makeup. This project uses buried pig cadavers to analyze the effect of climatic factors on decomposition and the effectiveness of electrical resistivity to locate the graves throughout the stages of taphonomy.

The first set of pigs were buried in October 2026, near Lawrence, KS, weighing 98 and 124 lbs. The second set, buried in January 2026, weighed 454 and 504 lbs. With each set, one pig was buried at a depth of 1 m in native Pawnee clay loam and the other in sand, while control graves using native soil and sand were excavated and filled in October and January, respectively. Four soil sensors—measuring soil temperature, moisture, and conductivity—were placed in the bottom of each pig grave, with one in each of the control graves. A rain gauge, thermometer, and humidity sensor were placed at the field site. Weekly electrical resistivity surveys were collected for the first six months following burials with an ABEM Terrameter using a dipole-dipole configuration and 0.25 m electrode spacing. With each set of pigs, one survey is collected perpendicularly across the two pigs and control grave, and two are collected parallel over each pig. Following six months, surveying on the first set of pigs was reduced to monthly due to negligible fluctuations in resistivity values within the grave.

We present ten months of soil sensor, atmospheric, and electrical resistivity data to analyze the effect of atmospheric conditions on the stages of decomposition. Overall, the results of this work are expected to assist future forensic investigations by providing expected responses for grave detection in similar environments.

title: Going, Going, Gone: Machine Learning Based Detection of Sus domesticus Using Electrical Conductivity and Soil Sensor Data
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: McDaniel, Alleh [1], Townsend, Ky [2], Steinauer, Kaitlin [3], Schneider, Blair Benson [4]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(4) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
abstract:
The use of geophysical surveys to discover unmarked burial sites is a relatively new approach in the forensic field. These methods allow for rapid, cost-effective results without disturbing the local terrain. Manner of burial, geological setting, and climate must be considered as these factors impact decomposition and thus data collection. Sus Domesticus are excellent proxies because of their physiological similarities to human cadavers. Two pigs, approximately 90-100 lbs, were buried at 1 meter depth on October 12th, 2025, in a 10 x 10 meter grid. Two more pigs were added, approximately 450-500 lbs, on January 15th, 2026, expanding the grid to 10 x 15 meters. The burials were performed at the Kansas Field Station initially in native clay loam soil, with cadaver burial in clay loam, a cadaver burial in sand, and a control grave. Our purpose was to refine machine learning models to make accurate and interpretable predictions of grave presence inside the survey grid.

Conductivity was collected via a Geophex GEM-2 on a 0.5 meter spaced grid in a north-south and east-west orientation to improve sampling density on a weekly basis. Meanwhile, at regular 5-30 minute increments, soil sensors collected data from four locations per cadaver grave and one location per control. Data from soil sensors was averaged on each day that GEM data was collected and merged into a complete data set.

Machine learning was conducted in R with the Tidyverse and Caret packages, with 80% of the data used as a training set and 20% used as the test set. Four linear models, a decision tree, and a random forest model were all constructed, each with five fold cross validation for stability. The best model was selected based on accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity.

The model that had the best results and highest interpretability was a pruned decision tree. This model provided high accuracy (88% and 86% respectively) on the sand and clay graves, with no statistically significant difference between the two. The best results occurred in the first three weeks, with sensitivity increasing as decomposition progressed. Data is still being collected and analyzed with the aim to assist forensic investigations by providing an efficient method for locating graves.

title: Integrating Thermal, Multispectral, and LiDAR Drone Mapping to Monitor Seasonal Fish Movement and Relative Abundance in Shenandoah Valley Streams.
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Meaney, Luke [1], Walsh, Coyt [2], Wijesinghe, Dhanuska [3], Leslie, Stephen A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(4) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
abstract: Thermal variations within stream systems greatly influence fish distribution, particularly in relation to cold-water shelters and structurally complex habitat zones. Monitoring these movements traditionally requires intensive field surveys, which are effective but have limited spatial coverage. This study evaluates how effectively drone-based thermal imaging, integrated with LiDAR and multispectral imaging, can detect temperature anomalies in streams, ultimately enabling detection of whether these temperature variations are associated with groundwater inputs or variations in surface geologic features such as fractures. Identification and location of areas with thermal anomalies will aid in determining patterns of fish relative abundance. The study area consists of two streams: North River near the JMU Farm and the South Fork of Shenandoah River near Stanley, Virginia. Data collection utilizes a DJI Matrice 300 RTK equipped with a Zenmuse H20T radiometric thermal sensor and an integrated LiDAR module (Zenmuse L2), while a DJI Mavic 3 collects multispectral imagery for vegetation analysis. All the flights were georeferenced using an RTK base station to ensure accuracy. Radiometric thermal imagery is used to map fine-scale surface temperature variability and identify thermal anomalies. LiDAR data were used to develop high-resolution digital elevation models to evaluate channel morphology, stream depth variability, and bank geometry. The multispectral imagery was used to develop vegetation indices, such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), to estimate canopy density around the stream and shading effects on stream temperature. Preliminary findings from the initial surveys have identified water-temperature anomalies that appear consistent with fracturing and faulting shown on existing geologic maps. This was especially evident in the Stanley location. The analysis has also identified instances in which drone or sensor error produced temperature miscalculations, demonstrating the importance of calibration, repeated surveys, and comparison with independent datasets. A more recent survey conducted at the Stanley location (July 28) does not show the thermal anomaly that was observed earlier. The next phase involves conducting multiple scans at both locations to determine whether these anomalies are genuine or artifacts. These repeated surveys, along with ground-truthing through stream temperature measurements, will enable us to identify areas with temperature anomalies, which will help determine whether a relationship exists between fish abundance and these thermal anomalies.

title: A spectrum of volcanic & plutonic rocks across the Elkhead Mountains of Northwest Colorado
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Tikku, Anahita A. [1], Day, Warren C. [2], Mercer, Cameron M. [3]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
(2) US Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysic,s and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
(3) US Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
The Miocene (~15 to 6 Ma) Elkhead volcanic field in Northwestern Colorado is a result of widespread volcanism associated with diffuse extension after the Laramide Orogeny (< 40 Ma). The region experienced uplift of ~1 km and denudation since the Late Miocene (<10 Ma), leaving a portion of the Elkhead Mountains as sub-volcanic plutons. The compositions of the igneous rocks range from alkali basalt, trachyandesite, trachydacite, to rhyolite.

Recently collected (2024-2025) high resolution USGS Earth MRI airborne magnetic and radiometric data significantly improve our ability to geophysically identify and characterize the spatial distribution and size of igneous bodies, faults, and mineralizing systems of the Elkhead Mountains. There are sizable magnetic susceptibility contrasts between the volcanic rocks and surrounding older host rock, as well as distinct potassium anomalies associated with some known outcrops. In 2025 and 2026, we collected magnetic susceptibility measurements, and rock samples for both geochronology and mineralogical characterization to better describe and map the various exposed volcanic features.

One preliminary highlight of our study is the identification of multiple lava flows around the Black Mountain – Mt. Oliphant, and Bears Ears Peaks regions that are coincident with magnetic anomalies. Bears Ears Peaks were previously mapped as a Tertiary intrusion, but we observed ~200 m of lavas with entablature style columnar A second highlight is the recognition of two distinct dike orientations (N45°W and N70°W) across the volcanic field from the magnetic data. Field observations corroborate the near vertical dikes interpreted from the magnetic data. The two dike orientations appear to map temporally distinct regional stress fields. We are working on identifying the ages and magmatic composition of the dikes to gain insight into the evolving magmatic system. A third highlight is the observation of widespread argillic alteration and the presence of a broad (~4500 m diameter) magnetically quiet region centered around Hahn’s Peak, with ~200 nT positive anomalies coincident with faults bounding the northern and southern edges of the Hahn’s Peak local horst block. Hahn’s Peak is identified as a hydrothermally altered porphyry body and was mined for gold, silver, lead, and zinc.

title: Tracking Fluid-Rock Interactions in Ultramafic Lithologies in Orogenic Systems
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics
authors: Cooperdock, Emily H. G. [1]
affiliations: (1) Brown University, Providence, RI,
abstract: Constraining the timing of fluid-rock interactions in serpentinized ultramafic rocks is critical to understanding how associated physical transformations, such as reduced rock strength, lowered density, and volume expansion, contribute to plate boundary deformation. Additionally, because serpentinized peridotite water content ranges from 0 to > 12 w.t.%, these units act as major fluid sources or sinks depending on metamorphic conditions. While fluid-mobile element and isotope systems effectively trace fluid movement, dating these interactions remains difficult due to limited geochronological tools. Here, we combine new geochronology, fluid-mobile element chemistry, and textural context to resolve complex, multi-stage fluid-rock interactions at the hand-sample scale. Our results demonstrate that different minerals and fluid-mobile elements can record distinct fluid episodes, highlighting a key challenge in interpreting fluid histories from the exhumed rock record.

title: A Process-Based Understanding of Soil water Evaporation and Pedogenic Carbonate Triple Oxygen Isotope Records
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements
authors: Peshek, Catherine [1], Breecker, Daniel [2], Sharp, Zachary [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(2) Jackson School of Geosciences, The Univerisity of Texas, Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(3) Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
Soil carbonate inherits the oxygen isotope composition of soil water and is used as a proxy for ancient meteoric water sources. The processes driving carbonate saturation ultimately moderate the preserved soil water isotopic signature. Transpiration and evaporation are the two main processes resulting in water loss and calcium carbonate saturation where evaporation is known to impart a significant isotopic offset from meteoric water.

Triple oxygen isotopes provide additional information on the kinetic effects due to the diffusion of water vapor in air and are thus useful for interrogating soil water evaporation processes. To investigate how soil water evaporation is recorded by soil carbonates we monitored the triple oxygen isotope composition of soil water with depth over time during a 100-day sand column drying experiment. The experiment was used to calibrate a one-dimensional numerical model that simulates the triple oxygen isotope composition of soil water undergoing evaporation. A sensitivity analysis of the main atmospheric and soil parameters show that the rate of liquid loss (or evaporation front lowering) is controlled primarily by the soil temperature, the liquid water contents (and the porosity) while the extent of kinetic isotope fractionation from meteoric water is driven by atmospheric humidity.

We applied the model to two soil carbonate triple oxygen isotope profiles from Albuquerque, New Mexico and the Mojave Desert, USA. We show how the estimated soil water for either location does not track the full extent of kinetic isotope fractionation due to soil water evaporation. We interpret this from a process-based perspective where soil carbonate formation occurs as the drying front moves downward over time, thus capturing an intermediate isotopic composition between meteoric water and the ‘most evaporated’ soil water that occurs at the front. When considering the time-dependent nature of carbonate solubility in soils, near surface (<40cm) saturation occurs (depending on the initial conditions) within weeks due to both evaporation and transpiration, whereas deeper samples form over much longer time periods, likely due to transpiration only. Based on this finding, deep soil carbonates may more faithfully record the isotopic composition of precipitation. Because the degree of isotopic offset is related to the degree of evaporation relative to transpiration, a connection between the isotopic composition of the soil carbonate and relative humidity is unclear.

title: New Constraints on the Paleozoic Tectonic Evolution of Central New England from Metamorphic Petrochronology
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Pansera, Genavieve [1], Castro, Adrian E. [2], Yao, Jannitta [3], Viete, Daniel Ricardo [4], Brenner, Dana C. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(2) Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA,
(3) Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH,
(4) Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD,
(5) Johns Hopkins University, Earth and Planetary Sciences, Baltimore, MD,
abstract:
The crystalline bedrock underlying Central New England has been thought to preserve a signature of deformation and metamorphism dominated by the accretion of Avalonia onto the Laurentian margin during the (Neo)Acadian orogeny (c.420–360 Ma). Understanding the nature of the tectonics in this region has strong implications for orogenic evolution, exhumation rates, paleoclimate reconstruction, topography, and petrogenesis of economic minerals.

Competing models for Acadian tectonism in central Massachusetts include: 1) a high elevation, low relief altiplano, characterized by periods of crustal thickening (50–60 km; 410–380 Ma), cooling (380–330 Ma), and rapid exhumation (330–300 Ma), and 2) a thin-skinned thrust nappe emplacement model. The plateau model suggests that the rocks underlying central Massachusetts, from the Iapetan suture to the Bloody Bluff fault, record essentially the same pressure-temperature-time (P–T–t) evolution, whereas the thrust nappe model implies the existence of relatively thin and distinct metamorphic zones recording distinct P–T histories in different parts of the orogen. Here, we employ equilibrium thermodynamic modeling in the MnNCKFMASHTi chemical system, petrography, and quartz-in-garnet Raman inclusion barometry to constrain robust P–T histories for three samples from Central Massachusetts.

Sample 21-EM-02 is a garnet-staurolite schist from the Littleton Formation near Erving, MA, with peak conditions at 550–650 °C and 5–8 kbar. West of this sample, 25-AP-01A is a garnet-kyanite schist from the Mt Mineral Formation near Pelham, MA, which records a counterclockwise P–T path with peak conditions at ~700 °C and 8 kbar constrained by quartz-in-garnet Raman inclusion barometry. Garnet rim isopleths indicate cooling during burial to ~625 °C and 9 kbar. 25-AP-02A is a garnet-kyanite migmatite gneiss also from the Mt Mineral Formation that records peak conditions of at least 800 °C and 11 kbar, determined by garnet rim isopleths.

These results suggest a significant decrease in metamorphic grade from W-E of ~1–4 kbar and 400 °C, over <2 km perpendicular to strike. The peak P–T conditions constrained here are generally higher P–T than previous work. We therefore favor tectonic models involving diachronous emplacement of ductile thrust nappes through the Late Pennsylvanian. These results will be bolstered with additional in situ monazite U-Pb dating and bulk garnet Sm-Nd geochronology.

title: Cenozoic magmatism within the Appalachian Basin: Subsurface architecture revealed using new Earth MRI aeromagnetic data
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Shah, Anjana K. [1], Gray, Alexander A. [2], McAleer, Ryan Joseph [3], Doctor, Daniel H. [4], Moore, Jessica [5], Dinterman, Philip [6]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(5) West Virginia Geological and Economic Survey, Morgantown, WV,
(6) West Virginia Geological and Economic Survey, Morgantown, WV,
abstract:
Eocene intrusions and volcanics in the Appalachian Basin, emplaced far from contemporaneous plate boundaries or hot spot traces, were discovered decades ago but remain enigmatic. These features exhibit potential for geothermal and possibly geologic hydrogen resources, and are hypothesized to be related to the >1000 km-long 38th parallel lineament and its associated mineral deposits. Previous studies have employed surficial geologic mapping, sample petrology, and mantle/Moho imaging, but little is known about the crustal architecture associated with these igneous features. Furthermore, the extent of the system is challenging to determine given dense vegetation; mapped occurrences have been limited to a handful of knobs up to ~80 m high and outcrops mostly along or near roads.

An Earth MRI airborne magnetic and radiometric survey was flown over this system in 2024-2025. The new magnetic data exhibit circular anomalies up to ~1 km in diameter associated with mafic intrusions, including several not previously mapped but verified in the field. Over 200 such anomalies have been identified after correcting for anthropogenic sources. About 75% of these show reverse magnetization, consistent with previous measurements of sample remanent magnetization. The reverse-magnetized anomalies mostly lie within an ellipsoidal area ~80 km EW and ~40-km NS centered ~10 km east of Monterey, Virginia. In contrast, the positive anomalies extend >100 km EW and some are associated with hot springs ~95 km southwest of Monterey near a survey boundary; there may be additional anomalies farther west. The positive anomalies may indicate a separate pulse of magmatism; new geochronology will help evaluate this possibility.

The magnetic data also show a system of negative magnetic lineaments interpreted as dikes; several have been verified in the field. The dikes exhibit a quasi-radial pattern with two sections separated by ~20 km ENE-WSW and each fanning outward ~30 degrees to the ENE and WSW. Topographic lineaments extend farther outward from the dikes for both sections. These lineaments show no relation to Mesozoic dikes mapped south of Harrisonburg, Virginia, which strike 115°-145°. We interpret the Eocene dike system as the result of a subsurface magma diapir that created or deformed shallow to surficial structures into which the dikes were emplaced. These data thus suggest a more voluminous event than previously recognized. Ground truth data collection and verification are ongoing.

authors: Al-Qattan, Nasser M. [1], Rech, Jason A. [2], Currie, Brian S. [3]

abstract: Unlike the modern hyper-arid conditions across most of the Arabian Peninsula, the region experienced pronounced humid phases during the Quaternary, supporting a dense vegetation cover. Although there is abundant evidence that the area once experienced wetter intervals, it is unclear whether these pluvial events were driven by incursions of a tropical ocean monsoon (summer) or by enhanced Mediterranean (winter) westerlies. This study investigated the use of soil petrocalcic horizons in Kuwait, interpreted to be relict features that formed under a vegetated and more humid landscape, to determine the time-averaged source of moisture over the late Quaternary. Soil calcic/petrocalcic were first examined geochemically, petrographically, and mineralogically to determine if the calcite was pedogenic, and to determine if there was any allogenic carbonate as detrital clasts or as eolian sediments. After excluding samples with dolomite and eolian carbonate grains, petrocalcic horizons have δ¹³C values that range from -5.5 to -9.2‰ PDB and average -6.8‰ PDB and δ¹⁸O values that range from -8.1 to -12‰ PDB and average -9.1‰ PDB. These values indicate a landscape covered predominately with C3 vegetation and a moisture source that is highly depleted. The most parsimonious interpretation of relict soil petrocalcic horizons with these isotopic values is that Kuwait was largely covered by forests and rainfall was primarily sourced from the tropical monsoon system. Although there is no age control at present on the soil petrocalcic horizons, they are believed to be early to Middle Pleistocene in age.

abstract: The Apex Chert of the Pilbara Craton in Western Australia has some of the oldest known Archean age rocks that have been studied for evidence of early life, such as carbonaceous material, and hydrothermal alteration. Previous investigations on the Apex Chert have identified two visually distinct populations of carbonaceous material with hematite associated in it, but the mineralogical differences between hematite populations present has not been fully examined and characterized. This study investigates the presence of hematite within the Apex Chert, focusing on the characterization of hematite populations using Raman spectroscopy for primary analysis and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for secondary, elemental analysis to evaluate any differences in crystallinity, structure, and composition. Preliminary Raman spectra results suggest the presence of multiple hematite populations exhibiting distinct spectral characteristics consistent with separate mineralization events or alteration conditions. This research aims to reconstruct the paragenetic history of hematite formation within the Apex Chert through mineralogical and elemental analysis and further improve understanding of hydrothermal processes in early Earth environments.

abstract: Water security is a growing challenge in peri-urban Africa, where many communities depend on shallow groundwater systems that are increasingly threatened by seasonal rainfall variability, surface-water contamination, and rising water demand. In the Franschhoek Valley of South Africa, perennial rivers are connected to unconfined alluvial aquifers, but the relationship between streamflow and groundwater-level responses, and its potential role in transporting contaminants from the adjacent informal settlement into the aquifer, remains poorly understood. The objective of this research was to investigate surface water–groundwater interactions along the Stiebeuel River in the upper Berg River catchment by examining winter-season changes in river flow and groundwater levels, while assessing whether these interactions could facilitate the movement of pollutants from the river into the shallow aquifer. To examine this relationship, water-level loggers were installed in five boreholes drilled at the Water Hub adjacent to the Stiebeuel River. Local rainfall data were compared with river-discharge and groundwater-levels and samples were collected from both the river and boreholes and tested for orthophosphates and ammonium-nitrates, to evaluate whether changes in groundwater chemistry correspond with rainfall-driven river responses. Preliminary data indicate that precipitation events are associated with changes in groundwater depth below the surface. Corresponding increases in orthophosphate and ammonium-nitrogen concentrations following rises in river stage further suggest that rainfall-driven recharge may provide a pathway for surface-water contaminants to enter the shallow aquifer. Clarifying how rainfall-driven river flow influences groundwater recharge and pollutant transport can support nature-based solutions and more sustainable groundwater management in the Franschhoek Valley, and can also improve the understanding of river-connected aquifer vulnerability in peri-urban regions. that are facing growing climate and water-security pressures.

authors: Schmalstieg, Benjamin [1], Judge, Lauren [2], Kohl, Jove [3], Juarez Rivera, Marisol [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Science, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA

abstract:
The study of microbial mat derived structures in sedimentary deposits continues to be an active and promising area of research. In particular, non-stromatolitic structures aren’t well understood and they require further study to identify and interpret. Being able to distinguish various microbially derived structures in the sedimentary record holds potential for paleoclimate and paleoenvironment interpretation. Modern lacustrine microbial mats are common in the perennially ice-covered lakes (PICLs) of the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica, the largest ice-free area on the continent. These unique lakes provide important modern analogues for Neoproterozoic (snowball earth) glaciations and other periods of intense glaciation. Lake Fryxell in the Taylor Valley is one of the most studied of these PICLs and its benthos is covered with microbial mats where photosynthesis is viable. The microbial community and morphology of the active mats in the lake vary with depth and available oxygen (Jungblut et al., 2016). These morphologies include mat liftoff structures, formed from gasses nucleating on the mat surface, at relatively shallow depths and honeycomb and pinnacle structures at deeper depths. Carbonates commonly precipitate at the mat-water interface and within sediments, preserving mat structures. These morphologies can also be preserved in microbial laminations and other small sedimentary structures.

Lake Fryxell has experienced lake level rise of about 2.7 meters, since manual recording started in 1971, due to an increase in glacial melt and fluvial inflow (Doran and Gooseff, 2026). Using Micro X-Ray Computer Tomography (XCT) imaging, we can observe microbially derived structures in sediments non-destructively. Numerous sediment cores collected from Lake Fryxell over the last two field seasons have been imaged, and we observed the changes in preserved mat morphology moving up-core. This includes liftoff structures overlain by honeycomb and pinnacle morphologies in the same sediment core, indicating a change in depositional environment. Using XCT imaging, we have been able to directly observe the changes in microbially derived structures through changing lake levels and how these structures are preserved in a sedimentary sequence. This research supports the use of XCT as a useful and non-destructive observation method to help interpret paleoenvironmental changes in lacustrine deposits. Understanding microbially derived structures, their context, and how they change with climactic shifts is essential for interpreting lacustrine deposits from similar environments.

abstract: In cities, lead has been used for hundreds of years, with use increasing consistently over time, particularly after 1900. New York City grew extensively since the 19th century, largely during the heyday of lead use. Indoor dust is usually seen as the primary source of lead exposure. Because leaded paint is an indoor source, most resources are devoted to mitigating lead exposures from peeling paint, which can result in significant lead exposures. Assessing risks posed by indoor dusts in NYC buildings requires improved knowledge of the sources of lead to indoor dusts, whether from internal (paint) or external sources (paint in other buildings, soil dust, etc.). We have collected a wide range of paired samples of indoor dust and outdoor dust sources as part of this work. These elemental concentrations of each sample (analyzed using X-ray fluorescence) were used to identify sources of contamination, and the bioaccessibility of the lead within the sample was determined using a simulated gastric acid digestion of a small mass of selected samples. The interquartile range for the indoor total lead samples are from 44 to 734 ppm with the highest reported concentration at 49515 ppm lead. The outdoor dust samples from the same sites are uncorrelated to the indoor dust at the same sites, suggesting that the typical soil environment outside the home is generally not the source of indoor dust, particularly for dust samples that are high in lead. That said, the chemical composition of the outdoor and indoor samples have groupings with similar composition. Consistently high lead samples had chemical compositions that suggested the lead was derived from construction and demolition materials (such as lead paint) mixed with soils and other sources. These materials had reasonably high bioaccessibility. The high quantity of lead in these materials point to them being transported from other sites rather than originating directly from interior sources. We see construction sites as playing a role in these materials and we should aim to minimize dust emissions from construction materials.

abstract: The National Landslide Hazard Reduction Program is a coordinated Federal effort to reduce landslide risks and losses. Created in 2021 by the National Landslide Preparedness Act (“the Act”), the Program aims to bolster national capacity to (a) assess landslide hazard and risk, (b) coordinate landslide risk reduction activities, (c) prepare and plan for landslide impacts, and (d) respond to damaging landslide events. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is the lead Federal agency for Program implementation. To support implementation, the Act established two coordination and governing bodies: (1) The Interagency Coordinating Committee on Landslide Hazards (ICCLH), with representation from the USGS, National Weather Service, National Science Foundation, Federal Emergency Management Agency, U.S. Forest Service, Department of Transportation, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and other Federal partners; and (2) the Federal Advisory Committee on Landslides (ACL), comprised of external advisors from state, Tribal, territorial, and local geological and emergency management organizations, academic institutions, and the private sector. The ICCLH enables coordination of resources and activities across the many Federal agencies whose missions include landslide hazard and risk. The ACL provides advice and guidance on Program implementation to the USGS and its Federal partners, supporting Program effectiveness, transparency, and accountability. This governing “superstructure” enables regular and sustained coordination across multiple governmental and non-governmental sectors, elevating landslide risk reduction to a level comparable to that for other natural hazards. Complementary to these two groups, the new USGS-led National Landslide Hazard and Risk Reduction Work Group brings together local and regional practitioners to share best practices and develop common approaches to landslide hazard and risk management. USGS efforts over the past 5 years have built a multi-level, multi-sector coordination structure facilitating landslide loss reduction at a national scale. Feedback and input from participants in this session will be vital as we take the next steps in implementing the National Landslide Hazard Reduction Program.

abstract: We have produced a detailed, age-constrained δ 13 C (organic) profile revealing the Valanginian carbon-isotope excursion (CIE) or “Weissert Event” (WE) from an ~11 m-thick composite section of the alluvial and palustrine Yellow Cat Member (YCM) of the Cedar Mountain Formation. The YCM in our study area (Poison Strip, Grand County, Utah) contains pervasive evidence for long intervals of pedogenesis. Our profile is amply constrained by two cryptotephra CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb ages (Joeckel et al. Geosciences , https://doi.org/10.3390/geosciences13020032). The structure of the WE in our YCM composite δ 13 C (organic) profile from the salt-tectonic Yellow Cat basin correlates remarkably well with one produced from ~200 m of Panthalassan marine strata in northeastern Japan reported by T. Tomaru et al. 2025, ( Newsletters in Stratigraphy , https://doi.org/10.1127/nos/2025/0868). They identified multiple constituent minor CIEs of the WE, naming those segments of their profile as NP2, PP4, NP3, NP4, PP5, NP5, and PP6, in ascending stratigraphic order. All seven of these features are readily identified in our profile as well, despite an eighteen-fold difference in stratigraphic thickness. This remarkable correspondence in the detailed structure of the first major CIE during the Cretaceous Period leads us to conclude that, at least in this case, the chemostratigraphic record “compensates” for a highly incomplete sedimentary record in conferring a means of correlation between stratal packages of vastly different scale in the terrestrial and marine realms. Accordingly, we encourage a significant paradigm shift in how disparate stratigraphic, and chemostratigraphic records are interpreted, compared, and correlated.

abstract: Reconstructing feedbacks in Earth’s climate system using paleoclimate archives requires precise, accurate geochronological methods. Marine sediments can be dated using radiocarbon for the last 50,000 years, but absolute chronologies beyond the radiocarbon timescales have remained elusive. While aragonitic corals can be used to date sea level change and provide snapshots of deep-sea conditions, paleoceanographers lack archives that can be precisely dated in continuously accumulating marine sediments. Pteropods are marine planktonic organisms that produce aragonitic shells and are found in marine sediments around the globe. However, the geochronological potential of their fossil shells has not been fully explored. We present an investigation into the robustness of U-series dating of fossil pteropod shells. We have tested primary vs. secondary uptake of U, cleaning techniques for isolating radiogenic 230 Th from adsorbed and detrital 230 Th components, and agreement of U-series dates with radiocarbon ages. U-Th and radiocarbon dates of pteropods from the same core intervals agree within error. However, some downcore samples displayed enriched 234 U/ 238 U ratios relative to seawater, suggesting that open system and/or alpha recoil correction models may be necessary.

abstract: The Climate Adaptation and Resilience Monitoring Alliance (CARMA) team utilizes NASA’s STELLA (Science and Technology Education for Land/Life Assessment) device to study the impacts of climate change on plant health in a variety of vulnerable environments. The CARMA team uses STELLA to determine the health of the plant before it shows visible signs of decline by observing reflectance across twelve unique near-infrared (NIR) and visible wavelengths. Ideally, a healthy plant should absorb red light for photosynthesis and reflect high levels of NIR irradiance. Therefore, when examining a healthy plant, the STELLA should measure high levels of NIR irradiance as well as green irradiance due to the plant’s chlorophyll, with relatively low levels of red and blue. By using a STELLA, researchers can determine the extent to which plants are being affected within their own communities or other areas of interest. CARMA is testing STELLA in a variety of environments; urban/campus, areas impacted by wildfires, state park lands, rural agricultural lands, and an in-house greenhouse in which to test the impact of various conditions on plant growth and health. Recent greenhouse experiments have been conducted to observe how plant spectral signatures and health indicators fluctuate in response to drought conditions. A handheld spectrometer like STELLA would allow ranchers and farmers to monitor the conditions of the crops and fields that feed their communities. CARMA is focusing on a rural ranching property devoted to conservation practices. Investigations into the difference in plant health across keyline-treated and untreated soil, as well as the influence of commercial mycorrhizal inoculant plant health, are ongoing projects. CARMA is actively conducting research on Colorado wildfire risk assessment via evaluation of soil moisture content and leaf water content by using STELLA’s NIR readings to create calibration curves that relate reflectance to these metrics. STELLA was originally intended for educational community science purposes but has proven the potential to contribute to professional research and sustainability efforts. NASA’s mission to educate the youth about the importance of monitoring climate change would be enhanced by continued support of STELLA’s research potential.

abstract: Terrestrial records of climate at the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) are sparse, compared to those from marine sediments. Paleoglacier extents are routinely used to assess past climate conditions, as the equilibrium line altitude (ELA) of a glacier is indicative of local annual precipitation and summer temperature conditions. Since the 1990s, hundreds of alpine glaciers moraines have been constrained to the LGM using 10 Be dating of moraine boulders. I first used an existing cosmogenic nuclide database – ICE-D – to identify alpine glacier moraines from around the world that dated to the LGM. I then used glacial mapping and an ArcGIS tool – PaleoIce – to reconstruct hundreds of paleoglacier surfaces and ELA. I will present these ELA reconstructions along with paleoclimate inferences, providing a new global terrestrial archive of LGM climate in glaciated areas worldwide.

title: Defining Magma-Flux State: Linking Thermal Budget, Melt Connectivity, and Eruptibility in Silicic Systems
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics
authors: Michelfelder, Gary S. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, Missouri, USA
abstract:
Silicic reservoirs are, most of the time, crystal mush bodies. Whether a mush is eruptible depends on whether it is above or below a rheological threshold (the rheological critical melt percentage), ~40–50 vol% melt, below which crystal networks lock. The body behaves as a solid rather than a mobile magma. The determining factor in whether a melt is eruptible is the thermal budget: continuous or repeated magma/heat recharge (high flux) keeps the reservoir warm and melt-rich for long periods, whereas low or episodic flux rates keep the system crystal-rich and non-eruptible. However, volcanic behavior cannot be explained by the magma supply rate alone. The evolution of silicic magmatic systems is better understood through the concept of the magma-flux state, where a given silicic reservoir resides along a continuum from melt-dominated (hot, melt-connected, eruptible) to crystalline (cold, crystal-locked, non-eruptible), as set by the balance between the rate of thermal/mass input (magma flux) and the rate of heat loss to the surrounding crust. Therefore, the magma flux state is defined as the thermal-rheological condition of a magma reservoir, determined by the ratio of magmatic/heat input rate to conductive heat loss rate, which governs melt fraction, melt connectivity, and the mechanical eruptibility of the system at a given time.

We develop magma-flux state by integrating complementary zircon and mineral chemistry records of magmatic evolution from long-lived silicic systems in the Central Volcanic Zone of the Andes and the Azores. Zircon’s ability to record timescales and crystallization conditions provides a baseline flux and thermal perturbations that define baseline flux states, meaning the age spectrum serves as a proxy for the duration and continuity of the reservoir's sub-liquidus history . In contrast to the long-term record of zircon, mineral diffusion chronometry provides the ‘speedometer’ for immediate, high-energy triggers and incubation times, capturing the episodicity of highly transient flux states. Spatial patterns within a single crystal distinguish between remobilization occurring as a single event and that occurring over prolonged heating, informing shifts in flux state. Examining silicic magmatic systems from the perspective of the magma-flux state connects crystal-scale observations to magma storage in the crust. This approach provides a mechanism to evaluate the longevity, eruptive behavior, and evolution of silicic volcanic systems.

abstract:
In 1927, the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC) was established to manage community development, protect natural and cultural resources, and provide recreational experiences for the public in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties, Maryland, USA. Prince George’s County has a rich fossil record, spanning from the early Cretaceous to the Pleistocene, with units preserving globally significant events, like the end-Cretaceous Mass Extinction and Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum. However, for many decades, fossil resources on park property were mostly ignored by M-NCPPC and left unregulated and underutilized.

This changed in 2009 when M-NCPPC opened Dinosaur Park as their first site dedicated to paleontological conservation and public recreation. Dinosaur Park includes a portion of a former iron mine and one of the only terrestrial early Cretaceous sites on the east coast of the United States. Public interest following the discovery of a bone bed at Dinosaur Park between 2021 and 2023 led M-NCPPC to further invest in paleontology. In 2025, after nearly 100 years, Prince George’s County Department of Parks and Recreation established a Paleontology Unit to manage fossil resources on the ~30,000 acres of park property, as well as to conduct/facilitate scientific research and implement educational programs throughout the county.

All onsite educational programs are centered around authentic community science, in which the public are active participants in our mission to conserve paleontological resources. At Dinosaur Park, we offer three types of onsite programs: free community Open House programs, paid Educational Group programs, and paid Fossil Dig programs. During these programs, participants get hands-on learning experiences, assisting with surface collecting, screenwashing, excavating, and field cataloging. The Paleontology Unit also offers free offsite community outreach programs, visiting schools, libraries, museums, and other organizations to share our work and encourage more participation in our community stewardship efforts. title: Greenhouse Warming Without Bottom-Water Deoxygenation: Multiproxy Evidence from the Southern Ocean During the Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum (MECO)
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part II)
authors: Egunjobi, Kehinde Joseph [1], Riedinger, Natascha [2], Quan, Tracy Michelle [3]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(3) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: The Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum (MECO) represents one of the most significant transient global warming events of the Cenozoic and provides an important natural analogue for understanding marine biogeochemical responses to sustained greenhouse climates. Although previous studies have documented changes in ocean circulation, carbonate chemistry, and productivity during the MECO, the response of high-latitude Southern Ocean redox conditions remains poorly constrained. We generated a high-resolution multiproxy geochemical record from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Hole U1514 in the Mentelle Basin, southeast Indian Ocean, integrating sedimentary trace metal geochemistry, carbonate content (CaCO₃), total organic carbon (TOC), and bulk organic carbon and nitrogen isotopes (δ¹³C org and δ¹⁵N org ) across the pre-MECO, MECO, and post-MECO intervals. Strong positive correlations between Al and lithogenic elements, together with inverse relationships between CaCO₃ and lithogenic element concentrations, indicate that variations in bulk sediment geochemistry are primarily controlled by dilution of the lithogenic fraction by biogenic carbonate. Redox-sensitive trace metals show no significant authigenic enrichment, TOC contents remain uniformly low, and δ¹⁵N org exhibits no systematic changes across the MECO. Together, these independent proxy records consistently support predominantly oxic depositional conditions throughout the studied interval, with no evidence of persistent oxygen depletion. Despite persistently oxic depositional conditions, CaCO₃ concentrations record substantial perturbations to the marine carbonate system, including transient carbonate dissolution and prolonged reductions in carbonate saturation. A post-MECO negative δ¹³C org excursion (CIE) likewise occurred without corresponding changes in redox-sensitive trace metals, TOC, or δ¹⁵N org , suggesting that the CIE was not accompanied by measurable changes in sedimentary redox conditions. Overall, the Hole U1514A record indicates that major perturbations to the marine carbonate system during MECO were not accompanied by persistent bottom–water deoxygenation.

title: Colorado School of Mines’ Approach for Integrating Professional Readiness Competencies into the Curriculum
session_title: Learning to be a Geoscientist: Professional Exposure, Agency, and Transferable Skills in Undergraduate Education.
authors: Houlton, Heather Renee [1], Marshall-McKelvey, Kira [2]
affiliations: (1) Trefny Innovative Instruction Center, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Trefny Innovative Instruction Center, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The professional workforce is shifting rapidly, characterized by Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), a volatile economic outlook for low-to-moderate wage earners ($85,000/year or less) in a “K” shaped economy (Miller et al., 2026), and a “near-zero” labor force growth in 2026 (Murray and Vidangos, 2026). Because the U.S. lacks a government-funded system to address major shifts strategically, workers facing job loss may experience disparities in health, educational attainment, and public safety (Frueh, 2025). Consequently, institutions of higher education must cultivate future employees’ professional readiness competencies, human-based skills and dispositions that GenAI cannot emulate or replace.

Colorado School of Mines (Mines) surveyed employers and alumni, identifying key professional growth areas for graduates. In response, Mines is piloting a new model integrating professional readiness competencies throughout the undergraduate and graduate experience. Impacting over 600 undergraduate and 300 graduate students per year studying geoscience-related disciplines, the initiative supplements Mines’ technical curriculum with three key professional readiness pillars: 1) communication, 2) networking, and 3) bringing “ideas to reality” via experiential learning (doing, practicing, failing and reflecting). Cultivating this ubiquitous ecosystem requires campus-wide collaboration across Student Life, Academic Affairs, the Foundation, and Marketing/Communications, operationalized through eight subcommittees.

To support classroom integration, the Trefny Innovation Instruction Center, Mines’ center for teaching and learning, developed a “faculty toolkit.” For example, we developed “Take-n-Teach” activities; and a syllabus template outlining a commitment to modeling professional communication in the course, contextualizing networking skills, and demonstrating the value of experiential learning. Additionally, we’ve developed language for GenAI prompts for faculty to integrate related course learning outcomes, assessment rubrics, and experiential learning activities into their courses.

This toolkit is one component of Mines’ broader initiative; by embedding these competencies, we equip our graduates with both top-tier technical aptitude and the essential professional skills to navigate an unpredictable workforce.

title: Zircons from Lambadalsfjall Volcano, Iceland: Insights into the Generation of Early Silicic Magmas
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Warnick, Genna E. [1], Banik, Tenley J. [2], Blum, Tyler B. [3], Meister, Paul A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(2) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(3) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(4) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
abstract: Iceland is a unique geologic location: it sits on top of a divergent plate boundary and a mantle plume, a setting unreplicated on modern Earth. Magma production is higher than at a ‘typical’ ocean island or a mid-ocean ridge alone, and silicic rocks are more abundant (~10%) in Iceland than on other ocean islands. Iceland’s oldest rocks (~15 Ma) are found in the Westfjords region and are understudied compared to those in the neovolcanic zones. Here, we map and investigate the petrogenesis of silicic rocks from Lambadalsfjall, an extinct volcano in the Westfjords, providing the first geochemical constraints on this system’s magmatic evolution. Zircon crystals were extracted from a rhyolite sample and imaged via cathodoluminescence prior to and after analysis. U-Pb ages (n=9) and trace element (n=10) compositions were acquired via SHRIMP-RG at Stanford University and O isotope compositions (n=21) were measured via SIMS at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Zircon U-Pb ages range from ~13.4 Ma to ~15.1 Ma with a weighted mean age of 14.5 ± 0.3 Ma. These zircons have uniformly low δ¹⁸O values; 20 grains range from 0.9–1.4‰ and one outlier has δ¹⁸O = -2.9‰. The median of all grains is 1.2‰, which is 2‰ lower than the median δ¹⁸O of all other zircon originating from across Iceland, which is 3.1‰ (Carley et al., 2020). Zircon trace element compositions include median U (37 ppm), Nb (9 ppm), Hf (9692 ppm), and Ti (16 ppm); median U/Yb is 0.15. When compared to other Tertiary volcanoes from the Westfjords (i.e., Hrafnsfjörður, Árnes, and Kaldalón), Lambadalsfjall zircon consistently clusters at higher Ti (vs. 10 ppm), lower Hf (vs. 8995 ppm), and lower U/Yb (vs. 0.22 ppm) (Banik et al., 2023). Taken together, these zircon data point to the Lambadalsfjall rhyolite resulting largely from partially melted, geochemically enriched, and hydrothermally altered bedrock—in contrast to other Westfjords systems whose melts result dominantly from fractional crystallization of new mantle inputs with little involvement of pre-existing crust. These baseline observations allow us to gain a better understanding of silicic rock generation in Iceland. However, it raises the question of how silicic magma generation may be unique to certain parts of the Westfjords, and how it varied in Iceland’s early lifetime.

title: Quantifying Interspecific Shell Shape Variation in Glycymeris gigantea and Glycymeris maculata Using Geometric Morphometrics

authors: Harrison, Logan Neill [1], Srivastava-Losey, Shravya [2], Moss, David Kelton [3]
affiliations: (1) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX, USA
(2) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX,
(3) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX, ; Natural History Collection, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX, USA
abstract: Systematic descriptions of fossil species often require comparison with extant representatives, but diagnostic characters identified in living taxa are not always preserved in the fossil record. The bivalves Glycymeris gigantea and Glycymeris maculata exemplify this challenge as their previous species descriptions have relied primarily on qualitative comparisons of modern specimens. A principal diagnostic character has been the difference in shell color pattern, a character with poor taphonomic potential in the fossil record and thus not useful when studying fossil representatives. Complicating the matter further, these two species co-occur in both modern and fossil settings. Previous work has not treated these species using a quantatitve approach. To remedy this situation, we applied two-dimensional geometric morphometrics to identify morphological characters that are applicable to both fossil and extant specimens. Analysis of modern individuals (n=20 for each species) was performed using specimen images from both species with a well-preserved shell interior. Most of the morphological variation was interspecific. Canonical variate analysis identified elongation of the adductor muscle scars, increased maximum shell length, dentition plate curvature flattening and longer ligamental area as the primary characters changing from G.maculata to G.gigantea . Principal component analysis recovered the same pattern of morphological differentiation. Fossil specimens (n=9 for G.maculata and n=10 for G.gigantea ) were analyzed using the same approach and likewise exhibited large interspecific variation. Canonical variate analysis of the fossil dataset considers adductor muscle scar length, maximum shell length, dentition plate curvature and ligamental area length as distinguishing characters between the two species. These results demonstrate that reliable species-level differences extend beyond shell color for G. gigantea and G. maculata and can be recognized in both extant and fossil material. Morphometric analysis therefore provides a quantitative framework for identifying diagnostic morphological characters that are relatively well preserved in fossil record, improving systematic descriptions and facilitating direct comparisons between fossil and modern representatives of a target species.

title: Geochemical Signatures and Paleoecological Shifts on the Eastern Niger Delta Shelf: Emergence of Late Pleistocene Lowstand Dynamics and Holocene Marine Transgression
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Garcia, Keagen [1], Adojoh, Onema Christopher [2], Trabal, William Christopher [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Natural Sciences, Northwest Missouri State University, Maryville, Missouri, USA
(2) School of Natural Sciences, Northwest Missouri State University, Maryville, MO, USA
(3) School of Natural Sciences, Northwest Missouri State University, Maryville, MO, USA
abstract: This research investigates the environmental transformation of the eastern offshore Niger Delta, Eastern Atlantic Ocean, through an integrated analysis of sedimentological, geochemical, and micropaleontological records obtained from three gravity cores (GC1–GC3). By combining lithofacies observations, granulometric profiles, Ti/Zr elemental ratios, and foraminiferal community assessments within an age-constrained framework, the study reconstructs a sequence of major paleoenvironmental transitions spanning the last ~18,000 years. The earliest core intervals indicate a prodeltaic and delta-front landscape, marked by coarse sediments, elevated Ti/Zr ratios, and abundant benthic foraminifera (notably Melonis spp., Uvigerina spp., and Ammonia sp.), pointing to dominant riverine input under low sea-level conditions. During the Holocene transistion, a pronounced shift is detected: Ti/Zr ratios decline, mud content increases, and planktonic foraminifera (such as Globigerinoides ruber and Globorotalia tumida) become more prominent, reflecting the landward movement of the shoreline and progressive marine flooding. The uppermost core layers are typified by fine-grained shelf deposits, reduced terrestrial influx, and a surge in planktonic foraminiferal abundance, indicative of a stable mid-Holocene highstand. Multivariate statistical techniques: Pearson correlation, principal component analysis, and hierarchical clustering corroborate the major role of post-glacial sea-level rise in shaping sediment dispersal patterns, depositional environments, and biological communities across the shelf. Collectively, these findings elucidate the evolution of coastal and marine systems in the Niger Delta region and enhance our understanding of how tropical Atlantic shelves responded to Late Quaternary climatic fluctuations.
