title: Why Melts Differ Across the Azores Triple Junction: Lithospheric and Source Controls on Basalt Geochemistry
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Doran, Angel [1], Michelfelder, Gary S. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
abstract: The Azores archipelago exposes a central ambiguity in the interpretation of ocean-island basalt: is inter-island geochemical diversity a record of mantle source heterogeneity, or a signature of lithospheric architecture filtering where melting stops and magmas stall? In the Azores, the two are geometrically inseparable: the isotopic enrichment gradient runs parallel to the lithospheric thickness gradient. Here we test which control is first-order using a screened nine-island whole-rock compilation (278 samples), together with new XRF and ICP-MS analyses and olivine EPMA, anchored to published receiver-function lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary depths. Garnet retains Yb far more than Gd, making Gd/Yb a garnet-sensitive index less inflated than La/Yb by light-REE source enrichment; primitive-mantle-normalized values climb from 2.37 at Faial, above a ~40 km lid, to 3.15 at São Miguel, above ~80 km, while adjacent plume-influenced Mid-Atlantic Ridge basalts anchor the ridge endpoint near 1.5 and extend the trend (r ≈ 0.79 among the islands, ≈ 0.88 with the ridge anchor). The eruptive and crystal records are consistent with contrasting delivery histories. Faial whole rocks reach 12–14 wt% MgO and at the crystal scale one Faial sample carries disequilibrium, reverse-zoned olivine cargo while two São Miguel samples contain host-equilibrated olivine recording ~1180–1290 °C. The sharpest test lies where the gradients diverge: Terceira and São Miguel share an ~80 km lid, yet Terceira erupts lower-Gd/Yb lavas. Recent seismic tomography images segmented crustal magma bodies beneath Terceira’s Santa Bárbara and Guilherme Moniz–Pico Alto systems, while crystal-zoning evidence documents multilevel storage, recharge, and mixing along its active rift; São Miguel preserves higher garnet-field ratios consistent with a different plumbing history. These results identify lithospheric architecture modulated by island-scale structure as a first-order control on melt chemistry, with source heterogeneity acting within that framework rather than instead of it. Sr-Nd data across all nine islands (259 paired analyses) document real source heterogeneity, but the island-scale Gd/Yb pattern remains more closely associated with the lithospheric framework than with the isotopic-enrichment gradient it parallels. Clinopyroxene barometry, in progress, will test whether the studied lavas record the storage levels already imaged beneath Terceira and how those levels compare with São Miguel.

abstract: Remote sensing provides valuable insight into the ecological health of Earth’s systems by measuring reflected and emitted electromagnetic radiation. The extreme drought conditions induced by a changing climate result in a vast shift in ecological trends, and handheld spectroscopic devices like STELLA are integral in understanding them. This is pertinent in sensitive areas where the minimization of environmental disturbance is key. The interactions between light and the pigment within plants can be measured using sensors. This data allows researchers to calculate reflectance values to predict the activity of pigments, and subsequently, the stress response of plants. The intention with this study is to utilize the STELLA spectrometer to corroborate and contribute to prior ecological research in Yellowstone National Park. STELLA is a handheld spectrometer developed by NASA, which measures 12 electromagnetic bands across the visible and near infrared (NIR) spectrum ranging between wavelengths of 450-860 nm. Although NASA’s Landsat satellite identifies broad trends, it cannot isolate the finer trends within individual plant communities. Complementary to Landsat and other published data, STELLA can monitor those acute shifts in Yellowstone’s ecological health without any physical disturbance to the environment. These experiments are based on three prior research studies about climate change-induced ecological shifts in Yellowstone National Park. The subjects of these studies are aspen recovery following the reintroduction of wolves, responses of wetland vegetation to drought, and drought resilience of the unique grass D. Lanuginosum (Hot Springs Panic Grass). This data will help answer three primary questions: Do STELLA health assessments of aspen stands reflect the state of recovery that other metrics, such as new aspen count and tree height, do? Are the broad ecological trends discovered in wetland communities via large-scale remote sensing reflected in ground-based monitoring accomplished with point-based spectroscopy? Does the symbiotic relationship that allows D. Lanuginosum grass to tolerate extreme temperatures allow it to maintain a healthy photosynthetic rate at these temperatures and in the face of drought? The research conducted in Yellowstone will be used to corroborate and enhance the breadth of data that has been collected within the park, and in so demonstrate the applicability of the STELLA device in ecological research fields.

session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Gervais, Bailey E. [1], Garvey, David [2], Arens, Nan Crystal [3]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Hobart & William Smith Colleges, Geneva, NY,
(2) Computer Sciences, Hobart & William Smith, Geneva, NY, USA

abstract: The Paleocene and Eocene epochs are characterized by significant global warmth, with higher temperatures and more precipitation than observed today. A valuable climate proxy for estimating and reconstructing terrestrial climates is leaf physiognomy, the study of leaf characteristics and how these traits relate to environmental factors like climate. In this study, 15 dicot leaf fossil localities (including localities found in Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Tennessee, Washington, Oregon, California, Idaho, Nevada, Wyoming, North Dakota, and British Columbia) from published literature and one unpublished locality from the Gulf Coastal Plain of southwestern Alabama were analyzed using the Climate Leaf Analysis Multivariate Program (CLAMP). CLAMP compares fossil leaf morphology with modern vegetation samples from known climates based on a multivariable relationship between leaf physiognomy and local climate. In addition to this analysis, eight additional localities whose flora had been analyzed through CLAMP were included in the reconstruction. The resulting paleoclimate reconstructions had mean annual temperature (MAT) values ranging from 9°C to 25°C, and annual precipitation ranged from 770 mm to almost 3000 mm. The paleoclimatic conditions of the localities were spatially interpolated using GIS to create MAT and GSP surfaces. The warmest and wettest conditions were found in the Gulf Coast region of the United States, followed by the Pacific Coast. The driest, coldest conditions in the north-central United States. Both MAT and GSP differed significantly from modern values, supporting previous findings of substantially warmer and wetter conditions during the Eocene. There was an average difference of more than 5°C in MAT between the Eocene localities and their modern-day climates, and GSP was 1428 mm more on average. Future work will apply the same methods to Paleocene-aged localities to compare climate conditions and patterns between the Paleocene and Eocene.

title: Trace fossils of the Liberty and Saluda intervals of the Cincinnatian Series (Late Ordovician) at Madison, IN: Assessing bioturbation levels and environmental controls

abstract: The Ordovician Cincinnatian Series (OH, IN, KY) is one of the most documented and analyzed geological sequences in the world, renowned for its pristinely preserved fossils from the Katian (Late Ordovician). This project aims to analyze the trace fossils and their depositional context in the Liberty and Saluda intervals of the Cincinnatian Series at Madison, IN. Our goals are to assess the amount of sediment mixing by animals during this time period and evaluate possible environmental stress factors affecting bottom waters and the seafloor. A 15 m-thick section was logged, and 20 samples were collected. Samples were embedded in epoxy, cut, and polished to improve trace fossil characterization. An ichnological analysis consisting of ichnotaxa and ethological characterization and quantification of the bioturbation index provided the basis for an ichnofabric analysis. The studied succession displays calcareous and mixed mudstone, bioclastic floatstone and rudstone, coral framestone, and dolostone, representing a prograding succession that ranges from shoreface mixed (carbonate-siliciclastic), shell beds and mudstones, through coral buildups, lagoonal organic-rich silty carbonates and mudstones, and culminating in intertidal laminated dolomitic siltstones. Six ichnofabrics have been identified within the logged sections: highly bioturbated with Chondrites, Nereites, Palaeophycus, Planolites, and Teichichnus; moderately bioturbated with Nereites, Palaeophycus, and Planolites; moderately bioturbated with Chondrites; sparsely to moderately bioturbated with Skolithos; sparsely bioturbated with Teichichnus; and sparsely bioturbated with Zoophycos. Preliminary findings show lower ichnofossil diversity within the intertidal zone and higher in the subtidal facies, with the highest in the shoreface mixed. Furthermore, the description of highly bioturbated ichnofabrics supports the idea that mixed carbonate and siliciclastic seafloors were fully mixed by the Late Ordovician.

title: The Role of Cryptic Plutons in Barrovian Metamorphism: A Case Study from the Funeral Mountains Metamorphic Core Complex
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Autrey, Suzanne [1], Montanez , Keanu [2], Wells, Michael L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, IL, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, IL, USA

abstract: Regional Barrovian metamorphic gradients in contractional orogens are commonly interpreted as products of crustal thickening and tectonic burial, yet localized magmatic heating may substantially modify these gradients and complicate tectonic interpretations. This effect may be especially important in the Funeral Mountains, a metamorphic core complex in the western U.S. Cordillera. Aluminosilicate-bearing schists exposed locally in the Echo Canyon field area interrupt the regional Barrovian metamorphic field gradient that spans the northern Funeral Mountains. Newly mapped mineral isograds, phase equilibria modeling, petrography, U-Pb rutile geochronology, and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar muscovite geochronology indicate that localized heating by a cryptic pluton disrupts the northwest-increasing Barrovian metamorphic gradient across the northern Funeral Mountains produced by Jurassic retroarc underthrusting. Phase-equilibria modeling of andalusite- and kyanite-bearing schists requires temperatures of at least 540 °C, substantially hotter than adjacent lower-greenschist facies rocks. Rutile and muscovite ages from the proposed contact aureole record Jurassic cooling at ca. 160-163 Ma, whereas lower-grade chloritoid-bearing schists preserve older rutile U-Pb dates interpreted to record prograde Jurassic metamorphism. Although the causative pluton is not exposed at the surface, the mapped metamorphic zonation, thermal structure, and geochronologic data collectively support the presence of a concealed Jurassic intrusion beneath Echo Canyon. Together with previously documented Cretaceous metamorphic overprinting in Monarch Canyon, the Echo Canyon aureole indicates that the Funeral Mountains preserve a composite tectono-thermal history in which localized magmatic heating overprinted a regional Jurassic Barrovian metamorphic gradient. These results demonstrate that cryptic plutons may locally perturb regional Barrovian metamorphic gradients in contractional orogens and suggest that magmatic heating may contribute to anomalously high thermal gradients in other Cordilleran metamorphic terranes.

title: Short Records, Longer Consequences: How Data Gaps Shape Subsidence Forecasts
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Saberi, Leila L [1], Ellis, John [2]
affiliations: (1) INTERA Incorporated, Chicago, IL, USA

abstract: Many subsidence models are calibrated using limited subsidence observations but somewhat longer groundwater-level histories—a common condition for GSAs across California. This presentation quantifies how shortened monitoring records affect subsidence model calibration and predictive uncertainty by systematically truncating long-term groundwater-level and subsidence datasets and recalibrating 1-D MODFOW CSUB models. Multiple scenarios are explored, including full subsidence and water-level records, short subsidence records paired with long water-level histories, and cases where both records are limited. Results demonstrate that long groundwater-level histories alone are insufficient to constrain key subsidence-related parameters such as elastic and inelastic skeletal storage, interbed vertical hydraulic conductivity, and preconsolidation head. In particular, incomplete subsidence records reduce the model’s ability to distinguish elastic from inelastic deformation and to characterize lag behavior, leading to biased estimates of critical head and increased uncertainty in future subsidence forecasts. The analysis highlights the importance of capturing multiple stress cycles and rebound periods and provides insight into how data limitations propagate uncertainty into long-term predictions used for SGMA planning.

title: USGS Geochron Database: AI Assisted Data Compilation
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data (Posters)
authors: Thomson, Kelly David [1], Gilmer, Amy K. [2], Morgan, Leah [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, DENVER, CO,
(2) U. S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO,

abstract:
The USGS Geochron Database is a publicly accessible repository containing geochronological dates and data for more than 40,000 samples. Focused primarily on the United States, these samples collectively represent over 300,000 individual analyses derived from 16 different geochronological and thermochronological methods. These methods span a broad temporal range, from Quaternary techniques such as radiocarbon, luminescence, and cosmogenic nuclide dating, to deep‑time approaches including 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, Rb-Sr, and U‑Th-Pb geochronology. Data incorporated into the database originate from a wide variety of sources, including USGS data releases, State geological survey contributions, and published academic or industry literature. The majority of data in the database have been compiled by USGS compilers, State geological survey employees, and academic researchers. As the database grows, we aim to incorporate automated compilation techniques into this workflow.

Compiling legacy geochronologic data from older publications presents significant challenges due to the diversity of data reporting styles, non‑digital or outdated table formats, and inconsistent file types. Many older documents exist only as low‑quality scans, further complicating the extraction of reliable numerical and metadata fields. To address these obstacles, we have begun experimenting with artificial intelligence (AI) tools to streamline the data compilation workflow. These efforts supply large language models with our database schema, compilation templates, and instructional guidelines as context, paired with detailed prompts designed to extract data from scanned articles and map key fields into our standardized templates. Results varied more by field type than by document and varied substantially across the tools tested. Analytical values and ages were often extracted successfully, but sample metadata proved considerable harder. Some tools failed to map values into the correct template columns, could not? reliably mine descriptive metadata distributed through body text, and did not consistently capture uncertainty levels. However, some large language models produced highly accurate and immediately usable compilations. All AI-assisted output is verified by an expert compiler against the source publication before entering the database. We treat these tools as an aid to compilation rather than a substitute for it, and the metadata failures described above are precisely the errors least likely to be caught without that review. As models continue to advance these tools are becoming a valuable asset for accelerating geochronological data compilation.

abstract: Groundwater depletion driven by irrigated agriculture threatens the long-term sustainability of food production systems across the semi-arid western United States. Developing reliable groundwater models is essential for sustainable groundwater management but is often limited by uncertainty in key model inputs (e.g., pumping rates and groundwater recharge) and aquifer parameters (e.g., storage properties). This study demonstrates how satellite-based remote sensing products and a national-scale hydrologic model can improve groundwater model development by providing more accurate model inputs and additional calibration constraints. We use irrigation mapping datasets (IrrMapper and LANID) combined with OpenET evapotranspiration estimates to distribute regional annual groundwater withdrawals among individual irrigation wells based on irrigation consumptive use, enabling estimation of monthly pumping rates. Initial groundwater recharge estimates are obtained from the National Agroecosystem Model (NAM), a physically based hydrologic model developed for the contiguous United States using publicly available datasets. In addition, we incorporate land subsidence observations derived from Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) as an additional calibration target to better constrain aquifer storage parameters and reduce parameter non-uniqueness. We apply this framework to develop and calibrate a MODFLOW groundwater model for Parowan Valley, Utah. Remote sensing-based estimates of well-level groundwater pumping substantially outperform simpler approaches for distributing regional groundwater withdrawals. Compared with transmissivity-weighted and uniform allocation methods, the remote sensing approach improves agreement with pumping estimates derived from power consumption records, increasing R 2 from -0.48 and -0.15 to 0.63, respectively. Using recharge estimates from the calibrated NAM also significantly improves groundwater model performance relative to recharge estimates from the uncalibrated NAM, reducing head simulation bias from 28.22 to 5.55 m, RMSE from 30.14 to 12.60 m, and increasing R 2 from -3.95 to 0.14. Incorporating InSAR-derived land subsidence into model calibration further improves model performance during the testing period, decreasing head simulation bias from 5.66 to 4.43 m, RMSE from 10.36 to 9.09 m, and increasing R 2 from 0.44 to 0.57. These results demonstrate that leveraging remote sensing observations and a national-scale hydrologic model can substantially improve groundwater model inputs, parameter characterization, and predictive performance, providing a practical framework for groundwater modeling in data-limited, groundwater-dependent agricultural regions.

title: Paleobiogeography of Paleozoic Paracrinoid Echinoderms
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology (Posters)
authors: Altier, Elizabeth B. [1], Potter, Erin [2], Limbeck, Maggie [3], Panzik, Joseph E. [4], Sheffield, Sarah L. [5]
affiliations: (1) Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA

abstract:
Paracrinoids are a small, enigmatic group of blastozoan echinoderms from the Middle to Late Ordovician. Their morphology deviates from other stemmed echinoderm groups, with a highly variable amount of ambulacra, flattened thecae, and diverse respiratory processes. While recent phylogenetic analyses have indicated they likely represent a monophyletic group, there are still many questions about their evolutionary history within Blastozoa.

Of particular interest within the paracrinoids is their limited geographic range and rapid diversification in a relatively short geologic time span.(477 to 449 Ma). The temporal, species, and geographic distribution of paracrinoids is far more restricted than other high-level taxonomic groups within Blastozoa, many of which, such as the diploporans or blastoids, reached a near-global range with large numbers of species, across a broader time span of the Paleozoic.

In this study, we explore the diversification of paracrinoids across Laurentia by performing a mutli-method phylogenetically informed biogeographic analysis. Using previously published phylogenetic hypotheses, we explored dispersal and speciation patterns of 24 taxa from across 10 localities in Laurentia. We performed biogeographic analyses using two approaches in R, one using ‘BioGeoBEARS’ and the other in ‘SBEARS’. We compared the results from each of the models to explore the efficacy of each method in reconstructing the biogeographic history of paracrinoids from a limited geographic range but high number of formations.

Initial results show increased speciation in the Late Ordovician, at the same time as the Taconic orogeny, with vicariance predominating before and dispersal predominating after. A great deal of uncertainty remains around paracrinoids and their evolutionary history, but these results expand our understanding of their movements through the upheaval of the Late Ordovician before their extinction.

abstract:
Releases of radioactive elements in the environment pose a serious threat to environmental and human health. While many studies have examined anthropogenic radionuclide mobility on short spatial and temporal scales, few address the long-term (decadal) fate of radioactive isotopes in watersheds. Here, I will focus on biogeochemical processes influencing plutonium (Pu) and cesium-137 ( 137 Cs) in two case studies from Savannah River Site (SRS), SC and Nevada National Security Site (NNSS), NV.

Pond B, a monomictic reservoir at SRS, was part of the secondary cooling loop of R Reactor, which produced weapons-grade Pu, from 1961 to 1966. During this period, the pond received documented releases of 10’s to 100’s of MBq of Pu and 137 Cs, which are still measurable today. Two consecutive years of monitoring demonstrated the occurrence of highly correlated concentration profiles of arsenic, iron, aluminum, plutonium, and dissolved organic matter, all of which increased in concentration by 1–2 orders of magnitude within the anaerobic hypolimnion. Plutonium appears to have become incorporated into the natural iron and carbon cycles with the highest concentrations in water observed at the start of stratification, with the majority released from shallow waters associated with Fe(III)-particulate organic matter.

In contrast to the saturated Pond B system, we studied radionuclide transport in an ephemeral wetland at NNSS. Over the last 65 years, the E-Tunnel ponds have continuously collected groundwater discharging from a tunnel where several underground nuclear tests were conducted from the 1950’s to the 1970’s. Variably saturated pond sediment profiles of Pu and 137 Cs show that Pu remains immobilized, but 137 Cs is largely transported through the pond sediments. Interestingly, column and batch experiments indicate that natural organic matter in the groundwater has the potential to mobilize Pu through the sediments. Therefore, Pu entering the ponds must be in a recalcitrant form and inaccessible to organic matter complexation. Prepared by LLNL under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344.

authors: Polcari, Mikyle [1], Gervais, Bailey [2], Fawad, Arshi [3], Garvey, David [4], Arens, Nan Crystal [5]

abstract: The Early Eocene experienced among the warmest temperatures in the Cenozoic, producing tropical and subtropical conditions globally. The Hatchetigbee Formation at Hatchetigbee Bluff, Alabama preserves Venericardia hatcheplata fossils used to reconstruct a mean annual temperature of 27°C. In 2019, fossil leaves were also discovered, which can serve as an additional line of paleoclimate evidence. The Hatchetigbee Bluff flora consists of about 200 specimens of about 20 morphotypes. Morphotypes were described and assigned species based on published descriptions of Eocene flora. Angiosperms dominate the flora, with families including Fabaceae (legumes), Juglandaceae (walnut family), Moraceae (fig family), Celastraceae (bittersweet family), Sapindaceae (soapnut family), Sapotaceae. These are consistent with tropical to subtropical climates. Several species and two families (Juglandaceae and Fabaceae) were shared with the roughly coeval Red Hot Truck Stop locality of Mississippi. The sediment in which leaf fossils were preserved is poorly consolidated and friable, yielding many fragmentary specimens, which complicates leaf physiognomy-based paleoclimate reconstruction. To develop the most accurate reconstruction, we apply three techniques together: the Climate Leaf Analysis Multivariate Program (CLAMP), Leaf Margin Analysis (LMA), and Digital Leaf Physiognomy (DiLP). This analysis provides additional context to temperature estimates based on marine bivalves.

title: Pressure-temperature-time path evidence for low-pressure, high-temperature Acadian metamorphism in the Rye Complex, southeastern New Hampshire
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Autrey, Suzanne [1], Wintsch , Robert P. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Enviornment, Northern Illinois University, Dekalb, IL,
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Science, Wesleyan University, Middletown, CT, USA
abstract:
The Rye Complex is a narrow band of poorly understood, high-grade pelitic metamorphic rocks located in coastal New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. It is in fault contact with low-grade Silurian-Devonian rocks of the Merrimack terrane, so its relationship to other metamorphic terranes is not known. We present a pressure-temperature-time (P-T-t) path to help give context for this terrane among others in northern New England. The metamorphic petrology here is consistent with a low-pressure P-T-t path. Centimeter-scale andalusite porphyroblasts showing undulatory extinction are common in a biotite (Bt) ± sillimanite (Sil) schist matrix. These porphyroblasts also contain rare inclusions of staurolite that do not occur in the schist matrix. Their xenoblastic outlines together with smaller inclusions of biotite porphyroblasts suggest that biotite and andalusite together are reaction products of the reaction: muscovite (Ms) + staurolite (St) = andalusite (And) + Bt + quartz (Qz). Inclusions of quartz grains and biotite porphyroblasts in the large andalusite grains define an earlier S n-1 foliation. The andalusite porphyroblasts, some rotated, are surrounded by a strong foliation, Sn, defined by Ms + Bt + Sil. Relic andalusite grains in some Sn folia are small and lobate and were probably reactants in the sillimanite-producing reaction. Other cm-scale subhedral andalusite grains overgrow Sn rather than being truncated by it, showing that they constitute a second generation of andalusite growth. Later foliations shred and boudin biotite grains in a host of dynamically recrystallized quartz, demonstrating protracted shear strain.

Textures suggest a progression from St → And → Sil → And. Phase equilibria pressure-temperature modeling constrains staurolite to have formed at 525 – 650 °C, andalusite to have formed at 500 – 650 °C at pressures of 0.3 and 0.4 GPa, and sillimanite to have formed at 560 – 670 °C, followed by second-generation andalusite. Monazite petrochronology identifies two distinct populations with dates at 401 ± 2 Ma and 375 ± 2 Ma, consistent with the Acadian orogeny. These mineral assemblages define a clockwise P-T-t path at low pressures that does not resemble other Acadian P-T-t paths in New England. Thus, the Rye Complex is a unique block tectonically emplaced into the Merrimack terrane in post-Devonian times.

title: Only So Many Fish in the Sea: Using ichthyoliths to investigate post-OAE2 Labrador Sea fish community dynamics at IODP Site U1407
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Posters)
authors: Norris, Eun-Jae Miyon [1], Clemente, Jean N.R. [2], Sibert, Elizabeth C. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geophysics, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, Massachusetts, USA; College of the Atlantic, Bar Harbor, ME, USA
(2) MIT-WHOI Joint Program in Oceanography, Woods Hole, Massachusetts, USA; Geology and Geophysics, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, Massachusetts, USA
(3) Geology and Geophysics, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA, USA
abstract:
Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2; ~94 million years ago) was a period of widespread marine anoxia and other climatic disturbances that widely altered marine ecosystems in the Cretaceous, triggered by widespread marine volcanism. While the fossil record indicates that high- and low- trophic level organisms (i.e., marine reptiles and calcareous plankton) were negatively impacted by OAE2, its effects on mid-trophic level organisms such as fish are less known. Aspects of fish community ecology such as population size and morphological diversity can be estimated using microfossils called ichthyoliths that accumulate in seafloor sediments. We extracted ichthyoliths from sediment cores taken at IODP Site U1407 in sediment drifts near the Newfoundland Ridge, paleogeographically in the proto-North Atlantic, and analyzed fish tooth count and morphology.

This study measures ichthyolith concentrations as a method of exploring pelagic fish community dynamics in the period following OAE2. We find that ichthyolith deposition rates dropped during OAE2 and remained low for at least 5 million years following reoxygenation at this location, indicating longer-term suppression of fish populations following the anoxic event. Despite this, tooth morphology did not change appreciably during the interval, suggesting that while abundance remained low, there was some stability in fish community composition in the North Atlantic during and after OAE2. The results of this study shed light on the morphological diversity and population dynamics of fish in a post-OAE2 ocean and indicate that oxygen levels may have long-term impacts on fish abundances. More broadly, long-term paleoecological datasets provide a unique opportunity to investigate practical applications of ecological theory, including potential patterns of ecosystem and community evolution after disturbance.

abstract: This study investigates the spatial distribution and extent of legacy metal contaminants—primarily Lead (Pb), Zinc (Zn), and Iron (Fe)—within the Missouri portion of the Tri-State Mining District (TSMD). Operating from 1848 to 1970 across Missouri, Oklahoma, and Kansas, the district's extensive extraction of Mississippi Valley-type (MVT) deposits hosted in the karstified limestone and chert of the Boone Formation has left a persistent, harmful environmental footprint across the Springfield Plateau. To assess where contamination remains, sediment samples from active and dry streambeds and soil samples from high-activity local parks were collected at depths of up to two inches across areas near and far from historical mining sites. Samples were disaggregated, sieved to the fine fraction, and analyzed using X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) spectrometry—with 20% verified via Inductively Coupled Plasma-Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS)—to generate concentration distribution maps in ArcPro. Preliminary results confirm that legacy metals have mobilized far from historical mining centers through the fractured carbonate landscape, with Pierson Creek yielding peak concentrations of 119 mg/kg Pb, 2,386 mg/kg Zn, and 15,540 mg/kg Fe.

title: The Thermodynamic Data Gap in Critical Mineral Systems: A Challenge for Modern Mineralogy
session_title: Early career investigators in mineralogy and crystallography
authors: Scharrer, Manuel [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA
abstract:
Thermodynamic data provide the quantitative foundation for understanding mineral stability, phase equilibria, and element partitioning. Despite major advances in mineral characterization, crystallography, computational approaches, and experimental techniques, many mineral systems relevant to critical resources remain thermodynamically poorly constrained. This limitation is particularly evident for non-oxide minerals, including sulfides and sulfosalts, as well as rare earth-bearing and hydrated mineral systems. These phases are challenging to characterize thermodynamically due to factors including complex bonding environments, metastability, synthesis difficulties, sensitivity to experimental conditions, and most importantly, the time-intensive nature of obtaining reliable measurements.

Experimental measurements remain essential for developing robust thermodynamic descriptions of complex mineral systems, but individual datasets represent only one component of a complete understanding of phase stability. An example from the Ni-Co-Fe sulfide system will illustrate how new experimental thermodynamic constraints can refine our understanding of mineral stability and highlight the need for integrating experimental data with phase equilibria and thermodynamic modeling approaches to develop comprehensive descriptions of critical mineral systems.

Addressing remaining thermodynamic data gaps for critical mineral phases will require coordinated efforts across mineralogy, experimental petrology, crystallography, computational modeling, and thermodynamic database development. Developing improved thermodynamic frameworks for complex mineral systems will enhance our ability to understand mineral formation, evolution, and element distribution in natural environments.

abstract:
The Hanna Basin in south-central Wyoming is a rapidly subsiding basin in the Cretaceous to Eocene Laramide foreland. After the Western Interior Seaway retreated from this area the emerging basin was occupied with swamps, rivers, inundated floodplains and shallow lakes, leading to the deposition of extensive coalbeds, carbonaceous shales and sandstones with some conglomerates. The upper part of this succession, comprising the Paleogene Hanna Formation, deposited when the uplifts along the basin margin increasingly isolated the drainage system. Rapid sediment accumulation rates yielded a thick, nearly continuous, undisturbed stratigraphic record across the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM, ~56 Ma), a significant global warming event driven by rapid carbon release into the oceans and atmosphere.

Exposures of the PETM were identified using leaf macrofossils, palynological analysis and a negative δ¹³C isotope excursion (CIE). Recently, we added important time control to the stratigraphic framework by identifying the paleomagnetic reversal for 25N to 24R. Via a novel method that uses fossil cuticles preserved in the carbonaceous shales, we also looked at canopy cover changes during the CIE. Two new cores were drilled across the CIE, that will add additional information in the future about fire markers, methane proxies and the hydrologic cycle as results are collected.

Following the onset of the CIE, canopy cover declined swiftly, preceding a shift in depositional environments with the expansion of a basin-wide channelized interval, a significant sedimentary response showing the importance of vegetation on bank stabilization and sedimentation. From the coring we learned that red-mottled paleosols are abundant in the CIE interval. Well-drained soils are rare elsewhere in this swamp-dominated sequence, and indicate significant drying. Once δ¹³C values returned to baseline in the recovery of the CIE, the sedimentary environments reverted to swamps again.

title: Fish and shark community dynamics from microfossils during the late Cenozoic cooling from a North Pacific red clay sediment core
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Alejos, Keila [1], Sibert, Elizabeth C. [2]
affiliations: (1) College of Letters and Science, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA
(2) Geology and Geophysics Department, Woods hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods hole, MA, USA
abstract: Marine communities are increasingly threatened by rapid climate change, with rising ocean temperatures altering fisheries seasonal yields and marine ecosystems. Intensifying coastal weather can significantly impact communities reliant on fish as primary source of nutrition and amplify coastal hazard impacts on established coastal communities. The late Cenozoic marks a period of significant climatic shifts contributing to the transformation of ocean circulation in the Pacific during the transition of cooling and descent into the current icehouse conditions of today. The Pacific is a critical large body of water for transport of global heat, primary production and is one of the largest reservoirs for carbon exchange making it an ideal analog for understanding how fish communities respond to large- scale environment change. This study uses microfossil ichthyoliths - fish teeth and shark denticles, preserved from a 3m deep sea gravity core retrieved from one of the oldest crustal regions of the Western North Pacific plate, to reconstruct fish and shark community dynamics from late Miocene to present. Ichthyoliths size distributions and assemblages were observed to analyze changes in community structure through the cores time scale. The proportion of small teeth increases to the present, suggesting that small-bodied fish increased in relative abundance with the long-term cooling of the late Cenozoic. This is the first high-resolution record of late Cenozoic ichthyoliths from this remote, under-studied region of the Pacific ocean, and provides critical insight into how global change impacted marine communities in the open ocean, and suggests that fish communities were able to adapt to the changing conditions of the icehouse world in the deep pelagic Pacific Ocean.

title: Science for All: Demystifying and Diversifying Research With Accessible Science Communication
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation (Posters)
authors: Friedman, Ella [1], Fino, Danielle [2], Kostel, Kenneth [3], Sibert, Elizabeth C. [4]

abstract: Science plays a crucial role in building an informed society, and yet it is greatly diminished without the use of strategic science communication. Research outcomes mean little in public perception when audiences are alienated by inaccessible communication techniques. The issue holds especially true in our relatively novel digital environments that are inundated with a constant flow of new information. While digital formats are incredibly valuable, their use for science communication often excludes much of the population whose disabilities limit their capacity to access digital materials. Disabled people constitute the largest minority group in the United States, encompassing more than 25% of adult Americans. Including the disabled population in science through universal design, such as captions, multimodal delivery, etc., in turn benefits both those within the disability community and millions of others who extend beyond it. Accessible science communication therefore serves as a vital tactic not only to create clarity amid the threat of information overload but also to diversify the audiences who engage with science. Here we develop a portfolio of digital geoscience communication projects focused on disability access to expand the audiences traditionally reached by STEM, along with sharing lessons learned and guidelines developed in the process. Jargon-free, multilingual articles provide more accessible means of receiving information and participating in the scientific process. Social media content similarly reaches wider audiences with alternative text, image descriptions, and colorblind-friendly palettes. This work highlights the importance of accessibility in the modern age for proper inclusion and transparency between researchers and public audiences.

title: Insights from Mapping Europa’s Geology with JunoCam
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Sacks, Leah E [1], Leonard, Erin J [2], Phillips, Cynthia B [3], Lesage, Elodie [4]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(2) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA

abstract:
As the Europa Clipper spacecraft continues its journey to Jupiter, it is critical to continue working to identify the most meaningful measurements and images to collect during the upcoming prime mission. These efforts rely on an up to date and detailed understanding of Europa, including its surface and geology. Most of our modern knowledge of the moon, including the global geologic map of Europa, is based on data from the Galileo mission, which visited the moon between 1996-2000. However, 4 more recent images from the JunoCam instrument on the Juno mission, which encountered the moon in 2022, provide the newest look at the surface. These four visible light (red, green, and blue filter) images show largely the same slice of Europa’s surface, with resolutions between 1 and 4 km/pixel. We have termed this area of the moon’s surface the “JunoCam Region.” In this presentation, we showcase our ongoing geologic mapping of the JunoCam images, at the regional level. This detailed work gives insight into areas mapped at lower resolutions previously, with the Galileo images of Europa, and supplements our understanding of surface processes at Europa.

The JunoCam dataset has already provided two new pieces of information. Directly, there are coverage gaps in the high-resolution images from Galileo in this region. At ~ 15°E, 25°N, there is an area that was never imaged at better than 7.4 km/pixel by Galileo. JunoCam images fill this gap at ~ 1 km/pixel. Additionally, a feature thought to be a crater has been shown to be an intersection of several sets of ridges in the JunoCam data (Hansen et al, 2024). As we began detailed mapping, we observed several differences between the current map and the geologic map of Europa, as they are done at different mapping scales. However, the discrepancies provide understanding into aspects of the surface geology that are absent in the wider map and are found instead in regional mapping. The JunoCam images have distinctly different lighting geometries than the Galileo images, highlighting specific surface morphologies. We specifically note features, including pit and arcuate depression features, that are more easily observed in the JunoCam data. We will also use our mapping to add to the understanding of the complex sequence of events on Europa’s surface.

title: Skeletal Abundance and Diversity through the Middle Ordovician in Nevada’s Antelope Valley Limestone

abstract: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE) has been heavily studied, but there is limited data on the expansion of skeletal biomass throughout the Darriwilian, particularly in the southwestern United States. To better understand this aspect of the GOBE in offshore settings on the northwest margin of Laurentia, ~376 meters of the Middle Ordovician Antelope Valley Limestone at Meiklejohn Peak near Beatty, NV were logged and sampled. The total section was sampled in three parts: 29 thin sections from ~89 meters of the Antelope Valley Limestone Lower and Middle Members, 55 thin sections from ~233 meters of the Middle and Upper Members, and 21 thin sections from the uppermost ~54 meters of the Upper Member. The Lower Member consisted mostly of mudstone and wackestone, the Middle Member wackestone and packstone, and the Upper Member mudstone, packstone, and wackestone. Point count analysis provided quantitative data on rock composition, skeletal biomass, and biodiversity in the Antelope Valley Limestone, and presence/absence of fossil grains was noted for each thin section. Overall, 8% of all points counted were skeletal, with skeletal grains making up 11% of the Lower Member, 10% of the Middle Member, and 7% of the Upper Member, with the percent of skeletal material making up each thin section ranging from 2–32%, 0-32%, and 0-25% in the Lower, Middle, and Upper Members respectively. Although the Upper Member had lower skeletal abundance overall, it increased to 10% in the final ~10 meters below the contact with the Eureka Quartzite. Skeletal biomass varied throughout the stratigraphy, potentially due to environmental shifts such as shallowing and deepening in the offshore setting recorded by this succession. This work demonstrates that local environments may be a dominant control on skeletal biomass through the GOBE, and further work on this section will enable us to connect these results to data from coeval successions across the western United States and globally.

title: Ready 2 Rock: Preparing Undergraduate Geoscience Students for Professional Conferences, Networking, and Career Pathways

abstract:
Attending a national geoscience conference for the first time can be an overwhelming experience, yet early exposure to professional meetings offers transformative opportunities for undergraduate students. Presenting at a professional geoscience conference allows undergraduates to develop scientific identity, build professional networks, and explore graduate school and career pathways. Ready 2 Rock is an independently designed workshop series created to prepare undergraduate researchers for a successful and meaningful experience at their first professional conference.

The program targets undergraduates engaged in research who are entering their final year and considering graduate school or entering the workforce. Beginning in January, approximately eight undergraduate students began participating in monthly workshops hosted through the academic year and continuing through the fall to the conference. Each workshop is co-facilitated by the program coordinator and a departmental faculty member with relevant expertise. Topics progress through the full arc of conference preparation: an introduction to professional geoscience conferences and their value, research design and problem statement development, scientific writing and abstract composition, poster layout and design tools, professional networking strategies, and a low-stakes poster practice session within the department.

The program is supported through departmental funding for travel and lodging, supplemented by external funding opportunities that students are encouraged to pursue. The proximity of the 2026 GSA annual meeting to our institution provides a timely opportunity to expand undergraduate participation while minimizing costs.

Ready 2 Rock was motivated by the program coordinator's own transformative experience attending GSA as an undergraduate, an experience that shaped professional identity and facilitated lasting connections. This program aims to demystify the conference environment, build transferable professional skills, and ensure that first-time attendees arrive prepared and confident. Insights from the in-progress Ready 2 Rock model will be shared to support others interested in adapting this approach for their own departmental contexts.

abstract: Transpression along strike-slip faults produces high topography and influences fault geometry. The Cenozoic Denali fault, the longest strike-slip fault in North America, is exceedingly narrow along much of its length (<500 m), despite preserving >450 km of net dextral separation. To distinguish fault-localized from regional exhumation, we applied thermochronology to fault-perpendicular transects across plutonic piercing points. Because these plutons share a common origin, divergence in their cooling histories is attributable to fault-related processes rather than inherited differences in crustal level or magmatic history. We acquired 41 new 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronologic ages on hornblende, biotite, and feldspar along transects within 20 km of the fault. The Foraker (South) and Schist Creek (North) plutons were emplaced along the active Denali fault around 36-38 Ma. Previous work demonstrates similar age, geochemical, and isotopic characteristics between the two plutons, establishing them as piercing points offset by ~155 km, thus providing a common starting point for diverging thermal and exhumation histories. Hornblende 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages overlap with zircon U-Pb ages. South of the fault (Foraker), biotite ages are constant at ~35 Ma at 10-20 km from the fault, whereas to the north (Schist Creek), they are 35-37 Ma and young only within 3 km of the fault. Integrated feldspar 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages are more sensitive to position relative to the fault. Feldspar ages on the south side are ~30 Ma far from the fault and young to <25 Ma within 10 km of the fault. On the north side, feldspar ages are within uncertainty of the intrusion age 20 km from the fault, and young monotonically to ~20 Ma within 1 km of the fault, with a steep gradient <5 km. Younging of biotite/feldspar ages towards the fault indicates elevated temperatures being sustained by exhumation focused on the fault. Thermal modeling shows rapid cooling from crystallization temperatures to ~350 °C in <2 Myr for all samples, near and far from the fault. The 350-200 °C cooling occurred in 1-5 Myr >10 km from the fault, but up to 15 Ma within 5 km, which we attribute to fault-focused exhumation at 30-20 Ma. We conclude that the highly localized nature of the Denali fault results from persistent exhumation directly along the fault, impeding fault broadening or secondary network development.

abstract:
In the Late Cretaceous, the globe was relatively warm and there was a shallow temperature gradient of ~0.3-0.4 ℃/°latitude, compared to ~1.0 ℃/°latitude today. This greenhouse interval was marked by high sea level, creating epicontinental seaways on every major landmass. One such Cretaceous continental seaway was the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) of North America, which connected the Arctic Ocean to the proto-Gulf of Mexico. Within the WIS, cool polar waters mixed with warm southern waters and created a steep temperature gradient within the basin. However, the steepness of the gradient on land is debated, ranging across data sets from 0.6 to 1.5 ℃/°latitude.

Using Digital Leaf Physiognomy (DiLP), we reconstruct mean annual temperature and rainfall from five sites across three formations within the Western Interior Basin (WIB) – the Almond, Neslen, and Kaiparowits formations – filling a gap in terrestrial temperature reconstruction spanning 47.3-50.9° paleolatitude.

The Almond Formation crops out in southwestern Wyoming (50.9° paleolatitude) and was deposited as the WIS receded during the Late Cretaceous. We describe a new collection of ~300 leaves represented by 32 morphotypes. We interpret the depositional environment to be estuarine based on the presence of poorly bedded fine sediment, storm deposits, and Teredolites . Previous paleobotanical collections from the Almond Formation were fern and gymnosperm dominated, whereas this site is angiosperm dominated.

The Neslen Formation crops out in eastern Utah in the Book Cliffs (49.4° paleolatitude). These rocks preserve fluvial and nearshore environments from ~75 million years ago. We describe and apply DiLP to two new angiosperm dominated sites, each preserving 150-200 leaves.

The Kaiparowits Formation in Southern Utah (47.4° paleolatitude) preserves well-studied fluvial strata from the middle Campanian. Fossil plants from two sites, Lost Valley and Caveat Friendship, were previously described. Those sites are diverse and dominated by woody dicots with ~45 morphotypes each, which make them good candidates for DiLP.

Preliminary results from DiLP indicate that these sites are warm with very little variation in mean annual temperature. Between these three formations, the temperature gradient is similar to average global values.

abstract: Silicic magma reservoirs are increasingly interpreted as long-lived crystal-mush systems, yet the relationships among magma flux, magma storage, and eruption in ocean-island settings remain poorly constrained. We use zircon U–Th geochronology, analyzed on unpolished surfaces by SHRIMP-RG, from four trachytic pumice falls: Ribeira Chã (8-12 ka), Pisão (4.76 ka), Fogo ‘A’ (4.6 ka), and Fogo ‘B’ (3.24 ka) of the Água de Pau volcanic system (São Miguel, Azores), and from four syenite xenoliths within the Fogo ‘A’ pumice fall to investigate the timescales and processes of silicic magma storage and rejuvenation and to determine magma flux rates. Zircon crystallization ages range from 26.1±6 ka to 259±96 ka for the pumices and 10.6±4 ka to 145±26.5 ka for the syenite xenoliths. All zircon crystallization ages substantially predate the eruption ages, suggesting prolonged magma residence within a thermally active magmatic system. Broad zircon age spectra, antecrystic populations, and distinct crystallization histories among eruptive units record repeated rejuvenation and recycling within a heterogeneous crystal-mush reservoir. Zircon saturation temperatures and Ti-in-zircon temperature constrained magma-flux modeling, reproduces the observed zircon age distributions with two contrasting storage regimes: a lower-flux regime associated with the large-volume Plinian Ribeira Chã and Fogo ‘A’ eruptions (1.0x10 -5 km 3 /yr and 2.6x10 -5 km 3 /yr, respectively) and a higher-flux regime associated with smaller sub-Plinian Fogo ‘B’ and Pisão pumice falls (1.08x10 -3 km 3 /yr and 6x10 -4 km 3 /yr, respectively). Syenite xenoliths represent long-lived, low-flux (1.12-3.63x10 -5 km 3 /yr, n=3) crystal-rich domains that remained thermally active for extended periods before entrainment. The association of the Plinian eruptions (Ribeira Chã, Fogo "A") with lower modeled magma fluxes indicates that eruption magnitude tracks the duration of mush maturation rather than the rate of magma recharge. The sustained low-flux conditions allow cryptic recharge, supplying heat and volatiles rather than large melt volumes to progressively remobilize crystal-mush domains over tens of thousands of years, accumulating eruptible melt within a compositionally heterogeneous, vertically extensive mush system. Higher-flux regimes (Pisão, Fogo ‘B’) reflect shorter maturation windows resulting in smaller eruptive volumes. These results demonstrate that magma flux exerts a fundamental control on zircon crystallization histories, reservoir evolution, and eruptibility, and establish Água de Pau as an important example of long-lived silicic magma storage in an ocean-island volcanic system.

abstract:
In 1937 Barnum Brown collected the first vertebrate fossils from the Upper Cretaceous Almond Formation of southwestern Wyoming. Renewed exploration has since yielded numerous vertebrate localities that fill an important temporal and geographic gap between the better-known Campanian-Maastrichtian faunas of northern and southern Laramidia. Here we present the first detailed assessment of taxonomic diversity at “Turtle Hill,” a new vertebrate microfossil site in the Almond Formation. The assemblage is preserved in coastal plain facies deposited near the shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway.

More than 1,500 vertebrate fossils have been recovered through surface collection and excavation. These methods yielded a fauna dominated by fish, with rare semiaquatic and terrestrial vertebrates, including turtles (e.g., Basilemys , Adocus ), crocodiles (cf. Brachychampsa ), mammals, and dinosaurs. As part of a preliminary Keck Geology Consortium project, we processed bulk samples for the first time at Turtle Hill, recovering more than 5,000 vertebrate bioclasts, many identifiable to major vertebrate groups. Preliminary data indicate that the sieved assemblage is dominated by osteichthyans (92%), with chondrichthyans (7%) and rare amphibians, squamates, turtles, crocodylians, and mammals (~1%). Multituberculate, therian, and eutherian mammals are represented by teeth. Other identifiable taxa include Coriops , Lepisosteus , Melvius , Myledaphus , Paralbula , Restesia , and Texatrygon .

Bulk sampling reveals greater taxonomic diversity than traditional collection alone, particularly among small-bodied taxa. For example, amphibians and squamates are largely absent in the excavated sample, but more abundant in the bulk sample. Likewise, minute teeth of at least three distinctive sharks, including two orectolobids ( Restesia and cf. Cantioscyllium ) and the sclerorhynchiform, Texatrygon , are abundant in the sieved sample but absent in the excavated sample. Comparisons with well-known Campanian Judith River Formation vertebrate microfossil bonebeds from Montana indicate that Turtle Hill contains fewer terrestrial taxa, and a greater abundance of salt-tolerant taxa. These results demonstrate that bulk sampling substantially expands estimates of vertebrate diversity in the Almond Formation and provides a framework for comparing coastal vertebrate communities and ecosystem change along the paralic margins of the Western Interior Seaway in the Late Cretaceous.

title: A Comparison of Chemical, Physical, and Isotopic Baseflow Separation Methods to Investigate Groundwater and Surface Water Interactions in the Chippewa River (WI)
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Draves, Wyatt Matthew [1], Schneider, Cyd Jayne [2], Meyers, Zachary P [3]

abstract:
Streams and rivers integrate water from multiple sources that possess distinct geochemical and isotopic signatures. Characterizing these endmembers is essential for baseflow separation. A better understanding of groundwater-surface water interactions improves our ability to evaluate contaminant transport and safeguard aquatic ecosystem health in Midwestern river systems. This study investigates the Chippewa River, which drains the second largest watershed in Wisconsin. The downstream portion of the Chippewa River supports a greater number of rare species and more native prairie than any area of comparable size in Wisconsin. Despite the regional importance of the Chippewa River, studies of source contributions to streamflow are sparse. In this study we conducted temporal hydrological sampling following snowmelt (i.e., late spring) through the variable summer season to capture a broad range of hydrologic conditions, including periods of low discharge dominated by baseflow and high-flow episodes driven by storm events. Sampling locations included the Chippewa River near Eau Claire (WI), a small tributary, a hillslope seep, a nearby spring, and several wells to represent potential streamflow endmembers. We utilized a multi-tracer approach combining field geochemistry (e.g., specific conductance, pH) with laboratory measurements of chloride, bromide, nitrate, water stable isotopes, and Radon-222. Streamflow records were retrieved from local USGS gauging stations on the Chippewa River.

Preliminary results from the Chippewa River reveal an inverse exponential relationship between Radon-222 concentration and stream discharge. Spatial and temporal patterns of nitrate and chloride among endmembers provide insight into watershed-wide anthropogenic influences on water quality. Future analyses of water stable isotopes will provide an additional constraint on streamflow endmember contributions. Pending work will compare temporal baseflow contributions derived from water stable isotopes, Radon-222, and specific conductance with results derived from stream hydrograph baseflow separation methods. Together, these findings will advance understanding of local watershed hydrology and provide valuable information for water resource management.

abstract: Tetrafluoroboric (HBF 4 ) acid is a versatile, non-oxidizing, acidic reagent that has been used as an alternative to hydrofluoric acid (HF) digestion to achieve leaching of trace elements and rare earth elements from siliceous samples without complete dissolution of silicates. Although HBF 4 digestions lead to partial dissolution of silicates, the merits for determination of trace amounts of silicon in biological samples, such as plants and tissues, have not been investigated. In this work, the suitability of HBF 4 for determination of silicon and trace elements was investigated as a method for analyzing plant and tissue samples by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). First, silicon volatility was examined by heating solutions containing 100 µg/mL silicon to dryness at 120 ℃. Silicon loss was substantial, indicating evaporation of HBF 4 digests was not feasible to eliminate HBF 4 from analysis solutions. However, dilute solutions of HBF 4 were found to be benign with quartz sample introduction components when nitric acid (HNO 3 ) blanks containing up to 10% HBF 4 were aspirated through sample introduction setup made up of a perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) spray chamber, Teflon nebulizer and sapphire or quartz injector. Silicon background signals from the PFA-quartz setup were not significantly different than that from the PFA-sapphire setup. This result indicated that digests of HBF 4 could be directly analyzed without experiencing any deleterious effects on silicon results. Considering this information, samples of several silicate-containing soil, plant and tissue certified standard reference materials (SRM) were digested using a microwave-assisted digestion scheme utilizing HNO 3 , HCl and HBF 4 and analyzed by ICP-OES and ICP-MS. The results indicated that leaching of silicon from the SRMs was incomplete (around 50%), even for plant and tissue SRMs. Leaching was successful for several trace and major elements, including Ba, Ca, Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, K, Mg, Mn, Mo, Ni, Pb, Sr, V and Zn. Arsenic (As) results from soil digests were accurate, but determination was adversely affected from plant and tissue samples due to high As blanks. The results imply that HNO 3 -HCl-HBF 4 digestion offers stronger leaching potential than HNO 3 -HCl, but care must be taken to avoid reagent contamination from trace element impurities in commercially available HBF 4 solutions.

title: Excess Water Precludes The Generation of Mineralized Granitic Pegmatites
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics
authors: Fonseca Teixeira, Ludmila Maria [1], Bachmann, Olivier [2], Ackerson, Michael Robert [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA

abstract:
Granitic pegmatites are key hosts of many critical elements in the upper crust (e.g. Li, REE, Nb, and others). Traditionally, pegmatites are viewed as a “residual-melt”, formed after prolonged crystallization of granitic magma and that, due to fractionation, inherit high concentrations of incompatible elements, as well as water and other volatiles. Nevertheless, fewer than 2% of pegmatites are rich in such elements.

We propose that pegmatite fertility is controlled partly by the timing of volatile exsolution and segregation from the parental magma. Thermodynamic constraints indicate that silicic melts containing >6–8 wt.% H₂O at the liquidus can reach water saturation while still relatively hot and poorly fractionated. Separation at this stage produces “early pegmatites” whose compositions remain close to those of their granitic sources and are consequently depleted in economically important rare elements.

We illustrate this concept through an analysis of granites and pegmatites from the Bergell intrusion (Switzerland), an I-type granite that hosts several barren pegmatites. Quartz, apatite, and zircon reveal overlapping crystallization histories for the granite and its barren pegmatites, including significant crystallization near and below the water-saturated haplogranite solidus. Our data supports the idea that cold and water-rich I-type magmas may produce barren pegmatites through early segregation, whereas the comparatively drier magmas associated with S- and A-type granites can undergo greater fractionation before pegmatite formation and may therefore have higher mineralization potential.

abstract: Alkaline magmatism of the Eastern Mexican Alkaline Province (EMAP) extends from the Gulf of Mexico to the Mexico–U.S. border. Despite its regional extent, the rare-metal endowment of its northernmost sector remains largely unexplored. Here, we describe the mineralogical and petrogenetic evolution of alkaline complexes exposed in the Sierra Maderas del Carmen region, focusing on syenites enriched in eudialyte-group minerals (EGM), which represent the most prospective lithologies for Zr-Nb-REE mineralization. The magmatic succession records progressive differentiation from alkali gabbros and intermediate intrusions to both silica-saturated and silica-undersaturated syenites. Geochemical signatures indicate derivation from enriched, OIB-like mantle magmas emplaced in an intracontinental tectonic environment. The EGM-bearing syenites form narrow dikes, sills, and small intrusions and are locally surrounded by calc-silicate skarn aureoles. Five syenite varieties were distinguished, encompassing fine-grained agpaitic and transitional-agpaitic assemblages composed mainly of EGM, aegirine-augite, alkali feldspar, and sodalite, locally accompanied by analcime. The most strongly mineralized varieties record early crystallization of EGM, alkali feldspar, and aegirine-augite, followed by late albite-calcite-gittinsite assemblages. This crystallization sequence reflects advanced magmatic differentiation under relatively dry and reducing conditions. Continued differentiation increased melt peralkalinity and enhanced the partitioning of Zr, Nb, REE, Th, and Ti into late-magmatic and magmatic-hydrothermal mineral assemblages. Scanning electron microscopy identified a diverse rare-metal mineral association that includes eudialyte, britholite-(Ce), thorite, pyrochlore, ancylite-(Ce), gittinsite, and baddeleyite. These minerals occur within both the syenitic intrusions and the spatially associated skarns. At the regional scale, the inferred emplacement interval of approximately 48–28 Ma overlaps with slab detachment beneath northeastern Mexico, suggesting a genetic connection between intraplate alkaline magmatism and the development of rare-metal-fertile magmatic systems. These results highlight the northern EMAP as an underexplored province for agpaitic-related Zr-Nb-REE mineralization in the North American Cordillera.

abstract: This study addresses seasonal heavy metal dynamics and contamination sources in lakes and ponds across the Missouri River floodplain in the Midwestern United States, utilizing an integrated suite of statistical and geospatial approaches. Sampling campaigns conducted in Summer 2024, Fall 2025, and Spring 2026 provided water chemistry data covering twelve trace elements and key physicochemical characteristics (pH, temperature, electrical conductivity, and total dissolved solids). Results highlight persistent exceedances of benchmark concentrations for cobalt, manganese, aluminum, sulfur, lead, and cadmium, with mean Heavy Metal Pollution Index (HPI) values (181.26) signaling widespread water quality impairment. Pollution levels and source patterns were quantified using U.S. EPA exceedance ratios, contamination factors, and HPI calculations, while multivariate methods including Spearman correlation, principal component analysis, hierarchical and K-means clustering, PAM, Gaussian mixture modeling, and geospatial mapping revealed clear lithogenic and anthropogenic input gradients. The analysis consistently pinpointed Lake Manawa as the region's primary contamination hotspot and identified Steinhart Park pond as chemically unique and high-risk. By synthesizing pollution indices, regulatory exceedance, contamination frequency, and spatial clustering, the research introduces a novel environmental risk profiling strategy that streamlines hotspot detection and management prioritization. The framework delivers practical insights for adaptive water resource oversight and serves as a transferable model for freshwater systems confronting intensifying human and climatic pressures.

abstract: Understanding climate and ocean history in deep time often requires hundreds or thousands of individual foraminiferal specimens to be identified and picked for geochemical analyses. This manual processing is time-consuming and requires significant training in micropaleontology. We present a prototype that performs automated foraminifera sorting, identification, and picking. The goal is to achieve faster sample processing without sacrificing the precision that later imaging and analysis demand. The system has two main components: a deep-learning framework that quantifies the uncertainty of microfossil classification, and a robotic system that images, positions, and picks up the targeted species. Three deep-learning models, Monte Carlo Dropout, a Bayesian Convolutional Neural Network, and Deep Kernel Learning, are trained on the Endless Forams dataset of modern planktonic foraminifera. Unlike standard deep-learning models, which produce a single confidence score per label per sample, our models produce a range of confidence scores per label per sample. This allows the system to quantify its own uncertainty, which significantly reduces false-positive and false-negative classifications. Robust decisions from the model ensemble allow the robot to pick target species with high accuracy. The robotic system coordinates the deep-learning models, imaging, positioning, and pickup process together. The camera automatically adjusts focus to keep each specimen sharp even when lighting across the sample tray is uneven, and a calibration step maps what the camera sees to real-world coordinates the robot can move to, correcting for any distortion or misalignment between the camera and the stage. Images of the tray are scanned and sent to the deep-learning models for classification. Once target species are identified, the robot positions itself with an accuracy of approximately 20 micrometers to pick up the specimens and sort them into collection vials. Though still at an early stage, this system has the potential to ease a major rate-limiting step in paleoclimate reconstruction.

abstract: Flocculent organic sediments (floc) commonly located at groundwater-surface water interfaces represent an often overlooked but potentially important component of shallow freshwater ecosystems. Floc forms a porous, organic-rich layer at the sediment–water interface where hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological processes converge in low-energy environments, such as wetlands, lakes, rivers, and floodplains. Yet, despite decades of sporadic study across multiple disciplines, floc remains inconsistently defined and poorly integrated into freshwater science. Here, we synthesize the literature on floc across freshwater ecosystems to evaluate its formation, physical and biogeochemical properties, ecological functions, and spatiotemporal variability. The reviewed studies show that floc develops through coupled physical, chemical, and biological processes and has characteristics that distinguish it from both suspended particulate matter and consolidated sediments. Floc is also found broadly around the world and has low density, high porosity, high surface area, mixed organic-mineral composition, and high microbial reactivity. These traits position floc as a potentially important site of many ecosystem functions (e.g., nutrient transformation, carbon processing, contaminant retention, and greenhouse gas production) like better documented groundwater-surface water environments (e.g., hyporheic and riparian zones). However, progress towards scalable or transferable understanding of floc has been limited by fragmented terminology and definitions, ecosystem-specific research traditions, and inconsistent methods of sampling and characterization. We conclude that there are three key research needs to reveal the roles of floc: 1. Recognize that floc should be treated not merely as a sedimentary feature, but is a reactive ecological interface and potential ecosystem control point in shallow freshwaters; 2. Establish a minimum set of quantifiable criteria to be included in the definition of floc; and 3. Establish an integrated research framework that links structure, composition, and function of floc across different types of freshwater ecosystems. To start addressing these needs and opportunities, we provide a set of quantitative criteria for defining floc and an interdisciplinary research framework. It is time to establish an understanding of the formation and function of floc, so we can determine if it is an overlooked component of freshwater ecosystems and their groundwater-surface water interactions.

title: Submarine Faults Strongly Impact Age and Salinity Distributions in Offshore Freshened Groundwater Systems
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Zhang, Yi-Peng [1], Kurylyk, Barret [2], Paldor, Anner [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN,
(2) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering, Centre for Water Resources Studies, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS,
(3) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN,
abstract: Coastal aquifers provide a vital connection between land and ocean, where groundwater flow and solute transport are influenced by the interacting effects of hydrogeological, morphological, climatic, and marine forcings in an era of sea-level rise. Previous studies of coastal and subsea aquifers have generally focused on continuous geological structures, overlooking submarine faults and other geological discontinuities. However, faults likely play a significant role in controlling groundwater flow and the distributions of salinity and groundwater age in many systems. We investigate the understudied influence of submarine faults by simulating a generalized coastal aquifer–aquitard system containing faults. Importantly, we consider realistic sea-level rise over paleohydrogeological timescales rather than adopting steady-state assumptions. Our results show that faults reduce the extent of offshore freshened groundwater (OFG), regardless of their location. Faults proximal to the coastline serve as pathways for freshwater discharge, whereas those located farther offshore act as conduits for seawater intrusion. Counterintuitively, both mechanisms reduce the extent of OFG. Fault-induced groundwater discharge creates upward freshwater plumes containing older groundwater in the upper unconfined aquifer, thereby indirectly controlling the age and potentially the chemistry of submarine groundwater discharge. In addition to fault location, fault orientation influences the distribution of OFG, groundwater fluxes to the ocean, and the salinity and age of groundwater discharge. These findings suggest that special attention should be paid to submarine faults, which can strongly influence offshore freshwater resources and biogeochemical reactions in coastal and marine environments.

title: From the Cradle to the Grave: Larval Development and Extinction in Conoidean Neogastropods from the Plio-Pleistocene of Florida
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: Wright, Nathan L [1], Hendricks, Jonathan R [2]
affiliations: (1) Milwaukee Public Museum, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA
(2) Milwaukee Public Museum, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA
abstract:
Larval development mode is a fundamental functional trait in marine invertebrates which has important implications for dispersal ability and sensitivities to a variety of biotic and abiotic pressures. Among marine gastropods, a species’ larval mode can often be categorized into two distinct types: Planktotrophic larvae, which feed in the plankton for extended periods before settling, and lecithotrophic larvae, which are typically non-feeding and have a shorter larval period. These larval modes can often be distinguished in fossil taxa through measurements of the size and number of whorls of the larval shell (protoconch).

Conoidea is a hyperdiverse superfamily of predatory marine gastropods, comprising the cone snails (Conidae), auger shells (Terebridae), and the turrids (17 families). Among Conoidea, the turrids are notoriously taxonomically challenging and fossil turrids are understudied. Fossil turrids are identified to the species level less than other neogastropods, and fossil turrid data often contain errors or outdated assignments at the family level.

In this study, we described the diversity and larval morphology of conoidean gastropods sampled from the Early Pleistocene Caloosahatchee and Plio-Pleistocene Nashua formations of Florida. We captured new images of more than 100 conoidean type specimens and used them to identify or confirm identifies of more than 40 species of conoidean gastropods from our study samples. We captured detailed protoconch morphology data from well-preserved specimens and used these data to characterize larval shell features and developmental mode for many of these species for the first time.

A significant turnover event occurred in the Plio-Pleistocene of the US Atlantic Coastal Plain, recognized by considerably elevated extinction and origination rates among mollusks. Among the conoidean species identified in our samples, we compared protoconch characteristics and larval development mode with extinction metrics derived from a large dataset comprising the molluscan collections of the Florida Museum of Natural History and modern OBIS data. At the family level, we find that planktotrophic larval modes are significantly correlated with increased average species duration across the Plio-Pleistocene of the Southeastern US among turrid families, but not among Conoidea as a whole.

authors: Moore, Kelsey R [1], Helms, Lucy [2], Khan, Sabrina [3], Sanders, Cecilia Brooke [4], Talgatbek, Aibolat [5], Mustapayeva, Sezim [6], Mamanov, Yerkhozha [7], Smith, Emily Frances [8]
