abstract: Hydrothermal environments are important targets for studies surrounding the early evolution of life on Earth because they are nutrient rich environments with extreme and dynamic chemical and physical conditions. As a result of these environmental factors, hydrothermal environments often host diverse microbial and eukaryotic ecosystems. Although they are widely recognized as potential cradles for early life, there are few documented examples of Proterozoic hydrothermal deposits. Here, we expand the record of fossiliferous hydrothermal deposits to include the Tonian Chichkan Formation of southern Kazakhstan. The Chichkan Formation is a richly fossiliferous deposit that is extensively silicified. We combine outcrop-scale, petrographic, and geochemical analyses of the four silica-rich facies in the Chichkan Formation to constrain the mechanisms and relative timing of silica deposition and characterize the depositional environment of the Chichkan basin. Based on the petrographic fabrics and relationships, we interpret the majority of silica in the Chichkan Formation as two early generations of silica – primary and early diagenetic. These abundant early generations of silica suggest that the Chichkan Formation was deposited in a restricted basin in which both the basinal and shallow pore fluids contained elevated concentrations of silica. These early generations of silica preserve a suite of redox sensitive accessory minerals that indicate that the basinal and shallow pore fluids were characterized by steep redox and pH gradients, features consistent with hydrothermally influenced environments. Together, these petrographic and geochemical results and the facies relationships are most consistent with deposition in a restricted hot spring environment. Based on this reinterpretation, we place the Chichkan Formation fossil assemblage within this environmental context. These findings expand the known habitat range of Proterozoic ecosystems to include hydrothermal environments. Importantly, the fossil assemblage and its environmental context together provide direct evidence for a Proterozoic ecosystem adapted to the extreme and dynamic chemical and physical conditions of a hydrothermal system.

title: Investigating the Mappability of the Red Pine Shale in the Uinta Mountains, Utah.
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: Patton, Harrison [1], Dehler, Carol M. [2], Reeher, Lauren [3], Eggert, Victoria [4], Anderson, Zach [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA; Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(2) Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(3) Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA; Department of Geology & Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(4) Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, USA; Utah Geological Survey, Utah, USA
(5) Utah Geological Survey, Utah, USA
abstract:
The Uinta Mountain Group (UMG) is an upper-Tonian succession of sandstone, conglomerate, siltstone, and shale covering an area greater than 500 km2 in northeastern Utah. The UMG was deposited into an active rift basin during the incipient breakup of the supercontinent Rodinia (<766-729 Ma). During subsequent Laramide shortening (~90-40 Ma), the preexisting basement shear zones of the Cheyenne Suture Zone that once accommodated subsidence and deposition were reactivated as thick-skinned reverse faults, uplifting the Uinta Mountains and exposing the UMG at the surface. Subdividing the stratigraphy of the UMG into appropriate and mappable formations has proven exceptionally difficult for three key reasons: 1) complex basin dynamics created a varied sedimentological record of interfingering fluvial, deltaic, and marine deposition, making the identification of coherent and correlatable stratigraphic units across the range challenging, 2) the entirety of the UMG is remarkably thick, upwards of seven kilometers, making measuring and categorizing this volume of rock an immense task, and 3) widespread Tertiary and Quaternary cover units obscure exposure and limit windows into the bedrock of the already remote and physically demanding Uinta Mountain wilderness.

As the Utah Geological Survey (UGS) prepares for 1:24,000 and 1:62,500 scale geologic mapping throughout the range, questions on how best to represent the UMG on geologic maps must be addressed. Previous studies have made progress on subdividing and formalizing formations within discrete geographic areas, but difficulties arise in the correlation of these units across the entire range. We investigate the ability to laterally correlate and map the uppermost formation of the UMG, the Red Pine Shale (RPS), representing less than ~20% of the total stratal thickness of the UMG. We characterized and assembled five sections of the uppermost UMG that span most of the length of the UMG outcrops (~110 km). Within these sections we observe dramatic facies changes along strike, an undulating and erosional upper contact with Paleozoic rocks, and a gradational and sometimes enigmatic lower boundary. These relationships are complex and, compounded with the access and exposure limitations, suggest range-wide correlation and definition of the RPS may warrant reevaluation before further mapping proceeds. These observations and challenges are corroborated by previous studies in stratigraphically lower parts of the UMG.

title: 1:62,500 scale geologic map of the Northern Snake Range metamorphic core complex, Nevada
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee (Posters)
authors: Lee, Jeff [1]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
abstract: Exceptional exposures and a well-known stratigraphic framework make the late Eocene to middle Miocene northern Snake Range an archetypal metamorphic core complex (Mcc). This 1:62,500 scale geologic map of the entire (~1563 km 2 ) northern Snake Range Mcc is a compilation of 10.5 published 1:24,000 scale 7.5’ quadrangle geologic maps. The principal structure in the range is the low-angle top-to-the-SE normal slip décollement, the northern Snake Range décollement (NSRD), that juxtaposes a lower plate of metamorphosed and ductilely thinned and stretched Neoproterozoic to Ordovician metaclastic, marble, and calc-schist rocks intruded by Mesozoic and Cenozoic plutons and dikes beneath an upper plate of normal faulted weakly metamorphosed to unmetamorphosed Middle Cambrian to Permian miogeoclinal rocks unconformably overlain by unmetamorphosed Tertiary sedimentary and volcanic rocks. Across the range, the NSRD defines an NNW-trending asymmetric dome with ~1600 m of relief. Exposures of ductilely thinned and horizontally stretched metamorphosed Neoproterozoic to Ordovician strata in the lower plate possess a mylonitic foliation and stretching lineation which record WNW-ESE ductile extension and vertical thinning. Ductile extensional deformation in these strata record a strain increase across the range from the west, where strata have been thinned to ~40% of their original stratigraphic thickness, to the east, where strata have been thinned to as little as ~5% of their original stratigraphic thickness and extended horizontally as much as ~2400%. In the northwestern part of the range, the ductile extensional strain dies out in the lower plate and older, Late Cretaceous foliations, intersection lineations, isoclinal recumbent folds, and minor thrust faults are exposed. In the upper plate, at least two-generations of normal faults, that record primarily WNW-ESE extension, cut Middle Cambrian to Permian miogeoclinal rocks, and unconformably overlying Tertiary sedimentary and volcanic rocks. The late Eocene to middle Miocene Sacramento Pass Basin, located along the southern flank of the range, and isolated middle Miocene sediments along the eastern flank of the range, record the exhumation and unroofing of this Mcc. Geochronology and thermochronology age data from across the range document late Eocene to middle Miocene ductile and brittle extension.

authors: Perry, Amelia A. [1], Corsetti, Frank [2], Lund, Steven P. [3], Celestian, Aaron [4], Frantz, Carie [5], Mahseredjian, Taleen [6], Spear, John [7]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(3) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(4) Natural History Musuem Of Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(5) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(6) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA

abstract: The Green River Formation records the evolution of a long-lived series of intermontane lakes across Wyoming, Colorado, and Utah during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum (~52–50 Ma), Earth’s last major hothouse period. Because lakes, especially hydrologically-closed basins, are highly sensitive to environmental variability, their sediments are excellent archives of climate change. Here, we present preliminary results from a ~10 cm-thick stromatolite from the LaClede Bed of the Laney Member. The stromatolite was analyzed via micro-X-ray fluorescence, magnetic susceptibility and previously collected δ 13 C and δ 18 O. Ca and Si are strongly inversely correlated across the record (R 2 =0.75), consistent with fluctuations between carbonate-rich stromatolite growth and intervals of greater siliciclastic input. Fe is also inversely correlated to Ca, and weakly correlated with Si. In the lower portion of the stromatolite, δ 13 C and δ 18 O covary, a characteristic of hydrologically closed basins. We therefore interpret the lower part of the stromatolite as deposition in closed-basin conditions. In the uppermost portion, δ 13 C and δ 18 O are decoupled, which is interpreted as a transition towards a more hydrologically open or balance-filled system. The magnetic susceptibility maximum is located towards the bottom of the section, with two additional peaks towards the top. The relationship between magnetic susceptibility and elemental and isotopic records suggests that the magnetic signal reflects sediment supply and potentially secondary magnetic mineral growth under reducing conditions. In the lower portion of the stromatolite, MS and δ 18 O are anticorrelated, consistent with falling lake level decreasing the fluvial delivery of magnetic minerals and δ 18 O being primarily influenced by evaporation. Up-section, MS and δ 18 O generally covary as the lake became more open and riverine input increased, linking sediment delivery more directly with δ 18 O. The preliminary results may indicate that the LaClede stromatolite did not form under a single stable lake condition; instead, this stromatolite records repeated shifts in lake level, carbonate production, siliciclastic influx, and water chemistry during a transition from a hydrologically closed lake to a more open system. These preliminary findings support the use of the LaClede Bed stromatolite as a high-resolution archive of environmental change within Lake Gosiute and establish magnetic susceptibility as a valuable paleoclimate proxy in the Green River Formation.

title: An Unusual Eurypterid-Dominated Arthropod Fauna from the Silurian Eramosa Lagerstätte of Canada
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Lamsdell, James Christopher [1]
affiliations: (1) Biology and Marine Biology, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
abstract: Eurypterids were major components of shallow marine communities during the Silurian, during which they reached the peak of their taxonomic diversity and attained a global distribution. Despite their relative abundance, the majority of Silurian eurypterid localities host monospecific occurrences, with diverse communities known from only a handful of localities including the Bertie Waterlime of New York, Kokomo Limsetone of Indiana, and the Scottish Lagerstätten of Lesmahagow and Pentland Hills. Each of these communities are dominated by different taxa – Eurypterus and Acutiramus in the Bertie Waterlime, Kokomopterus and Carcinosoma at Kokomo, Erettopterus and Cruinnopterus at Lesmahagow, and Stoermeropterus and Drepanopterus in the Pentland Hills – with very little in the way of taxonomic overlap. These communities are also representative of distinct environments ranging from the upper shoreface to the continental shelf; as such, it is unclear whether these differences in community composition are due to geographic or environmental factors. Eurypterids are, however, consistently associated with an arthropod fauna typically comprised of phyllocarid crustaceans and synziphosurine chelicerates. Eurypterids have been known from the Silurian Eramosa Lagerstätte of Ontario, Canada, for 19 years but have yet to be fully described. Study of the 98 available specimens held in the Royal Ontario Museum and Yale Peabody Museum reveals a diverse community of five eurypterid species. Interestingly, the faunal composition of eurypterids includes a combination of taxa found across the other Silurian localities, including a species of the stylonurine Kokomopterus , otherwise known from Kokomo, and the carcinosomatid Cruinnopterus and pterygotid Erettopterus , which both occur at Lesmahagow. The associated arthropod fauna also includes a unique combination of taxa regularly found alongside eurypterids (including synziphosurines, scorpions, phyllocarids, and chasmataspidids) and species widespread in the Cambrian but unknown from contemporaneous localities. The Eramosa fauna greatly expands our knowledge of Silurian eurypterid communities and provides a link between biota in Scotland and the American Midwest as well as providing evidence for the persistence of Cambrian predators in a reduced role during the Silurian.

session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research
authors: Wilson, Sarah [1], Weekly, Robert [2], Bravo, Tammy [3], Parafina, Sophia [4], Sweet, Justin [5], Hubenthal, Michael [6], Trabant, Chad [7]
affiliations: (1) Earthscope Consortium, USA

(3) EarthScope Consortium, USA

abstract:
Modern geoscience visualization increasingly relies on specialized software, cloud-hosted datasets, and reproducible computational workflows. Installing, configuring, and managing authentication for these tools can create significant barriers for both research and instruction. GeoLab, a cloud-computing environment provided by the NSF National Geophysical Facility operated by EarthScope, is a browser-based JupyterHub environment that provides immediate access to the NGF’s petabyte-scale seismic and geodetic data archives. As the archives are lifted into the cloud, new cloud compute resources and strategies create opportunities for researchers to conduct larger analyses on a more rapid scale, and share them more easily with students and collaborators.

GeoLab is designed to minimize cloud configuration barriers with free, browser-based access. The platform supports interactive visualization workflows using PyGMT, ObsPy, and other Python-based libraries, allowing users to explore seismic waveforms, geodetic time series, mapping tools, and derived spatial products within a homogenized environment. The default environment is optimized for Python notebooks and pre-loaded with geophysics domain-specific libraries, while offering the flexibility for users to extend their environments with additional Python packages during their compute session. More complex software, such as QGIS or R-based environments, can be installed in custom images that can be reused and shared with collaborators. GeoLab also includes the EarthScope API and SDK, which streamline credential management and programmatic data access. For users with heavier compute needs, a Dask Gateway, scalable CPU and memory allocations, and GPU-backed servers are available upon request.

Reproducible and customizable environments have made GeoLab an invaluable tool for teaching. Over the past two years, the platform has hosted eleven educational workshops and technical courses serving over 625 learners on topics ranging from GNSS strain accumulation and inversion modeling to machine learning and massive parallelization frameworks. Prior to each course, instructors configure the required software and computational resources, then distribute identical cloud environments to every participant through a web browser. This creates a common, reproducible starting point for every participant, reducing technical barriers due to differences in local installations or individual computers’ hardware specs, and ensuring all learners can immediately engage with the course activities. By combining cloud-native computing with reusable instructional environments, GeoLab enables visualization tools developed for research to be used directly in classrooms, workshops, and self-paced instruction, strengthening the connection between research and geoscience education.

title: Critical Mineral Distribution Across Oil, Produced Water, and Reservoir Rock in the Permian Basin
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources
authors: Webster, Kamryn Orianna [1], Elliott, Brent [2]
affiliations: (1) The Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) The Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract: Critical minerals are essential for energy technologies, transportation, electronics, and national security, creating increasing demand for secure domestic supplies. Produced waters generated during oil and gas operations have emerged as a promising unconventional source of lithium and other critical minerals. This study evaluates the partitioning of critical minerals between co-located produced water, crude oil, and reservoir rock to better understand how these elements are distributed. Preliminary results are based on 93 paired oil and produced-water samples and demonstrate that elemental distribution is strongly phase dependent. Most analyzed elements, including lithium, boron, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, strontium, rubidium, cesium, and barium, are substantially enriched in the aqueous phase, consistent with their occurrence as dissolved ionic species in highly saline formation waters. In contrast, selenium, vanadium, nickel, chromium, and lead exhibit greater relative enrichment in crude oil, suggesting stronger affinity for the hydrocarbon phase or association with organometallic compounds. Formation-specific differences are also observed, with Delaware Mountain Group oils exhibiting elevated selenium, vanadium, and nickel concentrations relative to Wolfcamp and Bone Spring oils, while produced waters from all three formations remain enriched in the majority of dissolved critical and trace elements. Ongoing integration of reservoir rock geochemistry will provide the first comprehensive evaluation of critical mineral partitioning among oil, produced water, and reservoir rock. These results improve understanding of critical mineral occurrence within petroleum systems and provide a geochemical framework for future critical mineral resource assessments.

title: Examining Kyanite-Quartzite Petrogenesis in the Virginia Piedmont via in situ Oxygen Isotope Analysis
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems (Posters)
authors: Jones, Kayla N. [1], Hamelin, Clementine [2], Kitajima, Kouki [3], Bonamici, Chloe E. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia, USA
(2) Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(3) University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(4) University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI,
abstract:
The largest kyanite (Al 2 SiO 5 ) mine in the world is located in the Chopawamsic Terrane of the Virginia Piedmont and is unique for containing up to 30 wt.% kyanite. The protolith of Willis Mountain and neighboring deposits is debated as being either sedimentary or igneous. In this study, we examine the oxygen isotope signature of coexisting kyanite and quartz in four kyanite-quartzite localities across ~50km. Our goal is to (1) compare isotopic variation between geologic setting and kyanite chemical composition, (2) calculate the temperature of kyanite and quartz oxygen isotope equilibration, and (3) examine possible fluid sources associated with protolith formation and/or kyanite crystallization during metamorphism. Oxygen isotope analyses were performed in situ at the University of Wisconsin–Madison WiscSIMS lab by secondary ion mass spectroscopy.

Values of δ 18 O(Ky) range from ~2-10‰, and δ 18 O(Qz) values range from ~5-11‰. Cathodoluminescence imaging revealed CL-dark cores and CL-bright rims within kyanite grains. Kyanite growth rims displayed higher δ 18 O values than cores with δ 18 O values varying by ~1.5-3‰ in individual samples. Trace elements like chromium and iron influence the appearance of blue and blue-green kyanite, whereas white kyanite is relatively pure. However, no relationship is observed between blue versus white kyanite and their corresponding δ 18 O values. δ 18 O values of kyanite and quartz decrease from northeast to southwest following the Chopawamsic terrane. Calculated oxygen isotope equilibrium temperatures yield ~580-750ºC, although some mineral pairs yield unrealistically high temperatures of ~800-1,200º. This suggests a level of isotopic disequilibrium only evident through in situ textural analysis as whole grain analyses would not capture the range of δ 18 O values recorded. Calculated δ 18 O for fluids in equilibrium with kyanite and quartz range from ~4-10‰, indicating potential mixing of seawater (~0‰) or meteoric fluids (<0‰) with magmatic-derived fluids (~5.3-11‰) to account for the lower δ 18 O(H 2 O) values. Our data suggests that the O-isotope signatures reflect interaction with fluids involved in the transformation of the protolith at elevated temperatures, either during hydrothermal alteration or metamorphism, rather than original protolith values. This data supports the hypothesis of a mafic to intermediate igneous protolith that interacted with externally-derived fluids. Differing protolith compositions, fluid sources, and fluid-rock ratios will affect the alteration history and the δ 18 O values of kyanite and quartz crystallized during metamorphism.

title: The Enigmatic Biscayne Aquifer: Field, Laboratory, and Computational Approaches
session_title: GSA Hydrogeology Division Birdsall-Dreiss and Lamoreaux International Distinguished Lecture Series
authors: Sukop, Michael C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
abstract:
The Biscayne Aquifer of southeastern Florida supplies water to approximately 6 million people. The Pleistocene eogenetic karst unconfined aquifer is characterized by meter-thick strata of dense networks of 2-cm burrow ichnofossil vugs. Porosity can be 50% or more and the rock can be difficult or impossible to core. Large pores and high porosity likely result in non-Darcian flow under quite low gradients (>10 -5 ) and contribute to extremely high hydraulic conductivities ( K s) that are challenging to quantify.

Multiple independent lines of investigation have been followed to address these challenges. Standard petrophysical laboratory measurements yield exceptionally low K s (~10 -5 m s -1 ) probably due to intrinsic test limits. The K of intensely burrowed zone rocks has been shown to be ~15 m s -1 through high viscosity glycerol laboratory measurements on a 0.1 m diameter 3-D printed core, consistent with analytical Poiseuille flow solutions for a 2-cm pipe. Lattice Boltzmann flow modeling corroborates the experimental results. Lattice Boltzmann simulations of flow in the 0.1 m core were extended to a Reynolds number of approximately 100 and reductions in the apparent hydraulic conductivity were used to fit a Forcheimer model. Subsequent laboratory measurements using water and flows with Reynolds numbers of 1,000 to 10,000 were exceptionally well predicted.

Lattice Boltzmann modeling was applied to an atypically large 0.4 x 0.4 x 17-m block of the aquifer simulated geostatistically and conditioned on high resolution borehole imaging data. The estimated K was 50 m s -1 . Biscayne Aquifer slug tests frequently show underdamped oscillatory responses indicative of inertial flow. A literature search shows that reported results of any underdamped slug tests never exceed K of ~0.1 m s -1 . Careful aquifer tests on the Biscayne Aquifer conducted and published in the 1950s and 1990s yielded minimum estimates of the high end of the K range of the Biscayne Aquifer of 0.1 to 0.2 m s -1 .

Agreement of laboratory and Lattice Boltzmann results at the 0.1 m scale suggests that the K of burrowed zones is well constrained in the 10 to 50 m s -1 range. Aquifer tests are inconclusive and are prohibitive if not impossible to conduct conclusively. Slug tests yield unexpectedly low K s; further examination of the standard approaches for analysis of oscillatory slug tests seems needed.

title: Paired Occurrence of the Trace Fossil Rosselia from the Cambrian–Ordovician Los Cabos Group, Spain: a New Ichnotaxa or Rosselia prolifera?
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Grossenbacher, Paige [1], Paz, Maximiliano [2], Mangano, Maria Gabriela [3], Buatois, Luis A [4], Campetella, Débora [5], Gougeon, Romain [6], Pérez-Pueyo, Manuel [7], Shillito, Anthony [8], El Albani, Abderrazak [9], Mazurier, Arnaud [10], Piñuela , Laura [11], García-Ramos, José Carlos [12]

abstract: The middle Cambrian to Lower Ordovician Los Cabos Group from Asturias, northern Spain, constitutes a ~5700 m-thick succession deposited in the margin of northern Gondwana. The succession is represented by sandstone and mudstone, recording deposition in deltaic systems affected by tides, waves, and storms. An unusual occurrence of the trace fossil Rosselia was studied to understand its morphology, potential producers, and ethology. Rosselia is typically represented by a single vertical tube that has a concentric infill, whereas the studied specimens are found in a paired form. The specimens occur in ripple cross-laminated, flaser, very fine- to fine-grained sandstone interpreted to be deposited in a tide-dominated siliciclastic coast. They consist of vertical to inclined U-, Y-, and arcuate-shaped burrows with a funnel-shaped aperture that tapers down to a cylindrical tube. The burrows contain a concentric infill in its upper part with a central causative tube. The causative tube has a diameter ranging between 0.25-1 cm and is 2-6 cm deep, and is 0.5-2cm far from the paired shaft. The bulbs are 0.5-5 cm across and 0.5-3 cm deep. The likely tracemaker for Rosselia is detritus-eating terebellid polychaetes, though more work should be done to consider if the newly described morphology also supports the terebellid polychaete. The studied specimens could be accommodated within different ichnotaxa. U- and Y-shapes are similar to the overall morphology of Rosselia prolifera (Knaust 2021), a newly erected ichnotaxon for previous occurrences of Polycylindrichnus prolifer (Fournier et al., 1980); however, the holotype has at least four branching bulbs. The studied arcuate shapes may belong to a new ichnospecies due to the distinct funnel-shaped bulbs distinguishing it from Cylindrichnus . More research of the morphology is needed to clearly assess if the specimens can be accommodated in Rosselia prolifera , Altichnus isp ., or if they belong to a new ichnotaxa.

title: Effect of Weathering on Rare Earth Element Mineral Hosts and Extractability in Mine Waste from the Pea Ridge Iron Oxide-Apatite Deposit
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources
authors: Wright, Emily G [1], Bao, Bethany [2], Catalano, Jeffrey G. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO, USA
(3) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO, USA
abstract:
The vulnerable supply chain of and increasing demand for rare earth elements (REEs) necessitates the identification of novel secondary resources. In particular, mine wastes from iron oxide-apatite (IOA) deposits often contain elevated REE concentrations, particularly more valuable heavy REEs (HREEs). However, while the bulk REE contents of such materials are known, it is unclear whether weathering of mine wastes impacts REE mineral hosts and thus extractability. More broadly, limited knowledge of REE environmental behavior further inhibits predictsion of the effect of weathering on REE mobility.

We sampled mine wastes for macroscopic and microanalytical characterization from the Pea Ridge IOA deposit in southeast Missouri, which has experienced variable degrees of weathering. Materials were sampled from barren surface locations, vegetated surface locations, and from 100 ft deep within the waste. The most abundant REE mineral hosts identified with SEM-EDS are REE-containing apatite, monazite, and xenotime, which will be further investigated by EPMA. Gradual weathering has decreased the pyrite content and produced jarosite in surface samples. In unvegetated samples, this is further accompanied by the formation of hexahydrite.

Sequential leaching releases a greater proportion of all REEs in earlier, less aggressive steps in near-surface samples compared to a sample from deep within the tailings pile. This variation suggests that chemical weathering has released REEs from primary, chemically resistant phases into more easily extractable forms. Leaching apatite recovers the majority of the HREEs in all samples, but some light REEs remain sequestered in monazite. A long-term leaching experiment indicates that even low, environmentally relevant citrate concentrations can release REEs, suggesting promising extraction technologies and indicating the importance of ligands in mobilizing REEs in natural systems.

Our results support mine waste from the Pea Ridge deposit (and IOA deposits more broadly) as promising future resources for obtaining REEs, particularly HREEs. Weathering of these materials, likely a result of acidity generation from pyrite oxidation, has preferentially corroded apatite over REE phosphates, resulting in a fraction of easily extractable REEs. Future extraction efforts should target apatite because it is a major host for HREEs at Pea Ridge and is more easily digested than monazite and xenotime. Additionally, REEs released into the environment from weathering of IOA deposits will follow the REE pattern of apatite, not the bulk rock containing more resistant monazite.

title: Cirque-like alcoves in the northern mid-latitudes of Mars as evidence of glacial erosion
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Li, An Y. [1], Koutnik, Michelle [2], Brough, Stephen [3], Barr, Iestyn [4], Spagnolo, Matteo [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences with Astrobiology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(3) School of Environmental Sciences, University of Liverpool,
(4) Department of Natural Sciences, Manchester Metropolitan University, United Kingdom
(5) University of Turin, Italy
abstract:
Viscous flow features known as glacier-like forms on Mars often emerge from alcoves that resemble glacial cirques on Earth. However, many alcoves on Mars lack associated glacier-like forms, and these features have never been analyzed at a population scale. On Earth, cirques are primarily formed by wet-based glacial erosion, although cold-based glaciers can also contribute to minimal headward and sidewall retreat. Here, we present evidence that cirque-like alcoves on Mars, similar to terrestrial cirques, are shaped by glacial erosion.

We mapped a population of ~2000 alcoves in Deuteronilus Mensae, a region in the mid-latitudes of Mars characterized by mesas surrounded by glacial remnants. Based on visual characteristics and morphometrics, we refined our dataset to 434 “cirque-like alcoves”–nearly six times the number of glacier-like forms in the region. High-resolution imagery reveals icy geomorphic evidence of glacial occupation within these cirque-like alcoves, including flow features, linear terrain, mantling material, moraine-like ridges, mound-and-tail terrain, polygonal terrain, moraine-like ridges, rectilinear-ridge terrain, and washboard terrain.

Most cirque-like alcoves face south to southeast, similar to gullies poleward of 40°. Two possibilities to explain this trend are that southward facing cirque-like alcoves in the northern mid-latitudes were more favorable for ice accumulation during periods of high obliquity, or alternatively, increased insolation and meltwater is necessary for cirque-like alcove erosion. Using wet-based glacial erosion rates, the timescales estimated for martian cirque-like alcoves align with both glacier-like forms (millions to tens of millions of years) and other viscous flow features such as lobate debris aprons (hundreds of millions of years). In contrast, cold-based erosion rates for cirque-like alcoves are only consistent with the older ages of lobate debris aprons. By mapping cirque-like alcoves at a large scale for the first time, we expand the catalog of features attributed to glacial erosion on Mars.

title: Late Oligocene to Present-day slip along the southern Sierra Nevada normal fault, California: Implications for uplift of the Sierra Nevada
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Lee, Jeff [1], Phillips, Fred M. [2], Blisniuk, Kimberly [3]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA; Dept. of Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
(2) Earth & Environmental Science Dept., New Mexico Tech, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
(3) Geology Dept., San Jose State University, San Jose, California, USA
abstract: The uplift history of the Sierra Nevada, California, and the processes that drive that uplift, are topics of long-standing disagreement. Models of normal faulting indicate that uplift of the footwall may occur during fault slip. Such models, applied to the east-dipping, Cenozoic southern Sierra Nevada normal fault (SNNF), which defines the spectacular eastern escarpment of the southern Sierra Nevada, indicate that footwall uplift may be an important contributing factor to uplift of the Sierra Nevada. Furthermore, numerous studies have shown that mountain ranges bordered by normal faults within the Basin and Range are highest where the normal fault vertical displacement rates are the highest. From these observations stems the general consensus that footwall uplift during normal faulting must contribute some component to mountain elevation. Our field mapping, structural geology, geomorphology, thermochronology, and geochronology studies along the SNNF, located at the base of impressive topographic relief along the eastern Sierra Nevada range front, highlight its late Oligocene to present-day history of normal fault slip that bear on the uplift history of the Sierra Nevada. Our studies focused along a ~95 km long section of SNNF and illustrate the style, geometry, and timing of normal fault slip. Field studies along the SNNF describe the bedrock fault structure and extensive apatite (U-Th)/He thermochronometry on samples collected from the footwall of the SNNF that indicate late Oligocene and middle Miocene normal fault slip on a steeply east-dipping fault. Geologic mapping, tectonic geomorphology, and cosmogenic radionuclide geochronologic data document late Pleistocene and Holocene normal fault slip histories along fault scarps of the SNNF. A plausible, but not unique, interpretation of the AHe age data, combined with published sedimentary and volcanic rock tilt data from the western flank of the Sierra Nevada, indicate that late Oligocene and middle Miocene normal fault slip along the SNNF contributed to westward rigid tilting and uplift of the Sierra Nevada. Normal fault slip along the SNNF from the Pliocene to present-day also contributed to the uplift of the Sierra Nevada if we assume that SNNF fault slip rates since the late Pleistocene remained constant since the Pliocene.

title: Strontium and Neodymium Isotope Data Constrain Seafloor Alteration and Fluid Sources in the Protolith of the Catalina Schist Metabasalts
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Loska, Deven Eyleen [1], Lindquist, Peter Carl [2], Nelson, Bruce K [3], Cantine, Marjorie [4], Condit, Cailey Brown [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(3) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(4) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(5) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
The amount of water carried into subduction zones by oceanic crust influences the cycling of elements through the Earth, and water released into the forearc and subarc controls deformation and melting processes. However, this dehydration is directly controlled by pre-subduction hydration patterns, which remain underconstrained. We explore the magnitude and spatial pattern of pre-subduction vs. subduction hydration of metabasalts in the Catalina Schist (Pimu/Santa Catalina Island) using Sr isotope ratios as a proxy for hydrothermal alteration and εNd to distinguish between MOR alteration and hydrothermal processes in the subduction zone. The Catalina Schist (Pimu’nga/Santa Catalina Island, California) is an ancient exposure of underplated oceanic crust resulting from the subduction of the Farallon Plate under the North American Plate during the Cretaceous. We use MC-ICP-MS to analyze whole-rock 87Sr/86Sr ratios and εNd of samples from the Epidote Blueschist unit of the Catalina Schist. Initial Sr isotope ratios range from 0.702 to 0.705, with some samples more shifted from a value indicative of unaltered mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB; 87Sr/86Sr ~ 0.702) towards a value indicative of Jurassic seawater (87Sr/86Sr ~ 0.708). Initial εNd values of the metabasalts range from 9 to 10, falling within the typical range for MORB, indicating little input from sedimentary-derived fluids. We conclude that the alteration these rocks experienced was driven by seafloor hydrothermal interaction prior to subduction, likely providing an important source of water for later metamorphic dehydration reactions.

Isotopic systematics indicate a water/rock ratio consistent with that of basalts hydrated in modern mid-ocean ridge systems. Heterogeneity in the 87Sr/86Sr ratios coupled with relatively unaltered MOR εNd values suggests a heterogeneous pattern of initial hydration, likely as a product of spatial variability in oceanic crustal fractures, and a lack of pervasive fluid flow in this portion of the slab during subsequent metamorphism. This work provides isotopic evidence from the exhumed subduction rock record of large but spatially variable amounts of seawater-rock interaction in the oceanic crust prior to subduction. In the Catalina Schist, these mid-ocean ridge hydrated basalts would have provided an important fluid source at the base of the subduction seismogenic zone.

title: Compositional Zoning in Tourmaline as a Monitor of Prograde Mineral Reactions in Metapelites
session_title: Early career investigators in mineralogy and crystallography
authors: Roach, Mary Elaine [1], Dutrow, Barbara [2], Henry, Darrell [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
abstract:
Metapelitic metamorphic rocks contain mineral assemblages and mineral chemistries that are sensitive to pressure, temperature, and bulk-rock composition used to interpret metamorphic evolution. Tourmaline, a common but often overlooked accessory mineral in metapelites, typically exhibits compositional zoning that reflects its chemical responsiveness to changes in, and its equilibrium with, the host-rock environment. Through integrated petrography, backscatter-electron imaging, and electron-probe microanalysis, tourmaline zoning can be correlated to the major discontinuous mineral reactions in the matrix of staurolite-zone metapelites from west-central Maine, USA.

These tourmaline grains typically consist of a detrital core surrounded by three compositionally distinct overgrowths. All metamorphic tourmalines are schorl-to-dravite and predominantly hydroxyl dominant. The earliest metamorphic overgrowth, which nucleated on the detrital core, exhibits decreasing X Mg (Mg/Mg+Fe) and Al from its interface with the detrital core to its margin with the next overgrowth. In contrast, subsequent overgrowths display the opposite trend with increasing X Mg , Al, and X -site vacancy. The second overgrowth is compositionally asymmetric, exhibiting growth polarity in which the c - -pole is enriched in X Mg , Ca, Ti, and depleted in Al relative to time-equivalent growth at the c + -pole. The outermost rim is homogeneous, consistent with growth at staurolite-zone conditions. Systematic partitioning of major elements shows that matrix minerals and tourmaline have approached chemical equilibrium during metamorphism such that variations in tourmaline compositions record changes in evolving matrix mineral compositions.

The chemistry of each tourmaline overgrowth reflects the host rock’s metamorphic-mineral assemblage at the time of its growth. Chemical discontinuities between successive zones, (e.g., zones 1-2, zones 2-3) coincide with major changes in the matrix mineral assemblages. These compositional breaks can be interpreted in the context of discontinuous and continuous prograde metamorphic reactions during heating at ~3.2 kbar. The earliest overgrowth likely formed under chlorite-zone conditions (<400 °C). Discontinuity (1) likely records the garnet-in reaction (460±50 °C), 1.5Chl + 2Ms + 3SiO 2 = Grt + 2Bt + 3H 2 O. Discontinuity (2) records the staurolite-in reaction (500±50 °C), 2Grt + 1.5Chl + 3Ms = St + 3Bt + 8SiO 2 + 4H 2 O. These systematic compositional trends are consistent across all staurolite-zone samples. This study demonstrates that compositional zoning in tourmaline records major matrix-mineral reactions, and underscores tourmaline’s utility as a robust indicator of prograde metamorphic evolution in low- to medium-grade metapelites.

title: Petrografía y geocronología U-Pb en zircones de granitoides en los alrededores de Isla Tiburón (Sonora) y San Felipe (Baja California): Conexiones intra Golfo de California
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part I)
authors: Acevedo Flores, Jesica Paulina [1], Iriondo, Alexander [2], Barron, Arturo J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geologia, Universidad de sonora, Hermosillo, Sonora,
(2) UNAM-Instituto de Geociencias, Queretaro, QRO,
(3) Universidad de Sonora, Hermosillo, SON,
abstract:
Los márgenes del Golfo de California registran una compleja evolución magmática y tectónica cretácico-cenozoica, asociada a la subducción de la placa Farallón y al posterior rifting del Golfo de California. Este margen continental alberga un importante cinturón batolítico cuya continuidad espacial y temporal ha sido fragmentada por la apertura asociada a la provincia extensional del Golfo de California.

Los estudios en los cinturones batolíticos de San Felipe y la costa de Sonora e Isla Tiburón muestran edades de cristalización de 95 a 63 Ma. En este estudio presentamos nuevos fechamientos U-Pb en zircones que representan edades de cristalización de granitoides expuestos en la costa central de Sonora e Isla Tiburón, así como en la región de San Felipe, en el noreste de la península de Baja California. Con el objetivo de caracterizar composicionalmente estas rocas, y determinar sus edades de cristalización para correlacionarlas con unidades regionales previamente documentadas, se realizó un análisis petrográfico mediante conteo de puntos en granitoides, el cual revela una composición de los intrusivos que varía de monzogranitos dominando las granodioritas a tonalitas. Asimismo, se presentan nuevos datos geocronológicos U-Pb en zircones por ablación láser (LA-ICP-MS) obtenidos a partir de nueve muestras representativas de granitoides. Los resultados muestran edades de cristalización cretácicas, que fluctúan entre ~150–76 Ma. Estos nuevos datos aportan información clave para refinar las reconstrucciones paleogeográficas y los modelos de apertura tectónica intra-Golfo de California, permitiendo una correlación directa entre los intrusivos de la costa de Sonora-Isla Tiburón y los expuestos en San Felipe. Al comparar este registro con los datos regionales previamente publicados para el Cinturón Batolítico Peninsular y el Batolito Costero de Sonora, este estudio contribuye a determinar la continuidad original de las cámaras magmáticas antes de la apertura del Golfo de California y se aporta información clave para refinar los modelos de reconstrucción paleogeográfica y precisar la dirección de la migración del arco magmático cretácico en el noroeste de México.

title: From Outcrop to Model: Integrating Field Mapping, Geophysics, and Geochemistry For Urban Subsurface Characterization in Montréal
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Perrot, Morgann Gwenva [1], Frost, Natasha [2], Pinon, Héloïse [3], Musajo, Claire [4], Tremblay, Alain [5], Ducat, Thibault [6], Halverson, Galen P. [7], Davies, Joshua [8]
affiliations: (1) McGill University, Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Montreal, Qc, Canada; Sciences de la Terre et de l'atmosphère, Université du Québec à Montréal, Montréal, Québec, Canada
(2) McGill University, Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Montreal, Québec, Canada
(3) UQAM, Department des science de la terre, Montréal, QC,
(4) McGill University, Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Montréal, Québec, Canada
(5) Sciences de la Terre et de l'atmosphère, UQAM, Sherbrooke, QC, Canada
(6) Dahrouge Geological Consulting Ltd, Montréal, Québec, Canada
(7) McGill University, Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Montreal, QC,
(8) Science de la Terre et de l'atmosphère, UQAM, Department des science de la terre, Montréal, QC, Canada
abstract:
Geological mapping and field observations remain foundational tools in the geoscientist's toolkit, yet their contributions are increasingly undervalued relative to newer approaches such as remote sensing, geophysics, and data analytics. Here we reassert the relevance of field observations as a complement to modern methods, demonstrating how direct field observations anchor, validate, and enhance analytical workflows. We apply this approach to mapping the subsurface geology in the Island of Montréal, Québec, Canada.

In Montréal, subsurface geology directly controls the feasibility and cost of urban infrastructure. The bedrock is composed of carbonate and siliciclastic units from the St. Lawrence Platform, and it is cut by faults whose geometry, kinematics, and displacement are poorly constrained. These units are also interbedded with weak bentonite horizons that, combined with the faults, pose geotechnical hazards when intercepted during construction. Without a reliable structural and lithological framework, geophysical surveys or 3D models cannot be confidently generated. Geological observations provide the basis for this framework where surface and subsurface structural observations define fault orientations and kinematics and establish the geometry and sequence of the bentonite horizons.

Building on the field observational foundation, we have integrated surface outcrop observations with borehole geophysics and spectral gamma surveys to extend structural observations into the subsurface, used U-Pb geochronology of syn-kinematic calcite cements to constrain the timing and phases of fault activity, and applied geochemical fingerprinting of apatite and zircon in bentonite layers to correlate marker horizons across the urban area and into adjacent regions. Together, these methods reveal dominantly normal faulting in E-W and NW-SE orientations and document a protracted and previously unrecognized history of tectonic activity in the Montréal area from ca. 150 Ma to near-recent.

Our results contribute to an evolving 3D model of the subsurface, critical for planning future tunnels, foundation engineering, and geothermal wells. Our case study shows how field mapping and observations are not a preliminary step to be replaced by more technologically advanced methods, but the basis by which those methods gain their meaning.

title: Repurposing State Well-Permitting Records to Detect a Diffuse, Five-Decade Decline in Shallow Groundwater Across Louisiana's Florida Parishes
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Munim, Mustuque Ahmed [1], Jahan, Shakura [2], Uddin, Ashraf [3], Uddin, Md Riaz [4]
affiliations: (1) Energy Institute, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(2) Mass Spectrometry Stable Isotopes & Energy Expenditure Lab, Pennington Biomedical Research Center-Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL,
(4) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
abstract: Louisiana's eight “Florida Parishes” overlie the Southern Hills regional aquifer system and range from the state’s most urbanized parish to some of its most rural. Outside the Baton Rouge Industrial District, most residents rely on unregulated domestic wells, and the region has no dedicated groundwater-level monitoring network, leaving water-table trends poorly constrained despite decades of uneven population growth. We repurpose 56,116 public water-well registration records from Louisiana’s SONRIS database (wells completed 1970–2025) as a chronosequence proxy for long-term groundwater conditions, using static water level recorded at well completion. Restricting the primary analysis to domestic wells completed in the region’s dominant shallow aquifer (Upland Terrace Aquifer; n=17,930, six parishes), OLS regression with a year-by-growth-group interaction term reveals a statistically significant water-table decline of 1.76 ft/decade (95% CI 1.46–2.07; p<0.001), from a modeled 27.6 ft in 1970 to 37.4 ft in 2025 (8.4 to 11.4 m; a 9.7 ft / 3.0 m drop). This decline rate does not differ significantly between fast-urbanizing and population-stable rural parishes, arguing against a simple local-pumping explanation and pointing to a region-wide signal. East Baton Rouge Parish’s well records let us benchmark this pattern against the well-documented, concentrated drawdown of the Baton Rouge Industrial District’s deep sands within the same dataset: depth to water there is three- to twelve-fold greater than in the shallow regional aquifer. These results show that state well-permitting archives, though never intended for scientific monitoring, can serve as a low-cost complement to sparse formal networks, with direct relevance to unregulated rural domestic-well users.

title: UAV-Based Digital Outcrop Basemaps for Geological Interpretation: Workflows, Case Studies, and Lessons
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Meng, Jiannan [1], Kusky, Timothy [2], Wang, Lu [3], Ning, Wenbin [4]
affiliations: (1) Badong National Observation and Research Station of Geohazards, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, Hubei, China

(2) Badong National Observation and Research Station of Geohazards, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, Hubei, China; State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, Center for Global Tectonics, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, Hubei, China
(3) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, Center for Global Tectonics, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, Hubei, China
(4) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, Center for Global Tectonics, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, Hubei, China
abstract:
Conventional field investigations often cannot fully reconstruct the spatial relationships among geological units along extensive sections and within geometrically complex outcrops. To address this limitation, our group began applying UAV photogrammetry in 2019 and gradually developed workflows for generating high-resolution orthomosaics and three-dimensional digital outcrop models. Rather than treating these products as final outcomes, we use them as spatially referenced digital basemaps for the rapid identification, tracing, and mapping of lithologic boundaries, structural contacts, faults, and surface ruptures.

Following the 2023 Türkiye earthquake sequence, quantitative UAV surveys began 10 days after the earthquakes. A DJI Phantom 4 RTK was used to acquire detailed georeferenced imagery at key surface-rupture sites. Combined with field observations, these datasets supported the extraction of fault displacement, kinematic characteristics, and surface-rupture features. It documented surface before it was substantially modified by rainfall erosion and post-earthquake reconstruction, while also providing basemaps for the vectorization and spatial analysis of coseismic ruptures. In the Shangying ophiolitic mélange of the eastern Hebei Complex, North China Craton, digital outcrop products assisted in tracing contacts between garnet clinopyroxenite and the surrounding metagabbro. During fieldwork in Australia, rapidly generated high-resolution imagery was used to update field basemaps, refine survey routes, and identify priority outcrops.

Our applications indicate that two-dimensional orthomosaics are particularly effective for continuously tracing lithologic boundaries and surface ruptures across relatively low-relief terrain, whereas three-dimensional digital outcrop models are better suited to extensive sections, steep exposures, and complex spatial relationships among geological units. Depending on the required accuracy and processing time, either rigorous photogrammetric reconstruction or rapid field-based image mosaicking can be adopted. UAV-derived digital basemaps provide an effective link among image acquisition, field observations, and geological interpretation; however, survey and processing strategies should be selected according to the geological objective, outcrop geometry, spatial-control conditions, accuracy requirements, and operational efficiency.

title: Structural architecture and tectonic evolution of the Okcheon Belt, Korea: A new tectonic model from integrated structural, stratigraphic, and geochronological constraints
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse (Posters)
authors: Kim, Changyeob [1], Jang, Yirang [2], Kwon, Sanghoon [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth System Sciences, Yonsei University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
(2) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Korea (The Republic of)
(3) Department of Earth System Sciences, Yonsei University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract:
The Okcheon Belt of the Korean Peninsula is one of the major fold–thrust belts in East Asia that preserves a prolonged tectonic record from Neoproterozoic basin development to subsequent Phanerozoic orogenesis. However, its tectonic evolution remains controversial because the timing of sedimentation, structural development, and tectonic framework have largely been interpreted from lithostratigraphic correlations with limited integration of structural, geochronological, and paleontological constraints. Here we present a new tectonic model for the Okcheon Belt based on integrated regional structural mapping, balanced cross-sections, zircon U–Pb geochronology, biomarker analysis, paleontological constraints, and cross-cutting intrusive relationships. The revised stratigraphic framework distinguishes primary depositional successions from structurally repeated strata and demonstrates that much of the exposed Okcheon Supergroup was deposited during the late Paleozoic rather than the Neoproterozoic. Together with the Cambrian–Ordovician Joseon Supergroup of the Taebaeksan Zone, these results define two contrasting tectonostratigraphic domains that were subsequently incorporated into a single regional fold–thrust belt. Structural analysis reveals fundamentally different deformation styles between the two domains. The Okcheon Zone is characterized by cover-dominated thrusting, fault-related folding, and localized basement involvement, whereas the Taebaeksan Zone preserves folded thrust surfaces, tectonic windows, doubly plunging culminations, fold-interference patterns, and large-displacement thrust systems. These structural relationships indicate that the principal fold–thrust architecture developed during the Permo–Triassic Songrim Orogeny following late Paleozoic sedimentation and was subsequently modified by Jurassic deformation during the Daebo Orogeny. These results establish a new tectonic framework in which the present-day architecture of the Okcheon Belt primarily reflects Permo–Triassic crustal shortening superimposed on inherited Neoproterozoic–Paleozoic tectonostratigraphic domains and subsequently modified by Jurassic deformation. This tectonic model demonstrates that inherited tectonostratigraphic architecture exerts a first-order control on the geometry, structural style, timing, and preservation of polyphase basement-involved fold–thrust belts, providing a broadly applicable framework for understanding the evolution of complex orogenic belts.

session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping (Posters)
authors: Hoxey, Andrew KR [1], Ash, Jason [2], Walker, J Douglas [3]
affiliations: (1) George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
(2) Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(3) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
abstract: The options for exporting data from StraboField projects now include a tool that generates Geologic Map Schema (GeMS)-formatted files. The new export module creates an efficient bridge between the digital collection of field data and the required USGS geodatabase standards for publishing geologic maps. StraboField is an open-source data collection app designed for field investigations and geologic mapping on iOS and Android mobile devices. The GeMS-compliant geodatabases standardize geologic map publications and is the required format for publicly funded geologic map productions (e.g. USGS STATEMAP program, USGS EdMAP program, etc.). StraboField projects and GeMS geodatabases store data in significantly different formats; StraboField uses a graph structure that enables large-scale data queries, and GeMS uses a table structure that is typical of conventional GIS applications. As a result, using both applications necessitates the translation of Spots from StraboField to their equivalent feature class fields and attributes, a time-consuming process in most GIS workflows. To expedite the translation process, the StraboSpot web interface now includes a GeMS-compliant export option. The export module uses Python dictionaries to generate JSON files that include all Spots within the dataset, include links to StraboSpot server data (i.e. images and sketches), and are organized with GeMS-compliant attributes. Users can modify symbol codes and descriptions of features when necessary to maintain quality control. Importing JSON files into a GeMS geodatabase is seamless with a standard geoprocessing toolbox and complements existing workflows. Here we present a description of the processing, the user interface, and recommended workflows for integration of StraboField into STATEMAP geologic mapping programs.

title: Crustal structure and lithosphere thermal state in central-southern Asia
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling
authors: Artemieva, Irina M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Zhejiang Deep-time Digital Earth International Research Center, Hangzhou, China
abstract:
Thermal structure of the lithosphere reflects its long-term evolution and controls its rheology, expressed in crustal and mantle anisotropic layering as observed in many seismic tomographic models globally and for Asia. Estimates of lithosphere thermal thickness, which defines lithospheric geotherms, show significant differences depending on the method and the employed lithosphere definition. While lithosphere thermal structure is often constrained by borehole heat flow values, the approach requires exclusion of tectonic provinces with non-steady-state thermal state. These requirements are not satisfied for ca. 75% of the Asian continent.

This study presents a new lithosphere thermal model for the central-southern Asia (15-50 N/70-135 E) based on an alternative approach (Artemieva, 2019a,b) and constrained by a new model of crustal thickness in Asia. The results are discussed in relation to regional geological and geodynamic evolution that shaped the region from Archean to present, including reworked and fragmented Precambrian cratons, the Paleozoic Central Asia Orogenic Belt and the Meso-Cenozoic Tethyan Belt.

title: Exceptionally preserved earliest Cambrian macroalgae from the Yanjiahe Formation, South China

authors: Lole Durbin, Orin [1], Song, Zuchen [2], Vayda, Prescott J. [3], Guo, Junfeng [4], Anderson, Ross P. [5], Xiao, Shuhai [6]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA

abstract: Marine macroalgae (seaweeds) are an important component of oceanic ecosystems today and have been since the beginning of the Phanerozoic. Paleontological evidence supports an ecological turnover in animals across the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, but whether the record of macroalgae exhibits a similar pattern is poorly understood. Early Cambrian deposits can provide important insights into the evolution of macroalgae during this critical transition, helping to reveal how their modern ecological role evolved at the base of the Phanerozoic. To further our understanding of early Phanerozoic macroalgae, we describe ~700 macroscopic, ribbon-like fossils from the Cambrian Yanjiahe Formation ( Purella biozone) exposed in Changyang County, Hubei Province, South China. Macroscopically, these fossils morphologically resemble members of the problematic genus Vendotaenia , common in Ediacaran–Cambrian strata. Fossils are documented throughout an interbedded succession of carbonates and shales interpreted to represent shallow marine deposition within a restricted intrashelf basin. They form mass accumulations of ribbon-shaped compressions, reconstructed as tubes, on the bedding surfaces of shales. The fossils vary between 0.2–2 mm in width with lengths of up to 10 cm. The population of width measurements is best characterized by two normal distributions, potentially supporting the presence of more than one species within this deposit. Thin sections of exceptionally preserved fossils revealed cellular-level preservation showing internal tissue differentiation within the filaments, analogous to modern algae, supporting a green algal affinity for at least some of these macrofossils. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analysis suggests preservation as compressed carbon-rich films, held within an aluminosilicate matrix, primarily via sulfurization of organic matter. The morphological similarity between the macroalgae of the Yanjiahe Formation and Vendotaenia specimens reported from many Ediacaran deposits worldwide suggests relative stability in macroalgal communities across the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary.

title: Importance of Eclogites from Cratonisation to the Phanerozoic Explosion of Onshore Life
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Thybo, Hans [1], Xia, Bing [2], Wang, Gaochun [3], Zhou, Zhipeng [4], Artemieva, Irina M. [5]
affiliations: (1) Zhejiang Deep-time Digital Earth International Research Center, Hangou, China
(2) Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of Oceanology, Qingdao, China
(3) Yangtze University, Wuhan, c, China
(4) China Earthquake administration, Beijing, China
(5) International Lithosphere Centre, Denmark, Sakskobing, Denmark,
abstract:
Eclogite formation from lower crustal rocks requires high pressure at relatively low temperature in the presence of water. Due to the high temperature regime in the early Earth and the sparse observations of eclogitic rocks at the surface, it is generally expected that such rocks are rare in cratons. Our recent results show that large amounts of eclogitic lower crustal rocks are present below the seismic Moho in the Baltic Shield 1 . Such eclogites in various metamorphic grades may explain the high topography of the Scandes mountain range in northern Fennoscandia 2 . Our findings suggests that the amount of sub-Moho eclogite can be generally underestimated globally!

Eclogitization may also play a major role in plateau formation in Tibet, where new addition of mafic underplate to the overthickened crust may immediately transform into eclogite, which founder each time the eclogite layer exceeds a critical thickness 3 . The whole continental crust in the central Lhasa Block has low seismic velocity (<6.7 km/s), which indicates that this thickest crust on Earth is felsic down to the Moho at 80 km depth, explaining half the present topography by isostasy. However, underplating and partial melt in the crust are also required to explain the high elevation of the Tibetan Plateau and other major plateaux worldwide 4 .

By interpretation of >18,000 km of seismic profiles, we document that a mafic crustal layer is generally preserved in Proterozoic orogens but absent in Phanerozoic orogens 5 . This indicates a change in the global subduction style at the onset of the Phanerozoic, which caused massive eclogitization of lower crust in orogens and recycling of the eclogitic rocks into the mantle. The resulting buoyant felsic crust lifted continents above sea level, which enabled onshore life to develop, thus explaining the Neoproterozoic oxidation event and the explosion of life in the Phanerozoic.

title: Top down vs bottoms up: We’ve looked at Alaska from both sides now
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Pavlis, Gary [1], Pavlis, Terry L. [2], Ridgway, Kenneth D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Indiana University, Bloomington, IN,
(2) University of Texas El Paso, El Paso, TX,
(3) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
abstract: In a GSA Today article in 2019 a group of us called on a need to integrate investigations based on mantle tomography (bottom up) and surface geology (top down) into a coherent framework to solve fundamental issues in tectonics. In that spirit we have integrated the geologic record of the northern Cordillera together with Earthscope imaging to evaluate the history of the margin from early Eocene to the present day with a focus on the role of the Yakutat terrane in the evolution of the margin. This analysis also allows for a reassessment of the plate tectonic record of the margin by constraining allowable plate geometries through use of pinning points like ridge-trench interactions, strike-slip fault system timing, and reanalysis of the Pacific plate magnetic anomalies. Our initial results include: 1) Mantle imaging indicates the flat slab region overlies a mantle scale lithospheric fold. Kinematic modeling of the imaged geometry indicates the flat slat originated prior to at least 25 Ma to as early as 40 Ma. We correlate the western transition from the flat slab to normal subduction with the likely location of a slab window during Kula times. We suggest one factor in the origin of the flat slab may be anchoring of eastern side of the slab window in the transition zone interacting with the large plate motion change as Kula merged with the Pacific plate. 2) Based on our plate reconstructions we conclude that the Transition fault originated as a sinistral Kula-Farallon transform that developed just prior to the demise of the Kula plate and evolved into a Pacific-Farallon transform that formed a mirror-image Mendocino type triple junction that migrated northward along the Queen Charlotte transform from at least 41Ma to ~25Ma. 3) Although an additional north Pacific plate is allowable, our analysis indicates a Kula-Farallon-Pacific system can explain all major Cenozoic tectonic events along the margin.

title: 90+ years of mapping and field education at the Yellowstone-Bighorn Research Association Field Station
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Sisson, Virginia B. [1], Robinson, Alexander [2]
affiliations: (1) Dept of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, TX,
(2) Dept of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, TX,
abstract: The Yellowstone Bighorn Research Association (YBRA) field station is a locus for geologic mapping, science education, and research in the Greater Yellowstone region. Since 1936, ~8,000 individuals have participated in field camps and courses and conducted research from this location. This experience was and still is transformative and critical to launching successful careers in government, academia, and the resource and environmental industries. Princeton’s Geology Department initiated the “Red Lodge Project” in 1930, choosing Red Lodge because of its superb geologic setting in an area that was then relatively unknown. In 1935, construction of a permanent field station began and by 1936 there was a lodge, shower house, and fourteen cabins. YBRA was incorporated as a not-for-profit organization in July 1936. Since the 1950s, YBRA has hosted field courses and annually hosts over 10 University and research groups. While some field activities have changed over the years (plane table mapping and pace-and-compass exercises long abandoned), most field projects at YBRA still focus on making geologic maps, generally still on paper base maps. Modern field projects also increasingly integrate remote sensing databases (satellite images and high-resolution DEM’s) with digital mapping apps such as StraboField and FieldMOVE becoming invaluable tools. These maps form foundations for students to explore 3-D geometries and structures responsible for the map patterns through cross-section analysis, some using seismic data. To construct geologic histories, traditional stratigraphy now incorporates geochronology such as detrital zircon data, Be 10 and U/Pb of igneous rocks. Looking to the future, field schools at YBRA are increasing their scope, moving away from strictly bedrock mapping to projects such as geomorphic mapping studying landscape evolution. The UH-YBRA field camp also developed a neotectonic fault mapping and landscape analysis project in southwest Montana. Students use high-precision RTK GNSS measurements across fault scarps combined with terrace soil profiles to assess regional seismic risks. At YBRA, geologic mapping remains the primary focus of most groups even as techniques change and are modernized, while broadening of field-based projects better prepares students for their future.

title: Linking the Yakutat terrane to sources and ridges: A revised north Pacific plate tectonic model and origin of the Transition Fault
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Pavlis, Terry L. [1], Ridgway, Kenneth D. [2], Pavlis, Gary [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas El Paso, El Paso, TX,
(2) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
(3) Indiana University, Bloomington, IN,
abstract: One of John Garver's favorite fishing areas contains a key assemblage for reconstruction of the Cenozoic paleogeography of the Cordillera. The Cretaceous-Paleocene Yakutat Group is a forearc accretionary complex that lies in thrust contact with ~56Ma mafic rocks interpreted as an oceanic plateau that formed in the Pacific basin and accreted to the Cordilleran convergent margin at ~50-40Ma at more southerly paleolatitudes. This composite Yakutat terrane was subsequently carried northward along the transform margin and is now colliding into southern Alaska. Early studies correlated the Yakutat Group with the Chugach terrane and inferred an origin along the BC margin. Garver et al (2015) showed, however, that the provenance of the Yakutat Group was distinct from Chugach and interpreted a southern CA source, although others challenged that interpretation and suggested a metamorphosed Belt Supergroup source in the Pacific NW. Either constraint when tied to reconstructions of the oceanic spreading center(s) that subducted beneath Chugach plus provenance data for Eocene strata on the Yakutat terrane places tight constraints on allowable plate geometries despite nearly complete destruction of the Kula plate and the spreading ridge that separated it from Farallon. Using new plate reconstruction scenarios we suggest Yakutat Group was initially accreted by subduction at paleolatitudes near northern CA and it, along with the Chugach terrane and inboard terranes were transported northward along dextral fault systems driven by highly oblique Kula and Farallon convergence at 56-40Ma. Northward motion of Chugach terrane and the subducting Kula-Farallon spreading allowed the Chugach terrane and Chugach metamorphic complex to get “out of the way” of the Yakutat collision by ~50Ma, but not the Yakutat Group. Continued oblique convergence from 50-40Ma drove Chugach northward with the Yakutat terrane following along an evolving plate boundary that involved at least one triple junction that was a mirror image of Mendocino with the Transition fault as an offshore sinistral arm of the triple junction.

title: Impact of Hematite Morphology on Coating Architecture of Sandstone and Limestone
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology (Posters)
authors: Ren, Wei [1], Xu, Tingying [2], Zhang, Yipeng [3]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(3) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract:
Mineral coatings are important components of both carbonate and clastic sedimentary systems, where they can modify pore-surface properties and fluid-rock interactions. Detrital and authigenic iron oxides are widespread in sandstone and carbonate reservoirs and may undergo reductive dissolution, recrystallization, redistribution, and phase transformation during burial diagenesis and hydrocarbon migration. These processes can generate iron oxides with distinct crystal phases, particle morphologies, and surface properties, potentially altering pore geometry, reactive surface area of reservoir rocks, interactions with polar crude-oil components, and reservoir wettability. However, how iron oxide morphology interacts with host-rock surface architecture to control coating development, and how the resulting coating patterns affect pore-scale transport, remain poorly understood.

Hematite is one of the most abundant iron oxides found on Earth’s surface and in the shallow crust, which has been commonly found in both sandstone and carbonate reservoirs. Platelet and cubic hematite particles expose different dominant crystal facets and surface functional groups, potentially leading to morphology- and facet-dependent adsorption, attachment, and coating development on reservoir-rock surfaces. To evaluate these controls, we compared hematite coating development on Berea sandstone (BS), Colton sandstone (CS), Indiana limestone (IL), and Edwards Brown limestone (EBL). Under identical coating conditions, platelet hematite formed broadly continuous coatings on all four substrates, whereas cubic hematite produced patchy, substrate-dependent coatings with coverage ranging from approximately 36% to 71%. Quantitative SEM analysis further revealed differences in coating distribution and spatial texture among hematite morphologies and host-rock types. The observed coating patterns are being incorporated into pore-scale models to evaluate their potential effects on fluid transport and displacement.

This workflow provides a reproducible approach for quantifying coating-related surface heterogeneity in porous geologic materials when direct measurements of surface topography or wettability are limited. Together, these results will provide a basis for linking mineral-coating architecture to pore-scale transport and fluid displacement in clastic and carbonate reservoirs.
