title: Three-Dimensional Hydrogeologic Characterization of the Canadian River Alluvial Aquifer Using High-Resolution Time-Domain Electromagnetic Imaging
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Correll, David [1]
affiliations: (1) Ensolum, LLC, DALLAS, TX, USA
abstract:
Groundwater occurrence within alluvial aquifers is controlled by the geometry, continuity, and hydraulic connectivity of fluvial deposits. Because these deposits are highly heterogeneous, drilling alone rarely provides sufficient subsurface control to characterize aquifer architecture. Boreholes provide only discrete observations, leaving significant uncertainty between control points. This study integrates high-density time-domain electromagnetic (TEM) data, lithologic information, and three-dimensional resistivity modeling to characterize the Canadian River Alluvial Aquifer beneath the McClain County Rural Water District No. 8 well field in central Oklahoma.

A total of 4,466 TEM soundings were collected across approximately 185 acres using a TEM2Go system. Data were processed using a laterally constrained inversion workflow to produce two-dimensional resistivity sections along each survey line. Interpretation was constrained using regional geologic mapping, nearby groundwater well records, and lithologic logs from exploratory borings completed within the study area. The interpreted sections were imported into RockWorks and interpolated using inverse distance weighting to generate a three-dimensional resistivity model.

The model delineated variations in alluvial thickness, mapped the underlying Permian bedrock surface, and identified laterally continuous resistive bodies interpreted as coarse-grained sand and gravel deposits. Three-dimensional visualization of these features improved interpretation of aquifer geometry and hydraulic continuity beyond what could be inferred from drilling alone. The model was used to guide exploratory drilling and production well siting. Subsequent drilling confirmed the predicted distribution of coarse-grained alluvial deposits, providing field verification of the geophysical interpretation.

The results demonstrate that integrating high-density TEM data with targeted lithologic control can resolve the three-dimensional architecture of heterogeneous fluvial deposits and substantially reduce uncertainty between boreholes. This workflow provides a defensible approach for developing hydrogeologic conceptual models and improving groundwater exploration in alluvial aquifers where the distribution and connectivity of coarse-grained deposits largely control aquifer productivity.

title: Tectonomagmatic Evolution of Northwestern Mauritania Based on SHRIMP U-Pb Zircon Protolith Ages and Whole-Rock Geochemistry

abstract: The Ediacaran tectonomagmatic evolution of the western margin of the West African Craton remains controversial, particularly in northwestern Mauritania and southern Western Sahara, where contrasting models have interpreted the widespread magmatism as the product of rifting, subduction-related magmatism, or even a transition between both regimes. The southernmost segment of the Souttoufides, exposed in the Northwest Chami Thrust Belt (northwestern Mauritania), is one of the least studied segments. We report new SHRIMP and LA-ICP-MS zircon U-Pb ages integrated with petrographic observations and whole-rock major- and trace-element geochemistry from representative igneous rocks exposed along a regional transect across the Northwest Chami Thrust Belt. The new geochronological dataset identifies two magmatic episodes: (i) a Mesoarchean event (ca. 3.0–2.9 Ga), represented by TTG-like granitoids that constitute the crystalline basement of the western West African Craton, and (ii) an Ediacaran event (ca. 621–604 Ma), comprising mafic, intermediate, and felsic intrusive rocks. The Ediacaran igneous suite is characterized by calc-alkaline affinity, enrichment in large-ion lithophile elements, and negative Nb and Ti anomalies, consistent with a subduction-related arc/back-arc setting. The joint consideration of previous geological, geochronological, and geochemical data from the Oulad Dlim Massif (Western Sahara) supports correlation of the Mesoarchean basement of the Northwest Chami Thrust Belt with its Eastern Archean domain. In contrast, the Ediacaran igneous rocks are more difficult to correlate with the Oulad Dlim Massif due to slightly older (c. 20 Ma) ages in northwestern Mauritania and the different cartographic pattern, which suggest a spatial and temporal migration of Ediacaran magmatism along the western margin of the West African Craton. Our results support a subduction-related magmatic tectonic scenario along the western margin of the West African Craton at Ediacaran time. The geochemical signatures closely resemble those reported from several peri-Gondwanan terranes, including the Anti-Atlas, Iberia, Cadomia, Avalonia, Meguma, and Carolina, thus supporting regional-scale tectonomagmatic correlations and reinforcing the interpretation of an arc/back-arc (Avalonian/Cadomian) tectonic setting along the northwestern margin of Gondwana.

title: Separating paleoenvironmental and post-depositional fluid signals in stable isotopes (δ13C and δ18O) of paleosol carbonates from Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade (Posters)
authors: Lee, Bryan [1], Kelson, Julia [2], Herrmann, Edward [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
(3) Far Western Anthropological Research Group, Davis, California, USA
abstract: Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, is a key early hominin site in East Africa. Contextualizing the paleoclimatic history of Olduvai Gorge is crucial to understanding the relationship between early hominins and their environment. Previous Olduvai pedogenic carbonate studies have used stable isotope values to investigate paleoenvironments and have reported large variation within single nodules, which was attributed to formation in meteoric and lacustrine waters. In this study, we revisit this observed range in δ 13 C and δ 18 Ο of pedogenic carbonates and use clumped isotope thermometry to better understand the fluid histories. We collected 19 paleosol carbonate samples, including nodules and rhizocretions, from four sites, FLK-N (Loc. 45a), SHK (Loc. 91), VEK (Loc. 85), and RHC (Loc. 80), that range from Upper Bed I (~1.91 Ma) to the top of Bed II (~1.14 Ma). We observed that the nodules have complex carbonate textures, suggesting several generations of carbonate formation: nodules from SHK and FLK-N are predominantly micritic with cross-cutting veins, while nodules from VEK are radially layered crystalline calcite. Some nodules have a micritic core that we hypothesize represents primary carbonate formation at the initiation of paleosol formation. The observed morphologies and calcite textures have distinct stable isotope values. Micritic calcite in nodules (n=10) has δ 13 C VPDB and δ 18 O VPDB values ranging from -3.83 to -0.58 and -7.67 to -3.31 ‰, respectively. Crystalline calcite in nodules (n=18) has δ 13 C VPDB values ranging from -7.75 to -1.98 ‰ and δ 18 O VPDB values ranging from -10.10 to -2.94 ‰. Rhizocretions (n=4) have a smaller δ 13 C VPDB range, with values ranging from -5.24 to -1.48 ‰, and a larger δ 18 O VPDB range from -15.88 to -0.86 ‰. Both nodule and rhizocretion values differ drastically from the surficial modern carbonate δ 13 C VPDB and δ 18 O VPDB values of -0.95 ‰ and -2.37 ‰. We will use carbonate clumped-isotope thermometry (Δ 47 ) to explore how this isotopic variation relates to different generations of carbonate formation via meteoric, lacustrine, or volcanic fluids. The diagenetic history and formation temperatures of carbonates will complement other paleoclimatic studies and facilitate temperature reconstructions at Olduvai Gorge.

title: The Future for Mineralogy (and Mineralogists) is Bright
session_title: MSA 2026 Awardees Lectures and Presidential Address
authors: Bodnar, Robert John [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA; Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA
abstract:
The future of mineralogy, sensu lato , has been a topic of much discussion within the mineralogical and geosciences communities in recent years. An analysis conducted in 2008 showed that 79% of geosciences departments required a course in mineralogy to earn a BS degree in geology, and 16% required optical mineralogy. A 2022 analysis showed that the number requiring mineralogy had decreased to 69% and optical mineralogy was not required by any program. Mineralogy was one of three courses (Sed/Strat & Paleo) that showed a >20% decrease between 2008 and 2022.

The critical minerals "revolution" provides a golden opportunity for the mineral sciences. Of the 60 critical minerals (elements) included in the USGS 2025 list, more than half are produced as by- or co-products during mining of some other material. These elements often occur as minor or trace components in ore minerals being mined to produce the dominant metal/element of interest. As an example, an ore mineral for the elements cadmium (Cd), gallium (Ga), germanium (Ge) and indium (In) is sphalerite (ZnS), and Cd, Ga, Ge and In occur as trace to minor components by substituting for Zn in the crystal structure. Additionally, these same elements occur in zinc ferrite (ZnFe 2 O 4 ) that forms during thermal and chemical processing of the zinc ores, where they replace Zn and/or Fe in the crystal structure.

Recent analyses suggest that an enormous critical mineral resource exists in various types of mine wastes that have been generated during more than two centuries of mining in the U.S. In order to develop efficient and cost-effective processes to extract the critical element of interest from the host phase in these waste materials, it is necessary to know the manner in which the elements are hosted within the ore mineral, including the mineral structure, crystallographic setting, distribution, and thermodynamic properties of the host phase and its contained trace and minor element budget. These topics represent the playground of the mineralogist, and our community is in an unprecedented position to lead the way in developing cost-effective methods to characterize and extract critical minerals from mine waste to meet expected increased demand for these materials. The future of mineralogy is bright IF we take advantage of the opportunities that are being presented.

abstract: Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity worldwide, raising questions about how rapidly ecosystems will respond to disturbance under a changing climate. In 2012, a wildfire burned approximately 42 km 2 of the Afroalpine zone within the Rwenzori Mountains, Uganda, which was found to be the first fire in the area since deglaciation about 13.2 ka, and was linked to subsequent destructive downstream flooding and landslides. Here, we investigate the ecological response and regional sedimentary signature of this event using pollen and charcoal records from three lakes within and outside the burn area: Lower Kitandara Lake (outside the primary burn area), Lake Kopello (upper burned catchment), and Lake Africa (burned mid-catchment). All lakes showed an increase in macrocharcoal of an order of magnitude above pre-fire baselines. At Lake Africa, this event was accompanied by elevated microcharcoal concentrations that persisted through an extended sediment interval from 21-10 cmblf. At Lake Africa, a new 210 Pb chronology, and reduced pollen concentrations above the base of the macrocharcoal peak, indicate substantially increased sediment influx following the fire, suggesting prolonged post-fire erosion and charcoal transport into the basin. Vegetation-fire responses suggest that endemic plants associated with the flat boggy valley floors surrounding Lake Africa declined markedly following the fire. In contrast, dominant woody taxa, including Dendrosenecio and ericaceous heath, showed little persistent change, despite visible and extensive fire damage in the modern landscape. However, multivariate analysis indicates distinct pre-fire, disturbance, and post-fire communities, suggesting that although the ecosystem has undergone substantial recovery during the twelve years since the fire, it has not yet returned to its pre-fire state. Combined with long-term Holocene records of pollen and charcoal from these sites, our results demonstrate that, not only was the 2012 wildfire unprecedented within at least 13.2 kyrs, but also that vegetation recovery following these events is slow and accompanied by significant reorganization of lacustrine deposition.

abstract:
Silicic arc melts can produce catastrophic eruptions, yet the processes responsible for their silica enrichment remain contentious. Are these melts generated by the infiltration of slab-derived silicic components into the mantle wedge, or are they derived from mafic mantle melts via crustal differentiation? Because arc magmas commonly undergo crustal-level mixing, tracing individual component melts relies on early-forming phenocrysts like pyroxenes or olivine. Orthopyroxenes are ideal for this purpose because they crystallize over a wide compositional range, and high-Mg# [= molar ratio of Mg/(Fe 2+ +Mg)] varieties reflect early crystallization from primitive, high- Mg# silicic melts.

In this study, we investigated orthopyroxenes from an olivine- and orthopyroxene-phyric, high-Mg# (68) hybrid andesite flow (61.2 wt% SiO 2 ) from the Quaternary monogenetic Guespalapa Volcanic Complex, Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt. Previous He-Os-O isotope studies on olivine from this flow confirmed the presence of mantle-derived component melts (Ahmadi et al., 2025, Chem. Geol. ). We selected euhedral orthopyroxene crystals (500-1000 µm) for EPMA elemental mapping, alongside spot analyses for major elements (Si, Mg, Fe) and selected trace elements (Ni, Al, Ca) via EPMA and LA-ICP-MS.

The high-Mg# of the orthopyroxenes (~84 to 88, corresponding to the melt Mg# of ~ 66 to 79) and high Ni concentrations (>1000 to ~2000 ppm) suggest that orthopyroxene crystallized coevally, and even slightly prior to, olivine. Furthermore, the variable Mg# range in orthopyroxene reveals a broader spectrum of primitive melt compositions than indicated by the bulk rock. Normal, reverse, and complex zoning patterns indicate that these phenocrysts record the assembly and mixing of multiple distinct batches of silicic mantle melts. Altogether, our data demonstrate that the Guespalapa andesite originated via the hybridization of andesitic component melts formed directly in the mantle wedge through melt-rock reactions between peridotite and infiltrating silicic slab components. These findings confirm that primary silicic melts can generate within the mantle wedge.

title: Preferential Manus Preservation of Quadrupeds in the Campanian Kaiparowits Formation, Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, Utah
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments (Posters)
authors: King, Michael Ryan [1], Tucker, Ryan Thomas [2], Brackett, Robert Jeffrey [3], Song, Carla [4], Zanno, Lindsay [5]
affiliations: (1) Natural & Environmental Sciences, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(2) Stellenbosch University, Department of Earth Sciences, Stellenbosch, South Africa
(3) Natural & Environmental Sciences, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(4) Department of Earth Sciences, Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch, South Africa
(5) NC Museum of Natural Sciences, Paleontology, Raleigh, NC,
abstract:
Vertebrate tracks are very rare in the Campanian Kaiparowits Formation of southern Utah, possibly because the waterlogged conditions that characterized many of its depositional paleoenvironments promoted sediment collapse, slumping, and deformation that obscured fine track morphology. One track-bearing interval within the formation contains at least twenty-one tracks preserved as natural casts across several horizons in rippled, fine-grained sandstone interpreted as overbank deposits. Poorly preserved ornithopod and theropod tracks are present, but the most abundant and morphologically distinct specimens consist of steeply inclined impressions (32-90 degrees) containing at least four digits arranged in an arc spanning 134-151 degrees. Sediment deformation extending posteriorly and slightly laterally from the digit impressions preserved on fallen blocks suggests that these features represent manus tracks produced by a quadrupedal animal. The manus track morphology is consistent with a possible ceratopsian trackmaker, although incomplete ankylosaur tracks lacking preservation of the medially-directed digit (I) cannot be entirely excluded because preservation on small, displaced blocks prevents complete verification of the digit’s absence.

The absence of well-defined pes morphologies may reflect the unequal distribution of body weight between the forelimbs and hind limbs of quadrupedal dinosaurs, such as ceratopsians. Greater loading of the pes could have produced deeper, more extensively deformed impressions, whereas the more lightly loaded manus may have formed shallower tracks that retained clearer digit morphology. The pes impressions may therefore be represented by deeper, more amorphous areas of sediment deformation that cannot be confidently identified as individual tracks. Displacement of the track-bearing blocks have obscured the original spatial relationships between the manus and potential amorphous pes, preventing them from being confidently reassociated as manus-pes pairs.

The central digit impressions occasionally contain a deeply recessed, posteriorly convex structure along their anterior portions. These features could represent pronounced sediment-collapse structures produced within the tracks during withdrawal of the manus. However, such extensive collapse may be unexpected given the relatively shallow depth of the digit impressions (<9.3 cm). Alternatively, the structures may indicate that sand beneath the true track surface was displaced downward and subsequently amalgamated with the sand that infilled the track. These manus tracks add to the sparse vertebrate track record of the Kaiparowits Formation and document a previously unreported combination of taphonomic and toponomic features.

title: Linking Pedogenic Ferromanganese Concretions to Soil Climate using Micron-scale Spatial Chemistry – Evidence from a Vertisol Climosequence
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science
authors: Richards, Devin Michael [1], Stinchcomb, Gary E. [2], Nordt, Lee C. [3], Beverly, Emily J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science Department, University of Memphis, Memphis, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Memphis, Memphis, TN, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(4) Earth & Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
abstract:
Bulk geochemical methods for predicting paleoclimate are flawed because other environmental factors (e.g., parent material) can affect the chemistry, interfering with the climate signal. Measuring chemistry of pedogenic soil features preserved in thin section may reveal elemental trends which record the chemical history of a soil feature in response to climate without additional parent material influence. Although untested, benchtop micro X-ray Fluorescence (μ-XRF) instruments offer a possible solution by spatially resolving chemistry in the soil or paleosol at the micron scale, which would allow isolation of pedogenic features more directly related to soil climate, particularly moisture regime. The non-destructive analysis of pedogenic soil features within billets and thin sections could provide insights more directly linked to soil climate dynamics than bulk geochemistry methods alone.

This study revisits a Texas Vertisol climosequence where the soil forming factors apart from climate are relatively constant. A subset of the climosequence sites with differing mean annual precipitations (MAP) and soil moisture regimes (SMR) were selected for study: Victoria Series (894 mm yr -1 , Ustic SMR), Lake Charles Series (1,124 mm yr -1 , Udic SMR), and League Series (1,411 mm yr -1 , Oxyaquic Udic SMR). We used an AtlasX μ-XRF to characterize micron-scale cross-section chemistry of ferromanganese concretions to quantify changing abundances of redox-sensitive elements (Fe & Mn). Preliminary results have replicated previous work correlating Fe abundance with rainfall and μ-XRF has increased the precision this method through the addition of previously unidentifiable diffuse concretions. Scanning elemental chemistry of pedogenic feature cross-sections shows that the maximum ratio of Fe/Mn within a concretion is positively correlated with MAP. The strength of this correlation varies with depth and is highest in the subsurface horizons, and lowest in the bottom horizons. Concretions sampled in the ustic SMR are Mn-dominant (>50% Mn), but those sampled from udic and oxyaquic udic SMR are Fe-dominant. These results are encouraging and will be used to develop a model that links ferromanganese concretion formation at different depths as a function of climate in modern Vertisols. Future work will include modern Vertisols with varying ages and parent material to test the robustness of the model.

title: A Clade Estranged – Investigating Historical Biogeography of Horseshoe Crabs
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Congreve, Curtis Raymond [1], Lamsdell, James Christopher [2]
affiliations: (1) NC State University, Raleigh, NC,
(2) University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
abstract: Xiphosurids (horseshoe crabs) are aquatic chelicerate arthropods with a 455 Myr evolutionary history. The four extant species have a markedly disconnected geographic distribution, with Limulus polyphemus occurring along the eastern coast of North America (inhabiting the western North Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico) while Tachypleus gigas , Tachypleus tridentatus , and Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda have a combined range encompassing the eastern coastline of India to the southern tip of Japan (inhabiting the Bay of Bengal and South China Sea). How these species ended up in their respective regions – at the opposite ends of two oceans, separated by a continent – remains a major untested question. Previous hypotheses posit that modern horseshoe crabs are relics of a global distribution after the breakup of Pangaea, or that the Asian species are the result of migration across Europe from North America. In order to test these hypotheses we conducted a BioGeoBEARS biogeographic analysis of 41 species using an existing Bayesian phylogenetic topology. We also use the results of this study to comment on the impact of incomplete sampling on the utility of modelling jump dispersal (the J statistic) in biogeographic analyses.

title: Humanizing STEM: A Framework for Building Neurodivergent-Affirming Partnerships Between STEM Students and Instructors
session_title: Making Sense of Methodologies and Theoretical Frameworks in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Lepore, Taormina [1], Hunter, Erin E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Mallinson Institute for Science Education and Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(2) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
abstract:
Humanizing pedagogies have been applied in STEM fields for the last two decades, driven by a mindset where students and instructors are seen as whole people and partners in learning, rather than empty vessels of learning or strict purveyors of content. Humanizing STEM (HSTEM) was forged by undergraduate student action in light of racial injustice in the United States, and has resulted in STEM instructors and students working together to co-build these more humanizing environments in college STEM. Implementing aspects of HSTEM can take many forms, including Universal Design for Learning, culturally responsive teaching, building empathetic and action-based learning communities, and more. As a framework, it has been applied through the lenses of multiple intersectional identities such as race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, but rarely through neurodivergent identity as a main focal point.

This talk explores humanizing STEM as a framework and vehicle for building neurodivergent-affirming partnerships in the geosciences, with neurodivergent STEM students and instructors working together as the primary drivers of potential change in STEM academic environments. Reflections from a student focus group following our recent neurodivergent student-instructor HSTEM partnership will be briefly underscored. Preliminary reflexive thematic analysis codes within these reflections center on STEM sense of belonging, believing and implementing accommodation needs, and and more visible representation and diversity in STEM. This talk will share key recommendations for implementing HSTEM in discipline-based geosciences education research, based on the broad STEM partnership, which included geoscience partners. Humanizing STEM and neurodivergent-affirming partnerships can be used in tandem with critical theory to guide research that more fully incorporates students, and neurodivergent people, as full partners rather than subjects of research design.

title: Heterogeneous Grain-Boundary Glasses in Granulite Xenoliths from the Geronimo Volcanic Field, Southeastern Arizona: Evidence for In Situ Melting
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Parker, Slade A. [1], Kempton, Pamela D. [2], Hindall, Andrew G. [3]
affiliations: (1) Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
(2) Kansas State University, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS,
(3) Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS,
abstract:
Two-pyroxene, two-feldspar granulite xenoliths from the Geronimo Volcanic Field, Arizona, are known to contain rare rhyolitic melt inclusions hosted in plagioclase feldspar [1]. Many of these same xenoliths also containgrain boundary glasses, raising questions about the origin(s) of the precursor melts and the relationship, if any, to the melt inclusions. Are the glasses indicative of infiltration by the host alkali basalt during ascent to the surface, or do they represent in situ melting that occurred sometime prior to entrainment? Here we use standard transmitted light petrography combined with scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) to address this question.

In plane-polarized light, the glasses show significant variation in color on the scale of microns, ranging from colorless to dark brown. Colorless glasses tend to occur as thin films up to tens of mm thick along grain boundaries, particularly adjacent to quartz and feldspar; these colorless glass films can be traced as continuous networks over large portions of a thin section in some cases. In contrast, brown glasses tend to form larger ‘pools’, occurring in interstitial areas adjacent to pyroxenes and/or oxides. In some cases, the two glass types are observed grading into one another. SEM-EDS analyses suggest that the colorless glasses are compositionally similar to the entrapped melt inclusions, being strongly enriched in K 2 O and Na 2 O with low FeO and MgO. Thermodynamic modeling by [1] suggests that these compositions are consistent with eutectic melting in this system. The compositional similarity between grain boundary glasses and melt inclusions suggests a similar formation mechanism, but the different modes of occurrence suggest they may have formed at different times; in general, grain boundary glasses are not observed in contact with entrapped melt inclusions. In contrast, brown glasses have higher FeO, MgO, and CaO contents but lower total alkalis (Na 2 O + K 2 O), consistent with a contribution from mafic minerals adjacent to the melt pools. The brown glass compositions are also distinct from the host alkali basalts. In combination with the observed compositional heterogeneity, we interpret the brown glasses as the product of localized in situ melting prior to entrainment and not the result of infiltration from the host basalts during ascent.

[1] Hindall et al., 2026, Goldschmidt Conference 2026, Paper ID: 37795.

title: Lessons learned from a CURE for an upper-level Paleontology Course
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Moss, David Kelton [1], Srivastava-Losey, Shravya [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX, ; Natural History Collection, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, Texas, USA
(2) Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX,
abstract: Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences, whereby a large portion of a traditional course is focused on providing students with authentic research opportunities, have shown to improve student learning outcomes. Such experiences also provide valuable skills desired by employers such as data analysis, working in groups, and scientific communication. Here, we present lessons learned and survey results from a first attempt at CUREing an upper-level Paleontology of Invertebrates class. This class ran during the spring 2026 semester and had an enrollment of 15 students. Our goal was to introduce the CURE concept, while also covering some of the traditional topics in paleontology. To facilitate student research projects, all students participated in a six-day field trip featuring localities in Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida. Students also visited the Florida Museum of Natural History and were given behind the scenes tours by museum personnel. While in the field, students focused on collecting bulk samples from Cenozoic units for use in projects related to taxonomy, predation, and life history questions. Students were divided into groups of three and prepared posters for an on campus undergraduate research symposium, where they were given formal feedback and evaluations by faculty members from other STEM departments. At the end of the semester, students were asked to complete a survey with 10 Likert style questions (1 = do not agree at all; 5 = agree a great deal) aimed at understanding student experiences, self-efficacy in research, and improvement in research skills and knowledge. In addition, the survey had three open-ended questions aimed at improving the course moving forward. Of the 15 students enrolled, nine completed full surveys. Survey responses indicate that for the majority of students, this was their first authentic research experience (average 3.8/5). Students indicated that they improved their research skills over the course of the semester (4.5/5) and their ability to properly conduct scientific inquiry (average 4.3/5). Most students also agreed that they gained a basic understanding of paleontological concepts (average 4.3/5) and that they could apply research techniques they learned during the CURE to other courses (average 4.5/5). Finally, for improvements to the course, responses focused on balancing time between the research project and lecture topics. These data suggest a successful CURE with room for improvement in the next iteration.

abstract:
Airborne magnetic data acquired across northeastern Minnesota through the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) will image the geologic framework of the Midcontinent Rift at unprecedented resolution. Whether bedrock is exposed or beneath patchy glacial cover, magnetic anomalies constrain the subsurface geometry of intrusive complexes and volcanic successions. These include intrusions hosting magmatic Cu-Ni-Co-PGE sulfide and Fe-Ti oxide mineralization. Realizing this potential requires rock property data that remain sparse across the rift's diverse lithologies. In the Duluth Complex, remanent magnetization typically dominates induced magnetization (Koenigsberger ratio Q > 1), so processing and modeling approaches that assume magnetization parallel to the present field will not be successful without constraints on remanence.

As part of hands-on training on state-of-the-art instrumentation at the Institute for Rock Magnetism Summer School, participants characterized a single drill core that intersects the South Kawishiwi intrusion, whose basal zone hosts magmatic Cu-Ni-PGE sulfide mineralization above footwall granitoids of the Archean Giants Range Batholith. Their measurements quantify natural remanent magnetization (NRM), susceptibility, and Q, and constrain magnetic mineralogy, domain state, coercivity, and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS).

The main augite troctolite composing most of the intersected intrusion is magnetically consistent, with remanence carried by low-Ti titanomagnetite and Q > 1 throughout. The mineralized basal zone is markedly heterogeneous. Ultramafic horizons—marker units associated with oxide concentrations and elevated PGE values—have the highest NRM intensities in the core and are most strongly remanence-dominated. Hematite becomes the principal carrier in granophyre and oxidized troctolite, while footwall granitoids pair relatively high susceptibility with low Q. Remanence directions and AMS fabrics are consistent with modest post-emplacement tilting.

These data anchor interpretation of the intrusion's aeromagnetic expression: remanence must be incorporated into anomaly models of this mineralized district, and the contrast between the consistent troctolite interior and heterogeneous basal zone is a petrophysical fingerprint for tracing mineralized stratigraphy in the subsurface—a step towards the much larger foundation needed to fully leverage Earth MRI aeromagnetic data across the rift.

authors: Rubins, Avery Helen [1], Guido, Lauren Elizabeth [2], Rengers, Francis Kevin [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA

abstract: Wildfire in steep and severely burned terrain can increase the likelihood of debris flows that are fueled by excessive surface-water runoff and sediment erosion. However, there are not large existing databases that show exactly where debris flows begin or where they start to deposit, making it difficult to develop statistical models that can identify potential initiation/deposition locations based on the geomorphology of a site. In this study, we contribute to creating this type of database by mapping postfire debris-flow initiation points, as well as points marking the onset of debris-flow deposition. We used field-verified debris-flow channels, as well as previously unidentified debris-flow channels in 14 burn scars in Arizona, Southern California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, and Oregon. We used digital elevation model differencing from before and after debris-flow events and high-resolution aerial imagery, as input data to guide the identification and mapping of the initiation/deposition points. Initiation points with the highest confidence ratings had discrete morphologic signatures, with change detection displaying incision greater than 25 cm, channel widening more than 1 m, and over 50 m of continuous erosion. Points marking the onset of deposition with the highest confidence ratings demonstrated change detection showed deposition greater than 25 cm in depth and channel widening greater than 1 m. These mapped points resulted in a dataset that will help analyze the specific geomorphic settings where debris flows initiate and begin to deposit.

abstract: On present-day Mars, the condensation and sublimation of seasonal ices drives landscape evolution by creating new surface features or altering existing ones. To better understand ice-induced landscape evolution, we need remote sensing observations capable of discriminating between CO 2 and H 2 O ices, as each affects the surface differently. However, most remote sensing datasets capable of identifying martian ice compositions have coarse resolution or limited spatial coverage. In this work, we aimed to understand whether the visual appearance of ice-covered sand dunes could be diagnostic of ice composition within the northern mid-latitudes (30-65 ᵒ N), thus providing an alternative method to determine ice composition at the landform scale. We reviewed 700 visible-wavelength HiRISE images to infer ice composition based on patterns in dune-ice morphologies. The inferred ice compositions were then compared with known ice compositions from prior seasonal ice mapping results, as well as surface temperature and spectral observations at the location of each dune field. Ultimately, we determined that dune ice with high surface brightness and sublimation-induced spots and cracks is consistent with CO 2 ice composition, while dune ice without these features indicates H 2 O ice composition. These results open new opportunities to study the martian seasonal water cycle at high resolution while also improving ice composition interpretations at the landform scale, adding to our understanding of ice-induced landscape evolution.

abstract: Newly recognized covariation between rare earth elements plus yttrium (REY) and germanium (Ge) in coal-associated non-coal strata of the Powder River Basin (PRB), Wyoming, raises questions about the origin of this geochemical association. Its persistence across multiple lithologies, locations, and sequential leach fractions suggests that this signature may reflect an inherited source-rock signature rather than independent enrichment during deposition or diagenesis. Alkaline igneous complexes exposed in uplifts surrounding the PRB represent plausible sediment sources to the basin, and existing whole-rock geochemical data from the nearby Bear Lodge Alkaline Complex exhibit similarly strong REY-Ge covariation. Apatite-group minerals are a potential mineralogical link between these systems because they are common in alkaline and carbonatitic rocks and are structurally able to incorporate REY and Ge via coupled substitutions. This ongoing study investigates REY and Ge occurrence in apatite and other potential host phases from three Wyoming igneous centers: the REY-enriched, carbonatitic Bear Lodge Alkaline Complex; the REY-depleted, carbonatitic Rattlesnake Hills Alkaline Complex; and the Laramie Anorthosite Complex, including the REY-enriched, non-carbonatitic Red Mountain pluton and the REY-depleted, non-carbonatitic Poe Mountain anorthosite. We present preliminary whole-rock geochemistry, petrography, electron microscopy, and in situ mineral chemistry to evaluate whether REY-Ge covariation is observed at the mineral scale and to identify the phases responsible for coupled enrichment. Comparisons among complexes are used to assess the roles of silica activity, volatile content, redox conditions, melt evolution, and hydrothermal alteration in promoting or disrupting REY-Ge coupling. Our findings contribute to the understanding of critical mineral partitioning in compositionally unusual magmatic systems.

title: Securing Field Camps for the Present and Future: Collaborative Action and Sustainable Field Education Models from Friends of Field Camps (FOFC)
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Reynolds, A-Lan [1], Appelbaum, Bruce [2]
affiliations: (1) Friends of Field Camps, USA; Reynolds Field Station for Education & Science Research, New Mexico, USA
(2) AAPG, Houston, TX, ; Friends of Field Camps, USA
abstract:
Geologic mapping underpins critical interpretations across energy, water resources, environmental engineering, hazards mitigation, and mineral exploration. However, the foundational training ground where future mappers develop spatial reasoning and observational discipline—university field camps—faces severe challenges. Declining enrollments, escalating operating costs, and diminishing institutional support threaten the survival of field programs nationwide. If field education falters, who will train and become the mappers of tomorrow?

To address this field skills crisis, the Friends of Field Camps (FOFC) coalition emerged in 2025 as a national alliance of professional societies and foundations, government agencies, geoscience faculty, and industry partners. FOFC is taking coordinated action across several key pillars to help field education survive and thrive:

● Student Recruitment & Access: Developing a central national clearinghouse website featuring an AI-powered search engine (in partnership with AGI) to streamline how students discover camps, evaluate program attributes, and access scholarship support.

● Web Forum for Field Camp Directors and Faculty: Developing a national member web portal for field camp directors, faculty and department chairs to network, share best practices in methods and safety, exchange cost-saving strategies and identify resources.

● Advocacy: Engaging and informing universities, state and national governmental agencies and industry regarding the critical role of field and mapping skills now and in the future.

● Career Development: Encouraging curricula that balance rigorous solid-earth mapping fundamentals with modern digital tools, such as drone imagery, GIS, and high-precision GPS metadata. Demonstrating alignment with evolving professional licensing standards (GIT/PG) highlights the career value of field training to students and university administrators.

● Sustainable Business Models: Developing and piloting innovative, financially solvent field camp frameworks, such as regional consortia to pool student and faculty cohorts and to reduce costs, shared infrastructure, modular or split-session options (e.g., 3+3 weeks) to reduce student opportunity costs, and best practice examples of grassroots alumni engagement strategies to fund capital expenses.

To meet future mapping demand, field education must broaden beyond traditional boundaries to encompass the full spectrum of modern geosciences. This talk invites faculty to engage with FOFC’s shared resources, assess adaptable program models, and participate in a unified effort to inspire, train, and secure the next generation of field geoscience mappers.

abstract:
Morphological Variation in Linear Vertebrate Trace Fossils from the Turonian Ferron Sandstone, Central Utah

Montgomery, Mackenzie; Gillam, Rachel; Hatch, Mazzy; Walsh, Reghan; Smith, Kaylan; Sloan, Dhara; Indigo, Liam; Struski, Raegan; and King, M. Ryan

Western Colorado University, 1 Western Way, Gunnison, CO 81231

Four morphotypes of vertebrate trace fossils occur in the Turonian Ferron Sandstone of central Utah. These traces are distributed among three localities within 650 meters of one another and occur within a 5-meter-thick stratigraphic interval. All four morphotypes contain parallel linear furrows, but they differ in preservation, feature number, relative length, and spacing. These morphotypes demonstrate variations in trace morphology that are dictated by trackmaker foot anatomy and behavior.

Morphotype 1 is preserved as a natural mold and consists of two prominent linear features of nearly equal length within a broader depression that terminates against a topographically raised margin. Unlike the elongate traces typically associated with swimming locomotion, Morphotype 1 may record irregular movement, sediment disturbance, digging, or foraging behavior. This trace fossil’s occurrence on a surface dominated by Amblydactylus , Iguanodontipus , and Therangospodus tracks suggest that it was produced by a tridactyl dinosaur.

Morphotypes 2 through 4 are preserved as natural casts on sandstone bed soles and are interpreted as swim traces comparable to Characichnos . Morphotype 2 contains three similarly sized, evenly spaced linear features, suggesting that three digits of similar length contacted the substrate approximately equally. Morphotype 3 also contains three similarly spaced features, but the central feature is longer and more prominent. This morphology is consistent with a tridactyl trackmaker possessing an elongated central digit, potentially a theropod. Morphotype 4 contains three linear features, with two positioned closer together and the third separated by a wider interval. This asymmetrical spacing is indicative a crocodylian trackmaker.

title: Probabilistic 3D Mapping of Critical Minerals Using Hard-and-Soft Conditioned Diffusion Models
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Yoon, Hongkyu [1], Xu, Guangping [2]
affiliations: (1) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have driven new approaches for subsurface energy and critical mineral resource evaluation. Accurate 3D characterization of these subsurface systems is essential for estimating total resource tonnage, determining economic viability, and optimizing targeted recovery operations. However, integrating multiple sensing modalities presents multifaceted challenges. These include a scarcity of direct measurements, massive unsampled volumetric gaps, and severe spatial resolution mismatches—contrasting highly accurate but spatially limited point data (e.g., well logs, core samples) with coarse, wide-area remote sensing (e.g., seismic surveys, hyperspectral imagery). Furthermore, characterizing critical minerals and rare earth elements is inherently difficult due to their exceptionally low localized concentrations and trace distributions. In this work, we advance 3D subsurface resource estimation by fusing heterogeneous datasets via multivariate generative diffusion models. We utilize localized, point-based observations as hard conditioning data, while integrating wider spatial sensing and geological priors (e.g., lithofacies, geophysics) as soft conditioning data. By performing joint distribution learning, the diffusion model effectively synthesizes trace element data concurrently with structural priors. Crucially, the stochastic nature of the diffusion process generates probabilistic ensembles that preserve spatial heterogeneity, accurately recreating sharp geological boundaries and high-grade structural pockets. We demonstrate this hard-and-soft conditioned framework using multiscale, multimodal laboratory data, highlighting its utility for assessing economic resource potential and informing extraction strategies in complex geological formations. title: Deep Time: The Past and Future of Geology and Society
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Lutz, Tim [1], Srogi, LeeAnn [2]
affiliations: (1) West Chester University, West Chester, PA, USA
(2) West Chester University, West Chester, PA, USA
abstract:
As Americans were proclaiming their independence from Britain 250 years ago, another revolution was underway: Hutton and Playfair, and later Lyell, proposed that Earth’s history was much longer than acknowledged by European scientists. This temporal revolution showed that a complete conception of Earth’s past has to include processes as quick as an asteroid impact and as slow as the movement of plates, playing out over Earth’s 4.54 billion year history. The temporal revolution succeeded by discovering and objectively quantifying Earth’s deep history, providing useful knowledge for society.

Now another temporal transformation is brewing – the Anthropocene Revolution (AR). The AR is an awakening of society to planetary change that is not only “now” but that arises in the context of Earth’s deep history, and it portends human influence extending into a geologically long future. AR concepts have emerged from the geosciences, social sciences, humanities, and arts, and the discussions are mainly independent of when or whether there is formal stratigraphic recognition of an Anthropocene epoch or event. As the AR proceeds, society will require geology to speak more clearly to humanity’s relation to earth’s deep past and to anthropogenic change in a deep future. During the next 250 years deep time will need to be more accessible, relevant, and meaningful to all.

We show how to make three improvements to our thinking about deep time. First, by reexamining a philosophy of time which reflects the scientific advances of the last 250 years but that can be expanded to aid the AR. Second, by improving the analogies we use to understand and convey deep time. Linear analogies fail to create perceptually powerful experiences from abstract chronological data and they promote a false conception that deep time is incomprehensible. Volumetric analogies better reflect the realities of geologic change and bring the scope and pace of earth’s history to human scale. Third, by developing pedagogies that make the deep past and deep future present in our classrooms. As a chapter in a textbook or a line on a syllabus, “time” is reduced to a topic separated from the geology that gave rise to the timescale. Thoroughly embedding deep time analogies in our classes brings us into the context of earth’s past and its emerging future.

title: Niche Partitioning Between Small-Bodied Insectivorous Mammals During Early Eocene Climate Fluctuation, Willwood Formation (56-52 Ma), Bighorn Basin, WY
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Kuhn, Reagan [1], Nichols, Kimberly A. [2], Bown, Thomas M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Anthropology and Geography, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Anthropology and Geography, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA

abstract: The early Eocene (56-52 Ma) is a paleontologically significant time period characterized by the appearance and proliferation of ancestors and relatives of modern mammalian groups as well as climate fluctuations analogous to modern climate instability. Analysis of modern and fossil taxa is instrumental for understanding early Eocene faunal ecology and adaptations, and the results in turn can be used to inform conservation efforts for modern mammals. Focusing on Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, Willwood Formation, fossil taxa, this study examines the potential for competition and niche partitioning between two early Eocene faunivorous small-bodied mammals: Haplomylus , an extinct relative of today’s elephant shrew (Order Macroscelidea) in Africa, and omomyid primate Tetonius in the lineage that gave rise to modern tarsiers in Asia along with modern monkeys, apes, and humans. It compares characteristics including distribution, locomotion, diet, activity, and body mass responses to well-documented thermal temperature fluctuations (PETM) using literature review, analysis of Haplomylus and Tetonius dental morphology, and geospatial analysis of fossil distribution using specimens and data from the Colorado State University Primate Origins Lab. Results show partial niche overlap in areas of diet, distribution, and body mass alongside diverging adaptations in other areas. This indicates indirect competition and increasing niche partitioning related to environmental stressors, which informs these animals’ evolutionary pathways and responses to significant climate fluctuations, thus providing insights applicable to conservation strategies for their modern descendants.

title: Petrology of a Franciscan garnet lawsonite blueschist from the southern Diablo Range (California, USA) and Automated Mapping of Inclusions in Garnets Utilizing ArcGIS and SEM-EDS Phase Maps

authors: Regnier, Lucien Duque [1], Page, F. Zeb [2], Flood, Clara Margaret [3]
affiliations: (1) Oberlin Geoscience Department, Oberlin College, San Rafael, California, USA

abstract: Existing petrologic studies of high-grade tectonic blocks hosted by the Franciscan Formation are largely focused on samples from the more northern reaches of the formation. Here, we report on a garnet lawsonite blueschist found as a small boulder weathered out of Franciscan mélange near Pacheco Pass in the southern Diablo range (California, U.S.A.). Thin sections were analyzed petrographically and by SEM-EDS. Samples are composed of glaucophane, garnet, sodic pyroxene (Jd 62 Ac 11 ), quartz, lawsonite, epidote, sphene, rutile, and apatite. Small (~0.5-1.2mm) euhedral to subhedral garnets are predominantly almandine, while displaying minimal major cation zoning other than in Mn (Sps 9.8 cores and Sps 0.1 rims). Glaucophane has thin rims slightly enriched in Fe. Garnets contain inclusions of jadeite, glaucophane, lawsonite, quartz, rutile, and sphene, ranging in size from 10 to 50 μm. Lawsonite makes up 20% of bulk rock as subhedral crystals in the matrix as well as part of late veins with quartz. Chlorite is notably absent. Some matrix sphene crystals preserve relict rutile in their cores. Modeling using Equilibrium Assemblage Diagrams (EADs) unsurprisingly does not reconstruct the full observed assemblage. However, a garnet, glaucophane, lawsonite, pyroxene, rutile, quartz assemblage is predicted at ~500˚C, >15kbar. Further modelling to assess the effects of changing f O2 and Ca-metasomatism are ongoing.To better understand the distribution of inclusions in garnet, SEM-EDS phase maps were analyzed using custom scaling in a Geographic Information System (GIS) to measure their distance from the 2-D garnet centroid. By scripting the procedure, 25,000 inclusions were measured in a single thin section. Probability density functions for all five inclusion phases have individual peaks with modes between 40-70%. The asymmetry of the inclusion distribution is very similar to the distribution of melt inclusions in migmatites as measured by X-ray computed microtomography (Parisatto et al., 2018). Ongoing research will apply microscopic computed tomography scanning to analyze radial distances of garnet inclusions in 3D in these samples.

abstract: Ediacaran–early Cambrian mixed siliciclastic and carbonate successions of the southern Canadian Cordillera are widely exposed across the northern Cariboo Mountains of British Columbia. Despite this, these strata still lack a modern sedimentological and chronostratigraphic framework. Here, we integrate new measured stratigraphic sections with paleontological and chemostratigraphic data from the Cunningham and Yankee Belle formations of the Cariboo Group across a transect of the northern Cariboo Mountains. We recognize twelve distinct facies in these units that predominantly reflect deposition in upper slope to inner ramp carbonate-dominated settings with local fluvio-deltaic intervals. Carbonate carbon isotopes from the Cunningham and Yankee Belle formations range from approximately -6 to +6‰ and exhibit several excursions that may be correlative with similar isotopic data from other successions globally. This includes an approximately -6‰ negative excursion in the Yankee Belle Formation that may represent the basal Cambrian carbon isotope excursion (BACE). These data are supported by an unpublished detrital zircon maximum depositional age of ca. 548 Ma from the upper Cunningham Formation, but more work is underway to refine these geochronological constraints. Together, these data help establish the nature and timing of carbonate sedimentation in the Cariboo Mountains and refine regional and global correlations of Ediacaran–Cambrian strata in the Canadian Cordillera.

abstract: The identification of the hydrated mineral ikaite (CaCO 3 ·6H 2 O) and its polymineralic pseudomorph, glendonite, is frequently used as a proxy for cold water temperatures in ancient sedimentary successions. In recent years, however, experimental work has shown that a variety of other factors, such as methane release, may drive metastable ikaite precipitation in marine sediments without requiring near-freezing conditions. We discovered abundant glendonites throughout the type area of the Lower Cretaceous Mount Goodenough Formation in the Aklavik Range of Northwest Territories, Canada. In addition to being the first detailed report of these features in Cretaceous rocks of the Beaufort Sea area, the glendonites are also intimately associated with methane and/or hydrocarbon seep carbonates and local tephra horizons. Here, we characterize the sedimentology and stratigraphy of the Mount Goodenough Formation in its type area. Second, we present new whole-rock geochemical results from Mount Goodenough mudstones, as well as new carbonate carbon and oxygen isotopic data from the glendonites and seep carbonates. Finally, we present new zircon U-Pb ages from the Mount Goodenough tephras that confirm its Barremian depositional age and point to potential distal volcanic products from the High Arctic large igneous province (HALIP). These new data ultimately provide new insight into the reliability of ikaite as a temperature proxy and provide new paleoclimatic information for the Canadian Arctic margin in the Early Cretaceous.

abstract: Secure supplies of critical minerals and materials (CMM) are essential to industrial competitiveness, energy technologies, and national security. This study explores whether rocks already developed for oil and gas production could also become a future source of these valuable elements. The Woodford shale is a major hydrocarbon-producing formation and contains elevated CMM inventories. Leveraging existing petroleum infrastructure to inject engineered fluids could enable in situ CMM recovery from unconventional reservoirs. We conducted column flow-through experiments on Woodford shale grains at 90°C and 90 bar to evaluate chelation CMM extraction under reservoir-relevant conditions. 0.2 M Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid solution was injected continuously for 12 days, and daily effluents were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma optical spectroscopy (ICP-OES) to quantify dissolved CMM concentrations and calculate element-specific extraction efficiencies. X-ray micro-computed tomography (XMT) was conducted on the shale-grain column before and after the experiment to quantify changes in grain size distribution, specific surface area, and porosity. Chromium, manganese, strontium, vanadium, zinc, titanium, lithium, yttrium, cerium, lanthanum, and neodymium were able to be extracted. Overall, manganese and zinc had the highest metal extraction efficiency (MEE%) around 50%. Titanium was the lowest value, 2.18%. Strontium extracted 25.79% from the source rock in the first day, with minimal values afterwards. As for rare earth elements, cerium had the highest MEE% of 9.12% while lanthanum was the lowest at 1.44%. Most of the rare earth elements had the most extracted on day one, while yttrium extracted the most on day 7. Data suggests manganese is extracted from the clays or sulfides, zinc from the organics, and strontium from the carbonates. XMT data is consistent with the ICP-OES findings, showing minimal difference in the grains before and after the extraction. Coupling effluent chemistry with micro-CT-derived structural metrics provides a basis for assessing the feasibility of engineered-fluid in situ mining of CMMs from Woodford shale.

title: The Evaluation of Three-Dimensional Shapes of Sand Grains Using Microfocus X-Ray Computed Tomography: Implications for the Discrimination Between Fluvial and Foreshore Environments
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Maeda, Yushiro [1], Ohta, Tohru [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Resources and Environmental Engineering, Graduate School of Creative Science and Engineering, Waseda University, Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
(2) Faculty of Education and Integrated Arts and Sciences, School of Education, Waseda University, Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
abstract:
The shape of clastic grains has been considered as an essential indicator of the depositional environments and hydrodynamic experience that grains have undergone. Therefore, many studies have been pursued to quantify the shape of clastic grains.

For example, Suzuki et al. (2015) applied elliptic Fourier principal component analysis to two-dimensional sand-grain outlines and showed that grains from glacial, fluvial, foreshore, and aeolian environments could be quantitatively discriminated.

However, this scheme is based on arbitrary two-dimensional projections of grains, which cannot fully capture their three-dimensional shape. Microfocus X-ray computed tomography enables three-dimensional characterization of modern grains and may permit nondestructive analysis of ancient grains within sandstones. This study investigates whether three-dimensional grain shape can discriminate between modern fluvial and foreshore environments.

Approximately 30 sand grains of 0.5–2.0 mm grain size were analyzed at each of twelve fluvial sites along the Shinano River, central Japan, and seven foreshore sites scattered in Japan. Three-dimensional surface models of sand grains were acquired using microfocus X-ray computed tomography (ComscanX Mini90-1616, Comscantecno Co., Ltd., Yokohama, Japan). We conducted visual inspections of sand grains by stereo microscope and confirmed that all 3D images used in this study were accurate. Volume-equivalent diameter, elongation ratio, flatness ratio, sphericity, and solidity (concavity) were calculated for each grain.

Standardized Principal Component Analysis was performed on the individual-grain values to produce the composite indices of macroscopic grain shape parameters. Principal Component 1 (PC1) showed positive correlations with sphericity and solidity. Therefore, PC1 represented a composite shape index, with positive scores indicating more spherical and less concave grains and negative scores indicating less spherical and more concave grains.

PC2 was mainly associated with volume-equivalent diameter as a positive load and elongation ratio as a negative load. Therefore, PC2 captured grain-size variation. Six of the seven foreshore sites had positive PC1 scores, whereas nine of the twelve fluvial sites had negative scores, indicating that foreshore grains were generally more spherical and less concave than fluvial grains. Little separation was observed along PC2, indicating that the environmental separation was associated primarily with three-dimensional grain shape rather than grain size.

This preliminary study indicates that 3D analysis of sand grains are promising and may enable discrimination of depositional environments by further studies.

abstract: Beginning with the 2007 discovery of endogenous (original) protein preserved within the femoral midshaft of a 67-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex , paleomolecular research has increasingly explored the preservation of original soft tissues and biomolecules in the fossil record. Recent studies have recovered cellular and soft tissue microstructures morphologically and molecularly consistent with those of modern vertebrates, including osteocytes (bone cells), blood vessels, and traces of proteins. However, most such investigations have examined a single fragment of dense cortical bone from a limb bone midshaft based on a long-standing assumption that this region offers the greatest potential for preserving endogenous soft tissues and biomolecules. Consequently, little is known about the spatial heterogeneity of biomineral and molecular preservation within individual skeletal elements. To address this knowledge gap, 12 cores were circumferentially excised from around the epiphyses and midshaft of a complete tibia of an Edmontosaurus annectens , the preservation of which were evaluated via trace element analyses, demineralization assays, and histological analyses of vascular density. Sum rare earth element (ΣREE) concentrations varied substantially among sampling locations, occasionally differing by nearly an order of magnitude. The greatest degree of geochemical alteration occurred within the distal epiphysis, whereas the proximal epiphysis possessed the lowest ΣREE concentrations. Burial orientation also influenced geochemical signatures: bone surfaces that faced stratigraphically upward consistently exhibited higher ΣREE concentrations than downward-facing surfaces. Comparisons of geochemical data with soft tissue recovery revealed a negative correlation between ΣREE concentrations and osteocyte preservation, with the highest yields of preserved bone cells deriving from samples exhibiting the lowest ΣREE concentrations. In contrast, vascular density showed no consistent relationship with soft tissue preservation. In some cores, porous cancellous bone yielded preservation equivalent to—or better than—that of dense cortical bone, suggesting that vascular density alone does not govern endogenous soft tissue preservation. These results represent the first comparative investigation of spatial variability in trace element geochemistry, cellular and soft tissue preservation, and vascular density within a single fossil bone. Our findings demonstrate that fossilization and molecular preservation are inherently heterogeneous within a single bone, challenging the assumption that dense midshaft cortex represents a universally optimal target for paleomolecular investigations. This highlights the importance of employing spatial sampling strategies in future studies.

title: New Geologic Mapping of the Ladycomb Peak and Van Horn Basin 7.5” Quadrangles, SE Oregon: Detailing a Newly Discovered Layered Mafic Intrusion of the Columbia River Basalt Group
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Collins, Rachel Anne [1], Streck, Martin J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Portland State University, Vancouver, WA, USA
(2) Geology Department, Portland State University, Portland, OR,
abstract:
New 1:24,000-scale geologic mapping of the 310 km² Ladycomb Peak and Van Horn Basin 7.5” quadrangles in the Pueblo Mountains of southeastern Oregon documents the distribution, stratigraphic relationships, structural geology, and intrusive architecture of volcanic, intrusive, metamorphic, and surficial deposits along the Oregon-Nevada border. Mapping was done as part of the U.S. Geological Survey EDMAP project and focused on a newly discovered mafic intrusion, here named Ladycomb Layered Mafic Intrusion (LLMI). The project integrated detailed field observations with petrography, whole-rock geochemistry, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, and critical mineral analyses to refine the understanding of this previously understudied portion of the Columbia River Basalt Province and to establish the relationships among regional volcanism, intrusive magmatism, and hydrothermal alteration.

Field relationships, petrography, whole-rock geochemistry, and an 40 Ar/ 39 Ar age of 16.656 ± 0.048 Ma demonstrate that the intrusion is associated with Columbia River Basalt Group magmatism, and in particular with Steens Basalt magmatism. The Ladycomb Layered Mafic Intrusion (LLMI) is a differentiated mafic intrusion emplaced into lava flows of the Steens Basalt. The LLMI represents the first recognized layered mafic intrusion associated with Columbia River Basalt Province magmatism. The intrusion is broadly divided into Border, Layered, and Feeder Series based on its mapped morphology and intrusive relationships. The Layered Series is further subdivided into Upper and Lower Zones that contain contrasting successions of olivine gabbro, gabbronorite, leucogabbro, and oxide-bearing cumulates.

The revised geologic framework also refines the structural evolution of the Pueblo Mountains and documents the interaction between Miocene magmatism and subsequent Basin and Range faulting, as well as instances of magmatic and hydrothermal mineralization. Weak orthomagmatic oxide-apatite mineralization enriched in Ti, V, and P within the LLMI, as well as structurally controlled low sulfidation epithermal Cu-Ag-Au mineralization, indicate greater critical mineral and precious metal potential than previously recognized. These results provide a revised geologic understanding for future investigations of Columbia River Basalt magmatism, Basin and Range tectonics, and mineral resources in southeastern Oregon.

title: Paleozoic Goldilocks: Distinct Lithofacies and Paleoenvironments As Loci of Intense Sediment Mixing in Cambro–Ordovician Successions of Western Newfoundland, CA
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Rivas, Ashley Y. [1], Pruss, Sara B. [2], Gill, Benjamin C. [3], Tarhan, Lidya G. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(3) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(4) Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
abstract: The Cambrian–Ordovician mixed carbonate-siliciclastic succession of western Newfoundland provides a valuable window into marine animal ecosystems along the eastern Laurentian margin during the interval leading up to the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. Additionally, these strata record a range of seafloor settings, from peritidal to continental slope, facilitating assessment of not only temporal but also paleoenvironmental patterns in early Paleozoic ecological development. Previous studies have suggested that the development of bioturbation (burrowing and sediment mixing by seafloor-dwelling animals) was protracted throughout this interval but may have begun to accelerate earlier in nearshore settings. Here, we present bioturbation intensity data from the Upper Cambrian and Lower Ordovician St. George groups near the Port au Port region and the Middle Ordovician Table Point and Table Cove formations in northwestern Newfoundland. We use statistical analyses of high-resolution ichnofabric index and lithofacies data (in total, ca. 350 m) collected at the decimeter scale to assess relationships between lithofacies, inferred paleoenvironment, and bioturbation intensity throughout this succession. Our results show that bioturbation intensity is highest in wackestone-dominated carbonate facies. These analyses also indicate that middle-shelf paleoenvironments may have served as a locus of the most intense levels of sediment mixing. Additional paleoenvironmental characterization of these data in stratigraphic sequence indicates that shallow-marine settings during this interval were, relative to deeper-water settings, characterized by greater variability in bioturbation. The intensity of bioturbation also increases in shallow-marine environments at a stratigraphically lower horizon than in deep-water settings. Overall, these data highlight that a complex interplay of paleoenvironmental, evolutionary, and preservational factors shaped records of Cambrian–Ordovician bioturbation.

title: Age, Stratigraphy, and Provenance of the Beaucoup Formation and Endicott Group, Central Brooks Range, Arctic Alaska Terrane
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Geier, George R. [1], Stukel, Caitlin S. [2], Bruxvoort, Samson [3], McClelland, William C. [4], Connors, Christopher D. [5], Crowley, James L. [6], Strauss, Justin V. [7]

(2) Geisel School of Medicine, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(3) Dahrouge Geological Consulting, Centennial, CO, USA
(4) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA

(7) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
abstract: Recent studies from the northeastern and southern Brooks Range of Alaska have reported evidence for Middle to Late Devonian subduction-related sedimentation and volcanism in the Arctic Alaska terrane. These results contrast with current tectonic models for Arctic Alaska that invoke widespread Middle Devonian continental rifting followed by passive margin development. In the central Brooks Range, Devonian rocks are widely exposed in the Endicott Mountains allochthon (EMA), including the Beaucoup Formation and Endicott Group; yet these critical successions have not been fully integrated into modern tectonic models for the Brooks Range. We investigated the stratigraphy, age, and provenance of the Beaucoup Formation and overlying Endicott Group in or adjacent to their type areas of the Philip Smith Mountains and along the Dalton Highway corridor. In the type area of the Beaucoup Formation (Philip Smith Mountains), we found that rocks previously mapped as the underlying Ordovician to Devonian “Skajit Limestone” instead locally form a discontinuous carbonate unit within the basal part of the Beaucoup Formation. This stratigraphic relationship highlights ambiguities regarding the basal contact of the EMA and its connection to the Hammond subterrane. Detrital zircon U-Pb geochronological and Hf isotopic data show strong similarities between the Beaucoup Formation in its type area and correlative units in what is mapped as the Hammond subterrane near the Dalton Highway, including the presence of significant ca. 450–410 and 2000–900 Ma age populations. Biostratigraphic and detrital zircon U-Pb data also reveal an important Middle–Late Devonian disconformity within the upper Beaucoup Formation, potentially indicating a regional shift in tectonic setting. Along the Dalton Highway corridor, the Nutirwik Creek metavolcanic rocks, which are intercalated with metaclastic rocks that resemble the Beaucoup Formation, yielded single-grain chemical abrasion-isotope dilution-thermal ionization mass spectrometry (CA-ID-TIMS) zircon U-Pb ages of ca. 396–392 Ma and whole-rock trace element geochemistry with volcanic arc signatures. Together, these results provide evidence for Middle Devonian subduction-related volcanism in Arctic Alaska, emphasize potential stratigraphic and provenance linkages between the Hammond subterrane and EMA, and provide additional context for the tectonic setting of the Endicott Group.

title: A floristic transition, not angiosperm diversification, drove peak insect family diversity
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Swain, Anshuman [1], Januario, Matheus [2], Labandeira, Conrad C. [3], Jouault, Corentin [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; Museum of Paleontology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(2) Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; Museum of Paleontology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(3) Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC,
(4) Oxford University Museum of Natural History, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom
abstract: The widely accepted narrative that the Cretaceous radiation of angiosperms triggered an unprecedented explosion of insect diversity, supported by species-level phylogenies of phytophagous lineages, observations of modern angiosperm-rich communities, and analyses conducted at finer taxonomic scales, is compromised by the pull of the recent. When interrogated at the family level using bias-corrected Bayesian birth-death models for three well-documented major plant-associated orders (Coleoptera, Hemiptera, and Hymenoptera; over 75,000 species-level fossils), a different picture emerges. Total beetle family diversity essentially plateaued from the Cretaceous onward despite the later ecological dominance of angiosperms, and the onset of current levels of insect diversity for all three orders occurred not during angiosperm dominance but during the gymnosperm-to-angiosperm transition (~145–100 Ma), when both plant groups co-occurred at relatively high diversity. We term this transformation the florotone, a temporal floral ecotone, in which gymnosperm decline and angiosperm rise generated a transient but exceptional ecological condition. Post-transition trajectories diverged predictably based on sensory and feeding ecology: gymnosperm-specialist beetle suborders declined; Aculeate Hymenoptera diversified through visual–olfactory coupling with angiosperms; Hemiptera followed a decline-and-recovery pattern tied to sequential changes in seed plant phloem chemistry. Our work confirms that floristic succession, not angiosperm dominance, shaped insect diversity at the deepest taxonomic levels.

title: Depositional environment in the Pennsylvanian, the Lower Morrow Formation, Woodward and Dewey Counties, Oklahoma, USA
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Tamaki, Hanon [1], Chiyonobu, Shun [2], Ando, Takuto [3], Mita, Isao [4], Hood, Kent R. [5], Urushima, Takuto [6], Alletag, Gregg S. [7]
affiliations: (1) Graduate School of International Resource Sciences, Akita university, Akita, Akita, Japan
(2) Graduate School of International Resource Sciences, Akita university, Akita, Akita,
