abstract:
The Pennsylvanian Morrow Formation is one of the most significant natural gas reservoir intervals in the Anadarko Basin in Oklahoma. The Morrow Formation can be divided into the lower and upper parts (Totten, 1956). Notably, the Lower Morrow Formation in Woodward and Dewey Counties is a site for iodine production, along with natural gas.

The depositional environment of the Upper Morrow Formation on the northwestern shelf of the Anadarko Basin has been extensively modeled as a glacio-eustatic incised valley-fill system (Puckette et al., 2008). Although the Lower Morrow Formation is a significant target to produce iodine and natural gas, it is essential to further our detailed understanding of its depositional environment.

This study aims to reconstruct the depositional environments of the Lower Morrow Formation by using core description and petrographic analysis. We build upon previous studies of the petroleum geology of the Morrow Formation in the Anadarko Basin using interpretations of the depositional environment that is placed in stratigraphic context, and present new core, and petrographic data. We also utilized a 30-meter core from a well drilled in Woodward County, Oklahoma that consists of sandstone, shale and conglomerate in the Lower Morrow Formation.

Based on core description and thin section analysis, the succession was classified into five lithofacies units. Unit I consists of channel lags, fossiliferous coarse-grained sandstone, and carbonaceous shales, indicating a temporary estuarine environment. Unit II consists of matrix-supported conglomerates and coarse-grained sandstones with cross-bedding and mud clasts, interpreted as fluvial deposits. Unit III is dominated by lenticular-bedded and carbonaceous shales containing abundant plant debris, recording a transition from a tidal flat to a marsh. Unit IV consists of channel lags and fossiliferous coarse-grained sandstones with cross-bedding, suggesting high-energy tidal currents. Unit V features fine- to coarse-grained sandstones with herringbone cross-stratification and marine shell fossils. Thin section petrography analysis also reveals significant calcite cementation indicating a shallow marine environment.

To summarize, these lithofacies clearly record the evolution of an incised valley formed during the regression as it transitioned from a fluvial to estuarine and shallow marine environment during transgression.

title: A Regional Compilation of Sedimentary Charcoal Records from the White Mountains, NH: Initial results
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Pendleton, Simon [1], Doner, Lisa A. [2], DelBove, Maggie [3], Hoyer, Emmett [4], Conley, Bryan [5], Moore, Virginia [6], Hastings, Elizabeth [7], Gifford, Aiden [8], Neely, John [9], Guiterman, Christopher [10]

abstract: As climate change and other anthropogenic activities increase wildfire risk across the United States, including the Northeast, a larger proportion of the population and ecosystems are projected to be impacted by large, damaging fires. As federal, state, local, and private forest stakeholders develop future best practices, including the use of fire as an ecosystem management tool, records of past fire occurrence, utilization, and impact are crucial in the development of forest management. To help provide this context, we present initial results from sedimentary charcoal records from 5 lakes and bogs in the White Mountains of New Hampshire covering the period of deglaciation at each site (~13-14 ka) to modern. Amongst all the cores, charcoal particle concentrations fluctuate but are persistent throughout each sediment record, indicating the consistent, though variable, presence of fire on the landscape. Thus far, several cores show higher, and more variable, charcoal concentrations immediately following deglaciation before decreasing to lower, less variable concentrations at ~7.5 ka. These lower concentrations persist through to modern, punctuated by discrete peaks; some of which are shared between cores. Separation and analysis of charcoal particles sizes (125-250, 250-500, >500µm) broadly show coherence within each record, although some peaks in the 125-250µm particle size are not mirrored in the larger grain sizes. These particle size relationships suggest that lake and bogs are generally capturing more local fire events, with periodic larger, farther afield events recorded across multiple records. Additionally, comparison of these charcoal records to tree-ring fire scar records from adjacent fire adapted tree stands will provide further insight into the preservation and interpretation of sedimentary charcoal. We continue to investigate chronological issues related to bog sedimentation and interpretation of charcoal peaks given the limits of our sampling resolution (~20-70 yr cm -1 ). Forthcoming pollen assemblage analyses will add to these results and provide ecological trends, relationships, and responses to fire regimes. The finished sedimentary charcoal records, tree-ring fire scar histories, and pollen analyses will provide important context for the development of forest best management practices under projected climate and ecological changes.

title: Tectonomagmatic History of Grenvillian Crustal Carbonatites: Insights from U-Pb Geochronology of Apatite
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Ahmadi, Jamshid [1], Rakovan, John [2], Emproto, Christopher [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA; New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami Universit, Oxford, OH, USA; Section of Minerals and Earth Sciences, Carnegie Museum of Natural History, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
abstract:
Grenville-aged rocks record the largest known continental collision in Earth's history, forming terranes across North America. In Ontario, Quebec, and New York, these terranes host crustal carbonatites — historically named "vein dikes" — which, unlike mantle derived classical carbonatites, are thought to form by melting of crustal carbonate rocks such as marbles and limestones. These carbonatites host numerous occurrences of critical and industrial minerals and gemstones and are thought to have been emplaced during collapse stages of the Grenville orogenic cycle. Our recent study discovered geochemical trends in Grenville crustal carbonatites linked to migrating collapse fronts. However, few crustal carbonatites have been dated, leaving the current geochronological framework poorly resolved. Here we present LA-ICP-MS U-Pb dating of apatite from crustal carbonatites in the Bancroft, Frontenac, and Wilberforce areas of the Grenville Province, to correlate their temporal distribution with the documented geochemical trends and investigate connections to regional tectonomagmatic regimes.

Preliminary results show U-Pb ages spanning 1040–790 Ma, clustering into three groups: 1040–980, 940–900, and 840–790 Ma. Comparison of these ages with previously U-Pb-dated minerals such as titanite and zircon shows that the apatite ages record delayed cooling relative to the original emplacement of these crustal carbonatites, reflecting protracted thermal conditions during the Grenvillian orogeny that persisted for tens of millions of years after the main orogenic pulses. Integrating these ages with trace element geochemistry, petrological observations, geographic distribution, and regional structural relationships is further consistent with these emplacement events occurring in a pulsed, episodic manner along migrating collapse fronts during the late and post-Grenvillian orogenic stages, with hydrothermal alteration persisting through the post-Grenvillian period and recurring during Rodinia breakup, resetting the apatite ages. We interpret these results as reflecting a spatiotemporal progression of orogenic collapse in the Grenville Province that generated the magmas, fluids, and pathways for crustal carbonatite emplacement, illuminating the confluence of structural and geochemical controls on the formation of these mineral resources.

title: Machine Learning Classification of Texas Aquifer Systems Using Spatial, Geomorphic, and Well Completion Attributes from the TWDB Continuous Monitoring Network
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: Imarhiagbe, Osayamen Julius [1], Fabusiwa, Ayodeji [2], Maju-Oyovwikowhe, Efetobore Gladys [3], Mohammed , Abdulqudus Onimisi [4]
affiliations: (1) Division of Earth Sciences and Geography, RWTH Aachen University, Aachen, NRW, USA; Department of Geosciences, University of Texas Permian Basin, Odessa, Texas, USA
(2) Division of Earth Sciences and Geography, RWTH Aachen University, Aachen, NRW, USA
(3) Department of Geology, University of Benin, Benin, Edo, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, University of Texas Permian Basin, Odessa, TX, USA
abstract:
Groundwater managers rely on accurate aquifer identification, but it's still unclear how much geographic position, surface geomorphology, and well completion details actually contribute to telling one aquifer apart from another across Texas's varied geology. We ran both unsupervised and supervised machine learning on 390 continuously monitored wells from the Texas Water Development Board network, covering 126 counties, 24 aquifer designations, and elevations from 5 to 5,308 ft.

K-Means clustering (k = 6, chosen by elbow analysis) sorted the wells into six spatially distinct groups without ever being told which aquifer each well belonged to, and the groups line up remarkably well with Texas's real physiographic provinces. A Panhandle cluster is almost entirely Ogallala wells at high elevation; a Trans-Pecos/Far West group sits at similarly high elevation but draws on Edwards-Trinity Plateau, igneous, and Pecos Valley aquifers; a Gulf Coast cluster of unconsolidated sediments sits near sea level; the largest group spans the Hill Country and Balcones Fault Zone; a North-Central Texas cluster mixes Trinity, Carrizo-Wilcox, and Woodbine wells; and a small, much deeper cluster (mean depth over 2,400 ft) picks out the confined Trinity and Gulf Coast wells beneath Dallas–Fort Worth and Houston. PCA backs this up, with the first two components capturing 79% of the variance.

We then trained a Random Forest on just four numbers, the latitude, longitude, well depth, and surface elevation and it predicted aquifer type with 84% cross-validated accuracy. Elevation carried the most weight (38.5%), followed by latitude and longitude, while well depth barely mattered (7%). A quick regression confirmed depth and elevation are essentially unrelated (R² = 0.07), meaning how deep a well goes has more to do with the target formation than the ground surface above it.

Aquifer identity in Texas is written into geography and topography far more than into completion depth, and a model this simple, built entirely from public well records, can flag likely aquifer type even where stratigraphic logs don't exist. Next steps are adding water-level trends and water chemistry to sharpen classification in the transition zones, especially Edwards-Trinity and Ogallala-Dockum, where the model struggled most.

title: Spatial Clustering of Landslides in the Himalaya: A Local to Regional Perspective
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies
authors: Bhandari, Bharat Prasad [1]
affiliations: (1) Central Department of Environmental Science, Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu, Bagmati, Nepal
abstract:
Cluster landslides frequently occur in the Himalayas, thus increasing the multi-hazard risk. The onset of cluster landslides in the Himalayas is predominantly influenced by monsoonal precipitation, frequent earthquakes, and road development, collectively instigating several slope failures in specific areas. This research investigates the geographical distribution of clustered landslides in the Lesser and Higher Himalayan regions of Central Nepal, focusing on five local and five regional areas selected at random. The landslides were identified in the satellite imagery and subsequently incorporated into the GIS layer. ArcGIS 10.7 spatial statistics tools were employed to examine the geographical distribution and clustering of landslides. The Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) was conducted to ascertain the clustering of landslides. Moran's I was employed to assess the spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, hotspot analysis (Getis-Ord Gi) was performed to pinpoint the high-risk regions for landslide incidents.

The Average Nearest Neighbor (ANN) analysis revealed that landslides at the local level exhibit a statistically significant clustered spatial distribution, whereas the regional-scale distribution indicates a relatively weaker but still discernible tendency toward clustering. The spatial analysis further demonstrated that landslide-prone areas are predominantly concentrated near settlements and recently constructed road segments. Similarly, higher landslide densities and statistically significant hotspots were predominantly distributed on slopes exceeding 35° in the higher Himalayan region, highlighting the strong influence of steep terrain on landslide occurrence. The 7.8 ML Gorkha Earthquake of 2015 and its subsequent aftershocks contributed to the initiation and spatial clustering of numerous landslides within the study region. The analysis also indicated that approximately 102 households across 12 villages are potentially exposed to the impacts of cluster landslides, emphasizing the significant risk to local communities. This research the spatial characteristics and controlling factors of clustered landslides and offers an important scientific basis for local governments and relevant stakeholders to develop and implement evidence-based disaster risk reduction, land-use planning, and landslide risk management strategies in the study region.

title: Mineralogical and Microstructural Controls on CO2 Trapping Potential in the Silurian Lockport Dolomite, Appalachian Basin
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology (Posters)
authors: Bonsu, Samuel [1], Weislogel, Amy [2], Sharma, Shikha [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(2) Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(3) Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
abstract:
Carbonate formations are attractive targets for subsurface carbon storage, yet mineralogical heterogeneity and diagenetic overprinting complicate prediction of pore evolution and fluid-rock interaction. The Silurian Lockport Dolomite in Wayne County, West Virginia, Appalachian Basin, is being evaluated as a potential reservoir within the Tri-State CCS Hub CarbonSAFE project (DOE Award DE-FE0032441). This study integrates bulk X-ray diffraction (XRD; n = 10) and field emission gun scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (FEGSEM-EDS; n = 15) on continuous core from well API #4709901549 to characterize mineral composition, diagenetic fabrics, and pore-network architecture.

The interval is dominated by non-stoichiometric dolomite with subordinate calcite, quartz, anhydrite, and trace pyrite, and is subdivided into three zones: (1) a dolomite-dominated upper zone (dolomitization index 97-100%), (2) a transitional zone containing the most calcite-rich and Fe-dolomite-rich samples, and (3) a mixed calcite-dolomite lower zone. These zones reflect six diagenetic stages, from early marine conditions through reflux dolomitization and meteoric dissolution to burial and late-stage modification.

FEGSEM-EDS imaging reveals a complex pore system comprising intercrystalline, fracture-controlled, dissolution-enhanced, and inter-plate microporosity. Stylolites are pervasive and exert dual control on reservoir quality, locally occluding porosity through clay- and pyrite-rich residues while enhancing permeability along dissolution seams that act as fluid pathways.

These diagenetic features control mineral reactivity and pore accessibility, with implications for CO 2 -brine-rock interaction. Calcite dissolution may buffer fluid acidity and release Ca 2+ , whereas reactions involving dolomite and Fe-dolomite may promote mineral trapping through secondary carbonate precipitation. These results demonstrate that diagenetic heterogeneity drives spatial variability in reservoir quality and reactive potential within the Lockport Dolomite and highlight the importance of sedimentological and microstructural characterization in evaluating carbonate reservoirs for subsurface fluid storage.

title: Late Pleistocene pyroclastic fall activity at Pico de Orizaba volcano
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Sourisseau, Delphine [1], Arce, José Luis [2], Macías, José Luis [3], Carrillo-Mondragón, José Juan [4]
affiliations: (1) Instituto de Geología, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Ciudad de México, Mexico
(2) Instituto de Geología, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Ciudad de México, Mexico
(3) Instituto de Geofísica Unidad Michoacán, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Morelia, Michoacán, Mexico
(4) Posgrado en Ciencias de la Tierra, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Ciudad de México, Mexico
abstract: Pico de Orizaba is an andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano in the easternmost part of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, active from ~650 ka to historical times. It is the highest peak in Mexico (5,636 m a.s.l.) and the second-highest in North America. Most pyroclastic falls described from this volcano occurred within the past 9 ka BP. Several older deposits have also been identified, including T-I and Orizaba I-II, though their precise ages remain uncertain. Recent field studies further indicate that this record is incomplete and that several units remain undescribed. Based on new stratigraphic descriptions, componentry analyses, and two new 14C radiometric ages from charcoal, we reconstruct the stratigraphy of pyroclastic activity from stratigraphic sections west of Pico de Orizaba. Preliminary results indicate that more than 10 explosive eruptions occurred over the past 43.5 ka BP, producing well-defined pumice-fall units. Major- and trace-element analyses of pumice glass, obtained by EPMA and LA-ICP-MS, enabled characterization of the chemical fingerprints of the pumice-fall units. These glass compositions were compared with a newly developed database covering several explosive eruptions of Mexican volcanoes. Statistical tools such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) were used to distinguish their chemical signatures. Components and pumice glass data suggest that several of these units originated from Pico de Orizaba, indicating a higher frequency of explosive activity during the terminal stage of the volcano than previously recognized.

title: A Block with Many Facies: The Complex P-T-Fluid History of a Franciscan High-Grade Rock
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Whitney, Donna L. [1], Brandt, Sarah A [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
abstract:
A large (~20 x 30 x 12 m) metabasalt block in the Central Belt of the Franciscan Complex (Mendocino County, CA) preserves an overall clockwise P-T path, including a path segment from eclogite to garnet amphibolite to blueschist, with late cross-cutting zoisite veins fringed by lawsonite + chlorite. The block, known as Syke Rock, is similar to other Franciscan high-grade blocks in bulk composition; mineral assemblages, composition, zoning; and evidence for metasomatism, although counter-clockwise paths have been interpreted for some otherwise similar blocks.

Metasomatic features include replacement of eclogite/amphibolite by garnetite or chlorite + garnet. These metasomatic zones contain neocrystallized garnet, atoll garnets, and partially birefringent garnets, and grade into a talc + actinolite layer that is discontinuously preserved around the block. The talc-actinolite layer indicates that metasomatism at the block margin was likely driven by reaction between metabasalt and serpentinite. However, the occurrence within the block of large cross-cutting vein systems composed of Ca-Al silicates (zoisite fringed by lawsonite), as well as the presence of minor local quartz- and mica-rich zones, indicates other fluid sources (e.g., metagraywacke, metabasalt) were involved later in the metamorphic history and affected the block interior. Whereas the serpentinite-metabasalt reactions occurred under garnet-stable conditions, lawsonite ± chlorite in and near the zoisite veins partially replaced garnet following the cessation of garnet growth.

The onset of hydration reactions/metasomatism may have corresponded to the detachment of the eclogite/amphibolite from the subducting slab and its development as a block embedded in a serpentinite matrix, with subsequent fluid-rock interaction in the block interior as the mélange evolved. An interesting feature of lawsonite in Syke Rock is that it contains a substantial amount of ferrous Fe (up to 60% of total Fe), in contrast to more typical lawsonite, which contains ferric iron that substitutes for Al. We are investigating whether the presence of ferrous Fe and other aspects of lawsonite composition are indicators of the fluid source(s) that produced the zoisite/lawsonite veins.

abstract:
Reconstructing the paleogeography of Baltica during the Ediacaran (635–539 Ma) has proven persistently difficult: paleomagnetic poles from this interval are sparse and, where data exist, they often show large, rapid directional swings that are hard to reconcile with a stable geocentric axial dipole field. These discrepancies have fueled competing explanations including extreme plate velocities, anomalous geomagnetic field behavior, rapid true polar wander, and compromised paleomagnetic recorders. Each explanation carries distinct implications for Earth's tectonic and geomagnetic history.

Two alkaline-carbonatite complexes in western Baltica, Fen (southern Norway) and Alnö (central Sweden), are central to this problem: both formed in the mid-Ediacaran (ca. 580–590 Ma) yet yield strikingly different paleomagnetic signals and are routinely excluded from regional pole compilations and reconstructions as a result. We present new paleomagnetic, rock magnetic and petrographic data from both complexes, integrating conventional techniques with scanning electron and quantum diamond microscopy to better understand the magnetic carriers and their magnetization history. Our results show that both complexes are highly susceptible to remagnetization: Fen carries a pervasive Permian overprint tied to Oslo Rift tectono-magmatic activity, while Alnö is dominated by a Cenozoic/recent overprint linked to uplift of the Fennoscandian Shield.

After isolating these secondary components, we identify a dual-polarity, shallow-inclination signal common to both complexes. This signal is weak and concentrated in previously unstudied rock types (mainly damtjernites and alnöites, i.e. ultramafic lamprophyre intrusions) that we interpret as a primary Ediacaran magnetization. Poles derived from this shallow component place Baltica at low to equatorial latitudes at ca. 580–590 Ma, offering a new, internally consistent constraint on Baltica's enigmatic Precambrian position. We discuss how these results help resolve long-standing conflicts between paleomagnetic records for eastern and western Baltica, and what they imply for Baltica's role in Neoproterozoic paleogeographic reconstructions and for the broader debate over geomagnetic field behavior during this critical interval of Earth history.

title: Box stromatolites: A new form of microbialite from the Flaky Dolostone of the upper Tonian Chuar Group, Grand Canyon

authors: Xiao, Shuhai [1], Boan, Phillip Charles [2], Dehler, Carol M. [3], Porter, Susannah M. [4], Crossey, Laura J. [5], Karlstrom, Karl E. [6], Hagadorn, James [7]

abstract: Stromatolitic carbonates serve as key stratigraphic markers in the predominately siliciclastic succession of the upper Tonian Chuar Group (770–729 Ma) in the eastern Grand Canyon of Arizona. One of these is the so-called Flaky Dolostone, a marker bed at the base of the Walcott Member of the Kwagunt Formation. The unit is regionally extensive, about 2-3 meters in thickness, and underlain and overlain by highly fossiliferous organic-rich shales. It contains microbial laminae that are preferentially silicified as are interlayered pisolite beds. Reworked microbial laminae occur as silicified and sometimes deformed flakes in the unit, giving it its name. Viewed in vertical profile, in-situ microbial laminae occur as sharp crests (centimeters in relief) separated by centimeter- to decimeter-wide troughs. On the top bedding surface of the Flaky Dolostone, these microbial structures form rectangular boxes, each with a concave-downward floor, an open top, and four vertical walls corresponding to the crests as observed on vertical profiles. The boxes are aligned in rows, typically with the short edge of the boxes parallel to the row, which has an average E-W trend. These box stromatolites represent a previously unknown form of microbialites. We hypothesize that they nucleated on centimeter- to decimeter-sized interference ripple marks in a hydrodynamically energetic setting. The box stromatolites were drowned or suffocated at the top of the Flaky Dolostone, when a rapid transgression event occurred with abundant supply of fine-grained siliciclastic sediment to the basin. In contrast to previous interpretations that posited late diagenetic, post-dolomitization silicification of microbial laminae in the Flaky Dolostone, we propose that these microbial laminae were selectively silicified probably during early diagenesis at or just below the water-sediment interface, and partially silicified microbial laminae were subjected to fragmentation, reworking, and deformation by waves and storms. The microbial structures in the Flaky Dolostone offer an opportunity to constrain the depositional environment of the upper Chuar Group and environmental context of early eukaryote evolution.

abstract:
The Almond Formation of southwestern Wyoming preserves vertebrate, invertebrate, and plant fossils in a paralic succession of strata that accumulated in close proximity to the Cretaceous Interior Seaway. Recent fieldwork has led to the discovery of several new fossil localities, including dinosaur sites and an extensive multi-taxic bonebed containing fish, turtles, crocodilians, and dinosaurs. Two vertebrate microfossil localities have also been identified. The taphonomy of one of these, the “Turtle Hill” microsite, was studied by a team of Keck Geology Consortium Gateway student researchers.

Turtle Hill is stratigraphically and taphonomically complex, with three discrete fossiliferous horizons over a vertical span of approximately 1 m yielding vertebrate, invertebrate, and plant fossils. Here we focus on the basal bone-bearing layer, a 2–3 cm thick bed of fine-grained, loosely cemented sandstone. Vertebrate bioclasts (bones, teeth, scales, rare otoliths) are intermixed with millimeter-scale carbonaceous plant debris and rare invertebrate fossils, including bivalve shell fragments and gastropod opercula. We sieved bulk samples collected from this horizon to augment existing surface and quarry collections, and we compared the preservational quality of the resulting assemblage with collections from vertebrate microfossil bonebeds from the Campanian Judith River Formation (JRF) of Montana.

Turtle Hill yields an exceptionally dense concentration of tiny vertebrate bioclasts (500 µm–2 mm), with a yield of over 5,000 specimens per kg of matrix. Importantly, ~36% of the bulk-sampled bioclasts are assignable to broad vertebrate groups, compared with ~18% in the JRF. Fish (osteichthyans and chondrichthyans) account for ~99% of identifiable specimens, whereas terrestrial vertebrates are present but exceedingly rare. Turtle Hill bioclasts are also smaller on average than those recovered from the JRF (1.3 mm versus 1.6 mm), and their shape distribution is strongly skewed toward flat elements such as scales, reflecting the dominance of fish remains. As in the JRF sites, many Turtle Hill bioclasts preserve traces of feeding, including pits, punctures, scores, and parallel furrows. Some bones show surface modification consistent with digestion (e.g., gar scales stripped of ganoine and evidence of pitting and dissolution), and small phosphatic coprolites consistent with carnivorous/piscivorous diets are common. Ongoing work aims to decipher the formative history of this unusual and highly productive coastal vertebrate microfossil assemblage.

title: Storage Depths of Recharge Magmas Feeding Newberry Caldera, Central Oregon
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Small, Elizabeth [1], Scruggs, Melissa A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA

abstract: Newberry Volcano ranks among the most hazardous in the United States, yet it remains one of the least petrologically studied. The 1,300-year-old Big Obsidian Flow (BOF), Newberry's most recent eruption, offers the best available window into where these recharge magmas might be stored. Geophysical surveys have imaged a single rhyolitic magma reservoir consisting of 8-12% partial melt spanning 3 to 5 km depth (Beachly et al., 2012; Heath et al., 2015), but BOF contains magmatic enclaves, whose existence requires the injection of a mafic recharge magma. Linneman and Myers (1990), still one of the very few petrologic studies of Newberry, described these enclaves and used two-pyroxene thermometry to place their crystallization near 1050°C, but did not resolve storage depth. Surviving thin sections from that study have been reanalyzed by electron microprobe alongside a newly collected enclave (BOF-I-42). The enclaves are basaltic andesite to andesite (58.6-60.7 wt.% SiO 2 whole rock), while interstitial glass adjacent to enclave pyroxenes is rhyolitic (69.6-74.6 wt.% SiO 2 ). Two-pyroxene thermobarometry, restricted to pairs confirmed as spatially co-located, yields P-T estimates of ~6 ± 6.4 kbar and ~1102 ± 140°C, and estimates made using clinopyroxene-only barometry yield crystallization P of ~4 ± 6.2 kbar, together placing the mafic recharge in the mid crust (~15 to 23 km, ± ~23.7 km), well below the imaged shallow reservoir. This places the recharge source below the resolution of existing geophysical imaging. These results are consistent with previously determined temperature estimates while resolving, for the first time, storage depths of recharge feeding one of the Cascades' most hazardous and understudied volcanoes.

title: Tectonic Evolution of the Late Triassic-Jurassic Talkeetna Arc from Subduction Initiation to Maturation along the Kodiak Archipelago-Alaska Peninsula Transect
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada (Posters)
authors: Keough, Brandon [1], Ridgway, Kenneth [2], Eddy, Michael [3], Johnson, Lauren [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(3) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
The Late Triassic-Jurassic Talkeetna Arc of southern Alaska is one of the best-preserved oceanic arc crustal sections on Earth. Most previous studies have examined magmatic and volcanic processes recorded by Jurassic rocks exposed in the northern Chugach and southern Talkeetna Mountains. In this region, Cenozoic flat slab subduction and associated exhumation along strike-slip fault systems has resulted in exposure of a near-complete composite crustal section. This section has proved ideal for petrologic studies of trans-crustal magmatic processes. However, post-magmatic tectonic dismemberment resulted in two main limitations of this record: (1) erasure of the earliest records of arc processes including subduction initiation; and (2) structural juxtaposition of rocks from different crustal levels, often with contrasting or unconstrained ages. By contrast, the western portion of the Talkeetna Arc on the Kodiak Archipelago and Alaska Peninsula contains a less-studied yet more coherent Late Triassic-Middle Jurassic record better suited to reconstructing upper crustal and surface processes through time.

Here we summarize the results of recent studies along the Kodiak Archipelago-Alaska Peninsula transect of the Talkeetna Arc with three key outcomes: (1) a volcanic record of subduction initiation processes between ca. 235-230 Ma (middle Carnian); (2) volcaniclastic and structural records of arc maturation under an extensional regime from the early arc front to an active backarc basin (ca. 230-210 Ma); and (3) subsequent inboard migration from the latest Triassic-Early Jurassic where the early backarc basin transitioned to a forearc depocenter. Based on rapid inboard migration of the magmatic front, subduction erosion played a key role in shaping the plate boundary and removing much of the Late Triassic forearc region. Our results also provide clarity on the importance of late Paleozoic arc crust which parts of the Talkeetna Arc were built on. In our model, extension and slab rollback during subduction initiation resulted in the formation of supra-subduction zone oceanic crust trenchward of late Paleozoic arc crust. The magmatic front first localized within this Late Triassic crust before migrating inboard and intruding late Paleozoic arc crust. This model for the evolution of the Talkeetna Arc is similar to models proposed for extensional fringing arc systems that formed along the western margin of Laurentia in the Late Triassic.

title: Progressive Underplating and Development of an Inverted Metamorphic Gradient in the Easton Metamorphic Suite, northwest Washington
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Mulcahy, Sean R. [1], Chan, Jeni [2], Schermer, Elizabeth R. [3], Smit, Matthijs [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(2) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(3) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA

abstract:
The Easton Metamorphic Suite of northwest Washington preserves an inverted metamorphic gradient that records the progressive construction of a Jurassic subduction interface. The Gee Point Amphibolite (700-800 °C, 1.0 GPa) structurally overlies a High-Grade Blueschist unit (500-550 °C, 1.0 GPa), which in turn overlies regionally extensive lower-grade units of the Shuksan Greenschist and Silver Phyllite (<450 °C, 0.7 GPa). Similar inverted metamorphic sequences have been interpreted to form through episodic accretion within a thermally evolving subduction zone. We apply this framework to the Easton Metamorphic Suite through integrated structural mapping, microstructural analysis, thermometry and geochronologic analysis.

The High-Grade Blueschist occupies a critical structural position between the Gee Point Amphibolite and regional blueschist-facies units. Garnet Lu-Hf ages show that amphibolite-facies metamorphism accompanied subduction initiation at ca. 183 Ma, whereas prograde to peak metamorphism of the High-Grade Blueschist occurred at ca. 173 Ma followed by underplating, recording addition of a high-pressure unit roughly 10 Myr after subduction initiation.

Titanite, amphibole, and mica ages ranging from 168-158 Ma indicate that the Gee Point Amphibolite and High-Grade Blueschist cooled together and were partially exhumed shortly after their assembly and prior to subduction of the regional blueschist units. Field and microstructural observations demonstrate a high-strain contact between the High-Grade Blueschist and underlying Shuksan Greenschist, marked by a penetrative foliation and localized retrograde overprinting of High-Grade Blueschist unit, that records a younger episode of underplating between 140 and 136 Ma.

These results demonstrate that the Easton Metamorphic Suite was assembled through episodic underplating of discrete tectonic slices over more than 40 Myr. The High-Grade Blueschist preserves a critical intermediate stage in this history, linking subduction initiation, deep underplating, partial exhumation, and later accretion of lower-grade units. The inverted metamorphic gradient reflects the progressive growth of the subduction interface through multiple underplating events during the thermal evolution of a nascent and evolving subduction zone.

title: Evaluating potential structural and lithologic control on varying debris flow behaviors in the Swannanoa Mountains, Appalachian Blue Ridge

authors: Prince, Philip [1], Hartman, Courtney [2], Fuemmeler, Stephen [3], Bauer, Jennifer [4]
affiliations: (1) Appalachian Landslide Consultants, PLLC, Asheville, North Carolina, USA

abstract: The Swannanoa Mountains of southeastern Buncombe County, North Carolina, experienced a catastrophic debris flow outbreak on the morning of September 27, 2024, with the passage of Helene’s most intense precipitation bands. The southeast face of the range hosted the Craigtown debris flow complex, the deadliest and most voluminous debris flow event of the storm. Notably, debris flows on the northwest side of the range were more numerous but systematically less voluminous, with shallower scour developed over shorter runout lengths. Extensive field reconnaissance supported by lidar change detection imagery suggests lithologic and structural distinctions, with associated variations in topography and colluvial soil development, dictated the contrasting character of debris flows on respective sides of the Swannanoa range. Long-runout (>3 km), high-volume debris flows of the southeast face of the range initiated in thick colluvium derived from phyllitic rocks in the footwall of the Brevard Fault Zone. South face colluvium is dominated by weathered, platy clasts in a tan, mica-rich matrix, with initiating landslide failure depths approaching 3 m. Colluvium rests atop dip slope foliation surfaces. South face slopes are systematically gentler than north face slopes, rarely exceeding 30 degrees. The more numerous, but less voluminous and mobile, debris flows of the north face initiated on steeper slopes (>35 degrees) in thinner colluvium, which often exhibits a dark, organic-rich matrix. North face debris flows show reduced runout and a greater tendency to deposit coarse debris, including metagraywacke boulders largely absent from the south face, at steep channel gradients. The apparent coupling between slope steepness, colluvium character and depth, and debris flow volume and runout supports previous studies suggesting more moderate slopes with landslide potential may source larger and more impactful debris flows due to a greater storage of colluvium overburden to be mobilized. These observations merit consideration in landslide hazard mapping, as the steepest topography may not necessarily exhibit the greatest long-runout debris flow potential. Other topographic variables, such as stream channel confinement and longitudinal profile, may also be potential controls on debris flow runout behavior.

title: Geologic Knowledge Versus Public Perception of the Driftless Area of the US Midwest
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations
authors: Carson, Eric C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey, Madison, WI, USA
abstract:
The Driftless Area of southwest Wisconsin and northwesternmost Illinois is a ~26,000 km 2 region that was not covered by any of the Quaternary glaciations, resulting in an atypical (for the US Midwest) landscape of dendritic rivers that have created deep valleys by incising into the local Paleozoic strata. The Driftless Area is bounded on various sides by glaciations of different ages, resulting in some places where the boundary between glaciated and unglaciated terrain is abundantly clear and some places where the boundary is much less apparent. The geomorphic origin of this region’s landscape was originally recognized by Chamberlin and Salisbury (1885), who identified the geographic boundaries of the region with admirable accuracy for the time of the publication even in areas where the most recent adjacent glaciation was early or middle Quaternary.

In recent decades, a cultural awareness and cachet have developed regarding the Driftless Area that centers on outdoor activities (canoeing, kayaking, hiking, bird watching, trout fishing, etc…) and associated tourism. As this has happened, glaciated areas of southeast Minnesota and northeast Iowa that have very similar topography to the adjacent unglaciated landscape have increasingly become included in the public mind as part of the Driftless Area. While this ‘cultural Driftless Area’ is a valid entity, the public still clings to using Chamberlin and Salisbury’s glacial identification of the true Driftless Area to describe the larger region. This mismatch of glacial geologic origin and geographic area creates an opportunity for geological education.

Quaternary geologists from the Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota, and Wisconsin geologic surveys recently collaborated to publish a brief factsheet (Carson et al., 2023) that reiterated the original definition of the Driftless Area as proposed by Chamberlin and Salisbury and supplemented by over a century’s research in the four states. Subsequent public presentations on the material in the publication routinely draw large and interested audiences. However, the fundamental misunderstanding of the geographic extent of the non-glaciated terrain persists, highlighting the gap that can exist between established geologic knowledge and effective communication of science to the public.

abstract:
Haywood County, North Carolina, has a long history of landslides that have impacted homes and structures, closed interstates and critical transportation corridors, and caused fatalities. In September 2024, the North Carolina Geological Survey (NCGS) was awarded a grant from the USGS Landslide Hazard Program National Strategy for Landslide Loss Reduction for The Haywood County, NC Landslide Hazards Project. The results of this project will address the USGS Priority Risk Reduction Areas (P1) Landslide hazard mapping and assessment, (P2) Planning and coordination, and (P3) Education and outreach. The NCGS contracted Appalachian Landslide Consultants, PLLC (ALC) to carry out this two-year project.

The remnants of Hurricane Helene hit Western North Carolina nine days after the contract for this project was signed, triggering thousands of landslides region-wide and over 1,350 mapped landslides in Haywood County (as of July 2026). ALC has field verified 222 of these post-Helene landslides, providing Haywood County Development Services, Emergency Management, and the Planning Department with information to help assist residents that were impacted. The NCGS and ALC have worked with the National Weather Service to refine landslide-related actions in their flash flood watches and warnings. Some areas impacted by Helene also experienced a debris flow outbreak in August 2021 with the passage of Tropical Depression Fred, allowing evaluation of landscape response to repeated catastrophic precipitation events. ALC has worked with the Haywood County EM Public Information Officer to create and distribute social media-friendly videos and messaging and blogs that were distributed periodically and during Hurricane Preparedness Week. This talk will discuss the variety of landslide types and impacts observed in the field, in addition to the outreach efforts to increase awareness of this natural hazard that continues to impact citizens of Haywood County.

title: Red Beryl Gemstone is a U-Pb Geochronometer
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Courtney-Davies, Liam [1], Henry, Rhiana [2], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [3]
affiliations: (1) San Diego State University, San Diego, CA, USA
(2) Gemological Institute of America, Carlsbad, CA, USA
(3) University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Rarer than diamond and more valuable than gold, red beryl is an elusive gemstone found in vugs (lithophysal cavities) or alteration fissures in specific topaz rhyolite layers in the southwestern USA. It is unique among beryls as it forms during vapor outgassing (e.g., the final phase of magmatic activity) and contains anomalously high lattice bound U (100’s to 1000’s ppm). We tested the gem’s utility as a U-Pb geochronometer via LA-ICP-MS, and use dates to reevaluate formation assignments between rhyolite units hosting to the world’s largest beryllium deposits in UT.

Surprisingly, results yield precise, often concordant dates, indistinguishable from other coexisting geochronometers. Downhole fractionation appears negligible when compared with zircon reference materials. Red beryl provides direct age constraints on vapor outgassing, capturing the climax of magmatism not recorded by conventional igneous geochronometers (e.g. sanidine, zircon). Our results indicate that if beryl or other gem minerals have elevated U, they are worth targeting as possible geochronometers and can provide unique insights into magmatic and mineralization histories

title: Deformation of the Rocky Mountain Erosion Surface Controls Post-Laramide River Courses and Landscape Evolution across Colorado and Parts of Neighboring States.
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: Sterne, Edward Joseph [1]
affiliations: (1) Littleton, CO, USA
abstract:
The Rocky Mountain Erosion Surface (RMES) is mapped continuously across Colorado and parts of neighboring states as a composite surface involving multiple unconformities overlapped by upper Eocene to Pleistocene strata. In areas devoid of overlap deposits, the RMES is mapped at or slightly above current topography. The RMES beveled preexisting uplifts and basins starting ca. 45 to 37 Ma between the end of Laramide contraction and the advent of extension and volcanism of the ignimbrite flare-up. Two areas on opposite sides of the Continental Divide contain the best and earliest constraints on the surface and its deformation.

East of the divide, Pikes Dome stretches 500 km from the Thirtynine Mile Volcanic Field east into western Kansas. Its rise starting at the end of the Eocene, reversed the Castle Rock paleoriver that flowed southeast across the Denver Basin, and reversed the ancestral South Platte River that flowed south out of South Park to Canon City and beyond, rerouting it first to the east then to the northeast into its current course around the northern dome margin. Pikes Dome forms the prominent topographic high, the interfluve between the South Platte and Arkansas rivers.

West of the divide, the Cimarron Uplift axis extends 100 km from the Silverton-Lake City area of the San Juan Volcanic Field to the north where it crosses the Gunnison River at the Black Canyon. This post-Laramide uplift has reversed west-flowing paleorivers in the upper Eocene Telluride Conglomerate, and folds Oligocene ancestral Gunnison River gravels and overlying Oligocene to Miocene volcanics. Timing of the uplift may be as young as the Pleistocene, given when tributaries to the Black Canyon were abandoned. Such indications of recent uplift point to the spectacular Black Canyon being cut by an antecedent Gunnison River during rise of the Cimarron Uplift.

These and other areas across Colorado demonstrate relief on the RMES is structural. Where deformation rates exceed incision rates, rivers are routed into synclines in the RMES. Conversely, where incision rates exceed deformation rates, rivers maintain their courses while cutting canyons across anticlines in the RMES. New detrital zircon and detrital sanidine analyses of paleorivers on the RMES demonstrate the timing of deformation, the resultant drainage reorganization, and help us understand the evolution of the landscape we inhabit.

title: Contrasting boron isotope signatures of Triassic and Cretaceous serpentinites from the Romeral Fault System, Colombian Andes

abstract:
Subducted serpentinites transport significant amounts of fluid-mobile elements (e.g., B, Li, and As) from the oceanic lithosphere into subduction zones. They therefore play a key role in fluid circulation, elemental recycling, and controlling the composition of arc magmatism. During subduction, progressive dehydration of the oceanic crust reaches a critical stage at temperatures above ~700 °C and depths of ~100–120 km, where these elements are released into the mantle wedge. Serpentinization of mafic and ultramafic rocks, followed by their emplacement along continental margins, can be investigated through whole-rock geochemistry, Raman spectroscopy, and in situ boron isotope compositions.

In the Colombian Andes, serpentinites are mainly exposed along the Romeral Fault System, a ~2,000 km-long tectonic suture that extends from Ecuador to Colombia. Along this regional fault system, Triassic and Cretaceous ultramafic complexes have been interpreted as having been emplaced along the northwestern South American margin during subduction, terrane accretion, and strike-slip deformation. This study integrates petrography, Raman spectroscopy, mineral chemistry, and boron isotope data from serpentinites of the Colombian Andes to constrain the origin of serpentinizing fluids and unravel their contrasting tectonic history: (1) the Triassic Angelópolis Ultramafic Complex (AUC), interpreted to have formed in a debated forearc or back-arc setting, and (2) the Cretaceous Filadelfia Ultramafic Complex (FUC), interpreted as part of a subduction-related metamorphic complex. The AUC comprises lherzolites, dunites, gabbros, and rodingites. Primary mantle assemblages consist of olivine (Fo90), enstatite, and Cr-spinel with magnetite rims, whereas serpentine occurs as both pseudomorphic and non-pseudomorphic textures composed of lizardite and antigorite. In contrast, the FUC consists of foliated serpentinites, metagabbros, and black schists under greenschist- to amphibolite-facies conditions. The serpentinites preserve porphyroclasts of olivine (Fo95), and Cr-spinel with magnetite rims within an antigorite-rich matrix containing chrysotile veins. The two complexes display contrasting δ¹¹B signatures reflecting different serpentinization environments. The AUC yields δ¹¹B values ranging from ~ 0‰ to +14‰, which is the typically observed in supra subduction zones ophiolites, whereas the FUC records values between –12‰ and +5‰, testifying from serpentinization by a fluid released from the subducting oceanic crust. These isotopic differences are consistent with the observed contrasts in field relationships, petrography, mineralogy and textures, demonstrating that the Angelópolis and Filadelfia ultramafic complexes represent distinct serpentinization histories, reflecting fluid-rock interactions in contrasting tectonic environments.

abstract:
The ~6 million year (Ma) Lemudong’o Formation in southern Kenya preserves fossil-bearing deposits distributed across several laterally separated exposures spanning ~9 km (E/W) by 4 km (N/S). Establishing stratigraphic correlations among exposures is essential for reconstructing the paleobasin’s depositional history and contextualizing paleoenvironments during a critical period for early human evolution. Documenting the volcanic sequences at each site is integral to establishing tephrostratigraphic correlations and chronologies. Enamankeon is a key exposure in the study area, located on a prominent isolated flat-topped hill. The section preserves ~120 m of lacustrine, paludal, tufa spring, fluvial deposits and paleosols with numerous interbedded tuffs hypothesized to correlate among nearby outcrops across the paleobasin. Here we describe the geology of Enamankeon, focusing on the volcanic record, and expand the geochemical dataset through new analyses of nine tephra samples.

The volcanic succession at Enamankeon includes at least eleven eruption events, preserved as layers of glassy gray ash, sandy tuffs, and ignimbrites, including a prominent 9 m thick cindery tuff bed and an impressive waterlain pumiceous ash deposit. Recent 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dating shows that deposition at Enamankeon began earlier than ca. 6.0 Ma and ended by ~6.1 Ma, suggesting rapid sedimentation within the basin. Nine tephra samples collected in 2023 were analyzed for major and minor elements using an electron microprobe. Data were compared with geochemical datasets collected by our group in 2019-2023. Results indicate that tephra from Enamankeon are trachytic to dacitic in composition and geochemically differ from glass shards analyzed thus far from other local sites. Comparisons to similarly aged volcanic sequences throughout Kenya will strengthen our understanding of the regional volcanic and depositional history, and help identify potential volcanic sources. Correlations among outcrops will provide a more complete picture of depositional environments across the Lemudong’o Formation paleobasin during a critical period in early hominin evolution.

title: Evaluation of Plume-Induced vs. Forced Subduction Initiation for the Talkeetna-Bonanza Arc System and Implications for Permo-Triassic Paleogeography of the North American Cordillera
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Keough, Brandon [1], Eddy, Michael [2], Ridgway, Kenneth [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(3) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
The mechanisms by which new subduction zones form remain one of the most fundamental problems in plate tectonics. Proposed mechanisms include underthrusting of oceanic lithosphere through crustal shortening (forced initiation), lithospheric collapse along transform systems (spontaneous initiation), and foundering along the margins of mantle plume heads (plume-induced initiation). In this study, we use Permo-Triassic stratigraphic data from across the Insular (super)terrane to evaluate potential mechanisms for Late Triassic initiation of the Talkeetna-Bonanza Arc system. New mapping of Permian and Upper Triassic strata on the Alaska Peninsula suggest a period of uplift and unconformity development followed by extension and subsidence as the arc system initiated at ca. 235-230 Ma (middle Carnian). Regional extension following subduction initiation was contemporaneous with eruption of the Wrangellia flood basalts, widely interpreted as plume-related. Integration of these findings with a synthesis of Permo-Triassic stratigraphic relationships in southern Alaska, southwestern Yukon, and coastal British Columbia shows that pre-initiation unconformity development occurred at the plate scale, with deformation and erosion concentrated along the inboard margin of the Insular terrane.

Based on this record, two potential mechanisms include: (1) forced initiation involving a subduction polarity reversal; or (2) plume-induced subduction initiation. Based on pre-initiation unconformity development, we prefer a forced mechanism as the main driver, though initiation could still have been influenced along part of the margin by a mantle plume. A forced initiation mechanism has several implications for the tectonic development of the Insular terrane and western North America more broadly. Available evidence suggests that the most likely scenario is a polarity reversal from late Paleozoic west-dipping subduction to east-dipping subduction associated with the Talkeetna-Bonanza Arc. We propose that this event resulted from convergence between the Insular terrane and either the Laurentian margin or another large Cordilleran terrane(s). In our preferred model, the Insular terrane shared a plate margin with the Intermontane belt during oblique arc-continent collision associated with the Sonoma Orogeny. Subduction initiation in the Late Triassic then resulted in rifting of the Insular terrane from its collider and opening of a marginal backarc basin. This model invokes an earlier shared history between the Insular terrane and Laurentia than prior studies and links development of the Talkeetna-Bonanza Arc to Late Triassic fringing arc systems that formed along the length of western Laurentia.

title: Conch in a Bucket: Diurnal Carbon Cycling by an Epilithic and Euendolithic Microbial Ecosystem
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Trower, Lizzy [1], Lincoln, Tyler [2], Lingappa, Usha [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Coulder, Colorado, USA
(3) California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, California, USA
abstract: Diurnal variations in rates of photosynthesis and respiration of shallow marine benthic organisms like corals or seagrasses can drive substantial shifts in the carbonate chemistry and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) δ 13 C values over the course of a day. These diurnal patterns can influence the temporal distribution of calcification (both abiotic and biotic) and potentially bias carbonate mineral δ 13 C values relative to longer term average seawater DIC δ 13 C values. We wanted to know whether these same diurnal changes can be driven by mineral-hosted shallow marine microbial communities: epiliths (microbes that live on mineral surfaces) and euendoliths (microbes that live in cavities within minerals that they create via active dissolution). To answer this question, we designed a field experiment we called “Conch in a Bucket”. We conducted this experiment at the Smithsonian Carrie Bow Cay research station, which is part of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef system in Belize. The intertidal and shallow subtidal zone adjacent to Carrie Bow Cay is characterized by many skeletal carbonates that are heavily colonized by euendolithic chlorophyte algae and cyanobacteria, in addition to epilithic algae. We selected a conch shell with a visually diverse epilithic and endolithic microbial community and placed the conch in a clear 5 L Cambro container filled with seawater. We tracked temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, and photosynthetically-active radiation (PAR) continuously in situ and sampled for major ions, DIC (concentration and δ 13 C values), and alkalinity hourly for 24 hours. After the experiment was complete, we extracted the euendolithic microbial community from the shell using a gentle EDTA leach and characterized them by microscopy and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. To provide environmental context, we also collected a similar dataset from the adjacent seagrass meadow. Our data reveal substantial shifts in the carbonate chemistry of the water across a diel cycle driven by the microbial community on and in the conch shell. These dynamics looked significantly different than the dataset from the seagrass meadow, in which the signal of respiration was much stronger than the signal of photosynthesis. Our data demonstrate that shell-hosted epiliths and euendoliths can represent hotspots of productivity and have the potential to drive significant diurnal shifts in ambient seawater carbonate chemistry.

authors: Porter, Susannah M. [1], Tydings, Aidan [2], Tingle, Kelly [3], Lahr, Daniel [4], Riedman, Leigh Anne [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA

abstract: Vase-shaped microfossils (VSMs), thought to be the tests of arcellinid testate amoebae, are widespread in late Tonian strata, typically preserved as mineralized casts and molds. Here we report diverse new assemblages of organically-preserved vase-shaped microfossils (VSMs) from ~750 Ma mudstones in the upper Awatubi and lower Walcott members of the Chuar Group. Twenty species have been tentatively identified. Seven have already been reported from the Chuar Group: Bonniea dacruchares , Cycliocyrillium simplex , Melanocyrillium hexodiadema , Melicerion poikilon , Pakupaku kabin , Trigonocyrillium fimbriatum , and T. horodyskii . An additional species, Dictyocyrillium erythron , known from the Elbobreen Formation of Svalbard and the Black River Dolomite of Tasmania, is newly reported here, as is a single specimen of Taruma rata , known previously from the Urucum Formation of Brazil. In addition, eleven new species have been provisionally identified. These include a species with a slit-shaped aperture; a species with a spherical test and triangular aperture; a species covered in ~2–4 micron bumps, and similar in appearance to a pickle; and a species covered in short, <1 µm-wide hollow bumps that is reminiscent of a strawberry. Numerous specimens across seven species preserve what appears to be a cell. The cell is pliable and protrudes from the test aperture. It exhibits a ~25 µm-diameter hole at its apex, the edge of which appears as if torn. In specimens assignable Cycliocyrillium simplex , the cell is associated with a ring of tentacle-like structures ~5 µm long and ~1 µm wide; in a specimen of Trigonocyrillium horodyskii the cell is retracted but the tentacles protrude from the aperture. To our knowledge, similar cellular features are not known to occur in modern arcellinid testate amoebae. This raises the prospect that either early arcellinid amoebae possessed a non-amoeboid stage in their lifecycle, or that at least some Tonian VSMs species, including C. simplex , T. horodyskii , and T. fimbriatum , do not belong to the arcellinid testate amoebae.

title: The Northern Snake Range Metamorphic Core Complex (NSRMCC) and Detachment Fault (NSRD): Celebrating Jeff Lee’s Contribution to its Mapping and Interpretation
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Miller, Elizabeth L. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA
abstract:
Mapping most of the many quadrangles that cover the NSRMCC culminated in Jeff Lee’s remarkable, just published, 1:62,500 color synthesis map (NBMG, 2025). His research on quartz mylonites beneath the NSRD led to the designation of the NSRMCC as a UNESCO World Geologic Heritage Site (I.U.G.S, 2022). Jeff’s early contributions on strain measurement, quartz fabrics and geo/thermochron were fundamental to understanding how this MCC evolved and include: 1. The mylonites are not confined to a “zone” but represent the deforming top of a hot and rising mass of rock with strain continuing at increasing T’s with greater depth in the crust. 2. The mylonites/strains are linked to slip on the NSRD and stretching of the upper plate based on strain progression, strain % and parallelism of strain axes. 3. U-Pb zircon ages on dikes bracket deformation in the NE as post 37-38 Ma and in the SW, pre 22.5 Ma. 4. The progressive west to east mica argon ages from ~ 80 to 20 Ma have a complex origin; their mostly disturbed spectra do not directly date lower plate mylonites. 5. His thermochron studies are evidence for a temperature difference across the range within the same structural horizon where lower plate rocks to the NW cooled below 300°C by 46 Ma and reached 115°C by 20 Ma, whereas lower plate rocks in the eastern parts of the range remained or were heated to temperatures above 300°C until 19 Ma. These observations are compatible with a deeper and/or hotter location of the eastern part of the lower plate and/or successive Oligo-Miocene pulses of formation and uplift of the mylonites.

Many divergent ideas on the evolution of the NSRMCC have been proffered, with continuing debate about the lower plate rocks of the NSRD and its motion history - how deep, how hot, when and why hot, how much up, when up, the age of the mylonites, and amount of slip on the NSRD. With the publication of the new map of the entire NSRMCC and Jeff’s foundational studies of the strain, its mylonites and timing/thermal history, may the research and debate continue to be interesting and lively in the years to come!

title: Surface and Subsurface Runoff Partitioning in Response to Winter Warming Across the Great Lakes Basin

authors: Karimi, Fatemeh [1], Qiu, Han [2], Hyndman, David [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Sustainable Earth Systems Sciences, School of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas, USA

abstract:
In snow-affected temperate regions, groundwater recharge depends on how snowmelt is partitioned between infiltration, runoff, and subsurface storage. As winters warm, seasonal snowpack becomes less persistent and midwinter melt events become more frequent, altering hydrologic processes across cold and temperate regions. Although changes in snowpack and streamflow timing have been widely investigated, how winter warming influences the partitioning of meltwater between surface runoff and subsurface flow pathways across watersheds remains less well understood.

This study investigates hydrologic responses to winter warming across the Great Lakes Basin using a multi-dataset framework combining gridded hydroclimatic products, land-surface model outputs from NLDAS-2, and hydrologic observations for water years of 1980-2025. Winter conditions were classified using a framework based on thawing degree days (TDD) and freezing degree days (FDD) to distinguish warm and cool winters.

Preliminary results indicate a basin-wide shift toward more thaw-dominated winters, accompanied by spatially variable hydrologic responses. Long-term snow-season Qs/Qsb ratios were highest in northern, snow-dominated watersheds, reflecting a greater relative contribution from surface runoff. Warm–cool comparisons showed higher surface runoff in parts of the northern basin but lower surface runoff across many southern and eastern watersheds. Modeled subsurface runoff was generally higher during warm winters across much of the basin, although statistically significant differences were spatially limited. Consequently, warm winters generally had lower Qs/Qsb ratios, suggesting a shift toward a greater relative contribution from modeled subsurface runoff in many watersheds, with northern exceptions.

This work will provide a basin-scale assessment of how changing winter conditions alter runoff partitioning across the Great Lakes Basin and will establish a foundation for evaluating implications for groundwater recharge, storage, and streamflow under future climate conditions.

abstract:
FossilSketch is an interactive digital learning application that introduces students to micropaleontology through educational videos, mini-games, and guided exercises highlighting its geoscience applications. This qualitative study investigated instructors' experiences using and implementing FossilSketch in high school, laboratory, or university settings.

High school teachers (n=13) participated in a School of Rock outreach workshop, where they watched a demonstration of FossilSketch functionality, explored the application on their own, and provided feedback through a survey. University instructors and researchers were recruited based on their interest in using FossilSketch in their courses, with five out of six instructors having implemented the application in their teaching. These users participated in semi-structured interviews. Participants in both groups described FossilSketch as a user-friendly and beneficial resource for students.

Four university-level instructors used FossilSketch in a broad range of undergraduate courses including Paleoceanography, Paleontology, Biodiversity, Ecology, and Conservation, and one researcher reported using it to train PhD students. Instructors noted that the application provided access to authentic scientific materials that would otherwise be difficult to replicate in traditional classroom settings. They observed that students enjoyed learning through FossilSketch and highlighted its meaningful educational benefits, such as understanding the applications of microfossil research, and the use of microfossils as proxies for paleoreconstructions, such as reconstructing past water oxygenation levels. Two of the instructors also pointed out the importance of looking at morphologically diverse groups of organisms and learning ways to distinguish between them, and thus understanding the basics of taxonomy. Participants also valued the application's ease of use for instructors with limited micropaleontology background. Instructors also recommended future enhancements, including the incorporation of additional exercises and features, such as short videos explaining differences between certain morphological characteristics, or groups of microfossils, and adding exercises on areas like phylogeny. Instructors also suggested increasing the database of 3D interactive images.

These findings demonstrate the applicability of FossilSketch to diverse geoscience and biology learning settings and highlight the potential of interactive digital tools to increase access to authentic geoscience experiences. The results also provide practical guidance for the design and implementation of future digital resources that support geoscience education and outreach.

title: Hidden Geothermal Systems in Southern Idaho: Geologic Controls, Masking Mechanisms, and Exploration Implications

abstract: Southern Idaho sits at the intersection of the northeast-migrating Yellowstone–Snake River Plain hotspot track, active Basin and Range extensional faulting, and widespread Cenozoic volcanism. All these conditions can create high regional heat flow and significant geothermal potential. Despite this region’s favorable tectonic setting, geothermal development remains limited. A key factor is the prevalence of hidden, or "blind," geothermal systems: subsurface hydrothermal resources that lack surface thermal expression and are therefore invisible to conventional exploration methods. Surface manifestations such as hot springs, fumaroles, and geysers are often absent in southern Idaho due to several overlapping masking mechanisms. Thick sequences of Quaternary basalt associated with the Eastern Snake River Plain overlie and recharge one of North America's most productive aquifers, which dilutes and cools ascending geothermal fluids before they reach the surface. Structurally complex fault systems, many of which are sealed by impermeable cap, further suppress hydrothermal fluid migration. Rhyolitic volcanic cover along the margins of the ESRP adds additional insulating and sealing capacity. In combination, these factors prevent geothermal fluids from reaching the surface, masking subsurface heat anomalies and rendering conventional indicator-based exploration ineffective. This study synthesizes published geological, geochemical, geophysical, and geothermal data to characterize the distribution, geologic controls, and masking mechanisms of hidden geothermal systems in southern Idaho. Using structural mapping, heat flow data, hydrogeologic models, and geochemical proxies, we identify where geothermal potential is most likely underestimated and outline the conditions under which blind systems are expected to occur. This work is intended to guide future Play Fairway Analysis (PFA) and field-based investigation, including a planned case study near Lava Hot Springs, Idaho. Southern Idaho provides a natural laboratory for understanding hidden geothermal systems in extensional tectonic settings. This synthesis advances exploration approaches, explains the geologic basis for Idaho's under-utilized geothermal resource, and supports efforts for expanding low-carbon energy development in communities across the region.

title: Detecting Deep Time Ocean Acidification Events with High-Precision Calcium Isotope Measurements
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part I)
authors: Jacobson, Andrew D. [1], Sageman, Bradley B. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL,
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL,
abstract: Earth Scientists have long hypothesized that CO 2 outgassing during large igneous province eruptions can acidify seawater, perturb carbonate mineral saturation states, and suppress biocalcification. To test this hypothesis, our group has worked over the past decade to generate and interpret high-precision TIMS δ 44/40 Ca records spanning multiple candidate ocean acidification (OA) events, including Ocean Anoxic Event 1a (OAE1a), the Aptian-Albian Boundary Interval (AABI), Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2), the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary (K-Pg), and the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM). When aligned relative to accepted event boundaries/onsets, most records resolve similar fine-scale signals that oscillate around different average δ 44/40 Ca values. The isotopic pattern comprises positive-to-negative shifts before the boundaries, negative-to-positive shifts that begin before and peak at the boundaries, negative excursions after the boundaries, and positive recoveries. Two K-Pg records yield the only exception, where peak δ 44/40 Ca values occur immediately prior to the Chicxulub impact. The consistently repeated pattern is striking given that the records represent different depositional settings, CaCO 3 archives, and mineralogies (calcite and aragonite). Our dataset includes supporting measurements (e.g., δ 88/86 Sr, Os i , and Sr/Ca), paleontological observations, and model calculations, which allow us to constrain the pattern’s origin and meaning. The high-fidelity preservation of primary kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) offers the best explanation. Higher δ 44/40 Ca values imply slower biocalcification rates, whereas lower δ 44/40 Ca values imply faster biocalcification rates. Alternative explanations, such as diagenetic overprinting and rapid changes in the Ca isotope composition of seawater due to enhanced chemical weathering and/or reduced carbonate burial, appear less likely. The AABI dataset systematically eliminates these alternative explanations. Among multiple insights, we contend that discrepant views of the δ 44/40 Ca tracer reflect artifacts of variable data quality and model assumptions that conflict with empirical evidence. Our findings illuminate the candidate OA events as volcanically triggered biocalcification crises. Implications exist for several first-order topics, including, but not limited to, linkages between solid and surface Earth processes, climate change, mass extinctions, OA dampening mechanisms, biomineralization, and even development of novel CO 2 removal strategies, such as artificial ocean alkalinization.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Willow Creek and South Crestone Creek Glacial Histories in the Sangre De Cristo Mountains, CO

abstract: Glacial erosion and glacially derived sediment can have an outsized impact on landscape evolution, sediment transport, and riparian habitat; yet, the degree of erosion and sediment production can vary greatly between neighboring drainages. Here, we investigate the drivers of differential glacial erosion and sediment production at North Crestone and Willow Creek, which are two adjacent glacial valleys on the western slope of Colorado’s Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Despite their proximity, Willow Creek ends in >800 ft terminal moraines while North Crestone Creek lacks any terminal moraines. Previous studies have focused on climatic differences on either side of the range; but there has been no explanation for the variable glacial deposits between western slope valleys. We used newly available lidar imagery and field observations to outline paleoglacier extents, and we created a geomorphic map of the region, which was paired with statistical analysis of sediment inputs. These features were cross analyzed with previously mapped faults, folds, and geologic units to identify patterns between sediment input, lithologic controls, and structural controls. We find that the longitudinal extents of both glaciers were shown to be incredibly similar, but the North Crestone Creek Glacier covered twice the area as the Willow Creek Glacier. Yet, Willow Creek has significantly more sediment input than North Crestone Creek, due to the strong structural control exerted by the Gibson Peak Syncline that promoted more glacial plucking in lower Willow Creek and bolstered rockslide occurrences in upper Willow Creek. Our results show that bedrock orientation has a significant influence on sediment production within glacial valleys to the extent that a glacier half the size of another can produce similar volumes of sediment. It also implies that structural features such as synclines may set the position of glacial valleys and thus of large drainage divides.

title: FURTHER PROOF OF A UNIFIED AVALONIA: LOWER CAMBRIAN “WORM-REEFS” LINK “WEST” AND “EAST” AVALONIA INTO NON-GONDWANAN RIBBON CONTINENT WITH SYNDEPOSITIONAL STRIKE-SLIP (NOT RIFT) FAULTING
