abstract: Avalonia forms the SE margin of the Appalachian (Acadian)–Caledonian orogen in NE North America, southern Britain, and north-central mainland Europe. It is a terrane defined by a distinctive terminal Ediacaran–Ordovician cover sequence unconformable on a late Proterozoic basement collage of arc, continental, and oceanic blocks. Exclusive of the Avalonian offshore Meguma belt, Avalonia’s SE margin is the inner platform, invariably with a thin (ca. 2 m to rarely12 m thick), generally red limestone exposed from eastern Massachusetts through Atlantic Canada to Shropshire. This limestone (Foster’s Point Formation, FPF) is a time-stratigraphic marker. It forms a 120 km-wide blanket across the Avalon Peninsula. This distribution counters the claim of as many as nine syndepositional half-grabens/rifts in SE Newfoundland, and is consistent with deposition in a strike-slip regime. The FPF is correlated chemostratigraphically with the CARE δC 13 excursion and by microfossils into lower trilobite-bearing strata in Siberia, China, Morocco, and South Australia (ca. 517.5 Ma), but lacks trilobites. Its correlation proves the diachronous lowest occurrence of mineralized trilobites, which appear in the rock record with the change from an aragonitic to a calcitic ocean. Indeed, the FPF unconformably underlies the Brigus Formation with Callavia broeggeri Zone trilobites, with a ca. 300 Ka hiatus. The more offshore (i.e., specifically the NE inner platform) FPF in “west” and “east” Avalonia (Cape Breton, SE Newfoundland, Shropshire) features an almost monospecific biofacies in nodular griotte of in situ (vertically embedded), calcareous (originally aragonite), tiny (to 1.5 mm diameter), slender tubes of the metazoan “worm-grade” (a polychaete?) Coleoloides typicalis . Densities of up to 550,000 individuals/m 2 (perhaps reflecting asexual reproduction) occur in griotte mud mounds that extend at least 1,600 km along “west” and “east” Avalonia (Cape Breton to Shropshire), which is exceeded in length only by the Great Barrier Reef. Vertically embedded C . typicalis (a polychaete?) and earlier Ladatheca ? cylindrica (and orthothecid hyolith) in Avalonian mud mounds are unknown in Gondwana, where these high latitude bioconstructions are replaced by tropical archaeocyath-algal build-ups.

title: Evaluating Basin-Scale Controls on River Avulsion Using a Global Database
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Reaves, Corey Blaine [1], Gearon, James Hooker [2], George, Sarah Winspeare Merriam [3]
affiliations: (1) Environment, Ecology and Energy Program, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA; Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA
(2) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA
(3) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA
abstract: River avulsion occurs when a river relocates from its channel onto an adjacent floodplain. Avulsions can cause catastrophic loss of life, infrastructure damage, and landscape alteration. Beyond their surface hazard potential, avulsion deposits are a major component of the alluvial stratigraphic record. While the local conditions behind avulsion setup (superelevation and gradient advantage) are linked to high channel-belt sedimentation rates, these data are not widely available and do not appear to explain all observed basin-to-basin variation in modern avulsion occurrence. Prior work explains avulsion from the perspective of local topography and cross-sectional morphology. However, these properties are fundamentally related to the characteristics of their upstream catchments. Whether basins that contain avulsing rivers are distinguishable from similar basins that do not is unknown. To test this, we compare climatic, hydrologic, physiographic, and geomorphic parameters from 93 basins with observed avulsions to matched control basins with no documented avulsions. Control basins were selected by minimizing the combined differences in upstream drainage area and mean annual precipitation, allowing other basin characteristics to be compared while accounting for two major controls on river size and water availability. This approach seeks to identify the basin-scale characteristics associated with downstream avulsion susceptibility, providing a framework for recognizing avulsion-prone catchments rather than only individual at-risk river reaches. Quantifying these indicators provides a method for evaluating broad avulsion risk, which can in turn inform hazard, infrastructure, and land-use management decisions in vulnerable regions where avulsions preferentially occur.

title: Building and Reworking Delta Plains Under Rising Seas: Experimental Insights into Delta Aggradation and Erosion
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Swaby, Trista [1], Steel, Elisabeth [2], Chun, Byong-suk [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences and Geological Engineering, Queen's University, Kingston, Ontario, Canada
(2) Geological Sciences and Geological Engineering, Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada

abstract: River-dominated deltas are complex geological landforms that connect and influence both fluvial and marine processes. The movement of sediment and water across the delta surface alters delta plain topography and affects local ecosystems as well as coastal communities. Once buried, sediment deposited by distributary channels can be preserved, creating pathways for subsurface fluids, forming reservoirs and aquifers. Previous studies describe autogenic cycles, that encompass periods of channelized flow followed by sheet flow on the delta topset. This cyclicity is a fundamental component of aggradation and channel migration across the delta topset, which strongly influences subsurface architecture of the delta. This study utilizes a physical laboratory experiment (QCDS24) to investigate how sustained sea-level rise drives spatial and temporal trends in delta plain aggradation and erosion. The QCDS24 experiment simulates a river-dominated delta with a stable and continuous influx of water and sediment, while undergoing constant steady sea level rise. The sediment mixture contained quartz sand, glass beads, ceramic microspheres and bentonite. The experiment ran for a duration of 300 hours with a constant sea-level rise of 0.5 mm/hr and a constant sediment (0.00022 L/s) and water flux (0.22 L/s). Data from the experiment was collected in the form of topographic scans, overhead images and physical sediment samples taken as peels from the final deposit. The dataset obtained from this experiment will allow for the investigation of links between autogenic cycles, distribution of aggradation across the delta surface and the corresponding subsurface stratigraphy. We will present preliminary results of spatial and temporal trends in aggradation and erosion of the surface and how this relates to the mobility of channels. Future work will focus on combining the temporal and spatial surface data to the subsurface architecture.

title: Does Morphology Record Environmental Stress? A Case Study of Turborotalita quinqueloba from the Messinian Salinity Crisis

abstract: The Messinian Salinity Crisis (MSC, 5.97 to 5.33 Ma), was a period of extreme salinities in the Mediterranean Sea driven by tectonic restriction of exchange with the Atlantic Ocean. The detrimental effect these extreme changes had on marine life remains a difficult area of study due to the limited record of marine life, specifically foraminifera, during this interval. Here we examine the impact of rising salinity associated with the MSC on foraminifera through the morphological variation of one species, Turborotalita quinqueloba , recovered from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 401 Site U1611A in the Alborán Basin, western Mediterranean Sea. This record is unique because this marginal basin of the main Mediterranean sustained planktic foraminifera despite the rising salinities during the MSC. To determine whether specific environmental stressors affect test morphology, we measured size and shape metrics of Messinian T. quinqueloba specimens. Tests of this species exhibit an increase in circularity and decrease in compactness prior to the onset of the MSC. However, we do not observe any significant size variation before or after the onset of the crisis. To investigate potential causes for these shape changes in the Mediterranean, we measured specimens of modern T. quinqueloba collected from depth-stratified plankton tows off the coast of Oregon, for which we have data of the precise environmental conditions of their collection sites. Measured temperature, salinity, and density with depth at each site do not differ from each other significantly; however, increases in fluorescence—a proxy for chlorophyll-a—and oxygen content occur at different water depths at each site. Additionally, sites have different proximities to the coastline and may be bathed in different water masses and ocean currents. We studied if environmental factors in living T. quinqueloba can explain the shape variations recorded in the fossil record. Preliminary results in modern T. quinqueloba specimens may indicate a nonlinear, site-dependent relationship between environmental variables and morphology. Further study could determine whether the shape variation in the fossil population records a pre- or early-MSC restriction event.

title: Patterns and Dynamics of In-Stream Large Wood Following Wildfire
session_title: Understanding and Facilitating River Corridor Resilience to Wildfire
authors: Kemper, John Trusal [1], Belmont, Patrick [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(2) Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT,
abstract: The cascade of disturbances that commonly occur following wildfire often culminate in elevated erosion risks, threatening critical infrastructure and natural resources within and downstream of burned areas. In-stream large wood may have several crucial functions that serve to mitigate these hazards in post-fire settings, including increased retention of sediment and enhanced habitat resilience and recovery. However, though past work has demonstrated that large wood loading generally increases following fire, the dynamics and trajectory of wood supply and impact following fire remain poorly understood. Quantitative field data on wood-sediment interactions following fire are similarly scarce. Here, we measure wood in nearly 400 stream segments in burned areas across the state of Utah that span gradients in topographic setting, forest characteristics, burn severity, and time since fire (1~25 years). Preliminary results suggest that fire measurably increases wood loading to streams within burned areas, with ~90% of individual wood pieces showing evidence of burning and ~95% of jams containing visibly burned wood. Similarly, wood volumes in burned reaches were statistically significantly greater than literature reported values for similar forest types. A majority of jams within burned areas (~75%) had an observable geomorphic impact, and, of these, roughly 70% stored measurable sediment, indicating that more than half of jams within burned areas impact downstream sediment transport. Stored sediment was primarily coarse gravel, and storage volumes measured in a subset of jams ranged across five orders of magnitude (10 -2 – 10 2 m 3 ), with a median of ~2 m 3 . Wood volumes appeared to be a function of valley morphology, burn severity, forest characteristics, and post-fire history (debris flow occurrence, time since fire). Together, results indicate that a) large wood has the potential to mitigate sediment export from burned watersheds, but storage volumes may be relatively minimal in most locations and b) topography and burn severity together control post-fire wood supply, suggesting that wood supply can be empirically modeled at the watershed scale using techniques like machine learning. Results should also help to inform targets for post-fire management actions, including erosion mitigation and stream restoration via wood addition to streams.

title: From Daily Tasks to Professional Wins: Lessons Learned from a Five-Year-Old Internship Program
session_title: Learning to be a Geoscientist: Professional Exposure, Agency, and Transferable Skills in Undergraduate Education.
authors: Adams, Elizabeth [1], Swallom, Meredith Leigh [2], Haneberg, William C. [3], Tobin, Benjamin W. [4]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY,
(3) William C. Haneberg, LLC, Albuquerque, NM,

abstract:
Through a generous gift from the late Dr. Paul Edwin Potter, the Kentucky Geological Survey (KGS) has supported 28 undergraduate and graduate students to explore geoscience research and professional goals through a 10-week summer internship program. The program comprises several components, including student-mentor matching, professional seminars, field experiences, and oral and poster presentations by interns to the local geoscience community. Established in the summer of 2022, the program has evolved over the years based on feedback from exiting cohorts and program mentors. However, the core goals of providing “new-to-them” skills and research topics, fostering soft skills for career readiness, and broadening perceptions of geoscience and geologists have remained constant.

Since its initiation, the program has received 157 applications (~18% acceptance rate) with steady annual growth year after year. So far, selected participants represent seven disciplines from ten institutions of higher education across three states, and 16 KGS research staff have volunteered as project mentors. Growing the cohort size and continuing to expand institution and discipline representation would allow for an increased acceptance rate and a broader scope of work for participating students.

As the program completes its fifth year in 2026, we have undertaken a five-year program evaluation study to capture the impacts of participation, evaluate how participation affected perceptions of geoscience as a career, and inform future program design. The study involves an IRB-approved protocol to administer a brief 10-question survey in year five to record self-reported benefits, perceptions, and impacts from the program’s participants. The study aims to capture impacts experienced during and years after participation, identify key components not replicated by other experiences, and evaluate the program’s effectiveness at preparing students for future academic and professional goals. The results of the study will be presented along with demographic information and program history as a workforce development and recruitment tool for geoscience professions.

title: Plutons and the rocks that surround them: minerals, structures, compositions
session_title: GSA Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Division Awards Session
authors: Barnes, Calvin G. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract:
It is a great honor to receive the MGPV Distinguished Geological Career Award. One might wonder, how does a kid from eastern Nebraska end up studying crystalline rocks? Perhaps the curiosity was already there, but an introduction to hard-rock geology during a week of field camp in Ruby Mountains, two seasons in Antarctica with excellent, if gruff, undergraduate advisor Sam Treves, and an MS thesis on Cascade volcanoes set the stage. The opportunity to work on USGS wilderness resource evaluations in the Klamath Mountains led to a shift in focus to plutons and their host rocks, and I never looked back. In those days, U of Oregon was not “into” granitic rocks. A.R. MacBirney’s advice was two-fold: “Everything you need to know about granite is in The Geology of Donegal ”, and “All granites are cumulates”. Nevertheless, field work with an amazing group of colleagues provided a real appreciation for the intricate relationships between plutons and their host rocks; insight that has guided our research ever since. This early work included recognition of tilted plutons, from moderate tilting to 90° rotations. Seeing the “vertical” variations in plutons resulted in an appreciation of the “where” and “when” of possible and improbable processes such as mixing, assimilation, partial melting, and stoping.

My mid-career crisis came when the Klamaths became boring. It was resolved with projects in north-central Norway and the Ruby Mountains (NV). The former was a beautiful contrast to Cordilleran geology, and the latter pushed me to come to grips with “true” granite.

Over time, I came to pay attention to Mac’s advice about granites as cumulates, which coincided with a new research emphasis: using trace element data on mafic minerals to attempt reconstruction of melt compositions. The approach led to a deeper understanding of liquid lines of descent, dimensions of magma batches, mass balance relationships, and the tectonic settings of volcanogenic sandstone. In many instances, the importance of crystal accumulation became obvious, at least to me.

Along the way, I have had the privilege of working with excellent students and have benefited, both personally and professionally, from the opportunity to work with fantastic collaborators. To all of them, and all of you in the MGPV community, I extend my heartfelt thanks.

title: Comparing Climate Change and Biological Invasion as Drivers of Holocene Megafaunal Extinction on Madagascar
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Hixon, Sean Wolf [1]
affiliations: (1) Integrative Biology, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA; Archaeology, Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology, Jena, Thuringia, Germany
abstract: Aridity can exacerbate threats to endemic biodiversity, and arid intervals during the last couple of millennia may have contributed to endemic large herbivore extinctions on Madagascar. However, regional palaeoclimate records spanning multiple millennia are limited, and the tolerance of extinct taxa to past water scarcity is poorly known. To infer changes in the diet and habitat aridity of extinct pygmy hippos and giant tortoises during approximately 6000–1000 years ago, I used carbon and nitrogen isotope ( δ 13 C and δ 15 N) data from 49 directly radiocarbon-dated bones collected around Tampolove, southwest Madagascar. Fluctuations in bone δ 15 N values through time in both species indicate tolerance of dry habitat during intermittent drying trends, including around a dry period known as the ‘4.2 ka event’. However, taxon-specific differences in the covariance of bone δ 13 C and δ 15 N values suggest that the diets of pygmy hippos and giant tortoises changed in different ways during these past arid intervals. This suggests that past aridification had different effects on these taxa. Thus, I argue that hypotheses for past extinction that involve a synergy among climate drying and forest clearance, hunting, and biological invasion must consider taxon-specific responses to past aridity.

title: Understanding the dynamics of phosphorus sorption onto microplastics and soils under clay minerals
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part II)

abstract: Microplastic pollution in aquatic ecosystems and agricultural soils is a significant concern in the United States. Agricultural soil serves as the primary sink for microplastics and acts as a carrier for various pollutants. Microplastic (MP) pollution in soil disrupts nutrient cycling and reduces nutrient bioavailability for plant uptake. Therefore, this study aims to understand phosphorus sorption onto MPs and competitive interactions with soils under varying clay minerals. Adsorption of Phosphorus has been investigated at varying phosphate concentrations (0-10 mg/L), MPs (0-50 mg), soils (0-1 g), and clay minerals (0-100 mg/L) at varying pH and ionic strengths. Various MPs, such as polystyrene (PS), polypropylene (PP), and polyethylene (PE), are commonly found in agricultural soils in the United States. In this study, phosphorus adsorption has been investigated under hematite, goethite, and kaolinite at the soil-MPs interface. This work summarizes how small quantities of MPs can adsorption significant phosphate and can affect its bioavailability for plant uptake. Furthermore, this work focuses on understanding phosphate adsorption in a cocktail of soil-MP systems under varying solution chemistries to address real-world challenges related to MP pollution in agricultural soils and nutrient management.

title: Mechanical Heterogeneity and Fold Kinematics in the Alta Thrust System: An Integrated Field and Digital Mapping Workflow for Complex Outcrops
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Conger, Abigail [1], Reeher, Lauren [2], Anderson, Zach [3], Patton, Harrison [4]
affiliations: (1) Utah Geological Survey, Millcreek, UT,
(2) Utah Geological Survey,
(3) Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT,
(4) University of Utah,
abstract:
The Alta and Columbus thrusts are stacked, moderate- to small-displacement thrusts exposed near Alta, Utah. These thrusts are unique in that they are east-directed but currently east-dipping, and are exposed in a structural high between the Charleston-Nebo and Wyoming salients of the Cordilleran thrust belt. The structural block bound by these thrusts contains a highly folded section of Cambrian Tintic Quartzite conformably overlain by the Ophir Shale. We measured and characterized folds within this block to understand: 1) the structural response of mechanical heterogeneity, 2) strain gradients near contacts and faults, and 3) the kinematics of the thrust faults.

The two units display distinct mechanical behaviors. The strong, medium-bedded Tintic Quartzite exhibits meter- to decimeter-scale folds, whereas the weak, laminated Ophir Shale accommodates strain through centimeter- to meter-scale folding. Deformation intensity increases towards the upper (Columbus) thrust contact, where the Ophir Shale is intensely and complexly folded.

Initially, these Ophir outcrops appear so chaotically folded that deformation patterns are not obvious. To extract meaningful kinematic data from these folds, we developed a systematic workflow to record georeferenced fold data for multiple small-scale folds. An orthomosaic image of the outcrops captured by a UAV provided a high resolution basemap to identify and georeference field localities exhibiting meter-scale folds, which are commonly accompanied by multiple scales of parasitic folding. Physical labels applied directly on the outcrop were used to delineate fold hinge axes, limbs, and different beds at each locality. These features were then photographed, measured, and geolocated with the Clino Field Move app. Furthermore, we utilized the LiDAR scanning capabilities of iPad Pro with CloudCompare to build virtual outcrops and extract additional data. This workflow can be used to analyze other small complex folding in the region.

Our analysis reveals that both calculated and measured fold hinge axes within the highly deformed Ophir Shale display a moderate plunge to the northwest, consistent with the geometry of the larger folds in the Tintic Quartzite. This structural alignment suggests that despite extreme local strain, small-scale folding in the mechanically weak Ophir Shale reliably records the broader kinematic framework of the Alta thrust system, providing critical insights into the region's tectonic evolution.

title: VSWIR Reflectance Spectroscopy of Hydrated Volcanic Glass: Assessing Bonding Sites Linked to δD values in the Campbell Creek Tuff
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California (Posters)
authors: Zinzer, Bailee [1], Rader, Erika [2], Cassel, Elizabeth [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
(2) University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
(3) University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
abstract:
Felsic volcanic glass is a valuable paleoaltimetry proxy because it captures the hydrogen isotopic composition (δD) of meteoric water shortly after deposition. However, the method to prepare glass to obtain δD values is time and laboratory intensive. A remote sensing technique sensitive to the water content of glass could potentially speed up this process and allow for a broader application of the glass-paleoaltimetry technique. This study tests whether visible near-infrared and shortwave infrared (VSWIR 350-2500nm) reflectance spectroscopy can identify specific bonding sites for protium and deuterium within the spectra and link δD values to absorption features in volcanic glass.

Ten glass separates from the 28.9 Ma Campbell Creek tuff (Nevada) were scanned using an ASD TerraSpec Halo spectrometer. Preliminary spectral profiles show water-related absorption features near 1155, 1415, 1910, and 2225 nm, and we are investigating how the depth, width, and area of these features relate to δD value. Of particular interest is the 2225 nm features associated with Si-OH since it is thought that deuterium prefers to bond to that site, a relationship that, if present, should reflect how this feature responds to δD values. Thus far preliminary results show that the 1910 nm and 2225 nm features have the strongest correlation with δD value, with deeper absorptions corresponding to more negative δD values. We also examine whether VNIR absorption features remain less sensitive to increasing hydration than SWIR features, which are expected to broaden and deepen with overall water content, and whether overall reflectance tracks hydration in a similar way.

To further assess how this relationship presents itself, we compare spectra from whole-rock samples of the Campbell Creek tuff to the glass separates, testing whether hydration features remain distinguishable from mineral absorption features and whether a spectral relationship to δD value persists despite mineral overlap. This is a key step toward determining whether VSWIR is suitable for identifying vitrophyre and estimating δD values without requiring glass separation. These preliminary results investigate whether portable VSWIR spectroscopy could be used as a rapid, field-deployable tool for screening volcanic glass suitability for paleoaltimetry and estimating δD values; while also answering how hydrogen isotopes partition to specific bonding sites and how that is portrayed in spectra.

title: Appalachian Mountaintop Removal Coal Mines as Harmful Engineered Systems: An Example from the 2022 North Fork Kentucky River Floods
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Haneberg, William C. [1]
affiliations: (1) William C. Haneberg, LLC, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract: Mountaintop removal coal mines, which are environmentally destructive and ultimately unreclaimable engineered systems, have disturbed more than 5900 km 2 of Appalachian landscape across 59 counties in Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Virginia. The mines have been associated with negative health outcomes among nearby residents (e.g., birth defects, cancer, cardiovascular and respiratory disease), landslides on ostensibly stable engineered slopes, downstream surface water quality and habitat degradation, and increased flood severity. Previously published results have shown that mountaintop removal mined lands may have increased cumulative discharge by 21% to 41% in four watersheds during late July 2022 floods along the North Fork Kentucky River resulting from rain that in some areas exceeded 1000-year recurrence thresholds. The modeled variability was due to a combination of spatially variable rainfall and mine footprints, leading to recurrence intervals ranging from 2 yr to 851 yr at three gages along the North Fork. The work described in this presentation 1) shows how significant variability in flood discharge and recurrence intervals at gages along a single river can be understood using a simple probabilistic routing model, 2) uses peak discharge stream gage data and modeled cumulative discharge values to further quantify the impact of mining through changes in estimated flood recurrence interval increases, and 3) makes a ~300 yr estimate of the July 2022 flood recurrence interval for Troublesome Creek, an ungaged tributary of the North Fork. Among the four watersheds analyzed, Troublesome Creek 1) received the highest average rainfall during the storm (22.6 cm), 2) had the highest percentage of mining-disturbed terrain (25%), 3) had the highest increase in modeled cumulative discharge attributed to mining (41%), and 4) was the location of 42% of the flood fatalities while comprising only 13% of the affected watershed area. Consequences like those of the 2022 North Fork Kentucky River flood raise important ethical questions about the role of geologists and engineers as advocates for and implementers of engineered systems for which an emerging body of literature shows a disproportionately high ratio of societal and environmental harms to benefits.

title: The Metallogenic Provinces of Wyoming and their Tectonic Origins
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits.
authors: Biasi, Joseph [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, Wyoming, USA
abstract: The U.S. state of Wyoming records a long and multifaceted geologic history, which has led to the formation of varied and overlapping metallogenic provinces. These provinces were formed in a variety of tectonic settings over the last 3.5 b.y., and deposit formation continues in Wyoming to the present day. This study presents an overview of the major ore-forming periods in Wyoming’s geologic history and provides tectonic and geographic context for these events. Collectively, these metallogenic provinces host a wide variety of deposit types — from magmatic PGE deposits, to orogenic gold, to roll-front uranium. These provinces, however, are not random in their occurrence or distribution, but are unique products of their tectonic environments of formation. Some provinces, like the Cheyenne Belt, have a protracted history of ore formation and modification extending back to the Archean. Other provinces such as the Laramide Basins and Distributed Alkaline provinces are products of more recent geological and tectonic processes. Finally, I discuss how a new metallogenic province may be actively forming beneath the Yellowstone Plateau.

title: Py_Glacier: A QGIS Plugin for Glacier Mass Balance and Ice Flow Modeling
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations
authors: Li, Yingkui [1], Plummer, Mitchell [2], Leonard, Eric [3]

abstract: Glacier modeling is of essential importance for understanding past and future climate impacts on glacier dynamics, yet existing models often require advanced programming skills and have software dependencies, creating barriers for many researchers. We present Py_Glacier, an open-source QGIS plugin that provides a friendly graphical user interface for running coupled mass balance and ice flow models directly within a widely used open-source GIS platform. This plugin integrates two components: a pure Python implementation of a distributed energy balance model that computes surface mass balance by incorporating snow accumulation and melt, solar radiation with shadow effects, longwave, shortwave, and turbulent heat fluxes, and avalanche redistribution; and a wrapper for an executable ice flow model that simulates ice deformation, basal sliding, and thickness evolution over time. The plugin handles input parameterization, generates model-configuration files, executes the model simulation, and visualizes model outputs in QGIS with real-time log messages and progress tracking. Py_Glacier has been tested and verified through comparison with Plummer and Phillips (2003)'s ArcView model outputs. By integrating sophisticated mass balance and ice flow models within the leading open-source GIS platform, Py_Glacier lowers technical barriers and enables researchers and educators to focus more on scientific questions rather than model processing complexities, promoting reproducible research and collaboration within the glacier research community.

title: Constraining Magmatic Timescales and Evolution During the Onset of the Continental Ignimbrite Flare-Up at the Platoro Caldera Complex Using Zircon Geochronology and Geochemistry
session_title: Continental magmatic-volcanic flare-ups: multidisciplinary investigations on their causes and consequences
authors: Liedtke, Brice [1], Tierney, Casey [2], Amundsen, Benjamin [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
(2) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA

abstract:
The Southern Rocky Mountain Volcanic Field (SRMVF) in southwestern Colorado is the product of a continental ignimbrite flare-up that erupted >60,000 km³ of lavas and ignimbrites between ~38 and 23 Ma. The 20 × 20 km Platoro Caldera Complex records some of the volcanic field's earliest volcanism, beginning with eruption of the Conejos Formation (~35–31.5 Ma; 40 Ar/ 39 Ar), a sequence of predominantly andesitic lavas. Previous geochronology suggests a subsequent ~1.4 Myr volcanic lull, wherein the upper-crustal magma system(s) and surrounding continental crust may have thermally and chemically incubated, before eruption of the six caldera-forming Treasure Mountain Group ignimbrites in quick succession (~30.1–28.8 Ma).

My research aims to utilize zircon separated from Conejos lavas and the earliest ignimbrites to investigate the timescales and evolution of the upper-crustal magma systems at Platoro. Of particular interest is when flare-up magmatism initiated in the area and how the magma system(s) and crustal storage conditions evolved leading up the eruption of the Conejos lavas, and also during the potential incubation phase prior to the ignimbrite eruptions.

U-Pb crystallization ages and trace element concentrations were obtained by Split-Stream LA-ICP-MS analysis of >350 zircon rims from four samples (two lavas and two ignimbrites). Zircon from the Conejos lavas record a continuous spectra of rim ages from eruption to ~40 Ma, indicating flare-up magmatism began by at least this time and may predate known Conejos volcanism by ~5 Myr. The youngest zircon rims, which provide a proxy for eruption timing, from one sampled Conejos lava dates to ~30 Ma. This overlaps with zircon rim and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar eruption ages from the earliest ignimbrites and suggests that previous sampling and age constraints may underestimate the duration of Conejos volcanism, and no volcanic lull may have occurred.

In zircon from both the lavas and ignimbrites, Ti and Th/U decrease through time, indicating cooling and progressive melt evolution. Whereas decreasing LREE/HREE could suggest progressively shallower magma storage. Increased trace element heterogeneity in the youngest zircon rims may record rejuvenated magma recharge or mixing near-eruption. Mesoproterozoic (1200–1500 Ma) zircon xenocrysts in both Conejos lavas and early ignimbrites indicate assimilation of the granitic basement. Future work includes utilizing thermochemical modeling with the zircon age spectra to constrain magmatic fluxes through time.

abstract: Rapidly urbanizing areas, such as Austin, Texas, face a multitude of compounding factors that impact water quality, such as aging infrastructure, continued development driven by increasing population density, and climate variability. Aging infrastructure leads to municipal water (supply water [or drinking water] and wastewater) leakage, resulting in the release of contaminants into surface waters. Wastewater poses a threat to human health and the environment, as it can introduce emerging contaminants (ECs) and pathogenic microorganisms into watersheds. Whereas traditional geochemical parameters (e.g., major ions) and isotopic tracers (e.g., Sr isotopes) are effective tracers of municipal water contributions to Austin-area streams, distinguishing between municipal supply water vs. municipal wastewater contributions remains a challenge. Prior studies have identified some ECs as effective signals of both raw and treated wastewater. We apply here traditional geochemical parameters as well as Escherichia coli ( E. coli ), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), pharmaceuticals, artificial sweeteners, and virus markers to assess the extent and potential sources of contamination in eight Austin watersheds that exhibit a range of urbanization extents and drain into the Colorado River as it flows through the city. We find that the extent of water quality degradation relates to the extent of watershed development, whereby highly urbanized watersheds (Waller and Boggy Creeks) exhibit higher concentrations of E. coli and some ECs (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFHxS) compared to rural and developing watersheds. We also find that concentrations of some PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFHxS), pharmaceuticals (carbamazepine, sulfamethoxazole), artificial sweetener (sucralose), and wastewater-associated ions (NO 3 , SO 4 ) increase downstream in the Colorado River as it passes through Austin’s urban core and adjacent to several industrial facilities. We also find an increase in PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFDA, PFHxS, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFHpS, PFBA, PFBS, PFPeA, 6.2FtS) concentrations in a semi-urbanized watershed (Onion Creek) as it passes by the international airport. These preliminary findings highlight the negative impact of expansive urbanization on surface water quality and demonstrate the value of a multi-tracer approach in identifying major contaminant transport pathways, improving the delineation between treated and raw wastewater inputs, and providing key insights to improve infrastructure and watershed management for the city of Austin and policymakers.

abstract: Extreme precipitation during storm events such as hurricanes and atmospheric rivers can cause widespread landsliding. Rapid estimation of the associated hazard can provide situational awareness to help practitioners and emergency managers make informed decisions about resource allocation when information is limited. Using Hurricane Helene as a test case, we evaluate the performance of the landslide hazard maps created by the USGS during the 2024 event response against a suite of maps produced using alternative modeling approaches to determine the most effective method for use in future responses. Using only data that would have been available before the hurricane, six groups were tasked with creating landslide initiation hazard maps of the region. The different model types include regional adaptations of: (1) semi-mechanistic models of rainfall-infiltration effects on slope stability using TRIGRS software, (2) the leaky bucket soil moisture framework paired with susceptibility, (3) heuristic combinations of rainfall and susceptibility, (4) a bivariate susceptibility and rainfall threshold map, (5) variations of NASA's statistical LHASA model, and (6) an empirically based frequency ratio model. All alternative modeling approaches used precipitation estimates from the Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor System (MRMS), and the 2024 response models used data provided by the National Weather Service at the time of the response. Models were assessed based on their ability to predict landslide occurrence, be applied rapidly anywhere in the United States, provide situational awareness, and be useful and interpretable by emergency managers. We used both quantitative and qualitative assessment methods to balance the need for accuracy and rapid implementation post event. Testing against the Hurricane Helene post-event landslide inventory, preliminary results suggest that the most promising models for performance and feasibility are the semi-mechanistic TRIGRS and leaky-bucket approaches, but further development and testing would inform the transferability of different approaches for routine nation-wide hazard assessments. An ad hoc model used in the Helene response, which multiplied a nationwide susceptibility map by total storm precipitation and aggregated the result, performed comparably to more complex approaches and could be readily refined and standardized for interim use.

title: Pliocene Laminated Sediments from Lake El’gygytgyn, NE Arctic Russia
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling
authors: Brigham-Grette, Julie [1], Shapiro , Daniel [2], Lapointe, Francois [3]
affiliations: (1) Dept of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts-Amherst, Amherst, MA, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Geographic and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts-Amherst, Amherst, MA, USA

abstract: Lake-bed sediment records are often key datasets for scientific inference of paleoclimates. Even more so if the lacustrine environment produces an annual layering cycle, or varves, which can give yearly fidelity of past climates, especially during the warm Pliocene. Lake El’gygytgyn is a lake situated in a meteorite impact site in northeastern Arctic Russia. The impact is dated to 3.6 million year BP. The lake has provided several lacustrine sediment cores ranging from the Quaternary to the Pliocene. The core sample analyzed for this project comes from ICDP site 5011-1, hole C, and originates in the Pliocene segment of this sediment record, approximately spanning 3.550 to 3.551 mya. Annual varves in Pliocene sediments are rare. The aim of this research is to determine if the laminae present in the core segment represent annual varves as well as any evidence of known cyclicity, such as the sun-spot cycle. Analysis is being conducted based on the existing thin-sections that were sampled from the lower half of the core. This involves the counting of the laminae in each thin-section via ImageJ and a custom made program. This counting is conducted optically, with spectral analysis being performed on the resultant data in R and the PAST software. This spectral analysis has indicated the possible presence of an 11-year sunspot cycle. The laminae of the nine thin-sections analyzed comprise approximately 48.8 cm of the core, starting at the bottom and ascending towards the mid-point. In total 517 laminae were recorded with the average thickness of the laminae recorded was approximately 1 mm. According to the chronology established by Brigham-Grette et. al (2013, Science) this bottom section accounts for approximately 600 years. This chronology roughly aligns with the total layer count, possibly indicating the laminae being varves. Should this core be an example of lacustrine varves it would provide a new source of climatic and environmental information from the mid-Pliocene.

title: Groundwater: One of the Energy Resources
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Lin, Yu-Feng Forrest [1]
affiliations: (1) Illinois Water Resources Center, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL, USA; Illinois State Geological Survey, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL, USA
abstract:
Groundwater has traditionally been evaluated according to its quantity, quality, and ecological functions. This presentation focuses on another fundamental and evolving service that should be explicitly recognized: groundwater’s ability to function as an energy resource through its natural thermal characteristics. Such a perspective is increasingly relevant as global expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, and other energy-intensive industries requires not only abundant electricity but also highly reliable, efficient, and resilient energy systems.

Public discourse on energy policy commonly emphasizes electricity generation capacity, measured in megawatts or gigawatts. Equally important is the management of thermal energy throughout the energy cycle, including heat rejection, storage, transport, and recovery. Groundwater possesses a unique combination of properties that directly support these functions. Extensive saturated aquifers maintain relatively constant temperatures, water has exceptional heat-storage capacity that varies with water chemistry, and groundwater movement naturally or artificially transports thermal energy. These characteristics distinguish groundwater from other subsurface materials and create opportunities for geothermal exchange, underground thermal energy storage (UTES), district energy systems, and thermal management of critical infrastructure. Fortunately, several coupled thermohydrologic models have been developed since the 1980s. The recent development of the Groundwater Energy-Transport (GWE) model for MODFLOW 6 provides open access to the modeling capability and future code development to simulate and evaluate these groundwater thermal processes and services.

Recognizing groundwater as an energy resource also reshapes the traditional water-energy nexus. Nearly every major form of electricity generation depends on dependable water supplies for cooling, processing, or manufacturing, making water availability a primary consideration in energy infrastructure development. Yet the groundwater community has largely portrayed itself as supporting the energy sector rather than as an integral contributor to energy security. Decades of international research have been demonstrating that groundwater provides services extending well beyond water supply. This presentation will use a new UTES project in Illinois as an example and propose that groundwater resource management should explicitly incorporate thermal energy as a core resource alongside water quantity and quality, thus expanding the role of hydrogeology in future energy policy, resilient infrastructure and sustainable development.

abstract:
The Williams Fork Formation is the youngest terminal formation of the Late Cretaceous Mesa Verde Group and is representative of a near marine or deltaic environment. Here, a preliminary review of fossils from multiple anthill localities from Moffat County, Colorado - collectively called “Blue Mountain” - are reported. Vertebrate materials from the Blue Mountain localities are interpreted to be from a freshwater, fluvial-to-periodically brackish environment based on the common presence of lepisosteid teeth, frequent Pseudomyledaphus teeth, rare occurrences of Paralbula teeth, and freshwater gastropods and molluscs lower in section. Marine vertebrate and invertebrate fossils are wholly missing from all anthills across Blue Mountain. Terrestrial materials recovered from the Blue Mountain localities include teeth and limited postcranial microfossils of dromaeosaurs, troodontids, hadrosaurids, thyreophorans, thescelosaurids, pachycephalosaurs(?), and indeterminate caudata. Terrestrial taxa recovered from the Blue Mountain anthill localities are more numerous in absolute numbers and taxonomic variety than in other recently published microvertebrate studies.

The presence of common, unabraided terrestrial microvertebrate materials suggests that the horizon the fossils are originally recovered from is representative of a predominantly freshwater fluvial system that reflects smaller and juvenile or perinatal terrestrial taxa. Larger amounts of terrestrial microvertebrate taxa imply the localities that make up Blue Mountain – and perhaps the wider Williams Fork Formation across Moffat County and nearby Rio Blanco County, Colorado – consist intermittently of larger amounts of diagnosable terrestrial faunas. This supports other recent research on the Cretaceous microvertebrate fauna of the local area, but these new microvertebrate localities are novel in that the recently discovered materials provide higher resolution to Late Cretaceous non-avian dinosaur, and potentially Caudata, taxonomy that is identifiable down to the genus-level near freshwater environs.

abstract:
Magmatism in the late Ediacaran to Cambrian Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen (SOA) provides a well-preserved record of continental rifting related to the opening of the southern Iapetus Ocean. Within the Wichita and Arbuckle Mountains, the exposed igneous framework comprises the Carlton Rhyolite, Raggedy Mountain Gabbro, and Wichita Granite Groups, along with pervasive diabase dikes; the adjacent subsurface preserves extensive basalts. To help constrain the evolution of this system, we present major- and trace-element geochemistry for 30 new samples of Carlton Rhyolite, late-stage diabase dikes, and small gabbro bodies from the Wichita Mountains.

The mafic units exhibit moderate LREE enrichment and lack significant europium anomalies. They plot within fields for within-plate tholeiitic to alkaline basalt compositions on standard discrimination diagrams. On the Nb/Yb versus TiO₂/Yb diagram of Pearce (2008), almost all samples plot in the OIB field, indicating that the magmas were derived from relatively deep-seated partial melting of garnet-stable mantle. On the Th/Nb versus TiO₂/Yb discrimination diagram of Pearce et al. (2021), all samples plot within the plume array, indicating a significant contribution from a mantle plume source. At a local scale, two diabase samples from the extreme west and east margins of the study area plot together on discrimination diagrams but are geochemically distinct from the other samples, suggesting a locally complex plumbing system for these mafic magmas.

The rhyolites display pronounced negative europium anomalies and LREE enrichment and plot in fields for within-plate A-type felsic rocks on standard discrimination diagrams. On the Y-Nb-Ce discrimination diagram for A-type felsic rocks of Eby (1992), the samples fall partly in the A1 field for felsic magmas derived from OIB-type sources and partly in the A2 field for magmas derived from sources modified by arc magmatism (perhaps in the distant past). This is consistent with a mantle plume source for the felsic rocks as well as the mafic ones. A rhyolite dike beneath the thickest flow in the Wichita Mountains exhibits a trace-element profile identical to the overlying flow, identifying it as the first recognized feeder conduit for the Carlton Rhyolite Group. Furthermore, a rhyolite dike intruding younger Wichita Granite shares this chemical signature, indicating a similar petrogenetic history for these rhyolites over an extended period of time.

abstract: Intermittent rivers and ephemeral streams (IRES) comprise up to 78% of the global river network and shape downstream water quality and quantity by controlling hydrologic connectivity, nutrient and solute pulses, and habitat availability. However, despite their abundance and influence on downstream rivers, IRES are seldom monitored relative to perennial rivers, leaving a gap in our understanding of river drying behavior and consequences for downstream water resources. To address this gap, we harmonize streamflow presence time series from ~850 sensors across 45 non-perennial headwater catchments spanning the continental United States. We pair these observations with contemporaneous outlet discharge, remotely sensed climate data, and static watershed attributes including topography, soils, geology, and land cover. We use these data to evaluate spatial and temporal drying patterns, and their drivers, across diverse watersheds. We demonstrate that topography, geology, and land cover are most predictive of where streams dry, while climate variables including temperature, precipitation, and evapotranspiration are most predictive of when streams dry and rewet. This work establishes a hierarchy of drying controls informed by synthesis across catchments spanning broad climatic and geologic gradients.

abstract: The Arctic archipelago of Svalbard consists of three prominent Proterozoic basement domains assembled during the middle-late Paleozoic Caledonian orogeny. The origin and displacement histories of these crustal fragments are critical to our understanding of the modern North Atlantic region during the assembly and break-up of Rodinia. The Northeastern Basement Province (NEBP), exposed across northeastern Spitsbergen and Nordaustlandet, has traditionally been divided into two “terranes” – West Ny-Friesland and Nordaustlandet – separated by the Caledonian Eolussletta Shear Zone. The West Ny-Friesland terrane consists of high-grade metamorphic rocks of the Mosselhalvøya Group and Atomfjella Complex. The Nordaustlandet terrane, which is the focus herein, is characterized by a >8 km thick package of Neoproterozoic–Ordovician sedimentary rocks that has traditionally been referred to as the ‘Hecla Hoek’ succession. These rocks presumably rest on deformed Tonian and older basement of the Brennevinsfjorden Group and Kapp Hansteen volcanics (and associated felsic intrusions), where deformation has been attributed to far-field “Grenville” or “Valhalla” orogenesis. Neoproterozoic–early Paleozoic rocks of the Nordaustlandet terrane have been correlated via multiple datasets with similar-aged successions in East Greenland, supporting oft-cited low-latitude Tonian paleomagnetic poles from the Akademikerbreen Group. Here, we revisit some of these foundational relationships through a compilation of field observations and new geochronological, geochemical, and paleomagnetic data to provide an updated synthesis of regional magmatism, deformation, and sedimentation in the NEBP. Lithostratigraphic and geochronological data clarify simple correlations between northeastern Spitsbergen and Nordaustlandet and argue against the need for separating these rocks into separate stratigraphic successions across Hinlopenstretet. In addition, geochronological and geochemical data suggest ca. 970–960 Ma Kapp Hansteen calc-alkaline magmatism was short-lived and unrelated to “Grenville” crustal thickening. A new expansive regional provenance dataset bolsters broad connections with East/Northeast Greenland and provides additional support for a Cryogenian–Ediacaran phase of basin reorganization associated with regional extension. Finally, new paleomagnetic data reveal complex ferromagnetic carrier assemblages in the Akademikerbreen and Polarisbreen groups, suggesting pervasive remagnetization of the NEBP sedimentary succession. Consequently, the Neoproterozoic paleolatitude of the NEBP and the regional evidence for Tonian true polar wander remain unresolved. Together, these data provide important new constraints on the regional geology of the North Atlantic, with implications for the tectonic evolution of Rodinia.

title: River silica concentrations rise with warming temperatures: potential geochemical mechanisms

authors: Warix, Sara [1], Singha, Kamini [2], Navarre-Sitchler, Alexis [3]

abstract: Dissolved silica (SiO₂ (aq) ) in rivers is a primary product of silicate weathering. We observed increases in river SiO₂ (aq) over multi-decadal scales in diverse landscapes and climates across the continental United States (CONUS) that mirror warming atmospheric temperatures. We hypothesize that temperature impacts on mineral kinetics and solubility are causing increasing river silica. To test this hypothesis, we first analyze long-term stream chemistry records from 1015 watersheds and find widespread, statistically significant increases in SiO₂ (aq) , particularly in summer months and in watersheds underlain by igneous and metamorphic silicates and sandstone. We constructed reactive transport simulations to quantify how warming temperatures affect silicate solubility in a linearly warmed one-dimensional column. The simulations show that under warming conditions, dissolved silica concentrations are primarily controlled by reactive silicate surface area. Overall, we demonstrate that the magnitude and timing of river silica increases are consistent with warming temperatures, but that the response is variable across spatiotemporal scales because of slow reaction kinetics and long subsurface transit times. Enhanced silicate weathering may have implications for other processes including carbon sequestration, in-stream biogeochemical processes, and enhanced clay precipitation which can impact subsurface structure.

title: Geochemical Characterization of Coal and Its Combustion Byproducts from BarapukuriaThermal Power Plants in Bangladesh: Distribution, Pollution, and Potential Ecological and Human Health Risks
session_title: Advances in Understanding and Predicting the Geochemical and Microbiological Conversion and Transport of Hydrogen in Deep Geological Repositories (Posters)
authors: Saha, Subrota Kumar [1], Mahmud, Tashfia Binte [2], Rahman, Md Aminur [3]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh
(2) Dept. of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh
(3) Institute of Mining, Mineralogy and Metallurgy, Joypurhat, Bangladesh
abstract:
This study investigates the coal and coal-combustion byproducts from Barapukuria Thermal Power Plant with emphasis on element distribution, pollution status, ecological risk and human-health implications. Coal, coal dust, dry ash, wet ash, power-plant coal, surrounding soils were examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray Fluorescence (XRF), field-emission Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy-Dispersive Spectroscopy (FESEM-EDS), while Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) was performed on selected solid samples to determine trace and rare earth element concentrations. Supplementary water-quality data from the Barapukuria mine-drainage and groundwater system were also evaluated to understand the possible link between solid residues and the surrounding hydrological environment.

The XRD results show that the Barapukuria coal and coal dust are mainly characterized by quartz, clay minerals and minor accessory phases, whereas the ash samples contain combustion-derived phases such as mullite and Fe-oxide minerals. The XRF data indicate that the Barapukuria ash is dominated by SiO₂ and Al₂O₃, reflecting an aluminosilicate-rich composition. FESEM-EDS observations further confirm differences in particle morphology and chemistry, with ash particles showing aluminosilicate and Fe-bearing compositions and coal particles retaining more carbon-rich characteristics.ICP-MS analysis of the Barapukuria dry ash, coal dust and soil samples shows variable enrichment of major, trace and rare earth elements. The REE distribution is dominated by light rare earth elements, particularly Ce, La and Nd, with normalized patterns indicating fractionation between LREE and HREE. Pollution indices, including contamination factor, geo-accumulation index, enrichment factor and pollution load index, show that some elements are enriched above crustal background, especially in ash and coal-dust samples. Ecological-risk and toxic-unit assessments identify selected toxic metals as the main contributors to environmental concern, while non-carcinogenic and carcinogenic health-risk calculations indicate that risk is controlled mainly by a limited number of elements with established toxicity values. The water-quality assessment shows circum-neutral but Fe–Mn-bearing mine drainage and groundwater, suggesting that redox-sensitive metals may be mobilized in the Barapukuria mining environment.The study provides an integrated geochemical and risk-based evaluation of coal and combustion byproducts in Bangladesh and highlights the need for regular monitoring, controlled ash management, and further leaching and speciation studies to better assess long-term environmental impacts.

title: Quantifying Soil Redistribution along Hillslope Using Fallout Radionuclide Tracers in Khagrachhari Hill District, Bangladesh
session_title: Advances in Understanding and Predicting the Geochemical and Microbiological Conversion and Transport of Hydrogen in Deep Geological Repositories (Posters)
authors: Saha, Subrota Kumar [1], Basak, Gobinda [2], Tushar, Mahmud Al Noor [3], Majumder, Ratan Kumar [4]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh
(2) Dept. of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh
(3) Dept. of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh
(4) Institute of Nuclear Science and Technology, Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract:
Hillslope soil erosion and sediment redistribution are among the most critical yet under-quantified land degradation processes in the hilly agricultural landscapes of Bangladesh. In the Chittagong Hill Tracts, particularly Khagrachhari Hill District, intense monsoonal rainfall, dissected terrain, shallow erodible soils, vegetation disturbance, and increasing land-use pressure have accelerated the removal and redistribution of fertile topsoil. This study presents a field-based dual-tracer assessment of hillslope soil redistribution using fallout radionuclides, specifically ¹³⁷Cs and ²¹⁰Pbex. Two representative hillslope transects were investigated, and 48 depth-wise soil samples were collected from upper, middle, lower-middle, and lower slope positions at 5 cm intervals to a depth of 30 cm. The samples were prepared through drying, sieving, homogenization, airtight sealing, and high-resolution HPGe gamma spectrometric measurement. Soil texture was also determined using the combined sieve–hydrometer method to support interpretation of erodibility and radionuclide retention.

Gamma spectrometric analysis identified both fallout and naturally occurring radionuclides, including ¹³⁷Cs, ²¹⁰Pb, ²¹⁴Pb, ²¹⁴Bi, ²²⁸Ac, ²⁰⁸Tl, and ⁴⁰K. The vertical distribution of ¹³⁷Cs showed discontinuous and irregular profiles, with surface depletion and subsurface enrichment in several samples, indicating erosion, deposition, burial, and soil mixing. In contrast, ²¹⁰Pbex displayed stronger and more continuous activity throughout the profiles, reflecting its greater sensitivity to recent and ongoing redistribution processes. The ¹³⁷Cs-derived rates revealed contrasting hillslope behaviour: Line 1 was mainly deposition-dominated, ranging from slight upper-slope erosion to lower-slope deposition of −12.9 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, whereas Line 2 was erosion-dominated, with the highest erosion rate of 9.1 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ at the upper slope. The ²¹⁰Pbex-derived rates further revealed a more complex recent redistribution pattern, including strong deposition at the Line 2 upper slope −43.4 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ and erosion at the Line 2 lower slope 11.2 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹.

The findings demonstrate that soil redistribution in Khagrachhari hillslopes is highly spatially heterogeneous and controlled by slope position, runoff connectivity, soil texture, vegetation condition, land-use disturbance, and tracer-specific time scale. The combined application of ¹³⁷Cs and ²¹⁰Pbex provides complementary evidence of medium-term and recent soil movement, enabling the identification of both erosion and deposition zones within the same hillslope system. This study advances the application of fallout radionuclide techniques in Bangladesh and provides a methodological foundation for evidence-based soil conservation planning in erosion-prone hilly agricultural environments.

title: K-feldspar megacryst thermal histories reveal a replenishing long-lived, large, and hot magma chamber in the interior of the Tuolumne Intrusive Complex
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part II)
authors: Durning, Sadie [1], Memeti, Valbone [2]
affiliations: (1) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA
(2) California State University, Fullerton, CA,
abstract:
Thermal conditions of magma chambers in space and time are key to understanding magma storage conditions and their connection to volcanic eruptions. Models of pluton construction and magma storage are commonly framed as two endmembers: (1) cold storage typically involving high crystallinity magma chambers that only briefly get rejuvenated to produce any size active magma chamber capable of eruption, and (2) magma chambers residing in hot storage with frequent and/or large replenishing intrusions that sustain large, long-lived magma reservoirs capable of producing high-volume eruptions over extended periods of time.

Potassium feldspar megacrysts (MKfs) from the 1,100 km 2 , 10-myr-long-lived Tuolumne Intrusive Complex (TIC) contain a rich geochemical record of the conditions of the magma chamber they crystallized in, both within the MKfs, and their hornblende inclusions. We used field relations of the MKfs-containing units in the interior of the TIC, Zhang et al. (2022) Ti-in-Kfs and Putirka (2016) hornblende thermometry, MELTS modeling, and mineral trace elements to determine magma processes and magma crystallinity during MKfs growth.

Updated TIC mapping reveals a wide gradation of up to 8 km with two mineralogically and texturally distinct transitions between the 90-88Ma pHD and 88-85Ma CP, i.e. the pHD-CP hybrid and transitional CP. MKfs and hornblende inclusion trace elements reveal the units underwent linked magma processes, including magma replenishment, fractionation, and defrosting. MKfs Ti-in-Kfs thermometry indicates fluctuating temperatures during MKfs growth with temperature jumps 0-130°C between adjacent spots and overall temperatures in single MKfs ranging from up to ~865°C to minimum temperatures near the solidus, suggesting frequent and hot magma chamber replenishments. Temperatures across MKfs suggest that they remained much above the solidus throughout most of their growth in all units, especially the pHD and pHD-CP hybrid. Average Ti-in-Kfs MKfs temperatures gradually reduced toward the interior, more evolved magmas from ~840°C in pHD to 770°C in CP. MELTs modeling indicates that most of the thermal fluctuations occur in >50% melt, therefore low crystallinity magma. Considering TIC ages and our updated TIC map, thermometry, mineral chemistry, and MELTS modeling, the gradational zone between pHD and CP was an active, episodically re-injected magma chamber over up to 700km 2 of the TIC interior for up to 3-5 myrs, supporting a hot storage model and making the TIC capable of feeding large volcanic eruptions.

title: Reassessing Early Cretaceous Crustal Thickness in the Western Metamorphic Belt, Sierra Nevada, CA Using Melt-based Mohometry
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California (Posters)
authors: Durning, Sadie [1], Ardill, Katie Erin [2]
affiliations: (1) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
(2) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
abstract:
Arc crustal thickness is intrinsically linked to magma generation, storage, and eruption. Bulk-rock geochemical proxies of crustal thickness (e.g., Sr/Y and La/Yb) use this petrologic relationship to provide insight into ancient paleo-crustal thickness. However, Sr/Y and La/Yb from deep fractionation or partial melting can be subsequently modified by magmatic processes in the crustal column, such as crystal accumulation. Consequently, there are large uncertainties in estimates of paleo-crustal thickness (±10-20 km).

We investigate the single mineral geochemistry of quartz diorites and tonalites from the Western Metamorphic Belt (WMB) to quantify the effect of crystal accumulation on bulk-rock Sr/Y and La/Yb signatures and describe the temporal evolution of the Early Cretaceous Sierra Nevada. Compiled geologic and bulk-rock geochemical data from the WMB describe the initiation of crustal thickening from ~30-50 km, between ca. 150-120 Ma, and the transition from submarine to subaerial arc deposition prior to the Cretaceous arc flare-up, when crustal thickness reached >70 km.

We analyzed hornblende from the Bass Lake, Ross Creek, and Millerton Lake tonalites, of the WMB, to reconstruct melt compositions. The resulting hornblende-derived equilibrium melt compositions are in equilibrium with rhyolitic melts, despite petrographic evidence indicating a more intermediate bulk composition. Hornblende temperatures range between ~720-820°C. In the Ross Creek tonalite, the presence of pyroxene allowed comparison of hornblende-equilibrium rhyolitic melts with pyroxene-equilibrium andesitic to dacitic melts. The differences in reconstructed melt compositions may reflect distinct stages of magma evolution. This is supported by petrographic evidence that indicates pyroxene crystallized before hornblende, as well as higher pyroxene temperatures (~900-1050°C). Trace element analyses will test this interpretation further, while analyses of additional high-temperature minerals from more WMB plutons will help reconstruct early-stage, high-temperature melts and better constrain the evolution of magma compositions through time.

Sr/Y and La/Yb values of melts in equilibrium with hornblende and pyroxene will be calculated, applied to existing calibrations and compared to bulk-rock ratios and geologic observations. The resulting values will be a melt-based approach to calculating paleo-crustal thickness through time in the Sierra Nevada arc. Understanding the effects of magmatic processes on chemical mohometry is important to define the petrologic relationship between magma composition and crustal thickness.

title: Refining igneous stratigraphy and geological controls on mineralization in the Serpentine deposit, Duluth Complex
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Kennedy, Cinthia Gisselle [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Abts, Miranda [3]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, Bolivia
(3) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Serpentine deposit is a large, undeveloped magmatic Cu-Ni-Co deposit located within the 1.1 Ga Duluth Complex in northeastern Minnesota. The deposit comprises an indicated mineral resource of 21.6 million metric tonnes grading 0.46% Cu, 0.16% Ni, and 0.014% Co, with an inferred mineral resource of 279.9 million metric tonnes grading 0.37% Cu, 0.12% Ni, and 0.007% Co. Disseminated sulfide zones are located within ultramafic and mafic rocks assigned to the South Kawishiwi intrusion, which is one of several intrusions making up the Duluth Complex. In the Serpentine area, the footwall to the South Kawishiwi intrusion is comprised of metasedimentary rocks of the ~1.90-1.87 Ga Animikie Group. Injection of sulfide melts into the footwall rocks has resulted in the development of low-tenor massive sulfide bodies.

Small-scale lithological variability makes the recognition of igneous stratigraphy within the South Kawishiwi intrusion challenging. In addition, subtle variations in cumulate mineralogy and mineral abundances are difficult to recognize in drill core. This study aims to refine the igneous stratigraphy of the Serpentine deposit and evaluate its relation to sulfide mineralization through petrographic classification of drill core and thin sections, integrated with continuous X-ray fluorescence core scanning. The data sets are combined to identify lithologic contacts and define units that can be used for multi-hole stratigraphic correlation within the South Kawishiwi intrusion. The spatial distribution of sulfur and base metals is evaluated relative to the refined stratigraphic framework to better constrain geological controls on mineralization. The refined stratigraphic framework will support more effective correlation between drillholes and provide a geological basis for future resource evaluation and exploration targeting at Serpentine.

title: Fossils of the Pleistocene Turlock Lake Formation, San Joaquin Valley, California, with Emphasis on the Middle Irvingtonian Fairmead Landfill Locality
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic (Posters)
authors: Anderson, Chase D. [1], Dundas, Robert G. [2]
affiliations: (1) Applied Earthworks, Pasadena, California, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, California State University, Fresno, California, USA
abstract: Consisting of fluvial and lacustrine sediments, the Turlock Lake Formation was deposited along the eastern half of California’s San Joaquin Valley during the mid-Pleistocene. Fossil plants, invertebrates and vertebrates occur throughout the formation. The unit’s most prominent fossil site is Fairmead Landfill, ten miles north of Madera, California. The mid-Irvingtonian (0.78–.55 Ma) Fairmead Landfill locality produced thousands of specimens representing 72 taxa (2 fish, 2 amphibians, 3 reptiles, 6 birds, 29 mammals, 1 bivalve, 1 gastropod, 12 plants/palynomorphs, and 16 diatoms). Fossils occur in sediments representing distal alluvial fan channel, distal fan overbank flood or sheetflood, and marsh/lacustrine deposits of the upper unit of the Turlock Lake Formation. A broad range of taphonomic conditions is represented. Fossils occur in facies ranging from conglomerate to clay. Specimens typically occur as isolated element fragments, but sometimes as groups of associated elements from single individuals and in bone beds of commingled specimens from multiple individuals and species. Articulated anatomical units sometimes occur, often as vertebral segments, parts of legs, or feet, but no complete or near-complete skeletons have been uncovered. The fauna is a carnivore-mediated attritional assemblage modified by fluvial transport and concentration. Elements are usually fragmented, and some exhibit carnivore gnawing. Most bone breakage likely resulted from carnivore activity or trampling by large herbivores. Fossils have been collected geographically from over 40 acres and stratigraphically from depths of 4 m to 20+ m below ground surface. Vertebrates include: Archoplites interruptus , Catostomus occidentalis , Urodela, Anura, Actinemys marmorata , Xerobates agassizi , Colubridae, Athene cunicularia , Branta canadensis , Tadorna tadorna , cf. Aythya sp., Cygnus columbianus , Zenaida macroura , Sorex sp., Paramylodon harlani , Nothrotheriops shastensis , Megalonyx wheatleyi , Canis latrans , Canis dirus , Vulpes velox , Homotherium sp., Smilodon sp., Miracinonyx sp., Panthera sp., Lynx rufus , Taxidea taxus , Arctodus sp., Spermophilus sp., Neotoma sp., Peromyscus sp., Microtus sp., Thomomys sp., cf. Dipodomys sp., Lepus sp., Mammuthus columbi , Equus sp., Camelops sp., Hemiauchenia sp., Tetrameryx irvingtonensis , Capromeryx sp., Odocoileus sp., and Platygonus vetus . Large herbivorous mammals dominate the fauna, particularly open-country grazers and mixed feeders such as Equus , Camelops , Mammuthus columbi and Paramylodon harlani . The pollen record is dominated by grass, although pine and juniper are common, and riparian, wetland, and halophytic forms also occur in some samples, indicating a mosaic of plant communities nearby.

title: Geoscience Challenges and Opportunities in Securing America’s Critical Mineral Supply Chains
session_title: Mineral Resources and Society
authors: Williams, Colin F. [1]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA, USA
abstract:
Critical minerals, those essential mineral commodities for which the United States has supply chains vulnerable to disruption, dominate current debates about resource strategy and drive substantial Federal government investments across the economy. These investments are intended to make mineral supply chains more resilient through increased production and more efficient use of critical minerals and their downstream products by the U.S. and its reliable trading partners.

The focus on critical mineral resources has developed during a period of American energy independence – an independence based primarily on fossil fuels. Could a renewed national commitment to an energy transition away from fossil fuels threaten energy independence and increase mineral supply chain vulnerabilities? And if so, how can the geosciences help the U.S. avoid that scenario?

The U.S. has abundant solar, wind, and geothermal resources, but converting those resources into usable energy requires a critical mineral intensity greater than that required for fossil fuels, despite the fact that production and use of fossil fuels has its own critical mineral dependencies. Securing the cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, nickel, platinum group elements, rare earth elements, and other critical minerals required for energy transition applications presents significant challenges but also presents opportunities for geoscientists and others to make decisive contributions that will identify new resources, enable greater production from known resources, minimize environmental impacts, support improved governance, and inform responsible land management.

Examples from recent USGS studies highlight these challenges and opportunities, which span the geosciences and related disciplines. The USGS, along with its Federal, State, Tribal, academic, and private partners, leads America’s mapping and resource science. USGS global mineral supply chain analyses underpin the List of Critical Minerals and inform economic, technological, national security, and global trade strategies. Onshore, the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative is transforming the surface and subsurface mapping of America’s geology and resources through advanced geological, geochemical, and geophysical survey and analysis techniques. Offshore, the USGS is collaborating with Federal partners to provide scientific information and critical mineral resource assessments that are foundational for seabed resource management decisions. In both onshore and offshore environments, the USGS is developing AI tools to streamline workflows for mineral resource assessments and is investing in academic programs to rebuild America’s minerals workforce.
