title: Triassic Fishes of Pennsylvania: A Summary of The Common Genera for Geologists
session_title: PALEONTOLOGY, BRYOZOANS, DINOSAURS, REEFS, STRATIGRAPHY, AND MILITARY GEOLOGY: IN HONOR OF ROGER CUFFEY AND HIS ECCLECTIC CAREER
authors: Cuffey, Roger J. [1], Lane, Jennifer A. [2], Lutz, Anne B. [3], Cuffey, Clifford A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Emeritus (Deceased), Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Division of Paleontology (Vertebrate), American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA; Department of Natural Sciences, Baruch College, City University of New York, New York, New York, USA
(3) Pennsylvania Geological Survey, Retired, Harrisburg, PA, USA
(4) Cliff's GeoTours LLC, Midland, TX,
abstract:
Most geologists working in eastern Pennsylvania and/or northern New Jersey encounter the fossil fishes reported from the Newark Basin and associated areas only as Latin taxonomic names not immediately attached to visual images, and thus have little appreciation of how those ancient faunas would have appeared in life. Various fossil assemblages elsewhere have been illustrated in non-technical pamphlets (such as the fossil shark teeth of the Chesapeake Bay region), and those publications have proved quite useful for both professional (but non-specialist) and amateur visitors to those areas. Our intent here is to provide geologists/paleontologists who are not paleoichthyologists with an overview of the Triassic fishes of this area (eastern Pennsylvania/northern New Jersey) to hopefully stimulate further interest in these important fossils should they encounter them in the course of their fieldwork.

We provide an overview and classificatory framework of fish genera rather than species, which are often numerous, known only from fragments, and as yet unreconstructed. In contrast, most genera are better known anatomically, have been reconstructed visually, and the number is small enough to provide a helpful overview.

We emphasize the early Late Triassic Lockatong Formation in northeastern Pennsylvania,but also include some materials from higher Triassic and basal Jurassic formations into northern New Jersey.

Almost all of the Newark fishes are actinopterygian osteichthyans, except for one Coelacanth ( Diplurus ) and one hybodont shark ( Carinacanthus ). Presence of a shark could indicate a temporary marine connection. The actinopterygians represented include the semionotids Lepidotus and Semionotus ; the parasemionotid Parasemionotus ; the saurichthyid Saurichthys ; the perleidids Perleidus and Cleithrolepis ; the pholidopleurid Pholidopleurus ; the ptycholepid Ptycholepis ; the paleoniscoid Turseodus , and the redfieldiids Cionichthys , Dictyopyge , Redfieldius , and Synorichthys . Many of the coprolites from the Lockatong black shales have been attributed to Diplurus , interpreted by some authors as a ‘top predator’ that fed on the anchovy-like redfieldiid chondrosteans in the deeper parts of the Newark lakes.

Finally, we find the term “Newark” has been used with inconsistent meanings in some of the literature (alternatively referring to the geographic area immediately surrounding that city; the area of NE Pennsylvania and northern New Jersey underlain by Upper Triassic and basal Jurassic rocks; the time interval represented; etc.), which should be addressed to improve accuracy of future reporting on these fossils.

title: Reconstructing Phosphorus Dynamics in the Precambrian Ocean Using Independent Component Analysis of Shale Geochemistry
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Nagao, Ryosuke [1], Komiya, Tsuyoshi [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo, Hongo, Tokyo, Japan

(2) Department of Earth Science & Astronomy, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, The University of Tokyo, Komaba, Tokyo, Japan; Department of Earth and Planetary Science, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo, Hongo, Tokyo, Japan
abstract:
Phosphorus is widely regarded as the ultimate limiting nutrient for marine primary production over geological timescales, governing organic carbon burial and, ultimately, the accumulation of atmospheric oxygen. Because the atmosphere was persistently oxygen-poor in the Precambrian, the ocean is commonly inferred to have been depleted in phosphorus. A mechanistic basis for this inference exists: in a ferruginous water column, Fe(III) oxyhydroxides efficiently scavenge dissolved phosphate at the redox boundary, and P/Fe ratios in iron-rich rocks and bulk P concentrations in shales, compiled from the literature, are indeed low and comparatively constant throughout the Precambrian, rising sharply in the Neoproterozoic.

However, the compilations rest on bulk-rock chemistry, which represents a mixture of detrital, organic, carbonate, sulfide, and oxide components. Only the chemical precipitates were directly related to the coexisting seawater, so bulk measurements dilute and potentially bias the seawater signal. We, therefore, applied Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to a large shale geochemical database (SGP database) to isolate a Fe-oxide phase, potentially hosting marine phosphorus. Unlike PCA, ICA does not impose orthogonality among components, a constraint with no geochemical justification. ICA was applied independently to age-binned subsets spanning 2000–0 Ma using 13 elements (TOC, Mg, P, S, Ca, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Zn, Mo, U, Zr), and 100 runs with different random seeds were clustered by cosine similarity to identify stable components because ICA is non-deterministic.

Geochemically interpretable components, including carbonate, organic, iron sulfide, and iron oxide phases, are resolved in most age bins. Rather than reading P/Fe directly from the component vector, which is not strictly quantitative, we selected samples scoring above the 75th percentile on the Fe-oxide component and obtained their median P/Fe. These ICA-filtered P/Fe ratios remain broadly constant from 2 Ga to the present, indicating that the Fe-oxide-bound P reservoir was not systematically depleted during the Precambrian. Given that elevated dissolved silica would have suppressed phosphate adsorption onto Fe-oxyhydroxides, the equivalent P/Fe ratios of iron oxides to the modern values imply an even larger seawater DIP reservoir than in the Phanerozoic. We suggest instead that low Mo availability restricted nitrogen fixation, making N rather than P the ultimate limiting nutrient.

title: Late Neoproterozoic arc/back-arc magmatism along the western West African Craton: Insights from the northern Mauritanides
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Jimenez Borrego, Roberto [1], Martinez Poyatos, David [2], Azor, Antonio [3], Accotto, Cristina [4], Gonzalez Menendez, Luis [5], Jabaloy Sanchez, Antonio [6], Gonzalez Lodeiro, Francisco [7], Hamoud, Ahmed [8]
affiliations: (1) Geodynamics, University of Granada, Granada, Spain
(2) Geodynamics, Univ. Granada, Granada, Spain
(3) Geodynamics, Univ. Granada, Granada, Spain
(4) Engineering, Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, Lima, Peru
(5) Instituto Geologico y Minero de Espana, Oviedo, Spain
(6) Geodynamics, Univ. Granada, Granada, Spain
(7) Gedynamics, Univ. Granada, Granada, Spain

abstract:
The northern Mauritanides preserve one of the least explored records of the Neoproterozoic evolution of the western margin of the West African Craton. Despite the abundance of igneous rocks within the Inchiri Complex in the Akjoujt area, their age, petrogenesis, and tectonic significance remain poorly constrained. We present new SHRIMP U–Pb zircon geochronological and whole-rock geochemical data from representative igneous rocks of the different units of the Inchiri Complex, providing the first integrated characterization of late Neoproterozoic magmatism in this sector.

The new geochronological dataset reveals two distinct magmatic episodes. An older late Cryogenian event (ca. 645 Ma) is recorded by MORB-like mafic rocks of the Agoualilet Unit, whereas widespread magmatism developed during the middle Ediacaran (613–572 Ma) within the Hajar Dekhen-Kleouat and Choueima units. Several samples also contain inherited Paleoproterozoic zircon grains (ca. 2.2–1.8 Ga), documenting recycling of an Eburnean crust derived from the West African Craton.

The whole-rock geochemical data indicates that the Ediacaran mafic rocks form a low-K tholeiitic series, whereas the felsic ones have calc-alkaline affinity and geochemical characteristics typical of I-type granitoids formed through partial melting of continental crust triggered by mantle-derived magmas. The Ediacaran mafic rocks are enriched in large-ion lithophile elements (particularly Ba and Pb), show pronounced negative Nb and Ti anomalies, low Nb/U and Ce/Pb ratios, and elevated Th/Nb, Th/La, and La/Nb ratios, suggesting metasomatism of the mantle wedge by subduction-derived fluids and/or melts. Furthermore, trace-element discrimination diagrams reveal transitional MORB–IAT affinities and compositions comparable to modern back-arc basin basalts, consistent with a mantle source modified by subduction-derived fluids or melts. In contrast, the Cryogenian Agoualilet Unit displays a MORB-like geochemical signature, which can be interpreted as a fragment of pre-existing oceanic lithosphere.

These results can be integrated in a model dominated by a long-lived supra-subduction arc/back-arc along the western margin of the West African Craton during Gondwana assembly. In this scenario, we interpret the late Cryogenian Agoualilet Unit as a fragment oceanic lithosphere formed prior to subduction initiation, whereas the younger middle Ediacaran bimodal magmatism records the establishment and evolution of a supra-subduction zone arc/back-arc system. This tectonomagmatic evolution strengthens regional correlations of the northern Mauritanides with coeval Pan-African and Cadomian belts throughout northwestern Gondwana.

session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Kojima, Kotaro [1], Ohta, Toru [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Resources and Environmental Engineering, Graduate School of Creative Science and Engineering, Waseda University, Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Resources and Environmental Engineering, Graduate School of Creative Science and Engineering, Waseda University, Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
abstract:
Shapes of clastic grains record transportation and depositional history, as well as post-depositional diagenetic modification. Using elliptic Fourier–principal component analysis (EF–PCA), Suzuki et al. (2015) defined two indices: REF1, a macroscopic measure of grain elongation, and SEF, a microscopic measure of grain-surface smoothness. These indices discriminate sand grains from glacial, fluvial, foreshore, and aeolian environments. However, reproducibility may be affected by image acquisition and particle-outline extraction when incomplete focus obscures fine boundary irregularities. This study aims to improve the reproducibility of EF–PCA and reassess its applicability to depositional-environment discrimination.

We analyzed 250–355 μm quartz grains using focus-stacked two-dimensional images acquired with a digital microscope (VHX-5000, Keyence Co., Osaka, Japan). Elliptic Fourier analysis of binary grain outlines up to the 100th harmonic produced 397 Fourier descriptors. PCA using the variance–covariance matrix yielded REF1, which indicates elongated grains when negative and circular grains when positive. PCA using the correlation matrix yielded SEF, which indicates smoother and more abraded boundaries at higher values.

A reference model was constructed from 1,245 grains from glacial, fluvial, foreshore, and aeolian deposits. REF1 explained 49.20% of the total variance and differed significantly among depositional environments, except between glacial and foreshore grains. SEF explained 30.17% of the amplitude variance and significantly segregated all depositional-environment pairs. Traditional and renewed indices were compared using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s tests with Holm correction. The same grains photographed using conventional single-focus and focus-stacking microscopy produced different SEF values, indicating improved reproduction of natural microscopic grain boundaries.

On the renewed SEF–REF1 diagram, the four grain types produced distinct clusters. We also applied the diagram to a glacial sand outlier undergoing soil modification at Zmutt Glacier, Switzerland, and a foreshore sand outlier reworked by aeolian abrasion since the Last Glacial Maximum in Tottori, Japan. The former plotted between the glacial and foreshore fields, whereas the latter plotted between the foreshore and aeolian fields. This method therefore discriminates standard grain origins and reveals overprints of different depositional histories. These results demonstrate that focus stacking and digital outline extraction improve the reproducibility of two-dimensional EF–PCA while preserving its ability to evaluate depositional environment and sedimentary history. A remaining concern is that two-dimensional grain characteristics can change with orientation.

title: Late Pleistocene-Holocene Non Steady State Erosion in a Hyper Arid Carbonate Catchment Revealed by 36Cl Concentrations in Alluvial Sediments and Bedrock
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution (Posters)
authors: Kuzmenko, Alyona [1], Kapp, Paul A. [2], Matmon, Ari [3]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Earth Sciences, Hebrew University of Jerusaelm, Jerusalem, Israel
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(3) Institute of Earth Sciences, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
abstract:
The mode of erosion of carbonate terrains is known to be controlled by annual precipitation. In hyper arid terrains mechanical erosion dominates while in wetter environments (>100 mm/yr) chemical weathering is dominant. Erosion rates in carbonate rocks can be calculated by measuring in-situ produced cosmogenic 36 Cl, assuming nuclide production profile has reached steady state. However, slow erosion rates in hyper arid regions impose long response times to achieve steady state profiles in eroding bedrock, raising the question of the legitimacy of the steady state assumption in such settings. The Shehoret catchment in the hyper-arid (~30 mm/yr) southern Negev, Israel, drains an area of ~12 km 2 into the Arava rift valley. Cretaceous carbonate lithologies comprise the upper part of the catchment. Precambrian crystalline rocks are exposed at its lower reaches.

36 Cl concentrations were measured in carbonate bedrock, sediment in the active channel, and sediment of known depositional age in an alluvial terrace. Bedrock and catchment average erosion rates were calculated using CRONUScalc v2.1. Massive limestone yielded rates of 39±7 and 37±9 mm/ka. Marly limestone yielded a rate of 10±2 mm/ka. Sediment from the active channel yielded an erosion rate of 60±16 mm/ka. A Monte Carlo model, based on the CRONUScalc framework, was written to calculate pre depositional 36 Cl concentrations in alluvial sediments of known ages (18±4, 30±9, and 123±28 ka) and known burial depths. These modeled concentrations were then used to calculate catchment paleo-erosion rates. Terrace sediments yielded erosion rates of ~59±21 mm/ka, similar to the modern rate. Thus, over the past ~120 ka, calculated catchment erosion rates systematically exceed bedrock erosion, indicating the contribution of 36 Cl poor clasts into channels and fluctuations in erosion rate. Possible sources are shielded faces of boulders that fall from cliffs during repeated earthquakes, and recycling of older sediment from alluvial terraces. These observations suggest that the 36 Cl production profile in bedrock may not be in steady state throughout the entire basin, and that caution is needed when calculating 36 Cl derived erosion rates in such hyper arid and tectonically active environments.

title: P-T constraints on eclogite-facies metamorphism in the southernmost Souttoufides (western Mauritania)
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Jimenez Borrego, Roberto [1], Lopez Sanchez-Vizcaino, Vicente [2], Martinez Poyatos, David [3], Azor, Antonio [4], Accotto, Cristina [5], Jabaloy Sanchez, Antonio [6], Gonzalez Lodeiro, Francisco [7]

abstract:
The southernmost exposed segment of the Souttoufides is preserved in the Northwest Chami Thrust Belt (western Mauritania) along the western margin of the West African Craton. This study reports the first discovery of eclogites in this segment of the belt, where they crop out at a major -suture-related- tectonic contact between the Neoproterozoic Saouda Complex and the Oued Dibilal Complex.

The eclogites preserve a metamorphic assemblage made up of garnet, two generations of omphacite (Omphacite-1 and Omphacite-2), Amphibole-1, Fe³⁺-bearing epidote, rutile, quartz, and minor white mica. Despite partial retrogression to amphibolite facies conditions, primary textures are remarkably well preserved. Retrogression is mainly expressed by the partial replacement of Omphacite-2 by Amphibole-2–quartz symplectites and the local growth of late Amphibole-3. Nevertheless, the primary eclogitic minerals display little or no intracrystalline compositional zoning, indicating that the effective bulk-rock composition remained representative of equilibrium during high-pressure metamorphism. Mineral chemistry reveals significant compositional differences between Omphacite-1 and Omphacite-2, whereas garnet exhibits little or no compositional zoning. The preservation of equilibrium textures, together with homogeneous mineral compositions and chemographic relationships among garnet, omphacite, and Amphibole-1, supports the application of phase-equilibrium modeling. To do so, P–T pseudosections have been obtained for the effective bulk-rock composition, yielding peak metamorphic conditions of 1.77–2.15 GPa and 550–600 °C. The coexistence of Omphacite-1, Omphacite-2, and Fe³⁺-bearing epidote, provides key constraints on the stability field of the peak assemblage. In contrast, the mismatch between the observed and modelled compositions of Omphacite-2 and Amphibole-1 likely indicates that these minerals underwent partial post-peak recrystallization during retrograde amphibolite-facies overprinting.

The estimated temperatures are consistent with previous studies of eclogites from the southern prolongation of the Northwest Chami Thrust Belt, whereas the significantly higher pressures obtained in this study most likely result from a better preservation of jadeite-rich Omphacite-1. These new data document a previously unrecognized high-pressure suture-related unit and provide precise P-T estimates for eclogite-facies metamorphism in the southernmost Souttoufides. They are placed in the accretion/evolution of northwest Gondwana.

title: Integrated stratigraphy and international correlation of the Aptian–Albian forearc basin successions of the Yezo Group, northern Japan

abstract:
The mid-Cretaceous Aptian–Albian interval was characterized by a peak in igneous activity and frequent Oceanic Anoxic Events (OAEs). To understand the linkages between igneous activity and environmental changes during this period, a goal of our collaborative research over the past 10 years is to provide a precise radioisotopic age model.

The Yezo Group of Hokkaido, Japan is a continuous hemipelagic marine succession spanning from Barremian to Maastrichtian that represents the middle–upper Cretaceous succession in the northwestern Pacific region. Because it contains numerous intercalated silicic tuff beds derived from subduction magmatism of the Asian continental margin, this succession has significantly contributed to refining the Cretaceous timescale; for instance, the radioisotopic age of the Albian/Cenomanian boundary in GTS2020 has relied on the ages of tuffs within this group. Although the Yezo Group yields abundant macro- and microfossils, the occurrence of index fossils common to the Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Points (GSSPs) in the Tethyan region is discontinuous. Consequently, previous international stratigraphic correlations of this sequence with representative Tethyan successions, which relied solely on biostratigraphy, lacked sufficient resolution.

Alongside the compilation of macro- and microfossil biostratigraphy, we have established high-resolution carbon and osmium isotope stratigraphy for the Aptian–Albian interval of the Yezo Group in Hokkaido that is anchored by dozens of U-Pb zircon and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar sanidine age determinations. Our multi-proxy approach enables precise identification of stratigraphic horizons in the Yezo Group equivalent to OAE 1a, Fallot OAE, OAE 1b (Jacob, Kilian, Paquier, and Leenhardt), OAE 1c, and OAE 1d, as well as the Barremian/Aptian, Aptian/Albian, and Albian/Cenomanian boundaries. Moreover, numerous silicic tuffs intercalated within these OAE horizons and stage boundaries offer potential for this succession to significantly contribute to future improvements in the accuracy and precision of the next generation Cretaceous timescale.

title: Bivalves replaced brachiopods through environmentally mediated competition
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Malanoski, Cooper [1], Roper-Smith, Tom [2], Shipley, Benjamin [3], Farnsworth, Alexander [4], Valdes, Paul [5], Saupe, Erin [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Oxford University, Oxford, (None), United Kingdom
(2) Museum of Natural History Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom
(3) Monash University, Melbourne, Australia
(4) University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom
(5) University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom
(6) Earth Sciences, Oxford University, Oxford, United Kingdom
abstract: Competition is often proposed as a key driver of clade replacement, yet its role over evolutionary timescales remains uncertain. A classic example is the apparent replacement of brachiopods by bivalves over the Phanerozoic. Here we analyse brachiopod–bivalve richness dynamics in a spatially and environmentally explicit framework using a newly curated dataset of more than half-a-million fossil occurrences to test for putative signals of competition. We find no clear inverse relationship between brachiopod and bivalve richness within constrained geographic regions before the Permian-Triassic mass extinction. However, we recover a significant negative relationship after the Permian-Triassic boundary, accompanied by increased segregation of brachiopod–bivalve occurrences. This inverse relationship persists after accounting for additional environmental and ecological covariates, including temperature and depth preferences. Although differences in environment do not account for the observed inverse richness relationship between brachiopods and bivalves, they may explain why it emerged after the Permian–Triassic mass extinction. We find brachiopods were more vulnerable than bivalves to elevated temperatures, consistent with end-Permian hyperthermal conditions eroding brachiopod incumbency and opening ecological space for bivalves. Together, our results suggest that climate-driven change first disrupted Paleozoic brachiopod incumbency, allowing bivalves to gain an ecological foothold, after which competition reinforced one of the most iconic clade replacements in the marine fossil record.

abstract: For the past decade, the Kentucky Geological Survey (KGS) has conducted landslide hazard research through several federal funding opportunities. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) hazard mitigation grants and U.S. Forest Service agreements have fueled improvements in our landslide inventory mapping and allowed for the production of landslide susceptibility maps. A large, statewide National Science Foundation EPSCoR agreement has allowed for the establishment of an extensive slope hydrologic monitoring network across eastern Kentucky. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Program has funded three projects focused on landslide inventories, elevation differencing for landslide event mapping, and additional landslide susceptibility modeling. Thousands of mapped landslides and currently 13 counties with landslide susceptibility have practical applications across Kentucky for those at risk from landslide hazards. This presentation will focus on our approaches and the results of the USGS program projects, discussing newly mapped landslides and best practices for leveraging inventory data for all aspects of KGS landslide hazards research. In addition, our engagement with the USGS National Landslide Hazard Risk Reduction (NLHRR) Working Group has allowed us to share best practices with other landslides experts around the county, presenting results and exchanging ideas. The NLHRR Working Group is critical for fulfilling the goals of the National Strategy for Landslide Loss Reduction, bringing together professionals focused on landslide mapping, modeling, landslide loss assessment, landslide forecasting, event response, and outreach and education. The benefits of the NLHRR Working Group reach geoscientists in the early stages of landslide hazard investigations and those with long histories of research and collaboration. Sharing work with others in the working group strengthens collaborations among researchers and practitioners, emphasizing applied efforts to reduce landslide risk.

title: Temporal Migration of a Salinity Transition Zone Along a Coastal Salt-Marsh Channel, Carpinteria, California
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Gove , Jacob B. [1], O'Neill, Sage [2], Fung, Megan K. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, California Lutheran University, Thousand Oaks, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, California Lutheran University, Thousand Oaks, CA, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, California Lutheran University, Thousand Oaks, CA, USA
abstract: Our research examines temporal changes in water quality across six fixed sampling sites in Santa Monica Creek within Carpinteria Salt Marsh, California. Water quality parameters, including temperature, dissolved oxygen, specific conductance, salinity, pH, oxidation-reduction potential, and turbidity, were measured in March 2025, January 2026, and May 2026 using a YSI ProDSS water meter. GIS and LiDAR-derived measurements of channel distance, width, and confinement are used to evaluate whether channel morphology influences the location of the salinity transition zone. Results show that salinity generally increased downstream during all three sampling events, but the location of the strongest transition shifted. Mean salinity across all sampling locations was 8.83 ppt in January, 21.64 ppt in March, and 26.94 ppt in May. The largest adjacent-site increase occurred between Sites 2 and 3 in March (13.50 ppt), Sites 4 and 4.5 in January (7.88 ppt), and Sites 1 and 2 in May (26.41 ppt). The May transition, between Sites 1 and 2, accounted for 90.9% of the total salinity change across the channel. Dissolved oxygen saturation generally decreased downstream and averaged 107.0% in January, 101.8% in March, and 150.4% in May. Mean turbidity ranged from 6.05 NTU in March to 28.53 NTU in May. These results suggest that the salinity transition zone migrates along the channel between sampling events. Combining water quality data with GIS and LiDAR measurements provides a hydrogeomorphic framework for understanding environmental variability in Carpinteria Salt Marsh and establishes a baseline for future micropaleontological analyses (e.g. foraminiferal test size, ostracod carapace size).

title: The Effect of Fluids on Geochronology
session_title: MSA 2026 Awardees Lectures and Presidential Address
authors: Timmerman, Suzette [1]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Geological Sciences, University of Bern, Bern, Bern, Switzerland
abstract:
The presence of fluids can affect the closure temperature of isotopic systems in minerals. In this talk I will show how fluids can also reset some (but not all) isotopic systems in xenocrysts in cooling magmas, with a focus on inclusions in diamonds recovered from kimberlite. For understanding processes in the Earth’s mantle, diamonds are a vital sample due to its chemical inertness and thus preserving pristine information in inclusions in diamond. Diamond formation ages are crucial to our understanding of carbon mobility. Yet, different isotopic systems have yielded a range of ages of which some are related to the kimberlite eruption time. This has given rise to a debate surrounding the interpretation of ages and the events they denote.

Here, I present an example from measured Rb-Sr, Sm-Nd, U-Pb isotope systematics of lherzolitic garnets in diamonds from the Victor kimberlite as well as isotopic modelling on garnet [1]. Sm-Nd isotope systematics of two populations yield isochron ages of 818 ± 251 and 624 ± 248 Ma, comparable to the ~720 million-year-old Re-Os age of peridotitic sulfide inclusions from the same location [2]. Rb-Sr and U-Pb isotope systematics of the same garnet inclusions point to a younger time, within uncertainty of the kimberlite eruption age of 177 Ma [3]. A fluid film is recorded at the garnet inclusion – diamond interface via 2D Raman mapping and the presence of such a fluid can induce parent/daughter fractionation. Partition modelling of the Rb-Sr, Sm-Nd, and U-Pb parent/daughter ratios at 700-1200 °C shows Sm-Nd are fully diffused from the fluid film back into the garnet inclusion during cooling of the host magma below 800 °C, giving the original Sm-Nd diamond formation age. Rb, Sr, and Pb however are variably incompatible in garnet between the closure temperature and 800 °C, resulting in partial to full resetting to kimberlite eruption age. Therefore, considering the presence of fluids is crucial to the interpretation of ages.

[2] Aulbach et al. (2018), EPSL 490, 77-87

[3] Januszczak et al. (2013), In Proceedings of 10IKC V2, 157-171

title: What’s the Point? Quantifying the Spatial Accuracy of Mineral Site Locations to Support High Standard Critical Mineral Assessments
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Zach, Terri A. [1], Rosera, Joshua M. [2], Case, George N.D. [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Geology, Energy & Minerals Science Center, Reston, VA, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Geology, Energy & Minerals Science Center, Reston, VA, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Alaska Science Center, Anchorage, AK, USA
abstract:
Understanding the quantity and distribution of domestic critical mineral resources is an important step in ensuring future supply, informed U.S. Government policymaking, and international relations. Through the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and other efforts, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and state partners are collecting and compiling new high-resolution geophysical, geochemical, spectral, and geological data to support efforts to map and quantify critical mineral resources. These data can be used to construct mineral prospectivity models to aid USGS assessments of critical minerals. However, training and validating mineral prospectivity models requires data on known mines, deposits, and occurrences – collectively called mineral sites. Most mineral site data are held in legacy datasets, such as the USGS Mineral Resource Data System (MRDS). Although it is generally understood that the locations of mineral sites in MRDS are often approximate, no study has attempted to quantify its spatial uncertainty. This study addresses that gap to better evaluate the level of effort, and justification, required to improve and verify mineral site data for critical mineral assessments.

We analyzed mineral site information from two independent mineral resource assessments: 1) pegmatite-related mineral sites in the Black Hills, South Dakota, and 2) a national dataset of graphite mineral sites. Both studies deduplicated MRDS records and improved locations for mineral sites using historical documents, topographic map-derived data, and modern digital elevation models. We compared the improved mineral site data to legacy coordinates to quantify spatial accuracy. Preliminary results showed that in the Black Hills (374 sites) the spatial deviation in the legacy locations had a median of 250 m, and a first-quartile (Q1) and third-quartile (Q3) of 100 m and 475 m, respectively. The national graphite dataset (516 sites) had similar distances of 350 m (median), 200 m (Q1), and 625 m (Q3). For comparison, mineral prospectivity mapping uses modern high-resolution datasets such as 1-meter lidar, 50-meter geophysical data, and 1:100,000-scale geologic mapping with ca. 50-meter resolution. These results demonstrate that less than 25% (i.e., Q1) of the studied mineral sites are accurate to within 100 m. Map scale and data resolution influence how mineral prospectivity models are fit and utilized. Improving mineral site locations can enhance model performance because it ensures that the target variables are aligned with high-resolution datasets.

title: Ancient Fault Populations on Mercury: A Record of Early Planetary Processes and Deformation
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Crane, Kelsey T [1], Riggs, Jamie D [2], Kirchoff, Michelle R. [3], Fincher, PJ [4]
affiliations: (1) Seres Engineering & Services, LLC, Brandon, MS, USA
(2) Thomas Jefferson University, College of Population Health Studies, USA; Northwestern University, School of Professional Studies, USA
(3) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
(4) Seres Engineering & Services, LLC, Charleston, SC, USA
abstract:
The oldest tectonic landforms preserved on a planetary surface record some of the earliest active processes on that body. Changes in orientation and planetary radius, tidal stresses, rotation rate, and internal dynamics may all be recorded within an ancient fault population; however, these landforms are often difficult to identify at the scale of global mapping studies due to degraded geomorphologic expressions and overprinting by younger impact craters.

This study presents the results of a detailed (1:750K), global mapping campaign of Mercury’s oldest preserved faults, those superposed by Calorian or older impact craters. Each of the 1,903 tectonic landforms mapped was split into 5 km-long segments (33,161 total), and latitude, longitude, strike, vergence (direction of tectonic transport), relief, width, and superposing crater were recorded for each segment.

Mapping shows that faults are preferentially preserved in the southern hemisphere. Preserved ancient structures have median and mean reliefs of 1.7 and 2.0 km, respectively, compared with 0.29 km and 0.37 km for all structures in the newly released MerCatSS dataset. The oldest faults have a median length of 69 km and a mean length of 84.6 km. Their greater relief and relief to length ratios indicate that the largest tectonic landforms are preferentially preserved and remain recognizable, even where impacts obscure their total length.

Vergence and strike data show most preserved ancient fault segments exhibiting northward and southward tectonic vergence (171- and 349-degrees azimuth), consistent with predominantly east-west strikes. These strikes are perpendicular to the attitudes of the global fault population, implying that stress orientations changed drastically over time.

For each tectonic landform, we will use crater-counting techniques to estimate model ages for fault-superposing craters, thereby establishing upper limits on the timing of ancient tectonic activity. Out of 926 craters larger than 20 km in diameter superposing faults, 93, 303, and 165 have previously been classified as Pre-Tolstojan, Tolstojan, and Calorian, respectively. The rest are unclassified (365).

We also aim to refine geomorphic measurements with machine learning techniques to estimate width and relief more precisely and relate our observations to predicted patterns in tectonics resulting from specific global and regional processes. With quantitative age estimates and detailed morphometrics for these tectonic landforms, our results may indicate types and intensities of processes active in Mercury’s early history.

title: Subsurface Systems Modeling: From Petroleum to New Energy and Mineral Systems
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Burton, Zachary Florentino Murguía [1], Wygrala, Bjorn [2], Palmowski, Daniel [3], Hantschel, Thomas [4]
affiliations: (1) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT,
(2) Cologne, Germany
(3) Terranta GmbH, Aachen, Germany
(4) Terranta GmbH, Aachen, Germany
abstract:
For over half a century, basin and petroleum system modeling (BPSM) has evolved to become an essential component of exploration workflows in global oil and gas companies. Its role in exploration is comparable to the role of reservoir modeling in production. BPSM enables investigations of all controlling properties and processes resulting in the formation of conventional and unconventional oil and gas accumulations. Methods include quantitative, multi-dimensional reconstructions of sedimentary basin and fluid system evolution over geologic timescales, including burial histories, rock properties, tectonics, thermal histories, pressure, fluid generation, fluid migration, and the trapping, accumulation, and preservation of fluids and associated resources. Spatial scales range from basin to play to prospects, and timescales range from over a billion years to less than a hundred years.

These proven concepts are now being increasingly invested to improve efficiencies in exploration for subsurface energy resources, such as geothermal and hydrogen, and for mineral systems. The key benefits are very similar to those achieved in petroleum exploration and include: significantly improved understanding of the geological properties and processes that control resource formation; more rigorous data collection, quality controls, and mapping; and the ability to perform process modeling (including reactive transport modeling, though requiring new physics implementations to handle aqueous transport) on all timescales that impact resource development. A final benefit is the ability of the modeling process to improve communications both within multidisciplinary teams and between technical and management teams.

However, despite clear parallels between numerous of the fundamental processes controlling petroleum system evolution and sedimentary basin-hosted mineral system evolution, the adaptation and application of powerful BPSM capabilities to the exploration and study of ore deposits is but nascent. Here, we present frameworks for modeling basin-hosted mineral systems. Alongside hydrogen, CCS, and mineral system case studies, BPSM-style workflows are discussed as well-suited to sediment-hosted copper (e.g., Central African Copperbelt; Europe’s Kupferschiefer), sedimentary-basin/oilfield lithium brine (e.g., Alberta Basin; USA’s Smackover Formation), geothermal-basin lithium brine (e.g., Upper Rhine Graben; California’s Salton Sea), Mississippi Valley-type lead-zinc (e.g., Missouri’s Viburnum Trend; Canada’s Pine Point; the Irish orefield), and basin-hosted uranium systems, with additional applicability to sedimentary-exhalative zinc-lead-silver (e.g., Australia’s McArthur River, Mount Isa; Alaska’s Red Dog), closed-basin lithium brine (e.g., South America’s Lithium Triangle; Nevada’s Clayton Valley), and, potentially emerging basin- or brine-hosted rare earth element systems.

authors: Haagsma, Autumn [1], Pearson, Sara [2], Scott, Ashley [3], Ives, Libby R.W. [4], Quigley, Ashley [5], Erber, Nathan Ray [6], Conner, Amber [7]

(7) Michigan Geological Survey, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
abstract:
The United States faces an increasing need for a highly skilled geoscience workforce capable of addressing complex societal challenges related to energy security, critical mineral supply chains, groundwater resources, climate resilience, geologic hazards, environmental contamination, and sustainable land-use planning. Federal initiatives have similarly emphasized workforce development to support emerging priorities such as carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS), geologic hydrogen, critical minerals, water resources, contaminant hydrogeology, and advanced geologic mapping. The Michigan Geological Survey (MGS) has developed a multifaceted student training model designed to prepare the next generation of geoscientists through mentored research, hands-on technical training, and applied scientific investigations.

MGS supports workforce development through three integrated pathways: a mentor-based summer internship program, summer field assistant positions, and year-round student research opportunities funded through state and federal projects. Students work alongside professional geologists, faculty, and research staff on multidisciplinary teams addressing real-world scientific and societal needs. Research areas include CCUS, geologic hydrogen, geologic mapping, groundwater resources, karst characterization, critical minerals, aggregate resources, subsurface data modernization, and contaminant occurrence, transport, and remediation, including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Student-led PFAS research contributes to understanding contaminant sources and behavior while supporting improved investigation and remediation strategies.

Students gain experience with GIS, digital mapping, core description, geologic field methods, geophysical surveys, X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), petrography, sediment analysis, laboratory instrumentation, database development, and scientific communication. Participants also build professional networks through collaboration with state and federal agencies, industry, regulators, research institutions, and academic partners. Many projects intentionally foster interdisciplinary collaboration among geologists, engineers, environmental scientists, data scientists, and other specialists, helping students understand how diverse expertise is integrated to address challenges related to energy, natural resources, environmental stewardship, contamination, and infrastructure planning.

Workforce development extends beyond internships and research assistantships through partnerships with faculty that integrate active Survey projects into university coursework. Students apply advanced analytical techniques to Survey-provided samples and datasets to address real research questions, allowing them to connect classroom learning with applied scientific problem-solving.

This presentation highlights the structure, outcomes, and lessons learned from MGS’s workforce development model, demonstrating how mentor-driven research experiences can advance scientific objectives while developing a skilled and adaptable geoscience workforce prepared to address national priorities in energy, resource security, environmental protection, and resilient communities.

title: Tracing sediment origin and organization of late Paleozoic Michigan Basin sandstones using detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Allen, Rose C [1], Bowen, Adeline G [2], Stevens Goddard, Andrea L [3]
affiliations: (1) Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract:
The Michigan Basin is an ideal location for identifying how tectonic events along a continental margin can influence sediment organization in the continental interior. We present detrital zircon U-Pb geochronologic data from sandstone deposited in the Michigan Basin during periods of active tectonism along the eastern margin of Laurentia including Acadian (~410-365 Ma) and Alleghenian (~360-300 Ma) orogenesis. Our target sandstones include the Devonian Sylvania (~390-380 Ma) and Berea (~360-370 Ma) Sandstones, the Mississippian Marshall Sandstone (~350-345 Ma), and the Pennsylvanian Saginaw Formation (~300-310 Ma).

The tectonically stable Superior Craton (3,000 – 2,500 Ma) and tectonically active Grenville provenance (1,300-1,000 Ma) and Appalachian orogens (480-300 Ma) are the most prominent sources present in the analyzed samples. Sediment organization varies spatially and temporally across the basin, with the Superior Craton being the most prominent source in the middle Devonian Sylvania Sandstone and the Grenville provenance being the most prominent source in the late Devonian – Pennsylvanian Sandstones. Appalachian sources are most abundant in the northeast of the basin during Acadian orogenesis, and southeast of the basin during Alleghenian orogenesis. These geochronologic data will be used to target age populations for pending (U-Th)/He thermochronology.

title: Using High-resolution Aeromagnetic Data to Refine the Precambrian Tectonic Evolution of the Southern Lake Superior Region USA
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Cannon, William F. [1], Drenth, Benjamin [2], Salerno, Ross [3]
affiliations: (1) Interior, United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(2) Interior, United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(3) Interior, United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
abstract:
The southern Lake Superior region is an area with sparse bedrock exposure that has had an extraordinarily complex 2.5-billion-year history of multiple superimposed orogenies. A high-resolution (150 m line spacing, 100 m nominal terrain clearance) aeromagnetic survey conducted by the USGS Earth MRI program in 2025, combined with high-resolution data acquired by the USGS in 2016 and 2018 with the same specifications, provides Rank 1 coverage for nearly all of the western Upper Peninsula of Michigan and parts of northern Wisconsin. The new data provide a wealth of information on the complex Precambrian geology of this region greatly improving accuracy in defining boundaries of the myriad tectonic terranes of the region and mapping features internal to those terranes that were not evident from older, more generalized, geophysical data. Highlights include: 1) improved resolution of the trace of the Niagara fault[CS1] , a terrane boundary between the southern margin of the Archean Superior craton and Paleoproterozoic arc volcanics obducted onto it, 2) an increase in the mappable extent of the Paleoproterozoic Bush Lake fault revealing that it is also an important tectonic boundary between areas of contrasting structural and metamorphic history, 3) detailed resolution of the flood basalt sequences of the Midcontinent Rift, including previously unresolved structural complexities within the thick basalt flow sequence, 4) refinement of the location and extent of domes of uplifted Archean gneisses and surrounding iron-rich Paleoproterozoic sequences in a region in northern Wisconsin and adjacent northern Michigan that is nearly devoid of outcrops, 5) revelation of several distinct sets of diabase dikes, probably ranging in age from Archean to circa 1.1 Ga, 6) extension of exposed Precambrian geologic features eastward for nearly 100 kilometers beneath thin Paleozoic sedimentary cover.

The improved spatial resolution of geologic units provided by the new high-resolution aeromagnetic data, combined with a wealth of recent geochronologic constraints on igneous, metamorphic, and tectonic events, is spurring a vastly improved understanding of the prolonged and complex geologic and regional metallogenic framework of this region where multiple orogenies that were superimposed through 2.5 billion years have left behind an extraordinarily complex odyssey of geologic history.

title: ASSESSING HYDROGEOCHEMICAL PROCESSES OF A HYDROLOGICALLY MODIFIED MANGROVE WETLANDS, SOUTHEAST FLORIDA
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Lara, Melaney [1], Price, Rene M [2], Ogurcak, Danielle E [3], Ross, Michael S [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environment, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(2) Earth and Environment, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(3) Earth and Environment, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(4) Earth and Environment, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
abstract: Mangrove wetlands are found at the intersection of land and sea, facing harsh conditions such as fluctuating salinity, alternating water levels, temperature changes, and anaerobic soil conditions. As increased urbanization pressures these ecosystems, mangrove wetlands are facing issues such as pollution, habitat fragmentation, and hydrologic disconnection from natural sources of water that deliver nutrients and deposit sediment. In the Biscayne Bay Coastal Wetlands in southeast Florida, mangrove wetlands are experiencing the effects of urbanization, with the wetland divided by structures such as canals and levees. These wetlands experience tidal influence in both dwarf and fringe structure zones, but in some locations, dwarf mangrove zones are experiencing increased freshwater discharge from canal sources via culverts. These hydrologically modified mangrove forests may experience a change in nutrient and biogeochemical cycling due to an increase in anthropogenic sources of water (e.g. canal water). This study focused on two structural zones of mangroves (dwarf and fringe) within six different transects (blocks) of mangrove wetlands; three blocks received canal water via a culvert, whereas three blocks did not have a culvert linking the canal and the wetland. This study investigated the nutrient and hydrogeochemical exchange of pore water and surface water within a hydrologically modified mangrove wetland receiving canal water inputs. Water sample collections occurred during the dry and wet seasons within the year 2024-2025. Environmental parameters such as salinity, specific conductivity, temperature, water depth, and pH were measured. Nutrient (total phosphorus and nitrogen) concentrations, stable isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen, cations and anions, and alkalinity analysis of the pore water and surface water were completed. Water sulfide concentrations and oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) were measured simultaneously with pore water collections only. The results of this study highlight the importance of water management practices that increase nutrient availability and decrease salinity in the dwarf mangroves by increasing canal water inputs into the blocks versus those that did not receive consistent canal water inputs. Using stable isotopes and metal tracers, groundwater and canal water inputs were higher in the dry season than in the wet season as well, where the blocks had significant influence from Biscayne Bay (brackish) and canal water inputs. The significance of this study informs coastal wetland managers of the hydrogeochemical dynamics of a valuable ecosystem and its restoration progress.

title: Integrated Characterization of Precambrian Core from the Michigan Basin: Applications to Geologic Mapping, Geologic Hydrogen, and Critical Mineral Resource Assessment
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources (Posters)
authors: Haagsma, Autumn [1], Harrison, William [2], Scott, Ashley Brooke [3], Conner, Amber [4], Crandall, Dustin [5], Isom, Shelby [6], Paronish, Thomas [7], Lammes, Anne [8]
affiliations: (1) Michigan Geological Survey, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(2) Michigan Geological Survey, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(3) Michigan Geological Survey, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA

(8) National Energy Technology Laboratory, Morgantown, WV, USA
abstract:
The Precambrian crystalline basement underlying the Michigan Basin remains one of the least understood geologic units in the region despite its importance for understanding basin evolution, geologic mapping, critical mineral resources, and emerging energy opportunities. Recent interest in geologic hydrogen, domestic critical mineral supply chains, and rare earth element (REE) resources has further highlighted the need for improved characterization of Precambrian lithologies, structures, alteration history, and petrophysical properties. To address critical data gaps, the Michigan Geological Survey (MGS) initiated a comprehensive effort to characterize available Precambrian core and compile existing subsurface information into a unified database.

Approximately 200 ft (61 m) of Precambrian core from 10 wells distributed across the Michigan Basin were identified and analyzed through a partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL). Core characterization included high-resolution multi-sensor core scanning, medical-scale 3D computed tomography (CT) imaging, and targeted subsampling for micro-CT imaging and micro-permeability measurements. These analyses provide new insights into lithologic variability, fracture occurrence, mineralogical heterogeneity, and physical properties within Michigan’s crystalline basement. In parallel, published studies, historical reports, geophysical interpretations, well records, and existing analytical data were compiled into a comprehensive Precambrian database to support future research and statewide mapping efforts.

Preliminary results reveal significant variability in basement lithology, texture, and internal fabric, while advanced imaging techniques provide a non-destructive framework for identifying structural features, alteration patterns, and potential fluid pathways. The integrated dataset establishes a foundation for future investigations focused on refining Precambrian geologic frameworks, calibrating geophysical models, and improving interpretations of basement structure and composition. Ongoing applications include support of U.S. Geological Survey STATEMAP projects, evaluation of geologic hydrogen generation potential, identification of controls on hydrogen migration and storage, and assessment of the distribution of critical minerals and rare earth element (REE)-bearing lithologies within Michigan’s crystalline basement. These data will also support future mineral resource assessments and provide critical calibration points for regional geophysical datasets used to characterize the basin's subsurface.

This study represents one of the first coordinated efforts to systematically characterize Michigan Basin Precambrian core using modern imaging and petrophysical techniques and demonstrates the value of legacy core collections for addressing contemporary scientific and energy-related questions.

title: Evaluation of Critical Mineral Enrichment in Permian Evaporite Deposits of Kansas
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Andrzejewski, Kate [1], Kalbas, James [2], Eltom, Hassan [3], Smith, Rachel [4]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(4) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
The vast Permian bedded evaporite deposits of Kansas have long been mined as a natural resource, yet the geochemical trace element characterization of these deposits and their stratigraphic extent is still poorly constrained. This study aims to systematically identify, evaluate, and map zones of critical mineral enrichment within the Permian bedded evaporite deposits. Integrating systematic geochemical evaluations, sedimentological analyses, and three-dimensional subsurface assessments within a high-precision stratigraphic framework, the distribution and concentrations of critical mineral accumulations can be quantified for regional evaporite successions.

Preliminary results highlight systematic evaluation of three cores spanning three evaporite successions: the Hutchinson Salt Member of the Wellington Fm., the Flower-Pot Shale, and the Blaine Fm. Each unit is primarily comprised of bedded halite, gypsum, and anhydrite. Compositional and geochemical analyses required a combination of tools including initial screening with a Multi-Sensor Core Logger (including handheld pXRF), handheld LIBS device, X-ray diffraction, and ICP-MS. High-resolution core descriptions were then combined with well-log datasets to identify, delineate, and map surfaces within Schlumberger’s Petrel Software Package. Geochemical results show little if any enrichment in critical minerals within the targeted evaporite deposits. However, elevated elemental concentrations of lithium (>250 ppm) and cesium (>100 ppm) are measured in the interbedded mudstones contained within the Permian deposits. The results suggest that while the shallow Permian basin served as a mineral sink, limited input of critical minerals to the closed basin resulted in minimal enrichment. Mapped subsurface horizons of the Hutchinson Salt Member reveal thick (> 450ft) and laterally continuous evaporite deposits in south-central KS most notably in Clark, Comanche, Barber, Kiowa and Pratt counties. The Hutchinson Salt Member then gradually thins to the north, east, and west eventually terminating along complex dissolution fronts that act as the bounding edges of the deposit. This framework model provides new insight into the sequence-stratigraphic relationships of these units and will aid in utilization of bedded salt units in Kansas for a range of industrial uses including subsurface energy storage.

title: Connecting the Upper Cretaceous Austin Chalk and Niobrara Formation in the Western Interior Seaway—Reconciling Different Facies and Sequence Stratigraphic Interpretations
session_title: Cretaceous Mudstones of the Western Interior Seaway: New Insights into Sedimentary Inputs and Processes Impacting Geologic Resources Potential
authors: Griffith, Christine M. [1], Pope, Michael C. [2], Donovan, Arthur D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA
abstract: The Upper Cretaceous Austin Chalk and the Niobrara Formation in the Western Interior Seaway are coeval but have very different facies and sequence stratigraphic interpretations. The Austin Chalk in Texas was deposited as a carbonate ramp, with light-colored, thoroughly burrowed chalk updip, and laminated organic-rich or marly chalks downdip. Sequence boundaries occur within chalk units, and maximum flooding surfaces occur within marls or organic-rich chalks. The Niobrara formation consists of basinal organic-rich marl and chalk units that grade into siliciclastic formations on the western flank of the seaway. The legacy Niobrara sequence stratigraphic interpretation focusses on facies relationships on the western flank of the basin. Laminated, organic-rich marl units in the basin axis are interpreted as regressive deposits containing sequence boundaries. Maximum flooding surfaces occur within chalk-rich units. A new sequence stratigraphic interpretation based on the Austin Chalk analog emphasizes shallower water chalk facies on the low-relief eastern flank of the seaway. These facies occur in 1) well-bioturbated sandy and scoured facies in the basal Niobrara Fort Hays Member, above a regional angular unconformity and in 2) well bioturbated chalk facies near the Sioux uplift in South Dakota and Nebraska. The seaway deepened and became more restricted through time, forming the dysoxic/anoxic facies of the upper Niobrara Smoky Hill Member. Austin Chalk sequences in Texas are highly asymmetric across the San Marcos Arch, indicating that sequences were controlled more by regional tectonism than eustacy. Similar regional tectonism in the central Western Interior Seaway is invoked as controlling alternating chalk and marl sequences in the Niobrara Formation. Episodic thrust loading would have caused the basinal axis to shift westward and trap siliciclastics. Pelagic organisms flourished and accumulated east of the axis, forming an eastern carbonate ramp that extended into the dysoxic basin. Between thrust loading events, siliciclastics advanced eastward beyond the basin axis, forming organic-rich marl units that lap out eastward. These lapouts represent maximum flooding surfaces between shallower-water eastern chalk sequences. The underlying Greenhorn Formation also may be interpreted using this new Niobrara stratigraphic model. Like the Fort Hays Member, the base of the Bridge Creek Limestone is interpreted as a sequence boundary, the basal benthonic foraminiferal zone is a transgressive chalk, and overlying siliciclastic-rich sediments contain the maximum flooding surface.

title: A LOOK INTO THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN LATE TRIASSIC VERTEBRATE FOSSIL ASSEMBLAGES AND SEDIMENTARY STRUCTURES OF TWO SITES IN THE DOCKUM GROUP
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Crowns, Madison Rose [1], Holbrook, John Rose [2], Martz, Jeff Rose [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental and Geological Science, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, TX, USA
(2) Department of Environmental and Geological Science, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, TX, USA
(3) Curator of Vertebrate Paleontology, Museum of Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA; Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract: The Dockum Group is of palaeontologic and sedimentary significance due to the fossils and preserved sedimentary structures. The Dockum Group contains a vast variety of Late Triassic vertebrates ranging from aquatic and amphibian to early mammals and dinosaurs and preserved upper-flow-regime structures. The opportunity to study how upper flow regimes effect fossil assemblages’ preservation makes the Dockum Group a unique study area. Observed outcrops come from two sites, Boren Ranch and OC Ranch. Boren Ranch outcrops represent an upper flow regime river and flood plain system, and OC Ranch outcrops represents a lower flow regime system that includes floodplains and lakes. Fossils at both sites are typically found in mudstone units representing floodplains, fossils are disarticulated and partial, suggesting pre-burial decomposition.

title: Exposing Undergraduates To Professional Conferences Through Geology Travel Studies
session_title: Learning to be a Geoscientist: Professional Exposure, Agency, and Transferable Skills in Undergraduate Education.
authors: Van Boening, Angela [1], Dunagan, Stan [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Agriculture, Geosciences, and Natural Resources, University of Tennessee at Martin, Martin, TN, USA
(2) Department of Agriculture, Geosciences, and Natural Resources, University of Tennessee at Martin, Martin, TN, USA
abstract:
Professional conferences expose undergraduate students to current research, graduate and employment opportunities, and professional development early in their academic careers. Yet, students may not have an opportunity to attend a conference unless they are presenting research. The geoscience program at The University of Tennessee at Martin has developed a model that combines conference attendance with faculty-lead field trips allowing students to attend professional meetings, gain regional field experience, and earn academic credit. The model uses an existing 3 credit hour course designated as “Travel Studies in Geology” which has traditionally been used for geology field trip courses. The semester-long course includes pre-travel meetings focused on the regional geology, assignments, and trip logistics, followed by post-travel student presentations and trip reflections. The conference travel studies typically consist of 4 days of conference attendance and 3 to 4 days of field excursions. Before the trip students choose a relevant geologic topic to research and present a site talk on the field trip. At the conference they are required to attend a set number of presentations to discuss upon return. Previous iterations have included GSA meetings in San Juan, Vancouver, Anaheim, and San Antonio, with field excursions along to Puerto Rico, the Pacific Cascades, Southern California, and the Texas Hill Country, respectively.

Utilizing the existing Travel Studies course allows partnership with the university’s Travel Studies Office for logistics and budget approval as well as access to travel study scholarships, college-level support, and university donors via gift funds. Student costs are typically $1800-2000 before financial assistance and pays for airfare, lodging, transportation, etc. Students earn 3 upper-division credit hours toward their degrees and financial aid may be applied to tuition. Student feedback has been overwhelmingly positive. Participants have made connections leading to employment, graduate school, and professional organizations. They gain firsthand exposure to the broad scope of geoscience research while experiencing geology in regions they might not otherwise visit. Recent travel alumni have also become first-time donors to the geology gift funds reflecting the lasting impact of these experiences. The UTM model integrates conference participation, regional field experiences, and professional development into a single course while reducing barriers to undergraduate participation. The approach is easily transferable to other programs seeking to expand student access to professional meetings.

title: From Contours to Flight Paths: A UAS Mapping Protocol for Complex Cliff Faces
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data
authors: Millo, Amit [1]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Woods Hole Coastal and Marine Science Center, Woods Hole, MA, USA
abstract:
Advances in unmanned aircraft system (UAS) technology have transformed geologic mapping by enabling the creation of low-cost, high-resolution digital outcrops using structure-from-motion. However, steep cliff faces featuring clefts and gullies, which are difficult or impossible to map using traditional satellite- or crewed aircraft-based remote sensing, remain challenging for UAS surveys because their complex geometry leads to image overlap inconsistencies and flight safety constraints.

This presentation introduces a field-tested UAS mapping protocol designed specifically for complex cliff environments. The workflow automatically converts topographic contour lines from a digital elevation model into terrain-adaptive flight paths that maintain a nearly constant stand-off distance from the cliff face. Combined with optimized oblique image acquisition, the protocol maximizes surface coverage, maintains consistent image geometry and overlap, and minimizes data gaps caused by complex relief.

Case studies from the Gay Head Cliffs on Martha’s Vineyard and Meteor Crater in Arizona demonstrate how the protocol produces high-resolution digital outcrops suitable for structural measurements, stratigraphic analysis, and change detection. By standardizing flight planning, data acquisition, and processing, this approach improves the quality of close-range remote sensing surveys. The resulting dataset expands the utility of digital outcrops for geologic research, hazard assessment, and long-term monitoring of inaccessible rock exposures.

title: Controls on Organic Matter Enrichment and Preservation across the Cenomanian-Turonian Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 Interval in USGS #1 Portland and Innes-1 Cores: An Integrated Sedimentologic and Organic Petrology Analysis
session_title: Cretaceous Mudstones of the Western Interior Seaway: New Insights into Sedimentary Inputs and Processes Impacting Geologic Resources Potential
authors: Li, Zhiyang [1], Flores, Eric [2], Minisini, Daniel [3]
affiliations: (1) Texas A&M International University, Laredo, TX, USA
(2) Texas A&M International University, Laredo, Texas, USA
(3) ExxonMobil, Spring, TX, USA; Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
abstract:
Many mixed (siliciclastic-carbonate) fine-grained distal offshore deposits in the Western Interior Seaway across the Cenomanian-Turonian Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2) interval contain high total organic carbon (TOC). To evaluate the controls on the enrichment and preservation of organic matter (OM), this study applied an integrated sedimentologic and organic petrology analysis to deposits across the OAE2 interval in the USGS #1 Portland (“Portland”) core and the Innes-1 (“Innes”) core. A total of 19 (Portland) and 16 (Innes) samples were collected, and a polished thin section and whole-rock pellet were prepared from each sample for optical petrographic and organic petrology analysis, respectively. This new dataset was supplemented by previously published carbonate content and TOC data from the two cores.

The onset of OAE2 in both cores approximately corresponds to a distinct shift from more laminated marl/mudstone facies to more bioturbated, carbonate-rich facies. The pre-OAE2 samples are characterized by distinctly higher TOC content than samples from the OAE2 interval, but the dominant maceral type in pre-OAE2 samples from both cores is bituminite (commonly micrinized; Type II OM). OAE2-interval samples contain a higher proportion of Type I OM (alginite and liptodetrinite) but overall lower TOC content. The proportion of Type III OM (vitrinite and inertinite) is commonly elevated in carbonate-rich (i.e., limestone) facies.

Results from organic petrology suggest that bottom currents and sediment accumulation rate exerted key controls on OM preservation and enrichment. In both cores, dominant bituminite in the pre-OAE2 interval reflects seafloor reworking by bottom currents, which supplied detrital sediment and recycled OM; the resulting relatively high sedimentation rate helped preserve labile OM, leading to higher TOC content but diluting Type I OM with Type II OM. The dominance of bituminite over Type I OM also argues against bottom-water oxygen deficiency as the dominant control on OM preservation during the pre-OAE2 interval. The less common bituminite in the OAE2 interval reflects reduced bottom-current reworking during sea-level rise (Greenhorn transgression); the resulting lower sedimentation rate led to degradation of labile OM through bioturbation and early diagenesis, elevating the proportion of Type III OM but yielding overall low TOC content. These results demonstrate that integrated sedimentologic and organic petrology analyses provide process-based insights into the controls on OM preservation and enrichment in fine-grained sedimentary rocks.

title: Reconstructing Paleohydrology of Eocene-Oligocene Transition Lakes in Western South Dakota
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Keenan, Sarah W. [1], Beeler, Scott R. [2], Kortenbusch, Riley A. [3], Khatri, Samantha [4], Pagnac, Darrin [5]
affiliations: (1) South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(3) South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(4) South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(5) South Dakota School of Mines, Museum of Geology, Rapid City, SD, USA
abstract: Lacustrine carbonates record the prevailing hydrologic, geochemical, and paleoenvironmental conditions present during the lifespan of the lake. Stable carbon and oxygen isotopes from primary carbonates precipitated from lakes have been used in modern and ancient systems as a proxy for lake hydrology, including open vs. closed basin behavior and lake residence time. The White River Group, which outcrops extensively in western South Dakota, preserves terrestrial, sedimentary deposits spanning the Eocene-Oligocene Transition (EOT), including spatially and stratigraphically isolated lacustrine carbonates. The terrestrial record of the EOT in the North American Midcontinent presents conflicting records ranging from significant cooling (~8°C) to no cooling, and significant aridification to no change in mean annual precipitation. To address these conflicting records, we examined stable carbon and oxygen isotopes from a total of nine lacustrine deposits spanning the EOT, geographic, and elevation gradients. Broad temporal trends in carbonate δ 18 O from Eocene to the Oligocene sites indicate a 2.2‰ increase, which would correspond to ~10.5°C cooling if the isotopic shift was the result of only temperature changes. However, hydrologic variability, notably the degree of hydrologic openness between sites, is also an important control on the δ 18 O composition of lacustrine carbonates. Most lakes exhibit hydrologically open behavior, characterized by low (r < 0.7) covariance between δ 18 O and δ 13 C. Lakes at higher elevation (~900 to 1200 m present day) and further to the west displayed the weakest covariance (r < 0.1) and relatively invariant δ 18 O (~2‰), indicative of hydrologically open-systems. In contrast, the two lowest elevation (~800 m) and furthest east sites displayed strong covariance (r > 0.8), strongly indicative of closed-basin behavior. Of the two sites, one is the youngest examined (Oligocene-aged Poleslide Member) and represents the last known lacustrine site from the region. The site is characterized by strongly enriched δ 18 O (range: -4.1 to -7.3‰) and depleted δ 13 C (range: -7.3 to -8.3‰) compared to the other sites, suggestive of cooling. A shift to hydrologically closed-basin behavior would align with increased aridification and isolation of lakes into the Oligocene as fluvial input from the Black Hills uplift to the west ceased in the more distal, eastern locations. Understanding larger, regional scale variability as well as local, basin-specific trends can help resolve the magnitude of climatic change during the EOT.

title: Preliminary results linking chlorite geochemistry to temperature via correlative electron probe microanalysis and Raman spectroscopy
session_title: Early career investigators in mineralogy and crystallography (Posters)
authors: Shtabnoy, Alisa [1], Stokes, M. Rebecca [2], McAleer, Ryan J. [3], Jubb, Aaron M. [4], Leprêtre, Rémi [5], Bourdelle, Franck [6]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(4) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(5) CY Cergy Paris Université, Cergy, France
(6) CY Cergy Paris Université, Cergy, France
abstract:
Chlorite commonly forms in rocks which experienced diagenetic to low-grade metamorphic conditions with a chemical composition sensitive to the temperature at the time of mineral growth. Hence, the geochemical composition of chlorite can be used as a geothermometer for recording subsurface temperature during mineralization.

Electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) can determine chlorite chemical composition at the micron-scale. When paired with site-filling criteria, EPMA data can be used to assign occupancies at tetrahedral and octahedral sites and function as key inputs into chlorite geothermometers. Raman spectroscopy is another method capable of detecting chemical substitutions in minerals and could serve as a potential alternative in the geothermometric analysis of chlorite. Several empirically and thermodynamically calibrated chlorite geothermometers are based on the atoms per formula unit (APFU) values of tetrahedral and octahedral cations, and rules have been empirically formulated through correlating EPMA-derived APFU values to individual Raman-band positions in chlorites (Bourdelle, 2021; Lamm et al., 2023).

This work further explores correlations between chlorite composition and related Raman characteristics towards building a Raman-based chlorite geothermometer. Four samples from the Ardennes mountains with Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous materials temperatures ranging from 258°C to 558°C were studied. Correlative EPMA and micro-Raman analyses were conducted on twenty chlorite grains per sample of varying size and occurrence, and empirical relationships were constructed using multiple-linear regression of Raman peak properties (i.e. peak center and width) and EPMA compositional values. Preliminary analysis shows poor correlations between individual Raman peak properties and chemical composition but does show strong correlations using multiple concurrent peak properties within our samples, highlighting the complex interplay between chlorite composition and its Raman response. We explore the possibility of linking Raman peaks to specific cation substitutions and discuss our findings in the context of existing geochemical chlorite geothermometers. Future work could expand this approach to lower temperature chlorite in petroleum reservoirs, where constraining subsurface temperature is vital for assessing energy resources.
