title: The Cool (Water) Carbonates of Sweden: Archives of Local Marine Redox Conditions and Faunal Dynamics of the Middle Ordovician Baltoscandian Carbonate Shelf
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part I)
authors: Barnes, Gwen L. [1], Lindskog, Anders [2], Owens, Jeremy D. [3], Young, Seth A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science and National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
(2) Department of Environmental Science, Kristianstad University, Kristianstad, Sweden
(3) Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science and National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Ocean & Atmospheric Science and National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
abstract:
The Ordovician Period (~487– 443 Ma) represents an interval of profound change within the Earth system, as evidenced by shifts in the global climate state, paleogeography, and marine biodiversity. Organismal diversity and abundance substantially increased during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE), along with a complete transformation in marine ecosystem dynamics. Also accompanying the rapid rise in biodiversity is a documented significant increase in skeletal carbonate production during the Middle Ordovician. Questions still persist regarding the drivers of these complex ecological innovations and restructurings, yet several hypotheses invoke oxygen, sea level, paleogeography, and climatic cooling in helping initiate and maintain biodiversification.

Here, we seek to test the extent to which local ocean oxygenation and ecosystem complexity are correlated using a paired geochemical-sedimentological approach on four sections across the Ordovician Baltoscandian carbonate shelf. Skeletal marine carbonates reflect the chemical and physical conditions of an environment as well as the abundance and diversity of calcifying organisms, making these rocks invaluable archives for reconstructing paleoenvironments. We assess the relationship between carbonate microfacies data (i.e., point counts of carbonate textures and fossil assemblages) and local marine redox data using iodine-to-calcium ratios (I/Ca), a local carbonate-based redox proxy. Our new results from central and northern Sweden suggest spatial and temporal heterogeneities in locally oxic regions of the Baltic shelf throughout the Ordovician. Fossil grain assemblages appear to show overall similar faunal patterns across sections when I/Ca exhibits little variation, even when carbonate texture varies. However, trends in I/Ca can also correlate with changes in microfacies data. These findings provide insight into the relationship between abundance and diversity of skeletonizing organisms across this region during the GOBE in relation to oxygen. Broadly, the results support the importance of local marine redox conditions and depositional environment in contributing to the elevated ecosystem complexity and habitability through this critical evolutionary interval.

abstract: Kenya’s growing population and urbanization have generated increased demand for housing, infrastructure, goods, and access to water, electricity, and transportation. As part of Vision 2030, the Government of Kenya aims to transform the country into a middle-income economy with improved living standards and employment opportunities across all sectors, particularly those focused on natural resource acquisition. Kenya is a country rich in natural mineral resources that have the potential to transform the economy and workforce of the country. Utilization of rock and mineral resources is currently underexplored or poorly managed and there are not enough graduates from geology programs to fill employment needs, leaving significant challenges to national growth. In collaboration with the US Embassy in Nairobi, Taita Taveta University (TTU), Voi, Kenya, recognized a need for geoscience curriculum and programmatic development to address workforce shortages. Through the Fulbright Specialist Program, we collaborated on the design of a new Bachelor of Science (BSc) in Geology degree at TTU, which, when active, will be the second such degree program in Kenya. We met with stakeholders from the Kenyan government, future employers in the mining sector (small-scale and large-scale), and faculty, students, and staff at TTU to develop coursework that would not only prepare graduates for employment within Kenya but as part of the global workforce. Students will benefit from hands-on and holistic learning opportunities afforded by the close proximity to one of Kenya’s most mineral-rich zones in Taita Taveta County. The program will also have strong linkages with industry partners as trainers. In designing a geology curriculum that leverages existing strengths in mining engineering and environmental sciences, graduates will directly contribute to the sustainable growth of the natural resources sector with environmental stewardship as a guiding force. The successful development of a new BSc in Geology program in Kenya will help to transform TTU into a premier hub for mining and geology research and innovation, and will directly contribute to Kenya Vision 2030’s Economic and Social Pillars.

title: Hellas, Ken and Me: Adventures in Exhumation and Inundation
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Moore, Jeffrey M. [1]
affiliations: (1) National Aeronautics and Space Administration, Moffett Field, CA, USA
abstract:
Hellas is the largest and deepest basin on Mars. A 1993 study by Moore and Edgett (GRL, 20, 1599-1602) noted that Hellas undergoes net dust erosion. Thus, the exposed surface must represent whatever lag or rock surface and could not be removed by the strong winds blowing at these low elevations. The particle size distributions and particularly the rock or boulder population in this lag was thought to be potentially useful for distinguishing between processes that formed the lithologic units that comprise Hellas Planitia. Earlier studies had suggested the Hellas floor might be paved with basalt or glacial deposits. Ken, who at the time was working with Viking Orbiter IRTM data knew that there were late mission observations of the Hellas floor acquired though clear skies. His derived thermal inertia from these observations strongly suggested that the abundance of particles larger than coarse sand was very low. Hence, our study concluded that the floor deposits were, among other possibilities, ancient loess or lacustrine deposits.

In 2001 a subsequent study on the Hellas basin by Moore and Wilhelms (Icarus, 54, 258-276) proposed that the basin was once a site of an ice covered sea, based on a series of circum-basin scarps that follow constant elevations as well as other landforms seen my Mars Global Surveyor’s MOC (an instrument that Ken played a major role in daily operations and data analysis) and topography derived from MOLA. Subsequently the best contiguous observations of the Hellas basin have been acquired from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s Context Camera, which again Ken has been a central player in its operations. Much of what we know about the grain-scale sedimentology of martian lacustrine deposits comes from the Curiosity Rover’s Mars Hand Lens Imager (which Ken was the PI through development and original operations within Gale crater). Under Ken’s watch several members of the Murray Formation were determined to be deposited in a lacustrine environment. A conclusion strongly demonstrated by MHLI imaging.

My personal relationship with Hellas isn’t over. The Europa Clipper flew directly over the Hellas basin including its deepest regions. Ther REASON Ice Penetrating Radar system collected data during this flyby ostensibly for calibration, yet the quality of the observations may yet provide new discoveries from Hellas.

title: Spatial Variability in Drivers of Light Attenuation Across Massachusetts and New Hampshire Coastal Waters
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Moon, Krio [1], Singh, Harshit [2], Ranasinghe, Sachini [3], Tierney, Sophia [4], Fichot, Cédric G. [5]

abstract: Seagrass survival, productivity, and distribution depend critically on the quantity and spectral composition of ultraviolet (UV) and visible light reaching the seafloor. Because water-column constituents selectively absorb different wavelengths, understanding the drivers of vertical UV–visible light attenuation is essential for predicting seagrass habitat quality in coastal waters. Chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM), non-algal particles, and phytoplankton are the primary contributors to light attenuation in nearshore waters, yet their relative importance and spatial variability across the coastal ecosystems of Massachusetts and New Hampshire remain poorly quantified. Here, we investigated the controls on the spectral diffuse attenuation coefficient of downwelling irradiance, K d (λ), across the Plum Island Estuary, Great Bay, Essex Bay, and Waquoit Bay. We collected water samples and in situ K d (λ) profiles between June 2019 and July 2026 and obtained laboratory measurements of CDOM ( a g (λ)), phytoplankton ( a ph (λ)), and non-algal particle ( a d (λ)) absorption from 250–700 nm. CDOM was the primary driver of K d (λ) in the UV, blue, and green spectral regions, accounting for a median of 84.9%, 63.1%, and 45.2% of total absorption, respectively (R² = 0.88–0.99), whereas non-algal particles became the dominant predictor in the red (R² = 0.80). Despite this overall pattern, marked regional differences emerged. Absorption by CDOM varied by location due to river- and marsh-delivered terrigenous inputs and tidal flushing. This is reflected in the decreasing linear relationship between salinity and K d (λ) at 340 and 443 nm (R 2 = 0.82–0.83). Waquoit Bay exhibited substantially greater non-algal particle contributions to UV–green attenuation compared to other regions, likely due to decomposed algal biomass and limited riverine CDOM inputs. Although phytoplankton generally played a limited role in light attenuation in the studied coastal sites, it exhibited a greater influence in offshore Great Bay, Plum Island Estuary, and Essex Bay stations. These findings demonstrate that although CDOM governs benthic UV–green light availability, regional differences in organic matter sources produce distinct underwater light environments likely to influence seagrass habitat suitability and productivity.

title: Assessing the Effects of Differing Acid Dissolution Methods on Bulk Carbonate Trace Element Analyses
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Kortenbusch, Riley Allan [1], Keenan, Sarah Wheeler [2], Beeler, Scott Randall [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, South Dakota, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA

abstract: The elemental composition of carbonate rocks provides an archive of paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental conditions throughout Earth’s history. Elemental analysis is commonly performed on acid digests of rocks using solution inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). For this approach, partial digestion methods are frequently used to target carbonate minerals and exclude detrital components such as silicate minerals. However, methodologies utilized vary widely and geochemical comparisons generated using different methods remain limited. This study investigates how the choice of digestion method affects the major and trace element composition of acid leachates analyzed by solution ICP-MS. Specifically, the effects of acid type (acetic vs. nitric), acid concentration (5% vs. 10% acetic acid), heating method (hot block vs. microwave), sample mass (200 mg vs. 400 mg), and sequential vs. bulk digestion on five rocks containing a range of lithology were evaluated. When comparing the acetic acid-based methodologies, acid concentration and sample mass had minimal impact on measured geochemical compositions. In contrast, choice of acid had a greater impact as use of nitric acid in place of acetic acid showed increased K, Al, Fe, and Ti concentrations, indicating leaching of non-carbonate phases. Similarly, the microwave digestion method exhibited signs of enhanced non-carbonate phases dissolution indicated through increased K concentrations compared to hot block methods. However, microwave digestion methods resulted in lower Fe concentrations and comparable Al concentrations compared to hot block methods indicating potential loss of analytes through secondary reactions or discriminate leaching of different non-carbonate phases. Sequential methods resulted in lower concentrations of Al, K, Ti, V, Cr, Fe, Cu, Ba, and Pb in comparison to other methodologies indicating minimal non-carbonate digestion but potential non-representative digestion of carbonate phases. Comparison of results between lithologies indicated that choice of dissolution method had a greater impact for samples with complex mineralogy compared to relatively pure carbonate samples. Additionally, the effect of reporting method (ug/g of total mass, ug/g of soluble mass, and normalization to Ca) was compared and found to affect both the spread in data across digestion methods and observed compositional differences between samples. These results highlight how the selection of digestion and reporting methodology, particularly for carbonates with high detrital silicate content, can affect the resulting elemental concentrations, and, in turn, affect the interpretations of paleoclimate and paleoenvironment proxies.

abstract:
The Late Cretaceous to Paleogene evolution of western North America has been interpreted in terms of either continuous, east-dipping subduction or northward strike-slip displacement of the exotic Baja British Columbia terrane (Baja B.C.) along its margin. We tested these models by compiling (1) zircon U-Pb crystallization ages for igneous rocks older than 40 Ma from British Columbia to central Mexico; (2) detrital zircon ages for Cenomanian to Eocene forearc basin and subduction zone strata from northern California to central Baja California; and (3) detrital zircon ages for modern river sands from California.

The igneous ages define remarkably continuous belts along the length of the Cordillera, with only minor gaps or overlaps. This pattern is difficult to explain if the Coast Mountains batholith of Baja B.C. overlapped latitudinally with the coeval Sierra Nevada and Peninsular Ranges batholiths between 100–85 Ma. Furthermore, there is no obvious change in magmatic patterns anywhere along the margin at 100 Ma, the commonly proposed time of Baja B.C. collision. Laramide-age igneous rocks (80–40 Ma) can be divided into a southern segment (southern Arizona to Mexico) with pronounced inboard jump in the locus of magmatism, two central divisions (Sierra Nevada and Mojave) with magmatic shutoffs, and a northern section (British Columbia to Idaho) with modest inboard migration of magmatism. This arrangement is consistent with prior interpretations of low-angle to flat subduction during the Laramide orogeny.

Forearc basin and trench strata and modern river sands are dominated by Jurassic and Cretaceous zircon derived from the western to central belts of the Sierra Nevada and Peninsular Ranges (provenance type A). Type A sediment is locally accompanied by other sediment types with sources in the southeasternmost Sierra Nevada (type B) or regions inboard of the Sierra Nevada and Peninsular Ranges, including the Mojave Desert and vicinity (type C) and Idaho (types D and E). The different extraregional sediment types occur in forearc basin and subduction rocks at comparable latitudes. The commonalities between the forearc basin and subduction zone rocks, and clear ties to sediment sources in the adjacent magmatic arc, provide further evidence in favor of continuous east-dipping subduction and against Baja B.C. models, particularly versions that place Baja B.C. as far south as southern California or Baja California.

title: Tracking Pesticide Change and Human‑Health Implications in US Surface and Groundwater Resources
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part II)
authors: Stackpoole, Sarah [1], Breitmeyer, Sara [2], Hinman, Elise [3], Miller, Sam [4], Shoda, Meg [5]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) US Geological Survey, Pennsylvania, USA

abstract: Pesticides are widely used in agricultural, urban, residential, and industrial settings. Several chemical characteristics of pesticides, including fast degradation rates and adsorption to soil particles, are thought to limit runoff to rivers and leaching to groundwater. However, pesticides often persist in the environment beyond the site of application and period of use. Starting in 1992, the US Geological Survey (USGS) established long-term monitoring networks and analytical methods to assess pesticide occurrence, distribution, and toxicity in surface water (rivers and streams) and groundwater of the conterminous United States. Since that time, the USGS has analyzed over 100,000 water samples collected at dozens of surface water sites and 25 principal aquifers that supply water to roughly 13% of the US population. Recent studies showed commonly used herbicides (atrazine, glyphosate, and metolachlor) and several transformation products were detected in surface water or groundwater. We analyzed trends in concentrations and them to regulatory and non-regulatory benchmarks, such as the US EPA maximum contaminant levels, US EPA Human Health Benchmarks for Pesticides, and the US Geological Survey Health Based Screening Levels. Surface water pesticide concentrations were more likely to be increasing compared to decreasing. In contrast, the percentage of wells that had moderate groundwater pesticide concentrations (defined as greater than 10 percent of the human health benchmark (HHB) but less than or equal to the HHB) decreased over the sampling period. Mixtures of multiple pesticides occurred at individual monitoring locations in both surface water and groundwater, including both parent compounds and transformation products. Parent compounds rarely exceeded benchmarks, but we were unable to evaluate the potential risk posed by transformation products or pesticide mixtures, largely due to a lack of benchmark information. Assessments that integrate surface water and groundwater quality datasets are valuable, because changing conditions in one medium may impact the other. Additional benchmark information, for transformation products and mixtures in particular, would enable a more complete evaluation of the potential risk of these changes in water quality conditions on human health.

abstract: The Surficial Geologic Map of the Kayenta and Pinon 30-minute by 60-minute quadrangles, Arizona, and Utah contributes to a growing East–West transect of 1:100,000-scale geologic maps centered along the 37th parallel from the Great Plains to the Sierra Nevada—synthesized in the Seamless Integrated Geologic Mapping (SIGMa) extension to the Geologic Map Schema (GeMS). This map lies in the Canyon Lands and Navajo sections of the Colorado Plateau. Surficial deposits range from alluvium in the floor of Monument Valley to the mesa tops, colluvium and mass wasting deposits emanating from the Black Mesa and other sedimentary rock cliffs, and extensive eolian sands blanketing much of the map area. Modern satellite imagery and 1-meter digital elevation models from lidar coverage in places enables contact location and certainty to be refined relative to previous mapping, previously lumped map units to be split, and new mapping to fill gaps in existing bedrock-focused or coarser-scale maps. For example, from Tsegi Canyon and along Laguña Creek in the northeastern part of the map, lidar shows distinct arroyos cut into Holocene alluvium and floored by what is interpreted to be modern to historic alluvium. Such alluvium is characterized by inset geomorphic relations in this map—improving on nearby geomorphic studies and maps that include the Naha, Tsegi, and Jeddito Alluvium, and the arroyos that cut them. Additionally, this map separates units that in previous mapping were combined into undifferentiated alluvium and eolian deposits. Satellite imagery and lidar, where present, distinguish deposits that may have originally been formed in eolian environments but were subsequently reworked into alluvium, eolian deposits that have dune landforms, and where those dunes are either vegetated or not—with implications for their potential stability versus mobility. This map also incorporates geochronology from recent publications, such as the early Pleistocene age of the White Mesa alluvium, the highest alluvial deposits on the western edge of this map. Importantly, this SIGMa GeMS database contains detailed information beyond that which is traditionally printed on a geologic map. Complementing the generalized print map symbols and description of map units, each line and polygon in this database includes additional digital attributes such as feature-specific characteristics, notes, mapping method, certainty, previously assigned map unit(s), and the data source(s) from which mapping was compiled.

title: Decision-Making in Educational Design Research: An Example from a Workshop Engaging Secondary Teachers in Reasoning About the Food-Energy-Water Nexus
session_title: Making Sense of Methodologies and Theoretical Frameworks in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Scherer, Hannah H. [1]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Ag, Leadership, & Community Education, Blacksburg, VA,
abstract:
The Food-Energy-Water (FEW) Nexus is promising for driving socio-ecological systems thinking, serving as a potential response to calls for addressing complex systems at K-12 levels. Thus, there is a need for, and promise in, designing professional learning opportunities for teachers that support their understanding of the FEW Nexus. In this project, our team implemented the unifying theme “Using Systems Thinking to Address Complex Real-World Problems in the FEW Nexus” as an overarching framework to guide reflection, synthesis, and sensemaking within a four-day immersive professional development program for secondary teachers. In this study, I focused specifically on exploring the efficacy of our design in supporting teachers’ socio-ecological systems thinking within the FEW Nexus, in service of the long-term aim of transfer to their classrooms.

The methodological approach used in this study was educational design research, in which the design of interventions is based in current research and theory, and the researcher seeks to generate new knowledge through careful study during implementation of the intervention. I first developed a conjecture map that illustrates the hypothesized relationships and processes in the design that might lead to the desired outcomes. I then chose to conduct a design study to test the design conjecture (part of the larger conjecture map) that if teachers engage in the workshop activities as designed (i.e., design embodiment), then reasoning about the FEW Nexus and socio-ecological systems thinking (i.e., mediating processes) will emerge. A qualitative content analysis of artifacts from collaborative structured reflection sessions, guided by a coding frame based on the conceptual framework used in the design, revealed ways in which participants displayed the desired reasoning and areas where they were challenged. This careful attention to what occurred during the intervention allowed me to develop recommendations for practice, both for this program and for others. I had limited resources for research in this project, which contributed to the decision to focus solely on artifacts, not observations, interviews, and other data sources which would have strengthened the findings. Nonetheless, this study is a promising entry point that will inform ongoing design research in an underexplored area.

title: Reexamining the Timing of the End-Permian Mass Extinction Recovery Using Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Insights from the Spathian-Aged Virgin Limestone, Southwest Utah
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record (Posters)
authors: Stanard, Sydney C. [1], Monarrez, Pedro M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(2) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
abstract:
The biotic recovery following the End Permian Mass Extinction (EPME) has long been considered protracted, lasting up to 9 million years and extending into the early Middle Triassic. However, researchers have increasingly discovered fossil localities that preserve complex marine ecosystems from the Smithian–Spathian (250-247 MA), approximately 2-5 million years following the extinction event. These new discoveries are often labeled as “refugia” communities or localities with uniquely good taphonomic preservation. The discrepancy between these findings and the current scientific consensus around the timeframe of the post-EPME recovery period calls for a reexamination of the Smithian-Spathian interval.

In this research we focus on the Spathian Virgin Limestone Formation, a member of the larger Moenkopi Group, which stretches from southwestern Utah to southeastern California, U.S.A. We describe exposures of the Virgin Formation in the Hurricane Hills of Utah, which represent the most proximal sections and preserve a fossiliferous carbonate ramp and associated arid mudflats. Reevaluation of the stratigraphy and facies preserved in the Hurricane Hills indicates that the Virgin Formation exhibits thin (1–10m) shallowing-upward sequences. The previously reported fossiliferous horizons at these localities occur in the deepest water facies, representing tidal inlet fill and shallow and deep subtidal facies, whereas the shallowest water facies (restricted shallow subtidal/lagoonal and tidal flats) are devoid of body fossils. This discrepancy indicates relatively high alpha diversity in the lower, deepest facies and overall low beta diversity for the locality, due to facies-controlled preservation.

Previous work suggests that low beta diversity of fauna in these localities resulted from the dominance of generalist taxa with low interspecific competition. However, our preliminary results suggest instead that stratigraphic structure exerts a strong control on the preservation of fossil fauna in these localities, rather than intrinsic biotic factors or deleterious environmental conditions contributing to the low beta diversity found here. Future work will extend westward to further place the fossils from the Virgin Formation within a larger basin-scale context and reevaluate how the recovery of the EPME has been interpreted in the southwestern U.S.

session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Scherer, Hannah H. [1], McCarville, Katherine [2], Lombardi, Doug [3], Burgess, Jerry L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Ag, Leadership, & Community Education, Blacksburg, VA,
(2) Minot State University, Minot, ND,
(3) University of Maryland, College Park, MD,
(4) Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD,
abstract: Food-Energy-Water (FEW)-Nexus-based education supports understanding complex relationships in FEW systems, promoting socio-ecological systems thinking and informed decision-making about natural resources and sustainability challenges. With applications across informal, non-formal, K-12, and higher education spaces, there is considerable potential for use by geoscience educators. In this study, the perspectives of educational practitioners from multiple related disciplines, including the geosciences, were used to define and describe FEW-Nexus-based education and identify challenges with its implementation. Directed content and thematic analyses of artifacts generated during workshops (including a short course at GSA Connects) resulted in a proposed framework consisting of ontological and epistemological dimensions and themes organized into four categories. The framework provides a conceptual foundation for organizing educational goals, instructional design, and future research across diverse FEW-Nexus learning contexts. Findings have implications for geoscience education and geoscience education research. Within the ontological dimension, a crosscutting theme of Scale, Complexity, and Systems highlights the complex systems nature of the FEW-Nexus, aligning with efforts to support geoscience learners’ complex systems thinking. The category Social Dimensions of the FEW-Nexus included themes, including Equity of Access and Interdependence and Governance, Policy, and Decision-Making, that support teaching of the geosciences in the context of societal issues. In the epistemological dimension, participants emphasized the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, inclusive pedagogy, and place-based engagement. Collective Beliefs about FEW-Nexus Education included themes such as Relevance of FEW to Curriculum and Student Futures, aligning with efforts in geoscience education to support workforce preparation and real-world problem-solving. Finally, themes within the Social Contexts of Formal and Informal FEW-Nexus Education category emphasize the emergent nature of FEW-Nexus-based education, calling for attention to student diversity, needs of educators, and external factors in ongoing and future educational practices and research. Geoscience educators and educational researchers can use findings from this study to strengthen existing FEW-Nexus-based education efforts and/or identify entry points into this novel and rapidly expanding interdisciplinary community.

title: Providing Undergraduate Students with Research Experience Through Macroscopic Charcoal Analysis of Lake Sediments
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Bunbury, Joan [1]
affiliations: (1) Geography & Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin - La Crosse, La Crosse, Wisconsin, USA
abstract: A course on past environmental change was developed specifically to provide students with a course-based undergraduate research opportunity. Since spring 2017, more than 50 students have produced geophysical and geochemical data from a lake sediment core collected from southeastern Wisconsin. The broader goal of this project is to develop a paleoclimate record spanning the post-glacial period for the upper Midwest. In spring 2024 and spring 2026 course offerings, students were trained in the processing and identification of macroscopic charcoal from the sediment core for the purpose of developing a record of fire history from the region. Student-generated data of sediment organic and carbonate content and sediment particle sizes exist and complement the macroscopic charcoal record. Individual student work is assessed through feedback on a scientific paper during the semester, whereas group work is evaluated via the preparation and presentation of a poster at the university’s annual undergraduate research symposium. Assessment results, and the benefits and challenges associated with this course-based research opportunity will be presented as well as a preliminary paleoclimate record spanning the past 5,000 years.

title: Tandem Mass Spectrometry Approaches for Low-Level Actinide Analyses in Complex Matrices
session_title: U-series Disequilibrium Geochronology: Advances, Applications, and Emerging Frontiers
authors: French, Amanda D. [1], Hobbs, Kirby P. [2], Hilton, Connor D. [3], Douglas, Matthew [4], Metz, Lori A. [5]
affiliations: (1) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, USA
(2) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, USA
(3) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, USA
(4) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, USA
(5) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Washington, USA
abstract:
U-series measurements require analytical approaches that can resolve low-abundance actinides from complex spectral backgrounds while preserving sensitivity and throughput. This presentation highlights tandem mass spectrometry strategies for low-level actinide analyses using both quadrupole ICP-MS/MS and MC-ICP-MS/MS, with emphasis on applications relevant to U-series geochemistry. Low-abundance actinides carry valuable chronologic, forensic, and environmental information, but are often limited by isobaric/molecular interferences, abundance sensitivity, environmental backgrounds, and lengthy separations. Tandem mass spectrometry provides new opportunities to address these challenges through controlled gas-phase chemical reactions to remove multiple types of interferences.

This presentation will focus on the advantages and remaining challenges of applying MS/MS methods to low-level actinide measurements. Our team has investigated fundamental ion-molecule reaction behavior to guide method development and improve interference removal, matrix tolerance, and measurement efficiency. Recent work has demonstrated the utility of MS/MS approaches for analyses with minimal sample preparation, including U isotope measurements in complex matrices and 241 Am/ 241 Pu age dating without prior Am/Pu separation. As analyte concentrations decrease, instrumental backgrounds become increasingly important, particularly for MC-ICP-MS/MS measurements where high-precision isotope ratios are necessary. Recently published work has identified sources of these backgrounds and strategies to reduce the overall backgrounds. We are also extending MS/MS techniques toward combined Th/Pa/U measurements to evaluate whether gas-phase separations can reduce sample preparation requirements for future U-series applications. Together, these approaches demonstrate how tandem mass spectrometry can strengthen applied isotope systems relevant to U-series-adjacent geochronology, nuclear forensics, environmental tracing, and complex-matrix geochemistry.

title: In situ-produced cosmogenic 10Be reveals erosion patterns and topographic persistence of synclinal mountains in the southern Appalachians
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Huang, Xianmei [1], Granger, Darryl [2], Luo, Lan [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(3) Department of Physics and Astronomy, Purdue Rare Isotope Measurement Laboratory, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA
abstract:
The persistence of high relief in the tectonically quiescent Appalachian Mountains is commonly explained by Hack’s dynamic equilibrium model, in which hillslopes adjust across rocks of contrasting erodibility so that erosion balances river incision. In layered fold-thrust belts, however, structural geometry can impose spatially heterogeneous erosion and the growth of relief, particularly in synclines, where the synclinal core remains isolated from local base level.

We evaluate the distribution of erosion rates at Butt Mountain and Fork Ridge, two adjacent synclinal mountains in the Valley and Ridge province near the New River, Virginia. Previous studies constrain Pleistocene incision of the New River to ~30 m/Ma, providing a long-term base level lowering rate to which hillslope response can be compared.

We quantify millennial-scale erosion rates using in situ -produced cosmogenic 10 Be in both fine-grained quartz from shale/siltstone and sand-sized quartz from sandstone. Point denudation rates were derived from 23 soil samples and one bedrock sample distributed across ridge crests and mountain flanks, and basin-averaged erosion rates were inferred from stream sediment in 4 headwater basins. We also mapped the abundance of resistant caprock-derived boulders on hillslopes.

Point denudation rates range from ~3 to 32 m/Ma and show no relation to local slope angle, but instead track boulder cover. Caprock-upheld ridge tops and boulder-mantled flanks erode at ~3 to 10 m/Ma, whereas comparably steep slopes with sparse boulder cover erode two to three times faster. Basin-averaged rates are highly variable, ranging from ~14 to 58 m/Ma and increasing with basin steepness.

We interpret the steep, rapidly eroding basins as recording transient adjustment to increased New River incision in the Pleistocene. Most hillslopes that we sampled appear to be relict surfaces, eroding at rates governed more by caprock debris supply than by slope angle. The contrast among ridge-crest lowering, basin erosion, and base-level lowering is consistent with a long-term pattern of slow syncline erosion punctuated by localized stream dissection in the Pleistocene.

title: Terrestrial Photogrammetric Monitoring of Dinosaur Track Preservation, Morrison Formation, Dinosaur Ridge, Jefferson County, Colorado
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding (Posters)
authors: Atwater, Amy [1], Anderson, Donna S. [2], Morgan, Matthew [3], Fitzgerald, Francis S [4]
affiliations: (1) Friends of Dinosaur Ridge, Morrison, CO, USA
(2) Consultant, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Colorado Geological Survey, Golden, CO, USA
(4) Colorado Geologcial Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Lakewood, CO, USA
abstract:
The Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation takes its name from exposures at Dinosaur Ridge near Morrison, Jefferson County, Colorado, where the first dinosaur discoveries in the 1870s launched more than 150 years of paleontological investigation in Colorado and across western North America. On the west flank of Dinosaur Ridge, these type-area exposures also preserve dinosaur track surfaces protected within the Morrison Fossil Area National Natural Landmark since 1973 and visited by approximately 250,000 people annually. Preserving these track sites is a continual struggle against mechanical and chemical weathering. The outcrops are fully exposed to freeze-thaw cycling, runoff, root wedging, and gravitational failure. Although grain-scale weathering occurs gradually, episodic mass-wasting events pose the greatest threat because they can remove tracks entirely. A repeatable, quantitative monitoring framework provides a baseline to assess site degradation, detect change, and guide preservation efforts.

We apply survey-grade handheld terrestrial photogrammetry to two track-bearing Morrison Formation sites at Dinosaur Ridge, the Brontosaur Bulges and Raptor Tracks, to establish a low-cost, centimeter-scale weathering baseline using change mapping. Surveys were conducted using PIX4Dcatch on a LiDAR-equipped iPhone paired via Bluetooth with an Emlid Reach RX2 GNSS receiver under NTRIP corrections. Ground control points established with the Reach RX2 and recovered through automatic tag detection constrain each survey to centimeter-level accuracy in a common reference frame. Captures were repeated at approximately monthly intervals from December 2025 through August 2026, spanning a full seasonal cycle that included winter freeze-thaw. Datasets were processed in PIX4Dmatic into scaled dense point clouds, meshes, and orthomosaics, then compared between survey epochs using cloud-to-cloud and mesh-to-mesh differencing.

Sub-centimeter weathering remains below the resolution of the method, but block detachment, spalling, slumping, and other mass-wasting processes can be readily identified. We report the change time series, the empirical detection limit, and any surface loss exceeding it, treating a well-constrained null result as a meaningful baseline rather than a failed measurement.

This study establishes a repeatable monitoring framework that can be continued by Friends of Dinosaur Ridge and adapted to other vulnerable geoheritage sites. The resulting datasets provide quantitative information to inform future preservation planning and funding efforts. An accompanying ArcGIS StoryMap makes these models accessible to the public while expanding their educational and interpretive value.

title: Testing for Ecological Crowding in the Paleozoic Crinoid Fossil Record: A Metatree Approach
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Chupongstimun, Sapon [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geophysical Science, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA
abstract: Ecological crowding is one of the leading hypotheses for controls on diversification rates, wherein we expect that taxa with more similar ecomorphologies should be subject to lower taxonomic diversification rates. I test this pattern using a dataset of Paleozoic crinoids by looking at the associations between genera’s taxonomic rates with their distances in morphospace at the lineage-level. By comparing taxonomic diversification among lineages rather than among time bins, this approach allows for issues such as confounding temporal trends in rates or disparity to be circumvented. I also built a metatree of ~200 Paleozoic crinoids with sources from the literature, which is needed to test for the effects of crowding on origination. Simulations show that this analysis is quite insensitive to both incomplete stratigraphic ranges and phylogenies. Overall, there is support for ecological crowding, but only in the Carboniferous, suggesting that the crowding may only take effect when taxonomic diversity is high. Further work is needed to test for the mechanisms behind this, and whether they operate differently for origination and extinction.

title: Episodic and Incremental River Channel Dynamism Associated With In-Channel Wood
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Triantafillou, Shayla [1], Richardson, Owen [2], Clark, Noël [3], Sinning, Kelley [4], Blehm, Lindsey [5], Sellers, Ben [6], Knaggs, Luke [7], Wohl, Ellen E. [8]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, USA
(3) Department of Ecosystem and Conservation Sciences, University of Montana, Missoula, Montana, USA
(4) Department of Ecosystem and Conservation Sciences, University of Montana, Missoula, Montana, USA
(5) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(6) Covering Ground Mapping, Bellvue, Colorado, USA
(7) Department of Ecosystem Science and Sustainability, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(8) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,
abstract: Natural rivers are dynamic over space and time due to variations in water, sediment, and wood fluxes. In addition to the influences of water and sediment on river corridor dynamism, wood can be a first-order control on river form and process in forested regions. Wood can play a role in many elements of channel dynamism including island formation, meander migration and cutoff, secondary channel creation, and avulsion. However, the relationship between in-channel wood and magnitudes of channel dynamism is poorly understood. As airborne and satellite imagery has become more frequently collected, of higher quality, and more widely available, analysis of river dynamism across large areas has become possible at the decadal timescale. We use up to 20 years of aerial imagery from 7 sites across North America with relatively unaltered wood regimes to investigate the effects of in-channel large wood on channel dynamism. Channel dynamism was quantified as the change over time of i) sinuosity, ii) shoreline complexity, and iii) floodplain creation and destruction. Preliminary results suggest that there is an association between the area of wood accumulations present and the magnitude of change to river form; large wood accumulations were associated with dynamic channel and floodplain change. Additionally, we characterized two types of channel dynamism: episodic channel adjustment was associated with large wood accumulations whereas reaches with incremental adjustment primarily stored individual pieces of wood. These findings imply that wood accumulations can trigger high-magnitude changes in otherwise homogenous river systems.

title: Characterization of Uranium Mineralization within the Fluvial Miocene Oakville Sandstone, Southern Gulf Coastal Plain, Texas
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics
authors: Reed, Robert M. [1], Ambrose, William A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Economic Geology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Bureau of Economic Geology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
Roll-type uranium deposits are present in some of the Paleogene–Neogene fluvial sandstones of the Texas Gulf Coastal Plain, including the Miocene Oakville Sandstone from Live Oak County, Texas. In the study area (Brown and Felder mines), the Oakville Sandstone is fluvial in origin. Study samples consist in part of sandy bedload fluvial channel fill interbedded with thin mud layers that represent abandoned bar forms or intrachannel pond fill. Sandstone grain size is dominantly medium, with some beds reaching lower coarse-grained. Accessory features include sparse clay clasts that represent either ripped-up floodplain or intrachannel pond deposits. Oakville sandstones are poorly consolidated by clay cement. Exceptions are some layers which also contain moderate to pervasive calcite cement. Minor localized cements include pyrite and zeolite. Previous workers determined that Oakville sandstones consist primarily of litharenites and feldspathic litharenites. In the southern coastal plain, including Live Oak County, the dominant lithic component is volcanic rock fragments. Other less common sandstone grain types include recycled Cretaceous fossils and glauconite, and cherts. Color differences indicate that both oxidized (brown) and reduced (gray) sandstones are present in the study area.

Uranium mineralization is present within both sandstones and thin mud layers but is localized to limited parts of the section only. Several uranium-bearing minerals (i.e. autunite, calcurmolite, brannerite, umohoite, and uraninite) have been identified in sandstones using energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy on the scanning electron microscope. Uranium-bearing phases are typically micrometer scale in size or less. Uranium minerals are preferentially located in three places, associated with clay coats on sand grains, within clay clasts, or within volcanic rock fragments. For example, brannerite occurs primarily as a replacement of titanium-bearing phases in volcanic rock fragments. Uranium-bearing powellite occurs as a cement around some grains. Uranium species vary between samples, reflecting variation in localized chemical environment. This investigation has demonstrated that detailed microscale analysis helps to characterize the uranium-bearing phases of these sandstones.

title: Understanding the relative timing and style of orogenic gold systems along the northern margin of ancestral North America: A case study at the 3Aces prospect, Hyland Valley, SE Yukon, Canada
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part II)
authors: Chehowy, Kathryn [1], Frieman, Ben M. [2], Goldfarb, Richard J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(3) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract: The relative timing of orogenic gold deposits which developed during Jurassic-Cretaceous amalgamations along the margin of ancestral North America remain poorly constrained, particularly within the Intermontane regions of Yukon, Alaska, and British Columbia. To establish the timing of mineralization relative to tectonism in the southeastern Yukon, this study integrates mapping with statistical and kinematic analysis of subsurface and drill core data at the 3Aces prospect of the Hyland Valley. Investigations focused on the Spades and Hearts targets within the Central Core zone at 3Aces. This work identifies four quartz vein morphologies: planar veins, irregular stockworks, podiform to irregular quartz bodies, and fault-shear veins. Field observations yielded three fault groups; an older set of thrust faults, an intermediate set of strike-slip faults, and a late set of normal faults. The dominant set is the intermediate strike-slip faults. These are predominately steeply dipping and northwest-trending with dextral oblique kinematics, although a subordinate, conjugate set is also observed. These strike-slip faults crosscut mineralized quartz bodies and are interpreted to be related to the regionally extensive Upper Hyland fault. The earlier reverse faults and later normal faults record east-directed contraction and post-collisional extension, respectively. Gold mineralization is interpreted to have occurred during the contractional deformation, likely during a transition from shortening to translational kinematics. Drill core observations indicate low-grade mineralization (<1 ppm) is spatially associated with steep north- to northwest-trending and moderately southeast-dipping planar to podiform veins. In high-grade zones petrographic observations indicate that dendritic gold occurs along breccia clast margins within podiform quartz styles. Further, arsenopyrite is abundant in planar and shear-hosted veins and commonly displays brecciated textures. Regardless of quartz vein morphology, mineralization is sulfide poor, consisting predominately of pyrite and arsenopyrite with local pyrrhotite, galena, chalcopyrite, and sphalerite. Preliminary results suggest that high-grade gold was emplaced during a limited number of hydrothermal events during peak- to post-peak contraction, likely as part of a transition from shortening to translational kinematics along the Hyland Valley fault system. Continued strike-slip activity and later Paleogene extension complicates deposit-scale continuity and correlation among prospective zones along strike to the northwest and southeast. Ongoing work seeks to generate a revised model for orogenic gold mineralization for the Intermontane regions of southeast Yukon through integration of the surface, subsurface, and micro-textural observations.

title: Unsteady sediment deposition plays a major role in the weakening of the anaerobic methane oxidation filter in coastal sediments
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)
authors: Gomes, Maya L. [1], Baker, Isabel Rose [2], Hantsoo, Kalev [3], Fike, David A. [4], Lapham, Laura [5], Malkin, Sairah [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD,
(2) Earth, Marine, and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(3) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
(4) University of Washington, St. Louis, MO,
(5) Chesapeake Biological Laboratory, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, Solomons, MD, USA
(6) Horn Point Laboratory, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, Cambridge, MD, USA
abstract: While it can be tempting to assume that stratigraphic geochemical variations record secular changes in seawater conditions, it is well known that changes in depositional environments can also drive variations in geochemical parameters without any major change in the marine realm. This does not mean that these geochemical records are not useful, just that they are telling a different story. We present geomicrobiological data from a modern setting of enhanced organic matter burial – The Chesapeake Bay – where eutrophication and land-use change have led to increased anoxia and sedimentation rates. Deposition of 34 S-enriched pyrite at the sulfate methane transition zone occurs at two sites close to the predominant source of terrestrial material. Methane is effectively oxidized aerobically with sulfate at the site with more terrestrial organic matter and less sulfate. At the site with more sulfate and planktonic organic matter, demand for sulfate for organoclastic sulfate reduction reduces the efficiency of anaerobic methane oxidation coupled to sulfate reduction. Other, less common pathways of anaerobic methane oxidation occur at the site, but they cannot keep up with methane production. The ingrowth of 34 S-enriched pyrite at the sulfate methane transition zone is similar between sites and occurs tens of centimeters below where sediment is being deposited today. While it may not be possible to discern if methane oxidation was efficient at ancient sulfate methane transition zones, this work documents that elevated anoxia and sedimentation rates can result in pyrite sulfur isotope values similar to (or perhaps exceeding) seawater sulfate sulfur isotope values.

title: Do basins have memory? Proterozoic inheritance and Caledonian evolution of the Baltic Basin
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Plink-Bjorklund, Piret [1], Bjorklund, Lennart [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy & School of Earth, Space and Planets, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden
abstract:
The Baltic Basin is a Phanerozoic pericratonic basin commonly interpreted as a non-orogenic epicontinental sea. Yet its stratigraphic record indicates pronounced changes commonly considered linked to tectonic rejuvenation. We integrate sedimentological, mineralogical, stratigraphic, provenance and structural data to evaluate the basin’s origin and Caledonian evolution.

We show that the Phanerozoic basin geometry corresponds to the distribution of Paleoproterozoic to early Mesoproterozoic rapakivi granite–anorthosite complexes within Paleoproterozoic Svecofennian amphibolite- and granulite-facies belts. This relationship suggests that inherited crustal heterogeneity and lithospheric mantle rejuvenation localized later subsidence and deformation. Phanerozoic structures record repeated intrabasinal uplift and subsidence under northwest–southeast compression with a strike-slip component. The principal deformation episodes coincide with accretion and subsequent collapse of the Scandinavian Caledonides.

The carbonate-dominated Ordovician–Silurian marine succession is overlain by thick, coarse-grained Devonian estuarine to deltaic siliciclastics, suggesting reorganization of the basin and its drainage system. Facies distributions and paleocurrent indicators show that the voluminous Devonian and the episodic Ordovician–Silurian fine siliciclastic sediment were derived from the northwest. Sediment composition shifted from Proterozoic basement-derived material toward increasingly mature sediment containing up to 99.9% quartz. These changes together with structural evidence suggest initial erosion of basement exposed on the forebulge of the Scandinavian Caledonian foreland basin, followed by cannibalization of foreland-basin deposits into a back-bulge depozone. Influence from the southwestern Avalonia–Baltica collision margin is limited to volcanic-ash input and southern Baltic Basin depth.

The Baltic Basin thus retained a long-lived tectonic memory – its geometry and deformation were conditioned by Proterozoic lithospheric grain repeatedly reactivated by far-field stresses from the Scandinavian Caledonides. This work suggests that crustal inheritance and far-field orogenic stresses should be considered in other nominally non-orogenic basins.

title: Physical Characterization of Ejecta from Impacts into Iron Meteorites
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: Brooks, Chandler Mathew Zane [1], Alexander, Amanda [2], Marchi, Simone [3], Elkins-Tanton, Lindy [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Astrophysical and Planetary Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, Boulder, CO,
(2) Department of Space Studies, Solar System Science & Exploration, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
(3) Department of Space Studies, Solar System Science & Exploration, Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
(4) Space Sciences Laboratory, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, California, USA
abstract:
Impacts onto astronomical bodies, such as asteroid (16) Psyche, excavate and ballistically eject material during the impact process. This material is then attracted back to the body through gravity. As the fragmented particles settle around the impact crater, an ejecta blanket is formed. The fragment structure of ejecta on metal-rich bodies is not well understood, nor are their degradation timescales.

Here, we present a study of metallic ejecta formed by, and collected following, hypervelocity impact experiments into iron meteorite samples. We performed X-ray computed tomography followed by analytical segmentation and separation with the Dragonfly image processing software [1] on collected ejecta fragments from three iron meteorite types: Campo del Cielo [2], Seymchan [3], and Gebel Kamil [4]. From these data, we derive quantitative physical characteristics of the ejecta fragments for each experiment (e.g., fragment size, volume, sphericity).

We find that the collected ejecta exhibit sharp, shrapnel-like texture that have low sphericity. Fragments range in size from several mm to micron sized. Fragment size distribution is variable among the meteorite types for nearly identical impact conditions. Ejecta formation therefore is likely dependent on chemical composition and crystal structure. Thus, fragment sizes in ejecta and regolith may be indicative of composition. The Psyche mission is expected to arrive at asteroid (16) Psyche in 2029 [5], and these data may help interpret ejecta blankets and regolith on metal-rich planetary surfaces.

title: Sedimentary Archives Reveal 3,200 Years of Tsunami History in the Central Aleutian Islands
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Blanco, Chris [1], Hawkes, Andrea [2], Klotsko, Shannon [3], Donnelly, Jeffrey [4], Maio, Chris [5], McKeon, Kelly [6], Bogardus, Reyce [7], LaClair, Chris [8]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Ocean Science, University of North Carolina, Wilmington, North Carolina, USA
(2) Earth and Ocean Science, University of North Carolina, Wilmington, North Carolina, USA
(3) Earth and Ocean Science, University of North Carolina, Wilmington, North Carolina, USA
(4) Seafloor Samples Laboratory, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Massachusetts, USA
(5) Department of Geosciences, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, Alaska, USA

abstract: The recurrence, magnitude, and regional extent of coastal hazards along the central Aleutian Islands remain poorly constrained because instrumental observations span only the past century, and few sedimentary archives preserve longer-term records. Consequently, the long-term hazard history of the region remains unknown, limiting our understanding of earthquake and tsunami recurrence. To address this gap, we evaluate whether south-facing sill-bounded coastal basins within the Andreanof Islands preserve reliable sedimentary records of coastal hazards and whether tsunami deposits can be distinguished from those generated by storms or volcanic eruptions. Sediment cores were analyzed using a multi-proxy framework including grain-size distributions, organic matter, X-radiographic imagery, lithostratigraphy, radionuclide dating ( 210 Pb and 137 Cs), hydrodynamic analyses of in situ wave observations, and comparisons with modern instrumental and historical records. Collectively, the absence of preserved modern storm deposits despite frequent storms in the region, substantial attenuation of storm-wave energy from outer to inner basins, and correlation of coarser-grained event deposits with historically documented earthquake-generated tsunamis indicate that this basin preferentially records only the largest wave events, most likely associated with near-field tsunamis. We identify twelve event deposits most likely representing tsunami inundation from a sediment record from Quail Bay, Kagalaska, yielding a mean tsunami recurrence interval of ~263 years (95% credible interval: 120–485 years). These findings establish central Aleutian coastal basins as robust archives of coastal hazards and provide the first multi-millennial tsunami reconstruction from the central Aleutian Islands, offering new constraints on the recurrence and regional behavior of great earthquakes along the Alaska–Aleutian megathrust.

title: Magnetic Properties Identify Heavy Metal Contamination at Pig’s Eye Park, St. Paul, Minnesota
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Regan, Angelina Michaela [1], Pinto, Stella Grace [2], Feinberg, Joshua M. [3], Snell-Rood, Emilie C. [4], Jelinski, Nicolas A. [5], Penn, R. Lee [6]
affiliations: (1) Manchester, CA, USA

(3) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(4) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(5) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

abstract: Methods for characterizing heavy metal contamination in soils are often costly and time-consuming, which impedes efficient widespread monitoring. The objective of this study is to evaluate the use of magnetic susceptibility as a proxy for heavy metal content to assess the extent of contamination at our study area: Pig’s Eye Park in St. Paul, Minnesota. Previous studies have attempted to use magnetic susceptibility as an environmental monitoring tool, but ambiguities can arise if various inputs are not well understood beforehand. If this method can be calibrated to the needs of individual sites, then it can reduce costs and sample processing time and be a less destructive method for future contamination studies. Pig’s Eye Park is located on the floodplain of the Mississippi River, where it served for decades as a general landfill for the city of Saint Paul and a repository for sludge ash from the adjacent wastewater treatment plant. Consequently, the soils and groundwater at the site show high concentrations of heavy metals and other pollutants. Initial remediation efforts in the early 2000s involved the removal of the most hazardous materials and the installation of a clay cap to prevent subsequent contaminant transport, but widespread contamination still remains and site managers do not have a clear sense of where lead (Pb)-rich sludge ash is located. We collected 384 geospatially-tagged soil samples across the site and measured magnetic susceptibility at two different frequencies (300 A/m at 465 Hz and 4650 Hz). Each sample’s elemental composition was also measured using a portable X-Ray Fluorescence spectrometer. Comparing our in-phase susceptibility values against elemental concentrations revealed strong positive correlations (Spearman coefficients >0.7) with Pb, copper (Cu), tungsten (W), and zinc (Zn). There is also a strong positive correlation (Spearman >0.7) between the absolute frequency dependence and these elements, suggesting that finer grain sizes carry higher heavy metal concentrations. Electron microscopy reveals that this relationship is linked directly to the occurrence of wastewater sludge ash. Thus, handheld magnetic susceptibility meters can rapidly map the location of persistent heavy metal contamination at this site. With further validation of this method for heavy metal detection, this approach could become a standard tool for quick and cost-efficient contamination assessment at similarly impacted sites.

title: Developing a Domain-Specific Large Language Model (LLM) for the Spanish Peaks in South-central Colorado
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Penn, Brian S [1]
affiliations: (1) Divide, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Traditionally, the path for a MS and PhD dissertation is to publish a few articles. Some make it to the internet; most don't. The author moves on and the papers are forgotten except by a few specialists in the field.

In 1994, the website, The Igneous Petrology of the Spanish Peaks, came online during the infancy of the internet. Based on today's standards, it was crudely constructed using HTML on a Silicon Graphics workstation. At the time, it was unusual because it presented all the information from my eponymously named PhD dissertation which included sample locations, geochemistry, etc. The website is a repository for the data collected from the dissertation.

Technology has evolved. While a portion of the original dissertation involved using Neural Networks to map dikes in satellite imagery, nothing prognosticated the direction machine learning would take or the role it would play today. Currently, we are in the midst of a revolution of Large Language Models (LLMs). The first of which was ChatGPT from OpenAI. Now there are hundreds of such models.

These models are quite dynamic, providing all sorts of information. Some of it is purely made up because of the completion problem, i.e., very few models respond with IDK, so they just make stuff up. Every query has to answered. Part of the problem is that when an LLM is queried, it has to go out and collect information. It starts from zero, every time. Several people have recognized this limitation, one of the first was Andrej Karpathy. He suggested something different. What if an LLM created a wiki previously discovered and/or synthesized that could be referred to later instead of recreating that information?

Taking this idea, a Spanish Peaks wiki was created. All the information about the Spanish Peaks was fed into CoPilot (another LLM) including the dissertation, abstracts, published articles, excel files, etc. These data were organized as a Karpathy Wiki. Since there are other models available, e.g., GeminiLM, and Perplexity, they were fed the same information. The amalgamated information is available for interactive queries from each of these models by the author. In this way, the information on the Spanish Peaks is preserved in context. This can provide an easily accessible repository for one's entire knowledge on a topic.

title: Simulation of Groundwater Flow in the Moab-Spanish Valley, Utah
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Taylor, Brooklyn [1], Lachmar, Thomas [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Water, Earth and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(2) Department of Water, Earth and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
abstract:
Groundwater is a critical resource in the Moab–Spanish Valley, a northwest-southeast trending valley in southeastern Utah. Continued population growth and projected climate change raise concerns regarding the long-term sustainability of groundwater resources in the valley.

A three-dimensional, numerical, groundwater-flow model was developed in MODFLOW-USG to evaluate groundwater availability, and to assess potential future impacts of climate change and increased groundwater demand. The model consists of seven layers. Three of the upper four layers represent the aquifers: the unconfined valley fill aquifer (VFA), the underlying unconfined Glen Canyon Group aquifer (GCGA), and the confined deep Glen Canyon Group aquifer (DGCGA). The three lowest layers represent relatively impermeable rocks, as does the third layer, which represents a confining unit between the GCGA and the DGCGA.

The model was calibrated under both steady-state and transient conditions. Steady-state calibration was performed to represent hydrologic conditions during November, and transient calibration simulated groundwater conditions from January 2022 through April 2024. The final values for the mean residual error (MR), mean absolute error (MAR), and root mean square residual error (RMSR) were -1.05 and -0.07 m, 8.68 and 9.31 m, and 20.92 and 16.23 m, respectively, for the steady-state and transient calibrations. Residual heads were less than 4 m each for 16 of the 20 wells used to calibrate the steady-state model. Sensitivity analysis identified recharge, evapotranspiration and horizontal hydraulic conductivity as the most influential model parameters.

Following calibration, nine forecasting scenarios were developed to evaluate varying levels of climate change impacts and groundwater pumping over a six-year time period from 2022 to 2028. The model results suggest that future groundwater availability in the Moab–Spanish Valley will be strongly influenced by climate change, particularly within the VFA, but that increased groundwater demand will have a lesser effect, especially on the DGCGA, which is the aquifer producing the most groundwater from wells in the valley. The calibrated model provides a useful tool for evaluating future management strategies and supports long-term groundwater planning.

title: Zircon Element Zoning Reveals Complex Pluton Crystallization Processes During the Assembly of the Tuolumne Intrusive Suite: Insights from Laser-Ablation Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part II)
authors: Kylander-Clark, Andrew [1], Johnston, Scott [2], Adamson, Morgan [3], Cottle, John [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo, CA, USA
(3) Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(4) Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
abstract:
In this study, we use element images produced by laser-ablation time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ToFMS) to complement an existing database of cathodoluminescence images and >6000 spot analyses of zircon from the Tuolumne Intrusive Suite, Sierra Nevada to better understand the role of zircon crystallization during pluton emplacement processes.

Existing 25-micron spot data from cores and rims from individual units within the suite show several characteristics. First, the zircon display a broad trend from low Th/Yb and Yb/Dy in the oldest, outermost unit to moderate values in the middle unit, to high Th/Yb and Yb/Dy in the younger, inner unit; this regional pattern represents differences in bulk chemistry and/or co-crystallizing phases between units. Second, low-Yb/Dy, Th/Yb cores in zircon from younger units indicate incorporation of antecrystic cores from older units, and autocrystic ‘cores’ differ from ‘rims’ in that they are lower in U/Yb and U/Th. Finally, few rim analyses indicate late-stage growth of high-Hf, high-U/Yb, low-Th zircon.

After spot analyses, LA-ToF 5-µm-pixel-resolution maps were made using an ESL ImageGeo laser and Nu Instruments Vitesse ToF-ICPMS at to add additional textural insight. Opposed to maps made with other microprobe techniques, LA-ToFMS mapping produces high-resolution maps of 10s of elements quickly; ~2-mm square maps (50+ coarse zircons) were made in ~2 hrs. Several discoveries illustrate the utility of fine-scale chemical analysis of zircon:

1) Although CL primarily shows oscillatory zoning, zircon are sector zoned in element ratios such as U/Yb and U/Th (highest in pyramid tips), indicating different distribution coefficients for different growth directions. The observed difference between ‘core’ and ‘rim’ spot analyses of autocrystic grains is not a trend in crystallization history but a result of the difference in distribution coefficients between zircon crystal faces and tips.

2) In all samples, many zircons have thin (<10 µm) high-Hf, high-U/Yb, low-Th/U rims, similar to hydrothermal zircon and zircon in leucocratic bodies. This suggests that final stages of crystallization occurred during a late-stage pulse of, and/or change in, magma/fluid chemistry.

3) Zircon inclusion type and proportion vary by sample, indicating which minerals crystallized prior to zircon. Furthermore, chemical halos around inclusions distinguish local changes in chemistry and/or diffusion of elements into zircon from the hosted inclusion.

title: Calibrating the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary: New U-Pb Constraints from Alberta, Canada

authors: Green, Theodore [1], Grasby, Stephen E. [2], Apen, Francisco [3], Eddy, Michael P. [4], Ickert, Ryan [5], Schoene, Blair [6]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(2) Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, AB, Canada
(3) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(4) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

abstract: The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary (KPB) has been extensively studied, with particular emphasis on the timing and relative contributions of the Chicxulub asteroid impact and the Deccan Traps large igneous province to this most recent mass extinction interval. However, the age of this crucial boundary is still debated. Ar-Ar geochronology, U-Pb geochronology, and astrochronology have been applied to this boundary in sections around the world and have resulted in suggested KPB ages ranging from 65.8 to 66.1 Ma. While there was more consensus on a 66.0 Ma age for the KPB in GTS 2020, recent astronomical tunings and some ages of the Ar-Ar Fish Canyon sanidine standard produce KPB ages of 65.8 Ma, which are offset from U-Pb ages by ~200 kyrs and reopen questions about discrepancies between different chronometers at this boundary. A recent Bayesian calculation of the K decay constants and a correspondingly recalculated Fish Canyon sanidine age result in a KPB age that more closely matches existing U-Pb constraints but further emphasizes the need for agreement on standard ages and intercalibration between chronometers. High-precision geochronology of additional KPB sections is necessary to better constrain this interval for comparison to the timing of potential extinction causes like the Deccan Traps large igneous province and the Chicxulub impactor as well as for the intercalibration of Ar-Ar, U-Pb, and astronomical chronometers that will be important for future updates to the Geologic Time Scale. Here we present zircon U-Pb TIMS dates from a series of ash beds above and a sandstone below an iridium anomaly marking the KPB in a core from the Luscar Coal Valley in central Alberta, Canada. Our new data are consistent with an age of >66 Ma for the KPB, which matches U-Pb geochronology from the Denver Basin and invites additional discussion on how to approach the offset between these ages and those from recent Ar-Ar geochronology and cyclostratigraphy. These dates also provide constraints on the location of the KPB in the Alberta region and can be used to correlate biostratigraphic, magnetostratigraphic, and climatic records of this extinction interval across this region and with other continental and marine sections globally.

title: Modern Calibration of Bulk Carbonate Stable Isotopes Along a Hydroclimatic Gradient in Loess-Derived Soils of Tajikistan (Central Asia)

authors: Khormali, Farhad [1], Tabor, Neil J [2], Robbins, John A [3], Valizadeh Navi, Saman [4], Schneider, Ramona [5], Buylaert , Jan-Pieter [6]
affiliations: (1) Roy M. Huffington Department of Earth Sciences, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, TX, USA
(2) Roy M. Huffington Department of Earth Sciences, Southern Methodist University, Dallas, TX, USA

abstract:
Pedogenic carbonate is widely used to reconstruct Quaternary terrestrial environments, yet the climatic significance of bulk soil carbonate remains uncertain because it commonly contains mixtures of inherited lithogenic and pedogenic carbonate. Modern calibrations from Central Asia remain limited. We hypothesize that increasing soil water availability progressively increases the pedogenic contribution to the bulk carbonate pool, thereby improving the utility of bulk soil carbonate as a hydroclimatic proxy.

Stable carbon (δ¹³Cbc) and oxygen (δ¹⁸Obc) isotopes of 54 bulk carbonate samples, together with 54 soil organic carbon isotopes (δ¹³Coc) samples, were analyzed from nine modern loess-derived soil profiles spanning a hydroclimatic gradient in Tajikistan (<200–1000 mm mean annual precipitation, 4–16°C mean annual temperature, and elevations of approximately 500–2600 m). The soils represent Aridisols, Entisols, Mollisols, Inceptisols, and Alfisols developed under C3 vegetation.

Profile-mean δ¹³Cbc values range from ~0‰ to −8.5‰ VPDB, whereas δ¹⁸Obc values range from ~−5.5‰ to −14‰ VPDB. δ¹³Cbc and δ¹⁸Obc values are strongly correlated with Aridity Index (P/PET), a measure of soil water availability (R² = 0.89 and 0.85, respectively), whereas δ¹³Cbc values decrease logarithmically with elevation (R² = 0.90). Carbonate δ¹⁸Obc also decreases logarithmically with elevation (R² = 0.80), from ~−5.5‰ at 500 m to ~−14‰ at 2600 m, equivalent to an observed isotopic depletion of approximately 4.0‰ km⁻¹. The magnitude of this depletion exceeds that expected from equilibrium calcite–water fractionation alone, indicating that progressive Rayleigh distillation of precipitation during orographic uplift, together with increasing snowfall contributions at higher elevations, exerts the primary control on carbonate δ¹⁸O. Both δ¹³Cbc and δ¹³Coc values are enriched with depth, whereas profile-mean δ¹³Cbc values become progressively depleted with increasing soil water availability, consistent with biologically derived pedogenic carbonate becoming the dominant component of the bulk carbonate pool.

These results demonstrate that bulk soil carbonate preserves complementary hydroclimatic information: δ¹³C primarily records increasing pedogenic carbonate contributions associated with greater soil water availability, whereas δ¹⁸O records the isotopic evolution of meteoric water along the elevational gradient. Together, these observations establish a modern calibration and process-based framework for interpreting Quaternary loess–paleosol records across Central Asia, extending our previous findings from Iranian loess-derived soils and improving reconstructions of paleopedogenesis, hydroclimate, and terrestrial environments.
