title: AMERICA’S OLDEST SHOW CAVE REIMAGINED: CELEBRATING 220 YEARS OF CAVE MAPPING OF GRAND CAVERNS
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: García, Ángel A. [1], Petrova, Maria D. [2], Wahlquist, Scott [3], Young, Mia Grace [4], Shank, Austin [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA

abstract:
Caves are significant geologic resources that support geotourism and local economies worldwide, generating billions of dollars annually through recreation while also advancing education, scientific inquiry, and community engagement. In the continental United States, Grand Caverns occupies a unique place in the history of cave tourism. Originally known as Weyer’s Cave, it began operating as a tourist attraction in 1806 and remains the oldest continuously operating show cave in the nation. Beyond its historical significance, Grand Caverns has served as a natural laboratory for karst and speleological research for more than a century, attracting generations of scientists, surveyors, and visitors.

One of the cave’s most remarkable yet often overlooked resources is its cartographic legacy. Mapping efforts began more than 220 years ago and document changing perceptions of the cave through the evolution of surveying techniques, from early compass-and-tape methods to modern digital technologies. Historical maps not only record advances in scientific practice but also reveal how explorers and researchers interpreted and represented subterranean landscapes through time. As surveying methods evolved, each generation of maps provided new insights into the cave’s geometry, passage relationships, and notable geological features.

This presentation reviews the history of mapping at Grand Caverns and highlights the evolution of cave-surveying methods over more than two centuries. We present the results of a newly completed map that uses LiDAR-SLAM to construct high-definition point clouds along with historical records, providing the most comprehensive spatial representation of the cave to date. The new map refines our understanding of passage morphology and spatial relationships while revealing previously unrecognized details within a cave long considered well documented.

title: High-Throughput Inclusion Analysis in Accessory Minerals by LA-ICP-TOF-MS
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems
authors: Cottle, John [1], Adamson, Morgan [2], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [3]
affiliations: (1) University of California, Santa Barbara, CA,
(2) University of California, Santa Barbara, Goleta, CA,
(3) UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA,
abstract: Minerals including zircon, titanite, apatite, monazite, and garnet are key petrochronology targets, yet the mineral and melt inclusions they host remain an underexploited record of the environment in which their host crystallized. Inclusions potentially preserve useful information on melt composition, coexisting phase assemblages, volatile budgets, and the evolving trace element reservoir of a magmatic or metamorphic system through time. Characterization anf statistical analysis of inclusion populations is currently limited by the throughput of conventional electron- and ion-beam methods, which permit analysis of only a few inclusions per sample and often struggle to resolve inclusions at the micron scale. Here, we apply high-speed laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOF-MS) to rapidly characterize large numbers of inclusions in accessory minerals at micron-scale resolution. Quasi-simultaneous acquisition of the full elemental mass spectrum at every pixel, with semi-automated processing and visualization, enables inclusions to be identified, classified, and compositionally characterized without prior knowledge of their location or mineralogy, while ultrafast washout and acquisition rates allow hundreds of inclusions to be surveyed in a fraction of the time required by traditional approaches. Drawing on igneous and metamorphic examples, we demonstrate how inclusion populations record the compositional evolution of the host system and constrain trace element partitioning and phase saturation. Combining large inclusion datasets with the petrochronologic context of the host affords a means to reconstruct the geochemical development of magmatic and metamorphic rocks, thereby improving our understanding of magmatic differentiation, metamorphic reaction history, and the trace element budget of the continental crust.

title: The Ghost in the Granite: Tracing a Mafic, Yavapai-Inherited Mantle Source Through 1.4 Ga Magmatism in Colorado and Wyoming

authors: Gilmer, Amy K. [1], Hillenbrand, Ian W [2], Thompson, Ren A. [3], Premo, Wayne R. [4], Thompson, Jay M. [5], Lowers, Heather [6]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA

abstract: Voluminous ferroan ca. 1.4 Ga granitic magmatism across the southwestern USA is commonly interpreted to reflect basaltic underplating, differentiation, and partial melting of the lower crust, yet direct evidence for mafic magmatism is scarce. We show that coeval mafic to intermediate magmatism, though individually minor in volume, is pervasive across the region. We synthesize new and compiled geologic mapping, U-Pb geochronology, whole-rock major- and trace-element geochemistry, and Nd-Sr-Pb isotopes for mafic dikes, stocks, and plutons across more than 30 localities in Colorado and Wyoming. Regionally consistent arc-like trace element patterns including Nb-Ta depletion, elevated Th/Yb and Pb/Ce, and steep REE patterns suggest derivation from garnet-bearing, subduction-metasomatized lithospheric mantle. Nd model ages (1.7–2.1 Ga) and a ca. 1.4 Ga Pb-Pb isochron intersecting model evolution curves at ca. 1.8 Ga indicate that the mantle source was metasomatized during Paleoproterozoic Yavapai subduction. Continuous major element trends with ferroan granitoids, together with isotopic modeling, support these mafic magmas as viable parental melts via fractional crystallization and assimilation of Paleoproterozoic crust. Within the Gunnison block, ultrapotassic alkaline and lamprophyre magmatism is enriched in Ba, Sr, and REEs (2–10x average continental crust) potentially reflecting heterogeneous mantle metasomatism beneath this more isotopically evolved, REE-fertile lithospheric domain. Together, these results indicate that Picuris orogeny-related tectonism triggered delamination and melting of previously subduction-metasomatized lithospheric mantle rather than a mantle plume. More broadly, these results suggest that arc-like geochemical signatures in Cenozoic magmatism may reflect inherited Proterozoic metasomatism rather than requiring Laramide flat-slab subduction.

title: Stable Diversity amidst Population Collapse in Pelagic Fish Communities across Cretaceous Ocean Anoxic Event 2
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Clemente, Jean Nikolas Reyes [1], Norris, Eun-Jae Miyon [2], Sibert, Elizabeth C. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA, USA; Earth, Planetary, and Atmospheric Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) College of the Atlantic, Bar Harbor, ME, USA

abstract:
Cretaceous black shales chronicle episodic ocean deoxygenation in the extreme greenhouse world of the Mesozoic. The largest of these Ocean Anoxic Events, OAE2 (Cenomanian-Turonian boundary event, ~94 Ma), dramatically reorganized marine ecosystems, driving turnover and notable extinctions in communities ranging from microscopic plankton to large predatory reptiles. Yet, the evolutionary dynamics of middle-trophic communities like fishes—which critically mediate energy transfer between such producers and predators— remain uncertain.

This enigmatic history stems largely from a sparse whole-body fossil record for fishes, despite their ecological dominance in modern open-ocean ecosystems. Recent works, however, highlights how certain disarticulated fish microfossils (“ichthyoliths”) like fish teeth offer insight into the evolutionary response of fish communities writ large to extreme marine perturbations. Because they are highly abundant and taphonomically resistant in sediments, ichthyoliths can provide a uniquely high-resolution, community-scale view of pelagic ecosystem evolution.

Here, we present a ~3.5-million-year record of late-Cenomanian/early-Turonian ichthyoliths from the proto-North Atlantic (IODP Site U1407) to reconstruct changes in pelagic fish abundance, diversity, and turnover across OAE2. Ichthyholith accumulation rates, interpreted as a first-order proxy for fish abundance, abruptly decreased near the onset of anoxia and remained suppressed for at least ~2 million years after the recovery of oxic conditions. Nonetheless, despite this near five-fold decline in production, the morphological diversity (richness and evenness) of post-OAE2 teeth remained nearly identical to pre-OAE2 assemblages, with both intervals sharing similar “core” communities. Thus, the ichthyolith record of the proto-North Atlantic demonstrates a remarkably stable fish community in spite of its population crash in OAE2, revealing resilience in the function and architecture of pelagic ecosystems amid severe oceanographic change. Ongoing work aims to verify the spatial and temporal extent of these trends, and to constrain the cause(s) of the apparent permanency of reduced populations in spite of the biogeochemical recovery of Cretaceous oceans.

title: Pleistocene fan aggradation, incision, and landscape resetting constrained by luminescence and 10Be exposure dating of transverse fan and terrace surfaces, Zereg basin, western Mongolia
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Vaughan, Nora [1], Pazzaglia, Frank J. [2], Ganbold, Baatarsuren [3], Corbett, Lee B. [4], Bierman, Paul [5]
affiliations: (1) Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA,

abstract: Mongolian Altai orogenesis intensified Central Asian aridification since the Pliocene and more broadly controls Northern Hemisphere climate; yet the Quaternary history of Altai landscape evolution remains poorly constrained. The late Pleistocene deformation record is encoded in six mapped fan and terrace surfaces (Qf1–Qf6) of the Zereg Basin, western Mongolia. Here, we develop an age model using relative soil development, luminescence dating (feldspar, n=3), cosmogenic 10 Be exposure dating (quartz, n=4), and drone-based structure-from-motion topography. Lateral propagation of thrust faults from a transpressional bend in the right-lateral Har-Us-Nuur fault drives uplift and folding of a northeast-verging, thrust-cored hanging-wall anticline. Fan-surface profiles record progressive but unsteady deformation, with tread gradients of ~44–98 m/km that generally increase with relative surface age. Soils on Qf6 through Qf4 exhibit expected trends of increases in thickness, clay accumulation, rubification, and pedogenic carbonate. Luminescence ages of the underlying alluvium also increase with stratigraphic age, from 84.1±9.4 ka to 73.1±7.8 ka to 55.7±6.3ka on Qf4 through Qf6, respectively. These ages indicate repeated fan aggradation and terrace formation at approximately 10–20ka intervals during MIS 5a–4. In contrast, the stratigraphically older Qf1-Qf3 surfaces have progressively less-developed soils, and 10 Be boulder exposure ages do not increase with relative surface age. The Qf4 10 Be age of 94±1.6ka overlaps within the uncertainty range of the luminescence age of its underlying alluvium, whereas 10 Be ages of 75±1.7ka and 86±1.8ka on Qf2 and Qf3 are reversed relative to stratigraphic order. Collectively these results indicate a period of Qf4 through Qf6 fan aggradation and surface stability during MIS 5a-4 that also reworked the surfaces of the older, perhaps middle Pleistocene fan deposit complex that host the Qf3 through Qf1 surfaces. Qf4 may represent a local surface preservation threshold determined by MIS 5–4 paleoclimate, and/or an autogenic response to declining infiltration and enhanced runoff over increasingly mature argillic and calcic horizons. This chronology extends previous work building paleomagnetic, biostratigraphic, and cyclostratigraphic age models for the underlying Mio-Pliocene synorogenic growth strata. Assuming the Zereg piedmont is representative of regional Altai deformation, the combined record indicates shortening across this part of the Great Lakes Depression at approximately 1.7 mm/yr and provides a paleoseismic framework relevant to seismic-hazard assessment and infrastructure development in western Mongolia.

title: Resolving groundwater storage changes using inverse modeling of geodetic datasets in two aquifer settings
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: Carlson, Grace [1], Werth, Susanna [2], Shirzaei, Manoochehr [3], Girotto, Manuela [4], Massari, Christian [5], Dionigi, Marco [6], Modanesi, Sara [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(4) University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA
(5) National Research Council (CNR), Institute of Geosciences (GEO), Perugia, Italy
(6) National Research Council (CNR), Institute of Geosciences (GEO), Perugia, Italy
(7) Institute of Geosciences (GEO), National Research Council (CNR), Perugia, Italy
abstract: Groundwater resources are increasingly essential to meeting global freshwater needs. However, accurate, high-resolution estimates of groundwater storage change remain challenging due to sparse in-situ data, hydrological models that do not accurately or fully account for all subsurface processes, and coarse-resolution satellite observations, such as those from the GRACE missions. Both total water and groundwater storage induce land surface motion and dense observations of surface deformation, recorded by networks of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) displacements and high-resolution multi-temporal Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), may offer a potential pathway to monitor groundwater at spatial scales that sparse wells and coarse satellite gravimetry cannot resolve on their own. In confined-to-semi-confined sedimentary aquifers, groundwater decline induces stress on the sedimentary matrix, causing pore-space closure and surface subsidence. Water mass change, on the other hand, induces elastic loading and unloading, generating measurable land surface uplift (subsidence) associated with mass loss (gain). In this talk, I demonstrate a multi-sensor inverse model that integrates these two measured components of surface deformation, elastic loading of water mass and poroelastic aquifer deformation, to solve for water and groundwater storage change during the 2019 to 2021 drought in California, and particularly over the intensively mined Central Valley aquifer system. Results show that this approach recovered groundwater storage changes at a finer resolution than gravimetry alone and agreed well with available water-level records. I then turn to ongoing work in the Euro-Mediterranean. There, I take a related approach, drawing on geodetic and gravimetric observations to estimate changes in groundwater storage. Early results suggest that observations of this kind can constrain storage change across regions with different network density, aquifer structure, and climate forcing. Together, these cases demonstrate how integrating geodetic surface observations with remote sensing and geophysical models can advance operational groundwater monitoring and support water management.

title: A Database-Driven Approach to Synthesizing Subsurface Geologic Data
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Johnstone, Sam Adam [1], Smout, Brooklyn [2], Sweetkind, Donald S. [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(2) United States Geological Survey,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract:
In 2020, Congress mandated the USGS “bring together ... 2D and 3D [geologic] information” produced by state and federal geologists to better serve this data to stakeholders across the country. Traditionally, geologic information has been “brought together” using two strategies; first is the cataloging of stand-alone products, in physical and/or digital catalogs, and second is new compilations, in which geologist(s) interpret detailed maps into new, often generalized maps. When it comes to “2D” information, the advent of digital geologic maps gave birth to a third strategy, the “multi-map”. Multi-maps unite individual maps into a single dataset without altering the interpretations of primary sources, often serving this content over the web. Multi-maps represent a compromise: these datasets allow users to access the information from individual maps across publication boundaries but require those users accept a “cost” that there are often inconsistencies across these boundaries. In the US, the State Geologic Map Compilation, Macrostrat, and the Cooperative National Geologic Map have shown the utility of the multi-map strategy, but multi-maps have seen minimal, if any, adaptation for subsurface geologic data. Here we propose a system for creating a multi-map of subsurface geologic data.

We review the costs and benefits of different strategies for bringing together geologic information and discuss the challenges with adapting the multi-map concept to subsurface geologic datasets. We develop a general strategy for deriving an integrated representation of many subsurface data sets, primarily interpreted geologic horizons, relevant for national-scale exploration and discovery. Our strategy uses a prototype schema for modeled geologic horizons, the Subsurface 3D schema (s3ds), for the standard formatting of input and the capture of key attributes described by this subsurface geologic data (e.g., what aspect of the geometry of a horizon is being measured and in what units). Alongside the s3ds schema, the critical development for the multi-map component relies on spatial aggregation of horizon altitudes across standard attributes. This spatial aggregation, and a structure of standardized attributes inherited from the Cooperative National Geologic Map, allows users to spatially explore typical properties of modelled horizons across depth ranges, or examine the typical (or bounding) depths of geologic horizons associated with a standardized age or lithology (e.g., the uppermost elevation of Precambrian units).

title: Assessing River Health Using Diatom Communities Across a Pollution Gradient
session_title: Nature-based Solutions Research for Water Security in Peri-Urban Africa (Posters)
authors: Tanner, Jayden [1], Scherer, Noah [2], Kerwin, Michael W [3], Winter, Kevin J. [4], LaVanchy, G. Thomas [5], Hoover, Joseph H. [6]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science, University of Southern Indiana, Evansville, IN, USA
(2) Geography & the Environment, University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(3) Geography & the Environment, University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(4) Future Water Institute, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa
(5) Geography, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(6) Environmental Science, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract: Freshwater pollution threatens river ecosystems through eutrophication, oxygen depletion, and the spread of invasive species, highlighting the need for effective monitoring. Conventional water quality parameters (e.g., pH, electrical conductivity, and dissolved oxygen), however, often fail to capture long-term ecological impacts. In Franschhoek, South Africa, the Berg River catchment is affected by rapid informal settlement growth, inadequate sanitation and waste management, and intensive irrigation. The Stiebeuel River becomes polluted as it flows through the informal settlement before entering the Franschhoek River. Downstream, it passes through the Water Hub, a former municipal treatment plant now used as a living laboratory for sustainable water treatment. We hypothesized that diatom community composition would differ along the pollution gradient and show increasing evidence of ecological recovery with greater distance downstream from the Stiebeuel River confluence. Seven sampling sites were selected in the Franschhoek River system. Two sites were located upstream of the Stiebeuel River confluence to represent reference conditions, two sites were located within the Stiebeuel River to characterize the pollution source, and three sites were located incrementally downstream of the confluence to assess dilution and ecological recovery. Diatom biofilms were collected from streambed stones using a toothbrush and analyzed under a light microscope. Consistent with our hypothesis, diatom community composition changed along the pollution gradient as water was diluted downstream. However, downstream communities remained distinct from upstream reference sites, indicating that recovery was incomplete over the study reach. These findings demonstrate the potential of diatoms as indicators of ecological condition in the Berg River catchment and support further investigation into their use alongside conventional physicochemical monitoring.

title: New Sedimentological, Geochemical, and Carbon Stable Isotope Records of the Mid-Cenomanian Event and OAE2 from the HOT-DAM #1 Core in Central, KS
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Andrzejewski, Kate [1], Kroeger, Megan [2], Kalbas, James [3], Smith, Rachel [4]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Larwrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(4) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
The Kansas Geological Survey (KGS) HOT-DAM #1 core from central Kansas provides a new, high-resolution dataset capturing the onset of the Greenhorn Cyclothem and providing key insights into the evolution of the eastern margin of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS). Furthermore, the data and observations obtained from the core provide crucial insight for interpreting depositional environments and building a sequence stratigraphic framework for the Dakota Fm., Graneros Shale, and Greenhorn Limestone, key units that comprise the upper portions of the Dakota Aquifer System which serves as an important groundwater resource in Kansas.

High-resolution core observations and measurements reveal a marked transition from coastal plain deposits of the Dakota Fm. consisting of fluvial sandstones and paleosol deposits, to tidally influenced sandstones and marine argillaceous mudstones of the Graneros Shale, recording transgression of the WIS. Within the Graneros Shale, multiple observed parasequences reveal the successive drowning of the margin and can be correlated to nearby outcrops using the prominent “X-Bentonite” marker bed. The transition from the Graneros Shale to the overlying Greenhorn Limestone is marked by an abrupt shift from siliciclastic dominated to carbonate-dominated sediment which is observed both in gamma ray log patterns and geochemical pXRF datasets collected from the KGS multi-sensor core logging tool.

Additionally, high-resolution organic δ 13 C org profiles of the Graneros Shale and Greenhorn Limestone reveal pristine records of the Mid-Cenomanian Event (MCE) and Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2) carbon isotope excursion events. Within the Graneros Shale, the MCE is marked by positive 4 per mil shift followed by an abrupt decrease in baseline δ 13 C org values reflecting the transition from terrestrially-dominated to marine-dominated organic matter. The Greenhorn Limestone contains a pronounced positive 4 per mil shift representing the rising limb and onset of OAE2. Collectively, the δ 13 C org profile appears to capture the entire OAE2 excursion including the Plenus Cold Event. Together the high-resolution sedimentological, geochemical, and stable carbon isotope datasets record the onset of the Greenhorn Cyclothem and provide crucial insight into the sequence stratigraphic succession that directly impacts the vertical and lateral connectivity of the Dakota Aquifer System.

title: George Perkins Merrill’s Analyses of Chondrules and Chondritic Meteorites
session_title: The Astro-Geoheritage of the Solar System: Past Explorations and Future Considerations
authors: Drummond, Carl N. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Science, Department of Physics, Purdue University Fort Wayne, Fort Wayne, IN,
abstract: George Perkins Merrill (1854–1929) was the preeminent American meteoriticist of the first quarter of the 20 th Century. He applied to that science his pioneering knowledge and skill in the petrographic analysis of chondritic meteorites. Throughout his long and distinguished career with the United States National Museum, now the Smithsonian Institution of Washington, D.C., Merrill authored over seventy publications on meteorites. While many of those contributions described new irons and stones which had come into the museum’s collection, a pair of papers concerning the origin of chondrules and the evidence for and causes of metamorphism of chondritic meteorites led directly to his selection as the second recipient of the J. Lawrence Smith Medal which was awarded by the National Academy of Sciences in 1922 for outstanding accomplishments in the study of meteorites. The origins, primary arguments, and subsequent reception of those two landmark papers will be reviewed. Particular attention shall be given to how (1) Merrill’s hypotheses on chondrule formation and (2) the evidence for thermal and dynamic metamorphic alteration of chondrites, have come to underpin and advance modern understandings of the early history of the solar system.

title: An Initial Environmental Site Assessment for Global Water Consortium for Installation of Bottled Water Plant Installation for the City of Chattogram, Bangladesh
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Posters)
authors: Harris, Emily E. [1], Thomas, Renie [2], Hart, Maura [3], Wudke, Hannah [4], Krekeler, Mark P. S. [5]
affiliations: (1) Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(3) Miami University, Oxford, OH,
(4) Duke University, Liberty Township, OH, USA
(5) Miami University, Oxford, OH,
abstract: The Global Water Consortium (GWC) is a nonprofit organization working toward installing local drinking water facilities in water-stressed areas internationally. GWC has approximately 20 sites identified for small-scale bottled water production; however, there is a need for an environmental site assessment to better understand water resources in general and to better use funds generated from the water plant installations for humanitarian use. Chattogram, located on the coast of the Bay of Bengal, is the second-largest city in Bangladesh, with a population of just over 3 million, and is designated as a GWC site. Regionally, water quality issues like bacteria, nitrates, and metals have been documented in the supply water and are perpetuated by a lack of infrastructure, which can only service around 30% of the city's population. This lack of sanitation coverage leads to widespread annual outbreaks of cholera and mosquito-borne diseases. In-ground tube wells have historically been used by outreach programs and local government bodies as an alternative to contaminated surface water. Arsenic contamination is a well-documented geogenic problem across much of the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) floodplain shallow aquifers. Given the site-specific and spatial variability of the aquifer and the nature of arsenic occurrence in the aquifers of the Chattogram region, the literature study suggests GWC conduct targeted water sampling (for As, Fe, Mn, salinity, heavy metals) at specific sites before well installation and water treatment plant construction, with regional literature informing site-specific interventions. Complexities in well installation may arise from pollution from the local river (the Karnaphuli River) and seawater intrusion, and thus a more detailed hydrogeologic study to address this issue is suggested. This site analysis provides the GWC with critical information to inform the development of drinking water infrastructure for local communities.

title: Reconstructing Terrestrial Primary Productivity Through Time: Net Primary Productivity in the Late Cretaceous Moreno Hill Formation
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials
authors: Taylor, Ian Alexander [1], Lupia, Richard [2], Hodges, Caitlin [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 100 E Boyd St. 73019, Norman, OK, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 100 E Boyd St 73019, Norman, OK, ; Sam Noble Museum of Natural History, University of Oklahoma, 2401 Chautauqua Ave. 73072, Norman, OK, USA
(3) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 100 E Boyd St 73019, Norman, OK, USA
abstract:
Net primary productivity (NPP) is a measure of the amount of carbon fixed by photosynthetic autotrophs and stored as biomass over an interval of time. NPP is an important measure of both the energy available within terrestrial ecosystems and the dynamics of the carbon cycle. While NPP can be directly measured or constrained in modern ecosystems, estimating productivity in deep time is considerably more difficult. Previously, we developed a probabilistic model that uses organic carbon preserved in paleosols to estimate a range of likely NPP values while also explicitly accounting for uncertainty in the parameters needed to make these estimates. As part of ongoing research, we are applying and adapting this model to examine changes in NPP through the Late Cretaceous Moreno Hill Formation of western New Mexico.

The Moreno Hill Formation spans approximately 90.9–88.6 Ma, from the late Turonian into the early Coniacian, an interval that follows some of the warmest conditions of the Cretaceous and is associated with a broader trend of declining atmospheric CO₂ and cooler global temperatures. Paleosols collected through the formation preserve differences in organic carbon content and degree of soil development. By applying the NPP model to that series of sample, we examine changes in likely productivity through time rather than reconstructing productivity across a single ancient landscape.

One of the major challenges in applying organic carbon-based productivity models to paleosols is determining how much of the original soil carbon remains after burial and diagenesis. To better constrain this uncertainty, we are also exploring the preservation of different organic carbon pools within the Moreno Hill Formation fossil soils. Building on relationships between mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) and total soil organic carbon observed in modern soils, we are evaluating whether preserved carbon fractions can provide additional constraints on original soil carbon content and reconstructed NPP.

Applying the model through the Moreno Hill Formation allows us to begin examining how terrestrial productivity changed over geologic time while explicitly considering uncertainty in the preservation of the paleosol carbon record. Ultimately, these productivity estimates can be correlated with fluctuations in vegetation and environmental conditions to investigate how this terrestrial ecosystem responded to the Angiosperm Terrestrial Revolution.

title: Does resin impregnation control lignin preservation in coal-ball wood? Confocal fluorescence screening of thin sections and mounted peels.
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections (Posters)
authors: Bober, Katherine Mae Maxine [1], Raymond, Anne [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
abstract:
Confocal laser scanning microscopy offers a rapid, non-destructive screen for residual biopolymers in permineralized plant tissue. We report preliminary observations from Pennsylvanian coal-ball wood imaged on a Leica SP8 confocal microscope with 405 nm excitation and emission collected at 430–550 nm, in both petrographic thin sections and mounted cellulose-acetate peels.

In a thin section, tracheids of a cordaitean root in a Pennsylvanian coal ball from the Kalo Formation of Iowa, which appear to be resin-filled, show blue autofluorescence consistent with residual lignin. No comparable signal was detected in a cordaitean stem from another Kalo Formation coal ball, which had pervasively separated or ‘pulled-apart’ tracheid walls, indicating selective decay of the lignin-rich middle lamina by fungi.

These observations motivate a testable relationship: wood fossils without lignin should exhibit tracheid wall-degradation textures diagnostic of lignin decomposition by fungi, including separated tracheid walls indicating selective decay of the lignin-rich middle lamina, and broken cells walls indicative of simultaneous decay. Wood fossils that preserve lignin should have exquisitely preserved cell walls. Likewise roots, which are intruded into peat and may become captured in a coal ball while living or shortly after death, are more likely to preserved lignin in coal balls than stem and branch wood, which experiences fungal decomposition on the surface of the peat prior to burial.

Work in progress includes testing whether and confirming that we can use auto-fluorescence techniques to detect lignin in mounted cellulose-acetate peels in addition to thin sections, a priority, as archival peel collections vastly outnumber thin sections. We will use FTIR to confirm the identity of the resin in the cordaitean root that shows lignin-consistent autofluorescence. Currently, possession of wood resin is a shared derived character of conifers, which are sister to cordaiteans. Finally, we will extend the search for wood resin and preserved lignin to other cordaitean wood fossils, in which ray cells but not tracheids appear resin filled, and to Miocene wood from a concretion collected on the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Spectral (lambda) scans will test whether blue emission is attributable to lignin rather than to co-occurring polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as perylene. If lignin-consistent emission proves restricted to resin-associated tissue, resin impregnation may be a significant control on lignin preservation in coal balls.

title: New LA-ICP-MS U/Pb isotope ages from the Jurassic De Roux unit and Paleogene igneous rocks from the central Cascades, Washington state.
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Ariza, Sophia [1], MacDonald, James H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(2) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
abstract:
Laser Ablation Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) was used for U/Pb dating of zircons from two samples collected in the central Cascades of Washington State. Sample DRJM 34 is a foliated, porphyritic metadacite from the De Roux unit, a group of undated metaigneous and metasedimentary rocks. DRJM 34 yielded 51 zircons. This sample has calc-alkaline, volcanic arc geochemistry and is pilotaxitic in texture and shows a lower greenschist overprint. Of the 51 zircons yielded from sample DRJM 34, all but 10 zircons were discordant. One of the 10 concordant zircons is a 1.9 Ga xenocrystic zircon, which was excluded from the data used to acquire the concordia and weighted mean ages for the sample. The 50 zircons from DRJM 34 yielded a concordia age of 165.32 ± 0.85 Ma with an MSWD of 0.063, and a weighted mean age of 165.3 ± 1.8 Ma with an MSWD of 0.34. The 9 most concordant zircons from DRJM 34 yielded a concordia age of 166.3 ± 1.5 Ma with an MSWD of 0.3, and a weighted mean age of 166.1 ± 1.7 Ma with an MSWD of 2.

Sample DRJM 29 intrudes the De Roux unit and is an intermediate quartz diorite with adakite geochemistry. DRJM 29 is hypidiomorphic-granular in texture. DRJM 29 yielded 14 zircons that could be categorized into three separate age groups. The 4 youngest zircons from DRJM 29 are Eocene-Paleocene with a radial plot age of 56.06 ± 0.48 Ma and a concordia age of 56.08 ± 0.45 Ma with an MSWD of 0.0036 Ma. Additionally, 5 xenocrystic zircons from DRJM 29 are Upper Cretaceous with a radial plot age of 80.0 ± 1.3 Ma. Lastly, 5 more xenocrystic zircons from DRJM 29 yield Ediacaran ages, with a radial plot age of 612.5 ± 8.1 Ma. The Middle Jurassic (~166 Ma) age for the zircons from sample DRJM 34 is the first ever age from the De Roux unit. This ~166 Ma age supports the De Roux unit’s correlation to the western mélange belt. The ~56 Ma age for the adakitic sample DRJM 29 is rare in Washington state, but there are two other ~56 Ma igneous samples found in Washington state.

title: Using Cost Effective Remote Sensing Data, GIS, and Machine Learning to Identify Cave Localities in the Northwest Himalayas
session_title: Geoinformatics and Data Science: A Showcase In Undergraduate and Graduate Student Research (Posters)
authors: Witten, Alex [1], Furtner , Margaret [2], Sagwal, Sumit [3], Li, Justin [4], Sekhon, Natasha [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Occidental College, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) National Cave and Karst Insitute, Carlsbad, New Mexico, USA; New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Carlsbad, New Mexico, USA
(3) National Centre for Earth Science Studies, Thiruvananthapuram, India
(4) Department of Computer Sciences, Occidental College, Los Angeles, California, USA
(5) Geology, Occidental College, Los Angeles, California, USA
abstract:
This preliminary study evaluates the proficiency of Random Forest (RF) models to identify cave entrances in the Northwestern region of the Himalayas. Approximately 29 remotely sensed parameters derived from multispectral imagery (i.e. NDVI, NDWI), topographic data (i.e. elevation, slope) and surface information (distance to drainage paths, sink presence, etc.) serve as input variables. Positive training data consists of 17 known cave locations, from which 153 30m pixels were isolated on or adjacent to the cave entrances. Negative training locality data consists of 1000 randomly generated background pixels in the same general area of interest.

Using a 10 fold cross validation method, the RF model performed with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of .949 an accuracy of 90%. A high theoretical precision (90%) and low recall (37%) indicate that the model is extremely cautious in its positive predictions, which is useful for a time and resource-limited survey context. These results indicate that even in its early stages, this incredibly cost effective method has the potential to aid in the discovery of caves in highly complex topography. Permutation importance tests conducted on individual variables indicate that distance to drainage and vector ruggedness measure (VRM) are the most important features for the RF model’s success.

Future work will run the RF model using a more comprehensive set of variables (such as including geologic data) and will compare RF performance against more complex machine learning frameworks (e.g. Convoluted Neural Networks and Maximum Entropy models). The most successful models will be applied to the larger NW Himalayan region to aid in-field survey efforts searching for previously unrecorded cave localities.

title: Gallium from Coal Waste: Assessing a Vital Critical Mineral
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Fashina, Bidemi Tokunbo [1], Banerjee , Debasis [2], Ghosh, Koushik [3], Rigali, Mark [4], Xu, Guangping [5]
affiliations: (1) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(2) Sandia National Laboratories, Livermore, New Mexico, USA
(3) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(4) Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(5) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
Gallium (Ga) has been listed as one of the critical minerals of importance to energy and national security in the United States. Currently, the U.S is 100% reliant on foreign countries for Ga supply. This poses a threat to national security and the economy because a 30% disruption in the market supply is estimated to cascade into a decline of more than 2% in the gross domestic product. It is projected that the demand for Ga in the U.S will double between 2025 and 2035 mainly driven by Ga’s application for energy. To reduce reliance on imports to meet the future Ga need, it is imperative to evaluate the potential of domestic feedstocks as sources of Ga. In this study, the potential of over 20 coal ash samples as domestic sources of Ga was investigated. The samples were collected from New Mexico, Arizona, Ohio, and Utah. The Ga concentrations were determined using Instrumental Neutron Activation Analysis. The mineralogy compositions were determined by X-ray Diffraction coupled with Rietveld refinement, and Scanning Electron Microscopy is used to study morphology as well as identify the mineral phases that host the Ga in the coal ash samples.

title: Analysis of Molluscan Diversity, Extinction, and Origination Across the Pliocene-Pleistocene Record of Southeast Virginia and Northeast North Carolina.
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Posters)
authors: Denton, Hannah D. [1], Ryan, Kaitlyn R. [2], Turner, Edward W.H. [3], Dowsett, Harry [4], Spivey, Whittney [5], Utsunomiya, Masayuki [6], Lockwood, Rowan [7]
affiliations: (1) Dept of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(2) Dept of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia, USA
(3) Dept of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(4) Florence Bascom Geoscience Center, US Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(5) Florence Bascom Geoscience Center, US Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(6) Geological Survey of Japan, AIST, Tsukuba, Iraraki, Japan
(7) Dept of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia, USA
abstract:
The Plio-Pleistocene record of the U.S. Mid-Atlantic Coastal Plain provides insight into how marine mollusks responded to past climate change and extinction, with direct relevance to future anthropogenic change. Sedimentary units from this time interval contain a well-preserved and sampled abundance of macroinvertebrates and microfossils, making it possible to combine a revised biostratigraphic and paleoenvironmental framework with assessments of molluscan community and diversity shifts. In this study, we analyzed how new foraminiferal and nannofossil data affect biostratigraphic and paleoenvironmental reconstructions for the Chowan River Formation; how extinction and origination rates vary from the Chowan River to today; and how molluscan richness, diversity, and community structure shifted across the mid to late Pliocene and Pleistocene.

Data from 23 bulk samples were compiled from field, museum, and literature sources for Pliocene (Yorktown, Chowan River, and Bear Bluff Formations) and Pleistocene (James City Formation) units, totaling 22,394 individuals, 287 species, and 185 genera. All field and museum samples were sieved to ≥4mm; bivalves and gastropods were identified to species level and taxonomically updated. To quantify abundance, specimens were counted as minimum number of individuals. Hill numbers were used to estimate richness and diversity, while a detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was used to assess changes in community structure. Extinction and origination rates were estimated from faunal lists in previously published monographs.

Preliminary results suggest that extinction rates were highest from the James City Formation to Recent. DCA revealed moderate shifts in community structure through time, with significant faunal turnover associated with the James City fauna. Taxon richness varied from low levels in the early Yorktown and James City Formations, to significantly higher levels in the middle Yorktown and Chowan River Formations. Planktic foraminifera placed Chowan River type locality samples within zone PL5. Common- to abundant (13-65%) occurrences of small Gephyrocapsa suggest these sediments are most likely deposited after re-entrance of small Gephyrocapsa (~2.5 Ma). Benthic foraminifera suggest shallow, warm, relatively high nutrient, well-oxygenated bottom waters, with strong coastal water influence.

title: Some Meta-cognition on Modeling, with a View Toward the Legacy of Randy Hunt
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Summers, Paul [1], Cardiff, Michael [2], Hart, David [3], Muldoon, Moe [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(2) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
(3) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey (Emeritus), Madison, WI, USA
(4) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey (Emeritus), Madison, WI, USA
abstract:
Every groundwater modeling project should start with the intent to answer a question – the modeling purpose. From that point forward the modeler is left with a near-infinite array of choices about how to create their model and how to spend their limited time and effort on meeting their modeling purpose. A modeler, whether they realize it or not, is thus performing constrained, high-dimensional integer-programming based optimization under substantial uncertainty – the hardest type of optimization known to man. It’s no surprise, then, that the search for “optimums” (i.e. best practices) in how we build a model to address a modeling purpose remains a subject of major ongoing debate. My hope for this talk is to continue to draw Randy Hunt into further debates about modeling.

In this presentation I will describe efforts to modify an existing model (appropriately enough, one created by Dr. Hunt) to meet a new modeling purpose. The Village of French Island, WI has experienced groundwater contamination of its shallow aquifer by PFAS from a nearby airport, with residents now reliant on bottled water for the past 5 years. As French Island works towards a new municipal water system that taps the deeper Mt. Simon sandstone for water supply, a clear modeling purpose was evident: the Village needs a model to assess impacts of deep pumping on PFAS transport and predict future pathways for PFAS movement. Working from Dr. Hunt’s initial regional model of La Crosse County, we developed a Python-based workflow that incorporated parameter estimation and prediction uncertainty, particularly focusing on the poor availability of data for local confining units. The legacy of Dr. Hunt in this effort was not only present in our use of his regional model, but in conversations with him and the way we considered uncertainty, the use of prior information, groundwater / surface water interactions, and the overall modeling process. Therefore, I will close with some reflections on the overall field of groundwater modeling and the value our continual arguments on how to model well (of which I hope Dr. Hunt will continue to be a part).

title: Cracking the Carbonate Clock: Aragonite to Calcite Neomorphism and U-Pb Dating
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Kainz, Sabrina [1], Cantine, Marjorie [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
The growing use of carbonate uranium-lead (U-Pb) dating demands robust criteria to distinguish reliable from unreliable dates and to identify the processes that drive open-system behaviour capable of resetting or modifying the U-Pb system. This study investigates how the neomorphism of primary aragonite to calcite affects carbonate U-Pb dating by applying petrography and geochemistry to exceptionally well-preserved marine carbonates.

Permian biolithoherms of the Bursum Formation in the Orogrande Basin of southern New Mexico preserve botryoidal seafloor cements originally precipitated as aragonite, now neomorphosed to calcite. These are found alongside fossil-rich sediments with skeletal bioclasts of original aragonitic or calcitic mineralogy. We combine petrography, cathodoluminescence (CL), U-Pb geochronology, and trace element geochemistry to elucidate the distinct histories of these two phases. Botryoidal seafloor cements, originally aragonite, are CL-dark and contain heavy rare earth element (REE) enrichment with negative cerium anomalies, consistent with precipitation from oxygenated seawater. Syndepositional, reproducible, and relatively high precision (down to 3% 2sd) U-Pb dates are measured on these phases. Conversely, fossil sediments produce scattered U-Pb dates inconsistent with biostratigraphic age constraints, are enriched in middle REE, and are bright orange and mottled in CL. These results suggest that fossil sediments are highly diagenetically altered, likely by reducing pore fluids post-deposition.

Preliminary results indicate that botryoid pseudomorph cements make promising targets for paleo-ocean reconstructions. They appear to have remained relatively closed systems, despite conversion to calcite. Although fossil components must have been formed synchronously with botryoidal cements and have also experienced neomorphism, they have experienced greater diagenetic alteration and reflect open-system mixed signals. We hypothesise that retention of primary geochemistry may be controlled by the fluid to solid ratio prior to neomorphism, such that components with high fluid content (i.e. fossil sediments) remain in open-system exchange for longer periods of time. This study provides a framework for identifying carbonate facies that can preserve reliable U-Pb dates of precipitation from primary seawater.

abstract:
Colorado River system integration and incision drive exhumation of the Colorado Plateau, but Desolation Canyon on the Green River tributary separates differential exhumation depth, such that upstream exhumation is <1 km while Canyonlands (downstream) exhumation reaches 2 km. High relief Desolation Canyon and surrounding lower-relief topography are eroded into variably resistant Eocene-age deposits of the laterally and stratigraphically variable sand- and mud-stone facies in the Wasatch Formation and the Green River Formation.

New in-situ cosmogenic erosion rates within Desolation Canyon and along the Book Cliffs are 150 to 300 m/Ma and match regional incision rates (~150 -200 m/Ma, derived from estimated strath terrace ages ranging up to 11 Ma), while erosion rates on the Tavaputs Plateau are ~40 m/Ma (~3 to 6x lower). Topographic analysis of Desolation Canyon and the surrounding Tavaputs Plateau shows normalized channel steepness within the canyon to be ~4-5x (k sn = 160 -200) higher than the plateau; however, the Book Cliffs east and west from Desolation Canyon in the same units show channel steepness values only ~2x (k sn = ~40 – 80) higher than the plateau surface. Mapping and helicopter-based photos over ~70 km of outcrop show substantially more sandstone within Desolation Canyon than surrounding lower-relief topography all within the Wasatch Formation. Field seismic rock-strength measurements indicate sandstones are circa 4x stronger than local shales. These data indicate that Desolation Canyon is a lithologically-induced transient knickpoint where the river and tributaries upstream of the canyon have not been reached by the full amount of Colorado River base-level fall since Colorado River integration.

title: Food Web Restructuring Across the Mesozoic Marine Revolution Driven by Increasing Energetics
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy
authors: Tyler, Carrie [1], Dineen, Ashley A. [2], Banker, Roxanne M.W. [3], Ess, Madeline P. [4], Roopnarine, Peter D. [5]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) University of California, Berkeley, CA,
(3) Providence College, Providence, RI, ; California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA, USA
(4) Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, USA
(5) California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA,
abstract:
Predators influence community structure and dynamics in many modern ecosystems, yet the importance of predation on macroevolutionary timescales remains controversial. To identify changes in ecosystem and trophic structure associated with the Mesozoic Marine Revolution (MMR), a proposed major reorganization of marine ecosystems attributed to increased predation pressure, we constructed five stage-level food webs from western Tethys spanning the Early Triassic to the Late Cretaceous.

To compare food web structure across the MMR, we generated 100 species-level food web models for each of the five communities to account for the uncertainty in the precise set of interspecific interactions in the fossil record. We examined a variety of common food web metrics, and compared body sizes within four predator clades (fishes, predatory marine reptiles, cephalopods, and predatory gastropods). We found that structural properties of food webs and predator body sizes differed across the MMR, but changes were non-linear. We also employed a Multinomial Logistic Regression to identify the main drivers of differences in ecosystem structure using the following predictors: the maximum species trophic position per guild, maximum body size, median number of predators per guild, median number of prey per guild, the total number of species per guild, and the longest trophic chain. We find that the main signal of the MMR was significant trophic restructuring and expansion associated predominantly with metabolic and physiological ramping up via increasing to higher mean and maximum trophic positions and longer trophic chains. In addition, while changes in taxonomic richness occurred, this did not translate to corresponding changes in food web structure, such as more guilds, functions, interactions, or greater complexity.

These results are consistent with an asynchronous MMR across different faunal groups and regions, with complex, non-linear changes in ecosystem structure and functioning. The examination of ancient food webs presents an opportunity to determine whether trophic organization has changed, and to understand the evolutionary mechanisms that have contributed to historical patterns of community structure.

abstract:
The southern Illinois Basin potentially contains one of the most complete Lower to Middle Devonian carbonate successions in North America. However, establishing the position of conodont biozone boundaries has been notoriously difficult, particularly near the base of the succession. The 300 m-thick interval contains a range of facies from laminated peritidal to cherty deep marine mudstones and bioclastic carbonates with the Dutch Creek Sandstone setting off the upper quarter of the succession. Integration of new chemostratigraphy andbiostratigraphic results provides increased constraints on age distributions and new insights into the formation of this extraordinary succession.

Chemostratigraphic profiles for eight subsurface sections in the southern Illinois Basin were generated usingportable X-ray fluorescence and carbonate carbon stable isotope analysis at the Illinois State Geological Survey. Archived core and cuttings samples were powdered prior to analysis. Results were evaluated for data quality and profiles were plotted stratigraphically. Conodont biostratigraphic range data was integrated with the chemostratigraphic profiles in cross sections parallel and oblique to depositional dip.

The new integrated stratigraphic framework provides high confidence chronostratigraphic interpretation. The upper Pridoli and lower Lochkovian (Klonk) δ13C carb excursions are clearly divided enabling identification of the base of the Devonian near the first appearance of the pelagic crinoid Scyphocrinites. Pragian and lower Emsian δ13C carbexcursions are also easily identified in an interval of well-developed conodont biozonation. The base of the EifelianStage occurs within the Dutch Creek Sandstone where the upper Emsian and lower Eifelian δ13C carb excursions are amalgamated. Stable isotope values decrease through the Grand Tower and Lingle formations and the succession is capped by an abrupt +2‰ positive excursion that may represent the Kačák-otomari event near the base of the Givetian Stage. The succession is capped by a paleokarst surface at the contact with the upper Givetian to Frasnian Blocher Member of the New Albany Shale. The new chronostratigraphic framework reveals onlap-offlap patterns related to Devonian sea level fluctuations and inherited basin morphology following Silurian platform progradation.

title: Tracing Water Sources Through Time and Space in an Urban Environment Using Sr, O, and H Isotopes
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: Kamenov, George [1], Kamenov, Emma [2], Curtis, Jason [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA
(2) University of South Florida, St. Petersburg, Florida, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA
abstract: Strontium (Sr) in natural waters is derived primarily from water-rock interaction in the watershed or aquifer, and Sr isotopes can be used to trace water origin. Water supply in a modern urban environment can involve multiple sources, including natural springs, wells and dams. For water source apportionment, the isotopic compositions of the potential sources should be distinct and preserved over long timescales. In Sofia, Bulgaria the main supply of drinking water is from a large dam “Iskar”. Other water sources are also utilized, including a smaller dam, and thermal mineral water springs. Mineral waters from two of the springs are commercially bottled and sold locally and internationally. Sequential sampling of waters in Sofia analyzed in 2023 show similar isotopic compositions to samples analyzed in early 2000s and in 2025, demonstrating remarkable isotopic stability on short (weeks) to long (years) timescales. The mineral waters show distinctly low Sr isotopes (as low as 0.7043), compared to the main tap water source “Iskar” (0.7085). Commercially bottled mineral waters show identical isotopic compositions to the source springs. Although meteoric origin is evident in the O and H isotopic compositions, the major types of Sofia waters exhibit distinct stable isotope compositions and can be distinguished from each other. Furthermore, the locally bottled mineral waters show some of the lowest Sr isotopes observed in mineral waters in Europe. Therefore, Sr can distinguish not only the major drinking water sources on a local scale, but also can be utilized to verify authenticity claims for commercially sold mineral waters internationally. In cases where there is overlap in Sr isotopes, O and H isotopes can be used to additionally verify the water origin. This is important because mineral waters are preferred for drinking due to purported health benefits. Comparison of the local mineral water chemical composition to the tap water reveals major differences. Although it is unclear if the chemistry of the mineral waters can support the purported health benefits, the chemical differences between the water types in the region can also be used to distinguish between water sources. Overall, the distinct isotopic and chemical signatures in waters in an urban environment can be preserved on a long timescale, and can be useful tracers for water source apportionment.

abstract: Beginning on December 8, 2025, a series of atmospheric rivers delivered historic precipitation across Washington, triggering widespread flooding and landslides throughout the state. In response, Washington Geological Survey (WGS) activated the December 2025 Atmospheric River Landslides Clearinghouse with the aim of providing state and federal disaster-response managers, affected organizations, the scientific community, and the public with prompt information on landslide impacts. Clearinghouse efforts focused on documenting the distribution and characteristics of landslides in the Cascade Range and post-wildfire areas statewide through remote sensing and field reconnaissance. The Clearinghouse operated for five months during which 174 clearinghouse forms were submitted and 767 landslides were identified. The Clearinghouse demonstrated the value of coordinated landslide reconnaissance during a major disaster while also identifying important lessons learned that will strengthen future emergency response, data collection, and interagency coordination.

affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA

abstract: Geoscience enrollments and diversity are low and solving one of those challenges likely involves solving both. Many efforts aiming to address these challenges have focused on urban populations, where diversity tends to be greatest, but there are also rural communities with student populations that are underrepresented in geoscience. To help reach those students, we created a geoscience recruiting network between a 4-year university and two community colleges and then tested the hypothesis that we can increase interest in geoscience and the diversity of geoscience students in a rural agricultural landscape by demonstrating the relevance of geoscience to the students’ lives through a co-curricular program of groundwater quality monitoring. Our program ran from 2023-2025 and included a university campus visit, a field experience, remote data analysis and poster preparation workshops, a community presentation event, and $3,000 scholarships. We evaluated the effectiveness of our program using retrospective and longitudinal surveys. Retrospective surveys were completed by 50 of the 55 participants and showed that most students did not participate because they wanted to explore their interest in geoscience. The top three reasons were to gain hands-on research experience (82%), enhance their resumes (80%), and earn money (74%). Most respondents agreed or strongly agreed that they gained a greater understanding of geoscience (94%), applications of geoscience in everyday life (92%), and educational and career opportunities in geosciences (80%). Students were also mostly satisfied with program events and mentoring. Most students also agreed or strongly agreed that they enjoyed learning about geosciences (96%) and would like to learn more (64%). However, only five students (10%) indicated that they would change their academic plans and none of the changes involved switching their major to geoscience. Instead, they were planning to adjust specialization areas or add minors. Findings from ongoing longitudinal tracking surveys have been hindered by low response rates, though the results obtained are consistent with the retrospective surveys. Although the project has not increased geoscience enrollment and diversity thus far, it has helped the student participants gain valuable research experiences and a greater appreciation of geoscience and water challenges. Furthermore, the groundwater quality data we generated is helping the broader public gain awareness of contamination issues and the efforts of geoscientists to address the problem.

title: Harnessing Fungi and Plants as Nature-Based Solutions for Stiebeuel River Water Remediation in Franschhoek, South Africa
session_title: Nature-based Solutions Research for Water Security in Peri-Urban Africa (Posters)
authors: Whitmore, Chrisa [1], Winter, Kevin J. [2], Hoover, Joseph H. [3], Kerwin, Michael W. [4], LaVanchy, G. Thomas [5]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA

abstract: Rapid urbanization and migration in South Africa have contributed to the expansion of informal settlements in and around major cities and towns. Limited access to sanitation services compels residents to dump human waste outside their homes that eventually flows into nearby river systems. Consequently, freshwater ecosystems are increasingly exposed to xenobiotic compounds and pathogenic microorganisms, posing significant risks to ecosystem integrity and the health of communities living near these water bodies. Nature-based solutions (NbS) offer an alternative to conventional wastewater treatment methods by harnessing biological processes to remediate polluted water. Microorganisms, such as fungi, have been studied as NbS for degrading complex organic pollutants while simultaneously improving the physicochemical quality of water. By integrating mycoremediation with phytoremediation, this project aims to pilot-test a low-cost, sustainable treatment system for improving freshwater quality and reducing contaminant loads in Fall 2026. This project proposes the development and evaluation of an integrated bioremediation system that combines mycoremediation, using fungi ( Pleurotus ostreatus or Trametes versicolor ), and phytoremediation, using duckweed ( Lemna minor ) and crop plants such as spinach and carrots, to remediate contaminated river water through the degradation, uptake, and removal of contaminants. The experimental design compares untreated Stiebeuel river water with biofiltered river water using parallel treatment systems consisting of soil substrates and soil substrates with an addition of biochar. Both water types will first undergo fungal mycofiltration pretreatment before being applied to the treatment systems. Water quality will be evaluated before and after mycofiltration to assess changes in physicochemical properties, nutrient concentrations, microbial indicators, and selected xenobiotic contaminants. The treated water will then be applied to soil-based systems containing duckweed or edible crops to evaluate plant growth and overall treatment performance. Comparisons among treatments will identify the most effective low-cost nature-based remediation strategy. The outcomes of this study will contribute to the development of scalable nature-based water treatment strategies that support sustainable water management and water reuse in resource-constrained communities.

title: Constructing Georeferenced HDPCs of Butler Cave as Datasets to Advance Machine Learning Applications in Cave and Karst Science
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science
authors: Young, Mia grace [1], Garcia, Angel [2], Crowell, Bryan [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Earth Sciences, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Earth Sciences, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(3) Butler Cave Conservation Society, VA, USA
abstract:
Modern computer-assisted mapping of karst features creates opportunities to conduct more detailed surveys than traditional mapping methods. Traditional mapping requires extensive knowledge of caving techniques and significant time investment involved in hand-mapping, whereas modern technologies such as LiDAR provide an efficient alternative. Previous research has demonstrated that machine learning combined with LiDAR can successfully identify cave entrances in forested environments, supporting the application of similar methods for analyzing cave systems

Butler Cave (BC), located in Bath County, Virginia, contains more than 18 miles of mapped passage hosting numerous unique features including maze and sinuous cave passages, geological structures such as: depositional layering, synforms, and evidence of changing environment. The abundance of these features and speleothem growth makes BC an ideal location for developing machine learning algorithms. This study aims to apply georeferenced High-Definition Point Clouds (HDPCs) collected from BC to train machine learning models. HDPC’s are the result of developing mass point-cloud data collected from LiDAR scans into visual 3D models of every point received from the LiDAR scanner.

Initially, a georeferenced HDPC containing more than 1.8 × 10⁹ points was constructed using a handheld LiDAR-SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) ZEB-Horizon system. The resulting dataset extends over 1.5 km of cave passage with more than 100m of elevation gradient. In addition, a georeferenced surficial LiDAR scan has been aligned with the cave HDPC to highlight structure and compare surface features to the alignment of the passages. This process aims to teach machine learning algorithms to refine interpretations of how surface characteristics including hydrology, epikarst development, and dolines, influence subsurface observations. Feature-recognition algorithms can be trained by reviewing bare HDPCs, those containing no distinct speleothems, and HDPCs containing anomalies including speleothems, water, and other unique formations. The algorithms distinguish unique features by identifying variations in shape and dimensions that are absent in bare HDPCs.

Machine learning algorithms have the potential to create detailed analysis of karst features while preserving the accuracy of HDPC datasets. This approach creates opportunities for developing advanced tools in cave and karst science, digital mapping, and geologic analysis. Future work will focus on improving speleothem identification, refining cave-mapping techniques, and generating higher-quality HDPC datasets. Machine learning represents only the beginning of a new generation of cave exploration, mapping, and karst geology research.

authors: Curl, Douglas C [1], Ramsey, Ryan [2], Johnson, Sarah [3], Crawford, Matthew M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Kentucky Geologcal Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(3) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY,

abstract:
Landslides are a persistent hazard in eastern Kentucky, where steep colluvial slopes and intense hydroclimatic events combine to threaten infrastructure and communities. To improve understanding of hydrologic triggering conditions, the Kentucky Geological Survey (KGS), as part of the Kentucky NSF EPSCoR CLIMBS (Climate Resilience through Multidisciplinary Big Data Learning, Prediction and Building Response Systems) initiative, installed and operates a network of 24 slope hydrologic monitoring stations across the region. Each station records volumetric water content, matric potential, and soil temperature at two depths, along with precipitation and other meteorological variables.

To make these data immediately accessible and interpretable, KGS developed a public, web-based dashboard (kgs.uky.edu/slope-monitoring) that displays near-real-time and historical conditions across the network. Station data are retrieved from the Zentra Cloud API on a ~45-minute cycle by a lightweight PHP caching layer, minimizing API load while keeping the map current. The interactive map is a custom application built with the ArcGIS JavaScript SDK. The map symbolizes each station by relative soil saturation (current water content normalized to the maximum observed at each sensor), a metric more directly interpretable for landslide-triggering potential than raw water content. This follows an approach developed for the Puerto Rico Soil Monitoring website by the USGS and University of Puerto Rico–Mayagüez. Users can toggle a lidar-derived KGS landslide susceptibility layer, overlay live NEXRAD precipitation radar, and step through 14 days of soil saturation and rainfall history with an animated time slider. Station detail panels provide multidepth time-series charts and downloadable records, and an automated open-data archiving pipeline is in development to publish daily observations to a public repository.

This presentation highlights the network design, web application architecture, API integration strategies, and data-visualization approaches, providing a transferable model for low-cost, real-time hydrologic monitoring dashboards supporting regional landslide hazard assessment.

title: WAS THE UPPER MISSISSIPPI RIVER VALLEY A SIGNIFICANT LOESS SOURCE DURING MIS 2?
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Schaetzl, Randall J. [1], Carson, Eric C. [2], Pruder, David [3], Post, Alanna [4], Farkas, Beata [5]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Environment, and Spatial Sciences, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA
(2) Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey, Madison, WI, USA
(3) Anthropology and Geography, Minnesota State University, Mankato, MN, USA

(5) Geography and Earth Sciences, University of Pecs, Pecs, Hungary
abstract:
Many studies have documented the west-to-east transport of loess and eolian sand in the upper Midwest, during and immediately after MIS 2. In southern Wisconsin, loess on the bluffs east of the Mississippi River valley (MRV) can exceed 5 meters in thickness. Loess here thins, predictably, to the east. Thus, for as long as loess has been studied, the MRV – a glacial spillway during MIS 2 – has been assumed to have been a significant loess source. However, loess to the west of the MRV, in eastern Iowa and Minnesota, is also thick, and gets progressively thicker to the west. This loess was primarily derived from the Iowan Erosion Surface (IES) and Des Moines Lobe meltwater. Thus, we examined the extent to which loess in western Wisconsin was sourced from Iowa and Minnesota, vis a vis the MRV.

To address this question, we cored thick loess adjacent to (east of) the MRV in western Wisconsin. For five of these cores, loess was sampled every 20 cm and analyzed for 15 elements, using X-Ray fluorescence (XRF). XRF data were then compared to data from loess samples in two different “source” areas – 40 samples from thick loess in Iowa and Minnesota, immediately downwind from the IES, and 30 samples from loess in northwestern Wisconsin, downwind of the Chippewa and St. Croix Rivers and their tributaries. These rivers are tributaries of the Mississippi River; they drained MIS 2 ice that flowed out of the Lake Superior Basin. Discriminant analysis of the elemental data for the loess from these two source areas confirmed that the two loess “types” are vastly different, especially with regard to Mn, Ti, P, and Ca contents.

Discriminant analysis of principal components of the XRF data from the five cores confirm that loess in western Wisconsin was derived almost entirely from sources west of the MRV, specifically the IES and the Des Moines Lobe. We attribute this to the abundance of shale in the upstream areas of the Des Moines Lobe, and the paucity of silt-rich sediment in the glacial sediments of northern Wisconsin. We conclude that the MRV was not a significant loess source during MIS 2, even in upstream areas and in areas downwind of reaches that aligned with the dominant WNW winds.

abstract: In 2015 I started ill-fated and overly ambitious dissertation research on the soil and biotic legacies of gravel mulch agricultural technology in the Upper Rio Grande. The only part of this study that worked was the soil component. I present this study as a tribute to Rolfe Mandel, who provided the crucial education in geomorphology and soil description that I depended on so heavily. Gravel mulch was an important component of Puebloan cotton agriculture, but its function and soil legacies are not well understood. Since water management was likely a critical feature of gravel mulch, this research examines soil variables affected by changes to water supply. Gravel mulch analyzed in this study was found to have a substantial impact on the surface soil particle size distribution, but other aspects of soil quality were unaffected. The depth profiles of base cation ratios in mulched and unmodified locations suggest that gravel mulch continues to enhance water infiltration. Based on the timing of cotton development and inferred infiltration depths associated with gravel mulch soils, gravel mulch technology is well suited to the monsoonal precipitation regime of the region and the phenology of cotton.

title: Evaluating Ecological Degradation in the Upper Berg River Catchment (South Africa) Using miniSASS
session_title: Nature-based Solutions Research for Water Security in Peri-Urban Africa (Posters)
authors: Scherer, Noah [1], Tanner, Jayden [2], Kerwin, Michael W. [3], Winter, Kevin J. [4], Hoover, Joseph H. [5], LaVanchy, G. Thomas [6]
affiliations: (1) Geography & the Environment, University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(2) Environmental Science, University of Southern Indiana, Evansville, IN, USA
(3) Geography & the Environment, University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(4) Future Water Institute, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa
(5) Environmental Science, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(6) Geography, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: Freshwater access, especially in the Global South, is increasingly threatened by anthropogenic changes. In South Africa, the rapid growth of informal settlements and challenges with adequate sanitation and waste management have caused highly contaminated pollution to flow into many rivers needed for irrigation and domestic uses. In the upper Berg River catchment of the Western Cape, the historically perennial Franschhoek River is threatened by both the overuse of surface and groundwater in addition to point source pollution from the highly contaminated Stiebeuel River which drains from the informal settlement of Langrug. To address these challenges, research is being organized around The Water Hub, an outdoor laboratory experimenting with different forms of nature-based solutions to clean and monitor water from the Stiebeuel River. As a part of a 5-week international research experience at the Water Hub, we investigated the rate of ecological health recovery along the Franschhoek River (using miniSASS assessment) above and below polluted discharge from the Stiebeuel River. Results show that while both miniSASS scores and species biodiversity increased with pollution source distance, ecological health had not yet returned to its pre-polluted state. Furthermore, miniSASS scores showed significantly higher health values post-rainfall, indicating swift changes in river ecology. These findings suggest that despite dilution occurring, adverse ecological health continues to persist far down river and could have harmful effects on both downstream users and the riparian environment.
