title: Trends in Precipitation and Groundwater d-excess Across the Colorado Front Range: Variability and Comparisons to δ18O
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Martinez, Ethan [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: Stable isotope measurements such as δ2H and δ18O have a long history of use as tracers for modeling the flow of water through hydrological systems and investigating the functioning of the water cycle from global to local scales. D-excess is a second-order stable isotope parameter that can be used as a tracer for water movement, as well as an indicator for the influence of various controls on the water cycle, including point-source relative humidity, regional moisture recycling, and evaporative influence. To examine the sources of precipitation and groundwater along the Front Range, we conduct an analysis of d-excess values in precipitation, groundwater, and stream waters across the Front Range. We utilize a water isotope dataset spanning from late 2021 to present, generated by a combination of samplers maintained by us as well as collaboration with citizen scientists from up and down the front range. Using this dataset, we analyze data across 14 discrete collection sites that include both precipitation and groundwater samples from the Colorado Front Range as well as one collection site from northern Wyoming. We find that d-excess in groundwater exhibits a greater degree of variability than δ18O, and that there is a tight correlation between the d-excess value of groundwater and elevation of the well head. A similar, but less constrained correlation is also observable in groundwater δ18O values. We also find that precipitation exhibits a unique signature in d-excess on the Front Range in which seasonal peaks take place in early Summer and early Fall, with a sharp drop to an annual minimum in the middle of Summer and another minimum occurring in the winter. These findings indicate that d-excess likely has a greater sensitivity to certain environmental/climatological influences than δ18O, indicating a need for further research into the function of d-excess in this region.

title: Correlation of the Cycladic Blueschist Unit: Comparative Detrital Zircon U-Pb Geochronology from Penteli and Evia, Greece
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Nguyen, Preya [1], Turek, Sage [2], Stockli, Daniel F. [3], Soukis, Konstantinos [4], Laskari, Sofia [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(4) National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece
(5) National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece
abstract: The Attic-Cycladic Crystalline Complex (ACCC) is a geologic region spanning mainland Greece and the Aegean Sea characterized by well-preserved blueschist- and eclogite-facies rocks that underwent two notable exhumations: syn-orogenic extension from the rollback of the Hellenic subduction zone in the mid-to-late Eocene (40-35 Ma) and post-orogenic extension in the Oligo-Miocene (23-10 Ma). The tectonostratigraphic and structural histories of the ACCC are debated by virtue of the timing of metamorphism in the exhumed metamorphic core complexes and the mechanisms of exhumation. The Cycladic Blueschist Unit (CBU) refers to a sequence of rocks within the ACCC that were subducted and exhumed in a high-pressure, low temperature (HP/LT) environment, whereas the Basal Unit was subducted after and exhumed before the CBU at lower pressure and temperature conditions. Mount Penteli represents a portion of the Northeast Attica Unit (NEAU), which has been characterized as belonging to both the CBU and the Basal Unit. We aim to describe the geologic setting of the NEAU at Penteli with respect to the CBU and Basal Unit. Detrital zircon analysis of Penteli metaschist samples yielded U-Pb maximum depositional ages (MDAs) and provenance. Compared with known CBU samples from the Styra Unit on Evia Island, these data provide evidence that the NEAU constitutes part of the CBU. Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) plots of the Penteli samples (MDA range = [98.2, 310.8] Ma) resemble those from the Styra Unit (MDA range = [155.5, 422.4] Ma). We infer that both sample groups were sourced from similar provenances and share a similar tectonic history; future work will increase the amount of geochronologic data in Attica for verification. This study can aid in advancing knowledge of the tectonic evolution of the ACCC alongside broader HP/LT subduction and exhumation dynamics.

title: Some New Insights into the Bioaccumulation of PFAS in Ohio Waterways: Findings from a Public Data Set.
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Moore, Andrew Patterson [1], Dietrich, Matthew [2], Krekeler, Mark P. S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) Minera Logic, Cincinnati, Minnesota, USA; Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(3) Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), commonly referred to as forever chemicals, are synthetic compounds used since the 1950s to make hydrophobic products and firefighting foam. As their nickname implies, they are highly resistant to environmental degradation, leading to persistence and accumulation in both the environment and organisms. These compounds can lead to adverse human health effects and disrupt ecosystems through similar effects to organisms. Because these compounds are widely used in industry and they cannot be easily broken down, PFAS is a pervasive threat to human and ecological health. Due to the large number of different PFAS chemicals and lack of established toxicological data on many, regulatory frameworks are evolving rapidly and better understanding of PFAS bioaccumulation may help with future toxicological risk assessments. Because PFAS often ends up in waterways from runoff processes, we aimed to study the extent of PFAS contamination and bioaccumulation trends in Ohio rivers by examining water, fish, and macroinvertebrate sample data collected by the Ohio EPA Large River Study. This was accomplished by examining the concentration trends of prevalent PFAS chemicals across different species, while also comparing results from Ohio with similarly sourced data from New Hampshire and a global meta-analysis. Through examination of the data, we found an overall positive correlation between bioaccumulation factors (BAFs) and PFAS chain length across all Ohio species. One specific example was in Ohio bluegill, where longer- chain compounds such as PFOS (perfluorooctanesulfonic acid) had considerably higher BAFs when compared to short-chain compounds. Additionally, BAFs differed significantly across Ohio fish species and macroinvertebrates for several PFAS chemicals, related to the type of sampling (whole body versus fillet tissue) and potential trophic-level interactions. Across the Ohio, New Hampshire, and global meta-analysis data, PFOS concentrations displayed the greatest variability in fish and water samples, while other similar compounds displayed less variability. Differences in land use may contribute to greater PFOS concentrations in Ohio versus New Hampshire, as PFOS could be sourced from agricultural runoff and Ohio has a much greater agricultural footprint than New Hampshire. These findings support our hypothesis that PFAS chemicals with longer chains of fluorinated carbons will show greater bioaccumulation in river organisms because of their tendency to accumulate in tissues and organs, and that bioaccumulation varies between species.

title: Co-seismic selective rock pulverization in the footwall of a Miocene low-angle normal fault
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Masoch, Simone [1], Rowe, Christie D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, ; Nevada Seismological Laboratory, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Nevada Seismological Laboratory, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, ; Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
abstract: Evidence of earthquake rupture propagation and resulting off-fault damage along detachment faults or low-angle normal faults (LANFs) is scarce in the rock record, limiting our understating on how damaging earthquakes propagate along LANFs to the surface. Here we document the presence of pulverized rocks (marker of paleo-earthquake rupture propagation), coexisting with pseudotachylytes (quenched frictional melts), related to final stages of slip of the Miocene Waterman Hills detachment (Mojave extensional belt, California). Rock pulverization affects only stiff meta-chert bodies in the uppermost ~30 m of the detachment footwall, becomes progressively more intense closer to the detachment, from shattered rocks to gritty and consolidated power, and has a patchy distribution across the footwall damage zone. The higher stiffness, finer grain size and progressive damage-induced mechanical weakening of the meta-chert compared to the other footwall rocks promote selective pulverization under transient stress conditions. Microstructural observations of the pulverized meta-cherts demonstrate a cumulative record of grain-scale shattering and progressive fracture-surface generation followed by fluid-assisted fracture healing between earthquakes. Our documentation represents a rare natural record of cumulative off-fault energy dissipation during multiple earthquake ruptures propagating along the shallow portion of a LANF, showing how elastic stiffness, inherited damage and fluid-assisted fracture healing modulate dynamic fragmentation over repeated seismic events.

title: Sensitivity of headwater watershed hydrology to subsurface properties and their spatial heterogeneity
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Oladoja, Victor [1], Wang, Lijing [2], Warix, Sara [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Willimantic, CT, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
abstract: Although more than 70% of the total stream network length in the United States lies within headwater watersheds, our ability to understand and predict hydrologic processes in these systems remains limited. Because headwater streams are strongly influenced by groundwater, fully integrated, distributed hydrologic models that can simulate surface-subsurface flow interactions offer a promising framework for improving process understanding. However, accurately parameterizing these models remains challenging because of uncertainty in subsurface properties and their spatial heterogeneity. Using Albion Basin in the Wasatch Mountains of Utah as a case study, we investigate which watershed subsurface characteristics, such as porosity, permeability, and depth to bedrock (DTB), exert the greatest control on streamflow throughout the watershed and at the outlet. We also evaluate the degree of spatial heterogeneity required to reproduce observed hydrologic behavior. We simulate watershed hydrology using the Advanced Terrestrial Simulator (ATS), a fully integrated distributed surface-subsurface hydrologic model developed by the U.S. Department of Energy. Model realizations are parameterized using open-source datasets, published literature, and field observations, including geophysical surveys, and are evaluated using distance-based generalized sensitivity analysis. Preliminary results indicate that peak flow, baseflow, and groundwater storage are most sensitive to DTB compared to porosity and permeability, highlighting the dominant role of subsurface water storage capacity in regulating headwater watershed behavior. These findings provide guidance on which watershed properties to prioritize for field observations to better parameterize integrated hydrologic models and improve understanding and prediction of headwater hydrology.

title: Origin of Xenocrystic Zircon from Galapagos Plume-Related Lavas
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Stanley, Rei Naomi [1], Banik, Tenley J [2]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(2) Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
abstract:
The Galápagos mantle plume has existed for ~90 Myr (e.g., Trela et al., 2015). In several mantle plumes, including the Galápagos plume, xenocrystic zircon that pre-dates their host lavas have been reported (e.g., Galápagos Islands, Easter Island/Rapanui) (Rojas-Agramonte et al., 2022, 2024). The presence of these older zircons has been explained by the contamination of the asthenosphere by subducted material (Rojas-Agramonte et al., 2022), then survival of zircon over extended time periods in a relatively stationary mantle. Here, we present geochronological and geochemical analyses of xenocrystic zircon from two Galápagos plume-related sites to investigate the origin and transportation of these older zircons.

We extracted zircon from two picrites—one from the Tortugal suite, Costa Rica, and one from Curaçao—that were previously studied by Trela et al. 2017 and Trela et al. 2015, respectively. The zircon grains were analyzed by SHRIMP-RG at Stanford University for trace element compositions and U-Pb ages.

Zircon U-Pb ages from both samples (n=22) have a weighted mean age of 732 +/- 6Ma and a median of 768 Ma; Curacao is slightly older with a weighted mean age of 726 +/- 8 Ma, while Tortugal zircon has a weighted mean age of ​771 +/- 10 Ma, both with one outlier rejected. Both samples’ zircons have median Ti = 18 ppm, Hf=9,360 ppm, and Th/U= 0.61.

While ~2/3 of the zircons between 950 and 560 Ma appear to have MOR-like affinities, the remaining zircon compositions straddle the continental, mid-ocean ridge, and ocean island domains of Grimes et al. (2015), complicating interpretation of their genesis and history. This suggests that their genesis is likely two-fold, with some grains resulting from local basement rocks, while others appear to be related to the rifting of Rodinia. Regardless, all zircons are substantially older than their Cretaceous host lavas. These results are comparable to other recent studies that indicate long-lived zircons in the Galapágos hotspot.

title: Leveraging the new LaICa Geodatabase for Regional-Scale Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Campania Region (Italy)
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Calcaterra, Domenico [1], Bausilio, Giuseppe [2], De Vita, Pantaleone [3], Di Martire, Diego [4], Shafi, Sedra [5], Guerriero, Luigi [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental and Resources Sciences, University of Naples Federico II, Naples, Italy

abstract:
Landslides are among the most significant geohazards in the Campania Region (southern Italy), where nearly 60% of the territory is susceptible to slope instability. Regional-scale susceptibility assessment has long been constrained by fragmented inventories, inconsistent classifications, and heterogeneous mapping criteria.

To address these limitations, we developed the Landslide Inventory of the Campania Region (LaICa), a harmonized geodatabase integrating 83,284 landslide records from the Southern Apennine Hydrological District, the Italian IFFI inventory, and published studies within a standardized classification framework. A key feature of LaICa is the explicit distinction between detachment/source areas and transit/accumulation zones, enabling more robust representation of landslide initiation processes. Nevertheless, some movement types inherited from the source inventories (e.g., creep) cannot be unambiguously reconciled with internationally adopted classification schemes, representing a residual source of uncertainty that will require further harmonization in future versions of the database. From the mapped detachment/source areas, maximum-elevation points were extracted as reproducible proxies for landslide initiation locations. These points were combined with an equal number of non-landslide background samples, producing a balanced dataset of 88,108 observations. Each sample was associated with regional-scale morphometric, geological, geomorphological, hydrological, rainfall, soil, and land-cover predictors. Random Forest models were trained using an 80/20 training-testing split to evaluate both overall landslide susceptibility and susceptibility for five movement types.

The global susceptibility model achieved a hold-out ROC-AUC of 0.818, while movement-specific models yielded ROC-AUC values ranging from 0.796 to 0.937, with the highest predictive performance for falls, rotational slides, and rotational flows. Comparison between the global model and the combined movement-specific susceptibility maps highlights areas where process-specific modeling substantially alters predicted susceptibility.

These results demonstrate that the homogenized LaICa inventory provides a robust foundation for regional-scale susceptibility assessment, improving spatial consistency and predictive performance relative to legacy inventories. The proposed framework supports territorial planning, civil protection, and spatial decision-support applications, while providing a transferable methodology for landslide-prone regions across the Apennines and the Mediterranean.

title: Preliminary Bedrock and Surficial Geologic Map of the McGaheysville 7.5-Minute Quadrangle in Northern Virginia
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Carver, Rebecca [1], Shannon, Carly [2], Phelps, Isabella [3], Isaacson, Bjorn [4], McKenzie, Kirsty [5], Whitmeyer, Steven J. [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA

abstract: The McGaheysville Quadrangle in northern Virginia extends from Page Valley in the northwest into Shenandoah National Park in the southeast. The geology consists of Quaternary alluvial and colluvial deposits, Cambrian to Ordovician bedrock within Page Valley, and Pre-Cambrian to Cambrian bedrock within the Blue Ridge Province. Current mapping has focused on the southeast portion of the Quadrangle, where we have identified five bedrock units and one surficial deposit. The oldest unit is the Swift Run Formation, an arkosic phyllite that has undergone greenschist facies metamorphism. The Catoctin Formation lies above the Swift Run Formation and is a metamorphosed basalt with prominent foliation, chlorite mineral lineations, and localized epidote veining. We also commonly observe lenses of the Catoctin Formation interbedded with the Swift Run Formation. Above the Catoctin Formation we observe the Weverton, Harpers, and Antietam Formations. The Weverton Formation is a coarse-grained, quartz-rich sandstone, with occasional quartz pebble horizons. The Harpers Formation is a grey to brown phyllitic shale interbedded with sandstones, with sandstone beds ranging in thickness from cm to m scale. The Antietam Formation is a quartz-rich sandstone to quartzite which commonly contains Skolithos. One surficial deposit has been observed along Gap Run, consisting of mature sub-angular to sub-rounded cobbles that are moderately sorted. Field data collection is being conducted digitally using the StraboSpot application and a USGS LiDAR-derived hillshade map. We present a preliminary geologic map created using ArcGIS Pro. Future work will focus on structural and bedrock mapping into the northwest portion of the Quadrangle and ground-truthing LiDAR-based mapping of surficial deposits.

title: Beyond Cataloging: Developing Sustainable Curatorial Practices for University Natural History Collections
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Hines, Ember Raine [1], Eichler, Carla M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Natural Sciences, West Texas A&M, Canyon, TX, USA
(2) West Texas A&M University, Amarillo, TX,
abstract: Beyond Cataloging: Developing Sustainable Curatorial Practices for University Natural History Collections West Texas A&M University houses an extensive collection of geological, paleontological, mineralogical, and comparative biology specimens that represent a valuable resource for teaching, research, and public outreach. Ongoing efforts have focused on developing and implementing a standardized curatorial methodology to preserve and improve access to geological, mineralogical, paleontological, and comparative biology collections. This work extends beyond digital cataloging by integrating museum curation principles into classroom collections through specimen stabilization, archival storage, standardized metadata, hazard identification, taxonomic verification, and the development of searchable digital records linked to physical specimens using QR technology. The project engenders long-term stewardship of natural resources by establishing protocols that reduce specimen degradation, improve traceability, and facilitate instructional use while minimizing unnecessary handling. Reorganization of legacy collections has recovered numerous unidentified and improperly stored specimens, allowing these resources to be reincorporated into laboratory instruction, undergraduate research, and community outreach. By combining physical conservation with modern digital collection management, this methodology provides a scalable framework for institutions seeking to revitalize teaching collections without requiring extensive museum infrastructure. This ongoing engagement demonstrates how systematic curation strengthens the educational and scientific value of university collections while promoting responsible management of natural heritage resources. The framework developed at West Texas A&M University offers a practical model for protecting, preserving, and expanding access to geoscience collections that support both current instruction and future research efforts.

title: Assessing Nutrient and Water Quality Dynamics Across a Nature-Based Treatment System in the Franschhoek Valley, South Africa
session_title: Nature-based Solutions Research for Water Security in Peri-Urban Africa (Posters)
authors: White, Ariel [1], LaVanchy, Cade [2], Winter, Kevin J. [3], Hoover, Joseph H. [4], Kerwin, Michael W. [5], LaVanchy, Thomas [6]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Computer Science, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Future Water Institute, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa
(4) Environmental Science, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(5) Geography & the Environment, University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(6) Geography, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: Surface water quality degradation is an ongoing global challenge that may be addressed using adaptive, nature-based approaches. Situated in the peri-urban Franschhoek Valley of South Africa, the Water Hub was created to address contamination of the Stiebeuel River using sustainable treatment methods in a living laboratory setting. Samples were collected from seven sites: five spread throughout the biofiltration systems of the constructed wetlands, one within the Stiebeuel River, and one from water filtered through the biofiltration systems and fed to the irrigation tank used for the Water Hub's gardens. Samples were measured for ammonia-nitrogen and orthophosphate before and after rainfall events, and these results were compared against dissolved oxygen (DO), electrical conductivity (EC), pH, and turbidity to assess treatment success. Post-rainfall data showed a significant reduction in both orthophosphate and ammonia-nitrogen levels. Comparing these results to pre-rainfall data from the 2025–2026 summer season, the increase in precipitation into the surface water system was consistent with dilution of water nutrients, as reflected by a notable decrease in EC alongside the observed reduction in ammonia-nitrogen and orthophosphate. The Stiebeuel River site showed the most pronounced change, with mean ammonia-nitrogen and orthophosphate decreasing by 39.1% and 44.9%, respectively (16.806 to 10.235 mg/L and 4.654 to 2.563 mg/L). These water chemistry shifts suggest that water quality degradation was lessened following rainfall events. The combined effect of rainfall and nature-based treatment on surface water pollutants highlights the potential of such systems to reduce pollutant loads and improve river health. These findings offer a scalable model for addressing water treatment challenges in South Africa and in similar peri-urban settings worldwide.

title: Evaluating 2-D Electrical Resistivity Tomography for Detecting Buried Objects in Conductive Soils at a Geophysical Test Site
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Crane, Matthew [1], Elshalkany, Muhamed [2], Rodriguez, William [3], Douglas, Audrey [4], Narimani, Roya [5], Murgulet, Dorina [6]
affiliations: (1) State University of Oneonta, Brooklyn, NY, USA; Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, NY, USA
(2) Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA

abstract: Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) is a well-established geophysical method used for imaging the subsurface by mapping resistivity contrasts that can help to identify changes in lithology, water-bearing formations, buried infrastructure, or contaminant plumes. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of ERT at detecting metallic and non-metallic objects of known sizes and depths (0.5-3 m) in a conductive clay-rich geophysical test site (GTS) at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. Seven ERT surveys were collected, one over each target line, with buried materials including steel drums, manhole well covers, plastic drums and buckets (empty, tap water filled, or 2% saltwater filled), and steel pipes. A Dipole-dipole array with 56 electrodes at 1 m spacing paired with an AGI SuperSting R8 was used in the field, while EarthImager2D was used to analyze and produce inverted resistivity sections (RMS values range from 4.04-4.90%). Results show that ERT detected 35 of 39 objects by mapping their contrasting resistivities as relatively high compared to the surrounding clay soil (<1 Ω-m). Steel drums and manhole well covers were consistent in providing strong contrasting resistivity anomalies (up to 4.6 and 3.3 Ω-m, respectively). While plastic drums and buckets were still detectable, they yielded less consistent results and weaker contrasting resistivity anomalies, possibly due in part to their material type and contents (up to 4.5 Ω-m). Whereas steel pipes were not effectively detected, possibly due to their small dimension (5.08 cm inner diameter) and unfavorable orientations to the survey line (up to 6.1 Ω-m). In addition to material type, the depth and dimension of the buried objects were important factors to ERT’s success, with small sizes and objects buried near the shallow resolution limit (0.5 m) of the 1 m electrode spacing producing weaker or absent anomalies. A possible explanation for additional anomalies at the surface that complicate interpretation includes mud cracks. Overall, these results highlight the importance that material, burial depth, dimension, as well as environmental conditions have on ERT’s effectiveness.

title: A Seesawing Laurentide Ice Sheet: The Surficial Geology of the Arcade and Sardinia 7.5’ Quadrangles, Western New York
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Grasing, Sean P. [1], Briner, Jason P. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, New York, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, New York, USA
abstract: Mapping the surficial geology of glacial landscapes provides insights into the behavior of past ice sheets, aides in finding future sites to study, and is beneficial to society but in western New York no surficial geologic and landforms maps have been formed since the 1970s. We mapped the Arcade and Sardinia 7.5' quadrangles using 1-meter LiDAR, field work, and well logs. In this mapping, we found the Laurentide Ice Sheet advanced and retreated five times between ~28 and 16 ka. These five advances, from oldest to youngest, are as followed: Olean, Kent, Lavery, Defiance, and Lake Escarpment. The Olean advance is represented with a Plum Point Interglacial organic-rich silt deposit along Cattaraugus Creek. The drift associated with the Kent advance is within Cattaraugus creek and in the southernmost portion of the mapping area. After the Kent, as the ice sheet receded it dammed water in Cattaraugus Creek, creating a lake. The advancing ice sheet during the Lavery overrode this lake forming a clast-deficient clay-rich drift. A period of retreat was followed by the short-lived Defiance readvance that began to form the widespread outwash deposits in the region. The receding ice sheet advanced again, in a group of minor readvances called the Lake Escarpment morainic system. This system of advances left the greatest impact on the region. It built moraines, widespread hummocky topography, and a vast outwash plain. We mapped multiple levels of Pleistocene-aged alluvial terraces that grade to glacial lakes in Lake Erie.

abstract:
During the 1960s and early 1970s, the Apollo astronaut field training program consisted of nearly 200 field trips to various lunar analog sites across the USA, Canada, Mexico, Iceland, and Germany. As an essential component of human and robotic investigations of the solar system, these analog sites fit within the geoheritage framework and possess significant scientific, educational, cultural, historical, economic, aesthetic, and recreational values. Collectively, these lunar analog sites represent a diverse collection of volcanic features, impact structures, artificial crater fields, intrusive complexes, and canyon systems offering vital clues to the Moon and beyond. Given that many of the astronauts were test pilots who lacked geologic experience, the need for a concise instructional plan grew increasingly clear to ensure the Apollo crews could successfully explore the geology of the lunar surface while enduring the physical, psychological, and physiological demands of each mission. Today, several of these analog sites continue to inspire or teach future generations and serve as valuable links bridging previous missions with future exploration.

Although the Apollo lunar analog sites are intrinsically scientific and educational in nature, many of these sites are situated within cultural landscapes or represent geologic features that have broader historical, economic, or recreational contexts. For example, many of the analog sites throughout the American West and Hawai’i share deep connections to Indigenous Peoples and are recognized as sacred localities utilized for ceremonial practices, oral traditions, resources (e.g., food, medicine, tools, building materials), shrines, burials, and ongoing cultural use. In the remote Nevada desert, nuclear crater fields of the Nevada National Security Site are relics of the Cold War but offered astronauts rare insights into freshly made crater features and morphologies. Field visits to Sudbury, Canada, provided beneficial information about impact cratering mechanics as they relate to the Moon, but the impact structure is responsible for and associated with the mineralization of valuable Ni, Cu, Co, and Pt ore deposits. Additionally, several analog sites—including Grand Canyon National Park, Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, and Barringer Meteor Crater National Natural Landmark—are administered by the U.S. National Park Service and overlap with popular travel destinations visited by millions of tourists annually.

title: From Sediment Routing to Exhumation in the Southern Appalachian Foreland: Integrated Detrital Zircon U-Pb–Hf Provenance and (U-Th)/He Thermochronology of the Cumberland Plateau, Tennessee
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Posters)
authors: Morris, Abigail [1], Bhattacharya, Gourab [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
abstract:
Grenville-dominated detrital zircon U-Pb age spectra are widespread in upper Paleozoic strata of eastern Laurentia, but their nonuniqueness makes it difficult to distinguish first-cycle orogenic detritus from recycled sedimentary cover and reconstruct foreland-basin sediment routing. We address this ambiguity by integrating U-Pb ages with Th/U ratios and Hf isotopes in eleven sandstone samples (n = 3022 concordant analyses) from Upper Mississippian to Lower Pennsylvanian strata of the Cumberland Plateau, Tennessee, in the southern Appalachian basin. All samples are polymodal and share a first-order architecture of dominant bimodal Grenville, subordinate Alleghanian–Acadian–Taconic, Granite-Rhyolite, Yavapai-Mazatzal, and Neoarchean populations, and pairwise comparison of age distributions yield consistently high similarity across the succession. Zircon εHf(i) values are dominantly juvenile to moderately evolved, with a subordinate tail of strongly evolved compositions concentrated in specific stratigraphic intervals.

Despite this first-order similarity in U-Pb age distributions, non-negative matrix factorization resolves a small number of distinct source end members whose proportions change systematically upsection, defining a multi-phase dispersal history across the Mississippian–Pennsylvanian transition. Comparison with coeval strata in the Black Warrior basin indicates that regional sediment routing was more spatially partitioned than single-trunk axial models imply. An Ouachita source is not required at any stage. Integrated Hf and Th/U data therefore resolve dispersal changes that are not apparent from U-Pb ages alone.

Zircon (U-Th)/He thermochronometry on the same succession shows that 21 of 50 dated grains are thermally reset, indicating variable degrees of thermal resetting across stratigraphic units. Inverse thermal modeling (HeFTy) of the reset grains indicates maximum burial temperatures of ~140–200 °C across the plateau and cooling between ca. 320 and 250 Ma, coincident with the late stages of the Alleghanian–Ouachita orogeny and most plausibly recording regional exhumation of the southern Appalachian basin. Together, the provenance and thermochronologic records link changing sediment sources in the Carboniferous foreland to burial and subsequent unroofing of the basin itself, providing an integrated view of how orogenic loading, drainage reorganization, and late Paleozoic exhumation were coupled along the southern Laurentian margin.

title: Trilobite Behavior and Evolution Over the Precambrian-Cambrian Boundary in the White-Inyo Mountains and Death Valley (CA, NV)
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination (Posters)
authors: Dodd, Lily [1], Bottjer, David J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
Here we present evidence of suggested biotic interactions between the earliest Cambrian trilobites and worms from lower Cambrian strata of the White-Inyo Mountains and Death Valley area in western Nevada and eastern California. This research examines the differences and similarities between trilobites, their evolution and behavior over the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary between two depositional environments. The depositional environment of the lower Cambrian Campito Formation of the White-Inyo Mountains is considered to be relatively shallow, located distally on the continental slope of a passive margin, likely between fair weather wave base and storm wave base. Conversely, the depositional environment of the Wood Canyon Formation in the Death Valley area represents a more proximal environment to the shoreline. Both formations contain some of the first trilobite body fossils found in the United States. However, arthropod trace fossils occur in much older Precambrian strata at both locations. Therefore, it is commonly believed that trilobites evolved prior to their appearance in the fossil record from an unmineralized Precambrian ancestor.

This project examines not only the first trilobite body fossils, but also the first arthropod traces, to learn more about trilobite evolution and behavior prior to and during the Cambrian Explosion. Methods of investigation include analysis of early Cambrian trilobite body fossils and Precambrian-Cambrian arthropod trace fossils reposited at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County and the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, as well as thin section analysis of these specimens. This project is unique in that it is the first to integrate investigations of the paleontology and sedimentology of these formations on a microscopic scale.

Preliminary results from trace fossils show evidence of biotic interactions between Precambrian-Cambrian arthropods and worms. There appears to be a close and common relationship between arthropod traces and worm burrows at both depositional environments. This suggests that arthropods and worms have had a biotic relationship since before the mineralization of trilobites in the early Cambrian. Additionally, the presence of microscopic Planolites burrows associated with trilobite-bearing strata, further suggests a biotic relationship between trilobites and the trace makers. Though it is commonly accepted that trilobites preyed on worms during the Cambrian, it is unclear what the relationship is between Precambrian arthropods and worms. Further study is needed to confirm this relationship.

abstract: Approximately 15% of the U.S. population relies on groundwater as a source of drinking water; however, comprehensive assessments of both conventional and emerging contaminants in private wells remain limited. This study evaluates private well water quality across five counties along the Texas Gulf Coast spanning an urbanization gradient, from the highly urbanized Houston metropolitan area to less developed coastal regions of central Texas. The study also includes wells located near industrial facilities and Superfund sites. Preliminary results indicate that total coliform was the most frequently detected contaminant exceeding drinking water guidelines. Elevated aluminum concentrations were likely associated with local geological conditions, while exceedances of EPA secondary drinking water standards, particularly for total dissolved solids and sulfate, were more common in wells located near the coastline. Initial nano- and microplastics analyses detected PVC and PET, indicating the presence of microplastics in well water and suggesting that well plumbing materials may contribute to their occurrence. PCB and PAH concentrations were below applicable drinking water guidelines in all wells analyzed, while ongoing PFAS analyses will further evaluate the occurrence of emerging contaminants, particularly in wells near industrial and Superfund sites. This comprehensive assessment will improve understanding of groundwater quality across the Gulf Coast and provide information to support private well owners, local agencies, and groundwater management strategies.

title: An Alternative Drainage Evolution of the Colorado Plateau for the Past 10 Million Years
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Ganahl, Rolf R. [1]
affiliations: (1) 455 Duffy Drive, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Colorado River is mapped flowing through Canyonlands since Late Miocene time (e.g. Hunt, 1956, 1969). Recent reports show that the river should have reached the Bidahochi area of northeastern Arizona (e.g. Hé et al., 2026; Karlstrom et al., 2026; Dallegge et al, 2003). Many reports suggest that there should have been a lake ponded along Glen Canyon east of the Henry Mountains, and/or north of Navajo Mountain (e.g. Hunt, 1956; Hill and Polyak, 2015, 2020); the lake’s existence uncertain as deposits have not been found. Deposits of Bidahochi area have been documented (e.g. Hack, 1942; Repenning and Irwin, 1954; Repenning et al,. 1958; Dallegge, 1999); Repenning et al. dividing the Bidahochi formation into a lower lacustrine, a middle volcanic, and an upper fluvial member; with Dallegge further separating these into six members. According to Repenning et al. deposition of both lower and upper members must have come from a source located to the northeast .

Gravel deposits near Gateway, Colorado (Balco et al., 2013), are interpreted to show that the ancestral Grand River (former Colorado River, here aGD) should still have been present in Unaweep Canyon ~2.3 million years ago, with geomorphic evidence suggesting that such drainage should have flowed south from the canyon exit — rather than following the generally assumed northern route. This evidence is used to propose an aGD route along future Dolores River towards southwestern Colorado, and into northwestern New Mexico, eventually reaching the Bidahochi area in Arizona from the expected northeasterly direction! An ancestral Green River (aGR) would join this ancestral drainage with a route from Green River (Utah) via Dewey Bridge, along future Dolores to join the ancestral Grand in the Gateway area. As will be shown, neither aGR nor aGD would flow near Canyonlands until much later. Based on the DZ profiles (Hé et al., 2026; Karlstrom et al., 2026) a Grand and (Utah-) Green River source can be attributed at circa 6 Ma, perhaps as early as 11 Ma, with a plausible route of the sources along the proposed course. Progressive drainage changes since cutting of the Kaibab Upwarp (6-5 Ma) will allow headward erosion towards the Canyonlands area (Marble, Glen, Cataract Canyons), eventually opening a new route for aGR at ~3 Ma, and incorporating aGD at ~2.2 Ma.

title: Stereogram: A modern and integrated structural analysis software
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research (Posters)
authors: Thacker, Jacob Oliver [1], Stahl, Julian [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology Program, Rocky Mountain College, Billings, MT, USA; Sigma Geoscience, Billings, MT, USA
(2) Sigma Geoscience, Billings, MT, USA
abstract: Current structural analysis software provides powerful tools but various limitations in analytical scope, price/accessibility, and/or modernity. Compounding limitations include data-centered rather than spatially-focused user interfaces, disconnected data collection methods, and complicated data entry or import requirements. Consequently, students and researchers are forced to chain together numerous apps and programs in order to perform a comprehensive structural analysis. These limitations can overwhelm users, especially undergraduate students, who are tasked with learning not only purpose and analytical best practices, but also how to operate multiple platforms with unique workflows. To promote efficiency and accessibility we developed Stereogram, a structural analysis software with accompanying data collection app for iPhone. The mobile app allows users to collect geo-located structural data, field notes, and photos, and perform simple stereonet and rose diagram operations. The Stereogram software is a web-hosted cloud-based application that allows access to the program and users’ data anywhere there is internet access. Data may be imported into Stereogram through a sync operation directly from the mobile app, or through an iterative importer that can read diverse spreadsheet layouts. Data structure in Stereogram is twofold: the Data Library, a repository for user data, and Analysis Datasets, a user-defined collection of data for analysis. Data in both can be displayed spatially from which users may target desired data for analysis (e.g., domains) or non-spatially by other properties (formation, age, etc.). A comprehensive suite of analytical tools are provided: stereonet and rose diagram plotting and operations, fault kinematic analysis, as well as histograms and 2D/3D scatter plots. All tools harbor advanced functionality, including statistical analysis, data overlays, and a rotatable stereonet to aid in visualization. Stereogram allows students and researchers to easily go from data collection and/or import to diverse data analysis through a modern user interface that is integrated, intuitive, and spatially focused. The efficient workflow and platform allows students to effectively focus on learning and analyzing 3D geoscience data whereas researchers may streamline and maximize their analytical output.

title: The Worth of the Ichnofossil—How CT Scans of Vintage Cores can Help Solidify Working Hypotheses for the Clinton Sandstone in Ohio
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections
authors: Thomas, Mindy [1]
affiliations: (1) Ohio Department of Natural Resources, Ohio Geological Survey, Columbus, OH,
abstract: The Silurian Grimsby Formation, perhaps more widely known as the “Clinton sandstone,” is a potentially viable target for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) and enhanced oil recovery (EOR) across the Appalachian Basin of eastern Ohio. CCUS primacy is becoming a reality for the State of Ohio with the recent passage of House Bill 170, which grants exclusive authority of carbon storage to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources. Therefore, a detailed understanding of our potential geologic storage reservoirs is more important than ever for proper management of our subsurface resources. The Ohio Geological Survey’s core repository holds a wealth of cores from all over the state, including numerous vintage cores from the Clinton sandstone interval. Original core studies of the subsurface Clinton interval aimed to identify lithologies, cementation, porosity/permeability, sedimentary structures, and the existence of any burrows. These core studies theorized a variety of depositional environments ranging from shoreface deposits to shelf bar complexes to deltaic deposits. In this study, twelve existing Clinton cores from the geologically complex Gore Consolidated Oil Field (GCOF) in southeastern Ohio have been thoroughly examined and redescribed using new data types and methods. Advances in technology have allowed us to obtain XRF data and computed tomography (CT) scans of the cores captured by the U.S. DOE’s National Energy Technology Laboratory. CT imagery revealed a variety of trace fossils in the Clinton interval that had either been historically overlooked or rudimentarily described as simply horizontal vs. vertical burrows. With the CT scans and the ability to view cores in both vertical and horizontal 3D slices, we can further identify fossil types, diversity, abundance, and sizes. Integrating the trace fossil data into the core descriptions has allowed us to recognize marine ichnofacies (or lack thereof) for each facies type described, which aids in solidifying interpretations of the depositional environments throughout the Clinton interval. With more robust evidence for each depositional environment within the Clinton, we can now more definitively create a sequence-stratigraphic correlation model and stratigraphic framework that support a tidally influenced paleogeographic deltaic model within the GCOF. With these models defined, high-resolution mapping of the Clinton interval can be completed, which will be crucial for implementation of CCUS/EOR in the Clinton sandstone reservoir.

title: Geochemical Analysis of Chalcedony and Quartz from Florida’s Ocala Limestone Using Petrographic, X-Ray Diffraction, and EPMA Techniques: First Identification of Moganite and Quartzine
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Wilke, Elizabeth [1], MacDonald, James H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(2) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
abstract:
Thirteen samples of silicified, late Eocene Ocala Limestone containing chalcedony and quartz were collected from a quarry in Center Hill, Florida. Processing of samples revealed vugs of chalcedony with drusy, macrocrystalline quartz. Petrographic analysis indicated the presence of both chalcedony (length fast) and quartzine (length slow) in radial, alternating bands. A single quartz crystal was isolated for SCXRD analysis at 100 K, and yielded cell lengths a=4.8965Å and c=5.3929Å. The sample was identified to be left-handed quartz. PXRD analysis was conducted on two chalcedony samples. Small peaks around 24° and 31° 2θ indicated the possibility of trace amounts of the polymorph moganite. Rietveld refinement analysis allowed for differentiation of potentially overlapping peaks of chalcedony and moganite. The refinement yielded a significant (~20%) presence of moganite in the samples.

Quantitative point analysis of trace elements was performed via election probe microanalysis (EPMA). When possible, chalcedony and quartzine were differentiated during analysis. Chalcedony has Fe ranging between 1.4 and 52.3 ppm, with an average of 15.1 ppm. Quartz has Fe ranging between 2.6 and 298.2 ppm, with an average of 58.8 ppm. Chalcedony has Ca ranging between 12.3 and 189.8 ppm, with an average of 106.3 ppm; while quartz ranges in Ca between 6.0 and 141.5 ppm, with an average of 59.5 ppm. Chalcedony has Mn ranges between <1.4 and 28.7 ppm, with an average of 10.0 ppm; while quartz ranges in Mn between <1.4 and 15.6 ppm, with an average of 6.1 ppm.

The elevated Fe concentration in quartz compared to chalcedony suggests dissolution of iron oxides during later stages of silicification. This is consistent with pyrite inclusions visible in petrographic analysis. Higher Ca and Mn concentrations in chalcedony suggest its precipitation during early silicification of limestone as calcite was still dissolving. Macrocrystalline quartz crystals represent the last stages of silicification, as lower Ca and Mn concentrations suggest precipitation after carbonate replacement had already occurred. The presence of moganite is consistent with low-temperature diagenetic silica precipitation. This study represents the first documented occurrence of moganite and quartzine in the Ocala Limestone.

title: Initial Investigations of the Yellow Groove Bamboo’s Heavy Metal Bioaccumulation Capabilities in a Coal-Mining Landscape, New River Gorge, West Virginia
session_title: Hydrogeology Discipline Session
authors: Voorhees, Elizabeth Renee [1], Lytle, Marion L. [2], Rader, Shelby True [3], Krekeler, Mark P. S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(3) Indiana University, Bloomington, IN,
(4) Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Recent studies indicate that several bamboo species have potential for phytoremediation; however, limited studies have been conducted in an uncontrolled field setting. The New River Gorge, WV, offers a suitable location to study real-world bamboo-metal interactions due to the heavy metal contamination remnant from extensive coal mining and the presence of the bamboo species Phyllostachys aureosulcata . Fifteen bamboo samples from two privately owned localities with different sized bamboo were collected for analysis and dissected into four parts (roots, stem, branch, leaves). Corresponding soil samples were collected at root depth near the base of each sample. Samples were digested using vegetation-specific and soil-specific methods. High-resolution inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (HR-ICP-MS) was used to determine metal concentrations. Values were used to calculate the bioconcentration factor (BCF; plant tissue-to-soil concentration ratio) and translocation factor (TF; aboveground-to-root concentration ratio) to assess phytoremediation potential for metal species of interest. Results identified metal quantities in bamboo tissues as follows: Hg (0.27 -14.55 ppm), Zn (4.21 - 259.54 ppm), Ba (1.68 - 458.61 ppm), Cu (1.89 - 140.43 ppm), and Pb (0.01 - 15.30 ppm) with quantities largely varying with tissue type and site. Mercury accumulates primarily in roots and leaves; however atmospheric deposition cannot yet be ruled out as the potential source. Nearly all sample and tissue types had a high BCF and low TF, except for four leaf samples having a high BCF and high TF. This indicates efficient accumulation throughout the whole plant and limited translocation. Barium accumulated primarily in the leaves of the samples, with nearly all leaf samples having a high TF and low BCF, indicating high translocation to leaves and lower overall significant accumulation. Zinc displayed high TF and low BCF values across all tissues, indicating high translocation throughout the whole plant and lower overall significant accumulation. Copper had variable results, but generally high root BCF values and low TF values, indicating accumulation is primarily occurring in roots. Lead produced low BCF and TF values for all tissue types, suggesting inefficient uptake. Future work will include scanning electron microscopy analysis to identify the morphology and distribution of metal particles within samples, and X-ray diffraction to identify minerals present within soil samples and ensure soil minerals are consistent with local lithology.

abstract: Debris flows are devastating natural, and sometimes human exacerbated disasters. The Oregon Cascade Range is prone to debris flows and the frequency of these events will likely increase with climate change due to changes in the frequency and magnitude of atmospheric rivers and forest fires. A detailed history of past debris flows is foundational to modeling hazard zones, predicting future events, and implementing risk reduction. The purpose of this study was to create a 35-year inventory of debris flows in the Oregon Cascade Range. This was accomplished using serial statewide orthophotos from 1995 to 2024. The aerial imagery was grouped into ~5-year epochs, allowing us to create seven datasets covering each epoch. We observed events in the orthophotos that persisted at least 5 years, so we estimated that we could see events from approximately 5 years prior to the first set of orthophotos (1995), making the first epoch ~1990-1995 and thus the total timeframe of 35 years. The mapping process consisted of mapping two spatial components: (1) a point in the central upper area of the debris flow initiation site (or other landslide type), and (2) a line along the center of the transport/inundation path in the case of a channelized debris flow. There is almost complete LiDAR topographic coverage for the study area, which complimented interpretation of the orthophotos and greatly improved locating the debris flows. To date, we have mapped approximately 5,000 debris flows and landslides; mapping is still underway for 2014-2020 and 2020-2024. We identified 1,263 debris flows or other landslides in the ~1990-1995 epoch, 2,178 in 1995-2000, 202 in 2000-2005, 423 in 2005-2009, and 894 in 2009-2014. There are an average of 992 debris flows and landslides per epoch and epochs with large storm events generally had larger numbers of debris flows. For example, the 1995-2000 epoch included a series of atmospheric rivers in February 1996, had more than twice the average. These data are essential for modeling hazard zones which can be used to implement risk reduction in the Oregon Cascade Range.

title: Mapping the Cretaceous Terrestrial Rock Record of the Western United States to Evaluate Bias Across the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: Menton, Bayden [1], King, Michael Ryan [2], Zanno, Lindsay [3]
affiliations: (1) Western Colorado University, Superior, CO,
(2) Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO,
(3) NC Museum of Natural Sciences, Paleontology, Raleigh, NC, ; Department of Biological Sciences, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA
abstract:
This project develops a digital geospatial dataset of Cretaceous outcrops in the western United States to evaluate how the distribution and exposure of sedimentary rocks may bias interpretations of biodiversity across the Cenomanian-Turonian Cretaceous Thermal Maximum (KTM). Geologic context is essential for relating fossil occurrences to depositional environments and assessing stratigraphic biases produced by incomplete preservation and limited surface exposure.

A replicable workflow was developed to compile and digitize geologic-unit boundaries from 47 online maps published by the United States Geological Survey and Utah Geological Survey, preferentially using 1:24,000-scale maps. Units were digitized in ArcGIS Pro, with emphasis on terrestrial, fine-grained clastic deposits that may have greater potential to preserve fossils. Most boundaries were digitized manually, although several Utah maps were available as existing digital datasets.

The compiled data is affected by the discontinuous nature of the Lower Cretaceous because of widespread unconformities and the preserved Turonian strata are dominated by marine deposits associated with the Western Interior Seaway. Outside the Naturita Formation/Dakota Sandstone, terrestrial units relevant to contextualizing the KTM are largely concentrated in east-central Utah and western Colorado, with smaller exposures in Montana, southern Nevada, and western Arizona. Data gaps remain along parts of the Utah-Colorado border, and some smaller-scale maps combine targeted units with the Dakota Sandstone.

The resulting dataset provides a foundation for quantifying mid-Cretaceous outcrop area, evaluating depositional and preservation biases, identifying poorly mapped regions, and guiding future field research through integration with land-ownership and access data.

title: Timing and Deformation of Permian Subduction Metamorphism in the Vedder Complex, southern British Columbia and northwest Washington
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Rayburn, Sydney Elizabeth [1], Mulcahy, Sean R. [2], Apen, Francisco [3], Epstein, Gabe [4], Wang, Jordan W. [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(2) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(3) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(4) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(5) University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
High-pressure/low-temperature (HP/LT) rocks along the western margin of North America record subduction metamorphism from the Paleozoic through the Cretaceous, however, the timing and duration of Permian-Triassic subduction remains poorly constrained. This study integrates detailed structural analysis with titanite and rutile U-Pb geochronology and amphibole and white mica 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dating to constrain the evolution of HP/LT rocks in the Vedder Complex of southern British Columbia and the Groat Mountain Complex of northwest Washington. Both occur as tectonic blocks within the Cretaceous Bell Pass mélange of the Northwest Cascades–San Juan Islands thrust system and have published K-Ar and Rb-Sr ages that range from 286 to 198 Ma.

The Vedder Complex consists of garnet-epidote amphibolite, actinolite schist, and graphitic-garnet schist that preserve a polyphase deformation history: relict S 1 foliation within garnet and albite porphyroblasts (D1), a dominant regional S 2 foliation with intrafolial F 2 folds (D2), and outcrop scale F 3 folds (D3). The Groat Mountain Complex preserves quartzose schist and amphibole schist with greenschist/blueschist to lower-amphibolite facies metamorphism and a comparable deformation history

New geochronologic data constrain peak subduction related metamorphism to the Permian. U-Pb ages coupled with 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages from both regions indicate prograde to peak metamorphism between 292 and 275 Ma, followed by cooling and exhumation until circa 212 Ma. This implies Permian subduction metamorphism occurred over a relatively short ~10 m.y. interval rather than the ~76 m.y. span previously inferred from legacy K-Ar and Rb-Sr ages, many of which likely record cooling rather than metamorphism.

New igneous and detrital zircon U-Pb ages and whole rock geochemistry refine regional correlations. The data support existing correlations of the Vedder Complex amphibolites to the Garrison Schist of the San Juan Islands. Gabbro juxtaposed with the Vedder Complex amphibolite is correlated with the Devonian Turtleback Complex and sedimentary rocks structurally juxtaposed against the Vedder Complex correlate with the Bell Pass mélange.

The resulting ages reveal an approximately 100 m.y. gap between subduction metamorphism in Permian Vedder Complex and nearby Jurassic-Cretaceous Easton Metamorphic Suite. This can be explained either by a long record of discontinuous subduction and accretion along this portion of Cordilleran margin or by an incomplete record of the Permian and younger subduction history preserved in the Vedder and Groat Mountain Complexes.

title: From Iceland to Alpha Regio: Rehearsing DAVINCI’s Descent over Venus Analog Terrains
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: Kohler, Erika [1], Garvin, James B [2], Scheidt, Stephen P [3], Slayback, Dan A [4], Ravine, Michael [5], Arney, Giada [6], Getty, Stephanie [7], Johnson, Natasha M. [8]

abstract:
NASA's DAVINCI mission will conduct near-infrared descent imaging over Venus's Alpha Regio tesserae in the early 2030s, providing the first high-resolution optical images of Venus's surface from ~21 km to touchdown. The Venus Descent Imager (VenDI) will enable quantitative evaluation of geological processes and rock compositions. However, no high-resolution optical data from Venus currently exists to inform descent imaging strategies or interpret sub-cloud deck observations. To address this gap, we conducted an extensive UAS-based imaging campaign over the Sandfellshaed lava shield and other sites in Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula. These terrestrial analog sites serve as "training landscapes" for DAVINCI data pipelines, establishing spatial discrimination thresholds for interpreting Venus surface processes from descent imagery and derived Digital Elevation Models (DEMs).

Over four active field days, our team deployed uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) to collect georeferenced imagery across ~1 km² of the Sandfellshaed complex and fresh Svartsengi lavas. We employed flight modes replicating DAVINCI scenarios: (1) wide-area terrain mapping flights (4 cm/pixel GSD) for comprehensive DEM generation via Structure-from-Motion (SfM), (2) simulated descent imaging sequences from maximum permissible altitude mimicking DAVINCI's trajectory, (3) Super-Low Altitude Mode (SLAM) traverse flights capturing sub-centimeter surface detail, and (4) targeted imaging of specific volcanic features. Processing over 800 overlapping frames using commercial software and custom NASA SfM pipelines, we generated multi-scale DEMs ranging from 5 cm regional grids to sub-centimeter local patches.

The Sandfellshaed monogenetic lava shield provides an exceptional analog for Venus's volcanic plains and tessera inter-ridge systems. The site's combination of smooth lava surfaces, rugose textures, and structural lineaments offered ideal conditions for establishing feature recognition thresholds relevant to VenDI's objectives.

This campaign produced benchmark descent sequences and multi-scale topographic datasets essential for interpreting future Venus observations at scales inaccessible from orbit. We established critical spatial scale dependencies, from centimeters to meters, for volcanic landscape discrimination, directly supporting VenDI experiment planning. The multi-scale approach developed here bridges the gap between orbital radar data and surface observations, providing vital "training data" for automated feature recognition algorithms. These methodologies will enhance DAVINCI's operational planning and establish protocols applicable to future comparative planetary studies.

title: Microbial mat primary productivity and pore water microenvironments controlled by changing ice cover attributes in a perennially ice-covered lake of the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Mackey, Tyler James [1], Kohl, Jove [2], Juarez Rivera, Marisol [3], Judge, Lauren [4], Takacs-Vesbach, Cristina [5], Morgan-Kiss, Rachael [6], Doran, Peter [7], Dugan, Hilary [8], Lawrence, Jade [9], Gooseff, Michael N. [10]

abstract:
The majority of net primary productivity in the polar desert ecosystems of the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica, takes place in microbial mats of meltwater streams or perennially ice-covered lakes (PICLs), which have seasonal liquid moats on the lake edge and perennial liquid water under the ice cover. Microbial mats across these habitats are sensitive to changing climate of the region, including both increased stream melt with resulting lake level rise and variation in the thickness of the perennial ice cover. In this contribution, we investigate the relative role of lake level and ice cover on benthic mat primary productivity in Lake Fryxell to assess the potential implications of future change on these microbially-dominated ecosystems. Conditions in regional lakes have been monitored by the McMurdo Dry Valleys Long Term Ecological Research project since 1993, and long-term data sets demonstrate that ice cover thickness and transmissivity has a stronger control on total surface area for net mat growth than changes in lake level.

Changes in ice cover thickness also affect the patterns of sedimentation in PICLs; aeolian sands are deposited on the PICL ice cover, and grains annually melt through thinner ice covers but accumulate within thicker ice covers before episodically working their way through the ice to form discrete sand mounds. Patterns of sand deposition have the potential to affect the local light environment in benthic mats, and we characterized spatial relationships among sand layers, microbial mat annual laminae, and carbonate precipitation with X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT). XCT observations and measurements of annual biomass accumulation indicate that thin mm-scale sediment layers are sufficient to significantly reduce photosynthetic activity within the benthic mats. Taken together, the thickness and associated transmissivity of the Lake Fryxell ice cover exert a strong control on the potential for benthic mat photosynthetic activity through both the amount of photosynthetically active radiation reaching the lake bottom and the patterns of sand sedimentation that control light transmission into the benthic mats. Anticipated changes to the Lake Fryxell ice cover and those of other PICLs could accordingly affect the overall primary productivity of these polar desert ecosystems.

title: Base level fall, erosion, and orogenesis in western Mongolia from new alluvial 10-Be cosmogenic measurements and erodibility-corrected inversions of fluvial topography
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Pazzaglia, Frank J. [1], Vaughan, Nora [2], Ganbold, Baatarsuren [3], Rugenstein, Jeremy Kesner Caves [4], Corbett, Lee [5], Bierman, Paul R. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA, USA
(3) Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics, Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia
(4) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(5) Community Cosmogenic Facility, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
(6) Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
abstract: The Mongolian Altai of central Asia currently intercept the prevailing westerlies, driving aridification in the Gobi, and contributing to the long-term cooling of global climate, but the timing of uplift remains unclear. New alluvial 10 Be terrestrial cosmogenic nuclide measurements from nine watersheds ranging in size from ~10 – 1000 km 2 in the Mongolian Altai and Khangai Mountains of western Mongolia help resolve the timing by reconstructing the history of base level fall for rivers that drain into the Great Lakes Depression (GLD). Erosion rates (E) in the Khangai Mountains determined from the 10 Be data are slow at 9+/-1, 10+/-0.2, and 11+/-1m/Myr, independent of catchment size, and consistent with other published geomorphic and thermochronologic data. Stream power based inversions of fluvial topography for Khangai catchments using both uniform and variable erodibility (K) assumptions reveal similar base level fall histories characterized by near steady rock uplift for the past 50 Ma at a rate of ~10-15 m/Myr and consistent with the 10 Be results. In contrast, catchments of the Mongolian Altai indicate a wider range of erosion rates ranging from 40+/-3 to 51+/-5 m/Myr for small range-front catchments on major transpressional blocks and 8+/-0.2 to 19+/-2 m/Myr for large catchments that drain the glaciated hinterland of the range. Small catchments sourced in lesser transpressional blocks have erosion rates of 19+/-2 to 33+/-3 m/Myr. The 10 Be measurements appear to be influenced by catchment size, indicating significant sediment storage and remobilization of older basin sediment in the larger catchments. Inversions of Altai fluvial topography with these E data, particularly those that consider rock-type distribution driven variations in K, generate unsteady base level fall histories with accelerations at ~30, 10, 5, and 2 Ma, consistent with unconformities and facies changes documented in a new age model for GLD synorogenic growth strata. Collectively, the 10 Be data, fluvial inversions, and comparison to the stratigraphy in the GLD suggest GLD subsidence and initial Altai uplift associated with the opening of Lake Baikal at ~30 Ma, followed by continued extension and local footwall uplift from ~20-6 Ma, then inversion of the normal faults and onset of crustal shortening accommodated by transpression. The transpressional Mongolian Altai ultimately grew to a width and elevation capable of intercepting significant meridional moisture in the Plio-Pleistocene.

title: Beyond Compliance: Building a Culture of Digital Accessibility at the Kentucky Geological Survey
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation (Posters)
authors: Curl, Douglas C [1], Hohman, Cheynne [2]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
abstract:
State geological surveys communicate science through sprawling collections of digital assets: websites, searchable databases, interactive maps and ArcGIS StoryMaps, PDF publications and maps, presentations, images, and audio and video media. When any of these are inaccessible to people using assistive technologies, the science they contain is effectively unavailable to part of the public it is meant to serve. Prompted by the April 2026 federal deadline requiring conformance with WCAG 2.1 AA standards under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Kentucky Geological Survey (KGS) undertook a comprehensive effort to make its digital resources accessible and, just as importantly, to build an internal culture where accessibility becomes a routine part of how staff create and publish content.

This presentation shares KGS’s practical experience from July 2025 through April 2026 and beyond. We describe a phased approach that began with adopting a formal accessibility work plan,cataloging all digital asset types, and deploying several accessibility tools for evaluating our digital content. We detail remediation strategies tailored to distinct asset types: correcting the most common web issues (insufficient color contrast, missing alternative text, unlabeled form elements, absent language tags, and keyboard navigation) by leveraging shared code and AI-assisted coding tools; a PowerPoint-based technique for converting complex geologic maps into accessible PDFs; producing accessible alternative publications; and generating transcripts and captions for KGS YouTube videos and the KGS podcast, The Big Blue Rock Pod.

Equally central was developing KGS staff buy-in. We delivered a series of three staff training workshops, built a shared library of accessible templates and resources, and established clear guidance for archived materials. Several lessons emerged from this work: compliance follows culture, progress matters more than perfection (especially for complex assets like maps), human assistance should always be easy to find, and accessibility is a sustained effort rather than a one-time project. The KGS experience offers a transferable model for other geoscience organizations to make their digital assets accessible to all users.

title: UAV-Based Digital Outcrop Modeling for Stratigraphic Correlation Across the Carboniferous Succession of the Southern Appalachian Basin, Tennessee
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Babbit, Gabriel S. [1], Seiling, Asher A. [2], Roberson, R. Philip [3], Bhattacharya, Gourab [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee, USA
(3) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
(4) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
abstract:
Large roadcut exposures preserve critical records of depositional environments, facies changes, bedding variations, and lateral stratigraphic continuity. However, steep geometry, height, and highway safety constraints often limit direct field observation and physical measurement. Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based photogrammetry enables the generation of high-resolution, three-dimensional (3D) digital outcrop models (DOMs) for investigating stratigraphic relationships in otherwise inaccessible portions of an outcrop.

We surveyed and modeled six prominent roadcut exposures across the southern Appalachian Basin in Tennessee using an Autel EVO II Pro 6K RTK V3 UAV. Individual exposures reach up to 210 m in length and 35 m in height. For each outcrop, we captured ~700–800 high-resolution images with ≥80% spatial overlap. Image sets were processed using OpenDroneMap on a high-performance computing cluster to generate georeferenced 3D point clouds. The resulting point clouds were post-processed in CloudCompare to remove vegetation, noise, and non-geologic artifacts prior to interpretation.

Integrating field measurements with spatial calibration in the DOMs enabled tracing of marker beds, assessment of bed-thickness variations, identification of formation contacts, and stratigraphic correlation across paired opposing roadcut faces. The datasets include paired outcrops which expose the Upper Devonian Chattanooga Shale and Lower Mississippian Maury and Fort Payne Formations, as well as paired exposures of the Upper Mississippian Pennington Formation. Additional standalone models document the Lower Pennsylvanian Warren Point Sandstone of the Gizzard Group, and strata of the Lower Pennsylvanian Crab Orchard Mountains Group, formerly assigned to the Fentress Formation. Collectively, the DOMs capture a key Carboniferous stratigraphic transition from organic-rich marine shale and carbonate-bearing Lower Mississippian strata to fine-grained Upper Mississippian carbonate and siliciclastic deposits up to resistant Lower Pennsylvanian coal-bearing sandstone units.

These DOMs establish a high-fidelity digital archive of Carboniferous exposures across Tennessee’s Eastern Highland Rim and Cumberland Plateau, supporting remote quantitative stratigraphic analysis, cross-roadcut correlation, and virtual examination beyond normal field-access limits. They also preserve geologic information from the southern Appalachian Basin that is vulnerable to weathering and modification during highway maintenance.

title: New Surficial Geologic Map of Nebraska Synthesizes Data and Provides New Interpretations at a Synoptic Scale
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: Barrette, Nolan Conroy [1], Johnstone, Sam Adam [2], Joeckel, R. M. (Matt) [3], Hanson, Paul R. [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(3) University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE,
(4) University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE,
abstract:
More than 87% of Nebraska is mantled by unconsolidated Pliocene, Pleistocene, and Holocene sediments, of which are mostly eolian sand and silt. These sediments are conduits for groundwater recharge, are sources of construction materials, are nutrient sources and substrate for crops, and support critical habitats along the Central Flyway. Nebraska is situated in a unique location between the Rocky Mountains and the heart of the glaciated Central Lowland. Because of this, the Conservation and Survey Division (CSD) has been focused on detailed geologic mapping in the state at 1:24,000 scale since the mid-1990s, rather than smaller scale maps. Additionally, due to this unique geographical setting, Nebraska was one of the only states not covered by a statewide surficial geologic map. Instead, CSD circulated a statewide bedrock geologic map.

Our new statewide Surficial Geologic Map of Nebraska (1:500,000) is an important step forward in surficial geologic mapping. CSD personnel at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and the USGS cooperated to integrate local geologic knowledge from the CSD with data management and GIS techniques from the USGS to formulate new geologic interpretations and draft a new statewide map. This cooperative mapping effort utilized existing geologic, soil, and geomorphic maps, and took advantage of statewide lidar-derived elevation models from the USGS 3DEP program. The Surficial Geologic Map of Nebraska documents our understanding of regional geomorphology around the intersection of the Great Plains and Central Lowland physiographic provinces, highlighting geologic features that exist near the margins of the glacial sediments in the east and the mountains in the west. The map provides a broad view of Nebraska’s varied landscapes, thereby supporting interdisciplinary analyses and documenting aspects of the state’s geology at a new and synoptic scale.
