title: Assessment of undiscovered, conventional oil and gas resources in the Buda Limestone of Texas, 2025
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Lohr, Celeste D. [1], Doolan, Colin A. [2], Merrill, Matthew D. [3], Craddock, William H. [4], Gardner, Rand [5], Anderson, Christopher P. [6], Le, Phuong A. [7], Mercier, Tracey J. [8]

abstract:
The U.S. Geological Survey recently assessed the potential for undiscovered, technically recoverable, conventional oil and gas resources in the Cenomanian Buda Limestone of Texas. This geologic formation, which comprises a 30-160-foot-thick, extensive, low-energy, coccolith-rich limestone, was previously assessed in 1995 and 2010. In 2025 the formation was reassessed to account for increased horizontal drilling and production since the 2010 assessment; the expansion of several major producing field areas; its stratigraphic proximity to the Eagle Ford Group, which has recently been proven as a prolific hydrocarbon producer and is considered the primary source of the hydrocarbons that migrated into the Buda Limestone; and to include the East Texas basin.

Hydrocarbon accumulation in the tight limestone requires extensive fractures, fault-induced brecciation, or some matrix porosity and occurs where large fractures or higher effective porosity and permeability intervals are present, stratigraphically trapping the hydrocarbons against an impermeable rock such as the overlying Eagle Ford Group. Growth faults or folded anticlines also trap hydrocarbons within the limestone. The geologic model is similar for the East Texas basin, though oil produced from its northern area may be sourced from Jurassic rocks whereas to the south oil and gas may be sourced from the Eagle Ford Group and Jurassic rocks, respectively. Jurassic salt diapirs emplaced into the Buda Limestone may also serve as an additional trapping mechanism.

Two assessment units (AUs) were delineated to evaluate the resource potential. The Buda Limestone Oil and Gas AU boundary was defined to the south by the Lower Cretaceous shelf edge; to the west by the U.S.-Mexico border; and to the north and east by the updip limit of the Upper Jurassic-Cretaceous-Tertiary Composite Total Petroleum System, the Balcones and Mexia-Talco Fault Zones, the East Texas Basin Province, and the absence of the formation. The East Texas Basin Buda Limestone Oil and Gas AU boundary was defined by the basin’s geometry, the Mexia-Talco Fault Zone to the west, and absence of the formation to the north and east. Estimated mean resources for the Buda Limestone Oil and Gas AU are 8 million barrels of oil (MMBO) and 158 billion cubic feet of gas (BCFG) and are 4 MMBO and 26 BCFG for the East Texas Basin Buda Limestone Oil and Gas AU.

title: Physicochemical and Isotopic Evidence for the Controls on Longitudinal Carbon Sourcing and Cycling in a Tidal Creek along the Land-Estuary Interface in a Tropical Mangrove Estuary
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Delgado-Moore, Azalia R. [1], Sunjo, Claris N. [2], Atekwana, Eliot A. [3], Agbogun, Henry M. [4], Njilah, Isaac K. [5]
affiliations: (1) Land, Air, and Water Resources, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA

abstract: We investigated physicochemical and isotopic properties along a 13 km stretch of a tidal creek during tidal ebbing and flooding at the land-estuary interface in a tropical mangrove estuary. We aimed to evaluate the factors controlling longitudinal carbon sourcing and cycling during the dry season. We made physical measurements of water clarity, dissolved oxygen (DO), turbidity, and salinity. We collected samples, which were analyzed for stable isotopes of oxygen and hydrogen (δ¹⁸O and δD), silica, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) components (alkalinity, total DIC, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO₂)), and stable carbon isotopes of DIC (δ¹³C DIC ). We found that water properties exhibited a consistent longitudinal trend from the open estuary into the headwater of the tidal creek. For example, DO, turbidity, salinity, and pH decreased, while clarity, alkalinity, DIC, and the pCO 2 increased. The salinity during tidal flooding was lower than during tidal ebbing, indicating that tidal intrusion brought fresher water into the tidal creek from the open estuary. The small difference in the range of the water isotopes (e.g., 0.4‰ in δ¹⁸O) indicates a dominance of terrestrial (river) water in the tidal creek. A hydrologic mixing model indicates a freshwater-dominated mixed seawater–freshwater source from the open estuary and freshwater in the headwater/interior of the tidal creek mixed with terrestrial groundwater influx at this land-estuary boundary. A Keeling graphical analysis indicates that longitudinal DIC evolution was from mixing between water from the open estuary to 3 to 6 km into the tidal creek and CO 2 exchange between the tidal creek and the atmosphere for the rest of the transverse. Miller-Tans graphical analysis further showed that the isotopic composition of the controlling DIC reservoir was -14.7‰ during tidal flooding and -13.6‰ during tidal ebbing. We attribute the observed longitudinal variability in water properties to the combined influence of mixed seawater-river water influx during tidal flooding, freshwater discharge in the headwaters of the tidal creek, and continuous submarine groundwater discharge from land into the tidal creek. Our findings provide critical insights into the role of tidal creeks in land-estuary carbon flow and in tropical mangrove estuarine carbon studies.

title: Strengthening of Quartzites Due to Synkinematic Partial Melting
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Holyoke, Caleb W. [1], Razo, Maria [2], Wehner, Karl [3], Mahan, Kevin H. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA
(3) Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA
(4) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
abstract:
Partial melting of rocks in Earth’s lower-continental crust is thought to weaken the crust by forming zones of melt and changing deformation mechanisms. We performed a series of general shear and axial compression deformation experiments to determine if partial melting affects water contents and the strength of common crustal rocks. The shear experiments used a natural, fine-grained, muscovite-bearing (10 vol%) quartzite (d~30 μm) at a range of temperatures (800-975 o C), pressure of 1.5 GPa, and strain rate of 6*10 -5 /s. The pressure-stepping axial compression experiment used a coarse-grained (~200 μm) natural quartzite with minor muscovite (<1 vol%) and was deformed at T = 900 o C, pressure of 1.5 GPa and strain rate of 2x10 -6 /s to measure water contents near melt pockets.

Yield stresses of fine-grained quartzite slices decreased as a function of increasing temperature from ~960 to ~300 MPa and increasing melt content (0-1 vol%). However, only the quartzite slice without melt strain weakened after yielding and all quartzites with melt strain hardened to 150-200% of the yield stress after yielding. The coarse-grained quartzite was deformed at three pressures and differential stresses increased as a function of decreasing water fugacity, consistent with previous work. Microstructures in both quartzites are consistent with dislocation creep. Melt in the sheared quartzite was mixed with recrystallized grains in bands oriented at ~20° to the shear zone (i.e. C’ shear bands). Melt pockets in the coarse-grained quartzite were parallel to the compression direction. FTIR analysis of the sheared quartzite is not possible due to the small grain size. However, water contents in quartz grains adjacent to melt pockets in the coarse-grained quartzite were <200 H/10 6 Si and were >2000 H/10 6 Si in the melt pockets. These results indicate that water diffused out of the quartz grains into the adjacent melt during deformation. This dehydration process may contribute to strengthening of the protolith after water-rich magma has migrated toward the surface, which can have long term implications for the physical and chemical evolution of continental crust. Natural examples of such long term strengthening may be recorded in dry lower crustal granulites such as those in the East Athabasca mylonite triangle of the western Canadian Shield.

title: Calcite and sulfur mineralization within the Boling Dome Cap Rock, northern Gulf Coast Basin: Implications for carbon sources and divalent metal availability
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology (Posters)
authors: Ortega-Sanchez, Sonny [1], Loyd, Sean [2], Richard, Kyle J [3], Woods, Adam [4], Phelps, Patrick [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Science, California State University, Fullerton, Fullerton, California, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, Fullerton, Fullerton, California, USA
(3) Department of Geologic Sciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(4) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, Fullerton, Fullerton, California, USA
(5) Department of Geological Science, California State University, Fullerton, Fullerton, California, USA
abstract: Salt domes are subsurface vertical piercement structures that commonly are mantled by cap rock zones of anhydrite, gypsum, and calcite that may include elemental sulfur and metal sulfides. These cap rocks are thought to form from fluid-hydrocarbon-microbial interactions that promote mineralization. This study explores the mineralization pathways of cap rock from Boling Dome (Wharton County, Texas, USA), the former largest Frasch sulfur producer in North America. Hand sample and petrographic examination reveals an abundance of elemental sulfur and multiple generations of calcite. High abundances of elemental sulfur are relatively uncommon in other geologic settings, which are instead often dominated by metal sulfide minerals. Low dissolved metals within salt dome environments may limit metal sulfide precipitation and promote the formation of elemental sulfur. In addition, the reducing potential of cap rock fluids may be related to the carbon source responsible for calcite formation. Crude oil and methane have been identified as possible carbon sources, and these exhibit different oxidation states and thus have different reducing potential. Preliminary calcite δ 13 C ranges from ~ -30 to -15‰ (VPDB) indicate hydrocarbon sources likely dominated by crude oil. Preliminary calcite-bound metal analyses reveal moderate manganese, low iron, and very low lead, zinc, and copper contents. A paucity of divalent metal ions may limit metal sulfide precipitation and allow elemental sulfur accumulation. Additional carbon isotope, elemental, and SEM-EDS analyses will help better define mineralization pathways in Boling cap rock. Ultimately, this work will lead to a better understanding of economic mineral accumulation in salt dome cap rock.

title: Porphyritic cobbles in the Frontier Formation sourced from mid-Cretaceous porphyritic intrusions in the Beartooth Mountains of the northern Laramide foreland (MT/WY): Implications for local to regional tectonism
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Thacker, Jacob Oliver [1], Brailer, Nicholas [2], Michelfelder, Gary [3], Shaulis, Barry [4], Attia, Snir [5], VanderLeest, Rebecca [6], Cunningham, Eddy [7]

abstract: Orogenic magmatism and sedimentation provide crucial constraints for deciphering tectonic processes and lithospheric evolution of convergent margin settings. In the northern Laramide foreland system, porphyritic cobbles in the Cenomanian Frontier Formation in Bighorn basin bear striking resemblance to porphyritic intrusions now exposed in the Beartooth Mountains. Paradoxically, deposition of these cobbles precedes appreciable tectonism in the area by ca. 20-30 million years. We utilized geologic mapping, petrography, geochemistry, and geochronology to compare rocks from both locations and test the provenance of these cobbles and further consider the tectonic significance of this magmatic and sedimentologic record. Mapping on Line Creek Plateau in the Beartooth Mountains shows at least three types of intrusions with porphyritic phenocrysts consisting dominantly of plagioclase (Kpp), plagioclase + potassium feldspar (Kpkp), and plagioclase + quartz (Kpq). Embayed quartz, opacitic rims, and zoned plagioclase are evident in petrographic analysis. Geochemistry characterizes the intrusions as trachydacite/trachyte with LREE enrichment and slightly depleted HREE trace element signatures relative to primitive mantle. Zircon U-Pb dating shows a prevalence of Archean inheritance and ca. 104−92 Ma dates, with some samples showing multiple mid-Cretaceous date populations. Porphyritic cobbles from Bighorn basin exhibit similar mineralogy, geochemistry, and overlapping Archean inheritance and mid-Cretaceous dates. Geochemistry of the porphyritic cobbles best matches basement-hosted porphyritic intrusions now exposed in the Beartooth Mountains and is dissimilar to mid-Cretaceous porphyritic sills hosted in Cambrian shale at the Beartooth front and coeval Idaho batholith magmatism upstream in the Frontier Formation depositional system. We therefore interpret the cobbles to have been sourced from the porphyritic intrusions in the Beartooth Mountains, however stratigraphic evidence does not support kilometer-scale exhumation at that time to expose the basement-hosted intrusions, and we therefore present a volcanic hypothesis to bring these rocks to the surface. Far inboard, mid-Cretaceous magmatism (and possibly volcanism) is unexplained by current tectonic models of the north-central Laramide foreland, and thus we further consider the spatial association of the intrusions compared to coeval magmatism in North America and possible tectonic controls for their formation.

abstract:
The paleontology collection of The University of Alabama Museums Research & Collections (UAMRC) houses more than half a million fossil specimens, representing >150 years of collection efforts and ~500 million years of geologic time. This collection is a valuable source for research, teaching, exhibits, and outreach, and includes irreplaceable specimens from historical sites in Alabama where additional collection is no longer possible. The UAMRC houses substantial vertebrate, plant, and trace fossil collections, but the invertebrates are the largest portion of the paleontology collection and the majority of them are Cenozoic in age. Despite the importance of the collection, most invertebrate fossils remained uncatalogued and unorganized, limiting the discoverability of specimens by interested researchers.

As part of an ongoing 2-year project, we are revitalizing this invertebrate paleontology collection. With the help of a full-time collection manager and two undergraduate student interns per semester, nearly 100,000 specimens have been identified, counted, cataloged, labeled, and rehoused thus far. Ongoing work includes the physical reorganization of specimens into broad taxonomic groups. Future work will include uploading specimen data to a searchable online database and the development of a small exhibit highlighting notable specimens discovered in the collections. In addition to providing collections-related training and experience for up to eight students, the project is enhancing the collections by rescuing and conserving data from historical labels and by increasing the searchability and accessibility of the collections for research and other purposes.

title: Near-Surface Carbon Storage in Organic-Rich Soil Profiles of an Old-Growth Hemlock and White Pine Forest, Eastern Maine
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science (Posters)
authors: Tanner, Benjamin [1]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science and Studies, Stetson University, Deland, FL, USA
abstract: Old-growth forests store substantial carbon in living biomass, but soil carbon pools in remnant northeastern forests remain less well characterized. Near-surface carbon storage was quantified in an approximately 32-ha old-growth eastern hemlock ( Tsuga canadensis ) and white pine ( Pinus strobus ) forest in eastern Maine. Soil samples were collected above mineral-dominant horizons from 30 soil profiles along transects and overstory composition was recorded using the point-intercept method. Larger roots, gravel, and other coarse material were removed before analysis. Bulk-density and loss-on-ignition measurements were used to estimate organic carbon concentrations and stocks in the collected soil samples. Hemlock or white pine dominated the overstory at most sampling locations. Organic-rich layers averaged 10.3 cm thick and contained an estimated mean carbon stock of 50.1 megagrams of carbon per hectare. These preliminary results demonstrate substantial near-surface carbon storage in this minimally disturbed conifer forest and provide a baseline for comparison with adjacent stands affected by timber harvesting.

title: Reconstructing 300 years of environmental change in the northern Chesapeake Bay with high resolution radionuclide analysis of a sediment core
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Walker, Elizabeth G. [1], Kaste, James M. [2], Klug, Paige [3], Hupp, Brittany N. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, William & Mary College, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(2) Geology Department, William & Mary College, Williamsburg, VA,
(3) Department of Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
(4) Department of Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
abstract:
The Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States and has been subjected to increased sedimentation from land-use change and cropland erosion, along with deposits from major storms for centuries. Analysis of sedimentary sequences is useful for reconstructing paleoclimate and environmental change. Development of a robust age-depth model and calculation of mass accumulation rates is a prerequisite for sediment core reconstruction. Using high resolution low-background gamma spectrometry, we analyzed one sediment core from the Northern Chesapeake Bay to create an age-model and reconstruct sedimentation rates for further biogeochemical analysis.

We collected a 190 cm gravity core from the northern Chesapeake Bay. This core was sliced into 1cm sections and dried prior to analysis. We analyzed slices for 40 K 137 Cs, 210 Pb, 212 Pb, 214 Pb, 226 Ra, 228 Ac and 234 Th activity with non-destructive photon counting. The 137 Cs peak was attributed to the year 1963 from the Cold-War era atmospheric nuclear bomb tests which dispersed cesium and americium isotopes globally. We determined excess 210 Pb by subtracting supported (geogenic) 210 Pb from total 210 Pb activity as calculated by the 186 226 Ra and 352 214 Pb keV gamma lines. We then used 137 Cs as a chronostratigraphic marker to create a piecewise constant rate of supply model (SERAC) to determine age by layer. Initial results indicate a sharp subsurface 137 Cs maxima at 40 cm which we use to calculate an average annual sedimentation rate of 0.68 cm since 1963. Radionuclide and geochemical analysis can provide insight into sediment provenance and sourcing. Combined with sedimentation rates, our data support the reconstruction of historical salinity, regional pollution history, sea-level fluctuations and other human and climate-forced variations preserved in the Chesapeake sedimentary record.

title: Expected and unexpected results from strataR: a coupled nonmarine–marine stratigraphic model for stratigraphic paleobiology
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Holland, Steven M. [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Georgia, Athens, GA,
abstract: Stratigraphic models are the basis for predictions in stratigraphic paleobiology, so it is critical to evaluate whether their output is reasonable. strataR is a coupled nonmarine-marine siliciclastic model that incorporates sediment flux, tectonic subsidence, eustasy, and geometric rules for deposition based on equilibrium profiles, and it has proven useful for simulating stratigraphic architecture. Deposition occurs where accommodation perches an equilibrium profile above the current land surface, with erosion where the reverse occurs. strataR incorporates temporally varying sediment flux and eustasy, as well as temporally and spatially variable tectonic subsidence. strataR is written in R and is available on GitHub. The model is inspired by Holbrook et al.’s (2006) model of buttresses and buffers and is designed for time scales above the compensation scale of Straub et al. (1992), over which allogenic sedimentary processes dominate. Most aspects of the strataR’s output match intuition, theoretical models, and field observations. For example, marine systems tracts (LST, TST, HST, FSST) align with the nonmarine systems tracts (HAST and LAST) as expected, with late HST and early LST favoring LAST in nonmarine settings, whereas times of high accommodation (TST) favor a HAST nonmarine architecture. Rapid rates of accommodation sequester sediment in the nonmarine realm, causing sediment starvation and the formation of flooding surfaces in marine areas. This is particularly enhanced in basins in which subsidence increases towards the sediment source, such as foreland basins and the hanging wall of extensional basins. Relative sea-level falls at the shoreline trigger fluvial incision. Although eustatic falls, counterbalanced by greater tectonic subsidence rates along the shore, do not generate fluvial incision, they do generate a LAST nonmarine architecture. strataR predicts thick marine FSST deposits, and this behavior is caused by incision along the entire fluvial profile instead of an upstream-migrating knickpoint. The scarcity of real-world thick FSSTs suggests that fluvial systems may continue to aggrade and store substantial amounts of sediment upstream of the erosional knickpoint. strataR also does not exhibit the autoretreat behavior of Muto and Steel (1992), primarily because delta foresets are not constrained to extend and thereby consume more sediment over time. As a result, stacking patterns in strataR directly reflect variations in the A:S ratio.

abstract: This study provides a preliminary analysis at how forest fires may have shaped terrestrial ecosystems in Colorado following the end-Cretaceous mass extinction (ECME) at the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and plant waxes to reconstruct large scale shifts in fire regime, occurrences of conifers and wood-eating fungi, and shifts or stability in plant communities. While vegetation changes did not generally correlate with changes in fire regimes, a large and rapid increase in the dominance of long-chain plant n-alkanes across the Danian P2-P3 pollen transition corresponds with an increase in fire frequency, indicating a potential drying event. Collaborators have found a contemporaneous increase in plant diversity, with the drying and potential stress from increased fire frequency driving diversification. Other observable trends included a lowering of fire intensity following warming events and the sudden appearances and disappearances of conifer biomarkers show a complex and constantly shifting ecosystem following the mass extinction.

title: Formation of Playas and Lunettes by Eolian Deflation in the Late Pleistocene, Nebraska, USA
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Hanson, Paul R. [1], Joeckel, R. M. [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE, USA
(2) University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract: Playas and lunettes are common features on the Great Plains, where they formed on multiple geological substrates, including alluvial sands, loess, and soft bedrock. These features are very common in Nebraska and assume at least three morphologies: (1) small basins that are typically round and lack lunettes, (2) small to medium and elongate (NW–SE) basins that also lack lunettes, and (3) medium to large and ovoid basins with roughly NE–SW long axes that are ~1 to 2.5 km in length. Ovoid basins, which in some cases enclose one or more smaller basins of similar shapes usually have lunettes on their southeastern and/or southern margins. Lunette crests are 8 to 12 m above the floors of adjacent playas. Such playas are referred to as “rainwater basins” on the extensive plains south of the Platte River in southcentral Nebraska. We collected 25 cores from 8 lunettes and playas and generated 22 OSL ages from them. The entire region, including the playas, is mantled with a variable thickness of Peoria Loess, which was deposited during MIS 2. Therefore, the playas formed prior to loess aggradation by the deflation of sandy alluvium on the abandoned braidplain of the northward-migrating Platte River. Our OSL ages constrain the deposition of sand (deflated alluvium) within the lunettes to between 20 and 51 ka, indicating that the basins formed during MIS 3 and early in MIS 2. We propose that arid conditions during MIS 3 resulted in dune migration atop the abandoned braidplain, as well as eolian deflation of the playas and the aggradation of the lunettes at their leeward margins. Intermittent wetter climates during this time facilitated basin remodeling and elongation of the larger basins by wave activity when they held water. Subsequent deposition of 4 to 12 m of Peoria Loess during MIS 2 subdued the relief of the basins and lunettes and stabilized the landscape. Our results underscore prior interpretations of the Nebraskan rainwater basins as products of eolian deflation.

title: Assessment of Soil Ecosystems During Eocene–Oligocene Transition from Paleosols of the White River Group, Colorado
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science
authors: Oligmueller, Andrew R. [1], Hembree, Daniel I. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract: Soil ecosystems contain diverse communities of organisms which play a significant role in soil formation and productivity. The composition and diversity of soil communities is closely linked to climate. As a result, understanding how long-term variations in temperature, precipitation, and seasonality due to climate change can affect soil communities is critical from both a scientific and socioeconomic standpoint. The Eocene–Oligocene transition was a global climate shift involving broad-scale trends in cooling and drying, resulting in the expansion of open habitats in continental interiors. Strata deposited during this transition are present in the Colorado Piedmont in northeastern Colorado represented by the Horsetail Creek (Eocene), Cedar Creek (Eocene-Oligocene), and Vista (Oligocene) members of the Chadron and Brule formations of the White River Group (WRG). These units consist of stacked successions of paleosols along with associated fluvial and eolian deposits. In this study animal and plant ichnofossils in these paleosols were examined to assess changes in the composition and activity of soil communities through the transition. Ichnofossils have been utilized in other studies as indicators of trophic and taxonomic diversity within ancient soil ecosystems, allowing for the assessment of environmental stresses based on changes in their abundance, diversity, morphology, and distribution. Ichnofossils within the paleosols of the WRG were described by their ichnotaxobases, relative abundance, maximum depth, and spatial distribution. Ichnofossil assemblages were described by their composition, ichnodiversity, and ichnodisparity. Identified animal ichnofossils include Planolites , Edaphichnium , Fictovichnus , Rebuffoichnus , Pallichnus , and backfilled burrows representing locomotion, feeding, reproduction, and pupation behaviors of annelids and various soil arthropods. Rhizoliths range from scattered to dense concentrations of small diameter (~1 mm), horizontally to vertically branching calcareous rhizotubules to large diameter (~1-6 cm), downward branching, vertical root casts. Low diversity assemblages characterized by backfilled burrows, Planolites , Pallichnus , and rhizotubules are present throughout the WRG section. Higher diversity assemblages also contain Fictovichnus, Rebuffoichnus, Edaphichnium, and large root casts are present in the Cedar Creek and Vista members. In general, ichnodiversity and disparity increases up section whereas abundance and spatial distribution are similar throughout the section. Changes to the ichnofossil assemblages suggest a general up-section shift from an open, unstable landscape to a more closed, stable landscape, resulting in the establishment of more complex soil communities.

title: Geologic Framework of a Consolidated Rock Aquifer System Using Airborne Electromagnetic and Borehole Data, Adelaida Area, San Luis Obispo County, California
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Neuhaus, Sarah [1], Cromwell, Geoffrey [2], Ball, Lyndsay [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Sacramento, CA, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, San Luis Obispo, CA, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Groundwater is the only source of water in the Adelaida area of northern San Luis Obispo County, California. Groundwater is extracted for residential and agricultural use from a consolidated rock aquifer system. Population growth and an increase in irrigated agriculture has impacted groundwater levels and availability. Currently, the Adelaida area is not designated as a groundwater basin by the California Department of Water Resources; thus, no comprehensive evaluations of groundwater resources have been conducted and little is known about the subsurface hydrogeology. Here, we present a preliminary three-dimensional (3D) geologic framework of the area to help understand the hydrogeology of the aquifers of the Adelaida area. The framework was built using borehole lithologic data and construction information, geologic maps, and resistivity profiles from an airborne electromagnetic (AEM) survey.

The Miocene Monterey Formation is the primary aquifer, although groundwater is also extracted from the underlying Miocene Vaqueros Formation and Cretaceous sandstone. The study area is structurally complex, and the overarching structural trend is a syncline plunging to the southeast. Faults bound the study area to the northeast and southwest along the strike of the syncline, and many minor anticlines and synclines are found throughout.

We identified surface and subsurface geologic contacts for all units in surface geologic maps, borehole lithologic and geophysical logs, and AEM resistivity profiles. The boreholes provided detailed point data and regional coverage of the study area and were supplemented with AEM data collected in August 2021 by the California Department of Water Resources. We developed new models of the AEM data to better represent the bedrock geology and topographic conditions of the Adelaida area. Interpretations of geologic contacts were iteratively made between the boreholes and AEM profiles, with care taken to evaluate the AEM results with respect to groundwater salinity and other parameters that may affect resistivity. Structural contours and synthetic control points were added as input data to enforce the conceptual understanding of the geology and geologic rules. The 3D framework was constructed using geologic-modeling software and geographic information system software. These results are intended to inform water management decisions for the Adelaida area and provide a useful template for future studies in similar consolidated rock aquifer systems.

title: AI-Enabled Prediction of Climate-Driven Seawater Intrusion Across Global Coastal Aquifers
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: Jiang, Su [1]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Carnegie Mellon Univesity, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
abstract:
Reliable prediction of seawater intrusion requires models that represent the diverse geologic, geometric, and hydrologic conditions controlling groundwater flow and salinity transport in coastal aquifers. Global assessment is challenging because coastal systems vary widely in topography, hydrogeology, recharge, and exposure to sea-level rise. Furthermore, conventional numerical simulations are too computationally expensive to explore the broad range of coastal settings and uncertain future climate conditions.

In this work, we develop an AI-driven framework for efficient prediction of coastal aquifer salinization. Coastal geometry and hydrologic forcing are parameterized using global geospatial, hydrogeologic, and climate datasets. High-fidelity numerical simulations generate physically consistent training and validation data across a range of aquifer geometries, hydraulic properties, recharge conditions, and sea-level scenarios. A geometry-aware neural operator is then trained to predict the spatial and temporal evolution of groundwater levels and salinity.

We evaluate the framework across diverse coastal environments and uncertain climate scenarios. The surrogate reproduces the major patterns of groundwater and salinity response while substantially reducing the computational cost of prediction. This efficiency enables large ensembles that quantify uncertainty and distinguish the effects of recharge change, lateral seawater intrusion, and coastal inundation. The proposed framework demonstrates how AI, process-based groundwater modeling, and global geospatial data can be integrated to provide scalable predictions of coastal groundwater vulnerability under a changing climate.

title: Environmental and nutrient controls on the rise of eukaryotes in Tonian oceans
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records
authors: Rizzo, Adriana Isabel [1], Bekker, Andrey [2], Xiong, Yijun [3], Karlstrom, Karl E. [4], Poulton, Simon [5], Love, Gordon Davidson [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, Riverside, California, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, Riverside, California, USA; Department of Geology, University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa
(3) School of Earth and Environment, University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom
(4) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
(5) University of Leeds, School of Earth and Environment, Leeds,
(6) UC Riverside, Earth and Planetary Sciences, Riverside, CA,
abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that the late Tonian period (~820-720 Ma) was an important interval for the evolution of complex life, with eukaryotes radiating into new environments and new modes of life concurrently with changing climate and tectonics. Changes in the carbon number patterns and abundance of regular (4-desmethyl) steranes, lipid biomarkers primarily sourced from eukaryotes, have been widely used to track the emergence and rise of different eukaryotic lineages throughout the environmental turmoil of the Neoproterozoic. Regular steranes first consistently appear in the fossil record circa 800 Ma, but Tonian strata are dominated by C 27 steranes, with the first appearance of C 29 steranes poorly constrained to sometime later after the Sturtian glaciation. The Tonian rise of eukaryotes has been linked to increased marine phosphorus inputs driven by the breakup of Rodinia, but more detailed molecular records are needed to tie the sterane record to such global changes. Here we present new lipid biomarker data from the Lena-Anabar Basin of Siberia, which has sedimentary rock samples spanning the Tonian to earliest Cambrian periods, with Cryogenian strata absent, as well as from the Tonian Chuar Group, USA. We additionally constrain local environmental conditions using iron speciation, trace element geochemistry, and phosphorus speciation to understand the local seawater redox and phosphorus availability which prevailed during deposition. Our data capture a strong C 27 sterane dominance in all Tonian samples, which together with moderately elevated S/H ratios (~0.3) in the Chuar Group suggest a predominantly red algal source for Tonian steranes. The Tonian strata from Siberia are characterized by low total organic carbon (TOC) and very low sterane/hopane (S/H) values formed under chronically phosphorus-limited conditions demonstrated by phosphorus speciation, a suite of characteristics symptomatic of strongly oligotrophic marine settings. Our data show regional variation in S/H between basins during the Tonian Period that covaries with TOC and productivity indicators, but not obviously with water column redox conditions – suggesting a primarily nutrient control on marine eukaryotic abundance. These findings support the notion that phosphorus and other nutrient species availability controlled the rise of Neoproterozoic algae and the environmental abundance of eukaryotes, but also underscores the importance of local environmental and ecological drivers which have sustained chemical and biological heterogeneity within the global ocean system across geological time.

title: Ages and origins of low-Ti iron ore from the Chateaugay mine, northeastern Adirondacks, New York, USA
session_title: Geochronology of Ore Deposits Containing Critical Minerals: Analytical Advances and Applications
authors: Aleinikoff, John [1], Walsh, Gregory [2], Taylor, Ryan [3], Thompson, Jay [4], Lowers, Heather [5], Dare, Sarah [6], Pillers, Renee [7]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) US Geological Survey, Montpelier, VT, USA
(3) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(4) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA

abstract:
Mesoproterozoic low-Ti iron deposits occur throughout the high-grade Adirondack Highlands, NY and have been the subjects of study for at least 180 years. In general, considerable controversy still exists regarding the origin(s) of these highly Fe-enriched occurrences world-wide. Interpretations of igneous and(or) hydrothermal processes have been ascribed to these very pure magnetite-rich rocks.

The Chateaugay mine in the northeastern Adirondack Highlands operated until 1968, extracting magnetite from two major tabular bodies. Five representative samples of the main geologic units at the mine were collected for geochronological and geochemical studies. Both SHRIMP and LA-ICPMS analytical techniques were utilized for dating of zircon and titanite. These units are: (1) host Lyon Mountain Granite Gneiss (1161 ± 8 Ma), (2) leucogranite gneiss (1064 ± 7 Ma), (3) magnetite-enriched granitic gneiss (so-called “lean ore”, 1054 ± 10 Ma), and (4) cross-cutting pegmatite (1037 ± 3 Ma). A sample of magnetite ore (so-called “rich ore”) produced anhedral-subhedral zircon grains with a variety of zoning patterns displayed in cathodoluminescence (CL). Most of the grains are relatively unzoned and yield ages of about 1005 and 955 Ma. A small percentage of zircon grains show fine oscillatory zoning and yield an age of 1032 ± 12 Ma, interpreted as the time of original igneous high temperature (>800˚ C) emplacement of the protolith of the rich ore, coincident with the age of late pegmatite. Ages younger than ~1032 Ma record times of subsequent lower temperature metamorphism and(or) hydrothermal activity. Geochemical data indicate that the magnetite was almost entirely statically recrystallized, removing evidence (except for rare older zircon) of the original igneous emplacement. The ~1032 Ma zircon age from magnetite ore agrees with age data from other deposits interpreted as igneous elsewhere in the Adirondacks.

Previous interpretations of magnetite formation related to hydrothermal activity during late-stage emplacement of the Lyon Mountain Granite Gneiss protolith are untenable because the granite is about 125 m.y. older than the magnetite deposits. Instead, an igneous source is favored, based on the occurrence of oscillatory zoning in zircon and intrusive cross-cutting contacts of rich ore into country rocks. Our results are consistent with the current paradigm for high temperature igneous emplacement of immiscible Fe-P-rich melts or Fe-rich hydrosaline liquids.

title: Impacts of Recharge Patterns and Magnitudes on Particle Deposition and Physical Clogging in Managed Aquifer Recharge
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions (Posters)
authors: Magar, Sunita [1], Zhang, Yipeng [2], Xu, Tingying [3], Chen, Xiaofeng [4]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(3) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(4) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: Aquifer clogging due to deposition and accumulation of suspended particles transported with recharge water is one of the key challenges during Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR). Natural precipitation patterns are often highly variable through time. The momentum of transient flow caused by episodic runoff events can detach particles from grain surfaces, suspend them, and redistribute them within pore spaces. Compared with the constant recharge, the time-varying recharge results in a more dynamic particle transport, where the deposited particle mass fluctuates in response to changing attachment and detachment forces. In this study, we investigated the controlling factors on clogging by varying recharge magnitudes and patterns using a numerical model of groundwater flow coupled with solute transport and particle deposition developed in COMSOL® Multiphysics. The simulation shows that, over the same simulation period, the overall reduction in normalized hydraulic conductivity (K/K 0 ) due to clogging under the constant recharge scenarios is 9-15% greater than that under the time varying recharge. However, when compared under equal total particle loads, the reduction in K/K 0 under the constant recharge is only 3-7% greater than time-varying. Reducing the recharge rate by 50%, the overall reduction in K/K 0 is 17% less under the constant recharge and 21% less under the time varying recharge. Furthermore, for the same total suspended particle load, replacing a high-magnitude constant recharge strategy with a low-magnitude periodic recharge reduces clogging by 13% in the shallow aquifer layer and by 16% in the deeper layer. These results demonstrate that both recharge magnitude and temporal variability strongly influence the evolution of physical clogging. Optimizing recharge strategies by adopting lower magnitude, periodic recharge can significantly mitigate clogging while maintaining equivalent particle loading, providing practical guidance for improving the long-term efficiency and sustainability of MAR operations.

abstract: Understanding how erosion rates are influenced by tectonics, climate, and lithology is crucial for interpreting the evolution of Earth’s topography. Previous research has investigated the influence of rock erodibility on the relationship between erosion rate and landscape steepness by analyzing erosion rates and steepnesses across individual catchments. However, the correspondence between rock erodibility and rates of erosion in mountains across entire continents and, by inference, during the geologic history (ontogeny) of mountain ranges has received less attention. Here, we examine the association between erosion rates derived from ¹⁰Be cosmogenic nuclides and channel steepness across orogens of different ages in the conterminous United States. Orthogonal log-log regressions of basin-averaged normalized channel steepness ( k sn ) on basin-averaged erosion rate derived from 10 Be cosmogenic nuclide data show a positive covariance within each province but differ systematically across the continent. When adjusted for channel steepness, erosion rates are lower in the older orogens of the eastern U.S.; conversely, when adjusted for erosion rate, channel steepnesses are lower in the younger orogens of the western United States. We expanded the initial analyses on United States orogens to the entire OCTOPUS v2.3 database, which includes 5,500 measurements of basin-averaged erosion rates from orogens around the world, and found similar patterns, plus new insights into the lifespan of global orogens. These associations of channel steepness, erosion rate, and orogen age are replicated within landscape evolution models that simulate a decrease in rock erodibility with increasing duration of orogen exposure and exhumation over tens of millions of years. Differences in topography and erosion rate among geologic provinces are strongly related to variations in rock erodibility which is dependent on degrees of exhumation during the ontogeny (life span) of orogens.

abstract: Sea-level rise presents more than surficial flooding hazards in low-lying coastal areas. Coastal groundwater systems are dynamic and responsive to sea level rise through rising seasonal static water levels, increased discharge to drainages, and/or rearrangement of groundwater flow paths. These changes in groundwater flow and discharge locations can alter contaminant migration pathways, while rising water tables and saltwater intrusion may modify geochemical conditions that affect contaminant mobility. For polluted sites, this poses an extra challenge for cleanup activities and the need for adjustment of long-term remediation goals. We developed and applied a groundwater flow model of the Zeneca site in Richmond, California to test how sea-level rise may control groundwater-based pollutant fate and transport. We simulated sea-level rise scenarios built on the current groundwater response over a decade time span utilizing recharge data, mean tide data, and monitoring well data for model calibration. Particle tracking analyses were conducted for these scenarios to identify shifts in flow pathways and discharge locations in the remediation areas. Model results indicated that groundwater flow paths and discharge locations are sensitive to projected sea-level rise, with some flow paths redirected toward new discharge areas as hydraulic gradients evolve. These findings suggest that remediation strategies designed for current hydrogeologic conditions may need to be adjusted in anticipation of future groundwater flow changes if the pollutants persist long into the future. The deviations in flow paths and dynamic groundwater levels at the Zeneca site can help guide long-term management and planning at other coastal remediation sites and indicate the need to the develop resilient and adaptable remediation plans that quantitatively address spatiotemporal groundwater responses to sea-level rise.

abstract: The Tomahawk obsidian deposit of the central Black Hills, SD presents a geological puzzle. Although two independent geochronology studies (each published in Science ) yielded ages of 55 Ma (Kirchner, 1977) and 10 Ma (Redden et al., 1983), both ages are problematic for preservation of volcanic glass given expected timescales for devitrification of volcanic glass in the natural environment. How did this glass escape the expected devitrification process over millions of years? The deposit consists of a dense network of anastomosing perlitic veins (0.1-3 mm) that delimit regions of unaltered, amber-colored glass (<1 cm wide). We use XRF and SEM to characterize the major and trace element geochemistry of the glass. In addition, we present FTIR and LOI analyses that show the glass to be the most water-rich natural glass (>8.5 wt% H 2 O) we’ve ever analyzed (by nearly a factor of 2). The relative concentrations of hydrous species (HOH vs X-OH) reveal a temperature of hydration at 200 °C, which is significantly lower than values reported for other natural volcanic glasses. We explore how the unique chemistry of this truly unusual obsidian glass might contribute to its exceptional long-term preservation.

abstract:
Despite decades of progress, lead (Pb) remains a pressing global health concern. Lead in the Environment (Reviews in Mineralogy and Geochemistry, volume 92) examines the fundamental geochemistry of Pb, its health impacts, and sources of Pb to the environment, both legacy and emerging. In reviewing the historical and modern sources of Pb use and their effects, a tension between its utility and toxicity emerges. This tension has created a cyclic pattern of 1) adopting new technological uses that disperse Pb in the environment, 2) human exposure to Pb with toxicological effects, followed by 3) the eventual removal of Pb from that use. This pattern has been repeated throughout history and continues today. Societal tension originates with the unique physical and electrical properties that make Pb highly useful and the toxic effects of Pb on many organismal systems, including the nervous and circulatory systems. Recognizing this cycle may be an important part of limiting global Pb exposure, particularly because the use of Pb is unlikely to be curtailed in the immediate future, especially due its use in lead-acid batteries that are critical to transportation and energy storage.

This presentation will highlight important X-ray techniques that have provided insight into Pb cycling and exposure to humans and wildlife in natural and manmade environments. Portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) has revolutionized the ability to study Pb in environmental samples because it is an easy to use, relatively low-cost instrument, with minimal per sample costs. As a result, pXRF has been used to identify Pb sources in residential areas associated with elevated blood lead levels and to conduct soil surveys to map the distribution of Pb in surface soils. A more specialized technique, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) directly probes the Pb atomic coordination environment and can identify the Pb-hosting phase, even in complex, heterogeneous samples with low Pb content. A new XAS variant, high-energy resolution fluorescence detection (HERFD) with X-Ray Absorption Near Edge Structure (XANES) spectroscopy enables collection of spectra that are significantly more featured and diagnostic than traditional fluorescence measurements, particularly for high atomic number elements, such as Pb. This presentation provides a novel synthesis of literature related to these techniques as well as examples of the improved spectral resolution offered by HERFD-XANES.

abstract:
The Eocene Green River Formation in Wyoming, Colorado, and Utah, USA, is a Lagerstätte particularly world-famous for abundant, well-preserved fish fossils. Also present with the fish are numerous morphologically diverse coprolites that reflect a variety of feeding behaviors by fish and other vertebrates. We examined coprolites from the 18-inch layer of the Fossil Butte Member of the Green River Formation at Fossil Lake in southwestern Wyoming that can potentially yield insight into paleoecologic trophic food webs of the Green River lacustrine system. We examined two similar large coprolites via microanalysis using optical microscopy, Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM), and Energy Dispersive Spectrometry (EDS).

The coprolites are 11.0 × 4.5 cm and 6 × 3 cm. The coprolite matrix sediment consists of laminated dolomitic micrite with rare quartz grains. Laminations are depressed below and drape over the coprolite. The sediment flowed from the margin of the coprolite. Under optical microscopy, the coprolite is structureless and isotropic, with rare, possibly fragmented bone and scale inclusions. Additionally, a zone of opaque minerals is present several mm interior to the coprolite margin. EDS analysis of the Au-Pd-coated specimens indicates that the surface of the coprolites consists of unknown organic carbon compounds. Randomly distributed pores up to 10 μm in diameter were found throughout the specimen, probably from trapped gases produced by microbial decomposition. The coprolite was of relatively low viscosity because the coprolite flowed onto the sediment surface upon impact. The lack of plant inclusions and the presence of bone and scale fragments suggest that the coprolites derive from a carnivore. Based on size, it probably represents a tetrapod.

abstract: The separation of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans by the Isthmus of Panama during the Mio-Pliocene resulted in shifts in marine biodiversity and ecology. While the Pacific sustained a high primary productivity, Atlantic Caribbean productivity decreased. Many questions remain concerning the effects of the formation of the isthmus, including how these productivity differences affected predator-prey interactions. Dredged modern bivalve and gastropod shells were used to explore predation patterns in mollusk assemblages. This collection of 15,963 specimens was surveyed for frequency of damage associated with successful predatory attempts (complete drill holes) and survived attempts (incomplete drill holes and repair scars). Drill holes dominate among predatory traces (96%). The Pacific exhibits a higher proportion of shell damage (11.0% of specimens) compared to the lower-productivity Caribbean (5.5%), linked to a higher proportion of gastropod drillers (Naticidae and Muricidae) among mollusks in the Pacific (1.8%) compared to the Caribbean (0.7%). Infaunal bivalves exhibit the highest proportion of drill holes among habitats in both waters, and the infaunal naticids appear more commonly than the epifaunal muricids. Repair scars are more common among epifaunal bivalves. Semi-infaunal gastropods exhibit a higher proportion of damage than epifaunal ones in the Pacific, but less in the Caribbean. In both waters, suspension-feeding bivalves and carnivorous gastropods were most frequently drilled. While prey sizes are the same, drill-hole diameter (predator size) and predator-prey size ratios are significantly larger on the Pacific side. These results suggest that environmental shifts associated with closure of the isthmus may have impacted regional mollusk predation.

title: Comparative Quantification of Ammonite Ornament in 3D Morphospace

authors: Palazzo, Gaetano Jose [1], Clapham, Matthew [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA, USA; Children’s Natural History Museum, Math Science Nucleus, Fremont, CA, USA

abstract: Over the course of their ~344 million year evolution, ammonoids exhibited a vast array of shell forms reflecting environmental, functional, and evolutionary controls on morphological diversity. Previous morphological research has an extensive history which has primarily focused on the quantification of whorl shape and whorl expansion rate. Shell ornament has been categorized quantitatively, but there is currently no mode of quantitative assessment universally used by cephalopod workers. Previous attempts have employed qualitative scoring methods, the expression of whorl expansion as a single sine wave, and 3D rugosity indices. Collectively, these methods capture general relief, but do not consider trends in the dimensions of specific forms of ornament. Additionally, these methods often exclude incomplete specimens and heteromorphs. We propose the use of 3D geometric morphometrics (GMM) to resolve these issues, as it has been the standard for morphological comparison among other taxa for decades. GMM has previously not been used in ammonoids because ornamental structures are not considered homologous with one another. While structural features themselves are not homologous, all ammonoids possess a lateral surface between the middle venter and umbilical shoulder on the outer whorl. Across over 700 3D scanned specimens from the Cretaceous, we assigned a high resolution landmark and semilandmark grid (41x41) to this lateral surface in Stratovan Checkpoint©. Principal Component Analysis and subsequent data transformations like outer landmark locking, fast fourier transform, and thin plate spline produce a morphospace that represents a nexus of the methods that have come before it. The morphospace adequately compares ammonite ornament; wherein the x-axis reflects overall rugosity and the y-axis shows ornamental spacing. Some potential applications of these methods may eventually be used to investigate sexual dimorphism, ontogeny, intraspecific variability, and the role of environmental stress in the construction of ammonite shells.

abstract:
The Clementine porphyry copper prospect in southwestern Montana is characterized by central mineralized breccia vein gossans and a distal ring of hydrothermal actinolite-titanite assemblages in host sedimentary rocks. The prospect is at the nexus of several mapped granites, including the Butte Granite (ca. 77–74 Ma) of the Boulder batholith, the undated Big Hole Canyon pluton, and undated smaller intrusions. However, previous U-Pb dating of hydrothermal titanite (ca. 71 Ma), interpreted as coeval with Cu mineralization, suggests there is a discrepancy between the age of mineralization and proximal granite emplacement. This study uses Earth MRI airborne geophysical data, U-Pb geochronology, and stable isotope geochemistry to evaluate the spatial and genetic relationships between Cretaceous magmatism and mineralization.

Magnetic inversions reveal a zone of high magnetic susceptibility on the southern edge of the prospect that is related to the Parker Creek stock. The high susceptibility zone appears to connect to the Big Hole Canyon pluton at depth, possibly consistent with a late stage differentiate of the cooling pluton. LA-ICP-MS U-Pb zircon geochronology of the Parker Creek stock and Big Hole Canyon pluton yield weighted mean ages of ca. 75, supporting a genetic connection between the intrusive units. Additionally, U-Pb zircon ages for other compositionally variable sills and stocks in the area indicate that magmatism was coeval with intrusions proximal to the Clementine prospect, but all predate hydrothermal titanite.

A central source of heat and fluids from the Clementine area intrusions is supported by stable isotope geochemistry. δ 13 C VPDB values of graphite in shale of the Cretaceous Kootenai Formation indicate contact metamorphism. Light δ 2 H VSMOW values of hydrothermal actinolite and thermodynamic models of redox equilibria suggest formation following magmatic H 2 outgassing during thermal advection from the parental intrusion. However, magnetic modeling finds no evidence of an undiscovered magnetic body underneath the Clementine prospect.

Other distal intrusions have ages more consistent with titanite formation (e.g., the Pioneer batholith ca. 72-64 Ma), such that additional dating of proximal and distal granitic intrusions will seek to resolve the magmatic source. Additional oxygen stable isotopes of breccia veins will seek to characterize the hydrothermal fluid source. This study demonstrates the utility of combining geophysical, geochemical, and geochronologic methods with thermodynamic theory to understand sediment-hosted porphyry copper formation in complex magmatic-hydrothermal environments.

abstract: The Mohawk Valley of central New York regulated and carried glacial meltwater outflow. Ice advance into the Mohawk Valley plugged an eastern outlet for the Great Lakes, sending their waters towards the Gulf of Mexico via the Mississippi River. Ice retreat from the Mohawk Valley allowed Laurentide Ice Sheet meltwater to escape to the North Atlantic, where it could weaken the Atlantic Ocean circulation system by increasing density stratification. Despite the broad importance of this relatively small region to our understanding of North American deglaciation, a significant discrepancy exists in our understanding of ice-margin fluctuations. Local studies, based on field measurements of stacked till, glacial lake, and outwash sequences, placed in time with the aid of magnetic-declination correlations, indicate cycles of ice advance and retreat. The most recent continental scale ice-margin reconstructions, however, depict monotonic ice retreat across the region because the radiocarbon and cosmogenic constraints all give minimum-limiting ages, thereby discouraging inference of readvance. In order to resolve this discrepancy, it was essential to improve the chronology of the stratigraphic record. To do so, we gathered samples of fluvial and river-fed deltaic sands from across the Mohawk Valley and performed single-grain infrared-stimulated luminescence (IRSL) on 17 samples. We likewise updated magnetic-declination correlations against the North American Varve Chronology – these were not included in the continental scale reconstruction – and folded in more distant radiocarbon constraints. Our new combined record begins with ca. 25–30 ka glacial outwash deposits predating the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) ice advance. Fluvial gravel deposits above glacial till date 17–18 ka, correlative with post-LGM ice retreat during the Erie phase, opening eastward meltwater routing at the same time a positive δ 18 O excursion (i.e., meltwater reduction) is recorded in the Gulf of Mexico. Magnetic-correlation-dated tills constrain ice-readvance phases between 17 and 15.5 ka, which partly blocked the Mohawk River valley and returned most Great Lakes meltwater to the Mississippi. Following this, the IRSL record adds information on the timing of progressively lower river-fed delta deposition, eventually leading to abandonment of the Mohawk River as a glacial meltwater spillway at 13 ka. Based on these data, we propose an ice-margin chronology that includes Erie-phase retreat and subsequent readvances, with implications for our understanding of ice dynamics, meltwater routing, and ocean–meltwater-mediated climate.

abstract: Concretions (preferentially cemented areas in sedimentary rocks) are diagenetic sedimentary features, but they may have an underappreciated potential to inform us about primary environmental conditions. Typically, they form as byproducts of microbial degradation of organic matter and may contain geochemical signals indicative of the microbial pathway. Here, we examine concretion-bearing strata in Muller Canyon, Nevada, deposited after the end-Triassic mass extinction (ETME), using geochemical and sedimentological data. Field investigation reveals that Thalassinoides burrows circumnavigate the concretions, implying the concretions were present before burrowing. Petrographic examination shows that concretions contain a high abundance of bioclasts compared to the host rock. Concretion δ¹³C carb values are similar to Early Jurassic seawater, and distinct from δ¹³C carb values typical of microbially induced reactions. The burrow-concretion relationship indicates the concretions formed at or near the sediment-water interface, very early in the diagenetic sequence. The relative lack of bioclasts in the host rock versus the concretions implies the bioclasts may have been subsequently dissolved from the host rock after the concretions formed. Although not diagnostic in isolation, the δ¹³C carb values near early Jurassic seawater values imply that mineralization was not driven by microbial organic matter degradation reactions. Concretions in broadly correlative strata from Levanto, Peru, also record δ¹³C carb values near Jurassic seawater, potentially indicative of regional, primary depositional controls on concretion formation. Distinguishing between carbonate concretion formation mechanisms has broader implications for interpreting geochemical signals across mass extinction events. We hypothesize that the Muller Canyon and Levanto carbonate concretions, although diagenetic in nature, may contain information related to the ETME, and that by studying these concretions we can further untangle ancient carbonate systems in the aftermath of mass extinction events.

abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) was established by Congress in 1879 and shortly thereafter authorized to undertake chemical and physical investigations into the geology of the United States. Central to this mission is the creation of a publicly accessible geochemical archive of analytical results obtained from geological and geochemical research studies conducted over the decades. Today, this responsibility resides with the National Geochemical Database (NGDB) Project, managed by staff at the Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center (Denver, CO), which assembles, formats, corrects, archives and releases these data to the public. In January 2026, the USGS published the most complete compilation to date of legacy and new geochemical data—collected from rock, sediment, soil, and mineral samples within U.S. state, territory or Economic Exclusive Zone (EEZ) boundaries—through the USGS data deliver platform, ScienceBase. This release represents a substantial subset of the NGDB, reflecting current operational and research priorities. The data span over 60 years of research (1962-2023) and support ongoing assessments of critical mineral resources and a wide variety of geologic and geochemical studies. The Geochemical Data Portal, an Esri-based web-mapping application, allows users to explore, filter, and download the data. We will share background on the 2-year effort to compile and release the data, describe its structure, and present a demo of the Geochemical Data Portal.

abstract: Depositional ages of sedimentary strata can be obtained through uranium (U)–lead (Pb) dating of authigenic minerals, such as calcite and apatite, that comprise carbonate and phosphorite sedimentary rocks, respectively. Primary U–Pb dates of these authigenic minerals are susceptible to post-depositional resetting via fluid interactions during regional and/or local metamorphism, which may conversely inform diagenetic histories of U and Pb mobility. Here we report laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) U–Pb isotopic data of Ediacaran–Cambrian phosphorites from the Kheseen Formation of the Khuvsgul terrane in northern Mongolia. Samples were collected along strike across 140 km of lateral distance, and from different thrust sheets associated with Paleozoic collision along the western margin of the Tuva-Mongolian Terrane. Analyses targeted microcrystalline apatite of laminated and re-worked granular phosphatic facies. While some samples retain Ediacaran–Cambrian depositional dates that are within error of chemostratigraphic age constraints for the Kheseen Formation, many samples exhibit apparently reset isotopic ratios, consistent with post-depositional resetting that likely occurred during subsequent regional metamorphic and/or deformational events. We coupled our analyses with petrography and LA-ICP-MS trace element data to characterize and link the U-–Pb dates with distinct textural and/or geochemical domains. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework to bolster the application of LA-ICP-MS geochronology for sedimentary phosphorite deposits.

abstract:
Boron isotope ratios (δ 11 B values) in carbonates are commonly used as a proxy for past seawater pH, but their reliability can be affected by diagenetic processes. Well-preserved fossil foraminifera in the geological record have enabled reliable estimates of surface ocean pH throughout the Cenozoic. However, extending pH reconstructions further back in time requires a better understanding of more complex shallow-water bulk carbonate materials. This study examines δ 11 B values in extensively dolomitized carbonates from the mid-Eocene Avon Park Formation (Florida, USA) to assess the extent of diagenetic alteration and its impact on boron incorporation. The δ 11 B values of Avon Park Formation carbonates show low variability with an average value of 13.8‰. Boron concentrations show greater variability and correlate with Mg content, suggesting a lithological control in which dolostones are enriched in boron relative to limestones. Based on trace elements concentrations and traditional stable isotope ratios (δ 13 C, δ 18 O) analysis, our results indicate that the Avon Park Formation carbonates were altered during early marine diagenesis by fluids with a composition similar to seawater.

The δ 11 B values and boron concentrations were used to reconstruct the characteristics of the diagenetic fluid indicating a pH range from 7.4 to 7.8, consistent with the pH ranges of modern pore water. These results suggest the influence of multiple factors on the isotopic composition of these bulk carbonates, such as local sedimentary pH and carbonate composition. Our mass balance model show that more than 80% of the boron in the diagenetic fluid was derived from seawater, with a smaller contribution likely originating from the dissolution of carbonate minerals. Additionally, we show that desorbed boron from clays has a minimal impact on the δ 11 B values in this system, shifting them by no more than +0.6‰. Thus, our results highlight the potential for boron isotope overprinting during early marine diagenesis. These findings suggest that while δ 11 B values in diagenetically altered bulk carbonates, particularly dolostones, may not reliably record past seawater pH, they may serve as a useful tool for reconstructing local diagenetic fluid pH and composition.

title: Limits on Large, Slow Impactors as a Source for Impact Basins on the Saturnian satellites
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Denton, C. Adeene [1], Rhoden, Alyssa [2]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Analysis of craters across Saturn’s mid-sized moons has shown evidence of an additional planetocentric impactor population [1-3]. In addition, many of the largest craters appear relatively young [1]; as large impactors are likely rarer over time, these basins may be planetocentric in origin. Mimas, the smallest (r = 198 km) and innermost of Saturn’s mid-sized moons, is heavily cratered with a large impact basin, Herschel (D ~140 km, d~10 km [4-5]) that formed within the last ~10% of Mimas’ history [1]. The velocity discrepancy between heliocentric and planetocentric impactors may be up to an order of magnitude [6-7] at Mimas, which raises significant questions for crater formation. In particular, previous work has suggested that large planetocentric debris, traveling at unusually slow speeds, could have produced Herschel in a fully frozen (and cold) Mimas [7-8], whereas impacts at higher velocity require a warm or ocean-bearing interior [9-10].

To determine whether Herschel can be produced from a large, slow impactor, we simulate impacts into a frozen, Mimas-like target for a range of large impactor sizes and velocities. We also incorporate a range of ice shell thermal structures for a fully-frozen Mimas. Our results indicate that formation of Herschel from a large, slow impact into a frozen Mimas is unlikely, potentially supporting the ocean hypothesis, as previous work found that higher-velocity planetocentric impacts (15 km/s, [9-10]) could only produce a Herschel-like crater if Mimas possessed an ocean or was near-melting at the time of impact. Large, slow debris may have produced other craters on the mid-sized moons, however; such craters possess a distinct morphology: unusually large simple craters far beyond the simple-to-complex transition.

title: Solving a stratigraphic mystery: using pXRF to field locate an unconformity by detecting abrupt provenance change in sandstones from the Narragansett Basin of Massachusetts

authors: Cook, Sarah Grace M. [1], Benner, Jacob S. [2], Knecht, Richard J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA

abstract: The Narragansett Basin of Southeastern Massachusetts contains the Wamsutta Formation, assigned to Late Carboniferous (Bashkirian) age based on plant fossils in its uppermost strata. A previous study dated a rhyolite flow within lower strata suggesting a portion of the Wamsutta Fm. was ~60 million years older (U-Pb; 373 +/- 2Ma); therefore, an unconformity must exist between the lowermost and uppermost terrestrial redbeds. We used portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) to characterize visually and structurally indistinguishable strata and to delineate a potential unconformity, predicting that a shift in sediment provenance would appear in the bulk geochemistry of the sandstone units. We measured freshly broken fine to coarse sandstones from the basin’s northwestern Wamsutta outcrop area with pXRF 5-10 times each. We derived data correction factors from linear regressions on standard reference materials and applied them to raw concentration values. We assessed and retained corrected elemental data within each sample suite based on their quality using Tukey’s Interquartile Range method, then transformed it to centered-log-ration values. Our resulting dataset was restricted to six provenance-relevant elements (Sr, Nb, Rb, Ti, Y, and Zr) plus Si and Fe for testing grain size, sorting, and matrix effects. Results of a principal components analysis (PCA) at the 6-element level were significant, explaining a combined 66.9% of total variance on two axes. PC1 was driven primarily by Sr, Nb, and Rb, while PC2 was driven by Ti and Y. A k-means cluster analysis recovered two distinct geochemical groups (0.496 silhouette) separated by only a few vertical meters. This boundary lies above the Devonian rhyolite and indicates a major provenance shift from K-feldspar (high Rb) rich to plagioclase and Ti-oxide-bearing sources (carrying Sr and Nb), likely reflecting a change in sediment supply from intrabasin volcanics and Quincy Granite-like lithologies to those with more mafic components. We determined grain size and sorting not to be a factor in the analysis, as it varied minimally across all sandstones sampled, and elements associated with heavy minerals were not correlated with changes in grain size or sorting. While a shift in provenance does not in itself indicate an unconformity, one this significant (PC1 p=0.0000) and abrupt is unlikely to have been generated without one. Index fossils, if discovered above and below the geochemical boundary, could confirm our hypothesis.

title: Tracing paleo-redox evolution and diagenesis in marine basins: Advances in LA-ICP-MS trace element geochemistry of carbonate fluorapatite
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems
authors: Martinez, Priscilla Rosemary [1], Kirk, Jason D. [2], Carrapa, Barbara [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
abstract:
Marine phosphorites are critical archives of Earth's biogeochemical cycles, recording major oceanographic and ecological reorganizations across geologic time. The understanding of phosphogenesis, the authigenic precipitation of carbonate fluorapatite (CFA), in marine sediments has undergone a fundamental paradigm shift over the past several decades. Early models invoke anomalous oceanic phosphorus cycling to explain intervals of widespread phosphorite deposition, whereas current frameworks recognize phosphorite deposits as the preserved expression of a convergence of redox, hydrodynamic, tectonic, and oceanographic boundary conditions. CFA sensitivity to seawater redox conditions and porewater chemistry at the sediment-water interface, coupled with its widespread preservation across continental margins, has opened new avenues for using CFA-bearing sedimentary successions to reconstruct the evolving redox conditions and nutrient cycling of ancient ocean basins across major Earth system transitions. However, the degree to which CFA trace and rare earth element (TREE) systematics preserve primary paleoenvironmental signals versus diagenetically overprinted signatures remains a central and incompletely resolved problem.

In situ LA-ICP-MS elemental mapping has emerged as a powerful analytical approach for addressing this problem, enabling spatially resolved quantification of TREE distributions at the scale of individual CFA grains and discrimination of primary seawater-derived signatures from diagenetic overprints. Normalized TREE systematics of ancient phosphorites compared against modern seawater compositions can elucidate on benthic redox conditions, upwelling intensity, and porewater chemistry during CFA precipitation, while Ce anomalies, LREE/HREE fractionation trajectories, and Y anomalies fingerprint the style and extent of post-formational modification. Here, we compare Miocene–Pliocene phosphogenic sedimentary sequences from the southeastern Pacific margin, which reveals that Chilean phosphorites preserve ubiquitous negative Ce anomalies consistent with oxic precipitation, whereas Peruvian phosphorites yield negligible Ce anomalies reflecting more reducing conditions, despite comparably elevated phosphorus availability driven by Humboldt Current upwelling along both margins. This suggests that local basin-scale redox conditions, and the depositional setting in which phosphorites form and are preserved, are primary controls on TREE proxy fidelity. These findings highlight the utility of integrating spatially resolved TREE geochemistry with high-resolution U-Pb CFA geochronology to directly link phosphogenesis timing to paleoenvironmental conditions preserved within discrete CFA domains. Applied across the diverse tectonic settings in which phosphorites occur, this coupled LA-ICP-MS framework represents a broadly transferable approach for reconstructing basin-scale phosphorus cycling and paleoceanographic evolution through time.
