title: Decapod Body Size Evolution is Best Modeled as an Unbounded Random Walk from a Moderately Sized Origin
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Daunoras, Vanessa [1], Khan, Nafeesa [2], Novack-Gottshall, Philip M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Biological Sciences, Benedictine University, Lisle, IL,
(2) Biological Sciences, Benedictine University, Lisle, IL,
(3) Biological Sciences, Benedictine University, Lisle, IL,
abstract:
As powerful predators, scavengers, and nutrient recyclers, decapod crustaceans have played critical roles in marine ecosystems throughout their history. However, their body size evolution is poorly understood. Here, we use an updated database of decapod body sizes for more than 1000 decapod fossil and extant genera to document their size evolution through time. Despite tremendous diversification during the “Mesozoic marine revolution,ˮ the average body size of decapods has maintained moderate sizes since their Devonian origin. During this history, maximum and minimum body sizes have expanded symmetrically across six orders of size magnitude. Maximum-likelihood statistics confirm the ordinal trend is best modeled as an unbounded, unbiased random walk (URW), which is also consistent with the persistent mean and continuous bidirectional expansion of smaller and larger body sizes from a moderately sized origin. Size trends in decapod subgroups also tend to be best supported by the URW model. A directional size increase cannot be ruled out for Dendrobranchiata and Brachyura, especially during the Mesozoic. Notably, decapod body size is remarkably unchanged during both Triassic and Cretaceous mass extinctions, despite substantial diversity losses at the K/Pg. These patterns are an exception to the generalization that Cope's rule applies across most animal groups, and sheds important light on body-size decapod evolutionary history.

The first two authors contributed equally. This research has been supported by NSF grant #2322080.

title: Reassessing a Metamorphic Core Complex and deformation style along the Bullfrog Hills-Fluorspar Canyon Detachment Fault, Beatty NV.
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee (Posters)
authors: Underwood-Aguilar, Ruben [1], Kirkpatrick, James [2], Jowitt, Simon [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA; Center for Research in Economic Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, Nevada, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, NV,
(3) Center for Research in Economic Geology, Nevada Bureau Mines & Geology, Reno, NV,
abstract:
The Bullfrog Hills–Fluorspar Canyon detachment (BHFCD) fault in western Nevada, just south of Beatty, has previously been proposed to be a metamorphic core complex (MCC). The surrounding mining districts host structurally controlled Au ore deposits of Miocene age that are historically—and currently—viable resources. However, significant Paleozoic and early Mesozoic thrusting have intensely folded and potentially rotated footwall rocks south of the BHFCD, complicating deformational history. Understanding the tectonic history and specific structural context of the BHFCD is critical for mineral exploration in the region. In this study, we re-investigate the rocks north and south of the BHFCD to document deformation variation, relative timing relationships, and fault kinematics. Specifically, we are conducting detailed mapping (1:3,300 scale) of undifferentiated lower-plate rocks. Lower plate rocks have been postulated to have rotated during Miocene extension, yet typical MCC features—such as pervasive mylonites and high-temperature basement rocks—are sparse to non-existent in the Beatty area. Mylonitic fabrics, though rarely exposed along the BHFCD, remain poorly understood. Instead, the footwall rocks exhibit complexly folded Paleozoic strata with predominantly N-S fold axes, which are inferred to result from Paleozoic and early Mesozoic convergence, though crenulations and refolded folds indicate complex kinematics. Currently, field data collected have focused on intensely refolded Paleozoic strata to untangle the amount of extensional folding during Miocene unroofing. We plan to use microstructural analyses to construct grain-size and thermal profiles from upper to lower plates to test if the BHFCD originated form an MCC and to establish the kinematics of deformation.

Previous work suggests that the BHFCD connects to the Boundary Canyon Detachment (BCD) in the Funeral Mountains to the southwest, which sits atop a well-characterized MCC. Reconciling the isolated BHFCD mylonites with the nearby Funeral Mountains MCC is challenging, leaving the BHFCD's tectonic affinity ambiguous. By clarifying the relationships between brittle and ductile deformation, we test whether the BHFCD represents a structurally isolated detachment system or, alternatively, a reactivated thrust system overprinted by Miocene extension. Furthermore, this project will test whether Au-bearing faults initiated prior to the Miocene and whether similar structures exist along the BHFCD that share this pre-existing inheritance. Ultimately, these findings will improve our understanding of regional deformation, providing new constraints for structurally controlled ore deposit exploration.

title: How is Systems Thinking Conceptualized, Operationalized, and Assessed in NGSS-Aligned Research: A PRISMA Systematic Literature Review
session_title: Making Sense of Methodologies and Theoretical Frameworks in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Cheek, Kim [1]
affiliations: (1) Teaching, Learning, and Curriculum, University of North Florida, Jacksonville, FL, USA
abstract:
Literature reviews make important contributions to a field by synthesizing findings from multiple studies and suggesting directions for future research. Reviews on constructs like systems thinking are especially valuable due to its critical importance in geoscience and beyond. In the past decade, there have been several literature reviews of systems thinking. Yet, none of those reviews explicitly investigated whether or how systems thinking is conceptualized and assessed in relation to the crosscutting concept systems and system models in the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). Thus, it is currently unclear what type of NGSS-aligned instruction might explicitly improve systems thinking in K-12 education.

This systematic literature review aims to address that gap. While there are many types of literature reviews, PRISMA systematic literature reviews rely on a specific protocol, clear inclusion and exclusion criteria, and methods to assess the risk of bias in studies included in the review. PRISMA reviews are highly regarded for their transparency, standardization, and thorough methodology, making them especially important for developing future research agendas in a field. In addition to a discussion of the results, this talk will highlight the steps involved in conducting a PRISMA systematic literature review, including how inclusion and exclusion criteria and search terms were developed, how transparency was maintained, and risk of bias assessed.

Research questions for this in-process review focus on how NGSS-aligned empirical studies define, operationalize, and assess systems thinking and the extent to which there is coherence among the elements. Three databases and citation searching identified 579 records in peer-reviewed articles from 2014-2026. After duplicates were removed and initial screening of titles and abstracts, full texts of 83 articles were screened. Studies were limited to ones mentioning systems thinking, complex systems, or system models. Next Generation Science Standards, NGSS, three-dimensional learning, crosscutting concepts, science and engineering practices, and performance expectations were used to identify NGSS-aligned studies. Studies within and beyond geoscience were included to increase the number of reports. While data analysis is in-process at abstract submission, screening indicates that K-12 systems thinking research may not be aligned with the NGSS systems and system models. Results and opportunities for future research to increase coherence in how systems thinking is conceptualized and assessed for three-dimensional learning, especially in geoscience, will be discussed.

title: Outcrop Affinity: Building an Open Geospatial Database of Roadside Geologic Outcrops across the Appalachians
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Bhattacharya, Gourab [1], Moore, Robert [2], Doane, Franklin [3], Schelling, Kaci [4], Busby, Conner [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
(2) Harpeth Valley Utilities District, Nashville, TN, USA
(3) Computer Science, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
(4) Center for Earthquake Research and Information, University of Memphis, Memphis, TN, USA
(5) Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
abstract:
Geologic outcrops are fundamental to field-based research, mapping, and education, yet regional-scale inventories of accessible exposures remain largely absent from geoscience data infrastructure. Outcrop Affinity addresses this gap through an automated geospatial workflow and open-access web database for discovering and cataloging roadside-accessible geologic outcrops. The algorithmic approach integrates publicly available 1-m LiDAR-derived digital elevation models and U.S. Census road-network data to quantify spatial and topographic relationships between high-relief terrain and roadways. Automated processing within ArcGIS Pro integrates local-relief analysis, threshold optimization, terrain classification, vector filtering, and spatial analysis to identify candidate roadside exposures.

Application across 14 Appalachian states from Maine to Alabama demonstrates the scalability of the approach, producing a regional database of roadside-accessible outcrop locations with direct Google Street View links for rapid remote examination. Independent validation in rural Tennessee and western North Carolina yielded true-positive rates of 83–86%. Accuracy was lower and more variable in urban settings (59–87%), where buildings, retaining walls, bridges, and other anthropogenic features commonly resemble natural high-relief terrain.

The resulting Outcrop Affinity web platform enables users to explore outcrop locations alongside geologic information and provides a framework for community-contributed field observations and photographs. The workflow is readily transferable beyond the Appalachians to other regions where suitable high-resolution elevation and road-network datasets are available. Outcrop Affinity demonstrates how open geospatial data, automated spatial analysis, and web-based cyberinfrastructure can transform scattered geologic exposures into a discoverable and extensible digital resource for field geology, research, and education.

title: Developing AI solutions to accelerate mineral resource assessment workflows

authors: Goldman, Margaret A. [1], Rosera, Joshua M. [2], Graham, Garth E. [3], Watkins, David [4]

(2) US Geological Survey, Herndon, VA, USA

abstract:
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) conducts critical mineral resource assessments (CMRAs) to inform land use planners and public stakeholders about domestic resource potential. Recent legislation directs the USGS to complete comprehensive national assessments of each critical mineral by 2031. The traditional approach to conducting CMRAs, developed and adapted by the USGS over the past 50 years, is labor- and time-intensive due to the large amount of data compilation and preparation required. A typical assessment takes 1-2 years from start to finish. To complete comprehensive assessments of all critical mineral commodities would likely require decades with existing staff and techniques. This prompted the USGS to enter a partnership with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) in spring 2022 to accelerate CMRAs and ultimately increase availability of timely, data-driven undiscovered resource estimates and maps. Following an initial scoping effort that included a machine learning competition aimed at extracting data from scanned geologic maps, DARPA, USGS, and the Advanced Research Project Agency – Energy (ARPA-E) launched the Critical Mineral Assessments with AI Support (CriticalMAAS) program. CriticalMAAS spanned 18 months, from August 2023 to February 2025, and included 4 technical areas: 1) data extraction from maps; 2) mineral feature engineering from documents and datasets; 3) mineral prospectivity mapping; and 4) human-in-the-loop learning. Nearly two dozen AI tools supporting the compilation and preparation of geoscience data and the execution of advanced machine learning models to create mineral prospectivity maps were developed. Most of these tools were made accessible to assessment scientists through no-code interactive web applications. The program also produced a centralized data repository (CDR) to facilitate integration of datasets and tasks employed in assessment workflows.

The CDR and the Polymer web application, designed to facilitate the curation of geologic map data for assessments, were the most mature tools at the program’s conclusion. In the past year, commercial AI software and cloud services supporting data extraction pipelines have continued to advance. The USGS is currently working to operationalize the CDR and Polymer, integrating these recent advances as well as some of the CriticalMAAS mineral prospectivity mapping tools to provide USGS geoscientists with modern assessment tools. We will present the system’s status and plans for continued maintenance and integration of new data supporting CMRAs and mineral resources research.

title: Relationship Between Fractures, Faults, Karst Features, and Groundwater Flow in Sinking Valley, Pennsylvania
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Steinhilber, Taylor [1], Pirhalla, Kathryn [2], Anhe, Daniel [3], Ridenour, Brooke [4], Hurd , Todd [5], Behr, Rose-Anna [6], Crowell, Bryan [7], Walsh, Talor [8]
affiliations: (1) Millersville University Earth Sciences, Millersville, PA, USA
(5) Department of Biology, Shippensburg University, Shippensburg, Pennsylvania, USA
(6) Pennsylvania Department of Conservation of Natural Resources, Pennsylvania, USA
(8) Millersville University Earth Sciences, Millersville, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
The orientations of fractures, faults, and bedding planes can play a critical role in controlling the development of secondary permeability within karst aquifers. We investigated the relationship between geologic structure, groundwater flow, and the development of karst features in Sinking Valley, a karst valley hosting middle Ordovician carbonates in Blair County, Pennsylvania.

Mapping of geologic structures was conducted in Tytoona Cave, Field Trip Cave, and an adjacent roadcut and documented thrust faults, strike-slip faults, joints, veins, and en echelon vein arrays consistent with the established deformation sequence found within the Appalachian Valley and Ridge.

To evaluate groundwater flow pathways, sodium fluorescein dye was injected into a swallow hole within Sinking Run, a sinking stream that loses its flow into the subsurface upstream of its confluence with the Little Juniata River. Water samples collected over 2.5 days in the Little Juniata River and were analyzed using a spectrofluorophotometer. The dye discharged from a single source, a riparian spring on the bank of the Little Juniata River. Dye was first detected 24 hours after injection. This rapid travel time and localized discharge indicate that the spring is fed by a karst conduit.

The structural and hydrologic data together indicate that geologic structures influence conduit development within Sinking Valley. Cave passage orientations in Tytoona Cave correspond to regionally extensive joint sets and veins, suggesting that speleogenesis occurred by preferential dissolution along previously existing discontinuities. Furthermore, the inferred groundwater flow path must crosscut the Coburn and Loysburg limestones into the Bellefonte Dolostone before discharging at the riparian spring, indicating that lithologic solubility alone does not control conduit development. Instead, the orientation of fractures may drive conduit formation even in less soluble lithologies. These results suggest that dye tracing combined with the evaluation of geologic structures such as fractures and faults can improve models of groundwater flow in karst aquifers, where heterogenous permeability makes fluid flow difficult to characterize.

title: Temperature Monitoring and Comparative Analysis of Rock Glacier and Non-Glacial Streams in the Bridger-Teton National Forest

authors: Hanley, Brett Coyne [1], Marks, Samantha [2], Snyder, Justin [3]
affiliations: (1) USDA Forest Service, Bridger-Teton National Forest, Pinedale, WY, USA

abstract: The Bridger-Teton National Forest (BTNF) is situated in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem and currently contains 328 mapped rock glaciers (Johnson et al., 2021). These may serve as reliable cold water sources in a changing climate due to the presence of ice insulated by debris cover (Brighenti et al., 2021). Despite several rock glacier studies being conducted at broad scales, the current impact of BTNF rock glaciers and their meltwater streams on the local ecosystem is relatively unknown. This study aims to investigate whether rock glacier-fed streams in the BTNF differ substantially in temperature from non-glacier-fed streams and therefore represent priority cold water refugia for land management agency actions. To accomplish this, baseline data from rock glacier meltwater fed streams and streams without perennial ice sources will be collected at a local scale within the BTNF. This information will then be analyzed to see if it is useful and feasible to collect at a BTNF-wide scale given the complexity of the terrain, restrictions of designated wilderness areas, and limited capacity of employees. The successes and failures of the methodologies from this study will be used to create a monitoring plan for rock glaciers in the BTNF. Understanding the distribution of rock glaciers and their influence on downstream plants, animals, people, and infrastructure is essential when considering management decisions, priorities, and protections (Brighenti et al., 2021).

title: Exploring Stressors Leading to Increased Rates of Teratology Across the Mississippian Pella Formation of Iowa
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Cerami, April C. [1], Petsios, Elizabeth [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
abstract: Morphological abnormalities can provide an organism-level window into how extinct taxa responded to environmental stress. This work focuses on the Middle Mississippian (Visean) Pella Formation of Iowa, which has been referenced as having a large frequency of abnormal invertebrate fossils. Horowitz et al. (1986) describes teratological defects in the blastoid Pentremites pulchellus from the Pella Formation which occur at a rate of 2.7%. Hessler (1962) additionally references several trilobites belonging to the species Kaskia wilsoni (formerly Griffithides wilsoni ) with abnormal segmentation from the same site. Horowitz et al. (1986) did not include any photographs of the observed abnormal blastoids and Hessler (1962) included only one photograph of an abnormal Pella Formation trilobite as an example. This study aims to describe and consider potential drivers leading to the abnormalities observed in the invertebrate paleocommunity of the Pella Formation. To do this, bulk samples have been collected from the portions of the Pella Formation exposed at Lacey-Keosauqua State Park in Keosauqua IA and the Russell Wildlife Area in Oskaloosa IA. Abnormal macrofossils collected from these site as well as from the Pella Formation museum collections at the University of Iowa have been photographed and their abnormalities have been classified. Ostracods were used to constrain salinity levels and wavelength dispersive XRF elemental analysis was performed on the fossil matrix to test for redox sensitive trace elements as a proxy for water column oxygenation. This work has yielded multiple abnormal blastoids, crinoids and trilobites, making this the first multi-phylum invertebrate community to be observed with high rates of abnormality. The ostracod community at the site yielded only normal marine taxa, indicating that salinity stress is likely not the main driver. Elevated trace metal concentrations can be observed in some Pella Formation samples, suggesting that local oceanographic conditions may play a role in the heightened frequency of abnormal growth. Further work is needed to elucidate the relative importance of environmental factors such as water column anoxia, heavy metal toxicity, or thermal stress on these communities.

abstract: While larger eruptions tend to be prioritized when studying magmatic cyclicity, a more holistic perspective can be gained from studying the small, intervening eruptions alongside these larger eruptions. Here, we target small-volume explosive eruptions preserved as airfall deposits in New Zealand’s Taupō Volcanic Zone (TVZ) between two major eruptive events, the Whakamaru supereruption (~350 ka, ~1500 km³) and the Chimp eruption (~310 ka, ~100 km³), to resolve magmatic behavior directly after, between, and leading up to major eruptions. Field examination of a representative tephra sequence identified 15 tephra horizons between the Whakamaru and Chimp eruptions. There are 6 reworked and 9 pristine tephra horizons, in addition to 5 paleosols. The reworked sections occur just after the Whakamaru and just before the Chimp eruptions. Major-element analysis performed via Scanning Electron Microscope with Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) was conducted on matrix glass from 7-17 clasts of ash- to lapilli-sized pumice clasts for each of the 15 tephra horizons (total 161 clasts). All glass is high-silica rhyolite with SiO2 ranging from 75.7-78.0 wt.%. While not all horizons demonstrate homogeneous compositions, there are four major compositional groups, primarily distinguished by SiO2 and CaO. These tephra are similar to glass compositions from the 310-240 ka TVZ flare-up compositions, notably overlapping with Whakamaru type A magmas. The Downer Road Tephras do not overlap with Chimp type A, and there is no direct overlap with Chimp type B, but type B is within the range of heterogeneous sections in SiO2 vs. CaO. These distinct glass populations suggest multiple magma bodies produced these smaller eruptions during a period of relative quiescence between large eruptions. Ongoing work aims to differentiate magma bodies and potentially trace these eruptions to eruptive centers active during this period. These small eruptions help to build a comprehensive picture of long-term volcanic cyclicity in one of the most active silicic regions in the world.

title: Investigating Fracture Networks and Connectivity in the North American Midcontinent Rift, Northeast Minnesota
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems (Posters)
authors: Daniels, Nathan Edward [1], Braunagel, Michael John [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Science, University of Minnesota Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, Duluth, MN, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Duluth, MN, USA
abstract:
Magmatic rift systems are important sources of metal and energy resources, including hydrothermal copper, geothermal energy production, and ultramafic bodies that can produce geologic hydrogen through serpentinization. The generation and distribution of many of these potential resources in rift systems are controlled by fracture networks, which provide the pathways and potential traps for fluid and gas migration in otherwise impermeable igneous rocks. Fracture networks in rift systems are complex, and may form in response to different applied stresses, including tectonic stresses, fracturing in the vicinity of pressurized intrusive bodies, and exhumation and unroofing. Although these rifts have proven to be vital, understanding the deep fracture network in these systems can be difficult due to the landscape and tectonic history.

The ~1.1 Ga North American Midcontinent Rift has a complex tectono-magmatic history, which resulted in abundant critical resources. However, the fracture networks of the Midcontinent Rift are poorly constrained. Rocks of the rift’s Duluth Complex can provide insight into the fracture network and geomechanical behavior of deep rift rocks, since they have been exhumed to the surface. To this end, we quantitatively characterized the fracture network of units in the complex by measuring fracture orientation, connectivity, compressive strength using a Schmidt Hammer, and identifying the abutting and cross-cutting relationships between fracture sets. This dataset allows us to constrain which fracture sets are critically stressed for fluid flow under the current stress regime, and provides for an understanding of the history of fracture network evolution within magmatic rift systems that may aid in extrapolation worldwide.

For each study site representing different intrusive bodies and the host rock of the Midcontinent Rift, we isolated major fracture sets based on consistency in orientation and used cross cutting relationships of the different fracture networks to better understand the relative ages of major fracturing events relative to the previously constrained ages of emplacement for each intrusion. Our preliminary data shows that the intrusive units of the Duluth Complex, consistently have a lower fracture density than the surrounding crystalline host rock, despite similar compressive strengths, and there are three distinct fracture sets across all sites. Based on relative age analysis, the most discontinuous set, which we interpret to be the youngest, strikes ~090, and the oldest, most continuous set, strikes ~150.

title: Exhumation Across the North Canterbury Fold and Thrust Belt: Implications for the Evolution of the Marlborough Transfer Zone, South Island, Aotearoa New Zealand
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Huising, Madison S. [1], Niemi, Nathan A. [2], Amos, Colin B. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(2) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(3) Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
abstract:
The North Canterbury Fold and Thrust Belt (NCFTB) is located south of the dominantly right-lateral Marlborough Fault System (MFS) on the South Island of Aotearoa New Zealand and accommodates the transition from subduction to transform deformation in the Marlborough Transfer Zone (MTZ). Existing thermochronometric data from the MFS record a two-phase evolution consisting of compressional deformation and exhumation along the present-day traces of MFS faults during the late Eocene to mid-Miocene, followed by their successive reactivation as strike-slip faults with attendant regional exhumation at ~2 Ma.

We present new low-temperature thermochronologic data from across North Canterbury, including apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe) and zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe) ages, combined with paleo-thermal burial temperature estimates from Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous materials (RSCM).

The Plio-Pleistocene-aged Kowai Formation independently constrains the onset of exhumation in the NCFTB and contextualizes the thermochronometric ages. AHe ages immediately south of the Hope Fault are ~5 Ma and fully reset, while ages throughout the rest of the NCFTB range from ~24-120 Ma. We interpret these ages as partially reset based on Early Cretaceous depositional ages of sampled strata. ZHe ages are ~100-180 Ma across most of North Canterbury and interpreted as unrest, but ~25-65 Ma ages south of the Hope Fault appear partially reset. Peak burial temperatures from RSCM range from ~165-195 °C.

A distinct boundary between younger ages near the MFS and substantially older ages across most of the NCFTB coincides with faults that ruptured during the 2016 Mw 7.8 Kaikōura earthquake. This boundary also separates domains of predominantly oblique-slip faults with right-lateral top-to-the-east displacement within the MFS from west-vergent structures in the NCFTB, clearly differentiating strike-slip and compressional regimes.

These datasets, combined with other constraints, indicate million-year exhumation rates of ~1.3-2.2 mm/yr on structures throughout the NCFTB. These rates are comparable with late Pleistocene terrace uplift rates derived from differential incision and OSL dating. These results clarify our understanding of the exhumation history of North Canterbury and suggest that the onset of shortening and exhumation in the NCFTB is temporally coincident with regional exhumation across the MFS, providing insight into how fault systems interact and evolve at plate boundaries with migrating subduction zone terminations.

title: Tectonic Development of a Mesozoic Composite Terrane: The Western Mélange Belt, Washington.
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: MacDonald, James H. [1], Dragovich, Joe D. [2], DuFrane , S. Andy [3], Anderson, Megan L. [4], Sauer, Kirsten B. [5]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(2) Dragovich Geo-Consulting, Lacey, WA, USA
(3) University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada; Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM, USA
(4) Washington Geological Survey, Olympia, WA, USA
(5) Winthrop, Wa, USA; University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
abstract:
The western mélange belt (WMB) consists of generally low-grade metaigneous and metasedimentary rocks exposed in the Cascade Mountains foothills, Washington. We used field mapping, geophysics, whole-rock geochemistry, petrography, and detrital U-Pb zircon age dating to better understand the tectonic development of the WMB. Field mapping and geophysics has identified three nappes within the WMB which were disrupted by Tertiary and younger, high-angle faulting. The highest nappe includes metasediments including volcanic lithic sandstones, metavolcanics, rare phyllite, quartz mica schist and marble. The middle nappe, termed Lake Chaplain nappe, consists of 172–148 Ma metagabbro with lesser metagranitoids that are locally gneissic. The lowest nappe consists of metasediments, including distinctive arkosic metasandstones, and metavolcanics. True disrupted mélange structure only occurs in the middle nappe. Metaplutonic and metatuffs are predominantly metaluminous, magnesian, and have arc affinities. Metavolcanic rocks have arc affinities except for one E-MORB and one OIB. Metaigneous samples are from depleted mantle sources, with a small group having more enriched sources.

Geochemically, sediments display little recycling and plot in fields defined by modern back-arc basins. Arkosic sandstones and accompanying argillites have intermediate provenances. Lithic sandstones and accompanying argillites have mafic-to-intermediate provenances. Four lithic and four arkosic sandstones have been analyzed for detrital zircon U-Pb ages. Detrital zircon U-Pb maximum depositional ages (MDA) for sandstones fall into three groups: Upper Jurassic; Lower Cretaceous; and Upper Cretaceous. The Jurassic sandstones are lithic and lack pre-Mesozoic zircons. The Lower Cretaceous sandstones are lithic and include older Mesozoic, Paleozoic, and Precambrian zircons. The Upper Cretaceous sandstones are arkosic, include Mesozoic, few Paleozoic, and abundant Precambrian zircons. One arkosic sandstone has an MDA of 74.2±1.3 Ma.

Current information suggests the WMB consists of at least three arc terranes which range in age from Late Jurassic to Late Cretaceous. The arcs transition from juvenile to mature as they progress in age, assemble, and form a composite terrane feature. As the older terranes accreted, they likely provided detritus to the younger arc depositional basins. The three internal nappes may reflect original accretion of multiple terranes against each other as the accretionary prism collapsed over time. After accretion, this composite terrane translated to the north and was emplaced as a thrust sheet in the Northwest Cascades thrust system after 74 Ma.

title: Taking the Pulse of the mid-Cretaceous Sevier Fold-Thrust Belt: The Iron Springs Formation of Southwest Utah.
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Quick, James Daniel [1], Hogan, John Patrick [2], Wizevich, Michael C. [3], Crowley, James L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(2) Missouri University of Science and Technology, Retired, Durham, NH,
(3) Earth and Space Sciences, Central Connecticut State University, New Britain, CT, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
abstract:
We present results from geologic mapping, measured sections, and detrital zircon (DZ) analyses to reinterpret the age and tectonostratigraphic significance of the lower Iron Springs Formation (ISF) at its type locality The Three Peaks. Here, lower ISF records initiation of a piggyback basin during rapid advancement of the Sevier thrust front as part of a Cordilleran-wide, mid-Cretaceous tectonic event.

Initial movement on the Iron Springs thrust at ca. 103 Ma generated accommodation along the trailing limb of the associated fault-propagation anticline to form a piggyback basin. Initial sediments preserved in this basin, at the type locality, are lacustrine limestones and seismically-triggered subaqueous debris flow limestone breccias of the Marshall Creek Breccia (MCB; basal member of the ISF) interbedded with sandstones and quartzite conglomerates. DZ provenance analysis suggests detritus was derived from both the hanging wall of the Iron Springs thrust to the east and the Wah Wah thrust to the west. A DZ maximum depositional age of 103.1+/-1.9 was determined for the MCB. As initial slip on the Iron Springs fault waned, an influx of siliciclastic material derived from the Wah Wah thrust arrived as a basal cobble conglomerate of the (informal) Sage Hills member (SHM), overlain by the 100.18 +/-0.04 Ma Three Peaks Tuff Member (Quick et al., 2020). We suggest this couplet is correlative with the basal conglomerate-~100 Ma tuff couplet of the lower Iron Springs in Gunlock, Utah. In The Three Peaks, this couplet is overlain by a series of lenticular bodies of sandstone alternating with laterally persistent beds of variegated blue-gray (fresh) silty and sandy limestone of the SHM. The limestone increases in siliciclastic content up-section and the top of the member is defined by the last continuous silty-sandy limestone bed. Progressive unroofing of Jurassic strata in the hanging wall of the Iron Springs thrust led to a subtle shift in provenance between the MCB and overlying sandstones and conglomerates of the SHM. A DZ maximum depositional age of 98.6+/-1.8 Ma was established in the upper SHM. The lower ISF, deposited between ca. 103 Ma and 98.6 Ma, preserves a record of the early episodic strain history of the Iron Springs and Wah Wah thrusts that coincides with the mid-Cretaceous magmatic flare-up of the Cordilleran arc.

title: A Celebration of the Pennsylvanian in the Subsurface at National to Sedimentary Basin Scale
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n)
authors: Sweetkind, Donald S. [1], Smout, Brooklyn [2], Goldberg, Judd [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
State and federal geological survey organizations use national- to basin-scale three-dimensional (3-D) modeling and subsurface mapping studies to support resource assessments, numerical process models, basin-scale tectonic and stratigraphic studies, and land management decisions. Pennsylvanian strata and the Pennsylvanian time interval are important components in these subsurface maps and models; here we celebrate Pennsylvanian rocks in the subsurface as we describe their incorporation into digital 3-D geologic models at varying scales.

At the national scale, a wealth of subsurface geologic data is benchmarked in the legacy paleotectonic and stratigraphic atlas published in 1975 as U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Professional Paper 853, "Paleotectonic Investigations of the Pennsylvanian System in the United States". This atlas presents, in diagrammatic form, subsurface geologic data that bears on sedimentation and tectonic events of the Pennsylvanian system through isopach, supracrop, subcrop, generalized lithologic, and paleotectonic maps. Many of these maps have been digitized and re-released as spatial data by the USGS, serving as an important set of subsurface digital data for the Pennsylvanian in a national-scale 3-D framework model.

Pennsylvanian rocks of the interior cratonic platform of the United States were deposited in two contrasting basin settings, intraplate basins such as the Illinois and Michigan Basins and proforeland flexural basins that developed in front advancing thrust fronts, such as the Appalachian and Denver Basins. In the Denver Basin, Pennsylvanian Lyons and Fountain Formations record alluvial fan sediments shed off the rising Ancestral Rocky Mountains; eastward, these clastic sediments interfinger with dolomites and anhydrites of the Stone Corral Formation deposited on a stable carbonate platform. A 3-D model of the Denver Basin must reconcile these differing Pennsylvanian depositional processes while preserving a constant unit stacking order within the digital model.

In the Illinois Basin, the Pennsylvanian section is bound at its base by the regional sub-Absaroka sequence unconformity. In this cratonic basin setting, this unconformity records the far-field effects of Pennsylvanian tectonism; the unconformity itself is not reported in well logs but must be deduced by missing section. The unconformity is an important framework element in 3-D basin scale models because it separates strata of differing lithologic and material properties.

title: Depth Profiling Zircon Rim Chemistry from the Last Chance Stock, Bingham Canyon Mining District, UT
session_title: Granite-related mineral systems: Advances in understanding their genesis, distribution, and exploration implications (Posters)
authors: McSweeney, Daniel [1], Beckman, Renan [2], Schoonover, Erik Jeffery [3], Moser, Desmond [4], Reimink, Jesse [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(4) Department of Earth Sciences, Western University, London, ON, Canada
(5) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract:
Copper is becoming an increasingly essential element to modern industry with the proposed growth of green energy sources leading to a projected increase in the metal’s demand. The majority of global copper resources currently come from Porphyry Copper Deposits (PCDs). PCDs involve a complex array of magmatic and hydrothermal processes, which require further investigation to understand the mechanisms that lead to PCD formation. An increasing number of publications focus on zircon geochronology and geochemistry as a mechanism for understanding magmatic and hydrothermal processes related to PCD development and, ultimately, the processes governing giant ore-body formation.

Our research group has been working to develop novel geochemical analytical protocols that target zircon rim-growth chemistry. Rim-ward growth tends to occur at lower temperatures, thereby recording late-stage magmatic, or even hydrothermal, processes. However, rim growth zones are nearly impossible to measure with standard methods. We have been focusing on using depth profiling to characterize the typically inaccessible rim chemistry, and the chemical growth trajectory inward from the rims.

In this presentation, we show new zircon geochemical analyses from zircon extracted from the Last Chance Stock, Bingham Canyon, Utah, which is spatially associated with the Bingham Canyon Cu-Mo-Au Porphyry Deposit, one of the largest PCDs in the world. We have performed Laser Ablation Split-Stream Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (LASS-ICP-MS) depth profiling for trace element chemistry. To understand and visualize the chemical depth profile through the zircon, we removed the analyzed zircon grains, rotated them 90 o about the c-axis, then remounted and polished the mounts to expose the depth profiles. We then mapped them using Cathodoluminescence (CL) spectroscopy and Backscatter Electron (BSE) imaging. This allowed us to integrate time-series chemical data with internal grain zoning for a full characterization profile. Ultimately, we present preliminary data from the Last Chance Stock, compare it to zircon extracted from other ore-bearing and non-ore-bearing systems, and explore the implications of our data for PCD development in one of the largest ore systems known.

title: Methods for Construction of a 14-Layer Geologic Framework Model of the Cratonic Continental Interior of the United States
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Sweetkind, Donald S. [1], Smout, Brooklyn [2], Johnson, Benjamin G. [3], Kinney, Scott [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, DENVER, CO, USA
abstract: Three-dimensional (3-D) geological information is an essential component in addressing many current and emerging geoscience issues. The U.S. Geological Survey constructs regional and national 3-D models and subsurface geologic datasets to support resource assessments, numerical process models, basin-scale tectonic and stratigraphic studies, and land management decisions. 3-D geologic framework models can represent stratigraphic-based model units by defining boundaries computed from unit elevation, thickness, extent, and the effect of faults. However, construction of the boundary elements for a national scale 3-D framework is hindered by the comparative lack of subsurface data outside energy-rich basins and by the regional-scale stratigraphic synthesis required to correlate the many geologic units reported in state and national well databases. A new 14-layer geologic model of the cratonic continental interior was constructed using national-scale thickness maps at the period/system level from legacy paleotectonic and stratigraphic atlases. Unit extent shown on these maps was modified to match mapped surface exposures on geologic maps to link the subsurface and surface expression of each model unit. Thickness maps were then positioned in 3-D space by hanging the thickness grid on an appropriate elevation datum. Elevation control for any time slice is at best regional in scope and the collection of elevation datums becomes a patchwork that is completed by locally stacking thickness grids to fill the 3-D volume. A companion approach to developing a national subsurface model involves using formation tops reported in oil and gas well databases to assign and aggregate stratigraphic ages at the period/system level. Stratigraphic ages are assigned by matching formation names to a national standard lexicon of stratigraphic names and ages. Formation tops and their associated depths are then grouped by geologic age and aggregated as derivative maps by period/system. Although these approaches differ in methodology, both are ultimately rooted in interpretations of borehole and geophysical data, providing complementary perspectives that balance expert regional synthesis with the broader but more heterogeneous interpretations preserved in national well databases. The resulting 3-D models from these companion approaches are a first step towards a national-scale volumetric 3-D geologic model.

title: Critical Mineral Potential of Metamorphic Shear Zone Hydrothermal Systems
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Taylor, Ryan D [1], Hofstra, Albert H [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) Colorado, USA
abstract:
Metamorphic shear zone hydrothermal systems include orogenic gold±antimony±arsenic±graphite and Coeur d’Alene-type polymetallic sulfide±antimony±uranium vein deposits. These mineral systems form through the metamorphic devolatilization of thick successions of volcanic or siliciclastic sedimentary rock sequences, with the metal-laden hydrothermal fluids focused and moved upwards along crustal-scale faults. Both base- and precious-metals are produced from these different mineral deposits, and the prospect of critical mineral byproduct production exists.

Newly collected and legacy samples were examined by high-precision methods that analyzed at least 64 elements, some of which were previously not systematically analyzed for or reported, and results were evaluated for byproduct critical mineral potential. As byproducts would be produced from primary ore producing metals such as Au, Ag, and Zn, a cutoff grade was applied for sample inclusion within this study. A 0.5 ppm Au cutoff was applied to orogenic gold samples, a 250 ppm Ag cutoff was applied to silver-rich Coeur d’Alene-type samples, and a 3 wt.% Zn cutoff was applied to zinc-rich Coeur d’Alene-type samples. Critical mineral concentrations in ore are compared to average upper crustal abundance.

Orogenic gold ore was found to have elevated Ag, As, Co, Cu, Mn, Sb, Te, and W. Of these, the most enriched critical minerals are As, Co, Sb, Te, and W, although Co (and Ni and Pb) enrichment appears to be dependent upon host rock type and fluid-rock interaction. Silver-rich Coeur d’Alene-type ore has elevated Ag, As, Bi, Cu, In, Mn, Sb, Pb, and Zn. Zinc-rich Coeur d’Alene-type ore has elevated Ag, As, Bi, Co, Cu, Ga, Ge, In, Mn, Pb, Sb, and Zn, although the concentration of Bi, Ga, Ge, and In are considered economically insignificant from a byproduct standpoint. These critical minerals largely reside in arsenopyrite (As), scheelite (W), siderite (Mn), sphalerite (Zn), tetrahedrite (Ag, As, Sb), stibnite (Sb), and telluride (Te) minerals.

These potential byproduct critical minerals exist in ore but may also be found in associated mine waste. For example, our calculations for Coeur d’Alene, ID, suggest over $2,500,000,000 USD worth of As, Mn, Sb, and Zn may still reside in remnant tailings within gangue minerals and untreated ore minerals.

title: Zircon Trace Element Discrimination Using PCA Applied to the Big Bear Lake Intrusive Suite, California
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems
authors: Richter, Maximillian David [1], Barth, Andrew P. [2], Eddy, Michael Patterson [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Indiana University Indianapolis, Indianapolis, IN,
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Indiana University Indianapolis, Indianapolis, IN, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
The Big Bear Lake Intrusive Suite (BLIS) is a Late Cretaceous granitic intrusive suite in the San Bernardino Mountains. Interest in the BLIS stems from its normal compositional zoning structure paired with its relatively large size, with 440 km 2 of exposure and an estimated volume of 3300-5100 km 3 . The BLIS comprises 9 cogenetic units - 7 granitic units in the main intrusive mass and 2 mafic satellite plutons. Previous work by Barth et al. 2016 assessed isotope and trace element (TE) signals left by source vs emplacement level processes through characterizing the diverse zircon domains in the BLIS, identifying two relevant to this study: early magmatic zircons defined by low U & Th and high Ti, with bright luminescent cores or overgrowths; and main phase magmatic zircons rich in U & Th with oscillatory zoning. Their emplacement model for the BLIS involved an early phase of low intrusion rates producing diverse sheeted intrusions followed by an increase in flux rates rapidly assembling the main intrusive mass through sheet stacking.

This work draws upon a larger body of zircons (611) from more whole rock samples (11 samples) collected in 2022; zircon TE and geochronological analyses were done using LASS-ICP-MS, and XRF for whole rock geochemistry. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was employed in two different ways: to identify distinct clusters within the BLIS zircon population using KCA; zircon discrimination using a global dataset of zircons. One cluster matched the early magmatic zircons described by Barth et al. 2016, with TE signatures suggesting crystallization from a hotter more mafic melt; however, these zircons are concentrated within the most evolved granitic units of the BLIS. Rhyolite-MELTS was used to model predicted Ti-in-zircon concentrations with respect to temperature; the individual whole rock models were in good agreement with their respective main phase zircons, but not for their early magmatic zircons. Rerunning Rhyolite-MELTS using the satellite pluton compositions produced results in agreement with the early magmatic zircons, suggesting a similar dioritic source magma for these early magmatic zircons, as corroborated by zircon discrimination using PCA. Further work is being done to reconcile the TE and geochronologic data.

title: Tephra Deposits Hold the Key to Mafic Eruption Styles
session_title: Using mafic and ultramafic deposits to decipher volcanic and magmatic processes
authors: Cashman, Katharine [1], Mckay, Daniele [2], Deardorff, Nicholas [3], Johnson, Emily Renee [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oregon, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Oregon, Bend, OR, USA
(3) Anthropology, Indiana University of Pennsylvania, Indiana, PA, USA
(4) U.S. Geological Survey,, Cascades Volcano Observatory, Vancouver, WA, USA
abstract: Unlike the products of silicic eruptions, the products of mafic eruptions - landforms, spatial distribution and constituent parts - are unusually sensitive to eruption conditions, and therefore provide detailed records of eruptive processes. Landforms include tephra sheets, scoria cones and lava flows; the relative importance of each form provides a general means of classifying eruption types, with tephra formed by strong explosions, scoria the product of weak explosions and lava flows the result of effusion. The size distribution and morphology of pyroclasts vary with eruption intensity and fragmentation conditions, in turn modulated by the efficiency of gas escape from vesiculating magma. Thus clasts created by lava fountains, Strombolian bubble bursts, Vulcanian explosions and unsteady vs. steady explosive activity can be attributed to formative eruptive processes. Stratigraphic variations in pyroclast form and size record temporal changes in the dynamics of eruptive activity, including the relative importance of true juvenile, recycled and lithic clasts. Finally, internal vesicle and crystal textures reveal details of magma ascent and decompression prior to disruption by fragmentation. Here we illustrate relations between landforms, deposit-scale characteristics (spatial distribution and grain size), stratigraphic variations in grain size and component type, and internal textures and external clast morphology using examples from Holocene (non-observed) mafic eruptions in the Cascades. We constrain interpretations of these deposits using constraints from well-observed subaerial eruptions (Parícutin, Mexico; Kīlauea, Hawaii). We then show ways in which these relations can be extended to mafic submarine eruptions, where deposit-scale analysis is not possible, by relating observed variations in eruption style to changes in the proportions of pyroclast components and internal characteristics. Together these examples illustrate not only the sensitivity of eruption products to eruption style, but also the close correlation between deposit-wide characteristics and individual deposit components.

abstract: Weapons manufacturing at the former Twin Cities Army Ammunition Plant in Arden Hills, MN resulted in the release of trichloroethene (TCE) and 1,4 dioxane into the Prairie du Chien and Jordan units of the deep bedrock aquifer, forming a ~5 mile long contamination plume. Remedial actions have included soil removal and soil vapor extraction near the source areas in the 1980s and 1990s and “pump and treat” efforts that are ongoing. The U.S. Army Environmental Command initiated a project with the U.S. Geological Survey to better understand the behavior and fate of the plumes, and to guide ongoing remedial pumping. A 16-layer MODFLOW 6 groundwater flow model was developed using detailed bedrock and Quaternary mapping from the Minnesota Geological Survey. The model simulates a complex groundwater flow system influenced by buried valleys, aquifer heterogeneity, numerous lakes, high-capacity pumping, and the geometry of the Mississippi River. Mass transport is simulated in a locally refined area of the model grid, using the MODFLOW 6 Groundwater Transport Model. Inherent uncertainties in the source terms and groundwater flowpaths through heterogeneous and fractured media were considered with an ensemble of plausible model realizations developed using the Iterative Ensemble Smoother in PEST++. Flow and transport model parameters for the ensemble were estimated simultaneously, allowing observed concentrations and the plume shape to inform uncertain hydraulic parameters. Results capture observed decreasing concentration trends in many places and indicate that the current pump and treat system is likely containing nearly all of the contaminant mass on-site. To maintain containment, some continued pumping is likely needed through 2042. Multi-objective optimization under uncertainty may help improve pumping efficiency.

title: Anthropogenic Materials in American Robin Nests in Arkansas: Preliminary Findings and Future Directions
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: Mader, Jordan [1], Skypala, Amy [2], McFerran, Willow [3], Kelley, Emily [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical Sciences, University of Arkansas - Fort Smith, Fort Smith, Arkansas, USA
(2) Department of Biological Sciences, University of Arkansas - Fort Smith, Fort Smith, Arkansas, USA
(3) Department of Biological Sciences, University of Arkansas - Fort Smith, Fort Smith, Arkansas, USA

abstract:
Anthropogenic (artificial) materials are common in the natural environment, and American Robins ( Turdus migratorius) , a common suburban bird, readily incorporate such materials within their nest. Therefore, nests may act as indicators of the abundance of such material in their localized environment.

During the spring and summer of 2025, eighteen American Robin nests were collected in Sebastian and Crawford counties, Arkansas, USA. Nests were photographed, weighed, and deconstructed to assess for the presence of anthropogenic nesting materials (ANM). If such materials were found, they were categorized by type, color, and position within the three layer components of the nest (outer grassy cover, clay-based mud cup, fine inner lining).

Of the 18 nests collected, 89% of them had some amount of ANM, including plastic (sheets, strips, and filaments), paper, yarn, and string. Materials were of a variety of colors. Most of the ANM was found in the outermost layer. We examined one layer of the nest, the middle mud cup, to assess for the presence of microdebris (potentially microplastics). Such debris was found in 11 of the 18 nests, but the inclusion of procedural blanks will be necessary for confidence.

With additional samples, plans include the refinement of our assessment of microdebris and the utilization of ATR-FTIR and Raman microscopy to chemically identify the material types more specifically. We will compare any microdebris components from the mud cup layer to that found in soil samples in the area of each nest, and we will compare the amount and types of ANM and microdebris in nests collected from areas with differing intensities of human usage.

This approach may elucidate the potential risks to birds of inclusion of man-made materials in nests. These risks could include entanglement of nestlings with larger items of ANM or the potential ingestion of microplastics by adults during the nest building process. More broadly, birds’ nests may provide a natural sample to assess anthropogenic material in the terrestrial environment.

title: Changes in Eocene–Oligocene Pelagic Carbonate Production and Preservation in the South Atlantic Based on Laser Grain Size and SEM Analyses
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Mackin, Caroline [1]
affiliations: (1) Institute for Geophysics, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
abstract: Pelagic carbonate production is an important part of the global carbon cycle, accounting for roughly half of annual carbonate production. Changes in the relative abundance of pelagic calcifiers like planktic foraminifera and calcareous nannoplankton can alter carbonate flux and the composition of deep-sea sediments. Traditional methods used to reconstruct carbonate production and burial, such as CaCO₃ weight percentage and carbonate mass accumulation rates, cannot distinguish the relative contributions of different plankton groups. Although sieving can separate broad size fractions, it is time-consuming and lacks the resolution needed to capture finer changes within plankton groups (e.g., a shift to larger foraminifera). Because deep-sea carbonate sediments are almost entirely biogenic, grain size offers a way to estimate the relative contributions of different carbonate-producing groups. Here, we utilize laser grain size analysis as a method for reconstructing changes in pelagic carbonate production. This approach quickly quantifies both coarse (>20 μm; planktic foraminifera) and fine (<20 μm; calcareous nannoplankton) carbonate fractions, as well as trends within those fractions. We applied this method to samples spanning the Eocene–Oligocene Transition (33.7–34.5 Ma) from Ocean Drilling Program Site 1265, International Ocean Discovery Program Site U1558, and Deep Sea Drilling Project Site 516 to create a South Atlantic transect spanning approximately 1-3 km water depth. At all three sites, calcareous nannoplankton dominate throughout the interval, comprising ~80–90% of the carbonate fraction, whereas planktic foraminifera make up <10%. Foraminiferal abundance peaks in the late Eocene before declining in the early Oligocene. SEM imaging was used to verify the grain size results and assess preservation. Despite high and relatively constant carbonate weight percent, SEM images show extensive foraminiferal dissolution, with depauperate assemblages mostly composed of large dissolution-resistant taxa such as Globigerinatheka dominating the late Eocene. In contrast, Oligocene samples contain more small planktic foraminifera, suggesting improved preservation, consistent with observations from other South Atlantic sites. These results show that laser grain size analysis, combined with SEM imaging, can detect changes in carbonate preservation and foraminiferal dissolution even where bulk carbonate concentrations remain relatively constant, providing information that cannot be resolved using %CaCO₃ or qualitative preservation estimates alone.

title: Comparing Methods to Quantify Groundwater Evapotranspiration by Willows in a Montane Riparian Ecosystem, Cache la Poudre River Watershed, Northern Colorado

authors: Seymour, Logan Michael [1], Ronayne, Michael [2], Rathburn, Sara [3], Rugenstein, Jeremy Kesner Caves [4], Cooper, David [5]
affiliations: (1) Colorado State University, Geosciences, Fort Collins, CO, USA

abstract:
Mountain watersheds often contain wide valley segments where floodplains store and transmit groundwater that supports stream baseflow and riparian ecosystems. Phreatophytes (plants that can root to the water table) typically dominate these ecosystems and can transpire groundwater, reducing groundwater contributions to streamflow or inducing stream losses. Groundwater evapotranspiration (ETg) is poorly understood despite its importance in mountain stream-aquifer water budgets. This study investigates the ETg flux induced by willows ( Salix geyeriana and S. monticola ) in a typical wide mountain valley, the South Fork Cache la Poudre River watershed in northern Colorado.

We use two ground-based methods to quantify groundwater-vegetation interactions: (i) analysis of diurnal water table fluctuations (DWTFs) in monitoring wells to quantify ETg; and (ii) measurements of transpiration (T) as water flux through plant stems using sap flow sensors. These two methods produce different fluxes; DWTF methods include groundwater evaporation in addition to transpiration, and ET from all plant species present. Sap flow solely measures transpiration by the selected individual Salix plants. Because willow roots occur in both the unsaturated and saturated soil zones, total transpiration includes transpiration derived from groundwater (Tg) in addition to soil water (Ts) recharged by precipitation. To distinguish plant water sources and constrain Tg, we use the stable isotopes of oxygen (δ 18 O) and hydrogen (δ 2 H) in groundwater, soil water, and plant xylem water. Lastly, we compared our results with commonly used remote sensing methods for ET estimation.

Preliminary stable isotope data indicate that xylem water plots on a mixing line with groundwater and soil water end members at sites with a shallow water table. At sites with a deeper water table, δ 18 O and δ 2 H values in plant xylem are higher than both groundwater and the soil water sampled from 20 to 40 cm depth, suggesting water-stressed phreatophytes may draw from highly evaporated near-surface soil water. Comparison of ground-based and remote sensing methods shows agreement among methods with respect to timing of peak fluxes in a season. However, the DWTF method reports significantly greater estimates of ETg, which we attribute to potential contributions of groundwater evaporation not captured by other methods, transpiration from other phreatophyte species, and uncertainty in the specific yield parameter used in the DWTF method.

abstract: The Penokean orogeny (1890-1830 Ma), best exposed in the Lake Superior region of Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, is a discrete event marking accretion of the Wisconsin Magmatic Terranes to the southern margin of Laurentia. However, new geochronology indicates deformation and metamorphism in the Penokean belt continued throughout the Paleo- and Mesoproterozoic, after the locus of accretionary activity in southern Laurentia had shifted hundreds of kilometers to the south. Whether this later period of deformation in the continental interior is coupled with these distal coeval accretionary events remains an outstanding, but central question, for understanding the drivers of intracratonic reworking in proto-North America. We test if and how far-field accretionary tectonics following the Penokean orogeny contributed to prolonged modification of crust in central Laurentia by integrating pressure-temperature-time-deformation (P-T-t-D) histories using high-precision and spatially resolved geochronology. In central Minnesota, detrital zircon U-Pb ages show protoliths of metasedimentary rocks were deposited by ~1820 Ma, and garnet Lu-Hf and monazite U-Pb geochronology indicates quick burial to amphibolite-facies conditions by ~1800 Ma. Microstructural relationships between garnet, monazite, and matrix fabrics indicate as many as four periods of fabric development, the last coinciding with uplift of cratonic basement in the McGrath Gneiss dome. This metamorphism and deformation immediately precede juvenile granitic magmatism in the adjacent East-Central Minnesota Batholith starting at ~1790 Ma. Farther east in the Penokean orogenic belt, kyanite-bearing rocks record higher grade metamorphic conditions slightly earlier at ~1820 Ma, followed by more protracted cooling through ~450°C by ~1740 Ma. These results, with previously published P-T-t-D data elsewhere in the Penokean belt, illustrate far-field accretionary tectonics following the Penokean orogeny played a major role in modifying the cratonic interior. The ages of prograde-to-peak metamorphism reveal crustal thickening lasting at least to ~1750 Ma, likely propagated from younger convergence far south of the Lake Superior region. Overlapping prograde and cooling ages between 1830-1750 Ma reflect exhumation during thickening, indicating crust modification via several cycles of synorogenic collapse. Additionally, the spatiotemporal relationship between magmatism and basement uplift in central Minnesota suggests orogenic collapse may have been aided by magmatic and/or thermal crustal weakening. Together, these processes reveal far-field stresses from continued convergence on Laurentia’s southern margin drove a dynamic orogenic system in the continental interior throughout the Paleoproterozoic.

title: Metasediments with mantle peridotite inclusions in continental lower crust: Global examples and new observations in the North Cascades
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Kelemen, Peter Boushall [1], Murray, Joshua [2], Smye, Andrew [3]
affiliations: (1) Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, NY, USA
(2) Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, NY, USA

abstract:
Metasediments interlayered with lenses of metaperidotite are commonly observed in exposed sections of lower continental crust (>25 km depth). These mixed assemblages are unlikely to have been transported deep into the crust via burial. Mixed metasediment and peridotite lenses are common in forearc accretionary prisms. Lower crustal peridotite inclusions in metasediments often lack spatial association with other potential components of subducted oceanic plates, and some retain high temperature mantle deformation fabrics. Thus the peridotites were probably derived from the mantle wedge above a subduction zone, and their host metasediments were probably subducted and then “relaminated” (as defined by Hacker et al. EPSL 2011): via (1) thrusting of forearc material into or just below arc crust, (2) buoyancy-driven ascent of subducted material in a subduction channel or (3) diapirs (review in Kelemen et al Treatise on Geochem 2025, K25). Well documented examples recording lower crustal depths include the Ivrea Zone (e.g. Quick et al Geology 1995), Val Malenco (e.g. Hermann et al. JGR 1997), the Gruf metamorphic complex (e.g. Galli et al Swiss J Geosci), the Sanbagawa belt (e.g. Aoya et al. Geology 2013), and in the US: the North Cascades crystalline core (e.g. Haugerud & Taber USGS 2009), Orocopia-Pelona-Rand schist (e.g. Haxel et al Int Geol Rev 2014), Condrey Mtn schist (e.g., Tewkesbury-Christie et al Tectonics 2024), and even Teton gneisses (e.g., Frost et al Geosphere 2018). The proportion of such assemblages at depth is difficult to discern, since many of the peridotite lenses are hydrated, and/or smaller than the length scale of seismic observation, while geophysical properties of metasediments overlap those of a broad range of igneous rocks (K25). Where peridotites are less hydrated, small-scale mixtures of peridotite with high seismic P-wave speeds (Vp) plus felsic rocks with low Vp have higher SiO 2 contents, at intermediate Vp, compared to large volumes of homogeneous rocks (K25, Figure 6B). Similarly, peraluminous metasediments with a given Vp have higher SiO 2 contents compared to most igneous rocks. These factors potentially lead to an underestimate of mid- and lower-crustal SiO 2 in some regions and global averages.

To further quantify these observations, we present new data on the proportion, length scale and composition of interlayered metaperidotites and metasediments in the North Cascades crystaline core (0.6 to 1.2 GPa), as well as a review of literature data.

title: Phosphate (U-Th)/He Thermochronology of Apollo 14 Melt Breccia 14311 Reveals Late-Stage Impact History
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials
authors: Diaz, Connor Antonio [1], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [2], Crow, Carolyn A. [3], Metcalf, James R. [4], Economos, Rita C. [5], Erickson, Timmons [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA

abstract:
Our ability to confidently characterize the impact history of the inner solar system is limited by discrepancies in radiometric dates and age interpretations for lunar samples. Here we present the first phosphate (U-Th)/He thermochronology of a lunar sample, Apollo 14 impact-melt breccia 14311, to investigate its long-term impact and transport history. Because phosphate (U-Th)/He has a substantially lower closure temperature than commonly used lunar chronometers, it can detect lower-intensity thermal events that may otherwise be unresolved.

Apatite and merrillite grains were identified by scanning electron microscopy, characterized by X-ray computed tomography, and analyzed for He, U, Th, and Sm. Phosphate (U-Th)/He dates span ~15-3712 Ma, broadly mirroring previous zircon (U-Th)/He dates from the same sample. Apatite dates correlate positively with effective U concentration (eU), suggesting that radiation damage primarily controls He retentivity, as commonly observed in terrestrial apatite. Merrillite dates show no relationship with eU, suggesting that crystal-chemical factors and pervasive shock-induced intragranular fractures dominate He retention.

Apatite thermal-history modeling supports a thermal pulse at ca. 110 Ma, perhaps associated with Tycho, and places tighter constraints on the post-Imbrium history of 14311. For preferred cooling durations of days to months, the apatite data are compatible with thermal conditions similar to those required by the zircon system, indicating that both chronometers record the same impact-related thermal pulse. The apatite data also place tighter upper bounds on potential intermediate thermal events between the ~3.9 Ga Imbrium impact and ca. 110 Ma. This work demonstrates that lunar phosphate can serve as a new sensitive thermochronometer for resolving lower-intensity impact events and the long-term thermal and transport histories recorded by lunar samples.

title: Simulating Stratigraphic Architecture and Fossil Preservation in Nonmarine Extensional Basins
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Loughney, Katharine M. [1], Holland, Steven M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Watershed Studies Institute, Murray State University, Murray, KY, USA
(2) Department of Geology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
abstract:
Extensional basins are common tectonic settings and have the potential to preserve extensive nonmarine fossil records. Although individual basins may have complex histories, extensional basins tend to display similar trends in accommodation and sedimentation that result in predictable facies development along depositional and elevational gradients. However, the tectonic boundary conditions of extensional basins cause accommodation and sedimentation to vary spatially across the footwall and hanging wall, and resulting facies stacking patterns should be out of phase across fault blocks. Patterns of fossil occurrence are therefore predicted to differ greatly across extensional basins, potentially complicating stratigraphic and paleontological correlations. We used sedimentary basin simulations in R to evaluate the temporal and spatial changes in accommodation and sedimentation, the distribution of high- and low-aggradation systems tracts (HAST, LAST), and fossil-occurrence patterns under typical scenarios of tectonic and lake-level controls in nonmarine extensional basins.

Stratigraphic architecture, species diversity, and elevation track temporal and spatial variations in accommodation across the basin simulations. Tectonically driven changes in accommodation result in similar temporal architecture trends across simulated basins, but accommodation changes driven by lake level result in disjointed architecture across fault blocks. In all simulations, footwall architecture is overall HAST-like, whereas hanging-wall architecture varies from LAST-like updip to increasingly HAST-like downdip. Overall species diversity on the footwall is nearly twice as high as hanging-wall diversity, and footwall occurrences are four times greater than hanging-wall occurrences. Footwall species diversity and occurrences decrease downdip with decreasing accommodation, whereas on the hanging wall, they increase downdip with increasing accommodation. Species’ elevation and water-depth preferences and rates of change in accommodation influence turnover patterns: slow rates of accommodation change result in slow turnover and averaging of elevation or water-depth preferences in fossil assemblages, whereas rapid rates of change result in rapid turnover marked by increases in first and last occurrences at downlap surfaces and subaerial unconformities.

title: Modeling the Evolution of Animal Locomotion During Snowball Earth
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology and Geomicrobiology (Posters)
authors: Hoeft, Evan [1], Simpson, Carl [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA

abstract: How did animals evolve the ability to move? Among the clades that evolved complex multicellular bodies, only animals are able to actively locomote. This circumstance starkly contrasts with the unicellular world, in which many groups across bacteria, archaea, and eukarya have independently evolved various types of taxis (motility directed towards or away from a stimulus). Both the earliest animals and their unicellular ancestors likely swam using flagella and responded to stimuli such as oxygen gradients (i.e., aerotaxis). We sought to understand whether the tactic strategies employed by unicells (e.g., run-and-tumble) remain effective when placed in a stochastic multicellular context—or if developmental organization, intercellular signaling, and other complex multicellular adaptations were prerequisites for motility in early animals. To evaluate these hypotheses, we expanded on previous work modeling the aerotactic responses of choanoflagellates, facultatively multicellular protozoans that are the closest relatives of animals. Our approach simulates the collective effects of cells independently following a run-and-tumble strategy on the motion of a stochastic 'rosette' colony across an oxygen gradient. We found that rosettes can retain aerotaxis performance in a variety of colony configurations and scenarios, demonstrating that multicellular locomotion can evolve directly from unicellular behaviors with minimal behavioral modification. Additionally, aerotaxis performance is positively correlated with colony velocity and slope of the oxygen gradient. In the context of the frigid Cryogenian oceans where multicellular animals likely evolved, smaller colonies and unicells would have been disproportionately slowed by high water viscosity, hampering their ability to navigate oxygen gradients. Simultaneously, these gradients could have been especially steep in cold water with low diffusivity, increasing both the viability of aerotaxis and its fitness benefit. Selection for aerotaxis may have therefore complemented other drivers of increased multicellular size during the emergence of animals.

title: Depth gradients in modern oceans and the dynamics of Sepkoski’s evolutionary faunas
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Gavirneni, Siddharth [1], MARSHALL, CHARLES R. [2]

abstract: The classical view of faunal turnover in the paleontological record is that evolutionary faunas originate onshore and subsequently drive their predecessors further offshore. Viewed through an energetic lens, this pattern can be interpreted as the large-scale competitive displacement of older faunas from shallow water, high-productivity environments. Modern representatives of groups like brachiopods and crinoids, which are characteristic of the Paleozoic fauna, tend to be found primarily in deeper waters, where the scarcity of energy and resources places abiotic constraints on more energetically ‘powerful’ modes of life. However, analyses of trilobite diversity by Westrop and Adrain (1998) show minimal change in shallow water alpha diversity between the Cambrian and Ordovician, suggesting that older evolutionary faunas may have been ‘diluted’ rather than displaced, and calling into question the interpretation of the onshore-offshore pattern as a product of competition. The extent to which biotic interactions such as predation and competition are major constraints on species distributions in the marine realm is thus still disputed. Here, we assess the diversity and abundance of taxa categorized into Sepkoski’s Paleozoic and Modern faunas across depth gradients in occurrence data from the Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS). We link these distributions to changes in factors including nutrient availability and dissolved oxygen, which are tied to metabolism and energetics. Preliminary results indicate that clades in the Modern fauna exhibit their highest diversity in shallow waters, while peak diversity tends to occur at depths of around 1000 meters for Paleozoic fauna taxa, a pattern consistent with displacement, rather than dilution. The distribution of clades in modern oceans can offer insight into the shifts in the composition of benthic marine ecosystems over the Phanerozoic, and the nature of interaction between evolutionary faunas in deep time.
