abstract: The Colorado River is a critical water resource for the western United States that supports public water supply, agriculture, ecological services, energy/mineral resource development, power generation, and recreation. A hydrological, chemical, and geospatial assessment was conducted in the Upper Colorado River Basin (UCRB) for contaminants of global concern (CGC), including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which are resistant to degradation and can persist for long transport distances. Measuring and modeling tools were developed to identify natural and anthropogenic sources of inorganic and organic CGC, with a focus on the influence of municipal and industrial wastewater reuse on streamflow and water quality. Geospatial models were used to evaluate municipal and industrial wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) discharges and other presumptive PFAS sources to predict environmental concentrations for each stream reach in the UCRB and determine potential vulnerability scores. Wastewater reuse begins in the headwater tributaries at the first WWTP effluent discharge and accumulated wastewater (ACCWW) continues to be contributed along the flow path with inputs from additional facilities (in 2020, there were 170 municipal and 188 industrial WWTPs). Of the 195,944 stream kilometers in the UCRB, 3.7% receive streamflow contributions from WWTP effluent discharges. At the most downstream Upper Colorado River streamgage (near Potash, Utah) ACCWW accounted for 2.2% of the mean-annual stream discharge. Between 2021 and 2024, stream water was sampled and analyzed for PFAS, pharmaceuticals, major ions, trace elements, dissolved organic carbon, and optical properties. River water inorganic and organic chemical composition increased in complexity along the flow path due to natural and anthropogenic sources. A holistic approach was used to assess the evolution of water quality across the landscape using chemical and optical proxies of various sources. Although there was widespread potential for PFAS contamination from wastewater reuse, predicted concentrations generally were below levels of concern for human health and ecosystem effects. Measurement and modeling results were consistent, with only sporadic detections of a limited number of PFAS at low concentrations. Despite the focus on contaminants such as PFAS, it is important to consider co-occurring CGC that can provide a greater understanding of water-quality impacts. Linking hydrological connectivity of contaminant sources at the basin-scale allows resource managers to identify areas of concern.

title: The Porewater Enrichment and Sediment to Seawater Flux of Uranium-234
session_title: U-series Disequilibrium Geochronology: Advances, Applications, and Emerging Frontiers (Posters)
authors: Pavia, Frank [1], Present, Theodore Michael [2], Johnson, Daniel [3], Adkins, Jess [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Oceanography, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Caltech, Pasadena, CA, USA

abstract:
The radiogenic uranium isotopic composition ( 234 U/ 238 U) of the ocean has been a curiosity for over 50 years, as it is ~15% elevated above secular equilibrium. The discharge-weighted U flux and 234 U/ 238 U ratios of rivers can only account for half the excess 234 U found in seawater, requiring alternative sources of 234 U to the ocean. Processes including glacial meltwater inputs, submarine groundwater discharge, and fluxes from sedimentary pore fluids have been suggested as additional 234 U sources, but quantifying these fluxes, particularly those from sedimentary pore fluids, has remained elusive.

We present pore fluid U concentration and ( 234 U/ 238 U) from four cores, spanning a range of lithologies, sedimentation rates, and oxygenation conditions. We find extreme porewater 234 U/ 238 U values, up to activity ratios of 2.4 at a low accumulation rate, fine-grained, completely oxic site in the North Atlantic gyre. We use the 234 U concentration gradient in the upper porewaters to calculate a 234 U flux to seawater that is an order of magnitude higher than previous estimates, suggesting that porewater fluxes have a more important role to play in setting both modern and past seawater 234 U/ 238 U ratios. We will discuss the possibility of changing bottom water oxygen concentration in modulating porewater 234 U release as a mechanism to explain changing seawater 234 U/ 238 U during the last deglaciation.

title: Regional Geologic Mapping Surrounding the Marius Hills Pit as the Basis for Potential Future Lunar Exploration
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Scully, Jennifer E. C. [1], Leonard, Erin J. [2], Fraeman, Abigail A. [3], Kerber, Laura A. [4], Elder, Catherine M. [5]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA,
(2) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA,
(3) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(4) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(5) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA,
abstract: The Marius Hills pit (14.1 °N, 303.2 °E) is within the large Marius Hills volcanic plateau on the Moon (e.g., Greeley, 1971; Head and Gifford, 1980; Wan et al., 2022; Whitford-Stark and Head, 1980) and is often interpreted as a lava tube entrance, making it a feature of interest for future human exploration (Haruyama et al., 2009; Robinson et al., 2012; Wagner and Robinson, 2022). It is a scientifically interesting site because its walls would provide access to a stratigraphy of bedrock layers and the vicinity contains diverse volcanic features (e.g., Robinson et al., 2012; Wagner and Robinson, 2014; Nesnas et al., 2023). We present our regional geologic map of the area surrounding the Marius Hills pit to provide a contextualizing geologic history. We describe in detail broad domes, as well as steep domes with summit depressions, representing an earlier stage of higher viscosity volcanism. We map younger cratered plains and rille floors/walls that are consistent with lower viscosity volcanism. The pit is in the floor of a rille and may be formed by collapse into an underlying lava tube, suggesting lava tube stacking. Some of the youngest features we map are tectonically-formed ridge scarps. We also describe variations in material composition throughout our map area and with time. Using our geologic map and relevant datasets, we develop suitability models for potential future landing sites and traverses, which would visit key locations for scientific exploration while avoiding hazards. We therefore provide a foundation for potential future exploration of this pit, which is timely given the current interest in non-polar locations for future lunar exploration and because such lunar pits provide a tantalizing option for human settlement protected from many of the hazards of the lunar surface.

title: The Surface Expression of a Modern-Day Epithermal System: Investigating the Hydrothermal Plumbing of Yellowstone’s Crater Hills Thermal Area
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Alexander, Erin R. [1], Stanbro, Ayden [2], Shock, Everett L. [3], Arrowsmith, Ramon [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(2) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(3) School of Earth and Space Exploration, School of Molecular Sciences, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(4) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
abstract:
Yellowstone National Park (YNP) hosts a massive hydrothermal system that acts as a modern-day analog for critical mineral deposit formation. In the subsurface, rising volcanic gases and heat combine with downwelling meteoric waters to form hydrothermal fluids. These fluids ascend, react with volcanic rocks, glacial sediments and soils, and mix with surface waters to produce a variety of chemical compositions. The many hot springs are the surficial expression of a subsurface plumbing system and provide insights on the formation and evolution of ancient epithermal deposits.

How should we approach mapping the structures and contacts of thermal areas? Thermal areas are rapidly resurfaced by sinter deposition, acid erosion, and hydrothermal alteration, making field mapping alone difficult. To address this problem, we adopt a multidisciplinary approach incorporating field mapping, hot spring geochemistry, hydrothermal mineralization, and geophysics to constrain the pathways controlling hot springs.

This study focuses on YNP’s acidic Crater Hills Thermal Area, where sulfurous springs exhibit a bimodal geochemical signature from highly concentrated to extremely dilute fluid. The thermal region sits atop a previously unmapped fracture radiating from the Sour Creek Dome. This fracture apparently channels hydrothermal fluid up, cementing overlying glacial deposits. In Crater Hills, the cemented area expands around the fracture zone, altering a hilly belt nearly a kilometer wide riddled with fumaroles, collapse pits, and sunset-colored mineral veins. Fluid flow is controlled by three cemented sedimentary units: sandy gravel, which hosts all hot springs; silty sand, which acts as an impermeable surface for spring run-off; and pebble conglomerate, in which fumaroles and veins form without present liquid water. We integrate field mapping with mineralization lab work to map surface contacts and probe alteration across units. Geochemical data indicate subsurface boiling partitions upwelling fluid into concentrated acid chloride springs and dilute steam-condensate springs; overlain on our surficial maps, concentration decreases with increasing distance from the fracture. These insights inform the interpretation of USGS Airborne ElectroMagnetics data to project surficial contacts into the ground. Layering these methods, we create a three-dimensional model of hydrothermal fluid rising along deep fractures before being separated by near-surface layers into shallow steam and deep acid chloride fluid. We then connect modern spring activity to past mineralization and track the evolution of an active thermal area into an epithermal system.

title: What Drives Antarctica’s Largest River? Linking Machine Learning and Causal Fixed-Effects Models of Streamflow in the Onyx River of the McMurdo Dry Valleys
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Gooseff, Michael N. [1], Li, Zhi [2], Maguire, Joseph J. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
(2) University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Streamflow in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys (MDVs) is generated almost entirely by glacial meltwater, making it acutely sensitive to the region's amplified, non-linear climate. Streamflow has been measured at over a dozen streams for several decades by the MDVs LTER group. We have developed an LSTM model that forecasts Onyx River discharge up to seven days ahead using meteorological and stratospheric ozone records. This model achieves strong short-term forecasting skill, and feature-importance analysis reveals that stratospheric ozone (an independent proxy for surface UV-B flux) becomes an increasingly important predictor at longer lead times. However, these architectures optimize predictive accuracy rather than causal attribution, limiting their use for mechanistic interpretation or scenario-based projection under continued ozone recovery and climate change.

To address this gap, we present a complementary causal-inference approach: a two-way fixed-effects panel regression linking meteorological drivers to streamflow, drawing on panel identification strategies used to isolate causal drivers in other Earth-systems settings. We construct a multi-site panel of MDV stream gauges (Wright Valley and Taylor Valley streams), with site and water-year fixed effects absorbing time-invariant and basin-wide confounders. Continuous drivers including air temperature, incoming radiation, a self-generated Landsat-derived glacier surface albedo record, ozone, and a wind speed-temperature interaction term capturing melt versus sublimation-dominated regimes, are regressed against log-discharge to estimate their independent contributions to streamflow variability.

Here we present preliminary fixed-effects results alongside the LSTM forecasts, directly comparing which drivers each approach identifies as important and where the two frameworks agree or diverge. We argue that pairing high-accuracy machine learning forecasts with interpretable causal estimates gives a more complete picture of MDV hydrologic sensitivity than either approach alone, with direct relevance to anticipating regime shifts in snow-free, glacially fed cold-region catchments.

title: Avian Track Taphonomy at Three Stratigraphic Horizons of the Maastrichtian El Molino Formation (Torotoro National Park, Bolivia) and Their Paleoecological Implications
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments
authors: Llempen, Nelson A. [1], Nick, Kevin E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth & Biological Sciences, Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA
(2) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA,
abstract: Vertebrate tracks are high-resolution, post-sedimentary features whose survival depends on a narrow range of substrate and diagenetic windows. The Maastrichtian El Molino Formation (Torotoro National Park, Bolivia) preserves a rich avian ichnological record across its lower and middle members, surpassing many equivalent Gondwanan units. This study analyzes taphonomic controls on high-density avian tracksites across three stratigraphic horizons: QG (lower member), CV, and CP9 (middle member). Methods included field and experimental sedimentological analyses, track measurements, thin section and SEM petrography of the upper 1cm of the track-bearing surfaces and overlying beds. Results indicate a strong correlation between high preservation quality and early carbonate cementation in the middle member (CP9, CV). These levels preserve primary textures, including isopachous, fibrous calcite crystals within detrital nested-ostracod grains and ooids, with minimal clay or evidence of microbially induced sedimentary structures (MISS). Intergranular volume (IGV) analysis against modern analogs demonstrates minor compaction, confirming that early cements stabilized the original framework. Additionally, these surfaces exhibit nearly pure carbonate horizontal laminae, wave ripples, simple vertical burrows, and desiccation cracks. In contrast, the lower member (QG) exhibits a distinct diagenetic path where dominantly clastic detrital grains are coated by thin quartz overgrowths, localized anhedral carbonates, and iron oxides. If originally present, early carbonates are not currently present. Here, late-stage equant, sparry calcite locally corrodes detrital quartz grain surfaces and syntaxial quartz overgrowths. Elongate, fabric-selected pores suggest early cement dissolution followed by overprinting under unique diagenetic conditions. Furthermore, coeval or modern weathering significantly influenced current morphology; the friable clastic matrix at QG enhanced the loss of diagnostic track features (e.g., hallux, phalangeal pads). Conversely, CP9 and CV exhibit a range of preservation modes skewed toward suboptimal to optimal resolution, reflecting limited subaerial exposure. These deposits represent shallow water to saturated mixed substrates along marginal settings subject to episodic water-level fluctuations. Taphonomic controls, combined with in-situ track distribution, reveal diverse avian behaviors—from synchronized foraging patterns to randomized, multi-morphotype assemblages. Ultimately, early freshwater phreatic calcite cementation is identified as crucial in controlling track formation, providing a high-resolution window into Maastrichtian avian paleoecology.

title: Casa da Pedra: A Model for Sustainability and Geoconservation Through the Reuse of Mining Waste in the Araripe Basin, Brazil
session_title: Webinar 2: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives
authors: Caetano, Lívia Manuela Gomes [1], Carvalho, Ismar de Souza [2], Henriques, Maria Helena Paiva [3]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Geosciences, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
(2) Institute of Geosciences, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal
abstract: The Araripe Basin, in the semiarid interior of northeastern Brazil, is internationally recognized by the exceptionally preserved fossils of the Crato Formation, which has drawn geoscientists to the region and sustained research by the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) since 1969. Among the outcrops of this formation occurs Pedra Cariri, a laminated limestone widely used in vernacular and contemporary architecture across Santana do Cariri and neighboring municipalities, where its extraction is the main economic activity. Because only slabs meeting market standards of thickness and quality are sold, quarrying generates large volumes of rejected stone, discarded within the quarrying sites, degrading the landscape and squandering a resource of considerable scientific, cultural, and economic value. It was in this context that Casa da Pedra emerged, a hub of UFRJ's Institute of Geosciences built to support research, teaching, and outreach across the Araripe Basin. Guided by geoconservation and sustainability principles, the initiative turned quarry waste into its primary building material: rather than relying on conventional materials, the station was built almost entirely from blocks and slabs of Pedra Cariri rejected during quarrying. Beyond reducing waste and mitigating the environmental impacts associated with quarry waste, this approach highlights a defining element of regional geodiversity, reinforces a local architectural identity long associated with Pedra Cariri, and demonstrates how circular economy principles can be applied to mining through the reuse of materials once considered commercially worthless. Since its 2016 inauguration, Casa da Pedra has become a permanent hub for research, teaching, and community engagement, hosting Brazilian and international researchers while promoting fieldwork, courses, workshops, guided visits, and heritage education. The concept of education by the stone turns the building into a teaching tool, letting students and visitors grasp geology, paleontology, geoconservation, and sustainable resource use as one integrated experience. This fusion of science, education, heritage, and community earned international recognition in February 2026, when Casa da Pedra was named among the first eleven initiatives worldwide honored by UNESCO's MOST-BRIDGES programme for transdisciplinary sustainability science. Casa da Pedra demonstrates how geodiversity can become a catalyst for sustainable development, transforming mining waste into scientific, educational, cultural, and social value, and showing that local geological heritage can inspire innovative solutions capable of strengthening both communities and the sustainable management of natural resources.

title: Bridging Mineralogical and Biological Sciences to Understand How Microbes Make Minerals
session_title: MSA 2026 Awardees Lectures and Presidential Address
authors: Chan, Clara S [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Delaware, Newark, DE, USA
abstract: Life has evolved to make and transform minerals, driving biogeochemistry in soils, wetlands, oceans and more. Scientists have long debated whether microbes catalyze iron oxidation and mineral formation on a geologic scale. The most well-known debate centers on iron formations, but the same question applies to modern soils, sediments, and waters. Are microbes important catalysts of rusting on Earth, and if so, how do they do it, and what are the consequences? I will discuss how we integrate mineralogical/geological and biological sciences to study iron biomineralogy and iron-oxidizing microbes. Field studies combined with kinetics experiments show that microbes are likely the primary driver of iron oxidation at redox transition zones common to many environments. Studies of microbial isolates, omics, and biochemistry reveal that microbes oxidize iron (dissolved and mineral-bound) by extracellular electron transport. These mechanisms are commonly encoded in genomes, suggesting that microbial iron oxidation is widespread. Our ongoing research aims to improve detection and quantification of microbial iron oxidation and its impacts on carbon and nitrogen cycling. We are applying our knowledge to develop new hybrid organic-inorganic materials, understand effects on wetland nutrient cycling and crops, and recover critical minerals.

title: Seasonal Atmospheric Carbon Dynamics in a Tropical African Grassland Revealed by High-Frequency CO₂, CH₄, and δ¹³C Measurements
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: Sunjo, Claris N. [1], Atekwana, Eliot A. [2], Wotchoko, Pierre [3], Ngwabi, Sheila Y. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA
(3) Geology, Higher Teacher Training College, University of Bamenda, Bambili, Cameroon
(4) Geology Mining and Environmental Sciences, University of Bamenda, Bambili, Cameroon
abstract: Tropical grasslands are a major carbon sink and play an important role in regional carbon dioxide (CO₂) cycling. However, long-term atmospheric high-frequency CO₂ concentration and stable carbon isotope (δ¹³C-CO₂) measurements remain scarce in African grasslands. We conducted a 12-month high-frequency ground-based monitoring study at a tropical sub-Saharan African grassland site, complemented by 24-hour diel campaigns during the rainy and dry seasons. Our goal was to document temporal variations in atmospheric CO₂, methane (CH₄), and δ¹³C-CO₂, and to identify the processes controlling seasonal carbon cycling. We found that the mean CO₂ concentrations increased by 5-80 ppm during the rainy season and exceeded ambient atmospheric (428.95 ppm) levels by more than twofold during the dry season. The mean CH₄ concentrations increased by 1-2.8 ppm in the rainy season and reached up to 38 times ambient atmospheric concentrations ( 1.9 ppm) during the dry season. The mean δ¹³C-CO₂ was more enriched during the rainy season but shifted significantly toward depleted δ¹³C-CO₂ values in the dry season. The CO₂ and CH₄ concentrations showed a 57-day lag during the rainy-to-dry transition (November-December) and a 107-day lag during the dry-to-rainy transition (March-June). Similar patterns in environmental variables such as the air quality index correspond to shifts in δ¹³C-CO₂ and support the delayed responses. Keeling and Miller-Tans' graphical analyses identified C₃ vegetation as the dominant CO₂ source in all seasons. We infer that enriched δ¹³C-CO₂ during the rainy season reflects high soil moisture, enhanced microbial activity, increased soil CO₂ efflux, and strong photosynthetic uptake. In contrast, depleted δ¹³C-CO₂ during the dry season was driven by intense bushfires, pyrogenic CH₄ oxidation, reduced microbial activity, lower soil CO₂ efflux, and weaker plant CO₂ uptake. Our findings demonstrate that local anthropogenic bushfires are substantial greenhouse gas sources in tropical grasslands, with important implications for greenhouse gas budgets, improving satellite retrieval algorithms, and understanding greenhouse gas dynamics in tropical grasslands.

title: Farouk El-Baz Award: Critical Zone Aeolian–Ecological Feedbacks at Multiple Scales in Drylands
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution
authors: Okin, Gregory S. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geography, University of California, Los Angeles, CA,
abstract:
The critical zone is commonly conceptualized as a vertically coupled system, but in drylands its behavior also depends on horizontal exchanges among vegetation patches, landforms, and regions. Wind makes these exchanges especially nonlocal: ecological structure controls aeolian transport, while the redistribution of sediment, nutrients, and seeds modifies soils, vegetation, and subsequent transport. Here I synthesize field experiments, spatial analyses, remote sensing, and conceptual models to show how these reciprocal interactions operate from meters to continental scales.

At patch scales, vegetation partitions wind shear stress and interrupts sediment-transport pathways. Consequently, the amount and spatial arrangement of bare ground—not vegetation cover alone—govern the connectivity of erosion and deposition. Precipitation-by-connectivity experiments in the Jornada Basin demonstrate that manipulating transport pathways changes plant establishment and cover, with effects contingent on water availability and ecosystem state. The Pulse–Interactions–Reserves–Feedbacks–Community–Trajectory (PIRFCT) framework places these responses in a longer-term context: pulses alter interactions and redistribute reserves; those changes modify feedbacks, reorganize communities, and shape trajectories. Aeolian transport therefore propagates local responses through space and can reinforce patchiness, thresholds, lags, and hysteresis during grassland–shrubland change.

At landscape and regional scales, this same mechanism amplifies seemingly modest land-surface change. Across an agricultural–steppe gradient in Niger, satellite estimates of exposed soil combined with reanalysis winds show that relatively small differences in soil exposure can produce much larger differences in potential aeolian transport because vegetation sheltering is nonlinear. Land-use and vegetation change can therefore reorganize source areas and regional dust loading before changes in total cover appear dramatic.

At continental scales, land–atmosphere coupling can close the loop. In the Sahel, vegetation loss can increase local dust emissions and reduce atmospheric moisture recycling; dust may also suppress precipitation, creating the potential for a low-rainfall/high-dust state. At the same time, circulation links rainfall to remotely sourced Saharan dust, making feedback strength context dependent. Together, these results suggest that aeolian transport is simultaneously a response to ecological structure, a driver of critical zone reorganization, and a pathway through which land surface change can influence climate. Recognizing these nested feedbacks is essential for predicting dryland landscape evolution and identifying when local management of connectivity can alter broader ecosystem trajectories.

title: Insights from Three-Dimensional Models of Early Jurassic Dinosaur Track Assemblages of the Moenave Formation at the St. George Dinosaur Discovery Site, Southern Utah, USA
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments (Posters)
authors: Crowell, Jennifer Kailoa [1], Platt, Brian F. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS,
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
abstract: The St. George Dinosaur Discovery Site at Johnson Farm (SGDS), Utah, USA, is a unique site that offers a rare glimpse into an Early Jurassic (~200 Ma) lacustrine ecosystem considered to fall within the Triassic-Jurassic transition, a time of intense Earth system changes including climatic shifts due to increased volcanism, the separation of Pangea, and the end-Triassic mass extinction event. The SGDS contains both body and trace fossils, including a variety of invertebrate and vertebrate traces, most notably well-preserved dinosaur tracks. Dinosaur tracks from the SGDS represent a variety of locomotion behaviors, including well-known behaviors like walking and running, as well as uncommonly preserved behaviors such as crouching and swimming. The SGDS is perhaps best known for its over 3,000 non-avian dinosaur swim tracks, many of which have been thoroughly documented both traditionally and digitally through photogrammetry. As part of museum conservation efforts in 2004-2005, a large track-bearing bed (including many swim tracks) was excavated as a series of over 50 sandstone blocks. Due to limited museum space, these blocks were stored outside behind the museum with individual protective wooden coverings. The wooden coverings were meant to be a temporary solution, but they still remain outdoors and are the only structure in place to protect the track blocks from the elements. While some blocks have been digitized through photogrammetry, the entire mosaic of track blocks has not been digitized and reassembled for study and preservation. Museum volunteers are currently working to clean the track block surfaces for archival, high precision LiDAR scanning with a Riegl VZ-600i LiDAR unit in late fall 2026. RiSCAN PRO software will then be used to digitally reassemble the track blocks and reveal the entire track-bearing surface for the first time. In the meantime, data from photogrammetry and results from neoichnological experiments involving domestic chicken and turkey tracks will be used to produce preliminary interpretations of Moenave Formation paleoenvironment and substrate conditions in order to better understand the preservation mechanisms.

title: Shallow aquatic sediment heat tracing of subdaily groundwater-surface water exchange patterns
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions
authors: Briggs, Martin A. [1], Rey, David [2], Moore, Henry [3], Sohn, Robert [4], Tucker, Annie [5], Day-Lewis, Fred [6]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Water Mission Area, Hydrologic Remote Sensing Branch, Storrs, CT, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Water Mission Area, Hydrologic Remote Sensing Branch, Denver, CO, USA
(3) University of Bremen, Germany
(4) Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(5) US Geological Survey, Water Mission Area, Hydrologic Remote Sensing Branch, Menlo Park, CA, USA
(6) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, USA
abstract: We demonstrate the ability of recursive-estimation heat tracing methods to accurately recover intricate sub-daily groundwater flux signals, including abrupt reversals in flux direction. Such flux estimates have been made across multiple environments with highly dynamic groundwater-surface water exchange fluxes, such as the intertidal zone with extensive bidirectional tidal pumping, and streambank seepages influenced by evapotranspiration. We apply these methods to instrumented seepages in the mountain headwater Neversink Reservoir Watershed in NY, USA, the tidal beach areas of Hen Cove, MA, and McAllister Landfill, RI, USA, along with the Herring Brook salt marsh in Wellfleet, MA USA. Specific discharge time-series estimates from the field sites are assessed using complimentary data, including soil moisture, evapotranspiration flux, pore water pressure, and streamflow, to develop process-based understanding. We also use synthetic data to quantify the accuracy with which specific discharge patterns with strong diel or semi-diurnal periodicity can be resolved (based on how well signal phase and amplitude is reproduced) by the Extended Kalman Filter and the Rauch-Tung-Striebel Smoother vertical flux estimation methods. While both modeling filters well-define a wide range of subdaily specific discharge flux patterns, the timing (phase) of those signals is generally more accurately estimated by the Rauch-Tung-Striebel Smoother. Finally, we investigate the influence of the ‘process variance’ modeling parameter on model output and provide guidance for appropriate parameter selection in varied settings. This body of work highlights the utility of advanced heat tracing methods for measuring intricate, rapidly changing hydrologic exchange patterns, bridging a critical gap in process-based research in mountain headwater and coastal intertidal systems where groundwater and surface waters interact.

title: Biomechanical performance across diverse morphologies of the echinoid feeding apparatus
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology
authors: Hebdon, Nicholas [1], Leavey, Alice [2], Thompson, Jeffrey Robert [3], Petsios, Elizabeth [4]
affiliations: (1) Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(2) University of Southampton School of Ocean and Earth Sciences, Southampton, USA
(3) University of Southampton School of Ocean and Earth Sciences, Southampton, None, USA
(4) Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
abstract: Natural selection is expected to favor morphologies that enhance ecological performance, yet structurally suboptimal forms exist throughout the history of life. These morphologies may represent evolutionary intermediates or dead-ends, clades trapped on local adaptive peaks due to phylogenetic constrains, or ecological trade-offs not captured by simple measures of structural performance. The fossil record of regular echinoids provides a unique opportunity to distinguish among these possibilities. The perignathic girdle, an internal skeletal structure that anchors the protractor and retractor muscles of the Aristotle's lantern, plays a pivotal role in feeding behavior by providing leverage for movement of the whole feeding apparatus. Here, we quantify the biomechanical performance of extinct and extant girdle morphologies across the evolutionary history of regular echinoids using finite element analysis and taxonomically constrained muscle force estimates. Forces were estimated at the ordinal level from muscle volume measurements obtained using MRI and diceCT scans of extant specimens. These forces were then applied to 3D models of extinct and extant echinoid tests to simulate stress distributions across the perignathic girdle structure. Mesh-weighted Von Mises peak stress and stress distribution was used to compare structural optimality across girdle forms. We find substantial differences in biomechanical performance among girdle forms, with comparatively “poor-performing” girdles, characterized by gracile pegs with limited skeletal bracing, being common in several regular euechinoid clades. These performance differences cannot be fully explained by broad differences in feeding ecology, at least at the resolution that can currently be inferred from the fossil record. Ecological trade-offs therefore remain a plausible explanation, but resolving their influence will likely require finer-scale characterization of niches than in the current study. Still, it appears that structural optimization alone cannot explain the evolution of the diversity of perignathic girdle shapes, highlighting the importance of ecological factors and historical contingency in shaping morphology.

title: Geologic Mapping on Europa: Connecting regional and global scales
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Patthoff, Alex [1], Leonard, Erin J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Science Institute, La Habra Heights, CA,
(2) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, CA,
abstract: Jupiter’s icy moon, Europa, displays one of the most complex surfaces in the solar system. One of the keys to evaluating the potential habitability below that surface is understanding the geologic processes that drive the interaction between the outer icy shell and the interior liquid water layer. Here we discuss the progress on our regional geologic mapping of Europa, six areas that have been imaged at relatively high resolution by the Galileo spacecraft: “Flows” (107 m/pixel), Moytura Regio (180 m/pixel), Conamara Chaos (180 m/pixel), Leading and Trailing pole-to-pole mosaics (220 m/pixel), and Wedges Terrain (233 m/pixel). Together, these regions cover approximately 10 percent of the surface. Our mapping, presented here, is the first to apply a consistent mapping scale and set of units across each of those regions and tie the regional units to the global units published USGS global map of Europa (Leonard et al., 2024). The six areas we map contain all of the units identified at the global scale. The overall aim of this work is to produce a total of nine geologic map products: 3 new geologic maps produced at a scale of 1:2M from the USGS Global Europa basemap; 3 digitized geologic maps from the literature (Figueredo and Greeley, 2004; and Prockter et al., 1999); and 3 modified versions of the digitized maps that are made consistent in terms of units, linework, and scale with the 1:2M regional maps. The resulting consistent set of regional-scale units and their stratigraphic relationships can also serve as input to geologic and geophysical models to better understand how the surface of Europa has evolved over time.

title: Testing Maximum Depositional Age estimates for the SW Montana foreland basin with U-Pb geochronology of interbedded tuffs in the Lower Cretaceous Kootenai Formation
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools (Posters)
authors: Barstad, Owen Campbell [1], McClelland, William C. [2], Dorale, Jeffrey A. [3], Finzel, Emily S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(2) University of Iowa, Schenectady, NY,
(3) University of Iowa, Geoscience, Iowa City, IA, USA
(4) University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
abstract:
Testing Maximum Depositional Age estimates for the SW Montana foreland basin with U-Pb geochronology of interbedded tuffs in the Lower Cretaceous Kootenai Formation

Constraining depositional ages within a foreland basin setting can be challenging due to limited biostratigraphic markers, and because estimated maximum depositional ages (MDA) based on U/Pb analysis of detrital zircons in fluvial strata may poorly represent the depositional timing of a unit. However, foreland basin deposits formed proximal to convergent margin settings, such as the Cretaceous foreland basin in the North American Cordillera, may include tuffs that can potentially provide more robust estimates for depositional ages. A 10-cm thick volcanic ash bed collected in the Lower Calcareous unit of the Lower Cretaceous Kootenai Formation exposed in Frying Pan basin located in Southwestern Montana provides an opportunity to establish a direct temporal constraint on sedimentation based on igneous zircon analysis and to evaluate the reliability of MDA estimates for the section. Zircons separated from the tuff are elongate, colorless, and euhedral with well-developed oscillatory zoning defined in CL images. U/Pb analysis of 60 zircon grains by LA-ICP-MS at the Arizona LaserChron Center yielded a weighted mean 206 Pb/ 238 U age of 115.5 ± 1.1 Ma (2 σ; MSWD=0.7; probability=0.93; n = 38). This age is consistent with previous MDA estimates based on detrital zircons separated from a limestone layer in the Lower Calcareous unit at the Ziegler Gulch locality (ZG-150m). Euhedral zircon from ZG-150m defines a youngest probability peak (YPP) of 115 Ma and a weighted mean 206 Pb/ 238 U age of 114.9 ± 1.8 Ma (2σ; MSWD=0.7; probability=0.71; n = 12) reported by Finzel and Rosenblume (2021, Geology). Further analysis of additional tuff units in the Lower Cretaceous section as well as high-precision CA-TIMS U/Pb analysis of select grains from the zircon suite will be conducted to further constrain the depositional ages of the Kootenai Formation in Southwest Montana.

title: Tracking Thermal Evolution Through Simple-to-Complex Transitions: A Case Study of Dione
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Fuhrman, Bethany E S [1], Denton, Adeene [2], Rhoden, Alyssa [3], Ferguson, Sierra Nichole [4], Siegler, Matthew [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Hawaii at Manoa / School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology, Honolulu, HI,
(2) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
(3) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, Boulder, CO,
(4) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
(5) University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI,
abstract:
The surface of Dione, a mid-sized moon of Saturn, possesses heavily cratered terrain and tectonically altered/resurfaced areas, suggesting it has experienced variable heating and internal geologic activity throughout its evolution [1-3]. The simple-to-complex transition diameter on Dione ranges from ~16.8 – 25 km [1,4], yet some similarly sized craters within a shared region vary in morphology, with some displaying clear central peaks and others lacking central structures. Because ice strength is strongly temperature-dependent, varying the ice shell’s thermal structure alters its strength profile and may affect the final crater shape, offering a possible explanation for the observed discrepancy in crater morphology. In this study, we model crater formation on Dione across diameters of ~15 – 40 km, varying the subsurface thermal gradient to identify the thermal conditions that produce complex craters at a given diameter or match a given simple-to-complex transition diameter. Under the conditions modeled, the observed simple-to-complex transition range on Dione requires a thermal gradient through the conductive portion of the ice shell as high as ~15 – 19.5 K/km, which corresponds to a conductive lid thickness of ~8 – 12 km depending on the basal temperature. This gradient is far higher than expected for Dione’s ice shell today, based on current estimates of ice shell thickness [5]. Although the impactor flux at the Saturnian system is not well-characterized, complicating efforts to determine when these conditions occurred [6], the largest craters generally predate smaller ones. Given that most 15 – 40 km craters on Dione are complex, the ice shell was likely substantially warmer during most large crater formation and has cooled since, explaining the presence of the relatively few simple craters within this diameter range, which likely formed more recently under colder conditions. Future work will include comparing modeled results with DEMs, relative age-dating large craters, exploring lower velocity impacts, and identifying conditions that could produce a relatively thin conductive lid in Dione’s past.

title: From Mineral Grains to Mountain Rivers: Tectonics, Surface Processes, and Landscape Evolution in the Eastern Himalaya
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Huntington, Katharine W. [1], Lang, Karl [2], Morey, Susannah [3], Shobe, Charles M. [4], Turzewski, Michael [5], Duvall, Alison [6], Santana, Gabriel [7], Nath, Srinanda [8]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(2) Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA,

(5) Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN,
(6) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(7) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(8) Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA,
abstract:
Mountain landscapes emerge from interactions between tectonics and surface processes spanning orders of magnitude in space and time—from million-year rock exhumation to individual episodes of erosion and deposition. The Tsangpo Gorge region of the Eastern Himalaya provides a natural laboratory for examining this interplay across scales. Here, one of Earth's most localized zones of rapid rock uplift and exhumation coincides with exceptional relief, an extremely steep bedrock river, and repeated outburst floods. We synthesize observations and models to address two linked questions: (1) What caused localized rapid deformation and exhumation? (2) How have extreme floods shaped the geomorphic expression of that forcing?

The spatial coincidence of localized rapid exhumation with one of Earth's steepest river gorges motivated hypotheses that fluvial erosion drives lithospheric deformation. However, detrital mineral thermochronology and provenance show the Yarlung-Siang-Brahmaputra River was established through the Gorge region millions of years before rapid exhumation began. These observations rule out proposed late-Cenozoic river capture and Quaternary climate change as triggers of the exhumation anomaly, supporting instead tectonic forcing of localized rapid rock uplift. Fluvial erosion thus appears to have responded to tectonically driven rock uplift, rather than driving the lithosphere-scale deformation responsible for the rapid-exhumation anomaly.

Quaternary megafloods (≥10 6 m 3 /s) generated by glacial dam failures likely played a major role in eroding the zone of localized rapid rock uplift and shaping the geomorphic evolution of the region. Integrating field observations of flood deposits, sediment provenance, hydraulic simulations of historical and ancient outburst floods, and geomorphic process models reveals not only the extraordinary erosive power of these events, but the long-lived legacy of their deposits. Megaflood boulders create channel disequilibrium that persists for millennia and compounds across successive floods, fundamentally altering channel evolution. These results highlight the importance of episodic sedimentation, alongside discharge variability, in mountain river evolution. Downstream, megafloods influenced the course of the Brahmaputra River and transported material from the zone of localized rock uplift >2,000 km offshore to the Bengal Fan, extending their influence across one of Earth's largest sediment-routing systems.

Together, these results link processes operating over minutes to millions of years, demonstrating that tectonics drives localized rock uplift, whereas rare, catastrophic floods govern how that tectonic signal is expressed in landscapes and ultimately preserved from source to sink.

authors: Sun, Mingzhao [1], Archer , Corey [2], Sweere , Tim [3], Shen , Yanan [4], Algeo, Thomas [5], Gill, Benjamin [6], Dahl, Tais [7], Zhang , Feifei [8], Wei, Guangyi [9], Cheng , Meng [10], Dickson, Alexander [11], Kender, Sev [12], Xiao , Shuhai [13], Jiang, Ganqing [14], Takahashi, Satoshi [15], Scholz, Florian [16], Sperling, Erik [17], Vance, Derek [18]

abstract: The evolution of Earth’s biosphere since the late Precambrian has played out and been partially driven by a changing surface Earth environment. Studies of the interactions between the changing environment and the biosphere it houses have often focused on spectacular, somewhat singular, evolutionary events, such as catastrophic mass extinctions, the Cambrian radiation of animals, or the appearance of vascular plants on the continents. But this evolutionary history is also characterised by long-term temporal trends and long wavelength variability. Though the details of the ways in which environmental change has influenced long-term biological evolution are still vigorously debated, studies of the interactions between tectonics, climate and the carbon cycle have focused attention on two particular drivers, with the biosphere itself feeding back into both: gradual surface Earth oxygenation punctuated by periodic reversions to oceanic anoxia, and the impact of physical and chemical weathering of rocks on climate, ocean chemistry, and continental regolith generation. Here, we present a new nickel (Ni) isotope record for the ocean over the entire Phanerozoic, based on analysis of ~500 organic-rich sedimentary rocks. Though oceanic Ni isotopes, a relatively new isotope tracer, are at least partially controlled by ocean redox via the preferential sequestration of light isotopes to sediments underlying an oxic water column, we show that the quantitative evolution of the oceanic mass balance must have been strongly impacted by temporal changes in the riverine flux from the continents, controlled by tectonics and the rate, pattern and intensity of chemical weathering. By coupling these new data to multiple complementary records of the surface Earth, we document changes in redox and the nature and rate of chemical weathering. In particular, we use records and mass balance models of multiple metal isotope systems to deconvolve the importance of multiple Earth system processes in controlling their behaviour. We document slow, sometimes transient, emergence from oceanic anoxia in the Ediacaran-Paleozoic, a fundamental reset of the Earth system at the Permian-Triassic boundary (~252 Ma), a Mesozoic Era characterised by variable environmental conditions, and the move to a modern environment through the Cenozoic Era.

title: Constraining the Most Recent Deformation on the Needles Fault System, Arizona Utilizing Surficial Mapping, Geochronological Dating, and Surficial Offset Analysis
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape (Posters)
authors: Muggli, Blake [1], Regalla, Christine [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(2) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
abstract:
The active Needles fault system, located near the Arizona-California-Nevada border, is one of the only identified fault systems in the region and poses a hazard to nearby infrastructure, but key parameters for seismic hazard modeling are unconstrained. These parameters include how far to the north, towards Davis Dam, this system extends and whether the timing, deformation rates, and geometry remain the same across the fault system. We investigate these parameters in the northernmost 4 km of the fault system, which contains a diffuse network of NW-SE oriented normal faults and a sub-parallel monocline totaling 20 km in length. We used tectonogeomorphic mapping to identify the location and relative age of fault scarps and the monocline, and elevation data to determine the magnitude of displacement across them. We will also use stream profile analysis to determine if monoclinal tilting is active, and luminescence geochronology to calculate the rate of monoclinal tilting.

Thus far, tectonogeomorphic mapping has constrained the location, length, and orientation of fault scarps, and relative ages of offset alluvial and fluvial units.. This mapping indicates that there has been at least one earthquake since ~12-20 ka based on inferred fan ages. Elevation data collected across fault scarps has constrained the vertical separation per event to between 0.3 m and 1 m. To further constrain fault displacement, additional elevation profiles will be extracted using LiDAR data. Our mapping has also identified potential tilted beds in this northern region that indicate the monocline extends farther north than previously known. We plan to further test the extent of the monocline by extracting elevation profiles across potentially folded alluvial fans, and longitudinal profiles of streams that cross the proposed monoclinal axis. Collectively, this research fills the identified gaps by contributing data to the geometry, timing, and deformation rate parameters for seismic hazard modeling of the Needles fault system.

title: Improving Inquiry Level, Utility, and Vocabulary Use in Labs Through Data-Informed Revisions
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Kortz, Karen Melissa [1], Rogers, Rachel A [2], Hart, Roger M [3], Smay, Jessica [4]
affiliations: (1) Community College of Rhode Island, Lincoln, RI, USA
(2) Community College of Rhode Island, Warwick, RI, USA
(3) Community College of Rhode Island, Lincoln, RI, USA
(4) San Jose City College, San Jose, CA, USA
abstract:
ESS Scaffolded Inquiry Labs are a collection of scaffolded, inquiry-focused lab activities we are developing for earth and space science (ESS) courses. These labs leverage online data sets and can be used asynchronously online or in-person. Our goal is to develop easy-to-implement labs that support students to achieve high levels of inquiry while reducing learning barriers created by specialized vocabulary. Labs with high levels of inquiry have students take part in more steps of the scientific process (e.g., procedures, analysis, communication). Labs with high utility require less instructor time (including preparation, teaching, and grading) and material costs. Labs with fewer vocabulary terms require less cognitive load for students. We created nine labs and analyzed them for level of inquiry, utility, and number of vocabulary terms. After this initial analysis, we used our findings to revise the labs to increase the inquiry and decrease specialized vocabulary use.

Regarding inquiry level (on a scale of 0=confirmation to 6=authentic), our revisions increased the overall inquiry average of the labs from 3.9 to 4.8 (guided/open inquiry). When looking at individual parts of the lab, our revisions increased the average of each part from 2.3 (structured) to 2.5 (guided). No parts were rated as confirmation. Revisions reduced the parts rated as structured to 44% and increased the parts rated as guided inquiry to 43% and open inquiry to 12%. When analyzing the labs with the Lab Utility Rubric, our labs averaged 28 out of 30, falling into the category of high utility. Regarding vocabulary use, our revisions decreased the total Tier 2 and 3 vocabulary use to an average of 42 terms per lab from 53. Importantly, we reduced the number of vocabulary terms used once or twice to an average of 9 per lab from 22. Our results demonstrate that systematic, data-informed revisions can decrease vocabulary barriers while simultaneously increasing the inquiry level. Following revision, our labs demonstrate high inquiry, high instructional utility, and low cognitive load through vocabulary.

title: An Integrated Groundwater Projection Model for The Greater Phoenix, Arizona Metropolitan Area
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Barber, Nicholas Dewitt [1], Price, Alexander James [2], Chakraborty, Madhumita [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciecne, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Phoenix, AZ, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, Virginia, USA
abstract:
Water supplies in the Phoenix, Arizona Greater Metropolitan Area are under intensifying pressure from urban growth and a warming, variable climate. Over five million people live accross around 3,000 km² of low-infiltration urban land in the Sonoran Desert, parts of which received only 107mm (4.2in) of rain in 2023. The Arizona Department of Water Resources (ADWR) attributes roughly 60% of municipal supply to snowmelt on the Salt-Verde system and 40% to the Colorado River, with groundwater covering overdraft and local deficits. Repeat-gravity and water-level monitoring in the Phoenix Active Management Area (Kennedy et al., USGS, 2025) indicates that present withdrawal rates are unsustainable under plausible future demand.

We are creating a coupled SWAT+/MODFLOW6 model, and applying it to the Verde-Salt system spanning around 32,000 km 2 . We couple SWAT+ 61.0.2 and MODFLOW 6.7.0 at a daily timestep, where SWAT+ percolation and channel discharge are written into MODFLOW memory each day as recharge and SFR6 reach inflow. Streambed leakage is limited by routed streamflow, and MODFLOW sends aquifer-stream exchange back to SWAT+ for channel routing. The exchange occurs in memory, and does not write files at each timestep.

Inputs include PRISM 4-km climate data, USGS-3DEP, gSSURGO, NLCD, USGS-NWIS, ADWR’s Groundwater Site Inventory, ADWR’s Wells55 database, and Central Arizona Project delivery records. We calibrate the model with a flow-duration-curve segmented objective and reject runs that fail water-balance criteria.

In the completed Verde River component of the model spanning around 17000 km 2 , daily coupling raises monthly streamflow prediction skill at USGS gauge 09504000 from NSE 0.61 for standalone SWAT+ to 0.70. It also recovers the ~1.7 m³/s of dry-season baseflow that SWAT+ alone structurally cannot supply, where an identically parameterized run scores NSE ≈ 0, showing that longer exchange intervals dilute storm pulses below the stream network's infiltration capacity.

The planned 50-year future scenarios test urban expansion, changing water demand, surface-water allocation, and pumping regulation. Even when surface water meets projected demand across the basin, business-as-usual pumping continues to deepen drawdown beneath fast-growing areas.

Major uncertainties currently involve deep-aquifer properties and the top-of-Redwall contact because of unclear and disagreeing logs. We ground-truth against USGS seepage runs, long-term water-level hydrographs, and published baseflow estimates.

title: Autochthonous Carbon Accumulation Across Tidal Zones in the Wax Lake Delta, Louisiana
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution
authors: Aalto, August [1], Breecker, Dan [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
Louisiana is experiencing a land loss crisis. Levees, dams, and other human modifications to the Mississippi River have restricted sediment delivery to the state’s coastal plain. As a result, Louisiana has lost over 25% of its coastal wetlands since the 1930s, an area the size of Delaware. The rapidly prograding Wax Lake Delta (WLD), the product of a river diversion dredged by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in 1942, is one of the few areas of the Louisiana Gulf Coast building land. The WLD serves as an iconic field model for studying processes driving delta maintenance and growth, and for evaluating how river diversions can be used as effective tools for coastal restoration. However, the processes driving soil development and their role in maintaining and growing deltaic islands remain understudied, even for the well-researched WLD.

To study soil development in the WLD, we collected 3-m vibracores from 14 sites along a chronosequence of subaerial land development, and sampled dominant plant species at each site. Cores were split, imaged, described, and sampled at regular intervals for dry bulk density (DBD), organic carbon content (%OC), stable carbon isotopes (δ 13 C), radiocarbon (Δ 14 C), 210 Pb activity, and grain size. DBD and OC content were multiplied to calculate OC concentration profiles. Plant samples were measured for δ 13 C. Depth profiles were normalized to the mean lower low water tidal datum using a new WLD lidar survey. In the subtidal zone, δ 13 C profiles are similar between cores, and OC loadings (OC/SSA) are typical of riverine sediments, with trends in OC concentration primarily controlled by mineral surface area. In the intertidal and supratidal zones, decreasing δ 13 C, increasing OC/SSA, and increasing Δ 14 C values are consistent with the deposition of OC from in-situ vegetation. We used a δ 13 C binary mass-balance mixing model with plant and recent mineral deposit endmembers to find that half of the OC in the intertidal and supratidal zones is autochthonous. We found a linear relationship between δ 13 C-δ 13 C 0 and ln(C/C 0 ) for these zones, which is more consistent with a time-dependent mass-balance mixing model influenced by the Suess effect than isotopic fractionation from microbial decomposition. These findings reveal a shift from mineral-surface-area-driven OC trends in subtidal deposits to vegetation-driven OC accumulation trends in young soils as deltaic islands emerge and mature.

abstract: Zircon (ZrSiO4) from hypervelocity meteorite impact structures often display {112} deformation twins with a 65° rotation about the <110> axis and lamellae. {112} twinning in zircon (ZrSiO4) has only been reported from terrestrial and planetary impactites, but it is not considered impact-diagnostic due to a lack of experimental work to calibrate formation conditions. These microstructures have been reported to exist in the same grain of zircon alongside its high pressure polymorph reidite. {112} twinning in zircon has been previously recreated in the lab using a diamond anvil cell, but it has not recreated in dynamic shock experiments.. Here we report the first successful synthesis of {112} twins in natural zircon using a multi anvil press. Two experiments were conducted: Sample B was run at 11 GPa and 1127 °C for 30 minutes in a Walker-type press and Sample J was run at 14 GPa and 600 °C for 60 minutes in a DIA-type press. Crystallographic orientation relationships and microstructure were characterized using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Both experiments resulted in planar {112} twins. Notably, Sample B yielded planar twins, whereas Sample J produced curviplanar twins, possibly indicating that peak pressure, temperature, and heating duration influences twin morphology. Our results indicate that {112} twins in zircon can be formed under static high-pressure conditions, such as those found in the deep Earth, but further work is needed to constrain the conditions under which the twins are preserved and determine the dynamic high pressure conditions under which {112} twins form and whether {112} twinning in zircon can be considered impact-diagnostic. Constraining the static thermodynamic conditions under which these microstructures form and are preserved could help validate their utility as reliable impact shock barometers in impacted rock.

title: GLAAS - a new FAIR data information system for tephra and geochemistry laboratory research
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era (Posters)
authors: Kuehn, Stephen C. [1], Nalesnik, Abigail [2], Parcheta, Debra [4]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Concord University, Athens, WV, USA
(2) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Concord University, Athens, WV, USA
(3) University of Colorado, Denver, Denver, CO, USA; Concord University, Athens, WV, USA
(4) University of Colorado, Denver, Denver, CO, USA; Blue Marble Enterprises, Aurora, CO, USA
abstract:
A prominent barrier to adopting open science and FAIR data practices is the large workload required for generating and sharing well-documented data and metadata, especially for legacy datasets generated via workflows not designed with FAIR data publication in mind. The Geological Laboratory Analytical Archive System (GLAAS) directly minimizes this barrier by (a) facilitating the operational capture of metadata as it is being generated while supporting laboratory workflows, and (b) integrating that with ingested legacy data. This approach eases the process of archiving and publishing FAIR data with rich contextual metadata following research community best practice standards. This system takes inspiration from Sparrow (https://sparrow-data.org/) for analytical lab data and Strabo (https://strabospot.org/) for field data. GLAAS has completed a first year of collaborative development which has established core functionality and is beginning a second year aimed at refinement and feature enhancement.

The current schema includes key data and metadata along with their relationships: people, user roles, projects, funding sources, physical sample cataloging, sample and sub-sample curation, sample preparation, analytical target cataloging, bulk and in-situ microanalytical geochemistry, analytical methods and instruments, grain size analysis, volcanological componentry, optical images, SEM images, and resulting publications. The ability to capture rich contextual information makes it possible to create well-structured datasets ideal for machine learning applications. An authenticated-access web interface allows users to securely access and input data. The designated project owner can manage their project(s) and sample/data visibility (denoting projects as public or private ), and they can configure multiple levels of project data access and management for their collaborators and members of the public. Datasets designated public are accessible to all other registered users, helping to foster and promote open science.

The development of this multi-component system and relational database gained valuable insight and direction from previous tephra community workshop participants, NSF-supported best practices development (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01515-y), IEDA EarthChem and SESAR collaborations, and early stage Concord University undergraduate student contributions. The intention is to make GLAAS available for the broader tephra-mineralogy-petrology and analytical lab community. Data export capabilities will facilitate archiving in data repositories (e.g. EarthChemLibrary) and discoverability through the Tephra Information Portal (TIP https://www.iedadata.org/communities/tephra).

title: Comparing the Number of Vocabulary Terms Used in Earth and Space Science Labs
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Quezada, Dorian [1], Kortz, Karen Melissa [2]
affiliations: (1) Community College of Rhode Island, Warwick, RI, USA
(2) Community College of Rhode Island, Lincoln, RI,
abstract: Earth and space science laboratory manuals are designed to reinforce concepts introduced in lecture and to develop scientific reasoning skills. Scientific vocabulary plays a key role in understanding and communicating these concepts, yet large numbers of academic terminology may increase students’ cognitive load and reduce attention from scientific reasoning. Tier 3 vocabulary consists of terms specific to a scientific discipline (e.g., tectonics), while Tier 2 vocabulary includes general academic language used across multiple disciplines (e.g., analyze). To better understand the vocabulary demands placed on students, we analyzed three sets of Earth and space science labs by comparing the total number of Tier 2 and Tier 3 terms, how frequently they appeared, and the number and percentage of terms used only once or twice. The newly-developed ESS Scaffolded Inquiry labs consist of nine labs designed to support scientific inquiry and scientific and quantitative literacy using online datasets. These labs were compared with three open-access labs (Deline, Harris & Tefend, 2015) and four widely-used published labs (Cronin & Tasa, 2026). We found that the ESS Scaffolded Inquiry labs contained an average of 41.7 Tier 2 and Tier 3 terms per lab (range of 31-61), compared with 90.0 terms in the open-access laboratory manuals (range of 81-99) and 148.0 terms in the published laboratory manuals (range of 98-205). On average, 9.1 (21.3%) terms per ESS lab appeared only once or twice, compared with 47.0 (52.0%) terms per open-access lab and 68.3 (46.4%) terms per published lab. Our findings demonstrate that the ESS Scaffolded Inquiry labs had fewer Tier 2 and Tier 3 vocabulary terms than the open-access and published laboratory manuals, reducing the overall vocabulary demands placed on students. Overall, by introducing fewer Tier 2 and Tier 3 terms, these labs may allow students to spend more time developing scientific reasoning skills and engaging in inquiry.

title: Exploring the Effect of Plankton Ecological Dynamics on Proterozoic Geochemical Models
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age (Posters)
authors: Sjosten, Sara [1], Daines, Stuart [2], Lenton, Tim [3], Roopnarine, Peter D. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Exeter, EXETER, United Kingdom

abstract: The early-middle Proterozoic marks the first appearance of plausible eukaryotes and algae in the fossil record, and prior ecological modeling of this record suggests that plankton communities were already diversifying in feeding mode and community structure by this time. The effects of such ecological diversification on ocean geochemistry have long been a subject of speculation, from changes in organic matter reworking driven by the biological pump to the role of larger eukaryotic cells and, later, sponges in altering carbon delivery to the deep ocean and seafloor. Despite this, models commonly used for deep-time geochemical reconstruction rarely resolve plankton community structure directly. Since shelf sediments account for most global phosphorus burial, shelf burial rates control long-term carbon and oxygen cycling. This burial is directly sensitive to plankton community structure through the impact of size and sinking on remineralization depth. Here, we present a computationally efficient 1D shelf sea model that couples a size-structured plankton community to an ocean and sediment column, allowing water column redox, organic burial, nutrient burial, and sediment geochemical signals to respond directly to changes in plankton community structure. Overall, this model provides a novel tool for linking plankton ecological dynamics to phosphorus and redox signals preserved in Proterozoic shelf sediments, and enables the integration of geochemical reconstructions with questions of paleobiological interest.

title: Newly Attributed Letters from Vincenzo Durante to Athanasius Kircher: Early Empirical Observations of Fossiliferous Strata in Umbria, 1661
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Parcell, William C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Wichita State University, Wichita, KS,
abstract:
Unsigned letters addressed to Athanasius Kircher, S.J., preserved in the Archives of the Pontifical Gregorian University, Rome (APUG 559, ff. 130r–131v; APUG 564, ff. 128r–129v), are here newly attributed to Vincenzo Durante on the basis of handwriting comparison with signed Durante correspondence and contextual evidence within Kircher's broader correspondence network. The letters document fossil-bearing strata near Orvieto and Monte Peglia, Umbria. Written in 1661, they predate Niels Stensen's (Steno's) Italian fieldwork by five years and his Prodromus (Florence, 1669) — a foundational text in stratigraphy and paleontology — by eight.

Durante frames his observations within a diluvial interpretation, attributing the strata to the Biblical Flood. Despite this theological framework, his descriptions show a systematic, empirical approach to field observation that antedates later stratigraphic methods. The letters capture an early stage in geological thought in which field observation, correspondence networks, and scriptural interpretation operated together rather than in tension.

Read within Kircher's broader correspondence network, these letters support a distributed, collaborative model of the emergence of geological observation in the seventeenth century — one in which practices later formalized by Steno were already circulating, in nascent form, among correspondents years before their formalized articulation. This new attribution and analysis add an underexamined data point to the historiography of early modern earth science and underscore the value of archival correspondence in reconstructing the prehistory of stratigraphic thinking.

title: Scaffolded inquiry labs that highlight the process of science and scientific and quantitative literacy
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Smay, Jessica [1], Kortz, Karen Melissa [2], Hart, Roger [3], Rogers, Rachel [4]
affiliations: (1) San Jose City College, San Jose, CA,
(2) Community College of Rhode Island, Lincoln, RI,
(3) Community College of Rhode Island, Lincoln, RI, USA
(4) Community College of Rhode Island, Lincoln, RI, USA
abstract:
Earth and Space Science (ESS) Scaffolded Inquiry Labs are a collection of labs designed with progressively reduced instructional scaffolding to guide students through authentic scientific research strategies while practicing scientific and quantitative literacies. The collection of nine modular labs spans entry-level topics in geology, oceanography, astronomy, and earth science. Because they use browser-based data sets, the labs bypass the need for specialized software or costly materials and make them easily adaptable for both in-person and online students. Each lab features 5 to 8 standalone parts, allowing instructors to adapt them for shorter lab periods or as brief in-class activities to enhance lectures. To prompt metacognitive awareness, we included embedded reflection questions that require students to identify their current stage in the process of science. Furthermore, each lab includes 3-7 targeted questions that focus on 2 or 3 scientific and quantitative literacies such as calculating averages, reading graphs, and distinguishing between observations and interpretations.

We conducted a pilot study of non-STEM majors in introductory ESS courses at a two-year college. After each lab, 83% of students across 276 lab completions reported they were better at applying and analyzing steps in the process of science. 76% of students reported they were better at the scientific and quantitative literacies highlighted, ranging from 66% to 83% for the different literacies. The positive student metrics underscore the value of this lab-writing strategy. These flexible, easy-to-implement labs are a resource for instructors seeking a versatile way to integrate scientific and quantitative literacy into introductory science courses. By using browser-based open educational resources, this set of labs makes scientific inquiry with real data sets available to all students in a variety of modalities. These open-access labs will be available to download on SERC’s Teach the Earth portal.

title: Lithology Impacts Borehole Breakout Directions: Examples from Central California
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Titus, Sarah J. [1], Hackenmueller, Hannah [2], Carson, Amelia [3], Posner, Max [4], Davis, Joshua R. [5]
affiliations: (1) Carleton College, Northfield, MN,
(2) Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA

abstract:
Borehole breakouts provide an important record of stress directions at shallow crustal depths. We investigate wells from central California, where breakout directions have been used to support the weak-fault hypothesis for the San Andreas fault. We revisit wells used in previous studies and report data from new wells. Our sites each include additional well records such as dip logs to infer bedding directions and electrical and mud logs to make lithologic inferences.

We observe the impact of lithology in three concrete ways. First, some breakouts start or stop at a lithologic boundary. Most commonly, breakouts are better developed in fine grained units, such as shale and mudstone, and terminate in coarse grained units, such as sandstone. Second, the width of breakouts may be impacted by lithology. Breakouts in shales are often wider than those in sandstones from the same well and may have washouts superimposed on them. In sandstone intervals, breakouts may be too narrow to match the World Stress Map criteria, although all characteristic patterns are met other than the width constraint. Third, bedding sometimes impacts breakout directions, especially in wells with moderately dipping beds. In several wells where bedding directions change with depth, there are corresponding changes in breakout directions.

From the dataset we have compiled, we find more variable breakout directions than those reported in the World Stress Map across central California. Local structures, such as faults and folds, appear to influence breakouts, creating directions that are, in some cases, inconsistent with a dextral plate boundary system. Taken together, our findings suggest that rock anisotropy may play a role in breakout development. Thus, stress directions inferred from breakouts may not always reflect a regional stress field.

title: The Caribbean Geosciences Conferences: More than Seventy Years of International Research Communication, Collaboration, and Networking
session_title: International Collaborations in the Geosciences: Celebrating Science Without Borders
authors: Laó-Dávila, Daniel A. [1], Weber, John C. [2], Mitchell, Simon Francis [3], Coutou, Richard A [4]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,
(2) Geology Department, Grand Valley State University, Allendale, MI,

abstract:
Since its inception in 1955 with 37 attendees in Antigua, the Caribbean Geoscience Conference (CGC)—formerly known as the Caribbean Geological Conference—has provided an important venue for geoscientists working in the Caribbean to communicate, collaborate, and network across international boundaries. Evolving from its roots in the English-speaking Caribbean, the CGC evolved with the inclusion of academic, marine, industry, petroleum, and mineral researchers and professionals from across the Caribbean, the Americas, and Europe. Renamed in 2025 to reflect an inclusive, multidisciplinary scope, the CGC has hosted 21 conferences across 11 countries, averaging 155 attendees (peaking at over 300), with contributions presented in English, Spanish, French, and Dutch. The conferences are held every 3-4 years except for a 10-year hiatus between 2015 and 2025. The 21 st conference was held in conjunction with the Geological Society of Jamaica’s 65 th Annual Meeting in Kingston, Jamaica. One notable participant in the first (1955) and second (1959) CGCs was Professor Harry Hess, an early proponent of the theory of seafloor spreading, a key part of the theory of plate tectonics.

Lacking formal legal standing, membership dues, or permanent funding, the CGC operates through volunteer effort and informal governance. Operations and continuity are overseen by a Standing Committee, while each conference is planned and executed by a rotating local Organizing Committee (typically from host geological surveys or universities). Targeted tasks, such as outreach or branding, are managed by ad hoc working committees. Host selection and new committee chairs are determined through informal discussions and consultation with the Standing Committee.

Each conference is financially self-sustaining, funded through registration, workshop, and field trip fees supplemented by generous government, industry, and academic sponsorship. Research presented at CGC meetings is preserved through printed and digital Transactions, extended abstracts, and special volumes.

For over 70 years, the CGC has made possible regional collaborations across international and political borders with the mission of advancing Caribbean geoscience research and practice and with key historic implications to the global understanding of geoscience.
