abstract: Burn severity is a key control on the magnitude of fire-enhanced runoff and sediment transport. Many hydrologic and geomorphic models used to assess postfire flow hazards rely directly on using burn severity as an input or indirectly to parameterize fire effects on input parameters. Empirical models used to assess postfire debris-flow (PFDF) likelihood, for example, require burn severity metrics, such as the differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR), to make predictions. dNBR is a remotely sensed metric used to inform the rapid postfire assessment of soil burn severity. While rapid postfire debris-flow hazard assessments have become an invaluable tool for identifying PFDF hazards, decision-making, and prioritizing resources, there is also much that can be gained from prefire assessments of PFDF hazards. Prefire assessments can provide additional time to develop and implement mitigation and risk reduction strategies. These assessments, however, require estimates of the severity of a future fire. This study develops a machine learning ExtraTrees regression model to predict dNBR from fire intensity metrics derived from FlamMap, prefire vegetation characteristics, and topographic information. The model is developed using data from five fires burned between 2018 and 2024 in forested areas of Arizona and New Mexico, USA. The predicted dNBR maps are then used as input to a PFDF likelihood model developed for the Southwest USA. Finally, we compare modeled PFDF likelihood using simulated and observed dNBR following a 2026 fire in western New Mexico to assess the ability of the model to estimate PFDF hazards. Results provide decision-makers with information on PFDF hazards that can inform mitigation efforts before a fire occurs.

abstract: The Cuatro Ciénegas Basin (CCB) in Coahuila, Mexico is a globally unique endorheic basin where groundwater upwells through faulted Cretaceous carbonate rocks to sustain a vast network of over 200 pozas. The CCB holds significant ecological and geological importance, hosting numerous endemic species, rare freshwater stromatolites, and unique gypsum dunes, a manifestation of a key phenomenon within the system where sulfate evaporites precipitate from sulfate-rich groundwater. However, it continues to face threat from groundwater overexploitation for regional agriculture and municipal demand. In this study, we use geochemical measurements to quantify the chemical makeup of different groundwater and surface water to understand the underlying causes of chemical variations within the shallow subsurface. We hypothesize that sulfur evaporite deposits heavily influence groundwater chemistry, effectively creating a sulfate dominated groundwater system. We established a network of monitoring wells across three major waterbodies within the CCB, where water quality was measured periodically and bottled samples were taken at several subsurface sampling points and surface water bodies to determine anion, cation, and alkalinity concentrations. We found that small differences in elevation (<0.1-0.25 m compared to surroundings) produced a high degree of variance in TDS and specific ions present, likely due to cyclic precipitation and dissolution of evaporite minerals in topographically low areas. We observed elevated levels of sulfate across the basin, meaning evaporite dissolution is a dominant geochemical process throughout the system. Additionally, we found that the source of water for most of the shallow subsurface was strongly chemically connected. Our results show that the shallow subsurface is chemically characterized by the same groundwater source. Our findings help to connect rainfall, water-evaporite interactions, and variations in topography with chemical variations in shallow groundwater. These results can be coupled with hydraulic head data to more accurately represent the processes taking place in the CCB under water-stressed conditions and how it affects the biological endemism as well as nearby communities that rely on the groundwater of the region.

abstract: Research over the last decades has demonstrated that methane (cold) seeps were much more common than previously recognized. Fossils within seep limestones indicate that seeps were inhabited by a variety of organisms, including facultative and obligatory inhabitants, often at higher abundance and diversity than in surrounding rocks. We focus on Cretaceous (Campanian) seeps from the Western Interior Seaway and Alaska, as shown by a combination of biogenic limestone structure reminiscent of seep limestones, low stable carbon isotopes values, and faunal components common at seeps. A survey of museum collections and field work have yielded rich assemblages. In the Pierre Shale of South Dakota and Wyoming, mollusks (bivalves, gastropods, cephalopods) tend to dominate seeps; other macrofossils include echinoderms, worms, sponges, corals, brachiopods, algae, bryozoans, vertebrates, and crustaceans. Trace fossils in bivalves demonstrate the presence of octopods. The decapod assemblage consists of Brachyura and Axiidea of at least seven species, all facultative inhabitants known from outside the seeps too. While preservation is usually mediocre, one remarkable crab shows mineralized soft tissues. Several lines of evidence showcase predation provisionally attributed to crustaceans. Unlike for South Dakota, seeps from Alaska are poorly known. A newly recognized seep from Alaska has yielded bivalves including chemosymbiotic lucinids, gastropods, worms, and decapods. Though mollusks dominate, the sole anomuran decapod species is abundant and is thought to be a stem-lineage taxon for a family living exclusively in seeps and hydrothermal vents today. Jointly, we suggest that seeps were an integral component of Campanian marine ecosystems in North America.

title: Integrating Electrical Resistivity Tomography, Spatial Interpretation of Paleogeomorphology, and Well Logging to Optimize Water Supply Well Placement in Rocky Mountain National Park

abstract:
Securing reliable groundwater supplies in high-elevation montane environments presents unique hydrogeological challenges due to complex glacial geology, thin overburden, and extreme spatial heterogeneity in aquifer materials. In Colorado’s Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP), developing sustainable groundwater supply infrastructure for park operations requires precise characterization of subsurface stratigraphy to locate adequate water-bearing zones while avoiding non-productive crystalline bedrock and low-permeability glacial till.

This technical investigation presents an integrated geophysical and geospatial framework combining two-dimensional surface electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) surveying and modeling, surface spatial analysis, and observing in-situ subsurface samples collected via rotosonic drilling methods to identify buried water-bearing paleochannels and optimize water supply well location and design.

Subsurface resistivity profiles were acquired using multiple overlapping ERT survey lines across potential replacement well sites. The intersecting grid geometry enabled three-dimensional interpretation and extrapolation of subsurface features. By integrating these inverted resistivity models with satellite imagery, digital elevation models (DEMs), and existing well logs, we established a comprehensive spatial framework for paleochannel mapping. Pronounced electrical property contrasts among stratigraphic units enabled clear subsurface delineation. Spatial interpolation of the resistivity profiles defined the primary paleochannel axis, regional water bearing layers, and depth to high-resistivity bedrock. Furthermore, the models resolved the spatial distribution and thickness of alluvium, glacial till and low-resistivity clay layers.

Combining ERT subsurface imaging, landscape observations, and well logging allowed for real time adjustment of exploration borehole locations and the final siting and design of two new groundwater supply wells. Subsequent pumping tests confirmed adequate groundwater yield from the targeted coarse-grained surficial alluvium and paleochannel at predicted depths. This integrated methodology highlights the efficacy of coupling geophysics and field observations to inform groundwater supply development in complex hydrogeological settings.

abstract: Snow water equivalent (SWE) is widely used as the primary predictor in operational streamflow forecasts across snow-dominated basins, but the relationship between SWE and runoff varies considerably in space within a single watershed. Recent large-sample analyses have shown that targeting new snow measurements at spatially variable "hotspot" locations improves water supply predictions more than basin-wide snow mapping, yet the physical mechanisms driving hotspot locations remain largely unexplained by simple terrain attributes. We investigate this gap in the East River basin, Colorado, using a pixel-scale comparison of runoff efficiency (RE) against a SWE-only baseline forecast. This analysis identifies spatial hotspots where local RE deviates from basin-average behavior across a wide range of SWE values, indicating that factors beyond snow accumulation govern hotspot occurrence. To evaluate candidate mechanisms, we compare an independent-pixel bucket model representing purely local water balance controls against the spatially distributed Watershed ECOHydrology (WECOH) model incorporating topographically-driven lateral subsurface throughflow, forced with identical snow and evapotranspiration inputs. Results indicate that lateral connectivity contributes meaningfully to the spatial pattern of simulated runoff efficiency, while local storage and evapotranspiration heterogeneity also play a secondary role, consistent with multiple landscape controls jointly shaping runoff generation rather than a single dominant mechanism. This work moves beyond correlative identification of hotspot locations toward a process-based understanding of their controls, providing a foundation for evaluating whether these controls will remain consistent as snowmelt-dominated systems experience continued warming.

abstract: The rapidly growing demand for rare earth elements (REE), combined with economic and geopolitical developments surrounding these materials, has deepened interest in finding new and alternative supply sources. REE bearing waste materials containing carbonates and phosphates are a promising potential source of recoverable REE compounds. Among the mineral phases present in these ore compound, REEOHCO 3 kozoites are of particular interest because they occur as secondary hydroxycarbonates precipitated in small cavities in alkali environments under low temperature alteration conditions. However, kozoites are not well studied, especially with regards to their structural and thermodynamic properties. In studies, we present a comprehensive thermodynamic investigation of kozoites endmember structures across the lanthanide series and yttrium. Different calorimetric techniques are used to determine the enthalpies of formation, heat capacities and the absolute entropy to evaluate the thermodynamic stabilities. abstract: The Valles Caldera, at the western margin of the Rio Grande Rift in New Mexico, USA, erupted at 1.25 Ma through Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Jemez volcanic field. The caldera has been continuously modified since this eruption by rhyolite lava flows and dome emplacement, debris flow activity, lacustrine sedimentation from several intra-caldera lakes, and rivers that incised the landscape and deposited multiple generations of alluvial fans. Groundwater-fed wetlands called fens occur along San Antonio Creek in the northern caldera, where the Summer of Applied Geophysical Experience program has conducted geophysical investigations since 2019. In this area, ~8 Ma precaldera volcanic flows form a constriction that was breached by the creek, causing groundwater to rise to the surface and sustain fens upstream and within the constriction. Our 2026 investigation combined mini-vibroseis seismic, electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), and transient electromagnetic surveys (TEM) to define subsurface controls on two of these fens. Refracted seismic arrivals constrain the lateral extent and depth to the top of bedrock, and the geometry and physical properties link these refractors to nearby volcanic rock outcrops. Models derived from ERT and TEM data indicate pronounced resistivity variability throughout the site. High-resistivity zones at elevated topography correspond to coarse lacustrine gravels and unaltered dacite, while underlying low-resistivity layers are interpreted to be clay-rich, pervasively altered volcanic flows that are exposed locally. Dipping and subvertical contacts between low- and high-resistivity layers occur beside each fen, suggesting that a permeability contrast between altered and unaltered volcanic rock redirects groundwater to the surface. Similar resistivity offsets are imaged across a mapped fault and suggest that one or more unmapped faults juxtapose units of contrasting permeability at the studied fens and help localize fen development. By combining multiple geophysical methods and field observations, this study presents an integrated subsurface interpretation of volcanic groundwater barriers and fen hydrogeologic controls, while providing a transferable approach to wetland investigations in complex volcanic terrains worldwide.

abstract:
Lake Tanganyika is the oldest and deepest rift lake in Africa, the second largest lake by volume (18,880 km³), and the second deepest lake in the world (1,470 m). Formed approximately 10 million years ago, it is home to hundreds of endemic species, including cichlid fish, mollusks, and ostracods. Human activity on and around the lake threatens these species, particularly through deforestation-driven siltation, which can blanket nearshore habitats and damage these ecosystems. To better understand these impacts, we analyzed the taphonomy and abundance of ostracod valves from mollusk shell beds and adjacent habitats at four locations with varying levels of anthropogenic impact: one in the northern subbasin (Luiche-LT), one in the central subbasin (Mitumba-MT), and two in the southern subbasin (Utinta-UT and Nsumbu-NT).

Samples were collected along nearshore transects via SCUBA and ponar grab sampler, then sieved and analyzed for ostracod abundance, juvenile-to-adult ratio, species richness, valve breakage, and reduction/oxidation staining. Fisher's diversity index and principal component analysis revealed consistent contrasts among sites. First, UT and NT (southern subbasin) generally showed higher species richness and diversity than LU and MT, with diversity and richness peaking at shallow-to-moderate depths (10–20 m) and declining with depth. Second, MT had the highest percentage of shell beds (81.8%), while NT had the lowest (27.2%). Third, mollusk shell-bed presence correlated with higher organic matter and distinct ostracod species associations — for example, G. alata was associated with mollusk beds at the UT/NT sites, while G. coheni and G. downingi were associated with non-mollusk-bed settings.

Importantly, lower- and higher-impact sites differed regardless of shell-bed presence, indicating that anthropogenic activity affects species diversity and abundance independent of this habitat feature. Luiche had the highest amount of reduction staining, indicating burial in organic-rich sediment, as well as oxidation staining, indicating exposure on the lake floor. These correlate with Luiche’s greater amount of human activity. These results will be instrumental in examining and understanding newly acquired sediment cores from these four sites to address questions about climate-driven changes in Holocene lake level and can be used by stakeholders to better understand the impact of climate change to the watershed.

abstract: Discovered in October of 2018, the TTT group of anthills preserve a rich biota from the Lance Formation of the Late Cretaceous, including some previously unreported materials. The expected Lance Fm micro fauna was discovered at the sites. Some of the most common discoveries are recorded as Lepisostidae (gar fish) with an estimation of 6,906 partial to complete scales. Along with the more common finds the ant hills produced a diversity of dinosaurs and other non-dinosaur reptiles, amphibians, fish, and some potential fossil bird claws were also discovered. Some of the most notable discoveries include 402 egg shell fragments, of dinosaurs and possibly birds. Prior to this only one fragment of eggshell has been recorded from the Lance Fm of Wyoming. Also a total of 253 mammal teeth, jaws, and bones were discovered. Furthermore many invertebrates were collected including 906 snail operculum and four snails. Lastly a potential amphisbaenid premaxilla was found which could be the first Cretaceous specimen from this taxon. Based on the collected material from the TTT ant hills a total of about 12,480 fossils were identified to one of the faunal groups listed above.

title: Hydrogeological Modelling and Health Risk Assessment in Ganga-Yamuna Floodplain, Kaushambi, India
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part II)
authors: Kushawaha, Jyoti [1]
affiliations: (1) Ramanujan College, University of Delhi, New Delhi, Delhi, India; School of Environmental Sciences, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, Delhi, India
abstract: In Rural India, the primary source of water for consumption and cultivation is groundwater. However, water quality is now strained by heavy groundwater use, which may further degrade it. Poor groundwater quality threatens human health, especially when hazardous and toxic metals are dissolved in groundwater. The study has used the water quality index, along with other irrigation indices, to assess groundwater quality for all major ions. A total of 130 groundwater samples were collected over different months before and after the monsoon in 2021. All the samples were examined for physicochemical parameters, including electrical conductivity (EC), pH, Na + , K + , Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , F - , Cl - , HCO 3 - , NO 3 - , PO 4 3- , SO 4 2- , and dissolved silica. Among the major ions, 37% of the samples exceed the BIS permissible limit for F - . The remaining major ions are within the permissible limits set by BIS and WHO. The Piper plot suggests that Na- or K-type water is dominant in the cationic facies, and bicarbonate-type water in the anion facies. Based on the diamond plot, the Ca-Mg-HCO 3 facies is the dominant, followed by Na-HCO 3 -Cl and Na-HCO 3 in the study area. Silicate weathering is the dominant phenomenon controlling groundwater chemistry. Groundwater has been classified as excellent based on the WQI calculation. Whereas the irrigation indices show variation in irrigation water use. Groundwater samples have also been analyzed for Al, As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Fe, Mn, Mo, Ni, Se, and Zn. Approximately 52% of the samples were categorized as having a high Heavy metal pollution index value. All groundwater samples have a total hazard quotient above 1, indicating detrimental health effects for children and adults. The water quality index and health risk assessment provide an overall estimate of the impact of water quality on health and offer researchers and policymakers a better understanding for further studies and policymaking.

title: Reconstructing Seawater Carbonate Saturation Through Time
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)
authors: Wang, Jiuyuan [1], Yan, Xiaoyu [2]
affiliations: (1) Peking University, Beijing, Beijing, China
(2) Peking University, Beijing, Beijing, China
abstract: One of Brad Sageman’s enduring scientific contributions has been to illuminate the processes that regulate carbon burial and the feedbacks by which they shape Earth’s climate and ocean chemistry. Together with organic carbon burial, the formation and burial of marine carbonates constitute the other principal pathway by which carbon is transferred from the ocean-atmosphere system to the solid Earth. Central to this process is the carbonate saturation state, which governs the rate and magnitude of carbonate precipitation, and the evolution of the marine carbonate factory, thereby influencing marine biogeochemical cycling, atmospheric CO 2 , and climate. Yet despite its fundamental importance, the scarcity of empirical constraints on the magnitude and tempo of secular changes in carbonate saturation has led to divergent views of how seawater carbonate chemistry has evolved through Earth history. In this talk, using minimal widely accepted assumptions together with observational constraints, we present a new numerical framework for reconstructing secular variations in seawater carbonate saturation through geological time. Our results provide testable constraints on the evolution of seawater carbonate saturation, and offer a complementary perspective on the long-term co-evolution of carbon burial, Earth’s surface environment, and life.

title: Snowball, Hothouse, Repeat: Rethinking the Sturtian Glaciation
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records
authors: Minsky, Charlotte [1], Wordsworth, Robin [2], Johnston, David T. [3], Knoll, Andrew H. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Science and Engineering, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Department of Environmental Science and Engineering, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA; Department Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
(4) Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract:
Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth glaciations mark the most extreme climate transitions in Earth's history, yet basic questions about their initiation and duration remain unresolved. Why was the Neoproterozoic uniquely prone to Snowball events when the preceding billion years were not? What triggered the Sturtian glaciation? And why did it last roughly 56 million years, an order of magnitude longer than the Marinoan and far beyond what canonical Snowball or Slushball models can sustain?

The central result presented here resolves the duration question. Using a carbon-oxygen-phosphorus box model, we show that the Sturtian's 56-Myr duration reflects not one continuous glaciation but a "limit cycle" of repeated Snowball-hothouse transitions, driven by incomplete weathering of the Franklin Large Igneous Province. As long as reactive basalt remains after a deglaciation, weathering resumes through the following hothouse until another Snowball is triggered, repeating until the Franklin's weatherability is exhausted. Across a broad, geologically plausible parameter range, this mechanism reproduces the full 56-Myr duration, matches the alternating diamictite/non-diamictite pattern observed in Sturtian sections, and lets atmospheric oxygen persist throughout, since biology only has to survive short, 4-Myr Snowballs rather than one prolonged event.

This duration story sits alongside two related results: a mechanistic weathering model showing that Franklin emplacement was itself a plausible trigger for the Sturtian, and general circulation model simulations showing that increasing solar luminosity, more than paleogeography, made the Neoproterozoic background climate especially sensitive to triggers like this. Together, these results offer an account of why the Sturtian happened, why it lasted so much longer than the Marinoan, and how a complex biosphere survived 56 Myr of recurring glaciation.

title: When Ontogeny Meets Phylogeny: Insights from Silicified Lower Ordovician (upper Tremadocian; Tulean) Asaphid Trilobites from the Great Basin, Western USA
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Camus, Titouan [1], Adrain, Jonathan [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
abstract: The Family Asaphidae Burmeister, 1843, was the most diverse and geographically widespread trilobite group during the Ordovician, yet its phylogeny and early evolutionary history remain poorly understood. A major challenge in reconstructing asaphid relationships is the frequently effaced morphology of adults, which obscures characters critical for cladistic analyses. Because effacement tends to appear late during ontogeny, juvenile asaphids frequently express characters absent in mature specimens. Tulean (upper Tremadocian) deposits of the shallow-water northern Laurentian paleo-margin (present-day western North America) contain abundant asaphid material, most of which has historically been assigned to two species with ambiguous affinities: Asaphellus? quadrata Hintze, 1953, and Asaphellus? venta Hintze, 1953. This material, subsequently assigned to the genus Aulacoparia Hintze & Jaanusson, 1956, is revised here, based on new silicified material collected over the last three decades from western Utah and southeastern Idaho. High-resolution sampling has revealed previously unsuspected high diversity, including seven new species of Aulacoparia and ten new species of Aulacoparina Hintze & Jaanusson, 1956 , in addition to the two already established species. This material includes exquisitely preserved larvae, juveniles, and adults, allowing the description of the first complete ontogenetic sequence for an asaphid, and documenting the oldest specifically identified larval material for a representative of the family. Cladistic analyses incorporating ontogenetic characters recovered two main subclades within the Aulacoparia/Aulacoparina group, each associated with very distinct morphologies. One subclade is characterized by relatively large, weakly dorsally convex, strongly effaced holaspids. In this group, the smallest specimens are uneffaced, whereas larger juveniles display a morphology close to that of the adults. The second subclade comprises more strongly vaulted taxa that retain important relief in adults and possess well-developed coaptative structures used by the animal during enrolment. In this group, juveniles are essentially miniature versions of the adults, with little modification of the shape during the development. Our results illustrate for the first time different patterns of development in asaphids and highlight the central importance of ontogenetic data for resolving phylogenetic relationships in taxa exhibiting convergent adult morphologies.

abstract: The informally named ‘Graf Phosphorite’ at the base of the Upper Ordovician Elgin Member of the Maquoketa Formation in northeastern Iowa, and adjacent areas in Wisconsin and Illinois, is a highly prospective and undeveloped cratonic sedimentary phosphate deposit. These types of phosphate deposits form by nutrient rich deep-water upwelling and/or continental-sourced ravine discharge into a restricted epicontinental basin, enhanced marine productivity concentrating organic matter and phosphate-rich sediment, and distinct chemocline boundaries controlling phosphate preservation or mobilization. Some phosphate deposits (> 4% P 2 O 5 ) have elevated rare earth element (REE) concentrations, particularly heavy REEs (HREEs). The Graf Phosphorite, deposited during the late Katian, is anomalously thick (up to 60 feet) in the vicinity of Dubuque, Iowa and shows enrichment greater than 1,300 ppm total REEs with nearly 50% HREEs. However, lateral trends in REE concentrations and resource grade is poorly constrained. With funding from the USGS Earth Mapping Resource Initiative and the STATEMAP program, the Iowa Geological Survey has drilled 15 boreholes penetrating the Maquoketa Formation and uppermost Galena Group. Here we present a preliminary lithologic and geochemical evaluation of the Graf Phosphorite deposit in Dubuque and Jackson counties (Iowa). This work builds on years of multi-state collaborative regional and local characterization of Upper Ordovician strata in the U.S. Midcontinent. Lithologically, the Graf Phosphorite can be divided into a lower basal peloidal phosphorite with diminutive fauna and sculpted phosphate-impregnated hardgrounds, a middle organic-rich shale interlaminated with argillaceous dolostone, and an upper granular, dolomitic phosphorite interbedded with argillaceous dolostone, nautiloid packstones, and dolomitic shales. More than 4,000 pXRF spot analyses were collected to construct semi-quantitative geochemical profiles of each core. These data demonstrate that the middle shale unit pinches out such that the upper and lower phosphorite intervals merge and rapidly thin southeastward into the Illinois Basin. This lateral change could represent topographic relief on the underlying Galena Group carbonates to allow thicker accumulation of phosphatic material or the concentration and consolidation of phosphatic material via winnowing by storm and gravity currents into deeper water settings. Furthermore, these pXRF data were used to identify zones with elevated phosphate and yttrium (a tracer for HREEs) to select samples for more quantitative whole rock elemental composition and petrographic analyses via ICP-OES, ICP-MS, WDXRF, and SEM-EDS, respectively.

title: Arctic River Morphodynamics in a Changing Environment
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Kirpalani, Deven [1], Pehlert, Isabella [2], Guo, Xiwei [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA

abstract: Arctic rivers are increasingly attracting global attention as rapid changes in climate, ecosystems, and land cover reshape these high-latitude environments. Through the delivery of significant water, sediment, and nutrients, Arctic rivers both respond to and influence regional and global environmental change. However, their remote locations and the lack of sufficient gauge station constrain our ability to predict how rivers evolve under intensified permafrost thaw, extreme weather, and direct human modifications. To address this, this work characterizes the morphological characteristics and dynamics of major rivers in Alaska, the Canadian Arctic, and Siberia over multi-decadal timescales. Specifically, we processed sequential satellite imagery to quantify channel migration, bank erosion and accretion, and assess spatial variability of channel morphodynamics. We demonstrate that all rivers showed stable, dominant vegetated multi-channel patterns, with considerable width variability among individual channel threads. The observed channel change reflects two competing processes: increased permafrost thaw promotes bank erosion, while eroded sediments redeposit along downstream river sections, causing deposition and island formation and/or expansion. These rivers showed positive correlations between anabranching intensity and channel change, along with a relationship between anabranching intensity and channel stability. As remote-sensing missions such as SWOT continue to improve spatial coverage and data accuracy for hydrologic monitoring of Arctic rivers, our work provides a geomorphic foundation for data integration and systematic understanding of these high-latitude environments.

title: The Mineral Cup: Gamifying Mineralogy to Enhance Engagement and Communication
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Deuerling, Kelly [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography & Geology, University of Nebraska Omaha, Omaha, NE, USA
abstract:
Since Fall 2023, Mineralogy students at the University of Nebraska Omaha have participated in the Mineral Cup as a means of class engagement that focuses on creativity and science communication. There are two competitions each year: a functional mineral cup and an interesting mineral cup. Students are challenged to explore minerals and must choose distinct minerals on a first-come first-served basis. There can be no repeat minerals within a single competition and no repeat minerals from the previous two years. I provide a variety of source materials including mineralogy textbooks, vetted social media accounts, and mindat.org for students to explore to make their choices. The project is scaffolded into four phases: 1) mineral identification, 2) mineral research and justification of choices, 3) draft production and peer-review, and 4) final products. Project products include a playing card and persuasive speech for each mineral.

The playing card is essentially a character card a la Pokémon that includes mineral facts such as hardness, luster, fracture/cleavage, chemical formula, etc. (“Stats”), formation conditions (“Affinities”), weathering conditions (“Vulnerabilities”), and flavor text that reflects the justification of why the student chose the mineral. The picture on the card must include a depiction of the mineral on a background that reflects the formation environment.

The persuasive speech is the student’s chance to justify to the class why their mineral is the most functional and/or interesting. The timed speech must include basic information about the mineral including physical properties, formation environment, diagnostic features, and mineral associations. Students must incorporate their justification of mineral choice into the presentation and include three facts about the mineral.

The final week of class is reserved for the Mineral Cup competitions. I set randomized brackets and students compete in knockout rounds. Each round involves the students giving their speeches in front of the backdrop of their playing cards. Following both speeches, each student is allowed one additional minute to provide feedback based on their competitor’s speech. The class anonymously votes and the mineral that receives the greatest number of votes advances to the next round. Once victors are declared in both Cups, a final round of voting recognizes the overall winner. Past winners include trona (2023), sylvite (2024), and ice (2025).

title: Proto-Siletzia beneath the Columbia Basin, and creation of the Columbia Embayment
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: Humphreys, Eugene [1], Wells, Ray [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Portland State University, Portland, OR, USA
abstract:
Seismic imaging resolves sections of the flat Farallon slab that subducted beneath the Pacific Northwest prior to Siletzia’s accretion 50 Ma. Tomographically resolved fast lower crust is very prominent beneath the Columbia Basin, even at the scale of the western U.S. We suggest this crust is proto-Siletzia metagabbro and mafic granulite that subducted ~60 Ma, and the velocity step imaged with receiver functions at 35-40 km depth is where mafic granulite has transformed to garnet granulite and eclogite. This proposed history accounts for the ~5 km of Columbia Basin subsidence and sedimentation that began 60 Ma. In support of this model is the remarkably rapid 3-5 km of subsidence that occurred during Columbia River flood basalt ponding within the Columbia Basin 16 Ma, which we attribute to pressure-induced garnet formation at and below the Moho.

East of the Columbia Basin, receiver functions resolve the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary being ~20-km deeper in the area immediately east of the very fast lower crust. We interpret this as a remaining fragment of flat Farallon slab. To the north, east and south of this apparent flat slab, upper mantle tomography images what must be dangling curtains of delaminated Farallon slab. We associate the north and east curtains with 55-50 Ma delamination that drove asthenosphere upwelling and the Chalis-Kamloops ignimbrite flareup, and the southern curtain to delamination from eastern Oregon during the Columbia River flood basalt event.

The ~60 Ma subduction of proto-Siletzia was coincident with the northern escape of the Intermontane terrane away from the Blue Mts terrane. A ~12-km thick middle crust in the Columbia Basin is thought to be the extended and thinned Intermontane crust, upon which the Columbia Basin sediment fill rests. An orocline of Mesozoic accreted island arc terranes enclose Columbia Basin, which defines the Columbia Embayment. This encompassing orocline formed in stages, with the post-Siletzia rotation of the Pacific NW being the most recent and most significant.

abstract: Hyperarid soils are valuable archives of paleoclimate. To advance beyond the over-simplified linkages between hyperarid pedogensis and mean annual precipitation, we used six years of continuous temperature, moisture and relative humidity (RH) measurements down the profile of ~12 and 70 ka gypsic-salic Reg soils in the hyperarid (< 50 mm/yr) Negev Desert to demonstrate that continuous, dynamic interaction between hygroscopic salts and soil RH exert primary and previously overlooked controls on pedogenesis in such environments. Namely, we show that repeated cycles of salt dissolution through deliquescence and subsequent re-crystallization within confined gravel voids, both in response to fluctuations in atmospheric RH, are the main drivers of intense gravel cracking commonly observed in the top 50 cm of hyperarid Reg soils. Gypsic-salic Reg soils developed in the Atacama Desert under similar precipitation conditions (< 55 mm/yr), but with significantly drier atmospheric RH fluctuations, lack the diagnostic horizon of cracked gravel in their top decimeters because conditions are too dry to repeatedly drive deliquescence of salts in the soil. Thus, in addition to precipitation, paleo-climatic reconstructions from saline Reg soils in hyperarid landscapes may also inform the RH regime in the soil and in the atmosphere under which the soils developed.

abstract: Faunal interchange between Cretaceous Asia and North America has been proposed for several major dinosaur lineages based on close phylogenetic relationships between taxa from the two continents. Among these groups, Thescelosauridae is a small-to-medium sized neornithischian dinosaur lineage that has undergone substantial expansion in taxon sampling over the past decade, altering the understanding of its phylogenetic relationships. However, their biogeographic history has not been formally tested using these updated datasets. We performed a Bayesian tip-dated phylogenetic analyses derived from alternative recent morphological character matrices, and conducted an ancestral-range estimation in BioGeoBEARS under different time-stratified dispersal settings. The results were then compared against previously proposed dispersal intervals for other dinosaur lineages. Across alternative datasets, reconstructions consistently supported an Asian origin for Thescelosauridae, followed by an Asia-to-North America dispersal of Thescelosaurinae and Orodrominae, with Orodrominae showing an additional, more complex dispersal history. The inferred dispersal interval consistently fell around the mid-Aptian–mid-Albian across analyses. These results support repeated faunal interchange between Asia and North America during the Early Cretaceous, consistent with previously proposed patterns in other major dinosaur lineages, and place Thescelosauridae within this large-scale intercontinental exchange.

abstract:
The East African Rift System is a natural laboratory for evaluating carbon storage in tectonically active basins, yet rift-basin reservoirs remain largely absent from global CCS assessments. This study integrates 3D seismic reflection data, wireline logs from three exploration wells, and post-stack seismic inversion to assess the CO₂ storage potential of the Mid-Miocene syn-rift Kakara Formation in the Semliki Basin, western Uganda.

Petrophysical analysis identified thin but laterally persistent reservoir sandstones within a dominantly fine-grained succession, with moderate porosity and a low net-to-gross ratio. Model-based inversion, calibrated to well ties, produced a three-dimensional acoustic impedance volume, and a logarithmic impedance–porosity transform mapped the spatial porosity distribution across the reservoir.

Structural interpretation defined a fault-bounded anticlinal closure on the eastern basin margin. Volumetric estimation yields a P50 primary storage capacity of approximately 4.9 to 7.8 million tonnes of CO₂, with additional secondary capacity in the surrounding porous rock.

The Kakara Formation possesses the essential elements for CO₂ storage, though lateral facies heterogeneity, limited well control, and the active tectonic setting remain key uncertainties. The workflow provides a transferable approach for screening storage potential in frontier rift basins.

abstract: Comparison between Permian-Triassic terrestrial records of North China and eastern Kazakhstan plates provides clues on paleogeographic, tectonic, and paleoclimatic evolution during closure of Paleo-Asian Ocean (PAO). Three measured sections in 50 km 2 at northern Helan Mountains, northwesternmost Ordos Basin are 1225 m in total thickness. 269 high-order cycles (HCs) are defined by repetitive environmental changes and belong to four types: braided- and meandering-stream and lacustrine deltaic and limestone-bearing fluctuating-profundal. A low-order cycle (LC) contains similar HCs and reflects long-term environmental, climatic, and/or tectonic trends. Eight LCs are delineated, named after current, approximately correlative lithostratigraphic formations, and assigned to approximate ages based on preliminary LA-ICPMS dates. The lower-Cisuralian uppermost Shanxi LC contains deltaic HCs deposited under humid and tectonically stable conditions. The upper-Cisuralian Lower Shihezi LC contains meandering-stream HCs with common quartzite gravels, plant fossils, Argillisols, and Gleysols in the lower part, indicating source-sink reorganization under humid conditions. Overlying deltaic and volcanic deposits indicate overfilled lakes and active volcanism. The latter induced another episode of meandering-stream development followed by deltaic and volcanic deposition of lower-Guadalupian Upper Shihezi LC under humid-subhumid conditions. The lower-Lopingian Sunjiagou LC contains meandering stream HCs with fluctuating-profundal HCs in the upper part, indicating another episode of source-sink reorganization. Mature Calcisols and Vertisols suggest subhumid-semiarid conditions. The Lopingian-Induan Liujiagou LC contains thick “super” meandering-stream HCs, signifying renewed reorganization, providing additional metamorphic and volcanic sediments under similar climatic conditions. The Induan-Olenekian Heshanggou LC contains super meandering-stream HCs with significant reduction in grain size, thick overbank deposits, and stacked mature Calcisols, indicating enlargement and stabilization of drainage basin. Finally, the thick mid-Triassic Ermaying/Zhifang LC composed of conglomerate-rich braided-stream HCs signifies final reorganization. Five unconformities at the bases of Lower and Upper Shihezi, Sunjiagou, Liujiagou, and Ermaying LCs indicate major uplift and reorganization events, probably related to episodic closures of PAO in early and middle Permian and mid-Triassic. They are approximately correlative to events in Bogda Mountains of Junggar Basin in eastern Kazakhstan. The climatic transition from humid-subhumid to subhumid-semiarid conditions between Shihezi and Sunjiagou LCs in mid-late Permian, however, differs from the Bogda record showing semiarid conditions in early-middle Permian and Early Triassic but subhumid-humid in late Permian. Temporal and spatial variations in paleotopography and paleolatitude likely caused the differences.

abstract:
Understanding hydroclimate variability and monsoon dynamics in Southeast Asia across millennial scale events is essential for evaluating long-term Indo-Pacific climate variability. Here, we present five new multi-proxy uranium-series dated speleothem records from the Philippines. Our new records from Palawan (Puerto Princesa Subterranean River, Natuturingam Cave, stalagmite GG-1; ~68–96 ka BP, MIS 5b–4; and overlapping stalagmites GP-0, GP-1 and GP-3, ~4-48 ka BP, MIS 2-3) and Bohol (Hinagdanan Cave, stalagmite BH1; ~28–51 ka BP, MIS 3) reconstruct tropical hydroclimate dynamics and interrogate remote teleconnections across the Late Pleistocene. To decouple regional monsoon strength from local karst hydrology, all records include high-resolution oxygen and carbon stable isotopes and trace element ratios (Mg/Ca, Sr/Ca, and Ba/Ca), with co-variations among trace elements and carbon isotopes isolating epikarst prior calcite precipitation (PCP).

This work demonstrates millennial-scale hydroclimate shifts, connecting tropical Southeast Asia precipitation with high-latitude freshwater forcing (Heinrich Stadials; HS) during MIS 5b–4 (HS9 to HS7a) and MIS 3-2 (HS5 to HS1 and Younger Dryas). These abrupt dry episodes reflect southward displacements of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and variable suppression of the regional monsoon. In the interglacial Palawan GG-1 record, the expression and magnitude of these stadial droughts is mediated by background climate boundary conditions, including global ice volume, sea level, and insolation. In the overlapping GP-0, GP-1 and GP-3 records from Palawan we observe a mixed response to HS 5 to 1, likely due to regional drought from Sunda Shelf exposure, stalagmite growth hiatuses during the Last Glacial Maximum and a strong response during the Younger Dryas. In the Bohol BH-1 record, rapid oxygen isotope and trace element shifts occur during HS 3 and 4 but not HS 5. Taken together in the context of other records from the region, this suite of new records provides new constraints on abrupt teleconnection mechanisms in Southeast Asia.

abstract: Perennial paleolake deposits in the Western US indicate that the Pliocene Epoch (~5.3 to 2.58 Ma) was warmer and simultaneously wetter than today, presenting a paradox as climate model projections under elevated atmospheric CO2 predict subtropical drying. The PLIOWEST International Continental Scientific Drilling Program (ICDP) project targets Pliocene to present double-cored lacustrine sequences along a 6° latitudinal transect (~1,380 km) in western North America to resolve Pacific climate dynamics. PLIOWEST cores two lacustrine basins. The northern site at Butte Valley, CA (41°N) targets ~200 m of carbonate-bearing siliciclastic lacustrine sediments extending into the early- to mid-Pliocene strata. The southern site at Searles Lake, CA (35°N) targets a ~710 m carbonate mud and evaporite sequence covering the mid-Pliocene to Holocene. Key targets include the M2 glacial (~3.3 Ma), the mid-Pliocene Warm Period (3.3–3.0 Ma), the Pliocene-Pleistocene Transition (3.0–2.5 Ma), and Pleistocene super-interglacials. Our framework tests two hypotheses for subtropical wetting. Reduced zonal sea-surface temperature gradients driven by permanent El Niño-like conditions displace the subtropical jet equatorward to increase winter precipitation in southern mediterranean regions, affecting the southern site. Alternatively, reduced meridional sea-surface temperature gradients caused by polar-amplified warmth weaken the Hadley circulation, reducing subtropical moisture divergence and boosting seasonal monsoonal rainfall at both locations. Our team will use an integrated multiproxy approach including isotope geochemical, organic, and microfossil proxies, and tephrostratigraphic and paleomagnetic dating. PLIOWEST also incorporates climate modeling and hydrogeologic modeling, as well as parallel research on the deep biosphere and critical mineral resources such as lithium brine dynamics in closed-basin evaporite systems. The ICDP project has been recently approved and the team will share the lithostratigraphy of both lake basins, outline the project objectives, solicit feedback and invite further collaboration at the meeting.

title: A revised timeline for construction of the Appalachian-Ouachita orogen?
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part II)
authors: McKay, Matthew [1], Jackson, William Thomas [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA
(2) Tennessee Geological Survey, Memphis, TN,
abstract:
The Paleozoic Appalachian orogen has been historically broken into 3 stages of mountain building. (1) The Ordovician Taconic orogen and (2) Silurian-Devonian Acadian orogen were driven by a hybrid of Cordilleran-style accretion of microterranes and Andean-style subduction along the eastern U.S. (3) The Pennsylvanian-Permian Alleghanian orogen throughout the Appalachians and Mississippian-Pennsylvanian Ouachita orogen reflect Alpine-style collision of Gondwana and Laurentia during the closing of the Rheic Ocean and amalgamation of Pangea.

We present a revised timeline for the Acadian and Alleghanian orogens in the southeastern U.S. based on recent and historic geologic mapping, regional stratigraphy, available metamorphic P-T estimates, and geothermochronology from Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina. These integrated datasets suggest that there is no distinct break in tectonism between the Acadian and Alleghanian orogens in the southeast, and observations of two events reflect a transition between Andean-style orogenesis and Alpine-style mountain building. Deformation in the southeasternmost Valley and Ridge and Blue Ridge was well underway by the middle Devonian and was overprinted during the Pennsylvanian-Permian. We postulate that Devonian-Permian deformation was out-of-sequence and deformation may have been controlled by earlier phase fault reactivation, orogenic wedge development, preexisting basement structures, and regional transpression.

abstract:
Alkaline magmas become progressively enriched in both HFSE and REE through a range of magmatic and late hydrothermal processes. We explore the evolution of one unit portrayed as a single magma batch in the Larvik Plutonic Complex (LPC) of the Permian Oslo Rift, Norway, using trace elements in diopside, a mineral stable in all lithologies. The LPC was emplaced between 299 and 288 Ma (Mansur et al., 2025; NGJ 105; Ramo et al., 2022; J. Pet. 63) as part of the Oslo rift and behaved mostly as a closed system (Buelens et al., 2024; Lithos 484-485). The LPC is composed of ten intrusive semi-circular imbricated units, identified based on the presence of “chilled” margins associated with depressions in the topography (Petersen, 1978; Geo. Rund. 67). The units are younger toward the northwest and vary from silica-saturated to nepheline-bearing silica-undersaturated.

Unit 9, focus of this study, ranges from a medium-grained nepheline-bearing olivine diopside magnetite monzodiorite with poikilitic hornblende in the north to a coarse-grained nepheline olivine diopside biotite magnetite ilmenite syenite in the south, where nepheline reaches 30 normative percent. The transition between the two units is gradational and marked by the arrival of large rhomb-shaped alkali feldspar phenocrysts, making the texture porphyritic. Several 1-2 m wide sub-vertical corridors where feldspar phenocrysts are oriented parallel to the contact cut the isotropic coarse-grained nepheline monzonite. A contact zone, at the border with unit 8, is composed a 10-30 m-wide zone where comb layering texture, perpendicular to the contact, alternates with fine-grained apatite-rich olivine monzodiorite with late poikilitic diopside containing networks of 2-4 cm euhedral rhomb-shaped alkali feldspar and nepheline, locally bounded by a 3 to 20 cm-large nephelinite layer.

Zirconium, Nb, REE, Mn and Zn concentrations increase in diopside from nepheline monzodiorite to the nepheline syenite, whereas Sr, P, Ti decrease, consistent with a system dominated by fractionation of olivine, diopside, apatite, magnetite, alkali feldspar and feldspathoids. Interstitial zircon attests to its late stabilization in the melt. Diopside from corridors shows wide chemical variations, which indicates that both differentiated mush and more primitive mush moved through these structures. This study illustrates the processes behind the enrichment of alkaline magmas in HFSE and REE through fractional crystallization.

title: Evaluating Agentic AI for Reproducible Shale Gas Analytics: Independent Workflow Reconstruction with VibeResearch and Claude Code
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Xiao, Yitian [1], Zeng, Lijuan [2], Ying, Zhiwen [3], Zhang, Gege [4]
affiliations: (1) DeepTime Digital Earth Zhejiang International Research Center, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China
(2) Zhejiang Lab, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China

abstract: Reproducing a published computational study provides a stringent test of agentic AI because success requires more than code generation: the system must interpret a scientific workflow, select compatible data, implement multiple algorithms, evaluate uncertainty, and explain geological differences. We evaluated two tool-using AI research environments—VibeResearch, developed by Zhejiang Lab, and Claude Code from Anthropic—by independently reproducing a hybrid shale-gas production analysis originally developed for the Fuling field, China. The target workflow combines random forest, gradient-boosted decision trees, XGBoost, fivefold stacking with a Ridge meta-learner, Tree-SHAP feature attribution, individual conditional expectation analysis, and particle swarm, differential evolution, and Bayesian optimization. Because the original industrial dataset was unavailable, both systems used the same public dataset of 506 North American shale-gas wells. Each independently generated a full analytical pipeline and completed all eight major methodological components. On a common single train-test split, Claude Code achieved a test R² of 0.9122 for the stacked model, whereas VibeResearch achieved 0.9006; the VibeResearch gradient-boosted model reached 0.9202. Differences among corresponding models were below 0.02. Repeated-split results converged further: stacked-model R² was 0.864 ± 0.064 for Claude Code (30 runs across all models) and 0.870 ± 0.055 for VibeResearch (100 runs for the stacked model). Both systems identified proppant loading and lateral length as the dominant controls in the North American data and independently reproduced the optimizer ranking differential evolution ≥ particle swarm optimization > Bayesian optimization, also observed in the original Fuling study. In contrast, the original Fuling analysis was dominated by geological variables, demonstrating that the workflow adapted to regional data rather than mechanically reproducing prior rankings. VibeResearch additionally generated narrative interpretation reports, whereas Claude Code produced more modular and reusable code. These results show that agentic research environments can reconstruct complex, end-to-end geoscience machine-learning workflows with comparable predictive performance and methodological completeness. Expert oversight nevertheless remains essential for dataset comparability, statistical design, geological interpretation, and code-quality assessment.

title: Update on Diagnostic Criteria used to Confirm Terrestrial Impact Structures
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Koeberl, Christian [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria
abstract:
Confirming meteorite impact origin for a terrestrial structure remains challenging, despite ~70 years of research (e.g., [1]). Part of the problem is that, in contrast to other planetary on Earth impact structures are rapidly eroded or covered up due to terrestrial geological processes. Also, in there was often controversy due to inconsistent application of diagnostic criteria, and lack of oversight by any official organization. To provide guidance on this issue, the Impact Cratering Committee (ICC) of the Meteoritical Society was established in 2020 and started work in 2023. The ICC has a mandate to (1) maintain and update a database of confirmed terrestrial meteorite impact structures, (2) define and update criteria used for identification of impact structures and related deposits, and (3) evaluate new submissions for approval and inclusion in the ICC database - in analogy to the Meteorite Nomenclature Committee (also led by the Meteoritical Society), which evaluates and confirms new meteorites. Before establishing a list of “approved” craters, the ICC evaluated all impact-diagnostic criteria. The ICC currently recognizes three categories of unambiguous impact-diagnostic evidence: (1) Shock metamorphic features within rocks or minerals that on Earth have only been reported to occur in impactites, and whose formation conditions (high pressure-temperature) have been demonstrated through experiments to only form at conditions created during hypervelocity impacts; (2) Meteorites that are spatially and chronologically associated with a site suspected of being an impact structure; and (3) Geochemical elemental or isotopic detection of an extraterrestrial signature in melt rocks or breccias associated with a site suspected of being an impact structure. Other mineral and rock features have been reported from impact structures that are important to document, but they do not represent irrefutable or unambiguous evidence of impact. These criteria, and information on how to apply and document them, have just been published [2] and thus the next step, establishing a “confirmed crater list” is being tackled, and first work shows that some craters that are currently held to be of impact origin will need additional studies and data.

[1] French B. M. and Koeberl C. (2010) Earth-Science Reviews 98, 123-170.

[2] Cavosie A.J. et al. (2026) Meteoritics & Planetary Science 61, 1538–1565, doi.org/10.1111/maps.70163.

title: Alleged Recent Impact Events: From the Ice-Ages to the Biblical Flood, Satan and Nostradamus
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Koeberl, Christian [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria
abstract:
Evaluating and confirming if a terrestrial geological structure has a meteorite impact origin is a challenging task that requires the detection and documentation of unambiguous impact-diagnostic evidence, as described in the geological literature for decades and summarized in a recent consensus report [1]. This has, however, not prevented publication of some more outlandish (and not scientifically confirmed) ideas about some past (relatively recent) alleged impact events. A recent peculiar example is the reinterpretation of Dante’s Inferno in which Satan rashes into Earth and forms “a massive, circular, terraced crater that reaches to the center of the earth” [2]; no geological evidence (or logic) is involved. For some time there have been claims that 12.9 thousand years ago an impact, or a series of impacts, caused cataclysm and climate change at the Younger Dryas. As discussed in several critical assessments, there is no clear evidence for any of this, and “criteria” are used by proponents in an ad-hoc way. As an aside, there have been publications that there is a huge crater structure called Hiawatha underneath the Greenland ice sheet, supposedly of Younger Dryas age; this was not confirmed. Maybe less well known is that some decades ago, it was proposed [3] that Noah's flood was caused by series of comet impacts about 10,000 years ago in the process also destroying a hypothetical Atlantis civilization. (The main proponent, a professor of geology at the university in Vienna, was also active as a regional politician of the Green Party, and later embraced esoteric topics, predicting a global catastrophe for the year 2000, based on Nostradamus prophecies, and when the world did not end at the time and he was asked if he made a mistake, he responded that not he, but Nostradamus was wrong!). Needless to say, there is no evidence at all for such “flood impacts” and that hypothesis was immediately and thoroughly rejected by the geological community [4]. This shows there is not, and has not been, a shortage of strange unverified “impact ideas”.

title: When carbonate archives misbehave: Formation and paleoclimatic limitations of fluvial oncoids in a Jamaican tufa system
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Husinec, Antun [1], Bowman, Audrey L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Saint Lawrence University, Canton, NY, USA
(2) Geology, Saint Lawrence University, Canton, New York, USA
abstract: Fluvial oncoids have been interpreted as archives of past environmental and climatic conditions, yet the processes controlling their growth, preservation, and geochemical signatures may produce complex and potentially misleading records. This study examines modern oncoids from Dunn’s River near Ocho Rios, Jamaica, a high-energy tufa-depositing system characterized by cascading waterfalls and stepped pools developed over Miocene and Pleistocene limestones. Oncoid-bearing sediment was collected from seven shallow pools below the falls. Grain size, morphology, and internal structure were characterized using granulometric and petrographic methods, and selected laminae were microdrilled for radiocarbon dating, stable-isotope analysis, and X-ray diffraction. The sand- to pebble-sized oncoids are spherical, ellipsoidal, or irregular, with external morphology partly controlled by the shape of their nuclei. Most nuclei consist of low-Mg calcite, although chert and other non-carbonate rock fragments also occur. Internally, the oncoids display alternating light and dark carbonate lamina sets arranged around the nucleus. Individual laminae are commonly discontinuous, poorly defined, and highly variable in thickness. Irregular grain shapes, truncated laminae, and the limited number of preserved lamina sets in some specimens indicate repeated abrasion and reworking within shallow, high-energy pools rather than uninterrupted concentric growth. Stable-carbon-isotope values (mean −9.97‰ VPDB) indicate a strong contribution from soil-derived CO₂. Conventional radiocarbon ages range from 3,095 to 3,225 BP despite the modern depositional setting, and outer lamina sets are 55–80 radiocarbon years older than corresponding inner sets. These anomalously old ages likely reflect incorporation of carbon derived from older tufa deposits, producing a freshwater reservoir effect. The results show that fluvial oncoids record alternating episodes of carbonate accretion, abrasion, and reworking rather than uninterrupted growth. Their discontinuous internal architecture and inherited radiocarbon signatures demonstrate how carbonate archives may “misbehave,” limiting their reliability as straightforward chronological or paleoclimatic records.

abstract: Managing science training programs for students, such as internships, REUs, and in-classroom undergraduate experiences, requires a challenging blend of administration, mentorship, and pedagogical expertise. To support program leaders, the Earth System Science (ESS) Faculty Community at the U.S. National Science Foundation National Center for Atmospheric Research provides a space for these professionals to cultivate connections, engage in creative problem solving, and share resources. The ESS Faculty Community was developed through an iterative design, evaluating and utilizing participants’ feedback regarding program challenges, and offering scalable insights for building sustainable early career learning programs in STEM education. This community consists of two main approaches combining a new digital platform along with regular virtual programming. During the community’s kick-off meeting, participants identified a critical need for structured peer support and collective troubleshooting. To address this, the community offers biweekly, advisor-led informal drop-in hours for immediate peer consultation, and monthly formal meetings featuring subject matter experts and community-building periods. Complementing these active virtual events, the digital platform provides networking spaces and a curated repository of programmatic resources. In this presentation, we will share upcoming activities and ways to engage with the ESS Faculty community.

abstract:
Since our collaboration began in 2008—building from the pioneering synergy between Bill Cobban and John Obradovich—advances in 40 Ar/ 39 Ar and U-Pb geochronology, astrochronology, biostratigraphy, and chemostratigraphy have transformed understanding of the chronology and paleoceanographic evolution of the Cretaceous Period. Our overarching aim has been to reduce temporal uncertainty sufficiently to resolve the sequence and rates of Earth-system processes during the Cretaceous. Beginning with the first direct intercalibration of radioisotopic and astronomical time scales across the Cenomanian-Turonian boundary in the Western Interior Basin, this research established a chronologic framework that integrated independent geochronometers while substantially reducing uncertainties in numerical ages. Subsequent expansion of this framework through the Turonian-Campanian interval refined the ages of Cretaceous stage boundaries and demonstrated that integrated radioisotopic, astrochronologic, and biostratigraphic approaches provide the most robust calibration of the geologic time scale. These advances also resolved longstanding discrepancies between 40 Ar/ 39 Ar and U-Pb chronometers through astronomical calibration of the Fish Canyon sanidine standard.

The resulting temporal framework enabled quantitative investigation of Cretaceous Earth-system processes. High-resolution chronostratigraphy and chemostratigraphy constrained the timing and duration of Oceanic Anoxic Event 2, demonstrated near-continuity of Western Interior Basin reference sections, and established the temporal relationships among volcanic activity, osmium- and carbon-isotope excursions, and environmental change. Extension of high-precision geochronology into the Albian-Cenomanian interval refined correlations among North American, European, and northwest Pacific successions in Japan, culminating in an updated synthesis of the Western Interior Basin and global timescales. Most recently, integrated U-Pb, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, carbon-isotope, and osmium-isotope records from Hokkaido, Japan, have provided new constraints on the age of the Albian-Cenomanian boundary and the timing of Oceanic Anoxic Events 1a and 1d, strengthening evidence that large igneous province volcanism exerted a primary influence on multiple Cretaceous carbon-cycle perturbations. Ongoing efforts are expanding this approach to Valanginian through Barremian strata in Japan.

Together, these studies illustrate how progressively improving temporal resolution has shifted Cretaceous research from establishing numerical ages to quantifying the rates, durations, and causal relationships of major paleoceanographic events. The resulting chronostratigraphic framework now provides a foundation for global correlation and for testing hypotheses linking large igneous province volcanism, carbon-cycle perturbations, oceanic anoxia, and biotic change during one of Earth's most dynamic greenhouse intervals.

title: Pleistocene-Holocene Sediment Transport from the Southern Alps to the Deep-Water Taranaki Basin, Aotearoa New Zealand

abstract:
Rapid exhumation of the Southern Alps of New Zealand over the past ~4-6 Myr has resulted in large quantities of sediment entering the Tasman Sea, with more than 70 Mt/yr of suspended sediment estimated for modern rivers. Although much of this sediment is likely diverted into large submarine canyons that incise the western continental shelf of the South Island, it is unclear to what extent Southern Alps-derived sediment is responsible for rapid outgrowth of the continental shelf farther north in the Taranaki Basin over the last ~5 Myr. Mapping of seismic reflection datasets has revealed repeated occurrence of large (i.e., up to ~4000 km 3 ) submarine landslides. Establishing a link between mountain building and growth of the shelf, if there is one, would provide important context for understanding the origin of these submarine landslides, which could produce damaging tsunamis if they occurred today.

We compare new analyses of nine river and beach sand samples with 10 core and dredge samples to infer the provenance of sediment deposited within the Taranaki Basin over the last ~60 kyr. Modal point counts of the sand-sized fraction reveal that Taranaki Basin samples show a strong resemblance to northern South Island beach sediment but are less enriched in lithics relative to sand from the central North Island and western South Island. Volcanic glass shards and pumice were found in several of the core samples, indicating that the basin received input of volcanic tephra. Heavy mineral assemblages in the Taranaki Basin samples are similar to the Farewell Spit of the northern South Island, including abundant garnet, epidote, blue-green hornblende, and titanite, while also having clinopyroxene and hypersthene. We interpret mixture modeling of detrital zircon U-Pb data in combination with (U-Th)/He cooling ages to indicate that a large majority (66-86%) of Taranaki Basin zircon were derived from recently exhumed rocks along the Alpine Fault in the central South Island. Taken together, these data suggest that the latest Pleistocene–Holocene Taranaki Basin was dominantly strike-fed, with sediment transported northwards along the coastline from at least 700 km to the south. These results suggest that sediment supplied from regions of high exhumation in the central Southern Alps may have played an important role in outgrowth and episodic failure of the Taranaki shelf.

title: Boron Isotope Ratio Analysis of Aqueous Samples by Laser Ablation MC-ICP-MS of Evaporites
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales (Posters)
authors: Rutherford, Danny [1], Pribil, Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Aqueous stable boron (B) isotope ratios (δ 11 B) are typically measured by thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS) or multiple collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (MC-ICP-MS). In both cases, separating B from sample matrices using column chromatography is frequently required. In the case of MC-ICP-MS, sample introduction techniques often require hydrofluoric acid, stabilizing agents, and long washout times between samples. A laser ablation MC-ICP-MS method for δ 11 B analysis of aqueous samples has been documented in the literature with excellent results. However, replicate analysis requires loading multiple sample volumes, limiting the space within the laser’s sample housing for different samples and increasing the frequency of lengthy laser prep procedures. Additionally, the method requires parafilm ablation, posing potential challenges in sample contamination and signal identification.

In this work, an alternative method was developed for δ 11 B determination of aqueous samples by laser ablation MC-ICP-MS that utilizes multiple ablations of sample evaporites. In summary, sample evaporites were prepared by evaporating sample volumes at ambient temperature, dissolving in minimal water, aliquoting to tracks machined into epoxy pucks, and evaporating in a laminar flow hood. Further improvements were achieved by reducing aliquot volumes and shielding aliquots from air turbulence while evaporating.

The method was applied to a set of 75 water samples associated with coal-fired power plant products, resulting in δ 11 B values ranging from -17.5‰ to 38.1‰ with uncertainty from 0.01‰ to 3.48‰ (1SD) and an average standard deviation of 0.75‰. A subset of 12 samples were previously analyzed by TIMS and results from the evaporite laser ablation method were in agreement with the TIMS data.

Detailed evaluation of method development challenges, including evaporite containment and δ 11 B variation across evaporite surfaces, will be presented along with consideration for application to other laser ablation amenable isotope systems (i.e., Pb, S, Sr, etc.).

authors: Carlton, Kenz M [1], Tikoff, Basil [2], Bauer, Annie [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA
(2) StraboSpot Data System, ; Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA

abstract:
The Huron Mountains of the Upper Peninsula, Michigan, are part of an Archean granite-greenstone terrane (Northern Complex). The Huron Mountains are separated from Archean outcrops of the Canadian shield in Canada by the 1.1 Ga Mid-continental rift. To the south of the Huron Mountains is the Marquette district.

Recent field mapping documents an amphibolite basement intruded by compositionally variable granitoids. Thin section analysis of two plutons indicates variable fabrics and compositions, usually ranging from tonalite to quartz-rich monzogranite. The basement is an amphibolite-rich banded schist that may represent a strongly metamorphosed mafic protolith. A pervasive regional fabric generally displays a northwest strike and northeast dip, although foliation is variable even within a single outcrop. The contacts between the schist and intruding granitoid plutons vary in expression over relatively short distances and, in some cases, can be traced from a planar contact into a 50+ m wide transition zone. Traceable exposures of the schist-pluton contacts are parallel or subparallel to foliation. Additional structures found in outcrop include meso- to micro-scale faults and meso-scale to map-scale shear zones.

Whole-rock major- and trace-element geochemistry indicates that all granitoids have SiO 2 >70%, LREE enrichment, and very low HREE values. The main pluton bodies range from calcic to calc-alkalic, and a smaller, separated body is alkalic. In thin section, the granitoids show microstructures consistent with solid-state deformation, including internal grain deformation, cuspate-lobate grain boundaries, and myrmekite. The amphibolite schist groundmass is tholeiitic with trace-element ratios suggesting ocean island arc or mid-ocean ridge origin. We interpret that the granitoids were emplaced into an oceanic-sourced metamorphosed mafic basement during regional deformation.

title: Icehouse Conditions Significantly Predated The End-Ordovician Mass Extinction

abstract: The severe end-Ordovician glaciation likely played a major role in the end-Ordovician mass extinction. An open question is the extent to which icehouse conditions preceded this glaciation. Here, we document the latitudinal temperature gradients using carbonate oxygen-isotope paleothermometers (3,405 well-screened proxy values) to constrain the equatorial temperatures and steepness of the gradients through the Ordovician. We show that temperatures crossed the threshold to icehouse conditions ~13 Myr before the end-Ordovician extinction (~Darriwilian-Sandbian boundary) with a temperature gradient similar to the Last Glacial Maximum. We find even colder temperatures and a steeper LTG at the end of the Ordovician. The Ordovician, with a transition from extreme hothouse conditions to severe glaciation, likely driven by tectonics-driven pCO 2 drawdown, coupled with biodiversity changes, provides an ideal time interval for examining the relationship between environmental change and biodiversity.

title: Quantitative metamorphic petrology and monazite and xenotime petrochronology constraints on the Grampian terrane, Scotland, with implications for the evolution of the Great Glen Fault
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Morse, Sarah [1], Thigpen, Ryan [2], Mako, Calvin Andrew [3], Law, Richard D. [4], Moecher, David P. [5], Cavellier, Jillian [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA

abstract:
The Northern Highlands (NHT) and Grampian (GT) terranes, Scotland, separated by the sinistral Great Glen Fault (GGF), record a polymetamorphic history that culminated in the Paleozoic Caledonian orogeny, which has traditionally been subdivided into the Grampian (Ordovician) and Scandian (Silurian-Devonian) phases. However, focused work over the past two decades has demonstrated that the tectono-metamorphic evolution of these terranes may be more complex. Recent monazite (Mnz) and xenotime (Xtm) petrochronology studies in the southern NHT have identified a protracted high temperature (680-640°C) metamorphic event spanning ~465-435 Ma and peaking at ~450 Ma, albeit with at least two phases of continued prograde garnet growth occurring post-450 Ma. However, similar geochronology studies in the GT have remained scarce. Here, we present new quantitative metamorphic analyses integrated with Mnz and Xtm laser ablation split-stream petrochronology from the GT.

Throughout the GT, the dominant foliation varies between N-S to NE-SW, with lineations trending down dip. In the eastern GT, the traditional Grampian event is recorded in monazite U-Pb dates that yield a weighted mean age of 467±4 Ma. In the central GT, monazite yields a younger weighted mean age of 446±1 Ma, and Mnz-Xtm thermometry indicates an increasing temperature trend, from 519±25°C at 455±10 Ma to 670±25°C at 437±10 Ma. Mnz that yields an age of ~440 Ma has long axes aligned with inclined mica shear bands that indicate top-to-the-SSE displacement. Further west, Xtm U-Pb dates range from 468-393 Ma, with weighted mean ages of 453±3 Ma and 438±2 Ma for grain cores and rims, respectively. Xtm rims have long axes aligned with the top-to-the-NW foliation and yield dates of 444-437 Ma. Proximal to the GGF in the western GT, Mnz yields a weighted mean age of 445±2, and Mnz-Xtm thermometry exhibits a decreasing temperature trend, from 673±25°C at 455±11 Ma to 438±25°C at 436±10 Ma. These results indicate a younger 455-430 Ma deformation and metamorphism event in the western GT that is consistent with studies across the GGF in the southern NHT, including the timing of high-T Mnz growth at c. 450 Ma. This population is not recorded in the eastern GT samples, indicating that the NE-SW oriented transpressional shear zones, including the GGF, may have contributed to the c. 440 Ma deformation and metamorphism in the western GT.
