title: The Obstacles Behind Compiling a Critical Repository of Volcano Activity Reports for the Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation (Posters)
authors: Bertha, Kaila Rose [1], Bennis, Kadie [2]
affiliations: (1) Global Volcanism Program, Smithsonian Institution, Falls Church, VA, USA

abstract: The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program (GVP) has been accumulating, archiving, and summarizing information about global volcanic activity for scientists and the public since 1968. One of GVP’s products, the Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network (BGVN), is a comprehensive narrative covering 4-6 months of activity. This project focuses on volcano activity data collection and archival from official volcano observatory websites in order to maintain the primary source data and add events to the eruption chronology. Original activity reports were organized in File Explorer, and other report formats were copied and pasted into Microsoft Word documents to maintain authenticity. Notable data include alert level changes, ash plume heights, pyroclastic flows, lahars, lava flows, and sulfur dioxide flux. Each volcano presents its own challenges when collecting data, with unique hazard events (e.g. seismic tremor, pyroclastic flows, lava flows, etc.), and different primary sources that vary in accessibility. More specifically, plumes may not be defined, images are not always captioned or contain a scale, the time zone is not defined, and current activity can be mixed with forecasted reports. Despite the challenges associated with inconsistent reporting methods, data preservation hosted from a single resource is valuable when accurately informing the public about global volcanic activity and maintaining a complete eruption history archive.

abstract: Recent studies with orbital and rover-based investigations have detected the presence of carbonate minerals in a variety of locations and geologic settings across the surface of Mars. A set of outcrops of great geologic interest in the Noachian-aged terrains of Mars are the weathering profiles or “clay stratigraphies” where Fe/Mg smectites are overlain by Al phyllosilicate minerals. Until recently, there has been no definitive detection of carbonates in association with these outcrops. The finding of siderite on the slopes of Mt. Sharp in Gale crater by the Curiosity rover, where there has been no evidence of its presence from orbital spectroscopy data suggests that spectral absorptions of carbonates near 2.3 and 2.5 microns could be masked by other phases with stronger absorptions. Bultel et al. (2019) made use of the 3 to 4 micron region in CRISM data to map out the stronger carbonate absorption near 4 microns. Those authors reported on the suspected presence of carbonates in the Mawrth Vallis region and also in the Eridania Basin and in NE Noachis Terra. Without observing additional confirming spectral features, these detections can be viewed as tentative. However, through the use of feature analysis/target transformation (FA/TT) technique, used to good effect with CRISM data by Thomas et al (2017) and Amador et al (2018) subpixel exposures of carbonates can be found with higher confidence. Here we report on the presence of carbonates, nominally siderite, in between the Fe-Mg smectite and upper Al phyllosilicate layers in Mawrth Vallis and other clay stratigraphies where carbonates occur in association with Fe-Mg smectite and Al phyllosilicate minerals. Their presence is strongly indicated by strong FA/TT matches as well as by spectral shape in the 3 to 4 micron region. We are using the presence of carbonates in the middle of these clay stratigraphies to try to distinguish between origin scenarios for the stratigraphies, notably whether they represent ancient paleosol sequences or whether they result from lacustrine deposition or groundwater diagenesis.

title: Provenance and Maximum Depositional Age of the Nueva Segovia Schist of the Chortis block in Nicaragua: Implications for Orogenic Gold Potential in Central America
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits.
authors: Cuti-Guillen, Benjamin Leonel [1], Frieman, Ben M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
abstract: The largest continental block of the Caribbean plate, the Chortis block, is thought to have originated as part of the Gondwana supercontinent. However, its position during and after supercontinent breakup is poorly constrained. In northwestern Nicaragua, the Nueva Segovia schist (NSS) is the primary supracrustal succession that hosts widespread orogenic gold mineralization, which is inferred to have formed during mid-Cretaceous tectonic activity. Due to structural complexity and a paucity of isotopic dating, the relative age of this succession is unknown. Thus, stratigraphic correlations and interpretation of tectonic configurations in the Jurassic-Cretaceous that culminated in gold mineralization remain enigmatic. To address these knowledge gaps, U-Pb isotopic dating of detrital zircon by LA-ICP-MS was conducted on five representative samples of the NSS, the host for the San Albino orogenic gold deposit. A total of 273 concordant analyses provide robust statistical constraints on the provenance and maximum depositional age of the NSS. Based on the 16 youngest concordant analyses, a maximum depositional age of 182.2 ± 1.2 Ma was calculated by the Maximum Likelihood Age method. This indicates that the NSS is at least Toarcian (late Early Jurassic) in age, and is correlative to the Agua Fria formation, which occurs as a lesser deformed sedimentary and volcanic sequence in the Central Highlands of Honduras. Four dominant age groups at approximately 1200–1000 Ma, 470 Ma, 260 Ma, and 190 Ma comprise the U-Pb zircon results. Monte Carlo mixing of the intrasample patterns provides a composite signature for the NSS, which is used to compare with Triassic-Jurassic and Cretaceous sequences in proximal terranes. Statistical analyses, including correlation matrices, multidimensional scaling, non-negative factorization, and unmixing models, were utilized to compare detrital zircon patterns of the temporal groups from nine associated geographic domains. The statistical analysis indicates a shared tectonic evolution among the Chortis block and terranes comprising central to southwestern Mexico, the southern Maya Block, the Gulf Coast, and northwestern Colombia. This suggests that, in the Early Jurassic, the Chortis block records deposition in an extensional setting prior to terminal amalgamations that resulted in orogenic gold mineralization. Given this correlation, it is suggested that prospective Mesozoic orogenic belts locally occur throughout central to southern Mexico, Central America, and northwestern South America, which were fragmented during more recent Tertiary tectonic activity.

title: Topographic and Zoogeographic Evidence for River Network Reorganization Within the Southern Appalachian Mountains
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Farmer, Anna M. [1], Johnson, Bradley G. [2], Stokes, Maya F. [3], Culley, Alexis V. [4]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Studies, Davidson College, Davidson, North Carolina, USA

abstract: Drainage divides that separate fluvial systems in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina are dynamic because of differences in potential energy across the Blue Ridge Escarpment. Atlantic-draining rivers are steeper and erode faster than neighboring rivers that drain towards the continental interior leading to drainage reorganization across a variety of mechanisms. These changes may influence the distribution of aquatic organisms; when geographic connectivity of fluvial ecosystems is lost due to drainage reorganization, previously connected species become isolated. Gene flow is inhibited, and populations may experience genetic divergence and eventual speciation. At the same time, drainage reorganization can connect previous isolated populations. This is apparent in the Blue Ridge where there are a variety of sites where freshwater fishes and crayfishes exhibit disjunct geographic distributions and genetic connectivity across drainage divides. Yet, our understanding of historic interactions between river networks, and therefore connection points for aquatic populations, across basins remains relatively unknown. Here, we evaluate an assortment of possible paleo fluvial connections across drainage divides and between major river basins along the margins of the Linville, Green and Toxaway rivers systems with the goal of better understanding previous drainage patterns and possible historic connections between drainages. Specifically, we interrogate topographic evidence for possible stream captures and drainage reversals in areas where aquatic organisms exhibit disjunct distributions and evidence of cross-divide gene flow. To do this, we use χ and long-profile analyses, and document drainage divide asymmetry, evidence of capture elbows, and qualitative topographic observations to evaluate the likelihood of historic connections that may explain the observed genetic connectivity across drainage divides. These findings improve our understanding of how drainage reorganization influences the evolution and distribution of aquatic organisms, and more broadly, how escarpments retreat over time.

title: From micron- to mountain-scales: Advances in (U-Th)/He and U/Pb chronology unlock geological problems
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling
authors: Flowers, Rebecca M [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
abstract:
(U-Th)/He and U/Pb chronologic methods are under continuous development. Recent advances enable dating of previously undateable minerals, provide improved spatial resolution, and enhance data throughput and the affordability of the techniques. These improvements offer increasing opportunity to tightly couple (U-Th)/He and U/Pb analyses in new and novel ways and unlock the ability to address previously-inaccessible geological problems.

Here a suite of case studies will be showcased from collaborative research in the University of Colorado Boulder Thermochronology Research and Instrumentation Lab. Our recent technique-development work has included the design and construction of a custom 4He extraction and measurement system, development of laser-ablation (LA)-(U-Th)/He methods, implementation of LA-U/Pb analyses to complement our (U-Th)/He capabilities, and analysis of unconventional minerals via whole-crystal (U-Th)/He dating. Collaborative applications include paired (U-Th)/(He-Pb) dating of kimberlitic zircon megacrysts to determine when kimberlites erupted and links (or not) with megacryst genesis, pyrite (U-Th)/He analyses to date metallogenic deposits and sedimentary units, detrital magnetite (U-Th)/He dating as a sediment provenance tool for porphyry Cu systems, hematite U/Pb dating of iron ore formation and of sandstone injectites that record Snowball Earth meltwater events, in situ (U-Th)/He analysis of oxide phases (e.g., hematite, rutile) to avoid analytical issues and acquire robust data for texturally complex samples, and detrital zircon LA-(U-Th)/(He-Pb) analyses of the classic Sierra Nevada gold-bearing gravels to understand their sources. Leveraging geological data and the sample context are crucial for interpretation of geochronologic data and for developing geologically valid thermal history models of thermochronologic results. This approach – careful analytical work at the micron-scale collaboratively integrated with geological information and other datasets at macro-scales – can yield powerful new insights into Earth history and processes.

title: Clay Mineral Alteration by Natural Acid Sulfate Waters under Mars-Analogue Conditions: Implications for Clay–Sulfate Assemblages on Early Mars
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Lefticariu, Liliana [1], Specht, Jerome F. [2], Pentrak, Martin P. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, IL, USA
(2) Geology, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, IL, USA
(3) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA
abstract:
Orbital and rover observations have revealed widespread occurrences of phyllosilicates (clays), sulfates, iron oxides, and silica across Martian surface, indicating complex aqueous alteration histories that evolved from clay-forming to increasingly acidic, sulfate-rich environments. To evaluate mineralogical pathways behind this shift, we exposed Mars-relevant clays (kaolinite, illite, chlorite, Al-montmorillonite, Mg-saponite, and two Fe-rich nontronite: NAu-1 & NAu-2) plus an amorphous silica control to natural acid rock drainage (ARD) in field flow-through experiments for up to 5 months. Natural ARD is rich in sulfate and dissolved cations (Fe, Al, Mg, Ca, K), providing a realistic analogue for Martian fluids and enabling complex alteration reactions that are unrealized in simple sulfuric acid solutions at equivalent pH. Upon retrieval, reacted solids were extracted from intact dialysis membranes for characterization. We used X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor layer stacking and crystallinity, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) to detect tetrahedral (Si–O) and octahedral (OH) structural changes, and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) to track cation leaching from reacted clays.

ARD exposure induced structural and/or chemical alterations across all samples. Kaolinite remained essentially unaltered, while illite underwent progressive structural alteration initiated by interlayer K release. Chlorite showed limited octahedral alteration, though Fe oxidation and partial Mg release occurred while preserving the crystalline structure. Swelling clays (smectites) exhibited variable structural responses alongside secondary Fe-Al precipitation. Among smectites, nontronites underwent initial tetrahedral distortion followed by structural reordering; montmorillonite exhibited moderate alteration alongside amorphous silica precipitation; and trioctahedral saponite experienced heavy leaching of octahedral Mg and tetrahedral Si. Consequently, clay stability under sulfate and Fe-rich acidic conditions follows the order: Kaolinite > Chlorite > Nontronite 2 > Illite > Nontronite 1 > Montmorillonite > Saponite. Unlike pure-acid solutions, natural ARD promotes adsorption, secondary metal precipitation, and structural reorganisation due to high ambient cation activities, leading to rapid surface passivation and demonstrating that complex fluids preserve clay frameworks for far longer during Martian acid alteration.

These results imply that clay persistence in Hesperian and Amazonian acid-sulfate units does not require brief or mild fluid exposure, as cation-rich acidic fluids naturally buffer clay destruction. The established stability ranking provides a predictive framework for rover and orbital observations, explaining how localized silica and iron sulfate deposits can form via selective leaching while preserving resilient clay frameworks across Martian sedimentary basins.

authors: MA, Xiaoli [1], Deng, Yiying [2], Zhang, Linna [3], Isson, Terry [4], Montañez, Isabel P. [5], Fan, Junxuan [6]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences and Engineering and Frontiers Science Center for Critical Earth Material Cycling, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China; State Key Laboratory of Critical Earth Material Cycling and Mineral Deposits, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China

abstract: The Ordovician was a pivotal interval in Earth history, marked by major biodiversity diversification and extinction events linked to climate change. Robust palaeotemperature reconstructions are essential for understanding its climate evolution, yet reliable fossil isotope archives are scarce, while abundant bulk-carbonate oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) records remain challenging to interpret due to high susceptibility to diagenetic alteration. Here, we develop a transparent multi-criteria quality-control framework integrating stratigraphic, petrographic, sedimentological, and geochemical constraints to evaluate the preservation of individual isotopic proxy values. Applying this framework, we construct OrdoTemp , a curated dataset of 5,299 screened proxy values from 15,406 measurements, including bulk-carbonate and fossil δ 18 O (96.5%), and also a smaller subset of carbonate clumped isotope (Δ 47 ) data (3.5%). With high temporal coverage (~60 kyr median age spacing), OrdoTemp enables high-resolution Ordovician temperature reconstruction and provides a reproducible framework for deep-time δ 18 O proxy synthesis.

abstract: One of the best-preserved successions of Tonian rocks is the 770 to 729 Ma Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon, U.S.A. This siliciclastic and carbonate succession is divided into three formations (the Nankoweap, Galeros, and Kwagunt) and contains abundant, paleontologically significant microfossils. Understanding the environmental conditions that enabled these ecosystems to develop and thrive provides insight into the biosphere of late Tonian oceans. Microbialites afford an important record of these conditions, as their morphologies reflect interactions between microbial communities and their depositional environments. Five conspicuous, m-scale, laterally extensive microbialites intervals are present in the Chuar Group, each appearing only once, and are arranged stratigraphically from oldest to youngest: Inzeria , the “ polygonal bed ”, Baicalia , the “brain bed” ( Boxonia) , and “the Flaky dolomite”. Here, we describe these stratigraphically unique microbialite intervals and explore the environmental conditions that influenced their formation. Specifically, we examine the charismatic “brain bed” at the base of the Awatubi Member of the Kwagunt Formation. The “brains” are ~2-m-scale diameter domes sitting on top of ~1.75 m tall densely pack parallel bifurcating columnal stromatolites that form extensive bedding planes that extend for tens of km across the entire Chuar Valley and are dated to ~755 Ma. Based on the lack of continuity between the columnar and overlying domal structures, as well as the significantly different facies associated with these microbiolite morphologies, we interpret the brain beds’ distinctive morphology to reflect a rapid facies change associated with shifting environmental conditions.

authors: Duncan, Avery [1], Grothe, Pamela [2], Cobb, Kim [3], Ibarra, Daniel [4], Morris, Chandler [5], Lockwood, Rowan [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Mary Washington, Fredericksburg, VA,

abstract: Marine proxies from the central tropical Pacific (CTP) are critical for contextualizing normal climate variability in a region dominated by El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) variability. Previous studies from the CTP have relied on high-resolution δ 18 O records from Porites corals, providing critical snapshots of statistically weaker ENSO variability throughout the Holocene, compared to last five decades. However, much work remains to approximate the full range of natural ENSO variability, which is critical for understanding future ENSO variability predictions under enhanced greenhouse gas warming. While Porites corals are considered the highest fidelity archive for ENSO reconstruction in this region, a multispecies approach may provide a more robust reconstruction. Porites coral skeletons are easily altered by diagenesis; they may reduce their growth rates during thermal stress events, and they are becoming increasingly difficult to sample across all preindustrial time periods. Alternatively, the giant clam, Tridacna maxima , which has a long lifespan and a fast growth rate, is not as susceptible to diagenesis and is commonly found throughout the CTP. Similarly to corals, Tridacna clams have a calcium carbonate skeleton that incorporates the geochemistry from the seawater at the time they grew. Here, we present the δ 18 O from several modern and radiocarbon-dated fossil Tridacna maximum shells collected from Kiritimati Island, CTP (1.8°N, 157.4°W). We first compare the δ 18 O from the modern clam shells with both instrumental sea surface temperature (SST) and published Porites δ 18 O records. We then analyze two radiocarbon-dated fossil clams. The δ 18 O samples were drilled using a computer-automated drill at 0.2 mm increments to get monthly resolution. Our results show that the modern clam shell δ 18 O values are strongly correlated with both SST and Porites coral δ 18 O, and that the seasonal cycles are well preserved in the fossil clams, suggesting their application as suitable archive for ENSO reconstruction. This work aims to expand the archive for a more robust paleo-ENSO reconstruction through a multi-species approach.

authors: MacLellan, Lauren [1], Gosse, John C. [2], Hidy, Alan J. [3], Piro, Marie-Cécile [4], Woodley, William [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada

abstract:
Quantifying crustal erosion rates over million-year timescales in cratons remains challenging because tectonic stability, resistant lithologies, and low relief result in slow time-averaged erosion. To determine average denudation rates for the past few million years, we apply vertical muon paleotopometry by analyzing depth-dependent concentration patterns of terrestrial cosmogenic nuclides (TCN). Concentrations of 10 Be and 26 Al (quartz) and 36 Cl (feldspar) in a 250 m drill core through compositionally homogenous granophyre in the Sudbury Igneous Complex were compared with modeled profiles for various erosion scenarios to identify the best-fitting history. Below the upper few metres, TCN production transitions from neutron-dominated processes to production by high-energy penetrating muons, reducing any influence of temporal geomagnetic field variation or transient surface conditions such as sediment cover or lakes. These advantages make hectometre-scale depth profiles well suited to reconstructing long-term erosion histories but require accurate modeling of muogenic production.

A key challenge is modeling the depth-dependent increase in apparent attenuation length for TCN production, which is commonly approximated using constant attenuation lengths of 1,500 g cm -2 for slow muons and 4,320 g cm -2 for fast muons. The measured 10 Be profile from Sudbury indicates an attenuation length exceeding 40,000 g cm -2 at 250 m. Measured attenuation lengths are compared with those predicted using the muon propagation codes PROPOSAL and MUTE to simulate underground muon flux and energy, coupled with Geant4 simulations of TCN production. Particle transport is modeled through site-specific geometries, incorporating topography, geochemistry, density, and depth. Dominant nuclear pathways producing 10 Be, 26 Al, 36 Cl, and other TCNs are quantified, revealing how the relative contributions of muogenic production mechanisms evolve with depth. The muon flux inferred from the TCN measurements is then compared with the modern flux estimated by MUTE for the present sample depths and constrained by muon measurements at the nearby 2 km-deep SNOLab. The discrepancy between these fluxes provides an independent estimate of the missing shielding depth (erosion) required to reconcile the measured and modeled TCN concentrations.

These developments establish a framework for vertical muon paleotopometry while improving models of muogenic production. This approach enables long-term erosion to be constrained where conventional methods are unsuitable and will inform policy regarding erosion over the next million years above a proposed Canadian Shield repository for the long-term management of Canada’s nuclear waste.

abstract:
Natural asphalt seeps are not only sites of preservation of past life (i.e., fossils from "tar pits"), but are alsoliving ecosystems home to extremophile organisms. The oil fly, Diasemocera petrolei (Coquillett, 1899), is an ephydrid fly whose larvae develop exclusively in liquid asphalt. We hypothesize that the distribution and genetic structure of extant oil fly populations have been shaped by both Late Quaternary hydrocarbon geologic evolution and more recent petroleum extraction activities, which may have expanded their habitat.

To test this hypothesis, we built a genomic sequencing, distribution modeling, and connectivity modeling pipeline, using California oil flies as a case study. We generated low-coverage whole genomes for 24 oil flies from seven asphaltic sites overlying Miocene Monterey-type formations between Santa Clara and Los Angeles counties. We then evaluated the statistical influence of factors such as Late Quaternary fault activity, sea level change, and radiocarbon-based records of seep development, alongside contemporary climate, asphalt seepage, and oil extraction activities on the biogeographic patterns and genetic differentiation of populations. We tested the influence of hydrocarbon variables on species distribution by comparing their descriptive power within species distribution models (e.g., Maxent, a machine learning approach). Using Circuitscape and Omniscape, we built models of oil fly population genetic connectivity with each variable, allowing us to identify which model best predicted observed gene flow between oil fly populations through linear modeling.

Our results suggest that the oil fly’s present distribution and genetic structure in California is influenced by both contemporary surface oil availability and longer-term variability in oil seepage throughout the Pleistocene. Oil fly species distribution models indicate that 19th-21st century human oil extraction and natural oil seepage are equally important predictors of the oil fly’s distribution, implying that human oil extraction enhances oil fly population connectivity by promoting gene flow. Our analysis of oil fly genetic structure suggests that gene flow may be well constrained along faults distributed over oil bearing formations in California, but this warrants further exploration pending a more complete genomic dataset. Beyond our study scope, these methods provide a blueprint for future research to explore how past geologic and landscape evolution shape contemporary biogeographic patterns.

title: Application of In-situ Sulfur Isotopes to Constrain Rare Earth Element Enrichment in the Elk Creek Carbonatite, USA
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Verplanck, Philip L. [1], Pribil, Michael J. [2], Lowers, Heather A. [3]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(2) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(3) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract:
Carbonatites are the primary source of the world’s light rare earth elements (REEs) and niobium and are potential sources of other critical elements. Magmatic, hydrothermal, and weathering processes play important roles in the enrichment of REEs in carbonatites, but distinguishing their role during REE mineralization remains challenging. Sulfur isotopic systematics can aid in constraining the origin of REE mineralization in carbonatites, as sulfide and sulfate minerals form throughout most of the carbonatite paragenetic history and may be co-genetic with REE mineralization.

We focused on the Elk Creek carbonatite, southeastern Nebraska, where we integrated pyrite and barite sulfur isotopic data with detailed mineralogical and textural data. The multi-lithologic Elk Creek carbonatite is part of an alkaline intrusive complex buried by >200 m of Pennsylvanian marine sedimentary rocks and Quaternary glacial till, such that all samples are from drill core. The carbonatite, reported to be the largest niobium resource in the United States, contains zones enriched in REEs, Sc, and Ti. Rare earth element mineralization primarily consists of fluorocarbonate minerals (parisite, synchysite, and bastnaesite) and monazite and is associated with barite.

Sulfur isotopic compositions were measured in-situ by laser ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer at the U. S. Geological Survey High Resolution Laboratory. The δ 34 S VCDT isotopic composition of pyrites ranged from -14.5 to 0.0‰. Corroded and embayed pyrites consisted of a narrower range of -4.6 to 0.0‰ (magmatic), while euhedral to subhedral pyrites ranged from -14.5 to -6.1‰ (hydrothermal). δ 34 S values of barites ranged from -6.4 to 25.2‰. Integrating this large range in sulfur isotope values with morphology, barite veins associated with REE mineralization appear to be hydrothermal (-2.9 to 9.3‰). The δ 34 S values (-6.4 to -4.2‰) measured in grains of barite in the upper portion of the carbonatite and associated with small clusters of secondary, REE phosphates appear to be supergene in origin. A set of barren barite veins that crosscut all lithologies formed during a later event and have the highest δ 34 S values (14.7 to 25.2‰). Overall, the S isotopic results demonstrate that much of the carbonatite formed by magmatic processes, but REE mineralization is primarily linked to hydrothermal fluids. Supergene barite is associated with fine-grained REE mineralization.

authors: McKenzie, Kirsty A. [1], Rosa, Sophia [2], Dunlap, Bronwyn [3], Rittenour, Tammy M. [4], Kelsey, Harvey M. [5]

abstract:
Marine terraces preserved along subduction coastlines can record the interplay of eustatic sea level changes, long-term tectonic uplift, and local tectonic activity such as upper-plate faulting and folding. Along the Cascadia subduction zone, near Alsea Bay, Oregon, previous work utilized the elevation and spatial distribution of marine terraces to investigate long-term tectonic uplift of the Cascadia forearc and locations of upper-plate faults including the Waldport fault.

Using a LiDAR-derived digital elevation model from the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries we revisit the coastal region from Alsea Bay to Yachats, Oregon, and develop a high-resolution map of marine terrace platforms and upper-plate faults. We have also determined 7 new infrared stimulated luminescence (IRSL) burial ages of marine sands, overlying marine terrace platforms preserved along either side of the Waldport fault. Six of the seven preliminary IRSL ages range from 75.0 ± 9.1 ka to 124.6 ± 13.5 ka, and suggest the terraces preserved near Alsea Bay formed during marine isotope stages (MIS) 5a, 5c, and 5e. We also determined an anomalously low age of 59.0 ± 6.7 ka for the lowest elevation surface, possibly reflecting terrace reoccupation or erosion of the surface following burial. Our preliminary results suggest that the terraces exposed along this stretch of the coastline are younger than previously interpreted by Kelsey et al., (1996). The terrace morphology, new terrace age assignments, and spatial distribution of IRSL ages indicate a history of upper-plate faulting along the Waldport and surrounding faults that has produced a complex pattern of terrace development, potentially associated with contemporaneous megathrust and upper-plate fault activity.

abstract:
Flat slab subduction is an ephemeral tectonic process operating over <10% of Earth’s active subduction margins but is commonly invoked to explain a variety of orogenic features in modern and ancient ocean-continent convergent margin systems, including (1) intracontinental shortening, (2) migration and shut-off of arc magmatism, (3) hydration and removal of the continental mantle lithosphere, and (4) large volume accretionary underplating of sediments in forearc regions. These inferences suggest that episodes of flat slab subduction, however transitory, may have profound effects on the long-term thermal, mechanical, and chemical evolution of overriding continental lithosphere.

In this study, we examine the thermal and mechanical conditions of flat slab subduction recorded in Triassic blueschist-bearing siliciclastic rocks of the Central Qiangtang Metamorphic belt (CQMB). Mapping in two new areas extends the western known limit of subducted and exhumed rocks in the region by >100 km and support previous observations that blueschist-bearing rocks of the CQMB occur in the footwalls of domal, low-angle normal faults and brittle-ductile shear zones where they are juxtaposed beneath Carboniferous-Permian continental passive margin strata of Gondwanan-affinity. Previous studies established ages of peak metamorphism and metamorphic cooling for high-pressure rocks (mostly blocks-in-mélange) in the CQMB to be between ca. 244 and 223 Ma and for exhumation to have occurred between the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic. New detrital zircon U-Pb results from samples of lower plate mélange matrix and coherent siliciclastic rocks from the westernmost field area yield Late Triassic MDAs ca. 214 Ma, demonstrating that subduction accretion (underplating) continued during upper crustal extension and exhumation of the CQMB. Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material (RSCM) thermometry of seven lower plate samples yield temperatures between 375 and 495 °C, consistent with relatively warm conditions expected along the slab top during shallow angle subduction. We pair these new temperature estimates and kinematic constraints with microstructural observations of lower plate sandstones and quartzite-hosted shear zones to characterize the strength of a sediment-dominated subduction interface during flat slab subduction.

title: Investigating In-Channel Silt Preservation in Glaciated Versus Non-Glaciated Gravelly Braided Rivers of the Alaska Range and Brooks Range, AK, USA
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping (Posters)
authors: Solar, Anna [1], Chamberlin, Ellen [2], Hajek, Liz [3], O'Halloran, Molly [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Geosciences, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, USA

abstract:
Fine-grained sediments (< 63 microns) are readily carried in suspension in gravelly braided rivers and thought to be deposited only on floodplains or in channels during low-flow conditions. However, studies have shown in-channel mud deposits can form under high-discharge conditions, and the extent of mud deposition correlates with fine-sediment supply. In many gravelly braided rivers, very large volumes of silt-sized fines are produced by glacial grinding in headwaters. We test the hypothesis that in-channel fines deposition is more extensive and more silt-rich in rivers with glaciers in the catchment, compared to comparable-size rivers without glaciers.

Comparative field analysis of in-channel fines of two glacially fed river systems: the Gerstle and Johnson Rivers (southeastern Alaskan Range, AK); and two rivers with no significant glaciation since the Pleistocene: the Dietrich and Atigun Rivers (Brooks Range, AK). We investigated three goals: 1) in which depositional settings are fine-grained sediments preserved on gravelly braid bars; 2) how do the grain size, thickness, and distribution of fine-grained deposits differ between glaciated and non-glaciated river systems; and 3) could in-channel silt content be an indicator of paleo-glaciation in ancient deposits?

From field results, we identify five fines facies preserved on braid bars across all four river systems: between pebble and cobble transverse ribs, behind woody debris, as low-energy fallout drapes, and within stratigraphy of dry channel chutes. Across all river systems, the thickest deposits occur behind woody debris and range from 1.0-23 cm, with thickest deposits found in the Atigun River. On average, fines facies are thicker and have higher silt content in the glaciated rivers. For example, mean thickness of fines between transverse ribs (in cm) was 3.7, 2.6, versus 1.8 and 1.9 for the Gerstle, Johnson, Dietrich, and Atigun Rivers, respectively. The matrix of gravel deposits at all sites is poorly sorted, however, glaciated sample matrix is finer (medium upper) with higher silt content, whereas non-glaciated samples have coarser matrix (coarse lower) with lower silt percentages. These comparisons indicate that glaciated and non-glaciated braided rivers preserve in-channel fines in similar depositional settings, with differences in thickness and grain size. Therefore, in-channel silt content could be used as an indicator of glaciated watersheds in ancient deposits where paleoenvironmental conditions are contested, including the Pleistocene Nenana Gravels in central Alaska.

title: From Legacy Collections to Extended Specimens: Integrating Physical, Chemical, and Digital Data in Geological Collections
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Widga, Chris [1], Wood Finkle, Patti [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Mineral Sciences Museum, Penn State University, University Park, PA, USA

abstract:
Geological collections are increasingly functioning as data ecosystems, where specimens serve as anchors for interconnected chemical, spectral, imaging, analytical, and digital datasets. By applying an extended specimen concept to legacy geological collections, museums can transform characterization, digitization, and even destructive analysis into opportunities to expand the long-term scientific value of collections rather than diminish them.

For earth materials collections, the extended specimen encompasses not only the physical object, but also a growing network of associated data and derivatives, including geochemical and mineralogical analyses, spectral signatures, 2D and 3D imagery, analytical standards, thin sections, powders, and linked digital records. These data products can become as valuable to future researchers as the original specimen itself. As collections increasingly support research in areas such as critical minerals, geochemistry, paleontology, and planetary science, stewardship practices must account for both preservation of physical specimens and long-term management of their associated digital and analytical assets.

We present an emerging framework that integrates specimen documentation, characterization, data management, and destructive analysis within a unified stewardship model. Emphasis is placed on preserving both the physical characteristics of specimens, including morphology, texture, and internal structure, and their chemical and mineralogical characteristics through baseline analytical characterization and permanent linkage of resulting datasets to collection records. By treating destructive sampling as a transformation of specimen information rather than a simple loss of material, the extended specimen framework provides a practical pathway for supporting research access while enhancing the long-term scientific value of geological collections.

abstract:
Oracle Ridge Mine is a historic Cu skarn deposit in the Santa Catalina Mountains of Arizona, USA. Ore is hosted in altered Paleozoic carbonate rocks and can be found in both calcic and magnesian skarn horizons, however the majority of high-grade Cu mineralization occurs in the dolomitic carbonate units of the Martin Formation, Abrigo Formation, and Escabrosa limestone. Sulfide minerals include chalcopyrite, bornite, and chalcocite, with magnesian skarn zones hosting more abundant high Cu/Fe ratio minerals than calcic skarn.

The fine interbedding of strata at Oracle Ridge provides a unique opportunity to observe the alteration characteristics of a variety of protoliths proximally to distally from the causative intrusion. Calcic skarn displays the well-documented phenomenon of proximal to distal garnet color zoning, whereas this study documents a sequence of first occurrences of minerals in Mg skarn relative to the causative intrusion: proximal olivine, intermediate diopsidic pyroxene, distal tremolite, serpentine, brucite, and talc, and finally ludwigite occurring most commonly at the marble front of the altered zone.

Additionally, five skarn-related garnet samples were dated by LA-ICP-MS U-Pb, yielding ages between 67.58 ± 0.88 and 72.45 ± 0.72 Ma, with a mean age of 69.78 Ma. This age overlaps with the accepted U-Pb zircon age of the Leatherwood intrusion and confirms that skarn-hosted mineralization coincided with the emplacement of the underlying Leatherwood granodiorite during the Laramide Orogeny.

title: Cutoff Geometry Dictates the Infilling and Longevity of Oxbow Lakes

authors: Edmonds, Douglas [1], Jing, Ye [2], Shoemaker, Dylan [3], Li, Yuan [4], Islam, Muzahidul [5], Konsoer, Kory M. [6], Constantine, Jose [7]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Science, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA

abstract: Oxbow lakes are critical ecological habitats and effective sediment and contaminant sinks on meandering river floodplains. However, the factors driving the wide variation in their lifespans—ranging from a few years to several centuries—remain unclear. Oxbow lakes are formed when plug bars seal each channel entrance, stopping the flow of sediment into the channel. Several hypotheses have been proposed to understand what controls the creation, and the persistence of oxbow lakes. Classical work suggests that plug bars form when the bifurcation angle from the main channel into the soon-to-be abandoned channel is large, whereas further work has suggested that the angle asymmetry, the upstream bend and the length ratio of the new cutoff and soon-to-be abandoned channels can also be important to the formation of plug bars. Here, we analyze Landsat imagery (1984–2025) to quantify infill histories and cutoff geometries for recent cutoffs in the Amazon Basin (1985-2021), supplemented by 57 global control cases. We show that oxbow lakes formed by neck cutoffs exhibit half the short-term (10-year) infill proportion of those created by chute cutoffs, leaving a larger open-water fraction that directly promotes long-term (30 years) lake persistence. Among candidate controls, channel length ratio clearly differentiates cutoff types and serves as the primary control on infill proportion ( R 2 = 0.6), with higher length ratios predicting lower infill; angle asymmetry acts as a secondary control. Using a one-dimensional numerical model, we reveal the underlying mechanism that how the length ratio controls the creation of oxbow lakes: a higher length ratio creates a slope advantage in the new channel, generating a diffusive wave that scours the upstream reach and transfers sediment into the abandoned bend to form the plug bar. These findings demonstrate that initial cutoff geometry exerts fundamental control over oxbow lake longevity, providing essential insights for managing water resources, biodiversity vulnerabilities, and carbon storage in the Amazon basin.

abstract: Glaciation in the northwest United States (U.S.) during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) was restricted to alpine glaciers and ice caps, unlike the surrounding areas, which were covered by the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets. It is hypothesized that southerly migration of the jet stream would have made mountain glaciers in Sawtooth Valley, Idaho, particularly sensitive to precipitation due to the regional cool but dry climate. By recreating the paleo-equilibrium-line altitudes (ELAs), we can understand the climatic conditions required for these glaciers to reach their LGM extent. Comparing the intrabasinal differences between adjacent glaciers can inform the role of small-scale changes in non-climatic influences or timing within the valley. To do this, we applied the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM) to the Sawtooth Valley, then varied the climate parameters: ELA depression and an accumulation scaling factor relative to the present. Here, we show how these results connect the effect of accumulation on the paleo-ELA of the Sawtooth Valley glaciers. Our results contribute to the knowledge of an area sensitive to changes in atmospheric circulation caused by the large ice sheets in the surrounding areas and the conditions required to grow a healthy glacier.

title: Depositional Environment Controls Biotic Patterns across the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event in the Western USA
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Morgan, Natalie E. [1], Stigall, Alycia L. [2], Pruss, Sara B. [3], Benjamin, Abigail [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract:
During the Ordovician, marine and oceanic environments experienced global cooling, shifting circulation patterns, and increased tectonic activity and oxygenation that profoundly impacted biotic systems, culminating in the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE). The GOBE is best expressed in Middle Ordovician strata and was characterized by dramatic taxonomic diversification resulting in niche evolution and higher ecosystem complexity. One poorly understood aspect of the GOBE is how the global diversification trend is derived from an accumulation of basinal-level patterns and how these patterns vary across regional depth transects. To address this gap, we have developed a detailed bed-level dataset of faunal diversity during the Middle Ordovician in the Great Basin. The localities represent near-shelf, mid-shelf, and outer-shelf environments, which provides a framework to analyze temporal and spatial changes in diversity in a cross-shelf context.

Bedding plane data from Floian through Darriwilian intervals were collected by quadrat sampling at three Great Basin localities. At Meiklejohn Peak, NV, data were collected from 28 beds across the Lower–Upper Antelope Valley Limestone. At Arrow Canyon Range, NV, 24 bedding planes were analyzed in the Opd and Opf subunits of the Pogonip Group. Near Ibex, UT, 40 beds were examined from the Wah Wah through Lehman formations. Taxa exposed on bedding plane surfaces were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level and assigned to a functional guild. This community composition data was statistically analyzed to quantify taxonomic diversity and ecosystem structure through time. Diversity was assessed using rarefaction and Simpson’s evenness indices. Ecosystem structure was assessed using ordination, cluster, and guild analyses. Diversity and ecological metrics were compared among localities and through time to develop a framework to examine how depositional environment impacts diversity and ecological trends through the GOBE in this region. Trends were further examined against lithology and geochemical proxy data to assess environmental impacts through time and space.

Initial results indicate clear differentiation of diversity and ecological trends across the depth gradient suggesting that local environmental impacts were important for structuring biotic changes within the Great Basin during the GOBE. Stratigraphic palaeobiological studies at the basinal scale, such as this one, can contribute key insights for linking basinal, regional, and global patterns, which is essential for a holistic understanding of globally recognized events like the GOBE.

abstract: The Arctic coralline alga, C. compactum, can be used to generate sub-annual resolution climate records of sea-ice cover and sea surface temperature. However, age model development for this species has relied heavily on visual counting of annual growth bands and geochemical proxy cycles of live collected (i.e., actively growing) algae, which constrains record development up to a specimen’s first growth hiatus. While limited U-Th dating has been conducted on C. compactum , no standardized approach currently exists. In this study, we apply U-Th dating methods to four C. compactum from the coast of Eastern Kingitok Island, Nunatsiavut (Labrador Sea). Specimens were screened for secondary calcification and diagenesis using visual examination of high-resolution images and X-ray diffraction analysis. Areas with relatively low detrital Th concentrations (<600 ppt), as detected by laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS), were identified for U-Th age subsampling. Subsamples were drilled using a diamond tipped handheld drill, avoiding reproductive conceptacles and sample cracks that could potentially harbor detrital material and secondary calcite deposits. Samples were digested, spiked with a mixed 236-233-229 tracer, centrifuged to separate U and Th from sample matrix, and loaded onto anion exchange columns. Separate uranium and thorium liquid extracts were measured on a multicollector ICP-MS (Thermo Neptune Plus) via peak-jumping mode on a secondary electron multiplier. Chemical blanks and instrument backgrounds were monitored continuously and corrected from final results (<79 ag of 230 Th, <207 ag of 234 U, <0.16 pg of 232 Th and <0.53 pg of 238 U). In all four specimens, δ 234 U sample fell within uncertainties of δ 234 U seawater . U-Th dating results agreed with manual band count estimates: 312 ± 8, 288 ± 87, 127 ± 24 and 38 ± 7 (years BP). Ages for all three specimens with multiple U-Th dates fell in stratigraphic order. Future work will include constraining sample 230 Th/ 232 Th initial ratios, anchoring band-counted chronologies with absolute U-Th ages, and producing a precisely dated, annual-resolution sea-surface temperature master chronology.

title: A Half-Century of Glacier Retreat: Reconstructing Glacier Change using Geomorphic Evidence from Wyoming’s Wind River Range
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations (Posters)
authors: Clayton, Massimiliano [1], Li, Yingkui [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) University of Tennessee Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract: Examining recent glacier changes in Wyoming’s Wind River Range reveals a pattern of substantial reduction in surface area and volume consistent with Late Quaternary deglaciation trends. Yet existing inventories contain temporal gaps and often mix glaciers with seasonal snowpack. This study uses geomorphological mapping and classification techniques to compare glacier boundaries created using high-resolution 2006 satellite imagery in Google Earth with inventories from 1966, 2015, and 2020. To distinguish glaciers from snowpack, Welch’s t-test was applied to find significant differences in elevation changes within and surrounding mapped boundaries based on digital elevation models from 2013 and 2021. Results show an 11% decrease in mapped glacier features from 1966 to 2006 (476 to 423), with a 19% reduction in boundaries classified as glaciers (210 to 170). Total glacier area declined from 45.1 km² in 1966 to 31.02 km² in 2006, while volume decreased from 0.955 km³ to 0.658 km³. From 1966 to 2015, area and volume losses reached 51.95% and 54.03%, respectively, consistent with accelerated regional retreat following the Little Ice Age. An unusually low decrease observed in 2020 data highlights methodological inconsistencies between existing inventories. This study underscores the need for standardized mapping protocols and robust classification between glaciers and snowpack to accurately refine glacial chronologies, document glacier changes, and assess their impact on water resources.

title: Coaxing Climate Inference from Dicot Leaves: A Test in the Rainforest of Queensland Australia
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Arens, Nan Crystal [1], Humphries, Nicholas Benjamin [2]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Hobart and William Smith, Geneva, New York, USA

abstract: Fossil dicotyledonous angiosperm leaves have been used to reconstruct paleoclimate since 1915, when botanists Irving W. Bailey and Edmund W. Sinnott recognized a correlation between the proportion of entire-margin leaves in a region’s flora and mean annual temperature (MAT). Such non-taxonomic climate reconstruction techniques rely on convergent evolution of leaf size and shape in response to climate conditions. However, they can be vulnerable to phylogenetic and biogeographic contingencies. The most basic method, leaf margin analysis (LMA) quantifies the relationship between the proportion of entire margin leaves and MAT to develop a least-squares predictive model. Simple to use and effective for fragmentary fossil material, LMA is sensitive to its training set and reconstructs only one paleoclimate variable. Improvements in computing power allowed consideration of more leaf features and more climate variables using canonical correspondence analysis in the climate leaf analysis multivariate program (CLAMP). Although CLAMP has evolved to include a global training set, its presence-absence scoring method has been criticized as difficult to reproduce. Improvements in digital image manipulation and hypotheses about the functional underpinning of leaf form-climate correlations led to digital leaf physiognomy (DiLP), which uses continuous measurements of leaf size and shape analysed with a custom R function. DiLP has shown promise, warranting a comparison between it, CLAMP and LMA. With development of these paleoclimate proxies weighted toward the northern hemisphere, calibration datasets tend to produce incongruent results for Southern Hemisphere applications, leading to multiple training set for CLAMP, and multiple LMA equations to account for biogeographic variation. A known-answer validation of these methods is overdue. We sampled leaves from 23 locations in Queensland, Australia. Samples were taken to mimic fossil assemblages, including 20-30 species growing in close physical proximity within primary rainforest. LMA, CLAMP and DiLP climate reconstructions were compared against actual climate measurements elicited from averaging 10 years of 0.5° x 0.5° gridded climate data.

title: Influence of Geologic Setting on Elevated Shear Strength Along Active Continental Margins
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections (Posters)
authors: Towoju, Victor [1], Reece, Julia [2], Childress, Laurel [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geologgy and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA

abstract: Sediments along active continental margins frequently exhibit elevated shear strength compared to those on passive margins, a phenomenon traditionally attributed to seismic strengthening. However, the precise influence of localized geologic setting on this strength elevation remains poorly quantified. Using undrained shear strength measurements collected using automated vane shear (AVS), penetrometer (PEN), and torvane (TOR) devices across > 70 drill sites from 10 Integrated Ocean Drilling Program and International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) expeditions included in the LIMS with Lithology (LILY) database and 13 Ocean Drilling Program (ODP) expeditions, we evaluated the spatial variability of shear strength across different geologic settings on active margins (specifically the incoming plate, frontal prism, forearc slope and basin, rear-arc and back-arc region). Our findings confirm that active margin sediments generally display higher shear strength than passive margin sediments, though the rate and magnitude of this strengthening vary significantly by geological setting. Along subduction zones, the highest shear strength increase occurs within the frontal prism and, to a lesser extent, in the fore-arc region. Conversely, sediments on the incoming plate and back-arc basin of these active settings typically exhibit shear strengths more comparable to passive margin sediments, except where localized overconsolidation has been induced by landslides or tectonic uplift. This pattern aligns with expectations that the frontal region of subduction zones may be influenced by lateral compression, whereas the back-arc region is typically dominated by an extensional regime. Overall, these results highlight that while seismic strengthening may contribute to enhanced sediment strength on active margins, local geologic setting and stress state exert primary controls over the evolution of undrained shear strength across ocean basin sediments.

title: Wood Dynamics and Ecogeomorphic Processes in Two Gravel-Bed River Floodplains
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Lininger, Katherine [1], Bertoldi, Walter [2], Ruiz-Villanueva, Virginia [3], Siviglia, Annunziato [4], Welsh, Josie [5], O'Callaghan, Marc [6]

abstract:
Wood in river corridors (channels and their floodplains) modifies flows, sediment transport, and geomorphic form, but most research on wood in fluvial systems has focused on wood within channels, ignoring floodplain environments. Understanding channel-floodplain wood fluxes and floodplain wood dynamics is necessary to predict wood transport and storage, close wood budgets, and support management decisions aimed at improving floodplain habitat and ecosystem services. We present field data on floodplain wood and organic matter loads and characteristics on two dynamic gravel bed river floodplains: the Tagliamento River (drainage area: 2580 km 2 ) in Italy and the Sense River (drainage area: 432 km 2 ) in Switzerland.

We measured large wood (>1m in length and >0.1m in diameter) and coarse particulate organic matter (CPOM; material finer than large wood) in accumulations (i.e., jams; n = 242) across the floodplain and in the active channel. In both floodplains, wood and CPOM loads (m 3 ha -1 ) on the floodplain close to the active channel and on vegetated islands were similar to or higher than loads in the active channel, highlighting the importance of floodplains for wood retention and storage. Some of the highest floodplain wood and CPOM loads were in preferential floodplain flow paths (e.g., side channels); wood and CPOM loads were lowest on the oldest floodplain surfaces farthest from the main channel. Living vegetation, including relatively small flexible vegetation (e.g., Salix spp. , Populus nigra ), effectively trapped wood and CPOM.

Floodplain relative surface age estimates from historical aerial imagery coupled with plot-based floodplain wood load measurements point to interesting interactions between geomorphic processes and wood decay rates that likely govern floodplain wood loads. Much of the Tagliamento floodplain area has been stable for multiple decades and wood likely decays relatively quickly, resulting in very low wood loads on older surfaces farther from the main channel. In contrast, much of the Sense floodplain area is comparatively young due to frequent shifting of the main channel location across the valley bottom, and wood pieces may be more resistant to decay due to the dominant tree species present; this likely contributed to observations of decayed wood jams on the Sense. Our results provide insight into floodplain ecogeomorphic interactions, with implications for floodplain carbon storage and management of floodplain habitats.

title: A Sabre-tooth at the Tar Pits, a Fossil Whale in Australia, Petroleum Forming Within Corals, and Other Important to Really Incorrect Geological Findings and Interpretations of William Denton (1823–1883), America’s Prominent Spiritualist Geologist
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Hannibal, Joseph T. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA; Cleveland Museum of Natural History, Cleveland, Ohio, USA
abstract:
Willian Denton was an English-born, self-taught geologist who made the United States his home. His oeuvre includes really important to unexceptional—as well as really wrong—findings and interpretations. His two big discoveries were the occurrence of fossil insects in the West, and that the bones at the La Brea tar pits were fossils and that they included a maerichidian (sabre tooth). Also notable were his early geological descriptions of Colorado. Denton was an ardent Spiritualist, and a prominent practitioner of the arcane art of psychometry. His best works and interpretations were based on his intense reading of the geological literature, standard observations, and study of museum specimens. Conversely, his findings based on information obtained using psychometry, including those based on his “sensitives” published in the 3-volume The Soul of Things co-authored with his spouse Elizabeth M.F. Denton, have not fared as well. For instance his view that petroleum formed in situ within the chambers of tabulate corals, which he included in geological reports, and which was verified with psychometry, were wrong and have been ignored. Denton’s discovery of a fossil whale at Beaumaris in Australia would have been an important discovery had it been described and published, and not disassembled by members of a public field trip he led.

Denton’s real forte was public speaking (on geology, Spiritualism, temperance, etc.) and debating. His most famous debate, centered on the Development Theory, was held over five days at the end of 1858. He was opposed by future President James Garfield, who would become a great supporter of geology as a congressman. In 1883 Denton became ill in New Guinea and died after he unwisely refused food and quinine. Denton’s books and lecture slides included reasonable as well as fanciful reconstructions of prehistoric organisms by his son Sherman, many based on Sherman’s psychometric observations. Sherman and his brother Shelley would leave Spiritualism, and Sherman would supply biological illustrations for US Fish Commission and paleontological illustrations for his father’s friend paleoentomologist Samuel Scudder. Their sister Carrie would teach standard geology at Teachers’ School of Science of the Boston Society of Natural History.

title: Investigation of Tidal-Bore-Induced Surface Water and Hyporheic Zone Mixing Using Paired Geophysics and Heat as a Hydrologic Tracer

authors: Lavender, Vanessa [1], Tackley, Hayden [2], Kurylyk, Barret [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering and Centre for Water Resources Studies, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
(2) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering and Centre for Water Resources Studies, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
(3) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering and Centre for Water Resources Studies, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada
abstract:
Tidal bores are progressive waves induced by flood tides funneled into narrow coastal rivers. They create powerful turbulent waves that drive sediment transport and mixing of heat, nutrients, salinity, and other surface water constituents. These conditions strongly influence ecosystem productivity and estuarine fluvial geomorphology. Despite their importance, tidal-bore mixing processes in integrated channel-hyporheic zone systems have received relatively little research attention because bores are uncommon, localized, and potentially hazardous to work in.

The Bay of Fundy borders the state of Maine and the Canadian Maritimes and is home to among the world’s highest tides. The Salmon River, a 40-kilometer estuary that empties into the Bay of Fundy’s Cobequid Bay, is a dyked, macro-tidal river that experiences semi-diurnal tidal bores. During high tides, seawater propagates upriver against the natural freshwater flow direction. To investigate tidal bore mixing in the surface water column and underlying sediment, a 500 m reach of the estuary was instrumented with conductivity-temperature-depth loggers (Solinst LTC), water temperature loggers (RBR SoloT, Onset Hobo Tidbit), and vertical sediment temperature probes (iButtons installed at multiple depths in stakes). These sensors were installed in cross-shore and longitudinal channel directions to characterize the spatiotemporal temperature patterns throughout the reach and were programmed to record at relatively high frequencies. These water temperature time series were complemented with water temperature maps collected from a drone-based thermal infrared survey to observe the bore arrival (DJI Matrice 300 UAV equipped with a Zenmuse H20T sensor). Frequency-domain electromagnetic geophysical surveys (Geophex GEM-2) were also conducted to map resistivity patterns and infer mixing dynamics. All data were recorded in the late summer 2026 during spring tides, when the bore was most pronounced, and during warm atmospheric conditions to maximize the thermal contrast between the Bay of Fundy and the Salmon River. These recently collected data will be presented to highlight our preliminary interpretation of the bore mixing dynamics in the channel and hyporheic zone as well as the implications for physical and biogeochemical processes in this distinctive, macrotidal setting.

abstract: The Western Cape of South Africa is home to termite mounds known as heuweltjies that are typically 30-40 m in diameter and 2 m high. Some of these mounds, particularly in more arid regions, possess pedogenic carbonate layers in a landscape otherwise devoid of carbonates. These calcareous layers impact soil biogeochemistry and comprise a sizeable carbon sink, but the rates and mechanisms driving their accumulation remain obscure. Paired field-based measurements of soil pore space O 2 and CO 2 can be used to investigate active biogeochemical processes such as soil respiration and carbonate formation/dissolution. In particular, Apparent Respiratory Quotient (ARQ = CO 2 /O 2 *0.76) values for soil gas measurements can point to the dominant processes (e.g. aerobic respiration, ARQ = 0.9-1.0; oxalate carbonate pathway, ARQ = 2.0, etc.). A custom-built soil monitoring station was assembled on top of an uncultivated termite mound near Koringberg, South Africa. This automated station measured soil CO 2 and O 2 daily at various depths from carbonate-bearing soil on the mound as well as carbonate-free off-mound soil. Soil respiration was higher at all locations during the wetter and cooler growing season than during the hotter and drier off-season, and the center of the mound maintained higher respiration rates than the edge or off-mound soils across all seasons. During the transition between wetter winter and dry spring, ARQ increased in the carbonate-bearing on-mound soils (from 0.85 in the winter to 1.0 in the spring), while average ARQ at the off-mound wells remained relatively stable. The ARQ increase observed on-mound indicates excess CO 2 , possibly driven by carbonate precipitation. ARQ occasionally rose slightly above 1.0 at the center of the mound with an overall maximum of 1.74, By using the off-mound ARQ signals as a carbonate-free control, we assess possible drivers of other metabolic processes that could drive higher ARQ values on the mounds, such as the oxalate-carbonate pathway or reprecipitation of existing soil carbonate. Overall, the data collected from this field site show that soil carbonate formation may be detectable using soil gas measurements, particularly during the transition period between winter and spring when aerobic respiration slows in response to declining soil moisture.

title: Karst bauxites as archives of shallow thermal histories: coupled hematite and goethite (U–Th)/He thermochronology from Provence, France
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Boschetti, Louise [1], Schwartz , Stéphane [2], Gautheron, Cécile [3], Rolland, Yann [4], Balvay, Mélanie [5], Cogné, Nathan [6], Mouthereau , Frédéric [7], Jepson, Gilby [8]

abstract:
Reconstructing post-depositional thermal histories in carbonate-dominated basins is challenging because conventional thermochronometers are scarce. Here, we demonstrate that karst-hosted bauxites provide an alternative thermal archive through coexisting hematite (Hm) and goethite (Gt). We report the first paired Hm and Gt (U–Th)/He dates, HHe and GHe, respectively, from Provence karst bauxites (France), together with thermal inversions based on the HHe data.

The karstic bauxites from this study were formed during tropical weathering and trapped within carbonate karst cavities at ca. 120–105 Ma, before being buried beneath Upper Cretaceous sedimentary successions and thrust sheets system during the Pyrenean compression (85-40 Ma). Analyses of 133 Hm and Gt grains yielded reproducible dates ranging from 85 ± 6 to 12 ± 1 Ma. These dates are younger than bauxite formation, indicating post-depositional thermal resetting. HHe dates are consistently older than coexisting GHe dates, ranging from 85 to 40 Ma and from 32 to 12 Ma, respectively, reflecting greater He retentivity in hematite.

HHe thermal modeling, consistent with regional geological constraints, reveals two successive cooling events. The first involved cooling after a maximum reached temperature of 90–120 °C at 60–45 Ma associated to exhumation during Pyrenean compression. The second involved reheating to 50–60 °C between ca. 35 and 15 Ma associated to a rifting event in the region. This younger event partially reset some HHe dates and fully reset all the GHe dates. The agreement between the HHe-derived thermal modeling history and the complete resetting of GHe suggests that the GHe thermochronometer is sensitive to temperatures below approximately 80 °C.

These results establish karst bauxites as robust archives for reconstructing shallow thermal histories in carbonate-dominated basins.

session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: MCKENZIE, IAN MICHAEL [1], Halihan, Todd [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geology, Oklahoma State Univ, Stillwater, OK, USA

abstract: Electrical Resistivity Imaging (ERI) produces large datasets that can be difficult to interpret. The objective of this research was to examine whether AI could be useful in identifying zones of interest at a light non-aqueous phase liquid (LNAPL) impacted site and improve subsurface characterization. Rather than using only manual or statistical analysis, the goal was to evaluate how effectively AI could process the large datasets and if it could accurately make decisions about anomalies of interest. AI demonstrated a very clear advantage in efficiency. The AI models excelled at completing repetitive or time-consuming tasks such as isolating the highest and lowest resistivity values and locating them along the ERI line. Automating this step of interpreting the data reduces the need for manual coding and accelerates an initial interpretation. However, several limitations to the AI method became apparent. Many AI platforms withhold their full capabilities behind a paywall by imposing file-size restrictions, thus preventing the full ingestion of the datasets and reducing the accuracy of the interpretation. Additionally, the AI was more efficient with images of datasets that utilize the raw pixel data rather than files of raw data. The most reliable results occurred when the AI outputs were using paid AI engines and integrating results with the known hydrogeologic model. While AI could prove to be a powerful tool in geophysics it should not replace human judgement and interpretation but can be a useful aid in processing large amounts of data across sites.

abstract: Gale crater was selected as the Mars Science Laboratory Curiosity rover’s landing site, in part, because of orbital detection of secondary minerals in ~3.5 Ga sedimentary rocks. Secondary minerals include Fe/Mg-smectite, hydrated Mg-sulfate, and hematite. The observed transition from clay minerals to hydrated Mg-sulfate going up stratigraphic section through the Mount Sharp Group was interpreted to signify a change in climate that may have occurred across Mars. The CheMin X-ray diffractometer on Curiosity has analyzed dozens of drill samples from units with secondary mineral absorptions from orbit. Quantitative mineralogical results from CheMin demonstrate spatially abrupt changes in mineral assemblages that may be from variations in depositional, early diagenetic, and late diagenetic environments. We hypothesize that smectite is a marker of fluvial-lacustrine depositional environments and that Fe(II)-carbonate, hydrated Mg-sulfate, gypsum, and halite represent early diagenetic products of near-surface groundwater freezing/evaporation in eolian environments. We present a late-diagenetic groundwater mixing model in which warm, oxic and acidic basinal brines ascended through fluvial-lacustrine and some eolian strata to cause the formation of Fe(III)-oxides, -oxyhydroxides, and -smectite and mobilization of transition metals. These warm brines mixed with cool, reducing groundwater at a local aquiclude called the Amapari Marker Band, causing high concentrations of Fe, Zn, and Cl.

title: ServoSipper: a Low-Cost, Flexible, High-Capacity, Long-Duration, Automated Water Sampler
session_title: Hydrogeology Discipline Session (Posters)
authors: Chapin, Thomas [1]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract: The ServoSipper is a low-cost (<$400 USD parts), low-power, portable, 3D printed multi-port pinch valve and peristaltic pump platform designed for automated, high-capacity, long-duration water sample collection in remote locations. ServoSippers offer tremendous sampling flexibility via user selectable features, such as sample volume, container type and size, and preservation methods. It also offers the capability for discrete/composite sampling and multiple sampling frequencies. The standard ServoSipper configuration fits in a weatherproof 5-gallon bucket, collects 96 15-mL samples or 32 50-mL samples and can operate unattended for 12 months. Larger volume samples (100 to >1000 mL) can be collected in a larger box or cooler. The sampling flexibility and high sample capacity allow different water sampling methodologies and different sample types to be automatically collected in a single ServoSipper deployment (e.g. unfiltered + filtered, metals + stable isotopes, multiple filter fractions, multiple depth sampling, multiple nutrient species). The Submersible ServoSipper collects 24 50-mL samples inside a waterproof housing and operates under ice for over-winter sampling. ServoSippers have primarily been deployed for automated, long-duration sample collection for toxic metals in remote acid mine drainage locations and selenium sampling in lakes and rivers providing multi-year records of contaminant concentrations. The flexible ServoSipper design concept of low-cost peristaltic pump and numerous multi-port pinch valves can easily be adapted to water sample collection for other analyte classes (e.g. organics, nutrients, stable isotopes, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, micro/nano plastics, eDNA, biologics, etc.).

title: Calling out the Small But Mighty: A Deep-Learning Model for Europa’s Microfeatures
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Haslebacher, Caroline [1], Olmstead, Elise [2], Rhoden, Alyssa R. [3], Singer, Kelsi [4], Bickel, Valentin T. [5], Schenk, Paul [6]

abstract: The surface of Jupiter’s moon Europa shows microfeatures, a term describing small-scale (~100 km 2 ) pits, uplifts, spots (spot-like albedo variations), small chaos patches, and hybrid forms. Their formation directly informs the subsurface structure including the thickness of Europa’s ice shell with implications for habitability. Therefore, geologic mapping of microfeatures is a means of constraining ice shell thickness and the variation thereof, and their formation mechanisms. Here, we are training a neural network, MicroMapper, at a regional scale to map microfeatures (instance segmentation). To prevent misclassification of (negative relief) pits and (positive relief) uplifts, we fuse Galileo optical images with topographic information before feeding the data into the neural network. A stitching algorithm during post-processing allows the creation of georeferenced output. Finally, this work prepares for the arrival of Europa Clipper when automated mapping becomes indispensable.

title: What Does it Take to Make a Large-volume, Silicic Magma Reservoir?: Observations from the plutonic record
session_title: GSA Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Division Awards Session
authors: Eddy, Michael Patterson [1], Mehra, Akshay [2], Pamukcu, Ayla [3], Klein, Benjamin [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(3) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
(4) Geosciences and Environment, University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
abstract:
Voluminous eruptions of silicic magma (up to 10 3 km 3 , >63 wt.% SiO 2 ) indicate that large volumes of eruptible silicic magma can exist within the Earth’s upper crust. An intrusive record of these reservoirs likely remains within the great granitoid batholiths. However, intrusive equivalents of large-volume caldera forming eruptions have been difficult to identify. Instead, high-precision U-Pb zircon geochronology has shown that many granitoid plutons are an amalgamation of many magmatic increments that are largely independent in time. The boundaries between these increments can be hard to identify, making it a challenge to delineate individual fossil magma reservoirs. These observations have led to the widespread view that upper-crustal granitoids represent mushes that can grow slowly over hundreds of thousands to millions of years. However, this is thermally challenging in a cold upper crust.

A key variable that has emerged from geochronologic studies of granitoids is the magma emplacement rate, a time-averaged estimate for the rate at which magma intruded during incremental pluton construction. This variable is important because only rapidly assembled intrusive centers can keep portions of the system above the solidus between different emplacement events. Here we evaluate the significance of magma emplacement rate, as calculated from map and geochronologic data. We show that the rate strongly depends on the time over which it was measured with the highest rates restricted to the shortest periods of time. This relationship arises from log normal distributions of magma increment size and hiatus durations, similar to the distributions of eruptive volume and repose times at volcanoes.

We suggest that development of large, upper crustal, silicic magma reservoirs is unlikely to occur through the steady accumulation of melt over prolonged >10 5 -10 6 periods of time. Instead, the largest reservoirs were probably built more rapidly. This inference is supported by the presence of large-scale geochemical gradients indicative of gravitationally-driven crystal settling in only the most rapidly emplaced granitoid intrusions.
