title: National Mine Waste Inventory: U.S. Geological Survey and State Geological Survey Collaboration
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Karl, Nick [1], Taylor, Ryan D. [2], Murzyn, John Anthony [3], San Juan, Carma A. [4]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(3) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(4) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract:
Locating critical mineral resources continues to be a high priority for both government and industry groups. This interest extends beyond lode resources and includes identifying surficial mine waste features that may contain critical mineral resources. As part of the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative’s focus on determining potential critical mineral resources, the U.S. Geological Survey is collaborating with State Geological Surveys to develop a comprehensive database of non-fuel and above ground mine waste features that will aid in research and development of these unconventional critical mineral resources.

The National Mine Waste Inventory (NMWI) database aims to answer primary questions such as: (1) How many mine waste features are found in the U.S.? (2) Where are they located? (3) What type of mine waste is present? (4) How much total material do they contain? and (5) What are the commodity characteristics of the material? The NMWI database provides general information pertaining to feature type and location to answer the first three questions. Footprints of geospatial features can be coupled with digital elevation models to estimate volumes of individual features using recently published software (Jones et al., 2026), providing valuable data on waste material tonnage. The features are further characterized by defining the deposit type that was exploited for the mine, what commodities were produced, and what ore and gangue minerals are present. This data provides insight into what critical minerals may exist. All database entries are derived from publicly available sources. Features captured in the inventory have a spatial extent of 2,000 m 2 in area or larger.

Version 1 of the published NMWI database contains 764 mine waste features inventoried at 181 mine sites within Arizona, Colorado, Kentucky, Michigan, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Utah, and Virginia. Version 2 of the NMWI database will be published in the fall of 2026 and incorporates additional sites from Alaska, Arizona, California, Idaho, Kansas, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. The NMWI database will integrate new geographic areas in versioned updates.

Jones, J.M., Smith, A.S., Gaynor, S.P., Mauk, J.L., 2026, Geospatial tool for mine waste volume calculations from remote sensing source code, v1.0.0: U.S. Geological Survey Software Release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P14P7CJG

title: Paleozoic Stenolaemate Bryozoan Skeletal Responses to Seawater Carbonate Saturation
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Pfenninger, Lindsey [1]
abstract: Drivers behind the evolution of skeletonization in paleoreefs are poorly understood. Bryozoans became dominant reef builders in the Late Ordovician and are among the first organisms to develop carbonate skeletons at a time when ambient seawater saturation state (Ω) was high, making it an ideal model to understand early evolution of skeletonization. I examine the relationship between abiotically derived Ω, stenolaemate and trepostome bryozoan skeletal index (BSI), and reef number throughout the Paleozoic and Triassic to understand the influence of Ω on bryozoan skeletal investment and reef abundance. The results reject that the evolution of skeletonization in bryozoans was only dependent on ambient Ω and support that reef abundance and reef builder biomineralization are biotically controlled, indicating that stenolaemate bryozoans did not adjust skeletal material to ambient seawater Ω. These findings contribute to the knowledge that biomineralizers maintained skeletal investment across a range of ambient Ω conditions throughout the Paleozoic.

title: From Coppice to Colonization: A 6,000-Year Pollen Record of Vegetation Change at Watling's Blue Hole, San Salvador Island, The Bahamas
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Hopps, Connor [1], Michelson, Andrew [2], Park Boush, Lisa [3], White, Lauryn [4], Leonard-Pingel, Jill [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(2) Marine Environmental Sciences, State University of New York Maritime College, Bronx, NY, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(4) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(5) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
abstract:
Reconstructed floral communities provide insight into past environmental conditions, ecological shifts, and localized community changes. These records help to define natural baselines, used in conservation as benchmarks of pre-human environmental conditions, and the tolerance of communities to environmental and human stressors. Such reconstructions are relevant to areas that experience human impact and are projected to see ever-increasing effects of contemporary climate change, such as The Bahamas. Bahamian pollen records are well-suited to document floral communities through time, with San Salvador Island offering an ideal setting due to its unique climatic history, relatively recent human habitation, and abundance of lacustrine catchment sites associated with significant archaeological records. Watling’s Blue Hole (WBH) is an inland blue hole near both Lucayan and colonial settlement sites, allowing for the integration of the sediment core record with the known history of human occupation and activity. Thus, WBH pollen data documents both natural and anthropogenic shifts in plant community composition.

Sediment core transects were recovered from WBH using a square-rod piston coring system capturing an approximately 6,000-year record. Core sediments yielded pollen that indicates a diverse floral community consisting of coppice species such as hardwoods ( Swietenia mahagoni and Bursera sp .) and epiphytes ( Tillandsia sp .). This community remained relatively stable throughout various environmental fluctuations, indicated by accompanying proxy records (e.g. sedimentology, ostracodes, XRF, grain size and LOI). Pollen counts indicate that the floral community began to gradually decrease in diversity ~1600 cal yr BP, ending with a more rapid decrease in diversity after ~700 cal yr BP. Core top pollen indicates a terrestrial floral community dominated by Asteraceae and Coccoloba sp ., which likely coincides with land clearing from European colonization and plantation efforts. This community progression differs greatly from Bahamian pollen records from more northern islands, demonstrating the diversity of flora across the region. The WBH records allow us to reconstruct climatic conditions and ecologic shifts on San Salvador throughout time and define a local ecological baseline that can help determine how modern plant communities have been shaped by human influence, goals for restoration efforts, and the susceptibility of local plant communities to climatic stress.

title: Ponds, Pines, and People: 6500-Year Record of a Wetland Floral Community from Poisonwood Blue Hole, New Providence, The Bahamas
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Hopps, Connor [1], Kjellmark, Eric [2], White, Lauryn [3], Goodson, Jacob [4], Leonard-Pingel, Jill [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(2) Department of Biology, Florida Southern College, Lakeland, FL, USA
(3) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(4) Department of Evolution, Ecology and Organismal Biology, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(5) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
abstract:
The Bahamas is projected to experience significant effects of contemporary climate change, such as sea level rise and increased hurricane intensity. There is no precedent to how local terrestrial environments will respond to these predicted climatic shifts, as many Bahamian islands have few, if any, pre-human terrestrial fossil records. Data preceding human influence is important for determining an ecological baseline which can be used to understand how communities shift in response to both natural and anthropogenic factors. Pollen records are direct proxies of plant community shifts throughout time and indirect proxies of local environmental conditions. To determine how Bahamian floral communities have shifted due to environmental flux and anthropogenic stress, we analyzed the pollen record of Poisonwood Blue Hole (PWBH) located on New Providence Island, The Bahamas; creating the first palynological record from this island.

Within the PWBH pollen record, there are four distinct zones defined by differing floral diversity and abundance. The bottom-most zone, beginning ~6500 yBP, is defined by an abundance of the wetland fern Acrostichum aureum and accompanied by hardwood tree species like Swietenia mahagoni and Picrodendron baccatum , suggesting the presence of a wet hardwood coppice. The next zone is defined by the appearance of the freshwater species Sagittaria lancifolia , indicating a permanent flooding of the area by freshwater. The following interval is defined by a shift to overwhelming dominance of Pinus sp ., a well-known signal of initial Lucayan colonization and agricultural burnings. The last zone, defined by the loss of all hardwood species and increase in disturbance species, is representative of European colonization and land clearing. Utilizing this pollen data in conjunction with other proxy records (XRF, LOI, etc.) we are able to define an ecological baseline for New Providence Island, determine the tolerance of the plant community to environmental and anthropogenic stress, and make informed suggestions on potential local conservation efforts.

title: Regional Controls on the Morphology and Activity of Alluvial Fans in the American Bottom, Illinois
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans
authors: Muhlbaum, Lily [1], Constantine, José A. [2], Masteller, Claire [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
abstract: Both active and inactive alluvial fans influence sediment transport, channel avulsion, and flood hazards. Although alluvial fans along the American Bottom of the Upper Mississippi River Valley have long been recognized and mapped, their regional geomorphic characteristics, controlling factors, and modern activity have never been systematically evaluated. We use high resolution LiDAR to develop the first quantitative inventory of alluvial fans across the American Bottom, examining relationships among fan morphology, drainage basin size, spatial distribution, and underlying bedrock. Sediment analyses further constrain sediment transport, depositional history, and present geomorphic activity. Preliminary analyses reveal systematic regional variation in fan morphology and activity that appears to reflect differences in drainage basin characteristics and geologic setting. This regional framework is then applied to an engineered alluvial fan channel to evaluate how culvert construction has altered channel behavior relative to other alluvial fan systems in the American Bottom. By placing this site within its broader geomorphic context, we assess the role of channel avulsion, sedimentation, and infrastructure in generating flood hazards. This work provides the first systematic geomorphic characterization of American Bottom alluvial fans and demonstrates how regional landscape analysis can improve understanding of flood hazards where human infrastructure intersects active alluvial fan systems.

title: Late Ordovician-Early Silurian Orogeny in the Scottish Caledonides: Tectonic Drivers and Models
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Strachan, Rob [1], Kirkland, Chris [2], Lamont, Thomas N. [3], Law, Richard D. [4], Thirlwall, Matthew [5], Hughes, Rosie [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Portsmouth, Portsmouth,

(4) Virginia Polytechnic Institute & State University, Blacksburg, VA,

(6) Dept of Earth Sciences, Royal Holloway University of London, Egham, Surrey, United Kingdom
abstract: Caledonian orogenesis in Scotland and Ireland (Laurentia) has been regarded as due to oceanward SE-directed subduction of Iapetan oceanic lithosphere followed by Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician (c. 490-470 Ma) arc-continent collision and ophiolite obduction. This resulted in regional deformation and Barrovian metamorphism of Dalradian and Moine successions (Grampian orogenic event), as subduction flipped to NW-directed with development of a continental arc on the leading edge of Laurentia (Connemara and NE Scotland) and in the Midland Valley, and the Southern Uplands accretionary prism. Later early Silurian (c. 435-425 Ma) continental collision (Scandian orogenic event) and ductile reworking of the Northern Highland Terrane (NHT) occurred during collision with Baltica. Large-scale sinistral strike-slip along the Great Glen Fault (GGF) then juxtaposed the NHT against the Grampian Terrane (GT) to the southeast. New datasets cast doubt on this two-stage Grampian/Scandian tectonic model. In the NHT, isotopic and microstructural data indicate a prolonged Late Ordovician-Early Silurian orogenic event involving widespread crustal thickening and high-grade metamorphism (up to 740-780°C and 1.0-1.3 GPa) at c. 450 Ma, including displacement along the regionally extensive Sgurr Beag Thrust. New and extant data from the GT identify an important tectonothermal event at c. 450-445 Ma, likely corresponding to upright ‘D3’ folding of Grampian nappes in the northwest of the terrane. Differences in Caledonian orogenic history across the GGF thus appear to be significantly less than previously considered. Baltica is not required as a collider and sinistral megashear models along the North Atlantic Caledonides are thrown into doubt. The Scottish margin of Laurentia must have faced open ocean at c. 450 Ma and hence instead of a collisional model we invoke low-angle (‘flat-slab’) NW-directed subduction of Iapetan lithosphere at c. 450-430 Ma as a driver of crustal thickening across the NHT. The Scottish Caledonides thus evolved between the Late Ordovician and early Silurian as a Cordilleran-style orogen, coeval with the Scandian continental collision between Greenland and Scandinavia along strike to the north, which was more protracted, lasting

title: Constraining the Sources of Calcite in the Ultramafic Lamprophyres of the Western Kentucky Fluorspar District
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics
authors: Anderson, Thomas [1], Dietsch, Craig [2], Widom, Elisabeth [3], Kuentz, David [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA
(2) Department of Geology, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA
(3) Institute for the Environment and Sustainability, Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(4) Institute for the Environment and Sustainability, Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
abstract:
The Western Kentucky Fluorspar District contains REE-enriched alkaline ultramafic lamprophyres that have long been interpreted as possible surface expressions of a deeper carbonatite-related magmatic system. No carbonatite body has been directly confirmed, however, and the origin of calcite in the lamprophyres remains unresolved. Calcite may represent carbonatitic carbonate, carbonate deposited from hydrothermal fluids exsolved from the lamprophyric silicate magma, or secondary carbonate emplaced by regional Mississippi Valley-type basinal brines. Distinguishing among these possibilities is critical because calcite may influence whole-rock trace-element patterns and interpretations of REE enrichment, volatile mobility, and alkaline magmatism in the District.

This study tests calcite origin using Sr-Nd-Pb isotope and trace-metal analyses of calcite separated from texturally distinct vein types. Targeted end-members include diffuse calcite veins/segregations that appear potentially carbonatitic, coarser calcite veins interpreted to be formed from silicate magma-exsolved hydrothermal fluids, and calcite ± fluorite ± sphalerite veins consistent with MVT-style mineralization from regional basinal brines. Calcite was isolated from selected lamprophyre-hosted and crosscutting vein samples through controlled leaching with 2% acetic acid, allowing the carbonate component to be analyzed separately from the silicate-dominated host rock. Initial results show carbonatitic end-members have a Sr isotope ratio ranging from 0.703578 to 0.704798, consistent with mantle values, while the other end-members range from 0.706107 to 0.709506, the latter similar to seawater-precipitated limestones. Trace-metal data will be paired with Sr-Nd-Pb isotope compositions to evaluate whether individual vein types preserve signatures of mantle-like carbonatite, magma-derived fluids, or MVT basinal brines that interacted with carbonate country rock.

By comparing calcite chemistry across these vein-type end-members, our work provides a direct geochemical test of the carbonatite hypothesis in the Western Kentucky Fluorspar District. The results will also clarify how calcite affects interpretations of REE enrichment in alkaline ultramafic rocks and establish a useful procedure for identifying the presence of carbonatite in potentially economically viable REE-enriched igneous systems.

title: Comparison of Photogrammetry, Mobile LiDAR, and Wearable Egocentric Sensing for Three-Dimensional Geological Trench Documentation
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data
authors: Streker, Simon [1], Abbey, Alyssa L. [2], DeTone, Daniel L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, California State University Long Beach, Long Beach, CA, USA
(2) Earth Science, California State University Long Beach, Long Beach, CA, USA
(3) Reality Labs Research, Meta, Redmond, WA, USA
abstract:
3D modeling helps to preserve spatial relationships, stratigraphy, and structure of geological exposures, which may be reexamined post-field work. Recent developments in photogrammetry, mobile Light Detection And Ranging (LiDAR), and egocentric sensing via wearable devices have made 3D reconstruction more efficient and accessible. However, the relative performance of these methods in terms of reconstruction quality, processing efficiency, measurement capability, and field practicality has not been evaluated extensively. We compare 3D models from three methods for collecting and analyzing visual field data from a colluvial fault-trench, and assess relative differences in method useability, efficiency, and quality.

The first method employs photogrammetry in Agisoft Metashape Pro (v2.3.1) from iPad Pro photos, using Structure from Motion (SfM) point clouds to build a 3D mesh. The second method takes advantage of the LiDAR scanner on an iPad Pro with Scaniverse, which builds a 3D Gaussian Splat reconstruction. The third method involves data collection with wearable egocentric smart glasses (Project Aria), which use visual inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (VIO-SLAM) to build a 3D model. Egocentric data from smart glasses such as Project Aria from Meta represent a new class of wearable technology that enables hands-free 3D reconstruction.

The Agisoft Metashape method required long image acquisition and processing times, but successfully aligned all 320 photographs taken and achieved a low 0.853-pixel reprojection error. Agisoft also produced the highest visual fidelity, preserving structure, color contrasts, and legibility of handwritten labels pinned to the trench walls. The Scaniverse method provided the fastest and most intuitive workflow, producing a complete model within minutes and enabling direct distance measurements. However, Scaniverse’s texture resolution was insufficient to clearly resolve the label inscriptions. Collection with Project Aria was the easiest as the wearer can remain hands-free and move around the space naturally. Initial qualitative results from this method show it is capable of generating 3D reconstructions on par with handheld scanning devices.

Future analysis with in-situ field tape measurements will enable comparison of the three methods quantitatively using manual annotated pairwise 3D metric distances marked in the trench wall. Our preliminary comparison shows trade-offs among the three approaches: photogrammetry provides high visual detail, mobile LiDAR enables rapid and intuitive field reconstruction, and wearable egocentric sensing offers flexible hands-free data collection.

abstract:
Subduction-related complexes have the potential to act as geological archives of convergence history in active margins. In the Northern Andes, metamorphic units grouped in the Arquia Complex relate regionally to a subduction complex that records the Cretaceous convergent history in northwestern South America. Two main episodes of metamorphism associated with subduction and collisional tectonic events have been proposed during the Early Cretaceous and Late Cretaceous–Paleocene, however, few attempts have been made to understand the evolution of the metamorphic record associated to these events, especially timing and linkage to P-T conditions.

We present petrography, geochemistry, Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material (RSCM) and in-situ multi-geochronology to characterize the Arquia metamorphic rocks in the western flank of the Central Cordillera of Colombia (Filadelfia-Caldas) and evaluate their implications for the convergence evolution of the Colombian Andes during the Early Cretaceous.

In Filadelfia (Caldas-Colombia), the Arquia Complex comprises metabasic and pelitic schists, and amphibolites associated with serpentinites, exposed along a NNE-trending structural belt. Mafic protoliths are predominantly of MORB affinity. In the southwest, pelitic schists show white mica (Si: 3.4 apfu), quartz and epidote-group minerals, with or without chloritoid, graphite and garnet retrogressed to chlorite, while metabasic shists comprise actinolite, albite, chlorite, occasionally preserving inclusions of garnet and white mica (Si: 3.3–3.4 apfu) within plagioclase porphyroblasts. RSCM yields temperatures between 452–486 °C, indicating low- to moderate-temperature conditions. To the northeast, hornblende and oligoclase-bearing amphibolites record higher metamorphic conditions. In-situ white mica Rb-Sr, titanite U-Pb and garnet Lu-Hf ages from pelitic and metabasic schists in the southwest range within ca. 132–123 Ma, whereas to the northeast pelitic schists and amphibolites yield titanite U-Pb and white mica Rb-Sr ages of ca. 117 and 115 Ma, respectively.

Our data suggest that rocks of the Arquia Complex underwent a diachronous thermal evolution tracking changes in the thermal regime of the subduction zone before Late Cretaceous collision, represented by an event at ca. 132-123 Ma under moderate-temperature conditions, followed by retrogression to lower-temperature conditions. Garnet and white mica inclusions in albite porphyroblasts suggest an earlier growth stage probably associated to higher pressure conditions. To the northeast, amphibolite-facies conditions at ca. 115 Ma suggest a shift toward a hotter thermal regime, possibly associated with a change in the subduction angle and roll back.

title: Tracking the hidden exhumation signals of the Caribbean Plateau collision with the NW South American margin
session_title: Pre–Neogene Tectonic evolution of South America
authors: Zapata Henao, Sebastian [1], Cardona, Agustin [2], Calderon Diaz, Laura Cristina [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Science and Engineering, Universidad del Rosario, Bogotá, Bogotá, Colombia
(2) Processes and Energy, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Medellin, Colombia
(3) School of Science and Engineering, Universidad del Rosario, Bogotá, Colombia
abstract:
Orogenic erosion and the associated rock exhumation are some of the main consequences of upper-crustal deformation and tectonically driven rock uplift. Consequently, thermal histories inferred from thermochronological data have been widely used to reconstruct past deformation events, in which cooling is commonly interpreted as a proxy for rock exhumation. However, not all deformation phases have a clear cooling record. These discrepancies can be related to the lack of vertical block displacements, inefficient erosion, or major modifications of the crustal thermal structure. An example of decoupling between rock cooling and deformation is the collision of the Caribbean Plateau with the NW South American margin, one of the major accretionary events in Andean tectonic history. This collisional event occurred between 72 and 62 Ma, as suggested by pre-collisional and post-collisional magmatism. This event drove a shift from marine to continental sedimentary systems in response to topographic growth, and formed a tectonic suture characterized by embedded blocks of both continental and oceanic crust. Despite the ample geological record of this collision, no significant syn-collisional cooling has been identified in the regional thermochronological record.

This contribution presents a regional compilation of low-temperature thermochronology along the NW South American margin, including newly acquired data from accreted oceanic crust and thermo-kinematic modeling in the northern segment of the Central Cordillera of Colombia. Results reveal only minor, scattered evidence of cooling during the Caribbean Plateau collision. Specifically, the northern segment of the Central Cordillera, adjacent to the accreted basement, presents a unimodal, post-collisional age distribution between 65 and 55 Ma, recorded by multiple low-temperature thermochronometers. Thermo-kinematic modeling suggests that the abundant post-collisional ages may reflect Eocene thermal relaxation and rock cooling following intense advection during the Caribbean Plateau collision, itself driven by fast rock uplift and significant topographic growth. Although these results reveal a thermal consequence of this event, this thermochronological signature cannot be extended to the rest of the orogen, and additional processes or paleogeographic configurations need to be considered.

title: Origin and Development of Terra Rossa Soils of Central Texas
session_title: Karst Sedimentary, Paleoclimate, and Historical Records (Posters)
authors: Oordt, Andrew [1], Soreghan, Gerilyn [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK,
(2) University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK,
abstract:
The karstic Edwards Plateau in Central Texas was covered by a reddish, silty clay soil thought to have developed during the Pleistocene. Today, remnants of this soil mantle exist in discrete patches atop the Cretaceous Edwards and Glen Rose Limestone formations, with erosional remnants also found in the underlying karst. These relict soils share many characteristics with terra rossa soils developed on karstic limestone throughout the Mediterranean region. Previous investigation of the Edwards Plateau red soils inferred an autochthonous origin, derived from in-situ weathering of the Del Rio Formation, a clay-rich unit overlying the Edwards Limestone. However, a potential allochthonous (eolian) parent for these soils is also possible. In this study, we investigate the hypothesis of an eolian origin for these relict soils of the Edwards Plateau. Discriminating between autochthonous and allochthonous origins is important because these soil-forming processes record distinct geomorphic histories and paleoclimatic conditions on the Edwards Plateau.

Here we present initial particle size analysis, geochemistry, and petrographic thin section data. Particle size distributions for two soil profiles show bimodal grain size distributions, with primary modes around 24 µm (silt) and subordinate modes around 0.2 µm (clay). The Del Rio Clay lacks this medium silt fraction, suggesting a different source for the silt. Given the dearth of other local siliciclastic units, eolian contributions remain a possible candidate for the silt. Continued investigation will assess provenance using both bulk geochemistry, and detrital zircon geochronology. Additionally, the soil mineralogy will be analyzed to look at variations in soil weathering history across the region.

The development of deeply weathered soils in Central Texas provides an opportunity to assess the Pleistocene paleoenvironment of the Edwards Plateau. These soils have geoheritage value as they may represent a period of wetter climatic conditions and thus are a physical expression of the climatic history of the region. Additional investigation is warranted to examine the age, weathering history, source, and relationship of the soils to the underlying karst. This study serves as a springboard for deeper investigation of this valuable geoheritage resource.

abstract: Microplastics, defined as anthropogenic polymer particles < 5mm in size, are pervasive in freshwater lakes. This raises concerns for the services lakes provide to ecosystems and communities within their watersheds. Microplastic fibers, alongside manufactured natural fibers, make up the majority of freshwater contamination. These anthropogenic fibers are easy to identify and offer a useful proxy for total microplastic contamination. In this study, we compare three Finger Lakes to assess the influence of watershed development and precipitation by quantifying levels of anthropogenic fiber contamination. Seneca, Hemlock, and Canadice lakes vary in their watershed characteristics, and have different possible sources controlling their anthropogenic fiber abundances. Seneca lake has the most developed watershed, receiving treated wastewater, primary runoff from urban areas, and various human activities. Hemlock and Canadice lakes have forested watersheds and undeveloped shorelines, do not receive treated wastewater, and host limited recreational use. From 2023-2026 water samples were collected from the surface and bottom of each lake’s water column, these samples were then filtered and anthropogenic fibers were identified and quantified. Statistical comparison of the anthropogenic fiber levels in each lake revealed no statistically significant difference (Kruskal Wallis: H = 0.135, p = 0.94). Seneca lake’s median fiber count was 19.4 ± 20 fibers/L, 20 ± 18 fibers/L in Hemlock, and 20 ± 20.5 fibers/L in Canadice. These results show that treated wastewater and watershed development do not positively influence anthropogenic fiber levels in Seneca Lake. In contrast, we found a strong, positive correlation between rainfall and anthropogenic fiber contamination (Pearson’s Correlation: t = 8.86, p < 0.0001). This implies that, in the humid climate of the Finger Lakes region, the atmosphere is the most influential source of a lake’s fiber concentration, rather than the make up of an individual watershed.

abstract: Recovery of ancient DNA directly from sediments ( sed aDNA) complements archaeological science by capturing broad ecosystem level changes and by identifying anthropogenic activity in the absence of preserved fossil material. Despite recently published and ongoing sed aDNA analyses providing novel paleoenvironmental insights, its application to archaeological sites is still in nascent stages. The relationship between DNA preservation and depositional context remains unresolved. Central topics about ancient DNA taphonomy in archaeological contexts include 1) what are the main sources of DNA in terrestrial sediments, 2) to what degree does sed aDNA capture local environmental signals compared to traditional methods of paleoenvironmental reconstruction, and 3) how to identify potential vertical and horizontal movement of DNA molecules within terrestrial deposits? Here, we provide recommendations for applying sed aDNA analysis to archaeological sites using case study evidence from Bluefish Caves, Yukon, Canada to reconstruct changes in floral and faunal community composition during the Pleistocene-Holocene transition. We explain how to collect sediment samples to address different research questions, highlight various methods of data generation and associated bioinformatic challenges, and offer considerations and potential pitfalls when interpreting the sed aDNA signal from archaeological deposits. These novel molecular techniques advance archaeological science and facilitate the growth of geoarchaeology as a field into the future.

title: Timing and Spatial Pattern of Cenozoic Exhumation in the Eastern Tibetan Plateau from Detrital Zircon (U-Th)/He Thermochronology

abstract: The details of the space-time patterns by which the Tibetan Plateau reached its present elevation remain poorly understood. In eastern Tibet, evidence for initial mountain building in Eocene-Oligocene time appears to be localized to fault-bound ranges, whereas rapid cooling and exhumation appear to have been widespread by Miocene time. Here we employ thermochronology of detrital minerals from modern fluvial sediments to estimate first-order patterns of cooling and exhumation from catchments across the eastern plateau margin. We combine a suite of detrital zircon (U-Th)/He ages with thermal modeling to reconstruct cooling and exhumation histories of five tributary catchments spanning from the margin to the interior of the eastern Tibetan Plateau. Detrital age distributions (n = 482 grains) reveal two main cooling phases at ~30–25 Ma and ~10–5 Ma. Thermal modeling indicates that all catchments experienced onset of rapid cooling and exhumation during the Oligocene (typical rates of ~90–240 m/Ma), followed by accelerated exhumation in the Late Miocene (at rates up to ~800–1800 m/Ma). Catchments draining the high relief massifs in the Longmen Shan hinterland record exceptionally high exhumation rates (up to ~1800 m/Ma), likely reflecting focused exhumation during crustal thickening against the margin of the Sichuan Basin. Our results are consistent with initial plateau growth involving upper crustal shortening followed by a transition to distributed deformation associated with lower crustal flow.

title: Building the Grid for Artificial Intelligence: Community Perspectives on Data Center Expansion in Northern Virginia
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Harder, Keira [1], Constantine, José A. [2], Carrasquillo, Anthony J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Studies Program, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
(3) Department of Chemistry, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA; Environmental Studies Program, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
abstract: Northern Virginia has become the world's largest concentration of hyperscale data centers, driving rapid expansion of substations, transmission corridors, and energy infrastructure. While discussions of artificial intelligence often emphasize computing capacity and energy demand, considerably less attention has been paid to how the infrastructure supporting these technologies is reshaping local landscapes, governance, and surrounding communities. This research examines the social and policy dimensions of data center expansion through qualitative interviews with residents, utility representatives, industry representatives, and community advocates in Virginia. Participant observation at stakeholder meetings and field documentation of energy infrastructure complement these interviews. Preliminary findings suggest that conflicts surrounding data center expansion extend beyond electricity demand to encompass competing priorities related to land use, infrastructure planning, public participation, and responsibility for cumulative impacts. Rather than representing a conflict between communities and technology, these findings reveal a complex network of stakeholders navigating rapid technological change within existing systems of land use and energy governance. As artificial intelligence drives unprecedented growth in electricity demand, understanding how communities experience and respond to the expansion of supporting infrastructure will become increasingly important for science-informed policy and long-term energy planning.

title: Science for Hazards, Impact Evaluation, and Long-Term aDaptation (SHIELD): Bridging the Divide Between Geoscience Research and Operations

abstract:
Earth hazards (such as floods, droughts, heatwaves, wildfires, hurricanes, storm surges, sea level, earthquakes, landslides, and volcanic eruptions) have profound impacts on human life and infrastructure. These extreme events sometimes occur together or in sequence (i.e., cascading), exacerbating and prolonging socio-economic impacts. Some Earth hazards can result from chronic conditions or gradual changes, accumulating damage over a long period of time. Others are acute, occurring quickly and seemingly with few warning signs. Understanding, monitoring, predicting, and mitigating these Earth hazards and their associated risks is crucial for society.

The Jackson School is home to many world-leading experts on various aspects of Earth hazards. This new program named: Science for Hazards, Impact Evaluation, and Long-Term aDaptation (SHIELD), aims to improve the collective impact of our research by taking a more integrative approach to understanding the physics of these hazards and how they translate to risks to infrastructure and people. The primary goal of the SHIELD program is to develop lasting mechanisms and platforms for a societally relevant, interdisciplinary Earth hazard research program that reduces the barrier of adoption by operational stakeholders.

The SHIELD program is organized across five Earth hazard themes: hydroclimate extremes, solid earth hazards, wildfires, heatwaves, and coastal hazards. The ultimate goals are to coalesce and amplify current and future Jackson School research into an effective and leading program in understanding Earth hazards and risks. SHIELD will achieve these goals by enhancing Jackson School collaborations, bringing together global leaders and stakeholders (industry, academics, policy makers), and developing pilot research projects related to these hazard themes. The pilot projects are currently under formulation and will leverage the unique and existing Earth hazard science and technological capabilities at the Jackson School to support operational agencies in meeting the challenges of Earth hazard management across the United States and beyond. These pilot projects are co-developed with management agency stakeholders to support decision-making before, during, and after Earth hazards. Through the SHIELD project, with strong cohesion with stakeholders, there is strong potential to increase the impact of research and reduce the burden of adoption for operations.

title: Time Distribution in the Abandoned Channel Belts of the Rio Grande Delta
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Obregon, Annette M [1], Dong, Tian Yang [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environmental, and Marine Sciences, The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Edinburg, TX, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environmental, and Marine Sciences, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Edinburg, TX, USA
abstract: The Rio Grande delta (RGD) in south Texas, USA, and northern Tamaulipas, Mexico, preserves numerous abandoned channel belts, locally known as resacas, that contain many oxbow lakes and record the evolution of the fluvial-deltaic landscape. Despite their abundance, the timing and spatial distribution of channel-belt abandonment remain poorly constrained, limiting our understanding of avulsion dynamics and floodplain evolution for the RGD. Thus, this study investigates the temporal distribution of abandoned channel belts by quantifying the geomorphic characteristics and spatial arrangement of oxbow lakes throughout the RGD, using metrics of normalized oxbow distance, abandonment, and cutoff timescales. High-resolution satellite imagery and digital elevation models were used to map abandoned channels and associated oxbow lakes in the RGD using ArcGIS Pro. For each oxbow lake, geomorphic attributes including centerlines, neck midpoints, endpoints, lengths, nearest-neighbor spacing, distance to the modern active channel, and meander radius were extracted and analyzed. A total of 38 abandoned channel-belt segments were identified, with 17 containing preserved oxbow lakes. Preliminary mapping indicates a greater abundance of oxbows on the northern (U.S.) side of the delta compared to the southern (Mexico) side, suggesting spatial differences in channel-belt preservation and abandonment history. The extracted morphometric dataset is then used to evaluate the spatial organization of oxbow lakes as a proxy for the relative timing of channel-belt abandonment. Distances between neighboring oxbows and their position relative to the active Rio Grande channel belt are compared with theoretical relationships describing meander-belt evolution to reconstruct floodplain time distributions. These analyses provide a quantitative framework for assessing whether channel-belt abandonment occurred as isolated events or in temporally clustered episodes associated with avulsions and channel migration. This work represents the first systematic application of oxbow-lake morphometry and spatial statistics to reconstruct the relative chronology of abandoned channel belts in the RGD, providing new insights into channel migration and floodplain development.

title: Paleo-Depositional Reconstruction of Cockspur Island, Fort Pulaski National Monument.
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling (Posters)
authors: Dahal, Kritik [1], Lo, Edward [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Georgia Southern University, Statesboro, Georgia, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Georgia Southern University, Statesboro, Georgia, USA
abstract:
Sedimentary sequences preserved in fluvial Channel Islands at the marine transition zone provide valuable records of environmental change, sea-level fluctuations, and sediment dynamics. However, the subsurface depositional history of Cockspur Island at Fort Pulaski National Monument, Georgia, remains poorly constrained despite the site's ecological, geological, and archaeological significance. Addressing this knowledge gap raises an important question: How did depositional environments at Cockspur Island change before and after European colonization, and what do these changes reveal about the evolution of the Savannah River Estuary?

A continuous ~3 m sediment core was collected from the southern margin of Cockspur Island using a truck-mounted GeoProbe 5400 direct push system. The core was described, photographed, and subsampled for laboratory analyses in the Sedimentary Environments Analysis Laboratory at Georgia Southern University. Grain-size analysis is being used to identify changes in depositional energy and sediment transport, while total organic carbon (TOC) measurements provide information on organic matter accumulation. Elemental geochemistry determined using energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (ED-XRF) is being used to evaluate variations in sediment composition and possible changes in sediment provenance. Radiocarbon dating will be conducted to establish sediment accumulation rates before and after European settlement and develop a chronological framework for the sediment record.

Initial core descriptions reveal noticeable changes in grain texture, sediment color, and organic-rich intervals, indicating shifts in depositional conditions through time. Ongoing laboratory analyses are integrating sedimentological, geochemical, and chronological datasets to identify changes in tidal influence, marsh development, and estuarine sedimentation. This data will allow interpretation of temporal variations in depositional environments and provide insight into the processes controlling sediment accumulation within this dynamic coastal system.

This study will contribute to a better understanding of late Holocene environmental change along the Georgia coast while providing baseline sedimentological and geochemical data for future research. The results will also support resource management at Fort Pulaski National Monument by improving knowledge of shoreline evolution, marsh stability, and the preservation of culturally significant archaeological resources.

title: Mining Heritage in the United States
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Casadevall, Thomas [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Advisory Group for Geoheritage, Lakewood, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The United States is a country with great geodiversity, expressed in its range and age of rock types, mineral deposits, fossils, soils, landforms, and geological processes from glaciation to tectonism, and from volcanism to fluvial and wind erosion. Where this geodiversity is revealed or expressed in unique ways, we recognize its heritage values- geoheritage – and we select these features, deposits, and processes for geoconservation, and manage these elements of geodiversity for these geoheritage values. The United States has a long history dealing with mining heritage as well as with conservation of previously mined areas.

“Mining heritage” is a term which has come into increased usage over the past several decades. “Mining heritage can be defined as the set of immovable and movable structures, documents, objects and intangible elements linked to past mining activities, to which a broad social group attributes historical, cultural or social values. Apart from its undeniable link with the geological heritage, since mining operations are developed on mineral deposits and rocks, this statement implies connections with both the historical, archaeological and industrial heritage, as well as with economic, technological and social history." (Carcavilla et al, 2007, 2019)

In the United States, the term “mining heritage” is used broadly to include sites, features, and areas with mining activity in the past up to the present day with the focus on the historical, industrial, economic, and cultural aspects of this heritage (Twitty, 2002). Conservation of the geoheritage values of mining areas or environments has generally not been included as a part of “mining heritage”. More recently concepts of geoheritage and geodiversity have been linked to mining heritage in the U.S. and principles and best practices of geoconservation (Henriques et al, 2011; Gordon, 2019; Crofts et al, 2020; Gordon et al, 2021) can be applied to the recovery, reclamation, and restoration of mining environments. Thus “mining geoheritage” in the United States expands the more traditional definitions of “mining heritage” found in wide use elsewhere in the World. In this session we explore from the U.S. perspective how the principles and practices of geoconservation are being introduced to recovery, restoration, and reclamation of mined landscapes and how scientific discoveries related to mining underpin our modern understanding of mining heritage.

abstract:
The Spirit Lake tectonic zone (SLTZ) forms the southern boundary of much of the Superior Province, juxtaposing Archean crust on the north with Paleoproterozoic crust on the south. The western Spirit Lake tectonic zone (WSLTZ) is informally defined as that portion of the SLTZ extending from the 1.1 Ga Midcontinent Rift System (MRS) on the east to the ~2.0-1.8 Ga Trans-Hudson orogen on the west. The WSLTZ region is thought to have significant potential for undiscovered deposits of critical minerals, including Ni-Cu-PGE-Co sulfides, Fe-Ti-V oxides, and REE-bearing carbonatites, among other deposit types. However, the Archean and Proterozoic rocks of interest are entirely concealed beneath hundreds of meters of sedimentary cover, and previous mapping studies were hampered by the low quality of public aeromagnetic data. To address mapping needs, a very large (274,100 line km, covering ~100,000 km 2 ) aeromagnetic survey sponsored by the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) was flown in 2023-2024 with 400 m line spacing and 100 m nominal terrain clearance.

Here, we highlight several aeromagnetic anomalies of interest. The WSLTZ is characterized by numerous subparallel, northeast-trending gradients, pattern breaks, and elongated anomalies that are likely produced by faults and crudely aligned dikes. Archean rocks north of the WSLTZ include many strongly magnetized intrusions and produce generally stronger anomalies than Paleoproterozoic rocks to the south. A suspected Mesoproterozoic massif-type anorthosite complex positioned along the WSLTZ near Spencer, Iowa, produces complex magnetic lows and highs. Along the South Dakota-Nebraska border a series of complex, high-amplitude anomalies are crudely aligned with the WSLTZ trend, likely produced by a large volume of poorly understood mafic/ultramafic intrusive rocks. The Sioux Falls area is characterized by smooth anomalies produced by thick, weakly magnetic Sioux Quartzite overlying deeply buried magnetic rocks. Across the survey region, Mesoproterozoic granitoids intruding Paleoproterozoic rocks south of the WSLTZ produce numerous sub-circular highs. Smooth anomalies lie over MRS flanking basins along the eastern and southeastern margins of the survey area, reflecting deep burial of magnetic crystalline rocks under weakly magnetized MRS sedimentary rocks. Rocks of the Trans-Hudson orogen produce relatively gentle, northwest-trending anomalies in the western part of the survey area, west of Yankton, SD.

abstract: Reduced oxygen availability and increased metabolic demand caused by climate warming are known to compress animal habitat during mass extinctions but the role of this mechanism during cooling intervals remains uncertain. The Late Devonian Kellwasser Event (~372 Ma) provides a test of whether physiological traits can be used to estimate extinction if deoxygenation is instead driven by enhanced nutrient loading and accompanied by global cooling. We identified candidate Kellwasser environmental transitions by evaluating the skill of Earth system model simulations spanning a range of atmospheric CO₂ concentrations and marine phosphorus inventories in reconstructing geochemical proxy records of subsurface regional hypoxia (I/Ca) and global marine anoxic extent (δ 238 U). For each valid pair of simulations fitting background and Kellwasser states, extinction was predicted quantitatively using the Metabolic Index, a measure of environmental oxygen supply to demand. The model-predicted genus-level latitudinal extinction gradients were compared with observed gradients calculated from Paleobiology Database fossil occurrence data. The best-supported transitions (i.e., extinction scenarios) are, on average, characterized by ~6 °C of global cooling and a ~1.5× increase in marine phosphorus inventory, consistent with independent proxy estimates. Enhanced nutrient loading expanded tropical deoxygenation while cooling increased dissolved oxygen concentrations at higher latitudes. The observed homogenous ~ 45% genus extinction intensity across sampled latitudes can be explained by temperature-dependent physiological constraints and biogeography. These results strengthen the case that physiological traits and biogeography link climate change to extinction selectivity across Earth’s history.

title: Too much of a good thing: stability-reducing strategies in cephalopod evolution
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Peterman, David Joseph [1], Anderson, Tasha Jane [2], Coppess, Caleb [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA

abstract: Over the last half a billion years, cephalopods have experimented with incredibly disparate morphologies. Each morphology expresses distinct hydromechanical properties that fundamentally constrain life habits and ecology. The earliest neutrally buoyant cephalopods had conical shells that distributed the air chambers (phragmocone) above the soft body. This configuration optimally separates organismal mass from the center of buoyancy, producing a highly stable condition (i.e., hydrostatic stability several orders of magnitude higher than most fish to ever exist). This condition generates a large restoring torque that resists change in orientation due to 1) external forms of energy, and 2) energy generated by their own jet thrust (the latter allowing a wider swath of jetting angles that produce backwards movement). However, this condition also reduces maneuverability and can restrict specific swimming strategies, presenting a classic functional tradeoff. Throughout the Paleozoic and Mesozoic, cephalopods displayed several evolutionary trajectories, which have been historically interpreted as attempts to reduce hydrostatic stability and improve maneuverability. These strategies are briefly summarized in the following categories: 1) counterweights in the form of cameral deposits (Orthoceratoidea), endosiphuncular deposits (Endocerida), and belemnite rostra, 2) dorsally distributed buoyancy apparatuses (e.g., Ascocerida and cuttlefish), 3) increased conch coiling (e.g., early ammonoid evolution), and 4) reduction and removal of the conch, entirely (e.g., Coleoidea). We evaluate these strategies using computer reconstructions and hydrostatic modeling. We find that the internalized counterweights, like cameral and endosiphuncular deposits, do not reduce stability beyond any meaningful threshold (under most conditions). Dorsally distributing the buoyancy apparatus can considerably reduce stability while producing more horizontal postures (to varying extents). Conch coiling can considerably reduce stability, but only if the whorl expansion rate is low. Finally, the air-filled buoyancy apparatus is roughly three orders of magnitude less dense than any other organismal component, and strongly repels the center of mass. Thus, simultaneously removing denser shell and the air-filled voids considerably reduces stability, improves maneuverability, and enables an entirely different range of swimming strategies.

abstract: Aeolian and coastal processes interact to shape the near-shore landscape. Although previous work has focused on beach dune systems, the role of aeolian processes in other coastal environments, particularly river deltas, remains limited. As river deltas are critical landscapes for humans and ecosystems, understanding the potential impact of wind on sediment deposition and erosion will shed light on the mechanics of delta evolution. This study examines the characteristics of lunette dunes (locally known as lomas ) on the Holocene Rio Grande Delta (RGD) plain, using remote sensing and field observations. We hypothesize that these dunes form through wind deflation of hypersaline tidal flats and shallow bays formed between abandoned RGD channels. These lakes are thought to be inundated primarily during extreme tides and runoff events, but experience prolonged dry periods, during which the lake beds act as a local sediment source for the formation? of lomas . Holocene sea-level rise likely increased the inundation periods, reducing sediment available for loma stabilization. To test these hypotheses, we mapped 195 dunes in the RGD via satellite imagery and a LiDAR-derived elevation model. The lomas have a mean area and volume of 3.11 x 10 2 ±2.869 x 10 2 km 2 and 1.14 x 10 3 ±1.34 x 10 3 km 3 (±1σ), respectively. Lomas were classified based on their relationship to nearby lakes, with single lomas being one dune per lake, and compound lomas being two or more dunes per lake. Their relationship to nearby lakes classified Lomas as single (one dune per lake) or compound (two or more dunes per lake). A volume-based sediment budget indicates that ~60% of dune sediment could originate from the lakes, supporting our hypothesis. Five accessible lomas were sampled for grain size and dated with 14 C and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL). Grain-size results support previous interpretations, with lomas consisting primarily of silt (~40%), 8–27% clay, and up to 35% sand, with a median grain size of 10–40 μm. 14 C and OSL ages indicate that deposition of the lomas occurred between 700 and 3300 years BP. Field observations suggest that, at present, these landforms are stabilized by vegetation but are susceptible to localized reworking through gully erosion. These findings indicate that aeolian processes have been an important driver influencing sediment redistribution of the Holocene RGD.

title: The influence of metal cations and organic molecules in calcium carbonate biomineralization

affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Division of Natural and Built Environments, University of Missouri-Kansas City, Kansas City, Missouri, USA

abstract:
Anthropogenic environmental changes threaten the stability of calcium carbonate biominerals (e.g. aragonite, calcite, and sometimes vaterite) that organisms utilize to construct shells and endo/exoskeletons. These minerals preserve geochemical signatures of past environmental conditions, which makes understanding the factors that govern formation critical. This study investigates how the incorporation of metal cations and the development of mineral-organic composites may influence mineralogy, composition, morphology, and stability of calcium carbonate biominerals. A suite of calcium carbonate mineral, including calcite, aragonite and vaterite, was synthesized using varying concentration of Mg, Mn, and Co in combination with amino acids and chitin. Mineralogical, quantitative compositional, and spatial characterization were performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS), and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES).

Comparable saturation states of calcite and aragonite were set across all experimental conditions. Metal cation incorporation exerted strong influences on crystal precipitation kinetics, morphology, and unit cell parameters. Mg promoted aragonite formation, and Mn and Co ions preferentially incorporated into calcite-structures at an accelerate rate, producing characteristics of diffusion-controlled growth. Presence of amino acid modulated precipitation through increase nucleation density and produced smaller, less euhedral crystals with higher densities of growth hillocks, spiral steps, and additional crystallographic faces. Additionally, differing amino acid incorporation has resulted in a mineralogical variation with the development of vaterite, a metastable calcium carbonate phase. This suggests the carbonate mineral growth is not solely controlled by thermodynamics, but also kinetics processes, which are influenced by the various functional groups of organic compounds and presence of different cations. These results demonstrate that the coupled effects of metal cations and organic molecules controls carbonate mineral phase, composition, and morphology. This work provides new insights into biomineralization processes, improves interpretation of carbonate biominerals as paleoenvironmental archives, and informs the development of carbonate-based bioremediation strategies under changing environmental conditions.

abstract: New research suggests Uranus’s moon Ariel once hosted, or may still contain, a deep subsurface ocean beneath its icy crust. Does this result, if confirmed, require tidal friction as a source of heating within Ariel? We analyzed more than 1,300 3D thermal evolution calculations consistent with Ariel and, vary the radius of the ice-rock boundary, density of the ice shell and rocky core, and initial temperature, while using the present-day mass, moment of inertia, and surface deformation history of Ariel as constraints. Beginning from a differentiated state with a rocky core, holding all the radiogenic elements, and (possibly) convecting icy mantle, find that many of the calculations have a temperature at the base of the mantle (CMB) exceeding the freezing point of water ice, consistent with a subsurface ocean during their evolution and 21 have CMB temperature exceeding the melting point of water ice after 4.5 Ga of model time, consistent with recent findings of a deep subsurface ocean. These all have moment of inertia factors less than 0.3. As a rule, a present-day subsurface ocean more likely with a higher initial temperature and larger ice-shell viscosity. The effect of core size is less obvious, while this increases the total amount of heat producing elements, it also reduces the likelihood of ice-shell convection that could draw heat away from the core. Models where the ice-shell never convects are likely to have internal temperatures above the melting point of water ice yet are inconsistent with the proposed young cryovolcanic features as well as the possible existence of endogenic chemical species at the surface of Ariel. Models with active ice shell convection, while consistent with surface deformation, do not have present day oceans. Models with surface deformation and present-day oceans remain elusive.

title: Mining Heritage and San Juan County, Colorado – engagement at the community level
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Rich, Beverly [1], Jones, William [2], Fetchenhier, Scott [3], Casadevall, Thomas [4]
affiliations: (1) San Juan County Historical Society, Silverton, Colorado, USA
(2) San Juan County Historical Society, Silverton, Colorado, USA

abstract:
The San Juan Mountains of southwestern Colorado represent a major Oligocene-Pliocene volcanic province. Their rich metallic ore veins have produced over $500 million in gold, silver, and other metals since the late 19th century. Geological research here has advanced our understanding of Western Cordillera tectonic development, volcanology, hydrothermal mineral deposits, and the cultural history of the American West. Efforts to preserve this unique geological and mining heritage include various formal designations, ranging from individual historic structures to the entire Town of Silverton, which became a National Historic Landmark District in 1961.

In 1964, the San Juan County Historical Society was founded to collect, preserve, display, and interpret the region’s past. Today, it operates the non-profit San Juan County Mining Heritage Center across three main facilities:

· Mining Museum: Houses an array of local historical and mining artifacts.

· Archive Building: Preserves photographs, correspondence, and mining maps. Subsurface and geological maps are actively being digitized to assist with modern environmental remediation.

· Mayflower Mill: A 1929 ore-processing facility designated as a National Historic Landmark, offering tours featuring original processing equipment and an aerial tramway.

The region is accessible via two national scenic byways—the Alpine Loop and the San Juan Scenic Byway. Another prominent attraction is the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, which has operated continuously since 1882. Originally built to transport supplies in and ore out, it now serves as a scenic tourist route following the decline of mining in the mid-20th century. Visitors can also experience underground operations and historic equipment at the Old Hundred Gold Mine Tour. A recent educational program is the effort to archive and digitize surface and subsurface maps from mines in the district. Geological and engineering maps - especially from the subsurface – are proving to be a key contribution to addressing some of the modern environmental impacts of the mines.

Together, these attractions illustrate the complete economic system that sustained the region from the 1870s until the final mine closed in 1991. Since active mining has ceased, tourism centered on geoheritage and historical sites has become the area's primary economic engine. However, maintaining these assets remains challenging due to high upkeep costs and environmental remediation efforts that risk altering or erasing historic mining features.

abstract:
Rolfe Mandel is best known for his work on soils and geomorphology at archaeological sites across the globe, but his wide range of research interests and professional connections have ensured that he is never at a loss for odd jobs to offer his numerous graduate students. This is how I ended up studying proboscideans and paleoenvironments in the Big Bend Region (BBR) of southwest Texas as Rolfe’s umpteenth “final” PhD student. Under Rolfe’s mentorship, I have learned that there are many ways to understand the archaeological record and the people that created it through geoarchaeology. In the absence of abundant archaeological evidence, one can turn to the accompanying geologic, paleoenvironmental, and paleontological records to understand the environmental parameters set on peoples of the past, which influenced settlement and subsistence opportunities.

Recent archaeological investigations by the Center for Big Bend Studies and the Odyssey Archaeological Research Program at the Genevieve Lykes Duncan site have confirmed a deeply buried Clovis component at ~12,800 cal. BP in the BBR. This is the first buried Early Paleoindian site in the region, confirming human presence in the BBR during the terminal Pleistocene. This discovery warrants an investigation of Big Bend proboscideans as a high-value resource for early peoples in the region. In addition to a characterization of proboscidean paleobiology in the region, stable isotopic data derived from dated animal bone specimens will inform on environmental conditions in the BBR during the terminal Pleistocene. Here, I will present preliminary results of my dissertation project and discuss how Rolfe’s mentorship has enabled me to conduct research that I am truly passionate about.

abstract:
This study evaluates the potential of geological H 2 systems across Texas using numerous remote sensing and in situ data. Co-existing H­­ 2 -relevent generating rocks, reservoirs, seals, timing relationships, depth, and temperature conditions were assessed from an exceptional volume of surface and subsurface data, including well gas analyses, seismic and geophysical surveys, and characterization of igneous and basement rocks. These conditions were integrated using Boolean logic and weighted subcomponent analysis to generate statewide prospectivity maps. Overall, geological H 2 potential was found to concentrate in West and North Texas where source rocks (iron- and radiogenic-rich) coincide with favorable reservoir and seal lithologies.

Following the identification of potential H 2 systems, soil gas surveys were conducted across major structural features of West Texas. These surveys highlighted surface anomalies along the footwall of the Ouachita Thrust Belt in the Marathon region, along Pecos intrusion-rooted faults, and above thinner evaporite sequences in the Delaware basin. The basement in these regions comprises of a complex assemblage of Fe-rich igneous and metamorphic Mesoproterozoic lithologies that are hypothesized to favor H 2 generation through hydration reactions involving Fe 2+ oxidation (e.g., serpentinization and arfvedsonite oxidation), as well as radiolysis. These regions highlight the potential migration and trapping interactions that could promote the generation of a geological H 2 resource. Results from the Franklin Mountains and Llano Uplift, also revealed promise for geological H 2 generation. However, the potential source rocks are at significantly shallow depths, limiting the potential for geological H 2 reservoir generation. Alternatively, the shallow source depth allows analysis into the ability for continued H 2 production and flux rate in the future.

Work is ongoing to expand our ability to detect surface seeps across Texas using remote sensing datasets including satellite-based infrared spectroscopy and Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), and seismic interpretation to identify sub-circular depressions (SCDs). It is hoped that these analyses, along with long-term monitoring to assess temporal (diurnal and seasonal) variations, will better constrain the link of surface expressions to the subsurface H 2 system. These investigations provide new insights into the subsurface potential for geological H 2 in Texas and establish a framework for future exploration of emerging geological hydrogen systems.

title: Cooling-Controlled Aqueous Mineral Evolution and the Retreat of Habitable Environments on Mars
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Liu, Jiacheng [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Please Select State, China; Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island, USA
abstract:
The Martian surface records a broad temporal mineralogical transition from early clay minerals, through middle-aged sulfates, to young ferric phases and associated hydrated minerals. This sequence has traditionally been attributed to progressive environmental drying and/or oxidation. Here, I emphasize that long-term climate cooling, through its control on the phase state, mobility, and reactivity of water, played a first-order role in governing the style of water–rock interaction and, consequently, the evolutionary trajectory of hydrated minerals throughout Martian history. Within this framework, clay minerals primarily formed via subaerial, top-down chemical weathering under warm climatic conditions (T > 0°C) on early Mars; sulfates predominantly resulted from freeze–thaw cycles at low-latitude to equatorial regions (T ≈ 0°C) on middle-aged Mars; and young ferric phases, along with associated hydrated minerals, likely originated from (ground) ice–magma/volcano interactions on young Mars under frigid climate (T < 0°C). This staged mineral evolution not only records the trajectory of surface temperature decrease on Mars, but its associated evolving pattern of water–rock interaction also implies a progressive retreat of habitable aqueous environments into the subsurface over time.

abstract:
Groundwater from private domestic wells is an important source of drinking water for many rural communities in Kansas, yet these wells are not routinely monitored for contaminants. Agricultural activities, including fertilizer application, livestock operations, and septic systems, have contributed to elevated nitrate concentrations in groundwater throughout agricultural regions, posing potential risks to human health and water quality (Singh & Craswell, 2021; Nolan & Hitt, 2006). Chloride is also a useful indicator of anthropogenic impacts on groundwater and can help identify contamination pathways associated with agricultural and human activities.

This study evaluated nitrate and chloride concentrations in private domestic wells in Ellis, Kansas, to establish baseline groundwater quality conditions. Groundwater samples were collected from private wells throughout the study area and analyzed for nitrate and chloride concentrations. The resulting data were compared with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency drinking water standards and evaluated to identify patterns in groundwater quality across the region.

This investigation established a baseline assessment of groundwater quality in Ellis, Kansas, that can serve as a point of reference for future monitoring of seasonal variability and long-term changes associated with land use and climatic conditions. The study contributes to a better understanding of groundwater vulnerability in a semi-arid agricultural region and provides information that may assist private well owners, local communities, and resource managers in protecting groundwater resources and guiding future monitoring efforts.

abstract: Subaqueous dunes are prevalent throughout fluvial-tidal transitions and thus dictate channel bed bathymetry and the character of subsurface deposits. Their size, shape, and scale depend on flow characteristics (magnitude, duration, and style) and sediment transport mode (bedload vs suspended load dominated). Thus, varying combinations of sediment size and flow type (unidirectional, oscillatory, bidirectional) lead to changes in the mode of sediment transport, which is reflected in dune morphology and preserved cross-strata. Most riverine and fluvial-tidal transition studies have only investigated dune morphology and have ignored linking how their morphology may be reflected in their preserved cross-strata and if these deposits provide a unique signature that can be used to identify changes in flow and sediment dynamics. Therefore, this study aims to identify how changes in the morphology of dunes affect preserved cross-strata within a fluvial-tidal transition. To accomplish this, we utilize high-resolution multi-beam bathymetric maps in conjunction with subbottom (parametric echosounder) seismic data to compare the morphology of fluvial-tidal dunes with the geometries of their recent subsurface deposits.

abstract: Early eukaryotic fossils, including non-biomineralizing macroalgae, provide important constraints on Proterozoic marine ecosystems. However, macroalgal fossils are rarely preserved with enough morphological characters to assess their taxonomic affinity. The ca. 950 Ma Dolores Creek Formation of the Mackenzie Mountains Supergroup (Yukon, Canada) contains macroalgal fossils including Archaeochaeta guncho at two different sites. The sites are 10 km apart and represent different paleoenvironments. Hematite Creek North has higher oxygen availability and a depositional environment above the shelf break while the fossils recovered at Hematite Creek South were deposited below storm wave base. Here, we evaluate how paleoenvironmental conditions influence the preservation and composition of the two fossil assemblages. Each assemblage includes over 300 individuals with A. guncho as the most abundant taxa while the other fossils differ between sites. A new, unnamed macrofossil that could represent cyanobacteria or macroalgae has been identified at only at one site. Scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy demonstrate that preservation by pyritization and clay templating is common at both sites. However, the quality of the preservation and abundance of holdfasts preserved differs between sites, suggesting different taphonomic pathways. These differences are interpreted as driven by local paleoenvironmental conditions including variation in oxygen availability and amount of clastic sediment deposition during fossil burial. Investigating the preservation of macroalgal assemblages will help to further untangle ecological from taphonomic trends during the expansion of eukaryotic life in the Tonian Period.

abstract:
Improvements in thermodynamic databases and accompanying software over the last two decades has led to the widespread use of programs like Gibbs, Perple_X, Theriak-Domino and Thermocalc to calculate mineral equilibria in rocks. These programs are now routinely used to estimate the mineral assemblages, modes, and compositions present as a rock migrates along a P-T path during metamorphism. However, the equilibrium thermodynamic approach does not provide insight into the meaning of the wide variety of sizes and spatial distributions of minerals that are present in metamorphic rocks. These textural patterns are related to kinetic processes that govern the nucleation and growth (or dissolution) of metamorphic minerals in response to rates of change in temperature (T), pressure (P) and composition (X) as metamorphism proceeds. Variation of dT/dt, dP/dt, and/or dX/dt in a rock influence crystal size distributions by controlling mineral nucleation rates, transport between reaction sites, and reaction rates during metamorphism. Simple kinetic relationships can be used to model these processes and gain insight into how they behave in a rock following a particular P-T-t path. The procedure allows investigation of constraints such as rapid vs slow reaction-overstepping, wet vs dry grain-boundaries, metastable vs equilibrium reactions, and nucleation patterns as a function of dT/dt, dP/dt, or dX/dt.

The technique will be illustrated by forward modelling metapelites crossing the garnet, staurolite and aluminum-silicate isograds along several different P-T-t paths. Each path specifies rates of overstepping (dT/dt + dP/dt) for each isograd, allowing the interplay between nucleation rate, material transport, and reaction affinity to be examined for each mineral as metamorphism progresses. The calculated size and position of each garnet, staurolite and aluminum-silicate in three-dimensional rock volumes are tracked continually along the P-T-t path as the model proceeds. Visual output is in the form of time-series videos that show how textures develop in 2-D cross-sections of the rock volume. This mimicks a thin-section view of minerals as they grow or dissolve along a specified P-T-t path. Final output includes the size and position of all minerals in the 3-D volume. Comparison of modelled textures with those from real rocks provides a tool to investigate overstepping rates as isograds are crossed along a proposed P-T path.
