title: Appalachian Pasts, Arctic Futures: Lessons from Frozen Critical Zones
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution
authors: Del Vecchio, Joanmarie [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
abstract:
Climate influences the evolution of Earth's critical zone by modulating temperature and moisture in rock and soil, which in turn control chemical and physical weathering and biota. However, due to the frequency of Quaternary climate shifts and the integrative nature of the critical zone, isolating and quantifying evidence for temperature control on long-term landscape evolution remains challenging. Here I will present data from both modern and ancient permafrost landscapes demonstrating the unique control that temperature exerts on hydrology, erodibility, and hillslope form in both the Arctic and mid-latitude sites adjacent to former ice sheets.

In Arctic landscapes, we show that hillslope flux from solifluction and inhibited incision from frozen ground together reduce drainage density and store carbon on permafrost hillslopes, and warming is likely to instigate channel network expansion and carbon release. I show that we can infer changes to thermal and hydrological conditions in the subsurface via satellite-derived vegetation indices, coupled with field observations of vegetation and temperature, allowing us to remotely monitor these critical zones. I connect the processes active on modern permafrost landscapes to the legacy of periglaciation south of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, where ancient critical zones can be reconstructed from cored sediments. I show that high regolith production from frost cracking and increased hillslope flux during thaw influence hillslope morphology and erosion rate, and that structurally controlled basins in Appalachia record ecological and landscape response to the Pleistocene-Holocene transition.

title: Using Hydrochemical Trends to Evaluate the Hydraulic Effects of Aquifer Depletion in the Middle Claiborne Aquifer, Mississippi Embayment Aquifer System

authors: seck, Sophia [1], Befus, Kevin M. [2], Ruhl-Whittle, Laura [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences Department, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Geosciences Department, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi Gulf Water Science Center, Fayetteville, Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA; Geosciences Department, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract:
The Mississippi embayment aquifer system underlies a large region of the south-central United States and supports groundwater use for agriculture, industry, and public supply. In this region, groundwater withdrawals have increased substantially over the past century, contributing to aquifer depletion and groundwater-level decline across several major aquifers. The Middle Claiborne aquifer, often referred to as the Sparta or Memphis Sand aquifer, is an important groundwater resource within the Mississippi embayment and has experienced long-term groundwater-level decline in response to intensive pumping. Because much of the region depends on groundwater for irrigation and water supply, pumping-driven depletion may affect not only groundwater availability but also groundwater quality. Although previous studies show that aquifer depletion and intensive pumping can alter groundwater chemistry, identifying the connection between depletion and observed chemical changes at specific locations remains challenging. Similar hydrochemical trends can result from different hydrogeologic processes, including saline or mineralized water migration, mixing of recharge with deeper or adjacent groundwater, or pumping-driven flow-path changes that shorten groundwater residence time and reduce water-rock interaction.

In this study, we investigate chemical observations from roughly 2,500 wells sampled between 1940 - 2026 to determine whether groundwater chemistry changes significantly through time and to identify how groundwater chemistry is affected by groundwater withdrawals. Groundwater-chemistry data from the U.S. Geological Survey’s Water Data for the Nation are combined with modeled drawdown and groundwater-flow information from the USGS Mississippi Embayment Regional Aquifer Study (MERAS) groundwater-flow model. We evaluate hydrochemical indicator groups associated with saline or mineralized-water migration, geochemical evolution and deeper groundwater mixing, and recharge or shorter-residence-time conditions. These indicators are evaluated alongside modeled drawdown, particle-tracking analysis, and statistical tests using a multiple-lines-of-evidence approach. By linking water-chemistry patterns with hydrologic change, this study identifies where groundwater chemistry is changing through time and where aquifer-depletion processes are most consistent with the observed spatial and temporal patterns.

abstract:
The Brule Spillway (Brule) and St. Croix River valley (St. Croix) were meltwater pathways for the retreating Laurentide Ice Sheet and several proglacial lakes following the last glacial maximum in the Lake Superior (LSB) and upper Mississippi River basins (UMR), USA. Significantly, these systems drained proglacial lakes in the western LSB and the ambiguous Glacial Lake Grantsburg (GLG). Building upon decades of deglaciation research and mapping, we address the remaining uncertainty regarding timing, frequency, magnitude, and geomorphic effect of meltwater discharge events. We synthesize prior data with new LiDAR-based DEM analysis, ground-penetrating radar (GPR) surveys, and geochronological data (OSL and cosmogenic nuclide depth profiles). With these multiple data sources, we elucidate morpho-stratigraphic relationships, interpret sedimentary structures, and constrain the sequence of deglacial drainage events.

Initially, the Brule aggraded outwash across its modern location. Subsequently, Brule incision produced inset terraces constrained by OSL between ~15.7 ±1.75 and 13.5 ±1.79 ka. We hypothesize these terraces correlate to Brule base level lowering as GLG levels fluctuated downstream. Prior to 13.5 ka, we interpret a basin-scale erosional event, consistent with results from prior work. This event deeply truncated GLG deposits and underlying till. We speculate this resulted from final drainage of GLG scouring the landscape, supported by geochronologic and morphologic data from high-magnitude flood landscapes downstream. Subsequently, an alluvial fan prograded ~130 km from the Brule to the southwest, partially refilling (5-30 m aggradation) the St. Croix between 13.5 and 12.1 ±2.2 ka, possibly as late as 10.9 ±1.1 ka (this study; Young 2008). Renewed incision abandoned this fan 20-30 m above the valley floor. The Lake View/Marquette glacial readvance (~11.5 cal yr BP; Lowell et al., 1999) likely dammed the Brule. Subsequent retreat permitted high-magnitude drainage, potentially followed by sustained drainage, until lower, eastern outlets opened. It is likely this final drainage carved much of the St. Croix below the aggradational fan, including the famous St. Croix Dalles and its’ potholes. A 14C date (~10.3 cal yr BP; Blumentritt et al., 2009) in wood atop gravels in UMR provides a minimum-limiting age for this final excavation of the St. Croix. This study reveals the inherent complexity in understanding outburst floods and ice-marginal landscapes.

abstract: The type locality for the Irvingtonian North American Land Mammal Age (1.8 mya - 250 kya) was once an active gravel quarry in what is now Fremont, CA. Much of the quarry was leveled in the late 1960’s by the state of California to construct the I-680 freeway. This halted any future paleontological or geological investigation. Although the assemblage of mammalian megafauna was described in great detail, their remains were not collected with precise stratigraphic information. Biostratigraphic correlation with related deposits is presently near impossible, which obscures a more complete understanding of megafaunal evolution and extinction in Northern California. Additionally, invertebrate and plant fossils that may have provided further insights on paleoclimate and paleoecology were not described and many recovered specimens have been lost. These factors contribute to limited perspectives on how ecosystems in the San Francisco Bay Area changed through the Pleistocene. Here, we report a section of the original quarry that was rediscovered by comparing historical photographs, aerial images, and geologic maps. This section represents pit 4 of the original quarry, which remains exposed and continues to yield scientifically significant fossils. However, pit 1 is a major locality that is on private land and currently at risk of being sold to developers. For the continuation of active research and natural resource protection, we propose recreating an active dig site and constructing a new facility dedicated to California’s natural history. The property with the exposed section contains a warehouse that would provide ample collections space for new, stratigraphically collected specimens from the proposed dig site. The University of California Museum of Paleontology (UCMP) possesses a large collection of the Irvington fauna and many other central California fossils, which would be the basis of exhibits in the proposed museum. Partnership between multiple organizations (Math Science Nucleus, UCMP, California Natural Resources Agency, Cal Trans) and funding from outside sources are required to realize this project. The construction of a proposed fossil museum emphasizing the Irvington type locality presents endless opportunities for paleontological research, education and outreach, and careers for geobiologists in one of the most populated regions in the world.

title: Brittle Fault Slip Analysis and Kinematic Availability Assessment of Laramide Faults to Determine the Influence of Precambrian Structures in the Black Hills, South Dakota
session_title: From outcrop to orogen—field-based perspectives on stratigraphy, structural geology, and mineral resources in the Rocky Mountain region—a session in honor of David A. Lindsey
authors: Tyler, Niah [1], Waldien, Trevor Scott [2], Katzenstein, Kurt W. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA

abstract: The Black Hills in western South Dakota are the product of older Precambrian suturing and intracratonic extension events as well as a younger Paleogene uplift known as the Laramide orogeny. The general structural style of the Laramide orogeny takes on the form of thick-skinned deformation and basement-cored uplifts, which the Black Hills exhibit. It remains debated as to whether the Precambrian structures influenced the mode of uplift in the Black Hills, and there are currently no published studies describing the slip sense of eastern brittle faults in the Precambrian core. However, there are mapped brittle faults on the eastern side of the basement core with reverse sense of motion that cut the Phanerozoic strata and the Great Unconformity, suggesting that Laramide deformation interacted with these Precambrian faults. We used brittle fault slip analysis to test the hypothesis that Precambrian faults were reactivated during the Laramide orogeny in the Black Hills. We also investigated the influence of select fault surfaces, and their associated discontinuities, on the kinematic availability of multiple slope failure mechanisms. Preliminary results include a NE-SW shortening direction on reverse slip fault surfaces, which is compatible with the Laramide stress field. Many fault surfaces also exhibited both older normal brittle slip indicators and younger reverse slip indicators, providing further evidence for fault reactivation. Preliminary kinematic availability assessments yielded that subvertical NW-SE fractures present on slip surfaces are susceptible to toppling failure. This structural data contributes to the understanding of the formation and existing hazards posed by brittle faults in the Black Hills.

abstract: Groundwater stored in alpine watersheds sustains perennial flow from springs, supplies baseflow to streams, and supports aquatic ecosystems and downstream aquifers, making it an increasingly important freshwater resource in regions undergoing rapid glacier retreat. As glaciers continue to retreat, predicting how mountain groundwater systems will respond to continued glacier loss requires an improved understanding of groundwater storage and flowpath connectivity. However, these hydrogeologic processes remain poorly quantified in alpine watersheds. This study investigates groundwater storage and flowpath connectivity in Glacier National Park, Montana, USA using strontium isotopic ratios ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) and chlorine-36 ratios ( 36 Cl/Cl). Three distinct groundwater groups associated with groundwater flow through different hydrostratigraphic units were identified in the 87 Sr/ 86 Sr dataset. The groupings defined using the 87 Sr/ 86 Sr dataset were also present in the 36 Cl/Cl dataset. Springs that have 87 Sr/ 86 Sr associated with flow through the high-elevation carbonate bedrock formations exhibit lower 36 Cl/Cl than springs that have 87 Sr/ 86 Sr associated with flow through mid- and low-elevation alluvium. In fact, 36 Cl/Cl ratios increase with decreasing elevation, where the highest elevation springs have 36 Cl/Cl similar to those from glacial ice and snow measured in this study, and the springs emerging at the lowest elevations are discharging a small component of bomb-pulse 36 Cl/Cl. The persistence of the groupings could represent either 1) distinct storage in different lithological units or facies or 2) transfers of groundwater from different facies across the mountain block. A dedolomitization plot supports the latter explanation where geochemical evolution is continuous. These findings indicate that hydrostratigraphy is a primary control on groundwater storage and flowpath connectivity in Glacier National Park such that groundwater processes are strongly constrained to the high-elevation carbonate bedrock, resulting in limited groundwater storage, restricted spatial connectivity, and limited groundwater circulation depths in the mountain block. These data provide valuable new insights into how glacial meltwater is stored and transmitted through the alpine bedrock aquifers and improve our understanding of how the groundwater system has responded and may continue to respond to ongoing glacier retreat. For example, this dataset provides an explanation for the observed spring desiccation and impacts to baseflow in Glacier National Park and suggests that the remaining springs and streams may have the same fate approaching an ice-free future.

abstract: Constraining the kinematic evolution of the frontal High Himalaya is critical for understanding interactions between tectonic and surface processes because it lies at the intersection of rapid erosion, extreme topographic relief, and high uplift rates. Previous studies have identified several thrusts within the Greater and Lesser Himalayan sequences based on the juxtaposition of rocks that often record markedly different pressure-temperature evolutions. In central-eastern Nepal, multiple studies have documented a pronounced discontinuity in peak metamorphic conditions (>300°C and >4 kbar) within Greater Himalayan rocks. However, the structure(s) responsible for juxtaposing these units, variably interpreted as the Main Central thrust, the Chomrong thrust, the Langtang thrust, and/or the Ramgarh thrust, has remained enigmatic, as the presumed fault zone often lacks a thick footwall mylonitic shear zone expected for a major ductile thrust, raising the possibility that this relationship instead reflects younger brittle faulting and subsequent exhumation. Here, we investigate the structural and exhumational history of the middle to upper crust in the frontal Himalaya crossing these interpreted thrust zones and the major topographic transition to the Lesser Himalaya, variably referred to as the Physiographic Transition II (PT2) or the High Himalayan Topographic Front (HHTF), using apatite U-Pb and zircon (U-Th)/He thermochronology. We model data from eight samples collected along the Seti Khola valley that span this structural section. By integrating these geo- and thermochronologic data with inverse thermal history and thermokinematic modeling, we reconstruct the exhumation history of this part of the frontal High Himalaya since ca. 27 Ma. This approach is designed to evaluate whether the observed metamorphic break(s) is best explained by long-lived ductile thrusting, younger brittle faulting, passive emplacement of the sequence above a ramp on the Main Himalayan thrust, or some combination of these, providing new constraints on the tectonic evolution of the Himalayan middle crust.

abstract:
We developed an inquiry-based, web-browser-hosted educational experience with ASU’s NASA-Center for Education Through Exploration that demonstrates how climate change reshapes animal habitat and biodiversity patterns through its influence on ocean temperature and oxygen content, which govern the ability of marine animals to meet their respiratory needs. The public is often exposed to the conclusions of climate science but has limited opportunities to engage with the underlying data and reasoning that produce those conclusions. This educational experience aims to improve climate literacy by helping users connect observable changes in marine habitat with the physical and physiological mechanisms that drive them through direct engagement with scientific tools.

We achieve this aim by introducing users to the quantitative principles of animal physiology and Earth system modeling that scientists use to evaluate habitat suitability and predict patterns of extinction selectivity. Users navigate the "Big Five" mass extinction events from the perspective of representative marine animals, discovering how species-specific physiological traits govern habitat suitability and extinction risk. They then apply these principles to predict how anthropogenic climate change threatens modern coral reef ecosystems. This experience was designed with the underlying limitations and uncertainties of climate reconstructions in mind. Through transparency about those limitations, users can gain inferential skills in interpreting outputs from real Earth system simulations.

abstract: The storage and transport of water in high mountain catchments is vital to downstream water supply and critical to the chemical weathering processes that control long-term climate and condition hillslopes for landsliding. The depths and timescales over which recharge passes through mountain catchments are modulated by the structure and hydrological properties of the near surface, which remain challenging to characterize. Landslides themselves heighten these challenges by disrupting hillslopes, yet much remains unknown about how they systematically alter water routing and storage at the catchment scale. We investigate the impact of landslides on infiltration and runoff dynamics using a hydro-geophysical observatory network in a steep mountain catchment in central Nepal as a natural laboratory (the Nepal-FRES observatory in the Melamchi River Valley). Using multiscale datasets, we evaluate the segregation of water pathways through fractured bedrock and surficial deposits with particular attention to variable recharge mechanisms and the role of landsliding in partitioning surface and subsurface flow and weathering of hillslope materials at the catchment scale. Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) surveys and seismic interferometry ( dv/v ) are used to infer subsurface water pathways and hydrological structure, while a deep borehole through the Kyul landslide provides direct calibration of slope material properties and weathering states with geophysical measurements. Time-series hydrological monitoring, including δ 18 O water isotopes and dissolved solute concentrations from springs, along with stream discharge and precipitation records, provide information on groundwater recharge, subsurface response times, and groundwater reservoir storage capacities. We find that landslide disturbances govern a dual-flow regime, where rapid stream discharge peaks correspond to shallow flow pathways through landslide colluvium, and slow, prolonged stream response is facilitated by a deeper fractured bedrock. Evidence that the deeper reservoir is fed by recharge at high elevations suggests that these reservoirs are largely segregated, and that precipitation on mid- and lower hillslopes is limited to the shallow reservoir. We posit that this hydrologic behavior is facilitated by sharp permeability contrasts introduced by landslides, which strip hillslopes of regolith and deposit permeable unconsolidated colluvium; these contrasts promote flow above the landslide base, preventing vertical movement into deeper reservoirs. These findings suggest that landslides play an active role in the storage and transport of mountain groundwater, providing a novel perspective on the movement of hydrological fluxes through steep mountain catchments.

abstract: Students from Minority-serving institutions (MSIs) are considered an underrepresented segment of the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) workforce. Traditional programs that equip students for research and STEM careers usually occur as extracurricular activities. However, many MSI students, such as those at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), have non-traditional, first-generation, and/or low-income backgrounds, which limit their opportunities outside instructional time. Through “Remote-sensing & Analytics for Integrating Science Education (RAISE)” funded by NASA, this study employs a pilot model to restructure the curriculum, providing students with enhanced experiential learning opportunities with incentives to improve their workforce readiness. Remote sensing data and data analytics were incorporated into the classroom to enhance students’ skills in practical applications of Earth and Environmental Sciences (ESS). Furthermore, scientists from R1 universities and NASA centers were invited to share their research and career journeys through seminar presentations. Students were able to foster connections with potential advisors and employers while gauging their interest in ESS research. Students were compensated for their time spent outside of their normal class schedule for these seminars. We then partnered with Johnson Space Center (JSC), Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and the University of Texas at Austin to send UTRGV students to 10 week-long summer internships. Surveys were conducted after each component to evaluate the program's effectiveness. The course survey revealed that 100% of students considered the course activities at least moderately relevant to real-world projects. 84% of participants reported feeling better prepared to embark on STEM-related academic or career opportunities after attending the seminar series. Lastly, students reported gaining practical skills, confidence, and career readiness in STEM after the internships. Given that this is a pilot study, the survey outcomes will aid the development of future curricula at UTRGV and peer MSIs/institutions to better prepare the future workforce for the public and private sectors, including NASA and various industries. Ultimately, implementing a similar framework can help MSIs strengthen STEM engagement and increase career opportunities for students.

session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Houchin, Shane Kenyon [1], Tissot, François [2], Ibanez-Mejia, Mauricio [3], Lanzirotti, Antonio [4], Newville, Matthew [5], Tappero, Ryan [6]

abstract:
Zircon is one of the most important archives of crustal evolution due to its physical and chemical resilience, widespread occurrence, and ability to record multiple episodes of magmatism and metamorphism. Extracting redox information from zircon has been challenging, however, because most zircon-based oxybarometers rely on trace-element concentrations that can also be influenced by temperature, melt composition, and co-crystallizing mineral assemblages. X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy overcomes many of these limitations by directly probing element oxidation states within mineral phases. In particular, U M 4 -edge XANES spectroscopy is emerging as a powerful tool for reconstructing magma redox conditions during zircon crystallization through empirical calibration of the relationship between uranium valence in zircon and the oxygen fugacity of their host rocks [1].

Here, we review the development of the zircon U XANES oxybarometer and its expanding applications to questions in crustal petrology. The high spatial resolution of this technique (≤5 µm) allows analyses to target individual growth domains, revealing intragrain variations in U valence state associated with evolving redox conditions during primary igneous crystallization or secondary growth during magmatic and/or metamorphic reworking. This spatial resolution also allows XANES results to be linked to geochronologic, geochemical, and isotopic measurements from the same growth domains, providing valuable context for interpreting the origin and geological significance of these signatures. At the conference, we will present examples from diverse tectonic settings and spanning in age from the Hadean to the Phanerozoic to illustrate how this method can be used to investigate tectonomagmatic processes across space and time, from variations within individual crystals and the evolution of single plutons or eruptions, to long-term secular changes in the redox state of the continental crust.

title: The DeForest Formation: A Stratigraphic Framework That Revolutionized Midwestern Geoarchaeology
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part II)
authors: Bettis, E. Arthur [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Iowa, School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Iowa City, IA, USA
abstract: During the late 1970’s and 1980’s addressing inadequacies in techniques used to discover and evaluate buried cultural resources in valley landscapes emerged as a focus for geoarchaeology. Projects in Iowa, Kansas, Missouri, and Illinois pointed to recurring patterns in the physical properties, distribution, and age relationships of alluvium in the region that would provide a detailed stratigraphic framework (the DeForest Formation) for the late Pleistocene and Holocene. A long collaborative effort among archaeologists, geoarchaeologists and other earth scientists, including an on-going key role by Rolfe Mandel, used the DeForest Formation to revolutionize theoretical frameworks and methods used to assess the record of the human past in the Midwest and beyond. Over the past couple decades the regional occurrence of DeForest Formation properties and distribution has also gained traction as an important frameworks for addressing bank and bed stability analysis and other environmental engineering challenges.

title: Breaking Up is Hard to Do: Coronae, Hotspots, and Superplumes on Earth and Venus
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: King, Scott D. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA
abstract: Courtillot and colleagues suggest that volcanic hotspots on Earth may have three distinct origins: those originating from the deepest part of the lower mantle (i.e., whole mantle plumes), others originating from the bottom of the transition zone at the top of the large transient domes that correspond to the Pacific and African superswells (on Earth Caroline, McDonald, Pitcairn, Samoa, and Tahiti are good candidates for these secondary hotspots) and the remainder being upper mantle features linked to the asthenosphere. The “diapirs” that form coronae on Venus may form via deep superplumes within Venus similar to Courtillot’s secondary plumes on Earth (i.e., originating from the transition zone atop large superplume structures in the lower mantle. Experiments by Davaille and colleagues show that simultaneous generation of superplumes and whole mantle plumes can arise naturally from thermochemical convection in a heterogeneous fluid requiring only chemical density anomalies at the base of the fluid (i.e., the core mantle boundary). On Earth, chemical density anomalies inferred from seismic data and mineral physics studies (on the order of 2%) could produce both modes. Do such chemical anomalies above the core mantle boundary exist on Venus? The mixed plume mode (superplumes and hotspot plume) seems to require thermochemical convection. If so, how did these form? Could Venusian superplumes break up in the same way Earth’s superplumes apparently have? I address these questions using 3D spherical geodynamic models.

title: Modernizing Puerto Rico's Geological Inventory: Integrating Rock Characterization, Legacy Data, and Digital Workflows
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Santiago Pijuan, Yasmin Nikauri [1], Palmieri, Mary [2], Quintero, Raiza Raquel [3], Hudgins, Thomas [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Puerto Rico, Mayaguez, Puerto Rico, USA
(2) University of Puerto Rico, Mayaguez, Puerto Rico, USA
(3) Universidad de Puerto Rico, Mayagüez, PR, USA
(4) University of Puerto Rico, Mayaguez, PR, USA
abstract:
As part of the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI), our team at the University of Puerto Rico at Mayagüez is developing a modern digital inventory of the island’s industrial mineral resources. The goal is to provide critical data that aids post-disaster recovery, improves infrastructure planning, and builds long-term hazard resilience. The most comprehensive assessment of Puerto Rico’s industrial mineral resources which included 450 industrial mineral mines and occurrences was completed by Bawiec, 1998. No updated centralized digital inventory currently exists. Over the past decade, severe weather (e.g. hurricanes Maria and Irma in 2017; Fiona in 2022) along with the 2020 M6.4 seismic sequence highlighted Puerto Rico’s exposure to both geologic risks and likely climate change-intensified storms (Balaguru et al., 2023). Hurricane Maria alone triggered >70,000 landslides (Hughes and Morales-Velez, 2021) and required $33.8 billion in recovery funds to repair external damage (FEMA, 2021). These events underscore the urgent need to document, characterize, and catalog the island’s industrial mineral resources to support future post-disaster reconstruction, particularly given the island's geographic isolation and the logistical challenges of importing construction materials following major disasters.

This project integrates legacy geologic information, rock characterization, geospatial datasets, and digital workflows into a comprehensive GeMS-compliant geodatabase. Historical reports, Mineral Resources Data System (MRDS) records, 1:20,000 geologic quadrangle maps, high-resolution LiDAR, topographic datasets, orthophotography, ArcGIS World Imagery, and publicly available GIS datasets are compiled, standardized, and integrated within a common spatial framework. Active and historical quarry information and operations are identified and incorporated through literature reviews, fragmented government databases, geospatial analysis, and targeted field verification. We present our preliminary resource inventory, methodologies, and analytical workflows for characterizing Puerto Rico's industrial minerals. The geodatabase integrates field mapping with petrographic, geochemical, volumetric, and spatial datasets to establish a standardized framework for rock analysis and resource management.

Our preliminary inventory captures over 65 operating industrial mineral facilities, over 120 historical extraction sites compiled from legacy MRDS records, and initial prospective targets identified via remote sensing that await field validation. This workflow establishes a modern geological baseline to support future resource assessments, geologic mapping, emergency response planning, and resilient infrastructure development across the island.

title: Basaltic to dacitic volcanic and hypabyssal intrusive complex in a Devonian submarine island-arc sequence in the northern Sierra Navada, California
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Mindrup, Quinton [1], Hanson, Richard [2]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
(2) Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, Texas, USA
abstract:
Meter-scale mapping in excellent glaciated exposures of relatively deep-marine island-arc strata exposed in cross section within the Upper Devonian Sierra Buttes Formation (SBF) in the northern Sierra Nevada, California has revealed a complex interplay of extrusive and subvolcanic intrusive processes in a submarine arc setting. Twelve lithofacies made up of five lithological types of basaltic to dacitic rock numbered 1-5 based on relative age are recognized in the study area.

Types 1, 2 and 3 hyaloclastites consist of angular, originally glassy shards showing abundant jigsaw-fit texture consistent with nonexplosive quench fragmentation. Emplacement of Type 1 hyaloclastite was followed by the eruption of Type 2 basaltic to andesitic lapillistone containing lapilli with dominantly unbroken droplet-like shapes indicating formation from submarine lava fountains. Type 2 hyaloclastite then flowed over the lapillistone, locally mixing with it and trapping pockets of lapilli within the hyaloclastite. A long period of time then elapsed during which at least some of the overlying arc strata including radiolarian chert, volcaniclastic turbidites, ash-fall tuff, and subaqueous debris-flow deposits accumulated. Renewed magmatic activity emplaced Type 3 intrusions into the overlying strata and formed a zone of dacitic peperite and intrusive hyaloclastite along the contacts.

We interpret dispersed fluidal bodies within the abundant hyaloclastites to have formed by disruption of branching tubular feeder networks that supplied magma to the growing hyaloclastite deposits and likely developed due to high extrusive magma pressures. Aqueous quenching, collapse of insulating vapor films along tube margins, and mechanical forces generated by ongoing magma injections led to the breakup of the originally interconnected feeder tube systems.

Types 1-4 coherent intrusions occur both as large and small discordant bodies throughout the study area, and we infer that they represent parts of a complex subsurface intrusive array that fed this part of the arc sequence. Type 4 coherent dacitic intrusions were emplaced into all the previously emplaced igneous lithofacies, and destroyed the basal contact of the complex with underlying SBF strata, but did not extend into the overlying SBF strata. Type 5 basaltic and andesitic dikes occur throughout the study area and extend into the base of the arc strata. Fluidal shapes and peperitic contacts indicate the dikes were emplaced while the host hyaloclastites and arc strata were still wet and unconsolidated.

authors: Kamran, Sarah [1], Nadeem, Shamaila Inayat [2], Javed, Asif [3], Khan, Ikram Ullah [4], Wahab, Abid [5]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Sciences, Kinnaird College for Women University, Lahore, Pakistan., Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan

(4) Hazara University, Mansehra, KP, Pakistan., Mansehra, KPK, Pakistan
(5) Higher Education Commission (HEC), Pakistan., Pakistan
abstract: Ionic liquids, also known as “Green Solvents”, have potential uses in diverse areas and several notable properties, which makes them safer and sustainable replacements for Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs). The major aim of the study was the synthesis of Ionic liquid along with their in-vivo and in-vitro toxicological activities. An ammonium-based salt tetrahexyl ammonium bromide was taken in the form of a hydrogen bond acceptor whereas decanoic acid was taken as a hydrogen bond donor to synthesize deep eutectic solvent. For the toxicity analysis, the fish species Cyprinus carpio was used and two strains of bacteria were studied to appraise the anti-bacterial activity ( Bacillus substilis for gram positive) and ( Klebsiella pneumoniae for gram negative), and the anti-fungal activity was examined against the Candida albicans . Both the antibacterial and antifungal activities were tested after culturing the microorganisms on different types of agars using prepared inoculums. Then, the serial dilutions of S13 were prepared and the toxicity analysis was performed using the disk diffusion method where antibiotics and antifungal solutions were used as control groups. The cytotoxic activity of DES was examined on NIH-3T3 cell line, derived from a 17 to 19-day old Swiss Albino mouse embryo using MTT Assay, and the antioxidant activity was examined using Catalase Assay and DPPH Assay. The DES showed strong anti-microbial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, however, was less toxic towards fungal strain at lower concentrations. Furthermore, the toxicity of DES was evaluated on fish ( C. carpio ), and DES had an LC50, less than 100 mg/L, and was found to be slightly toxic. The results clearly showed that DES some extent of toxic behavior, despite being labeled as green and might prove to be hazardous towards several organisms when released as a waste. However, its strong anti-bacterial, non-cytotoxic, and potent antioxidant behavior still makes it a primary contender to be used in different industries. Combining AI and Machine Learning-based predictive toxicology with experimental in vitro and in vivo testing is anticipated to create a comprehensive approach for faster screening, rational design and development of safer and more sustainable DESs.

title: Bedload Textural Characteristics of Late Quaternary Braided Versus Meandering Phases of the Lower Oconee River, Atlantic Coastal Plain, Georgia, USA
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Suther, Bradley E. [1], Leigh, David S. [2], McDonald, Jacob Michael [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Anthropology, Kennesaw State University, Kennesaw, GA, USA
(2) Department of Geography, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
(3) Lewis F. Rogers Institute for Environmental and Spatial Analysis, University of North Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
abstract:
Braided terraces dating to 30-17 ka occur along many rivers of the southeastern Atlantic Coastal Plain that reflect regional channel response to high sediment loads and bank instability associated with the colder, drier paleoclimatic conditions of the Late Pleistocene. Although these terraces are well-documented in Georgia and the Carolinas, few studies provide quantitative data on the sedimentology of braided channel deposits and its relationship to that of other fluvial sediments in the region. Thus, this research uses particle size analysis and field morphological descriptions to evaluate textural differences in the bedload of late Wisconsin (35-17 ka) braided versus terminal Pleistocene (17-11 ka) and Holocene (11-0 ka) meandering channel deposits of the lower Oconee River valley in southeast Georgia, a locality with a wide array of late Quaternary fluvial landforms that is representative of other alluvial valleys in the region.

Along the Oconee, braided river bedload facies are 8 to >10 m thick and comprised of gravelly coarse sand that was deposited in lower braid bar and channel bed environments. In their upper 1 to 3 m, these deposits grade to medium sand that reflects sedimentation in middle and upper braid bar positions. In contrast, meandering channel bedload deposits are 2 to >6 m thick and predominantly composed of coarse sand associated with channel lag and lower point bar settings. Somewhat similarly, these sediments fine upward in their upper meter to medium sand that represents deposition in upper point bar positions. Although the gravel contents of uppermost bed sediments for braided and meandering channels are comparable (2-3% by weight), the gravelly sand that constitutes most of the braided river bedload averages more gravel than the channel lag and lower point bar deposits of meandering channels (16 vs. 10%). Greater gravel content in basal bedload sediments of braided versus meandering channel deposits is consistent with the higher bed sediment loads and possibly higher stream powers (relative to later meandering forms) inferred by previous studies for Late Pleistocene braided rivers in the region.

Work is underway to identify additional grain size parameters useful for differentiating braided versus meandering channel deposits along the Oconee River. Results should help to better inform lithofacies interpretations and geologic mapping efforts in late Quaternary alluvial valley fills of the southeastern Coastal Plain.

title: Searching for Biosignatures Within Fluid Inclusions in Bedded and Displacive Halite From the Mars-Analog Permo-Triassic Spearfish Formation of North Dakota
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Hernandez, Katrina Abigail [1], Onah, Comfort E. [2], Benison, Kathleen C. [3]
affiliations: (1) Chemistry, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, West Virginia, USA
abstract:
Ancient acid brine systems are essential for interpreting past environments on Earth and understanding ancient Martian environments. Evaporite minerals from hypersaline lakes, such as halite (NaCl), have recently captured the attention of astrobiologists because of their ability to rapidly trap and preserve surface water, air, microorganisms, and organic compounds during precipitation. Here, we investigated biosignatures preserved within fluid inclusions in halite from the Permo-Triassic Spearfish Formation in the Halite #1 core from McKenzie County of western North Dakota. The Spearfish Formation contains both bedded halite, which precipitated from lake waters, and displacive halite, which grew syndepositionally within shallow acid-brine groundwater. Samples were examined using transmitted and UV-vis light microscopy at magnifications ranging from 6.3× to 2000×. Bedded halite hosted abundant primary fluid inclusions containing water, vapor, accidental daughter crystals, suspect cells, and organic compounds, as well as secondary fluid inclusions, many of which were filled with liquid hydrocarbons. In contrast, displacive halite contained only rare, isolated fluid inclusions. Primary fluid inclusions were examined for suspect cells, which appeared as single or clustered orange, yellow, and clear spheroids that fluoresced pale to bright yellow under UV-vis light. Some vapor bubbles fluoresced blue or yellow under UV-vis light, suggesting the presence of organic compounds coating the vapor phase. Fluorescent responses of organic material and the vapor phase were documented, and images were compiled for digital analysis to automate hue co-variation sorting.

Disparities in the distribution of inclusions and organic material between bedded and displacive halite were observed. This preliminary petrographic comparison of fluid inclusions in bedded and displacive halite demonstrates that bedded halite is a more promising target for preserving cells and organic compounds than displacive halite. Therefore, bedded halite on Mars should be an important exploratory target in the search for evidence of past life.

title: Complex Magma Storage and Assembly from Crystal Melt Disequilibrium In Faial, Azores
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Lee, Erica [1], Dickensheets, Ava [2], Pimentel , Adriano [3], Michelfelder, Gary [4], Ramos, Frank C. [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM, USA
(2) Geology, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM, USA
(5) Geology, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM,
abstract:
The Azores archipelago is a volcanically active island group in the central North Atlantic formed through the interaction of mantle upwelling associated with the Azores hotspot and complex tectonic setting near the Azores Triple Junction, where the North American, Eurasian, and African (Nubian) plates meet. Faial lies along an active volcanic ridge between Faial and Pico Island, where tectonic deformation and crustal fractures influence the movement of magma. This combination of mantel derived magmatism and active tectonic deformation provides an important setting for investigating the storage and evolution of magma beneath volcanic islands.

This study investigates trachytic deposits, groundmass, and alkali feldspars from three eruptions of the Cerdos Volcanic Complex C6 (~2110± 50 yr BP). C9 (~1600 ± 60 yr BP), and C11 (~980 ± 50 yr BP). These were collected and individually analyzed to understand the pre-eruptive histories of their host magmas. Crystals that are in equilibrium with their host melt are expected to reflect conditions of crystallization within the magma system, whereas crystal melt disequilibrium indicates that crystals may have formed under different physical or chemical conditions than those represented by the melt in which ultimately erupted. Such disequilibrium can preserve evidence of processes including multiple stages of crystallization magma recharge, magma mixing, crystal accumulation, storage, and remobilization of crystal rich magma.

By examining crystal compositions and their host melts this study aims to determine the extent to which alkali feldspars preserve pre-eruptive magmatic histories beneath Faial Island. Disequilibrium between crystals and host melts suggests that the erupted magmas may have incorporated crystals formed during earlier stages of magma evolution or within chemically distinct magma reservoirs. These observations provide insight into the complex and potentially prolonged magma storage system beneath Faial, revealing processes occurring beneath the island that cannot be observed directly at the surface. Comparisons among the C6, C9, and C11 eruptions may further determine whether these processes represent localized behavior within individual magma systems or reflect broader characteristics of magmatism at Faial.

title: Was Rapid Intermediate-T Cooling at the end of High-T Metamorphism in Sri Lanka Related to Thermal Relaxation after Gondwana Construction or Orogenic Collapse?
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Rider, Emily Nicole [1], Holm, Daniel [2], Ranasinghe, Pradeep Nalaka [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Kent State University, Kent, OH, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Kent State University, Kent, OH, USA
(3) School of Chemistry, Environmental, and Geosciences, Lake Superior State University, Sault Ste. Marie, MI, USA
abstract: The Neoproterozoic crustal block of Sri Lanka is well suited for investigating how volcanic arcs are transformed tectonically via accretion/collisions, UHT metamorphism, intense deformation, and ultimately stabilized into continental crust. Abundant zirconology over the past five decades has greatly enhanced our understanding of the tectono-metamorphic history of Sri Lanka during its construction, yet a dearth of information exists on the post-polymetamorphic intermediate temperature (500-300 C) thermal history. Recent concordant hornblende and biotite plateau Ar/Ar ages from near the eastern suture zone in southern Sri Lanka suggest rapid cooling through intermediate mid-crustal temperatures in the early Ordovician (490-480 Ma), similar to prior Rb-Sr biotite ages and one hornblende age clustering ~470 Ma from the central Highland Complex and ~450 Ma from the bounding arc terranes. The Ar/Ar ages are synchronous with the cessation of high-T zircon and garnet growth, and with late pegmatite crystallization and hydrothermal gold formation. We are evaluating whether this rapid cooling might be related 1) to the end of the construction phase of Gondwana, perhaps marking the cessation of thrusting and the onset of thermal relaxation, or 2) to post-thrusting orogenic extensional collapse associated with isostatic re-equilibration. The temporal linkage between the end of long duration (600-500 Ma) UHT metamorphism followed shortly by rapid intermediate-T cooling is consistent with thermal relaxation following thrust cessation. Alternatively, recent work in terranes formerly peripheral to Sri Lanka (East Antarctica and India) are identifying late extensional structures which post-date Gondwana contractional features. Similarly, in Sri Lanka, doubly plunging dome-and keel-type structures in the western Central Highlands were recently reinterpreted to have formed during post-orogenic intraplate extension, although their timing is poorly constrained. To test between thermal relaxation and extensional collapse induced rapid cooling, we have collected samples from a wider geographical area, including from the Vijayan Complex in the south, and from the Central Highland and Wanni Complex to the north. The absence of intermediate temperature ages younger than ~450 Ma from both Rb-Sr and Ar-Ar systematics is consistent with a lack of petrologic evidence for low-grade metamorphic overprinting in Sri Lanka, making it likely that more thermochronologic mineral ages will yield robust post-Gondwana primary (and not younger reset) cooling ages.

title: Microscopic Fluid Flow Networks, a Tale of Two Quartzites
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits. (Posters)
authors: Maher, Dr. Harmon D. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Geology, University of Nebraska, Omaha, NE, USA
abstract: The Sioux quartzite is a relatively undeformed but very mildly metamorphosed Precambrian quartz arenite found mostly in South Dakota and Minnesota, with a bit in northwest Iowa. The Carboniferous Billefjorden Group exposed on Spitsbergen, Norway is composed of abundant quartz arenite strata intercalated with coal measures. Billefjorden Group strata are locally involved in subsequent Carboniferous rifting and in Tertiary folding and thrusting, but are unmetamorphosed. Despite their separation in space and time they share the following widespread traits: 1) abundant post-depositional fluid inclusion planes (FIPs) in multiple preferred orientations, 2) micro-veins aligned with the FIPs, 3) abundant evidence of pressure solution, and 4) a network of very thin and irregular phyllosilicate seams that mostly follow highly modified depositional grain boundaries. Post-depositional FIPs come in a variety of types in addition to the initially more obvious trans-granular planes. Within each quartzite common orientations, linking and truncation geometries, and timing relationships suggest that all of these four features overlapped in time. They are interpreted to be part of two similar, penetrative, micro-fracture fluid flow networks that developed independently in the quartzites. The microfractures must have healed on geologically short time frames given the rock body retained its integrity. How far traveled the fluids moved in these two cases is unknown, but of distinct interest. In some cases, distances must be large enough to explain local significant pressure solution volume loss seen. One tentative possibility is that the network formed due to volume contraction associated with cooling and/or erosional unloading. This explains the multiple directions. The network-produced micro-fabric also strongly influenced subsequent macroscopic joint development. A transition between two different fluid flow regimes is suggested. Initially fluid flow was through detrital pore spaces. Through pressure solution related compaction and cementation this porosity became negligible and overpressures could build. Subsequently a dynamic porosity/permeability consisting of self-healing microfractures dominated. Examples of other quartzites described in the literature that also have widespread FIPs and some of the other three features suggest that such dynamic micro-porosity networks may be a more widespread phenomenon. How fluids move along penetrative self-healing microfracture networks is worthy of continued scrutiny.

title: Arsenic on the Playa: Spatial Mapping and Geochemical Comparison of Exposed Great Salt Lakebed Sediment
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Kelly, Naomi M. [1], Miller, Lindy V. [2], Sorensen, Mary [3], LeMonte, Joshua J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigam Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigam Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(4) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
abstract:
The Great Salt Lake has been steadily shrinking, exposing over 750 square miles of lakebed sediment referred to as the playa (Perry et al.). Prevailing wind patterns have been tracked blowing the top layer of this sediment towards the populated Wasatch Front. This has become a major public health concern in the area as it has been found that lakebed sediment and subsequent dust contain heavy metals including As (Perry et al.). Due to the high stakes and high interface with the local population, a deeper understanding of the geochemical makeup and interactions across the lake is needed. While it is known that there is As in the sediment, the more bioavailable and reduced form As(III) is of more concern than the oxidized form As(V) because it is more easily absorbed by the body. Having a better understanding of how As interacts spatially and what other elements is the next step to being able to address these concerns.

To do this, we will be creating geochemical maps of the spatial distribution and correlation matrixes of other elements. We sampled 30 sites across the lake taking 10cm and 2 ft cores. Sites were reached using fat tire bikes allowing us to get a comprehensive view of the whole playa not just isolated regions. Samples were immediately vacuumed-sealed in the field and then processed in an anaerobic glove box to preserve conditions. Following acid digestion and dilution, inductively coupled plasma (ICP-OES) analysis was used to determine total chemical breakdown.

Results from the top 1cm revealed that on average the total As is 10 times higher than EPA industrial standards of 3ppm (U.S. EPA, 2024). Geochemical data will be mapped and put into a comparison matrix to identify hotspots and areas of concern and better understand possible speciation by looking at chemical colocation. This data will ultimately allow stakeholders and policy makers in the area to create targeted interventions for the region involving Great Salt Lake dust and subsequent water management.

title: High-Resolution Doppler Lidar Observations of Offshore Internal Boundary-Layer Development Across a Coastal Land–Ocean Transition
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Solari, Mojtaba Shams [1], Roy, Sayahnya [2], Moss, Coleman [3], Cinquino, Eve [4], Kirincich, Anthony [5], lungo, Giacomo Valerio [6]
affiliations: (1) Wind, Fluids, and Experiments (WindFluX) Laboratory, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, USA
(2) Wind, Fluids, and Experiments (WindFluX) Laboratory, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, USA
(3) Wind, Fluids, and Experiments (WindFluX) Laboratory, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, USA
(4) Department of Physical Oceanography, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(5) Department of Physical Oceanography, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(6) Wind, Fluids, and Experiments (WindFluX) Laboratory, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, USA
abstract:
Coastal transitions produce abrupt changes in surface roughness and thermal forcing that reorganize the atmospheric boundary layer and generate an internal boundary layer (IBL). Although offshore IBL development directly affects coastal transport, air–sea exchange, and wind-resource characterization, its spatial evolution remains difficult to observe because conventional towers provide measurements at only a few fixed locations. This study investigates offshore IBL formation using high-resolution scanning Doppler lidar observations collected near Nantucket, Massachusetts, during the Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project (WFIP3).

A range–height indicator scan was continuously aligned with the mean offshore wind direction to resolve flow evolution from the coastline to approximately 3 km offshore. Each 15-min period encompasses 104 repeated scans, each consisting of 18 lines of sight. The measurements provided radial wind velocities at approximately 1,800 locations along the offshore transect, sampled at 1.5-m intervals with an effective range resolution of 24 m. Following quality control and statistical-convergence assessment, profiles of mean wind speed and turbulence intensity (TI) were constructed at successive offshore fetches. The IBL height was identified from the local maximum in TI, equivalently represented by a zero crossing in its vertical gradient, and was compared with the traditional velocity-kink method.

The observations show a distinct TI reduction within the developing marine IBL and a pronounced maximum near its upper boundary. This turbulence-based signature is more consistently identifiable than the wind-speed kink, particularly where the mean velocity profile adjusts gradually across the coastline. Above the IBL height, identified by the TI maximum, both the wind-speed and TI profiles retain characteristics like those of the upstream boundary layer over land, indicating that the flow has not yet fully adjusted to the ocean surface. Below the IBL, wind speed accelerates as the flow adjusts from the rougher land surface to the smoother ocean, while the turbulence structure progressively develops toward marine conditions.

These findings demonstrate that repeated scanning-lidar measurements can resolve coastal boundary-layer adjustment at spatial scales inaccessible to conventional measurement systems. The proposed turbulence-based diagnostic provides a practical framework for quantifying offshore IBL growth and improving the understanding and prediction of coastal atmospheric flows.

title: Enhancing Recharge on Flat, Freezing Landscapes – Application in the Rural Midwest
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Cardiff, Michael [1], Kershner, Samantha Charlotte [2], Brockschmidt, Samuel [3]

(2) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA

abstract: Rural land overlies the majority of the US by area, and thus the majority of available aquifer volume for water storage. Despite generally high water availability, in the rural Midwest, landscapes are increasingly being stressed by nutrient pollution, more intense stormflows, and increased occurrence of mid-winter melts. Enhancing aquifer recharge in this region has value, then, in potentially diluting existing aquifer contamination and reducing intensity of runoff. We have recently tested shallow, small-diameter drywells as an approach for enhancing recharge in areas with low-permeability surficial soils. Results from our test in Wisconsin indicate that these systems perform well at enhancing recharge throughout a year of operation, despite no pretreatment and experiencing freeze-thaw conditions. In areas with naturally high water quality, such as forest and shrublands, arrays of such installations may provide an opportunity to further protect groundwater resources while operating with a minimally-invasive footprint.

title: When Salt Changes Everything: Geochemical Modeling of Heavy Metal Behavior under Fresh to Hypersaline Conditions
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Posters)
authors: Schmidt, Caden Chad [1], Miller, Lindy V. [2], LeMonte, Joshua J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(3) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
abstract: Redox reactions are fundamental processes in environmental chemistry, driving nutrient cycling, mineral formation, and the transformation of toxic heavy metals. However, hydrologic disturbances such as overuse of groundwater, sea level rise, tidal influence, and agricultural runoff can alter redox dynamics and, through changes in chemical speciation, influence the mobility and toxicity of heavy metals. Many of these hydrologic shifts directly affect ionic strength (salinity), a key factor in redox behavior. However, the full impact of ionic strength on redox conditions is not fully understood. Recently, a study was conducted in both Wilmington, Delaware, and the Great Salt Lake, Utah, analyzing the behavior of arsenic (As) and iron (Fe) in seawater, river water, and lake water across a range of pH and redox levels. This paper aims to build upon these studies by quantifying speciation in this system through thermodynamic modeling in PHREEQC to better understand the direct impact of ionic strength. Results showed that as ionic strength increases in these systems, it enhances the release of As due to the compression of the Electrical Double Layer. However, this only remains true under reducing conditions where As(III) is loosely bound in outer-sphere complexes. Ionic strength at these levels was also discovered to have little direct impact on speciation, but can still influence the rate of reduction, which, along with pH, is a primary driver of speciation.

title: Characterizing Arsenic in Playa Dust: Reducing Uncertainty in Health Outcomes Through Arsenic Speciation and Particle Size Distribution
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales (Posters)
authors: Miller, Lindy V. [1], Carling, Gregory T. [2], Kerry, Ruth [3], Tappero, Ryan V. [4], LeMonte, Joshua J. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(3) Department of Geography, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(4) National Synchrotron Light Source II, Brookhaven National Lab, Upton, NY, USA
(5) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
abstract:
Over 90 million Americans live in regions where year-round particle pollution levels exceed EPA air quality standards (American Lung Association, 2024). Compared with other pathways of contaminant transportation, dust has the highest capacity for transporting nonvolatile contaminants at regional and global scales; it can travel these distances at high speeds (Csavina et al., 2012). Shrinking water bodies contribute significantly to dust generation with playas accounting for 34% of global dust emissions (Parajuli and Zender, 2017). Playas, especially terminal lake playas, are natural areas of contaminant accumulation, showing increased concentrations of salts and heavy metals. Arsenic is of particular concern because of its widespread occurrence and its toxicity at low levels (Csavina et al., 2012). In a recent global health impact assessment, it was named as one of the six most toxic pollutants threatening human health (McCartor and Becker, 2010). The toxicity of arsenic depends largely on speciation. Despite the potential human health impact from exposure to As in dust, the form and bioavailability of As in playa dust is poorly understood.

This research characterizes arsenic speciation in playa dust sampled at the Great Salt Lake and at two nearby cities in northern Utah using synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES), and links speciation to particulate size distribution. Preliminary µXANES speciation findings show heterogeneous As speciation – reduced and oxidized forms – across and within sites. Arsenic concentrations are higher in finer fractions. This has important implications for public health, since the mobility and bioaccessibility of As depend on its oxidation state, and finer particles can penetrate deeper into the respiratory system. Planned in vitro tests using synthetic lung fluid will assess post-inhalation As desorption, offering insight into sorption behavior under physiological conditions. These findings will improve future decision making by providing more accurate insight into the health risks of arsenic-laden dust emissions. As playas continue to expand globally, understanding the composition, transport, and health impacts of playa-derived dust is increasingly critical.

title: A Critical Assessment of Anthropogenic Slags and Petroleum Pyrogenetic Glasses in the Southeastern United States: Petrology and Misidentification as Natural Melts
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Harris, R. Scott [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA; Georgia Space and Rocks (GASPAR), LLC, Loganville, GA, USA
abstract:
Many of the controversial claims that have been published over the last two decades regarding evidence of impacts or airbursts at the Younger Dryas Boundary have cited and relied upon comparisons to melt breccias collected around Blackville, South Carolina, described by Bunch et al. ( PNAS , 2012). As someone acknowledged by those authors as providing “critical” samples (and as a co-author of the Firestone et al. (2007) YDB article), I am uniquely qualified to give testimony that those glasses are slags from an abandoned railroad. The lead authors were aware of the clear evidence of that before publication.

I could argue that to the extent subsequent claims of YDB glasses, and other more recent Holocene samples, convincingly demonstrate similarities to the Blackville slags, those claims of impacts or airbursts that rely on the comparison, properly should be retracted. Remarkably, many of the Bunch at al. (2012) authors joined with Bindi et al. (2026) seemingly to endorse the conclusion, after fifteen years of saying otherwise, that they are uncertain whether the glasses were, “…produced by natural processes or anthropogenesis.” But how can there can be any doubt when the coordinates of the sample studied by Bindi (2026) map to the center of a railroad berm composed largely of construction aggregate.

No amount of circumspection prevented many of the authors from drawing on Bunch at al. (2012) to make definitive assertions of a YDB impact near Perkins, Louisiana (Fitzenreiter et al., 2025). I was asked by one author to examine samples from the site in advance of publication. My preliminary petrography suggested quench rates slower than those typically observed for small-scale impacts or short-duration airbursts. I reported that they either were anthropogenic or, less likely but plausibly, might be ejecta eroded from older impact strata that do occur up-gradient. However, a subsequent tour of the site and additional samples graciously provided by the lead author, revealed evidence that these glasses are most like those produced by petroleum fires. The Perkins site, in fact, sets in the middle of an area with abundant pimple mounds , which have been linked to gas extrusions.

title: Impact of sea level on estuarine biogeochemistry in the Western Interior Seaway
session_title: Cretaceous Mudstones of the Western Interior Seaway: New Insights into Sedimentary Inputs and Processes Impacting Geologic Resources Potential
authors: Lattea, Abigail [1], Gallagher, Timothy M. [2], Tessin, Allyson [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, Kent State University, Kent, OH, USA
(2) Kent State University, Kent, OH,
(3) Kent State University, Kent, OH,
abstract: The biogeochemistry of coastal wetlands is highly dependent on changes in sea level. These estuarine environments function as a unique boundary between the terrestrial and marine realms and are hotspots for global carbon burial. During the late Cretaceous, extensive black shale deposits were characteristic of Oceanic Anoxic Events. These black shale deposits indicate an increase in preservation, representative of both terrestrial and marine organic matter. The goal of this project is to understand how changes in sea level affect the biogeochemistry of estuarine environments and their ability to sequester carbon and nutrients. Estuaries are complex environments that are constantly changing. The Late Cretaceous Straight Cliffs Formation of the Kaiparowits Plateau, which was deposited on the western coastline of the Western Interior Seaway, provides an ideal opportunity to investigate how sea level change impacts long-term estuarine carbon burial and nutrient dynamics. It contains estuarine, floodplain, and shoreface sediments deposited during periods of both sea-level rise and fall. For this research, samples were analyzed from two cores (the more proximal SMP-1-91 and more distal CT-1-91) that record multiple oscillations in regional sea level. Bulk sulfur content declined upsection, indicating a declining marine influence through time. Organic carbon-rich samples (TOC >2%) were analyzed via ramped-pyrolysis to help characterize the composition and quality of organic matter. Hydrogen-index values ranged from 54-264 mg HC/g TOC and oxygen-index values ranged from 13-454 mg CO 2 /g TOC. This data indicates the organic matter present in these samples is a mixture of marine and terrestrial, with the greatest marine influence (high HI values) and best preservation (low OI values) observed during a transgressive sequence lower in the formation. Extremely large amounts of sedimentary iron were deposited at sea-level inflection points (>20 wt. %), and reactive iron and sulfide data will be compared to RockEval data to constrain the impact of sedimentary iron cycling on the preservation of organic carbon and sequestration of phosphorus.

title: From Forests to Farmhouses: A Stable Isotope Perspective on Holocene Synanthropy in the Middle Mississippi River Valley
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Pearson, Maxwell [1], Koch, Paul L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Marine Sciences, Univ of California-Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA,
(2) Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Santa Cruz, CA,
abstract:
Animals that thrive in human-engineered ecosystems, or synanthropes, have adapted to anthropogenic changes in habitats and resource availability over timescales short relative to their evolutionary histories. In response to novel human-associated resources and environments, synanthropic taxa may specialize within, expand, or shift their ecological niches. Although these transitions have been extensively studied in the Old World, where interactions between Homo species and native fauna have a long history, their development in the Western Hemisphere remains comparatively poorly understood. The middle Mississippi River Valley preserves a rich archaeological, paleontological, historical, and modern record spanning the middle and late Holocene. Here, carbon and nitrogen stable isotope analyses reconstruct changes in the isotopic niches of four synanthropic mammals—raccoons ( Procyon lotor ), Virginia opossums ( Didelphis virginiana ), fox squirrels ( Sciurus niger ), and eastern gray squirrels ( Sciurus carolinensis )—and evaluate how these changes correspond with major human cultural, technological, and land-use transitions during the past 8,500 years.

Among raccoons, carbon and nitrogen isotope values document progressive incorporation of anthropogenic resources associated with agriculture and irrigation, forest clearing, the Green Revolution, and urbanization. Mean δ¹³C values increased from −21.5‰ at 8,500 yr BP to −16.4‰ in modern individuals, paralleling isotopic shifts observed in local human populations following increased cultivation of maize, a ¹³C-enriched C₄ crop, by Indigenous and later Euro-American communities. Raccoon δ¹⁵N values decreased between 8,500 and 2,000 yr BP, increased from 2,000 yr BP through the 1970s, and subsequently declined. These patterns are consistent with changes in regional nitrogen cycling associated with irrigation, nitrogen-fixing plants such as beans, manuring, and later industrial fertilizer use. Meyer Cave, a paleontological site, provides a baseline for evaluating isotopic variation at archaeological sites. The Apple Creek Indigenous site (2,000 yr BP) exhibits niche specialization, with an isotopic niche smaller than and nested within that of the Meyer Cave population. Data from early European settlement and historical collections indicate a partial transition toward anthropogenic resource use, whereas modern raccoons exhibit a complete isotopic niche shift relative to the Meyer Cave baseline. Ongoing analyses of the remaining three species will test whether similar isotopic trajectories characterize synanthropization across taxa.

title: Evidence of post-Pinedale earthquakes in western Wyoming
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape (Posters)
authors: Reedy, Tabor [1], Ellett, Nicholas [2]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract: New lidar coverage east of the Teton Range contains scarps that serve as evidence of large, post-Pinedale earthquakes. Previous researchers identified short segments of faults with evidence of post-glacial deformation, and named them the Uhl Hill, Davis Hill, Baldy Mountain and Togwotee Lodge faults. Here, we utilize the new lidar data and field verification to map additional scarps and geomorphologic surfaces at select sites along the faults. Our mapping shows that these faults are significantly longer than previously considered, reaching up to ~50 km, though the scarps that serve as evidence of surficial rupture are generally discontinuous. The Togwotee Lodge fault at the North Buffalo Fork River and various sites along the Baldy Mountain fault show evidence of multiple post-Pinedale (~16 ka locally) earthquakes, similar to what has been demonstrated for the Uhl-Davis Hill faults. Topographic profiles along the Togwotee Lodge fault show vertical displacements of up to ~20 m in Pinedale-age deposits, suggesting a post-Pinedale rate comparable to the Teton fault. Displacements measured on the Baldy Mountain and Uhl-Davis Hill faults are roughly 2-10 meters in Pinedale-age deposits. Many of the scarps have exceptionally sharp morphology, suggesting youthful ruptures, but the timing of earthquakes on these faults remains unknown. The region lacks a clear landscape scale signature of these faults, calling into question how representative these faults might be of long-term deformation. Regardless, our new mapping suggests these faults may have hosted multiple very large earthquakes. Our new mapping and preliminary slip rates augment our understanding of post-glacial surface ruptures and better inform seismic hazard studies in the region.

title: Using the Book Creator Application to Give Students a Tectonic Identity
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Melzer, Leonard M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Manhattan International High School, New York City Department of Education, New York, NY, USA
abstract:
In today’s highly diverse urban classrooms, students find themselves learning about information that can at times seem unrelated or unimportant to them. The subjects of plate tectonics and lithospheric-dynamics offer an excellent opportunity for students to incorporate their unique and specific life experiences, while engaging in a content-rich classroom setting.

As an Earth science educator at an international high school for over twenty years, one of my goals was to think of ways for students to generate differentiated/individualized and culturally-responsive project based assessments using real-world data. The subject of plate tectonics and lithospheric-dynamics naturally lends itself to these types of assessments, specifically due to many students' past experiences with earthquakes.

Shortly after learning the basics behind the reasons for plate-motion and interactions, students are asked to learn more about how these interactions directly affect them and the people of their home countries. Students then discover several basic yet essential pieces of information that will ultimately help them form their tectonic identity; a unique story that helps develop an understanding for current, past, and future tectonic events.

Recently acquired by Kami in 2025, the Book Creator application can be an excellent tool for students to use when working individually or collaboratively. With Book Creator, students can easily add text, images, videos, and recorded audio samples designed in such a way so that the finished product feels like a fresh and captivating educational e-book. Perfect for teachers and the classroom, the application allows all student work to be saved with cloud storage, which can also easily be organized into different sections (displayed on a virtual bookshelf for each class). When finished, students have the ability to publish their books based on the permission settings applied by the teacher (this can be limited to the class, school, or the general public).

It is paramount that students not only “learn for the sake of learning,” but also to gain a sense of importance and relevance when applied directly to their places of origin and pathways forward. With a tectonic identity, it is my hope that students complete their plate tectonics and lithospheric-dynamics unit with a renewed sense of pride and awareness; one they’d be proud to share with each other, and perhaps the world.
