title: Assessing Magma Storage Conditions in On-Rift and Off-Rift Volcanic Centers in Iceland
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics (Posters)
authors: Hall, Parker R. [1], Harmon, Lydia J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Occidental College, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Occidental College, Los Angeles, CA,
abstract: Determining where and how magma is stored prior to volcanic eruption is critical, particularly for hazard assessment and for conceptualizing magma storage in the crust. While substantial progress has been made for systems in various tectonic regimes, rhyolites in Iceland are uniquely positioned to elucidate the conditions of silicic magma storage in a rifting, extensional regime. We collated published glass compositions from five volcanic systems from on-rift (Askja, Krafla) and off-rift (Ӧrӕfajӧkull, Hekla, Katla) centers, to assess the effects of tectonic regime on geochemical variation. Most rhyolites are metaluminous, but there are appreciable differences between on-rift and off-rift systems in major-element glass geochemistry. Using a subset of the data from Schattel et al., 2014, we utilize Rhyolite-MELTS to assess magma storage conditions between the off-rift Ӧrӕfajӧkull and on-rift Askja systems. To validate our modeling, we compare the observed mineral assemblage and calculated f O2 to the model results. Off-rift Ӧrӕfajӧkull results indicate the magma was stored at shallow ~120 MPa depths. In contrast, preliminary results from on-rift Askja indicate much shallower storage conditions ≤ 50 MPa. While the modeled mineral assemblage includes phases consistent with the observed mineral assemblage, modeling the on-rift Askja system at fluid-saturated versus fluid-undersaturated conditions significantly affects the results. In combination, there are substantial differences in magma composition and storage for the systems investigated. Future work will expand the storage depth modeling to the other volcanic centers to probe how on-rift and off-rift settings influence magma composition and storage depth in Iceland.

title: Sclerochronological Investigation of Shellfish Harvesting from an Early Spanish Colonial Archaeological Site in Coastal Georgia, USA.
session_title: Geoarchaeology (Posters)
authors: Rossman, Gavin M [1], Andrus, C. Fred T [2], Blair, Elliot H [3], Napolitano, Matthew F [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA

abstract: This presentation reports a sclerochronological investigation of clam shell remains excavated from a large shell-filled pit feature excavated at the North End Field Site (9MC81), located on the northeastern end of Creighton Island, Georgia, USA. The characteristics of this and multiple similar features within the site are highly unusual, leading to questions of depositional behavior. This site holds significance as it is believed to be Santa Clara de Tupiqui, a Spanish colonial mission located in the province of Guale from ca. 1595-1674. Artifacts found in the pit (Altamaha series pottery and Spanish olive jars) and radiocarbon dating indicate an age of ca. 1640/1650 for the feature. The goal of the project was to assess if the pit represented an accumulation of refuse over a long period of time or was the product of a short-term event, e.g., feasting. To address this question, two methods of analysis involving different sample species were employed. Method one consisted of growth band analysis of Mercenaria spp. recovered from the feature. Growth bands in the shells were analyzed to determine the season of capture for samples taken from the pit. Samples were sectioned along the axis of maximum growth to expose internal growth increments. These bands were digitally scanned, and their widths were measured to identify growth patterns and estimate the season of collection. Results indicate the Mercenaria spp. were harvested in all seasons, suggesting continuous collection rather than a single event. These findings will be independently tested using a second method applying sequential oxygen isotope analysis of stout tagelus razor clam (Tagelus plebeius) shells recovered from the same site. This represents the first measurement of season capture using stout tagelus. Comparing results of the isotope derived season of capture and the growth band interpretations will improve assessment of the processes and duration of site formation. These analyses provide additional anthropological insight, providing interpretations for shellfish harvesting practices and resource use.

title: Accelerating Glacier Retreat along the Colorado Front Range
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers
authors: McGrath, Daniel [1], Ulmer, Harlan [2], Raup, Bruce [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Ecosystem Science and Sustainability, Colorado State University, Fort Collin, CO, USA
(3) National Snow and Ice Data Center (retired), University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: Colorado's Front Range hosts 16 named glaciers and perennial snowfields, most smaller than 0.1 km² and perched at high elevations (~3600 m) in east- to northeast-facing cirques. We present a multi-decadal geodetic mass balance record for a subset of these glaciers spanning 1963 to 2025, synthesizing historical aerial images, airborne lidar, and structure-from-motion photogrammetry from low-altitude aircraft surveys. At Andrews Glacier, geodetic mass balance rates reveal a pronounced acceleration in mass loss: -0.02 m w.e. yr⁻¹ (1963–2010), -0.16 m w.e. yr⁻¹ (2010–2020), and -0.94 w.e. yr⁻¹ (2020–2025), consistent with regional summer warming trends documented in ERA5 climate reanalysis data. For Arapaho Glacier, the rate of mass loss is even more marked, increasing from -0.35 m w.e. yr⁻¹ (2010–2020) to -1.2 m w.e. yr⁻¹ (2020–2025). Local topographic controls—including shading, debris cover, wind redistribution of snow, and avalanche inputs—modulate the pace of retreat between individual glaciers despite comparable regional climate forcings. Extrapolating current thinning rates against ground-penetrating-radar-measured ice thicknesses suggests that several of these glaciers may disappear within the next 25–65 years. These findings are the longest available observational record of alpine glacier change along the Colorado Front Range and underscore the vulnerability of small glaciers to ongoing atmospheric warming.

title: NextStep Geosciences: Building Geoscience Identity and Expanding Participation Through a Theory-Informed Undergraduate Research Experience
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part II)
authors: Simurda, Christine [1], Vasquez, Veronica [2], Rowling, Jessica [3]
affiliations: (1) Jackson School of Geosciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Jackson School of Geosciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(3) Jackson School of Geosciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
The geosciences continue to face longstanding challenges in recruiting and retaining the next generation of professionals from vast educational, socioeconomic, and personal backgrounds. While undergraduate research experiences are widely recognized as high-impact educational practices, less attention has been given to the educational theories that should guide their design. NextStep Geosciences, a summer undergraduate research program at the Jackson School of Geosciences at the University of Texas at Austin, was intentionally developed using established learning and persistence frameworks to support student engagement, identity development, and pathways into geoscience careers. Annual evaluation techniques were implemented to assess the success of the program structure and understand the best implementation of these theories. The program specifically seeks to expand access for students with fewer opportunities to participate in authentic scientific research.

The program design draws upon four complementary theoretical perspectives. Situated Learning Theory and Communities of Practice theorize that students learn by participating in authentic disciplinary activities and gradually move from peripheral participation toward full membership within a professional community. Social Cognitive Career Theory emphasizes the importance of research experiences, mentorship, and mastery experiences in building self-efficacy and informing career decisions. The Science Identity Framework highlights the role of competence, performance, and recognition in helping students see themselves as scientists, while Tinto's Theory of Student Persistence underscores the importance of academic and social integration in promoting long-term engagement and retention. Together, these frameworks informed decisions related to research project structure, faculty mentoring, cohort formation, community-building professional development activities, scientific communication training, and opportunities for professional recognition.

Annual evaluations from the last two years indicate positive gains in students' sense of belonging within the geoscience community, confidence in conducting research, and interest in pursuing graduate education and geoscience careers. Rather than viewing research solely as a vehicle for technical skill development, NextStep Geosciences positions undergraduate research as a process of professional identity formation and community integration. Students engage in authentic faculty-mentored projects while participating in a structured cohort-based professional development experience designed to foster belonging, peer support, scientific confidence, and exposure to geoscience career pathways. This program demonstrates how educational theory can be translated into intentional program design and offers a transferable framework for institutions seeking evidence-based approaches to increase participation and strengthening persistence in the geosciences.

abstract:
The research data life cycle is a concept widely used to describe data-centric phases of decision-making and tasks throughout the research process. These phases are frequently labeled Plan, Acquire, Process, Analyze, Preserve, Publish, and Reuse. Here, we adapt the generic research data life cycle for collections-based paleontological data. We highlight domain-specific considerations in each phase, and we contextualize the value of the data life cycle for paleontological researchers. We also point to commonly used resources–including data standards–and roles in order to make this perspective practical.

Critically, we aim to illustrate the cyclical nature of collections data: from initial capture to data mobilization and publishing, refinement and use in research products, and finally reintegration of resulting data back into the original collections data system for future discovery and reuse. Closely examining the entire life cycle of paleontological collections data ensures that each phase is optimized to best support ongoing stewardship, broad use, and coordination with research efforts. In addition, it facilitates alignment with key data principles, leading to data that is more FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) in the long run.

abstract: Lake Seminole, a reservoir managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), was first impounded in 1954. The lake floods the confluence of the Chattahoochee and Flint Rivers, and these form separate arms of the reservoir. These two rivers have similar watershed sizes (~20,000 km 2 ). The Chattahoochee River is one of the most heavily managed systems in the country, with 14 dams along its mainstem, including two with large flood-control capacity and several that are used for hydropeaking electricity generation. By contrast, the Flint River has only two mainstem dams, neither of which alter the hydrology. Furthermore, Lake Seminole is managed so that the water level remains relatively constant in time, varying ±0.3 m in elevation. These characteristics make Lake Seminole an outstanding laboratory for studying reservoir sedimentation. Strikingly, the Chattahoochee arm exhibits a sandy subaerial delta, which prograded at 0.12 km 2 /yr, based on aerial photographs from 1994 and 2015, and aggraded 1.5±0.5 cm/yr, based on differencing lidar surveys from 2007 and 2018. Repeat cross-section surveys by the USACE since 1957 and sediment cores collected in 2023 show sedimentation rates up to 12 cm/yr in the former channel and 0.5-3 cm/yr on the inundated floodplain of the Chattahoochee River. By contrast, the Flint arm has no subaerial delta, with sedimentation rates up to 2.5 cm/yr in the paleo-channel and 0-0.9 cm/yr across the paleo-floodplain. We speculate that these contrasting styles result from a combination of (1) greater and sandier sediment load delivered by the Chattahoochee River; (2) differing geometries of the inundated river valleys; (3) daily fluctuations in discharge due to hydropeaking; and/or (4) differing degrees of sediment trapping and altered flood hydrology by upstream dams. We explore these hypotheses with estimates of sediment provenance from Rb-Sr isotope measurements of reservoir sediments, and a two-dimensional, depth-averaged, process-based morphodynamic model. Overall, the estimated volume of reservoir sediment accumulated from 1954–2023 is 7.1×10 7 ±4.7×10 5 m 3 , which represents a storage capacity loss of ~0.23% per year, or ~16% of the original capacity. While this rate is modest compared to reservoirs in high-relief regions, the sedimentation is impacting river morphology and flood risk both upstream and downstream of the reservoir.

abstract:
Extensive Large Igneous Province (LIP) volcanism during the Cretaceous ‘greenhouse’ caused elevated atmospheric CO 2 levels, warm climates, weakened ocean circulation, and widespread ocean deoxygenation. LIP-triggered short-term global carbon (C) cycle perturbations termed Oceanic Anoxic Events (OAEs) show characteristic carbon isotope (δ 13 C) excursions and have been identified by widespread deposition of black shales enriched in organic carbon (>1 wt.%) in the rock record. The Early Aptian OAE1a (Selli Event, ~119.5Ma) and Cenomanian-Turonian OAE2 (Bonarelli Event, ~94Ma) are the two most significant and extensive OAEs. In this study, we synthesize new δ 13 C bulk , calcium isotope (δ 44/40 Ca), and osmium isotope (Os i ) records for OAE1a from the Les Sauzeries core (Vocontian Basin, SE France) and for OAE2 from south-central Mexico with existing δ 13 C, δ 44/40 Ca, and Os i records for these events from other locations. Collectively, the new dataset represents multiple globally distributed sites (e.g., Western Interior Seaway, Tethys, and proto-Atlantic), varied depositional settings, and different carbonate archives.

The sites are chemostratigraphically correlated, with confirmation from published biostratigraphy where available. The Os isotope records support assertions that CO 2 emissions during LIP eruptions caused ocean acidification (OA), which is expected to reduce carbonate production and increase δ 44/40 Ca values. Accordingly, the δ 44/40 Ca records for OAE1a and OAE2 resolve distinctive negative-to-positive shifts that begin before and peak after abrupt excursions to unradiogenic Os i values, which precede the δ 13 C-defined event onset. Several features of the δ 44/40 Ca records are consistent with the high-fidelity preservation of primary kinetic isotope effects. Observations include: 1) different δ 44/40 Ca records for OAE1a and OAE2 show similar stratigraphic signals that oscillate around different absolute values, despite large separations in space and time; 2) δ 44/40 Ca and Os i records for OAE2 exhibit synchronous precursor shifts, even though t Ca = 10 2 -10 3 ´t Os ; and 3) δ 44/40 Ca values for R. cushmani increase as tests become smaller and malformed leading into OAE2. We interpret these δ 44/40 Ca records to reflect similar responses of the carbonate factory to changing ocean chemistry driven by LIP volcanism during both OAE1a and OAE2.

abstract:
Scientific ocean drilling cores and associated data, housed in three international repositories and numerous databases, provide an unparalleled opportunity to investigate Earth's history using legacy materials in new ways. Repository-based expeditions, modeled after shipboard science expeditions, enable researchers to re-examine cores collected during nearly 300 drilling expeditions over more than five decades. By integrating these legacy collections with modern analytical techniques, researchers can address new scientific questions that were not envisioned when the cores were originally recovered.

Four 21st Century Drilling workshops were held at Kochi Core Center (2023); Bremen Core Repository (2024); and Gulf Coast Repository (2025). Site 266 was investigated at KCC. The Bremen workshops, conducted as mini–Legacy Expeditions, investigated Sites 704, 1090, and 1092; the GCR workshop used Sites 1095 and 1096 to train and help participants develop future repository-based research projects.

We share two examples of how the legacy expedition approach can impact scientific investigations: 1) age model (re)development and 2) collecting new physical properties data on aging core. To update biomagnetostratigraphy, datums are compiled from shipboard and postcruise research, updated and integrated into recent time scales and biozonations. Additional samples are collected and analyzed for at least some microfossil groups. Once the age model is revised, high resolution records can be developed from both non- destructive measurements such as scanning XRF and Section Half Image Logger (SHIL), which in turn can be used to refine age models, and from core photographs.

Comparison of original core photographs (DSDP and ODP) with newly collected SHIL data provide an opportunity to compare initial and current core conditions. This is useful during core redescription and interpretation of new datasets such as XRF. Data can be inferred from original photographs (e.g., L*) and comparison of the inferred record to newly acquired SHIL and Section Half Multisensor Logger (SHMSL) data permits evaluation of the fidelity of the inferred L* record and a sense of the impact of core aging on L*. Further comparisons to shipboard CaCO 3 measurements and newly collected scanning XRF data (e.g., Ca) aid in evaluation of the L* records.

title: Concretions in Cleveland: Lithological and Geochemical Trends Associated with Fossil Bearing Concretions of the Devonian Cleveland Shale
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Roselli, Maya [1], Marroquín, Selva [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(2) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
abstract:
Decades of research has documented and described the exceptionally preserved fish and shark fossils of the Devonian Cleveland Shale. These fossils are most often preserved within concretions, however the quality of preservation varies, with only some fossils preserved with original soft-tissue. Interestingly, the concretions containing fossils are limited to a few specific geographic locations within the city of Cleveland, Ohio despite widespread occurrence of the Cleveland Shale throughout Ohio and Kentucky. This pattern suggests that these specific areas may have featured unique environmental conditions which facilitated the formation of fossil bearing concretions. With this work, we aim to uncover any spatiotemporal patterns associated with the presence or absence of fossils preserved with soft-tissue in concretions. Here, we begin to investigate the geochemistry and lithology at multiple Cleveland Shale localities in the Cleveland area.

From our initial field work we collected two five meter drill cores from two field sites, one with (Rocky River Metropark) and one without (Euclid Creek Metropark) previously documented occurrences of fossil bearing concretions. We undertook initial analyses with detailed lithologic descriptions and total organic carbon (TOC) and organic carbon isotope (δ13Corg) to establish a chemostratigraphic framework. This will serve as the backbone for further geochemical analyses to categorize the spatial patterns in local redox conditions to determine environmental drivers for concretion formation. Future work will include iron speciation analyses and detailed geochemical analyses of the fossil bearing concretions themselves.

title: Toxic Carbonates and Synsedimentary Tectonics: their Influence on Basin Structure, and Anhydrite Facies Distribution (Duperow Formation, Upper Devonian, Intracratonic Williston Basin)
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Irofti, Doina [1], Egenhoff, Sven Olaf [2]
affiliations: (1) University of North Dakota, College of Engineering and Mines, Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Grand Forks, ND, USA
(2) University of North Dakota, College of Engineering and Mines, Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Grand Forks, ND, USA
abstract: Carbonates are generally seen as reflecting hospitable living conditions, yet some of them in the Duperow Formation reflect toxic conditions. This study explains how this can happen and link it to zones of synsedimentary tectonics and the set-up of an intracratonic basin. It will highlight how also anhydrites mirror this basin geometry and define the basin center equally well as carbonate facies. The Upper Devonian Duperow Formation in the Williston Basin shows reef carbonates following the contours of the basin and also growing on a N-S-trending tectonically elevated zone. When sea-level falls, the area behind the reefs gets cut off from freshwater supply and develops unhealthy conditions where few if any animals can survive, reflected in the absence of burrowing and body fossil remains, yet perfectly developed bedding features and ripples. Maps of synsedimentary features and thickness distributions show that this N-S-running synsedimentary structure existed throughout Duperow times and divided the basin into two sub-basins. When sea-level fell over a certain threshold during lowstands, the basin became isolated from the open sea and switched from carbonate to evaporite sedimentation and became saline. The resulting anhydrite also reflect sedimentary conditions with sabkha anhydrites in shallow, and laminated anhydrites in basinal parts of the Williston. These basinal anhydrites, just as the most distal carbonate facies, outline the basin center perfectly showing its prominence in both sub-basins, but also displaying the lack of basinal facies on top of the elevated zone separating these two sub-basins.

abstract: Accurate ice sheet model histories after the Last Glacial Maximum are needed to understand ice sheet sensitivity to past and future climate changes. Relative sea level data are a useful comparison dataset to validate ice sheet histories. Large spatial data gaps remain around the Greenland Ice Sheet and limit a comprehensive data-model comparison. Here, we present two relative sea level curves from northeast and northwest Greenland that fill spatial data gaps and showcase the spatial heterogeneity of sea level histories in Greenland. We use sediment cores from isolation basins and marine embayments at numerous elevations to capture Holocene sea-level changes. To track marine and freshwater sediment transitions, we use XRF and macrofossil assemblages; we use radiocarbon ages to date the timing of these transitions. Additionally, we will present new modeling of sea-level histories to fully quantify uncertainties. In northeast Greenland, we find that between deglaciation (~12.7 ka) and ~10 cal ka BP, sea level was either falling slowly from a 58 m marine limit or rising to a marine limit that post-dates deglaciation. After ~10 cal ka BP, sea level fell at a faster rate before slowing once more in the past 5 ka. We do not find evidence that sea level fell below the present in the Late Holocene. In contrast, in northwest Greenland, we found that sea level was >8 m lower than modern sea level following the last deglaciation. Sea level reached ~3.5 m below sea level 1.5 cal ka BP and subsequently rose to the present level, which is the local marine limit. The sea level history in northeast Greenland highlights a system dominated by the Greenland Ice Sheet and ice-sheet oscillations may have influenced the earliest part of the record. In northwest Greenland, evidence suggests the post-glacial trend of sea level rise is due to subsidence of the forebulge from the Laurentide and Innuitian ice sheets that was situated under northwest Greenland during the Last Glacial Maximum. This work will add to the broader ice sheet reconstruction and sea level community via the RAD-CI Project, a new community-driven cyberinfrastructure for polar radiocarbon.

title: LEVERAGING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HYDROLOGY TO PROCESS CITIZEN SCIENCE PHOTOS OF WATER LEVELS
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Lowry, Chris [1], Manandhar, Abhinna [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
(2) University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
abstract:
The increasing need for hydrologic data in ungauged watersheds has led to the growth of citizen science initiatives, such as the CrowdHydrology project, where participants submit observations of water levels. While traditionally based on text-messaged numerical data, the widespread use of smartphones has resulted in an influx of unprompted photos of staff gauges, creating an opportunity for image-based processing and quality control. This research develops a methodology to extract water levels and station identification from these images using Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically designed to lower the barrier to entry for professional scientists who may lack expertise in computer vision.

The developed workflow employs a multi-stage process starting with Region of Interest (ROI) extraction using the YOLOv8 object detection model to isolate the staff gauge and the station label. Images are then preprocessed through grayscaling, contrast enhancement, and morphological filtering to reduce noise. A crucial step in the pipeline involves identifying the visual waterline through binarization and scanning, which is then marked with a horizontal red line before being passed to the Gemini 2.5 Flash LLM. The LLM utilizes structured responses via Pydantic data models to return validated numerical values for both water level and station ID.

Results indicate that while "naive" processing of raw images resulted in a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 0.89 feet, the addition of the visual waterline label significantly improved accuracy, reducing the RMSE to 0.25 feet. Furthermore, the LLM demonstrated a 98% accuracy rate in correctly identifying station IDs. To address potential hallucinations or reasoning errors, the system integrates a human-in-the-loop framework, allowing citizen scientists to verify and update processed contributions. This research demonstrates that leveraging the raw potential of established LLMs can streamline field-based hydrologic observations with minimal technical complexity, though current limitations in image resolution and font size on gauges suggest these methods may be best suited for higher-order streams

abstract: The Mississippian-age Greenbrier Group in West Virginia is a major Paleozoic transgressive period characterized by a thick, heterogenous package of well-developed carbonates. During deposition, this area underwent both temporal and lateral changes as the Appalachian foreland basin shifted episodically, resulting in thickening to the south-east where the Appalachian foredeep was located. In addition, minor periods of glaciation resulted in intermittent flooding of the foreland ramp, causing additional complex changes in the depositional patterns of the carbonate ramp environment. This complexity creates challenges when identifying and naming members over a regional area, as evidenced by changes in unit nomenclature. In the southeastern portion of the state where the unit is thickest, it is composed of the basal Hillsdale Limestone, Denmar Formation, Taggard Formation, Pickaway Limestone, Union Limestone, Greenville Shale, and Alderson Limestone. This carbonate package thins northeastward into the central portion of the state from 1,000 to 400 feet [305 to 122 meters] to as little as 100 feet [30 meters] in the north-central portion of the state. In areas bordering Pennsylvania and Maryland, a different stratigraphic nomenclature developed (the basal Loyalhanna Formation, Deer Valley Limestone, Savage Dam Member, and the Wymps Gap Member) that more effectively divides the Greenbrier Group in the north; thereby greatly complicating correlations across the entire region. Further studies have compounded these complications by showing that the Greenbrier Group in central West Virginia is not well suited to either northern or southern nomenclature and often cannot be divided into individual members. Lithostratigraphic correlation charts can be used on a state-wide level to better determine the trends of these basin-wide changes. In the quest to improve overall bedrock maps in the state, the ambiguity of the Greenbrier Group has driven the West Virginia Geological and Economic Survey to undertake a multi-year study to trace and understand its heterogeneity, resolve complications in its nomenclature and subdivisions, as well as map the overall unit in a more detailed manner.

title: Reef-building Contributions of Microbes and Metazoans in the Lower Ordovician
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Mikhailova, Marina [1], Ibarra, Yadira [2], Marenco, Pedro J. [3], Marenco, Katherine N. [4]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, San Francisco State University, San Francisco, CA, USA
(2) School of the Environment, San Francisco State University, San Francisco, CA, USA

abstract:
Reef ecosystems underwent major ecological reorganization during the Cambro-Ordovician, yet the relative contributions of microbial and metazoan framework builders during this transition remain poorly quantified. This study examines reef framework composition in the Lower Ordovician Fillmore and Wah Wah formations of the Ibex region, western Utah, spanning approximately 8 Myr of deposition. Petrographic thin sections, high-resolution scans, and systematic point counting were used to quantify the relative abundance of skeletal components, microbial fabrics, and altered microbial textures through the succession.

Twenty-three thin sections were analyzed using an average of 324.5 ± 54.1 points per sample. Point counts included micrite, microspar, spar, peloids, voids, burrows, oxides, microbial fabrics, and skeletal fossils. Because microspar commonly occurs in close association with microbial textures, a combined microbial + microspar category was used as an interpretive proxy for altered microbial framework.

Framework composition varies through the succession but remains consistently dominated by microbial material and carbonate matrix. Skeletal components increase from an average of 2.7% in the earliest interval to approximately 8% in the middle and latest intervals. In contrast, the combined microbial + microspar category averages 48.9%, 43.8%, and 58.9% across the three intervals, indicating that microbial fabrics remained the principal framework constituent despite increasing skeletal abundance. Additional petrographic observations document diverse microbial fabrics, including laminated and grumose textures, as well as Girvanella sheets, Epiphyton , and microbial fabrics associated with fenestrae and oxide-rich veins.

These data suggest that the Ibex reef system was characterized by persistent microbial influence and substantial diagenetic overprint, rather than by a simple replacement of microbial frameworks by skeletal builders. The recognition of complex microbial textures challenges earlier interpretations of these deposits as structureless mud mounds and indicates that Early Ordovician reef construction in western Utah was more texturally and biologically heterogeneous than previously recognized. Ongoing analyses will further evaluate the stratigraphic expression of these fabrics and the extent to which they record primary biological construction versus early diagenetic modification.

title: From Hillslope to Microscope: Linking LiDAR, Mineralogy, and Microstructure to Landslide Susceptibility in Appalachian Kentucky

affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Atmospheric Sciences, Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green, Kentucky, USA

abstract:
In Appalachian hillslopes of Kentucky, rapid mass wasting events such as landslides results from the combined effects of steep relief, layered sedimentary bedrock, weathering, groundwater movement, and storm-driven slope response. In the Williamsburg and Somerset areas, landslides pose a persistent threat to infrastructure, communities, and natural ecosystems. While terrain variables including topographic and hydrological data are commonly incorporated into susceptibility investigations, mineralogical and microstructural actors that contribute to material weakening are often overlooked. This study integrates geomorphic mapping based on a 61-cm-resolution LiDAR-derived digital elevation model with laboratory characterization of slope forming soils and rocks. More than 100 potential landslide locations were identified from morphologic markers including scarps, hummocky terrain, and downslope deformation, visible in multidirectional hillshades and slope maps. Ten accessible locations were selected for field investigation and sampling, yielding 29 soil and rock samples for petrographic and microstructural analysis. These samples were analyzed using optical petrography, scanning electron microscopy, back-scattered electron imaging, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.

Initial observations show that many rock samples from Somerset are calcite-rich, with microcrystalline and sparry calcite cement locally occluding primary pores. In contrast, rock and soil samples from Williamsburg contain little or no calcite, and consists primarily of detrital quartz, feldspar, and clay-bearing phases. Mineral textures and elemental compositions in Somerset rock samples are consistent with presence of illite- and chlorite- bearing minerals, whereas locally observed expandible clay-like phases may indicate moisture sensitive materials. Williamsburg soil and rock samples reflect a broadly similar mineralogy, although ongoing work utilizing X-ray diffraction is needed for definitive clay-mineral identification. Microcracks, clay-rich coatings, stylolitic dissolution seams, alteration rinds, and cement-filled pores record diagenesis, weathering, and fluid–rock interaction. These features may promote instability where dissolution, weathering, or clay accumulation weakens bedding planes, discontinuities, and rock–soil interfaces. Linking LiDAR-derived landslide inventories with mineralogical and microstructural evidence provides a framework for refining susceptibility models in Kentucky and similar humid, dissected sedimentary terrains.

abstract:
Abstract: Neck cutoffs on large meandering rivers usually disconnect from the active channel within 2 to 10 years as plug bars build up at the abandoned bend entrance and exit junctions. At Pumps Bend on the lower White River, Arkansas, a neck cutoff formed in 2013 has remained hydraulically connected for more than a decade, with traditional plug bar conceptual models not accurately predict patterns and rates of sedimentation. The elongate subparallel planform geometry of the site redirects flow nearly 180 degrees through the new cutoff channel; yet the role of unsteady discharge on sediment redistribution inside the abandoned bend is not well understood. This study uses Delft3D FM to simulate sediment flux and bed change under three 31-day discharge scenarios: steady flow, a single flood pulse, and two successive flood pulses. All three scenarios have the same total water and sediment input, such that differences in deposition can be attributed primarily to hydrograph dynamics. In the steady case, the upstream limb accumulates roughly twice the sediment of the downstream limb. A flood pulse inverts this pattern with the downstream limb receiving about 30% more sediment than the upstream limb. One of the mechanisms for this shift is a brief reversal in the water-level gradient at the exit junction near peak discharge, which redirects sediment toward the loop entrance. During the rising and falling limbs, the entrance-side gradient dominates and pushes sediment downstream. Additionally, prominent zones of flow recirculation within the entrance and exit of the bend also substantially limit the amount of sediment transported into the abandoned bend and thereby limit the growth of plug bars and the full disconnection to the active channel. Movable-bed runs also show a 20 to 40% reduction in cumulative sediment flux compared to fixed-bed runs, as bed aggradation limits how much sediment can enter later in the simulation. These findings have important implications for predicting planform dynamics of meandering rivers and the alluvial architecture of floodplains.

Keywords: Neck cutoff, Flood pulse structure, Meander loop connectivity, Sediment partitioning, Morphodynamic modeling

title: Integrated Trends in Groundwater, Streamflow, and Stream Temperature Across the United States
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Johnson, Zachary [1], Walvoord, Michelle [2], Ebel, Brian [3], Stagnitta, Timothy [4], Ayers, Jessica [5]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Washington Water Science Center, Tacoma, WA, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Earth System Processes Division, Denver, CO, USA

(5) The Nature Conservancy, San Francisco, CA, USA
abstract:
Understanding water availability requires integrating signals across groundwater, streamflow, and stream temperature. We synthesize two national multi-decadal trend analyses – one linking groundwater and streamflow and one linking streamflow with stream temperature – to develop a cohesive picture of hydrologic change across the United States. Both studies apply trend tests to large observational datasets and evaluate spatial patterns across three periods (1980–2020, 1990–2020, and 2000–2020).

The groundwater-streamflow analysis reveals contrasting tendencies: increasing low streamflow (wetting) and deepening groundwater levels (drying), with regional aggregation and longer timeframes improving trend agreement. Regionally, unified drying emerges in the West/Southwest, wetting in the upper Midwest, and directional mismatches persist in the High Plains and Mississippi Alluvial Plain. Aggregation by Hydrologic Landscape Regions yielded the strongest alignment between groundwater and streamflow trends, suggesting that climate, relief, and geology collectively drive coupled responses more than geography or geology alone.

The streamflow- temperature analysis documents and compares decadal and seasonal trends, assessing external drivers – land cover, precipitation, air temperature, and baseflow fraction. While most trends were uncertain or unlikely, significant positive correlations emerged between air temperature and stream temperature, as well as precipitation and streamflow. For 2000–2020, streamflow generally increased, attributed to higher winter/spring precipitation and lower spring/summer baseflow fraction. However, earlier periods showed more widespread streamflow decreases, particularly in the South and West. Regional case studies demonstrated nuanced relationships: Midwest streamflow increases linked to precipitation and reduced baseflow fraction, California-Nevada decreases associated with higher baseflow fraction and air temperature, and Atlantic Coast stream temperature trends tied to air temperature variability.

Integrated, multi-characteristic frameworks can prove indispensable for trend assessments of groundwater, streamflow, and stream temperature. Taken together, these results demonstrate that climate and anthropogenic factors drive divergent and often regionally specific changes in hydrologic metrics, with implications for water resource management and ecological sustainability. This work advances understanding of how groundwater, streamflow, and stream temperature respond to environmental drivers, supporting the development of holistic water availability assessments and adaptive management strategies.

title: Refined Latest Pleistocene Water-Level Record of China-Searles Lake System, Eastern California Based on New Luminescence Dating of Shoreline Deposits
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution (Posters)
authors: Duncan, Maggie E. [1], Bacon, Steven N. [2], Rodrigues, Kathleen D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Graduate Program of Hydrologic Sciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA; Division of Hydrologic Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Division of Hydrologic Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
(3) Division of Earth and Ecosystem Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
abstract:
During the late Pleistocene, the paleo-Owens River system included a chain of four pluvial lakes along the southern Sierra Nevada between Owens Valley and Panamint Valley in eastern California. Searles Lake is the third in this hydrologically connected system, receiving overflow from upstream China Lake. During exceptionally wet periods the two lakes coalesce between ~665 m and the overflow level at 690 m. Using sequence stratigraphy and infrared stimulated luminescence (IRSL) dating of well-preserved beach ridges, this study provides the first direct chronological constraints of shoreline deposits in China and Searles Lake basins, yielding new insights on the timing and magnitude of latest Pleistocene–early Holocene lake-level fluctuations and paleohydrologic change in the region.

Seven beach ridges underlain by bedded, sand-rich lacustrine and terrestrial deposits at 570, 585, 594, 607, 645, 670, and 680 m were investigated in the northern and southern sectors of Searles Lake basin. Preliminary IRSL dating of eleven samples yielded a range of mean ages for the following depositional environments: beach ridges at 569–667 m from ~17.0 to 11.8 ka, back-barrier aeolian sand sheets at 637–667 m from ~15.9 to 12.4 ka, and alluvium at 595–599 m from ~25.9 to 16.8 ka. Additional IRSL dating in China Lake basin of beach ridge deposits at 670 m yielded ages of ~12.9 and 13.0 ka.

Preliminary results indicate at least three major transgressive-regressive cycles occurred above 570 m between ~24.0 and 11.8 ka. The earliest is constrained between ~23.7 and 16.8 ka, reaching a minimum elevation of 607 m. A second transgression occurred after 16.8 ka, rising above 645 m, before dropping to at least 570 m by ~16.1 ka. The third and latest transgression reached at least 670 m between ~13.0 and 12.0 ka forming a coalesced China-Searles Lake, followed by a regression to 594 m by ~11.8 ka. Planned IRSL dating of samples collected at 680 and 690 m in Searles Valley and ~676 m in China Lake basin will constrain the timing of highstand water levels and potential overflow episodes of China-Searles Lake. Ultimately, these results will be integrated with existing shoreline chronologies from previous studies to refine the latest Pleistocene lake-level history of China-Searles Lake.

abstract:
Age models that relate stratigraphic or chronostratigraphic position to numerical time are the backbone geologic time. Over the past c. 15 years, the have been considerable advances Bayesian age modeling methods that are able to directly incorporate prior information about stratigraphic sections (e.g., sedimentation rates, superposition) as well as a variety of geochronologic data including radioisotopic dates, astrochronology, and biozones. While development of new statistical methods is critical to developing better age models, the best way to improve age models is to is to improve the data they are conditioned on. Adding new chronostratigraphic tie points, refining the numerical age of existing points, and adding new types of geochronologic data dramatically improve age model quality.

We demonstrate the magnitude of these improvements via a case study of the Altajme drill core (Gotland, Sweden). The core is a key section on which much Silurian biostratigraphy is based. Carbon isotope excursions from the core also define the Ireviken and Mulde events, two large scale ocean anoxia events. Earlier work by Cramer et al. (2012) produced 3 CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb dates for the core. We collected new CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb ages for these bentonites and using the ET2535 tracer solution. The new ages on average ~1 Myr younger than those previously reported and when combined with 5 new dates from the core allowed us to generate a highly resolved Bayesian age model. The new model systematically shifts the age of the core by approximately 2 Myr. Critically, while this core was used in the calibration of the 2020 Geologic Time Scale, the new age model does not overlap that of the GTS. Finally, the age model allows us to refine both the timing and duration of the Ireviken and Mulde events, necessary information for estimating perturbations to the Silurian carbon cycle. Together these data show not only the importance of updating our modeling methods (splines to Bayesian) but also the value of adding new data and revisiting old data for even well studied sections.

abstract:
Hypervelocity impact cratering is a fundamental geological process, but accurately dating terrestrial impacts remains challenging. Recrystallized, granular zircon associated with impactites suffers variable lead-loss and has been used to date impacts. Some of these granular zircon crystals exhibit systematic orientations, which have been proposed as impact-diagnostic microstructures formed by transformation of zircon to its polymorph reidite during shock, followed by reversion to zircon during post-shock high temperatures (known as the FRIGN zircon mechanism). However, this mechanism has not been experimentally tested. The crystallographic orientation relationships observed between natural and experimentally shocked reidite and host zircon where ({110} r ||{001} z , {110} z ||{001} r , {110} r ||{110} z ) are theorized to result in three mutually orthogonal orientation clusters, which coincide on the {001} and {110} in systematically oriented granular FRIGN zircon. We experimentally tested the FRIGN mechanism by transforming a single-crystal natural zircon to reidite at 13 GPa/1400 K for 8 hours using a multi-anvil press, followed by calorimetry for which we heated the reidite sample above the expected reversion temperature. We used electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to characterize the sample.

We achieved full transformation from single-crystal zircon to polycrystalline reidite. Reidite crystals were elongated perpendicular to the sides of the original zircon block, indicating nucleation originated at the edges of the block. The majority of reidite crystals were elongated perpendicular to block edges. Reidite grains display considerable spread in crystallographic orientations, with strong correlation between alignment with expected crystallographic orientations and smaller crystal size. Larger crystals likely nucleated and grew incoherently. Preliminary calorimetry data shows the heated sample was likely partially or fully reverted to zircon. We will also present a comparison of the pre- and post-annealing samples.

Our results provide experimental evidence for FRIGN zircon as an impact-diagnostic shock microstructure. Reidite formed in the deep Earth would likely lose crystallographic orientation relationships with its parent zircon over the long heating times expected in a tectonic environment.

abstract:
The end-Triassic mass extinction (ETME; ~201.6 Ma) coincided with emplacement of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP), one of Earth's largest large igneous provinces. Although CAMP volcanism is widely regarded as the primary driver of environmental change during the ETME, the relative importance of direct volcanic input versus enhanced continental weathering remains poorly constrained. We present new high-precision highly siderophile element (HSE; Ir, Ru, Pt, Pd and Re) and mercury (Hg) data from the Triassic–Jurassic Global Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) at Kuhjoch, Austria, to investigate the relationship between volcanism, weathering, and environmental recovery.

HSE concentrations increase near the Marshi carbon isotope excursion, remain elevated through the lower Tiefengraben Member, and decline higher in the succession. Most HSE enrichments correlate with siliciclastic proxies (Al, Ti and Zr), indicating that lithology exerts a primary control on absolute concentrations. After normalization to lithology, however, distinct HSE enrichments remain within the T-bed and lower Tiefengraben Member. These intervals coincide with elevated Hg/TOC values that have previously been interpreted as evidence for CAMP volcanism.

Comparison with published HSE records from other ETME sections demonstrates that Kuhjoch shares the characteristic Ir and Pt enrichments observed globally. However, Pt/Ir and Pd/Ir ratios overlap those of both CAMP basalts and upper continental crust, showing that these crossplots alone cannot uniquely distinguish volcanic from crustal sources.

Instead, our results demonstrate that integrating HSEs with Hg and lithological proxies provides a more robust framework for interpreting volcanic and weathering signals. Elevated Hg/TOC ratios record relatively short-lived volcanic degassing, whereas sustained HSE enrichments reflect both direct volcanic input and prolonged continental weathering following CAMP emplacement. These complementary proxy records suggest that CAMP volcanism initiated the environmental perturbation, while enhanced silicate weathering contributed to post-extinction carbon-cycle recovery.

title: Coupled Time-of-Flight and LASS-ICPMS U-Pb Dating of the Sturtian Cap Carbonate in Southern Oman

authors: Tasistro-Hart, Adrian [1], Adamson, Morgan [2], Koran, Isabel [3], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [4], Macdonald, Francis A. [5]

abstract: The Sturtian and Marinoan Neoproterozoic glaciations are ubiquitously sealed by carbonate sequences — “cap carbonates” — whose basal portions should be the same age under the hypothesis of globally synchronous Snowball Earth deglaciation. This synchronicity has been established with a handful of records where volcanic tuffs in proximity to the cap carbonates permit precise U-Pb zircon dating. Recently, in-situ U-Pb carbonate dating of Marinoan cap carbonates has yielded results overlapping with the zircon ages. Despite the lower precision of in-situ U-Pb carbonate dates, the ability to generate accurate ages from carbonates could be used to distinguish Sturtian from Marinoan caps in ambiguous successions, refining local age models and facilitating stratigraphic correlation. However, carbonate U-Pb dating often suffers from difficult-to-resolve complexity in open system behavior of the chronometer, which generates uncertainty in the geologic meaning of resulting ages. Here, we apply detailed spatial maps generated by time-of-flight (ToF) mass spectrometry to aid interpretation and identify geologic sources of analytical dispersion of LASS-ICPMS in-situ dating, thereby demonstrating an end-Sturtian affinity of the Ayn Formation cap carbonate in Mirbat, southern Oman. We analyzed both coarse, void-filling cements as well as laminated, barite-bearing and organic-rich carbonates. Detailed, 15 μm/px ToF elemental maps of U, Pb, and Al of the laminated carbonates revealed abundant disseminated siliciclastic material, which we interpret to be responsible for the excessive dispersion of U-Pb analyses for those samples, consistent with abundant Al and Si measured during LASS-ICPMS. ToF mapping of syn-depositional dolomite and early diagenetic calcite cements, on the other hand, permitted identification of homogeneous U-rich domains, enabling precise targeting for ICPMS to yield a coherent isochron with a lower intercept 95% confidence interval of 652.5-666.6 Ma. This lower intercept date overlaps with the ca. 661 Ma age for Sturtian termination, precluding a Marinoan interpretation for glacigenic diamictites of the underlying Ayn Formation. By integrating these methods, we demonstrate how ToFMS multi-element mapping can identify sources of analytical dispersion, direct U-Pb analyses, and improve the geologic interpretation of dates from stratigraphically ambiguous successions.

abstract: The occurrence of tocopherols in the sedimentary record, notably in OAE1a, reflects their biosynthesis by photoautotrophs to serve as anti-oxidants to counteract production of free radicals during photosynthesis. Enhanced production of tocopherols by photosynthetic algae represents a direct response to environmental stressors. Chromans are structural analogs of tocopherols that lack a phenolic hydroxyl group but possess similar anti-oxidant properties. Examination of 'aromatic hydrocarbon' fractions of samples from two Italian OAE2 sequences collected at Vispi and Furlo revealed that they contained familiar suites of aromatic steroidal hydrocarbons, methylphenanthrenes, and benzohopanes, but their two most abundant components were a-chroman (trimethylMTTC or trimethyl-2-methyl-2-(4,8,12-trimethyltridecyl)chroman) and a diaryl isoprenoid not previously reported. a-Chroman is the major component of the Vispi samples, whereas the Furlo samples are dominated by the unknown diaryl isoprenoid. The relative abundances of the two compounds are remarkedly consistent among each of the sequences, yielding strong correlations (r 2 = 0.94 for Vispi, r 2 = 0.81 for Furlo), which suggests a common biological source or similar environmental controls on their production. The mass spectrum of the unknown resembles those of tocopherols and chromans exhibiting a molecular ion (M +. at m/z 374; C 28 H 38 ) and two prominent fragment ions (m/z 159, 119/118) that, coupled with its elution position are consistent with expectations for a symmetric, diaromatic hydrocarbon, tentatively assigned as 1,4-bis[2,5-dimethyl-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronapthal-2-yl]butane. Sequential cyclization and aromatization of squalene represents a viable biosynthetic pathway for formation of this compound, which seems more probable than generation by diagenetic alteration. The d 13 C composition (-29 ‰) of the unknown is consistent with production by photoautotrophs and excludes a possible origin from anoxygenic sulfur bacteria that are known to produce C 40 aryl isoprenoids (e.g., isorenieratane). Significantly, its structural affinities to tocopherols, related chromans, and carotenoids suggest that this unknown undoubtedly serves a similar function and its dual aromatic rings likely make it more effective anti-oxidant than chromans. The prominence of these anti-oxidant compounds in the aromatic hydrocarbon fractions from Furlo and Vispi likely represent a direct response to environmental stressors, including high light intensity, elevated amounts of heavy metals, high temperatures, and low dissolved CO 2 , while the higher abundance of the unknown in the Furlo sequence perhaps reflecting a greater influence of these stressors relative to Vispi.

abstract:
Glacial geologic records and tree-rings are both influenced by summer temperatures and moisture. Previous studies have provided a framework to compare these proxies, from coastal settings, symmetrically along the shores of the North Pacific Gulf of Alaska (GOA) with the Southern Hemisphere’s Patagonia Icefields. Climate modes in the Pacific Basin including the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) are reflected in glacier mass balance and tree growth in both hemispheres. Therefore, these modes can potentially drive glacial variations and tree growth along the GOA and in Patagonia symmetrically across the equator, possibly yielding insights into the climate forcings of ice fluctuations and forest growth.

Tree-ring chronologies in both regions span thousands of years and have been used to reconstruct temperature. Building on the seminal work of R. Villalba (Mendoza Tree Ring Lab), our recent comparisons show a strong correlation between a coastal Alaska ( Tsuga merte nsiana ) tree-ring series and similar records from Northern Patagonia ( Nothofagus pumil io ). Comparisons yield a correlation of 0.42 (N=348 years) for year-to-year comparisons, as previously reported, and a correlation of 0.50 (N=348) where the Patagonia record lags Alaska by two years. Ongoing research will compile and compare glacier records to further investigate how the ocean-atmosphere modes of ENSO and PDO might be linked to the trees and glaciers in Alaska and Patagonia.

title: Phase-equilibrium constraints on fluid release in Archean orogenic gold systems

authors: Ramos Galarza, Santiago Ismael [1], Hernandez Uribe, David [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA

abstract:
Metamorphic devolatilization of Archean metabasalts is the widely accepted mechanism for forming orogenic gold deposits. While recent models suggest auriferous fluids can be released at high temperatures without partial melting, the specific mineralogical controls and the role of initial protolith hydration remain poorly constrained. Here, we use phase-equilibrium modeling across three geothermal gradients (500, 750, and 1000 °C/GPa) and three Archean basaltic compositions to evaluate P-T silicate-hydrous mineral equilibria. Fluid generation data were coupled with recent gold solubility models for metabasite-derived fluids to quantify Au release.

During metamorphism of water-saturated Archean basalts, chlorite breakdown at the greenschist- to amphibolite-facies transition (460–510 °C) acts as the primary engine for fluid generation. Our models show major fluid pulses releasing up to 1.6 wt.% H2O, yielding cumulative releases of 0.91 to 1.55 ppb Au before reaching the solidus. By contrast, in water-unsaturated Archean metabasalts (modeled with half their saturated H2O content), amphibole (>50 vol.%) is the dominant hydrous phase, and fluid production drops drastically. Notably, along a cold geotherm, specific unsaturated protoliths fail to release any free H2O or Au. Even under warmer gradients, the maximum cumulative Au release is restricted to <0.25 ppb Au.

Our results demonstrate that while chlorite breakdown is highly efficient at mobilizing Au, the protolith's initial hydration state ultimately dictates mobility efficiency. If the system is water-undersaturated, the source rock traps the gold during prograde metamorphism, highlighting the necessity of pre-metamorphic hydration for the formation of orogenic gold systems.

abstract: Students often find that some of the most difficult geoscience concepts to grasp require the development and practice of spatial reasoning in three dimensions. The difficulty possibly arises from little training in spatial thinking and 3D visualization early in their education and insufficient practice with applicable scientific examples. We use Visible Geology to create teaching modules that help introduce students to 3D models of various geoscience concepts and build intuition about spatial relationships. Visible Geology is a free online application (https://www.visiblegeology.com/). We have partnered with SERC (Science Education Resource Center) to create new educational resources with Visible Geology to help faculty integrate the application and spatial thinking skills into their courses. We have created eight new teaching activities that range from ~1 hour of time to longer labs or multi-class sessions (3+ hours). Our activities cover topics like the rule of V’s, folds in maps and stereonets, fold interference patterns, cross-sections, basin correlation, and reservoir stratigraphy, and are intended for use in classes like field methods, structural geology, and sedimentology/stratigraphy. These activities enable spatial reasoning growth in students through the creation of 3D models, hypothesis testing, and self-guided exploration. The modules are peer reviewed and freely available through Teach the Earth including teaching notes, student examples, and answer keys making them an approachable resource for instructors who aim to increase the development of spatial thinking and 3D visualization skills from a geoscience context.

abstract: Increasing the number of datable thermochronometric minerals ensures coverage of a wide range of rocks and thermal sensitivities. Monazite is a widely used chronometer for (U-Th)/Pb dating, but the underlying mechanisms controlling the variation in closure temperature (Tc, 200-300 °C) for (U-Th)/He remain poorly understood. This variability has been attributed to monazite's broad compositional range, the potential presence of complex chemical zoning, and the previously unstudied effect of radiation damage (α). Furthermore, monazite α kinetics differ significantly from those of well-understood minerals like zircon and apatite, as α damage anneals more readily at lower temperatures. Therefore, monazite requires a new method of calibration for α and Tc to establish a routine double dating workflow. We analyzed the 554 and 44069 monazite standards, as well as detrital monazites from the Upper Paleozoic Paganzo Basin in Argentina, to evaluate the controls on He diffusion kinetics across various thermal histories. To characterize α, we generated monazite Raman maps, focusing on the Full Width at Half Maximum (Γ) and peak positions around the ν1 (PO₄) band near 974 cm⁻¹. These grains were Th-Pb dated, and their T/REE concentrations were measured using LA-ICP-MS. EDS was used to map intragranular chemical variability and guide site selection for electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). Combining EPMA and Γ data allowed us to assess α differences within and between grains. These grains then underwent step-heating experiments with varying complexities in their heating schedules. Step-heating results produced a Tc range of 203-244 °C, with one grain containing multiple He diffusion domains akin to the K-feldspar 40Ar/39Ar system. These distinct domains were successfully documented using the combined EPMA-Γ. Moreover, Tc and α are inversely correlated between grains as constrained by the EPMA-Γ data, and this same relationship was documented in grains that experienced multi-cycle heating as α anneals during the analysis. Based on findings from various complex heating schedules, the last three samples were step-heated using a schedule that includes two prograde cycles and one retrograde cycle between 300 and 600 °C. This successfully shortened the experiment time while constraining diffusion parameters without modifying them. Ongoing work involves implementing a machine learning algorithm to predict Tc directly from T/REE data, to establish routine monazite (U-Th)/He dating procedures that may bypass time-consuming step-heating analyses.

abstract:
The U.S. Geological Survey is identifying geologic features with significant scientific, educational, cultural, economic, and aesthetic values to bring awareness to our national geoheritage and the critical role geodiversity plays in society. These geoheritage values are illustrated at numerous geologic sites that have played a role in scientific discovery and research, formal and informal geoscience education, as well as possess deeply rooted cultural significance and an aesthetic appeal that attract scientists and artists alike. Often, these locations also have an economic significance with historical connections to mining, including natural resource discoveries and production driven by societal needs at the time. To communicate these societal connections to our geology, we designed a web map application geared towards education and outreach called the Geoheritage Sites of the Nation Explorer, or Geoheritage Explorer, to inform the public about unique geologic features across America’s iconic landscapes. These geoheritage sites have been selected from Federally designated public lands and are characterized by their significant geoheritage values. This presentation will explore geoheritage sites with connections to the extraction of natural resources and their influence on human histories.

Within the Geoheritage Explorer, locations with related 1) coal mining history (e.g., New River Gorge of West Virginia and Little River Canyon of Alabama); 2) legacy metal mining (e.g., areas near Tar Point of Minnesota and La Coca Falls of Puerto Rico); 3) protected geothermal features (e.g., Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park); 4) geologic settings of oil and gas reservoirs (e.g., Guadalupe Peak and the nearby Permian Basin in Texas and the first oil well west of the Mississippi River in Garden Park Fossil Area of Colorado); and 5) other energy resources (e.g., uranium resources in the Grand Canyon area of Arizona) are highlighted and linked to scientific reports, geologic maps, and informational products geared towards a less technical audience to further enhance understanding of these sites. By exploring the interconnected scientific and societal histories related to resource extraction, the Geoheritage Explorer presents opportunities to educate the public about our vital geologic resources and how they have shaped U.S. history. These opportunities have the potential to spark the curiosity of the next generation of geoscientists who will be essential in addressing future societal needs related to our natural resources.

title: NO GUTS, NO GLORY: THE IMPORTANCE OF CONSUMULITES (FOSSIL INFILLINGS OF THE GI TRACT)
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Hunt, Adrian P. [1], Lucas, Spencer G. [2]
affiliations: (1) Flying Heritage Combat Armor Museum, Everett, WA, USA
(2) New Mexico Museum of Natural History & Science, Albuquerque, NM,
abstract: Consumulites represent material ingested and preserved material within the gastrointestinal tract of fossilized animals. Consumulites include aspirationalites, oralites, esophagolites, cropalites, proventralites, gastrolites, cololites, intestinilites, enterospira and evisceralites. The majority of consumulites are gastrolites (stomach contents). A matryoshkalite is a consumulite within a consumulite, and there are only three currently known examples, from the Permian of Germany and the Eocene of the United States and Germany. The preservation of consumulites is favored by a longer gut retention time and a lower digestive acidity. Consumulites are principally associated with, or at least recognized in the context, of articulated skeletons, the majority of which are from aquatic environments, as are many consumulites. Articulated skeletons are common in Lagerstätten that preserve vertebrate fossils. The vast majority of consumulites represent carnivorous animals because plant material is usually finely macerated during digestion, and it is much easier to recognize a bone as a foreign object than carbonaceous debris. Large body size favors the recognition of consumulites. The combination of large body size and an aquatic lifestyle results in an extensive record of consumulites in large Mesozoic marine vertebrates, notably ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and mosasaurs. Consumulites should receive ichnotaxonic names, but there are currently only four named ichnotaxa. Consumulites provide information on evolutionary and paleoecological issues, notably the evolution of digestive systems, including the function and location of organs, the chemistry of digestive systems, the evolution of diets within clades and the ontogeny of feeding. Consumulites preserve a wide range of organic elements with a poor fossil record, ranging from lepidopteran wings to hair, and thus represent micro-Lagerstätten. There is an extensive and under-appreciated fossil record of vertebrate consumulites starting in the Middle Silurian. Marine and nonmarine strata from the Cretaceous Period have a notable abundance of consumulites.

title: Pollution Sensitivity in Benthic Macroinvertebrates as a Parameter of Water Quality: A Preliminary Investigation of Ohio-Indiana Border Tributary Streams
session_title: Hydrogeology Discipline Session (Posters)
authors: Kandel, Britain Blue [1], Leong, James Andrew [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract:
Comparative ecohydrology can establish a timeline of system damage after contaminant spills, marking transport through the system by population fluxes of benthic arthropods, molluscs, annelids, and flatworms based on pollution tolerance. In the Midwest, agriculture and the manufacturing industry contribute non-point pollution from runoff and drainage into streams, introducing phosphates, nitrates, and trace metals. These passive contaminants differ from large spill events as their effects can take much longer to appear. The continuous introduction of contaminants leads to minute ecological changes, which can be compared across regional streams.

Common water quality parametersーconductivity, pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), biological oxygen demand (BOD), trace metal analysesーprovide ample information on the status of tributary streams. Less commonly are the inhabitants of the stream used as an indicator of stream health. Using these parameters and traditional kick-net sampling of benthic macroinvertebrates, six HUC-12 tributary streams located in the Ohio-Indiana border region were sampled biweekly during Summer 2026 to determine indices of pollution tolerance in aquatic organisms and geochemical stream health. Field probes were used for conductivity, pH, DO, and BOD, and High-Resolution Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (HR-ICP-MS) will be used to identify the presence of trace metals. Stream pH values ranged as follows: Four Mile Creek (8.14-8.53), Sevenmile Creek (8.10-8.38), Indian Creek (8.35-8.59), Rush Run (8.03-8.38), West Fork Mill Creek (8.24-8.26), Laughery Creek (8.09-8.82). Conductivity values (uS/cm) ranged as follows: Four Mile Creek (477-551), Sevenmile Creek (627-662), Indian Creek (535-559), Rush Run (636-690), West Fork Mill Creek (657-948), Laughery Creek (329-372).

Given these results, pH and conductivity indicate that wet to dry season stream changes can be tracked. As surface flow decreases, base flow introduces dissolved ions into the system; in limestone-dominated regions, CaCO3 dissolution into streams incrementally raises the pH. Furthermore, this ion influx can increase conductivity; in other streams, less runoff decreases the amount of total dissolved solids in the stream, affecting the conductivity and decreasing it over time. Future expected results of this study are negative correlations between suspended trace metals and pollution-sensitive organisms. As this research finalizes, more conclusions can be drawn between these systems, displaying the complex interplay of aquatic geochemistry, contaminant transport, and macroinvertebrate populations.

title: Mapping Geologic Thermal Energy Storage Potential Across the United States
session_title: Hydrogeology of Geothermal Resources: From Shallow Systems to Deep Reservoirs
authors: Pepin, Jeff D. [1], Burns, Erick R. [2], Cahalan, Ryan C. [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Portland, OR, USA
abstract: Storing thermal energy underground for later use in electricity production or direct-use heating/cooling is a promising green energy option. Reservoir thermal energy storage (RTES) is one such approach that stores energy in underutilized permeable strata with low ambient groundwater flow rates and more geochemically evolved waters (e.g. brackish/saline) relative to overlying aquifers. The U.S. Geological Survey is assessing the national potential of RTES by focusing on five generalized geologic regions in the United States: Basin & Range, Coastal Plain, Illinois Basin, Michigan Basin, and Pacific Northwest. Reservoir models are developed for the following eight metropolitan areas to evaluate RTES performance across different climates and subsurface environments: Albuquerque, New Mexico; Charleston, South Carolina; Chicago and Decatur, Illinois; Lansing, Michigan; Memphis, Tennessee; Phoenix, Arizona; and Portland, Oregon. Evaluated metrics include required well spacing, thermal storage capacity, and thermal recovery efficiency through time. Potential complicating factors considered for each reservoir include reservoir depth, free convection, and groundwater salinity. This work focuses on direct-use cooling because the need for cooling representative modern office buildings (25,000 square-feet, two stories) greatly exceeds that for heating in most parts of the country; however, the evaluated metrics are also relevant to heating and electricity applications. Results indicate that favorable RTES conditions exist in every region, with the Coastal Plain and Basin & Range being particularly favorable for thermal storage capacity, while the Pacific Northwest and Michigan Basin excel at energy recovery for the evaluated cooling application. The results underscore the utility of developing maps of thermal storage capacity, subsurface temperature models, and volumetric estimates of thermal storage capacity to serve as potential key RTES resource classification standards. Overall, this pre-assessment provides an initial understanding of RTES potential in several cities and geologic regions throughout the country and could aid further evaluation of national RTES efficacy.

title: Earth MRI from the State Geological Survey Perspective: Building the Geoscience Framework for a Mineral-Secure Nation
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Day-Stirrat, Ruarri James [1]
affiliations: (1) Oregon Department of Geology & Mineral Industries, State of Oregon, Portland, OR, USA
abstract:
The Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) has changed how the United States develops the foundational geoscience information needed to understand its mineral resources. From the perspective of the state geological surveys, its central achievement is not simply the acquisition of new data, but the creation of a durable federal–state partnership that links national priorities with local geologic knowledge.

Many of the most important mineral-resource questions cross jurisdictional boundaries, require multiple data types, and exceed the practical capacity of any single organization. Earth MRI makes these projects possible by combining USGS coordination and modern geophysical acquisition with the field capability, geologic mapping, samples, historical records, and place-based knowledge maintained by state geological surveys. This structure allows projects to move from regional reconnaissance to targeted investigation while retaining the geologic context needed to interpret geophysical, geochemical, mineralogical, and subsurface data.

The benefits extend beyond mineral exploration. Earth MRI investments improve geologic maps, preserve and modernize legacy data, expand public access to precompetitive information, train the next generation of geoscientists, and strengthen relationships among federal agencies, states, Tribes, universities, and industry. In Oregon, Earth MRI-supported work is improving understanding of nickel-bearing laterites, lithium-bearing volcanic systems, cobalt bearing systems, as well as mine waste, and other prospective geologic environments while also generating information relevant to groundwater, geothermal resources, natural hazards, and land-use decisions.

The next phase of Earth MRI should build on this collaborative model. Significant gaps remain in geologic mapping, high-resolution geophysics, geochemistry, mineralogy, and subsurface characterization. Closing those gaps will require sustained funding and continued investment in state geological survey capacity. Earth MRI should be viewed as a multi-decadal investment in opportunity.

A mineral-secure nation must first be a geologically informed nation. Earth MRI provides the framework for that understanding and demonstrates that national-scale geoscience is most effective when federal leadership and state expertise are designed to work together.

title: P-value Pulse of Türkiye as a Global Sink for Geochronology Data
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data (Posters)
authors: Sinoplu, Ozan [1], Onat, Kaan [2], Vermeesch, Pieter [3], Gildir, Semih [4], Yu, Hao-Cheng [5], Qiu, Kun-Feng [6], Donmez, Cahit [7], Pang, Jianzhang [8], Karatas, Burcu [9], Sarikaya, Oral [10], Keles, Ozlem [11], Kaya, Mustafa [12], Kocaturk, Huseyin [13], Tamer, Murat [14]
