abstract:
Geochronological datasets are fundamental to reconstructing Earth's tectonic and thermal evolution, yet their reliability depends on the statistical transparency of reported ages. The rigid application of p-value thresholds, alongside variance filtering and p-hacking, can obscure genuine geological complexity under artificial statistical conformity. To expose these trends, we present a comprehensive audit and spatial analysis of Türkiye's geochronological archive, evaluating data from 61 international laboratories across five continents. This compilation is significant for measuring p-value trends across Türkiye's tectonic zones and enabling a worldwide audit of laboratory signatures, necessitated by scarce domestic analytical facilities.

Compiling 202 articles with 656 U–Pb and 468 fission-track (FT) samples (20,009 individual grain analyses), our statistical evaluation reveals significant deviations from theoretical expectations. U–Pb datasets predominantly exhibit statistical overdispersion indicative of retained, complex petrogenetic histories. However, inconsistent MSWD and p-value reporting frequently obscures interpretation, and ~11% of U-Pb data remains under-dispersed. Conversely, FT datasets demonstrate severe underdispersion. Strikingly, ~45% of FT samples yield extreme p-values approaching 1.0 (p > 0.95), and ~90% exhibit variances that are "too good to be true." This pattern is consistent with observer bias, truncation, and homogenization arising during human-intensive manual data acquisition. Benchmarked against prior compilations—where 21% of high-profile journal U-Pb analyses and 30% of geochron.org FT samples enter the forbidden zone—the Turkish U-Pb archive mirrors the global norm, whereas its FT archive is three times more underdispersed. Disaggregating the repository reveals a clear pattern between statistical conformity and origin facility. We hypothesize this reflects a globally synchronized analytical culture where the p-value transformed from a variance measure into an institutional target, manifesting Goodhart’s Law, driven by aligned author, laboratory, reviewer, and publisher incentives.

To analyze how these artifacts affect tectonic interpretations in Türkiye, we used kernel density estimation heatmaps to identify regional clusters of extreme statistical conformity across major tectonic domains. Flagged U-Pb ages (p ≥ 0.95) cluster most strongly in northeastern Anatolia, and flagged fission-track ages in central and western Anatolia. The culmination of this research is the Geochronology P-value Map of Türkiye, an interactive web platform (https://www.chronostat.earth) that integrates statistical metadata with geographic context. This living database provides a scalable framework to visualize radiometric dating uncertainty, expose analytical homogenization, and guide more spatially informed future sampling.

title: Dehydration Melting of Amphibole-rich Lower Crust During Crustal Thickening Generates Super Wet Magmas: Implications for Porphyry Copper Deposits Formation

authors: Donoso-Tapia, Damian [1], Tassara, Santiago [2], Hernandez Uribe, David [3], Olivares, Arnaldo [4], Inostroza, Alan [5]

abstract: We use petrological modeling to investigate the effects of crustal thickening on the fate of structurally bound H 2 O in amphibole-rich, lower-crustal cumulates. Our results show that these lithologies undergo dehydration partial melting during burial associated with crustal thickening, at deep crustal conditions (~1.0-1.4 GPa and ~800-1000 °C), producing volumetrically relevant super-wet melts (>6-14 wt. % H₂O). This process does not require the influence of externally derived fluids and operates over a range of bulk compositions and geothermal gradients. We hypothesize that temporal variations in the compressional regime can trigger the episodic extraction of these super-wet melts, generating transient pulses of exceptionally hydrous magmatism that fertilize arc magmatic systems and promote the formation of large porphyry copper deposits (PCD). Overall, our findings suggest that crustal thickening can act as an active driver of volatile release from crustal rocks, providing a mechanistically grounded framework linking deep crustal processes to PCD formation.

title: Correlating the Eifelian/Givetian stage boundary (Middle Devonian) across the Appalachian Basin using conodonts and magnetic susceptibility data from the Marcellus subgroup (New York) and Delaware Formation (Ohio)

authors: Waid, Christopher B.T. [1], Over, D Jeffrey [2], Brett, Carlton E. [3], Ruggiero, Joseph A. [4], Farrugia, Vincent C. [5], Ver Straeten, Charles A. [6], Danielsen, Erika M. [7]
affiliations: (1) Ohio Geological Survey, Columbus, OH, USA

abstract:
Chronostratigraphic correlation of the mid-Eifelian through lowest Givetian stages has been problematic in the Marcellus subgroup (proximal Appalachian Basin) and the approximately coeval uppermost Columbus through Delaware formations (distal Appalachian Basin), in large part because of limited conodont data. Of the seven conodont zones comprising this interval, only the costatus and kockelianus zones have been identified within the Marcellus subgroup in previous studies. Similarly, only the costatus , australis , and eiflius zones have been recognized in past studies of the uppermost Columbus through Delaware formations. No conodonts indicative of the lowest Givetian hemiansatus Zone have been recovered in either unit, but macropaleontological evidence indicates that the Eifelian/Givetian boundary occurs within the East Berne Member of the Oatka Creek Formation of the Marcellus subgroup. Furthermore, the limited conodont data makes identifying the stratigraphic position of the globally recognized Kačák Bioevent ( ensensis Zone, latest Eifelian) difficult in the Appalachian Basin.

To improve chronostratigraphic correlation between the proximal and distal basin and better constrain the position of the Eifelian/Givetian boundary, we collected additional conodont samples and developed magnetic susceptibility curves (δMS) from the Marcellus subgroup and upper Columbus through Delaware formations. These new conodont data allow for the recognition of the Eifelian pseudofoliatus Zone in the uppermost Columbus and lower Delaware formations, and the ensensis Zone in the upper Delaware Formation and the Cherry Valley Member of the Oatka Creek Formation. No hemiansatus Zone conodonts were recovered. Sharply rising δMS values from the top of the Cherry Valley through lower East Berne members, and within much of the upper Delaware Formation, are similar to those that occur within the ensensis Zone at the Givetian GSSP and which coincide with the global Upper Kačák Bioevent. As at the Givetian GSSP, we place the Eifelian/Givetian boundary at a negative δMS deflection just above this initial rise. In Ohio, this deflection occurs just above the highest occurrence of the conodont Icriodus stelcki , which does not extend into the Givetian. Combined, the new conodont and δMS data from New York and Ohio improve chronostratigraphic correlation of the mid-Eifelian through lowest Givetian strata of the Appalachian Basin and constrain the position of strata correlating to the Kačák Bioevent.

title: From Skin to Stone: A Review of Three-Dimensional Soft Tissue Fossilization in Paleontological Research
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record (Posters)
authors: Maddox, Hannah Marie [1], Keenan, Sarah Wheeler [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD,
abstract: Fossilized integument provides some of the most direct evidence of the paleobiology of extinct organisms, yet the processes responsible for its preservation in the rock record remain poorly understood. Fossils with associated, three-dimensional soft tissues are rare, require expertise to recognize when soft tissue is present, require extensive time to excavate, prepare, and curate, are difficult to loan out for research, and may have complex ownership histories due to their perceived novelty. As collection and preparation techniques improve, we are observing an increase in three-dimensional fossil “mummies” globally, suggesting that soft tissue preservation may be more common, or more frequently recognized, than we currently realize. Inherent structural differences between the integument of major clades, such as increased keratinization within the stratum corneum of reptilian skin compared to that of mammals, have the potential to explain some of the patterns we see in soft tissue fossilization. Actualistic decomposition experiments have demonstrated that reptilian skin can last for over a year within a humid, temperate environment, suggesting that the potential for soft tissue preservation does not require the presence of unusual environmental conditions to last on the open landscape. Although three-dimensional skin tissue associated with fossil remains has been recognized since the mid-19 th century, most literature regarding fossilized tissue has been confined to brief references within larger studies or morphological description. The past few decades have seen a resurgence of interest in soft tissue research with a more in-depth histological, sedimentological, and geochemical focus. Recent analyses have suggested that multiple taphonomic pathways for soft tissue fossilization exist, ranging from iron-mediated direct mineralization of skin tissue to impression-style “clay-mask” preservation. However, the lack of widespread use of geochemical analytical techniques in soft tissue analyses likely leaves the full picture of soft tissue taphonomy unfinished, as most published specimens are only known from morphological analyses, while many more potentially scientifically important specimens remain undescribed within museum collections. A preliminary literature meta-analysis revealed that over half of sampled articles (~69%) described fossilized skin tissue with the generic term “impression”, regardless of any geochemical confirmation as such. Integrating more geochemical analyses with actualistic taphonomic experiments across vertebrate clades will be essential for our ability to identify and categorize the biological and environmental controls governing soft tissue preservation in the rock record.

abstract:
The Blue Earth River (BER) basin, Minnesota, USA, has undergone a conversion from prairies and wetlands to extensive row crop agriculture and artificial drainage over the last two centuries. This has resulted in well-documented geomorphic change accompanied by increased sediment and nutrient loading which is further exacerbated by changing precipitation regimes. The Rapidan Dam (RD) was constructed on the BER in 1908-1910, ~19 km upstream from the confluence with the Minnesota River. RD represented a ~16 m local base level high, resulting in rapid sedimentation within the reservoir that was near capacity at the time of failure. On June 24, 2024, following ~20 cm of rainfall over three days, the BER spilled around the western edge of RD, causing an avulsive failure. Media coverage and observations of the event provided a unique opportunity to investigate fluvial response to both dam failure and abrupt base level change. As the failure evolved, it became evident that this was akin to natural spillover processes that create transverse drainages – a fundamental mechanism in reorganizing drainage networks.

Over the past ~2.5 years, repeat LiDAR, structure-from-motion surface models, and cross-sectional transects were used to quantify the geomorphic response of the BER. The rapid lowering of base level following the event triggered the development and migration of knickpoints through underlying alluvial, glacial, and Paleozoic sedimentary strata, with some traveling upwards of 130 m hr -1 . These knickpoints excavated 1.6 million m 3 of hillslope and reservoir sediment within 2 km upstream of the dam. The downstream portion now exhibits near-braided morphology as large volumes of remobilized sediment move through the system. Longitudinal profile analysis indicates that the BER continues to approach a graded profile, but the majority of this adjustment occurred within one week of spillover. The result of this event is the transverse gorge through which the BER now flows.

We suggest this ongoing study is a powerful example of avulsive-style dam failure and transverse drainage development that can aid both geomorphologists and municipalities. The potential for this type of event is increasing with changing hydroclimatic regimes and aging infrastructure, driving the need to better understand the geomorphic implications of these events to protect people and the environment. This study also exemplifies the unprecedented geologic impact human activities have on landscape evolution.

title: Legacies of Extraction: Unearthing Ethics in Mining Frameworks
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Huss Llenos, Sophia [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA
abstract: While mining industries power nearly every aspect of our daily lives, they have long been associated with ethical controversies involving land use, environmental degradation, Indigenous rights, and community impacts. These legacies, which are embedded in both historical and contemporary mining practices, continue to influence approaches to remediation, restoration, reclamation, and rehabilitation. In recent decades, the global mining sector has introduced a range of frameworks intended to promote responsible, sustainable, and ethical practices. However, the adoption and effectiveness of these frameworks remain inconsistent, and they often fall short of addressing the full scope of sociocultural, economic, and environmental concerns. This study presents a systematic literature review examining how ethics are conceptualized and operationalized in mining, with attention to both historical practices and contemporary governance frameworks. By analyzing responsible, sustainable, and related mining frameworks, this work identifies key overlaps and gaps in how ethical considerations are addressed. Findings indicate that while ethical principles are often implicitly present in these frameworks, they are rarely framed explicitly as “ethics,” and the concept of “ethical mining” itself is largely absent from the literature. Furthermore, existing frameworks tend to overlook the specificities of mined materials, geographic contexts, and fenceline communities, while disproportionately privileging western ethical perspectives and offering minimal engagement with Indigenous knowledge systems. These omissions limit their effectiveness in guiding meaningful approaches to the long-term stewardship of mining-impacted landscapes. The gaps identified in this study can serve as opportunities to integrate community-based and culturally grounded ethical approaches in order to address the persistent sociocultural, economic, and environmental challenges associated with mining. Such integration can strengthen geoconservation practices and support more just engagement with mining-impacted environments and communities, while also acknowledging and preserving the historical and scientific significance of our shared mining heritage.

authors: Velez Lewis, Lily [1], Patounakis, Katerina Anne [2], Shteynman, Leah [3], Bowey, Sean Martin [4], Shuman, Mohamed A [5], Queener, Maxwell Gregor [6], Sharp, Thomas G [7]

abstract:
Zircon (ZrSiO 4 ) is a geologically important mineral found in meteor impact crater sites that transforms into its polymorph, reidite, under the high pressure and temperature (PT) conditions of an impact. The transformation from zircon into reidite is important to understand in order to constrain the PT conditions of impact. Reidite reverts to zircon after decompression if it is annealed above 1200°C. It is hypothesized that former reidite in granular neoblastic (FRIGN) zircon, a systematically oriented microstructure found in impactites, forms from the transformation to and reversion from reidite. This backtransformation has not been replicated experimentally, so the FRIGN model assumes that the reversion of reidite to zircon follows the same crystallographic pathways as the transformation of zircon to reidite.

The purpose of this study was to understand the crystal growth and nucleation processes of the zircon-reidite transformation using static high-pressure experiments. Two multi anvil experiments were conducted using a natural zircon block packed with zircon powder at 13 GPa and 1400K with varying heating durations. One sample was heated for thirty minutes, producing a partial transformation to reidite along the edges of and fractures within the block, while a second sample was heated for eight hours, resulting in full transformation. Reidite nucleated heterogeneously and grew into elongated grains, perpendicular to the boundary lines of the zircon block. This was likely due to a lower activation energy needed for nucleation on these sites. This pattern of grain growth and elongation was observed in both the partially and fully transformed samples, with an estimated minimum growth rate along the edge and fracture line of the zircon single crystal to be between 2.8-4.2 μm/min.

Our results support FRIGN zircon, a systematically oriented granular microstructure of backtransformed zircon found in impactites, as likely impact-diagnostic. It is unlikely that FRIGN zircon could form and be preserved within the Earth’s mantle. Our results indicate that under the static conditions of the upper mantle, incoherent growth and/or recrystallization of reidite would erase the crystallographic orientation clustering from the zircon-reidite transformation.

title: Capturing Caprock Heterogeneity with Continuous Scratch Testing: Implications for Geological CO₂ Storage in the Michigan Basin
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Zakharova, Natalia V. [1], Kim, Boyoung [2], Treece, Cailey [3], Burns, Aidan [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mt Pleasant, MI, USA
(2) Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, Michigan, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI, USA
(4) Deparment of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, Michigan, USA; University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
abstract:
Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) is a key strategy for reducing atmospheric CO₂ emissions, but its successful implementation depends on a thorough understanding of the petrophysical and mechanical behavior and heterogeneity of reservoir-caprock systems. This study investigated the geomechanical properties of Cambrian and Ordovician formations in the Michigan Basin using new-generation instrumented scratch testing. Unlike conventional laboratory strength tests, scratch testing provides minimally destructive and nearly continuous estimate of unconfined compressive strength and related mechanical properties directly on the core, allowing characterization of geomechanical variability at centimeter-scale resolution without extensive sample preparation. Scratch-derived strength profiles were integrated with lithologic, petrophysical, and stratigraphic data to evaluate the integrity and spatial variability of potential reservoir and sealing formations. Results demonstrate that both regional and small-scale heterogeneity are significant features of Michigan Basin storage systems.

Target caprock formations within the Michigan Basin, e.g., the Eau Claire and Glenwood formations, exhibits pronounced regional and local differences and a wide range of geomechanical properties. The Eau Claire Formation changes significantly west to east: with relatively uniform but consistently low strength in the west and highly variable but overall more competent intervals in the east. Within the Cambrian carbon storage system, the Trempealeau Formation exhibits the highest average compressive strength, indicating that it is the most mechanically competent caprock. The Ordovician Glenwood Formation is characterized by high mechanical variability, including localized intervals of very low strength associated with black shale and white sandstone facies containing green vertical burrows, highlighting the need for more site-specific caprock assessment. The Trenton-Black River limestone forms a relatively competent caprock, whereas the Utica Shale represents the weakest sealing unit evaluated to date. These results demonstrate that continuous scratch testing provides a powerful approach for capturing geomechanical heterogeneity that is often missed by conventional discrete laboratory measurements. In addition to unconfined strength, scratch testing allows estimating fracture toughness and establishing site- and/or formation-specific velocity-strength relationships, potentially facilitating log-based strength assessment and geomechanical extrapolation beyond cored boreholes. The resulting high-resolution mechanical characterization improves reservoir and seal evaluation, supports more reliable geomechanical models, and reduces uncertainty in CCUS site selection and risk assessment.

title: Fossils and Fantasy: A New and Engaging Way of Merging Pop Culture and Science
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Bennett, Cassandra C. [1], Schiffbauer, James D. [2], Vassmer, Sara [3], Huber, Christal [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA; Sternberg Science Camps, Sternberg Museum of Natural History, Hays, Kansas, USA
(2) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(3) The Connector, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(4) The Connector, University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA
abstract: In times of low student enrollment, geoscientists are looking for new and engaging ideas to recruit students and encourage young scientists to consider the Earth sciences as a viable future career path. In many ways, informal education is a gateway for students to explore various fields and make enjoyable memories that can influence their future endeavors (Kim and Dopico, 2016; Mohr-Schroeder et al., 2014; Kitchen et al., 2018). At the University of Missouri, we are seeing a steady decline in both undergraduate and graduate geology majors. Thus, finding ways to connect to young students is critical in recruitment efforts, perhaps now more than in the past. While we have ample scientific outreach opportunities, many of our activities are basic and rely on lecturing students on fun facts, rather than engaging them in a memorable experience. Combining pop culture with science is not a new idea; there have been a variety of programs and activities, including University of Lincoln’s SciPop Talks (Burks et al., 2017), Patterson’s cosplay booth at San Diego Comic Con (2023), and the most prevalent, Cosplay for Science, a nonprofit educational initiative (Santos [JS1] et al., 2019). With the rising popularity of the tabletop role-playing game Dungeons and Dragons (D&D), we have a unique opportunity to capitalize on a growing trend in pop culture. Fossils and Fantasy is a preliminary educational activity that relies on combining the fantastical creatures of D&D and an immersive experience with actual scientific practices used in paleontology. This activity was showcased at both Columbia Young Scientist Symposium and Art in the Park. Students engaged with a 2-dimensional representation of a rock outcrop preserving fossils of the game’s fantasy creatures. Students would pick out fossils and match them to their corresponding creature. Each student was provided with a booklet describing how paleontologists identify fossils, how organisms and their parts fossilize, what the fantasy creatures look like, and short-answer activities that help students think deeper about how these creatures look (and how to identify them!) when fossilized. Preliminary results suggest that students were happy to engage in an activity from media that they knew and recognized. Future work will incorporate realistic props and immersive environmental design elements to support experiential, play-based learning and promote sustained student engagement.

title: Planetary Geoarchaeology: Exploring Site Formation Processes Beyond Earth
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Holcomb, Justin A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract: Since the crash of Luna 2 into the Moon's surface in 1959, humans have interacted with the surfaces of ten other celestial bodies, leaving behind artifacts (e.g., scientific equipment, rovers, landers, impactors, cultural items), features (e.g., rover and human trackways, sampling locations), and archaeological sites (e.g., impacts, landings and crashes), which collectively form the archaeological record of the Solar System. From a contemporary archaeological perspective, the vast quantity of debris scattered across the solar system represents the material footprint of our species’ history of dispersal – first out of Africa and, ultimately, beyond Earth. I argue that this material offers a unique opportunity to extend geoarchaeological approaches to off-Earth environments. Geoarchaeologists seek to understand how natural and cultural processes operating within diverse depositional environments shape the archaeological record (i.e., site formation processes). Drawing on recent research, I provide examples of how geoarchaeologists can study site formation processes on other celestial bodies, such as Earth’s Moon, Venus, and Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko (67P/C-G). This paper demonstrates how geoarchaeological principles can be applied beyond traditional archaeological contexts to address contemporary challenges, such as our current dispersal across the Solar System.

title: The effect of thermal annealing and chemical abrasion on laser ablation U-Pb and trace element analysis of five reference zircon
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications
authors: Oleson, Ethan W. [1], Sharman, Glenn R. [2], Malkowski, Matthew A. [3], Crowley, James L. [4], Shaulis, Barry J. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas-Faytteville, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas-Fayetteville, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Bosie State Univeristy, Boise, ID, USA
(5) Trace and Radiogenic Isotope Laboratory, Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas-Fayetteville, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract: The use of laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) for joint U-Pb and trace and rare earth element (TREE) analyses of zircon and other accessory minerals is a widely used technique in studies of tectonics, provenance, and economic geology. In recent years, discussions about pretreating zircons using both thermal annealing and chemical abrasion to improve the accuracy of age estimates in LA-ICP-MS workflows have increased. Inherent in the use of both thermal annealing and chemical abrasion for LA-ICP-MS U/Pb + TREE is the creation of standardization brackets to correct analyses from the effects of instrumental drift and quantify systematic bias. However, there has been little study of the effect of standardization with pretreated reference material on TREE concentrations in unknowns. The use of treatments on zircon may change not only radiogenic isotope ratios and TREE concentrations but also the ablation behavior (e.g., rate, depth, ejection efficiency). Therefore, it is necessary to understand how pretreatment of reference zircon affects LA-ICP-MS results of samples. We present a comparison of the effects of thermal annealing and chemical abrasion on both the U-Pb age and TREE compositions of five zircon standards ranging in age from ~200 to ~1100 Myr. Preliminary results suggest that the age difference between treatment types for each reference zircon is highly dependent on the standard's crystal structure and effective alpha dose. These preliminary results also suggest that thermally annealed standards display an apparent enrichment in certain TREE concentrations relative to untreated zircon. The impact of age offset and TREE concentrations in pretreated reference zircons on unknowns will be discussed using three samples of differing alpha doses. We will also discuss the implications of standardizing unknowns to differently treated zircons and comparing datasets of zircon U-Pb + TREE that have undergone different pretreatments. As more studies implement zircon pretreatment to improve the accuracy of LA-ICP-MS U-Pb geochronology, it is important to also understand the effects of each treatment type on TREE chemistry of both the standards and unknowns.

title: Heat input during the Great Basin ignimbrite flareup did not drive the initial extension of the Nevadaplano: insights from time-temperature histories from the Northern Snake Range (eastern Nevada, U.S.A.)
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Rosenberger, Aurora E [1], Long, Sean P [2], Flowers, Rebecca M [3], Thomson, Stuart N [4], Metcalf, James R [5], Soignard, Emmanuel [6]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
(2) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA; Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(3) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(5) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(6) Eyring Materials Center, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract:
The thermal architecture of orogenic crust can exert a strong control on the style, magnitude, and location of deformation. Therefore, quantifying the thermal history of orogenic crust can provide an important context in which to interpret successive deformation events. The western U.S. portion of the North American Cordillera experienced Jurassic-early Paleogene contraction followed by mid-Paleogene-present extension, making it ideal for examining the influence of crustal thermal conditions on the mode and timing of deformation. In eastern-Nevada and western-Utah, Cordilleran shortening had constructed a high-elevation plateau (‘Nevadaplano’) by the Late-Cretaceous. Starting at 37-35 Ma, the Nevadaplano in east-central Nevada began to be dismembered by extension, which was approximately contemporaneous with the southwestward sweep of the Great Basin ignimbrite flareup through this region. The factors that drove the transition of the Nevadaplano to an extensional regime are debated, with some hypothesizing that crustal thermal weakening during the ignimbrite flareup was a major factor.

Here, we test this hypothesis by quantifying cooling histories of hanging wall rocks in the Northern Snake Range core complex. We collected zircon (U-Th)/He, apatite fission-track, and apatite (U-Th)/He dates from eight samples of the Ordovician Eureka Quartzite, which range between 664-215 Ma (demonstrating a lack of full resetting following deposition), 72-61 Ma, and 61-25 Ma, respectively. Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material thermometry constrains the peak temperatures of stratigraphically adjacent Ordovician carbonates to 137-194 °C. Thermal history modeling reveals cooling from peak temperatures at 85 Ma to 85-45 °C by 70 Ma (3.7-7.3 °C/Myr), followed by slower cooling (0.1-2.1 °C/Myr) to the present. We integrate our cooling histories with published time-temperature paths from the footwall of the core complex and adjacent ranges to the west, north, and south, which demonstrate gradual cooling from 85 Ma to the present. Based on the lack of evidence for thermal perturbation before, during, or after the 37-35 Ma sweep of volcanism through this region, we interpret that heat input into the crust during the Great Basin ignimbrite flareup was not a driving factor for extension. Instead, thermometry and low-temperature thermochronometers demonstrate that the brittle upper crust was cold, thick, and therefore strong at this time. Relaxation of the compressional stress regime during Farallon slab-rollback was likely the primary driving mechanism for extension.

title: Analyzing Cryptotephra from Volcanic Ash Beds in the Renova Formation of Southwest Montana
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Conrad, Lucia [1], Joyce, Eliza [2], Kenderes, Elizabeth [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Scieces, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract:
The Western United States has experienced Cenozoic volcanism related to the Cascades, Snake River Plains, Basin and Range extension, and slab rollback of the Farallon plate. Ash from these explosive volcanoes can travel hundreds of miles, leaving behind deposits of unknown origin, called cryptotephra. The chemical composition of cryptotephra can be used to correlate to the magma chamber of the volcano from which it erupted.

We focused on cryptotephra found in the Oligocene-Miocene Renova Formation of Southwest Montana. The Renova Formation is an extensional basin deposit, 0 to 3,500 feet thick. It is composed of interbedded pebbly mudrock and sandstone with locally abundant rhizoliths and vertebrate fossils. Most notably, it contains discontinuous volcanic ash beds, which is the source of our samples. We collected and analyzed 9 ash samples and separated the glass pieces under a microscope to analyze trace elements with an MC-ICP-MS. We isolated volcanic glass for analysis because this most closely represents the bulk rock composition of the original eruption. Through comparisons with trace element data of bulk volcanic rock from EarthChem database of the same age, we determined that our samples best match the Snake River Plain volcanics in Southern Idaho. The chemical composition, however, is based on bulk glass composition from multiple grains within a sample.

To account for possible mixing of sources, we conducted Raman spectral analysis to compare individual glass fragments from within each sample, telling us whether the sample contains cryptotephra from one eruption or from multiple eruptions. Initial results indicate that the cryptotephra does originate from multiple eruptions, meaning the MC-ICP-MS data will have combined element data from multiple eruptions and is therefore less reliable. We are currently also using the Raman data to predict the eruption viscosity after Giordano et. al. (2019), which will help determine how far ash may have travelled. It is possible that cryptotephra may have been remobilized through further erosion.

Based on these current data, we aim to model how volcanic ash from the Renova Formation moved throughout the atmosphere and potentially through additional fluvial or eolian erosion during the Oligocene and Miocene. Ultimately, this helps us understand how widespread the effects of these volcanoes were on factors such as climate and wildlife and better predict movement of future explosive volcanoes.

title: Lunar Impact Glasses: Big Science from Small Samples
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials
authors: Zellner, Nicolle [1]
affiliations: (1) Physics, Albion College, Albion, MI, USA
abstract: Lunar impact glasses, pieces of melted lunar regolith created by energetic impacting events, can offer information about the Moon’s impact history, its geology, and its evolution in general. These samples possess the composition of the target material and formation ages can be determined by various radiometric dating systems, including the 40Ar/39Ar (argon) system. Understanding the ages of impact glasses, along with their compositions, allows us to begin to piece together information about the rate of impact events in the inner Solar System and their effects on Earth. Important questions that can be answered include determining the form of the large-impact distribution with respect to time (e.g., smooth decline versus cataclysmic spike); whether there is periodicity in Earth-Moon cratering history; the effects of impacts on the distribution of regolith materials; the rate of delivery of biomolecules; and the applicability of the lunar record to other planets (including Mars). This talk will provide a summary of the science supported by investigations of lunar impact glasses and propose new ideas that have yet to be explored.

title: The Evidence is in the Rocks: Why Massif Anorthosite-Ferroan Granite Suites Did Not Form in Arcs
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Frost, Carol Denison [1], Frost, Bryce Ronald [2], Lindsley, Donald H. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
(2) University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
(3) Stony Brook University, South Setauket, NY,
abstract:
The AMCG (anorthosite-mangerite-charnockite-granite) suite of massif anorthosite, monzonite, and ferroan granite occurs almost exclusively in the Proterozoic, and Phanerozoic analogs are extremely rare. Accordingly, the tectonic environment in which they occur is not obvious, and some authors have proposed an origin by arc magmatism above subduction zones. However, petrologic evidence in the rocks themselves precludes this origin. The composition of the likely parent magma to anorthosite, high-Al gabbro, is unlike basalt from MORB, oceanic plateaus, or subduction zones. AMCG high-Al gabbro most closely matches basalt from the Galapagos plume. Experimental phase equilibria studies suggest that melting took place at 10-12 kbar, shallower than arc melting. The mafic rocks in the AMCG suite are compositionally distinct from those in arcs: AMCG gabbros have olivine with Fo 65 or less whereas arc gabbros have more magnesian olivine (<Fo 70 ). AMCG gabbros have plagioclase with An 65 or less, whereas arc gabbros have relatively calcic plagioclase (>An 75 ).

Ferroan granites of the AMCG suite are alkalic to alkali-calcic, unlike magnesian, calcic to calc-alkalic arc magmas. Ferroan granites are relatively reducing, crystallizing at or below FMQ, whereas arc magmas tend to be relatively oxidizing, having crystallized at oxygen fugacities 1-2 log units above FMQ. Ferroan granites have lower water contents and crystallize at higher temperatures than do arc magmas. Where ferroan granitic magmas intrude crust with isotopic compositions distinct from contemporary mantle, it is clear that these magmas have a dominantly mantle origin.

The long-lived Nuna-Rodinia supercontinent persisted throughout the Proterozoic and may have insulated the underlying mantle and caused large areas of mantle upwelling that produced the AMCG magmatic suites. If instead the origin of the AMCG suite were related to an arc setting, it must have involved large amounts of magma not at all typical of known arc magmas. Impossible? No. Implausible? Yes!

title: Putting the Rocks Back in the Stratigraphic Section: The Geology of the Florissant Fossil Beds in a Box
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation (Posters)
authors: Quinlan, Katherine A [1]
affiliations: (1) National Park Service, Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument, Florissant, CO, USA
abstract: The National Park Service preserves significant cultural and natural resources for the enjoyment and education of future generations. The Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument is one of the few national park units to be established for the express purpose of preserving and interpreting its fossil resources. When considering the National Park Service’s goal audience of fifth graders, we must consider how to communicate complex information, like a two-dimensional stratigraphic section, to increase understanding and enjoyment of these resources for the target audience. A critical component to the interpretation of these fossils is their geological context, which is best understood through the study of stratigraphy. Stratigraphic sections are invaluable tools for geoscientists to understand the geology of a given area. However, two-dimensional stratigraphic sections lack the in-person observation required for rock identification, such as texture, cleavage, and color. As an intern in the Scientists in Parks program, I created a hands-on, interactive stratigraphic section of the Florissant Fossil Beds’ geology using interpretive geological samples representative of informal units in the Florissant Formation, Wall Mountain Tuff, and Pikes Peak Granite to present to visitors. The section, titled “Geology of the Florissant Fossil Beds in a Box,” was modeled after a stratigraphic section used in educational resources throughout the park. The section followed the same general shape and color scheme of the two-dimensional section. Samples were stabilized in foam with rock units outlined in the similar colors used in the two-dimensional section. Additionally, fossiliferous rock units were marked with drawings of common fossils noted in published literature with pictures of real examples of fossils sized to scale. Using the Geology of the Florissant Fossil Beds in a Box, visitors were able to make direct observations about different rock types including texture, color, structure, and grain size using sight and touch. This learning aid was facilitated as part of a touch table with fossil replicas and display boxes of fossils to inspire connections between the larger context of geology in the area and more specific study of fossil organisms. Through continued visitor interaction, the Geology of the Florissant Fossil Beds in a Box can engage visitors with different levels of geology knowledge and promote understanding of fossil resources at the Florissant Fossil Beds and other geologically rich areas.

title: Critical mineral potential of mine waste: Earth MRI’s journey in national mine waste characterization
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Campbell, Kate Marie [1], Seal, Robert R. [2]
affiliations: (1) USGS, Geology, Geophysics, and Geochemistry Science Center, Denver, CO, USA
(2) USGS, Geology, Energy, and Minerals Science Center, Reston, VA, USA
abstract:
Mine waste is an important potential resource that has been historically under-characterized in the search for unconventional sources of critical minerals and other commodities. Materials that were not viable in the past and were sent to waste may be considered a resource today as extraction technologies improve and ore grades decrease. Additionally, many elements that are currently on the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2025 List of Critical Minerals had limited or no use in the past but co-occur with primary commodities. These byproduct elements historically went to waste and warrant re-evaluation in light of their economic and strategic value. Mine waste has the advantage of generally being above-ground and having gone through significant processing, such as crushing and milling. Further, reprocessing and re-disposal may provide important environmental benefits. Given the substantial data gaps regarding the composition of critical minerals and other commodities in existing mine waste, the Earth Mapping Resource Initiative (Earth MRI) initiated a mine waste characterization component in 2023 in partnership with State Geological Surveys to provide standardized, on-the-ground sampling of mine waste nationwide. A foundational aspect of this program was to develop standardized sampling protocols for a variety of mine waste types (Campbell and others, 2025) and a standard set of comprehensive geochemical and mineralogical analyses to ensure high-quality data for elements on the critical mineral list. This effort resulted in hundreds of new samples of a wide variety of mine waste types across 21 states. In this presentation, we will discuss the process of developing a national mine waste characterization program, highlight some of the results at individual sites, and how we are linking the characterization results to the parallel Earth MRI mine waste inventory endeavor. Ultimately, the goal of the work is to create the basis for a national mine waste critical mineral assessment.

title: Quantifying Seismic Hazard on Hispaniola: Slip Deficit Rates from GNSS-InSAR Strain Fields
session_title: Imaging, measuring, and characterizing the Earth’s changing surface through remote sensing (Posters)
authors: Lee, Yi-Chieh [1], Maurer, Jeremy [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, Missouri, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, Missouri, USA
abstract: Hispaniola sits at the oblique boundary between the North American and Caribbean plates, which converge at a rate of ~20 mm/yr. This convergence drives a complex fault system and poses a severe seismic hazard to the island. Quantifying the slip deficit rate (SDR) across this fault network is essential for understanding that hazard. Our prior work, using a combined GNSS and InSAR surface velocity field, estimated a total moment deficit rate of 3.72–10.18 × 10 18 Nm/yr, depending on assumed crustal thickness (20–40 km), equivalent to an annual Mw 6.35–6.64 earthquake. We then apply the Slip Deficit From Strain (SliDeFS; Johnson et al., 2024) method, which estimates SDR directly from the observed strain rate field without needing to specify a block model and far-field plate motion, a key advantage in tectonically complex regions like Hispaniola, where block motion models may not capture distributed crustal deformation. Peak maximum shear strain rates concentrate along the Septentrional-Oriente Fault Zone (SOFZ) and the Hispaniola Fold-and-Thrust Belt (HFTB). Moment accumulation on the SOFZ totals ~2.7 × 10 18 Nm/yr across its three segments, equivalent to Mw 7.91 event over 300 years, while the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden Fault Zone (EPGFZ) shows a moment deficit rate of ~0.46 × 10 18 Nm/yr, equivalent to Mw 7.39 event over 300 years. Our modeling results reveal high slip deficit along the central and eastern segments of the SOFZ, consistent with the paleoseismicity records. The accumulated strain over three centuries on the SOFZ would be sufficient to produce an Mw 7.91 earthquake, which is consistent with the historical earthquake accounts and represents a major regional seismic hazard.

title: Ensemble Methods for Assimilating Subsidence Information: How the Sausage is Made
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges

abstract:
Land subsidence in Central Valley has been studied extensively and monitored at many sites for decades. Still, many efforts to simulate the historic and possible future patterns of land subsidence struggle to appropriately represent observed historic subsidence and compaction, a potential “red flag” for model predictive skill. These struggles are likely due to a combination of factors including: model scale and resolution, subsidence process representation and simplification, as well as inverse problem design and implementation.

This talk will introduce some concepts around model purpose, design, and simplification, then present some theory and concepts related to using ensemble methods to assimilate subsidence and compaction information, with care given to parameterization, objective function design, and coping with nonlinearity. A case study from a simple 1-D column model of a long-term monitoring site will be used to demonstrate concepts.

title: Reading the Roots of REE Mineralization: A Multi-mineral Petrochronologic Framework for the Mojave Province
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits.
authors: Hillenbrand, Ian [1], Miller, David M. [2], Thompson, Jay M [3], Watts, Kathryn E. [4], Mahan, Kevin H [5], Karlstrom, Karl E. [6], Lowers, Heather [7]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Moffet Field, CA, USA
(3) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Spokane, WA,
(5) University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(6) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
(7) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract: Exposures of the deep continental crust provide important insights into crustal evolution, tectonic reworking, and magmatic and hydrothermal processes linked to mineralization. The deep crustal rocks of the Mojave Province, composed predominantly of ca. 1.8–1.6 Ga orthogneiss and paragneiss, host the ca. 1.4 Ga Mountain Pass intrusive suite and world-class rare earth element (REE) mineralization. We present a multi-mineral petrochronologic record for these rocks by integrating in situ LA-ICP-MS/MS analyses of garnet (Lu-Hf), apatite (U-Pb/Lu-Hf), zircon (U-Pb), titanite (U-Pb), monazite (U-Pb), and mica (Rb-Sr) with thermobarometric constraints from petrological modeling. These data constrain more than 400 Myr of lower crustal evolution and establish the tectonic context for REE mineralization at Mountain Pass. Our results indicate that >1800 Ma metasedimentary rocks were buried, metamorphosed, and intruded by arc plutons during the ca. 1780–1750 Ma Kokoweef orogeny. Following emplacement of isotopically juvenile mafic dikes, all rocks experienced regional granulite facies metamorphism (700–850°C) at ca. 1710–1680 Ma during the Ivanpah orogeny, with peak pressures reaching ~0.6 GPa in the Ivanpah Mountains and ~1.0 GPa in the New York Mountains. These rocks experienced slow, protracted cooling (~2–3°C/Myr) recorded by paired apatite Lu-Hf and U-Pb dates and upper amphibolite facies mylonitization at ca. 1620–1590 Ma (U-Pb titanite, U-Pb monazite). Eastward younging in apatite Lu-Hf and U-Pb cooling ages, together with the increase in peak pressure, indicates that the middle- to lower-crustal roots of the Ivanpah orogen are exposed in the eastern Mojave Desert. This difference in presently exposed crustal level may reflect subsequent tilting or disruption by unidentified faults. Localized greenschist-facies ca. 1400 Ma deformation records oblique convergence associated with the Picuris orogeny synchronous with the Mountain Pass intrusive suite and REE mineralization. Mesoproterozoic deformation localized along older structures suggests that crustal architecture inherited from Paleoproterozoic assembly and orogenesis remained mechanically susceptible to reactivation. These mechanical anisotropies may have focused magmatism and fluid flow associated with REE mineralization.

abstract: Hurricane Helene was an extreme precipitation event for much of the Blue Ridge Mountains with peak precipitation > 750 mm and much of the region receiving > 500 mm. Extensive flooding and numerous landslides were reported throughout the region. Saturated soils and high winds with peak gusts from 30 to 50 m/s created ideal conditions for a generational tree mortality event across the Blue Ridge. Large blowdowns (concentrated areas with high tree mortality) were common across the Blue Ridge after Helene with individual blowdowns up to 20 km2 in size. Within these blowdowns, the majority of trees are dead and most are fully uprooted ‘tree throws’ with large holes. Here, we seek to better understand the regional extent of blow downs and the impact that they have had on soil development, hillslope morphology, and broader landscape evolution. To do this, we have examined hundreds of blowdowns in the field including documenting tree diameter, hole volume, and direction of fall. Our field work sets a baseline for understanding how tree throw holes evolve through time and how hillslopes ‘heal’ after blowdown events. We also compare our field results with remote mapping of more than 16,000 tree throws observed from aerial imagery. By combining this data, we can begin to estimate the total soil disturbance caused by blowdowns in Helene. Specifically, data on tree mortality density and tree pit volume presented here helps us as we work towards the long-term goal of understanding the total extent of blowdowns across the region. To accomplish this, we work towards an automated mechanism for counting total tree mortality in post-Helene aerial images. Our results will improve our understanding of hillslope evolution and how hillslopes are impacted by tree mortality events that are relatively common over geologic timescales. Further, our study helps to explain previous work in the region that has noted a lack of soil development on colluvial hillslopes.

title: An Anomaly at the Base Of The Sauk Sequence: Rapid Erosion-Driven Basement Cooling In The Early Ordovician, Florida Mountains, SW New Mexico
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Copeland, Peter C. [1], Lawton, Timothy [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sci, University of Houston, Houston, TX,
(2) Geosciences, Univ. of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract:
The base of the time-transgressive Sauk sequence in the southwestern US is typically Cambrian to Ordovician strata deposited on continental basement rocks formed 1.8 to 1.4 Ga. Paleotopography of the basement surface on which the Paleozoic rocks were deposited has been interpreted to be the combined result primarily of long-wavelength crustal deformation, varied resistance of substrate rocks, and marine planation.

The basal unit of the Sauk sequence at Capitol Dome in the Florida Mountains of SW NM, which lay near the early Paleozoic continental margin, is the Bliss Formation, a medium- to coarse-grained sandstone with local boulder conglomerate. The depositional age of the Bliss in the Floridas is not well known but comparison to fossiliferous localities elsewhere in southern NM suggests deposition during or immediately after the Skullrockian Stage (~488 to 477 Ma).

Nearshore Bliss deposits nonconformably overlie granite and syenite at Capitol Dome. Geochronologic data from the granite include a CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon age of 510.83±0.20 Ma (Holland et al ., 2023), and hornblende and biotite 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages of 486±5 and 491±5 Ma, respectively (Ervin, 1998). The ~20 m.y. difference in zircon and hornblende ages indicates this pluton was intruded into country rock at temperatures above 500 °C. The coincidence of the hornblende and biotite ages from the granite and the depositional age of the Bliss require an episode of rapid erosion at the begining of the Ordovician. Depending on the closure temperature of Ar in biotite, geothermal gradient, and depositional age of the basal Bliss at Capitol Dome, these data indicate average erosion rates of 1-7 mm/year sustained for 14–2 million years. Rapid cooling of the Capitol Dome granite suggests basement unroofing during crustal extension of the type observed in Mesozoic to Neogene core complexes in Arizona and California.

The Florida Mountains formed an island during much of the Sauk transgression. Onlap of the Sauk III sequence (mid-late Cambrian to Early Ordovician) elsewhere took place along the flanks of the Transcontinental Arch and the edges of the Canadian shield (Sloss, 1988). Delayed onlap of Cambrian basement, brought to the surface in the early Ordovician near the edge of the craton, makes the Florida Mountains location a significant anomaly in the regional character of the Sauk sequence in North America.

abstract:
The Mount Vernon 7.5-minute quadrangle in eastern Tennessee is along the boundary between the Appalachian Valley and Ridge and Western Blue Ridge provinces. East dipping thrust faults juxtaposed Precambrian, low-grade metamorphic rocks of the Walden Creek Group above Cambrian rocks of the Chilhowee Group, Shady Dolomite, and Rome Formation in the Bullet Mountain thrust sheet. The Bullet Mountain thrust sheet replicates lower Cambrian stratigraphy against Cambrian-Ordovician rocks of the Shady Dolomite, Rome Formation, Conasauga Formation, Knox Group, Athens Shale, Holston Formation, and Bays Formation. The Cambrian-Ordovician rocks in the footwall of the Bullet Mountain fault are folded into the Tellico-Sevier syncline.

Traditional field mapping for this project is paired with neural network construction to create a predictive lithology map. LiDAR, aerial imagery, LandSat and data stations were used to create secondary data products including curvature, slope, false color, and contoured lithology maps. Using field data, we defined the range of characteristics of each unit and constructed neural networks to assign pixels as high or low similarity to each unit. Based on these derivative predictive maps, we construct a machine-learning-based geologic map and compare and contrast the results to a traditional, hand-drawn geologic map.

title: The Ladycomb Layered Mafic Intrusion: A Newly Recognized Intrusion of Steens Basalt Magma, Columbia River Basalt Group
session_title: Using mafic and ultramafic deposits to decipher volcanic and magmatic processes
authors: Collins, Rachel Anne [1], Streck, Martin J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Portland State University, Vancouver, WA, USA
(2) Geology Department, Portland State University, Portland, OR, USA
abstract:
The Ladycomb Layered Mafic Intrusion (LLMI) is a newly recognized middle Miocene layered mafic intrusion exposed in the Pueblo Mountains of southeastern Oregon. The intrusion was mapped on a 1:24,000-scale for a U.S. Geological Survey EDMAP project during which field relationships were established and analytical data acquired consisting of whole-rock geochemistry, petrography, and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar age dates. The intrusion is exposed over approximately 12.5 km along strike and is structurally dissected by Basin and Range type faulting. The intrusion is bound by Steens Basalt lavas on the top and the bottom although the bottom is poorly exposed. The intrusion is divided into Border, Layered, and Feeder Series based on its mapped morphology and intrusive relationships. The Layered Series is further subdivided into Upper and Lower Zones that contain contrasting successions of olivine gabbro, gabbronorite, leucogabbro, and oxide-bearing cumulates. Field relationships indicate emplacement as a small, shallow chonolithic intrusion fed by a centrally located feeder system and subsequently modified by Basin and Range extension. Relationships between the Feeder Series and the Upper and Lower Zones of the Layered series indicate at least one episode of magma recharge during construction of the intrusion.

Whole rock data closely correlates with the composition of lavas of the Steens Basalt, except for samples affected by crystal accumulation, such as samples of the olivine-rich Marginal Facies, which contain up to 23.1 wt. % MgO. Intrusion samples of the Megacrystic Border Series Leucogabbro align with lava flow samples and have the following compositional ranges: MgO wt. % between 4.4-8.3, Zr ppm between 92-65, and La/Yb between 5.0-6.1. Emplacement of the intrusion during Steens Basalt magmatism (16.9 to 16.4 Ma) is established by a sample of the layered series that yielded an age of 16.656 ± 0.048 Ma on plagioclase separates while a nearby overlying trachytic lava flow yielded 16.723±0.039 Ma.

The LLMI is spatially associated with multiple styles of magmatic and hydrothermal mineralization, including orthomagmatic Fe-Ti oxide-apatite enrichment within the LLMI, and structurally controlled low-sulfidation Cu-Ag-Au mineralization localized along northwest-trending fault systems. Recognition of the LLMI expands our knowledge of the intrusive component of Columbia River Basalt Group magmatism and is a case study for investigating magma storage, differentiation, and mineralization of continental flood basalt provinces.

title: Decoupling the Optical and Structural Evolution of Organic Matter in Orogenic Systems: A Comparative Study of %VRo and RSCM in the Greater Caucasus
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Marks, Chloe [1], Niemi, Nathan A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
abstract: We present new Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material (RSCM, n=82) and vitrinite reflectance (%VRo, n=17) geothermometry results from the Greater Caucasus, an actively developing orogenic system. Low-temperature geothermometers, like %VRo and RSCM, have historically been derived using organic matter (OM)-bearing rocks from sedimentary basins because of their ability to determine petroleum source rock potential. Although these two methods are commonly used to answer similar questions, they rely on fundamentally different aspects of OM evolution: %VRo is the quantification of the optical evolution of OM, while RSCM quantifies the structural evolution of OM. When exposed to the same P-T histories, the optical and structural evolution of OM have different kinetics, leading to complexities in recovering the thermal history and state of maturation of a source rock. Therefore, how %VRo and RSCM can be used to study systems with geologic histories other than single-phase burial in a sedimentary basin (for example: compressional tectonism and regional metamorphism) is not well constrained. In the Greater Caucasus, we find that RSCM temperatures (147°-474°C) increase towards the hinterland and record distinct steps in temperature associated with major structural boundaries or changes in metamorphic grade observed in the field. Temperatures derived from %VRo, measured on a subset of the same rocks analyzed for RSCM, yield a narrower range of peak burial temperatures (160°-270°C) from a %VRo-mean range of 1.45%-4.81%. We find that at ~270°C the optical evolution of OM plateaus, while the structural evolution continues to progress. In sedimentary basins, the slowed optical evolution of OM is attributed to a phenomenon called reflectance suppression. This process can be controlled by maceral type, lithology, or overpressure, and can lead to an underestimation of thermal maturity. In orogenic belts, it is possible that this suppression is exacerbated by high differential stress and lithostatic over-pressure. While %VRo can be an effective geothermometer at lower temperatures, RSCM is applicable across a broader range of temperatures (150°-600°C) that are more useful for understanding the thermal evolution of orogenic systems. Therefore, we suggest that RSCM is a more viable method for assessing the thermal maturity of rocks in tectonically active settings, and we should be cautious when considering %VRo as an independent mechanism for estimating thermal maturity in tectonically deformed settings.

abstract: Toronto is Canada’s largest city and home to over seven million people. The regional geology features Pleistocene glacial sediments that overlie Ordovician shallow marine deposits. These rocks are not always exposed at surface but they have a profound and often unappreciated influence on people’s everyday lives. To highlight Ontario’s geology, and to communicate the importance of geological materials to the public, the APGO Education Foundation have developed a comprehensive website with virtual resources that include geoscience walking tours (e.g., GeoWalks) and field guides (GeoHikes, GeoPaddles, available at geoscienceinfo.com). Here, we describe targeted efforts to reach the next generation of geoscientists by creating a children’s book series highlighting geological features in our local region. The goal of this book series is to ensure accurate geoscientific information is available for K-12 students and teachers in accessible and engaging formats. The first book in the series, “ Rocky the Raccoon explores the Niagara Escarpment” follows Rocky on the Chedoke Radial Trail (Hamilton, ON, GeoHike) as he learns about rocks, minerals, and fossils, guided by a crinoid named Lily. In the newly released second book in the series, “ Rocky the Raccoon explores Toronto”, Rocky visits the big city where he once again teams up with Lily to learn about critical minerals on the subway, building stones at the university, and hidden rivers. In addition, he visits the Royal Ontario Museum to learn about famous fossils from the Burgess Shale that document the origin of animals, as well as meteorites, and dinosaurs. He completes his journey at the Don Valley Brick Works, a former quarry, that has been restored to a green space where he realizes there is always more to learn. This book series provides a guide for those developing other Geoheritage sites and K-12 content aimed toward young students, sparking curiosity and stimulating interest in geoscientific discoveries and future careers.

abstract: Semi-arid endorheic lagoons act as long-term sinks for trace metals from agricultural runoff, upland erosion, and settlement drainage, yet integrated source-pathway-risk frameworks remain limited. This study employed a combined hydrological-pathway, entropy-weighted transfer-risk, and probabilistic exposure framework for Bustillos Lagoon, Chihuahua, Mexico, using surface-water data from 20 stations sampled in 2018-2020 (n = 60). Eight trace metal(loid)s (As, Cd, Cu, Cr, Mn, Mo, Ni, Pb) were evaluated using stream-network analysis, an entropy-weighted risk transfer model (EWTRM), and Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations) to assess non-carcinogenic hazard and arsenic cancer risk under a precautionary exposure scenario. EWTRM results showed a shift in dominant risk contributors: arsenic drove risk in 2018 (61.1%) and 2019 (44.0%), while manganese dominated in 2020 (89.6%), coinciding with a tenfold increase in maximum RiskScore (~1.4 to 17.8). Spatial analysis indicated lagoon-wide risk intensification in 2020. Precipitation anomaly data identified 2020 as the driest year (2000–2020), suggesting reduced inflow, weak flushing, and evaporative concentration amplified trace-metal risk. Monte Carlo results supported this pattern: mean adult hazard index increased from <0.07 (2018-2019) to 0.31 (2020), with exceedance probabilities of 0.92% (adults) and 1.20% (children). Arsenic cancer risk remained within the 10 -6 -10 -4 range, with no exceedances above 10 -4 . The integrated framework distinguishes persistent contamination from drought-amplified risk, providing a robust approach for managing trace-metal exposure in semi-arid lagoon systems.

abstract:
The Afro-Arabian large igneous province (also referred to as the Ethiopia-Yemen LIP) is distributed across the conjugate rifted margins of Yemen and Ethiopia, Djibouti, and Eritrea. The main pulse of LIP magmatism occurred between ~33 and 29 Ma and was characterized by widespread basaltic volcanism followed by an intense period of explosive silicic volcanism and ignimbrite emplacement. This magmatic pulse has long been causally linked to Oligocene isotopic perturbations and global cooling events, but more recent geochronology has called this correlation into question.

Although much of the volcanic stratigraphy has been disrupted by post-emplacement faulting associated with continental break-up, Yemen preserves a nearly continuous volcaniclastic succession. Four large-volume volcaniclastic units from northern Yemen (~360 to 2,700 km 3 minimum total eruptive volume, dense rock equivalent) were previously dated using high-precision U-Pb zircon geochronology and found to contain a substantial proportion of antecrysts and xenocrysts, consistent with mineral-melt and mineral-mineral equilibrium assessments.

New 40 Ar/ 39 Ar feldspar ages further provide evidence for prolonged magma residence and crystallization during the ~100 kyr proceeding eruption. Together, mineral-scale observations and high-precision dating indicate that these large-volume magmas were generated through multiple episodes of rapid crystallization and remobilization prior to eruption. These findings provide important constraints on the timescales and mechanisms of silicic magma generation and underscore the importance of integrating detailed mineralogical characterization with high-precision geochronologic data when reconstructing magma evolution.

abstract: Quantifying time averaging across taxa, fragmentation status, and depositional environments provide valuable insights into the differential taphonomic behavior of skeletal remains and the factors that influence their preservation. Here, we utilize calibrated radiocarbon ages to estimate time averaging for whole and fragmentary remains of irregular echinoids and bivalve mollusks collected from multiple marine ecosystems in the Gulf of Mexico. Posterior probability distributions generated for the radiocarbon ages of 641 specimens were used to develop error-corrected age-frequency distributions (AFDs) via a weighted-bootstrap approach. The median specimen age and the standard deviation of specimen ages were then used as estimates of median age and time averaging (TA), respectively. Across the three sampled mixed-siliciclastic depositional environments, whole irregular echinoid tests were generally the youngest (median = 21.9 years BP) and least time averaged (TA = 982.0 years), followed by echinoid fragments (median = 383.5 years BP; TA = 7015.8 years), whole mollusk shells (median = 421.7 years BP; TA = 7478.4 years) and mollusk fragments (median = 2053.5 years BP; TA = 7651.2 years). This rank order is consistent with that observed in our previous work (Torres et al., in review), in which the mass-based relative abundances of echinoid-mollusk death assemblages suggested a durability gradient among skeletal remains (whole echinoid tests: 1.0%; echinoid fragments: 11.5%; whole mollusk shells/valves: 13.3%; mollusk fragments: 74.2%). However, the disparity between whole echinoid tests and the other specimen types was significantly less pronounced at the deeper Carrabelle sites (CB-D: water depth = 14.6–25 m; n = 2) than at the shallower Carrabelle (CB-S: water depth = 6.4–8.2 m; n = 3) and Cedar Key (CK: water depth = 4 m; n = 1) sites. These results suggest that although intrinsic factors, such as skeletal durability, strongly influence the preservation potential of remains in time-averaged sediments, extrinsic environmental factors can mitigate the severity of the resulting taphonomic biases. Consequently, faunal compositions derived from heavily time-averaged fossil assemblages may still underrepresent whole skeletons of echinoids and other fragile taxa. In contrast, fragments of these relatively fragile taxa seem to be time averaged over timescales comparable to those observed for more durable remains, suggesting that their inclusion in paleoecological analyses may mitigate the impact of taphonomic biases.

abstract: Solid matter consists of three-dimensional arrangements of individual atoms predominantly organized in repeating patterns (motifs). We can directly relate properties of materials, both of natural and synthetic origin to their structural arrangement, regardless if they belong to the classes of organics, polymers, or inorganics. For example, the arrangement of carbon atoms leads to the stark difference between diamond and graphite. The large-scale analysis of crystal structures is fundamental to discovering structure–property relationships that can be employed for the design of new materials.As crystallographic databases continue to expand, the need for powerful computation tools to harness their information has become critical. The Crystallographic Information File (CIF) is the standard for disseminating this data, yet researchers face a significant bottleneck in its programmatic use. Manual data extraction is tedious, and syntactic inconsistencies in CIF files complicate high-throughput analysis, forcing researchers into fragmented workflows.To improve reproducibility, we have developed crystract, an open-source R package designed to provide an efficient solution for the batch processing and statistical analysis of CIF files. Built around R's data.table paradigm, crystract streamlines the extraction of metadata, unit cell parameters, atomic coordinates, and symmetry operations. A key feature of the package is its ability to determine first-neighbor bonding environments around each symmetrically independent atom using multiple algorithms, including minimum distance, Brunner, Econ (Hoppe's), Voronoi, and CrystalNN. Furthermore, crystract rigorously propagates experimental uncertainties (estimated standard deviations) through derived quantities, such as interatomic distances and bond angles. It also includes comprehensive post-processing tools to handle structural disorder, utilizing filtering functions to eliminate non-physical distances associated with positional disorder and calculating occupancy-weighted average distances for occupational disorder. By outputting all extracted and calculated data as tidy data frames directly within the R statistical environment, crystract provides a seamless workflow designed to facilitate the preparation of crystallographic data for large-scale statistical analysis and machine learning applications. As a fully open-source package, crystract promotes reproducible, data-driven research in the material and Earth sciences.

abstract: Seasonal freeze–thaw processes strongly influence groundwater recharge in cold regions by controlling the storage and movement of water between the land surface and the subsurface. This study investigates the physical interactions among snow accumulation, soil thermal dynamics, ice formation, and groundwater recharge using the coupled surface–subsurface model Amanzi-ATS for a soil column in the Karhinkangas aquifer in central Finland. Model simulations were evaluated against observations of snow depth and near-surface soil temperature for four winters (2011–2015). The simulations reproduced the observed seasonal evolution of snow accumulation and soil temperature and were used to investigate the physical mechanisms controlling winter recharge. Results demonstrate that the timing of persistent snow accumulation relative to the thermal state of the soil strongly influences soil freezing and thawing. Snow insulation reduced heat exchange between the atmosphere and the soil, but its effectiveness depended not only on snow depth and persistence, but also on soil temperature when the snowpack became established. Frozen soil limited groundwater recharge during much of the winter, whereas thaw conditions promoted infiltration. The highest recharge rates were generally associated with rain-on-snow events, during which rainfall and snowmelt combined to provide abundant liquid water for infiltration into thawed soils. These findings improve the understanding of the coupled hydrologic and thermal processes controlling winter groundwater recharge and provide a physical framework for evaluating future climate-driven changes in cold-region groundwater systems.

title: The Potential of Ex-Situ CO2 Mineralization in a Flow Through Reactor Using Midatlantic Mine Wastes

abstract: Ex-situ mineral carbonation is considered one of the most promising approaches for secure and permanent CO₂ storage. Unlike geological carbon sequestration, ex-situ mineralization is conducted under controlled conditions, eliminating the need for long-term monitoring while offering opportunities for potential economic benefits by valorizing waste materials, such as quarry fines and mine tailings. This study simulates ex site CO₂ mineralization using two different mineralogical compositions of Mid-Atlantic mine waste in an industrial-scale flow-through reactor. The reactor has a total volume of 250 m³ (10 m × 5 m × 5 m), with a porosity of 30% and a permeability of 10⁻¹³ m². Simulations were performed at 25 °C and 200 kPa, with aqueous CO₂ injected through five inlet cells and discharged through a gravity drainage outlet located at the opposite end of the reactor. Each simulation was conducted over a period of five years. Two mine waste mineralogical compositions were evaluated, each represented by three particle-size distributions (fine, medium, and coarse) and three fluid flow rates. The first mineralogy is dominated by olivine and pyroxene, whereas the second contains dolomite in addition to these silicate minerals. The simulation results demonstrate that variations in mineralogical composition, reactive surface area, and fluid injection rate significantly influence the overall carbonation efficiency. Magnesite was identified as the dominant secondary carbonate phase, accompanied by the formation of amorphous silica as a by-product, indicating a clear reaction pathway from silicate mineral dissolution to carbonate precipitation. Furthermore, the reactive transport system produced distinct spatial variations in mineral precipitation, highlighting the influence of fluid transport on the distribution of reactive zones within the reactor. Overall, these findings provide a robust framework for the long-term sequestration of CO₂ through ex-situ mineral carbonation in engineered flow-through reactor systems.
