title: GIS AND THIEM MODELING OF THE POTENTIAL IMPACTS OF A PROPOSED QUARRY ON GROUNDWATER IN A CRYSTALLINE BEDROCK AQUIFER, CHAMBERS COUNTY, ALABAMA (USA)
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Akinyemi, Ayomiposi Oluwakemi [1], Barineau, Clinton [2], Keller, Troy A [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Columbus State University, Columbus, GA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Columbus State University, Columbus, GA, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Columbus State University, Columbus, GA, USA
abstract: Quarry development has the potential to negatively impact aquifers when rock removal coupled with dewatering results in drawdown of local groundwater levels. In crystalline bedrock aquifers (e.g., metamorphic rock), groundwater flow is predominantly controlled by bedrock secondary fracture porosity and the thickness of overlying regolith. Despite their low hydraulic conductivity and porosity, crystalline bedrock aquifers are important sources of local groundwater in rural communities. Consequently, the cone of depression resulting from dewatering quarries in these areas can have negative impacts on well productivity. This study evaluated the potential hydrologic impacts of a proposed quarry on a semi-confined, crystalline bedrock aquifer in east-central Alabama (Chambers County). Static water-level measurements from surrounding private wells were used to model groundwater elevation (Inverse Distance Weighting), which was then used to create a flow-direction map in ArcGIS Pro. The map indicated that the site lies above a divide that causes the subsurface and surface waters to flow north and south, away from the proposed quarry site. To simulate quarry development, GIS was used to model scenarios in which a “well” was placed at the center of the proposed quarry site, with aquifer drawdown modeled for quarry depths between 70m and 170m. AQTESOLV software was used to estimate aquifer transmissivity from well recovery data (n=3) in the study area. The steady-state Thiem model predicted a cone of depression extending up to 2,000 m (1.24 mi) away from the quarry center based on estimated transmissivity values ranging from 0.0116 to 0.6484 m²/day. The model suggests the quarry would affect at least five private wells and one agricultural well within its cone of depression. Additionally, long-term, local groundwater flow is likely to reverse towards the quarry, with the potential to negatively impact groundwater seeps south of the proposed quarry site. This integrated GIS and analytical approach provides a practical framework for environmental assessment and groundwater-management decisions in similar hydrogeologic settings.

title: Investigating the structural and petrographic characteristics of the Pelona schist in the northern Crafton Hills, Southern California
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Rannis, Matthew Dean [1], Pimentel, Diana [2], Valencia, Ashley Juliet [3], Bidgoli, Tandis S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, San Bernardino, California, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, San Bernardino, California, USA
(3) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, San Bernardino, California, USA
(4) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, San Bernardino, California, USA
abstract:
The Pelona-Orocopia-Rand schists of southern California are widely interpreted as records of Late Cretaceous shallow subduction and subsequent exhumation along the Cordilleran margin. Although the major exposures of these units are well studied, smaller exposures in the San Bernardino region remain poorly characterized. This study integrates detailed geologic mapping, structural analysis, and microstructural characterization of Pelona schist in the northern Crafton Hills to evaluate its deformation history and relationship to regional exhumation and younger tectonic overprints.

High-resolution mapping documented lithologic variations, contacts, foliation patterns, fold and fault geometries, and shear sense indicators. Fracture orientations (n=247) were measured from four 1-m² areas to examine younger structural overprint. Orientation data was analyzed using equal-area stereonets to identify deformation patterns and quantify the geometry of foliations, folds, and faults.

Pelona Schist in the study area is dominated by muscovite–albite–quartz schist, with chlorite–albite–actinolite greenstone locally beneath mylonitic rocks of the Vincent thrust, a regionally significant shear zone placing granitoids above the schist. Schistose fabrics exhibit a dominant foliation (S 1 ), striking 120° and dipping 40-50°SW, and primary bedding was not identified. Tight to isoclinal folds, with axial planes striking 136° and dipping 37° SW (S 2 ), have limbs inclined in the same direction as foliation, indicating that the foliation has been folded. These folds are parallel to foliation in the Vincent thrust mylonite together recording a consistent southwest-inclined structural grain.

This framework is overprinted by several fracture and minor fault sets. One consists of N- to NE-striking, moderate- to steeply dipping fractures, parallel to extensional faults bounding the Crafton Hills. A second comprises E-W-striking, moderate- to steeply dipping fractures that may record contraction related to the San Bernardino strand of the San Andreas fault. The youngest set includes weakly developed subhorizontal fractures and small faults, likely reflecting landslide-related deformation. Thin-section analysis will refine lithologic variability, metamorphic assemblages, and microstructures.

title: Satellite Observations Reveal Contrasting Groundwater–Surface Water Responses to Anthropogenic Drought Across the Colorado River Basin
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: Oyedele, Esther [1], Werth, Susanna [2], Carlson, Grace [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(3) Geography, Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract: Groundwater is an essential component of water security in the Colorado River Basin (CRB), yet its response to prolonged drought and increasing water demand remains spatially heterogeneous and difficult to quantify at basin scales. We integrate GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite gravimetry with hydrological datasets to evaluate terrestrial and groundwater storage variability and their relationship to surface-water deficits across the CRB from water year 2004 to 2023. To characterize these groundwater–surface water interactions under drought conditions, we employ a joint framework combining copula-based dependence modeling with statistical inference to quantify probabilistic relationships among storage-based drought indicators. Results indicate persistent groundwater depletion throughout the basin, with accelerated losses since 2019 and during the 2020–2022 drought. Contrary to expectations, and as a new basin-scale finding, groundwater losses during this period were substantially greater in the Upper CRB (17.5 ± 3.5 km³) than in the Lower CRB (9.4 ± 6.5 km³), despite the Upper Basin historically exhibiting greater hydrologic resilience. Dependence analysis further reveals strong coupling between groundwater drought probability and surface-water deficits in the Upper CRB, whereas weaker statistical dependence in parts of the Lower CRB suggests groundwater depletion increasingly reflects sustained anthropogenic withdrawals under chronically limited surface-water availability. These findings demonstrate the utility of integrating satellite observations with probabilistic statistical approaches to diagnose groundwater vulnerability and improve understanding of hydroclimatic and human controls on water storage dynamics in large managed river basins.

title: Are Microwave Observations of Venus Consistent with Large-Scale Compositional Layering in the Plains?
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: Akins, Alex [1], Ganesh, Indujaa [2], Butler, Bryan [3], Siegler, Matthew [4]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(2) Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA,
(3) National Radio Astronomy Observatory, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(4) University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI, USA
abstract:
At longer wavelengths than observed by Pioneer Venus or Magellan, Venus’ microwave emission drops well below its surface temperature; Mohan et al. (2019) find an upper limit to the planet’s disk-integrated 1.3 m brightness temperature of 320 K. Antony et al. (2022) posit (based on results from a non-scattering radiative transfer model) that this could result from the presence of a layer of high dielectric material, comparable to that inferred in the highlands, under a meter of fine basalt regolith. A perhaps more geologically plausible interpretation, given plains surface images from the Venera landers (Garvin et al. 1984), would be scattering from large-scale blocks in a low-loss background regolith, as has previously been postulated to explain the emissivity of the highlands (e.g. Tryka and Muhleman, 1992). Whichever it is, this is a global scale phenomenon, and perhaps diagnostic of the vertical structure of the shallow subsurface in Venus’ lowland plains.

To investigate this, we have undertaken a joint analysis of long-wavelength radar and radiometric observations of Venus with the VLA (Akins et al. 2025), GMRT (Mohan et al. 2017, 2019) and Arecibo (Hagfors and Campbell 1974, Campbell and Campbell 2022). VLA and GMRT observations made at wavelengths >50 cm are disk-integrated, but multi-angle polarimetry is available other datasets. Of particular interest are both the low values of linear polarization in the 70 cm Arecibo radar returns and the high values in the GMRT 50 cm emission. We will present the results of our radiative transfer modeling comparisons to the available observations and discuss their general implications for the near-surface composition and structure of Venus’ plains material.

title: Eye to Eye in 10 Years: Impact of Direct Landfalls of Hurricanes Joaquin (Category 3; October 2015) versus Melissa (Category 1; October 2025) on Coastlines of San Salvador Island, The Bahamas
session_title: Contemporary research in geomorphological hazards
authors: Glumac, Bosiljka [1], Curran, H. Allen [2], Cullen, Eloise [3], Wheeler, Hanna Teruko [4], Savarese, Michael [5], Dexter, Troy A. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(5) Department of Marine & Earth Sciences, The Water School, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(6) Gerace Research Institute, University of The Bahamas, San Salvador Island, Bahamas
abstract:
Hurricanes Joaquin and Melissa passed directly over San Salvador, 10 years apart (October 2015 and October 2025), following a similar S-N path. This allowed closer comparison between Category 3 (120-130 mph winds) vs Category 1 (75-90 mph winds) hurricanes, respectively, in the context of long-term monitoring of storm impacts on this small (163 km 2 ), low-relief island, located on the easternmost carbonate bank of the Bahama Archipelago. Such monitoring of coastlines vulnerable to increasing impacts of climate change can provide valuable insights for improving societal resilience.

In January 2016, after Hurricane Joaquin that damaged ~80% of buildings on the island, significant changes to coastal boulder deposits were observed at two sites monitored since 2012: 1) Singer Bar Point (SBP) along the relatively low-energy, gently seaward-sloping ramp on the lagoon- and reef-protected north coast; and 2) rocky cliff bench, 3-5 m above sea level, at The Gulf (TG) on the high-energy south coast. Storm waves overtopped TG cliffs and modified the sharp-crested, narrow boulder ridge into a broad, vegetation-free field. New boulders up to 3 m in diameter were emplaced on the cliffs, and 1-3 ton blocks from prior storms were moved up to 26 m inland. A small reentrant at TG was enlarged and mostly emptied of large boulders that filled it before the storm. Sandy coastlines also experienced significant erosion. On the east coast, the seaward-facing wall of Fortune Hill Cemetery was destroyed and replaced by a ~2 m vertical foredune scarp. Some dune scarps showed signs of repair months after the storm, and 10 years later, the dune and beach system adjacent to the cemetery was fully recovered from Joaquin erosion.

Observations from June 2026 included amalgamated effects of Hurricane Melissa and 2026 northerly winter storms, that modify SBP site on a seasonal basis, and subsequent natural recovery. A ~0.5 m beach scarp, most likely produced by Melissa, was present along the east coast, but dunes showed no evidence of erosion. The pattern of boulder transport and vegetation damage on TG cliffs was similar to that of Joaquin, but less intense. Within TG reentrant, Melissa’s waves piled up most of the remaining boulders along the northwestern wall, marking the possible start of reentrant infilling by smaller intensity storms in between higher-energy erosional events.

title: Using element mapping and in-situ 40Ar/39Ar dating to constrain magmatic–hydrothermal pulses at the Filo del Sol Cu–Au–Ag Porphyry–Epithermal System
session_title: Geochronology of Ore Deposits Containing Critical Minerals: Analytical Advances and Applications
authors: Jicha, Brian R [1], Sojo, M. Camila [2], Merino, Guido [3], Rezeau, Herve [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA

abstract: The Filo del Sol (FDS) is a giant porphyry-epithermal Cu–Au–Ag deposit straddling the Argentina–Chile border. The duration of ore formation at FDS has been primary constrained by molybdenite Re-Os dates clustering around 14.6 Ma together with a few, imprecise alunite K-Ar ages from 13.9 ± 1.6 to 12.0 ± 2.4 Ma, thereby providing limited constraints between <1 to >3 million years. Moreover, the temporal relationship between high-sulfidation epithermal mineralization at FDS and the underlying porphyry is not well established. Prior to attempting to constrain the timing of mineralization at FDS via in-situ 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, samples were carefully characterized to identify biotite and K-feldspar formed during the porphyry mineralization and the overlapping generations of alunite and sericite with respect to the micro-scale spatial relationships amongst the ore mineral assemblages in the epithermal mineralization. Element mapping (K, Al, Si, S, Fe) and EDS spot analyses revealed the distribution of K-bearing alteration minerals, many of which were only 100-300 microns wide in numerous samples. These screening steps enabled precise target site selection for in-situ 40 Ar/ 39 Ar laser ablation, which has seldomly been used, thus far, for dating porphyry-epithermal deposits. Thirteen to fifteen in-situ 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates were obtained per sample including transects across samples and ablations of alunite that likely would not have been able to be isolated using traditional mechanical separation techniques. New in-situ and bulk 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages on alunite, biotite, sericite and K-feldspar range from 14.3 to 11.3 Ma with peaks in the age populations at ~14 and ~13 Ma. The ~13 Ma group of alunite ages along with the 11.3 Ma age suggest late-stage ore-forming fluids were released either during the waning stages of magmatism or from unrecognized, younger intrusions at depth. Overall, FDS records episodic hydrothermal pulses and a protracted dynamic evolution, both of which allow us to improve our knowledge about the mechanisms for the enrichment of precious and critical minerals in the upper continental crust.

title: Mapping Hydrothermal Alteration Halos with Multispectral Drone Imagery: Predicting Mineralization at the Hummingbird Mine, Uncompahgre Uplift, Colorado USA

affiliations: (1) Physical & Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA

abstract: Drone-based multispectral imagery was used to identify hydrothermal alteration halos at the Hummingbird Mine area, Unaweep Canyon, western Uncompahgre Uplift, Colorado. The study area hosts a Nancy Hanks-type epithermal vein system characterized by quartz, amethyst, fluorite, illite, and pyrite localized along fault-controlled fluid pathways. Three multispectral band-ratio indices were derived from multispectral drone (sUAS) imagery (450–840 nm): Red Edge/Red for iron oxide alteration, Red/Red Edge for silicification, and NIR/Green for broadband silica brightness. Vegetation was removed using NDVI masking prior to spectral anomaly mapping. At the first site, the Red/Red Edge and NIR/Green indices delineated nearly identical silicification anomalies of 259 m² and 257 m², respectively, whereas the Red Edge/Red index identified a smaller 56 m² iron oxide anomaly, consistent with an iron oxide halo surrounding a silicified core. Multi-index convergence (where several indices indicated similar anomalous regions) guided field verification to two mineralized locations where hydrothermal vein conduits and adjacent alteration halos were confirmed. A mapped spectral polygon of 93 m² closely matched a field-measured alteration zone of 80 m². At the second site, a silicified dike was spectrally distinguishable from the adjacent Wingate Formation using the Red/Red Edge index, providing independent validation of the silicification mapping approach. The hypothesis was partially supported: multi-index convergence zones successfully predicted mineralization locations, but lithologic reflectance—including diagenetic iron oxides in the Chinle Formation and primary silica in the Wingate Formation—limited the ability to distinguish hydrothermal alteration from formation-level spectral signatures without field verification. These results demonstrate that drone-based multispectral imagery provides an effective first-pass tool for targeting hydrothermal alteration, while highlighting the continued importance of field observations in geologically complex terrains.

title: Capturing Daily Variability in Microplastic Transport Across a Piedmont River Network
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part I)
authors: Chapman, LeeAnna [1]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Studies, Davidson College, Davidson, NC, USA
abstract: Small tributary streams and confluences serve as critical conduits routing terrestrial plastic pollution into river basins. However, daily variations and short-term microplastic transport remain poorly understood. High-frequency daily sampling is necessary to capture storm-driven fluxes and cross-channel transport variability. This study collected stream surface grab samples daily for 30 consecutive days across three locations on the West Branch Rocky River in the Piedmont of North Carolina: two small tributary streams and their downstream confluence. At each location, samples were collected in duplicate from both the stream bank and mid-channel. Local stream velocity was measured daily alongside obtaining regional daily stream gage height, precipitation, and discharge. Samples underwent density separation before sequential size-fractionated filtration through 30 μm and 5 μm filters. Under microscopic examination, microplastics were quantified and categorized into five distinct morphotypes (fibers, fragments, films, styrofoams, and pellets) along with total particle counts. Daily spatiotemporal variations in particle concentration and morphotype composition were observed across the stream network. Analyses including daily concentration spikes evaluated against discharge and precipitation, size comparisons between 5 µm and 30 µm filters, cross-sectional differences between bank and mid-channel sites, and morphotype distributions will be discussed during the session. These findings highlight essential sampling considerations for accurately modeling microplastic dynamics in Piedmont stream systems.

title: Mafic Recharge Primes Mingled Lava Eruption in the Searchlight Magmatic System, Nevada
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Miller, Rachel [1], Eddy, Michael Patterson [2], Miller, Calvin F. [3], Gualda, Guilherme [4], Hinz, Nicholas [5], Pamukçu, Ayla [6], Wallrich, Blake [7]
affiliations: (1) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

abstract: Mafic recharge can renew the eruptive potential of upper crustal magma reservoirs. Evidence of magma recharge is extensive in the volcanic and plutonic records and includes increased magma temperatures recorded in crystals, pre-eruptive changes in magma isotopic composition recorded in phenocryst rims, mineral disequilibria, magmatic enclaves, and physical and compositional evidence of magma mingling and mixing within upper crustal plutons. However, there are few locations where both the plutonic and volcanic record of a recharge-triggered eruption are preserved. The Miocene Searchlight magmatic system in southern Nevada includes a well-mapped paleo-vertical upper crustal plutonic section, where there is exposure of dikes rooted in mingled gabbro and granite that traverse the pluton towards an overlying, coeval volcanic section. These dikes are phenocryst-rich rhyolite porphyry with abundant mafic enclaves that locally have mafic margins. At least one dike can be traced into the volcanic section, where previous work considering field relations, glass and mineral geochemistry, and mineral textures suggests that it fed a rhyolite porphyry lava flow containing extensive mafic enclaves. This exposure provides a unique opportunity to study a vertically integrated record of eruption triggered by mafic recharge. Here, we present new high-precision U-Pb zircon dates that further demonstrate that the pluton, dike, and eruptive records were contemporaneous, as well as field, petrologic, and geochemical data to better understand the mafic recharge systematics.

title: Burned: What can char debris tell us about the paleoecology and paleoclimate of Pennsylvanian coal-ball swamps?
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Jackson, Christian Daniel [1], Raymond, Anne [2]
affiliations: (1) Texas A&M University, Weslaco, TX,
(2) Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
abstract:
Coal balls preserve permineralized peat from Pennsylvanian swamps, providing a detailed record of ancient swamp ecology with implications for Pennsylvanian paleoclimate. We use patterns of fossil preservation to investigate the nature of wildfire in Pennsylvanian peat swamps. Medullosans are early seed plants that contributed 4 – 20% of the plant debris in most Pennsylvanian coal-ball swamps and 40% in some. The most common medullosan fossils are the branches of their compound leaves known as Myeloxylon, which are hypothesized to have produced large amounts of plant resin, making medullosans vulnerable to fire. To test this, we compared the percentage of charred Myeloxylon to the percentage of charred cordaitean wood or lycopsid periderm in coal balls collected between 1930 and 1980 from three stratigraphic intervals, now in the Phillips collection (IGS) or Thompson-Darrah collection (Harvard). In all three, significantly more Myeloxylon debris was charred than cordaitean wood or lycopsid periderm (Chi-squared test of independence, p 0.02).

The three stratigraphic intervals fell on a rainfall gradient from seasonal in the early mid-Pennsylvanian Kalo Formation, wetter in the mid-Pennsylvanian Fleming Coal, to very wet in the late mid-Pennsylvanian Herrin Coal. However, all three localities had similar char percentages (Chi-squared test of independence, p 0.37). The percentage of charred debris in Pennsylvanian coal balls is not a reliable proxy for relative precipitation or length of the low-rain season.

The organ composition and taxonomic affiliation of charred debris in Kalo Formation coal balls suggests that this debris resulted from canopy, rather than surface or ground fire. We censused 1186 pieces of charred debris in 78 randomly selected coal balls from the Kalo Formation. Whereas roots are 49% of Kalo Formation peat, all identifiable char belonged to aerial organs).

In 90% of coal balls with char, the taxonomic composition of identifiable char matched that of the unburned debris in the coal ball, suggesting that char derived from local vegetation, consistent with canopy fire. Our sample contained 31 layers of charred debris, each interpreted as resulting from one fire. In all cases, the organ composition of peat above and below the charred layer matched, suggesting that charred layers resulted from small, local fires, and that fire did not drive ecological succession in Kalo Formation swamps.

title: Stream Capture and Landscape Transience Reveal Post-Orogenic Rejuvenation in the Wet Mountains, Colorado, USA
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens (Posters)
authors: Sugerman-Brozan, Lev [1], Schanz, Sarah Anne [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
abstract: Traditional landscape cycles showcase steady erosional reduction of mountain belts post-orogenesis in which fluvial systems reach a dynamic equilibrium. Yet, post-orogenic landscapes globally preserve signals of topographic dynamism, including relief production, sediment flux, and fluvial incision. In particular, erosional and geomorphic markers suggest topographic dynamism in the last 5 Ma in the Southern Rocky Mountains (SRM), though the timing and mechanism of such uplift is highly debated. Here, we quantify the direction and timing of late Cenozoic landscape transience and drainage reorganization in the Colorado Wet Mountains (CWM) using remote sensing, field observations, numerical modeling, and infrared-stimulated luminescence dating (IRSL). We found persistent southwest-oriented drainage divide migration, two stream capture events, and anomalous chi/elevation relationships occurring between 3300 and 3450 meters in elevation in the CWM, indicative of a wave of upstream-migrating incision. Valley width to drainage area relationships demonstrate underfit streams on the captured side of the drainage divide. Drainage divide migration has driven cross-divide stream capture, but stream capture has also occurred within the southwest side of the main drainage divide, suggesting a more complex pattern of uplift. The spatial coherence and directionality of drainage reorganization are most consistent with epeirogenic tilting in the CWM rather than lithologic or climatic controls. Thus, we provide the first field evidence of late Cenozoic landscape transience showing that the SRM are undergoing continued adjustment to tectonic tilting.

abstract:
The Baringo Basin, located in the Eastern African Rift in Kenya, contains the Pliocene-Pleistocene Chemeron Formation consisting of fluvio-lacustrine sediments. A 227 m sediment core (HSPDP-BTB13; 3.29 to 2.56 Ma) records times of hominin evolutionary transitions and two major global climate events– the mid-Pliocene Warming Period (mPWP; 3.25 to 2.95 Ma) and the onset of the Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (NHG; ~2.75 Ma). The paleosols (n = 78) in HSPDP-BTB13 preserve past climate conditions that can be correlated with other paleoclimate proxies to develop an understanding of the paleoenvironment of Baringo Basin while early hominins occupied the region. Stable (δ 13 C PC and δ 18 O PC ) and clumped isotopes from paleosol carbonates (Δ 47 ) track environmental and climatic changes including paleotemperature, woody cover, and paleohydrology, which shift throughout the mPWP and NHG. δ 13 C PC (-13.2‰ to 4.5‰ VPDB) shows a transition from shrubland/ wooded grassland to C 4 grasslands as the NHG intensified. δ 18 O PC (-17.9‰ to -0.3‰ VPDB) serves as a proxy for paleoprecipitation and changing seasonality due to shifts in the Eastern African Monsoon (EAM) – the region’s dominant precipitation regime. Fifteen Δ 47 samples, spaced by depth every ~20m, were analyzed with four replicates each to reconstruct paleotemperature, which ranged from 15.7 to 45.5℃ with a mean of 29.3 ± 2.34℃.

Overall, the changes in paleotemperature, paleohydrology, and paleovegetation indicate that the EAM weakened during the mPWP and strengthened during the transition from mPWP to NHG before weakening once more as temperature cooled. δ 18 O PC values from the mPWP suggest that precipitation decreased and seasonality increased along with an increase in the abundance of paleo-Vertisols, a soil order indicative of seasonality. Other paleosol features, including horizonation, bioturbation, and redoximorphic features, support the interpretations that paleotemperature and water availability in the Baringo Basin increased in the mPWP and then decreased during the NHG. In addition, paleosol mineralogy– determined using X-Ray Diffraction– shows shifts in the presence/abscence of quartz, feldspar, and clay minerals that correspond with shifts in weathering intensity and environmental conditions that match the changes also observed in the stable isotope records. These results indicate that the strata in Baringo Basin record local paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental responses to global climate change which may have affected early hominins.

(3) Earth & Environmental Sciences,, Wesleyan University, Middletown, CT, USA; Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Heaven, CT, USA
abstract:
The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM; ~56 Ma) represents one of the best-documented episodes of rapid global warming, during which global temperatures increased by approximately 5–9°C over a few thousand years, remaining high for ~200kyr. The PETM coincided with the Benthic Foraminiferal Extinction Event (BEE), one of the most severe deep-sea biotic crises of the Cenozoic, resulting in the global extinction of 30–50% of benthic foraminiferal species. The western South Atlantic is an exceptional setting to investigate the response of benthic foraminiferal assemblages to the PETM, recording changes in deep-water circulation, carbonate dissolution, and the recovery of benthic ecosystems.

This study compares benthic foraminiferal assemblages across the PETM using data from ten industry wells along the Brazilian continental margin and DSDP Sites 356 and 20 (Hole 20C). The BEE was identified at all study areas; but better documented at the DSDP sites, due to sampling resolution. Calcareous taxa were disproportionately affected among the extinct taxa, at 83%. Extinction intensity was lower in the marginal basins (~16%) compared with the more distal and deeper DSDP sites (~35%), reflecting the higher proportion of calcareous taxa in the open-ocean assemblages.

Following the PETM, in the early Eocene, benthic assemblages in most Brazilian marginal basins shifted abruptly from agglutinated- to calcareous-dominated faunas. The exception was the Campos Basin, where agglutinated taxa remained dominant throughout the Eocene. This faunal turnover likely reflects the combined influence of passive-margin progradation, and shoaling, increased siliciclastic input driven by tectonic and climatic processes, and a possible deepening of the carbonate compensation depth (CCD) along the continental margin.

The transition from agglutinated- to calcareous-dominated assemblages occurred in the Sergipe–Alagoas, Mucuri, Santos, and Pelotas basins but not at the open-ocean DSDP sites. These contrasting patterns indicate that local environmental changes, particularly increased siliciclastic sediment supply associated with continental margin progradation, strongly influenced benthic foraminiferal distribution and modulated the ecological response to the PETM in the western South Atlantic.

title: Reexamining Ages of Marine Terraces Using Lidar Topography and Mapping Along the Gaviota Coastline, Southern California
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens (Posters)
authors: Morgenthaler, Naomi [1], Morell, Kristin [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA,
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA,
abstract:
Long-term uplift of the westernmost Transverse Ranges in Southern California is recorded by marine terraces along the Gaviota coastline, a ~60 km stretch from Isla Vista to Point Conception. However, disagreements in age dating of the first emergent terrace by Morel et al. (2022) and Muhs et al. (2026) introduce uncertainty into these uplift rates. Both studies agree that the Isla Vista terrace corresponds to Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 3 (~50 ka), but they differ on the terrace ages between Tajiguas and Point Conception, proposing MIS 3 and MIS 5a (~80 ka), respectively. These age differences between Morel et al. (2022) and Muhs et al. (2026) significantly affect calculated uplift rates and regional tectonic models.

Assuming constant uplift in time and space, an MIS 5a terrace from Tajiguas to Point Conception should occur at substantially higher elevation than the MIS 3 terrace at Isla Vista (>50 m higher uplift). This study seeks to test this hypothesis using high-resolution LiDAR, well log report data, and alluvial sediment thickness measured at the sea cliff to map terrace inner edge elevations along the coast at key areas. This analysis reveals little change in along-coast inner edge elevation, with at most 20 m of gradual variations in elevation. These findings suggest either a sharp change in uplift rate in space, which could be caused by an active fault, and/or temporal variations in Quaternary uplift rate. We do not find evidence for active fault(s) in the key region needed to explain the inner edge elevation patterns. The results suggest that additional age dating is needed to resolve remaining uncertainties and refine tectonic uplift models.

title: Reconstructing Paleovegetation from Complex Leaf Wax Biomarker Mixtures Using Machine Learning
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Flanagan, Evangeline [1], Ponton, Camilo [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA,
(2) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
abstract:
Plant leaf wax n -alkanes are widely used to reconstruct terrestrial vegetation and paleoclimate, yet few studies validate biomarker reconstructions against the plant macrofossil record. Here, we use statistical learning models trained on modern leaf wax n -alkane distributions to deconvolve mixed biomarker signals from the Paleocene–Eocene Chuckanut Formation (western Washington) into vegetation endmembers. The abundant plant macrofossils preserved in the Bellingham Bay and Padden members provide an ideal test of biomarker-based vegetation reconstructions.

n -Alkanes were extracted from sedimentary rocks and analyzed by GC-MS. Machine learning successfully resolved complex n -alkane mixtures into vegetation endmembers, providing a more complete reconstruction of forest composition than chain-length analyses alone. Results show that subtropical flora dominated the Chuckanut Formation throughout the late Paleocene and early Eocene, consistent with the globally warm climate. From the late Paleocene Bellingham Bay Member to the early Eocene Padden Member, conifers increased while angiosperms declined.

These results are in partial agreement with the macrofossil record, which also shows an increase in conifers but does not preserve the dominance of subtropical vegetation in the Padden Member. This difference may reflect preservation bias, as palms and ferns are less likely to be preserved than conifers because of differences in habitat and fossilization potential. Model performance is also expected to improve as modern n -alkane training libraries expand to include more species and greater taxonomic diversity. Despite these limitations, our results suggest that leaf wax biomarkers capture a broader picture of regional vegetation than macrofossils alone, including plant communities that may be underrepresented in the fossil record. More broadly, this study demonstrates the potential of machine learning to extract vegetation signals from complex biomarker mixtures, offering a promising new approach for reconstructing past ecosystems and climate.

title: Lithium and potassium partitioning during low-temperature disordered dolomite precipitation
session_title: Early career investigators in mineralogy and crystallography (Posters)
authors: Downey, Autum R. [1], Valencic, Nathan Rae [2], Fang, Yihang [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Missouri, Kansas City, MO,
(2) University of Missouri, Kansas City, MO, USA
(3) University of Missouri, Kansas City, MO, USA
abstract: Carbonates exhibiting dolomite stoichiometry with little to no Ca-Mg ordering, hereafter referred to as disordered dolomite, are widely interpreted as the metastable precursor to ordered sedimentary dolomite and therefore represent a critical intermediate in low-temperature dolomite formation. Quantifying Li and K partitioning during disordered dolomite precipitation is particularly important because these elements are increasingly used to investigate fluid evolution, water-rock interaction, and critical element cycling in many carbonate-bearing systems. Low-temperature precipitation experiments were conducted across a range of dissolved Li and K concentrations to evaluate their influence on Ca-Mg carbonate precipitation. X-ray diffraction analysis reveal that all experiments produced similar mixed carbonate assemblages consisting of near equal proportions of calcite and disordered dolomite, with no systematic variation in mineralogy as a function of Li or K concentration. Preliminary SEM-EDS analyses demonstrate a positive relationship between dissolved K concentration and K associated with the carbonate precipitates while indicating a homogeneous spatial distribution of K throughout the precipitates. Ongoing development of a sequential leaching protocol, coupled with adsorption isotherm experiments will resolve phase-specific Li and K distributions and distinguish surface-associated from structurally incorporated Li and K. Together, these experiments establish the foundation for quantifying phase-specific Li and K partitioning during disordered dolomite precipitation and provide a framework for interpreting trace element incorporation during early dolomite formation.

title: Securing Graphite Supply through International Collaboration: Outcomes of the 2026 Graphite Summit, Sri Lanka
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Case, George [1], Stokes, Rebecca [2], Gamage, Kusali [3], Stowell, Harold H. [4], Toma, Jonathan Alan scott [5], Stewart, Emily M. [6]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey Alaska Science Center, Anchorage, AK, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey Geology, Energy, and Minerals Science Center, Reston, VA, USA
(3) Austin Community College, Austin, Texas, USA
(4) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL,
(5) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(6) Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL,
abstract:
Natural graphite is a vital raw material for battery anodes and defense applications, yet the United States relies on imports for its supply. Hydrothermal vein graphite is the purest (>99%), and rarest, variety and is only produced in Sri Lanka, though geologic evidence implies potential for more resources in both there and the U.S. In April 2026, a U.S. National Science Foundation-funded summit at the University of Peradeniya, Sri Lanka, established collaborations and shared knowledge between academic, industry, and government scientists from both countries. The U.S. contingent included academics from the U.S. Geological Survey, National Laboratory of the Rockies, eight universities, and three State geological surveys. Sri Lankan attendees included the Geological Survey and Mines Bureau and faculty and students from the University of Peradeniya. Also present were exploration, mining, and application experts from both countries. The summit focused on vein ore genesis, best mining practices, and modern market access. Here, we summarize the outcomes of the summit and opportunities for new graphite research.

Ore genesis models of graphite vein deposits are still debated. Sri Lanka’s deposits are thought to be related to orogenic graphite mineral systems that were active late in the amalgamation of Gondwana ca. 600-500 Ma, deriving their carbon and fluids from either supracrustal or mantle reservoirs. To elucidate these sources, scientists visited all three operating mines at Bogala, Kahatagaha, and Ragedara during the summit to collect samples of veins and wall rock. The samples will enable geochronologic and isotopic analyses that may constrain carbon and fluid sources and vein formation age. Such results will inform mineral system models essential to exploration and assessment of yet-undiscovered vein graphite resources in Sri Lanka and the U.S.

In addition to ore genesis research, the summit highlighted the need for future collaboration in the areas of material quality, geologic data preservation and modernization, standard reference materials and laboratory instrumentation, mining methods, and policy development. For example, lack of digital geologic maps, geochemical data, and known occurrence information discourages exploration investment, and outdated mining techniques limit production and access to U.S. markets. Continued work on these topics can improve scientific understanding of vein graphite deposit genesis, reduce their associated mining and investment risks, and ultimately increase the security of the U.S. graphite supply chain.

authors: Mercer, Celestine N. [1], Thompson, Jay M. [2], Mercer, Cameron M. [3], Monteleone, Brian D. [4], Eastman, Kyle A. [5], Gaynor, Sean P. [6], McIntosh, Julia A. [7], Attia, Snir [8]

abstract:
Advances in in-situ analytical techniques enable integration of multiple methods on individual tourmaline samples, offering insights into magmatic-hydrothermal processes in ore-forming systems. Tourmaline is a common mineral in igneous and hydrothermal systems and varies from an accessory phase to a major gangue mineral. While tourmaline abundance is not a proxy for mineralization potential, it may be a valuable recorder of magmatic-hydrothermal evolution and proxy for mineral system fertility. By characterizing tourmaline using multiple in-situ datasets from barren and mineralized deposits within and around the Boulder batholith, Montana, we test tourmaline as an integrative recorder of granite-related mineral systems. This mineral-scale perspective complements ongoing Earth MRI efforts including regional geologic mapping, geophysical surveys, whole-rock geochemistry, and geochronology across the Boulder batholith.

This study uses representative tourmaline from deposit types across the Boulder batholith (e.g., pegmatites, polymetallic veins, skarns, breccias, stockwork veins) to evaluate variations in tourmaline chemistry and petrogenesis. We aim to integrate petrography, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, in-situ B and Pb isotopes, and major (EPMA) and trace element (LAICPMS) datasets to constrain the timing of tourmaline crystallization, boron and magma sources, magmatic-hydrothermal evolution, fluid-rock interaction, and mineral system characteristics.

Preliminary SEM results (n=17) reveal tourmaline abundances in thick section (7–66 area%) and varieties include Fe-rich black schorl, Mg-rich black/green/brown dravite, and Ca-rich black uvite. Textures vary from massive, graphic, prismatic, fibrous, to acicular. 40 Ar/ 39 Ar analyses (n=11) yield well-defined plateaus but contain excess 40 Ar; therefore, we favor isochron ages indicating Late Cretaceous tourmaline crystallization between ~78–73 Ma. These ages reveal tourmaline varieties are coeval with early batholith formation through the emplacement of the Butte Granite, the main batholith phase. SIMS analyses (n=9) reveal isotopically light boron (δ¹¹B = -1.8‰ to -11.6‰) overlapping with continental crust, clastic metasediments, and porphyry Cu-Mo-Au deposits. δ¹¹B in tourmaline from the Bluebird–Pen Yan Au-Ag-Cu(-Pb-Zn) mine is like pegmatitic tourmaline (-6.8 ± 0.9‰), supporting geologic interpretations that this deposit formed from metal-rich fluids focused at the roof of the batholith. δ¹¹B values from the Tourmaline Queen Au-mineralized breccia are relatively lighter (-10.8 ± 0.7‰) while those from gray sericite-altered stockwork quartz-pyrite veins are heavier (-2.8 ± 0.6‰). Preliminary results indicate that integrated in-situ tourmaline datasets will provide a powerful mineral-scale framework for reconstructing magmatic-hydrothermal evolution and evaluating granite-related mineral systems.

title: Monitoring and Modeling Temperature of a Central New York Stream
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes (Posters)
authors: Baker, Emily A [1], Gutierrez, Emily [2], Hahn, Amelia [3]
affiliations: (1) Hamilton College, Clinton, NY, USA
(2) Hamilton College, Clinton, NY, USA
(3) Hamilton College, Clinton, NY, USA
abstract:
Stream temperature is a key water quality parameter that influences physical, chemical, and biological processes, thereby affecting aquatic ecosystem structure and function. Unfortunately, stream temperature is directly impacted by air temperature, which is expected to rise as climate change continues. Rising summer air temperatures and increasing heat wave frequency will therefore impact stream temperatures, potentially putting ecosystem function at risk and threatening the health of cold-water organisms. In central New York, this is a concern for freshwater fish populations, particularly wild trout inhabiting headwater streams. To evaluate current thermal conditions and vulnerability to future warming, stream temperatures along Oriskany Creek were monitored. Oriskany Creek is a premier fishing area that is a wild trout stream in its upper reaches. Temperature sensors were deployed at seven sites along the 53 km stream, recording stream temperature at 15-minute intervals during the summer of 2026. Meteorological and groundwater temperature data were also collected within the catchment, along with stream discharge data at multiple locations along the creek, to evaluate controls on stream temperature.

We found that summertime stream temperatures typically increased along the length of Oriskany Creek, indicating that solar heating exceeded cooling contributions from groundwater inputs. During June 2026, temperatures exceeded 20°C, a threshold associated with heat stress in brown trout, in only 1.5% of measurements at the upstream site compared with 51% at the downstream site. Similarly, temperatures exceeded 24°C, a threshold associated with severe thermal stress and increased mortality risk, in 0% of upstream measurements and 10% of downstream measurements. At the end of June, downstream locations experienced a seven-day period during which stream temperatures remained above 20°C continuously, including overnight. These prolonged periods of thermal stress are expected to become more frequent under future climate warming. Lastly, these data were used to calibrate a stream temperature model and assess how increases in air temperature and periods of prolonged elevated temperatures may alter stream temperatures along Oriskany Creek.

abstract:
A new structure map of the Middle Devonian Columbus Limestone provides insight into the stratigraphic relationships of the Marcellus shale interval and surrounding Devonian strata in the subsurface of eastern Ohio and is the first step to improving maps of this interval in the distal Appalachian Basin. In the subsurface of eastern Ohio, the Columbus Limestone is overlain by the Marcellus shale and forms the top of the drillers’ “Big Lime.” This represents the same chronostratigraphic surface and lithostratigraphic transition as the top of the widespread Onondaga Limestone, a key datum for Middle Devonian subsurface mapping in the Appalachian Basin. To the west, however, the Marcellus shale grades into the Delaware Limestone; at this point, the Delaware has been mapped as the top of the “Big Lime,” despite it overlying the Columbus Limestone. This has resulted in basin-wide maps of the top of the Onondaga Limestone which represent the base of the Marcellus throughout most of the Appalachian Basin, but which represent the top of Marcellus-equivalent strata in the distal Appalachian Basin. To resolve this, we mapped the Columbus Limestone from the westernmost edge of the Appalachian Basin eastward into the subsurface.

The Columbus Limestone and overlying Delaware Limestone have been mapped through traditional bedrock mapping where they are exposed in the central Ohio outcrop belt. To extend the mapped surface farther east into the subsurface, we applied several geophysical and chronostratigraphic techniques (stable carbon isotope and conodont biochemostratigraphy) to core and outcrop samples to ensure accurate correlation and differentiation of the units using lithological and geophysical means. We described the Columbus/Delaware contact interval in 14 cores and 4 field locations. All cores were scanned with a Geotek core logger to collect bulk density and gamma-ray data, and outcrops were scanned with a handheld gamma-ray spectrometer. We used GeoGraphix software to correlate outcrop, core, and well-log data across our mapping area. Here, we present the resulting structure contour map on top of the Columbus Limestone, which integrates the existing bedrock map with our subsurface mapping area. Future work will include extending the top Columbus Limestone surface eastward, mapping the top of the overlying Delaware Limestone and Marcellus shale, and delineating the facies boundary between these units.

authors: Elliott, Caroline M. [1], Call, Bruce C. [2], Jacobson, Robert B. [3], Mansfield, Michael P [4]
affiliations: (1) U. S. Geological Survey, Columbia, MO,
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Columbia, MO, MO, USA

abstract: The Lower Missouri River downstream of Sioux City, South Dakota, is a 1,200-kilometer-long engineered navigation channel designed to be self-scouring. Dynamics of sand transport and bedforms within the navigation channel are poorly understood. Sand can be deposited by flood events causing problems for navigation that can require channel maintenance. We mapped fluvial bedforms in a reach of the channelized Lower Missouri River to explore the relationship between flow and bed sediment dynamics. Mapping consisted of 15 repeat multibeam bathymetric surveys of a 2-km long reach consisting of a cross-over and a bend near Missouri River mile 176 in central Missouri between 9/28/2023 and 11/25/2024. These surveys occurred during the regular Missouri River navigation season, which typically runs from April 1 through November 30. Surveys included a high-flow event with a peak of 6,088 cubic meters per second (a flow event with a 3 percent daily flow exceedance probability). Results show some locations in the navigation channel over the course of the year had variations in bed elevation as much as 4 m; the mean variation in bed elevation was 2 m. We calculated mean dune dimension metrics (i.e., amplitude, wavelength, and lee slope) for each survey date using 3 different methods: a polygon in the reach consistent with all survey footprint areas, a profile on the navigation line, and a profile through the largest dunes for each survey date. Bedform dimensions show changes in size with discharge; seasonal variability indicates probable lags in adjustment to hydraulics and effects of varying sediment supply. Surveys during and after the flow peak showed that net bed erosion occurred during this event, although there were also areas where deposition occurred. Following the high flow event, surveys were less frequent but show a general trend of sediment deposition on the bed. Between the first and last survey there is a general trend of deposition on the upstream part of the reach (crossover) and a moderate amount of erosion in the downstream portion of the bend. Net bed elevation change over the course of the year for the whole reach was much lower than between individual surveys indicating seasonal sediment transport patterns and transport dynamics that wouldn’t be captured in a single survey or preserved in the sedimentary record.

title: Paleodrainage history of the northern and central Sierra Nevada from new in-situ detrital zircon U-Pb and (U-Th)/He analysis of Eocene – Oligocene gravels

authors: Borders, Nicholas Ryan [1], Cassel, Elizabeth J. [2], Kortyna, Cullen David [3], Allard, John [4], Flowers, Rebecca Marie [5], Cecil, Robinson [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, ID, USA

abstract:
The Sierra Nevada of eastern California is an extinct Mesozoic continental arc system with a complex post-magmatic depositional and erosional history. The range exhibits distinctive geomorphology, including deep east–west canyons and increasing elevation and relief to the south, prompting debate over the relative roles and spatial patterns of erosion and tectonics. Buttressed along the valley walls of the northern and central Sierra are Eocene – Oligocene (E-O) auriferous gravels. The gravels provide a record of early Cenozoic erosion and topography, offering key insights into the evolution of the range and the broader convergent system.

Previous workers have used detrital zircon (DZ) U–Pb dating in the northern Sierra to better understand the provenance of the gravels and the erosional history of their source catchments. The ages of source domains, however, are non-unique, making it difficult to differentiate between local and extra-regional sources with DZ dates alone. To address this, we performed laser-ablation (LA)-U-Pb-He double dating on zircons from five samples within basal auriferous gravel beds in the ancestral Yuba and American river systems. These new double dates refine provenance interpretations and provide unroofing histories of the gravels’ sources. LA-(U-Th)/He dates from grains with pre-Cenozoic U–Pb ages record Mesozoic cooling, which we interpret to reflect local sediment derivation and widespread Mesozoic exhumation. Furthermore, to better understand early Cenozoic drainage systems in the central Sierra, we conducted new DZ U-Pb analyses on two additional gravel samples in the ancestral American and Tuolumne river drainages. Maximum depositional ages from basal central Sierra gravel zircons become progressively younger to the south, which may be the result of gravel preservation through burial beneath progressively younger ignimbrites to the south.

The data presented here serve as a foundation for future detrital U-Pb-He analyses of pre-volcanic gravels in paleochannels farther north and south within the Sierra Nevada, as well as eastward in western Nevada, with the goal of comprehensively characterizing early Cenozoic erosion and drainage evolution across the region.

affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Western University, London, Ontario, Canada

abstract: Human wastewater contains a wide range of contaminants including fecal pathogens, nutrients, and emerging contaminants that pose risks to human and ecosystem health if released to surface waters. Onsite wastewater treatment systems (OWTSs) are widely used globally for the treatment and dispersal of domestic wastewater, serving approximately 14% of Canadian households and 20% of households in the United States. Although well-functioning OWTSs can provide substantial contaminant attenuation within and below the soil drainage bed and during transport through groundwater, poor design, installation, siting, or maintenance can reduce treatment effectiveness, potentially increasing contaminant inputs to groundwater and nearby surface waters. Preliminary evidence suggests that shallow drainage infrastructure may provide an important pathway for the rapid delivery of OWTS contaminants to surface waters. However, the prevalence and significance of this pathway remain unclear, including the physical and socioeconomic conditions under which it is most important. This study addressed this uncertainty by conducting widespread sampling at more than 100 residential, agricultural, and storm sewer drains discharging to streams across the Canadian Lake Erie Basin. Samples were analyzed for human-specific wastewater tracers including artificial sweeteners (acesulfame, saccharin, sucralose) and the microbial DNA marker HF183, as well as phosphorus, nitrate, E. coli, and chloride. Data revealed elevated wastewater contaminants in all types of drains, suggesting that each type may be important conduits for short-circuiting OWTS wastewater contaminants to streams. Statistical analyses were conducted to examine associations between the prevalence of drains with notable OWTS contaminant signatures and physical (e.g., soil permeability, topographic slope) and socioeconomic (e.g., household age and income) variables. The findings highlight the need to consider subsurface drainage infrastructure in designing, siting and reinspection programs for OWTSs, and in predicting inputs of OWTS wastewater contaminants to surface waters.

title: Surface conformation as a control on nickel bioavailability in a deep-sea hyperthermophilic methanogen
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Downey, Autum R. [1], Gorman-Lewis, Drew [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Missouri-Kansas City, Kansas City, MO,
(2) University of Washington, Earth and Space Sciences, Seattle, WA,
abstract: Nickel, though a minor element in Earth’s crust, is essential for methanogens because methanogenesis requires the nickel-containing cofactor F₄₃₀ to catalyze the final step of methane production. As a result, nickel abundance in the rock record has been proposed as a biosignature for methanogenesis throughout Earth history. For example, declining nickel concentrations in late Archean banded iron formations have been linked to the Great Oxidation Event, given the strict anaerobic requirements of methanogens. Resolving such connections between nickel availability and methanogen activity requires a detailed understanding of how this metal interacts with cells. Metal uptake begins with adsorption to the cell surface, where functional groups act as the first step in bioavailability. Here, we probe the molecular-level interactions underlying nickel adsorption onto the surface of the deep-sea hyperthermophilic methanogen Methanocaldococcus FS406-22 using attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy. Prior ATR-FTIR work on FS406-22 showed evidence of divalent cation-driven conformational changes to surface layer proteins, triggering significant changes to protonation behavior of the cellular envelope. Building on this, we examined nickel adsorption with and without conformationally induced surface changes, as a function of nickel concentration and pH. We observed distinct nickel-induced spectral shifts when concentrations exceeded 12 ppm, with the largest changes near pH 6 and shifts persisting, though reduced, at pH>6; notably, these shifts did not occur in NaCl solutions, highlighting the role of protein conformation in nutrient acquisition. Together, these findings demonstrate that nickel adsorption is fundamentally linked to solution chemistry and protein conformation, a potential adaptive mechanism attuned for metal acquisition at the organism’s optimal growth conditions. These data hint at the adaptability of methanogens to fluctuating solution chemistries through Earth history and to the geochemical signals they imprinted in the rock record.

abstract:
Montana’s water resources are facing increased pressure, while climatic variability is resulting in uncertain water supplies, leading to greater interest in Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR). Because MAR has not been widely researched in Montana, the Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology (MBMG) conducted suitability analyses at various scales, including (1) a statewide surface MAR evaluation, (2) three aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) evaluations conducted in selected basins, and (3) six local surface MAR evaluations. All analyses used a consistent, GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis framework that incorporates peer-reviewed literature and publicly available datasets. We also developed interactive web applications that communicate the methodology and allow users to explore results with other GIS datasets.

We have refined our approach over this three-year effort, and four key lessons emerged. First, clearly defining the scope helps keep the analysis focused and achievable. We limited our analyses to hydrogeologic factors, allowing us to apply our expertise and maintain a manageable set of criteria. This allows others such as regulators, geochemists, and engineers to build upon the analysis based on their expertise. Second, the analysis approach must be adjusted based on the availability and quality of existing data; the same approach is not appropriate or possible for every setting. Third, scale matters. Statewide mapping was effective for a preliminary screening of surface MAR potential, whereas ASR assessments required basin-specific analyses. At the local scale, high-resolution datasets and project-specific objectives improve the defensibility of constraint mapping and allow unsuitable areas to be excluded with greater confidence. Finally, it is important to embrace iteration. Suitability maps are screening tools that improve through repeated evaluation, refinement, comparison, and incorporation of new information.

title: Diagnosing Flowpaths to a Rock Glacier Outlet Stream

authors: McDonough, Maya P. [1], Anderson, Suzanne P. [2], Ruef, Juliana M. [3], Anderson, Robert S. [4], Ge, Shemin [5]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA; Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(2) Dept. of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, ; Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, Boulder, Colorado, USA

abstract: How do rock glaciers affect alpine stream hydrology? We examine flowpaths to the outlet stream emerging from a rock glacier in the San Juan Mountains of Colorado to address this question. Working in Imogene Basin, we deployed a stream gage in the outlet from a 0.15 km 2 rock glacier in a 0.23 km 2 catchment from mid-June to mid-August in 2025 and collected monthly water samples until October 2025. We ran two-component mixing models to partition discharge into supraglacial flow through the rocky debris carapace on the rock glacier and groundwater flow under the rock glacier. The best model separation, based on specific conductivity, shows that supraglacial flow declined as the snow cover on the rock glacier surface declined, while the groundwater component remained relatively steady. By July 30, snow cover on the rock glacier was depleted and the supraglacial flow component was negligible. Integrating the supraglacial discharge to that time yields 0.43 m of supraglacial flow from the 0.15 km 2 rock glacier area, an amount equal to approximately 80% of the snow water equivalent (SWE) measured at Red Mountain Pass SNOTEL, ~75 m below and 5 km SE of our field site. Supraglacial flow was revived by a subsequent ~12 mm rain event, yielding an additional 0.035 m of supraglacial flow from the rock glacier through the end of our gage record on August 11. The relatively steady groundwater discharge component yields 0.24 m of runoff from the full 0.23 km 2 catchment, an amount much less than the SNOTEL SWE. If instead we assume that groundwater recharge occurs only in the 0.08 km 2 above the rock glacier, the groundwater specific discharge totals 0.69 m. As the upper catchment is >300 m higher in elevation than Red Mountain Pass SNOTEL, greater annual SWE in the groundwater recharge zone is not unreasonable. These precipitation-driven flow components to the rock glacier outlet reasonably account for all the discharge, and do not require an additional water source from melt of the rock glacier ice. We conclude that no measurable rock glacier ice melt is occurring. Instead, we attribute flow from the rock glacier to snowmelt flowing in a supraglacial path above the ice permeability barrier and to subglacial groundwater recharged in the catchment above the rock glacier.

title: The Forgotten Togiak Arc Terrane of Southwest Alaska: Integrated Petrographic, Geochemical, and Geochronologic Constraints on Arc Evolution
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada (Posters)
authors: Patton, Alex [1], Regan, Sean P. [2], Waldien, Trevor Scott [3], Hofmann, Florian [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK, USA
(2) University of Alaska, Fairbanks, AK, USA
(3) South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD,
(4) University of Alaska, Fairbanks, AK,
abstract:
The Togiak arc terrane of southwestern Alaska is one of the least characterized volcanic arc terranes in the northern Cordillera. Despite the rapid advances in terrane analysis techniques, the timing, petrogenesis, and tectonic setting of the Togiak arc remain poorly constrained, resulting in an incomplete dataset for terrane reconstructions. During fieldwork in 2025, we mapped and sampled shore exposures within Wood-Tikchik State Park for petrographic thin section analysis, whole-rock geochemistry, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, and U-Th-Pb LA-ICP-MS zircon geochronology.

The rocks exposed in Wood-Tikchik State Park are composed of two main packages: 1) Paleozoic chert-sandstone mélange, basalts, and limestones of the Tikchik complex and 2) Triassic to Early Cretaceous Togiak arc, composed of volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks. Petrography documents regional low-grade incipient metamorphism in both units. The top of the Tikchik complex is composed of pillow basalts and local scoria, consistent with both subaqueous and subaerial eruptions. Detrital zircon analysis of local conglomeratic units within the basalts yields a maximum depositional age of 226 ± 10.4 Ma, consistent with Upper Triassic fossils identified within laterally discontinuous limestone units. U-Pb zircon geochronology from the overlying Togiak arc indicates principal volcanism extending throughout the Jurassic and into the early Cambrian. Both components exhibit minor detrital and inherited zircon with a continental affinity, indicating proximity to continental basement. The bulk-rock major and trace element geochemistry exhibit depletions in high field-strength elements and large-ion-lithophile enrichments consistent with an arc origin for both units. Togiak terrane is therefore interpreted to preserve punctuated phases of arc volcanism built on mixed continental-oceanic substrate evolving from a marine setting with atolls to a more extensive subaerial eruption environment during the Jurassic. The Togiak arc rocks were structurally imbricated over upper Paleozoic substrate.

Most 40 Ar/ 39 Ar step-headed spectra showed evidence of significant excess argon. All samples yielded plateau and isochron ages of 42-74 Ma, interpreted to reflect widespread resetting during regional magmatism at that time, perhaps corresponding to the regionally extensive incipient metamorphism that overprints both the Togiak arc and the underlying Tikchik complex. Given the punctuated volcanic history, continental-oceanic detrital record, and extensive argon resetting, the Togiak arc is an example of a structurally imbricated volcanic arc terrane whose magmatic and metamorphic record has widely been overprinted by regional tectonism.

title: Rethinking Geological Knowing Through Distributed Fieldwork
session_title: Iris Moreno Totten Research in Geoscience Education Session
authors: Cox, Michael [1], Marshall, Anita [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
abstract:
Geoscience fieldwork is the discipline’s signature pedagogy, yet research on virtual and in-person field education has largely focused on learning outcomes and modality comparisons. Less understood is how these modalities can be integrated to support collaborative knowledge production. This gap matters when participation spans on-site and remote positions, where students contribute different forms of access, evidence, and expertise. The question of whether remote students learn as much as those in the field overlooks a more fundamental question: what knowledge can distributed teams produce that neither cohort could accomplish alone?

Drawing on distributed cognition, we propose that geological knowledge is not produced solely by individual learners, but emerges across people, technologies, artifacts, and environments. Traditional field requirements have historically excluded students with disabilities from full participation in geoscience, making accessible field programs a distinctive window into what distributed participation can produce. We ground this argument in an ongoing qualitative case study of students participating in GeoSPACE, a hybrid planetary geology field course built accessible by design and deployed across northern Arizona’s San Francisco Volcanic Field. Nine students from the 2026 cohort with disabilities participated. The deployment engineered a low-latency multimodal network for real-time distributed field collaboration, enabling synchronous audio, video, and chat across modalities. During a collaborative investigation on an unmapped crater, remote students analyzed geophysical and remote sensing data while on-site students investigated directly, sharing observations and measurements that refined remote interpretations.

This case provides three empirical illustrations of a distributed system in practice. First, geological interpretation emerged through the distributed system. Integrating remote data with field observations enabled the team to interpret the geologic history of the crater. Second, participants described shifting from observers to genuine contributors, developing epistemic agency and embodied connection through real-time direction of field activity. Third, the digital workspace functioned as cognitive infrastructure and enabled heterogeneous evidence to be shared, compared, and integrated across the team. Participants described the investigation as something they could not have achieved alone, and several noted it was the first time they had seen themselves as geoscientists. These patterns suggest that accessibility can be understood not simply as expanding participation, but as reconfiguring the cognitive architecture of fieldwork. Designing field education around distributed agency may therefore reshape what field teams can know and accomplish together.

title: Interaction between Megathrust Locking and Upper Plate Architecture Controls Forearc Sliver Development
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Morell, Kristin [1], Newman, Andrew [2]
affiliations: (2) Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
abstract: Understanding the processes that govern deformation within the overriding plate is fundamental to models of subduction zone evolution and seismic hazard. At convergent margins, oblique plate convergence generates a trench-parallel component of relative plate motion, which is often partially accommodated within the overriding plate. Previous studies have proposed that forearc sliver faulting develops under conditions of high convergence obliquity, defined as the angle between trench normal and relative plate convergence. However, subduction zone segments with only moderate obliquity can also exhibit fully developed forearc slivers, suggesting that convergence obliquity alone cannot explain how deformation localizes within the overriding plate. Here we compile a catalog of active terrestrial strike-slip trench-parallel faults in the arc and forearc from eight active subduction zones, together with published geodetic estimates of the downdip limit of megathrust locking. Where geodetic locking models are unavailable, we use independently constrained seismogenic zone depth as a proxy for the downdip extent of locking. We find that coherent forearc slivers develop only where the distance between the active volcanic arc and the downdip limit of locking is less than ~150 km, regardless of convergence obliquity. At these margins, trench-parallel deformation localizes onto a single strike-slip fault within the volcanic arc that accommodates a substantial fraction of relative plate motion. Where the arc lies farther from the downdip limit of locking, deformation is instead distributed across one or more shorter, discontinuous forearc strike-slip faults, each accommodating a small portion of relative plate motion. To investigate the mechanism underlying this relationship, we use a simple elastic dislocation model to predict the distribution of trench-parallel elastic shear strain generated by megathrust locking. The model predicts that shear strain is concentrated above the downdip edge of a locked megathrust. Based on these results, we propose that when this predicted zone of maximum strike-slip shear coincides with the mechanically weak volcanic arc, deformation localizes to form a coherent forearc sliver. When the volcanic arc lies farther landward, trench-parallel shear is instead accommodated by distributed slip on inherited forearc faults rather than by a single structure. These results suggest that megathrust locking geometry governs the location of maximum elastic trench-parallel shear, but the rheological structure of the overriding plate governs how that strain is accommodated by brittle upper plate faulting.

title: Resolving Rapid Climate Change: Exceptional Preservation at the Onset of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Wright, James D [1], Miller, Kenneth G [2], Schaller, Morgan F [3], Katz, Miriam E [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers Univesity, Piscataway, NJ, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers Univesity, Piscataway, NJ, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(4) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ, USA; Geosciences Dept., Union College, Schenectady, NY, USA
abstract: The meaning of rapid climate change depends on the age of the event because it is constrained by the temporal resolution of the geologic archive. Late Glacial and Holocene climate changes can be resolved at annual to decadal scales using ice cores and varved sediments. In contrast, older events rely primarily on open-ocean sediment records with accumulation rates commonly averaging only 1–2 cm kyr⁻¹, limiting the ability to distinguish geologically instantaneous events from those unfolding over millennia. Here, we test the hypothesis that the onset of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) was effectively instantaneous on geologic timescales. The PETM is marked by a large negative carbon isotope excursion and profound environmental and biotic change, yet the duration of its initial carbon release remains debated. The Marlboro Clay of the New Jersey Coastal Plain preserves an unusually detailed record of this transition. Its 1–2 cm rhythmic layers have been interpreted as rotary-drilling artifacts or secondary deformation. We demonstrate instead that they are likely primary depositional structures produced during rapid emplacement of fluidized mud deposits. A push core from Medford, New Jersey, preserves identical layering independent of rotary drilling, while grain-size analyses show that layer contacts coincide with subtle grain-size maxima. Rotary drilling merely "biscuited" the cores by preferentially fracturing along these coarser horizons. The exceptional preservation of the layering, together with abundant, well-preserved planktonic foraminifera and the near absence of bioturbation, indicates rapid deposition and burial. We propose that an effectively instantaneous PETM onset rapidly intensified the hydrologic cycle, destabilized terrestrial landscapes, and generated exceptional sediment fluxes that preserved fluidized mud deposits before they could be bioturbated or reworked. Independent evidence from the Atlantic Coastal Plain, including abundant charcoal and widespread wildfires, is consistent with rapid landscape disturbance. Together, rhythmic layering, exceptional fossil preservation, extraordinary sediment accumulation rates, and evidence for widespread wildfires fail to reject the hypothesis of an effectively instantaneous PETM onset and are difficult to reconcile with a gradual onset over several millennia. The Marlboro Clay may therefore provide one of the highest-resolution marine archives of the onset of this major global warming event.

title: Graphite for Battery Applications
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Harrison, Katharine [1], Fink, Kae [2], Rowland, Steven [3], BURRELL, ANTHONY [4]
