abstract: Graphite is the predominant anode material used in lithium-ion battery anodes. Global graphite demand is growing rapidly, driven largely by demand for battery applications. Batteries typically utilize graphite blends comprised of high-quality synthetic graphite and large flake, high-crystallinity natural graphite. Graphite feedstocks are heavily processed to tune the performance for battery applications, which typically involves additional processing beyond conventional synthesis for synthetic graphite or beneficiation and separations for natural graphite. These additional steps include graphite particle shaping (spheronization), classification (particle size selection), purification, and coating before the particles can be fabricated into electrodes and batteries. In this talk, we will discuss the importance of graphite in battery applications, processing and material requirements for graphite battery applications, and National Laboratory of the Rockies capabilities and projects related to graphite for batteries. The National Laboratory of the Rockies has experience in several areas of graphite battery research including: (1) modeling graphite battery supply chains and recycling; (2) developing synthetic graphite processes, primarily focused on bio-derived feedstocks processed via catalytic graphitization and evaluating for battery applications; (3) recovering mixtures of natural and synthetic graphite from spent batteries and recycling it into new battery graphite through separation, purification, shaping, re-graphitization, coating, and battery testing processes; (4) processing natural graphite through shaping to optimize the morphology for battery applications; (5) holistic and multi-modal characterization of the physical, chemical, electronic, and electrochemical properties of graphite from the atomic to electrode scale; and (6) accelerating graphite validation to decrease adoption time through graphite material and electrochemical characterization coupled with machine learning approaches that enable predicting battery performance trajectories from early data.

title: Dual-Target Calibration Using Flow Direction and Hydraulic Head Observations to Constrain Groundwater Flow Models of Increasing Complexity
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling (Posters)
authors: Davis, Sydney [1], Lowry, Chris [2]
affiliations: (1) University at Buffalo, Amherst, New York, USA
(2) University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY,
abstract: Groundwater flow modeling is a practical tool used in the fields of water resource management, environmental consulting, and energy resources to simulate and predict how fluid moves through the subsurface. An issue many modelers face during model development is simulating accurate, unique solutions to the inverse problem while having limited observation data to construct and calibrate models. To address these data limitations, a new class of calibration data incorporating groundwater flow direction as an additional target during the calibration process is proposed. For this research, four models (two synthetic and two real-world systems) of varying complexity are calibrated using the following target calibration scenarios: 1) head, 2) flow direction, and 3) head and flow direction. Along with calibration scenarios, the selected models vary the method of parameterization using piecewise constancy and pilot points. Performance of each calibration scenario and parameterization method is assessed and compared using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE), and residual ranking. Despite the common application of multi-target calibration, the use of flow direction as target data in recent research has had limited attention. The results of this research directly address underdetermined, ill-posed models and quantify the effectiveness of groundwater flow direction as a data type used in model calibration. By expanding and diversifying the available observation dataset for model calibration, the research aims to generate unique solutions to the inverse problem and improve model accuracy.

title: Central Texas Graphite District: Characterization and Ore Body Modeling using Legacy Data for a Domestic Flake Graphite Resource
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Short, Shelby R. [1], Elliott, Brent A. [2], Kyle, J. Richard [3]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(2) Bureau of Economic Geology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(3) Dept Earth & Planetary Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
Flake graphite is an essential anode material for lithium-ion batteries, and the United States remains heavily import dependent, with domestic production only recently re-established at demonstration scale. The Central Texas Graphite District, situated within the Llano Uplift, represents a significant but underexplored terrane with potential for critical mineral development. The uplift exposes the largest area of Mesoproterozoic basement in the southern U.S. and is composed of deformed and metamorphosed sedimentary and igneous rocks formed during the Grenville orogeny (1.2–1.1 Ga). Graphite is primarily associated with the Honey Formation of the Packsaddle Schist, a metapelitic to semi-pelitic unit that experienced upper amphibolite-facies metamorphism during Grenville deformation (1.1 Ga). At least eleven documented graphite localities occur within the district.

The largest and most thoroughly documented of these localities is the Southwestern Graphite Mine, discovered in 1913 and worked intermittently from 1918 to 1979. Chelf (1943) placed the deposit within a broader NW–SE-striking, steeply dipping schist band. Exploration drilling, completed in 1926 and compiled onto prospect maps by Southwestern Consolidated Graphite Co., outlined three ore zones (West Quarry, Middle/East Quarry, and a North Ore Body) from holes 50–100 ft deep with composite assays over 5-ft intervals (Fealy, 1933). Needham (1946) reported pre-1930 exploration indicating 2–2.5 Mt of ore, and Fogg and Boyle (1987) documented 1.6 Mt mined between 1949 and 1979 at 5.2% flake graphite, yielding roughly 75,000 metric tons of high-grade product. Despite this legacy record, controls on grade distribution remain poorly constrained and the district carries similar unknowns regarding continuity, geometry, and grade at depth and along strike.

Historic drill data are used to build a geologic model of the mined deposit and is validated against reported historic production. The model is then examined for possible relationships between higher-grade graphite and nearby structural features such as dikes and folds. Airborne and ground-based electromagnetic data are considered for similar settings elsewhere in the district, offering a possible way to screen for additional areas of interest and to illustrate how geophysical surveys could help characterize undrilled graphite localities moving forward.

authors: Menozzo da Rosa, Eduardo [1], Flaig, Peter P. [2], Hattori, Kelly E. [3], Ko, Lucy T. [4]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Economic Geology (STARR), Jackson School of Geosciences, Austin, TX, USA

abstract: Mixed siliciclastic–carbonate systems display pronounced vertical and lateral heterogeneity from bed to basin scale. The Middle–Upper Pennsylvanian (Desmoinesian–lower Missourian) Strawn Group is an important conventional hydrocarbon reservoir on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin, Texas. However, predicting facies distribution remains challenging because of its heterogeneous stratigraphic architecture and the absence of a high-resolution subsurface sequence stratigraphic framework. This complexity reflects both the mixed nature of the depositional system and cyclic sedimentation controlled by autogenic processes, including basin morphology, carbonate buildup development, and deltaic sediment supply, together with allogenic controls such as tectonic subsidence, high-frequency glacioeustatic fluctuations, and variations in sediment influx. This study establishes a stratigraphic framework for the upper Strawn Group in the KMA Field (Wichita County, Texas), where deposition was influenced by repeated interaction between the Haskell Delta–Knox–Baylor trough system and the Red River carbonate platform. The dataset integrates facies analysis of 880 ft (270 m) of core from seven wells with wireline-log correlation, ichnology, and whole-rock XRF geochemistry to characterize facies architecture, high-resolution sequence stratigraphy, and evaluate controls on mixed siliciclastic–carbonate deposition during the Late Paleozoic Ice Age glacioeustatic regime. Core description identified siliciclastic, carbonate, and mixed lithofacies together with 20 ichnotaxa. The succession contains eight to nine fourth- to fifth-order depositional sequences, approximately 11–70 ft (3–21 m) thick. Sequence boundaries are recognized by subaerial exposure features, including microkarst, paleosols, pedogenic alteration, and intertidal exposure surfaces, as well as firmgrounds assigned to the Glossifungites ichnofacies, intraclast lags, and colonization surfaces. Transgressive surfaces are commonly expressed by carbonate-cemented sandstone firmgrounds. Many sequence boundaries cut across lithostratigraphic contacts, emphasizing substantial lateral facies variability. Mixed reservoir facies, including ooid grainstones, skeletal–ooid grainstones, sandstones, and crinoid-rich sandstones, exhibit strong vertical and lateral heterogeneity governed by grain composition, sorting, cementation, and bioturbation. These deposits accumulated within a tide-influenced system of migrating mouth bars, tidal conduits, and ooid shoals that promoted repeated reworking and interfingering of siliciclastic and carbonate sediments. Continued integration of petrographic and biostratigraphic (fusulinid and conodont) data will refine depositional ages, improve recognition of key stratigraphic surfaces, and demonstrate key elements for correlating high-frequency depositional sequences between siliciclastic-dominated and carbonate-dominated domains in mixed systems

title: Lower Ordovician Reef Mounds as Oxygen Oases in the Aftermath of the Stairsian Extinction Event
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Posters)
authors: Pruss, Sara B. [1], Gill, Benjamin Charles [2], Tarhan, Lidya [3], Barnes, Gwen [4], Young, Seth [5], Owens, Jeremy D. [6], Ferraro, Jillian A. [7]
affiliations: (1) Smith College, Northampton, MA,
(2) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA

(5) Florida State Univ, Department of Earth, Ocean & Atmospheric Science, Tallahassee, FL, USA

abstract:
During the later Cambrian and Early Ordovician, marine environments experienced fluctuations in temperature, sea level, oxygen concentrations, and other factors that affected ecosystems. In this interval of time, a series of biomere extinction events also occurred, potentially caused by changing marine oxygen levels, which affected diversity and abundance of marine animals. The record of one such event, the Tremadocian Stairsian extinction, consists of a carbon isotopic excursion coupled with trilobite turnover. In its aftermath, in a few horizons in unit Opa of Arrow Canyon Range of southern Nevada and the lower Fillmore Formation in the Ibex area of Utah, sponge-microbial patch reefs occur. Here, we utilize geochemical and fossil point count data from these reefs to analyze the environmental conditions in the aftermath of this event.

Carbon isotopes and iodine-to-calcium ratios (I/Ca) a local carbonate-based redox proxy, were measured from facies within and outside of the patch reefs, and these samples were also analyzed for animal abundance. In general, animal abundance in the reefs was low overall, around 6% of all points counted, with sponges being most abundant within reef mounds and the problematic alga Nuia being the most abundant fossil outside of the mounds. I/Ca values in the mound and surrounding facies were elevated (up to 2.78) compared to previous studies on similar sections (up to 0.45), so while these reefs formed in areas of lower-oxygen levels, they may have served as oxygen oases, possibly due to local microbial processes. However, the carbon isotope data from the reef mounds and adjacent facies are similar suggesting these microbial processes had limited isotopic influence on the local carbon cycle. Nevertheless as microbial communities expanded, they constructed and maintained reef mound structures and potentially chemically altered their surroundings by impacting the oxygen concentration of the waters, making them more habitable for other organisms and fostering local patch reef ecosystems.

title: Beyond "more data:" Natural history specimens for methods validation and student training

authors: Thompson, Carmi Milagros [1], Leeson, Morgan Sabrina [2], Klompmaker, Adiël A. [3], Finnegan, Seth [4], O'Dea, Aaron [5], Leonard-Pingel, Jill [6]

abstract:
Biodiversity data have utility ranging from fundamental taxonomic studies to applications of public health research; thus, it is important that these data are discoverable and have useful metadata to avoid duplication of effort. Here, we present a case study integrating collection of biodiversity data from natural history specimens with training of students in data management and specimen curation.

Collections from the Panama Paleontology Project (PPP) offer possibility for provision of vast sets of body size data rapidly, using high throughput imaging methods. These large specimen collections also allow students to have practice in collecting biodiversity data. Here, we utilized a sample of 1000 Chione bivalve specimens from the Ground Creek faunule (~2 Ma) , measured both by calipers, and digitally to validate the accuracy of the digital method. This genus was selected because it is morphologically simple and had an abundant sample size, thus allowing for a meaningful comparison of methods. After measurements were collected using calipers by a student trainee, we then used a digital camera and a rail stacking tool to collect digital measurements. When possible, specimens were imaged with those of similar sizes to minimize misalignment between specimen photos. Specimens were given a unique number, which allowed for comparison between hand measurements and digital measurements. Following the acquisition of photographs by student trainees, image stacks were processed using the AutoMorph software developed by Hsiang and collaborators (2018). 2D measurements were close between digital and manual, while 3D measurements were more variable.

There is always a need for physical specimens and collections – these serve as the basis for fundamental biodiversity research and for continuing collections. This project highlights a supplemental modality for investigating biodiversity collections. It also serves as a case study for integrating biodiversity training with natural history collection specimens – teaches interns valuable lessons about data management, specimen handling practices, and data preparation.

abstract:
The larval mode of individual gastropods can be inferred from shape, size, and morphological characteristics of the protoconch, or larval shell. The size is tied to larval mode, which is often related to primary productivity. In the Neogene southwestern Caribbean, environmental change initiated by the formation of the Isthmus of Panama impacted oceanographic conditions (warmer temperatures, higher salinity, and a decrease in productivity). Previous work on gastropod ecology shows that there are documented broad-scale decreases in predatory gastropods during this time. However, we still do not have a complete picture of how decreases in primary productivity may have impacted gastropod communities. Beyond changes in trophic structure, gastropod communities may have experienced other ecological or evolutionary changes driven by changes in primary productivity. This protoconch study continues to provide additional insight into individuals that live in the communities of this changing ecosystem.

Here, we look at the protoconchs of Nassarius (family: Nassariidae). This genus was selected because it is abundant across samples collected from fossil localities in the Isthmus and because of its trophic position. We anticipate that larval mode of this genus will switch developmental strategy from lecithotrophic to direct as the Isthmus closes. For our preliminary survey, we have collected some measurements of protoconchs of Nassarius using an AXIO Zoom.V16 microscope and Zen core 3.16 software. Magnification varied from 100x to 250x, depending on the size of protoconch of the organism (and overall size of the shell). Specimens were imaged on a dark background for contrast. Following collection of images, FIJI was used to extract measurements of diameter and number of whorls, which can be used to infer larval mode. These measurements will be used to explore our hypothesis.

title: Spiral valve morphology in ancient chondrythians as revealed by cololite morphologies
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Lobb, Mathias G [1], Selly, Tara [2], Jacquet, Sarah [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA; X-ray Microanalysis Laboratory, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA
(3) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract:
Spiral and scroll cololites represent fossilized intestinal tracts characterized by ribbon-like coils, and are frequently attributed to chondrythian taxa. Within the Niobrara Formation (Late Coniacian to Early Santonian) of Kansas, among the abundant vertebrae and macroinvertebrate remains, is a plethora of bromialite trace fossils, including a distinct group of spiral cololite forms. In this study, seven spiral specimens were investigated representing three morphotypes, including heteropolar (n=5), amphipolar (n=1), and scroll forms (n=1). We hypothesize that the interior spiral morphology of these cololites preserve the intestinal valve morphology of the producer.

Coprolites were imaged using µCT at the X-ray Microanalysis Lab at the University of Missouri-Columbia, and reconstructed using Dragonfly Comet 3D analysis software, where they were segmented using an AI-trained algorithm. Examination of coprolite exterior and interior surfaces revealed minimal skeletal inclusions, with CT-data showing a predominantly amorphous, chalky matrix. Internally, the arrangement of the coils differs markedly between forms, with each displaying variably funneled and scroll valve morphologies. Directionality of the anterior and posterior complicates the distinction between funnel valve morphotypes, which dominate the sample. Moreover, no columnar morphologies were observed. Despite the limited sample size, variation in gross morphology and valve structure suggest that these coprolites were attributed to multiple producers. Ongoing analysis with 3D modeling of internal valve arrangements and rudimentary flow analysis may reveal further information about the organisms that produced them.

title: From Digital Outcrops to Virtual Field Environments: Tools for Structural Analysis and Instruction
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data
authors: Needle, Mattathias D. [1], Crider, Juliet G. [2]
affiliations: (1) Bellevue College, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
Digital outcrop models can be used for more than visualization when users can query the model and extract structural data. We present virtual field experiences developed with the Structural Geology Query Toolkit, a Unity-based set of pre-coded modules for first-person-perspective interaction with 3D geologic models. The work began with the Whaleback Anticline virtual field experience, which placed a photogrammetric model of an exceptionally well exposed fold into a browser-accessible, video-game-style field environment for open-ended structural exploration. Users move through the terrain and select where to make observations of the geologic structure.

Beyond this open-ended navigation, the Toolkit allows users to measure surfaces and distances, fly over outcrops, view topographic profiles, plot orientations, and export data for further analysis. For planar measurements, users can click three points on a surface to generate a plane and calculate strike and dip; for rapid surface-orientation measurements, the pole tool samples and averages local mesh normals and plots the resulting poles to planes on a stereonet. In one application, we used a high-resolution Whaleback model to measure fault-normal extension along transects parallel and perpendicular to the fold axis and calculate mesoscale extensional strain. These data demonstrate that digital field simulation tools can support structural analysis as well as education.

We have extended these workflows to real field-area models, simplified conceptual field areas, and other 3D geologic objects. Drone-derived models originally collected for field-course mapping products have been adapted into smaller virtual field trips and missions. Because these environments are open-ended, instructors can adapt the same field experience for introductory geology, structural geology, and field methods exercises involving mapping, planes, poles, and stereonets. We have also incorporated 3D scans of fossils into historical geology activities, embedding specimen-scale models within larger field and map-area contexts. These examples frame virtual field experiences as queryable environments for digital outcrops, field-area models, and conceptual geologic terrains.

abstract: Climate change is increasing the size and severity of wildfires in the western United States, requiring the development of new fire management practices; concurrently, endangered Chinook salmon and steelhead are losing critical habitat, necessitating co-management strategies that protect both fire resilience and aquatic species in western watersheds. Zena Creek Ranch sits atop a 97,000 m² alluvial fan east of McCall, Idaho. As part of the Zena Creek Fish Passage Project, crews will remove a 1950s-era earthen dam at the site in fall 2026, reopening over 4 miles of high-quality salmonid spawning and rearing habitat. Through dam removal and subsequent installation of beaver dam analogs (BDAs), this private-public partnership aims to enhance fire resilience while restoring critical habitat in Zena Creek. Our objective in year 1 was to describe baseline stream conditions by characterizing channel morphology, hydrology, riparian vegetation, and macroinvertebrate community structure prior to dam removal and BDA installation. During summer 2026, we (in conjunction with the Zena Creek Field School) established four cross-stream transects along a 1-km downstream reach of Zena Creek. Data were also collected at two additional transects to assess changes at the pond and a large abandoned side channel. At each transect, we constructed cross-sections and measured slope using an auto level and level rod, calculated discharge, characterized substrate composition with the Wolman pebble count method, and quantified canopy cover using 50m line-point intercept transects. We collected aquatic macroinvertebrates with drift nets and Surber nets across varied microhabitats. Three pressure transducers were installed to monitor water level continuously over the next year. Baseline measurements revealed stream discharge of 6.41 to 8.43 cfs, with stream slope of 0 at the pond to 5.8%. Stream temperatures ranged from 14.1 to 15.2°C, canopy cover varied from 0 at the pond to 98% just below the spillway. Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera (EPT) comprised 48–77% of the macroinvertebrate community. Cross-sectional areas and substrate D50 are still being calculated at this time. In summer 2027, we will repeat measurements and install BDAs in an attempt to inundate abandoned side-channels and increase riparian habitat. It is our hope that this 'win-win wetlands' approach offers a scalable solution in future co-management restoration efforts across the western United States.

title: Remotely Sensed Postfire Hydrological Changes in mid-Klamath Tributary Watershed
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society (Posters)
authors: McKoy, O'Dane St. Orbyn [1], Mahmood, Taufique [2]
affiliations: (1) University of North Dakota, Harold Hamm School of Geology and Geological Engineering, Grand Forks, ND, USA; University of North Dakota, Center for Water Research, Grand Forks, ND, USA

abstract: Wildland fires are becoming increasingly problematic, particularly with global climatic shifts and land use changes. While their impacts on habitats, infrastructure, and agriculture are well documented, their effects on ecohydrological systems are often underreported. Wildland fires remove extensive vegetative canopy cover and can create hydrophobic soils, intensifying runoff, streamflow, and flooding. Here, we present an assessment of the post-fire hydrological responses to two wildfires, the Natchez Fire (2018) and the Slater Fire (2020), within the Indian Creek Watershed (ICW), a subbasin within the broader Klamath River Basin (KRB) of northern California. We aimed to investigate whether runoff ratios increased in the post-fire environment and, if so, whether the increase was greater following the higher-severity Slater Fire (2020). The differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) was utilized to determine the burn severity of both fires. Runoff ratios were calculated using streamflow and precipitation data from two independent meteorological stations, Crazy Peak Station and Slater Butte Station. Additional streamflow data were obtained from a USGS stream gage within the basin. Results suggest that runoff ratios were higher after the Slater Fire than after the Natchez Fire. In addition to dNBR, elevated runoff ratios are also attributed to increased throughfall due to lower leaf area index. This multivariable remote sensing analysis provides insights into post-fire hydrological responses and demonstrates the potential of remotely sensed data as an effective tool for water resource management within wildfire-affected watersheds of the KRB.

title: Pressure-Temperature Conditions of a Fossil Brittle-Ductile Transition in the Great Common Fault Zone, Norumbega Fault System, Maine, USA

authors: Johnson, Sophia [1], Levy, Drew A. [2], Condit, Cailey Brown [3], McPherron, Emberlee [4], Peterman, Emily [5], West, David [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA

abstract:
Evaluating the pressure-dependent brittle behavior and temperature-dependent ductile rheology are key to understanding earthquake processes and crustal rheology and thus require constraints on the pressure and temperature (P-T) conditions. The Great Common fault zone, associated with the regionally extensive Norumbega Fault System, is a world-class exposure of an exhumed deep seismogenic zone localized in the Rye Complex, a distributed ductile shear zone developed in polymetamorphosed rocks. Field observations of mylonitized pseudotachylyte suggest the current exposure represents a brittle-ductile transition (BDT), but the exact conditions of this transition remain poorly constrained. We use petrography, electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) on quartz, and phase equilibria modeling to quantitatively constrain the P-T conditions of metamorphism, distributed ductile deformation and localized brittle-ductile cycling.

We petrographically distinguish textures and mineral assemblages corresponding to prograde (M0), peak (M1), ductile fabric development (M2), and retrograde (M3) metamorphic events in eight samples across the fault zone. Using pseudosections constructed in Perple_X, we match observed equilibrium mineral assemblages with phase stability fields and measured mineral compositions with isopleths to obtain P-T estimates for each episode.

We interpret the garnet cores, large biotite and muscovite grains, resorbed staurolite, and andalusite clots to represent M0 heating from 450–550 ºC at 2.5–3 kbar. Sillimanite wrapping around andalusite and in the foliation places peak (M1) conditions in the sillimanite zone. The foliation is defined by elongate biotite, muscovite, and sillimanite, which are offset by C’ shear bands, and in chemical equilibrium with euhedral garnets. Foliation parallel quartz veins exhibit subgrain rotation dynamic recrystallization and grain boundary migration. Quartz c-axis pole figures show centered CPOs recording prism <a> slip, which corresponds to amphibolite facies temperatures. Preliminary constraints on M2 conditions are 575-625 ºC and 3.25-5.25 kbar. The path from M2 through brittle-ductile cycling to M3 is challenging to constrain. M1 and M2 are variably overprinted by incomplete retrograde (M3) chlorite. Preliminary chlorite thermobarometry records temperatures between 370-400 ºC.

Taken together, preliminary findings suggest peak metamorphism reached sillimanite zone conditions, distributed ductile deformation occurred at near peak conditions and mid-crustal depth, and brittle-ductile cycling occurred following M2 into M3. These P-T constraints indicate cyclic brittle-ductile deformation was occurring at temperatures hotter than but depths comparable to the conditions of modern seismicity along active strike-slip faults.

title: Challenges at the science-policy interface for groundwater governance in freshwater lenses, salt wedges, and offshore aquifers

authors: Kurylyk, Barret [1], Yu, Shengchao [2], Cantelon, Julia [3], Michael, Holly [4], Maselli, Vittorio [5], Nedimović, Mladen [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Resource Engineering and Centre for Water Resources Studies, Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada

abstract:
Long-term groundwater depletion is an increasingly global challenge, with concern amplified by the extreme droughts affecting many regions in 2025 and 2026. Sustainable groundwater pumping remains the holy grail of groundwater management, yet determining appropriate pumping rates is particularly challenging in complex hydrogeologic settings. Governance paradigms from one region may not translate well to another due to localized differences in the ‘forcing, fabric or function’ of groundwater systems. For example, coastal and offshore aquifers present unique governance challenges because of hydrogeological complexity imposed by saltwater–freshwater transition zones, variable-density groundwater flow, and oceanic forcing. This presentation will highlight how groundwater policy should be informed by hydrogeological understanding using three distinctive aquifer settings along the onshore–offshore continuum as illustrative examples: (1) freshwater lenses, (2) salt wedges, and (3) offshore aquifers.

Freshwater lenses beneath sandy barrier islands have limited storage capacity and are highly vulnerable to sea-level rise and coastal storms. Groundwater withdrawals from freshwater lenses are largely sourced through ‘submarine groundwater discharge depletion’. In these flashy hydraulic systems, geophysically mapped salinity distributions can often better inform long-term aquifer change assessments or model-based groundwater management than continuous head measurements. Salt wedges along marine coastlines are increasingly exploited to supply saline groundwater for land-based aquaculture. High-capacity pumping permits in these jurisdictions are commonly based on meteoric recharge and groundwater storage concepts that do not directly apply to salt wedges. Although strong hydraulic connections to the ocean can provide an effectively unlimited water source, excessive wedge pumping may induce undesirable impacts, including subsidence, active saltwater intrusion, and migration of coastal contaminant plumes. As droughts intensify and water demands increase, interest in offshore freshened groundwater as a supplementary water resource is growing in densely populated coastal regions and offshore industries. Offshore aquifers can be broadly classified as active or relict freshened groundwater systems. Pumping from relict systems constitutes groundwater mining, while pumping from hydraulically connected, active offshore aquifers can produce cascading hydraulic and salinity impacts across the subsurface land–sea continuum. Illustrative examples of these three aquifer types will be presented based on field investigations and numerical modeling in the Canadian Maritimes to demonstrate that sustainable groundwater governance in coastal environments must be guided by a rigorous understanding of coastal and submarine hydrogeological processes and vulnerabilities.

title: Influence of Large Wood on Flow Permanence in Non-Perennial Headwater Streams
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Johnston , Wes Jasper [1], Scamardo, Julianne [2]
affiliations: (1) Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(2) Utah State University, Logan, Ut, USA
abstract:
Non-perennial streams, which lack year-round streamflow, make up approximately 75% of stream networks by length in the intermountain western United States. As climate change alters hydrologic dynamics by decreasing snowpack and increasing temperatures, non-perennial streams are expected to experience fewer wet days. Although precipitation, lithology, and topography are recognized controls on flow permanence, the influence of in-stream large wood (LW) remains poorly understood.

In perennial systems, LW is known to scour pools, pond water, reduce flow velocity, and enhance surface–groundwater exchange, but its role in controlling bed topography and drying dynamics in non-perennial systems remains poorly quantified. We investigated how large wood influences streamflow permanence in non-perennial headwater streams across contrasting mountain environments, the Bear River Mountains (UT) and Smoky Mountains (ID). Between 2025 and 2026, we surveyed 824 pieces of LW and 238 LW jams across both study areas. Despite a lower frequency of jams, 78.8% of the total measured wood volume were contained in jams, highlighting the importance of fluvial transport and jam formation for LW storage, even in non-perennial streams. Jams and individual pieces acted as a hydraulic control, with 64.1% oriented perpendicular to flow and 58.2% spanning the active channel. Large wood generated geomorphic complexity with 55.1% of pieces and 63.7% of jams forming plunge pools, while 25% of individual pieces and 38.3% of jams created upstream ponding. Observations from 2025 suggest that reaches with a greater LW density remain wet longer, potentially due to increased pool frequency and water storage associated with wood-induced scour and upstream ponding.

Longitudinal streamflow surveys were paired with continuous wet/dry signals measured by HOBO TidBit sensors in randomly selected LW ponds and pools. Multiple sensors remained wet when the channel dried, with observations suggesting that downstream plunge pools were more likely to stay inundated than upstream pools. These observations suggest features created by large wood may enhance localized water storage and additionally prolong surface water persistence during seasonal drying. These findings provide preliminary support for quantifying the role of LW in regulating streamflow resilience within drying stream networks.

title: The Influence of the Concentration of Trace Element dopants on Clinopyroxene/Melt Partitioning

authors: Christiansen, Ian J. [1], Ustunisik, Gokce K. [2], Nielsen, Roger L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, Rapid City, South Dakota, USA

abstract:
Understanding the dynamic processes by which igneous systems evolve (e.g., fractionation, partial melting, mixing, and degassing) requires that we are able to predict what phases are present and how specific major and trace elements are distributed between them. The most commonly applied metric for calculation of the how trace elements behave is the partition coefficient (D). Past experimental studies have worked to develop models of partitioning behavior that accommodate changes in temperature (T), pressure (P), melt composition (X), and oxygen fugacity (fO 2 ). Rare earth elements (REEs) were of particular interest in many of these studies due to their systematic behavior and the differences in their partitioning among different phases - ranging from highly incompatible (plagioclase) to compatible (garnet). Before the development of laser inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy (Laser ICP-MS), measurement of the concentration of REEs in phases present in experimental charges was challenging due to their low natural concentration. To address this, experiments were doped with wt.% levels of specific REE to reach detectible concentrations by electron microprobe (EMP). High dopant levels are known to suppress the liquidus and may result in violation of Henrian behavior 1,2 .

Understanding the systematics Clinopyroxene-Melt D i is important due to the relative compatibility of REEs and its role in controlling the trace element budget. However, the extent to which doping affects Clinopyroxene -Melt D REE is not well known. This raises a fundamental question “does doping a single REE at the % level, change the behavior of the other elements in the series.” To address this question, we re-analyzed experiments with doping between 0.1 wt.% and 3 wt.% for specific REE 1, 2 with the goal of determining the influence of doping on the clinopyroxene/melt partitioning behavior of the REEs. Analyses of the doped elements were done by EMP at the time the experiments were conducted, but values were obtained only for the doped elements. We analyzed those experiments by Laser ICP-MS and compared the results of doped and undoped trace elements. Our results indicate that Clinopyroxene-Melt D REE of adjacent REE is not influenced by dopant level. For any individual experiment, partition coefficients of doped REEs are within analytical error of values for undoped REEs.

2 Nielsen et al. (1992) Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology, 110, 488-499

abstract: The presence of an aridity gradient across equatorial Pangea in the late Paleozoic has been suggested by fossil flora and paleosol morphology of strata throughout North America, which straddled the equator in a slightly rotated paleogeographic configuration at this time. We use paleosol carbonate d 13 C measured from coeval deposits to assess the utility of this proxy as an archive of past plant productivity, which in turn reflects local moisture limitations. We employ a data compilation of over 100 upper Pennsylvanian through lowermost Permian paleosol carbonate stable isotope values from across North America. We also present 50 new paleosol carbonate stable isotope values collected from contemporaneous formations across Colorado. d 13 C measured from the samples in both datasets was used alongside estimates of atmospheric CO 2 from this period to calculate soil respiration rates at each location. Combining this new data with our compilation, we infer spatial patterns in soil respiration rates recorded by these paleosols to compare with previously published estimates of aridity gradients across North America. Using a set of probable high (700 ppm) and low (200 ppm) values of atmospheric CO 2 for the interval of study, we show that calculated soil respiration rates continue to follow a spatial pattern consistent with other proxies of aridity in this region. This agreement between d 13 C and other proxies indicates that soil CO 2 production, rather than atmospheric CO 2 , was the predominant factor influencing the stable isotope record in this region. We utilize this data in tandem with other lines of proxy evidence to generate a narrative of terrestrial paleoclimate in terms of relative regional moisture states. In all, the data suggest drying across Pangea’s equatorial zone, with western North America experiencing at least seasonally drier conditions and lower levels of productivity than in the east. We suggest that this record of productivity is driven by regional moisture availability and can thus be utilized to evaluate gradients in terrestrial paleoclimatic conditions in the late Paleozoic. Our application of d 13 C to perform broader paleoenvironmental analyses beyond atmospheric CO 2 reconstructions allows for more effective interpretations of land—atmosphere interactions across a range of climate states.

abstract: Hemlock and Honeoye Lakes are two of the smaller Finger Lakes in Western New York and represent two distinctly managed ecosystems. Hemlock Lake, a mesoligotrophic water body, is located within the Hemlock-Canadice State Forest and is heavily monitored by the City of Rochester for over 100 years as the main drinking source for the city. Honeoye Lake, a mesoeutrophic water body, serves as both a residential and recreational lake for the region, resulting in continuous human influence and activity. Working in collaboration with the City of Rochester and the Honeoye Lake Watershed Task Force, a live-dead benthic survey was conducted to assess the status of aquatic invasive benthic invertebrates in the north and south basins of both lakes. By comparing the living communities (LC) to the death assemblages (DA), this study aims to assess the ecological memory of a protected ecosystem (Hemlock) in comparison to a more impacted ecosystem (Honeoye). Surface benthos samples were collected along a shore-to-basin 40 meter transect using an Ekman dredge. Sampling depths varied between 0.8 to 6.7 meters deep. Subsamples were dyed with Rose Bengal to distinguish live and recently dead organisms from dead remains. Sediments were sieved, separated, and macroinvertebrates were identified. Benthic macroinvertebrates include annelids, arthropods, bivalves, gastropods, and ostracodes. Zebra Mussels, Dreissena polymorpha, were found to be the dominant species present in both LC and DA, with a distinct lack of native mollusks in both lakes. Fidelity analyses and diversity indices between LC and DA in both lakes will be done to determine how aquatic invasive species impact the long-term memory of lake benthos in two different managed lakes.

title: The Evolution of Late Pleistocene Climate Dynamics in Tropical Southeast Africa

abstract: The relationship between tropical southeast African climate systems and global climate change remains poorly constrained, and this scientific uncertainty poses significant challenges for human communities and ecological systems in the region under modern anthropogenic forcing. The hydroclimatic sensitivity of tropical southeast Africa to globally warm extremes remains particularly uncertain, as the region is variably sensitive to a wide range of regional and global forcings and feedbacks. To better understand how tropical southeast African temperature and precipitation regimes will respond to abrupt global change, we turn to lacustrine sedimentary archives in the region to reconstruct long-term paleoclimate dynamics during past periods of significant global climate change. Here we present organic geochemical records of temperature and hydroclimate from two cores collected by the 2005 ICDP Lake Malawi Drilling Project (MAL05-1 and MAL05-2A), which together include the past 140,000 years of climate evolution in tropical southeast Africa. We analyze branched and isoprenoid glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraethers (GDGTs) to quantify the magnitude of temperature change during two glacial terminations and to refine GDGT-based paleothermometry methods at the site. Our records display strong coherence with global climate fluctuations, capturing peak interglacial warmth during Marine Isotope Stage 5 (130-100 ka), cooling into the Last Glacial Maximum, and early Holocene warming across two basins of the lake. We additionally analyze plant wax deuterium isotopes to reconstruct hydroclimate dynamics at Lake Malawi. Our results suggest that Malawi’s hydroclimate is both sensitive to low-latitude insolation and global climate fluctuations, with a distinct antiphase relationship between our hydroclimate record and similar records from East African sites north of the equator emerging after the Last Glacial Maximum and into the Holocene. These findings better constrain the relationship between regional temperature, hydroclimate, and their overlapping sensitivities to low-latitude forcings and global climate dynamics throughout the past 140,000 years, ultimately lending critical insight into how tropical southeast Africa responds to abrupt global climate change.

abstract: Osorno is a predominantly basaltic andesitic-andesitic volcano that began to erupt dacitic domes, lava flows, and tephra during the Holocene. We integrate new 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages of late Pleistocene-Holocene lava flows (119.0 to 1.3 ka) and existing 14 C ages (11 ka to 200 a) for tephra deposits with new petrologic observations and thermodynamic modeling to understand what, if any, impacts the slow growth between 35 and 18 ka, and rapid retreat between 18 and 16 ka, of the Patagonian ice sheet had on the underlying magma plumbing system. During the Holocene, dacitic domes or lava flows erupted at 8.9 ka on the south flank, 2.4 ka on the north flank, and on the east flank. In the south dacite dome and dacitic lava flows on the north and east flanks, andesitic quenched magmatic inclusions (QMI) surrounded by vesicles evince magma mingling and volatile transfer. The dacites each contain glomerocrystic aggregates of clinopyroxene-olivine-plagioclase-oxides with rhyolitic interstitial glass (>72% SiO 2 ). More recent intermediate to silicic explosive eruptions include a 1.1 ka andesitic pyroclastic flow and a previously undescribed airfall tephra deposit zoned from dacite at the base to basaltic andesite at the top. Glomerocryst and autocryst plagioclase in the south dacite are ~10% more anorthitic than in the north dacite. Plagioclase autocrysts and microlites in the QMI within the south dacite are similar in composition to those in the host dacite suggesting that magma mixing occurred between the dacite and a recharge magma. Thermobarometry and Rhyolite-MELTS modeling suggests a multistage process wherein basaltic andesite sourced from a reservoir at 32 to 24 km depth ascends to depths of 15 to 12 km where it stalls, cools, and further differentiates. The south dacite dome reflects eruption from the shallow reservoir at 8.9 ka when recharge was underway, whereas the north dacite tapped into a cooler more differentiated portion of the reservoir less impacted by magma mixing at 2.4 ka. We propose that the transition toward silicic eruptions over the past 9 ka is a result of increased thermal maturity of the plumbing system promoted by an intracrustal stress perturbation due to growth of the Patagonian ice sheet. This caused basaltic andesite magma to stall, differentiate, and generate small silicic magma reservoirs within the upper crust.

abstract: The Flat Top 7.5’ quadrangle is in Gunnison County in Colorado and is immediately north of the Gunnison quad and the town of Gunnison. The quad is dominated by the ~10 Ma basalt and basaltic andesites that make up Flat Top mesa (3050-3220 m). Outcrops of weakly cemented Tertiary sandstone to boulder conglomerates are intermittently exposed under Flat Top. The lithology of the gravels includes an assemblage of Precambrian and Paleozoic clasts closely matching the modern Gunnison River gravel composition, and so we infer these gravels are a paleo Gunnison River deposit. The gravels sit on the ~30 Ma West Elk Breccia and are under the ~10 basalt flows capping Flat Top. To further narrow the depositional age of these gravels we took 6 samples for detrital sanidine dating and are awaiting results. The West Elk Breccia is composed of multiple volcanic mudflow facies derived from the West Elk volcano to the west. The breccia is juxtaposed against pre-existing topography and thins from ~400 m to nothing across the quad. Poorly exposed outcrops of Mancos Shale are under the Tertiary gravels and West Elk Breccia and cover a large portion of the quad. Mesaverde Formation overlies the Mancos in the northwest. Multiple generations of mass movements have occurred on the Mancos Shale. Some of these mass movements originate near the Flat Top escarpment and appear young, while others are reactivated slides of former landslide and debris flow bodies and range from young to much older morphologies. Most mass movements, regardless of age, have basalt and/or gravel clasts in them. The abundance of mass movement on the Mancos Shale and our frequent inability to determine if Mancos Shale was in place or also moved, required us to use a combined Qc/Km or Qls/Km unit over much of the quad.

title: Investigating active structures in the forearc of Southern Peru: Geometry and kinematics of the Incapuquio Fault System
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Gomersall, Jackson M. [1], Perez, Nicholas [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA

abstract: A ~460 km structure in Southern Peru forms a distinct topographic expression that marks the transition from the low relief forearc to the high relief Western Cordillera arc. To the north this expression is named the Western Andean Escarpment and to the south it is referred to as the Incapuquio Fault System. Previous interpretations of the Incapuquio Fault System and the Western Andean Escarpment propose an oblique-reverse fault, left-lateral strike-slip fault, NE-dipping left-lateral oblique-reverse fault, SW-dipping reverse fault, SW-dipping normal fault, and a SW-dipping right-lateral oblique-normal fault. The timing of activation of the Incapuquio Fault System ranges between the lower Tertiary and the Holocene. Results from new field mapping from three locations along 355 km of the Incapuquio Fault System and new U-Pb zircon geochronology provide constraints on the geometry and sense of displacement along the Incapuquio Fault System. This work demonstrates the variable nature of the Incapuquio Fault System as it transitions between deformation styles from north to south. The northern end of the Incapuquio Fault system is characterized by a single SW-dipping normal fault. The middle segment of the system develops into a broad 100-200 m wide SW-dipping normal fault zone. Finally, the southern end of the Incapuquio Fault System transitions into a series of both oblique-normal and steep reverse faults. This work has major implications for copper porphyry mineralization and seismic hazards.

authors: Mann, Aatish S. [1], Kary, Steve [2], Collom, Christopher J. [3], Daniels, Benjamin G. [4], Johnston, Paul A. [5]
affiliations: (1) Mount Royal University, Dept of Earth & Environmental Sciences, Calgary, Alberta, Canada

abstract:
Irregular echinoids are exceedingly rare in Upper Cretaceous marine deposits of Western Canada. The only previously documented species, Cassidulus taylori Warren, 1926, is known from seven poorly preserved endocasts from Birch Lake, Alberta, that lack most diagnostic test features. In 2023, new irregular echinoid specimens were collected from the upper Bearpaw Formation southeast of Drumheller, Alberta, on the Historic Graham Ranch between East Coulee and Dorothy. Unlike the C. taylori material, these specimens preserve much of the test, allowing detailed comparative morphological and cladistic analyses, which together support the erection of a new genus and species within the extinct family Faujasiidae (Neognathostomata, Clypeasteroida). The new echinoid closely resembles C. taylori , and the two taxa are interpreted as closely related, though differences in test morphology, including the position of the apical system, support recognition of a distinct taxon.

The new genus and species is the only North American faujasiid from farther north than Colorado, extending the family's known range within the Western Interior Seaway. Faujasiids are otherwise known almost exclusively from limestone and chalk deposits, so its recovery from fine- to medium-grained siliciclastics also expands the group's ecological range. Faujasiids have been proposed as the most primitive stem group of Clypeasteroida (sand dollars and relatives), derived from cassiduloid echinoids in the Late Cretaceous, though this transition remains poorly understood due to their scarcity and poor preservation. The new species has a highly derived morphology, with a suite of features intermediate between cassiduloids and clypeasteroids, including test flattening, reduced petals, and a more centrally positioned peristome, offering a rare data point for this transition.

The echinoid-bearing interval occurs approximately 3 m above the Dorothy Tongue and 34 m below the Zero Coal. Associated molluscs and trace fossils, together with the stenohaline physiology and functional morphology of the new species, indicate deposition in a moderate-energy, nearshore marine setting under stable euhaline conditions. This is the first detailed systematic study of an irregular echinoid from the upper Bearpaw Formation and documents a previously undescribed associated body-fossil assemblage. These results refine previous paleoenvironmental interpretations of the upper Bearpaw Formation, which relied largely on sedimentological and ichnological evidence, and demonstrate the value of integrating shelly fauna into reconstructions of the final stages of marine deposition in the study area.

abstract:
Professional identity development is a central outcome of undergraduate geoscience education, shaping how students understand their abilities, their place within the discipline, and their capacity to contribute as geoscientists. Community-engaged learning may support this development by placing students in authentic public settings where they apply disciplinary knowledge, communicate with diverse audiences, and connect geoscience to local needs. Despite growing interest in community-engaged learning, less is known about the developmental processes through which these experiences support professional identity development in geoscience.

This qualitative case study examined student experiences across two community-engaged geoscience courses at a Hispanic-Serving Institution in the U.S.-Mexico border region. Unlike courses that incorporate community engagement as a single project or instructional component, these courses were organized entirely around sustained partnerships with community organizations. Guided by Communities of Practice and Borderlands Pedagogy, the study drew on pre- and post-course surveys, focus groups, written reflections, classroom and field observations, and student-generated artifacts. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis.

Four interconnected themes emerged: science communication as disciplinary practice, identity and confidence development, place-based and culturally situated learning, and learning through ambiguity, collaboration, and authentic problem solving. Students described moving from uncertainty to increasing confidence as they communicated geoscience with public audiences, collaborated with community partners, and connected geologic knowledge to the landscapes and communities of the U.S.-Mexico border region. Through these experiences, students increasingly came to see themselves as geoscientists, demonstrating that sustained community-engaged practice supported professional identity development through authentic participation in the discipline.

This study demonstrates that community engagement can function as more than a supplemental instructional activity. When community engagement serves as the organizing principle of a course, it creates sustained opportunities for students to develop professional identity through authentic disciplinary practice while strengthening connections between geoscience and society.

title: Late Cretaceous (Campanian) Clumped Isotope (Δ47) Paleothermometry Based on Inoceramid Prisms from the Pierre Shale Formation: “The Ugly, The Bad and The Good(?)”

authors: Altenberg, Thais A. [1], Kelly, D. Clay [2], Petersen, Sierra V. [3]

abstract: The Western Interior Seaway (WIS) of North America is an iconic feature of the Late Cretaceous world. However, use of traditional oxygen isotopes (δ 18 O) in biogenic carbonates for paleoenvironmental reconstruction in the Late Cretaceous WIS has been plagued by uncertainty stemming from overprinting by spatiotemporal variation in seawater δ 18 O w and/or diagenetic alteration. Here, we evaluate the potential of clumped isotope (Δ 47 ) measurements on calcite prisms from inoceramid clams for reconstructing Campanian bottom-water temperatures and δ 18 O w in the WIS. Inoceramid prisms were taken from cores drilled through the Pierre Shale (Gregory, Crow Creek, Degrey Members) in the town of Presho and Aurora County, South Dakota. We first report the ugly/bad results from the Presho section where Δ 47 analyses yielded implausibly hot bottom-water temperatures (~40-60⁰C). By contrast, the “good” news is that inoceramid Δ 47 analyses for the Aurora section yielded more plausible temperatures that fall within the range of published Δ 47 -based temperatures derived from Maastrichtian/Campanian molluscan (bivalve, gastropod) shells in the WIS (Petersen et al., 2016). Comparative analyses of frosty (opaque white) versus translucent prisms taken from the same Aurora samples revealed that the former returned implausible Δ 47 -temperatures (~50⁰C) while the latter registered tenable Δ 47 -temperatures (15-35°C). We suspect that deeper burial depths (thermal reordering of isotopologues) may be the cause of the erroneous Δ 47 -temperatures in the Presho record. In the well-preserved Aurora samples, we find that bottom-water temperatures and δ 18 O w rapidly decrease during the Late Campanian, suggesting a southerly incursion of cooler, δ 18 O w depleted boreal waters sourced from the circum-Arctic region. These results imply that, given the availability of well-preserved specimen, Δ 47 paleothermometry has the potential to reveal short time-scale oceanographic changes.

abstract: Upper Cretaceous dinosaur nesting site localities across different latitudes (10° between Kaiparowits and Two Medicine, with St. Mary’s River closer in proximity to Two Medicine) and depositional settings can reveal dietary and hydroclimatic information through fossil eggshells. This is pertinent to understanding how these conditions vary across regions and species, as well as if fossil eggshells can be used as a proxy to further our understanding of paleoclimate. Diet and vegetation of the region influence the eggshell carbon isotope composition during formation, so fossil eggshells can be used to reveal dietary information or even trophic level; in contrast, humidity and source water influence eggshell 𝛅18O values, so fossil eggshells can be used to indicate past hydroclimatic conditions if temperature and diagenesis can be constrained. We drilled and measured 𝛅18O and 𝛅13C values of 26 fossil eggshell samples of different taxa (drilled at multiple sites as the isotopic value may vary based on which area of the eggshell was more diagenetically altered). Across known species, variation in 𝛅13C values is observed, with omnivores showing more enriched values than herbivores. Across regions, variation in 𝛅18O values is observed, with enriched values indicating drier conditions for Kaiparowits and depleted values with wetter conditions for Two Medicine and St. Mary’s River, under the assumption that temperature is consistent and diagenetic alteration is limited. Optical and cathodoluminescence microscopy has been used to ascertain the fidelity of the 𝛅18O values, with varying results and degrees of erosion to the thin sections showing plausible signs of diagenesis.

title: Reading the Heat: Developing a Quartz Luminescence Proxy for Wildfire Soil Heating
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution (Posters)
authors: Rodrigues, Kathleen [1]
affiliations: (1) Division of Earth and Ecosystem Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
abstract:
Quantifying subsurface soil heating during wildfires is critical for understanding post-fire changes to soil properties, hydrology, and ecosystem recovery, yet direct measurements of soil temperature are rarely available. Quartz is a ubiquitous mineral in soils and exhibits changes in luminescence sensitivity following heating, suggesting that it may provide a quantitative proxy for reconstructing wildfire-induced soil heating.

To evaluate this hypothesis, quartz (32–63 μm) separated from unheated soils collected at the RRR-2 wildfire study site was subjected to controlled laboratory heating experiments spanning temperatures representative of wildfire conditions. Samples were heated for durations ranging from 5 minutes to 1 hour, after which quartz sensitivity was measured.

Results indicate little change in luminescence sensitivity below approximately 350 °C, followed by a transition between 350 and 400 °C and a pronounced increase above ~400 °C. Although heating duration exerts a secondary influence, the luminescence response is primarily controlled by maximum temperature, suggesting that quartz records thermal thresholds even when fire residence time is unknown.

Additional burn chamber experiments using instrumented soil profiles with embedded thermocouples are being conducted to compare luminescence sensitivity directly with independently measured soil temperatures. Together, these experiments demonstrate the potential for quartz luminescence sensitivity to serve as a quantitative proxy for wildfire-induced soil heating and provide the foundation for reconstructing subsurface fire severity in natural wildfire and prescribed burn settings.

abstract: Leucogranites in the New York Mountains, NV, have previously been identified as hosting significant enrichment in U, Th, and rare earth elements (REE). Mineralization in this region has only been studied at the reconnaissance level highlighting Paleoproterozoic plutonic evolution in relation to the Ivanpah orogeny. However, there remains no coherent petrogenetic model for ore formation, nor data that quantify how this occurrence might be temporally and/or genetically related to other mineralized domains in the Proterozoic southwestern USA. This study employs detailed field mapping, along with petrology, geochemistry, and geochronology by high-spatial-resolution in-situ Laser Ablation Split Stream and Time of Flight Mass Spectrometry (LASS-MS and ToF-MS) to investigate distinct actinide- and REE-enriched domains. Textural, geochemical, and U-Pb geochronologic analyses of ore-forming REE-phosphates and -silicates, reveal complex microstructures suggestive of a late-stage syn-magmatic genesis during Paleoproterozoic magmatism associated with the Ivanpah orogeny. Oscillatory zoning, identified via cathodoluminescence (CL) imaging, in coeval zircon supports the idea of a syn-magmatic relationship between REE-mineralization and regional-scale plutonism. Textural analysis also indicates that primary REE-phosphates are variably overprinted by secondary REE minerals, with abundant evidence of fluid-mediated dissolution and re-precipitation reactions. Initial geochemical modeling suggests that fluid release during the final stages of pluton emplacement facilitated the mobilization of incompatible elements. Ore grade was subsequently enhanced by focused, structurally controlled fluid flow, resulting in discrete domains of mineralization. This integrated analysis provides new insight into the magmatic mechanisms driving initial REE enrichment during leucogranite crystallization, clarifies the timing of mineralization relative to regional Paleoproterozoic plutonism, and highlights the crucial role of fluid-mediated alteration in the formation and distribution of primary and secondary REE minerals.

title: In-Situ Ar/Ar Dating of Shocked Meteorites: Redistribution of K and Anomalous Shock Ages
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials
authors: Sharp, Thomas George [1], Karageozian, Mara E. [2], Van Soerst, Matthijs [3], McDonald, Christopher [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA

abstract:
The impact history of the Solar System is recorded in shocked meteorites, and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology is fundamental to interpreting that history. However, natural shock effects in meteorites are heterogeneous and result in non-uniform release of radiogenic 40 Ar*. Nonintuitive behavior of K and Ar in shock melt has resulted in anomalous 40 Ar/ 39 Ar shock ages, as first reported for the Peace River L chondrite (McConnville et al. 1988). Here, we present in situ UV laser ablation microprobe (UVLAMP) argon mass spectrometry data and petrographic analysis of the L chondrite Mbale to illustrate how the behavior of K and Ar during shock results in anomalous 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages. Mbale is an L5/6 ordinary chondrite fall with shock stages S5 and S6 and a bulk 40 Ar/ 39 Ar age of 479 ± 7 Ma. Our Mbale section is composed of ~25% shock-melt vein (majoritic garnet and wadsleyite with metal-sulfide droplets) with entrained clasts of partially transformed olivine and enstatite (wadsleyite and majorite). The host contains plagioclase that is completely transformed to maskelynite adjacent to the shock vein and partially transformed farther from the shock melt.

Three UVLAMP profiles were measured across the shock vein, producing relative ages from 444 ± 10 Ma to 6145 ± 137 Ma. The oldest ages occur within the quenched shock vein and the youngest ages in the host. WDS and EDS data show that the shock vein is nearly K 2 O-free whereas the maskelynite adjacent to the shock vein is enriched with ~ 2.0 wt% K 2 O. In general, the shock heating results in the release of radiogenic 39 Ar and resetting of 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages in shocked meteorites. However, S6 shock veins, which quench rapidly during the shock pulse, trap Ar while expelling K into adjacent maskelynites. This loss of K results in 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages that are older than the ~470 Ma impact event that shocked Mbale. While 40 Ar/ 39 Ar step heating of shocked L chondrites produces well-defined plateau ages of ~ 470 Ma, corresponding to the breakup of the L-chondrite, many step-heating data sets also have late-release ages that are older. These older late-release ages likely come from quenched shock melt that lost K but retained Ar.

title: Evolution of the Ancestral Gunnison River and Post-Laramide Deformation in the Gunnison region of western Colorado, U.S.A.

authors: Aslan, Andres [1], Sterne, Edward J. [2], Heizler, Matthew T. [3], Cole, Rex D. [4], Schwartz, Darin [5]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA

abstract:
Fluvial conglomerates interpreted as representing the ancestral Gunnison River system overlie Proterozoic basement rocks in western Colorado at elevations of ~675–850 m above the Gunnison River. We determine maximum depositional ages (MDAs) of these fluvial conglomerates and interpret those ages alongside ages of younger volcanic rocks to constrain the timing of landscape changes that include: 1) post-Laramide erosion of the Gunnison uplift and development of the Rocky Mountain Erosion Surface (RMES), 2) early Oligocene establishment of the Gunnison River, 3) Oligocene–early Miocene volcaniclastic aggradation, and 4) Neogene deformation and accompanying Gunnison River incision.

MDA estimates of the fluvial conglomerates at two locations (Poverty Mesa, Black Mesa) are based on detrital-sanidine (DS) 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates (n=637), detrital-zircon (DZ) U-Pb dates (n=186), and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dating of two volcanic clasts. At Poverty Mesa, the DS MDA estimate is 29.691 ± 0.030 Ma (n=1 grain). At Black Mesa, the DS MDA estimate is 29.064 ± 0.090 Ma (n=4 grains). The age estimates are consistent with the presence of the overlying ca. 28.7 Ma Blue Mesa Tuff and are supported by a DZ MDA (28.7 ± 2.50 Ma; n = 3 grains) and the youngest volcanic clast date (29.75 ± 0.07 Ma).

DZ data (~52% of the dates are ca. 1800–1400 Ma) and the abundance of volcanic and granitic clasts in the conglomerates suggest that the early Oligocene Gunnison River flowed west from sediment sources including the Sawatch Range, the Gunnison uplift, and the West Elk and San Juan volcanic fields. The presence of the early Oligocene fluvial conglomerates atop basement rocks of the Gunnison uplift requires that 2–2.5 km of Mesozoic sedimentary strata were eroded from the uplift >30 Ma. Oligocene–early Miocene volcanism caused subsequent aggradation.

The RMES rises to the west across the Cimarron uplift, a north-south oriented RMES structural high whose axis crosses the Gunnison River at the Black Canyon. The early Oligocene conglomerates deposited by the west-flowing ancestral Gunnison River as well as the overlying Oligocene–early Miocene volcanic rocks, rest atop an eastward dipping RMES. This observation is interpreted as evidence for Neogene deformation. Continued regional uplift, including development of the Cimarron uplift, has driven deep Gunnison River incision into Proterozoic basement rocks to form the spectacular Black Canyon.

title: Multivariate Geochemical Assessment of Groundwater in the Cherokee Basin, Southeastern Kansas.
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Posters)
authors: Onwuagba, Fidelis Chinaemelum [1], Seybold, Erin [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, University of kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA; Assistant Scientist, Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
abstract: Groundwater quality is a reflection of the complex interactions between natural processes, such as mineral weathering and redox reactions, and human activities, including fertilizer application, industrial discharge, and legacy mining. Analyzing the geochemical signature of groundwater using multivariate statistical techniques provides valuable insights into these dynamics. In particular, correlation analysis can be used to assess potential co-mobilization between major ions and trace metals, while Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces the dimensionality of large datasets, enabling the identification of dominant geochemical processes and controlling factors (Helena et al., 2000; Shrestha & Kazama, 2007). This is particularly important for assessing the mobility of redox-sensitive elements, as transitions from oxic to suboxic or anoxic conditions significantly affect the solubility and transport of contaminants (Chapelle, 2001). This study investigates the relationships between redox conditions, trace metal mobility, and possible anthropogenic influences in groundwater. Groundwater samples from domestic wells in southeastern Kansas were analyzed for major physicochemical parameters and trace metals, with statistical analyses revealing key correlations. The results indicate that the geochemistry of groundwater in the study area is influenced by a combination of redox processes, the dissolution and precipitation of minerals, and the dynamics of sorption and desorption.

title: Resolving the timing of Laramide uplift and sedimentation in the Powder River Basin, Wyoming, using detrital heavy mineral geochemistry
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools (Posters)
authors: Brodale, Matthew A. [1], Finzel, Emily S. [2], Horkley, L. Kenneth [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(3) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA, USA
abstract: Thick-skinned deformation associated with the Laramide orogeny has been linked to flat-slab subduction of oceanic lithosphere beneath western North America from approximately 80-40 Ma. The relative timing and spatial pattern of Laramide deformation has not been fully resolved. Some models predict a broad wave of inboard deformation whereas opposing models suggest a relatively narrow corridor, while other work has proposed multiple stages of Laramide deformation with reversing direction of migration associated with slab removal. The Powder River Basin (PRB) in northeastern Wyoming is a large broken foreland basin in which Paleocene-Eocene strata, with sediments sourced from the adjacent basement-cored uplifts, were deposited coincident with the Laramide orogeny. Here we use detrital heavy mineral suites from these strata to resolve the relative timing of basement daylighting across the region. The earliest Paleogene PRB deposits include the Paleocene Fort Union Formation and the overlying Eocene Wasatch Formation. The Fort Union Formation is composed of the early Paleocene Tullock, middle Paleocene Lebo Shale, and late Paleocene Tongue River members. Samples of each Fort Union Formation member and of the Wasatch Formation were collected from outcrops across the western, southern, and eastern margins of the basin. These fluvial and lacustrine sandstones and shales were disaggregated before being submerged, centrifuged, and partially frozen in sodium polytungstate, a heavy liquid with a density of ~2.9 g/cm 3 . The heavy mineral fractions obtained from this separation were analyzed in a scanning electron microscope equipped with two energy dispersive spectrometers (EDS). AZtecGeo software with a modified database was used to classify the heavy minerals present in each sample based on elemental parameters. Our results are compared to the same type of data collected from sediments in modern rivers draining the exposed Precambrian cores of potential source areas in the Beartooth, Bighorn, Laramie, and Medicine Bow Mountains. These data contribute to the development of mineralogical and geochemical fingerprints for each of the basement uplifts that allow us to then determine very specific sediment source area contributions to the Paleocene-Eocene strata in the PRB over time and a sequence of uplift at the eastern margin of the Laramide Province which can be used to evaluate the various models of Laramide deformation.

title: Cryogenian collision and stitching plutonism in the northwestern Arabian-Nubian Shield preceded final closure of the Mozambique Ocean
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Zhang, Yiming [1], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [2], Schmitz, Mark D. [3], Zoheir, Basem [4], Macdonald, Francis A. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN,
(3) Boise State University, Boise, ID,
(4) King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
(5) University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
abstract: The East African Orogen is commonly framed as the product of terminal collision between East and West Gondwana that assembled the Arabian–Nubian Shield. However, an alternative interpretation is that the majority of contraction is associated with collisions that occurred prior to the terminal closure of the Mozambique Ocean. In the Eastern Desert of Egypt, ca. 700 Ma ophiolites record oceanic-lithosphere formation at a time when regional tectonic models commonly depict the western Arabian–Nubian Shield terranes as already amalgamated. Their subsequent obduction and collision must predate widespread late Cryogenian, post-collisional magmatism. We present high-precision zircon U–Pb ID-TIMS dates from the post-collisional Kadabora pluton and two crosscutting rhyolite dikes. A granite sample yields an age of ca. 636 Ma, establishing latest Cryogenian pluton emplacement. Two rhyolitic dikes that crosscut the pluton yield indistinguishable ca. 546 Ma ages. The ca. 636 Ma age demonstrates that collision-related deformation had ended locally by that time and links Kadabora to the plutonic pulse documented across the shield from Egypt through Ethiopia to Saudi Arabia during the latest Cryogenian to earliest Ediacaran. The regional distribution of these granitoids across deformed arc assemblages and suture zones is consistent with widespread stitching plutonism associated with regional crustal thickening. Together, ca. 700 Ma back-arc oceanic crust and ca. 636 Ma stitching plutonism bracket major arc-terrane collision and ophiolite obduction within an interval of ~65 Myr. Records of arc activity within the Arabian-Nubian Shield as well as passive margin marine sedimentation in Oman indicates that the Mozambique Ocean remained open at this time. These records reveal that the East African Orogeny is better understood as resulting from terrane collision prior to the terminal suturing of Gondwana. We put forward a more nuanced paleogeographic reconstruction of the Arabian-Nubian Shield during the assembly of Gondwana.

title: Subsurface Microbe-Rock-Fluid-Critical Mineral Systems: from Observation towards Prediction
session_title: From Deep Earth to Digital Twins: Artificial Intelligence in Earth System Science and Predictive Subsurface Systems
authors: McIntosh, Jennifer [1]
affiliations: (1) Hydrology & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract: Application of AI/ML to predict multiple uses of the subsurface (e.g., water supplies, energy extraction and storage, critical mineral resources, CO 2 sequestration, etc.) and potential contamination requires process-based understanding of subsurface microbe-rock-fluid systems (SMRFS), including how they have evolved over geologic time. It also requires physical, chemical and biological datasets that are few and far between beyond a few 100 meters depth and outside oil/gas producing zones. This talk will explore how landscape evolution (i.e., changes in geologic, hydrologic, and climatic forcings) across the Colorado Plateau has driven deep subsurface fluid flow, fluid-rock reactions, and microbial processes, with implications for critical minerals (e.g., Li, Cu), He, and natural H 2 , as well as geogenic sources of contamination (e.g., As). We will hypothesize how spatial-temporal patterns of rapid exhumation, river incision, and bleaching and mineralization over the past few million years may be combined with relatively common measurements of fluid chemistry and microbial activity in an AI/ML framework to make predictions of hydraulic gradients, permeability distribution (e.g., removal of confining units; joints/faults activation), fluid and solute fluxes, accumulation and/or flushing of reservoirs, and microbial habitation. Insights into paleo- to modern-fluid flow and reaction may also be used to refine preliminary ML-GIS models of arsenic mobilization in groundwater.
