title: Boulders and Boulder Tracks in Permanently Shadowed Regions of the Lunar South Pole
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Racek, Gillian [1], Lamantia, Anthony [2], Adepoju, Olufunke [3], Baughman, Emma [4], Luna, Jeannette Wolak [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN,
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee,
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee,
(4) Department of Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee,
(5) Department of Earth Sciences, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, Tennessee,
abstract:
This project maps boulders across the Lunar South Pole (LSP) using complementary datasets from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) and Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter ShadowCam (SHC). While NAC imagery provides excellent coverage of illuminated terrain, permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) cannot be adequately observed. ShadowCam imagery supports boulder mapping in these previously inaccessible regions, allowing for a complete boulder inventory across the LSP. Because PSRs receive little to no direct solar radiation, weathering processes are expected to differ from those operating in illuminated terrain.

Using ArcGIS Pro, individual boulders were digitized as point features and boulder tracks as line features at a mapping scale of 1:1,500 to 1:3,000 across the LSP. Using the NAC dataset, 90,060 boulders and 782 boulder fields were identified across 9,878.51 square km. Nine regions of significant shadow were identified and mapped using ShadowCam. These regions cover 2,166 square km, with the largest region encompassing the combined area of Henson and Sverdrup craters at approximately 1,061 square km.

Preliminary mapping in shadowed regions identified 12,223 boulders across 2,166 square km of terrain. Boulder distribution varied considerably among the mapped regions, with densities ranging from 0.03 boulders per square km in areas where boulders were sparse to 39.44 boulders per square km where they were closely spaced. In addition, 29 significant boulders were identified, averaging 32 meters in length, with the largest measuring approximately 71 meters. Boulder tracks were concentrated primarily within Shackleton, with Sverdrup representing the only other mapped region containing tracks despite its much gentler slopes (<5°) compared to Shackleton (~30°). Future work will focus on using this expanded boulder dataset to compare illuminated and shadowed terrains and evaluating how temperature fluctuations and illumination influence the abundance, size, and preservation of lunar boulders.

abstract: A critical mineral or material is essential in a modern engineered material, component, or system; it also is subject to short-term supply-chain risks or longer-term concerns about availability - or both. This talk focuses on the economic, geopolitical and public policy dimensions of these minerals and materials. In particular, it evaluates how the world is re-imagining globailization and how the United States and Europe are-embracing industrial policy.

title: Cuffey Confronts Creationism
session_title: PALEONTOLOGY, BRYOZOANS, DINOSAURS, REEFS, STRATIGRAPHY, AND MILITARY GEOLOGY: IN HONOR OF ROGER CUFFEY AND HIS ECCLECTIC CAREER
authors: Ross, Marcus R. [1]
affiliations: (1) College of Arts & Sciences, Liberty University, Lynchburg, VA, USA
abstract:
Among Roger Cuffey’s many geological and paleontological endeavors, his early career featured a notable interest in science-faith dialogue and a particular emphasis on articulating the case for biological evolution. From 1969 to 1972, Cuffey published no less than seven comments, reviews, and dialogues in the Journal of the American Scientific Affiliation ( JASA ), where he defended evolution and conventional geological perspectives of Earth history against anti-evolution challenges from both young-Earth and old-Earth creationists. These forays at the dawn of the modern creation-evolution controversy culminated with Cuffey’s 1973 debate with Dr. Duane Gish of the Institute for Creation Research. The event took place on Penn State campus and reportedly drew over 1,500 attendees. Much of the debate centered on evidence from the fossil record, and Cuffey’s greater command of paleontology and Earth history was met with Gish’s considerable rhetorical skills. Cuffey viewed the experience rather negatively and, perhaps not coincidentally, he abstained from further engagement with creationism for over two decades. The one notable exception during this time was the inclusion of his 1972 JASA paper on the evidence for evolution in the fossil record in Ashley Montagu’s influential volume Science and Creationism , published in the wake of the 1981 McLean vs. Arkansas Board of Education and prior to the 1987 US Supreme Court case Edwards vs. Aguillard .

After a long hiatus, Cuffey returned to the topic of creationism in 1999 as a panelist and contributor to The Creation-Evolution Controversy II , a GSA short course conducted by the Paleontological Society. In keeping with his early writings, Cuffey’s contribution was primarily educational and peer-oriented as he outlined his approach to teaching evolution in undergraduate paleontology courses. His perspectives and recommendations bore the experiences of a seasoned career, characterized by his consistently congenial manner, his gracious care for students, and his longtime emphasis on seeing and handling paleontological evidence.

title: Development of a Machine Learning Model for Identifying Fragmentary Irregular Echinoid Fossils
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: Liyanagedara, Pamod Heshan [1], Kowalewski, Michal [2], Portell, Roger [3], Torres, Luis [4], Jang, Hyungjoo [5], Porto, Arthur [6]
affiliations: (1) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, Florida, USA; Department of Biology, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA
(2) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, Florida, USA

(5) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, Florida, USA; Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA
(6) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, Florida, USA
abstract: Skeletal fragments are often ignored in invertebrate paleontology, despite being more abundant than whole specimens in fossil assemblages and potentially containing meaningful taxonomic information. To assess potential biases toward whole specimens and the underrepresentation of fragments in the fossil record, we conducted a survey of published monographs (n=25). The results revealed that 76.8% of described invertebrate fossil species were based on whole specimens, whereas only 6.05% were based on unique fragments. The remaining 17.15% were based on partially complete specimens. This bias mainly results from the difficulty of accurately identifying fragments. To address this issue, a machine learning model to accurately identify fragments was developed. Our preliminary model focused on five irregular echinoid genera: Clypeaster (n=101), Encope (n=932), Leodia (n=164), Mellita (n=123), and Meoma (n=30). Instead of mechanically creating fragments, we programmatically generated a dataset of polygonal fragments including systematically controlled proportions of the test area (100%, 50%, 25%, and 12.5%). To assess how classification accuracy changes with the fragment size, we trained a pre-trained ResNet-18 classifier on these fragment datasets at the genus level. Encope showed the highest classification accuracy at the 100% fragment size (99.91%), whereas Meoma showed the lowest (81.81%). Classification accuracy declined as fragment size decreased, with all genera except Encope showing accuracy below 30% at 12.5% fragment size. Encope retained a classification accuracy of 93.38% even at 12.5% fragment size, likely due to its larger sample size. These results indicate that sample size has a positive effect on classification accuracy and that even smaller fragments retain important taxonomic information. Regional heatmaps suggest that certain areas of the test are more taxonomically informative than others. We expect this model to provide the foundation for more advanced models that incorporate both irregular and regular echinoids and taphonomically altered fragments. With larger training datasets and advanced models, there is great potential to recover meaningful taxonomic information from small fragments which are usually overlooked in paleontological studies.

title: 40Ar/39Ar Eruption Age Estimation Via Bayesian Mixture Modeling
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data
authors: Carter, Jack Norman [1], Morgan, Leah [2], Renne, Paul R. [3], Jicha, Brian R. [4], Keller, C Brenhin [5], McLean, Noah [6], Schoene, Blair [7], Schmitz, Mark D. [8], Sprain, Courtney Jean [9]
affiliations: (1) Berkeley Geochronology Center, Berkeley Geochronology Center, Berkeley, CA, United Kingdom; Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, CA, United Kingdom
(2) USGS, United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, United Kingdom
(3) Berkeley Geochronology Center, Berkeley Geochronology Center, Berkeley, CA, United Kingdom; Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, CA, United Kingdom
(4) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Middleton, WI, USA

abstract:
As the analytical precision of 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology has improved, single-crystal datasets from volcanic ejecta, including tephra deposits and lavas, have increasingly revealed geological complexity within individual samples. Not every crystal necessarily records the eruption event of interest. Individual grains may yield older or younger apparent ages because of inheritance, incomplete degassing, alteration, argon loss, or other geological and analytical processes.

Comparable challenges have emerged in U–Pb geochronology, where improved analytical resolution commonly reveals extended and complex crystallization histories rather than a single, discrete eruption age. This recognition has motivated the development of probabilistic approaches such as Bayesian eruption age estimations. The increasing complexity resolved within single-crystal 40 Ar/ 39 Ar datasets similarly requires interpretative methods that can account for multiple geological age populations while recovering a meaningful eruption age.

Currently, these datasets are commonly interpreted using weighted means calculated from subsets of analyses selected according to statistical or subjective criteria. Such approaches include low-MSWD filtering, weighted-mean filtering, goodness-of-fit tests for a normal distribution, and the manual exclusion of grains interpreted as outliers. Although useful, these methods generally require analyses to be classified as either included or excluded before the eruption age is calculated.

Single-crystal age distributions are instead well suited to a mixture-model framework, in which the observed data are interpreted as combinations of distinct age populations rather than as a single population to be averaged after subjective or statistical filtering. We present a Bayesian mixture model for estimating eruption ages from 40 Ar/ 39 Ar single-crystal datasets using only the measured age and analytical uncertainty of each crystal as inputs. The model treats each analysis probabilistically as belonging to an eruption-age population, an older population, or a younger population. It thereby estimates the eruption age while propagating both analytical uncertainties and uncertainty in the population membership of individual grains, avoiding the need to make fixed, binary decisions about which analyses should be retained.

title: Assessing Ecological Effects of the Late Ordovician Richmondian Invasion Event on Brachiopods Using Three-Dimensional Geometric Morphometrics
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Comas, Sofia V. [1], Saines, Spencer [2], Christie, Max [3], Sclafani, Judith A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science & Environmental Change, University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA
(2) School of Integrative Biology, University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA
(3) Department of Earth Science & Environmental Change, Univeristy of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA
(4) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, The University of the Pacific, Stockton, CA, USA
abstract:
Invasive species can dramatically affect ecological communities and are often detrimental to native species. Analyzing the effects of ancient invasion events preserved in the fossil record may help us assess long-term ecological impacts of modern invasion events. We focus on the Late Ordovician Richmondian Invasion event, when several new taxa invaded the Cincinnati area, to assess changes in brachiopod morphology.

Morphological diversity and phenotypic plasticity are important for the ability of organisms to cope and adapt to changing environments. This is particularly relevant in sessile brachiopods, which primarily interact with their environment through the shape of their shell. Here, we investigate changes in the three-dimensional morphological diversity of brachiopods across the Richmondian Invasion to understand ecological impacts of major changes in community composition.

We collected Late Ordovician brachiopod fossils along an environmental depth gradient of deep to shallow subtidal in the Cincinnati Arch from before (C2 sequence) and after (C5 sequence) the Richmondian Invasion event. To quantify changes in shell shape, Structured Light Scanning is used to digitally construct the 3-dimensional shape of brachiopods using the Revopoint INSPIRE2 scanner. The software ‘Revo Metro’ is used to build 3D models of the dorsal valve of each brachiopod. Fixed landmarks and semi-landmarks are placed across the surface of the shells using the software ‘3D Slicer’. General Procrustes Analysis and Principal Components Analysis (PCA) are performed in ‘R’ using the package ‘geomorph’ to determine shape changes.

Preliminary results on Rafinesquina show significant shape changes after the invasion event, with post-invasion specimens showing weaker convexity of the pedicle valve and stronger rounding of the distal ends of the hingeline. PCA shows pre-invasion specimens occupy a greater range of morphospace, contrasted with tight clustering and a decrease in morphological diversity exhibited by post-invasion specimens. There is little to no overlap between the two groups within the morphospace. Analyses for Cincinetina specimens are currently being conducted. We expect to see similar patterns of decreased morphological diversity after the invasion, alongside shape changes across the environmental gradient from deep to shallow subtidal.

title: How well do class activities and assessments ask students to develop research skills in first-year and upper-level CURE courses?
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Kenderes, Elizabeth [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
abstract: Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) have long been encouraged by the National Research Council (NRC, 2012) and have been included in the National Association of Geoscience Teachers’ Community Framework for Geoscience Education Research – specifically Grand Challenge #5: “How can we better engage learners as co-discoverers of knowledge and co-creators of new instructional strategies in geoscience?” My work seeks to assess how well assessments in two CURE-based courses address NRC learning goals for authentic student research. Specifically, how well my class activities and assessments ask student to (1) ask scientific questions, (2) develop and use models, (3) plan and carry out investigations, (4) analyze and interpret data, (5) use mathematics and computational thinking, (6) construct explanations, (7) engage in argument from evidence, and (8) obtain, evaluate, and communicate information (NRC, 2012). To assess this, I look at two courses: a freshman research experience called “The Science of Climate Change” (N=18) and an upper-level igneous and metamorphic petrology course (N=15). The freshman research class is a full semester dedicated to the research project, whereas the CURE in the petrology course is a semester-long term project that supplements the course materials. To assess how well my courses target NRC learning outcomes, I adapted a conceptual framework for measuring the effectiveness of CUREs in biology courses. I used this framework to develop a way to code assignments to determine whether I am truly assessing student research skills. I am building in a coding system to then determine how well student products meet those objectives. Through this work, I make recommendations for incorporating scaffolding and TiLTed assignment instructions consistently in CURE courses to help students focus on the entirety of the learning outcomes of each assignment and the course as a whole.

title: Efficacy of Urban Road Salt Reduction Strategies on Public Supply Well Quality
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Rudolph, David L [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada
abstract: Long-term road salt application has increased chloride (Cl - ) concentrations in public drinking water wells in many cold climate communities. A range of Best Management Practices (BMPs) have been adopted to mitigate the impact of road deicing compounds on groundwater quality. Chronic increases in chloride levels have been observed in several municipal well fields within the southern Ontario Regional Municipality of Waterloo (RMOW). In response, the RMOW and City of Kitchener implemented a plan to reduce salt application on roads by 25% within the local capture zones of one of the impacted well fields, the Greenbrook Well Field. Here the influence of salt reduction BMPs on subsurface water quality are examined by documenting changes in pore water Cl - concentrations and stored salt mass in vadose zone core samples collected at sites near the well field both before and after the implementation of the BMPs. The data indicate that ~6 years after salt reduction measures were initiated, average Cl - pore water concentration and average cumulative stored chloride mass in the vadose zone had decreased by approximately 60% and 40%, respectively. Groundwater samples collected from shallow monitoring wells installed at each field site showed similar post-BMP reductions in shallow groundwater Cl - concentration (~35%). Long-term (1973–2022) trends in raw water Cl - concentration data from the deeper public drinking water supply wells clearly demonstrate a slow, time-lagged response of the municipal supply wells to the salt reduction BMPs. The combined results suggest that controlled reductions in road salt applications within vulnerable, capture zone regions of public supply wells can reduce the impact of road salt deicing practices on municipal groundwater supplies over time.

abstract: The Cuatro Ciénegas Basin (CCB) in Coahuila, Mexico is a rare endorheic desert oasis where thermal groundwater upwells through faulted Cretaceous carbonate rocks to support over 200 pools, or pozas, home to many endemic species (Felstead et al., 2015). Extensive regional groundwater pumping for agricultural and municipal use has triggered water table declines exceeding 30 meters, threatening the survival of these spring systems (Pedrozo-Acuña et al., 2026). This study evaluates the physical and hydraulic characteristics of the shallow subsurface to determine the resilience of these aquatic habitats to continued groundwater overexploitation. We hypothesized that the shallow subsurface is relatively homogeneous and highly electrically conductive, and pozas are generally in losing conditions and lack significant natural buffering against external hydrologic shifts. We installed monitoring wells at Rio Mezquites and Poza La Becerra, using RTK-GPS and Total Station surveys for precise topographic mapping. Subsurface structures and saturation were assessed through Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT), in-situ Guelph permeametry, and falling-head core analysis. Pressure transducers and stream gauging with acoustic Doppler velocity meters provided high-resolution data on head fluctuations and reach-scale mass balances. ERT results showed a highly conductive and physically homogeneous shallow subsurface. Water table levels rose rapidly (8-16 cm) following meteoric events, indicating a highly sensitive system with short recharge lag times. While localized gradients typically indicate losing conditions, precipitation events can temporarily reverse flow direction. These findings suggest that the lack of subsurface heterogeneity limits hydraulic resistance, leaving these springs highly vulnerable to continued groundwater extraction.

title: The Goodenough unit of western Colorado: A sedimentary record of middle Eocene uplift, erosion, and formation of the Rocky Mountain Erosion Surface
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding (Posters)
authors: Tuck, Adam [1], Ruffner, Jordan [2], Aslan, Andres [3], Cole, Rex D. [4], Heizler, Matthew T. [5], Schwartz, Darin [6]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
(2) Dept. of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
(3) Dept. of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA

(6) Dept. of Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, Idaho, USA
abstract:
Up to 300 m of fluvial-lacustrine deposits of the informally named Goodenough unit are present in the southeastern Piceance Basin and consist of volcanic and arkosic sandstone, smectitic mudrock, and minor carbonate. The Goodenough unit has previously been mapped as the Eocene Green River Formation, but it is sandstone rich, contains volcanic pebble conglomerate and red mudrock, and lacks oil shale. In areas where the Goodenough unit is recognized, it overlies the Green River Formation.

40 Ar/ 39 Ar and U-Pb geochronology was used to date detrital sanidine (DS) (n=847) and detrital zircon (DZ) (n=425) in four conglomeratic samples collected near the base of the Goodenough unit. DS maximum depositional ages (MDA) range from 42.19 ± 0.0093 Ma (n=9 grains) to 41.64 ± 0.037 Ma (n=5 grains). Fourteen 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates of volcanic clasts yielded ages of ca. 45–42 Ma. These basal age constraints for the Goodenough are consistent with an 40 Ar/ 39 Ar date (34.9 ± 0.09 Ma) on tephra located near the top of the Goodenough unit. 98% of the DS grains in the samples are <45 Ma, which suggests that the DS MDA estimates may approximate the depositional age of the basal Goodenough.

DZ U-Pb age spectra with dominant modal peaks at ca. 1400 Ma and 1700 Ma (~85% of all the DZ dates) indicate erosion of Precambrian basement rocks of the Gunnison uplift and Sawatch Range. The volcanic clast and DS dates suggest erosion of a nearby middle Eocene volcanic field although no such terrain exists today. One possibility is that middle Eocene volcanoes existed in the Sawatch Range but were subsequently eroded leading to exhumation of plutons such as the ca. 42 Ma Twin Lakes pluton.

The timing of Goodenough deposition (ca. 42-35 Ma) and formation of the Rocky Mountain Erosion Surface (RMES) are similar. RMES formation across the Gunnison uplift, as well as erosion of the Sawatch Range, was probably triggered by post-Laramide uplift and explains the composition of the Goodenough unit.

Uppermost Goodenough(?) sediments have a DS MDA of ca. 13 Ma, and unconformably overlie the main body of the Goodenough unit. These late Miocene deposits mark the final episode of sedimentation in the Piceance Basin prior to the development of the ancestral Colorado River ca. 11 Ma.

title: Building stories about ancient landscapes across space and time: data selection and resolution in marine geoarchaeology
session_title: Geoarchaeology of the Land–Sea Interface: Processes, Preservation, and Palaeolandscape Reconstruction
authors: Rivera-Collazo, Isabel [1], Clark, Loren Rachel [2], Garcia-Colon, Javier [3], Rodriguez-Delgado, Eric [4]
affiliations: (1) Scripps Center for Marine Archaeology, University of California San Diego, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, La Jolla, CA, USA; Anthropology Department, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA

(3) Anthropology Department, UC San Diego, Scripps Center for Marine Archaeology, La Jolla, CA, USA

abstract: Geoarchaeology, the study of people and landscapes through time using concepts and methods from the Earth Sciences, seeks to analyze the geomorphological contexts in which past human decision-making occurred. This requires identifying and integrating multiple lines of evidence to unravel how the land has changed over time and space. There is no single recipe for reconstructing past landscapes, as these investigations are constrained by the scale of human processes and the characteristics and interconnections of relevant climatic, environmental, and geological/geomorphological variables. Therefore, recovering stories of the past requires grounding in clear and concrete research questions and a surgical, purposeful approach to data selection, recovery methods, data analysis, and the accurate braiding of compatible datasets. In this presentation, we focus on examples from our work tracing the land/water interface since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) in the Caribbean basin to discuss multiproxy data selection, compatibility, resolution, and eventual braiding. Starting from the present at a decadal scale, we tell the story of the effects of storms and flooding after sea level stabilization to understand landscape morphology and social vulnerability in Manati, Puerto Rico. We then shift to a century scale in Guayanilla, Puerto Rico, to understand how the dynamics of sea level rise, compounded with fluvial and marine sediment transport in an enclosed basin, impacted and were also affected by human activity from the Mid-Holocene onwards. Finally, we zoom out to the millennial scale to consider how post-LGM sea level rise and ongoing taphonomic and post-depositional processes affected human and faunal access in Late Pleistocene/Early Holocene cave systems in Quintana Roo, Mexico. Overall, geoarchaeologists should be primarily archaeologists: our goal is to understand people. Only after we build relevant stories from the past can we look at the present and the future to guide education and the preservation of these dynamic environments.

abstract: Associated with a co-alluvial fan within the Ozark National Scenic Riverways (Carter County, Missouri), the Spring Valley Site (23CT389) is a multicomponent site spanning the Middle Paleoindian through Middle Archaic periods. Geoarchaeological investigations co-occurred with excavations in 2017 under the supervision of Dr. Rolfe Mandel. The goals of the investigation were to determine whether the site retained its stratigraphic integrity, and to define site formation processes. The study integrated description of soils and sediments, particle-size analysis, coefficient of linear extensibility, clay mineralogy via X-ray diffraction, radiocarbon dating, artifact refitting, debitage size-sorting, and 3D spatial analysis of piece-plotted artifacts and features. Results indicate that while post-depositional mixing occurred, many larger artifacts maintained strong vertical and horizontal spatial integrity. Most notably, discrete Late Paleoindian and Early Archaic occupation surfaces were successfully defined, demonstrating significant stratigraphic preservation despite a magnitude of pedoturbation processes.

abstract: Fossilized faunal remains from Willwood Formation localities in the Bighorn Basin, WY, dated to 56-52 Ma, demonstrate a broad vertebrate assemblage within an early Eocene subtropical habitat. Analysis of the squamate fossils of a sample of this assemblage reveals unexpected diversity. The study sample was collected during the 2013-2026 field seasons (ANTH 470: Paleontology Field School, CSU, Dept Anthropology & Geography). This project analyzes the squamate assemblage in order to: (1) identify and classify fossil specimens, (2) evaluate the geographic and stratigraphic context of the specimens, and (3) infer paleoenvironmental conditions. Evidence is obtained from taxonomic data, analysis of osteoderm and dental morphology, and paleoenvironmental information. These results provide insights on early Eocene squamate diversity, ecology, inter-species relationships. In addition, we report on remarkable specimens from the assemblage that include a tiny, intact squamate skull and associated mandible as well as another specimen with uniquely well-preserved osteoderms.

title: Evaluation of managed aquifer recharge impacts in the San Joaquin Valley, California using the Central Valley Hydrologic Model Version 2
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Pensky, Jennifer [1], Platt, Logan [2], Traum, Jonathan [3], Faunt, Claudia [4], Adera, Saalem [5]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, California Water Science Center, Santa Cruz, CA,

abstract: The San Joaquin Valley, California, has experienced decades of groundwater level decline, land subsidence, reduced aquifer storage, and depletion of interconnected surface waters. Under California’s Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), groundwater sustainability agencies have developed plans that propose managed aquifer recharge (MAR) projects to mitigate groundwater depletion and its associated impacts. However, the cumulative and regional-scale impacts of these projects remain uncertain, particularly with respect to future hydrologic variability. The Central Valley Hydrologic Model Version 2 (CVHM2) was used to evaluate the impacts of proposed MAR projects in San Joaquin Valley groundwater sustainability plans. MAR projects from these plans were compiled and categorized by different project parameters, including type (such as recharge ponds, injection wells, in-lieu recharge), water source and volume, proposed benefit, and location. The project parameters were then incorporated into CVHM2 and simulated using historical conditions and projected future hydrologic scenarios. These model simulations can be used to evaluate: 1) how proposed MAR projects influence groundwater levels, subsidence, aquifer storage, and stream-aquifer exchange; 2) how different MAR types vary in effectiveness and spatial impact; and 3) how the effects of MAR compare to other water management actions. These preliminary results can provide a regional-scale assessment of MAR effectiveness under proposed SGMA implementation and demonstrate how integrated modeling tools such as CVHM2 can support the evaluation of water management strategies.

title: Quarrying Geoheritage: Challenges and Opportunities in Charnwood Forest Geopark, UK
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Matthews, Jack J. [1]
affiliations: (1) Charnwood Forest Geopark, United Kingdom; Oxford University Museum of Natural History, United Kingdom
abstract:
The resource extraction industries have long presented a conundrum for the protection and promotion of geological heritage. On the one hand, quarrying has the potential to damage and destroy geoheritage, and on the other, many features have only been discovered, described, and designated because they were first exposed by quarrying. And this potential conflict isn’t disappearing: quarrying remains an essential industry as society seeks the resources needed for a greener economy.

Charnwood Forest Geopark in Leicestershire, UK, has a rich quarrying history, dating back at least 2000 years to the Roman period. The region is also home to some of the oldest animal fossils ever found, some of which are associated with sites of stone extraction.

Charnwood Forest contains five active quarries, three of which include nationally designated sites for geoconservation. While this may appear – at face value – to be an unusual and contradictory situation, there need not be a conflict between preserving geological features and regulated active quarrying, as will be detailed.

This presentation will describe how geological heritage and quarrying are co-managed in Charnwood Forest, using examples from across the Geopark. The legislative and regulatory underpinning to geoconservation in quarries will be explained, alongside details of how the Geopark has shaped bespoke development conditions to ensure both continued conservation of geological features, and increased public engagement. The protocols and projects developed in Charnwood Forest may provide a useful case study for other regions seeking to conserve geoheritage in areas of active quarrying.

title: From Estuary to Impoundment: A Geological Archive of Anthropocene Water-Quality and Ecosystem-Service Change Before and After Damming of the Nakdong Estuary, South Korea
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Sauceda, Miranda [1], Ross, Ashley D. [2], Dellapenna, Timothy [3], Adyasari, Dini [4]
affiliations: (1) Marine and Coastal Management and Science, Texas A&M University at Galveston, Galveston, Texas, USA
(2) Marine and Coastal Management and Science, Texas A&M University, Galveston, TX, USA
(3) Oceanography, Texas A&M University, Marine Science, Galveston, TX,
(4) Marine and Coastal Management and Science, Texas A&M University, Galveston, TX, USA
abstract:
Estuarine dams reorganize the systems they impound, converting free-flowing, tidally flushed estuaries into poorly circulated, lake-like basins that accumulate fine sediment and associated contaminants. This interdisciplinary study integrates coastal-geological analysis with a social-ecological ecosystem-services framework to reconstruct how one such transition restructured the water quality of the Nakdong River Estuary in southeastern South Korea.

Following closure of the Naksan Dam in 1934, the West Nakdong was isolated from river flow and tidal exchange was suppressed. Prior work documents that this alteration drove sediment convergence and an energy-regime shift, part of a broader pattern of Anthropocene estuarine loss in which South Korea has reclaimed roughly 60 percent of its estuarine area. Dated sediment cores recovered downstream of the dam are analyzed for grain size, heavy-metal geochemistry, and 239+240 Pu geochronology, which anchors the stratigraphy and assigns each down-core shift a calendar date.

Grain-size analysis is expected to record a transition from a sand-dominated, tidally energetic channel to a mud-dominated basin, evidencing the loss of tidal flushing that follows tidal-prism reduction. Heavy-metal stratigraphy (Cu, Cd, Zn, Ag, and Hg; lithium-normalized) is expected to show enrichment above pre-damming background, reflecting reduced contaminant export and increased retention in the finer, poorly flushed substrate. Change-point detection, pre- versus post-boundary comparison, and correlation analysis are used to locate and characterize these shifts.

To complement this stratigraphic and geochemical record, the study applies a social-ecological resilience framework, interpreting the biophysical changes as an ecosystem service tradeoff. Provisioning objectives such as flood control, agricultural and industrial water supply, and reclaimed land were secured at the measurable expense of regulating services such as tidal flushing, water purification, and salinity regulation.

By pairing sediment archives with an ecosystem-services lens, this study frames the Nakdong as a geological archive of Anthropocene change in a dam-altered coastal basin. It offers a transferable, interdisciplinary framework for regions weighing comparable flood infrastructure, and demonstrates how stratigraphy and geochemistry can quantify the water quality dimension of ecosystem services tradeoffs.

title: From Spoil to Supply: Rare Earth Element Potential of the Windber Coalfield, Pennsylvania
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources (Posters)
authors: Gasior, Ian v. [1], Kerrigan, Ryan [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences and the Environment, University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown, Johnstown, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Geosciences and the Environment, University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown, Johnstown, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
The discovery of rare earth elements (REEs) in coal refuse piles has generated renewed interest in legacy coal due to the potential economic and environmental benefits. Two coal refuse piles in Western Pennsylvania were examined during this study: Eureka No. 35 mine in Windber, PA and Miller Shaft in Portage, PA. Both operated for over 50 years within the Windber coalfield, targeting the lower Kittanning coal seam until their closures in the 1950s. Since then, the discarded subeconomic tailings have been open to the environment, polluting local waterways with acid mine drainage (AMD). With the growing demand for REEs, which serve as critical components in many electronics and renewable energy applications, an additional domestic source of REEs would be advantageous to remain competitive in the global market.

The coal refuse piles were characterized through field mapping, sampling, whole-rock geochemistry (major, minor, and trace elements), and LiDAR-derived volumetric analysis. Integration of our characterization with current REE market valuations provides for a determination of the economic potential harbored within these refuse piles. Forty-seven samples were collected from the two study sites; observed lithologies included shale/claystone, sandstone, coal, and acid mine leachate (in order of abundance). Twenty-six representative samples (14 from Eureka No. 35 and 12 from Miller Shaft) were submitted for whole-rock geochemical analysis of major, minor, and trace elements. The geochemical analyses revealed a wide range of major and minor element compositions; however, REE patterns were consistently enriched except for some minor outliers. Whole-rock geochemistry revealed consistently enriched REE concentrations, averaging 260 ppm (SD = 96.6 ppm), with the highest values occurring in coal, clay-rich, and oxidized materials. LiDAR-derived volume calculations determined the following metric tonnage: Eureka No. 35 = 1,792,000 and Miller Shaft = 115,000. Integrating volume, elemental concentrations, and economic value allows for a first order approximation of the net value stored in the piles. The presence of critical minerals in both sites may provide additional economic incentives for remediation efforts. Even without economically feasible REE recovery, remediation of these refuse piles is essential to address legacy contamination, safeguard surrounding ecosystems, and restore impacted landscapes.

abstract: Landslides are severe geohazards that impact communities, ecosystems, and landscape evolution globally. In the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, steep slopes and extreme rainfall events commonly trigger landslides and debris flows. In September of 2024, Hurricane Helene, coupled with a preceding rainfall event, caused catastrophic flooding and extensive landsliding across the region. Wilson Creek, a fourth-order stream along the Blue Ridge Escarpment, drains 168 square kilometers and experienced high rainfall during Helene, triggering landslides throughout the basin. Using LiDAR change detection, satellite imagery, and site visits, we have mapped over 500 landslides within the Wilson Creek drainage basin and into Avery County more broadly. Our mapping contributes to the broader inventory initiated by the USGS LASER program and now continued by the NCGS. This preliminary map indicates that failures have preferred east and southeast facing slopes, although failures occur on all aspects. The majority of failures occurred on modified slopes, and many landslides impact the streams below. We observe a variety of slide types including landslides, debris flows, and blowouts. A complete inventory of landslides caused by Helene is crucial in comparing past events, understanding the factors that drive these landslides, and predicting future failures. As climate change continues to affect rainfall intensity, landslide research is vital in order to preserve property and human life.

title: Was “Barrovian” Metamorphism in the Manhattan Prong, New York, USA, Driven by Mantle Heating?
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Castro, Adrian E. [1], Viete, Daniel Ricardo [2], Brigham, John Mark [3], Jaret, Steven J. [4], Spear, Frank S. [5], Roberts, Nicolas M. [6], Weed, Riley [7], Baxendell, Nivale [8], Baxter, Ethan [9]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(2) Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD,
(3) Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA,
(4) Kingsborough Community College (CUNY), Brooklyn, NY,
(5) Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY,
(6) Hamilton College, Clinton, NY,
(7) Wellesley College, Wellesley Hills, MA,

abstract:
Though regional Barrovian metamorphism has long been recognized as a fingerprint of collisional orogenesis, the sources of heat needed to reach peak pressure-temperature (P–T) conditions remain ambiguous. Recent work has suggested that the P–T conditions of Barrovian metamorphism may require significant basal heating of thinned crust, followed by collision and thickening. This model would produce a two-stage P–T path characterized by low P/T followed by intermediate P/T metamorphism. Evidence of the earlier event, however, may be obscured if rocks spend protracted time at peak temperature. Thus, evidence of this two-stage path is most likely to be preserved in rocks that experienced transient peak temperatures. Some of the rocks underlying the Manhattan Prong in the Central Appalachians, USA have recently been shown to preserve evidence for rapid and pulsed metamorphism during the Devonian Acadian orogeny, and thus are an excellent natural lab to explore the drivers of Barrovian metamorphism.

Here we present results from two garnet-bearing metapelites of Manhattan Schist sampled from Manhattan, New York City. Sample MAT-2017-01a is a garnet-kyanite migmatite schist which has been previously reported to record peak conditions of ~750 °C and 9 kbar and a bulk garnet Sm-Nd age of ~386 Ma. Sample GWB-01a is a garnet-kyanite-staurolite-sillimanite schist with garnet porphyroblasts typically >1 mm in diameter. Garnet grains preserve inclusion-poor cores, sillimanite-included mantles, and kyanite-included rims. Garnet cores and mantles preserve typical Mn-growth zoning, whereas rims are depleted in Mn and enriched in Ca. The synthesis of this data with thermodynamic modeling and QuiG barometry suggests a two-stage P–T path: (M1) low P/T metamorphism at ~650 °C and 6 kbar, and (M2) burial intermediate P/T metamorphism at ~675 °C and 9 kbar. Bulk garnet Sm-Nd dating retrieved a growth age of c.377 Ma. Preliminary Mn-in-garnet diffusion modeling suggests peak conditions persisted for <10 m.y.

Taken as a whole, these data suggest the Manhattan Prong records early back-arc metamorphism (M1) followed by crustal thickening to peak conditions (M2). These results also suggest the transition from back-arc to thickening to cooling likely occurred on the order 10–50 m.y. These results will be supplemented with whole rock geochemistry of synmetamorphic amphibolites and 2D thermal modeling to further refine our interpretations.

title: Tephrochronology for Geologic Mapping
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation
authors: Walkup, Laura Casey [1]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA, USA
abstract:
Tephra layers are excellent chronostratigraphic markers because they are deposited rapidly and can be preserved in a wide variety of depositional environments, making tephrochronology a powerful tool for dating, correlating, and mapping diverse sedimentary sequences. While some tephra layers contain dateable comagmatic minerals, not all do, and distal deposits often lack these phases or the crystals are too small for analysis, necessitating correlation via glass chemistry to more proximal, datable equivalents or to other deposits with additional geologic context. In addition, tephrochronology allows us to determine whether similarly-aged tephra deposits are from the same eruption or from different eruptions that occurred during similar timeframes.

The USGS Tephrochronology Laboratory specializes in geochemically characterizing tephra and establishing geochemical correlations between tephra layers and their source eruptions via analysis of volcanic glass. Volcanic glass forms when fragmented molten magma is rapidly quenched in the air during explosive eruptions. This volcanic glass retains the geochemical signature of its parent magma chamber at the time of the eruption. Due to its low density and loftable shapes, volcanic glass can be widely dispersed while retaining its geochemical fingerprint regardless of how far from the eruptive center the tephra is deposited, enabling local, regional, and even intercontinental correlations. Tephra correlation is particularly helpful for time-transgressive deposits since tephra deposition occurs rapidly.

The USGS Tephrochronology Lab supports geologic mapping and research across the western United States by providing temporal control and deposit linkages through tephra correlation. Our internal tephra glass geochemical database is central to this work. It contains glass compositions from over 7,000 samples with which we can compare new samples. For complete tephrochronological interpretation; independent age control, stratigraphic positions, field and petrographic characteristics, eruption heterogeneity, and mineralogy are also considered. This growing resource enables identification of unknown tephra layers by chemically matching them to previously analyzed samples and known eruptions, thereby improving the chronology of the sedimentary sequences in which they are found. Each new sample is added to the database along with its geological context, enhancing the database’s utility for future studies.

abstract:
Freshwater mollusk communities in Florida’s spring-fed river systems have undergone considerable changes driven by anthropogenic activity, rising sea levels and salinity intrusions, climate shifts, and variable success of introduced taxa. To study these changes, three types of samples were collected: living mollusks (live assemblages), shell accumulations (death assemblages), and in situ bank sediments (fossil assemblages from the Late Pleistocene-Holocene) along the Wakulla and St. Marks rivers in Florida. Between 2017 and 2026, 293 samples containing 61,259 mollusks from 16 taxa were collected.

Live and fossil assemblages have an equivalent species richness of 11 taxa. However, nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) indicates that fossil mollusk communities are compositionally distinct from the live mollusk communities of both the Wakulla and the St. Marks rivers. These differences can be attributed to the presence of a native, euryhaline species ( Vitta usnea ) and two introduced species ( Melanoides tuberculata and Corbicula fluminea ) in live assemblages that are absent in the fossil assemblage. Additionally, four native, freshwater species present in the fossil assemblage are absent from live assemblages. NMDS also reveals compositional differences between live assemblages of the upper Wakulla River (the headspring and upper 5 km of the river) and those of the lower Wakulla and St. Marks rivers. Vitta usnea constitutes between 80-100% of the sampled live assemblage at sites in the lower Wakulla and St. Marks rivers, but is entirely absent from the upper Wakulla River. In the upper Wakulla River, live assemblages contain only freshwater taxa, dominated by a combination of the native Elimia floridensis , the introduced M. tuberculata , and lesser numbers of other taxa. Death assemblages are compositionally intermediate to fossil and upper Wakulla River live assemblages, as they are likely formed from both sources. However, the live assemblages of the lower Wakulla and St. Marks rivers are distinct from their respective death assemblages, suggesting changes to these live assemblages are relatively recent as they are not yet reflected in the death assemblages. These community shifts likely reflect the impact of local and regional anthropogenic and climatic disturbances on Florida’s freshwater spring and river ecosystems.

abstract:
Vertebrate microfossils from localities DNM 94 and DNM 96 in Dinosaur National Monument were incorporated into a course-based undergraduate research experience involving eighteen students. Both localities occur within the Brushy Basin Member of the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation. Students examined microfossil concentrates derived from historically processed material and newly disaggregated and sieved mudstone. The project introduced students to authentic paleontological research practices while generating specimen data from previously unsorted material.

The activity followed a scaffolded instructional sequence. Before sorting, students worked in groups of three to examine twenty printed examples of commonly encountered vertebrate microfossils, including dinosaur teeth, crocodylian and turtle material, and fish scales. Each group developed a classification system based on observable two-dimensional morphology. The class then combined these systems to establish shared descriptive criteria. Because no standardized photographic reference set existed for these localities, the system was refined into four broad categories as new materials were encountered.

Students sorted concentrates with fine-tipped brushes under a stereomicroscope at 8× to 35× magnification and placed selected objects into 24-well slides or small vials. The wells were suitable because most recovered microfossils measured less than 2 mm in diameter and remained below the slide covers. Approximately three slides and one vial were used per student. Containers were labeled with the locality number, sorter initials, and a classification code. “V” designated readily recognizable and potentially significant vertebrate specimens, particularly teeth; “I” indicated objects with potentially identifiable morphology; “O” represented dark fossil material lacking recognizable morphology; and “N” contained material interpreted as non-fossiliferous.

Procedural refinements improved specimen recovery and accountability. Sorting trays had a tapered margin so objects could be guided directly into wells without being lifted. White plastic tablecloths beneath work areas improved recovery of dark specimens displaced by static electricity or handling. An instructor reviewed all slides and vials to identify misclassified material and ensure that potentially informative specimens were not placed in lower-priority categories. Two students then photographed the most diagnostic specimens from the class-wide “V “and “I” collections using a stereomicroscope-mounted camera. Preliminary identifications included teeth from small crocodylians, theropod dinosaurs, and an ornithischian dinosaur.

The project provided experience in collaborative classification, microfossil sorting, specimen labeling, curation, quality control, and scientific imaging while demonstrating that classroom-based research can produce usable paleontological data.

title: No allochthons allowed: Detrital zircon provenance contradicts Mesozoic terrane accretion in central Chile (~28–34°S)
session_title: Pre–Neogene Tectonic evolution of South America (Posters)
authors: Cramer, Amarissa C [1], Ronemus, Chance [2], Sundell, Kurt [3], Hazelbush, Parker [4], Hursh, Tiana Belle [5], Murillo, Ismael [6], Graham, Stephan A. [7], Dobbs, Stephen C. [8]

(2) Idaho State Univeristy, Pocatello, ID, USA

abstract:
Plate reconstructions based on seismic tomography have revived the provocative idea that the Mesozoic arc of coastal Chile is an intra-oceanic terrane accreted to South America along a cryptic Late Cretaceous suture, perhaps coinciding with the Central Valley. This proposal stands in stark contrast to the dominant view of long-lived east-dipping subduction beneath the continent since late Paleozoic time. These two models make distinct predictions for the provenance of Triassic–Early Cretaceous sedimentary rocks in coastal Chile, which should lack Gondwanan basement input in an allochthonous scenario. We test these predictions with 4,224 new detrital zircon U-Pb ages (after data-quality filters) from 15 samples of Triassic–Cretaceous sandstones collected in two latitudinal transects (28–29 and 32–34°S) crossing the proposed suture (Coastal to Frontal Cordillera), alongside a compilation of zircon U-Pb ages from coeval deposits and potential source terranes (>12,000 ages).

Within each transect, samples yield multimodal age spectra that are similar both across the proposed suture and through time. Dominant age populations are consistent with South American sources, including the Permo–Carboniferous Elqui-Limarí arc (~290–310 Ma), Ordovician Famatinian arc (~450-480 Ma), and Mesoproterozoic Sunsás basement (~1.0-1.1 Ga), with subordinate syndepositional and Archean ages. We find no anomalous age populations indicative of an exotic terrane. Statistical dissimilarity between sample composites paired across the proposed suture (median Kuiper V = 0.15; cross-corellation R2 = 0.89) does not exceed intraformational variability, and no sample resembles a synthetic non-Gondwanan spectrum constructed to simulate an exotic arc (median V = 0.88).

Similar detrital zircon age spectra across the proposed suture from the Triassic through the Cretaceous indicate shared Gondwanan sediment sources, contradicting terrane accretion models and recording generally consistent provenance across ~150 Myr of margin evolution. These findings constrain models of Andean crustal assembly and suggest that Central Chile represents a single, long-lived, west-facing continental margin. This study refines tectonic reconstructions of the southeastern Pacific margin and requires reconsideration of tomography-based models for the plate tectonics of Mesozoic South America.

title: Dynamic marine redox evolution and transient oxygenation at 1.64 Ga: Constraints from a thallium isotope spatial transect
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales (Posters)
authors: Zhou, Anwen [1], Owens, Jeremy D. [2], McGoldrick, Peter [3], Adiatma, Yoseph Datu [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
(2) Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL,
(3) University of Tasmania,
(4) Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL,
abstract:
The mid-Proterozoic (1.7–0.7 Ga) ocean has long been regarded as persistently anoxic, whereas emerging evidence suggests episodes of transient oxygenation. However, the spatial extent of these oxygenation events remains poorly constrained. Thallium (Tl) isotopes (ɛ 205 Tl) serve as a robust paleo-redox proxy, primarily tracking manganese oxides (Mn oxides) burial and providing insights into marine redox conditions. Tl isotope records from the early Mesoproterozoic remain sparse, limiting our understanding of global redox architecture. Here, we investigate the ~1.64 Ga Barney Creek Formation (McArthur Basin, Australia) using three stratigraphically equivalent drill cores (H6, BC3 and BMR2). These cores span a proximal to distal gradient relative to the seafloor hydrothermal system associated with the supergiant McArthur River (HYC) Zn-Pb-Ag deposit.

A key feature of our spatial transect is the extreme negative Tl isotope excursion recorded at the proximal H6 site (~2 km from the hydrothermal center). Here, ε²⁰⁵Tl reaches −5.4, distinctly different from the hydrothermal input Tl isotope composition (~−2.0) but close to the modern fully oxygenated ocean value (ε²⁰⁵Tl ≈ −6.0). The extremely negative Tl isotope signal likely reflects Mn oxide burial in the Mesoproterozoic McArthur Basin. This pattern implies that, despite the predominantly anoxic state of the Mesoproterozoic ocean, localized oxygenated niches (i.e., oxygen oases) may have developed, providing favorable conditions for Mn oxide precipitation and subsequent burial. However, the distal BMR2 core (~23 km from the hydrothermal center) records a distinct Tl isotope signature, with relatively stable ε²⁰⁵Tl values (−2.6 ± 1.8, 2SD), close to previously reported Mesoproterozoic seawater background values, The intermediate BC3 core records ε²⁰⁵Tl values that fall between proximal H6 and distal BMR2, revealing a systematic spatial gradient in Tl isotope compositions across the transect. We therefore propose a two-endmember mixing model, with the H6 signature representing an Mn oxide evolved endmember and the background seawater representing another endmember, to explain the observed Tl isotope gradient across the transect.

title: Rapid sulfurization and biomarker preservation in a transient euxinic environment: insights from Trunk River Lagoon, Cape Cod.

authors: Dumit, Diana [1], Moynihan, Molly A [2], Husain, Fatima [3], Vanderscheuren, Hannah [4], Liu, Xiaolei [5], Ruff, S. Emil [6], Summons, Roger E. [7]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Florida Atlantic University, Boca Raton, Florida, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Atmospheric an Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(4) Ecosystems Center, Marine Biological Laboratory, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(5) School of Geosciences, The University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA

abstract:
Lipid biomarkers derived from anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria are widely used as indicators of ancient photic zone euxinia (PZE) and ocean anoxia. Here, we present a biomarker study of the Trunk River Lagoon (Falmouth, MA), a shallow, oxygenated estuary that transiently turns euxinic and hosts blooms of blooms of anoxygenic phototrophs. Although these microorganisms are considered strict anaerobes and are typically restricted to permanently euxinic settings, they colonize an initially oxygenated water column in this particular case. The Trunk River Lagoon thus represents a valuable modern system for investigating PZE biomarker signatures that are formed transiently in shallow water.

We sampled the water column during an active bloom across a vertical profile spanning the lagoon’s surface water, the water-bloom interface, the bloom core, and the bloom-sediment interface. Using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOF) and gas chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (GC-MS/MS), we conducted a comparative analysis of carotenoids of three lipid pools: functionalized (intact) lipids, sulfur-bound lipids, and geolipids (fossil biomarkers). Our results reveal distinct carotenoid distributions among these pools. Notably, the sulfur-bound lipid pool contains biomarkers including steroids, hopanoids, and carotenoids, and demonstrates that sulfurization occurs rapidly within the water column.

These findings challenge the assumption that euxinic biomarker signatures are markers of persistent anoxia, and they highlight the sulfur-bound lipid pool as an essential and underexplored archive for reconstructing modern ancient euxinic environments. The Trunk River Lagoon demonstrates the utility of transient phototrophic bacterial ecosystems for calibrating the formation, transformation, and preservation of geobiological signals.

title: Characterization of the Alta Thrust System, Utah, USA: Evaluating the Connection of Cordilleran Salients and Superimposed Tilting
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Anderson, Zach [1], Reeher, Lauren J. [2], Conger, Abigail [3], Patton, Harrison [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Natural Resources, Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
(2) Department of Natural Resources, Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, Utah,
(3) Utah Geological Survey, Millcreek, UT,
(4) University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
abstract:
The Alta thrust system exposed near Alta, UT, is composed of three stacked thrusts known as the Alta, Columbus, and Reed & Benson thrusts. These thrusts provide a unique opportunity to understand Cordilleran shortening within the core of the Uinta-Cottonwood arch, a structural high between the Wyoming and Charleston-Nebo salients of the Sevier thrust belt. Building off foundational work by Calkins et al. (1943) and Crittenden (1967), we present new geologic mapping, kinematic data, and fault branchline maps to better characterize the kinematics and origin of these structures.

The thrust faults dip 10°-30° east, ramp upsection to the east, and have moderate to small (100’s of meters) stratigraphic separation that decreases to the north, south, and east. Kinematic indicators (e.g., slickenlines) on the faults suggest an overall dip-slip, top to the east motion. Folds within the thrust blocks plunge moderately to the northwest, and have axial planes that dip moderately southwest. These thrusts represent thin-skinned shortening structures that developed either during early phases of the Cretaceous Cordilleran orogeny as footwall imbricates to the Charleston-Nebo salient, as southern extensions of frontal thrusts of the Wyoming salient, or as an independent system that bridged a gap between thrust salients. All thrusts are cut by Eocene-Oligocene intrusive rocks and high-angle normal faults related to Basin and Range extension.

Post-thin-skinned deformation has variably tilted all structures to their current orientations. We evaluate three potential drivers for this post-thrusting tilting: 1) Laramide (thick-skinned) structural relief extending west from the Uinta arch, 2) eastward tilting in the hanging wall of the Wasatch normal fault, and 3) potential crowding and folding associated with the emplacement of the Cottonwood and Alta stocks. Untangling these superimposed tilting events is critical for accurately restoring the initial geometry of the thrust sheets and fully understanding their role in accommodating regional shortening.

title: Tracing Emerging Contaminants from Convective Storms to Karst Aquifers: An Integrated Study of Microplastics, PFAS, and Stable Isotopes
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part I)
authors: Nordstrand, Thomas Edward [1], Gao, Yongli [2], Afzal, Amna [3], Weathers, Michael Zachary [4], Fu, Qi [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA
(3) University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA
(4) University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA
(5) University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA
abstract:
Understanding the pathways by which emerging contaminants move through the atmosphere and hydrologic system is critical for assessing environmental exposure and informing water-resource management. Over the past several years, we have investigated the occurrence, transport, and fate of microplastics and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) across multiple components of the hydrologic cycle in Texas using complementary geochemical and isotopic approaches. Our work includes analyses of precipitation, hail, surface water, springs, and karst recharge features, providing a unique opportunity to examine contaminant transport from atmospheric deposition to groundwater.

Previous studies demonstrated that precipitation efficiently scavenges atmospheric microplastics, while stable isotopes constrain moisture sources and storm evolution. More recent analyses of hailstones collected during severe convective storms reveal that hail acts not only as an archive of atmospheric microplastics but also as a selective scavenger, preferentially incorporating larger and denser particles while allowing smaller particles to remain suspended for longer-range transport. Concurrent monitoring within the Edwards Aquifer region shows widespread occurrence of PFAS and microplastics in springs, rivers, and recharge features, with elevated concentrations associated with urbanized watersheds and wastewater-affected reaches.

Together, these studies demonstrate that extreme weather, atmospheric deposition, and rapid recharge in karst terrains are closely linked components of the transport pathway for emerging contaminants. Integrating isotopic tracers with measurements of microplastics and PFAS provides a process-based framework for identifying contaminant sources, transport mechanisms, and environmental fate across interconnected precipitation, surface water, and groundwater. This integrated perspective supports improved conceptual models of contaminant transport and provides scientific information relevant to groundwater protection, monitoring strategies, and future regulatory decision-making in vulnerable aquifer systems.

abstract: Skin impression trace fossils provide rare evidence of dinosaur external anatomy, but isolated specimens are difficult to identify without associated skeletal material. This study evaluates two skin-impression molds, BB1 and BB2, from the Brushy Basin Member of the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation in Curecanti National Recreation Area to determine whether their scale morphology is consistent with sauropod integument. Maximum scale length, width, and relief depth were measured with calipers, and the shape of polygons were noted on both specimens. These measurements were compared with a cast of Barosaurus lentus forelimb skin from Dinosaur National Monument and with published sauropod skin-impression data. BB1 contains large, deeply relieved polygonal scales averaging 38.5 mm long, 32.5 mm wide, and 5.7 mm deep. BB2 preserves smaller polygonal scales averaging 22.8 mm long, 17.0 mm wide, and 3.1 mm deep. The Barosaurus cast has smaller, more tightly packed, rounded scales averaging 13.0 mm long and 1.6 mm deep. BB2 falls within published sauropod scale-size ranges and exhibits the characteristic non-overlapping, honeycomb arrangement of sauropod skin. Its mixture of scale sizes and packing densities may represent a transitional region between a flexible limb and a more rigid body surface. BB1 exceeds most published sauropod scale dimensions, but its morphology resembles large hexagonal impressions previously attributed to sauropods from the Morrison Formation. Although a non-sauropod origin cannot be excluded, the polygonal arrangement and regional comparisons support a sauropod affinity for both specimens.

title: Critical Need: Sustainable Development of Mineral Resources and the Mining Workforce
session_title: Mineral Resources and Society
authors: Runyon, Simone [1], Stavast, William [2], Canby, Mac [3]
affiliations: (1) Freeport-McMoRan, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(2) Freeport-McMoRan, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(3) Freeport-McMoRan, Tucson, Arizona, USA
abstract:
The energy transition, expansion of data infrastructure, and general global economic development continue to increase demand for mineral resources. Recent attention has focused on critical minerals that historically had limited global demand (e.g., rare earth elements). However, traditionally mined base metals, such as copper, are also experiencing persistent, strong demand growth. Global refined copper use exceeded 28 million tonnes in 2025, reflecting its essential role in the clean energy transition, communications, and manufacturing. A study released in 2026 by S&P Global reports that copper supply is anticipated to fall 10 million metric tons short of demand by 2040.

Meeting these needs will require addressing complex scientific and operational challenges. In response, the minerals industry is advancing new approaches to exploration, mining, processing, and workforce development to improve efficiency, sustainability, and resilience. New discoveries are increasingly being made at greater depths, and the brownfield growth that will help secure domestic mineral supplies will occur in long-lived mining districts with declining average ore grades. Industry is advancing technologies such as large-scale data integration, autonomous mining systems, and improved leaching methods that enhance resource recovery while reducing environmental impacts.

Continued industry innovation requires a skilled and diverse workforce. Since the early 1980s, undergraduate geology enrollment in the United States has been highly variable, and currently job demand exceeds the supply of trained graduates. Industry, academia, and government must work together to expand educational pathways, address workforce shortages, and broaden participation in the geosciences and mining professions.

Maintaining public trust is also essential to strengthening the mining workforce and supporting responsible resource development. Industry initiatives such as the Copper Mark and the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) promote responsible production practices, community engagement, and sustainability. Building public trust requires both education about modern mining practices and consistent demonstration of responsible performance.

Collaboration across disciplines, sectors, and communities is necessary for responsible mineral resource development. By advancing geoscience, fostering innovation, investing in people, and more effectively engaging with society, we can sustainably secure the mineral resources needed for future generations.

title: Integrated Geophysical and Remote Sensing Investigation of Two Contrasting Landslide Systems in Southern California: Palos Verdes Peninsula and the San Gabriel Foothills
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies
authors: Robles-Ernst, Jacquelyn [1], Alam, Md Iftekhar [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Cal Poly Pomona, Pomona, Ca, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Cal Poly Pomona, Pomona, California, USA
abstract:
Slope hazards across Southern California arise from different mechanisms, but often share the same controlling factors: rock and soil structure, moisture, and land use. This study looks at two contrasting sites: the Palos Verdes Peninsula, where coastal bluff retreat and deep-seated landslides are tied to marine terrace sediments and wave erosion, and the Sierra Madre foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains, where post-fire debris flows depend on wildfire severity and nearby active faults. Drought and instrumental meteorological records spanning the past century were used to understand the impact of the climatic variables on the stability of both landforms.

An integrated geodatabase was developed incorporating USGS and NASA geophysical and remote-sensing datasets. Modern and traditional land use, archival aerial imagery, fire burn perimeters, geological maps, and historical meteorological data were integrated to evaluate hazard controls at both sites. Planned field surveys will complement these datasets by characterizing shallow subsurface lithology, density, and moisture conditions at selected sites. Field sites in both areas have been selected based on geologic setting, hazard history, and proximity to homes and road infrastructure.

Preliminary results show that debris-flow susceptibility at Sierra Madre varies across drought, atmospheric river, and El Niño/La Niña conditions. At Palos Verdes, geophysical anomalies line up spatially with mapped historical landslide boundaries. These results demonstrate the value of integrating geophysical and geospatial datasets to improve hazard characterization, support accessible communication of natural hazards, and establish a framework for future risk and exposure modeling grounded in measurable environmental observations

abstract: The drainage history of Glacial Lake Hitchcock encompasses a long-evolving narrative that has been studied for over two centuries. Recent investigations have integrated radiocarbon (¹⁴C) dating, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) exposure ages, and the North American Varve Chronology (NAVC) to refine the lake’s temporal framework. Along the western shore in north-central Connecticut, the Farmington River delta was established as an ice-marginal feature between approximately 17.9 and 17.6 cal ka. Previous mapping suggests three separate depositional phases for this delta, each corresponding to lake-level changes driven by meltwater stream discharge variability and the evolution and failure of the sediment dam at Rocky Hill, Connecticut, amid regional isostatic rebound. We utilize a new outcrop, sediment cores, and ground-penetrating radar (GPR) data from the late-stage easternmost portion of the delta to evaluate whether these three distinct depositional phases withstand modern geophysical reinterpretation. Stratigraphy in the upper 3 meters is consistent with braided rivers carrying silt, sand, and fine gravel within a topset environment. GPR profiles reveal numerous large, linear paleochannels downcutting across the post-stable stage delta, which field observations confirm are filled with medium-to-fine sand. Rather than the regional lake-level shifts proposed by Stone et al. (2015), we interpret these channels and their sand fill as products of local lake-level fluctuations potentially driven by seasonal outburst floods and rapid deglaciation. To establish a precise timeline, representative samples from the paleochannel fill and an adjacent relict sand dune will undergo OSL and ¹⁴C analysis. Integrating these site observations with forthcoming geochronology and paleoclimate proxies will refine the temporal framework of Glacial Lake Hitchcock, further resolving its late-stage sedimentation and drainage history.

title: Critical minerals mapping across the United States under the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI)
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Jones, James V. [1]

abstract:
The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) collects modern, high-quality geoscience data nationwide to support a wide range of applications including the identification of domestic critical mineral resources. Earth MRI began in 2019 with the collection of new, high-resolution topographic data, airborne magnetic and radiometric surveys, and geological and geochemical mapping by USGS-funded state geological survey partners. The USGS works closely with state surveys to identify and prioritize data needs, and data collection is prioritized over areas of known or suspected critical mineral potential. From 2022 through 2026, Earth MRI data collection activities were substantially augmented by five years of supplemental congressional funding ($320M total), which expanded projects, accelerated data collection, and also allowed for the addition of airborne electromagnetic surveys, regional- and district-scale hyperspectral remote sensing surveys, and national inventory and characterization of critical mineral potential of mine waste sites. This generational investment and the resulting data and maps are collectively transforming our understanding of the nation’s bedrock geologic framework. Earth MRI data directly support identification and assessment of critical mineral potential through resource prospectivity mapping across the nation while also supporting regional energy resource studies (particularly geothermal and geologic hydrogen), informing the identification and assessment of natural hazards, and providing key insights for modeling groundwater availability and vulnerability. This presentation will provide an overview of the national-level Earth MRI-supported projects featured in this session and include status updates, recent outcomes, and strategic directions for the initiative.

All Earth MRI data, maps, and reports are made publicly available through USGS and state geological survey websites. More information on Earth MRI can be found at https://usgs.gov/special-topic/earthmri.
