title: Unexpected Heterogeneity of Successive Communities of the Ediacara Biota Preserved Within the Ediacara Member, South Australia
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: McCandless, Heather K. [1], Droser, Mary L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
abstract: Fossils of the soft-bodied Ediacara Biota occur within the Ediacara Member (Rawnsley Quartzite, South Australia) where entire communities of Earth’s earliest animals are preserved as in situ casts and molds on the base of successive bedding planes. This style of preservation results from extensive organic mats that stabilized Ediacaran sediments and prevented reworking or amalgamation of discrete event horizons. At dig site 1T within Nilpena Ediacara National Park (NENP), nine fossil beds have been excavated from a 1.3m thick succession of the Oscillation Rippled Sandstone Facies. All excavated beds are fine-grained and range in average thickness from approximately 2-10 cm. Beds are largely planar to ripple laminated and are interpreted to represent deposition above storm wave base. Of the nine excavated sandstone fossil beds, beds 1T-LB2, 1T-LB3, and 1T-NA have evidence of relatively immature organic mats, but beds 1T-LB2 and 1T-LB3 each preserve only a single body fossil while 1T-NA preserves a diverse population of relatively abundant fossils. The six remaining beds all have evidence of mature mats. Bed 1T-BOF is dominated by dense macroalgae, bed 1T-T is dominated by abundant Tribrachidium , and bed 1T-A is dominated by Parvancorina and Ikaria specimens that are almost exclusively under 5mm in length. Beds 1T-LS and 1T-F preserve dense and diverse fossil communities with high evenness, and bed 1T-LB1 preserves almost no fossils. Mat maturity is interpreted to be a function of the duration between sedimentation events and is typically correlated with species richness and density in beds. The high degree of difference among fossil communities preserved on similarly mature mats within the 1T succession reflects true patchiness on the Ediacaran seafloor within a tightly constrained environmental framework. This unexpected level of variation within a small stratigraphic range provides unique insight into the original heterogeneity of the Ediacaran seafloor prior to the advent of bioturbation and the consequential time averaging of the fossil record.

title: Big River Versus Volcanic Arc—The Arc Almost Wins in the Pliocene Diversion of the Columbia River through Wallula Gap, Washington
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: O'Connor, Jim E. [1], Cannon, Charles [2], Staisch, Lydia Marilyn [3], Schwid, Maxwell [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Portland,
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Portland, Oregon, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Portland, OR,

abstract:
The Columbia River is globally unique—a continental river transecting a volcanic arc. The resulting Columbia River Gorge is the river’s long-held path through the active Cascade volcanic arc since before emplacement of the ~16-10 Ma Columbia River Basalt Group (CRBG). Yet a major post-CRBG diversion is evident east of the Cascade Range, where quartzite-rich gravel trace a former route west from Pasco Basin in eastern Washington up the Yakima Valley and then southwest into the eastern Columbia River Gorge where it intercepts the present river path. A diversion after the 10 Ma emplacement of the youngest CRBG flows displaced the river >50 km south to the present route through Wallula Gap, the Umatilla basin, and into the Dalles basin in the eastern gorge.

Recent geologic mapping, clast provenance studies, and detrital zircon geochronology show no evidence of the Columbia River in the Dalles basin until after 5.4 Ma. Moreover, detrital zircons in deposits marking the river’s prior pathway are as young as 3.5 Ma, indicating diversion after then. This timing and local stratigraphic relations indicate emplacement of the Simcoe Mountains volcanic field, active along the eastern flank of the volcanic arc between ~4 Ma to 0.6 Ma, triggered the shift. We propose canyon-filling Simcoe lavas blocked the Columbia River along the southern margin of the volcanic field, thereby causing lacustrine conditions recorded within the Ringold Formation of Pasco basin after 4.8 Ma. The last episode, about 3.4 Ma, raised the Ringold lake to a new outlet saddle in the Horseheaven Hills anticline bounding the southern margin of Pasco Basin, thus directing the river south, incising Wallula Gap through the Horseheaven Hills, and then west on its new course through Umatilla and Dalles basins.

These results imply substantial post-3.5 Ma rock uplift, signaled by Columbia River deposits, formerly near-sea-level, now found as high as 900 m above sea level on the crests of Yakima folds. We also speculate that this diversion was a close call; a less voluminous Columbia River at the time of impoundment could have led to a terminal Ringold Lake rather than an overtopping one, thus separating the Columbia River from the sea and giving the arc victory, apparently the eventual outcome in most arc versus river scenarios.

title: The Simsboro Formation: A Diagenetic Quartz Arenite Resulting from Aggressive Eogenetic Weathering During the Paleocene-Eocene Transition
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Dworkin, Steve I. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Science, Baylor University, Waco, Texas, USA
abstract:
Outcrops of the central Texas Simsboro Formation were deposited in a nearshore fluvial setting and are part of the thick package of Gulf of Mexico fluvial and deltaic clastic sediments spanning the Paleocene-Eocene transition. Previous work on zircon geochronology indicates that Simsboro sands have a mixed provenance and this is consistent with petrographic observations made in this study. This includes 7% of quartz grains being polycrystalline, indicating a metamorphic source as well as a large contribution of locally derived volcanic sediment indicated both by euhedral and embayed quartz grains. The texture of the detrital grains also indicates direct volcanic input because 40 % of the framework grains are angular indicating that they could not have sustained any significant fluvial transport.

Simsboro sandstones are composed of 51% detrital grains, 33% cement, and 16 % porosity. Framework grains are overwhelming composed of quartz (97 %), with minor amounts of metamorphic rock fragments and trace amounts of muscovite and feldspar. The cement is exclusively composed of kaolinite. The majority of the porosity is intergranular although secondary porosity makes up 4% if the rock volume.

Kaolinite is the only cement and comprises 33% of the whole rock. Kaolinite occurs as a grain replacement that fills oversized intergranular areas and some of the adjacent intergranular areas. The abundance of oversized pores and oversized intergranular areas filled with kaolinite equate to a loss of 30% of the original framework grains. Therefore, the Simsboro is a diagenetic quartz arenite that has undergone extensive meteoric diagenesis that destroyed all of the labile grains. The lack of Fe and Mn oxide cements indicates that kaolinite formed under low oxygen conditions in the shallow subsurface. Modern day environments where kaolinite is formed near the Earth’s surface have mean annual precipitation exceeding 40 inches of rain per year confirming that central Texas conditions during the PETM transition were considerably wetter than today.

title: Revisiting Legacy Ocean Drilling Cores to Reevaluate Global Controls on Silica Diagenesis
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections
authors: Aiello, Ivano [1], Johnson, Nalina [2]
affiliations: (1) Moss Landing Marine Laboratories, San Jose State University, Moss Landing, California, USA
(2) Moss Landing Marine Laboratories, San Jose State University, Moss Landing, California, USA
abstract:
Legacy DSDP, ODP, and IODP core collections provide an exceptional opportunity to revisit fundamental geological questions using analytical methods unavailable when the cores were originally recovered. We are using archived marine sediment cores to test long-standing hypotheses on the controls governing the transformation of biogenic silica (opal-A → opal-CT → quartz), one of the most important rheological transitions in the shallow subseafloor. This reaction produces large reductions in porosity, increases sediment brittleness and permeability, influences fluid migration, and has implications for basin evolution and the deep biosphere.

Current kinetic models of silica diagenesis were developed largely from laboratory experiments and early ocean drilling observations during the 1970s and 1980s. Although these models have guided interpretations for more than four decades, numerous drilling expeditions have documented silica phase transitions occurring outside their predicted stability fields, including opal-A preserved in unusually hot subseafloor environments and opal-CT forming under unexpectedly low-temperature conditions. The global scientific drilling archive provides a unique empirical dataset to evaluate these discrepancies across diverse lithologic and thermal settings.

Our work also illustrates the challenges and opportunities of archive-based research. Early sampling based solely on requested depth intervals frequently failed to recover silica-rich horizons, emphasizing that successful studies require lithology-guided sampling of archived cores. We therefore developed an integrated workflow combining handheld XRF screening, quantitative X-ray diffraction, SEM characterization of opal-CT microfacies, and archived shipboard datasets including in situ temperatures, geothermal gradients, sedimentation rates, physical properties, and pore-water geochemistry.

Preliminary results indicate that host lithology influences the onset of silica diagenesis. Carbonate-rich and clay-rich successions exhibit different thresholds for the initial precipitation of opal-CT, producing distinct intercepts in crystallographic ordering versus temperature relationships. However, once opal-CT precipitation begins, the increase in crystallographic ordering (measured by XRD d-spacing) with temperature follows remarkably similar trends across contrasting lithologies despite major differences in burial history and thermal regime. These observations suggest that lithology primarily controls where silica diagenesis begins, whereas subsequent ordering is governed by a common temperature-dependent pathway. This study demonstrates how legacy scientific drilling collections can generate new global datasets that refine long-standing kinetic models and reveal previously unrecognized controls on subseafloor mineral transformations.

title: Investigating Changes in Floodplain Soil Carbon at an Unnamed Tributary of Pine Creek in Woodward, PA Seven Years After Stream Restoration and Live Staking
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Pedrotty, Abigail [1], Chamberlin, Ellen [2], Bergeron, Allison [3]
affiliations: (1) Bucknell University, Department of Geology and Environmental Geosciences, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Bucknell University, Department of Geology and Environmental Geosciences, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) Bucknell University, Department of Environmental Geosciences, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
Livestaking is a common and low-cost stream restoration method wherein cuttings are taken from native trees and planted with the goal of revegetating stream banks to reduce floodplain and bank erosion, reduce water temperatures, and provide riparian habitat. However, long-term monitoring of live staked sites is limited, and the extent to which they improve channel stability and sediment storage is unclear. Here we investigate the impact of live stakes on soil properties (including organic carbon) at an unnamed tributary of Pine Creek in Woodward, PA, which is a first-order stream that was previously channelized through agricultural land, causing incision, poor water quality, and stream impairment. From 2018 to 2020, live stakes were planted on the floodplain and hard structures were placed along the channel. In 2021 and 2026, 90-cm soil cores were collected along five transects perpendicular to the tributary, with sites spaced at 5, 15 and 25m distances from each channel bank, to determine soil type and collect samples for soil organic carbon (SOC) analysis (completed on a LECO CHN 628 analyzer at Bucknell University). We also collected RTK-GPS data using a Trimble TSC510 to measure changes in floodplain elevation and channel slope.

Soil observations from June 2026 show that the typical floodplain soil is grayish brown to dark grayish brown silt loam with orange mottling and roots, similar to 2021 soil data. CHN results show that the average SOC is 2.04% site-wide, which is a 0.27% increase from 2021 and brings floodplain soil into the expected range of 2% to 5%. The upstream-most transect had the greatest increase in SOC (+0.56%) and it is located within the most successful patch of live stakes; elsewhere at the site, live stake survival was not high due to drought. However, this SOC increase was inconsistent across the floodplain and across soil depths; at three transects, average surface SOC decreased between 2021 and 2026 while average SOC at depth increased. Overall, these results show small improvements in the soil carbon over a 5-year period, with the best improvements located near successful live stake plantings.

abstract: High-latitude coastal groundwater systems are typically conceptualized by tidally modulated exchange that pumps saline ocean water into permeable sediments along coastlines. Yet new observations from a glacierized Alaskan fjord reveal a short-residence, seasonally restricted mechanism active only during the summer meltwater period: tidally recirculated glacier meltwater. This process was identified through a multi-season monitoring effort that combined high-resolution time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography, a shore-perpendicular transect of multi-level instrumented wells, and a coastal ocean sensor positioned to capture freshwater signals from a proximal river outlet and from discharging groundwater at ebb tide. These patterns vanish outside the melt season, demonstrating that tidal recirculation depends on the seasonal abundance of surface meltwater in the estuarine environment. Well transect data reveal tidally reversing hydraulic gradients and residence times of hours to days, consistent with rapid subsurface storage and release in high-energy deposits. Concurrently, the ocean sensor records distinct pulses of fresher, cooler water during ebb tide, including meltwater signatures traceable to the nearby river plume, confirming that both locally infiltrated and river-derived meltwater contribute to this SGD flux. Stable water isotopes (δ¹⁸O, δ²H) and major‑ion chemistry from wells and coastal waters further corroborate these findings, showing clear seasonal shifts toward glacial and riverine meltwater endmembers that recirculate via tidal pumping during the glacial melt season, revealing distinct geochemical modification during subsurface transit. Together, these datasets show that tidally pumped meltwater can represent a substantial portion of total SGD to proglacial estuaries, modifying meltwater chemistry through sediment-water interactions and altering nutrient, metal, and carbonate fluxes to nearshore ecosystems. Recognizing this seasonally forced mechanism expands conceptual models of coastal hydrology in high-latitude environments and underscores the importance of tidal-glacial coupling under accelerating cryospheric change.

title: Reassessing Recharge Seasonality in the Intermountain West Using Groundwater Stable Isotopes
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Rey, David [1], Walvoord, Michelle [2], Green, Christopher T. [3], Scholl, Martha A. [4], Hecht, Jory [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,

abstract: In the mountain western United States (U.S.) recharge is commonly attributed to winter precipitation and snowmelt occurring during periods of low evapotranspiration demands. However, stable isotope signatures from shallow groundwater (less than 60 m below ground surface) across the Upper Colorado River Basin (UCRB) and adjacent western U.S. subbasins reveal a more nuanced picture of seasonal recharge. This study integrates newly developed high-resolution seasonal precipitation isoscapes with groundwater δ²H and δ¹⁸O measurements to quantify spatial patterns in long-term seasonal recharge bias and winter recharge fraction. Together, these two indicators characterize the effectiveness of seasonal precipitation for generating groundwater recharge and the volumetric contribution of precipitation occurring in each season to recharge. Results show substantial spatial variability, challenging the assumption of universally winter-dominated recharge. Aggregated HUC8-scale data indicate an inverse relationship between the proportion of winter precipitation and winter recharge bias. In fact, groundwater stable isotopes from many high-elevation, snow-dominated subbasins suggest relatively balanced recharge, with both winter precipitation and summer convective storms contributing effectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) across the broader UCRB and adjacent subbasins reveals a climate-elevation gradient driving most variability in seasonal recharge metrics, while a secondary axis captures the influence of the North American Monsoon. Contextualizing PCA results using CMIP6 LOCA2 downscaled climate projections suggest a future domain-wide shift toward more winter-biased recharge under warming scenarios. Collectively, these findings underscore the complexity of recharge processes in the western U.S. and highlight the historical importance of summer contributions to mountain groundwater—an influence that may diminish under future warming.

abstract:
SedimentSketch is a bi-lingual (English and Spanish), interactive, web-based teaching application designed for undergraduate sedimentology courses. The goal of the project was to develop an instructional resource that incorporates active learning and scaffolded instruction to support students’ understanding of key sedimentology concepts in an online environment. The application was developed around the curriculum of undergraduate sedimentology courses and includes four instructional modules: Grain Texture and Siliciclastic Components, Carbonate Components, Sedimentary Structures, and Sedimentary Environments. Each module integrates educational videos, interactive mini-games, and guided exercises that reinforce conceptual understanding and provide instantaneous feedback to users.

To evaluate the educational effectiveness of SedimentSketch, we developed and validated a sedimentology conceptual assessment that measures students' understanding of core concepts. We used control (without use of SedimentSketch) and test (using the application) groups, to assess effectiveness of SedimentSketch in undergraduate courses. The assessment was administered as both a pre- and a post-test in control and test sections of the two courses, Sedimentology and Stratigraphy and Geology of Petroleum at Texas A&M University. Students in these two courses had different levels of prior knowledge, with the first course including mostly geology majors with high-level of prior knowledge, and second being mostly engineering students with little to no prior knowledge in geology concepts.

Students in the control group received traditional instruction, whereas students in the test group supplemented classroom instruction with SedimentSketch activities. No statistically significant differences were observed between pre- and post-assessment scores in the control group. In contrast, students who used SedimentSketch demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in conceptual understanding from pre- to post-assessment in both courses.

These findings suggest that integrating interactive and active learning based digital tools into undergraduate sedimentology courses could impact student learning and provide an effective supplement to traditional instruction. SedimentSketch offers a scalable approach for incorporating active learning into geoscience education while improving students' conceptual understanding of sedimentological processes.

abstract: Eocene Lake Gosiute in southwestern Wyoming met its demise as an influx of volcaniclastic sediment ultimately filled the basin and ended lacustrine deposition. Early research hypothesized that the source of this volcaniclastic sediment originated from the proximal Absaroka volcanic province to the north, while more recent research invokes an ancient river system that sourced the Challis volcanic province of central Idaho to the northwest. Determining the source of this sediment has remained challenging because the Absaroka and Challis provinces temporally overlap, rendering provenance interpretations based on age as nonunique. We present new detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology and trace element geochemistry in the context of a measured composite stratigraphic section of the Bridger Formation in the southwestern greater Green River Basin; samples within this volcaniclastic horizon were also collected across the basin. Bridger basin strata reflects a mixed fluvial-deltatic environment with a fluctuating sediment supply, intermittent carbonate deposition, and periodic volcanism. Trace element geochemistry successfully discriminates between potential sediment sources through a non-Naïve Bayesian classification routine, with optimal chemical ratios chosen using a greedy selection algorithm. This multivariate approach was bootstrapped to ensure classification robustness by providing confidence intervals for individual analyses. Results classify >80% of detrital zircon from the volcaniclastic deposits as being sourced from the Absaroka volcanic province, thus permitting mixed sediment sourcing dominated by a south-flowing fluvial system with lesser tributaries tapping central Idaho to the northwest.

abstract: The California Geological Survey (CGS) Reported Landslide Database (RLD) is a publicly available dataset that compiles reported landslide events throughout the state and displays them on an online map for public use. Since inception, the RLD has acquired data from many sources; however, the declining availability of reliable data sources has limited the diversity of landslide reports. The California Highway Patrol (CHP) has consistently provided landslide data and has recently become the primary source for events added to the RLD. Previous methods of acquiring CHP reports required CGS staff to actively monitor and download time-limited reports as they appeared on the CHP Traffic Incident Information Page (CHP TIIP). To increase efficiency and completeness, CGS developed the CHP AutoFeed, which uses AutoHotKey to automatically download, format, and store reports from the CHP TIIP. This new approach enables CGS staff to review CHP reports well after they have been removed from the CHP TIIP, increasing the completeness of the datasets while reducing staff time. With the implementation of the CHP AutoFeed, CGS has increased its capacity to record landslides during storm events and to provide continuous coverage between storms and during small, isolated storms that CGS staff might previously have missed. Efforts are ongoing to incorporate precipitation data into the RLD, improving understanding of potential triggering rainfall conditions. We calculate precipitation accumulations for landslide events over various intervals (i.e. 15min, 30min, 1hr, 3hrs, 6hrs, 12hrs, 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, water year to date) based on the reported event time. We use a Python script to download raw precipitation data via the Synoptic Weather API, format the data, and calculate the precipitation accumulation for each interval. In addition to gathering event-specific data, we compare the cumulative number of landslides with accumulated precipitation within the California counties and National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Climate Divisions. Using CHP AutoFeed data collected during the current water year (2025-2026), we observe relationships between accumulated precipitation and the number of landslides recorded within both California counties and NCEI Climate Divisions. These results demonstrate the value of the CHP AutoFeed for documenting landslides and investigating potential precipitation-related triggering conditions.

title: Delineating the Contributions of Mantle Source Heterogeneity to the Pb and Sr Isotopic Variability of Basaltic Lavas from the Black Rock Desert Volcanic Field, Utah
session_title: Using mafic and ultramafic deposits to decipher volcanic and magmatic processes
authors: Rogers, Caroline [1], Rivera, Tiffany [2], Renson, Virginie [3], Schwartz, Darin [4]
affiliations: (1) Pine City, NY,
(2) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO,
(3) University of Missouri, Research Reactor Center, Columbia, MO,

abstract:
Basaltic volcanic fields throughout the Basin and Range Province provide important constraints on source heterogeneity and magmatic processes within continental extensional settings. Previous workers have shown that several Quaternary basalts of the Black Rock Desert volcanic field (BRD), Utah, preserve significant variability in whole-rock Pb, Sr, and Nd isotopic chemistry despite their broadly similar eruptive style and major-element compositions. The spatial and temporal variations in trace elements and radiogenic isotopes can be used to investigate the processes responsible for this variability. In this contribution, we integrate new Pb and Sr isotope analyses with existing whole-rock major and trace element geochemistry and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology from the BRD and other volcanic fields spanning a ~600 km north-south transect across Utah to investigate the petrogenesis of Quaternary basalts.

Most lavas are tholeiitic yet have distinct 87 Sr/ 86 Sr (0.7035-0.7075) and 206 Pb/ 204 Pb (16.8-18.4) compositions that correspond to individual eruptive centers despite overlapping eruption ages (0.3 to 2.5 Ma), indicating that spatial variation in source composition dominates over temporal evolution. Trace element systematics within an eruptive episode suggest magmatic differentiation trends; however, assimilation-fractional crystallization modeling using representative granitoid and sedimentary crustal lithologies fails to reproduce the observed trace element and isotopic trends, suggesting that shallow crustal contamination of these components alone cannot explain the geochemical diversity of the lavas.

Our results indicate that spatial variations in source reservoirs exert a stronger control on basalt chemistry than shallow crustal processes. We propose that Quaternary basaltic magmatism in Utah was generated from compositionally heterogeneous asthenospheric mantle that interacted with variable Precambrian lithospheric domains and limited subduction-modified subcontinental lithospheric mantle. These results suggest that small-scale heterogeneity within the lithosphere-asthenosphere system governs the chemistry of continental basalts beneath the eastern Basin and Range.

abstract: A well-known large deep-water microbial mound known as the Meiklejohn mudmound is located approximately 10 kilometers from Beatty, Nevada and is part of the Middle Ordovician (Dapinigian) lower Antelope Valley Limestone. The mudmound contains classic examples of textures known as stromatactis and zebra banding, which are typical of Middle Ordovician to recent carbonate mudmounds. Stromatactis and zebra rock textures are thought to be the result of the decay of microbial communities, among other proposed explanations. Here, we report a new analysis of this mudmound that examined facies along 3 separate transects. Samples along transects were each selected for the presence of cements, stromatactis, zebra banding, and fossils. Thin sections of various facies revealed an abundance of echinoderms, ostracods, and trilobites. There were also less abundant sponge spicules, cephalopods, the putative red algae Halysis, gastropods, calcitarchs, brachiopods, Nuia, and microbial textures. In addition to thin section analyses, cement, micritic and microbial facies were selected and drilled for iodine-to-calcium (I/Ca) local redox proxy analyses and carbon isotopes. The I/Ca preliminary results reveal low values across facies, similar to I/Ca records from nearby lower Antelope Valley sections. Carbon isotopes range from -0.51 to 0.64, also consistent with previous carbon isotope analyses from outside the mudmound. These analyses support the hypothesis that this mudmound likely formed in a deep water environment, perhaps in the presence of limited light and low oxygen. Additionally, thin section analysis confirms the mudmound framework is microbial with sponges being locally important. Future work on the Meiklejohn mudmound will focus on determining the unique environmental conditions which allowed for its development and how its formation fits into the broader understanding of Middle Ordovician mudmounds and mudmounds across geologic time.

title: Pedogenic Carbonate Isotopic Constraints on the Paleoclimate and Burial Histories of the Early Cretaceous Wayan Formation
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Marchant, Sarah [1], Burgener, Landon [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(2) Geology, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
abstract:
Atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations are increasing due to anthropogenic emissions, shifting Earth’s climate away from the glacial-interglacial cycles that dominated the Quaternary towards a warmhouse climate. Paleoclimate studies focused on previous warm periods such as the Cretaceous are a critical tool for understanding and predicting the magnitude of future climate changes. However, our understanding of past greenhouse periods is hampered by a mismatch between proxy data and climate model simulations for these periods. This discrepancy is often referred to as the Equable Climate Problem and suggests a fundamental limitation in our understanding of greenhouse climates.

The Early Cretaceous Wayan Formation, located on the leeward side of the Sevier Orogen, represents a unique case study of upland environments during the runup to the mid-Cretaceous Thermal Maximum. The Wayan Formation is coeval with more well-known formations, such as the Cedar Mountain Formation (Utah) and contains abundant pedogenic carbonate nodules, allowing for stable, clumped, and triple-oxygen isotope reconstructions of local paleoclimate conditions. In this study, the clumped isotope composition of pedogenic carbonate nodules and XRF analysis of bulk paleosol sediments will be used jointly to reconstruct mean annual temperature, mean annual range in temperature, mean annual precipitation, and growing season precipitation. Triple oxygen isotopes of pedogenic carbonate nodules will be analyzed to reconstruct evaporative effects and shed light on the local and regional hydrologic cycle. Traditional stable isotopes will be used to provide information on the likelihood of water mediated diagenesis and to differentiate water mediated diagenesis from solid state reordering—if the temperatures derived from clumped isotopes indicate that the samples are not pristine. The results of this study will increase our understanding of how the unique geography of the Wayan Formation may have impacted local climate and shed light on regional climate paleoclimate patterns in the western United States during the mid-Cretaceous, adding to our understanding of warmhouse climate systems as a whole.

abstract:
Coal balls are diagenetically altered, calcium carbonate concretions containing plant materials from the Carboniferous. In many coal balls, preservation is exceptional, preserving cellular level detail of fossil plants. The University of Illinois’ Phillips Coal Ball Collection houses the largest collection of coal balls in the world, consisting of around 50,000 collected by the late Dr. Tom Phillips.

This collection is threatened by pyrite disease, which occurs when pyrite absorbs oxygen and water and chemically reacts to produce sulfuric acid (Tacker 2020). Over time pyrite disease can destroy coal balls. Recent work has developed a scale for grading coal balls in terms of their pyrite disease severity, with zero being near perfect preservation and five being largely destroyed (Rosko et al. 2026 [In press]). This study uses scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to quantify the composition of coal balls along this scale.

We selected an initial set of six coal balls of varying levels of pyrite disease for SEM analysis. Pieces of roughly a centimeter were broken off of the coal balls and encased in a puck of resin. The pucks were polished and scanned on a Tescan Vega SEM with an EDAX octane x-ray analysis system. A representative sample of the coal ball was chosen to undergo an elemental map at 108x magnification. The study compared sulfur, aluminum, silicon, iron, and magnesium abundance and distribution among samples at different levels of degradation, with sulfur showing the clearest trends to date. Preliminary results suggest sulfur is largely absent in well-preserved samples (Level 0) but is present in all samples showing signs of pyrite disease. The spatial distribution suggests that in lower levels of severity, sulfur is isolated in the sample and increasingly becomes more distributed in more severe specimens. We are currently expanding our sample set to more coal balls. This work may lead to strategies to help preserve collections susceptible to pyrite disease in the future.

title: GEOCHEMISTRY OF SOUTHERN LOUISIANA WATERS AND IMPLICATIONS FOR RUM PRODUCTION
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: Cummings, Jayde [1], Elkins, Joe [2]
affiliations: (1) USA
(2) University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO, USA
abstract: Louisiana has supported commercial sugarcane agriculture since the eighteenth century, yet its rum industry has been comparatively limited relative to those of the Caribbean. This study examines whether the geochemistry of natural waters in southern Louisiana affects their suitability for rum fermentation and distillation. Water samples were collected from water and groundwater sites associated with the Atchafalaya Basin and Mississippi River region. Field measurements included pH, total dissolved solids, and electrical conductivity. Samples were analyzed for Ca, Fe, K, Mg, Mn, Na, and Zn using ICP-MS and ICP-OES. Elemental concentrations were mapped in ArcGIS and compared statistically with previously collected water-chemistry data from Barbados, the ‘birthplace’ of rum. The chemistry of Louisiana waters exhibits spatial variability. Calcium concentrations range from below detection limit to 146 mg/L. Sodium displays the greatest range from 6 mg/L to 511 mg/L, while magnesium varies from 0.8 to 64.2 mg/L. Fe, Mn, and Zn are consistently low or near analytical detection limits. Of the measured elements, only Potassium differs significantly between the Louisiana and water samples from collected Barbados. Louisiana samples have a higher mean K concentration (21.44 mg/L; n = 9) than Barbados samples (7.10 mg/L; n = 8). This variability likely reflects differences between silicate-rich alluvial deposits of southern Louisiana and the carbonate geology of Barbados. These findings indicate that Louisiana water chemistry does not preclude rum production, but its geographic variability should be considered when selecting water sources and building fermentations.

title: Re-Examining Meteor Crater's Rock Flour
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: Laferriere, Anjelina [1], Leben, Cambria [2], Shteynman, Leah [3], Sharp, Thomas George [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA

abstract: One of the striking features at Meteor Crater near Flagstaff, Arizona is the large amount of pulverized Coconino sandstone (>95% quartz), known as “rock flour” or “silica”, in the impact ejecta. However, the limited existing literature on rock flour, which was written before the acceptance of terrestrial impact cratering as a fundamental surface process, was limited to basic optical microscopy and sieving. The material was described as fine-grained, angular crystalline quartz resembling “crushed” fragments of glass, but it is unclear where samples were sourced, and a comprehensive and spatially resolved study of the material across the crater has not yet been published. It is not yet known whether the rock flour is a primary shock product or produced by weathering of shocked Coconino sandstone. This project aims to utilize X-ray diffraction (XRD), optical microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to sample and recharacterize rock flour across the crater, in order to better understand its composition and origin. We also present a comparison of rock flour collected at the crater with a selection of “potential rock flour” samples in the Meteor Crater Drill Hole Sample (MCDH) Collection housed at the USGS Astrogeology Science Center. XRD analysis of the rotary drilled samples, shows out of the 12 samples, 8 were 100% quartz, identifying them as potential rock flour in the collection. The other 4 samples had significant amounts of dolomite or calcite, meaning they were likely sourced from non-Coconino target rocks. Optical grain mount microscopy of the drilled (100% quartz from XRD) samples was conducted using immersion oil with a refractive index of 1.458 at 20x magnification. We analyzed MCDH #40 (9’ - 10’) just south of the crater rim, and MCDH #4 (8’ - 10’) just east of the silica pits. MCDH #40 grains were angular, platy, and <40 µm. MCDH #4 grains were angular, stubby-tabular, and >40 µm. MCDH #154 (0’- 1’) and MCDH #4 were similar in grain characteristics and location. Our results indicate that rock flour may have been sampled in the MCDH collection. We have collected a suite of rock flour samples from Meteor Crater and will also present XRD and microscopy results comparing them to the MCDH samples.

title: Environmental Variations in Feeding Ecology and Ecomorphospace Occupation of Late Ordovician (Katian) Crinoid Communities
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology
authors: Bell, Nicolas J. M. [1], Cole, Selina R. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA; School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(2) Sam Noble Museum, Norman, OK, ; School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
abstract:
Crinoids are an incredible model group for the study of community paleoecology, including niche space occupation, feeding ecology, and species interactions. Ecomorphological traits can be used to model resource use and niche occupation of species and to evaluate species interaction and structure within crinoid communities. The ecomorphological traits of crinoids reflect their filter-feeding habits through traits including calyx size and filtration fan area and density.

To effectively model the evolution of crinoid communities over time, we must also understand the degree to which environmental factors such as habitat filtering control the distribution of crinoids within communities. I analyzed the feeding ecology of crinoids from seven paleocommunities from the Katian stage of the Late Ordovician Period (453.0-445.2 Ma) to quantify the similarities and differences in crinoid feeding ecology between various sedimentary environments and evaluate relationships between crinoid ecomorphology and environment. I employed functional morphology methods to collect ecomorphological trait measurements and quantify crinoid feeding ecology and niche space occupation.

The results of this study show that there is a measurable directional control on the feeding ecology of Katian crinoid communities by depositional environment. Across an environmental gradient from deep, low-energy settings to shallow, high-energy settings, as well as a gradient from predominantly siliciclastic to predominantly carbonate settings, ecomorphological disparity increases toward the shallow, carbonate end of the gradient. Habitat filtering thus plays a major role in controlling the ecological structure and taxonomic composition of crinoid communities by preferentially excluding species with ecological strategies that are ill-suited to certain environmental conditions.

abstract: The Paleobiology Database (PBDB) is one of the most impactful and widely used digital representations of the fossil record, capturing the age, location, taxonomic identity, and geological context of fossils. Although the research and educational impact of the PBDB is far-reaching, there are key issues with the current infrastructure, which was first designed and implemented in late 1990s and early 2000s. To provide a modern technical development trajectory, better integrate with other community-curated data systems, and expand the user base, it is necessary to refactor key elements of the system. In 2025, our team received funding from the NSF Geoinformatics program to undertake a complete technological overhaul of the PBDB. Numerous improvements will arise, in part, through coupling with the Integrative Paleobotany Portal (PBot), whose cutting-edge conceptual framework allows explicit support for uncertain taxonomic classification, a more specimen-forward approach to organizing fossil data, inclusion of high quality specimen images alongside other data, and workbench capabilities that support projects from inception to publication. We have four primary objectives: 1) update the PBDB’s data model, database, and application logic to integrate PBot functions, streamline data entry, and improve technical sustainability; 2) create a more capable application programming interface; 3) construct a new web application that leverages these back-end upgrades to facilitate new science; and 4) host community events and activities to assess progress, train new members, mobilize data, and produce new educational/outreach materials focused on plant fossils. In this presentation, we introduce to the broader geosciences community our vision for the PBDB 2.0 and solicit feedback.

title: Temporal Trends of Net Primary Productivity in the Moreno Hill Formation (Turonian–Coniacian, Cretaceous), New Mexico
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials (Posters)
authors: Jackson, Aiden [1], Taylor, Ian Alexander [2], Lupia, Richard [3], Hodges, Caitlin [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 660 Parrington Oval, Norman, OK 73019, Norman, Oklahoma, USA

(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 660 Parrington Oval, Norman, OK 73019, Norman, Oklahoma, USA; Paleontology/Paleobotany, Sam Noble Museum of Natural History, 2401 Chautauqua Ave, Norman, OK 73072, Norman, Oklahoma, USA

(3) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 660 Parrington Oval, Norman, OK 73019, Norman, OK, USA; Paleontology/Paleobotany, Sam Noble Museum of Natural History, 2401 Chautauqua Ave, Norman, OK 73072, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
(4) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, 660 Parrington Oval, Norman, OK 73019, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
abstract:
Total organic carbon (TOC) preserved in paleosols may provide a proxy for evaluating relative net primary productivity (NPP) in ancient terrestrial ecosystems. The late Turonian–early Coniacian Moreno Hill Formation of western New Mexico records terrestrial ecosystems during an interval of declining atmospheric CO₂ and continued angiosperm diversification, providing an opportunity to investigate stratigraphic changes in terrestrial productivity. Here we explore whether relative NPP can be reconstructed from paleosol-derived TOC within a probabilistic modeling framework.

A previously developed probabilistic NPP reconstruction model was applied to measured TOC values from individual paleosols to estimate plausible NPP distributions for each horizon. Rather than interpreting these estimates as absolute productivity values, reconstructed productivity is expressed as deviations from the median productivity of the sampled stratigraphic interval, allowing relative changes in productivity to be evaluated through the section. Emphasizing relative rather than absolute productivity reduces the influence of uncertainties associated with long-term organic carbon preservation while preserving stratigraphic patterns within the succession.

Pedogenic features, including root traces, argillans, redox mottling, homogenized sedimentary fabrics, and slickensides, were documented post hoc for each sample to identify paleosols and provide an independent framework for evaluating reconstructed productivity. Preliminary analyses indicate that reconstructed relative NPP exhibits structured variation through the sampled succession rather than a simple stratigraphic increase or decrease. Ongoing analyses are assessing how reconstructed productivity relates to pedogenic development and additional paleoenvironmental proxies within the Moreno Hill Formation.

These preliminary results demonstrate the utility of probabilistic paleosol-based productivity reconstructions for resolving stratigraphic variability in terrestrial NPP and establishing a quantitative framework for integrating sedimentologic, pedogenic, and palynological evidence. Ongoing work will expand sampling throughout the Moreno Hill Formation and incorporate palynological data to investigate how changes in vegetation and paleosol development relate to reconstructed productivity.

abstract: The Elliot Formation in South Africa preserves a fossiliferous record spanning the Late Triassic-Early Jurassic, a time marked by significant environmental perturbation related to the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) and the end-Triassic extinction event (ETE). Despite its importance, the Elliot Formation remains poorly constrained due to limited chronostratigraphic markers. Globally, the Triassic-Jurassic boundary is characterized by a pronounced negative carbon isotope excursion dated to 201.56 Ma that is linked to CAMP volcanism and acts as a chronostratigraphic tie-point for the ETE. This study investigates whether the Elliot Formation records this characteristic negative C-isotope excursion at the Qhemegha fossil locality in the Eastern Cape of South Africa. Bulk organic C-isotope values were measured using isotope ratio mass spectrometry to create a high resolution isotope profile of the Elliot Formation at the Qhemegha locality, where samples were collected approximately every 50-100 cm. The sampled section yielded a mean δ¹³C value of -24.83‰ with a standard deviation of 2.18‰. A pronounced negative C-isotope excursion spanning 4.125 meters was identified just above 200 m in the section, within the lower Elliot Formation, where δ¹³C values reached a minimum of -30.73‰. Detrital zircon maximum depositional ages ranged from Norian at the base to Sinemurian at the top of the section, with a Rhaetian maximum depositional age constraint occurring approximately 14 m below the negative C-isotope excursion. These data together suggest that this negative C-isotope excursion may represent the ETE. Higher resolution sampling and Bayesian age modeling will be utilized to further resolve the origin of the C-isotope excursion at the Qhemegha locality. This will improve understanding of local chronostratigraphy, the effects of CAMP volcanism in southern Gondwana, and better constrain the timing of extinction and evolution across the Triassic-Jurassic boundary.

title: Serrated Ovipositor in a Mazon Creek Apterygote Insect: A New Basal Record of Endophytic Oviposition in Insects
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Carr, Thomas John [1], Young, Andrew [2], Wittry, Jack [3], McCoy, Victoria E [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI, USA
(2) The David and Sandra Douglass Collection, Evanston, IL, USA
(3) Earth Sciences, Negaunee Integrative Research Center, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, IL, USA

abstract: The fossiliferous concretions of the Mazon Creek Lagerstätte host an incredible variety of insects and plants, giving us great insight into the unique diversification of insects and development of complex plant-insect interactions during the Late Pennsylvanian. In particular, the fossil plants from the Mazon Creek fossil site preserve an abundance of ovipositional scars, suggesting that endophytic oviposition—the act of laying eggs within plant tissue—was common at this locality. The earliest evidence of endophytic oviposition in the fossil record is from the Early Pennsylvanian of Ukraine, only slightly older than examples in the Mazon Creek fauna. To date, endophytic oviposition in modern and fossil ecosystems has been attributed only to pterygote (winged) insects, suggesting that this behavior originated in that group. Within extant insects, only pterygotes are known to carry out endophytic oviposition; and among extinct insects, only pterygotes have previously been recorded as possessing the serrated ovipositors necessary to perform endophytic oviposition; therefore, endophytic ovipositional scars on fossil leaves, although they cannot be directly linked to the insect that produced them, are commonly attributed to coeval pterygote insects. Here, we present a scanning electron microscope analysis of a fossil apterygote (wingless) insect from the Mazon Creek fossil site, identified as Dasyleptus sp. We demonstrate that it possesses a specialized serrated ovipositor, indicating that it likely engaged in endophytic oviposition—the first record of an apterygote adapted for endophytic oviposition. Thus, endophytic oviposition may have originated in apterygote groups, such as Dasyleptus sp., and then been later lost and eventually regained in pterygote insect groups. Alternatively, the unique environmental challenges of the Late Pennsylvanian ecosystems may have led to an origination of endophytic oviposition in apterygote insects entirely independent of its origination within pterygote insects. This discovery changes our understanding of the development of complex egg-laying strategies in early insects and shows that these strategies were present in more basal insect groups than previously thought.

title: Reconstructing Paleofire Activity and Its Environmental Controls across the Pleistocene–Holocene Transition, Lake Izabal, Eastern Guatemala, Central America.
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: OGUNSAKIN, Oluwakunle Moyofoluwa [1], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(2) Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
abstract: The Lake Izabal region, a tropical biodiversity hotspot in eastern Guatemala, faces increasing wildfires driving forest loss, biodiversity decline, and soil erosion. Establishing baseline patterns of natural wildfire occurrence and its environmental controls is essential for contextualizing these modern trends. We present a high-resolution record of biomass burning using macroscopic fossil charcoal counts (>125 μm; MFCC) and charcoal morphological analysis (MA) from a ~12.2 m sediment core from western Lake Izabal, focusing on the latest Pleistocene–early Holocene transition (12.2–10.1 m). We integrate fossil charcoal, bulk sediment geochemistry, X-ray fluorescence data, magnetic susceptibility (MS), and bulk density to identify environmental controls on past fire activity. Two zones with distinct fire regimes are observed. In Zone 1 (12.2–11.05 m), a dense green clay with calcitic nodules, MFCC are low and variable (~6 particles/cm³), with no charcoal recovered where calcitic nodules are abundant, while MA indicates prevalence of leafy, herbaceous assemblages reflecting an open, low-biomass ecosystem. Low total organic carbon (TOC), total nitrogen (TN), sulphur (S), and elevated bulk density reflect a low-productivity setting with minimal terrestrial organic input, while calcitic nodules, marked by high calcium-to-titanium log ratios [log(Ca/Ti)], indicate evaporative conditions. Zone 2 (11.05–10.1 m) comprises a thin, poorly sorted coarse-sand bed overlain by a peaty interval and capped by a carbonate layer, with gastropods and ostracods at the peat–carbonate transition. Here, MFCC exceed 300 particles/cm³, while MA indicates a shift to predominantly woody assemblages, with root and grass contributions, recording a transition from herbaceous to woody biomass. An MS spike and low log(Ca/Ti) values at the green clay–coarse sand transition likely reflect a flooding surface, while the overlying peaty interval, with high TOC and TOC/TN ratios, suggests establishment of a productive freshwater wetland. The charcoal record therefore documents a shift from suppressed fire activity in a drier, low-biomass, herbaceous-dominated ecosystem to markedly increased fire activity in an organic-rich, woody-dominated ecosystem under wetter conditions. Fire activity likely tracked fuel load and biomass type, with wetter conditions promoting rather than suppressing biomass burning by increasing woody fuel availability. This study provides baseline data on natural fire activity across the Pleistocene–Holocene transition in the Izabal region, offering a valuable dataset for modeling fire behavior in Central America.

authors: Antoshechkina, Paula [1], Riches, Amy [2], Nguno, Anna [3], Bohrson, Wendy A. [4], Brown, Guy [5], Spera, Frank J. [6]
affiliations: (1) Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(2) SETI Institute, Mountain View, CA, USA; Principal Cosmochemistry and Planetary Science Consultant, Glasgow, United Kingdom
(3) Geological Survey of Namibia, Ministry of Industries, Mines and Energy, Windhoek, Namibia

abstract:
The Magma Chamber Simulator (MCS) is a thermodynamic model for computing the open-system, polybaric evolution of magma storage regions that includes crystallization, stoping, assimilation of crustal melts, mixing of magmas, mush entrainment and rejuvenation, and magma ascent and eruption [1]. easyMelts is a modern graphical user interface to the MELTS family of algorithms by Mark Ghiorso and co-workers that runs natively on all Mac, Windows and Linux platforms. easyMelts was designed by Einari Suikkanen (who also created the MCS Visualizer), implements built-in plotting, and exports results to Excel, making it an excellent introduction to thermodynamic modeling for users without coding experience. Recently, we have incorporated easyMelts into the open-source codebase used to maintain the MELTS component of MCS [2]. Upgrades to easyMelts simplify the workflow, increase interoperability with other MELTS software, and add support for mantle melting simulations. Here, we use easyMelts and MCS to remodel the early Cretaceous tholeiitic suite of picrite-to-rhyolite dykes, Spitzkoppe, Namibia, which proved central to our earlier work [3].

For most major oxides and trace elements (Al 2 O 3 being an exception), observed data from the dyke swarm fall between trends previously modeled with (p)MELTS for (a) closed-system fractional crystallization, dominated by conductive heat loss, and (b) heat-balanced assimilation and fractional crystallization, with local granitic crust as the contaminant. Unlike the original MELTS liquid calibration, the rhyolite-MELTS and H 2 O-CO 2 mixed fluid model successfully predicts the major element compositions of the more evolved Spitzkoppe dykes. Fractional crystallization models (without assimilation) that match the Al 2 O 3 trend slightly overestimate Fe 2 O 3 T at low MgO, and vice versa, but the overall fit to the major elements is significantly improved compared to [3]. We use easyMelts to evaluate the effects of oxygen fugacity and volatile content on modeled liquid lines of descent and MCS 1.0 to interrogate the model space between scenarios (a) and (b), iterating to generate a family of models that simultaneously explain major and trace element trends, and isotopic signatures of the Spitzkoppe suite. With MCS 2.0 we explore assimilation coupled with crystallization that may be fractional, equilibrium, or concurrent (some crystals removed and others remaining in equilibrium with melt) while ensuring thermal equilibrium between magma and cumulate.

title: Alaska's Mining Heritage
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Frederick, Phil [1], Wilson, Frederic [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Anchorage, Alaska, USA
abstract:
The exploration of Alaska’s wild beauty is steeped in stories of resource discoveries and gold rushes. This rich history of the exploration and mining of gold, copper, lead, zinc, and other metals is part geology and part societal effects. Geology determines what can be mined and where; societal effects dictate what is mined and when. This discussion focuses on some of the important societal effects that shaped Alaska’s mining history.

Two major eras of mineral exploration and mining occurred after Alaska Natives’ use of stone and native copper (and Russian coal mining). The first era, from about 1890 to World War II, consisted of wide-ranging reconnaissance across Alaska as gold discoveries in the territory and adjacent Yukon led to rushes and the discovery of all major gold placer districts and few lode gold mines. By the beginning of World War II, more than 25 million fine ounces of gold had been produced in Alaska. Other discoveries led to production of copper, silver, zinc, lead, antimony, mercury, and tungsten. However, the War Powers Acts of World War II held the price of gold at $35 per ounce and most placer and lode gold mines were no longer economically viable. The second era of widespread mineral exploration began in the 1970s, and major lode deposits, such as Red Dog (zinc, lead, silver), Fort Knox (gold), Greens Creek (silver gold, lead, zinc), Kensington (gold), Pogo (gold), and other yet undeveloped deposits were discovered. Catalysts for this reinvigorated exploration were the ending of the fixed convertibility of dollars to gold in 1971 and the passing of the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 and the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980. These societal effects led to a rising price of gold and resolution of land and resource ownership issues important to mineral exploration. The U.S. Geological Survey’s Alaska Mineral Resource Assessment Program began fieldwork in 1975 and produced many maps and folios on Alaskan mineral resources for use by government agencies and industry. Mineral exploration has been a continuing part of Alaska’s history, and although historically known as a gold producing State, the total production value of zinc has outstripped the value of gold mined in Alaska since 1989.

title: Analysis on the Origination Selectivity for Body Size of Bivalvia
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination (Posters)
authors: Levy, Joshua Leonard [1], Heim, Noel A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Climate Sciences, Tufts University, Medford, MA, USA
(2) Earth & Climate Sciences, Tufts University, Medford, MA, USA
abstract:
Earth’s biodiversity is directly impacted by the gaining and loss of new and existing taxa. The cycle of origination and extinction has greatly changed the marine organisms that exist today. Much of the biodiversity is a function of taxonomic additivities, morphologies, and ecological modes of life. Much of the previous work in the cycle of origination and extinction focuses mainly on the extinction side of the equation; there are relatively few quantitative studies of the selectivity of origination. The overall goal of the study is to determine trends in origination selectivity patterns with respect to body size and motility in the molluscan class Bivalvia.

This study uses nearly 2000 Phanerozoic marine bivalve genera with body sizes and stage-resolved stratigraphic ranges. We also incorporate the level of bivalve motility in our analyses. The primary analysis is a multiple logistic regression to assess the impact of body size and motility on the origination of new genera. Our results show that bivalves show nearly an order of magnitude increase in average body size between the Ordovician and Jurassic. This sustained increase is followed by a decrease through the Paleogene. Motility followed the Bambach and Bush (2007) ecospace framework. To simplify analyses, we converted coded motility as a binary variable: non-motile and motile. Motile genera include those who are fully motile and facultatively motile in the original ecospace framework. During most of the Paleozoic, the proportion of motile and non-motile genera is approximately equal. However, starting in the Pennsylvanian, the relative proportion of motile genera increases substantially.

Our logistic regression analysis shows that over the Phanerozoic, new genera tend or originate at small body sizes, while there is no strong preference over newly originating genera being motile. Consistent with previous studies, an analysis of extinction selectivity shows that small genera also tend to morevulnerable to extinction, while motile genera are more likely to go extinct. These results suggest high turnover at small body size within bivalves.

title: Drone LiDAR Surveys of Precariously Balanced Hoodoos Constrain Seismic Ground Motion in Western Colorado, USA
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Marso, Samuel Anthony [1], Baker, Gregory S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(2) Earth, Energy, and Environments, University Of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract: Precariously balanced rocks (PBRs) act as natural seismoscopes because their continued survival constrains the maximum ground shaking a site could have experienced. This study uses drone-based LiDAR to quantify 21 precariously balanced hoodoos near the base of Mount Garfield in the Book Cliffs of western Colorado (USA) to establish first-order upper bounds on seismic ground motion in an intraplate region with limited instrumental earthquake records. The hoodoos consist of Mesaverde Group sandstone caprocks perched on pedestals of the shale-dominated Mancos Formation. Pedestal erosion rates based on previous studies suggest the present balanced configurations have developed over approximately the past millennium. High-resolution LiDAR was used to measure hoodoo geometry, including rock height, width, and pedestal contact diameter. These measurements were used to calculate overturning thresholds, the minimum peak ground acceleration (PGA) required for overturning, and the corresponding earthquake moment magnitude (Mw) using standard ground-motion attenuation relationships under the conservative assumption of a fault rupture directly beneath each site. Calculated overturning thresholds ranged from 0.45 to 2.64 g (mean = 1.42 g), corresponding to Mw 5.3–7.3 (mean = 6.5). Because all 21 hoodoos remain intact, no earthquake has exceeded the lowest calculated overturning threshold of 0.45 g (equivalent to Mw 5.3 under the assumed rupture geometry) at this location during approximately the past 1,000 years. This constraint is consistent with the regional seismic record, in which no earthquake within the Grand Valley’s approximately 120-year instrumental history has exceeded M4.7, while Colorado’s largest documented historical earthquake (1882; M6.5) is comparable to the mean calculated threshold. These results demonstrate that drone LiDAR provides a repeatable, non-contact, and scalable alternative to traditional manual PBR surveys and extends PBR-based paleoseismic analysis to sedimentary hoodoo terrains. The resulting constraints provide new information relevant to regional seismic hazard assessment, infrastructure planning, and land-use decisions in western Colorado.

title: Limited Biotic Homogenization During the Plio-Pleistocene Transition in North America
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Boricha, Shrutik Arvind [1], Jukar, Advait Mahesh [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Biology, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA; Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, Florida, USA
(2) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, FL,
abstract:
Understanding how biological invasions and climate change drive biotic homogenization is critical for predicting modern ecosystem responses. During the Plio-Pleistocene, the Great American Biotic Interchange (GABI) and concurrent climate-driven environmental shifts resulted in faunal turnover and changes in diversity. Previous studies show that GABI immigrants were filtered by ecological and physiological traits, however, local co-occurrence assembly rules remained remarkably conserved despite this influx.

It remains unclear if this massive taxonomic reorganization erodes regional community distinctiveness. We tested whether immigration and climate shifts would homogenize communities through the selective extinction of habitat specialists and the continent-wide spread of generalists. While recent studies evaluated local immigrant proportions or explicitly controlled for geographic distance to assess functional co-occurrence, our study uniquely treats distance as a primary variable. Unlike analyses that utilized broad multi-million-year temporal windows or multidimensional functional trait spaces, we employ distance-decay and beta-diversity partitioning to explicitly test for spatial homogenization across North America. We compiled occurrence data from FAUNMAP and Paleobiology databases for the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, retaining sites with over five species to limit sampling bias. Dividing this interval into five ~900,000-year time bins, we conducted multi-site beta-diversity analyses on large herbivores, small mammals, and combined datasets. We calculated turnover, nestedness, Jaccard similarity, and distance-decay relationships.

Contrary to our predictions, all taxonomic groupings maintained exceptionally high beta diversity. Turnover consistently dominated over nestedness, proving that species replacement, rather than nested subsetting, drove community differentiation. Jaccard similarity remained persistently low (<0.25), and distance-decay slopes showed minimal variation across all time bins.

Our spatial approach demonstrates that geographic distance maintained its structuring influence throughout the GABI. Despite extreme taxonomic turnover and climatic perturbations, North American mammalian communities successfully resisted spatial homogenization. These patterns have important implications for understanding modern ecosystems, suggesting that regional communities may retain distinct ecological identities rather than converging toward homogenized assemblages, though the rate and magnitude of current changes may produce different outcomes.

title: Size disparity among Karoo Basin tetrapods tracks synchronous basin-wide environmental change before and after the Permo-Triassic mass extinction in residents, but not in immigrant taxa

authors: Huttenlocker, Adam [1], Abbott, Caroline [2], Angielczyk, Kenneth [3], Botha, Jennifer [4], Pinto, James [5], Smith, Roger [6], Tse, Yuen Ting [7], Viglietti, Pia [8]

(2) Committee on Evolutionary Biology, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
(3) Negaunee Integrative Research Center, The Field Museum, Chicago, IL, USA
(4) Evolutionary Studies Institute, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa

abstract: Recent geochronological research in South Africa’s Karoo Basin has clarified the timing of tetrapod turnover during the Permo-Triassic mass extinction (ca. 251.9 Ma; PTME), providing a framework for understanding the extinction’s effects on terrestrial diversity and community structure. Prior analyses of body size disparity in Karoo tetrapods have demonstrated Triassic “Lilliput” phenomena–i.e., post-extinction body size reductions that have been attributed to a variety of causes–but only in a limited number of taxa (e.g., therocephalians and Lystrosaurus ) and lacking detailed geospatial information. We investigated patterns of body size disparity across the PTME from a sample of 863 specimens collected from two major study sites in the vicinity of Nieu Bethesda and Bethulie and addressed the following questions: 1) Did large-bodied taxa have shorter lineage durations (and, thus, were more prone to extinction) than smaller taxa during “background” intervals? 2) Did body size disparity in Karoo tetrapods decrease with secular climate drying and warming synchronously throughout the basin? 3) How did extinction responses vary between resident and immigrant taxa? We show that lineage durations are random with respect to size and display no size-selectivity before the extinction. However, there was a slight decrease in size disparity in the Palingkloof Member with the greatest reduction occurring across the PTME at both study sites. Size disparity across the basin remained low during Triassic hyperthermal conditions and did not return to pre-extinction levels until Cynognathus Assemblage Zone times, at least 2.6 million years after the extinction. Logistic regressions indicate that large-bodied taxa had a higher probability of extinction during the PTME than small-bodied taxa. However, residents were most affected by reduced disparity, whereas immigrant taxa filled vacant niche spaces such as the large predatory gorgonopsian Inostrancevia and the archosauriform Proterosuchus in the latest Permian and earliest Triassic, respectively. These spatial patterns–particularly the roles of residents and immigrants–mirror other terrestrial mass extinctions, such as North American K-Pg mammal communities, and shed light on the “rules” of extinction and recovery during similar major biodiversity crises.

abstract: ColoradoStratigraphy.org (CS) has been providing indispensable information and data pertinent to Colorado’s varied and fascinating stratigraphic record. Colorado Geological Survey (CGS) joined CS in preparing graphics and making these resources available to the public and geoscience researchers. Our most recent products include stratigraphic panels that illustrate relations between formations along border-to-border transects. The intent is to show variations and relations to major tectonic features that influenced depositional environments. Panels illustrate changes in formation thicknesses using a datum of base of the Mesozoic. Not only do the panels provide insight into relations of stratigraphic patterns to major tectonic features, but they also serve as a reference resource for users. Data used in preparation include measured sections; deep well logs and correlations; publicly available well tops data; and mapped outcrop patterns. Locations of individual reference sources are shown as are type locations of units along the transects. Points of Geologic Interest (POGIs) are included to provide guidance for users to find good exposures of stratigraphic intervals in easy to access locations. Lastly, panels are prepared in a dynamic digital format where online users can “click” on data sources to be directed to accompanying digital data.

title: Discriminating between multiple metasomatic events in the Big Maria Mountains, CA
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Droubi, Omar Khalil [1], Craddock Affinati, Suzanne [2], Hoisch, Thomas D. [3], Kitajima, Kouki [4], Blum, Tyler [5], Schoonover, Erik Jeffery [6], Nachlas, William O. [7], Bonamici, Chloe E. [8]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA
(2) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ,
(3) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ 86011, AZ,
(4) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA
(5) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA
(6) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA,
(7) University of Wisconsin - Madison, Department of Geoscience, Madison, WI,
(8) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
abstract:
The migration of fluids within the crust plays a significant role in crustal evolution, driving metasomatic reactions that change rheology or induce melting, and transporting and concentrating critical metals. The Big Maria Mountains (BMM), in southeastern California, expose metasomatic calc-silicate rocks with protoliths correlative to the Paleozoic-Mesozoic sedimentary sequence in the Grand Canyon. These supracrustal rocks and associated Jurassic granitoids were deformed and metamorphosed as part of the Late Cretaceous Maria Fold and Thrust Belt, forming a map-scale nappe structure with strata locally attenuated to ~1% of their original thickness. Syn- and post-deformational Late Cretaceous leucogranite dikes occur in a swarm in the western BMM. The calc-silicate rocks have experienced varying degrees of complete to partial wollastonitization and decarbonation (quartz + calcite reacting to wollastonite + CO 2 ). Previous modeling of these reactions produced calculations of a large (≥17:1) fluid-rock ratio assuming pervasive fluid flow across the BMM from an unresolved source. To resolve metasomatic events and fluid sources in the BMM, we study the petrography, major-element mineral compositions, geochronology, and oxygen isotope records for BMM metasomatic rocks.

The metasomatic rock types include 1) calc-silicate gneisses with layering defined by variable amounts of wollastonite, K-feldspar, diopside, grossular-andradite, quartz, and calcite; 2) epidote-andradite ± diopside ± amphibole skarn, which occurs as lenses, layers, and pods folded and boudinaged within the dominant calc-silicate fabric; and 3) a Late Cretaceous kyanite quartzite. Titanite U-Pb geochronology reveals two populations; Jurassic titanite are found in most outcrops, while Late Cretaceous titanite are generally restricted to outcrops proximal to leucogranite dikes. In the most comprehensive SIMS oxygen isotope survey of calc-silicate phases to date, we observe inter-sample d 18 O variabilities in diopside (up to 8‰), wollastonite (up to 7‰), garnet (up to 5‰), feldspar (up to 4.5‰), and titanite (up to 4‰), and intra-sample mineral d 18 O variabilities of 1–3‰, suggesting widespread d 18 O heterogeneity at the grain-scale and outcrop-scale. Reconstructed bulk-rock d 18 O values (~4–11‰) indicate widespread lowering of d 18 O relative to sedimentary protoliths, providing evidence for spatially heterogeneous interactions with lower d 18 O fluids. Although our oxygen isotope data cannot rule out a Farallon slab fluid source (~3–6‰), the abundance of metasomatic K-feldspar suggests fluids sourced from nearby Jurassic and Cretaceous granitoids (7-8‰) and/or pluton-associated meteoric-hydrothermal systems (≤0‰) over two periods in the BMM.
