title: Faulted and Twice Drowned: Fluvial to Deep-Marine Deposition Across the Triassic–Jurassic Boundary at the Edge of Gondwana (~32° S, Chile)
session_title: Pre–Neogene Tectonic evolution of South America (Posters)
authors: Hursh, Tiana Belle [1], Ronemus, Chance [2], Hazelbush, Parker [3], Cramer, Amarissa [4], Sundell, Kurt [5], Graham, Stephan A. [6], Dobbs, Stephen C [7], Murillo, Ismael [8], Rodriguez, Maria Pia [9]
affiliations: (1) Idaho State Univ, Geology, Pocatello, ID, USA
(2) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA; University of Calgary, Calgary, AB, Canada
(3) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(4) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(5) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(6) Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
(7) Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
(8) Servicio Nacional de Geología y Minería, Santiago, Chile
(9) Universidad Andres Bello, Santiago, Chile
abstract:
The Late Triassic–Early Jurassic tectonic evolution of the proto-Andean margin is debated. Competing models involve slab roll-back, post-accretion subduction transference, or transform faulting. Early Mesozoic development of the paleo-Pacific continental edge recorded in little-studied basins of the Chilean Coastal Cordillera (~32 °S). To help distinguish among tectonic hypotheses we measured ~1.8 km of stratigraphy and detrital zircon U-Pb age distributions from the Middle(?)–Upper Triassic El Quereo, Upper Triassic El Puquén, and Upper Triassic–Lower Jurassic Los Molles formations.

The El Quereo Formation overlies an angular unconformity atop Carboniferous–Permian metasedimentary basement, adjacent to a syndepositional normal fault. This formation consists of a basal colluvial breccia succeeded by fluvial sandstones that transition abruptly into turbidites, which shoal upward to shallow-marine deposits. These deposits are overlain by bimodal, low-K, tholeiitic lavas and tuffs (Pichidangui Formation) and deltaic deposits with syndepositional normal faults (El Puquén Formation). A second cycle of basin deepening is recorded by shelf to deep-marine turbidite, debris flow, and mass-transport deposits of the Los Molles Formation. Paleocurrents (N=17; n=242) record W-NW transport in El Quereo fluvial deposits and axial NE dispersal in Los Molles turbidites; SE-dipping mass-transport complex paleoslope determinations (N=7; n=53) suggest slumping of the basin margin.

Detrital zircon U-Pb distributions (N=11; n=2,905) shift from Devonian–Ordovician and Neo–Mesoproterozoic modal ages in basement samples to dominant late Paleozoic ages in the basin fill, recording a change from distal to more proximal sources. Maximum depositional ages indicate the basin fill is locally ≤ 235 Ma and align with biostratigraphic ages for all formations except the Los Molles, which lacks syndepositional zircon. Conglomerate clast counts (N=9; n=993) transition from basement- to volcanic-dominated within the El Quereo Formation and consist mainly of quartz and intra-formational rip-up clasts in the Los Molles Formation. These data are consistent with the dissection of the Carboniferous arc and accretionary complex and dwindling input from syndepositional magmatism.

Syndepositional normal faulting, two cycles of basin deepening, bimodal volcanism, and locally derived detritus support fault-controlled subsidence under extensional to transtensional tectonics. Thus, upper-plate extension here was established between ca. 235–220 Ma and persisted into the Early Jurassic, providing a constraint that tectonic models for this interval must satisfy.

title: From conceptual Models to Decision Tools: Advances in Regional Groundwater Simulation in Wisconsin
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Bradbury, Kenneth R. [1]
affiliations: (1) Wisconsin Geological Survey, Brooklyn, WI, USA
abstract:
From the 1980s to the present has been an era of important collaboration between the Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey, U.S. Geological Survey and local and state agencies in developing regional groundwater models in Wisconsin. Randy Hunt was a collaborator in much of this work, and his enthusiasm and leadership coupled with his never-ending quest for newer and better simulation methods contributed much to our current understanding of the hydrogeology of the state. These regional models become operational tools that support regulatory decision making and powerful educational tools that help citizens and government personnel better understand groundwater movement. Two examples illustrate these advances.

In an effort to understand one of the largest regional cones of depression in the US, construction of a regional flow model of southeast Wisconsin (including the urbanized belt from Chicago to Milwaukee) helped redefine and test the hydrostratigraphic understanding of this region and relationships between regional water use, a deep sandstone aquifer, shallow dolomite and glacial aquifers, a regional aquitard, and surface water, including Lake Michigan. This model helped guide decision making for water supply in SE Wisconsin, was later expanded to include much of Lake Michigan, and supported decision making leading to the important Great Lakes Compact. It also spawned additional research on aquitard hydrogeology, radium movement in the deep aquifer, groundwater-surface water relationships, and other topics.

Motivated by concerns over development and land use, two county-scale flow models of Dane County focused on simulating flow to high-capacity wells supplying the Madison urban service area and included detailed transient simulations of groundwater-surface water exchange with the Madison lakes. These models supported wellhead protection analyses and county-level planning decisions. By incorporating new (at the time) modeling capabilities such as improved solvers, lake-stage simulation, streamflow routing, borehole flow, pilot points, autocalibration and linked-array computing these models pushed the envelope of modeling practice and gave Wisconsin hydrogeologists experience with these new techniques.

Our modeling approach in Wisconsin has always included educational follow-up with technical reports and public meetings with interested parties including regulators, consultants, and citizen groups. The success of these efforts has built trust in models and has led to the funding and construction of regional models over much of the state, and these efforts continue today.

title: Interpreting Mg-carbonate signatures and geochemical properties in Martian analog lakes using VNIR/SWIR reflectance spectroscopy
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Cloutier, Sydney Marie [1], Horgan, Briony Heather Noelle [2], Bryant, Roger [3], Raudsepp, Maija [4], Wilson, Sasha [5], Olson, Stephanie [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
(3) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(4) Department of Physical Science, MacEwan University, Edmonton, AB, Canada
(5) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Science, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB,
(6) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
On Mars, magnesium carbonates have been detected in numerous settings and provide key insights into potential habitable and past aqueous environments. However, Mg-carbonate spectral detection is limited by its co-occurrence with clays and sulfates. This phenomenon arises when diagnostic carbonate absorptions are obscured—a process known as spectral masking. Since visible/near-infrared to shortwave infrared (VNIR/SWIR; 0.35–2.5 µm) spectroscopy is the primary technique used to identify carbon-bearing deposits from orbit, understanding how mixed mineral assemblages influence spectral signatures is essential for reconstructing ancient Martian environments. We investigate whether VNIR/SWIR reflectance spectroscopy can distinguish magnesium carbonate-producing alkaline lakes with varying geochemical conditions and evaluate the extent to which sediment spectra preserve information regarding depositional context.

A total of 37 Earth analog sediment samples from the Cariboo Plateau, Canada and Lake Salda, Turkey were analyzed using VNIR/SWIR reflectance spectroscopy, spectral parameter calculations, quantitative X-ray diffraction (XRD), and comparisons with published geochemical datasets. Principal component analysis separated six statistically significant spectral clusters (silhouette score = 0.61; PERMANOVA pseudo-F = 31.26, p = 0.001) corresponding to discrete mineral assemblages and lake chemistries. The clusters differentiate spectrally weak, moderate, and strong Mg-clay assemblages, hydromagnesite-bearing sediments, and sulfate-dominated sediments, while preserving trends in lake geochemistry. Alkalinity (F = 30.15, p < 0.001, η² = 0.829) and sulfate concentration (F = 831.73, p < 0.001, η² = 0.993) emerged as the strongest controls on spectral properties and mineralogy.

Reflectance spectra preserve relevant geochemical information beyond mineral identification but also reveal notable limitations for carbonate detection in VNIR/SWIR. Mg-carbonate absorptions were heavily masked by Mg-clays and sulfates, even in sediments containing up to ~60 wt% carbonate, demonstrating that abundant carbonate does not automatically exhibit a diagnostic spectral signal. Despite this masking, spectral clustering remained consistent with mineralogical and geochemical data—indicating that physical conditions can encode within the overall spectral response. These findings suggest that weak or absent carbonate absorptions in Martian orbital datasets should not immediately be interpreted as evidence for carbonate-poor environments but may instead reflect mineral mixing. By quantitatively linking reflectance spectra with lake geochemistry and mineralogy, this work provides an improved framework for interpreting CRISM observations of carbonate-bearing terrains, including Jezero crater, and strengthens the use of terrestrial alkaline lakes as analogs for ancient habitable environments on Mars.

title: Mapping Hydrothermal Alteration Mineralogy Using Hyperspectral Core Scanning Data on Research Drill Core from Norris Geyser Basin in Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Posters)
authors: Ensign, Derek [1], Monecke, Thomas [2]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract: Hyperspectral core scanning is a powerful tool allowing mapping of the distribution of alteration minerals in geothermal systems. In the late 1960’s, the U.S. Geological Survey conducted a drilling campaign in Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming as part of a broader initiative to understand geothermal systems. All 13 drill cores from Yellowstone were archived at the Core Research Center of the U.S. Geological Survey in Denver, Colorado. In 2015 and 2016, the U.S. Geological Survey contracted Corescan to image the cores using a Mark III Hyperspectral Core Imager which covered the visible and near infrared through short-wave infrared spectral range (450-2500nm). This legacy data was processed with the U.S. Geological Survey’s Material Identification and Characterization Algorithm to map spectrally active minerals along the core. In Norris Geyser Basin, the vertical drill holeY-9 reached a depth of 247.8 m. Hyperspectral imaging mapped kaolinite and smectite in varying proportions along the entire length of the Y-9 core. Hole Y-12 penetrated to a depth of 331.6 m. In this core, alunite and kaolinite were mapped near surface with varying amounts of hydrated silica within the top 50 m. Further down hole, transitions through zones dominated by kaolinite, kaolinite and smectite, smectite, and muscovite were observed. Hyperspectral mineral classification has identified minerals with temperature stability ranges that conform to the reported subsurface temperature gradients constructed from measurements during drilling. The alteration mineral assemblages correspond to steam-heated advanced argillic and argillic alteration assemblages. In core Y-9 only argillic alteration is noted. In contrast, Y-12 exhibits steam-heated alteration near surface with argillic alteration at depth. The distribution of the steam-heated alteration is related to the position of the water table with respect to the drill sites.

title: Investigation of Continental Trace Fossils, Sedimentology, and Stratigraphy of the Paleogene Lacustrine Claron Formation in Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Rea, Amanda Sumatra [1], Roberts, Eric M [2], Garrard, Rhiannon M [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) National Park Service, Bryce Canyon National Park, UT, USA
abstract:
Bryce Canyon National Park, located on the Paunsaugunt Plateau in Utah, is known worldwide for its concentration of hoodoos associated with the Claron Formation. Described as a carbonate-rich fluctuating alluvial-lacustrine system initiated from the Laramide Orogeny, the Claron Formation is contemporaneous with other lake systems of the Paleogene such as the Unita, Piceance, and Green River Basins. Despite the relation to these well-studied basins, little is known about the paleoenvironment and paleontology of the Claron Formation. Continental trace fossils are abundant in the Claron Formation, including the enigmatic ichnotaxon, Eatonichnus, which is traditionally described as dung beetle traces. This study builds upon previous paleontological surveys within the park to include a newly discovered “ Eatonichnus horizon” in the Pink Member of the Claron Formation and new localities of Eatonichnus and other continental trace fossils in the White Member. The goal of this study is to re-examine the continental trace fossils of the Claron Formation to understand their genesis, re-evaluate possible trace makers, and reconstruct the depositional environments.

Eatonichnus has not been described in situ within the Claron Formation before. However, we report at least two laterally extensive horizons of Eatonichnus , in both the Pink and White Members. The “ Eatonichnus horizon” in the Pink Member extends laterally for >0.5 km 2 reveals a close packing of Eatonichnus in a single 25-35cm thick peloidal palustrine bed. Eatonichnus is an expanding spiral of packed mud around a wide central chamber that is <2.0cm wide with some chambers exposed at one end and others terminating at both ends. The 2-7cm wide spiral burrows vary significantly in length, from ~6-15cm long with 4-9 spiraled segments. Celliforma and other traces cross-cut Eatonichnus burrows in places, while orange mottling, slickensides, and weak ped structures suggest the “ Eatonichnus horizon” in the Pink Member developed during or after lake shore regression and represents a powerful paleoecological recorder of paleo-lake/water table levels. Observations from the “ Eatonichnus horizon” in the White Member suggest a similar depositional scenario, however the traces are distinctly smaller. The dense concentration of traces in these two horizons associated with a regressive lakebed setting is consistent with formation following subaerial exposure and subsequent paleosol development, but the origin of the trace maker remains unclear and dung beetle trace makers is questioned.

title: Comparing the Responses of Coastal Urban and Rural Shallow Aquifers to Sea-Level Rise
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Amin, Md Al [1], Russoniello, Christopher J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Planning, and Design, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, RI, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Planning, and Design, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, RI, USA
abstract:
Low-lying coastal areas are global hotspots of settlement and economic activity, and their hydrologic connection to the ocean makes them among the landscapes most vulnerable to sea-level rise (SLR). Coastal infrastructure was largely built to function under present-day sea levels - designed to remain dry or experience only seasonal contact with fresh surface water and groundwater. Ongoing SLR raises groundwater tables, thins the unsaturated zone, and drives saltwater intrusion into coastal aquifers, increasing threats to buried infrastructure, freshwater resources, and ecosystem resilience.

Previous studies have primarily focused on groundwater potability and freshwater sustainability in rural or natural coastal settings, leaving a gap in how urbanized coasts respond. Urban environments fundamentally alter groundwater systems through extensive impervious cover and recharge, engineered drainage networks, buried infrastructure, and transboundary water transport. This results in hydrologic conditions that differ substantially from undeveloped landscapes.

We address this gap with variable-density groundwater flow and transport models of Warren, RI, a representative of a low-lying coastal town on Narragansett Bay. These models simulate urban infrastructure - sewer system, impervious land cover, transboundary water supply, and reduced recharge - control and are impacted by groundwater flow and saltwater intrusion under projected SLR and climate forcings. We contrast these urban impacts with rural analogs to identify configurations most vulnerable to compounded SLR impacts.

Preliminary results indicate that urban infrastructure, particularly sewer drainage systems, generally increases the risk of saltwater intrusion under projected SLR compared to rural setting. However, the magnitude of this effect depends on local drainage characteristics and groundwater recharge conditions.

title: Attracting students to careers supporting the mining industry using hot topics in mine water geochemistry
session_title: New approaches and emerging technologies for the prevention, control, and remediation of acidic rock drainage and legacy mine waste
authors: Castendyk, Devin [1], Jones, Daniel [2], Verburg, Rens [3], Figueroa, Linda [4]
affiliations: (1) Colorado Geoenvironmental, SRK Consulting, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Mine Water and Environment, WSP, Redmond, WA, USA
(4) Environmental & Mining Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
The mining industry faces a growing need for geoscientists with expertise in mine water geochemistry, mine waste characterization, and predictive environmental management. However, many students in geoscience and engineering related programs receive limited exposure to mining-related geochemistry. This disconnect creates a workforce challenge at a time when demand for critical minerals, mine closure planning, abandoned mine land remediation, and sustainable water management is increasing.

The Acid Drainage Technology Initiative, Metal Mining Sector (ADTI-MMS) has identified several areas where demand for geoscientists and engineers is particularly strong. Established practice areas include characterization of mine wastes using mineralogical and geochemical testing; prediction of drainage quality from waste rock, tailings, heap leach facilities, underground mines, and pit lakes; and development of water management strategies that adapt to changing mine plans, expansions, and closure scenarios.

Emerging opportunities are reshaping the field and creating new career pathways. These include calibration and validation of long-term geochemical predictions throughout the life of mine including closure and relinquishment, assessment of alternative tailings storage approaches, and evaluation of links between geochemical processes and geotechnical stability of tailings and mine waste facilities. Increasing attention is also being directed toward economic recovery of critical minerals from legacy mine waters and mine wastes, application of machine learning, artificial intelligence, and autonomous vehicles to real-time characterization and monitoring, investigation of emerging contaminants, and advancement of biogeochemical treatment systems. Additional growth areas include supporting remediation of abandoned mine lands, transitioning mines into post-closure beneficial land uses, improving predictions of evaporation and climate-related changes to mine water balances, and developing carbon sequestration strategies using mine wastes.

Geoscientists trained in these topics are sought by mining companies, environmental consulting firms, and federal and state regulatory agencies. In addition, these topics demonstrate that mine water geochemistry is no longer focused solely on acid rock drainage prediction and treatment; it has become a multidisciplinary field spanning geochemistry, hydrogeology, microbiology, data science, environmental engineering, and resource recovery. ADTI-MMS members are available to collaborate with faculty and academic departments to develop classroom materials, field exercises, guest lectures, and student engagement opportunities. Our goal is to increase awareness of rewarding career paths in mine water geochemistry and help prepare the next generation of geoscientists to address the environmental and resource challenges facing the mining industry.

title: Hydroclimatic versus Source-Proximity Controls on PFAS Composition in South Texas Coastal Estuaries and Groundwater: A Multivariate and Machine-Learning Assessment

authors: Anyanwu, Ifeanyi Emmanuel [1], Narimani, ROYA [2], Felix, Joseph David [3], Murgulet, Dorina [4]

abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as “forever chemicals”, are persistent contaminants whose distribution in coastal systems reflects competing hydroclimatic and source-driven controls. We investigated PFAS composition across the Nueces estuary, including Corpus Christi, Nueces, and Oso bays in South Texas, sampling six surface-water sites and three groundwater monitoring wells monthly from May 2022 to April 2023 (n = 108). Fifteen PFAS analytes were quantified and log-transformed, and samples were classified by water matrix (surface water versus groundwater) and precipitation regime (high versus low). We integrated multivariate models, machine-learning, and driver-attribution approaches to identify the controls on compositional variation. Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities showed strong separation by water matrix but none by precipitation. PERMANOVA corroborated these findings, with water matrix explaining 35.2% of compositional variance versus 0.3% for precipitation. Similarity-percentage (SIMPER) analysis identified PFOS (13.8%), PFPeA (13.4%), PFHxA (11.9%), and PFBA (11.4%) as the principal discriminating compounds. A four-dimensional variational autoencoder (VAE), trained separately by precipitation regime, extracted nonlinear structure and enabled source apportionment by correlation with proximity to four PFAS source classes. Under high precipitation, latent dimension three tracked wastewater proximity, shifting to landfill proximity under low precipitation, indicating precipitation-driven source apportionment. Support vector regression (SVR) was integrated to quantify which hydroclimatic and environmental factors drive PFAS abundance. Groundwater PFAS was highly predictable (R 2 = 0.74) and dominated by source-proximity terms such as distance to superfund sites and industrial-waste sites whereas surface-water PFAS was governed by landfill proximity, with antecedent 7-day evapotranspiration, streamflow, and tidal level emerging as the leading hydroclimatic drivers. Overall, fixed source proximity, controlled secondarily by transient hydroclimatic forcing showed the most influence on PFAS composition and abundance, thus informing targeted coastal PFAS monitoring and management need.

title: Geological Hazard Assessment and the Effects of Anthropogenic Activities Using GIS and RS
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Zhou, Wendy Wei [1], Idowu, Dorcas [2], Lowry, Benjamin Lowry [3], Baker, Scott [4]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA

abstract: Geological hazards, or geohazards, are processes near the Earth's surface that pose risks to human lives, property, or infrastructure. Examples include mass-wasting events such as landslides, rockfalls, debris flows, and mudslides, as well as earthquakes, volcanic hazards, and floods, all of which affect surface features and landscapes. Field reconnaissance and investigation of geological, hydrogeological, and geomorphological features are essential for understanding geohazards and collecting valuable data for ground truthing. Technologies such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing (RS) provide distributed spatiotemporal data, enable rapid hazard mapping, and support near-real-time monitoring, making assessments more efficient and cost-effective. This presentation highlights the applications of GIS and RS in geohazard assessment and the impact of anthropogenic activities through case studies, including (1) a land use and land cover (LULC) change assessment over 35 years in the context of flood hazard in Nigeria; and (2) a landslide study using 3D modeling combined with Advanced Land Observing Satellite-1 (ALOS-1) Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) techniques in Colorado, USA. The results of the first case study revealed a 69% decrease in wetland area and a 94% increase in developed area over 35 years. While wetland was a primary land cover type in 1986, it became the least common land cover type in 2020. These LULC changes could be responsible for the rise in flooding in the State. Most LULC changes result in the conversion of wetland areas into developed areas and in unplanned development in very high- to moderate-flood-hazard zones. The second case study reviewed the destruction of Colorado State Highway 133 between 1986 and 1987 during different reactivation phases. Additionally, the study focused on the ALOS-1 InSAR analysis, which detects ground displacement at very-slow-to-extremely-slow velocities and has a notably larger spatial extent.

abstract:
The Late Cretaceous tetrapod record of Peru remains poorly documented compared with that of other regions of South America. To expand the fossil record of this understudied area, recent field expeditions to the Peruvian Andes were conducted in 2025 to the Vilquechico area (Puno Region) and in 2026 to the Bagua syncline (Amazonas Region).

In southern Peru, material recovered from the middle member of the Vilquechico Formation (middle–late Campanian) includes numerous turtle carapace and plastron fragments, isolated crocodyliform postcranial elements, and a partial mandible with some preserved teeth assigned to Peirosauridae (Notosuchia). The latter significantly expands the known geographic range of the group northward within South America. Most notably, the assemblage includes a nearly complete skull referable to Dyrosauridae (Neosuchia) with preserved teeth, lacking the mandible. Sedimentological and micropaleontological evidence indicates deposition in a marginal-coastal setting that included brackish lacustrine environments.

In northern Peru, fieldwork in the Bagua syncline yielded abundant dinosaur remains from the Pongo de Rentema Formation (Campanian–Maastrichtian). These findings include isolated theropod teeth, vertebrae, and possible carpal elements, a large (~one meter long) indeterminate dinosaur femur, isolated dorsal and caudal titanosaur (Sauropoda) vertebrae, several dinosaur eggshell fragments associated with titanosaurs and an unusual concentration of at least 40 associated osteoderms also referable to Titanosauria. Sedimentological and stratigraphic evidence suggests a continental fluvial depositional setting.

Together, these discoveries and ongoing research in Peruvian localities provide new evidence of tetrapod diversity and habitat occupation across contrasting marginal-coastal and continental fluvial ecosystems, offering key insights into the biodiversity of an understudied region of South America prior to the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction.

title: Rainfall-Induced Landslide Susceptibility Assessment through Soil Mineralogy, Microstructural Analysis, and Logistic Regression Modelling in Namchi, Sikkim Himalaya, India
session_title: Contemporary research in geomorphological hazards
authors: Naskar, Ria [1], Chowdhury, Arindam [2], Sharma, Milap Chand [3], De, Sunil Kumar [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Disaster Management, Techno India University, Agartala, Tripura, India
(2) Geomorphology, Faculty of Science, Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic
(3) Centre for Study of Regional Development, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, India
(4) Geography, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong, Meghalaya, India
abstract:
Landslides pose a significant natural hazard in the mountainous terrain of Namchi, Sikkim Himalaya, India. This study investigates landslide susceptibility in this geologically fragile region, which is underlain by the Gondwana Supergroup and the Daling Group of rocks, where frequent landslides are primarily triggered by intense rainfall events. An integrated approach combining Logistic Regression Modelling (LRM), X-ray Diffraction (XRD), and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) was employed to develop a landslide susceptibility map, determine the mineralogical composition of slope materials, assess their susceptibility to chemical weathering, and examine microstructural characteristics associated with slope instability.

The logistic regression model indicates a marked increase in landslide probability when daily rainfall exceeds 20 mm. XRD analysis reveals a high Al/Si ratio, indicating intense chemical weathering of the parent rocks and the subsequent formation of clay minerals. The presence of these clay minerals enhances water absorption, leading to reduced shear strength and increased slope instability. SEM analysis further reveals significant microstructural alterations, including particle disaggregation and fungal-like (fugal) growth induced by rainwater infiltration. These changes weaken soil cohesion and increase pore-water pressure, thereby substantially increasing the likelihood of landslide occurrence.

The integrated results from the susceptibility modelling, mineralogical analysis, and microstructural investigation demonstrate that prolonged rainwater infiltration accelerates both chemical weathering and microstructural degradation, ultimately compromising slope stability in the study area. The findings underscore the importance of continuous monitoring of rainfall patterns and soil characteristics for effective landslide hazard assessment, risk management, and the development of sustainable mitigation strategies in the Namchi region of the Sikkim Himalaya.

title: New Data Fills a Gap for Understanding the Cretaceous-Paleogene Coastal Batholith in Northern Peru
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Posters)
authors: Clausen, Benjamin [1], Martinez-Ardila, Ana Maria [2], Pompe, Lance R. [3], Voos, Alex [4]
affiliations: (1) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA; Geoscience Research Institute, Loma Linda, California, USA
(2) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA

(4) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, California, USA
abstract:
Minimal geochemical and geochronological data have been available for the northern part of the Cretaceous-Paleogene Peruvian Coastal Batholith (PCB) at 9-5°S. Newly collected samples aim to fill this gap. Our previous work on the PCB has looked at: (1) magma sources, changes in mantle input, different types of basement, changes in crustal thickness, crustal assimilation, mantle/crust fraction, and extent of differentiation (Martinez et al., 2023, Lithos), (2) episodic flare-ups and lulls in magmatism, magma addition rates for the crust, and a comparison with the Eastern Cordillera of Peru (Pompe et al., 2026, JSAES), and (3) arc trends for plutonic rocks of the PCB and the associated volcanics (Voos et al., 2026, IGR).

The studies used field work, geochemistry, bedrock ages, and detrital zircons. The geochemistry classifies the volcanics as island arc tholeiites. Attempts have been made to correlate magmatic data with tectonic data such as tectonic setting, arc migration, change in dip angle, and other subduction parameters. The results show spatial and temporal geochronological and geochemical trends along and across the arc, younging from south to north and west to east. Zircon ages confirm that the volcanic rocks are part of an integrated volcanic-plutonic system rather than a separate host rock for the PCB plutons (Voos et al., 2026).

The new data extends these trends to the very north of Peru at 10-4°S along the coast and in the Andean foothills. The data also yield some new observations. Sampling of Precambrian basement and metamorphosed Paleozoic country rock provides data about possible source of contamination for PCB magma. The Tahuin terrane presents a different crustal contamination source than the Paracas and Arequipa terranes further south. The presence of pillow lavas, altered in places, are compatible with submarine volcanism documented in central Peru and linked in intra arc settings (Polliand et al., 2005, IJES). Other field observations include PCB contacts with volcanics and the Precambrian, a zoned pluton, xenoliths, dike swarms, and hypabyssal textures. In places, volcanics showed ignimbrites, columnar basalt, and olivine and plagioclase phenocrysts. Tectonic features include drag folding, faulting, and uplift. These new data refine the volcanic-host rock architecture of the northern PCB and test how basement heterogeneity, tectonic segmentation, and arc migration shaped magmatism along the Peruvian margin.

title: Hyperspectral Mangrove Signatures on the Florida West Coast from the 2010 AVIRIS Flight Campaigns
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Simon, Anika D [1], Bell, Tom W [2], Lee, Pamela J [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Atmospheric and Geological Sciences, State University of New York at Oswego, Oswego, NY, USA
(2) Department of Applied Ocean Physics & Engineering, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, Massachusetts, USA

abstract: Mangals, or mangrove forests, are wetland ecosystems found in tropical latitudes that serve as marine estuaries, blue-carbon sinks, and provide natural shoreline protection. The roots of mangroves stabilize coastlines by trapping sediments and reducing turbidity and erosion, thereby influencing coastline morphology. Remote sensing of mangals enables scientists to observe the health and diversity of species on a scale that is more beneficial to mangrove conservation and management groups. With tropical storm intensities increasing and the expansion of human activities along coastlines, large-scale studies of mangals can provide a more complete depiction of inhomogeneous mangal degradation, identify deforestation hotspot regions, and determine which mangrove species are most endangered. However, there is a lack of research on applying remote sensing techniques to larger spatial areas of U.S.-based mangals. AVIRIS, or the Aerial Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer, is a remote-sensing, aircraft-based instrument with 224 continuous bands, covering 400-2500 nm spectral range, with a 15-20 m ground spatial resolution. This study uses hyperspectral imagery from AVIRIS to assess the variability in mangal density and spectral diversity in 2010 across the mangrove-inhabited region of the western Florida shelf. From the hyperspectral reflectance data, vegetation indices are calculated, including Enhanced Vegetative Index (EVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), Structure Insensitive Pigment Index (SIPI), and Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE). These are then applied to the mangrove strands along the Florida coastline. Unsupervised K-means clustering and species-specific spectral signatures are then used to differentiate between potential classification variations. Clustering based on canopy density, provided by vegetative indices, and spectral signatures is the first step toward creating a comprehensive map of the four mangrove species inhabiting the western Florida shelf (red, white, black, and buttonwood mangrove). Understanding how mangrove species are distributed within a forest strand provides insight into the overall health and occurrence of mangrove species, highlighting where conservation efforts are needed most.

title: Decadal changes in large wood volume and mobility in headwater streams following catastrophic forest blowdown
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers
authors: Scamardo, Julianne [1], Kemper, John [2], Shobe, Charlie [3], Triantafillou, Shayla [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Science, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(3) U.S. Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fort Collins, CO, USA

abstract: Large-scale forest disturbances, including catastrophic forest blowdown and fire, are mechanisms for infrequent yet mass recruitment of large wood (LW) to headwater channels, potentially elevating LW volumes for decades. These long-term effects on wood storage post-disturbance, and subsequent impacts to local channel morphology and sediment storage, depend on wood mobility and decay. Portions of the Routt National Forest in northern Colorado experienced catastrophic blowdown in October 1997 followed by a wildfire in 2002. Following these events, we hypothesize that (1) LW volumes would have increased following the initial blowdown and again following fire, due to compounding disturbance and additional recruitment, but that (2) LW will have decayed in the past two decades, becoming more mobile and returning wood loads to a pre-disturbance state. To test these hypotheses, we compile data on LW volumes, characteristics, and locations collected in 1998, 2010-2011, and 2025-2026 in two headwater streams in the Routt National Forest: South Fork Lost Dog and Agnes Creeks. Wood volumes substantially increased in both creeks in 1998 following the 1997 blowdown (from 69 m 3 /ha to 402 m 3 /ha in Agnes Creek and from 30 m 3 /ha to 613 m 3 /ha in South Fork Lost Dog) and have been steadily declining in subsequent surveys, suggesting that compounding disturbances may have a diminishing effect on wood recruitment. Wood volumes recorded in 2025 were still 4x and 11x higher than pre-disturbance volumes for South Fork Lost Dog and Agnes Creek, respectively. The different post-disturbance wood load responses at the two sites may reflect differences in logging history between watersheds. Approximately 500 pieces of LW were tagged or retagged per creek (~1000 total) in 2010, of which 338 (33%) were resurveyed in 2026. Approximately 50% of resurveyed LW had moved >1 m and 10% had moved >30 m, with a maximum surveyed movement distance of 350 m. The true maximum travel distance is likely longer, as tagged logs may have been exported out of the original reach and were not resurveyed. Although resurveyed pieces were shorter than in 2010 and fewer were bridged above the channel, approximately 50% of surveyed LW pieces were incorporated in jams, potentially limiting future mobility. Transport limitations may keep LW volumes elevated in post-disturbance streams for decades to come.

title: Numerical Model of the Generation of the Gediz Vallis Fan Stratigraphy: Implications for Interpreting Debris Fow Fans on Mars and Earth
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Dietrich, William Eric [1], Miao, Runze [2], George, David L. [3], Barnhart, Katherine R. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA,
(2) Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, California, USA
(3) United States Geological Survery, Cascades Volcano Observatory, Vancouver, Washington, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Landslide Hazards Program, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Imaging during the Curiosity mission revealed a thick exposure of deposits that extends from the underlying bedrock to the ground surface along the remnant Gediz Vallis (GV) fan in Gale Crater. Most of the deposits are coarse, poorly-sorted sediments interpreted to be debris flow deposits. In a 70 m exposure, the dip of the layers is nearly constant at about 4 degrees downslope. These layers are deposited on an underlying bedrock profile surface that is steeper than 8 degrees. Puzzled by these observations we asked some simple questions: (1) what sets the nearly constant slope of the deposits, (2) how would the depositional slope compare with fan surface slope (not preserved at this site), and (3) how can the gently sloping deposits simply climb a much steeper bedrock surface as the fan develops?

We employed D-Claw, which solves two-dimensional depth-averaged equations that track fluid depth, moment, solid volume fraction and basal pore-fluid pressure and which include the role of segregation that produces levees. Here we report runs based on simplified geometries. We modeled a straight steep channel that delivers debris flows across a broad gently sloping plain. A selected volume of sediment was repeatedly released downslope, progressively building a fan up to 50 meters high. The first flows stopped on the imposed downslope plain. Progressive deposition and the resulting shifting of flows left and right of that built the fan and led to a wide range of depositional slopes. However, as the overall fan form emerged, the fan took on a nearly constant average slope. Fan apex deposition led to the growth up the steep source channel, generating a nearly constant, relatively gently sloping stratigraphy underneath (similar to that observed in the GV fan). This growth led to a steepening of the developing average fan slope. These runs indicate that a wide range of depositional slopes can, collectively, lead to a common average slope of deposition. The results also show that fan slope depends on the ascent of the apex, which is strongly influenced by the lateral shifting process during deposition and growth. Simply changing gravity from Earth to Mars leads to distinctly different fan forms and stratigraphy.

abstract: Carbonate sediment texture and composition reflect interactions among benthic carbonate production, hydrodynamic energy, and sediment redistribution, yet the relative importance of these controls may vary across shallow-water environments. This study compares sediments from six transects across two contrasting lagoons on Ambergris Caye, Belize: the reef-facing windward lagoon (transects A–C) and the protected leeward lagoon at Secret Beach (transects D–F). Field observations documented water depth, substrate, and benthic habitats, whereas dry-sieve granulometry and petrographic point counting were used to characterize sediment texture and grain composition. Both lagoonal settings contain polymodal, poorly sorted medium sand, but the leeward sediment is slightly coarser and contains a substantially larger gravel fraction. Mean grain size is 306 μm leeward and 291 μm windward, whereas gravel constitutes 5.4% and 1.7%, respectively. Both sediments are poorly sorted, although the leeward sediment is slightly more poorly sorted than its windward counterpart. Grain composition shows a pronounced but contrasting pattern. Peloids dominate both assemblages but are more abundant leeward (~82%) than windward (~69%). Windward sediment contains a larger and more diverse skeletal fraction, including approximately 19% molluscan grains and 4% Halimeda , compared with approximately 6% mollusks and negligible Halimeda leeward. Foraminifera are somewhat more abundant leeward (~8%) than windward (~4–5%). These compositional differences are consistent with field observations of dense seagrass, abundant Halimeda , and diverse benthic communities in the windward lagoon, in contrast to the predominantly open sandy substrate and more restricted benthic habitats leeward. Despite greater wave exposure windward, the leeward sediment is coarser and more gravel-rich, whereas the windward sediment contains the larger and more diverse skeletal fraction. This opposing pattern indicates that compositional diversity does not necessarily correspond to coarser sediment or greater hydrodynamic exposure. The windward–leeward contrast demonstrates that grain texture and composition may record partly independent aspects of sediment production and redistribution within a single carbonate-lagoon system.

title: From Collection to Classroom: Developing a Raman Spectral Library for Research and Geoscience Education
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Schumacher, Emilie [1], Eichler, Carla M. [2]
affiliations: (1) West Texas A&M, Amarillo, TX,

abstract:
Raman spectroscopy is a powerful, non-destructive analytical technique for identifying minerals through their unique vibrational spectral "fingerprints." Yet, natural history collections at many universities lack the reference databases needed to fully utilize this technology. At West Texas A&M University, an institution without the resources to purchase a commercial spectral database, we are addressing this gap by developing an in-house Raman spectral reference library using the university's extensive Ward's mineral collection. As an initial step, Raman spectra are being systematically collected for all rock-forming minerals using a Horiba Raman spectrometer and verified against the RRUFF Project database.

In addition to creating a practical reference library for WTAMU, this project establishes a standardized operating procedure (SOP) for the Raman spectrometer, providing a reproducible workflow that other resource-limited institutions can adapt to develop their own spectral databases. The project also has a strong educational component by engaging undergraduate researchers in analytical instrumentation, database development, and scientific methodology while creating resources that can be incorporated into geology instruction and K–12 outreach.

Once the reference library for rock-forming minerals is completed, the workflow will be expanded to additional specimen types within the collection, including bone, feathers, and teeth. As part of the Texas Panhandle Natural History Digital Archive, this project enhances the research value of an existing but underutilized collection while creating an accessible resource for research, education, and public engagement. The resulting workflow and spectral database are intended to serve as both a practical institutional resource and a transferable model for similar regional collections.

title: River Health and Human Interference: A Study of the Haora River, Tripura, India
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Bandyopadhyay, Shreya [1], De, Sunil Kumar [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Maharaja Nandakumar Mahavidyalaya, Kalyanchak, Purba Medinipur, India
(2) Geography, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong, Meghalaya, India
abstract:
Traditionally, the term ‘River Health’ depends solely on the measurement of physical, chemical and some biological characteristics of the river. It is usually applied to the assessment of river conditions and is often found analogous to human health. River health is a relatively new branch within Geomorphology, Hydrology, and Environmental Science. The present study aims to define the term ‘river health’ and its application to the river Haora, which flows between two countries, India and Bangladesh.

The Haora River is widely regarded as the lifeline of Agartala, the capital city of Tripura. Originating in the Baramura Hills, the river descends onto the rolling plains at Chandrasadhubari, near National Highway 44, before flowing south-westward into Bangladesh, where it ultimately joins the Titas River. Since the 1950s, rapid population growth and urban expansion within the Haora River basin have imposed increasing pressure on the river system. Although the overall course of the Haora River remained largely unchanged between 1932 and 2005, significant channel modifications have been observed in three distinct reaches. The changes observed in the first reach are primarily attributed to localised tectonic movements and structural controls that altered the channel alignment. As a consequence, the Katakhal, one of the principal tributaries of the Haora River, has progressively become disconnected from the main channel. These geomorphic adjustments have also resulted in a shift in the confluence of the Haora River with the Titas River within Bangladesh. In contrast, the channel modifications observed in the other two reaches are predominantly the result of intense human intervention, including urban expansion, encroachment onto the floodplain, channel modification, construction activities, and other anthropogenic disturbances. These alterations have affected the geomorphic stability, hydrological behaviour, and ecological functioning of the river, thereby influencing its overall health.

title: Oman Ophiolite as a Potential Analogue for Early Mars Habitability and Life Detection
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology (Posters)
authors: Stoebenau, Ayli [1], Srivastava, Anushree [2], Steele, Andrew [3], Wang, Chenying [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Science Department, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada; Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Science, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Science, Washington, DC, USA
(3) Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Science, Washington, DC, USA
(4) Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Science, Washington, DC, USA
abstract:
Can organic matter associations with manganese dendrites and hematite in Oman ophiolite serpentine inform our understanding of early Mars habitability? Serpentinization is a hydrothermal alteration of ultramafic rocks that produces serpentine, magnetite, or brucite, and hydrogen (H₂) (Joseph, 2023; Shen et al., 2024). H₂ generated during serpentinization fuels hydrogenotrophic and chemolithotrophic microbes and promotes abiotic organic synthesis from dissolved CO₂, potentially supporting microbial populations dominated by Methylotrophic organisms (Steele et al., 2022; Colman et al., 2025). This could create habitable conditions on early Mars (Shen et al., 2024).

Complementary analytical techniques were used to investigate the presence of organic matter in the samples. Raman spectroscopy was performed using a WITec alpha300 confocal Raman microscope on natural surfaces and thin sections to characterize mineralogical and organic signatures. Scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM; ZEISS Auriga) was used to investigate areas previously analyzed by Raman to localize organic signals and their association with mineral textures.

Raman spectroscopy revealed manganese dendrites, hematite, and carbonaceous material, including beta-carotene and CH 2 /CH 3 stretching consistent with cell membranes, associated with serpentine. While manganese dendrites and hematite can oxidize through biotic or abiotic processes, the presence of beta-carotene and possible cell membrane components appears more consistent with a biological origin. SEM investigation also revealed cell-like morphologies in serpentine associated with an exopolymer-like material that secures them to the surface, which is more consistent with a biological origin. Magnetite was also detected by Raman spectroscopy, a known byproduct of serpentinization of iron-rich ultramafic minerals such as fayalite, which is present in this sample. Additionally, Raman mapping allowed single-cell detection. The cell concentration was estimated at 2.5 x 10 5 cells per cm 2 .

Microbially mediated oxidation of dissolved or mineral-bound Mn(II) may have contributed to the formation of Mn-oxide dendrites and the transformation of magnetite to hematite (Neubeck et al., 2025; Brown et al., 1997). This requires further investigation using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, GC-MS, XRD, and DNA extraction to understand the microbe-mineral associations. Serpentine and hematite have been identified on Mars (Tosca et al., 2025; Hynek et al., 2002). If the oxidation responsible for forming manganese dendrites and hematite could be definitively linked to microbial activity, their presence in serpentine on Mars could represent a potential biosignature.

abstract: The Altai Mountains of western Mongolia currently rise over 4 km above sea level, casting a substantial local rain shadow while also modifying Northern Hemisphere climate and dust fluxes. Historical >8 Mw earthquakes are evidence of ongoing tectonism throughout the region. The ambiguous timing of Altai uplift—variously placed in the Mesozoic, late Paleogene, or the Neogene—obscures the potential underlying tectonic mechanisms that drove uplift and our ability to reconstruct how growing Altai topography shaped past climates. We present new results from an ongoing international collaboration to constrain the timing and mechanisms of Altai uplift and trace the associated climatic impacts through time. We integrate new paleomagnetic and cyclostratigraphic data to build a well-constrained age model anchored by biostratigraphic constraints of fluvial and lacustrine sediments in two western Mongolia basins—Hyargas Nuur in the immediate lee and Zereg to the south. We map new and previously published authigenic carbonate stable isotope data to this refined age model to describe the climate evolution of western Mongolia. A thin veneer of Oligocene sediments is present in only one location, with a region-wide unconformity ending with the onset of widespread Neogene sedimentation in the middle to late Miocene, followed by a pronounced unconformity in the late Miocene. Simultaneously, carbonate d 18 O decreases at Hyargas Nur, which we interpret as increasing distillation of moisture over growing topography to the west. In both basins, carbonate d 13 C increases, indicating continued aridification. To contextualize our observations, we performed an idealized experiment with a regional climate model forced with both lower and modern topography and evaluated the simulated changes in climate against our geologic and geochemical data. Elevating the Altai in the climate model concentrates annual precipitation in the summer and substantially increases surface wind speeds over the core part of the Gobi Desert to the south and east. Interpreted together, these results demonstrate that substantial topographic growth occurred in the latest Miocene and Plio-Pleistocene, as initially Oligocene extensional faults were inverted by ongoing compression associated with the India-Asia collision. The timing of this uplift potentially implicates the Altai in documented changes in dust fluxes and ocean circulation that occurred during the Pliocene and suggests that the modern-day Gobi Desert has its origins in the Plio-Pleistocene.

title: A Reanalysis of the Extinct Guitarfish Protoplatyrhina Yields New Insight into Cretaceous Rhinopristiform Diversity and Evolution
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Goode, Benjamin Spencer [1]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Paleontological Society, Mesa, Arizona, USA
abstract: Guitarfish within the order Rhinopristiformes are represented by a rich and diverse fossil record dating back to the Early Jurassic, with many paleotaxa described solely from isolated teeth; one such taxon is the Late Cretaceous genus Protoplatyrhina . Presently, two species have been described: the type species Protoplatyrhina renae , and P . hopii , initially described from the Campanian Judith River Formation of Montana and the Turonian Toreva Formation of Arizona, respectively. Reanalysis of material from the type locality of P . hopii , along with teeth from the Judith River Formation and the Santonian Hosta Tongue of the Point Lookout Sandstone in New Mexico has revealed new insights into Protoplatyrhina evolution and systematics. Initially described lacking a lingual crown uvula (a common characteristic present among rhinopristiform dentitions), P . hopii has now been found to on occasion present this feature, albeit small when represented, helping solidify its placement into the genus. P . renae is marked for its higher degree of heterodonty, particularly concerning crown height; anterior position teeth possess tall, blunt, cuspidate crowns notably distinct from P . hopii or the teeth from the Point Lookout Sandstone. The lingual uvula on anterior and lateral position teeth are much more salient than seen in P . hopii or the Point Lookout Sandstone specimens, as is the lingual protuberance on the tooth base. The Point Lookout Sandstone teeth, first reported as Protoplatyrhina aff. P . renae , are distinct in possessing an intermediate level of crown height heterodonty compared to P . hopii and P . renae , without the cuspidate nature of anterior files as present in the latter. Additionally, the uvula morphology of anterior and lateral files is more pronounced than on stratigraphically older P . hopii , while less pronounced than on younger P . renae , while being morphologically distinct in its sharp protrusion lingually, rather than a rounded lingual protrusion that extends further basally as found in P . renae specimens. Thus, the Point Lookout Sandstone specimens may represent an intermediate taxon within the Protoplatyrhina lineage. Morphological similarities with teeth of Pseudohypolophus and Angolabatis suggest close intrafamilial relationships between the three genera, with a lack of the plesiomorphic trait of a prominent transverse keel on the crown of all tooth positions separating the three taxa from the previously attributed Hypsobatidae.

title: Constraints on the Genesis of the Hod Maden Au–Cu Deposit, Eastern Pontides, Turkey: Timing of Massive Sulfide Formation and Polymetallic Quartz Veining
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part II)
authors: Bilgin, Bader [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Reynolds, T. James [3], Uludag, Osman [4]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines Geology & Geological Engineering, Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Golden, Colorado, USA; Exploration, SSR Mining Inc, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines Geology & Geological Engineering, Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Golden, Colorado, USA
(3) Colorado School of Mines Geology & Geological Engineering, Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Golden, Colorado, USA; FLUID INC, Denver, Colorado, USA

abstract: The Hod Maden Au-Cu deposit in the Eastern Pontides of Turkey comprises semi- to massive sulfide ore bodies containing proven and probable mineral reserve of 7.714 million metric tons of ore grading 7.6 g/t Au and 1.3% Cu, containing a total of 1,896 koz of gold and 223.1 million pounds of copper. The volcanogenic massive sulfides are hosted by a succession of Late Cretaceous submarine volcanic rocks assigned to the Kızılkaya Formation. The stratigraphic footwall to the sulfides has been affected by pervasive chlorite alteration, whereas white mica alteration is dominant in the stratigraphic hanging wall. The volcanic succession is crosscut by polymetallic veins containing abundant pyrite, sphalerite, or chalcopyrite. These veins exhibit textures distinct from typical stringer veins, and their timing and origin remain debated. Detailed petrographic studies and lithogeochemical investigations indicate that the semi- to massive sulfides are hosted by volcaniclastic deposits of andesitic composition. Sulfide precipitation occurred by subseafloor infiltration and replacement. Re-Os geochronology indicates sulfide formation occurred at 86.88 ± 0.32 Ma, consistent with the age of the submarine volcanic host rocks. Field observations and drill core logging revealed that the polymetallic quartz veins are stratigraphically controlled and predominantly occur in the footwall of the semi- to massive sulfides. Quartz in the veins displays mosaic textures, flamboyant grains characterized by inclusion-rich cores, and prismatic grains showing feathery domains. These microtextures suggest that the quartz formed through maturation of a noncrystalline silica precursor by quenching of the hydrothermal fluids. The fluid inclusion inventory of the quartz has been affected by post-entrapment modification, suggesting that quartz formation predated regional metamorphism. This interpretation is supported by the deformation and recrystallization textures observed in both the semi- to massive sulfides and the polymetallic veins. The study demonstrates that polymetallic veins are unlikely to be related to an Eocene hydrothermal overprint.

title: Flood duration controls the detectability of multiscale bedforms in preserved cross strata
session_title: Morphodynamics and preservation of bedforms across scales and environments
authors: Das, Debsmita [1], Ganti, Vamsi [2], Mahon, Robert [3]
affiliations: (1) University of California Berkeley, Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Berkeley, California, USA

(2) University of California Santa Barbara, Department of Geography, Santa Barbara, California, USA; University of California Santa Barbara, Department of Earth Science, Santa Barbara, California, USA
(3) University of Wyoming, Department of Geology and Geophysics, Laramie, Wyoming, USA
abstract:
Floods reorganize river channels and reshape sedimentary deposits, yet only a subset of flood events survive the filtering effects of sediment transport and reworking to leave a stratigraphic imprint. Identifying which floods are preserved and which get erased is central to reconstructing hydroclimatic variability from the fluvial rock record. Migrating bedforms on sandy riverbeds deposit cross strata whose geometry encodes formative flow and sediment transport conditions, making them a key tool for inferring paleoflow. Classic preservation theory predicts that under steady flow these bedforms generate exponential-tailed cross-set thickness distributions. Natural rivers, however, are unsteady and host multiscale bedforms that reorganize with the sediment transport stage during floods. Yet it remains unclear how flood duration controls the stratigraphic signature of these multiscale bedforms.

We addressed this gap using physical experiments of bedform evolution in a 15-m-long, 2-m-wide, 1-m-deep sediment-and-water-recirculating flume. We prepared a 0.25 m deep sediment bed of unimodal quartz sand and set the flow depth to ~0.35 m above it. We ran six symmetric flood-hydrograph experiments that shared identical base (0.29 m³/s; u*/w s <1) and peak discharge (0.41 m³/s; u*/w s >1) but spanned durations from 20 minutes to 20 hours, and one steady-state experiment at the baseflow. We captured high-resolution bathymetry every 2–4 minutes with an underwater laser scanner over a 5 × 0.75 m section throughout each run. From these bed-elevation profiles we constructed synthetic stratigraphy, computed set-thickness statistics, and compared them to scour-depth distributions from the bedform profiles.

Our results indicate that, for floods of a given magnitude, the duration sets the threshold for their detectability in preserved cross strata. Floods shorter than the turnover timescale of smaller-scale bedforms are shredded by internal variability of the bedform field, leaving strata indistinguishable from baseflow. Intermediate-duration floods drive partial reorganization of the bed, producing deeper scours and thicker cross-sets, while only floods exceeding the turnover timescale of large bedforms fully reconfigure the bed into large dunes with superimposed bedforms, generating the deepest scours and thickest preserved sets with preservation biased toward falling-limb deposits. These results show that only floods long-lived enough to exceed the turnover timescale of the largest bedforms are detectable in the stratigraphic record.

title: The nature and age of deformation along the northwestern boundary of the New England Avalon Terrane in Eastern Massachusetts
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part II)
authors: Arolkar, Nikhil [1], Kuiper, Yvette D. [2], Link, Frederik [3], Long, Maureen [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Institute of Geosciences, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Mainz, Rhineland Palatinate, Germany

abstract: The New England Avalon terrane’s (AT) accretion to the southeastern margin of the Nashoba terrane (NT), the trailing edge of Ganderia, marks the Acadian orogeny’s onset (~420 Ma) in New England. Northwest-side-down folds at high structural levels and symmetric folds at lower levels are documented in the northwest-dipping NT. High-grade, partially melted NT rocks are juxtaposed against lower-grade rocks of the Merrimack belt and AT to the northwest and southeast, respectively. Previous studies contend that the NT underwent channel flow and ductile extrusion to the southeast onto the AT during the Acadian orogeny. Furthermore, a northwest-dipping transition in crustal structure, potentially representing the base of the channel flow zone, is visible across the NT-AT boundary in cross-sections produced from data collected by the GENESIS array of broadband seismometers. Folds with northwest-side-down asymmetry are expected at the bottom of a channel flow zone. However, these were not found in the southeastern part of the NT. A ~26 km by ~11 km area in the northwestern part of the AT, adjacent to the NT, was structurally mapped to test whether the base of the channel flow zone was located in the AT adjacent to the NT. Based on deformation styles, the study area was divided into ductile-dominated and brittle-dominated zones (DDZ and BDZ, respectively). The DDZ exhibits moderately to steeply northwest-dipping isoclinal folds and foliations. Lineations plunge northeast and southwest. Mylonite zones dip northwest and show various shear directions and senses. Fault planes and slickenlines are parallel to foliations and lineations, respectively. Rocks in the BDZ contain more faults than the DDZ. Foliations, lineations, mylonite zones, faults, and slickenlines exhibit various orientations. Folds are not observed. Fault movement in both the DDZ and BDZ is predominantly normal. Ediacaran (~590 Ma, ~593 Ma, and ~602 Ma) U-Pb LA-ICP-MS zircon ages from migmatites suggest that high-grade metamorphism and partial melting in the AT predate the Acadian orogeny. Furthermore, 365 Ma zircon crystallization ages from a granite crosscutting a mylonite indicate that mylonitization occurred before the early Carboniferous. Evidence of widespread faulting, coupled with the lack of evidence for channel flow during the Acadian orogeny, may indicate that a fault cut off the bottom of the hypothesized channel flow zone.

title: Evidence for Phylogenetic Continuity Among North American Crocodylians and Faunal Replacement in Europe Across the K–Pg Boundary
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Posters)
authors: Tarailo, David A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Biological Sciences, Fort Hays State University, Hays, KS,
abstract: The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) mass extinction substantially reorganized vertebrate communities, but the dynamics of crocodylian survival and recovery remain poorly understood. I compared phylogenetic structure across the K-Pg boundary in Europe and North America to test whether the two regions experienced different patterns of faunal continuity versus replacement. A composite phylogeny was assembled for crocodylian taxa occurring within approximately 10 m.y. of the boundary, in order to examine the relatedness of crocodylians pre- and post-extinction. This was quantified using mean taxon distance (MTD) across all pre- and post-extinction pairs, and mean nearest-taxon distance (MNTD) between the closest cross-boundary relatives. Statistical significance was evaluated using size-matched permutation tests which compared the observed metrics with those of randomly assembled global faunas. Europe consistently exhibited larger cross-boundary phylogenetic distances than North America. Species-level MTD was 19.5 in Europe and 14.3 in North America, and MNTD was 8.7 and 4.1, respectively. The regional contrast was found at both the species and genus levels and persisted after the removal of phylogenetic outliers, indicating that it is not explained by differences in taxonomic lumping versus splitting or the presence of particularly phylogenetically distinct taxa. North American MTD and MNTD fell within the lowest 3-4% of null distributions obtained from permutation tests, whereas European values generally exceeded null means. This demonstrates markedly greater phylogenetic continuity across the K-Pg boundary in North America, contrasted with more extensive faunal replacement in Europe. The observed pattern is consistent with enhanced persistence of resident lineages in North America, coupled with increased immigration into Europe during Paleocene recovery.

title: Short-Term Fieldwork, Long-Term Impact: Building Community, Self-Efficacy, and Skill Development to Improve Geoscience Retention
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation
authors: Flynn, Wendilyn [1], Keeler, Jason [2], Kluver, Daria [3], Johnson, Matthew [4], DeYoung, Collin [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mt. Pleasant, MI, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mt. Pleasant, MI, USA
(4) Department of Counseling, Educational Leadership, & Higher Education, Central Michigan University, Mt. Pleasant, MI, USA
(5) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mt. Pleasant, MI, USA
abstract:
Student Training for Observational Research in Meteorology (STORM) is an intensive, week-long collaborative field experience designed for undergraduate meteorology students who are rising sophomores. This demographic has been identified as a critical point of attrition among atmospheric science majors. Few empirical studies in the geosciences have examined the impacts of short-term project interventions on students’ affective development and long-term retention. This project seeks to bridge that gap, through cultivating student personal development alongside technical skills in meteorological instrumentation. In this presentation, we will detail the methodological framework and pedagogical construction of STORM and share preliminary outcomes.

This mixed-methods study employs a pre- and post- survey design to measure affective domain changes such as science identity, sense of belonging, self-assessed perseverance in the major and specific impacts of this experience. Student participants are selected based on application responses to affective domain questions rather than GPA or academic standing, as we seek to include students that have a higher likelihood of being influenced by the experience. Living arrangements, organization of student fieldwork teams, team-based data analysis, and planned, optional social activities are intentionally designed to build community during the student experience. In-person and remote activities in subsequent semesters help sustain and strengthen the interpersonal connections formed during the experience. Goals of this project include mitigating student attrition in the geosciences and deepening our understanding of the role of student affective domain in retention through short-term high-impact experiences.

title: Fossil Camel bones from the Pliocene San Diego Formation, California, with numerous Shark tooth marks
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record (Posters)
authors: Bogart, Destin [1], Prothero, Donald R. [2], Deméré, Thomas A. [3], Olson, Sara [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, CPP, pomona, CA, USA
(2) California Polytechnic State University, La Crescenta, CA, USA
(3) San Diego Natural History Museum, San Diego, CA, USA
(4) Geology, CPP, Pomona, CA, USA
abstract: Shark bite marks in fossil bones are uncommon in the fossil record but have been reported in a number of cases. The Pliocene San Diego Formation in southern California, a shallow marine unit, has already yielded whale bones with bite marks attributed to the great white shark, Carcharodon sulcidens . In addition to other examples of shark-bitten whale bones, there are shark bite marks on a humerus of an associated front limb attributable to the extinct giant camel Megatylopus sp. (these same specimens are misidentified as Camelops in the literature and online) that apparently came from a bloat-and-float event. These bones bear clear grooves with shark-tooth marks. On the humerus, there are a total of 8 marks, with an average length of 16.375 mm, and an average orientation of 61.5° ± 0.93° with respect to the long axis of the bone, or nearly perpendicular. These marks occur on all sides of the humerus, suggesting the bone was likely impacted by both upper and lower teeth. In addition, one mark preserves a set of fine parallel ridges and grooves indicative of damage caused by a tooth with serrated margins. This evidence suggests the trace maker was likely Carcharodon sulcidens , since the only other shark known from the San Diego Formation with teeth large enough to create the observed overall pattern of bite marks is a species of mako shark, Isurus sp., whose teeth are not serrated. This is the first known and described occurrence of extinct shark-tooth marks in extinct camelid remains.

title: Beyond Jadeitites: Garnet-bearing Quartz Albitites Define a New Archive of High-pressure Subduction-zone Fluids
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Strickland, Anna H. [1], Flores, Kennet E. [2], Gazel, Esteban [3], Hull, Sarah W. [4], Requena, Jaime [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Marine, and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(2) Earth, Marine, and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, USA; Earth and Planetary Sciences, American Museum of Natural History, New York City, NY, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
(4) Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
(5) Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Guatemala City, Guatemala, Guatemala
abstract:
Fluid-rock interaction governs mass transfer and metasomatism along subduction interfaces, producing a diverse suite of metasomatic vein-rocks including jadeitites, omphacitites, albitites, phengitites, and lawsonitites that have long been interpreted to reflect differences in fluid composition, host-rock composition, and reaction pathways. However, because most of these lithologies are near monomineralic, making them unsuitable for quantitative thermobarometry, the pressure-temperature conditions of fluid-rock interaction remain poorly constrained. As a result, interpretations of the physical conditions of vein formation have relied primarily on petrogenetic stability fields; which for jadeitites in the North Motagua Mélange (NMM), Guatemala, yield broad constraints of ~300–450 °C and ~0.5–1.2 GPa.

Here we identify garnet-bearing quartz albitites, a previously unrecognized subduction-related, vein-rock lithology formed during interaction between slab-derived fluids and serpentinite in the NMM, that unlike jadeitites and most other metasomatic vein-rocks, preserve equilibrium mineral assemblages permitting the P-T-t reconstruction of fluid-rock interaction. We combine petrography, mineral chemistry, whole-rock geochemistry, U–Pb zircon geochronology, Ti-in-zircon thermometry, and quartz-in-garnet elastic thermobarometry to constrain their P-T-t evolution. U–Pb zircon ages demonstrate that the quartz-albitites formed contemporaneously with NMM jadeitites (~90 Ma). These coeval ages and similar zircon trace-element compositions indicate formation from related slab-derived fluids and permit direct comparison between these vein rocks. Thermobarometric results indicate that fluid-rock interaction occurred at 1.4–2.2 GPa and 650–750 °C, significantly higher pressures and temperatures than those previously inferred from jadeitite stability fields.

The higher P-T conditions recorded by garnet-bearing quartz albitites, despite their formation from fluids comparable in age and composition to the coveal jadeitites, demonstrate that paragenetic vein rocks formed from related slab-derived fluids can record markedly different physical conditions of fluid-rock interaction. These results indicate that the diversity of subduction-related metasomatic vein-rocks reflect not only differences in fluid and host-rock composition, but also the evolving physical conditions in which slab-derived fluids react with the mantle. By preserving equilibrium mineral assemblages needed for integrated P-T-t reconstruction, garnet-bearing quartz albitites provide the first quantitative constraints on one stage of this evolution, linking the timing, pressure-temperature conditions, and geochemical signature of fluid-rock interaction within a single vein-rock lithology. Together with jadeitites and other subduction-related vein-rocks, they provide a more complete record of how slab-derived fluids evolve, migrate, and drive metasomatism along subduction interfaces.
