abstract:
Water tracks are a critical hydrologic feature spanning permafrost environments, where the impermeable permafrost limits fluvial incision, leading to linear to curvilinear subsurface flowpaths draining hillslopes into larger water bodies. These flowpaths contribute to a significant amount of drainage area in these environments while both transporting nutrients and supporting productivity. Furthermore, water tracks can release significant amounts of greenhouse gases due to promoting thaw and, as climatic disturbance is introduced, can develop into thermoerosional gullies, making them significant geomorphic and climate indicators. However, despite these broad impacts, large scale remote sensing identification remains underdeveloped due to the varying morphologies of water tracks both within and between different permafrost environments. Thus, this project seeks to develop a deep learning image segmentation methodology that can delineate individual water tracks using high-resolution satellite data, such that water track abundance and type can be efficiently monitored across time and space.

We manually segmented water tracks from the well-studied Seward Peninsula, Alaska utilizing RGB and NDVI data from Worldview-2 as well as elevation and slope data from ArcticDEM. This dataset is converted into image label pairs, which we used to test several trained and untrained segmentation applications designed for geologic and remote sensing use. After attempting various programs, a manually trained U-Net model produced the most promising results, which accepts various hyperparameter configurations and multispectral imagery while returning easily transferable model weights.

This successful model is applied to large areas surrounding the training data in the Seward Peninsula to monitor performance over similar water track morphology. The model is then upscaled to detect water tracks in both varying seasonalities and in different, well-studied regions of the pan-Arctic to assess performance as water track morphology differs. We hypothesize that the model will succeed at capturing similar locations and times to the training data, but will worsen as water track features begin to differ over time and space. Future work will focus on creating both improved and varied datasets, as well as additional models where one begins to fail, potentially resulting in the use of ensemble methods to detect all morphologies.

abstract: The interaction of hydrothermal fluids with fault rocks throughout seismic cycles can result in hydrothermal alteration, modifying fracture networks, permeability, and ultimately influencing both subsurface fluid flow and future fault reactivation. Determining the categories and sequential relationships between preexisting and concurrent hydrothermal alteration along faults provides important insights into fault nucleation and propagation along preexisting structures. In this study, we focus on the 2019 Ridgecrest earthquake sequence, where numerous faults were activated along preexisting dike contacts. We compare surface slip with field and satellite mapping of dikes, which displays variable fault activation over the length of meters to kilometers along dike intrusion contacts. To further understand why faulting occurs on only some sections of an individual contact, we perform structural and geochemical analyses along transects orthogonal to the dike contact at two locations, one with faulting present and one without. We map out fractures through field and photogrammetric analysis, and conduct mineralogical and chemical characterization using petrographic imaging, X-ray diffraction, and X-ray fluorescence. Mineralogical analysis reveals enhanced concentrations of phyllosilicates and calcite growth along faulted dike contacts, producing a weaker zone in the granites close to the dike. In contrast, the portion of the dike that has not been reactivated as a fault shows reduced levels of hydrothermal alteration and phyllosilicate formation, and an absence of calcite. The presence of micas and sericite along the faulted section of the dike suggests localized phyllic alteration in the granite, which is frictionally weak compared to the less altered dike contact with no fault reactivation. Our results suggest that variations in hydrothermal mineral alteration along dike contacts dictate varying degrees of fault reactivation and initiate positive feedbacks wherein progressive deformation accelerates further alteration. This study leads to a better understanding of the impactful presence of fluid within fault zones and provides insights to help better predict long-term chemical evolution and changes in fault strength.

title: The Significance of Orogenic Cores and Associated Detachment Systems
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse
authors: Teyssier, Christian [1], Whitney, Donna L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota - Twin Cities, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota - Twin Cities, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
abstract:
During the orogenic cycle, crustal accretion may take 10-100 Myr, whereas the collapse of thickened crust, resulting flow of deep crust, and emplacement of metamorphic core complexes (MCC) and migmatite domes, is short lived (1-10 Myr). Material transfer during collapse is achieved by lateral flow near the base of the thickened crust, where highly sheared partially molten rocks (migmatites when crystallized) either remain buried or are exhumed in domes. Migmatite domes commonly include mafic layers or pods that are valuable recorders of the provenance of partially molten crust. In some domes, mafic pods are eclogite or high-pressure (HP) granulites that were metamorphosed in the deep orogenic crust, and the age of HP metamorphism is close to the age of migmatite crystallization. In other cases, eclogite formed in subduction zones and was later incorporated in partially molten crust. The presence of orogenic eclogite in migmatite suggests that the partially molten crust is sourced at near-Moho depths and is extremely mobile, traveling rapidly laterally (>100 km) and vertically (from near-Moho to near-surface). This also implies that partially molten crust exists under a normal geotherm and does not rely on additional heat sources to explain the occurrence of high-T rocks at the low to moderate depths of emplacement.

MCCs are bounded by detachment shear zones that record large strain and steep metamorphic gradients as well as effective fluid-rock interaction enhanced by intense deformation and recrystallization processes at the grain scale. Stable isotope analyses across detachment systems have delineated the limit between a zone dominated by surface-derived (meteoric) fluids above and a zone of prevailing metamorphic fluids below. In some cases, the meteoric fluid is consistent with a surface fluid that precipitated at high elevation and was involved in convective flow from the surface down to the detachment shear zone, likely during the initial stages of orogenic collapse. Therefore, both migmatite domes and detachment zones present in the core of orogens retain essential information about the flow of the deep crust, the provenance of partially molten crust, the history of metamorphic and meteoric fluids, and the deep to shallow processes that reflect the stabilization of orogenic crust.

title: Downfan Process Variation in a Multi-Process Dryland Alluvial Fan: Insights from the Cretaceous Jeokgakri Formation, Korea
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans

abstract: The downfan variation of depositional processes is well documented for single-process-dominated alluvial fans, but remains poorly constrained for multi-process, composite fan systems. The Cretaceous Jeokgakri Formation of mid-eastern Korea preserves a small-scale, dryland alluvial fan succession recording four depositional processes (cohesive debris flow, hyperconcentrated flow, stream flow/sheetflood, and overland flood flow), providing a favorable target for examining this problem. Thirteen sedimentary facies were documented at 16 localities and grouped into proximal, medial, and distal sectors using a relative proximity classification based on maximum clast size and the proportion of fine-grained deposits. Proximal sectors are dominated by amalgamated, boulder-bearing debris flow sheets; medial sectors show a marked increase in hyperconcentrated flow and stream flow deposits within concave scour, and low-relief gravel sheets; and distal sectors are dominated by fine-grained deposits, with gravelstone comprising only a subordinate fraction. Notably, hyperconcentrated flow and stream flow deposits decline more rapidly toward the distal sector than debris flow deposits, a pattern not fully explained by the downfan decrease in slope gradient alone. We interpret this as reflecting differential infiltration resistance among processes: debris flows, which trap interstitial pore water and require a comparatively low water fraction to remain mobile, are less susceptible to infiltration-driven discharge loss, whereas stream flow and hyperconcentrated flow progressively lose transport competence through downfan infiltration. Supporting evidence includes clay coatings on grains that predate calcite cementation, convex gravel sheet geomorphology consistent with short-lived hydrographs, and pervasive reddish pigmentation with calcrete development indicating a persistent vadose zone. These results indicate that downfan process variation in multi-process dryland alluvial fans is governed not only by slope gradient but also by process-dependent infiltration resistance, offering a depositional model applicable to other multi-process alluvial fan systems and to flood hazard assessment in arid regions.

abstract: Hillslopes in northern Vietnam's mountainous terrain are highly unstable and, when intensely saturated during the monsoon season, especially along the trajectories of tropical cyclones, become hot spots of landslide activity. Historical data suggest the phenomenon is recurrent, but its spatiotemporal prediction is highly uncertain. Using field and remote sensing data, soil laboratory analyses, and machine learning techniques, we explored several aspects of landslide activity in the study region: landslide types and their driving factors, as well as soil and terrain features that increase the likelihood of landslides. Soils on steep, vegetated, or frequently agriculturally altered hillslopes move downslope under gravity and groundwater pressure. Landslide features varied across the geological bedrock, which was frequently deeply weathered. The majority of forms were classified as debris avalanches and flows, and they all formed quickly during periods of high cumulative precipitation. Examples include regions such as Ho Bon and Xuan Minh, where clusters of landslides formed during well-defined rainfall events. At certain spatial resolutions, geological bedrock and precipitation are the most important predictors for landslide susceptibility mapping. In addition, the distances to faults, roads, and streams are important features explaining landslide densities and probabilities. However, static predictors are insufficient to inform landslide hazard assessments, and modern approaches require dynamic, time-dependent variables such as rainfall sums, changes in vegetation cover, and land-use/land-cover features. At the soil profile scale, we suggest that soil and weathering-material features, such as particle-size distribution and clay mineral content, have controlled landslide formation in the study region by influencing groundwater flow and pressure. The study has been supported by the National Science Center (project no 2023/49/B/ST10/02879).

abstract: Detrital mica ⁴⁰Ar/³⁹Ar and zircon U-Pb geochronology record reorganization of regional river systems in response to early Eocene collision of the Siletz oceanic terrane with North America in SW Oregon. The Umpqua Group (UG; ~53–49 Ma) filled a peripheral foreland basin during collision of Siletzia, and the overlying Coos River group (CRG, informal name; ~48–40 Ma; includes the Tyee Formation) records subsidence during post-collision reorganization of the convergent margin. This transition was marked by a westward jump of the trench to form the modern Cascadia subduction zone, slab rollback, extension, and clockwise rotation of Siletzia and its Eocene sedimentary cover (Wells et al., 2014). Previous studies proposed a provenance shift from proximal sources in the Klamath Mountains to distal sources in the Idaho Batholith, but published detrital mica datasets lacked a UG baseline needed to test alternative provenance hypotheses. We present 1,120 single-grain 40 Ar/ 39 Ar total fusion ages of detrital mica from eight samples spanning the UG and CRG. Two additional samples characterize potential sediment sources: modern sand from the Payette River which drains the Atlanta lobe of the Idaho Batholith, and the Cretaceous Cape Sebastian Sandstone to evaluate sediment recycling. These data provide the first continuous grain-scale record of this tectonic transition using integrated 40 Ar/ 39 Ar and U-Pb methods. The Tenmile and Whitetail Ridge formations (middle UG) are dominated by mica ages with a single peak at ~150 Ma, consistent with a source in the Klamath Mountains. The Camas Valley Formation (upper UG) shows a dispersed, transitional spectrum of mica ages. The CRG lacks ~150-Ma mica and zircon and records a distinctly different spectrum of younger ~80–60-Ma populations compatible with input from western Idaho. Depositional age constraints from detrital zircon show that this change took place in ≤2 Myr, between deposition of the basal Camas Valley Formation (~50 Ma) and basal Tyee Formation (~48 Ma). We interpret that this provenance shift records a brief phase of post-accretion topographic reorganization when proximal rivers sourced in the Klamath Mountains were replaced by a large river system that delivered detritus from the continental interior to the evolving margin. The new paleoriver appears to have crossed the Klamath Mountains without entraining Klamath-derived mica, a result that raises new questions about post-collision landscape evolution.

abstract: The end-Ordovician mass extinction profoundly disrupted benthic marine ecosystems, yet post-extinction recovery is generally viewed as a largely temporal process rather than one structured along environmental gradients. Here we report abundant wrinkle structures from the Lower Silurian Daxichang Formation of Guizhou, South China, a siliciclastic shelf-transition succession deposited between shallow-water carbonate platforms and deeper graptolitic black shales. Graptolite biostratigraphy indicates that the wrinkle-bearing interval is latest Rhuddanian, immediately following the extinction interval. Unlike coeval shallow-water carbonate successions, where shelly benthos and the earliest coral–stromatoporoid reef communities had already begun to recover, deeper offshore black shales remained largely devoid of benthic metazoans. We propose that the Daxichang shelf-transition environment represents an ecological intermediate, where metazoan grazing and bioturbation remained suppressed, yet environmental conditions were sufficiently favorable to support extensive microbial-mat development and preservation. This pattern suggests that microbial mat expansion following the end-Ordovician mass extinction was not uniform across marine environments, but instead reflected a depth-selective ecological release. In this model, microbial mats reached their greatest ecological importance within a bathymetrically restricted transition zone situated between rapidly recovering shallow-water ecosystems and environmentally stressed offshore settings. Rather than representing ecosystem collapse alone, these matgrounds may have temporarily stabilized substrates, concentrated organic matter, and provided ecological opportunities for surviving and opportunistic benthic organisms before the re-establishment of fully bioturbated seafloors. This recovery model differs fundamentally from the widespread and prolonged microbial resurgence documented after the end-Permian mass extinction, suggesting that microbial ecological release after mass extinctions may be highly dependent on environmental gradients and the spatial heterogeneity of benthic recovery. The Daxichang Formation therefore provides a new perspective on how microbial ecosystems and metazoan communities interacted during one of the earliest Phanerozoic recovery intervals.

abstract:
Wildfires affect substantial areas of Mediterranean mountain environments on an annual basis. Most studies aiming to understand the in situ adverse effects of fire focus on the immediate post-fire period or, at most, a two- or three-year window until the vegetative cover begins to recover. The objective of this study is to conduct a detailed monitoring of a mountain hillslope in the Mediterranean region (Central System, Spain) using LiDAR data—acquired via manned aircraft in 2011, 2018, and 2023, and via UAS-LiDAR in 2024, May 2025, and December 2025—alongside their derived products (DEMs, connectivity models, hillshades, etc.). Additionally, in situ soil sample analyses and precipitation data from a nearby meteorological station were utilized. Soil erosion on the hillslope was subsequently modeled using the Water Erosion Prediction Project (WEPP) model to benchmark the magnitude of the observed changes.

The results demonstrate high and widespread erosion rates during the first period (2011–2018), corresponding to the response to a wildfire that occurred in 2016. In 2019, a debris flow (DF) occurred, mobilizing 2,867 m 3 of sediment and forming a channel 310 m long, 12 m wide, and 2 m deep on average, depositing the coarser material into the existing channel at the base of the slope, whose trajectory was substantially altered. The UAS-LiDAR data acquired throughout 2024 and 2025 reveal that erosion rates remain elevated nearly a decade after the wildfire, far exceeding the estimates produced by the WEPP model (195 vs 87.5 ton·ha -1 ·y -1 ). The observed topographic modifications have significantly altered hillslope connectivity, enhancing it and accelerating the loss of water and sediment. Analysis of precipitation data indicates that the event triggering the DF exhibited an Intensity–Duration threshold substantially lower than the previously established threshold for the Central System (I=38D -0.7077 vs I=127.93D -0.7077 ) underscoring the severe impact of the wildfire and vegetation cover reduction. This study demonstrates that the wildfire and the subsequent DF have driven long-term changes on this hillslope, significantly altering its hydrosedimentary connectivity and sustaining remarkably high soil erosion rates.

abstract: Megathrusts are interplate faults that accommodate deformation under low effective stress in a fluid-rich environment. The stress state and the origin of fluids of ancient, exhumed megathrusts can be investigated from syntectonic veins. The Sestola–Vidiciatico Unit (SVU) in the Northern Apennines (Italy) was the plate boundary shear zone (200–400 m thick) between the Ligurian prism and the Adria microplate during the early–middle Miocene, active up to temperatures of ~170 °C. The SVU is composed of kilometre-scale slices of marls, shales and sandstones derived from the Ligurian prism and its sedimentary cover, thrust along a basal décollement onto younger Adria foredeep turbidites. We studied a well-exposed outcrop of the basal décollement of the SVU. The footwall consists of sandstones and siltstones of Langhian age, overthrust by a slice of Aquitanian marls, and by an upper slice of Priabonian claystone. We performed structural mapping, microstructural and geochemical analyses (stable and radiogenic isotopes, trace and major element geochemistry), and fluid inclusion studies on calcites cementing shear and extensional veins and tectonic breccias. Thrust surfaces are very sharp and decorated by multistage shear veins. Off the thrusts, marls and claystone are crosscut by pervasive shear fractures bounding flattened and elongated lithons defining a low angle foliation. Deformation in the footwall includes oblique cleavage, bedding-parallel shear planes, and a conjugated set of subvertical transtensional faults mutually crosscutting with the basal thrust of the SVU. Calcite shear veins mark thrust surfaces, whereas transtensional faults in the footwall are marked by shear and extension veins, and calcite-cemented breccias. Two main calcite phases have been observed: an early-stage calcite rich in host-rock inclusions and a later inclusion-free calcite. Geochemical and thermometric results point to two groups of distinct mineralizing fluids circulating through the fracture network: (1) diluted seawater precipitating early-stage calcites at low temperatures (< 50 °C up to 70 °C); (2) an external low-salinity fluid precipitating later-calcites at higher temperatures (~80-100° C). Data suggest a transition from low temperature, low salinity fluids, possibly from mixing between seawater and clay dehydration-derived fluids, to the ingression of moderately hot fluids (up to 120 °C) external from the system. The opening of fluid circulation by faulting was modulated by the progressive embrittlement of the megathrust at increasing burial.

abstract:
Lava rheology exerts strong controls on the style of eruption and the rate of lava flow emplacement. Unlike other physical properties, it can vary by many orders of magnitude from vent to flow toe. Most cooled lava samples contain three phases: liquid/glass, crystals, and bubbles. We are currently developing experimental techniques for three-phase rheological measurements at the temperature and strain-rate conditions of flow emplacement (Halverson & Whittington 2025 Geology). Here we compare our preliminary experimental results with the predictions of current models for liquid and suspension viscosity, and consider their uncertainties.

Step 1 is to calculate the viscosity of the liquid, which varies with temperature and composition. Several models are now available but all have uncertainties ~0.5 log units (a factor of 3) at the ±1 sigma level. Additional uncertainties arise from temperature, composition, and model calibration.

Step 2 is to include the effect of crystals, which depends on crystal size and shape distribution, and strain rate, as well as total volume fraction. Uncertainties for relative viscosity (i.e. viscosity of suspension / viscosity of just the liquid phase), in the 40-60% crystallinity range are orders of magnitude.

Step 3 is to include the effect of bubbles, which are deformable at high capillary number (high strain rates) so they can increase or decrease magma viscosity, but their interactions with crystals are poorly understood.

Preliminary results on lavas from Kīlauea and Mauna Loa volcanoes, Hawai’i, and Carrizozo, New Mexico, indicate that deformable bubbles can offset viscosity increases due to modest amounts of crystals, so that three-phase lavas can potentially be as fluid as the melt alone. Three-phase lavas are typically more strongly shear-thinning than crystal-liquid suspensions without bubbles. This enables very rapid emplacement of crystal-poor lava near the vent. The observation of uniform spherical bubbles in a highly crystalline matrix in the Mauna Loa 1880 flow indicates that textures may continue to evolve after flow has ceased, making experimental measurements at eruption conditions even more important for estimating emplacement rates.

abstract:
Mediterranean Mountain Areas (MMA) are highly vulnerable to Global Change, severely impacting landscape stability and hydro-sedimentary regulation. This research quantifies soil erosion dynamics within the Jerte Valley catchment (Extremadura, Spain) by contrasting two geomorphological hotspots: Pasil, a mid-elevation area of terraced cherry orchards, and Asperones, a steep high-mountain environment featuring a 2019 active debris flow.

Hydrology and erosion mechanics were simulated using the GeoWEPP model. The framework integrated 1m UAS-LIDAR Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) with localized environmental data, validating sediment yields through DEMs of Difference (DoDs) and statistical metrics such as R 2 and NSE.

Results revealed erosional dynamics strongly conditioned by landscape features. In the Asperones area, using the initial UAS-flight DEM (October 21, 2024) and historical land-use data, a 10-year simulation yielded a soil loss of 45.5 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 . However, incorporating 2022 land-use data—which captures the active debris flow and increased exposed rocky substrate—dramatically escalated the estimated soil loss to 87.5 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 . Conversely, the Pasil hotspot exhibited significantly lower and more consistent erosion rates. Using its initial UAS-flight DEM (December 16, 2024) with 2022 land-use data, the estimated soil loss was 10.8 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 , remaining nearly identical (10.3 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 ) when applying historical land-use data. This negligible variation reflects Pasil stable agricultural land use, contrasting sharply with the severe geomorphological instability driving larger soil loss in Asperones.

Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that terraced agriculture maintains relatively moderate erosion rates. At approximately 10 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 , this soil loss sits at the threshold between moderate (2-10 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 ) and high (10-20 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 ) categories according to the European Joint Research Centre (JRC) classification. Under current environmental conditions, agricultural terracing proves to be more beneficial for soil conservation than highly disturbed high-mountain and forest land uses. However, the subsequent implications of these agricultural practices on local water resources and hydrological dynamics remain a critical aspect that needs further investigation.

abstract: Lithium isotopes fractionate strongly during water-rock interactions associated with chemical weathering and clay formation, making seawater δ⁷Li a sensitive tracer of continental weathering. Marine carbonates can preserve this seawater δ⁷Li signal after accounting for carbonate-seawater isotopic fractionation, providing a proxy for long-term continental weathering history.Proterozoic carbonates investigated to date display a persistently low δ 7 Li signature. However, diagenesis and detrital contamination can substantially alter carbonate mineralogy and chemical components, making it difficult to distinguish primary seawater δ 7 Li values from secondary overprinting. Here, we integrate petrographic, mineralogical, elemental, and isotopic screening approaches to identify Proterozoic marine carbonates that faithfully record primary seawater δ 7 Li. SEM and XRD analyses first exclude samples containing more than 50 % quartz, retaining carbonate-dominated material for subsequent geochemistry. Major, minor, and trace elemental ratios then flag residual detrital contamination and diagenetic alteration, whereas rare earth element patterns help identify hydrothermal signatures. Finally, paired carbon (δ¹³C) and oxygen (δ¹⁸O) isotope analyses indicate negligible meteoric diagenesis for selected samples. After screening, only samples preserving primary marine signatures are retained for δ 7 Li analysis. Coeval seawater δ 7 Li values are reconstructed by correcting for carbonate-seawater isotopic fractionation associated with mineralogical and vital effects. Our results indicate that the Proterozoic seawater δ 7 Li values range between ~ –6 to +21 ‰, far below the modern seawater value of ~+31 ‰. In detail, the early Proterozoic exhibits slightly lower seawater δ 7 Li values than later intervals. We therefore propose that the reconstructed changes reflect a combination of mechanisms, with different processes dominating at different times. This study presents an integrated screening framework that combines multiple approaches to enhance the fidelity of seawater δ 7 Li reconstructions from ancient marine carbonates, enabling a more robust interpretation of long-term continental weathering and the global lithium cycle. Our study also provides new insights into carbonate diagenesis by leveraging elemental and isotopic ratios to evaluate the imprint of diagenesis on the mineralogical and geochemical records preserved in ancient marine carbonates.

abstract: The Dinarides formed during the Cenozoic from the collision and subduction of the Adria microplate with Eurasia. However, there remain questions about the geodynamic mechanisms that created this subduction orogen. These different mechanisms predict different topographic responses through time; therefore, constraints on the elevation of the Dinarides in the past may elucidate how subduction of the Adria microplate has interacted with the overlaying Eurasia plate to produce topography. Within the Dinarides, a series of intramontane basins formed freshwater, carbonate-rich lakes in the Early Miocene. The oxygen isotope composition (δ 18 O) of authigenic lacustrine carbonates is commonly used as a paleo-altimeter to reconstruct past elevations. Stable-isotope paleoaltimetry is based on the concept that, as moist air parcels are forced upwards by orography, 18 O is preferentially removed by the resulting precipitation, resulting in lower δ 18 O at higher-elevations and in the lee of ranges. We collected authigenic lacustrine carbonate and clay samples from eight basins in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina that span the range from sea-level to high-elevation and measured these samples for δ 18 O. In addition, we also collected stream samples that span the range to constrain the modern change in δ 18 O across the Dinaric Alps. Today, meteoric water δ 18 O is high (~ -6‰) at the coast and lower at the crest of the range (~ -11‰). However, Middle Miocene lacustrine carbonate δ 18 O is high (~ -3‰) at the crest of the range and lower (~ -6‰) at the coast. To account for the effect of evaporation on Miocene lacustrine carbonates, we analyzed a subset of our samples Δ′ 17 O, which is sensitive to the degree of evaporation. These data show that these lakes were evaporatively impacted, resulting in higher δ 18 O in carbonate marls. We then reconstructed the unevaporated δ 18 O of the meteoric waters that formed the lacustrine carbonates using a Bayesian Monte Carlo simulation and a model of lake evaporation. We find that reconstructed, unevaporated δ 18 O was largely constant across the range in the Miocene, suggesting little change in δ 18 O between coastal sites and interior sites. This suggests the development of the high topography of the Dinarides post-dates the Middle Miocene.

title: Testing competing hypotheses for the collision of the Ontong Java Plateau with the Solomon Islands Arc
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Furness, Clara [1], Rosenbaum, Gideon [2], Ubide, Teresa [3], Musgrave, Robert [4]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia
(2) School of the Environment, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia

abstract:
The collision of the Ontong Java Plateau with the Solomon Islands Arc is commonly cited as the classic example of a flipped subduction zone, whereby the arrival of a thick oceanic plateau leads to subduction congestion that triggers the formation of a new subduction zone with an opposite polarity. Nonetheless, the tectonic history of this collision is a contentious issue, mainly because the timing of collision is poorly constrained. The most popular model (Hypothesis 1) is based on the assumption that a hiatus in arc volcanism in the Solomon Islands occurred at 20–10 Ma. Hypothesis 1 thus invokes that collision occurred during the Early Miocene (at 25–20 Ma), although evidence for contemporaneous collision-related structures is lacking. It has therefore been referred to as ‘soft docking’. Hypothesis 2 assumes that the plateau collision occurred much later (at <5 Ma), and Hypothesis 3 considers an earlier emplacement of a piece of an oceanic plateau fragment (Malaita Terrane; a rifted fragment of Ontong Java Nui) at ~35 Ma, followed by a plateau collision at ~10 Ma. By contrast, both Hypotheses 1 and 2 assume the Malaita Terrane to have been contiguous with the rest of the plateau until the final plateau collision.

We tested the alternative hypotheses by determining the age and origin of volcanic ash and volcaniclastic sandstone samples from the Malaita Terrane. Our samples show a calc-alkaline geochemical affinity, consistent with arc magmatism. Furthermore, our samples yielded abundant zircon grains with Miocene ages, ranging from ~17 to ~10 Ma. This interval lies within the supposed volcanic hiatus of Hypothesis 1. Our results, therefore, refute Hypothesis 1, indicating that the arc was active until at least 10 Ma. This implies ongoing subduction of the Pacific Plate during the Miocene. The study calls for a re-evaluation of the ‘soft docking’ model. Based on our results, the Ontong Java Plateau more likely collided with the Solomon Islands Arc at 10–8 Ma, triggering arc polarity reversal and subduction of the Indo-Australian Plate since the Late Miocene. Furthermore, the presence of Early–Middle Miocene volcaniclastic rocks on the Malaita Terrane shows that emplacement of this terrane preceded plateau collision, invalidating Hypothesis 2. Out of the three hypotheses, Hypothesis 3 is the only one consistent with all data.

title: Boxworks in Terrestrial Sedimentary Environments
session_title: Boxwork and Fracture Halos: Changes in mineralogy and erosion resistance around fracture features on Earth, Mars, and across the Solar System
authors: Potter-McIntyre, Sally [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth Systems and Sustainability, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, IL, USA; Section 4.3 GeoEnergy, Helmholtz Center for Geosciences, Potsdam, Brandenberg, Germany
abstract: Boxworks are common features in sedimentary rocks that result from a variety of formation mechanisms. These features are found in many different sedimentary lithologies such as limestones, siliciclastics, and salts, and range in size from micron- to kilometer-scale. The simplest are secondary sedimentary structures formed in unlithified sediment such as mudcracks (cm- to m-scale). These can then be infilled with sediment or cement that produce positive topographic features when overlying strata are eroded. Other formation mechanisms are initiated during burial diagenesis such as fractures with subsequent cementation or magmatic intrusions (mm-km scale). When exposed via erosion, these subsurface features become topographically upstanding boxworks. Recognizing the formation mechanism is crucial to understanding the depositional, diagenetic, and erosional history of the rocks, particularly because many of these mechanisms occur via water/rock interaction and thereby influence—and subsequently preserve the record of—subsurface habitability. This work explores the variety of means by which boxworks form in terrestrial environments to provide a framework for understanding similar features on other solar system bodies. The focus will be on the formation mechanism and identifying features such as morphology, mineralogy, and geochemistry. The mechanisms of emplacement, in turn, affect subsurface habitability. For example, when fractures form in the subsurface, they become preferential flow paths for reservoir fluids owing to enhanced permeability relative to the surrounding host rock. When reservoir fluids meet and mix with fluid(s) of different chemistry, cement minerals can precipitate. These fractures become hubs of habitability compared to the host rock because of increased and focused fluid and energy source influx (e.g., redox reactions for chemotrophs). Alternatively, if the boxworks are caused by intruding magma, the surrounding metamorphic halo is sterilized. Nevertheless, any time an ecological niche is created by an extinction, organisms rush in to colonize and evolve in that space. Combined with the incursion of elements from the magmatic fluid, the zone surrounding magmatic intrusions would become a hyper-habitable environment as soon as it cooled to temperatures conducive to life.

title: Top-down: Perspective of Lithospheric Foundering from Surface Geology
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: He, John [1]
affiliations: (1) University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
The viscous removal of dense, gravitationally unstable lithosphere beneath thickened plateaus is increasingly recognized as a fundamental process of intraplate tectonics. Yet lithospheric foundering is transient, leaving only indirect evidence in present-day geophysical observations, and difficult to study except via numerical geodynamic simulations. Over the past decade, a growing number of studies have proposed that foundering-induced dynamic topography may produce sedimentary basin records that preserve evidence of lithospheric removal. However, distinguishing such basins from more conventional tectonic basins remains an unresolved challenge.

Existing sedimentary basin models were developed primarily for basins generated by flexural loading, extension, or strike-slip deformation and do not explicitly account for localized dynamic topography associated with lithospheric removal. As a result, interpretations of “dynamic rebound basins” often invoke foundering to account for unexplained subsidence, leading to ongoing debate over whether these basins are best explained by lithospheric removal.

In this talk I explore the requirements for a testable sedimentary basin framework linking lithospheric removal to observable surface deformation, stratigraphic architecture, and thermochronologic signals of exhumation. Although such a model must necessarily be simplified and provisional, it provides a set of working hypotheses that can guide targeted geological fieldwork and enable comparisons among orogenic systems. Ultimately, the goal is to determine when, and with what confidence, the sedimentary and structural record can reveal otherwise hidden episodes of deep lithospheric foundering.

title: Atlantic-Derived Moisture in High-Andean Headwaters: Stable Isotopic Evidence from Streams, Springs and Rock Glaciers in the Arid Aconcagua Region of Argentina (32–33°S)
session_title: High mountain headwaters: Snow, ice and alpine hydrology
authors: Fennell, Lucas Martin [1], Rey, Agustín [2], Pérez Argañaraz, Patricio [3], Calvi, Carolina Rosa [4], Sagripanti, Lucia [5], Hren, Michael T. [6]
affiliations: (1) INGEIS (UBA-CONICET), Buenos Aires, N/A, Argentina

abstract:
Moisture source identification in modern waters draining from mountain ranges is essential for addressing paleotopographic, geomorphological, and paleoclimatic problems at geological timescales, as well as evaluating the impacts of climate change on water resources at human timescales. Different atmospheric origins, transport distances, and regional topography leave unique isotopic fingerprints in precipitation, making stable isotope studies in high-mountain headwaters a key tool for tracing water sources. Available studies indicate that precipitation on the Andes between 32°S and 33°S at elevations above 2,000 m asl is largely derived from a westerly Pacific source, whereas eastern slope lower elevations exhibit a mixture of Pacific and easterly Atlantic sources. However, most regional studies have focused on major drainage basins, leaving smaller, high-elevation catchments poorly characterized due to geographical remoteness and rugged terrain.

In this study, we report 55 new stable isotope values from streams, springs, and rock glaciers in small high-altitude catchments across the arid Aconcagua Region of Argentina. Values range from -10.0‰ to -21.4‰ for d18O and from -69‰ to -160‰ for d2H, with the lightest values representing the most isotopically depleted waters ever measured in this region. The variations observed in these data mostly show a clear correlation with elevation, indicating an altitude effect on both east- and west-facing slopes. Comparing these measurements with published regional datasets reveals a previously unrecognized Atlantic-derived moisture component reaching the highest elevations in the area.

Our findings demonstrate that high Andean headwaters are not purely sustained by winter snowpack of Pacific origin, but are also significantly replenished by summer precipitation events originating from the Atlantic. The integration of isotopic signatures from rock glaciers, streams, and springs confirms that this eastern moisture source directly feeds both surface runoff and groundwater baseflow in these critical catchments.

Recognizing this dual-moisture origin is vital for regional water management and climate resilience. As global warming shifts large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns, altering the intensity and frequency of both westerlies and easterlies, the relative contributions of Pacific winter snow and Atlantic summer rains will likely change. Uncovering this Atlantic moisture component fundamentally alters our understanding of mountain hydrology in the high arid Andes, highlighting the need to incorporate summer convective precipitation into future water availability models.

title: 25 Years of Field Study at Acid Salt Lakes in Western Australia: Why Visiting a Salt Lake Once or Twice is Not Enough
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Benison, Kathleen C. [1], Bowen, Brenda B. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, West Virginia, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract:
Ephemeral acid salt lakes on the Yilgarn Craton of southern Western Australia are both spatially and temporally dynamic. Here, we share field observations of the changes in sedimentology , mineralogy, and water geochemistry that we’ve documented over multiple time scales from 10 field campaigns between 2001 and 2026, with a focus on five lakes near Hyden, Norseman, and Salmon Gums.

Atmospheric conditions play a significant role in the state of a lake at any one time. Specific pHs, salinities, and temperatures are not sufficient to predict exact minerals and sedimentary features. We have found different products in the same places at different times under the same geochemical conditions.

A long-held question about the rate of growth of bottom-growth gypsum was addressed with new field observations made in January 2015, January 2026, mid-March 2026, and late March 2026. We estimate that bottom-growth gypsum crystals, many of which are swallowtails, may grow faster than 5 mm/yr.

We propose that a single visit to an ephemeral acid salt only gives a snapshot of the range of potential geochemistry, mineralogy, and sedimentary processes and products. Understanding these extreme environments and their Earth system interactions requires multiple field campaigns that capture various time ranges, including hours, days, months, seasons, years, and decades.

title: Preservación del registro tectonotérmico paleoproterozoico en el Complejo Metamórfico Bámori (Sonora, México): Nuevas edades 40Ar/39Ar en hornblenda y mica blanca

abstract:
El Complejo Metamórfico Bámori (CMB), ubicado al sur de Caborca, en el noroeste de Sonora, constituye el afloramiento de rocas ígneas y metamórficas más antiguo reconocido en México y representa un segmento clave del basamento paleoproterozoico del margen suroccidental de Laurentia. Estudios previos de geocronología U-Pb en circones de los protolitos indican edades de cristalización de hasta ca. 1780 Ma; sin embargo, la cronología del metamorfismo y el grado de preservación del registro tectonotérmico paleoproterozoico permanecen inciertos debido a la prolongada evolución geológica del basamento y a la posible sobreimpresión causada por el magmatismo y la deformación laramídica.

Con el objetivo de establecer la cronología del metamorfismo y evaluar el efecto de los eventos tectonotérmicos posteriores, se obtuvieron tres docenas de edades Ar-Ar en hornblenda, mica blanca, biotita y feldespato potásico (FK) de las principales unidades metamórficas del CMB. Las hornblendas definen edades entre 1717 y 1569 Ma (media de 1654 Ma), interpretadas como el enfriamiento posterior al pico metamórfico. Las micas blancas presentan edades entre 1652 y 1531 Ma (media de 1623 Ma), aunque algunas muestran evidencias de perturbación, posiblemente durante el Mesoproterozoico. Por su parte, las biotitas y los FK muestran espectros con pérdida parcial de Ar y edades aparentes paleozoicas, jurásicas y otras más jóvenes, entre 78 y 65 Ma, lo que evidencia un rejuvenecimiento isotópico asociado a reactivaciones tectonotérmicas posteriores. La comparación entre minerales con diferentes temperaturas de cierre permite distinguir el enfriamiento paleoproterozoico de las sucesivas reactivaciones paleozoicas, mesozoicas y cenozoicas, lo que permite reconstruir la evolución térmica completa del complejo.

Los resultados demuestran que el sistema isotópico Ar-Ar del CMB no fue completamente reiniciado durante la evolución cordillerana, como ocurre en numerosos segmentos del basamento cristalino del noroeste de México, sino que preserva un registro robusto del enfriamiento paleoproterozoico en algunos de sus minerales. Integradas con las edades U-Pb de los protolitos, las nuevas edades Ar-Ar demuestran que parte del basamento paleoproterozoico del margen suroccidental de Laurentia conservó su registro térmico a pesar de la intensa reactivación tectonomagmática mesozoica-cenozoica. Estos resultados ponen de manifiesto que el sistema Ar-Ar puede preservar información del enfriamiento paleoproterozoico incluso en basamentos policíclicos afectados por una importante reactivación tectonotérmica posterior, ampliando su potencial para reconstruir la evolución temprana del margen occidental de Laurentia.

abstract:
Arsenic in drinking water is a human health concern worldwide. Rural communities across the Colorado Plateau rely on groundwater from the Navajo Sandstone Aquifer, which is known to contain elevated dissolved As, yet the sources and mobilization mechanisms of dissolved arsenic unrelated to mining are relatively unknown. Groundwater in the modern Navajo Aquifer is fresh to brackish and relatively oxic. Previous studies in other oxic sedimentary aquifers show that As can be adsorbed onto iron and aluminum (oxyhydr)oxide mineral surfaces and released to groundwater through changes in pH, alkalinity, and cation concentrations. Arsenic concentrations also increase along flowpaths with greater water residence times. To investigate the geogenic sources of As and hydrogeochemical conditions that may lead to elevated dissolved As in the Navajo Aquifer, this study combines water chemistry, solute isotopes, and age tracers of well water, field XRF and laboratory analyses of Navajo Sandstone and adjacent formations near Escalante and Bluff, UT, and reactive transport modeling (RTM).

We found As concentrations beyond the US EPA maximum contaminant level (10 µg/L) and up to 74 µg/L in well water close to discharge zones of the Navajo Aquifer System (e.g., near the Escalante and San Juan rivers) that have residence times at or beyond radiocarbon dating limits (~49,000 years old). Geochemical modeling shows that the oxyanion arsenate (HAsO 4 2- ) is the primary As species in the oxic aquifer. Elevated As is associated with higher Na/(Ca) 0.5 molar ratios and HCO 3 - concentrations, suggesting ion exchange and desorption reactions with iron oxide and other clay minerals may release As to groundwater. This hypothesis is consistent with RTM results showing Na-dominant water enhances As desorption from aquifer sediments. Preliminary XRF results show that As in the bulk Navajo Sandstone is generally low (1-16 ppm), while the underlying Kayenta and Chinle formations contain relatively high As (>1600 ppm). Groundwater with elevated As have 87 Sr/ 86 Sr ratios that plot between the Navajo Sandstone and underlying Upper Paleozoic formations, and evidence of crustal 4 He and deeper saline fluid inputs (Cl/Br ratios), suggesting upward migration of As-bearing fluids from underlying formations in discharge zones. Results of this study will be used to revise preliminary ML-GIS models of arsenic in well water across the Colorado Plateau to improve geogenic contamination prediction.

abstract: Quantifying the impact of warming sea surface temperature (SST) and/or freshening sea surface salinity (SSS) in the central tropical Pacific (CTP) from anthropogenic climate change is challenging due to limited continuous instrumental and paleoclimate records before 1950 CE. Current paleoclimate records from Kiritimati Island (1.8° N, 157.4° W), an atoll in the heart of the CTP, lack centuries-long high-resolution records from the reliable coral climate proxy Porites , shifting the focus to shorter Porites coral rubble sequences. However, this coral rubble approach requires dozens of overlapping samples and would benefit from the addition of other coral genera as the spatial and temporal distribution of Porites corals alone can be a limiting factor in paleoclimate reconstruction. Work with large skeletal architectural corals in the Caribbean suggests that similar types of corals in the CTP may be used as recorders of climate, providing an expanded archive of coral genera used for paleoclimate reconstruction. Here, we test both Dipsastraea speciosa and Hydnophora microconos , collected from the reef on Kiritimati Island. The δ 18 O and Sr/Ca of the coral skeletal material were analyzed along the main growth axis and compared with instrumental sea surface temperature (SST) and sea surface salinity (SSS) data. We find consistent variability in δ 18 O timeseries in both Dipsastraea speciosa and Hydnophora microconos. However, Sr/Ca timeseries show more variability, both in the single coral and multi-coral reproducibility tests, suggesting the incorporation of Sr and Ca is more sensitive based on the type of skeletal material. We then test young fossil corals from Hydnophora microconos found on the rubble fields of Kiritimati Island and U/Th dated from the mid-1900’s that overlap existing Porites paleoclimate records from the same rubble fields. Hydnophora microconos δ 18 O time series are correlated with both Porites δ 18 O and instrumental SST records where they overlap and are incorporated into an updated coral-based climate record from Kiritimati Island. This research helps us expand the coral paleoclimate archive on Kiritimati Island to create a nearly continuous high-resolution climate record back to 1800 C.E. This record is critical to quantify the impact of anthropogenic climate change on this region and to support climate models for future climate predictions under greenhouse gas forcing.

abstract:
55 samples of greenstone, greenschist, and metagabbro from the Caucomgomoc Lake Inlier of northwestern Maine were analyzed by XRF and ICP-MS. These meta-igneous rocks are associated with mélange and olistostromal units. The samples fall into two groups on chondrite-normalized diagrams: 1) depleted to moderately enriched in LREEs (MORB to E-MORB-like) and 2) strongly-enriched in LREEs and a negative slope (WP-like). Both groups show negative Ta-Nb anomalies on MORB-normalized diagrams. The large majority of analyzed samples are group 1 rocks that come from the Avery Brook and Hurd Mountain formations along the western side of the inlier, and the Loon Stream and Caucomgomoc Lake formations in the east, all inferred to be Cambrian to Ordovician in age. The few group 2 rocks are scattered around the inlier and do not show good correlation with map units.

The group 1 rocks vary from MORB to E-MORB, but otherwise plot together in trace element discrimination diagrams suggesting they come from a similar mantle source but have experienced varying degrees of fractionation. Supporting this is an unnamed, late, but likely-related intrusive tonalite that probably represents an even more fractionated unit. On some trace element discrimination diagrams (Ti-V, Cr-Y), group 1 rocks plot in MORB fields, while on others (Hf-Th-Ta, Th/Yb-Ta/Yb) plot in arc fields. On Ce/Nb-Th/Nb and Y-La-Nb diagrams group 1 rocks plot in back-arc basin fields. These patterns are similar to those seen in the Dry Way Volcanics and Bean Brook Gabbro of the Chesuncook Dome, Bluffer Pond Volcanics of the Munsungun Inlier, Stacyville Volcanics of the Weeksboro-Lunksoos Inlier, and possibly the Lobster Mountain Volcanics of the Lobster Mountain Anticlinorium.

The group 2 rocks are highly enriched in LREEs similar to within-plate volcanics. However, on trace element discrimination diagrams they consistently plot in arc fields. This group strongly resembles the Siluro-Devonian volcanics of the West Branch Formation in the Chesuncook Dome, Spider Lake Volcanics of the Munsungun Inlier, Flagstaff Complex and The Forks Formation of the Lobster Mountain Anticlinorium.

The chemical similarity of Cambrian through Devonian meta-basalts and -gabbros with those of other northern Maine inliers indicates that they are probably related to the volcanic and intrusive sequences of the other inliers.

abstract:
The Blue Ridge Escarpment (BRE) is a NE-trending belt of rugged topography (>1000 m relief) and abundant rock slopes within km-scale arcuate reentrants and trench lineaments, making it prone to precipitation-driven natural hazards. The Chimney Rock study area straddles the WNW-oriented Hickory Nut Gorge (HNG) trench lineament and adjacent Shumont reentrant and has a >100 year history of documented slope failure events. A stalled cold front preceding tropical storm Helene (Sept. 25-27, 2024) resulted in catastrophic flooding and >40 debris flow initiation zones (IZs) over a ~5 km 2 area. Most IZs formed on SW-facing HNG slopes and E- and SE-facing Shumont reentrant slopes. The integration of LiDAR (2017, post-event 2025), aerial photography (pre- and post-event), and geologic mapping, offer a valuable opportunity to examine relationships between bedrock geology and the ~35 unmodified slope failures.

Bedrock is comprised of a ~100-m-thick body of mostly amphibolite gneiss between bodies of granodioritic Henderson Gneiss in transitional contact with felsic gneiss (HG-FG), arranged by m- to 100m-scale intrafolial folds helping to define the gently SE-dipping transposition foliation. Pervasive steep, planar NW-, NE-, and E-striking joint sets are larger and more widely spaced in HG-FG, where sets are locally connected by steep curved fractures. Rock slope failure in HG-FG has produced unvegetated cliffs with narrow fracture-controlled drainage pathways above steep slopes with thin boulder clast-supported, vegetated, colluvium. In the upper Shumont reentrant slopes, joint set intersections in HG-FG form concave arcuate cliffs that help define 0.5 km-scale colluvial catchments. Along HNG, joint set intersections help define narrow colluvial catchments.

Ongoing work indicates most IZs formed in HG-FG colluvium within steep fracture-controlled drainage on HG-FG slopes, both above and below the amphibolite gneiss unit. Some IZs formed ~10m below hollows visible in pre-event (2017) LiDAR. Runout tracks followed existing pathways: initially fracture-controlled – including >45° turns – then into incised channels within mid- and lower-slope colluvium. These preliminary results suggest that IZ formation was (partly) runoff-generated and favored narrow bedrock structure-controlled locations during the conditions of this weather event, versus forming within shallower and broader colluvial hollows. If so, further study of fracture-controlled runoff and infiltration, failure criteria in clast-supported rock slope colluvium, and the role of antecedent moisture, will improve understanding of slope failure processes and hazards along the BRE.

abstract:
Artemis II marked humanity’s return to lunar space in more than 50 years with Commander R. Wiseman, Pilot V. Glover, Mission Specialist C. Koch, and Canadian Mission Specialist J. Hanson. Artemis II was a test mission, designed to launch humans on the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket for the first time, test performance of the Orion spacecraft, and return the crew home safely. The mission also enabled the integration of lunar science objectives into the mission architecture. Artemis II science was accomplished by crew-driven verbal observations, images, and annotations of the lunar surface and other Solar System targets, supplemented by images and video taken with the Orion vehicle-mounted cameras. Observation and imaging plans were developed by the Lunar Science Team to take advantage of the unique trajectory and perspective the Artemis II mission. The crew was trained in science imaging objectives as part of their mission training.

Inside the Integrity spacecraft, the crew had access to multiple imaging systems including Nikon D5 and Nikon Z9 cameras with 35mm, 14-24mm, and 80-400mm lenses, and each crewmember was issued an iPhone 17 Pro. The interior crew handheld cameras were supplemented by external modified GoPro Hero 4 Black vehicle cameras, primarily used for spacecraft and engineering assessments, mounted on the exterior Solar Array Wings (SAW). Operation of these cameras and downlink of the data required close collaboration between the Lunar Science Team and the Flight Operations Directorate (FOD), the FOD Intravehicular Activity (IVA) Photo/TV team, and the Image Science Analysis Group (ISAG) at the NASA Johnson Space Center. Through collaboration with these groups, Artemis II intentionally collected spectacular images during the mission that inspired the world and added new context to decades of imaging science accomplished with robotic spacecraft.

abstract: This study explores historical wildfire activity in the White Mountain region through analysis of sedimentary charcoal from Echo Lake located in Echo Lake State Park in Conway, New Hampshire. The research focuses on fire history reconstructions that provide greater context for forest management within our changing climate. A 6 m core was retrieved from the 6-ha Echo Lake kettle basin located in the southeastern region of the White Mountains. Loss on Ignition (LOI), magnetic susceptibility (MS), and particulate charcoal analysis provide an assessment of watershed productivity, sediment influx, and the frequency of past wildfire events, respectively. Coarse sediment in the base of the core captures deglaciation of the basin by the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This period of deglaciation is also captured by low LOI and high MS values. LOI analysis provides insight on lake organic content and landscape behavior throughout the Holocene by burning off the organic content through furnacing. LOI percentages stay in the 15-20% threshold in the first half of the core and begin to drop off in the latter half. MS is a proxy for the mineral content present in each centimeter of the core which increases dramatically in the bottom ~200 cm of the Echo Lake Core, working in conjunction with LOI to capture the deglacial to Holocene transition of the lake environment. Charcoal analysis shows relatively low charcoal concentrations in the upper ~200 cm, punctuated by periodic peaks. Thus far, the record below ~200 cm contains relatively higher charcoal concentrations and more variability. The charcoal results so far indicate fire has a consistent presence on the landscape though the character of fire regime appears to shift partway through the analyzed record. We are awaiting the completion of the charcoal counts and the radiocarbon ages to more fully interpret and compare this fire record to others in the region. Further counting is necessary to finish the charcoal record. This research is part of a larger collaborative project with the U.S. Forest Service aimed at improving the record of historical fires on the New England landscape to provide important context for forest management in the future.

abstract: Developing clean sustainable drinking water sources is a global challenge and is a major focus of numerous governments, companies, and non-profit organizations. Detailed assessments of water chemistry are integral to such leading edge efforts in underserved communities, however are not often undertaken in the early stages of efforts. Large segments of the population of Honduras are facing pressing water quality and accessibility issues impacting human health. Rural communities are at extreme risk, in part due to inadequate infrastructure for both sanitation and distribution to homes. GWC Projects is a non-profit operating in west central Honduras and has conducted observational and initial sampling trips. Adolescents can experience tooth decay and other dental problems, potentially linked to the water they drink. This study investigates the geochemical composition of a limited number of potential drinking water sources across multiple regions of west central Honduras to assess potential health implications, including dental health concerns linked to fluoride and mineral content. A large number of water samples were collected and provided to a third party non-profit who failed to do meaningful analyses. Other water samples were collected from seven sites and analyzed after shipping to Miami University using ion chromatography (IC), high resolution - inductively coupled plasma - mass spectrometry (HR-ICP-MS), and pH measurements to characterize major ion chemistry, trace metal concentrations, and redox conditions. Results indicate that groundwater in the study area is predominantly of calcium-magnesium-bicarbonate type, consistent with interaction with carbonate and silicate lithologies of the Chortís Block. Bicarbonates potentially impact water quality parameters such as pH, in this region. Eh-pH analysis places all samples near the ferrous iron and hematite stability boundary, suggesting mildly reducing, near-neutral conditions. Cation-anion balance of water analyses is, however, somewhat problematic and may have resulted from degassing, precipitation, or biological activity. No significant concentrations of metals of health concern (e.g., Pb, Cu, Hg) were observed in HR-ICP-MS data in the available samples, and preliminary data indicates metals may not be of high concern at least initially. These findings provide a geochemical baseline for evaluating water safety and informing targeted infrastructure and treatment interventions in underserved Honduran communities. Geochemical results are promising and suggest that a larger, more systematic sampling is warranted.

abstract: Archaeocyath sponges are among the earliest animal reef builders, constructors of both small patch reefs and larger reef complexes in the early Cambrian. In addition to the archaeocyath-microbial consortium that characterizes most of these Cambrian reefs, other enigmatic calcareous organisms have also been documented in these ecosystems. These include cryptobiotic species, coralomorphs, and encrusters, but these organisms have received comparatively less attention than the archaeocyaths themselves. The lower Harkless Formation from two fault blocks near Gold Point, Nevada contains previously undescribed archaeocyath reef beds ranging from 0.5 - 1.5 m thick. These occur as small patch reefs ~34 m from the base of the section, primarily composed of archaeocyaths, but also containing small shelly fossils and what appear to be a variety of enigmatic branching calcareous fossils that are up to several centimeters long. In thin section, the enigmatic fossils are intensely recrystallized, which has made it difficult to further identify them. Additionally, microbial fabrics are not present in any reef samples, but archaeocyaths are well preserved. Trilobites and chancelloriids are minor components of the reef thin sections. Overall, the discovery of these enigmatic organisms in the lower Harkless reefs supports the notion that these reefs created habitats for not just framework builders, but a variety of organisms, much like modern coral reefs. Future work will focus on constraining the identity of these calcareous organisms and characterizing the inhabitants and ecology of the lower Harkless reefs.

abstract:
The Calloway Creek Formation is a carbonate-dominated stratigraphic unit within the Cincinnatian Series (Upper Ordovician), occupying the uppermost Edenian and lowermost Maysvillian stages. Exposed along the eastern and western margins of the Cincinnati Arch in central Kentucky, the formation consists of lophophorate-dominated bioclastic limestone interbedded with calcareous shale of variable lateral thickness. Analysis of measured sections has identified distinct biofacies and depositional sequences that permit stratigraphic correlation throughout the unit. Sedimentary structures, lithology, and bedding characteristics indicate deposition within a shallow, subtidal, storm-dominated marine environment.

A distinctive bryozoan-rich biofacies occurs at multiple localities and is characterized by abundant specimens of the otherwise uncommon cryptostome bryozoan Escharopora hilli , together with Fenestella and Chasmatopora . Associated fauna include Hebertella , Vinlandostrophia , Strophomena , Constellaria florida , and Escharopora falciformis , indicating a Maysvillian age. Ecological interactions are common and include encrusting bryozoans ( Prasopora ), bioclaustration structures ( Catellocaula ), and Cornulites worm tubes attached to skeletal substrates.

Field observations indicate that this interval extends from Washington County in the west to Montgomery County in the east and occupies a consistent stratigraphic position within the Calloway Creek Formation. Its lateral continuity, distinct faunal assemblage, and mappability distinguish it from adjacent strata.

This interval is herein designated the Paint Lick Member, named for its type locality near Paint Lick in Madison County, Kentucky, where it is best exposed. Correlation with coeval strata, including portions of the Fairview and Leipers formations, will require further investigation. Future work will focus on reconstructing the depositional history of the member and evaluating its relationship to adjacent units within the Calloway Creek Formation.

abstract:
Upper Paleozoic (Pennsylvanian-Permian) strata on the Mogollon Rim were termed the Supai Formation in 1910; we refer to them as Supai Group. Since 1910, creation of a complex, in part duplicative, and largely miscorrelated stratigraphy has obscured understanding of late Paleozoic deposition and paleogeography across much of Arizona. Since 2018, we have undertaken stratigraphic and sedimentological studies of Supai strata across the Rim to arrive at a new understanding of these strata and their geologic history. A key conclusion is that deposition in the Grand Canyon embayment was not connected to deposition on the Rim, so extension of Grand Canyon stratigraphic units to the Rim, particularly the Hermit Formation, lacks justification. Some Mogollon Rim stratigraphic names are unnecessary, such as Schnebly Hill and Cibecue, and can be abandoned. Two sets of lithostratigraphic nomenclature should be applied to upper Paleozoic Supai Group strata: (1) to the east (ascending): Amos Wash, Big A Butte, Fort Apache and Corduroy formations; (2) to the west (ascending): Packard Ranch, Oak Creek, and upper Supai (unit to be named) formations.

Deposition across the Rim thus took place in two different areas genetically connected to marine deposition in the Pedregosa basin of southeastern Arizona. In east-central Arizona, from near Payson to the Fort Apache Reservation to north of Holbrook, Pennsylvanian (Desmoinesian-Virgilian; mid-Moscovian to Gzhelian) deposition was mostly marine on the Pedregosa shelf. To the west (near Payson through Sedona), on the Mogollon shelf, the upper Paleozoic strata are much less marine, with only one significant (Desmoinesian; mid-Moscovian) transgression, and some minor marine deposition as far north as Jerome. By Late Pennsylvanian time nonmarine deposition dominated the Mogollon shelf and gave way in the middle Leonardian to an erg, while evaporite deposition took place in the Holbrook basin to the north of the Pedregosa shelf. Nevertheless, the middle Leonardian Fort Apache Formation marine carbonates are present from the Fort Apache Reservation to Sedona, though west of Cibecue they thin dramatically and change facies. The Fort Apache records an extensive mid-Kungurian transgression that can be traced from Texas to Arizona. A mixed marine/ nonmarine late Paleozoic depositional system extended from the Pedregosa basin across parts of central and northern Arizona as the primary focus of marine and nonmarine deposition over most of the state.

title: Field Campaign to Locate and Sample Olivine-Bearing Basaltic Dikes in the Adirondack Highlands and Lowlands: Assessment of the Applicability of Ni-Based Olivine-Melt Thermometry/Hygrometry at the Liquidus

authors: DeBrosse, Geo M [1], Brehm, Sarah K [2], Nagel-Myers, Judith [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, St. Lawrence University, Canton, NY, USA

abstract:
Numerous crosscutting mafic dikes are observed throughout the Adirondack Highlands, Lowlands, and the Hudson Highlands. These intrusions record a prolonged history of mafic magmatism and are interpreted to reflect extensional tectonics and may be linked to the early stages of Iapetan basin formation. Basaltic dikes are windows into the mantle source conditions at the time of their birth and emplacement and may help constrain the number of magmatic events and the injection of significant heat and dissolved H 2 O content into the overlying crust. Basaltic dikes from the region reflect a range in geochemistry that suggests mantle source heterogeneity. Proterozoic dikes have a geochemical signature that indicates an asthenospheric mantle source, whereas Mesozoic dikes show large ion lithophile enrichment that is consistent with subduction modified lithosphere. Diffusion-limited growth textures in olivine (i.e. skeletal/dendritic) are observed in a subset of ADK basalts, which are consistent with rapid phenocryst growth during ascent. This provides an opportunity to apply olivine-melt thermometry/hygrometry by pairing the most Mg-rich olivine and the whole-rock composition as a proxy for the initial liquid using the method established by Brehm and Lange (2020). Olivine-melt pairs are evaluated for chemical equilibrium using the Fe-Mg K D (olivine-melt) and Mg-Mn K D (olivine-melt) liquidus tests. This study consists of an extensive field campaign to collect and analyze olivine-bearing Proterozoic dikes from the ADK Highlands and Lowlands to assess the applicability of the Ni-based olivine-melt thermometry/hygrometry method developed by Brehm and Lange (2020).

Preliminary petrographic analysis reveals that a subset of dikes is olivine-bearing and range from fine-grained altered diabase and olivine diabase containing plagioclase, olivine, and clinopyroxene. Preliminary results by Reina and Brehm (2026) indicate that a single Proterozoic basalt from the Bennies Brook Slide passes equilibrium tests and yield a temperature and dissolved melt water content consistent with a dry asthenosphere source. It is anticipated that additional Proterozoic basaltic dikes collected in this study will reflect a similar rift signature. Future application of this method aims to determine variations in temperature and dissolved H 2 O content between Proterozoic basalts from the asthenosphere and Mesozoic basalts from subduction modified lithosphere. Widespread application of this method will contribute to our understanding of mantle source heterogeneity and mantle evolution during the prolonged and complex tectonic history of eastern North America.

title: Does the Deformation of the Harney Peak Granite Record Transpressional Folding in the Black Hills, South Dakota?
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Steup, Kadie Joi [1], Waldien, Trevor [2]
abstract: The southern Black Hills of western South Dakota expose a core of Precambrian metasedimentary rocks that record multiple overprinting foliations (D1 and D2) and deformation by left lateral pure shear dominated transpression (D3) from 1730 -1715 Ma. The Harney Peak Granite (HPG) intruded into the metasediments at 1715 Ma ± 3 Ma and is associated with localized folds near the contact that deform previous fabrics (D4). Previous geochronology indicates that folding associated with emplacement of the HPG overlapped in time with transpressional deformation, however it remains unclear whether the deformation of the HPG and transpression are kinematically linked. This study presents structural data from the northern margin of the HPG, where metasedimentary rocks are highly attenuated in a ~10-km-wide ENE-WSW corridor adjacent to the HPG. Preliminary results show a regionally consistent sub-horizontal foliation that locally contains recumbent folds of HPG dikes. Stretching lineations within the foliation trend ENE-WSW and are parallel to fold axes. Some HPG dikes that cross cut the foliation are boudinaged and display curved lineations along the margins of pegmatite dikes, suggesting dikes were also stretched ENE-WSW after emplacement. This field data suggests that rocks adjacent to the north side of the HPG experienced high strain associated with simple shear folding during the emplacement of the HPG. Forthcoming analysis in mutually perpendicular oriented thin sections will relate microstructural shape fabrics to outcrop scale deformation structures. The preliminary data suggest that syn-emplacement deformation along the northern side of the HPG is compatible with simple shear deformation. Prior distinction between D3 and D4 deformation in the Black Hills Precambrian may result from the orientation of pre-existing fabrics that localize strain relative to regional relative block motion.

title: Exploring the Effects of Vegetation on Inorganic Soil Carbonate Activity
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Williams, Sha'Heen [1], Gallagher, Timothy M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Kent State University, Kent, Ohio, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Kent State University, Kent, Ohio, USA
abstract: Soils exchange carbon with the atmosphere primarily through plant- and microbial-driven processes. Carbonate minerals that form in-situ are a common feature in many dryland soils. These soil carbonates are a huge reservoir of carbon and a critical archive of past environments, but uncertainty persists about the ultimate control on their formation. We need to understand the controls on soil carbonate dissolution and formation to understand how it will respond to modern global change and to improve our ability to interpret soil carbonate paleoclimate records. To investigate the influence of plants on carbonate formation and dissolution, we installed 12 pots under grow-lights in the lab to isolate the impact of plants on soil carbonate formation. Six pots have plants (Canadian Wild Rye) and another six serve as plant-free controls. Pulverized limestone at 10 weight percent was mixed into the soil between 5 and 15 cm depth in three of the pots with plants and three of the plant-free controls. The remaining pots are carbonate-free controls. The gas wells are connected to an automated system that directs flow every four hours to a FOXBOX gas analyzer that measures high-precision CO2 and O2 values. The use of carbonate-free pots and a paired gas approach enable us to separate CO2 changes driven by soil respiration (produces CO2 & consumes O2) from those driven by calcite dissolution (consumes CO2, no O2 change) and precipitation (produces CO2, no O2 change). Unlike previous field and laboratory experiments, clear dissolution and precipitation signals have yet to be observed over the first two months during plant establishment. Respired CO2 levels have been relatively stable and low (3,000 to 6,000 ppm), suggesting rapid increases in respiration are required to drive carbonate dissolution. While average daily ARQ values (CO2 produced/O2 consumed) have been stable (0.92 – 1.01), four-hour sampling resolution has revealed a surprisingly large diurnal cyclicity in soil respiration and ARQ values (e.g. 0.85 – 1.1) that may be linked to temperature driven changes in soil metabolisms or physical modifications of gas ratios.

title: Novel Signatures For Identification of Subtle Martian Paleolakes
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Williams, Rebecca M. E. [1], Irwin, Rossman Philip [2], Berman, Daniel C. [3], Hill, Jonathon [4]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Science Institute, Tucscon, AZ,
(2) Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC,

abstract:
Past studies have documented hundreds of lake basins across Mars, with a concentration on the ancient southern highlands. However, with the planet’s pronounced history of burial and erosion, the full lacustrine record is underreported. Further, questions persist about the duration of standing water, a key constraint on climate conditions. Here, we highlight new approaches to search for subtle martian paleolake signatures to expand the inventory of sites and identify lake level.

(1) The vast majority of paleolakes on Mars are topographically bound by crater rims. How can paleolacustrine sites be identified in highly eroded terrains where the confining basin or contributing valley networks have been erased? One landform interpreted as an erosional remnant of crater lakes are low, circular features (<50 m relief) thought to preserve intercrater lacustrine fill. Such circular features require careful examination of visible-wavelength images because there is often minimal tonal difference relative to the surrounding terrain. Within a test region in northeastern Arabia Terra, we observed a distinct color signature of circular pedestals in multispectral Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) infrared images when band 9 (center wavelength 12.57 μm), band 6 (10.21 μm) and band 3 (7.93 μm) are mapped to red, green and blue, respectively. This 9-6-3 combination illustrates the maximum spectral variability within THEMIS data in a 3-band set. Coincidence of circular shape and purple color in THEMIS-9-6-3 serves as a rapid method for identifying paleolake sites elsewhere.

(2) Paleochannel ridges, often called ‘inverted channels,’ are the erosional remnants of fluvial deposits. Based on an Earth analog at Californian Lake Coyote, some ‘inverted channels’ can form subaqueously in lakes. We illustrate martian case studies to demonstrate how this insight can be used for constructing lake hydrographs.
