title: Insights into the K-Pg boundary from studies of outcrops on the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Landman, Neil [1], Allmon, Warren [2], Myers, Corinne [3]
affiliations: (1) American Museum of Natural History, New York, New York, USA
(2) Paleontological Research Institution, Ithaca, New York, USA
(3) Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences 1 Northrop Hall, MSC03 2040, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) asteroid impact hypothesis—the first credibly suggesting that mass extinction events could occur extremely rapidly—is now widely accepted, and it has evolved over time from near total rejection, to testing and re-examination, to regular appearance in textbooks and popular culture. This is a remarkable transition, for both paleontology and Earth science in general, comparable to plate tectonics in its scope and significance for our understanding of the history of life and the planet.

While research on the K-Pg event has been global, a significant dataset has been accumulating on the US Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains (GACP), where the number of known K-Pg sections has increased from fewer than a dozen to more than 30. These sections provide some of the most detailed records anywhere of what happened just before, during, and immediately after the impact.

The high temporal resolution and outstanding preservation of sediments and fossils in these sections have taught us things about the K-Pg that we could not have learned from other sections: they show us details of what happened in shallow shelf environments geographically proximal to the impact; they reveal the sedimentological chaos resulting from the impact, suggesting reinterpretations of some sections elsewhere in the world; they confirm that ammonites survived for a brief period after the impact, and that evolutionary rates immediately post-K-Pg may have been extremely rapid (e.g., foraminifera).

More broadly, the wide acceptance of the impact hypothesis and the extraordinary level of temporal resolution that is now possible in GACP and other boundary sections support a robust assessment of the role of this event in Earth’s biological history. The event abruptly pruned branches of the evolutionary tree. The lineages that survived did not do so because they were better adapted to existing conditions than those that experienced extinction, but because of idiosyncratic, non-adaptive characters such as geographic and environmental distribution or having a dormancy state in ontogeny. The evolutionary results of this pruning were growth and diversification along new and unpredictable trajectories, with contingency and exaptations playing major roles. The consequent changes in life were irreversible. But within a few hundred thousand years at most, the planet had physically returned to pre-impact state. Sea floor spreading, global climate change, and sea level were unaffected.

authors: Anyanna, Linus Victor [1], Oboh-Ikuenobe, Francisca E [2], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [3], Jaramillo, Carlos [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, Missouri, USA

abstract: Paleoclimate records from Central America are dominated by archives from the dry interior basins of northern Guatemala and the Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the vegetation history of the wetter Caribbean margin poorly constrained. We present a pollen record spanning ~9,300–12,700 cal yr BP from a composite sediment core from Lake Izabal, eastern Guatemala, which receives ~3,000 mm of annual rainfall. Palynological analysis documents a progressive transition from a near-barren latest Pleistocene landscape to a diversifying early Holocene tropical forest. The basal interval (~11,800 –12,700 cal yr BP) coincides with a green-colored sediment facies containing pedogenic carbonate nodules interpreted as a paleosol, indicating subaerial exposure and extremely sparse vegetation. This is followed (~10,600n –11,800 cal yr BP) by rapid floristic reorganization dominated by Typhaceae and Pinus , reflecting an open, seasonally stressed landscape. The subsequent interval (~10,000–10,600 cal yr BP) documents the initial expansion of evergreen and deciduous forest taxa, while the uppermost interval (~9,300 –10,000 cal yr BP) registers peak diversity, including the first occurrence of montane taxa, which is consistent with a warming, increasingly humid early Holocene period. Detrended Correspondence Analysis (DCA) of the pollen record confirms a directional shift from open vegetation toward closed-canopy forest. These results provide new constraints on the latest Pleistocene to early Holocene vegetation dynamics along the humid Caribbean margin of Central America and fill a critical gap in the regional paleoclimate record.

abstract:
Various tools are used by Mars rovers to remove dust and weathered surface coatings from rocks, exposing fresh material for scientific investigation. Here, we describe the abrasion process used by the Perseverance rover and present preliminary observations suggesting that specific abrasion patterns are linked to target rock composition. In particular, embedded tool marks preserved in abrasion cuttings may serve as an early indicator of clay-bearing rocks. Such mineralogical clues in abrasion images are valuable for prioritizing spectroscopic investigations within the time-constrained rover operations schedule.

Perseverance uses the corer mechanism mounted on its robotic arm to produce a 5-cm-diameter abrasion patch. The abrading bit contains three tungsten carbide teeth of different lengths, creating three distinct abrasion zones. The sequence begins with percussion to chisel approximately 2 mm into the rock, followed by clockwise rotation to a maximum depth of 16 mm. A high-speed counterclockwise clear-out step then disperses cuttings to the patch perimeter, after which compressed-air puffs remove remaining debris. Finally, the arm-mounted WATSON (Wide Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering) camera acquires high-resolution images of the abrasion patch for petrographic analysis and spectroscopic target selection.

Between sols 1 and 1938 (February 2021–July 2026), Perseverance completed 65 abrasion patches. Although the objective is to produce a smooth, dust-free surface for spectroscopic observations, some abrasion cuttings display cohesive behavior, forming clumps or adhering to the rock as radial stripes that preserve the abrading tooth pattern. These embedded tool marks occur in multiple geologic settings, including the delta front, upper delta, Neretva Vallis, on the crater rim, and the Lac de Charmes plains, but are absent from abrasion patches on the Jezero crater floor. The patterns are most pronounced in fine-grained rocks, including sandstone and mudstone. Similar tool marks formed during JPL testing on pure hydrated sulfate samples; however, Martian sulfate-rich fine-grained targets (e.g., Berry Hollow and Uganik Island) do not exhibit this texture. Instead, preliminary analyses indicate a stronger correlation between the apparent stickiness of abrasion cuttings and hydrated phyllosilicate-bearing rocks (X-ray fluorescence detection). Although other minerals, including carbonate and sulfate phases, may contribute to this behavior, embedded tool marks appear to be a useful predictive indicator of clay mineral presence.

title: Is the Kootznahoo Formation in Southeastern Alaska Terra Firma for the Chugach-Prince William Terrane?
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Davidson, Cameron [1], Gale, Clara [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
abstract:
The Paleocene to Miocene age Kootznahoo Formation is a predominantly nonmarine clastic unit deposited in pull-apart basins on the Wrangellia composite terrane in southeast Alaska. As part of a 2009 Keck project involving nine undergraduate students, John Garver worked with the group on these spectacular rocks. One of the goals of the project was an attempt to collect a record of the unroofing history of the Coast Mountains Batholith complex using detrital zircon U/Pb geochronology. In 2009, John Garver was standing on Kupreanof Island looking pensively (but joyfully) west out over the Queen Charolette transform fault to the Pacific Ocean and asked out loud: “I wonder if the Chugach-Prince William terrane was out there when these rocks were being deposited?” That elegantly simple question launched a flurry of activity for the next 15 years involving multiple Keck projects and a minimum of 47 undergraduate students from 14 different intuitions.

In this contribution we compare the detrital zircon U/Pb signal preserved in the Kootznahoo Formation from Southeast Alaska with coeval units within the outboard Chugach-Prince William terrane (CPW) in Prince William Sound. We also compare these data to possible source terranes including the underlying Alexander terrane, Gravina belt, Coast Mountains Batholith, and Admiralty Island volcanics. In the Kootznahoo Formation, maximum depositional ages (MDA) range from 86-23 Ma with most samples deposited ~ 55 Ma. Three distinct stratigraphic groups are identified: The Hamilton Bay group has an MDA of 85 Ma and appears to be derived from adjacent Late Cretaceous age plutons of the Coast Mountains batholith. The Keku Straight and Pybus Bay group has MDAs of 57-51 Ma and correlate with similar age rocks of the CPW. The Porcellainite beach group is dominated by grains from the Admiralty Island volcanics and have an MDA of 26 Ma. Overall, the Kootznahoo Formation has a strikingly similar grain-age distribution to the Orca Group of the Chugach-Prince William Terrane. High cross-correlation coefficients and multi-dimensional scaling results show that the Kootznahoo Formation is more closely related to the Orca Group than the rocks they are deposited on, and suggests that the Orca group was outboard of the Kootznahoo Formation in the late Paleocene to early Eocene.

abstract: Fluornatropyrochlore [(Na, Pb, Ca, REE, U) 2 Nb 2 O 6 F] within the Agua de Pau São Miguel Island, Azores ejecta has long been known to the gem and mineral community but is rarely mentioned in the Azores literature. It occurs in both glomerocrysts and in interstitial cavities as euhedral, reddish-orange, hexoctahedral crystals up to 3 mm in diameter. Crystals are adamantine and isotropic. The mineral has a white streak and a calculated density of 5.275 g/cm 3 . Fluornatropyrochlore is isometric with a fluorite-type structure, space group Fd3̄m, with a= 10.5053(10) Å. This phase is part of the pyrochlore-supergroup minerals (A 2 B 2 X 6 Y), composed of two prefixes and one root name. The first prefix refers to the dominant anion, fluorine, in the Y-site. The second prefix relates to the dominant cation, sodium, in the A-site. Within the pyrochlore-supergroup, fluornatropyrochlore belongs to the NbO-pyrochlore group. Outside of the Azores, fluornatropyrochlore is a very rare phase found exclusively in rare-metal deposits. It is associated with zircon, dalyite, astrophyllite in a matrix mainly of albite, aegirine, and quartz.

title: OneStrata: A foundation model for deep-time biodiversity and mass extinction reassessment
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Shen, Shuzhong [1], Zhang, Shuhan of [2], Leng, Jiacheng [3], Fan, Junxian of [4], Erwin, Douglas H. [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
(2) School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China
(3) Zhejiang Lab, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China

(5) Santa Fe Institute, Santa Fe, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
The canonical "Big Five" mass extinctions have long been regarded as the principal drivers of Phanerozoic marine biodiversity history. This paradigm, however, was built upon taxonomic range compilations and stage-level time bins that cannot resolve ecological dynamics operating on timescales of thousands to tens of thousands of years. Here we present OneStrata, a transformer-based AI foundation model that learns a shared probabilistic representation of geological time directly from fragmented stratigraphic observations. Unlike conventional correlation methods such as CONOP, which formulate stratigraphic correlation as a combinatorial optimization problem whose computational cost becomes prohibitive when datasets exceed approximately 10,000 fossil species, even on modern supercomputers, OneStrata reformulates the problem as a representation-learning task. The model integrates within-section stratigraphic superposition, species co-occurrence patterns, temporal windows, and radiometric age constraints into a unified probabilistic framework that scales to global databases.

Applied to a global dataset of 31,044 stratigraphic sections, 183,514 species, and 2,845,815 fossil occurrences, supplemented by 449 high-precision ID‑TIMS dates, OneStrata reconstructs marine biodiversity at an imputed average temporal resolution of thousands of years across ~600 million years, from the Ediacaran to the early Neogene. The resulting biodiversity trajectory challenges the classical "Big Five" paradigm: only the end‑Ordovician and end‑Permian events emerge as profound global biodiversity collapses, whereas the Late Devonian, end‑Triassic, and end‑Cretaceous extinctions appear comparatively weak or diffuse.

Beyond revising the mass‑extinction narrative, this study demonstrates how AI foundation models can transform fragmented geological observations into a continuously improvable probabilistic representation of Earth history. OneStrata establishes a scalable temporal infrastructure that can integrate paleontological, stratigraphic, geochronological, and environmental data within a unified deep‑time reference system. The framework is designed as a general infrastructure for deep‑time Earth‑system analysis rather than a biodiversity‑specific application, opening a pathway toward a predictive digital Earth for investigating the long‑term co‑evolution of life and the planetary environment.

title: Late Permian to Triassic record of trench retreat in the Colombian Andes: timing, effects and mechanisms
session_title: Pre–Neogene Tectonic evolution of South America
authors: Cardona, Agustin [1], Zapata, Sebastian [2], Bedoya, Alejandra [3], Valencia, Victor A. [4], Zapata Villada, Juan Pablo [5]
affiliations: (1) Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Processes and Energy, Medellin,

(3) Universidad del Rosario, Bogota, Colombia, Colombia
(4) Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA

abstract:
Trench retreat has been considered as a major process of continental crust formation and evolution in convergent margins characterized by long-term subduction. Different tectonic mechanisms have been related to this tectonic switching, including slab migration through the mantle in a constant slab dip (rollback) or slab steepening. Each of these settings is responsible for different signatures in the upper plate that must be understood in order to precisely reconstruct the geodynamic evolution of a continental margin.

Although the Triassic tectonic history of the northern Andes of Colombia and Ecuador has been related to well defined phase of extension, a detailed discrimination of the effects associated to trench retreat, its timing and specific mechanism are still debatable. We integrate published geological constraints with new U-Pb zircon geochronological from magmatic, sedimentary and metamorphic units from the northern segment of the Central Cordillera of Colombia to reconstruct the geological record between the Late Permian and the Triassic. Late Permian red beds document the initiation of extension of the former Permian arc between 262 and 258 Ma. Late Permian to Middle Triassic granitoids are associated with widening of the magmatic arc, which by the Middle to Late Triassic included bimodal magmatism, with dikes and locally associated with migmatites. New and previous results from the plutonic component of ophiolite remnants in the western flank of the Cordillera indicate formation of oceanic crust between 230 and 226 Ma, and possibly until 216 Ma. This tectonic configuration over imposed the Permian margin and can extend to Ecuador. It’s suggested that this geological evolution can be related to a trench retreat setting, in which the widespread distribution of magmatism and ophiolite formation in a continental margin can be associated to a slab rollback mechanism that promoted a margin wide tectonic response with and the strong mantle input and the melting of the fertile and previously thick Permian crust that end with the formation of a suprasubduction ophiolite. After this extensional history and as short-term Late Triassic quiascence, the continental margin switch to a more compressional arc setting in the Early Jurassic and the older record was deformed, metamorphosed, and tectonically and magmatically dismembered.

title: Evaluating thermal processing of a carbon-rich slate to concentrate and high-grade semigraphite and vanadium
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Stokes, Rebecca [1], Barsukov, Igor V [2], Doninger, Anna [3], Mahin, Robert [4], Quigley, Ashley [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA,
(2) American Energy Technology Co., Wheeling, IL,

abstract:
Natural crystalline graphite is a critical mineral and an important component in steel and foundry functions, aerospace and weapons systems, and technology applications like battery energy storage systems. For these applications, natural graphite is typically sourced from flake deposits in which amphibolite facies or higher metamorphism generates graphite with high crystallinity and particle size. Few flake graphite deposits are known in the United States (e.g. Coosa, Alabama; Graphite Creek, Alaska), motivating investigation of sub-amphibolite facies carbonaceous rocks as unconventional sources. This study evaluates if slates containing semigraphite can be processed to yield graphite of sufficient crystallinity and particle size to substitute for flake graphite, and yield other critical minerals, like vanadium (V), as byproducts.

The Paleoproterozoic Michigamme Formation in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan is a sequence of greenschist-to-amphibolite facies metasedimentary and metavolcanic rocks. Certain intervals of this package are carbon-rich, with C graphite contents as high as 29 wt.% and V concentrations exceeding 3,000 ppm. For this study, ~100 kg of outcrop Michigamme Fm. material (C graphite = 9.5%; V= 3,026 ppm) was collected in the highest metamorphic grade region (staurolite grade, ~500°C). The sample was processed by particle size reduction using roller mill press crushing and wet ball milling, followed by three rounds of froth flotation and calcining in nitrogen at 1000°C. Following the primary beneficiation steps, thermal purification in nitrogen at 2800°C was performed on the concentrate which increased the grade from ~80 to 99.95+ wt.% C graphite . Raman spectroscopic analysis of the graphitic flakes revealed D1/G amplitude ratios decreased from 0.28 in the natural semigraphite to 0.02 in the thermally processed graphite, indicating a significant improvement in structural ordering. Particle sizes also transformed with thermal treatment from a bimodal to near unimodal distribution, and the median particle size increased from 163 µm to 299 µm. These graphite characteristics (particle size, purity, and crystallinity) are similar to those achieved for processed natural flake graphite. Vanadium was not detected in the thermally processed graphite, however off-gas residues created during thermal treatment contained ~2000 ppm of V. Results from this study indicate that thermal processing of semigraphite-rich slates such as from the Michigamme Fm. creates a mostly unrealized graphite resource. Additional testing like conductivity and battery coin-cell testing could provide further guidance for potential applications.

abstract: Cenozoic basins along the Bangong-Nujiang suture zone (BNSZ) in central Tibet record a protracted history of upper crustal shortening and deformation, roughly 290 km north of the India-Asia suture. Reconstructing basin formation processes are key to understanding the dynamics of continental collision and the evolution of the broader Tibetan Plateau. One prominent example along the central BNSZ is the Nima Basin, an east-west trending basin with late Cretaceous to Miocene strata, structurally overturned by basin-bounding thrust faults. Basin formation is interpreted to be driven by flexural subsidence associated with crustal loading along reactivated faults associated with continued Lhasa-Qiangtang shortening. Another model to explain the formation of basins further north of the BNSZ suggests localized subsidence may have been induced by the sinking of lithosphere drips, in addition to flexural loading. Another possible mechanism is subsidence associated with transtensional/strike-slip faulting. However, few other Cenozoic basins have been investigated in detail in the region. Here we present the results of new geologic mapping, cross section reconstruction, measured stratigraphic section, structural observations and geochronology, from an Eocene basin along the western BNSZ, the Awenco Basin. We compare new observations from preliminary fieldwork to previously studied basins (Nima, Lunpola, Dongco, etc.) within the BNSZ and in the Qiangtang terrane.

session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)

abstract: Pegmatite typically represents the last stages of a melt during plutonic placement, but their relationship to the overall magmatic system may be difficult to determine. Pegmatite intrusions exist within the Searchlight pluton in southern Nevada, though their association with the general system (specifically the middle Searchlight Monzonite) is unclear. Here we present new whole rock geochemical and petrographic analysis of four pegmatitic dikes from the middle and lower Searchlight monzonites to identify the relationship of the pegmatite to the quartz monzonite and the processes that formed these intrusions. We suggest that there are two different stages of crystallization characterized by two distinct dike sets: a very coarse grained and a finer (but still coarse) grained set. The very coarse-grained series consists of feldspars 1-3cm in diameter, hornblende, and trace minerals. The fine-grained series is composed of feldspars 0.5-1.5cm in diameter, hornblende, and trace minerals. The very coarse-grained dikes represent late stage melt from the middle Searchlight Monzonite, and the fine-grained dikes represent the north-south trending dike swarms that intrude the entire pluton.

title: High-precision U–Th geochronology on the Neoma MC-ICP-MS: a hybrid SEM–10^13 Ω Faraday approach

authors: Simões Pereira, Patric [1], Moseley, Gina E. [2], Edwards, R. Lawrence [3], Cheng, Hai [4], Spötl, Christoph [5]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Geology, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria

abstract:
U–Th geochronology provides high-precision ages for carbonate archives, but measurement of low-abundance 234 U (and 230 Th) isotope relative to 238 U remains difficult without trade-offs; static measurement of all U isotopes on Faraday cups requires large sample masses to obtain sufficient 234 U signal on high-ohmic resistor amplifiers, while dynamic secondary electron multiplier (SEM) peak-jumping requires diluting 235 U to avoid non-linearity, increasing measurement time. Hybrid approaches measuring 234 U on an SEM while collecting 233 U- 235 U- 238 U on Faraday cups rely on standard-sample bracketing for SEM yield, requiring drift tracking and error propagation.

Here we present a hybrid (static/dynamic) approach, developed for the ThermoScientific Neoma MC-ICP-MS with high-ohmic resistor amplifiers, Aridus 3, and autosampler, in which SEM–Faraday yield is determined within each analytical run. Tests were performed at the recently inaugurated Herbert W. Franke Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory, University of Innsbruck. 234 U is measured statically on the SEM while 233 U and 235 U- 238 U isotopes are collected on 10 13 Ω and 10 11 Ω Faraday cups, respectively. A dynamic peak jump to 233 U on the SEM provides an in-run yield determination under the same sample conditions. This principle is applied to Th, measuring 230 Th on the SEM and 229 Th on a 10 13 Ω Faraday cup, with a peak jump to 229 Th on the SEM providing within-run yield. Measurement duration is ~10 minutes each.

Within-run SEM yield precision is typically 1–1.5‰ for U and ~3‰ for Th. SEM-yield-corrected NBL-112A gives δ 234 U = −38.6 ±0.6‰ (2SE, n = 23, over two months), consistent with accepted values. Using ~40-50 ng U, we achieve 0.6–0.9‰ internal precision on δ 234 U and 1.2–2‰ on 230 Th/ 229 Th, with age precisions of 0.3–0.4% for clean carbonates spanning 5–150 ka. Analysis of speleothem SPA59 gives 133.1 ±0.5 ka, agreeing with independently determined University of Minnesota age from the same powder (132.4 ±0.8 ka, n=6), confirming inter-laboratory consistency. The SPA59 powder was, however, not homogenous, and replicates with naturally lower [U] than measured in Minnesota yielded ~131–134 ka. Error propagation shows that within-run yield correction makes a small contribution to uncertainty as 230 Th and 234 U counting statistics remain the dominant limitation.

Within-run SEM–Faraday yield determination with autosampler analysis enables high-precision U–Th measurements from small sample masses while reducing reliance on standard-sample bracketing. This approach is suited to higher-throughput, high-precision U–Th dating of carbonate archives.

title: Elevated Marine Phosphate Availability During the Tonian Period

authors: Ingalls, Miquela [1], Urist, Amanda [2], Trower, Lizzy [3], Crockford, Peter [4]

abstract:
Phosphorus (P) is considered the ultimate limiting nutrient for Earth’s biosphere over geological time, but ancient seawater phosphate ([PO 4 3- ]) concentrations remain poorly constrained. Reconstructing Proterozoic P availability is critical for understanding whether biological expansion, eukaryotic diversification, and shifting primary producer communities during the Neoproterozoic Era were facilitated by relaxed nutrient limitation. Carbonate-associated phosphate (CAP) provides a semi-quantitative proxy for dissolved inorganic phosphate ([DIP]) in ancient shallow marine environments. We analyzed CAP across four Tonian-aged carbonate platforms—the Little Dal Group (~1.00-0.78 Ga, Canada), Akademikerbreen Group (~0.82-0.74 Ga, Svalbard), Otavi Group (~0.75-0.72 Ga, Namibia), and the Beck Spring Dolomite (~0.78-0.72 Ga, Death Valley, USA) and Chuar Group (~0.77-0.74 Ga, Grand Canyon, USA)—and three mid-Proterozoic platforms as a baseline comparison—Rocknest Formation (~1.90 Ga, Canada), Bylot Supergroup (~1.05 Ga, Canada), and Crystal Springs Formation (~1.08 Ga, USA). We integrated these into a global dataset of >1,600 CAP measurements from the Neoarchean to the Cenozoic.

Neoproterozoic CAP concentrations represent peak global values across Earth history even within the uncertainties of differing analytical approaches and the context of global carbon cycle perturbations. In addition, we used ooid-size-based estimates of pH (8.49-8.68) and CAP values to reconstruct seawater [DIP] of 1.4-14.1 µM for the Akademikerbreen Group, 3.8 to 7.0 µM for the Beck Spring Dolomite, and 6.5 to 9.8 µM for the Chuar Group, exceeding modern P-limited ocean surface levels by up to sevenfold. Together, these findings have implications for both global climate and biogeochemistry. Reconstructed [DIP] falls below the threshold for calcite nucleation inhibition, indicating elevated [DIP] alone cannot account for ikaite persistence in warm waters supporting a cool late Tonian climate. In addition, CAP variations across the Bitter Springs carbon isotope anomaly and globally distributed platforms demonstrates phosphate availability reduced biosphere nutrient limitation and sustained primary productivity prior to animal radiation.

abstract:
The Reserva de la Biosfera Marismas Nacionales (RBMNN) located in Nayarit is one of the largest mangrove-dominated wetland systems along the Pacific coast of Mexico. This study uses sedimentological, geochemical, and biological proxies to identify potential storm overwash deposits and reconstruct paleoenvironmental and paleoecological changes, providing new insights into the long-term history of tropical cyclone activity and coastal evolution in Western Mexico.

In June 2025, 15 sediment cores were collected along a ~5 km transect extending inland from the Pacific Ocean using vibracoring, push coring, and peat boring, while 37 surface samples were taken from ocean, beach, wetland, ridge, and swale environments to establish modern sedimentary and geochemical signatures for comparison with the core records. Multiproxy analysis featuring loss-on-ignition, X-ray fluorescence, and magnetic susceptibility were applied to characterize sediment composition and identify storm- or flood-related horizons.

Core 04 (extracted ~3 km away from the beach) is divided into three sedimentological zones. Zone I (22-166 cm) consists of alternating dark and light brown sand, indicating deposition under more energetic conditions than today. Ti and Fe concentrations covary and display peaks at 125-130, 95-110 and 40-50 cm suggesting episodic increases in terrestrial sediment delivery. Zone II (15-22 cm) consists of an abrupt change to a distinct silt layer which suggests an instantaneous depositional event from an extreme event, likely a severe hurricane or tsunami. The top of the core (Zone III, 0-15 cm) consists of black clay interpreted as a low energy mangrove-wetland sediment.

Additional multi-proxy analysis is currently ongoing. Microfossils are being counted and analyzed to reconstruct ecological changes, while grain-size will characterize sediment transport processes and depositional energy. Scanning electron microscopy will examine grain morphology and microtextures to help distinguish marine and terrestrial sediment sources.

abstract: Cenozoic basins along the Bangong-Nujiang suture zone (BNSZ) in central Tibet record a protracted history of upper crustal shortening and deformation, roughly 290 km north of the India-Asia suture. Reconstructing basin formation processes are key to understanding the dynamics of continental collision and the evolution of the broader Tibetan Plateau. Three models have been proposed to explain the formation of these basins: 1) Basin formation is interpreted to be driven by flexural subsidence associated with crustal loading along reactivated faults associated with continued Lhasa-Qiangtang shortening; 2) localized subsidence may have been induced by the sinking of lithosphere drips, in addition to flexural loading; 3) subsidence is associated with transtensional/strike-slip faulting. However, few Cenozoic basins have been investigated in detail in the region. Here we present the results of new geologic mapping, measured stratigraphic section, structural observations, and preliminarly geochronology from an Eocene basin along the western BNSZ, the Awenco Basin.

title: ACCURATE AND ROBUST PREDICTION OF WATER QUALITY USING MACHINE LEARNING
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: Uprety, Grishma [1], Adhikari, Nabin [2], Hwang, Gisuk [3], Wang, Xiaoheng [4], Wasomi, Nicole [5], Swindle, Andrew [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(2) Computer Science, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(3) Mechanical Engineering, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(4) Public Administration, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(5) Public Administration, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(6) Wichita State UniversityDepartment of Geology, Wichita, KS,
abstract:
Groundwater quality is vital for human health, ecosystem stability, and sustainable water management. Shallow alluvial aquifers respond quickly to hydrologic fluctuations, making it important to forecast key water-quality parameters that signal shifts in aquifer conditions. Motivated by this need, we analyzed a high frequency dataset from nine monitoring wells at the Wichita State University Ninnescah Reserve to identify physical controls on groundwater behavior and evaluate machine‑learning approaches for predicting water‑quality dynamics.

The monitoring network shows a consistent 2.55ft hydraulic gradient from southwest to northeast, with MW-7 showing localized influence from river-aquifer interactions. Hydraulic gradient and flow direction are defined jointly by well location and hydraulic head: spatial coordinates establish the relative positions of wells, while elevation differences between them determine which wells are upgradient and downgradient. Neither variable alone captures the aquifer's flow structure; it is the spatial arrangement of head values across the monitoring network that defines gradient direction and magnitude.

We tested Bayesian Neural Networks (BNN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) using 21,600 spatiotemporal samples. Because gradient driven flow depends on the joint spatial- elevation relationship between wells, we used well locations and time as model inputs; outputs were water elevation, temperature, salinity, TDS, conductivity and pressure. All models achieved excellent accuracy for temperature with Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) below 4% and MAPE 0.015% for water elevation. For salinity and TDS, SVM and Bi‑LSTM achieved MAPE < 5% when trained on larger datasets, with Bi‑LSTM providing the highest overall performance.

These consistently low MAPE values demonstrate that key groundwater‑quality parameters in this alluvial system are highly predictable when hydrologically meaningful features are included. Elevation‑based spatial structure combined with high‑frequency temporal information provides a robust foundation for forecasting water‑quality behavior in sensitive alluvial aquifers.

title: Disruption of Complex Life Cycle Parasite-Host Interactions Among Trematodes and the Bivalve Genus Gemma Across the Plio-Pleistocene Extinction Event in the Southeastern US
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part II)
authors: Barkoviak, Hannah [1], Huntley, John Warren [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract: Parasites are often treated with instinctual repulsion and for good reason, they can be a severe detriment to their host’s health and overall fitness; capable of stealing nutrients, damaging tissues, and even affecting host behavior. Perhaps surprisingly, parasites are a vital component of a healthy ecosystem. Their roles can broadly influence aspects of a community's natural selection pressures, population sizes, biodiversity, and trophic level interactions. Despite the growing awareness of their importance, little is known about how complex life cycle parasites have responded to extinction events. The Plio-Pleistocene transition of the western Atlantic is characterized as a climate-influenced biotic turnover of bivalves, with an estimated extinction rate of 65%. The abundant, r -selected genus Gemma survived this extinction, commonly exhibits the characteristic shell malformations induced by complex life cycle trematodes, and is a strong candidate for addressing how parasite-host interactions were affected by climate change and extinction. Here we analyze prevalence, intensity, and aggregation of trematodes in Gemma across the Plio-Pleistocene transition utilizing the Florida Museum of Natural History’s invertebrate paleontology collections. We collected data from 2,234 valves of six species from 55 lots representing 11 formations along the southeast coast of the US, recording parasitic traces and measuring host and trace size. When considering all taxa, prevalence increases monotonically from the Pliocene through the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene whereas intensity decreases significantly in the Late Pliocene and rebounds slightly in the Early Pleistocene. Gemma magna , the most abundant taxon in our dataset (39%), displays a significant decrease in prevalence in the Late Pliocene followed by an increase to Pliocene values in the Early Pleistocene. Similarly, trematode intensity decreased significantly in the Late Pliocene with a less dramatic increase in the Early Pleistocene. Aggregation of trematodes decreased monotonically through time with a significant decrease between the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene with greater variation in the Late Pliocene. Our initial results suggest fundamental shifts in the parasite-host interactions across this extinction event. Ongoing modeling efforts will allow us to examine these patterns while accounting for potentially confounding factors including body size distribution, lithology, and latitude.

title: Application of Machine Learning-Based Analysis of Rainfall–Hydraulic Head Dynamics in a Karst Aquifer: Case Study from Jamaica
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: , ARPITA MANDAL [1], PAYNE, KARL [2], WILLIAMS, KELYSIA [3]
affiliations: (1) DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES, MONA, KINGSTON, Jamaica
(2) CERMES, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES, CAVE HILL, CAVE HILL, Barbados
(3) DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES, MONA, KINGSTON, Jamaica
abstract:
Groundwater is a major source of water resource for the island of Jamaica in the Caribbean. It accounts for ~80% of the island’s water resource and is confined in the karstic limestone and alluvium aquifer. Understanding the temporal relationship between rainfall and groundwater hydraulic head is fundamental for sustainable groundwater management, particularly in karst aquifers where recharge processes are highly heterogeneous and nonlinear. As the island faces the extremes of the hydrological cycle it is essential to understand and model groundwater flows with limited data availability. This research targets a hydrological basin in Jamaica, the Rio Cobre basin that has an extensive karstic aquifer which could be used for future water resource as the island’s surface water resources bear the brunt of the ongoing El Nino event. Traditional statistical approaches often struggle to capture the delayed, threshold-dependent, and complex interactions between meteorological forcing and groundwater response. This study proposes a machine learning framework to model and predict hydraulic head dynamics using rainfall and hydrogeological observations from the Rio Cobre basin in Jamaica.

Time-series datasets consisting of rainfall, hydraulic head, and supplementary hydrogeological variables, including antecedent rainfall, groundwater level trends, seasonal indicators, and climatic variables, were integrated into a unified predictive framework. Prior to model development, exploratory data analysis, lag-correlation analysis, feature engineering, and data normalization were performed to identify the dominant recharge-response timescales and improve model performance. Multiple machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks, were evaluated for their ability to reproduce observed groundwater fluctuations. Model performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R²), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE). The resulting models were used to investigate recharge dynamics, identify periods of rapid groundwater recovery, and estimate hydraulic head under varying rainfall scenarios. The models demonstrated good predictive performance, with an R 2 value of 0.8 indicating that a substantial proportion of the variability in the observed data was explained by the model. The framework of combining rainfall observations with historical groundwater records, enables accurate short-term hydraulic head forecasting and is readily transferable to groundwater systems where continuous monitoring data are available and can complement traditional physically based groundwater models.

title: Modeling the Source of Evaporated Soil Waters Using δ17Ο, δ18Ο, and δ2H
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Jorgenson, Annika [1], Kelson, Julia [2], Bowen, Gabriel J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract: Soil water’s stable oxygen and hydrogen isotope compositions reflect that of its source water, which depends on seasonality of recharge and is subsequently modified by evaporation. Deciphering source water, seasonality, and evaporation from δ 18 O in paleosol minerals remains a challenge for paleoclimate workers. Triple oxygen isotope geochemistry, evaluated with the parameter ∆ 17 O, may help disentangle these hydrologic processes: ∆ 17 O is sensitive to evaporation and can be measured in paleosol carbonates. Bowen et al., (2018) developed a Bayesian approach to model δ 18 O and δ 2 H of source water and seasonal contributions of recharge using δ 18 O and δ 2 H of evaporated terrestrial waters by considering the magnitude of evaporation, the slope of the evaporation line, and the local meteoric water line. Here we modify this model to include ∆ 17 O to expand its applicability to calcic paleosols. We use meteoric and soil water (depths 0 to 100 cm) stable isotope data (δ 2 H, δ 18 O, ∆ 17 O) from four locations in the US to test the model skill at predicting δ 18 O of source water. Each location represents a different climate regime: winter-wet, arid Reynolds Creek (ID), bimodally-wet, hyper-arid Mojave Desert (CA), summer-wet, semi-arid Jornada Basin (NM), and summer-wet, humid Edwin S. George Reserve (MI). Overall, the model tends to predict δ 18 O of source water that is lower than observed mean weighted precipitation δ 18 O values for soil water samples collected at depths > 40 cm. The offset is smallest for the humid MI site vs. the arid sites (median offset of 0.9‰ vs. 1.7‰). For the summer-wet sites (MI, NM), the model predicts that summer precipitation contributes > 50% to the source, while for the winter-wet sites (CA, ID), the model predicts that winter precipitation contributes > 50% to the source. We hypothesize that the model-observation offset in source δ 18 O reflects a combination of statistical bias to lower δ 18 O values and true hydrological differences in the effectiveness of recharge during certain seasons. For the shallow soil samples, the offset between modeled source δ 18 O values and mean weighted precipitation varies greatly (-7.3 to +4.3‰), reflecting dynamic near-surface processes including infiltration, mixing, and evaporation that reset stable isotope values near the surface. This Bayesian model may be used to better constrain interpretations of δ 18 O from pedogenic carbonate, with implications for paleoclimate research.

title: MICA GROUP K/RB ANALYSIS ACROSS ZONATION IN THE EMMONS PEGMATITE, GREENSWOOD, ME.
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Hecksher, Kaleb Otto [1], Falster, Alexander [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, West Chester University, West Chester, PA, USA; Maine Mineral and Gem Museum, Bethel, ME, USA
(2) MP2 Research Group, Maine Mineral and Gem Museum, Bethel, ME, USA
abstract:
Mica species are a key mineral group in studying the geochemical signature of pegmatites. Compositional variations suggest different formation conditions and help to better understand the formation of pegmatite. The K/Rb ratio in pegmatitic micas is linked to the degree of fractionation which shares an inverse and linear relationship, where a lower numerical value of the ratio suggests a higher degree of geochemical evolution of the particular pegmatite zone.

The Emmons pegmatite, located in Greenwood, Oxford County, ME, is a highly evolved pegmatite with well developed zoning. The anatectically formed pegmatite ( Webber et al ., 2019) is a boron-lithium-cesium-tantalum enriched pegmatite part of the Oxford pegmatite field. The K/Rb ratio of mica was used since it is present in each zone. Samples were taken across 6 different sites, including the core, core margin, intermediate zones, and hanging wall wall zone. Elemental analysis was performed using a Bruker S1 Titan X-ray Fluorescence Spectrometer (XRF).

A widespread heterogeneity in micas’ of K/Rb was found throughout the 6 sites. The evolving melt is expected to continuously increase in incompatibles, including Rb. In the less evolved outer zones of the pegmatite, high K/Rb values were found. Conversely, the core had higher Rb substituting for K and thus lower K/Rb values, which corresponds with the K/Rb progressional zoning. The pegmatite has a max K/Rb value of 85.39, and a minimum of 4.81. Whereas the pegmatites zoning supports the K/Rb hypothesis, each zone had a range of K/Rb values. Multiple sites contain isolated decreases in Rb, dramatically increasing the K/Rb value for a single measurement. These outlier samples go against the gradual zonation progression along strike. This study supports the idea of K/Rb ratios being useful to comprehend the complexity of a pegmatite system, while also displaying the variability of microchemistry environments.

title: Using Laser Ablation ToF-ICPMS High-Resolution Geochemical Maps to Define Zoning in Zircon from the Granodioritic Tuolumne Intrusive Suite, Sierra Nevada Batholith
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Posters)
authors: Johnston, Scott M. [1], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [2], Adamson, Morgan [3]
affiliations: (1) Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo, San Luis Obispo, CA,
(2) UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA,
(3) University of California, Santa Barbara, Goleta, CA,
abstract:
Laser ablation ICPMS allows rapid measurement of trace element concentrations in minerals. However, conventional procedures on accessory phases like zircon are limited by laser spots of 20 µm or more that are unable to resolve finer-scale geochemical zoning characteristic of various geologic processes. Here, we compare 5-µm resolution geochemical maps acquired by laser ablation Time-of-Flight (ToF) ICPMS with 25-µm laser ablation split stream (LASS) ICPMS spot data in zircon sampled from Tuolumne Intrusive Suite (TIS) granodiorites in the Sierra Nevada batholith.

As a proof-of-concept, the ToF-ICPMS yields trace element concentrations that broadly reproduce the LASS-ICPMS spot data, except with much higher spatial resolution. When combined with geochemical discriminant diagrams, the ToF-ICPMS data maps discrete geochemical domains within individual TIS zircon grains. Notably, zircon from younger, interior units of the TIS include xenocrystic/antecrystic cores characterized by moderate U/Yb and Lu/Y, primitive autocrystic cores characterized by low Hf, U/Yb, and Lu/Y, and autocrystic mantles and rims with higher U/Yb and Lu/Y.

The ToF-ICPMS maps also reveal the presence of sector zoning in zircon from all TIS units that is not readily visible in CL. This zoning is strongest in zircon with lower Ti-in-zircon temperatures, and most easily observed in maps of trace element ratios that indicate higher U/Yb in pyramid tips—the result of higher U and lower Yb—than prism faces. Because LASS-ICPMS spot data targeted grain centers and tips, and thus inadvertently sampled prism faces and pyramid tips, respectively, the recognition of sector zoning clarifies the interpretation of geochemical zoning. For example, it is now clear that the 2X increase in U/Yb from grain centers to tips in interior TIS zircon, displayed by the LASS-ICPMS spot data, reflects sector zoning rather than magma evolution. Instead, rimward line profiles across ToF-ICPMS maps of prism faces and pyramid tips from these same samples indicate constant U/Yb, flat or subtly increasing Lu/Y, and gradually decreasing Th/U. ToF-ICPMS maps also display 5–10 µm rims on many grains characterized by abruptly increasing Hf, U/Yb and Lu/Y with decreasing Th/U that were not clearly resolved in LASS-ICPMS spot data. This study demonstrates the utility of high-resolution data when using trace elements to probe magmatic evolution, and further integration of these two techniques should help our understanding of the TIS.

abstract: Most Cretaceous stage boundaries are based on bio- and carbon isotope stratigraphy in Tethyan sections of Europe. However, these are bereft of tuffs that can be radioisotopically dated, and only Late Cretaceous strata in North America contain well-dated marine fossils. In contrast, during the Cretaceous Northern Japan was located along the East Asian subduction zone that produced fossil-rich mudstones intercalated with hundreds of silicic tuffs. These sediments offer extraordinary opportunities, not only to improve the global age model and uncertainties associated with Valanginian through Campanian stage boundaries, but also to resolve the timing and potential drivers of paleoenvironmental perturbations, including OAEs. We integrate U-Pb zircon CA-ID-TIMS and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar sanidine ages of tuffs with advances in bio-, carbon-, and osmium isotope stratigraphy in Hokkaido and Northern Honshu. Examples here will highlight recent contributions and future prospects for an open science Cretaceous time scale. U-Pb zircon ages of tuffs in the Yezo Group, Hokkaido, where Leupoldina cabri occurs above synchronous carbon and osmium isotope excursions, indicate that OAE1a began at 119.55 ± 0.08 Ma and lasted 1116 ± 90 kyr. These findings imply that Ontong Java volcanism is a probable driver of OAE1a and facilitate precise correlation with Tethyan and South Pacific Ocean records. U-Pb and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates from Yezo Group tuffs also yield an Albian-Cenomanian boundary age of 100.74 ± 0.10 Ma. This age relies on correlating distinctive 13 C excursions of the Albian-Cenomanian boundary event, including OAE1d, from the Mt. Risou, France GSSP to those in Yezo Group strata where Thalmanninella globotruncanoides first appears. A subdued osmium isotope excursion suggests a role for Kerguelan LIP volcanism in driving the Albian-Cenomanian boundary event. Importantly, the ICS Cretaceous sub-commission is considering a proposal to redefine the base Aptian to the carbon isotope excursion demarcating the onset of OAE1a at Cau, Spain. Our radioisotopic ages for OAE1a/base Aptian stage and the Albian-Cenomanian boundary can be used to anchor a recently published astrochronologic age model spanning from 121-100 Ma extracted from the Poggio le Guaine core, Italy. A Cretaceous open science time scale will benefit from organizing and cross-linking radioisotopic, orbital tuning, biostratigraphic, and chemostratigraphic metadata from these and future contributions that can be integrated, evaluated and updated by next generation geoscientists.

title: Flow-Connectivity Improves Stream Temperature Predictions in a Karst Watershed: A Spatial Stream Network Approach
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Curtis, Daniel [1], Orr, Lexie [2]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania,
(2) Biology, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract: Stream temperature drives chemical and biological processes, so accurate predictive models are essential for stream-network management. However, karst systems are challenging to model because cool-spring groundwater discharge affects downstream surface water via flow connectivity. Previous regression and Euclidean modeling techniques do not explicitly represent this directional thermal transport. This study applies a moving-average, flow-connected stream network model to Spring Creek, a mixed-land-use karst watershed in central PA, and compares its performance with Euclidean and nonspatial regression approaches under high thermal variability. Initial models use long-term temperature observations and available site and watershed-level predictors, but ongoing model development will evaluate additional hydrologic, groundwater, and landscape controls. Among the models evaluated to date, the tail-up model had the strongest fit and predictive performance, reducing cross-validation prediction error by ~25% and ~20% relative to the nonspatial and Euclidean models, respectively. These results highlight the value of incorporating flow-connected thermal transport when predicting thermal conditions in karst stream networks and provide a foundation for identifying thermally important reaches for targeted monitoring and management.

abstract: Reconstructing the climate of Earth's arid continental regions can be challenging due to a lack of continuous sedimentary archives. Dust blown from the continents offshore to the oceans carries molecules of land plants with it, thereby allowing for past conditions on land to be studied from ocean sediments. In 1986, ODP Leg 108 recovered Plio-Pleistocene sediments from the tropical eastern Atlantic Ocean offshore northwest Africa. Situated beneath the path of the African Easterly Jet, Site 660 receives dust from the Sahara/Sahel region of central North Africa. In this study, plant wax deuterium and carbon isotopes are used to examine hydroclimate (wet vs arid) fluctuations and past shifts in the dominant vegetation type (C 3 versus C 4 plants), respectively, during the past ~4 million years. While prior studies of dust flux suggested that northern Africa became progressively more arid during the past 3 million years, new data from ODP 660 plant wax hydrogen isotopes reveals high variability but no overall long-term trends in hydroclimate. However, a long-term shift in the dominant vegetation type from more C 3 plants in the Pliocene to more C 4 plants in the Pleistocene is noted. A similar pattern in C 3 /C 4 shifts during the Plio-Pleistocene is noted between western and eastern Africa. During the Plio-Pleistocene, changes in the dominant vegetation type across the northern African continent were likely driven by changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations rather than changes in rainfall amount.

abstract: Conodonts were recovered from bedding planes in black shale intervals from two 10 cm (4 inch) diameter drill cores from central Alabama. In the Cain 6-6 #1 core the occurrence of Palmatolepis bogartensis ? (Stauffer 1938), Pa. extensa Ziegler and Sandberg 1990?, Pa. rhenana Bischoff 1956, and Pa. boogaardi Klapper and Foster 1993 were recovered from a 3.5 m thick interval in the Chattanooga Shale, indicative of the highest Frasnian Zone 13. In the Weyerhaeuser 2-43-2402 core Pa. per. perlobata , Pa. clarki , and Pa. del. delicatula in a lag bed in the Chattanooga Shale indicates the Pa. min. minuta to Pa. crepida Zone. These conodonts indicate Frasnian and Famennian strata in the Chattanooga Shale in the southern Appalachian Basin of the Alabama subsurface. The Floyd Formation (Carboniferous) in the Weyerhaeuser 2-43-2402 core contained a full and an incomplete assemblage of Gnathodus bilineatus ssp., and a single incomplete assemblage of two Sb1 or Sb 2 elements, two indeterminate S elements, and one Sc1 element from an Idioprioniodus sp. The morphology of the Idioprioniodus sp. specimen, as well as the time constraints provided by G. bilineatus, make the species indeterminate and possibly transitional between I. healdi and I. conjunctus .

abstract:
Mafic enclaves are often cited as evidence that a reservoir has been recently recharged by a less-differentiated magma at or near its liquidus. In some systems, petrographic and compositional variations within enclaves are attributed to differing degrees of undercooling within the recharge magma during mixing. Other systems yield enclaves with petrographic textures and mineral compositions that can only be produced by a prolonged thermal history, with their presence attributed to the syneruptive breakup of a mushy magma body. At Newberry Volcano, a back-arc shield volcano within the Cascade Range, the presence of mafic enclaves within the 1.3 Ka Big Obsidian Flow (BOF) has previously been attributed to mixing between older rift basalts and BOF rhyolites.

A new suite of mafic enclaves was collected from BOF during Summer 2025. Petrographic textures, mineral compositions, and bulk rock 143 Nd/ 144 Nd and 87 Sr/ 86 Sr isotopic compositions of variably-mixed basaltic-andesite enclaves, xenoliths, and host lavas preclude this binary mixing origin for BOF mafic enclaves. Fine-grained enclaves are more radiogenic than their resident host lava and are better reproduced by a primitive calc-alkaline basalt mixing with or assimilating melts isotopically similar to earlier-erupted Holocene rhyolites, whereas our coarsest-grained enclave is much less radiogenic than BOF host lavas. Fine-grained enclaves likely represent a batch of recharge magma stored at depth that evolved by assimilating melts derived from a radiogenic, high-SiO 2 source before being mixed with BOF rhyolites.

Two pyroxene and pyroxene-only P-T estimates of fine-grained enclaves indicate recharge magmas were stored near their liquidus in the middle crust; crenulated enclave margines and petrographic texturesw suggest this enclave population was <7% crystalline at the time of mixing. Petrographic textures and crystal morphologies within medium-grained enclaves are indicative of a disaggregating crystal mush, while petrographic textures and mineral and glass compositions of our coarsest-grained enclaves suggest a cumulate origin, bolstered by new storage estimates at low- T within the upper crust. Alongside the dataset of Linneman & Myers (1990), our mafic enclaves preserve a record of Newberry's magmatic system unresolved by geophysical methods. Mushy bodies and multiple magma batches appear to be the norm, and Newberry's magmatic system is no exception.

title: Tools for Attracting Students to your Geoscience Department: Emphasize Altruism and Salary on your Department Website

abstract:
Geoscience has a marketing problem. Despite workplace growth and comparatively high salaries, the number of recent Geoscience graduates has decreased, and some Geoscience departments have closed or are facing the threat of closure. In addition, many people consider Geoscience to be outdated and/or environmentally damaging. How can we market Geoscience to represent the true breadth of the field and attract students to the discipline?

We surveyed more than 2,000 students from high schools (30%), 2-year colleges (14%), and a 4-year college (56%) in Northern California to determine what aspects of the Geosciences are attractive to students and how they prefer to get information about majors and careers so that we can tailor marketing materials to their preferences.

We found that students are attracted to altruistic aspects of the Geosciences, such as solving pollution problems, protecting the environment, minimizing the effects of natural disasters and protecting local and global communities. Students are also financially conscious. When presented with Geoscience job information, students are attracted to the salary and career outlook of the discipline as well as the range of job opportunities.

From our survey results, we determined that students prefer to get information from department websites (57%) and counselors/advisors (50%), even more than from social media (18%). This presents a challenge for many Geoscience departments because the people in charge of websites may lack time and/or expertise to update the website. Additionally, there might be institutional restrictions on how a department may modify its own website.

We have used the results of our survey to begin creating a set of materials for attracting students to Geoscience that can be tailored to a department’s needs. Materials for websites and social media are intentionally designed to be easily modified using common software and will be freely available online.

title: Geogenomic approaches for inferring paleo-river networks
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Stokes, Maya F [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Science, Florida State University, Tallahassee, 32303, USA
abstract: Geogenomics relies on the premise that some geologic processes have a causal relationship to biological evolution and thus information about the pace and spatial patterns of biological diversification can be inverted to investigate the history of geologic features. In this presentation, I will discuss geogenomics approaches for inferring the history of river network reorganization at different spatial and temporal scales. Drainage divides, the topographic boundaries of river basins, are dynamic landscape features. As they shift gradually or abruptly, dispersal pathways for sediment and freshwater taxa are disrupted. The abrupt movement of a drainage divide via river capture, for example, can isolate evolutionary lineages of freshwater taxa which may lead to speciation while also allowing for dispersal between previously disconnected regions. Freshwater biologists have found examples in which continental-scale evolutionary relationships amongst riverine fishes are more consistent with paleo-drainage networks than modern river networks. Meanwhile, geologists often use topographic and sedimentary-provenance analyses to infer historical or ongoing river network reorganization. I will discuss how biological and geologic lines of evidence can be analyzed jointly to reconstruct the history of North American river network reorganization at deeper to more recent timescales. I will first present a novel method for inferring continental-scale river network connectivity that combines U-Pb provenance data with an ancestral area reconstruction of a time-calibrated phylogeny of Centrarchidae (basses and sunfishes). Next, I will discuss topographic, zoogeographic, and population-genetic evidence for pulsed river captures across the Blue Ridge Escarpment. The presentation will highlight the challenges and promise of geogenomics tools for investigating the history of river network reorganization.

title: Dilution Versus Authigenesis: Disentangling Detrital and Redox Controls on Trace-Metal Enrichment in Paleozoic Phosphatic Shales, Oklahoma
session_title: Metals in Motion: Trace metal heterogeneity, speciation, isotopes, and cycling across varying spatial and temporal scales (Posters)
authors: Morris, Noah S. [1], Hunt, Lindsey Elise [2], Hayman, Nick [3]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK,
(2) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK,
(3) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK,
abstract: Molybdenum, uranium, and phosphorus enrichment are widely used to infer water-column anoxia and phosphogenesis in black shales, but their expression reflects not only redox state but also rate of detrital dilution during deposition. Preliminary analysis of core from five Paleozoic shale units across Oklahoma demonstrates this directly. In the Woodford Shale (Devonian–Mississippian), sustained, minimal detrital input (Ti, Zr enrichment factors ~0.3–0.6x average shale) coincides with extreme, basin-scale enrichment in molybdenum (up to ~100x) and uranium (~11–12x), consistent with a starved basin in which authigenic metals accumulated with little clastic dilution. In Pennsylvanian cyclothem shales (Cherokee and Checkerboard), by contrast, Ti/Zr enrichment is near baseline (~0.7–0.9x), and Mo, U, and P values are muted, but within narrow (<5 ft) intervals, Ti and Zr drop sharply (to ~0.2–0.4x) precisely where Mo, U, and P spike (Mo to ~71x), showing bed-scale brief reductions in detrital input, not increases in anoxia alone, permit authigenic concentration. An Ordovician interval (Upper Simpson Group) contrasts a dilution-only explanation: despite low detrital input, it shows negligible metal enrichment, indicating genuinely oxic deposition rather than a starved-anoxic setting. A Mississippian Caney Shale core adds an independent pathway, with strong phosphorus-uranium co-variation (r ≈ 0.8) reflecting authigenic uranium uptake during apatite formation rather than a purely redox-driven mechanism. The results indicate trace-metal enrichment in shales cannot be interpreted as a redox proxy in isolation; pairing with a detrital proxy is necessary to distinguish oxic from anoxic signals suppressed by dilution, and may control phosphogenesis.

title: Abundant Evidence for Reworking of Materials in and around Jezero Crater
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Kah, Linda C. [1], Minitti, Michelle E. [2], Williams, Rebecca M. E. [3], Kennedy Wu, Megan R. [4], Yingst, R. Aileen [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,
(2) Planetary Science Institutes, USA
(3) Planetary Science Institute, USA

abstract:
MAHLI and WATSON are 2-megapixel, color cameras that support handlens-scale science on the Curiosity and Perseverance rover missions (Edgett et al., 2012). These cameras can focus on targets at working distances from 2.1 cm to infinity, have a best-resolution of approximately 14 microns/pixel, and a more typical resolution of ~18-20 μm pixel. Because unique identification of a single grain typically requires more than 4-5 individual pixels, this resolution is sufficient to accurately resolve individual grains in sizes consistent with very fine sand (62.5 to 125 μm), thereby discriminating them from grains that are silt-sized or smaller (<62.5 μm), which are not clearly resolvable. Individual pixel color, however, is often sufficient to mark the presence of silt-sized and smaller grains.

Jezero crater was chosen as a landing site for the Perseverance rover, in large part, because of the potential array of geologic materials both inside and outside of the crater. These include potential coarse and fine-grained igneous materials exposed along the crater floor, both coarse-and fine-grained materials exposed within a large sedimentary fan deposit, and a variety of materials (e.g., igneous, sedimentary, impactoclastic/volcanoclastic) in the Jezero crater rim and outside of Jezero crater. Here we use WATSON images to explore the extent and behavior of ‘fine-grained’ materials exposed within Jezero crater, Mars, with a focus on targets that have undergone abrasion by the Perseverance rover’s abrasion bit, and post-abrasion clearing by the gDRT (gas Dirt Removal Tool). The majority of the‘fine-grained’ materials—which in this case are broadly defined as having individual grains identifiable only because of variation in pixel color—have been interpreted as sedimentary or impactoclastic/volcanoclastic (air fall) deposits. WATSON images show that the majority of these ‘fine-grained’ materials are actually composed of composite grains. Most composite grains fall within the scale of fine-to-medium sand (125-500 μm), although several have grains as large as very coarse sand (1-2 mm). Fine-to- medium grain sizes suggest the potential for flocculation in the martian atmosphere and/or surface waters, and coarser grained components are consistent with a broad range of reworking of previously emplaced materials, both inside and outside of Jezero crater.

title: Fossil planktic foraminifera microstructure reflects deep equatorial Pacific carbonate ion saturation since the Last Glacial Maximum
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Fehrenbacher, Jennifer S [1], Fritz-Endres, Theresa [2]
affiliations: (1) College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(2) College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
abstract:
Reconstructing deep ocean carbonate ion saturation (ΔCO₃²⁻) is essential for understanding carbon cycling and storage in the climate system across glacial–interglacial timescales. In this study, we develop a core-top calibration for the equatorial Pacific to quantify deep ocean ΔCO₃²⁻ using foraminifera dissolution data derived from micro-computed tomography (microCT) scans. Core-top samples spanning a natural ΔCO₃²⁻ gradient demonstrate strong correlations between microCT metrics and measured bottom water ΔCO₃²⁻, forming the basis of regional calibration equations for the species Neogloboquadrina dutertrei , Pulleniatina obliquiloculata , and Trilobatus sacculifer .

We apply the N. dutertrei calibration to reconstruct bottom water ΔCO₃²⁻ during the deglaciation and Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). Our results indicate better preservation in deglacial specimens, with reconstructed bottom deep ocean ΔCO₃²⁻ values 10–15 μmol/kg higher than those from the Holocene and LGM. These results are consistent with other regional records and support the hypothesis that variations in deep ocean carbonate chemistry contributed to changes in atmospheric pCO₂ over this interval.

Because poor preservation in the deep central Pacific has previously limited ΔCO₃²⁻ reconstructions, this dataset provides new regional constraints on deep ocean carbonate chemistry since the LGM and enhances our understanding of deep ocean carbon cycling during major climate transitions. By establishing a quantitative link between microCT-derived data and ΔCO₃²⁻, this work also demonstrates the utility of high-resolution imaging for paleoceanographic reconstructions.

abstract:
With growing interest in mining of deep-sea polymetallic nodules to meet raw material demand, it is important to understand the various ecosystems where these nodules occur and how they may be affected by mining operations. To do so, various assessments of the seafloor geology and chemistry have been conducted to establish benthic baselines in advance of these activities.

These assessments include using High Purity Germanium (HPGe) gamma detectors to measure a suite of radioisotopes that can be used as particle tracers, geochronometers, and to determine apparent diffusion flux. Radioisotopes in the U-238 decay chain from Ra-226 and below (daughter products) have elevated activity in sediment cores collected in the Clarion Clipperton Zone (CCZ) NORI-D contract area and in the Cook Islands CIC CBG4 exploration license area. These elevated activities are not found in the radioisotopes above Ra-226, indicating that the radioisotopes in the U-238 decay series are not in secular equilibrium. The elevations of Ra-226 are on average 17x higher than expected based on the supported Th-234 levels in these regions. This elevation in Ra-226 may be due to polymetallic nodules, but the specific chemical or mineral responsible for the disequilibrium is unknown.

To ascertain the cause of any elevated radioisotope activity, X-ray diffraction (XRD) was employed to identify the mineral composition of the sediments, and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) was used to determine the elemental composition. Direct comparison of these results will show which elements or minerals drive elevated radioisotope activity, contributing to a better mechanistic understanding of the geochemical setting in which deep-sea nodules form and supporting refinement of monitoring tools used to assess mining activity, such as benthic plume detection. This supports broader impact assessment efforts by quantifying abiotic variables that can be tied to biotic responses.

title: Tracking the Marine Sulfate Reservoir Through OAE1a
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Posters)
authors: Herlinger, Jillian F. [1], Tretina, Veronika C. [2], Podrecca, Luca G. [3], Sageman, Bradley B. [4], Hurtgen, Matthew T. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA

(4) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA

abstract:
One of the largest negative seawater sulfate sulfur isotope (δ 34 S) shifts of the last 130 million years (~-5‰) coincides with Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a (OAE1a; the Selli Event). Although an excursion of this magnitude has highly significant implications for biogeochemical cycling in the Early Aptian, the specific drivers of the event remain unresolved. One hypothesis attributes the shift to the addition of 34 S-depleted sulfur associated with large igneous province (LIP) volcanism, whereas another invokes a decrease in global pyrite burial resulting from extensive sulfate removal through evaporite deposition linked to the opening of the South Atlantic Ocean. However, these processes affect marine sulfate concentrations differently: increased volcanism enhances sulfate delivery to the ocean, whereas evaporite deposition removes sulfate through calcium sulfate precipitation. From an Earth-systems perspective, this distinction matters because seawater sulfate levels regulate pathways of organic carbon remineralization and thus influence nutrient recycling, ocean redox, methane production, and alkalinity generation, all of which affect carbon-cycle feedbacks and climate.

This study presents new δ 34 S records for pyrite and sulfurized organic matter from a section that captures OAE1a in southeastern France (Vocontian Basin, Western Tethys). We integrate these records with redox-sensitive trace-metal and iron and phosphorus speciation data to reconstruct changes in local redox conditions and sulfur cycling during OAE1a. Together, these data help constrain local sulfate availability and provide insight into the state of the global marine sulfate reservoir and its influence on biogeochemical cycling during the event.

title: Ephemeral Saline Lake Systems as Analogs for Martian Crater Lakes: Insights from Shoemaker Crater, Western Australia

authors: Tagle, Natasha B. [1], Kah, Linda C. [2], Bartley, Julie K. [3], Schmoyer, Sonja M. [4], Sumrall, Colin D. [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA

abstract:
Crater lakes are prime targets in the search for ancient Martian habitability, yet they are often modeled as single, long-lived evaporative basins producing concentric “bullseye” mineral zonation and thick deposits of evaporative facies. Facies relationships in Gale crater, Mars, for instance, show a more complex history of lacustrine, aeolian, and diagenetically overprinted deposits indicative of episodic flooding, evaporation, and groundwater interaction rather than simple basin-wide desiccation.

Reconstructing this dynamic depositional and diagenetic history requires a terrestrial analog that captures comparable hydrologic complexity. Shoemaker crater, Western Australia, is a ~25 km diameter, Fe-rich and sulfur-bearing impact crater that hosts multiple ephemeral saline lakes. These lakes develop prominent color variation during drying, precipitate gypsum and halite, and are surrounded by gypsiferous soils reflecting mixed lake/groundwater contributions. However, these systems remain essentially undocumented. We will be addressing this gap in understanding by (1) characterizing the geochemical evolution of Shoemaker’s lakes across wet and dry seasons and (2) documenting spatial and temporal variability in lacustrine sedimentary fabrics and facies across the basin.

Here, we report on lake behavior based on multi-year surveys of LANDSAT images and show results from our initial field season in mid-May to early-June 2026. Comparison of LANDSAT images to regional rainfall shows a complex relationship between input fluids and longer-term lake behavior. Initial in situ reconnaissance of dried lakes shows a range of characteristics, with the lakes on the crater rim displaying a hardened, mud cracked surface and little evidence for evaporite deposition at the surface. By contrast, other lakes record a variably soft surface of generally uniform efflorescent halite salts, with regions of depressed topography marked by a gypsum crust. Trenching of the lakes and their inlet channels showed gypsum precipitating in sediment pores in upper subsurface, displacive lensoidal gypsum above the water table, and groundwater present at about 30-40 cm depth. We suggest the ephemeral saline lakes within Shoemaker crater—which preserve evidence of wet-dry hydrologic variability in their evaporite mineralogy and sediment fabrics—may serve as a useful analog for episodic, groundwater-influenced lake systems proposed for Gale crater’s sulfate-bearing units.

title: Geochronology and geochemistry of an overprinting Porphyry-Epithermal Au-Pb-Zn-Cu mineralization system: A case study from the Biga Peninsula (NW Turkey), Tethyan Metallogenic Belt

authors: Davis, Zachary [1], Yasar, I. Dogancan [2], Kamenov, George D. [3], Sayit, Kaan [4], Miller, Brent [5], Heizler, Matthew T. [6], Curtis, Jason [7], Billor, Mehmet Zeki [8]
