abstract:
Western Anatolia underwent post-collisional extension during the Miocene, driven by slab rollback of the Aegean Sea Plate and westward strike-slip escape of Anatolia. As a result of this extension, widespread magmatism and related porphyry, epithermal, and skarn mineralization systems populated western Anatolia, creating various ore deposits as a part of the Tethyan Metallogenic Belt. Within the Tethyan Metallogenic Belt, the Biga Peninsula (NW Turkey) region contains the Catalcam Au-Pb-Zn-Cu mineralization, interpreted to have formed as an Au-Cu porphyry that was later overprinted by Pb-Zn epithermal mineralization. The system is hosted by the Yuntdag Volcanics, consists of calc-alkaline porphyritic andesite, basaltic andesite, trachy-andesite lavas and pyroclastic rocks. Here, we present new zircon Hf isotopic data from the host rocks, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology of biotites and sericitized groundmass, and O-isotopic data from the dolomitic ore vein material that includes the epithermal products of the system. The results provide new insights into the complex evolution of the Biga Peninsula and the Catalcam mineralization system.

Our previously reported LA-ICP-MS analysis of zircons from three andesites yielded U-Pb concordia ages of 19.51-19.65 Ma, whereas an andesitic tuff yielded a U-Pb concordia age of 20.26±0.12 Ma. These ages constrain Early Miocene post-collisional continental arc-like magmatism of the Yuntdag volcanics to a duration of ~1-million-years. New LA-MC-ICP-MS zircon Hf isotopic analysis of the zircons yielded εHf (t) values ranging between -15.4 – -1.4, providing further evidence of crustal contamination of the magmatic source for the Yuntdag volcanics, previously established with bulk-rock Sr-Nd-Pb isotopes. New laser incremental heating analysis of sericitized groundmass and biotites from the host rocks revealed 40 Ar/ 39 Ar plateau ages of 19.80±0.09–18.65±0.12 Ma, and 20.11±0.05–18.91±0.18 Ma, respectively. These ages are interpreted to constrain hydrothermal activity and related alteration during the porphyry-to-epithermal stage of the Catalcam mineralization. Furthermore, our new O-isotope analysis of the dolomitic vein material that includes the sphalerite ore revealed δ 18 O values ranging between -13.73 – -11.93‰, consistent with low-sulfidation epithermal systems dominated by meteoric fluids.

Ongoing work aims to precisely constrain the timing of epithermal ore mineralization via solution Rb-Sr sphalerite isochron dating and ore metal sources via Pb isotope analysis of sphalerite.

title: Coal Balls: A Hi-Fi Record of Swamp Deposition and Extreme Diagenesis Revisited
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections (Posters)
authors: Rubin, Lillian N. [1], Christie, Max [2], Punyasena, Surangi W. [3], Elrick, Scott [4], Johnson, Thomas M. [5], Sivaguru, Mayandi [6], Fouke, Bruce W. [7]

abstract:
Coal balls are diagenetically altered remains of Late Pennsylvanian (Carboniferous~ 300Ma) swamps that preserve a high fidelity cellular-level record of fossil plant tissues that experienced extensive syn- and post-depositional diagenetic alteration in dys- to anoxic sedimentary environments. While the floristic composition of coal balls has been well-studied, details of their depositional history and diagenetic alteration remain minimally understood and hotly debated. For example, some previous studies suggest coal balls form in terrestrial freshwater settings, while others propose deposition in marine environments. The goal of the present study is to revisit coal ball taphonomy by integrating next-generation 140 nm-resolution optical microscopy techniques with established approaches in energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and isotope geochemistry. As a pilot study, here we focus on a single coal ball from the Sahara Mine in southern Illinois, before expanding to a larger sample set available for analysis in the comprehensive coal ball collection assembled by Professor Tom Phillips at Illinois. From this single pilot specimen, we microdrilled powders for carbon, oxygen, and strontium stable isotope measurements and prepared a doubly-polished 20 mm-thick petrographic thin section of the sampled area. This integrated geobiology approach permits coal ball composition to be dynamically linked with its petrography.

Super resolution petrographic analyses on a Zeiss LSM 980 reveal a robust paragenetic sequence in which pyrite preferentially forms on plant material. This is followed by multiple generations of fibrous through blocky calcite cements, with concentric crystal zonations under cathodoluminescence (CL) and fibrous crystals exhibiting triangular cross-sections associated with freshwater meteoric diagenesis (Siewers and Phillips, 2015). EDS of these calcite cements shows elemental heterogeneity at the cellular level, consistent with CL zonations. Stable carbon isotopes exhibit high variability, ranging from δ¹³C −34‰ to −17‰ (VPDB), with areas of carbonate cement showing more negative values than plant material. Stable oxygen isotopes were negative and relatively stable, δ¹⁸O −8‰ to −5‰ (VPDB), suggesting fresh water sources. ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr isotope ratios were stable and higher than the secular seawater curve for the Carboniferous. This petrographic and geochemical evidence implies early diagenetic alteration in reducing freshwater environments that may have impacted by microbial methanogensis during ongoing sediment shedding and runoff from the central Pangean mountains exported strontium to swamps.

abstract: Magnetic susceptibility (MS) was measured through the Upper Devonian Cleveland Shale Member of the Ohio Shale at high resolution in three drill cores: OGS 2811 (Ross County: RC), OGS 2736 (Delaware County: DW), and OGS 6426 (Cuyahoga County: CH). Multitaper spectral analysis (MTM) and TimeOpt sedimentation rate optimization were applied to identify Milankovitch-band periodicities in depth-domain MS. Biostratigraphic control places the lowermost Cleveland Shale in the aculeatus Zone based on the occurrence of Bispathodus aculeatus antiposicornis in the uppermost Huron Shale along with other taxa representative of this zone in the basal Cleveland. Long-ranging species of Bispathodus, Branmehla, Palmatolepis, and Polygnathus were recovered through the entire Cleveland interval, none of which are diagnostic of higher zones. All three cores preserve sedimentation rates of approximately 1.07-1.25 cm/kyr and record orbital cycles consistent with precession (~16.85-22 kyr) and obliquity (~37-41 kyr). The obliquity cycle is expressed at every ~1.5 m, while the precession occurs at every ~0.68 m. The two longer cores (RC and DW) additionally resolve short-eccentricity cycles of ~95-126 kyr. Spectral comparison of the complete CH record against the uppermost 8 m of the RC and DW cores reveals identical Milankovitch cycles at the same depth-domain frequencies, which indicates that only the upper portion of the Cleveland Shale is preserved and that the base of the Cleveland Shale is diachronous.

title: An Investigation of Tropical Angiosperm Relative Genome Sizes from the Aptian-Cenomanian Une Formation of Colombia

authors: Smith, Bryton [1], Zhang, Xiaoqing [2], Shi, Gongle [3], Jaramillo, Carlos [4], Carvalho, Mónica [5], Herrera, Fabiany [6]
affiliations: (1) Committee on Evolutionary Biology, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA; Earth Sciences, Negaunee Integrative Research Center, Field Museum, Chicago, Illinois, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Negaunee Integrative Research Center, Field Museum, Chicago, Illinois, USA

(3) State Key Laboratory of Palaeobiology and Stratigraphy, Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology and Center for Excellence in Life and Palaeoenvironment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing, China
(4) Center for Tropical Paleoecology and Archaeology, Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, Ancón, Panamá, Panama

abstract: Ancestral character estimation suggests that early angiosperms had small genome sizes relative to gymnosperms and ferns. In extant angiosperms, genome size and guard cell size are generally positively and significantly correlated. Small genome sizes likely benefited angiosperms physiologically and ecologically relative to gymnosperms and ferns. The potential benefits include a greater capability to adjust anatomical and physiological traits such as guard cell size, stomatal density, leaf vein density, and stomatal conductance rate in accordance with environmental factors (e.g., light). While there are some guard cell size data from early angiosperms, we lack guard cell size data from early low-latitude angiosperms. Abundant gymnosperm and angiosperm cuticles from the low-latitude Aptian-Cenomanian Une Formation of Colombia provide a unique opportunity to use guard cell sizes to infer the relative genome sizes of early tropical angiosperms compared to co-occurring gymnosperms. We therefore collected guard cell size data across angiosperm and gymnosperm morphotypes to address the current knowledge gap on early tropical angiosperm relative genome sizes. Our results suggest variation in guard cell size among specimens and morphotypes, perhaps partially reflecting differences in genome size. Moving into the data analysis phase, we are contextualizing our results within the concept of the Angiosperm Terrestrial Revolution. We hope that our work will promote further research into early angiosperm relative genome sizes leveraging collections with fossil plants from additional regions around the world.

title: Comparative Analysis of Fluid Pathways in Shear Zone Using Structure-from-Motion Photogrammetry and Field Measurements
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Davis, Niya Kasmonique [1], Gottardi, Raphael [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(2) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
abstract: Fluids play a crucial role in weakening the rheology of shear zones and the lithosphere in general. However, our understanding of how fluids permeate shear zones and interact with deforming rocks remains limited, especially regarding meteoric fluid infiltration beyond the brittle-ductile transition. We propose that extensive fault and fracture networks in the brittle upper crust act as migration pathways for surface fluids to reach the middle crust. However, obtaining detailed structural data of faults and fracture populations remains challenging, stemming from exposure and accessibility issues. To address this, we use remote sensing techniques, including satellite imagery and drone-based surveys, along with fieldwork for structural analysis. Specifically, structure-from-motion photogrammetry will help create high-resolution 3D models of outcrops, enabling a broader structural assessment. Our virtual measurements are then compared with actual field data for comparison. To test our approach, we use two well-exposed shear zones, the Miocene Raft River detachment shear zone (Utah), and the Alexander City fault zone (AL). Our preliminary results suggest that the remote sensing approach using structure-from-motion provides a more comprehensive characterization of the complete fault and fracture population, which is otherwise limited by field accessibility.

title: U-Pb zircon geochronology and geochemistry of Proterozoic magmatic rocks from the Yavapai, Mazatzal and Picuris Orogenies of northern New Mexico
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Urda, Diana Jean [1], Sylvester, Paul J. [2], Souders, Kate [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA
(2) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX,
(3) US Geological Survey, Denver,
abstract:
Paleoproterozoic Yavapai and Mazatzal magmatism is widely interpreted to have formed by convergent plate margin processes along the southern cratonic margin of the North American craton during the accretion of juvenile crust between 1.8 and 1.6 billion years ago. However, it is unclear if the timing of the transition from the Yavapai to Mazatzal events was synchronous along the plate boundary or varied geographically. Also, geochemical differences between Yavapai and Mazatzal magmatic rocks, which may reflect different processes of crustal genesis, are not well-documented. The geochemistry of enigmatic Mesoproterozoic Picuris magmatic rocks hosted by Yavapai and Mazatzal units is also not well-known.

Twelve total samples of Yavapai, Mazatzal and Picuris magmatic units ranging from gabbro to granite, were sampled from the northern part of the Taos Range, the Picuris Mountains, and the Las Vegas region of northern New Mexico. Although variably metamorphosed up to amphibolite facies, these samples provide the opportunity to determine the timing of magmatism and its compositional characteristics. U-Pb zircon ages were determined by laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS). Whole rock compositions were determined by ICP-MS and – optical emission spectroscopy of acid-dissolved fusions of rock powders.

In the studied region, Yavapai-age samples are ~ 1.75-1.73 Ga. They display a broad compositional range, extending from diorite to granodiorite compositions. Most Yavapai samples are metaluminous, although minor peraluminous compositions are also present. Their modified alkali-lime indices are calcic. Sr/Y ratios are variable ranging from ~3 to 11. In contrast, Mazatzal-age samples are ~1.70-1.68 Ga. Their compositions are more restricted to granite and alkali-granite and are consistently peraluminous to strongly peraluminous. Their modified alkali-lime index is generally calc-alkalic. Sr/Y ratios are mostly lower (<3), perhaps reflecting shallower crustal sources. Picuris-age samples are ~1.47-1.40 Ga. They are compositionally variable, including both metaluminous gabbro and peraluminous granite compositions.

These results demonstrate that the older Yavapai magmatism was more diverse than Mazatzal magmatism, possibly due to more heterogenous mantle-crustal melt sources, more extensive crystal fractionation, and/or crustal assimilation during the Yavapai event. These new data will be compared to larger published geochronological and geochemical databases of Yavapai, Mazatzal and Picuris magmatic units to determine if results from northern New Mexico are consistent in other regions along this ancient convergent margin boundary.

title: Petrogenesis and Thermotectonic Evolution of the Granite Harbour Intrusives Suite (Central Transantarctic Mountains, Antarctica): Implications on the Ross Orogeny
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Yasar, I. Dogancan [1], Kamenov, George D. [2], Sayit, Kaan [3], Miller, Brent [4], Fosdick, Julie [5], Davis, Zachary [6], Zou, Haibo [7], Hames, Willis E. [8]

(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(3) Department of Geological Engineering, Middle East Technical University, Ankara, Turkey

abstract:
The Granite Harbour Intrusives (GHI) suite occurs as widespread voluminous granitoids emplaced during several stages of the Ross Orogeny. Here, we present bulk-rock geochemistry, bulk-rock Sr-Nd-Pb isotope geochemistry, and laser incremental heating 40 Ar- 39 Ar ages for samples from the GHI, providing insights into the tectono-magmatic and -thermal evolution of this syn-to-post-collisional magmatism at the paleo-Pacific margin of Gondwana during the early Paleozoic.

The bulk rock chemistry of GHI samples (n=50) indicates distinctive groups of granite and granodiorite-to-diorite with A-type and I- to S-type signatures, respectively. For both groups, trace element systematics display enrichments in LILEs-Th-LREEs over HFSEs and HREEs coupled with negative Nb and Ti anomalies, typical of continental arc-related magmas. However, where the dioritic variety has Ta depletion coupled with Nb, the granitic variety lacks that signature. The mixing of pelitic and mafic melts is evident for both varieties through major and trace elements and Sr-Nd-Pb isotopic compositions. Even though Sr-Nd coupling does not discriminate the two varieties, it does indicate crustal contamination. The Pb isotopic data from the GHI Suite indicates a higher amount of crustal material is involved in the source of the granitic magmas. The tectono-magmatic signatures of the GHI Suite indicate magmatism occurred in two modes: 1) as Andean-style dioritic continental arc magmatism along the paleo-Pacific margin of Gondwana followed by 2) granite generation through re-melting of crustal material (including the diorites) due to later stage extension of thickened crust caused by slab rollback of the subducting oceanic lithosphere.

Multi-crystal laser incremental heating analysis of hornblende from dioritic and granitic varieties of GHI plutons yielded 40 Ar- 39 Ar plateau ages (n=11) of ca. 499-485 Ma. These ages are interpreted to represent cooling through ca. 500 °C and are conformable with available zircon U-Pb ages. From both groups, single-crystal incremental heating analysis of biotite yielded ca. 495-460 Ma 40 Ar- 39 Ar plateau/integrated ages (n=18) recording cooling through ca. 280°C. These ages support the overlap and shift in the chemical signature and represent cooling through mid-Ordovician time. Ranges of estimated cooling rates implied by these hornblende and biotite data are interpreted to represent variation in emplacement depths of these plutonic bodies and/or variation in exhumation along the Central Transantarctic Mountains.

title: The Holocene as a Testing Ground for Developing Truly Actionable Extinction Lessons
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Mychajliw, Alexis M [1], Turvey, Samuel T [2]
affiliations: (1) Biology / Environmental Studies, Middlebury College, Middlebury, Vermont, USA; Samuel Oschin Global Center for Ice Age Research, La Brea Tar Pits & Museum, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Institute of Zoology, Zoological Society of London, London, United Kingdom
abstract:
Of all the mass extinction events to unfold on our planet, only today’s involves a conscious attempt to avert it. Studies of ancient mass extinctions have not only captured the imagination of our global society but have meaningfully allowed us to diagnose the magnitude of our ongoing biodiversity crisis and motivate recognition that action should be taken. But, the temporal and spatial scales of data used to describe mass extinctions are profoundly decoupled from the scale of data employed in context-specific conservation decision-making. Can these scales ever be bridged?

We propose that the Holocene represents the ideal testing ground for identifying which conservation problems can benefit from the insights offered by the fossil record. To illustrate this, we developed a new global dataset of Holocene mammal extinctions to explore the differing conservation information-content of past environmental archives, including revised last appearance dates for >300 postglacial mammal species losses. These data reveal that even in near time, extinction data quality varies extensively in geographic, temporal, and taxonomic, information content, hindering our ability to fully contextualize the present with both ancient mass extinctions and even geologically recent historical diversity. We identify key data incompatibilities and discontinuities that complicate direct transfer of conservation-relevant information between past and present. These differences are inherent to 1) extinction as an evolutionary process; 2) the types of data available to paleontologists and neontologists; and 3) the training and lived experiences of people working across biodiversity disciplines.

Yet, we also identify many opportunities in which Holocene datasets have been vital to conservation efforts on global and local scales. Drawing from experience with the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Species Survival Commission, we provide concrete examples of how fossil records have informed IUCN Red List and Green Status frameworks and highlight ways that paleontologists can play larger roles in such assessments. On the scale of regional wildlife management, we share how Holocene fossil records can be crucial components of reintroduction and rewilding discussions through collaborative work with agencies and non-governmental organizations. Moving forward, we encourage paleontologists to critically interrogate how the scales and biases of their fossil datasets may align with or diverge from existing policy frameworks and management programs, and to seek out transdisciplinary conservation communities of research and practice.

title: Long-Term Trends in Groundwater Levels, Recharge, and Precipitation in Western Kentucky
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Sesay, Alhaji M. [1], Fryar, Alan E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
abstract:
Reliable recharge estimates are needed to support groundwater management in western Kentucky, where groundwater supplies irrigation, public water systems, and ecological resources. This study evaluates long-term groundwater recharge at the USGS Viola monitoring well in Graves County, Kentucky. The 106-ft-deep well is completed in the unconfined Claiborne Group of the Mississippi Embayment aquifer system. It has the longest groundwater-level record in western Kentucky, spanning 1951–1984 and 1989–2026. The well is not significantly affected by nearby pumping, making it well suited for long-term recharge analysis.

Depth to water ranged from 4.89 to 19.17 ft below land surface from 1951–2023. Annual mean groundwater levels showed statistically significant rising trends during both study periods. Water levels rose by approximately 0.158 ft/year during 1953–1984 (Kendall's tau = -0.697, p = 0.002) and by 0.123 ft/year during 1989–2023 (tau = -0.743, p < 0.001). Across the full record (1951–2023), groundwater levels rose by approximately 0.145 ft/year (tau = -0.842, p < 0.001). Seasonal fluctuations were superimposed on these long-term increases.

Daily groundwater-level records from 1953–2023 were analyzed using the water-table fluctuation method. A 7-day moving average was applied to identify recharge events. Annual recharge was estimated using representative specific yield (Sy) values of 0.398 and 0.436. A total of 319 recharge events were identified, and 310 passed the quality-control criteria.

Mean annual recharge ranged from 24.5–26.8 inches during 1953–1984 and from 39.3–43.0 inches during 1989–2023, depending on the Sy value. Mann-Kendall trend analysis of the annual recharge estimates indicated increasing recharge during both periods. Neither trend was statistically significant (p = 1.000 for 1953–1984 and p = 0.0608 for 1989–2023). Sen's slope ranged from 0.136–0.150 inches/year during the earlier period and from 0.466–0.511 inches/year during the later period. These results indicate greater annual recharge during the later period and suggest a stronger rate of increase despite the lack of statistical significance.

Annual precipitation at the Paducah weather station also showed increasing trends during both study periods. The trend was statistically significant during 1953–1984 (tau = 0.266, p = 0.0336), but not during 1989–2023 (tau = 0.096, p = 0.426). These precipitation trends provide climatic context for interpreting the observed groundwater recharge patterns.

abstract: The Frasnian-Famennian boundary marks the end of the Kellwasser Crisis, one of the “Big 5” mass extinctions. The boundary is recognized at the top of the Pt. Gratiot Bed, the Upper Kellwasser Bed equivalent, in the Beaver Meadow Member of the Hanover Formation in western New York State. Three drill cores, two in the valley of Eighteenmile Creek and one in the Buffalo Creek Valley, through the Beaver Meadow Member, in an east to west transect where the Pt. Gratiot Bed and the Beaver Meadow Member thicken eastward, were sampled at 1 cm intervals and analyzed for magnetic susceptibility (MS). Fourier Transform Analysis resolved two distinct cycles at 0.4-0.6 cycles per meter and 2 cycles per meter that correspond to Milankovitch band obliquity and precession cycles. Millennial-scale cycles are superimposed on the longer cycles. In the overlying Dunkirk Formation, which marks the onset of the IIE transgressive cycle, the MS values are lower and cycles are muted, but detectable in the same frequencies.

authors: Gernon, Thomas M [1], Hincks, Thea Katherine [2], Rugen, Elias [3], Brune, Sascha [4], Braun, Jean [5], Marshak, Stephen [6]

abstract: The Grand Canyon encompasses two billion years of Earth history, but more than half of this record is absent across a regionally extensive erosional surface known as the Great Unconformity. This enigmatic surface has been linked to multi-phase regional tectonics accompanying supercontinent assembly and breakup and to Cryogenian glacial erosion. Although rift-related uplift during the breakup of Rodinia has long been implicated in erosion associated with the Great Unconformity, we argue that exhumation in the Grand Canyon region was focused along a continent-scale rift-flank escarpment. This "Great Escarpment of Laurentia", initiated ca. 800–750 Ma, occupied a position analogous to major escarpments generated during Mesozoic Gondwana breakup and experienced similar magnitudes of exhumation. Our landscape evolution models simulating rift-driven topography suggest that rocks within several hundred kilometers of this feature endured substantial erosion, reaching ca. 8 km near the escarpment and decreasing to ≤2 km at lateral distances of ca. 200 km from its peak. Such differential erosion, evidenced in prior thermochronology models, necessitates exhumation of mid-crustal basement lithologies including along reactivated crustal fault blocks. This model thereby helps explain the variable magnitude of erosion associated with the Great Unconformity in the southwestern United States.

title: Authigenic Carbonate Stable Isotope Evidence for a Climate and Environmental Response to the Mid-Pliocene Warming Period in the Albuquerque Basin

authors: Walsh, Adam Clark [1], Rugenstein, Jeremy Kesner Caves [2], Bernstein, Rachel [3], Koning, Daniel J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Colorado State University - Fort Collins, CO, Fort Collins, CO, USA

abstract: Multiple paleoclimate proxies indicate that southwestern North America was wetter during the Pliocene, when atmospheric CO 2 was higher than in preindustrial conditions. There is ongoing debate about whether these wetter conditions were due to more winter precipitation from a consistent El Niño-like climate or an enhanced summer North American Monsoon. The mid-Pliocene warm period (mPwp), between ~3.3 and 3.0 Ma, is often used as a comparison for possible future climate scenarios because it was the last time CO 2 levels were comparable to today's (above 400 ppm), and mean annual temperatures were 1.8 to 3.6 ℃ warmer. Authigenic carbonate stable isotopes are sensitive to changes in precipitation seasonality and plant productivity, and thus useful for interpreting paleoclimate and paleoenvironmental responses to changes in climate forcings. In this study, we use authigenic carbonate δ 18 O and δ 13 C values from middle Pliocene through lower Pleistocene strata of the Santa Fe Group in the Albuquerque Basin to interpret these responses in terms of rainfall seasonality and plant productivity. We selected stratigraphic sections whose ages are well constrained by paleomagnetic data and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar analyses of tephras to constrain changes in δ 18 O and δ 13 C from 3.45 to 1.5 million years ago. We interpret changes in δ 18 O as reflecting a shift between wintertime precipitation and the summertime monsoon. The lowest authigenic carbonate δ 18 O values appear near the start of the mPwp and increase to their highest values in the early Pleistocene. There is a notable δ 13 C minimum during the mPwp followed by an increase after 2.9 Ma and into the Pleistocene. Changes in δ 13 C are interpreted as shifts in plant primary productivity, with lower values suggesting greater vegetation growth. These findings suggest that during the mPwp, warmer global temperatures led to more wintertime precipitation and increased primary productivity in the Albuquerque Basin.

title: Characterizing Natural Gas Generation from the Illinois Basin Using Carbon and Hydrogen Stable Isotope Ratio
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Shiozaki, Chiyori [1], Willette, Donna Caraway [2]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA
(2) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA
abstract:
The Illinois Basin is a structural basin that covers Illinois, Indiana, and Kentucky. It was formed on a failed rift system from the Cambrian and deposited shallow marine sediments from Cambrian to Pennsylvanian. It has been producing oil and gas since the 19 th century, with more than 20,000 oil and gas wells in Illinois. Despite this rich hydrocarbon resource, natural gas in Illinois was viewed as a byproduct of oil and coal, not as a valuable resource and a potential reservoir driver to deliver more oil to the wellbore. This resulted in producers to ‘flare’ it or vent it to the atmosphere in the early days of hydrocarbon production. A consequence of natural gas being overlooked as a resource resulted in a dearth of research and compositional analyses within the basin.

In this study, we present a compositional, isotopic, and geospatial analysis of natural gas sampled in Illinois. The sample data were compiled from an older dataset published in 1981 and modern well data sampled predominantly in southern Illinois. Gas data from the 1981 dataset did not contain isotopic analyses, so the isotope analysis was only performed on the modern data. The data was then normalized to remove O 2 and N 2 due to air contamination. Data was then plotted using compositional and isotope metrics to determine gas source and composition. The compositional analysis yielded mostly methane-rich gas from shallow wells in northern Illinois, and heavier (longer chain alkanes), thermogenic gas from deeper wells in southern Illinois. The isotopic analyses revealed mostly mixed microbial and thermogenic gas from the dataset of modern wells. At least one well with characteristics of a coalbed methane source was documented from Pennsylvanian stratigraphy which contains abundant coal seams. The application of this data in research constraining basin evolution and hydrocarbon migration across the Illinois basin will assist resource development and storage opportunities in the future.

title: The Case for a National Cooperative Subsurface Assessment Program
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Kalbas, James L. [1], Wellman, Dawn [2], Rhodes, Greg [3], Regier, Margo [4], Shuster, Mark [5], Anderson, Scott [6], Myers, Mark [7]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Savannah River National Laboratory, Savannah, Georgia, USA
(3) Fervo Energy,
(4) National Petroleum Council, Washington D.C.,
(5) Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
Every pathway to a secure energy future in the United States — conventional oil and gas alongside geothermal, nuclear, wind, solar, hydrogen, and hydropower — ultimately depends on our quantitative understanding of the subsurface. However, our geologic framework remains insufficiently characterized relative to its strategic value. Growing pressure to secure domestic energy supplies, critical minerals, subsurface storage capacity, and water resources means the nation can no longer treat subsurface characterization as a secondary priority. Sustained, coordinated efforts among industry, academic, and state and federal partners are necessary to reduce exploration risk and unlock new opportunities.

A recent National Petroleum Council (NPC) study, commissioned by the Department of Energy with support from the Department of the Interior, looks across sectors and resource use cases – essential minerals, geothermal energy, geologic hydrogen, oil and gas, coal, and subsurface storage – to weigh the practical value of the nation's publicly available subsurface data and assessments. Defined broadly as the appraisal of a buried resource’s distribution and internal makeup, subsurface assessments can be understood as a layered ecosystem of public and private effort. Government generated data and regional evaluations provide foundational information and often set the stage for industry's basin- and prospect-specific work. Across public and private enterprises, robust, well-curated subsurface data must be combined with advanced technologies and analytical workflows by highly skilled experts in order to produce impactful evaluations.

The NPC report lays out a plan for a National Cooperative Subsurface Assessment Program that addresses cross-cutting opportunities to expand understanding of U.S. subsurface potential. Implementation will require focused efforts to: develop an integrated, holistic multi-resource assessment framework; develop comprehensive and robust baseline datasets through legacy data preservation and strategic data acquisition; broaden access to subsurface data held by various entities; expand standardized, interoperable datasets; align assessment methodology and emerging technologies; and expand U.S. subsurface geoscience workforce expertise in data science, modeling, and geospatial skills. Implementing the Program would translate directly into faster resource identification, lower development costs, and better-informed choices across government, industry, and the public.

abstract:
Recent analysis of the Rainstorm Member of the Johnnie Formation (approx. 585-579 Ma) (Witkosky and Wernicke, 2018) conducted near the Western Talc Mine southeast of Death Valley, CA, and in the Spring Mountains, NV, reveals distinct crossbedding trends within the oolite and underlying quartzite strata. When quartzite bedding is adjusted to paleohorizontal, the foresets trend in a southeastern strike–at an average of 140.6° azimuth ±24.3॰, and dip average of 13.7° ±7.18॰. When oolite bedding is adjusted to paleohorizontal, crossbeds within dip either to the west or east at an average of 9.6°. These beds strike at a respective average of 196° azimuth (south), or 357.4° azimuth (north), though more specific measurements and sampling of interbed structures within the oolite is necessary to perform more comprehensive statistical analysis and hypothesize details of deposition, which could be influenced by tsunamigenic wave action indicated by differences in the attitude of the quartzite and oolite.

This Ediacaran continental shelf region is an area of interest, as recent work has drawn a possible temporal correlation with its time of deposition and that of the Acraman impact in South Australia (Rodriguez et al. 2025). We aim to further analyze the Upper Johnnie Formation and establish an understanding of shoreline orientation and aquatic conditions to explore possible indicators of tsunamigenic wave action near the high Iridium concentration region measured along the oolite marker bed. Existing interpretations of the paleoshoreline direction this area range from east-west (e.g. Bergmann et al. 2011) to more north-south trends (e.g. Stewart, 1970). The variation between these interpretations is a key point of interest to future work because of their near 90° difference. Future work will collect additional measurements of correlating strata in an expanded region of localities, with an emphasis on measuring multidirectional oolite crossbedding and herringbone quartzite foresets in order to build a clearer model of the paleo-flow and shoreline orientation of the western margin of Laurentia at the time of the Acraman impact.

title: Investigating a Mysterious Encruster and the Reefal Subfacies it Occupies in Cores of the Pleistocene Owl’s Hole Formation, San Salvador Island, The Bahamas
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Griffing, David H [1], Lynip, Johanna H [2], Glumac, Bosiljka [3], Curran, H. Allen [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, Hartwick College, Oneonta, New York, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, Hartwick College, Oneonta, New York, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, Massachusetts, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, Massachusetts, USA
abstract:
Largely positioned above current sea level, Last Interglacial or Eemian (MIS 5e) coral reef deposits have been extensively documented around the world. By comparison, older Pleistocene reef deposits are poorly known beyond rock cores. Detailed examination of shallow marine coral-rich deposits within cores that penetrate the Owl’s Hole Formation on San Salvador Island, including portions dated as MIS 7, reveals a subfacies distinct from those observed in younger Eemian Grotto Beach Formation deposits. This subfacies is characterized by extensive coralline red algae crusts, commonly interlaminated with fenestral, silty microbialite and covered in fairly large masses of a diverse array of encrusting foraminifera. The most distinctive component among these encrusters bears a preserved skeletal structure not easily attributed to Pleistocene or modern reef-builders.

Although these older reef deposits lie below closely-spaced caliche crusts with rhizoliths and display moldic porosity, crusts of an “alveolar” skeletal structure have survived extensive meteoric modification. Recognized largely from thin-section, these relatively rare structures are up to 2 cm thick and composed of an irregular network of angular to subrounded, elongate to equant, fitted pores approximately 0.05 to 0.6 mm in diameter (most between 0.1-0.25 mm) separated by thin, dark (micritic) arcuate walls. Skeletal walls display crude laminations within some thin-sections. Although most of the pores are currently open, the walls are truncated by macroborings, suggesting either an original rigid structure or synsedimentary lithification. The texture crudely resembles that of calcified demosponges, suggesting one possible affinity for the unidentified organism. In this study, we examine this and other interpretations for the mystery encruster.

Given that sponges are a common component of most modern reef systems, it is peculiar that we have not yet found any evidence for their presence in the overlying Eemian Grotto Beach Formation reefal deposits. A focused petrographic search may result in their documentation in other parts of the succession. It is also possible that abundant microbial encrusters on MIS 5e corals suppressed sponge encrustation. Finally, the delicate sponge structures may not have been preserved in the uppermost portions of the Pleistocene carbonate successions due to diagenetic alterations during prolonged subaerial exposure.

title: Timing, Kinematics, and Deformation Conditions of the Towaliga Fault Zone in Eastern Alabama
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Posters)
authors: Clarke, Benjamin William [1], Gottardi, Raphael [2], Steltenpohl, Mark G. [3]

(2) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA

abstract: The Towaliga Fault Zone of the southern Appalachian Piedmont is a major structural feature interpreted to be similar to the subparallel Brevard Fault Zone located to its' south, a crustal-scale structure that records phases of prolonged ductile deformation followed by later brittle reactivation during Paleozoic Appalachian orogenesis. The Towaliga Fault Zone is commonly interpreted as either a branch of the broader Eastern Piedmont Fault System or a kinematically related structure with similar deformation history. At its core the Towaliga Fault Zone is characterized by mylonitic and ultramylonitic rocks associated with a damage zone of partially mylonitized schists, gneisses, and quartzites; together they form a heterogeneous shear zone up to ~6 km wide bounded to the Northwest by the Towaliga fault. Petrologic and microstructural analyses indicate that deformation along the Towaliga fault occurred under amphibolite- to greenschist-facies conditions and later transitioned from brittle–ductile to brittle regimes during exhumation of the fault surface. Timing of late-stage movement and post-deformational cooling sourced from sparse 40Ar-39Ar cooling ages indicates a relative age of 277 Ma or younger for late-stage faulting, placing it within the Alleghenian orogeny. However, these cooling dates do not resolve the timing of earlier ductile shearing, pre-Alleghenian metamorphism, or subsequent reactivation. Here we present preliminary results that combines field structural analysis, microstructural characterization, thermobarometry of minerals in equilibrium, and thermochronologic data to better constrain the timing of deformation, trace kinematic evolution, and isolate the pressure–temperature conditions of fault zone activity. Our results provide new insight into the role of the Towaliga fault zone in strain partitioning and tectonic evolution of the southern Appalachian Piedmont.

authors: Butler, Caleb [1], Eichler, Carla M. [2]
affiliations: (1) West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA

abstract:
The abundance of quartzite pebbles within the Texas Panhandle Ogallala gravels makes them a key asset for reconstructing the formation’s sedimentary provenance. I am currently researching the provenance of quartzites found within the Ogallala Formation of the Texas Panhandle.

Based on preliminary point-count analysis of thin sections collected from across the Panhandle, I hypothesize that the pebbles were transported from their source area in northern New Mexico, specifically the Sangre de Cristos, to the Ogallala via alluvial fan lobes shed from the southern Rockies, consistent with models proposing either a single dominant fan lobe or a three-lobe system, with downhill water flow driving pebble transport to their present resting place. This interpretation is supported by the presence of sillimanite and kyanite, along with an abundance of opaque heavy minerals identified through the Dickinson-Gazzi point counting method. In addition to mineralogy, I determined multiple textural populations, including but not limited to granoblastic texture, highly strained texture, and bimodal grain size.

Because of the fact that several distinct quartzite types occur within northern New Mexico, I will determine whether the pebbles derive specifically from the Ortega Quartzite, as well as to compare and contrast the samples in terms of their respective accessory minerals and overall structural fabric.

abstract: Following the 2024 Wapiti fire in central Idaho, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) published a post-fire debris flow (PFDF) hazard assessment that estimates the likelihood of debris flow initiation and potential volumes in burned watersheds given a specified precipitation intensity. The M1 likelihood (M1) and Emergency Assessment Volume (EAV) modeling frameworks were originally formulated with data from southern California and may provide less accurate estimates when applied outside of the region where the model was developed. For example, a study in a tirbuary drainage of the South Fork Payette found that the M1 model predicted numerous false positives and the EAV overestimated debris flow volume by 17%, following the 2016 Pioneer fire. These models can be improved through the inclusion of PFDF characteristics from different regions. This study will focus on PFDF’s in the headwaters of the South Fork Payette drainage, which is underlain by highly erodible Idaho batholith granite where PFDF volumes between ~5700–13400 m 3 have been reported by previous studies. Our goals are to: 1) Compare debris volumes measured with high-resolution repeat LiDAR point clouds (LPC) and ground-based survey methods to volumes predicted by the EAV and the recently published WEST model. 2) Analyze the spatial variability of precipitation during debris flow producing storms using forecasted precipitation from synoptic weather models. 3) Create an inventory of post-fire debris flow events throughout central Idaho including PFDF volumes that have been previously published in the literature but have yet to be included in national inventories. We present preliminary results of this inventory and describe some of the 30 debris flow events that have been cataloged so far.

title: Sub-communities in fossil food webs suggest core processes of community assembly in modern marine ecosystems already present in the Middle Triassic
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Banker, Roxanne M.W. [1], Ess, Madeline P [2], Dineen, Ashley A. [3], Roopnarine, Peter D. [4], Tyler, Carrie L [5]
affiliations: (1) Biology Department, Providence College, Providence, RI,
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Geoscience, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, USA
(3) University of California Museum of Paleontology, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
(4) Department of Invertebrate Zoology and Geology, California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA,
(5) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV, USA
abstract: Species interactions in a community form a network of interconnected food chains, or a food web, and patterns of interactions ultimately make a community more or less stable in the face of disturbance. One understudied food web characteristic is modularity, the tendency for food webs to self-organize into more densely linked sub-communities. In other words, taxa within a given module in a food web are more likely to interact with one another than with members from a separate module. Modularity is hypothesized to be important because modules may prevent the propagation of extinctions, thereby enhancing system resilience and stability in the face of large scale perturbations (e.g., global change). To empirically assess modules, we reconstructed food web networks from five Mesozoic Stages that spanned a broad gradient of environmental and ecological change, the Triassic (Anisian, Carnian), Jurassic (Bathonian), and Cretaceous (Aptian, Maastrichtian) using fossil occurrence data. We examined food webs as old as the 247 Ma (Anisian) and all communities had either 3 or 4 modules. Body size distributions and functional diversity composition within modules were similar between Mesozoic communities and modules studied from modern marine food webs. The organization of ecological functions into modules appeared consistent among communities through time, supporting the role of biotic interactions dictating higher level community structure. Interestingly, the module that contained a higher proportion of lower trophic level (e.g., filter feeding) groups showed less ecological turnover between successive Mesozoic stages than did the module that was dominated by predators; this aligns well with the observed ecological escalation of organisms during the Mesozoic, particularly among predatory taxa. Taken together, these patterns indicate that while different communities had different numbers of modules, modules and the core processes of community assembly that operate in modern ecosystems were features of food webs as soon as the Triassic. Modules may have been present earlier in Paleozoic communities, but have not yet been described. Overall, these results further underscores the utility of the fossil record in understanding community evolution and the role of modularity in community structure and persistence. A better understanding of how modules mediate the flow of energy and recycling of materials in food webs can help us to better understand ecosystem stability and persistence in past and present ecosystems.

title: Adapting Image-Based Grain-Size Analysis Techniques to Characterize Poorly Sorted Regolith on Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars (Posters)
authors: Sikes, Daniel [1], Siebach, Kirsten Leigh [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Rice Univ, Dept of Earth Science, Houston, TX, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, TX, USA
abstract:
Martian regolith serves as a scientific archive while simultaneously dictating rover mobility and in-situ resource potential. A key characteristic of regolith is grain size distribution (GSD), typically gleaned from high-resolution imagery captured by proximity rover cameras like Curiosity’s Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). When targets are well sorted, GSDs can be characterized manually at one scale by either measuring every grain in an image or overlaying a grid onto the image and measuring the grain at each grid intersection as a representative subpopulation.

On poorly sorted regolith surfaces, grain sizes can span over three orders of magnitude, complicating GSD measurements. Image standoff distances that capture centimeter-scale rocks yield images with insufficient resolution to regularly measure micron-scale grains. Additionally, grid counting is hindered by spatial constraints: resolving relative grain proportions accurately requires 200-400 points spaced wider than the largest visible grain in the image. For heterogeneous regolith, this requires a grid layout larger than available image dimensions.

MAHLI's imaging of surfaces at multiple standoff distances enabled us to develop a method for characterizing heterogeneous regolith using two scales. We calculate the areal coverage of each grain size (rather than count-based or volumetric GSDs). First, using a 25 cm-standoff MAHLI image, we manually measure all resolvable grains down to a lower limit of five pixels (~500μm), drawing polygons around each grain. Next, using a representative 2 cm-standoff image within the 25 cm-standoff image, we use a grid count method to measure the fine grains, drawing polygons around individual grains at grid intersections. Given the higher resolution of that image, our 5-pixel limit allows us to measure grains down to ~100 μm. When completing the grid count, we exclude all polygonal areas already outlined in the 25 cm-standoff image. This generates two GSDs that may have overlapping size ranges (e.g., depending on dust, shadows, grain agglomerates, and/or cementation). We transition from count-based GSDs to areal GSDs by normalizing individual grain areas to the total grain area measured on the same scale image. We generate a single surface-wide GSD by merging the two distributions—weighting each population by its areal coverage calculated from the 25 cm-standoff image—then binning and plotting by long-axis length.

This technique enables 2D image-based grain size analysis of heterogeneous regolith targets where standard approaches fail.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Distance-Dependent Overbank Deposition on Avulsion Loci, Pathfinding and Fan Morphology in RiverWalk, a Cellular Model of River Avulsion
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Masetu, Jackline [1], Chamberlin, Ellen P [2], Martin, Harrison K [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Environmental Geosciences, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Geology & Environmental Geosciences, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, USA
abstract:
River avulsions are the abrupt relocation of a channel onto a new course on its floodplain and are the primary mechanism by which sediment and water are redistributed across aggrading alluvial landscapes; however, the extent to which floodplain deposition rates and styles impact avulsion locations and pathfinding is unclear. In this study, we build on RiverWalk, an existing cellular model of river avulsion and megafan growth, to test how distance-dependent floodplain rules impact avulsion processes and fan shape. In the original model, Martin and Edmonds (2022) incorporate floodplain dynamics in the form of abandoned channel attraction and repulsion rules, and they show that when abandoned channels repulse avulsing flow, avulsion locations shift farther downstream from the mountain front, but when abandoned channels attract flow, avulsion locations occur closer to the apex. Outside of abandoned channels, RiverWalk overbank deposition is uniform across the floodplain and varies only with distance from the mountain front; therefore, floodplain aggradation is decoupled from active channel location.

However, field and theoretical studies have shown that overbank deposition rates often decline with lateral distance from a channel as flow depth and transport capacity decrease. To address this, we add a new overbank deposition method in RiverWalk that incorporates a lateral distance-decay function based on the exponential formulation in Mackey and Bridge (1995), in which each floodplain cell’s deposition rate depends on its distance from the nearest channel margin. We test exponential decay (lambda) values ranging from 0.12 to 0.45 and distance rules ranging from 2-10 times the channel width to test model sensitivity to floodplain rules.

Preliminary results show that in the distance-decay method, avulsions increase in the distal fan, and the avulsed channel shows a clear tendency to return to previously occupied paths compared to the uniform floodplain aggradation models. This change in loci leads to a narrowing of the fan shape. Overall, our preliminary results show that incorporating more complex floodplain-filling rules influences avulsion behavior and fan shape in RiverWalk, suggesting that overbank deposition outside of abandoned channels is also important for avulsion dynamics and fluvial fan architecture.

title: Dating Smarter, Not Harder: Optimizing Sample Density for Age Model Accuracy and Precision
session_title: ‘GTS2030’ – Toward an Open Science Geologic Time Scale
authors: Cothren, Hannah R. [1], Cantine, Marjorie [2], Goldberg, Samuel [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(2) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA,

(3) Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Sciences, Department of Marine Geosciences, University of Miami, Miami, FL, ; Frost Institute for Data Science and Computing, University of Miami, Miami, FL, USA
abstract:
Accurate, precise age models built on high-precision geochronological data are crucial for placing stratigraphic records of environmental and evolutionary change into temporal frameworks. They allow rigorous interpolation of proxy data ages between dated horizons. Age model accuracy and precision depend not only on the precision and accuracy of individual ages, but also the density and stratigraphic distribution of dated horizons. Although age models generally improve with additional dated horizons, geochronological data acquisition is often constrained by analytical cost and sample suitability. In settings where datable material is abundant, chronostratigraphers must decide the number and stratigraphic position of dated horizons, yet how these choices affect age model accuracy and precision remains poorly quantified. We present a model that explores the relationship between sample stratigraphic position, dating precision, dating density, and resulting age model accuracy and precision.

We generate synthetic stratigraphy spanning 0.5-20 million years using a random walk model of deposition and erosion. We simulate radiometric dating of these records using the characteristic analytical precision of different widely used Phanerozoic geochronometers (U/Pb zircon 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, and Re/Os). Age-depth models are generated from these simulated dates using modifiedBchron, an open-source Bayesian age-modeling package in R that imposes priors of variable sedimentation rates and stratigraphic superposition. We also simulate common complications in U/Pb zircon age interpretation, inheritance and Pb-loss, to assess how unmitigated inclusion of such data affects model performance. Using these simulated records, we evaluate how dating density, distribution, and age uncertainty affect age model accuracy and precision. Accuracy is calculated as the offset between the modeled and true ages; precision is calculated from the modeled age uncertainty (95% HDI) of interpolated horizons.

Age model performance improves with additional dated horizons. Above a dating density of approximately 2-4 dates/Ma, age model accuracy and precision are limited by age uncertainty and shifts in sedimentation rate not resolved by dated horizons. For CA-ID-TIMS U/Pb zircon ages, which comprise >75% of radiometric ages in GTS2020, low dating densities (<1 date/Ma) produce age models offset from true ages by ≥0.3 Ma. All Phanerozoic periods and epochs in GTS2020 are constrained by less than one date per million years. These results offer a quantitative framework for optimizing chronologic investment and future sampling design.

title: Atmospheric pO2 modulates the intensity of tropical extinction during cooling events
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Finnegan, Seth [1], Monarrez, Pedro M. [2], Stockey, Richard G. [3], Pohl, Alexandre [4], Yohler, Ryan Michael [5], Arif, Evren [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Integrative Biology, University of California, Berkeley, CA, ; Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, Panama, Panama
(2) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(3) School of Ocean and Earth Science, University of Southampton, SOUTHAMPTON,
(4) Biogéosciences, CNRS, Dijon, France
(5) Integrative Biology, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
(6) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, CA, USA
abstract:
The theory of oxygen- and capacity-limited thermal performance holds that the thermal limits of aquatic ectotherms are determined by the interaction between temperature-dependent oxygen supply and demand processes. The oxygen supply/demand ratio is captured by the Metabolic Index, which predicts the biogeographic and bathymetric distributions of many modern marine species and has provided insight into the magnitude and selectivity of extinction during past hyperthermal events.

We apply the Metabolic Index framework to consider the expected magnitude and selectivity of extinction during global cooling events. Whereas warming events have a relatively straightforward effect by elevating metabolic oxygen demand while simultaneously decreasing environmental oxygen supply, the effects of cooling involve more complex tradeoffs: oxygen solubility increases and metabolic rates decrease, but cardiac output, ventilatory pumping rates, and molecular diffusion rates decline. Recent work has shown that many marine ectotherms exhibit distinct thermal optima in supply/demand, bounded not only by upper thermal limits at which metabolic oxygen demand exceeds supply capacity but also by lower limits where cold-induced declines in ventilation and circulation outpace reductions in metabolic demand, causing cold hypoxemia. This raises the possibility that the atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen (pO 2 ) may play an important role in modulating the impact of cooling on marine taxa and ecosystems.

Using simulated species with a wide range of ecophysiological traits and cGENIE Earth system models, we compare biogeographic responses to comparable cooling events under relatively high (100% PAL) and low (40% PAL) pO 2 . We consider only species with trait combinations permitting them to inhabit at least some portion of continental shelf and upper slope habitats during warm (pre-cooling) states at both low- and high-pO 2 conditions. Low pO 2 restricts the overall availability of aerobically viable habitat, but cooling relaxes oxygen limitation and permits range expansions of some high- and mid-latitude species. However, cold hypoxemia sharply reduces or outright eliminates viable habitat for many relatively active tropical and subtropical species. In contrast, the same species persist and even maintain wide geographic ranges during cooling when buffered by high pO 2 conditions. Numerous other factors are also involved, but the elevated vulnerability of tropical species to cooling under low pO 2 may contribute to the exceptional severity of apparent extinction during the Late Ordovician Hirnantian glaciation compared to subsequent cooling episodes.

abstract:
The Fiordland block in SW New Zealand exposes a nearly complete section of Cretaceous continental arc crust from paleodepths of ~5 to at least 50 km and locally ~65 km. The present architecture of the section was assembled mainly at 8-7 Ma when reverse faults inboard of the Alpine Fault uplifted and imbricated slices of lower, middle, and upper crust. These exposures allow direct examination of how arc magmatism built a thick, compositionally stratified column of continental crust above a subduction zone along the Mesozoic Gondwana margin. We combine structural analyses, new mapping of lower crustal plutons, published zircon Hf and O isotopes, and >100 published U-Pb zircon and titanite dates to reconstruct the patterns of pluton emplacement during two periods of high magma addition rates, including a terminal flare-up lasting ~14 m.y.

The results show that three inherited, lithospheric-scale discontinuities, spaced ~25-30 km apart, localized magma influx during emplacement of the Darran Suite at 147-136 Ma and the Separation Point Suite/Western Fiordland Orthogneiss at 128-114 Ma. The inherited structures coincide with distinct zircon Hf- and O-isotope domains, supporting their long-lived control on magma pathways. The younger of the two magmatic events peaked at 118-115 Ma when ~70% of the exposed lower crust was emplaced within ~3 m.y. Our mapping reveals five subvertical feeder zones, each up to ~5 km wide, that localized magma input along two of the discontinuities, forming overlapping mushroom-shaped plutons in the lower crust. Although magmatism migrated regionally from outboard to inboard between the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, successive pulses repeatedly reused and alternated between the same structural conduits. Plutons were emplaced at multiple crustal levels, precluding a simple bottom-up model of arc construction.

Repeated mafic recharge at the base of the crust, recorded by hornblendite and wehrlite sheets emplaced into lower crustal mushes, utilized the same inherited structures and mobilized felsic interstitial melts. These melts were extracted through compaction, channelized flow, and diking, and transferred upward along the inherited discontinuities into the middle and upper crust. These results indicate that inherited structures controlled where mantle-derived magma entered the crust, where lower crustal storage and processing reservoirs developed, and how evolved melts escaped to build a compositionally stratified column of arc crust.

title: Recrystallization in Syndepositional Dolomites: A Case Study in the Llandoverian Byron Formation, Michigan Basin, USA
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Ledbetter Ferrill, Nathaniel [1], Al-Musawi, Mohammed [2], Scott, Ashley Brooke [3], Norouzi, Saeed [4], Kaczmarek, Stephen E. [5]
affiliations: (1) Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(2) Chevron, Houston, TX, USA
(3) Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI,
(4) Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(5) Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI,
abstract:
Ancient carbonate platforms are complex archives of chemical and paleoenvironmental changes during sedimentation and post-depositional diagenesis. Accurately interpreting this archive in dolomitized rocks is further complicated by various proxy signals that are often confusing.

The current study utilizes an integrated multi-proxy approach to characterize four cores positioned along a dip-profile of a dolomitized Llandoverian-age carbonate ramp in the Michigan Basin with the goal of evaluating the timing, mechanisms, fluids, and conditions of platform-scale dolomitization. Previous research on the Llandovery succession in the Michigan Basin suggests that dolomitization occurred in evaporitic conditions and dolomite abundance decreases down-dip, grading toward zero in the basin center, consistent with the evaporative reflux model.

While sedimentological observations, such as abundant mud cracks, rip-up clasts, hardgrounds, algal laminations, limited fauna, and the presence of evaporites, suggest deposition of the Bryon Formation occurred in a restricted subtidal to supratidal setting, dolomite inclusions in anhydrite nodules indicate dolomitization occurred prior to the formation of depositional evaporites. Bulk-rock d 18 O and d 13 C values are in line with carbonates expected to have formed from near-normal Silurian seawater, but calculated D 47 clumped isotope temperatures range from 57-76℃, suggesting that at least some of the dolomites may have recrystallized during burial. XRD mineralogy data show that dolomites are poorly to moderately ordered and Ca-rich suggesting that recrystallization may have been relatively minor.

Together, these observations are consistent with a model of syndepositional dolomitization in near-shore restricted peritidal settings and subsequent recrystallization during shallow burial that presumably reset the isotopic and geochemical signatures resulting in elevated D 47 crystallization temperatures relative to expected surface temperatures, and isotopic values consistent with near-normal marine signatures. This study provides a valuable analog for platform-scale dolomitization and suggests that integration of multiple proxies provides the most reliable approach for obtaining the complex diagenetic history of dolomitized carbonates.

title: Reconciling Radiocarbon and Cosmogenic Chronologies of the Laurentide Ice Sheet Retreat Across Long Island, New York
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations (Posters)
authors: Elbaroudy, Laila [1], Ali, Guleed [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY,
abstract: Ice sheets regulate sea level and ocean circulation, and their sensitivity to climate forcing makes them critical components of the climate system. Understanding their response to external forcing requires robust records of past ice sheet behavior, particularly during intervals of rapid climate change. The Laurentide Ice Sheet, which extended across much of North America during the Last Glacial Maximum, reached its southeastern limit at the Ronkonkoma Moraine on Long Island, New York. This moraine provides a valuable record for constraining the timing of deglaciation. However, significant discrepancies persist between plant macrofossil radiocarbon ( 14 C) ages and cosmogenic exposure ( 10 Be) ages, with radiocarbon ages often appearing substantially younger. These offsets may reflect delayed plant colonization, incomplete sediment recovery, or nuclide inheritance and post-depositional processes, leaving the timing of ice retreat poorly constrained. To refine this chronology, we applied accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dating to plant macrofossils from a kettle basin exposed along the wave-cut cliffs of eastern Long Island. A wood sample yields an age of 14.2–14.9 ka calBP, providing a minimum constraint on ice retreat. Additional radiocarbon dating of plant macrofossils from lower levels in the same exposure is currently underway and will extend the chronology toward the base of the basin fill. These ages will test whether the offset from 10 Be chronologies reflects delayed colonization or a difference in the events being dated. By resolving these inconsistencies between radiocarbon and cosmogenic chronologies, this work builds toward a more robust timeline for deglaciation across Long Island and a clearer picture of ice sheet response to climate forcing.

title: Thermal and Chemical Fluid Evolution of the REE-rich Hicks Dome Carbonatite Breccia
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Posters)
authors: Jones, Victoria L. [1], Lamadrid, Hector M. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geoscience, University of Oklahoma, Sarkeys Energy Center, 100 E.Boyd St., Norman, OK, USA
(2) School of Geoscience, University of Oklahoma, Sarkeys Energy Center, 100 E.Boyd St., Norman, OK, USA
abstract: The transition to low-carbon energy technologies has increased demand for critical metals, particularly rare earth elements (REEs). They are essential for producing renewable and electronic technologies. The Hicks Dome deposit, located in southern Illinois between the Waukoukigous Igneous Province (WIP) and the Illinois-Kentucky Fluorspar District, is emplaced within a Paleozoic carbonate sequence. The Hicks Dome breccia is closely associated with Permian ultramafic intrusions and lamprophyre dikes. Hicks Dome mineralization is hosted within different hydrothermal breccias that evolve from sedimentary breccia clasts to a true carbonatite breccia deeper in the system. The breccia cements are primarily formed by calcite, dolomite, fluorite, quartz, barite, and REE minerals (phosphates and carbonates). Although the IKDF is globally important for fluorite production, the genetic relationships among carbonatite magmatism, brecciation, and MVT mineralization remain unanswered. This study examines fluid and melt inclusions in drill core samples from Hicks Dome and nearby MVT deposits to better characterize the mineralizing environment. Preliminary results reveal a diverse range of inclusion types, including aqueous liquid- and vapor-rich inclusions, halite-bearing inclusions, CO 2 -dominant inclusions, and polycrystalline inclusions thought to be melt inclusions. Raman spectroscopic analysis, combined with microthermometric measurements, indicates multiple volatile species like CO 2 , CH 4 , and other hydrocarbons, as well as SO 4 2- and CO 3 2- dissolved in the liquid phase. Microthermetric measurements of the fluid inclusions show a vertical thermal evolution from shallow cores with temperature ranges between 133-154°C to higher temperatures deeper in cores with temperature ranges between 210-300°C, some reaching 418°C. Interestingly, a subset of the aqueous fluid inclusions shows extreme metastability and never froze even at temperatures of -180 ºC. These results provide insight into the chemical and thermal evolution of the fluids responsible for the REE mineralization. Overall, our data aims to create a detailed petrological and geochemical framework linking carbonatite emplacement, breccia formation, and the relationship with the regional fluorite mineralization. Future work will focus on evaluating fluorine mobility, fluid sources, and the broader impact of the WIP on mineralization throughout the district, ultimately aiding in the development of improved exploration models for carbonate-hosted REE systems.

title: Predicting Future Vulnerability to Storm Ebb Surge Damage in Southwest Florida from Tropical Cyclones
session_title: Contemporary research in geomorphological hazards
authors: Savarese, Michael [1], Bhatt, Dhruvkumar [2], Hummel, Whitney [3], Daly, Chris [4], Ciarletta, Daniel J. [5], Palermo, Rose V. [6]
affiliations: (1) The Water School, Department of Marine & Earth Sciences, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(2) The Water School, Department of Marine & Earth Sciences, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(3) The Water School, Department of Ecology & Environmental Studies, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(4) The Water School, Department of Marine & Earth Sciences, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(5) USGS Saint Petersburg Coastal & Marine Sci Ctr, St. Petersburg, FL, USA

abstract:
Ebb surge-driven erosion and outwash, caused by seaward return of tidal water after storm winds wane, were unanticipated consequences of tropical cyclones in southwest Florida prior to Hurricane Ian (2022), leaving regional managers without historical precedent for adaptation planning to combat these effects. Hurricane Ian and two subsequent storms in 2024, Helene and Milton, all generated high-enough surge to cause ebb-surge erosion. Here, we show that the short return period of these events allowed for patterns to be discerned that have predictive value. To investigate the geographic predictability of outwash channelization, the distribution of channels across Sanibel Island, a highly developed barrier island, were mapped using a UAV-flown LiDAR sensor. Geospatial data were subjected to 3 analyses: (1) Predicted flow pathways were calculated for the pre-Ian digital elevation model (DEM) using ArcGIS’s hydrology toolset. The locations of inferred pathways were then compared against the erosional channels produced by Ian. (2) We compared the location of Ian and Helene/Milton channels, investigating whether Ian channels were reactivated after beach nourishment infilling or if the 2024 storms created channels in new locations. (3) The number and location of unvegetated dune crossover paths, a management practice regulated by municipal government, were compared against the ebb-surge channels caused by Ian. Based on post-storm observations, we hypothesized that unvegetated paths are more susceptible to erosion, and therefore, predisposed to ebb-surge channel erosion.

Results show that approximately 60% of the Ian-eroded channels were predicted by the locations of flow pathways on the pre-Ian topography. The remaining 40% were channels that would not have been anticipated. Of the 23 ebb-surge channels eroded by Helene/Milton, 19 were co-located with channels created by Ian (+/-5 m). Additionally, these 19 locations coincided with the predicted ebb-surge pathways in the first analysis. A total of 220 “extensive channels” (those extending across more than one strandplain ridge) were eroded by Ian; 203 (93%) of these were co-located on dune unvegetated walkover paths. The remaining 17 extensive channels formed along the soft edges against concrete foundations.

These analyses demonstrate that the location of ebb-surge erosion can be anticipated. A coastal community, equipped with a contemporary pre-event DEM and appropriate geospatial tools, can determine which locations behind or along the foreridge are vulnerable to outwash erosion.

title: Echinoderm species richness is largely unsampled, an example from the Mississippian (Visean) Pella Formation, central Iowa
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Sumrall, Colin D. [1], Amini, Laya [2], Hueser, Sydney [3], Reich, Mike [4], Thuy, Ben [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN,
(3) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN,
(4) State Natural History Museum, Brunswick, Brunswick, Germany

abstract: The Middle Mississippian (Visean) Pella Formation of Central Iowa has long been known for a rich, open-marine fauna including a variety of brachiopods, mollusks, bryozoans, corals arthropods and echinoderms. The described echinoderm fauna contains seven genera of crinoids, two genera of blastoids, one genus each of edrioasteroids, and echinoids. Furthermore, there is a report of unidentified asteroid material. However, like many Carboniferous faunas, the more fragile echinoderm taxa such as ophiuroids, holothuroids, and ophiocistioids have not been discovered as articulated skeletons and overlooked because of an inherent bias against investigating small, disarticulated material. Here we discuss an example where isolated skeletal elements add significantly to the echinoderm fauna. Samples were collected from in-place, weathered marl at the Russel Wildlife Area, an abandoned limestone quarry in Mahaska Co. Iowa. Samples were washed using standard micropaleontology methods, sieved, and picked for echinoderm microfossils. Ophiuroidea is by far the most abundant and speciose group with ~92 LAPs/g in the 0.5-0.25 mm fraction. Archaic taxa include three stenuroids ( Umerophiura, Antiquaster ?, and Eriniceaster ), three protasterids ( Strataster , Schoenaster , and an undescribed genus), four Furcasterids (three species of Furcaster and one species of Cholaster ), one cheiropterasterid ( Vandelooaster ) and two metophurids ( Suchaster and Sulphaster ). Holothuroids are represented by calcareous ring elements and associated wheel and hook ossicles of the body wall. Calcareous ring elements of three species of apodid holothuroids are common in the residues and rare wheel elements of an elasipodid have been recovered but calcareous ring elements have yet to be sampled. Furthermore, small, isolated goniodonts (or teeth) of the ophiocistioid Linguaserra are presented in the fauna being one of only a handful examples of the class from North America. While ophiuroid, holothuroid, and ophiocistioid ossicles are not rare in the Pella Fm., these elements are all less than a mm across making their recovery through micropaleontological techniques necessary. Regardless, the inclusion of these microfossils more than doubles echinoderm species richness in the Pella Fm. Similar patterns are seen in many Late Paleozoic fossil localities.
