title: But What Does "Accessibility" Actually Mean? Technical vs Meaningful Accessibility in the Geoscience Classroom
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Carlson, Ash [1], McDaris, John R. [2]
affiliations: (1) Science Education Resource Center, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
(2) Science Education Resource Center, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
abstract:
The US federal government has updated Title II of the American Disabilities Act (ADA), setting the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, Level AA as the new standard for web and mobile app accessibility for public entities. These guidelines were designed to set baselines for technical accessibility (e.g., alt text on images, screen reader friendly organization) and don’t provide instructions for application to education materials. There are also areas where the Title II standard is vague (e.g., what level of usage qualifies a resource as “archived"), and there is limited material support for implementation. These factors result in institutions of higher education taking various approaches to digital materials under their purview (including educational documents) and consequently providing varying guidance on how to go about meeting the new requirements, ranging from “you may not...” to “figure it out.” Many educators are left feeling like they don’t know where to begin.

To address the technical need of meeting the WCAG 2.1 Level AA, the Science Education Resource Center (SERC) at Carleton College has developed materials to strengthen understanding of the rationale for improving accessibility and how-to guides for updating common document formats (e.g., word, ppt, pdf). (https://serc.carleton.edu/249733) As stewards of one of the largest collections of open educational resources (OER) in the geosciences, SERC is committed to making the materials on its websites accessible to the widest possible audience. Given that the materials in the collection are created and submitted by individual faculty members, providing professional development on creating accessible materials is essential to meet that commitment.

Beyond technical compliance, there are larger questions that the geoscience community needs to engage with. Geoscience is a discipline with many fundamental skills existing at the intersection of multiple senses and physical abilities. Disciplinary norms and structures still primarily accommodate individuals without disabilities. Current and prospective geoscientists who identify as disabled do not have equal access. This moment is a new opportunity for the geoscience community to disrupt the cycle of inaccessibility and foster more meaningful inclusion.

We invite conversation around the larger, nontrivial goal of moving beyond technical accessibility of individual documents (“do my images have alt text?”) to meaningful accessibility (“do my activity design and educational materials facilitate positive learning outcomes for learners regardless of disability?”).

abstract:
Subduction zone great earthquakes (≥ M8) and their potential tsunamis are significant hazards for coastal regions, as evident by several catastrophic earthquakes over the past few decades, including 2004 Sumatra (M9.3), 2011 Japan (M9), and 2025 Kamchatka (M8.8) events. Unlike other subduction zones, the Cascadia Subduction Zone (CSZ) lacks instrumental records of any great earthquake and tsunami, which forces hazard assessments to be reliant upon paleoseismic records. Dendrochronology and coastal stratigraphy along the CSZ reveal evidence of the most recent great earthquake and tsunami to have occurred in 1700 CE. Even though detailed tsunami inundation maps play an important role informing hazard assessments, a lack of high-resolution paleotsunami inundation mapping exists along much of coastal Cascadia. Additionally, the limited number of sites with mapped paleotsunami deposits only represent the potential minimum reach of inundation, as recent tsunamis have shown that the tsunami sand deposition extent is only a fraction of the total inundation distance. To improve CSZ tsunami hazard maps and hazard assessments, additional high-resolution mapping of the tsunami sand and tsunami silt, is necessary.

Along Johns River, a tributary into Grays Harbor, WA, stratigraphy of 93 sediment cores were described up to ~5.5km upriver during summer 2026 fieldwork. Forty-seven fossil core samples were taken for additional lab analysis. Initial results show 1700 CE deposits thinning and fining inland, with sandier deposits extending up to ~3km upriver. In 9 cores, there is evidence of 2-3 thin (<3mm-thick) tsunami sand to silt sequences potentially representing wave pulses. High-resolution stratigraphic mapping, radiodensity imagery of fossil sediment cores, and grain size analysis indicate that the 1700 CE tsunami likely inundated at least ~1km farther inland than previous estimates suggested, based on how far the traceable tsunami sand deposit extends.

However, the 1700 CE coseismic subsidence contact is observable up to ~5.5km upriver. In addition, stratigraphic observations suggest main channel location changes, perhaps associated with 1700 CE coseismic subsidence. Data presented here can further constrain hypothetical earthquake and tsunami model scenarios and better inform hazard characterization.

title: Implications of off-axis hydrothermal alteration on Seawater Lithium Mass Budget: Insights from Marine Porewaters
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Shaikh, Juzer I [1]
affiliations: (1) Princeton University, Department of Geosciences, Princeton, NJ, USA
abstract: Silicate weathering consumes CO 2 and controls cation fluxes to the ocean, thus playing a critical role in modulating long-term seawater chemistry and climate. There are very few markers of seawater chemistry whose value has changed over time as a function of the uplift – weathering – subduction cycle. Lithium, being one such proxy, has been extensively utilised as a geochemical tracer whose long-term evolution of isotopic composition in seawater is a function of Urey’s tectonic cycle. Marine pore waters are an excellent archive utilized here to study the sedimentary processes affecting seawater chemistry. Utilizing a method developed in-house to separate Li from matrix and measure Li isotopes, I analysed porewater samples from IODP Leg 339 and Leg 379. At the porewater-sediment interface of continental margins, authigenic aluminosilicate clay (smectite) formation, also termed reverse weathering, removes Li from seawater/porewater. The process of reverse weathering preferentially uptakes 6 Li over 7 Li. Thus, porewaters are expected to be depleted in [Li] compared to seawater ([Li] PW < [Li] SW ), and the porewater Li isotopic composition is more enriched in 7 Li than seawater (δ 7 Li PW > δ 7 Li SW ). This process occurs in shallow sediment depths where smectite is the dominant clay and illitization has not commenced. However, most porewater profiles exhibit higher Li concentrations and lighter isotopic compositions, indicating clay transformation processes. During clay transformation caused by high pressure and temperature during burial, isotopically light Li is released from the clays. This release of isotopically light Li increases the porewater Li concentration while driving it isotopically light. During sediment subduction, a significant fraction of this clay-bound isotopically light Li is released as a part of clay dewatering. Our study of Leg 339 porewater samples with clay dewatering evidence and Leg 379 porewater samples in a silica-rich environment helps us to further constrain the Li seawater mass budget by constraining the mass flux and isotopic composition of recycled Li from sediments to seawater. I have also developed a set of equations to extrapolate my present findings to a global scale. This study of Li isotopic systematics of marine porewater helps constrain the complex dynamics of Li in seawater.

abstract: The U.S. Geological Survey’s National Seismic Hazard Model (NSHM) calculates the frequency of earthquakes across the country to estimate potential ground shaking. Outputs of the model are used to establish insurance rates, building codes, and public safety planning. The most recent update, published in 2023 (NSHM23), significantly expanded the number of active faults in the model. However, the simple depiction of faults in NSHM23 does not fully capture the complexities of real fault surfaces and sub-surface geometries. The next update, planned for 2029 (NSHM29), aims to address this by representing faults as three-dimensional meshes that account for variations in seismogenic depth, local topography, fault intersections, and dip uncertainty. Preliminary NSHM29 fault meshes were developed from NSHM23 faults and subsurface information using PyVista. We calculated fault areas to understand how corrections for seismogenic depth, topography, and fault intersections during mesh creation impacts geologic moment rate, which directly influences earthquake frequency within the NSHM. Analysis of the results was completed using scatter plots and maps that depicted ratios and absolute changes in area and moment rate. This research reveals how different assumptions influence fault area and geologic moment rate to varying degrees. Some faults showed substantial changes in geologic moment rate from the combined effects of seismogenic depth, topography, and possible fault intersections, while others showed comparatively little. Our approach improves the geometric modeling of faults in the next iteration of NSHM by adding greater geometric fidelity to the fault model and is a step forward in probabilistic seismic hazard modeling. This work was conducted as part of the Geo-Launchpad internship program, supported by the National Science Foundation's National Geophysical Facility operated by EarthScope Consortium.

abstract: Red beds of Central Tibet record paired surface and deformation processes from the Cretaceous to the Oligocene, both prior to and following the India-Asia collision, yet they remain poorly dated and are often grouped together. The Qiu Ru Ba Formation are nonmarine red beds in north-central Tibet that sit in the footwall of a north-dipping thrust fault beneath a complex hanging wall composed of older structures that juxtaposed Triassic blueschist-bearing mélange of the Central Qiangtang Metamorphic Belt with Carboniferous to Permian upper crustal strata of the Qiangtang terrane. Preliminary mapping suggests that the north-dipping thrust belt propagated south into the Qui Ru Ba Formation, possibly creating a series of fault-propagation folds with E-W trending axial traces. Previous researchers interpreted the Qiu Ru Ba Formation and its overlying thrust to be Eocene to Oligocene in age based on a correlation with similar structures in the Rongma area, where a tuff collected from the footwall red beds yielded a K-feldspar Ar/Ar age of ca. 35 Ma. Resolving the age of these and other local red beds and thrust faults in the region is crucial for determining the spatial distribution and propagation of contractional deformation in the Qiangtang terrane. Current age control is limited to a single detrital zircon sample which yielded a mid-Cretaceous maximum depositional age, which indicates a mid-Cretaceous or younger estimate for the onset of thrusting. Here we present detailed geologic mapping, structural analysis, age constraints, and measured stratigraphic sections to resolve the timing and style of deposition and deformation of the Qiu Ru Ba Formation.

title: Assessing the link between the Taconic orogeny and Late Ordovician glaciation with new constraints on silicate weathering rates
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Murray, Joshua [1], Jagoutz, Oliver [2]

abstract: Mafic and ultramafic terranes are ‘hotspots’ of modern global weathering, responsible for large fluxes of dissolved Ca and Mg. It has been proposed that the spatiotemporal variation in the uplift of these (ultra)mafic terranes, primarily through arc-continent collision, is responsible for secular changes in Earth’s climate. In this framework, the obduction and weathering of (ultra)mafic rocks within Earth’s tropical rainbelt increases global weatherability and draws down CO 2 . One type-example of this process in the ~450 Ma Late Ordovician glaciation which coincides with the Taconic orogeny. Here we present new constraints on the pre-, syn-, and post-collisional silicate weathering fluxes associated with the Taconic orogeny. We analyse the geochemistry of siliciclastic sediments derived from the weathering and erosion of the Taconic-age Bay of Islands ophiolite in Newfoundland, Canada. We use a new provenance method to constrain the protolith composition and, when coupled with sedimentation rate, we calculate the local flux of Ca and Mg. We find that Ca fluxes are well-correlated with the erosion of the Bay of Islands ophiolite, occurring in two distinct pulses associated with initial collision with the Newfoundland promontory and subsequent collision with the Québec embayment. Unlike the Ca flux, the high residual Mg concentrations within the sediments suggest only small changes in Mg flux, likely due to the formation of authigenic clay minerals on the continental margin. Combined, the total increase in silicate weathering is limited, implying that ultramafic rocks may have less leverage over Earth’s inorganic carbon cycle than previously assumed. Comparing to modern weathering fluxes, we suggest that Taconic silicate weathering is insufficient to single-handedly account for Late Ordovician cooling. Recreating the Ordovician climate variation, therefore, requires a complementary mechanism.

title: Revealing Los Angeles's Hidden Ocean: An Animated Film for Localized Geoscience Outreach and K–12 Engagement
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: Zhao, Judy [1], Soni, Priyanka [2], Kim, Diane Young [3], Bottjer, David [4], Smith, Kathy [5]
affiliations: (1) Expanded Animation Research + Practice, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) Wrigley Institute for Environment and Sustainability, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
(3) Wrigley Institute for Environment and Sustainability, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
(4) Wrigley Institute for Environment and Sustainability, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
(5) Expanded Animation Research + Practice, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
abstract:
Geoscience remains underrepresented in many K–12 classrooms despite its central role in understanding Earth's history and environmental change. In Los Angeles, this challenge is compounded by the misconception that geology is disconnected from students' urban environments, even though the region preserves an exceptional record of ancient marine ecosystems beneath the modern city in institutions like the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles Coun. Locally relevant educational resources can better connect students with their local geologic history, in turn increasing scientific literacy while fostering early interest in Earth and marine sciences.

To explore this effort, we are developing an educational animated short film and a story script that reconstructs Los Angeles's ancient ocean using fossil discoveries from across the city. The film combines paleontological research, geologic interpretation, and digital 3D animation to reimagine extinct marine ecosystems within recognizable Los Angeles landscapes, allowing students to visualize familiar landmarks as submerged environments millions of years ago. Scientific reconstructions of mammals and coastal invertebrates are informed by fossils recovered from Miocene to Pleistocene throughout the Los Angeles Basin and field investigations at sites such as the Palos Verdes Peninsula and the Los Angeles Metro station. The animation is created using the 3D program Blender and integrates scientific content with engaging visual storytelling designed specifically for K–12 audiences.

Upon completion, the film will be incorporated into youth education and outreach programming through the Natural History Museum, Cabrillo Marine Aquarium, and the USC Wrigley Institute, expanding access to relevant geoscience education beyond traditional classrooms. A post-video survey will allow the viewers an opportunity to provide feedback on knowledge gained and areas for improvement.

By transforming Los Angeles's fossil record into an engaging visual narrative, this project demonstrates how collaborations among geoscientists, educators, and artists can make complex geologic concepts accessible to diverse audiences. The film highlights the value of localized science communication for broadening participation in the geosciences, encouraging students to recognize Earth science within their own communities, and inspiring future interest in geology, paleontology, and marine science.

title: A Diverse Vertebrate Assemblage from the Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) Neslen Formation, Utah, USA and the Utility of Isolated Remains in Reconstructing Vertebrate Faunas

authors: Lively, Joshua Ryan [1], McKee, Michael Justin [2], Greaves, Whitney Ruth [3], Toscanini, Marcello [4], Grossart, Stephanie [5], Cone, Marjean [6]
affiliations: (1) Prehistoric Museum, Price, UT, ; Department of Geosciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(2) Department of Biological Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Wesleyan University, Middletown, CT, USA
(4) Western Slope Paleontological Services, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(5) Eocene Environmental Group, Draper, UT, USA

abstract:
The Campanian Neslen Formation, exposed in the Book Cliffs of eastern Utah, is a geologic unit that historically has not been heavily prospected for paleontological resources when compared to contemporaneous fluvial strata across the Western Interior Basin. The skull and skin impressions of the hadrosaur Rhinorex and a partial tyrannosaur hindlimb represent the only two vertebrates formally described from the formation. Ten expeditions to the Book Cliffs led by the Prehistoric Museum have produced an abundance of vertebrate remains. Although most of those are isolated bones and other fragmentary specimens, these data can be applied to large-scale paleobiologic and biogeographic questions.

Here, we describe the vertebrate body fossil assemblage using an approach that focuses on apomorphic characters to avoid circularity in identification and provide the most accurate representation of the fauna. One partial hybodontiform shark tooth, comparable to Meristodonoides , was discovered in estuarine deposits low in the formation. Turtles include members of the Adocidae (c.f. Adocus ), Nanhsiungchelyidae (c.f. Basilemys ), Baenidae indet., a plastomenine ( Hutchemys ), and two other trionychid morphotypes. Hutchemys ( Derrisemys ) was previously identified from the Campanian Kaiparowits Formation but is otherwise only known from the Maastrichtian and Paleocene. We recognize two morphotypes of crocodyliform teeth, including one assignable to the Mesoeucrocodylia. Elements from dinosaurs discovered thus far include dromaeosaur and tyrannosaur teeth as well as bones from saurolophine hadrosaurs, nodosaurid ankylosaurs, and ceratopsians. One ceratopsian specimen is an isolated postorbital horn that curves dorsolaterally from the orbital margin. Though not confidently assignable to any named taxa on its own, it shares some resemblance to Judiceratops from the Judith River Formation of Montana.

Our results support the presence of components from both the hypothesized northern and southern Campanian biogeographic provinces, indicating either a latitudinal gradient or zone of mixing between two provinces. Hutchemys represents a southern Campanian taxon that disperses northward during the Maastrichtian, whereas the published tyrannosaur was hypothesized to share traits with species from Montana and Alberta. The presence of a ceratopsian similar to Judiceratops also supports some northern Laramdian influence in the Neslen, though we use caution in assigning the Neslen specimen to that taxon. The fossil assemblage of the Neslen Formation underscores the utility of even isolated remains in providing data on paleoecology and paleobiogeographic patterns.

title: Its Time to go Digital -- Digital Geologic Mapping Has Arrived.
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Langford, Richard P [1], Ricketts, Jason P [2], Pavlis, Terry P [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Resource Sciences, University of Texas El Paso, El Paso, TX, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Resource Sciences, University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, TX, USA
(3) Earth, Environmental, and Resource Sciences, University of Texas El Paso, El Paso, TX, USA
abstract:
At the University of Texas at El Paso, we have, for nearly 20 years, incorporated digital techniques into a traditional field course. We offer three-week courses in winter and May, timed so students have most of the summer free for jobs and internships. While we emphasize use of digital methods in the field, the fundamental techniques are largely technology-independent. We emphasize observation and description. Data is recorded in digital or paper field notebooks, and technology assists with location and quick measurement.

We have adopted two technology suites that are dependable and low-cost. The lower-cost option combines phones and notebooks for data collection, where students work in Strabospot. Data is then transferred to laptops for creating maps and reports. The second workflow is to map directly in QGIS on inexpensive tablet computers. We use the open-source QGIS that supports custom forms for easy data collection and plug-ins for orientation data collection and quick cross-section construction.

We typically fly a drone one morning. Each student sets up and flies the drone over a small area (about 5 minutes). The actual map is larger and nearby, where we have previously flown a key area. We walk the students through data processing using Agisoft Metashape. We use drone imagery to map complex areas and for detailed geomorphic analysis.

Using technology allows mapping of larger and more complex areas. Students concentrate on observation and interpretation of the data. Quick creation of maps and cross-sections also frees time for interpretation and writing. Our typical workflow is mapping until late afternoon five days a week. Evenings are spent on step-by-step map and report construction. Usually after the first day, we have the students write their unit descriptions and ask that students show their initial map work. Most recently, we have leaned into AI, showing students proper use of prompts to help edit writing and suggest data that is missing from the first report sections. While there are difficulties associated with using digital mapping and writing, the benefits are numerous.

title: Constraining iron cycling in the Yellowstone hydrothermal system from iron and oxygen isotopes in hydrothermal fluids
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Miller, Andrew Evan [1], Sims, Kenneth Warren [2], Scott, Sean R [3], Cox, Alysia [4], St. Clair, Brian E [5], Timmer, Jacqueline [6], Boyd, Eric S [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
(2) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
(3) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA,
(4) School of Geosciences, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, LA, USA
(5) Independent Scientist,
(6) Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Montana Tech of the University of Montana, Butte, MT, USA
(7) Department of Microbiology and Cell Biology, Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
abstract:
Iron is one of the most abundant redox elements in hydrothermal systems, and its speciation, concentration, and isotopic composition are sensitive to both abiotic and biotic processes. Variations in iron isotopes reflect processes such as dissolution of aquifer rock (abiotic), secondary mineralization (abiotic), and microbial metabolism (biotic), making iron isotopes a powerful tool for tracing iron cycling. In continental hydrothermal systems, previous studies have focused on iron isotope behavior within individual hydrothermal features (Wu et al., Astrobiology, 2013; Fortney et al. Astrobiology, 2021). The cycling of iron across an entire hydrothermal system, comprising features spanning a wide range of pH and temperature conditions, remains poorly characterized.

In this work, we sampled features from the Yellowstone hydrothermal system spanning a range of pH (1.8 to 7.8) and temperature (20°C to 93°C). Our samples came from one calcium-bicarbonate, seven neutral-chloride, and ten acid-sulfate features located across Yellowstone National Park. We paired measurements of iron isotopes (δ 56 Fe and δ 57 Fe) with oxygen (δ 18 O) and deuterium (δ 2 H) isotopes in hydrothermal fluids to constrain the processes controlling iron cycling and fluid evolution across the Yellowstone hydrothermal system.

Our results show that iron isotopic compositions in hydrothermal fluids reflect abiotic and/or biotic processes. Most hydrothermal fluids analyzed have a limited range of d 56 Fe values from +0.3‰ to +0.7‰, which we attribute to abiotic bulk dissolution of the volcanic substrate. Some fluids exhibit d 56 Fe values up to +1.2‰, which we interpret as evidence of abiotic subsurface mineralization of iron (hydr)oxides or sulfides, in which preferential incorporation of 54 Fe into the mineral phase leaves the residual fluid isotopically heavier. Several fluids have d 56 Fe values as low as -1.0‰, indicating microbial metabolism of iron via dissimilatory iron reduction or iron oxidation. Trends in iron and oxygen isotopes show distinct groupings that we attribute to abiotic and biotic processes involved in the geochemical evolution of hydrothermal fluids.

abstract:
The StraboSpot database and applications (StraboField, StraboMicro, and StraboExperimental) enable the collection, storage, and sharing of geologic data from the field to the lab, maintaining spatial relations and geologic context across scales. Development of the StraboSpot ecosystem is community driven to meet the needs, workflows, and vision of geologic disciplines. One of the immediate community needs is to work collaboratively using digital data systems both across interdisciplinary collaborations and within working groups.

Collaborative workflows require the ability to share data while maintaining a record of data progression and individual contributions. Additionally, much collaborative work involves the dissemination of samples to multiple labs, which requires detailed logging of current specimen locations and a record of the data associated with a particular sample. To address these issues, and facilitate group collaboration across the StraboSpot ecosystem, new tools are in development, including:

Collaborative Group Workflows: New permission controls on the web version of StraboField allow project owners to grant view or edit access to collaborators. Privacy settings are not changed by this development.

Enhanced StraboField & StraboMicro Sample Management: “Rich Samples” in StraboField allow users to attach images, geologic units, structural measurements, and lithologic notebook pages directly to sample entries. A yellow interface and map-level starburst icons provide visual distinction between samples and spots. Legacy samples can also be upgraded to rich samples. StraboMicro (2.0) enables flexible linking and unlinking of samples between StraboMicro and StraboField across all projects and datasets.

Unified Strabo Samples Hub: A new centralized samples hub integrates all user samples from StraboField, StraboMicro, and StraboExperimental into a unified schema. This web-accessible database contains available sample metadata, links to parent projects, and tracks sample provenance, repository locations, ownership, transfers, and splitting history, thus allowing researchers to share individual sample records without exporting entire projects. title: Determining the Evolution of the Himalayan Thrust Belt
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Robinson, Delores M. [1], DeCelles, Peter G. [2]
affiliations: (1) Dept of Geological Sciences, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(2) Dept of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract:
In the past 30 years, geologists have been completing field work in the Himalaya at a remarkable pace to understand how the compressional system evolved. Dr. Jay Quade was at the forefront of that research. Jay’s research supported our understanding of how the Himalayan thrust belt eroded and the corresponding sediment distributed in basins. The Himalayan thrust belt extends from the Indus-Yarlung Suture Zone in Tibet, through the highest peaks in the world, through subtropical rain forests, to the Main Frontal thrust at the toe of the mountain belt in Pakistan, India, Nepal, Sikkim and Bhutan. Thus, research completed in the Himalaya takes place within extreme environments.

Beginning in the late 1990’s and early 2000’s, the use and proliferation of U-Pb ages of detrital zircon helped understand and revise the stratigraphy of the Himalaya. This was supported by months-long field campaigns in largely roadless regions. New balanced cross sections revealed the 2D structural architecture. Neodymium and Strontium isotopic data coupled with magnetostratigraphy helped to determine how the Himalaya were eroded, putting specific ages on the advance of the thrust belt. Next, we modeled the Himalayan thrust belt in 2D fields taking into account erosion and loading in the thrust belt and using medium temperature thermochronology – muscovite/argon cooling ages – to determine the time that the metamorphic rocks were brought toward the surface. Low temperature thermochronology, particularly apatite fission track, zircon fission track and zircon helium ages, added cooling ages and more depth into our understanding of exhumation and erosion. Finally, balanced cross sections, based in part on new seismic models, have been integrated into a thermokinematic model using thermochronologic ages to produce the most accurate 2D visualizations of the Himalaya possible. The research continues with more advances to come. Jay’s advice to young researchers was to pursue the questions that most intrigued our minds in regions where others said the work was impossible to do. This is where he made his most important breakthroughs and how he inspired a generation of Himalayan researchers.

title: IUGS HERITAGE STONES: A GLOBAL BRIDGE BETWEEN GEOHERITAGE AND CULTURE

authors: Canet, Carles [1], Kaur, Gurmeet [2], Mathew, Bobby [3]
affiliations: (1) Instituto de Geofisica, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, Ciudad de Mexico, Mexico
(2) Department of Geology, Panjab University Sector-14, Chandigarh, India

abstract:
The Heritage Stone (HS) designation is granted by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) to natural stones that have ‘been used in significant architecture and monuments, recognized as integral aspects of human culture’. Stones eligible for HS designation must fulfill at least one of the following four criteria: (i) international distribution, (ii) use in emblematic buildings/sites, (iii) traditional architecture, and (iv) unique character of the stone. The HS designation was officially established in 2021, following the approval of the statutes of the International Commission on Geoheritage; however, the recognition of these stones began years earlier, in 2016. To date, there are 69 total HS, which includes 47 declarations granted after the approval of the statutes, in addition to the 22 that existed prior to the statutory definition. The current list of designated HS covers all five continents and the primary rock groups (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic).

Seeking to highlight the connections between HS and cultural heritage and their symbolic impact across centuries, a comparison is made between two HS designated in 2024: Western Ghats Laterite (India) and Tezontle volcanic scoria (Mexico). Originating from contrasting cultural settings and distinct geological processes, these stones were selected not at random, but due to the striking aesthetic coincidence of their predominant reddish coloration and rough surfaces. This analysis explores a possible convergence in their usage and symbolism. Crucially, both HS exhibit connections with indigenous cultures, colonialism, responses to the Reformation, and Baroque architecture, particularly coinciding between the 16th and 20th centuries. Clearly, their use has been shaped by global political and cultural dynamics; therefore, these natural stones undoubtedly hold international significance, despite being geographically restricted to their regions of origin.

Parallel to the HS designation, numerous monuments constructed with these stones are registered on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The IUGS HS recognition itself enhances the visibility of geoheritage by bridging geology with historical and cultural elements through the holistic concept of ‘geocultural heritage’. Ultimately, this label is expected to foster conservation policies prioritizing original restoration materials, historical quarry protection, and geotourism programs.

title: Tracing PFAS Contamination in Streambed Sediments Using 19F NMR
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part II)
authors: Halverson, Charlie [1], Constantine, José A. [2], Carrasquillo, Anthony J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA

abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent fluorinated contaminants that have become widespread in aquatic environments. Although regulatory monitoring relies primarily on targeted mass spectrometry of surface and drinking water, streambed sediments may preserve longer-term records of contamination that water-column sampling alone cannot capture. We evaluate whether 19F nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of sediment extracts can identify and trace a known PFAS point source within a fluvial system. Sediment was collected along a 1.3 km reach of a northeastern U.S. river spanning a fluoropolymer manufacturing facility with a documented history of downstream PFAS contamination. 19F NMR analyses reveal no detectable fluorine signal upstream of the facility, a pronounced resonance immediately downstream consistent with terminal CF₃ groups characteristic of perfluoroalkyl compounds, and a persistent but diminished signal farther downstream. This spatial pattern parallels previously documented changes in dissolved PFAS concentrations while demonstrating that streambed sediments preserve the legacy of contaminant release. Although the current methodology is best suited as a qualitative indicator of PFAS occurrence and distribution, ongoing calibration demonstrates strong potential for quantitative estimation of sediment PFAS concentrations from spectral response. These results establish 19F NMR as a rapid, non-targeted approach for identifying fluorinated contaminant plumes archived within fluvial sediments and highlight the potential for river deposits to serve as long-term environmental records of industrial contamination.

abstract: The extents of Pleistocene glaciers are well known in numerous mountains of the western United States, developed chiefly from decades of mapping glacial sediments and landforms. Reconstructed ice extents have been digitized for mountains throughout the west, permitting viewing and analysis at various spatial scales in geographic information systems. The PaleoGlacier Inventory is a compilation of reconstructed mountain glacier extents during Quaternary glaciations from across the conterminous western United States and Hawaii drawn at scales ranging from 1:24,000 to 1:100,000. The inventory is available as a geodatabase consisting of attributed polygons for public access and is developed by contributions from published and unpublished sources. Here, we present updates to the inventory, including (1) the addition of detailed outlines from the southern Rocky Mountains, the Great Basin, the northern Basin and Range, and the Idaho Batholith, (2) generalized outlines to permit visualization of glaciated mountains over larger areas, and (3) a set of applications and document formats for viewing the inventory online and on mobile devices. abstract: A conodont biostratigraphic and carbon-isotope framework provides the background for placing the two pulses of the Late Ordovician Mass Extinction (LOME 1 and LOME 2) in stratigraphic context in the Williston Basin. Three closely spaced cores from the Williston Basin (1231, 9102, and 7612) were correlated based on conodont biostratigraphy and carbon-isotope stratigraphy. The Hirnantian Isotopic Carbon Excursion (HICE) and a smaller carbon-isotope excursion identified as the KaH were observed in the Stonewall Formation. The formation contains a conodont fauna indicative of the A. shatzeri - O. hassi North American Midcontinent conodont zones. Based on the position of the HICE, LOME 1 is provisionally correlated with the lower Stonewall Formation, approximately 25-40 m in the composite section, whereas LOME 2 is placed in the upper Stonewall Formation, approximately 15-18 m, on the falling limb of the HICE . This interpretation is based on the positions of LOME 1 and LOME 2 recognized in the Monitor Range in Nevada by Kozik and others (2022) and provides a framework for a more detailed analysis of geochemical trends across the extinction interval in the Williston basin. However, the base of Hirnantian cannot be placed with confidence within the conodont biostratigraphic framework because it is not well defined by the North America Midcontinent conodont zonation. Graptolites that define the base of the Hirnatian are lacking because of the perennially restricted, shallow-marine carbonate-evaporite depositional setting of the study area. The base of the LOME 1 may consequently occur somewhat higher in the section than suggested by the current correlation. Additional high-resolution geochemical data from this interval should help constrain its position with higher confidence.

title: Petrogenesis of the Korba Granites: implications for Mesoproterozoic tectonomagmatic evolution of the Central Indian Tectonic Zone(CITZ)

authors: Hsieh, Robert B. [1], Shellnutt, John Gregory [2], Hari, K. R. [3], Vishwakarma, Neeraj [4], Deshmukh, Shrinivas [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, National Taiwan Normal University, Taipei, Taiwan

abstract: Peninsular India is a result of the collision between Archean cratons during the Meso- to Neoproterozoic. The collisional belt between the cratons of southern India (Bastar, Dharwar, Singhbhum) and northern India (Bundelkhand) is referred to as the Central India Tectonic Zone (CITZ). There are a number of batholiths within the CITZ that record different stages of crustal evolution that culminated during the terminal stages of collision at 1000-850 Ma. The ‘Late Archean’ Chhotanagpur Gneissic Complex (CGC) of the CITZ includes ‘undifferentiated’ Korba granites and associated meta-sedimentary rocks, but very little is known about the granites including their petrogenesis and age. In this study, we report the first geochemical and geochronological results from the Korba granitic rocks. Granites, pegmatites, and meta-sedimentary rocks were collected from Korba District, Northern Chhattisgarh. The in situ zircon U-Pb geochronology results indicate an Early Mesoproterozoic (1565.9 ± 6.8 Ma) emplacement age. The granites (SiO 2 = 60-76 wt%) are peraluminous, alkali-calcic to calc-alkalic, ferroan in composition and have abundant LILE and slightly to moderate abundant in HFSE. The ɛ Hf ( t ) values of Korba granites range between -6.6 and +4.6. Furthermore, sillimanite-bearing pegmatites zones are found throughout the upper parts of the Korba granites suggesting that there was a period(s) of late stage Al-rich fluid fluxing. Blocks (1-10 m wide) of meta-sedimentary rocks are found within the granites and may represent a roof pendant of the series. The Korba granites are mineralogically and compositionally similar to granitoids derived by partial melting of sedimentary rocks during crustal thickening associated with collision. The results of this study suggest that there was a regional collisional event ~500 million years before the Neoproterozoic terminal collision, which is also likely recorded by the Sauser group at southwest side of CITZ. We suggest that the Korba granites were emplaced within rifted continental crust from the Southern India Craton that collided with the Northern Indian Craton during the Early Mesoproterozoic.

title: Palaeoenvironmental history of cold-climate aeolian dunes in the Vienna Basin, Central Europe
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Holuša, Jakub [1], Woronko, Barbara [2], Nývlt, Daniel [3]
affiliations: (1) Polar-Geo-Lab, Department of Geography, Faculty of Science, Masaryk University, Brno, Czech Republic; Conservation and Survey Division, School of Natural Resources, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
(2) Faculty of Geology, University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland

abstract:
Vienna Basin represents the northwesternmost part of the Carpathian Basin. Aeolian sand sheets and dunes are spread over 1,300 km 2 of the Basin, covering >10% of its total area. The northernmost part of the Vienna Basin served as a convergence zone for at least two atmospheric circulation patterns. Whilst the current wind pattern (westerlies) in most of the Basin has remained unchanged at least since the Last Glacial Maximum, some of the dunes were formed by katabatic winds blowing from north, propagating from the Scandinavian Ice Sheet. These winds ceased to exist once the Ice Sheet retreated northwards, probably during the GS-2.1 stadial (23.0–14.7 ka). This created a globally unique system of dunes corresponding to changes in atmospheric circulation during the Late Glacial period which now follow a zig-zag pattern.

OSL ages of the two largest dune fields in the Vienna Basin show episodical aeolian activity between 26 ± 2 ka and 13 ± 2 ka, peaking during the GS-2.1a/GI-1 transition (~14.7 ka). This chronology is in accordance with a pattern reported in other parts of the Carpathian Basin, but differs from the European Sand Belt, where the aeolian activity peaked during the GS-1 stadial (12.9–11.7 ka). This difference results from the presence of the Scandinavian Ice Sheet in the North European Plain, which overdue the dune formation in this area.

title: The Rare Earth Element Budget of the Red Mountain Pluton, Laramie Range, Southeastern Wyoming
session_title: Granite-related mineral systems: Advances in understanding their genesis, distribution, and exploration implications (Posters)
authors: Abram, Veronica Carmelita [1], Futcher, Phoebe Valerie Ann [2], Lewis, Madeline J. [3], Biasi, Joseph [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, Wyoming, USA
(2) Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
(3) Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
(4) Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY,
abstract:
Increased demand for domestic rare earth element (REE) resources highlights the need for improved understanding of mineral hosts in REE-bearing mineral systems. The Halleck Creek REE deposit in the Laramie Range of southeastern Wyoming, hosted in the Mesoproterozoic Red Mountain pluton, provides an opportunity to investigate REE distribution in an unconventional deposit type. The broadly monzonitic pluton is the youngest intrusion in the 1.43 Ga Laramie Anorthosite complex and contains bulk rock REE concentrations averaging ~0.2 wt.% total REEs, with some samples up to 65 times more enriched than typical continental crust. Allanite is considered the primary REE-bearing mineral in the Halleck Creek deposit, although accessory minerals zircon and apatite occur in modal abundances averaging around 0.5 %. Both zircon and apatite can accommodate several wt.% of REEs in their mineral structures, yet their contribution to the Halleck Creek deposit REE budget remains unconstrained.

We aim to quantify how much of the Red Mountain pluton whole rock REE budget is hosted in zircon and apatite, relative to the dominant REE-bearing mineral allanite. Additionally, we investigate relationships between REE grade and rock type within the deposit to address whether REE contributions from zircon and apatite vary relative to allanite across the plutonic lithologies. Total-alkali-silica classification of >2,100 whole rock analyses from the Red Mountain pluton indicates that the most abundant rock type in the pluton is syenite, though rock types range from monzogabbro to granite with SiO 2 contents ranging from 46–77 wt.%. The highest whole rock REE concentrations occur in the syenites and monzonites (58-66 wt.% SiO 2 ), with a maximum of 1.15 wt.% total REEs. Representative samples of each rock type in the Red Mountain pluton were selected for zircon and apatite analyses, coupled with corresponding whole rock compositions. REE concentrations in these minerals determined by laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS) will constrain the compositional variability of these minerals and their contribution to the overall REE budget in the Halleck Creek deposit. By combining bulk rock and mineral geochemistry, this study will improve our understanding of REE distribution among different mineral hosts and rock types in the Red Mountain pluton, informing future exploration and REE extraction from the Halleck Creek deposit and other magmatic REE resources.

authors: Luzzadder-Beach, Sheryl [1], Beach, Timothy [2], Tumanova, Olga [3], Scott, Elle [4], Pratt, William [5]
affiliations: (1) Geography and the Environment, University of Texas, AUSTIN, TX, USA

abstract: Dr. Rolfe Mandel inspires research into human and environment relations in the deep past, applying multiple tools of Geoarchaeology. He has opened the field into a “big-tent” for innovation and technology. For example, scientific knowledge on ancient Maya agriculture has evolved enormously in recent decades. This progression begins with early findings on Ancient Maya Wetland Agriculture in the 1970s and 80s from aerial photography and field research, and is now well-covered in more recent papers, especially after the LiDAR revolution in Maya Archaeology. Multiple aspects of ancient agriculture are explored in these works, from soil characteristics and chemistry to crop types to climate vulnerability, all elements of deep traditional environmental knowledge. However, only a handful of geoarchaeological studies consider water quality, including water chemistry, as a variable. Here we present the results from a detailed analysis of an ancient Maya Wetland field agroecosystem, the Birds of Paradise fields of Northwestern Belize, to test the hypothesis that the Ancient Maya were knowledgeable about water quality variations and their impacts on agroecosystems, and managed their water resources accordingly. These data are a portion of our long-term regional elemental water quality monitoring project in the Maya Lowlands, where ancient Maya settled and farmed for centuries. Water chemistry reflects the elemental geochemistry of the aquifers and basin geology that imprint on its character via throughflow. As geology does not normally change its elemental state rapidly, this provides a window into potential past regional water conditions, including those which affect human domestic and agricultural water use.

title: New Evidence of Late Pleistocene Reverse Faulting in the Wind River Basin
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape
authors: Ellett, Nicholas [1], Pierce, Ian [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Lakewood, CO, USA

abstract: Few faults in central Wyoming preserve clear evidence of late Quaternary surface rupture. Those that do strike generally east-west and record normal motion, implying north-south crustal extension at low slip rates (0.1 mm/yr or less). Here, we present evidence of a previously unreported east-west striking fault exhibiting reverse motion, implying north-south crustal shortening in the late Pleistocene. We mapped the apparently south-dipping Crow Creek fault along a 17 km trace near the northwest margin of the Wind River Basin. It demonstrates a consistent down-to-north sense of motion along conspicuous, uphill facing scarps without compelling evidence of lateral motion. Lidar-based vertical offset measurements range from 0.9 to 8.8 m in fluvial terraces, landslides, and hillslopes. Multiple generations of alluvial fan surfaces are progressively offset by 0.2 to 3.3 m. The displaced landforms lack radiometric age control but are tentatively estimated to be late Pleistocene or possibly Holocene based on geomorphic expression, implying preliminary slip rates up to approximately 0.1 mm/yr on this previously unreported fault.

title: MiNE: Mineral Network Explorer
session_title: Early career investigators in mineralogy and crystallography
authors: Ngo, Don [1], Burges, Jarrod [2], Hummer, Daniel Robert [3], Li, Yanzhang [4], Morrison, Shaunna [5], Ma, Xiaogang [6], Prabhu, Anirudh [7]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Science, Washington, DC, USA

abstract:
The complex interdependencies between minerals and their formational environments present a multidimensional challenge in the Earth sciences. Network analysis has emerged as a powerful tool for unraveling these relationships, allowing researchers to represent Earth's mineralogy as a mathematically rigorous system of nodes and edges. By leveraging both unipartite and bipartite graphs, researchers can visualize large-scale mineralogical trends and discover hidden patterns tied to Earth's evolutionary history. These graphs represent either direct connections between similar entities (e.g., mineral-to-mineral co-occurrence) or relationships across distinct classes (e.g., minerals and their localities).

Despite the widespread utility and success of network analysis in the geosciences, a barrier to its widespread adoption is the lack of accessible, user-friendly tools designed specifically for Earth science data. To bridge this gap, we have developed the Mineral Network Explorer (MiNE), a highly interactive, web-based visualization application built in TypeScript. MiNE provides researchers with an intuitive graphical interface to ingest, analyze, and dynamically visualize complex unipartite and bipartite mineral networks without requiring advanced programmatic expertise.

The application is built around a responsive, browser-based rendering engine that allows users to seamlessly navigate large-scale graph layouts. Core app capabilities include interactive filtering, enabling users to isolate specific mineral clusters, trace targeted formational environments, and dynamically toggle node and edge visibility based on underlying mineralogical properties. Furthermore, MiNE integrates robust network topology algorithms, allowing users to execute community detection (such as the Louvain method) and calculate network metrics on the fly directly within the user interface.

By centralizing force-directed layout visualization, algorithm deployment, and interactive data filtering within a highly accessible web application, MiNE accelerates the exploratory phase of data science in mineralogy. As an open-source tool, MiNE empowers the geoscience community to apply advanced graph-based analytics to crystallographic and geochemical databases, facilitating data-driven discovery in the Earth and planetary sciences.

title: Bivalve isotope geochemistry as an archive of Cretaceous climate and oceanography

authors: Jones, Matthew M. [1], Brown, Adriana [2], Petersen, Sierra V. [3], MacLeod, Kenneth G. [4], Huber, Brian T. [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Energy & Minerals Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA

abstract: Mollusk biostratigraphy anchors the Cretaceous timescale, providing a chronostratigraphic foundation for many studies of Cretaceous oceanic anoxic events (OAEs), stratigraphic correlation, and reconstruction of depositional environments. In many Cretaceous mudstone strata, macroinvertebrates also represent the main appreciably preserved archive for analysis using carbonate-based geochemical proxies. Here, we summarize results from a series of recent carbonate clumped isotope (Δ 47 ) analyses of bivalve fossils to test the paleothermometer’s wider application in Cretaceous strata for reconstruction of paleoclimatic and oceanographic conditions. One sample set (n=118) comprised Albian to Maastrichtian oyster specimens from strata of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) of North America, collected from outcrops spanning from the southern to northern gateways of the seaway. Additional sample sets of Turonian and Campanian inoceramid prisms (n=32) are from two sites cored in the Indian Ocean during International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) expeditions 369 and 392, which were located at the southern high latitudes during the Cretaceous. Results from the compilation highlight potential complicating factors particularly relevant to Cretaceous Δ 47 datasets. These include the potential for thermal reordering of skeletal carbonate Δ 47 signals during burial and possible clade-specific biases in Δ 47 temperatures, namely in inoceramids. Despite these potential concerns, our results collectively resolve spatial and temporal temperature gradients in the Cretaceous. The Cretaceous thermal maximum (KTM) is evident from the WIS and IODP datasets, with peak marine warmth (>30°C) in the Cenomanian to Turonian stages followed by later relative cooling through the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages. Latitudinal temperature gradients derived from the bivalve Δ 47 dataset of the WIS are minimal during the peak of the KTM and increase during the Campanian and Maastrichtian. Further, calculations of Cretaceous water oxygen isotope (δ 18 O w ) compositions from Δ 47 temperature and carbonate oxygen isotope data, provide geochemical evidence supporting hypotheses of mixing of distinct water masses in the WIS sourced from both the northern and southern gateways of the seaway. These findings demonstrate that Δ 47 analysis of properly screened bivalves can yield Cretaceous paleotemperature and δ 18 O w data. Where suitably preserved specimens can be recovered, bivalve Δ 47 datasets have the potential to quantitatively reconstruct climatic and oceanographic responses to OAEs and the KTM, as well as test hypotheses about potential cold snaps in the Cretaceous and reconstruct local depositional conditions in mudstone strata.

title: Remagnetization of the Nindam Formation reveals late-stage vertical-axis rotation during development of the Nanga Parbat syntaxis.

abstract: The continuation of convergence between India and Eurasia following closure of the Neotethys Ocean has resulted in deep indentation of the Indian subcontinent into Eurasia, producing major oroclines at the western and eastern syntaxes of the Himalaya. Understanding the relationships between oroclinal bending, structural reactivation, uplift, and convergence requires paleogeographic and kinematic constraints from allochthonous crustal elements. The timing of vertical-axis rotations relative to Indian indentation and uplift remain poorly constrained in the western Himalayan syntaxis. Here we present new paleomagnetic results from the Indus Suture Zone that constrain how orogenic paleogeography developed during the formation of the Nanga Parbat syntaxis. Our study focuses on the Nindam Formation, a volcaniclastic turbidite succession deposited in the forearc basin of the Kohistan–Ladakh Arc (KLA) during its accretion to the Indian margin. Demagnetization experiments isolated multiple secondary high-temperature remanences acquired at different stages of deformation. Although this pervasive remagnetization precludes the determination of a reliable primary paleopole, the secondary remanences provide new constraints on the paleogeography of the Himalayan fold-and-thrust belt during deformation. They constrain the magnitude of clockwise vertical-axis rotations within the Indus Suture Zone during development of the Nanga Parbat orocline. They also show that rotation took place after regional tilting associated with Nanga Parbat uplift, supporting a model in which the uplift of Nanga Parbat promoted oroclinal bending and late-stage strike-slip reactivation of suture-zone thrusts.

title: Advancing Landslide Risk Reduction through Collaboration: Interest Groups of the National Landslide Hazard Risk Reduction
session_title: The National Landslide Hazard Reduction Program (NLHRP): Advancing Landslide Hazard Reduction in the U.S. through Working Groups and Landslide Risk Reduction Grants (Posters)
authors: Hall, Sarah R. [1], Slaughter, Stephen L. [2]
affiliations: (1) College of the Atlantic, Bar Harbor, ME, ; U.S. Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA

abstract:
Eight landslide interest groups met regularly in 2025-2026 to focus on a range of topics with an overarching goal of reducing landslide losses by coordinating practitioners; sharing best practices; and co‑developing applied tools, information, and workflows that support risk reduction. This goal is common to all interest groups and contributes toward the shared national mission of the U.S. National Landslide Hazard Reduction Program. Broadly, the regionally and topically focused interest groups aim to advance specialized landslide topics, build regional networks and shared resource repositories, and organize collaborative work that feeds into national risk reduction efforts, including inventories, modeling methods, and communication strategies. Originating as sub-groups of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) National Landslide Hazard Risk Reduction (NLHRR) Working Group, the established interest groups include Event Response and Recovery, Mapping and Modeling, Outreach and Education, Mitigation and Preparedness, Forecasting and Warning, and Landslide Loss. Two additional groups, the Eastern Region and Intermountain West Region interest groups, emerged from member interest to address geographic needs. Led by volunteers, these groups typically meet virtually, though regionally focused groups aim to hold at least one in‑person meeting annually to strengthen collaboration and local engagement.

This presentation will showcase each of the interest groups, their goals, and their annual work plans, with the aim of broadening participation across the landslide risk reduction community. By highlighting ongoing efforts, emerging needs, and opportunities for collaboration, we hope to engage geoscientists, engineers, academics, students, planners, emergency managers, and other practitioners who are interested in contributing to landslide risk reduction. Growing the network of professionals involved in these interest groups across the country will expand national capacity to develop and share actionable landslide science, tools, and best practice to reduce risk and losses.

title: The Beane Crinoid Collection at Beloit College: Exceptionally Preserved Specimens of Broad Scientific Value
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Dirks, Lia Marin [1], McCully, Lillianne [2], Zambito, James Joseph [3]
affiliations: (1) Beloit College, Beloit, WI,
(2) Beloit College, Beloit, WI, USA

abstract:
Exceptionally preserved, articulated crinoids from the Maynes Creek Formation of Le Grand, Iowa, have provided key insights into crinoid taphonomy, arm regeneration from predatory attacks, taxon-specific organic molecules related to original pigmentation, and ecological tiering. Crinoids were first collected for scientific study from the Le Grand area in 1858. In 1874, a lenticular deposit of articulated crinoids formed the basis of initial taxonomic descriptions. Additional lenticular deposits were discovered in the early 1930’s; hundreds of slabs of articulated crinoids were excavated and prepared by amateur paleontologist B.H. Beane for his private collection. Beane subsequently sold the majority of his collection, with a portion purchased by Beloit College Trustee R.H. Solem who donated it to the college in the 1960’s. The Beane Crinoid Collection at Beloit College consists of over 500 slabs of various sizes ranging from dimensions over 1 m to 10 cm and containing 1000’s of articulated crinoids in total preserved in obrution deposits. Since its acquisition by the college the collection has been housed in various buildings and displays, half the collection has been inaccessible for nearly twenty years, and slabs have undergone disparate levels of study, curation, and additional preparation.

The B.H. Beane Crinoid Collection at Beloit College is currently undergoing a renewed curation effort with the overarching goal of improving accessibility for teaching, research, and outreach. Slabs are being reassembled from multiple storage locations, and those that had been inadequately stored are being cleaned and assessed for damage using historical photographs. Future guidelines and recommendations on how to care for the specimens, storage suggestions that aid in the collection's longevity and accessibility, and ensuring the specimens in this collection are properly represented in our college fossil collection database are included in this effort. Current student research and class assignments are focused on documenting hardground features observed in some slabs. Additionally, various records including correspondence between Beane and Solem as well as relevant publications, dissertations, and theses are being compiled and will form the basis for an article in the college magazine as part of our outreach efforts.

title: Multi-Stage Lithospheric Drips Drive Topographic Evolution of Sedimentary Basins and Orogenic Plateaus: Insights from Analogue and Numerical Modelling

authors: Andersen, Julia [1], Pysklywec, Russell [2], Göğüş, Oğuz [3], Heron, Phil J. [4], Şengül Uluocak, Ebru [5], Santimano, Tasca [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada

(4) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, University of Toronto Scarborough, Scarborough, ON, Canada; Department of Earth Sciences, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada

abstract: Seismic tomography surveys reveal regions of “missing” continental lithosphere that manifest as slow seismic wave speed in gaps of seismically fast mantle lithosphere or columns of seismically fast, cold/dense mantle lithosphere descending into the sub-lithospheric mantle. Such findings have been interpreted as evidence of lithospheric “dripping” whereby gravitationally unstable, high density anomalies in the mantle lithosphere sink or “drip” into the underlying sub-lithospheric mantle. As the mantle lithosphere drips, it thins, removing a portion and leaving a gap that is filled by upwelling sub-lithospheric mantle. This produces crustal tectonics where the dripping lithosphere induces surface subsidence, and horizontal tractions causing thickening, folding/faulting of the crust above the drip. Lithospheric dripping has been linked to the topographic evolution of sedimentary basins within orogenic plateaus, while simultaneously large-scale lithospheric removal has been linked to uplift of the plateaus themselves. Thus far, our understanding of the surface manifestations of deeper mantle processes remains unresolved. Furthermore, the link (if any) between basin scale deformation and plateau scale uplift through lithospheric dripping processes has not been established. Three dimensional, scaled, analogue models and high-resolution optical image correlation techniques are used in conjunction with two dimensional numerical models to demonstrate that basin topographic evolution and plateau scale uplift may be linked through a process of multi-stage dripping. Furthermore, the models demonstrate that lithospheric drips differ in their surface manifestations where some drips induce significant shortening in the crust, while others do not and are further differentiated by the scale (small or large) of lithosphere removed. These deeper mantle lithosphere processes may be identified by the topographic changes over time in the crust. This research provides insight into the dynamics between the mantle and upper crust and the tectonics that drive topographic evolution of orogenic plateaus.

title: Unfreezing Snowball Earth: The Basal Ediacaran Cap Carbonate Record in Northern Utah and Southeastern Idaho, USA

abstract:
The cap-carbonate records in northern Utah and southeastern Idaho provide a better understanding of the duration and style of Marinoan deglaciation and how it relates to global climate change and animal evolution.

This research evaluates sedimentary and stratigraphic features within new and formerly discovered cap carbonates that overlie Cryogenian glacial successions in the region. We conducted field work, detrital-zircon geochronology, and carbon-isotope analyses at nine Utah locations, within and around the Great Salt Lake and the Huntsville area, in the northeastern Wasatch Mountains. Although both Sturtian and Marinoan strata are recognized, only the Marinoan strata are capped by conspicuous carbonate facies.

Basal Ediacaran cap carbonates were previously described in the Pocatello Formation in southeast Idaho. This cap succession is a siliciclastic-bearing, buff- to pale-pink dolostone unit and includes features such as turbidities, bar forms, swaley cross beds, plane beds, and sedimentary breccias with an overall trend indicating decreasing accommodation space (e.g., post-glacial isostatic rebound). The overlying strata are argillaceous with rare interbeds of rippled micrite and rare cm-scale aragonite fans indicating post-glacial transgression. C-isotope values from the cap sections of Idaho range from -6 to -3 per mil. Detrital zircons from quartz sandstone within the cap carbonate at Scout Mountain, SE Idaho yield a U-Pb CA-ID-TIMS age suggesting basal Ediacaran deposition.

Cap carbonates in northern Utah show similar features to those in SE Idaho. The Salt Lake cap sections exhibit peloids and ‘giant wave ripples’. The cap carbonate on Antelope Island is a structural outlier and contains tubestone, sheet cracks, and cryptalgal laminations. Most Utah caps overlie and/or are interbedded with silicilastics. Stable-carbon isotope values also range from -6 to -3 per mil. The collective cap carbonate record in Utah and Idaho indicate dynamic changes in accommodation space and an interplay with siliciclastic sedimentation suggesting a more protracted deglaciation.

title: A new tale of shales: isotopic and molecular approaches for evaluating the biogeochemical control on black shale deposition in the Devonian and Cretaceous.

authors: Junium, Christopher K. [1], Cohen, Phoebe A. [2], Yang, Zonglin [3], Logie, Tyler [4], Uveges, Benjamin [5]
affiliations: (1) Syracuse University EES, Syracuse, NY,

abstract: The iconic black shales that typify the depositional record of the Cretaceous and Devonian during Oceanic Anoxic Events (OAEs) have captivated geologist and geochemists for many years. Diagnosing the causes, durations and environmental impacts of OAEs has been central to contextualizing these events and their relationship to climate variability and accompanying extinctions. The mode of the carbon cycle during the Late Devonian and mid-Cretaceous was tipped toward enhanced production and burial of organic matter under more reducing conditions and catalyzed by non-analog nutrient cycling regimes. Using examples with well-developed temporal chronologies (including astronomical time scales) we will present new and existing carbon, nitrogen and hydrogen [PAC1] isotopes on organic matter from specific compounds, bulk sediments, and other phases. These results paint a picture of or a nitrogen cycle that is dominated by the presence sub-surface waters rich in ammonium and respired carbon-rich that are variably accessed by primary producers. During mixing events, breakdown of water column stratification allowed upward excursions of nutrient-rich chemocline waters that resulted in enhanced organic carbon production that has strong 15 N depletion, and in some cases, 13 C depletion. Outside of the OAE events, proxy variations tend to follow orbitally controlled periods. What remains unclear is the degree to which these isotope excursions and the organic matter enrichment are caused by external input of terrestrially derived nutrients responding to terrestrial hydroclimate variability or through internally driven oceanic processes (wind-driven upwelling or overturning) occurring at Milankovitch periods. We will present new compound specific hydrogen isotope data on terrestrial leaf wax lipids to explore connections between terrestrial hydroclimate and marine redox variability in mid-Cretaceous black shales of the North Atlantic.

title: Mantle Waves Connect Rifted Margins and Cratonic Interiors
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling (Posters)
authors: Gernon, Thomas Michael [1], Brune, Sascha [2], Hincks, Thea [3], Braun, Jean [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Ocean and Earth Science, University of Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom; Geodynamic Modelling Section, GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, Potsdam, Germany
(2) Geodynamic Modelling Section, GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, Potsdam, Germany; Institute of Geosciences, University of Potsdam, Potsdam, Germany
(3) School of Ocean and Earth Science, University of Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom
(4) Earth Surface Process Modelling, GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, Potsdam, Germany; Institute of Geosciences, University of Potsdam, Potsdam, Germany
abstract:
Continental rifting is traditionally viewed as a spatially confined process, with impacts restricted to the rift zone itself. We present a body of work showing how rifting can instead trigger a chain of convective instabilities — "mantle waves" — that propagate hundreds to thousands of kilometres cratonward along the lithospheric root, with consequences persisting for tens to >100 Myr after breakup (Gernon et al., 2023–2026). These 'waves' progressively erode the base of adjacent cratonic keels, driving a sequence of mantle, and in turn, surface responses. The removal of some ~35 km thick keels of cratons promotes small-degree mantle melting, generating volatile-rich kimberlite melts, explaining the multi-million-year lag between supercontinent breakup and kimberlite eruption, and linking diamond-bearing volcanism directly to earlier rift dynamics. This removal of lithospheric keel drives isostatic uplift of craton interiors, coupling rift-flank escarpment retreat to plateau formation in continental interiors. Some of the removed, geochemically enriched keel is entrained into the suboceanic asthenosphere, fuelling ocean island and seamount volcanism even in some cases where mantle plumes are absent. The resulting wave of topographic uplift can further enable the nucleation of continental ice sheets (Abstract #2091183), thus linking rift-driven mantle dynamics to major climate transitions over 100 Myr later. Mantle waves represent a highly systematic physical mechanism through which rifting can reorganise mantle flow, cratonic architecture, and Earth's surface environment long after breakup, extending the reach of rifting processes, and their geologic and climatic implications, far beyond the rift itself.

title: Removal of Arsenic (As) from Mississippi Lakes using Raw Bauxite found in Northern Mississippi
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Dennison, Abigail [1], Widanagamage, Inoka Hasanthi [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
(2) University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
abstract:
Arsenic is being introduced to lakes within Mississippi due to multiple processes (e.g. runoff from farmlands or production waste). There are growing health concerns as most lakes are used recreationally by millions of people. Extended exposure to arsenic can lead to skin damage and multiple forms of cancer. Enid Lake, Mississippi, is used for fishing and swimming by locals. Using previous data, the lake has an average As level between 4 to 6 µg/L. The EPA sets the maximum contaminant level (MCL) is 10µg/L, but the maximum contaminant level goal (MCLG) at 0µg/L for As, so health effects can still be caused by extended exposure. Using bauxite, which is an abundant geological unit in northern Mississippi, is a more efficient and cheaper alternative to other treatment methods. This study will use raw clay-rich-bauxite to investigate the efficient removal of contaminants (e.g. As) following sorption models.

Fifteen water samples were collected; over 5 locations in Enid Lake. Physicochemical parameters such as pH, temperature, specific conductivity, ORP, and dissolved oxygen have been recorded at each sampling location. The average pH recorded at 7.22; temperature was 25.26°C; specific conductivity was 52.44 µS/cm; ORP was 104 mV; and 8.68mg/L dissolved oxygen. Two series of preliminary batch experiments were performed to remove arsenic. The first batch uses a solution containing 1 g/L of bauxite while the second batch uses 10g/L of bauxite. The lake samples were spiked with arsenic to reach the MCL and allowed 24-hour contact time with the bauxite. Every sample in the second batch shows 100% removal of As, while 50% of the samples show efficient As removal in the first batch with the lower bauxite dosage. The detection limit for both experiments was about 65%, but it is assumed at least 90% was removed from the samples. This confirms that raw bauxite sorption capacity is efficient in removing As.

Further sorption experiments will be performed in Ross Barnett Reservoir near Jackson, Mississippi area. The preliminary data indicates that raw bauxite has a high potential to be a cost-effective material to remove As efficiently from contaminated lake water.

title: U-Pb joint inversion for thermal history reconstruction
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Zhang, Yiming [1], Schmitz, Mark D. [2], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
(3) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
abstract:
Thermal histories that integrate geochronologic and thermochronologic observations can provide powerful constraints on the timing and duration of tectonic processes such as the duration and cooling of orogenesis involving high-grade metamorphism. In U-bearing accessory minerals, thermally activated diffusion of radiogenic Pb produces two complementary observables: spatial variations in U–Pb isotopic composition within individual grains and grain-size-dependent, volume-averaged ages. LA–ICP–MS depth profiles can resolve the former at high spatial resolution, whereas isotope-dilution thermal ionization mass spectrometry provides higher-precision whole-grain measurements of the latter. Jointly modeling these observations can leverage individual grain’s diffusion records that neither dataset resolves independently.

Integrating these datasets is complicated by differences in spatial sampling, precision, grain geometry, and uncertainty structure. In particular, interpreted depth profiles are sensitive to how the beginning and end of ablation are identified and how time-dependent instrumental fractionation is corrected. We present two linked, open-source packages that address these challenges. UPbRPy distinguishes the baseline, the signal plateau used for conventional spot-mean calculations, and the complete ablation-signal interval used for depth profiling. It aligns sweeps to the arrival of sample-derived material at the detector, calculates downhole fractionation corrections across the full signal, and applies session corrections using standard plateau means. The workflow retains sweep-level observations with explicit uncertainty propagation, separates spot-mean calculation from depth-profile derivation, and supports data processing for common-Pb-rich phases and calibration against standards with heterogeneous distribution of radiogenic isotopes.

UPbJointInversion uses reduced data from in situ and whole-grain analyses and provides forward and inverse modeling capabilities for radiogenic-Pb production and diffusion through candidate thermal histories. It supports depth-profile-only, whole-grain-only, and joint inversions using one-dimensional models or explicit three-dimensional grain geometries. Grain geometry, diffusion kinetics, boundary conditions, depth calibration, and associated uncertainties are incorporated explicitly rather than condensed into a single effective closure temperature.

We demonstrate the paired workflow using synthetic data as well as measured U-Pb data from the Adirondack Highlands that combine LA–ICP–MS depth profiles and whole-grain ID–TIMS analyses. Together, these tools provide a reproducible pathway from raw analytical data to thermal-history inference from minerals that experienced diffusive Pb loss.
