title: Provenance and Transport Pathways of Supraglacial, Englacial, and Subglacial Debris in a Fault-Bounded Glacier System
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations (Posters)
authors: Adamson-Endres, Elias Lee [1], Kopczynski, Sarah E. [2], Kar, Nandini [3]
affiliations: (1) SUNY, Brockport, Earth Sciences, Johnson City, NY, USA
(2) Glacier View, AK,
(3) SUNY, Brockport, Earth Sciences, Brockport, NY, USA
abstract: This project investigates the provenance, lithologic diversity, and transport pathways of glacially transported debris at the Matanuska Glacier in south-central Alaska. This glacier is suited for this study because the Border Ranges Fault cuts directly through its flowline, dividing the glacier between two distinct bedrock terrains: the Chugach Terrane made up of sedimentary and meta-sedimentary rocks such as phyllite, greywacke, and meta-greywacke underlying the upper half of the glacier, and the Peninsular Terrane made up of various igneous and meta-igneous lithologies such as tuffs, granites, andesites, and basalts underlying the lower half of the glacier to the terminus. Because of this, debris carried by the ice can be traced to their sources with great accuracy and differences in lithology can reveal transport histories. 709 samples were collected from transects at the glacier terminus and 50 samples have been collected from the largest medial moraine up-glacier towards the glacier’s origin. Lithologies were identified using hand-sample characteristics and accessory mineral analysis, while roundness was quantified with a standardized visual comparison chart. Fisher’s Exact Test was used to assess whether moraine-derived material is compositionally distinct, whether roundness varies by depositional zone, and if englacial material is distinct from subglacial material. Results show that provenance signals from the medial moraine are only partially preserved at the terminus, where debris mixing obscures more detailed lithologic differences, though broader patterns remain detectable. It was also found that lithologic composition clearly distinguishes between englacial and subglacial debris, while clast roundness does not. The fault-bounded terrane contrast at the Matanuska Glacier allows transport pathways to be distinguished using lithologic composition even where textural characteristics are indistinguishable. Understanding these processes contributes to glaciological knowledge of how debris is moved and deposited, with implications for reconstructing past glaciations, for analyzing behavior of glaciers today, and for predicting how glacial landscapes will change in the future with a warming climate.

title: Shining a new light on modern raptor pellets as taphonomic analogues
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Toon, Kyle A. [1], Selly, Tara [2], Jacquet, Sarah M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA; X-ray Microanalysis Laboratory, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract:
Fossil evidence indicates ancient animals have utilized regurgitation as a means of removing indigestible materials since the Early Permian (~290 Ma). Bromalites, which include coprolites (fossilized feces), cololites (gut contents), and regurgitalites (fossilized regurgitate materials), are the fossilized digestive contents of ancient organisms. Bromalites can provide insight into extinct or ancient predator-prey relationships, feeding habits, and predator digestive systems. This study pairs high powered imaging with the examination of modern raptor regurgitation pellets (RPs) to characterize regurgitate production, contents, and potential for preservation as a framework for interpreting fossil regurgitalites, and further reconstruct feeding ecology and trophic interactions of extinct communities.

RPs were collected from the University of Missouri’s Raptor Rehabilitation Project from Tyto furcata (American barn owl), Strix varia (barred owl), Haliaeetus leucocephalus (bald eagle), and Buteo lineatus (red shouldered hawk). These species were selected for their variety of digestive characteristics which includes stomach acidity. Regurgitate samples were imaged using X-ray microcomputed tomography (µCT) at the University of Missouri-Columbia X-ray Microanalysis Laboratory, allowing nondestructive, three-dimensional visualization of their internal structures and inclusions. Datasets were reconstructed using Dragonfly Comet 3D software and segmented using an AI-trained algorithm to identify and quantify tissue, fur, and bone elements and characterize their taphonomic grades. Preliminary results show that RP content preservation and element fragmentation, orientation and distribution vary between taxa, and in some cases within the same taxa. Contrary to traditional methods of physical (wet/dry) disaggregation, this non-destructive method preserves the ultrastructure of the pellet which may be useful in comparisons with fossilized analogues.

title: Pore-Water Salinity Alters the Geotechnical Behavior of Landslide-Prone Pittsburgh Red Bed Mudstones
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment (Posters)
authors: Ayo-Bali, Abiodun Emmanuel [1], Bain, Daniel J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA,
abstract: Clay-rich mudstones are an important control on landslide development in southwestern Pennsylvania, yet the influence of road-salt contamination on their geotechnical behavior remains poorly understood. A key unresolved question is whether salinization and repeated salt-flushing cycles can alter the engineering properties of failure-prone mudstones sufficiently to influence slope stability. Previous studies have largely focused on salt-related deterioration of infrastructure, leaving the response of clay-rich geologic materials comparatively understudied. To address this problem, we combined mineralogical characterization with laboratory geotechnical testing of Pittsburgh Red Bed mudstones subjected to increasing NaCl concentrations and repeated salinization-freshwater cycling. Quantitative X-ray diffraction indicates that the mudstones are dominated by low-swelling chlorite and illite with no discrete smectite, yet increasing salinity and repeated salt-freshwater cycling produced measurable changes in Atterberg limits and a progressive decline in swelling index (Cs) across successive treatment cycles. These results demonstrate that repeated salinization can progressively alter the hydro-mechanical behavior of clay-rich hillslope materials even in the absence of highly expansive clay minerals, suggesting that widespread road-salt use may contribute to previously unrecognized changes in landslide-prone slopes.

abstract:
On April 20, 2025, NASA’s Lucy spacecraft [1] completed its closest approach with main-belt asteroid (52246) Donaldjohanson [2]. Donaldjohanson appears to be a contact binary and is about 8.8 km long [2]. High resolution images from L’LORRI (Lucy Long Range Reconnaissance Imager) [3] throughout the flyby show linear clusters of depressions, or pit chains, across Donaldjohanson’s imaged surface.

The term “pit chain” is not diagnostic of formation mechanism, and these features can form from a range of processes including primary or secondary impacts, venting, or dilational faulting [e.g., 4–6]. We will discuss the most likely formation mechanism(s) for the pit chains on Donaldjohanson and compare the morphology of these features with that of pit chains observed on other small bodies such as (433) Eros, Phobos, (243) Ida, and (951) Gaspra [7–12].

Under the assumption that Donaldjohanson’s pit chains form due to the drainage of unconsolidated material into subsurface structures, we will use the depths of these pits to calculate a minimum thickness for a layer of unconsolidated regolith-like material on the surface of Donaldjohanson. We will compare this estimate with regolith thickness estimates from the study of impact craters on Donaldjohanson as well as estimates from prior studies of pit chains on small bodies.

title: Examining the trace element geochemistry of Globorotalia scitula as a potential tracer of past oxygen minimum zone intensity
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Hupp, Brittany N. [1], Fehrenbacher, Jennifer S. [2], Alcorn, Rachel C. [3], Davis, Catherine [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Atmospheric, Oceanic and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA

abstract: It is well documented that our oceans are experiencing deoxygenation. However, as the Earth continues to warm, it is unclear if oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) will continue to intensify or contract. Given this uncertainty, it is critical to have multiple robust proxies available to probe paleorecords for additional insight into processes modulating ocean oxygenation. Here we present intriguing results investigating the trace element geochemistry (i.e., Mg, Na, Sr, Ba, Mn, Zn) of modern specimens of planktic foraminifer Globorotalia scitula collected from the Northern California Current via plankton tow. The depth habitat of this taxon has been shown to intersect the oxygen minimum zone depending upon the vertical extent of the OMZ. Preliminary results suggest that the combined usage of Ba/Ca and Mn/Ca in G. scitula may serve as a tracer of dissolved oxygen levels in the subsurface water column. Specimens found living in environments where dissolved oxygen was <3 mg/L exhibit Ba/Ca and Mn/Ca values that are on average 5x and 3x higher, respectively, than shells collected from oxic conditions. Significant positive covariation is found between whole-shell Ba/Ca and Mn/Ca (R 2 =0.48; p < 0.0005), but not between any other trace elements examined. This positive covariance increases in strength when examined at the individual chamber level, particularly in older chambers (i.e., F2, F3). Lastly, both Ba/Ca and Mn/Ca were found to be highest in the oldest chambers (F3) and decreased with progressively younger chambers. Analysis of a larger dataset will further constrain Ba/Ca and Mn/Ca values across oxygenation levels. These results show great promise for the coupled examination of Ba/Ca and Mn/Ca in fossil specimens of G. scitula to delineate oxygen conditions in the subsurface, providing a novel approach for reconstructing OMZ intensity.

title: pH-Dependent Phosphate Oxygen Isotope Fractionation in Extremophiles: Refining Biosignature and Temperature Proxies
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry (Posters)
authors: Dhiman, Gareema [1], Moller, Spencer R. [2], Wostbrock, Jordan A.G. [3], Blake, Ruth E. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA; Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Behavior, University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(4) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT,
abstract:
The oxygen isotope composition of inorganic phosphate (δ 18 O P ) has recently emerged as a robust proxy to determine environmental and cellular/tissue specific temperatures, intracellular water oxygen isotope (δ 18 O W ) values, and the detection of life (e.g., biosignatures) in extreme environments. These applications are based on the temperature dependent, equilibrium oxygen isotope exchange that occurs within the intracellular dissolved inorganic orthophosphate (P i , including, PO 4 3- , HPO 4 2- , H 2 PO 4 - , H 3 PO 4 ) pool before P i is incorporated into phosphatic biomolecules. However, precise calibration of P i -H 2 O oxygen isotope fractionation has been limited to slightly basic (i.e. marine systems) or near-neutral pH conditions. The influence of pH on oxygen isotope fractionation in biological systems remains untested, despite a previous abiotic study reporting significant pH-dependent P i -H 2 O oxygen isotope fractionation.

Here, we evaluate the influence of pH on P i -H 2 O oxygen isotope fractionation in extremophilic microorganisms, including acidophilic, alkaliphilic, microaerophilic, anaerobic, and aerobic bacteria and archaea, using both δ 18 O P and triple oxygen isotope (TOI) analysis (paired δ 17 O-δ 18 O values). δ 18 O P values reflect the effect of pH on P i -H 2 O oxygen isotope fractionation, whereas the TOI measurements enable a clear distinction between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism as indicated by the amount of metabolic water contributing to the intracellular water pool that exchanges with intracellular P i . Aerobic organisms were incubated under both shaking and non-shaking conditions to examine the effects of aeration/oxygenation on metabolic water production and oxygen isotope signatures associated with aerobic respiration. Biomass was harvested during the early stationary growth phase, and P i was isolated and precipitated as Ag 3 PO 4 for oxygen isotope analyses.

Preliminary results demonstrate successful growth of bacterial and archaeal strains across the experimental pH range (pH 3–11). Biomass P i concentrations for initial shaking and non-shaking aerobic cultures, averaged 16.08 μmol/g P i and 21.79μmol/g P i , respectively. Wet biomass yields ranged from 33–49 g, indicating comparable P i recovery and biomass production between the two conditions. Ongoing isotope analyses will determine whether pH influences biologically mediated P i -H 2 O oxygen isotope fractionation and whether TOI values vary with metabolic style. These findings will refine the application of δ 18 O P values as a biosignature, temperature proxy, and tracer of phosphorus biogeochemical cycling while advancing the use of TOI measurements to understand metabolic pathways of extremophiles.

title: Holocene drought-driven re-mobilization of a barchan dune in the Nebraska Sand Hills
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Holuša, Jakub [1], Hanson, Paul [2]
affiliations: (1) Polar-Geo-Lab, Department of Geography, Faculty of Science, Masaryk University, Brno, Czech Republic; Conservation and Survey Division, School of Natural Resources, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
(2) Conservation and Survey Division, School of Natural Resources, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
abstract:
The Nebraska Sand Hills are the largest dune field in the western Hemisphere, covering approximately 50,000 km 2 . The dunes have been historically grass-covered, but the dunes which were active during the Late Pleistocene were also re-mobilized four times during four major Holocene droughts. These are evidenced by dune movements between 9.6-6.5 ka, and shorter drought events dated to ~4.1, 2.5 and 0.8 ka, the latter corresponding to the Medieval Climate Anomaly. The approximate timing of reactivation during those periods is established; however, the amount of re-mobilized sand during each of those events remains unknown.

We aim to generate a four-dimensional map of a large barchan dune to determine how the sand within the dune was re-mobilized and to quantify how much sand is preserved from these periods of dune movement. To do so, we will evaluate dune morphologies using LiDAR and subsurface materials using geological maps and soil data and we will collect cores to obtain samples that will be analysed using a sampling strategy for OSL dating. We will also characterize sediments and soils by particle size analysis. Furthermore, ground-penetrating radar profiles will be conducted over the barchan dune to cross-check the data obtained from our OSL dating results.

title: Revisiting the 2016 Sooner Lake Earthquake: An Updated Look at Fault Complexity and Stress Interactions
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Carpenter, Brett M. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
abstract: Induced seismicity continues to be a concern in regions of wastewater disposal, hydrocarbon production, carbon sequestration, and enhanced geothermal operations. The state of Oklahoma experienced widespread seismicity from 2009-2019, including the 2016 M5.8 Sooner Lake earthquake. The majority of this seismicity has been attributed to the reactivation of pre-existing and critically-stressed faults due to decades of wastewater injection. While the overall rate of seismicity has been at reduced levels, events, such as the 2024 swarm near Edmond (~20 events) and the 2024 M5.1 near Prague, show that Oklahoma’s basement remains susceptible to seismic reactivation. This work revisits the Sooner Lake earthquake by expanding our knowledge of fault geometry/complexity via seismicity mapping and then using that data in stress analyses. Multiple catalogs of seismicity and focal mechanisms were used to map and constrain fault geometry and complexity in the vicinity of the Sooner Lake Fault (SLF). In the course of this analyses, several new structures were identified. Utilizing Fault Slip Potential 2.0 and Coulomb Modeling 3.4 software, we then assessed foreshock stress transfer (triggering) related to two published hypotheses and the migration of seismicity following the mainshock. Our stress analyses show that: the time-dependent migration/pattern of seismicity along the SLF and nearby faults is consistent with stress transfer after the mainshock; and while both foreshock hypotheses are plausible, triggering from the June 8 event was more likely. Updated and improved earthquake catalogs allowed for the identification of additional structures, and their complexity, in the vicinity of the Sooner Lake Fault. With improved inputs, stress analyses allowed for the testing of foreshock hypotheses and improved understanding of seismicity migration after the mainshock. The combined results of this work highlight the importance of constraining structure and stress to better understand earthquake triggering and aftershock migration.

title: More Than Pretty Colors: New Airborne Geophysical Data Reveal the Geophysical Framework of Critical Mineral Systems in the South-Central United States
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Amaral, Chelsea M. [1], McCafferty, Anne E. [2], Connell, Dylan M. [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract: The South-Central US hosts multiple critical mineral systems, however, understanding of their geological framework is hindered due to concealment beneath sediments, alluvium, and vegetation. Airborne magnetic data provide valuable information for mapping geologic structures at and below the surface, whereas radiometric data map near-surface radioelement (K, U, Th) concentrations that may indicate zones of alteration and serve as vectors towards mineralization. As part of the US Geological Survey’s Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) effort to modernize the Nation’s geologic and mineral resource mapping, eight high-resolution magnetic and radiometric surveys have been flown across the South-Central region since 2019, and two additional surveys are ongoing. The surveys were designed with state geological survey partners to target known critical mineral systems and areas of high critical mineral potential. More than tripling the resolution of legacy datasets, these surveys are flown along flight lines spaced 150 to 400 m apart at a nominal 80 to 100 m above ground level. Recently completed (2024-2025) and active Earth MRI airborne geophysical surveys in the South-Central US cover the Ozark Plateau and Upper Mississippi River Valley regions, where overlapping mineral systems have produced world-renowned mining districts. The high-resolution data offer new perspectives of the Paleozoic sedimentary section and the architecture of the mostly buried Precambrian crystalline basement. In Missouri and eastern Kansas, magnetic data show subsurface structures that likely facilitated formation of Mississippi-Valley type (MVT) Zn-Pb deposits in the Tri-State Mining District. The new data also reveal anomalies in other parts of the Eastern Granite Rhyolite terrane with similar characteristics to known critical-mineral bearing iron-oxide-apatite (IOA) and iron-oxide-copper-gold deposits in the Southeast Missouri Metallogenic Province. The Pea Ridge IOA-rare earth element (REE) deposit in Missouri was previously mined for magnetite and iron ore. At the surface, the highest Th values in the entire survey area occur over the exposed Pea Ridge mine tailings and are attributed to apatite and other Th-REE-bearing minerals. These examples highlight valuable geologic and mineral deposit insights derived from Earth MRI geophysical data, with additional use cases in studies of energy and water resources, natural hazards, and infrastructure and land-use planning.

title: Beyond Flying Drones: Lessons Learned from an Interdisciplinary Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience in Geoscience
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Baker, Gregory S. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Energy, and Environment, University Of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
abstract: Small uncrewed aircraft systems (sUAS, aka drones) are becoming increasingly important tools in Earth and environmental science, yet many university courses emphasize drone operation and software rather than scientific investigation. This presentation describes lessons learned from four offerings of a course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) designed to use drone technology as a vehicle for teaching hypothesis-driven research. The course enrolled 8–18 students per offering and intentionally combined sophomores, juniors, seniors, and graduate students from diverse academic backgrounds. Approximately 30% of participants were geology majors, while the remainder represented a variety of disciplines including environmental studies, biology, ecology, business, physics, urban planning, and criminal justice. Rather than completing prescribed laboratory exercises, student teams developed original research questions, designed field investigations, acquired and analyzed drone-derived data, and communicated their findings through professional oral presentations and written reports. Research topics reflected wide-ranging student interests and included geologic mapping, sediment transport, critical mineral exploration, crime-scene footprint mapping, transportation infrastructure, parking-lot optimization, dinosaur track mapping, forest road planning, and environmental monitoring. A subset of students also presented their projects at the university’s undergraduate research symposium. Instructor observations, peer feedback, and audience evaluations consistently identified several themes across the four course offerings. Mixed-major interactions produced some of the strongest connections by combining complementary disciplinary perspectives and technical skills. Students generally mastered drone operation and data processing rapidly but required substantially more guidance in developing testable hypotheses and designing rigorous experiments. The greatest improvement occurred in scientific communication, with students demonstrating substantial growth in presenting quantitative evidence and defending conclusions. These experiences suggest that drone-based CUREs are most effective when technology serves as a platform for authentic scientific inquiry rather than the primary instructional objective. The instructional strategies and lessons learned provide a transferable framework for implementing interdisciplinary, hypothesis-driven geoscience CUREs that prepare students to apply emerging technologies to real-world Earth and environmental problems.

title: Tectonic Relations to Chert-Forming Silicification Processes of the Leithsville Formation of Sussex County, New Jersey
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Siqueiros-Gonzalez, Alfredo Isaac [1], LaPorta, Philip Charles [2], Brewer-LaPorta, Margaret Colette [3]
affiliations: (1) Indiana University Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, South Bend, IN,
(2) The Center for the Investigation of Native and Ancient Quarries, Middletown, New York, USA; Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, New York, USA
(3) The Center for the Investigation of Native and Ancient Quarries, Middletown, NY, USA; Pace University Department of Chemistry and Physical Sciences, Pleasantville, NY, USA
abstract: The Early-Cambrian Leithsville Formation of Sussex County, New Jersey, has three members: Califon, Hamburg, and Wallkill. The Califon is shale or dolostone and the Hamburg is alternating layers of dolostone and sandstone with interspersed shale horizons. The Wallkill Member is dolostone and has chert nodules/beds in certain locations. This investigation tested a hypothesis by LaPorta (2009) that attributed chert formation to the dissolution of silica during Taconic orogeny tectonic loading. Silica sources are thought to be cratonically derived clays, bentonitic ash, and marine transgressive quartz sand sequences. The hypothesis was tested using rock fabric measurements made from field observations, rock slabs, and thin section analyses. The presence of fracture cleavages in dolostone and chert in the Wallkill Member revises the hypothesis of tectonic loading as a chert-forming mechanism. The fractures suggest that cherts in the lower Wallkill were lithified prior to tectonic loading. However, field observation and slab analysis of the upper Wallkill cherts show a second phase of pressure solution silicification. Upper cherts have an internal lighter silicification phase with an exterior darker phase. Early-Cambrian faulting and stylolites provided channels for silica solution movement, with fracture cleavages providing additional permeability for the second silicification phase.

title: Can tourmaline vein mineralogy be an effective exploration vector for porphyry mineralization?: A case study of the Haib porphyry deposit, Namibia
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Friehauf, Abe [1], Friehauf, Kurt [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
(2) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
abstract:
The Haib porphyry copper deposit, hosted by the 1.88 Ga Paleoproterozoic Richtersveld Arc of southern Namibia, is one of the world’s oldest well-preserved porphyry deposits [Meng et al., 2021]. The deposit contains an indicated resource of 511 Mt averaging 0.33% Cu and 51 ppm Mo [Koryx, 2025]. Mineralization is centered on potassically-altered granodiorite porphyry, with peripheral chloritic and local sericitic alteration. Exploration drilling 2 km ENE of the proposed pit intersected a barren tourmaline breccia potentially related to late-stage or distal hydrothermal fluids. Tourmaline veins, commonly 5 mm wide (range 1–7 mm), cut feldspar porphyry and granodiorite porphyry.

We analyzed samples spanning 100m of the distal drill hole and one proximal sample from within the proposed pit using Field-emission scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectrometry and X-ray diffraction to assess vertical and lateral variations in vein mineralogy and tourmaline composition.

All tourmaline veins contain Fe-bearing chlorite, fluorapatite, quartz, and rutile. Distal veins additionally contain ubiquitous calcite, magnetite, muscovite, and ilmenite. Rare-earth elements occur in monazite in the shallow distal breccia with calcioancylite and synchysite at depth. The proximal sample contains chalcopyrite and K-feldspar/anorthoclase but lacks muscovite.

Tourmaline grains are mostly 30–100µm in diameter (locally 200µm) and average ~100µm long, reaching 500µm. Most tourmaline is hydroxy-dravite–schorl solid solution (Ca:Na <0.1). X Na ranges from 0.54 to 1.00, clustering at 0.9–1.0, with neither systematic vertical variation nor distal–proximal differences. Tourmaline contains no detectable F but is consistently associated with fluorapatite. Mg:Fe ratios are bimodal, with modes centered at 1.45 and 1.85. Higher Mg:Fe correlates with Al, while Fe correlates negatively with Al, suggesting Fe³⁺ substitution in the Z site. Individual grains exhibit zoning with varying Mg:Fe ratio, possibly recording variable and fluctuating redox conditions. Shallow samples span a wider Mg:Fe range, but average compositions remain constant vertically. Average Mg:Fe is higher distally (1.5) than proximally (1.25). Mn is near detection limits and shows no vertical zoning; proximal tourmaline lacks Mn. Ti ranges from 0 to 0.74 cations (Y+Z = 9), averaging 0.25–0.30 at all depths.

Our small dataset suggests tourmaline mineralogy and major element geochemistry in breccias would not be useful for mineral exploration vectoring in the Haib district (in contrast to trace element successes in other districts).

title: Bioleaching of critical elements from ultramafic minerals with synthetic biology
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources
authors: Gazel, Esteban [1], Klug, Jacob D. [2], Plante, Luke [3], Adair, James L. [4], Almansoori, Alia [5], Lee, Joseph J. [6], Murillo Maikut, Stephanie [7], Barstow, Buz [8]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell Univeristy, Ithaca, NY, USA
(3) Department of Chemical and Biological Science and Engineering, United States Military Academy, West Point, NY, USA
(4) Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
(5) Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
(6) Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
(7) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
(8) Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
abstract: As the world demand for critical elements needed for energy storage (e.g., Ni, Co, Cr) exponentially increases, the need for non-conventional sources becomes more urgent. Ultramafic minerals are an important reservoir of these energy-critical elements, but they are bound within silicate structures making it challenging to separate them, and thus most current mined sources are laterites. These deposits resulted from extensive weathering, taking geologic time scales for dissolution and concentration. Carbon mineralization of ultramafic rocks is also a promising approach for long-term carbon dioxide removal from the atmosphere. Therefore, a strategy for accelerating weathering of ultramafic rocks is fundamental. We investigated whether an engineered strain of Gluconobacter oxydans (B58 ∆pstS, P112:mgdh) can accelerate weathering to simultaneously bioleach critical elements (e.g., Ni) and sequester carbon from ultramafic minerals (olivine and enstatitie). These minerals were bioleached at low-temperature conditions (30 °C) and with 5% pulp density in direct contact with the engineered microbes and by separating the biolixiviant from the living cells. Experiments with direct interaction of G. oxydans with ultramafic minerals evolved from white to dark red/brown, witch likely resulted from a redox reaction (Fe 2+ to Fe 3+ ). This reaction has been observed where microbes oxidize Fe as an energy source or to limit Fe 2+ toxicity. We also found that G. oxydans interaction with ultramafic minerals also enables the precipitation of magnesium oxalate, a pathway with twice the carbon storage capacity of magnesite. Oxalic acid was identified in the biolixiviant produced by G. oxydans and Mg-oxalate formation was most efficient at low pH. SEM and XRD analyses indicate extensive olivine dissolution and coating by Mg-oxalate and amorphous silica. Mass balance calculations suggest that G. oxydans leached up to 75% of the Mg hosted in the starting materials, while only 11% of leached Mg reacted to sequester carbon as Mg-oxalate after 15 days. During this time the solution reached ~8000 pm Mg and ~80 ppm Ni, leaving only 25% of Mg in the residual olivine that did not react. The enhanced sequestration potential of Mg-oxalate, coupled with bio-accelerated critical element leaching presents a promising opportunity for global carbon storage and opens new, non-conventional, sources of critical elements.

title: STRUCTURAL CONTROLS AT CAVE HILL, VIRGINIA, REVEALED BY INTEGRATED LIDAR-SLAM CAVE MAPPING AND DRONE-BASED LIDAR SURVEYS
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science
authors: Petrova, Maria D. [1], García, Ángel A. [2], Adamassu, Yonathan [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA, USA
abstract:
Cave Hill, located in Grottoes, Virginia, contains more than 20 surveyed caves, including Grand Caverns, the oldest continuously operating show cave in the contiguous United States. The exceptional accessibility of these caves provides a unique natural laboratory for investigating the relationships among structural deformation, karst evolution, and cave development in the Appalachian Valley and Ridge province. This study integrates georeferenced high-density point clouds (HDPCs) acquired through LiDAR-SLAM surveys of Madison Saltpetre Cave, Grand Caverns, Forgotten Saltpetre Cave, Jefferson’s Cave, and Fountain Cave with drone-based LiDAR mapping of Cave Hill to evaluate links between cave geometry, bedding orientation, and surface geomorphology.

The resulting dataset comprises approximately 804.5 million georeferenced points and a high-resolution digital elevation model covering 1.61 km² at 6.72 cm pixel resolution. Analysis of the LiDAR-derived terrain model identified 27 dolines that exhibit substantial variability in morphology, orientation, area, volume, and base-level elevation. Comparisons of surface and subsurface datasets reveal pronounced differences between the northern and central-southern sectors of Cave Hill, including contrasts in cave elevation, passage orientation, bedding attitude, and doline distribution.

Structural measurements define two distinct domains. The Western Domain, encompassing Grand Caverns, Madison Saltpetre Cave, and Jefferson’s Cave, is characterized by steeply dipping, north-south-striking beds. In contrast, the Eastern Domain, represented by Fountain Cave and Forgotten Saltpetre Cave, contains gently south-dipping strata. These contrasting structural relationships are consistent with deformation associated with either a fault-bend fold or a fault-propagation fold, both implying an asymmetric fold geometry linked to a possible NNE-SSW-trending reverse fault. Such a structure may have influenced groundwater flow pathways and localized speleogenesis across Cave Hill. These results demonstrate the utility of integrated cave and surface LiDAR datasets for resolving structural controls on karst development, hydrologic connectivity, and landscape evolution in complex carbonate terrains of the Appalachian region.

title: Preliminary Pressure-Temperature Constraints on Migmatization Within the Norumbega Fault System, South-Central Maine
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Baxendell, Nivale E [1], Castro, Adrian E. [2], Roberts, Nicolas M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(3) Geosciences, Hamilton College, Clinton, NY, USA
abstract:
Deformation within active strike-slip fault systems is well documented in the shallow crust, and restraining bends are recognized as important sites of strain localization. However, the processes accommodating deformation in the deep crust remain poorly understood because they are inaccessible in active plate-boundary settings. The Androscoggin Riverlands State Park in south-central Maine exposes mid-crustal rocks within a restraining bend on a splay of the Norumbega fault system. This provides an opportunity to investigate the role of metamorphism and partial melting in strain localization during deep-crustal transpressional deformation. To constrain the conditions under which deformation occurred, we integrate petrography and phase equilibria modeling to reconstruct the pressure–temperature (P–T) history of migmatitic rocks.

We present preliminary results from two metasedimentary migmatites (NMR-24-04 and NMR-24-06). Sample NMR-24-06 is a strongly restitic migmatite characterized by abundant biotite, garnet-bearing leucosomes, and textures consistent with biotite-dehydration melting. Phase equilibria modeling indicates peak metamorphic conditions of approximately 725–750 °C and 4–7 kbar, with melt stable at peak conditions. Sample NMR-24-04 records a similar low-pressure, high-temperature mineral assemblage consisting of garnet, biotite, sillimanite, plagioclase, quartz, and muscovite, with petrographic evidence for both muscovite-out and biotite-out melting reactions producing peritectic aluminosilicate and garnet, respectively. Preliminary phase equilibria modeling suggests subsequent near-isobaric cooling from peak conditions.

These preliminary results suggest these rocks record a clockwise, low-pressure, high-temperature P–T metamorphism accompanied by partial melting within the restraining bend. The inferred conditions are consistent with thermal input from Devonian gabbro emplacement and suggest that migmatization may have weakened the middle crust, promoting localization of deformation into adjacent high-strain shear zones. This work will be supplemented with outcrop- and thin section-scale structural analysis, traditional thermobarometry, and zircon/monazite U-Pb petrochronology to further constrain the pressure–temperature–time–deformation evolution of these rocks and provide further insight into the interplay between metamorphism, anatexis, and deformation in the deep crust of a strike-slip system.

title: Distinguishing Between Seismically Induced and Flood-Derived Event Deposits in a Guatemalan Karst Lake
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: McEnaney, Trenton Nickalaus [1], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences & Engineering, Missouri University of Science & Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(2) Earth Sciences & Engineering, Missouri University of Science & Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
abstract: Lacustrine event deposits preserve a valuable record of past environmental change, but distinguishing seismically induced turbidites from flood derived deposits remains challenging. Lake Chichój, a karst lake situated adjacent to the Polochic Fault in central Guatemala, provides an ideal archive for evaluating sedimentary responses to tectonic and hydrologic processes along the North American–Caribbean plate boundary. This study uses sedimentological observations and high-resolution X-ray fluorescence (XRF) core scans to characterize event deposits and identify their dominant sediment provenance. Most turbidites display clear fining upward grain size trends that include erosional or scoured basal contacts, parallel laminations, and ripple cross laminations. Statistical analyses of the XRF dataset indicate differences in turbidite composition based on carbonate content and detrital elements with a secondary variability related to redox conditions. Three statistically distinct event deposits are distinguished based on geochemical clusters. The first turbidite group is defined by carbonate enrichment, reflected in elevated Ca/Ti and Ca/Rb, a signature consistent with remobilization of carbonate-rich lake-floor sediment during subaqueous slope failure. The second is defined by a stronger detrital signature, marked by high Rb/Sr and correspondingly depleted Ca/Ti, consistent with increased terrigenous influx from the catchment. The third group consists of a more complex geochemical signal complicating interpretations of possible origins. It is characterized by elevated Zr/Rb and highly variable Ca/Ti and occupies a correspondingly broad region in PCA space. The coarse grain size implied by elevated Zr/Rb, combined with the heterogeneous composition, is consistent with a mixed-source provenance. Integrating sedimentary facies, XRF-based geochemistry, and multivariate statistics provide a framework for distinguishing event triggering mechanisms and improves identification of earthquake generated turbidites in lacustrine paleoseismic records.

title: Taphonomic and Sedimentary Influences on Fossil Preservation from the Lowermost Jurassic of Nevada
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record (Posters)
authors: Justice, Ian M. [1], Monarrez, Pedro M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
abstract: The Ferguson Hill Member of the Lower Jurassic Sunrise Formation in the New York Canyon area in Nevada is one of just a few fossiliferous deposits that preserve a shallow marine environment in the immediate aftermath of the end-Triassic mass extinction. It has thus been studied extensively to better understand how benthic ecosystems recovered in the earliest Jurassic. However, the extent to which differential taphonomic conditions might create preservational biases in these assemblages has not been as thoroughly described. Assessing the taphonomy of the fossil material can help determine whether previously observed patterns of biotic recovery reflect true biological processes or if interpretations of recovery need to be reassessed. Here we preliminarily evaluate the taphonomy of marine benthic organisms from the Hettangian to lower Sinemurian of the Ferguson Hill Member of the Sunrise Formation within a stratigraphic and facies context to assess whether preservational biases are influencing interpretations of extinction recovery. We collected hand samples and created thin sections from throughout the Ferguson Hill Member to assess how the taphonomic condition of skeletal remains changed through time and across different facies. The Ferguson Hill Member represents a progradational parasequence, spanning offshore to shallow subtidal environments. Preliminary observations of macrofossils suggest preferential preservation of fossils with original calcite material (pectinids and brachiopods) and fossils that underwent silicification (e.g., corals, some bivalves), with aragonite-precipitating organisms primarily preserved as steinkerns and molds. Thin section analysis will provide insight into the nature of shell preservation that is not visible from hand samples. These results will provide insights into the current framework of understanding the recovery of the end-Triassic mass extinction in Nevada and the role taphonomy plays in our understanding and interpretation of post extinction recovery dynamics.

title: Analyzing Patterns in Morphology and Mineralogy of Interdunes at Olympia Undae, Mars
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Elalaoui-Pinedo, Dora [1], Bishop, Janice L. [2], Fenton, Lori K. [3], Gruendler, Markus R. D. [4], Itoh, Yuki [5], Yanez, Katya L. [6], Parente, Mario [7], Szynkiewicz, Ania [8], Zuschneid, Wilhelm [9], Gross, Christoph [10], Gibson, Tatiana [11]

abstract:
Olympia Undae is the largest dune field on Mars, partly encircling Planum Boreum, the north polar ice cap. Uniquely, its dark dunes contain a substantial fraction of gypsum, unlike most Martian dunes, which consist of basalt. Gypsum is typically found in ancient Martian terrains (>3.7 Ga), so its presence in these young dunes (<300 Ma) is puzzling. The dunes are also intriguing due to bright-toned material observed between the dunes that likely represents the underlying basal unit. Our study characterizes morphological and mineralogical differences of these interdunes across Olympia Undae to understand the character and origins of the gypsum and associated salts, as interdunes may preserve exposed materials and formation processes distinct from the dunes.

We analyzed 5 hyperspectral images from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) that were processed to minimize atmospheric components and reduce noise, spanning 1-2.65 μm. We used High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images to catalog overlapping CRISM and HiRISE coverage. Using JMARS, a geospatial information system, we mapped and categorized interdune morphologies into four types: megaripples (~5-40 m spacing); light polygonal terrain (relatively bright, fractured terrain, ~0.5-3 m polygons); dark polygonal terrain (relatively dark, fractured terrain, ~3-10 m polygons); and intermixed polygonal terrain (relatively bright, fractured terrain ~2-5 m polygons with overlying dune-derived sand). We collected interdune spectra from each morphological category at 1×1 pixel resolution (18 m/px) using ENVI, a hyperspectral image analysis tool.

Current findings demonstrate strong gypsum absorption bands in megaripples and light polygonal terrain within eastern interdunes, consistent with the gypsum composition of surrounding dunes. In contrast, spectra of intermixed polygonal terrain in western interdunes exhibit weak gypsum signatures and different spectral features, consistent with rozenite or other hydrated iron sulfates. These features are indicated by a strong ferrous iron slope from 1.0-1.6 μm and a shift in the hydrated sulfate feature from 2.48 μm (gypsum) to 2.53 μm (rozenite). Additionally, polygonal cracking within interdunes suggests a past evaporite deposit, with evidence of secondary salt precipitation. Studying interdunes within Olympia Undae's gypsum-bearing dunes offers insight into aqueous processes in the northern circumpolar region, including the possible presence of additional evaporite minerals, and advances our understanding of the climate history on Mars and present-day polar processes.

title: Extending Coastal Dune Mapping Beyond Southeastern Queensland: A Morphological Analysis of the Stockyard Dune Field, Australia
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Messenger, Lauren [1], Patton, Nicholas [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(2) Geology, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
abstract: Dune mapping permits aeolian systems to be placed in a chronological framework, thereby allowing us to infer the potential mechanisms that drive both their activation and stabilization. For example, coastal dune activity has been associated with changes in primary productivity, where vegetation growth prevents sediment availability and reduces wind speeds. More recently, extensive dating and mapping efforts in the Southeastern Queensland (SEQ) coastal dune fields have highlighted the role of sea-level variability and storm events, especially within the Holocene sections where these absolute dating techniques are more precise.This study aims to expand the mapping efforts on the east coast of Australia and determine if these observations remain consistent. The area of focus for this project is in Stockyard, a coastal town, 550 km north of Brisbane, Australia. We chose to map this area because of the close proximity to the SEQ dune fields (i.e., K’gari (Fraser Island), Cooloola, Moorgumpin (Moreton Island), and Minjerribah (North Stradbrook Island)), which are derived from a comparable quartz sand, and are inferred to have evolved in a similar manor. At least 80 dunes are within the area; most are parabolic dunes as indicated by the crest and trailing arms of each dune. The dunes here travel inland from the coast as far as 13 km, reaching up to 250 m above sea level from a consistent, southeasterly wind. We delineated individual dunes at the base of the trailing arms and crest, and placed them in morphological units according to onlapping and cross-cutting relationships, as well as topographic indices. The mapped area consists of approximately 140 km 2 with about 5 km 2 of currently active dunes on or near the coastline. As expected, older dunes were typically the largest, furthest from the coastline, had smoother topography, and were often covered by smaller, younger dunes with rougher topography. Extending the mapping of the coastal dune fields helps test this mapping approach while testing whether sea-level rise and fall played a similar role in dune activity outside of the SEQ dune fields.

title: Spatial Variations in the Abundance, Type, And Morphology of Microplastics in Rivers, Lakes, and Coastal Environments
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Posters)
authors: Perez, Nicholas D. [1], Moore, Gavin [2], Smolen, Justin A. [3], Jaiswal, Kuhu [4], Sundell, Kurt [5], Nielsen, Ryan [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Department of Chemistry, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(3) Department of Chemistry, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(4) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(5) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(6) Idaho State Univ, Geology, Pocatello, ID,
abstract: Microplastics are omnipresent across the environment and throughout the global civilization’s food web. Despite emerging evidence of their distribution throughout human bodies and potential linkages to disease, the sources and dispersal of microplastics have remained challenging to quantify. We developed new protocols for separating microplastics from environmental sediment samples, and new approaches to the identification and quantification of microplastics using integrated image analysis, micro-Fourier Transform Infrared (µFTIR) Spectroscopy, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network trained on a µFTIR dataset by similarity learning. Samples were collected from rivers in Texas and Arkansas, along the Lake Tahoe shoreline, and beaches in South Africa and Costa Rica. We find that there are differences in the abundance and types of microplastics across these environments, suggesting regional differences in the land use practices and pathways for pollution to enter rivers, lakes, and coastal settings. Abundances ranged between 7 and 1468 identified microplastics per 100 grams of sediment. Nylon was among the most abundant microplastic observed and variably contributed ca. 6–83% of microplastics in individual samples. In contract, polycarbonate was relatively rare in most samples (between 0.01% and 18%), except in the Brazos River near Navasota TX, where it accounts for 47% of all microplastics observed. Further, we observed spatial variations in microplastics along a single river such as the Trinity River, where polycarbonate is relatively more abundant upstream in Dallas and Fort Worth, but decreases at downstream locations. We hypothesize that the interplay between numerous sources of microplastics, storage and reworking of microplastics along active depositional environments, and the disparate rate of microplastic breakdown in natural settings all contribute to variations in spatial microplastics signature across different parts of the world.

title: Relative roles of magmatic and hydrothermal processes on the extreme light rare earth element (LREE) enrichment in carbonatites: A case study from Kamthai, Rajasthan, India
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics
authors: Dasgupta, Rajdeep [1], Gupta, Ayush [2], Paul, Debajyoti [3], Costin, Gelu [4], Sun, Tao [5], Banerjee, Anupam [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, India; Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
(3) Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, India
(4) Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
(5) Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
(6) Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, India
abstract:
The association of rare earth elements (REEs) with carbonatite is well-known. However, the relative roles of magmatic and post-magmatic processes in enriching REEs remain debated. Here, we used whole-rock major- and trace-element geochemistry, petrography, mineral chemistry, and stable carbon and oxygen isotope ratios of carbonatites and alkaline silicate rocks from the Kamthai carbonatite complex in Rajasthan, India, to investigate the relative contributions of various processes to REE enrichment. Two main varieties, low-REE and high-REE calciocarbonatites (CC; CaO: 40–52.4 wt.%), are identified, with the latter abundant in alkali REE carbonates (carbocernaite), whereas the former lacks carbocernaite. The SREE in low-REE and high-REE CC are 0.6–2.7 wt.% (La/Yb N : 34–306) and ~14.3 wt.% (La/Yb N : 2100–2950), respectively. The isotope composition of the least altered carbonatite ( δ 13 C VPDB : –5.11‰, δ 18 O VSMOW : +6.9‰) and triple oxygen isotope compositions of alkaline silicate rocks ( δ' 18 O VSMOW : +4.34 to +6.21‰, δ' 17 O VSMOW : +2.24 to +3.23‰) suggest that they are mantle-derived.

To assess the relative contributions of various petrogenetic processes to REE enrichment, we modeled the Kamthai carbonatite using a series of steps, supported by field, petrologic, and geochemical data. A carbonated silicate parental melt, generated by low-degree partial melting of a primitive mantle source, undergoes fractionation and evolves towards the liquid immiscibility field. Such carbonatite melt produced from immiscibility undergoes prolonged crystal fractionation, which can reproduce the level of LREE enrichment observed in the high-REE carbonatites. Fluid exsolution in high-REE carbonatites also contributes to the LREE enrichment. The petrography of high-REE carbonatites indicates some degree of hydrothermal alteration, implying the influence of an orthomagmatic fluid in secondary REE mineralization (bastnäsite, ancylite, synchysite, etc). Our geochemical modelling suggests that the relative contributions of petrogenetic processes for stepwise LREE enrichment in the melt relative to that of high-REE carbonatites are partial melting (0.2–0.6%), fractional crystallization of olivine and clinopyroxene from the carbonated silicate melt (0.25–1.4%), liquid immiscibility (2.6–6.3%), fractional crystallization of calcite (≤64%) and fluid exsolution (up to 32%). The fractionation and exsolution model is proposed as a plausible mechanism for the extreme enrichment of LREEs in such carbonatites. Our study provides a framework for assessing the LREE enrichment mechanisms in carbonatite and quantifying the relative contributions of various magmatic and hydrothermal processes.

session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Lewis, Carter [1], Hunt, Lindsey Elise [2], Hayman, Nick [3]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK,
(2) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK,
(3) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK,
abstract:
The Wichita Igneous Province (WIP) is a large igneous province exposed in Wichita Mountains of southern Oklahoma. The outcrop exposure of the WIP is broadly elongate in shape and trends in the WNW direction. In the subsurface, the rocks of the WIP extend from north central Texas across western Oklahoma and the Texas panhandle and reach at least 12 km in depth. The WIP was emplaced in the Southern Oklahoma Aulocogen (SOA), a failed rift structure related to rifting along the Laurentian margin. Geochronological age dating places the formation of the WIP in the latest Ediacaran – earliest Cambrian during the opening of the Iapetus Ocean at the southern Laurentian margin.

Rocks of the WIP reflect bimodal magmatism and volcanism and consist of a layered mafic intrusion, peralkaline granite intrusions, rhyolite flows, flood basalts (subsurface only), and diabase dike swarms. Additionally, slivers of metamorphic rock can be found along igneous contacts and as stoped blocks. Here, we present whole rock geochemical data acquired through USGS EarthMRI funded projects along with Harker, REE, tectonic discrimination, and petrological diagrams to further characterize petrological and magmatic processes. The ultimate goal of this study is to place the geochemistry of the WIP in a mineral systems framework to understand the concentrations of critical minerals.

title: The taphonomy and preservation of soft-bodied fossils in the Lower-Middle Cambrian Emigrant Formation, Goldfield Hills, Nevada
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record (Posters)
authors: Hassan, Mo A. [1], Tarhan, Lidya [2], Gill, Benjamin Charles [3], Pruss, Sara B. [4]
affiliations: (1) Smith College, Northampton, Massachusetts, USA
(2) Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(3) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(4) Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
abstract: The Cambrian Explosion saw the introduction of complex body systems, sensory organs, and complex predator/prey interactions, marking it as one of the most significant events in the history of life. Widespread Cambrian Lagerstätten, which host fossils of soft-bodied organisms, have provided a key window into the Cambrian Explosion. Here, we report a new occurrence of soft-bodied preservation from the basal lower Cambrian Emigrant Formation in the Goldfield Hills, north-central Nevada, including algae, potential vermiform organisms, and well-preserved hyoliths with possible gut traces. Minimal degradation in a deep marine setting may have enhanced the exceptional preservation of these organisms. Within the collected fossil samples, some characteristics include “halos” or oxidized areas around the fossils and visible traces of oxidized iron on bedding plane surfaces. When analyzed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS), individual fossils show peaks in Fe, Mg, Ca and O and are hosted in clay-rich shale. Trace amounts of S are, in some instances, associated with Fe, suggesting pyritization of soft tissues (later transformed to Fe oxides, which frequently act as secondary diagenetic mineral replacement in Burgess Shale-type (BST) preservation). Fe oxides, and their relationship to Mg, Ca, and K, are similar to what has been found in the lower Cambrian Kinzers Formation of central Pennsylvania, which contain fossil assemblages that appear to be preserved in a similar way to those of the Emigrant Formation. Future work will focus on uncovering the full diversity of fossils preserved in this unit and the taphonomic conditions that enabled their preservation.

title: Mistaken identity? Snowball refrigeration of the Earth’s crust mimics glacial erosion
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records
authors: Flowers, Rebecca M [1], Macdonald, Francis A. [2], Anderson, Robert S. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
(2) University of California, Berkeley, CA,
(3) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
abstract:
The Cryogenian (717-635 Ma) Snowball Earth glaciations mark a period of extreme change in Earth’s atmosphere, biosphere, and hydrosphere. Massive glacial erosion assumed to have occurred during this interval has been appealed to as the cause of the Great Unconformity across the continents and as inducing enhanced nutrient flux that promoted late Neoproterozoic biological evolution. In support of this model, some thermochronologic datasets have been interpreted as recording syn-Snowball rock cooling signals, attributed to 3-5 km of glacial erosion globally on the continents. However, integrated thermochronologic and geologic datasets from a variety of locations provide evidence that the Great Unconformity formed diachronously through the Neoproterozoic and into the Paleozoic, supporting its origin by regional geodynamic and tectonic drivers rather than global glaciation. Moreover, extremely cold temperatures from Snowball climate models imply cold-based ice sheets that would have caused little erosion. If syn-Snowball rock cooling signals are indeed present in some thermochronologic datasets, and if glacial erosion did not cause them, then what did?

Glaciation cools the crust by reducing the surface temperature to 0°C or well below. The durations of the Snowball events govern the depth in the Earth to which the refrigeration penetrates. We calculate the thermal histories and thermochronologic dates of the crust during the Snowball Earth glaciations and find that the glacial boundary conditions were in place for long enough to cool the entire crustal column and substantially modify thermochronometers in the upper quarter to half of the crust. Refrigeration, with little to no synchronous erosion, can yield rock cooling signals that are indistinguishable from up to 3-5 km of glacial erosion. It therefore appears inescapable that during Snowball Earth, a cold thermal wave migrated deep into the Earth and imparted a simultaneous and global refrigeration imprint on thermochronometers that could be misinterpreted as glacial erosion. If syn-Snowball rock cooling signals are preserved on the continents, they are more appropriately attributed to a Snowball refrigeration of the Earth’s crust instead of massive global glacial erosion. As glacial erosion does not appear to be a feasible mechanism to produce the Great Unconformity, it should neither be invoked to boost the late Neoproterozoic nutrient flux nor as a putative driver of biological evolution.

title: Sea Level, Drought, and Salt Marsh Migration
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Wilson, Alicia M. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of the Earth, Ocean & Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA
abstract:
Sea level rise is an obvious cause of salt marsh migration, but salt marsh migration in a Georgia (USA) salt marsh occurred in pulses during a series of droughts. In contrast with recent field studies that have identified drought-related hydrologic changes but have not yet linked these to plant zone migration, the Georgia marsh shows clear plant zone migration but lacked hydrologic monitoring at the time. We instrumented this marsh in 2018 to monitor water levels and (intermittently) salinity. Groundwater models were then calibrated to the field observations and used to reconstruct groundwater flow patterns and salinity from 1998 to 2022.

The models showed recurrent winter expansion of the fresh groundwater lens, and hence freshening at the forest-marsh boundary, which is consistent with field observations from marshes in a wide range of climate zones. This freshening was markedly reduced or absent during drought. However, the winter salinities during drought were not obviously different from summer salinities, raising questions about why salt-adapted perennials would be affected. In our conceptual model, salinities at higher elevations of the forest-marsh boundary are stabilized by fresh groundwater discharge from the upland, whereas salinities at lower elevations are stabilized by frequent tidal inundation. The transition between these regimes migrates during winter sea level lows, with the freshwater lens expanding to cover areas that are not reached by tidal inundation. During drought, however, the freshwater lens failed to expand. We propose that drought allows a gap to form between the edge of the freshwater lens and the zone of frequent tidal inundation, creating a zone that is vulnerable to large fluctuations in salinity controlled by rainfall (or lack thereof during drought) and evapotranspiration. Large fluctuations in salinity can shock otherwise salt-tolerant plants, causing plant zone migration.

title: Shake it Up: A 45-Minute Shake Table Demonstration for Teaching Resonance and Seismic Risk to Non-Geology Majors
session_title: Iris Moreno Totten Research in Geoscience Education Session
authors: Gansler, Kathryn [1], Schmerr, Nicholas C. [2], Huang, Mong-Han [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, Riverdale, MD, USA
(2) Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA
(3) Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, College Park, MD, USA
abstract: "Earthquakes don't kill people, buildings do" is a common adage in seismology, yet few short, hands-on activities give students outside of geoscience and engineering majors the tools to quantitatively investigate why. We present a 45-minute activity intended for an undergraduate general education geology course. Students integrate basic seismology concepts including wave frequency and amplitude, the relationship between wave frequency and earthquake magnitude, building response to ground shaking, and earthquake mitigation strategies. We designed the activity following Kolb's (1984) cycle of experiential learning, which describes learning as progressing through concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. Two model buildings of different heights with inertial measurement units (IMUs) attached to the top were secured to a hand-cranked shake table. The structures were shaken at varying frequencies, both with and without rudimentary tuned mass dampers attached. 62 students used time-series data recorded by the IMUs during in-class demonstrations to calculate an approximate average resonant frequency and maximum accelerations of the buildings, then answered three long-answer questions. They also completed a Google Form with 12 true/false concept questions, 14 questions on their opinions of the activity, and 6 demographic questions. We assessed measurement accuracy using equivalence testing and demographic equity using Fisher's exact tests with bias-corrected effect sizes, correcting for 150 simultaneous comparisons. Students consistently identified resonant amplitudes and frequencies within the allowable bounds from real data and performed well and approximately equitably across demographic groups on the true/false concept assessment; nearly all apparent demographic differences traced to subgroups of five or fewer students. However, they struggled to connect their direct observations to abstract reasoning and real-world applications. Non-significant demographic effects on one member of a paired concept question routinely vanished on its rephrased counterpart, suggesting localized misconceptions rather than random guessing. This is consistent with the well-documented gap between surface and deep learning, a dichotomy not yet widely examined in geoscience education. These results informed specific revisions to the activity's worksheet questions, aimed at more directly targeting the transfer from abstract conceptualization to active experimentation, a transition that proved most difficult for students. Beyond its undergraduate classroom use, this low-cost (~$400) activity can be easily adapted to outreach and informal education settings.

title: The differing response of cats and dogs to the terminal Pleistocene extinction
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Smith, Felisa A. [1], Elliott Smith, Emma A. [2], Tomé, Catalina [3], Restrepo Cortes, Esteban [4], Casiano Ruiz, Marina [5], Keller, Jonathan [6], Lyons, S. Kathleen [7]
affiliations: (1) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
(2) Center for Stable Isotopes, University of New Mexico, Santa Fe, NM,
(3) Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites, Indianapolis, Indiana, USA
(4) Biology, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(5) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(6) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(7) University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract: The significant extinctions in Earth history have largely been unpredictable in terms of who perished and what traits made them susceptible. This changed in the late Quaternary when human activities began leading to strikingly size-biased extinctions of large-bodied mammals and has accelerated in the modern. Such trophic and body size downgrading is leading to changes in the structure and function of modern ecosystems. Predicting the full effects of biodiversity loss is of obvious importance for effective conservation and management, but many indirect interactions can take decades, centuries or longer to play out. Here, we use the fossil record of the terminal Pleistocene megafauna extinction in the Americas as a proxy for characterizing the consequences of modern biodiversity loss. Using a mammal community in the Edward’s Plateau of Texas, we quantify the isotopic (δ 13 C and δ 15 N) and body-size niche before and after biodiversity loss to assess shifts in the ecology and ecological interactions of surviving species. Before the extinction, there was a rich and diverse community quite similar to modern African savannas. In particular, we find regular partitioning of carnivorian dietary isotopic niche with body size; families were largely non-overlapping. Moreover, the largest carnivores were highly specialized. Post-extinction, considerable body size and isotopic niche space were lost, carnivores became more generalized, and some shifted their dietary isotopic niche. We find the ecological roles megafauna play in the earth system are not replicated by smaller-bodied animals. Our work highlights the importance of integrating a paleontological perspective into modern conservation efforts to develop a more synoptic understanding of ecosystems.

title: Tracking Petrogenic Organic Carbon Oxidation during the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum using the Rhenium Proxy and Provenance Tracers
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change (Posters)
authors: Dean, Jess [1], Ramos, Evan J [2], Choi, Hwiseo [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
abstract:
The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) was a climate change event where global temperatures increased by 5-8°C in ~20,000 years and were sustained for an additional ~200,000 years before recovering. This duration is long compared to other climate events of similar magnitude in the Paleogene; one speculated cause is enhanced oxidation of petrogenic (or rock-bound) organic carbon (OC petro ). OC petro is stored in siliciclastic sedimentary rocks (i.e., shale), which can be oxidized during rock weathering, releasing CO 2 that can keep atmospheric temperatures elevated. Few geologic carbon cycle models directly account for OC petro oxidation, partly because few deep-time records of this process exist.

In this study, we produce records of OC petro oxidation in fluvial deposits spanning the PETM using the novel trace element proxy rhenium (Re), a transition metal that strongly associates with marine organic matter during deposition and mobilizes during oxidation of OM-bearing lithologies. We focus on 3 localities in the Bighorn Basin (Wyoming, USA) containing extensive PETM sediments but cropping out at varying distances from the basin axis. We hypothesize that landscape position modulates the provenance and proportion of shale- and igneous-bedrock-derived sediment each locality received from the hinterland, impacting the magnitude of OC petro oxidation. Immobile element tracers (Rb/Zr, Ti/Al) show distinct inputs of igneous-bedrock- and shale-derived sediment, with the location near the basin axis (Sand Coulee) having a greater proportion of igneous sediment than the more distal location (Polecat Bench). Re concentrations in sediment spanning the PETM (n = 9) at Sand Coulee range from 14 to 44 ppb, with post-PETM sediments generally having higher Re concentrations than pre-onset samples, perhaps due to lower temperatures after the event and consequently lower organic matter breakdown. Known Re concentrations of felsic igneous rocks (~2 ppb) and black shales (~150 ppb) suggest that Sand Coulee sediments must have received a significant proportion of sediment from basin-bounding shale, but the degree of oxidation they experienced will depend on measurements of Bighorn Basin bedrock samples. A July 2026 sampling campaign yielded a complete transect of the Sand Creek Divide locality, which is positioned farthest from the basin axis and contains greater proportion of fine sediment. Additional Re, trace element, and isotopic measurements (e.g., 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) will help clarify the local controls and magnitudes of OC petro oxidation during the PETM.

title: How Did Rhinoceroses Grow? A Systematic Analysis Of Growth Pattern in North American Rhinoceroses
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Santos, Sunshyne Mia [1], Prothero, Donald R. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, California State Polytechnic University, Pomona, California, USA
(2) California Polytechnic State University, La Crescenta, CA,
abstract:
Rhinoceros growth and development is not fully studied as a group. Despite the numerous fossil specimens available for research, it is not fully understood whether isometric or allometric growth takes place during their ontogeny (over the course of their lifetime) or phylogeny (over the course of their evolution). To get a good idea across the different groups across their ontogeny, I measured the limb bones of two species: the most robust of the group, Teleoceras proterum, as well as the most gracile, Menoceras arikarense . We measured diaphyseal length (minus the epiphyseal caps) and midshaft circumferences of the humerus, radius, femur, and tibia of both rhinos from several museum collections. We calculated the reduced major axis (RMA) slope for their growth, using PAST software. The slopes for most of the Menoceras limbs were slightly greater than 1.0 (slightly gracile), while most of the Teleoceras limbs had slopes less than 1.0 (slightly robust). However, these slopes are not significantly different from the isometric slope of 1.0 because the error estimates in the slope are large. This is consistent with the data from Kilbourne and Makovicky (2012), who found that even graviportal animals like the black rhinoceros ( Diceros bicornis ), as well as elephants and hippos, showed isometric growth in most of their limbs, despite their large body masses.

In addition, I conducted a separate analysis to see how Teleoceras limb bones evolved over time as their limbs got more and more stumpy. As predicted, the later species of Teleoceras show negative allometry, consistent with the idea that the limbs are growing thicker faster than they are growing longer. However, since these interspecific comparisons can use only means of species samples, there are only a handful of data points, so the correlation coefficient is quite low, and these results were not significantly distinct from the isometric slope of 1.0.

title: Mapping Flash-Flood Exposure in Kerr County, TX Using a LiDAR-Derived Building Inventory
session_title: Geoinformatics and Data Science: A Showcase In Undergraduate and Graduate Student Research (Posters)
authors: Jensen, Donovan [1], Zhang, Yiming [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science and Environmental Change, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA
(2) Bureau of Economic Geology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract: The July 4, 2025, flash flood in Kerr County stands as one of the deadliest flash-flood events in recent U.S. history, with officials confirming 119 fatalities and 2 individuals missing in Kerr County. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) 100-year and 500-year floodplain maps provide the standard baseline for flood exposure, yet numerous affected structures lie outside the Special Flood Hazard Area boundaries. Therefore, an accurate building inventory is needed to assess the threat that flash floods pose to Kerr County communities. Existing methods for identifying at-risk buildings often underestimate the number of properties in rural, undermapped areas. Advances in LiDAR technology now allow structures to be located more completely, including in places poorly captured by existing inventories. In this project, we build a LiDAR-derived building inventory to assess flash-flood exposure across the Kerr County portion of the Upper Guadalupe River Basin. LiDAR data collected in 2019 are classified to identify building structures, and NAIP (National Agriculture Imagery Program)-derived NDVI (normalized difference vegetation index) values are used to reduce false detections associated with vegetation. The buildings are overlaid with the FEMA 100-year and 500-year floodplains to identify exposed structures. The analysis quantifies the percentage of LiDAR-derived buildings within the study area that fall within flood exposure. Of the 67,639 LiDAR-derived buildings in the study area, 22.2% fall in the FEMA 100-year floodplain and 28.5% in the 500-year. Because the LiDAR predates the 2025 flood, the inventory does not include buildings constructed after the acquisition date. Despite this, the methodology provides a reproducible framework for future exposure assessments using updated LiDAR and flood-hazard models.
