title: Surprises in St. Charles Bay, Texas: Unexpected Assemblages and Yellow Tests
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Buzas-Stephens, Pamela [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado Museum of Natural History, Boulder, Colorado, USA
abstract: Examples of foraminifera living in what other organisms consider to be hostile habitats abound. Even with low to no oxygen, highly fluctuating environmental conditions, or at abyssal depths, a few genera can usually push thresholds and proliferate. This study is the first to document the foraminifera in St. Charles Bay, Texas, and focuses on living species. An inlet of Aransas Bay, St. Charles Bay is very shallow (2 m or less) and subject to the extreme temperature, salinity, and oxygen circumstances found in Texas Gulf Coast waterways. Samples were taken in August 2009, during a period when salinity reached over 52 ppt. Surprisingly, Ammotium salsum , most often considered a harbinger of brackish habitats, was the most abundant taxon at all four stations, with up to 700 living individuals present in 10 mL. Many A. salsum have what appear to be sulfur grains comprising their shells, and the same type of grains are scattered throughout the sediment. Other species, including Ammonia sobrina (calcareous), Quinqueloculina wiesneri , and Trochammina inflata (both agglutinated), also exhibit a yellow color. Are these yellow tests an indication of sulfur metabolism, or perhaps oxidation? Further investigation is required to begin answering these questions.

title: Power Play: Using Stream Power to Build Resilient Urban Riverscapes
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Boylan, Nora [1], Jones, AJ [2], Russell, Luke [3], Thorne, Colin [4], Wolfe, Marjorie [5]
affiliations: (1) Wolf Water Resources, Portland, Oregon, USA
(2) Wolf Water Resources, Portland, OR, USA
(3) Wolf Water Resources, Portland, OR, USA
(4) Wolf Water Resources, Portland, OR, USA
(5) Wolf Water Resources, Portland, Oregon, USA
abstract:
Urbanization and climate change are increasing the frequency and magnitude of stormwater runoff, exposing streams to greater erosive forces that drive channel incision, bank erosion, floodplain disconnection, habitat degradation, and increased risks to communities and infrastructure. Traditional stormwater management has focused on conveying runoff through engineered systems, often without addressing these downstream geomorphic impacts. As an alternative to traditional stormwater management, the resilient stream corridor approach focuses on reconnecting streams to their floodplains and restoring hydrologic and morphologic complexity. This strategy re-establishes natural fluvial processes that dissipate stream energy, lower flood stages, and extend time-to-concentration by increasing floodplain width and roughness. Morphologically, the approach fast forwards stream evolution toward a more stable and ecologically functional condition.

Effective implementation of resilient stream corridors requires quantifying the processes driving hydromodification. Specific stream power, which represents the erosive energy of streamflow acting on the bed, banks, and floodplain, provides a practical metric for assessing altered hydrology and identifying opportunities for resilience-based restoration. Evaluating stream power at the reach and watershed scales helps identify areas susceptible to degradation, prioritize locations for intervention, and inform development standards that reduce ecological degradation and infrastructure vulnerability.

To support these objectives, we developed a planning-level methodology for estimating resilient corridor widths using specific stream power. The framework introduces the concept of a Diminishing Returns Threshold, which identifies the corridor width at which additional widening produces only marginal reductions in stream power. Rather than prescribing a single erosion threshold, the methodology evaluates the relationship between corridor width and stream power to develop a risk-based framework that balances geomorphic function with real-world constraints such as existing development, valley space, and project objectives. Because the analysis relies on readily available hydrologic and topographic datasets, it can be applied across large drainage networks without extensive field investigations or hydraulic modeling.

The resilient corridor width framework provides a scalable decision support tool for watershed planning, stream restoration, and land use management by identifying the space streams require to maintain dynamic equilibrium under current and future hydrologic conditions. By working with natural fluvial processes rather than constraining them, the approach supports proactive corridor protection, complements conventional stormwater management, reduces long-term reliance on structural stabilization and maintenance, and advances nature-based solutions that improve watershed resilience while protecting communities and infrastructure.

title: Rock Glacier Response to Climatic and Seasonal Change in Colorado, USA: A Kinematic and Hydrologic Investigation
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Schanz, Sarah Anne [1], Berry, Juniper [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO,
(2) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
abstract: Documenting regional variation in rock glacier kinematics and hydrology is critical to understanding the changing cryosphere, and in particular, impacts on water resources. Despite being one of the most prevalent cryospheric features and potential water reservoirs in Colorado, contemporary knowledge of rock glaciers lacks a regional perspective on the variation of rock glacier surface speed and meltwater contribution to alpine watersheds across the state. Likewise, not enough is known about how rock glaciers across Colorado respond to drought events. We calculated 2D surface displacement for 12 rock glaciers across five major mountain ranges in Colorado to understand how rock glacier surface movement has changed from 2009-2019 and establish a baseline for regional variability in rock glacier kinematics. In order to constrain drought and seasonal meltwater response, we analyzed the hydrochemistry on four rock glaciers throughout the 2026 melt season. We find rock glacier discharge and temperature are consistent throughout the summer melt season while conductivity and pH generally increase throughout the summer, indicating a relative increase in ice melt. Our results show that rock glacier velocities can vary significantly across the Rocky Mountains and call for a regional perspective when evaluating cryospheric change and alpine water resources. Likewise, by taking advantage of the low snowpack in 2026, our results highlight the critical role that rock glacier melt has on sustaining alpine streamflows.

title: Life History Shifts in Anthropocene Seas: Variation in the Reproduction, Growth, and Physiology of Free-Living Bryozoans in Response to Coastal Eutrophication and Hypoxia
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Harnik, Paul [1], Cammarata, Madison [2], Creary, Kanish [3], Garcia, Jeriah [4], José, Emma [5], Unnone, Victor [6], Liow, Lee Hsiang [7], O'Dea, Aaron [8]
affiliations: (1) Colgate University, Hamilton, NY, USA
(2) Colgate University, Hamilton, NY, USA

(5) Colgate University, Hamilton, NY, USA

abstract: Changes in food availability over relatively fine temporal (million-year), spatial (basin), and taxonomic (species) scales are associated with functional shifts in a diversity of marine animals. To what extent have human-induced changes in nutrient cycling and primary productivity resulted in similar functional responses, albeit at much faster rates? To address this question, we investigated spatial and temporal variation in the life histories of two species of free-living bryozoan ( Discoporella depressa and Reussirella doma ) sampled along a eutrophication-hypoxia gradient in the northern Gulf of Mexico. Using light and scanning electron microscopy, we gathered data on the reproductive mode (clonal vs. aclonal), colony size, and orifice area of specimens sampled in death assemblages at multiple stations on the continental shelf. Lophophore size positively correlates with orifice area in some bryozoans, and lophophore size constrains the particle size a bryozoan can ingest. We hypothesized that increased food supply would be associated with greater frequencies of clonality, larger colonies, and larger orifice areas. To test these hypotheses, we compared assemblages sampled offshore of larger versus smaller watersheds (i.e., Louisiana and Alabama vs. Florida) and colonies within each region that varied in post-mortem age. Whereas R. doma was exclusively aclonal, greater frequencies of clonality in D. depressa occurred offshore of larger watersheds. Frequencies of clonality in D. depressa increased towards the present-day in regions with known histories of anthropogenic eutrophication (Louisiana, Alabama), but did not vary over time in shelf environments where eutrophication has not historically occurred (Florida). For both species, larger colonies were observed in more productive settings. D. depressa had larger orifices in more productive environments, whereas variation in orifice size was modest in R. doma and in the opposing direction (i.e., larger in less productive environments). D. depressa orifice area did not vary over time offshore of Alabama and Florida, but did decrease significantly in Louisiana, perhaps due to expansion of hypoxic conditions as a result of anthropogenic nutrient loading in the Mississippi River watershed. Our results illustrate the diverse ways in which colonial marine benthos can adjust their life histories in response to changes in food supply and oxygen availability, and the role of anthropogenic environmental change in shaping the functional diversity of coastal ecosystems over decadal to millennial scales.

title: Recent Insights Into the Behavioural and Ecological Diversity of Early Annelids
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Nanglu, Karma [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Riverside, Riverside, California, USA
abstract:
Annelida is one of the most speciose and ecologically diverse groups of animals, with a fossil record extending back to the early Cambrian. However, most of their anatomy (with the exception of their jaws) is soft-tissue, which precludes their preservation in most environments. As a result, understanding the total diversity and ecological disparity among annelids in a deep-time context is challenging.

In this talk, I will present a series of papers which detail recent insights into early annelid ecology, with particular focus on their behaviour and inter-specific interactions. I will begin with the first report of commensal annelids from the middle Cambrian Burgess Shale in Canada. These annelids are found within large, organic tubes that were likely built by stem-enteropneusts. The annelids themselves are small and thin, with short chaetae. Most notably, within the studied interval of the Raymond Quarry locality, 92% of all annelid specimens were found within these organic tubes, with up to eight co-inhabiting within a single tube. This suggests an obligate, symbiotic relationship rather than opportunistic habitation. I will then discuss a novel parasitic annelid from the Fezouata Shale Biota of Morocco. This new symbiotic interaction was described based on twenty two specimens of the Ordovician bivalve Babinka which show a highly characteristic, question mark-shaped boring structure. Many of these specimens were only discovered after using micro-CT scanning, which revealed a high density of additional parasitized shells buried within the matrix. Moving to the Silurian Waukesha Biota, I will describe the recent discovery of the first leech body fossil. This new species, Macromyzon siluricum, preserves exceptional soft-tissue detail, particularly of the diagnostic external annulations and caudal sucker. The age of this new species predates molecular clock estimates for hirudinidans by roughly 200 million years, and challenges the commonly held notion that the earliest true leeches fed on vertebrate blood.

Taken together, these studies demonstrate how much remains to be discovered regarding the place annelids had in early ecosystems. Whether through symbiotic relationships or as key members of their trophic webs, the significance of early annelids is made partially cryptic through fossilization bias, and can only be ameliorated with additional specimen-focused research.

title: Implications of a Large, Compiled Detrital Zircon U-Pb Age Dataset for the Mesozoic to Cenozoic Evolution of Sierra Nevada Topography
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Tye, Alexander [1], Attia, Snir [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
The paleotopographic evolution of the Sierra Nevada is vital to understanding the tectonic and geodynamic processes that affected the North American Cordillera from Mesozoic to Cenozoic time. We use a compilation of all available detrital zircon U-Pb age data from the Sierra Nevada (as of late 2025) and a representative dataset from the Great Valley Forearc Basin to constrain the paleotopographic evolution of the Sierra Nevada from Jurassic to Pliocene time.

A drainage divide was first constructed along the length of the Sierra Nevada arc during middle Early Cretaceous time and is recorded by a reduction in pre-Mesozoic zircon, sourced from inboard Laurentia, from ~50% of samples in Jurassic strata to <10% of samples from mid- to Upper Cretaceous strata. The construction of the drainage divide was roughly coeval with intra-arc shortening and major activity of the Sevier thrust belt.

Detrital zircon in Eocene deposits of west-flowing paleochannels in the northern Sierra Nevada constrain whether an Eocene drainage divide existed along the Sierra Nevada or farther inboard. Comparison of these detrital zircon age populations with potential sources in the Western Metamorphic Belt, the Sierra Nevada batholith, and central-western Nevada reveals that no samples require paleochannel headwaters east of the Sierra Nevada batholith. Further, a new quantitative analysis of palinspastically restored, hypothesized river drainage areas reveals that existing data are inconsistent with an Eocene divide in central Nevada even when allowing for the most extreme differences in zircon fertility and erosion rates recognized in modern analog settings. We infer that an Eocene drainage divide was located within, or very close to, the Sierra Nevada batholith. Correlation of Oligocene ash flow tuffs from central Nevada across the Sierra Nevada suggests that the Oligocene drainage divide was located farther east than the Eocene divide. We hypothesize that Farallon slab rollback and attendant ignimbrite volcanism, which reached central-western Nevada in early Oligocene time, drove topographic uplift that caused drainage divide migration.

Pliocene uplift of the Sierra Nevada due to hypothesized lithospheric foundering is inferred from apparent westward tilting of reconstructed Eocene drainage networks in the northern Sierra Nevada. The propagation of detrital zircon populations through the drainage network broadly supports these reconstructions.

The data suggest a high Cretaceous and Eocene Sierra Nevada and are consistent with hypothesized Pliocene tilting.

abstract: The Lower Miocene fossil locality of Locherangan preserves a robust fossil assemblage, including three primates, from west of modern Lake Turkana, Kenya. The distribution of outcrops at Locherangan is limited and discontinuous due to major structural reorganization of the area post-Miocene deposition. In order to better situate new fossil collections into their stratigraphic and environmental context, we mapped the exposures and tied them into the type section of the soon to be defined Locherangan Formation. Initial field observations reveal complex spatial relationships between sedimentary units, including lateral offsets, and apparent irregularities in lithologic contacts. These observations suggest that the expression of the sedimentary sequence is influenced by pre-existing topography of the underlying basalt and by possible faulting leading to apparent warping or discontinuity of the overlying sediments. We produced a high-resolution geologic map contextualizing the main fossil collecting areas through field mapping using hand-held GPS points combined with satellite-image interpretation. Key stratigraphic contacts, such as the base of the section, were mapped directly in the field where exposed in order to evaluate unit continuity and thickness. The new geologic map provides an essential framework for future geological and paleontological investigations, enabling paleontologists to determine relative age in the sequence based on where fossils are found. By distinguishing the influence of basaltic paleotopography, this work improves interpretations of the depositional context of Locherangan and the post-depositional tectonic activity at Locherangan and in the Turkana Basin more broadly.

title: Remote Sensing-Based Geologic Mapping of the Talcuna Mining District, Coquimbo Region, Northern Chile

authors: Smith, Nicole [1], Seymour, Nikki [2], Anthonissen, Christoffel J. [3], del Real, Irene [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Occidental College, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Occidental College, Los Angeles, CA, USA

(4) Departamento de Ingeniería de Minería, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Santiago, Chile
abstract: Copper makes up a large portion of the resource demand for photovoltaic solar, wind, and grid battery storage, and is therefore a key component of strategies to decarbonize the electrical grid, as well as the industrial and transport sectors. This resource can be derived from a number of ore deposit types, including iron oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) and related deposits. The mechanism behind the formation of IOCG deposits is disputed. While there is wide agreement that hydrothermal fluids are required, the fluids have been variably attributed to evaporitic or magmatic sources. Here we applied remote sensing methods to investigate the spatial relationship between alteration minerals and igneous units in the Talcuna mining district in the Coquimbo region of Chile. This region is located in an arid environment well suited to study by remote sensing methods. The district hosts several Cu-bearing deposits, including IOCG and stratabound Cu-Ag styles of mineralization. Band-ratio maps showing ferric oxide alteration, ferrous silicate minerals, and hydroxyl alteration were derived from ASTER and Sentinel 2 multispectral data. Principal component analysis (PCA) and Spectral Angle Mapping (SAM) of EnMAP hyperspectral data were used to produce surface maps of primarily hydroxyl alteration minerals. Carbonates, siliciclastic units, volcanic deposits, and intrusions showed distinct responses in PCA visualization. Our maps show strong lithologic agreement with bedrock mapping published by Emparan and Pineda (1999). Montmorillonite, illite, and kaolinite were the primary hydroxyl alteration minerals detected in the overall study area. Alteration present in igneous units are dominated by montmorillonite with minor pyrophyllite compared to altered sedimentary siliciclastic surrounding units, which record montmorillonite, kaolinite, and illite. The concentration of hydroxyl alteration minerals around and within igneous units supports the involvement of magma in the region’s mineralizing hydrothermal system. This work serves as a basis for ongoing study, including field-based characterization and targeted geochronology on the alteration and intrusions.

title: Recent and Deep Incision of the Western Andean Plateau Margin Driven By Basement-Involved Crustal Shortening
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Perez, Nicholas D. [1], McCain, Payton L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA; ExxonMobil, Houston, TX, USA
abstract: The Western Cordillera of southern Peru hosts three exceptionally deep canyons (Cotahuasi, Colca, and Tambo) that rank among Earth’s 10 deepest. In the >3 km-deep Cañon de Colca, new geochronologic and thermochronologic results from Jurassic and Cretaceous sedimentary rocks and Cenozoic plutonic rocks are coupled with new field-based geologic mapping and cross-section construction to investigate the timing and mechanisms for canyon incision. This contribution builds on work from Taylor Schildgen, Kip Hodges, and others who also investigated the timing and mechanisms for incision of these deep canyon systems over 15 years ago. In this new work, mapping results from upstream of the previous studies reveal a basement-cored anticline situated near the deepest and highest relief reach of Cañon de Colca, which is interpreted to have formed above a blind SW-dipping reverse fault rooted in metamorphic basement. Kinematic modeling is used to investigate fault geometry and detachment depth. Samples collected across this anticline from the canyon span >1700 m of elevation across > 5 km of structural relief and are distributed along a ca. 35 km stretch of the canyon. Reset zircon U-Th/He ages are youngest (13.4 Ma) across the core of the anticline, and become progressively older and unreset toward the SW backlimb of the fold. All apatite U-Th/He ages are reset, including those from Schildgen, Hodges and others downstream, and become progressively younger upstream from ca. 4.8 to 2 Ma. Zircon U-Th/He results are interpreted as evidence that fault motion caused rock uplift beginning at ca. 13.4 Ma. Apatite U-Th/He ages are interpreted as evidence for rapid Pliocene canyon incision that propagated upstream. These results demonstrate that the newly recognized phase of Miocene basement-involved out-of-sequence deformation must be considered in the context of tectonic uplift and long-term climate variability, all as potential drivers of canyon incision.

title: The challenge of telling geologic time in the aftermath of the greatest mass extinction on the planet: Using carbon and strontium isotopes to refine age estimates of the Lower Thaynes Formation (Early Triassic) in the Great Basin region, western USA
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part II)
authors: Edwards, Cole Tyler [1], Saltzman, Matthew R. [2], Clements, Alexa [3]
affiliations: (1) Appalachian State University, Boone, NC,
(2) Ohio State University, Columbus, OH,
(3) University of Northern Iowa, Cedar Falls, IA,
abstract:
The Permian-Triassic (PT) interval has been well-studied to understand the cause and effect of a mass extinction, but determining the age and tempo of bioevents presents challenges in the aftermath of a mass extinction without good age control. Without biostratigraphic control or the presence of datable radiometric materials, age estimates of some PT intervals may be possible using chemostratigraphy when compared to well-calibrated sections across the globe. Geochemical data must be thoroughly interrogated for diagenetic overprints prior to making chemostratigraphic correlations. Uncertainties due to alteration can be assessed with multiple kinds of geochemical data measured from various materials that behave differently during diagenesis.

In this study we measured stable carbon (d 13 C) and strontium ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) isotopes from carbonate rock and conodonts preserved in the Great Basin region, western USA. We studied the Permian Gerster Limestone and Triassic Thaynes Fm interval in the Confusion Range (UT), Palomino Ridge (NV), and at Spruce Mountain (NV) where we sampled for d 13 C (n = 182) and 87 Sr/ 86 Sr (n = 115) to characterize the geochemical record and determine how complete the PT interval is here. The basal Thaynes Fm contains a unique succession in the Confusion Range, not found elsewhere in the region, that hosts peritidal carbonates with features characteristic of shallow water conditions (tepees, oncoids, fenestral fabrics), indicative of possible diagenesis and erosion. Based on petrographic analysis, trace elemental concentrations, and comparison with published isotopic records, we developed an age model that suggests that approximately 1.5 Myr of time is missing here from the earliest Triassic (252–250.5 Ma). This omits the entire Induan and lowermost Smithian Stages from the geologic record, consistent with prior paleontological work. Deposition resumes to capture a large Smithian negative d 13 C excursion (d 13 C = -4‰, known as N3) before being capped by a large positive d 13 C excursion at the Smithian-Spathian boundary (d 13 C = 8‰, known as P3). This age refinement helps to answer questions about how (in)complete the PT record is in the Great Basin region, but now poses new questions such as what explains such a large d 13 C excursion (8‰) relative to other Tethyan sections?

title: Three Decades of Crossing Borders in Geoscience Education: International Geoscience Education Organisation
session_title: International Collaborations in the Geosciences: Celebrating Science Without Borders
authors: Locke, Sharon M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL, USA
abstract: The status of geoscience education in schools varies widely across the world. The U.S. has enjoyed increasing prominence of earth sciences in schools due to the Next Generation Science Standards. In many other countries, however, earth science concepts are embedded within geography courses and share curricular space with social sciences. To promote earth sciences in schools, in 1995 a group of educators founded the International Geoscience Education Organisation (IGEO). For the past three decades, this organization has created several flagship initiatives to raise awareness of the geosciences among educators and students and encourage students to consider geoscience careers. For students, the longstanding International Earth Science Olympiad is an event for high school students that combines individual competition with international team cooperative learning. For educators, the recently established Global Leadership in Earth Systems Education program brings educators from around the world together for a week-long inquiry learning experience. An important outcome is that each participant formulates a plan to promote earth sciences learning and systemic change in their own country. A second program for students, the International Geoscience Youth Leadership program, is a student-led organization to nurture student interest in geosciences. Touching different parts of the geoscience learning ecosystem, IGEO has grown over the years to include a core membership of 29 countries on six continents and overall participation of 40 countries in various events. IGEO’s affiliation with the International Union of Geological Sciences means that the organization will continue to lead and shape global conversations on geoscience education at a time when it is vital to expand geoscience pathways for students to prepare a highly skilled future generation of earth scientists.

title: Mineralogy and Geochemistry of Bethlehem Steel Slag Found Along the Lake Erie (NY) Shoreline
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Skowron, Simon [1], Farthing, Dori J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences Dept., SUNY Geneseo, Geneseo, New York, USA
(2) Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences Dept., SUNY Geneseo, Geological Sciences, Geneseo, NY, USA
abstract:
The Bethlehem Steel company (Lackawanna, NY) was once the world’s largest steel producer. At its peak, it annually produced more than 20 million tons of steel. The smelting activities also generated a waste product called slag that was dumped into piles on the Bethlehem property and into Lake Erie. The slag dumps expanded the shoreline westward by ~1,300 feet around the smelter property. Today, pieces of Bethlehem slag are found on public beaches and in the shallow waters south of the now remediated smelter site. An intensive slag study was carried out at one of these beaches, Woodlawn, with the goal of understanding how much slag is present, as well as the mineralogy and geochemistry of the slag. This data will help determine the potential hazard level associated with this waste material. This work involved field surveys, microscopy, XRD, EDS, and XRF.

Field-based point counting (n = 1000) suggests that <1% of the sediments at Woodlawn Beach are slag. The slag is light blue to white, phaneritic, and vesicular. Many contain inclusions of charcoal and brick. Freshly exposed interiors of the slag are often more intensely colored and may display cooling or weathering-related banding. One large slag piece was conglomeratic and contained banded phaneritic clasts held within a fine-grained cement. Mineralogically, all Woodlawn Beach slags are dominated by gehlenite/akermanite, wollastonite, pure iron prills, glass, and secondary iron oxides. The gehlenite forms as euhedral crystals that are intergrown with whiskers of wollastonite. The bulk chemistry of Woodlawn Beach slags are dominated by calcium and silicon (~40 wt% CaO and ~30 wt% SiO 2 ). This chemistry fits well with the dominance of gehlenite and wollastonite and also matches EDS analyses of glass. The slags also contain high concentrations of Sr (420 - 974 ppm), Ba (456 - 774 ppm), and Zr (142 - 301 ppm). The chemistry and mineralogy of the slag makes them easy to differentiate from natural beach sediments and the initial findings of this work do not indicate that the slag poses an immediate chemical threat to its surroundings.

title: A “peak” at the Stenian: Using high-n, high precision detrital zircon geochronology and geochemistry to investigate ca. 1.1 Ga detrital zircon in a Cambrian sandstone
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Muhlbauer, Jason G. [1], Mohr, Michael T. [2], Crowley, James L. [3], Schwartz, Darin M. [4], Holland, Mark Edward [5], Schmitz, Mark D. [6]
affiliations: (1) Pacific Centre for Isotopic and Geochemical Research, University of British Columbia Vancouver, Vancouver, BC, Canada
(2) Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
(3) Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
(4) Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
(5) Arizona Geological Survey, Tucson, AZ, USA
(6) Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
abstract:
North American detrital zircon signatures characterized via laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) commonly include a major unimodal or polymodal peak of Stenian age (1.0–1.2 Ga). The presence or absence of a ca. 1.1 Ga peak in Proterozoic–Phanerozoic formations, e.g. the “Grenville Flood”, has been used to interpret continental drainage patterns and timing of epeirogenic uplift. For example, the provenance of Stenian detrital zircons in early Cambrian sandstones of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico is tied to interpretations of the Transcontinental Arch. At the typical analytical resolution of LA-ICP-MS measurements a unimodal Stenian peak is commonly apparent; but is it a singular age and provenance signature? We provide a test with high-n, high precision geochronology of ca. 1.1 Ga detrital zircons from the Cambrian middle member of the Sixtymile Formation, Grand Canyon, AZ. A total of 47 new chemical abrasion–isotope dilution–thermal ionization mass spectrometry (CA-ID-TIMS) dates with paired trace-element data deconvolve the “Stenian peak” and establish a more temporally refined and geochemically characterized detrital-zircon signature. The dataset is critical for testing regional connections between Cambrian sandstones of the southwest and possible ca. 1.1 Ga sources in western and eastern North America.

At CA-ID-TIMS measurement resolution, the unimodal ca. 1073 LA-ICP-MS peak of the Sixtymile Formation is >6 resolvable modes each representing a separate source. Age peaks from 1064–1127 Ma, including major peaks at ca. 1073 Ma, ca. 1080 Ma, ca. 1088 Ma, ca. 1091 Ma, and numerous dates from 1108–1127 Ma, appear to match bedrock units in the Llano Uplift, Texas (1070–1116 Ma), Franklin Mountains (1112 Ma), and/or Pikes Peak batholith (1080–1088 Ma). Trace-element signatures for most age groups show similarity, with some outliers. Correlating each individual peak to a specific source rock with certainty is not yet possible; however, two 1112 Ma grains overlap in age with CA-ID-TIMS data from the Red Bluff granitic suite, TX and others overlap with recent high precision Pikes Peak batholith geochronology. Our results reveal that a unimodal LA-ICP-MS detrital zircon age peak may not represent unique provenance source when subject to further high precision analysis and provide a template to address the complexity of the Stenian peak in North America.

title: The Martian North Polar (Sand) Sea: Estimating Water Volumes in the Gypsum Sands of the Olympia Undae Dunes
session_title: Morphodynamics and preservation of bedforms across scales and environments
authors: Bretzfelder, Jordan M. [1], Rivera-Hernandez, Frances [2], Day, Mackenzie [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences, University of California Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
There is abundant geologic evidence for the presence of surface liquid water on Mars in the past, however constrainng the fate of this liquid water has proved complex. Mars' North Polar erg (or sand sea), known as Olympia Undae, is the largest dune field on Mars, and is known to contain gypsum (CaSO 4 *2H 2 O) sands. Gypsum contains structurally bound water, and requires liquid water to form. Thus, the gypsum in these dunes provides additional evidence for the past presence of liquid water on Mars, as well as acting as a reservoir for water that has not previously been accounted for in Mars' water budget. As an example, the gypsum dunes of White Sands National Park in New Mexico, USA, cover an area of ~72 km 2 , and contain approximately 807,200,000 metric tons of water. The Olympia Undae dunes cover an area of 470,000 km 2 , though unlike the dunes of White Sands, they are not composed entirely of gypsum, but a mixture of gypsum and basalt, leading to additional complexities in estimating the water volume. As the amount of water stored in the gypsum dunes is currently unknown, the water budget for Mars' northern polar region is not well constrained.

Our study combines orbital data from several instruments, including visible near-infrared (VNIR) data from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) and digital terrain models (DTMs) from the High-Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE), to help constrain the amount of water bound in the Olympia Undae gypsum dunes. By integrating these datasets, the water content of the entire north polar erg will be quantitatively estimated and contextualized with high- spatial and spectral resolution observations. This investigation improves our constraints on the Martian volatile budget, and the processes that have contributed to the sequestration of water on Mars throughout the evolution of its climate.

title: Bogs, Frogs, and Pollywogs: The Cooling Eﬀect of Hot Springs
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Fairley, Jerry P. [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Idaho, Moscow, ID, USA
abstract: In a recent paper, I published a model of advective and conductive heat transport in groundwater discharge zones that incorporates the eﬀects of evaporative cooling and convective heat loss to the atmosphere. Here, I apply the model to the analysis of near-surface conditions at two Basin and Range hydrothermal areas. In the ﬁrst case study, I use the model to make point estimates of discharge and geothermal heat ﬂux at Borax Lake Hot Springs, in southeast Oregon, USA. The model is applied to an area of diﬀuse discharge near the springs, but where there is no visible surface water, and evaporative cooling has lowered surface temperatures below the average annual air temperature. In a second example, I examine potential impacts of a reduction in discharge on a groundwater dependent ecosystem, loosely modeled on Dixie Meadows, in Dixie Valley, Nevada. Dixie Valley is a target for groundwater development and geothermal power production, as well as being the only habitat of the federally-listed Dixie Valley Toad. The model predicts no change in ground surface temperature as long as discharge exceeds the maximum evaporation rate. Once groundwater discharge decreases below the maximum evaporation rate, surface water disappears (i.e., the wetlands dry-out), and the land surface temperature increases due to loss of evaporative cooling. In spite of this warming, the predicted rise in temperature is not suﬃcient to impact toad breeding or brumation behavior. Therefore, as long as the total (convective plus advective) geothermal heat ﬂux remains constant, dry-out is a greater danger to the toad’s habitat than increasing ground temperatures. On the other hand, if discharge is held constant and the geothermal heat ﬂux is decreased, the model predicts that ground surface temperatures will decrease linearly until they are below the requirements for toad habitat.

title: Volcanic rifted margins without plumes: a tale of mantle refertilization and cooling timescales.
session_title: Using mafic and ultramafic deposits to decipher volcanic and magmatic processes (Posters)
authors: Hernandez Montenegro, Juan [1], Lee, Cin-Ty [2], Dasgupta, Rajdeep [3], Zhang, Yishen [4]
affiliations: (1) Rice University, Houston, TX,
(2) Rice University, Houston, TX,
(3) Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
(4) Rice University, Houston, Texas, USA
abstract: Volcanic rifted margins are associated with large igneous provinces that are emplaced over remarkably short intervals immediately before and during continental breakup. Because of their high estimated magma fluxes, these events are conventionally attributed to mantle plumes supplying a thermal anomaly, yet a plume is not demonstrably required everywhere. The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province lacks a hotspot track and records mantle potential temperatures only modestly above ambient, while in the North Atlantic Igneous Province the thermal anomaly alone does not explain the volume, timing, and distribution of magmatism. Here, we propose that voluminous rift magmatism reflects decompression melting of a progressively refertilized, heterogeneous mantle. Two fertile domains contribute to this magmatism: one formed during early extension as asthenospheric melts percolating into harzburgitic lithosphere dissolve orthopyroxene and precipitate clinopyroxene and garnet, depressing the solidus; the second comprises pyroxenitic and variably hydrated veins inherited from earlier subduction or orogenesis. Both domains remain subsolidus until continued thinning advects them upward. Where stretching outpaces conductive cooling, their melting adds to ongoing asthenospheric melt production and reduces bulk lithospheric viscosity, promoting necking in a positive feedback that culminates in continental breakup, alongside eruption of continental flood basalts and basaltic flows (seaward dipping reflectors; SDRs) at the continent-ocean transition. Once breakup is complete and a mid-ocean ridge is established, melting is dominated once more by ambient asthenosphere. This model accounts for the delay between rift onset and the magmatic climax, and predicts a systematic upsection decline in the pyroxenite-derived melt fraction through SDR sequences toward MORB-like compositions — a prediction we test with thermodynamic melting models and margin geochemical compilations. Magma-poor margins emerge naturally from this model when cooling outpaces advection, suppressing melting of pyroxenite veins in the mantle lithosphere and of the asthenosphere itself.

title: Ophiolites as archives of Jurassic seawater: triple oxygen isotopes of altered crust and hydrothermal minerals from the Josephine Ophiolite
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics (Posters)
authors: Sheik, Afrid Abdaly [1], Zakharov, David [2]
affiliations: (1) Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(2) Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI,
abstract: Seawater δ¹⁸O is a fundamental parameter in Earth system evolution, reflecting the balance between ¹⁸O-depleting continental weathering and ¹⁸O-enriching hydrothermal exchange at mid-ocean ridges. Because seawater itself is not preserved, this history must be reconstructed from proxies. Marine sediments, the most widely used of these, record a ~15‰ rise in δ¹⁸O since the early Paleozoic, but this cannot be uniquely attributed to rising seawater δ¹⁸O because sedimentary δ¹⁸O depends on both temperature and fluid composition and can be modified by diagenesis. Ophiolites record seawater–basalt exchange directly, yet bulk compositions integrate high- and low-temperature alteration at variable water/rock ratios, producing the same ambiguity. Mineral separates such as epidote instead precipitate during seawater-ophiolite interaction, and its small mineral–water fractionation (~− 0.37- +2.16‰) at relevant growth temperatures (250- 400 °C) makes it a near-direct recorder of that fluid. Here we report high-precision triple oxygen-isotope measurements δ′¹⁸O, Δ′¹⁷O, δD, and water contents along a continuous stratigraphic transect through the Jurassic Josephine Ophiolite to reconstruct the δ′¹⁸O of Jurassic seawater. Whole rock δ′¹⁸O increases systematically (+2.7-+11.3‰) up-section, but Δ′¹⁷O scatters broadly (−0.078 to −0.016‰) and resolves no unique seawater composition. In contrast, epidote separates yield fluid compositions (δ′¹⁸O = −3.2-+1.1‰, Δ′¹⁷O=−0.001- +0.014) broadly consistent with Jurassic seawater (δ′¹⁸O = −1‰, Δ′¹⁷O=+0.000‰), and quartz–epidote pair thermometry independently constrains growth to 250–342 °C. Epidote triple O-isotope systematics therefore provide an archive of paleo-seawater δ¹⁸O and a route to reconstructing its secular evolution from ophiolites through Earth history.

title: A Tale of Two Clams: Investigating Body Size Changes in Glycymerididae and Lucinidae from the Caribbean Neogene

affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(2) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA

(4) Department of Integrative Biology, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
(5) Department of Museum Research and Collections, UA Museums, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA

abstract: Paleontologists utilize body size as a proxy for productivity, as body size generally scales with nutrient demands; therefore, larger body sizes are generally found in higher productivity regions. Body size may also be an indicator of trophic position/ecological structure and is also a character on which natural selection acts. Despite the importance of body size data to paleontology, we still know little about how body size frequency distributions vary during periods of environmental change or across productivity gradients. The marine fossil record of the SW Caribbean, which captures the time of the formation of the Isthmus of Panama, provides a perfect opportunity to determine how changes in primary productivity impacted the body size of bivalves. After the Caribbean was isolated from the Pacific ~3.5 million years ago, upwelling in the Caribbean decreased, leading to lower planktonic productivity of the region and, therefore, less food sources for organisms, especially suspension feeders. We present body-size data from two families of fossil bivalves, Lucinidae and Glycymerididae, to understand how average body size has been impacted by planktonic productivity. Lucinidae are chemosymbiotic bivalves, as they have a symbiotic relationship with sulfur-oxidizing bacteria housed in their gills that provide them with energy. In contrast, Glycymerididae are suspension feeders, which means that their main source of energy comes from filter feeding. These specimens were collected from localities in Panama and Costa Rica and represent time periods before, during, and after the closure of the Isthmus of Panama. We obtained stacked digital images of individuals, then used the digital measurement software AutoMorph to obtain body size (length, height, width) from each image. Body size data were used to determine the mean body size and size frequency distributions for each family at each sample location. These size frequency distributions through time can be used to test our two hypotheses: 1) As productivity in the Caribbean decreased average body sizes of bivalves decreased and 2) The chemosymbiotic relationship may insulate Lucinidae from productivity changes, resulting in no change or even an increase in average body size. This research will help us to better understand the relationship between primary productivity and body size in marine benthic communities, which has implications for ecological and evolutionary responses of modern bivalves to a changing ocean environment.

abstract:
We present updated mapping and geochronology of potential late Quaternary faulting on the eastern margin of the Española Basin, Rio Grande Rift, New Mexico. The Española Basin is a ~60-km-wide, west-tilting half graben with low rates of geodetic extension, seismicity, and fault slip. Prior paleoseismic work has focused on demonstrating late Quaternary activity of the western-margin faults of the Española Basin, including the Pajarito fault system, which passes through Los Alamos National Laboratory, and most recently, the Puye fault that runs roughly parallel to the Pajarito fault, about 2-7 km eastward. In contrast, the paleoseismic history of faults along the eastern basin margin, broadly defined by the north-south-trending Picuris–Pecos fault system (PPFS), remains poorly constrained.

The PPFS records a complex and protracted history of deformation marked by multiple episodes of reactivation since the Proterozoic, and evidence of Quaternary deformation along the PPFS has been unclear. We integrate new neotectonic and geomorphic mapping on lidar-derived topography, field observations, and 10 Be cosmogenic exposure ages from offset moraines in the southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains to characterize Pleistocene deformation on the PPFS. Mapping and field observations show moraine crests that are individually displaced by ~1 m (down-to-the-west), with total vertical separation >2 m across multiple scarps, that we interpret as displacement on possibly active fault strands. We present preliminary 10 Be cosmogenic radionuclide exposure ages from glacially transported boulders on the moraine crests to constrain the timing of recent fault movement. Based on landscape position and preliminary ages, these moraines are likely associated with the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), implying the most recent surface rupture of the PPFS occurred since the LGM. Additional evidence supporting late Quaternary fault activity along the PPFD includes potential deformation of middle and early Pleistocene surfaces, topographic lineaments, fault exposures in outcrop, and aligned springs. Collectively, these observations suggest that the PPFS is a Quaternary-active seismogenic fault that should be considered in regional seismic hazard assessments.

authors: Mackaman-Lofland, Chelsea A. [1], Constenius, Kurt [2], McQuarrie, Nadine [3], York, Aidan James [4], Starkey, Ainsley [5], Fan, Majie [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,

abstract: The Cordillera of Montana and southern Canada represents one of the best-studied orogenic systems on Earth. Uplift and subsidence in this region have been primarily attributed to fold-thrust belt shortening, associated crustal thickening, and topographic development; and flexural subsidence in the adjacent foreland basin. However, the undeformed foreland has undergone >1 km of surface uplift and ~2–5 km of erosion and rock exhumation, as recorded by Upper Cretaceous marine strata now at ~1–1.5 km elevations and peak temperature data from basin stratigraphy. These patterns of rock exhumation and lithospheric deflection cannot be explained by supracrustal deformation or eustasy, and require the influence of deeper crustal, subducted slab-related, or mantle dynamic processes during evolution of the fold-thrust belt and foreland basin. We present new low-temperature thermochronology and peak temperature data spanning the Montana hinterland, fold-thrust belt (Sawtooth Range) and proximal-distal foreland basin, interpreted alongside preliminary flexural thermokinematic models, to 1) quantify the timing and magnitude of supracrustal deformation, structural/sedimentary burial, exhumation, and inferred topographic uplift, and 2) evaluate potential drivers of deep deflection. Apatite fission track (AFT) and apatite and zircon (U-Th)/He analyses (AHe, ZHe) yield partially to fully reset dates and constrain Late Cretaceous–Miocene burial heating and exhumation-driven cooling. Fully reset AFT and ZHe dates align with independent constraints on the timing of thrust motion in the Sawtooth Range, and require post-depositional heating to at least ~100–140°C or ~4–6 km depth (given a ~20–25°C/km geothermal gradient). These findings are consistent with flexural thermokinematic models that predict rocks currently exposed in the thrust belt were buried beneath >5–8 km of “phantom,” proximal foredeep deposits and the southernmost extent of the Lewis thrust sheet prior to exhumation. AHe dates are fully reset across the study area and span ~60–20 Ma, with the youngest dates (<40–20 Ma) collocated within the frontal fold-thrust belt and proximal foreland basin. The magnitude, distribution, and spatial progression of overburden removal indicated by these results reinforces thermal maturity trends defined by vitrinite reflectance data, and suggest that, while uplift and exhumation of the foreland may have initiated in response to subducted slab rollback, slab window subduction, and associated mantle convection (~55 to 40 Ma), foreland deflection continued to <20 Ma and potentially present day.

title: Baseline Study of Recent Benthic Foraminifera from an Understudied Mediterranean Coastal System: Al Hoceima Bay, Northern Morocco
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches (Posters)
authors: Hrida, Abdelghafour [1], Etebaai, Issam [2], Khameiss, Belkasim Kh. [3]
affiliations: (1) Team of Applied Geosciences and Geological Engineering, Faculty of Science and Technology, Morocco
(2) Team of Applied Geosciences and Geological Engineering, Faculty of Science and Technology of Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco, Morocco
(3) Oklahoma Geological Survey Sarkeys Energy Center 100 E. Boyd St., Suite, Norman OK, OK, USA
abstract:
Benthic foraminifera constitute a highly diverse and widespread group of marine microorganisms that are widely applied in micropaleontological research. This study presents a comprehensive taxonomic assessment of modern benthic foraminiferal assemblages from Al Hoceima Bay in northern Morocco, an area of the Mediterranean Sea that remains relatively poorly studied. A total of fifteen taxa were recorded, encompassing both benthic and planktonic forms, although the study primarily emphasizes the benthic component of the assemblages. The assemblages are dominated by calcareous benthic species, with the highest relative abundances observed in Ammonia beccarii (30.2%), Quinquiloculina limbata (16.7%), and Quinquiloculina seminulum (14.2%). Other frequently encountered taxa include Elphidium crispum, Textularia agglutinans, and Lobatula lobatula . Species richness varies between four and nine taxa per sampling station, indicating noticeable spatial heterogeneity in community composition.

The observed assemblages range from highly simplified communities dominated by Ammonia beccarii and miliolid taxa to more diverse assemblages where several species co-occur without a single dominant form. Cluster analysis supports this variability by separating stations into distinct groups based on their faunal composition. These differences in assemblage structure likely reflect environmental gradients such as water depth and sediment type, although the focus of this study remains primarily taxonomic.

Importantly, this represents one of the first detailed investigations of recent benthic foraminifera from Al Hoceima Bay. Establishing a baseline dataset from this understudied region is essential for several reasons. It improves regional biogeographic coverage of Mediterranean foraminiferal distributions, provides a modern reference framework for future paleoenvironmental and palaeoceanographic reconstructions, and supports environmental monitoring in a coastal area influenced by both natural variability and increasing anthropogenic pressure. In addition, documenting modern assemblages is critical for calibrating ecological indicators used in sedimentary and environmental interpretation.

Overall, the benthic foraminiferal communities identified in Al Hoceima Bay are consistent with typical assemblages reported from Mediterranean coastal environments. This study, therefore, provides a valuable taxonomic baseline for recent benthic foraminifera along the Moroccan Mediterranean coast and enhances the regional dataset available for modern foraminiferal distributions.

title: No Jacob’s Staff, No Problem: Automated Mapping of Stratigraphic Height for Field Investigation and Thickness Measurement
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools
authors: Tye, Alexander [1], McMillan, Mitchell [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(2) Earth, Oceanic, and Atmospheric Science, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
abstract:
Stratigraphic study involves arranging observations and data by stratigraphic height. The stratigraphic height of each observation, measurement, or sample location is a function of its position within the geometry of a folded or tilted package of sedimentary rock. Traditionally, stratigraphic height is measured using a Jacob’s staff. We present a new algorithm, called Skystrat, for calculating and mapping stratigraphic height across a study area landscape using only a digital elevation model (DEM) and several georeferenced bedding attitude measurements.

Our method creates a geometric model of folded stratigraphy to directly calculate the stratigraphic height of geospatial points. We use the classic, geologically intuitive arc cross section method of Busk (1929), in which folded beds are modeled as circle sectors on the fold profile plane. This geometry defines the stratigraphic height of any location on the profile plane. By projecting DEM grid cell centroids onto the profile plane, our method calculates stratigraphic height maps across a study area DEM. Example applications in the well-exposed San Rafael Swell of Utah and poorly exposed folded strata of western Pennsylvania indicate that the stratigraphic height maps are accurate and useful.

The stratigraphic height maps produced by our method can be loaded onto a mobile app for use in the field, so that researchers can see the stratigraphic height of their current GPS location in real time without having to measure with a Jacob’s staff. The algorithm presents a more flexible, accurate, and efficient alternative to traditional measurement with a Jacob’s staff. The precision of the algorithm is limited by DEM resolution and GPS accuracy, but is sufficient for large-scale basin studies.

The algorithm can also be used for precise stratigraphic correlations between laterally offset sample locations or to project sample locations onto stratigraphic columns. In this way, the method improves the precision and reproducibility of the correlations that undergird stratigraphic studies. We provide implementations for ArcGIS and QGIS.

title: The structural transition along the Canning displacement zone in the central to northeastern foreland of the Brooks Range orogen, Arctic Alaska
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Connors, Christopher D. [1], Craddock, William H. [2], Gooley, Jared T. [3], Lease, Richard O. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA; Geology, Energy & Minerals Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(2) Geology, Energy & Minerals Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
(3) Alaska Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA
(4) Alaska Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA
abstract:
The northward increase in topography and width from the central to the northeastern Brooks Range is one of the most prominent features of the mountain belt. This sinistral bend in the geometry of the orogenic belt, the Canning displacement zone, is associated with a pronounced northward step in Cenozoic contractional deformation that is manifest at the surface. We present a regional seismic interpretation of data north of the range, integrated with published geologic maps, biostratigraphy from wells, and new U-Pb geochronologic dating of outcrop and well samples to show a similar fundamental structural transition occurs in the subsurface foreland of the orogenic belt.

In the central part of the northern foothills, from the Colville River east to the Itkillik River, a W-E striking, north-directed, thin-skinned fold-and-thrust belt is well-expressed as predominantly north-vergent imbricate fault-bend folds, with local south-directed back thrusts. The Upper Jurassic–Lower Cretaceous Kingak Shale and overlying strata are commonly duplexed above a detachment at the base of this section and below upper detachment surfaces in the Lower to middle Cretaceous Torok Formation and composite Cretaceous pebble shale unit and Hue Shale. From the Itkillik River east to the Ivishak River, this thin-skinned fold-and-thrust belt continues, with the strike of thrusts changing to a WSW-ENE geometry. The upper detachment here is in the Upper Cretaceous Canning Formation and Hue Shale, and similar local south-directed back thrusts are present.

From the Ivishak River east to the Canning River, WSW-ENE striking thrusts involving Devonian and likely older Paleozoic strata mark a fundamental change in detachment levels and exhumation of the thin-skinned belt in the foreland. An upper detachment in the Lower Mississippian Kayak Shale acts as a roof thrust to allow slip to transfer back to the south, thus limiting the northern extent of contraction in the foreland at this area. East of the Canning River, the front of contractional deformation steps substantially northward. The Marsh Creek anticline, more properly described as a complex passive-roof duplex, limits transfer of shallow slip into the foreland, but large contractional folds in the Beaufort Sea indicate a deep detachment extends northward offshore. The Canning displacement zone is thus composed of several Cenozoic en echelon, thick-skinned thrusts that laterally transfer slip in a sinistral sense into the foreland.

title: Determining Cross-Shore Variation in Grain Size Using Image Analysis: A Case Study of Sand from Puerto Rico
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Abron, Gene Bea [1], Harper , Cameron [2], Zambito, James Joseph [3]
affiliations: (1) Beloit College, Beloit, WI,
(2) Beloit College, Beloit, WI,
(3) Beloit College, Beloit, WI,
abstract:
Various studies have demonstrated a relationship between grain size and depositional environment. For example, fluvial, beach, and dune samples have different grain size distributions as a result of the transport mechanisms and energy in these environments. However, traditional grain size analysis using sieves can be tedious. In contrast, laser granulometry can determine grain size distributions efficiently, but does not provide information on the composition of the grains that would come from visual inspection either with the naked eye during sieve analysis or subsequent microscopy. Image analysis for grain size on the other hand allows the researcher to not only determine grain size but also provides the opportunity to determine grain composition through visual inspection of microscope pictures of sample grains.

This study seeks to develop a method for characterizing sample grain sizes from microscope photos of sand samples collected along cross-shore transects from various beaches in Puerto Rico using the image processing software ImageJ. The primary goal is to differentiate foreshore (intertidal) from backshore (dune) sands based on grain size distribution. Initial attempts to automate the process of measuring grain size dimensions using ImageJ were unsuccessful, as polished biogenic carbonate grains often had a glare and were difficult to distinguish from the image background using image edits of contrast and color. A method of measuring grain dimensions from images manually using ImageJ was therefore developed, with the maximum and minimum dimension of at least 125 grains per sample determined. The minimum dimension of a grain was important in order to process the data in a simulation of traditional grain size analysis with sieves for comparison to previous studies. Not only was the method employed able to produce a grain size distribution that was in agreement with distributions from the expected environments as found in previous studies, but the grain size data collected using this method was also reproducible among two different undergraduate students with different amounts of training. Additionally, the collection of images allowed an efficient visual determination of grain composition, and thereby mineralogy, that is also in agreement with the location of the samples along the cross-shore transect.

title: Hydroclimate, ecosystem and wildfire change across the Eocene–Oligocene Transition on the western North Atlantic margin: a multiproxy organic geochemical record from Bass River, New Jersey
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling
authors: JAYACHANDRAN, AKSHAY [1], Wang, Zhao [2], Hren, Michael T. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA; Center for Environmental Sciences and Engineering, Storrs, CT, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA; Center for Environmental Sciences and Engineering, Storrs, CT, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA; Center for Environmental Sciences and Engineering, Storrs, CT, USA
abstract:
The Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT, ~34 Ma) marks Earth's transition from greenhouse to icehouse, yet terrestrial records integrating continental hydroclimate, vegetation and fire remain poorly constrained along the western North Atlantic margin. Here we present coupled leaf-wax hydrogen isotope (δ²H n -C₂₉ ), vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH; fire-markers) records reconstructing hydroclimate, ecosystem and wildfire history across the EOT from the well-dated Bass River borehole, New Jersey (ODP Leg 174AX).

δ²H n -C₂₉ varies in three phases an ~45–50‰ 2 H-enrichment preceding the transition, an ~25‰ 2 H-depletion coinciding with the EOT, and a ~50‰ enrichment rebound into the early Oligocene. The initial enrichment precedes the benthic δ¹⁸O shift and may reflect altered isotope hydrology under high CO₂ and temperatures combined with ecosystem reorganization affecting apparent leaf-wax–water fractionation. The subsequent depletion is consistent with cooling-driven changes in precipitation δ²H and clumped-isotope estimates of 4–6 °C cooling on the conjugate North Atlantic margin. However, sea surface temperature records from the Newfoundland margin and southern Labrador Sea indicate little resolvable cooling, so altered meridional vapor transport associated with North Atlantic circulation reorganization cannot be excluded. Molecular-inferred VPD doubles from 0.26 to 0.58 kPa before relaxing in the early Oligocene, indicating drying. Because rising VPD should enrich leaf waxes through evaporative fractionation, the underlying change in precipitation δ²H likely exceeds the measured signal. Retene, a conifer-derived biomarker, is an order of magnitude more abundant in the late Eocene than the early Oligocene and declines through the transition, indicating progressive loss of conifer and/or woody biomass, while hinterland pollen records establishment of Quercus–Carya mesophytic forest by the early Oligocene, suggesting a shift from conifer-rich to angiosperm-dominated ecosystems. The δ²H rebound coincides with this vegetation turnover and may reflect changing meridional vapor transport in the cooler early Oligocene and a shift in apparent fractionation associated with changing ecosystem type affecting the 2 H-enrichment. PAHs decline by an order of magnitude across this transition despite cooler and drier Atlantic margin conditions and a persistent closed mesophytic forest, suggesting that sustained burning required a critical dryness threshold.

We suggest that wildfire at temperate continental margins is influenced more by ecosystem changes rather than fire weather, and that δ²H n -C₂₉ integrates ecological as well as hydrological change across the EOT.

authors: Clarkson, Jasper [1], Patton, Katherine [2], Seymour, Nikki [3], Stockli, Daniel F. [4]

abstract: How much heat is needed in order to break a new ocean basin? Studies of the Tethyan magma-poor margin preserved in the western Mediterranean suggest Jurassic hyperextension resulted in a pulse of lower crustal reheating to >600 ºC in Corsica and the Ivrea zone at ~200 – 180 Ma followed by rapid cooling through ~400 ºC between 180 – 160 Ma. We investigated the spatial extent of this thermal pulse by investigating exposures of lower crustal rocks in Calabria, southern Italy. We present new LA-ICP-MS zircon, rutile, and apatite U-Pb ages from 23 samples across the Sila, Serre, and Aspromonte massifs. These data record a complex, long-lived history of western Mediterranean tectonics. Zircon data from the Sila and Serre massifs (n = 16) shows two distinct populations: detrital cores and single grains ranging from ~3218 – 350 Ma, and overgrowths ranging from ~350 – 227 Ma. The overgrowths are not restricted to one age peak and occur on all older age ranges, therefore they are interpreted to have formed during Variscan collisional metamorphism. Rutile data from the Sila and Serre massifs (n = 9) formed a “wedge” defined by upper and lower intercept ages ranging from ~206 – 121 Ma (upper intercept) and ~160 – 48.6 Ma, respectively. Upper intercept ages require that cooling through ~400ºC occurred coeval with or after the formation of the Tethys Ocean (190 – 150 Ma). The wedge-shaped distribution and lower intercept ages may record either subsequent partial resetting or recrystallization of rutile during Alpine deformation. Lower crustal apatite data from the Serre massif (n =3) record highly variable cooling ages of ~250 to 76 Ma. Upper crustal apatite from the Serre massif (n = 3) yielded ~260 and ~203 Ma ages, whereas upper crustal apatite from the Aspromonte massif (n = 3) yielded ~250, ~200, and ~106 Ma ages. While complex, preservation of Permian cooling ages indicates mid- to upper-crustal levels in Calabria have resided at T < 375°C since the end of the Variscan Orogeny. The lack of Jurassic metamorphic zircon growth in the lower crust with rutile upper intercept ages younger than ~206 Ma allow for a thermal event associated with Tethyan rifting, but suggest temperatures were not as high as seen in Corsica and the Ivrea Zone.

title: Establishing the Central Andean Arc Crust via Recycling of Supracrustal Materials
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Velázquez Santana, Liannie Coral [1], McLeod, Claire Louise [2], Brown, Kenneth [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Environmental Geoscience, DePauw University, Greencastle, IN, USA
abstract:
Thickened continental arcs are major sites of continental crust generation and modification, yet the composition and origin of their deep crustal roots remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate this using petrography, bulk geochemistry, and zircon U-Pb-Hf isotope systematics from granulite-facies xenoliths entrained in Plio-Pleistocene volcanic rocks in the Bolivian Altiplano, one of Earth’s thickest continental crustal sections (~75 km).

The Bolivian xenoliths comprise garnet-sillimanite-biotite-quartz granulites with supracrustal protoliths that experienced high-temperature metamorphism. A geothermal gradient of 25-30°C/km, combined with petrographic and geochemical observations, suggests equilibration at mid-crustal depths (~25-35 km). Regional structural reconstructions of retroarc thrusting during Andean shortening offer a plausible mechanism for burying these originally shallow supracrustal rocks. Bulk compositions and zircon populations resemble Paleozoic Eastern Cordillera units, which represent likely protolith sources.

Zircon U-Pb ages within the xenoliths span Paleoproterozoic to Phanerozoic ages with age peaks at ~1.9-1.7 Ga, ~1.2-1.1 Ga, ~0.61 Ga, and ~0.48-0.47 Ga, and predominantly sub-chondritic εHf values (-31 to +18), consistent with a detrital provenance from mostly evolved continental reservoirs. Within these groups, the Neoproterozoic-early Paleozoic zircon populations (~0.61, 0.48-0.47 Ga) are more abundant in the xenoliths than in the Central Andean detrital zircon records, providing evidence for selective preservation at depth. These populations correspond to regional tectonic events recorded across the proto-Andean margin, including Paleoproterozoic crust formation (~1.9-1.7 Ga), the Sunsás orogeny (~1.2-1.1 Ga), Puncoviscana basin rifting (~0.61 Ga), and Famatinian orogenesis with reaccretion of the Antofalla terrane (~0.48-0.47 Ga). Additionally, younger zircon populations show increasingly evolved εHf signatures consistent with reworking of older crust through successive tectonic events. Wide intra-sample εHf variability further indicates a heterogenous, incompletely mixed reservoir rather than a coherent terrane-scale block.

This material also contributes to arc-related silicic magmatism. A dacitic xenolith with young zircon crystallization ages (<20 Ma) records evolved Sr-Pb-Nd isotopic signatures that overlap with the host andesites and the regionally extensive Los Frailes ignimbrite suite. A subset of zircons from this xenolith yield inherited ages that match several of the basement populations identified here and directly link recycled crust to this young magmatic system. These results show that recycled supracrustal materials are important components of the crust beneath the eastern Bolivian Altiplano and serve as long-term archives of arc crust evolution.

abstract: The early Paleocene Wills Point Formation (Midway Group) has a very poorly known marine vertebrate fauna stratigraphically positioned (~62-64 Ma) after the end Cretaceous mass extinction and within the so-called Patterson Gap. However, recent efforts are uncovering a unique fauna demonstrating that this time period is key to understanding aspects of the Mesozoic to Cenozoic marine transition. The bony fish record (Osteichthyes) comprises vertebral and other skeletal fragments, but is mostly represented by a growing diversity of otolith taxa. Some of these otolith species ( Serranus ? caribbaeus , Ampheristus americanus , and Hoplostethus stringeri ) are known extinction survivors restricted to Texas and Arkansas. Their records in the younger Wills Point Formation extends their known survival in Texas for millions of years after the mass extinction. This survivorship of regional endemics relatively close to the impact in the Yucatan Peninsula in the western part of the gulf is unexpected. Much of the otolith diversity is centered among the percomorphs (members of Ophidiiformes, Scrombiformes?, Acropomatiformes) and helps support the Danian as a key interval of the post-extinction radiation of this group that is dominant today. The shark fauna (represented by isolated teeth) has a lower diversity, but comprises representatives of different clades including Carcharhiniformes (Triakidae) and Squaliformes (Squalidae and Etmopteridae?). The triakid appears to be a species of Palaeogaleus , but fragments of other tiny teeth with thin central cusps point to the possibility of a lamniform or even another squaliform lineage. The squaliform fossils of a species of Squalus and an Etmopterus -like taxon likely are the first records of this ordinal clade in the Danian of the Gulf Coast, and they support the interpretation of parts of the formation as being deposited in deep waters. Squalus is a mass extinction survivor, but at present Etmopterus and its closest relatives are known only later in the Cenozoic. The Wills Point fauna helps to demonstrate that the later part of the Danian was a key time in marine vertebrate evolution with: 1. a unique mixture of Cretaceous surviving species and lineages coincident with early records of post-extinction diversifying clades (such as the percomorphs); 2. the long-term survival of some regionally endemic fish otolith taxa; and 3. insights into deep water faunas on the Gulf Coast.

title: Beyond Baselines: The Relational Dimension of Conservation Paleobiology
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: DIETL, Gregory P. [1]
affiliations: (1) Paleontological Research Institution, Ithaca, New York, USA; Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, USA
abstract:
Conservation paleobiology is typically framed as a means of extending ecological baselines beyond the limits of contemporary observation. Here, I argue that this framing understates the field's broader value for conservation science. As conservation increasingly emphasizes rapid assessment, real-time monitoring, and short-term management outcomes, ecological change is often interpreted through compressed temporal frames that reinforce shifting baseline syndrome, eroding ecological memory. Drawing on Hartmut Rosa's theory of social acceleration, which describes how modern societies increasingly compress temporal experience and prioritize immediacy, I propose that the long-term perspective provided by geohistorical records promotes temporal deceleration by expanding the temporal frame of reference through which conservation practitioners interpret ecological change.

Biological invasions serve as a case study illustrating how temporal perspective shapes conservation thinking. Geohistorical records restore ecological memory across nested temporal scales, documenting invasion histories and long-term trends that place present-day invasions within a broader ecological context. Temporal deceleration alone, however, is not the endpoint. Rather, by restoring ecological memory, the expanded temporal perspective provided by geohistorical records may create conditions for resonance— in the sense of shaping how conservation practitioners interpret invasions before deciding how to act—as a counter to the effects of social acceleration.

The value of conservation paleobiology therefore extends beyond its informational role in establishing ecological baselines. By reshaping how conservation practitioners interpret invasions through expanded temporal perspective, conservation paleobiology has the potential to contribute to the relational dimension of conservation decision-making, reconnecting present-day ecological challenges with the deeper histories that continue to shape ecological futures.
