title: The Timing of Carbon Mobility in Metasedimentary Schist, an Example from the Alabama Graphite Belt
session_title: Geochronology of Ore Deposits Containing Critical Minerals: Analytical Advances and Applications
authors: Stowell, Harold [1], Toma, Jonathan [2], Bollen, Elizabeth [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(3) Geological Survey of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
abstract:
Most resource-grade flake graphite results from concentration and recrystallization of carbon during metamorphism of organic-rich sediments. Important examples with sediment sources include Balama (Mozambique), Mahenge and Nachu (Tanzania), Molo (Madagascar), Graphite Creek (Alaska, USA), and Zavalyevsiry (Ukraine). The concentration of carbon in these and other graphite occurrences requires significant carbon mobility during metamorphism or graphite concentration from partial melting and melt loss. Therefore, the metamorphic conditions and timing of carbon mobility are crucial for understanding mineralization.

The Alabama graphite belt contains flake and vein graphite in schist, gneiss, and quartzite of the Higgins Ferry and Poe Bridge Mountain groups, which extend across approximately 150 km in the eastern Blue Ridge (EBR). Flake graphite occurs in discontinuous schist layers up to 1.5 km thick, which contain < 0.1-m-scale lenses and local approximately 1 cm cross-cutting veins of graphite. Additionally, flake graphite is locally associated with medium- to coarse- grained vanadium-rich muscovite. The Higgins Ferry Group near the southwest end of the Alabama graphite belt reached up to 700°C at 6 to 9 kbar and locally contains leucosome veins and lenses indicating partial melting. Graphite Re-Os ages of 358.3 ± 0.8 and 350.1 ± 1.1 Ma and a garnet Sm-Nd age of 353 ± 3 Ma indicate that most flake graphite crystallized near synchronously with peak metamorphism. Additional graphite Re-Os ages indicate that later graphite veins and graphite growth associated with ductile to brittle veins occurred at approximately 338 and 282 Ma, respectively. These graphite ages overlap or postdate 40 Ar/ 39 Ar cooling ages for three schist and one pegmatite sample which yielded plateau ages of 342 ± 1, 345 ± 2, 337 ± 1, and 339 ± 1 Ma, respectively. This requires some carbon mobility below the Ar closure temperature in muscovite at approximately 350°C.

Published δ 13 C values for Alabama graphite belt metasediments indicate a crustal and likely biogenic origin for carbon; however, graphite veins were emplaced by CO 2 or CH 4 bearing fluids after peak metamorphism. Regardless, there is no evidence for large-scale mobility, and transport was likely centimeter scale. Our data are compatible with biogenic graphite, low carbon mobility, and limited oxidation from metamorphic fluids.

abstract:
Rice accounts for 20% of the world’s annual calorie consumption. Due to the rice crop’s unique physiology, it is susceptible to arsenic uptake from soil, leading to its accumulation within the grain. Arsenic is a toxic metalloid widely occurring in soils across the world. Seasonal flooding of rice paddies creates reducing conditions that can lead to the reductive dissolution of arsenic-bearing minerals, in particular iron oxides. Upon dissolution, these minerals can release arsenic into the pore water, allowing for its uptake into the rice grain. Arsenic is toxic to the rice plant, significantly reducing crop yield, and is toxic to humans who consume it.

To better understand the environmental factors that govern arsenic mobility within soils, as well as its subsequent accumulation within the grain, we sampled rice grain, leaves, soils, and water from paddies across a wide geographical range in Cambodia. The country’s reliance on rice for 60% of its caloric intake as well as the widespread traditional farming practices, make Cambodia an ideal location for this research. Soil reflectance measurements of nearly 200 rice paddies across Cambodia were made using a visible reflectance spectrophotometer. We also deployed synthetic iron oxide strips across a subset of these fields to assess their utility as indicators of reduction in soil (IRIS).

Here, we present the results of IRIS strip measurements and visible reflectance spectroscopy of soil, and link them to soil and rice grain arsenic levels. Our research suggests that spectroscopy of soil within the visible light spectrum is predictive of rice grain arsenic and soil redox conditions. In particular, we find that the spectral slope of reflected light at specific wavelengths correlates with soil arsenic concentrations. This research demonstrates the potential of spectroscopy in predicting rice grain quality before the crop is even planted in a field. Our findings can lead to increased public health and food security in nations like Cambodia where rice is a staple.

title: IOCG Deposits are Enigmatic and Fundamental Questions Demand Answers
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Thompson, John FH [1], del Real, Irene [2]
affiliations: (1) PetraScience Consultants, Vancouver, BC, Canada
(2) Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Santiago, Chile
abstract:
Iron oxide Cu-Au (IOCG) deposits are an economically important mineral deposit class defined by mineralogy – Cu sulfides, Fe oxides and K-Na-Ca alteration mineral assemblages; a broad classification that causes potential misclassification. Major groups of unequivocal IOCG deposits occur in metallogenic provinces formed from the late Archean to Cretaceous, commonly with a range of ages within provinces. Provinces may also contain, or be dominated by, iron oxide-apatite (IOA) deposits. The age range of IOCG provinces and mineralization styles differ significantly from porphyry deposits, implying contrasting formation and preservation histories.

IOCG-focussed research has established settings, mineralogical characteristics, structural controls, metal zoning patterns, and ages. Mineralogy is poorly suited to fluid inclusion studies, but geochemical and isotopic methods suggest a variety of fluid, and therefore, metal sources. Empirical data support a general spatial model that helps the evaluation of deposits, but the wide range of geometries and mineralization styles, and the inadequate genetic model hinder predictive exploration.

Fundamental unknowns need to be addressed to advance the understanding of IOCG and assist with the discovery of new deposits. The tectonic framework in the Andean belt is documented with strike-slip deformation, but the relative importance of transtension versus transpression are not well-understood. Subduction and transcrustal structures have been suggested in older provinces, but extension is also recognized. Magmatism is a critical component of the framework, and while documented to be co-temporal with mineralization in some deposits, mineralizing intrusive phases and associated processes have not been identified.

There is evidence to support magmatic sources of fluids and metals in several deposits, but continental brines and other fluids appear to play a role, and wallrocks may contribute to the long list of metals enriched in IOCG. The importance of brines is supported by evidence for evaporites and continental basins in some provinces. Both regional and deposit-focused alteration occur in most areas but may be of different ages and origins.

The relationship between IOCG and IOA deposits is uncertain, not helped by conflicting models for the latter. Similarly, the relationship, if any, to stratabound Cu-Ag and porphyry Cu deposits in the Andean belt is debated. Our inability to resolve these basic questions is unsatisfactory, hinders exploration, and demands further collaborative research in several global provinces.

title: Muck Matters in the Critical Zone: Greenhouse Gas Production Potential of Flocculent Organic Sediments
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes
authors: Fatima, Nudrat [1], Zarnetske, Jay P. [2], Finegan, Carly R. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA
abstract: Flocculent organic sediment, also referred to as “floc” or “muck”, accumulates at the groundwater-surface water interface in many shallow freshwater ecosystems. While floc is organic-rich, porous, and exposed to rapidly changing redox conditions, it is often an undocumented part of the critical zone due to the difficulties associated with studying it. We hypothesized that floc is an important biogeochemical hotspot because it has a greater greenhouse gas production potential than adjacent water and mineral sediment. To make the first-ever assessment of the greenhouse gas production potential, we conducted laboratory incubation experiments on floc, mineral sediments, and water collected from the Augusta Creek watershed, located in southwestern Michigan. The samples were collected from three types of freshwater ecosystems: a pond, a wetland, and a stream margin. These samples, along with controls, were incubated in sealed serum bottles for 72 hours, with headspace greenhouse gas content (CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O) measured by gas chromatography at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours. Headspace production rates were normalized to initial wet sample mass. Across all ecosystems, floc consistently produced more CO₂ than water and mineral sediment. Overall, mean 0-48-hour floc CO₂ production ranged across ecosystem types, but floc CO₂ production was 2.7-15.0 times greater than mineral sediment production and 16.3-77.5 times greater than water production. CH₄ production was more variable and dependent on ecosystem, floc properties, and incubation period. Wetland floc produced CH₄ at a rate approximately 71 times greater than water and 66 times greater than mineral sediment. N₂O production rates were less than CO 2 and CH 4 and more variable across all incubations. Together, these novel floc experiments support our hypothesis that floc is a reactive hotspot, especially for CO₂ production, compared to other parts of these ecosystems. Hence, explicitly recognizing and studying floc may improve estimates of shallow aquatic ecosystem greenhouse gas dynamics and help explain why they are significant sources of global greenhouse gases. More generally, this study demonstrates that floc likely contains many undocumented redox processes within the freshwaters of Earth’s critical zone.

title: Microfacial, Paleontological and Structural Analyses of the Middle Oligocene Abraq Formation, in Al Jabal al Akhdar, Libya.
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Posters)
authors: Al Kowafi, Anas A. of [1], KHAMEISS, BELKASIM [2], Khalifa , Ali [3]
affiliations: (1) 1The Libyan Academy – Ajdabiya Branch, Libya, School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Department of Geology, Ajdabiyah, Libya., Benghazi, Libya
(2) 3Oklahoma Geological Survey, Sarkeys Energy Center,100 E. Boyd St., Suite N131, Norman, OK 73019, NORMAN, Oklahoma, USA
(3) Faculty Member - Geology Department / College of Engineering Sciences Bright Star University, Libya
abstract:
Macrofossils are used largely as biomarkers to delineate specific stratigraphic horizons. This fact is applied to define the exposed Oligocene Abraq Formation at the Tansolukh-Abyar road-cut section in Al Jabal al Akhdar, northeast Libya. This Formation has been divided into six microfacies based on both depositional texture and paleontological contents, these from bottom to top: i) Echinocyamus-Nummulitic Packstone Microfacies ii) Nummultic Peloidal Grainstone Microfacies; iii) Nummulitic Echinoidal Packstone Microfacies; iv) Nummulitic Packstone Microfacies; v) Nummulitic Dolograinstone Microfacies; and vi) Silty-operculinid Packstone Microfacies. The supra-abundance of the small-sized infaunal echinoids “ Echinocyamus” has been documented for the first time from Libya. Based on the co-occurrences of the larger benthic foraminifers ( Eulepidina dilatata, Nummulites fichteli and Nummulites vascus ), the Nummulites fichteli – Nummulites vascus Biozone of Rupelian age is assigned to the Abraq Formation. According to the standard benthic Zones of the Tethyan realm, it is assigned to SBZ 21 (early Rupelian) and SBZ 22A (late Rupelian). The tiny Echinocyamus species are stratigraphically used in the correlation with the Echinocyamus- bearing horizons from other paleobiogeographical realms. The presence of vertebrate bony fish rib has been found in the Abraq Formation within Nummulitic Packstone Microfacies for the first time. The environmental significance of the middle-ramp setting of the six established Abraq limestone microfacies, and the stratigraphical relationships with the underlying Algal Limestone of the Al Bayda Formation and the overlying Al Faidiyah Formation have also been established. The recent documentation of noticeable structural deformations (folding and faulting) that were observed in the Abraq Formation, at Wadi Sidi Yousif Quarry and Wadi al Kuf roadcut sections, are considered of importance in understanding the structural configuration of the Al Jabal al Akhdar during Oligocene time.

title: Basal Cambrian Sediment Sourcing and Routing in the Western Laurentian Midcontinent, Iowa, USA

authors: Wendler, Tealyn Kay [1], Malone, Dave [2], Malone , Jack [3], Craddock, John [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Geography, & The Environment Department , Illinois State University, Normal, WI, USA

abstract: The Cambrian Mt. Simon Sandstone records the initial Paleozoic transgression of the Laurentian midcontinent. Here we evaluate detrital zircon U-Pb data from six drill core samples in Iowa in order to constrain sediment sourcing and routing in the western Laurentian midcontinent. Zircons were analyzed by LA-ICPMS at the University of Arizona Laserchron Center. In southeast Iowa, the FrissU core is dominated by a ~2700 Ma age peak, indicating a distal, northerly sediment source in the Archean Superior Provence. The FrissL core has a broad, age distribution dominated by ~1350–1450 Ma zircons, with secondary Paleoproterozoic (~1700–1850 Ma) and Archean (~2700 Ma) populations, recording a well-mixed transgressive fluvial system traversing Iowa. In southcentral Iowa, The KeithU core exhibits a broad age distribution from 1100–1400 Ma and a lesser Paleoproterozoic contribution (1780-1840 Ma), indicating mixed localized erosion of underlying Iowa basement rocks such as the Midcontinent Rift or Granite-Rhyolite Province and western sources from the Transcontinental Arch. The KeithL core has a prominent age peak of ~1400 Ma, indicating erosion of Iowa Granite-Rhyolite basement rocks. In northcentral Iowa, the MN6 core exhibits a bimodal signature with peaks at ~1850 Ma and ~2700 Ma, where the older population indicates sourcing from Paleoproterozoic and Archean basement along the Transcontinental Arch. The A1-2 NJ core contains a Mesoproterozoic cluster (~1100–1450 Ma) paired with a lesser ~2700 Ma peak indicating a mix of local basement and distal northerly sediment sourcing. Overall, the Mt. Simon in Iowa contains mostly zircons sourced from local basement rocks, with the Transcontinental Arch sourcing sediment. An interesting finding of this research is that most of these samples contain sparse late Neoproterozoic and early Cambrian zircons. The zircons occur only in core east and south of the southern boundary fault of the Midcontinent rift, indicating the presence of juvenile crust of this age in Iowa, such as the late Neoproterozoic to Early Cambrian (~540–500 Ma) Elk Creek Carbonatite. Alternatively, a younger shallower arm of the Illinois Aulacogen may occur in the Iowa subsurface.

abstract: The Mammoth Site of Hot Springs, SD (HSMS) is an active in-situ Pleistocene paleontological museum which has been in operation for over 50 years. Since 2002, HSMS has hosted an annual summer internship program for college-aged students and recent graduates. Today, the museum internship program is structured for interns to continually engage with the public while developing skills in excavation, in-situ conservation, fossil preparation, microfossil picking and sorting, and collections management. The internship program has shifted in structure and scope over the past 24 years, thus evaluating previous intern experiences provides valuable insight to understanding the past impact and future directions of the internship program. We emailed a self-reporting survey, consisting of a mix of multiple choice and write-in answers, to 106 former HSMS internship participants to evaluate how the internship program has evolved over its years of existence, and how a specific iteration of the program helped shape an intern’s career trajectory. We received 45 anonymous responses in which individuals were asked what year they participated in the internship program, the focus of their internship, their level of education at the time of the internship, their current employment, and highest current level of education obtained. Additionally, the survey asked respondents about their specific programs—how much of it was research focused, education focused, or if they worked in a mixture of both aspects—and about the influence that the program had on them. These metrics allow the Mammoth Site to evaluate the efficacy of the internship, both in terms of technical skills learned and in shaping future careers. Overall, 57.78% of respondents indicated that the internship had some-to-major influence on their future careers, with 20% reporting a major influence. Cumulatively, 28% of respondents stated science communication as the most beneficial skillset they developed while participating in the program, from guiding tours to teaching hands-on dig classes as tours become self-guided. Additionally, the opportunity for interns to delve into multiple aspects of paleontology and museum work was of great value. The experiences of past interns are of immense utility to The Mammoth Site as the internship program continues to evolve to provide benefit to participants while achieving and expanding its educational and research objectives.

title: Small Fans, Coarse Carbon: Woody Debris and the Underestimated Turbidite Carbon Sink
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections
authors: Ponton, Camilo [1], Okedoyin, Omololu E [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
abstract:
Submarine turbidite systems efficiently bury terrestrial organic carbon (OC), yet global estimates rest on a few well-studied large fans (Bengal, Congo, Amazon). Roughly two-thirds of the global riverine OC supply is routed through a vast residual population of small, largely unstudied systems whose burial efficiency is modelled rather than measured. Those most likely to depart from modelled values are small, high-relief, forested active margins, where turbidity currents deliver abundant coarse woody debris. Yet these are the least represented in global datasets, as sandy turbidites are difficult to core, and geochemical analyses conventionally target only the fine fraction.

The Nitinat Fan, Cascadia Basin, tests this bias. Analysis of turbidite samples from ODP Leg 146, Site 888B, separated into fine (<2 mm) and coarse (>2 mm) fractions, confirms a gymnosperm source for the woody debris (stable isotopes, elemental ratios, Raman microscopy), establishing a land–sea carbon pathway via turbidity currents. Wood-bearing layers contain six times more OC than non-wood-bearing sediments, 77% in the coarse fraction. The fan has sequestered ~1,200 MtC since the mid-Pleistocene, ~50% above estimates based on the fine fraction alone. One fan is minor globally, but the bias it quantifies likely propagates across the forested active margins that dominate the unmeasured population. Including coarse woody debris in OC budgets is necessary to constrain land–sea carbon fluxes.

abstract:
The Northern Great Plains is experiencing increasing hydrologic variability driven by shifts in precipitation and temperature associated with climate change. While extensive research has focused on the mountainous headwaters of the Missouri River Basin, the Missouri Plateau remains critically understudied despite its importance for regional water resources, agriculture, and Tribal communities. This study investigates the hydrology of the Cannonball River Watershed (CRW), a major tributary within the area, using field-based observations and a cold region hydrologic model (CRHM). To supplement the existing 15 climate stations, three rainfall and soil moisture monitoring stations were deployed across the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation within CRW. Field observations of soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and streamflow collected from 2024 to 2026 were used to evaluate the CRW CRHM model.

Results highlight strong interannual hydrologic contrasts between consecutive water years. The 2024–2025 season was wetter than 2025–2026, while both winters experienced below-average snowfall, limiting snowmelt contributions to streamflow. Spatial analyses of precipitation (18 stations over 11,000 km 2 ) reveal considerable variability across the watershed, with a pronounced east-to-west rainfall gradient during the wetter season. Streamflow response was more strongly influenced by precipitation occurring in the central portion of the watershed than by rainfall in the headwaters, indicating that storm location plays a greater role in runoff generation than previously assumed. During a major rainfall event in May 2025, river stage increased 2.61 m over four days, whereas by July 24, 2026, stream stage had declined to approximately 0.2 m under much drier conditions. Soil moisture also spiked due to major precipitation events and receded due to evapotranspiration. Modeled ET at the soil moisture stations ranged from 156.7 mm to 357.1 mm.

These findings demonstrate the importance of distributed field observations for improving understanding of climate-driven hydrologic variability and supporting hydrologic modeling in the Missouri Plateau while strengthening water resource management through collaboration between the University of North Dakota and the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe.

title: Fern Spores From Inland Lake Sediment Core Indicate Floral Change at Poisonwood Blue Hole, New Providence, The Bahamas

authors: White, Lauryn [1], Hopps, Connor [2], Leonard-Pingel, Jill [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(2) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(3) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
abstract:
The Bahamas supports a remarkable diversity of endemic plants, birds, reptiles, and marine life, but these ecosystems are threatened by climate change, including projected sea-level rise and increased hurricane intensity, as well as coastal development, pollution, and invasive species. Creating a natural baseline for Bahamian terrestrial communities and better understanding how these communities have reacted to environmental shifts in the past, can help inform conservation and management strategies in the present. Ferns are diverse and encompass a wide variety of habitats in The Bahamas, with preserved spore records offering a useful proxy to their past abundance. The Bahamas is an optimal setting for the study of these records due to its well-documented human habitation, diverse climatic history, and wealth of depositional sites. Analyzing trends in spore records allows us to track shifts in fern communities through time, infer past environmental conditions, and define ecological baselines: environmental conditions before human influence. A spore record obtained from a sediment core from Poisonwood Blue Hole (PWBH) on New Providence Island, The Bahamas, allows us to reconstruct the past environment, identify when and how the environment shifted naturally or as a result of human disturbance, and see how the plant community responded to these changes.

We have identified three major fern species in the PWBH sediment core record: Acrostichum aureum, Pteridium aquilinum, and Phlebodium aureum. We analyzed fern diversity and abundance over time and defined three distinct zones within the core. Beginning at the bottom of the core ~6500 cal yr BP, Zone 3 is dominated by wetland ferns (A. aureum) and likely represents a shallow wetland. Zone 2, beginning ~1150 cal yr BP, is defined by an increase in epiphytic (P. aureum) and coppice ferns (P. aquilinum). This zone occurs concurrently with spikes in charcoal and pine pollen seen in other floral records consistent with Lucayan habitation and agricultural burning. Zone 1 is defined by the loss of the previously mentioned epiphytic and coppice ferns and returned dominance of wetland ferns. Abundance of fern spores throughout the sediment core can help us reconstruct past environmental conditions, as well as floral shifts due to both natural and anthropogenic stress. Ecological baselines, which represent what the floral community was like, could be used to aid in local plant conservation efforts.

title: Field and Modeling Constraints on the Construction of Arc Crust
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Klein, Benjamin [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
abstract:
Exposed arc crustal sections represent unique locations to study the transport, storage, and differentiation of arc magmas from (near-)Moho depths to the shallow crust, offering ‘top-down’ constraints on arc construction processes that in modern arcs are only accessible through ‘bottom-up’ geophysical methods. Several well-studied paleo-island and -continental arc crustal sections exist, and they all show similar first-order structure: a lower crust dominated by mafic cumulates, and a relatively sharp transition to an intermediate to felsic middle and upper crust dominated by granitoid intrusions. Metasediments and other material representing either the pre-existing crust on which the arc was constructed, or tectonically added material, are present in nearly all crustal sections but constitute at most ~30% of the exposed middle and lower crust. Here I will examine models for the construction of arc crust motivated by these sections, focusing on the Bear Valley Intrusive Suite (BVIS), a continuous crustal section spanning from >9 to <3 kbars in the Southern Sierra Nevada Batholith (California). High-precision zircon geochronology shows that this entire section was constructed in <1.5 Myr, making the BVIS one of the few crustal sections where contemporaneous intrusions can be examined across all crustal levels.

Specifically, I will use the BVIS to examine two frequently discussed topics in arc magmatism: 1) trans-crustal, mush-dominated magmatic systems, and 2) magmatic flare-ups. First, it is increasingly thought that mush-dominated magmatic systems are the norm, but the transport of magma through these systems at crustal scales is not well understood. Construction of the BVIS likely required rapid transport of differentiated magmas from the lower to middle crust. I will examine possible mechanisms for this transport within a mush-dominated crustal section. Second, the transition from felsic plutons to mafic cumulates occurs at a shallower level in the BVIS than in the rest of the Sierra Nevada Batholith. This likely results from elevated magmatic fluxes during a flare-up, which raised lower crustal temperatures and allowed mafic magmas to ascend to shallower levels before stagnating and crystallizing. Together, these ‘top-down’ results demonstrate how field, geochronologic, and geochemical data from exposed arc crustal sections constrain the rates and mechanisms of arc construction and can be directly compared with ‘bottom-up’ geophysical images to build a more complete picture of arc crust assembly.

title: Exploring Pit Features on Europa Using JunoCam Imagery
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Greenwell, Sophie [1], Sacks, Leah [2], Leonard, Erin [3]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Geosciences, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, La Canada Flintridge, California, USA; Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana, USA
(2) Planetary Geosciences, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, La Canada Flintridge, California, USA
(3) Planetary Geosciences, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, La Canada Flintridge, California, USA
abstract:
The surface of Europa hosts a variety of fascinating geologic features for which we do not understand the formation mechanism, including multi-kilometer scale depressions called pits. Many existing studies of surface features on Europa, primarily based on 1996-2000 Galileo mission images, identify pits and propose possible formation mechanisms. The term “lenticulae” has often been used to collectively describe pits, spots, and domes due to their similar sizes, shapes, and close spatial associations in the Galileo imagery. This grouping implies a shared formation mechanism for these features. However, there is no consensus for how pits should be defined, how they form, or how they relate to other surface features such as ridges and bands. Advancing our understanding of pits will help contextualize and refine interpretations of Europa’s surface and internal processes.

In this project, we used ArcGIS Pro to map visible pits, here defined as any noticeable depression on the surface that is not an obvious or previously mapped crater or arcuate depression, in four JunoCam images of a small region of Europa from Juno’s 2022 flyby. We categorized the mapped features based on morphological similarities and analyzed their spatial distribution. We find that pits visible in the JunoCam images vary regionally in circularity, size, and orientation. Several large, approximately north-south oriented pits (greater than 750 km 2 ) are observed in the central region of the study area. This region also contains terrain that appears relatively undisturbed, with consistent apparent albedo and lineaments that continue uninterrupted through the pits. In contrast, the southern region contains many smaller pits (less than 150 km 2 ) with more variable orientations and apparent albedo, indicating the presence of chaos ter rain. Additionally, we have observed a continuum of morphology between several pits in the central region and arcuate depressions, or broad topographic lows that reach hundreds of kilometers in length. Our observations of regional differences in pit morphology support the possibility that multiple processes may be involved in their formation. We also note that many pits visible in the JunoCam images are not apparent in the Galileo images of the same region, and vice versa. This distinction highlights the challenges of remote sensing icy bodies, where image resolution and lighting angles can substantially impact the visibility and character of surface features.

authors: Soumano, Victoire Daniela [1], Badillo, Jackie [2], Daniels, Alecia [3], Shenoy, Neel [4], Owyang, Elaine [5], Godfrey, Jessie [6], Garcia, Joshua [7]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Systems, University of California Merced, Merced, CA, USA
(2) Garcia Lab, University of California Merced, Merced, CA, USA
(3) Agricultural, Health, and Natural Resources, Kentucky State University, Frankfort, Kentucky, USA

abstract: Rising urbanization generates a growing amount of organic waste, the management of which puts a significant strain on municipal budgets and land usage while also contributing to air and water pollution. One strategy for addressing this issue could be to redirect this waste to the production of organic amendments such as biochar and compost, both of which show potential for improving soil health and plant performance across diverse ecosystems. While the soil health benefits of these amendments are well-documented in contexts such as large-scale agricultural production and natural ecosystems, field studies examining their potential benefits in urban agricultural soils are lacking. In this study, we worked with Local Ecology and Agriculture Fremont, a small urban farm in Fremont, CA, USA, to evaluate the influence of locally sourced compost and biochar on physical, chemical, and biological soil health outcomes as well as crop productivity through an on-farm field trial. Preliminary data from samples collected three months after the start of our experiment show that the application of compost and biochar increased soil electrical conductivity relative to unamended soils, suggesting a potential increase in available nutrients. Additionally, we found that soils treated with mixed compost and biochar displayed increased microbial biomass carbon relative to unamended soils, suggesting that mixed compost and biochar could be effective in supporting microbial growth and activity in urban soils. We found that amended soils had lower labile carbon compared to unamended soils, which may be a result of microbial carbon consumption. Overall, our data suggest locally sourced organic amendments could alter soil health outcomes in urban agriculture and hold promise for supporting soil health and functioning in urban landscapes.

title: Marine or Not Marine: A Reinterpretation of the Stratigraphic Architecture and Depositional Setting of the Mesaverde Formation Fales Rocks Quarry, Natrona County, Wyoming

authors: Tenney, Zachary David [1], Wroblewski, Anton [2], McElroy, Brandon [3], Vietti, Laura [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA; Geology & Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
(2) Geology & Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
(3) Geology & Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA

abstract:
The Fales Rocks Quarry (UW V-81006) is the most extensively studied vertebrate locality within the Mesaverde Formation of Wyoming, yet its depositional and stratigraphic setting remains uncertain. The diverse vertebrate assemblage, including chondrichthyans, osteichthyans, amphibians, reptiles, dinosaurs, and mammals, has led previous studies to interpret the site as predominantly nonmarine fluvial and coastal deposits. However, recent field observations identified numerous trace fossils and sedimentary structures indicative of marine influence, prompting a reevaluation of the locality.

We conducted a detailed stratigraphic investigation of the Fales Rocks Quarry and a correlative section in the Ervay Basin, approximately 13 km to the northwest. The Mesaverde Formation in the study area comprises four members: the Fales Member, Wallace Creek Tongue, unnamed middle member, and Teapot Sandstone. Below the unnamed middle member, the Fales Member is composed of shoreface, delta front, and paralic deposits capped by the offshore Wallace Creek Tongue. The unnamed middle member includes carbonaceous mudstones and channel-form sandstones. At Fales Rocks, the vertebrate quarry consists of ironstone-cemented bone-pebble conglomerates with thin mud-draped foresets of trough crossbeds, suggesting tidal influence within the channel system. Overlying strata contain additional channel deposits capped by a climbing-ripple sandstone and an ironstone bed which are indicators of marine event bed deposition. Bergaueria , sea anemone trace fossils, occur in sandstones both below and above the Fales Rocks Quarry.

The majority of fish taxa within the Fales Rocks Quarry are either marine or have brackish water tolerance. Brackish intolerant species, such as amiids and amphibians, are most likely hydraulically transported downstream into inhospitable environments. The new data suggests the Fales Rocks Quarry is part of a complex progradational deltaic succession with frequent transitions from marine to paralic deposits. A significant reinterpretation from the fluvial freshwater meander belt depositional system that has been previously suggested. This study highlights the importance of reexamining historic localities using new stratigraphic methods to improve depositional models and environmental interpretations.

title: Cenozoic Elevation, Uplift, and Climate of the Northern Sierra Nevada, USA: Importance of 40Ar/39Ar Dating of Detrital and Rock K-feldspar in Paleovalleys
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Henry, Christopher D. [1], Heizler, Matthew T. [2], Wood, Jim [3], ONeal, Matt [4], Glasmann, Joseph Reed [5]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA
(2) New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Sierra Geological Services, Colfax, CA, USA
(4) California Geological Survey, Sacramento, CA, USA
(5) Willamette Geological Service, Philomath, OR,
abstract:
The long-debated uplift, elevation, and climate of the Sierra Nevada have relied heavily on the age and other characteristics of paleovalleys and their deposits. However, a presumed 50 Ma age of the “auriferous gravels” based on their contained Chalk Bluff flora has misled researchers for 80 years. Recent detrital zircon dating shows that some deposits are younger but is hampered by the overwhelming abundance of zircons from Cretaceous and Jurassic batholith. Our new detrital and rock dating, especially 40 Ar/ 39 Ar of detrital K-feldspars, demonstrates that the flora and host sediments are ≤40 Ma. Detrital Cenozoic volcanic sanidine is distinguishable from plutonic grains during hand picking, and precise 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates and K/Ca potentially can uniquely identify sources.

New geologic mapping, stratigraphic and mineralogic analysis, new and published detrital dates, and abundant, high-precision sanidine dates of ignimbrites indicate with variable certainty: The ancestral rivers and valleys probably formed by 80 Ma during erosion of a Late Cretaceous batholith highland. The rivers initially eroded, and deposition only occurred at the western marine boundary at the edge of today’s Great Valley. Initial, possibly v-shaped canyons evolved to wide, shallow valleys probably resulting from weathering in a warm, wet climate. Erosion changed to major deposition in the paleovalleys, although precisely when and why are unresolved.

Pre-volcanic deposits consist of lower, thin, kaolinite-rich, coarse gravel and sand of uncertain age (none are dated), and upper, thick sand, fine gravel, and mudstone with smectite proportion increasing upsection. The lower-upper division is difficult to distinguish in the field and can be either an erosional unconformity or gradational. Upper gravels commonly contain sparse 43-25 Ma zircons and are gradational to 31.5-23.0 Ma ignimbrites that erupted in central Nevada and reached the Sierra Nevada by channelized flow in paleovalleys. The scarcity of Cenozoic grains reflects great distances to sources, which, at 43-40 Ma, were no closer than northeastern Nevada and east of all proposed paleodivides to rivers that drained across the Sierra Nevada.

Although not resolving the relative contributions of ≥Eocene and latest Cenozoic uplift, our data indicate uplift between ~43-40 and 4 Ma is unlikely. Modern, deep, v-shaped canyons of the northern Sierra Nevada postdate ancestral Cascade rocks as young as 4 Ma, cut across paleovalleys, and did not re-excavate them.

title: A Landscape in Transition: Geoarchaeological Insights into Coastal Evolution and Neolithic Settlement at Atlit-Yam
session_title: Geoarchaeology of the Land–Sea Interface: Processes, Preservation, and Palaeolandscape Reconstruction
authors: Shtienberg, Gilad [1], Kanari, Mor [2], Friesem, David [3]
affiliations: (1) Anthropology, UC-San Diego, San Diego, California, USA; Geosciences Research Division, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, San Diego, California, USA
(2) Department of Marine Geology and Geophysics, Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research, Haifa, Israel; Department of Marine Geosciences, University of Haifa, Haifa, Israel

abstract: The submerged Pre-Pottery Neolithic settlement of Atlit-Yam, now found 8-12 meters below current sea level and ca. 0.5 km off Israel's Carmel Coast, offers a unique opportunity to investigate how Early Holocene coastal evolution shaped the development, persistence, and eventual abandonment of one of the world's earliest coastal farming settlements. We hypothesize that progressive shoreline transgression, rather than abrupt marine inundation, fundamentally altered the settlement's geomorphic and ecological setting, influencing human land use and long-term settlement sustainability. To test this hypothesis, we integrate high-resolution Chirp seismic data collected across and around Atlit-Yam with sedimentological, geochemical, and chronological records from a nearby coastal sediment core. Seismic profiles, acquired at 2-5-m spacing across the archaeological site and 30–50- m spacing across the surrounding landscape, are used to reconstruct drowned wetlands, transgressive sand bodies, ravinement surfaces, and buried paleo-landforms. Preliminary interpretations suggest that Atlit-Yam (ca. 9.6–8.4 ka) occupied an elevated geomorphic mound adjacent to a freshwater stream and wetland, while a north-south aeolianite ridge may have partially shielded the settlement from coastal sand encroachment and marine processes. We evaluate whether this landscape configuration reflects deliberate human niche construction, with selection of a naturally resilient setting that maximizes freshwater availability and ecological diversity while reducing exposure to coastal hazards. We further test whether continued sea-level rise, wetland migration, groundwater salinization, shoreline transgression, and increasing deposition of littoral sands progressively reduced habitable land and altered coastal ecosystems, ultimately contributing to settlement relocation prior to the site inundation. This ongoing study explores how integrating marine geophysics, coastal stratigraphy, and archaeology can provide a geoarchaeological framework for understanding the reciprocal evolution of coastal landscapes and Neolithic settlement systems, while extending the archaeological investigation to areas of sub-seafloor buried remains.

abstract: Sulfuric acid-driven carbonate dissolution is a rapid and dynamic weathering process that represents a net flux of CO 2 to the atmosphere. This process, and its consequences for karstification, can be directly observed in active sulfuric acid caves, which are sites of rapid carbonate corrosion and void development in the subsurface. Most research on limestone dissolution in sulfuric acid caves has focused on the phreatic zone; however, H 2 S degassing from springs and streams also drives substantial carbonate corrosion and secondary mineral precipitation above the water table. In this study, we are combining direct measurements of sulfide oxidation and carbonate dissolution with modeling and microbiological approaches to quantify this degassing-driven process in the vadose zone of the Frasassi cave system, Italy, and evaluate microbiological contributions to karstification in different cave regions. Tablet dissolution experiments showed that corrosion is most rapid close to sulfidic cave streams, but could still be detected at distances >10 m above the water table where H 2 S(g) concentrations are <1 ppmv. We are testing a method using a stable isotope tracer to measure sulfide oxidation rates on cave wall surfaces across this same spatial gradient, and to assess biotic versus abiotic contributions to sulfide oxidation. To study microbial activity in more detail, we combined rRNA transcript libraries with metagenomics, which showed that sulfide-oxidizing bacteria are abundant and active both in the active corrosion zone close to the sulfidic water table, but also further away where H 2 S(g) is not detectable in the cave atmosphere. Metatranscriptomic analyses, in progress, will reveal other active metabolic processes in zones that are removed from H 2 S degassing, in order to test the hypothesis that other lithotrophic and organotrophic metabolisms are more prevalent in these lower energy areas and to explore other microbiological processes that may continue to modify cave walls long after H 2 S degassing ceases.

authors: Rataizer, Jordana [1], Schwartz, Joshua J. [2], Miranda, Elena A. [3], Klepeis, Keith [4], Richter, Sadie [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State Univesity, Northridge, Northridge, CA, USA

abstract: How large volumes of continental crust are generated and emplaced remains a long-standing problem in geology. In continental arc settings, intermediate lower-crustal melts are transported upward through dike networks to build shallow-crustal granitic batholiths. Dikes therefore record evolving melt chemistry and vertical network connectivity. The Misty pluton in Fiordland, New Zealand provides an opportunity to investigate an exhumed and tilted vertical cross section of Cretaceous lower-arc crust. Our mapping divides the Misty Pluton into four structural zones. The deepest region (zone 1) occurs in the west, zone 4 in the east is the shallowest. We use applies amphibole chemometry on 14 intermediate-felsic dikes sampled across Zones 2–4, spanning ~20–35 km paleodepths, to test whether Misty Pluton melts contributed to the emplacement of the Western McKerr Intrusives, which occur in the mid-crust above the Misty Pluton. The dikes are ~0.5 to 10 cm thick, with some reaching ~1 m. Their textures range from coarse-grained to pegmatitic, and their mineral assemblages are dominated by plagioclase and amphibole, with abundant epidote and biotite, accessory apatite and Fe–Ti oxides, and quartz and titanite. Zone 2 Amphiboles are classified as pargasite, magnesio-hastingsite, and, rarely, tschermakite, with calculated crystallization temperatures of 820–940 °C. Their amphibole-equilibrium melts are dacitic. Zone 3 amphiboles are classified as tschermakite and yield estimated crystallization temperatures of 820–1000 °C. Their amphibole-equilibrium melts define basaltic-andesitic and dacitic-rhyolitic groups. Zone 4 amphiboles range from tschermakite to ferro-tschermakite and yield calculated crystallization temperatures of 825–925 °C. Their equilibrium melts are andesitic to dacitic. Harker diagrams comparing dike amphibole equilibrium melts with the Misty Pluton and Western McKerr Intrusives show that Zones 2 and 4 overlap with the Misty Pluton trend and bridge the two systems. Zone 3 melts form distinct mafic and felsic groups that do not overlap with the Misty Pluton but follow the same general trend; the felsic group bridges the two systems. Taken together, these results support a genetic connection between the two systems and suggest that evolved melts from zones 2-4 contributed to the growth of the Western McKerr Intrusives. Zone 3 mafic melts may record hydrous basaltic recharge in the lower arc crust.

title: New Material Referable to Stegosaurus armatus Marsh 1877, the Historical Type Species of Stegosaurus
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Mossbrucker, Matthew T. [1]
affiliations: (1) Morrison Natural History Museum, Morrison, CO, USA
abstract:
New material referable to Stegosaurus armatus Marsh 1877 has been identified from the Lakes-Marsh Atlantosaurus Beds at Morrison, Colorado. It includes an isolated proximal mid-caudal vertebra, a partial sacrum, and a dorsal plate, all partially exposed in matrix and under preparation. These elements do not duplicate the historical material and are consistent in scale with these specimens, all from the same quarry. Together, the new and historical collections provide further insight into this enigmatic type specimen.

Scores of Late Jurassic fossils were collected from these Morrison Formation outcrops during the 1870s for the Yale museum. O. C. Marsh acquired the specimens and described novel fossils from six localities. One yielded “Saurian No. 5,” the historical type of S. armatus , and became known as Quarry 5. The site is a fluvial, mostly grain-supported, poorly sorted quartz arenite with dispersed mudstone lag. These irregular clasts are commonly directly cemented, complicating preparation and examination.

Quarry 5 also contains mostly isolated remains of Allosaurus , Camarasaurus , and Apatosaurus material attributed to Diplodocus lacustris Marsh 1884, a nomen nudum . Marsh’s 1877 description of S. armatus consisted of three paragraphs without figures and included teeth now recognized as diplodocine, which he later attributed to D. lacustris . Accordingly, remains not confidently identifiable as Stegosauridae are excluded here.

A survey of the historical Quarry 5 collections sought to identify the original Stegosaurus material. Although much remains unprepared in separate blocks, indisputably identifiable postcrania include two isolated proximal caudal vertebrae; four articulated proximal caudals; four partially articulated mid-caudal centra; five articulated caudal neural spines; seven articulated caudal centra posterior to the mid-caudal series; several chevrons; one partial plate from the pelvic or proximal caudal region; and one isolated plate tip.

The caudal series preserves a distinctive stegosaurian suite of characters. The historical type of S. armatus is adequate to diagnose the taxon and includes tall neural spines from the tail base through the mid-tail, each terminating in a well-developed bicondylar apex. The restored partial dorsal plate resembles the broad-based, narrow-tipped plates of the Carnegie Quarry, Utah, stegosaur population. Continued preparation will further clarify this historically significant specimen.

title: Refinement of Continental Lower Crust by an Orogenic Density Filter
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Klein, Benjamin [1], Smye, Andrew [2], Müntener, Othmar [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
(2) Penn State University, University Park, PA,
(3) University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
abstract:
Estimates for the bulk composition of lower continental crust differ depending on the material considered: average compositions derived from granulite terranes are dominantly andesitic, while the average composition of lower crustal xenoliths is more mafic. Indirect geophysical constraints from e.g., seismic velocities and heat flow measurements are equivocal and permissive of either compositional estimate. Often, the discrepancy between the granulite terranes and xenoliths is attributed to preservation bias: that granulite terranes are more felsic because this material is buoyant and more readily exhumed, while felsic material is missing from the xenolith record due to dissolution of this material by the entraining melt. Here, we present and evaluate an alternative hypothesis that unifies these differing compositional estimates: 1) that ‘immature’ lower continental crust is primarily constructed in volcanic arcs and thus is dominated by mafic magmatic material. This component dominates the material most frequently sampled in xenoliths. 2) During subsequent ocean closure and continental collision, crustal thickening produces pressures sufficiently high for much of this mafic material to become density unstable, while at the same time temperatures are sufficiently high to enable rapid flow and delamination of this material.

We evaluate the viability of this model through a combination of phase equilibria modeling, geodynamic modeling and comparison to the rock record. Using phase equilibria modeling, we find that mafic lower crust is density stable when located in typical arc crust thermal structure, but becomes denser than underlying mantle when orogenic thickening increases crustal thicknesses to at least 55 km, corresponding to lower crustal pressures above 1.5 GPa. Geodynamic modeling shows that for typical lower crustal rheologies, temperatures of at least 850 °C are required for efficient removal of these dense roots on timescales comparable to orogenic events. Through this mechanism, dense mafic material can be efficiently removed, leaving a lower crust that more closely resembles the average composition in granulite terranes. Finally, we evaluate these predictions by comparing the bulk compositions of representative high-pressure granulite terranes to regions that were exposed to lower pressures and/or temperatures. Based on these findings, we explore the efficacy of the orogenic density filter to produce stable lower continental crust over Earth history, and to resolve the discrepancy between xenolith and granulite records.

title: Southwest North American Interglacials were Significantly Dustier than Glacials During the Middle Pleistocene: A Long-Term and High-Resolution Dust Record from the Valles Caldera, New Mexico
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Fawcett, Peter J. [1], Draven, Elias [2]
affiliations: (1) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
(2) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
abstract: Long-term dust records from polar ice cores and marine sediments show that Quaternary glacial periods were significantly dustier than interglacial periods in response to globally colder, drier, and windier glacial conditions. However, recent work from Stoneman Lake Arizona (Staley et al., 2025 Nat. Comms.) showed an opposite glacial-interglacial trend for southwestern North America. Here, interglacial dust fluxes were higher than glacial fluxes, as this region experienced drier interglacials relative to the wetter (pluvial) conditions during glacial maxima. In this study, we extend this analysis to the middle Pleistocene and further east into New Mexico to test the wet glacial – dry interglacial dust flux hypothesis for the southwest. A deep sediment core from the Valles Caldera (core VC-3), a large volcanic caldera that contained a large alpine lake during the mid-Pleistocene, provides an excellent long-term dust record. Core VC-3 extends in time from late MIS 14 (~552 ka) to early MIS 10 (~370 ka) with the age model constrained by Ar-Ar tephra dates and paleomagnetic field excursions correlated to well-dated marine events. We use sediment grain size analysis and results from XRF core scanning (Zr/Rb and Zr/Ti) to document changes in eolian input into the lake over time and compare this with already published paleoclimatic records from pollen analysis, molecular biomarkers, sedimentology and other physical core properties. We find that the aeolian dust flux is markedly higher during interglacials (especially MIS 11, an orbital analog for future climate change) as documented by higher Zr/Rb and higher fractions of coarse silt sized material consistent with modern dust grain sizes in the southwest. We hypothesize that wetter glacials, such as MIS 12, allowed a denser vegetation cover across dust source areas southwest of the Valles Caldera, which reduced the regional dust flux. Drier interglacials including MIS 11 developed reduced vegetation cover in the same source areas, allowing for a greater atmospheric dust flux even though the strength of prevailing winds was likely weaker than during the glacial periods. We also find that prominent wetter/drier substages within MIS 11 display reduced/enhanced dust fluxes, likely for the same reason.

abstract:
The physical and chemical state of magma reservoirs is difficult to constrain from active volcanic systems because their magma bodies are inaccessible to geochemical observation. Silicic plutons emplaced in the upper crust preserve information on intrusive magmatism, and may record information about the reservoirs that produced silicic eruptions. However, the extent to which the plutons represent cumulate residues associated with erupted magmas remains uncertain. Exposed shallow magma reservoirs and cogenetic erupted deposits provide an opportunity to consider both the architecture of volcanic plumbing systems and the nature of volcanic-plutonic relationships.

The Oligocene Freeman Creek pluton (central Nevada) represents the upper sections of a silicic magmatic system that was tapped by caldera-forming eruptions in the Stillwater caldera complex. The pluton is composite, with eight texturally and compositionally distinct intrusive units, indicating incremental emplacement of lithologies ranging from quartz monzonite to leucogranite (64.8-77.4 wt.% SiO 2 ). Whole-rock compositions and zircon geochemistry and geochronology indicate that some portions of the pluton are temporally and geochemically similar to the Tuff of Poco Canyon (~350 km 3 , 25.3 Ma), whereas separate mapped intrusions are consistent with the Tuff of Elevenmile Canyon (>2500 km 3 , 25.1 Ma). All major units in the pluton—quartz monzonites, biotite granites, and leucogranites—have geochemically similar counterparts in the erupted compositions, indicating that multiple magma batches were tapped by eruptions. Magma crystallization pressures and temperatures were constrained using rhyoliteMELTS geobarometry and Ti-in-zircon thermometry, respectively. Results indicate that the bulk of the intrusions differentiated between 260 and ~525 MPa before extraction from depth and ultimate shallow emplacement at 160–220 MPa. We use rhyoliteMELTS to estimate the crystal content of intrusions in the pluton, which suggests that the quartz monzonite and biotite granites were the most eruptible (lowest crystal content) magma batches during their ascent to the emplacement level. Leucogranite intrusions are interpreted as late-stage melts that were extracted from magma mushes at or near the emplacement level. The Freeman Creek pluton and associated eruptions demonstrate that incremental pluton assembly and the generation of large, mobile magma bodies capable of feeding caldera-forming eruptions are not mutually exclusive. The pluton preserves intrusions that are compositionally equivalent to the erupted tuffs, indicating that pluton construction and caldera-forming eruptions were supplied from a common magmatic source at depth.

title: A Tale of Two Paleocommunities: Functional Variation After the Permo-Triassic Mass Extinction
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Dineen, Ashley A. [1], Roopnarine, Peter D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Museum of Paleontology, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
(2) Invertebrate Zoology & Geology, California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA, USA
abstract: The Permo-Triassic mass extinction (PTME) is believed to have played a key role in shifting faunal dominance in the ocean from the Paleozoic Evolutionary Fauna (PEF) to that of the Modern Evolutionary Fauna (MEF). This transition indicates that the new Triassic ecosystems were distinct from Permian ones, being better described as restructured after the mass extinction rather than simply recovered. Whereas previous studies have primarily focused on the change of taxonomic diversity following the PTME, less consideration has been given to the functional differences between the surviving PEF and the new MEF members during this period. Here we quantify the functional diversity and trait space of two Early Triassic (Spathian) paleocommunities in the western US, that of the offshore Paris Biota from southeastern Idaho and the shallow onshore Virgin Limestone Member of southwestern Nevada. Despite occurring in the same time interval after the PTME, the two communities represent different depositional environments and what appears to be differing degrees of restructuring. Results indicate that while both communities were roughly equivalent in terms of functional richness, the distribution of that richness in functional ecospace varied. For example, whereas newly originated Triassic taxa shared ecospace with Permian survivors in the Virgin Limestone, and hence retained many PEF-style traits (i.e., passive, sedentary, suspension feeders, etc.), they differed significantly in distribution from the Paris Biota. Thus, the deeper water environment of the Paris Biota may have buffered environmental stresses, resulting in a paleocommunity shifting towards more MEF-style traits (i.e., active, mobile, omnivores and predators, etc.). This indicates that the Paris Biota may represent a more functionally complex ecosystem than has been previously documented in the early Triassic, and a community at the start of an ecological and macroevolutionary transformation. Overall, these results emphasize the need to examine both the spatial and temporal patterns of ecospace occupation after mass extinctions, as well as highlight the intricate connection between taxonomic and functional diversity through time.

title: Black Diamond Goes Ballistic: Reconstructing Reservoir Failure, Explosion Energy, and Ballistic Hazards from the 2024 Black Diamond Pool Hydrothermal Explosion

authors: Kondracki, Phillip J. [1], Hungerford, Jefferson D. G. [2], Gallen, Sean F. [3], Harrison, Lauren N [4]
affiliations: (1) Colorado State University, Greeley, CO, USA
(2) National Park Service, YNP, WY, USA
(3) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(4) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract:
On July 23, 2024, a hydrothermal explosion at Black Diamond Pool in Biscuit Basin, Yellowstone National Park, upended the thermal area and damaged nearby visitor boardwalks. The event represents the largest witnessed hydrothermal explosion in Yellowstone since the Excelsior Geyser explosion of the 1880s. Field investigations documented an ejecta field extending more than 70 m from the source. Ballistic blocks were preferentially distributed along a northeast-trending axis and consisted of diverse lithologies, including hydrothermally altered glacial sediments, laminated siliceous sinter, conglomerate, and breccia.

This study reconstructs the shallow subsurface system beneath Black Diamond Pool and evaluates the processes that allowed pressure to accumulate before failure. We hypothesize that progressive silica precipitation locally reduced porosity and permeability within a shallow, permeable reservoir, restricting fluid flow and promoting overpressurization. The resulting pressure increase eventually exceeded the mechanical strength of the overlying and surrounding materials, producing rapid decompression, flashing of hydrothermal water to steam, and ballistic ejection.

To evaluate this model, surface observations are integrated with subsurface stratigraphy, petrographic and geochemical analyses, ballistic calculations, and one-dimensional numerical modeling of hydrothermal pore-pressure evolution and reservoir failure. More than 1,000 mapped ballistic clasts are used to assess ejecta distribution, preferred transport direction, travel distance, minimum launch velocity, and kinetic energy. Subsurface architecture is constrained using newly developed lithologic logs and three-dimensional correlations of legacy drill cores Y-7 and Y-8, located within approximately 250 m of Black Diamond Pool. Thin-section petrography and electron probe microanalysis are used to correlate ejecta lithologies with specific core intervals and characterize the distribution of hydrothermal alteration and silica cementation. These observations are incorporated into numerical models of pressure evolution and ballistic transport to evaluate the conditions required for reservoir failure and to estimate the energy associated with the observed ejecta field.

By linking directly observed explosion behavior with ballistic mapping, drill-core stratigraphy, and numerical modeling, this study provides a rare reconstruction of the shallow hydrothermal system and the evolution of conditions leading to mechanical failure. The results improve understanding of how shallow hydrothermal reservoirs become sealed, pressurized, and destabilized while providing real-world context for evaluating ballistic hazards and informing future monitoring in heavily visited hydrothermal areas.

abstract:
Access to safe drinking water supplies is fundamental to economic development and public health. Groundwater arsenic is a major public health challenge disproportionately impacting populations in South Asia, including in parts of Bihar, India [1]. Although a number of remediation technologies exist, appropriate selection and management of optimal remediation strategies remains challenging, due, in part, to the intersectionality of technical, socio-economic, regulatory and other factors impacting implementation and sustainability. Here we explore the utility of a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) approach to comparatively evaluate groundwater remediation options commonly implemented in Bihar ( e.g. source switching, sand filtration, reverse-osmosis, disinfection) against criteria types including remediation effectiveness ( e.g. with regard to groundwater arsenic reduction potential), costs, feasibility, sustainability and equity. Input data includes primary field-generated data [2,3,4], and evidential reasoning based open-source MCDA software (Intelligent Decision Systems) [5] is used for MCDA modelling, including of exemplar stakeholder weighting scenarios, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis. The approach here follows a similar approach being developed in parallel for the prioritization of interventions to reduce the burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) [6,7]. Notwithstanding limitations, including assumptions and simplifications for MCDA, the approach demonstrates the highly context-specific nature of groundwater arsenic remediation selection, and enables more transparent evaluation of trade-offs among competing decision objectives. This exploratory investigation offers substantial opportunity for development and potential integration as a decision support tool for improved groundwater remediation.

abstract:
Niobium is a key geochemical identifier of arc magmas, as low Nb concentrations relative to other size-charge comparable trace elements (i.e., negative Nb anomalies) result from the fluid-immobile behavior of high field-strength elements during production of typical arc magmas. Coupled zircon U-Pb-Nb-Ti-eHf i geochemistry may be used to identify short-lived events during which atypically Nb-rich and atypically hot (i.e., high zircon Ti content) magmas are introduced into arcs. We suggest that these geochemical events provide a new view into the tectonic evolution of long-lived convergent margins such as the Sierra Nevada arc, which was active for almost 200 m.y.

In the southern Sierra Nevada, secular variation in Cretaceous zircon initial hafnium isotope ratios (eHfi) delineates a hafnium isotope draw-down interpreted to mark an increasing component of partial melts of continental crust as the Cretaceous arc matured. At approximately 102 Ma, highly variable zircon eHf i values signal the introduction of lower-crustal and depleted-mantle-derived melts into an extending upper arc crust. At ca. 100 Ma, elevated zircon Nb and Ti concentrations are consistent with introduction of partial melts of asthenospheric mantle and subducted oceanic crust into arc magmas.

These data may be explained by slab detachment at ca. 100 Ma, an interpretation consistent with models for mid-Cretaceous collision of the Insular superterrane against southern California. Assuming a ~10 m.y. lag time between collision and breakoff of the Bridge River slab, Cretaceous geochemical data are consistent with Insular superterrane collision at ca. 110 Ma during a relative lull in southern Sierra Nevada arc magmatism. A similar pattern of geochemical disturbance is recorded by the arc at the end of the Jurassic (ca. 148 Ma), where an abrupt, 40-unit variation in zircon eHf i values coincides with a ~100-ppm spike in zircon Nb content. During both the mid-Cretaceous and latest Jurassic geochemical disturbances, unusually Nb-rich zircons are found in high silica magmatic rocks, seemingly implicating the introduction of partial melts of foundering slab material and not sub-slab asthenospheric mantle, the preferred source of rare Nb-rich mafic rocks found in other arcs.

abstract:
Major features of our modern biosphere, including the development of bioregions and the latitudinal diversity gradient, may have begun as early as the Cambrian Period. Though the evolution and diversification of metazoan life predated the Cambrian, the Cambrian “explosion” may have been the evolutionary event which initiated the development of biosphere features observable today. One group that has become important to understanding the development of biogeographic patterns of the biosphere are trilobites. Trilobites, likely originating in the Early Cambrian, diversified rapidly throughout the Cambrian Period. However, the origins and biogeographic history of this group remain poorly understood. This study examines the historical biogeography and spatial evolution of Cambrian trilobites in a phylogenetic context across different biogeographic models. We utilized a previously published phylogenetic dataset and one maximum clade credibility tree which included 106 Cambrian trilobite species coded with 107 discrete characters. The R package ‘BioGeoBEARS’ was used to estimate ancestral states, infer dominant speciation types within each group, and identify global dispersal pathways. The best-fitting model for our phylogeny was the DEC+j model, a model which includes a parameter for founder-event speciation. This finding indicates the spatial evolution of Cambrian trilobites involved dispersal-mediated range expansions and episodic colonization of three distinct clade-related bioregions. Our results further indicate either (i) founder event speciation was an important mechanism implemented by trilobites and/or (ii) there are missing species from the fossil record and trees, thus masking true patterns of biogeography. We recognize that within the trilobite phylogeny, there is large uncertainty regarding the location where the earliest trilobites originated. Our results indicate peri-Gondwana as a potential origin.

This study furthers previous work by providing additional evidence for a possible ancestral area for trilobites in Western Gondwana in the mid-latitudes. Additionally, the initial break-up of Gondwana and potential species-species interactions contributed to dispersal and adaptation/origin via niche partitioning patterns, respectively. We anticipate our study will bolster previous evidence of a trilobite origin in Western Gondwana (Morocco, Spain, etc.) and provide a backdrop for which Early Cambrian trilobite studies may find useful. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of assessing the consistency and variation across multiple biogeographic models to tease apart true patterns from data noise.

title: Interaction of Local and Regional Fluvial Systems in the Pliocene Olla Formation, Southern California, USA
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology (Posters)
authors: Petersen, Aidan [1], Steel, Elisabeth [2], Steel, Ronald J. [3], Chun, Byong Suk [4]

abstract: Fluvial systems stratigraphy can record windows of Earth’s history, with systems ranging from small, local drainage networks to large, continental catchments that can be deposited across varying temporal scales. Spatial interaction between large- and small-scale fluvial networks can lead to deposits with lateral interfingering of sediments. The ultimate scope for this study is to understand how system interfingering is controlled by autogenic sediment storage and release cycles versus allogenic climate and tectonic forcing. The coeval deposition of two systems makes disentangling the controls that govern the architecture of these fluvial deposits challenging, due to the complex nature that the spatial and temporal distribution of the interbedded local and regional sediment presents. For this study, a detailed facies and stratigraphic analysis was conducted of the fluvial Pliocene Olla Formation in the Fish Creek Vallecito Basin (FCVB) of Southern California. The Olla Formation constitutes a unique case where exposure of local sediments deposited from a transverse braided river system (L-suite composition) are interbedded with regional sediment from the axial Colorado River (C-suite composition). Fieldwork, including two stratigraphic sections summarizing over 580 m of section, over 2500 outcrop photos, and satellite imagery show clear vertical alternation and relatively minor grain mixing between the two fluvial systems. C-suite intervals are dominated by paleochannels and floodplains of the Colorado river. Typical C-suite characteristics consist of very fine – fine grain size, quartzose composition, red mudstone layers, high density low angle – parallel lamination, and clear fining upward cycles. L-suite intervals are dominated by floodplains, sheetfloods and bar scale channelized flow. Typical L-suite characteristics consist of medium – coarse grain size, arkosic composition, dark brown – grey mudstone layers, large tangential crossbeds (0.5 – 2 m thick) and poorly-developed thickening and coarsening upward cycles. Through our ongoing work, we aim to quantify the degree to which the interfingering of L- and C-suite deposits varies vertically and laterally in the stratigraphy. The results of this study on stratigraphy and controls on fluvial mixing of large and small fluvial systems represents an important tool for understanding basin stratigraphy. Especially during the tectonically active phase, many basins develop a large basin-axial fluvial system which also receives sediments from basin-transversal smaller fluvial systems.

title: Tracking the Rheological Evolution of Ascending Silicic Magmas Provides Insight into Conduit Dynamics and Eruption Style
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Knesel, Kurt M. [1], Long, Charles [2], Gingerich, Morgan [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, Texas, USA

abstract:
Observations from recent rhyolitic eruptions have led to the suggestion that silicic volcanism is fundamentally pyroclastic in nature and that silicic lavas arise from sintering of fragmented magma during the final stages of ascent in shallow conduits. We attempt to reconcile this proposal with the petrologic observation that explosive activity is generally fed by silicic magmas within a restricted range of pre-eruptive dissolved water between ~4 and 5.5 wt. %, while water contents below or above this threshold tend to promote lava emission. Accordingly, we track the evolution of melt viscosity for three categories of pre-eruptive conditions (i.e., hot and dry magmas; cold and wet magmas; and magmas with intermediate water and temperature) using the viscosity and solubility models of Giordano et al. (2008) and Liu et al. (2005), respectively. As these magmas ascend and degas, their viscosities evolve along distinct paths. Hot, water-poor magmas approach the surface with melt viscosities up to two orders of magnitude lower than their cooler, water-rich counterparts. These viscosity paths govern the time required to relax shear stresses developed during flow and allow evaluation of whether each magma class ascends viscously or fragments during ascent.

The low viscosities and short relaxation times for hot, water-poor silicic magmas hinder strain localization and fragmentation. These magmas typically follow ascent paths conducive for outgassing via deformed, permeable bubble networks developed through conduit-wide laminar flow. This behavior may limit ascent velocity and promote non-explosive effusion of coherent lava. In contrast, magmas with intermediate to high water contents generally meet criterion for shear localization and melt rupture along conduit margins. Their ascent paths favor plug flow, rapid ascent, and explosive activity. However, the depth of fragmentation scales with initial dissolved water, potentially leading to different eruptive outcomes. Magmas with intermediate water contents tend to fragment at shallower depths in the conduit and are thus more likely to fuel dominantly explosive activity. Cooler and wetter magmas achieve fragmentation criteria at greater depth, increasing the potential for occlusion and sintering of fragmented magma prior to existing the vent primarily as extruded lava.

abstract:
Cosmogenic exposure dating of alpine glacial moraine sequences provides numerical ages for the timing of deglaciation and thus proxy information about changes in climate. However, exposure-age populations from moraines often contain outliers, making chronologic interpretation less certain.

To explore the chronology of Late Quaternary glacial retreat in the Rocky Mountains (western USA) and understand better the variability in exposure ages from moraines, we analyzed and sampled 10 boulders on two moraine sequences of different relative ages in the Wind River Range of Wyoming: one interpreted as Late Pleistocene and the other thought to have been deposited during the Little Ice Age based on weathering and soil development. We analyzed in situ produced 10 Be in quartz and calculated exposure ages.

The resulting age distributions each have a distinct mode but are oppositely skewed, yielding probability density functions that are mirror images. On the Little Ice Age moraine, 7 of the 10 samples produced two younger modes: a primary mode at 0.5±0.1 ka (n = 4) and a secondary mode at 1.1±0.1 ka (n = 3), as well as 3 older outliers. On the Late Pleistocene moraine, 7 of the 10 samples have similar ages, forming a unimodal peak of 12.5±0.6 ka, with 3 younger outliers.

We interpret outliers on the Little Ice Age moraine (all older) as caused by rockfall from above the ice, boulder exposure during the Holocene thermal maximum, and/or subsurface muon production. In contrast, on the Late Pleistocene moraine, the outliers are all young and likely reflect rockfall after moraine deposition, erosion of the moraine and exposure of once subsurface boulders, and/or boulder erosion after deposition. We infer that average ages on Late Pleistocene moraines are more likely to be biased young, while ages on Little Ice Age moraines are more likely to be biased old, at least for alpine glacier systems. This analysis allows us to not only refine Late Quaternary glacial chronology in the most concentrated area of glacial ice in the Rocky Mountains, but also to treat scatter as a meaningful signal that provides insight into the processes controlling age distributions.
