abstract:
Hands-on, place-based learning provides students with meaningful opportunities to develop scientific skills while connecting water resource science to their local communities. This approach was implemented through a water quality workshop at White Shield High School on the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation, where students learned to analyze and interpret water quality data using professional field instrumentation.

Through field-based activities, students learned the importance of clean water for human health, ecological function, and sustainable resource management. Using a Hanna Multiparameter Meter and an Apera Pocket Tester, they collected and analyzed water samples from their school's drinking water and a nearby pond, compared water quality between the two sources, and evaluated how water treatment influenced measured parameters. Through small-group investigations, students practiced field sampling techniques and interpreted environmental data.

Workshop effectiveness was assessed using post-activity surveys. Results showed that 92% of students learned at least one new scientific tool or concept, 75% reported an improved understanding of local water resources, and most notably, all students stated that the hands-on activities enhanced their understanding of the concepts presented.

These findings demonstrate the value of culturally responsive, place-based geoscience education for increasing scientific literacy and student engagement in Native-serving schools. By connecting science to local water resources and community priorities, the workshop fostered environmental stewardship while helping broaden participation in the geosciences and strengthening pathways into STEM careers.

abstract:
The Turkana Basin, Kenya, lies within the East African Rift System and preserves one of the world’s most important records of hominin evolution and paleoenvironmental change. On the eastern side of Lake Turkana, the Koobi Fora Formation (KFF) represents a ~560-m-thick stratigraphic succession spanning ~4.2 million years, and is chronologically constrained by 40Ar/39Ar dated tuffs. The most recent member of the KFF, the Chari member, contains the youngest well-dated tuff, the Silbo tuff (~750 ± 20 ka) [1] . Above the Chari is the Galana Boi Bed, a holocene deposit that occurs in unconformity. The stratigraphic interval separating the KFF from the holocene bed units remains poorly constrained chronologically, limiting our ability to resolve the relative influence of uplift, erosion, and Late Quaternary lake-level fluctuations on landscape evolution.

During our 2024 and 2026 field season in areas 3, 4, and 7 of the Ileret region of Turkana, we identified sedimentary packages within this interval that have potential to refine the depositional history of the basin, as well as the temporal context of nearby fossil-bearing and archaeological sites [2] . The objective of this study is to test the hypothesis that the stratigraphic interval between the KFF and the Holocene Beds preserves datable Mid-to-Late Pleistocene sedimentary records. To evaluate this, we apply both conventional and recently developed luminescence-based approaches on feldspars mineral grains to determine the age of their last exposure to sunlight (i.e. deposition age). In this presentation we will compare the robustness of these techniques, and discuss the challenges and strategies employed to obtain a more complete geochronological record for the region.

title: Quartz OSL and Feldspar IRSL Chronology of the Galana Boi Beds, Turkana Basin
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Ceesay, Roheyatou [1], Frouin, Marine [2], Cangemi, Dante Louis [3]
affiliations: (1) Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York, USA
(2) Stony Brook university, Stony Brook, New York, USA

abstract:
The Turkana Basin of northern Kenya, within the East African Rift System, preserves an important record of environmental change and hominin evolution 1 . While, historically, much of the geological and archeological research has focused on old deposits (Miocene, Pliocene, Early Pleistocene), the young (Holocene) sedimentary record and changes in the extent of Lake Turkana during the Holocene remain understudied. In the Ileret region on the eastern side of Lake Turkana, the Galana Boi Beds preserve sediments believed to have been deposited during the African Humid Period (14.8-5 ka), a time of increased moisture and major lake expansion across East Africa 2 . Reconstructing Holocene lake margins would help identify sites where archeological and faunal remains may be preserved, and contribute to a better understanding of past populations during this period.

During our 2024 and 2026 seasons, field observation revealed sedimentary facies with ripple marks, trough-cross beds, volcanic pebbles, graded bedding, and a gastropod-rich transitional bed. These observations suggest that the Galana Boi beds record a multitude of depositional environments, indicating more complex landscape dynamics than previously understood. We collected sediment samples from each distinctive horizon for luminescence dating analysis. Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz and infrared stimulated luminescence (IRSL) dating of potassium-rich feldspar has been applied to these samples. The comparison between OSL and IRSL results will help us refine the timing of sedimentation in the Galana Boi Beds and improve understanding of late Quaternary landscape evolution in the region.

title: Climate-Halokinetic Coupling During the Carnian Pluvial Episode: Paradox Basin, Utah

authors: Ross, Jonathan Daniel [1], Barbeau, David L. [2], Pullen, Alexander [3]
affiliations: (1) School of the Earth, Ocean and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA
(2) School of the Earth, Ocean and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA

abstract: Climatic perturbations that alter the hydrologic cycle may strongly influence salt deformation, affecting surface uplift and synkinematic sedimentation. The Carnian Pluvial Episode (CPE; 234 – 232 Ma) represents a major humid interval interrupting the otherwise largely arid Triassic and provides an opportunity to examine climate–halokinetic coupling. I am investigating the timing of Upper Triassic fluvial growth strata of the Chinle Formation preserved within actively subsiding salt-withdrawal minibasins between rising salt walls in the Paradox Basin, Utah. I hypothesize that CPE-related moisture contributed to the development of highly weathered paleosols within the lower Chinle Formation, while also accelerating salt withdrawal and minibasin subsidence rates via increased sediment generation. I am testing the hypothesis through the determination of maximum depositional ages of Chinle strata using laser-ablation U–Pb detrital-zircon geochronology. A robust maximum depositional age of 226.6 ± 1.8 Ma (n = 67/122) from strata immediately overlying the weathered interval is consistent with the interval being approximately coeval with the CPE, although additional age constraints are still required for strata within and below the interval. These results provide insights into the effects of climatic perturbations on salt tectonic systems and could improve predictions of geological hazards associated with existing salt structures in environments of rapid climate change.

title: Late Pleistocene activity on the Hoadley fault, an active fault in the Klamath Mountains Province
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape
authors: von Dassow, Wesley [1], Reedy, Tabor [2]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Technical Service Center, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Technical Service Center, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Shortening between the Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains is expected to drive deformation and active faulting in the transition region, yet few active faults have been identified. We present new constraints on the slip rate of two active faults in the Sacramento Valley-Klamath Mountain transition and discuss implications for ongoing strain accommodation in this region.

The Bear Creek fault is an east-west striking, north-dipping reverse fault located in the Sacramento Valley south of Redding, California.[RW1] The Bear Creek fault forms a ~17 km long north-side up escarpment offsetting a mid-Pleistocene terrace surface. This offset is consistent with north-south shortening across a reverse fault. We identify a basalt flow near the center of the escarpment that is vertically offset 15.3 ± 3.32 m. Argon-argon dating of the basalt yields an age of 274 ± 10 ka which we use to calculate a vertical offset rate of 0.055 ± 0.008 mm/yr.

The Hoadley fault is a northwest-southeast striking fault located in the Klamath Mountains northwest of Redding, CA. Although the Hoadley fault was previously mapped as a bedrock structure, we identify two debris flow fans transected by a discrete scarp of ~ 800 m length along the mapped bedrock trace. Scarps on both surfaces indicate north-side down displacement. Previous geologic mapping constraints and observation of sheared structures in underlaying bedrock indicate the fault dips to the north, suggesting a normal sense of motion. The upper and lower surfaces appear to record progressive displacement, though the lower surface is partially eroded which prevents confident estimates of offset. We resolve 26.5 ± 9.7 m of vertical offset across the scarp on the upper surface. Infrared stimulated luminescence dating of a sample collected ~6 m beneath the upper surface yielded an age of 86.3 ± 12.0 ka. These constraints suggest a vertical offset rate of 0.31±0.11 mm/yr in the Late Pleistocene. The relatively fast slip rate of the Hoadley fault, in conjunction with its relatively subdued expression in the modern landscape, suggests that signatures of active faulting in this region may be partially masked by high geomorphic rates. Collectively, these results help refine our understanding of active faulting and regional strain accumulation patterns inboard of the Mendocino Triple Junction.

title: Lithofacies Associations and Depositional Environments of the Eocene Aycross Formation, Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, USA

authors: Reynolds, Sydney N [1], Lundeen, Ingrid [2], Rodwell, Ben [3], Foreman, Brady Zangs [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA

abstract: The Aycross Formation is an approximately 350-meter thick sedimentary succession of Eocene-aged strata exposed in the Bighorn Basin of northwestern Wyoming, USA. Despite the Aycross Formation containing numerous mammal fossil localities, it remains a comparatively understudied formation within Laramide basins. In the field, we identified lithofacies types and lithofacies association patterns. We measured detailed stratigraphic sections that included bed-by-bed descriptions of grain size, grain sorting, bed contacts, sedimentary structures, bioturbation, and Munsell color. These data display six major lithofacies types including: (1) fine to medium-grained sandstones containing cross-stratification, marine invertebrate fossils, soft sediment deformation, and clay rip-up clasts; (2) fine-grained sandstones containing laminations, plant fossils, soft sediment deformation, and concretions; (3) massive, olive to grey mudstones containing uncommon fine laminations, organic debris, and rare burrows; (4) calcareous mudstones; (5) tuffaceous sandstones, siltstones, and claystones containing euhedral minerals, clay clasts, and zeolites; and 6) bentonitic mudstones that are massive to normally graded, display shrink-swell properties, and popcorn weathering. These lithofacies are interpreted as the following environments: (1) and (2) lake margin and deltaic deposits; (3) and (4) distal lacustrine deposits; (5) reworked volcaniclastic deposits predominantly within lake sub-environments; and 6) ash fall deposits. From the bottom to the top of the Aycross Formation these lithofacies form packages that appear to display three major progradation events of the deltaic system with sediment sources to the west. These data allow for comparisons of the Aycross Formation with other similar-aged Laramide basins, for example the Green River Formation in more southern basins. This study constrains the paleoenvironmental context and biostratigraphy of existing mammal fossil localities in the Aycross Formation, with many fossil localities occurring within the middle portion of the unit associated with deltaic facies rather than lacustrine facies. Moreover, it documents the depositional response to later Laramide deformation, eruption of the Absaroka Volcanics, and climatic shifts associated with the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

title: From Modern Distributions to Paleo Sea-Surface Temperatures: Applications of EcoCleanR to Paleobiology
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space (Posters)
authors: Shalaev, Elina [1], Soni, Priyanka [2], Bottjer, David J. [3], Hendy, Austin J.W. [4]
affiliations: (1) Occidental College, Los Angeles, California, USA; Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, California, USA

abstract: Ongoing ocean warming and increasing climatic variability are creating a rapidly changing future that is difficult to predict using models alone. However, Earth’s past warming periods preserve evidence of how marine ecosystems responded to changing environmental conditions. Reconstructing past sea-surface temperatures (SSTs) can therefore help us understand long-term changes in marine communities and coastal ecosystems and improve predictions of their responses to future warming. Numerous approaches have been developed, with various geochemical proxies and climate models providing some of the most direct records of environmental conditions experienced by organisms. In addition, modern analogs of fossil species, including their geographic distributions and environmental niche spaces—have long been used to interpret past climatic conditions and evaluate species' responses to climate variability through time, although often through a qualitative or anecdotal lens. The rapid expansion of global biodiversity databases (e.g. GBIF), including citizen science platforms, has created unprecedented opportunities to refine modern species analogs using millions of occurrence records. Advanced analytical tools have enabled the reconstruction of species' geographic distributions supporting studies in conservation, ecology, and evolution. Here, we use EcoCleanR, a reproducible workflow for occurrence data cleaning, to reconstruct species' geographic distributions and environmentally suitable (biogeographic) ranges. We defined geographic ranges as well as thermal tolerance of ~100 modern molluscan taxa that are reported from the fossil record of the last Interglacial of southern California. This approach reconstructs the first high-resolution, spatially continuous coastal sea surface temperature dataset for the study region, notably revealing a north-to-south (Point Conception to San Diego, CA) temperature gradient of 4 °C that closely matches the modern spatial temperature gradient. However, our reconstruction also captures microscale paleoceanographic variability, identifying an approximately 5 °C temperature difference between open shelves and protected embayments of the last Interglacial along the Los Angeles coast, and exhibiting a distinct nearshore-to-offshore temperature gradient. Our results demonstrate that modern biodiversity databases, when integrated with advanced analytical tools such as EcoCleanR, provide a powerful framework for reconstructing species' modern biogeographic patterns and extending these insights to paleoecological and paleoceanographic research.

abstract:
Geochronology is a critical tool in Quaternary Geology and Geomorphology research, but students at most institutions have limited access to the specialized facilities needed for sample preparation and analysis. Since 2018, we have used National Science Foundation funding to run a cosmogenic nuclide sample preparation facility focused on visitors. The Community Cosmogenic Facility provides specialized laboratories, student mentoring, and geochronologic expertise to users from around the world. Secondary goals include formulating reference materials, sharing methods, creating an online database, and making data widely available to the community.

Visitors to the Community Cosmogenic Facility have included people from a wide range of institutions, backgrounds, geographic regions, and areas of study. Over the past 8 years, we hosted 39 undergraduate students, 62 graduate students, 19 research professionals, and 29 faculty members, for a total of 149 laboratory users. Laboratory visitors came from 27 US states and from 13 countries outside of the US.

Datasets from the Community Cosmogenic Facility have been at the core of several dozen peer-reviewed papers and hundreds of conference abstracts focused on quantifying rates of geomorphic processes, understanding landscape evolution, and dating landscape features around the world. Users, most of whom are students, have studied a wide range of Earth surface processes including erosion, glaciation, soil development, and recent tectonic activity.

Although hosting visitors is at the core of our mission, we also aim to provide resources for other cosmogenic nuclide laboratories. All methods are available freely online, as are detailed plans for laboratory innovations. We created and distributed a new reference material for cosmogenic nuclide analyses (called UVM-A), which is currently being used in 19 different peer laboratories in 5 countries.

In order to make the cosmogenic data we have generated more accessible, including to those without research funding, we are developing an online database for storing and sharing 33 years of 10 Be and 26 Al analyses. Our aim is to not only improve data access, but also to identify and share unpublished data that could be of use to the community.

abstract:
Inorganic arsenic (As) is a carcinogenic metalloid that is found naturally in soils worldwide. Rice is highly susceptible to accumulating As within its grain due to the plant's unique physiology and the environmental conditions under which it is grown. In particular, the flooding of rice paddies can lead to anaerobic conditions that drive the reductive dissolution of arsenic-bearing iron oxides in the soils. Once As is mobilized from the soil, it can be taken up by the rice crop and accumulate in the grain.

Arsenic uptake into the rice crop reduces yields and poses serious health risks to those who consume the grain. However, there are difficulties in predicting rice grain As levels, which depend on the complex interactions of environmental factors, including rice paddy hydrology, climate, and soil properties. These factors result in highly variable As levels in soil and rice grain. Further complicating predictions of grain As is the fact that rice grain As levels are poorly correlated to bulk soil As concentrations. The ability to predict which fields have the potential for high As in rice grains is critical for mitigating As exposure.

This limited relationship between bulk soil As levels and rice grain As may be in part driven by variation in how solid-phase As is partitioned within the soil (e.g., weakly or strongly adsorbed, incorporated in mineral phases). To better understand this disconnect, we conducted a series of rapid laboratory incubations and rapid soil digestions on over 150 fields across a wide range of settings in Cambodia. Due to Cambodia’s largely traditional farming practices, which use minimal inputs (e.g., chemical fertilizers, herbicides, and irrigation), Cambodia provides a window into how environmental conditions affect As mobilization and uptake into rice. For Cambodians, As intake through rice is a significant health concern because of high As concentrations and their reliance on rice for over 60% of their caloric intake. In this study, we connect our soil incubations and digestions with rice grain As levels measured on these same fields. We find that these rapid and easy-to-implement methods shed light on As partitioning in the soil and the potential of a given rice paddy to produce high-As rice grain.

abstract: During the Quaternary Period episodic magmatism in western Colorado produced several volcanoes, one of which (Dotsero Crater) remains dormant. To understand how magmatic processes and storage evolved throughout the Quaternary, we investigated lava flows at Triangle Peak (1.98Ma), Willow Peak (280ka), and Dotsero Crater (4.15ka) using petrographic analysis and mineral compositional analysis via wavelength dispersive spectroscopy. Lavas from all localities contain the following mineral assemblage: plagioclase > clinopyroxene > olivine > Fe-Ti oxides. Xenoliths and xenocrysts were not recognized in Triangle Peak lavas. In contrast, Willow Peak basalts contain an abundance of granitic xenoliths. Apart from the previously recognized quartz xenocrysts in Dotsero basalts, coarse-grained xenocrystic biotite was also observed. Olivine phenocrysts in Triangle Peak lavas range from iddingsitized to unaltered, with iddingsitization more common in the earliest erupted lavas. Unaltered olivine grains in Triangle Peak have average core and rim compositions of Fo 78±5 and Fo 71±6 , respectively. Average groundmass olivine compositions (Fo 62±6 ) overlap with average rim compositions, but some are Fe-enriched. Triangle Peak clinopyroxene are unzoned diopsidic augites (En 38±2 Wo 47±2 Fs 15±1 ). Two compositionally distinct populations of plagioclase occur in Triangle Peak lavas: low-K (An 37±3 Ab 60±3 Or 3±1 ) and a less abundant high-K population (An 40±4 Ab 45±9 Or 14±7 ). Unlike Triangle Peak, lava erupted at Dotsero contains no iddingsitized olivine and only a single compositional population of more calcic plagioclase (An 72±2 Ab 27±2 Or 2±0.4 ). Both clinopyroxene (En 39±2 Wo 46±1 Fs 15±1 ) and olivine compositions (cores= Fo 80±1 , rims = Fo 76±2 ) are very similar in Dotsero and Triangle Peak lavas. Clinopyroxene-only geothermometry indicates crystallization temperatures of 1050- 1100°C for Dotsero basalt and 1050-1150 °C for Triangle Peak basalts. The difference in plagioclase compositions from Dotsero and Triangle Peak basalts indicates that Triangle Peak lavas were more evolved. The subordinate high-K plagioclase grains are potentially antecrysts that originated from a hotter, more alkaline magma that mixed into the reservoir prior to eruption. Willow Peak, and potentially Dotsero, basalts may have been stored at greater depths than Triangle Peak lavas in order to assimilate plutonic material. Integration of this dataset with additional geochemical analyses will enable further insight into how magma storage pressure, temperature and processes differed amongst different Quaternary eruptions in western Colorado.

abstract: An exceptional outcrop of the Coon Creek Formation, located in McNairy County, Tennessee, is a Late Cretaceous (76 Ma) Lagerstätte that contains abundant invertebrates, plant remains, and vertebrates (mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and sharks). Whereas the deposits are part of the Mississippi Embayment, and marine in origin, there have been questions about how far from the shoreline and how deep the ocean was at the location during the time of sediment deposition. Although mosasaurs existed across a range of temperatures, previous workers have noted their occurrence in strata where temperatures were colder. The Coon Creek locality is an ideal site for reconstructing paleotemperature because previous workers have inferred no diagenetic alteration of the fossil material. Here, we present mineralogical and elemental geochemical data for sediments across the site as well as stable isotopic geochemistry data from exceptionally preserved inoceramid bivalves. Mineralogy shows little variation across the locality, suggesting uniform depositional conditions. Elemental geochemistry was used to reconstruct pH, and carbonate δ¹⁸O values of inoceramids found proximal to the mosasaur excavations were used to reconstruct the paleotemperature of the site. These paleotemperature estimates are compared with those from other locations that contain both inoceramids and mosasaurs (such as Bentiaba in Angola) to discuss potential variability in mosasaur habitats.

abstract:
Sparse data exists on the microfossils of the Green River Group (GRG), particularly in Fossil Butte National Monument. Palynological samples were prepared to better understand the climate and biota of the Fossil Butte Member of the GRG. Sample material was collected from four sites within the Lower Sandwich Bed (~15 cm thick) which is bounded above and below by volcanic ash, so all the samples are from the same relative time in Fossil Lake history. Two of these sample sites were on the lake margin and two were from the center of the lake deposit. In the field, epoxy was used to bind the entire thickness of the bed together from which vertical slabs were cut through the bed. Ten equidistant samples were taken from the thickness of the bed. All samples numbered five and ten were processed by Global Geolab Limited (Alberta, Canada) and the other samples were personally prepared without the use of hydrofluoric acid.

Preliminary data has returned eleven total taxon and sixteen morphotype groups. All eleven of the taxa identified suggest humid temperate climates, though one of the eleven, a relative of Rocky Mountain Ponderosa Pine, implies a mountainous temperate upland climate. The most abundant taxon is Equisetum , a plant commonly found on stream and lake margins in humid temperate regions. Equisetum and many of the other taxa identified have also been found as macrofossils in the Fossil Butte Member of the Green River Group. Further work needs to be completed on the identification of both micro and macrofossil plant material in the GRG, especially the Fossil Butte Member, but preliminary results suggest a large amount of overlap between micro and macro fossil plants.

title: Lessons From an International Potable Groundwater Project in a Rural Community

authors: Ali, Hendratta N. [1], Sanuade, Oluseun [2], Prasad, Manika [3]

abstract: Barriers to clean water security around the world arise from both natural and human causes. These barriers include events such as droughts, over-extraction of groundwater, sufface and groundwater pollution, and human aspects such as conflicts, lack of infrastructure, insufficient resources both for technical expertise and financial access. Although the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals for 2030 identify access to potable and safe drinking water as one of its objectives, safe drinking water availability and access continue to be challenging for many communities globally. Professional organizations such as the SEG’s Geoscientists Without Borders program supports geoscientists to engage in humanitarian projects to help communities in need, including access to clean water. SEG supported our project to explore and provide potable groundwater access to a rural community in Cameroon. The outcomes of the project involved water sampling and analyses, geophysical surveying and mapping, student training, and constructing and installing a solar powered water supply system. During the project that spanned the COVID pandemic time, we successfully accomplished our goals and came away with new additional experiences in recruiting participants, coordinating with the local communities, training students, managing and handling instruments and equipment internationally, and interacting and engaging with the user community. However, in addition to the successful research and technical components of the project, our activities significantly involved training, negotiating, group dialogues and mediation. In the process, lessons were learned about the similarities and subtle differences between geoscience research focused fieldwork and applied humanitarian projects in the areas of logistics, recruiting, community engagement and teamwork.

abstract: Collaborating PIs and students from the Universities of Colorado and Akron are using field-based observations, microstructural analysis, and FTIR measurements from a natural shear zone and deformation experiments to help develop numerical models and test hypotheses related to the rheology of deep continental crust. The field setting is the Cora Lake shear zone, a km-scale strike-slip structure exhumed from 35–25 km paleodepths in the Canadian shield that hosts synkinematic granulite- to upper amphibolite-facies pseudotachylyte. Examples of ongoing projects include the following. 1) Investigating field-based spatial and causative relationships between crystal-plastic strain state, lithology and pseudotachylyte (Flynn et al., this session). This project also employs numerical modeling and trace water analysis of quartz and feldspar in natural and experimentally deformed samples to better understand its influence on rheology during dynamic recrystallization. Results support episodic brittle deformation via local stress enhancement from lithologic contrast influenced by synkinematic dehydration of rocks during deformation. 2) Experimental investigation of strengthening of quartzites due to synkinematic partial melting (Holyoke et al., this session). This series of experiments suggests that dynamic recrystallization of quartz in the presence of melt has a drying effect that could contribute to long-term strengthening of lower crust. 3) Constraining rheological flow laws for lower crustal aggregate lithologies using experiments on natural samples including pseudotachylyte (Oatman et al., this session). Preliminary results support field observations that felsic granulite is relatively weak compared to mafic granulite, which contrasts with some published experimental work. 4) Experiments on single crystal and synthetic and natural quartz aggregates to refine quartz flow laws as a function of both water content and fugacity with specific applicability to dry conditions. These multiple complimentary and collaborative approaches form the basis for theses and research projects for Colorado and Akron graduate and undergraduate students. Reciprocal experiences for both students and PIs between the Colorado-led field work and Akron-led deformation experiments enhance the exchange of ideas and broaden the students’ experience and skill development. The results are yielding valuable information applicable to broader community efforts in crustal rheology, including flow law development, approaches to numerical modeling of shear zone properties, and understanding transient deformation processes during continental crustal evolution.

title: Geologic Setting and Origin of Lithium-Clay Deposits in the McDermitt Caldera, Nevada – Oregon, USA
session_title: From anode to cathode: Mineral systems of battery commodities
authors: Henry, Christopher D. [1], Burns, Randal [2], Hatcherian, Javin [3], Hackley, Paul C. [4]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Lithium Americas Corporation, Reno, NV, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA

abstract:
The McDermitt caldera hosts possibly the world’s largest Li-clay deposits, which are contained in intracaldera tuffaceous sediments that have undergone closed-hydrologic system diagenesis (CHSD). Li-smectite deposits with maximum grades of ~4000 ppm occur throughout the caldera. Li-illite deposits with maximum grades of ~9000 ppm are only known in the southern, Thacker Pass part of the caldera. The origin of the Li-clay deposits, particularly the relative contributions of low-temperature CHSD versus high-temperature hydrothermal processes to Li enrichment, and the total source of Li are debated.

The ~40 x 25 km caldera resulted from the 16.4 Ma eruption of ~1000 km 3 of magma deposited as the McDermitt Tuff, which reaches intracaldera thicknesses of 600 m. A resurgent dome formed shortly after collapse, and minor icelanditic eruptions continued to 16.1 Ma, when caldera volcanism ceased. Rhyolitic tuffaceous sediments accumulated in a caldera lake between 16.4 and 15.7 Ma. During CHSD, rhyolitic glass dissolved to generate high-total dissolved solids and alkaline water that, further enriched by closed-basin evaporation, precipitated smectite, zeolites, authigenic K-feldspar, albite, and, based on our work, probably illite. Li mineralization continued to at least 15.7 Ma, the age of the youngest mineralized sediments. A 14.87±0.05 Ma 40 Ar/ 39 Ar date on authigenic K-feldspar in the illite zone at Thacker Pass suggests Li mineralization continued until then, long after any igneous heat source. However, others interpret that Li-illite formed during resurgence soon after caldera formation and required temperatures ≥230°C.

To evaluate maximum temperatures, we measured vitrinite reflectance (R o ) in smectitic and illitic Li-mineralized sediments. Preliminary vitrinite reflectance (Ro) measurements at Thacker Pass (n=8) range between 0.34 and 0.57% Ro, and one north caldera Li-smectite zone sample has a R o of 0.41%. These Ro values indicate maximum temperatures ≤60°C. Additional vitrinite reflectance analysis is underway in the context of petrographic evaluation for hydrothermal alteration. Qualitative illite crystallinity X-ray diffraction data are consistent with similar low temperatures of the Li-illite deposits. We are investigating what additional factors were present at Thacker Pass to generate the higher-grade Li-illite deposits.

Li-smectite deposits are widely present in Nevada in extensional basins containing diagenetically altered, rhyolitic tuffaceous sediments. The similarity of Li-smectite deposits in the McDermitt caldera and extensional basins is strong evidence that both formed through CHSD.

title: In Situ Rb-Sr Constraints on Ductile Shearing in the Norumbega Fault System, South-Central Maine.
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications (Posters)
authors: DeMarco, Natalie Mae [1], Johnson, Scott E. [2], Cruz-Uribe, Alicia Marie [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Climate Sciences, Univeristy of Maine, Orono, ME, USA
(2) University of Maine, Orono, ME, USA

abstract: The Norumbega fault system (NFS) in Maine is a dextral transcurrent fault initiated during Middle-to-Late Devonian time due to a shift in regional kinematics. Within south-central Maine, the Sandhill Corner shear zone (SCSZ) was exhumed from depths of ~10–15 km and represents the longest continuous strand of the Norumbega system. The duration of shearing is generally well-known, with the exception of its later phase of localized high-strain mylonitization that involved coseismic deformation. Current constraints on the shear history rely on traditional 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology published two decades ago suggesting an age range of dextral transpressive shear from ~380–280 Ma, a time period consistent with prolonged regional cooling and exhumation after low-pressure amphibolite-facies metamorphism. Timing of shear deformation and the processes that influence its recorded dates remain difficult to ascertain due to structural overprinting, lack of mineralogical preservation, and geochronologic limitations. Advancements in tandem mass spectrometry have enabled in situ Rb-Sr analyses of micas using laser-based sampling, which allows analyses of targeted mica textures in metamorphic rocks. Here we report in situ Rb-Sr dates from micas within and around the SCSZ to refine the ductile shear age context for this region. Preliminary Rb-Sr muscovite and biotite geochronology across multiple samples in one transect yields dates of 359–320 Ma, suggesting a ~40 Ma time span of mica growth and/or resetting during the Paleozoic cooling and exhumation evolution of the shear zone. We observe distinct dates between muscovite and biotite in many samples, and in some samples two muscovite dates can be resolved for microstructurally distinct textural domains. For example, one sample from the shear zone core spans the entire range of Rb-Sr dates reported here, with muscovite dates of ~359 and ~320 Ma. Data collection from a second transect <1 km northeast of transect 1 is ongoing and results will be presented at the conference. As demonstrated above, the SCSZ allows for a unique case study of Rb-Sr geochronometer behavior in ductile shear zone settings to improve temporal context between deformation and metamorphism in shear zones.

title: Testing Hillslope and Fluvial Topography Response Across Erosion Rate Gradients in the Tropics
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution (Posters)
authors: Siar, MK [1], Drobnich, Kate [2], Gallen, Sean F. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado,
(2) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,

abstract: The relationship between erosion rate and hillslope and fluvial topography is primarily understood in the context of temperate climates and felsic rock types, but implications of these interactions are largely unexplored in tropical climates, particularly in more mafic rocks. In this study, we bridge this gap using the tropical island of Puerto Rico as a setting to understand how erosion rate gradient influences topographic metrics across predominately intermediate to mafic bedrock. Specifically, we aim to understand how topography, via a suite of topographic metrics including channel steepness, slope-drainage area relationships, channel head location, drainage density, hilltop curvature, and hillslope length, relief, and gradient, changes as a function of erosion rates. Here, we conduct a controlled experiment, using 60 existing 36 Cl derived basin averaged erosion rates measured within a single geologic map unit and a 1-m resolution DEM resampled to a resolution of 3-m to extract topographic metrics for each basin to assess their response to changing relative base level lowering rates. We select only basins draining at least 80% of intermediate-to-mafic volcaniclastic bedrock that appear morphologically in equilibrium based on smooth concave upward longitudinal river profiles devoid of major knickpoints. From this experimental design, we will assess how this array of topographic metrics changes as erosion rate increases and expect to quantify the relative efficiency of hillslopes and river channels across an erosion rate gradient. Specifically, we aim to determine how changes in topographic metrics reflect the evolution of dominant geomorphic processes as a function of erosion rate. We anticipate that these results will have broader implications for understanding natural hazards due to changes in gradient, physical conductivity, and how sediment is produced and routed through fluvial systems.

abstract:
Since its inception in 1983, over 1000 students from around the world have participated in the Summer of Applied Geophysical Experience (SAGE) program for undergraduate and graduate students and working professionals. The EarthScope Consortium and its predecessor organizations, which operates the NSF National Geophysical Facility, have supported a wide variety of geophysics research and educational endeavors since 1984. Starting in 2026, SAGE and EarthScope have formed a new partnership with the goal of better supporting student geophysics field education and workforce preparation. Team science is a fundamental tenet of this partnership.

SAGE students use geophysics to address a scientific research question or applied geoscience problem of value to society, while operating as effective, professional members of a scientific team. SAGE’s motto is ‘Learning Geophysics by Doing Geophysics’. The central activity of SAGE is the acquisition, processing, and integrated interpretation of various geophysical datasets. SAGE integrates online learning, classroom and field lectures, geologic field trips, hands-on data acquisition, and team-based data processing, interpretation, and oral/written presentation. Teamwork is a crucial and integral component of SAGE. In the field, students are divided into squads that rotate together through different activities each day such that each student participates in collecting data for all the available methods over 6 field days. During the data processing and interpretation phase, students choose a particular method on which to concentrate while also participating in integrated teams focused on a common scientific question. Final presentations are organized by the integrated teams; each student presents a conference-style talk and extended abstract within the context of the overall team objective.

The SAGE-EarthScope team-based educational approach continues to evolve in a changing world while providing future generations of geoscientists with the foundational tools needed to tackle future challenges. This presentation discusses the current SAGE-EarthScope educational model, lessons learned, and challenges faced while striving to offer an inclusive and immersive learning environment to future geoscientists.

title: Transforming Earth MRI Regional AEM Survey Results into Watershed-Scale Brine Maps for Lithium Assessments in the Basin and Range Province
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities
authors: Ball, Lyndsay B [1], Gustafson, Chloe D [2], Bedrosian, Paul A [3], Crosbie, Jade W [4]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA

abstract: Lithium is critical for energy storage, transportation electrification, and numerous industrial processes. The Basin and Range Province is the most prospective region in the United States for lithium‑bearing brine and clay deposits, as well as hosting numerous mineral systems prospective for other critical minerals. Through the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI), over 30,000 linear km of airborne electromagnetic (AEM) data have been collected across 121,000 km² of the Basin and Range to improve our understanding of its three‑dimensional geologic framework. Because the high dissolved-solids concentration of groundwater brines results in high electrical conductivity, AEM surveys are uniquely well suited to identifying closed-basin brine deposits within the depth range most accessible for exploration, generally the upper 300 to 500 m. The Earth MRI AEM surveys used a 5-km line spacing in combination with basin-center tie lines through the surface extent of playa lakebeds; these supplemental tie lines play a key role in identifying smaller brine deposits as well as assessing the potential for subsurface groundwater flow between topographic watersheds. These regional AEM results were used to systematically evaluate closed basins in western and central Nevada for conductivity signatures consistent with subsurface brine. Basins were classified by the presence and shallow areal extent of brine deposits, providing a regionally consistent mappable criterion for mineral‑resource assessments. Although not all brines are expected to contain elevated lithium concentrations, when combined with other geologic factors, this framework can be used to support prospectivity mapping for economically significant lithium‑brine resources.

title: Mapping Ground Subsidence Caused by Excavation of a Rail Crossover Cavern and Twin Tunnels in Downtown Los Angeles Using Multi-sensor, Multi-platform InSAR

authors: Zhou, Wendy Wei [1], Wnuk, Kendall [2], Liu, Linan [3]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA

abstract: This presentation discusses two case studies in downtown Los Angeles: (1) subsidence linked to the excavation of a subway station and rail crossover cavern; and (2) ground subsidence related to twin-tunnel construction. In the first case, surface deformation measurements above the excavation were obtained through InSAR time-series analyses of data from sensors operating at different wavelengths, including the C-band Sentinel-1, X-band COSMO-SkyMed, and L-band UAVSAR. Data from these satellite and airborne SAR sensors revealed deformation around the 2nd Street and Broadway Subway Station and the nearby rail crossover cavern, with maximum vertical displacement reaching 2.5 cm and horizontal displacement 1.7 cm. In the second case study, ground subsidence associated with twin-tunnel excavation was mapped using the Persistent Scatterer Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PSInSARTM) technique. The vertical deformation rate in this study is derived by combining Line-of-Sight (LOS) deformation velocities obtained from Sentinel-1 SAR images in both ascending and descending satellite orbits. Local and uneven settlements of up to approximately 12 mm/year were observed along the tunnel alignment. Furthermore, a Machine Learning (ML)-based permutation feature-importance method is used in a parametric study to identify dominant factors associated with twin-tunneling-induced uneven ground subsidence. Among the six parameters selected for the parametric study, overburden thickness, i.e., the thickness of artificial fill and alluvium soils above the tunnel springlines, is the dominant factor, followed by the distance between tunnel centerlines, depth to the tunnel springlines, and building height. Two parameters, the distance to the tunnel and the groundwater level, play lesser roles than the others.

title: Variable Fabric Preservation but Uniform Geochemical Overprinting in Triassic Dolomites of the Zagros Basin, Iran
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Norouzi, Saeed [1], Kaczmarek, Stephen E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological & Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(2) Geological & Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
abstract:
Dolomite texture is routinely used in studies of the timing, fluids, and conditions of dolomitization. In particular, the well-preserved Ca-carbonate precursor fabrics characteristic of mimetic dolomite are often cited as evidence for early, near-surface replacement and preservation of primary geochemical signatures. This study tests that assumption using the approximately 305-m-thick, pervasively dolomitized Triassic Khaneh Kat Formation of the Zagros Basin, Iran. The succession is dominated by very fine- to fine-crystalline dolomite that exhibits variable preservation of depositional textures, ranging from mimetic intervals characterized by well-preserved allochems, laminae, fenestrae, and early cements to intervals in which depositional fabric is poorly preserved or completely destroyed. Thin-section petrography, cathodoluminescence, powder X-ray diffraction, trace-element analysis, stable-isotope analysis, and clumped-isotope thermometry were integrated to investigate the causes of the observed textural variations throughout the section.

Despite substantial differences in the degree of fabric preservation, mimetic and nonmimetic dolomites show no systematic differences in Sr, Na, Mn, or Fe concentrations, δ¹³C and δ¹⁸O values, dolomite stoichiometry, cation ordering, or cathodoluminescence characteristics. Fabric-preserving mimetic dolomites and fabric-destructive nonmimetic dolomites are composed of similarly stoichiometric, moderately ordered dolomite and commonly display uniform dull- to dark-red CL signatures. The lack of geochemical and mineralogical separation suggests that the different dolomite textures do not reflect distinct dolomitization events, fluids, or burial histories.

Cross-cutting relationships and preservation of depositional and early diagenetic fabrics indicate that dolomitization began early, prior to significant burial compaction. However, clumped-isotope temperatures of approximately 75–101°C in fine-crystalline matrix dolomite and calculated fluid δ¹⁸O values of approximately +5 to +10‰ VSMOW indicate subsequent interaction with evolved fluids during burial. These elevated temperatures, together with dolomite δ¹⁸O values lower than those expected for Triassic Tethyan marine dolomites, suggest alteration of the original isotopic record. Stylolites, fractures, and localized fluid pathways may have enhanced recrystallization and fabric destruction in some intervals, but the similarity of geochemical signatures across all textural classes indicates that burial overprinting was formation-wide.

These results demonstrate that mimetic texture may record early replacement prior to significant burial, but it does not necessarily indicate preservation of the original dolomitizing fluid composition or conditions of dolomite formation.

title: Prediction, Regulation and Remediation of High Arsenic Groundwater Sourced Drinking Water Utilising Hybrid Artificial Intelligence/Expert Approaches: Benefits, Limitations and Opportunities
session_title: From Deep Earth to Digital Twins: Artificial Intelligence in Earth System Science and Predictive Subsurface Systems
authors: Polya, David A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Science, School of Natural Sciences, Faculty of Science and Engineering, The University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom
abstract:
Hazardous high arsenic groundwaters utilised for drinking, cooking and irrigation remain a major source of health risks to the public across the globe, notably including in the USA, China, India and Bangladesh [1,2]. In the absence of relevant comprehensive granular data related to all of hazard distribution, exposure routes and receptor characteristics and susceptibilities, artificial intelligence (AI) models [3] are increasingly used for hazard [2-6] and health risk [7-8] prediction, as well as informing regulation and remediation [9]. There remain both data and model limitations to these approaches.

Drawing particularly on research and reviews from our Manchester group and collaborators, theoretical advances, limitations and opportunities in the application of AI to this ongoing health- and policy-related challenge are highlighted. Highlights include the use of more homogeneous sub-domains to improve spatial models [6], purpose-dependent cost-informed cut-off points [10] and the use of pseudo-contours [11] whilst key limitations include over-fitted models [3] and the relative lack of AI approaches to addressing data deficiencies related to exposure and receptors [12].

title: Sequence Stratigraphic Interpretation across Craton-Margin Hinge Zone in the Northern Great Basin, USA
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Stage, Lainey Reese [1], Koran, Isabel [2], Macdonald, Francis A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA

abstract: The Cordilleran margin of Laurentia preserves a Cryogenian to Cambrian rift-drift transition; however, the exact timing of the transition is unclear. Resolving the exact timing of rifting places important constraints on paleogeographic models for super continent cycles. Late Tonian to Cryogenian (780-635 Ma) deposits show geologic evidence for rifting including syn-sedimentary faulting, volcanism, and angular unconformities. It is debated whether overlying Ediacaran to Early Cambrian (635-530 Ma) sediments record rift reactivation, or whether they were instead accommodated by post-rift subsidence. These models make different predictions for the stratigraphy across the craton-margin hinge zone. In the post rift subsidence model, the hinge zone remained passive with sedimentary packages prograding and flexurally loading the margin. In the rift reactivation model, the hinge would have stayed active during the Ediacaran with the increase in subsidence accommodation accompanied by faulting. Here we test these models by constructing a basal Ediacaran to early Cambrian cross-section from Nevada to Utah. We propose new correlations of Ediacaran strata in a sequence stratigraphic framework across the craton-margin hinge zone. Geologic mapping paired with measured stratigraphic sections show multiple sequence boundaries throughout stratigraphy across wide regions. Using these sequence boundaries for correlation shows continuous siliciclastic successions that thicken westward, with no evidence of syn-sedimentary faulting. These observations are consistent with an increase in sediment supply near the Ediacaran–Cambrian transition that drove westward progradation and does not require rift reactivation to accommodate these successions.

authors: Hill, Maggie [1], Harmon, Lydia [2], Harris, Morgan [3], Smithies, Sarah [4]

abstract: The Taupō Volcanic Zone (TVZ) of New Zealand has produced some of the most devastating volcanic eruptions in the Quaternary. The largest ~350 ka Whakamaru supereruption is unusual compared to other TVZ eruptions not only in its size, but also in its mineralogy. It also lacks a basal fall deposit. Previous work has characterized four distinct magma types erupted through the Whakamaru supereruption, but the cause of its initiation is as yet unknown and its various distinct characteristics may indicate a different eruptive mechanism is at play. Here, we focus on the base of the supereruption to interrogate the characteristics and compositions of the material that erupted first. We present volcanological, textural, and compositional data for the only known basal outcrop of the Whakamaru ignimbrite. At the outcrop scale, we interpret a surge sitting atop the basement rock followed by an indurated ignimbrite that can be separated into 4 subunits based on textural changes. We present geochemical data obtained via X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) for whole-rock compositions and Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) for matrix glass compositions. The whole-rock data, while giving reasonable, self-similar compositions are somewhat surprising, as they do not compositionally overlap with previously published Whakamaru ignimbrite data. This could be explained by comparing bulk whole-rock compositions to individual pumice compositions, which are absent from the outcrop. Matrix glass compositions correlate to published airfall data of Type A, which erupted throughout the Whakamaru supereruption. This may indicate that the initial phase of the eruption was sourced from the Type A magma, but differences in geochemistry and their implications continue to be explored. Future work will focus on the mineralogy of the ignimbrite to determine its similarities with later-erupted Whakamaru deposits. With this future work, we hope to gain a more nuanced perspective and clarity on the composition of the first-erupted magma body of the Whakamaru supereruption.

abstract: The Cambrian witnessed the early diversification of calcified cyanobacteria which played a key role in the formation of more complex bioconstructions. In Australia, these early calcified forms are particularly prevalent in association with early archaeocyathid reefs including Girvannella, Renalcis, and Epiphyton , but are otherwise rarely reported within other lithologies. For the first time, we report Subtifloria delicata alongside other calcified cyanobacteria (including Girvannella and ? Epiphyton) from the lower Cambrian (Series 3, Stage 3-4) Third Plain Creek Member of the Mernmnerna Formation, Bunkers Range of South Australia. This carbonate-dominated unit is defined by interbedded limestones and sandy lenses, deposited along a marginal slope reflecting shelf progradation and an influx of allochthonous shelf-derived debris, as well as terrigenous sand and silt. Specimens of S. delicata reported herein are derived from three samples in the upper portion of the unit, exclusively the quartz-rich sandy intervals. They are characterized by well-preserved hollow calcified sheaths consisting of parallel unbranched tubular filaments of uniform diameter. Petrographic thin sections reveal the taxon is common, with more than 400 individual sheaths identified across the samples, corresponding to an average 0.07 individuals/cm 2 . Specimens of S. delicata reach up to 1300 µm in length, average 86.1µm in external diameter, and cell diameters of 8 µm. Documentation of the genus Subtifloria extends the known distribution of the taxon from Siberia and China to East Gondwana. Moreover, the occurrence of the Australian material in siliciclastic-dominated facies expands the known environmental range of the genus to include settings subject to high-energy conditions. Whilst the specimens documented herein were likely derived from shallower-water settings, their preservation demonstrates that these delicate structures can survive transport and subsequent burial in coarse-grained deposits.

authors: Jones, Marcus Logan [1], Groff, Stephen Christopher [2], Stoller, Mike [3], Walker, Sally E. [4], Lockwood, Rowan [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Geosciences, College of Charleston, Charleston, SC, USA
(2) Paleontology, Calvert Marine Museum, Lusby, MD,
(3) Paleontology, Charleston Center for Paleontology, Charleston, SC, USA
(4) Department of Geology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
(5) College of Arts and Sciences, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA,
abstract:
Petricolids are a globally distributed family of shallow-dwelling venerid bivalves. Many members of the family Petricolidae employ rock boring and nestling behaviors. Nestling species occupy crevices, cavities, and empty borings within hard substrates such as rock, coral, and shells. To date, only one species— Petricola ramirezi from the central coast of Chile—has been documented in the literature as inhabiting vacant Balanid barnacle shells in modern and Pleistocene collections, a behavior that has not been reported outside the eastern Pacific.

Here we describe a new occurrence of petricolid nestling clams inhabiting empty barnacle shells, including Pleiorytis calvertensis , a petricolid, a currently unidentified bivalve, and multiple species of Balanid barnacles from the Miocene sediments of coastal Maryland and Virginia, USA. Our specimens are currently known from Beds 16B, 17, and 19 of the Choptank Formation, and Beds 23E and 24 of the St. Marys Formation. Using Morphologic comparison, bulk samples, and targeted sampling, we have made observations regarding the frequency, size, and orientation of these clams, which may yield further insight into their life cycle and behavior. Our morphologic comparison of free growing and barnacle-nestled Pleiorytis has shown that the latter are highly stunted, though seem to orient themselves to occupy the greatest possible capacity of their restrictive environment. It is clear from our sampling that barnacle nestling is not the usual behavior among these clams, though more is needed to statistically determine frequencies. These specimens represent a substantial expansion of the known geographic and temporal range of petricolid–balanid nestling behavior. This is the first documented occurrence of this association along the Atlantic coast and extends the fossil record of this behavior by at least nine million years. Our specimens are rare and fragile and have historically been under-collected, resulting in a limited sample size; however, recent collecting efforts have yielded sufficient material for a preliminary study. Future work involving μ-CT, bulk sampling and examination of Neogene and Quaternary Atlantic specimens may further clarify the life-cycle, frequency and persistence of balanid-nestling and other similar behaviors across multiple oceans since the mid-Miocene.

title: Integrating Benthic Foraminiferal Biostratigraphy and Geochemistry to Investigate Siderite Formation in Late Pennsylvanian Cyclothems of Northeastern Kansas
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change (Posters)
authors: Khameiss, Belkasim Kh. [1], Ishman, Scott E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK, USA
(2) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
abstract:
The origin and depositional significance of siderite within Late Pennsylvanian strata of the Midcontinent region remains incompletely understood due to limited biostratigraphic and paleoenvironmental constraints. This study integrates benthic foraminiferal analysis with petrographic and geochemical investigations to evaluate the formation of siderite-bearing intervals recovered from the PNR#1 and Edmonds A1 cores in northeastern Kansas. The studied succession consists of cyclic coal beds interbedded with shale, limestone, and sandstone, containing siderite-rich horizons that record episodes of enhanced chemical weathering and iron accumulation within the depositional system.

Benthic foraminifera were examined to establish age control and reconstruct depositional conditions, providing critical stratigraphic information in a region where detailed micropaleontological studies are scarce. The recovered assemblages offer valuable insights into environmental fluctuations associated with Pennsylvanian cyclothems and help refine the biostratigraphic framework of Midcontinent strata. Mineralogical and geochemical characterization was conducted using petrographic observations and Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) to determine the elemental composition and distribution of siderite within the cores.

The combined micropaleontological and geochemical data indicate that siderite formed under low-oxygen, iron-rich conditions in brackish- to freshwater wetland settings associated with coal-forming environments. The presence and distribution of benthic foraminifera further suggest periodic marine influence during sediment deposition. These findings demonstrate the importance of benthic foraminifera not only for establishing the age of Pennsylvanian successions but also for reconstructing paleoenvironmental conditions in the Midcontinent region. The study provides new insights into the controls on siderite precipitation and enhances our understanding of the complex interactions among climate, sedimentation, and ecosystem dynamics during the Late Pennsylvanian .

title: Preservation Bias in Ophiuroid Lateral Arm Plates: Dissolution and Mechanical Weathering at Cedar Key, FL
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Hill, Stephen A [1], Sumrall, Colin D [2], Thuy, Ben [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Environmental and Planetary Sciences, The University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth Environmental and Planetary Sciences, The University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA
(3) Luxembourg Museum of Natural History, Luxembourg City, Luxembourg
abstract:
Emergent methods in paleontology utilizing Lateral Arm Plates (LAPs) have begun to greatly expand the Paleozoic fossil record of ophiuroids. However, taphonomic alteration may obscure diagnostic features and bias their preservation and recovery. Here we document taphonomic variability of modern LAPs from shallow-water sediments at Cedar Key, Florida, and evaluate the roles of chemical dissolution and mechanical weathering in their degradation. More than 500 LAPs were isolated from sieved surface sediments and examined by scanning electron microscopy. Cedar Key LAPs exhibit a continuum from pristine, unaltered stereom to severely degraded specimens with tunneling, peeling, and jagged edges, as well as loss of spine bases and other diagnostic features. This degradation contrasts sharply with typical Paleozoic LAP assemblages displaying nearly pristine ossicles with intact species diagnostic features.

Field measurements of pH in both the water column and sediment pore waters at Cedar Key indicate that low pH conditions in the sediment could be responsible for dissolution. This is consistent with the tannin-stained freshwater input from the Suwannee River and the observed resemblance between Cedar Key LAP textures and echinoderm ossicle dissolution features reported in other studies. However, Cedar Key is also a shallow, energetic coastal setting subject to wave, tidal, and storm-driven sediment transport.

Laboratory experiments designed to replicate textures observed on Cedar Key LAPs indicate that dissolution alone does not account for the full range of taphonomic features. Instead, the observed degradation likely reflects the combined effects of chemical and mechanical weathering caused by wave and tidal forces. Continued experimental comparison of altered LAPs with naturally weathered specimens will identify diagnostic textures associated with each process and assess how these taphonomic biases may affect the preservation and interpretation of LAPs in Paleozoic sediments. Understanding these processes will be critical to further utilization of LAPs beyond taxonomy in paleoecological studies.

title: Understanding mid-Cretaceous Terrestrial Climate using Palustrine Carbonates from the Newark Canyon Formation, Nevada
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Lewis, Corra [1], Fetrow, Anne C. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA
(2) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO,
abstract:
The mid-Cretaceous climate represents one of the warmest periods of the Phanerozoic, with global temperatures estimated to have been 6–12°C above modern conditions. However, climate reconstructions of this period are predominantly marine, with limited understanding of how terrestrial systems responded to these changes. The Newark Canyon Formation (NCF) in central Nevada preserves palustrine facies deposited between ∼123–117 Ma (Aptian) and ∼110–108 Ma (Albian), which captures a critical period of warming before the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum (95–90 Ma). This provides an opportunity to interpret how Cretaceous wetland systems recorded and responded to a warming hothouse climate. This study aims to reconstruct the evolution of depositional environments, assess changes in the hydrologic cycle, and constrain terrestrial temperatures. Petrographic and cathodoluminescence analyses were used to characterize facies and evaluate carbonate preservation. The upper section of the NCF Devil’s Gate section has previously been interpreted as representing an anastomosing river with associated palustrine environments. Sandy to pebbly micrite and non-calcareous mudstone are present. These are interpreted as palustrine and floodplain deposits, respectively.

Material interpreted to preserve primary carbonate was analyzed for stable carbon and oxygen isotopes (δ13C and δ18Ocarb) and clumped isotope thermometry (Δ47). δ13C values have an average of –3.62‰ and range from –5.23 to –2.63‰. δ18Ocarb values average –14.19‰ and range from –15.2 to –12.85‰. Clumped isotope thermometry (Δ47) was used to reconstruct carbonate formation temperatures, which average 18.8°C and range from 6.3 to 28.9°C across samples. Calculated δ18Owater values average –13.5‰ and range from –16‰ to –10.9‰. Preliminary cathodoluminescent observations reveal localized microsparite suggesting some diagenetic alteration and variable preservation throughout the section that must be considered when interpreting geochemical proxies. By combining optical and cathodoluminescence petrography with stable single and clumped isotope geochemistry, we will evaluate this record for diagenetic alteration as well as changes in depositional environment, evaporation, and temperature. With this work we aim to expand the terrestrial record of the mid-Cretaceous hothouse climate and improve understanding of wetland responses to a warming climate.

title: Fault Zone Permeability – Fluid Flow and Mineralization Within the Fault Damage Zone and Fault Core.
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
authors: Petrie, Elizabeth S [1], Loewy, Staci L [2], Skurtveit, Elin [3], Evans, James P [4], Høe, Makus [5]
affiliations: (1) NES-Geology, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Jackson School of Geosciences, Austin, TX, USA
(3) Norwegian Geotechnical Institute, Oslo, Norway; Department of Geoscience, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway
(4) Water, Earth, & Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(5) Artic Geology, University Centre in Svalbard, Svalbard, Norway
abstract:
Modelling subsurface fluid migration pathways within fault zones requires detailed characterization of the structure and composition of the fault core and the surrounding damage zone. We present integrated field and laboratory results of deformation-related permeability pathways in well-exposed outcrop of fault systems in southeastern Utah that provide evidence of long-term (~ 100 ka) CO₂ leakage. Modern high CO₂ fluxes are associated with calculated dilation tendencies ≥ 0.8 of the faults and damage zone fractures. These fracture networks document the history of fluid flow and changing deformation mechanisms across reservoir and seal lithologies.

We integrate structural transect data from the fault core and damage zone with vein petrography, geomechanical testing, and U-Th age determinations from symmetric veins. The studied lithologies preserve a record of repeated episodes of fluid migration through fractures. Cross-cutting relationships indicate that shear failure preceded the development of open-mode fractures, likely reflecting changes in rock mechanical properties driven by prolonged rock-fluid interactions. U-Th ages obtained from travertine, steeply dipping and bedding-parallel calcite veins, range from ~130 ka to ~12 ka and suggest that permeability pathways are open for periods of approximately 500 to 30,000 years. Age relationships also indicate that wider-aperture fractures seal more rapidly than narrower fractures.

Mechanical testing of fault gouge reveals that its permeability is dependent on mineralogy and stress. Increased carbonate mineralization within fault gouge results in the development of fracture permeability within the fault core. At this study site the fault damage zone is the primary conduit for fluid flow and the current fault gouge permeability varies as a function of calcite content.

This naturally overpressured, CO₂-rich system provides insight on fluid flow in fault zones. Study results document the complex history of vein formation and demonstrates that both the damage zone and, under certain conditions, the fault core, can sustain permeability and fluid flow over timescales significant to subsurface storage applications.

title: Impact of Legacy Oil and Gas Infrastructure on Methane Concentrations in South-Central Kentucky Karst
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science (Posters)
authors: High, Madison [1], Washburn, Alex Matthew [2], Erhardt, Andrea M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, Lexington, KY, USA; Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Kentucky Geological Survey, Burlington, KY,
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY,
abstract:
The landscape of south-central Kentucky is dominated by karst features, such as caves and sinkholes. The region has also had historical oil and gas production. Today, many of these wells have been orphaned or abandoned, and damaged or decaying infrastructure on legacy wells could be allowing for methane (CH 4 ) migration at depth, possibly introducing excess CH 4 into the region’s karst systems. The impact of CH 4 originating from oil and gas wells in karst environments has not been widely investigated. This study aims to investigate how emissions from orphaned oil and gas wells impact CH 4 concentrations in caves across south-central Kentucky.

Walkthrough surveys were conducted in caves with no known oil and gas influence ( n = 6) and a cave with a plugged abandoned oil well drilled through it ( n = 1). Real-time ambient gas concentrations were measured with an Aeris MIRA Pico, and cave temperature and barometric pressure were recorded. The seven caves that have been visited to date all had CH 4 concentrations ranging from 0 ppm to ~1.5 ppm, aligning with previous research showing that caves generally have sub-atmospheric concentrations (<~2 ppm) of CH 4 . These preliminary findings suggest that caves with properly maintained infrastructure or no connection to legacy infrastructure should have sub-atmospheric concentrations. Future surveys will be conducted in a cave with an unplugged abandoned well drilled through it ( n = 1) and a cave with a natural hydrocarbon seep ( n = 1). Time lapse measurements of CH 4 and other ambient gas concentrations will track background and active CH 4 sources in the caves and provide a better understanding of the caves’ responses to the active CH 4 sources.

In addition to the walkthrough surveys, CH 4 isotopes will be collected from ambient air samples in each cave to determine the origin of cave CH 4 . Methods are being developed to concentrate low CH 4 for δ 13 C analysis to further validate the origin of CH 4 . The measured methane concentrations from walkthrough surveys will be crucial for the δ 13 C analysis and to determine how emissions from oil and gas wells are affecting ambient cave gasses. Methane and other ambient gasses influence factors such as microbial development and mineral precipitation, so understanding the sources and amounts of ambient gasses in cave systems is essential to conserve cave systems.

title: Assessing the Reliability of Folia as Sea-level Indicators in Coastal Caves of the Yucatán Peninsula
session_title: Karst Sedimentary, Paleoclimate, and Historical Records (Posters)
authors: Rivera Ramos, Pedro Hernán [1], Vogtner, Juliet [2], Lopez Martinez, Rafael Antonio [3], Valera, Daisy [4], Lases Hernández, Fernanda [5], Kamenov, George D. [6], Beddows, Patricia A. [7], Oliveras Amador, Jessica [8], Severino Zorrilla, Matias [9], Dumitru, Oana [10], Onac, Bogdan P. [11]

abstract:
Constraining the rate and duration of future sea-level rise remains one of the central environmental challenges of our time. Past warm periods when sea level stood near or above present position provide valuable analogs for future coastal responses. Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 7 (~245-190 thousand years ago) remains relatively understudied because it has a weaker climatic optimum and a more complex structure than other late Pleistocene interglacials, with three warm peaks and poorly constrained ice-volume changes. A range of geological indicators, including corals, speleothems, marine terraces, and others, have been used to reconstruct past sea-level fluctuations during such analog periods.

Folia are speleothem calcite cave deposits that form in bracket shapes extending out and downwards from walls and ceilings in coastal caves of the Yucatán Peninsula, where they have also recently been observed forming on pre-existing speleothems. They form at the water-air interface, and their elevation closely tracks the position of the water table at the time of growth. In coastal cave settings, this water table is controlled by sea level. We posit that folia development requires the water table to remain stable, or to fall very slowly, to allow carbonate precipitation to keep up with sea-level change. [PB1] Consequently, the overlapping fin-like layers suggest that sea-level fall was not continuous but interrupted by intervals of near stability. This makes folia promising archives for reconstructing successive stages of long-term sea-level change.

To evaluate this potential, we analyzed ten folia samples collected from within 3 to 128 cm of the modern water table, from Garra de Jaguar and Río Secreto caves located south of the City of Playa del Carmen, within ~5 km from the Caribbean coast. U-series dating places all samples within MIS 7, and their age-elevation distribution is concentrated along the falling limbs of the associated sea-level highstands. This pattern suggests that folia may record successive short-lived sea-level stillstands during transitions from warmer to colder climate conditions, providing robust constraints on the timing of these events and the rates of sea-level fall in coastal regions.

title: Evaluating River Corridor Geomorphic Response to Large Wood Augmentation in the Southern Appalachian Mountains
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Hutchinson, Hope [1], Marshall, Anna [2], Curley, Mairin [3]
affiliations: (1) Geography & Sustainability, University of Tennesse, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Geography & Sustainability, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(3) Geography & Sustainability, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract: Large wood is a fundamental driver of channel complexity, sediment storage, and aquatic habitat in river systems. However, human activities have substantially altered natural wood regimes in many watersheds, reducing geomorphic complexity and disconnecting physical and ecological processes. Large wood restoration is increasingly used to enhance channel complexity and ecological function in degraded rivers, yet relatively few studies have quantified how logjam characteristics influence geomorphic adjustment over time. This gap is especially pronounced in Appalachia, where a legacy of deforestation and channel wood removal has constrained observations of wood dynamics in streams. Here, we assess the geomorphic response to wood augmentation in two tributary stream channels within the Citico Creek Watershed of the Cherokee National Forest in southeastern Tennessee. The Citico Creek Watershed is a highly diverse area that has experienced historic wood removal from timber harvests, degrading and disconnecting aquatic habitats, making it a priority for restoration. We examined two restored tributary streams within the Citico Creek watershed - the Little Citico Creek and Caney Branch - where large wood has been installed over the past several years. The streams differ in wood installation age, providing an opportunity to assess how both logjam characteristics and time since installation influence geomorphic response. We tested whether the older restoration site of the Little Citico exhibits greater geomorphic development than the recently augmented reach of Caney Branch. We quantified logjam geometry, porosity, blockage ratio, spatial distribution, and associated pool morphology to evaluate how logjam characteristics influence channel complexity and local geomorphic processes. Preliminary results suggest that the older restoration site has more variation in logjam characteristics and associated channel complexity than the recently restored stream, suggesting that geomorphic adjustment increases through time following wood augmentation. These results provide early evidence that logjam design and restoration age influence geomorphic adjustment following wood augmentation. Continued monitoring will improve understanding of restoration trajectories and inform process-based river restoration in mountain watersheds.
