title: An Ecometric Framework for Anticipating Reef Collapse and Recovery
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Williams, Claire M. [1], McGuire, Jenny L. [2], Bolden, Isaiah W. [3], Lawing, A. Michelle [4]
affiliations: (1) Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA; Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Ga, USA
(4) Texas A&M University, College Station, USA
abstract:
As coral reefs undergo rapid ecological change, there is an urgent need for approaches that can anticipate community dynamics and identify when and where ecological functions may be lost. Ecometrics addresses this challenge by providing a powerful quantitative framework that links community-level trait distributions to environmental conditions and creating a transferable framework for interpreting functional structure and change.

To our knowledge, this project represents the first application of an ecometric approach to coral reef ecosystems, using global coral reef assemblages to evaluate key coral traits (i.e growth form and corallite width) and assess the extent to which they covary with temperature. Community-weighted means and standard deviations of growth form and corallite width show significant predictable relationships with ocean temperature, providing a promising basis for applications across modern, fossil, and future systems; observed maximum ocean temperatures and temperatures estimated from the ecometric models were strongly positively related for both growth form (R 2 =0.717, r=0.847, p<0.001) and maximum corallite width (R 2 =0.723, r=0.850, p<0.001). Cooler temperatures were associated with greater representation of encrusting and massive growth forms and larger average corallite widths, whereas warmer temperatures were associated with greater variation in both traits. Using this approach, we can compare community trait composition predicted temperatures against observed climate, noting regions with greatest dissonance; in the Persian Gulf, both growth form and corallite width indicated communities more characteristic of cooler environments. Extending these models to fossil assemblages and projected environmental conditions will allow us to evaluate coral trait-environment relationships beyond the deteriorated modern ecological space represented by modern reefs, examine community organization across past episodes of environmental change, and anticipate how coral communities may reorganize, where functional disruption is most likely, and which trait configurations may persist or emerge in future oceans.

title: Flood Frequency Analysis of Big Creek, Kansas
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Funai, Ryan Saburo [1], Santoli, Jason T [2], Wainscott, Gunnar F [3], Zurn, Callen M [4], Ali, Hendratta N. [5]

abstract: The primary purpose of flood frequency analysis is to determine a timeframe of potential flood events. Analyzing flood frequency is a process that involves collecting years of quantitative data on discharge rates, calculating the probability of exceeding a certain rate of discharge, and calculating the average interval between events equaling or exceeding a certain rate of discharge. The Big Creek Watershed drainage area covers an area of 549 square miles in Western Kansas, including Ellis, Trego, Gove, and Sheridan Counties. This research analyzes 79 years of data collected manually and with automated sensors by the USGS at the intersection of Big Creek and US-183. This research aims to provide a statistical probability estimate for a period of time that major flooding events may occur within.

abstract:
Missions to small asteroids, including (101955) Bennu, (25143) Itokawa, and the Lucy spacecraft's flyby of the contact binary (52246) Donaldjohanson, reveal surfaces with a distinct deficit of small craters. To understand these crater-depleted surfaces, we apply a flux-agnostic proximity-to-saturation analytic model to evaluate crater retention on Donaldjohanson. Our analysis isolates size-dependent degradation regimes, revealing a degradation signature with a distinct structural slope break at approximately 120 m globally, with variation in the efficiency of size-dependent erasure between lobes.

Recent literature indicates that small bodies may possess seismically dissipative interiors. Consequently, global seismic shaking alone may not explain these crater deficits. Instead, we investigate how Donaldjohanson’s contact-binary geometry may act as a frequency-dependent seismic filter. We will investigate the effects of the bilobed shape on the ability of seismic waves to erase craters, exploring whether high-frequency seismic energy from localized impacts is trapped within the lobes to efficiently erase craters <120 m, while larger craters are only degraded by rarer, low-frequency seismic modes capable of propagating across the narrow neck.

This seismic agitation of highly mobile thin fallback regolith may continually tumble grains and expose fresh material beneath the weathered optical skin, effectively slowing space weathering and actively shaping the asteroid's overall optical maturity over geologic timescales.

The Lucy mission is funded through the NASA Discovery program (contract NNM16AA08C). Part of this work is funded by Participating Scientist award 80NSSC25K7725.

title: Viséan Carbonate and Shale Systems Revealed by Benthic Foraminifera: A Comparative Study of the Cyrenaica Platform (Libya) and Ardmore Basin, Oklahoma (USA)
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches (Posters)
authors: Khameiss, Belkasim Kh. [1], Stanley, Thomas M. M [2], Muftah, Ahmed of [3]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma Geological Survey, Norman, OK, USA
(2) University of Kansas, Norman, ok, USA
(3) University of Benghazi, Benghazi, Libya
abstract:
This study documents a Viséan benthic foraminiferal assemblage from a cored interval (6950–6980 ft) of the Shregat Formation in well A1-75/03 on the Cyrenaica Platform, northeastern Libya. Nineteen core samples were analyzed using micropaleontological and petrographic methods to reconstruct the biostratigraphy and depositional environment of the succession. The assemblage is dominated by small benthic foraminifera, particularly endothyrids and ammodiscids, including Endothyra bradyi, Chernyshinella cf. glomiformis, Plectogyranopsis cf. convexa, Laxoendothyra parakosvensis, Endostaffella parva, Euxinita aff. efremovi, Pseudochernyshinella aff. subrotunda, Ammodiscus spp., Hemidiscopsis caprariensis, and Earlandia sp,. This assemblage confirms a Late Mississippian (Viséan) age and indicates deposition in a shallow inner-shelf environment under normal marine conditions.

A comparable Mississippian benthic foraminiferal assemblage is recorded from the Caney Shale of the Ardmore Basin, Oklahoma, USA, including Plectogyra irregularis and Endothyra macra. Although both regions share similar foraminiferal taxa, this is indicative of an open marine shelf. The Caney Shale represents a more tectonically deformed, shale-dominated basin setting. These results highlight the strong biostratigraphic and paleoenvironmental utility of benthic foraminifera for correlating Mississippian marine systems across contrasting sedimentary and tectonic regimes.

title: Dynamics of Flat-Slab Subduction and the Effects on the Overlying Continent
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Currie, Claire [1], Liu, Xiaowen [2], O'Keefe, Amelia [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
(2) Department of Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
(3) Department of Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
abstract:
Transient episodes of flat-slab subduction have profoundly shaped the geological record of western North and South America. In the western United States, the development of Farallon flat-slab subduction during the Late Cretaceous drove an inboard migration of magmatism and basement-involved deformation to more than 1500 km from the plate margin. Subsequent foundering of the flat slab during the Late Oligocene was accompanied by widespread magmatism and rapid changes in surface topography. Although the first-order surface expressions of flat-slab subduction are well documented, its effects on the deep continental lithosphere remain poorly understood.

We use two-dimensional numerical models based on the tectonic setting of the western United States to investigate how flat-slab subduction modifies the thermal, mechanical, and compositional structure of the overlying continent. Models first examine flat-slab development, in which slab shallowing is driven by continental advance and subduction of anomalously buoyant oceanic crust (the Conjugate Shatsky Rise). As the slab flattens, it mechanically entrains the lowermost 20-50 km of the continental lithosphere, forming a keel that thickens as it is pushed inland. Flat-slab emplacement progressively cools the overlying lithosphere, suppressing magmatism, while continued slab dehydration metasomatizes the deep continent.

Slab removal is driven by an increase in oceanic plate density and/or a slowdown in continental advance. Models explore two modes of removal: (1) rollback as the slab progressively steepens and (2) vertical foundering following slab breakoff at the seaward edge of the flat segment. Both modes produce changes in surface topography, continental shortening, and magmatism, although the spatiotemporal patterns and magnitudes differ. The models predict that hydration of the continental mantle lithosphere during the flat-slab episode primes it for extensive melting following slab removal. In addition, the former flat-slab region is characterized by thinned continental lithosphere resulting from both earlier mechanical displacement and subsequent gravitational thinning. Our results demonstrate that flat-slab subduction can significantly modify continental lithosphere structure and that these modifications are consistent with present-day geophysical observations of the western United States lithosphere.

abstract: The Edwards and Trinity aquifers are crucial resources of drinking water for much of south-central Texas. This study provides a comprehensive hydrogeochemical characterization of Helotes Creek Watershed (HCW) in south-central Texas, evaluates hydraulic communication between the Upper Glen Rose (UGR) and Lower Glen Rose (LGR) units of the Trinity Aquifer, and characterizes rare earth elements (REEs) distributions. Seasonal groundwater samples from private HCW wells and comparison wells at the Edwards Aquifer Authority’s Field Research Park (FRP) are analyzed for physicochemical parameters, major ions, trace elements, total organic carbon and nitrogen (TOC/TN), dissolved organic matter (DOM), stable isotopes (δ¹⁸O, δD, δ³⁴S, δ¹⁵N), and REEs. Groundwater chemistry is dominated by carbonate and evaporite dissolution with clear hydrochemical separation between the UGR and LGR. The UGR is characterized by Ca-Mg-HCO₃ hydro-facies, lower conductivity and TDS, and stronger influence from rapid recharge. In contrast, the LGR is characterized by Ca-Mg-Cl-SO₄ hydro-facies, elevated conductivity and TDS, SO 4 2- , Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , B, and Fe, indicating stronger water-rock interaction, evaporite dissolution, and longer residence times. δ 18 O and δD variations indicate recharge by direct precipitation with limited evaporative trends. TOC/TN and DOM patterns reveal strong surface-water interaction with slight influence of wastewater that is primarily driven by organic soils and fertilizers applied to the lands. Trace elements and major ion concentrations are below WHO thresholds. REE concentrations are low, but PAAS-normalized patterns provide supporting evidence for groundwater evolution. FRP contains higher absolute ΣREE, whereas HCW and especially LGR wells displayed stronger HREE and MREE enrichment. Overall, the combined geochemical, isotopic, organic, and REE geochemistry evidence indicates limited hydraulic communication between the UGR and LGR, with localized mixing possible along specific flow paths or pumping-stressed zones.

title: Work Minimization as a Control on the Development and Spacing of Imbricate Thrust Systems
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics
authors: Brink-Roby, David D. [1], Walsh, Talor [2]
affiliations: (1) Marshall University, Huntington, WV, USA
(2) Millersville University Earth Sciences, Millersville, PA, USA
abstract:
Imbricate thrust systems, including duplexes and imbricate fans, influence slip transfer, crustal thickening, groundwater and hydrocarbon systems, seismic hazards, and the development of critically tapered fold-and-thrust belts. Although geometric and kinematic models describe the architecture of fold-and-thrust belts, they do not explain why fold-and-thrust belts have multiple faults (i.e., why do new thrust faults form instead of continued slip along existing faults?) Previous work-based models attributed imbrication to frictional strain hardening. This mechanism requires that the increased frictional work due to strain hardening offsets the added work of propagating new thrust faults and deforming intervening thrust sheets—an unlikely condition when elevated pore-fluid pressure, fluid-assisted alteration, phyllosilicate development, or grain-size-sensitive deformation occurs.

Here, we propose new kinematic work-minimization models that incorporate a dipping basal fault, a frontal ramp, and a critically tapered wedge. Our models include estimates of work due to fault propagation, frictional sliding, internal deformation, and gravitational work due to uplift. As a result of these geometric changes, the work due to gravity becomes an important factor in determining the formation and propagation of thrust faults. The models show that as basal-fault dip increases, deformation along a single fault results in more gravitational work than it does for a system with multiple imbricate faults. Above a threshold slope for the basal fault, the gravitational-work reduction from imbrication exceeds the additional work of fault-propagation and internal-deformation, making a new thrust fault mechanically advantageous.

We conducted sandbox analogue modeling experiments to test our kinematic results and hypothesis. When a critically-tapered sand wedge slips up a nondeformable frontal ramp, displacement remained localized along a single fault. When a comparable critically-tapered sand wedge is thrust over a deformable ramp, regularly-spaced imbricate thrust faults form in the footwall. In models where imbricate thrust faults formed, distributed faulting reduced the effective basal slope and produced a lower center of mass than the single-fault experiment, reducing gravitational work.

Our results were compared to balanced cross sections from the Sevier, western Taiwan, and Himalayan fold-and-thrust belts which geometrically replicate our results (e.g. imbricate thrust faults form at frontal ramps), demonstrating their applicability to natural fold-and-thrust belts.

abstract:
Global glaciations have long been proposed as major drivers of biological and environmental change during the Neoproterozoic. Cryogenian panglacial intervals are hypothesized to have reorganized Earth’s surface environments by disrupting the global carbon cycle and producing changes in atmospheric pCO₂, oceanic and atmospheric oxygenation, continental weathering, and nutrient distribution patterns. Testing for these changes enables an evaluation of whether Cryogenian climate change led to conditions (e.g., redox conditions and nutrient-cycling regimes) favorable for metazoan emergence.

One carbonate-dominated and two mixed siliciclastic-carbonate Cryogenian successions on the Congo Craton of Namibia were sampled from inner-platform, foreslope, and basinal settings, respectively. Carbonate samples were collected for coupled δ¹³C, δ²³⁸U, and rare earth element analyses to reconstruct the relationship between the platform’s redox structure and carbon cycling, enabling us to characterize differences in post-Sturtian seawater oxygenation between shallow- and deep-water settings. Redox-sensitive elemental proxies in shale samples from the basinal section, including U/Al, U/Th, V/Cr, and Mo/Al, indicate predominantly oxic to suboxic conditions through much of the nonglacial interlude, followed by the development of more anoxic conditions coincident with the pre-Marinoan Trezona anomaly. This preliminary interpretation will be tested using δ²³⁸U and Ce/Ce* records currently being generated from carbonate samples.

abstract:
he Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous (83–72 Ma) was a dynamic interval in the evolutionary history of North American ecosystems. Mammalian communities were diversifying and beginning to resemble the well-studied cimolodontan- and therian-dominated communities of the Maastrichtian. Several penecontemporaneous formations across the Western Interior Basin of North America preserve this interval and associated geology and paleontology. Despite the extensive history of fossil collection in these formations, studies have only recently achieved high-resolution chronostratigraphic correlation. Here, we propose a revised correlation of discontinuous outcrops and mammalian faunas of the Judith River Formation (JRF) near Rudyard and Havre in Hill County, Montana (MT).

A complete section of the JRF crops out in well-studied and sampled exposures of the JRF in the Upper Missouri River Breaks National Monument (UMRBNM), near Winifred, MT. Previous research established chronostratigraphic correlation across this region and beyond using significant surfaces and high-resolution U/Pb ages. In contrast, the discontinuous and incomplete exposures of the JRF in Hill County were, until now, loosely correlated and relatively undersampled for fossils, despite bearing several rich mammalian localities. Consequently, analysis of diversity dynamics of mammalian faunas from the JRF has previously not been possible. Recent field work conducted by a team from the University of Washington and Macalester College in these study areas has sampled and stratigraphically placed >30 new and existing localities and recovered a large collection of vertebrate microfossils (>10,000). We used a series of marker beds and distinctive bedsets, along with findings from previous studies, to place localities from the Rudyard field area into the lower ~45 m of the McClelland Ferry Member of the JRF and those from the Havre field area into the upper ~50 m of the Coal Ridge Member of the JRF. With these localities now integrated into the chronostratigraphic framework of the JRF, mammalian faunas can now be more readily compared to those in the UMRBNM.

This new stratigraphically ordered suite of fossil localities places fossil horizons from across the region into a temporal sequence that will facilitate study of taxonomic diversity dynamics of mammalian communities during the Campanian in north-central Montana. Ongoing recovery and study of mammals from this new temporal sequence will advance understanding of taxonomic and ecological dynamics of Campanian mammal communities in North America.

title: Gusherite: An Oil-Cemented Anthropogenic Deposit at the 1910 Lakeview Gusher Site, Midway-Sunset Oil Field, California
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Testa, Stephen Michael [1], Thompson, Vaughn [2]
affiliations: (1) Mokelumne Hill, CA, USA

abstract:
On 15 March 1910 the Lakeview No. 1 well, drilled to 2,225 ft in the Midway-Sunset oil field, Kern County, California, blew out and flowed uncontrolled for 18 months, discharging 8–9.4 million barrels of crude, the largest accidental liquid petroleum release in U.S. history. Although4.7–6 million barrels were recovered; the unrecovered 2.0–4.7 million barrels remained on the ground across the 60-acre containment works.

Preserved at California Historical Landmark No. 485, the site offers something the rock record almost never does: a deposit whose emplacement requires no inference. The fluid was 18–21° Baumé heavy crude; its evolution into a yield-strength slurry is on record with emulsion reaching 60% of daily production by January 1911 and sump emulsion remained unseparated in open air as late as July 1914; rock ejection and a crater-filling sand cone were reported, and photographs track the cone’s growth. Lakeview is a full-scale emplacement experiment with input conditions well documented.

The deposit is organized accordingly: a constructional cone whose beds dip radially outward from the collapse crater, discordant with the uniform northeast dip of the nearby Tulare Formation; a shrinkage-cracked river of oil toward the Buena Vista Lake lowland, bearing fluid- and gas-escape structures; engineered sumps; and thin distal crusts. The cone facies preserve beds and depositional structures (albeit without aqueous traction structures), is locally erosive, and records a yield-strength oil-sediment slurry. Also entrained are disoriented timber and hundreds of sandbag molds and partially preserved sandbag fabric, some apparently lithifying, as well as striking sandbag-induced flame structures.

We propose gusherite as an informal name for such blowout deposits. Petrographic analysis and lab testing on selected samples was performed to distinguish matrix-supported fabric (sediment carried within oil) from grain-supported (sediment soaked by standing oil): the aim being to calibrate the signature of catastrophic emplacement versus impregnated sedimentary units. Deposits interpreted as seeps or passive impregnation may for example include products of natural catastrophic seal failures with the Lakeview site supplying the reference section for recognizing such features in the geological record.

title: Exported Sediment Mineralogy Indicates Weak Hillslope–Stream Connectivity in First-Order Post-Glacial Watersheds of New Hampshire
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: McCloud, Connor [1], Kaste, James [2]
affiliations: (1) William and Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(2) William and Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
abstract: Soils are an essential natural resource that support food production, regulate water quality, sustain ecosystems, and store carbon, making accurate measurements of soil loss critical for understanding landscape susceptibility. A common way to measure erosion rates is by measuring the sediment removed from a landscape in rivers and extrapolating it over the watershed as the mass of soil material lost per unit area, assuming that sediment is derived from hillslope erosion and the landscape is lowering uniformly. However, in post-glacial New England, where resistant soils, high infiltration capacities, and thick organic horizons strongly limit hillslope erosion, streams continue to export measurable quantities of suspended and bedload sediment. I hypothesize that a significant amount of sediment is produced via in-channel weathering rather than hillslope erosion. Using the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest (HBEF) in New Hampshire as a research site, I investigate the provenance of particulate material exported from HBEF watersheds by using the degree of biotite weathering as a mineralogical tracer. In temperate climates, biotite vermiculitizes rapidly under soil-forming conditions and is therefore expected to be scarce or highly altered in upland soils, but relatively unweathered if derived from in situ weathering of streambed material. Clay-sized (<2 µm) sediments collected from weir stilling basins and hillslopes were analyzed using oriented X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify mineral assemblages. Initial XRD results reveal abundant biotite and kaolinite with trace amounts of chlorite and interstratified mica-vermiculite, but an absence of vermiculite characteristic of upland soils in the region. Additionally, the occurrence of relatively unweathered mafic minerals, including amphibole, in exported stream sediments provides further evidence for an in-channel sediment source because these minerals are highly susceptible to chemical weathering and are not expected to persist under soil-forming conditions. Together, the presence of unaltered biotite, weathering-sensitive mafic minerals, and absence of vermiculite in exported sediments, contrasted with the presence of vermiculite and absence of unaltered biotite in soil clay mineral assemblages, indicates that particulate material exported from the HBEF is derived predominantly from streambed weathering rather than erosion of upland soils. These findings demonstrate a disconnect between soil weathering and sediment export in this low-erosion, forested watershed and emphasize the importance of in-channel sediment production in controlling solid-phase watershed losses.

abstract: A previously unrecognized, 160-km long belt of small (0.5-7.2 km 2 ) monogenetic adakite volcanic domes crops out in the southern California–northern Baja California coastal region. The belt appears related to Neogene transrotational rifting of the inner southern California borderland caused by propagation of the East Pacific Rise into the region. Volcanism from 18-14 Ma attended peak rifting within the borderland. Adakites erupted along the eastern rift flank are somewhat younger based on new 40 Ar/ 39 Ar data (14-8 Ma). The adakite domes are compositionally distinct from the mostly calc-alkaline borderland volcanics in having higher Na- and Al-contents, higher Na/K, depleted HREE, depleted Y, and elevated Sr and Sr/Y. We propose that they were generated by lateral heat transfer from upwelling asthenosphere beneath the inner borderland into the rift flank, where low volume adakite magmas were produced by partial melting of the Cretaceous subduction complex beneath the western Peninsular Ranges arc. This conductive heat transfer operated at slower time scales lagging behind the more rapid advective processes active within the rifted borderland. Partial melts likely formed at 20-30 km depths for up to 6 Myr after the main phase of borderland rifting. The oldest and most mafic rocks of the coastal adakite belt occur closest to the coast while the youngest and most silicic occur farther inland. This is consistent with the higher temperatures, earlier melting, and larger melt fraction expected closer to the rift axis. We further recognize adakite from published whole-rock analyses from a dacite dome at Harris Point on San Miguel Island in the northern Channel Islands that may correlate with the Prisoner Harbor dacite atop the Santa Cruz Island volcanic section. Late cross-cutting dacite domes with adakite-like chemistry also occur in the Conejo Volcanics of the western Santa Monica Mountain. These occurrences suggest the same process that produced the coastal adakite belt may have also generated adakite along the northern Channel Islands/Santa Monica Mountains conjugate rift margin.

title: A Reanalysis of Temperature-Index Modeling of Climate During the Last Glacial Maximum in the Southern Rocky Mountains, U.S.A.
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations (Posters)
authors: Brugger, Keith A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology Discipline, University of Minnesota, Morris, Morris, MN, USA
abstract:
Proxy-based reconstructions of climate during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) in the southern Rocky Mountains are sparse. Glaciological modeling has therefore provided alternatives for quantitative estimates of LGM climate. However, there are inconsistencies in the foundational data and its parameterization used in these models. Moreover, these approaches suffer from a lack of knowledge regarding paleoprecipitation specific to study areas, and this is problematic in determining LGM temperature depression.

To address such shortcomings in temperature-index modeling of LGM climate, a reanalysis was performed using twenty (five new) reconstructed paleoglaciers in six different study areas in Colorado and New Mexico. The reanalysis updates previous work that was based on older gridded or other climatologies for modern climate, and to some extent some details in the modeling. In addition, instead of making arbitrary assumptions for possible changes in LGM precipitation, changes in the latter are informed by the CHELSA-Trace21k high-resolution downscaling of global climate. While in some study areas the new estimates of temperature depression are comparable to previous estimates, in others the magnitude of cooling increased significantly by nearly 2 °C. Regionally, preliminary results indicate the southern Rocky Mountains were ~9 °C cooler than today. Although this is contrary to studies that suggest a more modest LGM temperature depression in the region, it is more consistent with that derived from downscaled climate models.

authors: Flynn, Andrew G. [1], Milligan, Joseph N. [2], Peppe, Daniel J. [3], Geng, Jie [4], Secord, Ross [5], Williamson, Thomas [6], Brusatte, Stephen [7], Shelley, Sarah [8], Munyaka, Venanzio [9]

abstract:
Early Paleocene floral and faunal communities were substantially restructured as a result of the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction approximately 66.0 Ma. While events immediately adjacent to the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary have been widely studied, comparatively little research has looked at long-term patterns in terrestrial ecosystem recovery during the early Paleocene. The San Juan Basin (SJB), located in northwestern New Mexico, preserves exceptional, diverse, and geochronologically well-constrained early Paleocene floral and faunal records, making it an ideal location to investigate long-term recovery of early Paleocene terrestrial ecosystems. Here we present a high-resolution record of early Paleocene terrestrial ecosystem instability during the first ~1.5 Myr of the Paleocene using plant and vertebrate fossils coupled with bulk organic carbon δ 13 C and reconstructed leaf area index from the SJB.

Plant and vertebrate macrofossils in the SJB were collected from the lower Paleocene Ojo Alamo Sandstone and lower Nacimiento Formation spanning the first ~1.5 Myr of the Paleocene. Floral extinction, origination, and net diversification rates were estimated using the Pradel capture-mark-recapture (CMR) model from 66.0-64.5 Ma with 150 Kyr timesteps. Two early Paleocene intervals of decreasing floral diversity were identified: a lower interval of ~25% diversity decrease at ~65.5 Ma and an upper interval of ~40% decreased diversity at ~64.8 Ma. Two short intervals of rapid floral diversification were also identified at ~65.3 and ~64.6 Ma. The onset of both intervals of decreasing floral diversity are coeval with -1.5 to -2.5 ‰ bulk organic carbon δ 13 C excursions and a decrease in forest canopy density reconstructed from paleo-leaf area index. Both intervals of floral extinction immediately precede the first appearance Puercan 3 (Pu3) and Torrejonian 1 (To1) mammalian assemblages, respectively, in the SJB, suggesting coupled floral and faunal turnover.

We also applied the Pradel CMR model to coeval macrofloras from the Denver Basin (DB), Colorado and the Williston Basin (WB), North Dakota and Montana, respectively. The floral diversity patterns estimated from the DB and WB indicate intervals of increasing and decreasing floral diversity that are contemporaneous with the same intervals identified in the SJB. This suggests a regional driver in patterns of floral diversity change during the early Paleocene in western North America, reflecting prolonged terrestrial ecosystem instability following the K-Pg mass extinction.

abstract: This presentation reports stable nitrogen isotope data (δ15N) measured in the organic matrix of commercially important European flat oyster shells ( Ostrea edulis ) from the Adriatic Sea. Oysters are filter feeders and the protein matrices in their shells reflect the δ15N values of the environment they live in. Ancient samples may retain their organic matrices over long periods of time under some depositional conditions, protected by the calcite crystals that make up most of the shell. Analyzing δ15N in the shells from different time periods can enable insight into environmental conditions over time. This method has been applied in other environments but has not yet been studied in the Adriatic Sea, and this is also its first application in O . edulis . Shell δ15N values are compared between modern and Neolithic oyster samples. Modern samples were collected from wild oyster beds in the open North Adriatic Sea and from an aquaculture operation in Mali Ston Bay (south-east Adriatic). Archaeological oyster shell samples were excavated from the Ždrilo Cave site (middle region of the eastern Adriatic), in stratigraphic layers dated to the Neolithic period. The goal was to assess potential changes in nitrogen inputs from the long history of human settlements in the area. Data collected thus far do not detect any evidence of δ15N value increase over time. Similar published studies document that mollusk shell δ15N values often become heavier over time due to inputs of agricultural and urban waste entering coastal areas. These prior studies focused on nutrient-rich ecosystems unlike the oligotrophic Adriatic Sea where additional nitrogen may be more easily utilized.

authors: Olson, Hunter C. [1], Farrell, Úna C. [2], Sperling, Erik A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA, USA

abstract: Large quantities of Indigenous data exist within public repositories without permission or are of unknown provenance, and this has only increased with the adoption of the FAIR principles (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, Reusability). Geology and paleontology databases are no different, with large amounts of data collected from current tribal lands and former territories publicly available. The CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) for Indigenous data governance were proposed to complement the FAIR principles while centering indigenous rights and concerns over how data is collected and managed. While CARE principles are gaining more widespread recognition, in practice adoption has been slow in many areas. Geologic and paleontological data have direct impacts on indigenous peoples and can affect community health, economics, territorial control, and can perpetuate past injustices; thus implementation of CARE principles is critical in geoscience databases. The Sedimentary Geochemistry and Paleoenvironments Project (SGP) is a database-driven research consortium focused on answering questions of environmental change across Earth’s history through statistical analyses of the global sedimentary geochemical record. SGP stewards geochemical data, stratigraphic and broader geologic context data, and locality information. Like many other geoscience databases, SGP has data holdings from federal reservation lands in the United States. The SGP database is developing new strategies to adhere to the CARE principles as the database continues to grow. This includes a PostGIS-based spatial check in our data ingestion pipeline to flag new samples for review that may come from lands under U.S. Tribal jurisdiction, such that we can request proof of permission if needed (e.g., Tribal permit). Second, we have integrated the Native-Lands.ca API so traditional homelands and territories can be acknowledged when data is downloaded. Finally, we are directly reaching out to Tribal governments and creating opportunities for tribal representatives to contact SGP with concerns about data presentation and accessibility. This work represents initial efforts to establish CARE principles within the SGP database, and we aim to discuss some of the practical methods that may be more broadly applicable.

title: Early and Often: Scaffolding of CUREs to Enhance Learning

abstract:
Translating important but unfamiliar and unintuitive scientific concepts to practical, usable knowledge is one of the central challenges of teaching and learning in an introductory mineralogy class. Solid solution is a common phenomenon in most minerals, yet the idea that elements substitute for one another in a crystal structure is often foreign to students. Nevertheless, this concept is critical for understanding chemical zoning and more advanced topics including the use of minerals as geothermometers and barometers. To help bridge this conceptual barrier, a semester-long course-embedded undergraduate research experience (CURE) has been incorporated into the introductory, sophomore-level mineralogy course at LSU. After students are introduced to mineral chemistry, solid solution, and analytical instrumentation, they engage as research mineralogists in discovery-based learning by using the electron microprobe (EMP). Each student pair is assigned a thin section with a specific mineral for chemical analysis. The project begins with petrographic observations and acquisition of a full thin section scan. During the EMP session, students explore minerals in context, strengthen spatial skills by comparing BSE images with optical scans, evaluate chemical zoning through changes in the BSE grayscale, use EDS analyses to identify accessory phases and complete WDS analyses for complete mineral chemistry. Results quickly show that the ‘ideal’ mineral compositions are simplified representations and that natural minerals commonly display complex solid-solution behavior. Following the EMP sessions, students complete a series of exercises in which they quality-control the data, calculate mineral stoichiometry, and plot compositional data for additional discoveries. Student data can be combined via a jigsaw approach to determine the pressures and temperatures of mineral formation. Over the last two decades, informal assessment demonstrates that over 80% of the students identified the EMP lab experience as one of the top three components of the mineralogy course. The project improved conceptual understanding while providing the students with authentic research experience.

This introductory exposure to mineral research prepares students for more advanced CUREs in sequential courses, including Igneous-Metamorphic Petrology and Earth Materials, Energy and the Environment. In the latter course, each student analyzes a REE mineral from a world class locality. In addition to strengthening understanding and comprehension of scientific concepts, these scaffolded projects enhance student learning in spatial and penetrative thinking, use of advanced instrumentation, quantitative analysis, and scientific communication.

title: Discovery of a 2-meter Temperature Anomaly in the Lost River Valley
session_title: Hydrogeology of Geothermal Resources: From Shallow Systems to Deep Reservoirs (Posters)
authors: Albaugh, Madison Bryce [1], Anderson, Ryan [2], Bottenberg, Carrie [3], Vissotski, Haley [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA

abstract: Geothermal resources are an underutilized source of energy that represent a sustainable and economically viable option for addressing energy concerns in Idaho. The Lost River Valley has been highlighted as having a number of geologic features that are closely associated with geothermal systems elsewhere in the Basin and Range; however, detailed studies to characterize the geothermal potential of the Lost River Valley are lacking. This study produced a collection of data layers (Quaternary faults, gravity, geodetic, earthquake rate density, and favorable structural settings) to highlight regions that have a high likelihood of hosting a blind or hidden geothermal system. Ground temperature surveys consisting of 2-meter rods driven into the ground on transects throughout the valley were then carried out to detect shallow subsurface anomalies. The Lost River fault zone (LRF) has been active throughout the Quaternary, with evidence for Holocene activity in the northernmost sections, the most recent rupture being the 1983 Borah Peak earthquake. Preliminary analysis of available datasets identified the northern part of the valley as having a fault accommodation zone with a high earthquake rate density that is favorable towards geothermal systems. Younger faults and earthquake epicenters are lacking in the southernmost sections of the valley; however there is a higher density of Quaternary volcanic centers and elevated heat flow. The survey produced 104 ground temperatures at 2 meters depth, with an estimated background temperature of 12.2℃. Seventy points were above background, with the highest recorded temperature being 22.5 ℃. This study highlighted the area North of Willow Creek Summit as having a shallow temperature anomaly that coincides with other favorable geologic parameters (close proximity to a historic fault rupture within an accommodation zone, with a relatively high earthquake rate density). This study indicates a possible hidden geothermal system that should be further evaluated for geothermal and economic potential.

title: Determining the Provenance of Glacially Derived Gravel at Point Betsie Lighthouse Beach, Lake Michigan, Michigan
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Topper, Laureen Meade [1], MacDonald, James H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(2) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
abstract:
Point Betsie Lighthouse Beach, eastern shore, Lake Michigan in Benzie County, Michigan, contains a diverse assemblage of locally derived Paleozoic carbonate gravel and glacially derived gravel transported to Point Betsie by the Lake Michigan Lobe of the Laurentide ice sheet during the late Wisconsinan glaciation. The glacially derived gravel preserves the potentially long-distance transport from northern source regions during the Late Pleistocene deglaciation. This study investigates the provenance of representative gravel through lithological, petrographic, and mineralogical analyses. In particular, this study aims to evaluate whether representative gravel is consistent with older Canadian Shield terranes or with the lithologies associated with the Mesoproterozoic Midcontinent Rift system of Lake Superior. A secondary objective is to quantify the relative abundance of these glacially derived gravel compared with the locally derived carbonate rocks. To achieve this, a point count of 1,884 clasts was conducted along the shoreline of Point Betsie Lighthouse Beach using transects 6.6 meters long and set 2 meters apart and a PVC quadrat 49 cm 2 , to document lithological abundance. Representative samples were collected for further evaluation using petrographic microscopy and powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) to assess mineralogy and texture and to confirm lithology.

Glacially derived gravel comprises 30% of the assemblage compared to 68% of local carbonates. The samples range in size from fine pebbles to large cobbles, with very coarse pebbles (32%) and small cobbles (25%) comprising the dominant Wentworth sizes. The gravel at location 1 is: 39% sedimentary; 60% metamorphic; and 1% igneous. Location 2 is: 76% sedimentary; 21% metamorphic; and 4% igneous. Location 3 is: 81% sedimentary; 16% metamorphic; and 3% igneous. Location 4 is: 69% sedimentary; 27% metamorphic; and 3% igneous. Preliminary PXRD analyses have identified mineralogy that is consistent with the lithologic classifications made during the field study. The presence of albite and quartz in a graphic gneiss; quartz, orthoclase, albite, biotite, and chlorite in a tonalitic gneiss; and hornblende, orthoclase, and quartz in a sample of migmatite. The source for the gravel is predominantly local carbonate. Glacially derived gravel is mainly derived from metamorphic terranes. Metamorphic grains are mostly migmatites and metabasalts. Further petrographic and mineralogical data will be compared with published studies to identify potential source terranes and to reconstruct their glacial transport history.

abstract: The Goodwin Creek Experimental Watershed (GCEW) is one of the original USDA Agricultural Research Service Watershed Assessment Studies Benchmark watersheds. Located in the loess-mantled uplands of north-central Mississippi, this 2,100-ha watershed was chosen for its mixed land use, active upland erosion, and steep degrading channels with unstable banks. The watershed is a headwater tributary of the Yazoo River, which ultimately flows into the Mississippi River. Surface and internal soil erosion are common in GCEW due to loess soils, high ground-surface slopes (>10%), and focused subsurface flow. To complement ongoing research focusing on surface and in-stream hydrology that began in 1981, a groundwater research component was added. A multidisciplinary approach is being applied to define the spatiotemporal variability of surface-subsurface water fluxes along a transect covering a hillside pasture adjoining a flat, riparian, non-irrigated, row-crop field. The groundwater research site consists of a 0.5-km transect of five wells installed in 2024 in the surficial aquifer. Standard penetration tests (14-46 m deep) were conducted at each well. To guide well placement, an electrical resistivity tomography survey was conducted in 2022, showing a continuous aquifer underlying the creek, row-crop field, and pasture. The aquifer comprises 8-21 m of sand and gravel but averages only 6 m in saturated thickness. An integrated Remote Sensing/GIS–Analytical Hierarchy Process approach was applied to develop a recharge potential model, combining a depth-to-water-table map and surface layers (slope, elevation, soil type, land use/land cover, vegetation index, drainage density, flow accumulation, and rainfall) created from satellite images, field measurements, and existing national databases. Validation results are within 6-10% of baseflow estimates, with the model showing about one quarter of the watershed has high recharge potential and two thirds with moderate recharge. In GCEW, however, recharge potential does not equate to aquifer recharge, where baseflow is supported by interflow facilitated by the loess and underlying Pleistocene sand and gravel terrace deposits. The water table is 1-2 m below the creek bed and slopes outward, suggesting the creek is an important source of aquifer recharge. Future work includes installing sensors to monitor groundwater levels, soil moisture, and temporal dynamics of subsurface fluxes. Research supports assessment of conservation practices to improve the long-term productivity of U.S. rainfed agricultural lands and advance the prosperity of rural communities.

title: Students’ Perceptions of the Practice of Dispositions in Geoscience Courses
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Viskupic, Karen [1], Egger, Anne Elizabeth [2]
affiliations: (1) Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
(2) Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
abstract:
Dispositions such as collaboration, desire to learn, and flexibility are as important to geoscience employers as technical geoscience skills when hiring entry-level employees. The development and recognition of dispositions is therefore important for geoscience students. Geoscience faculty report using a variety of strategies in their courses to help students develop dispositions identified as critical for success in the geoscience workforce (attention to detail, collaboration, desire to learn, flexibility, initiative, integrity, organization, positive attitude, professionalism, work ethic). Surveyed faculty most frequently report intentionally asking students to practice collaboration, attention to detail, and organization, with faculty teaching upper-level courses (numbered 300 and 400) reporting more intentional practice of all dispositions than faculty teaching lower-level courses (numbered 100 and 200).

Geoscience graduates seeking employment will need to recognize where and how they have developed dispositions so that they can demonstrate them. We surveyed undergraduate students enrolled in geoscience courses during two semesters at a single institution, and asked them if they were provided opportunities to develop any dispositions. Students completed the survey for a specific course and could select all that applied from a list of dispositions. Students’ responses to the survey were compared with faculty responses for the same courses. Paired responses were available for 6 lower-level and 8 upper-level courses. The number of student responses for individual classes ranged from 1 to 16. Multiple student responses for a course were collapsed into a single value: if more than 50% of student respondents reported having opportunities to practice a disposition then we report that the disposition was practiced in that course as recognized by students.

In upper-level courses, students most frequently report having opportunities to practice collaboration, organization, and attention to detail, but overall report fewer opportunities to practice all dispositions than faculty report for the same courses, with the exception of organization and initiative. These preliminary results suggest that students in upper-level courses do not recognize all of the ways they are practicing and developing dispositions, which may hinder their competitiveness when entering the workforce. In addition, upper-level students report few opportunities to practice flexibility and initiative, which are highly valued by geoscience employers.

title: Pelona schist deformation adjacent to the San Andreas fault: Insights from Badger Hill and the Shandin Hills, San Bernardino, California
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Pimentel, Diana [1], Bidgoli, Tandis S. [2], Rannis, Matthew Dean [3], Valencia, Ashley Juliet [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, California, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, CA, USA
(3) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, CA, USA
(4) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, San Bernardino, California, USA
abstract:
The Pelona-Orocopia-Rand (POR) schist is a Late Cretaceous–early Tertiary metamorphic rock assemblage distributed through southern California and parts of southern Arizona and western Nevada. It preserves evidence of subduction-related metamorphism associated with the Laramide Orogeny and the transition of a subduction tectonic boundary to the San Andreas transform boundary system. This study investigates the structural characteristics of POR schist exposed at Badger Hill and a portion of the Shandin Hills in the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains to evaluate competing exhumation models and better constrain its tectonic evolution. Geologic mapping, structural analysis, and petrographic characterization provide the framework for documenting the sequence of deformation preserved within the study area.

At Badger Hill, the Pelona schist is dominantly a muscovite–albite–quartz schist. Field observations indicate that primary bedding, striking ~N30°W, represents the oldest preserved surfaces, S 0, that were subsequently folded into tight to isoclinal folds about S 1 axial planar surfaces oriented approximately parallel to the bedding and dipping ~88° NW. A penetrative foliation, planar surface striking approximately N15°E and dipping 30°-40° SE (mode of 36°), crosscuts the folded bedding and is in turn folded into recumbent folds about S 2 axial planar surface oriented ~N53°E, dipping ~10°. Fracture orientation data (n=454) collected from five 1 m 2 areas across Badger Hill represent the youngest recognized deformation events. Additional broad, low-amplitude folds with axial surfaces striking ~S35°W, with a steep dip of ~85° SE were also noted. Two dominant fracture sets were identified: ~S60°E, dipping ~45° NE and ~N10°E, dipping ~55° NW. The former set parallels the strike of the nearby San Andreas fault, located ~300 m north, whereas the latter is oriented perpendicular to the minimum stress direction associated with the fault, together suggesting a brittle overprint linked to this major structure. These preliminary structural observations establish a relative sequence of at least four deformation events and constrain the exhumation history and tectonic evolution of the POR schist within the San Bernardino Mountain foothills. Thin‑section analysis of samples from Badger Hill and the Shandin Hills is underway to refine lithologic variability, metamorphic mineral assemblages, and deformation microstructures.

title: Quantifying the Trophic Fidelity of Benthic Invertebrate Food Webs
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy
authors: Leung, Rebecca [1], Kowalewski, Michał [2], Tyler, Carrie L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) Florida Museum of Natural History, Invertebrate Paleontology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(3) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
abstract: Due to the ongoing global biodiversity crisis, it is paramount to evaluate how unaltered ecosystems that predate human disturbances functioned. Paleontological records have the potential to provide pristine reference conditions for conservation paleobiology, if they prove reliable at preserving ecosystem structure. As fidelity is often assessed narrowly by using single higher taxonomic groups with strong preservation potential (e.g., mollusks), it remains uncertain to what extent the fossil record accurately preserves diverse food webs. To quantify food web fidelity, here we utilized sympatric surveys of live and dead shallow shelf assemblages of macrobenthic invertebrates from 52 sites in Onslow Bay, North Carolina (USA). Food webs were constructed for: the Living Assemblage (LA), the Death Assemblage (DA), and a theoretical Fossil Assemblage of taxa with a known fossil record (FA). Structural similarity to the LA was assessed using a bootstrapping procedure to sample taxa from the LA and produce 9,999 randomized food webs that maintained observed species richness while preserving the original predator-prey relationships. This created a baseline of ‘perfect fidelity’ to measure taphonomic bias against. Observed food web metrics in the DA and FA were compared to null expectations using standardized effect sizes (Z-scores) and Bonferroni-adjusted significance tests. Across the DA and FA, broad-scale food web properties including connectance, compartmentalization, diameter, and mean total interactions were not significantly different from LA-derived expectations (ɑ = 0.05), suggesting that overall food web architecture was not significantly altered by taphonomic biases despite notable differences in preservation potential across taxa. However, interaction-specific distributions showed significant departures from null expectations. DA and FA exhibited significantly reduced variation in the number of prey per consumer (DA: Z = -7.73, p-adj = 0.004; FA: Z = -10.33, p-adj = 0.001), and strongly elevated variation in the number of predators per resource (DA: Z = 34.36, p-adj = 0.001; FA: Z = 38.25, p-adj = 0.001). These results indicate that taphonomic filtering and preservation biases are unlikely to substantially alter overall food web architecture, but may influence the distribution of species interactions represented in reconstructed ecosystems. This would validate the use of trophic structure and food webs derived from paleontological records to inform modern conservation and ecosystem management.

title: Scientists and Writers in the Same Boat: Exploring Transdisciplinary Science Communication
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part II)
authors: Pinter, Nicholas [1], Ziser, Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, California, USA
(2) Dept. of English, University of California, Davis, CA, USA
abstract:
Since 2002, UC Davis has offered immersive classes and field expeditions along wild and scenic rivers and coastlines from Arctic Alaska to tropical Mexico. These “Ecogeo” capstones include a classroom term followed by 1-2+ weeks of rafting or kayaking that brings cutting-edge research into the field. Some previous trips have trained Ecogeo students in communications, including mentorship with national journalists and science writers. In 2026, we explored a new, more assertively transdisciplinary model.

The 2026 Ecogeo class and trip were small, recruiting 4 PhD-level science students and 4 PhD and MFA student writers. Through the academic term, classes included: (1) lectures on disciplinary fundamentals and current research spanning geology, ecology, oceanography, climate science, etc.; and (2) scientist-writer collaborative writing and workshopping. Four two-week units covered four writing modalities: (1) science journalism, (2) nature writing, (3) science fiction, and (4) science writing for public policy. Each science student-writer pairing was different, and many of the assignments and pairings pushed students outside their comfort zones. Guidance came from the classroom instructors (Geology, English) and from guest experts in each writing modality.

This fusion of graduate-level writing and science was steered towards the annual Ecogeo expedition, which in 2026 was sea kayaking in the San Juan Archipelago of the Salish Sea, Pacific Northwest USA. All Ecogeo expeditions are famously experiential, bringing cutting-edge field science into the landscapes that inspire and inform it. In 2026, days included lectures on management challenges in the Salish Sea (e.g., post-glacial geodynamics, marine mammal conservation, water supply, climate change), and evenings included discussions about effective science communications, guided journaling, and even one evening of student-led poetry writing. As with most field expeditions, the experience pushed students: physically, intellectually, and creatively. Writing students reported that the capstone activities gave them a deeper of how scientific knowledge is developed and applied; the science students reported that they had never before engaged so deeply with the craft of communicating research and scientific context.

title: Simultaneous Determination of Germanium, Tin and Bismuth from Mine-waste by Hydride Generation ICP-MS

authors: Arslan, Zikri [1], Berry, Cyrus [2]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, Crustal geophysics & Geochem Sci Ctr, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, CICT, Denver, CO, USA
abstract: Hydride generation (HG) is a unique – analyte separation and sample introduction method for determination of hydride forming elements, such as bismuth (Bi), germanium (Ge) and tin (Sn). HG coupled to ICP-MS multielement detector offers tremendous sensitivity for ultra trace detection and determination of Bi, Ge, and Sn from very complex samples like mine-waste, without exposing ICP-MS instrument to elevated levels of unwanted matrix elements. In this work, a multi-element HG approach is developed for determination of Bi, Ge and Se by ICP-MS. A double-pass perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) double-pass spray chamber equipped with a Teflon nebulizer was used as a gas-liquid/separator. Gaseous hydrides were transported to an argon plasma via nebulizer argon gas. Rhodium was used as internal standard (IS) and IS solution aspirated via the nebulizer to correct instrumental sensitivity changes. Hydride generation conditions were examined by reacting 10 µg/L multi-element solution in hydrochloric acid (HCl) and nitric acid (HNO 3 ) and sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ) solutions with sodium borohydride (NaBH 4 ). HCl provided comparatively higher sensitivity and broader acidity range for Bi, Ge and Sn. Optimum HCl concentration was around 4% (v/v). Substantial carryover was observed for all elements. Various solutions of HCl, HNO 3 and combination of HCl and hydrofluoric acid (HF) or HNO 3 -HF were used as a carrier and washout solution. A solution of 2% (v/v) HCl and 0.5% (v/v) HF effectively removed the carry-over. A solution of 1% (m/v) potassium iodide (KI), potassium cyanide (KCN) and potassium ferricyanide (K 3 Fe(CN) 6 ) were examined as additives to alleviate transition metal interferences. KCN and K 3 Fe(CN) 6 were effective. Severe suppression on Bi and Sn hydride generation occurred from 1 µg/mL iron (Fe), copper (Cu) and nickel (Ni) in KCN medium. These interferences were eliminated using combined KCN + K 3 Fe(CN) 6 solution. A concentration of 1% (m/v) NaBH 4 was found optimum for multi-element hydride generation. Compared to solution nebulization, sensitivity was enhanced by factor of 50 to 150. The performance of the method will be presented for analysis of different standard reference materials (Hard Rock Mine Waste, SRM 2780 and bullet lead, C2416) by HG-ICP-MS for Bi, Ge, and Sn.

title: The Interpretation of Simultaneously Entrapped Quartz and Zircon Inclusions in Garnet for Elastic Thermobarometry: A Case Study from the Harcuvar Complex

authors: Gonzalez, Joseph P. [1], Walsh, Emily O. [2], Campomenosi, Nicola [3], Koch, Megan M. [4], Singleton, John [5], Wong, Martin S. [6]
affiliations: (1) Research and Collections, New York State Museum, Albany, NY, USA

abstract: The application of elastic models to inclusions with differing mineralogy entrapped in the same host mineral can yield thermobarometric constraints that are independent of chemical equilibrium. However, recent studies have shown that host-inclusion systems undergo elastic re-equilibration under specific P-T-t-X conditions and therefore must be considered in interpreting elastic thermobarometry datasets. In this study, we evaluated quartz-in-garnet (QuiG) and zircon-in-garnet (ZiG) elastic thermobarometry data in combination with phase diagram modeling and conventional thermobarometry in a metapelite from the Harcuvar metamorphic core complex in Arizona, USA. Phase diagrams and conventional thermobarometry indicate that garnet cores crystallized at 0.91±0.24 GPa and 739±55 °C, mantles at 0.79±0.21 GPa and 796±58 °C, and rims at 0.68±0.27 GPa and 660±69 °C. These P-T conditions were used to calculate the remnant inclusion pressures expected to develop (P inc exp ) in both QuiG and ZiG at each stage of garnet growth. The measured quartz and zircon inclusions are typically contained in garnet cores and have faceted negative crystal shapes. Measured remnant strains and inclusion pressures (P inc meas ) were determined using Raman spectroscopy in conjunction with the phonon-mode Grüneisen tensors of quartz and zircon. QuiG P inc meas values have an average of 0.07±0.06 GPa (1σ st.dev) and best agree with the P inc exp values from the garnet rim P-T conditions (-0.026 GPa). ZiG, however, has an average P inc meas value of 0.56±0.14 GPa and is lower than all the P inc exp values. Therefore, the P-T indicated by the intersection of QuiG and ZiG elastic equilibration curves (i.e., isomekes) is lower than those obtained from all other methods. This indicates that the remnant strains and stresses in QuiG and/or ZiG continued to re-equilibrate after garnet growth due to an external process that facilitated strain resetting at lower P-T conditions. Based on petrologic observations of the host garnets and consideration of garnet flow laws, we propose that ZiG underwent nonelastic resetting due to interaction with a metamorphic fluid after garnet growth. Therefore, the apparent intersection of QuiG and ZiG isomekes cannot be unequivocably interpreted as the P-T conditions of final elastic equilibration of both host-inclusion systems. This shows that it is important to consider the effects of the post-entrapment metamorphic history and decoupled elastic re-equilibration when interpreting elastic thermobarometric data from host-inclusion systems.

abstract: Accurate measurement of personal PM2.5 exposure is essential for understanding the health impacts of household air pollution. The GRAPHS (Ghana Randomized Air Pollution and Health Study) team uses personal air monitors to measure PM2.5 exposures among mothers and children. However, GRAPHS identified large particles (>> 2.5 µm) sporadically bypassing the size-selective cyclone inlet of UPAS v2+ monitors (Access Sensor Technologies) and accumulating on filters, biasing gravimetric PM2.5 measurements by median factors of 2-3. Field evaluations were conducted in Ghana to assess the effectiveness of several types of manufacturer-designed, precyclonic impactor inserts intended to improve removal of particles >2.5µm. Ninety-one mothers and children each wore two collocated monitors for 24–48 hours: one with the original cyclone-only inlet and the other with an updated impactor insert plus cyclone. These paired deployments addressed two questions: (1) whether precyclonic inserts eliminated large-particle breakthrough and (2) does the large particle composition inform the cause of the breakthrough or allow for a correction factor for the biased filters. Close visual inspections of the filters and inlets were performed in Ghana, leading to subsequent insert improvements and use of silicone grease. Monitors with precyclonic impactors collected one-half to one-third of the gravimetric mass measured on collocated cyclone-only monitors. Differences in elemental concentrations measured by energy dispersive XRF on collocated filters were used to estimate large breakthrough particle composition, while filters from units with later impactor inserts characterized PM2.5 composition. K&Cl and Si&Fe were strongly correlated and served as tracers for biomass combustion and crustal material, respectively. Assuming each pair of collocated monitors sampled the same PM2.5, elemental concentrations from the insert filter were subtracted from those of the collocated cyclone-only monitor to estimate large particle composition. Biomass tracer elements exhibited similar elemental ratios in large and fine particles but had lower concentrations in breakthrough particles, whereas crustal elements showed similar ratios and concentrations, indicating large breakthrough particles were dominated by crustal material and had a smaller biomass contribution than that measured in the PM2.5 fraction. Consequently, XRF analyses indicate there is nothing special about the large breakthrough particles nor suggest a correction method. Importantly, precyclonic impactors appear to largely eliminate large-particle breakthrough thereby preserving gravimetric PM2.5 measurements. Additional testing is ongoing.

title: Variability and Scale-Dependence in Molecular Evolution Rate Impacts Interpretation of Eukaryotic Evolutionary Histories
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology
authors: Tamre, Erik [1], Nelson, Lyle Lee [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract:
Molecular evolution is often modeled as proceeding at consistent rates over time, with some deviations accommodated by relaxed molecular clock models. Here, we quantify the full extent of variability in branch-specific substitution rates across eukaryotic phylogenies where divergence times are relatively well calibrated by fossil constraints, so that substitution rates can be independently measured. Our results reflect that punctuated change at the molecular level underlies evolution at the morphological level, where punctuated dynamics are more commonly recognized.

Further, we show how inferred substitution rates decrease systematically when measured across increasing time intervals. This scale-dependence persists over timescales of up to a billion years and across alternative clock models, calibration strategies, and prior assumptions, but disappears in simulated data evolved under a constant rate – suggesting that the phenomenon likely arises from time-varying substitution rates and reflects genuine properties of evolutionary histories rather than model artifacts. The observed pattern is analogous to the Sadler effect in sedimentary geology, where time-averaged rates decline with increasing measurement interval because sedimentation is episodic, with longer hiatuses occurring less frequently. We show how the scale-dependent bias in molecular evolution is not captured in current molecular clock models and significantly impacts inferences of evolutionary history, such as estimating the age of Metazoa and understanding the timing and nature of the Cambrian Explosion.

title: Hack’s Law-like Scaling Relations in the Channel Network of River Deltas
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Dong, Tian Yang [1], Vulis, Lawrence [2], Ma, Hongbo [3], Tejedor, Alejandro [4], Goudge, Timothy Andrew [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environmental, and Marine Sciences, University of Texas Rio Grande Valey, Edinburg, TX, USA
(2) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA

(4) Institute for Biocomputation and Physics of Complex Systems, University of Zaragoza, Zaragoza, Spain; Department of Theoretical Physics, University of Zaragoza, Zaragoza, Spain

abstract: River deltas create and sustain land by channeling water and sediment through branched networks. However, how the arrangement of distributary channels relates to the area of land they build remains not well understood. Drawing inspiration from Hack’s law in tributary systems, we explore whether a similar link exists between the length of distributary channels and the land area they support, known as the nourishment area, which acts as the land-building equivalent of the drainage area. Analyzing a global dataset of these networks reveals that channel length and nourishment area follow a scaling pattern very similar to tributary systems. Nonetheless, two different local behaviors are observed: Uniform Delta Networks maintain a consistent Hack-like relationship across scales, while Composite Delta Networks show a scale break, shifting from space-filling near the delta's source to nearly linear growth toward the coast. These patterns indicate that similar overall scaling can originate from various local growth processes and spatial organizations. In summary, the findings demonstrate that deltaic land formation exhibits both global regularity and local variability in its organization.

title: Defining the Ecomorphology of Enigmatic Cambrian Animals: The Swimming Habits of Vetulicolians
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Mendoza Maya, Ana Karen [1], Nanglu, Karma K [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Riverside, Riverside, California, USA
abstract:
Vetulicolians are a perplexing group of Cambrian organisms that inhabited the oceans for only approximately 20 million years. They are characterized by a bipartite body plan consisting of a barrel-shaped anterior section that bears a series of circular to rhomboidal openings along the lateral midline, and an elongated, segmented, tail. This unique body plan has led researchers to assign them to groups ranging from arthropods, to early deuterostomes, to stem-vertebrates. What has received relatively little attention, however, is the ecological diversity of this group. Their laterally compressed body along with their laterally flexing tail somewhat resembles the body plan of modern fishes, suggesting a swimming lifestyle. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether vetulicolians were active swimmers, or whether they occupied benthic, nektobenthic, or pelagic habitats.

In this study, we address these questions using a combination of morphometric approaches. First, we use geometric morphometrics to quantify shape variation in both the anterior body region and the posterior tail region. The results of our principal components analysis (PCA) suggest that in the anterior region, most of the variation in shape centers around the relative elongation of the antero-posterior axis, with a substantial amount of additional variation being related to the margin of attachment between the tail and the anterior. Variation in tail morphology is primarily divided between leaf-shaped tails which are widest at the mid-point, and thinner tails. We further investigated these results using linear morphometrics. This allowed us to increase the sample size of our dataset, and draw more explicit comparisons with extant fish morphometrics. Preliminary results suggest that, when using the same metrics that summarize fish ecomorphology, a combination of factors describing how streamlined the body is and total surface area of the caudal fin are the primary axes of variation.

In total, our results lead to two primary conclusions. First, there is considerable variation among vetulicolians in their morphology when we explicitly analyzed metrics related to swimming efficiency in fish. Second, these preliminary analyses suggest that the main differentiation is between stream-lined morphologies designed for rapid movement, and deeper shapes better designed for maneuverability.

title: Rough Around the Edges: Neotectonic Investigations Along the Margins of the Basin and Range Province
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Lifton, Zachery M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Idaho Geological Survey, Boise, ID, USA
abstract: Neotectonic investigations in the Walker Lane and central Idaho illustrate that active faulting along the edges of the Basin and Range Province (BRP) is more complex than simple extensional normal faulting. On the western edge of the BRP, the Walker Lane accommodates dextral transtension between east-west extension of the Basin and Range and northwest-directed shear of the North America-Pacific plate boundary. Geomorphic mapping, cosmogenic nuclide geochronology, and GNSS surveying along the White Mountains and Lone Mountain faults reveal a complex zone of strain transfer that varies in space and time. Distributed deformation across multiple faults obscured within basin-fill sediment likely accounts for a significant portion of the total slip budget and could result in underestimation of seismic sources during hazard assessment. At the BRP’s northern edge in central Idaho, active normal faults including the Sawtooth and Lost River faults accommodate northeast-southwest extension. Geomorphic mapping, paleoseismic trenching, geochronology, microseismicity, and InSAR analysis suggest that active faults along this margin of the BRP are truncated by the now-inactive Eocene trans-Challis fault system (TCFS). The 2020 Mw6.5 Stanley earthquake occurred near the intersection of the TCFS and the Sawtooth fault, but on a pair of blind faults with opposite dip direction and different sense of motion than the Sawtooth fault. This suggests that easily identifiable surface fault traces may not predict all earthquake sources, and moderate earthquakes can happen on unknown faults. Together, these results demonstrate that while the BRP accommodates simple extension, its margins become more complex zones of strain accommodation and release as they interact with existing crustal structure and tectonic boundaries.
