title: Climate-Driven Weathering Controls Lead Bioaccessibility Through Mineralogical Transformation in Legacy Mine Tailings
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part I)
authors: Root, Robert A. [1], Alghzawi, Ma'in Zaid [2], De Gracia , Xenia Medina [3], Chorover, Jon [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Science, The University of Arizona, TUCSON, AZ, USA
(2) Department of Environmental Science, The University of Arizona, TUCSON, AZ, USA
(3) Department of Environmental Science, The University of Arizona, TUCSON, AZ, USA
(4) Department of Environmental Science, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract:
Legacy polymetallic mine tailings are major sources of Pb-bearing particulate matter (PM), yet risk assessments still rely largely on total Pb concentrations, overlooking how mineralogy and speciation govern Pb mobility and bioaccessibility. We hypothesize that climate-driven weathering fundamentally alters Pb speciation and, in turn, Pb bioaccessibility and human exposure potential. To test this, we isolated particulate matter from tailings collected at 10-cm depth increments to 2 m in twelve 50- to 100-year-old polymetallic sulfide mine tailings piles spanning a climate gradient from the arid deserts of Arizona to the humid temperate forests of Oregon. Each profile was characterized across the vertical oxidative weathering front using total elemental concentrations, mass-transfer coefficients (τ) to quantify geochemical enrichment and depletion, two-stage in vitro gastric bioaccessibility (IVBA), and Pb and Fe speciation by synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) before and after IVBA extraction.

Weathering intensity varied systematically with climate, producing distinct vertical weathering profiles. Surface tailings consistently exhibited the lowest Pb bioaccessibility, whereas the parent material generally exhibited the highest values. Mass-transfer coefficients (τ) quantified climate-dependent redistribution of Pb, with chemically enriched (τ max ) horizons developing within the oxidative weathering profile. Although Pb was enriched within these horizons relative to the parent material, enrichment alone did not predict bioaccessibility. Instead, Pb bioaccessibility within the τ max horizons varied with climate, remaining below that of the parent material at humid to intermediate sites but increasing to match or exceed parent material values at the driest sites. Synchrotron XAS revealed transformation of primary Fe- and Pb-bearing minerals to secondary weathering products, with increasing incorporation of Pb into jarosite-group minerals corresponding to progressively lower Pb bioaccessibility. Tailings with pH <4 exhibited negligible Pb bioaccessibility, indicating that Pb incorporated into acid-stable secondary weathering phases is highly resistant to gastric dissolution.

Together, these results demonstrate that climate controls Pb bioaccessibility by driving mineralogical evolution during weathering, which in turn alters Pb speciation. Molecular Pb speciation, rather than total Pb concentration, is the primary control on bioaccessibility across weathered mine tailings. These findings provide a mechanistic framework linking climate, weathering, mineral transformation, and Pb bioaccessibility, with direct implications for risk assessment and remediation of legacy mining districts.

title: Lack of Standardize Process Hampers Establishment of Post Fire, Early-warning Stream and Rain Gage Networks
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies (Posters)
authors: Tillery, Anne C. [1], Rowden, Katherine L [2], Abshire, Kate [3]
affiliations: (1) USGS, United States Geological Survey, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) US Army Corps of Engineers, National Silver Jackets Program, Spokane, Washington, USA
(3) National Weather Service, Office of Water Prediction, Silver Spring, MD, USA
abstract: The combination of increasing fire severity, community vulnerability, and shifting precipitation patterns is amplifying post-fire hazards across the nation. Where there is a risk of post-wildfire flooding and debris flows, a robust and responsive early warning system is critical to effectively mitigate threats to life and property. The remote or mountainous terrain of many wildfire locations frequently contributes to spotty or absent radar detection of precipitation, hindering accurate and timely early flood warnings. Real-time observations from strategically placed stream and rain gages are therefore essential for early warning as they dramatically improve prediction of these post-fire hazards, giving emergency managers, first responders, and the public more time to take action to ensure safety and protect infrastructure. However, there is no standard, streamlined process for communities to quickly obtain, deploy, and maintain post-fire rain and stream gages and associated data. Significant gaps in funding, coordination, and technical capabilities hamper strategic and timely deployment of essential gaging equipment. Case studies are presented for wildfire incidents in 4 western states in which communities followed different paths to establish their early flood-warning stream and rain gage networks. The case studies demonstrate the challenges to communities working within a system that is not designed for the unique set of hazards that follow wildfires in the American west or in wildland-urban interface areas throughout the country. The lack of standardized processes for funding and procuring post-fire gages led to unnecessary delays in gage deployment and, in one case, early termination of a critical early-warning gage.

title: Tarping the Leak: A Flexible Protocol for Measuring Methane from Orphaned Wells
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Washburn, Alex M. [1], Hawksley, Andrew [2], Zierer, Deron [3], Rivers, Monte [4], High, Madison [5]
affiliations: (1) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA

(4) Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA

abstract: Measuring methane emissions from abandoned and orphaned oil and gas wells (OOGWs) is necessary for quantifying emissions mitigated through plugging and for developing criteria to prioritize wells for remediation. However, these measurements are complicated by variations in wellhead configuration, infrastructure condition and size, the number and location of emission points, and site accessibility. Conventional rigid chamber systems can be difficult to transport and may not readily accommodate complex or irregular infrastructure. To address these limitations, the Kentucky Geological Survey developed a tiered measurement protocol in which low-emitting wells may be evaluated using a static chamber paired with a LI-COR LI-7810 methane analyzer, whereas higher-emitting or structurally complex wells are measured using a SEMTECH High Flow 2, either directly at individual leak points or beneath a flexible tarp that collects emissions from multiple sources. This study evaluated the usability of this protocol under simulated well conditions. We hypothesized that tarp-assisted measurements would provide more complete methane recovery and closer agreement with reference release rates than untarped measurements while retaining the portability and adaptability needed for rapid field deployment. Four mock wellheads were constructed to represent an open borehole, a single flow line with multiple leaks, twin leaks 1 ft apart, and twin leaks 3.5 ft apart. Methane was introduced through each configuration at multiple controlled rates using a calibrated mass flow controller, and emissions were measured with and without the tarp. Reference measurements were collected immediately before and after each test by directing the methane flow into the High Flow 2 intake to characterize short-term variability and provide a basis for test-specific normalization. A separate experiment paired the static chamber with the LI-COR LI-7810 to evaluate the lowest release rate tested and compare its performance with the high-flow protocols. Preliminary results from 84 high-flow tests indicate that tarped measurements produced greater methane recovery, less negative bias, and improved repeatability across all simulated well configurations, with the greatest improvements where emissions originated from multiple or spatially distributed leak points. Untarped measurements more frequently failed to capture gas that bypassed the High Flow 2 intake. These results support incorporating a tarp into a portable and adaptable field protocol for complex or multipoint emissions while retaining the chamber-based approach as a complementary method for very low emission rates.

title: Reading Ancient Thermometers: Evidence for Extreme Late Permian Hothouse from Halite Fluid Inclusions
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Graham, Kathryn Grace [1], Lowenstein, Tim [2], Arnuk, William Donald [3], Guillerm, Emmanuel [4], Krüger, Yves [5], Meckler, Anna Nele [6], García-Veigas, Javier [7], Gibert, Luis [8], Lepchitz, Zachary [9], Powers, Dennis [10]

abstract:
The Late Permian was marked by the development of extensive marginal marine evaporite basins across Pangea and rapid climate warming immediately preceding and after the end Permian mass extinction. The Delaware Basin of New Mexico and Texas preserves thick halite sequences deposited during the Ochoan Series (~252 Ma), and the Polish Zechstein Formation of the European Permian Basin contains similar aged sequences of halite. Together, these deposits offer an opportunity to reconstruct paleoclimate during evaporite deposition on opposite sides of Pangea before Earth’s most severe mass extinction. Here, we use nucleation-assisted microthermometry on fluid inclusions in halite from both basins to constrain paleotemperatures.

Fluid inclusions trapped in primary halite preserve ancient brines that record the temperatures of crystal growth. We analyzed more than 2,000 fluid inclusions from Delaware Basin and Zechstein halite using a femtosecond laser to nucleate vapor bubbles and subsequently measuring homogenization temperatures. Petrographic characterization differentiated primary chevron halite from secondary recrystallized material and established the depositional setting of each sample.

In the lowermost Delaware Basin evaporites (Castile and lower Salado Formations), homogenization temperatures show narrow ranges (~10°C) with average temperatures near 25°C, which we interpret as having formed in deeper brines. Halite from the overlying Rustler Formation exhibits broader temperature ranges (~20°C) and higher average temperatures (25-35°C) that record diurnal temperature swings, indicating progressive basin shallowing and hothouse climate. Diurnal variation is especially clear when temperatures are mapped along crystal growth axes. The Polish Zechstein also records temperatures as high as 40°C, and even reaches 50°C during two intervals that coincide with a shift to Ca-rich brine chemistry. This suggests air temperatures may have exceeded 50°C during halite formation, consistent with extreme warmth during the Late Permian. A shift from SO 4 -rich to Ca-rich brine chemistry also occurs at the base of the Rustler Formation within the Delaware Basin, suggesting the two basins underwent similar chemical and temperature changes.

By comparing our results with modern analogs and existing paleoclimate reconstructions, we can evaluate the link between evaporite deposition and hothouse Late Permian climate. This study provides new quantitative paleotemperature constraints from Late Permian halite, documents episodes of extreme heat preceding the end-Permian mass extinction, and demonstrates that halite fluid inclusions are a valuable archive for reconstructing ancient climate.

title: Assessing Lithium Potential from the Fish Canyon Tuff, Mineral County near Creede, Colorado
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Smith, Craig [1], Leatherman, Mark [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Natural Sciences, Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, CO, USA
(2) Department of Natural Sciences, Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, CO, USA
abstract:
Does the size of volcanic eruptions correlate with higher deposits of lithium (Li)? Roughly 28 Ma ago, one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions—an 8 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) — occurred in the present-day La Garita Caldera in Mineral County near Creede, Colorado, to produce the Fish Canyon Tuff (FCT). The FCT is composed of layers of rhyolite, dacite, andesite & welded tuff. These rock types from similar eruption styles in intracontinental settings are known to carry Li, which is critically important since the rapid global transition to clean energy (i.e., electric vehicles & battery storage) has increased demand, necessitating the development of unconventional resources. This research is inspired by the recent discovery of the Li-rich deposit in the 19-16 Ma McDermitt Caldera (MDC), located on the Nevada-Oregon border. This deposit is estimated to contain between 20-40 metric tons of Li worth approximately $1.5 trillion in today’s market. This research attempted to mimic the naturally occurring leeching of lithium from FCT rocks with two separate tests with different acids from a volcanic environment, HCl & H 2 SO 4 .

The samples were crushed & digested using HF to break down silicates. Initial Li content was found using an Inductively Coupled Plasma - Optical Light Spectrometer (ICP-OES). The FCT andesite had the highest concentration at 0.176 mg/L. THE FCT dacite sample was next at 0.091 mg/L, while the FCT vitrophyre sample was lowest at 0.038 mg/L. The concentrations are tens of thousands of times smaller concentration than found at MDC. After placing the samples in acid-baths & testing again with the ICP-OES, HCl-bathed andesite extracted the highest Li content at 51.203 µg/L. The same rock sample with H 2 SO 4 bath yielded a 31.062 µg/L Li content. The dacite sample had the second highest Li yield with its HCl bath yielding 32.516 µg/L. Vitrophyre samples yielded the least Li content at an average of 8.810 µg/L. The depositional environment of the La Garita Caldera is drastically different than the MDC & drainage is a prominent factor. The limited Li potential at La Garita Caldera is most likely due to heavier weathering and erosion from superior drainage channels, lacking the more stagnant, evaporative environment of the MDC despite its high overall eruptive volume.

abstract:
With accelerated ice mass loss in West Antarctica, recent research has centered on areas adjacent to the rapidly receding Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers. Cranton Bay, a small bay located within the Pine Island Bay Polynya, is a newly explored and understudied area within the larger Amundsen Sea Embayment (ASE). Cranton Bay deglaciated by the Early Holocene and today is characterized by the highest levels of biological productivity of the ASE, even considering the productivity typical of polynyas offshore.

Here we compare multiproxy data from marine sediment cores NBP19-02 KC27 and NBP20-02 JGC74 (the latter was recovered from the same site as the previously published core NBP20-02 KC72), which had been retrieved from Cranton Bay during expeditions by the Thwaites Offshore Research Team of the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration. To identify blooms in primary productivity and their potential triggers, we analyzed the composition and structural features of the sediment cores using Computed Tomography scans, magnetic susceptibility data, stable nitrogen and carbon isotopes of the bulk sediments, Total Organic Carbon (TOC) and Total Nitrogen contents, benthic foraminifera assemblages, grain size distributions, and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) scanner data.

2 radiocarbon ages obtained from calcareous benthic foraminifera near the base of KC27 indicate that the northeastern part of the bay deglaciated by ca. 9.6 14 C kiloyears Before Present (ka BP, uncorrected). XRF data show variable Fe/K, Ca/Ti, and Si/Ti ratios in the early Holocene, followed by a spike in Ca/Ti ratios in the mid Holocene. Late Holocene-age sediments include up to 1.0 wt% of TOC, more negative sediment δ 13 C ratios, consistent presence of benthic foraminifera, and increased diatom abundance, supporting higher biological productivity in Cranton Bay during the Late Holocene. Ongoing analysis of XRF data alongside laser particle size distributions should reveal more detailed environmental information, allowing us to test whether increased iron supply by icebergs or meltwater plumes were the main initiator of productivity in Cranton Bay. Uncovering the drivers of such patterns and changes in biological productivity will be critical to predicting how accelerating deglaciation may impact the global carbon cycle and Antarctic marine ecosystems.

abstract:
Late Cretaceous atmospheric-ocean system global perturbations related to magmatic pulses and activity of Large Igneous Provinces resulted in massive carbon release, intensified hydrological cycles, and enhanced nutrient input to marine ecosystems. These global changes together with rapid sea level rise, triggered episodes of widespread marine oxygen depletion, the Oceanic Anoxic Events (OAEs). Cenomanian-Coniacian interval encompasses major ecological disruptions associated with OAE2 and subsequent recovery of ecosystems. These processes affected planktic communities, causing extinction of specialized taxa, temporary declines of groups, proliferation of opportunistic species, and later diversification of more specialized forms. In Mexico, studies of effects of these environmental perturbations on planktic microfossils are scarce.

Study of the stratigraphic successions of two subsurface cores, IRME-1 and IRME-2, from the Burro-Peyotes Peninsula and the Sabinas Basin, northeastern Mexico, documents paleoenvironments, changes in microfossil abundance, and succession of bioevents throughout Cenomanian-Coniacian, constrained by planktic foraminiferal biostratigraphy.

Both cores encompass the Buda Limestone and the Eagle Ford Formation. Buda Limestone consists of light grey bioturbated limestone containing abundant calcispheres and radiolarians, and scarce planktic foraminifera. Overlying Eagle Ford Formation is composed of organic-rich laminated mudstone and marlstone interbedded with limestone and bentonites, containing abundant planktic foraminifera spanning the interval from Rotalipora cushmani to Dicarinella concavata Zones .

Microfacies and microfossil assemblages indicate progressive deepening from outer-shelf to bathyal during late Cenomanian. The Burro-Peyotes Peninsula records deposition above storm wave base, whereas the Sabinas Basin represents a deeper setting below storm wave base. Abundant calcispheres and planktic foraminifera dominated by intermediate and mixed-layer dwellers in the base of the succession, indicate mesotrophic-eutrophic conditions and a weakly developed thermocline. Although thermocline dwellers remain scarce throughout the successions, their slight increase toward the top of the Eagle Ford Formation, indicate modest strengthening of water-column stratification. Also, filament events were identified within Rotalipora cushmani , Whiteinella archaeocretacea, Marginotruncana schneegansi and Dicarinella concavata Zones.

Across Cenomanian-Turonian the ‘ Heterohelix shift’ is recorded in the top of Rotalipora cushmani Zone. In the Sabinas Basin, this bioevent is preceded by radiolarians blooms and followed by a filament event apparently correlatable with the global basal Turonian event.

Succession of radiolarian blooms, ‘ Heterohelix shift’, and filament events in the Sabinas Basin, resemble patterns from OAE2 successions worldwide, highlighting the regional expression of global paleoceanographic perturbations in northeastern Mexico.

title: The Forearc Record of Late Jurassic to Mid-Cretaceous Tectonics of the Central North American Cordillera
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Surpless, Kathleen DeGraaff [1], Orme, Devon A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT,
abstract: High-resolution mantle tomography as well as increased recognition that changing relative plate motions influence the timing, locus, and style of upper-plate deformation have led to renewed debate about the Jurassic-Cretaceous development of the central segment of the North American Cordillera. Strata of the Upper Jurassic Galice and Mariposa Formations, the Upper Jurassic to Cretaceous Great Valley Group (GVG), and the Upper Cretaceous Hornbrook Formation and Ochoco Basin form an integrated record of tectonic processes along the margin. Middle to Late Jurassic Farallon slab rollback and associated extension during east-dipping subduction may have generated accommodation space for sedimentation and development of a fringing magmatic arc built on previously accreted terranes, or the Early Jurassic demise of the Mezcalera plate through double-sided subduction led to arc-continent collision and accretion of the western Sierran foothills and perhaps western Klamath terranes by Middle Jurassic time. Establishment of Farallon subduction beneath western North America or a return to a shallower angle of Farallon subduction by 160 Ma led to upper-plate contraction, rapid deposition of turbidites in the Galice and Mariposa basins, and syndepositional thrusting and metamorphism. Rapid northward drift of North America beginning 150 Ma may have led to sinistral transtension in the upper plate and another episode of slab roll-back and trench retreat that shifted magmatism westward. Early Cretaceous transtension along the margin included extensional growth faults in the Great Valley forearc that accommodated displacement of the GVG and underlying Coast Range Ophiolite and the forearc Klamath basement to the northwest, possibly shifting the Klamath block westward relative to the northern Sierran foothills. Rapid westward drift of North America beginning ca. 120 Ma resulted in nearly orthogonal convergence, development of an accretionary margin, and the Cretaceous magmatic flare up in the Sierra Nevada. Upper Cretaceous strata from the GVG, Hornbrook Formation, and Ochoco Basin may have formed a single marginal basin beginning ca. 85 Ma, with subsidence of the Klamath Mountains province, deep-water deposition in the Hornbrook and Ochoco systems, eastward migration of the Late Cretaceous GVG shoreline, an eastward shift in sediment sources, and uplift in the eastern Sierra Nevada and possibly Idaho arc and Lemhi basin in central Idaho. Collectively, these marginal basins provide a record of western North American tectonics from Jurassic through Cretaceous time.

abstract: The southern Appalachians represent a composite orogenic system, recording at least four orogenic events, including the Grenville (1.25-0.90 Ga), Taconic (480-440 Ma), Neoacadian (410-340 Ma), and Alleghanian (330-280 Ma) orogenies. Despite extensive study, the timing, conditions, and spatial extent of metamorphism and subsequent overprinting in the metamorphic “core” of the orogen have remained poorly constrained in parts of this system. This study presents new in situ U-Pb geochronological data from monazite and xenotime collected near the Brindle Creek-Jackson Lake fault in Georgia, to revise petrotectonic models of the Cat Square (CST) and eastern Tugaloo (ETT) terranes of the Inner Piedmont. ETT samples exhibit weak foliation, relict anhedral garnet fragments, and muscovite pseudomorphs after staurolite. Matrix monazites reveal complex chemical zoning; however, U-Pb dates show no systematic correlation with core-rim zoning patterns. WIP samples yield monazite weighted mean ages of 318.6±2 Ma and 322.1±1.1 Ma for cores and rims, respectively. Those samples yield xenotime weighted mean ages of 322.4±4.3 Ma and 313.6±2.7 Ma. Because surrounding units record peak kyanite-staurolite grade metamorphism previously attributed to Neoacadian prograde burial, we provisionally interpret our ETT samples as recording Alleghanian retrogression of a Neoacadian peak assemblage. CST samples from an area previously interpreted as sillimanite grade are characterized by heavily resorbed garnet porphyroblasts aligned with the dominant foliation. Two CST samples yield monazite weighted mean ages of 314.3±1.2 Ma and 302.7±1.1 Ma, interpreted as recording Alleghanian retrograde metamorphism. One sample contains a single xenotime date of 290.8±6.9 Ma and four concordant monazite dates with a weighted mean of 1000±12 Ma, indicating preservation of a detrital Grenville source. A third CST sample yields a monazite weighted mean age of 363.0±2.7 Ma, single concordant monazite outlier date of 311.5±8.1 Ma, and a xenotime weighted mean age of 296.8±5.2 Ma, highlighting preservation of the Neoacadian to Alleghanian metamorphic evolution in a single sample. Combined, these data document a complex polyphase metamorphic history for the ETT and CST in Georgia, consistent with similar findings along strike to the northeast, in North Carolina. Future work will address the spatial extent and conditions of Neoacadian and Alleghanian metamorphism in the ETT and CST of Georgia.

title: The Great Dulling: Climate, Thermal Physiology, and Mass Extinction Explain When and Why Global Communities Homogenize in Deep Time
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Al Aswad, Jood [1], Bazzi, Mohamad [2], Monarrez, Pedro M. [3], Penn, Justin L. [4], Deutsch, Curtis Anthony [5], Payne, Jonathan L. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, ; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA

abstract: Global biotic homogenization is a rare phenomenon in which the world's communities become dominated by the same few abundant species, regardless of how far apart these communities are. However, little is known about what drives global communities to become more similar over time. In this talk, we provide an explanation, anchored in physiology, for the most dramatic example of biotic homogenization, which occurred in the direct aftermath of the end-Permian mass extinction ~252 million years ago. Using a combination of fossil occurrence data, oceanographic modeling of temperature and oxygen change constrained by isotope proxies, and physiological data of tolerances to changes in oceanic oxygen and temperature constrained by experiments on living counterparts, we show that the global spread of survivors tracked their preferred aerobic niches from the equator to the poles. We extend this analysis by examining changes in the compositional similarity (Jaccard index) of communities across the globe for benthic organisms from one age to the next throughout the Phanerozoic. The two ages that show marked increases in Jaccard similarity are the Induan (the age following the end-Permian mass extinction) and the Hirnantian (the age following the first pulse of the Late Ordovician mass extinction). We propose that a combination of aerobic habitat homogenization associated with intense climate change and ecological release following mass extinction explain these unusual moments of global homogenization in deep time.

title: Towards Paleoproteomics from Amber: Experimental Protein Diagenesis in Tree Resin

abstract: The fossil record contains a wealth of paleobiological information about macroscopic organisms – and a select few microorganisms – in the form of body and trace fossils. However, the majority of microbes (including many that drive important biogeochemical processes) do not leave behind informative morphological fossils. For such taxa, molecular fossils can be our best set of clues to the biological past, and proteins are a promising class of molecular fossils – if their molecular diagenesis in various geological contexts were better understood. Amber (fossil tree resin), is one geologically-durable archive that can preserve delicate biological structures, potentially including biopolymers from microbial biomass trapped within. In this project, we developed novel techniques to extract identifiable protein fragments from resin-encased organic matter, and we performed diagenetic laboratory experiments with a range of proteinaceous materials , to clarify the molecular signatures of protein diagenesis in fossil resins. Results indicate that one of the primary polymer components of Hymenaea verrucosa resin is covalently linking in entrapped proteins, potentially providing a molecular diagnostic for ancient protein present in amber at the time of resin hardening.

title: The Relationship Between Environmental Conditions and Exceptional Preservation in the Middle Cambrian Depositional Systems of Montana
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Olson, Hunter C. [1], Monarrez, Pedro M. [2], Sperling, Erik A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA, USA

abstract: The middle Cambrian rocks of southwest and central Montana preserve a diverse assemblage of co-eval environments. These rocks exhibit highly variable fossil preservation, with many sections containing no fossil material, and one locality, Nixon Gulch, hosting rare soft-bodied fossils and better-preserved trilobites. Here we present new stratigraphic context, paired with geochemical redox proxies, Total Organic Carbon (TOC) concentrations, and mineralogical measurements, to reveal how paleoenvironmental conditions relate to the opening of a unique taphonomic window at Nixon Gulch. 12 stratigraphic sections were measured across southwestern and central Montana; 8 sections were sampled for sedimentary geochemistry and mineralogic analysis. The Nixon Gulch fossil horizon was deposited in a depocenter, as indicated by the thickness of the fossiliferous interval relative to the same horizon in adjacent sections. The fossil beds at Nixon Gulch also show elevated TOC concentrations compared to other stratigraphic sections, indicating favorable conditions for greater accumulation or preservation of organic matter. No sections show evidence of redox-sensitive trace-metal enrichments (uranium, molybdenum, vanadium), indicating likely oxic to dysoxic conditions. Moderate CIA (Chemical Index of Alteration) and high ICV (Index of Compositional Variability) values in other stratigraphic sections indicate that sediment sources were weakly weathered and compositionally immature, but the Nixon Gulch fossil horizon has some of the most compositionally mature and heavily weathered sediment, likely indicating increased clay content. Combining these lines of evidence provides a holistic view of the various environments present in the middle Cambrian of Montana and how environmental factors interact to allow for the preservation of soft-bodied fossils.

title: Capturing Critical Elements from Mine-waste using Different Layered Double Hydroxides
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Arslan, Zikri [1], Berry, Cyrus [2]
affiliations: (1) US Geological Survey, Denver, Crustal geophysics & Geochem Sci Ctr, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, CICT, Denver, CO, USA
abstract: Sulfide-based materials possess high affinity toward heavy metal cations and have emerged as efficient scavenging sorbents for soft heavy metal cations (Ag, Au, Pd, Pt, Te). Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are a well-known type of anionic clay consisting of positively charged host layers and ion-exchangeable counter-anions in the interlayers. This class of clay possesses strong intercalation and anion-exchange properties. In this work, two LDH materials (LDH-Sn 2 S 6 and LDH-MoS 4 were prepared by intercalating with soft Lewis basic sulfur species such as S x 2- (x = 2, 4) and MoS 4 2- in the positively charged layers of MgAl–LDH. The sorption performances of these sorbents for capturing critical elements and heavy metal cations were investigated using simulated aqueous waste solutions with a pH range of 3 to 9.5. LDH-Sn 2 S 6 resulted in a strong affinity to gold (Au), platinum (Pt) and palladium (Pd) between a pH of 3 to 4 with sorption efficacy >99%. Silver (Ag) and tellurium (Te) were captured effectively between pH 3 to pH 8.6 (>99%). LDH-MoS 4 showed strong affinity for Au, Pt and Pd (>99%) in acidic pHs (pH 3 to 4). Additionally, iridium (Ir) was effectively recovered between pH 8.5 to 9.5 (>99%). Tellurium was best scavenged between a pH of 5 to 9.5 (>99%). The sorption performances of the sorbents were verified at pH 4 and 8.6 for capturing critical elements from aqueous solutions of Hard Rock Mine Waste standard reference material (SRM 2780a) and mine tailings samples. In mine tailings samples, both LDHs showed strong sorption (> 98%) of Ag, Au, Pd, Pt and Te at both pHs. Iridium sorption was somewhat weak for both SRM and tailings (<50%).

title: The Evolving Significance of Fossil Specimens and Finding Future Value in Old Collections
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Nanglu, Karma [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Riverside, Riverside, California, USA
abstract:
Fossil collections represent a physical, directly observable record of both biotic and abiotic changes that have occurred. As such, they represent an irreplaceable resource for understanding the future trajectory of our planet, and the fundamental underlying structure of nature. However, these collections can sometimes be perceived as relics of an older “era” of research, or curiosities that no longer have direct relevance to cutting edge research programs. In this talk, I will discuss this perception, using specific examples wherein fossil material has found new value with newly available technologies and techniques, or in the context of changing perspectives in science more broadly.

New visualization methods stand out as a particularly impactful suite of techniques for breathing new life into old material. Elemental mapping on carbonaceous compression fossils, such as those found in Cambrian lagerstätte like the Burgess Shale, has been demonstrated to reveal anatomical details far beyond what traditional imaging methods would suggest. Nervous and circulatory systems have been described in several taxa using elemental mapping, and the list is ever-growing. Three dimensional visualization, including micro-computed tomography, is becoming increasingly common and now routinely reveals anatomical details that would have previously been impossible to access. These insights range from uncovering the detailed limbs of early arthropods, to nanometer-scale innervation pathways among early fish.

It is equally important to recognize cutting edge and costly techniques and methods are not necessary for “old” collections to find new value. As the broader scientific landscape changes, re-visiting assumed knowledge drawn from fossil collections is critical. Poignant examples come from the re-description of fossil taxa, particularly among invertebrate groups where our understanding of phylum and class-level relationships often remain unresolved. For these groups, fossils provide an incalculably significant source of information, and re-description of old material can be as significant as new collections.

Fundamentally, what these approaches share in common is an emphasis on the often untapped wellsprings of data that fossil collections represent. Whether it is through the advent of new technologies or thorough re-consideration of our long-held beliefs, we cannot perfectly presage the future value of a fossil collection, which is in and of itself part of their value.

abstract: The Permian-Triassic Great Extinction event left clear stratigraphic markers in its deposits, not only in the fossils but also in geochemical traces. The extinction event is represented in Northern Utah at the boundary between the Permian Park City Formation and the Triassic Dinwoody-Woodside Formation. Our study of conodonts from these strata in Northern Utah plus carbon isotope ratios and trace elements shows that all three of these stratigraphic markers can be used to identify the Great Extinction Event in Northern Utah strata. We have collected samples from sections of this boundary near Salt Lake City for study of conodonts and 13 C/ 12 C isotope ratios and certain trace element excursions shown in the literature. Life’s preference for 12 C over 13 C means there is a 13 C/ 12 C ratio characteristic in marine life. At an extinction event, an abundance of dead marine life settled into the sediment and this 13 C/ 12 C isotope ratio is expected to decrease in the sediment until life is re-established in the ocean. We observed this pattern in our sections. Carbon isotope ratios and certain trace element excursions are thus geochemical stratigraphic markers independent of fossils for recognition of the Permian-Triassic Great Extinction Event in Northern Utah strata.

title: Pliocene Deformation in the Central California Coast Ranges: Thrusting of the Cuesta Ridge Ophiolite Over the Franciscan Complex and Monterey Formation
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Shervais, John W. [1]
affiliations: (1) Utah State University, Logan, UT,
abstract:
The Coast Range Ophiolite (CRO) and Franciscan Complex (JKf) represent a classic forearc basement-subduction accretion assemblage formed during Jurassic subduction along the Cordilleran margin. These rocks are typically juxtaposed along the Coast Range fault, which varies from high-angle reverse or normal faults to low-angle detachment faults in the northern Coast and Diablo Ranges (e.g., Jayko et al, 1987, Tecontics).

Near San Luis Obispo, California, the CRO is represented by the Cuesta Ridge ophiolite, consisting of depleted mantle harzburgite, mafic plutonic rocks, pillow lava, sheet flows, and a mafic volcanic breccia. The mafic plutonic rocks include gabbro, quartz gabbro, and hornblende diorite, cut by late dikes of MORB-like basalt; the volcanic rocks include arc tholeiite and boninite. Overlying the igneous section is a sedimentary breccia containing dacite and rhyolite clasts (similar to the Crowfoot Point breccia), and ash-rich chert. This assemblage resembles CRO rocks found in the northern Coast Ranges. The CRO is overlain by the upper Jurassic-lower Cretaceous Toro formation (GVS), upper Cretaceous Atascadero (GVS), and Oligocene Vaqueros sandstone.

The Franciscan complex near San Luis Obispo comprises a classic “argille scagliose” with a matrix of highly sheared microgreywacke+clay containing blocks of chert, greywacke, and altered oceanic basalts (e.g., Port San Luis), with belts of sheared serpentinite mélange contain blocks of undeformed lherzolite. The Franciscan here is overlain unconformably by Miocene Monterey Formation and a locally exposed sandstone-silt-conglomerate thought to correlate with the Pliocene Pismo Formation. All of these units are overlain unconformably by a submarine fan deposit consisting of breccia derived from the CRO. This submarine fan breccia was formerly interpreted and mapped as landslide deposits from Cuesta Ridge but based on the occurrence of clasts of Monterey Formation near the base of the unit, we interpret it as a molasse deposit eroded off an allochthonous thrust sheet comprising the CRO and overlying formations.

The underlying Franciscan is missing Cretaceous through Eocene sediment, unlike the overlying CRO. In contrast, Miocene Monterey Formations is deposited directly onto Franciscan basement. The age of this thrust must be post-Miocene since it places the allochthon over Monterey formation, consistent with late Pliocene to Pleistocene deformation of the Central California Coast Ranges, as documented by Page et al. (1998, GSAB).

title: Rocks on the Move: Long-term Monitoring of Storm Impacts on Coastal Boulder Deposits from San Salvador Island, The Bahamas
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Wheeler, Hanna Teruko [1], Cullen, Eloise [2], Glumac, Bosiljka [3], Curran, H. Allen [4], Dexter, Troy A. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA

(4) Department of Geosciences, Smith College, Northampton, MA, USA
(5) Gerace Research Institute, University of The Bahamas, San Salvador Island, Bahamas
abstract:
Coastal boulder deposits have been monitored since 2012 at two contrasting sites on San Salvador Island, Bahamas: Singer Bar Point (SBP), a low-energy, gently seaward-sloping ramp protected by a reef and lagoon on the north coast; and The Gulf (TG), with 3-5 m cliffs on the high-energy south coast. The initial survey included photographing, describing and GPS locating of 15 large boulders at SBP and 12 at TG, as well as manual profiling of boulder ridges at both sites.

Smaller size and better roundness of SBP boulders indicate their more frequent movement, yet after Hurricane Sandy passed 80 km west of the island as a Cat. 1-2 storm in Oct. 2012, and Hurricane Joaquin made direct landfall as a strong Cat. 3 storm in Oct. 2015, all 15 monitored boulders remained at or near their original locations. In contrast, these storms moved all but one 4-ton boulder at TG. New boulders as large as 3 m in diameter were emplaced on TG cliffs, and 1-3 ton boulders moved up to 25 m inland with Joaquin’s waves. To aid in post-storm analyses, aerial imagery was first implemented in 2016, and >50 boulders and some cobbles were tagged at each site in 2019 using RFID technology. These advances allowed documentation of modifications at SBP by northerly winter storms in the absence of major hurricanes prior to 2025. During that time, TG cliffs remained mainly unaltered, except for post-Joaquin regrowth of vegetation and some sand transport.

Continued monitoring produced digital transects for comparison with 2012 manual profiles, and illustrated a 4-5 m landward movement of the seaward edge of boulder deposits at TG and their conversion by Joaquin’s waves from a sharp-crested ridge to a broad boulder field that covered portions of the coastal road. The monitoring also allowed a comparison with Hurricane Melissa, which in Oct. 2025 as a Cat. 1 storm followed a very similar path across the island to that of Joaquin 10-yrs prior. Melissa’s impacts were similar to Joaquin’s in terms of boulder transport, vegetation damage and coastal road inundation, but less extensive. Such long-term monitoring (2012-2026) provides critical information about vulnerability of coastal areas to storms, but its future is uncertain due to increasing complexities of working in The Bahamas.

title: 1:5,000-Scale Geomorphic Map of Indian Wells Valley, Eastern California: A Framework for Reconstructing Late Pleistocene Landscape Evolution and Spatiotemporal Variations in Fault Slip
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Duncan, Maggie E. [1], Bacon, Steven N. [2]
affiliations: (1) Graduate Program of Hydrologic Sciences, University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA; Division of Hydrologic Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Division of Hydrologic Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
abstract:
Indian Wells Valley (IWV), eastern California, is located along the eastern edge of the southern Sierra Nevada, forming a structurally-complex graben within an active dextral transtensional shear zone. The northern sector of the basin is crossed by four principal faults with late Pleistocene to historical activity: the normal Sierra Nevada frontal fault (SNFF), and the normal-oblique Little Lake (LLF), Airport Lake (ALF) and Paxton Ranch (PRF) faults. IWV is one of the most seismically active basins in eastern California with M4.9, 5.8, and 6.4/7.1 earthquakes occurring in 1982, 1995, and 2019, respectively. Although the basin has experienced repeated late Pleistocene deformation and historical surface rupture, the morphostratigraphic relationships of Quaternary deposits and the magnitude and distribution of faulting remain poorly constrained, limiting quantitative assessment of late Pleistocene tectonic deformation across the basin.

This study presents the first 1:5,000-scale geomorphic and fault map of western Indian Wells Valley, integrating high-resolution (1- and 2-m) digital elevation models, aerial imagery and detailed field mapping to delineate Quaternary alluvial fan, fluvial, and volcanic deposits, as well as fault scarps along a 26-km-long section of the valley extending from the Sierra Nevada range front to China Lake basin. Five alluvial fan units were differentiated and assigned relative ages: Qf1 (old), Qf2 (intermediate), Qf3 (intermediate-young), Qf4 (young), and Qf5 (active). Together with mapping of fault strands along the SNFF, LLF, and ALF, this map establishes a detailed Quaternary stratigraphic framework for western Indian Wells Valley, providing the geologic context for reconstructing late Pleistocene landscape evolution and basin-scale extension.

Ongoing analysis of 10 cosmogenic surface exposure ages from boulders on offset Qf2 and Qf3 fan surfaces will provide the first direct numerical age constraints on fan deposition along the Sierra Nevada range front in the valley. These ages, together with luminescence ages from newly dated shoreline deposits in China Lake basin, existing 10 Be exposure ages from alluvial deposits, and published 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages from basaltic flow rocks, will provide age control for fault scarp analyses of 40 transects across the major fault zones in the basin. The resulting chronology will allow for the first vertical slip rate estimates for the SNFF in IWV, and enable quantitative evaluation of distributed late Pleistocene vertical deformation and analysis of spatial variations in extension rate across IWV.

title: Recurrent Burial and Exhumation of a Laurentian Great Unconformity Surface: (U-Th)/He Thermochronology of the Montreal River Monocline
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Alemu, Tadesse B [1], Guenthner, William [2], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science Department, University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire, Eau Claire, WI, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science & Environmental Change, University of Illinois, Urbana, IL, USA
(3) School of Earth & Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
abstract:
The assembly and breakup of supercontinents are thought to have driven vertical motions of continental interiors that shaped the Great Unconformity, the surface across which Cambrian strata rest on Precambrian basement throughout Laurentia. Whether this surface records Cryogenian glacial erosion, dynamic topography tied to the supercontinent cycle, or diachronous tectonic exhumation remains contested, in part because most thermochronologic studies target crystalline basement lacking independent constraints on its burial history. The Montreal River monocline on the south shore of Lake Superior, a 35-km-thick crustal panel tilted to near-vertical during far-field Grenvillian contraction, is a rare exception: its Archean and Mesoproterozoic rocks are flanked by dated Mesoproterozoic (Oronto Group) and early Neoproterozoic (Jacobsville Formation and Bayfield Group) strata that anchor thermal history models at multiple points.

We present zircon and apatite (U-Th)/He data spanning the monocline's structural levels, synthesized through forward and inverse (Thermochron.jl) thermal history modeling. The results resolve three cycles of burial and exhumation of the basement surface, which we relate to stages of the Rodinia and Pangea supercontinent amalgamation and break-up. The oldest zircon dates cluster at ca. 1050–1000 Ma, recording rapid exhumation during contractional rift inversion in the Ottawan phase of the Grenvillian orogeny and indicating that far-field deformation associated with Rodinia assembly penetrated far into the cratonic interior. Apatite dates require subsequent reburial above 80 °C beneath a Jacobsville–Bayfield basin; preservation of pre-depositional helium in Freda Formation detrital zircon, combined with clumped-isotope reordering constraints from previously studied and dated fault calcite of Hodgin et al. (2024), caps that burial below ~130 °C, corresponding to 2 to 4 km of basin fill. A 688 ± 22 Ma apatite date-eU pediment records ensuing Neoproterozoic exhumation. The most radiation-damaged grains yield consistently Mesozoic zircon dates (230 ± 28 Ma), recording a final cycle of Paleozoic burial and Mesozoic erosion, implying Paleozoic strata once extended well beyond their preserved limits and linking their removal to dynamic uplift of Laurentia within Pangea. This basement surface is therefore a recurrent unconformity assembled across two supercontinent cycles rather than the product of any single erosional event.

abstract: In response to groundwater storage depletion, irrigation pumping restrictions are being implemented in some locations. However, the consequences of these pumping restrictions for groundwater quality are not well known. To help fill this knowledge gap, we examined groundwater quality in and near the Sheridan 6 Local Enhanced Management Area (LEMA) in northwest Kansas. Pumping restrictions within the LEMA were implemented in 2013 to help reduce the depletion of groundwater in the Ogallala Aquifer, with an average pumping reduction of 23.5% within the LEMA relative to a control area nearby. During summer 2026, we sampled 43 wells (domestic, irrigation, and livestock) and analyzed concentrations of major ions and trace elements, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), microplastics, herbicides, non-purgeable organic carbon (NPOC), total nitrogen (TN) as well as concentrations of groundwater age and recharge temperature tracers (sulfur hexafluoride (SF 6 ), 3 He/ 4 He, and noble gases) and water stable isotope ratios. Several analyses are in progress, but initial findings indicate groundwater in the study area is Ca-HCO 3 type with near-neutral pH (avg. 7.34), elevated dissolved oxygen levels and relatively low total dissolved solids (TDS) content (avg. 428 mg/L). Nitrate concentration was below the standard for drinking water in groundwater from all but three wells. Moreover, a preliminary comparison of inorganic chemical concentrations inside vs outside of the LEMA does not reveal significant differences in groundwater composition, indicating that a pumping reduction has not altered groundwater quality at least for the data we have so far. Our ongoing efforts will further test relationships between pumping and water quality by examining additional parameters and evaluating pumping rates on a finer spatial scale using historic pumping data from irrigation wells. We expect that our study findings will help improve management of water quality alongside water quantity in agricultural regions.

title: Zircon based petrogenetic modeling of contemporaneous tholeiitic and calc-alkaline rocks at Króksfjörður, Iceland
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Drager, Lillian [1], Banik, Tenley J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology & The Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(2) Geography, Geology & The Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
abstract: In western Iceland, the extinct Króksfjörður volcano is a complex and enigmatic magmatic system. Rhyolites and dacites with calc-alkaline (CA) and tholeiitic compositions were contemporaneously produced from ~10–12 Ma. Rocks of CA composition are unusual outside of subduction zones, a tectonic setting never experienced in Iceland. Previous petrogenic models (Jónasson et al., 1992; Willbold et al., 2009) discuss the role of partial melting and fractional crystallization of hydrothermally altered crustal basalts in producing deposits with CA and tholeiitic compositions. With a focus on zircon O isotope and trace element data, we reevaluate these models. We collected zircon (n=>100) δ 18 O isotope and trace element (TE) data from three CA and three tholeiitic units at Króksfjörður, then used the model of Claiborne et al. (2018) to model potential parent melt REE compositions. In Króksfjörður zircon, measured Ti values are 5–15ppm and Hf ranges from ~7,500–10,500 ppm in all samples. U/Yb is 0.1–1.0 and Gd/Yb values are 0.07–0.1. Our model parent melt based on the zircon data displays a U/Yb range of 0.5–1.9, with a Gd/Yb of 1.8–2.5. Measured whole rock compositions from which these zircon grains were extracted average U/Yb=0.29 for CA samples and 1.41 for tholeiitic samples. Gd/Yb in CA samples averages 1.5 compared to 2.2 in tholeiitic samples. Thus, the model parent melt largely encompasses the values displayed in the measured whole rock data, which supports the interpretation that the zircon parent melts are broadly represented by the whole rock composition. δ 18 O in Króksfjörður zircon ranges from 1.0–3.5‰ irrespective of CA or tholeiitic affinity, which suggests that some amount of hydrothermally altered material was assimilated into all zircon parent melts. To achieve these values, we conservatively estimate that ~20–40% of the zircon parent melt for both CA and tholeiitic samples results from anatexis of these hydrothermally altered, low- 18 O crustal materials, while the remainder is generated via fractional crystallization of mantle melts. Our results agree with those of Jonasson et al., 1992 regarding genesis of the tholeiitic rhyolites; however, the δ 18 O values and overlapping TE trends between the two groups complicate the interpretation of genesis of CA silicic melts at Króksfjörður.

title: Insights into Mixed-mode Brittle Failure in the Shallow Crust from Experimental Analyses
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Evans, James P. [1], Bauer, Stephen J. [2], Petrie, Elizabeth S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, LOGAN, UT, USA
(2) Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
(3) Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
abstract: Predicting the modes of brittle failure with pore pressures in heterogeneous sedimentary rocks requires analyses of three rock strength parameters in a range of rock types. We determine tensile, cohesive, and shear strengths for clastic and carbonate siltstone, sandstone, and thin-bedded limestones lithologies from the Organ Rock, Entrada, Tununk, and Carmel Formations that represent sealing or low-permeability reservoir rocks. Tensile strengths range from -2 to -11 MPa; calcite-cemented siltstone and sandstones are lowest, calcite-cemented mudstone and sandstone have intermediate values and fine-grained carbonates exhibit the highest tensile strength. Coefficients of friction range from 0.75 to 1.09, and cohesion ranges from 5.8 MPa for the siltstones to 13 MPa for carbonates in the Tununk Member. Plotting results in principal stress space rather than Mohr-Coulomb space more clearly define fields of tensile, hybrid, and shear failure modes under a range of stress states in a multilithologic stack of rocks. For stress conditions as deep as 3 km, low cohesion, low tensile strength rocks are predicted to fail at low pore pressure in hybrid open + shear modes; rocks with high tensile strengths and cohesion fail in nearly pure open-mode fractures at high pore pressures. Rocks with little or no cohesion are predicted to fail only in shear. Our results and compiled data from other rock-mechanics experiments show how sedimentary sequences may exhibit coeval open-mode veins, shear+ open mode surfaces, and simple shear failure that formed in the same macroscopic stress regime. In some cases, using a single set of values for tensile, cohesion, and frictional strengths for a heterolithic sedimentary sequence, or assuming that cohesion and tensile stress are zero, may not accurately represent failure for natural or injection-related pore-fluid pressure settings.

title: From Tectonic Compression, to Quiescence, to Extension: The Late Cretaceous to Neogene Early Andean Stages in Central Chile (31°-35°S)

authors: Muñoz-Gómez, Marcia [1], Charrier, Reynlado [2], Tapia, Felipe [3], Gerding, Vicente [4], Quiñones, Sergio [5], Mpodozis, Constantino [6], Rodriguez, Maria Pia [7]

abstract:
The Southern Central Andes (31°–35°S) record a well-recognized but complex history of alternating tectonic regimes. Integrating igneous geochemistry of mostly arc rocks, as a primary proxy for lithospheric conditions, with regional field observations and geochronology, we review a three-stage evolution from early, low-magnitude contraction, through prolonged tectonic quiescence, to major Cenozoic rifting.

The modern Andean cycle began with a mid-Cretaceous contractional pulse (ca. 105–90 Ma). Evidence includes the development of shear zones at ca. 100 Ma (Silla del Gobernador and Limahuída) and the accumulation of thick proximal foreland clastic successions (lower Las Chilcas Formation, Santa Virginia conglomerates, and the Brownish Red Clastic Unit). These features record E–W shortening, followed by renewed volcanism after ca. 90 Ma (upper Las Chilcas Formation, and Salamanca Formation). However, geochemical crustal-thickness estimates indicate that the crust remained moderately thin (ca. 30–36 km) and paleoelevations were probably near 1 km, suggesting only moderate uplift of the present-day Coastal Range following the closure of Early Cretaceous intra-arc extensional basins.

Following these events, the margin entered a ca. 40-m.y. interval of tectonic relaxation and relative quiescence between ca. 80 and 40 Ma. This stage is geochemically defined by bimodal arc suites, including the Late Cretaceous to early Paleocene Lo Valle and Plan de los Yeuques formations, and the Middle Eocene Tapado and Cordón de los Ratones units. These units are characterized by juvenile Sr-Nd-Hf isotopic compositions and geochemical signatures of low-pressure mineral assemblages. Persistently low accumulation rates (<120 m/m.y.) and stable, moderate crustal thicknesses (ca. 33–37 km) across the studied 31°–35°S segment confirm a state of arrested tectonic activity. This is mirrored in the Argentine retroarc by a significant depositional hiatus and sediment bypass.

A new tectono-magmatic regime began with the Late Eocene–Early Miocene Abanico rift (ca. 37–20 Ma). During this period, the composition of arc igneous rocks shifted toward tholeiitic affinities, and geochemical proxies record low crustal thicknesses (down to ca. 30 km). In addition, accumulation rates increased to ca. 200–240 m/m.y., consistent with rapid subsidence and sustained intra-arc extension.

In conclusion, the integrated record of arc geochemistry, field relationships, and geochronology highlights an early Andean evolution characterized by discrete stages of mild compression, prolonged stability, and extension before the onset of dominant Neogene shortening.

title: Evaluating AI-Assisted Vibe Coding in Hydrologic Sciences
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Gregg, Arianna [1], Davis, Sydney [2], Manandhar, Abhinna [3], Lowry, Christopher [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, New York, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, New York, USA
(3) Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, New York, USA

abstract: Advances in computing and the availability of large language models (LLMs) have created new opportunities for hydrologists to complete routine coding and data-analysis tasks more efficiently. However, many researchers still encounter challenges when writing code and understanding unfamiliar scripts. This research examines the potential of LLM-assisted vibe coding to support hydrologists in developing solutions, interpreting unfamiliar code, and more effectively utilizing computational tools. Participants were assigned to one of four leading LLM platforms, Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and tasked with completing a series of hydrologic coding exercises. Throughout the experiment, participants documented their prompts, exported generated code and outputs, and recorded observations regarding task completion and required user intervention. Results indicated that vibe coding can be an effective aid for computational tasks, although performance varies across platforms and is strongly influenced by prompt specificity and user interaction. This methodology showed great success in certain tasks such as hydrograph statistics, cross-correlation analyses, precipitation interpolation, and data pulls. However, more applied tasks such as developing unit hydrographs require more intervention and input from the user. As LLM capabilities continue to advance, vibe coding has the potential to become an increasingly valuable tool for updating legacy code, accelerating learning, and streamlining hydrologic research and workflows.

title: Investigating the Paleoecology of Insects from Florissant, Colorado, Using Carbon Isotope Geochemistry
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Posters)
authors: Zuccotti, Emma C [1], Fricke, Henry C. [2], Rossetto-Harris, Gabriella [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA
(2) Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
(3) Florissant Fossil Beds National Monnument, Florissant, Colorado, USA
abstract: Florissant Colorado is home to one of the most unique fossil deposits in the world, one that preserves a rare assemblage of plants (leaves & tree stumps), insects, fish, mammals & aquatic diatoms. These fossils are preserved in lake sediments deposited 18 miles from the latest Eocene Guffey Volcanic Field, and their study can provide a window into the ecological relations of this ancient forest-lacustrine environment. For this project, over 50 plant fossils and 15 insect fossils were collected from paper shale deposits located in and outside Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument. Fossils were sampled with the goal of using their carbon isotope ratios (d13C) to make paleobiological and paleoecological interpretations. Primary observations include: i) an isotopic offset between angiosperm and gymnosperm plants, and ii) isotope ratios of Hymenoptera (ants) and Diptera (flies) that overlap with angiosperm plants. The former is consistent with offsets in d13C observed between angiosperm and gymnosperm plants in modern forests, while the latter suggests that ants & flies relied primarily on angiosperms as food sources, either directly or indirectly. This study is the first to include carbon isotope data from Florissant plants, and to the best of our knowledge it is the first study of any kind to include isotopic data from fossil insects. As such, it provides a baseline for future studies of Florissant’s ancient ecology and environment.

title: Quantifying Uncertainty in Seepage Estimation: Toward a Reliable Understanding of Groundwater–Surface Water Interaction in the Middle Rio Grande.
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Nguyen, Tin Trung [1], Cadol, Daniel [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
The Low Flow Conveyance Channel (LFCC) is a drainage channel in central New Mexico that primarily delivers water into irrigation ditches, receives agricultural return flows, and incidentally collects groundwater seepage. Seepage fluxes have been estimated across numerous studies by taking differences in area-velocity discharges at sequential points down the channel (known as seepage runs). However, an uncertainty assessment of the methodology in terms of error margins has yet to be locally performed. This study conducted several field experiments: subsection width alteration, vertical velocity sampling methods, flow velocity steadiness over time, and spatial variation.

First, under the conditions of the LFCC, a subsection width of 0.5 meter is a suitable balance of precision and time efficiency, as its results closely align ±10% with the more detailed 0.25-meter measurement spacing while differing significantly from the 1-meter spacing. Second, methods of vertically averaged velocity measurement were compared among the single-point (0.6d), two-point (0.2d and 0.8d), and the fitted logarithmic curve to all three vertical positions: 0.2d, 0.6d, 0.8d. The results reveal negligible differences of less than 5% among calculated discharges. Third, sequential measurements of 20-second average velocity are highly steady, up to 5 samples (total of 100 seconds). Without flow obstructions, the measured velocity fluctuates by one resolution unit of the meter (0.01 m/s) and yields ensemble discharge estimates with less than 5% variability. In contrast, gauging in a reach with invasive emergent aquatic vegetation (Myriophyllum aquaticum, locally known as parrot feather) growth obstructing the flow path produces highly turbulent waters and increased variability of ensemble discharge (more than 10%).

Thus, in well-selected reaches, the uncertainty of individual discharge measurements is relatively constrained. However, because of low seepage fluxes in the LFCC, a margin of error from 5% to 10% in discharge measurement can generate an uncertainty of seepage rate up to 50%. As an illustrative case, closely spaced estimates of seepage fluxes along a 1-kilometer curved reach show high variability, which may be a consequence of uncorrelated estimate uncertainty between cross-sections. Therefore, the study suggests a potential approach using trend lines to quantify measurement uncertainty.

title: Project HOTSPOT, The Snake River Scientific Drilling Project: Looking Forward, Looking Back
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling
authors: Shervais, John W. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
abstract:
Project Hotspot was an international collaboration focused on understanding interactions between the Yellowstone mantle plume and continental lithosphere. Our funded goal was to investigate innovative approaches to geothermal energy exploration, but we were able to address significant scientific issues as well: how do mantle plumes interact with continental lithosphere and how does this interaction affect the geochemical evolution of mantle-derived magmas and continental lithosphere?

Project Hotspot completed three holes in the eastern, central, and western SRP: Kimama, Kimberly, and Mountain Home. We acquired 5324m of continuous core that documents the volcanic and sedimentary record of the hotspot track. The Kimama hole is dominantly basalt, while the Kimberly hole encountered alternating basalt-sediment, underlain by >1550m of rhyolite. These holes overlap in age, providing a stratigraphic record spanning ~8Ma. The Mountain Home hole penetrated ~640m of lacustrine sediment overlain (215m) and underlain (960m) by basalt; this hole also intersected an ~150C hydrothermal resource at 1745m. The project included water chemistry and geophysical studies comprising gravity, magnetic surveys, active source seismic surveys, vertical seismic profiles, and wireline logging of all three holes. Paleomagnetic inclinations were determined every 1.5m, supplemented by Ar-Ar and zircon U-Pb age determinations.

Our work shows that continental lithosphere forms a reactive filter which affects mantle derived magmas. The Kimama core contains 432 basalt flow units that document fractionation and recharge of mid-crustal magma chambers over 5.6Ma. Recharge magmas mix with residual magma from the previous cycles so that subsequent melts are more enriched than their parents. Paleomagnetic inclination data further show that both fractionation and recharge occur on timescales of a few decades to centuries (20-200 years). Similar cycles are documented in iron-rich basalts from Mountain Home (2.2-5.4Ma), which are coeval with basalts from Kimama (0.5-5.6Ma). The Kimberly core sampled two rhyolite lavas and a 1350m ash flow, as well as younger basalt flows.

Project Hotspot has generated nineteen publications and many geothermal conference papers. A GSA Special Publication with further results is in preparation. The core is now stored at LacCore (lake sediment) or at the USGS CRC in Denver, where it continues to be studied.

abstract: On 7 January 2025, the M W 7.1 Tingri earthquake ruptured the Lagoi and Dingmu Co faults in the Xianza-Dinggye Rift in the south-central Tibetan Plateau, China. This region is characterized by north-south trending rift systems that accommodate east-west extension across the Tibetan Plateau. We mapped coseismic surface rupture using manual mapping and sub-pixel optical image cross-correlation with the software MicMac on high-resolution (~0.5 m) WorldView-2 satellite images and post-earthquake digital elevation models (0.5-m resolution), and phase gradients derived from InSAR ALOS-2 images. The surface rupture is expressed as discontinuous dip- and oblique-slip scarps that extend for at least 35 km. The character of the surficial deposits and rupture expression varies along strike. Along the northern section of the Lagoi fault, the surface rupture is generally diffuse and discontinuous but sometimes narrowed through thin glacial and talus deposits over granitic bedrock. The southern section of the rupture along the Dingmu Co fault is characterized by discontinuous, distributed faulting and secondary surface deformation through thick alluvial-fluvial-lacustrine sediments overlying metasedimentary bedrock in the Dingmu Co Basin, with more localized faulting through older alluvial fan deposits along the rangefront. This variable surface rupture expression highlights the importance of surficial deposit type for identifying, preserving, and interpreting faults in the landscape record, as the surface rupture expression changed depending on the surficial properties. We also mapped pre-existing faults using pre-earthquake digital elevation models (8-m and 0.5-m resolution) and showed that the surface rupture coincides with pre-existing fault scarps for ~31% of the rupture length. When compared to the pre-existing fault landscape record, the location and distribution of these additional 69% of unanticipated surface ruptures may have resulted in a pre-event underestimation of fault activity. Retrospectively, this underestimation of fault length, complexity, and connectivity could affect seismic hazard assessments.

title: Evaluating the Radiation Stability of Meta-autunite Family Minerals for Nuclear Waste Storage
session_title: Mineralogical Insights from Modern Spectroscopic Techniques
authors: Krukowski, Marissa A [1], Dye, Chris A [2], LaVerne, Jay A [3], Hixon, Amy E [4]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, Indiana, USA
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, Indiana, USA
(3) Physics and Astronomy, University of Notre Dame, South Bend, Indiana, USA

abstract:
Uranium mobility in environmental and geologic repository settings is heavily driven by speciation, where soluble uranyl hydroxides and carbonates contrast sharply with low-solubility uranyl phosphate phases. Minerals of the meta-autunite group—such as meta-autunite and metatorbernite—act as critical solid-phase sinks that limit uranium migration at contaminated sites, making them promising candidates for long-term nuclear waste disposal. Consequently, evaluating their viability requires a thorough understanding of their long-term structural and chemical stability under self-irradiation. In this study, natural and synthetic meta-autunite and meta-torbernite samples were subjected to gamma irradiation to simulate radiation-induced aging, and their structural, elemental, and radical responses were evaluated using an integrated spectroscopic suite.

Crystal structures were verified via powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) for synthetic phases and single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) for natural specimens. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy was employed to probe transient and persistent radiation-induced radical species, providing insight into defect formation and radiation damage accumulation over long timescales. Complementary vibrational modes were mapped using Raman and Infrared (IR) spectroscopies to track subtle structural alterations, while X-ray fluorescence (XRF) confirmed elemental stoichiometry. By correlating radical generation with vibrational shifts and structural integrity, this multi-spectroscopic approach establishes a robust framework for predicting the long-term containment efficiency of uranyl phosphate minerals and can be broadly applied to study aging and structural stability in other radioactive mineral systems.

title: Untangling the Relative Climate and Tectonic Effects on the Long-term Exhumation History of the Khumbu Region, Nepal.

authors: Pye, Alexandra Eleanor [1], Schultz, Mary Hannah [2], Hodges, Kip [3], Whipple, Kelin X. [4], Ehlers, Todd A. [5], van Soest, Matthijs [6], McDonald, Christopher [7]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA

abstract:
Untangling the relative – and potentially coupled - effects of climate and tectonics on the spatial and temporal evolution of mountain ranges remains a key outstanding question. The Himalaya provide an excellent natural laboratory to explore the competing forces acting on mountain landscapes, and the potential feedbacks between climate and tectonics.

The physiographic edge of the Tibetan Plateau (PT 1 ) is sharply defined and marked by prominent knickpoints on major Transhimalayan rivers. PT 1 generally coincides with a major change in climate; the plateau is semi-arid and slowly eroding while the flank receives up to 4 m/yr precipitation and is rapidly eroding. The correlation with a dramatic climate gradient is clear, but the persistence of PT 1 may be attributed to active deformation and uplift patterns. Plio-Pleistocene aged normal-sense slip at the range crest has been documented at several locations in the central Himalaya and may be responsible for pinning knickpoints at PT 1 . Alternatively, the knickpoints at PT 1 could be migrating upstream, driven by a vigorous erosional response to increased thrusting at the mountain front. Whether the location and morphology of PT 1 reflects a fixed tectonic boundary, migrating erosion or is a manifestation of the dramatic precipitation gradient is uncertain. Additionally, the climate gradient may influence active tectonic processes. The potential for climate-tectonic coupling across PT 1 is both a complication and an opportunity to shed light on this elusive question.

Exhumation patterns along the Dudh Kosi river in the Khumbu region of Nepal provide insight into this problem. A major knickpoint has been documented at PT 1 , coinciding with a significant transition in the rainfall from >3 m/yr in the south to <0.5 m/yr in the north. We present data that show a dramatic break in cooling ages coincident with this knickpoint. Upstream zircon (U-Th)/He dates are 12-13 Ma, whereas those downstream are <4 Ma. Apatite (U-Th)/He dates record a similar break. The transition in rainfall could be responsible for this cooling pattern. However, the climate driven erosion must have triggered a tectonic response to cause this break, such as a normal-sense structure like those found at PT 1 elsewhere. However, no such fault has been documented. We explore these possible climate and tectonic drivers on the landscape, along with the effects of structures at the range front.

title: Seasonal Hydro-ecological Trajectory Regimes and Significant Vegetation–Moisture Changes in the arid Landscape of Western Rajasthan in India
session_title: Contemporary research in geomorphological hazards
authors: Siddiqui, Azizur Rahman [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, University of Allahabad, Allahabad, Uttar pradesh, India
abstract:
District Jalore is a part of Indian Arid ecosystem located in Western part of Rajasthan State in India, this desert arid tract are highly sensitive to seasonal hydro-climatic variability, particularly the pronounced contrast between monsoon and non-monsoon conditions. However, conventional trend analyses often assess trend persistence and magnitude separately, limiting the integrated interpretation of vegetation–moisture dynamics. This study applied a Hydro-ecological Trajectory Regime (HTR) framework integrating Kendall’s τ and Sen’s slope to characterize seasonal vegetation–moisture trajectories across Jalore District using Landsat 8-derived Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) composites from 2015–2025. Seasonal trends were quantified for two major hydro-climatic periods, monsoon and non-monsoon, and classified into recovery, stability, transition, and degradation regimes based on their integrated persistence–magnitude characteristics. The results revealed significant seasonal changes in vegetation and moisture trajectories, with clear differences between monsoon and non-monsoon periods. NDVI and NDWI exhibited spatially heterogeneous trends, reflecting significant changes in vegetation condition and surface moisture availability across the district. Significant differences were observed in the distribution of HTR classes between the two seasons, indicating substantial seasonal restructuring of vegetation–moisture dynamics. Topographic variability significantly influenced the spatial distribution of HTR regimes, while climatic validation confirmed significant hydro-climatic differences among the identified trajectory classes (p < 0.05). The findings demonstrate that the integrated HTR framework effectively captures significant seasonal changes in hydro-ecological conditions and provides a transferable remote-sensing approach for assessing vegetation recovery, transition, stability, and degradation in an arid landscape of district Jalore in India.
