abstract:
Great (>Mw 8.5) subduction zone earthquakes are among the world’s most devastating natural hazards. The Cascadia subduction zone (CSZ) has experienced several great earthquakes throughout the Holocene, with the most recent event occurring in 1700 CE. These prehistoric earthquakes are well preserved within the stratigraphic records of Pacific Northwest estuaries. However, despite this extensive record, the magnitude of prehistoric earthquakes and the inland extent of subsequent tsunamis are not well constrained. Currently, reconstructions of prehistoric tsunami inundation extents typically rely on tracking the inland limit of tsunami sand deposits. However, the extent of sandy tsunami deposits provides only a minimum inundation estimate because modern observations show that sand falls out of suspension before the tsunami wave stops its inland advance. Understanding the true inland extent of prehistoric tsunami events is essential for accurate earthquake and tsunami modeling, especially in regions like the CSZ which have not experienced a rupture since the development of modern instrumentation.

To better constrain the maximum sedimentary inundation limit of the 1700 CE tsunami, we evaluate the use of sedimentary environmental DNA (eDNA), which has successfully distinguished modern tsunami deposits from non-tsunami wash over deposits. However, this proxy has not been previously used to map a prehistoric tsunami’s inland inundation extent. Here, we analyzed an inland transect of sediment cores from the Salmon River estuary in Oregon to test if eDNA can be used to map prehistoric tsunamis further inland than the current 1700 CE sand derived limit. Sediment cores were sub-sampled in 1-cm intervals, spanning pre-earthquake, tsunami, and post-earthquake sediments. eDNA was extracted using a Quigen soil kit, before being sequenced on a MinION Mk1B Nanopore sequencer to a read depth of >7,500 reads per sample. Preliminary results indicate that tsunami deposits contain distinct microbial assemblages relative to pre- and post-earthquake deposits. This microbial signature is observed in every core along the transect and extends ~1km beyond the preserved sand limit, indicating that sedimentary eDNA can track subtle prehistoric tsunami sediment inland where obvious sand is absent. These results demonstrate the potential for sedimentary eDNA to provide an independent proxy for reconstructing prehistoric tsunami inundation and improving constraints on earthquake and tsunami hazard models.

abstract: Late Devonian mass extinctions, together constituting a ‘Big Five’ mass extinction of the Phanerozoic, were composed of multiple globally correlative biotic crises that occurred through the Frasnian and Famennian stages. In the latest Famennian, the Hangenberg Crisis strongly affected fauna that inhabited shallow epeiric seas and the marine-to-terrestrial transition zone, with a proposed driver of this extinction being the intrusion of toxic euxinic water into shallow seas during marine transgression. However, it can be difficult to reconstruct the exact timing and spatial extent of marine transgression relative to extinction pulses to determine potential cause-and-effect relationships. A proxy that can potentially facilitate reconstructing sequences of sea-level rise and fall relative to extinction horizons is the ratio of boron to gallium (B/Ga), a paleosalinity proxy applied to clay-rich siliciclastic rocks. Because clay minerals naturally absorb B in proportion to the salt content of the water they were formed in, higher ratios (>6) indicate marine conditions, intermediate ratios (>3&<6) indicate brackish conditions, and lower ratios (<3) indicate freshwater. Here, we present a paleosalinity analysis of field and core samples covering a transect from more distal (relative to the ancient Acadian Highlands) Famennian environments of Ohio (Cleveland Shale Member) to proximal localities in north-central Pennsylvania (Catskill, Lock Haven, and Oswayo formations). Preliminary data from northeast Pennsylvania field samples from an environment interpreted as west-facing rivers, estuaries, and deltas draining the ancient Acadian Mountains exhibit freshwater to brackish B/Ga paleosalinity values ranging from 2.2 (freshwater) to 4.4 (brackish), with these values implying lower salinity conditions than the brackish to marine gradient recorded in Ohio's Cleveland Shale. Paleosalinity interpretations are supported by primary physical observations such as sedimentary structures (e.g., symmetrical ripples vs desiccation cracks) and fossils (e.g., brachiopods vs root traces) that indicate deposition in distal fluvial channel-floodplain and tidal flat-channel environments. Our integrated paleosalinity, sedimentological, and paleontological data reveal previously undocumented relative sea-level fluctuations that may have influenced paleobiodiversity. Stratigraphic profiles will be developed for B/Ga paleosalinity in correlated Pennsylvania and Ohio Famennian sections of core and outcrop. Further analysis will include comparisons of B/Ga values with isotopic analysis of bioapatite from fish bone samples (independent paleosalinity proxy) to infer the salinity habitats of fish taxa and develop a robust multi-proxy reconstruction of changing sea-level during the latest Famennian.

title: Predictions and Geologic Implications of Europa’s Global Ice Shell Thickness Variations, Anchored by Juno Results
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Rhoden, Alyssa [1], Walker, Matthew [2]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Planetary Science Institute, USA
abstract:
The thickness of the ice shell overlying Europa’s global ocean has implications for the formation of Europa’s enigmatic surface features and the extent of material exchange between the ocean and surface. Recently, model fits to Juno microwave radiometer (MWR) measurements provided new constraints on Europa’s ice shell thickness. Observations across the six MWR channels were concentrated within the northern portion of the sub-Jupiter region. By optimizing the value of a single, uniform thickness over the entire observation region, Levin et al. (2026) found that 29±10 km produced the smallest total residuals.

Here, we reproduce the Juno-derived thickness at a reference location within the observation region using a 50-layer ice shell, conductive heat transport, tidal heating, and a near-surface temperature from Galileo data. We then identify the basal heat flux that can keep the ice shell in thermal equilibrium and use this value to assign basal heat fluxes across Europa. We explore both constant basal heat fluxes, as in previous work (Rhoden et al., 2026), and spatially-variable basal heat fluxes from models of ocean circulation. Then, we produce global maps of Europa’s ice shell thickness and surface heat flux, anchored by the Juno results.

We find that the region observed by Juno is consistently among the thickest regions on Europa due to its alignment with the tidal axis. Mid-latitudes, away from the tidal axis, are usually the thinnest due to the combination of tidal heating and surface temperature variations. Spatially-variable basal heat flows that include substantial tidal heating show the most distinct patterns in ice shell thickness variations, with thinner ice contours aligning very well with the locations of chaos terrains. These results suggest that chaos is not formed by solid state convection, which would be more likely to occur in regions of thicker ice. We find that spatial variations in surface heat flux can be diagnostic of local ice shell thickness and the relative contributions of basal and tidal heating to Europa’s thermal budget, with implications for future Europa Clipper observations.

title: Late Pleistocene Marine Ecological Change and Implications for Modern Climate Change Along the Southern California Coast
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Soni, Priyanka [1], Hendy, Austin J.W. [2], Bottjer, David J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA,
(2) Natural History Museum of Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA,
(3) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA,
abstract:
Earth has experienced significant climatic fluctuations through geologic time, including warming events of varying duration and intensity. These events leave behind evidence in the fossil record that can provide valuable insights into how biodiversity responded to past warming events, helping us better understand the ecological consequences of future warming trajectories.

The impacts of climate warming in the marine and terrestrial realms can be very different, resulting in highly variable extinction and survival patterns across different environments and taxonomic groups. Southern California serves as an ideal location to study potential linkages between land and sea in the context of climatic variability due to its excellent Late Pleistocene record, which preserves everything from terrestrial megafauna to marine micromolluscs. Several studies have shown vegetation and megafaunal responses to rapid climatic shifts during the last deglaciation, including range shifts and extinction. However, less is known about how coastal marine species responded to climate forcing, particularly whether they experienced extinction or avoided extinction through range shifts, local persistence, or survival in refugia.

Here, we investigate Late Pleistocene coastal molluscan assemblages from Southern California to examine how marine biodiversity responded to the Last Interglacial warming event. We find no major extinction among marine molluscs during this time. Instead, thermally anomalous species preserved in the fossil record provide evidence for an escape hypothesis, in which province-restricted taxa tracked suitable environmental conditions through range shifting. Range shifting taxa could establish populations in shallow, protected warm-water habitats that likely acted as refugia during warming phases, despite climatic instability on the open shelf. As much as 10% of Late Pleistocene molluscan taxa in Southern California exhibited this migratory response, suggesting that marine coastal ecosystems were dynamic and composed of taxa readily shifting their distributions. In contrast topographic complexity on land generates local entrapments, and increases the potential for local extinction.

Evidence from the fossil and stratigraphic record provides valuable insight into the potential impacts of ongoing climate change and biodiversity loss, linking past ecosystem responses to modern and future warming. These findings also highlight the ecological significance of warm-water embayments or protected habitats as shelters for migratory species during climate change.

title: Roger That, Over and Out (With Your Fossils): 40 Years of Strategic Specimen Acquisition
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: Means, Guy H. [1]
affiliations: (1) Florida Geological Survey, Tallahassee, FL, USA
abstract:
Over a distinguished 40 plus year career with the Florida Museum of Natural History (FLMNH), Roger W. Portell has fundamentally shaped our modern understanding of Cenozoic invertebrate paleontology. Through decades of meticulous fieldwork collecting, preserving, and curating countless fossil specimens, he transformed the FLMNH Invertebrate Paleontology Collection into an internationally recognized, world-class research repository. Portell’s research focuses on the systematics, paleoecology, biogeography, and biostratigraphy of fossil arthropods, echinoderms, brachiopods, and mollusks and is documented in more than 170 professional publications.

Roger has led or participated in numerous field expeditions throughout Florida, the southeastern United States and other parts of the world. His unmatched field expertise stems from developing relationships with pit and quarry owners to secure access to hundreds of new fossil localities. Portell has also conducted field work in the Caribbean and in many parts of Central and South America. Notably, his extensive work documenting the fossils at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, provided unprecedented insights into Caribbean marine paleoenvironments, and his discovery of the early Eocene quadrupedal sirenian Pezosiren portelli Domning, 2001 in Jamaica advanced our understanding of the evolutionary transition of dugongs from terrestrial to marine environments. Although Roger’s primary research interest focuses on invertebrates, he has made significant contributions in vertebrate paleontology, paleobotany, and other subdisciplines.

Beyond quantifiable metrics, Portell’s greatest contribution is his ability to bridge the gap between professional scientists and fossil collectors, breaking down academic barriers and inspiring public engagement. He has consistently dedicated his time to guiding students, volunteers, and early-career researchers. Reflecting on a 25-year working relationship, this presentation honors Portell’s enduring legacy by highlighting some of the collaborative work and major discoveries that have defined his outstanding career.

abstract: Due to the global reliance on critical minerals for emerging technologies and the green energy transition, the extraction of these commodities from unconventional resources has come to the forefront of geochemical research. Manganese (Mn) oxides can concentrate many critical minerals, including rare earth elements and yttrium (REYs), in ore grade concentrations. Both aqueous Mn and REYs are elevated in acid mine drainage (AMD), with Mn oxide minerals generated during passive remediation of AMD. This, in turn, concentrates critical minerals from AMD via adsorption and coprecipitation. Thus, passive remediation of AMD may serve as a potential method to extract REYs at low ore grade concentrations while improving ecosystem health. Passive AMD remediation typically promotes both geochemical and microbial processes to facilitate the precipitation of Mn oxides. This study aims to explore the role that biomass and biogenic Mn oxides play in REY adsorption and coprecipitation through both laboratory experiments and investigating real-world processes at the Sterrett and Kentucky Hollow remediation sites in Pennsylvania, USA. Experiments were conducted with two Mn-oxidizing fungi, Stagonospora sp. SRC1lsM3a and Paraphaeosphaeria sporulosa , AP3s5-JAC2a. To isolate the effect of biomass, REY uptake by Mn oxides formed in association with biomass was compared against Mn oxides formed in cell-free filtrates, in addition to Mn-free biomass experiments. Aqueous Mn and REY concentrations, along with pH were tracked for the duration of the experiments. We find fungi-free systems remove little to no REY from solution, while Mn-free experiments with biomass remove ~45% of the initial REY from solution. The addition of Mn substantially increases solid-associated REY, with the cell-free filtrate and Mn system removing 81% of REYs while the biomass and Mn system removes 99% of REYs from solution. Field studies involved deployment of reaction chambers with nylon mesh bags designed to permit or prevent microbial transfer between the chambers and AMD. Analysis of the resulting solids finds that the chambers preseeded with Mn-oxidizing microbes have elevated solid-associated REY relative to abiotic chambers. These results suggest that Mn oxides in combination with biomass may allow for the most productive sequestration of REYs. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into extracting critical minerals from contaminated sites, providing a potential pathway to harnessing greener energy while mitigating environmental hazards associated with conventional critical mineral extraction.

authors: Richter, Sadie Mae [1], Klepeis, Keith A. [2], Schwartz, Joshua J. [3], Miranda, Elena A. [4], Rhea, Gillian [5], Rataizer, Jordana [6]

abstract:
The Median Batholith in Fiordland, New Zealand exposes Cretaceous continental crust that formed in a Cordilleran-style magmatic arc along the Gondwana margin. The ~15 km-thick Misty pluton was emplaced at 120–115 Ma during a terminal magmatic surge at ~25–40 km depth. We integrated field mapping, serial cross-sections and quantitative fabric analysis to investigate the role of mafic recharge, dissolution-reprecipitation and compaction on the extraction of hydrous intermediate–felsic melts out of the deep crust.

Field data allowed us to reconstruct the 3-dimensional architecture of the Misty pluton. The reconstructions show that the Hawes Head Ultramafic Complex at the base of the Misty pluton consists of hornblendite, hornblende peridotite, and wehrlite sheets that intruded hornblende diorite mushes at ~9.5–10.5 kbar. These intrusions form discontinuous bodies that disaggregated within the dioritic host mushes and are spatially associated with comagmatic granitic segregations, suggesting that mafic recharge disrupted, reheated and mobilized trapped felsic melts within the dioritic mush. Deformed dikes and changes in foliation intensity measured across strain gradients indicates that coaxial shortening affected the deepest parts of the pluton. These results suggest that post-recharge compaction was an important mechanism for the extraction of granitic melts out of the lower crust.

Measures of crystallinity, mineral clustering, and shape-preferred orientations (SPOs) in thin sections from host and recharge-modified mush domains allowed us to further investigate the effects of mafic recharge and compaction. Preliminary results suggest that recharge-modified, melt-rich domains preserve weaker mineral SPOs and more disrupted grain distributions, whereas less melt-rich host mushes show stronger SPOs, greater crystal ordering, and textures consistent with compaction. Mineral-specific trends suggest that compaction was also accompanied by dissolution, redistribution, and recrystallization. Together, the field and textural observations support a model in which mafic recharge rejuvenated lower crustal mushes and subsequent compaction promoted the segregation and extraction of evolved melts from the deep crust.

title: A Reevaluation of the Severn Formation in Southern Prince George's County, Maryland, U.S.A (Implications for Paleoenvironmental/Ecological Studies on the Cretaceous East Coast)

abstract:
The Severn Formation of Prince George’s County, Maryland, U.S.A, is a Maastrichtian age (77.2-66 Ma) Cretaceous geologic unit that contains a wide variety of both invertebrate and vertebrate taxa. Arguably the most notable fossils found within the formation include a wide variety of reptiles such as Deinosuchus schwimmeri , Trionyx priscus, Cimoliasaurus magnus , and Mosasaurus sp. in addition to bony and cartilaginous fishes such as Enchodus sp ., and Squalicorax sp .. In a geologic context, notable characteristics can also be attributed to the Severn Fm such as changes in depositional environments and higher concentrations of elements like sulfur in specific outcrops. Many of the publications regarding both the geology and paleobiology of the Severn Fm. are over 20 years old and are in need of critical review. Since the release of those publications, new samples have been uncovered in established outcrops and a new, fossiliferous outcrop has been discovered (previously submerged) by the construction and waterway management in Piscataway creek, southern Prince Georges County.

The purpose of this study will be to evaluate new fossil material and describe the different depositional facies that these fossils occur in. Samples and specimens have been collected from these localities and will be compared with other Mid-Atlantic Maastrichtian formations. These comparisons will hopefully aid in future research to gain a broader understanding of the Mid-Atlantic region during the Late Cretaceous.

abstract:
The Trans-Pecos magmatic province of Texas hosts numerous Paleocene- to Miocene-aged intrusive and extrusive igneous bodies that formed during the transition from subduction-related compression to subsequent regional extension. A series of alkaline intrusions occur along a northwest–southeast-trending belt in the northern part of the province, encompassing compositions that range from mafic to highly evolved felsic magmatism.

The Bureau of Economic Geology conducts geologic mapping and geochemical sampling in support of critical mineral assessments within this region. GEOCHEMWTX (Trans-Pecos Texas Geochemistry Explorer) is an interactive GIS platform designed to visualize and disseminate geochemical data collected from the Trans-Pecos magmatic province of Texas and is accessible at https://maps.beg.utexas.edu/portal/apps/sites/#/geochemwtx. The platform provides sample locations, lithologic information, and whole-rock geochemical data. It also enables visualization of the distribution and variation of critical elements and selected major oxides across the different intrusive complexes. The datasets will be updated as new studies are completed and additional data become available.

title: Constraints on Ore-Forming Processes at the Hog Mountain Orogenic Gold Deposit from Apatite Textures and Geochemistry

authors: Iran Manesh, Sara [1], Bilenker, Laura [2], Poole, Joshua D. [3], Gottardi, Raphael [4]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA

abstract:
Hog Mountain is an orogenic-related gold deposit located in the southernmost Appalachians in central Alabama. It was an important target during historic gold mining, with efforts focused on gold hosted in quartz veins that crosscut a small tonalite body and often contain sulfides and Bi-Te phases [1]. The tonalite is surrounded by metasedimentary rocks of the Wedowee Group, which is thought to be the source of the ore-forming fluids. Apatite occurs across the deposit and is present as multiple generations in a range of crystal sizes (microns to millimeters), making it a promising record of ore forming processes and conditions at Hog Mountain.

The objectives of this study are to determine how many populations of apatite exist in the deposit, what their compositions are, and which geochemical signatures and mineral textures are consistent with gold mineralization. Analytical work on 12 samples combines petrography, scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), cathodoluminescence (CL), and laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) to determine the composition of apatite grains from each population. Preliminary work reveals that apatite occurs in three different hosts in the Hog Mountain deposit: (1) the tonalite, (2) quartz veins, and (3) the Wedowee rocks. The apatite within the tonalite is euhedral and coarse-grained with a yellowish-green color. Within the quartz veins, apatite grains are both aggregated and scattered and are hexagonal to cubic in whitish to bluish green. In the Wedowee phyllite, they are more rare and green-blue in color. They all have similar elemental compositions, rich in Mn, Fe, Na, and Yb. Mineral inclusions vary from xenotime to titanite and sulfide minerals like pyrite. While they are chemically homogenous in back scattered electron images and EDS elemental maps, heterogeneity is observed in CL. Ongoing analysis includes LA-ICP-MS and additional CL. This work will provide a basis for using apatite as an indicator at a local active gold prospect.

abstract:
Speleothems preserve climate signals over long timescales, can be dated precisely using U-Th methods, and record a wide range of geochemical proxies for reconstructing past environmental change. The Yucatán Peninsula is particularly well-suited region for paleoclimate reconstructions, as its karst landscape of caves, sinkholes, and underground drainage promotes rapid infiltration of meteoric water and sustained speleothem growth, while its location makes the region highly sensitive to Caribbean climate dynamics. Despite decades of speleothem-based research in the region, most existing records focus on the mid- to late Holocene, leaving the early Holocene comparatively underexplored.

Here we reconstruct early Holocene hydroclimate variability using stalagmite J3.3_Top (45.5 cm) from Garra de Jaguar Cave in northern Yucatán. To better link cave geochemistry with surface climate, we paired speleothem analyses with one year of drip-water collected beneath the stalactite that formed J3.3_Top using an SYP autosampler (Waikato Scientific Instruments). Local rainfall variability, including event frequency, intensity, and timing was monitored with a Pluvimate rain logger, and freshly precipitated calcite was collected from active drips for comparison with drip water and stalagmite isotopic compositions.

The stalagmite chronology based on 15 U-Th ages spans ~ 9.1–7.9 ka BP. Stable carbon and oxygen isotopes analyses of 216 powder samples reveal substantial variability in both δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C, indicating pronounced hydroclimatic change during this interval. By testing isotopic equilibrium, examining drip water-to-calcite transfer, and assessing hydroclimatic controls on δ¹⁸O, this research clarifies the processes governing speleothem growth and isotopic variability at Garra de Jaguar Cave. Together, the modern monitoring and J3.3_Top geochemical data provide an early Holocene perspective on hydroclimate variability in the northern Yucatán Peninsula.

abstract:
Although the Cascadia subduction zone (CSZ) has not experienced an earthquake in modern history, it has produced several great (>Mw 8.5) earthquakes throughout the Holocene, with the most recent occurring in January 1700 CE. While the 1700 CE earthquake and tsunami have been documented in the subsurface stratigraphy of many CSZ estuaries, the spatial extent of tsunami inundation remains poorly constrained because previous studies have largely relied on the inland limit of preserved tsunami sand as the primary indicator of inundation extent. However, observations from recent tsunamis, including the 2011 Tohoku and 2010 Maule events, demonstrate that tsunami inundation commonly extends beyond the landward limit of sand deposition, highlighting the need for high-resolution mapping using multiple sedimentary proxies.

Alsea Bay, Oregon, is an important site for constraining past tsunami inundation because previous work documented relatively small amounts of coseismic subsidence despite the presence of a distinct tsunami deposit. To refine tsunami inundation estimates we combine high-resolution mapping of tsunami sand deposits with detailed grain size and diatom analyses, extending our investigation inland beyond the preserved sand bed into silty sand and sandy silt deposits. Marine-brackish diatoms can be transported farther inland than sand during tsunami inundation, providing an independent indicator of marine flooding where sandy deposits become discontinuous or absent.

Fieldwork conducted in October 2025 included the collection of 33 sediment cores and systematic mapping of the 1700 CE buried soil and tsunami deposits throughout Alsea Bay and Lint Slough. Tsunami sand deposits were mapped and traced across Alsea Bay, ranging from 6 cm thick at seaward sites to <1 cm thick at inland sites. Sand deposits averaging 3 cm thick were also identified within Lint Slough, representing the first systematic mapping of tsunami deposits in the slough. Ongoing grain-size and diatom analyses show that finer-grained inland tsunami deposits contain anomalous marine-brackish diatoms and elevated sand content, indicating that the 1700 CE tsunami inundation extended approximately 1.25 km beyond the previously mapped minimum inundation limit defined by preserved tsunami sand within the bay. These new field observations refine the mapped extent of the 1700 CE tsunami at Alsea Bay, providing improved constraints on Cascadia earthquake rupture models and contributing to more accurate tsunami hazard assessments for the central Oregon coast.

title: Influence of aridity in grassland-shrubland (C4-C3) transitions in southern New Mexico during the Holocene
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade (Posters)
authors: Remian, Bethany [1], Kelson, Julia [2], Monger, Curtis [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM, USA
abstract: Shrub (C 3 ) encroachment is often attributed to overgrazing and increased aridity, but the long-term specific hydrologic drivers remain poorly understood. We use paleosol carbonates of Pleistocene and Holocene New Mexico to investigate relationships between water stress and vegetation (C 4 grasses vs. C 3 shrubs). Previous work identified an expansion of shrublands in the mid-Holocene. We hypothesize this expansion was driven by multiple hydrologic factors, including water stress. We collected Pleistocene and Holocene pedogenic carbonate samples from five sites in the Jornada Basin, and measured δ 13 C, δ 18 O, and 14 C values to constrain the timing, landscape-scale spatial variation, and drivers in shrubland expansion. The δ 13 C values range from -7.77 to -1.02‰ VPDB and record a shift from C 4 - to C 3 - dominant vegetation in the Holocene. The paleosol carbonates in the piedmont sites have a defined decrease in δ 13 C at the start of the Holocene and then return to higher δ 13 C values, indicating an increase and then decrease in the proportion of shrubs. The paleosol carbonates in the basin floor site also decrease in δ 13 C in the start of the Holocene, indicating shrubland expansion contemporaneous with the piedmont, but then the δ 13 C values remain low through late Holocene. At all sites, the δ 18 O values range from -9.61 to -2.46‰ VPDB. The δ 18 O increases for most of the Holocene but the signal is decoupled from δ 13 C, suggesting that changes in hydrology occurred after shrubland expansion. We will use triple oxygen isotope and clumped isotope geochemistry to further explore moisture source, evaporation, and temperature. Additionally, we discovered a sequence of Holocene sediments, the Big Meadow site, that is distinct from the other paleosol sites in color, texture, and isotope geochemistry. It is isotopically invariant (δ 13 C range: -3.01 to -1.40‰, δ 18 O range: -6.64 to -4.61‰) and has high 14 C ages (~14-30ka). Sr isotope ratios for samples at Big Meadow (~0.708) suggest that the Ca is derived from limestone in the San Andres mountain range upslope. We hypothesize that Big Meadow represents an erosion pulse rather than in-situ pedogenesis; its deposition history will be related to paleoclimate from the other paleosol sites. In conclusion, our data show that the Jornada was a mosaic of shrubs and grasses, and the relationship between vegetation response (δ 13 C), hydroclimate (δ 18 O), and sedimentation varied across the basin.

title: Resolving the Mesozoic Tectonic History of the Tyaughton-Methow Forearc Basin: Preliminary Results from Southwestern British Columbia
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: Boeman, Emma Z [1], Wang, Jordan W [2], Carrapa, Barbara [3], Kapp, Paul A. [4], Marulanda, Sebastian [5]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, The University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, USA
(3) Geoscience, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(4) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(5) Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
abstract:
The tectonic configuration of the Insular and Intermontane superterranes with respect to North America during the Mesozoic has important implications for our understanding of the subduction system along the western North American margin and for Cordilleran tectonics. To discriminate between competing models of subduction polarity and terrane paleogeography, we focus on the Upper Triassic to Cretaceous sedimentary record of the Mesozoic Tyaughton-Methow basin of southwestern British Columbia, between the Insular and Intermontane superterranes, which consists of a 6 km thick section of arc-derived detritus. These strata provide a unique record to resolve potential changes in basin dynamics and sedimentary provenance related to Insular-Intermontane collision and assembly with North America. Previous detrital zircon analytical work has been limited to Middle Cretaceous samples in the upper part of the basin, whereas the stratigraphy of the Lower Jurassic portion of the basin has not been studied in detail. Here we discuss a multi-disciplinary approach including low temperature thermochronology (zircon U-Th/He), detrital zircon geochronology, and geochemical analysis across five formations spanning the Upper Triassic to Lower Cretaceous, as well as new stratigraphic analysis and paleocurrent data for the Lower Jurassic Nemaia formation and explore the implications for provenance and subduction polarity during this time.

Detrital zircon U-Pb analyses were conducted on samples across the Middle Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous Relay Mountain Group and the Upper Triassic to Upper Jurassic Upper Cadwallader Group. These results include a range of Mesozoic ages, with each sample yielding either bimodal or unimodal age populations between ~231 and ~135 Ma. Older Paleozoic and Proterozoic ages indicative of input from the craton interior were absent in the dataset, suggesting either a topographic barrier preventing inboard detritus from the craton or a large distance between the Intermontane terranes and North America throughout most of the Mesozoic. Lu-Hf and trace and rare earth element analyses were conducted on selected detrital samples across these age distributions. These analyses reflect a highly juvenile source terrane signature and trace element composition consistent with an arc-derived source terrane from within the Canadian Cordillera. We explore the depositional context and potential source terranes of these deposits, providing important insight into the tectonic configuration and paleogeographic evolution of the western North American margin throughout the Mesozoic.

title: Is Multichannel GPR Worth Its Salt? Applications For Mapping the Extent of the Roman Saltworks of Galicia
session_title: Geoarchaeology of the Land–Sea Interface: Processes, Preservation, and Palaeolandscape Reconstruction
authors: Gontz, Allen M. [1], Curras Refojos, Brais X [2], Perona, Damian Romero [3], Corozon, Santiago Tunas [4]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Clarkson University, Potsdam, NY,
(2) Spanish National Research Council, Madrid, Spain
(3) Spanish National Research Council, Madrid, Spain

abstract:
Archaeological research carried out over the last two decades has documented extensive evidence of marine salt exploitation on the Atlantic coastline of the northwestern Iberian Peninsula. The positions of numerous occurrences of flat stone pavements with low stone walls and carved depressions have been documented and mapped. These features have been attributed to the Roman Empire and are related to the development of the salting industry. The exposed sections are often small, a couple of meters or less and represent a small glimpse into the entire complex construction.. While the strong winter storms expose the saltworks, these storms, coupled with sea level rise are destroying the saltworks. It is critical to map the occurrences of the saltworks in detail and characterize the construction and disturbance before they are lost to the sea. But how do you examine large areas of the coastal system and map the inland extent of these saltworks and document their occurrence and structure before their ultimate destruction by coastal processes?

This work applied high-resolution multi-channel ground penetrating radar in an attempt to map the extent of the saltworks. The GPR data were supported with LiDAR, photogrammetry, RTK-GPS survey and linked to previous excavations.

During early June 2026, a team of archaeologists and geophysicists surveyed three (3) sites in Galicia using an Impuls Radar Mini Raptor with 8 channels acquiring data at 500 MHz. The locations had known saltworks with storm-related exposures, minor coastal excavations or isolated trenches excavated during construction. At each site, the GPR was able to identify features that were consistent with saltwork construction - flat pavements of stone, bounded by low < 25 cm walls. The largest site included several different evaporating basins. The GPR data were linked to the excavation data using RTK-GPS and elevations were compared.

A campaign is under development to confirm the GPR interpretations through excavation.

title: What Controls the Longitudinal Trends in 129I/I Ratios along the Upper Wabash River, IN, USA? Lithology, Nuclear Fallout, or Dietary Iodine in Wastewater?

authors: Wickramasinghe, W.M. Srilani [1], Frisbee, Marty Dale [2], Caffee, Marc William [3], Chmiel, Greg J [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric & Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA

(3) Physics & Astronomy & Purdue Rare Isotope Measurement Laboratory, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(4) Purdue Rare Isotope Measurement Laboratory, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA
abstract: Iodine-129 ratios ( 129 I/I) were measured in river samples collected longitudinally down the Upper Wabash River in northern IN, USA to investigate using 129 I/I to date baseflow, specifically to identify components of bomb-pulse recharge stored in the watershed. Based on a previous multi-isotope study, our hypothesis was that elevated 129 I/I bomb-pulse signals would be preserved and transported longitudinally along the river during baseflow conditions owing to the larger groundwater fraction in the baseflow and the presence of bomb-pulse 129 I/I in aquifers in central IN (ranging from 4000 × 10 -15 to 22,000 × 10 -15 ). The 129 I/I ratios measured along the river ranged between 2,000 × 10 -15 to 700,000 × 10 -15 . The headwaters reach of the Wabash River has the lowest 129 I/I ratios and behaves differently from the rest of the river. The lowest ratio (2,203 × 10 -15 observed 142 km from the origin) represents dilution due to a combination of factors including dietary iodine from a wastewater treatment plant and possibly groundwater flow through a clay-rich, swampy area that is rich in organic matter. The higher ratios in the rest of the river likely indicate a discharge of a mixed groundwater signal that contains a component of elevated 129 I/I from nuclear fuel rod reprocessing and/or nuclear fallout. On average the river 129 I/I ratios were an order of magnitude higher than that of the aquifers in central IN and two orders of magnitude higher than the historically accepted background 129 I/I ratio of 1500 ± 150 × 10 -15 . In comparison, 129 I/I ratios of monthly aggregated local precipitation samples collected from March 2025 to March 2026 had even higher 129 I/I concentrations ranging from 355,000 to 13,280,000 × 10 -15 ; however, the average 129 I/I in precipitation lies within the range of 4,000,000 to 8,000,0000 x 10 -15 . This dataset shows that a mixture of 129 I sources related to nuclear weapons testing in the 1950s and 1960s, nuclear accidents and recent nuclear fuel rod reprocessing contribute to recharge and baseflow in the watershed, underscoring the complexities in the temporal variability of 129 I/I in modern precipitation which makes it challenging to use 129 I/I to date surface and groundwater in the Midwest.

title: From Conceptual Geologic Models to TOUGH Simulations: Lowering Barriers with PetraSim
session_title: Hydrogeology of Geothermal Resources: From Shallow Systems to Deep Reservoirs (Posters)
authors: Alcott, Alison [1], Azizian, Mitra [2]
affiliations: (1) RockWare, Inc., Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) RockWare, Inc., Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Numerical simulation of coupled multiphase fluid and heat transport is widely used to investigate geothermal systems, groundwater flow, geologic carbon storage, hydrogen storage, and other subsurface processes. The TOUGH family of simulators provides a robust framework for modeling these systems, but preparing input files, constructing computational meshes, assigning model properties, managing simulation runs, and interpreting output can present a substantial learning curve for new and occasional users.

PetraSim is a graphical modeling tool designed to make TOUGH-based simulation more accessible while retaining the capabilities of the underlying numerical simulator. It integrates model construction, mesh generation, material-property assignment, initial and boundary conditions, simulation control, and post-processing within a unified workflow. The software supports multiple computational grid types and TOUGH equation-of-state (EOS) modules, allowing users to develop models appropriate for a wide range of hydrogeologic, geothermal, and subsurface energy applications. Integrated visualization tools, including scalar and vector displays, facilitate evaluation of simulation results and model behavior while supporting export to common scientific visualization and data formats for additional analysis.

This poster presents the progression from conceptual geologic models to TOUGH numerical simulations using PetraSim. Representative examples illustrate how geologic framework models are translated into simulation grids and parameterized for analyses of subsurface processes. The featured applications include CO₂ injection into deep geologic formations and coupled heat and fluid flow in geothermal systems. By lowering practical and technical barriers to model construction and analysis, PetraSim can broaden access to multiphase flow simulation for students, researchers, consultants, and practicing geoscientists.

title: Evaluating Crustal Hydration as a Surface Uplift Mechanism for the Colorado Plateau from Xenolith and Seismic Studies
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Sims, Jacob [1], Mahan, Kevin [2], Goncalves, Philippe [3], Newell, Dennis [4], Schulte-Pelkum, Vera [5], Hernandez, Micah [6], Zawaski, Mike [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA

(3) Chrono-environment, Universite Marie et Louis Pasteur, Besancon, France
(4) Department of Geosciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA

abstract: The Colorado Plateau is one of several orogenic plateaus with an uncertain uplift history, and understanding its surface-uplift mechanisms could reveal important principles applicable elsewhere. The plateau’s surface has uplifted ~2 km since the Late Cretaceous, and the cause is poorly constrained. One hypothesis is that metasomatism of the continental lithosphere by fluids associated with shallow subduction of the Farallon slab reduced lower crustal density, causing the lithosphere to rise, raising surface elevation. Support for the Farallon slab as a fluid source comes from stable isotope data and late Cretaceous dates from secondary phases (e.g., actinolite, zoisite, muscovite, monazite, titanite). We test this hypothesis using crustal xenoliths from the Navajo Volcanic Field in the Four Corners region. Previous models of Plateau metasomatism have found 200-900 m of uplift. However, these studies have used geophysical models that do not explicitly depend on lithology, or they assumed a limited range of lithologies. We begin with a previously proposed multi-layer model for the Colorado Plateau crust with layer thickness, Moho depth, and lithologic proportions based on prior xenolith geophysical observations. We select xenoliths for each lithology and make textural observations to interpret the pre-hydration mineral assemblage of each xenolith. Each lithology is weighted by its relative proportion in the crustal layers, and pre- and post-hydration densities are compared to determine the net surface elevation change. Xenolith densities are calculated at pressures and temperatures that we estimate by petrological modeling, which we also use to constrain a cooler paleogeotherm than the modern Colorado Plateau. We then revise the model by evaluating the relative volume proportion of each lithology in the middle and lower crust by comparing calculated xenolith P-wave velocities to those observed from reflection surveys and using receiver functions from EarthScope stations to evaluate layer thickness and Moho depth. We find that the average crustal thickness of the central CP is 48 km, compared to the 43 km of the initial model crustal column. Hydration likely extended near the top of the middle crust, ~12 km below the surface, based on the interpreted depths of the metasomatized xenoliths. With these parameters, Laramide metasomatism resulted in a ~0.3 km of local uplift. This is ~15% of the total (2 km) uplift since the late Cretaceous, meaning other mechanisms are required.

title: Contrasting Road Salt Fate in Two Urban Watersheds in Omaha, NE
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Deuerling, Kelly [1], Gholami, Adelan [2], Berglund, Sam [3], Luokkala, Christa [4], Hribljan, John [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Nebraska Omaha, Omaha, NE, USA
(2) Central High School, Omaha, NE, USA
(3) Central High School, Omaha, NE, USA
(4) Central High School, Omaha, NE, USA

abstract:
Salinization of surface waters due to winter road salt addition is a pervasive problem across the globe. Previous work has shown that all trophic levels are affected by intensive road salt usage in freshwater ecosystems, though often at sublethal levels, nevertheless impacting ecosystem function. We explore the impact of road salt on two urban watersheds in Omaha, Nebraska: Elmwood Creek that feeds into Little Papillion Creek and Heron Haven, a springfed wetland flowing into Big Papillion Creek. Both watersheds include first-order streams each with a natural drainage area of ~1.5 km 2 and are extensively impacted by stormwater infrastructure significantly increasing drainage area and potential anthropogenic additions. We present high-resolution conductivity data from inlets and outlets of both watersheds between October 2025 and March 2026, as well as chloride spot samples during the same period. Omaha Public Works utilizes sodium chloride salt/brine, calcium chloride brine, and sand to maintain winter roads, depending on temperature and severity of storm events.

At Elmwood Creek, peaks in conductivity at both upstream and downstream sites follow snow events. The upstream site peaks at over 6000μS/cm and consistently falls over ~14 days back to background levels at ~900μS/cm. The downstream site also peaks following snowfall events but reaches peaks of ~3000μS/cm before returning to background levels. The lower conductivity noted at the downstream site is likely related to dilution as its watershed includes residential neighborhoods that are not as aggressively salted as well as green infrastructure designed to increase infiltration.

In contrast Heron Haven shows retention and/or dilution of road salt within the wetland. The groundwater retains consistently low conductivity (~900μS/cm). The anthropogenically impacted inlet, which drains a residential area and major roadway through stormwater infrastructure, does not respond directly to snowfall events. Instead, following an initial pulse where conductivity reached over 15,000μS/cm, values slowly decreased through time with a noted freshening during a mid-January rain event. Over the same period, the wetland outlet never exceeded ~1000μS/cm, though there is a noted increase in conductivity concurrent with the high conductivity at the anthropogenic inlet. These data indicate that the salt is retained within the wetland and future work will focus on where the salt is partitioned in the ecosystem.

authors: Moore, Adam V. [1], Hyland, Ethan G. [2], Gates, Terry A. [3], Zanno, Lindsay E. [4], Burgener, Landon K. [5]
affiliations: (1) North Carolina State University, Marine, Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Clayton, NC, USA

abstract:
Investigating seasonal temperature and precipitation paleoclimate trends associated with broader annual paleoclimate data is essential for understanding complete past temporal and spatial climate changes and their potential impacts on biodiversity. During the mid-Cretaceous, the upper Cedar Mountain, Naturita, and Straight Cliffs formations (~98-83 Ma) within a portion of the greater Western Interior Basin (WIB) in Utah, USA, underwent dynamic geological and environmental changes exacerbated, in part, by the regional transgression of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) and continued uplift of the Sevier Orogeny. These formations capture terrestrial archives of the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum (KTM) and corresponding Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE 2), as well as recorded regional dinosaur faunal turnover.

In order to more accurately determine the seasonal climatic shifts in these WIB formations, we examined B-horizon paleosol samples for geochemical (bulk) and carbonate clumped isotope (Δ 47 ) paleoclimate proxies through the utilization of a benchtop XRF and Dual Inlet Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry (DI-IRMS), respectively. Throughout these formations, the mean annual temperature (MAT) and mean annual precipitation (MAP) increased by ~4-8℃ and ~774-1,244 mm/yr, respectively, which indicates that the annual climate in Utah during the mid-Cretaceous was becoming warmer and wetter across the KTM. Seasonally, there was also an average decrease in the mean annual range in temperature (MART) of ~5℃, whereas summer extremes (temperatures during season of carbonate formation) increased by >15℃. This discrepancy is likely due to a shorter window in which carbonates formed as the MAP increased. Growing season precipitation (GSP) increased proportionally with MAP, and the ratio of GSP to MAP remained at ~75% over the studied interval. Furthermore, when examining samples of the same approximate age from multiple localities across a basinal transect, there are slight differences in the MAT, MART, GSP, and GSP/MAP values due to the proximity of the sample locality to the margin of the WIS. Overall, these data suggest that even though mid-Cretaceous Utah was becoming increasingly warm and wet (humid subtropical climate regime), seasonal climates in this region were becoming less extreme (MART) or remained approximately the same (GSP/MAP) through time.

abstract: Accurate identification of wildfire-prone landscapes is essential for improving hazard assessment, wildfire risk mitigation, and ecosystem management across the western United States. This study develops an integrated multi-source remote sensing and machine learning framework to assess wildfire susceptibility across Yellowstone National Park (YNP) from 2000 to 2025. Optical satellite imagery (Landsat 5–9 and Sentinel-2 MSI) was processed in Google Earth Engine to characterize wildfire disturbance using the differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR), with the 2016 Maple Fire serving as a reference event for calibrating burned areas. Environmental predictors representing terrain, vegetation, climate, hydrology, and geothermal proximity were compiled as long-term means and stacked into a 30-m multiband dataset. A Random Forest classifier was trained using stratified samples of burned and unburned pixels to generate a spatially continuous wildfire susceptibility probability surface. Model performance was evaluated using confusion matrix statistics and the Kappa coefficient, achieving an overall accuracy of 0.98 and a Kappa coefficient of 0.95. Feature importance analysis identified land surface temperature, enhanced vegetation index, soil moisture, and elevation as the most influential predictors, highlighting the combined influence of thermal, moisture, and topographic conditions on wildfire susceptibility across Yellowstone's geothermally active landscape. The resulting susceptibility map delineates persistent high-risk zones and provides a spatially explicit framework to support wildfire hazard assessment, environmental monitoring, and land management within YNP.

title: Floodplain Sediment Organic Carbon Response to River Restoration

authors: Johaneman, Taylor M [1], Lininger, Katherine B [2], Fields, Jordan F [3], Landis, Joshua D [4]

abstract: Carbon sequestration by river restoration has been pitched as a potentially important natural climate solution in recent years, but we currently lack the data and knowledge to predict the response of floodplain organic carbon (OC) dynamics to river restoration. We investigated the impact of river restoration on floodplain sediment OC storage and accrual rates on Ninemile Creek (Montana, USA) which was degraded by repeated placer mining over the last century. Restoration led by Trout Unlimited has restored channel-floodplain connectivity by resetting the valley bottom along different reaches of the creek from 2014 to 2024. Using a space-for-time approach, we evaluated floodplain sediment OC accrual and changes in storage across reaches restored at different times throughout the past decade. In each reach, we delineated ecogeomorphic units (EGUs) – floodplain patches characterized by distinct geomorphology and vegetation – to account for the potential difference in local fluvial ecogeomorphic processes that influence floodplain sediment OC dynamics. We collected sediment samples from EGUs in five reaches: three restoration reaches (restored in 2014, 2018, 2022), a reach that was not restored, and a reach that was not impacted by placer mining. To determine sediment OC storage, we used an element analyzer to measure OC content (percent by mass) and, using bulk density values and alluvial thickness measurements, we calculated sediment OC stock (Mg C per ha) for each sampling location. We utilized fallout radionuclides – 7 Be and 210 Pb – to determine deposition dates and estimate OC accrual rates of each EGU. Preliminary results show an increase in floodplain sediment OC storage with time since restoration. Total sediment OC stock in the 2014 restoration reach was greater than the unrestored reach and similar to that of the reach unaffected by placer mining. Our results provide evidence for increased floodplain OC storage as a co-benefit of river restoration. This work will inform resource management decisions regarding river restoration by providing insights into how sediment OC changes with restoration and over what timescales.

title: Basin and Range Faulting Bites into the Northern California Cascades: Offsets and Time Documented by Argon Geochronology of Faulted, Tholeiitic Basalt

abstract: The axis of the Cascade magmatic arc in northern California runs between the major volcanic centers of Mt. Shasta, to the west, and Medicine Lake, to the east, and this portion of the arc axis has erupted hundreds of times over the past 1500 kyrs (R.L. Christiansen, unpublished mapping). Arc-axis eruptions were mostly of calc-alkalic andesites that built small-to-moderate sized edifices, but 1500-950 ka the large Rainbow Mountain stratovolcano grew along the axis, before Mt. Shasta and Medicine Lake volcanoes existed. Rainbow Mountain ceased erupting 950-700 ka whereupon arc-front volcanism shifted 20 km west and began building Mt. Shasta along the westernmost identified Basin and Range normal fault. Medicine Lake Volcano likely commenced in the rear arc 700-500 ka. From 1500 ka to present, there have been at least ten voluminous eruptions of low-viscosity, low-potassium olivine tholeiite (LKOT). Each LKOT eruption was brief and temporally separate, as evinced the lavas’ distinct paleomagnetic directions and limited dispersion. Most LKOTs vented from a zone of regional normal faults trending generally N20°W, just east of the main arc axis; their eruptions effused 0.1-0.5 km 3 of lava that flowed to 40 km from source vents and covered to 90 km 2 of lowland areas. The broad areas, thin flows, and flat surfaces make the LKOTs excellent strain markers, contrasting with the abundant, small andesitic edifices that overlap irregularly, providing limited stratigraphic control. 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages permit calculation of the rates of vertical fault offsets. The basalt of McCloud River erupted northeast of Mount Shasta at ~27 ka and is now offset locally by normal faults to nearly 20 m. Farther east, the ~200 ka basalt of Tennant records offsets as great as 60 m. The ~400 ka basalt of Nitwit Camp is offset more than 50 m. The ~890 ka basalt of Algoma is offset up to 60 m. The ~1480 ka basalt of Dead Horse Summit is offset by as much as 90 m. LKOT eruptions generally progressed westward with time and may record incursion of the Basin and Range province into the Cascades over the past 1500 kyrs.

title: The Origins and Drivers of Methane Emissions from Orphaned Oil and Gas Wells
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Zierer, Deron [1], Fryar, Alan E. [2], Washburn, Alex Matthew [3], Reynolds, Amanda C. [4], High, Madison [5], Hawksley, Andrew [6], Rivers, Monte [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Kentucky, Kentucky Geological Survey, Lexington, KY, ; Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY,

(5) University of Kentucky, Kentucky Geological Survey, Lexington, KY, ; Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky,
(6) University of Kentucky, Kentucky Geological Survey, Lexington, KY, USA

abstract:
Kentucky’s tradition of oil and gas development spans more than 200 years, with the first discovery of oil in 1818. The Commonwealth currently has approximately 16,000 documented orphaned oil and gas wells (OOGWs). Many of these emit methane, a flammable and potent greenhouse gas. We are measuring methane emission rates and natural gas compositions of OOGWs across the state to better understand methane sources and identify if additional data may yield insights into methane emission trends. Measured OOGWs show variability in emission rates and emission compositions. Multiple factors, including gas sources, subsurface conditions, and surface mining, may contribute to this variability. To better predict emissions, a more in-depth geologic understanding of their origins is required. This information could ultimately be used in the prioritization of plugging and potential repurposing of OOGWs.

Kentucky can be split into three geologic provinces: the Appalachian Basin on the east and the Illinois Basin on the west, separated by the Cincinnati Arch. Methane emission rates have been measured at 450 OOGWs across all three provinces. Our measurements indicate a wide range of emission rates, from 6.0 × 10 −8 to 3,571.5 g/hr. Currently, the top 10% of wells account for 90% of the cumulative emissions rate.

To better understand the origins of these emissions, 16 representative samples have been collected for isotopic analysis. Natural gas samples from OOGWs have been analyzed for gas wetness, δ 13 C-CH 4 , δ 2 H-CH 4 , and δ 13 C-CO 2 to source the gas. Of the 16 analyzed wells, isotopic analysis suggests that the producing formation alone does not explain the variability observed and that the origin of gases is complex. For sampled gases, stable isotopic compositions ranged from −47.95 ‰ to −61.67 ‰ for δ 13 C-CH 4 , −179.8‰ to −291.9‰ for δ 2 H-CH 4 , and −11.9‰ to −21.3‰ for δ 13 C-CO 2 .

Sampled gases generally fell within the zone characteristic of thermogenic and microbial mixing. However, additional processes appear to contribute to the range of isotopic compositions, including biodegradation of petroleum and thermochemical sulfate reduction. Coal mining operations in proximity to OOGWs also have produced a dominantly microbial methane signal. Thus, our preliminary results suggest that both thermogenic and biologic sources contribute to methane emissions from OOGWs in Kentucky.

title: El Futuro del Uso de Energía Renovable y su Impacto Climático, Social y Económico en Tierra del Fuego, Sur de Chile
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part II)
authors: Mora-Klepeis, Gabriela [1], Klepeis, Keith A. [2], Klepeis, Peter J. [3], López-Maldonado, Jorge [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Geosciences, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
(2) Geography and Geosciences, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
(3) Geography, Colgate University, Hamilton, NY, USA
(4) López-Maldonado Consulting, Punta Arenas, Magallanes, Chile
abstract:
La implementación del uso de recursos naturales renovables requiere del entendimiento de la geología y del impacto en el cambio climático, social y económico de la región. Los depósitos sedimentarios en la Cuenca de Magallanes en Tierra del Fuego y los alrededores han sido la fuente primordial de hidrocarburos en la región. El acceso al mar y vientos de más de 120 kph junto con el préstamo del Banco Mundial al gobierno de Chile, fomentaron instalaciones de turbinas de viento que son necesarias para la producción de ‘hidrógeno verde’. Este proceso usa la fuerza eólica para la desalinización de agua marina que es necesaria para producir hidrógeno y oxígeno por medio de electrólisis. Compañías extranjeras (especialmente Europeas) empezaron a invertir en el desarrollo de esta tecnología en Tierra del Fuego. El enfoque de nuestro estudio es entender si existe un balance entre los beneficios y los impactos negativos en el paisaje natural y sus efectos en el ambiente, la sociedad y la economía de la región.

Entrevistas conducidas a residentes, agentes gubernamentales, científicos, representantes de diversas industrias y protectores del medio ambiente en los últimos 2 años muestran puntos extremos sobre la implementación de hidrógeno verde. Opiniones positivas incluyen el desarrollo económico, creación de trabajos y reducción de emisiones de carbón. En contraste se desconoce el grado de contaminación generada por la desalinización de agua marina, el impacto a las aves en peligro de extinción por las turbinas y la carencia de infraestructura para apoyar trabajadores. Los críticos consideran que este movimiento beneficia desproporcionalmente a los inversionistas extranjeros con gran costo a las comunidades locales y al medio ambiente.

Un mejor entendimiento de la transición al uso de energía renovable debe incluir estudios transparentes de las partes beneficiadas con este cambio. La impresión general es que la implementación favorece inversionistas europeos y líderes políticos de la industria chilena. Beneficios económicos y laborales a nivel local parecen limitados. Para facilitar la transición es importante consultar científicos ambientales, buscar un balance entre el desarrollo regional y la población local, integrar perspectivas de las partes afectadas y mejorar el desarrollo de la población. El cambio de gobierno este año presenta retos al futuro de la industria y al desarrollo económico de la región.

title: Disentangling Redox and Water-Management Effects on Rice Soil Chemistry
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes (Posters)
authors: Hanington, Connor [1], Mehling, Zoe [2], Day, Arionna [3], Vega, Michael [4], Rohila, Jai S [5], Reid, Matthew C [6], Maguffin, Scott C [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, NY, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, New York, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, NY, USA
(4) School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithica, NY, USA
(5) USDA-ARS, Dale Bumpers National Rice Research Center, Stuttgart, AZ, USA
(6) School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Cornell University, Ithica, NY, USA
(7) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, NY, USA
abstract:
Rice feeds roughly half the world's population, yet its cultivation must balance conserving water, limiting soil trace gas fluxes, curbing accumulation of toxic elements such as arsenic (As) and cadmium (Cd), and preserving grain micronutrients. Unlike the commonly used continuous flooding, alternate wetting and drying (AWD) can address several at once, but it drives redox swings that couple element and nutrient chemistry in complex, hard-to-disentangle ways. Dry-down oxidizes iron and manganese, precipitating oxides that can sequester oxyanions such as arsenate while shifting the availability of cationic micronutrients (Zn, Mn, Fe, Cu); reflooding reverses these changes. Our prior field studies documented these tradeoffs but were confounded by rainfall and seasonal weather, obscuring how redox and dry-down timing govern soil and grain chemistry.

To partition these effects, we reconstructed paddy environments in a controlled growth chamber, growing rice (cv. Katy) in two silt loam soils from contrasting U.S. rice regions, New York and Arkansas, under continuous flooding and AWD (a 2x2 design, three replicates). We continuously logged soil redox potential, volumetric water content, and temperature, and sampled pore water for pH and chemistry, testing whether intrinsic soil properties (organic matter, cation exchange capacity, reactive Fe/Mn content, and acidity) govern the rate and extent of redox shifts and, in turn, the partitioning of arsenic against essential micronutrients.

Under identical continuous flooding, the two soils established markedly different geochemical regimes: the Arkansas soil turned strongly reducing (mean redox potential near -380 mV) and circumneutral, whereas the New York soil stayed less reducing and more variable (near -250 mV, with recurring oxidizing excursions) and about 0.8 pH units more acidic. Because flooding was identical, this contrast isolates a soil-type effect; the AWD treatments will test the water-regime role. Grain and pore-water total-element concentrations and arsenic speciation are being quantified to test whether these soil-specific redox regimes open distinct dry-down windows that immobilize arsenic without stranding micronutrients. Resolving those windows will be a step toward site-tailored irrigation for safer, more nutritious rice.

title: The Fingerprint of Fire on Quartz Luminescence in the Critical Zone
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution
authors: Rittenour, Tammy [1], Tanski, Natalie [2], Johnstone, Samantha [3], Dib, Brooklyn [4], Phinney, April [5], Strange, Michael [6]
affiliations: (1) Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA

(3) Utah State University, LOGAN, UT, USA

abstract: Fire is an important agent in shaping critical zone processes related to ecosystem dynamics, sediment generation and transport and hillslope hydrology. Remote sensing, geomorphic and hydrologic tools have been deployed to assess regions of greatest post-fire hazards from debris flows and landslides and to characterize the impact wildfires on catchments. Key to understanding the magnitude of post-fire hazards is to characterize fire intensity (heat energy released by combustion), which is commonly reflected as a burn severity metric based on impacts to vegetation. The luminescence sensitivity (intensity of luminescence signal generated per dose of absorbed radiation) of quartz sand may provide an alternate metric to characterize fire intensity and identify thermal exposure of soils and sediment. Although quartz sensitivity is partly controlled by source rock type, it is also enhanced through repeated exposure to Earth-surface processes during weathering, transport, and sediment recycling. Exposure of quartz sand to high thermal temperatures has been shown to change quartz sensitivity, perhaps in proportion to the intensity and duration of heat exposure. Here we compile quartz sensitivity results from surface soils that were exposed to a range of fire conditions and compare with adjacent samples collected from non-burned settings. Results test if the quartz in burned soils have greater luminescence sensitivity and if the magnitude of sensitivity is related to burn severity.

title: Geologic Hydrogen in Iowa: Background, Evidence of Recorded Occurrences, and Additional Frontiers
session_title: Advances in Understanding and Predicting the Geochemical and Microbiological Conversion and Transport of Hydrogen in Deep Geological Repositories
authors: Clark, Ryan [1], Honings, Joe [2]
affiliations: (1) Iowa Geological Survey, Iowa Geological Survey, Iowa City, IA, USA
(2) Iowa Geological Survey, Iowa City, IA, USA
abstract:
Driven by energy security, diversification, and low-carbon emissions interests, the global exploration for geologic hydrogen is underway. Water-rock interactions within mafic and ultramafic rocks, primarily through serpentinization, results in the generation of natural hydrogen over geologic time. The Midcontinent Rift System (MRS) and the Northeast Iowa Intrusive Complex (NEIIC) both contain enormous volumes of mafic igneous source rocks, which has placed Iowa in the spotlight for hydrogen exploration efforts. In 1969, gas samples were collected from four wells in the Vincent Structure, a structural dome overlying the MRS in north-central Iowa. Two of the four wells sampled recorded 33.7% and 96.3% molar hydrogen. Although Iowa lacks a fossil energy production industry, and the wealth of deep geologic data it yields, legacy seismic reflection and petrophysical information from sparse petroleum exploration and natural gas storage structures over the MRS may provide a glimpse into the geologic hydrogen system.

Characterization of the Vincent Structure began in the late 1950s, with over 70 holes drilled but only 21 deep enough to intersect the MRS. After several rounds of natural gas test injections, the site was deemed unfit for commercial development and abandonment began in the early 1970s. The hydrogen occurrences and relative abundance of subsurface data made Vincent the focal point for attempting to characterize the geologic hydrogen system. Legacy down-hole geophysical information was modernized to improve interpretation and correlation between wells. The response of petrophysical logs within interpreted zones of hydrogen accumulation demonstrate that the now obsolete neutron-gamma logging tool is sensitive to the presence of geologic hydrogen, but ancillary resistivity, acoustic, and density logs are necessary for further interpretation.

Results indicate hydrogen shows in multiple wells occur within the upper carbonate facies of the Eau Claire Formation. Offset of sedimentary units overlying MRS mafic rocks identified by well log correlations and a legacy 2D seismic profile reveal a nearby fault zone that could serve as a migration pathway. Evaluating the hydrogen system at the Vincent Structure is complicated by potential disturbance of accumulated hydrogen by natural gas test injection operations, lithologic variability, and a lack of robust gas sampling across the structure.

title: Paired Organic and Carbonate Carbon Isotope Chemostratigraphy of the Ireviken Biogeochemical Event from Measley Ridge, Ohio
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Cramer, Bradley Douglas [1], Skelley, Emma [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
abstract:
During the Silurian Period, the Ireviken Biogeochemical Event (IBE) was a major disruption to the global carbon cycle including an expansion of reducing environments and an extinction event. The IBE spans the Llandovery-Wenlock boundary, and the initiation of the event serves as a useful chronostratigraphic marker for the base of the Wenlock Series. Specifically, the organic and carbonate carbon isotope excursions associated with the IBE are an excellent chronostratigraphic marker that have been widely utilized for global chronostratigraphic correlation.

The Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) for the base of the Wenlock Series is located at Hughley Brook in the United Kingdom, but this GSSP is currently under revision and a new location to place the GSSP is being sought. The current re-evaluation of the base Wenlock GSSP has initiated a search for potential Standard Auxiliary Boundary Stratotypes (SABSs) that may serve as important additional regional correlation tools for this position. The Measley Ridge outcrop in southern Ohio is a potential SABS candidate. Here, we present new paired organic and carbonate carbon isotope chemostratigraphy from the Measley Ridge section that clearly show the IBE in these strata and demonstrate that the carbon isotopic signature of this event can serve as an excellent chronostratigraphic marker for the base of the Wenlock Series.

title: Natural tracer study to identify sources of water supporting the Santa Cruz River headwaters and adjacent wetlands in southern AZ at the US-Mexico border
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Munari, Fernanda [1], McIntosh, Jennifer C. [2], Salywon, Andrew [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(3) Desert Botanical Garden, Phoenix, AZ, USA
abstract: Headwater streams and adjacent wetlands anchor riverscapes and are hotspots of plant and wildlife diversity. Yet the sources of water supporting them, and how those sources are changing under increasing stress, remain poorly understood. Spring-fed freshwater, mid-elevation wetlands (ciénegas) and baseflow in streams fed by regional groundwater (e.g., basin-fill aquifers) with relatively long transit times may be impacted by groundwater pumping and lowering of regional water tables. Surface waters and shallow groundwater recharged by more recent, local precipitation (e.g., alluvial aquifers) may be more sensitive to drought, shifts in precipitation patterns, and increases in evapotranspiration (ET). The San Rafael Valley (SRV) is one of the last untouched grassland ecosystems in the United States and contains the headwaters of the Santa Cruz River with adjacent ciénegas, serving as a critical wildlife corridor along the U.S.-Mexico border. Despite its ecological and hydrologic importance, few studies have characterized the source waters of the SRV’s regional and riparian aquifer systems. An initial study of sixteen wells, springs, and river sites across the SRV found that recharge is dominated by summer monsoon precipitation with little evaporative enrichment, and that tritium concentrations reveal a mix of modern and premodern groundwater, with premodern water more prevalent near springs and the Santa Cruz River. The SRV showed dominance of summer monsoon recharge compared to other basins across southern AZ, leading to questions about the fate of winter precipitation. This study is continuing to collect spatially-distributed water chemistry, isotope, and age tracer data from wells and springs across the valley and the Santa Cruz River to better characterize the locations, seasonality, and extent of groundwater recharge sustaining these headwaters, and how stressors such as groundwater pumping, drought, and vegetation change are altering them. Results of this study will inform how these biologically important riparian ecosystems, and the resources that depend on them, may respond to prolonged drought punctuated by more extreme monsoon storm events.

title: Raman Spectroscopy as a Novel Tool for Determining Apatite Halogen Compositions: Insights Into Halogen Migration Throughout the Subduction Cycle
