authors: Ferrell, Megan E. [1], Odlum, Margo [2], Haertel, Birk [3], Kazimierczak, Mina [4], Poulaki, Eirini M. [5], Condit, Cailey B. [6]
affiliations: (1) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
(2) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
(4) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
(5) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
(6) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract: Halogens are strongly incompatible, fluid-mobile, and volatile elements that enhance the ability of hydrothermal fluids to dissolve and transport metal ions, high-field-strength elements, large-ion lithophile elements, and rare-earth elements (REEs) between Earth’s reservoirs. During subduction, halogens are cycled out of enriched surface reservoirs into various hydrous mineral phases, where they are either released in halogen-bearing fluids during devolatilization reactions or transported back into the mantle as slab residue. However, the mantle remains relatively depleted in halogens, and current models of global halogen cycling reveal a deficit in arc outputs compared to trench inputs, highlighting significant gaps in our understanding of halogen transport and storage during subduction. Apatite readily incorporates fluid-mobile elements, including REEs and halogens. Combined with its susceptibility to dissolution-reprecipitation reactions and stability across a wide range of P-T conditions, this makes apatite a robust tracer of geochemical processes and halogen redistribution in subduction zones. This work combines Raman spectroscopy, a relatively new tool for estimating halogen concentrations in apatite, with electron probe microanalysis and apatite U-Pb petrochronology data from the Catalina Schist, Peninsular Ranges Batholith (PRB), and Point Loma Formation to investigate halogen behavior throughout the subduction cycle. Detrital apatite from the Upper Cretaceous forearc sediments of the Point Loma Formation preserves a range of halogen compositions representing pre-subduction trench inputs. In the Catalina Schist, apatite halogen compositions are similar within each unit but vary between units with different P-T conditions. Apatite from lawsonite- and epidote-blueschist facies rocks exhibits low Cl and OH contents consistent with low-grade devolatilization and dehydration. In contrast, metasomatic apatite from the Epidote-Amphibolite Unit is the most OH-rich, consistent with hydrous metasomatism by Ca-rich fluids during prograde metamorphism. Within the Amphibolite Unit, apatite from a migmatitic paragneiss is nearly anhydrous and F-rich, reflecting dehydration and crystallization during partial melting. Magmatic apatite from the PRB is predominantly F-rich but has higher Cl concentrations than apatite from the Catalina Schist. Our new observations support previous work suggesting that most Cl hosted in hydrous mineral phases is lost before or during blueschist-facies metamorphism and that apatite may record (de)hydration reactions during subduction. Together, these results reveal systematic changes in apatite halogen compositions during the subduction cycle, demonstrating the utility of apatite as a tracer for halogen redistribution.

title: A Total Evidence Phylogeny of Carcharhiniformes Sharks Since the Cretaceous Using Dental Morphological Characters and Genomic Data
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology
authors: Kane, Miriam Elaine [1], Gates, Terry [2], Simões, Tiago [3]
affiliations: (1) Biology, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA
(2) Biology, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA
(3) Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA
abstract:
Total evidence phylogenetics is a powerful tool that allows the inference of time-calibrated phylogenies of extant and extinct lineages using both morphological and genomic data in an integrated, simultaneous framework. Historically, total evidence phylogenetics has not been used on sharks due to the limited morphological data available from teeth—the predominant anatomical feature preserved in the fossil record and assumed high intraspecific variability of tooth morphology. Here we provide what is by far the largest total-evidence phylogenetic dataset of Carcharhiniformes sharks, incorporating 128 taxa (22 fossils) across 15 genes and 194 dental characters, assessed with relaxed-clock Bayesian inference in MrBayes (version 3.2.7a) under various partitioning schemes.

Within the total evidence tree, two polytomies appear: one located at the Carcharhiniformes root (directly following the split of the most basal taxa) and a second within the genus Carcharhinus. Resolving the polytomy at the Carcharhiniformes root and within Carcharhinus will require further fossil and genomic data. The current analysis posits the fastest evolutionary rate at the branch encompassing the clades Carcharhinidae, Sphyrnidae, Galeocerdonidae, and Hemigaleidae, which is dated by our tree at approximately 125.23 Ma. Fossil Negaprion (lemon shark) taxa are scattered throughout Carcharhinidae, Triakidae, and within more basal sharks, which we hypothesize is caused by their more generic dental morphology and could therefore represent the ancestral condition for these families. Additionally, in this study, Carcharhinidae is paraphyletic by the inclusion of Sphyrnidae. This ambiguous relationship between Sphyrnidae and Carcharhinidae is not without precedent, as the genus Carcharhinus has previously been classified within Sphyrnidae.

Compared to estimates from recent genomic models, the total evidence tree alters divergence times significantly, which represents its most substantial impact. The root age shifts from 251 Ma to 188 Ma in this study. Furthermore, the divergence between Lamniformes and Carcharhiniformes is relocated from 166.7 Ma to 182.24 Ma, which pushes the Carcharhinidae divergence back to 117.4 Ma, in contrast to the 61.6 Ma age estimated by genomic trees. Ultimately, integrating the prolific fossil record and contemporary molecular datasets via morphology opens the door to more accurate reconstructions of shark evolutionary history.

title: Connecting People to Place: A Community Engagement Model for Advancing Geoheritage Stewardship
session_title: GSA Noontime Lecture: Marilyn Russell and Sabrina Kainz
authors: Russell, Marilyn [1], Kainz, Sabrina Josephine [2]
affiliations: (1) La Veta Trails, La Veta, CO,

abstract:
Scientific research has the greatest potential to influence conservation when it is accessible, relevant, and connected to the communities who live within the landscapes it seeks to understand. The Geoheritage of Huerfano and Las Animas Counties Initiative is a partnership between La Veta Trails and the University of Colorado Thermochronology Research and Instrumentation Laboratory (CU TRaIL) that demonstrates how university-community collaboration can translate geoscience research into meaningful public engagement and long-term stewardship.

The initiative combines current geologic research with public trails, interpretive storytelling, regional history, and local culture to help residents and visitors develop a deeper understanding of the landscapes they experience. Community engagement efforts include a dedicated geoheritage web resource, interpretive trail guides that connect geologic processes to on-the-ground trail experiences, public presentations, guided hikes, and youth learning opportunities developed in partnership with the La Veta School. Together, these efforts help people move from experiencing a landscape to understanding its geologic story, strengthening their connection to place and encouraging stewardship.

This community engagement model positions geoheritage as a catalyst for education, collaboration, and conservation. By integrating scientific research with place-based learning and local partnerships, the initiative demonstrates how geoscience can foster community investment in protecting significant landscapes while offering a replicable framework for translating research into lasting public impact.

authors: Calvert, Andrew T. [1], Stelten, Mark Evan [2], Pivarunas, Anthony Francis [3], Grove, Marty [4], Burgess, Seth D. [5], Avery, Margaret [6]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA, USA

abstract:
Paleomagnetic, argon, and U-Th/Pb geochronologic laboratories work closely and iteratively with mapping geologists to correlate and reliably date disparate deposits, help compile them into coherent and age-ordered map units, and develop robust geologic histories. Following long histories in Menlo Park, the USGS laboratories were reestablished in 2024 at Moffett Field. Goals of these geologic maps and stratigraphic studies include understanding volcanic and seismic hazards, tectono-magmatic evolution, igneous and geothermal processes, and ore deposits. The laboratory work is generally iterative with the field mapping so discrepancies can be resolved.

The argon geochronology laboratory operates three mass spectrometers coupled with flexible extraction lines for heating single crystals and small (≤1 mg), moderate (100 mg), and very large (25 g) volcanic groundmass or mineral samples with lasers or furnaces. K-feldspar thermochronology is currently being implemented using continuous-ramp heated argon extractions for multi-domain diffusion modeling. The primary focus of the argon geochronology laboratory is on dating Miocene to Late Pleistocene (occasionally Holocene) volcanic materials, but we also work on older materials.

Trace-element characterization, and uranium-lead and uranium-thorium dating remains active at the nearby USGS-Stanford SHRIMP-RG facility. To supplement the in-situ work in instances when increased age precision is necessary, newly built clean room facilities at Moffett Field will enable preparation of low-blank splits for CA-ID-TIMS U and Pb isotopic measurements on the UC-Santa Cruz Keck Isotope Facility instrument.

The paleomagnetic laboratory utilizes an automated cryogenic magnetometer, thermal demagnetization ovens and shielded room for direction and intensity measurements, and a magnetic susceptibility system for basic rock magnetic characterization. The primary focus of this laboratory is correlating geologic units and assessing the rates of geologic processes. The automated capacities of this laboratory allow for rapid and inexpensive throughput that is valuable toward constructing geologic maps with stratigraphic frameworks constrained by spatially detailed mapping and precisely dated geologic units. Improved hand sample preparation and alternating field demagnetization methods are currently in development. Paleomagnetics is a highly complementary technique to both geochronology laboratories, since it can provide valuable relative refinements to the numerical ages produced by the radioisotopic methods.

abstract: Wildfire frequency in New Hampshire and New England has generally decreased in the past century, largely due to fire suppression and other anthropogenic land-management practices. This has led to an increase in natural debris on the forest floor, which could potentially be the kindling for increased fire risk and intense wildfires, especially considering projected climate changes in the region. Here we report on the radiocarbon dating, loss on ignition testing (LOI), magnetic susceptibility (MS), and charcoal analysis of a 4.9 m sediment core from Red Eagle Pond in Albany, NH. The sediments at the base transition from organic-poor silts, clays, and sands into organic-rich muds. This transition suggests the core spans watershed deglaciation following retreat of the Laurentide Ice Sheet (~14 ka) through the present. Initial MS measurements confirm this with higher minerogenic content lower in the core, transitioning to lower minerogenic content higher in the core. We are awaiting radiocarbon and 210 Pb ages to better constrain the core age model. Preliminary analyses indicate a consistent presence but variable concentrations of charcoal in the upper core sediments, suggesting that fire has persisted on the landscape in the younger portion of the record. Continued analysis of charcoal, LOI, and MS will give us a better understanding of Red Eagle Pond’s wildfire history. The completed reconstruction will improve our understanding of long-term wildfire variability and provide valuable insight for forest management strategies, prescribed burning practices, wildfire policy, and community resilience.

title: New Geochemical Analysis of Well-Preserved Cliff Outcrops of Seymour Island, Antarctica Provide Insights into Paleoenvironments Prior to the End Cretaceous Mass Extinction
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: Hautala, Isaac A. [1], Schoepfer, Shane D. [2], Lonski, Michaela [3], Heberlein, Marianne Gisela [4], Davis, Sean [5], Self-Trail, Jean M. [6], Lam, Adriane R. [7], Totten, Rebecca L. [8], Huber, Brian T. [9], Harwood, David M. [10], Coenen, Jason James [11], Tobin, Thomas S. [12]

(12) Department of Geosciences, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
abstract:
Seymour Island, located in the Weddell Sea of the NE Antarctic Peninsula, has an expanded stratigraphic record of the uppermost Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) through the lowermost Paleogene. Specifically, the López de Bertodano Formation (LBF), a shallow marine clastic shelf deposit, has been subject to decades of studies investigating the End Cretaceous Mass Extinction (ECME; ~66 Ma), including analyses of well-preserved macro- and microfossil records, and sedimentological and geochemical data. A major challenge to this work, especially for sedimentary geochemistry, is that a combination of intense freeze-thaw weathering at the surface and a deeper permafrost layer make acquisition of fresh samples difficult. Weathering affects geochemical data quality and obscures primary sedimentological features, particularly in unconsolidated mudstones. To address this shortcoming, the NSF funded CSI: Antarctica expedition aboard the R/V Sikuliaq sampled sediments from a cliff exposure along the southern shore of Seymour Island, where rapid erosion outpaces freeze-thaw weathering. New geochemical data from this exposure can evaluate the fidelity of prior studies and provide new insights about the environmental conditions leading up to and through the ECME.

In January/February 2026, we measured and sampled approximately 215 meters of stratigraphy spanning the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary (KPB). Bulk sediment samples (n=170) were sub-sampled for major and trace element concentration (XRF, ICP-MS) and subjected to grain characterization through thin section and grain size analyses. Preliminary XRF analyses reveal several intervals with elevated redox-sensitive trace element (V, U, As) concentrations indicative of anoxic bottom water conditions. Two of these intervals correspond to the glauconitic horizons at the base (~40 m; ~20% glauconite) and top (~200 m; ~30%) of “Unit 9” of the LBF, the latter of which is coincident with the KPB. Here, we hypothesize that anoxic conditions are indicative of ferruginous conditions due to the abundant iron-rich glauconite. Redox-sensitive trace element enrichments are present at a concretionary (~65% carbonate) horizon within “Unit 9” (~110m). We hypothesize that this horizon is a cold methane seep, with methanogenesis near the sediment-water interface reflecting low-oxygen conditions in sedimentary porewater.

The coincidence of iron-rich glauconite (suggesting an abundant supply of reactive ferrous Fe) with evidence for low-oxygen conditions and methanogenesis is consistent with low seawater sulfate concentrations during the Maastrichtian at Seymour Island. Future work includes further grain characterization and coupled ICP-MS data.

title: The Rusting Horton River - Climate Warming and Permafrost Thaw Driving Acidification of Water Ways in Arctic Canada
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Grasby, Stephen E. [1], Smith, I. Rod [2], Yuan, Wanju [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Survey of Canada, Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, AB, Canada
(2) Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
(3) Geological Survey of Canada, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
abstract: In the Smoking Hills (Ingniryuat) of Arctic Canada naturally occurring streams and ponds of hyperacidic (pH <−2) metal-rich brines (total dissolved solids up to 394,000 mg/L) are formed though oxidation of pyrite and metal-rich mudstones of the Late Cretaceous Smoking Hills Formation. Acid generation occurs through mass wasting of Smoking Hills Formation mudstones due to coastal erosion and stream undercutting, as well as permafrost thaw and ground-ice melt. Water which comes in contact with the slumped mudstones rapidly changes chemistry, becoming acidic, metal-rich, and opaque orange due to precipitation of Fe-sulfates.These hyperacidic metal-rich waters discharge to larger river systems and are transported to the Arctic Ocean. We suggest that climate warming may increase slumping and associated debris flows, impound more surface ponds and stream courses, generate more acid waters, amplify toxic-metal flux to the environment, and ultimately be a driver of "river rusting.”

title: Project EMPRESS – Electron Microscopy of Primitive Remnants of the Early Solar System – Recruiting Young Scientists Through Research Experience
session_title: Planetary Potpourri (Posters)
authors: Kropff, Heidi [1], Friehauf, Kurt [2]
affiliations: (1) Chemistry, Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
(2) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
abstract:
Contrary to common misconception, being an effective scientist is less about memorizing facts and more about making mindful observations and thinking creatively (i.e., asking novel questions, creatively posing possible explanations, and designing methods to objectively test hypotheses). Most of the process of research is spent in a state of heightened uncertainty, and for people willing to weather the discomfort of that uncertainty, the reward of discovery is exhilarating!

We propose that middle and high school students who experience the reward of weathering through such uncertainty will be motivated to consider lives as scientists and may be more successful as scientists because they chose the path with realistic expectations.

Project EMPRESS provides high school students (participants) with hands-on research experience using high-tech instrumentation to experience firsthand what scientific research feels like. This experience aims to help young people develop confidence in scientific research and discover that science is driven by curiosity, not the need to have all the answers.

Pre- and post-experience surveys characterized participants’ perceptions of science. College students (mentors) guided participants in operating both the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and the Energy Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS).

Participants studied four types of meteorites: chondrite, metallic, pallasite, and achondrite, representing four major materials in the early solar system. We weren’t focused on teaching the information – Meteorites were just a venue chosen because space is a topic that naturally interests many students.

Mentors emphasized that participants drive the inquiry – choosing what to analyze and interpreting the data – to maximize the immersive experience. College mentors guided participants using a Socratic approach – asking questions rather than proclaiming answers. Participants described orally and in surveys their discomfort with not knowing the “right answer,” but maintained close engagement throughout the experience.

After completing their analyses, participants designed large-format research presentation posters using their own SEM imagery and chemical data. Participants kept their printed posters for sharing with their classmates at their schools.

Future iterations of Project EMPRESS will involve longer and more research times, keeping in mind potential challenges of scheduling conflicts with after-school activities. We also plan to work with a class remotely (operating the instrumentation through the internet with imagery projected onto the classroom screen). This could be particularly helpful for reaching young people in rural communities.

title: A new species of compsemydid turtle from the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah, USA
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Rollot, Yann [1], Lyson, Tyler [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Denver Museum of Nature & Science, Denver, Colorado, USA; Department of Biomedical Sciences, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University, Athens, Ohio, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, Denver Museum of Nature & Science, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Compsemydidae is a clade of extinct, aquatic turtles from North America and Europe. Compsemys Leidy, 1856 was the sole genus known for nearly 150 years based on fossils from the Campanian to early Paleocene of North America, and only over the last 15 years have new taxa been described from the Late Jurassic to Paleocene of Europe. In its most inclusive definition, the group includes up to eight species, but its phylogenetic relationships and the taxonomic affinities of some of these taxa are still debated. Compsemys victa is a relatively common component of the fossil record of turtles in North America that can easily be distinguished from other turtles by its unique shell surface ornamentation, which consists of a dense pattern of round and flattened tubercles separated by narrow grooves. However, complete shells are rare and the vast majority of remains reported in the literature consist of isolated fragments, which prevent thorough study of the anatomy and evolutionary history of the group in North America. While it is likely that more than a single taxon lived from the Late Cretaceous to Paleocene of North America, all of the Campanian to early Paleocene fragmentary fossils have been attributed to Compsemys victa pending the discovery of more complete specimens.

We here provide the description of a new compsemydid turtle based on three partial shells from the Kaiparowits Formation (Upper Campanian) of Utah. This new taxon notably shares with Compsemys victa the presence of a cervical scute, a humeral-pectoral scute sulcus that crosses the entoplastron, and a sinuous midline scute sulcus on the plastron, but differs from the latter by the presence of two suprapygals and a novel arrangement of the tubercles on the shell surface. Our phylogenetic analyses retrieved the new compsemydid as sister taxon to Compsemys victa , and these two taxa are the most derived compsemydids. Finally, we also discuss variation in shell ornamentation and highlight different arrangements of the tubercles on the surface of the shell of compsemydids.

title: El Uso de Isótopos Estables de Carbono para Aclarar la Producción Primaria de Microbialitos de la Formación Gamohaan (2.52 Ga), Sudáfrica
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part I)
authors: Alatorre-Acevedo, Eduardo [1], Sumner, Dawn Y. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California,Davis, Davis, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA,
abstract:
In modern microbial mats, autotrophic and heterotrophic microbial communities each influence the local Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC) pool as they metabolize carbon and cycle nutrients. Local changes in DIC can be preserved in the stable carbon isotope ratio of calcite (δ 13 C cal ). The δ 13 C cal can preserve evidence of metabolisms that were active through time and space within a microbial mat. Modern microbialites growing in lakes of the Antarctic McMurdo Dry Valleys are analogous to fenestrate microbialites from the 2.52 billion year old Gamohaan Formation, South Africa. These modern analogs are a guide for targeted δ 13 C measurements of different structures within ancient fenestrate microbialites.

Samples from 4 stratigraphic locations in the Gamohaan Formation were microdrilled to collect carbonate powder from three textures within the microbialites: microspar, herringbone, and bladed/blocky calcite. The microspar calcite is associated with organic inclusions that define vertically oriented planar structures called microbial supports by prior researchers. Herringbone calcite is interpreted as a marine cement that directly precipitated on the seafloor, including on microbial communities. Bladed/blocky calcite precipitated on herringbone calcite and is interpreted as a burial void-filling cement. The microspar calcite has a δ 13 C range of -1.12‰ to 0.80‰ and an average δ 13 C of 0.09‰ vs bladed/blocky calcite, which had a range of -0.60‰ to -0.06‰ and an average of -0.35‰. The herringbone calcite has a δ 13 C range of -0.69‰ to 0.46‰ and an average δ 13 C of -0.10‰. All δ 13 C cal values are reported in standard delta notation relative to VPDB. ANOVA and Tukey's HSD tests show that there is a statistically significant difference between δ 13 C of the microspar calcite and the bladed/blocky calcite with a P-value of 0.00.

In combination with other published geochemical and sedimentological data, we interpret the δ 13 C enrichment found in the microspar calcite of the microbial supports as a signature for an autotrophic metabolism, likely oxygenic photosynthesis. This interpretation implies that an oxygen oasis was present within the deep subtidal facies of the 2.52 billion old Gamohaan Formation, approximately 100 million years before the oxygenation of the Earth’s atmosphere.

title: Finding the Haystack Before the Needle: DORA as Geoarchaeological Method and Pedagogy in the Search for Late Pleistocene Sites
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Davis, Loren [1]
affiliations: (1) Oregon State University, Department of Anthropology, Corvallis, OR, USA
abstract: Archaeological discovery can be aided by embracing the “Dirt of the Right Age” approach, or DORA. As one of the pillars of geoarchaeological method and theory, DORA practitioners recognize that the search for early sites begins with understanding where deposits, soils, and landforms of the appropriate age are preserved, exposed, buried, eroded, or absent. These contexts may contain archaeological materials directly or preserve stratigraphic associations with them. Rolfe Mandel’s work in the Great Plains helped establish this approach as a practical framework for targeting Late Pleistocene archaeological sites, where archaeological visibility depends as much on landscape history as on human behavior. This paper builds on that foundation by considering DORA as both a research strategy and a teaching framework for geoarchaeology and First Americans archaeology. The search for DORA begins with a simple but powerful question: where are Late Pleistocene deposits preserved, exposed, buried, eroded, or absent within a given landscape? Rather than assuming that early artifacts will be visible on the modern ground surface, or even within reach of manual test excavations, the approach first seeks to identify sedimentary contexts that could contain or be associated with archaeological materials of the right age. This deposit-first strategy is especially useful in landscapes where early archaeological records are deeply buried, discontinuous, or obscured by later site formation processes. Drawing on research from the Willamette Valley of western Oregon, this paper presents two case studies that demonstrate how DORA can guide the search for Late Pleistocene archaeological contexts. As pedagogy, DORA helps students move beyond artifact-focused discovery models and toward a deeper understanding of archaeological visibility, site formation, geomorphology, and landscape history. It teaches students that finding early sites requires learning how sediments record time, process, and preservation. In this sense, DORA reflects and extends Mandel’s contributions to geoarchaeology by treating the search for Late Pleistocene sites as both a meaningful scientific and educational process: find the dirt of the right age before looking for the artifacts.

title: From Science to Scoring: United States Federal Cleanup Priority and Groundwater Transport Assumptions in Fractured-Rock Systems
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Hinojosa, Blanca E [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Colorado Boulder, Environmental Studies, Boulder, Colorado,
abstract:
CERCLA’s Hazard Ranking System (HRS) is the United States federal scoring mechanism that determines Superfund cleanup priority. Its groundwater pathway relies on transport assumptions developed for continuous, porous-media aquifers in humid climates. In fractured rock and arid regional settings such as the Colorado Plateau, contamination instead moves through discrete fracture networks and can surface at springs, seeps, or private wells located outside the distances these assumptions anticipate. This talk examines how that difference in transport behavior interacts with HRS’s scoring criteria.

Using statutory and regulatory analysis alongside documented case studies, this talk describes how HRS’s municipal well definitions and fixed evaluation zone radii determine which groundwater sources are scored under the groundwater pathway. In one site, a community’s shallow-well drinking water source fell outside these criteria and was not scored under the groundwater pathway despite documented uranium contamination. I present this and comparable cases to illustrate how current evaluation zone distances may not capture contamination transport patterns observed in fractured-rock hydrogeology.

Based on this analysis, I propose extending HRS’s standard groundwater evaluation radius from four miles to ten miles for sites in fractured-rock and arid-region settings, a change consistent with existing CERCLA statutory authority. This talk presents the technical and regulatory basis for that proposal and is intended for hydrogeologist, agency scientists, and policy researchers working on groundwater characterization and federal cleanup criteria.

title: Mineralogical and Elemental Characterization of Niagaran Group Reef-Flank Facies for Lateral Confining Potential, Kalkaska Co., MI
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Price, Mallory [1], Scott, Ashley [2], Haagsma, Autumn [3], Conner, Amber [4], Atilhan, Mert [5], Kaczmarek, Stephen [6]
affiliations: (1) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, Michigan, USA
(2) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, Michigan, USA; Michigan Geological Survey, Kalamazoo, Michigan, USA
(3) Michigan Geological Survey, Kalamazoo, Michigan, Uzbekistan
(4) Michigan Geological Survey, Kalamazoo, Michigan, USA
(5) Chemical and Paper Engineering, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, Michigan, USA
(6) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, Michigan, USA
abstract:
The Pinnacle Reefs of the Silurian Niagaran Group have been the focus of numerous petroleum and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) studies throughout the Michigan Basin. The reef structures have been prolific oil and gas producers and are actively used for CO 2 enhanced oil recovery (EOR). Despite the attention received, few studies have focused on evaluating lateral characteristics of the reefs, as most work has been focused on the central reef reservoirs and their vertical confining units. Understanding the lateral flanks of the reefs is essential information for drill permitting and subsurface management.

This study utilizes a high-resolution approach to evaluate lateral mineralogical and elemental variability of two cores along the Northern Reef Trend: State Kalkaska 1-15, located on the windward distal reef flank, and the Kalkaska 1-23 positioned in the regional inter-reef zone. Carbonate mudstones, wackestones, and conglomerate facies comprise both cores. Bulk-rock elemental analysis using portable X-Ray Fluorescence (PXRF) show higher magnesium (Mg) concentrations in the reef flank facies, and lower Mg concentrations in the more distal inter-reef facies. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) identified relatively high abundance of dolomite [CaMg(CO 3 ) 2 ] in the reef flank core facies, which corresponds with the increase in Mg concentrations compared to the inter-reef region. Preliminary results show that intervals with more dolomite correlate with higher observed porosity.

This study highlights the advantage of a high-resolution elemental and mineralogical characterization in core work. Identification of patterns and trends in compositional data provides a framework that, when paired with thin section petrography, porosity, and permeability measurements, allows for a data-driven evaluation of the potential utility of these facies as lateral confining units in the Northern Reef trend of the Niagaran Group.

title: A diverse Early Ordovician (Floian) trilobite fauna from the Eleanor River Formation, Nunavut, Arctic Canada, and resolution of century-old systematic issues
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Laird, Joshua D. [1], Adrain, Jonathan M. [2], Westrop, Stephen R. [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(3) University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Ingersoll, ON, USA
abstract: The trilobite fauna of the Early Ordovician (Floian; Blackhillsian) Eleanor River Formation of the Canadian Arctic has not been systematically treated since Poulsen’s initial work in 1946. New collections were made at historically surveyed localities at Sanddöla Creek and Bartlett Bay on eastern Ellesmere Island, and at Dundas Harbour on southeastern Devon Island. All three localities originally had published faunal lists indicating the presence of low diversity trilobite assemblages. The trilobite material is mostly disarticulated with few partially articulated individuals. Specimen preservation is generally good and without considerable exfoliation, despite variable abrasion and compaction in the dolomite mottled lime mudstone-wackestone matrix. The new collections reveal a species-rich shallow water fauna characteristic of the bathyurid biofacies. At least sixteen species are present, including asaphids, bathyurids, a cheirurid, dimeropygids, and pliomerids. Only Ischyrotoma anataphra Fortey, 1979, previously described from the Catoche Formation of Newfoundland, is known from elsewhere. Seven additional species are sufficiently well represented to be formally named. The two sampling regions are separated by over 500 km, but share multiple species. No species in the sampled interval on eastern Ellesmere Island are conspecific with those previously described from the correlative Nunatami and Canyon Elv Formations across the Nares Strait in Washington Land, Avannaata, northwestern Greenland. The fauna is similar in genus composition to many shallow water Floian assemblages of the eastern and southern Laurentian margins. Two longstanding systematic issues are resolved. A new genus is proposed for a group of species previously assigned to Jeffersonia Poulsen, 1927, and subsequently Cullisonia Loch, 2007. In addition, a new genus is proposed to replace Strotactinus Bradley, 1925, which we restrict to its lost type specimens. Reexamination of the Eleanor River Formation suggests that some available literature-based occurrence records of trilobite species richness may significantly underestimate the diversity present.

title: Taxonomy of Small Shelly Fossils from the Middle Cambrian Deadwood Formation, Black Hills, South Dakota
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Guilfoyle, Margaret [1], Selly, Tara [2], Bykova, Natalia Lee [3], Jacquet, Sarah M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA; X-ray Microanalysis Laboratory, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(4) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract:
The lower member of the Deadwood Formation was deposited in the Middle to Late Cambrian during the initial flooding of the craton from the Sauk II transgression. At Little Elk Creek near Nemo, South Dakota, a 20 m exposure of the lower member consists of a massive basal sandstone overlain by bioturbated maroon siltstones that grade upwards into greyish green glauconitic carbonates with sandstone interbeds. The upper portion of the section contains limestone intraformational conglomerates with glauconitic rinds, interbedded with glauconitic packstones. Previous work on the Deadwood trilobite assemblages place the Little Elk Creek outcrop within the Cedarina dakotaensis and Crepicephalus faunal zones within the Guzhangian Stage of the latest Middle Cambrian. Although previous work on Little Elk Creek trilobite assemblages is extensive, the broader paleocommunity, particularly its small shelly fossils and their unique taphonomy, warrants further investigation.

In total, 16 hand samples from the fossiliferous upper 9 m of sandstones and carbonates were macerated, and phosphatic and glauconitic microfossils picked from the residues. Herein an initial report of the taxonomic composition reveals abundant brachiopod, echinoderm, and small shelly fossil material; this is the first report of echinoderms from the Cambrian of South Dakota. Brachiopod genera typical of the upper Middle Cambrian, like Stilpnotreta and Dicellomus , are abundant. Identifiable echinoderm plates include edrioasteroid interradial oral frame plates and ambulacral flooring plates. Though abundant, the remaining echinoderm elements cannot be assigned with confidence due to poor preservation or non-distinctive morphology. These elements are left in open nomenclature. Elements of the paraconodont Prooneotodus rotundatus have also been recovered. The remaining fossils are more broadly assigned, or enigmatic, their identification complicated by unusual preservation. These include orthothecid hyoliths, chancelloriid spicules, and concave indeterminate plates. The latter are multi-layered plate-like elements with concave surfaces, concentric ribbed ornament, and rounded edges; these fossils are undocumented in the literature. Initial SEM EDS analyses reveal preservation of small shelly fossils via calcium phosphate, glauconite, and in some cases, both within the same fossil. This report expands the known diversity of the Deadwood Fm. and documents previously unreported taxa and preservational pathways, providing new insight into the history of Cambrian shallow-marine ecosystems.

title: Unraveling the Alteration of Early Earth Ecosystems: Metamorphosed Stromatolites from the 2.1 Ga Nash Fork Formation, Wyoming
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Cirigliano, Taylor M [1], Shapiro, Russell [2]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Chico, Chico, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science Department, California State University, Chico, Chico, CA, USA
abstract:
The purpose of this study was to analyze Paleoproterozoic stromatolite fossils within the Nash Fork Formation (Snowy Range, Wyoming) that have been subjected to multiple events of regional mountain building, localized diabase intrusions, and post-lithification weathering. The goal is to unravel the 2.1 billion year metamorphic and diagenetic history to build tools to understand the original condition of these stromatolites as geobiological targets.

The Nash Fork Formation is a prime target for study because it hosts relatively unaltered stromatolites adjacent to their metamorphically altered forms, providing a gradation of alteration. The Nash Fork Formation is the carbonate-rich unit of a thick sequence deposited on the southern margin of the Wyoming Craton in the Paleoproterozoic. Rifting occurred soon after formation of the stromatolites, and led to diabase intrusions. The entire margin was then subjected to regional greenschist metamorphism during the amalgamation of the Laurentian craton.

Data was collected during field mapping with a focus on relationships of stromatolite samples to variously thick diabase intrusions. Field data was analyzed with QGIS software to best quantify field relationships. Several dozen hand specimens were chosen from outcrops with a focus on the least surface weathered samples. Each was prepped with standard techniques to produce polished thin-sections for petrographic, reflected-light and scanning electron microscopy as well as elemental dispersive x-ray spectroscopy.

While all samples show some degree of alteration and loss of microfabrics, the variability was most pronounced in the level of secondary silicification, and the replacement of stromatolite lamination by actinolite and tremolite. Amphibole orientations are both aligned with lamination and preserved at an angle to bedding. The amount of amphibole replacement and iron content is directly related to distance from the intrusion.

This study will better inform our collective geologic knowledge and can aid in future identification of altered fossil structures. Throughout most of Earth history, the rock record has been in some way altered physically and chemically, and it is our objective to undue that alteration to better understand the story behind what we are seeing. Thus these results will impact studies of early Earth geobiology and potentially extraterrestrial macrostructural targets.

title: Paleoenvironmental Interpretation of the Upper Devonian Gordon Sand: Possible Record of the Dasburg Event
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Witt, Rowan [1], Weislogel , Amy [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
abstract:
The Gordon Sand is an informal unit of the Upper Devonian Venango Group that has been extensively drilled in several oil fields across northern West Virginia (e.g., Wileyville, Jackson-Stringtown), permitting a high-resolution stratigraphic correlation of these units across this part of the Acadian basin. To extend this correlation ~80 km toward the south within the context of a depositional model, we performed a detailed examination of a 41 ft Gordon Sand core extracted from a wildcat well (API# 4700701140 ) located in Braxton county, West Virginia.

Analysis of the core was performed through detailed cm-scale measurement and description.

Ten lithofacies were identified, with most lithofacies composed primarily of thick bedded (~0.5 m) fine-grained well-sorted sandstone, ranging from gray to purple to tan color. These sandstone beds often exhibit horizontal to inclined cross-lamination, and contain layers of rounded quartz pebbles and dark mud rip-up clasts at the base of beds. Sandstones were interbedded with thick (~0.3 to ~1m) dark wavy-lenticular laminated very fine sandstone and siliciclastic mudstone, along with thinner beds of black to purple laminated mudstone ranging from <2 cm to several centimeters in thickness. Mud-dominated intervals exhibited rare small marine fossils (brachiopods) along with a few trace fossils. In addition, mud-dominated intervals contained rounded granule to pebble clasts in thin horizontal laminations and thin conglomerate beds of 1-2 cm thick, along with rare load structures.

Overall the interpretation of these facies indicate a tidally-influenced shallow marine shelfal environment positioned along the southern extent of the Gordon Sand shoreline, with conglomerate representing coarse-grained influx during increased energy associated with storm weather conditions. Depositional environments record environmental change in response to sea level fluctuations, with sandstone beds deposited during lower sea level and interbedded mudstones deposited in anoxic offshore environments that developed during shoreline transgression. Based on prior conodont biostratigraphy of the Venango Group, the Gordon Sand records environmental conditions of the Dasberg event, a period associated with a minor extinction, ocean hypoxia and sea level fluctuations.

Further work to identify metal enrichment in shales through XRF analysis could support the proposition that the Gordon Sand is a record of the Dasberg event.

affiliations: (1) Climate Resilience Collaborative, School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI, USA

abstract:
Urban Honolulu, and Waikīkī specifically, was developed through large-scale early 20th century filling of coastal wetlands, and a dense network of underground infrastructure, including sewer mains, electrical and telecom conduits, storm drains, and basements, was subsequently constructed into that fill, much of it predating modern flood-resilience design standards. Local relative sea level has since risen roughly 0.15 m, based on the century-scale Honolulu tide gauge trend, raising the shallow water table and introducing a hazard distinct from surface inundation: direct groundwater contact with buried infrastructure, and associated changes to corrosion.

We characterize this process using eight shallow monitoring wells installed or occupied across Honolulu's Primary Urban Core in partnership with the Honolulu Board of Water Supply, six sited on artificial fill and two on native geology, to compare hydrogeologic behavior between fill and native substrate. Wells on fill already show critically shallow groundwater, less than 1.5 m below the surface. Each well's record is decomposed into component drivers, tides, non-tidal ocean forcing, rainfall recharge, and barometric pressure, using UTide harmonic analysis paired with Pastas transfer-function-noise modeling. Because tide and other stresses are collinear at wells with weak tidal signal, producing implausible results if estimated jointly, the tidal gain is fixed from independent harmonic analysis rather than estimated freely. Calibrated response functions are driven forward under NOAA's Intermediate Sea-Level Rise Scenario to project groundwater levels through 2100, classifying each well by decade as unaffected, storm-driven, chronically cyclic, or continuously submerged relative to infrastructure burial depths.

Fill wells already show storm-driven to continuous submersion of buried infrastructure at present, intensifying with sea-level rise to sporadic surface inundation beginning by the 2030s. Preliminary geochemical sampling has detected predominantly anoxic conditions at Waikīkī sites. At wells where specific conductance was measured over multiple months, it remained stable at 65–70% of seawater's strength, an extremely high corrosion risk for buried metal infrastructure. This is motivating ongoing work with the UH Corrosion Lab to relate substrate type and hydrogeologic regime to corrosion mechanisms affecting buried infrastructure in reclaimed coastal settings. These results offer a transferable framework for groundwater-driven infrastructure risk in reclaimed coastal cities worldwide.

title: Linking Remotely Sensed River Reflectance to Suspended Sediment Concentration in the Upper Colorado River Basin

abstract: Suspended sediment concentration (SSC) plays a critical role in river systems, influencing ecosystem health, water quality, and reservoir capacity. Measuring SSC within a reach remains challenging and time-consuming making basin-wide measurements infeasible. However, a river’s reflectance (i.e., color) can be monitored from remotely sensed images, where the reflectance is a combination of SSC, organic matter, and other particulate pollutants carried by the river. Here we focus on pairing individual sites within the Colorado and Green River basins with high-resolution SSC records (+10 years of 15-minute data) with remotely sensed imagery (Landsat and Sentinel) to determine which spectral variables, bands, and indices best predict SSC. Critically, we explore a collapse of the remotely sensed sediment relationships across sites by accounting for channel hydraulics, river discharge, near-channel attributes, and grain size. This single-site modeling approach enables robust sediment concentration estimation from reflectance data, from which patterns of changing sediment dynamics can be directly observed basin-wide. The high-resolution informed basin-wide snapshot represents a key step toward leveraging remote sensing for sediment flux prediction, concentration monitoring, and watershed management.

title: Leucogabbro in Lunar Meteorite Northwest Africa (NWA) 5000: Revisited
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials
authors: Treiman, Allan H. [1], Nagurney, Alexandra [2], Humayun, Munir [3], Petruccelli, Brianna [4]
affiliations: (1) Science, Lunar & Planetary Institute, Houston, TX,
(2) ION Clean Energy, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL,
(4) Dept. Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
The lunar meteorite Northwest Africa (NWA) 5000 consists mostly of fragments of leucogabbro – an impact melt rock that formed at ~4.2 Ga (Irving et al., 2008; Nagurney et al., 2016; Grange et al., 2016). The leucogabbro consists of approximately 70% anorthite, 11% olivine, 11% augite, 7% hypersthene, and 1% Fe-Ni metal. Mineral compositions are homogeneous across our sample, implying an extended post-igneous thermal history. Mineral compositions are consistent with a Mg-suite gabbronorite rock (An93, Mg#=75); the high proportion of anorthite suggests instead that the leucogabbro is mixture of gabbronorite and ferroan anorthosite (An96). The anorthite and olivine occur as euhedral-subhedral grains; the pyroxenes form vermiform extended crystals enclosing anorthite and olivine. Most of the metal is as circular or hemispherical masses, suggestive of molten droplets; merrillite all is in, or adjacent to, the metal. The metal composition is consistent with derivation from an ordinary chondrite impactor (e.g., Re/Os > CI; Pd/Pt < CI), with addition of W from the silicates and loss of P to merrillite.

Only ~2% of the lunar surface exposes leucogabbro-like rock (Sun et al., 2021), most of which is associated with the impact craters Tycho and Giordano Bruno. Both craters are too old to be ejection sites of NWA 5000, and Tycho’s impact melt pool is too young to be the source of the leucogabbro. A possible source for the leucogabbro is the ancient Lomonsov-Fleming basin (NW lunar farside), which is near the Giordano Bruno crater and could reasonably be the source of its leucogabbro ejecta. NWA 5000 would then have been ejected from a younger crater within the Lomonsov-Fleming basin. If so confirmed, NWA 5000 would provide ‘ground truth’ for an unexplored corner of the lunar surface.

abstract: Here, we introduce PBot, the Integrative Paleobotany Portal (PBot; pbot.paleobiodb.org), a free online software platform designed specifically for fossil plant data management, analysis, and exploration. Fossil plants provide an essential record for understanding ancient terrestrial environments, yet they remain severely underrepresented in major online scientific databases. Until now no online data-management infrastructure could accommodate the full range of informal and formal naming practices used in paleobotany, incorporate trait and descriptive data, or facilitate the comparison and synonymization of taxa across regions, time periods, or research groups. PBot was designed to solve these fundamental gaps in the digital landscape while complementing existing resources, working in conjunction with the Paleobiology Database, existing museum specimen portals, and digital image repositories. PBot’s graph-based architecture supports a rich network of data, linking informal and formal taxa directly to fossil specimens and references. These specimens are tied to precise geographic, geologic, and sampling data, with options for images, text descriptions, and scored character traits and measurements. By integrating this data into a single platform, PBot acts as free data management software for researchers to directly organize, manage, and share their research with the public. Through the PBot Workbench, registered users can enter and edit data, build custom dynamic character schemas, and manage collaborative datasets and data privacy from project inception to publication. The PBot Explore portal enables anyone to view public fossil plant data and to perform flexible, multi-parameter searches across geographic, geologic, and descriptive data. By bridging critical data infrastructure gaps and bringing paleobotany's hidden data to light, PBot sustains the meaningful inclusion of fossil plants in large-scale synthetic studies of global biodiversity, paleoecology, and evolutionary biology.

abstract: Recently, Mineral Association Analysis (MAA) used the Apriori algorithm to predict previously unknown localities of several economic mineral species in the United States of America by analyzing patterns in the Mineral Evolution Database (MED). This method mines association rules based on large scale trends of mineral co-occurrences within the database, with the first model based on minerals across the United States. Our reference dataset included 93,419 localities across the United States of America, which spanned 2,622 different mineral species and generated 8,139,004 association rules. This method was previously applied at Mars analogue sites like Tecopa Basin, California, in preparation for planetary applications. One excellent dataset to apply this model to is the set of minerals identified by the NASA Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) CheMin (Chemistry and Mineralogy) X-ray diffraction (XRD) instrument. This XRD on the Curiosity rover is the most robust mineralogical instrument we have sent to another planetary body. By assessing crystallographic information from CheMin, we have high confidence in the mineral interpretations coming from Gale Crater. In this study, we apply the MED MAA model to these minerals identified in Gale crater to predict previously unknown mineral occurrences of known martian minerals and hypothesize the presence of species not yet found on the red planet. In future work, refined subsets of the Mineral Evolution Database will be mined with the Apriori algorithm to create more Mars-specific models. By understanding possible additional mineral phases in Gale crater, we gain insights into Mars’ geologic history, environmental change, and aqueous activity. In our modern age of large-scale data availability, this research illustrates one instance of advancement and possibility in mineral informatics. This research shows that mineral association rules generate statistically sound and geologically insightful predictions.

title: Formation of Fibrous Chalcedonic Quartz in Epithermal Deposits
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part II)
authors: Soberano, Omar Baculna [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Reynolds, T. James [3]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA

abstract:
Epithermal deposits are an important source of high-grade gold and silver ores. High-grade ores are found in banded quartz veins where mosaic, flamboyant, and prismatic quartz dominate. Recent studies have documented that the original silicate precipitates were noncrystalline opal-A G , which is composed of aggregates of silica microspheres (1-5 µm). In contrast, fibrous, chalcedonic quartz dominates interlayered barren bands. Previous studies suggested that the fibrous quartz had been directly precipitated from solution.

Observations in pipes from geothermal systems, which are modern analogues of epithermal deposits, show that silica precipitates are also noncrystalline. Opal-A G is common, but so is opal-A N that is not composed of microspheres but occurs as translucent colloform bands that are glass-like and lack the characteristic microspherical texture of opal-A G . Initial maturation of the material results in the development of anisotropic features characterized by conical extinction patterns and fine concentric banding. In addition, opal-A N affected by incipient maturation can show conical fiber bundles resembling those in the fibrous quartz bands in epithermal veins.

Based on these initial observations, it is hypothesized that bands with fibrous microtexture in epithermal veins, particularly those with conical fiber bundles, may have been derived from the maturation of opal-A N . Alternating bands of fibrous quartz and mosaic, flamboyant, or prismatic quartz may simply be products of the maturation of two different noncrystalline silica precursors.

title: Detrital Zircon Geochronology of the Middle Ordovician St. Peter Sandstone in the Western Midcontinent Basin
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Huisman, Matthew [1], Malone, John E. [2], Malone, David H. [3], McLaughlin, Patrick I. [4]

abstract:
Quartz arenites are a distinctive feature of the early Paleozoic stratigraphic record in the Laurentian midcontinent. The St. Peter Sandstone was deposited during the Middle Ordovician Tippecanoe transgression. The provenance of the St. Peter Sandstone was studied in the central and eastern midcontinent and new data from five cores in Iowa and Missouri refine sediment sourcing in the western midcontinent basin. We test the hypotheses that the Transcontinental Arch and Ozark Dome were sediment barriers and source areas.

Samples were collected from the Camp Quest, WPF, Arthur Brown, Wisnom, and Roy Lewis cores archived by the Iowa Geologic Survey. Zircons were analyzed by LA-ICPMS at the University of Arizona Laserchron Center (Zn=836). Previous work on the St. Peter Sandstone in the eastern Laurentian midcontinent revealed three principal sources area that variably supplied sediment, the Superior Province (distal to the north), the Grenville Orogen (distal to the east) and recycling of the Neoproterozoic Jacobsville sandstone (proximal to the north). Our goal was to determine whether the Ozark Dome and Transcontinental Arch were supplying sediment to the western midcontinent basin. The Camp Quest (westernmost sample) has prominent 1830 and 2700 Ma age peaks, which were likely derived from Trans-Hudson/Penokean and Superior Province rocks exposed along the Transcontinental Arch to the west. The other four samples have a mix of Grenville (1000-1300 Ma) and Superior (2700 Ma) age peaks. The Arthur Brown and Wisnom cores cluster with the regional Superior Province chronofacies, whereas the WPF and Roy Lewis cores cluster with the Grenville chronofacies. None of the samples have 1300-1500 Ma age peaks, which indicates that no Ozark Dome sediment source area existed during St. Peter deposition. Our hypothesis that the Transcontinental Arch supplied sediment to the western midcontinent depositional basin is supported by our data, and a fourth St. Peter chronofacies is herein established.

abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) are critical minerals vital to modern technologies due to their unique properties. To meet escalating demand, domestic sourcing efforts have increasingly targeted unconventional feedstocks, such as coal and coal mining waste (CMW). However, conventional metallurgical extraction remains commercially unviable due to high operational costs and environmental impacts. Microbial biomining offers a promising, sustainable alternative to recover REEs from CMW. Specifically, bioleaching combines high REE selectivity and recovery yields (>80%) with low environmental toxicity. CMW provides an ideal substrate for bioleaching: their organic matter content can sustain microbial growth, leading to the secretion of organic acids that solubilize REE-bearing phosphates (monazite, apatite) into soluble REE complexes. However, compositional variations among CMW types, along with key physicochemical parameters like pH, strongly govern microbial dynamics and subsequent REE recovery. This study evaluated how the organic and inorganic matrices of CMW influence REE extraction during bioleaching. CMW samples collected from abandoned coal mine sites in southern Illinois were comprehensively characterized for their organic petrology, mineralogy, and geochemistry prior to bioleaching with indigenous phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms. The results show that the total organic carbon (TOC) ranges from 2.61% to 76.74%, and REEs content varies between 32.9 ppm and 229.94 ppm. The mineralogy comprises quartz (20.5% - 73.7%), kaolinite (0.7% - 23.3%), illite/mica (2.9% - 36.4%), pyrite (0.2% - 6.3%), and jarosite (0.2% - 19.6%) and the organic fraction is mainly composed of the vitrinite maceral group, followed by inertinite and liptinite. This compositional heterogeneity of CMW directly influenced REE release, since higher REE concentrations in the leaching supernatant were associated with high-carbon material and near-neutral pH, whereas REE-rich, silicate-dominated coarse refuse yielded lower recovery. The enrichment of Comamonadaceae , Beijerinckiaceae , and Pseudomonadaceae bacterial families correlated with enhanced REE mobilization under substrate-supplemented leaching conditions. Overall, these findings demonstrate that organic carbon availability in CMW, as well as the buffering capacity to neutral pH, serves as a primary control on microbial community development and subsequent REE extraction efficiency.

title: Whence the Lustrous Stones? Provenance of the Paleogene Rodados Lustrosos Gravel Lag in the Andean Foreland Basin (~35–37 °S)
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools
authors: Ronemus, Chance Baylor [1], Howlett, Caden James [2], Fennell, Lucas Martin [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
(2) Department of Environmental Sciences, University of Montana Western, Dillon, Montana, USA
(3) INGEIS, UBA-CONICET, Buenos Aires, Argentina
abstract:
Depositional hiatuses mark important changes in tectonics and climate, yet sediment routing across them is difficult to study; they leave little behind. A major hiatus in the Andean (Neuquén) foreland basin is recorded by a thin lag (~1–3 m) of conspicuously polished gravel known as the Rodados Lustrosos (RL; “lustrous stones”) exposed between ~35 and 37.5°S. Its Paleogene depositional age coincides with a shift from retroarc shortening to hinterland extension proposed to have shut off flexural subsidence. We explore the basin response over this interval using the lithology, geometry, zircon U-Pb/εHf, and bulk geochemistry of RL cobbles—a detrital provenance toolkit at the clast scale.

We map the RL overlying a channelized disconformity cutting down-section southward from Eocene to Upper Cretaceous strata from 35–37.25°S and in angular unconformity over Eocene deposits at 37.5°S. It underlies uppermost Oligocene–lower Miocene back-arc volcanics and foreland basin fill. RL clasts exhibit superposed fluvial and eolian abrasion features, including rubbing and corrasion pits overprinted by percussion marks. We interpret the RL as a hybrid braid plain–desert pavement that developed under an arid climate with occasional floods.

Felsic volcanic clasts dominate all sites but decline northward (93–62%) as andesite increases (0–25%). Median clast size also fines northward exponentially (5.08–1.5 cm B-axis). Zircon U-Pb ages of two volcanic cobbles (183.3–189.3 Ma) and their εHf (median +2.7; 0.5–4.8 IQR) match igneous rocks of the Cordillera del Viento, ~75 km SW of our southernmost site and adjacent to an Oligocene intra-arc graben. A recycled sandstone clast yields a detrital zircon age spectrum consistent with Mesozoic cover of this same uplift (150 ± 2.9 Ma maximum depositional age). Both populations are sparse to absent in deposits above and below the RL, which record western arc and fold-thrust belt sources.

These data suggest Paleogene establishment of north-directed sediment routing across a transport surface beveling the abandoned foreland and frontal thrust belt. Inherited orogenic topography, potentially enhanced by rift-flank and/or dynamic uplift, shed durable detritus that survived as an ultra-mature lag; labile lithologies were destroyed, and fines were exported until renewed subsidence buried the RL at ca. 23 Ma. Sediment routing across a major hiatus can thus be read from its gravel lag alone.

abstract: Conventional cooling systems, particularly cooling tower-based systems, use large amounts of electricity and water. The rising demand for cooling data centers and districts in warm and humid coastal areas led to the idea of Geologic Sea Water Air Conditioning (GeoSWAC), which could potentially provide a sustainable option by using naturally cool saline groundwater from deep, permeable formations as a cooling source. Preliminary modeling in southeastern Florida suggests that the highly transmissive Boulder Zone in the Lower Floridan aquifer, with a transmissivity of 3-26 m 2 /s, allows cool seawater from the Straits of Florida to flow inland and therefore may be an attractive target for GeoSWAC. In this study, groundwater flow, solute and heat transport modeling is conducted to understand the distributions of pressure, salinity and temperature in the aquifer under static conditions prior to evaluating future extraction scenarios. A two-dimensional cross-sectional model is developed to examine how density differences and hydraulic properties control groundwater flow beneath the Miami area. The model examines regional groundwater heads, groundwater flow toward the coast, and the inland movement of deep saline water from the Straits of Florida through the Lower Floridan Aquifer and Boulder Zone. The 110-km-wide domain represents the eastern half of the peninsula and the adjacent offshore area and extends to 1 km depth. Simulated water fluxes include freshwater recharge and fluxes across coastal and offshore boundaries. A highly permeable Boulder Zone is represented below 800 m depth. MODFLOW 6 is used, which includes the capability to simulate groundwater flow, salinity transport, and energy transport. The Buoyancy Package links salinity and temperature to fluid density to represent variable-density flow. Preliminary simulations show that groundwater head decreases from about 12 m in the shallow subsurface near the center of the peninsula to sea level at the coast; salinity is low near the surface and increases to seawater-like values around 610 m below sea level; and cool seawater (4-10 °C) is present within the Boulder Zone. Results of this model will for the initial conditions for future transient simulations that will evaluate how groundwater head, salinity, and temperature distributions respond to cool-water extraction.

title: Locating Laurentia: A Paleomagnetic Study of Geography and Climate 1.4 Ga
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age
authors: Jay, Annabel F. [1], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [2], Zhang, Yiming [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota,

abstract: Climate and atmospheric oxygen shaped ecological conditions for eukaryotic diversification and innovation during the Mesoproterozoic, yet both remain difficult to reconstruct without reliable paleogeographic context. The Sibley Group, a 950 m hematite-rich sequence of Mesoproterozoic sandstones, silt-stones, and carbonates, in Ontario, Canada, serves as an important geochemical archive, recording a Mesoproterozoic terrestrial environment. Primary fluid inclusions in Sibley halite recently yielded direct constraints on atmospheric O₂ and CO₂ and depositional temperature, indicating an equable climate and oxygen levels sufficient for animal respiration long before animals emerged. Those interpretations, however, assumed a Sibley Basin location near 30°N, based on a previous reconstruction. In this study, we constrain the paleolatitude of the Sibley basin 1.4 Ga using paleomagnetism. Positive conglomerate and baked-contact field tests support a primary, detrital origin for the magnetic remanence, from which we calculate a new paleomagnetic pole and paleolatitude for the Sibley Basin. The result places the basin at a tropical latitude lower than previously assumed. Though consistent with field evidence of evaporites, this revised position places the Sibley Basin at latitudes slightly lower than expected for the formation of evaporites, suggesting evaporative potential closer to the equator for sediments in the continental interior, where evaporation exceeded precipitation. This new paleogeographic context strengthens interpretations of Mesoproterozoic atmosphere and climate, made from Sibley halite, evaporite, and stromatolite records, and improves comparisons with broadly coeval North American successions of the Belt Supergroup, Apache Group, and Troy Quartzite. Placing the direct atmospheric and climatic constraints in a more precise paleogeographic context, our results add to the interpretation of the environmental setting of Laurentia during a consequential interval of Earth-system and biological evolution during the Mesoproterozoic.

abstract: In September 2024, intense precipitation from a predecessor rainfall event followed by the remnants of Hurricane Helene produced record-breaking flooding and triggered more than 2,200 landslides and debris flows across the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina. Debris flow initiation zones were generally small and ranged from typical shallow landslides to “blow-out” features characterized by downslope overland flow and minimal initial scour. Despite their small sizes, many initiation zones evolved through coalescence and downstream entrainment to form long-runout (>0.5 km) debris flows, resulting in numerous fatalities and widespread damage. Existing regional debris flow susceptibility maps, like many landslide susceptibility maps, focus on the initiation zones and do not account for growth and potential runout. However, because most people live within potential inundation areas rather than source areas, delineating these hazard zones is critical to improve hazard planning and response. This study presents a first-order regional debris flow runout model created using Grfin Tools and calibrated using short- and long-runout debris flows in drainages in Buncombe and Yancey counties in North Carolina. Grfin Tools uses empirical approaches based on regional geomorphologic and topographic parameters readily acquired from digital elevation models, rather than specific material properties, to produce a first-order model. A key feature of Grfin Tools is its ability to model debris flow growth via entrainment using source area or stream channel length, simulating the numerous slope and channel-based processes that increase debris flow volume and ultimately control inundation extent. The extensive distribution of the 2024 debris flows provides a unique opportunity to evaluate first-order regional runout predictions, improve the delineation of debris flow hazard zones for future extreme rainfall events, and identify areas that require more detailed investigation.

title: Challenging the Ice-Free Greenhouse Paradigm: Sea-Level and Milankovitch Variations Suggest Episodic Early Eocene Glaciation
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Miller, Kenneth G. [1], Schmelz, William J. [2], Browning, James V. [3], Wright, James D. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sci., Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ, USA

abstract:
The Early Eocene (56-48.6 Ma), the warmest interval of the Cenozoic, is commonly viewed as an ice-free greenhouse world with atmospheric CO₂ concentrations of ~1000-1500 ppmv. We reassess this paradigm using paired benthic foraminiferal oxygen isotope (δ¹⁸Ob) and Mg/Ca records together with backstripped New Jersey relative sea-level (RSL) data to evaluate the contributions of deep-sea temperature (DST) and ice-volume change to the Early Eocene δ¹⁸O signal. Using a Bayesian framework, we decompose Pacific benthic δ¹⁸O records, which reflect mean deep-water conditions, into temperature and seawater δ¹⁸O components. The results indicate terrestrial Antarctic ice sheets and ice-driven (barystatic) sea-level (BSL) variability on both Milankovitch and million-year timescales.

Model results suggest orbitally driven BSL fluctuations of ~5-15 m at precession (19/23 kyr), obliquity (41 kyr), and eccentricity (95/100 kyr) periods, superimposed on million-year-scale variations of ~10-20 m. Wavelet analyses show that orbital-scale variability is strongly expressed in reconstructed BSL records during glaciated intervals, whereas modeled temperature records retain strong orbital variability during both glaciated and ice-free states. Independent constraints from backstripped New Jersey RSL records and sea-level estimates derived from Mg/Ca-based DST reconstructions indicate million-year-scale sea-level changes of ~10-30 m. However, preferred Bayesian model solutions generally favor amplitudes below 20 m.

Applying pH corrections increases reconstructed temperatures and reduces inferred ice volumes, highlighting the uncertainty and model dependence of ice-volume estimates. Nevertheless, even under warm end-member assumptions with large pH corrections, persistently ice-free conditions are difficult to reconcile with the data because the temperature signal required to explain benthic δ¹⁸O approaches or exceeds the upper 95% confidence limits of Mg/Ca-derived temperatures. Our results suggest that fully ice-free conditions were limited to peak hyperthermal events, with ice sheets re-establishing during background Early Eocene climates. We conclude that the Early Eocene was unlikely to have been persistently ice-free, but instead was characterized by dynamic ice-sheet growth and decay. These findings imply that other greenhouse climates, including the Mesozoic greenhouse and Miocene Climate Optimum, may also have supported continental ice sheets.

title: Olistoliths of Battle Mountain, Nevada: Bradoriids and the Earliest Ostracods
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: McMenamin, Mark A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geography, Mount Holyoke College, South Hadley, MA, USA
abstract: An unusual assemblage of lower Cambrian fossils occurs at Battle Mountain, Nevada, USA. The fossils occur in limestone olistoliths within an olistostrome at the top of the Valmy Formation (Ordovician). The Battle Mountain olistoliths are of interest as they represent an otherwise unknown fossil assemblage that contains both archaeocyaths and the putative cnidarian Aploconus . Fossil seed shrimp (= bradoriids + ostracods) were reported from the olistoliths in 1990 as “ostracodes” in thin section. Acetic acid maceration of newly collected (June 2026) Battle Mountain olistoliths has yielded silicified specimens, representing over 45 species, of both bradoriids and specimens interpreted here as the earliest ostracods to appear in the fossil record. Bradoriids belonging to Bradoriidae and Hipponicharionidae occur in the maceration residues. Also present is a bairdiid ostracod comparable to the ceratobairdiids. The bairdiid specimens form an ontogenetic series. Although bradoriid homoplasy (convergent on bairdiid morphology) cannot be completely ruled out, it seems likely that the bairdiid specimens are the first ostracods. If so, ostracods emerged from a diverse seed shrimp community associated with a lower Cambrian (Toyonian) archaeocyath-calcimicrobe- Aploconus marine assemblage.
