title: Utilizing XRF and Crush-Leach Analysis as Exploration Tools for Gem-Bearing Pegmatite Pockets in the Pikes Peak Granite, Colorado
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Shkolnik, Nikalina [1], Leatherman, Mark [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Natural Sciences, Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, CO, USA; Department of Geology & Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Department of Natural Sciences, Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Pikes Peak Batholith (PPB) is a prolific ~1 Ga granitic body that hosts pegmatites containing smoky quartz, amazonite, topaz, fluorite & others that attract prospectors worldwide. Exploration for pegmatite gemstone pockets traditionally relies upon surface clues such as “following float”, the presence of iron-rich clay, following zoning patterns & increasing euhedral crystal habit. Even with these clues, the discovery of pockets is still hit-or-miss, requiring time & labor. The pegmatites are classified as Niobium-Yttrium-Fluorine (NYF)-type pegmatites.

During the last stages of pegmatite formation, minerals crystallize from volatile-rich fluids in miarolitic cavities. Afterwards, the residual fluid can migrate into nearby fractures & crystallize as quartz veinlets containing indicator elements of LCT pegmatites such as Zr, Mo, Y, U & Rare Earth Elements (REEs). The veinlets erode to become part of the overlaying soil.

This project utilized soil geochemistry to attempt to identify unique geochemical signatures that can lead to gem-bearing pockets. Clay fraction sediment samples were collected from both known crystal-producing & non-producing pockets & analyzed using portable X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF), while quartz separates underwent crush-leach analysis for fluid inclusion composition. Results focused on calculating enrichment factors (EF) of the above elements compared against average crustal abundances.

The XRF results show significant enrichment in Mo & Zr (max EF values of 42.5 & 10.3, respectively) & moderate enrichment of Th, U, Y & Pb (max EF values of 13.1, 11.1, 7.6 & 7.9, respectively). Crush-leach data revealed minimal REE enrichment. However, other pegmatites within different districts of the PPB are known for enriched REEs (i.e. the South Platte District). The elevated Pb contents could indicate amazonite potential as it’s a contributing chromophore.

Differences between samples & grain sizes indicate that these elements are not uniformly distributed & may be concentrated in surface coatings, fractures, or fluid features rather than the crystal lattice. Combining XRF & crush-leach analyses provides a more complete geochemical picture, revealing both the composition & localized enrichment processes responsible for trace element variability & thus has good potential for exploration upon analyzing more sites.

title: Light Element Detection by Continuous X-Ray Fluorescence Core Scanning for Quantification of Hydrothermal Alteration Intensity
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Abts, Miranda [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Lundström, Annelie [3], Seyfarth, Alexander [4]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA

abstract:
Diamond drilling is key to understanding the subsurface geology and to determine the size and grade of mineral resources. During drilling campaigns, a team of geologists and technicians log the drill core to understand the distribution of lithology types, alteration, and mineralization. Sampling of the drill core is conducted for laboratory assay. The integration of core scanning into drill core characterization workflows using instruments such as the Minalyzer continuous X-ray fluorescence core scanner (CS) allows for a rapid and deeper characterization of drill core by providing depth-constrained high-resolution core images, colorized 3D LiDAR point clouds, non-destructive multi-element geochemistry, and high-resolution rock density data.

The Colorado School of Mines Core Research Laboratory houses a Minalyzer CS which has the capability to quantify light elements such as Na and Mg at detection limits below 0.5 wt%. The Minalyzer CS has the ability to quantify light elements to these detection limits by utilizing a He purge into both the 3D printed detector cone and the X-ray tube collimator to reduce primary X-ray beam attenuation. To capture the full suite of elements for geochemistry, two X-ray tube settings are used. One at 15 kV and 24 µA with a He purge to capture Na to Ca and another at 40 kV and 8 µA in air for K to Pb.

The instrumental configuration allows detection of light elements critical to the quantification of the alteration intensity in volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits and other base and precious metal deposits. Using exploration drill core from the world-class LaRonde Penna deposit in Quebec, it demonstrated that the Ishikawa alteration index and the chlorite-carbonate-pyrite index can now be determined rapidly at high precision and accuracy. Installation of the instrument on site would permit near real-time measurement and data delivery, enabling geologists to make more informed exploration decisions.

title: Mass-dependent titanium isotope variations in the roots of the Famatinian paleo-arc, Argentina: searching for a ‘missing’ Ti reservoir in the crust.

abstract:
Mass-dependent titanium isotope variations in the roots of the Famatinian paleo-arc, Argentina: searching for a ‘missing’ Ti reservoir in the crust.

Titanium isotope fractionation in the crust is mainly attributed to mass-dependent effects during crystallization of Fe–Ti oxides, driven by preferential incorporation of lighter Ti isotopes into oxides relative to coexisting melts. Fractional crystallization of these oxides should therefore produce an isotopically ‘heavy’ upper crust (high Ti 49 /Ti 47 ) and a complementary ‘light’ lower-to-middle crust (i.e., low Ti 49 /Ti 47 ). While heavy signatures are well documented in upper-crustal silicic rocks, the light counterparts have remained elusive and are largely inferred from mass-balance calculations. Yet, despite lacking direct evidence, this inferred light reservoir underpins long-term models of mantle-crust evolution [Deng et al., 2023, Nature 621].

In this study, we attempt to identify and characterize this “missing light reservoir” by determining the mineral chemistry, whole-rock major and trace element composition, and Ti-isotope signature of gabbroic rocks traversing the lower-to-middle crustal (0.7-0.5 GPa) Valle Fértil-La Huerta section of the Ordovician Famatinian arc, Argentina. This exceptionally well-preserved sequence records a continuous cumulate line of descent [Walker et al., 2015, J of Petrology 56], transitioning from Mg-rich, Ti-poor, ultramafic and mafic lithologies to Mg-poor, Ti-rich gabbroic cumulates, continuing into tonalitic and granitic lithologies.

Here, we test the hypothesis that early spinel-bearing cumulates have mantle-like isotopic signatures (i.e., unfractionated), whereas moderately evolved Ti-rich gabbroic cumulates (i.e., hornblende-bearing and hornblende-free gabbronorites and norites) are isotopically light owing to the accumulation of Fe-Ti oxides. Gabbroic rocks along this section have variable proportions of magnetite and ilmenite, sometimes as high as 7-8%, allowing us to evaluate the role of these oxides in producing the isotopically heavy signatures that are characteristic of evolved upper-crustal lithologies.

The presence of an isotopically light reservoir in plagioclase-rich lower-to-middle crustal cumulates has important implications for the Ti cycle, as it would: i) enable evaluating the mass balance of Ti and ii) allow testing the hypothesis that lower crustal foundering has been a driver of mantle Ti isotopic evolution over time.

abstract:
Coastal hazard science rarely translates into durable adaptation policy, in part because flood assessments that characterize where flooding occurs without resolving the physical mechanism behind it cannot support the mechanism-specific interventions planners and engineers actually need. Groundwater inundation, drainage backflow, wave overtopping, coastal erosion, and compound flooding follow distinct geomorphic and hydrologic pathways, respond to sea-level rise (SLR) along different trajectories, and require fundamentally different engineering responses, from subsurface dewatering to managed retreat.

We apply this framework to Waikīkī, Oʻahu, resolving each mechanism individually with dedicated physics-based tools, MODFLOW-2005 for shallow and emergent groundwater, CoSMoS-COAST for shoreline change, BARRACUDA for wave runup, and WRF-Hydro-CUFA for compound rainfall-marine flooding, across incremental SLR scenarios. Present-day groundwater conditions are already critical: 92% of buildings sit above critically shallow groundwater (<1.5 m), a threshold also met beneath 82% of the buried stormwater and sewer network. Results identify a 3-4 ft SLR threshold where mechanisms converge toward system-wide exposure simultaneously, with infrastructure exposure consistently outpacing areal flood extent, a nonlinear relationship reflecting the concentration of buried utilities and structures in the lowest-lying, often artificially filled, portions of the district.

Uptake of this mechanism-resolved output is already occurring across governance scales in Honolulu: the Primary Urban Center Development Plan and Climate Ready Oʻahu incorporate its hazard layers into zoning and capital improvement planning, the One Water Initiative targets the groundwater and drainage-backflow vulnerabilities it identifies, phased district-scale pathways under Adapt Waikīkī 2050 and the Waikīkī Resilience & SLR Adaptation Project assign mechanism-specific interventions, and site-scale design work translates its groundwater and inundation-depth output into amphibious and elevated structure typologies, together demonstrating a transferable geoscience-to-governance pathway for reclaimed coastal cities worldwide.

abstract: The Late Ordovician Mass Extinction (LOME) is unique among the Big Five mass extinctions as the only event tied to cooling. Geographic range and thermal breadth have previously been established as selective factors, but the physiological mechanism linking glaciation to selective genus-level extinction has not been quantified, nor has the deeper question of why no later cooling event produced equivalent losses. Here, we test whether aerobic physiology, measured by the factorial Metabolic Index (MI) under Katian and Hirnantian baseline ocean conditions, explains observed extinction patterns. We map 1,155 marine genera with ~17,500 occurrences from the Paleobiology Database onto previously published Late Ordovician cGENIE model climate fields. We measure the extinction selectivity of geographic range, thermal breadth, and aerobic physiology and confirm that geographic range (OR = 0.937, p < 0.001) and thermal breadth (OR = 0.834, p < 0.001) are the dominant predictors of extinction from the Katian to the Hirnantian. Katian-baseline aerobic scope, however, is independently significant when added to the model with geographic range and thermal breadth (LRT p = 0.0012, OR = 0.423). Extinction was highest among genera in low-latitude, low-pO2 shelf environments, which were nearest their aerobic limits, in an ocean at ~30–40% PAL. These genera went extinct not because cooling reduced their aerobic scope, but because they had the least aerobic physiological buffering capacity to withstand glaciation-driven habitat disruption. A traditional two-pulse comparison of the LOME reveals that this signal is specific to pulse 1 (end-Katian). The Katian shelf's ~20-fold dissolved oxygen gradient provided predictive power for aerobic scope independent of temperature (OR = 0.816, p = 0.001). The Hirnantian shelf was more uniformly oxygenated (~2.5-fold range), and the pulse 2 MI signal is fully mediated by temperature (LRT p = 0.669). Low Ordovician background oxygen was the critical enabling condition for aerobically selective extinction. As background oxygen rose through the Paleozoic, glaciation could no longer compound pre-existing aerobic marginality, potentially explaining why subsequent cooling events did not produce an equivalent biotic crisis.

title: Update on the Geological Map of Sedna Planitia, Venus: V-18 and V-19 Quadrangles
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: Buczkowski, Debra [1], Whitten, Jennifer [2], Matiella Novak, Alexandra [3], Jozwiak, Lauren M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Johns Hopkins U Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD,

abstract:
Sedna Planitia is a large area of low-lying regional plains material found to the south of Ishtar Terra, the east of Beta Regio, and north of Sif and Gula Mons. The majority of Sedna Planitia is covered by two map quadrangles: V-18 Lachesis Tessera (300 o -330 o E, 25 o -50 o N) and V-19 Sedna Planitia (330 o -360 o E, 25 o -50 o N). The V-18 Lachesis Tessera quadrangle covers the transition zone from Beta Regio, a major area of uplift to the west, to a major area of low-lying plains in the northeast, making it important to the overall investigation of the evolution of the surface and lithosphere of Venus. Similarly, the V-19 Sedna Planitia quadrangle covers the transition zone from the Eistla Regio uplift to the south and Ishtar Terra in the north, divided by the low-lying Sedna Planitia.

Here we present our progress on the 1:5M geologic maps of the V-18 and V-19 quadrangles. Geologic units include regional plains, lava flows, crater materials, maculae deposits, and fields of small shield volcanoes, among others. While V-18 was previously completed, we are revising the linework as needed to keep contacts consistent across the boundary between the two quadrangles.

In addition, we are creating maps of specific features at 1:500k, to take advantage of the highest resolution of Magellan radar data (75 m/pixel). These include maps of tessera inliers, coronae, volcanoes, and tectonic belts in V-18 and V19. Wrinkle ridges, graben, and lineament maps are also being constructed at this scale. Evaluating these structures, as well as their relationships to geologic units, may shed some light on which geomorphic features might represent different lithospheric thicknesses, which would have important implications towards our understanding of the history and development of the interior of Venus and how it differs from the other terrestrial planets.

title: Seismic Refraction Tomography Reveals Contrasting Shallow Hydrogeologic Controls on Flood Response Along the Texas Gulf Coast

authors: Elshalkany, Muhamed [1], Hinojosa, Hector R. [2], Rodriguez, William [3], Murgulet, Dorina [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA; Department of Geology, Suez Canal University, Egypt, Arab Rep.
(2) Cordillera Geo-Services, LLC, CEDAR PARK, TX,

(4) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
abstract:
Flood response in coastal environments is strongly influenced by shallow groundwater conditions and near-surface hydrogeologic properties, yet the effects of coastal geomorphic setting on subsurface architecture and depth to saturation remain poorly constrained. This study uses Seismic Refraction Tomography (SRT) to investigate shallow hydrogeologic conditions across three contrasting geomorphic and hydrogeologic settings along the Texas Gulf Coast: barrier islands (6 profiles), estuarine bay margins (6 profiles), and inland clay-rich coastal plains (3 profiles). Surveys were conducted using a Geometrics ES-3000 24-channel seismic system with 1–3 m geophone spacing and a sledgehammer energy source. Data were processed and inverted using SeisImager to generate two-dimensional P-wave velocity models. Where available, nearby groundwater-monitoring wells provided independent constraints on the interpreted depth to saturation.

Barrier-island profiles indicate the shallowest interpreted depths to saturation, generally 1–2 m below ground surface, consistent with sandy deposits and shallow water-table conditions. Bay-margin profiles show intermediate depths to saturation of approximately 2–4 m, and greater lateral variability, consistent with heterogeneous sediments associated with estuarine deposition. Inland clay-plain profiles exhibit the deepest interpreted depths to saturation, approximately 3.5–4 m, while several profiles lack a distinct velocity boundary attributable to saturation, despite reports from property owners that these locations remained flooded for more than one week following major rainfall events. The contrast between relatively deep groundwater and prolonged surface flooding is consistent with ponding controlled by low-permeability near-surface sediments and limited drainage rather than by a uniformly shallow water table. Estimated P-wave velocities range from 241–1,735 m/s for barrier islands, 163–1,740 m/s for bay margins, and 213–1,781 m/s for inland clay plains. All tomographic inversions produced RMS errors ranging from 0.6% to 2.5%, indicating close agreement between observed and modeled first-arrival travel times.

The comparative SRT dataset identifies a progressive transition in shallow hydrogeologic conditions from shallow saturation beneath sandy barrier islands, to increasingly heterogeneous bay-margin systems, and ultimately to clay-dominated inland environments where surface flooding can persist despite relatively deep groundwater levels. These findings indicate the importance of coastal geomorphic setting in controlling the mechanisms and persistence of flooding and demonstrate the value of integrating seismic refraction tomography with groundwater observations for hydrogeologic characterization and improved interpretation of flood susceptibility along the Texas Gulf Coast.

abstract:
Skarn deposits are a significant source of Fe, Cu, W, Mo, Zn-Pb, and Au; they are also an important source of critical minerals Co, Bi, Te, Be, B, Sn, fluorspar, and REEs (Einaudi et al., 1981; Rossetti et al., 2026). All but Fe, Mo, and Au appear on the 2025 U.S. List of Critical Minerals (U.S. Geological Survey, 2025), making skarn systems an increasingly strategic domestic exploration target as the U.S. works to reduce import reliance for these commodities.

Trans-Pecos Texas has a long mining history with many of the past mines producing minerals that are now considered critical including: silver at Shafter, zinc and lead at the Bonanza Mine, and fluorspar in the Eagle Mountains (Price, 1983). In the present, there are quite a few known rare earth prospects that are being worked including: Little Round Top, Round Top, and Sierra Blanca. Skarns are not a major ore deposit type in the Trans-Pecos, but occurrences are documented in the Quitman Mountains (Murry, 1980) and, in the Christmas Mountains (Joesten, 1974), and a newly explored skarn in the Hood Spring 7.5’ quadrangle, Texas. Characterizing these skarn systems is necessary to evaluate the region’s capacity to contribute to domestic critical mineral supply.

The Hood Spring 7.5’ quadrangle contains Cretaceous rocks intruded by plugs, dikes, and sills of rhyolite, trachyte, and basalt belonging to the southern Trans-Pecos suite of alkalic rocks (Graves, 1954). In the southeastern portion of the quadrangle, trachydolerite underlies what was most likely a trachyte sill emplaced in the Glen Rose Formation. The later intrusion produced a fault, and along the fault trace metamorphosed Glen Rose was brought in contact with Edwards Limestone (Graves, 1954). Recent field mapping has identified a skarn associated with this collapsed laccolith. This research presents petrographic and SEM analysis of the skarn system that gives insight into the mode of metamorphism and metasomatism that took place along with the geochemical makeup of the hydrothermal fluids.

Within the southeastern portion of the quadrangle, other possible buried intrusions have been discovered with recent aeromagnetic and radiometric surveys. This research provides a mineralogical baseline for evaluation of these intrusions as exploration targets.

abstract: The Cretaceous terrestrial fossil record of the Korean Peninsula is exceptionally rich in trackways, whereas skeletal remains are exceedingly rare. Recent discoveries from the mid-Cretaceous Ilseongsan Formation of Aphae Island (Aphaedo), southwestern Korea, have substantially expanded this record. The formation has yielded a diverse, theropod-dominated egg assemblage that includes Macroelongatoolithus , other elongatoolithid eggs, dendroolithid and prismatoolithid eggs, and Onggwanoolithus aphaedoensis, the first avialan egg reported from Korea. Onggwanoolithus represents one of the earliest known examples of an unornamented, three-layered eggshell resembling those of crown birds. The site also produced Doolysaurus huhmini , an early-diverging neornithischian dinosaur represented by a partially articulated skeleton comprising cranial and postcranial elements, as well as gastroliths, investigated by X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT). This specimen includes the first studied dinosaur cranial remains from Korea and indicates that the diversity of Korean Cretaceous dinosaurs was substantially greater than suggested by the previously known skeletal record. Notably, the skeletal and egg fossils from the Aphaedo site are generally well preserved, and several specimens show evidence of limited or no transport prior to burial. Nevertheless, no invertebrate fossils or trace fossils have been identified, apart from vitreous tubular structures tentatively interpreted as root traces. This apparent absence contrasts markedly with many other Cretaceous fossil localities in Korea and suggests that the Aphaedo deposits underwent a distinct taphonomic history. Together, the unusual fossil association, exceptional preservation, and limited evidence of transport identify Aphaedo as an important mid-Cretaceous terrestrial vertebrate locality and provide an opportunity to investigate depositional and taphonomic conditions that differed from those represented at other Korean fossil sites.

title: Organic Metal and Metalloid Complexes (OMMC): Analytical Method Development and Applications
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Kane, Tyler James [1], McCleskey, Richard Blaine [2], Barber, Larry B. [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Organic metal and metalloid complexes (OMMC), formed when aqueous metal(oid)s bind to organic ligands ranging from natural organic matter (NOM) and biological metabolites to industrial synthetic compounds, are likely an important control on the mobility and bioavailability of trace elements in the hydrologic environment. OMMCs may be especially prevalent in mining-impacted environments where elevated trace element concentrations co-occur with strong chelating agents such as ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and/or other synthetic acids often used in hydrometallurgical extraction processes. Yet these compounds are seldom measured in field samples and their consequences for metal(oid) fate and transport remain largely unknown. Analytical challenges have prevented routine quantification of OMMCs, leaving a critical gap in the ability to characterize trace element speciation, address research questions related to source tracking, and inform bioavailability and risk assessment models used by land and water resource managers.

Here we present progress toward a suite of analytical methods designed to measure inorganic and organic speciation of critical metals and metalloids in natural waters. Using high performance liquid chromatography-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (HPLC-ICP-MS), we assessed analytical protocols for redox speciation and OMMC of arsenic, selenium, antimony, and vanadium, and for separation of metal-EDTA complexes for cobalt, copper, and lead. Geochemical modeling (PHREEQC) was used to optimize method conditions and provide independent validation. Our results demonstrate that separation of organometallic complexes from free metal ions is analytically feasible for several elements, that quantitation of redox oxyanion speciation is especially promising, and that weakly bound metal-natural organic matter complexes are not sufficiently stable for the methods tested.

Once optimized, these capabilities could have broad application across use cases including critical mineral recovery from mine waste, wildfire-driven metal mobilization, municipal wastewater treatment, and harmful algal bloom biogeochemistry. By enabling source characterization through co-occurring anthropogenic chelating agents and improved speciation measurements, this work supports watershed management, contaminant source apportionment, and remediation strategies relevant to Tribal communities, regulatory agencies, utilities, and the broader research community.

abstract: The eastern Himalayas record the transition from collisional tectonics of the central Himalaya to hyperoblique convergence at the IndoBurman subduction zone. At the eastern terminus of the Himalayan orogen, the Burma terrane converges with India and Eurasia forming a triple junction of continental fault systems. While the eastern Himalayas are considered an archetype for collision to subduction transitions, few studies have focused on deformation related to the Noa-Dihing fault system (NDFS) located at the apex of the triple junction. To evaluate the broader influence of terrane accretion on indenter corner dynamics, we present new mapping, structural analyses, detrital Be-10 derived erosion rates, and detrital zircon (U-Th)/Pb (DZUPb) analyses to characterize the crustal structure and deformation rates within the NDF. The NDF is a major crustal structure that juxtaposes garnet and sillimanite bearing gneiss of Himalayan wedge in the hanging wall with Oligocene–Pliocene fluvio-deltaic deposits of the northern IndoBurman Ranges in the footwall. An ~100-m wide outcrop of crush breccia preserved along the Kamfei River represents the main strand of the NDF. Fault-slip measurements from this outcrop document northwest-striking faults with both right-lateral and top-southwest reverse sense-of-slip. The main fault strand is mappable along strike for >100 km in hillshade imagery from the TanDEMx 12.5m InSAR DEM. New DZUPb ages from small tributaries that cross the NDF in several locations along its mapped extent confirm that the hanging wall comprises both the Greater Himalayan Series and Tethyan Himalayan Series, with no apparent contribution from the Lesser Himalayan Series or Lohit Plutonic Suite. In the footwall, northwest-vergent thrusts of the IndoBurman Ranges are crosscut and folded by three southward propagating and south-verging splay thrusts of the NDFS, including the Manabhum fault. A train of south-verging, left-stepping, en-echelon folds associated with the footwall splay faults is consistent with right-lateral and reverse shear. Be-10 derived erosion rates of 1-1.75 mm/yr from the hanging wall of the Manabhum fault, combined with a structural model of the fault, yield slip rates of ~1-2 mm/yr. Results indicate contemporaneous slip along the Indo-Burman thrusts and NDFS, with the NDFS overprinting and propagating southward into the IndoBurman ranges. Our results highlight how sliver terrane accretion along the flanks of collisional orogens can modify the dynamics of indenting plate collisions.

session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Todd, Erin [1], Caine, Jonathan Saul [2], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [3], Bizimis, Michael [4], Lowers, Heather [5], Thompson, Jay Michael [6]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK,
(2) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(3) UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA,

(5) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,

abstract:
New field observations, geochemical, and isotopic data for mafic-ultramafic rocks near Kanuti River and Ray Mountains of interior Alaska help elucidate the nature and tectonic evolution of the Angayucham terrane and associated assemblages. The Angayucham terrane, an allochthonous assemblage comprising Late Devonian to Early Jurassic mafic rocks, has N-MORB to E-MORB composition consistent with an oceanic plateau-seamount setting. Ages are constrained by faunal assemblages in radiolarian chert and minor carbonates interbedded with volcanic rocks. Radiometric ages are generally consistent with fossil data, but few U-Pb crystallization ages exist owing to poor zircon fertility in primarily mafic magmatism.

Locally, Angayucham rocks are overlain by Jurassic allochthons of partial ophiolitic sequences representing either forearc or juvenile arc magmatism, possibly related to the Koyukuk arc terrane (informal). Existing models are ambiguous whether these suprasubduction ophiolitic assemblages were constructed on, or were later tectonically obducted onto oceanic Angayucham crust, or represent some combination of these end-member processes. It is also unclear when composite Angayucham+Jurassic ophiolitic sequences were thrust onto pericratonic Ruby terrane and Arctic Alaskan basement, along the southern and northern Yukon-Koyukuk basin (YKB) margins, respectively.

We present new whole-rock and mineral geochemical and isotopic data for a suite of igneous rocks from the southern YKB margin, including the Kanuti ophiolite, the Rampart assemblage (Angayucham terrane), and mélange assemblages between them representing a possible metamorphic sole. Kanuti rocks have a depleted mantle source and variable suprasubduction affinity, whereas local Angayucham rocks resemble E-MORB, with absent to slight Th enrichment relative to mantle, and are more isotopically evolved. The mélange includes rocks resembling both suites, but Rampart-like mafic rocks dominate.

In-situ Kanuti gabbro U-Pb ages (ca. 165–160Ma; zircon and primary titanite) are consistent with previous work. Titanite and apatite ages in the metamorphic sole are variable. The oldest (ca. 230–210Ma) come from rocks with compositions resembling Angayucham (Rampart) gabbro (ca. 235–224Ma). However, both Kanuti and mélange rocks near the metamorphic sole have U-Pb intercept ages ca. 150–140Ma, inferred to record local metamorphism associated with ophiolite obduction. Similar compositions and primary ages between Kanuti metamorphic sole and Angayucham suggest subduction initiation occurred within an intra-(Angayucham)oceanic environment. Younger intercept ages suggest that obduction of the composite Angayucham+Jurassic suprasubduction ophiolitic allochthons onto Paleozoic basement occurred within 10–20 My of initiation.

title: Prolonged Interactions between the Menefee Formation and Cliff House Sandstone Indicate a Dynamic Nearshore Environment During the Campanian

authors: O'Callaghan, Zeke [1], Chavez, Ronni A. [2], Baare, Madison [3], Smith, Heather [4], Adrian, Brenton [5]
affiliations: (1) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA

abstract:
The Western Interior Seaway (WIS) is one of the most studied Cretaceous systems in North America. Fossils from the WIS are well studied, and have influenced our understanding of biostratigraphy, punctuated equilibrium, and cladogenesis. However, less geological research has been conducted on nearshore deposits of the WIS preserved in the San Juan Basin of New Mexico, outside of identification and mapping of fossil fuel reserves during the 20th century. Examining the fossil record of the San Juan Basin, most research has centered on its dinosaur‑bearing units, while the interaction between the Campanian Menefee Formation and the overlying Cliff House Sandstone has received comparatively little attention. Fluctuations of the WIS during the Campanian have historically complicated ecological interpretations of these faunas, particularly within the transition from the primarily terrestrial Menefee Formation to the largely marine Cliff House Sandstone. Recent fieldwork in this transition at Tsaya Canyon has revealed a rich assemblage of chondrichthyans, actinopterygians, and marine reptiles, in addition to significant ichnofauna. The current study aims to characterize the nature of the contact between the two units to properly contextualize the fauna.

Three stratigraphic columns measured near and in Tsaya Canyon are reported here, and indicate complex interactions among highly carbonaceous Menefee-influenced lagoons and Cliff House Sandstone barrier islands. Both flaser and lenticular beds are present along laterally discontinuous sandstone beds, and a large sandstone body incising the final coal layer of the Menefee Formation. Flat discontinuous beds of the lower Cliff House Sandstone indicate washover fans, while crossbeds only appear at Tsaya Canyon above the large Cliff House Formation tongue that crops out within it. The lowest occurrence of crossbeds in the section appears to coincide with published data on distinct sandstone bodies in the Cliff House Sandstone. Float fossils from above this interval appear to contain deep-water faunas, consistent with previous interpretations. In particular, durophagous fauna from the basal part of the section suggest a nearshore environment, while fossils from above Tsaya Canyon are consistent with deeper ocean taxa. These findings support Tsaya Tongue as representing a lagoonal barrier island system, before retrogradation of the system to a lower shoreface facies.

abstract:
A recent paper (Rodríguez-López et al., 2026, Earth-Science Reviews) presented compelling sedimentologic evidence for subtropical tidewater glaciers during the early Campanian as mid-Cretaceous hothouse conditions waned. This Barrika glaciation, with global implications for accommodation and sedimentation in coeval basinal records, is associated with nannofossil biozone UC14, which is presently calibrated to 82.80–80.96 Ma (Geologic Time Scale 2020). However, potential Myr-scale stratigraphic uncertainty persists beyond the precision of the current 83.6 ± 0.2 Ma base-Campanian age (International Chronostratigraphic Chart).

In the Colville basin, a major Campanian unconformity (CU) is expressed in seismic reflection data and outcrop, yet the base-level fall drivers are unclear. Here, high-precision isotope dilution geochronology from several outcrops along a ~135 km depositional-dip transect, spanning non-marine through deep-marine environments, is integrated with sedimentologic and stratigraphic observations to render insight into the CU. At the most landward site southwest of Uluksrak Bluff (SWUB), the pre-CU shoreline is dated as ~82.1 Ma at ~14 m below a ~62-m-thick fluvial sequence that hosts four laterally extensive braided-channel packages collectively interpreted as an extended record of CU processes; zircon ages bracket this conglomeratic channel belt succession between ~81.3 and ~79.1 Ma. Farther east, the CU is seismic stratigraphically tied to shelf incision, suggesting the up-dip channel belts may reflect pulsed, downstream-controlled forced regression. We also constrain CU-associated shoreline regression at a Toolik River valley outcrop ~95 km down-dip of SWUB, with an ~80.1 Ma age from ~14 m above a marine–non-marine transition. At the distal end of our transect, a slope incision-fill element exposed along the Ivishak River yielded an ~80.4 Ma result, temporally tying that sandy deep-water section to the CU topset record.

A preliminary cyclostratigraphic assessment of the SWUB channel belts suggests CU regression was possibly paced by four long-eccentricity (~405 kyr) cycles. We hypothesize that the CU—with signatures of marked sediment supply and caliber, steepened fluvial gradients, incised valleys, pronounced bypass to deep-marine settings, and local dropstones—may be linked with Barrika glaciation if that cold spell is ~1.5(?) Myr younger than existing calibrations suggest. Critical correlations and causal interpretations are bolstered by precise, accurate numerical age control and thorough characterization and reduction of uncertainty associated with integrated stratigraphic frameworks and global boundary stratotype sections and points.

abstract: Rolfe Mandel has inspired and mentored geoscience and archaeology research projects of many types, including our own research in the American Midwest, the Mediterranean, and the Neotropics. Here we build from his themes to consider surface and buried soils from geomorphology and geoarchaeology studies in floodplains and other sinks from Belize. Our field records come from fluviokarst valleys of ancient Maya intensive wetland farming, including Belize’s Birds of Paradise Wetlands (BOP), Lamanai, and Wari Creek. These regions each have specific water chemistries, ranging from high to low calcium carbonate and sulfate loads that influence carbon storage and aggradation rates. These case areas are Ancient Maya wetland field complexes, where studies have documented multiple paleosols buried to over 5 meters in depth and over 5,000 years in age through 20 kilometers of floodplain. Carbon occurs in both organic and inorganic horizons in this area of variable water chemistry of high to low CaCO 3 and CaSO 4 ·2H 2 O. The organic layers range up to 100 cm thick in cumulic horizons of Histosols, Mollisols, and Vertisols soil orders and preserve more than 10% organic carbon. Here, carbon storage also includes CaCO 3 tufa and carbonate horizons (Bk or Ck) that are up to 100 cm thick and formed from accretion in the rhizosphere, especially associated with some tree species such as in the genus Ficus . This paper will present a preliminary assessment of the buried soil sequences in terms of their radiocarbon chronologies, carbon quantities, water and soil chemistries, environmental change implications, and conceptualizations of the Ck horizon formation processes. In each example, the floodplains indicate sequences of paleosols that become more stable from mid Holocene (4,000 BP) to the Late Holocene (post 1500 BP) as ancient intensive farming with wetland fields and terraced slopes propagated across the landscape.

abstract: The Galápagos Archipelago is a globally important hotspot of high productivity and biodiversity, primarily thanks to its location along the equator and its bathymetry contributing to strong island-driven upwelling. Despite this area undergoing long-term climatic changes, physical controls on phytoplankton distribution throughout the archipelago are poorly known on an interannual scale. Here, we investigate the impacts of island-driven upwelling and the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) on phytoplankton using satellite-based sea surface temperature and chlorophyll-a concentration products from September 1997 through December 2024. Our analysis uses sea surface temperature as a proxy for island-driven upwelling and for local ENSO impacts, and investigates the correlation between these physical factors and chlorophyll-a on both seasonal and interannual scales. Island-driven upwelling is associated with an increase in phytoplankton biomass. ENSO strength is associated with chlorophyll-a concentration, with El Niño events tending to demonstrate lower chlorophyll-a concentrations, and La Niña events showing higher concentrations. Advances in our understanding of the long-term impacts of physical controls on phytoplankton distributions are critical to predicting how life in coastal regions will respond to our changing climate.

title: Sediment Storage Dynamics in Headwater Catchments following the Hurricane Helene Extreme Precipitation Event
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers
authors: Tennent, Emma Rae [1], Marshall, Anna [2], Schaffer, Grace R [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Sustainability, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Department of Geography and Sustainability, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA

abstract: Hurricane Helene caused unprecedented flooding, landslides, and debris flows throughout headwater catchments in the Southern Appalachian Mountains in September of 2024, resulting in loss of life and extensive damage to downstream property. Despite the regional scale of Helene’s disturbance, downstream flooding and sediment deposition varied substantially among neighboring catchments, suggesting differences in river corridor capacity to store and attenuate sediment. Improved understandings of watershed response and downstream hazard cascades are increasingly important as extreme storms, like Helene, become more frequent and severe in this region. To identify factors which increase catchment capacity to absorb disturbance, we investigated the relationship between sediment storage, geomorphic complexity, and human use in hurricane impacted headwater catchments in the Pisgah National forest. Sediment storage is used both as a proxy for flood water attenuation and as a direct measure of catchment disturbance resilience. We predict that high-storage reaches will be characterized by greater biogeomorphic complexity, including multithread planforms, islands, logjams, and/or evidence of beaver activity, whereas low-storage reaches will exhibit simpler channel morphology. We further predict that high storage reaches will display greater variability in channel geometry and sediment size, reflecting an increased capacity to retain and store sediment during Helene. We use a combination of longitudinal profiles and cross sections to characterize reach scale sediment storage volume and geomorphic complexity, and pebble count surveys to characterize sediment storage type. Forest composition surveys were conducted near each reach, as a proxy for logging legacy and human use. Catchment scale characterization was conducted using pre- and post- event LiDAR and aerial imagery. Although catchments vary in total storage, preliminary results indicate that multithread planforms, islands, and log-jam presence correspond with zones of greater sediment storage in every catchment. Presence and scale of these geomorphic features appear to correspond with logging legacy and human-use, with more homogeneous forest compositions and greater human disturbance corresponding with less extensive storage reaches and fewer instances of wood in channels. These findings suggest that logging legacies and ongoing human-use are associated with differences in modern channel complexity, and influence sediment storage following disturbance events. By continuing to investigate the complex interactions between disturbance, ecology, and human-use, we will improve our ability to identify headwater catchments that buffer or amplify downstream flooding and sediment delivery.

authors: Sandefur, Lydia Sharon [1], Rhoades, Caden [2], LaDue, Nicole [3], Jaeger, Allison [4]

abstract: concepts by aligning a lesser-known “target” with a familiar “source.” The goal of the present study was to document analogies present in seven popular college-level introductory geology textbooks and to analyze their characteristics. The texts used in this study included three printed textbooks, two open-source online textbooks, and two print lab manuals. A set of search terms (e.g., like, such as, analogous) was used to identify potential analogies, yielding more than 2000 results. After multiple rounds of coding, a final set of 550 analogies was identified and categorized based on the number of mappings (simple, meaning one mapping, and enriched, more than one mapping), relational comparison (form or function), and source origin (everyday, geology, science). Generally, analogies were more frequently related to everyday concepts rather than scientific domains (94%). Moreover, a higher proportion of analogies focused on functional relationships (e.g., buoyancy, viscosity) than form relationships (e.g., shape of river systems, layers of Earth). An association between the book type and analogy richness was found ( χ ² (2, N = 550) = 26.34, p < .001, Cramer's V = .22). Post-hoc comparisons indicated that while printed textbooks contained more analogies ( n =376), they had a lower proportion of enriched analogies (10.4%) than both open-source textbooks (22.7%) and Lab Manuals (29.6%), which did not differ significantly from each other. Enriched analogies contained more functional relationships than form relationships ( χ ²(1, N = 504) = 13.49, p < .001, Cramer's V = .16). Qualitative examination of the source domains showed that source domains related to food and household objects were the most common. The target concepts varied; the most common were geologic structures ( n = 50), earthquakes ( n = 53), minerals ( n = 55), plate tectonics ( n = 58), and volcanoes/igneous processes ( n = 73). The analyses confirm the presence of analogies throughout college-level introductory geoscience texts; however, prior studies indicate that simple analogies are not the most effective means of teaching on their own. Instructors should familiarize themselves with the analogies in their textbooks so they can expand and enhance their meaning for students in their teaching.

abstract: The Goat Rocks Volcanic Cluster in Washington State is an extinct volcanic area southeast of Mount Rainier in the Cascades Volcanic Arc. The cluster consists of four main central composite volcanoes and several peripheral mafic volcanoes that span in age from 3.6 Ma to 65 ka, overlapping activity at nearby Simcoe Mountains volcanic field and neighboring composite volcanoes (Mounts Rainier, Adams, St. Helens). This study applies new approaches to existing geochemical datasets to improve understanding of pre-eruptive magma storage conditions. We focus on three mafic volcanoes on the north and east side of the cluster: the upper and lower units of Hogback Mountain shield volcano (1.1-1.0 Ma), Devil’s Washbasin volcano (3.0-2.7 Ma), and Miriam Creek volcano (3.6 Ma). Bulk rock major and trace element compositions and olivine and spinel microprobe analyses from Wall et al. (2025) were used for Magma Chamber Simulator (MCS) modeling and thermometry, with the aim to constrain magma storage pressures (depths) and temperatures. MCS modeling was focused on the two Hogback Mountain units and used the most primitive composition from each unit as input magma composition. The models that best fit each unit’s bulk rock compositions and mineral assemblages are those with pressures between 500 and 1000 bars (1.7 to 3.3 km; upper Hogback Mountain) and 500 and 4000 bars (1.7 to 13.2 km; lower Hogback Mountain), suggesting magma storage and crystallization in the upper crust for both units. The following temperatures were determined from liquid-only, olivine-liquid, and olivine-spinel thermometers: 956°C-1243°C (lower Hogback Mountain), 1097°C-1209°C (Devil’s Washbasin), and 1144°C-1254°C (Miriam Creek). These findings improve understanding of pre-eruptive magma storage conditions in the Goat Rocks area and complement recent and ongoing geochemical and diffusion chronometry studies.

abstract:
The tectonic regimes operating on the early Earth have typically been presented as a binary system, with either stagnant-lid or mobile-lid processes. Recently, geochemical evidence, particularly zircon trace element compositions, suggest Hadean and Archean crust were generated by the tandem operation of both stagnant- and mobile-lid processes (Mixon et al., 2024; Valley et al., 2026). However, the relationship between observed trace element ratios in Hadean and Archean detrital zircons and the actual processes of magmatism and differentiation are unclear. The translation of empirically calibrated proxies to Hadean settings further complicates interpretation.

We present linked trace element, oxygen isotope, and hafnium isotope data from 4.3 – 3.5 Ga detrital zircons from the Jack Hills, Western Australia. During the Hadean, there are three geochemically distinct periods of juvenile magmatism that are periodically reworked through the Eoarchean. Zircon U-Nb-Sc-Yb trace element proxies for tectonic provenance generally correspond to plume-like values in the first (oldest) array, mixed in the second array, and arc-like in the third (youngest) array. In other words, trace element proxies generally shift towards arc-like values over time, but these trends are better defined when contextualized by Hf model ages. Furthermore, while trace element proxies suggest a range of tectonic regimes at any given time, the tectonic character of juvenile magmatism becomes progressively more arc-like over the Hadean period. This supports a complex tectonic history for the Jack Hills source(s), and for the broader Hadean period, beyond a simple transition from stagnant- to mobile-lid regime.

title: Where and what is the front of the Variscan Orogenic wedge in western Ireland?
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Posters)
authors: Bloomquist, Maxwell J [1], Yoshinobu, Aaron S. [2]
affiliations: (1) department of geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(2) Geosciences department, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract:
New structural data from coastal exposures along the entire western shore of County Clare, western Ireland, combined with INFOMAR seabed imagery, reveal that deformation at the front of the Variscan orogenic wedge is marked by large-wavelength (100 m to km-scale) periclinal detachment folds, localized fault zones, and axial planar, anastomosing cleavages within Carboniferous deepwater through deltaic sedimentary rocks. Strain is partitioned into local high-strain zones which can be seen in variations in the density, distribution, geometry of folds and associated faults.

Coastal mapping demonstrates the following: Doubly-plunging periclinal folds range from kilometer to meter scale, with axial traces trending ~080–260°. Folds with wavelengths >100 m have interlimb angles of 70–120°, while smaller folds (<100 m) are open to isoclinal. Folding is accompanied by numerous m-displacement out-of-fold faults, flexural slip, buckling, and flexural flow, particularly where thick mudstones act as ductile layers. A spaced, anastomosing axial planar cleavage is well developed regionally in the southern half of County Clare. INFOMAR bathymetry reveals kilometer-scale domes, basins, and doubly-plunging folds cut by NE-striking faults (1–2 km long). Faulting along the limbs of periclinal folds display shearing which reflects non-plane strain movement. These structures mirror smaller-scale features observed onshore.

Correlation between offshore and onshore structures reveals the possibility of localized wrench fault systems propagating along strike of the orogen in localities such as Bridges of Ross, generating tight to open doubly plunging folds. Additionally, the presence of anastomosing cleavages preserved further north than previously estimated provides reason for a new estimate of the range and regional extent of the deformation at the toe of the Variscan orogenic wedge. Together, the data suggest greater deformation magnitudes within the orogenic wedge at this latitude than previously recognized. The findings challenge published strain estimates and imply that cylindrical fold models used in cross-section restorations may be invalid for this region.

title: Estimating Sedimentation in Small Reservoirs in the United States using a Random Forest Regressor Model
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Gavilan-Abanto, Maby [1], Konsoer, Kory [2], Langendoen, Eddy [3]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Anthropology, Louisiana State Univesity, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA
(2) Geography and Anthropology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA
(3) United States Department of Agriculture, Oxford, Mississippi, USA
abstract: Reservoir siltation constitutes one of the big threatening challenges in the current century. Over 12,000 small dams and reservoirs were built across the United States under the USDA Watershed Protection and Flood Prevention Program (PL-566), with most construction occurring prior to 1970. These dams were built with an expected operation lifespan of 50 to 100 years, and following the lifespan of individual dams, extensive maintenance and monitoring has been lacking. Traditional reservoir surveying of such a large number of sites is prohibitive and time consuming. Therefore, this study seeks alternative methods (e.g., regression, correlation, machine learning) to estimate the remaining capacity in reservoirs. While previous research has applied different machine learning algorithms to estimate reservoir capacity loss for some of the largest reservoirs in the US, similar studies for small reservoirs are lacking, creating a need to understand how environmental and watershed characteristics influence small-scale reservoir sedimentation and flood risk. The dataset used in these analyses includes 1544 reservoirs and 3644 sets of consecutive sediment surveys. Environmental, watershed, and reservoir parameters that are expected to influence the amount of sedimentation delivered and trapped by a reservoir were obtained from various sources, such as monthly precipitation, maximum temperature, elevation models, soil, and land cover. Different features were derived e.g.: monthly precipitation, mean slope, hydraulic soil conductivity. Following various statistical analyses and data reduction, a random forest regression model was trained, with results indicating that sedimentation rates for small reservoirs are driven primarily by hydroclimatic extreme events, sediment supply at a basin scale, and reservoir geometry rather than fine-scale topographic attributes. The findings suggest that small reservoirs are affected by intense, short-duration events, given their restricted storage and hydrologic damping. However, as these records include reservoirs distributed all over the United States, next steps for model development should explore different cross validation methods that can provide the model with a finer regional context, such as using ecoregions, physiographic province, or land management regions as part of the cross-validation stage.

title: Field-based Constraints on the Deep Crustal Evolution of a Tonalite Batholith; Insights From the Athabasca Granulite Terrane, Canadian Shield
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Sasso, Joseph Anthony [1], Fleischer, Noah [2], Dumond, Gregory [3], Williams, Michael L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Geographic and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
(3) Univ of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Geosciences, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(4) University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
abstract: Tonalite is a major component of ancient tonalite-trondhjemite-granite suites and modern arcs. Tonalite formation is critical for the evolution of continental crust. Experimental studies show tonalite is produced by melting hydrous mafic rocks at high pressure conditions which are met in lower crustal arc settings. The timing of the onset of modern subduction remains widely debated, as is the tectonic origin of ancient tonalite suites, which may predate plate tectonics. The Athabasca granulite terrane (AGT) in the Canadian Shield is one of Earth’s largest exposures of exhumed lower crust; it provides a natural laboratory for studying deep crustal processes. The Chipman domain of the AGT is dominated by a large body of heterogeneous and structurally complex tonalite intruded by the Paleoproterozoic Chipman dike swarm. Zircon geochronology from tonalite throughout the domain ranges from >3.0-1.9 Ga. New field mapping has yielded new constraints of the tonalite’s structural and petrochronological evolution. We identify a strain gradient increasing to the southeast based on grain size reduction and thinning foliation from centimeter- to millimeter-scale. This gradient coincides with the overprinting of an earlier tonalite fabric (S1) by a second, nearly orthogonal foliation (S2), and increased abundance of Chipman dikes. S1 is a subhorizontal fabric of 2-10 cm thick layers of hornblende-poor tonalite and rare amphibolite layers. S1 is isoclinally folded and sheared by S2, a steep SW-striking fabric defined by a hornblende-tonalite gneiss with abundant dextral porphyroclasts. The S2 foliation is subparallel to Chipman dikes. Some dikes are partially melted, producing tonalitic leucosome with dextral kinematic indicators. S2 orientation and kinematic indicators are consistent with slip along the Grease River shear zone ~1.9 Ga. We interpret that S2 developed syn-kinematically with the emplacement and metamorphism of the Chipman dikes. We interpret S1 to be a remnant of primary magmatic layering deformed and transposed by an unknown deformation event. Melting of Chipman dikes provides a model for tonalite formation consistent with modern subduction during the Paleoproterozoic. Structural evidence suggests the Chipman batholith was formed from two or more tonalite forming events. Ongoing work seeks to constrain the timing of tonalite formation and S1 fabric development to characterize the evolution of the Chipman tonalite across a billion years.

title: Selecting Well-Preserved Benthic Foraminifera for Geochemical Analyses: Developing a Modified Preservation Ranking Workflow

authors: Cantrell, Ripley C [1], Burkett , Ashley M [2], Hupp, Brittany N. [3], Penman, Donald E. [4]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Oklahoma State University,
(3) George Mason University, Fairfax, VA,

abstract: The selection of benthic foraminifera that retain their original microstructure and geochemical composition is fundamental for accurate analysis of trace elements and stable isotopes. However, diagenetic processes can alter test morphology and geochemistry, ultimately making specimen screening a critical yet undervalued process for palaeoceanographic research. This project has cultivated and applied a standardized workflow that evaluates the preservation of benthic foraminifera recovered from Paleocene-Eocene sediments before geochemical analysis. Individual specimens were examined under reflected-light microscopy and assigned to one of five preservation categories, ranging from glassy to frosted. The surface integrity was assessed independently using a first score (IS;3-5) based on the preservation of chambers, structures, pores, and overall test morphology. Because the original Foraminiferal Preservation Index (FPI) was created in relation to younger sediment, a modified assemblage preservation score was used to better accommodate older material in which recrystallization may have mimicked intermediate preservation states. Therefore, the resulting preservation scores were used to find the highest quality specimens for future analysis of stable isotopes and trace elements while also documenting the preservation variability among the samples. This project shows how standardized preservation assessments can improve specimen choice, increase reproducibility, and maximize the scientific value of geochemical datasets. In addition to providing support to ongoing palaeoceanographic research, this project also provided hands-on training in micropaleontology, microscopy, data management, and quality assessment.

title: Interspecific Allometry Of Late Miocene To Early Pliocene Giant Camels Of North America
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Oganesyan, Cruz [1], Prothero, Donald Ross [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, Cal Poly Pomona, Pomona, California, USA

(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State Polytechnic University Pomona, Pomona, California, USA; Department of Vertebrate Paleontology, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract: As an animal grows larger and subsequently heavier, it must also have limbs suitable enough to support their prodigious bodies. If they increased isometrically or otherwise gracile, they would be too flimsy and weak. The size of their limb bones must increase allometrically to achieve the needed strength. The same remains true for family Camelidae of the Ungulates. The evolution of Miocene to Pliocene North American camels from ancestral Procamelus occidentalis to descendant Gigantocamelus spatulus, Megatylopus gigas, and Megacamelus merriami saw them grow from approximately 1.2 meter at the shoulder to over 3.6 meters, and from an estimated 55 kg to over 4000 kg in the latter. In order to support this increased mass, the limbs grew faster in circumference than length. To test our hypothesis, we collected measurements from the long limb bones: humerus, radius, femur, tibia, and respective metapodials of 4 different continuous species of ancient dromedary camels for comparison. The results from the data we collected were negatively allometric and supported our hypothesis that the limbs became more stalky and less gracile as they evolved.

title: SPARTA: A Toolkit for In Situ Geomechanical Analysis of Small Body Regolith
session_title: Big Science from Small Worlds
authors: Anderson, Robert [1], Buczkowski, Debra [2], Wyrick, Danielle [3], Long-Fox, Jared [4], Sollitt, Luke [5], Aiken, Ava [6], Khan, Shezren [7], Ishida, Wesley [8]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA,
(2) JHU Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD,

(4) University of South Florida,

(7) San Diego State University,
(8) University of California, Berkley,
abstract:
The SPARTA (Soil Properties Assessment, Resistance, Thermal, Analysis) toolkit is an advanced, compact system engineered for the in situ measurement of key geomechanical properties, thermal conductivity, and water/ice content of planetary regolith. This multi-functional instrument integrates a cone penetrometer/vane shear device for geomechanical assessments, a dielectric probe for determining the dielectric constant and water content, and a thermal conductivity probe for evaluating the thermal properties of regolith materials. Operating at depths of up to 1 meter, SPARTA is specifically designed for applications in planetary exploration, providing crucial data for understanding surface and subsurface characteristics across a range of celestial bodies.

The toolkit’s modular design allows for versatility in exploring diverse planetary environments. The requirements needed for testing under small body conditions (including asteroids, comets, and icy moons) are being determined; SPARTA has already been extensively tested for Mars and Moon conditions. By measuring regolith compaction, shear strength, water content, and thermal properties, SPARTA provides a comprehensive dataset essential for evaluating the suitability of planetary surfaces for resource utilization, as well as long-term human habitation. These measurements are vital for NASA’s future exploration missions, especially those targeting in situ resource utilization (ISRU) on small bodies and sustainable human presence in the outer solar system.

The design architecture, functional capabilities, and potential applications of SPARTA are pertinent to NASA's exploration goals. Integrated data from SPARTA could guide the selection of landing sites, inform habitat construction, and support resource extraction strategies, ensuring a foundation for future planetary exploration missions. Additionally, SPARTA’s portability, ease of deployment, and ability to operate autonomously at various planetary sites make it a critical tool for advancing human exploration and permanent settlement in space.

title: Commotion in the Ocean: Tsunamis, Seiche Waves, and Sedimentary Responses to the Chicxulub Impact on the US Mid-Atlantic margin
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Miller, Kenneth G. [1], Sugarman, Peter J [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sci., Rutgers University, Pennington, NJ,
(2) Dept Earth Planetary Sci., Rutgers University, Piscatway, NJ, USA
abstract: The mid-Atlantic Coastal Plain preserves an exceptional record of the Chicxulub impact at an intermediate distance of approximately 2,500 km from the crater. Sections found beneath the modern outer shelf and continental slope contain major unconformities, collectively termed the East Coast Sequential Unconformity (Olsson and Wise, 1985), which were likely produced by slumping triggered by an impact-generated mega-earthquake estimated to have approached Mw 11-12 and by subsequent aftershocks. Across the New Jersey Coastal Plain, preservation of the impact record varies systematically with depositional setting. At the downdip Bass River site, deposited in a middle-shelf environment at approximately 75 m paleodepth, an undisturbed spherule layer is interpreted as ballistic ejecta that arrived within hours of impact. More updip sites, including Ancora (~50 m paleodepth), contain reworked spherules and sedimentary deposits attributed to swash-back and seiche activity. These sedimentary observations are consistent with tsunami or seiche waves reaching heights on the order of 15-20 m and disrupting the shallow (<50-75 m) seafloor. Farther updip, sections are commonly diastemic or preserve only weak and diffuse Ir enrichments that have been redistributed by bioturbation. The most proximal updip locality, the Campo-Buck Pit (proposed Millstone Geological Park), records the impact in a lower-shoreface setting at approximately 20-30 m paleodepth. A 50-cm-thick clay layer contains a pronounced Ir peak near its base and multiple thin siderite laminae near its top. These laminae are interpreted as concentrations of reworked impact spherules deposited by earthquake-generated seiche activity during the months to years following the impact. The laminae document repeated episodes of ejecta remobilization and help explain the heterogeneous preservation of K/Pg boundary deposits throughout the region. At the Edelman Fossil Park, deposited in paleodepths of 30-40 m, the Main Fossiliferous Layer (MFL; Obasi et al., 2011) contains abundant in situ Danian fossils mixed with reworked Cretaceous material. The MFL lies approximately 50 cm above the heavily bioturbated K/Pg contact, and neither horizon contains a significant Ir anomaly, suggesting removal of the primary fallout layer. We propose that the MFL at Edelman represents an early post-extinction recovery fauna containing reworked Cretaceous material. This assemblage was later buried by aftershock-induced seiche deposits years to decades after the impact rather than representing a death assemblage generated directly by the extinction event.

title: Occurrence and Characterization of Rare PGE and As-Bearing Phases in Chondrites
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials (Posters)
authors: Truman, Natalie [1], Scharrer, Manuel [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract:
Chondrites preserve records of the processes of the early Solar System that are typically obscured and overprinted in other Solar System bodies. Although chondrites have been studied extensively, several aspects of their formation and evolution remain poorly understood. Due to their uniqueness, rare phases enriched in PGEs such as sulfides, tellurides, and arsenides as well as other arsenides and sulfarsenides have the potential to provide new insight into the formation conditions and/or modification processes of these meteorites. However, these phases have been generally overlooked due to their small size and rarity, resulting in mostly vague descriptions of their presence in the limited literature that acknowledges them.

Sampling CK, CV, and R chondrites, where the occurrence of these phases has been described throughout a range of thermal metamorphism, allows for investigating a range of solar nebula aspects and allows the separation of systematics in the primary condensation of these elements and secondary redistribution effects that result in the present day systematics in petrology and chemistry of these phases. The mineral compositions and textural relationships of these phases in the chondrites is constrained by optical microscopy, SEM, and compositional analysis and the systematics between the chondrites in the abovementioned chondrites is presented. The occurrences, composition, and textural relationships are used to draw conclusions and allows for a better overall understanding of the PGE, As, and Te elements in the early solar system and subsequent overprinting due to nebula and parent body processes.

title: Evaluating the Influence of Microplastics on Health and Calcification of Benthic Foraminifera Ammonia confertitesta
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology and Geomicrobiology (Posters)
authors: Reed-Horn, Madeleine [1], Hoskison, Eli [2], Haynes, Laura [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science and Geography, Vassar College, Poughkeepsie, NY, USA
(2) Earth Science and Geography, Vassar College, Poughkeepsie, NY, USA

abstract: Plastic pollution is becoming one of the most ubiquitous and dangerous anthropogenic pollutants that poses a significant threat to the health of marine life. Plastic pollution further breaks down into microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs), which can enter marine ecosystems through lower trophic levels, although the effects of microplastics on the health and viability of these species remains understudied. Of particular importance are marine calcifiers, especially foraminifera: marine protists whose shells contribute up to 50% of calcium carbonate sediments globally, making them crucial players for long term carbon storage. Thus, the impact of microplastics on the health of foraminifera is of importance for understanding both their (1) ability to calcify and sequester atmospheric carbon while exposed to MP and NPs, and (2) their potential to transport MP and NPs through the food chain as basal species. In this study, we observed the abundant benthic foraminifera species Ammonia confertitesta found in the Long Island Sound, where anthropogenic pollution is known to accumulate. A. confertitesta are observed for their biological and behavioral response to various types and sizes of MPs, including fluorescent amino formaldehyde polymers. Fluorescence and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging will allow us to investigate interactions of foraminiferal rhizopodial network with MPs and general behavioral response to MP exposure.

title: Overview of the Gray Fossil Site flora (Neogene, Tennessee, USA)
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part II)
authors: Hermsen, Elizabeth J. [1]
affiliations: (1) Milwaukee Public Museum, Milwaukee, WI, USA
abstract: The Neogene Gray Fossil Site (GFS) is a sinkhole deposit located in northeastern Tennessee, USA. It preserves a rich paleobiota, providing crucial information about a time period that is poorly documented in the Central Appalachian region of the United States. In addition to a rich vertebrate fauna, the site preserves a diverse fossil flora made up of conifers and angiosperms represented by reproductive and vegetative structures (in this account, species followed by their authorities have been formally described). Conifer remains include bald cypress ( Taxodium , branchlets and seeds), as well as unidentified cone material. Angiosperm trees and shrubs include oak ( Quercus , nuts and cupules), hickory ( Carya tennesseensis Huang et al., nuts and husks), prickly ash ( Zanthoxylum , 2 spp., seeds), winter hazel ( Corylopsis grisea Quirk & Hermsen, seeds), bladdernut ( Staphylea levisemia Huang et al., seeds), tupelo ( Nyssa grayensis Noll, nom. ined., endocarps), raspberry/blackberry ( Rubus , endocarps), and birch ( Betula , catkins). Climbing plants include grape ( Vitis , 3 spp. described by Gong et al., seeds), passionflower ( Passiflora , 2 spp. described by Hermsen, seeds), a species in the moonseed family ( Sinomenium macrocarpum Liu & Jacques, endocarps), and Sargentodoxa (seeds). Remains of several herbs have been identified from the site, although some might be contaminants. One extinct angiosperm with unclear affinities is represented by endocarps, Cavilignum pratchettii Siegert & Hermsen. Vegetative structures include wood, grass stem fragments, thorns, and tendrils. Fungal fruiting bodies (cf. Annulohypoxylon ) and caterpillar frass occur amongst the plant remains. The plants identified from the site to date primarily have affinities to fossil and modern plant genera and/or species found in North America and Eurasia. Their biogeographic connections to Eurasia are consistent with the existence of land bridges between North America and Eurasia earlier in the Cenozoic, the occurrence of modern Eurasian elements in other Neogene floras from the eastern US, and the well-known “Tertiary relict” disjunct patterns observed in the modern flora of the Northern Hemisphere. The GFS flora has clear connections to the modern flora of eastern North America, including the US Southeast (e.g., Taxodium ), although at least one taxon ( Zanthoxylum cf. Z. americanum ) has a more northerly distribution today. The occurrence of Passiflora indicates a potential Neotropical connection, and Cavilignum is not known from other localities.

title: Rates of landscape change following the 1992 Landers earthquake
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape (Posters)
authors: Reitman, Nadine G. [1], Arrowsmith, Ramon [2], Rhodes, Dallas D. [3], Hatem, Alexandra [4], Schwarz, Madeline [5], Zuckerman, Malinda [6], Powell, Joseph [7]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Golden, CO,
(2) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
(3) R&R Consultants, Santa Fe, NM,
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, Golden, CO,

(6) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,

abstract: The landscape record of earthquakes is a primary tool used to interpret the location, displacement, and recency of active faulting. Landscapes change after earthquake rupture from both natural and anthropogenic causes (e.g., runoff, mass wasting, geotourism, dirt bikes), causing erosion and modification of vertical fault scarps and laterally offset features. The 1992 M7.3 Landers, California, earthquake offers an opportunity to quantify the degradation of lateral and vertical displacements that were documented post-earthquake (Arrowsmith & Rhodes,1994; McGill & Rubin,1999). We focus on a ~500-m-long section of the Emerson fault scarp south of Galway Lake Road that had up to 5 m right-lateral and 1.8 m vertical displacement with areas of localized and distributed deformation. We document landscape change over 30 years using vertical differencing of topography derived from 1992 USGS aerial photographs taken two days after the earthquake and 2022 UAS photogrammetry and geomorphic analysis of both elevation datasets, as well as field surveys. Geomorphic changes include extensive rills across the scarp (some with apparent left-lateral offset due to flow patterns), headward-eroding channels deeply incised into what were broad washes in 1992, formation of post-1992 channels on the downthrown block, and layback of the 1992 vertical scarp. Nine gullies with the most erosion in 2022 were formed from seven primary channels in 1992. In these channels, knickpoints have retreated ~8-12 m upstream, with a maximum of 18 m, but minor incision continues for 14-30 m up the channels. The volume of material removed since 1992 results in minimum rates of 0.04-0.11 m^3 per year, with seven of the nine channels clustering at 0.08-0.09 m^3 per year. The gully with the most erosion reflects a shifting watershed boundary that captured more area between 1992 and 2022. Catchment-wide erosion rates average an order of magnitude faster than measured in prior studies (e.g., Owen et al., 2011), reflecting the influence of sudden baselevel drop from vertical displacement in the 1992 earthquake and the spatiotemporally variable nature of geomorphic change. The results of this work will help parametrize landscape evolution models of active faulting and inform how landscapes are interpreted for evidence of active faults.

title: Modeling Slow-Slip Behavior in the Cascadia Subduction Zone
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources (Posters)
authors: Hosek, Madeleine Lillie [1], Hooker, John N [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Department of Atmospheric Science, Environmental Science, and Physics, University of the Incarnate Word, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
Since 2001, slow-slip events (SSEs) have become an important focus of subduction zone systems due to their potential effects on strain accumulation and stress transfer across fault systems. In the Cascadia Subduction Zone, heterogeneities in the mechanical properties of the subducting Juan de Fuca plate interface are thought to reflect variations in frictional behavior, producing distinct locked, episodic tremor and slip (ETS), and stable-slip (SST) zones. However, the relationship between aseismic SSEs, low-frequency earthquake swarms, and the stress conditions that govern megathrust earthquake cycles, as seen in the past, remains unclear.

This study investigates how hydrologic, mechanical, and geometric factors influence the magnitude and duration of SSEs within the Cascadia Subduction Zone. Seismic data from the USGS Earthquake Catalog were analyzed in MATLAB to characterize the temporal distribution of seismicity. Building upon the framework of Bürgmann and Dascher-Cousineau (2024), we use the Mineralization, Earthquake, and Fluid-flow Integrated SimulaTOr (MEFISTO) to simulate variations in pore-fluid pressure, frictional properties, slip rates, stress transfer, and fault geometry. These simulations are designed to evaluate how changes in these parameters affect SSE behavior, periodicity, and stress redistribution along the plate interface.

Preliminary results indicate that SSEs are characterized by unique conditions such as stress drops of only a few kPa, suggesting that relatively small stress perturbations may influence strain accumulation and stress transfer within Cascadia fault systems. Ongoing simulations are examining how variables such as fluid pressure, static: dynamic friction ratios, and plate-interface geometry can affect SSE recurrence intervals, duration, and magnitude. These results will improve the understanding of the physical conditions that govern slow-slip behavior and their potential role in stress evolution throughout the Cascadia earthquake cycle.
