title: Geologic Framework and Controls on Mineralization at the Venari Minerals Red Mountain Lithium Deposit, Nye County, Nevada
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics
authors: Gans, Phillip B. [1], Healy, Matthew [2], Abbott, Paul [3], Welch, Isabella B [4], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [5], Eden, Ryan [6]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Earth Science, UC, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) Suite 116, Level 1, 165-167 Phillip Street, Venari Minerals, Sydney, New South Wales, USA
(3) Suite 116, Level 1, 165-167 Phillip Street, Venari Minerals, Sydney, New South Wales, USA
(4) Dept of Earth Science, UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(5) Dept. of Earth Science, UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(6) UC Santa Barbara, Goleta, CA, USA
abstract:
The Venari Minerals Red Mountain Lithium Project (500Mt @1139 ppm Li for 3.03Mt LCE ) is hosted in lacustrine rocks of the Miocene Horse Camp Formation (HCF) ~50 miles SW of Ely, NV. The HCF is an E-tilted half-graben basin fill in the footwall of the Railroad Valley fault. New detailed mapping, logging of drill core, U-Pb dating, and XRD/SEM studies shed light on the basin evolution and Li mineralization. The ~ 2.5 km-thick HCF accumulated between ~16.5 and 15.0 Ma, with alluvial fan systems to the N and S feeding coarse detritus into the basin and a central trough of fine-grained lacustrine deposits. Accumulation rates were ~1.5 mm/yr in the nearshore and ~0.8 mm/yr offshore between 16.2 and 15.5 Ma, when fault slip outpaced sediment supply and water depths reached 900 m. Late infilling of the basin was dominated by fluvial and palustrine/playa deposits.

Logging of DDH holes in the upper part of the HCF differentiated 14 lithofacies based on grain size and composition, with high Li grades restricted to 3 of these: a) organic-rich marl (clay + calcite), b) intraformational conglomerate (rip up clasts in a muddy matrix), and c) laminated sandstone composed of clay pellets ± calcite. These represent diverse environments, including aeolian dust dunes (Parna deposits), palustrine/playa marshlands, shallow lacustrine, and delta fore-slope. The Parna deposits are the highest grade (3000 to >5000 ppm Li). The common feature of all Li-rich intervals is their high clay content, and high porosity/permeability. XRD and SEM analysis indicate the main Li-bearing phase is a high-Mg smectite (Welch and Gans, this vol) and is associated with calcite ± qtz ± kspar ± analcime± strontianite. We conclude that Li mineralization in the HCF resulted from fluxing by low-T hypersaline/alkaline Mg- and Li-rich brines though permeable horizons during diagenesis, with replacement of pre-existing clays by high Mg smectites/hectorite. The Red Mountain Project is considered a Volcano-Sedimentary type deposit, but lacks evidence for coeval volcanic activity in the vicinity. Rather, lithium was likely leached from the huge volumes of Eocene silicic volcanic rocks that contributed most of the basin detritus, and from the dozens of distal silicic ashes that rained down in the lake.

title: Chronostratigraphy of the Late Turonian System, Powder River Basin, WY: paleogeographic insights from integrated U-Pb geochronology, core-to-outcrop stratigraphy, and biostratigraphy
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part I)
authors: Sullivan, Patrick [1], Sonnenberg, Stephen [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA; United States Geological Survey, Central Energy Resources Science Center, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract: Upper Turonian strata of the U.S. Western Interior Basin contain an anomalous number of unconformity-bound marine sandstones interpreted as remnants of broader depositional systems. High precision geochronologic constraint is crucial to resolving enigmatic stratigraphic correlations of these units. Upper Turonian strata atop the composite Mid-Turonian Unconformity (MTU) in the Powder River Basin (PRB), Wyoming are investigated through study of shallow marine sandstones and shales of the Wall Creek Member of the Frontier Formation and the Turner Member of the Carlile Shale. Five new high-precision CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon ages, 41 whole cores, and 19 measured outcrop sections were correlated across the basin using compiled ammonite zones and digital well logs. A bentonite collected below the sharp base of the Wall Creek Member containing the Late Turonian ammonite Scaphites whitfieldi in the northwestern part of the basin yields a Cenomanian age 93.98 ± 0.07 Ma, documenting a hiatus of ~4 Ma. A bentonite collected in concretionary mudstones below the Wall Creek sandstone in the southwestern margin of the PRB, mapped as the Cenomanian-age Belle Fourche Member by previous authors yields an Upper Turonian age of 90.872 ± 0.013 Ma, correlative to the zone of S. warreni and documenting the preservation of older strata in the region than previously mapped. A bentonitic mudstone below the uppermost sandstone unit in the S. warreni zone in the eastern PRB yields a single-crystal age of 90.670 ± 0.09 Ma, suggesting a conformable relationship with the overlying S. whitfieldi unit in the Turner in the central PRB, which yields an age of 90.645 ± 0.016 Ma. Where a complete Upper Turonian succession is preserved, strata display five progradational episodes within an overall retrogradational sequence. Both the Wall Creek and Turner Members display identical stacking of nearshore to offshore sediments from S. whitfieldi to P. germari , although an additional unit consisting of S. warreni and P. macombi- age strata is only present in the easternmost PRB. Successively younger strata of both the Wall Creek and Turner members onlap a convex MTU towards a maximum hiatus along an apparent northwest-southeast-trending feature in the central PRB, likely created by differences in accommodation created by temporary forebulge-style lithospheric flexure in the backbulge during a documented 80 km eastward transfer from the Willard-Paris-Meade to the Crawford Thrust in the Sevier fold-and-thrust.

title: New Mapping and Characterization of the Deadwood Fault, West-Central Idaho
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape
authors: Vadman, Michael [1], Laabs, Benjamin J. C. [2], Lamont, Ellen A. [3], Slawson, Jacob [4], Liberty, Lee M. [5], Lifton, Zachery M. [6]
affiliations: (1) Seismology & Geomorphology Group, Technical Service Center, U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, CO, USA
(2) Seismology & Geomorphology Group, Technical Service Center, U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, CO, USA
(3) Seismology & Geomorphology Group, Technical Service Center, U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, CO, USA
(4) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(5) Boise State Univ, Dept Geosciences/CGISS/MS1536, Boise, ID, USA
(6) Idaho Geological Survey, Boise, ID, USA
abstract:
The Deadwood fault is a complex, north-south striking fault located in west-central Idaho. Mapping of faults in the Idaho Batholith has been historically challenging, but the availability of new lidar-derived topography has facilitated detailed studies along the Deadwood fault. We combine both digital and field-based mapping, paleoseismic trenching, and geophysical techniques to characterize different aspects of the fault. These techniques reveal a transtensional fault system, evidenced by stratigraphic and geomorphic observations along the fault trace including offsets of glacial and fluvial deposits. The northern and middle sections of the Deadwood fault accommodate oblique-normal to strike-slip motion while the southern section displays more evidence of normal faulting. In the southern section, normal fault strands west of the Deadwood reservoir were exposed in two paleoseismic trenches revealing offset units of late Pleistocene to Holocene age and evidence of at least two earthquakes in the last 22 ka. Seismic reflection profiles also show stratigraphic offsets along the same orientation.

Based on observations from paleoseismic trenches, vertical slip rates along the southern section of the fault are 0.2-0.6 mm/yr, which equal or exceed slip rates along some faults in the neighboring northern Basin and Range. The Deadwood fault lacks steep range-front relief and other geomorphic indicators of consistent vertical slip, however, suggesting that slip rates inferred from trench stratigraphy may overestimate longer-term slip. We suggest that the late Quaternary slip rate of the Deadwood Fault reflects changes in crustal stress along the fault from local ice cap growth and decay in the Salmon River Mountains. Our lidar- and field-based mapping suggest other faults in the western Idaho Batholith may feature similar transtension and evidence of late Quaternary activity. We discuss how this pattern of deformation may fit into regional tectonics.

title: Decreased Terrestrial Weathering Intensity in the Southern Hemisphere Topics during the Ireviken Biogeochemical Event
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: McNally, Anna [1], Stolfus, Brittany [2], Cramer, Bradley Douglas [3], Peate, David W. [4], Hill, Talia [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
(3) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
(4) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
(5) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA,
abstract:
The Ireviken Biogeochemical Event (IBE) includes a major perturbation to the global carbon cycle during the Silurian. Along with carbon, other geochemical cycles, including nitrogen and sulfur, were impacted, with each of their excursions coinciding near the onset of a biotic crisis. This extinction event affected a range of taxa including conodonts and graptolites. As more data emerges, it is becoming clear that the Ireviken is an example of an Oceanic Anoxic Event (OAE) driven by the expansion of reducing environments caused by enhanced primary productivity. The driver of enhanced primary productivity is currently unknown, but likely scenarios include enhanced terrestrial weathering delivering nutrients to the oceans or enhanced oceanic recycling of nutrients.

Here we studied changes in weathering intensity of terrestrial sources from two cores located in the southern hemisphere tropical belt during the Silurian (Gotland, Sweden, and Iowa, USA). We utilized a series of geochemical proxies including the Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA), the Chemical Index of Weathering (CIW), and the Plagioclase Index of Alteration (PIA) to evaluate changes in weathering intensity. The data sets show a clear decrease in weathering intensity immediately prior to the IBE and throughout the early to middle Sheinwoodian Stage. These data indicate that there was a reduction in weathering intensity within the southern hemisphere tropical belt, and that an increase in weathering intensity is not the source of nutrients to initiate the IBE.

title: Addressing “Undone Science” Through Community-Based Participatory Research (CBPR): A Transformative Approach to the Challenges of Legacy Soil Lead (Pb) and Urban Agriculture
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part I)
authors: Schofield, Suzanna [1], Kelemen, Adela [2], Lynch, Eliza Marie [3], Lynch, Bridget Elizabeth [4], Andrews, Danielle [5], Hayhow, Claire [6], Brabander, Daniel Joseph [7]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences Department, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(3) Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley Hills, MA,
(4) Geosciences Department, Wellesley College, Wellesley Hills, MA,
(5) The Food Project, Boston, MA, USA
(6) Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, ; Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, USA
(7) Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA,
abstract:
Pb contamination of urban soils is a biological and social toxicity in Boston, Massachusetts caused by historic and current industrial activity and legacy leaded paint and gasoline. Pb impacts neurological development and perpetuates distributional injustice in low-income communities and communities of color across generations. While urban growing is essential in promoting community activism and food justice, growers in Boston often face uncertain risks due to close contact with urban soils. The Food Project (TFP) is an urban agriculture and youth education program that employs 120 teenagers annually to help grow 150,000 pounds of fresh produce using best practices that increase soil health and limit heavy metal mobility. The Daniel J. Brabander (DJB) Lab has collaborated with TFP for twenty five years to co-develop and co-implement this mission by designing CBPR research studies that investigate undone science questions. Through two decades of youth-led workshops and community events that have impacted 120 undergraduate students, 240 high schoolers, and countless community members, the collaboration has expanded beyond its initial goals and is constantly evolving to address emerging community needs.

Our collaborations have developed both urban agriculture and CBPR best practices over time. For example, TFP and DJB designed and implemented a free raised beds program (“Build a Garden”) that has installed over 2,000 raised beds around Boston to support individual growers. Further, decadal long surveillance of Pb concentrations in compost delivered to urban growers has resulted in changes to the city program that have brought the Pb concentrations in this growing matrix down by 75% since 2012 when Pb concentrations were exceeding the 400 μg/g Environmental Protection Agency's soil benchmark. As of 2026, over 300 household urban gardens have been tested to quantify and isotopically identify Pb risk exposure, leading to new community-based interventions, such as updated guidance on raised bed height and placement.

This partnership demonstrates that long-term collaborations based in empathy, listening, and trust foster a cycle of question asking and answering that can shape research priorities, build diverse partnerships, and deliver community-centered deliverables that would not be possible within a non-CBPR format.

title: When Five Meters Isn't Always Five Meters: Complex History of Offset Channels in the Carrizo Plain, CA
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape
authors: Akciz, Sinan O. [1]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Fullerton, CA,
abstract: Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural disasters, and understanding whether faults produce only large or mixed-magnitude slip events is critical for improving hazard models. Offset stream channels are widely used to reconstruct slip-per-event and slip-rate histories along active faults, and measuring these offsets is straightforward. Determining whether a given offset records one earthquake or several is not. Numerical landscape evolution modeling shows mean measured offset can underestimate true slip once cumulative displacement exceeds channel spacing, and that fault-zone geomorphology degrades further with time since the last earthquake. Field-based 3D excavations corroborate this: some apparent offsets are instead deflections never tectonically displaced, or channels aligned across the fault only coincidentally. Catalogued offsets along the Carrizo Plain section of the San Andreas Fault cluster near multiples of ~5 m (5, 10, 15, 20, 25 m), historically interpreted as evidence that each rupture produced ~5 m of slip. However, at the fault's 45–145-year recurrence interval and ~36 mm/yr slip rate, most earthquakes should accumulate only 1.5–3.5 m, implying the ~5 m clustering reflects channel spacing and capture dynamics, or channels sampling several earthquakes per formation interval, rather than true per-event slip. We test this using pIR-IRSL dating of K-feldspar grains, which directly dates channel-fill deposition and avoids unreliable ages from detrital radiocarbon samples. Applying this method to a channel offset solely by the 1857 earthquake constrained the penultimate event's age more precisely than radiocarbon allowed. Extending the approach to channels with 10 m and 16 m of offset, we recover incision ages of 770 CE, 1260 CE, and 1760 CE, showing channels persist through multiple cycles and confirming that 1857 slip was ~5 m while earlier events were smaller. These ages imply a slip rate of only ~20 mm/yr over the last millennium, half the modern rate, requiring faster slip, perhaps exceeding 40 mm/yr, between 1,000 and 3,600 years ago to satisfy the ~36 mm/yr average at nearby Wallace Creek. Because offset measurements alone can mislead, hazard calculations should seek independent age control comparing offset features to known earthquake ages, or explicitly incorporate this uncertainty when such data are unavailable. Encouragingly, these assumptions are testable, and growing this chronologic approach across more sites offers a promising path toward more reliable slip-per-event and hazard estimates.

title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Total Water Storage in the Coastal Lowland Aquifer of Texas Using Downscaled GRACE/GRACE-FO Satellite Observations
session_title: Geoinformatics and Data Science: A Showcase In Undergraduate and Graduate Student Research (Posters)
authors: Jahan, Md Nasrat [1], Yarbrough, Lance [2], Yasarer, Hakan [3], Oommen, Thomas [4], Counts, Ronald C. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, University, MS, USA
(2) Department of Geology & Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, University, MS, USA
(3) Department of Civil Engineering, University of Mississippi, University, MS, USA
(4) Department of Geology & Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
(5) Department of Geology & Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA; Mississippi Mineral Resources Institute, University of Mississippi, University, MS, USA
abstract: The Coastal Lowland Aquifer of Texas is an important freshwater resource supporting municipal, industrial, and agricultural demands along the Gulf Coast. Although GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) satellite observations provide valuable information on total water storage (TWS), their coarse spatial resolution limits their use for regional and local assessments. This study examines TWS dynamics across the aquifer from 2003 to 2023 using machine learning–downscaled GRACE/GRACE-FO observations. Monthly TWS anomalies were downscaled from ~330 km to 800 m using an Artificial Neural Network model that integrated precipitation, temperature, evapotranspiration, normalized difference vegetation index, elevation, slope, soil type, and lithology. The resulting high-resolution dataset revealed substantial spatial and temporal variability across the aquifer. Persistent storage declines were observed throughout much of the study area, with the strongest depletion concentrated in the central portion of the aquifer, particularly in Karnes County and DeWitt County. In contrast, the northeastern and eastern regions generally exhibited smaller negative TWS anomalies. These spatial patterns were broadly consistent with available groundwater-level observations, an important component of TWS. Aquifer-wide linear trend analysis indicated a mean TWS depletion rate of −2.25 ± 2.64 mm year⁻¹ at the 95% confidence level. Although negative, the trend was not statistically significant, reflecting pronounced spatial and temporal variability across the aquifer. The downscaled dataset improves the regional applicability of GRACE/GRACE-FO observations and demonstrates the value of machine learning for monitoring long-term water-storage dynamics, drought conditions, and water-resource sustainability in coastal aquifer systems.

title: WERE CRATONS TRULY STABLE SINCE FORMATION? A GEOPHYSICAL STUDY ON LITHOSPHERIC SIGNATURE FOR NORTHEAST AFRICA: SAHARAN METACRATON OR CENTRAL SAHARA SHIELD?
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources (Posters)
authors: Abdelrahman, Ahmed M. [1], Knapp, James H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma State University Boone Pickens School of Geology, Stillwater, OK, USA
(2) Oklahoma State University Boone Pickens School of Geology, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: Does craton stability since Archean formation truly hold, or have cratonic regions been modified by later tectonism? A true craton requires a thick, buoyant mantle keel with crust >40 km and LAB >150 km to maintain long-term isostatic equilibrium. Northeast Africa offers the best natural laboratory to test this, hosting the Saharan Metacraton (SMc)—a vast Precambrian tract whose cratonic status remains debated. The conventional theory posits pre-Neoproterozoic continental crust partially remobilized and reworked during the Pan-African orogeny (Abdelsalam et al., 2002). Liégeois et al. (2013) proposed three cratonic remnants (Al-Kufra, Marzuq, Chad) beneath thick intracratonic sag basins, suggesting partial cratonic preservation, whereas de Wit et al. (2021) argue for a fundamentally collage of accreted blocks lacking coherent lithosphere. We tested these models using broadband seismic data from eight permanent and temporary stations with satellite gravity and topographic remote sensing. Our results reveal remarkably uniform crust (25–36 km) across the entire study area, incompatible with an Archean-Paleoproterozoic root. This thin crust, combined with the absence of a deep keel, implies the region lacks thick lithospheric support as required for classical cratons. Our gravity-inferred LAB map, carefully calibrated with seismic control points, shows shallow lithosphere throughout NE Africa, with only a small localized northern ~124-km zone—still far shallower than the canonical 150+ km keels observed in intact cratons globally. Our density slices from 0 to 100 km depth exhibit low-amplitude variations, quantitatively confirming no dense deep-seated cratonic mantle root. Our upward-continuation gravity maps at 50, 100, 150, and 200 km isolate the deep regional potential field, revealing broad long-wavelength anomalies that correlate with the major topographic and magmatic swells. These signatures coincide precisely with Cenozoic intraplate volcanic provinces—including the Jebel Marra (Darfur) Massif, the Tibesti Massif, and the Hoggar (Ahaggar) Massif—where asthenospheric upwellings thermally and chemically modified the lithosphere. This integrated fingerprint—thin crust, shallow LAB, muted density contrasts, and long-wavelength gravity anomaly—supports pervasive attenuation by asthenospheric upwellings, not a single deep plume. Our findings challenge the classical SMc cratonic-root interpretation and raise a fundamental question for global craton stability: was it never a craton, or has it been pervasively decratonized by Cenozoic events associated with these provinces? Resolving this requires integrated geochemical, isotopic, and high-resolution seismic imaging.

title: Practical Application of U-Pb Detrital Zircon Geochronology to Geologic Mapping with Examples from the Sevier Fold-Thrust Belt, Southwest Utah, and the Southern Appalachian Inner Piedmont, Western North Carolina
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation
authors: Quick, James Daniel [1], Hogan, John Patrick [2], Cattanach, Bart L. [3], Wizevich, Michael C. [4], Trantham, Brennan [5], Curry, Adam [6], Kaiser, Jason F. [7], Crowley, James L. [8]
affiliations: (1) North Carolina Geological Survey, Asheville, NC, USA
(2) Retired, Durham, NH,
(3) North Carolina Geological Survey, Asheville, NC,
(4) Central Connecticut State University, New Britain, CT,
(5) North Carolina Geological Survey, Candler, NC,
(6) North Carolina Geological Survey, North Carolina Geological Survey, Raleigh, NC, USA
(7) Southern Utah University,
(8) Boise State University, Boise, ID,
abstract:
U-Pb detrital zircon (DZ) geochronology has emerged as a rapid, cost-effective means to characterize the maximum depositional age and provenance of sedimentary and metasedimentary strata. Cyclic repetition of depositional systems, metamorphic overprinting, and complex faulting can juxtapose geologically disparate, but lithologically indistinguishable rocks, leading to spurious correlations. We demonstrate the utility of DZ analysis to resolve geologic mapping problems in contrasting tectonic settings: the highly metamorphosed Southern Appalachian Inner Piedmont and the (unmetamorphosed) foreland basin of the Sevier fold-thrust belt.

In the Southern Appalachian Inner Piedmont, the Brindle Creek thrust (BCT) places Silurian amphibolite-grade schist and metawacke of the Cat Square terrane above Cambrian-Neoproterozoic amphibolite-grade schist and metawacke of the peri-Laurentian Tugaloo terrane. Geologic mapping near Newton, NC (Byers, 2010; Gilliam, 2010) identified a tectonic window through the BCT exposing underlying Tugaloo terrane metasediments. However, DZ age spectra from a sample collected within the window (as previously interpreted) exhibits a prominent peri-Gondwanan-age population common in Cat Square metasediments and rare in Tugaloo metasediments. Additionally, multi-dimensional scaling analysis of multiple samples of Cat Square and Tugaloo metasediments demonstrates the sample within the window has clear Cat Square terrane affinity. This implies that the contact of the BCT defining the window is significantly (>1.5 km) further east than previously mapped. In SW Utah, the >1000 ft thick siliciclastic Iron Springs Formation, deposited in the proximal foreland basin of the Sevier fold-thrust belt, has recently been correlated, in large part, to the John Henry Member of the Straight Cliffs Formation. However, the prominent Yavapai-Mazatal DZ population intrinsic to the John Henry Member DZ spectra are conspicuously muted in the DZ spectra of the Iron Springs Formation. In addition, maximum depositional ages from DZ grains subsampled for euhedral grain geometry, paired with U-Pb zircon ages on interbedded airfall tuffs, constrain the deposition of the Iron Springs Formation to ca. 103 Ma (for the basal member) to ca. 88 Ma (for the upper member), weakening wholesale correlation to the ca. 88-82 Ma John Henry Member.

A multifaceted approach to DZ geochronology provides critical mapping insight across a range of tectonostratigraphic settings. These examples highlight the pitfalls of continuing to rely solely on lithologic similarity, and the power of integrating DZ analysis with geologic mapping.

title: The Salinology Approach: Joint Estimates of Lithology and Salinity Through Probabilistic Integration of Airborne Electromagnetic and Borehole Data
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Hoogenboom, Bennett [1], James, Stephanie [2], Minsley, Burke [3], Elsheikh, Ahmed [4], Knierim, Katherine [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Sacramento, CA, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Nashville, TN, USA
(5) United States Geological Survey, Little Rock, AR, USA
abstract:
Airborne electromagnetic (AEM) surveys are one of the primary methods capable of mapping aquifer structure and water quality at watershed-to-basin scales. AEM surveys complement borehole datasets that typically lack the spatial extent and density needed over large areas. However, interpretation of AEM datasets can be limited as both lithology and pore fluid conductivity (salinity) exert strong controls on bulk electrical resistivity, resulting in non-unique or ambiguous interpretations when both properties vary within a survey area. Traditional interpretations make assumptions about either lithology or salinity to infer distributions in the other, with minimal attention given to uncertainty propagation.

Here, we introduce a new probabilistic Bayesian workflow named “salinology” to jointly predict lithology and salinity, together with estimates of uncertainty, by incorporating AEM resistivity models, borehole observations, and a priori information (e.g., geologic maps, salt-water boundaries, etc.). The joint probabilities of user-defined lithology and salinity classes (e.g. fine to course and fresh to saline) are produced for every point in a 3D volume. Borehole observations are categorized into class probabilities and interpolated across the 3D volume, with uncertainty based on data quality and distance from boreholes. AEM resistivity models are mapped as class probabilities based on a petrophysical relationship that includes the influence of surface conduction (a proxy for lithology) and fluid conductivity (a proxy for salinity) on bulk resistivity. The combined product of the borehole and AEM probabilities, together with prior information, yields a posterior prediction of lithology and salinity classes throughout the model domain.

We demonstrate the “salinology” approach for the state of Louisiana and highlight its compatibility with independent lithology or salinity interpolation routines. Replacing the salinity well data with a predictive machine-learning model refines the workflow’s comprehensive assessment of hydrogeologic properties and water quality while also honoring observation and interpretational uncertainties. This approach directly addresses the non-uniqueness challenge to better inform decision-making in groundwater investigations.

title: Radiogenic Helium Generation in Organic-Rich Unconventional Reservoirs: In-Situ Source Potential of Six U.S. Shale Plays
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources (Posters)
authors: Gurbuz, Ibrahim Suha [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Helium is a non-renewable resource that is recovered mainly as a byproduct of natural gas production. Most economic helium is radiogenic 4He, produced by alpha decay of uranium and thorium over geological time. Because of its small atomic radius and high diffusivity, helium is easily lost unless trapped in low-permeability formations or structural closures. In conventional systems, helium is generated in uranium- and thorium-rich crystalline basement and migrates upward through faults and permeable carrier beds into overlying traps. In this model, sedimentary reservoirs are treated as passive storage units. Whether this framework applies to unconventional reservoirs remains poorly resolved.

Organic-rich shales differ from conventional reservoirs in important ways. They contain uranium bound to organic matter and fine-grained minerals deposited under reducing conditions, and they combine high total organic carbon (TOC) with nanopore networks and low matrix permeability. These properties suggest that shales may generate and retain radiogenic helium in place. This study tests the hypothesis that, in organic-rich reservoirs where external gas migration is minimal, the amount of in-situ radiogenic 4He can be quantitatively estimated from stratigraphic age, gamma-ray response as a uranium proxy, and TOC. If in-situ generation is the main mechanism, older formations such as the Ordovician Utica should show systematically higher in-situ 4He than younger formations such as the Late Cretaceous Niobrara.

The study focuses on six U.S. shale plays from the Ordovician to the Late Cretaceous: Utica, Marcellus, Bakken, Wolfcamp, Eagle Ford, and Niobrara. A two-stage approach is used. Stage 1 computes a theoretical closed-system 4He baseline for each reservoir interval using the alpha-decay equation, with uranium and thorium estimated from spectral or total gamma-ray logs. Stage 2 applies a machine-learning model that compares this baseline with measured helium from public gas-composition datasets and from new gas chromatography of Utica core samples. Each interval is classified as generation-, migration-, leakage-, or dilution-dominated, with uncertainty reported for every estimate.

The expected outcome is a framework that separates generation-dominated from migration-dominated helium systems, together with first-order helium-in-place estimates for each play. The results will either support the reclassification of organic-rich shales as active helium sources or refine the conventional basement-migration model with quantitative constraints. In both cases, this study provides the first systematic in-situ helium analysis across U.S. shale plays.

title: Upper Cretaceous foreland basin initiation and propagation in the southernmost central Andes of Mendoza, Argentina

authors: Balgord, Elizabeth [1], Perez Consuegra, Nicolas [2], Carrapa, Barbara [3], Mescua, José [4], Giambiagi, Laura [5]

abstract: The Andes Mountains are the type example of an active ocean-continent, subduction-related orogenic belt. Uplift in the Andes is temporally and spatially variable leading to questions regarding the underlying mechanisms controlling mountain building, particularly the balance of upper- versus lower-plate forcing and the interplay between the magmatic arc and crustal shortening on crustal thickening. The Aconcagua area (32-33˚S) is located at the northern edge of the Neuquén Basin and preserves an Upper Jurassic to Miocene sedimentary sequence, which includes the earliest record of Andean shortening and foreland basin development at this latitude. The region also contains the highest elevation peak within the Andes (Cerro Aconcagua, 6962 m), sits at the southern boundary of the modern zone of flat-slab subduction, and the transition from a magmatic gap to active arc magmatism to the south. The exact timing and the magnitude of different uplift events at this latitude have not been quantified, making it impossible to determine the rates over time and compare them with orogenic development along strike. This study presents new sedimentological and detrital zircon U-Pb and Hf isotope data from Upper Cretaceous sedimentary units in this segment of the Andes. The depositional environments, stratigraphic relations, provenance, maximum depositional ages, and isotopic ratios are used to evaluate the mechanisms of basin formation and its relationship to arc evolution. New maximum depositional ages show Late Cretaceous sediment accumulation within an evolving foreland basin that eventually contains interbedded pyroclastic flows indicating considerable eastward advancement of the volcanic arc in the Maastrichtian. Hf isotopic ratios from arc-sourced detrital zircons show relatively juvenile values at the beginning of the Late Cretaceous that trend to significantly more evolved as the arc migrates and shorting progresses. Coeval eastward migration of the volcanic arc, trends towards more evolved isotopic signatures along with fold-thrust belt shortening and foreland basin migration are also observed to the south, in the Malargüe area (35˚S) recording regional regularity in orogenic development.

title: Insights into the characteristics of subsurface deposits of the Pennsylvanian Upper Strawn Group, Permian Basin, Texas from an outcrop analog in the contemporaneous Bug Scuffle Member of the Gobbler Formation in the Sacramento Mountains, New Mexico

authors: Johnson, Isabel [1], Flaig, Peter P. [2], Hattori, Kelly E. [3], DeJarnett, Beverly [4], Carr, David L. [5], Rendall, Benjamin [6]

abstract:
The Desmoinesian Upper Strawn Group on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin, Texas (TX), contains oil/gas reservoirs that have produced for over a century. The Strawn comprises mixed carbonate-siliciclastic deposits recording relationships between deltaic point sources, a tidally dominated siliciclastic shelf, and a carbonate ramp during high-amplitude (>100 m), high-frequency (20-100 kyr) sea-level fluctuations of the Pennsylvanian icehouse. Glacioeustatic fluctuations combined with internal complexities in the evolution of deltaic systems and carbonate platforms produced highly variable vertical and lateral facies mosaics and key surfaces/transitions. While deposits of mixed carbonate-siliciclastic systems may be common in the rock record, their internal characteristics remain poorly documented at high-resolution, and controls on complex stratigraphic stacking patterns and facies transitions remain somewhat enigmatic, particularly in icehouse systems.

Sparse, non-analogous Strawn outcrops in TX mean that in the subsurface only rare core, localized wireline logs, and isolated seismic profiles inform depositional models. To provide a deeper understanding of the characteristics of the subsurface Strawn along the Eastern Shelf we first examine a series of publicly available drill core and a high-density wireline log dataset from near the Katz Field in Stonewall County, TX to develop a new model of the paleoenvironmental evolution of Upper Strawn deposystems. Next we analyze an outcrop analog from the mixed carbonate-siliciclastics of the Bug Scuffle Member of the Gobbler Formation in the Sacramento Mountains, New Mexico (NM). The Strawn and Bug Scuffle both contain deposits of outer, middle, and inner ramp environments (e.g. wackestone/packstones, ooid and skeletal grainstones), mixed carbonate-siliciclastic tidal channel deposits (e.g. fossiliferous trough cross stratified sandstones, oolitic sandstones), and mixed-process delta deposits and associated sub-environments Both successions record a siliciclastic wedge that prograded over a carbonate ramp. The Strawn and Bug Scuffle also contain select intervals of stratigraphy that are carbonate-dominated that alternate with more siliciclastic intervals. However, internal to these intervals carbonates and siliciclastics interfinger.

In both cases we interpret that stratal characteristics were governed by both allogenic processes, including high-frequency, high-amplitude sea-level fluctuations associated with the Pennsylvanian icehouse, and autogenic processes including delta lobe switching, delta front channel migration, variable sediment influx, and development of shorefaces or a tidal shelf and carbonates along the margins siliciclastic sources. Our results provide a test for pre-existing models for mixed carbonate-siliciclastic systems.

title: From Counts to Years: Open-Source U–Th data Reduction and Visualisation Software

abstract:
Uranium–thorium (U–Th) dating is widely applied to Pleistocene–Holocene archives. It requires relatively few, simple assumptions, so accuracy can approach precision, and is used in palaeoclimate, fossil, archaeological, and neotectonic studies. The technique has been refined over the last few decades in terms of measurement protocols and half-life values, such that sub-permille level precision on the low abundance isotopes ( 234 U and 230 Th) can be achieved with increasingly smaller sample sizes. U–Th data reduction and error propagation, however, has received less attention and, to many researchers relying on U–Th data, this process may remain somewhat of a black box.

To address this, we are developing open-source, Python-based software. The data reduction process requires making a series of corrections to measurements obtained by mass spectrometry including those for procedural (chemistry) blanks, instrumental backgrounds, peak-tails, mass fractionation, tracer impurities, distinct U and Th instrumental sensitivities, and any initial 230 Th present (i.e., 230 Th not produced by in situ decay). Additionally, determining accurate age-errors is arguably as important as the accuracy of the ages themselves. This requires rigorously propagating all sources of error through an unbroken chain—from raw measurements to the final activity ratios and ages—providing a robust error estimate.

We plan to include: flexible data input to accommodate diverse measurement protocols; user selectable options for statistically valid outlier rejection; rigorous, comprehensive linear and Monte Carlo error propagation; user selectable options for initial 230 Th corrections; and options for internal and external age-errors. We plan to provide visualisation tools to track sources of uncertainty in individual analyses for each step of the uncertainty propagation, e.g., how much of the final age uncertainty is because of the peak-tail correction on 234 U? The software will employ a modular structure so that users may make use of, for example, the module for calculating ages with different user-selectable initial 230 Thcorrection strategies without engaging with the entire U-Th data reduction workflow. At the presentation, we will seek community input on our efforts to date.

title: Geologic Mapping Using Imaging Spectroscopy
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: Myers, Madison [1], Cleghorn, Zane [2], DeMarais, Ceili A [3], Valli , Raqib [4], Redfield, Trista [5], Ketel, Jessica [6], Schweiger, Anna [7]
affiliations: (1) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT,
abstract: Mapping the distribution, composition, and types of rocks on Earth’s surface has important implications for society, including informing infrastructure decisions (road placement), regional hazards (landslides), and resource inventories (critical minerals). However, the ways in which we create these maps are resource intensive, requiring geologists to walk over the landscape and interpret the material at their feet, resulting in geologic maps of differing resolutions and reliability. For regions that are more challenging to access, maps are often less detailed and defined. Here we present a first attempt to reconstruct a recently published geologic map of the McDermitt Caldera in northeastern Nevada using spectral data collected by the EMIT imaging spectrometer mounted on the International Space Station. We use pixels of known geologic units to train predictive models and then apply the model to sort ‘unknown’ pixels (ignored during model training) into these units. Initial validation results showed mixed but consistent outcomes, where some units predicted with up to 90% accuracy, including both rhyolite and basaltic compositions, whereas Quaternary units were consistently predicted poorly. Interestingly, we found that predictability of poorly predicted units greatly improved by including pixels with substantial vegetation cover in our models. This points towards at least some chemical characteristics of the bedrock being preserved in the vegetation. Moving forward, we explore using our approach to predict the extent of geologic units in a difficult to access area of Yellowstone National Park, using training data from regions that have been previously visited to ground truth our model.

title: Building a Chemical Fingerprint Library for Tire Wear Particles Using LDIR Imaging System
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part II)
authors: Oo, Chit Wityi [1], Brown, Megan R.M. [2], Buczynska, Anna [3], Lenczewski, Melissa E. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, USA

abstract:
Tire wear particles are one of the most prevalent microplastics in environmental samples. Beyond potential health hazards associated with particulates, tire materials includes heavy metals and chemicals like N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′ -phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD) and its derivative 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q). Differentiating types of tires can help determine the source and transport of the particles.

Utilizing an Agilent 8700 Laser Direct Infrared (LDIR) Chemical Imaging System and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometer (ICPMS), we investigate the variations in polymer spectra and heavy metal concentrations among tire samples. Samples are collected from new and used auto and bicycle tires representing different brands, ages, and manufacturing locations. The samples are fragmented into microplastic-sized particles using cryomilling and individual particle infrared spectra are collected using LDIR analysis. The tire samples are analyzed using Shimadzu ICPMS-2030 to determine the concentrations of target trace metals and elemental signatures associated with tire materials. Preliminary results show slight variations in the LDIR spectra across particles from the same tire sample. Further, there are distinct differences in the LDIR spectra between both the tested brands of tires and tires from Asia versus the United States.

The goal of the research is to develop a reference library integrating LDIR spectral fingerprints and elemental compositions to identify source-specific characteristics of tire particles (i.e. brand, age, and manufacturing location) that can improve the identification and source tracking of tire-derived particles in environmental samples.

abstract: In this study, Mineral Association Analysis was used to predict occurrences of 70 mineral phases across Gale crater drill and scoop samples using historical mineral patterns in the Mineral Evolution Database. These phases include hydrated minerals that speak to the water history of Mars, several sulfides that could support a period of hydrothermal activity in Gale crater, and mineral phases that imply a possible history of metamorphism at modest pressure. MAA produced more possible locations for minerals already detected by the CheMin instrument as well as scores of other mineral phases not currently identified by the CheMin instrument. Not all these predictions guarantee the presence of the predicted mineral and some phases are likely the result of model bias, as our model is based on mineral localities in the United States. Although this version of the model is based on Earth data, it provides a launch point for considering possible additional mineral phases present at each of the CheMin drill hole sites. Some of these phases support water history that was of varying acidity (acidic: jarosite, kaolinite, marcasite, melanterite; alkaline: carbonates), S, Si, Fe, and Ca rich (gypsum, melanterite, sulfur, opal, hematite, magnetite, fluorite, calcite), of varying redox (oxidized: hematite, goethite, baryte, gypsum; reduced: ilmenite, siderite, pyrite, and other sulfides), hydrothermal (talc, sulfides, and phyllosilicates), and potentially accompanied by low-grade pressure or contact metamorphism (clinochlore, wollastonite, micas, actinolite, epidote). We conclude that with careful consideration of model biases, the predictions from MAA provide additional insights to the mineral diversity and geologic history of Gale crater.

title: Wave, Tidal, and Fluvial Influences in the Sedimentary Deposits of the Campanian (Late Cretaceous) Western Interior Seaway, USA

abstract: The Western Interior Seaway was a major epeiric marine body of water that linked the Arctic Ocean with the Gulf of Mexico during the last forty-million-years of the Cretaceous Period. The western coast of the Western Interior Seaway during the Campanian shows a wave and shelf bottom current-controlled association of lithofacies from the shoreface seaward to the relatively deep (less than 200 meters) basin. The facies associations comprise paralic, tide-influenced coastal environments; intensely burrowed, storm/wave processes-dominated prograding delta-fronts and shorefaces; heavily bioturbated glauconitic sandstones; and traction current-controlled, tidally influenced open-marine shelf and subaqueous delta deposits with dominantly southward paleocurrent directions. The persistence of southward paleocurrent directions indicates along-shelf sand-transport by strong bottom currents. Seafloor topography generated by Laramide block uplifts enhanced the transport of (often relatively coarse) sediments into the deeper parts of the basin, as well as controlled sediment dispersal patterns in this part of the seaway. The review of the typical Campanian depositional environments from paralic to shelf deposits suggest the common mix of fluvial, wave, and tidal processes at any given time with sea level as the main control of the locus of the dominant process, but with tectonics, geometry of the coast, and bathymetry amplifying a particular process locally.

title: Stratigraphic, geomorphic, and structural record of migrating slab tear during the past ~1 Myr in southern Calabria and NE Sicily, Italy

abstract: Southern Italy is well suited for studies of coupled deep Earth and surface processes because it preserves a well-documented record of deformation and uplift related to migrating collision, trench retreat, and tearing of subducted ocean slabs. However, mechanisms of mantle-driven uplift remain incompletely understood due to a lack of reliable ages for Pleistocene marine terraces >200 m above sea level (masl). To address this gap, we investigated regional stratigraphy, geochronology, geomorphology, and structural geology in southern Calabria and NE Sicily to assess rates and drivers of vertical crustal motions. Our results, combined with previous studies, reveal four regionally correlative stratigraphic units: (1) shallow marine Vinco calcarenite (~1.0 Ma at the top; age of base is uncertain); (2) bathyal marine claystone and marl (~1.0–0.48 Ma); (3) Messina Gravels and Sands Formation Gilbert-delta deposits (~480–120 ka); and (4) ~120-ka shallow marine terraces preserved at ~100–1,300 masl. 40 Ar/ 39 Ar step-heating experiments on fresh glass from volcanic tuff interbedded with claystone near the top of unit 2 yield reproducible age spectra with a mean age of 0.481 ± 0.019 Ma (± 2σ). Luminescence dating of marine terrace sands (unit 4) reveals burial ages that overlap across the full range of sampled elevations (~100–1,000 masl) with a weighted mean of 118.8 ± 8.7 ka (± 1σ). These ages, combined with surface mapping and fault-zone morphology, indicate that the marine terraces are erosional remnants of a single, once-continuous surface that has been offset by active normal faults and uplifted at rates ranging from <1 mm/yr near the coast to >12 mm/yr in the high Aspromonte Mountains, with time-averaged fault throw rates of 0.8–4.2 mm/yr. Rates of surface uplift and fault throw are 5–10 times faster than prior estimates that were based on a widely accepted but unsubstantiated age of ~1.0–1.2 Ma for marine terraces >1,000 masl. We infer that rapid post-120 ka uplift is an ongoing isostatic response to an active migrating tear in the subducted Ionian slab, consistent with recent geophysical observations and predictions of geodynamic models. The brief period of subsidence recorded in unit 2 (~1.0–0.48 Ma) is also predicted by numerical models for slab tearing, though the geometry and direction of tear migration currently are not known.

title: Anoxia-Driven Change in Community Composition at the Norian–Rhaetian Boundary in Panthalassa
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Lacherez, Lena Jude [1], Ramirez-Guasp, Fiorella S. [2], Bingham, Joseph D. [3], Tackett, Lydia S. [4], Dineen, Ashley A. [5], Banker, Roxanne M.W. [6], Roopnarine, Peter D. [7], Tyler, Carrie L. [8]

abstract:
Shallow‑marine ecosystems today are increasingly threatened by anoxia. Ancient intervals of oxygen stress, such as the Late Triassic Norian–Rhaetian Boundary (NRB), provide critical analogues for understanding long-term ecological responses. The Gabbs Formation (Norian-Hettangian) in New York Canyon (western‑central Nevada, USA) preserves a stratigraphically continuous fossil record across the NRB from eastern Panthalassa, allowing us to evaluate the effects of anoxia on marine ecosystems.

Here, we assess changes in community composition across the NRB by compiling taxonomic occurrences from the shallow marine Gabbs Formation representing 9 phyla. Bulk field sampling resulted in a total of 497 specimens, with 24 Norian samples containing 57 genera, compared to 9 Rhaetian samples containing 28 genera. Community composition was compared using Non‑metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS) based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, alongside cluster analysis and environmental correlation vectors of redox proxy data (Mn, Sr, δ¹³C, δ¹⁸O) and ecological traits (feeding and motility). PERMANOVA indicates minimal overlap in species composition between the Late Norian and Rhaetian intervals (p = 0.001). Community composition was weakly, but significantly, correlated with manganese concentrations (R² = 0.32, p = 0.03), an established proxy for anoxia, suggesting that worsening oxygen stress played a central role in community restructuring.

Across the NRB, 63% of taxa were lost in New York Canyon. Four motility types (sessile unattached, facultative slow, facultative fast, fully mobile slow) were significantly correlated with community change, suggesting motility was a strong predictor of survivorship. In addition, both the suspension feeders (R2 = 0.25, p = 0.001) and predatory lifestyles (R2 = 0.36, p = 0.001) had significant effects on taxonomic losses, while deposit feeders did not. This is likely caused by the limited mobility of many suspension feeders, while some highly mobile predators may have been able to forage outside of anoxic zones. Deposit feeders likely thrived in the early stages of the perturbation, as accumulating organic remains would have initially provided ample food sources. These results demonstrate substantial changes in an ancient shallow‑marine ecosystem under sustained deoxygenation, offering a deep-time analogue for modern coastal ecosystem decline.

title: Quantifying the Taphonomic Filters Governing Vertebrate Anatomical Information from the Earliest Triassic of Antarctica
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Stupakoff, Nissa Margaret [1], Woolley, C. Henrik [2], Sidor, Christian [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA; Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Department of Biology & Burke Museum, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(3) Department of Biology & Burke Museum, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract: The Fremouw Formation hosts the oldest record of tetrapod vertebrate fossils from Antarctica and figures prominently in paleontologists’ understanding of vertebrate assemblages at high paleolatitudes during Early Triassic times. Comparative work between the Fremouw and coeval assemblages at lower latitudes could uncover spatial heterogeneity in the tempo of recovery from the End-Permian Mass Extinction (EPME) across southern Pangea. However, to better understand the contribution of the Antarctic fossil record during the recovery of terrestrial ecosystems after the EPME, we must first characterize and quantify the geologic, taphonomic, and sampling filters that affect our ability to reconstruct ancient biodiversity and environments. In this study, we use a novel, semi-quantitative metric to quantify the skeletal completeness of over 600 specimens housed at the University of Washington Burke Museum of Natural History & Culture and the American Museum of Natural History, regardless of taxonomy and specific morphology, to assess taphonomic controls on the completeness and quality of anatomical information preserved in the Fremouw vertebrate assemblage. We then compare skeletal completeness with matrix lithology, depositional setting, taxonomic affinity, and specimen locality and find that the Fremouw fossil record is largely anatomically incomplete. However, we also find that specific depositional settings, body size, and identification biases play prominent roles in asymmetrically filtering skeletal information. By utilizing this depositionally and taxonomically indiscriminate methodology to assist in determining the overall completeness of fossil assemblages, this study lays critical groundwork for future basin-level interpretations and comparisons of the paleobiological history of fluvial foreland basins across southern Pangaea.

abstract: In the 1980s USGS geologist David A. Lindsey and his colleagues mapped >1,500 km 2 of the rugged and geologically complex Sangre de Cristo Range in southern Colorado at 1:24,000 scale, providing an outstanding foundation for many subsequent studies. We build on this pioneering work through geo/thermochronology and detailed (1:10,000-scale) geologic mapping of select areas between ~37.55°N and 38.18°N with the goal of understanding the geometry, kinematics, and timing of structures associated with the Pennsylvanian–Permian Ancestral Rocky Mountains (ARM) orogeny, the Late Cretaceous–Paleogene Laramide orogeny, and the Oligocene to Quaternary Rio Grande rift. Evidence for ARM deformation includes intraformational angular unconformities and growth strata in the Pennsylvanian–Permian Crestone Conglomerate associated with the Gibson Peak syncline and the transpressional Little Sand Creek fault system. In addition, stratigraphic and structural relations indicate an ARM origin for the oblique-reverse Sand Creek fault and older Marble Mountain thrust. ARM deformation was progressive, involving early foreland thrusts and later basement-involved transpression from NE-directed shortening. The extent to which these ARM structures were reactivated by Laramide contraction remains ambiguous, and Laramide structures preserved in Mesozoic strata along the eastern flank of the range also record NE-directed shortening. Along the western flank of the range, basement-involved structures including the Crestone thrust, Independence Mine shear zone, Deadman Creek thrust, and Mosca Creek thrust were locally reactivated as top-SW extensional shear zones during the early stages of the Rio Grande rift (~30–26 Ma). This early stage of rifting was coeval with late Oligocene plutonism that localized low-angle mylonitic shear zones characterized by top-SW normal-sense shear and coaxial-dominated shear. Oligocene bimodal magmatism was established along the western flank of the range by ~28–27 Ma and produced several contact aureoles reaching 400–650°C peak temperatures in the Pennsylvanian Minturn Formation. Extensional exhumation of the range and development of rift-flank topography occurred in the Miocene, initiating with normal-sense reactivation of the NE-dipping Laramide Alvarado fault along the eastern flank of the range and transitioning to slip along the W- to SW-dipping Sangre de Cristo normal fault system near the western flank of the range at ~14–11 Ma.

title: Petrologic Records of Magma Storage, Recharge, and Ascent Beneath Okmok Volcano, Alaska
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics
authors: Myers, Madison [1], Ross, Carly [2], Patel, Yamini [3], Hosseini, Behnaz [4]
affiliations: (1) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT,
abstract:
A key challenge in volcanology is identifying the processes and timescales that transform long-lived magma reservoirs into eruptible systems, particularly at volcanoes that exhibit limited precursory unrest [1]. Okmok Volcano, Alaska, is an ideal natural laboratory because it produces eruptions spanning VEI 1-6, basalt to rhyolite, and diverse eruptive styles. The only eruption of Okmok to occur with monitoring instrumentation began July 12, 2008, and was preceded by just ~5 hours of precursory seismicity, despite petrologic evidence that magma rejuvenation and mobilization occurred over decades to months prior to eruption [2]. Here we aim to expand our petrologic dataset for understanding the subsurface architecture of Okmok Volcano by exploring eruptions of different VEI levels. We combine petrologic constraints and diffusion chronometry from the 1997 Strombolian eruption (VEI 3) along with melt inclusion volatile and melt speedometry tools applied to the opening phase of the ca. 2050 yr BP Okmok II caldera-forming eruption (VEI 6) to reconstruct magma storage, recharge, and ascent across a spectrum of eruptive magnitudes.

Fe-Mg diffusion modeling in olivine from the 1997 eruption yields recharge-to-eruption timescales of 1.5-64 days (mean 10.6 days). The consistency of olivine zoning patterns and core and rim compositions signals that, in contrast to the 2008 eruption, the 1997 eruption of Okmok was initiated by a singular recharge event, where a batch of magma ascended from depth over a period of days to weeks and experienced limited (less than a day of) interaction with the shallow reservoir prior to eruption. For the Okmok II caldera-forming eruption, plagioclase-hosted melt inclusions indicate shallow storage at ~20-80 MPa that overlaps with the shallow center activated in the 2008 eruption. H₂O diffusion profiles preserved in olivine-hosted embayments yield ascent times of ~55-90 minutes, whereas bubble number density measurements record rapid shallow-conduit ascent over ~1-3 minutes. These results highlight how mineral- and melt-scale records can bridge the gap between long-term reservoir evolution and short-lived eruptive precursors, providing critical insight into the development of eruptibility in restless volcanic systems.

title: The Influence of Geospatial Mapping Methods on Sinkhole Morphometry and Size Distributions
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Romero, Perla [1], Covington, Matthew D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR,
abstract:
Sinkhole morphometry and size distribution offer valuable insight into the mechanisms driving sinkhole development and evolution. For example, distributions without a characteristic scale may signal positive feedback runaway growth, while distributions that cutoff above a certain scale may indicate negative feedback that caps sinkholes at a certain size. There is no general agreement within the literature regarding which scaling relationship best described observed karst depressions. Recent advancements in geospatial analysis have improved detection and mapping of sinkholes across large areas. Although this does not replace on-site verification, it provides a basis for investigation at low cost. High-resolution digital elevation models (DEM) are used to identify depressions and calculate geometric parameters for sinkholes such as area, perimeter, and depth.

In this study, we evaluate how differences in mapping approaches influence sinkhole morphometry across diverse environmental settings in the United States. In addition, mapped sinkhole datasets were compared against commonly described size distributions (power-law, log-normal, and exponential) to understand whether mapping approach influences the determination of size distribution. We compared two sinkhole datasets: (1) the USGS karst depression density dataset, and (2) the Mihevc & Mihevc US dolines dataset. The USGS dataset used a hydrologic flow-routing algorithm, while the Mihevc dataset used a machine learning algorithm.

QGIS and Python were used to quantify and compare morphometric parameters within a range of karst settings quantitively and qualitatively. Sinkhole polygons were smoothed to reduce pixelation effects associated with DEM resolution when calculating parameters such as circularity. Both datasets were compared to field-verified sinkhole polygons to assess detection accuracy and geometric differences. Preliminary data show distinct differences in morphometry between methodologies. The USGS dataset detects larger, more irregularly shaped sinkholes, while the Mihevc dataset detects smaller more circular features. Ongoing analysis of size distributions will help clarify the dominant mechanisms driving sinkhole development in each study area.

title: Exogeoheritage Eight Years On: Progress in Conserving Extraterrestrial Heritage
session_title: The Astro-Geoheritage of the Solar System: Past Explorations and Future Considerations
authors: Matthews, Jack J. [1], Fletcher, Clare [2], McMahon, Sean [3]
affiliations: (1) Oxford University Museum of Natural History, United Kingdom; Loughborough University, United Kingdom
(2) University of New South Wales, Australia
(3) University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom
abstract:
In 2018 the concept of exogeoheritage, alongside associated terms such as exogeoconservation, were introduced to promote a new holistic concept for the conservation of significant features in extraterrestrial environments.

On Earth, geoconservation is an accepted theoretical, practical and administrative approach to the protection of geological and geomorphological features of special scientific, functional, historic, cultural, aesthetic, or ecological value. Protected sites on Earth include natural rocky outcrops, shorelines, river banks, and landscapes, as well as human-made structures such as road cuts and quarries exposing geological phenomena.

Exogeoconservation is the proposal that geoconservation strategies used on Earth can be adapted to protect celestial bodies such as rocky and icy planets, rings, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, and comets, which present extraordinarily diverse, beautiful, and culturally, historically and scientifically important geological phenomena. This concept recognises that extraterrestrial nature is dominated by exogeodiversity, with no known biotic components. Features of significance are therefore recognised as exogeoheritage.

This presentation will review the additional research undertaken in the last eight years that has further developed the concept of exogeoheritage, and the growing need for an agreed framework in this area. We will outline how the ideas of exogeoconservation might be applied to future Lunar and Martian sampling missions, and discuss how any protocols need to be sensitive to the needs of scientific, industrial, and other potential human activities.

abstract:
Intensive lead (Pb) and zinc (Zn) mining during the 1900s at the Tar CreekSuperfund Site (Ottawa County, OK) has left the community with 67 million tons of mine waste (“chat”) and acid mine drainage (AMD) from mines. Flooding disperses heavy metals from chat and AMD onto residential floodplains. Research has focused on Pb, Zn, and cadmium (Cd), but manganese (Mn) remains understudied despite downstream floodplain soils reporting concentrations 10x the Ottawa County background level. Several studies have found that elevated Mn is correlated with lower neurodevelopmental scores at Tar Creek. Thus, investigation of spatial and temporal trends of Pb, Zn Cd, and Mn throughout the watershed is necessary to characterize exposure risk over time.

Using a Participatory Action Research approach with LEAD Agency, riverbank sediment cores and a soil trench were analyzed using benchtop X-Ray Fluorescence. Trace elemental fingerprinting using Mn/Uranium and 1/Uranium demonstrated that AMD and chat pile runoff both contribute Pb to the floodplain. Fingerprinting also suggested that there is a third, recent source contributing to an increase in Mn temporally constrained to the top 10 cm of the cores and trench.

To investigate this finding, we compared archival (2007) and contemporary (2023-2025) elemental analysis of three floodplain soil transects. Principal component analysis (PCA) of these datasets expressed that archival floodplain samples were more associated with Pb, Zn, Cd, Fe, Ge, Ti, and Fe, whereas contemporary floodplain soils were more associated with Mn, Mg, Al, and Si. Additionally, the 2007 dataset contained samples collected before and after a 100-year flood event, providing an opportunity to investigate the geochemical impact of flooding. While the PCA suggested that the flood event did not change the overall geochemical composition of the soils, differences in the concentrations of Pb, Zn, Cd, and Mn as a function of distance from Tar Creek suggests flood-driven geomobility.

The City of Miami has responded to flood-driven heavy metal deposition with engineered features on the floodplain to protect some low-lying areas. Differences between the archival and contemporary spatial distributions of Pb, Zn, Cd, and Mn suggest that these engineered features have reduced heavy metal deposition. However, in unprotected flood–prone locations, metal concentrations remain comparable to 2007 levels, indicating the need for further mitigation efforts.

title: Why Some Skarns Fail: Case Study of the South Dom Skarn, Ertsberg District, West Papua, Indonesia
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits. (Posters)
authors: Stahley, Rachel [1], Friehauf, Abe [2], Friehauf, Kurt [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
(2) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
The Ertsberg Intrusive Complex in West Papua, Indonesia hosts several world-class skarn deposits (e.g., 933.2 Mt East Ertsberg Skarn System, 470 Mt Kucing Liar, 70 Mt Big Gossan, and 32 Mt Original Ertsberg deposits [past production + reserves – PT Freeport, 2025]). Less studied are the Dom and South Dom skarns located on the southeast margin of the Ertsberg monzodiorite intrusion. The Dom skarn hosts an economic deposit with an estimated 61 Mt measured+indicated resources that average 1.42% Cu, 0.34g/t Au, 8.85 g/t Ag [PT Freeport 2022], but the South Dom skarn, just 600 meters to the south, is essentially barren. This study explores how the barren South Dom mineralogy compares with the Cu-mineralized Dom skarn.

Mertig [1995] described Dom ores to consist of high-temperature magnesian skarns with early barren monticellite, forsterite, vesuvianite, grandite garnet, and diopside gangue crosscut by magnetite and ore-stage Cu-Fe sulfides with quartz and calcite associated with retrograde phlogopite, talc, chlorite, and serpentine.

Analysis of drill core samples from the South Dom deposit using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) indicate the South Dom skarn consists of predominantly of Fe-poor forsterite and diopside, with minor spinel and Mg-Fe spinel, plus sparse pyrite and magnetite. South Dom samples in this study completely lacked chalcopyrite or bornite.

X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed the presence of forsterite, diopside, and calcite, as well as spinel, magnetite. XRD data also characterize retrograde skarn mineralogy as consisting of Fe +2 -bearing clinochlore, lizardite, eastonite, brucite, and some magnetite.

The South Dom has a mineralogy similar to the Dom skarn’s early high-temperature magnesian skarn. Copper mineralization in the Dom skarn overprints and destroys that early high-temperature calcsilicate assemblage, but although South Dom also has low-temperature retrograde alteration, late-stage South Dom retrograde fluids lack evidence for transporting metals and sulfur.

We suggest that, although early prograde conditions may have been similar at Dom and South Dom, late-stage retrograde fluids at South Dom lacked the salinity needed to transport metals, possibly due to the timing of magmatic hydrothermal fluid released from the intrusion (either relative to release of an earlier stage of hydrothermal fluid that removed Cl, S, and metals from the magma, or relative to the percent crystallization of the magma).

title: Corals, Climate, and Canoes: Archaeological Corals as Dual Archives of Environmental Change and Human Migration
session_title: U-series Disequilibrium Geochronology: Advances, Applications, and Emerging Frontiers (Posters)
authors: Nash, Kyle [1], Cantine, Marjorie [2], Pavia, Frank [3], Sinelli, Peter [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(3) School of Oceanography, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington, USA
(4) Department of Anthropology, University of Central Florida, Orlando, Florida, USA
abstract:
Understanding how past climate variability influenced human migration and adaptation requires accurate, precise chronologies of human activity and robust reconstructions of environmental change. In the Caribbean, uncertainties in archaeological age models and limited regional paleoclimate records hinder efforts to evaluate the climate context of human settlement and mobility. The Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI), carbonate islands at the southeastern terminus of the Lucayan archipelago in the North Atlantic Ocean, were occupied by the Indigenous Lucayan Taíno from the 8 th -16 th centuries CE. Initial migration by canoe into the TCI from the Greater Antilles in the 8th century CE is hypothesized to have been facilitated by higher precipitation during the Medieval Warm Period (MWP). However, Caribbean climate is dominated by a hydrologic dipole, such that heightened periods of rainfall in the south are accompanied by drier conditions in the north, causing regional variability in precipitation. The timing and spatial expression of past precipitation changes over the Common Era remain poorly constrained in the Lucayan Archipelago.

Existing chronologies of Lucayan occupation rely almost exclusively on radiocarbon dating of charcoal, marine shells, and bone fragments. However, the absence of a local marine reservoir correction for the TCI introduces significant uncertainty into these archaeological age models. Lucayan coral abrader tools recovered from archaeological sites provide a unique opportunity to refine settlement chronologies and reconstruct past environmental conditions. These coral tools can be dated using U–Th geochronology. Additionally, their aragonitic skeletons encode geochemical records of sea surface temperature, reflected in Sr/Ca ratios and Δ 47 values, and relative changes in precipitation, recorded by δ 18 O values.

We are investigating coral abrader tools from the Palmetto Junction archaeological site on Providenciales, TCI. We present preliminary results demonstrating the potential of these artifacts to establish a robust chronological and paleoenvironmental framework.

title: Pedogenic Carbonate—Its Move from Soil Survey to Paleoecology and the Global Carbon Cycle
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Monger, Curtis [1]
affiliations: (1) Plant and Environmental Sciences, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA
abstract: In the 1880s, Dokuchaev in Russia and Hilgard in the US had demonstrated that soil carbonate, unlike quartz, was not ubiquitous, but was instead a predictable mineral in arid and semiarid soils. Building on this observation, Marbut in the 1930s as Director of the US Soil Survey program used soil carbonate at the highest level in his classification system (Pedocals vs Pedalfers). Until the 1960s, soil carbonate was largely viewed as being inherited from parent material and therefore designated as “Cca” horizons (“Ccam” when indurated), which missed carbonate’s pedogenic origin. During the 1980s, the scientific importance of soil carbonate (now “pedogenic carbonate”) increased when its paleoclimatic significance was discovered and explored using (1) computer simulation modeling based on its depth in soil and (2) the discovery that pedogenic carbonate carries an isotopic signature of plants growing on land surfaces of the geologic past. Also in the 1980s, the importance of soil carbonate increased when its global amount was estimated at 800-930 PgC making it a larger carbon pool than land plants. For the last 30 years, hundreds of papers have been written using pedogenic carbonates to reconstruct ancient ecosystems, atmospheric carbon dioxide, and paleoelevations. Sequestering atmospheric carbon as soil CaCO3 using management practices has been debated with many of the sequestration claims for mitigating climate change recognized as being unrealistic. But this area of research continues to advance as does the use of pedogenic carbonates to better understand Earth’s biogeochemical evolution and astropedology.

abstract: Flooding events and frequency of impactful flood events in Kentucky have increased substantially since 2022. Development of resiliency to flooding events requires that we develop the capacity to engineer the built environment to withstand worst-case scenario flooding conditions. These are, however, very poorly understood, in part because the record of Holocene rainfall patterns for Kentucky is lacking. As part of the CLIMBS (Climate Resilience through Multidisciplinary Big Data Learning, Prediction, and Building Response Systems) Project 2: Paleoperspectives program, we are developing a record of Holocene flooding events relative to past rainfall patterns and land-use changes, both of which are reconstructed using palynology. Knox County, Kentucky, located in the Eastern Kentucky Coalfields physiographic region in the southeastern part of the Commonwealth has been repeatedly rattled by flash flooding, which has become increasingly common since 2022. The Mayla site, located adjacent to Stinking Creek, a tributary of the Cumberland River, contains a record of sediment deposition and land use prior to and following arrival of European settlers. Multiple drive hydraulic push cores were collected in 2024, and sub-sampled at 5-cm intervals for palynology in 2025. Samples were processed using low-acid protocols and resulted in an assemblage of palynomorphs, including abundant fungi. Palynology results were used to reconstruct ancient ecosystems present as well as past rainfall regimes. Palynomorph preservation was variable, with pollen scarce in core 1B, and abundant in core 1. This highlights the need for use of multiple palynomorph proxies in interpreting past rainfall regimes and ecological conditions.
