abstract: The Ozark dome and Arkoma basin of the foreland of the Ouachita orogen preserves the influence of the Paleozoic suture of Laurentia and Gondwana. Within this framework, a newly drilled Dare Creek #1 core from the Ozark National Forest in Arkansas (Griffis and others, 2026) provides a better understanding of the passive margin to active foreland succession across the Morrowan-Atokan (Early Pennsylvanian) boundary, and a better description of the Trace Creek Member of the lower part of the Atoka Formation. Distinctive delineation of the Trace Creek Shale utilizing LiDAR derivatives with supporting field inspections has allowed refinement of geologic mapping in the Fort Douglas, Sand Gap, Treat, and Simpson 7.5-minute quadrangles in the Boston Mountains. Preliminary mapping of Pennsylvanian Hale, Bloyd, and Atoka formations document several prominent deformation structures. The Mulberry fault is an E-trending down-to-the-south normal fault with a maximum throw reaching 1500 m. The Sugar Creek fault is a NE-trending down-to-the-northwest normal fault with 110 m of throw, and has an identical strike but opposite throw sense to the Confederate fault which is aligned to the northeast, indicative of a strain transfer along a controlling basement lineament. The Treat fault zone consists of a series of ESE-striking right-stepping en échelon faults with connecting monoclinal folds that accommodate left-lateral-normal oblique displacement and up to 170 m of throw. These observations are consistent with regional interpretations from geologic mapping and fault-slip analysis (Hudson and Turner, 2022) and modeling (Lutz and others, 2024) that detail a repeated pattern of E-trending foreland-migrating normal faults likely formed through flexural loading of the Ouachita fold-thrust-belt (ca. 335-306 Ma). These E-trending faults are segmented by NE-striking scissor faults which formed through strain transfer along inherited structures, or merge with ESE-trending normal-oblique fault zones with en échelon normal faults and connecting monoclines. Refined interpretations from detailed geologic mapping in the Ozark National Forest have important societal implications for groundwater and energy resource management, infrastructure planning, and risk mitigation from newly recognized landslides.

title: Forgive Us Our Transgressions: Landward Shoreline Migration Reduces Fresh Aquifer Volume Under Sea-Level Rise.
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Russoniello, Christopher J. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Science Planning and Design, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, RI, USA
abstract: Coastal aquifers can be classified as recharge-limited or topography-limited according to how their freshwater volume responds to sea-level rise (SLR). In recharge-limited systems, unsaturated accommodation space lets the water table rise with the sea, preserving fresh aquifer volume; in topography-limited systems, limited accommodation space suppresses water-table rise, so fresh volume declines. The models that established this framework assume a static, "armored" shoreline that did not move horizontally as seas rose. In natural coastal settings, however, the shoreline migrates landward with SLR, altering aquifer length, recharge area, and the position of the freshwater–saltwater interface tip—each of which governs fresh aquifer volume. Here we characterize how the dynamic shoreline migration that accompanies SLR reshapes the response of both recharge- and topography-limited aquifers. Using coupled variable-density groundwater flow and solute-transport models in MODFLOW 6 with time-varying ocean boundary conditions to represent a range of coastal aquifer configurations. Comparing static and dynamic shoreline scenarios across a range of SLR rates and topographic slopes isolates the effect of lateral shoreline migration on simulated aquifer response. Including migration reduces fresh aquifer volume in both system types especially when slopes are low, indicating that static-shoreline models understate freshwater loss. Topography-limited aquifers remain more vulnerable to SLR. As seas rise, shoreline migration emerges as a first-order control on coastal groundwater, with direct implications for predicting freshwater availability in low-lying coastal aquifers.

title: Habitat-specific death assemblages and taphonomic patterns across nearshore environments of Santa Catalina Island (CA)
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record (Posters)
authors: Norrell, Keira Lane [1], Soni, Priyanka [2], Hendy, Austin [3], Bottjer, David J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Dornsife, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) Dornsife, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(3) Malacology, Natural History Museum of LA County, Los Angeles, CA, USA

abstract: Molluscan death assemblages provide an important record of living community structure and are widely used to interpret past ecosystems, yet their ecological fidelity across nearshore habitats remains poorly understood. This study investigates how skeletal assemblages (e.g., composition, taphonomic signatures and habitat fidelity) vary among rocky reef, kelp, and adjacent sandy habitats around cove beaches of Santa Catalina Island. We chose to conduct our study on 3 sites including Cherry, Fourth of July and Isthmus Coves. Dead skeletal material were collected using systematic random transect surveys conducted by scientific SCUBA and subsequently assigned to habitat zones according to distance from shore (proximal, middle, and distal) to examine nearshore-to-offshore patterns, generally representing a transition from rocky reef to deeper sandy-bottom habitats within each cove. Specimens were identified to the lowest identifiable taxonomic level, assigned to habitat affinity (rocky, kelp, or sandy), and assessed for taphonomic preservation using abrasion, fragmentation, bioerosion, and encrustation indices. Based on the preliminary analysis of the ½-inch size fraction, the proximal and middle zones exhibited highest specimen abundance across the three study areas, averaging approximately ~35 specimens per 0.25 m², compared with ~15 specimens in the distal zone. Species richness was comparable among these zones, averaging fewer than 10 species per 0.25 m². Rocky-substrate taxa dominated the assemblages, accounting for approximately ~80% of specimens in the proximal and middle zones, whereas the distal zone still contained a substantial proportion of rocky-substrate specimens (~50%). The high proportion of rocky-substrate specimens in the distal zone (often pebble, gravel, or sandy substrates) suggests habitat mixing, through reworking and transportation. Taphonomic signatures differed from onshore to offshore. The proximal zone, which comprises nearshore rocky and kelp habitats with the most intense wave energy exhibited the highest abrasion, fragmentation, and bioerosion indices. In contrast encrustation was greatest in the distal zone, perhaps reflecting longer residence times and greater substrate stability that allows for epibiont colonization. These results highlight the value of fine-scale modern analogue studies for understanding death accumulations and habitat mixing under varying environmental settings, improving interpretation of fossil assemblages.

abstract:
Scientific computing skills are becoming essential across the geosciences, yet many learners struggle with barriers unrelated to the science itself, including software installation, computing environments, unfamiliar workflows, and limited programming experience. These challenges can reduce learner confidence and limit the development of workforce-ready skills.

The NSF National Geophysical Facility (NGF)'s Computing & Data Science Academy was established to reduce these barriers through a coordinated technical training program that combines shared cloud infrastructure, intentional instructional design, and community-developed courses. Rather than treating workshops as standalone events, the Academy provides a common instructional ecosystem that leverages a standardized cloud computing environment (GeoLab), reusable instructional resources, digital credentials, and learning pathways that support learners' progression from foundational computing skills to advanced scientific workflows.

To understand how these design choices support workforce development, the Academy is implementing a program-wide evaluation framework that examines technical readiness, learner confidence, participation, and continued engagement across multiple courses. Common learning outcomes and evaluation instruments support comparisons across courses while informing continuous improvement of curriculum and learner support. Early evaluation results suggest improvements in learner confidence and perceived readiness to apply computational workflows in research.

This presentation describes the Academy's instructional framework and emerging assessment strategy for scalable workforce development in computational geoscience. We discuss how shared infrastructure, intentional instructional design, and coordinated evaluation can strengthen workforce preparation while providing a model that can be adapted across geoscience education programs.

abstract: Understanding how reservoir rocks respond to CO2 injection is critical for predicting the performance and long-term security of geological carbon storage. We developed an in-house high-pressure, high-temperature experimental system to simulate supercritical CO2 -rock-brine interactions under reservoir conditions and applied an integrated analytical workflow to evaluate reaction-induced changes in five reference reservoir lithologies: Indiana Limestone, Carthage Limestone, Wisconsin Dolomite, Silurian Dolomite, and Berea Sandstone. Experiments were conducted for seven days at 140°C and approximately 10.3 MPa using synthetic brines and supercritical CO2. Initial X-ray diffraction analyses show that Indiana and Carthage limestones are composed of approximately 99 wt.% calcite, Silurian Dolomite contains approximately 99 wt.% dolomite, Wisconsin Dolomite contains approximately 80 wt.% dolomite and 18 wt.% quartz, and Berea Sandstone is dominated by quartz (88 wt.%). Pre- and post-experiment characterization included petrography, SEM-EDS, micro-XRF, micro-CT, porosity-permeability analyses, major-ion geochemistry, and isotopic measurements. Macroscopic, petrographic, and SEM observations demonstrate lithology-dependent reaction pathways. Indiana Limestone exhibits localized dissolution of blocky calcite cement, increased surface roughness, and minor enhancement of existing pore space. Silurian Dolomite records corrosion of pore-lining dolomite crystals and enlargement of pre-existing intercrystalline pores. In contrast, Carthage Limestone shows little evidence of alteration despite a similar calcitic composition, indicating limited carbonate dissolution under the experimental conditions. Wisconsin Dolomite and Berea Sandstone display alteration primarily within clay-rich laminae, mud lenses, and pore-lining coatings, while the primary rock-forming minerals remain largely unaffected. No significant secondary cement precipitation was observed. Despite clear petrographic evidence of mineral-fluid interaction, porosity changes range only from -0.9 to +1.1 porosity units, within typical analytical uncertainty. The results indicate that short-term exposure to supercritical CO 2 promotes localized dissolution and clay alteration but produces limited changes in bulk reservoir properties. Overall, these findings demonstrate that measurable mineral-fluid reactions can occur without producing substantial changes in bulk reservoir properties over short timescales.

title: Energy flow optimization in the bryozoan Parasmittina eccentrica: Applying a diffusion model to understand the arrangement of sources and sinks in a colonial organism

authors: Leventhal, Sarah [1], Samuels-Fair, Maya [2], Evensen, Claire [3], Shaw, Jack [4], Morrison, Rebecca [5], Simpson, Carl [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC, USA

abstract: Modular colonial organisms are made up of genetic clones, so the survival and reproduction of any individual increases the evolutionary fitness of all other individuals. As a result, some colonial organisms have evolved polymorphs: individuals within a colony have specialized morphologies for distinct tasks. Perhaps the most extreme example of polymorphism in a colonial organism, cheilostome bryozoans (Phylum Bryozoa, Order Cheilostomatida) exhibit highly divergent morphologies for feeding, reproduction, and defense. The arrangement of polymorphs in a colony exhibits spatial structure that varies across species and habitats, suggesting there are optimal configurations for colony fitness. Cheilostome polymorphs are identifiable in fossil specimens, so the evolution of polymorphs and polymorph arrangement can be studied in fossil time series. Individuals within a cheilostome bryozoan colony are physiologically connected through a shared circulatory-like system, and polymorphs are either feeding (energy sources that provide nutrients to others) or non-feeding (energy sinks that take nutrients from others). Here we model variable arrangements and metabolic costs of polymorph sinks and sources. We then compare the energetic uniformity of real colonies’ polymorphs to various hypothetical endmember polymorph arrangements. We find that real colonies’ polymorph arrangements avoid the extreme energetic gradients produced by other arrangements. This result suggests there is a fitness cost to extreme diffusion gradients. Future work should include both experimental manipulation of polymorph arrangement in living cheilostomes and observations of polymorph arrangement in the earliest polymorphic cheilostomes.

title: Regional Geologic Controls on Culvert Outlet Scour: A Statistical and Machine Learning Analysis
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Gupta, Keira Marie [1], Schanz, Sarah Anne [2], Mason, Brian [3]
affiliations: (1) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
(2) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
(3) Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, Fergus Falls, Minnesota, USA
abstract: Scour at culvert outlets is an ongoing issue, and can cause roadway damage, barriers to aquatic organism passage, and disrupt geomorphic stream stability. Previous studies have identified the most significant structural factors contributing to outlet scour, but there is little work on “external” factors, such as regional geology. Because of this, we examined the influence of Quaternary history on a) scour development and b) structural factors contributing to scour by comparing culvert survey datasets from two Minnesota watersheds using statistical analyses and machine learning (ML) methods. We found that Quaternary history places a slight lithologic control on scour formation, while scour severity and contributing structural factors are driven by differences in topography. Our classification and regression ML models, built for predicting scour presence and severity, respectively, performed better than their individual baselines. While this indicates that these models could be implemented to support culvert installation practices, these datasets would also likely benefit from more robust methods in the long-term. Furthermore, these models, in addition to our other findings, provide useful insights to help reduce future culvert outlet scour, thus supporting aquatic organism habitat and geomorphic stability in streams. Generally, our results suggest that regional geology plays a significant role in scour development and should be taken into account in future scour-related investigations to help minimize the negative impacts of culvert systems on the natural environment.

title: Insights into Lunar Basaltic Regolith Breccia Petrogenesis from the Dominion (DOM) Range 18678 Meteorite
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials (Posters)
authors: Bell, Jordan [1], McLeod, Dr. Claire [2], Shaulis, Dr. Barry [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(3) Trace Element and Radiogenic Isotope Laboratory (TRAIL), University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract:
The 2018-2019 NSF-NASA supported Antarctic Search for Meteorites (ANSMET) recovered eight lunar meteorites from the Dominion (DOM) Range. Previous mineralogical and geochemical studies of this lunar DOM suite has classified these samples as polymict regolith breccias composed of multiple clasts, minerals, and glass fragments. They are typically clast-poor with basaltic, gabbroic, granulitic, anorthositic clasts, 3-phase symplectites (fayalite, clinopyroxene, and silica), all ranging from 100µm-1mm in size.

This study will be the first to conduct a petrological investigation of sample DOM 18678 (mass: 11.6g). Work to date on a single thin section (1.6cm x 2cm) has been conducted via PLM and SEM, including BSE and EDS analyses. Clasts within DOM 18678 are predominantly basaltic, subhedral to anhedral, and vary in size, ranging from 50μm-1mm. These clasts are composed mainly of calcium-rich plagioclase (anorthite), clinopyroxene, iron-rich olivine (fayalite), minor Fe-Ti oxide (ilmenite), silica, and iron sulfide (troilite). Other clasts present include impact melt breccias, microbreccias, and 3-phase symplectites (fayalite, clinopyroxene, silica) consistent with previous work on this lunar DOM suite. These clasts are surrounded by a black to dark gray, fine-grained, glassy matrix. Throughout the brecciated matrix, glass is present in the form of glass spherules, melt veins, and as a variably vesiculated, 10-50μm thick fusion crust surrounding ~55% of the meteorite.

Guided by textural and chemical information acquired via SEM, in-situ analysis via EPMA will quantify major and minor element mineral chemistry to evaluate clast petrogenesis and their potential source regions on the Moon (e.g., plagioclase An# vs. pyroxene Mg#). This will be accompanied by EPMA data from mineral fragments and glass data to further evaluate breccia petrogenesis (e.g., CaO/Al 2 O 3 vs. MgO/Al 2 O 3 in glasses). Data collected via EPMA will subsequently inform accompanying in-situ trace element data to be acquired via LA-ICP-MS. By analyzing the potential petrogenetic relationships between basaltic components, and comparing clast, mineral, and glass chemistries to other lunar materials, this study will advance understanding of breccia petrogenesis and contribute to knowledge of this relatively new lunar meteorite suite.

title: Discrepancies in Central Himalayan Denudation Rates from Millennial to Million-year Timescales
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: McQuarrie, Nadine [1], Ghoshal, Suryodoy [2], Eizenhöfer, Paul R. [3], Ehlers, Todd A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Plymouth, Plymouth, United Kingdom

abstract: Himalayan denudation rates from catchment-­averaged cosmogenic radionuclide data reflect timescales of a few to tens of thousands of years. The geomorphology of catchments they were collected from are free from knickpoints and suggest a quasi-­steady-­state between uplift and erosion. When these millennial-scale rates are extrapolated to longer (million-year) timescales they provide a means to evaluate transients in denudation when compared thermochronology data. To do this, we use cross-section derived velocity fields as input into both thermokinematic and landscape evolution models and replicate measured thermochronometer ages, and topographic metrics in the central Nepal Himalaya. Simulations that replicate both low temperature thermochronometetric ages between 0.5-3 Ma, and the topographic form of the Marsyangdi drainage basin identify spatial and temporal variations in structural uplift, topography, and erosion. Model results show topography that is constantly changing, including advection of topography in the direction of transport, growth and decay of topography in response to changes in uplift location and rapid incision into formerly uplifted topography. At Himalayan convergence rates (~ 20 mm/yr) uplift can quickly outpace a rivers ability to incise, so high-relief develops from incision into previously uplifted topography. Modeled erosion rates also vary in space and time, but median rates remain very high (8-13 mm/yr) across the high Himalaya from ~ 3 Ma to Present. Denudation rates from these best-fit simulations are a factor of 2 to 3 times higher than those determined from a compilation of catchment-average denudation rates from cosmogenic radionuclides across the high Himalaya (2-4 mm/yr). Cosmogenic rates are replicated by the fluvial denudation component of the model, with the landslide component of denudation 2-4x higher. However, immediately south of the region of active uplift, modeled denudation rates, and catchment-mean erosion rates are similar at ~ 0.5-3 mm/yr. We discuss the discrepancies and similarities of transient denudation rates in the content of structural controls on river incision and denudation, the effects of Quaternary glaciations on denudation, and potential biases measured cosmogenic nuclide concentrations such as landslides, and grain size dependence.

title: From Mineral Isotopes to Orogenic Architecture: Testing Cratonic Stability in the Neoproterozoic Zalingei Fold Belt, Darfur, Sudan

abstract: How do orogenic systems modify continental lithosphere, and what controls long-term stability versus thermal and structural reworking? The Neoproterozoic Zalingei Fold Belt (ZFB)—exposed within the Darfur Dome of western Sudan—presents a fundamental puzzle in the assembly of Northeast Africa, variously interpreted as a partially remobilized metacraton (Abdelsalam et al., 2002) or an accreted mobile belt within the Central Sahara–Central African shield assembly (de Wit et al., 2021). Resolving this fundamental geodynamic debate requires linking deep-time crustal growth to post-orogenic thermal and exhumation pathways. Here, we integrate U-Pb zircon geochronology, Lu-Hf isotope geochemistry, and 40 Ar/ 39 Ar mica thermochronology across the ZFB to evaluate these competing tectonic end-members. Our U-Pb data document a protracted polyphase evolution spanning the Mesoproterozoic through Ediacaran: detrital zircon arrays in metamorphic hosts range from 1944 to 710 Ma, unfoliated granitoids yield crystallization ages at 930 Ma and 701 Ma, and syn- to post-kinematic foliated granitoids constrain final magmatic activity to 602–583 Ma. Strongly negative values (>90 % of analyzed zircons) demonstrate that Pan-African orogenesis was overwhelmingly dominated by extensive recycling of pre-existing continental crust, with negligible juvenile additions. To scale from mineral-scale petrogenesis to mountain-scale architecture, we employ mica 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology (closure T around 350°- 400°) to directly test two competing tectonic predictions: (1) Synchronous 40 Ar/ 39 Ar cooling ages at 580-600 Ma across distinct U-Pb domains would reflect rapid, coherent regional exhumation following collisional assembly as an accreted mobile belt, whereas (2) 40 Ar/ 39 Ar cooling ages that scale directly with individual U-Pb crystallization ages would indicate slow, localized in-place cooling without widespread regional unroofing, strongly supporting a metacratonic stability model. By systematically pairing magmatic isotopic tracers with low-to-intermediate temperature thermal paths, this integrated thermochronological framework provides critical insights into whether the lithosphere of Northeast Africa was structurally dismembered or rheologically modified during Neoproterozoic assembly.

abstract: Fire regimes in the Rocky Mountains have varied through time in response to changes in climate, including atmospheric warming, glacial retreat, increased summer insolation, and drought, as well as more recent human activities. Macroscopic charcoal preserved in lake sediments provides an opportunity to reconstruct these long-term changes in Grand Teton National Park. We analyzed a 7.17-meter sediment core from Jackson Lake (Wyoming) spanning the last ~6.5 cal ka BP. Sediment chronology was established using an age-depth model based on radiocarbon dating. The core was subsampled at 1 cm intervals, and 2 cm 3 samples were treated with sodium hexametaphosphate and sieved through a 106 μm mesh to recover macroscopic charcoal. Charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR; pieces cm⁻² yr⁻¹) were calculated using the R package tapas to reconstruct past fire activity. The signal-to-noise index indicated a reliable charcoal record (mean value 3.24). The record includes 59 fire episodes, averaging 8.9 episodes/1,000 years, with fire-return intervals ranging from 16 to 880 years (mean = 112; median = 60). Fire activity peaked ~4.9-4.1 cal ka (16 episodes) and increased again during the last millennium (12 episodes). The charcoal record indicates an apparent fire-free interval from ~5.8-4.9 cal ka. Ongoing analyses of samples from the Early Holocene (10.4 cal kyr BP) will extend the fire history record, providing the opportunity to evaluate long-term fire regime changes in response to climate variability.

title: Understanding Controls on Organic Carbon Enrichment in Permian Deep-Marine Siltstones of the Delaware Basin: A Tribute to Brad Sageman
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)

affiliations: (1) Applied Sedimentary Geology, Bozeman, MT, USA
abstract:
Organic carbon-rich siltstone (ORS) marker beds in the Permian Brushy Canyon and lower Cherry Canyon formations record organic carbon enrichment within a basin-restricted deep-marine system. This research integrates stratigraphic mapping of continuous shelf-to-basin exposures with geochemical proxy relationships to evaluate mechanisms controlling particulate organic carbon (POC) accumulation.

Organic carbon enrichment was driven chiefly by hydrodynamic concentration of POC within sediment gravity flows, rather than by suspension fallout in surface waters modulated by production, destruction, and dilution processes. Poor to negative correlations between POC and geochemical proxies for these processes, together with positive correlations between POC and the vertical and longitudinal interval thickness of ORS marker beds, indicate enrichment under high sedimentation rates and efficient burial. Across the 55-km exposure of the 450-m-thick deep-marine siliciclastic succession, 25 to 33 ORS marker beds mapped over 245 km 2 provide a stratigraphic framework for correlating organic enrichment trends across second- through fifth-order deepwater episodes.

Submarine canyons incised the carbonate shelf margin and directed sediment transport into down-profile fairway, interfairway, and extra-channel regions. Catastrophic floods generated hyperpycnal flows that delivered shelf-derived POC to the basin during sea-level rise, when external sand supply was low and shelf inorganic and organic carbon productivity was high. Slope enrichment reflects stripping from super-elevated flows, whereas channel-fairway enrichment supports a shelf-derived source. Together, these relationships indicate that sea level directly controlled sediment sources and indirectly controlled sediment flux by modulating flow initiation by flood or failure. More broadly, hyperpycnal sediment gravity flows provide a plausible mechanism for POC accumulation in onshore basins and where carbonate shelves source off-platform deep-marine settings.

abstract: Understanding West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) sensitivity to natural forcing requires detailed lithofacies classification and quantitative methods to resolve ice-marginal processes across glacial-interglacial cycles. We apply unsupervised multivariate clustering to quality-controlled, high-resolution XRF and shipboard physical property data from IODP Site U1525 (eastern Ross Sea continental slope) to build an objective lithofacies framework for Unit II, spanning the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT). We then examine orbital-scale variability in the lithofacies-discriminant proxies to explore how the Ross Sea ice margin responded to orbital forcing across glacial, deglacial, and interglacial periods of the MPT. Preliminary results show the clusters carry distinct geochemical and physical property signatures that significantly correspond to independently described lithofacies from traditional methods. The stratigraphic and temporal pacing of lithofacies reveals shifting roles and combinations of forcing factors on the ice margin across glacial-interglacial cycles, consistent with an orbitally sensitive marine-based ice margin during this interval. This approach offers a transferable framework for objective, reproducible facies classification in glaciomarine archives.

title: New Updates to Wildfire© Software Enable Multi-Phase Analysis of Illite Polytypes
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)

affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Biological Sciences, Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA

abstract:
Along with its sister program, Newmod, Wildfire © allows for the advanced modeling of X-ray diffraction patterns of clay minerals. The original version of the software, written by Reynolds (1993), was designed to calculate three-dimensional models of clays, but it did not have the capacity to seamlessly combine and match multiple polytype phases to an experimental pattern. We present preliminary updates to the Wildfire © program that enable this kind of multi-phase analysis of clay-rich samples. The software package includes modules for modeling ordered and disordered mica polytypes, as well as chlorite. Polytype phases are modeled individually and then added to a “multi-phase” list. The relative proportions of each individual phase are manually adjusted via sliders – or automatically adjusted via an “autofit” feature – to create a new composite model. This model can then be visually matched to experimental pattern data that are imported into the program. The capacity to plot individual phases in one window and view the composite model in a separate window is a significant upgrade to the user interface over previous versions of the software.

An AI Assistant (Anthropic's Claude Code) was utilized to design the “autofit” feature: modeled diffraction patterns from the multi-phase list are aligned across a unified 2-theta range, and an optimization routine is executed via the Apache Commons Math library. Following execution, the optimized weights for each model dynamically update and the composite curves are replotted. The routine is validated using three independent curves – each containing 310 data points – and optimized against an experimental reference curve. Computational execution is instantaneous, producing relative weights for each polytype that closely match expected theoretical values.

While clay polytypes have been long studied, their interpretations remain a specialized endeavor. Furthermore, different illite polytypes may be associated with a detrital or diagenetic origin, impacting depositional models for the rocks and sediments that contain them. We hope that these updates to the Wildfire © program will expand opportunities for interpreting clay minerals in the rock record.

abstract: Metamorphic dehydration of subducting oceanic crust controls deformation, melting, and element cycling in subduction zones. This is often quantified through phase equilibrium modeling approaches that calculate the stable mineral assemblages in various rock types and how these evolve along subduction pressure-temperature (P-T) paths. These models allow geologists to predict when, where, and how much water can be released by the subducting crust, which can be compared to evidence for such dehydration reactions in the natural rock record. However, the record of these reactions in metamorphic subduction rocks can be difficult to discern. Here we constrain the prograde metamorphic history of epidote-amphibolite facies metabasalts from an underplated and exhumed subduction plate interface preserved in the Catalina Schist in southern California, USA. In-situ LA-ICP-MS trace element analysis of the mineral products of dehydration reactions allow us to identify the likely reactants and provide empirical constraints on P-T paths followed by these rocks. The trace element data combined with textural context reveal four generations of epidote growth from pre-subduction hydrothermal alteration through prograde, peak, and retrograde metamorphism. Hydrothermal alteration of interpillow networks is evidenced by epidosite exhibiting strongly negative Ce-anomalies, and bulk-rock Sr-isotope ratios further indicate extensive seawater-rock interaction prior to subduction. Outside of interpillow networks, epidote-rich vein-like structures exhibit patterns of rare-earth element (REE) concentrations that suggest that this epidote grew as a result of pumpellyite breakdown. Phase equilibrium modeling of these basalts suggests that this pumpellyite-epidote reaction occurred near 300°C and liberated a large amount of mineral-bound water. We interpret the vein-like setting of this epidote to represent self-organizing porosity structures that provided conduits for the draining of dehydration fluids from the subducting slab. Additionally, epidote porphyroblasts throughout the metabasalt have distinct REE patterns, major element compositions, and mineral associations that suggest re-equilibration at peak to retrograde conditions. Retrogressive cooling of the epidote amphibolite metabasalts likely represents cooling of the unit following underplating. Our work provides insight into the initial hydration of the oceanic crust prior to subduction, the metamorphic evolution of subducted metabasalts including their dehydration early during subduction, and the final underplating and refrigeration of the Epidote Amphibolite Unit. Trace element data provide constraints on this metamorphic history and aid in the interpretation of structural elements that would otherwise remain enigmatic.

abstract:
The northeastern margin of the Uncompahgre uplift of the late Paleozoic Ancestral Rocky Mountains (ARM) preserves evidence for syndepositional deformation within the Pennsylvanian-Permian deposits of the Central Colorado trough. We present 1:20,000-scale geologic mapping of a ~130 km 2 area in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains near Crestone, Colorado, including parts of the Crestone thrust, Spread Eagle thrust, Independence Mine shear zone, and Sangre de Cristo normal fault. Primary objectives for this project aimed to investigate the geometry and kinematics of ARM structures and whether these structures were overprinted by Laramide contraction and/or Rio Grande Rift extension.

Approximately 4.2 km of the Pennsylvanian-Permian section is exposed in the study area, which transitions from the marine Pennsylvanian Minturn Formation to proximal terrestrial deposits of the Sangre de Cristo Formation. The lower Minturn Formation is exposed in a fault wedge bound by splays of the Crestone thrust with well-developed SW-dipping phyllitic cleavage and is locally folded in a tight overturned syncline-overturned anticline pair in the footwall of the Crestone thrust. Chloritoid is locally prominent in the lower Minturn in North Crestone Creek, exhibiting evidence for contact metamorphism associated with Oligocene magmatism along the western flank of the range. Geologic mapping within the Pennsylvanian-Permian section documents NE-vergent growth folding and two intraformational unconformities associated with the Gibson Peak syncline within the Crestone Conglomerate Member of the Pennsylvanian-Permian Sangre de Cristo Formation. This syncline is a NE-vergent, NW-trending fold located ~1–4 km northeast of the SW-dipping Crestone thrust, which juxtaposes Proterozoic crystalline basement and thin, overturned slivers of Mississippian, Devonian, and Ordovician strata in the hanging wall against Pennsylvanian-Permian strata in the footwall. Minor thrust faults within 250 m of the Crestone thrust record a mean subhorizontal shortening direction of 041°, oriented 88° from the mean fold axis trend of the Gibson Peak syncline, indicating kinematic compatibility between NE-directed thrusting and folding. We interpret the Gibson Peak syncline to be an ARM structure associated with the NE-directed thrusting of the Crestone thrust with minimal overprinting during Laramide contraction. Microstructural analysis of oriented samples collected from the Crestone thrust core shows evidence for top-SW extensional reactivation localized within carbonate units in the hanging wall. However, the Crestone thrust is locally intruded by late (?) Oligocene aplite dikes that postdate deformation.

title: Evolutionary consequences of asexual reproduction in fossil ostracodes
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Hunt, Gene [1], Smith, Chloe [2], Nadalin, Caroline [3], Puckett, Terry Markham [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC, USA
(2) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Williams College, Williamstown, MA, USA

abstract: Perhaps no questions in evolutionary biology have received more attention than those related to the origin, maintenance, and evolutionary consequences of sex. The central puzzle is that asexual reproduction is much more efficient than sex and yet the latter occurs in nearly all eukaryote lineages. Evolutionary thinkers have since the 19 th century ascribed the preponderance of sex to its variation-generating properties. Abundant variation increases the effectiveness of adaptation and thereby the ability of populations to respond to changing conditions, which is argued to decrease the risk of extinction. Here we describe ongoing work using the rich fossil record of cytheroid ostracodes from the U.S. Coastal Plain to test directly the consequences of reproductive mode in fossil species. We document the presence of sexual reproduction by assessing sexual dimorphism in valve size and shape in adult cytheroid species. In most cases, mixture models reveal the presence two significant clusters, readily interpreted as males and females. Rarely, however, we find populations that are best fit by a one-cluster model with low shape variance. Following common practice among ostracod workers, we interpret these populations as female-only and therefore asexual. We have analyzed over 250 species thus far, ranging in age from the Late Cretaceous through Eocene. We infer that asexual reproduction occurs in about 7% of species, similar to the proportion of asexual cytheroids found today in the marine waters surrounding the United Kingdom. We also present a case study of the genus Phacorhabdotus , which in this fauna has species with sexual, asexual, and mixed reproduction. Phylogenetic analysis reveals multiple transitions in reproductive mode within this genus and that the only strictly asexual species, P. bicostilimus , also has the shortest stratigraphic range. In addition, the best supported mixed effect linear model indicates that sexual populations evolved more in shape compared to asexual ones. These findings are consistent with the view the asexual reproduction may limit evolutionary potential.

title: Investigating the Effects of Human Alteration on Floodplain Carbon Storage in the Southwest and Midwest U.S.
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Thomas, Lauren [1], Lininger, Katherine [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geography, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
River corridors, which include channels, floodplains, and the hyporheic zone, are key pipelines for carbon (C) transport from the landscape to the ocean. Previous research has shown that floodplain organic carbon (OC) is primarily stored in riparian vegetation, downed large wood, and soil. Across the U.S., floodplain ecosystem services and functions have been affected by human modifications, including dams, water withdrawals, agriculture, and land development. Current understanding of floodplain OC storage is limited, as few existing studies quantify OC stocks in all 3 sources, assess the impacts of alteration, or estimate OC across large spatial scales. To quantify OC stocks and understand how they have been affected by human alterations in the Southwest and Midwest U.S., two regions where floodplain OC has not been comprehensively studied, we combined geospatial analyses and field sampling techniques to assess OC stocks along the San Pedro River, AZ and the Rum River, MN.

For each floodplain, we classified high-resolution ecogeomorphic units based on vegetation, hydrology, and morphology using publicly available datasets and ArcGIS Pro. We used additional geospatial analyses to categorize reaches as altered or unaltered based on land cover, levees, and water withdrawal datasets. We collected soil cores, alluvial sediment depths, vegetation surveys, and downed wood surveys across ecogeomorphic units and alteration levels. To estimate wood volume, we measured wood jams, accumulations, downed wood, and porosity using the census method at each site. We collected sediment cores and analyzed them for grain size, OC content, soil moisture, and mineral-associated and particulate OC fractions. We measured tree dimensions within plots to calculate aboveground biomass from allometric relationships. We used these field data to calculate OC stocks at 36 locations within each floodplain. We then used our OC stock measurements to estimate biomass, downed wood, and soil OC stocks at the floodplain scale based on alteration and ecogeomorphic unit classifications. We compare our floodplain-scale OC stocks to existing large-scale estimations of OC, derived from the TreeMap and SSURGO databases. Preliminary results indicate that floodplain OC stocks differ by climate zone, and some stocks differ by level of alteration and ecogeomorphic unit. This work provides a replicable workflow that can be used to scale-up floodplain OC stock estimates over broad geographic extents.

abstract: The Parowan Creek watershed (~150 km 2 ) is the principal water source for an endorheic extensional tectonic basin in southwestern Utah. The watershed serves as the primary water supply and aquifer recharge source for a growing rural community, has a history of wildfire and flooding, and is characterized by a diverse geology with active faults and strong structural control on topography. Parowan Creek and its tributaries are steep, gravel-bedded streams draining the Markagunt Plateau mountain block uplifted along a series of normal faults resulting in approximately 1600 m of topographic relief. These faults create horsts and grabens that influence local relief, expose different sedimentary and volcanic lithologies, affect runoff processes, and regulate sediment supply to stream channels. Hydrologically, the bulk of streamflow is derived from snowmelt, but the largest floods are caused by monsoon thunderstorms over steep terrain. Here we present a dataset from more that 20 sites within the watershed to understand the role of geology in shaping downstream changes in stream geomorphology and sediment transport capacity. Further, we explore how geologic structures affect downstream surface water-groundwater exchange via contemporaneous discharge measurements. Results show that both gaining and losing stream reaches are common, where losing reaches are generally associated with grabens underlain by Tertiary limestone, whereas gaining reaches and springs often occur where horsts expose older Cretaceous rocks. Downstream hydraulic geometry relations show significant scatter as post-fire floods caused channel widening in some reaches while other reaches remained relatively unchanged. Yet bankfull Shields stress values show a much more coherent pattern, with sediment transport capacity increasing downstream. This likely reflects increasing downstream sediment supply as streams pass through steep horst blocks near the mouth of the watershed and is supported by measurements of bed sediment lithology dominated by proximal source rocks. Despite the clear role of monsoon thunderstorms in generating sediment from steeper terrain in horst blocks, sediment transport modeling shows that long-duration snowmelt floods transport the bulk of the sediment at the basin outlet. Taken together, these results show that geology strongly influences the hydrogeomorphology of the watershed, with implications for mountain-block recharge of the downstream basin aquifer and morphological adjustment of stream channels following a fire-flood sequence.

abstract: Coastal, glacierized watersheds within the Gulf of Alaska are receding at an alarming rate, contributing vast amounts of physical and chemical weathering products to the ocean. These glacierized mountain catchments may export weathering products that either consume or generate CO 2 ; however, seasonal controls on these processes remain understudied in these environments. Therefore, we investigated five watersheds in Southeast Alaska that vary in glacier coverage (55-0%), proglacial lake coverage, and bedrock lithology. This study spans two melt seasons from April through October 2021 and 2022. River-water major ions, δ¹⁸O, ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, discharge, precipitation chemistry, mineralogy, and whole-rock geochemistry were integrated with MEANDIR Monte Carlo inverse modeling of carbonate weathering and pyrite oxidation. Seasonally, river-water composition changed; however, it did not follow conservative mixing trajectories between precipitation and whole-rock compositions. Calcium enriched stream waters indicate preferential dissolution of reactive minor phases. Seasonal ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr shifts were strongest in the heavily (55% and 42%) glacierized watersheds, where spring and summer variability may indicate evolving access to mineral sources as glacial drainage systems developed. Some river-water ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr values were more radiogenic than measured local bulk-rock values, indicating preferential weathering or implying weathering of an unmeasured phase. MEANDIR modeling results reveal seasonal weathering variability across the watersheds that may indicate changes in weathering sources. Modeled carbonate and sulfide contributions were only weakly related to discharge, indicating that seasonal chemical weathering changes may not be fully explained by dilution or runoff magnitude alone. A large proglacial lake within the Mendenhall watershed may contribute to the observed muted seasonal chemical weathering variability, despite large melt-season discharge variability. This buffering across the Gulf of Alaska may become increasingly prominent as glaciers rapidly recede and form or expand proglacial lakes.

abstract:
Since December 23rd, 2024, Kīlauea has been erupting episodically, producing 52 episodes of high lava fountains, as of July 2026. Fountaining episodes typically last <9 hours and vary in height, with a maximum of 540 m (1770 ft). The U.S. Geological Survey’s Hawaiian Volcano Observatory has collected over 250 samples of tephra and lava flows for near-real-time geochemical monitoring of the eruption. In collaboration with the University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo, an Energy-Dispersive X-Ray Fluorescence (EDXRF) spectrometer is used to analyze bulk rock geochemistry usually within 24 hours of sample collection. In addition, matrix glass and olivine are analyzed every month using scanning electron microscopy and electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). These data are used to monitor MgO as a proxy for the temperature of the magmatic system, which provides insights about magma storage, fluctuations in eruptive temperatures, and magmatic recharge.

Matrix glass analyses for the current summit eruption show a 1 wt% increase in MgO from its lowest extent in the 2020–2023 summit eruptions to the lowest extent in the ongoing eruption (from 6.0 wt% to 7.0 wt% MgO). Glass from the first 48 episodes of the current eruption had 7.0-7.8 wt% MgO, reflecting melt temperatures of 1165-1183℃. The increase in MgO wt% compared to the 2020-2023 eruptions is consistent with hotter magma entering the system. All episodes of the ongoing eruption have contained two populations of olivine: a dominant population of non-zoned Fo82-83 olivine and a population of normally zoned olivine with Fo88 cores and Fo83 rims. In episodes 44 and 46, a third population of normally zoned olivine with Fo83 cores and Fo81 rims was identified. Future diffusion chronometry will be conducted on the different olivine populations to provide insight into timescales of mixing between more primitive and evolved magmas within the reservoir system. Continued near-real-time geochemical monitoring of Kīlauea allows for the tracking of changes in the magmatic system.

abstract: Chacororé Lake is a shallow floodplain lake seasonally connected to the Cuiabá River in the Barão de Melgaço, northern Pantanal, Mato Grosso, Brazil. We characterized the modern lake using daily stage records from four gauging stations operated by the Brazilian National Water Agency, 47 surface sediment samples, water quality data, and the first freshwater sponge collections from the lake. Three stations record stage on the Cuiabá River: upstream of the lake, at the junction with the connecting channel, and downstream. The fourth station records water level inside Chacororé Lake. These data establish a hydrobiological baseline and provide an interpretive context for sediment core records. Lake stage follows the three river stations through the annual flood pulse, showing that lake level is strongly controlled by the Cuiabá River. In a dry-season survey in August 2023, surface water was neutral (pH 7.0), dilute (mean TDS 25 ppm), well oxygenated (80% saturation), and thermally uniform (20.6 °C), with a depth of 0.8 to 1.9 m, indicating a shallow, well-mixed system. Silt is the dominant grain-size fraction (mean 52.6%), but sand ranges from 1.1 to 93.5%, coarsest along the southeastern margin and finest in the central basin. Total carbon ranges from 0.27 to 4.74% (mean 1.30%), with the highest value in the north. SiO₂ (mean 66.3%) is highest in the north and east, and Al₂O₃, K₂O, and TiO₂ are highest in the southwest. Sponges were collected with a Van Veen grab from rock substrates in the lake and in the river. Eunapius fragilis (Leidy, 1851) occurs in the lake. Tubella variabilis (Bonetto & Ezcurra de Drago, 1973), T. repens (Hinde, 1888), and Corvospongilla seckti (Bonetto & Ezcurra de Drago, 1966) occur in the river. The two assemblages are consistent with differences in flow velocity and substrate between the lentic and lotic settings. Analyses of spicules preserved in lake-floor sediments are underway. The dataset is a baseline for interpreting paleoenvironmental records from the lake and for future assessment of river regulation in one of the world's largest tropical wetlands.

abstract:
Hyperspectral drill-core data, traditional nuclear wireline logging and portable x-ray fluorescence (pXRF) measurements from multi-sensor core logger (MSCL) yield multiple independent estimations of either elemental abundance or mineralogy. These methods offer potential for more rapid and cost-effective screening of resources as compared to more time-intensive inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry ICP-MS. Ideally, hyperspectral data, including visible-near-shortwave infrared (VN-SWIR) and longwave infrared (LWIR), will directly measure absorption features of certain minerals. Our initial approach focuses on the use of Gadolinium (Gd) and Titanium (Ti) recorded by the nuclear wireline tools as direct proxies for rare earth element and critical mineral abundance in formations of interest. Elemental abundances from wireline spectroscopy are integrated into petrophysical models and compared/calibrated to hyperspectral and pXRF derived mineralogy to evaluate resources.

We evaluate the potential of thinly bedded deposits in Pennsylvanian aged coaly strata of the Cherokee-Forest City Basin (CFCB) centered in eastern Kansas as part of a U.S. DOE supported interstate effort. In May 2024, 119 feet of conventional 4-inch core was collected from the Krebs interval of the lower Cherokee Group in the Peterson Trust #8-31. Triple-combo logs as well as geochemical spectroscopy logs were acquired over the same intervals. Elements of interest with elevated abundances are potentially transported by hot saline basinal brines that have migrated through the Mississippian formation. These elements are transition metals, post-transition metals and metalloids, for which there are proxies available from wireline spectroscopy.

Elemental abundance from wireline were calibrated using handheld pXRF core analysis and bulk-rock geochemistry via ICP-MS with comparisons to both VN-SWIR and LWIR derived minerology. This calibration enabled high-resolution estimates of in-situ Gd concentrations within the wireline tool's detection zone as well as confirmation of lithology of resource bearing zones. Gd concentrations were normalized to core-derived ICP-MS concentrations, resulting in a key reference dataset. Gd values were upscaled into a geocellular model and propagated across the surface and subsurface extent of the Pennsylvanian section in Kansas. These results culminated in a Gd-based resource potential map of the coal-bearing Krebs interval of the lower Cherokee Group. Similarly, geochemical wireline proxies may be identified that will aid in developing resource maps for transition, post-transition, and metalloids within the Pennsylvanian that were identified as elevated.

abstract: As part of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) STATEMAP program, the Colorado Geological Survey (CGS) compiled a new 1:100,000-scale geologic map covering approximately 4,200 square kilometers of the northern Colorado Front Range and western Colorado Piedmont, including Fort Collins, Loveland, Broomfield, Boulder, Longmont, Brighton, and Greeley. This map provides a synthesis of recently published geologic maps in the western part of the Colorado Piedmont geologic province, using data from both bedrock and surficial geology maps. We compiled 212 existing numerical ages for the surficial units and collected 32 new geochronology samples to constrain the timing of late Quaternary landscape evolution. This map showcases bedrock units of the Denver Basin, formed from sediments deposited in the late Cretaceous through the early Paleocene. Along the western map boundary, deformation associated with the Front Range uplift controls bedrock structure, while Front Range lithologies provide the source material for many piedmont surficial deposits. Fluvial incision and erosion by the South Platte River and its tributaries removed much of the Paleogene and Neogene section. Across much of the Colorado Piedmont, discontinuous Quaternary fluvial, eolian, and mass-movement deposits now form a veneer over older bedrock. Seventeen OSL and 15 14 C (carbon-14 analysis of bulk sediment) samples were collected from fluvial and eolian Quaternary deposits as a part of this study, yielding preliminary analytical results. 14 C ages range from ~1–13 ka and preliminary OSL ages range from ~3–44 ka. This map incorporates information from multiple geologic maps including 20 CGS 7.5’ quadrangles, 4 USGS 7.5’ quadrangles, 4 USGS 30x60’ quadrangles, and other miscellaneous scale maps. We prioritized using data mapped at 1:24,000-scale (7.5’ quadrangles) and incorporated other data at coarser scales where necessary. Mapping was primarily completed using 1-meter DEM-derived lidar hillshades combined with satellite imagery, and we conducted field visits to verify key areas. Unit descriptions were aggregated from source maps and combined and simplified for clarity. Detailed mapping of river corridors delineates excavated areas, artificial fill, and disturbed ground, providing a foundation for future aggregate-resource mapping. More broadly, the compilation provides a regional geologic framework for geologic hazard assessment, water-resource studies, land-use planning, and other resource evaluations across the northern Colorado urban corridor.

title: Rhyolite-MELTS Aplite Geobarometry: Effective Assessment of Pluton Depths
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part II)
authors: Miller, Calvin F [1], Lopez Acevedo, Marvin Alejandro [2], Gualda, Guilherme A.R. [3], Kelly, Liam J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Fisk-Vanderbilt Masters-to-PhD Bridge Program, Nashville, TN, USA
(3) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville,
(4) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
abstract:
Estimating depths of felsic magma crystallization in plutons has long frustrated petrologists and tectonicists. Such plutons generally lack either minerals with simple pressure-sensitive compositions or mineral assemblages that provide precise pressure constraints. Amphibole has been the favored mineral for pluton geobarometry (e.g., Hammarstrom & Zen Am Min 1986; Ridolfi et al CMP 2010; Mutch et al CMP 2016), but its occurrence in felsic plutonic rocks is limited; calculation of its lengthy formula is made more challenging because of dependence upon Fe 3+ /Fe 2+ ratio; and proposed barometers have been complicated and commonly imprecise and/or unreliable. Pressure sensitivity of highly silicic melt compositions, specifically at the quartz+plagioclase+alkali feldspar (Q2F)-saturated cotectic, has long been recognized as an indicator of depth of crystallization of felsic magmas (e.g. Tuttle & Bowen GSA Mem 74 1958; Blundy & Cashman CMP 2001). However, reliable thermobarometry based on this relationship requires well-calibrated Q2F+melt (Qz-Or-Ab-An) phase equilibria, and, importantly, compositions of plutonic rocks rarely represent Q2F-saturated melts.

We propose that application of Rhyolite-MELTS thermobarometry (Gualda & Ghiorso 2014, Gualda et al 2024) to aplites can yield relatively precise and accurate pressures (thus depths) of crystallization of many plutons. Unaltered aplites are almost ubiquitous in felsic plutons as relatively thin leucogranite dikes with sharp contacts against a granitic host. Such dikes, which are typically fine-grained, equigranular, and lack a sequential fabric, are widely interpreted to represent nearly crystal-free melts locally extracted from host granitoid. Thus, they provide the Q2F-saturated melt composition necessary for Rhyolite-MELTS modelling of ~ambient pressure.

We are testing the efficacy of Rhyolite-MELTS aplite geobarometry using typical dikes from granitic intrusive complexes, using their compositions as proxies for melt compositions and determining the Rhyolite-MELTS-modelled pressure where the three Q2F saturation curves most closely approach intersection. The Tuolumne Intrusive Complex, California, has been our primary initial focus (Lopez et al GSA abstract [this meeting]); 13 samples yield P ~190-240 MPa (~7-9 km depth), with individual uncertainties mostly ~±30 MPa (~1 km), well within the range of published estimates. We have further collected seven aplites from five metaluminous and peraluminous granitic intrusions in SE California, NW Arizona, and S Nevada with previously well-constrained, though imprecise, emplacement depths ranging from ~1 to 15 km (~30-400 MPa). Results to date are all promising – consistent with existing pressure constraints.

abstract:
StraboMicro is part of the StraboSpot ecosystem of digital applications for collecting, organizing, and sharing geologic data. StraboMicro specifically is a tool for organizing and analyzing micro-scale imagery and associated data that are easily linked with sample information from StraboField to preserve contextual information. The free, open-source StraboMicro application is community-driven. Re-envisioned in 2026 as a result of user feedback, it features a redesigned platform with improved usability, high resolution image tiling, image analysis tools, data versioning, and updated sharing capabilities. Depending on user needs, data can be shared, made public with DOIs, or kept private.

We present a StraboMicro use-case example from research on the Catalina Schist (southern CA, USA) in which optical and electron imagery are combined with chemical and electron backscattered diffraction data. Loaded with base low-resolution optical scans and higher-resolution images, StraboMicro facilitates the planning and execution of electron beam analyses, the data from which are then easily loaded into StraboMicro to be evaluated in their spatial context. StraboMicro streamlines these workflows, whereas the same work might be done between multiple files edited in separate vector graphics programs, GIS software, or spreadsheet software. In the research use-case, StraboMicro aided the petrologic and micro-structural interpretation of metamorphic evolution and deformation processes in the Catalina Schist. StraboMicro also has significant potential as a teaching tool, offering a versatile platform for students to practice a range of skills from basic annotation and analysis of petrographic images to more advanced integration of micro-scale datasets.

title: Relative roles of slab age, convergence rate, upper plate thickness, and asymmetric erosion in Cordilleran-type orogens: insights from numerical modeling

affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, CNSM/Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK, USA
(2) Department of Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
(3) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA

abstract: Long-lived Cordilleran-type orogens display diverse structural styles and orogenic wedge geometries resulting from interactions among converging plates. Along-strike variations in climate, plate properties, and convergence rates may influence upper plate deformation. We use a visco-elasto-plastic thermo-mechanical numerical model to simulate the effects of end-member subducting slab age (20 and 50 Ma), convergence velocity (2 and 7 cm/yr), and initial upper plate crustal thickness (30 and 50 km). We also couple the geodynamic model with a surface-process model to simulate end-member asymmetric erosion (10 times higher) focused on the foreland, focused on the forearc, or minimal erosion, to assess the effects of climate gradients. The parameter space is motivated by the Andes, where along-strike variations in orographic gradients, oceanic plate age, convergence velocity, and upper plate thickness result in an important transition toward a smaller and thinner orogen in the south (Patagonian Andes) compared with the Central Andes. Among our results, we show that oceanic plate age plays a major role in the amount of upper plate lithosphere removed by subduction erosion, with the older oceanic plate (50 Ma) transporting more upper plate material into the asthenosphere. Initial upper plate crustal thickness strongly controls upper plate deformation, where the thinner crust (initially 30 km thick) results in greater lithospheric bulk strain, with folding and tilting of the lithosphere. The initially thick crust, instead, results in a much more stable continent with only minor deformation. The effects of convergence velocity are more important with an initially thin crust, where faster convergence rates (7 cm/yr) result in greater deformation and subduction erosion. Effects of asymmetric erosion are only visible when enough topography is generated by deformation, as erosion is scaled to be a function of the topographic slope and drainage area, and thus, in several models it is negligible. A few models show that forearc-focused erosion helps prevent subduction erosion to some extent, whereas foreland-focused erosion can generate tilting and strain concentration in the foreland region. We thus highlight the importance of subducting plate age on subduction erosion, which has been largely overlooked in previous studies, and reinforce that lithosphere with thinner crusts are more prone to deformation, whereas asymmetric erosion exerts only a secondary influence under the explored conditions.

title: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition as Seen from the Eastern Equatorial Pacific: A 1.2 million year chronology and bottom water oxygen reconstruction
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Dorchinecz, Annaliese [1], Bown, Zoë [2], Jacobel, Allison [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Climate Science, Middlebury College, Middlebury, Vermont, USA
(2) Earth and Climate Science, Middlebury College, Middlebury, Vermont, USA
(3) Earth and Climate Science, Middlebury College, Middlebury, Vermont, USA; Institute for Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Mid-Pleistocene Transition (~1.25-0.75 Ma) marked a change in Earth’s climate system as glacial-interglacial cycles shifted from periods of 41 kyr to 100 kyr and glacial periods became more intense. While the mechanisms driving the transition are not well understood, leading hypotheses include changes to deep ocean carbon storage 1 . Reconstructing ocean change across this period is important for mechanistic representations of climate system processes and future climate modeling.

Working with a new splice from ODP Site 846 in the eastern equatorial Pacific, we analyze benthic foraminifera stable isotope ratios to better understand the carbon cycle dynamics before, across the MPT, and over the eight subsequent glacial-interglacial cycles. We constrain the age model for our splice using new δ 18 O from Cibicidoides wuellerstorfi and a Bayesian approach 2 that provides statistically defined uncertainties. We use the new age model to present the time-variant Δδ 13 C between C. wuellerstorfi and Globobulimina spp. This Δδ 13 C gradient has been previously calibrated to deep water oxygen 3 , allowing us to derive the first quantitative estimates of bottom water oxygen for the deep Pacific over this interval. In turn, we use our bottom water oxygen estimate to quantify changes in the dissolved inorganic carbon content of deep waters across the MPT. We pair this data with percent coarse fraction, a proxy for carbonate dissolution, to gain further insights into patterns of ocean carbon storage and their changes over the last 1.25 Ma.

abstract: The Chicxulub Impact occurred 66 million years ago on the Yucatán Peninsula (the K-Pg boundary). Its global effects included earthquakes, tsunamis, wildfires, ejecta fallout (“spherules”) and a mass extinction. The impact melted and vaporized crustal material, ejecting it into the atmosphere. The vapor cooled and condensed into spheroidal droplets, falling to the surface. After burial, the spherules are typically diagenetically altered into Ca/Mg-rich 2:1 layer aluminosilicate clays such as smectite. Preservation of unaltered ejecta is rare although glass spherules have previously been recorded at a few sites such as Beloc, Haiti; Gorgonilla Island, Colombia; and Tanis, ND, USA. Impact spherules documented at Wahalak Creek, Mississippi, USA (~1,500 km from the crater), at the top of the Prairie Bluff Chalk (PBC), are similarly glassy and represent the first recorded occurrence of preserved impact glass on the U.S. Gulf Coastal Plain. X-Ray Diffraction analyses of several glassy spherules indicate that they have an amorphous, non-crystalline structure. SEM-EDS and Raman Spectroscopy analyses of 10+ other glassy spherules, as well as altered clay spherules from the overlying Clayton Formation, show the presence of Ca, Mg, and Al, typical of impact ejecta noted at other K-Pg sites. Soft-sediment deformation (as a result of impact-related earthquakes) injected spherule-rich material into the underlying clay-rich PBC. We hypothesize that the low permeability of the PBC inhibited alteration of the original impact ejecta, preserving the spherules in a glassy, amorphous state. These glassy spherules can provide previously unrecorded regional information on the composition of the Yucatán crust, the impactor, and the condensation processes within the Chicxulub vapor plume.

title: A Pilot Study of the Implementation of the Digital Tool Visible Geology with a First-year Geological Mapping Laboratory

authors: Pedley, Kate [1], Hoult, Henry [2], Kennedy, Ben [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand
(2) School of Earth and Environment, University of Geneva, Switzerland; School of Earth and Environment, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand
(3) School of Earth and Environment, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand
abstract:
Spatial skills are an invaluable tool for geoscientists as they provide the basis for visualizing, projecting, manipulating and interrogating subsurface structures. 3D visualisation of geological features is a challenging component of first geology education at university. Classroom-based laboratories typically use 2D Maps, cross sections and drawings, physical block models, field photos, and PowerPoint slides to teach geological mapping.

Visible Geology, an initiative by Seequent, The Bentley Subsurface Company, is a free, browser-based tool for creating and manipulating virtual geological structures in 3D. Users can shape the topography of block models, add geological units, impose structures (e.g., folds, faults, intrusions) and view a geological history. Here, we pilot the integration of five Visible Geology-based lesson plans into first year mapping laboratory sessions to quantitatively and qualitatively assess its efficacy at improving student spatial skills.

Qualitative pre-course survey data show the majority of students have (1) little previous experience with geology, (2) hike less than once every six months, (3) do not have formal training in spatial software, and (4) play computer games more than once a month. Quantitative, pre and post-laboratory spatial skills tests show a small overall increase in student spatial skills. Post-laboratory survey responses frequently mentioned Visible Geology as useful, easy to use and explore, and it consistently ranked highly among preferred learning tools. We conclude that this type of visualization tool is a useful addition to the geoscience teacher’s toolbox. In addition, we encourage other instructors to utilise the free resources and explore more research into how the tool can be used to add value to the geoscience curriculum.

title: PLUME CHANNELIZATION AT THE YELLOWSTONE AND AFAR CONTINENTAL HOTSPOTS
session_title: Continental magmatic-volcanic flare-ups: multidisciplinary investigations on their causes and consequences
authors: Camp, Victor E. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, San Diego State University, San Diego, CA, USA
abstract:
Continental hotspots are typically defined by magmatic flare-ups of mafic to bimodal volcanism fed from crustal reservoirs at or near the site of mantle-plume impingement. Estimates on the crustal ratio of intrusive-to-extrusive volume typically range from ~5:1 to 1:1, or higher if one includes the presumed volume of crustal underplating thought to be associated with continental flood-basalts. These large igneous provinces (LIPs) are characterized by sustained high effusion rates over a short-lived main eruptive phase of 1–2 m.y. Geologic data demonstrate that LIPs, together with more dispersed basalt provinces, can erupt hundreds of kilometers away from the active plume center. This characteristic is typically attributed to flattening and equidimensional spreading of the plume source (i.e., pancake flow), and/or to forceful dike injection and the rapid lateral flow of magma in crustal dikes or interconnected dike-sill systems. However, channelized plume flow (i.e., viscous fingering) may also play a significant role in the lateral propagation of magmatism during plume emplacement. Such a process occurs at the base of heterogeneous continental lithosphere, where variably thinned zones and weakened structures, together with compositional, density and rheological instabilities are subject to thermomechanical erosion and the creation of preferential conduits of mantle-plume flow.

Plume channelization beneath ancient hotspots may be difficult to reconstruct, largely because the dynamic processes are no longer extant and therefore unresolvable by seismic tomography. In contrast, channelized plume flow is evident in the seismic tomography of the Yellowstone and Afar mantle plumes, the two most active continental hotpots on earth. The intent of this talk is to show how the tomographic record can be combined with interdisciplinary geologic and petrologic data consistent with channelized plume flow playing a significant role in the evolution of diverse volcanic fields linked to the active Yellowstone and Afar hotspots. This contemporary record of channelized plume flow may provide a template for past events associated with LIP formation and continental break up where tomographic data is obscured or incomplete.

abstract: Two of the most common Quaternary geochronometers, cosmogenic nuclides and radiocarbon, provide absolute dates that are pivotal for constraining numerous Earth surface processes from the recent geologic past, including glaciations, climate change, erosion, and sedimentation. Accurately capturing the nature and timing of these processes is critical for understanding how they will impact present and future society under expected climate change scenarios. We report on recent efforts through the Informal Cosmogenic-nuclide Exposure-age Database (ICE-D) and Radiocarbon Cyberinfrastructure (RAD-CI) Projects to centralize cosmogenic nuclide and radiocarbon measurements into accessible and transparent cyberinfrastructures that give users access to data for more efficient data discovery, analyses and visualizations, as well as control over how their data is maintained. We report on a few case studies currently in publication as well as future endeavors from team members with the aim to invite other community members to utilize these infrastructures for their own research.

title: Hazard cascades, mega logjams, and geomorphic response in mountain rivers
session_title: Understanding and Facilitating River Corridor Resilience to Wildfire
authors: Marshall, Anna [1], Johnson, Bradley G. [2], Tennent, Emma Rae [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,
(2) Davidson College, Davidson, NC,
(3) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,
abstract:
Hazard cascades, such as extreme rainfall-triggered landslides or wildfire-amplified debris flows, are increasingly recognized as major drivers of geomorphic change in mountain landscapes. Hurricane Helene illustrates this in the Southern Appalachians, where extreme precipitation in September 2024 triggered a compounding response of flooding, landslides and debris flows, bank erosion, floodplain deposition, and generational recruitment of large wood to channels. In several catchments, flooding and mass movements delivered pulses of wood that resulted in "mega logjams"—dense, 2-3 m tall, valley-spanning wood accumulations. These mega logjams fundamentally altered sediment routing, hydraulics, and downstream response during and after flooding. These features sit at a critical but poorly constrained link in the hazard cascade connecting hillslopes to rivers: mega logjams may buffer hazard cascades by trapping sediment, additional wood, and flood energy, or become future hazards as wood decays or is remobilized during subsequent floods. These gaps in knowledge reflect both the transient nature of wood deposits and the rarity of both timely post-event data collection and long-term monitoring. This is especially pronounced in Appalachia, where a legacy of deforestation and channel wood removal has constrained observations and theory of wood-mediated disturbance dynamics.

Using pre- and post-event LiDAR, aerial imagery, and field surveys across six sites in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, we document mega logjam morphology, spatial distribution, structural controls, and geomorphic impacts. Mega logjams formed in both wide, multi-thread reaches pinned by islands and in narrow valley pinch points. Preliminary results indicate these logjams initially act as major sediment and flood attenuators, dampening downstream geomorphic change. As we consider riverscapes in transition, understanding whether mega logjams function primarily as transient buffers, long-term sediment storage, or evolving hazards is critical for predicting the trajectory of hazard cascades and the resilience of forested mountain river corridors. Although motivated by Hurricane Helene, this research is broadly applicable to other disturbance-driven systems, including wildfire-affected watersheds where large pulses of wood may similarly reorganize river corridors.
