abstract: Natural disasters, especially flooding events, are increasingly common in Kentucky and place humans and infrastructure in harm’s way. One of the primary goals of CLIMBS (Climate Resilience through Multidisciplinary Big Data Learning, Prediction, and Building Response Systems) Project 2: Paleoperspectives is to build a record of paleoprecipitation regime end-members that can be applied to engineer infrastructure and human resiliency to flooding events. As a test of results from studies examining floodplain sediments, paleoprecipitation records from ponded environments must also be examined. Stump (also called Burchett) Pond in Clinton County, Kentucky occurs within a general region of marshes and wetlands developed on the St. Louis Limestone northwest of Albany, KY between present-day Lake Cumberland and Dale Hollow Lake. The pond falls into the eastern highland rim ecoregion and is surrounded by oak-hickory forests. Short cores held by the Kentucky Geological Survey were sub-sampled for palynology; sub-samples were processed using low-acid methods to ensure recovery not only of chemically resistant pollen, but also non-pollen palynomorphs, including fungi and arthropod remains. Past rainfall regimes were reconstructed using pollen presence/absence data in the CREST for R package. Ecological groupings present were reconstructed using cluster analysis in PAST. A diverse and abundant palynoflora was recovered. Arthropod and fungal remains are common, and charcoal is very sparse. The overall flora is consistent with deposition in ponded and wetland environments, while the pollen assemblage, specifically, provides insight into changes in rainfall seasonality.

abstract: Chondrites are a class of primitive, undifferentiated stony meteorites that best represent the early solar system and the formation of the Earth. Each are matrix that surrounds chondrules, spherical particles dominated by quenched silicate melt, olivine, pyroxene, and Fe-Ni Metal with varying degrees of internal metamorphism. The Kimbell School of Geosciences houses a small collection of chondrites, including one sectioned fragment of NWA 869 provided by the Monnig Meteorite Gallery at TCU. NWA 869 is an ordinary, low-iron chondrite that has undergone a degree of internal metamorphism, classified as type L3-6. It is represented by thousands of individual stones retrieved from an undisclosed location and sold in the markets of Morocco and elsewhere. We recently acquired an unclassified NWA specimen (UNK) that seemed comparable to our certified 869 meteorite. UNK was a 48 g deformed oblate spheroid (resembling a chicken nugget) specimen, with a long axis of 5.8 cm and a diameter of 2.7 cm. The specimen lacked a fusion crust, exhibiting a smooth brown, mottled exterior. We evaluated the in-tact piece through optical and electron microscopy, then carefully sectioned a 5.837 g, 3.5 mm slab to resolve the interior. Both the UNK section and the certified 869 were evaluated through optical and electron microscopy and in-situ semi-quantitative XRF for direct comparison. Acquired data were compared against published values in literature. We found UNK to be sufficiently similar to 869 both physically and chemically. Both are of comparable interior color and alike in their distribution and shape of chondrules and of iron and iron sulfide grains. Both are largely matrix made of clasts dominated by pyroxene with small amounts of glass. Irregular-shaped iron sulfide is typically found abutting native iron. Both specimens contain a range of chondrule types, including barred olivine. XRF analysis of 17 elements are similar between both; primary components are silica: 42.6 wt.% for 869; 42.5 wt.% for UNK; magnesia: 24.2 for 869, 24.3 for UNK; total iron as Fe 2 O 3 : 22.3 wt.% for 869, 22.6 for UNK, lime: 2.05 wt.% for 869, 2.32 for UNK; and sulfur: 1.6 wt.% for 869, 1.32 for UNK. Although this confirms UNK is likely another 869, we plan on assessing olivine and pyroxene compositions through SEM-EDS as a final comparison technique.

title: Multi-fault earthquakes and subduction megathrusts: new insights from central Aotearoa-NZ

authors: Humphrey, Jade [1], Nicol, Andy [2], Howell, Andy [3], Penney, Camilla [4], Langridge, Rob [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand

abstract:
Recent large earthquakes (e.g., >M w 7) worldwide rupture multiple faults and/or form earthquake sequences spanning months to decades. This spatial and temporal complexity is challenging to forecast but must be accounted for in time-dependent seismic hazard models. Here, we examine historical earthquakes, paleoseismic records and synthetic earthquake catalogues to investigate earthquake clustering on key faults along the central Aotearoa-New Zealand plate boundary. At the latitude of study, the plate boundary is dominated by subduction and strike-slip faulting in the overriding plate with slip rates of up to ~15 mm/yr.

Historical records in Aotearoa-New Zealand (post 1840 CE) show that almost all earthquakes >M w 7 involve multi-fault rupture. Although these events provide valuable analogues for future earthquakes, their long-term frequency is poorly understood. Comparison of ~5,000 year paleoseismic records of upper-plate faults and the Hikurangi Subduction interface indicates that many paleoearthquakes occurred in similar 100 to 200 year time intervals. However, uncertainties in the radiocarbon dating make it difficult to distinguish whether this clustering is a result of multi-fault ruptures and/or sequences of earthquakes closely spaced in time (e.g., <200 years). To examine the frequency, complexity and magnitudes of multi-fault earthquakes in central Aotearoa New Zealand we supplement geological records with synthetic earthquakes from a physics-based RSQSim model, which generates an event catalogue over 100 kyr. Co-rupture of the upper-plate strike-slip faults with the subduction interface is common in the historical and synthetic datasets, and consistent with the observations from the paleoseismic record. At magnitudes > M w 7 multi-fault earthquakes that involve the plate interface and at least one upper plate fault account for ~54% of synthetic events and suggests that these events may be more frequent than previously recognised. The precise impact of these large and geometrically complex earthquakes requires further exploration, particularly in consideration to cascading hazards and post-event recovery.

title: Analyzing Mineral Inclusions in Diamonds from Gahcho Kue, Canada to Uncover the Composition of the Mantle from Southeastern Slave Craton

authors: Ramirez, Reyli [1], Kiseeva, Ekaterina S. [2], Korolev, Nester [3], Seymour, Nikki [4]

(2) American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA

abstract: The Archean (4.02 – 2.5 Ga) Slave craton of the Northwest Territories in Canada consists of some of the oldest crustal rock and has been stable for around 2.6 Ga. The craton preserves multiple isotopic and petrologic mantle domains, which can provide insights into the processes responsible for the growth and stabilization of early continental crust. Petrology of mantle xenoliths by Kopylova & Caro (2004) from the economic Gahcho Kué (GK) mining district, located in the southeastern corner of the Slave craton, suggests multiple mantle lithologies are present, including altered eclogite, coarse garnet or spinel peridotite, and deformed garnet peridotite. However, hydrothermal fluids associated with the kimberlite pipes caused late-stage recrystallization of the primary minerals in the xenoliths. Diamonds, which form at high-pressure, low-temperature conditions typical of mantle domains, sometimes trap mineral inclusions during their growth, preserving the primary signature of the host rock. Here we present preliminary results from a detailed catalog of diamond-hosted mineral inclusions to identify the mantle composition and P-T conditions of diamond formation below the Gahcho Kué mine. 215 diamonds were characterized using optical stereomicroscopy. Diamond resorption and surface features posed challenges for optical methods, as surface resorption affected the ability to view inclusions within the GK samples. The degree of resorption for each diamond was recorded using a 1-6 scale defined by McCallum et al. (1991). Potential mineral inclusions were identified in 79/215 diamonds by a combination of optical petrographic methods and X-ray MicroCT scanning. The identification of mineral species in 30 inclusion-bearing diamonds was determined using Raman spectroscopy. 24 diamonds each hosted a single inclusion: 1 clinopyroxene, 1 orthopyroxene, 12 olivine, 3 coesite, 2 sulfide, and 5 as-yet unidentified minerals. The remaining 6 diamonds hosted multiple inclusions: one with garnet and clinopyroxene, two with multiple clinopyroxene, one with 3 garnets, and two with multiple olivine. The total number of individual mineral inclusions was 39. These findings suggest that GK diamonds sample primarily peridotitic lithosphere with a smaller contribution from an eclogitic mantle. Ongoing work includes EPMA analyses to determine the major element chemistry and LA-ICP-MS to reveal trace element signatures of the inclusions. These together will be used to constrain the P-T conditions of the southeastern Slave Craton during diamond formation.

title: Incorporating Research Experiences into an Introductory Geology Lab: A Mini-CURE Pilot Study

affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, American Museum Natural History, Dept Earth & Planetary Sciences, New York, NY, ; Department of Earth and Environmental Science, Columbia University, New York, New York, USA

abstract:
Providing students with actual research experience via a course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) early in their educational career has the potential to offer a large impact on their college trajectory. Previous work incorporating research experiences into the classroom setting has focused on upper division courses where enrolled students have already decided their major. Instead, this project incorporated a mini-CURE into an introductory geology lab course taught at Queensborough Community College (QCC), a 2 year community college in New York City with a diverse student population. The mini-CURE spanned the second half of the semester and was made up of 3 parts: (1) developing descriptions of a set of rocks sourced from a local water tunnel, (2) plotting and interpreting geochemistry data from the water tunnel rocks using Google Colab, and (3) presenting results in small groups.

To assess the effects of research experiences on student science interest and identity the Persistence Research In Science & Engineering (PRiSE) survey [1] was adapted so that items were geoscience focused. Surveys were administered to students before and after CURE-implementation. Additionally, open-ended questions and student interviews provided deeper insights into the student experience. Although the small sample size (n=20) of this project limited the statistical power of our results, the item assessing student science interest increased between surveys with a p-value that was marginally significant (p=0.053). However, changes in all other items were far less significant and some items displayed decreases in interest and identity measures. Student responses to open-ended questions reflect positive attitudes towards the mini-CURE and a strong preference for the mini-CURE labs compared to more traditional labs. These findings suggest that mini-CUREs may be a useful intervention for introductory courses, though further studies are needed to confirm effects on science interest and identity constructs.

abstract:
The Silurian Ireviken Biogeochemical Event (IBE) is comprised of one of the largest perturbations of the global carbon cycle during the Phanerozoic and a major extinction event that impacted conodonts, graptolites, ostracodes, and corals. The IBE spans the Llandovery-Wenlock boundary and serves as a stratigraphic marker for the base of the Wenlock. The base Wenlock Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) is being re-studied and the Subcommission on Silurian Stratigraphy is looking for a new location to place the GSSP golden spike. The Lusklint-1 section on Gotland is a candidate location for the new GSSP to be placed, and as a result, new data need to be generated from this section.

In 2024, a new core was drilled approximately 1km SE of the Lusklint-1 outcrop that will serve as a “behind the outcrop core” for the Lusklint-1 section. This new core, the Lusklint-1 core, will serve as an archival version of the Lusklint-1 outcrop, which is a sea cliff that must be trenched in order to be studied effectively. The IBE has been identified in the Lusklint-1 core and the stratigraphically significant K-bentonites preserved in the Lower Visby Formation at the Lusklint-1 outcrop have all been identified in the new core as well. Here, we present major- and trace-element geochemistry from the Lusklint-1 core to develop additional chemostratigraphic tools to evaluate the IBE as well as to aid in global chronostratigraphic correlation of the base of the Wenlock Series.

abstract:
The Wichita Igneous Province (WIP) marks the Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen, an Ediacaran-Cambrian rift presently trending WNW from the Laurentian-Iapetus margin. Magmatism produced an extensive mafic layered complex (GMLC) punctured by biotite-gabbro plutons of Roosevelt Gabbro (RG). This is overlain by widespread lava flows of Carlton Rhyolite Group (CRG), the base of which served to trap Wichita Granite Group (WGG) sheet plutons. We present additional high-precision CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon geochronological constraints for several of the main igneous units in the WIP, extending the range of recorded magmatism, refining age relationships, and providing the first high-resolution geochronological data for the westernmost exposed WIP.

Significant felsic magmatism predates mafic activity. Prior dating established the 539 Ma eruption of the eastern CR exposed in the Arbuckle Mountains. Eruptions continued nearly 6 million years later and 100 km inboard, as marked by the exposures of the voluminous Fort Sill rhyolite (CR) flow (533.26 ± 0.22 Ma) and hypabyssal intrusives (533.29 ± 0.19 Ma), predating the 532.5 Ma GMLC. Adjacent to the Fort Sill CR, the newly mapped Craterville pluton (the eastern portion of the Quanah Granite) intruded at 532.33 ± 0.17 Ma, roughly contemporaneous with the GMLC.

Prior dating indicates that intrusion of the Mount Sheridan gabbro (RG) followed at 532 Ma, as did a sequence of CR flows at Bally Mountain to its north, from 531.0 - 530.7 Ma. The bulk of WGG commences in the eastern Wichita Mountains at 530.6-530.2 Ma. As it concludes, plutonism is recorded in the northwestern-most WIP exposures. Here, two distinct units within the WGG emplacement are collectively mapped as Headquarters Granite: the Walsh Mountain pluton (529.95 ± 0.21 Ma), and the Brown Mountain pluton (529.56 ± 0.15 Ma). These are intruded by the WGG Reformatory Granite (529.10 ± 0.17 Ma), which in turn is cut by the widely distributed Lugert Granite (527.72 ± 0.23 Ma). This indicates that the WIP exposures preserve a 12-million-year history of intense, inboard-younging bimodal magmatism, punctuated by ~9 million years of rhyolite eruptive activity and a ~4.5-million-year period of sheet pluton emplacement.

title: Crustal Hydration Metamorphism during Laramide Flat-Slab Subduction

affiliations: (1) School of Earth & Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ 86011, AZ, USA

abstract: Fluids expelled from subducting oceanic slabs by metamorphic devolatilization are proposed to flux melting in the mantle wedge leading to arc magmatism and to hydrate the superjacent mantle. Flat-slab subduction involves shallow-angle truncation of the continental crust, creating the potential for upward migrating fluids to directly infiltrate and hydrate the continental crust. The Little Maria Mountains in southeastern California represent an exposure of mid-crustal rocks that were situated above the Laramide flat-slab subduction interface. We analyzed titanite in a sample of metamorphosed Jurassic granite from the southeastern Little Maria Mountains using a laser-ablation split-stream system to determine U-Pb ages and trace element abundances. The data displays arrays with lower intercepts of 166.5 ± 1.1 Ma and 70.3 ± 1.3 Ma, consistent with ages obtained locally from titanite and monazite in metamorphosed Paleozoic strata. Ce mapping revealed two domains: the Jurassic age spots (33) are located within a high-Ce domain, and the Late Cretaceous age spots (8) are located within a low-Ce domain. Spots analyzed within the Jurassic domain yielded REE patterns with low scatter and negative Eu anomalies and represent primary igneous compositions, whereas spots analyzed within the Late Cretaceous domain yielded REE, Th, Y and Zr abundances 0.5 to 1.5 orders of magnitude lower and Cr and Ba higher, with high scatter and both positive and negative Eu anomalies. Ce maps revealed the presence of small (5-20 μm) allanite epitaxial rims on epidote hosted entirely within the recrystallized Late Cretaceous domain, suggesting they formed during the Late Cretaceous recrystallization. Nucleation of allanite resulted from a hydration net transfer reaction and was stabilized by the release of REE. Metamorphism also involved albitization via breakdown of the plagioclase anorthite component and hydration to crystallize epidote. The conditions of metamorphism were determined from a nearby sample of garnet-bearing pelitic schist. Mineral compositions were analyzed by electron microprobe and used in conjunction with point counts to calculate a bulk composition and isochemical plot. Garnet displays simple growth zoning. Compositional isopleths for garnet core and rim yielded a path of 515°C at 4.0 kbar (core) to 550°C at 5.0 kb (rim) corresponding to depths of ~14-18 km. The hydration metamorphism is dated at ~70 Ma (titanite recrystallization age), coeval with Laramide flat-slab subduction.

abstract:
An expanded and continuous Cretaceous/Paleogene (K/Pg) boundary section containing an iridium anomaly is well exposed on Seymour Island, Antarctica (65°S paleolatitude). Macrofossils, foraminifera, and other microfossils were previously collected at 10 to 20-meter intervals through a measured ~1200 m composite section across the island, but each section was characterized by large gaps in calcareous microfossil recovery. We aim to increase stratigraphic resolution of calcareous microfossils across the upper Maastrichtian and lower Danian interval on Seymour Island.

To improve stratigraphic resolution, both 4-5 m-long drill cores and surface samples were collected in 2026 by the NSF-funded CSI: Antarctica expedition with shipboard support of the R/V Sikuliaq . The drill sites are located on the southeast side of the island and recovered a total of 16 m of core, spanning the uppermost Maastrichtian through basal Danian. Surficial samples were obtained across approximately 215 m of tilted and exposed stratigraphy, spanning the K/Pg boundary, with a target resolution of 0.5 m, though some intervals were not sampled due to unsafe conditions. Sampling locations and approach were chosen to minimize diagenetic effects from surficial freeze-thaw weathering that affected previous studies.

Smear slides were made to investigate calcareous nannofossil assemblages from cores (~10-cm resolution) and from all surficial samples. Smear slides examined from surficial samples are barren. By contrast, ~37% of the core samples analyzed contain calcareous nannofossils, though only in Cretaceous-age strata. We attribute the absence of calcareous nannofossils in surficial samples to rapid, modern oxidation of sulfides, producing acids that led to dissolution. Maastrichtian-age calcareous nannofossils recorded include Braarudosphaera bigelowii, Cribrosphaerella daniae, Nephrolithus frequens, N. corystus, and Prediscosphaera stoveri . Surficial cliff samples yield sparse assemblages of planktic, calcareous benthic, and agglutinated foraminiferal genera. Preliminarily, we observed planktic foraminifera including Planoheterohelix globulosa, Pl. planata, and Planohedbergella aspera , and benthic taxa including multiple nodosariids, gavelinellids, cibicidids, praebuliminids, and various agglutinated taxa. Many samples are barren of foraminifera despite minimal exposure to surface weathering. Foraminiferal and calcareous nannofossil analyses are ongoing, and we anticipate this work will yield additional microfossils that will allow detailed paleoenvironmental reconstructions across the Deccan eruption and K/Pg event intervals.

title: Insights into Arc-Related Magmatism During Petrogenesis of the Eocene Absaroka Supergroup, WY
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Aguirre, Danielly [1], McLeod, Claire Louise [2], Shaulis, Barry [3], Loocke, Matthew Phillip [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA

abstract:
Investigating the evolution of the lithosphere during arc-related magmatism contributes to our understanding of the Earth’s tectonomagmatic history. The Eocene-aged Absaroka Volcanic Supergroup (AVS, 53-43 Ma) located in NW Wyoming and southern Montana records a relatively recent cycle of tectonomagmatic activity associated with rejuvenated magmatism due to slab roll back, and subsequent extensional collapse. In the central region of the AVS, in eastern Yellowstone National Park, volcaniclastics and andesitic lava flows of the Trout Peak Trachyandesite are cross-cut by the intermediate intrusives of the Two Ocean and Langford Formation. In this study, the textural, mineralogical, and geochemical characteristics of these intrusives, along with their entrained xenolith populations, are investigated within the context of the AVS and evolution of the North American continental margin at the time.

Sample collection was completed during the summer of 2022 in eastern Yellowstone National Park. From the study of thin sections via PLM and SEM (including BSE imaging and EDS mapping), host intrusives are porphyritic, characterized by ~40–50% euhedral to subhedral plagioclase with visible oscillatory zoning, and ~10–20% euhedral to subhedral amphibole in a microcrystalline, feldspathic groundmass with minor magnetite and ilmenite. Entrained xenoliths are holocrystalline, characterized by ~40–80% subhedral to anhedral amphibole, ~10–30% subhedral to anhedral feldspar, and quartz, with minor apatite, biotite, ilmenite, and magnetite. From bulk powder XRD on the intrusives, major minerals are confirmed as amphibole (hornblende), plagioclase (andesine to labradorite), and quartz, with minor magnetite. Host intrusives are dioritic in composition (wt. % SiO 2 from 62.14 to 62.84 at wt. % Na 2 O + K 2 O from 6.49 to 6.56), and calc-alkaline based on the MgO-FeO-Na 2 O+ K 2 O ternary systematics. Bulk rock primitive mantle-normalized spidergrams exhibit a subduction-related signature as evidenced by LILE enrichment and Nb-Ta depletion, with chondrite-normalized profiles exhibiting LREE enrichment (La N /Lu N : 34.74–39.10).

Future work will focus on in-situ analysis of the amphibole populations throughout the sampled suite. Quantification of major and minor element compositions via EPMA will 1) determine amphibole type and 2) be applied to geothermobarometers to evaluate P-T-H 2 O conditions during this stage of AVS magmatism. This dataset will be coupled with in-situ minor and trace element analysis via LA-ICP-MS to further investigate amphibole populations, their petrogenesis, and lithospheric evolution during the Eocene.

title: The Role of Anatexis in the Formation of IOA Deposits and Related Metasomatism at Granulite Facies Metamorphism
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Posters)
authors: Weitzel, Michael A [1], Lamadrid, Hector M. [2], Guevara, Victor E. [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA

abstract: Iron Oxide-Apatite (IOA) deposits are an important source of Fe and, in some cases, of REEs. IOA deposits are formed in different geologic/tectonic settings and ages, ranging from the Paleoproterozoic to the Pliocene and at different depths of the continental crust. Recent studies have found the ubiquitous presence of carbonate, sulfate, and calc-silicate polycrystalline inclusions in fluid inclusion assemblages. These polycrystalline inclusions represent recrystallized molten salt inclusions that evidence the interaction between silicate magmas and sedimentary sequences. In the Adirondack Highlands of New York (USA) and the New Jersey Highlands (among other places), workers have found Iron Oxide-Apatite (IOA) deposits hosted in felsic to intermediate igneous rocks that are geographically and temporally associated with granulite facies metamorphism deeper in the system. Coincidentally, similar polycrystalline carbonate-silicate-rich inclusions have been described accompanying fluid inclusions in granulites and other lower-crust rocks. These inclusions have been interpreted as daughter and step-daughter minerals; however, in some cases workers have noted similarities with melt inclusions, suggesting they represent true carbonate-silicate-rich melts, not unlike what has been described in IOA systems. Moreover, granulite facies rocks are chemically depleted of trace elements like LILE, HFSE, REEs, and U and Th, elements that, in contrast, are enriched in IOA mineralizations. Carbonate-rich melts, either formed from the melting of metasediments (anatexis of evaporites and carbonates) or true mantle carbonatites, are highly mobile fluids, with very low dihedral angles (<30), and are excellent solvents, providing a mechanism for both transport and dissolution that could explain the depletion of some of these trace elements and the enrichment at higher levels of the crust. In this study, we will test the potential connection between these fluids and melts in these two systems by characterizing the mineralogy of the inclusions and the chemical and isotopic compositions of the fluids and melts hosted in the IOA deposits from the New Jersey and Adirondack Highlands, as well as the polycrystalline inclusions hosted in the neighboring high-grade metamorphic rocks.

title: From Magma Reservoir to Mesosphere: An Overview of the Evolution of the 15 January 2022 Hunga Eruption
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics
authors: Ukstins, Ingrid [1]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,
abstract:
The 15 January 2022 eruption of Hunga Volcano, Tonga, was the most explosive eruption of the twenty-first century and evacuated ca 6.5 km³ dense-rock equivalent during an ~11 h caldera-forming episode. Data from glass, bulk rock, phenocryst, melt-inclusion, ash morphology, and leachate data connect magma reservoir evolution with fragmentation and plume chemistry. Surtseyan activity from late December 2021 through 14 January 2022 tapped a shallow, relatively evolved andesitic magma (A2) similar to magma erupted in 2009 and 2014-2015. A sharp increase in eruption rate on 13 to 14 January coincided with the first appearance of a slightly more primitive, volatile-rich magma (A1), vent subsidence below sea level, and deeper decompression. Melt inclusions and phenocryst cores sample distinct magma batches, while micron-scale mingling records syn-eruptive interaction of a compositionally narrow andesitic suite. Primitive olivine, clinopyroxene, and calcic plagioclase cores, with normally zoned plagioclase and pyroxene rims, indicate rapid decompression, dehydration, and vesiculation rather than new, deep mafic recharge.

Juvenile ash ranges from dense blocky glass to variably vesicular dark and light pumice and is fine-grained and poorly sorted, recording rapid fragmentation and chilling during efficient magma-seawater interaction. Caldera-fault reactivation and seawater penetration into the depressurizing reservoir promoted runaway phreatomagmatism, amplifying eruption rate and driving a plume to ~58 km. Pristine ash is coated by NaCl and CaSO₄; sulfur- and chlorine-isotope systematics indicate that most ash-leachate sulfate and the plume’s Cl and Br were seawater-derived. Salt-enhanced aggregation promoted ash removal, whereas much of the magmatic sulfur entered the ocean in submarine density currents, explaining the anomalously low atmospheric SO₂ burden.

Hunga demonstrates that extremely explosive shallow-submarine eruptions can arise from feedbacks among resident magma withdrawal, reservoir decompression, structural failure, and seawater ingress. These coupled processes need to be integrated when assessing eruption triggers, ash dispersal, and atmospheric impacts of submarine calderas.

title: Comparative Analysis of Geological Settings, Safety-Relevant Structures, and Investigation Methods in Radioactive Waste Disposal Programs
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Na, Yeseong [1]
affiliations: (1) Princeton High School, Princeton High School, Princeton, NJ, USA
abstract:
Radioactive waste disposal programs must evaluate geological conditions over time scales that extend far beyond historical earthquake records. The purpose of this study is to compare how geological setting influences which faults, fractures, deformation zones, and how groundwater-conducting features are treated as safety-relevant and which investigation methods are used to characterize them. Four national cases were examined: the operating Wolseong Low and Intermediate Level Radioactive Waste Disposal Center in Gyeongju, South Korea; the proposed Yucca Mountain high-level waste repository in the Basin and Range Province of the United States; the Onkalo spent-fuel repository program in Finland; and the Forsmark spent-fuel repository program in Sweden. These cases represent contrasting intraplate, extensional, and crystalline-shield settings and differ in waste type, repository concept, and development stage. Information was organized using a three-part framework consisting of geological setting, safety-relevant structures, and investigation methods. The study shows that all four programs combine structural, seismic, subsurface, and hydrogeological investigations, but their relative emphasis differs. Wolseong facility emphasizes regional fault characterization and seismic-hazard assessment, while Yucca Mountain combines regional fault, paleoseismic, and probabilistic seismic investigations. In contrast, Onkalo and Forsmark place particularly strong emphasis on site-scale fracture networks, deformation zones, underground rock characterization, and hydrogeological analysis in crystalline bedrock. These results explain that differences among the programs reflect geological setting and repository context rather than a simple division between active and inactive regions. The South Korean comparison also indicates that future high-level waste site selection will require broader structural, paleoseismic, and deep-hydrogeological characterization than the investigation framework associated with the operating Wolseong LILW facility. Potential mechanical and hydrogeological consequences of the identified structures will be considered as a future extension of this comparative study.

title: Resolving Declining Seasonality in Alaska Rivers: Organized Hydrograph Deconcentration or Increasing Event Dominance?

authors: Jenckes, Jordan [1], Russo, Aeon [2], Muñoz, Sebastian [3], Munk, Jens [4], Munk, Lee Ann [5]
affiliations: (1) Computer Science and Engineering, University of Alaska Anchorage, Anchorage, AK, USA

abstract: Recent work across Alaska and northern Canada indicates contemporary river discharge is less dominated by seasonal variability than historical records suggest. This transition is often termed stochastic or the increasing influence of irregular runoff events. However, seasonal dominance can also weaken when runoff is redistributed across a longer, organized portion of the year. As precipitation regimes change and the cryosphere diminishes, runoff timing increasingly reflects overlapping contributions from snowmelt, glacier melt, rainfall, and groundwater. We evaluated hydrograph deconcentration, defined here as declining seasonal concentration accompanied by expansion of the flow season with or without a shift in its seasonal center, using daily discharge records from 31 U.S. Geological Survey stream gages distributed across Southeast, Southcentral, Interior, Western, and Arctic Alaska. For each water year, we quantified the shortest continuous interval conveying 80% of annual discharge, the seasonal concentration and center of discharge, and short-period variability. Of the 30 stations with sufficient temporal coverage, 19 exhibited significant elongation of the interval conveying 80% of annual discharge, and 21 showed declining seasonal concentration, indicating flow became more evenly distributed through the year. No station exhibited significant contraction of the principal flow season. Seasonal centers shifted at some stations, but timing changes were less consistent than changes in duration and concentration. Short-period discharge variability did not increase systematically, suggesting that weakening seasonality cannot be attributed solely to increasingly irregular flow. Together, these results reveal a widespread reorganization of Alaska river hydrographs: annual discharge is being distributed across longer intervals without a corresponding statewide increase in day-to-day variability. The pattern is consistent with earlier snowmelt, extended glacier melt, more frequent warm-season rainfall, and enhanced cold-season groundwater contributions acting in different combinations across regions. Hydrograph deconcentration therefore provides a complementary interpretation of increasing flow irregularity. It distinguishes loss of seasonal concentration from loss of temporal organization and offers a measurable basis for comparing how snow-dominated, glacier-influenced, rainfall-dominated, and permafrost-affected rivers respond to changing water sources. This distinction is important for reliably predicting regional changes in floods, low flows, aquatic habitat, and seasonal transport of sediment and solutes across high-latitude watersheds.

authors: Su, Lewei [1], Chen, Zhong-Qiang [2], Huang, Yuangeng [3], Roopnarine, Peter D. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Invertebrate Zoology and Geology, California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA, USA; State Key Laboratory of Geomicrobiology & Environmental Changes, China University of Geosciences (Wuhan), Wuhan, China

abstract: The latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG) is one of the most pervasive macroecological patterns of the biosphere, but its origins and drivers remain debated. The strength and direction of LDGs vary among modern marine invertebrate functional groups, raising the question of whether such groups also responded differently to environmental crises in deep time. Here, we used global marine fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database and Bayesian birth–death models to reconstruct genus-level diversity and diversification dynamics in equatorial and non-equatorial regions from the Late Permian to the Early Jurassic, comparing mobility groups across the end-Permian and end-Triassic mass extinctions. Our results show that marine LDGs shifted from a steep equatorial diversity peak in the Late Permian to a shallower gradient after the end-Permian extinction, recovered during the Middle Triassic, and inverted after the end-Triassic extinction. These trajectories differed among mobility groups. Swimming taxa exhibited a nearly flat LDG after the end-Permian extinction and a persistent inverse LDG after the end-Triassic event. Motile benthic taxa retained a strong equatorial diversity peak after the end-Permian crisis but also developed an inverse LDG after the end-Triassic extinction. Sessile taxa showed weakened gradients after both crises but did not develop a persistent inverse LDG. These results demonstrate that dispersal ability might modulate how marine invertebrates responded geographically to environmental disruptions, while their contrasting responses to the two crises suggest that the ecological and environmental controls on marine LDGs were not constant through time.

abstract: A global record of mountain glacier terminations during the last deglaciation (∼19–11 ka) dated by a large, uncurated data set of cosmogenic-nuclide exposure ages highlights a statistically significant asynchrony in termination ages between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. This interhemispheric offset in the timing of glacier terminations is consistent with previously correlated ice core records that show a systematic interhemispheric lag in the timing of abrupt climate events, with the Southern Hemisphere leading the Northern Hemisphere by ∼300–3,500 years. Our analysis (a) aggregates cosmogenic-nuclide exposure ages from a global data set of moraines to discern climatically driven peaks in moraine emplacement events, and (b) utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation based on a null hypothesis that moraine emplacement is interhemispherically synchronous to estimate the statistical significance of the observed offset. The observed lag of Northern Hemisphere emplacement events compared to the Southern Hemisphere is statistically significant and is consistent with the “bipolar seesaw” pattern observed in ice core records.

title: Bias in Basins: Investigating Preservational Megabias in a Simulated World
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Apgar, Alexandra Davis [1], Xing, Jiahua [2], Qiao, Huijie [3], Machado-Stredel, Fernando [4], Saupe, Erin [5], Peterson, A. Townsend [6], Soberón, Jorge Townsend [7], Moore, Jason Richard [8], Myers, Corinne [9]

abstract: Our interpretation of the terrestrial fossil record is obscured by several taphonomic megabiases, including that only terrestrial organisms that exist within a net-depositional sedimentary basin may potentially preserve for geologically long periods of time (hereafter, the basin-only megabias, or BOM). It is imperative, therefore, that we gain an understanding of how greatly this bias can impact our ability to accurately represent species traits, phylogenetic relationships, and ecosystem structures. To address this, we adapted an existing virtual world model simulating global conditions (including fluctuating precipitation and temperature patterns) across the past 120,000 years (Late Pleistocene to present) that was originally developed to delineate macroevolutionary patterns of organisms over time. Virtual species within this model were seeded into 7,774 km 2 grid cells randomly across the planet and were capable of extinction, speciation, and/or expansion of geographic range based on assigned values relating to dispersal ability and niche breadth. To understand the impact and extent of the BOM on phylogenetic relationships and species diversity within terrestrial settings, we added the real-world position of all sedimentary basins containing at least one fluvial megafan network active within the past 120,000 years post-hoc to simulation results, and pruned all lineages not within a basin (representing non-preservation). We then compared our biased diversities and phylogenies to their ‘real’ record. We further examined whether any relationship existed between these ‘preserved’ species and additional traits (e.g., niche breadth, dispersal ability, basin size). Finally, we reran our analyses with basin positions randomized, to investigate the influence of basin position and orientation. Preliminary results demonstrate that while the BOM results in overall record reduction regardless of virtual species’ traits, basin position, or basin size, additional potential paleoecological biases may exist – especially regarding species’ niche breadth and basin connectivity. If such biases are confirmed within the terrestrial fossil record, we could be required to alter our interpretations of prehistoric ecosystems across much of deep time.

abstract: Field observations and high-resolution topography data combined with 10 Be exposure dating on offset landforms indicate higher than expected fault slip rates and seismic hazard potential on the Santa Cruz Mountain section of the northern San Andreas Fault in the San Francisco Bay Area. Geomorphic mapping in Sanborn County Park near Saratoga reveals a progression of alluvial fans and debris flows dextrally offset from their upstream sources by 55 ± 10 m, 170 ± 20 m and 320 ± 20 m, respectively. Surface-exposure dating of large sandstone boulders in these deposits, which are derived from the Tertiary Vaqueros Formation, reveals three distinct depositional ages, ranging from 2.8 ± 1.3 ka, 7.7 ± 0.9 ka, and 12.3 ± 1.5 ka (2), respectively. Combining observed offsets with depositional ages indicates an average slip rate of 24.8 ± 3.0 mm/yr on this section of the San Andreas Fault, which is higher than the previously assumed rate of 17 ± 4 mm/yr. This higher slip rate on the fault suggests potentially higher seismic risk for this section of the San Andreas Fault and that slip may remain relatively constant for the northern San Andreas Fault from the North Coast to the Santa Cruz Mountain section.

title: Using bones to recognize the complex histories of hiatuses: micro-taphonomic and diagenetic evidence for marine condensation and cryptic subaerial exposure in the Miocene of Maryland
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Laker, Rachel [1], Kidwell, Susan M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Hanover College, Hanover, IN, USA
(2) University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
abstract: Understanding the architecture of the sedimentary record is necessary to accurately interpret the paleobiological or environmental information held within it. However, assessing the biological resolution of fossil assemblages associated with episodes of non-deposition can be challenging. Here, I evaluate the utility and sensitivity of bones as capsules of environmental and temporal information during hiatal events, using thin-section analysis to recognize early post-mortem and diagenetic evidence of often-transient seabed conditions. Bones should be uniquely excellent records of these conditions: they are geochemically reactive, have a complex and porous structure susceptible to taphonomic alteration and diagenetic infill, and are difficult to transport, remaining local despite winnowing and other erosion of finer sediment. To conduct this test, 28 cetacean bones with high stratigraphic confidence from the Miocene of Maryland (Calvert Cliffs, a notoriously thin record) were assessed for differences in taphonomic and diagenetic trajectories that might refine or refute existing sequence stratigraphic interpretations. The shallow-marine strata of the Calvert Cliffs are cut by a series of 3 rd -order sequence boundaries, often mantled by a condensed shell- or bonebed acting as the primary evidence of siliciclastic reworking, bypass, and/or starvation, with limited evidence of subaerial exposure. Thin section analysis reveals that bones acquire increasingly complex taphonomic histories depending on their context, which ranged from aggradational intervals to 4 th , 3 rd , and 2 nd order surfaces. Evidence of subaerial exposure was found along all proposed sequence boundaries, including a hypothesized cryptic sequence boundary superimposed on the 2 nd order surface of maximum transgression (PP2); evidence for subaerial exposure is most severe along the base of an IVF (CT0) and the base of a 2 nd order FSST (SM0), where significant incision occurs. The rates of observed taphonomic alterations are still poorly understood, as are certain environmental associations, prompting further investigations to vet these associations under natural conditions of time averaging.

title: Trace Element Analysis of Clinopyroxenite Xenoliths Record Extensive Melt-Rock Interaction in the Mantle beneath Uganda, East African Rift
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems (Posters)
authors: Dodson, Johnathan [1], Nelson, Wendy R. [2], Furman, Tanya [3]
affiliations: (1) Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
(2) Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
(3) Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
abstract: The East African Rift System (EARS) is a prime example of present-day continental rifting. However, before its current tectonic regime, the region experienced extensive subduction and collisional tectonics, most recently during the Pan-African Orogeny. This event left an indelible mark on lithospheric mantle both geochemically and lithologically, though the signatures varies significantly throughout the region. We can study the effects that ancient tectonics have on modern rifting directly through mantle xenoliths and indirectly through mafic lavas that result from the partial melting of the lithosphere. Despite extensive study of EARS lavas, analysis of mantle xenoliths – especially non-peridotite mantle xenoliths - is limited. In this study, we investigate the major and trace element signatures of clinopyroxenite xenoliths from the Bufumbira volcanic field located in southwest Uganda. Modally, the clinopyroxenite xenoliths consist of ³75% Mg-rich augite with olivine and/or phlogopite comprising the remaining macroscopic crystals. Cr-spinel is present as inclusions in olivine and some clinopyroxene while ilmenite and occasional apatite are present in phlogopite and as interstitial phases. Melt channels are present in some samples. Major elements were measured on olivine, spinel, and clinopyroxene; trace elements were measured on clinopyroxene. Samples measured displayed mildly depleted LILE and LREE relative to the otherwise negatively sloping normalized patterns. The xenoliths can be divided into two distinct groups based on relative depletions seen in Th, U, Nb, Ta, and Pb. Zr and Ti are inconsistently depleted. The depletion in these elements is controlled, in part, by low clinopyroxene partition coefficients. They may also be controlled by minor refractory phases (e.g. Fe-Ti oxides) that strongly incorporate those elements. We hypothesize that these xenoliths were formed initially during the Pan African Orogeny but experienced more recent melt-rock reaction with alkali magmas associated with modern EARS dynamics.

title: Investigating 3D crystal frameworks in 2D using optically continuous inverted pigeonite networks in the Dufek Intrusion, Antarctica

authors: Gallo, Rose Isabelle [1], VanTongeren, Jill A. [2], Bryan, Ashley [3], Holness, Marian [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Climate Sciences, Tufts University, Somerville, MA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Climate Sciences, Tufts University, Medford, MA, USA

abstract: The Dufek Intrusion, the second-largest known layered mafic intrusion in the world, located in the remote Pensacola Mountains of Antarctica, contains large sections of stratigraphy that display a conspicuous and unusual microstructure: optically continuous patches of inverted pigeonite that share a crystal lattice but are made up of networks of cumulus crystals with distinguishable original grain boundaries. The orientations of pre-inversion augite exsolution lamellae indicate that the lattice alignment occurred as part of the pigeonite inversion process, with inversion nucleating in one grain and propagating across crystal boundaries. The extent of optical continuity in thin section thus permits estimation of the degree of connectivity of the original pigeonite grains. This microstructure predominates in the lower portion of the intrusion, in gabbros containing as little as 11 volume % inverted pigeonite grains and in pyroxenites with as much as 72 vol %, but is rare higher in the stratigraphy where augite becomes the dominant pyroxene phase. Similar microstructures are observed in limited sections of the Bushveld Complex, and a few smaller intrusions around the world, but their prevalence within the Dufek Intrusion is much greater. Orthopyroxene networks are larger (0.2 to > 4.5 cm 2 ) in samples with > 35 vol % inverted pigeonite, while those in gabbros with 11-34 vol % range from 0.5 cm 2 to networks comprising just a few grains in visible 2D section. In all samples with > 35 vol % inverted pigeonite, > 99 % of the grains are part of a network, in agreement with modeling and 3D tomography studies suggesting 35 vol % as the threshold above which 80-90 % of grains of the same phase in a cumulate will belong to a single continuous framework. Above this threshold, the limits of an optical zone should be determined primarily by the nucleation kinetics of the inversion process. At lower inverted pigeonite volumes, network sizes are additionally controlled by the extent of 3D connectivity, which is dictated by grain sizes and orientations, and the presence of pre-existing clusters of pigeonite grains. We examine the impact of these factors on network sizes and consider what the prevalence of this texture suggests about the construction of the cumulate pile and the thermal history of the Dufek Intrusion.

title: An Atlas of Paleosatellite Images to Show the Evolution of Rocky Mountain Landscapes Through Deep Time
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: Petermann, Holger [1], Clement, Annaka [2], Bonner, Hannah [3], Sullivan, Patrick [4], Moss, Maggie [5], Raynolds, Bob [6], Hagadorn, James [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Denver Museum of Nature & Science, Denver, Colorado, USA

(3) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA

abstract:
We created a series of images that show the changing landscapes of the Rocky Mountain region from the Cryogenian to the Last Glacial Maximum and into the future. These map-like images, known as paleosatellite images, give a sense of what the region would look like as if viewed from 800 mi (1300 km) above. They represent the result of a stepwise iterative process that combines stratigraphic, geophysical, geochemical, paleontological, and paleoclimatological information into paleoenvironmental interpretations that are then peer reviewed.

The paleosatellite images were grouped into chapters that provide the context for each phase in the geologic history of the Rocky Mountain region. In total, we split this work into nine chapters. These chapters are the Cryogenian (Snowball Earth), the Cambrian-Mississippian (passive Laurentian margin), the Pennsylvanian-Middle Triassic (assembling Pangea), the Late Triassic and Jurassic (Pangea break up), the Cretaceous (Western Interior Seaway and Laramide orogeny), the Paleogene (building the foundation of the modern Rocky Mountains), the Neogene (shaping the Rocky Mountains), the Quaternary (ice ages shaping the landscape), and 10 Ma into the future (post-human recalibration).

Our goals are to provide these images to the community, so that they can help illustrate how our planet has looked in the past, how it has changed, and where knowledge gaps exist that offer opportunities for future investigation. We anticipate making this atlas of images and their underlying data available as an open-access publication. We envision this atlas as a progress report in paleogeographic mapping, and because we provide an explanation of techniques used to make the maps, we hope that users will improve upon and use them in new ways for their own scholarship, teaching, or outreach.

abstract:
Landslides represent a significant natural hazard in the Cincinnati area, where weak lithology, anthropogenic slope modification, and climatic conditions, such as intense precipitation and rain on snow events, can contribute to widespread slope instability. This study combines lidar-based mapping and field investigation to produce the first comprehensive landslide inventory for the region and evaluate the principal factors controlling landslide distribution within the urban environment. We derived a 0.25 m DEM from lidar point-cloud data acquired in 2021 through the U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program to enable delineation of fine-scale morphological features and support morphometric analysis. The DEM and its derivative layers were leveraged to create a landslide database for the Cincinnati area following the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries protocols. High-resolution DEM-based analysis enabled systematic identification and delineation of internal deformation structures, microterraces, and hummocky surface features in a densely urbanized environment, where infrastructure and anthropogenic slope modification complicate conventional landslide mapping.

Spatial analysis across lithological units revealed a clearly nonuniform distribution. More than 300 landslides were identified within the Upper Ordovician Kope Formation, which is predominantly comprised of shale, substantially exceeding the numbers recorded in other lithological units. While this formation is anecdotally known for landslides, verification is difficult due to a lack of studies accounting for area weighted occurrence. Representative sites were selected for detailed field investigations, verifying mapping and identification of rotational, translational, and complex landslides. Initial results highlight the dominant role of lithology, particularly the low strength and high susceptibility to water saturation of clay-rich materials, and dissected slopes exceeding 20–25° in controlling slope instability.

title: Groundwater availability and use in a consolidated rock aquifer system, Adelaida area, San Luis Obispo County, California

authors: Cromwell, Geoffrey [1], Moret, Geoff [2], Neuhaus, Sarah [3], Seymour, Whitney [4]
affiliations: (1) California Water Science Center, United States Geological Survey, San Luis Obispo, CA, USA
(2) USGS Nevada Water Science Center, Boulder City, NV,
(3) California Water Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Sacramento, CA, USA
(4) California Water Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, San Diego, CA, USA
abstract:
Groundwater is the only source of water in the Adelaida area of northern San Luis Obispo County, California. Groundwater is extracted for residential and agricultural use from a consolidated rock aquifer system. Population growth and irrigated agriculture in the area may have affected groundwater levels and availability. Currently, the Adelaida area is not designated as a groundwater basin by the California Department of Water Resources; thus, no comprehensive evaluations of groundwater resources have been conducted. Here, we present preliminary results of a groundwater availability and use study in the Adelaida area. This work is based on an integrated evaluation of groundwater-level monitoring data, water quality data, estimates of water-balance and water use, and a geologic framework.

Prior to this study there was no comprehensive understanding of the underlying hydrogeology of the area and few publicly available groundwater-level and water quality data from wells. Groundwater is extracted primarily from the Monterey Shale, and from underlying sandstones. Structural folds and faults in the study area may affect groundwater flow and may compartmentalize aquifer responses to groundwater recharge and pumping. To understand the current hydrologic system, new data were collected from 2022–2025, including: quarterly groundwater-level measurements from 60 wells, water quality samples from 15 wells and 5 stream and spring sites, and continuous surface-water measurements from 2 streamgages. These new data were integrated with State and National models of historical groundwater recharge and water use to evaluate the spatial, vertical, and seasonal variability of hydrologic conditions in the Adelaida area. The historical groundwater recharge and water use estimates also provide insight into the changing landscape of the Adelaida area and relative water balance as population increased and land use shifted from dry farming to irrigated agriculture.

In this presentation, we will share successes and challenges faced in designing and implementing this first-ever hydrologic investigation for the Adelaida area, as well as preliminary results on the hydrologic variability of the area with respect to the geology framework and historical changes in the relative water balance. These results are intended to inform water management decisions for the Adelaida area and provide a template for future studies in similar consolidated rock aquifer systems.

title: Using Soil Map Properties and Wind Erosion Testing to Understand Dust Emissivity in the Northern Great Plains, USA
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Rabac, Isabella Donna [1], Sweeney, Mark R. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Sustainability, University of South Dakota, Vermillion, South Dakota, USA
(2) University of South Dakota, Vermillion, SD, USA
abstract: The Northern Great Plains states are no stranger to dust storms and wind erosion, with the most notable period of dust storms occurring from 1930 to 1939, known as the Dust Bowl. Even now, drought conditions and periods of high wind lead to dust storms in this region. Many Northern Great Plains soils are derived from glacial parent materials and tend to be clay dominated, in addition to sandier fluvial, aeolian, and bedrock influenced parent materials. However, due to the removal of the native grassland prairie, fine textured soils have been susceptible to wind erosion since the early days of agriculture. Our goal is to investigate which soil-related properties are associated with areas of dust storms. Using state-wide historical data, we found counties known to have experienced wind erosion during the Dust Bowl including Ward County, ND, Sheridan County, MT, McPherson County, NE, and Goshen County, WY. We studied a variety of soil textures from sand to clay and orders including Entisols, Inceptisols, Mollisols, and Vertisols. In the field and lab, we measured the amount of dust each soil produced using the Portable In-Situ Wind Erosion Laboratory (PI-SWERL). Field sites were characterized using the Gridded Soil Survey Geographic Database (gSSURGO). Tabular soil characteristics assumed to influence dust production were tacked. Preliminary findings indicate that many soil factors are correlated to the amount of dust produced in Northern Great Plains soils. For example, soil texture, mean annual precipitation, drainage class, mean annual temperature, geomorphic position, and frost free days all influence the amount of dust produced by the soil. In the Northern Plains, the freeze-thaw process may be uniquely important because it creates sand-sized soil aggregates in clay-rich soils that are more susceptible to wind erosion and dust production. PI-SWERL tests indicate soils derived from glacial parent materials and dominated by aggregates produce more dust than sandier soils associated with fluvial or aeolian deposits. Detailed soil maps, when combined with PI-SWERL data, are a useful tool to understand the areas vulnerable to wind erosion. This work could help to inform land use decisions in the Northern Great Plains.

title: Exploring the Formation and Persistence of the High Himalayan Topographic Front
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part I)
authors: Whipple, Kelin X. [1], Hodges, Kip [2], Adams, Byron Allen [3], Forte, Adam Matthew [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(2) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University College London, London, United Kingdom
(4) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA
abstract:
Interpretation of the abrupt physiographic transition between the High and Low Himalaya, traceable over 1300 km along strike and termed here the High Himalayan Topographic Front (HHTF), is vigorously debated. The HHTF is variously interpreted as a steady-state topographic expression of a change in rock uplift rate across a steep ramp in the basal thrust, the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT), the manifestation of recurring, long-term out-of-sequence thrusting, or the result of topographic decay following advection over a more northerly MHT ramp.

The debate is partially fueled by different perspectives – a focus on seismic hazards versus a focus on long-term mountain building processes. As the primary seismic hazard is associated with rupture of the MHT flat south of the HHTF, the steady-state ramp model is a sufficient explanation in most cases. However, the devastating loss of life in the 2005 Kashmir earthquake highlights the importance of active out-of-sequence deformation for both orogen evolution and seismic hazard. Low-temperature thermochronometric data are not diagnostic and have been used to support all three models. Interestingly, constraints on longer-term pressure-temperature histories, often disregarded in this debate, strongly support a dynamic, evolving system with significant out-of-sequence thrusting associated with the HHTF since ~17 Ma. This deformation postdates emplacement of the Lesser Himalayan Klippen which are often used in support of the MHT ramp hypothesis. The implications are that (1) the thermal histories of the Klippen cannot be used to support a steady-state model, and (2) the MHT ramp model is only plausibly viable on a shorter timescale.

Here we examine topographic patterns, erosion rates, and cooling ages, in conjunction with seismic and geodetic fault-plane solutions of recent earthquakes, to test among the competing hypotheses. We focus on geologic and seismic receiver function crustal sections that have widely been used to support the MHT ramp model. In all cases where co-located fault plane solutions from recent earthquakes exist (the 1999 Mw 6.3 Chamoli, 2015 Mw 7.8 Gorkha, and 2015 Mw 7.3 Kodari earthquakes), the results require a re-assessment of the interpretation of seismic and geologic cross-sections. We suggest that observations are more consistent with either the out-of-sequence thrusting model or the topographic advection model than with a steady-state MHT ramp model.

title: From CUREs in Geosciences to Expanding HIPs across the Institution
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Visaggi, Christy C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA; Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning, and Online Education, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA
abstract:
Georgia State University (GSU) is a large, minority-serving public research institution that serves six campuses and over 53,000 students. Traditionally, awareness and opportunities for undergraduate students to engage in research have depended largely on department culture, interest by select faculty, and access to programs and experiences outside of the curriculum. Furthermore, participation in research for many of the students at GSU (e.g., first-generation, Pell-eligible, commuters) may be challenging if mostly limited to volunteer options beyond coursework. The previous strategic plan at GSU included a focus on increasing experiential learning at the institution resulting in more individual credit-bearing research opportunities for students. Through a new strategic plan and University System of Georgia initiative to prioritize High-Impact Practices (HIPs) as part of a student’s educational journey, more faculty have expressed interest in embedding research opportunities into their courses across all levels.

Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) have been long recognized as a valued approach for students to learn science by doing science. Through the Department of Geosciences at GSU, students have had access to different CURE models for nearly 15 years including literature, lab, field, as well as citizen science or community-based approaches to incorporating authentic research into a course. Students in these experiences engage in multiple aspects of the research process such as project design and methodology, analyzing data and interpreting results, and disseminating findings to local and national audiences. Models and outcomes featured in this presentation include community-based GIS collaborations in Belize, citizen-science projects in modern ecosystems both nearby in Georgia and in the Bahamas, paleontological research in partnership with the National Park Service, and studying Cenozoic fossils from a range of localities for addressing different research questions in paleoecology and conservation paleobiology. These varied approaches, often additionally incorporating aspects of place-based learning, have helped to set the stage for a suite of faculty development programming at the institution, initially in STEM, and now more broadly as part of scaling HIPs university-wide. Leveraging the HIPs and related elements framework from the American Association of Colleges & Universities as well as an array of resources available through CUREnet have helped to frame how best to guide and support faculty in bringing research into their courses with not only expanded successes in geosciences but across the institution.

title: Terrestrial Community Response to Aridification: Analysis of Lower Jurassic Fossil Tracks From Zion National Park
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments
authors: Bennett, Conner [1], Hembree, Daniel I. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Science, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
abstract: Zion National Park (ZION) is host to both rich paleontological data and an erosional rate roughly 400 m (1,300 ft) per million years. This causes new fossils to become rapidly exposed and weather quickly. In order to mitigate this rapid fossil turnover, ZION has utilized photogrammetry to monitor fossil site conditions and preserve site data in a digital repository. Using this digital repository, we studied the vertebrate fossil track record of the Moenave, Kayenta, and Navajo Sandstone formations to evaluate terrestrial vertebrate community response to environmental shifts caused by aridification. To accomplish this, 63 fossil track localities were visited, separated between the upper Kolob Canyon, middle Wilderness, and lower Zion main canyon areas. Ichnogenera found within the lower Jurassic section included Anomoepus , Brasilichnium , Eubrontes , and Grallator . The entire section possessed 15 Anomoepus tracks, 15 Brasilichnium tracks, 101 Eubrontes tracks, and 40 Grallator tracks. Ichnogenera were defined based on both track measurements (overall length/width, divarication angles, etc.) and overall track morphology. Fossil track assemblages were correlated to the respective paleoenvironment of each formation. Depositional environments shifted from fluvio-lacustrine within the Moenave Formation, fluvial in the Kayenta Formation, to extensive eolian dune and interdune complexes in the Navajo Sandstone. The Moenave and lower Kayenta formations possess 56 fossil track localities, consisting of 137 tracks and include the ichnogenera Anomoepus , Eubrontes , and Grallator . The upper Kayenta Formation holds 4 vertebrate fossil track localities and preserves 17 tracks including the ichnogenera Eubrontes and Grallator . The Navajo Sandstone holds 3 vertebrate fossil track localities which preserves 17 tracks including the ichnogenera Brasilichnium and Grallator . Abundant fossil tracks and greater ichnodiversity are evident within the upper Moenave and lower Kayenta, contrasted by the sudden decrease in abundance and diversity higher in the section. This decrease in fossil track abundance and diversity is likely due to the aridification of the region during the lower Jurassic. As the region dried, conditions became unfavorable for both track preservation due to substrate conditions and populations of large vertebrates (therapod and basal ornithischian dinosaurs) due to resource reduction. This caused fossil tracks of smaller vertebrates (tritylodontids) to become more dominant in the Navajo Sandstone of ZION.

title: A New Record of the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum in Desolation Canyon, Utah: An Analog for Anthropogenic Climate Change
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Prichard, Joshua Alexander [1], Penman, Donald E. [2], Thompson, Maya [3], Francis, Kate [4], Harper, Dustin T. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(2) Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(3) Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(4) Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(5) University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract:
The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM, ~56 Ma) was a 5-8 °C global warming event driven by rapid release of isotopically light carbon, manifested by a negative carbon isotope excursion (CIE) in sedimentary records. Globally, the PETM was characterized by hydrologic cycle modification, with varied impacts on regional terrestrial ecosystems and sedimentation. We undertook a sedimentological, chemostratigraphic, and paleobotanical study of the Colton Formation (Paleocene-Eocene, Uinta Basin, Utah) to understand the regional effects of the PETM in Eastern Utah. Sedimentary and fossil evidence from the Colton suggest a wet fluvial system bounded by the Laramide Orogeny, Uinta Uplift, San Rafael Swell, and Douglas Creek arch, creating a distributive fluvial fan draining into ancient Lake Uinta.

To determine the stratigraphic location of the PETM, paleosol carbonate nodules were collected for stable carbon isotope analyses from floodplain mudstones across the Colton Formation in Desolation Canyon. In the lab, samples were cut and micro-drilled, targeting amorphous micrite while avoiding recrystallized sparite. The powdered calcite was analyzed via mass spectrometry for carbon isotopes. The resulting record shows an interval of nodules with low δ 13 C values at outcrops near the mouth of Chandler Canyon, where further sampling was later conducted to increase resolution of this CIE, which we tentatively interpret as the PETM. Leaf fossils found within Chandler Canyon support a consistently wet ecosystem. The flora was largely comprised of broad-leafed plants with larger surface area requiring high water availability. Alongside these plants were gar fish scales. The paleosols are mostly red (oxidizing) with some gray and purple (reducing), suggesting mostly well-drained floodplain conditions with frequent flooding. These proxies combined indicate a hydrological refuge for resilient riparian life in the arid PETM landscape.

As anthropogenic climate change continues, studying PETM environments like the Colton Formation is becoming increasingly important. Recognizing how tectonic basins sustain freshwater ecosystems in a rapidly warming world allows us to identify potential resource rich regions for future generations.

title: Geochemical Evidence for Incremental Inflation of Massive Submarine Basalt Flows: A Case Study using IODP and ODP Legacy Cores
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections
authors: Nelson, Wendy R. [1], Burdt, Garrity [2], Dodson, Johnathan [3], Shervais, John W. [4]
affiliations: (1) Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
(2) Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
(3) Towson University, Towson, MD, USA
(4) Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
abstract:
The eruption of massive basalt flows (>3m thick) on the seafloor is a less recognized yet widespread component of seamounts and oceanic plateaus. Over the decades of DSDP-ODP-IODP exploration, massive basalt flows have been recovered in a number of ocean drilling expeditions. Many of these flows were sparsely sampled for on-shore geochemical work, often leading to the assumption that massive flows are geochemically homogenous aside from the effects of fractional crystallization. However, a recent study (Shervais et al., 2025) of massive basalt flows erupted along Walvis Ridge demonstrates that massive flows are not geochemically homogenous. Rather, high-resolution XRF core-scanner data quantified for major and trace element abundances clearly show that repeated pulses of magma were injected into an initially much thinner lava flow, and the composition of those injections can change over short timescales. This process inflated simple sheet flows into massive flows. In order to determine if flow inflation is a widespread process responsible for generating massive submarine basalt flows, we identified massive flows recovered from Shatsky Rise (ODP Leg 198, IODP Exp 324), the East Pacific Rise (ODP Leg 208, IODP Exp 309), and the Ontong-Java Plateau (ODP Legs 130 and 192) for further study. Legacy cores were scanned for major and select trace elements using the XRF Core Scanners at the Gulf Coast Repository at Texas A&M University. Three basaltic USGS standards were scanned along with the cores, allowing for quantification the XRF spectral data. We focused on massive flows with high recoveries. The thickness of measured flows varied from 5m to 29m. Compositional data plotted against depth show scalloped patterns inconsistent with whole-flow fractional crystallization. Instead, these geochemical variations likely represent repeated injections of fresh magma into the interior of the lava flow. This supports the flow inflation model observed at Walvis Ridge and demonstrates that it is a widespread process responsible for generating massive submarine basalt flows.

title: Expanding Macrostrat’s Multiscale Map Compilation: A Pipeline for Integrating Digitized Geologic Maps
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: Fromandi, Amy [1], Quinn, Daven [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
abstract:
Geologic maps constitute the primary spatial record of Earth's surface geology, yet they remain scattered across organizations, formats, scales, and legend conventions. Macrostrat addresses this heterogeneity by aggregating maps from diverse sources into a harmonized, multiscale framework accessible through a single machine-readable endpoint. Each map preserves its geological interpretation, while its attributes are linked to standardized definitions for lithology, age, stratigraphic names, and feature types. This synthesized map is correlated with other geological datasets (e.g., stratigraphic columns) for scientific analysis and interpretation. Macrostrat’s platform and applications now serve geologic maps to more than 100,000 users daily, positioning it as one of the most widely used platforms for accessing digital geologic maps.

Since its initial development (Peters et al., 2018), Macrostrat’s mapping system has integrated 288 geologic map datasets with global coverage. However, further integration stalled around 2020 because of limited staffing, computational overhead, and manual workflows. To renew the platform and extend it through community support (Quinn et al., 2024), we rebuilt Macrostrat’s ingestion system as a modular, reviewable pipeline.

In the renewed pipeline, GIS files enter a staging environment where polygon, line, and point features are prepared through reusable routines and a web interface. Data curators combine automated tools with geologic review to align map attributes with Macrostrat’s classification framework, including assigning explicit age boundaries to geological units. Unified datasets are integrated into a global topology, aggregated into layers, and served publicly as vector and raster map tiles. Normalized pipelines for common map products, including GeMS, bulk processing of similarly structured map series, and an iterative topology engine remove prior bottlenecks, enabling hundreds of maps to be processed in a single execution cycle.

Using this system, we integrated 374 maps from the Geological Survey of Japan’s 1:50,000 Quadrangle Series, 268 maps from the Arizona Geological Survey, and the USGS National Geologic Synthesis compilation (Johnstone et al., 2026). These additions more than double the number of publicly available maps in Macrostrat and improve high-resolution coverage in several key regions. With this system in place, we will continue to integrate new map sources into Macrostrat. Future developments will establish a community contribution and review process, improve referencing and styling for individual maps, and support more flexible delivery methods in GIS environments.

title: Major- and Trace-Element Geochemistry of the Ireviken Biogeochemical Event from Measley Ridge, Ohio
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Havens, Morgan L. [1], McNally, Anna K. [2], Cramer, Bradley D. [3], Peate, David W. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
(2) University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
(3) University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA

abstract:
The Ireviken Biogeochemical Event (IBE) was one of the largest perturbations to the ocean-atmosphere-biosphere system during the Paleozoic. The IBE spans the Llandovery-Wenlock boundary and includes an extinction event that affected conodonts, graptolites, trilobites, and other taxa, as well as a perturbation to the global carbon cycle that is expressed as a major positive carbon isotope excursion. The Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) for the base of the Wenlock Series is located at Hughley Brook in Great Britain and is currently under revision for potential replacement. This renewed investigation of the base Wenlock GSSP also includes a search for potential Standard Auxiliary Boundary Stratotypes (SABSs) that may serve to supplement the GSSP and aid in regional correlation of the boundary.

One potential SABS for the base Wenlock Series is the Measley Ridge outcrop in southern Ohio. There, the conodont biostratigraphy and carbon isotope chemostratigraphy clearly demonstrate that the IBE is present and well developed, and that this section can be easily correlated to the current GSSP and the important reference sections on Gotland, Sweden. Recent work on the geochemistry of the IBE has been focused on the excellent exposures of Gotland, but no similar major- and trace-element geochemical data sets have been generated. Here, we develop high-resolution major- and trace-element geochemical records of the IBE from the Estill and Bisher formations at the Measley Ridge outcrop and compare those records to previous studies from Gotland.
