title: The Clear Lake Aquifer: 40 years of Monitoring and Groundwater Development
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Johanson, Alex [1], Tharp, Kieran [2]
affiliations: (1) Groundwater Assessment Program, Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Butte, Montana, USA; Structural Geology and Tectonics Lab, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
(2) Groundwater Assessment Program, Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Butte, Montana, USA
abstract:
The Clear Lake Aquifer is a complex aquifer system in northeastern Montana composed of highly permeable Late Tertiary Missouri River alluvium and Pleistocene glacial outwash, interbedded with less permeable lacustrine and glacial till. It is the primary water source in a semi-arid region (< 15-in of precipitation/yr). Increasing irrigation development has raised questions regarding the long-term sustainability of the aquifer. Our research analyzed 40 years of precipitation data, irrigation withdrawals, groundwater-level measurements, water-quality data, and lithologic logs to assess the aquifer response to climate and groundwater development.

Spring peak groundwater levels closely track winter precipitation trends, indicating that long-term groundwater conditions are primarily controlled by climatic variability. Although irrigation development has expanded substantially during the past decade, groundwater-level declines are limited to the northern management area, where the aquifer is thinner and more than half of the irrigation withdrawals occur. Several pot-hole lakes overlie the aquifer. Detailed hydrogeologic cross sections and paired shoreline–groundwater monitoring wells indicate that shallow groundwater and surface water are generally hydraulically connected. Groundwater chemistry has remained stable throughout the period of record and is generally suitable for irrigation.

The results indicate that climatic variability remains the dominant control on groundwater conditions across most of the Clear Lake Aquifer, while irrigation-related impacts are localized to areas of concentrated development. This study demonstrates the value of long-term, high-frequency monitoring towards supporting sustainable aquifer management.

title: A Multi-Phase Record of Basin Restriction and Oxygenation during the Breakup of Southern Gondwana: Sedimentology, Chemostratigraphy, and Geochronology of the Early Cretaceous Rocas Verdes Basin
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: Clevenger, Griffin [1], Malkowski, Matt [2], Launderville, Emily May [3], Crowley, James L. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(2) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(3) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(4) Boise State University, Boise, ID,
abstract: Paleogeographic reconstructions of the south Atlantic opening during Gondwana breakup remain poorly resolved, limiting understanding of Early Cretaceous Southern Hemisphere hydrographic connections. The Rocas Verdes backarc basin (RVB), at the southern tip of South America, opened during the latest Jurassic–Early Cretaceous and occupied a critical paleogeographic position between the Pacific and developing Atlantic oceans, yet the timing and extent of marine exchange between them remain uncertain. At the Tyndall Glacier locality in Torres del Paine National Park, a ~1 km mudstone succession of the Zapata Formation preserves a record of basin evolution between 150 and 110 Ma and contains numerous volcanic ash horizons providing chronostratigraphic control. Whole-rock major- and trace-element geochemistry, integrated with sedimentologic observations and a Bayesian stratigraphic age model constrained by 11 zircon CA-TIMS and LA-ICPMS U-Pb ash-bed ages, records a multi-phase history of redox evolution, basin connectivity, and sediment provenance. We evaluate Mn enrichment as a proxy for marine connectivity because exchange with oxygenated marine waters promotes delivery and preservation of particulate Mn(III/IV) oxides, whereas persistent restriction and anoxic bottom waters favor reduction to soluble Mn(II), resulting in Mn depletion. RVB Mn chemostratigraphy records episodic marine exchange throughout basin evolution. At the base of the section, organic-rich carbonaceous shale with elevated TOC and depleted Mn records an initially restricted, anoxic basin, after which a transition to calcareous shale accompanied by increased Mn enrichment marks the onset of exchange with oxygenated marine waters. The transition from calcareous to overlying siliceous mudstone reflects basin deepening below the carbonate compensation depth, increased terrigenous dilution, or both, while persistent Mn enrichment indicates continued marine exchange. In the middle Zapata Formation, depleted Mn coincides with rhythmically interbedded siliceous-calcareous slump and debris-flow deposits interpreted as submarine canyon fill, recording renewed restriction and anoxic bottom waters. This restricted interval and an overlying disconformity may reflect tectonically driven basin reorganization, including basin narrowing or sill formation during incipient compression and backarc closure. Above the disconformity, siliceous debris-flow deposits coincide with renewed Mn enrichment, documenting reestablished marine exchange before grading upward into siliceous mudstone with declining Mn enrichment, consistent with progressively reduced interaction with the open ocean. This study illustrates how combining chemostratigraphy, sedimentology, and high-precision geochronology can identify transient marine connections in backarc basin successions that are otherwise cryptic.

abstract: The transition between the Cambrian Explosion (CE) and the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE) represents a dynamic interval in Earth history. However, the role and timing of local and global ocean redox conditions, and their links to early Paleozoic evolution, remain debated. Constraining long-term ocean redox dynamics throughout this interval is essential to further assessing the connections between oxygenation and early animal evolution. Although trace metal geochemistry in black shales is a robust proxy for local and global redox conditions, relatively few studies have utilized it to constrain long-term redox evolution during this interval. Here, we present new iron-speciation and trace metal concentrations from two black shale cores from Baltoscandia, spanning the Lower to Middle Ordovician, integrated with a new compilation of regional redox proxies spanning the upper Cambrian through the Late Ordovician. Iron speciation and Mn concentrations indicate persistently oxygen-deficient, predominantly ferruginous conditions on the deep shelf of Baltoscandia. In contrast, pronounced enrichments in V, and to lesser extent Mo, define repeated pulses of elevated trace metal inventories, implying intervals of contracted global marine anoxia. Our conservative numerical model suggests a contraction in anoxic seafloor from 2.7% to 0.6% (decreased by 7.3×106 km 2 ) during the Floian–Dapingian. In a longer temporal context, the new compilation reveals an oscillatory redox pattern, with phases of expanded anoxia coinciding with faunal turnover, and intervals of increased ventilation aligned with biodiversification pulses. These results demonstrate that early Paleozoic marine oxygenation did not follow a monotonic, linear trajectory but instead occurred through recurring redox oscillations that modulated extinction susceptibility and metazoan evolution.

title: Lab topics matter! Quantifying factors that improve maximize student learning in introductory geoscience lab courses
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Teasdale, Rachel [1], Ryker, Katherine [2], Bitting, Kelsey S. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, California State University, Chico, Chico, CA, USA
(2) School of Earth Ocean and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA

abstract: Laboratory activities play an important role in student learning in introductory geoscience courses. With smaller student to instructor ratios, hands-on activities, and more time for in-depth examination of concepts, laboratory activities are often expected to maximize learning. To quantify the factors that most impact learning, we evaluated the influence of lab topics, the level of inquiry, teaching assistant (TA), course format (online, hybrid or in person) and students’ situational interest in each lab. Data were collected from six introductory geoscience laboratory courses at five public research institutions for four semesters. Student learning was measured using pre- and post- course surveys for six lab topics, using three content questions per topic. Lab topics were selected by each course instructor and learning survey questions were aligned directly to the lab activities of each course. Odds ratio analyses indicate that of all factors considered, the topic of the lab activity and the TA are the strongest predictors of student learning. Impacts of TAs are likely related to a variety of factors, which are the subject of our additional study. Our detailed assessment of the lab topics indicates there are higher odds of student learning for lab activities on Minerals, Earth's Interior, Earthquakes, and Landscape Development. Students who also indicate strong interest in specific lab topics have higher odds of learning than students who do not indicate interest (e.g., they have an 88% increase in learning for Rocks labs and a 51% increase in learning for Rivers and Streams labs). The impact of lab format on learning also varies by topic. For example, students have higher odds of learning in Minerals and Topographic Maps labs when taught in person than when taught online, but there is no statistically significant difference in the odds of improved learning in labs taught in-person versus online for other topics such as Earthquakes, Landslides and Rivers & Streams. Our results illustrate that careful selection of lab topics and activity design are important considerations when developing lab courses in the geosciences.

title: Can Semi-Automated Machine Learning Methods Standardize Lunar Geologic Mapping and Improve the Efficiency of Exploration Site Characterization?
session_title: Planetary Potpourri (Posters)
authors: Serrano, Veronica [1], Hurtado, Jose M [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental and Resource Sciences, University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental and Resource Sciences, University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, Texas, USA
abstract: Geologic mapping provides the framework for interpreting planetary surfaces and is an essential part of planning future lunar exploration. However, manually producing detailed geologic maps from the growing volume of remotely sensed data is both time-intensive and subject to interpreter variability. In this study, I evaluate whether supervised machine learning can improve the efficiency and consistency of lunar geologic mapping while still preserving expert interpretation. We use remotely sensed datasets collected by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter for six candidate Artemis exploration sites near the lunar south pole. Existing geologic maps provide the labeled training data, while visible imagery, topography, and radar backscatter serve as predictor variables. The ML workflow combines ArcGIS Pro for data preparation with Google Colab and Scikit-learn for model development and evaluation. Model performance is assessed using overall accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, processing time, and expert review of the resulting geologic maps. Current work focuses on implementing and evaluating a Random Forest classifier. Preliminary results demonstrate that the workflow can successfully produce reproducible geologic classifications that are suitable for comparison with existing manually generated maps. Developing an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model will enable a direct comparison of classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and overall map quality. This work will help evaluate the potential of supervised machine learning as a tool to support future planetary geologic mapping and characterization of Artemis exploration sites.

title: Differentiating Drainage Capture from Climatic and Tectonic Signatures in Fluvial Topography
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Leonard, Joel S. [1], Whipple, Kelin X. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA
(2) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA
abstract: The goal of understanding the relative roles of climate and tectonics in shaping the fluvial topography of active orogens has motivated decades of research and intense debate. Isolating the effects of these drivers is challenging because each can impart similar morphological signatures, and because complex interactions between climate and tectonics are likely manifest in active orogens. More recently, significant interest has focused on the process of drainage capture and identifying diagnostic signatures of stream network disequilibrium. Capture events and drainage network disequilibrium more broadly may also ultimately have a tectonic or climate driver, and thus correct identification could provide important insight into a landscape’s history. However, apparent disequilibrium signatures can also arise as artifacts of common analysis methods and climate-driven effects from orographic rainfall patterns in particular can mimic expected signatures of recent drainage captures, even in stable drainage networks. Hence, misidentification of these signatures can lead to false impressions about the dominant processes shaping a landscape. Here, we present an analysis of fluvial topography of different orogens, including the Andes and Himalaya, and numerical modeling results to illustrate 1) the degree of similarity between signatures of drainage capture and gradients in climatic and tectonic conditions, 2) potential pitfalls of common analysis methods that could lead to misidentification, and 3) useful differences between signatures created by these forcings that researchers may target to differentiate among possible causes. We highlight divergent interpretations that follow from using standard drainage-area-weighted morphometrics (χ and k sn ) and rainfall-weighted versions, χ Q and k snQ , and show that these tools are best used in combination. Additionally, regional context gained from analyzing adjacent river networks may provide crucial diagnostic evidence.

title: 40Ar/39Ar Geochronology and Marker Bed Stratigraphy of Lacustrine Tuff beds in McDermitt Caldera, Oregon, USA

authors: Hess, Raegan L. [1], Cahoon, Emily Bogdan [2], O'Barr Rogers, Sophia A. [3], Tattitch, Brian [4], Dilles, John H. [5]
affiliations: (1) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA

abstract:
The McDermitt Caldera is an eruptive center related to early Yellowstone hotspot magmatism in southeastern Oregon and northern Nevada with historic Hg and U mining activity. McDermitt Caldera is now a promising Li resource within lacustrine clay-rich sedimentary sequences. The intracaldera lacustrine stratigraphy includes variably mineralized, well-bedded tuffaceous siltstones and sandstones, lacustrine airfall tuffs, and claystones with locally silicified zones along basement contacts with flow-banded icelandite. Key interbedded tuff units represent potential marker beds alongside Li-rich smectite (hectorite) claystone horizons, making correlations between subsurface drill cores and surface exposures possible. However, absolute ages of claystone deposition and lithium mineralization within the HiTech claim area require further refinement for possible correlation.

Previous single crystal 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages of anorthoclase constrains the underlying McDermitt Tuff at 16.39 ± 0.02 Ma, while authigenic K-spar 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages from the Thacker Pass Li-rich claystone section south of the HiTech claim area, dates Li-mineralization at 14.87 ± 0.05 Ma (Henry et al., 2017). Our Initial 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dating on tuffaceous units at surface returned ages of 16.39 ± 0.02 Ma at the base of the section with the youngest grains from higher in the section returning an age of 15.92 ± 0.08 Ma. Preliminary ages from drill core MDD010 returned ages of 16.361 ± 0.015 Ma to 15.772 ± 0.012 Ma from a depth range of 88.8m to 28.3m, respectively (Henry, written communication). We are attempting to further refine the transition between volcaniclastic activity and enrichment of lithium-mineralization. We will present 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages on sanidine in the key MDD010 interval along with 2 additional drill cores and nearby surface samples within the study area. Samples were crushed, sieved to 250-180um, separated by density, and cleaned with dilute HF. Suitable grains from six samples were handpicked, irradiated, will be analyzed via single crystal and incremental heating methods using the ARGUS-VI mass spectrometer at Oregon State University. We will present these 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages along with field relationships and stratigraphic context, with the goal of identifying tuffaceous marker beds located within Li-ore clay horizons and surface exposures of the same horizons and placing these key units into the broader history of volcanism, sedimentation and mineralization in the McDermitt Caldera.

title: Influence of Large-Scale Climate Teleconnections on Lake Michigan's Water Temperature
session_title: Geoinformatics and Data Science: A Showcase In Undergraduate and Graduate Student Research (Posters)
authors: Ambrose, Jenna Rae [1], Guo, Yiming [2]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(2) Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
abstract: Lake Michigan, one of the Laurentian Great Lakes, experiences substantial interannual to decadal variability in lake surface temperature (LST), which influences thermal stratification, ice cover, biogeochemical processes, and aquatic ecosystems. While local atmospheric forcing contributes to short-term variability, large-scale climate modes can modulate regional atmospheric circulation and influence long-term thermal variability in the Great Lakes. North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) are three major modes of climate variability that operate over ocean bodies surrounding North America, mostly involving air circulation and air temperature alterations. The effect of these patterns is observed through NOAA CoastWatch Great Lakes Node high-resolution satellite imagery, which generates data points containing information regarding Lake Michigan’s LST. Harmonic analysis removes the influence of seasonal cycles for the region to isolate the interannual climate variability. Climate-lake interactions were then analyzed for timing and strength quantification. Because of typical seasonal variation, large-scale climate modes over this region may have an altered effect. With the removal of the seasonal cycle for this region, an underlying pattern on an interannual cycle becomes more apparent, which suggests the effects of large-scale atmospheric variability occurring beyond the local region. These climatic influences have been found to display a lag in response and persistence to the local region being studied. Further analysis will uncover the seasonal dependence, temporal lag, and relative contributions of NAO, ENSO, and PDO to Lake Michigan’s thermal variability. This study offers a new perspective on the mechanisms by which large-scale climate variability influence Lake Michigan water properties using high-resolution satellite imagery. By identifying the influence of teleconnection patterns on regional climate variability in the Great Lakes region, an updated and improved understanding of the changing lake surface temperature and its relationship with the changing climate is possible.

title: Isotopic Stability of Nitrogen During Early Leaf Decomposition: Implications for Paleoclimate Reconstructions

authors: Purdue, Catherine [1], Bellich, Nicolas [2], Grajales, Alexandra Maria [3], Johnson, Benjamin William [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere, and Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA,
(2) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere, and Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA,
(3) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere, and Climate, Iowa State University, Washington, DC,
(4) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere, and Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA,
abstract: Fossil plants are useful paleoclimate archives. While decades of work have unlocked carbon content and isotope values as records, little work has been completed using nitrogen. Nitrogen is a critical nutrient for plants, especially in chlorophyll. The ratio of C:N in leaves correlates with pCO2, and N isotopes can reveal the presence or absence of symbiotic relationships with N-fixing bacteria. Yet the taphonomic processes leaf matter undergoes on its way to fossilization may alter its isotopic fingerprint, limiting use in paleoclimate and paleoecological reconstructions. To address this knowledge gap, a litter-bag study was carried out for 6 months in a controlled environment to track alteration in N and C isotopes as decomposition progressed. Leaves were used and gathered from nitrogen-fixing (alder, Alnus ) and non-nitrogen-fixing species (maple, Acer ) both pre- and post-abscission (i.e., leaf color change and drop). Samples were buried at differing depths of 2, 4.5, and 12 cm, as well as in both unsterilized and sterilized soil, in indoor containers. At regular intervals, leaves were unearthed and measured through a mass spectrometer for N and C geochemistry. Results showed noticeably lower amounts of nitrogen post-abscission, but no clear correlation between time spent in the litter bags and δ 15 N values. This may support the conclusion that in ideal conditions, isotopic change is not noticeable in the first six months of burial. Future studies could involve much lengthier studies and a variety of conditions that would help us piece together the transformation of biomatter from its time alive to its fossilized remains.

title: Service With a Smilodon: Climatic Niche Modeling of Smilodon and It’s Prey Genera
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space (Posters)
authors: Jones, Avery [1], Lyons, S. Kathleen [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
(2) School of Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract: Knowing how species respond to periods of drastic climate change is proving increasingly important in the modern era. Global temperatures have soared and populations of large mammals are declining. Understanding how this will affect Earth’s ecosystems is imperative. One method for predicting a faunal response to climate change is to study similar periods of climate change that occurred in the past. For the modern era, the Pleistocene offers a useful comparison point due to its periods of intense climate change and extinction of many mammalian megafauna. Here, we use ecological niche modeling techniques to estimate the ranges of suitable habitat for six ancient mammals and evaluate how they changed over the course of the Pleistocene. We focus on one highly successful predator genus and its potential prey to understand how a set of trophic interactions were affected by climate change during this time. Bioclim models were created to map the habitat suitability of the North and South American predator Smilodon , as well as six genera of its prey: Lestodon, Macrauchenia, Megatherium, Bison, Equus, and Mammuthus . Occurrences and climate data were divided into three distinct time periods based on South American Land Mammal Ages: the Lujanian (0.01-0.2 Ma), Bonaerian (0.2-0.55 Ma), and Ensenadan (0.55-2.15 Ma). We find that the suitable habitat ranges for each genera were reduced during the Bonaerian. Additionally, some genera (e.g., Macrauchenia and Bison ) had larger suitable habitat ranges in the Lujanian compared to the Ensenadan, while others showed the opposite trend (e.g., Lestodon ). The most suitable habitats (suitability > 0.75) for Smilodon and all of its prey genera tended to overlap in almost every time period with a few notable exceptions including both Bison and Mammuthus in the Bonaerian. These results indicate that while climate was changing, the geographic location of these genera’s suitable habitat overall was not. Our results suggest that modern mammals will attempt to maintain their ecological niche while being exposed to periods of intense climatic changes. Modern conservation efforts should prioritize maintaining potential dispersal routes between areas of suitable habitat for vulnerable species as climate changes.

title: Moss Community Composition Affects Mineral Weathering and Nutrient Release in Newly Deglaciated Arctic Environments
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology and Geomicrobiology (Posters)
authors: Ezukanma, Izuchukwu O [1], Lockwood, Emily [2], Salinas, Tatiana [3], Zupanska, Agata [4], Martin , Ellen E [5], Martin, Jonathan B. [6], McDaniel, Stuart F. [7]

abstract: Mineral weathering is a key driver of nutrient availability in recently deglaciated Arctic landscapes, yet the extent to which weathering processes are influenced by plant community composition is poorly understood. If individual species mobilize specific nutrients, landscape-level successional changes may predictably alter runoff water chemistry with implications for both trophic cascades between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems and understanding weathering-related carbon cycling. Here we tested whether common moss species differ in their capacity to mobilize nutrients from mineral substrates using a 16-month mesocosm experiment in which five moss species were grown on pulverized Greenlandic rocks with and without a co-culture of mutualistic N 2 -fixing cyanobacteria. Following harvest, we analyzed the substrate leachates for dissolved macro- and micronutrients (Na, Mg, Al, P, Ca, Mn, Mo, Fe, Cu, and Zn). We found variations in the elemental composition of the leachates that corresponded to distinct moss species and to the presence of cyanobacteria (MANOVA; p < 0.001), but no evidence of an interaction effect. Species-specific weathering signatures were primarily associated with differences in Mg, Ca, Mn, Mo, Fe, Cu, and Na mobilization, while cyanobacterial inoculation selectively altered Mg, Mn, Fe, Cu, and Na concentrations. Interestingly, cyanobacteria modified specific nutrient pools rather than inducing broad compositional shifts. Collectively, these results indicate that both the identity of moss species and the presence of cyanobacteria exert a strong influence on substrate-derived nutrient mobilization, potentially driving trophic cascades between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems and linking landscape-level biological processes to carbon sinks resulting from silicate weathering.

title: Climate control on the timing of meander cutoffs and terrace formation in the Oregon Coast Range, OR, USA
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Schanz, Sarah Anne [1], Breyak, Annie [2], Lin, Ya-shien [3], Yanites, Brian J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada
(3) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences Department, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(4) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences Department, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract: Bedrock river terraces form through periods of planation and incision, the timing of which reflects climatic and tectonic forcings and can inform uplift rates and styles along subduction zones. However, recent work suggests that autogenic processes, namely lateral beveling and incision through meandering, can drive similar terraces in the absence of any major change to climate or tectonics. Yet, meandering rates themselves likely respond to climatic perturbations such as changes in weathering potential and sediment supply. Here, we examine how meander cutoffs—an aspect of meandering that drives knickpoint formation and upstream incision—influence terrace formation in the Smith River, Oregon, USA, and whether the timing of cutoffs is related to changes in climatic forcings. In this relatively narrow bedrock valley, we mapped fluvial terraces, characterized knickpoint retreat styles and rates, and constrained incision rate histories. We find that knickpoints retreat consistent with n = 1 in the stream power law and applied this to estimate the relative proportion of terraces formed via upstream migrating knickpoints and those formed by changes in basin wide incision potential. We find that 44% of terraces have elevation patterns consistent with basin wide incision, with another 32% consistent with a migrating knickpoint. Basin-wide incision events at 14.2 and 72.5 ky correspond to periods of climatic instability when bedrock erosion potential is enhanced. Prominent meander cutoffs in the landscape date to 15.2, 19.5, 21.3, and 46.4 ky, and comparison with local climate and erosion records correlates these ages with intervals of enhanced weathering and sediment supply, all of which would drive increased lateral migration rates and increase the likelihood of a cutoff event. Thus, particularly in narrow bedrock valleys with limited lateral migration, cutoff events appear to be highly influenced by climate, and the terrace record reflects climatic rather than autogenic signals.

title: Modeling Mushes: Linking Compaction and Crystallization to Simulate Modal Variation in a Zoned Granitic Pluton
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Hirt, William H [1]
affiliations: (1) Biological and Physical Sciences, College of the Siskiyous, Weed, California, USA
abstract:
The Whitney pluton of the eastern Sierra Nevada is dominated by two major phases: a relatively coarse-grained interior phase and a finer-grained marginal phase that contains lower abundances of ferromagnesian minerals and quartz but a higher abundance of alkali-feldspar. Because many granitic rocks like these are interpreted as cumulates (Barnes et al., 2019) their compositions are best modeled as mixtures of early-formed crystals with later phases precipitated from trapped interstitial melts. To simulate how the modal differences between the interior and marginal phases of the Whitney pluton might have arisen, models for compaction and fractional crystallization were combined in a series of discrete steps that made it possible to track the compositions of crystal assemblages, melts, and mushes (magmas with ≥70 vol. % crystals) as an initially homogeneous intrusion solidified.

The simulation begins when a 5 km-thick model intrusion cools to 50 vol. % crystallinity and ceases to mix convectively. Crystals in the bottom 1 km of this intrusion then compact to 70% crystallinity and trap 30% interstitial melt. The remaining melt from this compacted layer is expelled upward where it lowers crystallinity in the uncompacted part of the intrusion and re-initiates convective mixing. When magma in the upper part again reaches 50% crystallinity, the cycle repeats. At the end of the simulation the pluton is made up of six compacted layers capped by a 714 m-thick layer that crystallizes and convects until it reaches 50% crystallinity, after which it solidifies without compaction.

The crystal assemblages and mushes in the first six layers define overlapping tracks on a Quartz-Alkali-feldspar-Plagioclase diagram that trend away from plagioclase towards a melt of nearly constant composition. This composition is initially buffered by the large volume of melt in the upper part of the intrusion, but as the convecting region shrinks melts expressed from the underlying compacted layers drive the remaining melt away from quartz and towards alkali-feldspar. The uppermost layer of the intrusion, which is a 50:50 mixture of this alkali-feldspar rich-melt and a relatively plagioclase-poor crystal assemblage, has a modal composition that is offset from earlier mushes in the same sense that the marginal phase of the Whitney pluton is offset from its interior phase.

title: Beneath the Ellipse: A Sedimentological and Geophysical Investigation of a Carolina Bay on the Delmarva Peninsula, Eastern Shore, VA
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Teeters, Corbin [1], Dufresne , Hunter [2], Oakley, Adrienne Jean [3], Cornell, Sean R. [4], Sherrod, Laura [5]
affiliations: (1) Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA,
(2) Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA
(3) Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA,
(4) Shippensburg University, SHIPPENSBURG, PA,
(5) Kutztown University, Department of Physical Sciences, Kutztown, PA,
abstract:
Carolina Bays (CB) are enigmatic geomorphic depressions found along the Atlantic Coastal Plain from NY to northern FL. These circular to elliptical features have raised rims and nearly flat bottoms. Though they have been extensively studied in the Carolinas, their origin remains in dispute and few studies have focused on CBs on the Delmarva Peninsula.

This study investigates a ~400m wide CB located at an elevation of ~10 m absl in Wattsville, VA. Bucket auger sediment cores and 250 mHz Mala X3M GPR reveal complex subsurface stratigraphy beneath the CB.

Overall, with the exception of the upper ~1m, reflectors in the GPR data do not follow the topography of the CB suggesting that the bay is a shallow feature. The deeper reflectors likely represent pre-existing surfaces, including overwash deposits, dunes, and a clay layer. A horizontal GPR reflector at 4-5 m below the bay floor coincides with a blue-gray clay horizon in our cores. This layer is interbedded with lenses of fine, oxidized sand containing large, >2cm clasts possibly indicating the presence of a paleochannel. The clay is overlain by a thick, sandy unit. Within these sediments, reflectors dip in the opposite direction to the CB topography and include foreset structures consistent with stacked dunes. 1.6-1.8 m below the rim of the CB, we found euryhaline benthic diatoms (Navicula spp. and Paralia sulcata) that are likely indicators of storm overwash. Medium-fine sandy sediments with rounded quartz pebbles further support high energy events.

The combined sedimentologic and geophysical evidence suggest a multi-stage development history for the CB. Rising post-LGM sea levels elevated groundwater tables and the low-permeability clay and silt layers promoted ponding in upland depressions between dunes. Subsequent shallow-water wave and aeolian processes formed the characteristic CB rim.

Our initial findings indicate that CBs on the Delmarva Peninsula preserve a more complex stratigraphic history than is evident in surface morphology alone. Future work will include micro and macrofossil identification, XRD analysis, and LOI to further constrain the depositional environments of the bay and underlying sediments. This study emphasizes the importance of subsurface investigations for evaluating models of CB origins and overall coastal evolution in the Mid-Atlantic Region.

title: Ilmenite-Magnetite Geothermometry and Oxybarometry of the Tieton Andesite Lava Flows, Goat Rocks Volcanic Cluster, Washington
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics (Posters)
authors: Harnett, Isabella G [1], Brunstad, Keith A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, State University of New York, Oneonta, NY,
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, State University of New York, Maryland, NY,
abstract: The Goat Rocks volcanic cluster is a deeply eroded, extinct volcanic system located in the south-central Washington Cascade Range between Mount Rainier and Mount Adams. The Tieton Andesite of Bear Creek Mountain erupted from the Goat Rocks between ~1.6 and ~1.3 Ma and comprises two of the longest andesite lava flows in the world (~74 km and ~52 km). By studying the Tieton Andesite flows, we aim to better understand the mechanisms that allow high-viscosity lava flows to travel anomalously long distances. This study applies ilmenite-magnetite geothermometry and oxybarometry to estimate crystallization temperatures and oxygen fugacity, thereby constraining the conditions under which ilmenite and magnetite coexisted and crystallized at equilibrium. Chemical analyses were conducted using a Hitachi 3030 SEM and Bruker QuantX 70 EDX, and ilmenite-magnetite geothermometry and oxybarometry were calculated following the methods of Spencer and Lindsley (1981), Ghiorso and Sack (1991), and Ghiorso and Evans (2008). Preliminary equilibrium temperatures range from 629 to 1015 °C, with corresponding oxygen fugacity (log f O₂) values ranging from -17.4 to -10.3. The highest temperatures likely reflect high-temperature magmatic storage and/or recharge by hotter mafic magma, whereas the corresponding oxygen fugacity values indicate moderately reduced conditions typical of intermediate arc magmas. Lower calculated temperatures likely record continued Fe-Ti exchange between coexisting oxides during prolonged subsolidus cooling, effectively resetting the Fe-Ti oxide geothermometer after magma emplacement. These preliminary findings provide new constraints on the thermal history of the Tieton Andesite and contribute to a broader understanding of the magmatic conditions that enabled the exceptionally long-distance emplacement of high-viscosity lava flows.

title: Modelling the Spatial and Temporal Variability of Rainfall over Jamaica using Satellite Rainfall Estimates and Rain Gauge Measurements
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: TAMBIE, JASON [1], MANDAL, ARPITA [2], Elliott, SOYINI [3], WILLIAMS, KELYSIA [4]
affiliations: (1) DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES , MONA, KINGSTON, Jamaica
(2) DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES , MONA, KINGSTON, Jamaica
(3) DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES, MONA, KINGSTON, Jamaica
(4) DEPARTMENT OF GEOGRAPHY AND GEOLOGY, THE UNIVERSITY OF THE WEST INDIES, MONA, KINGSTON, Jamaica
abstract:
The Small Island Developing States (SIDS) of the Caribbean are at risk to hydrometeorological events that affect life and livelihood. Jamaica, the third largest island in the region, has been exposed to droughts and floods which have increased in the last decade, exacerbated by impacts of climate change. A better assessment of the hydrometeorological events requires understanding of the rainfall variability (spatial and temporal) across the island. The challenge lies in data accuracy as there exists significant gaps and inconsistencies in the rain gauge records. In the absence of ground based station data, the closest proxy used is satellite rainfall estimates for predicting and analysing rainfall trends. This research examines the relationships between rain gauge measurements and satellite-derived precipitation from Precipitation Estimation from Remotely Sensed Information using Artificial Neural Networks (PERSIANN) Climate Data Record (CDR) in Jamaica. This pilot study utilises continuous quality-controlled daily rainfall data from 33 rain gauges over a ten-year period: 2000 to 2009. The study will be extended to 2025 in the final assessment, and incorporate data from additional rain gauges . Preliminary results revealed that the average correlation between rain gauges and PERSIANN-CDR was weak (r = 0.34), with PERSIANN-CDR generally overestimating rainfall along the dry north coast of Jamaica, and underestimating it in the wettest eastern region. The lowest root mean square error (RMSE), 9.48 mm occurred where the largest number of rain gauges were found within a satellite grid cell. Categorical metrics gave insights into how well rainfall was detected by the satellite product, with average values determined for probability of detection (POD = 0.66), false alarm ratio (FAR = 0.47), and critical success index (CSI = 0.41). The highest PODs (> 0.72) occurred where satellite grid cells overlaid the mountainous interior and the wet western region of the island. This research provides quantitative information on the spatial and temporal variability of rainfall in Jamaica, and explores the usefulness of PERSIANN-CDR as a potential alternative to ground-based measurements. Future work will examine intercomparisons among other satellite products in rainfall representation, and explore how satellite rainfall estimates can support applications such as hydrological modelling and drought assessments.

Keywords: Rainfall, PERSIANN-CDR, Rain Gauges, Small Island Developing States, Caribbean

title: ¿Las terrazas agrícolas previenen o provocan deslizamientos de tierra? Inferencias de estudios estadísticos en la Región de Moquegua, Perú
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part II)
authors: Ronda, Gonzalo [1], Santi, Paul M. [2]
affiliations: (1) SRK Consulting, Buenos Aires, Argentina
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
abstract: Comunidades montañosas de diversas partes del mundo han utilizado terrazas construidas para nivelar el terreno para extender terrenos cultivables. Si bien algunos investigadores han sugerido que la reducción de la escorrentía y la erosión que proporcionan las terrazas disminuye la ocurrencia de deslizamientos, demostramos que el aumento de la infiltración de agua puede favorecer el movimiento de deslizamientos debido al incremento de los niveles freáticos. Nuestra base de datos de prueba contiene más de 200 deslizamientos mapeados en un área de 250 km² en los valles cercanos a San Cristóbal, en el distrito de Moquegua, al sur de Perú. También mapeamos la ubicación de las terrazas en esta área y luego utilizamos teledetección, SIG y análisis deestabilidad de taludes para evaluar la relación entre deslizamientos y terrazas. La primera comparación aplicó un enfoque de matriz de confusión para identificar posibles correlaciones, utilizando deslizamientos de tierra como la clase real y terrazas como la clase predicha. Los resultados muestran una alta correlación espacial entre ambas características, con valores de precisión y sensibilidad entre el 64 % y el 81 %. La segunda comparación utilizó una serie de modelos de regresión logística múltiple para probar si la adición de la presencia de terrazas como un término en las ecuaciones mejoraba la capacidad predictiva y área bajo la curva (AUC) del modelo. Si bien los resultados no son estadísticamente robustos, muestran una mejora consistente en el rendimiento del modelo cuando se consideran las terrazas, elevando el AUC entre 0,01 y 0,05. Finalmente, utilizamos el modelado de elementos finitos para evaluar la estabilidad de taludes y mostrar que el factor de seguridad contra fallas materiales podría reducirse a niveles críticos (reducción de ~20 %) con tan solo 189 mm/año de infiltración de agua a través de terrazas, una cantidad razonable en comparación con la precipitación anual en el rango de 269 mm/año.

title: Late Holocene Paleoenvironmental Reconstruction of Chacororé Lake, Pantanal, Brazil
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)

abstract: Late Holocene paleorecords from Pantanal floodplain lakes remain scarce despite the sensitivity of these lakes to regional climate and river dynamics. We reconstructed environmental change in Chacororé Lake, a shallow floodplain lake connected to the Cuiabá River (Mato Grosso, Brazil), using a 106-cm sediment core analyzed for seven AMS radiocarbon ages, grain size, total carbon (TC), XRF-inferred geochemistry, phytoliths, sponge spicules, and diatoms. Stratigraphically constrained cluster analysis identified three environmental zones. Zone I (106–74 cm; ~5,540–3,060 cal yr BP) is characterized by relatively low TC (2.3–9.6 wt.%), high Al₂O₃, abundant lotic and lentic sponges, and sparse diatoms, indicating strong river influence and frequent sediment input. A hiatus in deposition at 74 cm represents a loss of approximately 1,800 years. Zone II (74–51 cm; ~1,230–920 cal yr BP) records peak organic accumulation (TC up to 28.4 wt.%), low concentrations of lithogenic oxides (SiO₂, Al₂O₃, K₂O, and TiO₂), abundant C4 mesic grass phytoliths, low Iph values, and planktonic Aulacoseira , indicating a persistently flooded lake with limited clastic input and possible disconnection with Cuiabá River. Zone III (51–0 cm; ~920–610 cal yr BP) shows declining TC, increasing K₂O, TiO₂, and MnO, higher proportions of bulliform and blocky phytoliths, rising Iph values, and the disappearance of freshwater sponges, indicating greater detrital input. These results show that Chacororé Lake alternated between organic-rich lacustrine conditions and river-dominated phases, reflecting centennial-scale changes in hydrological connectivity and floodplain dynamics in the northern Pantanal.

title: Sedimentology and Diagenesis of Curiosity’s traverse though the Boxwork-Hosting Altadena Member, Gale Crater, Mars
session_title: Boxwork and Fracture Halos: Changes in mineralogy and erosion resistance around fracture features on Earth, Mars, and across the Solar System
authors: Seeger, Christina [1], Siebach, Kirsten Leigh [2], Mondro, Claire A. [3], O’Connell-Cooper, Catherine [4], Schwenzer, Susanne [5], Gasda, Patrick [6], Dietrich, William Eric [7], Banham, Steven [8], Caravaca, Gwenael [9], Scuderi, Louis [10]

(2) Rice University, Houston, TX,

abstract:
From May 2025 through March 2026 (Sols 4534-4844 (Martian days)), the Mars Science Laboratory Curiosity rover traversed through a geologic unit distinct from the surrounding aeolian Chenapau member: the Altadena member of the Mirador formation. This unit is exposed vertically over ~60 meters on the slopes of Aeolis Mons (informally, Mount Sharp), the sedimentary mound that rises ~5km above the floor of Gale crater. From orbit, the Altadena member hosts a network of decameter-scale raised ridges with ~0.5-2m deep hollows between them, which has been interpreted to be the result of diagenetic fluids flowing through and cementing grains within a fracture network (see Siebach et al., this meeting).

In situ rover observations of the stratigraphy and diagenetic fabrics within this unit—including meter- and millimeter-scale imaging, plus chemistry and mineralogy data—provide key insights into the depositional and subsequent groundwater processes. We present evidence for primary deposition in a lacustrine environment, based on the observed host rock facies and relationships at stratigraphic contacts. Bedrock throughout the Altadena member is characterized by friable, fine-grained rock (likely mudstone, though grains below the scale of very fine sand are unresolvable with rover instrumentation) with faint mm-scale planar lamination. These deposits are occasionally punctuated by trough cross-stratified sandstone lenses interpreted to be fluvial or lake margin deposits. Curiosity also investigated stratigraphic contacts between the Altadena and Chenapau members both at the eastern and southern extent of the unit. Preliminary interpretations of a lateral pinch-out to the east and underlying relationship to the south further support the lake margin interpretation

Rover observations support orbital formation hypotheses and provide a more complex view of the diagenetic fabrics contributing to the Boxwork terrain. Ridges are characterized by a blocky laminated mudstone morphology with abundant veins with white fill material. Sparse mm- to cm- scale nodules near ridge centers increase in abundance towards ridge walls, which slope downwards into hollow floors. Where sparse outcrop is visible amidst sand cover in hollow bottoms, the rock tends to be heavily overprinted with nodules forming a knobby, flakey, or dendritic texture. This evidence for sustained groundwater interaction, coupled with evidence for surface water during lake deposition, has implications for a water-stable Martian climate higher in the stratigraphy—and therefore later in time—than previously hypothesized.

abstract: The ecological effects of the Cretaceous - Paleogene (K-Pg) mass extinction vary regionally and across taxa. We compare the pre-extinction and post-recovery ecological communities at Stevns Klint, Denmark, a UNESCO World Heritage site known for its exceptional exposure of bryozoan chalk reef-mound facies before and after the K/Pg boundary. We generate an image database of all marine invertebrate specimens > 2 mm (N = 5,853 specimens) from bulk sediment samples, imaged using digital light microscopy, spanning the pre-extinction and post-recovery intervals and across the mound habitat gradient. Non-bryozoan specimens include crinoids, irregular echinoids, regular echinoids, asteroids, ophiuroids, bivalves, brachiopods, serpulids, corals, gastropods, and calcareous sponges. We compare the composition of pre-extinction and post-recovery ecological communities at the phylum, class, and genus levels, as well as the diversity of echinoid spine morphotypes. We find change in community composition at the K/Pg is significant at all taxonomic levels, but diversity trajectories vary among taxa. Furthermore, we see that the stratigraphic member and time are better predictors of this ecological turnover than hypothesized nutrient availability based on mound microhabitats. We hope this image dataset will serve future work on taxonomic and paleoecological change surrounding the Cretaceous/Paleogene boundary and its applications to understanding current biodiversity loss and ecological cascades.

abstract:
Different regions of a lava flow experience distinct cooling conditions and vary in texture and mineralogy, with a flow’s surface experiencing rapid cooling compared to the interior. On Mars, such cooling differences may be obtainable from textural and mineralogical data, potentially aiding in identifying parts of a lava flow. This study characterizes the texture of experimental samples crystallized at two cooling rates. Using a 1-atm CO-CO2 gas mixing furnace, samples with a composition corresponding to Martian olivine-phyric shergottite Yamato 980459 were cooled from above the liquidus temperature (1500℃) to crystallization temperatures (Tc) at 35℃/hour to mimic a flow’s interior [1], and ~700℃/hour to mimic its surface. As detailed in [2], slowly cooled samples exhibit few, large crystals, including euhedral pyroxene and olivine, spinifex pyroxene, and dendritic pyroxene, compared to fast cooled samples, which contain abundant small euhedral pyroxene and olivine, and spinifex pyroxene. All samples also contain glass. Following the textural analysis method from [3], we determined surface area per unit volume (SPv) for each crystal type using backscattered electron (BSE) images calculated as twice the population intersections divided by the volume fraction. This method provides a better fit than CSD in geologic systems and experimental samples, which often have imperfect crystals [4].

Euhedral pyroxene and olivine exhibit a general increase of SPv with increasing Tc, similar to the overall SPv trend of the total crystal, euhedral crystal, and spinifex pyroxene populations. Total pyroxene populations tend to have higher SPv compared to olivine populations. For euhedral olivine and spinifex pyroxene, rapidly cooled samples showed a higher SPv compared to those cooled slowly. The data suggest SPv, which is related to crystal size, shape, and abundance, is strongly influenced by Tc, phase, and cooling rate, with faster cooling rates generally yielding higher SPv. Since cooling rate affects SPv, and thus crystal size and abundance, spectral data in the near-infrared and mid-infrared range acquired from orbit will be impacted. Future studies will explore this in detail.

abstract: The California Geological Survey’s (CGS) Forest and Watershed Geology Program (FWGP) has developed a new regional landslide mapping initiative to provide high-resolution landslide data to the public in regions of the State with a high proportion of industrial timber lands and other working lands. FWGP provides technical information and recommendations regarding erosion, landslides, and other geologic hazards on California's forested lands and watersheds where land-use decisions may affect water quality and fish habitat. FWGP is responsible for providing engineering geologic review of proposed Timber Harvest Plans, Vegetation Treatment Plans, and related activities to prevent slope stability or erosion issues that may impact public safety and the environment. These plans are expected to identify all known landslide and slope stability issues that may be impacted by vegetation management activities, but existing landslide data in these landscapes is typically limited. Plans are prepared by environmental professionals who may have experience with engineering geologic concerns but are not licensed Professional Geologists and may not consult with geologists during preparation of the plans. Many plans submitted for CGS review fail to recognize areas of concern, thereby delaying plan implementation. This new mapping aims to address that issue, while complementing landslide mapping by other CGS programs that focus on regions closer to population centers. This new mapping effort will provide critical management-relevant data to land managers, while also providing a baseline for monitoring and modeling future changes in landslide frequency expected with California’s changing climate. To facilitate this effort, up to four FWGP engineering geologists are mapping landslides and geomorphic features from lidar-derived topographic base maps at a scale of 1:2,000 within USGS 7.5-minute quadrangles following standard landslide inventory mapping protocols and feature attribution. Final products will be published as Landslide Inventory Map Sheets on compiled geologic map bases for each quadrangle with an associated pamphlet and digital database. Up to fifteen quadrangles along the north coast are expected to be published within the next year, with 3-4 maps published on an annual basis in subsequent years.

abstract: Although U.S. lithium production currently relies primarily on brines and volcanic sedimentary clay deposits, lithium-bearing rhyolites represent a potentially valuable but relatively understudied resource, particularly when developed alongside other critical minerals. Round Top Mountain, a rhyolitic laccolith in the Sierra Blanca Complex of west Texas, is interpreted to be a late-stage intrusive body that became enriched in incompatible elements during magmatic evolution. As a result, the deposit hosts significant concentrations of heavy rare earth elements (HREE) as well as other critical minerals, including lithium (~500 ppm), which is thought to reside mainly within mica. Commercial development of the Round Top deposit is scheduled to begin in 2028 using a sulfuric acid heap-leach process to recover REE, Be, Ga, Zr, Hf, and Li. However, differences in mineral reactivity suggest that valuable lithium may remain in the tailings after primary processing. Because REE-bearing fluoride minerals and fluorite dissolve more readily than several of the more resistant rhyolitic mineral phases, additional lithium may be recoverable after the initial heap-leach stage. To evaluate this potential, we conducted laboratory simulations of the planned sulfuric acid heap-leach process and characterized the critical minerals remaining after leaching. The simulated leaches recovered approximately 60% of the total lithium. We then investigated a range of chelating agents and organic acids as secondary extraction fluids to target the residual lithium with the long-term objective of achieving complete recovery.

title: Applying Debris-Flow Avulsion Research to Fan Hazard Management
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans
authors: Santi, Paul M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
abstract: Debris-flow deposits typically build fan-shaped landforms over time, as successive flows fill in low points in the topography. These shifting flow paths, known as avulsions, create frequent changes in the locations most vulnerable to debris-flow hazards, a concept not necessarily accounted for in hazard management. However, applied research has developed methods to identify the likely locations and probability of avulsion, which is the first step towards management. Databases of locations of avulsion show that they are generally associated with (1) channel obstructions, such as high availability of boulder-sized material, (2) topographic channel constrictions, (3) lobes of thicker or more viscous debris identified from previous events, (4) locations that enhance deposition of debris such as low lateral confinement of channels or decreases in channel slope angle, (5) high ratios of expected flow thickness to average channel slope, and (6) longer flow paths and locations farther down-fan. Avulsion likelihood can be predicted using stratigraphic analysis tools such as compensational stacking, which uses cross-fan exposures or stratigraphic columns from boreholes or channel walls to calculate the propensity of avulsion between successive flows. Flow runout and deposition modeling of avulsion at locations predicted by these factors helps to identify future hazard locations and is an important step beyond simply modeling runout of current conditions. The combination of these tools assists in important elements of debris-flow hazard management on alluvial fans: hazard identification, risk assessment, and delineation of inundation hazard.

abstract: Near IR-laser based, continuous ramp-heating (CRH) of foil-wrapped samples is a natural and efficient method for degassing basement K-feldspar and other anhydrous phases for 40Ar-39Ar thermochronology. CRH avoids pitfalls of incremental gas extraction via resistance-heating or CO2 laser methods including grain fracturing during rapid and repeated temperature cycling, non-optimal temperature control during short-duration heating steps, and differential coupling and partial grain fusion during a measurement sequence. CRH methodology and apparatus developed at Stanford have been re-commissioned at the USGS Moffett Field argon lab to pursue new applications. Flat, 3 mm diameter x 0.5 mm thick tantalum foil packets are heated with a focused 980-micron wavelength laser beam in a manner widely used in (U-Th)-He thermochronology. While analytical solutions of the diffusion equation exist for CRH for heating linear in inverse temperature, this results in very small 39Ar fractions at low-T and much larger 39Ar aliquots at high-T. We alternatively continuously increase temperature following a power-law relationship that helps to even out 39Ar release. Diffusion-weighted mean temperatures are calculated numerically for discrete gas aliquots using a 45 kcal/mol energy dependance. A 5-minute duty cycle for 40Ar-39Ar measurements enables 24-increment age spectra from 18 samples in 40 hours. This includes initial degassing, cooldown, and blank measurements. Temperature precision is generally < 1 degree Celsius over the 250-1500°C range. The accuracy of 2.3 micron wavelength optical pyrometer temperatures is assessed via 39Ar diffusion coefficients measured from neutron-irradiated, air-abraded beads of synthetic kalsilite glass. Reproducibility is <0.3 log10 unit with absolute values consistent with resistance heating results. Applications include thermochronology performed with basement K-feldspar, detrital K-feldspar, volcanic sanidine, and adularia. While the concentration of 40Ar ultimately limits age resolution, we present well-defined 18-24 step age spectra and Arrhenius plots for 10-100 microgram single crystals. The CRH method also permits determination of the 39Ar diffusion properties of volcanic sanidine and other anhydrous phases to evaluate ability to retain Ar during progressive eruption burial. Similarly, the thermal history significance of 40Ar-39Ar ages from hydrothermal adularia is evaluated.

title: Linking benthic microbial mats to exported biomass using depth-dependent genetic and isotopic signatures in ice-covered Lake Fryxell, Antarctica

abstract:
Perennially ice-covered lakes in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica serve as sources of organic matter to surrounding soils, which are among the most carbon-poor ecosystems on Earth. At Lake Fryxell, buoyant mobilization of benthic microbial mats (liftoff) beneath the ice drives biomass export. Bubbles nucleate within mats, enabling mats to float to and freeze into the overlying ice cover. Once within the ice, seasonal cycles of surface ice ablation and basal freezing cause the mats to move vertically through the ice, whence they are exported up to 10 years later.

We have shown that liftoff is driven by photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), which supports oxygen production and bubble formation. Consequently, the extent of the “liftoff zone” fluctuates with changes in PAR. During 2022-2025, we documented a large-scale disturbance event, with liftoff mats observed to 8.5 m depth and a doubling of the surface area supporting mobilization relative to 1980-1981 when lift-off was not observed below 8.0 m depth. To link benthic mats with exported biomass, we characterized microbial mat composition (16S rRNA) and stable isotopic signatures (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) along a depth transect and compared them to exported biomass. Principal coordinate analyses reveal distinct microbial communities between shallow (4.3-6.1 m) and deeper (>7.9 m) environments. Isotope signatures show that contemporary exported mats overlap with shallow benthic and moat mats, but not deeper environments.

These results show that contemporary biomass flux from lake to soil is sourced primarily from under-ice habitats shallower than ~6 m and the moat. The deeper mats are as yet unrepresented in exported material, which we infer to reflect the approximately one-decade lag for liftoff to migrate to the ice surface. Years with unusually large liftoff events are thus likely to enhance nutrient flux to surrounding soils, albeit some years later. Interannual variability in mat mobilization therefore represents a key process linking irradiance and organic carbon flux across these polar cryo-ecosystems.

abstract: Confining units regulate groundwater flow and aquifer vulnerability, yet their effectiveness is often difficult to quantify due to their heterogeneity. This study uses chemostratigraphy to evaluate the confining nature of the Zilpha Clay, a regionally extensive fine-grained interval, within the Middle Claiborne Group of the Eocene Memphis Aquifer system in the Northern Mississippi Embayment. Major, trace, and rare-earth element (REE) geochemistry from 185 samples collected from three continuously cored wells (AEM, MSA, EPA) across Shelby County, Tennessee, was integrated with sedimentologic descriptions of cores to construct a chemostratigraphic framework. Six lithofacies grouped into channelized, hemipelagic, and pelagic facies associations were identified, from river mouth to brackish water environment. Immobile element proxies and REE patterns indicated a broadly uniform felsic to intermediate upper continental crustal source across all wells, with minimal provenance variability. Sand- and silt-dominated channel facies showed elevated SiO₂ contents and reduced trace-element retention, whereas clay-rich facies show enrichment in Al₂O₃, TiO₂, Fe₂O₃, large-ion lithophile elements, and total REEs. Chemostratigraphic correlations identify laterally persistent marker horizons that distinguish the Zilpha clay beyond areas where the continuity was previously uncertain. Paleodepositional conditions indicate predominantly oxic to suboxic environments, with short-lived anoxic episodes. The regional extent and distinct geochemical signature of the Zilpha Clay suggest it may serve as a secondary protective layer for production wells screened below it, with implications for groundwater management.

title: Leveraging Trace Elements to Investigate Metamorphism and Petrogenesis of Kyanite Quartzites in the Virginia Piedmont

affiliations: (1) Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA

abstract:
Kyanite quartzites are economically and petrologically valuable rocks. The largest kyanite mine in the world, located at Willis Mountain in the Chopawamsic Terrane (central Virginia Piedmont) contains up to 30 wt.% kyanite and is vital to refractory industries. Kyanite quartzite from this and nearly localities are also important petrological markers for metamorphism and tectonic processes associated with continental collision and Paleozoic Appalachian orogenesis. Directly investigating records of metamorphism in these rocks using conventional geothermobarometry is challenging due to a limited assemblage of kyanite + quartz + rutile + zircon ± muscovite ± pyrite ± topaz ± staurolite. Proposed P-T constraints of ~600ºC, ~6.5 kbar for these rocks are derived from nearby garnet schist (Cochrane, 1986). However, controversies regarding the genetic association of kyanite quartzites–either with Chopawamsic metavolcanics and volcaniclastics or overlying metasedimentary units of the Arvonia formation–poses challenges to directly relating these P-T results to the kyanite quartzites.

This study aims to leverage trace element analyses to investigate P-T conditions of metamorphism directly from kyanite quartzites of the Chopawamsic Terrane. We combine textural analysis of kyanite (cathodoluminescence imaging and trace-element mapping via EPMA) with trace element thermobarometry (Zr-in-Rt and Ti-in-Qz) in kyanite quartzites from four locations in the terrane to (1) determine the number and sequence of kyanite (re)crystallization events, and (2) calculate P-T conditions of metamorphism recorded by kyanite quartzites to provide updated constraints on the metamorphic history of the terrane and conditions under which the kyanite ore formed. Quartz yields Ti < 20ppm (1s ± 2 ppm; d.l. = 3 ppm) and is zoned in Ti. Rutile yields Zr ~300-450ppm (1s ± 15ppm, d.l. = 26 ppm) with two localities yielding Zr as low as ~150 ppm. P-T results obtained from combining Ti-in-Qz and Zr-in-Rt fall broadly between ~550-750ºC and 6-16 kbar, and are carefully assessed based on petrographic and textural observations of distinct domains (inclusions in kyanite vs. matrix minerals). In addition, kyanite grains are zoned in trace element (Cr, Fe, V) that are broadly related to their color (blue, teal, white/grey) and correlate with core-rim kyanite CL-zoning. We discuss the significance of these trace element signatures with respect to discriminant diagrams proposed to identify kyanite quartzite protoliths based on trace element-based geochemical fingerprinting schemes.

abstract:
Ice sheets intermittently covered much of the Northern Hemisphere over the last several million years; yet, the degree to which they eroded bedrock and transported sediment remains poorly constrained. Here, we evaluate the landscape-scale effects of repeated Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS) glaciations across eastern North America using in-situ produced cosmogenic nuclides. We measured concentrations of 10 Be and 26 Al in quartz isolated from glacially deposited sediment (n=19) and bedrock (n=2) recovered from two deep sediment cores (89.9 and 134 m in length) along the eastern shore of Lake Michigan, and in deglacial sediment (n=14) from gravel pits, drillings, and stream cuts in New England.

Concentrations of 26 Al (3.4x10 3 to 3.2x10 5 atoms g -1 ; μ=1.2x10 5 ± 9.2x10 4 ; n=25) and 10 Be (6.4x10 2 to 5.4x10 4 atoms g -1 ; μ=2.3x10 4 ± 1.4x10 4 ; n=35) are pervasively low, independent of sample type and location. 26 Al/ 10 Be ratios are lower than at production (6.75) for 17 of the 25 samples for which we currently have 26 Al data. These low ratios suggest a short period of surface exposure followed by a prolonged burial. Across all core and gravel pit samples with dual isotope data (n=25), calculated exposure periods are short, <12 ky (μ=4.8±0.4 ky; median=4.0 ky), whereas burial times are long, up to 3350 ky (μ=510±660 ky; median=378 ky). The isotopic data mandate burial during or between exposure periods over multiple glacial cycles, likely reflecting ice sheet coverage and/or sediment storage in deglacial landforms. For the Michigan sediment cores, burial times and 26 Al/ 10 Be ratios are not stratigraphically consistent, suggesting that sediments contain nuclides produced during prior periods of near-surface, most likely interglacial, exposure.

In New England, only three gravel pit samples within the Connecticut Valley have measured 26 Al/ 10 Be ratios indistinguishable from surface production (OBC-090: 6.8±0.8, OBC-093: 6.4±0.8, OBC-097: 6.7±0.6), indicating the most efficient erosion and shortest duration of sediment storage occurred at the center of ice lobes. Four gravel pit samples, outside the Connecticut Valley (OBC-100: 4.8±0.6, OBC-110: 5.8±0.6, OBC-116: 5.5±0.7, OBC-091: 3.0±2.5), display ratios below constant exposure beyond uncertainty. Our dataset, like that of Cavnar et al. (2026) from eastern Canada, suggests that the LIS eroded and transported sediment inefficiently across much of eastern North America during the LGM.

abstract: Phenotypic evolution among lineages often proceeds in a mosaic fashion with different suites of traits, or modules, evolving at varying tempos and under different modes. This could be the product of a conserved developmental program that channels evolution in directions of greatest phenotypic (co)variation, but may also be the result of evolution across a complex multivariate adaptive landscape. These factors are not mutually exclusive and both are likely to contribute to mosaic evolution, within and between modules. The fossil record of the Miocene stickleback Gasterosteus doryssus from western Nevada provides an opportunity to evaluate the contributions of these processes to phenotypic change in a microevolutionary, within-lineage framework. Population-level trait (co)variation changes across a 16,000 year interval of marked evolutionary change, while trait-to-trait changes in means are best fit by different models of trait evolution, including OU and random walk processes. By examining the mosaic pattern of trait evolution, we document the complex microevolutionary route by which a phenotype is assembled during adaptation and gain insight into how this process shapes population-level patterns of trait (co)variation through time.

session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: Goeke, Hannah [1], Whittington, Alan [2]

abstract:
Located within Chile’s Atacama Desert, near the town of Pica, lies a discontinuous 5-centimeter-thick layer of green glass with a bulbous to grooved lower surface overlying unaltered sediment. These glasses could be one of the best preserved examples of a meteor airburst; a cosmic event where a meteor explodes in the atmosphere, releasing a cloud of extreme heat and magnitude capable of melting the ground below without leaving a crater. These glasses have been found in five small areas across a 90 km swath, atop ancient wetland sediments (Schultz et al. 2022) and radiocarbon dating places their formation in the late Pleistocene (~12,300 - 11,500 years ago).

For over a decade, scientists have debated the origin of the “Pica Glasses.” Were they forged in extreme wildfires sweeping across ancient wetlands (Roperch et al., 2017)? Or did they form in the intense heat of an airburst (Blanco and Tomlinson, 2012; map 6, Schultz et al., 2022)? Two lines of evidence support the airburst hypothesis: (i) zircon grains within the glass have partially decomposed into zirconia, requiring temperatures above 1670°C, which is far beyond the reach of wildfires or volcanic activity; (ii) their folded, vesicular textures indicate rapid cooling from a molten state, while their composition reflects a mix of local sand, organic material, and exotic fragments including nickel-bearing sulfides and calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions (Schultz et al., 2022). Most intriguingly, no related crater exists, a sign of airbursts where the explosion occurs in the atmosphere rather than on impact. Airbursts are far more common than crater-forming impacts, yet few have been recognized (Boslough & Crawford, 2008).

To test the origin of the glasses, we will heat similar desert sediment to 1400°C - 1600°C for 10 - 600 seconds (guided by models from Boslough & Crawford, 2008), then air-quench them, and compare texture and composition of the resulting glasses to those collected in the field using petrography and electron microscopy. We will also measure their viscosity, heat capacity, and thermal conductivity as a function of temperature, to aid in models for their formation and cooling.

title: Testing Models of Continental Sedimentary Rock Cycling in Northern Eurasia
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Posters)
authors: Mazko, Evgeny [1], Peters, Shanan E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(2) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
abstract: Sedimentary rocks archive the history of the Earth-life system and contain most of the surface-accessible mass of elements critical to life and climate. Understanding the formation and destruction of sedimentary rocks is, therefore, essential to understanding our sample of Earth history and the factors that govern it. The sedimentary rock cycle is typically posited to be at steady state, wherein total sedimentary rock quantity is invariant and age-independent destruction is persistent, resulting in exponential decline in surviving rock quantity with increasing rock age. Quantity-age data for sediments deposited on oceanic crust are consistent with this cycling model, but comparable data for sediments in North America suggest that the continental sedimentary rock reservoir has undergone non-steady state growth, with a lesser signature of destruction, especially among the marine sedimentary rocks comprising most of the surviving continental sediment volume. Here we use a new macrostratigraphic compilation of 166,007 rock units distributed among 2,312 regional columns spanning 15.3 million square km of northern Eurasia to assess continental sedimentary rock cycling models. On the East European Craton, sedimentary rock area peaks in the Late Devonian–Carboniferous, with pronounced minima in the middle Cambrian and Triassic–Jurassic. Marine deposits dominate the Paleozoic maximum, whereas non-marine strata predominate in the Neogene–Quaternary. On the Siberian Craton, sedimentary rock area peaks in the Cambrian, with marine deposits of this age covering nearly the entire platform; non-marine sediments are more prevalent in the Cenozoic. On both platforms and intervening areas combined, there is no decline from the Neogene to late Ediacaran in total sedimentary rock quantity with increasing age, suggesting a prominent signal of variable accommodation and a much lesser one for erosion. Although a late Ediacaran to Cambrian increase in preserved sedimentary rock quantity denotes a shift to a higher Phanerozoic baseline relative to the Precambrian, the increase in area from the Proterozoic occurs earlier and is less pronounced than it is in North America, owing to more widespread Meso- and Neoproterozoic sedimentary deposits. Within the Phanerozoic, first-order variability in sedimentary area attributable to the supercontinent cycle is similar to that in North America, but the relative magnitudes and phases of Sloss sequence-like second-order oscillations differ, suggesting more regional control on this scale of variability in the extent of sedimentation.

title: Probabilistic Flood Inundation Mapping Under Rainfall Uncertainty Using a Computationally Efficient 2D Hydrodynamic Model

authors: Munna, Md Saiful Ashraf [1], Huang, Tao [2], Savage, Bruce [3], Daniel, Brent [4], Li, Xue [5]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA

abstract: Flood inundation maps are critical tools for flood risk management, emergency preparedness, and infrastructure planning. However, current mapping practices, including Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs) developed by Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), rely on a single deterministic model configuration that does not account for uncertainty in rainfall inputs through the flood modeling workflow. Consequently, translating statistical rainfall estimates into meaningful flood inundation maps across different recurrence intervals and durations remains a challenge. This study presents a probabilistic flood inundation mapping framework based on a computationally efficient two-dimensional hydrodynamic model to quantify how uncertainty in NOAA Atlas 14 rainfall frequency estimates propagates into predicted flood inundation extents. The model was calibrated against 100-year FIRMs using the Fit Index (F) and Correctness Index (C). The top 20 parameter combinations, each run with five stochastic realizations, were used to generate a 100-member ensemble for each of the 48 rainfall scenarios comprising four return periods (50-, 100-, 500-, and 1000-year), four storm durations (1, 6, 12, and 24 hours), and three rainfall distributions (mean and 90% upper and lower confidence bounds). Model validation against 500-year FIRMs yielded F and C values up to 0.67 and 0.91, respectively. Across all scenarios, the 90% upper bound rainfall event produced inundation extents on average 20.2% greater than the mean rainfall estimate, while the lower bound produced 21.5% smaller than the mean. The resulting probabilistic inundation maps derived from the 100-member ensemble show that high-probability flood zones extend beyond the existing FIRM boundaries under upper-bound rainfall scenarios, indicating that deterministic maps may underestimate flood hazards in some areas for extreme rainfall events. Overall, the proposed probabilistic framework provides a practical approach for incorporating rainfall uncertainty into flood hazard assessments and informs better decision-making and policy planning, particularly in data scarce regions.
