title: Reconstructing Early–Middle Jurassic climate change from continental sedimentary successions in eastern Mexico
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: The Sedimentary Record of Climate Change
authors: Ruiz Urueña, Jorge Enrique [1], Martini, Michelangelo [2]
affiliations: (1) Programa de Posgrado en Ciencias de la Tierra, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, México Distrito Federal, México, Mexico
(2) Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Geología, Ciudad de Mexico, CDMX, Mexico
abstract:
The preservation of paleoclimatic signals in continental sedimentary successions is commonly complicated by the combined effects of provenance, sedimentary processes, hydraulic sorting, and diagenesis, which may obscure the original climatic signature recorded by detrital sediments. Consequently, evaluating the reliability of sedimentary archives is a critical step before reconstructing past environmental conditions. This study presents a multiproxy approach to assess the preservation of paleoclimatic information in three continental Jurassic successions of eastern Mexico (Huayacocotla, La Boca, and Cahuasas formations), deposited during the fragmentation of western equatorial Pangea.

The climatic signal was evaluated through the integration of sedimentology, modal petrography, heavy-mineral assemblages, and whole-rock geochemistry, within a U–Pb geochronological framework. Rather than relying on a single paleoclimate proxy, this integrated framework allowed us to distinguish climatic controls from compositional variations related to source-rock lithology, depositional processes, hydraulic fractionation, and post-depositional alteration.

The upper Huayacocotla Formation (Sinemurian–Pliensbachian) records alluvial fan deposits formed under humid tropical conditions, supported by depletion of labile minerals, moderate to high CIA and WIP values, coal-bearing intervals, and abundant plant remains. In contrast, the La Boca (Toarcian–Callovian) and Cahuasas (Aalenian–Callovian) formations record semi-arid to arid conditions characterized by abundant pedogenic features, preservation of labile minerals, and comparatively mild to moderate degrees of chemical weathering. Together, these successions document a regional climatic transition from humid tropical conditions during the Early Jurassic to predominantly semi-arid climates beginning in the Toarcian.

This climatic transition broadly coincides with tectonic reorganization associated with major structures (e.g., the North Oaxacan Transfer and Río Salado–Axutla fault) formed during the breakup of Pangea. Although paleolatitude remained a first-order climatic control and the studied basins remained within the tropical belt, the temporal correspondence between tectonic activity and the reconstructed climatic transition, together with the spatial distribution of humid and semi-arid environments, is consistent with paleotopographic reorganization having contributed to regional moisture redistribution across western equatorial Pangea.

abstract: Prior research on sediment cores recovered by the Olduvai Gorge Coring Project (OGCP) has established how biomarker signatures reflect paleoclimatic conditions during wet/dry cycles within Upper Bed I (~1.8 Ma). They record a stable terrestrial ecosystem with a consistent mix of woodland and grassland, while water resources were affected by the pronounced temporal variations in the hydrological cycle regulating the size and chemistry of Paleolake Olduvai. The second phase of the OGCP recovered further sediment sequences amenable to biogeochemical analyses. The cores recovered at Site 4A, located between Site 1A and 2A, included a series of lacustrine claystone beds from below the Bed I basalt from a stratigraphic unit older than any sediments exposed as outcrops in the gorge. Their aliphatic hydrocarbon distributions reveal a prominence of higher odd-numbered n -alkanes derived from plant waxes. The suite of samples shows variations in their n -C 33 / n -C 31 ratios from 0.56 to 0.77, which is comparable with most of Upper Bed I in OGCP Core 2A, except for the markedly higher values (avg. 1.04) for the Tuff IB to IF interval. Two samples from Section 78Q differ markedly from overlying sequences as they contain far higher proportions of C 27 and C 29 n -alkanes, suggestive of increased contributions from C 3 plants. Both samples possess series of des-A-triterpenoids derived from angiosperms, which were not observed in any Upper Bed I samples from OGCP Core 2A. These characteristics likely reflect a wetter climate than the overlying claystone intervals within Upper Bed I. In addition, the suites of hopanes and hopenes prominent in these samples suggest active bacterial cycling of organic matter.

title: Landslide Inventory Mapping in Portions of Yavapai County, Central Arizona: Abundant Landslides near Bagdad, Yarnell, Big Bug Mesa, and Jerome

abstract:
Landslides were mapped in portions of Yavapai County, central Arizona, with funding from the USGS Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Program. We selected four study areas (827mi 2 /2,140km 2 ) within Yavapai County (8,178mi 2 /21,180km 2 ) based on available lidar, known/suspected slides, and moderate–high landslide susceptibility from a recent nationwide susceptibility model.

The Bagdad study area hosts an active open-pit copper/molybdenum mine and is adjacent to a lithium-bearing clay deposit. US-93, the future Interstate 11 corridor, passes through the study area. Approximately 30 landslides were previously mapped in this area, predominantly along the edges of basalt-capped mesas. We refined the boundaries of these slides and identified 125 additional slides, primarily in areas underlain by a shrink-swell clay unit in the US-93/I-11 corridor and where mesa-capping basalt overlies rhyolitic tuff altered to clay north and east of Bagdad.

The Yarnell study area, which contains placer/lode gold deposits and a Paleoproterozoic copper mine, contained no previously mapped landslides. We identified 35 landslides in this area. Notable findings include the Antelope Peak slide ~1.5km southeast of Yarnell and landslides along Kirkland Creek, ~0.5km SE of SR-89, both in areas where basalt overlies fine-grained sedimentary units.

The Big Bug Mesa study area has an extensive mining history, but no previously mapped landslides. We identified 53 landslides, including large, deep-seated slides along the edge of Miocene basalt-capped Big Bug Mesa and slides along steep canyon walls and roadcuts in Paleoproterozoic metaigneous rocks.

The Jerome study area hosts two Paleoproterozoic volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits that produced over 3.7 billion pounds of copper. Jerome is now a popular tourist destination with over one million annual visitors. The main parking area in town sits atop a historic landslide with major movement in 1936–1937 that destroyed numerous buildings. The slide was previously mapped as 200m long, but lidar data and historical aerial imagery suggest landslide reactivation between 1943–1953 that mobilized >450m of the hillslope. We mapped 106 slides in this area, including several historically active slides.

This project increased the number of known landslides in Yavapai County from 200 to 520 and added ~38 km 2 of mapped landslide area to the Arizona Statewide Landslide Inventory Database to be utilized by land-use planners, emergency managers, landslide researchers, and the public.

title: Cross Comparison Between Raman Spectroscopy of Carbonaceous Material and Quartz Opening Angle Thermometry on the Phyllite-Quartzite Unit in Crete Greece
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Houghton, Grayson Kepner [1], Rahl, Jeffrey M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, Virginia, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
abstract: Quantifying the temperature history of rocks is essential for testing models for various geologic processes and understanding the tectonic history of an area. Two commonly employed methods for determining temperature are Raman Spectroscopy of Carbonaceous Material (RSCM) thermometry and quartz opening-angle thermometry. The RSCM thermometer is based on the Raman spectra of the organic material commonly found in metasedimentary rocks, which is progressively transformed from poorly organized organic material and to highly ordered graphite with increasing temperature. The quartz opening angle thermometer is based on the crystallographic preferred orientations of quartz, which commonly develop a cross-girdled appearance. The angle between the limbs on a pole figure is controlled by the relative activity of slip systems in quartz, particularly the competition between basal <a> and prism [c], and which are dependent on deformation temperature. Although both methods are widely used, there has been little systematic comparison of these two approaches, in part due to the challenge of finding samples suitable for both techniques. Here, we describe new RSCM and quartz opening angle data from samples of the Phyllite-Quartzite unit, a package of metasediments exposed in Crete, Greece. We find RSCM temperatures ranging from ~350-400°C and quartz opening angle temperatures from ~390-520°C. Direct comparisons from individual samples show that opening angles are consistently ~90°C hotter than estimates based on RSCM. Exploratory analyses into samples from other geologic terrains suggest that the temperature offset observed may be typical of the Crete rocks rather than a systematic bias in the two methodologies. One potential explanation for the observed mismatch is the geologic history of the Cretan rocks – which involved rapid subduction, burial, and exhumation – provided insufficient time for the graphitization process to proceed to equilibrium, producing lower-than-expected temperature estimates. Our ongoing work seeks to better document and interpret these observations.

abstract: Fire, canopy cover, hydrology, and salmonids are intrinsically intertwined in Idaho’s ponderosa pine-mixed conifer forests of the Pacific Northwest. Increasing wildfire intensity and severity across the western United States is swamping managers with multivariate land management decisions that beget collaboration amongst scientists, managers, tribal agencies, and landowners. As a part of the Zena Creek Field School, a team of scientists and professionals led university students in field data collection to bolster interdisciplinary knowledge and inform future beaver dam analog (BDA) placement in an effort to restore an incised mountain creek and increase salmonid habitat. BDA implementation will inundate historic side channels currently occupied by conifers, inducing mortality in some while increasing water availability for others. This mortality contributes large wood, an essential component of riparian complexity and salmonid habitat, to the stream system and joins fire, debris flows, and chainsaw treatment as a channel complexity recruitment mechanism. Canopy water-shading capacity, important to maintaining cold-water thermal refugia for salmonids, is being quantified via line-point intercept transects across four reference reaches, while fuel connectivity in the sub-acre inundation footprint will be assessed through a full census of affected trees (DBH, height, crown base height) to derive canopy fuel load, bulk density, and base height using the Forest Vegetation Simulator’s Fire and Fuels Extension. Comparing these metrics across the inundated area will allow managers to weigh crown fire hazard against thermal refugia benefit on a site-specific basis. A vouchered plant collection, completed with a botanist in July 2026, supports species-level identification across both efforts. These pre-treatment data will serve as a baseline for a multiple before-after-control-impact (MBACI) monitoring design following BDA installation. These findings will be integrated into a land manager and landowner toolkit to support more holistic management of multivariate riparian-fire systems.

abstract: Dust emission is controlled by complex surface and atmospheric interactions making accurate prediction challenging. This study integrates fractional vegetative cover derived from remote sensing spectral mixture analysis (SMA), Drought Severity Coverage Index (DCSI) data, and wind speed data between 2004 and 2024 to understand the drivers of dust emissions in the Escalante Desert (ED), Milford Flat (MF), and Dugway Proving Ground (DW) regions of Utah’s Great Basin. The estimated seasonal fractional vegetative cover reveals that non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV) dominates ED, ranging between 38 and 75%, while bare soil (BA) dominates both MF (26.7 - 75.6%) and DW (23.9 - 88.2%). ED showed elevated photosynthetic vegetation (PV) from 2014 to the later years compared to previous years with NPV peaking in fall. In MF, spring had highest PV fractions and fall had highest NPV fractions. DW shows more varying peaks of PV and NPV alternating between spring and fall. Across the study areas, seasonal analysis of most years revealed increased BA in summer with higher PV in the spring and fall. Dust events for the study occurred mostly in the spring and summer seasons with associated wind speeds of over 10 m/s. Dust-generating winds decrease with higher BA exposure and increase with higher vegetation cover. Drought reduces surface roughness by lowering vegetation cover and increasing soil exposure. However, dust events also occurred during periods without drought implicating anthropogenic disturbances such as possible military activities at DW and post-fire reseeding at MF. Thus, dust events in the study area are controlled by the interaction of land surface conditions and meteorological inputs rather than by drought alone. The integration of fractional covers, drought and wind data provides a framework for assessing dust emission potential. Our results highlight the differences in vegetation phenology and implications for seasonal dust emission susceptibility. It also reveals that remote sensing is a valuable tool for rapid environmental monitoring and air quality risk assessment in these regions.

abstract: As society continues to grow, the demand for critical minerals and rare earth elements (REEs) increase. Obtaining critical minerals and REEs, however, has become more difficult due to factors such as geographic abundance and geopolitics, creating a search for alternative domestic sources. Recently, byproducts of coal mining and coal power generation have emerged as one of these sources. Rocks associated with the Kittanning coal seams within the Middle Pennsylvanian Allegheny Formation of the central Appalachian Basin have been shown to be enriched in critical minerals, including REEs, which has attracted attention to the Kittanning as a potential critical mineral feedstock. Previous work has demonstrated enrichment in the Lower Kittanning was observed in coal ash, underclay and overburden materials, with total rare earth element content of Lower Kittanning coals correlates strongly with Si concentration, with light REEs likely derived from a clastic source and some heavy REEs bound to organic matter in the coal. In order to perform a more detailed test of the distribution of critical mineral enrichment in the Kittanning interval, this study investigates the sedimentology and geochemistry of core samples from the Upper, Lower, and Middle Kittanning coal products from the Upper Potomac Coal Field in western Maryland. These cores preserve floor and roof rocks, with rare preservation of the coal seam itself. Sedimentological description at the centimeter scale shows that the coal seams are associated with several variable facies, including dark gray laminated siliciclastic mud, medium gray very laminated siltstone to very fine-grained sandstone, and light-colored, poorly sorted medium-grained sandstone. Preliminary geochemical analysis was performed at a 10 cm sampling interval using a HITACHI X-MET8000 portable XRF and rock powder produced by a rotary drill. Results from 16 samples showed moderate abundance of lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium, and yttrium totalling a few hundred ppm. Thus far, the total concentration of these 5 critical elements in roof rocks ranges from 113 - 460 ppm (average = 305 ppm), parting rock ranges from 100 - 480 ppm (average = 282 ppm), and floor rocks ranges from 99 - 545 ppm (average = 214 ppm). These analyses will be compared with in situ portable XRF analysis of unprepared core material and ultimately ICP-MS analyses to determine the impact on assessment of the Kittanning coal interval as a critical minerals resource.

abstract: Fire-enhanced runoff and erosion can increase the likelihood and magnitude of postfire flow hazards (PFFH). PFFH include landslides, debris flows, flash floods, and surface runoff on hillslopes that can degrade water quality and threaten life and infrastructure. Burned landscapes are most susceptible to postfire flows in the first few months to a year after fire, leaving limited time to implement mitigation strategies. Here, we review approaches for evaluating postfire flow hazards within a prefire context, with an emphasis on methods and datasets commonly applied in the western US. We reviewed 36 reports and peer reviewed articles documenting prefire assessments of PFFHs in the US, Europe, Australia, and China from local (10 km 2 ) to regional scales (100,000+ km 2 ). Although objectives and scales vary, many prefire assessment frameworks share common elements, such as (1) defining objectives and values at risk, (2) estimating future fire probability, extent, and severity, (3) modeling hydrologic and geomorphic responses to fire, and (4) quantifying hazard, risk, and potential economic impacts. Methods for estimating the severity of future fires vary from the definition of idealized, decision-relevant scenarios to fire behavior modeling and data-driven approaches. Models employed to estimate postfire flow likelihood and magnitude are often empirical and can be implemented over large study areas in a geographic information system. Stakeholder engagement most commonly informed objectives and definitions of decision-relevant scenarios for future fire activity. Prefire assessments of PFFHs could be supported by improved methods for quantifying uncertainty through multiple models linked via input/output exchanges, increased engagement with decision-makers to identify the most useful modeling targets, and generalizable approaches for linking fire severity to input parameters used in flow models. Prefire assessments could play an important role in prioritizing mitigation opportunities and improving community resilience to postfire flow hazards.

abstract:
The Upper Cretaceous Tropic Shale of southern Utah captures oceanographic changes that occurred along the shallow (<80-100 m) western margin of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) during Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2). To resolve these changes at high temporal resolution (<5 ka), this study reports planktic and benthic foraminiferal assemblages in relation to calcareous nannofossils, stable organic carbon isotope (d 13 C org ) chemostratigraphy, and organic biomarker datasets compiled from a composite 35-m outcrop and core section spanning ~1.09 myr.

The onset of OAE2, identified by a distinctive d 13 C org signature, coincided with a rapid transgression and a brief interval of potential cooling as suggested by the abundance of nannofossil Biscutum constans . The tiny opportunistic planktic Guembelitra cenomana initially dominated surface waters and infaunal benthic species Neobulimina albertensis dominated at the seafloor. Other rare species of calcareous benthics, including Hoeglundina charlottae and Buliminella fabilis , demonstrate that this interval is correlative with the "Benthonic Zone" that marks an oxygenation event elsewhere in the WIS.

Epifaunal benthic Gavelinella dakotaensis proliferated as OAE2 intensified in the interval below Bentonite B during the late Cenomanian. The " Gavelinella acme" generally coincides with the widespread planktic “ Heterohelix shift”, the latter likely triggered by high productivity and/or photic zone euxinia. However, G. dakotaensis likely records seafloor ventilation, proposed to be a function of caballing (downwelling and mixing) along a strong Boreal-Tethyan oceanographic front. Such frontal conditions appear to have alternated with euxinic conditions--marked by abundances of green sulfur bacteria biomarkers and peaks of Planoheterohelix and --related to stratification as suggested by the nannofossil species Eprolithus floralis and Cyclagelosphaera margerelii . The peak of OAE2 is marked by an abrupt shift back to Neobulimina dominance in benthic assemblages in the latest Cenomanian as the oceanic front waned and stratification again became established with the incursion of oxygen-poor Tethyan waters. Elevated Biscutum abundances suggest potential surface water cooling during the early Turonian as OAE2 waned.

These results show the " Gavelinella acme" was longer-lived and Neobulimina dominance occurred earlier along the western margin of the WIS compared to studies across the seaway, suggesting that these bioevents were diachronous. The OAE2 interval in the WIS was characterized by dynamic changes in relative sea level and productivity, as well as by frontal mixing or stratification of Boreal and Tethyan-sourced water.

title: Evaluating the Presence of Atrazine, Glyphosate, and Metolachlor within a Midwestern USA Agricultural Watershed
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Flegel, Lauren E. [1], Lemke, Lawrence D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI,
abstract:
In the midwestern United States, where corn and soybeans are commonly grown, atrazine, glyphosate, and metolachlor are frequently applied as herbicides on agricultural fields. Each of these compounds has the potential to persist in soils, runoff into waterways, and negatively impact aquatic ecosystems. However, testing surface water for atrazine, glyphosate, and metolachlor is expensive (typically $300 or more per sample), and, despite their widespread use, they are not routinely included in laboratory pesticide screening analyses. Consequently, we set out to measure atrazine, glyphosate, and metolachlor concentrations in surface waters of the Little Swan Creek watershed (HUC 040500010402) in south central Michigan to evaluate how lake retention and surface water processes influence contaminant attenuation prior to groundwater recharge. 80% of the land use in this watershed is agricultural, with corn and soybeans as the primary crops. Hence, we expected to find atrazine, glyphosate, and metolachlor in the surface waters of the watershed.

On July 21, 2026, we collected samples under dry weather conditions at six locations chosen to represent watershed segments upstream and downstream of a drainage lake located in the approximate center of the 20,000-acre (81 km 2 ) watershed. Results detected atrazine at relatively low concentrations (0.1 ug/L) in one location downstream of the lake. Other locations were non-detect, indicating concentrations below the reporting limits for all three analytes.

Our results suggest that surface waters in the watershed are not subjected to prolonged high concentrations of atrazine, glyphosate, or metolachlor in mid-summer months. However, wet weather sampling could reveal short-term periods when concentrations may be higher. Alternatively, unseasonally high rainfall in April 2026 may have flushed these herbicides, which are typically applied early in the growing season, through the watershed prior to our sampling. In addition, natural degradation processes could have reduced herbicide concentrations. Future studies should also sample for the highly persistent degradates of these compounds, such as desethylatrazine (atrazine), aminomethylphosphonic acid (glyphosate), and metolachlor ethanesulfonic acid or metolachlor oxanilic acid, to investigate their environmental fate in surface water bodies.

title: Experiments on the Use of Hydrogen Peroxide to Control Disinfection Biproducts in Aquifer Recharge Water
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions (Posters)
authors: Howe, Julian [1]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, Washington, USA
abstract: Warmer winters in the Pacific Northwest have resulted in reduced snowpack and available snowmelt through spring and summer months, putting additional pressure on already hard to meet water demands. To help meet demands, surface water can be pumped into depleted aquifers in the winter, and pumped out when it is needed. This management practice, referred to as Aquifer Storage and Recovery (ASR), is being pursued by several municipalities throughout Washington state. Water quality criteria in Washington State require disinfection of “recharge water”, which can result in the formation of disinfection byproducts (DBPs), some of which can be toxic and carcinogenic. One group of DBPs of concern are Trihalomethanes (THMs) which form when organic matter interacts with the hypochlorite ion. It has been proposed that treating the recharge water with hydrogen peroxide before it is pumped into the ground can reduce the formation of THMs. Benchtop laboratory experiments controlling Total Organic Carbon (TOC) concentration, Chlorine dose, and hydrogen peroxide dose can help determine the efficacy of this proposed treatment as well as the optimal timing and dosage of hydrogen peroxide before in situ pilot studies are conducted.

title: An Argon Dating Data Repository (KArAr) Supported by the FIESTA Open Source Software Suite
session_title: Data-driven approaches for aligning geologic information in time
authors: Jarboe, Nicholas [1], Minnett, Rupert [2], Koppers, Anthony [3]
affiliations: (1) Jarboe Enterprises, Carbondale, CO, USA; via Oregon State University, Corvallis, CO, USA
(2) Cognese, Ft Lauderdale, FL, USA; via Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA

abstract:
FIESTA (earthref.org/FIESTA) is an open source software suite that powers the KArAr geochronology (https://karar.earthref.org/KArAr) data repository, the Magnetic Information Consortium's (MagIC - www.earthref.org/MagIC) geo, rock and paleomagnetic data repository and many others. FIESTA is open source software and is available on GitHub (github.com/earthref). It was developed to be configurable, enabling the creation of other data repositories with a much lower effort and cost than a bespoke data repository solution. The website front end, searching, uploading, DOI creation, validation, and archiving systems are reused. The main work needed to create a new repository is for a community to create and agree on a data model (the data that is required for a dataset to be added and the other optional data fields) and data file format conversion. AI coding assistants continue to improve at a rapid rate which also eases the cost of creating and maintaining data repository systems.

We have used FIESTA to create a data repository for 40 Ar/ 39 Ar and K/Ar rock ages (KArAr -karar.earthref.org) using the guidelines found in Renne et al., 2009 with additional fields informed from the MassSpec and ArArCalc 40Ar/39Ar data acquisition/analysis software. We hope to expand the FIESTA repository group to include other rock dating systems in the near future and welcome others who are interested in using FIESTA in their own projects to join us and collaborate on this project.

title: Electrical Conductivity of a Major Lithium Host, Spodumene, in the Crust: Implications for Detection
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Ashley, Aaron Wolfgang [1], Manthilake, Geeth [2], Muller, Remi [3], Falvard, Simon [4], Dominique, Jessy [5], Bouhifd, Mohamed Ali [6]

abstract: Critical minerals are essential for modern technologies and the transition to renewable energy systems. Among these, lithium (Li) is a key component of rechargeable batteries in portable electronics and electric vehicles, thus resulting in increasing demand for economically viable Li deposits. When exposed at the surface or still buried at shallow depths (typically less than a km), field observations and geologic mapping are essential to constraining the distribution and formation processes of such deposits. However, many Li-bearing deposits are formed from magmatic and/or hydrothermal processes that emplace the ore bodies deeper within the crust (often multiple km). Geophysical remote sensing techniques, such as magnetotelluric and seismic surveys, provide powerful tools to potentially detect, characterize, and study such deeper deposits. One challenge, however, is that geophysical observations are combined signals from the mineralogy, rock fabrics, and potential fluids and/or magma present within the subsurface. Laboratory-based measurements on the physical properties, such as electrical and elastic responses, of Li-bearing minerals are therefore crucial to deciphering their potential contributions to geophysical observations. In turn, these data can enable detection of the minerals and help elucidate their economic potential and formational histories. Here, we will present the first step in our investigation of a major Li-host, spodumene (LiAlSi 2 O 6 ), in which we experimentally measured its electrical conductivity at crustal pressures (P) ≤ 10 kbar (roughly ≤ 30 km depth) and temperatures (T) ≤ 900 °C. Our measurements constrain the combined P-T effects on the conductivity, allowing us to evaluate the potential to detect buried spodumene-rich resources from magnetotelluric observations. We also investigated the conductivity along the monoclinic crystallographic axes of spodumene. The results confirm the persistence of anisotropy in the electrical conduction to higher P-T, further enabling us to evaluate the effect of crystal orientation on magnetotelluric data.

title: Shallow subsidence steals elevation from U.S. Atlantic Coast marshes
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Hasan, Md Asif [1], Tornqvist, Torbjorn E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Tulane University, New Orleans, LA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Tulane University, New Orleans, LA, USA
abstract: Shallow subsidence (SS) can substantially reduce marsh elevation gain relative to sea level. While compaction and organic matter decomposition in marsh strata are well documented, direct measurements of net shallow subsidence remain sparse, and its spatial distribution across broad coastal gradients is poorly known. We analyzed SS rates measured from surface elevation table–marker horizon (SET-MH) records at 308 tidal marsh sites along the U.S. Atlantic Coast. SS rates are modest at most sites (25th–75th percentiles −2.4 to +2.6 mm/y), indicating that both subsidence and subsurface expansion occur within the coastal wetland landscape. Spatial patterns are pronounced. In the South Atlantic (North Carolina to Florida), 68% of sites are actively subsiding (25th–75th percentiles −0.1 to +2.6 mm/y). The North Atlantic (Massachusetts to Connecticut) is dominated by expansion, with only 34% of sites subsiding (−3.8 to +1.0 mm/y). The Mid-Atlantic (New York to Virginia) is intermediate, with 47% of sites subsiding (25th–75th percentiles −2.5 to +3.7 mm/y). This regional contrast likely reflects variation in soil composition and organic matter dynamics. One possibility is that southern marshes are more prone to decomposition and autocompaction under warmer temperatures and higher microbial activity, while cooler conditions, slower decomposition, and denser root structures sustain soil volume in northern marshes. An alternative, not mutually exclusive, explanation is that regional differences in mineral content govern the pattern, since southern marshes tending to be more minerogenic, with higher mineral fractions increase effective stress and compaction potential. Distinguishing between these mechanisms requires paired measurements of soil organic matter and bulk density across the latitudinal gradient. Regardless of cause, these patterns are consistent with conceptual frameworks in which shallow subsidence is driven by processes acting within the root zone and upper stratigraphic profile, meaning surface accretion alone does not reliably indicate vertical stability.

title: Mapping Martian Lava Flow Fields: Pāhoehoe Flow Morphologies in the Tharsis Volcanic Province
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Crown, David A. [1], Berman, Daniel C. [2], Scheidt, Stephen P. [3], Garry, W. Brent [4]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA
(3) University of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD, USA; Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA

abstract: This investigation examines the distribution, types, topographic attributes, and spatial and temporal contexts of pāhoehoe flow morphologies on Mars in order to assess lava flow emplacement processes and the development of Martian lava flow fields. We utilized high-resolution imaging and topographic datasets to characterize two regions within the peripheral plains that surround the Tharsis Montes: a) Southern Tharsis (10-40°S, 115-145°W), including lava flow fields that comprise the SW rift apron of Arsia Mons, and b) Eastern Tharsis (0-15°N, 85-107°W), where volcanic plains east of Ascraeus and Pavonis Montes include rift apron flows mixed with flows sourced at small local vents. In each study areas, we have identified pāhoehoe morphologies and mapped major flow field features. Study area maps show vents (where observed), central channels of rugged, elongate flows (‘a‘ā-like), distributary features for pāhoehoe (including lava tubes, narrow channels, and sinuous ridges), and plateau-like flows attributed to inflation. Sheet flows with smooth and platy-ridged surface textures are also noted. Following generation of regional flow fields maps, we conducted detailed analyses of flow characteristics at sites with representative pāhoehoe morphologies, utilizing HiRISE and CTX images and digital terrain models. Pāhoehoe-like characteristics and evidence for related flow inflation include plateau-like flow forms, sinuous ridges/plateaus, pitted surfaces, and lobate, irregular, and digitate margins with steep and stepped profiles. Branching/connective relationships and margin characteristics indicate compound flow behavior. Pāhoehoe-like morphologies are also found in association with ridged sheet flows with evidence for low viscosity interiors that feed breakouts as flows encounter changes in topography. Morphologic and morphometric attributes of pāhoehoe-like flows and the nature of their distributary features, which contrast with adjacent rough-surfaced, thick flows with central channel and lateral levees, indicate the occurrence of intermingled flow fields on Mars with end-member lava types analogous to Hawaiian basaltic flow fields and include features diagnostic of pāhoehoe lava flows. Flow inflation is common in these Tharsis study areas and occurs along pāhoehoe distributary features, with inflation plateaus increasing in abundance and forming large lava plains in southern Tharsis.

title: Examining Historical Events Through Modern Techniques, a Geochemical Analysis of the 1919-1920 Maunaiki eruption from the Southwest Rift Zone of Kīlauea volcano, Hawaii (U.S.A)

abstract: Kīlauea volcano (Hawaii, U.S.A.) has had 75+ eruptive periods in the last ~200 years; >10% of these eruptions have occurred from the Southwest Rift Zone (SWRZ) and/or south caldera (SC) region, with only four being well documented. SWRZ/SC eruptions have been short-lived (four days in 1971, six hours in 1974, and eight hours in 2024), are small in volume (each were less than one-million cubic meters), and are now covered by other deposits. In contrast, the SWRZ Maunaiki eruption (1919-1920) occurred over an eight-month period and erupted 46-million cubic meters of lava. The opening phase of the eruption, characterized by ‘a‘ā flows, lasted for ~one month, followed by three months of shield building and an additional four months of pāhoehoe and tube-fed flow field development. We integrate field observations, whole-rock geochemistry, and olivine petrography to compare different phases of the Maunaiki eruption to better understand this anomalously long SWRZ event. Whole rock analysis using energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence (EDXRF) shows an initial MgO concentration of 7.81 wt.% for the opening phase. This drops to 7.18 wt.% during shield building and increases to 7.30 wt.% during the final pāhoehoe flow field growth. Olivine crystals from the shield building stage were analyzed by electron probe microanalysis. We observe euhedral olivine crystals (0.5-2.0 mm) that are either normally zoned in forsterite (Fo; Mg/(Mg+Fe)x100; Fo core >Fo rim ; n=18) or have complex zoning with a reverse zoned interior followed by normal zoning toward the crystal-melt boundary (n=3). Olivine core compositions (n=21) range from Fo 84.4-90.2 . with 81% falling between Fo 86.5-89.5 . All crystal rims are Fo 80.5-83.2 . These preliminary results suggest that magma was stored prior to the eruption and that multiple injections into the storage system may have driven the multiple eruptive pulses. Future work will incorporate olivine analyses on the initial and flow field growth stages, modeling of compositional zoning for timescales of diffusive re-equilibration for each stage, and comparing these results to other SWRZ/SC eruptions.

title: Extending GBDB from Sections to Specimens: Reflections on Data Integration and Interoperability
session_title: Data-driven approaches for aligning geologic information in time
authors: Na, Lin [1], Li, Qi-jian [2], Zhu, Ming-hang [3], Lin, Yun-kai [4], Cui, Yu-han [5]
affiliations: (1) Big Data Center, Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Nanjing, China

abstract:
The rapid growth of digital collections, paleontological databases, and AI-enabled research is transforming how geological and paleobiological data are generated and used. As paleontological databases continue to diversify, many scientific questions increasingly benefit from combining complementary resources developed for different purposes. While community efforts have already made substantial progress toward improving interoperability through shared standards, identifiers, and vocabularies, our experience developing the Geobiodiversity Database (GBDB) has reinforced the practical value of designing data outputs that are straightforward to exchange, combine, and reuse.

GBDB was originally developed as a section-centered platform in which stratigraphic sections provide the framework linking lithostratigraphy, fossil ranges (FADs and LADs), and geological context. This architecture has proven particularly effective for integrated stratigraphy, biostratigraphic correlation, and diversity analyses based on correlated stratigraphic ranges. At the same time, the recent development of standardized occurrence outputs and application programming interfaces (APIs) has greatly improved the integration of GBDB with occurrence-based resources, expanding the range of analyses that users can perform without requiring detailed knowledge of the database's internal structure. Building on this experience, GBDB is now extending its architecture to incorporate specimen-level information while preserving its section-based foundation. Individual specimens remain explicitly linked to their precise stratigraphic positions while integrating photographs, thin sections, SEM and CT imagery, three-dimensional models, morphometric measurements, geochemical analyses, and other associated data. This development serves as one example of how increasingly rich and multimodal geological information can remain closely connected to its geological context while also being designed for broader reuse.

The evolution of GBDB, that is, from sections to standardized occurrences and now to specimens, has prompted us to reflect on a broader question. As paleontological infrastructure continues to diversify, continued attention to user-facing data exchange may be as important as advances in database architecture itself. We hope our practical experience from GBDB can contribute to the ongoing community discussion on how independently developed databases can remain specialized in design while becoming easier for researchers to connect, integrate, and reuse.

title: Paleontological Proxies Support a Brackish Paleoenvironment for the Mississippian-age Northview Formation (MO, USA)
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Casey, Spencer Ray [1], Rovey, Charles W. [2], Bassett, Damon [3], Tackett, Lydia [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Missouri State University, Springfield, MO, USA; Missouri Geological Survey, Missouri Department of Natural Resources, Rolla, MO, USA

abstract: The fossil fauna of the Northview Formation located in southwestern Missouri was left unstudied for a significant period of time until recent publication of depositional hypotheses. Utilizing paleontological descriptions as early as 1855 and current paleontological concepts alongside recent lithological analyses of the Northview Formation, it is the goal of this study to create a better understanding of the role fossil fauna play in determining the paleoenvironment of the Northview Formation. To accomplish this, fossil specimens were collected from various localities where the formation is exposed, measured, observed for specific morphological characteristics, and then subjected to the Shannon Index while some species were also subjected to the Berger-Parker Index. The results show significant evidence in support of a deltaic origin in the assemblages, size, growth characteristics, and biodiversity of present macrofossils. This study also questions the possibility of euryhaline brachiopod species within the Northview Formation. Although the paleontological evidence alone would fail to specifically indicate a deltaic depositional environment, this evidence when compared to the lithological characteristics from Rovey et al. (2021, 2024) strengthens their original hypothesis.

title: Mineralogy and Enrichment Mechanisms of Clay Hosted Lithium in the Red Mountain Deposit, Nye County, Nevada
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Welch, Isabella C. [1], Gans, Phillip B. [2], Zepeda-Rosales, Miguel [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) Earth Science, UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(3) Material Science, UC Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
abstract:
As the shift to renewable energy, electric vehicles, and smart devices continues to grow, so does the societal demand for lithium. Venari Mineral’s Red Mountain Lithium Project in east-central Nevada has identified widespread high grade lithium mineralization (up to 5,000 ppm) in clay rich horizons of the Horse Camp Formation, a Middle Miocene (~16.5–15 Ma) syn-extensional basin fill (Gans, 2017, this vol). The highest grade intervals are found within clay-rich palustrine, shallow lucustrine, delta fore-slope, and clay-rich parna deposits of the upper stratigraphic section (Gans,et al, 2026 this vol). Unlike other volcano-sedimentary Li deposits, (e.g. Thancker Pass, Rhyolite Ridge) the Horse Camp basin lacks proximal coeval rhyolitic volcanism. Instead, it apparently leached Li from Eocene silicic volcanic detritus and intercalated fallout tuffs raising questions about the mode of enrichment.

Clay minerals were separated from a suite of drill core and surface samples using Stokes law in preparation for XRD analysis. Mineralogy was determined using the XRD by correlating 2θ angle peaks with the associated D-spacing of known clay species. Clay samples were tested in air dried, hydrated, and heated states to constrain identifications. Analysis of clays separated from high Li grade intervals indicate that high Mg smectite clays (e.g. Hectorite) are the primary host of Li with standard 2θ peaks of ~7°. Detailed geologic mapping of the SE part of the basin fill at 1:2000m scale combined with 3 measured sections reveal abrupt lateral changes in lithofacies and clay mineralogy. Integrated field work and XRD /EDS analyses show probable kaolinite/illite mixed clays in subaerial/ fan delta conglomerate, siltstone and sandstone intervals and Mg-rich smectites in highly permeable and clay rich lithologies (subaqueous soft-sed breccias, clay rich sandstones/ marl, and claystone). These observations suggest that the incorporation of Li into Mg rich smectites occurred as a secondary process involving later diagenesis and fluxing of concentrated saline brines which altered pre-existing clays rather than a primary function of silicate weathering.

title: Building the Next Generation of Quantitative Micropaleontologists: Undergraduate Researchers Develop a Standardized MicroCT Workflow for Benthic Foraminifera
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence (Posters)
authors: Roush, Jackson [1], Burkett, Ashley [2], Bowser, Samuel [3], Goldstein, Susan [4]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
(2) Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
(3) Doghouse Laboratory, Schroon Lake, NY,
(4) department of geology, University of Georgia, Athens, Georgia, USA
abstract:
High-resolution X-ray micro-computed tomography (MicroCT) is transforming micropaleontological research by enabling non-destructive visualization of internal morphology and quantitative three-dimensional morphometric analyses. However, the large volume of data generated presents a significant processing bottleneck, creating an opportunity for undergraduate researchers to contribute meaningfully to active research while developing advanced technical skills. We developed a standardized MicroCT workflow that integrated undergraduate researchers into every stage of data processing for a large morphometric study of the Antarctic benthic foraminifer Cibicides antarctica.

Working within an active research project, undergraduate students processed more than 150 MicroCT datasets using standardized protocols for volume segmentation, artifact removal, surface reconstruction, and extraction of quantitative morphometric measurements. Rather than performing repetitive tasks, students were trained to recognize imaging artifacts, evaluate segmentation quality, troubleshoot complex specimens, and maintain consistency across the dataset through documented quality-control procedures. Their contributions produced research-grade datasets while establishing reproducible workflows that can be applied to future MicroCT studies.

Beyond technical proficiency, students gained experience working within a collaborative research environment, participating in discussions of experimental design, biological interpretation, and data reproducibility. The project exposed students to quantitative paleobiology, digital imaging, computational analysis, and scientific communication while demonstrating how undergraduate researchers can contribute directly to publishable research. This model illustrates how integrating undergraduate researchers into advanced imaging projects simultaneously accelerates scientific discovery, creates standardized analytical pipelines, and provides authentic workforce training in the computational and quantitative skills that are increasingly central to modern micropaleontology and geoscience research.

title: Monitoring Effects of Postfire Flows on Flood Mitigation Structures Below the 2022 Pipeline Fire Burn Area
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society (Posters)
authors: Beers, Rebecca Louise [1], McGuire, Luke A. [2], Youberg, Ann M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Arizona Geological Survey at University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(2) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(3) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
abstract: Communities in fire-prone areas are subject to significant, life-threatening, and costly impacts from wildfires and subsequent postfire flooding, prompting a need for enhanced community resilience through postfire flood mitigation. As postfire flooding becomes more prevalent in fire-prone communities and beyond, new flood mitigation strategies are being evaluated. Communities near Flagstaff, Arizona, USA, experienced significant flooding following the 2022 Pipeline Fire, prompting the construction of eight flood mitigation structures in watersheds upstream of impacted neighborhoods. The mitigation strategy involves reshaping alluvial fans and floodplains to create broad, low-relief surfaces to decrease flood-flow velocities and promote infiltration and sediment deposition. We assessed the efficacy of this mitigation strategy below the Pipeline Fire burn area during the 2023, 2024, and 2025 monsoons though repeat structure-from-motion surveys (SfM). During this period, three intense, short-duration rain events occurred over the headwaters of one of the structures, producing debris flows on 30 July 2023 and 12 August 2025, and a hyperconcentrated flow on 2 September 2023. Our SfM surveys indicate that although sediment was deposited across the upper third of the structure, erosion dominated the lower two-thirds following each event, resulting in a net sediment deficit, demonstrating that the structure became a sediment source rather than a sink. Concurrent monitoring of headwater soil hydraulic properties (SHPs) indicates hydrologic recovery trajectories that differ from those reported at other wildfire locations across the southwestern US. The magnitude and timing of hydrologic recovery could have influenced the observed, repetitive flood and debris flow responses. These observations provide insight into the limitations of this mitigation approach in steep, relatively confined, geomorphically active settings.

title: Tracking Modern Sediment Mixing and Provenance using Multi-Mineral Detrital Geochronology, Taranaki Basin, New Zealand
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Martin, Gabrielle [1], Sharman, Glenn [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas, USA
abstract: Provenance studies commonly rely on detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology to reconstruct sediment source areas and sediment routing systems, but differences in accessory mineral fertility among source rocks can bias interpretations because zircon is preferentially produced in felsic lithologies. Detrital titanite and rutile can provide complementary information by recording sediment contributions from metamorphic or more compositionally mafic igneous terranes that may be underrepresented in detrital zircon datasets. In addition, differences in U-Pb closure temperatures among zircon, titanite, and rutile allow each mineral to record stages of magmatism, metamorphism, and exhumation. This study evaluates how different detrital accessory mineral ages can be used to evaluate sediment sources and quantitative estimates of sediment mixing by using samples from modern river and beach sands from the North and South Islands of New Zealand and piston cores from offshore Taranaki Basin. U-Pb geochronology and trace-element analyses were conducted using LA-ICP-MS. Preliminary results from Farewell Spit, the Waiho River, and the offshore Taranaki Basin demonstrate contrasting age distributions. Zircon contains major Proterozoic, Devonian, Permian-Triassic, and Cretaceous populations, whereas titanite is dominated by Permian-Triassic and Cretaceous populations. Rutile analyses from the Waiho River contain abundant Cenozoic ages that are interpreted to reflect partial or complete Pb resetting of the U-Pb system during rapid exhumation of the Southern Alps. In contrast, the absence of young titanite ages is consistent with its higher U-Pb closure temperature. Rutile age distributions also differ between modern onshore and offshore sediments. The offshore Taranaki Basin sample contains a broader mixture of Cenozoic, Mesozoic, and Paleozoic age populations, while modern onshore samples with Cenozoic ages are related to resetting during exhumation. Although both titanite and rutile require a common Pb correction to calculate U-Pb ages, rutile analyses are more challenging due to low U concentrations. Additional titanite and rutile analyses are necessary for analyzing the relationship between age and corresponding terranes. We hypothesize that zircon age spectra preferentially record felsic Western Province sources, whereas titanite and rutile record greater sediment contributions from the more compositionally mafic Eastern Province sources, causing zircon records to underrepresent Eastern Province contributions and titanite and/or rutile records to underrepresent Western Province contributions.

title: Becoming a "real geologist": What field camp teaches students about belonging
session_title: Iris Moreno Totten Research in Geoscience Education Session
authors: Godin, Emily L. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract: Capstone field camps are widely regarded as transformative experiences in undergraduate geoscience education, yet they also communicate implicit expectations about participation and belonging within the discipline. This exploratory qualitative study examines student perspectives from a three-week capstone field camp through interviews and focus groups. Students described field camp as both a scientific and a cultural learning experience, shaping not only how they reasoned through geologic uncertainty but also how they understood the behaviors, attitudes, and expectations associated with success in the field environment. These findings suggest that field camp contributes not only to how students learn geology but also to how they come to see themselves as "real geologists." Understanding these experiences may help inform ongoing conversations about belonging, participation, and the future of field education.

title: Microfossils in Soft Sediment Clasts Reveal a Composite Cenozoic Stratigraphy in West Antarctic Basins
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Heins, Megan [1], Harwood, David M [2], Leventer, Amy [3], Coenen, Jason James [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Geosciences, Colgate Univeristy, Hamilton, New York, USA
(4) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
abstract: Understanding and identifying the history of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) is important to our understanding of its future responses to climate change. WAIS plays an important role in global climate dynamics, influencing sea level as the ice sheet shrinks and grows. In order to better predict future ice sheet responses to our changing climate, we must first understand the drivers and environmental factors of past ice sheet change. We can document past times of WAIS retreat through the identification of distinct ages of marine microfossils that grew in West Antarctic paleo-seas during times of decreased ice sheet cover. We interpret the presence of fossil marine diatoms recovered in discrete soft sediment clasts from glacial and glacimarine sediments to reflect primary diatom growth at various times during the Cenozoic. Traditionally, samples examined from subglacial sediment cores are composed of matrix sediments that contain diatoms of mixed ages. This mixing confused biostratigraphic interpretations and delayed development of a robust biostratigraphic framework. The character of subglacial strata that contributed to these mixed assemblages can be isolated through the examination of diatom-bearing soft sediment clasts. Due to the discrete nature of the diatom assemblages within the clasts, the biostratigraphic principles of taxon co-occurrence and presence/absence can be used to narrow biostratigraphic age interpretations for several discrete intervals of marine sedimentation, including portions of the early Oligocene, early Miocene, middle Miocene, and late Miocene. Key ‘index’ taxa and distinct cohorts of diatom assemblages are important in further development of an Antarctic shelf biostratigraphic framework. Contrasts in the paleobiogeographic distribution of fossil diatom taxa on the Antarctic Shelf, versus the Southern Ocean, can also be identified by studying the primary assemblages in sediment clasts from the West Antarctic interior. The character of dominantly reworked ‘residual’ assemblages of diatoms in the sediment matrix is reflected in the concentration of robust, heavily-silicified taxa, including Stephanopyxis spp., Paralia sulcata , Pseudammodochium (ebridian), Isthmia fragments, Actinocyclus ingens , Actinoptychus undulatus , Aulacodiscus browneii , Coscinodiscus , and Endictya , These taxa are absent or occurring in low abundance within soft sediment clasts.

title: Provenance of the Sepur-Soyaló turbidites as a record of the Late Cretaceous–Paleogene North American–Caribbean collision in Guatemala, Belize, and Chiapas (Mexico)
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Milián de la Cruz, Ricardo Enrique [1], Martens, Uwe C. [2], Sierra-Rojas, Maria Isabel [3], Solari, Luigi A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, UNAM - Instituto de Geociencias, Querétaro, Querétaro, Mexico
(2) Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, UNAM - Instituto de Geociencias, Queretaro, Queretaro, Mexico
(3) Los Andes University, Bogotá, Colombia,
(4) UNAM - Instituto de Geociencias, Queretaro, QRO,
abstract:
The Sepur-Soyaló turbidite deposits of the southern Maya block record Maastrichtian–Paleocene deposition in an underfilled foreland basin, produced by flexural loading associated with collision between the Greater Antilles Arc (Caribbean plate) and the North American continental passive margin.

Foreland basin conditions are first recorded in western and central Guatemala, where thin, fine-grained basal turbidites accumulated over latest Campanian platform limestone. In central Guatemala, stratigraphic relations and maximum depositional ages (72–67 Ma) indicate a Maastrichtian age for these turbidite deposits. Subsequent orogenic growth expanded the underfilled basin northward into northern Guatemala, Belize, and Chiapas. Here, turbidite deposition is constrained to the Paleocene, as turbidites overlie Maastrichtian limestone and K/Pg Chicxulub impact-related breccias, and detrital zircon maximum depositional ages range from 64 Ma to 59 Ma.

Maastrichtian turbidite sandstones are dominated by detritus consistent with calcareous and volcanic sources, and by a prevailing Cretaceous detrital zircon U-Pb age group (134–67 Ma) whose grains show igneous textures under cathodoluminescence. We surmise that the calcareous detritus was derived from Upper Cretaceous platforms in the southern Maya block and from carbonate platforms fringing the Greater Antilles Arc, while the igneous material was derived from the arc itself (extinct during the collision) and from the post-collisional volcanic belt produced in Jamaica and the Nicaragua Rise following subduction polarity reversal. In contrast, Paleocene turbidite sandstones are characterized by a highly heterogeneous provenance, including serpentinite and other metamorphic lithics, detrital glaucophane, and pre-Cretaceous detrital zircon age groups (1370–780 Ma; 480–420 Ma; 297–202 Ma), as well as detrital material related to the extinct arc, the post-collisional arc, and the Cretaceous platforms. We surmise that ultramafic nappes, high-pressure belts, Maya block continental-basement units, and recycled sedimentary successions of the passive margin became incorporated into the orogen during the Paleocene.

Sepur-Soyaló sandstone provenance data indicate a transition from a homogeneous sediment source in the Maastrichtian to more heterogeneous sources in the Paleocene, suggesting progressive unroofing of the orogen that eventually exhumed ultramafic nappes, metamorphic complexes, and sedimentary cover deposited on Maya block crust.

title: Evidence for Variable Cretaceous Sedimentary Burial and Tertiary Subcretion Across the Central-Southern Klamath Mountains from (U-Th)/He Thermochronology
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Brabant, Adaline C [1], Regan , Angelina M [2], Gallagher, Olivia K [3], Neal, Katalina L [4], Gonzalez, Angel M [5], Lewis, Xander C [6], Sousa, Francis J [7], Michalak, Melanie J [8], Baughman, Jaclyn S [9]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt, Arcata, CA, USA
(2) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt, Arcata, California, USA
(3) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt, Arcata, California, USA
(4) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt, Arcata, California, USA

(7) College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA
(8) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt, Arcata, California, USA
(9) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University, Humboldt, Arcata, California, USA
abstract:
The Klamath Mountains Province (KMP) is part of the Paleozoic-Mesozoic Cordilleran arc system that is currently situated in the southern Cascadia forearc. The KMP consists of Cambrian to Cretaceous-aged accreted terranes intruded by Jurassic-Cretaceous plutons. Following terrane accretion, the KMP experienced significant burial during a Cretaceous marine transgression and subsequent exhumation associated with regional tectonic events including Eocene collision of the Siletz terrane, Tertiary extension, and Miocene regional rock cooling.

Our cohort of six undergraduate students and faculty mentors investigated the extent and influence of these events on the central KMP using zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe, closure temperature (Tc) ~180°C, 2 samples; 10 individual dates) and apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe, Tc ~60°C, 5 samples; 24 individual dates) thermochronology and thermal modeling. We targeted plutons within the central KMP because, unlike the southern and eastern KMP, it lacks a preserved Cretaceous sedimentary record. Our results reveal significant spatial and temporal variations in the thermal history across the central-southern KMP. Individual ZHe dates in the central KMP are dispersed (~70-180 Ma), suggesting partial resetting through reheating, likely via burial, into the ZHe partial retention zone. In contrast, previously presented samples from the southern KMP yield fully reset, internally reproducible ZHe dates (~98-146 Ma), indicating a hotter and likely deeper burial history. These differences may reflect preexisting, uneven topography and/or differential sediment accumulation rates during the regional Cretaceous marine transgression. Ongoing ZHe analysis of preserved Cretaceous sedimentary rocks in the southern KMP will provide independent thermal histories that can be compared to that of local plutons. These results will help us test if regional contacts are depositional, as currently mapped, or the result of faulting related to later tectonic activity.

AHe dates define an eastward-younging pattern from 40 to 5 Ma. Along similar latitudes, samples in the western KMP yield older AHe dates, indicating progressively younger cooling toward the east. We interpret this pattern to reflect eastward migration of exhumation driven by subcretion of low-density material beneath the KMP, consistent with east-dipping subduction.

title: Lunar EVA Simulations: Evaluating Human Accuracy And Location Estimates In Analog Terrain
session_title: Planetary Exploration and Education: How We Learn About Our Solar System and Beyond
authors: Ford, Emily Joanna [1], Kobs Nawotniak, Shannon [2]
affiliations: (1) ISU Geosciences Department, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(2) ISU Geosciences Department, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
abstract:
Future Artemis IV astronauts will conduct extravehicular activities (EVAs) on the lunar surface without a GPS or tracking system; rather, they will rely on printed maps and terrain interpretations to estimate their positions. To better understand the complications with map-based navigation, we evaluated the accuracy of position estimates during field traverses in lunar analog terrain on the eastern Snake River Plain, Idaho, which includes Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, The Breaks, and Beartrap Cave.

During field campaigns conducted in 2024 through 2026, trained field geologists traversed lunar analog sites while recording their estimated positions at five-minute intervals using printed maps with alphanumeric grids. Researchers also collected GoPro footage, which was reviewed after the fact to make location revisions in keeping with revisions that would be done by members of Mission Control live-time during an actual EVA using suit video transmissions. A hidden GPS provided ground-truth locations, which were later analyzed to determine in-field and video-derived revision accuracy compared to the GPS. These datasets allowed direct comparison between field estimates, in-lab video estimates, and true GPS positions.

Navigation accuracy was strongly influenced by terrain characteristics. Position estimates were increasingly accurate near prominent topographic features, such as ridges, rims, and volcanic outcrops, with 1-2 meter-scale features like lava morphology changes and sagebrush providing very little apparent help to the field team despite the features being very visible in the aerial imagery. Errors increased in homogeneous terrain where few recognizable large landmarks were available. Abrupt elevation changes associated with steep slopes were helpful for along-feature navigation but corresponded to increased errors when teams actually went up or down slope. The 2025 field campaign demonstrated slightly improved overall accuracy, which could reflect the differences in traverse planning and familiarity with the study area. The comparison seen between the 2024 and 2026 fieldwork highlights the importance of understanding terrain, the differences between reaching the target, and the structure of navigation. By understanding these, we can continue to improve these traverses and in-field and in-lab performance.

title: The Geomorphology and Hydrology of Pre-Restoration West Fork Teanaway River, Kittitas County, WA
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Egan, Shana M. [1], Ely, Lisa L. [2], Gazis, Carey [3], Lipton, Jennifer [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA,
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA,
(3) Department of Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA,

abstract: The West Fork Teanaway (WFT) River in Kittitas County, WA is an alpine river with an entrenched bedrock river channel, disturbed floodplain geomorphology, and degraded riparian ecology. Two stream restoration approaches, “stage 0” valley bottom reset and engineered logjam installation, will be implemented at the WFT in 2026-2027 by collaborators at the Washington State Department of Fish and Wildlife and Mid-Columbia Fisheries Enhancement Group. The objectives of this study were to constrain the pre-restoration geomorphic and hydrologic conditions of the WFT, including the shallow floodplain aquifer stratigraphy, the hydrologic regime of the WFT River, and the groundwater/surface water interactions in the shallow floodplain aquifer. Monitoring of groundwater and surface-water levels with eleven floodplain piezometers and two in-stream stilling wells began in November 2024 and ended in May 2026. The timing of floodplain groundwater recharge, baseflow recession, and surface water-groundwater mixing were determined through analysis of stable isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H) and hydrographs of groundwater and surface water. The floodplain aquifer began baseflow recession into the WFT River by early June 2025 and ended by October 2025. Recharge of the WFT floodplain aquifer is sourced by surface water, and recharge timing occurred from October 2025 to mid-March 2026. The floodplain aquifer groundwater had a rapid, synchronous response to WFT River surface water, demonstrated by the hydrographs of the floodplain piezometers and stable isotope trends of surface water and groundwater. This relationship is most likely enabled by the coarse-grained stratigraphy providing preferential groundwater flowpaths in the floodplain aquifer. Alteration of the floodplain stratigraphy during restoration could impact this connection. These results will be used to determine hydrologic changes as a result from the two restoration approaches through future, post-restoration monitoring of the WFT study area

title: Metamorphic Soles to Ophiolites: Windows into the Thermal Regime of Megathrust Earthquakes?
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Lamont, Thomas Neil [1], Smye, Andrew J [2], England, Philip C [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Nevada Las Vegas, Las Vegas, Nevada, USA
(2) Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom
abstract:
Metamorphic soles beneath ophiolites are widely interpreted to preserve conditions along ancient subduction interfaces at depths of ~20–50 km (0.5–1.5 GPa). Temperatures near their tops are ~800–900°C and decline by several 100°C across the 10s-100s m immediately beneath. Some interpretations invoke processes that are atypical of present-day plate interfaces, for example rapid thrusting beneath young ocean floor and/or initiation of subduction. Here, we explore an alternative possibility, by examining the relationship between metamorphic soles and megathrust earthquakes, a ubiquitous feature of modern subduction interfaces over this depth range.

Our study is motivated by the metamorphic sole of the Tinos Ophiolite, Greece, which preserves a typical inverted thermal gradient yet formed beneath old (~80 Ma) oceanic lithosphere at a relatively slow convergence rate (~20 mm yr⁻¹). Co-seismic melts preserved at the top of the Tinos sole indicate that transient heating during Mw 7–8 earthquakes was the dominant heat source for metamorphism. Similar evidence for syn-deformational melting reported from other metamorphic soles hint that they, too, may be related to large earthquakes.

Ophiolite soles comprise metamorphosed sheets whose protoliths record the progressive underthrusting of abyssal oceanic crust (basalts and gabbros), continental rise (pelagic and terrigenous sediments), and continental margin (carbonates and siliciclastic sediments). This lithological progression is accompanied by a systematic change in mineral assemblages, from strong clinopyroxene–garnet–amphibole–plagioclase assemblages at the highest structural levels to weaker quartz–feldspar–mica–carbonate assemblages at the base. The maximum temperature experienced by a given mineral assemblage within a plate interface will be at its seismic-aseismic transition: when it is weak enough to absorb motion across the plate interface by ductile flow rather than by earthquakes. If metamorphic soles are formed within that environment, then the temperatures they record should be controlled by their mineralogy. As successively weaker lithologies pass beneath the base of the ophiolite they will accommodate the relative plate motion at successively lower temperatures.

We test this hypothesis using published rheological parameters to calculate transition temperatures for sole rocks whose P-T conditions and mineral assemblages are well characterized. The calculated temperatures agree with observed metamorphic temperatures to within 100°C, over the range ~400°C to 950°C. This agreement suggests that the thermal structures of at least some metamorphic soles are explained by processes that are characteristic of present-day plate interfaces.

title: U-daughter dating of sub-fossil eggshells

authors: Niespolo, Elizabeth [1], Kim, Noe-Heon [2], Miller, Gifford H. [3], Varricchio, David [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(2) Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA

abstract:
Without new dating tools, many fossil deposits remain unanchored in time, reducing confidence relating temporally dependent climatic and anthropogenic perturbations to faunal evolution and diversity. Megafaunal eggshells are effective for paleoclimate and chronological reconstruction in the archaeological and fossil records due to 1) a stable low-Mg calcite composition, 2) common occurrence in terrestrial sequences, and 3) useful paleoenvironmental proxy records [1]. Recent work has demonstrated eggshells of Pleistocene large flightless birds can be suitable to date fossil and archaeological deposits via 230 Th/U geochronology [1, 2]. We present trace element patterns from eggshells of extant and extinct flightless birds from three continents that range from Eocene to Holocene in age. Patterns in the “common” isotopes of uranium ( 238 U), thorium ( 232 Th), and lead ( 208 Pb) via laser ablation ICP-MS determine the time range over which U is retained and the potential for U-daughter dating in yet-untested eggshells and geographic ranges. 238 U tracks eggshell structures and has maximum values at the surfaces in contact with soil and local pore water but quickly decrease to stable concentrations in the palisade layer of calcite crystals, internal to the eggshell surfaces. 232 Th is also highest at the surfaces where ancient eggshells have been in contact with detritus, and it remains low in the interior palisade crystals of eggshell fragments. Unlike U and Th, Pb is present in modern eggshells; thus, common 208 Pb corrections must be constrained for U/Pb dating of older eggshells > 500 ka. In ancient eggshells, 208 Pb is variable but low in some areas internal to eggshell surfaces. To account for variable post-depositional U and Pb uptake from soil pore waters in older eggshell fragments, we evaluate U-Pb dating of dinosaur eggshell fragments from four independently dated Cretaceous formations. Although systematically younger than bracketing tephra ages, some U-Pb ages of dinosaur eggshells broadly approximate the depositional age and overlap with tephra ages, suggesting that dinosaur eggshells might provide minimum age constraints on host deposits.

title: Geographic Differentiation of Conodont Biofacies in the Early Mississippian (Kinderhookian) Siphonodella sandbergi Zone Marine Sequence in the Williston Basin, Northwestern United States
session_title: Microfossil Con Queso – Conodont Questions of Importance –North American Pander Society Meeting
authors: Hogancamp, Nicholas Jay [1]
affiliations: (1) BEHRO & Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY,
abstract: The regionally widespread Early Mississippian (Kinderhookian) marine sequence in the Williston Basin that comprises the Upper Bakken Member of North Dakota, The Upper Sappington Member of Montana and Wyoming, and the Mickelson Member of South Dakota have been previously correlated based on conodonts and were deposited during the S. sandbergi Zone. A review of new and previously published quantitative conodont abundance data revealed significant variations in the conodont assemblages that are preferentially distributed in different parts of the Williston Basin. Four conodont biofacies are recognized: The Siphonodella obsoleta and Polygnathus inornatus group biofacies is most common in the carbonates in South Dakota; the Polygnathus inornatus group biofacies is most common in the shale and siltstones of northcentral Wyoming; the Polygnathus communis group biofacies is most common in the shale and siltstones of northwest Wyoming; and the Siphonodella cooperi, Pseudopolygnathus, and Bispathodus biofacies is most common in the black shales of western Montana. These spatial biofacies variations within the same temporal interval (i.e. the same regional depositional sequence and biozone) likely represent ecological partitioning of conodont groups into different parts of the basin and depositional profile. Although most conodont biofacies focus on the genus-level this dataset display some species level differentiation, most notably within Siphonodella where species with smooth rostral platforms (e.g. S. obsoleta ) dominate carbonate facies in South Dakota but species with ridged rostral platforms (e.g. S. cooperi, S. quadruplicata ) dominate black shale facies. This compiled conodont data set is limited in the amount of other data types available that would be required to thoroughly test depositional environment and paleocological hypotheses, but the broad patterns observed here warrant further study that could refine our understanding of Kinderhookian conodont paleoecology.
