title: ~60-Million-Year Periodicity in the Volatility of the Geological Carbon Cycle and in Climate: Links to Biodiversity History, Mass Extinctions, and Tectonics
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Bush, Andrew M. [1], Tabor, Clay R. [2], Deneau, Taylor [3], Payne, Jonathan L. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(2) University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(3) University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(4) Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
abstract:
During the Phanerozoic, marine animal biodiversity fluctuated with a periodicity of about 60 million years, and similar periodic fluctuations occur in Sr and S isotopes, suggesting links between biodiversity, tectonics, and ocean oxygenation. Here, we document a similar periodicity in the volatility of the geological carbon cycle over the past 500 m.y., where volatility was calculated as the standard deviation of δ13C values of marine carbonates within a moving window, subsampled to standardize sample size. Intervals of time with numerous/large carbon isotope excursions (CIEs) have high volatility, and intervals lacking major excursions have low volatility.

As noted previously, carbon cycle volatility decreased during the Mesozoic, which has been attributed to more complete ocean oxygenation. Spectral analysis of the detrended time series reveals a significant ~60-m.y. periodicity in volatility, in addition to an ~80-m.y. signal. Intervals of high carbon cycle volatility generally correspond with lower biodiversity.

CIEs are commonly attributed to major events like expansions of marine anoxia or large igneous province eruptions, and they are often associated with climate change. Thus, CIEs represent major disruptions of Earth-surface environments and biogeochemical cycles. Periodicity in carbon cycle volatility can thus be interpreted as periodicity in global environmental stability on million-year timescales. These results help explain why biodiversity is periodic even though mass extinctions themselves are less regular: most mass extinctions have tended to occur during these extended intervals of increased biogeochemical instability and may contribute to the overall volatility but do not explain it on their own.

These results are consistent with Boulila et al.’s (2025, doi:10.1038/s43247-025-02370-6) suggestion that 60-m.y. biodiversity cycles relate to cycles in ocean oxygenation, as many CIEs are attributable to ocean anoxia and carbon burial. High temperature may contribute to the development of anoxia, and some Phanerozoic temperature data show evidence of a similar periodicity. These cycles could, in turn, be driven by cycles in tectonics and weathering, reflected in the strontium record. Links to reported periodicity in large igneous province eruptions are unclear.

title: Preliminary Joint Survey in the Central New York Appalachian Plateau: Implications for Groundwater Use for Datacenters and the Proposed Constitution Pipeline
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Gaston, Miles [1], Brunstad, Keith A. [2]
affiliations: (1) State University of Oneonta, Oneonta, NY, USA
(2) State University of New York, Maryland, NY,
abstract:
Groundwater contamination associated with the proposed Constitution Pipeline and the potential construction of new data centers represents an important environmental concern in central New York. Regional bedrock fracture networks may provide preferential pathways for contaminant transport; therefore, this study aims to characterize joint orientations across the Middle Devonian strata of the Appalachian Plateau to evaluate potential groundwater flow pathways. A primary objective is to distinguish joints controlled by regional paleostress fields from those associated with geomorphic processes, such as karst development, in order to assess whether fractures are localized within the shallow subsurface or extend through multiple stratigraphic units.

Preliminary field mapping was conducted throughout the region bounded by the I-81, I-88, and I-90 corridors in central New York. Joint orientations were measured at roadside, gorge, and stream, outcrops. Preliminary results indicate that joint sets in Chenango County and [KB1] Schoharie County predominantly strike NNE–SSW. In contrast, joint orientations in Otsego County are more variable, with dominant trends ranging from ESE–WNW to SE–NW. Southeast of Syracuse, joint sets primarily strike NE–SW and ENE–WSW, corresponding closely to the approximately 045–050° and 060° orientations of Sets II and III described by Engelder and Geiser (1980). Measurements collected within karst terrain adjacent to Manlius and Jamesville also reveal localized joint sets striking approximately NE–SW and ESE–WNW.

These preliminary results indicate that fracture orientations vary across central New York and likely reflect the combined influence of regional tectonic stresses and local geomorphic processes. Continued mapping will refine the regional fracture network and improve assessments of groundwater vulnerability associated with future infrastructure development.

title: Venus Volcanism, Occam’s Razor, and Computational Fluid Dynamics: It’s Probably Basalt
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: Sakimoto, Susan E. H. [1], Gregg, Tracy K. P. [2]
affiliations: (1) Space Science Institute, , Boulder, Colorado, USA; Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
abstract:
Volcanic deposits cover 70-75% of Earth, similar to that of Venus (80-85%), and both planets display a wide variety of volcanic landforms. However, Earth’s volcanism is currently dominated by plate tectonics, with around 70% of the volcanoes mafic (mostly at mid-ocean ridges), and Venus’s volcanism is probably basalt-dominated and driven by mantle plumes (a.k.a. hotspot volcanism). The similarities are significant enough that studying volcanic processes on either planet informs understanding of processes on both. Any Venusian volcanic feature with a morphology not obviously consistent with basalt generates significant interest, as there are widespread implications for planetary magma plumbing and melt generation. Pancake domes are suggested to be made of more viscous (perhaps silica-rich) lavas and the long (>10 3 km), narrow(<10 km) canali and lava channels are commonly cited as evidence for low-viscosity carbonatite and komatiite compositions.

However, non-basaltic compositions have been hypothesized based on models that, due to software or computational limitations, use greatly simplified inputs and model physics. For example, canali and channels have been modeled with several depth-averaged (1-D) lava models that assume turbulent flow with an isothermal interior, externally impose a flow rate or velocity, and only then solve for bulk viscosity. Under these assumptions, low viscosities and unrealistically high flow rates are essential for the models to reach observed flow lengths. However, evolved (silicate-rich) lavas, carbonatites, and komatiites are difficult to generate in the necessary volumes in hot-spot regimes, and proposed emplacement styles are typically unsupported by regional geology. In contrast, we find that 2-D or 3-D coupled flow and cooling models with basaltic temperature-dependent properties, along with Venusian ambient conditions, naturally produce both the pancake domes and the canali/channels. Thus, although a limited range of non-basaltic compositions are still possible in these more detailed models, they are no longer forced by the model. Additionally, we note that solving for internal velocity, viscosity, and temperature distributions, rather than imposing them, shows that many prior simplifying model assumptions (i.e. turbulent flow, and values for flow rate and cooling rate) are likely erroneous, and generate misleading results. We therefore suggest that Venusian volcanism is entirely consistent with basaltic or basaltic-adjacent compositions, and that other composition suggestions based on simplified models should be reassessed with modern modeling approaches.

title: Multimodal Assessment of Along-River Patterns in Erosion and Deposition Following Hurricane Helene-driven Flooding Across the Blue Ridge

authors: Masteller, Claire C [1], Lopez, Cesar G [2], Darafshi, Niku R [3], Bradley, Alexander S [4], Michaelides , Roger [5], Johnson, Bradley G. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St Louis, Missouri, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, Missouri, USA

abstract:
Extreme floods redistribute large volumes of sediment, yet the spatial organization of erosion and deposition along river networks remains poorly quantified. We present a multimodal remote sensing framework to evaluate channel change following Hurricane Helene across eight watersheds draining the Blue Ridge Escarpment and adjacent Blue Ridge Highlands. We trained an automated image segmentation model to identify gravel bars, the primary sites of transient sediment storage within river corridors, from pre- and post-flood 6-inch aerial imagery. These mapped features were integrated with lidar change detection (LCD) derived from pre- and post-event lidar-derived topography to quantify erosion and deposition associated with individual gravel bars. We then analyzed longitudinal patterns in sediment exchange and related these changes to pre-flood channel morphology.

Distinct along-river trends emerge across the physiographic boundary separating the steep Blue Ridge Escarpment from the lower-gradient Blue Ridge Highlands. In escarpment watersheds, gravel bars in headwater reaches exhibit net erosion, transitioning to net deposition downstream. In contrast, highland rivers display the opposite pattern, with net deposition in headwaters and increasing erosion farther downstream. These contrasting responses likely reflect differences in sediment supply, valley confinement, channel gradient, and stream power that govern sediment transport capacity and transient storage during extreme floods. Steep escarpment channels rapidly evacuate sediment from source areas before depositing it in lower-gradient downstream reaches, whereas the more gradual highland channels initially store sediment in upstream reaches before remobilization farther downstream.

Our results demonstrate that combining automated feature extraction from high-resolution imagery and with (LCD) derived from pre- and post-lidar allows for spatially explicit quantification of event-scale sediment redistribution over entire river networks. These findings provide new insight on controls on sediment routing during extreme floods and improve our ability to anticipate channel adjustment, flood-driven erosion hazards, and impacts to river corridors following increasingly frequent high-magnitude flood events.

title: A multimineral perspective on the provenance of the Mesoproterozoic Belt Supergroup and its long metamorphic history

abstract:
The Mesoproterozoic Belt Supergroup is a > 15 km sequence of predominantly siliciclastic sediments in the northern U.S Cordillera and adjacent Canada. These sediments were deposited in an extensional basin between western Laurentia and another continental mass during the breakup and/or reorganization of the supercontinent Nuna. Here we review recent work on the provenance and later metamorphic history of the western part of the basin by combining more traditional detrital zircon U-Pb dating and Hf isotope analysis with detrital zircon trace element analysis, detrital monazite and rutile U-Pb dating and trace element analysis, and Pb isotope analysis of detrital feldspar.

The Prichard Formation and Ravalli Group of the Belt have homogeneous detrital mineral age spectra, with a main zircon age peak at 1.61 Ga and monazite age peaks at 1.67, 1.60, and 1.50 Ga, whereas the overlying Missoula Group and Lemhi strata have a principal zircon age peak between 1.7 and 1.8 Ga, monazite age peaks at 2.43, 1.78, 1.73, and 1.68 Ga, and a rutile age peak around 1.63 Ga. The Prichard/Ravalli zircon and monazite age spectra (along with zircon Hf isotopes and trace element compositions) are most consistent with sources in the Gawler craton in southern Australia, and Belt rocks may have direct correlatives in Tasmania, with both points suggesting a modified SWEAT configuration for Nuna. Conversely, Missoula/Lemhi data are most consistent with provenance from the Mojave and Yavapai terranes in the southwestern US.

Belt Supergroup rocks experienced an eventful life after lithification. Several episodes of post-depositional metamorphic monazite growth occurred between ~1.38 and 1.00 Ga, generally aligning with published garnet Lu-Hf ages. The tectonic significance of these events remains obscure but may be attributable to the consolidation of Rodinia after Nuna breakup. Additional monazite growth episodes occurred locally in the southern parts of the basin at ~720 and ~513 Ma, which may reflect the thermal imprint of magmatism associated with Rodinia breakup and subsequent Early Paleozoic intraplate magmatism. Mesozoic metamorphic disturbances are also recorded across several minerals, with discordant detrital zircons projecting to a ~100 Ma lower intercept, sparse Mesozoic monazite growth, and whole-scale re-equilibration of the Pb isotope composition of feldspars throughout the basin. These Mesozoic events most likely reflect reactive fluid flow during Sevier and Laramide orogenesis.

abstract: Ensuring a safe and secure water supply is critical to human and environmental health and economic and social sustainability. Observational data are the foundation of any water management plan, and yet their design and implementation are often ad-hoc and reactive. In addition, groundwater, surface water, snow, and climatic monitoring programs are often developed and applied independently of each other, despite their clear connections through the hydrologic cycle. In this work, an existing observational network for hydrologic conditions, including groundwater, surface water, snow, and climate, across the Province of Alberta, Canada, are integrated to one framework to evaluate gaps, redundancies, and connections between hydrologic components. In addition, projections of future climate, population, and industrial growth are considered. Focusing on groundwater, several approaches to evaluate current availability, short and long-term trends, and interaction with surface water systems are compared, including statistical, numerical, and integrated methods. The results of this work directly inform water monitoring planning and support future water management decisions.

abstract: The Meeman-Shelby fault (MSF) is a north-northeast trending reverse fault in the northern Mississippi embayment with evidence of Quaternary activity. The MSF, along with similar faults in the region, may form a critical hydrologic boundary for Paleogene aquifer systems, including the Memphis and Fort Pillow (Wilcox) aquifers, which are primary groundwater resources. Electrical resistivity (ER) and airborne electromagnetic (AEM) surveys provided constraints on the MSF’s offset and geometry, which were previously debated based on seismic reflection profiles. Recent borehole cores corroborate the sense of displacement and offer further insights into the style and degree of deformation in the associated damage zone. Geophysical data show an approximately 40 m thick, low resistivity zone, attributed to the Eocene Cook Mountain Fm., offset roughly 30 m by a reverse fault zone nearly 25 m wide. These findings informed the placement of two boreholes drilled by sonic methods to 88 and 104 m, respectively, capturing the hanging wall and fault zone stratigraphy and structure. An apparent offset of the upper Cook Mountain Fm. of approximately 50 m is accommodated by multiple faults between the hanging-wall block and cored base of the faulted interval. The damage zone is approximately 17 m thick, evident by multiple m-scale-offset faults and extensive cm-scale-offset faults of weathered and rooted silty clay in the upper Cook Mountain Fm. Slickensides along faults indicate mainly vertical motion, but oblique motion is commonly evident. Evidence of late Quaternary reverse motion along the fault is indicated by 27 m of thickening of the Pleistocene-Holocene Mississippi River Valley alluvium above the fault zone. The initial results clarify the structure and orientation of the MSF, previously interpreted as having a north-northeast or north-northwest orientation, and provide a framework for evaluating the hydraulic characteristics of the fault zone. Two monitoring wells, screened in similar silty sand within the Cook Mountain Fm. and upper Eocene Memphis Sand, were constructed and are currently being developed for future sampling and hydraulic testing.

title: Evolution of surface deformation partitioning during experimental strike-slip faulting
session_title: Recurrence of what?
authors: Cawood, Adam J. [1], Wyrick, Danielle Y. [2], Stamatakos, John [3], Ulmer, Kristin [4], Woodworth, Daniel [5], Ferrill, David A. [6]
affiliations: (1) Syracuse University, San Antonio, TX, USA

(3) SwRI, San Antonio, TX,
(4) Southwest Research Institute, San Antonio, TX, USA
(5) Southwest Research Institute, San Antonio, TX, USA

abstract: Quantifying how coseismic surface deformation is partitioned between the principal fault trace and off-fault deformation (OFD) is important for earthquake cycle studies, geologic slip-rate estimates, and seismic hazard assessment. Although OFD is commonly treated as a single component of the surface displacement budget, it comprises two fundamentally different processes: distributed deformation and displacement on secondary fault strands. Here, we develop a quantitative, pixel-based framework – using twelve strike-slip analogue experiments monitored with digital image correlation – to partition surface deformation into four categories (i) primary fault slip, (ii) secondary faulting, (ii) distributed deformation, and (iv) aggregate off-fault deformation (the combined contribution of distributed deformation and secondary faulting). Incremental displacement fields were classified using displacement gradients to distinguish localized and distributed deformation. These classifications were combined with normalized displacement budgets to quantify the proportions of displacement accommodated by our four deformation categories throughout progressive fault growth. All experiments exhibit progressive strain localization, transitioning from broadly distributed deformation to localized slip on an established fault zone. Distributed deformation proportion of the total displacement decreases rapidly following fault nucleation before approaching a relatively stable plateau, whereas secondary faulting proportion of total displacement remains spatially heterogeneous and temporally variable throughout model evolution. Aggregate OFD exhibits substantially greater spatial and temporal variability than distributed deformation alone because it incorporates the highly variable contribution from secondary faulting. Despite substantial differences in model thickness, material properties, and layer configuration, all experiments exhibit remarkably similar first-order trends, indicating that fault maturity exerts the primary control on deformation partitioning, while fault geometry governs much of the observed along-strike variability. Reanalysis of published optical image-correlation displacement fields from the 2019 Mw 7.1 Ridgecrest and 2013 Mw 7.7 Balochistan earthquake surface ruptures reveal the same first-order behavior, supporting the broader applicability of the experimental observations. These results demonstrate that aggregate OFD should not be regarded as a single deformation process. Explicitly separating distributed deformation from secondary faulting provides a more physically meaningful framework for interpreting earthquake surface ruptures, geologic slip rates, and fault-displacement hazard assessment.

abstract: Uranium (U)-series geochronology is among the most precise and accurate geochronometers applied to Pleistocene timescales, achieving 2s uncertainties <0.1% for detritus-free samples (e.g., clean carbonates, low-thorium (Th) correction igneous minerals). Samples must be spiked with synthetic Th and U isotopes to track column chemistry efficiency and other measurement parameters using a mixed 229 Th- 233 U- 236 U, and ion beam intensities are calibrated using a mixed 232 Th- 238 U standard solution; most academic laboratories make their own mixed spike and standard solutions and calibrate them in-house. Given the diminishing supply of Th and U isotope-enriched materials and the logistical hurtles to obtain these materials, we have made a gravimetric 232 Th- 238 U solution in large quantities to share among interested U-series laboratories. High purity 232 Th and 238 U metals were weighed while monitoring all ambient conditions on precision mass balances. Th and U metals were dissolved in nitric acid (HNO 3 ) and hydrofluoric acid (HF); high purity boric acid was added to ensure no ThF 4 could precipitate over time. This solution comes in three 232 Th- 238 U dilutions (c. 2 wt.%, 5 ppm, and 12 ppb 238 U), all with the same molar 232 Th/ 238 U (~ 0.1), while the most dilute is ready for analysis in 2% HNO 3 + 0.01% HF. These gravimetric solutions allow direct calibration of new spike solutions and are available for distribution upon request.

title: Surprises and insights from Lake Bonneville’s deepwater carbonates
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: McGee, David [1], Steponaitis, Elena [2]
affiliations: (1) MIT, Earth, Atmos. and Planetary Sciences, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract: The Bonneville Basin held the largest late Pleistocene lake in the western U.S., and over a century of study of shoreline deposits and sediments has carefully documented the rise and fall of Lake Bonneville during the last glacial period and deglaciation. In the mid-2000s, Jay Quade identified a valuable new archive of Lake Bonneville’s history: dense, crystalline calcium carbonate deposits deposited in cavities of all sizes at water depths ranging from near-surface to over 200 m. These deposits have provided precisely-dated, high-resolution records of the lake’s isotopic (oxygen, strontium, uranium) and chemical composition throughout the last lake cycle – in effect forming a lacustrine equivalent of speleothems. We show how dense lacustrine carbonate deposits from a variety of locations and elevations provide reproducible records. We also explore what these records have to tell us about how precipitation patterns and water balance in the Bonneville Basin changed between 26 and 13 ka, including shifts of precipitation northeastward into the Wasatch Range in Heinrich Stadials 1 and 2 and a southward shift during the Last Glacial Maximum. Finally, we note how these pore-filling deep-lake carbonates complicate dating of tufas and other porous deposits, demanding careful screening of tufa-based radiocarbon and U/Th dates used for lake-level reconstructions.

authors: Chan, Christine F. [1], Gaffney, Amy M. [2], Boro, Joseph R. [3], Weber, Peter K. [4], Worsham, Emily A. [5], Gonzales, Matthew S. [6]

abstract:
U-series disequilibrium geochronology provides a versatile framework for constraining timescales from years to approximately 10 5 years across geological, environmental, and nuclear forensics applications. In nuclear forensics, radiochronometry can estimate the time since the last isotopic resetting or chemical purification of uranium-bearing materials. Conventional model-age calculations, however, typically assume zero initial daughter and closed-system behavior. In many real samples, measurable initial daughter and spatially heterogeneous parent-daughter distributions violate these assumptions and can produce discordant aliquot ages, even for a single chronometer such as 230 Th/ 234 U or 231 Pa/ 235 U.

Here, we evaluate an isochron-based model-age approach that explicitly accounts for nonzero initial daughter and corrects for the effects of impurity and sample heterogeneity. Implementing this approach requires linking sample-scale heterogeneity to subsampling strategy and analytical design, including FIB-SEM-guided microsampling and optimized ion-exchange separations for high-precision MC-ICP-MS analysis of small aliquots, ranging from individual particles to millimeter-scale fragments. We summarize the workflow, discuss practical considerations for characterizing heterogeneity and selecting aliquots, and demonstrate how isochron-based radiochronometry can recover robust ages from materials that are poorly suited to conventional bulk model-age calculations. More broadly, this work illustrates how U-series disequilibrium methods developed for complex geological systems can be adapted to anthropogenic materials and provides a transferable framework for obtaining reliable ages when conventional bulk model-age assumptions are not satisfied.

abstract: The volume of Cryogenian ice sheets and concomitant glacio-eustatic sea-level fall are poorly constrained and yet are key elements of the Snowball Earth hypothesis. Cryogenian continental margins potentially preserve key records of ice-sheet dynamics, sea-level change, and glacial erosion. Here, we present detailed geologic mapping and measured stratigraphic sections through the Abenab Subgroup of the Otavi Group across multiple shelf-to-slope transects that traverse the western continental margin of the Congo paleocontinent in NW Namibia. A gradual and distinctive facies transition occurs as the platformal Sturtian cap carbonate and overlying stromatolitic reef facies pass westward into a mixed siliciclastic-carbonate turbidite succession (informally termed the Ondole sequence). We interpret this facies change as evidence for progressive westward deepening from platform carbonates into foreslope deposits. At the platform margin, a prominent channel is incised c. 350 m into the underlying Abenab carbonates. The presence of the Marinoan cap carbonate at the base of the channel fill supports a glacioeustatic and/or glacial erosional origin rather than a tectonic detachment, as previously proposed. Further, we show that the Marinoan grounding-line wedge (Ghaub Formation) occurs 25-35 km seaward of the platform margin, constraining the position of the ice margin relative to the shelf break during channel incision and infill. Our results demonstrate that the western Congo craton margin preserves its primary depositional architecture, providing a new framework for reconstructing Marinoan sea-level change, glacial erosion, and ice-sheet extent.

abstract:
The biological degradation of organic matter is a key control on geochemical conditions that affect the deposition of minerals such as sedimentary sulfides, one of our longest-lived paleoenvironmental archives. Microbial sulfate reduction, a dominant modern control on the isotopic composition of sedimentary sulfides, is primarily controlled by cell-specific sulfate reduction rate, which is mainly affected by sulfate concentration and organic matter availability and speciation. Much of our understanding of the impact of organic matter on sulfur isotope fractionations from sulfate reduction comes from experimental work utilizing simple organic substrates and pure cultures, rather than the complex natural organic matter and mixed communities typical of sedimentary environments. In this work we investigated the impact of changing, complex organic matter on average sulfur isotope fractionation magnitudes at Tuckerton Marsh, NJ.

We performed microbial enrichment experiments using biomass derived from either cyanobacteria or eukaryotic algae, with or without an inhibitor of sulfate reduction. Fractionation values were indistinguishable for enrichments with both biomass sources. Similar volatile fatty acids were detected in inhibited and uninhibited enrichments for both biomass sources, but these cannot stoichiometrically explain the observed sulfate depletion, suggesting that other types of unanalyzed substrates are important electron donors at Tuckerton Marsh. The likely fermenting and sulfate-reducing taxa are similar between enrichments for both biomass sources. These results suggest that the delivery of electron donors by fermenting taxa is a dominant control on fractionation values in modern marine sediments.

We also directly incubated sediments from Tuckerton Marsh with and without an inhibitor of sulfate reduction. Sulfate depletion rates were slower in deeper, peat-dominated sediments, but fractionation magnitudes were indistinguishable from those in shallower sediments dominated by more labile organic matter. This contrasts a previous porewater sulfide sulfur isotope profile which exhibited more negative values in deeper sediments. Volatile fatty acid accumulation was very low (<10%) and is insufficient to explain the observed consumption, suggesting the presence of alternative electron donors. These results suggest that local isotopic signals of sulfate reduction are being overprinted by oxidative sulfur cycling, potentially involving cryptic microbial processes or metabolite transport.

title: Classical Test Theory Analysis of the Biogeochemistry Content Inventory

abstract: A key area in understanding teaching and learning in the geosciences is the development of concept inventories to assess student understanding of key areas. Biogeochemistry studies the flow of matter and energy through all parts of the Earth system, and an understanding of basic biogeochemistry is a key component of Earth System Science. Despite the importance of biogeochemistry in understanding the Earth system and global change, it is often not explicitly included in undergraduate geoscience curricula, and no instrument exists to assess knowledge of biogeochemistry content. Thus, it is important to develop tools to understand how biogeochemistry content knowledge develops in undergraduate geoscience classrooms. We developed the Biogeochemistry Concept Inventory (BGC CI) to assess undergraduate students’ biogeochemistry content knowledge. This study aims to provide an overview of the development of the instrument as well as to discuss the piloting and validation of this instrument. The instrument was developed using previous qualitative and quantitative data collected from student interviews and consultation with experts to develop a table of specifications. The instrument was administered in multiple iterations using Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (MTURK) ( n = 1004). Results of multiple administrations were analyzed using Classical Test Theory, a psychometric framework that uses metrics such as item difficulty and item discrimination to evaluate educational and psychological tests. This talk will provide tools for practitioners to apply elements of Classical Test Theory to the development of their own instruments and discuss how instruments like this can be deployed.

session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part II)
authors: Kocher, Simon [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Reynolds, T. James [3], Henderson, Paul [4], Kasprowicz, Filip [5]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA

abstract:
The historic Tonopah mining district in Nye County, Nevada, is amongst the most prolific intermediate-sulfidation epithermal districts worldwide, having produced 174 million ounces Ag and 1.86 million ounces Au since mining commenced in 1900. Ore zones are largely confined to structurally controlled quartz veins with high-grade ores displaying crustiform, banded and brecciated textures.

Textural characteristics of the vein quartz and the relationships between quartz and ore minerals, as well as the ore mineralogy itself were determined through a combination of high-magnification optical petrography in transmitted and reflected light, optical cathodoluminescence microscopy, field emission-scanning electron microscopy, and automated mineralogy.

Microtextural evidence suggests that much of the quartz formed via maturation from noncrystalline silica and is, therefore, not a primary precipitate. Characteristic textures include fine-grained mosaic quartz with interpenetrating grain boundaries, polygonal quartz, flamboyant quartz with radiating arrays of inclusions, and large prismatic quartz grains with feathery texture in splintery domains and recrystallization fronts defined by pseudoprimary inclusions. The large prismatic quartz crystals exhibit complex internal zoning patterns visible in optical cathodoluminescence. The microtextural observations provide evidence that the crystals grew in a gel-like substrate and that crystals were competing for space during conversion of the noncrystalline silica to quartz. The quartz in the veins hosts ore minerals, including acanthite, polybasite, pyrargyrite, and electrum that commonly have delicate, multi-branching shapes resembling dendrites in discrete bands. These dendrites originally formed in a matrix of noncrystalline silica and were subsequently enveloped by the quartz during maturation of the matrix. This resulted in textural modification of the dendrites, including grain coarsening and migration of ore minerals along grain boundaries of the enclosing quartz. Textural reequilibration of ore minerals during the waning of the hydrothermal activity and related cooling is indicated by exsolution of initially homogeneous phases. This includes the formation of symplectic intergrowths of aguilarite and galena from a homogeneous Ag-Pb-Se-S phase hosted in the noncrystalline silica matrix.

The microtextures indicate that the initial deposition of the noncrystalline silica in the intermediate-sulfidation epithermal vein at Tonopah and the growth of the ore mineral dendrites within the silica substrate occurred as a consequence to vigorous boiling of the hydrothermal liquids hundreds of meters below the paleosurface, leading to supersaturation of solutes in the hydrothermal liquids and rapid growth at far-from-equilibrium conditions.

title: A Mountain in Motion: Landslides Triggered by the 2024 Monsoon Flood in the Mahabharat Range, Nepal
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies (Posters)
authors: Eskew, Gabrielle [1], Bhandari, Basant [2], Murphy, Michael A. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Houston, Houston, Texas, USA

abstract: Intense rainfall events alter topography through erosion and slope failure, but determining controls on rainfall-induced slope failures remains a formidable challenge. High relief topographic slopes frequently approach critical conditions that allow for a triggering mechanism to initiate failure. This study will investigate the interaction between pre-event slope conditions and rainfall-induced changes during a 2024 record breaking rainfall event that triggered slope failures in the central Mahabharat Range, south of Kathmandu Valley. The Mahabharat Range is a highly populated frontal mountain range that extends across central Nepal, and receives the first pulse of monsoonal air mass as it makes it way northwest across the Himalaya. Pre- and post-flood imagery from the 2024 event are used to map sediment changes through NDVI and BSI changes, yielding failed slopes outside of channels occurring between 35° − 50°. Field observations indicate anthropically altered slopes are more susceptible to failure. Located on the southern side of the Mahabharat Synclinorium, the prevailing formation in the study area is the Tistung Formation, composed of folded lesser Himalayan sedimentary lithologies. Soil samples were collected and analyzed to calculate bulk density parameters for modeling. Current shallow slope stability modeling aims to identify spatial distributions of failures relative to induced rainfall. NASA Giovanni hydrology data was used to characterize antecedent and event hydrologic condition changes and was used in a modified SHALSTAB equation using observed landslide geometries. Our modified SHALSTAB calculations suggest the antecedent slope was unstable based on observed landslide geometries and assumed material friction parameters. This back analysis method aims to investigate the interaction between pre-event slope conditions and induced rainfall. Characterizing this relationship can improve our understanding of rainfallinduced slope failures and support future hazard assessment.

abstract: Amendment-based remediation of legacy mining-contaminated agricultural soils is typically optimized for a single soil condition, overlooking whether contamination and soil degradation severity modulate amendment efficacy. This study evaluated a binary mixture of pecan-derived biochar and bovine bone char (blend ratios 100:0, 75:25, 50:50, 25:75, and 0:100) applied at three doses (3%, 7%, and 11% w/w ) to two agricultural soils in San Felipe de Jesús, Sonora, México: a highly acidic soil (pH 4.9, EC 0.66 dS/m) located directly opposite the pollution source, and a more pH-neutral soil (pH 6.2, EC 0.24 dS/m) 130 m away and separated by a living tree barrier. A mixture-amount response surface model was fitted for pH, electrical conductivity (EC), and water-holding capacity (WHC) as functions of soil, dose, blend proportion, and their interactions. pH responded predominantly to total amendment dose (p<0.001), with limited sensitivity to blend composition, whereas EC exhibited soil-dependent curvature across both dose and proportion (p<0.05); the optimal composition for improving water retention remained consistent across both soils. Desirability-based optimization maximizing pH, minimizing EC, and targeting a 30% relative WHC increase identified soil-specific amendment optima: a bone-char-dominant blend (25:75) at 10% dose was ideal for highly acidic soil, whereas a 6% dose of 100% biochar was superior for soil with moderate conditions. This study demonstrates that optimal remediation of mining-contaminated soil via biochar-bone char blends requires soil-specific formulations, as optimal amendment ratios vary across contamination gradients, supporting soil-specific formulation strategies for successful soil remediation in mining impacted regions.

abstract: Suturing of Paleoproterozoic tectonic blocks in the Lower Granite Gorge of Grand Canyon took place across the Gneiss Canyon shear zone, a 13-km-wide NE-striking subvertical high strain zone. CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon ages show that multiple igneous units of the Diamond Creek magmatic arc to the east of the shear zone are 1735 ± 0.4 Ma whereas the 245-Mile granodioritic arc to the west is 1722 ± 1 Ma. Each magmatic arc is underlain by isotopically distinct crustal blocks: the near-juvenile 1840 Ma Elves Chasm block to the east and the isotopically evolved Mojave province to the west. Chemical mohometry indicates that the eastern arc plutonic complex formed in thin crust (30 ± 4 km) whereas the western arc plutonic complex formed in thick crust (61 ± 4 km). Kinematic indicators record west-up/ dextral transpressive thrusting of the Mojave block over the down-going eastern block during high-temperature shearing. Higher metamorphic grade (750 °C, 7–7.5 kbar) Mojave rocks were thrust over lower grade (575 °C, 4 kbar) eastern block rocks at 1.70-1.68 Ga, as indicated by syntectonic monazite and titanite in both blocks. Emplacement of the syn-D 2 Surprise pluton took place at 1697.6 ± 0.54 Ma in the 63 ± 4 km thick Mojave block crust. Newly mapped mylonite–pseudotachylyte dextral strike-slip shear zones reactivated the Gneiss Canyon shear zone ~ 1.4 Ga at lower temperatures. These discrete shear zones show intense grain size reduction, 300-400 °C microstructures, and are interpreted to have formed ~ 1.4 Ga based on mica 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates. The Quartermaster (1370 ± 1.1 Ma), Gold Butte (1372 ± 12 Ma) and ~ 1.39 Ga Peacock granites were emplaced in 49 ± 2 km-thick Mojave crust, reflecting 8-10 km of crustal thinning between 1.68 and 1.37 Ga. This transect provides a middle-crustal record of a Paleoproterozoic subduction system frozen-in, then reactivated, during accretion of the lithosphere of southwestern Laurentia. These analytical data complement a new 1:24,000-scale basement geologic map and cross section of the Lower Granite Gorge’s Proterozoic geology. The true scale cross section is embedded within a crustal section that shows its paleo 1.7 Ga middle-crustal position underlying the “Vishnu Mountains” and paleo-crustal thickness based on chemical mohometry and metamorphic data.

title: Comparative Morphometric Analysis of Riverscour and Non-Riverscour Watersheds: A Case Study of Little River Canyon and the Buffalo River
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Shehorn, William Brian [1], Shepherd, Stephanie L. [2], Adams, Jack [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama, USA
abstract:
Riverscour grasslands are unique, dynamic riparian habitats occurring along high energy bedrock streams in the Southeastern United States. Maintained by high velocity floodwaters and occasional ice scours rather than fire or grazing, these systems support a disproportionately high number of endemic and threatened plant species. While riverscours have received increasing ecological attention, their geomorphological characteristics remain poorly defined, and no standardized geomorphic framework exists for their identification. This study seeks to create a conceptual geomorphic model for riverscour grasslands using watershed and reach-scale morphometric analysis. High resolution (1m) lidar DEMs were analyzed in ArcGIS Pro to calculate 14 morphometric parameters for watersheds containing well documented riverscour grasslands, with the Little River Canyon, Alabama, serving as the primary case study. Morphometric characteristics of riverscour watersheds were compared to those of the Buffalo River, Arkansas, a geomorphically similar watershed lacking documented riverscour grasslands. Hydrologic analyses were also conducted to evaluate differences in flood regime characteristics between the two systems, and field investigations were used to document local geomorphic conditions at riverscour sites along the East Fork, West Fork, and main stem of the Little River.

Preliminary results indicate that riverscour grasslands occupy a distinct geomorphic setting characterized by differences in valley width, sinuosity, drainage texture, mean bifurcation ratio, overall watershed size and localized channel gradient. Field observations revealed that each documented riverscour in the Little River watershed occurred immediately downstream of a knickpoint, suggesting that localized increases in flow may play an important role in riverscour formation and maintenance. Hydrologic analyses indicated that the Little River flow regime is characterized by frequent and sustained moderate flood events, whereas the Buffalo River experiences less frequent but larger and shorter duration flood events. Together, these findings suggest that geomorphic configuration and flow regime influence the development and persistence of riverscour grasslands across the southeastern United States.

title: Garnet as an Archive of Appalachian Metamorphism: Microstructural and Geochronologic Evidence from Rowe-Moretown Schists in Chester, MA
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)

abstract: The geology of Western Massachusetts involves a complex sequence of tectonostratigraphic units associated with Ordovician island-arc/microcontinent accretions along the Laurentian margin. In the town of Chester, Massachusetts, layers of garnet-rich pelitic schist near the Rowe-Moretown boundary provide an opportunity to examine the mechanisms, conditions, and timing of the events related to the assembly, and later deformation, of the Northern Appalachian Orogen. In this study, we perform analysis of polished thin sections taken from three sample locations containing abundant garnet. We performed structural analysis of outcrops in the field, followed by hand-sample description. Thin sections were cut parallel to both strike and lineation directions from the best samples. Remnants of an earlier foliation perpendicular to the current foliation, as well as layered and sigmoidal oxide and quartz inclusion trails in garnet were identified using a petrographic microscope. Compositional maps were made on the electron microprobe to locate datable phases and to identify locations for quantitative traverses. We used geothermobarometry and forward modeling to constrain the changing metamorphic conditions in the area. Xenotime and monazite U-Pb geochronology placed temporal constraints on the metamorphism of these rock units. S1 and S2 fabric orientations and inclusion trails suggest at least two deformation events. We have calculated 6-7 kbars and 550-600°C for peak metamorphic conditions across multiple sample locations, and using multiple methods. Dates acquired from xenotime and monazite have shown remnant Taconic age (~450 Ma), with a dominant Acadian age (~380-370 Ma). It is likely that deformation during the Acadian orogeny has overprinted the Rowe-Moretown units previously accreted and deformed during the Taconic orogeny. This work contributes to the broader understanding of the Appalachian orogenesis of New England.

title: Climate Across the K-Pg Boundary: Evidence from δ¹⁸O of Freshwater Unionid Bivalves from Montana

authors: Mccraw, Jessie [1], Ward, David McCoy [2], Wilson-Mantilla, Gregory P. [3], Sprain, Courtney Jean [4], Renne, Paul R. [5], Tobin, Thomas S. [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, ; College of the Redwoods, Eureka, CA, USA

(5) Berkeley Geochronology Center, Berkeley, CA,

abstract:
Terrestrial climate change during the K-Pg extinction and subsequent recovery is not well constrained. Mass extinction models often emphasize mean annual temperature change, but seasonal extremes may have more direct biological effects on organisms. Individual freshwater unionid bivalves record seasonal δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C variation within their shells, sometimes truncated during peak summer or winter. We examine these shells (n=54) as an archive of seasonal isotopic change across the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary in the Hell Creek and Fort Union (Tullock, Lebo, and Tongue River members) formations of central and eastern Montana.

Unionid shells are often geochemically well-preserved, but many localities, particularly in the Lebo and Tongue River members, yield only fragments rather than whole valves despite pristine aragonite mineralogy. We tested the isotopic fidelity of fragmentary material by serially sampling whole valves, then pulverizing the remaining half and sampling a random array of fragments (≥30 per specimen). Fragmentary sampling reliably reproduces mean δ¹⁸O, but recovery of seasonal extrema is variable and does not consistently match serially-derived ranges, complicating extrema interpretation where records rely solely on fragments.

We find a statistically significant decrease in δ¹⁸O extrema from Hell Creek to Tongue River: average δ¹⁸O maxima decrease from -9.4‰ to -12.2‰ over the record (Jonckheere-Terpstra test on n=54, p<0.01), and average δ¹⁸O minima decrease from -14.6‰ to -19.3‰ (p<0.01). Mean δ¹⁸O shell shows no significant temporal trend, confining this signal of environmental change specifically to extrema. δ¹⁸O distribution shape shifts through the section, indicating the persistence of a bimodal δ¹⁸O distribution into the Paleocene, apart from the Tullock specimens which are distinctly unimodal.

Shells with more negative δ¹⁸O means tend to have larger δ¹⁸O ranges, a pattern present in both serially- and fragment-sampled shells, a pattern that persists after controlling for formation identity and sampling density. δ¹³C shows no comparable relationship.

δ¹³C remains unimodal and stable (mean ~-5‰) throughout, with no obvious temporal trend, though these values cannot be reliably interpreted in fragmentary material due to vital effects on the inner shell layer. Together, these results support changing hydrology and/or regional climate across the K-Pg boundary in this basin.

title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Instructor Perspectives on Geology Analogies
session_title: Iris Moreno Totten Research in Geoscience Education Session
authors: Rhoades, Caden [1], LaDue, Nicole [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, Illinois, USA

abstract:
Analogies are an important learning mechanism and pedogeological tool used across STEM disciplines, including geosciences. By connecting (mapping) familiar concepts (sources) with the concept being taught (target), analogies can facilitate student comprehension. These analogies can be particularly useful for the complex, abstract, and/or extreme scalar targets found in geoscience courses. While most existing research explores analogies through the student lens within the context of K-12 or introductory undergraduate courses, this study investigates geoscience instructor perspectives on analogy use in upper-level undergraduate courses. This mixed-methods study investigates the following research questions:

1. What types of analogies are used in upper-level geoscience courses?

2. Do geoscience instructors believe that analogies aid or harm student learning? Are there complications when using analogical examples in upper-level geoscience courses?

3. How do geoscience instructors engage students with analogies in upper-level geoscience courses?

A digital survey conducted in Spring 2026 investigated beliefs and collected 130 analogy examples from 50 geoscience instructors. Survey data shows that of the study participants, most geoscience instructors (88%) believe analogies to be “very effective” in upper-level courses and they report predominantly engaging students with their analogies while lecturing (39%) and/or by utilizing a visual aid (23%). Additionally, the provided analogy examples fall into a few overarching upper-level courses: Mineralogy and Petrology (42), Structure (33), Sedimentology and Stratigraphy (20). Semi-structured interviews with instructors of these 5 upper-level courses were conducted in Summer and Fall 2026 to build upon the primarily quantitative survey data. Preliminary findings from qualitative interviews with instructors suggest that instructors use many analogies during the course of instruction; however, the implementation of analogies does not align with best practices described in the cognitive science literature. One important outcome of this study is the identification of future directions for faculty professional development.

title: Rapid collapse of a Siberian landscape revealed by satellite imagery: widespread permafrost thaw slump failure occurs in days; downstream sediment transport is elevated for years
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Dethier, Evan N [1], Erikson, Christian M [2], Renshaw, Carl E [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences Department, Colby College, Waterville, Maine, USA
(2) GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, Potsdam, Germany
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, USA
abstract:
Warmer temperatures and changing precipitation patterns in the Arctic appear to be increasing erosion, but the spatial distribution and timing of increased erosion is not yet clear. In 2020, the Taymyr Peninsula, Siberia, Russia, experienced a historic heat wave that coincided with rapid expansion and generation of more than 1,700 large permafrost thaw slumps. We investigate this regional mass wasting event to better understand thaw slump timing and downstream geomorphic effects. We used repeat satellite imagery to identify slump failure with two approaches: 1) a machine learning algorithm identified slump occurrence from planform area changes, and 2) a record of suspended sediment concentration (SSC), generated from near-daily Sentinel-2 imagery, identified slump occurrence by changes in river sediment transport. Both approaches indicate widespread hillslope failure in August 2020, when temperatures were at a sustained maximum and a moderate precipitation event occurred (14 mm). Change-point analysis of the SSC record indicates a regionally consistent step change in SSC, with that change occurring at nearly all river sites on August 4 (10 sites), and August 5 (6 sites). Control rivers have either non-significant change points or change points distributed through the 2020 season. The temporal coherence of this widespread failure suggests that the region’s hillslopes failed en masse in just 1 to 3 days, creating the densest complex of thaw slumps on earth. SSC in the region continued to increase from 2021–2024, scaling with the percent of upstream area covered by slumps. The post-2020 period has the four highest average SSC years in the 40-year Landsat record (1985–2025). Channels downstream have continually adjusted for five years by widening, frequently switching channels, and aggrading.

These lines of evidence indicate that regional failure of a permafrost landscape can occur in just a matter of days, with long-lived geomorphic effects. It remains to be seen whether a combination of susceptible underlying geology and anomalous warm temperatures makes this a globally unique event. However, we find that the probability of such temperatures occurring has increased more than 1000-fold in Siberia since the mid-20th century, likely also the case elsewhere in rapidly warming high latitudes.​​​​​​​​​

authors: Panidapu, Apoorva [1], Jamgochian, Arec [2], Corso, Anthony [3], Delecki, Harrison [4], Mern, John [5], Bryk, Alexander [6]
affiliations: (1) Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA; Terra AI Inc., USA

abstract:
Exploration programs advance through a sequence of decisions made on incomplete subsurface information. Uncertainty is typically addressed within a single or handful of preferred interpretations, by varying contacts, dips, or physical properties within that interpretation. Geologists have long recognized, however, that the larger uncertainties often lie between interpretations (e.g.,whether a fertile intrusion is present at depth or whether ore-controlling faults merge along strike). These alternatives are structurally distinct geologies, and perturbing a single or handful of models cannot capture the full diversity of hypotheses.

We present an exploration framework that represents uncertainty as an ensemble of structurally distinct geologies, and evaluate it on a synthetic porphyry Cu benchmark. We begin by constructing a prior over geologies that spans competing interpretations of a mineral system. Hypotheses about a porphyry system, such as emplacement geometry, alteration zoning, intrusive order, post-mineral faulting, and cover thickness, are encoded in a probabilistic paragenetic sequence, which is sampled to produce internally consistent 3D geologies. Forward simulation of each subsurface geology produces the geophysical surveys (magnetics, gravity, DC/IP) and geological observations (outcrop and drillhole) that geology would yield. A generative model is then trained on these synthetic geologies (GeoPriors). Conditioning the priors on the data available at the site yields a posterior ensemble whose members honor all data modes simultaneously. This ensemble of data-conditioned geologies allows for quantitative analysis of subsurface uncertainty and supports drill planning against site and stage-specific objectives.

The workflow is applied to target definition on a fixed initial dataset: airborne magnetics and gravity, mapped surface geology, a ground DC/IP survey, and two shallow RC holes. We demonstrate the use of ensemble-based methods in drill planning through anomaly explanation, discovery, and delineation. Results show that the prior produces geologies of realistic complexity, that the ensemble supports decisions at all exploration stages, and that joint conditioning outperforms interpretation within any single data mode as well as conventional interpolation methods.

title: Geoheritage at GSA: A New Chapter for Geoheritage in the United States
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Sztein, Ester [1]

abstract:
U.S. geoheritage now has a home in the Geological Society of America (GSA). Concerted work towards the development of geoheritage as a discipline in the United States started in 2009 at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM). These activities included a series of technical events and symposia at GSA and other professional scientific societies and the 2013 and 2020-2021 seminal workshops on America’s Geoheritage and the resulting NASEM official proceedings. The 2015 establishment of the U.S. Advisory Group for Geoheritage led by Thomas Casadevall as a development activity of the U.S. National Committee for the IUGS served as a nucleus for U.S.-based geoheritage activities and a home for their practitioners. Members of the Advisory Group also provided advice to U.S. and international individuals and groups interested in the identification and protection of sites that are of significant scientific, educational, and cultural importance. In the meantime, GSA adopted a position statement on geoheritage in 2012, which was subsequently revised in 2017 and 2022.

Beginning in 2023, U.S. geoheritage activities became progressively incorporated within GSA. This relationship solidified through the integration of the Advisory Group within GSA’s History and Philosophy of Geology division, which in 2025 officially changed its name to GSA's History, Philosophy, and Geoheritage division. This integration allowed for the continuation of the original activities and catalyzed new opportunities and collaborations, such as important Pardee symposia, numerous technical sessions, field trips, short courses, webinars, and frequent articles on geoheritage in GSA Today . Some of these activities are the result of successful collaborations with the International Association for the Conservation of Geological Heritage (ProGEO). This presentation will provide a view on the evolution of this fascinating discipline in the United States and share ideas for future work at the national and international levels and open avenues for collaboration.

abstract: Springs are ecologically and geologically important due to being biologically diverse hotspots and revealing underground formations and bedrock lithology. With current climate changes – rain-snow transition line moving, snow accumulation lessening, and melt times coming earlier – this will affect springs' recharge rates, thus affecting life and water quality downstream. Our goal was to pinpoint the geologic units sources of spring water in the Gibson Jack Watershed in southeastern Idaho to understand the influence of geology on spring water chemistry with implications for downstream chemistry. We hypothesized that dissolved inorganic carbon would be correlated to strontium as an indicator of water-rock reaction. We collected 20 spring water samples during the winter baseflow and analyzed them for pH, specific conductivity, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and elemental compositions using a Thermo iCAP Q ICP-MS. Fifteen springs were associated with quartzites, two with limestones, two with landslide deposits, and one with shale/slate. In contrast to our expectations, DIC was weakly correlated with Sr and U (r 2 =0.6512), these were the strongest correlations found. The data showed there were specific groupings based on what lithological unit the spring water was sourced from - the limestone and quartzite made their own distinct groups in many of the elemental analyses based on DIC and ppb levels of the elements. There is an outlier in the quartzite that had high ppb levels of differing elements such as Sr, Ca, Mg, U, and Ti. The landslide deposits indicate a mix between quartzite and shale/slate based on the location and proximity to lithologic groupings. This work can be used in other watersheds in the area to fingerprint spring water sourcing.

title: Constraints on the age and hiatal duration of the unconformity at the base of the Muddy Incised Valley in the Golden/Morrison Area in the Denver Basin

abstract: In the Eastern portions of the Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway the Classic Greenhorn T-R Cycle is bounded by a basal unconformity that occurs at the base, or within, the Muddy Formation. A recent chronostratigraphic study of bentonites using 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, as well as U-Pb zircon, age dating techniques provided ages for the interpreted underlying and overlying strata, as well as context to the magnitude of the hiatus across this unconformity. This earlier chronostratigraphic work concluded that the Muddy Valley Fill in the paleo-geographically downdip Power River Basin is Early Cenomanian (approximately 99.5 mya), while the age of the interpreted Muddy Valley Fill in the paleo-geographically updip Denver Basin is older (approximately 104 mya), essentially Late Albian. Furthermore an associated hiatus of approximately 3 million years was interpreted in the Power River Basin, while a hiatus of approximately 670,000 years was interpreted in the Denver Basin. These results are puzzling, since basic sequence stratigraphic principles dictate that hiatal breaks should be greater, as well as overlying strata younger, in updip paleo-geographic locations. As a result of these puzzling chronostratigraphic relationships, a review of stratigraphy of the classic outcrop localities in the Golden-Morrison area along the western flank of the Denver Basin, where the recent bentonite samples were collected and dated, was conducted. This review revealed that none of the bentonite samples at the Dinosaur Ridge locality are from the Muddy (fluvial/estuarine) Incised Valley Fill, but were all collected from the open marine strata in the underlying (older) Skull Creek Formation. Fortunately, this recent chronostratigraphic study reported an Early Cenomanian (approximately 99.4 mya) age for a bentonite in the overlying Shell Creek/Mowry (TST) in the Denver Basin. This age would suggest, based on the ages assigned to the same strata in the Powder River Basin, an Early Cenomanian, not Late Albian, age for the underlying Muddy (Lowstand) Incised Valley at the Dinosaur Ridge locality in the Denver Basin. Finally, the stratigraphic reassignments in our interpretation also suggest that the associated hiatus across the unconformity between overlying Muddy Valley Fill and underlying Skull Creek strata at the Dinosaur Ridge locality in the Denver Basin is on the scale of 4 million years, not 670,000 years as previously interpreted.

title: Tale of Two Centrics: An Analysis of Diatom Paleoecology in Lake Core Records from Silver Lake and Shadow Lake, Sierra Nevada, CA
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Lundquist, Anna Katarina [1], Lyon, Eva [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, The College of Wooster, Houston, TX,
(2) Earth Sciences, The College of Wooster, Wooster, OH,
abstract: Diatom assemblages from lake sediment cores can be used as indicators for changing environmental conditions and can be used to study both regional and broader global climate and temperature changes. Shadow and Silver Lakes are both small, hydrologically open glacial lakes located in the eastern Sierra Nevada region of California. Despite these similarities, Shadow Lake is located higher in the mountains, where Silver Lake is located in a more populated region; due to this, these lakes are impacted by different levels of human settlement. This study will examine palaeoecological changes present in two short cores, one from each lake, with sedimentation rate from nearby June Lake suggesting that these cores preserve a record of around the past 200-500 years. Diatom assemblages from these two cores, as well as surface samples from both lakes which are used as a proxy for paleoenvironmental change. Preliminary smear slide investigations show that Silver Lake contains an abundance of fairly well-preserved diatom taxa, while the Shadow Lake diatoms are rarer, less diverse, and are generally more fragmented. Further investigations work with cleaned sediment samples, which are used to compile a voucher flora of taxa present, and diatom valves are counted to determine relative abundance throughout each core. Surface samples from the lake bottom are used to assemble a modern biogeographical profile of the lake, as well as providing a broader perspective on the diatom communities present. Changes in diatom ecology over time are used as a proxy for the influence of Euro-American settlement altering lake state over the course of the past ~200 years, with hypothesized greater changes present in Silver Lake, due to its closer proximity to human infrastructure. This leaves it more vulnerable to the impacts of pollution, eutrophication, and invasive species, which would in turn influence diatom communities present in the lake, with implications for better lake stewardship in the region. Palaeoecological changes shared between these lakes will also be examined to better understand the effects of anthropogenic climate change on this region as a whole.

title: A New Stereonet-Based Approach to Utilize 3-D Grain Shape of Detrital Zircon Populations to Identify Sediment Sources and Crystallization Conditions
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools (Posters)
authors: Wachob, Olivia M. [1], Ketcham, Richard A. [2], Malkowski, Matthew A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA

abstract: Analyzing the morphology of detrital zircon grains has been shown to provide helpful insights into the hydrodynamic sorting, mechanical abrasion, and sediment recycling effects of a given sample. Additionally, the arrangement of pyramidal and prismatic faces on a grain has been linked to crystallization conditions, providing a potential new vector for sediment source identification. Thus, the impact grain morphology analyses can have on detrital zircon applications has yet to be fully exploited. Traditional manual approaches are time-consuming and are subject to human error. Recent studies using 2-D imaging are promising for obtaining dimensional measurements but are limited in their ability to extract 3-D crystal face information of grains. Hence, we present a new method utilizing high-resolution micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) image data that generates stereonets representing the orientation, size, and condition of each crystal face for each zircon grain in a mount, often containing hundreds of grains. We then showcase the ability of deploying machine-learning based approaches to analyze these stereonets in support of detrital zircon applications. Initial results indicate that a machine learning approach using the images of each grain’s associated stereonet to classify zircon morphology can reproduce human scores, and that the accuracy of differentiating between similar morphology types may be related to noise stemming from human inconsistencies. Initial explorations using unsupervised approaches appear to be a promising avenue for avoiding this human-related subjectivity and can account for the natural variations of grain shape within a given sample or crystallization regime. The dispersion, symmetry, and orientation of crystal facets and interfacial angles displayed in each stereonet assists in interpreting grains as broken, euhedral, or rounded. Collating this information for each grain within a detrital population could characterize sediment sources or screen for sharply-faceted grains, which may aid in finding syn-depositional grains for maximum depositional age estimates. Furthermore, this technique shows promise in differentiating between 3-D shape parameters associated with original crystallization conditions and features developed through subsequent weathering or transport. Future work seeks to analyze the ability of this method to differentiate between crystallization sources and assess the role of crystal habit retention as a function of fluvial transport, while continuing to refine the stereonet classifier model to include a wider range of morphologies.

abstract: Surface loading due to thickening and thinning of ice sheets can impact the rates and composition of eruptions where the lithosphere is thin, as in Iceland. The influence of glaciation on continental arc volcanoes atop thicker lithosphere and crust is less well known. In this talk, we explore the role that glaciation and deglaciation have on two volcanoes in the Andean Southern Volcanic Zone (Chile), Villarrica and Mocho-Choshuenco before, during and after the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) at 35 to 18 ka. By coupling radioisotopic and cosmogenic dates ( 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, 14 C, 3 He and 36 Cl) with rock and mineral compositions, we show that the edifices are two to three times younger than previously thought, thereby changing the perception of volcanic risks each pose. Cliff-forming lavas terminating at 1400-1500 masl indicate that the Patagonian ice sheet was 1.5 to 2 km thick, consistent with paleoclimate models. During the peak of glaciation at 35 to 18 ka eruptive rates at both volcanoes declined three-fold. However, each volcano responded to the rapid retreat of ice between 18 and 16 ka differently. Mocho-Choshuenco erupted dacites and rhyolites long stored at great depth, ~14 km, following ice retreat at ~16 ka, whereas Villarrica mostly erupted basaltic andesite and andesites stored at 5 to 15 km depth. Mocho-Choshuenco produced a caldera-forming eruption at 11.5 ka, several millennia after glaciation whereas caldera collapse at Villarrica occurred at 16.8 ka, coincident with rapid ice loss. We suggest that Villarrica shows little compositional variation during the last glacial cycle because, despite sitting atop thermally mature crust, small reservoirs containing eruptible melt in the mid to upper crust are discrete, transient and not compartmentalized, therefore constantly interacting with one another. In contrast, the magma plumbing system beneath Mocho-Choshuenco volcano contains large shallow silicic reservoirs that are distinct from deep crustal basaltic-basaltic andesitic reservoirs. These findings —together with those from other nearby volcanoes—suggest that the response of continental arc volcanoes to regional external forcing, in this case via glaciation, is modulated by the duration of volcanism and maturity of the magma plumbing system.

title: Dynamic recrystallization induced dehydration contributes to strengthening and episodic seismicity in a lower crustal shear zone; western Churchill Province, Canada
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Flynn, Corey [1], Mahan, Kevin [2], Holyoke, Caleb [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA

abstract: Field-based and experimental studies of the effects of water on the strength of nominally anhydrous minerals indicate that dynamic recrystallization during dislocation creep causes water content to decrease. Some of these studies indicate that the strength of quartz-rich rocks is not affected by this decrease in water content, but their final water contents are still relatively high (>1000 H/10 6 Si). However, some field-based studies and recent experimental results indicate that the strength of these minerals increases as water content decreases below this amount. Additionally, few definitive studies exist on the rheology of plagioclase and the effects of water on its strength, despite it being one of the most abundant minerals in earth’s crust. The Cora Lake shear zone (1.89-1.87 Ga) of the western Churchill Province, Canada provides a natural laboratory to observe the relationships between strain and water content in nominally anhydrous minerals. The shear zone was active at transitional granulite-amphibolite facies conditions during exhumation as temperature decreased from 850 to 700°C and pressure decreased from 1.0 to 0.8 GPa corresponding to 35-25 km paleodepths. Variably mylonitized veins of pseudotachylyte are preserved within the highest strained regions of the shear zone and formed transiently during otherwise crystal plastic deformation dominated by dislocation creep. Intragranular, single point measurements of quartz and plagioclase grain interiors using Fourier Transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy yield very low water contents (0-400 H/10 6 Si) in ultramylonitized anorthosite and quartz-rich layers in mafic granulite. FTIR measurements on the same minerals in lower strain mylonitic tonalite have greater and more variable water contents (1227-23,000 H/10 6 Si). We complement these single point surveys by presenting new FTIR absorbance maps collected on porphyroclasts and recrystallized grain populations of quartz and plagioclase, the two minerals thought to have the greatest influence on the rheology of the shear zone. Our results indicate that water content in recrystallized grain domains decreases with increasing strain and decreasing grain size, consistent with water loss due to diffusion from grain interiors towards grain boundaries through dislocations and microcracking. Our results also show higher amounts of trace water in grain boundary regions than in grain interiors. Deformation-induced water loss locally strengthened the rocks in the Cora Lake shear zone and helped lead to episodic seismicity.

title: A Collapsed Labyrinth and the Origin of Equatorial Pits on Titan
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Malaska, Michael James [1], Schoenfeld, Ashley Marie [2], Schurmeier, Lauren [3], Lalich, Dan [4]
affiliations: (1) Blue Marble Space Institute of Science, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(2) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, CA, USA

abstract:
The depth of organic material in the mid-latitude plains of Saturn’s moon Titan is poorly constrained. Estimates range from 10 m to 300 m. The latter estimate is driven by measurements of the height of radial labyrinths in the mid-latitudes, which are thought to be uplifted indurated plains. In addition, the equatorial and lower latitude regions of Titan host over a thousand <10 m diameter pits scattered across the surface. The origin of these pits remain a mystery.

Re-examination of Cassini Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data revealed a feature located in the South Belet region of Titan that could provide clues to both the depth of the organic sediment layer and to equatorial pit formation mechanisms. This feature is interpreted as a partially uplifted organic plateau that has collapsed on the eastern side into a series of blocks and deep depressions. While the labyrinth plateau is elevated 300 m above the surrounding terrain, a large pit in the collapse region is 300 m below the surrounding terrain, giving a total elevation differential of 600 m. It is likely that the uplands will eventually erode down and the depressions infill to resemble typical pitted terrains as found in S Belet and in other equatorial and mid-latitude areas. The formation of the deep closed pit to a depth of 300 m (requiring at least 11 km 3 of accommodation) offers constrains on possible pit formation mechanisms. Potential mechanisms include: volatile organic sublimation, cryovolcanic blowout, melt-pool descent, dissolution, dissolution coupled with suffosion, and suffosion alone. Depending on the mechanism, and the residual organics left behind, this implies that the organic-rich sediments of these plains are between 300 and 600 m thick. The amount of organic material on Titan, especially contained in the vast mid-latitude plains has important implications for Titan’s organic production and astrobiological potential. We will present this fascinating feature, a synthetic 3D reconstruction, a likely evolution sequence, possible formation mechanisms and associated likelihood, and implications for the depth of the organic layer. It is possible that this feature may inform us of the general formation mechanism of equatorial pits on Titan.

abstract:
OpenSpace [1] is free, open-source interactive data visualization software designed to visualize the entire known universe, now in version 0.22.0. It supports live presentation of dynamic data from observations to space mission planning and operations. OpenSpace works on multiple operating systems with an extensible architecture powering many display formats, from laptops to planetarium domes. Expert users can integrate their own datasets for sharing with the OpenSpace community [2].

OpenSpace has supported 100s of interns who learn STEM skills and content [1]. Presentations have been shared via public programs at the AMNH and many informal science institutions (ISIs) and universities [3]. In 2025, OpenSpace was used in over 1,255 programs and 12 exhibits, reaching 1,050,023 individuals onsite. Over ten years, OpenSpace has driven 3,595 onsite programs, engaging 4.5M learners.

OpenSpace is an effective science teaching tool. It can be used to explore data at all scales with compelling visuals, including exploration of Moon, Mars, Earth, Venus, and Mercury using the most recent, highest resolution images on digital elevation maps and NASA TREKs layers. This allows in-classroom or virtual explanation of cratering and crustal processes, planetary morphology, lunar exploration sites and outcrops, and landscape evolution by both students and instructors [3, 4].

OpenSpace contains ephemeris data for over 1.36 million asteroids, in 12 separate orbital groups from Atira and Amor to inner-main-outer belts to Trojan and Trans-Neptunian groups. We have now added the Bus-DeMeo asteroid taxonomy [5], allowing the use of OpenSpace to explore visual-near-infrared characteristics across asteroid orbital groups. Meteor trajectories and strewnfield heat maps (as geojson and geotiff files) can now be integrated into OpenSpace (e.g., Wadsworth, 17-Mar-2026, Strewnify).
