title: Petrogenesis of mafic lavas from Tenerife, Canary Islands: Evidence for equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions during rapid ascent
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Kallahan, Tammi [1], Brehm, Sarah [2]
affiliations: (1) Atmospheric and Geological Sciences, SUNY Oswego, Oswego, NY, USA
(2) Atmospheric and Geological Sciences, SUNY Oswego, Oswego, NY, USA
abstract: Basaltic lavas provide insight into mantle sources and yield critical information about the source at the time of crystallization. This is significant for basalts associated with intraplate plumes such as the Canary Islands, as they often represent partial melts of mantle heterogeneities. Tenerife, the largest of the Canary Islands, has a history of mafic volcanism from 12Ma-present, consisting of high-MgO basanites, hawaiites, mugearites, alkali olivine basalts, and ankaramites. Samples in this study range from 13.2-8.3 wt % MgO and 249-86 ppm Ni. Trace element geochemistry indicates an asthenospheric source with no involvement from slab fluid. The presence of dense peridotite xenoliths between a 5-15 cm in diameter in erupted basalts precludes prolonged storage in crustal reservoirs and points to rapid ascent to the surface. Diffusion-limited growth textures are observed in olivine (e.g., dendritic/skeletal) and clinopyroxene (e.g., sector/oscillatory), which suggests rapid phenocryst growth during ascent. This provides an opportunity to apply olivine melt thermometry/hygrometry by pairing the most Mg-rich olivine with the whole-rock composition. The objective of this study is to apply olivine-melt thermometry/hygrometry to estimate T and the dissolved H 2 O content at the onset of crystallization. Results for a single hawaiite yield an Fe2+-Mg K D (oliv-melt) of 0.32, which is consistent with chemical equilibrium. Paired application of olivine-melt thermometry based on D Mg oliv/melt and D Ni oliv/melt is applied to estimate temperature at the liquidus. The Ni-thermometer is independent of dissolved H 2 O in the melt, and yields an actual temperature of 1140°C, whereas the Mg-thermometer gives an anhydrous temperature of 1203°C. A calculated ∆T (=T Mg – T Ni ) of 63°C represents the depression of the olivine liquidus due to 3.0 wt% dissolved H 2 O. Notably, three samples fail the Fe2+-Mg K D (oliv-melt) test for equilibrium. In one sample, the most Mg-rich olivine is too fayalitic to be in equilibrium with the whole-rock composition, indicating the sample experienced diffusive re-equilibration. For two additional samples the most Mg-rich olivine is too forsteritic to be in equilibrium with the whole-rock composition, and olivine populations are strongly bimodal. This suggests these may have an inherited high-MgO olivine population from magma mixing. However, diffusion-limited growth textures in olivine and clinopyroxene, as well as the presence of peridotite xenoliths, indicate magma mixing may be occurring during rapid ascent.

title: From Dike to Depth: Field-to-Lab rhyolite-MELTS Geobarometry of Aplites from the Tuolumne Intrusive Complex, California, U.S.A.
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part II)
authors: Lopez Acevedo, Marvin Alejandro [1], Miller, Calvin F. [2], Gualda, Guilherme A.R [3], Kelly, Liam J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Fisk-Vanderbilt Masters-to-PhD Bridge Program, Physical Sciences, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) Vanderbilt University, Earth & Environmental Sciences, Nashville, TN, USA
(3) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(4) Vanderbilt University, Earth & Environmental Sciences, Nashville, TN, USA
abstract:
Pressure estimates for felsic plutons remain difficult to obtain since evolved rock compositions often lack suitable mineral barometers and coarse granitoid whole-rock compositions rarely represent evolved liquids. Fine-grained, highly silicic aplite dikes present an opportunity as they are interpreted as crystal-poor melts extracted from nearby quartz-feldspar mushes (Miller et al GSA abstract [this meeting]).

We test this approach in the Late Cretaceous Tuolumne Intrusive Complex (TIC), California. Aplite-host granodiorite pairs were sampled from Cathedral Peak, Half Dome, and Kuna Crest units. Petrography confirms the presence of fine-grained, intergrown quartz + plagioclase + alkali feldspar (Q2F) assemblages. Whole-rock compositions obtained using XRF analysis define a narrow aplite population containing 75.9-77.5 wt% SiO2, with low values of Ca, Mg, Fe, Ti, and P relative to the granodiorite host rocks. Each aplite composition was modeled using rhyolite-MELTS (Gualda and Ghiorso, 2014) to identify the pressure closest to Q2F co-saturation; analytical uncertainty was propagated through 200 Monte Carlo compositions per sample.

Thirteen aplites yield pressures concentrated between ~190-240 Mpa (~7-9 km, assuming 2,700 kg/m^3 crustal density), with sample-level uncertainties mostly ~±30 MPa (~1 km). We find that solution quality depends not only on minimum residual magnitudes from co-saturation temperatures, but also on whether the residual curve defines a distinct internal ‘trough’; broad or ‘edge-bound’ residual curves define weak solutions. The strongest solutions cluster near ~190-220 Mpa and overlap independent TIC emplacement estimates from hornblende geothermobarometry, field constraints, and geobarometry syntheses (Ague and Brimhall, 1988; Žák and Paterson, 2005; Gray et al., 2008; Paterson et al., 2016; Memeti et al., 2022; Tomek et al., 2024). Three spatially associated Half Dome samples cluster at ~210–220 MPa, which supports reproducibility of the rhyolite-MELTS approach.

Currently, overlapping uncertainties preclude resolving systematic differences among TIC units. This suggests that the Cathedral Peak, Equigranular Half Dome, and Cathedral Peak units of the TIC formed at similar depths of ~7-9 km. Overall, our results support extraction of evolved aplite-forming liquids from the upper-crustal crystal mushes and demonstrate a field-to-laboratory workflow for obtaining reproducible pressure constraints where traditional mineral barometers are absent or ambiguous.

abstract:
Grand Mesa (2995-3452 m) is a prominent lava-capped landform in the Piceance Basin of western Colorado. The Greater Grand Mesa Area (GGMA) has an area of about 3900 km 2 and the remnant lava cap is about 155 km 2 . Mesozoic-Cenozoic strata (~3050 m thick) underlie the cap. Because of its strategic location, development of the Mesa provides important insight into the Cenozoic history of both the Southern Rocky Mountains and the Colorado Plateau.

The post-Laramide history of the GGMA began in the middle Eocene when it was at a lower elevation than today and had a much more subdued topography. Between 42 and 13 Ma (5 detrital-sanidine and -zircon MDA values), aggradational deposition occurred across the southern Piceace Basin, possibly filling relict Laramide basin paleotopography. A record of this depositional history, as preserved beneath the lava cap, consists of a 200-300 m sequence of fluvial and lacustrine sediment, informally called the “Goodenough” unit. Volcanic ash from late Eocene-Oligocene volcanic centers to the east-southeast also contributed to the Goodenough mass. Towards the end of the Goodenough’s history (late Miocene), aggradation diminished and erosion began. The Grand Mesa lavas flowed across the erosional surface.

The Grand Mesa volcanic field, which is the westernmost outlier of the mafic volcanism associated with the Rio Grande Rift in northwestern Colorado, was created by fissure-type eruptions between 10.74 and 9.82 Ma (21 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates). Magma/rock types ranged from basalt to latite (655 ICP-MS and ED-XRF analyses). Most of the lava flowed west into the paleo-valley of the ancestral Colorado River near present-day Palisade, CO. Following volcanism, regional uplift and incision by the incipient Gunnison, North Fork, and Colorado Rivers created a classic topographic inversion. Modern relief between the Colorado River and the lava cap is 1500 m, which equates to a long-term (10.7 Ma) incision rate of 140 m/Ma. The Mesa’s inversion history helps constrain the incision histories of the Black Canyon of the Gunnison and Unaweep Canyon, as well as the drainage-integration history of the upper Colorado River system.

As inversion progressed, the lava cap partially fragmented into numerous large slump blocks and during the Pleistocene, the GGMA was glaciated (ice caps) at least four times. Following deglaciation, numerous mass-wasting events occurred on the flanks of the Mesa.

title: Between Mantle and Crust: Sr–Nd–Pb Isotope Constraints on the Petrogenesis of the Cold Springs Breccia near Roosevelt, Oklahoma
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Newman, Jordan [1], Stern, Robert J. [2], Leybourne, Matthew [3]
affiliations: (1) Sustainable Earth Systems Science, University of Texas at Dallas, Plano, TX, USA
(2) Sustainable Earth Systems Science, University of Texas at Dallas, Dallas, TX, USA
(3) Queen's University, Kingston, ON,
abstract:
The Cold Springs Breccia (CSB) is a compositionally diverse igneous complex within the largely bimodal, 530 Ma Wichita Igneous Province of southern Oklahoma. The CSB’s unusual abundance of tonalite and granodiorite provides an opportunity to investigate the processes responsible for generating intermediate and felsic magmas during continental rifting. Radiogenic Sr–Nd–Pb isotope compositions were measured for representative CSB lithologies and compared with published data for regional basalts, diabase dikes, and gabbros to evaluate magma sources and test models involving fractional crystallization, liquid immiscibility, crustal melting, and magma mixing.

Initial εNd values define a systematic progression from relatively juvenile mafic rocks (+1.1 to +5.4) through intermediate rocks (−1.5 to +0.1) to granites (−2.2 to −1.3). Corresponding depleted-mantle model ages increase from 0.62–1.13 Ga in the regional mafic suite to 1.01–1.21 Ga in intermediate rocks and 1.13–1.73 Ga in granites, indicating progressively greater involvement of older continental crust with magmatic evolution. Lead isotope compositions similarly distinguish the mafic and felsic rocks while placing the CSB within an oceanic-island-basalt-like mantle field. The intermediate rocks generally occupy isotopic positions between hornblende diabase and granite. Initial Sr isotope compositions are more variable and were likely disturbed by post-magmatic fluid interaction, potentially including circulation of Rb- and Sr-bearing brines associated with Permian evaporite deposition and diagenesis. In contrast, Nd isotope compositions appear comparatively robust and Th/U and Pb/U systematics indicate limited U and Pb mobility.

The isotopic distinction between mafic and felsic rocks argues against derivation of CSB granites solely through fractional crystallization or liquid immiscibility from a mafic partial melt of lithospheric mantle. Although intermediate compositions record contributions from both mantle and 1.6 Ga continental crust, their isotopic and trace-element characteristics do not support simple local mixing of the exposed granite and diabase endmembers. Instead, the CSB records a dynamic and heterogeneous magmatic system involving mantle-derived magmatism, crustal assimilation and reworking, and deeper hybridization prior to emplacement. These results demonstrate that mechanical mingling at the present exposure represents a unique expression of a longer history of mantle–crust interaction during opening of the southern Iapetus Ocean.

authors: Wass de Czege, Jewel "Mica" K. [1], Sherpa, Tshering [2], Condit, Cailey Brown [3], Poulaki, Eirini M. [4], Tewksbury-Christle, Carolyn M. [5], Mulcahy, Sean R. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA,

(4) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA,

abstract:
During prograde subduction, dehydration reactions influence the rheology of the subducting slab. During subduction underplating and exhumation, fluid release can be intimately related to chemical and mechanical changes of the plate interface. Understanding the metamorphic evolution of exhumed subduction plate interface rocks can help illuminate how these processes occur and evolve. Ios Island, in the Greek Cyclades, comprises exhumed fossil megathrust/subduction plate interface rocks of the Cycladic Blueschist Unit (CBU). Prior detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology work on Ios indicates preservation of an imbricated repeating ~300 meters interval stack of CBU juxtaposed by cryptic thrusts. These structures are interpreted to represent underplating and syn-subduction early exhumation to greenschist-facies retrogression during the Oligo-Miocene (M2). The pre-exhumation prograde subduction history (M1) of these individual slivers remains unconstrained; it is not clear if they all reached similar P-T conditions before underplating, or represent variable depths of decoupling before subsequent underplating and stacking. We aim to determine whether rocks collected from separate slivers of the CBU record different pre-underplating P-T conditions during M1, and to understand the metamorphic evolution of the deep subduction plate interface (M1 to M2).

We present new results from Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous materials (RSCM) of 18 carbonaceous CBU samples along three transects on the north part of Ios Island. These are combined with detailed field observations, petrography, bulk rock geochemical data and phase equilibria modelling (pseudosections) to establish the (1) equilibrium conditions of M1 and M2 assemblages for samples from different CBU slivers, and (2) the relative sequence of metamorphic events that occurred during underplating and exhumation at the deep subduction plate interface.

Preliminary RSCM results indicate all the slivers reached peak temperatures of 532 ± 16oC with no statistical variation in peak metamorphic temperatures observed across the inferred cryptic thrusts . This indicates that in Ios, CBU rocks either 1) reached similar peak temperatures (and depths) and were eventually juxtaposed together by underplating or 2) sequentially reached similar peak temperatures together before underplating. Additional pseudosection models will aim to examine these tectono-metamorphic scenarios to characterize P-T evolution of CBU rocks exposed at Ios Island.

title: Associated Temporal Shifts In Functional Richness Between The Large Herbivore And Predator Guilds Of The North American Cenozoic
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic
authors: Doughty, Evan M. [1], Balisi, Mairin [2], Friscia, Anthony [3], Howenstine, Aidan [4], Jacquemetton, Christiane [5], Juhn, Mark Sunwoo [6], Marcot, Jonathan D. [7], Van Valkenburgh, Blaire [8]
affiliations: (1) Applied Earthworks, Inc., Alhambra, CA,
(2) Alf Museum of Paleontology, Claremont, CA,
(3) Department of Integrative Biology and Physiology, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA,
(4) Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA,
(5) Department of Biology, St. Mary's College of Maryland, Los Angeles, CA,

abstract:
The species richness of large mammalian predators positively correlates with that of their presumed large herbivore prey in both modern and fossil assemblages at continental (e.g., North America) and global scales. This relationship is strongest for predators exceeding 21 kg, but it remains unclear if this pattern represents an evolutionary response by predators to changes in the body mass distribution within the herbivore guild, a byproduct of other drivers, or stochasticity. We further explored the relationship between these patterns by subdividing the predator and herbivore guilds into ecologically significant body mass categories and tracking the species richness of these categories through time. We estimated the body mass of predators ( n =400 species) using the length of the lower carnassial (m1), and that of large herbivores ( n =1087 species) using the lengths and widths of the upper and lower cheek teeth; dental metrics were measured directly on specimens or, when inaccessible, were compiled from the literature. We partitioned each guild into five ecologically significant body-mass categories, then tested for significant temporal shifts in the distribution of richness among these categories. We compared the timing of shifts between the guilds and with environmental events.

The herbivore guild shows significant shifts at five distinct points in time that characterize a long-term transition from an assemblage dominated by chevrotain- and javelina-size (5-25 kg) herbivores to one dominated by antelope- (25-150 kg) and horse-size (150-500 kg) herbivores. These shifts chiefly occurred synchronously with, or following, major climatic or environmental transitions, suggesting widespread evolutionary responses to these events. Meanwhile, the predator guild exhibits four significant shifts. We identified that three of these (at 45 Ma, 31 Ma, and 17 Ma) lagged (≤2 Ma) after those of the herbivore guild. These three shifts were characterized by the proliferation of coyote- (7-21 kg), wolf- (21-100 kg), and/or lion-size (>100 kg) predators, and follow notable increases in the richness of antelope-size and larger herbivores. The correspondence of temporal shifts of body mass distributions in the two guilds corroborate earlier studies on taxonomic richness, and further suggests that the evolution of herbivores had a strong influence on the mammalian predator guild throughout the Cenozoic.

title: When is Ecological Change Evidence of Selective Extinction? Simulating the Effect of Random Extinction on Functional Diversity in Ecosystems with Variable Rank-Abundance Distributions
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Samuels-Fair, Maya [1], Finnegan, Seth [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(2) Integrative Biology, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
abstract:
Selective extinction by definition causes some groups to become extinct at higher rates than others and is thus often assumed to be the cause of functional diversity changes following mass extinctions. However, significant changes in functional diversity can occur even when extinction is nonselective (random). Counterintuitively, lack of functional diversity change can also be evidence of selective extinction. This can occur because (1) the number of taxa in each functional group varies and (2) the abundance of each functional group varies. Consequently, random removal of taxa or individuals disproportionately affects rare functional groups. We simulate random extinction with a range of initial rank abundance distributions, varying the number of taxa in each functional group and the evenness of abundances across taxa. We then measure change in functional diversity before and after random extinction using PERMANOVA. This generates a null distribution of how functional diversity would be expected to change under random extinction for each initial rank abundance distribution. Change in functional diversity outside the null distribution is then positive evidence of nonrandom extinction, nonrandom origination, or nonrandom changes in abundance.

We apply this approach to examine changes in the bryozoan fauna of Stevns Klint, Denmark following the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) mass extinction, using a dataset of 4,453 specimens from 13 pre-extinction and 7 post-extinction samples. We find that functional diversity changes significantly across the K/Pg boundary, but functional change is largely consistent with random extinction, followed by an increase in the abundances of the functional groups with the fewest taxa. Our approach thus allows us to differentiate between selective extinction and other mechanisms of functional diversity change, which can be applied to other extinction events.

title: Revision of the Morrison-Cloverly Contact in the Northern Bighorn Basin, Wyoming
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Dalton, Jack [1], Parcell, William C. [2]
affiliations: (1) Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(2) Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
abstract:
The Morrison and Cloverly Formations are crucial for understanding environmental and faunal shifts that occurred in Wyoming and Montana during the Upper Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous. A disconformable contact exists between these two units. Unfortunately, the lithologic markers of this contact are poorly-defined. The limited exploration of the uppermost Morrison in this segment of the Western Interior is a major reason for this. Additionally, there is significant variability in the extent of the stratigraphic interval removed by the Morrison-Cloverly disconformity. At some exposures, lower members of the Cloverly may be partially or fully-present. At others, these lower members are entirely absent.

Ongoing lithostratigraphic and chemostratigraphic work on stratigraphic sections in the Indian Pass 7.5 min Quadrangle in the Bighorn Basin of northwestern Wyoming has indicated the presence of a bentonite-dominated subunit in the uppermost Morrison. Thick accumulations of bentonite have also been identified at localities in the Bald Peak and Spence 7.5 min Quadrangles. As bentonite beds can also be prevalent in lower members of the Cloverly, this presents another challenge in identifying the Morrison-Cloverly contact.

Recent fieldwork conducted at seven localities in the Bald Peak, Indian Pass, and Spence 7.5 min Quadrangles has identified lithologic markers that can define contacts between bentonitic horizons of the uppermost Morrison and different members of the Cloverly. Markers for the contact between the Morrison and the Cloverly’s lower Pryor Conglomerate member are consistent with those established in the literature. Novel markers for contacts between the uppermost Morrison and the Cloverly’s Little Sheep Mudstone and Greybull Sandstone members are herein reported.

title: Geochemical fingerprinting of Snake River Plain volcanics deposited in the Renova Formation near Bozeman, Montana, USA
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Joyce, Eliza [1], Conrad, Lucia [2], Kenderes, Elizabeth [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
abstract: Volcanic ash and lithics can be expelled thousands of miles away from the eruption site following a volcanic eruption. Cryptotephra are microscopic glass particles and mineral fragments that can provide a geochemical fingerprint to trace ash deposits to their volcanic origins. Two samples of volcanic tuff were collected from Bozeman, Montana from the Miocene Climbing Arrow Member of the Renova Formation, an extensional basin deposit containing preserved ash beds and fluvial-mobilized volcanic material. Volcanic glass fragments were separated from bulk tephra under a microscope and analyzed for trace elements (Cr, Ni, Zn, Rb, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, Ba, Pb, Th, U, and REEs) using ICP-MS, which was compared to regional volcanic rock logged on the EarthChem database. The ages were estimated to be 9.33 – 10.35Ma based on ages of three previous samples with K-Ar sanidine dates. Trace element analysis shows a correlation to volcanics derived from the Snake River Plain. ICP-MS provides bulk chemical analysis, but these volcanic ash beds have the potential to be derived from multiple eruptive events. SEM analysis on individual glass grains was conducted to determine major element composition and mode of deposition. We found there were multiple distinct clusters of geochemical compositions per sample, suggesting reworking of ash by fluvial or aeolian processes. Approximately one-fifth of the glass grains clusters around 10-14wt.% K 2 O+Na 2 O and 60-65 wt.% SiO 2 content. About half cluster around 5-7wt.% K 2 O+Na 2 O and 63-70wt.% SiO 2 content, and the remaining fraction of samples has 2-5 wt.% K2O+Na2O and 44-54wt.% SiO 2 content. K-Ar sanidine dating of the Bozeman samples and repeating ICP-MS for more accurate geochemical data will be completed to narrow down a volcanic center within the Snake River Plain more precisely. Current age estimates of 9.33-10.35Ma and similar major element composition suggest the tephra originated from Twin Falls or Picabo, which had active volcanism 10.0 – 8.6Ma and 10.2Ma respectively. This study shows how cryptotephra can be used to model the patterns of ancient volcanoes and how volcanic material traveled following an eruption. These data can be used to help predict how a modern-day eruption may behave and how ash is transported that could help us prepare for and model future eruptions.

abstract:
Graphite is a globally recognized critical material, with demand growth driven primarily by the burgeoning lithium-ion battery market. Downstream processing of natural graphite for battery applications includes a shaping (i.e., spheronization) step, which is implemented to tune the graphite’s morphology, particle size distribution, and surface properties. This step enhances graphite’s electrochemical performance by facilitating lithium-ion diffusion, increasing packing density, and reducing electrode tortuosity - and is essential to meeting the stringent performance requirements of modern lithium-ion batteries, such as fast-charging. The shaping process imposes complex physical forces on graphite particles, which influence structural and morphological properties relevant to battery applications. Past studies probing the impact of varied shaping parameters on graphite properties and performance have predominantly been parametric, probing linear variations of single parameters within a specific milling system framework with limited variable tuning. Building a comprehensive tie between all tunable operating parameter combinations, the physical forces experienced by graphite during milling, the resulting physical properties of graphite, and the associated electrochemical performance is essential to achieving a true processing/property/performance optimization framework for battery-grade natural graphite.

To this end, our teams at the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) and Orbia have collaboratively developed a machine-learning (ML)-based optimization framework to enhance the efficiency of industrial-scale natural graphite shaping. We have employed a Taguchi design-of-experiments approach coupled with a ML-based regression model to rationally inform optimization of a low-cost, scalable shaping method (ball-milling). We have systematically investigated the effects of several key milling parameters on the morphological transformation of virgin natural graphite, and have quantified the tunability in graphite morphology and resulting properties as a function of processing conditions. Through multi-scale physicochemical characterization, we establish milling parameter optimization criteria using a range of morphological descriptors that are critically relevant to practical battery applications. We have also applied model-informed shaping optima to a range of purified recycled graphite materials, and highlight the challenges of directly translating parameter optima between disparate feedstocks. Our coupled ML/experimental approach lays a strong foundation for further optimization, enabling the cost-effective shaping of high-performing battery-grade graphite from diverse feedstock sources. Further, the quantitative methodology developed here to describe processing–structure–performance relationships may be extended to inform optimization of both alternative shaping methodologies and additional graphite processing steps.

title: Using Continental Scientific Drilling to Constrain the Source of Trace Metals in Drinking Water in West-Central Wisconsin
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling
authors: Zambito, James Joseph [1]
affiliations: (1) Beloit College, Beloit, WI,
abstract:
Most drinking water in the Upper Mississippi River Valley comes from the extensive Cambrian-Ordovician aquifer system. While municipalities regularly test well water, private well owners are less diligent. This is problematic because without regular testing no baseline exists for identifying when water quality changes and by how much. During a recent industrial (frac) sand mining boom in west-central Wisconsin, testing of unlined mine ponds found low pH and high trace metal concentrations leading to an increase in private well testing and water quality issue identification. However, it was unclear if these issues were new or preexisting. Other wells in the area drawing water from the same strata being mined had low pH and trace metal contamination before mining started. This suggested a common geogenic cause for both mine pond and groundwater contamination.

Low pH and proximity to Mississippi Valley Type (MVT) mineralization suggested sulfide minerals were the likely trace metal source. However, sulfides are not easily sampled at the surface because of oxidative weathering; this is especially true in west-central Wisconsin, part of the Driftless Area, where surface exposures have undergone oxidation for possibly millions of years. Continental Scientific Drilling was therefore critical for obtaining unaltered aquifer system sample material for analysis. Sulfide mineralization in core and cutting samples is observed as locally patchy but regionally distributed throughout the aquifer system. Mineralogical and geochemical analyses indicate that sulfides have two origins: trace metal-bearing sulfides typically occur as nodules and stratiform mineralization sourced from MVT fluids, while sulfides not enriched in trace metals are typically disseminated intergranular cements and burrow infills associated with Cambrian early diagenesis; the latter sulfides are also highly prevalent in strata recording the SPICE biogeochemical event. Additionally, during microbially-mediated oxidation of MVT and Cambrian sulfides, iron (hydr)oxides may scavenge trace metals present. The potential for trace metal contamination of groundwater is therefore site specific and primarily related to local sulfide and iron (hydr)oxide mineralization in combination with water table fluctuations that cause redox changes. Although most trace metal contamination of groundwater in the study area is likely geogenic, contaminated water infiltration from nearby unlined mine ponds as well as water table fluctuations caused by municipal, agricultural, and mine high-capacity well pumping or climate change can be a contributing factor.

title: Sedimentary Redox Responses Across the Last Two Deglaciations: Multiproxy reconstructions from new cores in the central equatorial Pacific
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Jacobel, Allison W. [1], Kosta, Kassandra M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Climate Sciences, Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT, ; Institute for Arctic and Alpine Research, University of Colorado Boulder,
(2) Marine Geology and Geophysics, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution,
abstract:
Deep ocean ventilation changes and respired carbon storage amplify insolation-driven glacial-interglacial climate change. Sedimentary redox proxies respond to both climate/circulation-driven changes in bottom water oxygenation (BWO) and local depositional conditions, including oxygen exposure time and organic carbon flux, complicating efforts to isolate and quantify the signature of bottom-water oxygen concentrations. Disentangling these controls is important for understanding when and where deep ocean ventilation signals are preserved, with implications for the spatial distribution of reconstructed oxygen changes 1 and efforts to reconstruct more quantitative BWO estimates 2 .

Here, we present new redox-sensitive metal enrichment records (Mn and aU) from a transect of cores in the Line Islands region of the central equatorial Pacific. Because the sites span a latitudinal transect (from just south of the equator to ~7°N), they also span the productivity gradient created by equatorial upwelling. The sites all occupy the same abyssal water mass, experiencing synchronous deglacial changes in BWO, so local differences in sedimentation and productivity can be evaluated independently of regional BWO 3 . Our sites record contrasting redox signals as a function of oxygen exposure time (and associated sedimentation rates) and organic carbon fluxes. We evaluate these controls using paired reconstructions of 230 Th-normalized Ba xs (productivity), and oxygen exposure time derived from 14 C- and δ 18 O-constrained age models 4 and dry bulk density 5 . Our results provide a framework for evaluating the fidelity of sedimentary redox proxies and identifying the depositional conditions under which changes in BWO are most faithfully recorded.

title: Geologic Map of the Mexican Hill Quadrangle, Northwestern Bighorn Mountains, Wyoming, USA, with Structural, Geochemical, and Petrologic Interpretations
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Gifford, Jennifer N. [1], Phelps, Lauren E. [2], Johns, Jessica T. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Mississippi,
(2) University of Mississippi,
(3) University of Mississippi,
abstract: The Bighorn Mountains (BHMs) of Wyoming show evidence of a long geologic history, beginning in the Archean. Past studies have found that intrusion of the northern igneous batholith took place in multiple pulses over ~200 million years, between ~2.7 Ga and ~2.9 Ga with the southern gneissic terrane being older. The formation of the mountains themselves resulted from the Late Cretaceous to Eocene Laramide Orogeny. The state of Wyoming’s current bedrock geologic map is at the scale of 1:500,000 and more detailed maps are needed to fully explain the BHM’s history. Mapping projects (1:24,000 scale), structural interpretations, and in-depth analyses of the granitoids in the Mexican Hill quadrangle (MHQ), have been performed in an attempt to further understand the petrogenesis of the northern batholith. Traditional field mapping methods combined with Field Move Clino were used to create a detailed geologic map of the quadrangle along with two interpretive cross sections. Once field samples were collected, thin section analyses, U-Pb geochronology, and major, minor, and trace element geochemistry were performed to better understand the intrusion ages and chemistry changes to identify whether the intrusion occurred as a single or multiple events. The MHQ contains one basement unit (monzogranite, granodiorite, tonalite, and quartz monzodiorite), two diabase dikes, and six sedimentary units (Flathead Sandstone (Ss), Gallatin-Gros Ventre (GGV) formations (fms), Bighorn Dolomite, Madison Limestone (Ls), and Amsden Formation (Fm)). Petrography reveals evidence of myrmekite, sericitization, hydrothermal alteration, and antiperthitic texture. The units in the MHQ demonstrate Laramide deformation through three major structures: monoclinal folding, a reverse/thrust fault, and a shallowly dipping anticline. The monoclines of the MHQ formed from a blind fault buried within ductile units rather than the major thrust/reverse fault. General trends in the dip of sedimentary units indicate that there was increased uplift in the southern half of the map area. The reverse/thrust fault terminated in the northeast corner of the MHQ and influenced flexural slip folding of the GGV fms and Bighorn Dolomite, which resulted in the anticline. U-Pb ages yielded an average of 2881 ± 5.6 Ma. The chemistry and geochronology suggest the Mexican Hill quadrangle basement is a subduction-zone granite from one intrusion event.

(2) University of Texas Institute for Geophysics, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
Airborne ice-penetrating radar systems from the 2023–2024 Dome A, East Antarctica field campaign that operate at different frequencies can reproduce the same broad ice geometry while emphasizing different reflectors. I compared coincident observations collected with the University of Texas Institute for Geophysics very-high-frequency (VHF) radar and the University of Kansas ultra-high-frequency (UHF) radar collected as part of the NSF COLDEX Science and Technology Center to evaluate how each system represents the surface, internal stratigraphy, and ice-bed interface. The Antarctic ice sheet shows radar horizons within the ice of constant age, which we compare across each system using the Open Polar Radar framework.

Overlapping flight observations were identified and matched using UTC acquisition times; paired radargrams were extracted and individual traces were aligned at the ice surface. Consistent automated surface and reflector Python picking scripts were applied, followed by manual evaluation and interpretation of reflector visibility. Of 66 candidate matches, 57 (86%) were successfully processed and reviewed.

Both systems reproduced the same broad ice geometry, but their dominant returns were systematically different. The bed was clearly visible in all reviewed UTIG records, whereas the KU bed was weak in 24 records (42%) and not visible in 33 (58%). The KU automatic picker selected a shallower internal reflector in all 57 records. The KU pick had a median of 8.317 μs below the surface and was tightly grouped across observations, with a standard deviation of 0.505 μs.

Among 54 comparisons with an identified candidate internal horizon, 45 (83%) KU files were within 1 μs, and 53 (98%) were within 2 μs of that horizon; 48 of 54 (89%) were closest to the 51 ka horizon. In the 33 comparisons with coverage of the interpreted 161 ka horizon, the KU pick was separated from it by a median of 11.963 μs, indicating that the picked reflector is unlikely to represent the 161 ka layer at these locations.

These results show that automated picks cannot be assigned geologic meaning from continuity and amplitude alone. Multi-frequency comparison and manual validation are therefore necessary to distinguish internal layers from the bed and improve interpretations of Antarctic ice thickness, basal geometry, and internal stratigraphy for NSF COLDEX exploration.

title: Delineating Specific Ignimbrite Units in the Sour Creek Dome, Yellowstone - A Multi Pronged Approach
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Ketel, Jessica [1], Myers, Madison [2], Redfield, Trista [3], Schweiger, Anna [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, Montana State University, Bozeman, Montana, USA
(2) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
(3) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
(4) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
abstract:
The two supereruptions erupted from Yellowstone volcano over the last 2 Ma are globally uncommon, with no modern example. Therefore, a thorough understanding of their deposits is required to understand the scale and behavior of eruption progression, to better comprehend the evolution of future unrest. Recent work in the Sour Creek dome (SCD) of Yellowstone has altered our understanding of both supereruptions. The Lava Creek Tuff (LCT; 0.631 Ma; 1000km 3 ) was originally split into members A and B, and overlied the older Huckleberry Ridge Tuff (HRT: 2.08 Ma; 2500km 3 ). New evidence shows that both of these interpretations were incorrect. First, the mapped HRT returns an Ar/Ar age of 631,000 years old, proving it is part of the LCT eruption. However, all outcrops visited in the SCD do not fit the descriptions of either mapped members A or B. Instead, these ignimbrites are now divided into four packages based on componentry (e.g., pumices, scorias, recycled clasts) and sanidine geochemistry. At this time, it remains unclear how these units project towards the eastern side of the dome. Samples taken from Stonetop Mountain were initially assumed to be part of Package 2, but quantitative validation is required prior to extending the unit.

Sanidine crystals were imaged via cathodoluminescence for zoning, then analyzed for major and trace element (barium - Ba) geochemistry with an electron microprobe. Stonetop sanidine have an average Ba concentration of 500 ppm while the other units have averages greater than 2,500 ppm. In addition, Stonetop sanidines have significantly more zoning (95%) compared to the other members (package 2 - 75%, package 3 - 79%, package 4 - 58%). Coupled with its rich componentry, we confirm that Stonetop Mountain is a separate ignimbrite package. The challenge remains as to what lies in the area between package 2 and 5. To address this gap, we used remote sensing. Spectral data gathered by Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation was used to train a statistical model and is being used to project these units into unexplored regions of the SCD. Only predicted pixels that were above 70% certainty were denoted as one of the known units, otherwise the pixel was marked as unknown. This method will allow us to prioritize unvisited areas for future field work to finalize a geologic map of the SCD.

title: RAPID CONSTRUCTION AND EPISODIC REJUVENATION OF LOWER-CRUSTAL MUSH IN THE MEDIAN BATHOLITH, NEW ZEALAND
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Schwartz, Joshua J [1], Tulloch, Andrew J [2], Ramezani, Jahandar [3], Klepeis, Keith A. [4], Miranda, Elena A. [5], Stowell, Harold H. [6]
affiliations: (1) California State University Northridge, Northridge, CA, USA
(2) GNS Science, Dunedin, New Zealand
(3) Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA,
(4) University of Vermont, Burlington, VT,
(5) California State University Northridge, Northridge, CA,
(6) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
abstract:
Lower-crustal magma systems beneath continental arcs are important for the chemical evolution of arc magmas, yet there is considerable controversy regarding the timescales over which deep-crustal arc magmas are stored, remobilized, and extracted. We investigate this problem through integrated field mapping, mineral thermometry, published garnet ages, and U-Pb zircon chemical abrasion thermal ionization mass spectrometry (CA-ID-TIMS) from ten samples across the lower-crustal Malaspina Pluton and adjacent Resolution Orthogneiss in the Mesozoic Median Batholith, Fiordland, New Zealand. The Malaspina Pluton represents a ~550 km² dioritic body which was assembled by numerous intrusions at 35-40 km depth. Magma was emplaced through two steep feeder zones along the Straight River shear zone, which acted as lithospheric-scale melt-transfer pathway. Most of the Malaspina Pluton was fed from a northwestern feeder zone, and dioritic magma spread eastward and southeastward into subhorizontal, isobaric sheets. A second feeder zone (Breaksea–Crooked Arm corridor) preserves a complex record of melt-reworked rejuvenated domains that are manifested by mafic recharge, leucocratic veins, peritectic garnet-bearing assemblages in melt-rich reaction zones, disrupted mush textures, and high-strain fabrics signaling open-system modification of lower-crustal mush.

New zircon geochronology reveals that low-strain dioritic sheets crystallized rapidly giving tightly clustered weighted-mean 206 Pb/ 238 U dates between 117.33 ± 0.04 and 117.05 ± 0.05 Ma consistent with crystallization in less than 0.3 Myr. In contrast, samples from rejuvenated domains along the southern Breaksea–Crooked Arm corridor preserve broader, overdispersed zircon populations with individual samples recording age spans of 0.4–5.6 Myr consistent with episodic rejuvenation extending locally to ca. 111.6 Ma. A sample from the Resolution Orthogneiss yields a tightly clustered zircon age of 115.85 ± 0.07 Ma, recording renewed dioritic intrusion in the Breaksea area while adjacent older mush was being rejuvenated. Published Sm-Nd and Lu-Hf garnet ages of 115.6 ± 2.6 to 110.6 ± 1.9 Ma date peritectic garnet growth in melt-rich reaction zones, independently linking the younger zircon record to melt-present mush rejuvenation. Our data show that lower-crustal magma systems comprise dynamically evolving mosaics of mush in which neighboring domains record distinct crystallization and rejuvenation histories. Thus, rapid batholith construction (10 5 yr) and prolonged magmatic rejuvenation (10 6 yr) are paired processes in the construction of lower-arc crust.

title: The Role of Production, Dilution, and Decomposition of Marine Organic Matter in the decoupling of δ13CTOC and δ13CCARB patterns during the Givetian-Frasnian Transition, Northern Appalachian Basin
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)
authors: Zambito, James Joseph [1], McLaughlin, Patrick I. [2]
affiliations: (1) Beloit College, Beloit, WI,
(2) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL,
abstract:
Sageman et al.’s seminal paper “A Tale of Shales” outlined the roles of production, dilution, and decomposition in controlling the formation of organic-rich strata in the Devonian Appalachian Basin, with key insights into black shale deposition throughout Earth history. As part of this and Sageman et al.’s companion papers, unique geochemical profiles associated with the Geneseo Formation in the Akzo #9455 Core were noted. For example, a ~2‰ negative shift in δ 13 C TOC during Geneseo black shale deposition was not related to changing proportions of marine versus terrestrial organic matter fluxes even though the detrital sediment influx proxy Ti/Al showed a slight increase through the Geneseo. This negative shift in δ 13 C TOC values has since been recognized as a global shift to some of the lightest δ 13 C values in the Devonian coincident with evidence for warming during the Givetian-Frasnian transition.

We build upon Sageman et al.’s work on the Akzo #9455 Core Geneseo Formation with a comparable dataset from the more proximal Cargill #17 Core that also includes a δ 13 C CARB profile that shows a negative shift to relatively extreme values near -5‰. However, in the Lansing #17 Core δ 13 C TOC values show a shift to lighter values only in the lower Geneseo equivalent. A decoupling of δ 13 C TOC and δ 13 C CARB patterns occurs in the upper Geneseo-equivalent, coarser-grained Sherburne Formation with a δ 13 C TOC shift to more positive values while δ 13 C CARB values become further depleted to extremely light values. Unlike the basinal settings of the Akzo #9455 Core, in proximal settings the influx of terrestrial organic matter, and dilution of marine organic matter, imparts enough of a signal to influence δ 13 C TOC values as seen in the Lansing #17 Core. Furthermore, the proximal record shows an increase in the detrital influx ratios of Si/Al and Ti/Al as well as a decrease in TOC values and Mo concentrations coincident with the transition to the coarser-grained Sherburne Formation and influx of terrestrial organic matter. Within the framework of Sageman et al.’s model for the formation of organic-rich strata, the decoupling of δ 13 C TOC and δ 13 C CARB patterns in combination with detrital influx and redox proxies suggests marine organic matter was likely influenced by increased dilution and possibly increased decomposition and decreased production during Sherburne Formation progradation in proximal settings.

title: Mafic arc cumulates in the mantle lithosphere -- one way to solve the crust composition paradox
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Rudnick, Roberta L. [1], Ortner, Sophia E. [2], Rubatto, Daniela [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science and Earth Research Institute, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(3) Institute of Geological Sciences, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland
abstract: The continental crust has an intermediate bulk composition, but mantle melts are basalt: the crust composition paradox. One way to solve this mismatch is for mafic cumulates that are compositionally complementary to the overlying crust to accumulate below the Moho. However, such cumulates, which are seen in some arc cross sections, are rare in continental xenolith suites, suggesting that any original mantle cumulates formed below oceanic arcs may have been lost to the deep lithosphere via density foundering at the time of arc-continent collision. This scarcity also raises the question of how important such deep differentiation is in building average continental crust, much of which may form above continental subduction zones. Texturally distinctive, mafic, kyanite-scapolite-clinozoisite-plagioclase-garnet-clinopyroxene-quartz-bearing granulite xenoliths from Big Slide, an Eocene diatreme in central Montana, have bulk rock compositions similar to plagioclase-rich arc cumulates (e.g., positive Eu and Sr anomalies; depletion in Nb and Ta relative to La). Equilibration pressures are high (1.5-2.2 GPa), corresponding to depths below the present-day Moho, which lies at ~45 km; plagioclase and garnet are zoned (lower An on plagioclase rims; higher Grs on garnet rims), reflecting a late pressure increase in the xenolith’s evolution. Garnet d 18 O values are homogeneous across grains and mantle-like (ave. 5.3 ± 0.9‰, n = 56). Thus, the xenoliths are interpreted as cumulates from mafic subduction zone magmas that formed in the mantle lithosphere, and which experienced recent thickening (perhaps during the Late Cretaceous Laramide orogeny). Late-stage brown chlorite, and possibly clinozoisite and scapolite (which forms rosettes around original sulfides in one sample) may reflect overprinting from fluids derived from the Farallon flat slab. There are no dateable U-bearing accessory minerals except rutile and apatite, the former of which defines the eruption age of 47 ± 2 Ma. We speculate that these cumulates formed below the antecedent continental(?) arc to the ~1.8 Ga Great Falls Tectonic Zone, which marks the closure of a Paleoproterozoic ocean, and were later modified by flat slab Farallon subduction. Their presence in the continental mantle lithosphere suggest sub-Moho basalt differentiation may indeed be an important process that could explain the continental crust paradox.

title: Quantitatively Exploring the Consequences of Open-System Magmatic Processes at Mid-Ocean Ridges
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part II)
authors: Bohrson, Wendy A. [1], Spera, Frank J [2], Strasser, Valerie [3], Estes, Bailey [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of California, Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(3) School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(4) School of Minerals and Subsurface Energy, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Petrochemical and geophysical studies indicate that mid-ocean ridge (MOR) magma storage zones are thin (~100-200 m), shallow axial melt lenses (AML) embedded within surrounding large-volume magma mush. The AML is replenished from below. Ongoing debate centers on the details of storage zone processes and the role of mantle versus crust in generating geochemical diversity, notably the source of incompatible trace element (ITE) variations. While there is unequivocal evidence that the asthenosphere is heterogeneous and therefore a source of ITE variation, crustal processes also affect AML petrochemistry.

Using the Magma Chamber Simulator (MCS), the impact of crustal processes on the mineralogy and geochemistry of mafic MORB (>6 wt.% MgO) is explored. Differentiation MCS models (n = 70, 0.15 GPa) combine fractional crystallization, recharge/magma mixing, addition of interstitial mush melt to resident magma, crustal assimilation, and eruption. Interstitial melts form in a solidification zone within the magma storage region, the modeled crust is MORB, and eruption is modeled via isentropic decompression.

All runs yield copious plagioclase with secondary olivine + clinopyroxene. Total crystallization is suppressed when assimilation and/or addition of in situ mush melt occur and is enhanced when recharge/magma mixing occurs. Compared to fractional crystallization, clinopyroxene is least abundant in simulations that include assimilation and interstitial mush melt; in addition, clinopyroxene resorbs during ascent. Despite these differences in total crystallization, at the same MgO, Al 2 O 3 , CaO, and Na 2 O are not dramatically affected by open-system processes compared to fractional crystallization-only. In contrast, FeO* and TiO 2 are lower, and SiO 2 and K 2 O are higher than in fractional crystallization-only runs, consistent with the addition of more evolved melts contributed by mush and crustal assimilation. Using K 2 O as a proxy for ITE behavior, enrichment in K 2 O (= K 2 O in 6 wt.% MgO melt/K 2 O in 10% wt. MgO melt) for fractional crystallization-only = ~2.6. In cases where interstitial mush melt is episodically added to a magma undergoing recharge-fractional crystallization-eruption, enrichment = ~3.8. Assimilation-fractional crystallization-eruption simulations yield a greater degree of enrichment = ~5.5.

These preliminary findings indicate that open-system processes in crustal storage zones can lead to significant chemical heterogeneity in relatively mafic MORB, particularly enrichments in ITE. Enabled by MCS's ability to model multiple open-system processes, including eruption, additional modeling, particularly focused on ITE, further illuminates how MORB petrochemistry is impacted by crustal processing.

title: Simulating Vertical Land Movement and Rising Sea Level in New Zealand Using MODFLOW-API
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Kitlasten, Wes [1], Chambers, Lee [2], Moore, Catherine [3], Narvaiza, Maria [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences New Zealand, Christchurch, New Zealand; University of Canterbury, Waterways Centre, Christchurch, New Zealand
(2) Earth Sciences New Zealand, Wellington, New Zealand
(3) Earth Sciences New Zealand, Wellington, New Zealand
(4) Earth Sciences New Zealand, Taupo, New Zealand
abstract:
Climate models predict rising global sea level and changes in atmospheric processes such as precipitation and evapotranspiration. The impacts of rising sea level on shallow coastal groundwater systems can be complicated by local vertical land movement, while changes in groundwater and surface water inputs are affected by on-land climate factors (i.e., precipitation and evapotranspiration). Evaluating the response of the shallow coastal groundwater system requires consideration of both large-scale on-land processes and high-resolution local-scale topography near the coast.

We present a workflow for evaluating the combined impacts of relative sea level rise (i.e., RSLS = vertical land movement + sea level rise) and changing atmospheric forcing (i.e., precipitation and evapotranspiration) on shallow groundwater systems near the coast. A history matched national-scale groundwater model is used to inform parameter values of higher resolution models along the coast, including groundwater and surface water flows along the inland boundary. The MODFLOW-API is used to modify the elevation of the upper boundary, controlling surface drainage, and the coastal boundary based on projection of RSLR from the NZ SeaRise project. The extent of shallow groundwater (<1m from surface) is evaluated using ensemble-based estimates of uncertainty.

We demonstrate the workflow across contrasting New Zealand case studies and management contexts, including socially, culturally, and agriculturally significant coastal areas, as well as tectonically active regions where vertical land movement strongly influences groundwater levels and drainage. For example, in low-lying urban environments such as Wellington, where even modest relative sea-level rise may substantially reduce the capacity of gravity-driven stormwater and wastewater networks, while exacerbating groundwater flooding with implications for infrastructure performance and adaptation planning. In agriculturally important coastal regions, the workflow can be adapted to evaluate changes in groundwater levels and salinity, supporting assessments of freshwater availability, drainage performance, and long-term land-use resilience. For this case study, the coastal boundary representation was improved using a density-corrected general-head boundary, in which equivalent freshwater heads and conductances were derived from paired variable-density cross-sectional models along the coastline.

title: A Morphological, Taxonomic, and Taphonomic Analysis of Canis from the Mid-Irvingtonian Fairmead Landfill Locality, Madera County, California
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy
authors: Iliff, Samuel Edmund [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, California State University, Fresno, Fresno, California, USA
abstract:
Fairmead Landfill in Madera County, California preserves a diverse middle Irvingtonian (0.78–0.55 Ma) vertebrate assemblage of 72 taxa that includes coyote ( Canis latrans ) and dire wolf ( Canis dirus ). This study examines the taxonomic placement, morphology, and taphonomic condition of Canis specimens from Fairmead Landfill through direct morphological comparison and metric analysis using modern coyote material, Rancho La Brea Canis dirus material, and published data from Nowak (1979), Kurtén (1984), and Merriam (1912).

Small-bodied specimens including UCMP 140413, MCPC A19, MCPC A1762, and MCPC A2606 exhibit gracile morphology and trenchant dentition consistent with Canis latrans . UCMP 140413 had wider M1 (18.6 mm) and M2 (13.3 mm) molars when compared to historical measurements, which could be explained by the larger size of large male pleistocene C. latrans as suggested by Nowak (1979) in other localities.

Large-bodied specimens including MCPC A948, UCMP 140265, MCPC A2209, UCMP uncat and MCPC A2202 exhibit robust dentition, enlarged carnassials, and reduced grinding cusps consistent with hypercarnivorous adaptations associated with C. dirus . MCPC A2209 preserves reduced metaconids and pronounced trigonid morphology most consistent with C. dirus . MCPC A2202 possesses a long left tibia (325 mm) relative to Rancholabrean specimens recorded in Kurtén (1984) and Nowak (1979). This longer tibia potentially reflects a greater morphological variability in Irvingtonian C. dirus populations relative to later Rancholabrean morphotypes.

Specimen MCPC A2202 is a partial skeleton composed of the left mandible with an incisor, canine, p1-p4, and m1-m2, partial right maxilla with canine and P1, partial right mandible with partial p2-p3 and m2, partial left and right scapula, atlas, left and right femora, left and right radii, left and right ulnae, left humerus, left tibia, partial right calcaneum, left astragalus, distal metacarpal II, miscellaneous bone fragments, and tooth fragments. Taphonomic features observed on MCPC A2202 includes circular punctures (3.6-10.4 mm in diameter) and furrowing located on the left distal humerus, left and right femora, and the right radius on the proximal and distal heads. These taphonomic traits are most consistent with repeated large canid gnawing behavior and marrow processing.

The Fairmead Landfill Canis assemblage provides important insight into the evolution, morphological variation, and ecological interactions of North American canids during the mid-Irvingtonian.

title: A revised calibration for Al-in-amphibole geobarometry based on the abundance of octahedral Al
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Guilherme, Gualda A. R. [1], Pamukcu, Ayla S. [2], Miller, Calvin F. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) Earth & Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
(3) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
abstract: Constraining the pressure of magma storage in the crust is of primary importance for our understanding of the architecture of the crust and magmatism within it. Amphibole is common in many granitoid and rhyolitic rocks, and while Al-in-hornblende geobarometry is a well-established method, the need to disentangle the effects of temperature and pressure has hampered our ability to use it in detail. Médard & Le Pennec (2022) propose an alternative approach based on the concentration of octahedral Al – rather total Al – in amphibole. While this approach is theoretically sound, the abundance of octahedral Al is strongly affected by the choice of amphibole mineral formula calculation procedure. Médard & Le Pennec (2022) assume that 20% of the total Fe is Fe 3+ , which is generally too inaccurate for natural amphiboles. We derive an alternative calibration using the same experimental dataset but employing the Schumacher_Max amphibole formula calculation procedure proposed by Gualda & Vlach (2005), derived from the method of Schumacher (1991). The pressures obtained using the new calibration for amphibole from Peach Spring Tuff (SW USA) high-silica rhyolite show excellent agreement with rhyolite-MELTS pre-eruptive storage pressures calculated using the composition of glass in contact with the same amphibole crystals. Al-in-amphibole pressures for the Searchlight Pluton (NV) show a systematic increase with inferred depth, consistent with the stratigraphic position of the samples within the pluton, lending support to the new calibration. Finally, pressures calculated for amphiboles from the Graciosa A-type Province (southern Brazil), which vary from calcic to sodic in composition, show the same pressure range irrespective of amphibole group – this suggests that Al-in-amphibole geobarometry using this approach is not limited to hornblende compositions, and can be applied more generally. We recommend using the Schumacher_Max amphibole formula recalculation procedure and our new calibration to estimate pressures for amphiboles commonly observed in granitoids and rhyolites. This approach also allows pressure determination for non-rim compositions, opening opportunities to investigate the depth-history of magmas over time. Robust determination of amphibole crystallization pressures using only amphibole compositions that can be determined using electron-beam techniques for a broad range of amphibole group minerals greatly enhances the possibilities of assessing the conditions of emplacement of silicic plutons and of pre-eruptive storage of rhyolitic systems, providing useful insight into the architecture of silicic magmatic systems.

title: SegmentEveryForam: Extending Segmenteverygrain for Automated Segmentation and Morphometric Analysis of Planktic Foraminifera
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches (Posters)
authors: Ojo, Gabriel Segun [1], Lowery, Christopher Michael [2], Sylvester, Zoltan [3], Martindale, Rowan Claire [4], Pamnani, Yash [5], Perez, Karina [6], Sanchez, Stephanie [7], Webb, Aniyah [8]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Institute for Geophysics, Austin, TX, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas at Austin, AUSTIN, TX, USA
(2) University of Texas, Institute for Geophysics, Austin, TX, USA

abstract:
Planktic foraminifera are among the most widely used proxies for reconstructing past oceanographic and climatic conditions. Quantitative morphometric analyses, however, remain labor-intensive because they require manual specimen identification, segmentation, measurement, and quality control. To address these challenges, we developed SegmentEveryForam, an open-source workflow that extends the Segmenteverygrain framework for automated segmentation and morphometric analysis of planktic foraminifera.

SegmentEveryForam combines deep learning-based image segmentation, Segment Anything Model (SAM) assisted refinement, interactive manual correction, automated scale calibration, and specimen-level morphometric extraction within a reproducible workflow. The current implementation measures derived metrics including area, perimeter, major and minor axis lengths, equivalent diameter, aspect ratio, circularity, roundness, elongation, and orientation, while automatically generating summary statistics, publication-quality figures, and downloadable datasets for downstream paleoceanographic analyses.

To improve segmentation performance on planktic foraminifera, the original Segmenteverygrain U-Net model was fine-tuned using 51 manually annotated microscope images and corresponding masks. The training dataset was divided into 7,140 image patches and trained using transfer learning. Evaluation of the fine-tuned model yielded a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.898, with class-specific IoUs of 0.996 for background, 0.955 for foraminifera, and 0.744 for specimen boundaries. Visual comparison with the original model demonstrates improved discrimination between specimens and background, producing cleaner segmentations and reducing the extent of manual correction required prior to morphometric analysis.

SegmentEveryForam provides a reproducible, extensible platform for high-throughput quantitative micropaleontology while maintaining compatibility with the Segmenteverygrain ecosystem. Future development will include expanded training datasets, a dedicated foraminifera-specific U-Net architecture, and a browser-based interface to facilitate broader community adoption. Ultimately, SegmentEveryForam will enable quantitative morphometric analyses at scales that were previously impractical. This capability creates new opportunities to investigate evolutionary, ecological, and paleoenvironmental changes in the fossil record.

title: Javelina Draw Folds: Stylolites and Slickenlines Tell the Story of Rock Deformation
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Piper, Amanda Rose [1], Kelsch, Jesse Moore [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Natural Sciences, Sul Ross State University, Alpine, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Natural Sciences, Sul Ross State University, Alpine, TX, USA
abstract: The Big Bend region of west Texas was subjected to a series of tectonic events that influenced the trend of exposed geologic structures. Most structures visible today in Big Bend National Park (BBNP) exhibit trends reflective of the most recent tectonic events, including the Cretaceous-Paleogene Laramide orogeny and Late Cenozoic Rio Grande rift extension. Javelina Draw, located on the western flank of the Sierra del Carmen in eastern BBNP, exposes meso-scale folding reflective of the shortening event associated with the Laramide orogeny, which was later exhumed during rift extension. The folds exposed within Javelina Draw in BBNP contain abundant fractures and slip surfaces that record the kinematic history of the structure. This study integrates structural analysis and high-resolution digital outcrop modeling (DOM) to analyze fractures within the folds exposed at Javelina Draw. Kinematic indicators such as fracture orientations and slickenline data from slip surfaces record the strain history of the fold structure. Fracture variability across the fold structure characterizes axes of strain during Laramide deformation, which contributes to the interpretation of the regional deformation history of BBNP. Fracture variability supplemented with outcrop-strength testing characterize how fracture patterns influence rock strength. Although the region has been mapped previously, a detailed structural analysis of the fold structures in Javelina Draw has yet to be published.

abstract: The Hyalite Peak Volcanics, part of the Eocene Absaroka Volcanic Field, consists of alternating members of andesite flows and volcanic debris flows. Within a basal conglomerate layer, a specimen of petrified wood was found exhibiting carbonization, silicification, and pyritization. The pyrite within the sample displays macroscopic cubic and octahedral crystals as well as evidence of cell structure preservation. Pyrite replacement of wood is uncommon and generally occurs only in marine or swamp deposits, with mineralization typically being caused by sulfate-reducing microorganisms. The current hypothesis regarding the pyritization of this specimen is replacement of material via hydrothermal activity. Supporting evidence for a hydrothermal origin includes the presence of copper mineralization in the same layer, as well as hydrothermally deposited hyalite opals throughout the region. To verify the hypothesis, we plan to measure sulfur isotopes in both the matrix and individual pyrite crystals. This sulfur reading will aid in identifying the sources of required chemical availability. Thin sections and ground polished sections of the wood will be taken across the transverse, tangential, and radial planes. These will allow for identification of tree taxa as well as a closer look at pyrite texture and cell preservation. We will also attempt to extract fossil pollen from the surrounding matrix to reconstruct the paleoenvironment. Finally, we plan to date the capping andesite flow as well as the pyrite to constrain both the temporal age of the volcanic conglomerate and the timing of the pyritization.

abstract: The geomorphic origin of the high-elevation, low-relief plateaus in the Scandes mountains—presently glaciated and dissected by deep, high-relief valleys—has remained a challenge to adequately resolve using conventional low-temperature thermochronometric techniques. It thus remains disputed whether these features are long-lived, uplifted relict erosional surfaces, or if they are Pliocene–Quaternary features formed in-situ at high elevations via (para)glacial processes. Motivated by theoretical predictions, we obtained a new, single-grain apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe) and apatite 4 He/ 3 He dataset from valley-bottom samples of the Jostedalsbreen region in Western Norway in an attempt to constrain the timing and magnitude of glacially induced erosion in the region. Thermal history inversions using 4 He/ 3 He data reveal that the observed diffusional distribution of radiogenic helium within a single apatite crystal with a 139 ± 35 Ma bulk AHe date is unique to a thermal history requiring prolonged and stable ~100 Myr residence in the AHe partial retention zone followed by a pulse of Pliocene–Quaternary crustal cooling to the surface with a magnitude of ~34 °C. Considering regional geothermal gradient estimates, the averaged magnitude of cooling from best-fitting models suggest erosion on the order of 1890 ± 300 meters above the sampling locality, which notably exceeds the total regional relief of ~1400 meters. This finding confirms that Pliocene–Quaternary erosion was not only focused within the fjords—erosion of the high-plateau of several hundred meters during this time is also required to satisfy the thermochronometric data, directly contesting the hypothesis that these broad low-relief surfaces reflect a long-lived geomorphological feature recording past tectonic events. Strategies employed here provide a future framework to adequately quantify baseline, climatically-induced erosional budgets within passive tectonic settings at million-year timescales, which may permit proper assessment of the proposed intensification of global scale erosion driven by Late Cenozoic cooling.

title: Archives Beneath the Cascades: A Speleothem Climate Record from Washington State
session_title: Karst Sedimentary, Paleoclimate, and Historical Records (Posters)
authors: Wilson, Avril Helena [1], Kainz, Sabrina Josephine [2], Cantine, Marjorie [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA

abstract:
Speleothems can provide valuable paleoclimatic geochemical and temporal data. In this pilot study, we investigate a new speleothem record from a karst-poor region: Western Washington state. The speleothem records most proximal to Western WA are in southern British Columbia and northern Oregon, reflecting both minimal karst terrain in Washington and the open potential for speleothem research in the region. Church Mountain Cave (CMC) is one of the few accessible karst caves in western Washington that hosts active speleothems. This pilot study investigates speleothems from CMC to evaluate their potential as paleoclimate records.

CMC provides an opportunity to reconstruct past atmospheric river (AR) activity in Western Washington. The Pacific Northwest is strongly influenced by AR each year, with a small number of AR storms delivering a large share of the region’s precipitation, which both replenishes water supplies and drives flood damages. Pilot data from Church Mountain Cave could lay a foundation to extend our understanding of past AR variability and could provide additional sources of information for flood-risk characterization in one of the most AR impacted regions in North America.

An initial field expedition, conducted under permit from the US Forest Service and with the engagement of the local caving grotto, yielded five speleothem fragments. Samples have been prepped and imaged, revealing recrystallized textures and dark grey/blue coloration in cathodoluminescence (CL). Ongoing work will pair U-Th geochronology with trace and rare earth element mapping, as well as carbon and oxygen isotope analyses.

abstract:
The Late Triassic was marked by intense climate change and prolonged biotic turnover culminating in the end-Triassic mass extinction (ETE). Marine faunas experienced extinctions and marked size reduction across the Norian/Rhaetian boundary (NRB) prior to the Triassic/Jurassic boundary (TJB) (Lucas and Tanner, 2018). However, the cause of these environmental changes remains unclear due to the limited bio- and chemostratigraphic constraints during the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic. Here, we present integrated radiolarian and conodont biostratigraphy together with whole-rock geochemical data, including major and trace element concentrations, organic carbon isotope (δ 13 C org ), and osmium isotope ( 187 Os/ 188 Os) records from the pelagic chert succession in the Sakahogi section, Japan, spanning the late Norian to the Early Jurassic (Sinemurian).

Our biostratigraphic analyses identified radiolarian zones from the Skirt F Zone (TR8C) to Bipedis horiae Zone (JR0B) and conodont zonation Misikella posthernsteini Zone. These biozones indicate that the studied succession spans from the late Norian to the Sinemurian. Furthermore, the TJB is recognized by the first occurrence of the radiolarian Pantanellium tanuense.

Enrichment factors of redox-sensitive elements (V, Cr, Mn) indicate the development of suboxic conditions during the latest Rhaetian, followed by oxic conditions. Weathering proxies (Chemical Index of Alteration and Weathering Index of Parker) consistently indicate four features: intensification of chemical weathering during the late Norian, temporary weakening across the NRB, re-intensification during the early Rhaetian, and weakening followed by re-intensification during the late Rhaetian. The δ 13 C org record shows three negative excursions in the late Rhaetian.

Measured 187 Os/ 188 Os ratios range from 0.5 to 0.8 and exhibit decreases during the latest Norian, the early Rhaetian, and the latest Rhaetian. These decreases coincide with enhanced chemical weathering, and the latest Rhaetian decrease also corresponds to three δ 13 C org excursions and the inferred redox transition. Integrated biostratigraphic and geochemical records suggest that major environmental changes associated with the ETE developed progressively from the NRB to the TJB rather than representing only a short-term environmental perturbation at the TJB. The decreases in 187 Os/ 188 Os ratios may reflect unradiogenic Os inputs associated with Late Triassic large-scale magmatism episodes, including the emplacement of the Angayucham oceanic plateau and the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Further studies are required to clarify the relationship between volcanism and environmental perturbations.
