abstract:
The mid-late Cenozoic spread of grassland vegetation made grasses (family Poaceae) among the most ecologically dominant plant lineages on Earth, with vast impacts on terrestrial biota, climate, and geochemical cycling. Nonetheless, the timing of the early diversification of Poaceae, starting in the Cretaceous, remains contested. Phytoliths, microscopic silica bodies that form diagnostic shapes within grass leaf tissue, offer one of the few direct lines of evidence for calibrating the grass phylogeny in deep time. However, traditional phytolith identification relies on 2-D, qualitative morphotype schemes, and it remains unclear how precisely these fossils can be assigned to modern taxonomic groups (subfamily, tribe, subtribe, or genus). This uncertainty limits confidence in using fossil grass phytoliths as calibration points for molecular divergence dating.

Here we combine a large modern reference framework of 3-D grass silica short cell phytolith (GSSCP) shape with fossil GSSCPs to test and refine calibration of the Poaceae phylogeny. Building a 3-D morphological database of GSSCPs from ~200 extant species spanning all 12 Poaceae subfamilies, we compare three complementary shape-analysis approaches, (a) landmark-based geometric morphometrics, (b) a pseudolandmark method, and (c) persistent homology applied to phytolith contours, to determine which best discriminates taxonomic groups. Using supervised classification, we evaluate how confidently modern GSSCP shape predicts subfamily, tribe, subtribe and genus identity.

We then use this quantitative framework to assess identifications fossil grass phytoliths from previously published and new samples: Late Cretaceous–Paleocene GSSCP from central India (67-66 Ma; Naskal, Rangapur, Gingurty) that are thought to derive from the grass subclades Oryzoideae, PACMAD, and BOP, and GSSCPs recovered from the early Miocene (21.73 Ma) Mush Valley locality, Ethiopia, interpreted to be from subfamily Pharoideae. By evaluating the taxonomic assignment of each fossil occurrence quantitatively rather than qualitatively, we assess which reported fossil grass records can serve as reliable minimum-age constraints on specific nodes of the grass phylogeny. This allows us to generate a revised set of calibration points for dating major diversification events in Poaceae.

title: Interactive Web-Based Visualization Tool for Global Sea Level Rise Risk Assessment with Population Vulnerability Estimates
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Price, Alexander James [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Phoenix, AZ, USA
abstract:
Sea-level rise (SLR) poses a critical threat to low-lying coastal regions worldwide, with impacts ranging from acute storm-surge flooding to chronic inundation and groundwater salinization. Decision-makers and researchers need accessible platforms to assess regional flood risk under various SLR scenarios.

This project develops a containerized web-based visualization system integrating three key components: (1) high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) tiles from DiluviumDEM (Dusseau et al. 2023), providing 30m x 30m coverage for the global coastline; (2) WorldPop UN-based population density data at 1 km resolution (2020); and (3) an interactive MapLibre GL-based interface with Web Mercator tile rendering for real-time SLR scenario analysis.

The backend employs spatial indexing to efficiently identify intersecting DEM tiles, mosaics multiple tiles where needed, and pre-processes reprojection to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) for seamless map integration. Flooded pixels are computed as cells where elevation is below or at a given SLR threshold and then traced via interchangeable connectivity calculation methods. The population affected is estimated by sampling WorldPop rasters at flooded coordinates, with support for cross-border multi-raster integration.

The tool enables users to interactively adjust SLR based on IPCC projection scenarios and visualize flood extent as semi-transparent blue overlay tiles. This system allows users to analyze regional statistics, including flood ratio by relative pixel count, and estimated population impact, providing uncertainty information from the source. The site presents five vulnerable case-study regions (Miami, New Orleans, Tokyo, Tabasco, and Bangladesh) through a "Story Mode" interface, and has the backbone for hundreds more.

Tile-based rendering with Least Recently Used caching enables the tool to scale with its host based on available resources. This open-source platform supports coastal hazard assessment, urban planning, climate adaptation research, and public engagement. The modular architecture accommodates alternative DEM sources (SRTM, GEBCO, COP-DEM) and population datasets. This system advances accessible, geospatial tools for climate impact visualization across much of the global coast over ESRI’s satellite basemap, providing easy to understand UI and visualization.

authors: Bos, Hailey [1], Garing, Charlotte [2], Milewski, Adam [3], Holland, Steven [4]

abstract: Increasing drought frequency and intensity in southwest Georgia warrant research into secondary sources of freshwater below the often overused Upper Floridan Aquifer. One of these alternative sources is the underlying Claiborne Aquifer, separated from the Upper Floridan by the Lisbon Confining Zone. The GA-FIT project aims to evaluate the properties of the Claiborne Aquifer and its potential connectivity to the Upper Floridan Aquifer. To characterize the sequence-stratigraphic architecture of the Claiborne and Lisbon, we use gamma, resistivity, and lithology logs from 42 wells and cuttings from 13 wells distributed along a north–south dip line, three updip east–west clusters, and one strike line. Lithologically, the Claiborne consists of variably shelly, silty to sandy, shallow-marine siliciclastics. There is substantial lithologic heterogeneity among wells, even those less than a kilometer apart, complicating correlation. The Claiborne contains at least five genetic sequences, bounded by flooding surfaces (following Galloway, 1989). Sharp-based sands in the gamma logs suggest the additional presence of multiple sandy valley fills within the aquifer, ranging from 15 to over 50 feet thick. The exact facies of these valley fills are unknown, as are their lateral extent and traceability, due to considerable variability among wells. The Claiborne–Lisbon boundary is conformable and consists of a retrogradational sequence set that passes upwards into a uniform shale. The shaly Lisbon is over 100 feet thick in updip counties (Webster, Terrell, Dougherty) but thickens and transitions to carbonate in downdip counties (Decatur, Mitchell, Grady). This heterogeneity within the Claiborne, notably its stacking pattern, valley fills, and updip–downdip variation, suggests laterally and vertically variable reservoir properties as well as connectivity between the Claiborne and Upper Floridan Aquifers. Updip, we find no evidence of connectivity between the Claiborne and Upper Floridan. However, updip pump tests indicate highly localized connectivity, which may suggest relief on the Lisbon–Upper Floridan unconformity (Hubert, 2026). Downdip, the shale-to-carbonate transition in the Lisbon may permit connectivity to the Upper Floridan. This possibility must be considered in groundwater management decisions in the context of high demand for freshwater in this agriculturally dominant region.

title: Trackways of a Striding, Bipedal, Non-Mammaloid Therapsid in the Lower Jurassic Navajo Lithosome of Western North America

abstract: We illustrate and describe a previously unrecognized ichnogenus that is common in the Aztec Sandstone of soiuhern Nevada and present but less common in the Navajo and Nugget formations of Utah and Wyoming. These three formations comprise the Navajo LIthosome. Only pes tracks appear to be present in this not-yet-named ichnogenus, and no conspicuous digit impressions are present. The tracks and trackways thus appear to record a pattern of plantigrade, bipedal locomotion. Individular tracks are round to slighty oval, approximately 1.0 to 1.5 cm in diameter, typically slightly wider than long. They are typically preserved in concave epirelief, usually with a small expulsion mound. Trackway width ranges from 2.6 to 4.5 cm. The stride is consistently 1.4 times longer than the trackway width. The trackways are wide gauge, with a conspicuous gap between the inner margins of the right and left pedes, indicating that the trackmaker had a sprawling gait. This indicates that the tracemaker was not a mammal; we infer it to have been a non-mammaloid therapsid. Pace angulation vaues are approximately 90 degrees. This ichnogenus is distinct from Brasilichnium in always having a gap between the inner margins of the right and left tracks, as well as having much lower pace angulation values, among other differences.

title: A preliminary analytical framework for estimating structural complexity in ancient reefs
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Mehra, Akshay [1], Helms, Lucy [2], Anderson, Ross Peter [3], Cohen, Phoebe A. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington Earth and Space Sciences, Seattle, WA,
(2) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(3) University of Oxford, OXFORD, Oxfordshire,

abstract:
Modern reefs are hotspots of biodiversity due in part to the structural complexity, or three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization, that biomineralizing metazoans provide. Such metazoan "framework" reefs are, by geologic standards, a recent innovation. For the entirety of the Precambrian, microbes, not animals, were the primary builders of reefs. To date, the structural complexity—and, therefore, capacity for biodiversity—of these early microbial ecosystems remains underconstrained. Addressing this knowledge gap will provide critical insights into the role of microbially constructed reefs as loci of biodiversity and drivers of evolution before the rise of biomineralizing metazoans.

It is nontrivial to measure structural complexity in extant reefs and even more challenging to extract such metrics from ancient examples. Therefore, the first step toward any estimate of structural complexity in Precambrian reefs must involve creating an analytical framework. To this end, we review metrics and methods that researchers use to describe the structural complexity of modern reef systems. Next, we leverage field observations, 3D digital reconstructions, polished slabs, and thin sections from three Proterozoic (2500 to 538.8 million years ago [Ma]) sedimentary successions—the Paleoproterozoic Pethei Group, the Tonian Little Dal Group, and the Ediacaran Nama Group—to explore what morphological properties workers can reliably extract from ancient reefs (e.g., estimates of synoptic relief across cm- to m-scales), as well as what challenges they may encounter. Using these insights, we establish a preliminary set of structural complexity metrics for ancient reefs that are analogous to those used in extant systems. Additionally, we propose a set of target features (e.g., stromatolite laminae) that researchers should measure to generate these metrics. Finally, we discuss how workers should contend with the uncertainty of these types of structural complexity estimates.

abstract: Modern deformation in the south-central Andes is concentrated in the San Juan Province of Argentina, where the Eastern Precordillera forms a seismically active, west-directed frontal thrust system adjacent to the city of San Juan. Despite the geologic hazard posed by this thrust system, a lack of absolute age constraints on Andean thrusting poorly resolves the structural and deformational history of this region. We integrate macro- to microstructural analysis, detailed geologic mapping, and fault rock calcite U-Pb and hematite (U-Th)/He geo-/thermochronology to determine the timing and distribution of deformation across the north-central Eastern Precordillera. Detailed geologic mapping of two study areas shows that the north-central Eastern Precordillera is composed of early Paleozoic platform carbonates exhumed along west-vergent, range-bounding reverse faults, overlain by late Paleozoic and/or Miocene siliciclastic strata. These reverse faults form large-scale, plunging anticlinal geometries that are internally complicated by minor faulting and parasitic folding. The presence of siliciclastic and carbonate strata facilitates the precipitation of syn- or prekinematic oxide and carbonate minerals amenable to thermochronometric and geochronometric analyses. Inherited Paleozoic structures in carbonate strata host calcite veins and masses associated with the protracted Phanerozoic history of the Andes; calcite U-Pb data record Ordovician and Jurassic deformation, and constrain the onset of Andean deformation in the Eastern Precordillera to ~7.4 Ma. Overlapping calcite U-Pb and hematite (U-Th)/He ages resolve Mio-Pliocene slip on the Sierra de Villicum Thrust, while latest Pleistocene hematite (U-Th)/He ages indicate that northern Eastern Precordillera ranges may remain seismically active, despite limited instrumental seismicity. Our results provide direct temporal constraints on brittle faulting in the Eastern Precordillera, and support the hypothesis that Andean faults in this region are reactivated structures.

authors: Wuertemburg, Alexus [1], Kohn, Matthew J. [2], Robinson, Delores M. [3], Corrie, Stacey L. [4], Long, Sean P. [5], Schwartz, Darin [6]

abstract:
Understanding the spatial distributions of peak metamorphic P-T-t conditions helps constrain models of orogenesis. Here, we quantified P-T conditions and peak metamorphic ages in Himachal Pradesh, NW India, along the Sutlej River valley and the nearby Pabbar valley. From structurally lowest to highest, metamorphic rocks consist of the Lesser Himalayan Sequence (LHS), the Greater Himalayan Sequence (GHS), and the Tethyan Himalayan Sequence (THS). Within the LHS, the Jutogh thrust emplaces Jutogh Group rocks over LHS, while the Main Central thrust (MCT) emplaces GHS over LHS. The South Tibetan Detachment System (STDS), a north-dipping normal fault system, drops the THS down onto GHS, but is not noticeably exposed in the study area. We calculated peak PT conditions using garnet-biotite thermometry and garnet-plagioclase barometry; we also measured peak ages using monazite U-Th-Pb, and coupled them to petrogenetic and P-T history through REE concentrations.

Within Jutogh Group rocks, P-T conditions increase upward towards the MCT, from ~575 °C and ~10 kbar at ~500 meters below the MCT to ~750 °C and ~12 kbar in the ~200 meter-thick section of uppermost Jutogh Group and lowermost GHS. Along the Sutlej Valley, PT conditions increase from ~600 °C and 9 kbar at the MCT to ~825 °C and ~13 kbar in the middle of the GHS, then decrease steadily through the upper GHS to ~500 °C and ~5 kbar into the THS. Lower GHS monazite gradually increases in HREE content from 40 to 25 Ma. Monazite from upper GHS migmatites shows low HREE from 29 to 23 Ma, then an abrupt increase in HREE to 21 Ma. THS monazite shows no trend of HREE, with ages spreading between 29 and 25 Ma.

P-T conditions are consistent with large lateral transport along the MCT (abrupt increases in P and T), but not across the GHS-THS contact; these data could be consistent with flattening strain distributed through the upper GHS and lower THS without a distinct STDS. Chronologic data suggest protracted high-T within the middle GHS from 40 to 25 Ma, and abrupt cooling and in situ melt crystallization in the upper GHS commencing ~23 Ma. This cooling could reflect either STDS movement or a flattening event. THS chronologic data are, as yet, too sparse for definitive interpretation.

abstract: The Central Andes in Bolivia are the archetype for Cordilleran fold-thrust belt systems and associated crustal shortening. Within the Central Andes in Southern Bolivia lie distinct, bowl-shaped synclines that are situated on the border of the Eastern Cordillera and the Altiplano. These folds, near Tica Tica, Bolivia, sit ~70 km to the east of the largest salt flat in the world, Salar de Uyuni, and are marked by their unique geometries that look remarkably similar to recognized salt-mini basins around the world. Previous studies provide conflicting interpretations of the area, including an east-verging thrust system (so-called “Calazaya nappe”) and a west-verging back-thrust system, part of the broader Central Andean Backthrust Belt. New geologic mapping and cross-section construction are paired with detrital zircon (DZ) U-Pb geochronology results to investigate possible unrecognized halokinetic deformation. Mapping and cross-section results demonstrate three isolated synclines, variable strike orientations, lateral thickness variations across synclines, interbedded evaporites and unconformities between Paleozoic and Mesozoic units. New DZ results provide maximum depositional age constraints to syncline hosted units, revealing recycling of Paleozoic units and a mix of intra and extra basinal sediment sources. title: Evaluating Uncertainty In North American Plate Tectonic Reconstructions From Lower Mantle Slabs
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Fuston, Spencer [1], Wu, Jonny [2], Colli, Lorenzo [3]
affiliations: (1) International New Ventures, EOG Resources, Houston, Texas, USA; Department of Earth And Atmospheric Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, Texas, USA

abstract: Tomographic images hold key constraints for North American Cordilleran plate tectonic histories but models that prioritize surface geology (i.e., top-down) or mantle tomographic slabs (i.e., bottom-up) show disparate conclusions. Here we highlight five key questions regarding assumptions and uncertainties for building North American Cordilleran plate reconstructions from tomography: (1) Which seismic anomalies under North America should be interpreted as subducted slabs?; (2) How should paleo-subduction zone absolute locations be determined from mantle constraints?; (3) How should paleo-subduction zone polarities be determined from tomography?; (4) How should slab constraints be integrated into absolute plate motion models?; and (5) How do inferences from lower mantle slabs compare to surface geologic remnants of accreted terranes along western North America? The lower mantle under North America shows five main slab-like, faster-than-average seismic anomalies; of these, four anomalies are generally interpreted as subducted slabs and the other anomaly is possibly a geophysical artifact. Comparison between interpreted subducted slabs from published tomography shows the interpreted slabs generally occupy similar mantle locations but slab dips may be highly variable between tomography. Thus, caution is needed when inferring paleo-subduction zone polarity or absolute locations directly from slab dips. Absolute plate motion models of offshore western North America during the Jurassic-Cretaceous implies a relatively fast, northeast-moving Farallon oceanic plate that precludes a stationary, long-lived (>40 m.y.a.), west-dipping intra- oceanic subduction zone. However, long lived east-dipping or bivergent (east- and west-dipping) intra-oceanic subduction zones are permissible. Alternative conclusions on North America Cordilleran paleo-subduction zone polarities and terrane-slab correlations stem from slab reconstruction approaches based on ‘vertical slab sinking’ and ‘non-vertical slab sinking’ hypotheses; future tests of these hypotheses will improve our understanding Earth’s mantle and its convective processes.

abstract: The appearance of the enigmatic Ediacara biota in the rock record represents an early experiment in multicellularity and has long been related to the oxygenation of the oceans and atmosphere associated with the Ediacaran Shuram Excursion (SE). The anomalously depleted δ 13 C values characteristic of the SE reflects a profound change in the redox landscape of Ediacaran seawater and has been interpreted as the crescendo of the protracted Neoproterozoic Oxidation Event (NOE), spanning the Tonian through the Cambrian. A main line of evidence for the SE as a ventilation event comes from carbonate uranium (U) isotopes, which record a shift to near-modern carbonate δ 238 U values coincident with the negative carbon isotope excursion in multiple SE sections worldwide. This observation directly contrasts with shale-based thallium (Tl) isotope data suggesting deep-water anoxia during the SE. Sedimentological observations of SE bearing carbonates globally and a Macrostrat-based carbonate quantity increase in North America during the SE suggest it occurred during a period of extremely high carbonate saturation, likely driven by intense continental weathering, supported by emergent carbonate lithium isotope data. In this study, we present new high resolution U isotope data from Siberia and model the effects of Ca 2+ and CO 3 2- ion concentrations on aqueous U speciation and thus its isotopic fractionation. Our results indicate that the neutral calcium-uranyl-carbonato species (Ca-UO 2 -CO 3 ) dominates under conditions of high carbonate saturation, thereby inhibiting the reduction of U(VI) to U(IV) and producing crustal δ 238 U values in seawater despite widespread ocean anoxia which is normally expected to drive seawater δ 238 U to lower values. We thus re-interpret the carbonate δ 238 U record of the SE as a reflection of high carbonate saturation in anoxic seawater associated with an increase in neutral Ca-UO 2 -CO 3 species (and not deep ocean oxygenation). This novel interpretation also provides a unified explanation for the time-series variations in other stable isotope systems (C, O, Li, Sr, Ca) during the SE that cannot be solely accounted for by diagenesis and contributes to our understanding of Earth system dynamics at the dawn of animal life.

title: Advancing the KGS mission through Science Communication

authors: Pruente, Ally [1], Schneider, Blair [2], Horinek, Hannah [3]

abstract:
Hundreds of projects take place behind the scenes at the Kansas Geological Survey (KGS) every year. From creating maps to collecting water samples and organizing core, each division of the survey is dedicated to its mission of “Advancing Science, Serving Kansas.” To truly fulfill this mission, however, we have to make sure we are conveying the work that we do for broader audiences. As times have changed and technology continues to advance, social media has become an important avenue to make this connection.

The KGS currently hosts multiple social media platforms: Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Youtube. These platforms have grown consistently over the last several years and the outreach team at the survey has been focused on identifying new and innovative approaches to gain new followers and spark conversation. For example, over the last 18 months, our Facebook page has increased engagement by over 500% with an increase in followers by 140% and our Instagram page has received over 512% new visits.

In order to reach these levels of engagement, each platform requires tailored content and media. This project will present an analysis of the different types of content provided, how it is tailored for each platform, and the resulting engagement as recorded by the platform engagement statistics. Some examples of the different types of content that will be explored include memes, press releases, staff spotlights, fieldwork highlights, and more. For example, our new “Staff Spotlights” features include interviews with scientists, staff, and students to highlight individual achievements at the survey. These interviews aim to increase feelings of belonging for staff, improve our public outreach, and increase both internal and external understanding of research and service. These spotlights are approximately 600 words long and are posted on the KGS social media platforms and website, which makes content more accessible. Within these content features, nested links lead readers to resources related to KGS research, increasing awareness of Survey initiatives. While still relatively new, Staff Spotlights have increased public awareness by highlighting important research and projects that often remain unseen. This successful content represents a key example of creative deliverables from geology related projects in our state and beyond.

abstract:
The geodetic and geophysical workforce is shrinking even as demand for precise positioning, timing, and hazard-monitoring expertise grows. This shortage is due in part to the limited presence of geodetic career pathways in secondary and undergraduate geoscience curricula. Faculty at two- and four -year institutions are uniquely positioned to close this gap as early exposure at this stage can shape whether students pursue geodetic and geophysical career paths.

This poster presents practical, low-lift strategies for integrating geodesy career awareness into existing geoscience courses without a full curricular overhaul. Attendees will gain practical entry points, including career spotlights, near-peer video testimonials, data-driven role-play scenarios, and internship messaging, that build students’ STEM identity and support efforts to address the national geodetic workforce shortage.

The Geodetic Careers Table compiled by NSF National Geophysical Facility, profiles geodetic career and job roles, their representative tasks, salary data, required education levels (from technical certificates through graduate degrees), and linked video profiles. Because the table spans multiple entry points, using this with quick and easy strategies can help students, including those in technical, non-four-year, or career-change pathways, envision working in the field.

The poster also highlights resources directly usable in the classroom. The Women in Geoscience video series, the Explore Your Future career panel webinar, and paid internship programs (Geo-Launchpad, RESESS, and Career Internship Program) that provide authentic research experiences and workforce pipelines for undergraduate and graduate level students. It also presents the Near Surface Instrumentation loan program providing faculty with opportunities to borrow GPS/GNSS- RTK, ERT, GPR, and seismic refraction equipment for educational purposes at shipping-only costs.

title: Departures from Spatial Homogeneity as Complementary Statistical Measures of Spatial Heterogeneity in Point Patterns of Sandstone Thin Sections
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology (Posters)
authors: Ju, Ziyue [1], Yang, Wan [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(2) Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
abstract:
Modal composition of a sandstone describes constituent proportions in a thin section, so does grain-size distribution for size frequencies; neither records spatial distribution of the studied objects. Sandstones with similar summary statistics may have different spatial arrangements, reflecting different depositional and/or diagenetic processes. Quantification of spatial heterogeneity requires a homogeneity reference and a departure measure from it.

We define spatial heterogeneity as the departure of the observed pattern of a sandstone attribute in a thin section from an analysis-specific probabilistic homogeneity reference. Using its centroid to represent an object, we compare Clark–Evans R of the observed pattern of an attribute with the mean value of empirical Monte Carlo null distribution and define Heterogeneity Index (HI) as the unstandardized departure [R obs − mean (R null )], and ZHI as standardized departure [HI/SD(R null )], where SD(R null ) is the standard deviation of R under the null distribution. Negative HI and ZHI values indicate clustering, zero randomness, and positive values regularity or dispersive. The Monte Carlo p-value measures tail extremeness. At a chosen significance threshold, a small p-value indicates statistically detectable heterogeneity relative to the homogeneity reference.

Using a mapped thin section, we demonstrated that HI and ZHI are complementary, not interchangeable, by comparing HI and ZHI values for the patterns of pore space and coarse-silt, very-fine-sand, and lithic grains. For all objects, HI and ZHI are negative, indicating departures toward clustering, relative to their respective homogeneity references. The HI values of coarse-silt (HI = −0.2150; ZHI = −21.84) and very-fine sand grains (HI = −0.2164; ZHI = −31.61) are only 0.7% different, but ZHI values are 45% different. In contrast, HI values of pore space (HI = −0.1735; ZHI = −38.58) and lithic grains (HI = −0.2287; ZHI = −38.28) are 32% different, but ZHI values are 0.8% different. Thus, similar HI values may correspond to substantially different ZHI magnitudes, and vice versa. For the pattern of a specific attribute, HI shows the magnitude and direction of departure from its homogeneity reference on the original R scale, whereas ZHI expresses the same departure relative to the standard deviation of the null distribution. Spatial heterogeneity should be an important aspect in sandstone petrography and be considered in sandstone classification.

authors: Schneider, Blair [1], Biebesheimer, Ellie [2], Houser, Rhonda [3]

abstract:
Despite its reputation as flat and boring, the state of Kansas is home to many interesting geologic features. From Little Jerusalem Badlands in Western Kansas to Schermerhorn Park and Cave in the Southeast, geologic sites span the entirety of the state. Many of these sites could easily be categorized as ‘geoheritage sites’, but there was no consistent way to organize these sites as such. Additionally, there was no compiled list or database of geoheritage sites in Kansas, let alone one that was easily accessible to the general public. With funding support from the USGS Statemap program, we have created an interactive map of geoheritage sites across Kansas to:

1. Give the public a way to find these sites and learn more about them (and perhaps be inspired to visit), and

2. To serve as a basis for future geoheritage projects in the state.

To accomplish this, we compiled a list of potential geoheritage sites from various sources available at the Kansas Geological Survey including field guides, public information circulars, education series, and the Kansas Geological Survey's GeoKansas website. We also found that social media and tourism websites contained a historic gold mine of information for potential geoheritage sites, especially since so much of Kansan land is private property. Once this list was compiled, each site was evaluated to based on the USGS Geoheritage Site of the Nation Explorer values (scientific, educational, cultural, economic, and/or aesthetic). We also developed sub-categories within each of the geoheritage values. This information was then all compiled into an interactive map hosted by the Kansas Geological Survey. The goal of this interactive mapper is to ensure that we have a live product that can be continuously modified and expanded as new potential geoheritage sites are brought to our attention. This mapper also servies as an accessible and comprehensive database of geoheritage sites for the public to enjoy and explore and to serve as a example for future geoheritage projects in other states or regions.

title: Behavioral response of Ammonia confertitestsa (foraminifera) of the Long Island Sound to minerals proposed for Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement

authors: Hoskison, Eli [1], Reed-Horn, Madeleine [2], Haynes, Laura [3]

abstract: Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) is a marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR) approach by which alkaline materials are added to the ocean to encourage production of bicarbonate. Olivine sand has been deployed at a small scale in the Long Island Sound (LIS), east of New York City, USA. It is important to consider both the direct and indirect effects of OAE on marine calcifiers, as their response has the potential to change the efficacy of the OAE. Foraminifera (forams), unicellular, calcareous-shelled eukaryotes, are a critical marine calcifier in the LIS, and in recent decades, the invasive Ammonia confertitesta has become the dominant taxa in the region. Previous work has suggested that coastal benthic foraminifera morphology is strongly affected by sediment grain size. Little is known about how A. confertitesta (1) would respond to the addition of olivine grains to their natural environment, (2) interacts with any sediment particles, or (3) possibly differentiates between particle size and type. This study aims to fill that gap by culturing and observing A. confertitesta in experiments with varying sizes of olivine, kaolinite, calcium carbonate, and glass beads. Results have indicated that smaller grained particles of any kind strongly inhibited A. confertitesta’ s metabolic processes. A. confertitesta has also shown a strong affinity for kaolinite, suggesting a potential ability to differentiate between particle types. Further work on how A. confertitetsa shell morphology changes during growth in the presence of different particle types and seawater chemistry through scanning electron microscopy will allow us to investigate the influence of particle type on their longer-term calcification response.

title: Impact to Terrestrial Environments after the Kasimovian-Gzhelian Warming Event: Paleosol Records from the Appalachian Basin
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Aguilera, Darren [1], Meadows, Kara [2], Weislogel, Amy [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(2) Agriculture and Natural Resources, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA

abstract: Much understanding of Late Paleozoic Ice Age (LPIA) climate dynamics has been obtained from well-dated marine intervals; however, similar investigation of terrestrial deposits is more challenging, as these records generally suffer from poor age constraints. In the proximal Appalachian basin foredeep it is possible to identify correlative terrestrial deposits within coal-bound cyclothems that formed just after an extreme warming event at the late Pennsylvanian Kasimovian-Gzhelian boundary (∼304 Ma ). Previous work on marine records have demonstrated an increase in atmospheric pCO2 concentrations from ~350 ppm up to ~700 ppm at the Kasimovian-Gzhelian boundary which caused an increase of ~4° C in ocean temperatures over a 300ky period. We have targeted 3 localities where paleosol intervals are exposed within the lower Casselman Fm. of the Conemaugh Group, above the Ames limestone, a regional marker bed recording maximum transgression during Kasimovian-Gzhelian, and below the Elk Lick coal that represents first regionally significant accumulation of peat after the warming event. Investigation of these three localities (Morgantown, WV; Clarksburg, WV and Amma, WV) can be used to assess paleoenvironmental conditions of across depositional strike in order to characterize conditions of low-latitude terrestrial environments just after the Kasimovian-Gzhelian warming event. Overall paleosol intervals are high chroma and mainly red in color with mottling of dark red, dark gray and orange, along with some low chroma dark gray paleosol intervals. Paleosols include root traces, vertic structures with slickensides, siderite nodules, and horizons of well developed pedogeneic carbonate nodules from 0.5->2cm in diameter. Paleosols include Spodosol, vertic Calcicsol, calcic Vertisol and Vertisol pedotypes. Preliminary estimates of mean annual precipitation rates from the depth to carbonate nodules suggest rainfall ~840 mm/year. Together this reflects soil development in a tropical dry forest landscape under a climate with wet and dry seasons. Additional elemental geochemical characterization of soil matrix to assess paleoweathering and paleobarometry from stable isotope analysis of pedogenic carbonate will be used to further constrain the impact to terrestrial environments from a large-magnitude warming event during Late Paleozoic Ice Age, which could be used to inform predictions about impacts to modern terrestrial environments as current atmospheric pCO2 concentrations increase.

title: Hidden Below Grade: Refining Waikīkī's Groundwater-Inundation Flood Models by Incorporating Undocumented Basements
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Hemstreet, Fiona [1], Habel, Shellie Linn [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
(2) Climate Resilience Collaborative, School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, Honolulu, Hawaii, USA
abstract:
Sea-level rise (SLR) poses a variety of flood risks to low-lying coastal cities, risks that are intensified by a concurrent rise in coastal groundwater levels. This SLR-induced shallowing of groundwater produces groundwater inundation (GWI), which corrodes and destabilizes conveyance infrastructure, roads, and below-grade construction such as basements. The Waikīkī area of Honolulu, Hawai‘i, is a densely populated, low-lying coastal district that already experiences shallow groundwater and GWI, with vulnerable areas expected to expand as SLR continues.

Prior studies by Habel et al. (2020) on Waikīkī have shown that digital elevation models (DEMs) and GWI simulations can be used to identify and map areas at risk of flooding. These DEMs, however, utilize LiDAR-derived elevation data and are therefore blind to below-grade spaces. This study addresses this gap by identifying buildings with basements and below-grade spaces across Waikīkī, in order to produce a more complete picture of areas vulnerable to GWI. Using virtual and on-site building evaluations, along with property records, we estimate the below-grade depth of buildings throughout the study area. These depth estimates were then incorporated into an updated DEM, which was used to simulate future SLR-driven flood scenarios with existing GWI models.

Of the 674 buildings surveyed in the study area, 21.5% were found to host below-grade spaces. Strikingly, only 7.63% of these confirmed basements were documented in existing property records. According to GWI simulations, current groundwater levels exceed the surface base in 98 of the 145 basements modeled. These results indicate that the large majority of below-grade spaces in Waikīkī are invisible to current flood models and government documentation alike. This suggests that flood-risk assessments underestimate GWI exposure in areas with significant below-grade construction. While this study is geographically limited to Waikīkī, the pattern of undocumented basement risk likely extends to other low-lying coastal communities with dense below-grade construction, such as San Francisco, Washington, D.C., and Southeast Florida.

abstract:
The ADVANCEGeo Partnership is an NSF ADVANCE funded project that focuses on broadening participation in the geosciences. This work is achieved through the development of evidence-based strategies to improve workplace climate. The ADVANCEGeo Workplace Climate Program is a pilot program of this project which aims to transform workplace climate in academic departments by creating and sustaining a shared vision for thriving research and training environments. In order to test the effectiveness of this strategy, we partnered with three separate earth science departments for one year each between fall of 2024 and spring of 2026. The desired outcomes of each year-long intervention included:

1) incorporating strategies for intentionally reducing the prevalence of hostile climates through community engagement and responsibility;

2) providing support for each department to create a thriving research and training environment; and

3) increase each department's potential to recruit and retain students, staff and faculty.

In order to maximize the impact for each case study, two ADVANCEGeo leaders were assigned as coaches for each case study. These coaches (n=6) worked with the department throughout the entire year to ensure consistency and continuity between sessions and product development. Here, we provide a qualitative analysis of the impact of this experience from the perspectives of both the department and the coaches. There was mixed engagement in the program both within and across departments, though most individuals who participated in the program indicated extremely positive outcomes. Coaching requires a significant time commitment, strong interpersonal skills, and a self-awareness to be able to establish boundaries with participating community members. The results of this analysis are intended to serve as a set of guidelines for both departments and professional scientists that are interested in engaging in this type of transformative workplace climate intervention.

title: Insights from Reaction Path Modeling into the Origin of Supergene Non-Sulfide Zinc Mineralization in the Jinding Deposit, Southwestern China
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Posters)
authors: Appold, Martin S. [1], Kyle, J. Richard [2], Gilg, H. Albert [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(3) School of Engineering and Design, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany
abstract:
The Jinding sediment-hosted base metal deposit is the largest Zn-Pb deposit in China with an original resource estimated at 220 million tonnes of ore grading 7% Zn+Pb. Primary mineralization consists of sphalerite, galena, pyrite, and marcasite as cements in sandstone pores and limestone breccias, as veins in fractures, and as replacements of limestone breccia clasts and calcite cements in Triassic, Cretaceous, and Paleocene host rocks. The upper 20 to 200 m of the primary ore have been oxidized to form secondary, supergene mineralization characterized by iron oxides and hydroxides, cerussite, hemimorphite, and smithsonite, the dominant secondary ore mineral. Supergene mineralization appears to be forming actively at Jinding and accounts for about 40% of the total ore, creating one of the largest non-sulfide zinc deposits in the world.

The purpose of the present study was to use reaction path modeling to test the hypothesis that modern groundwater infiltrating the Jinding deposit is effective at converting the primary sulfide mineralization to the observed smithsonite-dominant supergene mineral assemblage, based on the measured chemical composition and temperature of the groundwater. In the models, a cool, dilute, oxidizing, pH-neutral fluid representing shallow meteoric groundwater was allowed to react progressively with calcite, pyrite, sphalerite, O 2 gas, and CO 2 gas. The model was intended to represent the migration of meteoric groundwater through calcite-bearing rock in the vadose zone where the groundwater dissolved CO 2 , maintained access with atmospheric oxygen, and reacted with primary sulfide minerals. Sensitivity analysis was performed to test the effect of uncertainties in the amounts of reactants. The results of the modeling show that dilute, Zn-poor groundwater can produce a smith­sonite-dominant mineral assemblage by reaction with cal­cite and the primary sulfide minerals, pyrite and sphalerite, provided the groundwater is sufficiently oxygenated and the abundance of pyrite is not too high, which causes the fluid to become too acidic to allow Zn mineral precipitation. This scenario also produces an abundance of iron oxide mineralization, lesser but persistent hemimorphite, minor early-stage cerussite, and abundant late-stage gypsum, consistent with field observations.

title: Controls on the Stability of Different Ferromagnesian Phases in the Mono Craters (CA) High-Silica Rhyolites: The Role of Temperature, Oxidation State, Water Content and Pressure

authors: Taylor, Mackenzie C. [1], Lange, Rebecca A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA

abstract: The Mono Craters are a chain of high-silica rhyolite volcanic craters, domes and flows, which erupted between 42,000 and 600 years ago (Sieh and Bursik, 1986; Hu et al., 1994; Marcaida et al., 2019), adjacent to the Long Valley volcanic field in eastern California. Although some of the Mono Craters are aphyric, the remainder all contain phenocrysts of quartz, sanidine, plagioclase, hornblende, titanomagnetite, ilmenite, apatite, zircon and allanite. There is a remarkable variation in the additional ferromagnesian phase that is present in addition to hornblende, namely biotite vs fayalite vs orthopyroxene, despite similar major-element compositions. This points to the role of temperature, oxidation state, water content and/or pressure in controlling which of these three different ferromagnesian phases are stable in the Mono Craters high-silica rhyolites. In this study, numerous analyses of titanomagnetite, ilmenite, plagioclase and sanidine were obtained on 15 crystal-rich units. Temperatures and ∆NNO values were calculated using the model of Ghiorso and Evans (2008). The results show that the biotite-bearing units grew phenocrysts at the coolest temperatures (~715-745 ˚C) and were the most oxidized (∆NNO= -0.5 to -0.8), followed by the fayalite-bearing units (~764-777 ˚C; ∆NNO= -0.95 to -1.1), and the hottest being the orthopyroxene-bearing units (~794-798 ˚C; ∆NNO= -0.95 to -1.0). Application of plagioclase-liquid hygrometry (Waters and Lange, 2015) shows a trend of varying water content with the biotite-bearing units averaging 6.3 wt% H 2 O, followed by the fayalite-bearing units averaging 5.2 wt% H 2 O, and the orthopyroxene-bearing units averaging 4.4 wt% H 2 O during phenocryst growth. Pairing these results with whole-rock analyses allows pressure during phenocryst growth to be calculated (Wilke et al., 2017). The orthopyroxene-bearing units record the highest pressures (avg= 540 MPa) whereas the fayalite-bearing units (avg= 400 MPa) and biotite-bearing units (avg= 390 MPa) record shallower pressures. This may have allowed growth of orthopyroxene phenocrysts at slightly higher pressures relative to the other units, enabling stabilization of Fe-rich orthopyroxene in such low Mg# rhyolites, which otherwise are expected to grow fayalite at lower water contents or biotite at greater water contents.

title: Drainage Reorganization in the Kamas Valley: Aggradational Piracy of the Ancestral Provo River, Utah
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Atkins, Rachel M. [1], Kleber, Emily J. [2], Reeher, Lauren J. [3], Morriss, Matthew C. [4], Rittenour, Tammy M. [5], Larson, Phillip H. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, Utah Valley University, Orem, UT, USA
(2) Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT,
(3) Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
(4) Utah Geological Survey, SALT LAKE CITY, UT,
(5) Utah State University, Logan, UT,

abstract: The Provo and Weber Rivers originate in Utah's Uinta Mountains and ultimately discharge to the Great Salt Lake (GSL) but arrive via different routes. The Weber River flows north from the northern Uintas and enters GSL from the northeast. The Provo River, by contrast, runs southwest from the southern Uintas and into Utah Lake before reaching GSL via the Jordan River and Farmington Bay in the southeast. Despite this divergence, the two systems run close to one another near their headwaters, separated by the Kamas Valley — a low-relief basin in the Wasatch Back along the western flank of the Uinta Mountains. LiDAR and satellite data across the Kamas Valley floor reveal surface morphology suggestive of northwestern flow of glacial outwash, indicating the source from the upper Provo River drainage. This orientation is inconsistent with the modern southwest-flowing Provo and instead points to what we hypothesize as the former river configuration where the Provo River was the south fork of the Weber River and flowed north through Kamas Valley. Since then, the Provo headwaters have been captured and rerouted through the middle and lower Provo River. A distinct elbow of capture and a transverse reach mark the probable locus of capture. OSL ages of river terrace samples indicate that capture likely occurred in the Mid to Late Pleistocene (257.3 ± 41.5 ka to 151.8 ± 15.6 ka), though more sampling is needed across the fluvial system. We interpret the capture mechanism as aggradational piracy whereby alluvial fans formed in the Kamas Valley as Uinta glacial meltwater delivered sediment causing aggradation of the valley, impounding the ancestral north-flowing Provo behind a fan-dam complex. This diverted flow into an adjacent valley. The relative elevations of the Kamas Valley fill and transverse reach near the elbow of capture further support this possibility. Repeated fill-and-spill cycles eventually linked the upper Provo drainage to the channel network draining toward Utah Lake. To reconstruct this history, we integrate river terrace mapping, DEM-based morphometric analysis, and OSL geochronology. This work aims to explore when and how aggradational piracy in the Kamas Valley restructured headwater connectivity between the Provo and Weber systems, and what that reorganization implies for the broader drainage evolution of the Great Salt Lake Basin.

abstract:
Arsenic contamination in drinking water remains a major environmental health concern for Indigenous communities across the southwestern United States. Among the Diné (Navajo) and Hopi Nations, water insecurity is intensified by complex hydrogeology, limited infrastructure, historical trauma, persistent poverty, environmental injustice, and a legacy of Resource Colonialism.

This presentation examines how community-based participatory approaches can support arsenic mitigation and reduce environmental health risks. Effective risk reduction requires addressing linguistic, cultural, geographic, and regulatory barriers while engaging community members as equal partners in project design, implementation, and evaluation. This collaboration can build trust, improve communication, and strengthen the sustainability of interventions.

One case study examines a nonprofit organization affiliated with a local educational institution that partners with Hopi communities to deploy nanofiltration systems for arsenic removal. Arsenic concentrations in 8 of the 11 Hopi villages exceed federal drinking-water standards. Through sustained community engagement and shared ownership, this initiative shows how locally supported treatment technologies can reduce exposure while building long-term capacity for water-resource management.

The second case study examines risk communication and management on the Navajo Nation for people who must haul their water from local wells. Of 1000 known wells, 172 exceeded the federal arsenic standard of 10 ppb, while 355 remain untested for arsenic. These conditions increase the risk of long-term exposure for residents who rely on unregulated water sources. A local non-profit delivers water to at-risk families and installs rainwater-harvesting systems that can provide critical support during monsoon season when the dirt roads are impassable. The organization conducted a survey that documents the actual community water-use patterns which can be aligned with mitigation efforts. These findings support a user-centered remediation framework that targets drinking-water treatment with use-specific risk communication.

Community-Based Participatory Research offers a collaborative model where the community is an equal partner with scientists, building trust, ownership, and sustainability. This approach expands access to safe drinking water and provides a scalable model for arsenic mitigation globally in Indigenous and other underserved communities.

title: Exsolution Textures in Garnet Xenocrysts from the Colorado Plateau: Applications for Reconstructing Tectonic Histories Across Lithologies
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Keller, Duncan S. [1], Hess, Benjamin [2], Gonzalez, Joseph P. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Skidmore College, Saratoga Springs, NY, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom
(3) Research and Collections, New York State Museum, Albany, NY, USA
abstract:
Inclusions in garnets from diatremes give insight into the petrologic conditions of garnet formation and subsequent exhumation. We present analysis of a suite of garnet xenocrysts from the Garnet Ridge ultramafic diatreme in the Navajo Volcanic Field of the Colorado Plateau. The garnets contain combinations of rutile, ilmenite, clinopyroxene, Na-Ca clinoamphibole, and quartz as lamellar to acicular microinclusions (LAMs) oriented parallel to <111> garnet . We use large electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) datasets and lattice matching calculations to show that the oxide and silicate LAMs represent exsolved precipitates from high-Ti and majoritic garnets. The exsolution textures indicate that the garnets experienced slow cooling and/or decompression that reduced solubility of high-temperature and/or high-pressure chemical substitutions at sufficient temperatures for long-range diffusive transport of LAM-forming components. Electron dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analyses of major and trace element chemistry show that the garnets can be assigned to both mantle and crustal sources in the classification scheme of Schulze (2003) for garnet xenocrysts from kimberlites. The garnets with exsolved silicates have major element compositions consistent with majoritic garnets from natural samples and laboratory experiments on metasediment, eclogite, and ultramafic bulk compositions formed at 5-10 GPa (Thomson et al. 2021).

We contextualize our findings within the geologic history of the lower crust and mantle of the Colorado Plateau, particularly Navajo Volcanic Field xenoliths attributed to the geologically recent materials of the subducted Farallon Plate that passed beneath the Colorado Plateau lithosphere in the last 100 Myr. The decomposed majoritic garnets in our sample suite that are comparable to those known from eclogites and metasediments point to a role for deep subduction of surficial materials in assembling the lithosphere of the (proto-)Colorado Plateau.

title: Utah Coal Leasing Revisited: Geoheritage Values in Conflict in the Lake Powell Region
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Grew, Priscilla C [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Nebraska State Museum, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract:
For the past half century, the coal resources of the Kaiparowits Plateau in Utah, under the jurisdiction of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), have provoked intense conflicts involving energy policy, environmental values, and water resource implications for the Colorado River Basin. According to a Utah Geological Survey estimate in 2021, the Kaiparowits Plateau coalfield contains up to 9 billion tons of potentially recoverable coal in beds thicker than 4 feet and under less than 3000 feet of cover. Proposals for underground coal mining have included mine-site powerplants cooled with Lake Powell water and rail transport of coal either to a new powerplant in Nevada, or to California for export to Japan.

Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument (GSENM) was first designated in 1996 and was the first Monument to be assigned to BLM. GSENM was cut to half its size in 2017, then fully restored in 2021. On July 4, 2025, the Secretary of the Interior made 13 million acres of Federal mineral estate newly available for coal leasing, including 29,000 BLM acres in Utah that are either near or adjacent to Bryce, Zion and Capitol Reef National Parks and to the 2021 version of GSENM.

On July 13, 2026, a Presidential Proclamation reduced GSENM from 1.87 million acres to 181,500 acres. The new Monument will retain an isolated square of 8,900 acres called the “Kaiparowits Horizon Unit” that “includes fossils of dinosaurs, reptiles and mammals.” The Proclamation retains some prominent geoheritage features but excludes others. The Canyons of the Escalante Unit and the Wolverine Petrified Forest in the Chinle Formation are retained, but other features such as Grosvenor Arch, Devil’s Garden with Metate Arch, and the Wahweap Hoodoos are excluded from the new GSENM.

The scientific importance and geoheritage value of the paleontological resources of GSENM were emphasized in the July 9, 2017 comments filed by the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology (SVP) which argued that “altering or revoking” the boundaries of GSENM “would be disastrous for the science of paleontology.” SVP stated that Kaiparowits has “the richest record of Late Cretaceous life anywhere in the world… Five new types of horned dinosaur have come from GSENM, as have new duck-billed dinosaurs, tyrannosaurs, ankylosaurs, caimans, plesiosaurs, crocodylians, lizards, snakes, turtles, and mammals.”

title: A Subsurface Geologic Material Mapping System for the Beaumont Formation along the Eastern Texas Coast Using Driller Well Logs Reports
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: Campos, Juan Marcel [1], Dashtian, Hassan [2], Elliott, Brent [3]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Bureau of Economic Geology, Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin - Austin, TX, Austin, TX,
(3) Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
The Beaumont Formation underlies much of the Texas Coastal Plain and consists of interbedded clay, silt, and sand deposited in Pleistocene fluvial, deltaic, and coastal environments. Mapping potential aggregate resources within this formation requires lithologic information that extends beyond the two-dimensional representation provided by surficial geologic maps. This study develops a regional subsurface lithologic model of the Beaumont Formation in the Houston area using publicly available descriptions from Texas Submitted Driller Reports.

A Python-based toolkit allows users to define the target lithology, depth interval, and study extent. For each well, the cumulative thickness of a selected material and divided by the total evaluated depth interval to calculate a depth-constrained lithologic proportion. Followed by lateral interpolated proportions to estimate the continuous relative abundance of selected materials in a depth interval across the study area. Because driller logs contain inconsistent terminology, historical phrasing, and variable interpretations, the workflow also can evaluate the use of large language models to classify and standardize lithologic descriptions.

The resulting thematic maps show spatial variations in lithologic composition within specified depth intervals. Sand-rich zones are commonly associated with modern fluvial systems, suggesting preservation of older channels, bars, and related depositional systems. Clay-rich materials display greater spatial heterogeneity and less connection with modern drainage patterns. Collectively, the maps reveal possible depositional lobes, coastal-plain sedimentation patterns, and areas affected by subsequent landscape modification.

Combining multiple datasets and depth intervals supports the development of integrated thematic maps and three-dimensional voxel models for geological interpretation and aggregate-resource assessment. The success of the workflow depends on the interpretation for the selected material classes based on geomorphic setting and extraction criteria but without this well-log derivative achieving such precision would be impossible. This workflow has applications not only in aggregate-resource mapping but also in broader shallow-subsurface geological investigations.

title: Detrital Zircon Geochronology of the Mesoproterozoic Freda Sandstone: Northeastern Wisconsin and Upper Peninsula, Michigan, USA
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Ortman, Caleb Daniel [1], Baumann, Steven [2], Craddock, John P. [3], Malone, David H. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA

abstract: The Freda Sandstone of Michigan's Upper Peninsula and northeastern Wisconsin is a unit of interbedded arkosic sandstones and siltstones that provide insight into sedimentation following the failure of the Superior Province's 1.1 Ga Midcontinent Rift System (MRS). Historical studies posit that the entirety of the Freda was deposited by fluvial channels carrying sediments from the south and east into the Superior Province. However, the Freda varies texturally in basal sections of the unit and in outcrops west of the Porcupine Mountains. These textural variations have prompted consideration of subdivision of the Freda due to possible differences in provenance and competence between these hypothetical members. To determine whether subdivision is warranted, samples of the Freda were collected from three locations: an outcrop on the Presque Isle River, an outcrop east of Redridge, MI, and the St. Amour borehole in Alger Co., MI. These samples were processed for detrital zircons to determine U/Pb ratios via LA-ICP-MS. Analysis of detrital zircon populations using detritalPy and DZMDS have yielded results that further characterize sedimentation in the Superior Province during the Mesoproterozoic. Probability density plots of the collected samples display distinct zircon age profiles for each sample, with some similarities. Zircon populations in all three samples are low in rift-sourced zircons, most prominently in the Presque Isle River and St. Amour borehole samples. These samples display their largest age peaks at 1450 Ma, with minor peaks at 1650 Ma, indicating sourcing from the Picuris and Mazatzal orogenies. The Redridge sample, however, lacks zircons of these ages, and is instead characterized by Grenville-aged peaks at 1325 and 1200 Ma. These data indicate that sedimentation after the failure of the MRS was dynamic and variable, was subject to MRS-generated topography (such as the Porcupine Mountains), and that sediment supply was dominated by distal sources, burying units generated from the failed MRS.

title: Stories of Support: Experiences of Geoscientists from Historically Marginalized Genders in Geoscience
session_title: Iris Moreno Totten Research in Geoscience Education Session
authors: Lapkoff, Megan [1], Lazar, Kelly Best [2]
affiliations: (1) Clemson University, Hickory, NC,
(2) Clemson University, Clemson, SC,
abstract: The number of geoscientists who identify with a gender that has been historically marginalized in geoscience, including women and those who identify as genderqueer, has been proportionally increasing, with the number of women earning advanced degrees reaching approximate parity with men. However, geoscientists of minoritized genders still face a lack of opportunities and harassment that impacts their willingness to remain in the geosciences. Understanding the experiences of these individuals is important for improving representation and retaining trained geoscientists within the discipline. This work is centered on sixteen interviews conducted through snowball sampling, focusing on the experiences of geoscientists of minoritized genders in industry and academia, analyzed through the dual lenses of Critical Feminist Thought and Gendered Organizational Theory. One theme that was found is that geoscientists of minoritized genders still face power dynamics that produce gender-based harassment within industry and academia. In response to this, a navigational strategy that emerged is that many geoscientists of minoritized genders, when faced with harassment, lean heavily on support networks and may even change the people who are around them to be able to persist within the field. Those who have sufficient support structures speak more positively about their positions and their experience in the field. Conversely, those without sufficient support structures report feelings of isolation, dissatisfaction with their current position, and a desire to transition to a different position. Support structures have a significant impact on the experience of individuals whose gender has been minoritized in geoscience. Mentors and those in power have the opportunity to become allies for these geoscientists, and being a supportive mentor can help reinforce a student’s support structure. The experiences of the participants lead us to suggest that mentors should actively and intentionally work to provide support structures for their students before they graduate. This could be connecting them with communities that have shared identities or interests and introducing students to collaborators. Attending to student support structures while still at university can have lasting effects throughout a student’s career.

authors: Kairo, Suzanne [1], Stinchcomb, Gary [2], Lane, Joseph [3], Loomis, Karen [4], Ramirez, Vincent [5]
affiliations: (1) Kairo GeoConsulting LLC, Houston, TX, ; Department of Earth and Atmospheric Science, Indiana University, Houston, TX, USA

abstract:
A structurally isolated Pliocene formation in Railroad Valley, Nevada hosts a concentration of valuable elements (lithium, potassium, boron, tungsten) and is the largest critical mineral resource in the US. Mapped and stratigraphically correlated using seismic, logs, and core, the formation is interpreted as an evaporite lake deposit. Whole rock ICP elemental and solubility studies indicate much of the resource is within highly soluble rock. Petrologic understanding of rock components is crucial to predicting the abundance, distribution and extraction of the valued elements.

Subsurface analysis and interpretation indicate a paucity of siliciclastic detritus distal to paleoshorelines. Distal deposits in core from well N2-34 are the focus of this study and comprise salts (non-marine) intercalated and intergrown with mud-sized matrix. The presence, abundance, morphology, size, and diagenetic features of salt crystals, and the texture and components of the mud matrix were characterized by petrographic analysis of 35 sections representative of core lithofacies. Micro-XRF element mapping augmented petrography.

Macrocrystals of salt (mm-cm size) occur individually and as groups surrounded by mud, and as distinctly layered intergrowths of crystals with little or no associated mud. Smaller (<1mm) salt crystals with a range of size, shape, and abundance also occur in the mud. Distinct macrocrystal layers likely formed when salts precipitated from brine near a sediment-water interface, whereas isolated and small groups of crystals surrounded by mud grew within an unconsolidated, uncompacted matrix. Micro-XRF mapping indicates distinct X-ray densities indicate presence of Na, Ca, and Mg in the salts.

Detailed petrographic analysis of the extremely fine mud matrix revealed no depositional sedimentary structures. Disruption and desiccation features suggest deposition in a water body or wet setting, prone to drying. The mud exhibits little or no birefringence (amorphous?), though a diffuse, low-birefringent crystalline phase is sometimes present. Distributed throughout the mud are tiny particles, crystals (10’s of microns), and crystallites (<10 microns) dissimilar from evaporite salt crystals in shape and optical properties. Micro-XRF indicates a heterogeneous mud composition, with higher x-ray density signals for Si, Al, and K. As such, the mud is interpreted as very fine volcanic ash, deposited by air-fall into a lake or pond. Future integration of XRD, SEM-EDX, Raman, micro-XRF, and microprobe ICP-MS studies will advance understanding of mineralogy, diagenesis, and origin of these deposits.

abstract: We explore the impact that warfare has on environmental disturbance in riparian ecosystems and forests. The selected study region in northeastern France and western Germany witnessed a multitude of conflicts spanning the pre-industrialized era to industrialized and mechanized warfare. Thus, permitting an analysis for how environmental impacts from war change, or scale, across different types of warfare in the same ecoregion. We find that landscape disturbance from early modern period wars amplifies pre-existing natural disturbance patterns. Whereas landscape disturbance during the 19 th and 20 th centuries is higher density and occurs over smaller areas. Moreover, disturbance patterns from former conflicts are also amplified by subsequent conflicts when separated in time by less than 50 years, and where conflict occurs in the same region. However, these effects, not inclusive of other legacy effects such as heavy metal contamination or unexploded munitions, diminish within several decades following the cessation of warfare. During time intervals of persistent conflict, more than one conflict separated by brief intervals of peace, a time lag of approximately 60-80 years occurs between peak forest disturbance and peak landscape disturbance. This indicates that vegetation responses to conflict are more rapid, whereas landscapes respond to this type of disturbance on longer timescales. We find that advances in military technology do not directly affect environmental impacts of war. However, how these technological changes affect the trajectory of war from one state to another, e.g., insurgency or entrenchment, has a profound effect on the scale of landscape disturbance. Scaling relationships between area of disturbance versus total conflict area are robust for both landscapes and forested ecosystems, where these relationships predict commensurate increases in environmental disturbance should a conflict change to an insurgency or an entrenchment.

title: The Role of Minor Phases in Controlling the Rheology of Oceanic Crust Gabbros
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Osti, Rudi [1], Gottardi, Raphael [2], Deans, Jeremy [3]
affiliations: (1) Auburn University, Geology & Geography, Auburn, AL,
(2) Auburn University, Auburn, AL,
(3) University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS,
abstract: Strain localization mechanisms lead to the development of ductile shear zones that accommodate high proportion of strains at plates interfaces. Our understanding of these processes is therefore critical to understand the mechanical behavior of the lithosphere and their effects on plates interaction. Gabbroic rocks are the most abundant lithology in the oceanic and lower continental crust, yet their rheology remains poorly constrained, especially when considering the role of minor phases. The goal of this research is to characterize the influence of Fe-Ti oxides (i.e. magnetite and ilmenite) on the mechanical deformation of gabbroic rocks during oceanic lithospheric generation and destruction processes taking place at mid-oceanic ridges and subduction zones. Fe-Ti oxides are known to be mechanically weak compared to silicates and their crystal-plastic deformation mechanisms are active down to temperature as low as 400°C, and even though they are typically no more than 5% of a gabbro, can reach to abundances of 30%. Yet, their role has been marginally considered and contrasting results have been obtained, with some authors suggesting a possible connection between the presence of these phases and the occurrence of crystal-plastic fabric while others have questioned it. Here, we present the results of our investigation of the role of Fe-Ti oxides on deformation of gabbro from oceanic crust developed at slow spreading ridge. Using petrographic analysis combined with SEM-EDS, our preliminary microstructural and microchemical results demonstrate thatplastic deformation tend to be associated with the presence of Fe-Ti oxides. A striking textural contrast can be observed with oxide-deficient domains where the original magmatic structure is preserved, with little to no evidence for deformation, whereas oxides-rich domains are characterized by mylonitic fabrics. This is particularly evident within plagioclase domains where the recrystallization mechanisms and deformation intensity seem to vary with the mineralogical association while no appreciable variability of deformation conditions seems to be present. Fe-Ti oxides play a clear rheologic role in these rocks making them weaker and more likely to partition strain, making the overall plate boundary weaker and more able to accommodate extension, which in turn are still weak as they enter a subduction system.

abstract: Investigating alteration patterns around intrusion-related ore deposits represents a first order observation that constrains our understanding of ore-forming processes while guiding exploration and resource delineation. This study integrates multi-element whole-rock geochemical data with petrographic observations and hyperspectral short-wave infrared analysis on representative drill core samples to define geochemical trends, alteration mineral associations, and their paragenetic relationships relative to high-grade veins in the Surebet intrusion-related Au-Ag-Pb-Zn deposit, located approximately 40 km south of Stewart, British Columbia. The deposit comprises mineralized quartz-sulfide veins hosted by Jurassic-Cretaceous volcanic and sedimentary rocks of the Stikine terrane that are crosscut by Eocene granodiorite dikes. While the relative timing and ore paragenesis are well constrained, the proximal to distal alteration signatures of the hydrothermal system remain poorly understood. Geochemical indicators associated with mineralization greater than 1 ppm Au correlate with elevated As, Bi, Pb, Te, W, and Zn concentrations. These enrichments are best defined within narrow (1-3 m) zones around high-grade intervals, rarely extending up to 25 m. Hyperspectral analyses yield modal mineralogical data for samples collected at systematically increasing distances from mineralized veins. Distal to the veins (up to 100 m), sedimentary units are dominated by muscovite and biotite, whereas proximal zones (up to 7 m) contain higher proportions of epidote, chlorite, amphibole, and lesser carbonate. In contrast, a high proportion of epidote, chlorite, biotite, and carbonate characterize andesite units distal to the veins (up to 190 m), while proximal zones (up to 12 m) contain higher proportions of muscovite. Mineralized granodiorite dikes are characterized by amphibole-rich vein selvages. Optical microscopy and automated mineralogy further constrain alteration assemblages, indicating that proximal domains across the principal host lithologies, sedimentary units, andesites, and granodiorite dikes, contain locally abundant actinolite, muscovite, garnet, and wollastonite. The granodiorite host rocks also display systematic variations in plagioclase composition, with albite dominating the most altered domains within thin section-scale mineralogical textures. Together, these observations suggest that calc-silicate (amphibole ± epidote), potassic (muscovite ± biotite), and sodic (albite) alteration assemblages are most representative of proximal domains to mineralized zones, depending on the host rock composition. These mineral associations, combined with enrichments in Bi, Te, and W, represent key vectors toward mineralization. The alteration trends are consistent with the model for intrusion-related Au-Ag deposits, especially the presence of high-temperature alteration mineral associations.

title: The Tempo and Mode of Paleoecological Change
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Saulsbury, James G. [1], Hunt, Gene [2]

abstract: Simpson’s concept of the tempo and mode of evolution has been foundational to how paleobiologists think about evolution in the fossil record, shaping debates over topics ranging from punctuated equilibrium to evolutionary rate-time scaling and serving as the basis for a set of now-familiar evolutionary models representing drift, stasis, and more complex evolutionary scenarios. Paleoecology has lacked an organizing framework of this kind, but the introduction of one could provide powerful analytical and conceptual tools for addressing longstanding questions about ecological change in deep time. Here we use ecological neutral theory to develop models of drift and stasis in community composition that are closely analogous to the Brownian Motion (BM) and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) models that have become standard in paleobiology and evolutionary biology. A one-parameter model of local drift in species relative abundances acts as a BM model that has been adapted to the unique features of fossil community data, whereas a two-parameter model of drift plus migration from a metacommunity acts like an OU model where the state of the local community is continuously drawn towards that of the metacommunity. In our implementation, these models can be fit to timeseries of fossil community composition and are robust to incomplete sampling, variable timescales, and differences in community structure and diversity. Doing so allows us to decisively test questions about the pace and mode of ecological change, such as whether community composition in a given dataset meanders freely or instead fluctuates about an optimum. We demonstrate our approach by testing whether Quaternary pollen communities on remote islands exhibited weaker community stasis than those on the mainland.

title: Transforming Jackfruit Waste into a Sustainable Medium to Enhance Biomass Production and Astaxanthin Accumulation in the Green Microalga Desmodesmus sp.
