abstract:
ABSTRACT

Commercial microalgae cultivation depends on synthetic growth media that increase production costs and limit opportunities for recycling nutrient-rich organic wastes. This study investigated the potential of unsupplemented Digested Jackfruit Waste Medium (DJWM) as a sustainable alternative to synthetic Bold's Basal Medium (BBM) for cultivating Desmodesmus sp. within a circular bioeconomy framework. Batch cultures were grown for 16 days using a range of DJWM dilutions to identify the optimal balance between nutrient availability and osmotic stress. A 50% DJWM dilution produced dry biomass yields (0.64 g L -1 ) and specific growth rates (0.30 d -1 ) that were statistically indistinguishable (p > 0.05) from those obtained with BBM, while significantly increasing astaxanthin accumulation (7.05 mg g -1 ) (p < 0.05). The optimized medium also promoted rapid assimilation of nitrogen and phosphorus recovered from jackfruit waste, demonstrating efficient nutrient recycling. Replacing synthetic medium with DJWM reduced media formulation costs by approximately six-fold while diverting organic residues from landfills and recovering valuable nutrients that would otherwise be lost from the agricultural system. These findings demonstrate that jackfruit waste can serve as an effective, low-cost cultivation medium for microalgae while supporting nutrient recovery, waste valorization, and sustainable biomass production. The study highlights the potential of waste-derived growth media as nature-based solutions that integrate agricultural waste management with environmental biotechnology and circular resource use.

title: Peak Metamorphic Temperatures of the Ashe and Alligator Back Metamorphic Suites, Southwestern Virginia
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Posters)
authors: Winter, Jackson Frederick [1], Rahl, Jeffrey M. [2], Gao, May [3]
affiliations: (1) Washington and Lee University, Nellysford, VA,
(2) Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA,
(3) Washington and Lee University, USA
abstract:
The Ashe and Alligator Back metamorphic suites are composed of interlayered metasedimentary rocks, mafic metavolcanic rocks, and subordinate ultramafic bodies that experienced polyphase prograde and retrograde metamorphism during the Taconic, Acadian, and Alleghanian orogenic events. These rocks are part of the Eastern Blue Ridge and are exposed in a NE-SW trending belt stretching across southwestern Virginia and northwestern North Carolina. Mineral assemblages and mapped isograds have established upper amphibolite-facies conditions during Taconic metamorphism for both units, and quantitative thermobarometry in the Ashe has documented peak conditions of ~600–650 °C and ~7.5 kbar. In contrast, no comparable thermobarometric estimates exist for these rocks in southwestern Virginia. Here, we address this gap by applying Raman spectroscopy of carbonaceous material (RSCM) thermometry to metasedimentary rocks across southwestern Virginia, providing new quantitative temperature estimates.

We collected about 20 samples of the Ashe and Alligator Back metamorphic suites along a ~70 km-long, strike-parallel transect, running southwestward from Rocky Mount, VA. We measured the Raman spectra of 10-20 unique carbon-rich spots per sample, on either cut rock chips or thin sections. Data were processed using a MATLAB version of the IFORS peak-fitting software and the calibration of Lünsdorf and others (2017). Estimated peak temperatures cluster between ~480 and 540 °C, with no observable spatial patterns in the studied region. These temperatures extend the record of Paleozoic metamorphism in the Eastern Blue Ridge northeastward from North Carolina, providing insight into the degree to which regional variations in metamorphism reflect a continuous gradient or discrete structural discontinuities.

title: Closure of the Mozambique Ocean during Gondwana assembly constrained by southward Cryogenian motion of Oman
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Yao, Mary Yuanyue [1], Zhang, Yiming [2], Koran, Isabel [3], Macdonald, Francis A. [4], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [5]
affiliations: (1) Institute for Rock Magnetism, Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

abstract: The closure of the Mozambique Ocean marks a major plate tectonic transition from Rodinia breakup to Gondwana assembly. Relics of this ocean are preserved in the Arabian-Nubian Shield, which was associated with the margin of the Congo craton, and in eastern terranes such as Oman, which were associated with India and South China. Paleogeographic constraints on these terranes are needed to resolve the geometry, timing, and position of ocean closure. Such constraints on Oman additionally place Cryogenian glacial and biomarker records in a latitudinal framework. Previous paleomagnetic studies have shown that Oman was at mid-latitude in the Tonian on the northern margin of the Mozambique Ocean. Tectonic models have suggested that Oman moved towards the western terranes of the Arabian-Nubian Shield during the Cryogenian, closing the Mozambique Ocean during the late Ediacaran to early Cambrian. However, the paleolatitude of Oman during that time remains poorly constrained, hindering the development of a more precise tectonic model for Gondwana assembly. In this study, we develop paleomagnetic data from well-preserved siliciclastic sedimentary successions Mirbat Group of Oman. The glaciogenic Ayn and Shareef Formation of the Mirbat Group have been debatably correlated to the two Neoproterozoic Sturtian and Marinoan snowball glaciations. We develop new paleomagnetic data from the Arkahawl and Marsham formations that were deposited during the intervening interglacial as well as the Shareef Formation. Well-resolved magnetization from these units is consistent with being held by detrital hematite. We demonstrate that the two resultant paleomagnetic poles corroborate a Neoproterozoic age for all formations of the Mirbat Group, consistent with the Ayn Formation resulting from the Sturtian glaciation, and the Shareef Formation from the Marinoan glaciation. These results indicate southward motion of Oman toward the Arabian-Nubian Shield as the Mozambique Ocean closed and constrain the latitudes of the intervening arc terranes whose weathering could have modulated Cryogenian climate.

title: Quantitative Assessment of Microplastic Routing: A Case Study in the Snake River Watershed
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part I)
authors: Nielsen, Ryan [1], Sundell, Kurt [2], Perez, Nicholas [3], Smolen, Justin [4], Moore, Gavin [5]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(2) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(3) Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
(4) Chemistry, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
(5) Chemistry, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
abstract: Microplastics are ubiquitous and potentially dangerous particles transported primarily by streams. Although microplastic pollution and polymer types have been shown to be correlated to land use, little work has been done to quantitatively assess microplastic routing within waterways draining catchments of various land uses. Despite rapidly growing interest in microplastic research and recent advances in quantitative analysis, most studies report microplastic assemblages qualitatively. We quantify microplastic routing along a 100-kilometer section of the Snake River that makes up a portion of the Idaho-Oregon border and receives the Owyhee, Boise, Malheur, Payette, and Weiser rivers. These tributaries drain contrasting land uses (urban, agricultural, and wilderness), providing natural variation in potential microplastic sources. We use micro-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy to identify different polymer types in sediment samples collected from these five tributaries and along the main stem of the Snake River above and below each confluence. We then apply quantitative methods recently developed for detrital zircon geochronology, readapted to handle microplastic data. Specifically, we implement multidimensional scaling and top-down mixture modeling to estimate the relative contribution of each tributary to downstream assemblages. We hypothesize (1) that different streams have distinct microplastic assemblages, (2) that downstream microplastic assemblages represent the admixture of upstream sources, and (3) that a sub-catchment's land use is recorded in downstream microplastic assemblages. This new application of established methods allows us to rigorously assess microplastic routing in the Snake River watershed and may be extended to identify emitters in other watersheds or at different scales.

title: Correlating Surface Morphology and Thermophysical Properties of Martian Crater Ejecta Facies Using High Resolution Color-Infrared Imagery
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Piatek, Jennifer L. [1], Tornabene, Livio L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Central Connecticut State University, New Britain, CT, USA
(2) Centre for Planetary Science & Exploration (CPSX) and Dept. of Earth Sciences, Western University, London, ON, Canada
abstract:
Past studies have characterized the geomorphology and thermophysical properties of both well-preserved and modified ejecta from Martian impact craters near the simple-complex transition diameter (~10 km) [1,2]. Ejecta facies were mapped using thermal inertia modeled from nighttime brightness temperatures derived from data collected by the Thermal Infrared Imaging System aboard Mars Odyssey (THEMIS/MO). Examination of thermal inertia values from different mapped ejecta facies suggest that well-preserved deposits have relatively narrow ranges of thermal inertia, with moderate values for continuous deposits likely composed of blockier/more coherent material and lower thermal inertia values for radial discontinuous units consistent with finer-grained deposits. Modified ejecta deposits exhibit wider ranges of thermal inertia values, likely due to either removal or deposition of finer grained material.

We test these interpretations by examining higher spatial resolution color-infrared data, specifically images from the Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System instrument on Trace Gas Orbiter (CaSSIS/TGO) and the the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment onboard Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE/MRO). CaSSIS/TGO is a visible/near-infrared color stereo camera that acquires images in up to 4 broadband filters (BLU: 495 PAN: 678 RED: 836 NIR: 939 nm) with a spatial resolution of 4 m/pixel after post-processing [3,4]. HiRISE/MRO provides a narrow VNIR color swath (~1.1-1.2 km width) in 3 broadband filters (BG: 500, RED: 690, NIR: 870 nm) with an unbinned resolution as high as 0.25 m/pixel after resampling [5,6].

Mars spacecraft missions have returned petabytes of image data across wavelengths from the visible to the thermal infrared at varying spatial scales. These datasets have significantly advanced scientific study of the geology and geomorphology of Mars. These high resolution images reveal details of ejecta deposits that complement analyses of lower resolution thermal infrared data. The overall goals of our work are to identify ejecta characteristics associated with well-preserved ejecta to inform modeling of impact processes and to identify changes in ejecta associated with modification to provide clues to the changing environmental conditions on Mars.

title: Uses for the "Useless": Finding Utility in Specimens Without Collections Data
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Dalton, Jack [1]
affiliations: (1) Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
abstract:
A major problem for long-running fossil collections is the reliance on physical catalogs for keeping record of locality information and other types of collections data. If a physical catalog is the only repository for specimen information, its loss represents the erasure of crucial data for a vast number of specimens. Digitizing collection records can help prevent this from occurring. However, small universities and museums often lack the sufficient staff and funding to support the digitization process. Wichita State University is one such example. Its fossil collection was established nearly a century ago and, since then, collections data has been stored exclusively in physical catalogs and specimen cards. In recent decades, most of the catalogs and specimen cards were lost. The majority of WSU’s specimens now lack accessible collections data. Due to staff shortages, efforts to digitize the remaining physical records have only recently begun.

Ordinarily, specimens without collections data are viewed as having limited scientific utility. Without knowing where a specimen was collected, it becomes much more difficult to place it within a geologic framework. This precludes a specimen’s use in most types of paleontological study. However, there is another approach that can be taken to these specimens that gives them significant utility. Physical attributes, be they anatomical characters or erosional effects, are retained. This means that these supposedly-useless specimens can be used to help teach students the methods of paleontology. Such attributes also allow these specimens to be used to great effect in outreach. During the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 academic years, several outreach events were run on the WSU campus that utilized “useless” fossils to engage with students and the general public. Such events have proven a useful aid in fostering interest in geology and encouraging enrollment in geology courses. Thus, broadening the scope of specimen use in this manner can bring new “life” to old specimens.

authors: Waldeck, Anna R [1], Leapaldt, Hanna C [2], Mousseau, Benjamin [3], Olsen, Ellen K [4], Wan, Chuyan [5], Custado, Manuel Justin [6], Wostbrock, Jordan AG [7], McCormick, Michael L [8], Kump, Lee R [9], Jacobson, Andrew D [10], Ingalls, Miquela [11]

abstract:
Microbial life shapes carbonate mineral (CaCO 3 ) production and preservation, which in turn helps regulate Earth’s carbon cycle and climate. CaCO 3 preserves geobiological and environmental information in fabrics, mineralogy, elemental abundances, and isotopic compositions, yet the formation pathways and potential biogenicity of many CaCO 3 sediments remain elusive. Here we investigate microbially mediated CaCO 3 formation in a modern lake system, Fayetteville Green Lake (FGL; New York, USA), which is a widely recognized analogue for ancient CaCO 3 environments. FGL hosts multiple modes of CaCO 3 formation: (1) a months-long summer whiting event in surface water which produces fine-grained CaCO 3 , (2) microbial thrombolites which trap sediments and promote CaCO 3 cementation along the lake margins, and (3) authigenic CaCO 3 muds that infill sediment pore spaces. CaCO 3 from the whiting event forms in association with photosynthesizers ( Synechococcus and diatoms) and reflects a pure photoautotrophic CaCO 3 facies. Meanwhile, lake sediments host chemotrophs and heterotrophs and may include authigenic CaCO 3 precipitated alongside sulfur metabolisms that drive local increases in alkalinity.

Between 2020–2026, we examined CaCO 3 precipitation at FGL and constrained environmental changes associated with its formation. We conducted aqueous geochemical measurements to constrain metabolic activity and CaCO 3 saturation states, and paired CaCO 3 isotope measurements to understand how microbial and geochemical signatures are recorded in the mineral. We find that whiting event CaCO 3 is strongly influenced by microbial metabolisms, consistent with models of photosynthesis in FGL water: dual clumped (D 47 –D 48 ) signatures indicate a high degree of disequilibrium in the DIC pool; calcium isotope (d 44/40 Ca) signatures are consistent with kinetic fractionation during microbial CaCO 3 precipitation; and triple oxygen isotope (d 18 O-D' 17 O) signatures are more muted, suggesting rapid oxygen isotope re-equilibration. Clumped and triple oxygen isotopes in core-derived CaCO 3 sediments are consistent with potential mixing with authigenic and/or recrystallized CaCO 3 , yet primary calcium isotope signatures from the whiting are preserved in sediments.

title: Relating to Rocks: Guillory’s Geoscience Interpretation Strategy to Supporting Geoheritage, ACE Interpretation, and Geoscience Education within the National Park Service
session_title: The Astro-Geoheritage of the Solar System: Past Explorations and Future Considerations
authors: Guillory, Makenna Josephine [1], Parcell, William Christopher [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(2) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA
abstract:
Within the last 15 years, geologic heritage, or geoheritage, has become a widely supported and thriving concept, with many major organizations recognizing that geologic landscapes and features hold great significance and a diverse array of values for all who encounter them. A protector of many geologic resources, the National Park Service has taken the initiative to support and preserve the diverse geoheritage values of its sites, including the artistic, cultural, ecological, scientific, and educational values. The NPS’s geoheritage efforts followed a shift in interpretation with the development of Audience-Centered Experiences (ACE), through which park rangers’ interpretive programs focus on highlighting visitors’ lived experiences, creating connections to the site, and inspiring stewardship rather than delivering a mass of scientific and historical facts.

These developments in geoheritage preservation and audience-centered interpretation present an enriching future for geoscience within the National Park Service. However, there remains a lack of concise information on integrating these initiatives with geoscience education in individual interpretive programs. Although many park rangers have successfully designed geoscience programs that educate visitors about geology while highlighting visitors’ lived experiences and the resource’s geoheritage values, there is a need for a fundamental guiding strategy adaptable to a site’s unique resources.

This project aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate a strategy designed to integrate geoscience education, geoheritage, and ACE interpretation. Drawing on previous research, Guillory’s Geoscience Interpretation Strategy (GGIS) was developed around five fundamental objectives: Connecting Through Stories, Establishing Familiarity, Making Space, Finding Emotional Perspective, and Creating Kinesthetic and Visual Opportunities. In partnership with Grand Teton National Park, a geoscience interpretive program outline, script, and interactive materials were developed to achieve the five GGIS objectives. This program, “Stone, Ice, & You!”, was delivered twice at Grand Teton National Park in a 30-minute presentation to park visitors. To evaluate the effectiveness of GGIS, an online Qualtrics feedback survey was offered to program attendees, collecting perspectives and recommendations. Initial results indicate that most attendees “Strongly Agree” on a five-point Likert Scale when evaluated on areas such as increased engagement, learning, inspired stewardship, connection, and feeling valued. Responses also indicated opportunities to strengthen stewardship inspiration, variety of engagement techniques, and adaptation to audience engagement/interests. These findings will inform revisions to Guillory’s Geoscience Interpretation Strategy and future testing in additional NPS locations.

title: Volcanic fireworks during the mid Cretaceous in the Sierra Nevada and Idaho arcs
session_title: Geologic and tectonic evolution of the Sierra Nevada, California
authors: Tikoff, Basil [1], Nelson, Ellen M. [2], Coleman, Drew S. [3], Frazer, Ryan E [4], Rudolph, Kurt W [5]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI,
(2) University of Wisconsin– Madison, Madison, WI,
(3) University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC,
(4) University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC,

abstract:
Although deformation in the US section of the North American Cordillera was ongoing in the Early Cretaceous, there is a major increase in shortening rates in the Sevier fold-and-thrust belt starting at ca. 100 Ma. We define this increase as the initiation of the Sevier-Laramide orogeny. This time is known to correspond to initial phases of block uplifts in the western United States and the initiation of transpressional shear zones within the Sierra Nevada and Idaho magmatic arcs. Major volcanic activity occurred in both of the arcs at this time. In the Sierra Nevada arc, there is a mid-Cretaceous flare up of high-silica magmas. These occur along the central and eastern margin of the Cretaceous batholith, including the Alabama Hills granite, inconsistent with a smooth west-to-east progression of magmatism in the batholith. The plutons intrude at shallow crustal levels, consistent with the occurrence of miarolitic cavities and tabular fracture clusters in the Alabama Hills granite, but inconsistent with shallowing pluton emplacement trend with decreasing age in the Sierra Nevada arc. Similar to the Johnson granite porphyry in the Tuolumne Intrusive Suite, the central section of the Alabama Hills likely erupted. In the Idaho arc, the depths of exposure of all mid-Cretaceous plutons are too deep to use fabrics to determine if eruptions occurred. There is, however, record of abundant volcanism in the foreland basin of Wyoming, that was immediately downwind of the Idaho arc. In this setting, most of the detrital zircons have similar ages to those provided by independent biostratigraphic control; moreover, depositional ash beds, preserved as bentonite layers, are abundant. This volcanic depositional input ended by 80 Ma. Together, these events signal a major change in arc magmatism in the western United States at ca. 100 Ma.

This timing is coincident with proposed oblique (right-lateral) collision of the Insular superterrane in western margin of the western United States (and perhaps northern Mexico and southern Canada). The magmatic arcs were linear features on the North American margin, that were rheologically weak because of the presence of magmas and localized deformation. The resultant dextral transpressional shear zones within the arc were likely conduits for magmas, explaining the genesis and timing of the eruptive magmatism.

title: Laurentia at the Core of Rodinia: A Revised Apparent Polar Wander Path from Unimos Ocean Closure Through Tonian Rifting
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [1], Zhang, Yiming [2], Slotznick, Sarah [3], Zielinski, Laurie Antoinette [4], Eyster, Athena Elizabeth [5], Piispa, Elisa [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN,
(2) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN,
(3) Dartmouth College,
(4) Dartmouth College,
(5) Tufts University, Medford, MA,
(6) University of Iceland,
abstract:
Rodinia assembled around Laurentia through collisional orogenesis: the ca. 1080–980 Ma Grenvillian orogeny brought conjugate continental blocks against Laurentia's margin and left the craton at the supercontinent's center, where some 200 million years of quiescence followed. Rifting initiated along the western margin with the ca. 780 Ma Gunbarrel large igneous province and soon after along the eastern margin. Protracted extension through the late Tonian to Ediacaran isolated Laurentia from the assembling Gondwana. Because Laurentia sat at the center, its position anchors reconstructions of Rodinia and the transition to Gondwana. Laurentia's rich paleomagnetic record is sufficiently continuous that its latitude and orientation can be traced without hemispheric ambiguity back through this interval to ca. 1800 Ma. New paleomagnetic data, high-precision geochronology, revised chronostratigraphy, and thermochronology have substantially updated understanding of the interval spanning Rodinia's assembly and the onset of dispersal. We synthesize them in a new openly documented compilation built from the underlying site-level data, with each pole position reproducible from the data that constrain it and revisable as new results emerge.

Our understanding of Laurentia's motion leading up to Grenvillian collision and into the interval of Rodinia has advanced markedly: rapid equatorward motion exceeding 20 cm/yr from ca. 1110 to 1080 Ma slowed to ~2 cm/yr by ca. 1045 Ma — a slow-down predicted if motion resulted from closure of the Unimos Ocean, terminated by continent–continent collision. Slow motion persisted, with the craton drifting gradually into the earliest Neoproterozoic. Thermochronologic recalibration of remanence acquisition during Grenville orogen exhumation changes the timing of Laurentia’s journey to high southern latitudes known as the Grenville Loop from ca. 1000 Ma to ca. 890 Ma. This motion is a Tonian feature within an already assembled supercontinent, not a latest Mesoproterozoic one. By the late Tonian, a coherent record from widely separated parts of the craton and different lithologies places Laurentia at equatorial latitudes through ca. 720 Ma as rifting progressed along its margins.

This sharpened reference frame advances the basis on which conjugate cratons within Rodinia can be reconstructed. The resulting picture is a revised position for Laurentia — and therefore the supercontinent — from Grenvillian assembly into the Cryogenian and a Rodinia drifting slowly rather than rapidly through its interval of stability.

authors: RODRIGUEZ CONTRERAS, PERLA [1], CHAPMAN, JAMES B [2], JIMENEZ LOPEZ, LUIS ANGEL [3]

abstract:
Northwestern Oaxaca exposes a segment of the Mesoproterozoic Oaxaquia microcontinent, characterized by granulite-facies gneisses, AMCG intrusions, and pegmatite dike networks, all influenced by regional structural systems. The district hosts established mines and mineral occurrences of gold, mica, feldspar, thorium, and uranium, providing an appropriate setting to evaluate geophysical methods for multi-commodity mineral exploration. This study integrates airborne magnetic and gamma-ray spectrometric data with fieldwork matching, as well as geochemical analyses, structural interpretation, and the distribution of known mineralization to delineate prospective zones and refine the regional exploration model.

Magnetic data were enhanced using the first vertical derivative, analytic signal, Center for Exploration Targeting structural analysis, and three-dimensional Euler deconvolution. These processed datasets delineate contrasting magneto-lithologic domains, probable intrusive centers, and structural corridors that likely controlled magma emplacement and hydrothermal fluid flow. Euler solutions indicate that some magnetic sources extend to depths of at least 150 meters, supporting the presence of buried intrusive bodies. Radiometric data were analyzed using potassium, equivalent uranium, and equivalent thorium channels, ternary images, and element-ratio maps. Elevated uranium and thorium responses correspond with radioactive pegmatites, while potassium-rich and high K/Th zones define areas of potassic alteration and felsic intrusive or pegmatitic domains.

The Analytical Hierarchy Process was used to weight variables such as radioactive element ratios, magnetic and structural lineaments, analytical signal, and known mineral occurrences. The resulting prospectivity model delineates several high-priority zones where structural complexity, intrusive signatures, and radiometric enrichment coincide. Preliminary results demonstrate that this integrated geophysical framework can support exploration for precious metals, industrial minerals, and Th-U-REE mineralization. The model offers a regional tool for prioritizing geological verification, systematic geochemical sampling, and detailed ground-geophysical surveys in northwestern Oaxaca.

title: Geologic Controls of Calcareous Glades in the Tennessee River Valley

abstract: Calcareous limestone glades within the Tennessee River Valley contain abundant Silurian-aged and Devonian-aged marine fossils, along with rare grassland plants. While calcareous glades are studied for their botanical significance, their distribution within the Tennessee River Valley remains poorly understood. We hypothesize that variations in limestone lithology affect soil depth, groundwater retention, and nutrient availability, which direct the distribution of calcareous glades within the Tennessee River Valley. If our hypothesis is correct, calcareous glades will primarily occur within specific geologic formations rather than being randomly distributed. This research used three primary analytical techniques: Geographic Information System analysis, ground-truthing, and petrographic analysis. GIS analysis was used to map the occurrence of glades, ground-truthing verified lithology, and petrographic analyses examined the composition of calcareous units. Data from GIS analysis of the study-area showed that the glades were disproportionately concentrated in the Middle Silurian Brownsport Group comprising 58% of occurrences (χ²(9)=562.46, p < 0.001). Understanding the geologic controls on the distribution of the Tennessee River Valley calcareous glades will aid in locating unmapped glade occurrences, identifying potential fossil localities within the Tennessee River Valley, and supporting conservation of rare habitats. To continue this research, future work will involve travelling to glade sites to record detailed descriptions along with collecting data to reconstruct stratigraphic and sedimentary environments of the Tennessee River Valley. Petrographic and chemical analyses of calcareous units will also be completed to examine possible factors controlling glade development in the Tennessee River Valley.

title: Assessing Spatial and Temporal Carbon Dioxide Exchange Patterns in a Cave Affected by Chimney Effect Airflow
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science (Posters)
authors: Noble, Megan [1], Covington, Matthew [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract: The exchange of carbon dioxide between water and air in a cave environment influences the degree of carbonate dissolution or precipitation and, consequently, the rate of cave passage evolution. Exchange is driven by a concentration gradient of CO 2 between cave air and water. If air pCO 2 is greater than water pCO 2 , carbon dioxide dissolves and may react with water to create carbonic acid, the main dissolution agent in carbonate caves. Dissolution will occur if the water has not yet reached the calcite saturation index. Should water pCO 2 be greater than air pCO 2 , CO 2 will be degassed to the air, and calcite may precipitate and form speleothems. Available CO 2 is influenced by seasonal and spatial ventilation patterns. Boy Scout Spring Cave in Bella Vista, Arkansas is affected by chimney effect airflow, where density differences between the interior and exterior of the cave cause airflow to seasonally reverse directions. In warmer months, when the cave interior is cooler than the exterior, CO 2 -rich air enters through upper openings, cools, sinks, and exits through a lower entrance. In cooler months, when the cave interior is warmer than the exterior, air enters through the lower entrance and exits through upper openings. While temporal variations in carbon dioxide exchange have been well characterized, spatial variations have been explored less. This project aims to analyze the environmental controls on carbonate dissolution by investigating longitudinal patterns of CO 2 exchange in a linear cave over a year. CO 2 sensors have been deployed in the air and water at three locations along the stream that runs through Boy Scout Spring Cave. One station is downstream and strongly ventilated due to its proximity to the cave entrance; one station is upstream and relatively isolated from the atmosphere; and one is at an intermediate location. If ventilation is the primary control on carbon dioxide exchange and cave development, average downstream pCO 2 and dissolution rates will consistently be lower than those upstream. Seasonal patterns may also be strongly reflected downstream in comparison to upstream.

abstract: Airborne radar surveys have produced decades of legacy radargrams across Antarctica, but their data quality varies widely, and no consistent method exists to evaluate that quality without manually opening each file. This study developed a repeatable six-class qualitative classification system based on bed visibility and internal ice-layer clarity, applied to 267 flight lines across three Antarctic survey regions (WSB, WLK, ELM1) near Allan Hills. Quality ratings were joined to flight-line geometry in QGIS and compared against Bedmap2-derived terrain variables. Spearman correlation confirmed that radargram quality is significantly linked to ice thickness (ρ = –0.70), distance to open water/ice-shelf front (ρ = –0.58), and distance to exposed rock (ρ = –0.45, all p < 0.001), demonstrating that the classification reflects measurable environmental conditions rather than subjective interpretation alone. A parallel analysis comparing recorded flight altitude against radargram quality identified a clear operational threshold: data quality holds reliably below approximately 826 m, with sharp degradation above that altitude. Together, these results provide both a validated method for triaging legacy Antarctic radar archives and concrete, actionable guidance, a terrain-informed flight altitude ceiling, for planning the upcoming NSF COLDEX airborne field season over the Allan Hills old ice site, East Antarctica, helping ensure future surveys collect usable, interpretable radar data on the first pass.

authors: Blythe, Ann [1], Klisura, Shayne [2], Doyle, Maddy [3], Smith, Iris [4], Longinotti, Nicole [5], Khalsa, Sopurkh [6]

abstract: The Tehachapi Mountains, which are a southwest continuation of the Sierra Nevada, have a complicated tectonic evolution. Here we present a compilation of 5 datasets from undergraduate student research projects; these studies, when combined, give us a comprehensive look at the patterns of exhumation in the Tehachapi Mountains and insights into the evolving tectonic framework. The data sets consist of low-temperature thermochronology (zircon and apatite fission track and (U-Th)/He ages), as well as geomorphic analyses (K sn values) of range front rivers. The thermochronological samples were collected along 2 North-South transects, one in the eastern Tehachapis and one in the central Tehachapis), and from locations on both sides of the NE-trending Garlock fault. The thermochronologic data show: 1) moderate cooling (and exhumation) on both sides of the Garlock fault from ~70 to 50 Mya, 2) in the eastern, but not the central, Tehachapis, rapid cooling and exhumation is recorded north of the Garlock fault beginning at ~20 Mya, and 3) in both the eastern and central Tehachapis, rapid cooling and exhumation beginning at ~12 Ma is found only to the north of the Garlock fault. We interpret the cooling and exhumation from ~70-50 Myr to be a regional event associated with the emplacement of the Sierra Nevada batholith and Laramide subduction. The cooling event at ~20 Ma in the eastern Tehachapis is most likely the result of uplift and exhumation associated with the onset of Basin and Range extension, and the ~12 Ma cooling event appears to be related to the onset of initiation of the predominantly left-lateral strike-slip Garlock fault. The Garlock fault clearly plays a partial role in the exhumation of the Tehachapis, but the story is more complicated, as additional dip-slip faults are required to create the topography to the south of the Garlock fault. The normalized channel steepness (K sn ) values of streams flowing to the southeast in the Tehachapis indicate that modern uplift rates increase to the NE in the Tehachapis. K sn values suggest that the modern day uplift rate in the Tehachapis is lower than that of the southernmost Sierra Nevada, whereas the thermochronological data suggest that the rates in the Tehachapis were equivalent or higher than the rates in the southern Sierra Nevada in the past.

title: Geologic Mapping of the Lower Colonias Quadrangle with emphasis on late Paleozoic geology
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Johnstone, Charlie Brian [1], Sapkota, Gyanendra Raj [2], Sweet, Dustin E. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA

abstract:
The Taos trough is a sedimentary basin that formed throughout the Pennsylvanian and early Permian associated with the Ancestral Rocky Mountains (ARM) orogeny. Subsequent deformation associated with the Laramide orogeny and Rio Grande rifting have reactivated and overprinted many of these late Paleozoic structures making it difficult to isolate ARM-aged structures. Here, we use new geologic mapping of the Lower Colonias 7.5-minute Quadrangle to unravel late Paleozoic deformation from younger overprints.

The Lower Colonias Quadrangle is located in the southern part of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of northern New Mexico, and preserves sediments deposited in the southern end of the Taos trough. 1:24,000-scale bedrock mapping, structural measurements, paleocurrent analysis, and petrographic study were conducted to define stratigraphic relationships and characterize structural geometries throughout the map area.

Late Paleozoic sedimentary rock units consist of the Arroyo Peñasco Group (Mississippian undivided), the Sandia Formation, the Porvenir Formation, and the Alamitos Formation. The Arroyo Peñasco Group is thin and pinches out locally. It is a predominantly limestone unit with some sandstone. The Sandia Formation consists of locally cross stratified feldspathic sandstone and shale with northwest-directed paleocurrents. The Porvenir Formation conformably overlies the Sandia Formation and consists of massive limestone and interbedded shale with occasional sandstone. The Alamitos Formation is characterized by cross-bedded, arkosic sandstone and shale with interbedded limestone.

Precambrian crystalline rocks are exposed in the northeastern portion of the map area along the hanging wall of high-angle reverse faults. Throughout the map area, strata generally dip to the southwest, with local folding and faulting. The central and eastern portions of the map contain approximately north-south trending, high-angle reverse faults and associated folds. Evidence suggests that these structures originated during the Early Pennsylvanian and later reactivated during the Laramide shortening. Several east-west trending folds occur within the Alamitos Formation in the western portion of the map area. These folds are kinematically consistent with Middle Pennsylvanian deformation associated with dextral slip in the Picuris-Pecos fault.

These relationships indicate that although younger tectonic events substantially modified the structural framework of the area, portions of the late Paleozoic structural fabric remain well preserved, providing new constraints on the tectonic evolution of the southern Taos trough.

title: Geologic Mapping of the Deadman Creek thrust: Interactions between Laramide contraction and early Rio Grande rift extension and magmatism in the Sangre de Cristo Range, southern Colorado

authors: Primus, Miriam E [1], Singleton, John [2], Frawley, Dylan Liam [3], Broeder, Hunter Joseph [4], Malavarca, Samantha L. [5], Rahl, Jeffrey M. [6]
affiliations: (1) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,

abstract: Detailed 1:10,000 scale geologic mapping of the western flank of the Sangre de Cristo Range in southern Colorado documents the geometry and relationships of contractional and extensional structures that record the transition from Laramide shortening to Rio Grande rift extension. This area of the range contains exposures of Proterozoic gneisses and granitoids, slivers of Mississippian, Devonian, and Ordovician sedimentary rocks (MDO), Oligocene gabbro stocks and aplitic dikes, and greenschist-facies mylonites. The focus of the map is the Deadman Creek thrust – a top-NE directed thrust fault that juxtaposes Proterozoic crystalline rocks in the hanging wall and MDO in the footwall. Mapping reveals this structure has been deformed by subsequent NE-vergent fault-propagation folds and back-thrusts, locally reactivated as an extensional shear zone, and later dissected by brittle-plastic normal faults. One of these normal faults, designated as the Short Creek fault, is localized on the steep to moderately NE-dipping folded limb of the Deadman Creek thrust. In addition, the footwall of the Deadman Creek thrust hosts gently dipping mylonite zones with SW- and NE-plunging lineations and fabrics indicative of top-SW sense shear, opposite of the Laramide contractional regime. These zones are locally 10s of meters thick and are found proximal to locally strained range-front Oligocene granodiorite and gabbro intrusions, rather than along the contact of the Deadman Creek thrust, suggesting these mylonites are associated with Oligocene magmatism. Microstructural observations and quartz crystallographic indicate top-SW shear to coaxial strain under greenschist-facies conditions. We interpret the top-SW shear zones and the brittle-plastic normal faults to record the earliest stages of Rio Grande rift extension that was coeval with bimodal magmatism and preceded development of the range-bounding Sangre de Cristo normal fault system in the Miocene. These mapped relationships provide new constraints on the structural evolution of the western Sangre de Cristo Range and demonstrate that early Rio Grande rift extension locally reactivated older Laramide structures during emplacement of Oligocene intrusions.

abstract: The stratigraphic sequence at Olduvai Gorge, which spans approximately the last 2.1 million years, indicates dynamic intervals characterized by changes in vegetation, climate, lake alkalinity and salinity, hominin diversity, and tectonic and volcanic events. Our research aims to identify changes throughout the sequence that evidence paleoenvironmental changes, exploring temporal trends in isotopic and molecular proxies that reflect the vegetation response to changes in climate (δ13Corg; distributions and δ13C compositions of n-alkanes) in claystones from stone/sediment cores as well as archaeological outcrops while targeting the implications of these changes to the archaeological assemblages and sites at the gorge. For example, the Upper Bed I and Bed II sequence spans a time of major environmental changes, with drier yet variable conditions and a dominance of C4 grasses occurring prior to and around the time of the Oldowan to Acheulean technological transition (~1.7 Ma.). Collectively, the data suggest landscape aridification occurring throughout the gorge sequence, with broad and variable drying trends in Beds II and III and more recent indications of a drying climate since the younger Masek Beds. Hence, changes in tool technology and hominin diversity across the gorge may relate to changes in the availability of resources associated with a drier environment.

title: Constraining the Three-Dimensional Geometry of the Duluth Complex, MN: Insights from Magnetic Fabrics and Paleomagnetic Data
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Akin, Kathryn [1], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [2], Lorenzen, Marcus [3]

(2) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

abstract:
The Midcontinent Rift developed within the interior of Laurentia during a period of extension and magmatism from 1109 Ma to 1084 Ma. Emplaced during the development of the Midcontinent Rift, the Duluth Complex is interpreted as the second-largest exposed mafic intrusive complex on Earth. The Duluth Complex comprises an anorthositic series and a layered series of gabbro and troctolite cumulates. Despite the wealth of data on the geology, mineralization, structure, timing, and emplacement mechanisms of the Duluth Complex, there remains some uncertainty surrounding its thickness and, therefore, overall volume.

The tilt of the Duluth Complex is poorly constrained due to the absence of macroscopic igneous foliation over much of the complex, particularly in the anorthositic series. This research focuses on developing data on Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) parameters and paleomagnetic remanence directions compared with expected tilt-corrected directions. These data lead to new estimates of the Duluth Complex’s tilt and therefore its thickness, which exceeds 9 km in the center of the complex. Remanence directions estimate a consistent tilt of about 14 to 16 degrees to the southeast in the anorthositic and layered series, as well as the overlying volcanics, indicating that the Duluth Complex and overlying volcanics were tilted simultaneously as a coherent block rather than progressively during rift magmatism. AMS parameters are used in areas where igneous foliation is not measurable and provide tilt estimates consistent with those derived from remanence directions. Indication of uniform tilt from remanence directions justifies a slab simplification for thickness estimates, and consistency between AMS, remanence, and field-derived tilts provides confidence in these estimates. Variation in the geometry of the Duluth Complex along strike will require this method to be utilized across the complex when calculating an overall volume.

Together, the new susceptibility and remanence data provide important petrophysical information for interpreting new USGS aeromagnetic surveys in northeastern Minnesota. Koenigsberger ratios calculated from Duluth Complex samples are dominated by remanent magnetization. This result provides important ground-truth data for modeling the aeromagnetic data and highlights the importance of considering remanent magnetization rather than induced magnetization alone.

abstract: Arsenic (As) and fluoride (F - ) groundwater contamination is a global concern posing significant health risks, especially semi-arid regions where population growth and agricultural demand increase reliance on volcanic aquifers with limited recharge. The Independence Basin Aquifer System (IBAS), Mexico, serves as an ideal study location for this contaminant co-occurrence. Currently, the primary processes in the study area presumed to be causing high dissolved As and F - are anthropogenic overexploitation of the aquifer and geogenic geothermal influence in fault zones. Recent studies suggest that a chain of geochemical reactions responsible for mobilization begin with silicate hydrolysis, followed by oxyanion release from arsenic-bearing iron-oxides, and dissolution of F-bearing minerals. The influence of groundwater temperature, pH controls on solid-phase materials, and dissolved organic matter (DOM) impact on these contaminants are not well understood. The objective of this dissertation is to establish locations of elevated As and F - and to investigate potential mobilization drivers such as groundwater temperature, pH influence on leachates of soils and rocks, and DOM from groundwater, soil leachates, and rock leachates. Characterization of major and trace elements of groundwater, soil leachates, and rock leachates established a hydrogeochemical framework and a baseline for present contamination and solid-phase contributions of As and F - . Characterization of DOM composition and relationships with contaminants delineated the mobilization processes taking place in recharge flow paths and groundwater interface with lithology along fractures. Results demonstrated that elevated arsenic and fluoride are associated with elevated temperatures, alkaline Na-HCO 3 type waters, depleted calcium, prolonged residence times and longer water-rock interactions. This study also revealed that volcanic soils and rocks are viable contaminant sources. DOM facilitates the mobilization of arsenic, whereas fluoride was decoupled from DOM, highlighting that F - mobilization is primarily controlled by water-rock interactions. These findings provide an integrated conceptual model linking groundwater evolution, soil contents, volcanic lithology, and DOM dynamics within the Independence Basin. This research establishes a framework that is applicable to global analogue settings with semi-arid climates and volcanic aquifers experiencing As and F - co-occurring contamination.

title: When Definitions, Guidance, and Interpretation Hit the Fan: Clarifying Alluvial Fan Terminology
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans
authors: Orem, Caitlin Anne [1], Wasklewicz, Thad [2]
affiliations: (1) Stantec, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(2) Stantec, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Transferring and keeping terminology consistent amongst research scientists (academia, government, private, and industry) and practitioners is essential for clear communication, accurately characterizing hazard and risk, and ensuring legal and scientific clarity. However, pitfalls such as mistranslation, misinterpretation, and unnecessary terminology make common terminology difficult to achieve.

Mistranslation of terminology from scientific literature to applied science and industry (and vice versa), or between disciplines and countries, can happen, especially if those terms are updated or advanced through scientific discovery and/or have evolved to be a functional term via practitioners. Misinterpretation of landforms, processes, and terminology occurs in industry, but may occur in academics as well across different disciplines. Practitioners in industry and geology-related disciplines may not possess the experience and expertise to correctly interpret alluvial fan morphology, processes, terminology, and guidance. Unnecessary terminology, or " terminology creep " occurs in both academia and industry where terms to describe similar or the same feature(s) increase in number without clear definitions and explanation as to how and why they differ from existing terms. This leads to an overlap in terminology and confusion as to the most accurate term to use and/or causes confusion to practitioners that may not have the experience or expertise to decipher differences between terms.

These pitfalls can lead to unintended consequences such as the mischaracterization of hazard and under and over estimation of risk. For example, misinterpreting a fan lobe or surface as inactive/relict/disconnected and therefore not including it within a detailed study can lead to an area without documentation of the potential hazard (i.e., mapping, zoning, and/or description). Here, alluvial fan terminology is reviewed and discussed to identify differences and common short-comings and pitfalls. Our aim is to raise awareness and start a conversation about term definitions and applications in relation to academic and applied science guidance documents.

abstract:
Slip‑rate variability along the San Bernardino section of the San Andreas fault (SAF) reflects the interaction of multiple faults and fault strands, including the San Andreas and San Jacinto faults, which merge westward and contribute to a complex regional fault network. Documented late Quaternary slip rates range from ~25 mm/yr near Cajon Creek to 15–11 mm/yr farther east, but the distribution and activity of individual strands within this section remain incompletely resolved. This study focuses on high-resolution (1:10,000 scale) geologic mapping of the San Bernardino section of the SAF between Cable Canyon and Sycamore Canyon to refine fault geometry and improve the basis for future slip‑rate estimates.

The study takes advantage of publicly available LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) data and NAIP (National Agriculture Imagery Program) imagery, which enable detailed analysis of fault‑related geomorphic features. A 1‑m resolution DEM (from the USGS LPC CA SanBernardinoCo AreaA 2013 LAS 2018 dataset) was used to generate hillshade, slope, aspect, roughness, and curvature maps, which—combined with NAIP imagery—significantly improve confidence in mapping fault strands and Quaternary surface relationships. In addition, new terrestrial laser‑scanning (TLS) LiDAR and drone‑based photogrammetry data were collected between Badger Canyon and Sycamore Canyon, providing ultra‑high‑resolution topography for identifying subtle scarps, offset landforms, and subsidiary fault traces.

Current mapping reveals multiple previously unmapped fault strands within the San Bernardino section of the SAF. Several smaller strands exhibit more dip‑slip character than the dominantly strike‑slip main strand, a pattern that may help explain slip‑rate variability reported across this region. Continued mapping of fault strands and their relationships to Quaternary surfaces, alongside topographic profile analysis and scarp degradation modeling, will support more accurate slip‑rate calculations and improve understanding of strain distributions along this structurally intricate portion of the SAF.

abstract: The goal of agricultural conservation efforts is to reduce nutrient runoff into downstream aquatic systems. Despite this, excessive nutrient enrichment and persistent algal blooms remain challenges for local farmers. In agricultural watersheds, livestock slurry can introduce nitrogen overload that then migrates downslope and eventually into surface water; thus, understanding the spatial variability of nitrate concentration is vital to mitigating nitrogen enrichment in streams. The present study investigates the spatial variability of soil nitrate within an agricultural farm located in the 100-year floodplain of Long Glade Creek in the Shenandoah Valley Region of Virginia. Field sampling will be collected across multiple transects from upstream to downstream along the vegetated buffer zone (9-15 meters from left and right stream banks) within the 100-year floodplain in the fall of 2026. To determine the impact of slope, sampling intervals along transects will be adjusted (to a minimum of 3-4 meters) based on the gradient. The vertical nitrate transport will be estimated by extracting soil cores at three depth intervals: 0-15 cm, 15-30 cm, and 30-60 cm. The sampling approach will help us determine nitrate accumulation in both the surface soil and the root zone, providing insights into nitrate distribution and the potential for nitrate leaching into deeper soil layers. To reduce statistical bias and small-scale variability, 3 core replicates will be collected at each sampling point and combined into a single composite sample. Each sampling point will be georeferenced via a high-resolution Topcon Hyper VR GPS. Collected soil samples will be analyzed for soil nitrate concentrations (US EPA Method 353.2) along with soil texture (laser diffraction method), organic matter (loss on ignition method), pH (EPA Method 9045D), and bulk density (bulk density core method). The data will be analyzed using geospatial and spatial statistical techniques to identify patterns in soil nitrate variability and examine the impacts of slope and other variables on nitrate distribution. Understanding the vertical nitrate distribution patterns in relation to slope, elevation, and spatial location will help to determine how changes in field elevation and soil properties affect nitrogen storage and transport. The findings of the present study will support improved nutrient management and sustainable agricultural practices in agricultural farming systems located in floodplain environments.

title: Intraspecific Variation Over 10 million Years Shows Potential Effects of Mass Extinction and Recovery on Sex and Age Demography in the Permian Stem-mammal Diictodon feliceps
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Pinto, James L. [1], Kammerer, Christian F. [2], Rabe, Caitlin [3], Huttenlocker, Adam K. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA,

(3) Palaeobiology Research Group, Department of Biological Sciences, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa
(4) College of Veterinary Medicine, Western University of Health Sciences, Pomona, CA, USA
abstract: Intraspecific variation through time can result from environmental adaptation and/or reproductive selectivity. Demographic changes (e.g. percent of younger/older or male/female individuals) are potential species responses to long-term ecological processes, such as environmental stress and faunal turnover during mass extinctions. A sample of the middle-late Permian (~262-252 Ma) South African dicynodont Diictodon feliceps , totaling 718 measured crania, records potential anagenesis and demographic changes over 10 million years. We recorded linear measurements, which were paired with categorical variables to estimate demographics. Sex is diagnosed by presence or absence of canine teeth, though we also find evidence for sexual size dimorphism, with toothed individuals (presumed males) being ~18% larger than toothless ones (presumed females), with normal distributions of sizes in each sex, evidence against the morphs being ontogenetic stages. Each morph is found to co-occur in ~99% of localities with at least 5 individuals, and the two morphs also co-occur separately in Zambia and China, evidence against the morphs being separate species. D. feliceps survived the Capitanian Mass Extinction (CME), with pre-/post-extinction and post-faunal recovery subsamples available for study. Relative abundance of D. feliceps changes throughout its range, increasing from ~10-40% of collected fossils over biozones following the CME, and decreasing from ~40-10% after faunal recovery, indicating a “disaster-taxon-like” species history. Average basal skull length (BSL) increased by ~10% following the CME and decreased by ~20% at the abundance decrease. Individuals from smaller bodied assemblages also have proportionately larger orbits, suggesting size shifts reflect changing age demographics, as previously observed in Lystrosaurus following the end-Permian Mass Extinction. Male-to-female ratios vary through time, with the percentage of males decreasing from ~2:1 to 1:2. The proportions of the orbit and the preorbital region also differ between assemblage zones, with differences between males and females being larger in the lower relative abundance, lower BSL intervals. Regardless of whether the morphs represent sexes, individuals with teeth become less common, possibly indicating changing importance of a social trait through time. These results indicate that in stressful periods near a species’ extinction, larger, older and possibly male individuals may be selected against.

title: Did the Winter Monsoon Buffer Vegetation Against a Weakening Summer Monsoon? Biomarker Evidence from the Bay of Bengal
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Roy, Pranto [1], Ponton, Camilo [2], Flanagan, Evangeline [3], Ranasinghe, Pradeep Nalaka [4]

abstract: The Indian monsoon, one of the world's strongest climatic systems, affects 1.5 billion people across the Indian subcontinent through two seasonally reversing branches: the Indian summer monsoon (ISM), which delivers about 80% of its annual rainfall, and the Indian winter monsoon (IWM). Geochemical reconstructions from the central Bay of Bengal indicate that a weakened ISM during the glacial period reduced chemical weathering and terrestrial input, favoring physical erosion and highland sources, whereas a strengthened Holocene ISM intensified chemical weathering and floodplain input. Whether vegetation cover tracked this rainfall decline from the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) to the Holocene remains poorly constrained. This study uses lipid biomarkers from a sediment core in the central Bay of Bengal to reconstruct vegetation cover across the last glacial-interglacial transition. We use n-alkanoic acids to evaluate the Carbon Preference Index (CPI), Average Chain Length (ACL), and Terrestrial to Aquatic Ratio (TAR), compared with coeval XRF records of weathering and sediment composition. In contrast to the pronounced reduction in terrestrial input inferred from weathering proxies, our biomarker records suggest vegetation cover remained relatively stable across the transition. These results do not support a simple shift from LGM C 4 grasslands to Holocene C 3 forests, but instead point to a complex, non-linear response. One possibility is that IWM-derived moisture sustained vegetation in an otherwise arid region even as the ISM weakened.

title: Preliminary 1:24,000 scale geologic map of the La Plata Quadrangle, San Juan County, NM and the Hogback monocline
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee (Posters)
authors: Hoxey, Andrew KR [1]
affiliations: (1) George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
abstract:
The mentorship of Jeff Lee encouraged recognition of geologic maps as the fundamental dataset for interpreting Earth’s history and geologic processes. Producing a geologic map of a region cultivates an understanding that cannot be replicated or understated. As a result, the contributions from students under Jeff’s direction regularly included extensive field seasons and structural interpretations, many of which became contributions to state survey geologic map libraries. Beyond field excursions, Jeff used a fully-integrated approach that employed analytical tools like petrography and geochronology, developing skills in graduates that continues to empower his mentees.

The Hogback monocline is a regionally northeast-plunging fold that flanks the western margin on the San Juan basin in northwest New Mexico and Southwest Colorado. Preliminary geologic mapping in the La Plata Quadrangle, San Juan County, NM and fracture analysis considers the strain history of folding in the context of models for monocline formation. Regionally, the Hogback monocline exhibits right-handed stepovers that likely reflect structural complexity in the subsurface. Models for the development of right-stepping monoclines include oblique slip on the fold-coring fault driven by convergence obliquity, structural inheritance and reactivation of pre-existing en echelon faults, and irregularities the in the along-strike geometry of the lithospheric keel. Preliminary 1:24,000 scale mapping represents a significant update to the published map (1:100,000 scale) and will help characterize the timing, scale, and kinematics of deformation. Here we document joint and fracture orientations in an effort to differentiate between predominantly oblique or dip slip.

abstract: Our understanding of human influence on soil erosion often centers on agricultural development and urbanization. However, the effect of warfare on soil erosion is underexplored, with potentially significant consequences for the environment and contemporary geopolitics. This project addresses that gap in knowledge by examining early modern period conflicts in western Germany and northeastern France. Understanding how factors such as deforestation and troop movement shaped erosion during pre-industrial warfare is critical in doing so. Data from early modern period conflicts create a baseline for war-induced environmental disturbance. This baseline can then be used as a comparison with modern wars, showcasing how environmental impacts scale with time and technological development. The study focuses on the Rhine River watershed, a region that experienced a centuries-long era of repeated conflicts. To explore warfare’s impact, alluvial and colluvial stratigraphy is studied along the banks of river catchments within this area. A chronostratigraphic framework is presented that includes four new high-precision luminescence ages ranging from 0.13–0.40 ka. Soil equilibrium analyses are applied to each study point, which associate a numeric value with the soil erosion and development at a given location. These analyses allow us to visualize and compare impacts between continuous conflict and inter-war periods. Additionally, paleohydraulic reconstruction is used to distinguish stream flow background erosion from conflict-induced disturbance. To complement these methods, dendrochronological analysis is used throughout the study region, indicating that impacts of conflict scale dramatically from the early modern period to the 20th century. Current results from the early modern period soils display increased erosion sporadically throughout the river basin, indicating non-uniform effects from warfare. On the contrary, samples from the 20th century show more concentrated impacts. These both correlate with war strategy during their specific time periods, adhering to expected environmental disturbance.

title: Global versus local controls on marine sedimentary records and their implications for carbonate-based proxies across the PETM
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part II)
authors: Waldeck, Anna R [1], Fantle, Matthew S [2], Kirtland Turner, Sandra [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(3) Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
abstract:
The Phanerozoic is punctuated by discrete events of atmospheric carbon injection and subsequent carbon drawdown through global silicate weathering and organic carbon feedbacks. Records of these global carbon cycle events are preserved in marine sedimentary carbonates, whose preservation depends on local factors such as photic zone export and coretop particulate flux of carbonate and organic matter and controls on the carbonate saturation state of the deep ocean and pore fluids(i.e., temperature and [CO 3 2- ]). Given that local preservation factors can vary spatially, they complicate the interpretation of sedimentary carbonate and carbonate-based proxies that constrain the global carbon cycle.

In this study, we examine marine carbonate preservation across the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM, ~56 Ma), which contains a significant interval of carbonate dissolution consistent with a rapid release of carbon to the atmosphere–ocean system. We assess spatial controls on carbonate preservation across the PETM using a combination of Earth system modeling and isotopic approaches. Using the CGENIE model, we simulate carbon injection and Earth system recovery across the PETM subject to the modeled silicate weathering and organic carbon cycle feedbacks and analyze the spatial differences in carbonate proxy archives. In parallel model runs, we isolate the relative importance of temperature, weathering, carbon input flux, and primary productivity on carbonate proxies by holding each of these fluxes constant. We then evaluate the model output using a compilation of sedimentary wt. % carbonate records from shallow and deep ocean sites. Finally, we conclude which of modeled environmental controls (temperature, weathering, carbon input, and primary productivity) most influence marine sedimentary records by comparing modeled spatial trends with new carbon and calcium isotope records from globally distributed sites.

title: Early Calcification Preserves Microbial-Scale Internal Architecture in the Cambrian Calcimicrobe Renalcis: Insights from Modern Calcifying Microbial Communities
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Ibarra, Yadira [1], Sanon, Sonicah [2], Wang, Ruby [3], Hedlund, Brian [4], Rademacher, Laura K. [5]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, San Francisco State University, San Francisco, CA, USA
(2) School of the Environment, San Francisco State University, San Francisco, CA,
(3) School of the Environment, San Francisco State University, San Francisco, CA, USA
(4) School of Life Sciences, University of Nevada Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(5) Geological and Environmental Sciences, University of the Pacific, Stockton, CA, USA
abstract:
Renalcis is one of the most abundant calcimicrobes in Cambrian reef ecosystems, yet its biological affinity and mode of calcification remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the morphology, morphometrics, and taphonomic preservation of Renalcis from the Upper Cambrian Pilgrim Formation of Wyoming, USA, using integrated petrography, digital image analysis, and observations of early-calcified filamentous microbes from Willow Creek Spring—an active spring-associated carbonate deposit. High-resolution petrographic imaging was used to examine Renalcis preserved as microbialite-mound encrusters, grainstone cavity fillers, and reworked intraclasts. Over 400 internal rounded structures from several Renalcis colonies were measured using standardized image analysis. Equivalent diameter, circularity, and spatial relationships were quantified to determine whether these structures represent a reproducible primary microfabric or secondary diagenetic textures.

The internal round structures are restricted to the millimetric Renalcis colonies and exhibit a narrow, largely unimodal size distribution, with an overall median equivalent diameter of 5.1 µm and a mean diameter of 5.5 µm; most measurements fall between 3 and 8 µm. Morphometric variation is limited despite preservation in three contrasting settings, and median diameters do not differ significantly among microbialite encrusters, cavity fillers, and transported intraclasts. The persistence of statistically indistinguishable morphometric characteristics across all preservational settings indicates that the internal architecture was established before erosion and redeposition and survived subsequent diagenesis.

We propose that Renalcis formed through iterative growth and early calcification of saccate microbial lobes, producing mechanically coherent chambered colonies with characteristic V-shaped internal cavities. Early micritization stabilized the framework, whereas later syntaxial calcite filled microbial-scale molds and cavities. The early calcification of filamentous microbial communities at Willow Creek provides a process-based modern analog, demonstrating how early microbial mineralization can stabilize cohesive carbonate frameworks despite the absence of the characteristic saccate architecture of Renalcis. These results provide the first quantitative assessment of the internal microfabric of Renalcis across multiple ecological and taphonomic settings and offer new constraints on the biology, early diagenesis, and preservation of this characteristic Paleozoic calcimicrobe.

title: Where the Confining Unit Breaks: Comparing Infiltration and Subsurface Connectivity of Bluffline Alluvial Fans in the Mississippi Valley
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions (Posters)
authors: Bhandari, Arjun [1], Counts, Ronald C. [2], Parajuli, Sanjeev [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Mississippi, oxford, MS, USA
(2) University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS,
(3) University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS,
abstract:
Groundwater extraction from the Mississippi River Valley Alluvial Aquifer (MRVAA) currently exceeds natural recharge, and the spatial distribution and mechanisms of vertical recharge remain poorly constrained. Regionally extensive fine-grained, low-permeability floodplain muds restrict vertical infiltration across much of the Mississippi Alluvial Plain, so recharge is likely concentrated where this confining unit thins, is absent, or is disrupted. In the study area, coarse-grained bluffline alluvial fans built by streams draining the Loess Bluffs onto the alluvial plain are candidate recharge pathways; groundwater highs on the potentiometric surface beneath several fans are consistent with this. Airborne electromagnetic resistivity (AEM) models reveal resistive features beneath some fans and is consistent with this conceptual model, but the inferred connectivity has not been tested using ground-based geophysics or infiltration measurements.

This research is evaluating whether bluff line alluvial fans near Batesville, Panola County, Mississippi, are preferential pathways for infiltration and potential aquifer recharge by characterizing fan geometry, sediment thickness, depth to underlying Tertiary units, and the continuity of the floodplain muds using published U.S. Geological Survey AEM models integrated with electrical resistivity tomography, Ground penetrating radar, and horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio surveys. Double-ring infiltrometer tests across proximal, medial, and distal fan surfaces with paired control measurements on the adjacent floodplain-mantled alluvial plain will be done for comparisons with the interpreted subsurface framework to determine whether areas of elevated infiltration coincide with geophysically identified breaches or thinning of the floodplain confining unit. The study will produce a geomorphic-zone-based assessment of infiltration capacity, a geophysically constrained model of fan architecture, confining unit continuity, and field-based criteria for identifying locations where bluff line alluvial fans may promote focused recharge to the MRVAA.

title: Using SWOT Satellite Data to Estimate Hydraulic Resistance and Sediment Transport Capacity in Large Rivers
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Minear, J. Toby [1], Johnson, Joel [2], Harlan, Merritt [3], Lamb, Mike [4], Rowley, Taylor [5]
affiliations: (1) Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(2) Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(3) Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(4) Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(5) Williams College, Williamstown, MA, USA
abstract:
Sediment transported by large rivers is a critical component of the global sediment cycle and is central to a broad range of fundamental processes of the Earth system, including river flooding and floodplain sediment dynamics, nutrient and adsorbed contaminant transport, and coastal sediment supply and coastal land loss. Yet, monitoring of bed sediment and sediment transport in large rivers occurs only rarely, if ever. The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite mission offers a novel ability to coincidentally measure river water surface elevation, extent, and slope and therefore can provide many, but not all, of the variables used to estimate sediment transport capacity in large rivers. In addition, the SWOT mission provides estimates of remotely-sensed river discharge but these discharge algorithms do not account for sediment transport related effects on hydraulic resistance.

For this initial effort, we build on previous work by making use of field measurement data collected routinely by water agencies at in situ gauging stations, including bed sediment data. Using discharge field measurements and SWOT data, we empirically solve for three critical variables that SWOT does not measure directly: depth to the bed, hydraulic resistance, and grain size. We use gauging station data where discharge is already known, combined with SWOT data, to solve hydraulic resistance equations for both Manning's n and the coefficient of friction, Cf. We also solve for the total depth to the bed and channel cross-sectional area. From these inversions, we derive an expression for hydraulic resistance, area and depth, directly from SWOT data for unmeasured sites. These relationships are used to estimate bed shear stress and bedload sediment transport capacity when combined with SWOT water surface elevations, extent and slope data. Through these initial models for hydraulic resistance and sediment transport, formulated from SWOT data, we are attempting to improve SWOT river discharge products and estimate bed sediment transport capacity in large rivers.
