title: Hematite and Magnesioferrite Veneers in Lava Tubes as Analogs for Venus Basalt Alteration
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: McHenry, Lindsay J. [1], Childs, Dylan [2], Ruffini, Joseph [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Wisconsin- Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI, USA
(2) Stoughton, WI, USA
(3) Bellingham, WA, USA
abstract:
Lavas erupted on the surface of Venus would be immediately exposed to the hot, dry, CO 2 -rich atmosphere, and would solidify and cool under conditions significantly different from Earth. This could affect the mineralogy and spectroscopic features of the resulting veneers. Most experiments involving alteration of lavas under simulated Venus conditions used already crystallized and cooled terrestrial rocks and minerals, leaving the effects of alteration during high-temperature cooling poorly constrained.

To investigate these processes, we examined samples from the interior of lava tubes in Craters of the Moon, Idaho, and Kipuka Kanohina (Mauna Loa) and Pu‘u ‘Ō‘ō (Kilauea), Hawaii. Lava tube interiors can remain hot for months to years after formation, providing a natural process analog for alteration and elemental redistribution of basalt during prolonged cooling. Powdered samples and polished cross sections were analyzed by X-ray Diffraction (XRD) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) with Energy Dispersive Spectrometry (EDS) to determine the mineralogy of veneers formed under these insulating, volcanic gas-rich conditions.

Many veneers consist of thin (1-100 µm) hematite and/or magnesioferrite surface layers that produce a characteristic specular sheen. These oxide-rich veneers commonly overlie a Ca-Mg-Si-rich zone, compositionally consistent with diopside, which overlies basaltic glass (often enriched in Na) and phenocrysts. Hematite and magnesioferrite were identified by XRD and supported by EDS observations showing spatial associations of Fe, Mg, and O (or just Fe and O) within surface veneers. This pattern is consistent with high-temperature cation migration, in which Fe 2+ in the cooling basalt oxidizes, prompting the outward diffusion of Fe 2+ , Mg 2+ , and Ca 2+ cations and a matching inward flux of positive charge (electron “holes”). In some cases the specular veneers are overlain by later precipitates, including sulfate minerals (principally gypsum). Similar hematite-rich alteration veneers reported from Venus-temperature experiments (e.g. Filiberto et al., 2020) suggest that high-temperature cooling may play an important role in their formation.

While conditions in terrestrial lava tubes and the surface of Venus differ in key regards (e.g. atmospheric composition, pressure, availability of oxidants), we argue that the mineral assemblages formed in these insulated environments are more relevant than most terrestrial analogs. These results identify high-temperature oxidation-driven cation redistribution as a process that should be evaluated further in experimental and analog studies and considered when interpreting spectroscopic results of future Venus missions.

abstract: Glacial landforms preserved on volcanoes of the Southern Chilean Andes record repeated glacier fluctuations through the Late Quaternary, yet the timing and regional coherence of these advances remain poorly constrained. Developing well-constrained chronologies across multiple volcanic edifices is critical for evaluating the response of mountain glaciers to Holocene climate variability and for assessing the influence of volcanic topography on glacier evolution. Here, we combine geomorphic mapping and cosmogenic 3 He exposure dating of moraine boulders to reconstruct glacier histories at Villarrica and Mocho-Choshuenco volcanoes. Exposure ages from 44 moraine boulders collected at Villarrica (n = 25) and Mocho-Choshuenco (n = 19) identify glacier advances during the Early Neoglacial, Little Ice Age, and post-Little Ice Age, while revealing both regionally consistent and spatially variable patterns of glacier behavior among neighboring volcanoes. Because active volcanic environments can modify moraine preservation, we integrate chronologies from different glacierized volcanoes to provide a more accurate regional framework for glacier-climate reconstructions. Together, these chronologies expand the network of Southern Hemisphere glacier records and provide new constraints on Holocene climate variability in the Southern Chilean Andes.

title: Hydrochemical Regimes and Substrate Influences on Hydrated Sulfate Assemblages at Devil’s Kitchen, Lassen Volcanic National Park: Implications for Paso Robles–Class Soils in Gusev Crater, Mars
session_title: Mineralogical Insights from Modern Spectroscopic Techniques
authors: Carman, Nancy Alejandra [1], McHenry, Lindsay J. [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA

abstract:
Paso Robles–class soils in the Columbia Hills of Gusev crater contain heterogeneous Fe 3+ -, Mg-, and Ca-sulfates, silica enrichment, and chemical signatures of local volcanic materials, consistent with acid-sulfate fumarolic or hydrothermal alteration. Since their original fluids are gone, it remains uncertain which aspects of acid generation, substrate leaching, oxidation, and water availability can be reconstructed from the preserved minerals. Devil’s Kitchen (DK), Lassen Volcanic National Park, is a steam-heated acid-sulfate system where oxidation of reduced sulfur generates acidity and promotes interaction with andesitic–dacitic substrate. We test whether sulfuric-acid input, substrate reaction, fluid availability, oxidation, and surface water loss generate contrasting mineral assemblages that preserve relative hydrochemical conditions.

We paired 2024–2025 field measurements and dissolved major-ion chemistry of fluids with X-ray diffraction and X-ray fluorescence analyses of precipitates, crusts, muds, and altered volcanic substrates. Waters ranged from dilute (pH 5.07; 78 mg/L sulfate) to acidic, solute-rich conditions (pH 2.27; 3443 mg/L sulfate; 30 mg/L dissolved Fe). At comparable temperatures, hot, dilute springs (pH 5.07–5.50; 89–90°C) were associated with silica polymorphs, kaolinite ± smectite, sulfur, pyrite, and alunite, consistent with dilute, substrate-dominated alteration. In contrast, an 84.1°C spring at pH 2.6 contained higher dissolved Ca, Mg, K, and Fe and occurred beside margin precipitates containing alunogen, gypsum, jarosite, pickeringite, quenstedtite, tamarugite, and voltaite. The co-occurrence of Al-, Ca-, Mg-, Na-, K-, and Fe-bearing sulfates, including Fe 3+ and mixed-valence (Fe 2+ /Fe 3+ ) phases, is consistent with access to rock-derived cations and spatially variable oxidation conditions. XRF showed that muds were depleted in CaO, MgO, Na 2 O, and K 2 O relative to the least-altered substrate. These observations support a conceptual leach-then-concentrate model in which sulfuric-acid alteration mobilizes rock-forming cations, followed by localized oxidation and water loss that promotes sulfate accumulation. Thus, the assemblages constrain relative acidity, cation availability, oxidation, and concentration, but not temperature or a unique parent-fluid composition.

DK provides a field-based analog for interpreting Paso Robles–class soils after the original fluids are gone. Their spatial heterogeneity may record localized sulfur and iron oxidation, substrate leaching, transient fluid flow, and concentration rather than a single equilibrium state, while contrasting Fe–Mg–Ca-rich and Al-rich expressions suggest substrate control on the mineralogical outcomes of comparable acid-sulfate processes.

title: The Chipman Dike Swarm in Canada’s Athabasca Granulite Terrane: A Field Example of Magmatic Intraplating in the Lower Crust

authors: Fleischer, Noah [1], Willaims, Michael L. [2], Dumond, Gregory [3], Sasso, Joseph [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, Barboursville, VA, USA

(3) Geosciences, Univ of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Geosciences, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(4) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract: Magmatic underplating and intraplating, the accumulation of magma beneath the crust and the intrusion of magma into the lower crust, are fundamental processes in evolution of continental crust. The Chipman dikes of the Athabasca Granulite Terrane represent an exceptional field example of magmatic intraplating. The basaltic dikes were emplaced into the Chipman tonalite batholith at ca. 1.9 Ga, along a minimum strike-length of 800 km. The Chipman tonalite experienced at least two deformation events, D1, characterized by a gently dipping S1 and D2, which developed during NW-SE shortening. D2 structures include (dextral) porphyroclasts, S-C and S-C-C’ fabrics, and isoclinal folds and a steeply dipping S2 foliation. The dikes are steeply dipping and NE-SW-striking and crosscut S1 and S2 in the tonalite. The oldest dikes are partially melted, have S2-concordant internal fabrics, lobate margins, and some are dismembered and/or folded. The youngest dikes are straight-sided, crosscut the partially melted dikes, and have a penetrative internal fabric (S2) subparallel to S2 in the tonalite. Previous U-Pb zircon dating of tonalite segregations formed during the partial melting of the oldest dikes indicates that anatexis was reached at ca. 1.9 Ga, the peak of D2. Previous thermobarometry indicates that metamorphic conditions during emplacement reached temperatures and pressures of 750-850°C and 1.0-1.2 GPa, respectively. Based on the ca. 1.9 Ga leucosome formation, the presence of S2 fabrics/D2 structures in the dikes, the crosscutting relations between the oldest and youngest dikes, and evidence of peak metamorphism during D2, the emplacement of the Chipman dikes was a progressive process syntectonic with D2. New mapping reveals at least one, but possibly multiple generations of ‘dikes’ that pre-date and are crosscut by the Chipman dikes. Some of these ‘dikes’ are concordant with the S1 enveloping surface and many are dismembered and/or partially digested in the Chipman tonalite. Diking and tonalite generation was likely episodic (and progressive during each episode). The partial melting of the earliest Chipman dikes provides a model for tonalite formation; multiple generations of dikes suggest multiple tonalite forming events. Multiple episodes of underplating and intraplating may have occurred in the same region of the lower crust, and tonalite formation may have occurred episodically there, perhaps for over 1 billion years or more.

title: Geologically Young and Future Landscapes: When to use Modern Topography to Anchor Paleogeographic Maps

abstract:
Creating images of ancient landscapes, such as in paleogeographic maps, typically affords great liberty regarding the exact extent of mountain ranges, deserts, seaways, and lakes; the path of ancient river systems; and the amount and density of vegetation. However, there is a point when these ancient landscapes incorporate still-existing landscape features. Not only do these geologically-young images require greater precision, they also give us the opportunity to use modern topography as a starting point for constructing such imagery.

We present a method for creating geologically recent and future landscape images that starts with a digital elevation model (DEM) of the modern topography. We illustrate this process using the late Neogene to Last Glacial Maximum of the Rocky Mountain region. These satellite-like images represent a snapshot from 800 mi (1300 km) above ground. Adobe Photoshop (or other image editing software) can be used with a modern DEM derived surface texture to either enhance or denude uplifts by using topography-textured brushes and beveling effects. Likewise, incision by rivers or glaciers can be exaggerated or reduced to modify the existing topography. This method both grounds the reconstruction in reality and provides immense flexibility to the user to modify the landscape according to geologic data. We also present the feasibility of sculpting these landscape changes in game design software such as Gaia and Unreal Engine 5. This method represents an update to the method of paleosatellite reconstruction developed by Petermann et al. 2024 for recent or future paleogeographic map reconstructions.

abstract: Radiation damage plays an important role in determining the kinetics of He diffusion in zircon. Previous work has developed a functional form that describes the damage-diffusivity relationship, which has been applied explaining trends between zircon (U-Th)/He dates and effective uranium (eU). Several lines of evidence, including laboratory step-degassing results and atomistic simulations, have shown that certain aspects of the functional form are inadequate and raise questions about the broader applicability of the currently widely used damage-diffusivity model in all natural settings. Here, we describe a new functional form and parameterization based on a multiple pathway approach that includes coefficients that allow for He to be exchanged between the pathways. As we show in this presentation, a multi-path model better reproduces behavior observed in laboratory step-degassing experiments, improves the fit of trends between individual kinetic parameters (activation energy and frequency factor) and damage. We also explore the consequences of this new model approach for interpreting the thermal history significance of zircon (U-Th)/He date-eU trends.

abstract:
The San Andreas fault (SAF) system has translated and reorganized numerous sedimentary basins across southern California, including Miocene non‑marine deposits preserved in the Cajon Pass and Mill Creek areas of the San Bernardino Mountains. These deposits occupy a structurally complex portion of the SAF system and may record aspects of their original depositional environments as well as subsequent strike‑slip transport of 160–310 km along the southern SAF. This study aims to establish the provenance and geochemistry of the Cajon Valley and Mill Creek formations by pairing sandstone modal point count analysis with X‑ray fluorescence (XRF) and X‑ray diffraction (XRD) analyses. These datasets provide independent constraints on evolving Miocene sediment sources and enable tests of potential correlations with other displaced units along the SAF system.

To evaluate provenance and compositional variability, we analyzed nine sandstone samples from Units 2, 3, and 5 of the Cajon Valley Formation and three samples from the Mill Creek Formation using >400‑point count modal petrography following the Gazzi-Dickinson method. Preliminary results show systematic relationships between our new modal data and published QFL datasets from other Miocene basins in southern California. Both formations plot within quartz–feldspar–lithic fields consistent with continental block provenance, and several potentially correlative units—including the Branch Canyon Sandstone, Santa Margarita, Punchbowl, Paradise Springs, and Vasquez formations—exhibit similar feldspathic compositions marked by nearly equal proportions of plagioclase and potassium feldspar.

Lithic fragment compositions, however, show more limited correspondence. Mill Creek samples contain lithic assemblages characteristic of continental block sources and lack sedimentary lithic fragments, similar to Vasquez Formation samples. In contrast, Cajon Valley samples contain lithic populations dominated by magmatic arc fragments, a pattern shared by only a few published samples from other formations. These differences likely reflect distinct sediment dispersal pathways and variable source‑area weathering histories, despite similarities in feldspar proportions. XRF and XRD data processing is underway and will be used to further refine interpretations.

title: Petrographic interpretation of a large medium-grained mafic enclave from Big Obsidian Flow, Newberry Volcano, Central Oregon
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Robledo, Luis David [1], Scruggs, Melissa A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS, USA
(2) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS,
abstract:
Newberry Volcano is the 13 th most hazardous volcano in the country, making it a very high threat to surrounding areas. In addition, its magmatic system is relatively unstudied compared to the other volcanoes in the Cascade Range. Mafic enclaves from the vent of Big Obsidian Flow (BOF) can tell us about deeper parts of Newberry's magma plumbing system where recharge magmas are likely stored. Linneman and Myers (1990) studied the BOF enclaves, but their hand samples could not be located and few thin sections were salvageable. New enclave samples were collected during Summer 2025 from the vent area of BOF, including the largest (~30cm) medium-grained enclave to date, enclave BOF-I-18.

We present bulk rock major and trace element and mineral compositions alongside a petrographic description of BOF-I-18 to evaluate whether this enclave represents a liquid, a crystal mush, or cumulates. BOF-I-18 displays a mixed intergranular to intersertal texture and is medium-grained. Vesicles (15%), glass (20%), and small crystals occupy the interstitial space throughout the thin section. The mineral assemblage identified in BOF-I-18 is: clinopyroxene, orthopyroxene, amphibole, plagioclase, olivine, and Fe-Ti oxides. Clinopyroxenes and orthopyroxenes display a range of euhedral to subhedral, granular and elongated prism shapes. Olivine shows a subhedral granular shape and does not show alteration. Amphibole in BOF-I-18 takes a euhedral shape and is a primary phase, rather than an alteration product. Some of the plagioclase crystals are tabular-shaped, with some zoning and rare resorbed cores. Fe-Ti oxides in BOF-I-18 all display a subhedral granular shape. Based on the petrographic textures and crystal morphologies, we suggest that enclave BOF-I-18 represents a disaggregated crystal mush instead of a liquid recharge magma. Different pattern and textures can be seen in other BOF enclaves, leading us to reconsider our understanding of enclave formation in the Newberry system.

abstract: Cretaceous mammals are important in the history of life as some of them survived the catastrophic end-Cretaceous extinction and are the ancestors of modern mammals. Recovery of a mammalian jawbone with differentiated dentition from the Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation at Baisch Dinosaur Ranch near Glendive, Montana, has led to an investigation into its identity and taxonomy. The jaw is a right ramus that is broken into four pieces, with 4 articulated teeth, two molars and two premolars. Comparison of anatomy of the specimen, and other established species of small Cretaceous mammals, as well as identification of key diagnostic features within the specimen will allow full description and identification of the fossil.

title: Normal Stress Controls on True Contact Area During High-Speed Fault Sliding in Granite: Implications for Fault Mechanics
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics
authors: Guerrero Bonnett, Santa [1], Chester, Frederick [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA
abstract: Faults zones accommodate deformation through complex interactions among asperities across multiple scales. The evolution of these contacts influences fault strength, slip localization, and weakening during earthquake rupture. Understanding how fault surface geometry and normal stress modify asperity-scale deformation is therefore important for linking laboratory observations with the mechanical behavior of natural faults. We conducted high-speed friction experiments on Westerly Granite using initially flat and grooved fault surfaces over a range of normal stresses representative of shallow crustal conditions. Infrared thermography was used to quantify the evolution of the true contact area by identifying and measuring millimeter-scale thermal anomalies associated with load-bearing asperity contacts during seismic-rate sliding. The results show that increasing normal stress increases the true contact area, while fault surface roughness strongly influences the spatial distribution of contacts. Flat surfaces exhibit larger, more uniformly distributed contact areas, whereas grooved surfaces localize deformation along asperity ridges, resulting in greater contact heterogeneity and enhanced frictional weakening. High-speed sliding also produces gouge (wear material), which preferentially accumulates within surface grooves, modifying asperity interactions and contributing to changes in frictional behavior and contact evolution. These observations demonstrate that fault surface geometry exerts an important control on asperity-scale contact evolution and provide new experimental constraints on the mechanical behavior of rough faults during earthquake slip.

authors: Webb, Lucy C. [1], Olson, Hunter C. [2], Thompson, Maya O. [3], Woltz, Christina R. [4], Simpson, Carl [5], Mills, Daniel B. [6], Sperling, Erik A. [7]

abstract: Multicellular eukaryotes including early animals evolved and diversified in the Neoproterozoic, however the driving mechanisms behind these evolutionary transitions remain unclear. Geologists often suggest that limiting oxygen and/or nutrient concentrations prevented the evolution of multicellular eukaryotes until their requirements were met, thus explaining the timing of these transitions. In contrast, biologists commonly emphasize the mechanisms that positively selected for multicellularity, such as deterring predation or more efficient nutrient usage. To evaluate long-term trends in productivity potentially linked to these evolutionary shifts, we used total organic carbon, nickel, copper, iron in pyrite, and phosphorus concentrations from >22,000 fine-grained siliciclastic samples spanning 2050–400 Ma. When binned by era, the median concentration of all proxies was significantly lower in the Neoproterozoic than the Mesoproterozoic and Paleozoic. Higher temporal resolution analyses indicate that productivity decreased at the start of Neoproterozoic and increased near the end. These results indicate that eukaryotic evolution at the start of the Neoproterozoic occurred in the context of limited food and nutrient availability while the late Neoproterozoic ecological flourishing of eukaryotic life occurred during a period of increased food availability.

title: Alluvial fan hazards: Current understanding with an eye to practice
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans

abstract: Alluvial fans are part of a continuum of features that can be present within a watershed and are found adjacent to many mountain locations throughout the United States. Numerous states and counties have mapped or are actively mapping alluvial fans. The contemporary appreciation of alluvial fans as part of the spectrum of geohazards places greater impetus on identifying, assessing processes, and understanding the associated flood hazards and risk present in these features. While this may appear to be rather straightforward, alluvial fans are complex features resulting from physical processes operating in the watershed, external factors (climate, tectonics, etc.) impacting the broader environmental context, and internal controls within the alluvial fan that often play a significant role in the flood hazards. These items and others have been consistently and increasingly studied by the scientific community over the past 50 years. Here, we present the current state of knowledge on watershed and alluvial fan relationships, surficial patterns and topographic controls, alluvial fan stratigraphy and its relation to alluvial fan evolution, external and internal controls on alluvial fan development, and the role of humans on modifying the processes operating on alluvial fans. This is done through a lens of properly identifying and assessing the alluvial fan processes and hazards with the goal of promoting more informed modeling, and better decision making at state, county, and local levels.

authors: Jenckes, Jordan [1], Russo, Aeon [2], Munk, Lee Ann [3], Munk, Jens [4], Boutt, David [5], Gabriel, Aidan [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Alaska, Anchorage, Anchorage, Alaska, USA

abstract: High‑latitude coastal watersheds are warming rapidly, accelerating glacier recession and shifting hydrologic regimes from snow to rain dominated systems. In glacierized basins, permeable glaciofluvial deltas create dynamic pathways linking upland weathering, meltwater streams, and shallow coastal groundwater, yet these seasonal and interannual exchanges remain poorly resolved due to limited high‑frequency, multi‑season datasets. To address this gap, we integrate multidecadal climatic records with a long-term, high-frequency, multi-season dataset of specific conductance, stream discharge, and groundwater levels to perform event‑scale hysteresis analyses, alongside geochemical data including stable water isotopes (δ²H, δ¹⁸O) and major and trace elements (Mg²⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, HCO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻, Cl⁻, SiO₂). Seasonally, evolving hydraulic gradients reorganize groundwater–surface water exchange between the meltwater stream and adjacent shallow (1–2 m) groundwater from groundwater-supported baseflow during early spring to a losing-stream system as glacier melt intensifies, to bidirectional exchange during peak melt and autumn rainfall. These transitions are expressed by clockwise stream and counter-clockwise groundwater hysteresis during early melt, narrowing hysteresis during midsummer, and mixed hysteresis during late-season. Corresponding geochemical responses evolve from early-season solute flushing to midsummer dilution as runoff shifts from proximal snowmelt to distal snow and glacier melt, followed by late-season mobilization of weathering-derived solutes despite continued meltwater dilution. Interannually, snow‑rich years exhibit depleted δ¹⁸O and pronounced early‑season solute flushing, whereas rain‑dominated years show elevated HCO₃⁻, SiO₂ concentrations associated with late-season carbonate weathering, indicating groundwater flowpaths and weathering processes are strongly hydroclimate dependent. Despite contrasting hydroclimates, persistent Cl- enrichment in both the stream and groundwater suggests that sustained glacier-fed aquifer recharge moderates short-term hydroclimatic variability. Together, these observations indicate that hydroclimate controls not only the magnitude of meltwater input, but also the groundwater flowpaths and residence times that regulate weathering-derived solute transport across the watershed. Beyond confirming groundwater-surfacewater connectivity, this study resolves how hydroclimate shapes groundwater flow paths, thus altering the timing, direction, and geochemical processes of that connectivity across seasonal and interannual timescales. These findings establish a framework for predicting how continued glacier recession and the transition towards rain-dominated hydrologic regimes will alter groundwater flowpaths, groundwater-surface water exchange, and downstream solute export across rapidly warming subarctic coastal watersheds.

abstract:
Important aspects of displacement history on the San Andreas fault (SAF) system remain poorly constrained because correlations among sedimentary units and their provenance are uncertain. Numerous Miocene sedimentary basins have formed along the SAF and were subsequently displaced and dismembered by strands of the fault, complicating efforts to reconstruct their original positions and sediment pathways. One such basin contains the Cajon Valley Formation, which is exposed along fault slivers within the Cajon Pass area of the San Bernardino Mountains. Although this formation superficially resembles other SAF-adjacent Miocene units, its provenance and potential ties to displaced basins remains unresolved.

This project has two complementary objectives. First, we examine clast compositions in the early to middle Miocene Cajon Valley Formation to evaluate how its lithologic assemblages compare with published clast data from other Miocene basin deposits across central and southern California. Second, we test whether younger deposits in the Mecca Hills region—proximal to the Orocopia Mountains, a proposed source terrane for the middle Miocene Punchbowl Formation, Mill Creek Formation, and Potato Sandstone—record provenance signatures consistent with those older units.

Clast compositional data were collected from four sites in the Cajon Valley Formation and from the upper Palm Springs Formation and Ocotillo Formation in the Mecca Hills. Counts were conducted using the area method, tallying all clasts above >2 cm within a 1 m 2 grid. Additionally, long and short axes for clasts were measured. These new datasets are compared with published clast counts from Miocene units spanning the SAF system from the San Gorgonio Pass to west of Tejon Pass, including the Potato Sandstone and Mill Creek, Punchbowl, Mint Canyon, Tick Canyon, and Caliente formations.

Preliminary results indicate that the Cajon Valley Formation is dominated by granitoid clasts and lacks gneiss, unlike the other formations which contain higher proportions of gneiss and volcanicss. The Punchbowl, Mill Creek, and Potato Sandstone have abundant schist similar to the Palm Springs Formation and Ocotillo fans potentially tying these deposits to a source near the Orocopias. Comparisons with published clast count data are in progress.

Together, these analyses will strengthen constraints on the provenance of early to middle Miocene units displaced by the SAF and provide new opportunities to refine long-term reconstructions of basin evolution and cumulative strike-slip displacement.

title: Nonmarine Facies Analysis and Refined Chronostratigraphy for Campanian-Maastrichtian Formations in Central Wyoming and Implications for Paleobiogeography and Biostratigraphy of Laramidia

authors: Tenney, Zachary David [1], McElroy, Brandon [2], Currano, Ellen [3], Slattery, Joshua S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA; Geology & Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA

(3) Geology & Geophysics/Botany, University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA

abstract:
The Upper Cretaceous of the Western Interior of North America (Laramidia) is among the most fossiliferous and well-studied stratigraphic sequences in the world. During the Campanian and Maastrichtian, Laramidia contained diverse northern and southern biomes, but few studies have examined the transition zone between biotas in central Laramidia. Numerous fossiliferous nonmarine formations occur within Wyoming during this critical period and region. This study examines three questions: 1) What is the depositional system?, 2) What is the age of these units?, and 3) What is the potential for significant paleontological advances? Over 5,000 meters of lithostratigraphic sections were measured in the Mesaverde, Meeteetse, and Lance Formations with new fossil collections made throughout the sequence.

The typical depositional sequence throughout the Upper Cretaceous is offshore marine shale transitioning to deltaic and/or shoreface deposits, followed by paralic or delta plain carbonaceous shale, with coastal plain to fluvial plain channel sandstone and overbank mudstone deposits capping the sequence. Using ammonite biostratigraphy, the middle member of the Mesaverde Formation was constrained to the Baculites reduncus biochron (77.2 – 76.5 Ma). Peak extent of the Meeteetse Formation occurred in the Baculites baculus biochron (72.3 – 71.5 Ma). The Lance Formation likely represents four million years of deposition (66.9 – 66.0 Ma) in the Powder River Basin, based on Baculties clinolobatus occurring near the base with the K/Pg boundary at the top. Vertebrate fossils were relatively common within both the Mesaverde and Lance Formations with numerous new localities discovered. The Campanian and Maastrichtian deposits have significant potential to contain key fossils for advancing paleobiogeographic and stratigraphic studies of Laramidia. In conclusion, Wyoming has significant potential for paleontological and stratigraphic work to improve our understanding of Late Cretaceous ecosystems during the period of peak dinosaurian diversity and leading up to the K/Pg mass extinction.

title: Establishing the Geo-PAD Consortium: Scaling Successful Undergraduate-to-Graduate Pathways in the Geosciences
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Kar, Aditya [1], Brudzinski, Mike [2], McLeod, Claire [3], Malin, Joel [4]
affiliations: (1) Natural & Computational Sciences, Fort Valley State University, Fort Valley, Georgia, USA
(2) Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA

abstract:
The Geoscience Pathways to Advanced Degrees (Geo-PAD) initiative establishes a multi-institutional consortium co-led by Fort Valley State University (an undergraduate HBCU) and Miami University (a graduate research institution). Geo-PAD addresses projected national shortfalls of technical geoscientists and growing workforce demands in critical minerals, energy, and data science by scaling an established interinstitutional bridge model.

This initiative builds on the success of FVSU’s GEOPAths program, which has introduced over 50 students to the geosciences through summer research, paid internships, multi-faceted mentoring, and a newly established geology minor. However, despite accelerated undergraduate engagement, only 20% of these graduates historically matriculated into geoscience graduate programs. Qualitative observations reveal persistent systemic barriers: lack of awareness regarding graduate funding (tuition waivers and stipends), misconceptions about independent research, self-doubt regarding academic preparation, and familial financial pressure to enter the workforce immediately after college.

A recent pilot partnership between FVSU and Miami University directly targeted these obstacles. For example, an FVSU Biology major with a Geology minor completed an EarthScope summer internship, transitioned into Miami’s graduate program, earned an M.S. in two years, and is now employed as a geophysicist at a Fortune 500 energy company. While this pilot proves feasibility, the specific institutional and psychological factors that optimize student transitions require systematic evaluation.

During its planning phase, the Geo-PAD Consortium brings together higher education institutions, technical internship providers, professional societies, and industry partners to build a collaborative Community of Practice. Grounded in Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT), the project investigates the key drivers of graduate school motivation among students entering the geosciences from non-traditional pathways. Through regular interinstitutional convenings, shared resource networks, and collaborative advising, Geo-PAD systematically evaluates the combined impacts of structured mentoring, hands-on research, targeted financial support, and professional socialization. Ultimately, Geo-PAD aims to co-develop a scalable, transferable framework that broadens participation and prepares a diverse, workforce-ready generation of geoscientists.

abstract:
Northwestern Nevada preserves an extensive belt of Cretaceous plutons that span a critical, yet poorly studied ~400 km gap between the Sierra Nevada and Idaho batholiths. Emplacement history, magma sources, and tectonomagmatic evolution of these Nevada plutons are poorly constrained, limiting our understanding of along-strike variations in magmatism between arc segments with contrasting ages, compositions, and lithospheric architectures. This study presents an initial petrologic and geochemical investigation of Cretaceous granitoids emplaced within the Black Rock arc terrane in the Pine Forest Range (PFR) of northwestern Nevada.

The northern PFR contains the zoned Mahogany Mountain plutonic complex (MMPC; ca. 115-104 Ma; U-Pb zircon). The outer MMPC contains the older (ca. 115-110 Ma), more mafic Black Mountain, Cold Spring, and Lone Mountain phases, which display well-developed mylonitic fabrics recording dip-slip syn-plutonic deformation. These intrusions comprise a heterogeneous assemblage of hornblende gabbros, quartz diorites, quartz monozodiorites, and monzonites, with minor leucogranite. The internal Thacker Canyon and Rattlesnake Spring phases are younger (ca. 108-106 Ma) and more homogeneous biotite hornblende granodiorites to quartz monzodiorites. The MMPC core is occupied by the youngest (ca. 105 Ma) Mahogany Mountain phase, a leucocratic two-mica granite with minor garnet and orthoclase megacrysts. The central PFR, in contrast, is underlain by the voluminous Duffer Peak pluton (DPP; ca. 104 Ma), which consists of a uniformly coarse-grained, leucocratic biotite granodiorite to granite with locally abundant orthoclase megacrysts.

Bulk rock geochemistry reveals that PFR intrusions are predominantly magnesian, calc-alkalic granitoids with arc signatures defined by LILE enrichments and HFSE depletions. Within the MMPC, compositions evolve from more mafic and metaluminous granitoids in the outer zones to a felsic, peraluminous granitoid within the core. Although each phase exhibits compositional heterogeneity, the MMPC intrusions consistently contain high Sr (389-856 ppm) and Ba (487-1998 ppm), low Rb/Sr ratios (0.05- 0.28), elevated Sr/Y ratios (~20-160), and steep REE patterns (La N /Yb N = 8-30) with pronounced HREE depletions and minor positive to negative Eu/Eu* anomalies. The DPP shares similar geochemical characteristics to the Mahogany Mountain phase, but lacks the zoning of the MMPC. These geochemical patterns are consistent with a petrogenetic model involving partial melting of deep crustal sources in equilibrium with feldspar-poor, garnet-, clinopyroxene-, and amphibole-rich residues; however, this preliminary interpretation is being evaluated alongside alternative models.

title: Spatially Variable Thermal Evolution of the Northern Klamath Mountains During Siletzia Collision: Insights from Multi-Thermochronometry

(3) Cal Poly Humboldt, Arcata, CA,

abstract:
The Klamath Mountains Province (KMP) lies within the North American Cordillera and is a series of Paleozoic-Mesozoic accreted terranes intruded by Jurassic-Cretaceous plutons. The northern KMP (NKMP) preserves a record of Cretaceous forearc basin development followed by the early Eocene collision of the Siletzia terrane. However, the extent to which Siletzia collision influenced burial, deformation, and exhumation across the NKMP remains poorly constrained. We combine bedrock and detrital zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe; closure temperature, Tc = ~200–150°C), apatite fission track (AFT; Tc = ~110°C), and apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe; Tc = ~90–45°C) thermochronology to constrain the timing and spatial patterns of burial and exhumation across the dextral-oblique Canyonville and Valen Lake thrust fault systems.

NKMP ZHe dates (132–85 Ma) record widespread Early to Late Cretaceous reheating to ~200°C followed by cooling, consistent with regional-scale basin subsidence and inversion. The Canyonville fault records syn-collisional transpressive motion associated with Siletzia accretion, as indicated by displacement of the Umpqua Group (~52–49 Ma), but not the overlying Tyee Formation (~48–46 Ma). Eocene (46 Ma) AFT results suggest rapid cooling north of the Canyonville fault consistent with erosional exhumation of significant orogenic topography in the NKMP. These cooling ages are compatible with recent detrital zircon provenance studies indicating that erosion of the NKMP supplied sediment to the Umpqua Group. By deposition of the Tyee Formation, topographic relief was diminished sufficiently to permit sediment transport across the NKMP from extraregional sources like the Idaho batholith.

In contrast to rapid Eocene cooling north of the Canyonville fault, ZHe and structural data farther south in the footwall of the Valen Lake thrust support tectonic burial driven by Siletzia collision, reheating, and structural thickening of the Late Cretaceous Dothan Formation. Field observations of isoclinal folding and prehnite-pumpellyite facies metamorphism further support burial to temperatures exceeding ~200°C. Oligo-Miocene AFT ages support a switch from reheating and contraction to cooling and extension along the western margin of the NKMP. Across both fault systems, Miocene AHe dates indicate regional cooling. Together, these data suggest that Siletzia collision produced spatially variable burial and exhumation across the NKMP, with structural burial concentrated west of the Valen Lake fault and rapid syn-collisional cooling north of the Canyonville fault, followed by regional Oligo–Miocene exhumation via extension.

title: Plutonic Lithic Fragments as Records of Crystal Mush Processes in the Ohakuri Caldera Magma System, Taupō Volcanic Zone, New Zealand
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Acosta, Delilah [1], Anderson, Henry [2], Cummings, Kenna [3], Smithies, Sarah [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Macalester College, Saint Paul, MN, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Whitman College, Walla Walla, WA, USA
(3) Syracuse University Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Syracuse, Syracuse, NY, USA

abstract:
The Taupō Volcanic Zone (TVZ) in New Zealand is one of the most active silicic volcanic systems, yet the exact structure of the crustal magma plumbing systems and processes that drive eruptive behavior remain debated. In this project, we investigate the magmatic system beneath the Ohakuri Caldera, which, together with the Rotorua Caldera, evacuated >245 km3 of rhyolitic magma in the paired Ohakuri and Mamaku eruptions at 240 ka.

To investigate the Ohakuri magmatic system, we examine plutonic lithics entrained in the eruption. We interpret these as erupted mush fragments, providing direct samples of these otherwise inaccessible mush chambers. Petrographic observations, back-scatter electron and energy dispersive spectroscopy scanning electron microscope analysis of three lithic samples reveal amphibole and glass-bearing granophyric granitoids with preserved cross-cutting textures that reveal at least two distinct crystallization events. The first stage includes crystallization of plagioclase and quartz followed by quartz-feldspar granophyre produced during relatively rapid crystallization of melt within magma chambers under varying cooling conditions. Late-stage textures include interstitial glass and melt pockets of fine-grained amphibole, biotite, pyroxene and opaque minerals within cross-cutting fractures, indicating continued melt movement after initial framework formation. Preliminary amphibole barometry indicates a crystallization event at 180-200 MPa (~7 km depth).

Granophyre and glass coexistence indicates at least two cooling events. Cross cutting interstitial glass suggests a compositionally distinct melt mobilization event during late stage crystallization, occupying fractures through granophyric textures. This is consistent with previous studies discussing vertically extensive chambers beneath the Ohakuri caldera. Interstitial glass compositions differ from those of glass found in pumice from the Ohakuri ignimbrite, indicating that our juvenile melt is of a different type and may have quenched separately from the melt that was erupted. These results suggest a dynamic and interconnected magma system in which crystal-rich chambers undergo crystallization and melt migration prior.

title: Shocked, granular quartzose clasts from Wetumpka impact structure, Alabama
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: King, David T [1], Beardsley, Lucille W. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama, USA
(2) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama, USA
abstract: An unusual type of shocked, granular quartzose clast is found within the central breccia unit at Wetumpka impact structure, Elmore County, Alabama. This type of clast has a peculiar, homogenous granular texture and an exterior surface that is marked by curvilinear rills that distinguish these clasts from other kinds of Wetumpka quartzone clasts in the central breccia unit that have been found also to have shock effects within them. Thin-section analysis of these granular shocked quartzose clasts show that they consist almost entirely of intensively shocked quartz granules, i.e., grains in the granule size range with internal domains of pervasive, decorated PDFs that have multiple orientations. In addition, toasting, undulose extinction, feather features, and dark splotches are also common among the quartz granules comprising these impact-affected rocks. Wetumpka’s shocked granular clasts are generally limited to sizes in the range of 10 to 15 cm in longest dimension. The surface of the shocked granular clasts are characterized by curvilinear rills of less than 1 cm in depth. The rills are wider at the surface than at depth in the clasts, which suggests an origin by radial expansion. The clasts are irregularly shaped but tend to have at least one large surface that is roughly convex. This also suggests an origin by radial expansion, and infers that individual clasts may have been fragments of larger granular quartzose masses. Petrographic observation of the granular quartzose clasts shows that they are pervasively shocked, i.e., dozens of sets of decorated PDFs with various orientations cover nearly the entirety of each thin section. PDFs are mainly {10-12} and {10-13}, but there are some higher angle PDFs as well. In most instances, the PDFs of each quartz grain persist up to the boundary with the adjacent quartz grain, but in some instances, an ultra-fine microbreccia occurs at the granular boundary. This suggests at the actual impactite rock-forming process may have been post-shock, or occurred in part after the main shock event was subsiding.

title: Pint-sized Paleontology: Using Biosediments to Understand Seafloor Diversity and Significant Horizons in the Silurian Rockwood Formation, Tennessee, USA
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology (Posters)
authors: Pruett, Ariel E. [1], Clement, Annaka M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Geology, and Environmental Science, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, Chattanooga, TN, USA
(2) Biology, Geology, and Environmental Science, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, Chattanooga, TN, USA
abstract: The diversity and preservation of biosediments provide insight into both the broader paleoecology and near-seafloor geochemical conditions of fossiliferous deposits. The carbonate beds of the Silurian Rockwood Formation in southeastern Tennessee preserve an array of invertebrate and potentially vertebrate biosediments. Biosediments were extracted from bulk rock limestone at six horizons below the contact with the overlying Fort Payne Formation at a well-exposed section north of Chattanooga, Tennessee. Bulk rock samples were digested in a 5% buffered acetic acid solution to disaggregate the biosediment grains. The resulting residue was sieved into size fractionations. In this study the 1 mm to 250 µm size fraction was picked for the first two hundred biosediments encountered. Preliminary results indicate that the majority of biosediments reflect the content of the macrofossils, including brachiopods, crinoids, bryozoans, and gastropods. Biosediments also revealed the presence of ostracods, echinoids, and potentially fish. Two horizons also displayed abundant phosphatization of biosediments (50% and 98% of originally carbonate fossils). It is notable that bryozoan biosediments were highly abundant in non-phosphatized samples and rare in phosphatized samples. While fossil accumulations were common at the tops of carbonate storm beds in this interval, phosphatization was not common. Increased levels of phosphatization can indicate lowered pH, fluctuating oxygen levels, and/or stratigraphic condensation. This agrees with periodic deposition of both ironstones and black shales to the north and south of the field site in the Silurian, both of which invoke fluctuating oxygenation of the seafloor. Ongoing work will address the utility of biosediments in recognizing the onset of these conditions as well as integrating the broader sequence stratigraphy of the Rockwood Formation in Tennessee into frameworks from the Appalachian Basin, northern Alabama, and Georgia.

abstract: El origen del magmatismo del Jurásico Inferior-Medio en el noreste de México ha sido objeto de debate en los últimos años. Los modelos clásicos lo relacionan con un ambiente de subducción, mientras que otras interpretaciones proponen su desarrollo en un contexto de rift continental. En este trabajo se presentan nuevos datos de geoquímica de roca total, geocronología U-Pb, isótopos de Hf y elementos traza en granos individuales de circón procedentes de rocas volcánicas recolectadas en diversas localidades de Zacatecas, Coahuila y Durango. Las edades U-Pb en circones varían entre 177 y 163 Ma, lo que confirma que la actividad magmática registrada en el área de estudio se extendió desde el Jurásico Temprano hasta el Jurásico Medio. La geoquímica de roca total indica que los magmas poseen carácter predominantemente peraluminoso, evidenciando una participación cortical importante en la generación del magmatismo. Los circones de la mayoría de las localidades analizadas presentan valores de εHf predominantemente negativos, con excepción de una de ellas que posee valores principalmente positivos. Esta variabilidad isotópica sugiere la participación de fuentes magmáticas heterogéneas, que incluyen componentes corticales evolucionados y aportes juveniles. En conjunto, los resultados indican que este magmatismo tuvo diferentes fuentes, tanto corticales como juveniles, en un ambiente tectónico extensional. Financiamiento PAPIIT16101026.

abstract: The Jackson Dome in Jackson, Mississippi and the Midnight Volcano in Southern Humphrey’s County, Mississippi are two Cretaceous-aged volcanic centers buried beneath approximately 2,000-3,000 feet of Cenozoic sediments. Direct drilling to collect samples has not been completed since the late 1930s and early 1940s due to not being economically feasible because of the thick sedimentary cover, so there is a considerable lack of geologic data on the volcanoes in the region. Through this research, we hope to constrain the origins and eruptive history of both the Jackson Dome and Midnight Volcano to better understand the volcanic landscape of Mississippi during the Cretaceous period. One sample each from both volcanic centers will undergo acid digestion, clean-laboratory column chemistry, and ICP-MS analysis to determine their elemental and Sm-Nd, Pb-Pb, and Rb-Sr isotopic compositions. The resulting geochemical data will then be compared with data from well-known volcanic provinces such as Yellowstone, Hawaiian Islands, Galápagos Islands, Canary Islands, and Iceland. The comparison of these results allows us to evaluate whether the Mississippi volcanics are most consistent with a continental rift, a subduction zone, or an intraplate hotspot origin.

title: Geomorphic and Hydrologic Controls on Localized Meander Migration Along the Rio Grande in Colorado's San Luis Valley
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Pieper, Nicholas [1], Carr, Hayden [2], Pacheco, Augustine [3], Atencio, Tytus [4], Lahiri, Chayan [5]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Adams State Universtiy, Alamosa, Colorado, USA

abstract:
Understanding why some meander bends migrate while adjacent bends remain relatively stable is important for improving our understanding of river evolution and identifying reaches that may be more susceptible to future channel adjustment. This study focuses on an approximately 10-km reach of the Rio Grande within the Rio Grande State Wildlife Area in Colorado's San Luis Valley. This relatively undisturbed reach provides an opportunity to investigate meander migration under conditions with limited direct human influence. Historical aerial imagery indicates that one meander bend has undergone measurable migration over recent decades, whereas adjacent bends have remained comparatively stable. This study investigates the geomorphic and hydrologic factors associated with this contrasting behavior.

The objectives of this study are to quantify the magnitude and rate of meander migration using historical aerial imagery and to evaluate characteristics associated with the observed channel adjustment. Analyses will incorporate historical aerial imagery, LiDAR-derived topography, and long-term streamflow records to examine floodplain relief, slope, geometry, abandoned channels, and discharge variability. Bank sediment characteristics, subsurface geology, and bank strength are recognized as potentially important controls but are beyond the scope of the present study and represent opportunities for future field investigations.

By comparing the migrating bend with adjacent stable reaches, this study seeks to identify measurable geomorphic and hydrologic characteristics associated with localized meander migration. The results are expected to improve our understanding of channel evolution in relatively undisturbed alluvial rivers and may provide a framework for identifying river reaches with greater susceptibility to future channel adjustment, thereby supporting river management, restoration planning, and assessments of channel stability in similar fluvial systems.

abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are subject to atmospheric transport and subsequent wet deposition, providing a potential pathway for their transfer to surface-water systems and groundwater recharge zones. However, variations in PFAS concentration and composition profiles among the precipitation events remain poorly understood. This study investigated PFAS in 15 precipitation samples collected during eight winter and summer events in San Antonio, Texas. Twenty-three PFAS compounds were quantified using triple quadrupole liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC/MS-MS) following the EPA 533 method, and variations in total PFAS concentrations and chain-length compositions were evaluated. Results reveal that total PFAS concentrations varied substantially among precipitation events, ranging from 2.36 to 86.60 ng/L. Among the sampled events in 2022 and 2023, winter precipitation exhibited comparatively moderate concentrations and relatively balanced short- and long-chain profiles. In contrast, summer samples showed greater variability in both concentration and composition. Several summer precipitation samples were characterized by increased contributions from long-chain compounds, with the highest contribution (up to 77%) observed during the June 5 event. Preliminary HYSPLIT back-trajectory analysis revealed contrasting marine and continental transport pathways among the sampled events. These findings demonstrate pronounced event-scale variability in PFAS occurrence in precipitation, suggesting that the atmospheric transport pathway may influence PFAS concentrations and compositional profiles in south-central Texas

abstract:
The Waterman Canyon fault (WCF) is a westerly striking Quaternary active fault in the San Bernardino Mountains (SBM) that appears to splay from the San Andreas fault (SAF) about 10 km ESE of its junction with the San Jacinto fault. Its close proximity to California State Water Project facilities in Devil Canyon was the motivation for this study. We conducted desktop mapping with LiDAR and aerial imagery, detailed field mapping, roadcut and backhoe exposure logging, soil analysis in hand dug pits, geomorphic analyses, and IRSL dating of 14 samples from Quaternary deposits to characterize late Quaternary fault activity.

In Devil Canyon, the WCF is composed of three left-stepping, en-echelon strands, and to the west bifurcates with the NW-striking northern branch apparently the most active since the latest Pleistocene. The WCF has ruptured multiple times since c. 31 – 35 ka, and the most recent surface rupturing earthquake may be as young as latest Holocene based on an age of 4.88 ± 0.33 ka from a thick, cumulic A horizon that appears to be displaced. The WCF accommodates right-lateral strike-slip with a subordinate component of up-to-the-south dip-slip displacement. Available data does not allow a net slip rate estimate. However, detailed geomorphic analysis and new geochronological constraints allow us to constrain a local vertical-separation rate of ~0.2 – 0.4 mm/yr since c. 31 ka.

IRSL ages of coarse alluvial fan deposits (Qyf, Qof, and Qvof) range from about 10 to 65 ka within Devil Canyon. Relict Qyf surfaces, constrained between ages of 9.58 ± 0.7 ka and 4.88 ± 0.33 ka, appear to grade to a common Devil Canyon paleo-valley floor. This early to middle Holocene aggradation was followed by a major pulse of late Holocene incision that created the deeply incised canyons and drainages in the watershed. This rapid incision provided many of the exposures in Quaternary sediments exploited for dating in this study.

title: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum within Terrestrial North America: A New Framework for the Golden Valley Formation, Williston Basin, North Dakota
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Blount, James Douglass [1], Beverly, Emily Jane [2], Riley, Jack W. H. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

abstract:
The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) (~56 Ma), a ~200,000-year long hyperthermal, and the subsequent Eocene Climatic Optimum (54-49 Ma) lie within the Bear Den Member and Camels Butte Member of the Golden Valley Formation in the Williston Basin, ND. The early Eocene has been of interest due to its analogous conditions to present day climate change, where an overall warm climate saw rapid increases in pCO2 and temperature. The Golden Valley Formation is exposed in buttes across western North Dakota, where the characteristic “orange zone” and tri-color weathering pattern sits conformably atop the upper Paleocene (Sentinel Butte Formation). Research on the formation spans 50 years, with previous efforts focused on clay mineralogy, paleobotany, reconstruction of the paleoclimate during the PETM, and detrital zircon geochronology of sandstones. This study focused on revisiting previous sites within the literature, which are classified as channel and inter-channel depositional environments. We expand on the previous characterizations of the units, notably the siltstones and claystones. Previous literature identifies paleosols (fossilized or buried soils) but detailed paleosol characterizations are needed.

Sampling occurred during the Summer of 2026, at three localities: 1) Murray Ranch (MR), 2) South Killdeer Mountains (SKDM), and 3) Twin Buttes (TB), which form a 70 km west to east transect. The localities were trenched, measured, and sampled, with a 15 to 20 m thick exposure containing the upper Sentinel Butte Formation through Camels Butte Member. Color, texture, horizon, and fossil occurrence were documented and samples for particle size, bulk geochemistry, clay mineralogy, and magnetostratigraphy were collected at each site. Preliminary results identified one paleosol in the upper Sentinel Butte Formation and up to eight paleosols in the early Eocene Camels Butte and Bear Den Members. Paleosol thickness varied (0.2 - 2.0 m) across the sites, with thicker paleosols appearing in the furthest east TB site. We have identified paleo-Vertisols and paleo-Oxisols across all three localities, but the paleosols are not laterally continuous across the basin. Future study in the Williston Basin will compare the Paleogene paleoenvironments to other Laramide Basins and utilize the new paleoclimate record of the early Eocene’s hyperthermals to understand anthropogenic climate change.

title: Patterns of faunal change and stability in the Middle Devonian across eastern Laurentia: Evidence for coordinated depletions, extirpations, and invasions of benthic faunas during a late Eifelian (~392–388 Ma) interval of climatic volatility
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Welych-Flanagan, Martin [1], Brett, Carlton E. [2], Van Tassel, Thomas Robert [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH,
(2) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH,
(3) University of Cincinnati, Chatham, NY,
abstract: Reanalysis of Middle Devonian faunal data from the vicinity of the Findlay Arch in central Ohio within an updated stratigraphic and basinal framework show corresponding patterns to the proximal Appalachian foreland Basin (NY and PA), which together provide new insights into evolutionary paleoecology during the late Eifelian Age. Similarity in composition of relatively stable biotas and in the timing of faunal turnovers provides strong evidence for the continuity of two Ecological-Evolutionary Subunits (EESUs) across this area, the Onondaga and Hamilton faunas of EESUs D-5 and D-7. New litho- and biostratigraphic study suggests that the absence of the intervening Stony Hollow Fauna of EESU D-6 in Ohio is due to a late Eifelian unconformity, perhaps associated with the incipient uplift of the Findlay Arch. Detailed study of the lower Delaware Formation (upper Eifelian) indicates a period of loss of Onondaga Fauna biodiversity with no commensurate replacement during the Tortodus australis conodont biochron, probably associated with the deepening and widespread anoxia of the Bakoven Event, creating a depleted “Delaware-Bakoven Fauna” (EESU D-5B). The warming-associated Stony Hollow Event ( Tortodus kockelianus-Polygnathus eiflius conodont biochrons) consisted of the wholesale invasion of warm water Old World Realm (OWR) Cordilleran Province faunas and outage of a majority of Eastern Americas Realm (EAR) taxa across eastern Laurentia. However, revised stratigraphic study suggests the occurrence of a third bioevent in the Pol. eiflius to early Pol. ensensis biochron, possibly associated with the “lower Kačák” or otomari Event known from other regions, consisting of the extirpation of the entire OWR Stony Hollow fauna and a return of the EAR fauna. During the latest Eifelian to earliest Givetian these recurrent EAR faunas were integrated with temperate-adapted OWR Rhenish-Bohemian faunas including Tropidoleptus , several spiriferid brachiopods, and several mollusks during upper Kačák event, establishing the “Hamilton fauna” of EESU D-7. This updated chronology of bioevents indicate the complex and volatile conditions of the late Eifelian-early Givetian interval. Moreover, mass invasions, extirpations, and the return of suites of taxa following prolonged (sometimes over 1 my) outages indicates the major role of coordinated migrations controlled by shifting climatic gradients.

title: What's A Fake Fossil? The Problem Of Authenticity In Paleontology
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Fulgenzi, Reese [1]
affiliations: (1) CEVIHE/Department of History, Tufts University, Somerville, MA, USA
abstract: Fossils, evidence of past life on earth, have been collected, altered, valued, and exchanged for centuries. This talk traces evolving notions of what constitutes an inauthentic fossil, and suggests a typology that captures the spectrum of fossil inauthenticity. By tracing historical understandings of fossil authenticity--what makes a fossil authentic or inauthentic--I show that practices of casting, reconstruction, compositing, and reinterpretation make inauthenticity intrinsic to how paleontology produces and circulates knowledge. I propose a spectrum of fossil authenticity to capture the nuance of paleontological practice and circulation. Casts, reconstructions, and composites are constitutive of how fossils circulate, and thus of the production of paleontological knowledge more broadly. These practices have historically shaped exchanges among scientists, commercial actors, museums, and the public, and continue to do so today.

title: Shash bi Jaa' (The Bear's Ears): It's Time to Protect the Bear
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Williams, Louis D. [1]
affiliations: (1) Ancient Wayves River and Hiking Adventures, Blanding, UT,
abstract:
The Bear’s Ears (Shash bi Jaa’), is a place of geological wonder, exquisite beauty and rich cultural value. Located within the Bears Ears National Monument in southeast Utah just north of the San Juan River, sitting atop the “Monument Upwarp”, are where the two buttes known as the Bear’s Ears are located. This region is the ancestral lands to the Ute, Paiute, Dine and many Pueblo groups such as the Hopi and Zuni. Chief Manuelito, a leader of the Dine in the 1800s, was born in the Bear’s Ears region (a short distance east of the Bear’s Ears buttes).

The ancestral lands of the Bears Ears region have seen past mining operations from different eras. The Honaker Trail constructed in the late 1800s provides evidence of the gold-rush era. Abandoned structures from the period of oil exploration and extraction (early 1900s) are evident along the San Juan river. Many roads we travel in this region were constructed during the era of uranium extraction, such as the Moki Dugway. As a guide in this region, I get to see all this history every time I’m out there on the trails or the river.

As a native tour guide in this region, I’m able to share all this great outdoor classroom has to offer and promote the protection of the place. We respectfully visit ancestral sites that were inhabited roughly 1000 ya. The lands within the BENM are delicate. Cryptobiotic soil throughout the region is important to this semi-arid landscape, providing nourishment to the high-desert soil. Delicate habitats of native plants that we utilize for medicine and other uses keep us on the trails. We don’t want to disturb those unique and irreplaceable habitats.

The Bears Ears region is a place rich with Geoheritage. The Bear is known to be a protector in the Dine culture as we personify this special place. A place where our ancestors sang songs, hunted, gathered medicine, prayed and raised families. It is time we protect this sacred place.

title: Variability of pre-vegetation fluvial style on a tectonically stable craton: the Cambrian Jangsan Formation, eastern Sino-Korean Craton
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Kang, Donghyeok [1], Galeazzi, Cristiano Padalino [2], Woo, Jusun [3]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Data Innovation in Science, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
(2) State Key Laboratory of Oil and Gas Reservoir Geology, Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu, China
(3) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract: Pre-vegetation rivers are now known to have spanned a broad range of styles, yet the conditions that governed this variability remain poorly understood. The basal Cambrian Jangsan Formation of the eastern Sino-Korean Craton offers an opportunity to examine this problem on a tectonically stable craton, where accommodation was generated externally by eustatic sea-level rise during the Cambrian transgression. Integrated analysis of fifteen facies, six architectural elements, and 524 paleocurrent measurements indicates that the formation, traditionally regarded as a shallow-marine sandstone unit, is a basin-scale fluvial succession. Four facies associations record distinct fluvial styles: coarse, texturally immature deposits of proximal ephemeral streams (FA1); wide, shallow braided rivers in which sand-dominated thalweg dune fields were preferentially preserved (FA2); a deeper, more persistent braided-river system characterized by compound bars and stable channel pathways (FA3); and distal sandy sinuous channels with high paleocurrent dispersion, variable accretion styles, and repeated channel reoccupation (FA4). These associations are interpreted as coexisting elements of a single proximal-to-distal dispersal system that drained a low-relief sub-Cambrian peneplain interrupted by inselbergs and northeastern basement uplands. Their vertical stacking records progressive landward backstepping of this tract during transgression. Substantial variability in pre-vegetation fluvial architecture could thus develop on a stable craton through the interplay of inherited paleotopography and transgressive accommodation alone, without requiring major syndepositional tectonic or climatic control. Basal Cambrian sandstones of the North China Platform may likewise preserve terrestrial sediment-routing systems that operated before widespread marine flooding.

title: The Thomas A. Greene and Fisk H. Day Collections: Resurrecting 19th-century Silurian Fossils from the Reefs of Milwaukee and Chicago
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Mikulic, Donald George [1], Kluessendorf, Joanne [2]
affiliations: (2) Weis Earth Science Museum, Menasha, Wisconsin, USA
abstract:
Paleozoic reefs were first accurately identified in the Silurian rocks of Wauwatosa and Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Using both paleontological and lithological evidence, James Hall (1862) and Thomas C. Chamberlin (1877) documented a reef-controlled depositional and environmental transition from fossiliferous mounds to the surrounding deeper-sea floor. The diverse biota of these reefs and those from Illinois reefs have remained important in research for over 160 years. This research has primarily relied on late 19th-century comprehensive collections made by local naturalists, notably Thomas Arnold Greene (1827-1894), whose collection is in the Greene Gallery at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee, and Fisk Holbrook Day (1826-1904), whose collection is located in Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology and the University of Michigan. For many of these specimens, the quarry where they were collected is known, but little other documentation exists. Since 1900, most of these sites have disappeared, making it impossible to assemble new collections.

In the 1960s, the authors began a program to improve the documentation of these irreplaceable specimens. This included efforts to catalog both collections, establish the precise historical location and geological features of each site, reexamine all remaining reef exposures to verify the distribution of taxa, establish biotic associations, and document depositional and taphonomic features. Over 50 museums in North America and Europe with related specimens were also visited to locate additional research material. An important primary goal was to establish a lithostratigraphic, biostratigraphic, sequence stratigraphic, and chemostratigraphic framework for the entire Silurian of this region. This was accomplished through outcrop and quarry studies, bedrock core logging, and the examination of temporary rock excavations, including over 200 kilometers of bedrock tunnels. Biostratigraphic data was gathered through collaborative efforts with other paleontologists.

The project's results include documenting and curating over 50,000 museum specimens, recognizing the impact of glacio-eustatic sea-level change on reef development, and understanding the evolution and extinction of reef biotas. These sites and collections are significant to the region’s geoheritage. Some have been officially recognized by the U.S. National Park Service, the International Union of Geological Sciences, and other organizations for their scientific, educational, and cultural value. A Silurian reef diorama based on this work is displayed in several North American and European museums.

authors: Adsit, Aaron James [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Alattar, Zaid Tareq [3], Abts, Miranda R. [4], Koerting, Friederike [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA

abstract: The Kay volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) deposit is a brownfield exploration project located 70 km north of Phoenix, Arizona with an indicated resource of 9.28 million metric tonnes grading 0.97% Cu, 0.33% Pb, 2.39% Zn, 1.39 g/t Au, and 27.6 g/t Ag and an inferred resource of 0.86 million tonnes grading 0.87% Cu, 0.20% Pb, 1.68% Zn, 1.06 g/t Au, and 15.4 g/t Ag at a cut-off grade of 1.00% Cu equivalent. The Kay deposit is one of the most important VMS deposits in Arizona. It is hosted in the bimodal volcanic rocks of the Townsend Butte formation of the Black Canyon Creek Group which is a part of the larger 1.7 – 1.8 Ga Yavapai Supergroup. Massive sulfide formation was associated with intense alteration of the volcanic host rocks, including the development of an intense chlorite alteration zone in the stratigraphic footwall that grades outward into white mica alteration. The Kay deposit was subjected to high-strain structural overprint during the Yavapai Orogeny at approximately 1.7 Ga. The hydrothermal alteration halo was overprinted by regional metamorphism at greenschist-facies conditions. The deformation and metamorphic overprint make primary textural relationships difficult to discern. Assessment of mineralogical gradients across the alteration halo was accomplished by continuous core scanning hyperspectral imaging using a HySpex SWIR-384 camera mounted above a translation stage. Additionally, a HySpex Mjolnir VS-620 hyperspectral camera was mounted on a Harris Aerial heavy-lift H6HL uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) to conduct mineral mapping at a spatial resolution of ~6 x 6 cm per pixel. This revealed discreet hydrothermally altered zones that were previously unrecognized within the metamorphosed host rock succession. The case study shows that UAV-based hyperspectral mineral mapping can be conducted to map exposed surfaces at high spatial resolution at a rate of ~80 hectares per day. Coupled with subsurface analysis by continuous scanning of drill core, this provides effective results for target generation and vectoring during exploration. These techniques are ideal for deposits like VMS, which are characterized by comparably small alteration footprints and cannot be easily recognized on low-resolution satellite imagery at tens of meters of pixel sizes. The developed workflows can be used to guide exploration in highly deformed volcanic terranes.

title: The Missing Stratigraphic Record: Reconstructing Eroded Strata Across the Arkoma Foreland Basin System Using Thermal Maturity and Thermochronology Data

authors: Smith, Tyson M. [1], Hudson, Mark R. [2], Thomson, Kelly D. [3], Johnston, Michelle [4], Wageley, Holly [5], Hackley, Paul C. [6], Barrette, Nolan C. [7], Houseknecht, David W. [8]

abstract: Late- to post-orogenic exhumation of the Arkoma basin-Ouachita Mountain system resulted in removal of a significant portion of the syn- and/or post-orogenic sedimentary record with some researchers suggesting ≥4 km of total erosion. Among the most striking lines of evidence for these missing strata is the high thermal maturity of rocks presently exposed at the surface. To better characterize the thermal history of the Arkoma basin system and assess late Paleozoic-Mesozoic erosion, we compile new and previously published thermal maturity and thermochronologic data from the Ouachita Mountains in Arkansas to the Ozark dome in Missouri. We use down-hole trends from compiled subsurface reflectance data, % R o , to calculate paleo-geothermal gradients, estimate the overburden removed, and develop a model of missing strata from the Arkoma basin, as well as investigate potential zones of hydrothermally altered maturities. Surface and subsurface thermal maturity data (i.e., % R o ) reveal surface trends of maximum temperature throughout the Arkoma foreland basin system, and yield paleo-geothermal gradients. A longitudinal profile of R o and recent thermochronometric data – traversing an approximate dip-oriented, north-south section – demarcate a thermal regime boundary at the surface between the Arkoma basin and Ouachita Mountains. Pre-orogenic strata exposed in the core of Ouachita Mountain uplifts exhibit the highest burial temperatures (>290°C), whereas Upper Mississippian to Pennsylvanian strata of the Arkoma foreland basin experienced lower temperatures, ranging from >200°C in the south to ~40°C on the Ozark dome. Thermochronometric and thermal maturity data indicate that maximum basin temperatures were not achieved until the late Paleozoic or Mesozoic, reflecting the continued burial beyond the present stratigraphic record and protracted residence time at depth. These thermochronologic data provide timing constraints on the thermal history of the Arkoma basin, allowing us to interpret isothermal age horizons within the reconstructed wedge of removed strata. Spatial trends of thermal maturity suggest first-order structural control on maximum burial, but also highlight secondary maturity trends that may record regions potentially affected by hydrothermal fluid migration, which previous authors have suggested. Ultimately, these integrated data provide a unique window into ancient thermal regimes and a rock record that no longer exists.
