title: Surface Controls on Phosphorus Transport in the Sangamon River Watershed, Central Illinois.
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes (Posters)
authors: Alaran, Zainab Opeyemi [1], Seyoum, Wondwosen [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(2) Geography, Geology and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
abstract:
Excess phosphorus in agricultural watersheds contributes to eutrophication, yet predicting its movement remains challenging because transport depends on interacting hydrologic, erosional, and geochemical processes. This study evaluated relationships between total phosphorus concentrations and selected water-quality indicators, including discharge, suspended sediment load, turbidity, and pH, at three monitoring stations (Monticello, Fisher, and Route48) across the Sangamon River watershed. Historical U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) water-quality datasets were analyzed in R using Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses to evaluate relationships between phosphorus concentrations and these selected indicators.

Relationships between phosphorus and the evaluated indicators varied among monitoring stations. At Fisher, phosphorus showed a moderate positive relationship with turbidity (Pearson r = 0.53; Spearman ρ = 0.51; p < 0.001) suggesting that suspended particles may contribute to phosphorus transport at this location. Relationships between phosphorus and discharge varied among stations, suggesting that these relationships may be influenced by high-flow conditions rather than consistent trends. At Monticello, phosphorus showed a strong Pearson relationship with suspended sediment load (r = 0.66, p < 0.001), whereas Spearman correlation was not statistically significant (ρ = 0.11, p = 0.12), indicating that sediment-associated phosphorus transport may be influenced by high flow-event. At Route48, phosphorus showed weak relationships with turbidity, indicating that sediment mobilization and flow conditions alone may not fully explain phosphorus variability at this downstream location. Across all three stations, phosphorus consistently showed moderate, statistically significant negative relationships with pH, with the strongest correlations observed at Route48 (Pearson r = −0.47; Spearman ρ = −0.52; p < 0.001), suggesting that water chemistry may influence phosphorus availability and retention within the river system.

These findings indicate that phosphorus transport in the Sangamon River watershed is controlled by multiple interacting processes, including sediment-associated transport, hydrologic variability, and water chemistry conditions. Differences among monitoring stations highlight the importance of watershed-specific characteristics when evaluating phosphorus dynamics rather than generalized watershed models.

title: Multi-Thermochronometer Constraints on Cretaceous to Cenozoic Exhumation of the Northern Peninsular Ranges Batholith
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Bush, Madison A. [1], Odlum, Margo [2], Haproff, Peter [3], Sihpol, Tatiana A. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of California, San Diego, CA, USA
(2) University of California, San Diego, CA,
(3) Pomona College, Claremont, California, USA; University of North Carolina, Wilmington, North Carolina, USA
(4) UC San Diego, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, San Diego, CA,
abstract:
The Peninsular Ranges Batholith (PRB) preserves an important record of the magmatic and tectonic evolution of southern California from the Jurassic through the mid Tertiary. Although previous low-temperature thermochronologic studies in the PRB broadly indicate Late Cretaceous–Paleogene cooling, a dearth of low-temperature thermochronology constraints along the San Jacinto and Elsinore fault systems has limited the ability to distinguish exhumation associated with transform faulting from subduction-related processes. To address this uncertainty, we sampled along the traces of these faults to evaluate the spatial and temporal trends in pluton crystallization, cooling, and exhumation.

New zircon and apatite U-Pb geochronology, apatite (U-Th)/He thermochronology, and inverse thermal history modeling is used to constrain the timing of crystallization and exhumation within the northern PRB. Zircon and apatite U-Pb ages record mid- to Late Cretaceous pluton emplacement and cooling within the mid- to upper crust. Apatite (U-Th)/He dates range from ca. 76–7.2 Ma, with most ages between ca. 76–40 Ma, recording Late Cretaceous to middle Eocene cooling. Inverse thermal history modeling indicates two regional cooling phases, occurring at ca. 75–68 Ma and ca. 55–40 Ma, along with localized Miocene–Pliocene cooling at ca. 12–7 Ma. New and previous thermochronologic data show a strong inverse age versus distance trend eastward from the paleo-subduction trench and a positive age versus elevation trend. The Late Cretaceous cooling phase is interpreted to record uplift due to the transition from normal-angle subduction to shallow slab subduction. The Paleocene–Eocene cooling phase reflects associated regional uplift, denudation, and erosion during shallow subduction. Although modern topography of the region appears to be influenced by slip on the San Jacinto and Elsinore fault systems, new and previous thermochronologic data indicate that most exhumation predates displacement along the fault systems and is associated with paleo-subduction margin processes.

title: Paleo-Lacustrine Palynomorphs from the El Molino Formation (Maastrichtian/Danian), Torotoro National Park, Central Bolivia
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Roman, Maria A. [1], Nick, Kevin E. [2], Biaggi, Roberto E. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Biological Sciences, Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Biological Sciences Department, Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA
(3) Earth and Biological Sciences Department, Loma Linda University, Banning, CA, USA
abstract:
The El Molino Formation lies within the Subandean segment of the central Bolivian fold‑and‑thrust belt. The Middle and Upper El Molino span the Cretaceous–Paleogene (K–Pg) boundary and consist of sandy oolitic grainstones that host abundant dinosaur and bird tracks and are separated by fine mudstones. The El Molino is coeval, with the Yacoraite Formation in Argentina; and Vilquechico Formation in Peru and portions are proposed to be lacustrine. The mudstones were examined for their paleoenvironmental and biostratigraphic information from a 40 m stratigraphic section at the Río Sucusuma locality. This study presents the first palynological dataset, offering preliminary results that establish a site-specific microfloral baseline to support paleoenvironmental interpretation for the Eastern Cordillera.

The microfloral assemblage is dominated by freshwater taxa, particularly Pediastrum and Azolla , with subordinate occurrences of Botryococcus and Ovoidites . Additional noteworthy elements include a spore of Marsileaceae affinity, cf. Gabonisporis, tentatively assigned at the genus level based on its trilete structure and diagnostic ornamentation. Should future work confirm its identification as G. vigourouxii, the taxon would provide valuable chronostratigraphic control, as it is widely regarded as an age‑diagnostic palynomorph for the Maastrichtian.

The presence of Azolla and Pediastrum indicates a shallow, freshwater lacustrine system, likely situated within a floodplain. This microfloral composition accords with warm Maastrichtian lacustrine environments previously documented in northwestern Bolivia. Fungal remains and a diverse suite of terrestrial sporomorphs, including trilete spores and pollen types such as tricolpate, stephanoporate, and baculate forms, as well as Ephedra , further characterize the assemblage. Importantly, the absence of marine palynomorphs supports interpretation of a strictly continental depositional setting.

Overall, the palynoflora reflects a shallow, low‑energy, warm freshwater environment consistent with a floodplain‑associated lake. These results also fill in the geographic extent of the lacustrine model proposed for the coeval Yacoraite Formation in Argentina, where comparable continental palynofloras, rich in freshwater algae and aquatic ferns, occur in strata renowned for extensive dinosaur trackways. By linking the Eastern Cordillera to these wider regional patterns, this microfloral evidence provides a significant Andean contribution to reconstructions of continental ecosystems during one of Earth’s major biotic transitions.

title: Early Cretaceous volcanism recorded in basal tuffs of the Gyeongsang Basin, SE Korea: implications for basin-forming tectonics
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins (Posters)
authors: Kim, Sojeong [1], Woo, Jusun [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract: Along the active continental margin of East Asia, especially the Korean Peninsula, the Early Cretaceous has long been characterized by magmatic quiescence. Traditionally, the basal Sindong Group of the Gyeongsang Basin—a Cretaceous basin in Korea—has been interpreted as amagmatic. This interpretation is based on regional sedimentary petrographic surveys showing sparse volcanic quartz and volcanic rock fragments in the lowermost Nakdong Formation. However, newly discovered tuff deposits in the Hapcheon area, stratigraphically positioned between basement syenite and the overlying Nakdong Formation, record local volcanism coeval with the opening of the basin. To elucidate the basin’s opening, a multidisciplinary investigation was conducted, incorporating facies analysis, zircon U-Pb geochronology and whole-rock geochemistry. The tuff deposits comprise three pyroclastic facies (lithic lapilli tuff, stratified tuff, massive tuff) and one transitional tuffaceous sandstone facies. Lithic lapilli tuff indicates deposition in a granular flow-dominated flow boundary zone. Stratified tuff implies rapid sedimentation under a traction-dominated flow boundary zone. The massive tuff facies, lacking internal structure, records direct fallout-dominated sedimentation. Abrupt vertical and lateral facies transitions reflect deposition from vigorous pyroclastic density currents with dynamically fluctuating flow boundary zones. Zircon U-Pb dating of the lithic lapilli tuff and stratified tuff yields a weighted mean age of 119.55 ± 0.56 Ma (n = 8, MSWD = 1.57), placing the volcanism in the Aptian. This age is essentially synchronous with basin initiation. Geochemically, the tuffs range from andesitic to rhyolitic in composition. These results indicate that explosive volcanism accompanied the earliest stage of Gyeongsang Basin formation, at least locally. This volcanism may also have supplied early Cretaceous zircons found in the overlying formations of the basin. The apparent discrepancy with regionally low volcanic detritus suggests that early magmatism was spatially heterogeneous rather than absent. Existing tectonic models for the Gyeongsang Basin remain divided over whether the basin initiated as a forearc or a backarc setting relative to the arc associated with Izanagi Plate subduction. Regardless of this debate, most of these models have assumed a lack of volcanic activity during the opening stage. This new evidence suggests that volcanism accompanied basin initiation, a possibility not considered in existing basin evolution models. Resolving whether this reflects a forearc or backarc setting will require integrating these new age and geochemical constraints with future studies.

title: Unraveling human and natural controls on stream intermittency in a highly developed, humid catchment
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Adebayo, Moses Boluwatife [1], Dumont, Marc [2], Rathore, Saubhagya Singh [3], Herndon, Elizabeth [4], Singha, Kamini [5]
affiliations: (1) Hydrologic Science and Engineering Program, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland
(3) Environmental Sciences Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, USA
(4) Environmental Sciences Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, USA
(5) Hydrologic Science and Engineering Program; School of Earth, Space and Planets, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Intermittent streams—streams that cease to flow at some point during the year—comprise about half of global waterways. Human modifications contribute to the prevalence of these intermittent streams; over half of stream gauging stations in the U.S. with recorded intermittent flows have at least 10% human-modified land use (agricultural or developed). Isolating the effect of human modification on stream intermittency remains difficult because anthropogenic contributions are convoluted with the effects of natural drivers, making interpretation difficult. In this study, we investigate how human modification alters streamflow patterns by comparing an urban site with a nearby, minimally disturbed forested site in the humid East Fork Poplar Creek watershed, Tennessee, USA. Sharing similar regional geology and climate, these two sites allow us to evaluate human modifications against a natural baseline.

At the urban site, we combined electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) and distributed temperature sensing (DTS) to map subsurface structure and identify groundwater upwelling zones. We then used continuous self-potential (SP) monitoring alongside groundwater and stilling wells to identify patterns of stream-groundwater exchange. We further used the wells to monitor electrical conductivity, temperature, and water level in the stream and groundwater. ERT and DTS reveal that bedrock fractures sustain perennial streamflow in the downstream reach of the urban site, similar to the fracture-driven flow observed in the perennial reach of the forested site, highlighting the prevalent control of below-ground drivers on streamflow patterns across the watershed. SP and meteorological data further show that evapotranspiration drives water-table drawdown during low-rainfall periods, ultimately triggering natural streamflow cessation. However, in a section of the stream reach, anthropogenic water inputs override these natural controls, artificially shortening the duration of dry periods. The modified reach is also characterized by distinct, non-natural EC and temperature signatures. These findings demonstrate that human modification of stream intermittency can be evaluated, and that stream-water signatures can be used to identify reaches where the flow regime has been artificially altered.

title: Paleoxygenation Trends Reveal Environmental Conditions Caused Delays in Recovery: Evaluating the Virgin Limestone following the Permian-Triassic Mass Extinction
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Woods, Adam D. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, Fullerton, CA, USA
abstract: The Permian-Triassic mass extinction was the most devastating extinction in the history of the Earth. Biotic recovery from the Permian-Triassic mass extinction was sporadic across the Early Triassic, with diversification beginning in earnest only in the early Middle Triassic. Harsh environmental conditions, likely associated with the cause of mass extinction, persisted across the Early Triassic by way of global hothouse climates and anoxic conditions in the oceans. These environmental stresses narrowed the area of habitable environments and likely reset recovery multiple times. This study focuses on the Virgin Limestone at Lost Cabin Springs, NV locality, where interbedded carbonate and siliciclastic beds were deposited from the Smithian (middle Early Triassic) until the Anisian (early Middle Triassic) in a deep outer carbonate shelf environment. The Virgin Limestone offers a unique setting whereby environmental conditions can be determined by examination of shale interbeds, and the degree of biotic recovery can be estimated from the fossils and trace fossil content of the limestone interbeds. A total of 47 shale samples were subjected to trace element analysis to determine paleoxygenation via U, V, and Mo contents, while biotic recovery in intervening beds was estimated using ichnofabric indices. Initial results suggest that suboxic to anoxic conditions were often associated with deposition of the shale interbeds, and this biotic stress is reflected in ichnofabric indices, supporting the hypothesis that environmental conditions determined the timing and shape of recovery. Further study will refine recovery estimates and separate local environmental controls from longer-term recovery trends.

title: Tectonic implications of unconformities and flooding surfaces in the proximal Central Colorado Trough
session_title: From outcrop to orogen—field-based perspectives on stratigraphy, structural geology, and mineral resources in the Rocky Mountain region—a session in honor of David A. Lindsey
authors: Smith, Tyson M. [1], Saylor, Joel E. [2], Lapen, Tom J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences and Environmental Change Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences, University of British Colombia, Vancouver, BC, Canada
(3) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Houston, TX, University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA
abstract:
The record of many Ancestral Rocky Mountain (ARM) uplifts is obscured by subsequent geologic events that overprint this enigmatic late Paleozoic episode of deformation. However, intraplate basins that developed adjacent to these basement-cored uplifts provide windows into their composition and deformational history. We present a case study in the proximal Central Colorado Trough (CCT) where we identify provenance changes across tectono-stratigraphic surfaces (i.e., unconformities and flooding surfaces) that record discrete episodes of late Paleozoic deformation along the east-bounding Apishapa Uplift.

Lower Pennsylvanian to lower Permian strata were deposited in this region of the CCT by fluvial and deltaic systems whose flow directions transitioned from northward (axial) to westward (transverse) as the Apishapa Uplift grew and deformation encroached on the depocenter. Field and geochemical data document this multi-phase intraplate tectonic activity through characterization of sedimentary facies and unconfomities, along with paleocurrent data, detrital zircon geochronology and geochemistry, and sandstone petrography. We interpret these data to reflect advance of thrust-induced shortening on the western flank of the Apisha Uplift, which drove migration of flexural-influenced depozones. Furthermore, this punctuated thrust activity initially exhumed Cambrian igneous rock within the catchment and then later supplanted that source of sediment by exhuming Proterozoic basement.

We present a 3-stage synoptic reconstruction of tectonic activity and drainage reorganization within this proximal area of the CCT. Additionally, we use the geochemical and petrographic detrital record of the now-absent Cambrian igneous body that dominated this Apishapa Uplift catchment to describe its approximate location and character within the context of our tectonic reconstruction.

title: GIS-Based Python Toolbox Using Machine Learning to Identify Alluvial Fans in north Mississippi and west Tennessee
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans
authors: Lahiri, Chayan [1], Heal, Elizabeth [2]
affiliations: (1) Adams State University, Department of Geosciences, Alamosa, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi-Gulf Water Science Center, Dover, DE, USA
abstract:
Alluvial fans are common geomorphic features along the eastern margin of the Mississippi Alluvial Plain in north Mississippi and west Tennessee. These depositional landforms receive sediment delivery from upland watersheds and play an important role in floodplain evolution. Many of these are long-lived depositional landforms shaped by extended periods of landscape development. Over the past 60 years, land clearing, agricultural expansion, and stream channelization have altered sediment delivery from upland watersheds, contributing both to continued aggradation of existing fans and probably to the formation of younger alluvial fans in headwater tributaries.

Despite their influence on watershed morphology, sediment storage, wetland formation, and wildlife habitat, the regional distribution and extent of these landforms remain poorly documented. Present identification methods rely heavily on manual interpretation of topographic maps and aerial imagery, making large-scale inventories time-consuming and inherently subjective. Furthermore, the age and origin of smaller fans are often uncertain because historical mapping lacks the spatial resolution needed to determine whether they predate widespread land-use change or formed more recently.

To address this knowledge gap, and in cooperation with the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency, we are developing a GIS-based toolbox that combines high-resolution digital elevation models and terrain-analysis techniques with machine-learning algorithms to systematically identify alluvial fans across north Mississippi and west Tennessee. The toolbox will contain several tools, one for each step of the identification and delineation process. Processing steps include identifying the point at which channel confinement ends and fans emerge, delineating the conical surface of these fans, and calculating fan slope. The objective is to establish a consistent, reproducible methodology for mapping and characterizing fan morphology over broad geographic areas, providing land managers and researchers with a reliable framework for developing regional fan inventories and supporting future studies of sediment dynamics, geomorphic evolution, wetland development, and watershed management. Field investigations at selected sites will be used to validate mapped landforms, improve training sets for feature identification, and evaluate overall toolbox performance.

title: Use of Organic Micropollutants Combined with Inorganic Constituents to Discover Hydraulic Connections in an Underground Gypsum Mine, Germany
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Posters)
authors: Awad , Marwa [1], Scheytt, Traugott J. [2]
affiliations: (1) TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Chair of Hydrogeology and Hydrochemistry, Freiberg, Saxony, Germany
(2) TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Chair of Hydrogeology and Hydrochemistry, Freiberg, Saxony, Germany; TU Bergakademie Freiberg, Freiberg Center for Water Research, Freiberg, Saxony, Germany
abstract: Understanding groundwater recharge pathways and mixing processes is essential for effective mine water management in karstified carbonate environments. For many years, the underground gypsum mine in Lamerden, Germany has experienced continuous water inflow, which replenishes the primary sump, the northern sump, and two additional sumps situated to the east and west within the mine. This study investigates the origin of this water and the hydraulic connections between groundwater and surface water. The mine is developed within the Middle Muschelkalk and is bounded by the karstified perched Upper Muschelkalk aquifer and the confined Lower Muschelkalk carbonate aquifer, while the nearby rivers Alster and Diemel represent potential surface-water recharge sources. A total of 32 water samples were collected from mine, from groundwater, and from surface water during two sampling campaigns and analyzed for major ions, trace elements, and organic micropollutants. The hydrochemical results indicate that water–rock interaction, particularly gypsum and carbonate dissolution, is the dominant control on groundwater chemistry passing from the upper aquifer to the middle Muschelkalk (Ca 2+ avg = 549 mg/l; SO 4 2- avg = 1,206 mg/l). The West Sump water is hydraulically connected to the Upper Muschelkalk and river water which was shown by higher nitrate concentrations (NO 3 - avg = 40 mg/l), lower strontium concentrations (Sr 2+ avg = 7.6 mg/l) and wastewater-derived organic micropollutants (e.g., carbamazepine, acesulfame and cyclamat). In contrast, the North Sump exhibited low nitrate concentrations (NO 3 - avg = 2.3 mg/l), elevated strontium concentrations (Sr 2+ avg = 16 mg/l), and only limited occurrence of wastewater tracers, indicating that it is predominantly recharged by the confined Lower Muschelkalk aquifer. The combined use of major ions, trace elements, and organic micropollutants proved to be an effective multi-tracer approach for distinguishing groundwater recharge sources and identifying groundwater–surface water interactions in a complex karst mining system. These findings improve the understanding of mine water recharge mechanisms and provide valuable information for groundwater management and flood mitigation in mining.

title: A Comparison Between Observed and Modeled Hillslope Sediment Yields Following the 2011 Wallow Fire
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments (Posters)
authors: Barbian, Vivian [1], McGuire, Luke A. [2], Beers, Rebecca Louise [3], Robichaud, Peter [4], Srivastava, Anurag [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(2) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(3) Arizona Geological Survey at University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(4) USDA, Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station, Moscow, Idaho,
(5) The University of Idaho, Moscow, ID,
abstract:
Wildfires are an increasingly prevalent hazard in the Western U.S. Wildfires often affect surface water runoff and soil erodibility, leading to increased hillslope erosion. Greater hillslope erosion can contribute to sediment-laden floods and debris-flows, sometimes with deadly consequences. Numerical models designed to predict postfire sediment yield are one tool that can be used to support hazard mitigation and public safety. It is beneficial to understand the uncertainty associated with model predictions.

We assessed the performance of the USDA Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station Erosion Risk Management Tool (ERMiT), a web-based application based on the Water Erosion Prediction Project (WEPP) model, by comparing predicted hillslope sediment yields to observed hillslope sediment yields collected by the USDA Forest Service following the 2011 Wallow Fire near Greer, Arizona. Hillslope erosion was measured using silt fences that were cleaned out following rain events during the monsoon season in the three years after the fire.Our preliminary results indicate that the model may underestimate sediment yield in the first post-fire year.

The first series of rainstorms following the fire had peak 10-minute rainfall intensities with recurrence intervals of less than 1 year. The observed sediment yield associated with these storms exceeded the modeled 100-year sediment yields. Comparisons between ERMiT and observed sediment yields are complicated by several factors. First, observed sediment yields are often not associated with a single storm. Instead, they represent erosion associated with multiple storms. Second, ERMiT output represents the probability that a particular sediment yield will be exceeded. Therefore, ERMiT output cannot be directly compared with an observed sediment yield. The exploratory analysis done here could motivate future work using more advanced methods for model evaluation.

title: Extending the CURE Framework: A Cohort-Based, Curriculum-Integrated Undergraduate Research Model at a Primarily Undergraduate Institution
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Baughman, Jaclyn S [1], Michalak, Melanie J [2]
affiliations: (1) Cal Poly Humboldt, Arcata, CA,
(2) Cal Poly Humboldt, Arcata, CA,
abstract:
Undergraduate research opportunities at regional and primarily undergraduate institutions (PUIs) are often constrained by faculty mentoring capacity, limited funding, and inequitable student access. We designed and implemented an academic-year-long, curriculum-integrated research experience centered on a six-member undergraduate cohort that emphasizes a collaborative and peer-supported research community. The experience was co-mentored by two faculty members with overlapping expertise at one PUI. Students received two units of graded course credit that counted toward their degree, five hours of paid support per week, and the opportunity to present at a regional conference. Weekly cohort meetings provided structured research time and faculty workload credit. Students completed every stage of authentic tectonics and thermochronology research, from field sampling and laboratory work to data analysis, thermal modeling, and presentation of results. Selection prioritized student interest, career goals, collaboration, and lived experiences rather than GPA, class standing, or prior research experience.

Our cohort model extends the CURE framework by integrating authentic discovery, collaboration, and iteration with sustained faculty mentoring more typical of one-on-one research experiences. This structure supports our goals of broadening access to undergraduate research, fostering a sense of belonging, and helping students develop the skills and confidence needed for graduate school or the geoscience workforce while advancing rigorous research outcomes.

Across three cohorts, pre- and post-experience surveys indicated increased scientific confidence, graduate school preparedness, and sense of belonging within our university’s department and the broader geoscience community. In post-experience surveys, nearly all students reported a strong or very strong sense of belonging, and all students reported feeling at least moderately prepared to apply to graduate school. Qualitative responses consistently highlighted (i) increased confidence and stronger scientific identity, (ii) the importance of collaboration, shared accountability, and sustained engagement as critical to both learning and project completion, and (iii) the value of a complete scientific experience throughout the academic year.

Importantly, GPA, class standing, and prior research experience were not strong predictors of student engagement or research contributions. Students produced publication-ready scientific figures, original thermochronologic interpretations, and presentations at three GSA Section meetings. These outcomes demonstrate that a cohort-based, academic-year research model can broaden participation, enhance student development, support faculty research productivity, and provide a scalable approach for integrating authentic research into the curriculum at teaching-focused institutions.

title: The setting of the Burgess Shale reconsidered: the origin of the Cathedral Escarpment
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Gaines, Robert R. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Pomona College, Claremont, CA, USA
abstract: The Cathedral Escarpment looms large in the contemporary understanding of the Burgess Shale. At the original locality on Fossil Ridge, the archetypal Cambrian lagerstätte was deposited at the foot of a >300 m submarine cliff, a prominent shelf break that separated relatively shallow water platform settings from deeper basinal depositional environments. The classical interpretation of the Cathedral Escarpment as the sharp distal edge of a large, microbially constructed carbonate reef has provided a basis for ecological interpretation of Burgess Shale localities as a fore-reef complex, and has also underpinned assumed geologic and stratigraphic relationships in the region. The validity of this interpretation, however, has been called into question, due to the geologic complexity of the region. An intensive campaign of fieldwork over the last fifteen years has provided regional geologic and stratigraphic data which demonstrate that the Cathedral Escarpment did not form as the result of upward growth of a microbial reef that maintained a near-vertical edge at the platform margin, but, instead, was formed by catastrophic carbonate platform margin collapse. These data provide a new framework for interpreting the paleoenvironments of Burgess Shale fossil assemblages across the southern Canadian Rockies, for the correlation of Burgess Shale fossil localities in relative time, and require revision of stratigraphic relationships of platformal and basinal deposits across the Cathedral escarpment.

title: Connecting the Timing, Rate, Extent, and Elevation of the Lewis Thrust System with its Foreland Basin: Insights from a New Balanced Cross Section and Implications for Dynamic Topography
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling
authors: York, Aidan James [1], McQuarrie, Nadine [2], Mackaman-Lofland, Chelsea A. [3], Constenius, Kurt [4], Fan, Majie [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(2) University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(3) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA
(4) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(5) University of Texas, Arlington, TX, USA
abstract: The North American Cordillera in Montana and southwest Canada retains significant elevation and relief 50 Ma after shortening ceased, and it represents one of the most comprehensively studied orogenic systems on earth. Despite this, longstanding questions about the Lewis thrust (LT), a major thrust sheet within the Cordillera, remain. In particular, the amount of shortening associated with the LT, the magnitude of sedimentation associated with that movement, the age the LT initiated, and its easternmost extent, are all unknown. Though the LT overlies 75 Ma sedimentary rocks, providing a younger age constraint, the timing of thrust initiation remains unconstrained. The magnitude of sedimentation associated with the Lewis and later thrusts is unknown due to significant erosion of foreland basin material. Additionally, these foreland basin rocks currently sit at over 1 km in elevation, despite originally being deposited at sea level. In order to address these questions, we present a new balanced cross-section which spans from the Washington-Idaho border to the Bearpaw Mountains in central Montana. This cross-section expands the section of Fuentes et al. (2012) 300 km westward of the Rocky Mountain trench, and increases the magnitude of shortening in the system from 136 to 300 km. Flexural-kinematic modeling links shortening along the LT to the deposition of synorogenic foreland basin sediments, beginning with the Kootenai Formation at 125 Ma, and ending with lower Wasatch Formation deposition at approximately 56 Ma. New cross section interpretations kinematically link a proposed duplex beneath the Plains Anticline in western Montana to thrusting in the Sawtooth Range. Modeling the system produces a significant thickness of foreland basin material that must be eroded in order to accurately reproduce the surface geology in the Sawtooth Range and the foreland basin. Models quantify a potential thickness range greater than 4–6 km in the foreland basin at the location of the Oxy Larson 1-1 well (25 km east of the deformation front), which indicates greater than 3–5 km of overlying foreland basin sediment has been removed. In the Sawtooth Range, model results suggest removal of at least 5–8 km of overburden. The magnitude and timing of this uplift and associated erosion, constrained by thermochronometric data, can be been used to quantify the influence of mantle-driven processes on the formation of present-day topography.

title: Optimization and Standardization of Methods for the Extraction and Quantification of Microplastics in Soil
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part II)
authors: Valdez, Kesiah Olivo [1]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science, Stephen F Austin State Univ - Nacogdoches, Tx, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
abstract: Microplastics are an emerging environmental concern that may alter soil physicochemical properties and pose potential risks to terrestrial organisms and human health. The identification and quantification of microplastics in environmental matrices, including water, air, and soil, require reliable and standardized extraction methods to obtain accurate and comparable results. This study aims to evaluate and optimize different methods for the extraction and quantification of microplastics in soil and to develop a standardized procedure. Soil samples were initially dried and subjected to organic matter removal using varying amounts of hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), followed by evaporation using either a hotplate or oven. Density separation was subsequently performed using canola oil, castor oil, and a combined oil–NaCl system, with separation conducted using either an orbital shaker or separatory funnel. The recovered samples were then filtered and washed prior to microplastic identification and quantification using a digital microscope system. Preliminary findings indicate that drying soil samples in a 40°C oven for 48 hours is sufficient to achieve a moisture content of less than 2%. The amount of H₂O₂ required depends on the soil organic matter content, while the use of a hotplate showed potential for more efficient organic matter removal. Among the density separation approaches, the combined oil–NaCl system using a separatory funnel is being investigated for its potential to improve microplastic recovery. Further analysis will determine the recovery efficiency and overall performance of the evaluated methods. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of a more effective and reproducible method for microplastic extraction and quantification from complex soil matrices, supporting improved environmental monitoring and assessment of soil microplastic contamination

title: Estimating Neoproterozoic–Paleozoic Temperature Conditions with Chemical Weathering Proxies from Laurentia
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology
authors: Olah, Jaden Karl [1], Nelson, Lyle Lee [2], Brennan, Daniel Thomas [3], Link, Paul K. [4], Eyster, Athena Elizabeth [5], Webb, Lucy Cora [6], Mills, Benjamin [7], Zheng, Dongyu [8], Sperling, Erik A. [9]

(2) Earth Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(3) Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Butte, MT,
(4) Department of Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(5) Department of Earth and Climate Sciences, Tufts University, Medford, MA,

abstract: The late Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic saw major swings in global climate broadly coincident with the emergence and diversification of animal life as well as changes in oxygenation. Recent work in marine ecophysiology has established that the oxygen requirements for sustained metabolic activity are closely related to temperature. While examining marine oxygen and temperature dynamics together is critical to understand marine environmental habitability, accurately constraining Precambrian paleotemperature remains notoriously challenging in part due to uncertainties in interpreting oxygen isotope proxies. Here, we applied the Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) of fine-grained siliciclastic rocks as an alternative, qualitative paleoclimate proxy to investigate the temperature dynamics of the Neoproterozoic through the Paleozoic. CIA values are calculated as a ratio of the concentrations of immobile Al cations to more mobile cations of Ca, K, Na, and can be used as an estimate for the degree of chemical weathering and temperature. CIA values were calculated for ~5500 fine-grained siliciclastic samples from localities across western Laurentia from the Sedimentary Geochemistry and Paleoenvironments Project (SGP) database and new data reported in this study. Paleogeographic reconstructions place Laurentia at relatively consistent, tropical paleolatitudes throughout this time interval, so variations in CIA values likely reflect global climate change instead of relative plate motion. The compiled CIA values are variable in the Tonian with the highest values between ca. 800-775 Ma. CIA values decrease to 65 in the Cryogenian then increase to moderate values of 72 in the Ediacaran. The lowest values CIA are recorded in the late Cambrian to early Ordovician, though this may be due to potassium metasomatism. CIA values then rise to moderate values again in the late Ordovician, Silurian, and Devonian. The Cambrian does not show the chemical weathering hallmarks of an extreme hothouse world similar to that of the later Cretaceous through Eocene. Cambrian temperatures were likely moderate and cooling climatic conditions from the late Ediacaran through middle Cambrian may have played an important physiological role in the Cambrian radiation.

title: Evolution of Sandstone-Dominated Mixed Systems Between Carbonate Platform Deposits: The Early Ordovician Dongjeom Formation, Taebaeksan Basin, Korea
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Ahn, Seungbeom [1], Woo, Jusun [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental sciences, Seoul National Univeristy, Seoul, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract: Mixed siliciclastic–carbonate systems record complex interactions among siliciclastic sediment supply, carbonate production, and relative sea-level change. However, siliciclastic-dominated intervals intercalated within carbonate-dominated successions have commonly been interpreted as records of increasing clastic influx, and the internal evolution of sandstone-dominated mixed systems remains poorly understood. This study examines the spatio-temporal evolution of the Early Ordovician Dongjeom Formation in the Taebaeksan Basin, Korea, a sandstone-dominated mixed siliciclastic–carbonate unit intercalated within carbonate platform deposits. Detailed sedimentological observations and basin-scale correlation show that the Dongjeom Formation records wave-dominated shallow-marine deposition and comprises six facies associations: four siliciclastic facies associations, including lower offshore transition (FA1), upper offshore transition to lower shoreface (FA2), upper shoreface (FA3), and tidally influenced upper shoreface (FA4), and two carbonate facies associations, including shallow mid-ramp (FA5) and deep mid-ramp (FA6). Facies distributions and paleocurrent data indicate a northwestward-deepening basin physiography, with a proximal sediment source to the southeast. The facies associations form three facies successions, bounded by transgressive surfaces, that record repeated alternations between normal regression and transgression. Lower rates of relative sea-level rise allowed normal-regressive sandstone progradation, whereas higher rates of relative sea-level rise led to transgressive surfaces and rejuvenated distal carbonate deposition. The recurrence of sand input during relative sea-level rise tentatively suggests source-area uplift, without evidence of coeval tectonic deformation within the basin. The sandstone-dominated facies successions record the initiation, basin-wide expansion, and systematic contraction of siliciclastic deposition: FS1 formed laterally continuous basin-wide facies belts, FS2 became thinner and more discontinuous with proximal sandstone and distal carbonate deposition, and FS3 was restricted to the southeastern proximal area. This upward trend records progressive waning and proximal trapping of siliciclastic sand during long-term relative sea-level rise. The Dongjeom Formation, therefore, reveals that sandstone-dominated intervals within carbonate-dominated successions preserve complex internal facies evolution controlled by variable rates of relative sea-level rise, source-area uplift, and basin physiography.

title: From Caldera to Cone: Geochemical and Mineral-scale Constraints on Early Magmatic Evolution in the Goat Rocks Volcanic Cluster, Cascades, WA
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: O'Leary, Yusei [1], Shamloo, Hannah [2], Takach, Marie [3], Mattinson, Christopher [4], Wall, Kellie [5]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
(4) Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
(5) Geological Survey & Services, Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries, OR, USA
abstract:
The Goat Rocks Volcanic Cluster (GRVC; ~3.5–0.1 Ma) is a Cascade arc center in south-central Washington where erosion has exposed the full volcanic system through time. This study examines the units from two of the earliest eruptive periods. The ~3.2 Ma Devils Horns Rhyolite (DHR) includes rhyolitic ignimbrites and breccias. After ~100 kyr, the Tieton Peak stratocone stage (TP; ~3.1–2.6 Ma) produced rhyolitic, dacitic, and andesitic lavas, marking a transition to effusive eruptions and the GRVC’s first stratovolcano. We aim to reconstruct the magmatic evolution and pre-eruptive histories of these units and evaluate whether they are genetically related or represent distinct magmatic systems to understand the earliest magmatic evolution of a Cascade system.

We present whole-rock major and trace element geochemistry, petrography, electron microprobe and LA-ICP-MS analyses of feldspar, pyroxene, and Fe-Ti oxides. Bulk trace element compositions suggest distinct magmatic sources. TP samples define a typical fractional crystallization array, whereas DHR forms a separate cluster outside this trend, most clearly in Zr-Nb space. Starting with the earliest erupted unit, TP rhyolite contains reversely zoned plagioclase (An₂₅–₃₂ rims; An₄₀–₆₀ interiors). TP dacite contains normal, reverse, and oscillatory zoned plagioclase (An₄₀–₉₀), reversely zoned clinopyroxene (Mg# 70–75 rims; Mg# 64–68 cores), and reversely zoned orthopyroxene (Mg# 66–68 rims; Mg# 60–63 cores). Similar to TP dacite, TP andesite contains normal, reverse, and oscillatory zoned plagioclase (An₄₀–₉₀), two distinct clinopyroxene populations (Mg# 63–71 and 79–85 distinct in Dy concentration), and zoned orthopyroxene (Mg# 57–61). Fe-Ti oxides yield an average temperature of 722±40°C and oxygen fugacity of QFM +1 determined through oxygeothermometry. Mineral data for DHR will be determined.

So far, these results suggest that the TP system through time does not follow a closed-system magmatic storage model. Instead, the similar mineral ranges present in TP dacite and andesite might suggest the tapping of similar magmatic components upon eruption through distinct vents. Additionally, fractional crystallization and repeated magmatic interaction likely play a role in the building of the TP stratocone. Whole-rock MELTS modeling, geothermobarometry, and DHR mineral data will be used to further reconstruct pre-eruptive histories of these units. We look to understand the magmatic evolution of the first stages of a Cascades volcanic system.

title: Morphometric Variation in Neothauma tanganyicense from Lake Tanganyika, East Africa
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Burdett, Evelyn [1], Soreghan, Michael [2], Cole, Selina [3], Samyn, Yves [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
(2) University of Oklahoma,
(3) University of Oklahoma, ; Sam Noble Museum of Natural History,

abstract:
Neothauma tanganyicense is a freshwater gastropod endemic to Lake Tanganyika. There are extensive unconsolidated shell beds of N. tanganyicense on the modern lake floor that exhibit time averaged accumulations from 200-3000 years old. They are a crucial part of the lake environment as they support a littoral ecosystem for many fish and invertebrate species. The shells exhibit geographically related morphological variation. Historically there has been considerable scientific debate over the taxonomic designation of the genus Neothauma and whether the differences in morphology could be considered different species. The most recent analysis was published in 1953 by Eugene Leloup and consolidated Neothauma into the single species based primarily on collections from the western side of the lake . Additionally, morphometric studies on newer collections of Neothauma from the eastern coast of the lake have been conducted, providing a wider scope of data. Advances in quantitative morphometric methods and evolving taxonomic concepts have provided new ways to evaluate the taxonomy of this species since this previous work.

This study statistically compares morphological measurements of snails collected from museum specimens from the western coast of the lake to measurements from the newer collections from the east side of the lake. To re-examine the questions regarding species designation(s), we analyzed over 1200 shells using a combination of 2d geometric morphometrics of the plane of the aperture and traditional morphometrics including categorizing differences in keeling and sutures through character data. These morphological data, analyzed in R and PAST using multivariate statistical methods, allow testing of whether geographically distinct samples form distinct taxonomic groups or a scale of variation. The results will provide the first quantitative analysis of Neothauma taxonomy in over 70 years and are timely because recent studies have indicated that populations of live Neothauma have decreased over the last 100 years: a change that may profoundly affect the lake’s ecosystem. Future conservation actions will depend on sound taxonomy of the affected taxa/taxon.

abstract: The Selwyn Basin records coarse clastic deposition during the Late Devonian–Early Mississippian along the reactivated northwestern Laurentian margin. During this time, eastward subduction of Panthalassa oceanic crust generated an extensional back-arc system, separating the Yukon-Tanana Terrane from the continent as the Slide Mountain Ocean opened. This renewed magmatism and subsidence along the continental margin in the Selwyn Basin, resulting in the Earn Group composed of alkalic volcanic rocks at the base of the section and overlying black mudstone, sandstone, and chert-pebble conglomerate deposited in deep-water turbidite environments. The initial timing of magmatism and deposition remain loosely constrained by conodonts at various localities, suggesting ages ranging from Early Devonian to Late Devonian. Resolving this timing is key to correlating the magmatic and sedimentary evolution along the continental margin with arc magmatism in the Yukon-Tanana Terrane and opening of the Slide Mountain Ocean within a broader tectonic framework of the back-arc region. We present new igneous and detrital zircon U-Pb geochronologic ages from four localities of the Earn Group across the Selwyn Basin in present-day Yukon and Northwest Territories and northern British Columbia. U-Pb ages from volcanic rocks collected at the base of the Earn Group and interbedded tuffs at the Macmillan Pass locality in the Yukon Territory refine depositional ages previously bracketed between the Middle–Late Devonian by conodont ages. Detrital zircon results suggest that northern Earn Group strata in the Yukon and Northwest Territories were supplied primarily by recycled Neoproterozoic–early Paleozoic strata with minimal input from potentially co-magmatic sources, whereas southern strata in northern British Columbia were supplied primarily by Yukon-Tanana arc assemblages, highlighting significant along-strike variation in sediment source age. We suggest along-strike deposition of the Earn Group was diachronous (southward younging), possibly related to pre-rift basin geometry and along-strike variation in the opening of the Slide Mountain Ocean.

abstract:
Wildfires introduce a modified flux of major and trace elements in soils, with impacts on nutrients, soil physical properties, as well as the vegetation and hydrology of the impacted area. In this study, we assess the major and trace element chemistry of soils immediately following a fire, and subsequent fate of those elements in the pioneer vegetation establishing after the fire. This presents a first attempt at understanding the pre-fire and post-fire chemical mass balance in the soil environment. The case study presented here is with the November 2024 Jennings Creek Fire that affected portions of Passaic County, New Jersey and Orange County, New York. The fire occurred in an area of mixed hardwood forest within watersheds for the New York/New Jersey metropolitan area, thus addressing a relatively under-studied biome and region with respect to wildfires.

We sampled post-fire soils as well as pioneer vegetation from burned and adjacent unburned woodland in Long Pond Ironworks State Park. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) revealed increases in several ash-associated elements (e.g., Ca, Cu, Ba, Sr) and depletion of more volatile elements in the soils. To address the biological components of the environmental system, we developed a modified acid digestion and extraction method to assess the element chemistry of newly sprouted plants including ferns, sassafras, and aster from burned and unburned representative transects on comparable soils. These plants exhibited elevated amounts of the same elements found in the post-fire soils. Ongoing analysis will assess the persistence of these fire chemistry indicators

title: Surveying the damage: investigating the Paleozoic emergence of arthropod herbivory
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Frank, Tanner Matthew [1], Donovan, Michael P. [2], Hotton, Carol L. [3], Labandeira, Conrad C. [4]
affiliations: (1) Paleobiology, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC,

abstract: Herbivores are a central component of nearly all modern terrestrial ecosystems, but this may not always have been so. Roughly 100 Myr separates the appearance of terrestrial arthropods in the Silurian from the emergence of widespread specialized herbivory in the Pennsylvanian, an interval during which food webs are generally hypothesized to have been detritus-based. Three non-exclusive explanations can account for this gap: (1) it is an artifact of an incomplete fossil record; (2) bottom-up constraints imposed by tough, nutrient-poor land plant tissues; (3) top-down suppression of early herbivores by predators subsidized by aquatic productivity. Distinguishing them requires new primary data and assessment of damage trends through this under-sampled interval. We surveyed functional feeding groups and damage types (DTs) on plant compressions and cuticles, documenting: possible feeding puncture marks in Early Devonian cuticles from Gaspé, Canada, consistent with previous reports from permineralized material at the site; external foliage feeding, possible galling, and piercing-and-sucking in Mississippian assemblages, particularly the Price Formation of West Virginia and Virginia, USA; and possible skeletonization plus additional DTs new for the Pennsylvanian in the Drywood Formation of Missouri, USA. These records expand the sparse evidence for early terrestrial feeding damage and highlight the presence of herbivory during this apparent gap; animals have likely consumed live plant tissues nearly as long as they have been on land, at least facultatively. Because floral composition varies among assemblages, we additionally tracked damage across the final 12 Myr of the Pennsylvanian on a single abundant, widespread host, the medullosan Macroneuropteris scheuchzeri (~ 3000 pinnules, ~70 localities). Herbivory damage frequency increased significantly while DT richness did not. These results support a real expansion in herbivory intensity across the interval, while the decoupling from DT richness is more consistent with release of top-down suppression than a relaxation of bottom-up constraints. Intensity was also lower in assemblages associated with permanently wet coal-forming environments, as predicted under the aquatic subsidy hypothesis. However, the concentration of damage on seed plants across assemblages in our surveys and the literature, and the small maximum size of early external foliage feeding, also support a role for bottom-up control, suggesting both factors shaped the tempo of the early expansion of herbivory.

abstract: During the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM, ~26-18 ka), global and continental-scale climatic changes produced generally cooler and drier conditions across Africa, but substantial regional and local variability was superimposed on this broader signal. Understanding environmental change at these smaller spatial scales is particularly important because climatic changes likely altered vegetation and the availability of plant and animal resources for human populations; however, the extent to which these changes affected resource availability remains unclear. Kisese II rockshelter in north-central Tanzania documents both environmental and behavioral changes across this period, preserving extensive fossil fauna, ostrich eggshell (OES) fragments, as well as lithic and ochre artifacts recovered from Raymond Inskeep’s 1956 excavations. Prior OES δ¹³C values indicate stable variation within mixed C 3 /C 4 plant communities through time, while OES δ 18 O minimum values from ~18.1–4.2 ka indicate lower evapotranspiration (cooler and/or wetter conditions). OES nitrogen isotope (δ 15 N) data suggest that peak precipitation occurred earlier, around 22 ka. There is no significant change in enamel δ¹³C and δ 18 O values from 93 fossil herbivore enamel samples (30 taxa) when analyzed together and as separate feeding guilds, further supporting a lack of change in vegetation during this period. Preliminary phytolith data (n=3) from the Silty Sands with Micritic Calcite (SSMC) stratigraphic unit (26.1–16.6 ka) suggest C 4 grass dominance with C 3 Pooideae grasses increasing around 18 ka, aligning with the OES δ 18 O minimum and reinforcing evidence for a cooler and/or relatively drier interval. However, samples (n=3) from colluvial clayey sands (CCS, 8.25-6.9 ka) show transitions from moist to arid conditions with C 4 Chloridoideae grasses at Kisese II. Together, the phytolith, OES, and enamel records suggest that environmental responses at Kisese II were more complex than a simple local expression of broader LGM aridity, underscoring the importance of multi-proxy approaches for reconstructing paleoenvironmental conditions at the local scale. Future research integrating higher-resolution paleoenvironmental data with expanded taphonomic and site-formation analyses will help clarify the spatial and temporal relationships among these records and provide a stronger basis for evaluating ecological resource availability and human adaptive strategies through time.

title: Recent Advances in Alluvial Fan Process Identification and Flow Path Prediction
session_title: Applied Science and Insights on Alluvial Fans
authors: de Haas, Tjalling [1]
affiliations: (1) Physical Geography, Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands
abstract:
Alluvial fans are preferred sites for settlement in mountainous regions and are therefore highly susceptible to debris-flow and flood hazards. Debris flows can produce peak discharges up to 40 times greater than floods generated from catchments of the same size, making them generally the dominant hazard on alluvial fans.

Two key components of alluvial fan hazard and risk assessment are process identification and prediction of flow paths and inundation areas. Process identification is ideally based on detailed field investigations, but these are often impractical. Instead, geomorphic processes are commonly inferred from catchment and fan morphometrics, including the Melton index (catchment relief divided by the square root of catchment area), catchment length, and fan slope. However, morphometric thresholds used to distinguish debris-flow-dominated from flood-dominated alluvial fans are typically site-specific and inherently uncertain. Recent analyses of large datasets combined with modern machine-learning techniques now make it possible to explicitly incorporate this uncertainty into alluvial fan hazard and risk assessments.

Flow paths and inundation areas generally follow the active channel and the direction of steepest descent across the fan surface. However, avulsions can redirect flow, shifting the areas affected by debris flows or floods. The mechanisms driving avulsion differ fundamentally between debris-flow- and flood-dominated alluvial fans. On debris-flow fans, avulsions are particularly difficult to predict because they often result from the highly stochastic formation of channel plugs through in-channel deposition of debris-flow lobes or during individual debris-flow surges. These processes cannot yet be represented by the current generation of numerical debris-flow models. Recent research demonstrates that debris-flow avulsion is controlled by a combination of factors, including the magnitude–frequency distribution of debris flows, grain-size distribution, and the ratio of channel depth to debris-lobe thickness.

In this presentation, I will summarize recent advances in alluvial fan process identification, avulsion mechanisms, and flow path prediction, and discuss how these developments can improve alluvial fan hazard and risk assessments.

title: Quantifying Surface and Groundwater Interactions in the San Acacia Reach, New Mexico
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: Berjaoui, Racha [1], Coyte, Rachel Marylee [2], Rinehart, Alex [3], Cadol, Daniel D. [4]

abstract:
Understanding surface-groundwater interactions in the Middle Rio Grande Basin is required for effective water management. These processes remain poorly defined in the San Acacia Reach, where water losses affect the state's ability to meet Rio Grande Compact deliveries to Elephant Butte Reservoir. Within this reach, the Low Flow Conveyance Channel (LFCC), an engineered drain built to support compact compliance, strongly influences surface and groundwater exchanges. Because it lies below the riverbed, it acts as a sink, and captures water from shallow alluvium, deep basin groundwater, and Rio Grande/irrigation return flow. However, their relative contributions are unresolved. This study quantifies surface-water and groundwater inputs to the LFCC across contrasting seasonal hydrologic conditions.

Five drainage and environmental tracer surveys were conducted along the LFCC and Rio Grande during the 2025 irrigation and monsoon cycle (February – December). Groundwater fluxes to the LFCC were estimated using differential gauging and 222-Rn measurements. Water samples were analyzed for major ions, trace metals, δ18O, δD, and 87Sr/86Sr. A multi-tracer Bayesian mixing model was developed to resolve the contributions of surface water, shallow alluvium, and deep basin groundwater.

δ18O values are depleted during the pre-irrigation (February) season, reflecting snowmelt-dominated river inputs. Chloride concentrations increase in mid-irrigation and mid-monsoon seasons (July and September), indicating a shift toward greater influence of saline groundwater, as cumulative recharge elevates the water table and enhances seepage to the LFCC. During mid-irrigation, the LFCC exhibits a downstream hydrochemical evolution from Ca2+-dominated to Na+-dominated water, reflecting fresher discharge in the upper reach and ion-exchange with aquifer clays in the lower reach. Mid-monsoon (September) samples are marked by sulfate enrichment associated with gypsum dissolution east of the Rio Grande.

Mixing analysis of pre-irrigation through mid-irrigation identifies hydrothermal waters at sites near basin boundaries that account for as much as 22%. Shallow alluvial waters were associated with the main aquifer system and show a system-wide enrichment from 14% to 39% from pre- and early-irrigation to mid-irrigation season. The Rio Grande accounts for as much as 55% throughout the three seasons; however it shows a higher credible interval per sample than the groundwater sources. Our results show that LFCC chemistry responds to seasonal changes in irrigation return flow, monsoon recharge, and basin-scale groundwater.

title: Building a Multiscale Stratigraphic Synthesis Engine at Macrostrat
session_title: Data-driven approaches for aligning geologic information in time
authors: Quinn, Daven P. [1], Fromandi, Amy [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin – Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(2) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin – Madison, Madison, WI, USA
abstract:
Macrostrat (https://macrostrat.org; Peters et al., 2018) is a data system that tracks the fundamental rock units that make up Earth’s crust. At its core is a set of stratigraphic columns that collectively describe regional stratigraphy and form the basis for “macrostratigraphy” (e.g., Peters et al., 2021), a new approach to analyzing the Earth-life system through time. Within Macrostrat, digitally described stratigraphic columns contribute to a multifaceted geologic synthesis engine, allowing other geologic datasets (e.g., stable isotope analyses) to be analyzed alongside their rock record context.

The scale and coverage of stratigraphic columns hosted in Macrostrat limit the application of these synthetic approaches to new geologic systems. Macrostrat’s core stratigraphic dataset, covering North America, was assembled through extensive compilation efforts during the COSUNA project (Childs et al., 1985) and subsequently in Macrostrat. However, the primacy of North American data complicates generalization across the entire Earth system. Relatively coarse spatial and temporal resolution hinders links to high-resolution proxy datasets (e.g., geochronology, biostratigraphy, and geochemistry) and does not capture rapid changes in localized depositional systems due to tectonism and basin dynamics. To address these limitations, Macrostrat contributors are curating regional column datasets covering new geographic areas; in tandem, we are developing tools and processes to incorporate community contributions, particularly high-resolution measured stratigraphy (Quinn et al., 2024).

Here, we present ongoing initiatives to capture high-resolution stratigraphic records into Macrostrat, including deep-sea borehole records (eODP), terrestrial stratigraphic columns associated with geochemical proxy analyses, and published well-log compilations. These new scales of compilation enhance Macrostrat’s alignment with other compilation efforts such as the Sedimentary Geochemistry and Paleoenvironments (SGP) project, the Paleobiology database, and the Geobiodiversity database. New column-ingestion workflows are supported by prototype community-contribution tools, including spreadsheet templates and a web interface for column ingestion and editing.

With high resolution stratigraphy increasingly available to Macrostrat analytical workflows, we can begin to anticipate the task of synthesizing it into updates to Macrostrat’s generalized framework. New editorial approaches will be needed to digitally correlatestratgraphic datasets at different scales; such scientific work must be supported by new ways to view, align, and share digital stratigraphic data. Ultimately, we hope these digital tools and datasets will form a flexible substrate for stratigraphic analysis at all scales, enriching efforts to understand the Earth system through time.

abstract:
Sedimentary ancient DNA ( sed aDNA) provides a powerful tool for reconstructing past marine ecosystems and their responses to climatic variability. Here, we use eukaryotic and foraminiferal sed aDNA from a sediment core in Hornsund, Svalbard, to investigate changes in marine community composition over the last ~1700 years, with particular focus on the Medieval Warm Period (MWP) and Little Ice Age (LIA).

We identify pronounced changes in community structure associated with the transition between these contrasting climatic conditions. During the MWP, communities showed higher diversity and were strongly influenced by diatoms, with a pronounced diversity peak around ~1400 CE. Following the transition toward LIA conditions, diatoms declined and dinoflagellates became dominant, potentially reflecting their greater ecological flexibility under colder and nutrient-limited conditions. Diversity indices also show a relationship with periods of low sunspot activity, suggesting a potential link between solar forcing and marine biodiversity.

The eDNA-derived community trends are further supported by similar patterns in foraminiferal assemblages and a variation of geochemical proxies, demonstrating consistency between molecular and traditional palaeoecological approaches. Warm-water and Atlantic Water-associated taxa, including the blue jellyfish and the copeped Calanus helgolandicus , were also detected during the MWP; these species are currently considered recent arrivals in Svalbard waters.

Our results demonstrate the potential of sed aDNA to reconstruct past Arctic marine ecosystems at decadal scales and reveal ecological responses to natural climatic variability, providing important context for understanding ongoing anthropogenic warming. These shifts in marine community composition are also relevant to carbon burial, as changes in the abundance and composition of primary producers can influence the quantity and quality of organic and inorganic carbon exported to and preserved within marine sediments.

title: Re-analysis and Revision of the Reindeer Hills “Mélange,” South-central Alaska
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Fife, Keelyn Joan [1], Waldien, Trevor Scott [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
abstract:
Rocks in the Reindeer Hills in south central Alaska have been previously interpreted as a Mesozoic subduction channel. Our new mapping, structural analysis, and U-Pb geochronology demonstrate that the rocks in the Reindeer Hills are dominantly interbedded, fine-grained, marine chert and mudstone strata with intact bedding that that generally strikes NE-SW. Volcanic rocks within the sequence yield U-Pb dates of ca. 430 Ma and metasedimentary rocks yield maximum depositional ages of ca. 416 Ma. All strata are folded by an earlier phase of upright folds followed by recumbent folding. Mélange fabrics in the Reindeer Hills are present but limited in extent and show polyphase deformation with left-lateral, right-lateral, and lesser oblique thrust slickenside surfaces. Some slickenside surfaces parallel to the mélange fabric show right-lateral mineral fibers overprinting left-lateral cuspate features, indicating the right-lateral deformation followed the left-lateral deformation. Additionally, ca. 70 Ma dikes crosscut Early Cretaceous (ca. 120 Ma) sedimentary blocks in the left-lateral mélange fabric, but are involved in right-lateral deformation zones, bracketing left-lateral shear to ca. 120-70 Ma and right-lateral shear to post-70 Ma. Detrital zircon U-Pb dating and thin section petrography suggest that the Early Cretaceous sandstone blocks are dismembered fragments of the nearby Kahiltna Assemblage.

Our data collectively indicate that rocks in the Reindeer Hills are unlikely to represent a Mesozoic subduction channel between accreted terranes. Instead, the hills are dominantly underlain by a package of coherently bedded Paleozoic strata with preliminary dates that permit correlation with either the Farewell or Alexander terranes. Mélange fabrics in the Reindeer Hills are restricted to the northwestern section of the hills and record left-lateral shearing of the Paleozoic strata against the Kahiltna Assemblage between 120-70 Ma and reactivation in right-lateral shear since 70 Ma. The new data and associated interpretations suggest that rather than a Mesozoic subduction complex, the Reindeer hills may expose the Broad Pass fault – a cryptic strike-slip fault that has been mapped to the southwest.

abstract:
Over the Phanerozoic Eon, the age of a genus in the fossil record is generally positively associated with its probability of survival into the next stage. However, previous work has shown that mass extinctions have been exceptions to this pattern, with little to no association between extinction risk and genus age in some of the Big Five events. Here we investigate whether patterns of potential extinctions for modern (extant) marine animals are more similar to those of Phanerozoic background extinction or mass extinction stages with respect to genus age selectivity. To evaluate past Phanerozoic stages, we used a dataset of 26,000 genera from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB) and performed logistic regression of extinction status as a function of genus age. For modern genera, we do not yet know whether they will survive or go extinct in the immediate future, so we used IUCN Red List categories to estimate their probability of extinction. We then performed logistic regression of this estimated extinction probability as a function of genus age for 945 marine genera with both an IUCN Red List designation and a fossil record in the PBDB.

We focused on Arthropoda, Chordata, Cnidaria, and Mollusca, as these were the only phyla with sufficient representation in both the PBDB and the IUCN Red List. We thus calculated a logistic regression coefficient for each of these four phyla in each Phanerozoic stage and for modern genera. We then used principal components analysis and cluster analysis on these sets of coefficients to compare modern genera with those in Phanerozoic background and mass extinction stages. We found that estimated age selectivity of modern genera is similar to that of the Changhsingian (end-Permian) and Maastrichtian (end-Cretaceous) stages. In other words, modern extinction threats do not preferentially affect younger genera, as was the case for most Phanerozoic background extinction stages. Rather, modern extinction mechanisms may disproportionately threaten older genera, as was the case in two of the largest mass extinctions in earth history.

title: Erosional modulation of tectonically-controlled shelf-edge migration: Insights from Middle Miocene clinoform successions, Ulleung Basin, East Sea (Japan Sea), Korea
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology (Posters)
authors: CHO, EUNHYUN [1], Song, Hoon-Young [2], Woo, Jusun [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
(2) Domestic Exploration Department, Korea National Oil Corporation, Ulsan, Ulsan, Korea (The Republic of)
(3) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)
abstract:
Shelf-edge evolution in tectonically active basins reflects complex interactions between structural deformation, sea-level change, and sedimentary processes. This study investigates Middle Miocene clinoform successions (14.00-12.50 Ma) in the southwestern Ulleung Basin, East Sea, using 3D seismic data to examine how erosional processes modulate structurally-controlled shelf-edge migration patterns. Eight clinothems were identified, showing cyclic alternations between sigmoidal types (ascending trajectories) and thin-top sigmoidal/oblique types (flat-to-descending trajectories), possibly reflecting high-frequency relative sea-level cycles (4th-5th order). A reverse fault system in the southeast of the study area (DS A) formed monocline structure that created differential accommodation along strike. The structure caused reduced accommodation space favoring oblique clinothems in the uplifted proximal area and maintained more space resulting in thin-top sigmoidal clinothems distally. Conventional tectono-stratigraphic models often predict that such uplift enhances shelf-edge progradation, producing arcuate shelf-edge geometry. However, shelf-edge migration remained relatively linear without enhanced shelf-edge migration toward the reverse fault system, contradicting these established models. The interaction between the structural deformation and erosional processes on the shelf margins explains these shelf-edge behaviours.

The structural deformation (DS A) that controlled clinoform type variation also induced slope oversteepening that promoted erosional features at shelf margins within 20 km of this structure. These erosional depressions formed atop sigmoidal clinothems during early stage of sea-level fall, creating additional accommodation at the shelf margin that moderated shelf-edge advance. This "erosional modulation" process represents a compensatory mechanism where uplift-induced oversteepening creates preferential erosion sites that generate offsetting accommodation, preventing the expected translation of structural deformation into margin architecture. The recurrence of this process across multiple stratigraphic cycles suggests that erosional modulation operates as a persistent architectural control rather than independent random events. These findings provide new insights into how erosional processes can modulate shelf-edge evolution, particularly in tectonically active settings, complementing traditional models that assume direct translation of structural deformation into margin architecture.

title: Divalent Metals and HEPES Buffer Interactions with Mn Oxidation and Oxide Structure Catalyzed by Plectosphaerella cucumerina, an Ascomycete Fungus
