abstract: Plectosphaerella cucumerina DS2psM2a2 is a Mn(II)-oxidizing ascomycete fungus isolated from coal mine drainage treatment ponds that forms highly reactive biogenic manganese oxides (BMOs) capable of scavenging nutrients and toxic metals across environments. This study investigates how divalent trace metals Zn(II), Co(II), and Cd(II), and HEPES pH buffer, affect fungal growth, Mn(II) oxidation, and metal sequestration in solid and aqueous media, using growth assays and inductively coupled optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES). On HEPES‑buffered solid media, Mn(II) generally enhanced or did not impact fungal growth, and the formation of Mn oxides mitigated Cd(II) and Co(II) toxicity to the fungi. Cd(II) had little effect on Mn(II) oxidation, while Co(II) and Zn(II) increasingly inhibited Mn oxide formation at higher concentrations, suggesting interference with a multicopper oxidase‑catalyzed pathway. In buffered aqueous coprecipitation, Mn(II) was fully removed from solution within 14 days, with Zn(II) causing slower Mn(II) removal than Co(II), and both Zn(II) and Co(II) were substantially depleted from solution only when BMOs were present, indicating sequestration by the mycogenic oxides rather than by biomass alone. Future unbuffered experiments and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) analyses at the Argonne National Laboratory are planned to clarify how HEPES and trace metals control Mn oxide speciation, Mn oxide structure, and metal binding mechanisms in this fungal system.

title: The Assembly of Gondwana and Snowball Earth: Tectonic Framework for the Cryogenian Western Margin of the Congo Craton, NW Namibia
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Koran, Isabel [1], Renger, Ellery [2], Macdonald, Francis A. [3], Nelson, Lyle Lee [4], Kylander-Clark, Andrew Robert Cooper [5], Tasistro-Hart, Adrian [6]

abstract: The southwestern corner of the Congo craton in Namibia hosts the prototypical evidence for Snowball Earth—glaciogenic deposits on a low-latitude carbonate-dominated platform. Tectonic accommodation of these successions has previously been attributed to passive-margin subsidence in the wake of rifting of the supercontinent Rodinia. In this model, wide ocean basins to the west and the south endured until middle Ediacaran arc accretion, followed by late Ediacaran to early Cambrian continent-continent collisions that arrayed the Río de la Plata, São Francisco, and Kalahari cratons around Congo. Alternatively, Cryogenian strata accumulated within an accretionary setting, associated with closure of an ocean basin along the western Congo margin. The two tectonic models make specific predictions regarding the timing and sources of sediment delivery to the margin, which we test using new detailed mapping and detrital zircon geochronology. In a series of east–west transects, we document the emergence of a middle Cryogenian shelf–slope transition inboard of the thick-skinned Ediacaran Sesfontein Thrust, linking distal parautochthonous sections to the west with well-studied epicratonic platform strata to the east of the thrust fault. Utilizing this stratigraphic correlation and age model, we show that widespread deep-marine mafic volcanism on attenuated continental crust shortly preceded deposition of the Sturtian Chuos Formation. A small but persistent population of latest Tonian detrital zircon grains (~6% of total) appears in the overlying Sturtian strata. Above, middle–late Cryogenian deposits capture a shift in detrital zircon provenance to dominantly late Neoproterozoic sources. We attribute the mafic volcanism to late Tonian to early Cryogenian extension induced by backarc rifting above an east-dipping subduction zone, consistent with the presence of contemporaneous supra-subduction ophiolite belts (Charrua Ocean) described in southernmost Brazil and Uruguay. Middle Cryogenian closure of this backarc basin delivered sediment from the Coastal Terrane volcanic arc (now an allochthon in northwestern Namibia), accommodating the Marinoan Snowball Earth deposits within a retroarc foreland basin. This evolution long preceded renewed foreland subsidence and sedimentation in the late Ediacaran that was driven by Pan-African–Brasiliano continent-continent collision and orogenesis.

title: An integration of impact tectonics with plate tectonics: A case study of MAPCIS
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics
authors: Connelly, Daniel Patrick [1]

abstract: The MAPCIS structure in Australia offers a potential example of how large impact events may interact with plate tectonic systems. The Precambrian to Cambrian boundary interval records rapid changes in plate velocities and lithospheric architecture. MAPCIS, as a large impact structure, provides a framework for evaluating whether high‑energy surface events can influence crustal strength as well as craton movement. Geophysical and structural observations across the MAPCIS region reveal deep crustal disturbance consistent with a large transient cavity and modification stage, including circular regional geometry, deep crustal brecciation, rifting, anomalous gravity and magnetic signatures. When integrated with plate reconstructions, MAPCIS aligns with a major lithospheric boundary activity. This case study highlights how incorporating impact tectonics into plate tectonic models may help explain abrupt changes in plate velocities, enhanced margin subsidence, and early Paleozoic basin formation. MAPCIS illustrates the potential for large impacts to modulate or initiate tectonic behavior during a critical transition in Earth’s geodynamic evolution.

abstract: Eukaryotic life entered a key period of diversification and ecological expansion during the early Tonian. Molecular clocks suggest major eukaryotic clades emerged by 1,000 million years ago (Ma), and cholestane biomarkers in marine sedimentary rocks indicate the subsequent rise of red algae as primary producers. However, direct evidence from fossil eukaryotes is limited between the emergence of eukaryotic algae at ca. 1,000 Ma (e.g., Proterocladus ) and the apparent diversification of eukaryotes in fossiliferous later Tonian deposits, such as the Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon. Although previous reconnaissance work from the Dodo Creek Formation, an ~57.5-meter-thick succession in the Mackenzie Mountains of northwestern Canada, yielded well-preserved microfossils, these strata have remained understudied. Here, we report new Re-Os geochronological data from the overlying Stone Knife Formation that refines the minimum age of the Dodo Creek Formation to ca. 860 Ma, with its maximum age estimated at <1,005 Ma based on detrital zircon U-Pb data in the underlying Katherine Group. Within Dodo Creek mudstones, we report a new assemblage of exceptionally preserved microfossils, including diverse acritarchs and filamentous forms. Particularly informative from this assemblage is a potential coenobial green alga that displays an architecture that has implications for understanding both the diversification of early algal morphologies and ecologies, and how predation may have contributed to driving eukaryote evolution during the Tonian. The Dodo Creek biota refines constraints on eukaryote evolution during the poorly resolved early Tonian interval, reinforcing the notion that eukaryote-rich ecosystems were already well established by this time.

abstract: Mesoscale fractures, with lengths between meters and tens of meters, cannot be effectively characterized in the subsurface, due to limitations of borehole and geophysical datasets. On the other hand, large quantitative structural datasets can be collected on outcrops by combining direct observations and remote sensing (digital outcrop models DOMs). These data can be used to constrain geometrical models of subsurface fracture networks with the outcrop analogue approach. In this contribution we present a workflow that leverages DOMs with at least two perpendicular faces and combines multiple types of input data (point cloud, textured surfaces and orthophoto DOMs), to collect a suite of statistical parameters to be used as input in current stochastic 3D DFN (Discrete Fracture Network) models. Orientation data are collected with a semi-automatic procedure applied to point cloud DOMs of the vertical side of the outcrop to extract 2D polygonal facets. Fracture sets are defined with a clustering procedure and different orientation distributions are fitted and tested with goodness-of-fit tests. Fracture traces are digitized on textured surface or orthophoto DOMs. Topological parameters are calculated on the digitized fracture network on horizontal and vertical orthomosaics, also considering relationships between fractures and bedding. Trace length and height distributions are estimated with an innovative approach, accounting for the censoring bias with survival/reliability analysis. P21 (ratio between total fracture length and sampling area) is measured from traces digitized on the large horizontal outcrop, also allowing for the Representative Elementary Area (REA) to be assessed. Even if the height/length ratio cannot be measured on an outcrop by any means, we attempt to relate heights and lengths under the assumption that the two datasets are correlated, with the longest fractures being also the tallest. We discuss the applicability of our workflow on a large highquality fractured limestone outcrop in the Murge Plateau near Altamura (Puglia, Italy).

title: Microperthitic Lamellae-Bearing Bands in Alkali Feldspar Megacrysts
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics (Posters)
authors: Seo, Youngdeok [1], Song, Yungoo [2], Chung, Donghoon [3], Park, Chaewon [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth System Sciences, Yonsei University, Seoul, Korea (The Republic of)

abstract:
The syenitic intrusive body in the Seosan area of the Korean Peninsula is characterized by abundant alkali feldspar megacrysts approximately 1–2 cm in size. These megacrysts exhibit distinctive internal microstructures that have not been observed in the surrounding coeval syenitic bodies.

The alkali feldspar megacrysts generally consist of three structural domains: a core, an intermediate zone, and a rim. The intermediate zone surrounding the core contains several to over ten recurrent bands that broadly follow the crystal morphology. Although these bands resemble conventional oscillatory zoning, they contain albite-rich lamellae approximately 1 μm thick, which are regularly arranged with consistent orientations, morphologies, and spacing. These microperthitic lamellae-bearing bands alternate with lamella-free bands that have near-end-member K-feldspar compositions. The K-rich bands also contain approximately 1–2 wt% Ba. An irregular patch perthite is developed in the outermost rim of the crystals. This patch perthite crosscuts or overprints the pre-existing compositional zoning and consists of domains with compositions close to the K-feldspar and albite end-members.

These microperthitic lamellae-bearing bands are known to form through exsolution during progressive cooling, following the development of oscillatory zoning during crystal growth. In contrast, the patch perthite in the outermost rim suggests that it formed through reaction and replacement involving residual melt or late-stage hydrothermal fluids during the final stages of crystal evolution.

This study aims to systematically analyze the microtextures and quantitative chemical compositions of alkali feldspar megacrysts in order to elucidate the distinctive internal structures observed in the intrusion and their formation processes. It will also investigate the crystallization conditions and tectonic setting that may have contributed to the development of these microstructures.

abstract:
U-Pb geochronology of low-U minerals by laser ablation ICP-MS has vastly expanded capabilities to date a wide variety of rock types. This has implications for the study of tectonics in general, and specifically of ore deposits, critical minerals, and petroleum systems. Three examples from recent undergraduate research exemplify the approaches, successes and challenges of applying low-U to mineral deposit and petroleum systems.

U-Pb dating of a complex network of calcite veins (some showing evidence for oil as blue UV fluorescence) in the Permian Cutoff Formation in the western Delaware Basin of SE New Mexico was combined with fluid inclusion data. The calcite veins yield dates from ca. 240 Ma to ca. 9.5 Ma, coinciding with times of maximum burial and late extension and unroofing. With this repeated deformation and fluid flow comes the challenge of discerning which parts of the vein network belongs to which generation, e.g. veins of the same orientation yield different dates, some veins contain different calcite generations.

Andradite garnet is a major mineral in the Eagle Point tungsten mining claim in the Little Hatchet Mountains of southwestern New Mexico. It forms large, spectacular concentrically zoned crystals, along with magnetite, scheelite, diopside, epidote and calcite. Four samples yield identical dates with a wt. mean of 38.9±1.0 Ma for the mineralization, most likely connected to activity of the Granite Pass fault, crosscut by a 33 Ma Rapakivi granite.

The Magnet Cove igneous complex in Arkansas is known for its unique mineral specimen. Several rock types contain black schorlomitic garnets that yield well-behaved laser ablation discordia arrays. Garnets from one of them, from a former magnetite quarry are currently being tested as potential U-Pb reference materials by high-precision TIMS. The challenge for U-Pb garnet dating is that U-Pb fractionation factors obtained from discordia arrays of currently available reference materials scatter, which limits precision and accuracy and needs further investigation.

In summary, applications of a wide variety of low-U chronometers (also fluorite, anhydrite etc.) will enable us to more fully understand the history of ore and petroleum deposits, but need combination with other datasets, detailed petrographic, and well-characterized reference materials.

abstract:
The origin of ancestral normal-sense shear fabrics preserved within metamorphic core complexes (MCCs) remains a fundamental unresolved problem in continental tectonics. Although regional extension was responsible for the final exhumation of MCCs throughout the North American Cordillera and Alpine–Himalayan belt, the tectonic processes responsible for their pre-extensional evolution remain debated. Here we show that upper amphibolite-facies migmatites exposed at the deepest structural levels of the Naxos (Aegean) and western Arizona metamorphic core complexes record clockwise pressure–temperature–time paths, demonstrating that they formed during crustal shortening, thickening and partial melting prior to regional extension. Both localities also preserve shallowly plunging, unidirectional normal-sense shear fabrics associated with isothermal decompression that are structurally discordant to the younger detachment faults responsible for final MCC exhumation.

On Naxos, deformation and metamorphism progressed diachronously down the structural section during continued convergence. Following high-pressure metamorphism of the Cycladic Blueschists at ca. 50 Ma, the underthrust continental margin underwent kyanite-grade metamorphism (0.8–1.0 GPa, 600–750°C) between ca. 24–18 Ma. Subsequent isothermal decompression through the muscovite dehydration melting reaction to sillimanite-grade conditions (0.5–0.6 GPa, ~730°C) between ca. 17–14 Ma was accompanied by top-NNE normal-sense shear zones that were later uprightly folded and cross-cut by the extensional detachment responsible for rapid MCC cooling after ca. 15 Ma.

In the Harcuvar–Harquahala–Granite Wash Mountains of western Arizona, the origin of these ancestral shear fabrics is more clearly preserved. Late Cretaceous migmatites recording ca. 0.75 GPa and 780°C were tectonically emplaced above greenschist-facies rocks recording ca. 0.35 GPa and 500°C by southwest-directed thrusting, producing an inverted metamorphic field gradient that juxtaposes crustal levels originally separated by ~15 km, whereas top-NE normal-sense shear zones occur at higher structural levels. U–Pb zircon, U–Th–Pb monazite and in-situ Rb–Sr geochronology demonstrate that peak metamorphism, water-fluxed partial melting, southwest-directed thrusting and top-NE shearing were synchronous between ca. 76–70 Ma, while cross-cutting granitoids show that thrusting propagated upward during continued shortening. The coincidence of Farallon flat-slab subduction and widespread crustal melting indicates that slab-derived fluids induced water-fluxed melting, reducing lower-crustal viscosity and facilitating syn-convergent ductile extrusion. We conclude that ancestral normal-sense shear fabrics preserved within MCCs are inherited roof shear zones of weak, partially molten extrusion channels formed during crustal shortening, rather than recording an earlier phase of regional extension.

title: Variable delta-plain channel mobility during coastal transgression
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Chun, Byong-suk [1], Steel, Elisabeth [2], Steel, Ronald [3]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences and Geological Engineering, Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada
(2) Geological Sciences and Geological Engineering, Queen's University, Kingston, ON, Canada

abstract: River-dominated delta plains are continually shaped by movement of distributary channels (i.e., channel migration and avulsion). The long-term sustainability of these plains therefore depends largely on channel regulation of the distributed water and sediment. On prograding, fan-shaped delta plains, this regulation is expressed through gradual channel migration and repeated autogenic channel re-routing (avulsion), resulting in the construction of delta lobes beyond the shoreline as the river delta builds basinward. However, there has been less attention paid to the details of variable channel migration rates during the systematic landward retreat of river deltas. Here we present experimental observations detailing seven successive avulsions and channel migration associated with overall landward shoreline retreat. By utilizing an adapted Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) to map channel bank migration vector fields, we quantify channel migration rates during aggradation between these avulsion events. Physical modelling was conducted in a 3.8 ´ 3.8 m basin at the Queen’s University Coastal and Deepwater Sediment Laboratory using a cohesive sediment mixture. Over the 300-hour experiment, base level was raised by a total of 150 mm while sediment and water discharge were held constant. Under these conditions, the upstream migration of in-channel deposition dominated the delta plain, modulating channel mobility and causing nodal avulsions at the delta apex. Between successive nodal avulsions, delta plains evolved through a recurring four-phase sequence with variable duration: (1) sediment bypass through the main distributary channel, driving mouth-bar growth and shoreline progradation; (2) landward migration of in-channel deposition within the main distributary; (3) extensive delta-plain aggradation through high channel mobility driven by in-channel deposition; and (4) reorganization of smaller delta-plain channels prior to establishment of a new single main channel. Our preliminary results suggest that: 1) periods of elevated lateral channel migration rates occur during punctuated shoreline transgression, whereas low migration rates occur during regressive shoreline pulses, and 2) spatio-temporal variability in channel mobility directly correlates with aggradation rates across the delta plain.

title: Depositional Regimes: An Intermediate Framework to Local and Basinwide Stratigraphy
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections (Posters)
authors: Senderoff, Preston [1], Ouimet, William B. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut - College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, Storrs, Connecticut, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut - College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, Storrs, CT,
abstract:
Nearshore coastal deposits form across a broad range of spatiotemporal scales, and no current framework relates the local responses a single sedimentary archive preserves to the regional history the basin records. Furthermore, sequence-stratigraphic facies do not extend to the subregional and local dynamics that dominate unconsolidated deposits; per-describer site-stratigraphic units conform to no recognized framework; and soil science does not incorporate process-geomorphology. Therefore, correlating site-specific units between cores demands a justification these established frameworks cannot supply.

To bridge this gap, we have developed a progressively coarsening refinement chain: four tiers and three refinement steps, each relating otherwise unique elements under a broader class of dynamics. Cores are describer-authored sedimentary archives that are often recorded at the finest level through horizons or beds. These units resolve into depositional settings against the national bank of parent-material kinds ( Field Book for Describing and Sampling Soils, v4 ). A small, falsifiable set of stratigraphic rules groups related settings into depositional packages , each derived package admitting one national process group. Adjacent packages conceding the same group coalesce into emergent depositional regimes . Each tier is a coarsening of the one below so that any two blocks are nested or disjoint. At the final tier, preserved depositional regimes across all cores describe the partial orders of a region’s total stratigraphic superposition.

Applied to 713 nearshore cores from the 2022-2024 USDA-NRCS Long Island Sound – Coastal Zone Soil Survey, the chain places four process-defined emergent states, recognizes two recurring but too sparsely to place, and identifies one bearing no superpositional relation to that order. Each core contributes a local partial order to the regional totally ordered superposition; for the Connecticut data, that is glacial, eolian, organic, and waterlaid deposits.

Overall, our approach shows that in the limit of a totally-driven region — one where core recovery consumes every reach — the partial order observed in any real corpus of cores would emerge as a subset of the region’s totally ordered superpositional chain. Applying the order-extension principle (Szpilrajn, 1930) to stratigraphy makes regional correlation of unconsolidated deposits an emergent property of the dataset itself and shows that sediment cores preserve a net-depositional, process-filtered partial of the total stratigraphic superposition of the region from which they were collected.

abstract: The definition of a representative elementary volume (REV) or area (REA) for a target parameter is a fundamental step toward the upscaling of fracture network properties generated by discrete fracture network models (DFN) to an equivalent continuous medium for in situ applications in engineering geology, hydrogeology, and structural geology. The target parameter of this work is the areal fracture intensity (P21), a key metric often used as a stopping criterion in stochastic DFN simulations, that is derived directly from surface data collected at natural outcrops. We propose a novel approach to define the REA as a range bounded by a lower and an upper limit. The upper limit, often overlooked but nonetheless theorized, identifies the largest representative domain, which is crucial for optimizing computational efficiency. We evaluate the REA range based on three statistical parameters, namely: the shape, mean, and variance of the P21 distributions obtained with progressively increasing scan area sizes. Each statistical parameter is assessed by combining formal statistical tests and diagnostic plots. Within a multi-parametric framework, the method enables a detailed analysis of the statistical behaviour of the dataset, supporting informed decisions in defining the REA range. The methodology is tested on two fractured limestone outcrops with markedly different characteristics: (i) an abandoned quarry in the Murge Plateau (Puglia, Italy) and (ii) the Lilstock Benches in the southern Bristol Channel basin.

title: The Late Pennsylvanian time scale conundrum
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Posters)
authors: Laurin, Jiří [1], Opluštil, Stanislav [2], Davydov, Vladimir I. [3], Weislogel, Amy L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Geophysics, Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic, Prague, Czech Republic

abstract: The Late Pennsylvanian (307–299 Ma) represents a phase of major climatic and biotic perturbations associated with the final expansion of late Paleozoic ice sheets. A rich spectrum of sedimentary and paleontological records, including the iconic cyclothems of the U.S. basins, is constrained by both radioisotopic and astrochronological data within a conodont biostratigraphic framework. These conditions make the Late Pennsylvanian one of the most promising targets for studies of paleoclimate mechanisms in an icehouse climate. Recent advances in biostratigraphy and geochronology, however, raise new questions regarding the prospect of developing a detailed, integrated time scale. A million-year-scale mismatch is identified between published radioisotopic dates from the Urals and Donbas and a high-resolution astronomical time scale from South China (Naqing). We will evaluate possible solutions including a diachroneity of one of the key biostratigraphic markers (first occurrence of Swadelina subexcelsa ), condensation or hiatuses in the radioisotopically calibrated sections, and distortion of the astronomical signal. The most plausible ages for the candidate GSSP markers of the Middle/Late Pennsylvanian (Moscovian/Kasimovian) boundary will be proposed. The results should help to refine the timing of key events such as the Desmoinesian/Missourian vegetation turnover, astronomical-scale CO 2 perturbations, and glacioeustatic records of the U.S. Midcontinent, Illinois and Appalachian basins.

title: QG&G Career Award: A Multi-Million-Year History of Arctic Surface Processes and Landscape Evolution Preserved Under Greenland’s Ice and Beneath North Atlantic Waters
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Bierman, Paul R [1], Shakun, Jeremy [2], Corbett, Lee [3]
affiliations: (1) Rubenstein School of the Environment and Natural Resources, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
(2) Boston College, Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chestnut Hill, MA, USA
(3) University of Vermont, Burlington, VT,
abstract:
As the Arctic rapidly warms, understanding the geomorphic response of cold-region landscapes is critical for protecting communities and the ecosystems of which they are part. In this talk, I describe how sampling and multidisciplinary analysis of two geologic archives––frozen water and sediment from beneath Greenland’s ice sheet and deep marine sediment from around the island––allow our team to understand the processes and timing of landscape change over millions of years as the climate warmed and cooled.

Using measurements of in situ cosmogenic 10 Be and 26 Al in 97 samples collected from 4 marine sediment cores, we find that pre-glacial regolith, indicative of a stable but unglaciated landscape, was progressively stripped by glaciation over millions of years. During the last 5 million years, nuclide concentrations and 26 Al/ 10 Be ratios are low in glacially derived sediment around Greenland, indicating that sediment source areas were routinely ice-covered and only rarely exposed to surface processes and thus cosmic radiation. Our results suggest that some of the Greenland Icesheet is often, but not exclusively, stable in a warmer world, highlighting the need to better understand what factors control its fate, both in the past and today.

Isotopic, geochemical, and physical analysis of sub-ice material collected at Camp Century (1966, NW Greenland) provide a deeper understanding of geomorphic processes when the ice is gone from a single point on the landscape. Cosmogenic nuclide and OSL data reveal a land surface free of ice during MIS 11 (~ 400 ka) for between 8,000 and 14,000 years and that the upper part of the soil profile (~40 cm) was well stirred. Interstitial porewater extracted from the sub-ice core contains up to 100 mg/L Ca 2+ with lesser concentrations of Mg 2+ >Na + >K + indicating, along with the presence of kaolinite, that weathering was actively leaching cations from minerals. The sub-ice material contains well preserved parts of tundra plants, mosses, fungi, and insects indicating a matrix of surface environments – some dry, some moist, some rocky, some disturbed under July mean temperatures between 1 and 10 o C. CT scans reveal sedimentary structures and ice-filled cracks consistent with permafrost cryoturbation of surface environments.

Together, these data indicate the power of multidisciplinary analysis of multiple, different sedimentary archives to understand geomorphic processes and landscape change over time.

title: Physical Mechanisms Linking Glacial Cycles to Magma Storage and Transport in Continental Arcs
session_title: Volcano-climate interactions
authors: Townsend, Meredith [1], Moreno-Yaeger, Pablo [2], Harp, Andrew [3], Huber, Christian [4], Singer, Brad [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Lehigh University, Bethlehem, PA, USA
(2) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, California State University, Chico, Chico, CA, USA
(4) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
(5) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI,
abstract:
Growing evidence indicates that glacial cycles influence volcanic activity. In Iceland, ocean island arcs, and along the mid-ocean ridge system, surface loading can modulate mantle melting rates through isostatic adjustment and decompression. In contrast, continental arc volcanoes are underlain by much thicker lithosphere, limiting the direct influence of glacial cycles on mantle melting. Nevertheless, an expanding body of observations indicates that glaciation can affect not only eruption timing and volume, but also magma composition, eruption style, and the conditions of crustal magma storage.

Here, we present a case study from the Andean Southern Volcanic Zone that illuminates the physical mechanisms by which glacial loading can influence magma transport and storage within continental arc crust. Physics-based models suggest that magma reservoir failure is relatively insensitive to the modest crustal stress changes produced by glacial loading. Dike propagation, however, is substantially more sensitive to these stress perturbations. Topographically controlled variations in ice thickness generate crustal stress “pinch points” that discourage dike ascent from lower-crustal storage zones, thereby reducing magma recharge to shallower reservoirs. This mechanism provides a physical basis for observed glacial-cycle changes in eruption rate, eruption style, magma composition, and magma storage depths at volcanoes in the southern Andes.

title: Mass extinction but not rapid climate change drives permanent ecological state changes in marine fish communities
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Sibert, Elizabeth C. [1], Fagan, William [2], Swain, Anshuman [3]
affiliations: (1) Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Woods Hole, MA, USA
(2) Department of Biology, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA
(3) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI,
abstract: Human impacts on marine systems – from over-fishing to rapid climate change – have the potential to have profound and perhaps irreversible impacts on marine ecosystems. Modern ecosystems can exhibit ecological hysteresis, switching between states along an environmental change that are not reversible along the same environmental axis, hinting that there may be processes driving long-term ecological stability. Dynamic systems theory suggests that ecosystems should exhibit periods of stability marked by rapid transitions between stable states, but to date, there are very few empirical datasets that have sufficient temporal scope to capture these predicted ecological dynamics. Here, we demonstrate that despite only approximately 5% of fish tooth morphotypes going extinct at the end of the Cretaceous, the extinction marks the transition between two distinct stable states: the Late Cretaceous and Eocene, with a directed transitional ecological phase in the Paleocene. This dataset, which spans 75-42 Ma in the South Pacific Gyre, fulfills the five quantitative criteria required in dynamic systems theory to be considered “true” stable states: compositional distinctness, statistical separation, differential attractor geometry, directed transitional dynamics, and irreversibility over the entire record. These patterns are robust when accounting for evolutionary drift by considering the community composition based on large-scale morphological groups, which can be interpreted as ecological guilds, rather than individual morphotypes. The long-term stable state observed in the Eocene spans several major climatic events of the Paleogene, including short term warming events such as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum and other Early Paleogene hyperthermals, as well as long-term warming and cooling of the Early Eocene Climate Optimum, suggesting that at this scale, ecological stability is robust to both rapid and long-term climate perturbations, but can be disrupted by major extinction events, even when the total extinction is quite small. These results suggest that selective removal of specific parts of the pelagic ecosystem - including overfishing of large predators from whales to sharks to tunas and billfishes, may have a far more destabilizing impact on pelagic fish community stability than the rapid warming driven by anthropogenic activities.

title: Crystallographic preferred orientations in several distinct generations of brittle fractures along the Iron Mountain fault, southwest Virginia
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics
authors: Levine, Jamie S. F. [1], Casale, Gabriele M. [2], Tripp, Gerald R. [3], Merschat, Arthur James [4]
affiliations: (1) Appalachian State University, Boone, NC,
(2) Boone, NC,
(4) United States Geological Survey, Zionville, NC,
abstract:
Brittle fault rocks are typically characterized by zones of cataclasis and gouge, with angular fragments, a range of grain sizes, and an absence of a crystallographic preferred orientation (CPO). However, in recent years there have been an increasing number of studies that record a CPO in seemingly brittle fault rocks. The majority of these studies come from natural fault zones within limestones or experimental studies deforming calcite. A few studies have instead focused on quartz and propose the c-axis CPO may result from pressure solution and dissolution, grain boundary sliding, preferential growth in the extension direction, or a component of plasticity.

We collected samples from the NW-dipping Iron Mountain fault, a folded thrust fault at the leading edge of the Blue Ridge thrust sheet in southwestern Virginia, and document several CPOs in fine-grained (grain diameters ≤ 8 µm) quartz. Samples within the fault zone contain several generations of fractures, many of which are bounded by pressure solution seams, but contain different morphologies, grain sizes, and CPOs. We conducted an optical and electron backscatter diffraction investigation of quartz located within fracture zones that are filled with highly comminuted material in several samples from the Iron Mountain fault. We made detailed electron backscatter diffraction maps, with step sizes of 0.1-0.25 µm, to fully characterize the shape, orientation, and grain size of the finest grained fraction.

Our observations do not universally support any single deformation mechanism. We document one fracture zone with angular grains, grain sizes ranging from < 1 µm-50 µm in diameter, and a quartz c-axis pole figure that displays a girdle plotting between the Y and Z axes. In a fracture zone oriented parallel to the extension direction of the fault, we document dominantly equigranular, rounded and faceted grains with some 120˚ triple junctions, a uniform grain size of 5-30 µm in diameter, and a quartz c-axis point maximum that plots on the perimeter of the pole figure. We propose that different fractures within the same fault rock or fault zone can have different deformation mechanisms, and find evidence for different CPOs which we selectively attribute to preferential growth in the extension direction, pressure solution, and grain boundary sliding.

title: Integrated Planktonic Foraminiferal Bio- and Chemostratigraphy across the Mid-Cenomanian Event 1 (MCE 1): Contrasting Paleoenvironmental Responses in the Tethyan Vergons and Boreal Folkestone Sections

authors: Petrizzo, Maria Rose [1], Jarvis, Ian [2], Gale, Andrew [3], Grocke, Darren R [4], Kennedy, William J. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Milan, Italy, Milan, Italy
(2) Department of Geography, Geology and the Environment, Kingston University London, Kingston upon Thames, Surrey, United Kingdom
(3) School of the Environment, Geography and Geological Sciences, University of Portsmouth, Portsmouth, United Kingdom; Earth Science Department, Natural History Museum London, London, United Kingdom
(4) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Durham, Durham, , United Kingdom
(5) Museum of Natural History, Oxford University, Oxford, United Kingdom
abstract:
Mid-Cenomanian Event 1 (MCE 1) is a globally recognized positive carbon-isotope (δ¹³C) excursion of about +1‰ during the middle Cenomanian (Late Cretaceous). Characterized by a distinctive double-peaked δ¹³C pattern (peaks a and b), MCE 1 has been recognized in marine and terrestrial successions worldwide and records major perturbations of the global carbon cycle, ocean circulation, biological productivity, and ocean oxygenation.

This study documents a new record of MCE 1 from the expanded Vergons section (Vocontian Basin, SE France), focusing on planktonic foraminiferal assemblages and their paleoenvironmental significance. The middle Cenomanian succession is constrained through correlation with the Blieux section in the Vocontian Basin using ammonites, inoceramids, and stable isotopes, and with the Folkestone section (SE England), where comparable planktonic foraminiferal, macrofossil, and isotope records are available. Quantitative analyses of planktonic foraminifera, integrated with δ¹³C and δ¹⁸O data, allow comparison of MCE 1 across the Tethyan and Boreal realms.

Both sections span the upper Thalmanninella globotruncanoides , T. greenhornensis , and lower Rotalipora cushmani Zones. Planktonic foraminifera are continuously present, moderately well preserved, and comprise 40–50% of the total assemblage. Both records document the appearance of double-keeled Dicarinella species and diversification within the Rotalipora lineage from R. montsalvensis to R. cushmani , indicating rapid evolutionary turnover among single-keeled oligotrophic taxa.

Regional differences, however, are pronounced. At Folkestone, MCE 1 is marked by a temporary decline of oligotrophic Rotalipora and an increase in mesotrophic taxa, suggesting weakened water-column stratification and thermocline disruption. In contrast, rotaliporids persist throughout the Vergons section, while the earlier appearance of R. cushmani indicates accelerated evolution with limited ecological stress.

Integrated micropaleontological, isotopic, and sedimentological data reveal contrasting environmental responses. At Folkestone, cooling episodes during peak a and below peak b coincide with positive δ¹⁸O excursions and Boreal macrofaunal horizons, indicating incursions of cold, low-salinity Boreal waters into the Anglo-Paris Basin. Enhanced mixing likely increased nutrient availability and primary productivity, contributing to the δ¹³C excursion. At Vergons, similar δ¹⁸O cooling signals occur without Boreal macrofauna or evidence of strong vertical mixing. Its upper-slope position along the western Tethyan margin suggests only a distal Boreal influence, producing a weaker productivity response and limited ecological impact.

abstract: Karst aquifers are highly vulnerable to contamination because of their hydrologic connectivity to surface environments through sinkholes, losing streams, and well-developed conduit networks. Despite the growing recognition of microplastics as emerging contaminants, their occurrence in karst features remains poorly characterized, particularly in the extensive karst terrains of the midwestern United States. This study therefore investigates the distribution, abundance, and characteristics of microplastics in springs and cave streams in the Mitchell Plateau of southern Indiana, a region characterized by its extensive karst topography and unique subterranean ecosystems. Water and sediment samples were collected from perennial springs and cave streams at Orangeville Rise, Wesley Chapel Gulf, and seven sites within Spring Mill State Park. Water samples were analyzed for geochemical parameters (e.g., specific conductivity, turbidity, and nitrate), sediment samples were analyzed for grain size distributions, and both sample types were analyzed for microplastics. Suspected microplastics were classified by their size, morphology, and color using microscopy. Microplastics were detected in both environmental compartments at every site, with clear fibers as the dominant color-morphology combination. Microplastic concentrations in karst water samples ranged 10-45 counts/kg. Their highest abundances occurred at Orangeville Rise and the touristed section of Donaldson Cave, suggesting that human presence near these features may enhance microplastic concentrations in the water. Water microplastic concentrations also increased downstream through the connected Twin Caves, Bronson Cave, and Donaldson Cave system. Preliminary analyses of sediment demonstrate microplastic concentrations ~2.5 orders of magnitude higher than those measured in water samples, with a range of 5313-6672 counts/kg. Sediment microplastic concentrations along with other water contaminants (e.g., nitrate) decreased downstream through the connected cave system. Contrasting downstream trends in nitrate, suspended microplastics, and sediment microplastics indicate differing behavior of particulate contaminants compared to dissolved solutes in karst conduit systems, emphasizing the importance of considering transport and storage processes that are unique to microplastics. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that microplastics are ubiquitous in the Mitchell Plateau karst system, sediment contains more microplastics than water, and microplastic concentrations in water and sediment exhibit contrasting downstream trends, suggesting that different transport and storage mechanisms govern their distribution. The widespread occurrence of microplastics in springs and cave streams highlights the vulnerability of karst aquifers to emerging contaminants and establishes a regional baseline for future groundwater monitoring.

title: Stratigraphic paleobiology of nonmarine vertebrates following the final regression of the Western Interior Seaway in the Bighorn Basin (Wyoming, USA)
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Sweedler, Rory Elizabeth [1], Loughney, Katharine M [2], Tobin, Thomas S. [3], Davis, Ethan Stone [4], Farke, Andrew A. [5], Weaver, Lucas Nile [6]
affiliations: (1) Museum of Paleontology & Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences and Watershed Studies Institute, Murray State University, Murray, KY, USA
(3) Geological Sciences, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA; Alabama Museum of Natural History, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA

(5) Alf Museum of Paleontology at The Webb Schools, Claremont, CA, USA

abstract:
The Western Interior of North America is arguably the best record of terrestrial ecosystems approaching the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction (KPME) in the world; however, whether these ecosystems were stressed or thriving prior to the KPME remains controversial. In part, this uncertainty is related to the coeval final regression of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) which altered sedimentation patterns in the Western Interior. Microfossil bonebeds provide the most detailed window into vertebrate community structure in the Late Cretaceous, yet the local paleo-communities preserved and the bonebeds' genesis, abundance, and preservation are likely influenced by stratigraphy.

In the Bighorn Basin of northwestern Wyoming, the “Mesaverde,” Meeteetse, and Lance formations host nonmarine microfossil bonebeds spanning the early Campanian to latest Maastrichtian (ca. 83–66 Ma), providing an opportunity to investigate the influence of stratigraphy on microfossil bonebeds at the basin scale. Here, we present new stratigraphic sections measured through Upper Cretaceous strata from east to west across the Bighorn Basin, contextualizing vertebrate microfossil occurrences during the final regression of the WIS. The “Mesaverde” Formation (likely genetically distinct from the type section in Colorado) primarily consists of prograding offshore, shoreface, and nearshore tidal deposits. Most “Mesaverde” localities are preserved in marginal-marine lags. The Meeteetse Formation consists of isolated channel sandstones, hydromorphic paleosols, low-grade coals, and bentonites, likely representing a high-aggradation setting. The Lance Formation exhibits abundant multistory channel sandstones and scarce carbonaceous beds. Unlike those in the “Mesaverde” Formation, microfossil bonebeds in the Meeteetse and Lance formations occur in a wider variety of nonmarine depositional environments, including channel lags, abandoned channel fills, and pedogenically altered carbonaceous shales. Our preliminary results suggest stratigraphic stacking patterns do influence microfossil bonebed formation and constituency approaching the KPME: (i) “Mesaverde” bonebeds may represent significant time averaging between marine and nonmarine environments, (ii) Meeteetse bonebeds may more closely approximate paleocommunities due to high sediment accumulation, and (iii) Meeteetse and Lance bonebeds become increasingly dominated by terrestrial taxa upsection, potentially preserving an elevational gradient.

title: Microplastic Distribution, Abundance, and Characteristics in Belizean Surface Water and Groundwater Systems
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Landsman, Eli S. [1], Hasenmueller, Elizabeth A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Geospatial Science, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, MO, USA; WATER Institute, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, MO, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Geospatial Science, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, MO, USA; WATER Institute, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, MO, USA
abstract: The global prevalence of microplastic contamination in hydrologic systems is a growing concern for human and ecosystem health. However, few studies have addressed the movement and characteristics of microplastics across environmental settings, especially in tropical and developing regions with limited environmental monitoring infrastructure. This project therefore characterized microplastic concentrations across a diverse range of Belizean surface water and groundwater systems to establish baseline conditions, investigate the distribution of microplastics across interconnected tropical aquatic ecosystems, and advance our understanding of plastic pollution in an understudied biodiversity hotspot. Sampling sites encompassed a broad geographic and hydrologic range across Belize, including tidal creeks, freshwater streams, lagoons, wetlands, caves, and urban canals. Water samples were collected in glass bottles and transported to the United States for filtration through 0.45-µm cellulose membrane filters. Microscopy and established identification criteria were used to distinguish microparticles of anthropogenic origin from naturally occurring materials. These suspected microplastics were then characterized by their size, shape, and color and mounted on microscope slides for future material classification efforts with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy. Microplastics were detected in nearly all water samples, with a concentration average and standard deviation of 4.1±8.5 counts/L and range of 0.0-31.0 counts/L (compared to procedural blanks at 3.0±2.8 counts/L). Fibers were the most frequently observed morphology in our water samples (93% of all microparticles), while common colors included clear, blue, and brown. The highest microplastic concentrations were found near ecotourism sites and urban areas, which may be due to recreational activities and waste inputs into the sampled waterbodies. Additionally, although fibers with clear, blue, or brown coloration were the most often observed morphology-color combinations across all samples, sites near anthropogenic influence exhibited a greater diversity of microparticle morphologies and colors. These preliminary results indicate that microplastics are concentrated in Belizean surface water and groundwater systems near human-impacted areas. The prevalence of fibers in our samples also suggests a regional microplastics source that is potentially associated with textile use. Our data help establish baseline microplastic pollution conditions in understudied Belizean aquatic systems, while also providing insight into microparticle characteristics that may inform future monitoring and mitigation efforts.

abstract: Published high-resolution P-wave tomography of southwest Alaska and the Eastern Aleutians reveals a clear slab gap that appears as a low-velocity anomaly within the subducted Pacific slab at depths of ~200 to 500 km between ~158.5°W and 168°W longitude. We unfold the Pacific slab and integrate it into a quantitative plate-reconstruction model to show that the slab gap aligns with the extinct Kula-Pacific mid-ocean ridge. We infer that the extinct Kula-Pacific ridge related slab gap likely continues westward into tomographically less-resolved regions under the central-western Aleutians. The slab gap likely terminates westward near the remnant Kula-Pacific spreading ridge around the Near Islands, Aleutians, explaining the origin of a previously recognized slab ‘portal’ in the region. Initial subduction of the extinct Kula-Pacific ridge after the late Miocene ~8 Ma was concurrent with documented Aleutian Trench arc and Kodiak Island forearc exhumation between ~7 and 5 Ma. The nascent slab gap, formed by ongoing subduction of the extinct Kula-Pacific ridge, may explain uplift of the Bristol Bay and St. George Basins, slab-edge magmatism at the Quaternary Hayes volcano, and intraplate mafic volcanism at the Pribilof volcanoes. The modern slab gap controls the limit of deep Benioff seismicity along the Alaska-Aleutians, including the westward-shallowing Benioff zone along the Aleutians. Our results demonstrate how ancient plate boundaries contribute to the fragmented nature of subducted slabs and provide new insights for northeast Pacific Basin plate reconstructions.

title: Comparison of Land Use/Land Cover Effects on Streamflow Variation in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain Physiographic Provinces of the Southeastern United States

abstract:
Urbanization continues to reshape watersheds across the southeastern United States, and the hydrologic response of streams to land development varies strongly with physiographic setting. This study compares streamflow behavior in five Piedmont watersheds (Sope Creek, Mountain Creek, Marsh Creek, Little Sugar Creek, and Difficult Run) and four Coastal Plain watersheds (Santee River, Pee Dee River, Savannah River, and Roanoke River) over a 26-year period (1995-2021), using USGS gauging records and National Land Cover Database (NLCD) classifications from 2011 and 2016. Mean, low (25th percentile), high (95th percentile), storm, and base flow were computed annually for each site and evaluated against land cover composition (developed, forest, agriculture, and wetland percentages) and against time via linear regression.

Land cover change was generally modest across both provinces over the study period, though agricultural land increased more in the Piedmont, while forested area and wetland extent showed measurable shifts in the Coastal Plain, including an increase in wetland-classified area between 2011 and 2016. Piedmont streams displayed no statistically significant trend in flow metrics over time at most sites, though Little Sugar Creek showed a marginally significant increasing trend in average flow (p = 0.05). Piedmont streamflow patterns showed a common decline around 1999 and a peak near 2004, coinciding with major regional hurricane activity. Coastal Plain streams, by contrast, showed a shared decline in streamflow around 2004, along with substantial variability in high flow and skewed baseflow distributions, most pronounced in the Santee River. Correlations between baseflow and land cover percentage (developed, wetland, forest) were not statistically significant across sites. These results suggest that physiographic setting, more than land cover change alone, strongly governs streamflow extremes and variability across the region.

abstract:
The North American Interior preserves spectacular terrestrial deposits that span the Cretaceous-Paleogene (KPg) boundary and the end-Cretaceous mass extinction (ECME). Many sections also include evidence for the recovery of ecosystems in the aftermath of the ECME over the first million years of the Paleogene. Although geological evidence points to an extraterrestrial impact causing the ECME, the emplacement history of Deccan volcanism during the Danian (early Paleogene) may represent an important factor controlling climatic and environmental change, and therefore the rebuilding of ecosystems on land. Investigating the record of sedimentary mercury (Hg) has the capacity to resolve the timing of the impact and volcanic activity as well as biogeochemical feedbacks to these phenomena including changes in soil formation, wildfires, and rainfall patterns.

We present a latitudinal transect of high-resolution (cm- to dm-scale) sedimentary Hg and total organic carbon (TOC) concentrations, as well as, fossil and other geochemical data including U-Pb radiometric age dates of ash layers, across the study interval. This drill core- and outcrop-based transect, spans North Dakota to New Mexico, allowing us to reconstruct regional Hg cycling and remove any bias that singular sites have. There are widespread Hg and Hg/TOC enrichments surrounding the KPg boundary, but diagenetic alteration appears to have erased these enrichments at one site. In sites without a clear KPg boundary clay, Hg and Hg/TOC enrichments may or may not be present, which is likely controlled by sediment accumulation and preservation during this transient interval. We find clear evidence that secondary mineral formation after deposition may also impact the Hg and Hg/TOC records. New Hg isotope (Δ 199 Hg and δ 202 Hg) data from a section that preserves the highest resolution KPg boundary interval also supports a rapid drawdown atmospheric Hg in the aftermath of the impact, but is not what would be expected if Hg was sourced from Deccan volcanism. Based on this compilation, we find it unlikely that KPg terrestrial Hg records can be used to estimate Hg fluxes from Deccan volcanism due to the influence of local processes that lead to unique Hg geochemical records. More broadly, this research confirms and highlights that investigating multiple sites representing different depositional environments is required to properly apply the Hg geochemical proxy to sediments and sedimentary rock.

title: Shifting Ground: Career Literacy and Conceptual Change in Geoscience Students' Understanding of the Extractive Industry
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Debrah, Maame Opokua [1], Yager, Stacy L. [2], Nyarko, Samuel Cornelius [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Indiana Univ Purdue Univ Indianapolis, Indianapolis, IN, USA
(2) Earth And Environmental Sciences, Indiana University Indianapolis, Indianapolis, IN, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Indiana University, Indianapolis, IN, USA
abstract: Geoscience students are among the most likely future employees of the extractive sector, yet many enter their programs unwilling to work in this sector. Prior surveys report that most university students hold negative views of extraction formed largely from public narratives rather than direct experience. Additionally, existing educational approaches have several limitations: although field-based experiences effectively shift perceptions, they are difficult to scale; brief informational interventions tend to produce only short-term changes; and the effects of ethics coursework often fade over time without sustained reinforcement. Drawing on conceptual change theory, which views learning as the refinement and restructuring of prior conceptions rather than their replacement, this study investigates whether a short classroom intervention can support undergraduate geoscience students in developing a more integrated understanding of extractive industries. A two-session pilot was conducted at a Midwestern U.S. institution, combining a case-based group investigation of extraction sectors with an industry panel, and assessed through pre- and post-surveys and written reflections. Pilot results from unpaired group comparisons (n pre =18; n post= 21) showed that students’ overall impressions of the extractive industry remained predominantly negative (82% pre, 74% post), while understanding grew. Agreement that students understood the daily responsibilities associated with careers in the extractive industries increased from 28% to 63%, while strong agreement that they had a clear understanding of what extractive industries are rose from 22% to 53%. Views on whether the benefits of extraction justify its environmental costs shifted from near-unanimous disagreement (94%) to a more balanced distribution (47% disagreement, 37% neutral), suggesting a greater recognition of the trade-offs involved. Willingness to consider a career in the extractive industries also increased from 6% to 21%, while written reflections showed greater awareness of reclamation and sustainability-related roles despite persistent reservations. Together, these results suggest that even a short classroom intervention can enhance career literacy and foster more nuanced reasoning, providing a foundation for a full-scale study examining how geoscience curricula can prepare students to critically evaluate, and potentially pursue careers in the extractive workforce.

title: Lithium Isotopes in Earth Surface Systems: From Continental Weathering Processes to the Evolution of Phanerozoic Seawater
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part I)
authors: Liu, Xiao-Ming [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA
abstract:
Lithium isotopes (δ⁷Li) have become a popular tracer of silicate weathering and its role in long-term climate regulation, because clays and other secondary phases preferentially incorporate ⁶Li, driving remaining fluids to heavier compositions [1]. However, seawater δ⁷Li reflects a mass balance among four major terms: riverine input, hydrothermal input, low-temperature alteration of oceanic crust, and marine authigenic clay formation [2]. Therefore, any seawater δ⁷Li excursion can arise from a change in any one of them, or in its associated fractionation, rather than from continental weathering alone. Importantly, two of these terms are influenced by biological processes: marine authigenic clay formation is modulated by silica biomineralizers, and the riverine flux is influenced by rooted vegetation [3]. Thus, the Phanerozoic δ⁷Li record is as much a record of the evolving biosphere as of tectonics or climate. Another important problem is archive fidelity. Sedimentary δ⁷Li records mineral-specific uptake, and reported offsets between seawater and bulk carbonate could vary from 0‰ to 10‰ in fiber-retentive dolomite and aragonite bulk carbonate, respectively [4, 5], comparable in magnitude to the secular changes observed across the Phanerozoic [3]. In addition, phase contamination and diagenesis complicate the use of sedimentary proxies for seawater composition [6].

Here I separate controls on seawater δ⁷Li from controls on archive behavior. I argue that marine carbonates remain the most promising archive for reconstructing Phanerozoic seawater δ⁷Li, but only where mineralogy, depositional setting, and diagenetic regime are well characterized. Because the marine Li reservoir is well-mixed, seawater δ⁷Li resolves broad secular change over the Phanerozoic rather than short-lived perturbations at event timescales. Therefore, the most defensible interpretations require accurate, reproducible δ⁷Li measurements coupled with sedimentology, petrography, mineralogy, and companion tracers.

title: Why is Appalachian Crust Thinner than Grenville Crust?
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Karabinos, Paul [1], Bourke, Jim R. [2], Long, Maureen [3], Webb, Laura E. [4], Espinal, Kimberly [5], Luo, Yantao [6], Masis Arce, Roberto Jose [7]
affiliations: (1) Williams College, Williamstown, MA,
(2) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(3) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(4) University of Vermont, Burlington, VT,
(5) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(6) Yale University, Earth & Planetary Sciences, New Haven, CT,
(7) Rutgers State UniversityDept Geological Sci, Piscataway, NJ,
abstract:
The Mesoproterozoic Grenville orogen in eastern North America (ENA) evolved during multiple events from ca. 1.4 to 1.0 Ga during construction of the supercontinent Rodinia. Neoproterozoic rifting formed the Laurentian passive margin of ENA. Multiple collisions along the Laurentian margin created the Paleozoic Appalachian orogen from ca. 480 to 270 Ma and culminated in the supercontinent Pangea, which rifted in the Mesozoic to form the North American passive margin. Despite similar tectonic histories and present elevations, seismic evidence from ENA clearly indicates that Appalachian crust is commonly 10 to 20 km thinner than Grenville crust.

Isostasy demands that mantle lithosphere under Appalachian crust is thinner than under Grenville crust to account for the similar elevations. Espinal et al. (2024) reported shallow asthenosphere depths of 60-110 km under Appalachian crust while investigating the Northern Appalachian Anomaly, and other studies in the Appalachians suggest similar shallow depths to the LAB in regions without thermal anomalies. Appalachian crust is particularly thin in southern New England where an orogenic plateau existed from 380 to 330 Ma (Hillenbrand et al., 2021). Delamination, thermal erosion, and slab rollback have been proposed to explain thinning of mantle lithosphere beneath orogenic plateaus. However, Appalachian lithosphere in regions without evidence for plateaus is thinner than Grenville lithosphere, and there is evidence for orogenic plateaus within the Grenville orogen.

The greater age of the Grenville orogen does not explain these observations; although the mantle lithosphere might have thickened over time, it would not explain the thicker crust. Differences in upper vs lower plate rifted margin behavior might have thinned margins differently, however the Laurentian and North American passive margins probably included both. There is also no evidence that Mesozoic rifting thinned Appalachian lithosphere more than Neoproterozoic rifting thinned Grenville lithosphere, in fact the Laurentian margin may have been hyperextended. It is likely that accreted Appalachian terranes do not rest on their original mantle, but instead were thrust onto rifted Grenville lithosphere during Paleozoic orogenies. Mesozoic rifting may have exploited zones thinned and weakened by Neoproterozoic rifting resulting in thin mantle lithosphere. Appalachian crust, thickened during Paleozoic orogenesis, collapsed and was eroded to achieve isostatic equilibrium with its thin underlying mantle lithosphere.

title: Leaders creating the time and space for change: Lessons from the Traveling Workshops Program in the geosciences
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Plenge, Megan F. [1], Egger, Anne E. [2], Viskupic, Karen M. [3]
affiliations: (1) The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA,
(3) Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
abstract:
Academic departments and disciplines have distinct cultures that tend to act as stabilizing features that resist change. Acknowledging, working with, and addressing that culture directly is required for lasting change to occur. Making change happen from within a culture can be challenging, however, and leaders can benefit from external facilitation that is familiar with but outside of the culture.

Since 2014, the National Association of Geoscience Teacher’s (NAGT’s) Traveling Workshops Program (TWP) has facilitated customized workshops for more than 90 departments and programs in 33 U.S. states and one other country. Leaders of 54 of those departments from the full range of institution types requested workshops focused on building stronger departments and programs. End-of-workshop evaluations from those workshops had an average overall satisfaction of 8.9/10, with comments highlighting the benefits of facilitation and setting aside substantial time (typically two full days) to work together. Though the immediate positive impact of workshops was well-understood by both participants and facilitators, we sought to understand their long-term impact.

We designed a survey and interview protocol to examine how perceptions of the workshop’s effectiveness changed over time and identify workshop outcomes that persisted. The survey consisted of Likert-scale questions about workshop outcomes, and both instruments solicited open-ended responses about short- and long-term impacts in areas such as departmental collaboration and shared vision development, barriers to implementation of strategic plans, and emergent departmental challenges. The survey was distributed to all participants in the 54 workshops and had a 12% response rate (n=58). Interview requests were sent to the leaders who initiated the workshop and13 were interviewed.

Survey results indicate strong persistence of many workshop outcomes, including creating a shared vision and fostering discussion. Many open-ended responses reflect on positive impacts for departments that have undergone mergers or made major curricular changes. Interview results echoed these positive impacts, with several interviewees indicating that participation in another TWP could help them navigate current departmental challenges.

At all levels within an institution, geoscience leaders can use this evidence to provide support for facilitated workshops. NAGT’s TWP is both a resource and a model for academic leaders who wish to engage groups in effective planning for change in deeply embedded academic cultures.

title: Crystal Chemistry of Igneous Minerals in Jezero Crater, Mars from the First 100 PIXL Scans of Abraded Rocks on the Mars 2020 Mission
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Moreland, Eleanor Louise [1], Siebach, Kirsten Leigh [2], Jones, Michael [3], Treiman, Allan H. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Science, Rice University, Houston, TX, USA
(2) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Science, Rice University, Houston, TX,
(3) Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Australia
(4) Lunar & Planetary Institute, Houston, TX,
abstract:
The Perseverance rover has traversed a wide range and age of terrains during its exploration of Jezero crater, Mars. This includes relatively young cumulate lava flows, ancient Noahcian-aged rocks, crater rim impactites, altered and largely unaltered igneous terrains, and fluviodeltaic sedimentary rocks from conglomerates to mudstones. Deciphering the history of the complex geology in Jezero crater, Mars, requires an understanding of mineralogy, as minerals record conditions of surface and subsurface formation environments.

Perseverance does not have a dedicated instrument for determining silicate mineralogy, but it does obtain high-resolution ~120 micron spot size geochemistry with the Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry (PIXL) instrument, an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer. Throughout the mission, Perseverance has abraded, or ground away, the surfaces of rocks along its traverse to expose fresh material for characterization. PIXL retrieves one to three geochemical maps, typically ~3 mm x ~5 mm, on each of these abraded rocks. Here, we focus on the first 100 scans PIXL retrieved of abraded rocks through 1855 sols (Mars days of the mission), comprising over 200,000 individual geochemical analyses.

We use a four-step procedure to identify coarse, crystalline, silicate mineral grain candidates. We then extract mineral chemistry to assess the igneous conditions of mineral formation and correlate mineral sources across the traverse. We focus primarily on mineral species in feldspar, olivine, and pyroxene groups. Our procedure includes: 1) use the Mineral Identification by Stoichiometry (MIST) algorithm to filter for stoichiometric mineral compositions, 2) propagate analytical uncertainty via Monte Carlo to assess confidence, 3) use K-nearest neighbors to isolate spatial clusters, 4) correlate PIXL diffraction to confirm crystalline material. We find that about one-third of the rocks abraded by Perseverance and scanned by PIXL have at least one coarse igneous mineral for which we can derive precise crystal chemistry. These crystal chemistries and their spatial distribution allow us to interpret differences in igneous formation conditions and shifts in mineral provenance along the traverse.

title: Life in the Brine: In-situ modification of fluid inclusion gases by microbial activity
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: Hinmon, Hadley [1], Handel, Ava [2], Hudgins, Michael Naylor [3], Park, Justin [4], Schaller, Morgan [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Science, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(5) Earth and Environmental Science, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
abstract:
Fluid inclusions are excellent archives for understanding ancient aqueous environments and constraining Earth’s evolving atmospheric composition. These microscopic volumes of trapped air and parent brine preserve the chemical signature of the mineral’s formational environment. Primary inclusions in lab-grown halites accurately record atmospheric gases after accounting for gas partitioning between aqueous and gaseous phases. However, these systems are simplified and do not account for the chemical and biological complexity of natural evaporitic environments where microbial processes modify dissolved gases, carbon isotopes, and the parent brine before mineral precipitation.

We hypothesize that microbial activity changes seawater chemistry to the point that measurable differences will be observed between gases in fluid inclusions grown from natural seawater (with its full complement of microbial life) and those grown in synthetic solutions. To test this, seawater collected from the Atlantic Shelf off the coast of Delaware was divided into filtered and unfiltered aliquots. Halite was precipitated through controlled evaporation experiments, and the resulting crystals were examined petrographically to characterize growth and identify primary inclusions. Gas compositions of the parent solutions as well as those liberated from crushed halite were measured using quadrupole mass spectrometry to evaluate potential differences between solution, atmospheric, and inclusions gases. Raman spectroscopy is used to characterize fluid inclusion contents and assess if microbes or biological signatures are visible or preserved.

We will discuss the observed and expected shifts in dissolved and entrapped gases as a result of different microbial metabolisms, especially those associated with respiration, photosynthesis, methanogenesis, and related geochemical processes. Microbial activity is also expected to fractionate carbon isotope ratios, potentially altering the isotopic signatures within inclusions. This study will improve the fidelity of halite as a paleoenvironmental archive and tool for atmospheric reconstruction by quantifying the extent to which biological activity modifies fluid inclusion gas compositions. These results will provide an important framework for interpreting fluid inclusion gas records from natural evaporite minerals, and for distinguishing atmospheric signals from biosignatures.

abstract:
Groundwater resources near oil and gas fields can be exposed to degradation in quality from both natural and anthropogenic processes. Within dense operational zones, multiple risk factors often intersect, yet they are rarely assessed together in space and time, leaving critical gaps in our understanding of groundwater vulnerability. In California, overlapping water users such as agriculture, municipalities, industry, and oil operators create high water demand which intensifies reliance on groundwater. This study identifies the hydrogeological and operational features that pose risks to groundwater at the Cat Canyon Oil Field in Santa Barbara County, California.

To evaluate risk of contamination of groundwater we constructed a conceptual model to guide data compilation and analysis. The conceptual model involves characterizing four key elements, 1) extent of fresh and brackish groundwater resources, 2) sources of naturally occurring hydrocarbons and saline groundwater, 3) potential migration pathways, and 4) driving vertical and lateral hydraulic gradients. We integrated multiple datasets—including groundwater geochemistry, borehole geophysical data, geologic layer depths, oil-well construction information, and groundwater table elevations—using geospatial and geostatistical analyses to explore the locations where the four elements intersect.

Preliminary results show pronounced heterogeneity in groundwater risk. Higher risk occurs along the western margin of Cat Canyon where upward fluid gradients are present near older wells with open annular space, potentially linking deep zones with hydrocarbons and saline groundwater to overlying aquifers. Downhole temperature surveys support this finding, suggesting upward fluid migration through well annuli from oil-bearing zones in some wells. Conversely, risk may be lower in the middle of Cat Canyon Oil Field, where newer wells have fully cemented annular space. However, localized detections of thermogenic hydrocarbon gas and dissolved hydrocarbons in shallow groundwater suggest that groundwater in this area can still be affected, though the specific anthropogenic or natural migration pathway is unclear.

abstract: Solar photovoltaic (PV) arrays are rapidly proliferating across semi-arid and arid irrigated agricultural areas, largely driven by the generally sunny conditions predominant in those lands. While at first glance this would seem to threaten irrigated agriculture, these arrays actually offer an opportunity for critically overstressed regions to move toward sustainability. Solar PV arrays generate electricity and fundamentally alter the surface energy and water balance beneath them, converting latent heat fluxes into sensible heat. The resulting decrease in evapotranspiration (ET) leaves water available for other water cycle components, notably groundwater recharge. How an array is designed and operated governs the degree to which recharge can be enhanced beneath it. Beyond traditional design points such as array spacing and axis tilt control, racks can be designed for rainfall capture, which can then be concentrated at the surface or injected into the subsurface. Even greater recharge enhancement can be achieved via retiring irrigated fields, and their associated water rights. Perhaps the greatest potential lies in designing solar PV arrays for managed aquifer recharge, as these arrays can be flooded essentially permanently and continue to function. Agrisolar PV, that is the explicit incorporation of solar energy generation into agricultural landscapes, can thus provide a path toward greater food, energy, and water security. Here we present two contrasting and illustrative cases: 1) irrigated field replacement in the California Central Valley, and 2) a novel rainfall-capturing artificial recharge test array constructed in Southwest Kansas. These two cases quantify the potential for recharge enhancement, and highlight the tradeoffs between recharge, food production, energy generation, and land use. Through better quantification and understanding of these tradeoffs, hydrologists can help broaden and reframe the debate between solar PV and agriculture, and identify a more sustainable and resilient path for irrigated agricultural landscapes.
