abstract:
Ghost forests are increasingly common in low-lying coastal regions of the United States and are predicted to expand as climate-driven sea-level rise (SLR) accelerates. However, similar ghost forests can also result from tectonic processes, drought, and river dredging, making it challenging to identify the drivers of their formation. Here we use microfossils (foraminifera and thecamoebians) to determine the drivers of ghost forest formation using two coastal rivers as case studies: Smith Creek, near Wilmington, NC and Bone River near Raymond, WA. At both sites, modern microfossil distributions provide analogs for reconstructing the paleoenvironmental changes associated with ghost forest formation. At Smith Creek, microfossils support dendrochronological results to show that the current and expanding ghost forest primarily resulted from much expanded river dredging of the Cape Fear River since the 1950s, which increased tidal amplitude and salinity upriver and into Smith Creek. At Bone River, microfossil and grain size analyses indicate that the 1700 CE Cascadia subduction zone earthquake and tsunami caused rapid subsidence (i.e., rapid SLR) and paleo-ghost forest formation which are still observable across the landscape today. Microfossils also constrain the amount of coseismic subsidence and enable high-resolution tsunami inundation mapping at the site.

Both sites are also experiencing accelerated rates of climate-driven SLR, which will amplify the ongoing ghost forest formation at Smith Creek and make the Bone River coastal forest more vulnerable to future ghost forest formation as the next earthquake and tsunami loom on the horizon (Cascadia subduction zone is currently locked and building strain). At Smith Creek, expanded dredging proposed along the lower Cape Fear River will likely result in higher and saltier water levels for longer periods of time, increasing the hazard posed to the coastal communities adjacent to these waterways. In Bone River, the estimated subsidence and tsunami inundation extent for the 1700 CE event help to provide constraints on modeled earthquake/tsunami scenarios and improve coastal hazard mapping and community evacuation plans. Modern and fossil microfossils played an important role in understanding the paleoenvironmental changes of these two coastal ghost forests and will continue to be crucial as their spatiotemporal footprints spread.

title: A calibrated model of total organic carbon accumulation across the southern Denver – Julesburg Basin during the Cenomanian – Turonian boundary interval
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part I)
authors: Flaum, Jason A. [1], Birdwell, Justin E [2], French, Katherine [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA

abstract: Studies of carbon burial and the global carbon cycle during times of extreme climate events in the geologic past have recognized carbon sinks that are unaccounted for in scales ranging from basinal to global throughout the geologic record. This lack of accounting for carbon sinks is driven by the reliance on core and outcrop data to provide the primary source inputs for regional and global models. Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 occurs at the Cenomanian – Turonian boundary and represents a time in the geologic past that is globally recognized for extensive accumulations of organic-rich strata and a notable positive carbon isotope excursion reflected in the δ 13 C signatures of organic matter and carbonate. Cenomanian – Turonian strata of the southern Denver – Julesburg Basin represent a prime example of the need to expand carbon burial models beyond intensively studied core and outcrop locations. These strata have been evaluated at the Global Stratotype Point and Section in Pueblo, CO and extensively studied in the U.S. Geological Survey #1 Portland Core in Freemont County, CO. While data from these locales provide key insights into the drivers of carbon burial at the cm – dm scale, models derived from these studies are limited in scope to their specific location. In this study we utilize a detailed facies classification based upon high resolution geochemical data and sedimentologic and petrographic observations of the Cenomanian – Turonian interval in the U.S. Geological Survey #1 Portland core to develop a calibrated and geophysical log-based DeltaLogR model estimates of total organic carbon (TOC) concentrations. From this calibrated model, we mapped TOC concentrations for the Cenomanian – Turonian interval (averaging 125 ft in thickness) on over 30 geophysical logs in the southern Denver – Julesburg Basin (spanning an area over 1000 km 2 . This method and map provide a means of addressing missing TOC concentrations at the regional scale during extreme climate events and perturbations to the global carbon cycle throughout geologic history.

title: Integrating zircon chemistry and textural zoning using depth profiling from the porphyry Cu-related Ruby Star pluton, Pima mining district, Arizona

authors: Beckman, Renan [1], Rezeau, Herve [2], Schoonover, Erik Jeffery [3], Feineman, Maureen D. [4], Reimink, Jesse [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA

abstract:
The main global sources of copper are Porphyry Copper Deposits (PCDs). New PCDs are becoming more challenging to find, and major discoveries from the past decade are being found deeper in the subsurface. Ore-forming processes appear to occur during late-stage magmatic events, when hydrothermal processes become more dominant.

A long history of work has focused on accessory igneous minerals (e.g. zircon, apatite) within granitic intrusions associated with PCDs as recorders of magmatic and hydrothermal evolution. Zircon is a great petrochronometer and pathfinder for PCDs. It can record the temperature and redox state of the magma, making it very useful for assessing magma fertility. Zircon often records late-stage processes at grain rims and displays narrow growth zone textures, making it difficult to characterize with conventional spot analyses.

Here we use a different approach, we performed an analytical Laser Ablation Split Stream Inductively-Coupled Mass Spectrometry (LASS-ICP-MS) depth profiling campaign on zircon grains collected from the Ruby Star Granodiorite associated with the giant Sierrita porphyry Cu-Mo deposit, Pima Mining District, AZ. Our unique LASS zircon chemical depth profiles from rim towards the interior are combined with direct cathodoluminescence (CL) imaging of analyzed zircon growth zones by plucking, rotating 90º, remounting, and polishing to expose the depth profiles. This method provides both a unique chemical evolution trajectory and associated textures from zircon rims inward, allowing us to fully interrogate the morphology and growth history of individual grains and populations of grains.

Integrating CL imaging and LASS depth profiling can identify normal oscillatory zones, represented by shades of grey in CL and relatively consistent but fluctuating trace element concentrations. In contrast, anomalous trace element-enriched zones are dark in CL and show a complex pattern of trace element incorporation order in the depth profiling data. These dark CL zones have anomalously high trace element concentrations (e.g., wt% U and 1000s ppm REEs). Our initial analysis shows that enrichment occurs in a sequence similar to the relative magnitude of trace element diffusivity in the melt, suggesting that these enriched CL-dark zones represent disequilibrium growth in the magma. These new data show the uniqueness and origins of CL-dark zones and are discussed within the metallogenic framework as evidence linking them to magmatic fluid exsolution and possible copper deposition.

title: Global Distribution of Groundwater Carbon Fluxes To and From the Atmosphere
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Magnone, Daniel [1], Polya, David A. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Natural Sciences, Lincoln University, Lincoln, United Kingdom; H Fraser Consulting Ltd, Shrewsbury, United Kingdom
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, School of Natural Sciences, Faculty of Science and Engineering, The University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom
abstract:
Groundwater’s role in the global carbon cycle is poorly quantified compared to other carbon reservoirs, particularly on a global spatial scale. Here we show that the carbon stock of terrestrial groundwater is approximately equal to that stored in the modern atmosphere, and substantially exceeds that held in vegetation. Globally groundwater represents a natural net sink for atmospheric carbon equivalent in magnitude to the natural flux of carbon from the oceans to the atmosphere (circa -0.4 versus +0.6 PgC/yr, respectively) but that this is unevenly distributed. Furthermore, the regions with large groundwater carbon fluxes – either as CO₂ emissions or sinks – are in regions projected to undergo major climate driven hydrological change.

The largest natural groundwater CO₂ emissions occur in circum-Atlantic tropical basins (notably the Amazon and Congo basins) which account for more than half of global terrestrial groundwater CO₂ gas emissions; however, high recharge here largely offsets these emissions, rendering them currently near CO₂-neutral. In contrast, the greatest terrestrial groundwater carbon sinks occur in the extra-tropical regions of Southern Africa, Europe and the Mediterranean, along with tropical Madagascar, all of which are projected to experience substantial future changes in rainfall and evapotranspiration.

Understanding how such hydroclimatic shifts will alter groundwater–atmosphere carbon exchanges therefore represent a key opportunity for future research as well as contributing to science-informed policy in relation to groundwater resource management.

abstract: The North Dakota Geological Survey (NDGS) has been identifying and mapping landslides in varying capacities for over four decades. The landslide program at the NDGS accelerated in 2017 and the following years. All landslide mapping at the NDGS is presented at 1:24,000. Before 2017, mapping utilized stereoscopic aerial photography and digital aerial imagery to delineate landslides, referred to as Phase 1 mapping. As LiDAR was introduced across North Dakota, the NDGS began mapping all landslides on a QL3 LiDAR base. This stage of the program, called Phase 2, was completed statewide in 2023, with 1,464 quadrangles mapped. In 2021, as multiple LiDAR datasets were introduced statewide, Phase 3 mapping began, which utilized LiDAR differencing techniques to identify landslide movements that occurred between LiDAR collections, a period of typically 7-10 years. Currently, the State of North Dakota has LiDAR coverage at QL2 and QL3 statewide. Phase 3 landslide mapping will be completed during the Fall of 2026, allowing the NDGS to observe trends of “active” failures. All landslide series maps are presented at 1:24,000; however, due to time constraints from industry, not all Phase 1 and Phase 2 landslides were delineated in a detailed manner. Many maps were compiled at 1:12,000, whereas Phase 4 aims to delineate all landslides at 1:1,000 or better resolution. To date, the NDGS has produced 64 Phase 4 maps. The addition of new datasets, including statewide QL1 LiDAR coverage and NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data, gives the NDGS several opportunities to explore new directions for landslide detection and hazard mitigation.

title: Calcium Isotopes Link Ocean Acidification to Aptian/Albian Foraminiferal Extinctions
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part I)
authors: Chen, Jonathan [1], Jacobson, Andrew D. [2], Huber, Brian T. [3], MacLeod, Kenneth G. [4], Wan, Chuyan [5], Waldeck, Anna R. [6], Balestra, Barbara [7], Sageman, Bradley B. [8]

abstract:
The second-largest extinction event in the evolutionary history of planktic foraminifera occurred at the Aptian/Albian boundary, ~113.2 million years ago. Around 70% of planktic species disappeared in the latest Aptian, while just two species with small and thin-walled tests survived into the Albian. In contrast, benthic foraminifera appear largely unaffected. This extinction has been linked to environmental perturbations associated with Oceanic Anoxic Event 1b. Volcanic CO 2 emissions from the Kerguelen Plateau may have caused ocean acidification, driving extinctions of planktic foraminifera with more heavily-calcified tests.

We constructed high-precision calcium isotope (δ 44/40 Ca) records for planktic and benthic foraminifera and bulk carbonate sediments across the Aptian/Albian boundary at Deep Sea Drilling Project Site 511 (Falkland Plateau, South Atlantic). We also present the first δ 44/40 Ca measurements of secondary calcite, manually separated from the chambers of infilled benthic foraminifera. The Ca isotope composition of marine carbonates may track biocalcification rates through time. Slower calcification rates yield higher δ 44/40 Ca values, while faster rates yield lower values. Biocalcification rates, in turn, depend on the carbonate saturation state of seawater. Thus, δ 44/40 Ca measurements may help to identify episodes of ocean acidification in the geologic past.

Benthic foraminiferal δ 44/40 Ca values (measured for infill-absent or dissected tests) display a distinct sequence of negative and positive excursions, mirroring δ 44/40 Ca records of other geologic acidification events. Bulk sediments show similar negative-to-positive shifts, occurring in parallel with benthic δ 44/40 Ca variations. Secondary calcite yields δ 44/40 Ca values akin to bulk sediment, suggesting that authigenic precipitation occurred under closed system conditions. These observations indicate that the major excursions in our δ 44/40 Ca records reflect primary kinetic isotope effects. In planktic foraminifera, δ 44/40 Ca values increase dramatically across the Aptian/Albian boundary. We interpret this excursion, one of the largest documented in the Phanerozoic, as evidence for a major decrease in the calcification rates of planktic foraminifera. The excursion also coincides with substantial decreases in planktic diversity and test size. Therefore, geochemical and paleobiological observations collectively support the hypothesis that ocean acidification drove extinctions of planktic foraminifera at the Aptian/Albian boundary. The consequent decline in surface-water calcification would have enhanced ocean alkalinity, potentially buffering the effects of acidification on deep-sea benthic foraminifera and fostering the formation of secondary calcite.

abstract:
As Iceland’s Vatnajökull ice cap shrinks in response to climate change, subglacial volcanoes like Þórðarhyrna (“Thordarhyrna”) are increasingly exposed. Prior to this investigation, much of what was known about Þórðarhyrna could be gleaned from a geologic map. Its position in the Eastern Volcanic Zone suggests that it is young and potentially active. Its location between Laki and Grímsvötn has led to speculation that Þórðarhyrna is a secondary central volcano in that famous system. Its nunataks are rhyolite, a composition rarely observed at Vatnajökull. Several Icelandic systems experienced increased eruptive activity triggered by rapid ice loss following the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). We hypothesize that Þórðarhyrna may have been among them, and are motivated to better understand the history of this enigmatic volcano under thinning ice. We use zircon (U-Pb and U-Th disequilibrium dating, O isotopes, trace elements) as our primary investigative tool.

Sparse crystallization began as early as ~300 ka. One rhyolitic sample with exclusively “old” (>200 ka) crystals suggests an eruption predating the Weichselian glaciation. Beginning ~90 ka, as the Icelandic Ice Sheet assembled, zircon crystallization began to increase in Þórðarhyrna magmas, with a major pulse ~30 to 10 ka. The median age of this younger population is ~25 ka, aligning with the local LGM. The magmas from which these young zircons grew were likely trapped in the crust while it was loaded by thick ice. Though stuck, the zircon record reveals that these magmas were not stagnant. From 60 to 6 ka, δ 18 O values rose from <3 to >4‰, Ti rose from 2 to 10 ppm, and Hf dropped from 15,000 to 8,500 ppm. Together, these observations suggest less influence of hydrothermally-altered crust on magma chemistries (δ 18 O approaching, though still well below, mantle-equilibrated values) and more involvement of hotter (higher Ti), less-evolved (lower Hf), mantle-melt on Þórðarhyrna rhyolites from ~60 ka until eruption. Individual zircon grains with multiple age analyses, and an individual rhyolitic sample with exclusively “young” (<60 ka) zircon crystals, reveal the duration of magma storage, disruption, and eventual eruption at Þórðarhyrna to be ~15-20 kyr, up to ~50 kyr. Zircon crystallization tapers from ~25 to 6 ka, suggesting deglaciation-triggered eruption following the collapse of the Icelandic Ice Sheet. This volcano-climate scenario is again relevant–Þórðarhyrna deserves closer attention.

title: Exploring Impacts of Groundwater Interactions on Urban Stormwater Control Measure Performance
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Winston, Ryan [1], Hamby, Isabelle [2], Smith, Joey [3], Tirpak, Andrew [4]
affiliations: (1) Food, Agricultural, and Biological Engineering, Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(2) Food, Agricultural, and Biological Engineering, Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA

abstract: Stormwater control measures (SCMs) are designed to ameliorate flooding, limit stream erosion, and improve water quality from urban developments. Infiltrating SCMs, such as bioretention and sand filters, are often designed for groundwater recharge to supply baseflow to nearby streams. Two field monitoring campaigns, one at a large sand filter draining an industrial site near Columbus and another with four bioretention cells in a parking lot at Cleveland Metroparks zoo, were recently completed with notable stormwater-groundwater interactions. The sand filter was located on poorly draining soils with a known high-water table; water level loggers within the sand layers and significant increases in hardness showed extended dewatering times (>1 week after rainfall) and a unique connection with the groundwater table. For 20 sampled storm events, pollutant concentrations were significantly reduced for heavy metals (>80%), total suspended solids (72%), and nutrients in runoff, inclusive of dissolved forms like nitrate (48% reduction). Ongoing dissolved oxygen and dissolved organic carbon monitoring may support denitrification. At Cleveland Metroparks zoo, bioretention cells with varying plant palettes and loading ratios (i.e., ratio of catchment area to SCM surface area) were monitored over one year. While runoff volumes were substantially reduced by three cells (71-89%), effluent volumes exceeded influent runoff at the low-lying Tree cell. Suspected groundwater interactions were confirmed by soil borings, which revealed redoximorphic features below the underdrain. Similarly, though mean concentrations of TSS were effectively reduced (by 50-83%), nutrients (i.e., N and P) were discharged at higher concentrations in the bioretention effluent, indicative of leaching of organics from compost in the bioretention media blends. Collectively, these two field studies highlight the need to consider groundwater interactions in SCM design, particularly since labile pollutants might be transferred to groundwater.

title: The Viability of Fulgurite Vesicles to Capture Atmospheric Conditions at the Time of a Lightning Strike

authors: Handel, Ava [1], Hinmon, Hadley [2], Park, Justin [3], Hudgins, Michael Naylor [4], Pasek, Matthew [5], Schaller, Morgan [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA

abstract: When a lightning strike comes in contact with sand, the rapid heating and subsequent quenching of the sediments forms natural glass structures called fulgurites. The extreme conditions of formation produce vesicles within the fulgurite walls, which may encapsulate gases from the environment surrounding the strike. Previous studies have gleaned paleoecological information from the composition of the trapped gases confirming the presence of organic matter in the original soil as well as the production of NO along the lightning channel. However, there still lacks understanding of whether the gases contained accurately reflect the atmospheric or soil conditions at the time of the strike. Fulgurites gathered from two sand mines along the Lake Wales Ridge (Florida, USA) were examined, and the presence of vesicles was confirmed using microscopy. The sand mines from which the samples were collected are fairly young (est. 1998), but the sediment itself is estimated to have been deposited in the Plio-Pleistocene. Trapped gases were released by mechanical decrepitation and analyzed by a quadrupole mass spectrometer. A known mixture of gas was used to create a calibration curve for the major atmospheric species before the samples were crushed; these species were then quantified at mass-to-charge (m/z) ratios 14, 32, 40, and 44 (N2, O2, Ar, and CO2, respectively). We also monitored m/z 30 as previous research confirms the production of NO when the energy generated by lightning breaks N2 and O2 bonds. If the gases observed do not reflect known atmospheric ratios, the observed ratios can give more insight into the chemical reactions that occur along the lightning channel whose products may have been sealed into the vesicles. Preliminary results reveal variable gas compositions between samples, which appear near but not quite atmospheric, with higher mole fractions of N2 and lower mole fractions of O2. These observations may indicate O2 consumption resulting from NO formation during the chemical processes of the strike or the denitrification of organic matter in the sand. Ongoing experiments are expected to show similar trends across the fulgurite samples and should confirm N2/Ar, O2/Ar, and CO2/Ar ratios, which will give further insight into the viability of fulgurites to capture the surrounding atmosphere.

title: Coupling Floodplain Nourishment with Sediment Transport and Deposition in a Semi-Arid Region, Elephant Butte Reservoir, New Mexico

authors: Lyon, Cristina Luisa [1], Garcia, Sarah Catalina [2], Carlson, Brandee [3], Copeland, Peter C. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA

abstract:
Floodplain nourishment is driven by flooding, during which sediment and nutrients are delivered and stored across the floodplain. In semi-arid and arid environments, flashy hydrology and seasonal variations in discharge strongly influence whether deposited sediment is preserved or desiccated and reworked. Dams further modify these environments by retaining sediment upstream of impoundments and altering downstream sediment supply. The routing, deposition, and preservation of fine sediment across semi-arid floodplains remain poorly understood. This study investigates how seasonally driven flood events are recorded within the stratigraphy of a crevasse splay at the northern reach of Elephant Butte Reservoir (EBR), New Mexico, on the Rio Grande floodplain.

To understand sediment deposition across the crevasse splay, four L-shaped trenches were excavated 10, 20, 30, and 40 meters from the active bank, perpendicular to the primary flow direction of the Rio Grande River, and one sediment core was collected 130 meters from the riverbank. An advection-settling model was used to compare observed stratigraphy with predicted spatial variation in grain-size distribution across the crevasse splay. The trenches expose sand-dominated beds with bidirectional flow structures and erosional contacts. The sediment core contains alternating mud and sand beds separated by sharp contacts. These results indicate that the crevasse splay preferentially preserves coarse sediment near the channel, whereas fine sediment is readily reworked by subsequent floods or aeolian transport following desiccation, limiting its long-term retention within the proximal splay. Floodplain nourishment in this semi-arid system is therefore governed by flood stage and inundation frequency, which determines whether fine sediment reaches areas where it can be buried and preserved before desiccation and reworking to remove it.

title: Deep-Time Low-Temperature Thermochronology of the Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic Athabasca Basin and Surrounding Canadian Shield

authors: Powell, Jeremy W. [1], Tschirhart, Victoria [2], O'Sullivan, Paul B. [3], Metcalf, James R. [4], Stockli, Daniel F. [5]
affiliations: (1) Natural Resources Canada, Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada

abstract:
Due to their distance from active plate boundaries, cratonic interiors are commonly regarded as tectonically, thermally and erosively stable over geologic timescales. In northern Canada, crystalline rocks of the Rae and Hearne Provinces of the Canadian Shield are thought to have resided near Earth’s surface since deposition of regional Paleo-to-Mesoproterozoic sedimentary strata, such as the Athabasca Basin of northern Saskatchewan and Alberta. However, younger Mesoproterozoic magmatism and Paleozoic and Mesozoic sedimentary xenoliths in kimberlite pipes suggest a more dynamic regional tectono-thermal history. Within the Athabasca Basin, some of the world's largest high-grade uranium deposits occur at the intersection of deep-seated basement faults and the unconformity with the basin strata. Uraninite U-Pb dates from these deposits record episodic hydrothermal events from the Mesoproterozoic to recent that partially or completely reset the uraninite isotopic system, demonstrating the repeated reuse of these Proterozoic fault zones as thermal-fluid corridors. Given this prolonged residence within upper-crustal temperature regimes and record of punctuated thermal events, the Athabasca Basin and surrounding cratons provide an exceptional natural laboratory for evaluating the applicability of low-temperature thermochronology methods for reconstructing thermal histories of the cratonic interior through deep time.

We present new zircon fission track (ZFT; n = 7), apatite fission track (AFT; n = 11), zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe; n = 15) and apatite (U-Th)/He (AHe; n = 7) low-temperature thermochronology data for 23 samples that span the Athabasca Basin and surrounding cratonic region. ZFT dates from crystalline rocks yield consistent Mesoproterozoic dates of ~1.17 Ga, whereas the ZFT dates from Athabasca Supergroup sedimentary strata define populations at ~0.48 Ga and ~1.17 Ga. AFT data fail the χ² test and yield central ages ranging from 102 ± 25 Ma to 657 ± 83 Ma and exhibit complex relationships among single-grain dates, radiation damage and apatite composition. ZHe and AHe data are highly dispersed and exhibit variable intrasample relationships between date, radiation damage and grain size. We integrate these thermochronometers to identify the sources of date dispersion and evaluate best practices for interpreting and modelling such complex datasets. The resulting thermal history models provide new constraints on the previously poorly resolved Mesoproterozoic-to-recent evolution of the Athabasca Basin, including maximum burial temperatures and the timing and magnitude of episodic thermal events.

title: Calibrating Luminescence Rock Surface Erosion Rates with a Manual Erosion Experiment
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution (Posters)
authors: Brown, Nathan D. [1], Valenzuela Davila, Diana [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA
(2) University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA
abstract:
Within the past decade, workers have proposed using luminescence depth profiles within solid bedrock to estimate erosion rates. Theoretically, this method should reveal erosion rates on timescales of decades to millennia and would be sensitive to length scales of mm to cm. If true, this tool could be applied in a variety of geomorphic contexts, to develop heatmaps of erosion rates across hard rock surfaces. Or to estimate changes in erosion rates through time, by comparison against complementary techniques such as paired, in situ cosmogenic radionuclide analysis.

However, this technique rests on untested assumptions. To translate luminescence depth profiles into apparent erosion rates requires assumptions about the rock optical properties, site-specific sunlight conditions, and luminescence kinetics. Moreover, the technique has never been validated against surfaces of independently known erosion rates.

In this experiment, we periodically erode six lithologies over the course of seven months at four erosion rates: 10, 50, 100, and 500 mm/yr. Rocks were sawn, cored, cast in concrete blocks, then left on the rooftop. At different intervals (depending on the intended erosion rate), these blocks were taken down off the roof and eroded on a custom-built device. Following each erosion, the eroded length was measured in several spots by depth gauge to precisely document the actual removed length. At the end of this experiment, we extracted the rock cores, wafered them, and measured their luminescence depth profiles. By comparing the measured luminescence depth profiles against the known erosion rates, we evaluate the ability of the technique to accurately recover hard rock erosion rates.

title: Environmental Controls on Alluvial Fan Morphology
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Morgan, Alexander Michael [1], Palucis, Marisa Christina [2]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH,
abstract:
Alluvial fan morphometry is commonly described using power-law scaling relationships between fan area, catchment area, fan gradient, and catchment topographic ruggedness. Constraining the environmental controls on these relationships is required to accurately interpret paleoenvironmental signals preserved in terrestrial geomorphology and ancient stratigraphy, as well as to reconstruct past and present hydrologic conditions on Mars and Titan.

We compiled a morphologic database of several thousand alluvial fans from the literature and extracted corresponding catchment lithology, wettest-month precipitation, and structural kinematic regime data. We then utilized Bayesian mixed-effects regressions to account for intra-study correlation and methodological variance. Our models demonstrate that structural kinematic regime exerts a categorical control on fan geometry. Extensional regimes contract the baseline fan area by 26% and steepen the baseline fan gradient by 29%. Conversely, compressional regimes expand the physical fan area by 26%. Vertical slip rate has a null effect on horizontal area expansion. Catchment lithology also controls fan shape, with an increase in the fraction of coarse, massive source rock systematically steepening the baseline gradient by 15%. We did not find a systematic effect of lithology on two-dimensional planform area. Furthermore, modern precipitation parameters do not systematically affect the scaling exponent for fan gradient. However, modeled Pleistocene Last Glacial Maximum precipitation shows a clear positive interaction with the ruggedness scaling exponent. This indicates the geomorphic relaxation time for large alluvial fans can exceed the duration of the Holocene, and modern fan macro-topography retains a relict Pleistocene geometric signature. Rather than vertical subsidence rates or modern climate, our findings highlight that structural fault geometry and paleo-environmental conditions are the primary boundary conditions governing global alluvial fan morphology.

title: Otolith nitrogen isotopes record submarine groundwater inputs and fish ontogenetic movements on the West Florida Shelf

authors: Lueders-Dumont, Jessica [1], Sigman, Daniel [2], Ward, Bess [3], Wang, Xingchen Tony [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts, USA

abstract: Otoliths (fish ear stones) are unique among accretionary structures as they originate from high trophic level animals (fishes) and are commonly found in fossil and archaeological contexts. As such, they serve as a valuable source of ecological information about fish life history in both the modern ocean and throughout Earth history. Here, we undertook a modern pilot study to assess the nitrogen isotopic composition (d15N) of individual fish at various stages of their life. Otoliths of red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) and lane snapper (Lutjanus synagris) along the Gulf Coast of Florida were extracted, cleaned, and analyzed. Using a Dremel tool, powder was drilled from sequential growth increments of intact otoliths and then measured for d15N using persulfate oxidation and the denitrifier method. We found consistently higher d15N values in the younger, core section of the otoliths with up to 2.3‰ changes within individual otoliths. This pattern contradicts the expected increase in fish d15N with size due to a diet shift from lower to higher trophic level prey as fish grow. Instead, the observed decrease in d15N from the juvenile to adult stage can be attributed to the habitat shifts from nearshore to pelagic environments, which is characterized by a significant environmental (i.e., baseline) d15N gradient in the northern Gulf of Mexico. Nearshore in Florida, high baseline d15N are mainly due to high-d15N submarine groundwater discharge. Conversely, in the open Gulf of Mexico, baseline d15N is lower, influenced by the input of low-d15N nitrogen from N2 fixation in the (sub)tropical Atlantic and its subsequent transport. The trends in otolith d15N data for the snappers are consistent with their migration offshore and increasing reliance on pelagic food sources as they mature. Thus, this study supports the utility of single otolith d15N measurements for tracking environmental nitrogen isotopes. Using fossil otoliths, we plan to test for whether the modern, coastal d15N signal has increased compared to pre-industrial coastal d15N values.

abstract: Interaction of olivine in basaltic melts with magmatic fluids can result in partial to complete olivine transformation into a fine-grained mixture of alteration products referred to as iddingsite. Although iddingsitization erases geochemical information in olivine that is reflective of crystallization conditions, unaltered domains within partially iddingsitized grains may still offer useful insights into the conditions of olivine growth. Here, we establish the petrologic context of unaltered domains within partially altered olivine from a Miocene basaltic lava flow nearby Gypsum, Colorado that contains olivine with varying degrees of iddingsitization via integration of petrographic analysis and EPMA mineral/iddingsite compositional analyses. In contrast to complete olivine iddingsitization in an older, highly vesiculated part of the flow sequence, younger lavas contain euhedral olivine with iddingsitized cores and unaltered rims as well as unaltered groundmass olivine. Texturally, these younger lavas are holocrystalline and subophitic with variable vesicularity. Unaltered olivine rims and groundmass are compositionally indistinguishable (Fo 57±2 and Fo 52±4 , respectively) in vesicle-poor portions of younger lavas, whereas iddingsitized cores are notably Mg-depleted and Ca-enriched. Unaltered olivine-iddingsite core interfaces are gradational with widths ranging from 10-60 μm in both vesicle-rich and vesicle-poor parts of the younger flows. Following eruption of the younger lavas, groundmass crystallization consisting of an assemblage of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, olivine, and Fe-Ti oxides occurred around 1089 ±36 °C according to clinopyroxene-only geothermometry. Our data are consistent with previously proposed iddingsitization models in which fresh olivine rims heterogeneously nucleate and grow on altered cores alongside nucleation of new olivine grains during groundmass crystallization. However, the lack of a sharp interface suggests that crystallization and iddingsitization may have occurred temporarily concurrently following eruption. This interpretation is further supported by some samples that contain both altered and unaltered groundmass olivine. Parts of the lava flow(s) in which magmatic fluids, i.e., vesicles, are unable to escape into the atmosphere may enable iddingsitization to persist even during the early stages of groundmass crystallization. Under this scenario, unaltered olivine domains in partially iddingsitized grains are most likely formed post-eruption and caution should be exercised when extrapolating pre-eruptive storage conditions from their compositions.

title: Decoding Coastal Clays: A Machine-Learning Approach to Predicting CPT-Derived Soil Behavior Types from Electrical Resistivity Tomography
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Rodriguez, William [1], Elshalkany, Muhamed [2], Anyanwu, Ifeanyi Emmanuel [3], Narimani, Roya [4], Murgulet, Dorina [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
(2) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA; Department of Geology, Suez Canal University, Egypt, Arab Rep.

abstract: Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) is often used in subsurface investigations because it provides continuous, non-invasive imaging of subsurface electrical properties. However, the interpretation of variations in resistivity in terms of subsurface materials remains challenging, particularly in clay-dominated coastal environments where measured resistivity is influenced by multiple factors including soil texture, porewater salinity, saturation, and porosity. This study presents a machine learning workflow for predicting soil behavior types from ERT data using Cone Penetration Testing (CPT) as reference labels. Co-located ERT surveys and CPT soundings were collected at multiple sites along the Texas Gulf Coast, with the current dataset consisting of four paired ERT-CPT profiles. Additional sites will be incorporated in order to expand validation. CPT measurements were used to classify soil behavior types, while resistivity measurements were resampled at corresponding CPT depth intervals, allowing a more direct observation of the relationships between geophysical and geotechnical measurements. These paired datasets were used to train and evaluate a machine learning model capable of estimating soil behavior type across ERT profiles based on observed relationships between resistivity and CPT parameters. Preliminary results from an initial random forest model demonstrate the potential of this approach. It is able to capture the complex, non-linear relationships between resistivity and subsurface characteristics. Using a depth-based evaluation approach, the model achieved an R 2 value of 0.877 with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.136. This demonstrates the ability of ERT measurements to provide useful information for predicting soil behavior types. The proposed workflow provides a transferable framework for the integration of geophysical and geotechnical datasets to improve subsurface characterization for applications including coastal engineering, environmental assessment, and hydrogeologic investigations.

title: Overprinting Mid-Crust Shear Zones and Their Role in Metamorphic Core Complex Development in the Albion–Raft River–Grouse Creek Mountains, Idaho–Utah
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee (Posters)
authors: Frenia, Lindsey [1], Masoch, Simone [2], Lee, Terry [3], Zuza, Andrew [4], Sihpol, Tatiana [5]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(3) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(4) Nevada Geosciences, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(5) Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California, San Diego, San Diego, CA, USA
abstract: Metamorphic core complexes (MCCs) expose mid- to lower-crustal rocks that record multiple phases of deformation and metamorphism produced by overprinting tectonic processes, from orogenic crustal thickening to mobile mid-crust flow to continental extension. For example, both the Ruby Mountains, Nevada, and Albion-Raft River-Grouse Creek (ARG), Idaho-Utah, MCCs exhibit complex patterns of apparently distinct shear zones with N- and W-trending lineations of debated age and origin. Here we focus on the ARG MCC to investigate how the geometry and kinematics of mid-crustal shear zones evolve in space and time during polyphase crustal deformation. The N-S-lineated shear zone preserves top-N and top-S shear sense, which is deformed and overprinted by Cenozoic plutons and E- and W-directed shear zones. We conducted detailed structural mapping along three transects (Grouse Creek, Graham Peak, and Raft River) to document variation in kinematics and geometry of shear zones as well as crosscutting relations in proximity to detachments and plutons. Field and microstructural observations show that earlier fabrics with N-S-trending lineations are variably preserved at all study locations across different lithologies and structural levels, as previously documented. Oligocene plutons intrude and preserve pre-existing N-S fabrics along magmatic contacts and in xenoliths. The plutons themselves are isotropic except where mylontonized only beneath major detachments, indicating that the N-S-trending shear zone predates at least a portion of Cenozoic structures. At exposed structural levels, regions with no exposed plutons still exhibit N-S-lineations. N-S-lineations and fabrics containing both superimposed E-W- on N-S-trending lineations are largely preserved in lower strain domains as well as proximal to plutons, although are completely overprinted under high-strain Cenozoic detachments as evident by dominant E-W-trending lineations and preliminary vorticity and microstructural results. Rather than reflecting coupling between detachment faulting and deformation, the ARG records a polyphase history where inherited shear zones, plutonism, and extension produce complex overprinting relationships. Further field observations coupled with microstructural and EBSD observations and accessory phase U-Pb geochronology will further establish timing and kinematics of inherited mid-crustal shear zones and how they are influenced by Cenozoic MCC development.

title: Rocks, Budgets, and Broad Horizons: The Unique Qualifications of Geoscientists in University Leadership
session_title: Geoscience Education (Posters)
authors: Clark, Christine M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI,
abstract: Geoscientists are disproportionately represented in higher education leadership positions relative to their total proportion among faculty. Understanding the specific academic background of geoscientists helps explain this administrative prevalence. Relative to other natural science disciplines, geoscience curricula require coursework across multiple foundational fields, including physics, chemistry, and mathematics. Furthermore, the discipline inherently connects physical Earth processes to societal impacts, such as natural hazard mitigation and resource distribution. Consequently, geoscientists develop broad cross-discipline literacy and systems-thinking capabilities, an appreciation for the work and research being conducted by faculty outside of geoscience. When coupled with analytical minds that can work with budgets, this holistic training prepares geoscientists to effectively address complex institutional challenges and serve as highly qualified college and university administrators.

title: Two-thirds of global riverine chemical fluxes sustained by groundwater
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling (Posters)
authors: Su, Jintao [1], Luo, Xin [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
abstract: Groundwater sustains river flow and transports weathering products, nutrients, and carbon from terrestrial landscapes to downstream ecosystems, yet its contribution to riverine chemical fluxes remains poorly quantified at the global scale. Here, we integrate machine-learning predictions of groundwater chemistry, baseflow estimates, and hydrogeochemical observations from 28,956 groundwater samples and 5,888 catchments to develop a global framework for tracing groundwater-derived solute fluxes. Rather than treating river chemistry only as an endpoint, our approach links riverine export to subsurface sources and evaluates how climate, topography, catchment size, and hydrological residence time shape groundwater signatures. The results indicate that groundwater contributes a substantial share of riverine solute fluxes, with strong spatial variation among solutes and catchments. These patterns reflect not only hydrological partitioning, but also concentration contrasts and in-stream processes such as dilution, mineral precipitation, gas exchange, ion exchange, and biological uptake. The study highlights groundwater as both a water source and a biogeochemical reactor that regulates chemical export from continents. Quantifying this role is important for predicting how climate change, land-use alteration, and groundwater abstraction may affect freshwater salinization, carbon cycling, ecosystem services, and the resilience of coupled groundwater-river systems, and for prioritizing protection of headwater aquifers and regional groundwater flow systems.

title: Textural attributes of periglacial loess and floodplain muds
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Griner, Alexis [1], Soreghan, Gerilyn [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Oklahoma, Mewbourne College of Earth and Energy, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
(2) University of Oklahoma, Mewbourne College of Earth and Energy, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
abstract:
Loess consists of eolian silt, and is common in modern high-midlatitude regions, with subordinate deposits in the subtropics. Loessite (lithified loess) remains poorly recognized in deep time; in some cases, strata formerly interpreted as floodplain have been reinterpreted as loessite. We are surveying the textural attributes of loess deposits, and selected floodplain muds, to establish general trends that might help differentiate the origins of deep-time mudstones of ambiguous depositional origin.

We collected loess samples (largely or partly periglacial) from Washington (n = 3), Iowa (n = 16), Poland (n = 12), Nebraska (n = 4) and Serbia (n = 7), and floodplain samples from Peru (n = 3). After removal of macroscopic plant matter, all samples were processed with 30% H2O2 (24 hr) for removal of organics, 1 N HCl (24 hr) for removal of carbonate, then sonicated one minute with dispersant before measurement using a Malvern Mastersizer 3000 laser particle-size analyzer (LPSA).

Particle-size modes of loess range from ~25 to 69 µm (medium to coarse silt), all negatively skewed, and unimodal. Location-specific modes are: Nebraska 54-69 µm, Washington 38-48 µm, Iowa 24-33 µm, Poland 29-46 µm, and Serbia 27-61 µm. Floodplain muds exhibit finer modes of ~12 µm (fine silt), positive skewness, and are multimodal. Sorting indices calculated using the (D90-D10)/D50 approach average ~2 for the loess samples, whereas floodplain samples average ~7, indicating much poorer sorting for the latter. Loess samples average 76% silt, 15% sand, and 7% clay (<4 µm), whereas the floodplain muds average 66% silt, 16% sand and 16% clay.

Although preliminary, these results suggest that textural attributes can provide a means to distinguish between loessiticmudstone and floodplain mudstone in the deep-time record, when samples are sufficiently friable for disaggregation to enable LPSA analysis.

title: A Decade of Discovery: Sustaining an Independent Biogeochemistry CURE
session_title: Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) in Geoscience: Outcomes, Projects, and Training Strategies for a Successful Experience
authors: Schmitkons, Jonathan P. [1], Light, Caitlin J [2], Fegley, Megan E [3]
affiliations: (1) Binghamton University, Vestal, NY,
(2) First-year Research Immersion, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
(3) First-year Research Immersion, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA
abstract:
Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) have become increasingly common since the early 2010s because of their success in scaling authentic research. One of two structural models can describe most CUREs: independent (local) or network. Longitudinal datasets of independent CUREs are the least common of the two. The Biogeochemistry (BGC) Stream of Binghamton University’s First-year Research Immersion (FRI) Program is one such example of an independent/local/standalone, early-entry CURE in Geosciences.

While the Geosciences have a long tradition of undergraduate research through field experiences, independent projects, and honors theses; these usually occur at the end of undergraduate study and serve established majors. Conversely, the FRI Biogeochemistry stream introduces students to the field-based, interdisciplinary, and collaborative nature of Geoscience at the beginning of their undergraduate studies while they still have the opportunity to consider additional/alternate pathways.

This presentation will highlight key data from 10 cohorts and approximately 300 BGC students to highlight key trends in student persistence in STEM, post-program placements, graduation rates, and continuation to advanced degrees. We will also explore how having FRI-dedicated faculty, scaffolded mentorship, collaborations, and institutional support have helped with the longevity of this independent CURE.

title: Fear! Fire! Scale! Four strategies that need more attention to bring the urgency of climate change home and foster action
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation
authors: Haas, Don A. [1]
affiliations: (1) The Center for Climate Change Education, The Paleontological Research Institution, Ithaca, NY, USA
abstract:
Climate communication has not driven the scale of change needed to protect continued human thriving. I suggest four strategies to improve these efforts:

- strategic use of fear, coupled with efficacious action,

- increased attention to fire’s central role in the climate emergency,

- straightforward discussion of the difficulties people have with understanding scale and how the understanding of scale is essential for communicating the urgency of the climate emergency, and,

- connect to locally relevant climate phenomenon.

Thoughtful Attention to Fear:

Being frightened by climate change is rational and a key motivator for those working to address it. Many educators avoid using fear, yet we have a moral obligation to be honest: if people aren’t scared, they don't truly understand the crisis.

However, fear shouldn't stand alone. Being too scared can lead to a state of hyperarousal, where one cannot calm down, or it can lead to hypoarousal, where one is depressed and shuts down. In between these extremes is the “window of tolerance,” where they remain mentally engaged. We can do this by validating fear as a rational response and pairing it with efficacious, community-based action. Working together to address the problem doesn't just alleviate climate anxiety; it transforms paralysis into productive, collective effort.

The Central Role of Fire:

Modern climate change is primarily driven by humans burning stuff - mostly fossil fuels. Everyone has familiarity with fire. This is not true of greenhouse gases or how they warm the planet.

Highlighting fire’s role in climate change makes key solutions more obvious. Wherever we can fire fire in our energy system - replace it with cooler processes or simply stop using it - we reduce emissions and reduce economic costs in the long term.

Teach Scale

Huge numbers are common in climate communication, but most people misunderstand scale. When asked to mark one billion between zero and a trillion, most place it at ~30%—about 300 billion! Without grasping the difference among a thousand, a million, and a billion, people can't appreciate the implications of Americans burning 376 million gallons of gasoline daily or what a gigaton of CO2 means.

Bring it Home

If the audience is connected to a geographic region, use examples of how the local climate is changing. Extreme weather events of 2026 have made this straightforward.

title: Shifting global marine redox linked to an early Silurian (Aeronian) extinction event
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part I)
authors: Evenson, Nathaniel C. [1], Goodin, John T [2], Chen, Qing [3], Zhang, Junpeng [4], Hints, Olle [5], Eriksson, Mats E [6], Ahlberg, Per [7], Adiatma, Yoseph Datu [8], Owens, Jeremy D. [9], Young, Seth A. [10]

abstract:
An early Silurian (late Aeronian) extinction interrupted the biotic recovery and radiation that followed the Late Ordovician mass extinction. This event, termed the Sandvika/ sedgwickii extinction (SSE), was characterized by significant faunal turnovers in most marine groups, including an approximately ~41% decline among graptolite species and a ~30% decline among conodont species. The main phase of the SSE coincided with a global +6‰ δ 13 C excursion known as the late Aeronian positive carbon isotope excursion (LACIE). A leading hypothesis suggests a possible link between the extinction event and changes in marine redox conditions; however, the relatively short duration of the extinction event (<1 m.y.) has previously hindered a robust reconstruction of global marine redox dynamics when employing most traditional global redox proxies (e.g. uranium and molybdenum) due to their long residence times (>400 k.y.).

Here we report a new high-resolution thallium isotope (ε 205 Tl) record spanning the Aeronian Stage (ca. 440.5–438.6 Ma) of the early Silurian. The shorter residence time (~18.5 k.y.) of Tl in modern oceans enables us to better constrain changes in global bottom water oxygenation throughout this geologically brief event. ε 205 Tl was measured in Aeronian organic-rich shales from three drill cores representing two separate paleo-ocean basins, the Baltoscandian and South China basins. Both basins have been independently interpreted as anoxic, providing ideal conditions for preserving authigenic seawater Tl isotopes which record variations in global Mn-oxide burial (specifically birnessite) related to marine redox conditions. Our new ε 205 Tl record reveals an oscillating trend surrounding the LACIE and SSE, providing evidence for several (de)oxygenation events of varying durations (~40–510 k.y.). Additionally, comparisons with global sea level reconstructions suggest a possible link between negative shifts in our ε 205 Tl record (oxygenation) and eustatic sea level fall associated with two Gondwanan glaciations. Together, these results reveal a more complex pattern of marine oxygenation than previously recognized, with rapid fluctuations in ocean ventilation linked to biological turnovers during a period of climatic instability in the early Silurian. More broadly our results highlight the important role short term changes in oxygenation play in shaping the evolution of the Paleozoic biosphere.

title: Allies and Enemies of Brachiopod Ecosystems: an Analysis of Who and What Effects Late Paleozoic Brachiopod Ecology
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: Lindgren, Blake David [1], Wagner, Peter [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Nebraska, University of Nebraska State Museum, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA
(2) University of Nebraska, School of Biological Sciences, Lincoln, NE, USA; University of Nebraska, University of Nebraska State Museum, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract:
Brachiopods remain the dominant invertebrates in midcontinent Carboniferous and Permian assemblages. Brachiopods typically represent sessile epifaunal suspension feeders. As such, we might expect similar partitioning of resources among brachiopod species in different settings, which in turn predicts similar relative abundance distributions (RADs) within brachiopod communities. Here, we examine whether there is variation in RAD types among latest Carboniferous – Early Permian brachiopod communities from the Nebraska-Kansas-Oklahoma Chase and Council Grove groups. And whether this variation coincides with abiotic or biotic factors. For abiotic factors, we look at lithology, relative sea level, and temperature. For biotic factors we look at co-occurrence of taxa with brachiopod assemblages. The co-occurrence taxa are, encrusting Brachiopods, attaching Porifera, Bryozoa, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Cephalopoda, Trilobita, Echinodermata, Serpulopsis sp., Rugosa.

We use taxon counts gathered at the University of Nebraska State Museum from 126 localities and 11 formations and assess the best fit from four commonly used RAD models: Geometric, Log-Series, Lognormal and Zipf. Geometric or Log-Series are expected given “simple” ecosystem structure in which all species are competing for the same general set of resources, whereas Lognormal or Zipf distributions are expected given more “complex” ecosystems in which some species increase the total amount of resources available to individuals in a community. We rank models from most diverse distributions to least diverse distributions as: Zipf, Lognormal, Geometric, and Logseries.

Preliminary results indicate that when certain factors are present, brachiopod RAD models shift compared to when that factor is not present. Broadly, abiotic factors (lithology, relative sea level, temperature) seem to have little if any effect on what model each brachiopod community is. Some biotic factors (specifically, encrusting Brachiopods, Bryozoa, attaching Porifera, Bivalvia, and Rugosa) presence are correlated to significantly different RAD models, when comparing their absence to presence. Variation in brachiopod RADs does not seem to correspond to the presence of other taxa (Gastropoda, Cephalopoda, Trilobita, Echinodermata, Serpulopsis sp.). This implies that brachiopod community structures are stable relative to physical environment and most other taxa do not affect brachiopod community structure, but the presence of some epifaunal suspension feeders does have an effect.

title: Generalizable indices of soil development and their application to soil geomorphic research
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part I)
authors: Hirmas, Daniel R [1], Koop, Aaron N [2], Sullivan, Pamela L [3], Tomar, Simmi [4], Newcomb, Benjamin [5], Gray, Andrew [6], Ajami, Hoori [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Plant and Soil Science, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(2) Soils Research, Newton, KS, USA
(3) College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(4) Department of Environmental Sciences, University of California - Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
(5) Department of Plant and Soil Science, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(6) Department of Environmental Sciences, University of California - Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA

abstract: Since their introduction more than 40 years ago, semi-quantitative indices that score various soil morphological properties and aggregate those scores into a single numeric value describing the degree of soil development have relied on information about the parent material in the computation of the index. Although these indices have proven to be useful tools in soil geomorphic research, especially in the development of chronofunctions, this reliance on parent material limits their application to specific geomorphic systems where knowledge of the parent material can be determined from exposures of pedogenically unaltered regolith. Even in cases where such exposures exist, because they exist below the solum, they often do not reflect the properties of the original material within which the soil horizons have developed (e.g., fining-upward sequences in certain fluvial depositional settings) and, thus, may not reflect accurate information on the development state of the soil. Here we describe a generalizable index that relies on relative differences between specific soil formed horizons informed by the relevant pedogenic processes governing each property being assessed. These indices are highly flexible and can be applied in settings that span multiple parent materials to inform soil geomorphic research questions across a range of spatial and temporal scales. The derivation of this index and its application to specific landscapes—including fire-affected catchments of the chaparral-dominated Santa Monica Mountains in southern California and soils of two lithologies of the arid White Mountains in eastern California—will be presented and discussed. Ultimately, this generalizable index opens the door to greater quantitative assessment of soil development rates, soil age, stability of geomorphic surfaces, and pedogenic processes.

title: Tracking Terrestrial Cyclostratigraphy Across the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary, Kiowa Core (Denver Basin, Colorado)

authors: Hagerty, Parker Jameson [1], Segessenman, Daniel C. [2], Omar, Hamdi [3], Brisson , Marcia [4], Hinnov, Linda A. [5]
affiliations: (1) Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA

(3) Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, Virginia, USA
(4) Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, Virginia, USA
(5) Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
abstract:
Milankovitch-forced cyclostratigraphy is an important geological tool for building timescales and correlating stratigraphic sections. Astrochronology is reconstructed from cyclostratigraphy by calibrating the latter to an astronomical model in numerical (absolute) time. However, there are two complicating factors: (1) sedimentary sections with both cyclostratigraphy and in situ geochronology or chronostratigraphy, the latter providing independent time constraints, are rare; and (2) planetary orbit dynamics has a “chaos horizon” at ~60 Ma, before which time astronomical models are inconsistent and not reliable for astrochronology.

Here we present a comparative analysis between portable gamma ray spectrometry and pXRF measurements from samples of a key terrestrial section, the Kiowa Core (Denver Basin, Colorado), which has well documented magnetic reversals and high-precision U-Pb TIMS ages. Lithologies alternate between fine and coarse-grained clastic facies. The goal of the analysis is to develop cyclostratigraphic proxies along the core section for astrochronological modeling of the K-Pg Boundary (KPB; ~66 Ma).

Measurements of the Kiowa Core with a portable gamma ray spectrometer and pXRF provides a means to compare terrestrial elemental cyclostratigraphy from the late Cretaceous and early Paleogene. Results indicate good agreement between the portable gamma ray and pXRF data and differences in some of the elemental trends above and below the KPB. Research objectives of future analysis include: (1) development of an astrochronology for the Kiowa Core around the KPB; (2) correlation with ODP Site 1262, a KPB-bearing marine core with well documented cyclostratigraphy and magnetic reversals, and (3) comparison of KPB cyclostratigraphy with astronomical models to assess which model yields the best fit.

title: A Labyrinth of Lines: Exploring Potential Stress Field Sources of Significant Jointing in an Abandoned Limestone Quarry in Southwest Ohio (Oakes Quarry Park)
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Haines, Gloria Rose [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Cedarville University, Cedarville, Ohio, USA
abstract: Joints are in-situ cracks in rock that indicate stresses that have pushed the rock beyond its plastic, elastic, or brittle limits. Pairs of oblique lines indicating stress fields can often be traced back to local tectonics, isostatic rebound, or any kind of localized extension event. One of the most expressive features in the structural geology of Southwest Ohio is the Cincinnati Arch. Primarily due to the first order structures created by the major plate convergence of the Alleghenian orogeny, the uplift of this horseshoe-shaped dome is suspected to have begun first in the Cambrian and continued through the Silurian. On the fringes of the Cincinnati Arch, distinct joints split the surface of the exposed basal Silurian Brassfield Limestone within Oakes Quarry Park, 190 acres of abandoned quarry undergoing wetland restoration. The Brassfield Limestone consists mostly of carbonate rocks with interbedded shale and is believed to be an onlap feature of the uppermost Ordovician. The prominence and great number of the clearly defined joints littering the former floor of the quarry sparks immediate curiosity about their stress source. The local stress field of the Cincinnati Arch and the Alleghenian orogeny, rebound after removal of overburden, thermal expansion, and high energy blasting all present themselves as potential stress sources. Five hundred and thirty-five (535) joints, dispersed over three distinct exposures that make up 67 acres of the Oakes Quarry floor, were individually traced using GPS, measuring their strikes and lengths. The collected strike orientations indicated that most of the strikes fall into two primary ranges. The most common range of strikes gave an average of 265 ±8.4 degrees. These strikes were generally much longer on average than those of the second most common orientation which was at approximately 335±8.3 degrees and characteristically shorter and less defined. title: Ancient low-angle fault imaged beneath the Salton Trough: Subsurface evidence for early extensional faulting near the San Andreas plate boundary?
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Persaud, Patricia [1], Nardoni, Chiara [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy; Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia, Naples, Italy
abstract: Southern California is a complex plate-boundary region where the oblique motion between the Pacific and North American plates is accommodated across complex networks of distributed faulting. Active deformation along this margin extends across the Salton Trough and the southern San Andreas fault system to the Los Angeles metropolitan area, generating new crust and geothermal systems in the south and a series of deep sedimentary basins. The basins are known to produce strong spatial variations in seismic wave propagation with substantial implications for ground motions of major earthquakes. Less well-understood is the impact that inherited structures have on seismic hazard and to what degree these structures have shaped the 3D architecture of the current plate boundary and contribute to present-day crustal heterogeneity. Using ~20,000 earthquakes recorded by the regional network combined with recordings of 71 explosions at 2,375 temporary stations, we apply seismic attenuation imaging computing peak delay variations to determine the scattering properties of the crust beneath the southern Salton Trough. High-scattering volumes may indicate fractured fault-zone rocks, sharp lithological contrasts, or sedimentary basin fill. We found a prominent scattering contrast between the Peninsular Ranges basement and overlying rocks that is consistent with the hypothesized surface of the West Salton detachment fault, the northern portion of a series of low-angle normal faults of late Miocene-Pleistocene age that were part of the plate boundary system for ~250 km along strike (Axen and Fletcher, 1998). Slip on these faults was largely contemporaneous with major dextral slip on the San Andreas plate-boundary faults and improved knowledge of their 3D geometry is essential for testing paleogeographic and tectonic reconstructions of this margin. Deep high scattering anomalies in the central part of Salton Trough appear to extend below the Imperial Valley basin and are associated with the intensely fractured plate boundary zone. These regions generally underlie the geothermal areas, are associated with zones of seismicity, and potentially highlight deep fluid pathways. Imaging seismic attenuation thus contributes to an integrated view of how long-term tectonic deformation and short-term processes interact within a complex active plate-boundary setting.

title: Boom and Bust: Temporal Diversity Dynamics on a Quaternary Cold Water Coral Mound in the Alboran Sea
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record
authors: Korpanty, Chelsea A [1], Schwartz, Ruby [2], Lancaster, Emily [3]
affiliations: (1) Eckerd College, St. Petersburg, FL, USA
(2) Eckerd College, St. Petersburg, Florida, USA
(3) Eckerd College, St. Petersburg, Florida, USA
abstract: Spatial patterns and drivers of distribution are key to understanding the capacity of cold water coral (CWC) reefs as biodiversity hotspots in the deep sea. While these factors have been evaluated on modern CWC reefs, little is known about how reef diversity fluctuates relative to habitat variability over geologic time – the scale at which long-term habitat and ecological dynamics are captured. This study characterizes the taxonomic and functional diversity of benthic CWC reef taxa relative to variations in habitat structure by exploring lithologic, stratigraphic, and paleobiological relationships within a CWC reef mound. To do this, we quantitatively defined stratigraphic units in a reef sediment core spanning the last ~13,000 years from a CWC mound in the Alboran Sea (western Mediterranean). Stratigraphic units are defined by lithology and quantiative framework coral characteristics derived from CT scans. We then assessed temporal trends of benthic invertebrate diversity and assemblage composition relative to these units. Our results demonstrate that multiple phyla are preserved in the sediment core in varying abundances, including Arthropoda, Brachiopoda, Bryozoan, Cnidaria, and Echinodermata as well as Mollusca, which were part of a previous study. Our data indicates the species and functional diversities are relatively low in stratigraphic units when CWC growth rates are relatively high, and increase in units when CWC growth rates decline. Specifically, attached suspension feeders dominate assemblages that occur when CWC growth is rapid, representative of living coral zones on modern reefs. In contrast, sessile and mobile suspension feeders and grazers dominate assemblages when CWC growth is slow or negligible, comparable to modern live-dead and CWC rubble zones. These patterns align with those recently documented for molluscan assemblages in the same sediment core. These patterns also resemble those observed spatially across living CWC reefs – where competition for food prevents high reef biodiversity in the immediate vicinity of dense living CWCs. Overall, this study supports that ecological patterns of living CWC reefs are captured in reef sedimentary records and that the rate of CWC growth affects diversity patterns over time. These findings contribute to our understanding of what enables CWC reefs to be biodiversity hotspots, providing important implications for reef and deep sea diversity dynamics over geologic time.

title: Quantitative Descriptions of Microbial Fabric and Texture From the Tonian Little Dal Group, Mackenzie Mountains, Northwest Territories, Canada
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Helms, Lucy A. [1], Cohen, Phoebe A. [2], Nadalin, Caroline C. [3], Anderson, Ross P. [4], Strauss, Justin V. [5], Mehra, Akshay K. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Williams College, Williamstown, MA, USA
(3) Williams College, Williamstown, MA, USA
(4) University of Oxford, United Kingdom
(5) Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(6) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
Microbial reefs, which comprise in situ structures built by microbes on the seafloor, serve as important paleoenvironmental records of early life on Earth. The morphology and structure of microbial reefs respond to a wide range of processes operating at different spatial scales. For example, light intensity may impact microbially mediated mineral precipitation at the mm-scale, whereas the local basin architecture may control the dm- to km-scale nature and extent of reef growth. Thus, constraining microbialite morphology the micro-, meso-, and macro-scale is essential for accurately reconstructing and interpreting the growth history of a reef. However, morphological observations often rely on qualitative descriptions of microbial textures (i.e., the size, shape, and arrangement of components) and fabrics (i.e., the orientation of components). Such analyses can introduce subjectivity to interpretations, making it difficult to discern trends through time and space. Digital image processing techniques can enable quantitative analyses of texture and fabric, directly addressing this potential shortcoming.

Here, we demonstrate the power of quantifying microbial textures and fabrics by characterizing microbial reefs from the Knife Edge Central Reef, a 400-m-thick reef within the Tonian Little Dal Group, Mackenzie Mountains, Northwest Territories, Canada. Previous work examining the sedimentology of the Stone Knife Formation has identified five stages of reef growth that loosely correspond with the regional changes in sea level recorded by four shale-to-carbonate packages in coeval off-reef strata. By combining observations from thin sections and polished slabs with computer vision image classification techniques, we quantitatively measure the size, shape, arrangement, and orientation of microfacies components, such as micritic clots, filamentous tubules, marine cement, detrital sediment, microbial laminae, and geopetal structures. We test the hypothesis that the fabric and texture of Knife Edge Central Reef microbial facies is heterogeneous across periods of sea level change and distinct generations of reef growth. This approach to constraining the micro-scale features of these microbial reef-building facies will generate novel insights into the evolution of one of the best-preserved Tonian calcimicrobial reefs in the geologic record.

authors: Panzik, Joseph E. [1], Baer, Christina S. [2], McCarty, Shane [3], Light, Caitlin J. [4], Fegley, Megan [5]
affiliations: (1) First-year Research Immersion, Binghamton University, Binghamton, NY, USA

abstract:
Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) are becoming increasingly common in undergraduate STEM courses as an avenue to encourage students’ connection between material and application by faculty research. For 12 years, Binghamton University has had the First-year Research Immersion program, a specialized three-semester program that directly integrates first-year students into research as a series of CURE courses across many disciplines in STEM, including two geoscience- focused streams (labs). Students who participate in and complete these courses have higher graduation rates. In addition, these students have had success in attaining internships, presenting work at conferences, publishing articles, and continuing research in various fields. In one example, a student began a startup business based on their project within one of the geoscience streams.

The success of CUREs often depends on the ability of teaching assistants (TAs) or peer mentors to guide and direct students in the authentic research experience. This can lead to challenges where students need additional supervision and TAs/peer mentors require additional training. While many institutes utilize graduate students for this role, others may need to rely on undergraduate students for TAs/peer mentors. Undergraduate peer mentors (UGPMs)/TAs may need increased guidance in general mentoring strategies, especially in a near-peer setting.

Our First-year Research Immersion program at Binghamton University solely relies on undergraduate peer mentors (UGPMs) to assist with the CURE sequence. We have developed new mentor training for UGPMs across all three semesters. These trainings range from informal 1-on-1s with instructors and group check ins to formal mentoring courses, modules on learning management software (LMS), and mindset self-assessment guide. Herein we present some of the materials and strategies we have developed for mentoring UGPMs with some common pitfalls and solutions that have been successful in our program. We have found that providing UGPMs/TAs with appropriate and numerous ways to grow as mentors in CUREs has been key to the success of the FRI program.

authors: Harding, Reina [1], McCormick, Cole A. [2], Chanchai, Watsawan [3], Vayda, Prescott James [4], Lau, Kimberly [5], Keller, Brenhin [6], Strauss, Justin V. [7]
