abstract: The end of the Neoproterozoic Era records profound changes in the Earth system, including the radiation of complex animals and shifts in Earth’s atmospheric oxygen concentration. In carbonate successions where trace and/or body fossil preservation is scarce or absent, the BAsal Cambrian carbon isotope Excursion (BACE) has been widely used as a chemostratigraphic marker for the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary. However, the BACE has only been identified at a handful of sites globally, and no consensus has been reached on whether the geochemical record at these sites truly records ancient seawater chemistry or reflects diagenetic alteration. In northwestern Canada, the carbonate-dominated Risky and Algae formations, which cap the Neoproterozoic Windermere Supergroup, regionally shallow-upwards to a subaerial exposure surface that marks the “sub-Cambrian” unconformity. In the Mackenzie and Wernecke Mountains, a substantial decrease in carbonate carbon (δ 13 C) values occurs near the contact between the Risky Formation and the overlying Ingta Formation, which locally records the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary. This negative excursion has been interpreted as the BACE; however, these low δ 13 C values coincide with the aforementioned subaerial exposure surface and with widespread dolomitization, making their origin enigmatic. Here we present new detailed carbonate carbon (δ 13 C) and oxygen (δ 18 O) isotope data, together with major and trace element geochemistry and mineralogical observations, from multiple measured sections of the Risky and Algae formations exposed across a shelf-to-slope transect in the Wernecke Mountains. By constructing this paleobathymetric transect across the basin, we evaluate whether the negative carbon isotope excursion reflects primary seawater chemistry or diagenetic overprinting, and assess the fidelity of the BACE as a marker for the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary in northwestern Canada.

title: Where the Plastic Flows: Microplastics in Northern New York Lakes, Rivers and Freshwater Bivalves
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Posters)
authors: Khumalo, Zakithi [1], Nagel-Myers, Judith [2], Oldacre, Amanda [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, St. Lawrence University, Canton, NY, USA
(2) Biology & Geology, St. Lawrence University, Canton, New York, USA
(3) Chemistry, St. Lawrence University, Canton, NY, USA
abstract:
Microplastics are persistent contaminants and indicators of human impact, yet factors controlling their distribution in northern New York remain underexplored. This study examines microplastic concentrations in lakes and rivers with different levels of surrounding anthropogenic development and potential transfer into freshwater bodies and their bivalves.

Fifteen rural and urban localities were sampled in the Adirondack Park and St. Lawrence Valley. Three 50mL water replicates were collected at each site, stained with Nile Red and Evans Blue, vacuum-filtered through 0.4 µm gridded filters, and imaged by fluorescence microscopy. Bivalve soft tissues were digested with FeSO₄ and 30% H₂O₂, then stained, filtered, and imaged using the same procedure. Microplastic particles were quantified from composite filter images. pH, dissolved oxygen, temperature, current velocity, and surrounding development level were also recorded. Development level was classified as low, moderate, or high as observed from ArcGIS data.

Microplastics were detected at all localities. Water-column concentrations averaged 0.81 particles/mL in lakes and 0.58 particles/mL in rivers. Mean concentrations were 0.54 particles/mL at low-development sites, 0.60 particles/mL at moderate-development sites, and 0.82 particles/mL at high-development sites. Bivalve tissue concentrations ranged from 6 to 99 particles/g. Site-level means reached 57 particles/g at Piercefield and 15 particles/g at Madrid Dam. Mean bivalve tissue abundance was 30.8 particles/g at lake localities and 24.5 particles/g at river localities.

Our preliminary results suggest that lakes accumulate microplastics at higher rates than rivers. Similarly, areas with anthropogenic development show higher microplastic levels than rural localities, suggesting local input via runoff. On average, bivalve tissue showed higher levels of microplastics at lake sites, matching the trends observed from the water column. In contrast, microplastic levels in bivalve tissues were highest in rural localities, and visual observations suggested that microplastic sizes were smaller in bivalve tissues than in the water column. Next steps include analyzing sediment samples from these localities and adding more tissue samples to expand our dataset.

title: The Potential Role of Microbes in the Formation of Reduction Spheroids: Co-occurrence of Organic Matter and Metals in Devonian and Mesoproterozoic Redbeds.

authors: McKenrick, Mitchel [1], Jennings, Eleanor [2], Nehzati, Susan [3], Dunn, Edward [4], Hickman-Lewis, Keyron [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Natural Sciences, Birkbeck, University of London, London, United Kingdom

abstract:
The hunt for life on other planets has broadened our understanding of paleoenvironments on Earth and Mars. By using Earth as an analogue for modelling Martian environmental processes, we can expand upon data received by remote sensing and rover missions. In 2024, the Perseverance rover detected mm-scale reaction fronts termed “leopard spots” within mudstones in Neretva Vallis, the river channel feeding Jezero Crater. The leopard spots are considered analogous to reduction spots/spheroids, a phenomenon ubiquitous across many terrestrial redbeds. These redbeds provide excellent analogues for Martian sedimentary environments, which are also strongly enriched in ferric iron. Combined with the identification of organics within both Earth redbeds and Neretva Vallis sedimentary rocks, this becomes compelling evidence of potential life on another planet (“potential biosignatures”). Indeed, it has long been suggested that reduction spheroids may be microbially mediated. Reduction spheroids are readily identified in visible light imagery by their “halo”, caused by the reduction of Fe, which makes them an easily identifiable target to search for on current and future missions.

This study aims to characterize reduction spheroids in the Old Red Sandstone (~400 Ma) at Dingwall, Scotland, and the Bay of Stoer Formation of the Torridon Group (~1200 Ma). Using multiple techniques—including SEM-EDS/-WDS and µXRF (major and trace elements, including transition metals), and Raman microspectroscopy (organic mapping and characterization)—this study provides datasets for comparison with the Martian “leopard spots”, enabling the development of a model that explains the formation of these features. Using each of these techniques, organic carbon has been identified to be associated directly with cores containing redox-sensitive elements, such as transition metals. The quantification of elements identified, such as Ni, Cu, Zn, Mn, and Cr, is compared to similar data sets from PIXL, the Perseverance’s rover µXRF instrument. The presence of localised concentrations of organic carbon, detected for the first time using Raman microspectroscopic mapping of reduction spheroids, may implicate dissimilatory metal-reducing microbial colonies in the formation of reduction spheroids. This is corroborated by increased presence of metals directly adjacent to organic matter in some cores from each locality. Perseverance PIXL XRF data corroborate the importance of such elements on Mars, and this comparison will serve as a basis for Mars Sample Return analyses, particularly of the core “Sapphire Canyon.”

title: Age, Morphology, and Radiation Damage: A Multi-Proxy Detrital Zircon Approach to Provenance Change Across the Kinderhookian-Osagean Transition in the Appalachian Basin
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond

(2) Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC,
abstract:
Early Mississippian strata of the central Appalachian Basin record the sedimentary response to an abrupt Kinderhookian-to-Osagean climate shift. The lower-middle Tournaisian Price Formation includes fluvial-deltaic sandstone, siltstone, and shale with minor coal, and preserves indicators of a cool, humid paleoclimate, including chemically reduced iron phases, thin kaolinitic paleosols, and abundant terrestrial organic matter. In contrast, the overlying Maccrady Formation contains redbeds, evaporites, and sedimentary structures indicative of an arid climate, together with loess deposits recording eolian dust. Farther west, the Maccrady transitions into the Grainger Formation and Borden Group, recording a shift from continental to shallow-marine deposition together with a significant contribution of wind-blown sediment. We investigate the impact of this climate transition on sediment provenance using detrital zircons from eight samples of the Price Formation and overlying units. For every analyzed grain we obtained (1) a U-Pb age, (2) grain morphology (size and shape) via a semi-automated image-analysis algorithm, and (3) accumulated radiation (alpha) dose, calculated from the instrumentally corrected width (FWHM) of the zircon ν3 Raman band using established FWHM-dose calibrations, with the Eg or ν2 bands used as proxies when ν3 was poorly resolved (e.g., due to grain orientation).

U-Pb age distributions are broadly similar across all samples, with a dominant Grenville-age population (~1000–1200 Ma), a ~480 Ma (Appalachian) peak, smaller groups at ~670 Ma and ~1480 Ma, and few grains older than 1600 Ma. However, systematic differences across the climate transition indicate an accompanying shift in provenance: relative to the Price Formation, overlying units contain proportionally fewer Appalachian-age grains and more Grenville-age material. Grain size decreases upsection from the Price into the Maccrady, and again westward from the Maccrady into the Borden, consistent with progressive eolian transport. Grain shape follows a parallel trend, with grains becoming more rounded from the Price to the Maccrady and particularly in the Borden. Radiation damage increases from the Price (least damaged) through the Maccrady to the Borden (most damaged), mirroring patterns documented in other datasets. Additionally, across all units we identify a relationship between radiation damage and grain shape: heavily damaged grains are almost exclusively low-aspect-ratio (<~2), regardless of stratigraphic position. Together, these independent datasets corroborate one another and enable more refined tests of provenance and transport hypotheses across this major Mississippian paleoclimate transition.

abstract: Arsenic demethylation is a microbially mediated process that can decrease methylated arsenic in rice paddies, reducing the incidence of straighthead disorder in rice plants. Rice paddies are also a significant source of methane emissions globally, and recent work has established that methylotrophic methanogens contribute to arsenic demethylation. This contribution aims to expand our understanding of (i) the methylotrophic methyltransferase enzymes involved in arsenic demethylation, (ii) how methanogens detoxify toxic intermediates and products during arsenic demethylation, and (iii) whether complex organic matter can promote these important connections between methylotrophic methanogenesis and arsenic demethylation. At the microbial community level, we show that amending soil slurries with trimethylamine promoted non-specific couplings between arsenic demethylation and multiple methylotrophic methanogenesis pathways, and that several Methanosarcina metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) were dominant in methyltransferase gene transcription (and by inference, arsenic demethylation). In response to toxic (methyl)arsenite intermediates produced during arsenic demethylation, we observed that Methanosarcina MAGs simultaneously transcribed multiple arsenic detoxification pathways in parallel with methylotrophic methanogenesis genes, with arsenite efflux and methylarsenite oxidation being the dominant detoxification pathways in terms of both community-level transcription and MAG-resolved couplings with arsenic demethylation. In rice growth experiments in the greenhouse, we demonstrate that amending natural organic matter (i.e., dried leaves) to paddy soil favored greater net arsenic demethylation in porewater and resulted in less methylated arsenic accumulation in rice grains relative to soils without organic matter amendment. Porewater correlations between dissolved methane and arsenic species were consistent with the model of methanogenesis-mediated arsenic demethylation releasing inorganic arsenic into the extracellular porewater environment. Interestingly, there was no increase in inorganic arsenic in porewater or rice grains grown in organic matter amended soils, and rice root plaque extractions are underway to determine if organic matter amendment resulted in greater inorganic arsenic adsorption to rice roots. Across multiple scales, our findings highlight new advances in the microbial connections between arsenic demethylation and methanogenesis with implications for food security and climate change.

title: Tracking Changes in Fracture Morphology on Jupiter’s Moon Europa

authors: Royes, Leah [1], Allen, Emma R [2], Martin, Emily S. [3], Nichols-Fleming, Fiona [4], Collins, Geoffrey C. [5], Rhoden, Alyssa [6]

abstract: Europa, one of Jupiter’s four Galilean moons, has an icy shell and a subsurface saltwater ocean. Europa has a heavily fractured surface and is the only other body in the solar system with evidence of plate-like motion, The fracture history preserved in Europa’s surface is manifested as a variety of structures, with double ridges being the most common. However, the formation of double ridges is not fully understood. We aim to test the hypothesis that double ridges form through an evolutionary sequence of morphologies. The sequence suggests that double ridges begin as troughs, then evolve into double ridges, ridge complexes, and bands. We used a previously established geological map with inferred stratigraphy of the trailing and leading hemispheres of Europa, to create a digitized version in ArcGIS. The digitized map has five types of features: trough, single ridge, double ridge, and band; all features were identified and mapped at a map scale of 1:500,000. We utilized the digitized map to note a transition in morphology. Transitions were defined as a point where the morphology of one feature transitioned into another. We found that most of the transitions were as expected; however, the large amount of double ridge to band transitions could imply that bands are not a part of the evolution sequence. Further analysis is needed to better understand whether the band and double ridges are part of the same sequence.

title: Investigating the Role of Geological Architecture on Shallow Injection in the Delaware Basin with Integrated Outcrop Characterization and Discrete Fracture Network Modeling
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data
authors: Busetti, Seth [1], Calle, Amanda Z. [2], Smye, Katie M. [3], Hennings, Peter H. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA

abstract:
Active injection of produced water into shallow clastic intervals in the Delaware Basin, TX, has led to elevated pore pressures observed over a ~100 km-wide region. Whereas regional synthesis of geological and engineering data has enabled a range of basin-wide simulations, many geological features are under-represented when averaged across large (>1 km) grid cells. This study aims to assess the role of fractures, faults, and bedding in the shallow injection zone at the <1 km scale. Specifically, constraints on anisotropic permeability in flow units can be improved by resolving fracture stratigraphy at the bedding scale. Additionally, the presence of long lineaments and structural blocks observed in InSAR surface deformation data and instances of containment loss may be explained by discrete structural elements. We are developing a digital outcrop model to help constrain flow anisotropy in the shallow injection units and to assess conditions for pressure localization and fault block compartmentalization.

The field location in northwest Culberson County, TX, is in the uppermost shallow injection interval in the Bell Canyon Formation of the Delaware Mountain Group. Data include measured stratigraphic sections supplemented by thin-section petrography and field and drone-based fracture and fault characterization. Field data are integrated with prior subsurface core, well logs, and 3D seismic. Three deepwater facies were interpreted in outcrop: (1) structureless fine-grained sandstone (≤1.6 m beds, <19% porosity); (2) lenticular sandstone (<0.4 m beds, 16–22% porosity); (3) planar-laminated siltstone and sandstone (<2 cm beds, 1–10% porosity). Interspersed calcite-cemented sandstone beds (<1 m thick) show <7% primary porosity, reduced permeability, and host a 345°-trending opening-mode fracture set consistent with trends of large-scale Basin and Range structures just west of the outcrops. A through-going 046°-trending shear fracture set is also present at our site and semi-regionally, consistent with Laramide contraction along a NE-trending SHmax direction. We built a discrete fracture network model that contains key facies and layers with matrix properties conditioned by the outcrop and subsurface data and fractures digitized from 3D drone imagery. The model assumes isotropic flow within structureless and amalgamated sandstone units with more restricted flow expected across erosional surfaces and in planar-laminated facies. Preliminary flow simulations using both discrete fractures and upscaled dual-porosity indicate both bedding anisotropy and fracture-controlled flow are likely in analog subsurface settings.

abstract: Wetland restoration is a focal point of land management in conjunction with ecological conservation efforts; yet the rarity of long-term studies of restoration efforts presents a challenge in understanding decadal-scale impacts of refurbished wetlands on local ecosystems. We capitalize on the efforts of a 30-year restoration project in a till-dominated watershed in New Carlisle, Ohio that resulted as a wetland mitigation mandate during a development project. The addition of continuous monitoring of both new and former points for both groundwater and surface water levels for a total of six pairs of piezometers, along with groundwater flow modeling of the aquifer via MODFLOW, provides insight into groundwater-surface water interactions that have evolved through the progression of the restoration project. Paired analysis of bi-weekly samples of stable water isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H) from groundwater, surface water, and an adjacent precipitation gauge provide additional insight into contributions to the wetlands. Coupled analysis of water levels with precipitation records from three different meteorological stations provide further insight into thresholds of precipitation that impact groundwater-surface water interactions related to the wetlands. While spring-based groundwater discharge continues to provide inflow to the wetlands, regional analysis of water levels shows a gradual progression of declining water storage in the high-capacity glacial till that predominates the aquifer. Precipitation analyses support that this groundwater storage decline is a response from prolonged drought in the past decade. This decline also does not appear to impact groundwater recharge from the wetland, though groundwater flow simulations suggest less storage results in more focused upgradient inflow into the wetlands. Both modeling and isotopic analysis support that the restoration project is accomplishing the ultimate goal of the restoration project to induce groundwater recharge, but groundwater recharge primarily occurs on the edges of the wetlands that are parallel to groundwater flow rather than the downgradient area of the wetlands. Isotopic analysis further indicates that the most downgradient edge of the wetlands exhibits a seasonal signal of groundwater upwelling, which may be indicative of longer, regional flow paths. Simulations solely based on the shallow groundwater table cannot capture that deeper groundwater upwelling. These findings provide a useful basis for evaluating wetland functioning and highlight the importance of considering both the geologic and hydrologic setting of restoration projects for long-term success.

title: Evaluating magma flow controls on Ni-Cu-PGE enrichment in the South Kawishiwi Intrusion, Duluth Complex, MN, using anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Niemiec, Ashlin [1], Kruckenberg, Seth C [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA, USA
(2) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA, USA
abstract:
Magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE deposits form through complex interactions between magma transport dynamics and sulfide segregation, yet the physical flow regimes governing ore genesis in layered mafic intrusions remain difficult to constrain directly. The South Kawishiwi Intrusion (SKI), part of the Duluth Complex, is an ideal location to advance our understanding of this problem, as it hosts Ni-Cu-PGE mineralization concentrated along its basal mineralized zone (BMZ). While prior work in the region has proposed that mineralization style reflects differences in magma transport dynamics, the internal flow architecture of the intrusion has not been systematically evaluated. This study applies anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) as a petrofabric proxy to test whether magnetic fabrics preserve primary magmatic flow signatures associated with sulfide enrichment, offering a broader methodological framework applicable to layered intrusions elsewhere.

Low-field AMS measurements were obtained from 32 oriented samples along two structural transects spanning previously characterized mineralized and non-mineralized zones. Bulk susceptibility (Km), corrected anisotropy degree (Pj), shape parameter (T), and principal susceptibility orientations (K1, K2, K3) were compared across non-mineralized, open-style, and confined-style mineralized samples. Results show elevated bulk susceptibility in mineralized zones, with confined-style samples exhibiting the highest mean Km, stronger anisotropy, and a shift toward triaxial-to-prolate fabrics, in contrast to the weaker, oblate fabrics characteristic of open-style and non-mineralized samples. Principal susceptibility orientations differ systematically between domains: non-mineralized samples show steep, near-vertical K3 axes consistent with vertical compaction, whereas mineralized samples exhibit shallower K1 inclinations, indicating a shift toward laterally organized flow within mineralized zones, with open- and confined-style domains further distinguished by contrasting K1 declinations. These patterns indicate that magnetic fabrics record primary magmatic transport rather than post-emplacement deformation.

These findings support a genetic model in which confined-style mineralization develops under higher-velocity, spatially restricted flow conditions that promote sulfide-silicate interaction and metal upgrading, whereas open-style mineralization reflects lower-energy emplacement. Despite constraints on sample density relative to intrusion scale, this dataset spans a substantial spatial extent and establishes AMS as a robust, quantitative tool for linking magma flow dynamics to sulfide distribution in layered mafic systems more broadly. These results underscore the utility of magnetic fabric analysis as a diagnostic tool for reconstructing ore-forming processes across magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE systems worldwide.

title: From Site-Based Thermal Surges to Network-Scale Vulnerability in a Karst Watershed
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Orr, Alexandra [1], Curtis, Daniel [2], Boyer, Elizabeth [3]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Bucknell University, Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, USA

abstract: Groundwater commonly stabilizes stream temperatures, but in urbanized karst watersheds this stability may increase the thermal contrast between cool baseflow and heated stormwater runoff. We analyzed daily stream temperature and discharge records from 2016 to 2024 and sub-daily temperature observations from 2020 to 2024 across 14 sites in the Spring Creek watershed of central Pennsylvania. Groundwater-influenced reaches exhibited dampened seasonal variability, whereas reaches dominated by shallower flow paths more closely tracked atmospheric forcing. Thermal surges were concentrated in urbanized tributaries, with maximum surge magnitudes exceeding 10°C. Surge magnitude increased with developed land cover, impervious cover, and hydrologic flashiness, supporting a contrast-amplification mechanism in which groundwater buffering can enhance storm-driven warming by maintaining cooler pre-storm conditions. We are extending these site-based results across the stream network by modeling reach-scale thermal surge vulnerability from baseline thermal conditions, developed land cover, spring influence, and hydrologic size while accounting for flow-connected spatial dependence. This framework is intended to identify vulnerable reaches where groundwater-supported cold-water habitat and urban runoff converge, supporting targeted monitoring and stormwater management.

title: Drip Tectonics and Surface Deformation in Mountain Belts: Role of Crustal Flow and Lithospheric Strength
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling
authors: McMillan, Mitchell [1], Sim, Shi Joyce [2], Tye, Alexander [3]
affiliations: (1) EOAS, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA; EAS, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) EAS, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
abstract:
Lithospheric foundering is often hypothesized as an important tectonic process, but crustal deformation and surface uplift patterns during a lithospheric drip are poorly understood. Using 324 visco-elasto-plastic numerical models, we systematically vary the lithosphere's rheology and density structure and develop a framework for understanding the tectonic effects of dripping. Model behaviors form a continuum, in which we recognize four characteristic tectonic responses: upper crustal shortening and surface subsidence (Type 1), upper crustal extension and surface uplift (Type 2), a transitional type from subsidence/shortening to uplift/extension (Type 3), and an intermediate type that combines upper crustal shortening with surface uplift (Type 4).

We argue that the occurrence of the Type 1 vs. Type 2 endmembers depends on two competing timescales: gravitational instability vs. crustal flow. We develop predictive equations for these timescales and define the crustalf flow efficiency ( C ), a dimensionless paramter that describes how readily a given crust flows in response to a given drip. Sustained subsidence and shortening (Type 1) requires C to be less than approximately 0.2, while uplift and extension (Type 2) requires C > 0.2. This timescale analysis gives a physical basis for the critical crust/mantle viscosity ratio ( η' ) that produces surface uplift vs. extension in classic Rayleigh-Taylor instability analyses, and it further predicts a strong dependence of η' on crustal buoyancy.

In practice, the response type can be predicted from lithospheric strength profiles together with the instability timescale. For example, Type 1 requires "crème brûlée" profiles, in which most of the strength resides in the crust, while Type 2 dominates "jelly sandwich'" profiles, which have a strong upper mantle. We find that the mantle lithosphere's rheology exerts the strongest control on drip style, followed by eclogite density and rheology. Processes that modify mantle rheology, such as hydration/metasomatism, heating, melting, and melt extraction, could therefore alter the tectonic expression of dripping through time or along strike in large orogens.

title: Thermal Resetting or Differential Exhumation? In Situ Rb–Sr Mica Geochronology of Western Maine Plutons and Metasediments
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Arkula, Cemil [1], Bubier , Noah [2], Garber, Joshua M. [3], Cruz-Uribe, Alicia Marie [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Climate Science, University of Maine, Orono, ME,
(2) Earth and Climate Sicence, University of Maine, Orono, Maine, USA
(3) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of St Andrews, St. Andrews, Scotland, United Kingdom
(4) Earth and Climate Science, University of Maine, Orono, ME,
abstract: Western Maine records a complex tectono-thermal history involving Acadian regional metamorphism and the emplacement of numerous pre-, syn-, and post-tectonic plutons that display both I- and S-type characteristics and range from mafic to felsic compositions. Here, we expand the existing geochronological framework for western Maine plutons with new in situ Rb–Sr muscovite and biotite dates from twelve plutons. These dates define contrasting post-crystallization patterns that may record differential exhumation, later thermal resetting, or both. Some plutons, including the Flagstaff Lake Igneous Complex and the Redington pluton, yield overlapping U–Pb zircon and Rb–Sr mica dates; others, including the Mooselookmeguntic Igneous Complex and the Songo and Sebago plutons, yield Rb–Sr muscovite and biotite dates that become progressively younger relative to their U–Pb crystallization ages; and the Phillips pluton represents a third pattern, in which U–Pb zircon and Rb–Sr muscovite dates overlap, but Rb–Sr biotite dates are significantly younger. The progressive younging of Rb–Sr mica dates cannot be explained solely by reheating associated with younger post-tectonic plutons, because synorogenic plutons yield overlapping U–Pb zircon and Rb–Sr mica dates, whereas the latest, post-tectonic plutons show progressively younger muscovite and biotite dates relative to their zircon crystallization ages. However, the younger mica dates of post-tectonic plutons emplaced between ca. 385 and 350 Ma in southwestern Maine could reflect thermal overprinting by the southernmost and youngest Sebago Pluton (~300 Ma). De Yoreo et al. (1989) proposed this interpretation based on the spatial distribution of 40 Ar/ 39 Ar mica and hornblende dates and the crystallization-age estimates of plutons available at the time. To better understand the distribution and juxtaposition of these distinct age domains, we compile geochronological dates from subsequent studies and integrate them with our Rb–Sr mica dates from plutons and metasediments collected during structurally focused fieldwork between plutons with contrasting cooling histories.

authors: Baldwin, Abigail [1], Burbridge, Katie [2], Giancarlo, Leanna [3], Odhiambo, Ben Kisila [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Mary Washington, Fredericksburg, Virginia, USA

abstract:
Trace metal contamination threatens both aquatic ecosystems and human health, as elevated concentrations of even biologically essential elements can become toxic and bioaccumulate through food webs. This study investigates the distribution and concentration of Hg, Pb, As, Cu, Zn, Cd, Cr, Ca, Mn, and Fe using sediment grab samples and water samples collected from 22 sites along the South Fork Shenandoah River and its tributaries. Pollution indices including enrichment factor (EF), contamination factor (CF), and pollution load index (PLI) combined with GIS‑based hot spot analysis will be used to evaluate spatial patterns and pollution severity. Biodiversity will be assessed through environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis.

The South Fork Shenandoah River, flowing along Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains, supports diverse wildlife, agriculture, and recreational use, yet has a long history of both point and non‑point trace metal inputs. The most notable source is the former DuPont textile facility in Waynesboro, which discharged mercury into a tributary from 1929 to 1950. Preliminary results show mercury concentrations ranging from <0.05 ppm upstream of the plant to 14.7 ppm in sediments immediately downstream, underscoring the persistence of legacy contamination. This study provides an updated assessment of mercury levels and expands understanding of additional trace metals not previously examined in the watershed.

title: Quantifying Wildfire-Related Debris Flow Risk to Inter-Basin Water Transfers
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society (Posters)
authors: Cadol, Daniel D. [1], Fernandez-Leger, Abelino [2], Nelson, Riley [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
abstract:
Wildfires and post-fire debris flows are well known to threaten water resources in fire-prone landscapes. This threat is compounded in the Intermountain West by the interaction of debris flow risk with inter-basin transfers of water. Communities that receive water from these diversions across natural drainage divides are exposed to negative impacts of wildfires that occur far from their physical location and even outside of their watershed. Fires in the donating watershed of these inter-basin transfers can impair or curtail the water the receiving communities have grown to depend on.

In this analysis, we combined an updated geodatabase of trans-basin diversion infrastructure with a new estimate of post-fire debris flow risk to evaluate the most threatened inter-basin transfer projects. We utilized an existing North American database as a starting point for our diversion geodatabase, and then improved the digitization of infrastructure in our study area and added additional diversions for which we could find record in the states of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming.

The post-fire debris flow risk estimate is based on a regression produced by the US Geological Survey of slope, rainfall intensity, and burn severity. For rainfall we used a 2-year recurrence interval event. Future burn severity was estimated using a Bayesian analysis of past wildfire severity and predictive factors such as vegetation type, vegetation density, and topographic indices. This analysis produced estimates of debris flow risk conditional on a fire occurring. We also considered the location of the sub-watershed producing the debris flow relative to the inter-basin diversion infrastructure in evaluating the risk of water impairment. Finally, we combined this debris flow risk with existing estimates of burn probability to produce a summary metric of annual hazard for each diversion project. We then grouped all projects into high or low relative debris flow risk and high or low annual volume of diverted water. The high-risk, high-volume category is of greatest concern, and includes projects such as the San Juan-Chama project, the Weber-Provo project, and the Twin Lakes project.

title: Tripoli: New Cyberinfrastructure for Mass Spectrometry
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data (Posters)
authors: McLean, Noah M. [1], Bowring, James F. [2], Burdick, Scott [3], Ickert, Ryan B. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(2) College of Charleston, Mount Pleasant, SC,
(3) Wayne State University, Detroit, MI, USA
(4) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
abstract:
Modern mass spectrometers use digital detection systems and software controls to produce large volumes of digital data – ion beam intensities, isotope ratios, and instrumental parameters. For thermal ionization and solution multi-collector inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (TIMS and MC-ICPMS), analyses are often long, and the large amount of data requires some basic manipulation, like outlier rejection and corrections for baselines, isobaric interferences, and/or internal mass bias correction. The output results are summarized with average values and uncertainties, which themselves become input parameters into further geochemical or geochronological calculations, like estimating nucleosynthetic isotope anomalies or radioisotopic dates.

The software supplied with commercial mass spectrometers is effective at both operating the mass spectrometer itself and providing an initial examination of the data. However, commercial mass spectrometer software does not provide a mechanism for users to interact with the data or save subjective data rejection choices alongside corrections, and it does not adopt newer statistical tools, for instance compositional data analysis or Bayesian statistical techniques.

Tripoli is new open-source cyberinfrastructure built to fit into mass spectrometer laboratory workflows and fill the gaps identified above. It replaces a previous software package of the same name, providing updates to both the graphical user interface, cross-platform compatibility, and integration with new mass spectrometers. Tripoli was designed with community input and developed and tested collaboratively on the GitHub platform.

Recent developments in Tripoli include improvements to LiveWorkflow, where data are streamed to Tripoli immediately as they are measured on the mass spectrometer, producing real-time summary statistics, as well as new Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods applied to Bayesian models of beam growth and decay for both static and multi-dynamic or single-collector measurements. We have also developed native session-based data aggregation and interpretation workflows, which link the data interpretations for a larger project across files that may be stored in distributed locations. Future effort will concentrate on improving ways to visualize and interact with the most sophisticated Bayesian models, which are based on both the measured ion beam intensity data and models for mass spectrometer behavior and noise.

title: Constraining the Influences of Primary and Secondary Surface Processes on Grain Roundness on an Alluvial Fan: Implications for Interpreting Fan Deposits on Earth and Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Gibson, Tatiana M [1], Rivera-Hernández, Frances [2], Thompson, Sharissa Y [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
abstract:
Alluvial fans record a history of surface water flows on Earth and Mars, and sedimentary properties including rounding, grain size, and sorting are used to interpret past flow conditions including transport distance and dominant transport process. However, secondary, post-depositional processes are known to alter these primary textures, especially through clast fragmentation from thermal stresses. To understand the relative influences of primary versus secondary processes on texture, we investigated 3 surficial units on the Piper Canyon alluvial fan (Dyer, NV) of different relative ages. These surfaces were identified in previous relative age mapping efforts and include the modern alluvial channel, a late mid Holocene surface, and an early late Pleistocene surface. We performed pebble counts at nine sites: three downfan distances for each of the three units, where we gathered data on clast rounding, grain size, and rock varnish development. The degree of rock varnish development has commonly been used as a relative age indicator on fans. Manganese is abundant in rock varnish and was assessed by portable laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), an analysis technique also used by some Mars rovers.

We found that LIBS peaks associated with manganese are on average 2 to 3 times higher intensity on the oldest unit than the younger units. We also found a distinct roundness distribution for each unit: the mean roundness class of the youngest unit is subangular, the intermediate unit is angular, and the oldest unit is very angular. We suggest that relative age is a more significant influence on clast rounding on Piper Canyon fan, rather than down-fan distance, due to the effects of secondary processes. Our results suggest that fan deposits bearing both elevated manganese and featuring mostly angular to very angular clasts have been sufficiently altered by secondary processes so that transport distance cannot be as reliably interpreted. This suggests that clast rounding alone may not be a reliable indicator of transport distance in arid environments with strong thermal stresses. By assessing manganese with LIBS and using a rounding metric that can be determined in images, we demonstrate the possibility of using similar data sets for identifying relative age indicators in fan settings on Mars to assess possible post-depositional alteration when interpreting past water history from sedimentary textures.

abstract:
The lower Deadwood Formation at Little Elk Creek (LEC) in South Dakota records transgressive shallow marine sedimentation along the northern margin of the Laurentian craton during the Cambrian Guzhangian Stage. At LEC, the lower portion of the unit consists of a massive basal sandstone overlain with bioturbated siltstones. The siltstones transition upward into gray-green glauconitic carbonates interbedded with quartz-rich sandstone benches. The upper portion of the unit contains glauconitic packstones interbedded with intraformational conglomerates featuring miciritic limestone intraclasts with glauconitic crusts. Fossils are found throughout as original calcareous and organophosphatic remains alongside moldic and secondary phosphatic and glauconitic preservation. Although glauconite pellets are common in Cambrian shallow marine deposits, the pervasive and apparently taxonomically selective glauconitic replication of shelly faunas from this locality is a taphonomic process that remains poorly understood. This study thus examines taphonomic pathways within a late Middle Cambrian shelly fossil assemblage to disentangle the geochemical and paleoenvironmental conditions that facilitate glauconite associated fossilization.

Samples were collected from a 20 m measured stratigraphic section at Little Elk Creek, South Dakota. Bulk limestone samples were macerated in 7% dilute acetic acid, sieved, and residues were picked for microfossils. Select specimens were examined using light microscopy, X-ray tomographic microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Results show original, moldic, and replacive processes, and of particular interest, an abundance of glauconite and calcium phosphate throughout the echinoderm and small shelly fossil assemblage. We suspect that the timing of glauconite entering the taphonomic system may vary and thereby facilitate the fossilization process and modification of skeletal elements. Hence, further work will require resolving the taphonomic history of the assemblage to differentiate between biostratinomic processes and subsequent paragenetic overprinting.

title: Modeling Mine Dewatering Impact On Local Hydrology: Insight From a Calibrated Steady State Groundwater Flow Model
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling (Posters)
authors: Ijigade, Franklin Oseyemi [1], Milewski, Adam M [2]

abstract: Mining supplies raw materials needed for infrastructure, energy technologies, and economic development, but mine dewatering can alter local groundwater-flow systems. while studies have examined dewatering impacts on water resources sustainability associated with deep open-pit mines, less attention has been given to shallow heavy-mineral-sand mines developed within surficial aquifers. This study develops a three-dimensional steady-state groundwater flow model to evaluate the hydrologic impacts of dewatering within a shallow (6 m below ground surface) heavy mineral sand mine in South Georgia. The conceptual model consists of three hydro-stratigraphic units subdivided into seven layers and was developed in the Groundwater Modeling System (GMS) using data from geophysical surveys and thickness maps from South Georgia and Florida. The MODFLOW-NWT simulator was used overs 116.35 km² domain with a 75 × 75 m grid to model spatial groundwater level conditions. Mine pit were represented using drain boundary with a bottom elevation of 16 m. Steady-state simulations representing pre-mining, active-dewatering, and post-dewatering conditions were calibrated and evaluated using groundwater-level observations (9 piezometers and 13 piezometer wells) from 2013 and 2026. Model calibration produced an RMSE of 0.17 m, NSE of 0.99, and R² of 0.98. Sensitivity analysis identified hydraulic conductivity as the most influential parameter, followed by recharge. The post-mining steady-state simulation shifted the area of highest modeled groundwater heads from the central mine area to the southern portion of the model domain, where heads were approximately 0.8 m higher than in the pre-mining simulation. The active-dewatering scenario produced a maximum drawdown of 5.5 m adjacent to the mine pit. In the post-dewatering equilibrium simulation, modeled heads were within approximately 0.3 m of pre-mining conditions, indicating limited residual drawdown under the simulated long-term conditions. Because steady-state simulations do not represent the timing of drawdown or recovery, transient modeling is needed to quantify the rate and duration of groundwater responses. This modeling framework provides a practical tool for optimizing mine dewatering while fostering environmental stewardship which will serve as regulatory compliance sustainable groundwater management

authors: Riggs , Abby [1], Clary, Renee [2], Nagel, Athena [3], Haney, Christa [4]

abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) printing provides geoscience educators with opportunities to expand access to physical fossil specimens and develop reusable materials for hands-on laboratory instruction. However, creating physical 3D fossil models for educational purposes requires several considerations that extend beyond the technical process of 3D printing. This study developed physical 3D fossil models for use in an introductory physical geology laboratory at Mississippi State University and examined practical considerations involved in transforming digital fossil models into classroom-ready instructional tools. Fossil models were created by 1) scanning fossil specimens and utilizing existing digital models, 2) digital preparation, and 3) 3D printing using PLA filament. Printed models underwent extensive post-processing, including sanding, painting, and application of a protective coating to improve their durability for repeated handling by students. Through this process, several practical considerations emerged for educational applications, including balancing the preservation of pertinent morphological features with model quality while also considering fossil size and complexity, printability, production time, and long-term classroom usability. Throughout the development process, decisions to improve printability, durability, and production efficiency were often balanced against maintaining accurate morphological representation and the educational usefulness of the models. By documenting the development process and practical considerations associated with creating educational 3D-printed fossil models, this study provides insight for educators interested in developing accessible, reusable 3D-printed materials and incorporating them in geoscience instruction for hands-on student learning. This study demonstrated that the most effective educational 3D fossil model is not necessarily the most technically accurate or visually complex model, but rather one that accurately represents important morphological features while also being printable, durable, appropriately scaled, and usable within an instructional setting.

abstract:
Project TrapRock is a collaborative research effort led by the Carbon Containment Lab in partnership with the Washington State Geological Survey (WGS). The project is funded by Washington State Department of Commerce through the state’s Climate Commitment Act and by a grant from Breakthrough Energy Foundation. The objective is to better characterize the Columbia River Basalt Group (CRBG) as a potential reservoir for permanent geologic carbon sequestration.

Geophysical data collected during the project include airborne electromagnetics (AEM), aeromagnetics, ground-based relative gravity stations, passive seismic monitoring, and an active-source 3D seismic survey.

Some key results include:

A 3D image from inversion of the AEM data, covering about 1500 km 2 and extending to a depth of 600 meters below the topography, reveals the stacked nature of the CRBG, including interflow horizons with lower resistivity and likely greater permeability as well as a transition to a very low resistivity zone consistent with mineralized waters below the contact between the Wanapum and Grande Ronde basalt flows.

A 3D image from the active-source seismic survey, covering about 25 km 2 and reaching to depths > 8 km, shows the base of the CRBG, and reveals through-cutting, sub-vertical, dextral shear faults oriented NE-SW and the low angle HHH thrust fault.

Gravity and aeromagnetic anomalies in the seismic footprint suggest the presence of unmapped structures in the CRBG beneath Quaternary loess.

While the scope of the airborne data is regional, the focus of modeling is the footprint of the seismic survey. The goal is to combine the geophysical data with geochemical and rock-property data to create a digital twin of (a portion of) the CRBG to simulate the flow and mineralization of carbon dioxide injected into its highly permeable flow tops and interflow horizons.

title: A Workflow for Classifying Skeletal Fossil Abundances Within Stratigraphic Sections Using Convolutional Neural Network Architectures
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology and Geomicrobiology (Posters)
authors: Helms, Lucy A. [1], Robillard, Sophia [2], Thomas, Laura [3], Gietka, Dahlia [4], Mehra, Akshay K. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(3) Department of Applied Mathematics, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(4) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(5) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
As machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) approaches in science continue to develop, fundamental questions about the utility, implementation, and efficacy of such approaches remain unanswered. Here, we consider the application of ML/AI to image classification in sedimentology and paleontology, namely as a tool for enhancing the efficiency of point counting. Point counting is one of the standard methods for quantifying the composition of a rock and involves identifying the composition of the rock sample at discrete points across a thin section. Through point counting, researchers generate important datasets about the abundance and diversity of their sample set, and students learn important skills such as fossil and mineral identification, sedimentary structure recognition, and classification of lithology. Point counting (and, more generally, classification) can be readily automated via AI/ML. The question, then, is how one might incorporate such techniques while preserving the expertise of researchers and the educational transfer of skills for students.

We present a novel workflow for training and classifying skeletal fossil abundance that bridges the gap between traditional microscope point counting methods and future fully automated classification efforts. Our method involves user classification of a subset of thin sections to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) model, which then classifies an entire set of thin sections using either a whole-patch or a center-dot architecture. We explicitly designed our model to train on and learn stratigraphic section-specific features in order to reduce classification errors that may come from training on thin sections from different depositional environments or time periods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our classification model by testing the result of our workflow against manual point count abundance data collected from thin sections from the Lower–Middle Ordovician strata of the Arrow Canyon Range, NV. This workflow is suitable for both classrooms and research settings, as it develops fundamental skills in fossil and sedimentological recognition and classification, introduces the user to AI/ML architectures for usage in the Earth sciences, and prepares individuals to navigate the realities of scientific research in the age of AI.

title: Refuting the sensational claim of a Hopewell‑ending cosmic airburst with evidence-based research
session_title: Myths and Misrepresentations surrounding Cosmic Impact claims in Paleoclimatology, Paleontology, Paleoecology, Geoarchaeology, and Quaternary Research
authors: Murphy, Laura R [1], Lepper, Bradley T [2]
affiliations: (1) Washburn University, Topeka, KS, USA
(2) Ohio History Connection, Columbus, OH, USA
abstract: In February 2022, Nature Scientific Reports (volume 12) published an article by Tankersley et al. titled: "The Hopewell airburst event, 1699–1567 years ago (252–383 CE)." The Washington Post covered the article shortly thereafter with the headline: "Did an exploding comet help end an ancient Native American culture? Experts think the violent blast incinerated Hopewell settlements in what is now Ohio." This is an example of a popular pseudoarchaeology trend which claims comet airbursts are responsible for destroying ancient cultures. Since it is difficult to prove or disprove an airburst at any given time in the past, proponents cherry-pick data to stitch together so-called "cosmic catastrophism" click-bait. The Tankersley et al. paper was no exception; media coverage of a Hopewell-ending airburst resulted in public misunderstanding concerning the fate of Indigenous people who lived in the Middle Ohio River Valley between 1,600 and 2,000 years ago. In July 2022, Neuhäuser and Neuhäuser sounded the alarm with a "Matters Arising" contribution in Scientific Reports highlighting the uncertainties for a comet in the place and time proposed by Tankersley et al. In August 2023, Nolan et al., published an archaeological and geological critique also as a "Matters Arising" contribution, which ultimately led the editors of Scientific Reports to retract the Tankersley et al. paper by August 30, 2023. Here, we present an overview of the Nolan et. al. effort to provide the data that led to the Tankersley et al. retraction. We elaborate on the evidence-based research, particularly from the Turner Earthworks site, and show how the Hopewell archaeological record demonstrates continued habitation with gradual sociopolitical and economic reorganization (e.g., a cessation in large ceremonial earthwork construction) and changes in settlement patterns. Without evidence for a culture-ending cosmic catastrophe, we discuss the harms of such pseudoarchaeological beliefs. We will demonstrate how we have used this case study to boost scientific literacy through pedagogy in our classrooms and public outreach through community lectures, social media, and podcasts in new ways with the intention of expanding the reach of evidence-based research to promote the Ohio Hopewell Culture.

title: Rain-Fed Bioenergy Crops in Place of Irrigated Row Crops: Sustaining the Ogallala Aquifer
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Quinn, John J. [1], Zumpf, Colleen [2]
affiliations: (1) Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne, IL, USA
(2) Argonne National Lab, Argonne, IL, USA
abstract: The Ogallala aquifer extends across the U.S. Great Plains, from South Dakota to Texas. Irrigation dominates the use of the aquifer, with groundwater essentially being mined, as recharge occurs much slower than the consumptive withdrawals. Rain-fed perennial native grasses, such as switchgrass, can be grown in the region and offer an alternative to irrigated corn for the production of liquid biofuels or biomass-based products. In this study, we modify a highly detailed numerical groundwater flow model developed by the U.S. Geological Survey (Peterson et al. 2016, 2020) to examine the long-term effects of reduced irrigation pumping in the northern Great Plains. Relative to baseline predictions, results indicate the improved groundwater availability in future scenarios that include conversion of a portion of center-pivot irrigation systems to rain-fed bioenergy crops. Together with reduced fertilizer requirements, reduced crop management needs, and a wide range of ecosystem services associated with perennial grasses, the adoption of rain-fed bioenergy crops provides a solution for improving the sustainability of this important groundwater resource.

title: Static Terrain, Changing Watersheds: Integrating Post-Fire Susceptibility and Current Conditions in Boulder County, Colorado
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society
authors: Lovekin, Jonathan [1], Crandall, Amy [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Colorado Geological Survey, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract:
Post-fire hazard assessments commonly address either terrain-based susceptibility—where runoff and sediment mobilization may occur—or changing watershed conditions, assessed with rainfall thresholds and field measurements. Neither provides a complete assessment alone.

Ingram Gulch in Boulder County, Colorado, burned in the September 2010 Fourmile Canyon Fire and subsequently produced post-fire debris flows. Colorado School of Mines collaborators established a real-time geotechnical monitoring array that measures hydraulic and soil-strength conditions. The resulting multiyear record provides an opportunity to examine how antecedent hydrologic and mechanical conditions relate to precipitation, runoff, and sediment mobilization. Monitoring sites in the Calwood burn scar, which burned in October 2020, provide complementary observations from another wildfire-affected Boulder County landscape.

We use Ingram Gulch to examine how static terrain susceptibility and dynamic watershed condition can be evaluated together. Static information describes source areas, routing pathways, receiving landforms such as alluvial fans, and potentially exposed infrastructure. Dynamic information includes precipitation history, field measurements of hydromechanical soil conditions, rainfall-initiation thresholds, and satellite-derived surface conditions.

Sentinel-1 radar backscatter, Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture, and Global Precipitation Measurement Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals (GPM IMERG) precipitation were evaluated against multiyear site-specific ground truth. Sentinel-1 tracked in-situ soil moisture weakly; SMAP more closely tracked ground measurements. GPM IMERG diverged from the rain gauge and consistently overestimated cumulative rainfall. Gauge and field measurements remain reference for interpreting these satellite products.

In a recent assessment, field measurements, precipitation records, and a Sentinel-1 surface-condition signal indicated elevated antecedent watershed conditions at Ingram Gulch. At the same time, observed rainfall remained below the modeled initiation threshold. Together, these observations supported a qualified interpretation: watershed conditions were more favorable for hazard initiation than under typical seasonal conditions, but available evidence did not indicate that the rainfall threshold had been exceeded.

No individual measurement predicts a debris flow. The scientific value lies in determining whether independent observations support the same interpretation—and recognizing when they do not. This approach may also help evaluate runoff, sediment transport, fan deposition, and related downstream effects. The satellite-versus-in-situ comparison provides a starting point for evaluating satellite reliability at other post-fire sites in Colorado. This work is intended to improve the scientific information available to watershed programs, emergency managers, and local governments while preserving the distinction between scientific assessment and operational warning.

title: Del volcán al salar: Firma hidrogeoquímica y evolución de elementos traza en la cuenca volcánico-evaporítica de Pastos Grandes, Bolivia
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part II)
authors: Huallpara, Lizangela [1], Ormachea, Mauricio [2], Elmeke, Ida [3], Witalisson, Hanna [4], Alam, Mohammad Ayaz [5], Bhattacharya, Prosun [6]
affiliations: (1) Instituto de Investigaciones Químicas, Universidad Mayor de San Andrés, La Paz, Bolivia; Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
(2) Instituto de Investigaciones Químicas, Universidad Mayor de San Andrés, La Paz, Bolivia
(3) Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
(4) Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
(5) Departamento de Ingeniería Geoespacial y Ambiental, Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Santiago de Chile, Santiago, Chile
(6) International Groundwater Arsenic Research Group, Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
abstract:
Este estudio investiga la composición de la firma hidrogeoquímica y la evolución de elementos traza (ET) en diferentes cuerpos de agua dentro la cuenca volcánico-evaporítica de Pastos Grandes, ubicada en el Altiplano Boliviano, donde los sistemas evaporíticos andinos de gran altitud han adquirido importancia estratégica, vinculados a tecnologías energéticas emergentes sobre todo en la región del Triángulo del Litio Sudamericano. A pesar de esta importancia, los procesos hidrogeoquímicos que controlan la movilización, el transporte y la acumulación de elementos traza a lo largo de la trayectoria hidrológica desde la zona volcánica andina hasta el salar, no son comprendido en su totalidad. Se tomaron muestras de aguas termales, ríos, lagunas, bofedales y aguas salinas evolucionadas para determinar sus características fisicoquímicas y su composición geoquímica, posteriormente, empleando diagramas de interpretación hidroquímica, herramientas estadísticas y modelación geoquímica con PHREEQC poder evaluar la firma hidrogeoquímica de los diferentes cuerpos de agua y su evolución dentro de la cuenca.

Los resultados identificaron a las aguas termales reductoras de tipo Na-Cl como la principal fuente geogénica de litio (Li), boro (B), arsénico (As), rubidio (Rb), estroncio (Sr) y cesio (Cs). A medida que el agua se transporta desde el cinturón volcánico andino hacia las zonas evaporíticas, evoluciona cambiando consecuentemente sus concentraciones. Los cuerpos de agua meteóricos de baja conductividad eléctrica, al fluir hacia la parte baja de la cuenca se mezcla con aguas termales y sufre procesos de intensa evaporación que terminan formando lagunas salinas y salares con elevadas concentraciones de solutos. Los elementos presentan un enriquecimiento progresivo asociado a la interacción agua-roca, procesos redox, control mineralógico y concentración por evaporación, alcanzando sus mayores concentraciones en las zonas de descarga de la cuenca salina (hasta 350 mg/L Li, 132 mg/L Cs, 66 mg/L Sr, 57 mg/L B, 52 mg/L Rb y 6.8 mg/L As). La interacción hidrotermal agua/roca, los aportes redox, mineralógicos y de evaporación definen la firma hidrogeoquímica de la cuenca desde el Cinturón Volcánico en los Andes hasta la laguna salina de Pastos Grandes y confirman el origen predominantemente geogénico de estos elementos. Estos hallazgos son cruciales para distinguir la evolución y el enriquecimiento natural de ET con los posibles impactos antropogénicos asociados con la explotación de recursos de litio en la región.

title: Using plant wax hydrogen isotope ratios to reconstruct Central American moisture source variability over the past 1,200 years
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Gibson, Derek K. [1], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [2], Berke, Melissa [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Systems and Sustainability, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, IL, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(3) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, USA
abstract: Accurately attributing the drivers of isotopic variability is particularly important in regions like Central America, where multiple moisture pathways intersect and their relative influence shifts through time. To improve predictive modeling efforts, a more complete characterization of the factors that influence regional isotope-based records is required. To address this need, we reconstructed 1,200 years of precipitation and circum-Caribbean atmospheric circulation using sedimentary plant wax hydrogen isotope ratios and XRF spectroscopy from Lake Izabal, Guatemala. Warm intervals (e.g., the Medieval Climate Anomaly; MCA) were dry with 2 H-depleted precipitation, whereas the cooler Little Ice Age (LIA) was wetter and precipitation was 2 H-enriched – opposite to the conventional “amount effect.” We attribute this to shifts in dominant moisture sources. Specifically, during the MCA, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) was in a northern position, while the Caribbean Low-Level Jet (CLLJ) strengthened and shifted south, reducing the contribution of ²H-enriched Caribbean moisture while increasing the relative contribution of ²H-depleted Pacific moisture. During the LIA, a northern CLLJ and southern ITCZ enhanced Caribbean-sourced precipitation. Our results highlight that Atlantic-Pacific moisture-source balance exerts a primary control on regional isotopic signatures, demonstrating the potential of isotopic proxies to reconstruct past moisture-source variability.

title: Integrated Hyperspectral, Geochemical, and Isotopic Constraints on Dryland Surface Processes in the Arabian Peninsula
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Alshakr, Ahmed M. [1], Sultan, Mohamed I. [2], Emil, Mustafa Kemal [3], Sturchio, Neil C. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA; Geology, Ain Shams University, Cairo, Egypt, Arab Rep.
(2) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(3) Geological and Environmental Sciences, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, USA
(4) Earth Sciences, University of Delaware, Newark, DE, USA
abstract: Arid landscapes evolve through interacting eolian, evaporative, and groundwater processes, yet their regional distribution, sediment sources, and evolution remain poorly constrained. Using the Arabian Peninsula (AP) as a natural laboratory, we investigated dune and sabkha distribution, provenance, types, and origin by integrating hyperspectral mineral mapping from NASA's Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT) with field observations, X-ray diffraction (XRD), geochemistry, and Sr-Li isotope analyses. EMIT mineral abundance maps identified six diagnostic minerals (calcite, kaolinite, muscovite-illite, chlorite, hematite, and goethite) that trace sediment provenance and transport pathways. Combined with prevailing winds, relict fluvial networks, and mineral attenuation, these fingerprints delineate three provenance domains: (1) intracontinental sources from the AP Shield and Paleozoic siliciclastic rocks, (2) marginal inputs from carbonate and ophiolitic terranes, and (3) extra-basinal contributions from marine carbonate aeolianites and the Bitlis-Zagros orogenic belt. EMIT also distinguishes three evaporitic environments: (1) coastal marine sabkhas characterized by gypsum and carbonates, (2) groundwater-fed inland sabkhas of eastern Arabia dominated by montmorillonite with field-observed halite, and (3) Arabian alluvial fan-playa systems characterized by detrital illite/muscovite and kaolinite deposits. We propose an Ascending Brine Model in which inland sabkhas formed through discharge of deep saline groundwater during wetter paleoclimatic periods, supported by: (1) concentric mineral zonation from elevated montmorillonite-rich mudflats to gypsum-rich margins and low-elevation halite-dominated salt pans; (2) Sabkhas localized within structurally controlled depressions aligned with major reactivated basement faults; (3) widespread sapping, karst, and saline springs indicating persistent groundwater discharge; (4) groundwater ^87Sr/^86Sr ratios (0.70771–0.70874) matching Neogene formation waters but distinct from seawater; (5) increasing δ^7Li values from springs to salt pans indicating prolonged water-rock interaction and brine evolution; and (6) stable O-H isotopes recording paleo recharge followed by intense evaporation. Results show that Integrated EMIT and traditional data provides a powerful framework for resolving sediment provenance, sediment-routing systems, groundwater evolution, and evaporite formation across arid landscapes, with broad applications to desert regions worldwide.

title: Bridging Detrital Age Distributions and Thermal-Kinematic Inversions: Regional Exhumation Along the Eastern Sierra Nevada
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Giblin, Jacqueline L. [1], Hodges, Kip [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Phoenix, AZ, USA
(2) School and Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract:
Regional exhumation studies are frequently limited by the availability of bedrock thermochronology data. Detrital samples integrate mineral ages within drainage basins but lack the spatial context required for three-dimensional thermal-kinematic modeling. We have combined detrital zircon U-Pb (ZrnPb), hornblende 40 Ar/ 39 Ar (HblAr), apatite U-Pb (ApPb), zircon (U-Th)/He (ZrnHe), and apatite (U-Th)/He (ApHe) data with catchment hypsometry to model candidate bedrock age-elevation relationships for the eastern Sierra Nevada of California. ZrnPb populations provide a catchment-specific temporal framework for evaluating post-magmatic cooling, while a topographic sampling function translates thermochronology distributions into predicted transects. Channel coordinates then provide spatial constraints for Pecube models.

We applied this approach to 25 catchments. ZrnPb datasets preserve signatures of Mesozoic arc-building episodes. Most catchments contain populations of the youngest major Sierra Nevada magmatic pulse (ca. 80-100 Ma), while several preserve Jurassic (ca. 160-170 Ma) or older (>200 Ma) populations. Relationships between ZrnPb crystallization and high- to intermediate-temperature thermochronometers (HblAr and ApPb) vary among catchments and provide context for the timing and rate of post-magmatic cooling. Lower-temperature systems also vary along strike: ZrnHe modes increase from ca. 39 Ma in the southernmost catchments (35.4°N), to ca. 61 Ma in central and northern groups (36.5°N - 39.2° N), while ApHe modes are predominantly ca. 20 Ma across southern catchments and form an older ca. 35 Ma cluster in the north.

Pecube inversions of predicted transects from three catchments in the central Sierra Nevada resolve a consistent two-stage history. Relatively rapid Late Cretaceous exhumation (0.4 km/Myr) is followed by rates of <0.1 km/Myr through the Cenozoic. Two catchments draining similar Late Cretaceous plutonic rocks produce closely aligned histories, whereas a third records earlier cooling and exhumation associated with an older magmatic population and deeper inferred sources. These histories agree with independent thermal-history models and predicted ApHe ages agree with published bedrock transects at overlapping elevations. However, catchments likely underrepresent the lowest elevations, where localized late Cenozoic signals may be preferentially recorded.

Together, these results illustrate how detrital multi-chronometer data can provide constraints on long-term exhumation while retaining catchment-specific magmatic and cooling histories. The approach offers a scalable pathway for evaluating regional exhumation where dense bedrock transects are unavailable, while recognizing reduced resolution of short-duration or localized events.

title: Hydrologic and Geomorphic Controls on Flooding in Dryland Riverscapes
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Shallue, Michaela K [1], Patterson, Noelle [2], Scamardo, Julianne [3], Phillips, Colin B [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering & the Utah Water Research Laboratory, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(2) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering & the Utah Water Research Laboratory, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(3) Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT, USA
(4) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering & the Utah Water Research Laboratory, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
abstract: Flooding in dryland riverscapes is shaped by both hydrologic and geomorphic drivers. Dryland streams in the southwestern United States experience flooding in response to warm‑season monsoon storms that produce high‑magnitude, short‑duration precipitation, despite occurring in arid and drought‑prone landscapes. Standard flood‑recurrence methods, such as the Annual Maximum Series (AMS), can obscure true flood frequency in systems where several flood events may cluster within one monsoon season and then be followed by years of prolonged drought. Hydrologic flood‑recurrence approaches also fail to capture geomorphic drivers of flooding: bed aggradation can reduce channel capacity, elevate the water surface, and lower the discharge threshold needed to cause flooding. To better characterize flood frequency and magnitude in relation to both hydrologic and geomorphic drivers, we apply a Peaks Over Threshold (POT) method to high‑resolution (15‑minute) stage and discharge data from US Geological Survey gages. These data come from dryland rivers and streams in Arizona, Utah, New Mexico, and Nevada, spanning perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral flow regimes. Using topographically defined flood thresholds, we independently assess the frequency of high flow stages versus high discharges to isolate the relative contributions of hydrologic forcing and channel‑bed change. This approach highlights how dryland flood hazard reflects both the undercounting of wet years and the flooding potential of rivers experiencing drought due to high sediment loads and persistent bed aggradation. Improving flood‑hazard characterization in these geomorphically dynamic riverscapes is essential for understanding how dryland channels respond to hydroclimatic variability and for mitigating damages to infrastructure and loss of life in flash‑flood‑prone landscapes.
