title: Quantification of polyphase lower crustal viscosity and strain localization processes in naturally deformed granulites of the Mount Hay Block, Central Australia
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Kruckenberg, Seth C [1], Shea, Lauren [2], Burek, Olivia [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA, USA
(2) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA, USA
(3) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA, USA
abstract:
The rheology of the lower crust exerts a first-order control on lithospheric strength and deformation, yet remains difficult to quantify because most experimental flow laws describe single mineral phases rather than the polyphase rocks that dominate natural exposures. The Mount Hay Block, central Australia, preserves an exceptional record of naturally deformed lower crustal granulites exposed on Mount Hay, Ceilidh Hill, and the adjacent, kilometer-scale Capricorn Ridge shear zone (CRSZ) that overprints them. These granulites comprise interlayered mafic and felsic domains, composed primarily of plagioclase, pyroxene, and quartz, that preserve variable modal mineralogy across both localities, providing an opportunity to directly compare polyphase lower crustal rheology across two structurally distinct domains.

Using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)-based microstructural and textural analysis, grain-size paleopiezometry, and geothermometry, we determined differential stresses, deformation temperatures, and recrystallized grain sizes for quartz, plagioclase, enstatite, and diopside. These parameters were used to calculate effective viscosities from monophase flow laws for each constituent phase, which were in turn integrated using two distinct approaches – the Minimized Power Geometric mixing model and the Asymptotic Expansion Homogenization (AEH) method – to calculate the bulk polyphase effective viscosity of each sample as a function of its modal mineralogy.

At Ceilidh Hill, deformation temperatures of ca. 780–810°C and differential stresses of 34–54 MPa yield polyphase effective viscosities of 3.07 × 10²⁰ to 2.74 × 10²¹ Pa·s at a strain rate of 10⁻¹⁴ s⁻¹. Across the CRSZ, differential stresses range from 14–27 MPa (quartz), 21.8–63.9 MPa (plagioclase), 2.1–12.7 MPa (enstatite), and 7.9–25.2 MPa (diopside) at similar deformation temperatures, yielding polyphase effective viscosities of 9.1 × 10²⁰ to 1.8 × 10²¹ Pa·s at the same strain rate. Within the CRSZ, polyphase viscosity decreases toward lithologic boundaries, where strain-induced fabrics are most intense, indicating that strain accumulation there is accommodated in part by grain-size reduction.

When compared at an equivalent strain rate, the polyphase effective viscosities calculated for Ceilidh Hill and the CRSZ overlap substantially and fall within the same order of magnitude, despite their distinct structural settings and deformation histories. This consistency demonstrates that combined field and microstructural studies of deformed lower crustal terrains, when integrated with mixing models of existing flow laws, yield robust estimates of naturally deformed polyphase lower crustal rheology.

title: From Feeding to Fossil Feces: Connecting Enigmatic Trace Fossils to a Likely tracemaker in the Late Cretaceous Niobrara Formation of Western Kansas
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part I)
authors: Maltese, Anthony [1], Atwater, Amy [2], Everhart, Michael [3]
affiliations: (1) Triebold Paleontology Inc., Woodland Park, CO,
(2) Friends of Dinosaur Ridge, Morrison, CO,
(3) Sternberg Museum of Natural History, Hays, KS, USA
abstract:
Exploration of the paleontology of the Smoky Hill member of the Niobrara Formation has regularly occurred since E. D. Cope’s 1870 expedition to western Kansas. Hattin’s 1982 description of the Smoky Hill Chalk marker units established useful stratigraphic references based on lithology, addressing complaints of the lack of stratigraphic data collected with vertebrate macrofossils. The description of trace fossils has lagged behind, with few mentions in literature. Here we describe a new ichnofossil with implications for paleoecology and biostratigraphy.

Unique trace fossils composed of angular bivalve fragments are found between Hattin’s marker units 4 and 6. This brief interval of deposition closes with the disappearance of the inoceramid Volviceramus involutus and the end of the Coniacian stage (~85.5 Ma). These trace fossils, here interpreted as coprolites, are strictly found in association with the rare and poorly known ram-snouted fish Martinichthys ziphoides. These fish, primarily found as robust isolated rostra, only occur in this interval in Kansas. We interpret the coprolites as traces of Martinichthys feeding activity.

CT scans, photographs, and thin sections of the coprolites were analyzed to study their composition. Thin sections were compared to sliced samples of Volviceramus , Pseudoperna , Platyceramus and barnacles.These analyses indicate that Marthichthys used a percussive, durophagous feeding strategy. Martinichthys , restricted here to M. ziphoides , likely preyed on Pseudoperna congesta oyster communities anchored to hardgrounds on the soft seafloor. These include large inoceramids, the rudist Durania maxima and encrusting fauna on sunken driftwood logs. Individually variable beveled rostral tips are interpreted as wear facets from feeding. There are no external indicators of stress fractures. We hypothesize an effective face-ramming behaviour for M. ziphoides that smashes encrusting oysters against the hardground, enabling a fish that completely lacks crushing dentition to exploit a hard-shelled prey. The resulting pulp is then ingested and processed through the fish. The relative abundance of coprolites compared to body fossils highlights their potential as biostratigraphic proxies for Martinichthys . Other durophagus Cretaceous fish were evaluated as a tracemaker; however, they have broader geographic and stratigraphic ranges and no co-occurrence with crushed shell coprolites. This research enhances our understanding of Late Cretaceous paleoecology, revealing a highly specialized trophic niche in the Niobrara. By describing these coprolites and assigning them to Martinichthys , this study highlights paleoecology significance and biostratigraphic value.

abstract: The Perseverance rover has observed boxwork-like fractured bedrock in two locations (Oslobreen and Le Meix) along its traverse of the outer Jezero crater rim, both thought to be Noachian in age. These features might have been associated with hydrothermal or groundwater systems resulting from the impact that formed Jezero crater, so are important targets for studying geologic context and astrobiologic potential for early Mars. These relatively small exposures are characterized by intersections of ~0.5 to 1 m-wide bedrock ridges creating boxwork-like patterns that are identified and separated by recessed areas filled with regolith. The patterns were initially observed in orbital HiRISE images and are visible in surface images from Mastcam-Z. In both locations, Mastcam-Z multispectral data show that the fractured, ridge-forming rocks contain low-calcium pyroxene (LCP). Additional SuperCam visible-infrared (VISIR) spectroscopic data at Le Meix show evidence of LCP and hydrated sulfates. These ridges are also associated with rubbly, cobble-to pebble-sized, Fe-poor rock fragments situated within their interior that appear to be locally derived. Based on Mastcam-Z observations with supporting instrument data in other locations of the Jezero rim, this Fe-poor material could be consistent with either a high-Si phase or feldspar. Chemical data acquired by SuperCam LIBS within the Le Meix area show elevated chemical indices of alteration (CIA) indicative of open-system alteration. At an area 300 m away, SuperCam acquired VISIR data on a fracture-associated halo feature that showed an Al-phyllosilicate signature (~2.21 micron band) and high CIA values, which indicates that bedrock fractures likely acted as conduits for fluid flow generally in the region. Given the Noachian age and geologic setting, one plausible formation mechanism for these patterns and corresponding mineralogical signatures is impact- or volcanic-induced hydrothermalism, whereby warm fluids flow through a fracture system and deposit Fe-poor mineral precipitates. Subsequent aeolian erosion exploits the relative erosional weakness of the surrounding material to leave the observed boxwork-like pattern. Should Perseverance encounter more of these features on its continued exploration, we recommend a dedicated investigation using the entire payload to better understand the small-scale textures and detailed chemistry of both the ridge material and associated Fe-poor fragments. This would help us to further constrain their origin and compare them to other, more prominent boxwork patterns on Mars.

abstract:
Industrial air pollution is a significant environmental problem in Bangladesh, particularly in Gazipur, one of the country's most densely populated and industrialized areas. The rapid increase in the number of textile composite manufacturers, brick kilns, steel re-rolling mills, and power plants in Sreepur Upazila has led to a substantial rise in sulfur oxides (SOx) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions. The U.S. EPA's AERMOD model was used to determine pollutant dispersion and spatial concentration, using typical area emission and weather data.

We developed an emission inventory using standard emission factors and fuel-use data from various sectors as well as AERMET processed meteorological data including hourly wind speed (annual mean = 3.0 m/s), wind direction, temperature, and atmospheric stability. The wind rose study showed that the most common wind direction during winter was from the north-northwest, whereas during the monsoon season it was from the south. These winds had a big effect on plume transport and ground-level impact zones. Under neutral to stable conditions, model simulations suggest that the highest 24-hour average ground-level concentrations happen 0.5-1.5 km downwind. During winter standstill, peak SOx levels from brick kilns reached 135-160 μg/m³ at ~1 km, exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) 24-hour recommendation of 40 μg/m³. NO₂ levels from textile boilers. Levels from diesel generators ranged from 95-140 μg/m³ within 0.8-1.2 km, surpassing the WHO 24-hour limit of 25 μg/m³. Due to dispersion, concentrations dropped by 60-75% over 3 km. Winter mixing heights of 500-700 m boosted accumulation. Monsoon winds of at least 4-5 m/s increased dilution by up to 50%, though overlapping plumes made certain areas hotter.

These results indicate that Sreepur, Gazipur, requires immediate action to reduce emissions, improve stack design, and strengthen regulatory oversight to protect public health and ensure sustainable industrial growth. To help inform regulatory policy, improve air quality management, and reduce public health risks in Bangladesh, it is important to develop models of how air pollutants spread across industries.

Keywords

AERMOD; Industrial air pollution; SOx and NOx dispersion; Emission inventory; Sreepur–Gazipur, Bangladesh

title: Characterization of Groundwater Salt Plumes Discharging Along a Highly Urbanized Great Lakes Shoreline Using Electrical and Electromagnetic Imaging Techniques

authors: Zhu, Junwei Zhu [1], Robinson, Clare [2], Roy, James [3], Power, Christopher [4]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Western University, London, ON, Canada

abstract: High de-icing salt applications in cold climates are leading to increasing chloride (Cl) concentrations in urban groundwater and surface waters, posing risks to drinking water and aquatic ecosystems. Although groundwater discharge is known to influence urban stream salinization, its contribution to nearshore lake salinization along urban shorelines remains unclear. This study assessed the utility of geophysical techniques for characterizing groundwater salt plumes along the highly urbanized northern Lake Ontario shoreline, Canada. Electromagnetic induction (EMI) surveys were conducted along 27 shoreline areas (120 - 1600 m each) to identify locations with potentially elevated groundwater salinity. Two suspected hotspots, Sunnyside and Bluffer’s Park, were then investigated in detail using 3D electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), shallow (<2 m) groundwater and sediment sampling, and horizontal hydraulic gradient measurements. 3D ERT surveys revealed high groundwater salt plumes at both sites with groundwater sampling confirming Cl concentrations reach up to 2310 mg/L at Sunnyside and 553 mg/L at Bluffer’s Park within the plume zones. Hydraulic gradient measurements suggest higher groundwater discharge at Bluffer’s Park, suggesting that Cl loads to the lake may be higher there despite lower Cl concentrations. Overall, this study highlights the potential contribution of lacustrine groundwater discharge to nearshore lake salinization in urban cold climate areas and demonstrates the value of rapid, non-invasive geophysical techniques for identifying and characterizing salt plumes along urban shorelines.

title: Eclogite Localization in Continental Crust: Reactive Two-Phase Geodynamic Models and Fluid Catalysis
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: McMillan, Mitchell [1], Sim, Shi Joyce [2], Wilson, Cian [3]
affiliations: (1) EOAS, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA; EAS, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) EAS, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) EPL, Carnegie Science, Washington, DC, USA
abstract:
Lower continental crust undergoes a phase transition from granulite to eclogite assemblages. This eclogitization affects the buoyancy, rheology, and long term stability of the crust, with fundamental implications for tectonic processes such as mountain building. While the transition is controlled by high-pressure metamorphic reactions, field relationships are more complex than would be predicted by assuming pressure-temperature equilibrium at regional scales. Instead, eclogite is localized onto discrete structures at cm to km scales, with metastable granulite often preserved between eclogite-rich fingers. Feedbacks among fluid infiltration, reaction rate, densification, and pressure/temperature are thought to control such eclogitization, but the origin of localized eclogite fingers remains a topic of ongoing research.

We present a suite of reactive, two-phase, thermodynamic-geodynamic models that explore mechanisms for eclogite localization. The models simulate the coupled deformation of a poro-viscous solid and an aqueous fluid. The solid is composed of mineral phases, initially set to a granulite composition, that react according to thermodynamically consistent equations. The fluid is here assumed nonreactive, but, where present, catalyzes the solid reactions to represent the coupled dissolution-precipitation mechanism. Using this framework we explore two fundamental processes that may contribute to localization. First, a reduction in solid volume associated with densification can locally increase fluid-filled porosity in the two-phase system. Second, a solid rheology that weakens under volumetric decompaction can concentrate fluid into localized porosity waves. When reactions are catalyzed by fluid content, both mechanisms lead to localized eclogite production.

title: Cretaceous Tectonic Motion of North America: New Sites from Montana and a Novel Approach to Assess Rotation
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: Osorio-Afanador, Diego A. [1], Swanson-Hysell, Nicholas L. [2], Zhang, Yiming [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(3) University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA
abstract:
This contribution aims to elucidate the Cretaceous tectonic motion of North America, with an emphasis on the post-85 Ma period, whose paleomagnetic signature is obscured by rotations associated with orogenesis. We accomplish this by combining new and existing paleomagnetic records with a statistical approach that uses a global reference to screen for rotations. An updated compilation of Cretaceous paleomagnetic records from plutonic, volcanic, and sedimentary rocks reveals a high-latitude-seeking pole path that reaches a standstill at ca. 125 Ma. The continent’s paleomagnetic pole anchors near 70º N until 85 Ma, after which the pole resumes motion. Whether this subsequent motion directed the paleomagnetic pole towards higher or lower latitudes remains ambiguous because most available records are within or near deformation zones. To resolve this, we present new paleomagnetic data from ca. 75 Ma dikes in the Sliderock Mountain volcanics, an area relatively far from the Sevier deformation front in Montana. Results from 17 independent dikes locate the paleomagnetic pole at lower latitudes than the standstill, contrasting with results from the nearby Adel and Elkhorn volcanics of similar ages (closer to the deformation front) that place the pole at higher latitudes.

These conflicting results highlight the difficulty of using paleomagnetic records from deformed units to reconstruct continental motion when deformation is poorly constrained. To overcome this, we designed a workflow to assess the coherence of the paleomagnetic directions relative to the stable continent. To compile our data, we build on procedures that draw on individual sites rather than on formation averages. Then, to establish a baseline less biased by local orogenic perturbations, we use a global paleomagnetic database as a reference, rotated into North American coordinates via a plate circuit. We then screen North American records for deviation from this reference and reconstruct candidate apparent polar wander paths from the retained sites, examining how they vary with the choice of reference and acceptance threshold. Rather than asserting a single path, this approach maps the range of Late Cretaceous pole motions consistent with the global record, providing a reproducible framework for separating continental motion from local rotations in complex orogenic settings.

abstract:
La geoquímica de fluidos volcánicos permite determinar las características de los cuerpos magmáticos someros, detectar variaciones en el grado de actividad del sistema geotérmico y evaluar la capacidad térmica de sistemas hidrotermales. En Bolivia, existen pocos estudios relacionados con la geoquímica de fluidos volcánicos; un sitio de interés particular es la zona geotérmica que dista a 8 km al oeste del volcán Sajama (18° 5’ S – 69° 1’O) en la Cordillera Occidental de los Andes dentro de la Zona Volcánica Central.

Este estudio presenta la caracterización y la composición geoquímica de manantiales termales y sinters asociados; además, presenta la cuantificación de la emisión de CO 2 difuso dentro de la zona geotérmica Sajama.

Los manantiales termales (n=15) mostraron temperaturas en un rango de 44.5 a 84.2 ⁰C (promedio 71.1 ⁰C), conductividades eléctricas entre 5554 y 6744 μS/cm y valores de pH que varían entre 6.8 a 8.9 (promedio 7.7). En cuanto a la composición química mayoritaria los iones predominantes fueron el Na + y el Cl - (concentraciones promedio 1303 y 1832 mg/L respectivamente); otros elementos de importancia son el Si, B, Li y As con concentraciones promedio de 101, 26.0, 6.4 y 5.8 mg/L respectivamente.

Las elevadas concentraciones de Si y la desgasificación de CO 2 promueven la formación de depósitos de sinters, mineralógicamente se identificaron fases de sílice como ópalo-A, ópalo-CT y ópalo-C constituidos principalmente por micro y nano esferas de ópalo-A con bajo grado de orden estructural que evidencian una secuencia diagenética influenciada por factores ambientales y geoquímicos.

Finalmente se realizaron 159 mediciones de flujo de CO 2 del suelo, se encontró una población A de flujo alto con un promedio de 850.55 g/m 2 /d que constituye el 2.8% de la muestra y otras poblaciones B y C con promedios de 5.37 y 0.0035 g/m 2 /d y proporciones de 57.2 y 40% respectivamente. Simultáneamente se midió la temperatura del suelo en los mismos puntos de medición de flujo de CO 2 , encontrándose un rango de temperaturas entre 4.9 y 57.1⁰C e identificándose una anomalía de temperatura en un área específica del suelo de la zona de estudio.

Estos resultados son particularmente relevantes para hacer un seguimiento a la actividad volcánica y además de identificar el potencial geotérmico de la zona.

abstract:
Since 2019, the Extending Ocean Drilling Pursuits (eODP) project has liberated nearly a million marine fossil occurrences and their corresponding lithologic and stratigraphic information, making these data more usable for both researchers and the general public. To facilitate the most science from these data, we used two existing, well-supported database systems, the Paleobiology Database (PBDB, paleobiodb.org) and Macrostrat (macrostrat.org) to organize these data and make them much more accessible. A key goal of the project is conforming to FAIR data standards.

eODP imported and harmonized shipboard data from several sources in an intermediate database and informatics environment. All taxonomic names were checked, revealing spelling errors or other issues within the original data. After cleaning, these names and their taxonomic hierarchy (i.e., Kingdom, Phylum, etc.) were entered into the PBDB. The original data, cleaned data, and code to perform all data manipulations are available in open access repositories (github; https://github.com/eODP). Manual data entry for the PBDB resulted in the addition of 1,328 new references, 2,021 new taxonomic names, and 3,157 new taxonomic opinions into the PBDB. This quantity reflects a genus-level and above taxonomic hierarchy for all microfossil taxa in the eODP corpus, and a species-level taxonomic hierarchy for the planktic foraminifera. After ingesting lithological logs into Macrostrat, initial age models were constructed for all 1,710 holes within the eODP collection, resulting in a total of 92,451 lithological units which now have estimated ages in addition to geological properties.

Three distinct research directions will also be discussed. The first is a comparison of two other main databases of planktic foraminifera occurrences (Neptune and Triton), investigating potential differences between multiple representations of what is, ultimately, the same underlying record. The second research outcome is a global atlas of marine lithologies through the Cenozoic, the discussion of which will include the goodness of fit (or not) to previous interpretations. The final research direction is continued age model development, with the goal of increasing resolution from the Epoch-scale.

abstract:
Avian foraging and nesting activity in a coastal wetland may vary with hydrologic conditions operating at various timescales. At the Pu‘ewai Wetland on the windward side of eastern O‘ahu, endangered ae‘o (Hawaiian stilt) and ‘alae ‘ula (Hawaiian gallinule) are commonly present. The wetland, at Bellows Air Force Station, is alongside the Waimānalo Stream (locally referred to as Puhā Stream) and within 250 m of the Pacific Ocean. The water level in the wetland often fluctuates diurnally with the tide. However, coastal sedimentation processes can create a sand plug at the mouth of the stream, separating the wetland from the tidal flushing effect.

Since 2021, the natural hydrological dynamics of the wetland have been studied by collecting hourly water level data using probes at three surveyed locations. These data are accompanied by hourly photos using programmable cameras to obtain visuals of the wetland conditions and sand plug.

Results indicate the depth, duration, and seasonality of flooding due to a sand plug; the occurrence of either dry, stagnant conditions or freshwater flooding behind a sand plug; and the magnitude of tidal fluctuations in the absence of a sand plug. These hydrologic scenarios are compared to bird activity observations to assess the relationship.

This study serves as a complement for long-term avian and vegetation surveying of the Pu‘ewai Wetland. Altogether, the studies aim to analyze the ability of the wetland to provide ground-nesting and foraging habitat for the species of concern and identify possible management considerations.

title: Using Synthetic Fluid Inclusions to Study the Hydrolysis Reactions During Fluid-Phase Separation
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Posters)
authors: Fox, Braden Ryan [1], Lamadrid, Hector [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA

abstract: Nearly every geologic process is mediated by fluids. Fluids are especially important for the mobilization of critical metals in the Earth’s crust. Fluid inclusions allow us to better understand interactions between fluid and rock, providing insight into the chemical and physical properties of the host fluid. Since the 1980s, experimental work has shown that during phase separation (boiling), hydrolysis reactions occur according to the equation: H 2 O + NaCl -> NaOH(l) + HCl(v), where an acid component preferentially partitions to the vapor phase and a hydroxide partitions to the liquid phase. Though boiling serves as an important mechanism for critical metal deposition, key aspects of the boiling process have long been ignored in the literature. To better understand fluid evolution during boiling, we use synthetic fluid inclusions (SFI) to trap fluids of different compositions at different P-T conditions. Pre-fractured quartz crystals were loaded into a platinum capsule with fluids of known composition, welded shut, and set for several days to weeks at high P-T in a cold-sealed vessel; at high temperatures, quartz regrows, healing the fractures and trapping the fluid. We conducted experiments using different compositions of H 2 O-NaCl at temperatures from 400 to 700 ºC and pressures from 500 bar to 2 kbar to trap fluids in the liquid and liquid + vapor fields. Since acids and bases neutralize each other, in the H 2 O-NaCl experiments, we conducted vertical experiments in long 5 cm capsules to allow maximum separation of the vapor from the aqueous liquid. Moreover, we loaded two quartz cores separated by a thinner platinum tube into the capsule, with the objective of trapping the different phases (vapor in the upper core and liquid in the lower core). After synthesis, SFIs were analyzed with Raman spectroscopy and a heating/freezing stage to monitor compositional changes. Results show that during boiling, Raman H 2 O peaks of the vapor and liquid phases progressively change, noting a compositional evolution of the fluids. Moreover, microthermometric analyses confirm that the salinities evolve, which we interpret as reactions between the H 2 O, NaCl, and quartz. This strongly suggests that during boiling of salty fluids, if the acidic vapors escape, the remaining liquid composition becomes enriched in Na. Further evidence will be needed to better determine the effect of hydrolysis on element mobility and ore metal deposition.

title: Can the temporal and spatial controls affecting groundwater exceedances identified in Beaufort, SC, be transferred to another low-relief coastal environment?
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Abioye, Riliwan Damilola [1], Wilson, Alicia M. [2], Levine, Norman S. [3]
affiliations: (1) University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA
(2) University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA

abstract: Groundwater levels exceeding critical thresholds for septic systems in low-lying coastal environments are controlled by hydrologic processes operating across multiple temporal scales. Previous work in Beaufort County, SC, has demonstrated that these exceedances are driven by multiday rainfall, seasonal groundwater conditions, and year-to-year variability in rainfall and groundwater recharge. In addition, the risk is correlated with the baseline depth to the water table (DTW). Here we test the transferability of the methods and results from Beaufort County to Edisto Island, SC, a 176 sq km island located approximately 65 km from Beaufort County, SC. Twenty shallow monitoring wells were installed on Edisto Island between May 2025 and June 2026. Preliminary observations showed that a sustained average rainfall of 0.1 cm/d and a tidal range of at least 83 cm during the previous week created conditions favorable for exceedance events. These exceedance events (n = 8), associated with rainfall totals of 0.15 cm over three days, clustered primarily in August and September 2025, highlighting the importance of antecedent groundwater conditions. Simulated water levels using a time series modeling approach over 36 years (1990-2026) reproduced the observed behavior. Models using projected sea levels show that groundwater levels and exceedance frequency increase under both 2050 and 2100 scenarios on a millimeter-to-tens-of-centimeter scale, with the largest changes occurring when sea level rise is combined with projected rainfall increases. Both the observed and simulated water levels showed that DTW is a dominant spatial control on groundwater vulnerability, consistent with findings from Beaufort County, SC. This study demonstrates a transferable and practical approach for evaluating groundwater vulnerability and supporting adaptation of wastewater infrastructure under changing precipitation intensities and sea levels.

abstract: Contamination of heavy metals and metalloids (HMMs) remains a persistent environmental health concern in urban communities with historical industrial activity. In children, frequent hand-to-mouth behaviors and outdoor play increase their contact with HMMs in contaminated residential environmental media, making them particularly vulnerable to such exposure. In the Westside of Atlanta (hereafter Westside), initial identification of elevated residential soil lead (Pb) concentrations prompted collaborative sampling efforts with community members to investigate whether contamination extended beyond the original site. These community-engaged investigations revealed the broader extent of residential Pb contamination across the Westside associated with historical industrial slag and supported the U.S.Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) designation of the area as a Superfund site and subsequent placement on the National Priorities List. However, questions remained regarding children’s exposure to Pb from contaminated soil and other residential sources, as well as potential exposure to additional HMMs. To address these concerns, this community-engaged study aimed to better understand the magnitude ofHMM contamination and exposure pathways to HMMs in historically-impacted urban communities. Through community outreach events, we recruited children aged 6 months to 6 years living within and close to the EPA Superfund Site boundary in the Westside. We collected residential soil, dust, and paint, as well as children’s urine and blood to evaluate environmental contamination and children’s exposure to HMMs, with a focus on Pb. We developed individualized report-back materials and hosted several community meetings to discuss results with participants. The study identified multiple households with elevated residential soil Pb concentrations, contributing to subsequent remediation efforts. These findings call for continued community-engaged research and monitoring to address environmental health risks associated with legacy contamination.

title: Mineralogy of the South Bayan Obo Deposit – Ore from the South Limb of the Bayan Obo Syncline, Inner Mongolia, China
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics
authors: Messner, Todd [1], Friehauf, Kurt [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Kutztown University, Kutztown, PA, USA

abstract:
The giant Bayan Obo mining district hosts two well-studied ore bodies (Main Orebody and East Orebody), as well as important lower-grade stratabound West Orebodies in the northern limb of the Bayan Syncline – each deposit characterized by different geometries and Rare Earth Element (REE) endowments. Mineralization in the southern limb of the Bayan Syncline is more localized and only recently explored, and thus not well characterized in the published literature.

We analyzed samples of the South Bayan Obo Orebody (location approximating Dongjielegele Orebody of Li et al., 2023 – 800 m SSE of the East Orebody) using a Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope (FE-SEM) with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) to characterize the major mineralogy.

We classify samples into three main ore types: 1. Fine-grained dark brown dolomite with disseminated magnetite ± trace disseminated pyrite, 2. Banded dolomite//ferroan carbonate with very minor magnetite, and 3. Magnetite-rich banded silicate ore with trace purple fluorite.

South Bayan Obo samples tended to be strongly dominated by Nb minerals – mostly as pyrochlore and fergusonite – with Rare Earth Elements also occurring as subordinate bastnaesite, parisite, monazite, and fluorapatite.

Gangue minerals include magnetite, hematite, pyrrhotite, spinel, ferrokinoshitalite, fluorophlogopite, norbergite, and fluorite.

South Bayan Obo samples in this study lacked the aegirine-augite gangue abundant in the East and Main Orebodies. Much of South Bayan Obo’s fluorine occurs in silicates and apatite rather than as abundant fluorite which is characteristic of some East and Main ores. Although South Bayan Obo ores contained significant REE mineralization, South Bayan Obo ores in samples we studied were dominated by Nb-, Ti-, and Ba-rich phases. If our samples are representative of the bulk deposit, this difference in metal ratios may reflect either a different stage of mineralization or a regional metal zonation.

title: Archean Podiform Chromitite in the North China Craton: Tectonic Mélange, Crust-Mantle Recycling, and Thrust-Controlled Exploration Model
session_title: Geological Processes and Metallogenesis at Plate Boundaries: Integrating Multiscale Mechanisms and Quantitative Approaches for Critical and Rare Metals
authors: Wang, Lu [1], Zhou, Qiming [2]
affiliations: (1) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, State Key Lab of GPMR, Wuhan, Hubei Province, China
(2) State Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan, Wuhan, Hubei Province, China
abstract:
The Zunhua podiform chromitite, hosted in the North China Craton, is among the few known Archean chromite worldwide. Yet its age, tectonic affinity, and controls on mineralization have long been debated, which has seriously hampered exploration efforts. To address these questions, we combined large-scale structural–lithological mapping with geochronology, mineral chemistry, and microstructural analysis.

Our mapping shows that the Zunhua ore-hosting sequence is not a simple magmatic intrusion, but rather an imbricate thrust stack. The assemblage comprises ultramafic tectonic blocks that carry the chromitite bodies, mafic blocks, and a matrix of biotite-plagioclase gneiss—typical of mélange formed in subduction–accretion systems. Zircon U-Pb ages from the blocks, the matrix, and crosscutting undeformed granitic veins converge on a narrow age range of 2.6–2.5 Ga, pinning mineralization to the Neoarchean. These data also reveal that orebodies and their host rocks were tectonically dismembered during and after mineralization, then stacked into their present imbricate geometry during later orogenesis. This picture stands in marked contrast to the conventional magmatic-intrusion model that has long guided local exploration. Instead, we envisage that imbricate thrusts have sliced an originally continuous mineralized horizon into multiple, vertically repeated fault-bounded slivers.

If correct, this reinterpretation carries immediate practical consequences. It predicts that the most promising drill targets lie not along the strike of exposed pods, but down-dip beneath thrust planes. Encouragingly, initial deep drilling has already cut new blind orebodies at depth, supporting our model and opening up substantial new exploration space in the district.

Three main conclusions emerge from this work. First, we provide the first robust Neoarchean (2.6–2.5 Ga) geochronological framework for the Zunhua chromitites. Second, we show that Archean podiform chromitites can be hosted in tectonic mélange and can retain petrogenetic signatures of subduction-related deep crust-mantle recycling (Mantle Transition Zone). Third, we offer a revised exploration model that shifts attention from magmatic centers to imbricated mélange slices. More broadly, this approach may be applicable to other Archean orogenic belts that host podiform chromitites, and it underscores how easily post-emplacement tectonic reworking—often overlooked—can govern the present-day geometry and preservation of ancient critical-metal ores. Our findings ultimately highlight the value of integrating structural, geochronological, and geophysical data in deciphering the multi-scale tectonic machinery that drives metallogenesis at plate boundaries.

title: Integrated Geophysical Modeling of the Basin Architecture of the Southernmost Rio Grande rift, Southern New Mexico and West Texas
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Reyes, Martin [1], Lavery, Daniel [2]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Bureau of Geology, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) New Mexico Bureau of Geology, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
The Rio Grande rift is a north–south-trending continental rift that initiated during the Late Oligocene and extends from central Colorado through New Mexico into West Texas and northern Mexico. It is tectonically bounded by the Colorado Plateau to the west and the Great Plains to the east. The southern Rio Grande rift comprises the Jornada del Muerto, Tularosa, and Salt basins, which developed through the overprinting and reactivation of older structures associated with the Paleozoic Orogrande Basin. However, the basin architecture and sedimentary infill of its southernmost expression remain incompletely constrained due to limited subsurface data.

The model is constrained through regional gravity and aeromagnetic surveys, well logs, and surface geological mapping data. Additionally, serial cross-sections were constructed using borehole data (logs, cores, cuttings) to define sedimentary thicknesses and infer basin geometry. These interpretations were further evaluated through gravity and structural forward modeling.

Integrated interpretation reveals significant variations in basin depth and geometry along the southern expression of the Rio Grande rift. The models define asymmetric depocenters bounded by segmented normal faults and basement structural highs oriented parallel to the rift axis. Oblique structural lineaments locally compartmentalize the basin and coincide with abrupt along-strike changes in basin thickness and geometry. These relationships suggest that pre-existing basement fabrics were reactivated during Cenozoic extension, exerting a primary control on fault development, basin segmentation, and the evolution of the southern Rio Grande rift.

The resulting geological framework yields new insights into the evolution of the southernmost Rio Grande rift and demonstrates the value of integrating multiple geophysical datasets where seismic information is sparse or unavailable. This framework establishes a basis for future studies of geothermal resources, groundwater systems, critical mineral exploration, and geologic carbon storage in southern New Mexico.

title: Glaciovolcanism and Geothermal Resources of Mount Baker, Washington
session_title: Hydrogeology of Geothermal Resources: From Shallow Systems to Deep Reservoirs
authors: Florea, Lee J. [1], Stenner, Christian [2], Sobolewski, Linda [3]
affiliations: (1) Washington Geological Survey, Olympia, WA, USA
(2) Alberta Speleological Society, Calgary, AB, Canada
(3) University of Iceland, School of Engineering and Natural Sciences Institute of Earth Sciences, Reykjavik, Iceland
abstract:
Mount Baker (Kweq' Smánit) is a 3,286 m, andesitic stratovolcano in the North Cascades of Washington State. The edifice is mantled by glaciers, including a glacial plug in Sherman Crater. The volcano has a long Quaternary eruption history, experienced thermal unrest in 1975, and has two very active fumarole fields. The edifice is the most recent expression of arc-based volcanism in this part of the North Cascades, with edifices as old as 3.7 mya to the northeast; the result of clockwise rotation of the crust.

Play fairway studies of geothermal favorability identified the Mount Baker region as an area of high geothermal potential. To the east of the edifice is Baker Hot Spring and wells with elevated geothermal gradient. Geochemical and geophysical studies correlate these heat signatures with faulting. Standard geothermometers at Baker Hot Spring are at equilibrium with calcedony and a reservoir temperature of 120-140 o C. Thermal imaging and spring chemistry surrounding the volcano reveal no other expression of heat in the near surface. Non-thermal springs in surrounding volcanics, metasediments, and ultramafics have very low TDS. Carbonate springs actively precipitate travertine.

A 2025 expedition in Sherman Crater mapped 1.5 km of glaciovolcanic cave, conducted drone-based photogrammetry, collected thermal imaging scans, and sampled fumaroles and thermal springs for geochemistry. Fumaroles exceed 90°C, are high in hydrogen sulfide, and have an isotopic profile consistent with a volcanic source. Geochemical syntheses, including standard geothermometers, reveal that volcanogenic waters in Sherman Crater are separately sourced from Baker Hot Spring and have a reservoir temperature of 250-380 o C.

This work responds to Washington Senate Bill 6039 directing Washington Geological Survey to prepare studies for geothermal focus areas. Work in Sherman Crater was funded by Mazamas, the National Cave and Karst Research Institute, and the National Speleological Society.

title: Great Unconformity erosion increased sediment supply and amplified subsidence on the rifted passive margin of western North America
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Macdonald, Francis Alexander [1], Wernicke, Brian P. [2], Anttila, Eliel [3]
affiliations: (1) Berkeley, California, USA
(2) California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(3) University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
abstract: One of the outstanding problems in the tectonic evolution of Rodinia is the misfit between the timing of the Cryogenian to Cambrian rift-drift transition on the western margin of Laurentia. From Arctic Canada to California, geological evidence supports Tonian to Cryogenian (780-635 Ma) rifting followed by Ediacaran to Paleozoic passive margin deposition. However, many of these successions also record an increase in sediment accumulation rates through the late Ediacaran to Cambrian (550-500 Ma) which, when incorporated into thermal subsidence models, suggests renewed rifting and a delay in passive margin deposition by 85-150 million years. To distinguish between these models for the timing of rifting and supercontinent breakup, we developed a series of palinspastically-restored east-west transects of Neoproterozoic to Paleozoic strata between the Grand Canyon and the Sierra Nevadas. We then incorporated these transects into a flexural isostatic model and performed sensitivity tests for changes in sediment supply, sea-level, and sediment density. The stratigraphic architecture indicates that the margin was sediment starved in the early Ediacaran followed by extensive late Ediacaran to Cambrian progradation of the margin. We interpret the increase in deposition rate, the primary observable supporting 550-500 Ma tectonic subsidence, to result from increased sediment supply rather than tectonically-generated accommodation, and the strongly amplifying effects of accommodation space generated by (1) flexural isostasy, (2) sediment compaction, (3) the Sauk II rise in sea-level, and (4) the increase in mean sediment density at the margin-wide transition from siliciclastic to carbonate deposition at ca. 505 Ma. We propose that the Ediacaran to Cambrian increase in sediment supply (i.e., the primary catalyst of the increase in sediment accumulation) was associated with rifting of the southeast margin of Laurentia, which drove exhumation of the cratonic interior both through mantle upwelling and the emplacement of large igneous provinces, but also by providing a conduit for moisture into the interior that caused the continental divide to migrate westward, generating the Great Unconformity.

title: Petrographic and Geochemical Examination of Xenoliths found at Big Obsidian Flow, Newberry Volcano, Central Oregon
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Galliton, Kayleigh B. [1], Nichols, Johnathon [2], Schwartz, Julia F. [3], Scruggs, Melissa A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA
(2) Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA
(3) Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA
(4) Wichita State University, Wichita, KS,
abstract:
Crustal xenoliths provide crucial evidence of processes ocurring within a magma chamber while preserving otherwise inaccessible continental crust. Newberry volcano is a back-arc shield volcano located in Central Oregon that has been reported to have crustal xenoliths present in different flows. The most recent activity at Newberry was the Big Obsidian Eruptive Episode, which occured approximately 1,300 BP. This eruptive episode consisted of three distinct events: the Newberry Pumice, the Paulina Lake Ashflow, and finally the Big Obsidian Flow (BOF). Although Linneman and Myers (1990) analyzed BOF samples, much of the original samples set has since been damaged or lost, prompting the collection of new samples during the 2025 field season.

We report major and trace elements and isotopic compositions for newly collected xenoliths from the vent of BOF. Petrographic analysis suggests that these xenoltihs are ash deposits from the surrounding area. Xenolith compositions were compared to Newberry tephra and ash deposits from the literature (Kuehn, 2002). Trace element diagrams indicate that the composition of one sample, BOF-X-01a, can be closely approximated with those of the most recent eruption event, with the exception of La and Ce. Whole rock 87 Sr/ 86 Sr and 143 Nd/ 144 Nd compositions indicate that the other recovered xenolith, BOF-X-30b, is the most radiogenic sample collected to-date from the Big Obsidian Flow. These results suggest that the xenoliths represent either recycled material from within the Big Obsidian Eruptive Episode, or crustal contaminants incorporated through assimilation from Pleistocene eruptions, providing possible constraints on magma evolution beneath Newberry Volcano.

title: Paleoseismic Evidence for Late Pleistocene and Holocene Earthquakes on the Caballo Fault in Southern New Mexico, USA
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape (Posters)
authors: Williams, Randolph T. [1], Vadman, Michael [2], Cline, Michael Logan [3], Koning, Daniel J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, CO,
(2) Bureau of Reclamation, Denver, CO,
(3) Bureau of Reclamation, Pittsburgh, PA,
(4) New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM,
abstract:
We present results of paleoseismic investigations of the Caballo fault, southern Rio Grande rift, New Mexico. The Caballo fault is a >40 km long, west-dipping normal fault accommodating east-west extension in the Palomas basin. Scarps observed along the Caballo fault exhibit increasing apparent offset on surfaces of increasing inferred age, suggesting a history of recurrent ground-rupturing earthquakes throughout the late Quaternary. We excavated two trenches into arroyo cut banks (~20 km apart) through prominent fault scarps.

The northern trench provides a clear exposure of the fault surface cutting alluvial fan and wind-blown loess deposits. Carbonate development is abundant, with some older units exhibiting stage III accumulation. A singular, narrow fault zone is defined by abrupt, consistent unit truncations and sub-vertically aligned clasts. Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) of exposed units reveals ages from ~100 to 6 ka. The lowermost unit in the hanging wall was dated to ~70 ka and exhibits a minimum of ~3 m of offset, suggesting slip rates of >0.04 mm/yr during the late Pleistocene. Stratigraphic evidence in conjunction with additional luminescence ages permits two or three earthquakes in the last 70 ka in the northern trench. Sheared sands dated to 6 ka indicate that one of these events occurred in the Holocene.

The southern trench exposes a more distributed fault geometry, with at least three separate fault surfaces offsetting primarily alluvial fan deposits. Carbonate development is similarly abundant with older units exhibiting stage III accumulation. OSL dating of exposed faulted units reveals ages from ~75 to 50 ka. The lowermost alluvial unit in the hanging wall was dated to ~75 ka. Offset alluvial deposits in both the footwall and hanging wall are overlain by unfaulted colluvial deposits. The youngest of these colluvial deposits was dated to 50 ka, which may approximate the age of the most recent earthquake on the southern Caballo fault.

title: Did the Early Miocene Rise of Grassy Woodlands Set Ape and Human Evolution in Motion?
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic
authors: Uno, Kevin Toshio [1], Tweedy, Ruth Rosegrant [2], Rowan, John [3], Ferland, Troy Michael [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Human Evolutionary Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA; Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA

abstract: The early Neogene (~24-10 Ma) vegetation history of eastern Africa is poorly known despite its likely important role in shaping ape and hominin evolution. This is because carbon isotope proxies are ineffective in a world where both trees and grasses use C 3 photosynthesis. A new quantitative plant wax-based proxy for fraction woody cover (FWC) that distinguishes forest, woodland, and grassland ecosystems, enables us to reconstruct eastern African vegetation from ~25 Ma to the present. These FWC reconstructions reveal that dense woodlands dominated until C 3 grassy woodlands expanded around the Miocene Climate Optimum (~17 Ma), after which expansive open woodlands drove changes in ape dietary and locomotor adaptations and served as stable corridors enabling dispersal into Eurasia by ~16 Ma. Combined FWC and existing carbon isotope data show C 4 grasses appeared in eastern Africa just after 10 Ma. They initially replaced existing C 3 grasses and only after 6.8 Ma did they expand beyond their previous limits. This expansion in the wake of ~10 million years of stable grassy woodland habitats coincided with the earliest evidence for bipedal hominins, thus providing strong support for more open ecosystems being the primary selection mechanism for bipedalism.

title: Beyond streamflow: managing tradeoffs between economy and ecology in high-capacity well evaluation
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Pruitt, Aaron [1], Reeves, Howard William [2], Ferre, Ty A. [3], Fienen, Michael [4]
affiliations: (1) Water Use, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, Madison, WI, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, USGS Upper Midwest WSC, Lansing, MI, USA
(3) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA

abstract: In the Great Lakes region of North America, water is abundant. Streamflows and lake levels, however, are often in a tenuous balance with the shallowest portion of the groundwater system. Small reductions in groundwater levels may leave plenty of water volume in place but may interrupt supply to streams and lakes. This condition motivates US states in the region to use surface water impacts as key legal considerations when evaluating requests for high-capacity well withdrawals for public supply, industry, and agriculture. The cumulative effect of multiple wells in a watershed can be estimated using superposed analytical solutions. The python package pycap-dss implements analytical solutions and can simulate many wells in a watershed efficiently, enabling multi-objective formal optimization that quantifies a Pareto frontier, delineating the tradeoff between the amount of pumping in managed wells and the streamflow response in a river. Using the Little Plover River in Wisconsin, USA as a test case, we demonstrated the use of this analysis. Additionally, we converted streamflow to brook trout probability of occurrence and quantified the agriculture receipts in US Dollars as supported by agricultural pumping. These Pareto tradeoffs compare model results with management options in terms that are relevant to the societal decisions at hand. Such tradeoffs have the potential to enhance understanding and negotiations about responsible water use serving all needs. We adapted this modeling framework to develop a Masters-level curriculum project at the University of Arizona. We also discuss insights, challenges, and results from the participating students.

title: Going with the Flow: Using 3-Dimensional Digital and Field Mapping Techniques to reveal Ediacaran Lava Flows of the Catoctin Formation, Virginia
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Kasper, Anna [1], Bailey, Christopher M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
(2) Dept. of Geology, William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
abstract:
The Catoctin Formation is a geologic unit situated in the mid-Atlantic region where it undergirds many prominent mountains in the northern and central Virginia Blue Ridge. Previous U-Pb zircon geochronology indicates the Catoctin lava flows erupted during the Ediacaran, between 550 - 570 Ma, and are interpreted as a series of flood basalts associated with the opening of the Iapetus Ocean. These basalts have since been transformed into greenstones via low-grade regional metamorphism. Although these rocks experienced some recrystallization and deformation, original lava flow boundaries are commonly discernible. Understanding the modern extent and geometry of these flows will help unravel the complex geologic history of the Virginia Blue Ridge.

Previous researchers have attempted to map the stratigraphy of individual flows, but were constrained by poor exposures and the resolution of 1:24,000 topographic maps. In this project we use 1-meter resolution LiDAR imagery paired with novel 3D mapping methods to understand the geometry and stratigraphy of the Catoctin volcanics. LiDAR imagery is spatially analyzed using aspect, hillshade, topographic position index (TPI), and slope techniques to illuminate flow boundaries in the topography. We mapped lava flow boundaries with varying degrees of certainty, and generated cross-sections at various locations to analyze the internal structure of the Catoctin Formation. Field measurements, traditional 2D mapping techniques, and previous research were also used to supplement mapping efforts.

Preliminary results from both the Simmons Gap and Wintergreen areas offer insight to the geometry and thickness of the Catoctin volcanics. These locations reveal 9 to 14 lava flows ranging from 10 to 100 meters thick. Cross-sectional data highlights subsurface structural geometries created from post-Catoctin deformation, revealing upright layers that are broadly folded, as well as more complicated geometries. Topographic maps, geologic cross-sections, and stratigraphic columns are used to highlight the variance in thickness, geometry, and areal extent of each flow.

session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part II)
authors: Krause, Samantha Marie [1], White, Marie Nicole [2], Olivier, Gwen [3], Goedert, Tristan [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Environmental Studies, Texas State University, San Marcos, TX, USA

abstract: Reconstructing environmental change across New Mexico in the southwestern USA requires an integrated geoarchaeological approach. Our research group is currently working in several drainage systems across New Mexico, and here we present a series of alluvial and archaeological case studies distributed across northern, central, and southern New Mexico, to examine how fluvial systems responded to climatic fluctuations and anthropogenic modification over different key points throughout the Holocene. Taken together, these records provide a spatially expansive framework that showcases regional hydroclimate variability and connects local human land-use practices across space and time. Here, we focus on an overview of three of our case study sites across New Mexico: first the Rio Embudo in northern New Mexico which provides sedimentological and geochemical evidence of early Holocene landscape change starting around 10,000 years BP. Second, in central New Mexico, we document burn layers and soil development dating to the early and middle Holocene (9,000–7,000 years BP). The most extensive and dynamic record we focus on here comes from southern New Mexico along the Rio Tularosa. Alluvial materials here composed of interbedded paleosols, gravels, and organic-rich black mats span the middle and late Holocene (6000 BP to modern downcutting). Some of the sediments here correspond with evidence for cooler and wetter conditions and coincide with Mogollon activity at the adjacent Creekside Village archaeological site. During the Mesilla phase (200–1000 C.E.), Indigenous communities engineered irrigation canals, terraces, and a reservoir, fundamentally altering the Rio Tularosa floodplain. Multi-proxy analyses demonstrate how climatic variability and sustained water management reshaped the geomorphology of catchments across New Mexico during important cultural periods. This research underscores the importance for understanding long-term hydroclimate dynamics and Indigenous water engineering and plant use. This kind of research informs contemporary watershed management in an increasingly arid New Mexico.

abstract:
In 2022, we published preliminary work showing a compelling correlation between biomarker evidence of earthquake heating in excess of 700°C and K/Ar dates from associated clay minerals in samples taken from creeping sections of the San Andreas Fault Observatory at Depth (SAFOD) core (Coffey et al., 2022). Since then, we have probed the meaning of these dates and tried to isolate the most recent earthquakes by separating different size fractions and mineralogies, characterizing the clay composition, directly targeting apparent slip surfaces, and conducting a range of heating experiments to better understand both the biomarkers and the K/Ar geochronology on samples from the San Andreas, Japan Trench, and New Zealand, as well as others shared by our collaborators. We share updates from this project and discuss ongoing questions and challenges as we continue to pursue the question of what exactly these dates mean in terms of earthquake timing and magnitude and what implications they have for understanding seismic hazard from major earthquakes.

title: Organic Fossils in Proterozoic Carbonates: Case studies from the Tonian Little Dal Group and beyond
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age
authors: Cohen, Phoebe A. [1], Strauss, Justin V. [2], Mehra, Akshay [3], Wedlake, George O. [4], Anderson, Ross Peter [5], Nadalin, Caroline [6], Nelson, Emil [7]
affiliations: (1) Williams College, Williamstown, MA,
(2) Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA

(4) University of Oxford, Oxford, Oxfordshire,

(6) Williams College, Williamstown, MA, USA
(7) Williams College, Williamstown, MA, USA
abstract:
Most Proterozoic microfossils have been found in shales or early diagenetic chert nodules and horizons. However, over the last few decades, a robust assemblage of microfossils have also been found in Proterozoic carbonates. While these fossils have led to important discoveries, there are still open questions about how these fossils are preserved and subject to potential contamination. Here, we explore the taphonomy of carbonaceous microfossils in Proterozoic carbonates, with a focus on fossils from the Tonian Little Dal Group of Northwest Territories, Canada. Beyond examples from northwestern Canada, we also discuss the taphonomy of organic fossils preserved in the carbonates of the Cryogenian-Ediacaran Tsagaan-Olom Group, Mongolia, and what common traits may unite these examples.

Two separate environments of the Stone Knife Formation of the Little Dal Group preserve organic microfossils as seen in macerates and thin section - carbonate mudstones preserve abundant acritarchs and filamentous fossils, and reefal carbonates preserve diverse filamentous fossils and rare acritarchs. While the bounding carbonate minerals (i.e., crystallites) can sometimes be larger than the fossils they preserve, this is often a secondary diagenetic feature; these carbonates likely started as mud- or silt-sized particles (i.e., micrite) that were then neomorphosed to form coarser-grained textures. We hypothesize the primary muddy substrate led to better microfossil preservation, allowing recalcitrant organic matter to survive the process of neomorphism during carbonate diagenesis.

In mudstone facies, acritarchs are preserved solely in strata that also contain molar-tooth structures (MTS). We also report similarly preserved acritarchs and filaments in MTS-bearing strata of the Tonian Reefal Assemblage in the adjacent Ogilvie Mountains of Yukon, Canada. Although there is currently no consensus on how MTS forms, sediment-pore water anoxia and localized carbonate supersaturation likely play a role, features that would also promote the preservation of recalcitrant organic fossils. Because MTS are globally restricted to pre-Cryogenian strata, it may be that this represents a taphonomic window that closes at the end of the Tonian.

We compare these Laurentian assemblages with fossil-bearing carbonates of the Tsagaan-Olom Group, which do not contain MTS, but may have clay mineralogical profiles that aided in organic fossil preservation. Our work shows that organic fossils are preserved in a variety of carbonate settings in the Proterozoic and that such strata should be the focus of further paleontological investigations.

title: Gaps in the Fossil Record Provide New Insights into Extinction Dynamics of Mammoths and Other Pleistocene Megafauna
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Miller, Joshua H. [1], Simpson, Carl [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
(2) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: As mammoths ( Mammuthus sp.) and other Pleistocene megafauna went extinct, did their populations fail catastrophically (and ecologically instantaneously) or did they undergo protracted population declines? The probability of becoming a fossil is determined by a combination of geological, taphonomic, and biological factors, such as changes in preservation potential due to shifts in climate, depositional setting, and/or population size. While such factors may be particularly challenging to differentiate using regional- to continental-scale data, highly fossiliferous Late Pleistocene records can provide geographically, climatically and environmentally constrained fossil time series from which aspects of population demographics may be evaluated. This is particularly relevant for mammoths, for which thousands of directly dated specimens are useful for assessing extinction timing across North America and Eurasia. Using these fossil timeseries, we combined the temporal distributions of specimen ages with the distributions and sizes of temporal gaps between dated specimens to test for shifts in population trajectories through time consistent with either protracted population decline, or abrupt population failure. We found that sampling can be excellent during mammoth extinction intervals. For example, in northern North America and Siberia, the gap sizes between fossil occurrences during the extinction interval are consistent with expectations based on the prior ~40,000 years. This finding indicates that populations failed catastrophically and without dwindling over millennia. Results were similar for mammoth populations on Arctic islands, where they persisted for millennia after the extinction of their mainland cousins (and in the absence of humans). While we find that mammoth extinctions followed similar patterns across the Holarctic, the record for wooly rhinoceros ( Coelodonta antiquitatis ) indicate a significant increase in gaps sizes during extinction. In the absence of a sedimentological driver, this finding is consistent with a population undergoing long-term stress and protracted population decline prior to their extinction. The Late Pleistocene provides opportunities to evaluate extinction characteristics that are generally impossible to quantify from most of geologic time. While the fossils themselves tell much of the story, gaps in the fossil record can be equally revealing for evaluating species’ demographic histories.

title: The Straight Cliffs Formation as a Window into the Drivers of the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part I)
authors: Barclay, Richard S. [1], Cohen, Joshua E [2], Mahon, Elizabeth [3], Korasidis, Vera A. [4], Gallagher, Timothy M. [5], Weaver, Lucas N. [6]
affiliations: (1) Smithsonian, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Mount Saint Mary's University, Los Angeles, California, USA
(3) University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia
(4) University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia
(5) Kent State University, Kent, OH, USA
(6) Ann Arbor, MI, USA
abstract:
The beginning of the Late Cretaceous (ca. 100–90 Ma) was a tipping point for terrestrial ecosystems. Life on land exceeded the diversity of the marine realm for the first time, continents assumed their modern configurations driving the emergence of mountain belts and shallow epeiric seas, and global temperature reached its highest point since the Jurassic. Global sea level reached the Phanerozoic high stand at the Cenomanian-Turonian boundary (ca. 94 Ma), with terrestrial life packed into the smallest terrestrial area since the Cambrian. During this transition, terrestrial ecosystems emerged that are more comparable to the ones we have today, characterized by flowering plants, pollinating insects, and the major groups of modern mammals. This diversification event is termed the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution.

Southern Utah represents the ideal global location to unravel the mechanisms driving the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution. In particular, the Straight Cliffs Formation (ca. 92–84 Ma) preserves a low-relief coastal record of plant and mammal fossils living along the shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway, flanked by the rising North American Cordillera. These coastal environments were constantly disturbed by sea level transgressions and regressions, occurring at multiple scales, causing these ecosystems to migrate back and forth from the alluvial plain and the mountains over an 8-million-year long period.

Despite prior work, the palynoflora and macrofossil plant records are incomplete, especially given the wide diversity of habitats of these coastal systems. The vertebrate record is more widely sampled, but taxonomic identifications remain tentative due to undersampling. The middle-Turonian Smoky Hollow Member is the temporally best dated member, constrained at its base by ammonites of Collignoniceras woolgari and a radiometric date in the top 5 m (91.87 Ma). The John Henry Member remains poorly constrained chronologically and is under-sampled for both plant and mammal records. We have now begun to fill these gaps and is part of our ongoing research.

We suggest that the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution, which stimulated the rise of modern terrestrial ecosystems, was driven by the dynamic landscape changes—mountain uplift and associated sea-level oscillations—captured during Straight Cliffs deposition. By studying the Straight Cliffs as well as the bounding terrestrial rocks we can track changes in both plant and mammal communities from ca. 100 to 80 Ma, all within the same region.

title: X-ray Analysis of Eocene Ocala Limestone Samples Collected from Haile Quarry in Newberry, Florida
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Gordon, Emily P. [1], MacDonald, James H. [2], Wollney, Isabella [3]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(2) Environmental Geology Program, Florida Gulf Coast University, Fort Myers, FL, USA
(3) University of South Florida, Tampa, FL, USA
abstract:
The purpose of the study was to obtain data from ten limestones using X-ray analysis to better understand the Ocala Limestone from Haile Quarry in Newberry, Florida; and compare the data to the Ocala Limestone north of Lake Okeechobee. The Ocala Limestone formed during the Eocene. Six samples are from the upper Ocala Limestone, and four samples are from the more dolomitic lower Ocala Limestone. All ten Haile Quarry Ocala Limestone samples were analyzed using PXRD (powdered X-ray diffraction) and pXRF (portable X-ray fluorescence) instruments. The data acquired by PXRD indicates all ten samples are calcite. The Haile Quarry samples have the following elemental ranges based on data obtained using pXRF: Ca from 30 to 43 wt. %; Mg from 1.7 to 2.8 wt. %; Fe from 0.01 to 0.13 wt. %; Si from 0.02 to 0.95 wt. %; Zr from 5 to 15 ppm; Sr from 218 to 271 ppm, and Ni from 13 to 32 ppm. The Mg/Ca ratio is 0.049 to 0.088 and the Sr/Ca ratio is 0.5 to 0.73. The samples (both upper and lower) plot near the calcite end member on the carbonate classification diagram.

The PXRD for all samples being calcite, the samples plotting at calcite endmember composition, and the Mg/Ca ratio for all samples being less than 0.8 indicates that they are not dolostone. The Haile Quarry samples were compared with samples obtained from Ocala Limestone north of Lake Okeechobee. The Haile Quarry Ocala Limestone are enriched with Si, Zr, Ni, and Fe, suggesting minor terrestrial inputs into the depositional basin. Sr values of the Haile Quarry are lower than those of the Lake Okeechobee Limestone, suggesting the Haile Quarry samples may have formed in a marine environment close to a terrestrial source and Lake Okeechobee Limestone may have formed in a marine environment further from a terrestrial source.

title: The Mars Ocean Hypothesis 40 years and hundreds of thousands of spacecraft images later: Does it hold water?
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: parker, timothy Jay [1]
affiliations: (1) Other Orb, LLC, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
For decades it has been recognized that there are geomorphic and chemical signatures suggestive of a past ocean in the northern plains of Mars. A key part of present understanding is the geomorphic evidence of possible paleoshorelines that persisted for long periods of time and at heights of hundreds of meters to kilometers above the elevation of the northern plains. These proposed shorelines are typically expressed as subtle erosional terraces often associated with overlying mantle deposits with lobate margins, or as broad, degraded erosional terraces lacking a sharp contact and evident primarily in the regional topography. The global imagery and topography data (chiefly CTX and MOLA) provide consistent image resolution and topographic precision that are quickly accessible for both detailed regional and overall global evaluation of the features thought to be shorelines.

In addition to the morphologic expression of these features, their departures from horizontality are of interest, as this might suggest isostatic or tectonic adjustments since their formation. Long-wavelength variations in elevation do seem to suggest regional tectonic affects. Short-wavelength variations can be harder to discern. With the recent update of the Murray Lab’s CTX Global Mosaic to V 1.0 with its improved georegistration to the global topography, displacements of several tens of meters or more of the shorelines mapped on the beta version of the map with respect to the V 1.0 mosaic can be seen. This can result in sizeable scatter of extracted shoreline elevations, particularly when the proposed shoreline falls along a slope.

In recent years, much of the most important criticisms of the ocean hypothesis centered around plotting the elevations of previously-mapped potential shorelines. In my own investigations of these arguments, I’ve found that most of them are based on the earlier Viking-based localizations that are too low in resolution and too imprecisely placed to provide reliable elevation measurements. Even with modern imagery and topography data, care must be taken in mapping these features as accurately as possible with respect to CTX images and DEMs.

The proposed shorelines suggest that, if the hypothesis is correct, all successful US and Chinese Mars landers are on surfaces that were once under water. Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, and Zhurong have all described sedimentary deposits that are best explained as indicative of deposition in water.

title: A Monte Carlo Framework for Estimating Background Geogenic Soil Lead in Cacao-Producing Countries
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: McDannell, Kalin T. [1], Slagowski, Naomi [2], Dugan, Thomas [3], Boomhower, Steven R. [4]
affiliations: (1) Gradient, Boston, MA, USA
(2) Gradient, Boston, MA, USA
(3) Gradient, Boston, MA, USA
(4) Gradient, Boston, MA, USA
abstract: Elevated lead (Pb) concentrations reported in chocolate have raised food-safety concerns. One source of Pb in chocolate may be naturally occurring soil Pb, which can be transferred into cacao beans grown in various countries in West Africa, South America, and other regions. However, the contribution of natural (geogenic) bedrock Pb sources to potential Pb exposure from cacao beans remains poorly quantified in scientific studies, particularly for various cacao-producing countries. We present a Monte Carlo framework that estimates background geogenic soil Pb attributable solely to bedrock geochemistry, providing a quantitative baseline against which measured field values can be compared. Country-scale lithologic areal fractions were derived from a published global lithologic map (GLiM; average scale 1:3,750,000), classifying geology into igneous/metamorphic, sedimentary, and volcanic categories. Lithologic Pb concentrations were parameterized from Turekian and Wedepohl (1961) using log-normal distributions considering the positively skewed nature of Pb in geological materials. For each of the 31 cacao-producing countries evaluated, 10,000 Monte Carlo iterations combined randomly sampled rock-type Pb concentrations, weighted by areal fraction, to generate a probability distribution of total geogenic soil Pb. The resulting geometric mean soil Pb estimate for each country was then multiplied by an empirical soil-to-plant uptake factor for "protected" crops ( i.e ., plants with enclosed seeds, such as cacao), yielding a point estimate of geogenic Pb in cacao beans. Modeled geometric mean total soil Pb across cacao-producing countries ranged from ~2.5 to 15 parts per million. Corresponding plant-tissue Pb uptake estimates were two orders of magnitude below those values for all modeled countries. These results provide a quantitative, geology-based estimate of the minimum expected Pb contribution from bedrock. Notably, this framework offers a transferable approach for establishing geogenic ( i.e ., naturally occurring) background in multiple contexts, such as human health risk assessment, food safety, and evaluating regulatory compliance. This work illustrates how public geologic and empirical bioavailability datasets can be combined with Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation to support risk assessment and evaluating regulatory compliance where direct farm-level sampling is unavailable.

title: A stratified Orosirian ocean where eukaryotes inhabited shallow and giant filaments thrived deep
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age
authors: Zheng, Wentao [1], Porter, Susannah M. [2], Riedman, Leigh Anne [3], Lechte, Maxwell [4], Brengman, Latisha Ashley [5], Czaja, Andrew D. [6], Halverson, Galen P. [7]
affiliations: (1) University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
(2) University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA

(4) University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia
(5) University of Minnesota, Duluth, MN, USA
(6) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
(7) McGill University, Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Montreal, QC, Canada
abstract: The Great Oxidation Event (GOE; 2.4–2.1 Ga) is widely thought to have facilitated eukaryogenesis by elevating oxygen levels and enabling aerobic metabolism (Lyons et al., 2014; Mills et al., 2022). However, the absence of unequivocal eukaryotic fossils shortly after the GOE has hindered our understanding of the relationship between the distribution of fossil eukaryotes and oxygen levels. To test and expand upon the hypothesis that early (>1.75 Ga) fossil eukaryotes were already aerobic (Lechte et al., 2026), we have analyzed siliciclastic samples from the ca. 2.0–1.8 Ga Paleoproterozoic Pokegama and Virginia formations of the Animikie Group (Minnesota, USA) and Tooloo Group (Western Australia). Here, we describe microfossil assemblages from the shallow-marine and likely oxic Pokegama Formation and Tooloo Group that include the likely eukaryote Satka favosa along with cyanobacterial filaments belonging to Siphonophycus spp. In contrast, the deeper water, anoxic Virginia Formation hosts giant, rigid, and tapering filaments up to 130 μm in width and 1 mm in length that we tentatively interpret to represent sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. These findings reveal distinct shallow- and deep-marine microbial communities in a stratified Paleoproterozoic ocean and further support the idea that early eukaryotes were restricted to shallow, oxic habitats.
