title: Evaluating Constructed Vernal Pools as Nature-Based Solutions to Urban Nutrient Pollution
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Flach, Adeline R. [1], Poprawski, Anna [2], Sloan, John J. [3], Hasenmueller, Elizabeth A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Geospatial Science, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, Missouri, USA; WATER Institute, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, Missouri, USA
(2) National Great Rivers, East Alton, Illinois,
(3) National Great Rivers, East Alton, Illinois, USA
(4) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Geospatial Science, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, Missouri, USA; WATER Institute, Saint Louis University, Saint Louis, Missouri, USA
abstract: Urbanization increases impervious surface cover, generating storm-driven pulses of nutrient-rich runoff that degrade downstream water quality. Vernal pools, seasonally inundated wetlands that function as biogeochemical hotspots, can retain and transform nutrients through microbial processes and extended water residence times. Their wet-dry cycles also exclude fish populations, providing critical amphibian breeding habitat. Despite this ecological importance, these small, isolated wetlands receive limited regulatory protection and are steadily disappearing from landscapes. Constructed vernal pools offer a promising nature-based solution for urban stormwater and habitat management, but their effectiveness in nutrient processing remains poorly understood. Our ongoing study therefore compares nutrient cycling dynamics among natural, mature constructed (>30 years old), and recently constructed (~5 years old) vernal pools at an urban restoration site near St. Louis, Missouri. Through weekly monitoring, soluble phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations are being measured in the three vernal pools’ surface water and soil porewater to capture temporally dynamic and depth-resolved nutrient cycling processes. To simplify nutrient load estimates, we calculated phosphorus as orthophosphate and nitrogen as the sum of ammonium and nitrate. Initial data for April-June 2026 (11 visits per site) show mean surface water phosphorus and nitrogen both increased with vernal pool age, with respective values of 0.06 mg/L and 0.12 mg/L in the recently constructed site, 0.07 mg/L and 0.42 mg/L in the mature constructed site, and 0.48 mg/L and 0.71 mg/L in the natural site. These results suggest that vernal pool age may help predict surface water nutrient status. Similarly, mean porewater phosphorus concentrations increased with vernal pool age (recently constructed vernal pool = 0.00 mg/L, mature constructed vernal pool = 0.01 mg/L, and natural vernal pool = 0.07 mg/L). In contrast, mean porewater nitrogen concentrations were highest in the mature constructed site (10.33 mg/L), with lower concentrations in the recently constructed site (0.78 mg/L) and natural site (4.16 mg/L). We also observed a delayed and diminished nitrate pulse in the porewater relative to the surface water at the natural vernal pool following a residential runoff event, suggesting nitrogen load attenuation during subsurface transport. As sampling continues, these initial patterns will be evaluated for seasonal consistency and used to assess whether constructed vernal pools can achieve nutrient retention capacity comparable to natural systems.

title: Deltaic Geomorphology Governs the Transferability of Machine-Learning Coastal Hazard Models in Louisiana
session_title: Contemporary research in geomorphological hazards
authors: Hossain, Tanvir [1], Leitner, Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and ANthropology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA
(2) Department of Geography and Anthropology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA
abstract:
The Mississippi River deltaic plain is shaped by low relief, compacting Holocene sediments, extensive marshes, and a dense network of distributary bayous and canals. These conditions also control the spatial expression of flooding, land subsidence, storm surge, and salinity intrusion. We examined how such geomorphic and coastal controls influence both susceptibility patterns and the geographic transferability of data-driven hazard models in Terrebonne Parish, Louisiana.

A common stack of 65 environmental predictors at 30 m resolution was assembled from topographic, hydrologic, soil, coastal, climatic, anthropogenic, and remotely sensed datasets. Eight machine-learning and deep-learning algorithms were evaluated for each hazard. To distinguish apparent skill from genuine geographic transfer, models were tested using a blocked holdout, interleaved 5 km block cross-validation, and a stricter contiguous-zone design with a 5 km separation between training and test areas.

Holdout F1-macro ranged from 0.644 for salinity intrusion to 0.923 for flooding. Interleaved block cross-validation produced statistically similar results, indicating that spatial blocks alone did not remove short-range dependence. Under buffered contiguous-zone testing, however, F1-macro declined by 12-54 percentage points. Flood and storm-surge models retained comparatively greater skill because their predictions were controlled by physically portable terrain and coastal variables, including relative elevation, topographic wetness, and distance from the coast. Subsidence and salinity models degraded more sharply because they relied more heavily on regionally interpolated geodetic and water-quality fields. A stacked ensemble did not improve spatially validated performance despite requiring approximately five times the training cost.

The resulting multi-hazard index identifies southern Terrebonne Parish as the area of greatest combined susceptibility. More broadly, the findings indicate that the apparent transferability of geospatial hazard models depends not only on algorithm choice, but also on the geological meaning and spatial support of their predictors. In deltaic environments, validation designs that preserve nearby spatial information may substantially overstate how well models will perform across geomorphic and environmental transitions.

title: The Impact of Urban Tree Canopy Depletion on the Urban Heat Island in Greater Dhaka City, Bangladesh
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: Hassan, Muhammad Qumrul [1], Khandaker, Nazrul I [2], Raza, Jowaher [3], Sharmin, Hosne Ara [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, 1000, Bangladesh
(2) Department of Earth and Physical Sciences, York College of CUNY, Jamaica, New York, USA
(3) Department of Geology, University of Dhaka, Dhaka, 1000, Bangladesh
(4) Department of Environmental Science, Faculty of Science and Technology, Bangladesh University of Professionals, Dhaka 1216, Bangladesh
abstract:
Controlling the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect is essential for protecting public health, reducing energy demand, improving air quality, and enhancing overall thermal comfort in rapidly growing cities. As urban areas expand, impervious materials such as concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, elevating surface and air temperatures. Urban Tree Canopy (UTC) serves as a natural cooling system by providing shade, promoting evapotranspiration, and lowering surface temperatures. These ecosystem services significantly moderate urban heat. However, ongoing tree removal and the shrinking of green spaces are weakening this protective mechanism, making cities increasingly vulnerable to heat stress.

Greater Dhaka exemplifies this challenge. Rapid urbanization has transformed vegetated land into dense built-up zones, intensifying thermal stress across the metropolitan region. This study evaluates the relationship between UTC depletion and UHI dynamics from 2000 to 2023, with particular emphasis on the Uttara Residential Area (URA). Multi-temporal Landsat-5 TM and Landsat-8 OLI/TIRS imagery were used for Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) classification and Land Surface Temperature (LST) estimation, achieving classification accuracies between 80% and 92%.

The findings reveal substantial landscape transformation. Built-up areas expanded from roughly 35% to over 70% in major growth corridors, while vegetation cover declined from nearly 38% to below 20%. In some core sectors, tree canopy loss reached approximately 45%. Correspondingly, mean daytime LST increased by 2.8-3.6°C, with urban-rural temperature differences peaking at 5-7°C. More than 70% of the study area now falls within thermally stressed built-up categories. Statistical analysis indicates a strong inverse relationship between normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and LST (R² = 0.62-0.78, p < 0.05), confirming the critical cooling role of vegetation.

In URA, accelerated development has fragmented canopy cover, producing localized heat intensification. Areas with over 30% canopy reduction recorded the largest increases in temperature. Modeling suggests that a 10% decline in UTC may increase residential cooling demand by 4-6%, whereas restoring 20% canopy coverage in hotspot zones could reduce mean LST by up to 2°C.

Thus, there is an urgent need for strategic urban forestry, canopy restoration, and climate-responsive planning to strengthen resilience and ensure sustainable urban development in Greater Dhaka.

Keywords: Urban Tree Canopy, Urban Heat Island, Land Surface Temperature, Urbanization.

title: Documenting Evidence of Multiple Phases of Wichita Mountain Deformation Near Lake Elmer Thomas Dam, Medicine Park, Oklahoma
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Memmott, Charles [1], Carpenter, Brett M. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
(2) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma, USA
abstract:
The Wichita Mountains are a recognized aulacogen that developed during the breakup of Rodinia. The aulacogen created an inherent weakness in the crust that allowed for localization of further deformation. The Wichita Mountains are known to have a complicated and multiphase deformation history with three main phases of deformation. During the initial rifting phase of deformation, the Mount Scott Granite was emplaced at depths no greater than 2 km. We identified an outcrop of Mount Scott Granite adjacent to Lake Elmer Thomas Dam that hosts multiple structures that can provide insight into a portion of the deformation history and paleostress direction evolution of the Wichita Mountains. These structures consist of dikes, unloading fractures, reverse fault, and strike-slip fault(s). The relationship of these structures to the known phases of the Wichita Mountain deformation is poorly understood.

We completed an approximately 7-meter-long scanline and two 0.25m 2 2D grid maps within the identified fault zone to characterize the spacing and orientation of fractures. We then completed two approximately 20-meter-long scanlines on the east and west sides of the fault zone to characterize spacing and orientation of unloading fractures. We observed the unloading fractures to be spaced closer together west of the fault zone than east of the fault zone, suggesting two different deformation histories on either side of the fault zone. Generally, fractures within and outside the fault zone were observed to be similarly oriented. Within the fault zone we observed three zones of higher fracture density, two of which had ramp-flat-like geometries that appear to have taken advantage of the preexisting weaknesses associated with the unloading fractures. Our preliminary observations suggest reverse motion with SE–NW compression. 2D grid mapping of these ramp-flat-like geometries allowed for the interpretation of Reidel fracture geometry, supporting this hypothesis. Nearby subvertical fractures, one of which has clear evidence of strike-slip movement, strike approximately SE–NW. This strike-slip movement is structurally conformable with reverse motion within the main fault zone. This deformation is structurally conformable with the current stress field and third phase of Wichita Mountain deformation when stress was oriented ENE–WSW and strike slip faulting dominated deformation within the Wichita Mountains.

title: Assessing the Role of Earthworms (Lumbricus terrestris) on Lead Transport and Accumulation in Lead Contaminated Urban Garden Soils and Potential for Bioremediation
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part I)
authors: Cox, Patricia Colleen [1], Farver, John R. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, Bowling Green State University, Bowling Green, OH, USA
(2) Department of Geology, Bowling Green State University, Bowling Green, OH, USA
abstract:
Anthropogenic activities including use of lead-based paint and lead-gasoline have resulted in elevated legacy lead levels in most older cities in the US. Urban community gardens provide benefits to their communities but may also provide a ready source of contaminated soil. Our previous studies show that raised bed soils can become contaminated with Pb in a few years and lead transport by earthworms is a primary cause.

To evaluate Pb redistribution via earthworms, microcosms designed to mimic urban gardens in NW Ohio were constructed using a sandy loam with 5 wt% sphagnum moss, 0.1 wt% CaCO₃, and ~20% water. Lead as PbCO₃, the form found in lead paint, was homogenously mixed into the soils. Lead concentrations of 100, 200 and 400 ppm were used corresponding to EPA action levels.

The microcosms were filled with 28 cm of soil mixture, 24 adult L. terrestris were introduced, and a 2-3 cm thick layer of sphagnum moss was sprinkled on top to maintain moisture and to promote feeding and anecic burrowing behavior.

Experiments were run 2, 4, and 8 weeks. Afterwards, earthworm casts at the surface were collected and the top mulch layer was carefully removed. The soil was removed in 1 cm layers down to 5 cm from the soil-mulch interface. The remaining soil was removed and homogenized. Soil, depurated and non-depurated earthworms, egesta, and casts were collected and analyzed using FP-XRF or ICP-OES following standard EPA protocols.

Results show that L. terrestris can facilitate both Pb redistribution and accumulation in garden soils. For an 8-week experiment with 400 ppm soil Pb, casts and top mulch layer had 313 and 233 ppm Pb, respectively. Bioaccumulation factors for depurated worms ranged from 0.14 to 0.36 with a general increase with duration and soil Pb concentration. Egesta and casts have similar Pb concentrations. Overall, Pb concentrations in the underlying soil decreased (up to 17.6%) with transport of the lead to the surface and deposition in the mulch layer.

The overall reduction in lead within the underlying soils and deposition at the surface, where it could be easily collected, indicates that earthworms may provide an inexpensive bioremediation mechanism for contaminated urban gardens. However, surface deposition and accumulation of lead in earthworm tissues increases potential for human exposure and up-trophic transfer.

title: The Value of Field Spectrometers: Mineralogical Baselines and Hyperspectral Models for Tunnel Dike
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Hopwood, Lucy Twakala Keya [1], Hidalgo, Paulo J. [2], Mittal, Tushar [3], Currier, Ryan [4]
affiliations: (1) Georgia State Univ, Geosciences, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA,
(4) University of West Georgia, Carrollton, GA,
abstract: Field sampling in igneous settings relies on visual properties, which do not consider subtle mineralogical variability. Portable field spectrometers allow for the non-destructive, in-situ identification of mineral phases in real-time, yet there is a gap in the literature testing the reliability of this field method against laboratory-based mineralogical baselines. I hypothesize that through Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) modeling, hyperspectral data can produce mineral proportions comparable to established laboratory methods, such as XRD (i.e., no statistically significant difference). Research objectives are (1) conduct powder XRD analysis for a mineralogical baseline, (2) collect hyperspectral data with the OreXplorer on hand samples, (3) calibrate mixing models using MCMC to predict mineral proportions in each sample, and (4) evaluate commonalities between hyperspectral mineral proportion mixing models and laboratory-derived mineralogies. Nine Tunnel Dike basaltic hand samples were collected in a previous field season in the Columbia River Flood Basalt province and portions of these samples were powdered in February 2025. Statistically insignificant differences between model mineral proportions and benchmarks will validate the hypothesis, while dissimilar results will result in a rejected hypothesis. This study contributes to quantitative methodology by developing a statistically rigorous framework through Markov-Chain Monte Carlo probabilistic modeling application to hyperspectral data, then verifying outputs against known mineralogical techniques. Findings will inform future methodological standards for the field usage of portable spectrometers and can lead to more efficient field visits. Preliminary results will be presented at the meeting. This research is funded by the Lipman Research Award, a GSA Graduate Student Research Grant.

title: Supergene dissolution and precipitation of rare-earth element (REE) minerals in orogenic garnet amphibolite
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part I)
authors: Cao, Wentao [1], Larson, Kyle [2], Shrestha, Sudip [3], Mergelsberg, Sebastian [4], Massonne, Hans-Joachim [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Sciences, State University of New York at Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA; Buffalo Museum of Science, Buffalo, New York, USA

(4) Pacific Northwest National Lab, Richland, WA, USA

abstract:
Understanding REE enrichment mechanism is critical to guiding the future exploration of hosting ore deposits. However, common REE ores typically exhibit complex textures and petrogenesis, making it difficult to elucidate the concentration mechanism. We report our recent results from an orogenic garnet amphibolite with enriched REEs from the Neoproterozoic southern Brasilia Orogen and interpret its forming mechanism. This rock mainly consists of garnet, amphibole, quartz, ilmenite, and minor REE phosphates. Garnet is almandine with a core to rim compositional variation from Grs 27-28 Alm 54-56 Py 4-5 Sps 12-14 to Grs 26–29 Alm 59–63 Py 8–11 Sps 1–2 . Amphibole is calcic with slight compositional variation, as magnesio-hornblende, tschermakite, pargasite, and sadanagaite.

Total REE abundance of the bulk rock is comparable to common REE ore specimens, with REEs hosted in REE phosphates. These minerals occur in two different textural settings with distinctive chemistry. The first group (Group I) of REE phosphate appears as subhedral to anhedral grains in the matrix of the rock, while the second group (Group II) is anhedral and distributed along grain boundaries. Electron microprobe analysis yielded mineral chemistries with low analytical totals and negligible Th, characteristic of hydrous REE phosphates or porous secondary minerals. Group I is Y-rich with less light-REEs (LREE) and lower totals than Group II, interpreted as heavily leached xenotime or secondary churchite-Y, a hydrous yttrium phosphate. Wide-angle X-ray scattering analysis of one area on the specimen yielded spectra of churchite. In comparison, Group II displays an LREE enrichment, with elevated CaO content and stronger negative Ce anomaly (Ce* = Ce/sqrt(La*Pr)), which are interpreted to reflect mobilization by oxidized fluids and precipitation as secondary hydrous phases such as rhabdophane-(Nd). Laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass-spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) analysis shows that Group II REE phosphates display elevated Sr contents compared to Group I, corroborating the interpretation of their formation via fluid-involved process. U-Pb geochronology of Group I REE phosphate by LA-ICP-MS yielded a poorly constrained date of 15 ± 54 Ma, whereas Group II returned a 2.95 ± 0.67 Ma date. Together, we propose a model with fluid-rock interaction and elemental fractionation, which led to secondary REE mineralization under supergene oxidizing aqueous conditions.

title: Towards a Comprehensive Acknowledgement of the Role of Extractive Industry in our Collective Geoheritage
session_title: Webinar 2: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives
authors: Calder, John Hugh [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Saint Mary's University, Boutiliers Point, NS, Canada
abstract: The concept of geoheritage has become accepted by the geoscience community and organizations, and awareness is continuing to grow with the general public. In developing one of the first systematic geoheritage inventories in Canada, two aspects of geoheritage were recognized in Nova Scotia, informed by the recognition of World Heritage: natural geoheritage (traditional geological sites) and cultural geoheritage where the impact of geology is reflected in the identity of a region’s peoples. Two primary aspects of cultural geoheritage involve Indigenous traditions of interpreting the landscape and historical mining and resource extraction that shaped communities. Indigenous cultural geoheritage is not restricted to spiritual aspects of the geological andscape. It is important to acknowledge the use of stone, copper, silver, turquoise and many other minerals by Indigenous peoples both pre-and post-colonial contact. Coal mining shaped towns across eastern North America, silver and related minerals in the southwest, oil extraction widely. Quarries that have supplied some of the most treasured objects of art and the practice of skilled stone cutters and artisans directly link culture and geology. But what is our responsibility to not only acknowledge these, but to acknowledge mining disasters (as done in Nova Scotia), non-sustainable practices and even environmental disasters, and the role of mining booms on Indigenous peoples? Surely these too comprise the geoheritage legacy of mining and petroleum extraction. Acknowledgement of such examples offer the chance for geoscience to be seen not only as the champion of extractive activities, but also as honest brokers that share lessons of the past. For those engaged in extractive industry today, such balance offers an opportunity to acknowledge past lessons in striving for safer and more sustainable practice today and in so doing, to gain trust by the general public.

title: Post-Hurricane Helene landslide inventory mapping in Grayson County, VA: insights into geology, geomorphology, and landslide initiation
session_title: The National Landslide Hazard Reduction Program (NLHRP): Advancing Landslide Hazard Reduction in the U.S. through Working Groups and Landslide Risk Reduction Grants (Posters)
authors: Mangum, Holly E. [1], Witt, Anne C. [2]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Department of Energy, Charlottesville, VA, USA
(2) Virginia Department of Energy, Charlottesville, VA, USA
abstract:
On September 24-29, 2024, Hurricane Helene impacted the southeastern United States, causing severe flooding and triggering thousands of damaging landslides. While western North Carolina bore the brunt of the storm, an initial assessment of post-storm satellite imagery and reports from media, emergency management, and the Virginia Department of Transportation indicated that nearly 40 landslides occurred in southwestern Virginia. Grayson County along the North Carolina border was most affected. Rainfall totals from the National Weather Service indicate that Grayson received upwards of 11 inches of rain during a 72-hour period ending on September 28, 2024.

In response, the Virginia Department of Energy’s Division of Geology and Mineral Resources (DGMR) applied for funding through the USGS Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Program to produce a landslide inventory map of Grayson County. No regional landslide hazard maps exist for this part of Virginia, so landslide risk was entirely unknown.

DGMR mapped landslide features using a combination of desktop and field investigation. Since the only publicly available lidar dataset for this part of Virginia was flown between 2015-2016, a USGS Preliminary Landslide Inventory, VDOT reports, social media, news reports, Copernicus satellite imagery, and field observations were used to identify landslides triggered by Helene. More than 300 modern landslides and 1400 ancient landslide deposits have been identified in the project area with 73% identified as debris slides. Field data were collected at nearly 600 stations to characterize modern landslides and ancient debris deposits. Only 16 landslides were definitely identified as resulting from Helene, most initiating on modified slopes. County-wide, slopes with landslides were on average 29 degrees and 80% were unmodified. Thicker, widespread ancient deposits developed in higher elevation areas with rhyolite and conglomerate bedrock.

The goal of this inventory map is to advance the understanding of geological and topographic factors that influence landslide initiation and the risk to public safety from landslides in southwestern Virginia. Future work in Grayson County will include using this inventory to perform spatial statistics to develop a landslide susceptibility and inundation map. In addition to documenting landslide damage from Hurricane Helene, these mapping efforts are part of a larger ongoing effort to create a statewide landslide inventory in Virginia.

title: How good is the radiocarbon record of extinct North American megafauna?
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation
authors: Jukar, Advait Mahesh [1], Garcia, Amaya [2], Mychajliw, Alexis M. [3], Pardi, Melissa Irene [4], Lindsey, Emily Leigh [5], Widga, Chris [6]
affiliations: (1) Natural History, Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, FL,
(2) Biology, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA
(3) Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT,
(4) Illinois State Museum, Springfield, Illinois, USA
(5) La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles, CA,
(6) Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
The loss of megafauna, or species weighing over 45kg has been documented world over during the last 100,000 years. This extinction severely reduced the diversity of large mammals across many continents such as Australia and the Americas. North America lost 53 species of mammals, the majority of them being megafauna, representing a loss of ~74%. Understanding the pattern, process, and causes of this extinction has been an area of intense research and debate for over 50 years. Extinction is a spatio-temporal phenomenon where species decline in abundance across a landscape, resulting in range contraction until the species eventually goes extinct. In order to study this process, a well-resolved directly-dated chronology of the range contraction and extinction is necessary. However, previous work has shown that the number and distribution of radiocarbon dates available for extinct species is highly biased by geography, with directly dated specimens for some species coming from one or a handful of sites in a subset of their range. In this study, we aim to investigate the pervasiveness of this problem and answer the question of whether the radiocarbon record of extinct megafauna are spatially comprehensive so as to provide an accurate picture of the timing and pattern of extinction.

We assembled the most comprehensive compilation of late Quaternary extant and extinct mammal species dated using 14 C techniques from North America, resulting in a dataset of over 4000 dated specimens. Using this dataset, we show that of the ~70 recorded extinct species, only 32 of them were directly dated, and 16 of these 32 species had fewer than 10 directly dated fossils. The distribution of directly dated specimens was also not uniform across the sampled range of these species as represented in the Neotoma database. For example, Smilodon fatalis is known from Florida to California, but the 398 directly dated specimens came from 4 localities in southern California. Large parts of the continent such as the Southeast have produced few to no direct dates for megafauna severely biasing our understanding of this extinction on a seemingly well-studied continent. Lastly, we offer recommendation for future targeted sampling and research to close the gaps in the radiocarbon record of extinct North American megafauna.

title: Re-mapping the Mount Jefferson Meta-ultramafic Body of the Ashe Metamorphic Suite, NC
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Spallone, Rachael S [1], Johanesen, Katharine E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Juniata College, Huntingdon, PA, USA
(2) Geology, Juniata College, Huntingdon, PA, USA
abstract:
The Ashe Metamorphic Suite (AMS) in Northwestern North Carolina is composed mostly of metamorphosed ophiolites, and is home to not only meta-mafic rocks, but also numerous bodies of meta-ultramafic rocks. The ophiolite originates from the Taconic Orogeny with the closing of the Iapetus Ocean. Much of the metamorphism that occurred in this region happened during the Acadian Orogeny, slightly later than the collisions that occurred further north in the Appalachians during this time period. Peak metamorphism in the part of the AMS we are currently studying has reached up to amphibolite facies, with a strong greenschist facies overprint.

The focus of this study is the Mount Jefferson meta-ultramafic body, and our goal is to learn about the body’s mineralogy, conditions of metamorphism, and protolith, so that it can be compared to other studied AMS ultramafic bodies. It is composed of schist rich in chlorite and amphiboles, primarily tremolite and anthophyllite. Our work redefines the map, as historical mapping may have overestimated the size of the body. We distinguish at least two ultramafic units through field mapping and high-resolution DEMs combined with petrographic study: a chlorite-rich unit that form narrow ~10 meter wide ridges, and a more amphibole-rich unit that erodes more easily and does not stand out as ridges. The resulting revised map shows complex layering parallel to the regional foliation (striking roughly 70 degrees), which may indicate large-scale isoclinal folding.

Utilizing a scanning electron microscope (SEM) to conduct chemical analysis via energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), we have confirmed chlorite, amphibole (tremolite and/or anthophyllite, as not every sample has both), and ilmenite as the most common minerals. One anthophyllite-rich sample contains talc but no tremolite. Some samples contain zoned tremolite, with a few crystals having partial hornblende transitioning, other crystals have iron-rich anthophyllite rims, and some with both types of rims. Oxides are dominantly ilmenite with trace amounts of other oxides, including magnetite and chromite, in some samples. Apatite, zircon, and monazite were observed in small amounts in a few samples.

title: U-Pb Zircon Dating of Granitic Pegmatites in the Crystal Mountain District in the Northern Colorado Front Range
session_title: Proterozoic Tectonics of Western Laurentia: New Perspectives on Crustal Growth, Orogenesis, Mineralization, and Intracontinental Reworking
authors: Baird, Graham B. [1], Saldivar, Desmond [2], Thoutt, Kyle [3], Jacobson, Mark Ivan [4], Kortyna, Cullen David [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO,
(2) Department of Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO, USA
(3) Department of Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Northern Colorado, Greeley, CO, USA
(4) Department of Geology, Denver Museum of Nature and Science, Denver, CO, USA
(5) Earth Sciences, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO,
abstract:
The Crystal Mountain pegmatite district, located around the Big Thompson and Buckhorn Canyons in the Proterozoic rocks of the northern Colorado Front Range, typically contains quartz, feldspar, muscovite, tourmaline, garnet, beryl, and rare-metal trace accessory minerals. The pegmatites are classified as lithium-cesium-tantalum pegmatites, which are thought to be formed from the last fractionated melts of peraluminous granitic plutons. The nearby c.1.7 Ga Big Thompson Canyon tonalite, the c.1.7 Ga Northern Front Range granodiorite, and the c.1.4 Ga Silver Plume granite all have this composition, but no definitive evidence links the pegmatites to any of these plutonic suites or other magma sources.

Four samples of zircons from pegmatites across the district were U-Pb dated via laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectroscopy. Two samples from and near the Storm Mountain pegmatite produced highly discordant data with a range of dates. From one sample, the oldest cluster of dates produce a Pb-207/Pb-206 weighted mean of 1733+/-16 Ma, whereas a chord fitted through the youngest dates produce an upper intercept of 1452+/-24 Ma. A second sample collected directly from the Storm Mountain pegmatite contains an old cluster of dates with a Pb-207/Pb-206 weighted mean of 1771+/-26 Ma, and a young cluster of dates with a Pb-207/Pb-206 weighted mean of 1346+/-22 Ma. A sample from the Bull Elk pegmatite also produced mostly discordant data, but a cluster of 11 concordant analyses yielded a concordia age of 1419+/-6 Ma. A sample from the Black Tourmaline pegmatite likely contains common lead that produces c.4.4 Ga dates. However, a handful of analyses appear to be free of this issue and results in an old cluster of dates with a Pb-207/Pb-206 weighted mean of 1733+/-29 Ma, and a young cluster of dates with a Pb-207/Pb-206 weighted mean of 1440+/-25 Ma.

The Bull Elk pegmatite is thought to have formed at c.1419 Ma, whereas the other pegmatites are thought to have formed at c.1730 Ma, but were affected by lead-loss at c.1350-1450 Ma. The c.1771 Ma age of the Storm Mountain pegmatite is problematic as it is older than the country rock protolith. Regardless, the ages demonstrate that the district was formed by multiple processes that spanned the Proterozoic history of the area.

title: Trace Element Geochemistry of Ordovician Microfossils from Baffin Island, Canada: Revisiting a Museum Archive
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: McFadden, Anna [1], Haynes, Laura [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, Vassar College, Poughkeepsie, NY, USA
(2) Earth Science, Vassar College, Poughkeepsie, NY, USA
abstract: The Ordovician was characterized by large shallow seas and a warmer climate for most of its approximately 40 million year duration. This environment allowed for massive diversification of marine invertebrates, ones who left their fossilized remains behind to record the chemical composition of their environment. A sample of these fossils were collected from a site known as Silliman’s Fossil mount on Baffin Island, Canada, in the summer of 1947 by paleontologist A.K. Miller and geologist Walter Youngquist. A portion of these samples were given to their contemporary A. Scott Warthin, a professor at Vassar College, for microfossil analysis, particularly on ostracods. However, these samples were never published upon and became part of his museum collection. Walter and Youngquist dated these samples to the Upper Ordovician using species identification, millions of years before the anoxia of the End Ordovician Mass extinction. We revisited these samples using modern geochemical tools to investigate whether they could provide new insight into the conditions of the marginal marine environment of Laurentia in the Ordovician. SEM/EDS analysis revealed concentrated zones of mercury, cerium, lanthanum, molybdenum, and neodymium, among other rare earth elements. Bulk analysis via Direct Mercury Analyzer indicated Hg levels above values that have been recorded for Ordovician limestones and shales. These rare earth elements, as well as the levels of mercury that we measured, likely indicate that an anoxic event is preserved at Silliman’s fossil mount . Further chemical analysis of these samples, alongside a comparison study with fossil samples from the Trenton and Richmond formations of New York from the same time period will allow us to ascertain the nature of the anoxia recorded in the microfossils of Baffin Island.

title: Geomorphic and Erosional Patterns of the Great Escarpment, SE Australia, and Their Implications for Passive Margin Landscape Evolution
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens (Posters)
authors: Gong, Lingxiao [1], Ellis Curry, Magdalena [2], Zhan, Wenbo [3], Tremblay, Marissa M. [4], McMillan, Malcolm [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, North Carolina State Univ,, Raleigh, NC,
(2) North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC,
(3) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
(4) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
(5) School of Geography, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, The University of Melbourne,
abstract:
The Great Escarpment of SE Australia is a major geomorphic feature separating a low-relief, high-elevation plateau from a near-sea-level coastal plain. Understanding its long-term evolution remains a fundamental challenge in geomorphology. In particular, it is debated whether the escarpment reached its present position through continuous inland retreat since continental rifting or experienced rapid early retreat followed by prolonged stability.

We first investigate the fluvial morphology of rivers draining the escarpment and identify two populations of knickpoints. In most catchments, major knickpoints occur near the escarpment front at elevations of ~1000 m, marking a topographic transition between the plateau and coastal plain. In contrast, several catchments, e.g. Shoalhaven and Macleay, exhibit a second group of knickpoints at lower elevations (600-800 m), characterized by high knickpoint height and deeply incised river profiles. Using published catchment-wide denudation rates derived from cosmogenic 10 Be, we estimate lateral retreat rates of these rivers over kyr timescales and find a systematic increase from south to north, coinciding with the increasing development of the lower knickpoints. This spatial pattern also aligns with the distribution of younger apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He and apatite fission-track cooling ages toward the northern sector of the escarpment.

While these observations alone may not distinguish between competing models of escarpment retreat, given documented spatial variations in tectonic history across SE Australia, they provide important constraints on long-term landscape evolution. To evaluate competing scenarios, we integrate landscape evolution modeling (FastScape) with thermo-kinematic simulations (Pecube) to jointly interpret apatite fission-track, apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He, and new 4 He/ 3 He thermochronology data. The coupled framework directly links drainage evolution and surface erosion to subsurface thermal histories, enabling quantitative evaluation of plateau degradation and continuous escarpment retreat models. Our modeling results favor a plateau degradation scenario over continuous escarpment retreat. Combined with geomorphic observations of lower knickpoints and along-strike variations in lateral retreat rates, these findings suggest that the Great Escarpment may have experienced a long-lived topographic disequilibrium, with drainage reorganization and spatially variable tectonic influences contributing to its ongoing adjustment.

title: Upper Pennsylvanian Plant Communities of the Appalachian and Illinois Basins: Implications for Paleoclimate and Environmental Change
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy
authors: Elliott, William S. [1], Joest, Taryn [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Physics, and Environmental Science, University of Southern Indiana, Evansville, IN, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI, USA
abstract: Compression plant fossils from the Late Pennsylvanian (Missourian to Virgilian) were examined from surface exposures of the Bond Formation (Upper Pennsylvanian, Missourian) in Posey County, Indiana, in the historic collections of the Working Men’s Institute in New Harmony, Indiana, and from roof shales of the Bakerstown Coal (Upper Pennsylvanian, Missourian) from the Difficult Hill locality near Gormania, West Virginia and shales below the Pittsburgh Coal (Upper Pennsylvanian, Virglian) at the Fairfax Stone Knob locality near Thomas, West Virginia in the collections at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. Plant fossils were identified using reference materials and their abundance determined as common (more than 20 percent), moderate (10 to 20 percent), trace (5 to 10 percent), and rare (less than 5 percent). All localities are dominated by Pteridosperm specimens including Alethopteris sp. , Cyclopteris sp., Macroneuropteris sp., Neuropteris flexuosa , Neuropteris jacksoni , Neuropteris fimbriata , and Neuropteris ovata . Moderate abundant plants included sphenopsids such as Calamites sp. , Annularia sp., Sphenophyllum sp. , and leaves of Cordaites sp . At the Old Dam locality in Posey County, Indiana, branch and trunk impressions were examined from sandstone beds of the Bond Formation (Upper Pennsylvanian, Missourian) and included Calamites sp. , Cordaites sp ., and Sigillaria sp. There are rare occurrences of Pecopteris sp . in the Upper Pennsylvanian sediments examined at the studied localities. The plant communities identified in the Late Pennsylvanian of the Appalachian and Illinois basins are consistent with a change in plant communities from lycopsids-sphenopsid dominated flora of the Early Pennsylvanian to pteridosperm-dominated flora of the Late Pennsylvanian. These temporal changes in plant communities may be the result of lower base level leading to the subsequent dominance of upland vegetation, or an overall drying trend induced by either a continental interior setting and/or a rain shadow effect related to the rising Appalachian Mountains.

title: New Cassiterite Geochronology Results from Lithium-mineralized Pegmatites in the Northern U.S. Appalachian Orogenic Belt- Petrogenetic, Geodynamic, and Mineral Resource Assessment Implications
session_title: Tectonics, geology, and geophysics of mineral systems and controls on the localization of mineral deposits.
authors: Holm-Denoma, Christopher S. [1], Pianowski, Laura [2], Felch, Myles [3], Bradley, Dwight [4], VanTongeren, Jill A. [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) USGS, Denver, CO, USA
(3) Maine Mineral & Gem Museum, Bethel, ME, USA
(4) Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(5) Tufts University, Medford, MA, USA
abstract:
New U-Pb laser ablation (LA)-ICPMS geochronology results from cassiterite associated with several lithium-mineralized pegmatite districts in the northern U.S. Appalachians reveal two main periods of pegmatite formation (350-320 Ma and 285-255 Ma) encompassing up to eight distinct Mississippian-Permian mineralization events.

Li-mineralized pegmatites are concentrated along a ~500 km section of the northern (New England) Appalachian orogen in ~15 pegmatite districts and broadly intrude Silurian-Devonian syn-tectonic metasedimentary basinal units (e.g. the Central Maine basin). The region records two complete Wilson cycles: the Mesoproterozoic Grenville orogeny followed by Neoproterozoic breakup, and the Paleozoic Appalachian orogenies (Taconic, Acadian, Neoacadian, and Alleghanian), followed by Mesozoic breakup.

More than 15 Li-mineralized pegmatites were recently dated by cassiterite U–Pb LA ICP–MS geochronology. Within these, several age distinctive pegmatites are identified, including: Forgotten pegmatite (~352 Ma); Black Mountain (~333 Ma); Plumbago North (~327 Ma); Paris district (GE North; ~285 Ma); Greenwood–Waisanen (~264 Ma); Mt Mica (Main Pit ~256 Ma).

These pegmatites post-date major regional Appalachian orogenic, magmatic, and tectonic phases including the Acadian orogeny (~425–380 Ma); Acadian altiplano (~380–330 Ma); and Alleghanian orogeny (~300–265 Ma), supporting an anatectic origin rather than derivation from proximal intrusive rocks, or ‘parental magmas’, as residual melts of granites.

Most occurrences lie within the footprint of the Acadian (~380–330 Ma) altiplano, suggesting that protracted foundering and delamination of the altiplano and Appalachian orogenic belt supplied repeated thermal pulses necessary for anatectic pegmatite generation. The dated pegmatite events in this study may record the protracted foundering of the overthickened crust (up to >60 km) of the Acadian altiplano.

In addition to providing constraints on petrologic and geodynamic studies, direct geochronology of Li-bearing pegmatites provides critical constraints for mineral resource assessment, enabling the development of mappable criteria that integrate age, structural position, host rock composition, and P–T conditions across this Li-rich region of the northern Appalachians.

abstract:
The Miocene Cajon Valley Formation (CVF), exposed north of the Cajon Pass alongside a railroad near the San Andreas Fault (SAF). The formation contains ~2,500 meters of middle Miocene clastic strata that filled a basin along the evolving paleo-SAF. Previous work on the CVF has focused on broad stratigraphic analysis dividing the formation into six members. Due to dominantly sandstone and conglomerate facies, the CVF has been interpreted as a braided fluvial environment. However, detailed facies analysis of CVF strata is lacking. In this study we begin to address that gap by completing and interpreting a series of measured sections within three members of the CVF. Reconstructing detailed sedimentary records in tectonically active regions provides foundational information for understanding changes in sedimentary conditions, including subsidence rates and sources over time.

In January 2026, we measured three stratigraphic sections through portions of the CVF, totaling to ~490 meters of section, including 194 meters from member 2, 126 meters from member 3, and 170 meters from member 5. Our data document overall fining-upward clastic stratigraphy composed primarily of cross-bedded and horizontally bedded medium to very-coarse sandstones locally interbedded with cross-bedded to lenticular bodies of granule-pebble conglomerates. Preliminary interpretations of the sedimentary environment suggest that all members record channel deposits in a braided fluvial system. Member 2 records sandy channels and a major gravel-dominated channel-fill sequence, member 3 records local overbank deposits in between minor sand-dominated channels, and member 5 records minor sand-dominated channels and sand flat deposits. Future work will focus on investigating the influence of autogenic and allogenic processes in the CVF and comparing depositional environment interpretations in the CVF with other strata of similar age exposed in other basins along the SAF.

authors: Khandaker, Nazrul [1], Singh, Andrew [2], Singh, Omadevi [3], Chen, Jessie [4], Persaud, Haley [5]

abstract:
The City University of New York (CUNY) York College in Queens, offers a variety of K1-12 STEM programs designed to engage and inspire young students. Queens, New York is a diverse borough with significant socioeconomic diversity. Many students, particularly those from under-resourced backgrounds, lack access to quality STEM education, limiting their educational and financial potential.

The STEM workforce is vital for driving innovation, economic growth, and national security. Southeast Queens is undergoing a rapid transformation connected to the JFK Redevelopment Initiative, bringing thousands of new jobs such as: subsoil/geotechnical personnel, air traffic controllers, unmanned aircraft/drone pilot, surveyors, urban planners, and site geologists. Encouraging interest and involvement in STEM and aviation education can ensure local residents are well-equipped for these roles and allow them to achieve economic security.

The current program focuses on experiential learning, project-based education, and cross-disciplinary collaboration to prepare students for the dynamic and interdisciplinary demands of the modern STEM workforce. Topics covered include: robotics, rocketry, programming, cybersecurity, machine learning, artificial intelligence. Since the start of the program, over 100 students have started college and a dozen secured jobs in aviation and technology fields. York has been highly successful in garnering federal grants and establishing partnerships with local public and private sector entities to provide the community with STEM education programs. title: Showcasing Portable Luminescence Utility Through Diverse Applications: Four Case Studies Conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey Luminescence Geochronology Laboratory
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation (Posters)
authors: Krolczyk, Emma Taylor [1], Gray, Harrison James [2], Nicovich, Sylvia [3], Mahan, Shannon [4]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Golden, CO, USA
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Luminescence dating is widely used in Quaternary geology to determine the time elapsed since quartz and feldspar grains were last exposed to sunlight prior to deposition. Traditional optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating provides quantitative depositional ages but requires extensive laboratory preparation and analysis. Portable luminescence (portaOSL) measurements offer a rapid alternative for evaluating relative luminescence signals in the field or laboratory. PortaOSL produces an uncalibrated bulk luminescence signal that it is valuable for assessing relative luminescence variability, though cannot be used for direct age calculation. Systematically sampling sedimentary exposures can provide valuable information on spatial variations in luminescence intensity that reflect sediment bleaching, depositional processes, sediment provenance, and post-depositional stratigraphic relationships. These observations can be used to identify optimal sampling locations for traditional OSL dating and to improve interpretations of complex depositional environments.

We showcase four case studies conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey Luminescence Geochronology Laboratory that demonstrate the utility of portaOSL across diverse geomorphic settings. These studies highlight a range of applications, including (1) paleoseismic investigation of the South Granite Mountains fault system in central Wyoming, (2) eolian aggradation processes within Great Sand Dunes National Park, Colorado, (3) identifying optimal locations for traditional OSL sampling within arroyo outcrops of the Stinking Water Creek basin in northwestern Colorado, and (4) distinguishing sediment bleaching histories in trenches excavated within Apalachicola National Forest, Florida.

These case studies illustrate the versatility of portable luminescence as a tool for Quaternary research. By identifying relative luminescence patterns before collecting samples for laboratory analysis, portaOSL can improve sampling efficiency, reduce analytical uncertainty, and provide valuable insight into sedimentary processes that may not be apparent from field observations alone.

title: Quantifying the Extents and Alteration of America's Riverscapes
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Gilbert, Jordan [1], Wheaton, Joseph Michael [2]
affiliations: (1) Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT,
(2) Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, UT,
abstract: Historically, estimates of riverscape extent at national and global scales have relied on coarse geospatial datasets that primarily capture larger river systems. Because first-order streams constitute most of the drainage network, these approaches have underestimated the true extent of riverscapes. This underestimation limits our understanding of the cumulative effects of human modification, the magnitude of restoration opportunity, and flood hazards in areas lacking detailed flood hazard mapping. To quantify riverscape extents across the contiguous United States (CONUS), we used a cloud-computing platform called CyberCastor to apply the Valley Bottom Extraction Tool (VBET) to the entire drainage network. In addition to delineating valley bottoms, VBET segments riverscapes into discrete polygons and automatically computes a suite of geomorphic metrics within those polygons, providing a consistent framework for continental-scale analysis. We further quantified the anthropogenic alteration of each riverscape segment by estimating the proportion of riverscapes fragmented by transportation and other infrastructure, and converted to agricultural or urban land uses. This was accomplished by intersecting the valley bottom polygons with a nationally consistent transportation infrastructure dataset and a remotely sensed land cover raster dataset. Our analysis indicates that riverscapes occupy approximately 20% of the CONUS land surface and have an average size of 18.5 hectares per kilometer of valley length. Across different physiographic regions, riverscapes are highly variable in size (1.27 - 826 ha/km) and the proportion of the landscape they make up (4.6 - 63.7%). For all of CONUS, 29-46% of riverscapes have been fragmented by human infrastructure or land-use change. Because these metrics are calculated for individual riverscape segments, they can be aggregated to stream, subwatershed, watershed, regional, or national scales, enabling consistent assessment of riverscape extent, condition, restoration potential, and flood hazards across a wide range of management and planning applications.

title: Old Cores, New Questions: Utilizing Data Visualization to Analyze Legacy Datasets

authors: Castillo, René [1], Crowell, Brendan [2], Childress, Laurel B. [3], LeVay, Leah [4]

abstract:
Over the past 50+ years scientific ocean drilling has collected kilometers of marine sediment and rock cores and generated a massive volume of data including measurements such as physical properties, visual core descriptions (VCD), and downhole logging data. Much of this data remains untouched, ready for new questions long after the original expeditions have concluded. Realizing that potential depends on shore-based infrastructure that makes archived data easily accessible to revisit and integrate with newly and future collected measurements. Such infrastructure will lower the technical barrier to data access, which will facilitate increased use of legacy datasets and save these resources from being underutilized. Here we present a portion of our shore-based data integration effort centered on an Ocean Drilling Data Science Toolbox, built to make archived and future scientific ocean drilling data mutually explorable within a single workflow.

One of the toolbox’s primary interactive components, IODP Explorer Dashboard, ingests standard data products, including data of IODP LIMS (Laboratory Information Management System; JOIDES Resolution ), J-CORES (Japan Core Research Information System; Chikyu ), and PANGAEA (Mission Specific Platforms) as well as OCR-parsed VCD PDFs, and integrates them with physical properties and downhole logging data in a linked, browser-based interface. By eliminating the need for coding or manual data processing, the dashboard enables users to rapidly generate interactive visualizations from multiple data sources within a single environment. These quick-look tools can support efficient sample planning, collaborative efforts during workshops, or basic investigation of data relationships in research and proposal planning.

title: Using C and N Geochemistry to Constrain the Evolution of Microbial Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Grajales, Alexandra M. [1], Johnson, Benjamin W. [2], Wing, Scott L. [3], Kipp, Michael [4], Hall, Grace A. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of the Earth, Atmosphere and Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA, USA
(2) Iowa State University, Ames, Iowa, USA
(3) National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
(4) Duke University, NC, USA
(5) Duke University, NC, USA
abstract:
Nitrogen (N) is an essential element for protein production, including Rubisco, the enzyme in charge of C-fixation during photosynthesis. Many environments and ecosystems are N-limited. These conditions are suggested to create selective pressures which led to the evolution of symbiotic N fixation (SNF) in plant groups such as legumes, cycads, and alders, providing a direct mechanism for atmospheric N acquisition. However, little is known about the timing of the evolution of SNF within the N-fixing clade. This work proposes to help geochemically constrain the evolution of one lineage of SNF plants, Alnus sp , by analyzing various fossil specimens (n > 30) found in museum and field collections from Early Eocene deposits in the Big Horn Basin in Wyoming, and comparing them to non-SNF plants from the same locality, Platycarya (n > 13) and Averrhoites (n > 25).

Since SNF plants tend to have lower leaf C:N ratios than non-SNF plants and N isotope signatures (ẟ 15 N) similar to atmospheric (-2 to 0 ‰), we propose that leaf tissue can provide an excellent record of the presence of SNF in fossil specimens. We hypothesize that if Alnus had engaged in N fixation during this period, when compared to the other non-fixing species from the same location, geochemical results will yield lower C:N ratios and ẟ 15 N closer to atmospheric values in Alnus sp ., following modern patterns. Our results to date indicate that Alnus in the Eocene had distinct C:N and ẟ 15 N compared to non-SNF plants, however Alnus ẟ 15 N signatures were more enriched than atmospheric ẟ 15 N values . We have yet to interpret these results as further analyses are needed, however we speculate taphonomic alterations may have influenced these findings. We hope that this work helps develop methods to understand the evolution N fixation within all N-fixing lineages and provides further insight into the biological and ecological parameters that push and drive biological evolution in plants.

title: Thermal Modeling of Inverted Metamorphism in the Central Appalachian Piedmont of SE Pennsylvania.
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part II)
authors: Bosbyshell, Howell [1], Coats, Molly L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, West Chester University, West Chester, PA, USA
(2) West Chester University, Philadelphia, PA, USA
abstract:
Inverted metamorphism has long been invoked to integrate structural and metamorphic observations in the Central Appalachian Piedmont of southeastern Pennsylvania. In the West Grove Metamorphic Suite, the highest-grade metamorphic rocks occupy the highest structural level in a crustal block consisting of stacked, basement-cored nappes bounded by vertical transpressive shear zones. Published monazite geochronology indicates that metamorphism within this block becomes progressively younger from Silurian-aged, ca. 425 Ma, metamorphism in structurally highest, upper-amphibolite facies rock of the Mill Creek nappe, through early-Devonian in the Avondale (419 Ma) and West Chester (409 Ma) massifs, culminating in ca. 381 Ma metamorphism in structurally lowest, greenschist facies rock. We propose that the metamorphic ages reflect progressive stacking of thrust sheets with successive emplacement of higher-grade rocks contributing to the thermal budget of underlying rocks.

To test this hypothesis, we conducted thermal modelling of the Embreeville Thrust, the structurally lowest and youngest in the sequence of thrusts. Our modeling demonstrates that emplacement of amphibole facies (600 C, 700 MPa, ca. 400 Ma) hanging wall rock of the Doe Run Schist generated sufficient heat to drive metamorphism in the greenschist (500 C, 600 MPa, ca. 381 Ma) Peters Creek Schist in less than 10 Myr. The magnitude of footwall heating varies with velocity and dip angle. These results are consistent with recent modeling of Thigpen et al. (2021) who found that inverted metamorphic gradients form on similar time scales and should be a common feature in thrust-dominated orogenic systems.

Moreover, the 45 Myr interval required to produce the sequence of thrusts, as indicated by monazite ages, is consistent with the duration of such activity in orogenic belts globally (Cursi, et al, 2025). We propose a model wherein shortening in an overall sinistral transpressive regime occurred episodically in internals of less than 10 Myr. The Devonian monazite ages suggest that this is associated with accretion of peri-Gondwanan tectonic elements during the Acadian orogeny.

title: Apatite 4He/3He Thermochronology Reveals Syn- and Post-rifting Rapid Evolution of the Southeastern Australia Great Escarpment
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Zhan, Wenbo [1], Tremblay, Marissa M. [2], Gong, Lingxiao [3], Curry, Magdalena Ellis [4], McMillan, Malcolm [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(3) Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA
(4) Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA
(5) School of Geography, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, The University of Melbourne, Parkville, Victoria, USA
abstract: In southeastern Australia, a high-relief Great Escarpment runs subparallel to the continental-ocean boundary for hundreds of kilometers, separating a near sea-level coastal plain from the ~1 km high landward plateau of the Eastern Highlands. The formation and evolution of the Great Escarpment is central to the landscape history of this passive margin that formed since Gondwana rifting occurred at ~110-90 Ma. We applied apatite 4 He/ 3 He thermochronology to a bedrock transect perpendicular to the escarpment from the coast to the plateau to understand the most recent near-surface cooling history that is tied to the escarpment evolution process. The degassing profiles of most samples indicate their most recent near-surface cooling were relatively rapid. Thermal history modeling combining the new apatite 4 He/ 3 He data with existing apatite (U-Th)/He and fission track data indicates that near-surface cooling initiated ~120-70 Ma for most samples across the coastal plain, with average cooling rates of ~10 ºC and cooling that ceased between ~100-50 Ma. These cooling histories suggest that the escarpment initially formed during Cretaceous rifting and that the onset of exhumation of the present-day coastal plain was near-synchronous with rifting. From the cessation of cooling, we infer that the escarpment reached its current location by ~50 Ma and has since been stagnated. Comparing our results with established geomorphic models of escarpment formation and evolution, we find that a plateau degradation model best represents the bedrock cooling patterns we observe. As Great Escarpments characterize many other continental passive margins, our findings add new insight into our understanding of syn- and post-rifting surface processes shaping this tectonic setting.

title: Polychaete worm fossils in the Miocene Chesapeake Group
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Posters)
authors: Groff, Stephen Christopher [1], Nance, John Robert [2], Tokarski, Braum Dakota [3], Deltrove, Cory Clark [4]
affiliations: (1) Paleontology, Calvert Marine Museum, Solomons, MD, USA
(2) Paleontology, Calvert Marine Museum, Solomons, MD, USA

abstract: Polychaete worm fossils are known from Miocene of the Chesapeake Group. The known fossils consist of fecal pellets; encrusting Serpulid tubes, which are commonly found yet poorly described; and jaws, which were only recently discovered during microfossil collection. The ichnofossil Coprulus oblongus , consisting of fecal pellets infilling voids in other fossils, such as fish skulls and mollusk shells, is attributed to Polychaete worms. Serpulid tubes are commonly found encrusting mollusk shells, but also bones and other hard substrate. Encrusting Serpulid tube fossils are most notably found in the Little Cove Point Member of the St. Marys Formation, Bed 16B of the Choptank Formation, and Bed 10 of the Calvert Formation. The most commonly found variety has not been properly described in the literature, nor identified beyond the family Serpulidae. A less common variety, Spirorbis calvertensis , known from at least Bed 10 of the Calvert Formation, is inadequately described in the literature. Recent microfossil collection in the St. Marys and Calvert Formations has yielded the first documented occurrence of the jaw apparatus of Polychaete worms from at least two families. From the St. Marys Formation, the first maxillae of worms from the family Glyceridae, possessing the distinct pores for venom delivery, were found in preliminary sampling. Several morphologies are visible in the collected maxillae, indicating multiple species may be present. During preliminary sampling of microfossils from the Calvert Formation, the first and second maxillae of worms in the order Eunicida, likely from the family Dorvilleidae, were found. While the second maxillae are often fragmentary, the first maxillae are well preserved, and display a variety of morphologies, again indicating the possible presence of multiple species. Here we give a preliminary description of these yet to be described Glycerid and Dorvilleid worm jaws, and the first formal description of Serpulids from the Chesapeake Group.

title: AI-Driven Flood Impact Analysis on Agriculture in Pakistan using Remote Sensing
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Ahmed, Rameez [1], Sarfraz, Muhammad Shahzad [2], Tabassam, Ahmad Ali [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Computer Science, National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences, Chiniot-Faisalabad, Pakistan
(2) Department of Computer Science, National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences, Chiniot-Faisalabad, Pakistan
(3) Department of Computer Science, National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences, Multan, Punjab, Pakistan
abstract:
Regional flood maps show inundation, but agricultural review needs smaller crop areas for inspection. We evaluated a multi-sensor workflow to find such areas along the Indus corridor from southern Punjab to interior Sindh after Pakistan's 2022 monsoon floods. In Google Earth Engine, changes in Sentinel-1 radar backscatter at VV polarization mapped inundation between pre-flood and flood-period composites, and ESA WorldCover confined the search to cropland. Phenology-matched Sentinel-2 normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) comparisons paired August 2021 with August 2022 for rice and March 2021 with March 2023 for wheat. Field-by-field crop records were unavailable, so seasonal calendars and satellite imagery supplied the wheat and rice categories.

Cloud-filtered Sentinel-2 true-color imagery yielded 880 nominal 3-km tiles, 220 per class across affected and unaffected wheat and rice. Class-specific K-means clustering proposed regions within each tile. We inspected all tiles, correcting, replacing, or removing proposals as needed. The review produced 950 reference boxes and 139 background tiles. We fine-tuned a pretrained YOLO11m detector using a random file-level 70:15:15 split. On 132 held-out tiles with 139 boxes, precision was 0.794 and recall 0.733. Mean average precision was 0.768 at an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5) and 0.728 across thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95. Supplementary reference-centered IoU was 0.875. Detection was strongest for affected rice (mAP@0.5 = 0.938) and weakest for unaffected rice (0.478).

The workflow narrows a broad flood footprint to crop zones for detailed review; drawing field boundaries and calculating crop loss remain separate steps. Analysts can use the detections to decide where post-flood checks should begin when time or field access is limited. It contributes to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) by enhancing agricultural resilience and food security through rapid post-flood damage assessment, and SDG 13 (Climate Action) by improving climate hazard assessment and adaptation. It also contributes to SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by supporting disaster risk reduction and resilience planning. The scores measure agreement with manually reviewed boxes from this dataset, geographic transfer and field-verified damage remain to be tested.

title: Sandstones and Paleosols of the Mingus Shale (Desmoinesian, Pennsylvanian), Palo Pinto County, Texas
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Rogers, Aryah [1], Rosscoe, Steven J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Kimbell School of Geosciences, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA
(2) Kimbell School of Geosciences, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA
abstract: The Mingus Shale (Desmoinesian, Pennsylvanian) is a widespread shale below the Brazos River Sandstone on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin. At two localities in the outcrop belt a prominent, purple, sandy paleosol was observed. At the Ward Mountain (WMTN) locality, the paleosol is broken into two units; a lower white sandstone with well-developed vertical root traces and an upper mottled purple sandstone. At the Lake Palo Pinto Creek Spillway (MSPP), the paleosol consists of a thin, lower white sandstone with abundant horizontal roots and an upper thinner grayish purple sandstone. Paleosols at both localities were characterized by geochemical and petrological analysis. Thin sections were prepared for petrographic and EDS analysis. Powders were prepared for X-Ray Fluorescence and X-Ray Diffraction analysis. Total organic carbon analysis (TOC) was completed with powdered samples using the Loss on Ignition method. The distinctive purple color of the upper paleosol was caused by increased hematite concentration. The reddish hematite mixed with gray clays drive the unit color to purple. WMTN hematite concentrations were higher, thus displayed a more vibrant purple coloration. MSPP featured less hematite but had an increased iron content expressed as pyrite. The switch to pyrite and introduction of manganese in birnessite resulted in a duller, grayish purple color. Overall, the paleosol at WMTN is more quartz enriched and more birnessite depleted. The MSPP paleosol has greater mineral diversity, as displayed by lower quartz and increased birnessite, along with calcite and microcline. WMTN had an order of magnitude lower TOC than MSPP in the purple paleosol. Overall, the Mingus Shale in these localities reflects a coastal setting without substantial deltaic input as observed with a lack of deltaic sedimentary structures and finer sands. WMTN was drier, featuring well-developed vertical root structures in thicker sand bodies and overall thicker soil development. Lower TOC and more hematite indicate more oxidation. MSPP was swampier, presenting horizontal roots in thinner sand bodies as well as more carbonate material. Indication of less oxidation and organics was supported by increased TOC and more pyrite.

title: A Re(ef) Interpretation: Potential Algal Origins of Proposed Neoproterozoic Poriferan Body Fossils

authors: Nadalin, Caroline C. [1], Nelson, Emil J. [2], Mehra, Akshay K. [3], Wedlake, George O. [4], Anderson, Ross P. [5], Strauss, Justin V. [6], Cohen, Phoebe A. [7]
affiliations: (1) Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA

abstract:
Ancient microbial reefs represent a key environment for supporting the diversification of early eukaryotes. The Tonian Little Dal Group, located within the Mackenzie Mountains of Northwest Territories, Canada, hosts well-preserved microbial buildups and reefs in the Stone Knife Formation, making it an excellent target locality for studying early Neoproterozoic biological systems. Vermiform microstructures in Little Dal reef fabrics have been hypothesized to be the fossil remains of basal poriferans (Turner, 2021). This interpretation would predate the earliest undisputed poriferan body fossils by over 300 million years. Here, we further evaluate this interpretation by comparing paired reef material in macerate and thin-section from 57 samples spanning a 175-meter reef core interval in the type area of the Stone Knife Formation. Macerated material yields abundant organic filamentous structures, particularly in the upper horizons of the reef. These filamentous structures vary widely in diameter (between 5 and 30 μm) and are characterized by divergent, acutely angled branching patterns. Similar filamentous morphologies and branching have also been identified in thin sections and are commonly preserved in fine-grained, intra-cavity micrite sediment and secondary pore-filling marine cements. This branching mechanism differs from the anastomosing and polygonal networks described by Turner (2021), being more comparable to branching seen in modern algal analogs. By combining paleontological and petrographic analyses, we hypothesize that (1) the vermiform microstructures described by Turner (2021), regardless of their affinity, are very rare components of the Stone Knife reefs, and that (2) their rarity could be attributed to the fact that they may be the product of diagenetic alteration of the filamentous structures we describe here; similar carbonate features in younger rocks also have proposed diagenetic origins, such as fluid-escape structures, biofilm channels, and thermal overprinting. Narrowing our understanding of the origin of these structures in the Little Dal reef allows us to more accurately reconstruct early eukaryote communities, as well as better differentiate between biotic and diagenetic signatures in Proterozoic carbonates.

Turner, E. C. (2021). Possible poriferan body fossils in early Neoproterozoic microbial reefs. Nature, 596(7870), 87–91. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03773-z

title: Investigating Retrofits to Improve Water Quality and Reduce Streambank Erosion in Aging Flood Control Basins in Northeast Ohio
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Winston, Ryan [1], Tirpak, Andrew [2]
affiliations: (1) Food, Agricultural, and Biological Engineering, Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(2) Food, Agricultural, and Biological Engineering, Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
abstract: Streambed and streambank erosion, a particularly vexing problem in urban watersheds, occurs when the stream’s critical discharge (Qcritical) is exceeded and bed and bank material are mobilized. In many Ohio watersheds, especially those developed between 1980 and 2003, urban runoff is routed to stormwater basins designed primarily for flood control (i.e., shaving the peak discharge without meeting other stream protection goals). As a result, many older stormwater basins fail to retain and slowly release runoff during frequently occurring small storm events, providing little to no water quality benefits nor mitigating (in fact, often exacerbating) erosion in receiving streams. Simple retrofits these basins (e.g., adding orifices, weirs, and other flow mitigation features to existing outlet structures) could improve their water quality benefits while reducing the occurrence of downstream erosion and maintaining flood control capacity. An extensive pilot-scale modeling effort was undertaken to evaluate the benefits of retrofits to flood control basins in Aurora and Mayfield Heights, Ohio. Retrofit strategies were designed to meet current regulations (i.e., slowly release runoff from a 0.9-in storm event over a 48hr period) while reducing opportunities for exceedance of Qcritical. In Aurora, targeted retrofits, especially to the largest, most downstream basin, achieved significant reductions in peak discharge and met all design objectives, including reducing instances of Qcritical to below pre-development levels, safely passing runoff from the 100yr-24hr event, and meeting current water quality drawdown requirements without changing existing normal pool elevations. Conversely, modeling for a suite of stormwater retention ponds in a commercial area in Mayfield Heights, Ohio underscores the limitations of basin retrofits in highly developed watersheds with large outlet structures which provide little hydraulic restriction to flow. Even extensive structural modifications failed to meet design objectives, suggesting that retrofits alone may not be sufficient in such contexts. These outcomes emphasize the need for a watershed-specific approach that considers outlet design, drainage area size, and development intensity when evaluating basins for potential retrofits. Findings from this research can inform similar retrofit efforts targeting flood control basins to bolster their water quality benefits and mitigate downstream erosion caused by aging stormwater infrastructure designed under outdated regulations.

title: Resolving Eruptive Pulses Within the Uppermost Fall Unit of the El Cajete Eruption, Valles Caldera
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Montes, Jeffrey J [1], Clarke, Amanda Bachtell [2], Roggensack, Kurt [3], Wells, Tyler [4]
affiliations: (1) School for Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(2) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
