abstract:
The Valles Caldera in north-central New Mexico is an active volcanic system whose youngest eruptive deposits, the El Cajete sequence (ca. 50–70 ka), preserve evidence of rapidly changing eruptive conditions. This high-resolution stratigraphic study investigates the seemingly cyclic changes in the uppermost fall unit as evidenced by variations in grain size and pumice density. Here we use grainsize to constrain temporal variations in plume height and mass eruption rate (MER), and pumice characteristics to assess corresponding changes in fragmentation processes and magma ascent conditions.

A detailed stratigraphic column was constructed that subdivides the fall unit into six discrete zones interpreted as variations in eruption rate or individual eruptive pulses. Maximum clast size was measured for each subunit and will be used to estimate plume height and MER. Hundreds of lapilli were collected to quantify density variations among the subunits. These measurements will be compared with equivalent analysis conducted by previous researchers for the same unit treated as a single eruptive pulse. Thin sections will be analyzed to quantify microlite textures and vesicle characteristics, providing constraints on relative magma ascent rates, outgassing conditions, and fragmentation processes. Together, these datasets will document rapid temporal changes in eruption dynamics and identify potential causes. These results will provide insight into evolving conditions and dynamic processes active during sustained explosive silicic eruptions.

title: A Heat-Tracer Probe for Measuring Groundwater Velocity in Fractures
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: Salamanca, Andres Felipe [1], Devlin, John F. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
(2) Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
Fractures provide preferential pathways for groundwater flow and contaminant transport in the subsurface. Recent advances in point-scale groundwater velocity measurements have demonstrated the potential for rapid and reliable flow estimation in fractured rock. However, tracer injections in deep boreholes (e.g., >10 m) may be affected by cavitation within tracer delivery lines due to the large hydraulic head difference between the tracer reservoir at the surface and the probe at depth, while saline tracers can induce density-driven flow. Both effects increase measurement uncertainty. Using heat as a tracer eliminates these solution-related limitations by providing a controlled, probe-centered tracer input that is unaffected by hydraulic head variations.

In this study, we evaluate the feasibility of using heat as a tracer with a previously developed In-Well Point Velocity Probe (IWPVP), originally designed for porous media, for point-scale groundwater velocity measurements in fractured media. Experiments were conducted using a laboratory fracture apparatus with a constant fracture aperture of 1.5 mm. Groundwater velocity was independently measured by visually tracking a dye tracer, while thermal pulses of 5, 10, 20, and 30 s were generated using an electrical resistance heater embedded within the probe. Temperature breakthrough curves were recorded using fine-wire thermistors positioned 12 mm downgradient of the heat source, in the direction of flow within the fracture. Thermal-derived velocities compared well with dye-derived measurements.

A linear calibration relationship (R² = 0.99) was established between probe-derived flow velocities and the corresponding dye-measured reference velocities, which ranged from 25 to 300 m/day, yielding a calibration factor of 2.04 ± 0.05 (1σ). This calibration factor is consistent with the expected increase in flow velocity within the probe resulting from its reduced flow cross-sectional area relative to the fracture capture area. These results demonstrate that heat is an effective tracer for the IWPVP and provides a practical alternative to conventional tracer injections for point-scale flow velocity measurements in fractured media. The method is particularly well suited for deep borehole applications, where tracer injections can introduce measurement artifacts.

abstract: Ground-based geophysical methods were used in northern Illinois to constrain interpretations of helicopter time-domain electromagnetic (HTEM) data. Ground-based time-domain electromagnetic (TEM), 2-D electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), and microtremor horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR) methods were applied in the Troy Bedrock Valley (TBV). Prior knowledge of the geologic context, infrastructure, and previous geophysical mapping in the area informed site-specific approaches. In addition to the geophysical data, gamma logs and other borehole information were utilized to form more accurate geologic interpretations of the TBV. In general, we find that the use of multiple geophysical methods at a site reduces the uncertainty associated with geologic interpretations of the HTEM data. More importantly, ground-based geophysical data resolves geologic features at a finer scale, which can help inform and predict variability of those features in other areas of HTEM data.

title: Systematic Evolution of Rb–Sr Downhole Fractionation in Micas Used in Laser-Based Geochronology
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications (Posters)
authors: Arkula, Cemil [1], Garber, Joshua M. [2], Cruz-Uribe, Alicia Marie [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Climate Science, University of Maine, Orono, ME, USA
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland, United Kingdom

abstract: In situ Rb–Sr geochronology is an efficient approach that preserves the spatial and textural context of the analyzed material while avoiding many of the challenges associated with solution-based techniques. However, the contrasting volatilities of Rb and Sr produce downhole fractionation, which compromises the reproducibility and accuracy of dates obtained using laser-based applications. Here, we investigate the effects of ablation conditions and sample matrices on downhole fractionation by analyzing eighteen micas (Fe-biotite, phlogopite, muscovite, phengite, and lepidolite) and seven reference materials (nanopellet pressed powder pellet MicaMg, NIST SRM610, BCR-2G, and new phlogopite glasses) across a broad range of ablation conditions. The tested ablation conditions included varying repetition rates (5–15 Hz), laser fluences (2–5 J cm⁻²), spot diameters (30–125 µm), and spot geometries (circles and rectangles). Fractionation trends of all measurements were compared by normalizing each ablation signal to its stable plateau, allowing all measurements to be plotted on the same scale. Although absolute downhole fractionation patterns are influenced by laboratory-specific factors, our systematic comparison of ablation parameters allows us to determine the ablation conditions that minimize the magnitude of downhole fractionation. We observe a strong matrix dependence on downhole fractionation, with distinct patterns occurring even between specimens of the same mica type. Such specimen-level variability limits the applicability of model-based corrections. We therefore recommend a strategic selection of ablation conditions to minimize the extent of downhole fractionation, together with specimen-specific trimming of ablation signals during data processing. Although incomplete exclusion of the fractionated interval during signal trimming at first appears to have only a limited impact on direct isochron dating, we demonstrate examples in which its effects become substantially greater. Overall, these recommendations provide a practical approach that can be adopted across laboratories to minimize the influence of downhole fractionation while accounting for specimen-specific factors such as grain size and variability in Rb/Sr ratios.

title: Terrane translation in the northern North American Cordillera: North to Alaska
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond

affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Union College, Schenectady, NY, USA
abstract: There is overwhelming evidence that outboard terranes in the northern NAM Cordillera have experienced hundreds to thousands of kilometers of northward translation. Many of these displaced terranes have ended up in the Pacific Northwest and Alaska. The N-S orientation of the Cordillera means that some temperature-dependent fossils and also paleomagnetism can be used to evaluate latitudinal variation. Geologic piercing points along the margin - mainly established by detailed provenance studies - also allow reconstruction of displaced terranes. Since the Cretaceous, offshore plate motions have had a northward component of motion, and thus partial or full plate coupling has resulted in dextral motion along a myriad of strike-slip faults. The Chugach and Yakutat terranes occur outboard of Wrangellia ( s. lato ), and they provide information about the history of accretion and translation. The Chugach and Prince William (CPW) terranes are traditionally viewed as a composite terrane (CPW) that was an accretionary complex to Wrangellia. For decades, the site of deposition and translation history has been both complicated and controversial. Zircon provenance provides a key to understanding the original source and translation history. The CPW, as defined in the literature, contains several tectonostratigraphic units: 1) McHugh Complex (mid K and older); and 2) Valdez and equivalents that are mainly Campanian to Paleocene (also Shumagin, Kodiak, and Sitka); 3) Orca and equivalents include Paleocene-Eocene turbidites and mafic volcanics of the Prince William terrane. Yakutat rocks have a different provenance and are likely tied to the southern end of the Wrangellia block. Several observations concerning correlation of units and overall provenance emerge from detrital zircon data: 1) the source was a volcanic arc built on a metaplutonic complex; and 2) Orca-like clastic rocks contain significant material recycled from the underlying Valdez-like rocks. Older Chugach clastic units (mid K) have an alliance and stratigraphic tie with WR/AX/PN (Wrangellia superterrane). Valdez-like rocks (Camp-Maas) are dominated by grain ages of 71-73 Ma, that are slightly radiogenic (but positive eHf), which rules out the Coast Plutonic Complex and Idaho Batholith as a source. The Sierra Madre Occidental in Mexico is a candidate source terrane for the voluminous sediment in the Valdez. This provenance tie would suggest sediment and/or tectonic transport of >3000 km.

abstract: It has been five years since Colorado passed a landmark initiative to support post-fire hydrologic hazard identification and mitigation planning efforts – all before wildfires occur . Since then, over 25 Wildfire Ready Action Plans (WRAPs) have been or are currently being developed to better understand post-fire hydrologic, flood, hillslope erosion, debris flow, and fluvial hazards in some of Colorado’s riskiest watersheds. Wright Water Engineers, Inc. is a member of the state’s technical assistance team for their Wildfire Ready Watersheds program, and we are also a technical lead on several ongoing WRAPs around the state. Building on information presented during previous Geological Society of America conferences, we will use our platform and experiences to provide an update on recent program developments, the evolution of how susceptibility characterization and hazard mitigation are being approached from the watershed to point-of-impact scales, and how the final project identification and implementation phase of a WRAP is being addressed. Concepts will be illustrated with case studies from the Upper Cache la Poudre, Roaring Fork, and Grand Mesa WRAPs.

title: Accuracy and Precision of Groundwater Temperature Data Illustrated with Aquifer Geothermal Gradients
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Haygood, Lauren [1], Martinez, Mason [2], Halihan, Todd [3]
affiliations: (1) The Oka' Institute, Ada, OK, USA
(2) The Oka' Institute, Ada, OK, USA
(3) Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK, USA
abstract: Temperature is a widely collected data in environmental systems, providing insight into chemical and physical processes such as evaluation of geothermal gradients. The tools to measure temperature vary in groundwater systems from small transducers, handheld probes on reels and well logging tools. In karst aquifer systems, thermal gradients are often highly heterogeneous, making them difficult to resolve accurately. This study evaluates the accuracy and precision of field temperature data and quality assurance protocols to obtain reasonable field thermal data. Aquifer geothermal gradients were measured in a research well field in Oklahoma using multiple environmental temperature measurement methods. These included pressure temperature transducers, a temperature level conductivity (TLC) meter on a reel, and a well logging tool in an aquifer with unusual previous thermal datasets. All instruments were calibrated using a high-precision platinum resistance thermometer to reduce systematic bias. Results indicate that calibration significantly improves inter-instrument agreement and directly influences calibrated temperatures. An inverted geothermal gradient was consistently observed within the Arbuckle-Simpson Aquifer. These findings demonstrate that interpretation of temperature data is strongly dependent on measurement accuracy, while gradient data estimates are strongly dependent on precision. The well logging tool provided the most reliable resolution of temperatures and vertical gradients, while transducers exhibit lower accuracy despite capturing temporal variability.

abstract:
We report new work in progress on an enigmatic NW-trending Ediacaran to Ordovician intraplate igneous province extending across parts of southern Colorado. These rocks include several large intrusive complexes and numerous diabase, trachyte, phonolite, carbonatite and lamprophyre dikes. In the Wet Mountains in south-central Colorado, CA-ID-TIMS dating of zircon from samples of quartz syenite in the Democrat Creek complex has yielded 206 Pb/ 238 U ages of 514.83 ± 0.20 Ma and 515.92 ± 0.018 Ma. Syenite within the McClure Mountain complex yields a 206 Pb/ 238 U age of 523.436 ± 0.056 Ma, consistent with a published ID-TIMS zircon age of ~524 Ma for the same unit. These data establish the Wet Mountains as an important region of intraplate magmatism in this time frame. A nepheline syenite further west within the Powderhorn carbonatite-alkaline complex yielded normally discordant U-Pb systematics in CA-ID-TIMS dated grains, consistent with modern Pb loss, resulting in a 207 Pb/ 206 Pb age of 584.82 ± 1.22 Ma. This age is older than a previously reported U-Pb perovskite age for the carbonatite of ~573 Ma.

A prominent NW-trending tholeiitic to alkaline diabase dike swarm that contains over 100 dikes and postdates most of the other igneous rocks in the province extends from Unaweep Canyon near the Utah border to the Wet Mountains. 25 dike samples plot in fields for within-plate tholeiitic to alkalic mafic rocks in standard discrimination diagrams and generally show E-MORB type REE patterns. A diabase dike in the Powderhorn region has yielded a preliminary CA-ID-TIMS zircon date of ~537 Ma.

The available data support a model in which alkaline and carbonatitic magmatism in Colorado was focused along a NW-trending zone of lithospheric weakness, along which the diabase dike swarm also was emplaced. Previous workers have postulated that the Colorado intraplate province is linked to voluminous 539-528 Ma intraplate magmatism in the Southern Oklahoma aulacogen to the southeast, although further work in Colorado is needed to verify this hypothesis. The aulacogen also contains a widespread NW-trending diabase dike swarm geochemically similar to the Colorado diabases. In the "LIP printing diagram" of Pearce et al. (2021), diabase dike samples from both regions plot primarily in fields for a plume-dominated source, suggesting involvement of a mantle plume in production of these intraplate magmas.

title: Upper-crustal heat and active faults control meteoric geothermal circulation across the Himalaya–Tibet orogen
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse
authors: Craig, Jason W. [1], Klemperer, Simon L. [2], Crossey, Laura J. [3], Karlstrom, Karl E. [4], Winn, Carmen [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Scienes, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA

abstract:
Geothermal activity is widespread across the Himalaya-Tibet orogen, but the relative roles of active faulting, crustal heat, topography, magmatism, and mantle-derived fluids remain debated. We integrate temperatures, major-ion chemistry, stable isotopes (δ 18 O-δD), helium isotopes ( 3 He/ 4 He), and Quaternary fault mapping from 214 thermal springs to evaluate the sources and pathways of hydrothermal circulation.

Stable-isotope compositions cluster near the Tibetan local meteoric water line, indicating that meteoric recharge dominates the hydrothermal fluid budget, with little evidence for direct interaction with shallow magma. Helium isotopes define a regional transition from predominantly crustal signatures in southern Tibet to increasing mantle-derived helium in northern Tibet. However, 3 He/ 4 He ratios show no correlation with spring temperatures or reservoir-temperature estimates, indicating that mantle volatile input does not directly predict geothermal-system temperature.

Instead, active faults exert the principal control on hydrothermal circulation. Quaternary fault systems control at least 57% of the studied springs, and fault-controlled springs average 11°C hotter than springs without confirmed fault control. Fault-controlled sites dominate the hottest spring population, including many of the 35 systems with reservoir-temperature estimates above 120°C. High-temperature systems preferentially occur at localized extensional and transtensional fault geometries, including fault terminations, releasing bends, pull-apart basins, and displacement-transfer zones.

Southern Tibet contains the greatest density of high-temperature springs despite predominantly crustal helium and colder underlying Indian lithosphere. We attribute this pattern to elevated upper-crustal geothermal gradients, while Quaternary dilatational faults provide permeability for meteoric fluids to circulate through approximately 5-10 km of upper crust. These results show that structurally focused exploration strategies developed in extensional provinces also apply to geothermal systems within active continental collision zones.

title: Integration of apatite and titanite petrochronology to understand fertility on copper–forming magmas in Sonora, Mexico

authors: Ramos Galarza, Santiago Ismael [1], Enwia, Eshmael O. [2], Hernandez Uribe, David [3], Valencia-Moreno, Martin [4], Tassara, Santiago [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL,

(5) Department of Structural and Geotechnical Engineering, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Santiago, Chile
abstract:
Porphyry copper deposits (PCD) are the main source of copper in the world. The fertility of PCD-forming magmas is sensitive to their magmatic evolution. Accessory minerals serve as recorders of the magma composition evolution. In this study, we integrate trace-element and U-Pb geochronology from apatite and titanite to explore the conditions that drive magmatic fertility in the Sonoran porphyry belt in northern Mexico.

Apatite’s trace-element patterns exhibit light REE enrichment in barren granitoids, with high La/Sm and Sr/Y ratios, whereas ore-related porphyries display lower Eu/Eu*. By contrast, apatite’s heavy REE show lower concentrations in these samples.

Titanite displays a primary trend of light REE enrichment alongside heavy REE depletion, accompanied by negative Eu/Eu*. However, significant trace-element variations occur across different sample locations, including samples with light REE depletion, as well as samples with high La/Sm and Sr/Y ratios coupled with strongly positive Eu anomalies.

U-Pb geochronology in apatite yields c. 55 to 71 Ma, while titanite yields c.96–107 Ma and c.62–74 Ma. This indicates that apatite likely grew after the first titanite formation event but is broadly coeval with the second titanite growth event.

Our preliminary results show that apatite and titanite capture the variability in magma evolution, different stages of crystallization, and may serve as fertility proxies. Our study has implications for reducing exploration risk in Sonoran PCD systems.

title: The Indigenous Science Toolbox: Using the Medicine Wheel to Teach Geoscience Through Two-Eyed Seeing
session_title: Geoscience Education (Posters)
authors: Leonard-Pingel, Jill [1], Castillo, Rene [2], Lucas, Madeleine [3], Saup, Casey Morrisroe [4]
affiliations: (1) Ohio State University, Newark, OH,
(2) School of Earth Sciences, Ohio State University, Columbus, OH,
(3) Washington Sea Grant, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(4) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH,
abstract:
Indigenous scientists remain significantly underrepresented within the geosciences, a gap that stems in large part from a curriculum built entirely around Western scientific epistemology. Historically, there has been little room for alternative ways of understanding and knowledge systems in Earth Science classrooms. Here, we present the Indigenous Science Toolbox (IST), a K-12 curriculum grounded in Etuaptmumk, “two-eyed seeing,” which teaches Westernized and Indigenous scientific methods side-by-side rather than positioning one as a lens through which to interpret the other. The IST’s central organizing tool is the Medicine Wheel, which functions as a systems-thinking framework rather than a linear one. Its four directions (observation, connection, interpretation, and reflection) correspond to stages of the scientific method. Rather than moving students through these stages sequentially, the wheel requires them to hold multiple components of a system in view simultaneously and consider how those components interact. This structure opens investigation to more complex, less bounded questions than a linear method typically accommodates, and creates space for multiple contributors and multiple epistemologies to inform a single line of inquiry.

We developed and piloted the curriculum in partnership with the Quileute Nation at LA Push, Washington. The IST comprises two volumes: a foundational volume introducing the premise that Indigenous storytelling and scientific observation are not distinct enterprises, and a second volume applying the framework to tsunami physics, sediment stratigraphy, and coastal hazard mapping along the Cascadia Subduction Zone. This systems-based, two-eyed approach allows the IST to treat Indigenous knowledge as a constitutive framework for geoscience inquiry rather than a supplementary addition, with implications for broadening participation in the discipline and for how geoscience education more broadly might be restructured around non-linear, relational modes of inquiry.

title: Sexual dimorphism and reproductive mode in Middle Eocene Ostracoda from the U.S. Coastal Plain
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Citko, Jami [1], Hunt, Gene [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Department of Paleobiology, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC,
abstract: The means by which organisms reproduce is fundamental to their biology, but it is seldom inferable from their fossilized remains. Cytheroid ostracodes offer a rare exception to this limitation. Sexual dimorphism of the mineralized carapace presents as differences in shape and size between males and females; usually, males have a more-elongate carapace. By digitizing the outlines of ostracode carapaces, we not only can differentiate males from females but also can determine sex ratios, which can reveal the existence of asexual populations if no males are present. Here we present the results of a broad-scale examination of sexual dimorphism and sex ratios for Middle Eocene (Claibornian regional stage) cytheroid ostracodes from the U.S. Coastal Plain. From this fauna, we collected dimorphism and sex ratio data from over 100 populations representing more than 75 species and 30 genera. Sexual populations were compared to similar published data from earlier intervals (Late Cretaceous, early Paleocene) and younger Late Eocene faunas. Overall, Paleogene dimorphism is generally lower than that of the Cretaceous, with notably fewer species with dimorphism indicative of very high male investment in reproduction. In addition, we document four species that have female-only, presumably asexual populations. This incidence of asexuality is similar to that of other time periods in this region, and to the living cytheroid fauna found around the United Kingdom today. These results contribute to a greater understanding of the evolutionary history of ostracodes as well as the ways reproductive mode and sexual dimorphism evolve across marine taxa.

title: Mineralogy, Crystal Chemistry, and Surface Properties of Pure Cookeite: A Reference-Quality Multi-Technique Characterization of a Lithium-Bearing Di-Trioctahedral Chlorite

authors: Oladele, Segun Olabanji [1], Kumar, Ashish R [2], Ogunmodimu, Olumide Samuel [3]
affiliations: (1) John and Willie Leone Family Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
(2) John and Willie Leone Family Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) John and Willie Leone Family Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
abstract: Cookeite, a lithium-bearing di-trioctahedral chlorite-group mineral, has long resisted precise crystal-chemical characterization due to the scarcity of pure, well-crystallized specimens and the compositional variability introduced by its diverse formation modes. This study presents a reference-quality, multi-technique characterization of pure cookeite from the Golconda pegmatite (Minas Gerais, Brazil), integrating powder XRD, SEM, TEM-SAED, STEM-EDS, ICP-AES, FTIR spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, TGA-DTG, and BET surface area analysis on a single specimen of confirmed mineralogical purity. Rietveld refinement of the PXRD pattern reveals the co-existence of one-layer Ia and two-layer IIb monoclinic polytypes, attributed to local fluctuations in fluid chemistry and temperature during pegmatitic crystallization. SEM imaging documents well-preserved platy morphologies with individual plates of 1-5 µm lateral dimension, while TEM-SAED confirms long-range structural coherence and the absence of mechanical amorphization at the nanoscale, with a pseudo-hexagonal [001] zone-axis pattern reflecting the near-hexagonal behavior of the cookeite unit cell. ICP-AES establishes a precise structural formula dominated by Al 2 O 3 (50.97 wt%), SiO 2 (41.21 wt%), Li 2 O (4.37 wt%), and B 2 O 3 (1.42 wt%), with a near-complete Si occupancy of the tetrahedral sheet reflecting an evolved, boron-enriched pegmatitic environment. STEM-EDS, FTIR, TGA-DTG, and structural formula analysis together provide four convergent, independent lines of evidence for minor F-for-OH substitution (~0.021 apfu), among the more rigorous multi-technique demonstrations of this crystal-chemical feature reported for cookeite to date. FTIR and Raman spectroscopy yield diagnostic vibrational fingerprints, including a δ(Al–OH) bending band at 792 cm -1 that distinguishes cookeite from trioctahedral chlorites such as clinochlore and chamosite, and a T–O–T breathing mode at 445 cm -1 . TGA-DTG identifies a two-stage dehydroxylation pathway, centered at 575.71°C with a subsequent exothermic recrystallization pulse, and a total mass loss substantially below the theoretical hydroxyl content of ideal cookeite, consistent with the confirmed F substitution. BET analysis provides the first reported surface area for cookeite (2.71 ± 0.02 m 2 g -1 ), a low value consistent with its coarse platy morphology and indicative of a relatively refractory gangue phase during hydrometallurgical processing of spodumene-bearing pegmatite ores. Together, these results establish a comprehensive mineralogical and crystal-chemical reference for well-crystallized cookeite, resolving longstanding identification ambiguities and providing a quantitative fingerprint that distinguishes cookeite from closely related chlorite-group minerals, with direct relevance to lithium resource evaluation, mineral processing, and exploration workflows targeting critical minerals.

title: Sediment Provenance of the Lower Cretaceous Colville Foreland Basin, Arctic Alaska, Exhibits Widespread Distribution of Permian to Jurassic Detrital Zircon U-Pb Age Populations
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada
authors: Gooley, Jared T. [1], Lease, Richard Oliver [2], Connors, Christopher D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Alaska Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA
(2) Alaska Science Center, United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA
(3) Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA; United States Geological Survey, Reston, VA, USA
abstract: The ancestral Brooks Range orogeny and Colville foreland basin of northern Alaska are the product of a Late Jurassic–Early Cretaceous collision of the Angayucham terrane and Jurassic Koyukuk arc with the Arctic Alaska-Chukotka microcontinent. The earliest stratigraphic record of the collision consists of a diverse assembly of deep-water rocks (Okpikruak Fm.) deposited on top of progressively emplaced allochthons. Previous petrographic studies documented disparate transverse sediment sources for these units. However, Moore et al. (2015) investigated foreland strata in the western Brooks Range and inferred that Jurassic detrital zircon U-Pb (DZ) ages in higher allochthons were sourced from the Angayucham terrane but more common Permian–Triassic DZ ages were recycled from Triassic clastic strata of Chukotka and the Herald Arch. We present new DZ data for ten Okpikruak Fm. samples from the central Brooks Range foothills and three samples from klippen of similar Lower Cretaceous rocks in the eastern Brooks Range to further interpret sediment transport into the early foreland. Results show that age populations found in western samples persist eastward for another ~700 km, but abundances are variable with Permian–Triassic ages being the most widely consistent. These latter ages are not recognized within older allochthonous or coeval autochthonous rocks of Arctic Alaska. Additionally, DZ Lu-Hf analyses of a subset of samples yield juvenile εHf (+8 to +15) for Jurassic zircon, which we attribute to an Angayucham source, whereas Permian–Triassic zircons have a much wider range of evolved εHf (-30 to +12). A recycled Russian source of Permian–Triassic DZ to the northeast Brooks Range would require either >1000 km of longitudinal transport or, more likely, multistage eastward sediment recycling during allochthon emplacement. The latter is consistent with intermingled proximal petrofacies, clasts, and olistoliths derived from the Brooks Range allochthons. Alternatively, more proximal but cryptic Permian-Triassic DZ sources may be required. Possible sources could include Chukotka-equivalent Triassic clastic strata that extended to the northern Angayucham ocean, or a hypothesized Permian–Triassic arc that were accreted in the Jurassic to Early Cretaceous and fully exhumed during mid-Cretaceous extension of the orogen. Further study of isolated and enigmatic Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous rocks exposed in the southeastern Brooks Range may offer additional insights into the early evolution of the basin.

authors: Semken, Steven [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract:
Geologic processes operating through deep time have endowed some regions, the U.S. state of Arizona for example, with abundant scenic and storied geoheritage places as well as significant deposits of economically valuable minerals. In these regions there is typically sociopolitical tension between (a) preservation of geoheritage places for environmental and cultural sustainability, tourism, and recreation; and (b) mineral exploration and mining to obtain materials essential to modern society. However, these divergent interests sometimes converge in mining districts and communities (such as Jerome and Bisbee in Arizona) become attractive as artistic and touristic places owing to their history, architecture, and landscapes. In these places people may become interested in mining after the fact, but may fail to fully appreciate that these places owe their existence and at least some of their appeal to mining, and ultimately to the geologic origin of the mineral deposits.

As a longtime teacher and public interpreter of geoscience, I have observed and appreciated the boundless curiosity learners have about the processes and time intervals recorded in landscapes, rocks, minerals, and fossils. Education and interpretation of geoheritage in regions where mineral deposits are part and parcel of the storied geology—whether they are being or have been mined, or not—should include explanations of their origin and configuration. Learners, especially the public, should be helped to better understand how the same processes that formed the landscapes they value also dictated where mineral resources occur—sometimes in the same places. Further, some active mining districts should be designated as geoheritage places alongside former mining districts. Mining companies can contribute through increased public engagement at their sites. Whether or not this affects public attitudes toward mining, it will at least improve public understanding of mineral exploration, mining, and post-mining reclamation.

title: Carbonates through time, through time: A database of published carbonate U-Pb ages from the last decade and beyond
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: Cantine, Marjorie [1], Kainz, Sabrina Josephine [2], Gerdes, Axel [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(2) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(3) Goethe-Universitaet Frankfurt, Frankfurt am Main, Hessen,
abstract:
Over the past decade, in-situ uranium-lead (U-Pb) geochronology using laser ablation ICP-MS has become widespread, thanks to this technique’s high throughput and the abundance of carbonates in settings of geological interest. Major applications of this technique include dating brittle deformation, sedimentation and diagenesis, ore deposits, and speleothems. Interpretation of U-Pb carbonate data can be difficult because carbonates are typically low uranium, high common lead-bearing minerals that may exhibit complex open-system behavior. Water-rock interaction and alteration can mobilize U and Pb, mixing or partially resetting the U-Pb system, obscuring primary age information, and making it difficult to distinguish geologically meaningful dates from errorchrons. Here, we present a database spanning more than 2,000 U-Pb dates to understand trends in published carbonate U-Pb dates and to improve understanding of accuracy in carbonate U-Pb studies.

We compare records of seawater chemistry and carbonate petrography with the U-Pb carbonate record to explore primary controls on the reliability and accuracy of the carbonate geochronometer. Records of brittle deformation are pooled regionally to explore spatial trends in the timing of faulting. We also compare the volume and spatial extent of carbonates at Earth’s surface to the spatial extent of published U-Pb carbonate data to identify constraints and opportunities. We investigate some of the “impossible dates” that have been generated by U-Pb geochronology and consider both geological and analytical explanations. Finally, we explore modeling tools for detecting age mixing and errorchrons. Given the complexity of carbonates, we see a need for a set of tests for assessing the reliability and reproducibility of carbonate U-Pb data, and we make suggestions about what those questions could be.

abstract: Expanded excavations at White Sands National Park, located in the Tularosa Basin of south-central New Mexico, have unearthed 20 stratigraphic horizons containing in situ human footprints, megafaunal trackways, and linear features created by travois. Innovative radiocarbon dating of conifer pollen, combined with ages of aquatic seeds, refines the chronology of the footprint-bearing sequence to between 23.5 and 21.7 ka, and allows for the development of highly resolved paleoenvironmental and paleoclimatic records in a terrestrial setting. Multiple proxies, including biomarkers (leaf waxes and GDGTs), pollen and ostracode assemblages, mineralogy, and sedimentological evidence, were used to elucidate climate and environmental changes on local, extralocal, and regional spatial scales. Hydrogen isotopes of leaf waxes show a close correspondence between rainfall isotopes in New Mexico and the Greenland ice core, further solidifying the temporal placement of the White Sands footprint sequences and demonstrating that the hydroclimate at White Sands responded strongly to abrupt millennial-scale climate changes. Together, the proxy data indicate a complete overturning of the environment from a perennial lake to a playa and capture a large aridification episode coincident with Dansgaard-Oeschger event 2 at 23.2 ka, which shrank pluvial Lake Otero and allowed people to traverse the former shoreline area for nearly two millennia. This well-dated and highly resolved paleoclimate record provides compelling evidence that humans in North America experienced dramatic environmental changes during the Last Glacial Maximum.

title: Remote Sensing Detection of Produced Water from Oil and Gas Well Leaks and Ghost Lakes in the Permian Basin
session_title: From Abandonment to Opportunity: Identifying, Monitoring, Mitigating, and Repurposing Oil and Gas Wells
authors: Stengel, Victoria Grace [1], Wallace, David Sam [2]
affiliations: (1) USGS, USGS Geology, Energy & Minerals Science Center, Austin, TX, USA
(2) USGS, USGS Oklahoma-Texas Water Science Center, Fort Worth, TX, USA
abstract:
Pore pressure increases from wastewater disposal during oil and gas development (i.e., produced water) is associated with earthquakes and complex surface uplift and subsidence across the Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico. Pore pressure increases can weaken the integrity of plugged wells to the point of leaking. When these leaking wells are not remediated, they can grow into what are known as ‘ghost lakes.’ For instance, Lake Boehmer, north of Fort Stockton, TX, started leaking in the 1990s and is now a ~60-acre lake. Constituents of produced water, including high levels of dissolved salts, heavy metals, and radioactive materials, are associated with significant negative human and environmental health impacts. Leaking wells may also emit hydrogen sulfide gas, which can be fatal to flora and fauna even at low concentrations.

Advancements in remote sensing mapping capabilities can help detect and differentiate oil and gas produced water morphological features. Conventional random forest machine learning classification, applied to Google Earth Engine artificial intelligence-trained embeddings data, delivers novel and highly accurate (+90%) rapid mapping of oil and gas pads at the regional scale. Analysis of Landsat, Sentinel-2, and Planet satellite image collections allows for high-temporal-frequency earth observation monitoring across multiple decades. When multispectral water detection indices are applied to these image collections, ephemeral produced water well leaks and growing ghost lakes can be revealed. The aim of this approach is to establish a regional-scale remote sensing framework for detection and monitoring of well leaks from produced water in the remote Permian Basin region that could support future water quality research and aid stakeholders in situational awareness, inventory, and the development of environmental health mitigation strategies.

abstract: This project evaluates the nitrate removal efficiency of bentonite clays sourced from two geologically distinct U.S. regions: the Upper Cretaceous Tombigbee Sand Formation of Mississippi and the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming. The goal is to determine how regional mineralogical differences influence adsorption performance. Each clay sample was tested in its natural state and after thermal activation at 400°C and 700°C to assess how heat treatment altered surface area, porosity, and the availability of adsorption sites. Batch experiments were conducted using a controlled 150 ppm nitrate solution prepared by dissolving 0.20 g of sodium nitrate (NaNO₃) in 1.0 L of water, allowing for direct comparison of nitrate uptake across clay types and treatment conditions. Nitrate concentrations before and after treatment were measured using a Vis spectrophotometer, with nitrate test strips used as a secondary method to verify results and provide rapid, comparative readings. SEM and EDS analyses will be used to document compositional and textural changes associated with thermal activation. By integrating adsorption measurements with mineralogical characterization, this study aims to identify a low-cost, scalable bentonite material capable of reducing nitrate pollution before it enters major waterways. The results will support broader efforts to mitigate nutrient-driven hypoxia in the Gulf of Mexico and contribute to the development of practical remediation strategies for agricultural regions.

title: An Empirical Lower Bound on the Duration of Wet-Based Ice for the Sturtian Snowball Earth
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records (Posters)
authors: McDannell, Kalin T. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
abstract: Snowball Earth glaciations are among the most significant climate perturbations in Earth history, yet how dynamic and erosive the ice sheets were remains contested. The Sturtian snowball Earth (c. 717 to c. 660 Ma) was the longer and more severe of the two Cryogenian (720–635 Ma) glaciations. A persistent view holds that snowball ice sheets were frozen to their beds and minimally erosive, based on low Cryogenian sediment accumulation rates, the preservation of Neoproterozoic basin strata, and low apparent erosion rates in surviving rock sections. Initial models envisioned globally stagnant, cold-based ice sheets, yet geological observations and climate modeling over recent decades instead suggest dynamic, wet-based ice potentially capable of substantial erosion and sediment transport, though its nature and duration remain poorly constrained. We show that the cold-based inference is fundamentally biased, since localities that preserve a measurable record are precisely those where erosion was limited, meaning the most erosive, wet-based settings are systematically absent from the geologic record. Using an orbitally paced statistical model calibrated against published ice-sheet erosion rates, an empirical lower bound on the duration of wet-based glaciation is derived for the Sturtian between ~1.5% to ~4.3% (95% credible interval) of the total c. 56 Myr icehouse, suggesting at least ~0.8 to ~2.4 Myr of glacial dynamism. If the Sturtian were instead characterized by cyclical fluctuations between icehouse and greenhouse conditions, as recently proposed by Minsky et al. (2026; ﻿doi: 10.1073/pnas.2525919123), the proportion of time that ice sheets were wet based is expected to be higher by more than an order of magnitude. Even at the lower-bound duration, comparison with glacial erosion rate data averaged across 10 -2 -to-10 9 -year timescales suggests globally widespread kilometer-scale erosion is plausible during snowball Earth.

title: Development of an AI-Based Grain Size Analysis Method and its Application in a Fluvial Confluence Setting
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era (Posters)
authors: Powers, Nolan [1], Grothe, Pamela [2], Kisila, Odhiambo [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, Universtiy of Mary Washington, Fredericksburg, VA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, University of Mary Washington, Fredericksburg, VA, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, University of Mary Washington, Fredericksburg, VA, USA
abstract: Grain characteristics of clastic sediments are important for understanding paleoenvironments and hydrodynamic conditions of sedimentary deposits, as well as more practical applications such as engineering, coastal management, and pollution monitoring. Traditional methods of sedimentary grain characteristics require either expensive microscopy instrumentation or time-consuming manual sieving and grain tracing. Alternatively, advances in AI-based machine learning algorithms provide an opportunity to analyze large numbers of samples of sedimentary grain characteristics more efficiently at low cost. Here, we present a simple AI grain characteristic analysis method using a machine learning algorithm that can be downloaded and used on any computer for processing. First, images from fluvial sediments that are mostly pebble to very fine sand grain sizes are manually photographed using a light microscope and then automatically analyzed using an algorithm that traces the grain boundaries, producing polygons of each grain. The grain polygons are then analyzed in ImageJ to calculate shape parameters: area, perimeter, circularity, roundness, feret diameter, and major and minor axis. A typical sample would consist of 50 different images and approximately 3000 grains and can be analyzed in seconds. To test the validity of our AI-based grain characteristics method, we compare the results from five sediment samples of varying maturity from fluvial, estuarine, and beach environments with both traditional sieving and grain tracing methods as well as with a particle analysis instrument, the Morphologi G3. The AI-based method yielded grain characteristic measurements that showed differences greater than 5% from the manual tracing method in all five samples averaging around 10% difference. These results suggest the need for post-processing of the images before calculating the grain characteristics. Comparison with the Morphologi G3 particle analysis is still pending but will help refine the next steps to improve the AI-based grain characteristic results. To illustrate the potential utility of this application, we analyzed 86 samples from a river confluence on the Rappahannock and Rapidan Rivers in Virginia and show that the program processed over 4,000 images and 325,000 grains in less than 30 minutes of computer processing, providing over 1000% more individual grain analyses than the manual tracing method.

title: Evidence of Impact Melting in Ungrouped Iron Meteorites
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System
authors: Corrigan, Catherine [1], Andrews, Ben [2]
affiliations: (1) Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Washington, DC, USA
abstract:
Of the ~1250 recognized iron meteorites, ~10% are compositionally distinct, termed “ungrouped”. Iron meteorite impact melts are exceptionally rare, despite the fact that their parent bodies, exposed cores of larger differentiated protoasteroids, must have experienced a violent impact history. Notable among iron meteorites exhibiting impact melt features are Nedagolla and Tucson. A number of iron meteorites contain anomalously low volatile siderophile element concentrations attributed to impact devolatilization. Three-dimensional (3D) μXCT study of iron sulfide (troilite) inclusions in ungrouped irons N’Goureyma and Dronino suggest formation by diapiric rise of troilite through (partially?) molten metal after impact melting.

Compositional and textural analyses of Dronino and N’Goureyma were conducted at the Smithsonian Institution using the Nova NanoSEM for backscattered electron imaging, the JEOL 8530F+ electron microprobe and the GE Phoenix Dual Tube µXCT. Two pieces of Dronino (USNM 7203b) and one piece of N’Goureyma (USNM 559a) were analyzed.

Texturally, the inclusions strongly resemble diapirs formed when a buoyant liquid ascends through a denser material. The relative densities of troilite (~4.6 g/cm 3 ) and metal (~7.6 g/cm 3 ) are consistent with such an interpretation. The most plausible scenario for the formation of these features is that molten troilite ascended through molten metal. The relatively short, long dimensions of these particles suggest limited ascent distances, as these tails elongate during ascent. We suggest melting and subsequent cooling occurred rapidly during impact melting, consistent with this inferred thermal history and explaining why such morphologies are rare among iron meteorites. If true, the implication of complete remelting and rapid solidification might explain the absence of a distinct Widmanstätten pattern. An interesting feature of these meteorites is the distinct morphologies of the troilite inclusions suggest that the initial size and shape of a sulfide bleb prior to ascent has a strong outcome on its eventual morphology. Inclusions starting as spherical would have formed the elongate occurrences with bulbous ends, and oblate inclusions would have formed tubes or curtains. After impact melting, but before ascent of troilite blebs, it would not be surprising to find both spherical and oblate shaped troilite blebs resulting from the dynamic nature of impact melting.

title: Bayesian Geographic Range Inference from Stable Isotopes of Giant Squid (Architeuthis dux) Statoliths
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Linzmeier, Benjamin John [1], Kitajima, Kouki [2], Bolstad, Kathrin [3], Landman, Neil H. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL,
(2) WiscSIMS Laboratory, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI,
(3) AUT Lab for Cephalopod Ecology and Systematics, Auckland University of Technology, Auckland, New Zealand
(4) American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY,
abstract:
Modern cephalopod statoliths (small incrementally precipitated carbonate archives) are analogous to fish otoliths and contain proxy archives of environmental conditions like temperature and biological conditions like metabolism. These carbonate archives in cephalopods are more commonly studied in contemporary fishery research, although not to the extent that fish otoliths have been.

Here we present the results of secondary ion mass spectrometry measurement of oxygen and carbon isotopes across five statoliths from modern giant squid ( Architeuthis dux ) collected near Aotearoa New Zealand. We find a plateau in δ 18 O values near -3‰ (VPDB) in the core of each statolith and then a monotonic shift to +2‰ with the highest values at the rim of the statolith. We observe uniform δ 13 C of -7‰ in the core of each statolith, increasing to +2‰ by the rim, which implies that metabolic rate decreases through ontogeny.

We constrain the geographic range of each A. dux individual using a Bayesian inversion model that combines oceanographic conditions (temperature, salinity, current velocity, and dissolved inorganic carbon) with organismal characteristics (hypothesised swimming speed, thermodynamic metabolic scaling). The model suggests that A. dux juveniles inhabit shallower, warmer water closer to the equator and then migrate deeper and farther South as they mature. Thermodynamic metabolic scaling and changing δ 13 C with depth also predict the observed carbon isotope patterns.

Our Bayesian approach to constraining geographic range can be applied to existing fossil datasets when combined with paleoclimate model outputs and could better constrain geographic range of individual cephalopods in deep time. Expansion of these methods could provide better insight into shell drift and the dynamics of endemism in environments like the Western Interior Seaway.

title: Conodonts and the Dynamic Stratigraphy of the Pennsylvanian (Missourian) Dog Bend Limestone, Palo Pinto County, Texas.

authors: Rosscoe, Steven J. [1], Bader, Jeremy D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Kimbell School of Geosciences, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA
(2) Department of Physical Science, Tarrant County College, Arlington, TX, USA
abstract: The Dog Bend Limestone Member of the lower Salesville Formation demonstrates the dynamic stratigraphy along the margins of the Perrin Delta System on the Eastern Shelf of the Permian Basin. The Dog Bend, at its most well-known exposure (TX-4) consists of a lower and upper limestone bed separated by 2.5 meters of fossiliferous shale. The TX-4 locality is furthest from the influence of deltaic sedimentation with only a thin sand below, in the position of the Lake Pinto Sandstone (the prior major advance of the Perrin Delta to the west). At the Mineral Wells Fossil Park (MWFP) locality, the upper limestone of the Dog Bend caps over 5 meters of fossiliferous shale. The lower limestone is not exposed. MWFP deposition occurred in a restricted bay between two lobes of the Perrin Delta. At the newly discovered Highway 337 locality (337), the lower Dog Bend is a 10-centimeter vuggy sandy limestone overlain by a 12-centimeter micrite of the upper Dog Bend. The two are separated by approximately 20 centimeters of covered material. The 337 locality sits on top of the Lake Pinto deposits of the previous deltaic advance. Idiognathodus species have proven helpful in correlating these three distinct localities with I. turbatus , I. heckeli , and I. eccentricus confirming the correlation of the lower portion of the Salesville Formation with the Hertha Cyclothem of the Midcontinent Basin. The limestone facies is characterized by Idiognathodus specimens of reduced size, Idioprioniodus , and Adetognathus . Adetognathus dominates the fauna of the upper Dog Bend at 337. At TX-4, Adetognathus is less common while Idioprioniodus , and Idiognathodus more common. At MWFP, conodonts are rare. The shale facies is characterized by a diverse Idiognathodus fauna with rare occurrences of the other genera. The shale facies fauna is much more uniform across the localities than is observed in the limestone facies. The conodont data has proven to be of great importance in correlating strata across these vastly different facies and provided evidence that, when incorporated with lithological and geophysical data, has provided great insight into the dynamic depositional system of the Perrin Delta.

authors: Byron, Benjamin [1], Emery, Joshua [2], Spencer, John [3], Hamilton, Victoria [4], Christensen, Philip [5], Lyster, Duncan [6], Howett, Carly [7], Bierhaus, Edward [8], Costello, Emily [9], Mottola, Stefano [10], Noll, Keith [11], Marchi, Simone [12], Levison, Hal [13]

abstract:
The NASA Lucy mission [1] encountered main-belt asteroid (52246) Donaldjohanson on April 20, 2025 [2] with the purpose of assessing spacecraft and instrument performance in advance of the upcoming Trojan asteroid flybys. In this work, we analyze surface radiance measurements of Donaldjohanson from the Lucy Thermal Emission Spectrometer (L'TES; [3]), which enable us to investigate regolith thermophysical properties and improve our understanding of the processes that have shaped its surface.

We use the Lucy-derived shape model and the TEMPEST thermophysical model [4] to simulate surface temperatures for Donaldjohanson during the flyby, assuming an albedo of 0.103 [5] and an emissivity of 0.95. We convert the model surface temperatures to spectral radiance and compare the model values with the L'TES-observed radiance over the course of the flyby. Several factors complicate efforts to model temperatures and derive thermal inertia for Donaldjohanson. First is its long rotation period (~252 hr) relative to the timeline of the L’TES flyby observations (554 s), which means that L’TES observed the sunlit surface in thermodynamic equilibrium. Second is its non-principal axis rotation (i.e., tumbling), which affects the periodicity in insolation. Accounting for these complications is ongoing work, and here we present preliminary models and attempt to place constraints on thermophysical properties.

Donaldjohanson is a C-type asteroid and a member of the Erigone collisional family [6]. Its intermediate size (~8.8 km long with a greater than 2:1 axis ratio) places it in a transition zone between smaller (< 1 km) asteroids, which generally exhibit higher (> 500 J m -2 s -0.5 K -1 ) thermal inertia, and larger (> 100 km) asteroids, which tend to have lower (< 50 J m -2 s -0.5 K -1 ) thermal inertia [7-9]. Because thermophysical properties are largely dependent on the particle size and porosity of the asteroid regolith, our results provide insight into regolith evolution processes (e.g., impact gardening, thermal cracking) and help place it in context with other asteroids. The methods we applied here will also support comparative analyses of future Lucy Trojan asteroid targets, improving our understanding of the diversity and evolution of primitive small-body surfaces.

title: The Power of Pyroxenes: Spectroscopic Clues to Planetary Thermal Evolution
session_title: Mineralogy in the Solar System
authors: Klima, Rachel L. [1]
affiliations: (1) Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD, USA
abstract: Pyroxene is one of the most abundant and spectrally distinctive minerals in the solar system. The chemical compositions of coexisting pyroxenes, measured in the laboratory, have been used for decades to characterize the phase equilibria of igneous systems, and for geothermometry. Detailed analyses of Mg-Fe 2+ ordering between crystallographic sites in a pyroxene provide further constraints on the cooling rates and history of pyroxene-bearing rocks. Transition metal-bearing pyroxenes exhibit characteristic spectral features at visible, near and shortwave infrared wavelengths, which vary based on chemical composition as well as site ordering. In the thermal infrared, pyroxenes, like other silicates, exhibit distinguishing vibrational features, which also vary in position and shape based on the cation composition. The distinctive spectral properties, coupled with the variety of cations that can be hosted within a pyroxene structure, make pyroxenes particularly powerful for remotely characterizing the geochemical properties and thermal history of asteroids and planets. This work reviews some of the discoveries that harnessing the power of pyroxene spectroscopy has enabled on the Moon, Mercury, and asteroids, and looks forward to upcoming missions that will provide new clues to the solar system evolution.

title: N-REFI: A Neural Receded-Flood Index for Reconstructing Post Flood Extent from Multisource Satellite Observations
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era (Posters)
authors: Sohail, Mohammad [1], Chu, Tianxing [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Computer science, Department of Computer Science, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
(2) Conrad Blucher Institute for Surveying and Science, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi,, TX, USA
abstract: Accurate flood mapping is essential for disaster management, yet available data sources have important limitations. SAR can operate through clouds but may be affected by urban surfaces, vegetation, rough water, and acquisition timing, while multispectral imagery is often unavailable during peak flooding and may only become cloud-free after substantial water recession. Consequently, conventional water indices can underestimate maximum inundation, whereas high-resolution aerial and UAV imagery remain costly, difficult to acquire, and spatially limited. To address these limitations, this study proposed the novel Neural Receded-Flood Index (N-REFI), a data-driven and interpretable framework designed to reconstruct flood extents from pre- and post-flood Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Multispectral Imaging imagery (MSI). N-REFI learns complementary flood-residual and background evidence from water and vegetation-sensitive spectral indices, including Normalized Difference Water Index, Modified Normalized Difference Water Index, Automated Water Extraction Index, Multi-Band Water Index, Normalized Difference Moisture Index, and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, together with terrain information derived from the U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program. Reference flood extents from the USGS and FEMA, together with high-resolution aerial imagery (NOAA) were used for model training, calibration, and validation. N-REFI was compared with NDWI thresholding, SAR backscatter thresholding, pre–post SAR change detection, and machine-learning models including SVM, RF, GBM, and XGBoost. The framework was trained and validated using Hurricane Harvey (2017) data from North Houston, Texas, and independently tested across flood events in Louisiana, Mississippi and Florida. N-REFI consistently achieved strong flood-reconstruction performance, outperforming both rule-based methods and conventional machine-learning models. Across the independent test locations, N-REFI achieved a maximum overall accuracy of 93%, an area under the AUC of 98%, and a MCC of 88%. The findings showed that N-REFI can reconstruct flood extent despite missing peak-flood SAR or optical imagery, substantial water recession, unavailable high-resolution aerial data, and persistent cloud cover.

title: North Cascades Cretaceous Arc Crust may have been Less Than 45 km Thick
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Kelemen, Peter Boushall [1], Murray, Joshua [2]
affiliations: (1) Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, 211 Comer Laboratory, Columbia University, Palisades, NY, USA
(2) Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, New York, USA
abstract:
The thickness of North Cascades Cretaceous arc crust may have been 60km [1-4]. Alternatively, it could have been <45km thick, as in all oceanic and continental arcs [5] except the Chilean Northern (54km [5]) and Central Volcanic Zones (65km [6]).

The North Cascades crystalline core (NCCC), metamorphosed at ≤40km [7], overlies ~30km of crust [8]. Post-Cretaceous magmatic underplating is probably limited [2]. However, forearc sediments were thrust into Cretaceous lower crust [9,10, 11,12]. Similarly, most rocks beneath the NCCC may have been underplated after peak metamorphism.

Liquid-like NCCC plutons emplaced at 25-35km depth record ~2x variation in incompatible elements [4], requiring a similar mass of hidden cumulates. If the plutons comprise 30% of the volume over 10km depth, hidden cumulates could form 10km thick roots directly beneath the plutons, or sills a few km thick over the entire area. Moreover, dense cumulates founder into underlying mantle during arc magmatism, limiting crustal thickness [13-16].

Trace elements indicate residual garnet in forming NCCC plutons. [1] as cited by [2] claimed this occurred at 1.8 GPa. However, [17] demonstrated garnet crystallization in hydrous, mafic arc magmas at 1.2 GPa, and many arc magmas include melts of subducting material with residual garnet [14].

title: Was hydrothermal circulation a source or a sink of phosphorus to the Archean biosphere?
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry
authors: Johnson, Benjamin William [1], Som, Sanjoy [2], Anderson, Rika [3], Stüeken, Eva [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmosphere, Climate, Iowa State University, Ames, IA, USA
(2) Blue Marble Space, c/o NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA,

abstract: Phosphorus is a critical nutrient, but is often limiting since it can only be delivered from geologic reservoirs. While continental weathering is important in modern sites, this source was likely less large in the Archean due to limited crustal emergence. Recent studies have suggested that hydrothermal circulation of seawater through oceanic crust may have released substantial P into the ocean during the Archean. Modern hydrothermal activity, though, is a sink for P. Further, at high temperatures during alteration apatite can form, potentially trapping P. To assess this possibility, we used the 3.24 Ga Panorama District volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) to constrain the behavior of P in a well preserved hydrothermal setting. Panorama preserves 5 distinct hydrothermal cells, with units that capture the full depth of these cells, spanning the paleoseafloor down several km to a granitic intrusion which provided heat to drive circulation. We find that P and K are anticorrelated, suggesting potassic alteration at relatively low temperatures. In contrast, P correlates with C, with P:Ca ratios matching the stoichiometry of fluorapatite in high-temperature zones. Yet, reactive transport modeling indicates that phosphite may be liberated during reaction with andesitic rocks, which are also found at Panorama. Our work indicates that there may be competing effects on P during circulation, and that P released may have been phosphite, rather than phosphate.

abstract: As micro- and nano-plastics accumulate in the open ocean, it is critical to assess the impact on organisms and the role that they play in modifying, degrading, and sequestering these pollutants. Spinose planktic foraminifera are a group of marine protists that are passive feeders who collect prey with their sticky rhizopodial network and are therefore likely to interact with microplastic particles in the open ocean. Because their dense shells sink rapidly out of the mixed layer, foraminifera also represent a significant flux of alkalinity and carbon out of the surface layer. Thus, their response to environmental perturbations, such as plastic pollution, may alter the ocean-atmosphere carbon system. Here, we investigated the potential for living planktic foraminifera to interact with and uptake microplastics into their cytoplasm and shell, as has been observed previously in reef-dwelling large benthic foraminifera. Individual Orbulina universa , Globigerinoides ruber , and Globigerinella siphonifera were collected from net tows off the coast of Bermuda and cultured in the laboratory with sustained exposure to 1-5 µm-sized fluorescent thermoset amino formaldehyde polymer plastic beads. Foraminifers rapidly interacted with the beads via cytoplasmic streaming and concentrated them close to the shell. Within 6 hours, microbeads had been taken inside the shell and into the cytoplasm, identified via light microscopy. The presence of microplastics inside the cytoplasm was confirmed using fluorescence microscopy. After transfer into clean culture jars, the foraminifers were observed to be free of microplastics in their spines, but plastics remained concentrated in the cytoplasm until gametogenesis. While foraminifers retained microplastics in their cytoplasm throughout their lives, this did not prevent them from feeding on Artemia nauplii. This indicates that microplastic ingestion does not lead to immediate death, and that foraminifers that ingest microplastics in the open ocean setting are likely to migrate to depth with microplastics as they complete their life cycle. We will discuss the potential impacts on carbon and alkalinity cycling of plastic ingestion, as well as the ultimate fate of plastics themselves.

abstract:
Trace metal distributions are frequently used for reconstructing environmental conditions, microbial activity, and geochemical processes in marine and terrestrial environments. Trace metal behavior in marine systems is often determined by the oxidation state of the system, authigenic mineral formation and dissolution, and microbial metabolisms that cycle trace metals between the dissolved and solid phases. These processes can impart diagnostic geochemical signatures in trace metal relationships, including isotopic compositions, concentration patterns, and speciation. In tectonically and volcanically active environments, however, non-traditional depositional pathways, diagenetic processes, and microbial metabolisms can dominate elemental behavior during deposition and burial, adding complexity to biogeochemical interpretations of sedimentary archives.

The Christiana-Santorini-Kolumbo Volcanic Field (CSKVF) is an active volcanic center located within the South Aegean Volcanic Arc. International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 398 drilled within the Santorini caldera and surrounding extensional basins aiming to characterize the formation and eruptive history of the CSKVF and impacts of volcanism on the deep biosphere. Initial porewater analyses of salinity, major cations and anions, and minor and trace elements revealed complex geochemical trends, and isotopic analyses of water isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H), sulfur isotopes (δ 34 S-SO 4 2- ), and strontium isotopes ( 87 Sr /86 Sr) reveal multiple diagenetic controls on porewater geochemistry.

Trace metals in the CSKVF exhibit similar non-traditional patterns and significant spatiotemporal variability. Within the Santorini caldera, sedimentary and porewater enrichments of trace metals including arsenic, mercury, and vanadium are correlated with hydrothermal and volcanic events. In the extensional basins outside the caldera, additional controls affect trace metal behavior, including water column low-oxygen episodes, subsurface fluid flow, microbial metabolisms, and authigenic mineral formation. By integrating porewater and solid phase major, minor, and trace element concentrations, isotopes, and elemental ratios, we reveal the primary and diagenetic effects of an active and evolving tectonic environment on geochemical records. Volcanic and hydrothermal events supply trace metals through primary depositional pathways, while subsurface fluid flow and mineral alteration affect trace metal supply and consumption during burial and diagenesis. Furthermore, biogeochemical cycling in the deep biosphere, supported by metabolic substrates resupplied by subsurface fluid flow, can result in geochemical overprinting of primary depositional signals but also record complex depositional, diagenetic, and metabolic regimes that affect trace metal distributions over space and time.

abstract: The Troy Bedrock Valley (TBV) in Boone County, Illinois is deeply incised and filled with glacio-fluvial sediments. Helicopter time-domain electromagnetic (HTEM) profiles were flown in 2025 to characterize the geology and variability within the regional sand and gravel aquifer system in the TBV. Ground-based time-domain electromagnetic (TEM), 2-D electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), and microtremor horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR) methods were used to assess HTEM interpretations of the shallow aquifer systems and bedrock geology. We specifically highlight the ability of ground-based TEM to supplement HTEM in semi-urbanized areas where HTEM data cannot be acquired due to regulatory and physical constraints. Supplementing gaps in HTEM data acquired in the TBV allows for an improved understanding of the aquifer geometry and water resources on a local and regional scale. In addition to ground-based geophysical data, water-well records were used to establish local geologic relationships. The use of multiple methods allows for more accurate interpretations of the bedrock and aquifers in the region. Importantly, we see that even sparse ground-based data within gaps of HTEM data can provide relevant information to extrapolate geologic interpretations across those gaps.

title: A Multidisciplinary Approach to Understanding the Seismic Structure of Arc Systems
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Delph, Jonathan [1]
affiliations: (1) Purdue University, Lafayette, IN,
abstract:
Seismic techniques are a common way to resolve where melt resides throughout the lithosphere in an active magmatic system. However, they often struggle to constrain the presence of magma at depths where geochemical and petrologic studies indicate magma storage and differentiation takes place, particularly below the "big red blobs" that characterize the shallow portion of the magmatic system. This is because 1) seismic arrays often lack the aperture and station density necessary to resolve the translithospheric system at the necessary resolution, and 2) we generally have a poor understanding of how seismic measurements relate to spatial distributions of melt.

In this study, we will explore how seismic properties can be related to rock composition and melt percentage, and how we can integrate geochemical observations and petrological characteristics from both active and extinct magmatic systems to better understand their architecture and evolution. To do this, we turn to the large, long-lived magmatic systems of the southern Altiplano and Puna Plateau, where existing geochemical and petrological data are abundant and seismic data are sufficient to image the entire translithospheric magmatic system. In addition, the tectonic history of the region allows for along-strike variations in the margin to be related to the evolution of a thermally-maturing silicic magmatic system. Our seismic results provide spatiotemporal insight into the evolution of a silicic magmatic system that can be reconciled with the geochemical trends and the petrological features of exposed arcs. This study provides a framework to investigate more typical (i.e., smaller) arc magmatic systems, which may require alternative imaging approaches to delineate the distribution of melt in the crust, and will allow us to move toward a more comprehensive multidisciplinary model of arc magmatic systems.

title: Evidence for Decompression and Melting in the Lowermost Crust of the Southern Basin and Range: Symplectites in Granulite Xenoliths from the Geronimo Volcanic Field, SE Arizona
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Kempton, Pamela D. [1], Rader, Mikaela [2], Hindall, Andrew G. [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS, USA
(2) Environmental Health & Safety, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(3) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS, USA
abstract:
Eocene-Oligocene rollback of the Farallon slab is inferred to be the driving mechanism for lithospheric extension of more than 50% across the southern Basin and Range [1]. Given that crustal thickness in the region today is ~28-30 km, thickness prior to extension could have been more than 50 to 60 km. At these depths, lower crustal mineral assemblages typically contain garnet. However, the lower crustal granulite xenolith suite from the Geronimo Volcanic Field (GVF), SE Arizona, consists primarily of two-pyroxene, two-feldspar metadiorites and an assortment of one- and two-pyroxene mafic metacumulates that contain plagioclase but no K-feldspar. Temperatures of equilibration range from 908 - 988°C based on two-pyroxene geothermometry, consistent with entrainment from the current base of the crust (~30km) assuming an average geotherm of 30 o C/km. This raises the question of whether the present-day lower crust was originally part of the middle crust, with the lowermost crust lost through delamination, or whether the lower crust underwent significant uplift, tectonic thinning, and decompression in response to Cenozoic lithospheric extension. New petrographic observations from gabbroic (cpx + plag + sp ± opx ± amph) metacumulate xenoliths from GVF preserve symplectite textures consistent with the latter interpretation. The symplectites are of two types. Spinel-pyroxene symplectites are petrographically similar to symplectites from other crustal xenolith localities worldwide and are interpreted as the product of garnet breakdown [e.g. 2]. A more unusual texture, which appears to be unique to GVF, consists of a rounded spinel core surrounded by concentric alternating bands of plagioclase and euhedral magnetite + ilmenite intergrowths, with clinopyroxene forming a discontinuous band around the outside of the alternating plagioclase – oxide bands. This texture also appears to be associated with pockets of in situ melting. The melting was not the result of infiltration by the host basalt, but rather an in situ process, likely facilitated by influx of metasomatic fluids prior to entrainment. While we cannot preclude a role for lithospheric delamination during formation of the southern Basin and Range, the GVF symplectites provide evidence for decompression of the lower crust from depths greater than those required for garnet stability in these rocks (>30km).
