(9) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(10) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA; Los Alamos National Lab, Los Alamos, NM, USA
abstract:
Understanding how composition, crystal chemistry, and chemical bonding control thermophysical properties under extreme conditions is a shared challenge across geoscience and materials science. These relationships help constrain phase behavior in planetary interiors and impact environments while also guiding the design of refractory materials. Zirconium carbonitride, Zr(C,N), adopts the rocksalt structure and forms a continuous solid solution between ZrC and ZrN, making it a useful model for linking these perspectives. Refractory-metal carbonitrides such as Zr(C,N) and Hf(C,N) have been reported or predicted to exhibit melting-temperature maxima at intermediate compositions, implying nonideal changes in bonding and phase stability. To test whether intermediate compositions exhibit enhanced lattice stiffness, we combined neutron diffraction, high-pressure–temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), high-temperature laboratory XRD, combustion analysis, and electron-probe microanalysis (EPMA) to evaluate compositional changes in lattice parameter, thermal expansion, and bulk modulus across the ZrC–ZrN join.

Sintered Zr(C,N) disks were produced by spark-plasma sintering of ZrC and ZrN mixtures. Time-of-flight neutron diffraction data were collected at the NOMAD beamline at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Rietveld refinements constrained carbon and nitrogen occupancies on the anion sublattice. Combustion analysis provided independent bulk C and N measurements, while EPMA assessed local composition. Lattice parameters and thermal expansion were determined by high-temperature XRD using a Bruker D8 diffractometer with fused-silica capillaries. Bulk moduli were measured by synchrotron XRD in a multi-anvil D-DIA apparatus at the GSECARS sector of the Advanced Photon Source.

The ambient-pressure lattice parameter increases approximately linearly with carbon content, broadly consistent with Vegard’s law. Thermal expansion decreases overall with increasing carbon content but exhibits nonlinear behavior between approximately ZrC 0.5 N 0.5 and ZrC 0.75 N 0.25 , reaching a local minimum near ZrC 0.6 N 0.4 . The isothermal bulk modulus shows complementary nonlinear behavior, with a maximum near the same composition. The coincident bulk-modulus maximum and thermal-expansion minimum near ZrC 0.6 N 0.4 identify an intermediate composition with enhanced effective thermoelastic stiffness. Similar nonlinear elastic or thermal-expansion behavior occurs in other solid solutions, although coincident elastic stiffening and reduced expansion appear less common than cases dominated by local strain, excess volume, or magnetovolume effects. In Zr(C,N), the correspondence is consistent with composition-dependent electronic structure and bond-force constants, but direct vibrational or electronic measurements are required to establish the mechanism.

title: What Can Shear Wave Splitting (SWS) Analysis Tell Us About Mt. Spurr’s 2004-6 Unrest Episode?
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Kissee, Ciean [1], George, Ophelia [2]
affiliations: (1) San Joaquin Delta College, Stockton, CA, USA
(2) Department of Natural Science, Pensacola State College, Pensacola, FL, USA
abstract:
Between 2004 and 2006, Mount Spurr, Alaska, experienced unusual volcanic unrest that included the formation of an ice cauldron within the summit vent, episodic development of a roiling summit lake, debris flows, increased fumarolic activity, and expansion of exposed steaming rock. Although this unrest did not culminate in an eruption, its surface manifestations indicated substantial changes within the volcanic system. Examining such non-eruptive unrest contributes to the development of a broader shear-wave splitting reference framework that may ultimately help distinguish signals preceding eruptions from those associated with unrest that subsides without eruption.

We applied shear-wave splitting analysis to local earthquakes recorded by four three-component seismic stations surrounding Mount Spurr between 2004 and 2006. Of 1,515 event-station pairs from 989 unique earthquakes within the shear-wave window, 511 produced acceptable splitting measurements used in the final interpretation. Fast polarization directions and delay times were highly variable and showed no systematic temporal or depth-dependent trends. In contrast, apparent percent anisotropy varied strongly with earthquake depth. Shallow earthquakes exhibited a broad range of values, including the highest apparent anisotropy observed in the dataset, whereas earthquakes originating at greater depths consistently produced low apparent anisotropy throughout the unrest period.

These results indicate that anisotropy was not distributed uniformly throughout the full crustal volume sampled by the ray paths. The contrast between shallow and deep events is consistent with a relatively localized shallow anisotropic region whose contribution becomes proportionally smaller along longer ray paths passing through more weakly anisotropic crust. This study demonstrates how shear-wave splitting measurements from non-eruptive unrest can contribute to comparative assessments of subsurface volcanic processes. This work was conducted as part of the Geo-Launchpad internship program, supported by the NSF NGF operated by EarthScope Consortium.

title: Drivers of Trace Fossil Silicification Across the Phanerozoic
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Pippenger, Kate H. [1], Slaney, Noah A. [2], Tarhan, Lidya G. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Memorial University of Newfoundland, St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
abstract:
Silicified body and trace fossils are an important part of the fossil record, as silicification can exceptionally preserve small or delicate structures and increase preservation potential. On long temporal scales, the abundance and selectivity of silicified body fossils is controlled by the dissolution rates of different carbonate phases, and the distribution of silicified body fossil occurrences is strongly linked to the occurrence of siliceous sponges. However, we do not know which processes drive trace fossil silicification on these large spatial and long temporal scales, or whether there are significant lithologic, paleoenvironmental, ichnotaxonomic, or other patterns of trace fossil silicification.

To address this, we constructed a database of >130 geologic units containing silicified trace fossils in Phanerozoic marine carbonate units to perform a systematic analysis of silicification trends in the trace fossil record. The trace fossil Thalassinoides is preferentially silicified at a rate much higher than any other trace fossil, likely because silica sources (both biogenic and clastic) are readily concentrated within its open burrow network. Siliceous sponge spicules are commonly the primary silica source for trace fossil silicification, at a rate much higher than that of clastic sediments or radiolarians. Diatoms are not found in any units, and notably we find no silicified trace fossils younger than Eocene age. Finally, significant peaks in the abundance of units containing silicified burrows occur during the Ordovician, Permian, and Cretaceous; these maxima persist even when normalized to available carbonate outcrop area and length of period. In contrast, very few units containing silicified burrows occur during the middle Paleozoic and the Triassic.

Here, we evaluate the links between these temporal trends and potential drivers of trace fossil silicification, including marine dissolved silica concentrations, Wilson cycles and other paleogeographic changes, and radiations/extinctions of silicifying organisms, and consider the ways in which these trends may bias our understanding of the evolution of bioturbation over the Phanerozoic.

title: Timing and Kinematic Evolution of the Eastern Terminus of the Himalayas
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Howes, Ceci [1], Betka, Paul [2], Lang, Karl [3], Mukherjee, Shreya [4], Pye, Alexandra [5], Rakshit, Raghupratim [6], Chance, Dena [7]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA

(6) Geology, Jagannath Barooah University, Jorhat, Assam, India

abstract: The eastern terminus of the Himalaya is defined by the India-Eurasia-Burma continental triple junction, which marks a transition from the collisional tectonics of the central Himalaya to hyper-oblique convergence at the Indo-Burman subduction zone. While the eastern Himalaya is considered an archetype for collision to subduction transitions, few studies have focused on deformation related to the Burma terrane collision, or the resulting Noa-Dihing fault system (NDFS). We combine map, outcrop, microstructural and quartz crystallographic preferred orientation (CPO) analyses with in situ UVLAMP 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology and detrital zircon 238 U/ 206 Pb (DZUPb) analyses to constrain the structure, timing and kinematic evolution of the Himalayan wedge in the hanging wall of the NDFS. DZUPb spectra demonstrate that the major lithostratigraphic units in the study area have provenance signatures consistent with the Greater Himalayan Series (Lalpani and Mayodia Fms.) and Tethyan Himalayan Series (Tidding Fm.) of the main Himalaya. Results from several across-strike mapping transects, CPO analysis and microstructure kinematic analysis reveal a ~45° clockwise rotation of prominent fabrics within the study area from 320°, 45° with southwest-directed shearing in the north of the study area to 005°, 85° with west directed shearing ~15km to the south. Mineral stretching lineations have high rakes in the northern transects and become more oblique and varied closer to the NDF. In situ 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages of 18-23 Ma from synkinematic muscovite and biotite record early Miocene thrusting under greenschist to lower amphibolite facies conditions, consistent with the timing of deformation observed in the Himalayan wedge to the east of the study area. Ductile fabrics in the wedge are truncated by the by northwest- to north-striking brittle fault zones with components of both right-lateral and reverse senses of shear. These cross-cutting brittle fault zones splay from the NDFS and record a substantial component of dextral wrench faulting that is interpreted to be associated with the Burma terrane collision. The Burma terrane accretion modifies the eastern Himalaya in the brittle regime, implying a transition from early Miocene ductile thrusting to late Miocene brittle deformation likely related to the development of dextral shearing around the eastern Himalayan syntaxis.

title: Chelicerates in the Cradle: Ontogeny and Variation in Limulitella bronni
session_title: New Voices in Geobiology
authors: Ocon, Samantha B. [1], Jukar, Advait Mahesh [2], Kowalewski, Michal J. [3]
affiliations: (1) Natural Sciences, Santa Fe College, Gainesville, FL, ; Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(2) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, FL,

abstract: Horseshoe crabs (Xiphosura) are often invoked as unchanging relics of a bygone era due to their seeming morphological immutability over geological timescales. Investigation of their 480 million year long fossil record, however, reveals a complex evolutionary history shaped by environmental and developmental factors. Previous work elucidating macroevolutionary dynamics in Xiphosura has identified heterochronic trends within two lineages that also occupy nonmarine environments, Belinurina and Austrolimulidae. As heterochrony is defined as an evolutionary change in developmental timing, characterizing ontogeny within a lineage is key to pinpointing shifts in developmental trajectory and can assist in distinguishing between occurrences of evolutionary convergence and parallelism. Additionally, interpreting fossils with an ontogenetic lens is essential to proper species delineation, phylogenetic analyses, and understanding organismal life history. Of the two clades that display aberrant, heterochronic morphologies, only Belinurina has been subjected to extensive ontogenetic study. Here, I present the first evaluation of ontogenetic and morphological variation in an austrolimulid, using Limulitella bronni material from the Triassic Grès à Voltzia formation. Morphological variation is quantified using linear and geometric morphometric datasets, alongside qualitative observational data. We identify two morphotypes, each comprised of material from multiple developmental stages.

title: A view from the Ladder. Using a geological approach to address archaeological anomalies in the Chihuahuan Desert of Southwest Texas
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part II)

abstract: The small portion of the Chihuahuan Desert within what is now southwestern Texas has been the subject of considerable archaeological investigation, most centered on regional material culture. The most significant of these studies was an early project led by geologists Claude Albitton and Kirk Bryant, which concentrated on identifying and describing late-Quaternary lithostratigraphy. These descriptions later served archaeologists for various research purposes, including environmental proxy analysis and relative dating methods used to construct seriations of cultural artifacts within the described layers. The latter, in part, focused subsequent decades of research in the region on cultural-historical sequences—an artifact-based descriptive endeavor. The succeeding decades of research found patterns in the material record of human occupation, but also noticeable holes in the diagnostic material of the earliest periods of human habitation, which caused many to conclude this portion of the desert was the “ el despoblado ” or uninhabited by early humans. Returning to and expanding the original work of Albritton and Bryant, under the direction of Rolfe Mandel and the University of Kansas Odyssey Archaeological Research Fund, geologically focused research has explained why this early period appears to be absent from the material record. This presentation will cover several sites in Southwest Texas, demonstrating how geological methods more effectively address archaeological questions about the region's earliest inhabitants.

title: Uncovering the Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Deep-Seated Landslides in Oregon, USA, via Continuous Surface Monitoring
session_title: Dynamics of natural and built environments
authors: Fulmer, Erik Andrew [1], Leshchinsky, Ben Adam [2]
affiliations: (1) College of Engineering; School of Civil and Construction Engineering, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA
(2) College of Forestry; Forest Engineering, Resources & Management, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon,
abstract:
Deep-seated landslides are a persistent challenge at the interface of natural processes and the built environment, where active slopes regularly affect highways, utilities, local economies, and communities. Their behavior reflects interactions among geology, topography, hydrology, and changing stress conditions, but these interactions are difficult to resolve using periodic surveys or observations from a single location. Spatially distributed monitoring at high temporal resolution provides an opportunity to better understand how landslides respond to rainfall and other drivers, how movement varies across a landslide body, and when changes in behavior may indicate increasing hazard.

We use arrays of RTK-GNSS instruments to monitor several active landslides across Oregon. The systems record three-dimensional positional measurements at 30-minute intervals with centimeter-level accuracy, allowing us to track displacement, velocity, and changes in movement through individual storms and across multiple wet seasons. We compare movement with precipitation to examine how rainfall response varies among landslides, through time, and between different portions of complex landslide bodies. Here, we focus on selected landslides that exhibit a broad range of behaviors. Some respond consistently to several days of antecedent rainfall, whereas others show changing sensitivity over the course of the wet season or require larger storms before accelerating. Within individual landslides, movement may be relatively coherent or concentrated within distinct zones that accelerate at different times or rates. These differences reflect variations in landslide geometry, material properties, drainage, and internal structure, and demonstrate that a single rainfall or velocity threshold may not adequately represent the behavior of a complex slide.

By combining continuous displacement measurements with rainfall records and geologic interpretation, this work provides a clearer view of how active landslides evolve under hydrologic forcing. The results can support more informed monitoring strategies, improve interpretation of threshold exceedances, and help transportation agencies and communities anticipate how changing natural conditions may affect vulnerable infrastructure.

title: Testing Thermomechanical Models for Magma Generation in the Mojave Early Miocene Magmatic Belt
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Sasich, Alexandra [1], Schwartz, Joshua J. [2], Gans, Phillip B. [3], Swanson, Brian J. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University Northridge, Northridge, CA, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University Northridge, Northridge, CA,
(3) Department of Earth Science, UCSB, Goleta, CA,
(4) California Geological Survey, Santa Clarita, CA,
abstract:
Anomalous magmatism developed in the Mojave Desert during the Miocene transition from Farallon plate subduction to the Pacific-North American transform boundary, but the sources and processes responsible for this volcanism remain unresolved. As segments of the Pacific-Farallon spreading system entered the trench, continued divergence of the subducting plates opened a slab window, allowing hot asthenosphere to rise beneath the continent while potentially heating the young slab margins. In the Mojave Desert, volcanic activity was concentrated in a narrow west-east corridor active from ca. 24 to 19 Ma, termed the early Miocene magmatic belt (EMMB). Existing geochemical datasets from the belt commonly lack the trace-element coverage needed to distinguish among competing models of magma generation and evolution.

Ridge subduction creates two contrasting magma-generation pathways that can be tested within the EMMB. Decompression melting of asthenosphere rising through the slab window should produce depleted, MORB-like magmas that may be modified during ascent through continental lithosphere and crust. In contrast, thermal erosion and partial melting of the young oceanic slab margins should generate adakite-like melts characterized by elevated Sr/Y and La/Yb, low Y and Yb, and depleted heavy rare earth element patterns. We test these thermomechanical predictions to determine whether EMMB magmatism reflects asthenospheric melting, slab-edge melting, or contributions from both processes.

We examine basaltic through rhyolitic volcanic suites from the western and central EMMB using whole-rock major- and trace-element geochemistry and clinopyroxene chemistry. These datasets are used to distinguish source-related signatures from those generated during differentiation, alteration, and crustal assimilation. Initial whole-rock analyses suggest predominantly MORB-like magmatism variably modified by crustal contamination, with localized adakite-like affinities toward the central part of the belt. Ongoing mineral analyses will test whether this spatial variation reflects primary magma sources, slab influence, or crustal assimilation.

By integrating whole-rock and mineral-scale data, this study evaluates how mantle source, slab contribution, and crustal assimilation produced the compositional diversity of the EMMB. Emerging geochemical variability suggests that magma generation may not have been uniform across the belt, although the roles of asthenospheric upwelling and slab melting remain under investigation. This study places the EMMB within a broader framework of magmatic-system evolution by linking magma source to the thermomechanical consequences of ridge subduction beneath the Mojave Desert during the Miocene.

abstract:
Hierakonpolis (Nekhen), Egypt preserves evidence of occupation spanning Naqada II through Dynasty I (about 3600–2900 BCE). Since 1988, this important site is degraded by rising groundwater, driven by agricultural expansion in Wadi El Saya'ada to the southeast and, more recently, to the south. We integrate satellite-based SAR, optical, and hydrological time series, and extended ground-based hydrogeological surveys to evaluate deformation and moisture dynamics at this important archeological site.

Our initial InSAR time series analysis reveals a spatially confined subsidence anomaly of -9.1 mm/yr (cumulative about 90 mm, 2015–2024) centered on the drainage canal south of ancient town perimeter wall distinct from the broader temple-town enclosure signal (-1.0 mm/yr, -10 mm cumulative). An uplift zone (1.5 to 2.0 mm/yr) northwest of the site may indicate upward seepage pressures due to rising heads in the confined aquifer and enhanced groundwater recharge centered within and spreading northwestward from the Wadi El Saya'ada reclamation area. Independent Sentinel-1/2 time series (2015–2024) corroborate this signal: MNDWI wet-surface area expanded by 4% (increased approximately by 11 ha/yr), while SAR VV backscatter over the same zone decreased by 1.56 dB/yr, consistent with progressive soil saturation. Both series could possibly track the shallow and deep-aquifer recharge.

Seasonal and annual ground-based specific-conductance, salinity, and water-table surveys across the ancient site confirm this rising-groundwater signal at decimeter scale since early irrigation at the Wadi El Saya'ada site, revealing that the water table is not spatially homogeneous. Site complexity documented by piezometry reveals site-wide changes, broadened by advances in satellite imagery and sequence data.

Together, InSAR, optical/SAR hydrology, and field hydrogeology may reveal a groundwater intensification event drove transient uplift and elevated moisture, followed by ongoing reconsolidation and subsidence south of the Temple-Town site. This multi-sensor, non-invasive framework establishes baseline deformation and hydrological rates essential for site assessment and further definition of the hydrogeologic framework at Hierakonpolis.

title: Co-Occurring Geogenic and Anthropogenic Contaminants in Unregulated Water Sources Across the Navajo Nation: Community-Engaged Exposure Science and Health Frameworks
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part II)
authors: Rock, Tommy [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
abstract:
The geologic profile of the western United States naturally produces elevated levels of arsenic and uranium in groundwater, a condition often exacerbated by hard rock mining. Across the Navajo Nation, the largest contiguous Native American Nation in the American Southwest, this legacy of hard rock mining spans more than a century, compounding concerns about drinking water safety. Due to a critical lack of public water infrastructure, many residents rely on unregulated water sources, where uranium, arsenic, and co-occurring contaminants routinely exceed national drinking water standards. While natural background concentrations contribute to regional water chemistry, anthropogenic contamination from legacy mining poses severe public health and environmental justice challenges for affected Diné communities. Addressing these co-occurring contaminants requires robust scientific investigation paired with community-engaged research frameworks to inform public policy and support tribal leadership.

Recent regional studies have focused on quantifying elemental contaminants to assess public health risks across the Navajo Nation. Between 2014 and 2017, an extensive sampling initiative evaluated 294 water samples from the Arizona and Utah portions of the reservation for 21 elements. Analysis revealed that 14 elements exceeded national regulatory limits at least once, with vanadium, calcium, arsenic, manganese, lithium, and uranium showing the highest incidence of exceedances. Epidemiologic evaluations further underscore the urgency of these exposure pathways. In a targeted assessment of unregulated well water used for drinking, 5.4% of tested samples (10 out of 185) exceeded maximum contaminant levels established under the Safe Drinking Water Act. These empirical findings highlight that while uranium and arsenic remain primary concerns, a broader spectrum of heavy metals and trace elements poses simultaneous risks to local water supplies.

The societal and scientific implications of these elevated exposures are profound. Strong toxicologic evidence links uranium exposure to renal damage, reproductive toxicity, and cellular DNA damage. However, epidemiologic evidence on cardiovascular and oncogenic outcomes remains limited, largely because long-term cohort studies with individual-level exposure assessments are scarce. This gap underscores the need to integrate the rigor of exposure science with Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge and lived experience. Sustained community engagement and transparent data dissemination are vital to implementing effective mitigation strategies, upholding environmental justice, and securing safe drinking water infrastructure for Indigenous populations.

title: Campanian Marine Vertebrate Fossils from the Hatch Mesa Sandstone, Eastern Utah
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Salmi, Jay [1], Anderson, Evan [2], Sonheim, Ryan Jacob [3], King, Michael Ryan [4], Lively, Joshua Ryan [5], Kirkland, James I. [6]
affiliations: (1) Natural & Environmental Sciences, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA

abstract:
This study presents the first known report of a vertebrate fossil assemblage from the Campanian Hatch Mesa Sandstone near Green River, Utah. The fossils occur within localized, channelized, coarse-grained sandstone bodies of the Upper Cretaceous Mancos Shale. These sandstone bodies are interpreted as offshore marine channels that accumulated sediment coarser than the surrounding marine mudstones.

Seventeen undergraduate students participated in systematic surface collection through a cooperative effort involving a university, museum repository, and government agency. Three students volunteered to serve as field managers. With guidance from the instructor, these students reviewed scientific literature and satellite imagery to develop a strategy for surveying and surface collecting fossils from the localized sandstone bodies within a limited field period. They also developed a standardized specimen-numbering and documentation system for cohesive collection methods. All students worked in close proximity and remained under the direct oversight of the instructor throughout the field activity. Each student field manager assisted approximately one-third of the class by helping manage the sheer volume of surface-collected material and ensuring that each specimen was described on a specimen card and assigned a consistent field number.

Following collection, the student field managers developed a preliminary classification system based on specimen color, length, symmetry, serrations, striations, curvature, and surface texture. Of the sixty-four fossils with definable morphology, shark teeth dominate the surface-collected assemblage. Scapanorhynchus is the most abundant identified taxon, whereas teeth attributed to Squalicorax and Cretalamna are less common. Batoids are represented by a Texatrygon tooth and a Ptychotrygon dermal denticle. One possible hybodontiform tooth was also recovered. These preliminary findings document a diverse Campanian marine chondrichthyan assemblage and demonstrate how structured student field leadership can facilitate the surface collection and documentation of large quantities of fossil material within a short field period while contributing to original paleontological research.

title: Surficial Geologic Mapping of the West Half of the Petersburg 30- x 60-Minute Quadrangle, Virginia
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: Warrington, Laura Spencer [1], Nelson, Michelle Summa [2], Occhi, Marcie Elizabeth [3]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Department of Energy, Charlottesville, VA, USA
(2) Virginia Department of Energy, Charlottesville, VA, USA

abstract:
Surficial deposits in the west half of the Petersburg 30- x 60-minute quadrangle were mapped by the Virginia Department of Energy, Division of Geology and Mineral Resources (DGMR) through a cooperative effort with the USGS STATEMAP program. This area is a geomorphically and geologically diverse region along the Fall Zone south of Richmond, Virginia, where unlithified sediments of the western Coastal Plain overlap crystalline rocks of the eastern Piedmont. Many of the upper Coastal Plain units in this area are used for aggregate resources and are known hosts for Ti, and Zr-enriched heavy mineral sand deposits.

This 1:100,000-scale surficial map covers sixteen 7.5-minute quadrangles. Eight quadrangles were mapped at 1:24,000-scale between 2005 and 2026, with the earlier maps created pre-LiDAR. The surficial data from these source maps were compiled into a GeMS geodatabase and reconciled using LiDAR and verified in the field. New surficial mapping was completed in the eight western quadrangles. Several subsurface datasets were used to inform the map, including boring logs from the Virginia Department of Transportation, DGMR’s internal borehole database, and county water well records. The USGS Earth MRI aeroradiometric geophysical survey of the VA-NC Fall Zone (Shah and Connell, 2022) and soil survey data from NRCS were also used to delineate the upper Coastal Plain deposits.

This map includes Pleistocene(?) terraces to modern alluvium in the Appomattox and Nottoway River watersheds and Miocene(?) to Pleistocene deposits in the Coastal Plain. Unconsolidated Neogene map units to the west are generally discontinuous and become less dissected to the east. These deposits are interpreted to be of near-shore marine, estuarine, and fluvial origin and the result of multiple cycles of marine transgression and regression due to changes in baselevel. Differentiating between these deposits based solely on lithology is challenging because many share compositional similarities and exposure is limited. Mapping in the region typically uses elevation to demarcate the deposits and known paleoshoreline scarp topography. Future work will utilize this map to identify areas for geochronology of these western Coastal Plain deposits to better understand their temporal relationship. The surficial plate of the west half of the Petersburg 30- x 60-minute quadrangle will be published alongside the new bedrock mapping of seven of the western quadrangles.

title: Reconstructing Yellowstone Geyser Activity from Archival Records and Modern Datasets
session_title: Old Collections, New Tricks
authors: Reed, Mara H. [1]
affiliations: (1) National Cave and Karst Research Institute, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Carlsbad, NM, USA
abstract:
Exploring complex environmental relationships requires long-term monitoring data that is not always readily available. For example, the external drivers of multi-year variability in geyser activity are not well understood despite the need to characterize hydrothermal systems and their evolving hazards. In Yellowstone National Park, some geysers are currently monitored via temperature sensors and seismometers, but visual observations have been the primary monitoring tool for most of the park’s history. Few attempts have been made to combine historical information with newer datasets to synthesize long-term eruption interval histories for Yellowstone’s significant geysers.

Grand and Riverside Geysers are large, charismatic geysers in the Upper Geyser Basin that attract significant public attention. As part of an investigation into the links between geyser behavior and tree mortality near Grand and Riverside, I reviewed collections maintained by the Yellowstone National Park Heritage and Research Center, work by geyser historians, and crowdsourced observations from GeyserTimes to determine how these geysers’ eruption intervals have changed since 1871. I focused on locating or calculating the average, minimum, and maximum eruption intervals to represent geyser activity because these parameters were most consistently reported. The primary challenges included (1) locating relevant sources across collections, (2) frequent geyser name inconsistencies among early observers, (3) assessing observer credibility, and (4) determining whether reported observations were representative of eruption behavior.

Neither geyser was consistently observed until the 1920s and 1930s. Grand has undergone at least three dormancies and its annual average eruption interval spans 6.1 hours (2019) to 288 hours (1960). Riverside’s eruption intervals have been much more stable with nearly all reported intervals falling between 5 and 10 hours; the highest annual average interval is 9.3 hours (1939). There is enough information to construct similar eruptive histories for several of Yellowstone’s other large geysers. Though scientists and land managers must invest in long-term monitoring to generate robust datasets, this work demonstrates the merit of consulting imperfect historical and modern records to obtain useful information about environmental changes on multi-decadal timescales.

title: Paleoceanographic Implications of Warmer Water Planktic Foraminifera in the Latest Oligocene to Middle Pleistocene of the Ross Sea, Antarctica

abstract:
Warmer water planktic foraminifera present in sediments cored on the Ross Sea continental shelf provide biotic evidence for polar amplification in Antarctica at times warmer than present, including the latest Oligocene-early Miocene of DSDP Site 270, early to middle Miocene of IODP Site U1521, and DSDP Sites 273 and 272, late Miocene-early Pliocene of Site U1522, and Pliocene to mid-Pleistocene of Site U1523.

At Sites 270, 272, 273, and U1521, we note persistent occurrences of a presumed planktic foraminifer endemic to Antarctica ( Antarcticella antarctica ), as well as sporadic and rare species with wider biogeographic ranges, including Globoturborotalita druryi , Trilobatus trilobus, T. quadrilobatus , Dentoglobigerina globosa , Globigerinita glutinata, G. uvula , Turborotalita quinqueloba , Paragloborotalia siakensis, P. cf. pseudocontinuosa , Globorotaloides suteri , Tenuitella angustiumbilicata , and T. munda . These taxa occur during the pre-MCO, MCO (Miocene Climatic Optimum), and MMCT (Middle Miocene Climate Transition) intervals. More recently, the 2026 SWAIS2C Crary Ice Rise drill core at ~83 o S has yielded rare planktic specimens from the upper and lower Miocene.

At Site U1523 on the shelf edge of the Ross Sea, an interval of elevated abundances of Globigerina bulloides/falconensis in the mid-Pliocene (~3.75-3.65 Ma) correlates with interglacials MIS Gi7-Gi3 while the presence of multiple specimens of Globigerinoides ruber and Globoconella inflata in a single sample likely correlates with late Pliocene MIS G17 (~2.95 Ma). The last occurrence of G. bulloides/falconensis was ~1.82 Ma at U1523, and ~1.15 Ma at slope Site U1525. Warmer water planktic foraminiferal occurrences have been excluded from the Ross Sea since the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT) as the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC) and Antarctic Slope Current increased in intensity, revealed by increasing Trifarina earlandi abundances at Site U1523.

The very low abundance of these planktic species suggests that they were not living in the Ross Sea, but rather were transported by ocean currents. Their presence may signal times when the Polar Front (PF) was closer to Antarctica, the sea surface temperature gradient across the PF was weaker, and/or when the ACC was weaker. Alternatively, they were transported by incursions of warmer Circumpolar Deep Water into the Ross Sea. The sporadic occurrences of warmer water planktic foraminifera suggest polar amplification in the Ross Sea at times during the early Miocene and MCO, and interglacials of the MMCT, Pliocene, and early Pleistocene.

title: Geochemistry of Gem Peridot near Badger Creek in Park and Fremont County, Colorado
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Barkley, Alexander John [1], Leatherman, Mark [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Natural Sciences, Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Natural Sciences, Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Badger Creek area, located just northeast of Salida, Colorado, is a rare occurrence for gem peridot in the state wherein its specific geochemistry is not well documented. The peridot is hosted in Miocene-age basalt where collected samples range from 0.5-2mm in size, although facet grade material of up to 3 carats have been reported. The basalt is divided into 3 types: 1) a lower elevation black, dense unit with mainly microscopic peridot, 2) a mid-elevation gray, softer type hosting most of the gems, 3) an upper red-gray vesicular unit with dominant alluvial peridot with some in-situ within vesicles.

Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) and portable X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) were used to examine major & trace elemental compositions to evaluate the forsterite-fayalite nature of the peridot & host rocks. Type 1 basalt has an average composition of 40.8 wt% Si, 6.95 wt% Fe, 4.5% wt% Mg. Type 2 basalt has averages of 37.2 wt% Si, 6.2 wt% Fe & 4.7 wt% Mg. Type 3 basalt has averages of 38.4 wt% Si, 7.2 wt% Fe & 2.2% wt% Mg. Average peridot composition with type 2 basalt is 9.7 wt% Si, 2.3 wt% Fe & 10.0 wt% Mg, with average compositions associated with type 3 being 7.6 wt% Si, 1.5 wt% Fe & 7.6 wt% Mg. Results indicate that Badger Creek olivine is predominantly forsteritic. However, when compared with olivine from the prolific San Carlos region of Arizona, the Badger Creek olivine exhibits a higher iron composition.

The whole rock data is indicative of variations in cooling history, Si content & the concentration ratios of Fe and Mg within the basalt. Compared with the San Carlos locality, Badger Creek exhibits a higher Fe/Mg ratio despite overall lower concentrations of both elements. The San Carlos samples also display a more consistent Mg-Fe relationship between olivine & basalt, suggesting consistent equilibration between the mineral & host magma. In contrast, Badger Creek samples exhibit greater Mg–Fe non-linear variability, indicating a more complex petrogenetic history of multiple magma pulses and/or assimilation of crustal material. These differences suggest variations in the magmatic conditions & chemical evolution between the two localities despite similar geologic ages & tectonic settings. Further planned studies include petrography to deduce specific gem growth conditions and fluid inclusion microthermometry.

title: Rheology of Two Natural Granulites from the Cora Lake Shear Zone, Saskatchewan, Canada.
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Oatman, Ryan L [1], Holyoke, Caleb W. [2], Mahan, Kevin H. [3], Flynn, Corey [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Akron, Akron, OH, USA
(2) University of Akron, Akron, OH,
(3) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
(4) University of Colorado, Boulder, CO,
abstract: The rheology of the lower continental crust is dominated by feldspar-rich rocks with varying amounts of quartz, pyroxenes and garnet, such as felsic and mafic granulite. Recent studies have found that quartz-bearing felsic granulite was stronger than mafic granulite, which does not contain quartz but has a similar feldspathic composition. However, field-based observations from the Cora Lake shear zone in northern Saskatchewan Canada indicate that felsic granulite is weaker than adjacent mafic granulite deformed at lower crustal temperature (700 - 800 o C) and presure (~0.8 GPa). We performed experiments on a felsic granulite ultramylonite (plag+qtz+K-spar+gt) and a mafic granulite ultramylonite (plag+OPx+gt+CPx+K-spar) from the Cora Lake shear zone at temperatures ranging from 850-925°C, a pressure of 1.5 GPa, and strain rates from 10 -7 to 10 -5 s -1 , in a Griggs piston-cylinder rock deformation apparatus, to create predictive strength models of both rocks. At all conditions, the felsic granulite ultramylonite was weaker than the mafic granulite ultramylonite. The felsic granulite ultramylonite deforms by a diffusive mechanism at differential stresses <400 MPa and by dislocation creep at differential stresses >400 MPa. The mafic granulite ultramylonite deforms by dislocation creep at all conditions of this study which is consistent with previous studies. Microstructural analysis will be performed to further evaluate deformation mechanisms. Results of our experiments are consistent with field observations indicating felsic granulite is weaker than adjacent mafic granulite deformed at the same conditions.

title: Rodingite U-Pb Titanite Geochronology Records Multi-episodic Metasomatism of the Dun Mountain Ophiolite, Aotearoa/New Zealand

authors: Hams, Jacob A. [1], Gevedon, Michelle [2], Stockli, Lisa D. [3], Nistor, Claudiu [4], Barnes, Jaime D. [5], Dragovic, Besim [6], Stockli, Daniel F. [7], Coulthard, Daniel [8]

(2) Geology Department, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(4) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA

abstract:
Constraining the timing of ophiolite metasomatism is challenging because serpentinites rarely contain minerals suitable for radiometric dating. Rodingites, metasomatic rocks formed through interaction between Ca-rich fluids and mafic protoliths during serpentinization, can contain hydrothermal titanite that record radiometric ages and provide opportunity to directly date metasomatic processes in ophiolites. We investigated rodingites from the Whakatū/Nelson segment of the Permian Dun Mountain ophiolite, Aotearoa/New Zealand, using petrography, whole-rock and mineral major element geochemistry, and in situ LA-ICP-MS U-Pb titanite geochronology to constrain the timing of multiple rodingitization episodes.

Rodingite samples (n=29) record a complex, multi-stage history of metasomatism evidenced by rodingite sample types with distinct whole-rock petrologic texture and geochemistry. One rodingite type preserves relict pyroxene grains in a hydrogrossular matrix and is depleted in Ti. A second rodingite type has a fine-grained recrystallization texture with neoblastic titanite and diopside in a hydrogrossular matrix. Both rodingite types experienced variable subsequent metasomatism recorded first by chlorite formation, then by development of cross-cutting veins of rodingite minerals. Individual dikes record the same texture and geochemistry, however, there is no spatial relationship between rodingite types. Hydrothermal titanite is interpreted to form via dissolution-precipitation reaction during rodingitization. Titanite U-Pb analyses of 10 rodingite samples yield dates spanning approximately 70 million years (ca. 282 to 214 Ma) and record multiple episodes of hydrothermal titanite formation. Ages indicate rodingitzation was spatially localized and controlled by chemical gradients and fluid flow, rather than as a single penetrative event.

Rodingite ages improve understanding of the tectonic events related to suprasubduction zone formation and Gondwanan margin obduction of the Dun Mountain ophiolite. The oldest dates (ca. 282 to 268 Ma) correspond to ages of late-stage intrusive dikes that crosscut the ophiolite and suggest initial metasomatism occurred during suprasubduction-zone development. Ages between 250 to 230 Ma may represent metasomatism during ophiolite obduction, which is consistent with the timing of the interpreted closure of the overlying Maitai basin by ca. 237 Ma (detrital zircon) and subsequent exhumation (ca. 230 to 240 Ma, Ar/Ar K-feldspar), and a gap in coeval arc magmatism. The youngest age (ca. 214 Ma) records the timing of formation of a titanite vein and may reflect post-obduction metasomatism related to continued regional convergence.

title: Changing Weathering Intensity in Paleosols of the Columbia River Basalt Group Between ca. 16-10 Ma, and Implications for the Timing of Cascade Uplift.
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements
authors: Bader, Nicholas E. [1], Persico, Lyman P. [2]
affiliations: (1) Whitman College, Walla Walla, WA,
(2) Whitman College, Walla Walla, Washington, USA
abstract: The fossil record shows that the inland Pacific Northwest has experienced remarkable climate change during the Neogene. The key drivers of this change are the uplift of the Cascade mountain range and the resulting orographic rainfall barrier, and cooling following the Mid-Miocene Climate optimum (MMCO). While the timing of the MMCO is relatively well understood, the timing of the closing of the Cascades is unclear, although arguably more important in its effects on regional climate. We studied a series of paleosols developed on basalts of the Miocene Columbia River Basalt group (CRBG). While many flows occurred rapidly, some flows were separated in time by periods of quiescence that allowed soils to develop in equilibrium with contemporaneous climate conditions. Subsequent flows preserved these weathering environments, making the CRBG a detailed repository of Miocene terrestrial paleoclimate data. We applied a variety of measurements to reconstruct weathering intensity: field measurements, micromorphology, geochemical mass balance calculations from WDXRF measurements of weathered basalt samples, and the identification of secondary clay minerals via powder XRD. Based on more complete oxidation, cation loss, and the presence of 1:1 secondary clay minerals, we interpret moderate weathering from earlier sites developed on the Grande Ronde Basalt and the Lookingglass member of the Wanapum Basalt. Younger paleosols developed on flows of the Saddle Mountains Basalt, in contrast, are minimally weathered. A transitional period between these is evidenced by moderate weathering on paleosols developed on the 15.0 Ma Frenchman Springs member of the Wanapum Basalt, subsequently covered by the ~13 Ma Umatilla member of the Saddle Mountains Basalt. We infer that Cascade uplift completed during or shortly after this transitional weathering period.

title: Evidence for the Neoproterozoic Rifting of Rodinia in the Rocky Mountain Front Range
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records
authors: Murray, Kendra E. [1], Niemi, Nathan A. [2], Clark, Marin K. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University Of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
abstract: The late Neoproterozoic breakup of supercontinent Rodinia profoundly shaped the western margin of Laurentia, leaving a geologic record that temporally links continental rifting to biological change at the Ediacaran-Cambrian transition and may explain the unusual eastern extent of the Laramide orogeny. Sedimentary evidence for this rifting is preserved in parts of Idaho, Nevada, and California but absent to the east of the Cordilleran hingeline, leaving postulated tectonic-biologic-climatic links untested. Such links are now testable due to advances in low-temperature thermochronology, which enable unprecedented recovery of deep-time thermal histories from Precambrian crystalline rocks. Here we interpret Neoproterozoic to recent tectonic histories of Paleoproterozoic basement rocks from the Colorado Front Range using thermal history analysis of apatite (U-Th)/He ages (54 ± 7 Ma) and zircon (U-Th)/He (ZHe) ages (50–607 Ma) that vary with grain U-Th composition ([eU] = 400–2400 ppm). Our inverse thermal history models are constrained by geologic records that place basement rocks near Earth's surface at ca. 700, 500, and 300 Ma. Samples that have ZHe ages that spanning a wide range of U-Th composition resolve reheating to 240–285°C following near-surface Tavakaiv injectite emplacement at ca. 700 Ma. We interpret this reheating as evidence of burial beneath 3–9 km of sediment in a rift basin, providing the first quantitative thermochronologic evidence that Neoproterozoic rifting coeval with global glaciations extended onto the craton and was later inverted during Laramide shortening. Sensitivity tests confirm that our ability to document this post-700 Ma heating signal depends on the combination of Mesoproterozoic biotite Ar ages and reproducible 61 ± 7.5 Ma high-[eU] ZHe ages that correspond to Colorado Mineral Belt magmatism and Laramide exhumation. Additionally, we find that while magnitude and duration of reheating are well constrained by the thermochronologic data, the timing of subsequent Neoproterozoic-Paleozoic cooling directly depends on how the geologic evidence of near-surface conditions is leveraged in our thermal history analysis. Further documentation of the timing of post‐rifting exhumation in the Front Range region, above and beyond that provided by our work, is necessary to genetically link this kilometer-scale erosion to tectonic or glacial drivers.

title: Ecological and Environmental Controls on Diversity Dynamics Across the Late Ordovician Richmondian Invasion in the Nashville Basin
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Kundladi, Shymah Beegam [1], Stigall, Alycia L. [2], Edwards, Cole Tyler [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Environmental & Planetary Sciences, The University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Environmental & Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN,
(3) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Appalachian State University, Boone, NC, USA
abstract:
Biodiversity change through time reflects the combined effects of environmental change and ecological interactions. Abiotic changes can alter habitats and introduce environmental stress, whereas biotic interactions can restructure communities through greater success of some groups versus others. Because these processes often occur simultaneously, it can be difficult to determine whether diversity change is driven by abiotic factors, biotic interactions, or their combined effects.

The Late Ordovician Richmondian Invasion provides an ideal system for testing how environmental and ecological factors jointly shaped diversity. This Katian marine immigration event introduced more than 60 genera, including brachiopods, bryozoans, mollusks, and corals, into eastern Laurentia, most notably in the Cincinnati and Nashville regions. These immigrations reorganized marine communities by changing richness, dominance, and evenness. Although the ecological effects of the invasion are well documented, the relative influence of environmental change versus biotic restructuring has not been studied in Nashville Basin.

This study integrates stratigraphically constrained, genus-level occurrence data with stable-isotope records from the C1-C5 sequences exposed at the Vietnam Veterans Highway and Briley Parkway sections, Tennessee. Occurrences were compiled from new fieldwork, published literature, the Paleobiology Database, and iDigBio. Newly generated δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C records were supplemented with published data. Taxa were classified as invasive generalists, invasive specialists, native generalists, or native specialists. Environmental variation is represented by δ¹⁸O, which records changes in temperature and seawater composition, and δ¹³C, which reflects carbon cycling; ecological context is represented by the diversity trajectory of each group.

To distinguish environmental from ecological drivers, we use complementary multivariate birth-death (MBD) and birth–death neural-network (BDNN) models in PyRate. MBD estimates directional associations between each group’s diversity and the origination and extinction rates of the other groups while simultaneously evaluating associations with δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C. BDNN jointly estimates lineage- and time-specific origination and extinction rates from the combined occurrence dataset and evaluates nonlinear effects and interactions among isotopic conditions, group diversity, and ecological category while accounting for preservation and sampling variation.

Results indicate substantial diversity restructuring during the invasion: native groups declined while invasive groups increased. Ecological associations appear to explain diversification dynamics more strongly than environmental variation alone, emphasizing the importance of biotic restructuring during the Richmondian Invasion.

title: Origin and Tectonic Significance of Granitic Pegmatites in the Southeastern Pennsylvania Piedmont
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Kerrigan, Ryan [1], Hollan, Jessica [2], Valencia, Victor [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences and the Environment, University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown, Johnstown, PA, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences and the Environment, University of Pittsburgh at Johnstown, Johnstown, PENNSYLVANIA, USA
(3) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
abstract: Granitic pegmatite intrusions dispersed throughout the Piedmont physiographic province of southeastern Pennsylvania have eluded proper geochemical characterization; analyses, modeling, and isotopic dating offer insight into the events that have shaped the east coast of North America. The Piedmont province has undergone repeated cycles of crustal thickening and deformation; geochemical characterization aims to implicate which tectonic events played a role in the generation of the pegmatite intrusions in the Piedmont. Two fieldwork localities (Coatesville and Elk Creek, located in Chester County, PA) yielded pegmatite samples for geochemical and geochronologic analyses. A subset of six representative samples were analyzed for major, minor, and trace element geochemistry. Results indicated that the Coatesville pegmatites are peralkaline, whereas Elk Creek pegmatites are peraluminous; however, both localities exhibit Nb > Ta trends and depleted P and Ca, diagnostic of NYF-type (Nb-Yb-F) pegmatites. These data are consistent with an anorogenic, partial melt origin possibly within an extensional tectonic setting. Trace element distribution coefficients were used to model partial melts of adjacent granodiorites, gneisses, and schists. The resulting melt signatures were compared to pegmatite geochemistry to evaluate potential source lithologies. Samples were selected for zircon U/Pb geochronology, and zircon grains were separated and analyzed using laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS) to obtain concordant isotopic ratios. High-U concentrations due to incompatible element enrichment in pegmatites complicates U/Pb dating, but analyses still provided valuable context. These results integrate geochemistry, partial melt modeling, and zircon geochronology to advance the understanding of pegmatite genesis and regional Appalachian crustal evolution.

title: Death by Dirt, Updated: 19th-century Cows Devastated Thriving Scallops, Shell-gravel Communities, and Beta Diversity on the Southern California Open Shelf, a Pre-industrial Legacy Persisting to This Day
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: Kidwell, Susan M. [1], Tomasovych, Adam [2]
affiliations: (1) Geophysical Sciences, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
(2) Earth Science Institute of Slovak Academy Sciences, Bratislava, Slovak Republic
abstract: In 2017, we reported 14 C evidence from ‘dead-only’ occurrences that terebratulid brachiopods had thrived for millennia on the southern California middle and outer shelf only to enter a steep decline in the 19 th century, disappearing entirely by the early 20 th -century. Our explanation of this extirpation, occurring well before the onset of wastewater emissions, urbanization, and secular warming, was ‘death by dirt’, i.e. a slow-motion smothering by silt released to the shelf by intense, unchecked 19th-century agriculture on the adjacent coastal plain, dominated initially by livestock (Spanish 1770s ramping up to the 1820s, maintained by US to 1870s) and then by cultivation without full soil conservation until the 1940s. Here, we expand this dramatic story with age data from a larger area and set of taxa, demonstrating that (1) scallops also inhabited the mainland shelf continuously over the last seven millennia only to collapse during the 19th century like the brachiopods; (2) the reconstructed population trajectories of these epifauna contrast with those of the more detritus-focused, infaunal mollusks that dominate today; (3) the now-extirpated species created unique shell-gravel habitats absent from 20th-century peak-wastewater and recovery phases and (4) supported significantly higher beta diversity across all shelf depths, detectable despite the inherent damping effects of time-averaging of dead-shell assemblages. The benthic ecosystem of today’s overwhelmingly muddy mainland shelf, a stubborn legacy of pre-industrial land use, remains locked in a state where epifaunal communities are still rare or absent despite 50-100 years of abatement of siltation and other contamination, indicating hysteresis-like behavior, with lower functional diversity and less efficient nutrient cycling than the “pre-cow” ecosystem. Live-dead analysis, taking advantage of time-averaged skeletal remains, thus revealed a fundamental transformation that was unsuspected despite exceptional ocean monitoring, suggesting that the potentially anthropogenic origin and biological consequences of other “shelf mud belts” deserve closer examination: such stubborn footprints are not expected beyond estuaries and other immediate coastal sinks, nor where larval connectivity should be high, underscoring how different solid sediment is from other pollutants. The survival of shell-gravel communities around some offshore islands that still have sandy shelves places a premium on conservation there and demonstrates the potential for eventually re-establishing lost communities on the mainland shelf.

title: Professional Preparation for Teaching Geoscience Among Geoscience Faculty as a Function of Career Stage
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Arthurs, Leilani [1], Wilfong, Collette [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, USA
abstract:
Professional preparation for teaching geoscience among the college and university professoriate has largely an ad hoc activity. This study aims to increase our understanding of current geoscience faculty members’ decisions about whether to attend teaching-focused professional development (PD) programs and implement research-based teaching methods (RBTM). The theoretical framework of Bandura’s concept of triadic reciprocal determinism is used to discover and characterize insights into personal, behavioral (i.e., experiences), and environmental factors that influence geoscience faculty members’ decisions to attend PD and implement RBTM. This exploratory study takes a cross-sectional methodological approach, to glean possible trends or patterns across tenure-track career stages. Study participant recruitment was based on convenience sampling and data were collected using Zoom -based interviews. Thematic analysis of the data highlights personal, behavioral, and environmental factors most influential in instructors’ decisions to attend PD programs and implement RBRM as a function of their career stage. Behavioral factors, especially past experiences with PDD programs, are the most influential in determining whether instructors continue to attend such programs.

Personal, behavioral, and environmental factors contribute to instructor decisions about whether to implement RBTM in various ways. In terms of personal factors, senior faculty members are more likely to choose teaching methods based on personal preferences they developed as a student and/or teacher (inc. graduate student teaching). Early and middle career faculty, on the other hand, more frequently cited the personal goal of being “a good teacher” as informing their approach to teaching. Across all career stages, a key environmental factor determining whether instructors implement research-based teaching methods is peer discussions on teaching. This study contributes to our understanding of current geoscience faculty members’ experiences with PD and their implementation of RBTM. Recommendations are made for institutional policies and for how PD programs can be optimally leveraged to support instructor implementation of RBTM.

title: Reconstructing Aqueous Geochemistry and the Sedimentary Environment of Proglacial Paleolake Hitchcock using Carbonate Concretions
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Melara, Julio César [1], Piccione, Gavin [2], Edwards, Graham Harper [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(3) Earth & Environmental Geosciences, Trinity University, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
Modern climate warming has accelerated glacier retreat, resulting in the expansion of new proglacial lake systems that are highly sensitive to climatic and deglacial dynamics. Our work investigates the sedimentary and geochemical archives of an ancient proglacial lake to better understand these evolving environments. We focus on Glacial Lake Hitchcock (GLH), which occupied the Connecticut River Valley between approximately 18.2 and 12.5 ka, during the retreat of the Laurentide Ice Sheet after the last glacial maximum. While the sedimentary record has been well characterized by prior studies of the varved lake sediments, we examine carbonate concretions (which formed non-displacively within the varved sediments) to reconstruct the geochemical conditions of the proglacial sedimentary environment during and following deglaciation.

We both used visual observations and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to examine in situ geochemistry of concretions collected from varved GLH sediment outcrops in Connecticut and Vermont, representing earlier and later depositional periods, respectively. The Connecticut (southern) samples contain coarser-grained silicate and Fe-oxide detrital clasts as well as fine-grained, Fe- and Al-rich red clay minerals in a calcite-cemented matrix. The presence of coarse detrital grains indicates intermittent higher-energy depositional events capable of transporting larger clasts, or, more likely, transport and deposition of ice-rafted debris (IRD). In contrast, the Vermont (northern) samples are finer-grained and comprised of Al-rich clays in a calcite-cemented matrix, with concentric orange-brown growth rings that lack calcite cement, reflecting changes in redox chemistry in porewaters during concretion growth.

The fine-grained clays cemented by the concretions reflect extensive chemical weathering and low-energy depositional conditions. The IRD in the Connecticut samples both suggest more ice-proximal conditions and may also have supported nucleation sites for concretion growth. In contrast, the concentric banding in the Vermont samples reflect noncontinuous concretion growth, likely regulated by changing redox conditions. Ongoing work includes U-series geochronology to better constrain the timescales of concretion growth following deposition of varved lake strata as well as carbon and oxygen isotope analyses of ostracod tests to infer lakewater compositions. These data will further develop our environmental and geochemical understanding of GLH.

title: Evidence for Pervasive Invasive Lavas in the Medusae Fossae Formation and Implications for Ice Near the Martian Equator
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Kerber, Laura [1]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Laboratory / California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
abstract:
The Medusae Fossae Formation (MFF) is a voluminous, fine-grained formation that extends along the Martian equator. It has been observed to contain hydrated material at the surface and hypothesized to contain a significant amount ice at depth. If proven, this near-equatorial water resource would greatly influence our strategy for human exploration. The MFF is morphologically heterogeneous, and the hidden ice, if it exists, is not likely to be uniform throughout the deposit. Here we examine the boundaries of the MFF where it intersects with Amazonian lavas and report the range of morphologies that are created by the interaction between the two unit types. We suggest that in addition to embaying and burying Medusae Fossae outcrops, lavas pervasively invade these outcrops in some regions (i.e., intruding from the side). The MFF may also be draped and pushed aside by lava flows. In some cases, invasion or embayment by lava flows appear to have caused MFF outcrops to exhibit explosive behavior. This perspective provides a new framework with which to understand unusual parts of the formation, such as the Fish-Scale Terrain, and provides a roadmap for future suggested radar investigations to better determine the material properties of the MFF’s diverse component parts.

Interactions between lavas and the Medusae Fossae Formation fit into a range of categories. Normal embayment relationships are found in some places, particularly in regions with yardangs, where lavas passively embay serrated yardang edges. Strong evidence for lava invasion is found in Gordii Dorsum, where invading lava fills up web-like cracks in the MFF, creating warrens of slender intersecting polygonal ridges up to 50 m tall. We propose that this is the principal formation mechanism of the Fish-Scale terrain, which should affect its density and radar properties compared to the rest of the formation. In some places, instead of invading MFF outcrops, lava appears to push the material out of the way. In northern Aeolis Planum, rootless cones emerge from the tops of MFF yardangs, suggesting that explosions took place as a result of lava embayment. These interactions suggest that ice may have been present in the formation at the time of invasion in some areas of the MFF (but not others). Ice loss through heating by lava may explain many unusual textures.

title: Student sense of belonging, geoscience identity, and fieldwork perceptions following field experiences: Preliminary results
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Burton, Zachary Florentino Murguía [1], Reano, Darryl [2], Arora, Shreya [3], Minor, Rebecca [4]
affiliations: (1) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT,
(2) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
(3) Bates College, Lewiston, ME,
(4) Bates College, Lewiston, ME,
abstract: Our research team is conducting a study to explore how geoscience fieldwork experiences influence diverse perceptions of geoscience identity, self-efficacy, sense of belonging to the geoscience community, perceptions of geoscience fieldwork, and academic and career intentions. Here, we discuss our motivation and methodology and share preliminary results. Study data were self-reported via an aggregated survey instrument deployed online. Voluntary participants must have completed at least one formal geoscience course and at least one geoscience field experience. This presentation focuses on student perceptions of their sense of belonging (assessed via 7 survey questions, or items), their geoscience identity (10 items), and their fieldwork perceptions (13 total items, including 4 confident or hopeful items, 4 apprehensive items, and 5 items related to their perceived value of fieldwork itself) following field experiences. Preliminary assessment of initial survey data ( n = 27 respondents) suggests better-than-neutral perceptions of sense of belonging (average rating of 2.4 out of 5, with 3 being neutral and 5 being lowest, across 7 survey items; averages for each survey item range from 2.1 to 2.6) and of geoscience identity (average rating of 2.5 out of 5 across 10 survey items; averages for each survey item range from 2.0 for item “I am interested in learning more about geoscience” [same for geology majors versus non-majors] to 3.1 for item “Others ask me for help in geoscience” [different for majors versus non-majors]). Responses collected on a separate, 7-point Likert scale suggest overall positive perceptions of fieldwork, including higher-than-neutral confidence, lower-than-neutral apprehension, and higher-than-neutral perceptions of the value of fieldwork. Respondents largely indicated that they “chose to take [the] class/experience because it involves fieldwork” (average item score of 6.2 out of 7, where 7 is “Very true of me,” 4 is “Neutral,” and 1 is “Not at all true of me”), and rated most highly the statements “I think I learn better from fieldwork than from normal classroom work” (x̄ = 5.9/7) and “Doing fieldwork increases my interest in science, compared with learning science in class” (x̄ = 6.0/7). Next steps in this work include expanding the dataset to additional respondents and conducting further interviews, including to explore possible counter-narratives among students self-reporting lower sense of belonging, geoscience identity, or perceptions of fieldwork.

authors: Thompson, Samuel Madison [1], Pederson, Matthew G. [2], Gan, Tian [3], Remirez, Mariano N. [4], Farkas, Juraj [5], Rugen, Elias [6], Segessenman, Daniel C. [7], Dahl, Tais W. [8], Frei, Robert [9], Kaufman, Alan Jay [10], Gilleaudeau, Geoffrey J. [11]

abstract: The Ediacaran Period records profound changes in ocean chemistry, climate, and early ecology, including the appearance of the first complex macroscopic life and major perturbations to the global carbon cycle. The period is characterized by multiple large negative δ¹³C excursions, including the Shuram-Wonoka Excursion (SWE; ~579–564 Ma) and the Basal Cambrian Excursion (BACE, ~539 Ma), both of which are preserved in marine carbonate successions from a variety of paleoenvironments across multiple paleocontinents. The dolostone-dominated Portfjeld Group of North Greenland preserves a pronounced negative δ¹³C excursion comparable to either the SWE or BACE, along with phosphatized microfossils below the nadir resembling purported early embryo-like metazoans from the late Ediacaran Doushantuo Formation of South China. Bulk-carbonate δ²³⁸U analysis of the Portfjeld Group reveals a pronounced positive shift to values comparable to modern carbonates near the nadir of the δ¹³C excursion, then return to more negative values. Similar inverse relationships between δ¹³C and δ²³⁸U in other SWE-bearing sections have been interpreted as evidence of transient global ocean oxygenation. However, this relationship could also reflect changes in uranium reduction kinetics related to oceanic carbonate saturation state, the expansion of ferruginous ocean conditions, or even diagenetic alteration. Here, we expand the Portfjeld Group record using δ⁷Li, ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, δ⁸⁸/⁸⁶Sr, and new δ²³⁸U measurements from chromatographically separated U(VI) and U(IV) fractions. This approach allows us to further evaluate potential causes of the positive bulk carbonate δ²³⁸U shift recorded in the Portfjeld Group. Parallel U(VI) and U(IV) analyses of the Doushantuo Formation enables comparison between two similar, yet paleogeographically distant successions, with initial analysis showing both sections are largely dominated by the U(VI) fraction. A pronounced negative excursion in δ⁷Li to near crustal values at the nadir of the δ¹³C excursion suggests intense congruent weathering of the continents, an expression similar to the SWE of South China and Siberia. δ⁸⁸/⁸⁶Sr values remain elevated throughout the succession (some of the highest recorded in Earth history) and are potentially even more enriched coincident with the nadir of the δ¹³C excursion, suggesting the existence of a large 88 Sr-depleted sink somewhere in the oceans potentially related to rapid authigenic carbonate precipitation. Together, these proxies provide a framework for distinguishing global ocean redox change from local depositional effects and post-depositional alteration.

title: Beyond Pearson: Nonparametric Correlation Coefficients Quantify New Elemental Associations in a Porphyry Copper Geochemical Database
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Hadden, Karlie M. [1], Quesada, Lauren J. [2], Holley, Elizabeth A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Mining Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(3) Mining Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO,
abstract: Porphyry copper deposits (PCDs) and their associated mineralized environments, such as skarns and epithermal deposits, are the world’s largest sources of copper and molybdenum, major sources of gold and silver, and large contributors of critical elements such as tellurium and selenium. These high-tonnage, multi-commodity deposits make PCDs an attractive exploration target offering opportunities for coproduct production, byproduct recovery, and waste valorization of critical elements. To increase exploration success, mining companies rely on porphyry indicator minerals (PIMs), porphyry vectoring and fertility tools (PVFTs), and pathfinder elements. However, the correlation coefficients that underpin such tools have introduced a bias that has gone largely unexamined. This study represents the first application of Chatterjee’s correlation coefficient in tandem with Spearman's correlation coefficient to a large-scale porphyry-based geochemical data set. Both Chatterjee and Spearman correlation coefficients are nonparametric, rank-based, and characterize broader classes of associations without requiring distributional assumptions. Applied to a geochemical database, this approach reveals elemental associations that differ meaningfully from Pearson’s correlation coefficient, which is commonly used for geochemical vectoring and exploration targeting. Few elements in this dataset meet the assumptions required for classical Pearson-based inference. Where Spearman and Chatterjee’s coefficients diverge from Pearson’s, they frequently identify stronger or additional copper associations, including common byproduct critical minerals rhenium and selenium, which are recovered during porphyry copper processing methods. These results identify candidate pathfinder elements alongside the established suite and indicate that correlation coefficient choice carries direct consequences for both critical mineral-focused and copper-focused exploration targeting. We advocate broader implementation of Chatterjee’s and Spearman’s correlation coefficients, alongside rigorous evaluation of distributional assumptions, as standard practice in geochemical analysis.
