title: Crustal evolution of the Albany-Fraser Orogen, Western Australia, revealed by integreated U-Pb, Lu-Hf, and Sm-Nd isotope systematics of granulites
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Bedoya, Johan [1], Vervoort, Jeff David [2], Hammerli, Johannes [3], Valencia, Victor A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
(2) Washington State University, Pullman, WA,
(3) Washington State University School of the Environment, Pullman, WA,
(4) ZirChron LLC, Tucson, AZ,
abstract:
The Albany–Fraser Orogen (AFO) and its Mesoproterozoic assemblage of igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks records the final stage of the Precambrian evolution of Western Australia. This highly deformed orogenic belt preserves a long history of crustal growth, deformation, and reworking influenced by multiple tectonic events. Processes like accretion, crustal thickening, high P-T metamorphism, and widespread deformation characterise the AFO’s Stage I (~1.3 Ga); while the continuous deformation, intracrustal reworking, and high-temperature granulite-facies metamorphism are related to the AFO’s Stage II (1.2-1.1 Ga). However, this tectonic framework has largely been developed based on zircon U-Pb ages, which primarily record the timing of magmatic crystallization and may not accurately record and constrain the timing of deformation or peak metamorphism.

To better constrain the orogenic timeline and resolve the timing of metamorphic and tectonic processes, we integrate whole-rock and mineral Lu-Hf and Sm-Nd isotope systematics with zircon U-Pb geochronology. We focus on Granulite-facies gneisses from three different units of the Albany-Fraser Orogen - the Nornalup Zone (1.8 - 1.6 Ga), the Biranup Zone, and the Barren Basin (all 1.8 - 1.6 Ga).

Our preliminary zircon ages are consistent with previous reports, yielding crystallization ages between 1.6 and 1.2 Ga. Most garnet Sm-Nd ages overlap in a narrow range at 1.17 Ga, which corresponds to the Stage II metamorphic event. Similarly, most garnet Lu-Hf ages yield ages between 1.26 and 1.18 Ga. One of the Nornalup Zone samples, however, yields an older Lu-Hf and Sm-Nd garnet age: 1.35 Ga and 1.23 Ga, respectively, which indicates an earlier metamorphic event, mostly related to Stage I. These analyses indicate that individual rock units may preserve distinct stages of the orogenic history in mineral phases beyond zircon, enabling a more complete and precise reconstruction of the timing and evolution of the Albany-Fraser Orogen. In addition to our multi-phase, multi-isotope geochronological approach, we use garnet mineral chemistry and compositional mapping to link isotopic ages to specific metamorphic processes and develop a robust, well-constrained model of the metamorphic evolution of the Albany-Fraser Orogen.

title: Characterizing the Rheology of Serpentinized Metaultramafic Lenses in the Condrey Mountain Schist, California
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Ribble, Ethan [1], Tewksbury-Christle, Carolyn M. [2], Behr, Whitney M. [3], Sherpa, Tshering [4], Condit, Cailey Brown [5], Poulaki, Eirini M. [6]
affiliations: (1) Fort Lewis College, Durango, CO, USA
(2) Fort Lewis College, Durango, CO,
(3) ETH Zurich, Zurich,
(4) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(5) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(6) Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA,
abstract:
Transient accelerated motion along modern subducting plate interfaces results in long duration surface deformation (slow slip) and low frequency earthquakes (tremor). Although slow slip and tremor (SST) mechanisms remain enigmatic, mafic and/or ultramafic rheologies are hypothesized to facilitate SST. The Lower Condrey Mountain Schist (CMS), a Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous subduction complex, comprises hemipelagic protoliths punctuated by meter- to kilometer-scale fully serpentinized ultramafic lenses sourced from ophiolites in the overriding plate, all metamorphosed at epidote-blueschist facies conditions (ca. 460°C, 1 GPa). Lower CMS serpentinites have comparable length scales to modern tremor sources and deformed at conditions consistent with modern SST. The timing of serpentinization (pre-, syn-, or post-subduction) remains poorly constrained, resulting in potential shear zone rheologies ranging from peridotite to serpentine. To evaluate the prograde rheology of these lenses and their potential link to SST, we characterized deformation, serpentinizing fluids, and serpentine species using field observations, serpentine ∂ 18 O and ∂D isotopes, and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD).

These serpentinites have anastomosing foliations that wrap centimeter- to meter-scale blocks of massive, non-foliated serpentinite. Both massive and well-foliated serpentinites are primarily antigorite. Serpentine (±magnetite±brucite) veins occur sporadically throughout both massive phacoids and well-foliated serpentinites and formed pre-, syn-, or post-foliation development. Post-foliation veins crosscut the subvertical foliation, are primarily lizardite, and have no systematic orientation pattern. Preliminary stable isotope analyses on foliated and massive serpentinites are most consistent with low-temperature serpentinization in equilibrium with seawater. In a km-scale lens, ∂ 18 O increases towards the structural center and has no relation to deformation style (massive or sheared).

Preliminary results suggest pre-subduction seafloor serpentinization, implying that serpentine (antigorite) rheology governed deformation at peak P-T conditions. Post-foliation veins formed after peak conditions (<350°C based on lizardite stability at 1 GPa), but the timing is unclear due to the lack of systematic orientations. Preliminary spatial ∂ 18 O patterns suggest minimal interaction with metasediment-derived fluids that would indicate syn-subduction serpentinization, but additional stable isotope and serpentine-magnetite geothermometry results will further characterize the temperatures and origin of fluids during serpentinization and deformation. The kilometric length scales of serpentinite bodies in the CMS suggest that they could define tremor sources, with accelerated frictional slip concentrated along antigorite foliation planes and/or brittle fracture accommodated within syn-subduction vein networks in more massive serpentinite lenses.

title: Expanding Topographically Derived Groundwater Models for Coastal Infrastructure Assessment on Edisto Island, SC
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Dickert, John Chandler [1], Levine, Norman S. [2], Wilson, Alicia M. [3], Abioye, Riliwan Damilola [4]
affiliations: (1) Environmental and Sustainability Studies, College of Charleston, Charleston, SC, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Geosciences, College of Charleston, CHARLESTON, SC, USA
(3) School of Earth ,Ocean, and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA
(4) School of Earth, Ocean, and Environment, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA
abstract:
Topographically derived groundwater models provide a practical, low-resource alternative to traditional groundwater models such as MODFLOW and FEFLOW for assessing groundwater dynamics and infrastructure vulnerability in coastal environments. This study applies a GIS-based workflow, adapted from recent research in Beaufort County, South Carolina, to model groundwater elevation and depth-to-groundwater on Edisto Island, South Carolina. The methodology integrates NOAA 2-ft LiDAR-derived Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), Mean Higher High-Water (MHHW) data, C-CAP land-use classifications, and USGS hydrologic datasets to generate continuous groundwater surfaces using Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation.

The resulting groundwater model provides a flexible framework for evaluating present-day conditions and simulating future sea-level rise scenarios by adjusting coastal boundary conditions. When coupled with NOAA sea-level rise scenarios, this methodology can be used to develop predictive groundwater models that forecast changes in groundwater elevations and identify areas where future inundation is likely to impact critical infrastructure. Additionally, by incorporating Soil Conservation Service Curve Number (SCS-CN) rainfall-runoff modeling, the methodology also captures the combined effects of precipitation-driven runoff and elevated groundwater, creating a predictive tool for assessing compound flooding hazards. This approach enables planners and resource managers to better understand how rising groundwater tables associated with sea-level rise may affect vulnerable coastal infrastructure.

The integration of groundwater and runoff modeling offers new insight into the future performance of buried infrastructure, including building basements, underground utility corridors, pipelines, stormwater systems, and septic systems that are increasingly susceptible to groundwater inundation. Unlike traditional groundwater models that require extensive hydrogeologic characterization and computational resources, this topographically derived approach can be implemented using widely available geospatial datasets, making it well suited for local governments and coastal communities with limited resources. The methodology provides an efficient and scalable framework for forecasting groundwater responses to sea-level rise while supporting resilience planning, infrastructure management, and adaptation strategies for vulnerable coastal landscapes.

title: Learning on the Go: Investigating Secondary Science Teacher Development Through an Inquiry-Based Field Course
session_title: Iris Moreno Totten Research in Geoscience Education Session
authors: Gunnell, Nathan V. [1], Searls, Mindi L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
(2) Center for Science, Mathematics, and Computer Education, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract:
The Methods in Geoscience Field Instruction course at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln is a 16-day immersive professional learning experience for pre-service and in-service secondary science teachers. Grounded in inquiry-based pedagogy, the course engages participants in authentic geoscience investigations across Nebraska, Wyoming, and South Dakota. Teachers work as learners in the field, posing scientific questions, constructing interpretations from evidence, and grappling with uncertainty while consistently reflecting on the experience and its implications for their own classrooms.

This study investigates how teachers describe the immediate and lasting influence of this immersive experience on their pedagogical beliefs, epistemological orientations, affective experiences, and instructional practice. Final course reflections are being analyzed using maximum variation sampling to capture differences in discipline, grade level, school setting, and teaching experience. Initial reflections were analyzed inductively to identify emergent themes and develop a codebook, which was refined through independent coding and reconciliation. Retrospective interviews with participants who completed the course between 2016 and 2024 provide a complementary longitudinal perspective, allowing examination of how changes described immediately following the course persist and shape professional practice over time.

Preliminary findings suggest that participants closely connect their experiences as learners in the field with how they subsequently approach inquiry-based teaching. Reflections indicate increased comfort with uncertainty and productive struggle, greater appreciation for collaborative knowledge-building, enhanced confidence in facilitating inquiry, and shifts in how participants conceptualize science learning and teaching. Classroom transfer emerged as a prominent theme, with teachers describing ways they adapted both the practices and principles of field-based inquiry for use in their own classrooms. Interview data extend these findings by providing examples of how participants continue to draw upon course experiences years later when designing instruction, facilitating inquiry, and supporting student learning.

These findings suggest that immersive field experiences can support teacher development not only through geoscience content learning, but also through experiences that reshape teachers' perspectives as learners and educators. Ongoing analysis will further examine how inquiry, reflection, and field-based sensemaking contribute to lasting changes in professional identity and instructional practice and will identify design principles for future field-based professional learning programs.

title: Using Variability in Flow Characteristics to Identify Possible Source Locations for the Malpais Hills Volcanics in the Knight Range, Southwestern New Mexico
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Shuler, Larry Allen [1], Stevens, Liane M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Aviation Sciences, Stephen F Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
(2) Earth and Aviation Sciences, Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, Texas, USA
abstract: The Knight Range of southwestern New Mexico exhumes a sequence of Eocene to Oligocene ignimbrites and andesitic flows, capped by the intermediate to mafic flows of the 32.6 ± 0.4 Ma Malpais Hills volcanics. While originally mapped as the “Latite and Andesite of Malpais Hills,” recent work suggests that these rocks have slightly more mafic compositions, including basaltic andesites, basaltic trachyandesites, and latite-basalts. While the older, intermediate to felsic volcanic units in the Knight Range have been correlated with either the Bootheel or the Mogollon-Datil volcanic fields on the basis of geochronology, the age of the Malpais Hills volcanics prevents similar correlation with regional sources, and a local source(s) has been suggested. Fieldwork conducted in Knight Canyon in June 2026 focused on the hypothesis that compositional and textural variations and flow indicators could be used to identify unique flows, flow directions, and/or source locations for the Malpais Hills volcanics. Work included collection of oriented samples along the unit’s strike, collection of orientation data for flow indicators (e.g., flattened or elongate vesicles and amygdules; aligned phenocrysts), and identification of possible flow surfaces. In the study area the Malpais Hills volcanics are characterized by reddish-brown (10R 3/4) to gray (N7), fine-grained lava flows that may contain mm- to cm-scale flattened, elongate vesicles and/or amygdules, as well as mm-scale olivine and pyroxene phenocrysts. Brecciated layers that contain clasts of mafic-intermediate rocks appear to separate distinct lava flows within the Malpais Hills volcanics, consistent with autobrecciation. Previously undescribed layers of red-brown tuff within the Malpais Hills volcanics were also observed. Future work will include petrographic analysis of oriented thin sections, X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), and analysis of orientation data and map patterns using stereonets and QGIS in order to describe variation in mineralogy, geochemistry, and/or flow direction, and to identify individual lava flows and their (possibly unique) sources.

title: Elemental Signatures of Graptolite Internal Casts and Associated Iron-Rich Debris Below the Silurian Lau Event, Henryhouse Formation, South-Central Oklahoma
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record
authors: McCauley, Christopher Michael [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA
abstract:
The discovery of rare internal graptolite casts within the informal lower member of the Late Silurian Henryhouse Formation at two sections in the Arbuckle Mountains of Oklahoma has prompted new questions regarding what taphonomic and diagenetic conditions enabled the casts’ preservation.

Bulk rock processed through formic acid for the purposes of conodont study yielded insoluble residues containing the casts as well as other conglomerations of fine quartz sediment, limonite, and other iron-rich compounds. At the most complete section studied, the casts come from the lower-middle portion of Unit 3 of the lower member, within the Polygnathoides siluricus conodont zonation and approximately 2.5-3.5 meters below the top of the lower member and the disconformity locally associated with the Lau Event. A preliminary investigation has been initiated targeting the elemental composition of excess internal graptolite casts and the iron-rich debris associated with them, using HNO 3 -HCl digestion and a Shimadzu ICPMS-2030.

The iron-rich residue appears to preserve partial geochemical evidence of one or more taphonomic or diagenetic processes. The soluble fraction of the residue is strongly dominated by Fe and also contains abundant Ca, Mg, and Al. Substantial Zn and Pb occur with elevated V, Cu, Co, Ni, As, Mo, Se, Sb, and other trace metals. Repeated measurements and dilution comparisons support the broad Fe-rich and metal-enriched signature. The elemental association is most consistent with a mixed assemblage of Fe-bearing cements, altered sulfide phases, and secondary oxides or hydroxides that concentrated or retained trace metals during early diagenesis and later alteration.

These casts were likely created when the internal cavities of the organic graptolite rhabdosomes infilled with sediment, creating localized reducing microenvironments in which sulfate reduction and sulfide precipitation occurred and trace metals were concentrated. Later oxidation may have converted much of the original iron sulfide to oxide, hydroxide, sulfate, or carbonate phases while retaining part of a metalliferous bottom water signal.

Alternatively, a significant fraction of the metals may have been transported by a later metal-enriched diagenetic fluid. Additional samples from the lower and upper members of the Henryhouse Formation must be tested to establish whether the Fe-rich, metal-bearing signature intensifies toward the Lau Event, varies with fossil content, or occurs throughout the formation.

title: Evaluating Health Effects and Environmental Justice Concerns of Uranium and Arsenic Groundwater Exposure on Navajo Lands
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Rock, Tommy [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
abstract:
The geologic profile of the western United States naturally produces elevated concentrations of arsenic and uranium in regional groundwater systems, a condition that has historically been compounded by extensive hard rock mining. Across the Navajo Nation, the largest contiguous Native American Nation in the American Southwest, a century-long legacy of mining activity intersects with limited public water infrastructure. Consequently, many residents rely on unregulated water sources that pose ongoing human health risks from toxic metal exposure. Distinguishing between natural background concentrations and anthropogenic inputs remains a critical challenge, as past uranium mining continues to affect unregulated water supplies. Addressing these co-occurring contaminants requires long-term hydrogeochemical monitoring and community-engaged research frameworks that directly inform Navajo tribal leaders and residents.

Recent epidemiological literature highlights substantial concerns about uranium's chemical toxicity in drinking water. Toxicological evidence strongly links chronic uranium ingestion to renal toxicity, reproductive harm, and DNA damage. However, epidemiological evidence from human populations exposed via drinking water remains limited—particularly for cardiovascular and oncogenic outcomes—largely because long-term cohort studies with individual-level exposure assessments are scarce. Despite these observational gaps, environmental justice concerns remain acute, given the disproportionately high exposure levels borne by rural Indigenous communities. Field assessments confirm this hazard: in an analysis of unregulated drinking water wells across Navajo lands, 10 of 185 samples (5.4%) exceeded uranium maximum contaminant levels set by the Safe Drinking Water Act.

Since 2003, sustained community-engaged monitoring initiatives have systematically quantified uranium and arsenic concentrations in unregulated wells across the western Navajo Nation. These ongoing collaborative efforts serve a dual purpose: bridging critical scientific gaps in environmental exposure data and empowering tribal governance with actionable evidence. Combining rigorous water quality analysis with direct community partnerships ensures that health data are transparently shared and culturally contextualized. Ultimately, prioritizing exposure mitigation, infrastructure investment, and targeted research is vital to addressing historical environmental injustices and securing safe, sustainable groundwater for future generations on Native lands.

title: Functional Diversity Shifts Across the Ediacaran Period Suggest Multiple Drivers for the Rise of Complex Animals
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Craffey, Matthew Philip [1], Shupinski, Alex [2], Darroch, Simon A.F. [3], Lyons, S. Kathleen [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(2) Natural Resources Department, South Dakota State University, Brookings, South Dakota, USA
(3) Paläozoologie, Senckenberg Forschungsinstitut und Naturmuseum Frankfurt, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
(4) School of Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Lincoln, NE, USA
abstract:
The Ediacaran period witnessed critical evolutionary innovations and ecological transitions for animal life. These constitute assemblage-defining shifts in occupied habitat, species-habitat interactions, dominant morphological groups, and environmental pressures. However, the temporal and spatial impacts on animal diversity remains poorly characterized, particularly with respect to the functional diversity of Ediacaran paleocommunities which, per modern ecological theory, should have responded strongly to proposed shifts in environmental pressures and species interactions.

To address this, we used newly assembled occurrence and trait data to quantify how multiple indices of functional diversity changed across local and global spatial scales. We also tested how functional and taxonomic beta diversity changed between Ediacaran assemblages to identify how these components of biodiversity were distributed across space, and how distribution patterns may have changed over time.

At global scales, we find that Ediacaran functional diversity broadly follows patterns of macroevolutionary change. However, at local scales we find evidence for trait-mediated habitat filtering across the Ediacaran. This becomes acute in the latest Ediacaran where 1) local functional diversity drops precipitously compared to global functional diversity and 2) beta functional diversity sharply increases, indicating a change in the spatial distribution of traits.

These shifts may reflect the onset of new an integrated disturbance regime. For example, the onset of bioturbation and shifts in ocean anoxia may have stressed ecological communities but with significant spatial heterogeneity. Thus, late Ediacaran functional and taxonomic diversity was maintained through the occupancy of narrow ecological niches subject to more complex distribution patterns. Such a change may have promoted new ecological strategies able to exploit shifts in habitat availability over space and time. However, while a potential contributor to evolutionary change over the Ediacaran-Cambrian transition, we emphasize that this integrated disturbance regime represents a temporally restricted balance of ecological and environmental pressures. Late Ediacaran fauna are not merely a stepping stone to phanerozoic ecosystems but a unique biota in aggregate, expressing distinct patterns of functional and taxonomic diversity.

title: 2026 Status of a South Pole-Aitken Basin Sample Return and Exploration Rover Concept
session_title: Planetary Exploration and Education: How We Learn About Our Solar System and Beyond
authors: Kerber, Laura [1], Keane, James [2]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Lab, California Institute Technology, Pasadena, CA,
(2) Jet Propulsion Laboratory / California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(3) Jet Propulsion Laboratory / California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
abstract:
Endurance is a mission concept for a long-range, highly autonomous lunar rover designed to explore the farside of the Moon and the largest, oldest, and deepest impact basin: South Pole-Aitken (SPA). Sample return from the SPA basin represents an opportunity to address some of the highest priority questions in lunar science, including bounding the basin chronology of the Moon to assess the validity of the late heavy bombardment hypothesis, collecting deeply exposed samples of lunar lower crust or mantle material to determine how the differentiation of the Moon produced its chemical structure, and determining the effects of mega-basin formation on the crusts of planetary bodies. Endurance would traverse 2,000 kilometers, acquire a large volume of in-situ data, and collect up to 100 kg of samples for delivery to Artemis astronauts at the lunar south pole in the early 2030s. This concept represents a new way to explore, combining next-generation rover autonomy and a powerful partnership between human and robotic explorers. Endurance would address long-standing planetary science questions about the formation and early evolution of the Solar System and terrestrial worlds. Endurance was developed during the recent 2023-2032 Planetary Science and Astrobiology Decadal Survey, which identified this concept as the highest priority for NASA's Lunar Discovery and Exploration Program.

In 2025, NASA convened the South Pole-Aitken sample Return and eXploration (SPARX) Science Definition Team (SDT) to define requirements for the mission concept. In parallel to the SDT, there has been substantial progress with technology developments for the Endurance rover, culminating in a Mission Concept Review (MCR) at the end of June. Key challenges for the Endurance concept have included power and thermal designs that operate across a wide range of latitude (from central SPA at ~55°S to the Artemis basecamp at ~90°S), traverse planning, and autonomy. JPL has developed a new half-scale rover test platform to test these technologies, ERNEST (Exploration Rover for Navigating Extreme and Sloped Terrains), and has successfully performed field tests with autonomous, high-speed, day/night driving. Information presented about the Endurance rover concept is pre-decisional and is provided for planning and discussion purposes only.

title: Modelling Soil CO2: Assumptions, Approaches, Sensitivities and Key Concepts
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade
authors: Breecker, Dan [1], Cerling, Thure E. [2], Quade, Jay [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
(3) Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract: Modeling soil CO 2 and its stable carbon isotope composition is useful for the study of ancient terrestrial environments and modern soils. We first discuss some of the common assumptions made in soil CO 2 models, particularly the assumption of steady state. We show that most of the time, in most soils, the steady state assumption is probably associated with minimal error. However, during rapid perturbations, transience over a period of several days can result in steady-state inferred δ 13 C values of respired CO 2 that are several per mil lower than actual. In soils with high water contents and/or those buffered at a high pH, transience can persist for much longer. Therefore, whether or not transient state must be considered depends on the soil(s) and question(s) of interest. We provide examples in which the steady state (inferring shifts in the relative abundance of C 3 and C 4 plants on ancient landscapes from paleosol carbonates) and the transient state (investigating changes in the source of respired carbon in response to pulse precipitation events) approach are appropriate. We then discuss model sensitivities and show that the largest sensitivities are themselves sensitive to model input. These metasensitivities complicate the most common geologic applications of the model. Finally, we review some key concepts, including the distinctions between 1) net flux versus gross flux and 2) soil CO 2 (a concentration) versus soil-respired CO 2 (a flux). We end by introducing a web-based graphical user interface that is now available for the steady state model.

title: Colorful Colorado: Photochromic reactions and crystal lattice modifications in Colorado mineral samples
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Guerrero, Camryn Michelle [1], Kackstaetter, Uwe Richard [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Denver, CO,
abstract: Several minerals have been known to express a color changing property when exposed to sunlight. The term for this reaction is photochromism. The type of light that usually prompts this color response is ultraviolet (UV) light, since UV radiation can lead to permanent alterations to the crystalline structure in certain mineral samples. Color changes in minerals commonly found in Colorado were examined through multiple tests to determine if certain wavelengths of light produce a faster or more vibrant change in the hue of a sample. The minerals collected for this study include amethyst, barite, celestine, smoky quartz, and fluorite. These samples were exposed to infrared, shortwave UV, longwave UV, and natural sunlight for up to ten hours. Infrared radiation (700–800 nm) produced no observable color change in any sample. In contrast, fluorite and barite exhibited distinct color changes when exposed to shortwave UV light (254 nm), longwave UV light (365 nm), and sunlight. Amethyst, celestine, and smoky quartz showed no visible response under any of the tested conditions. X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis was conducted on both altered and unaltered samples of fluorite and barite to further examine the origin of the color changing reaction. The XRF data indicates that samples that contained trace elemental impurities exhibited a change in color. This demonstrates that the existence of color centers in the crystal lattice is associated with trace impurities found in the samples that changed color.

title: Remote Sensing and Field Observations of Ice-Surface Texture and Sediment Abundance at Lakes Joyce and Fryxell, Antarctica: Implications for Depositional Models of Perennially Ice-Covered Lakes
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology
authors: Rivera-Hernández, Frances [1], Mackey, Tyler J. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract: Constraining variability in ice-surface texture and sediment properties in perennially ice-covered lakes (PICLs) is important for interpreting lake-bottom facies and predicting impacts on benthic microbial mats. Ice surface roughness controls sediment accumulation, while sediment properties (grain size, albedo, and abundance) and ice thickness influence melt-driven migration through the ice. These processes control sediment amount, distribution, and depositional style on the lake bottom, as well as light transmission and sediment delivery to benthic microbial mats. However, long-term, lake-wide observations jointly characterizing ice-surface roughness and sediment abundance are lacking, limiting evaluation of depositional models and predictions of PICL responses to environmental change. Here, we combine field observations and remote sensing to characterize the ice covers of Lakes Joyce and Fryxell, Antarctica. We use airborne LiDAR and field observations to establish lake-wide ice-surface morphology and Sentinel-1 C-band synthetic aperture radar data (10 m/pxl; HH and HV polarizations) to evaluate temporal changes in ice surface radar texture. Radar texture is calculated as the local standard deviation of HH and HV backscatter within 3x3-pixel neighborhoods for individual observations and monthly median composites. We apply spectral mixing analysis to Sentinel-2 imagery (10 m/pxl) to map sediment abundance and compare with Sentinel-1 radar texture, ice-cover thickness, and under-ice photosynthetically active radiation (PAR). Preliminary results suggest that radar texture exhibits seasonal cycles, with lake-wide values highest during austral summer and lowest during austral winter. At Lake Joyce, HV exhibits a greater seasonal range than HH, although neither polarization shows an obvious long-term trend. Lake Fryxell also exhibits greater seasonal variability in HV than HH, but both show a sustained baseline increase starting in 2022. This shift in Lake Fryxell coincides with documented ice-cover thinning, an increase in sediment abundance in 2022 followed by a decline in 2024, and increased under-ice PAR. We hypothesize that elevated summer radar texture in these PICLs reflects increased ice-surface roughness due to seasonal ablation and sediment-induced melting. For Lake Fryxell, we further hypothesize that the 2024 decline in ice-surface sediment and PAR increase reflects increased sedimentation to the lake bottom and predict this will reduce ice-surface roughness over time. Ongoing work will test these hypotheses by completing remote sensing analyses and comparing results with field observations of the ice cover and lake-bottom deposits to inform PICL depositional models.

title: The Quest for Detrital Muscovite 40Ar/39Ar Ages of Zero - How Close Can We Get?
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Hames, Willis [1], Wijbrans, Jan [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences, Vrije Universitet, Amsterdam, North Holland, Netherlands
abstract: Detrital muscovite has proven useful in tectonic and sedimentological studies to providing a record of the distributions of cooling ages for exhumation of the mid-crustal lithologies within the catchment to a drainage system (Hodges et al., 2005). Single-crystal 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages for detrital muscovite crystals in ancient strata sensibly provide a maximum estimate of the time for deposition of ancient strata and allow a window on the surface geology at the time of deposition. Considering the youngest detrital muscovite ages observed in modern sediment are ca. 0.2-2.0 Ma (e.g., Gemignani et al., 2018), the mathematics and kinetics for argon diffusion in muscovite (to predict radiogenic 40 Ar-retention and hence isotopic ‘closure’ well above 400°C), and the statistical and instrumentation limits inherent to sector mass spectrometry, it appears that accurate resolution of detrital muscovite 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages is possible within or above the youngest ages reported (i.e., > 0.2-2.0 Ma). Such young detrital muscovite ages require astounding rates of exhumation (rates at or above 1 cm/yr integrated over ~ 10 6 years) and extreme tectonic environments, including extrusion in deep orogenic hinterlands ( e.g., G.E. Batt, 2001; E.J. Hill et al., 1992 ) and orogenic syntaxes where the incision of major rivers couples with tectonic instability to form ‘tectonic aneurysms’ (Zeitler et al., 2001). This presentation offers consideration of the myriad variables that define the younger limit to what we can presently expect to observe in detrital muscovite geochronology, with examples of modern and well-constrained ancient orogenic settings where these conditions align to form the youngest detrital muscovite. Although very young ages for such thermochronometers (that typically retain their radiogenic products within the mid-crust) are hallmarks of extreme tectonic environments, they are not atypical or isolated, but rather are coincident and distributed in time and space with Earth’s highest orogenic topographies.

abstract: The Sandal Shaft locality of the San Esteban Rockshelter in southwest Texas has yielded more than 20 perishable weapons dating to ca. 6,500 cal. BP and multiple superposed combustion features with ages ranging from ca. 11,000-15,500 cal. BP. Based on the stratigraphy of the Sandal Shaft, there are at least two separate occupational events: one during the terminal Pleistocene and another during the mid-Holocene. Interspersed throughout the various site occupations are thousands of faunal remains as well as packrat ( Neotoma sp.) middens. In this talk, I will present initial results as well as some problems encountered during our analysis of the faunal assemblage. The goal of our study is to: 1) gain a better understanding of how the physical environment of the Sandal Shaft locality changed through time, 2) how these changes effected the human use of space, and 3) what this can tell us about the human-environment relationships in the northern Chihuahuan Desert from the terminal Pleistocene through the Holocene.

title: Phosphatic Fossil Assemblages from the early Cambrian of northwestern Canada
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry
authors: Vayda, Prescott [1], Evans, Scott [2], Strauss, Justin [3], Xiao, Shuhai [4], Zhao, Alyssa [5], Lau, Kim [6], Garber, Joshua [7], Harding, Reina [8], Cobbett, Rosie [9]
affiliations: (1) Division of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA; Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(2) Division of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(5) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(6) Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(7) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland, United Kingdom
(8) Department of Earth Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(9) Department of Energy Mines and Resources, Yukon Geological Survey, Whitehorse, Yukon, Canada
abstract:
The early Cambrian is notable for the abundant preservation of invertebrate fossils closely associated with phosphatic minerals, including apatite skeletonization, cementation, and replacement. These fossils, often called small shelly fossils, are useful for biostratigraphic correlation and for the preservation of small and soft-bodied taxa that are often not otherwise preserved in the fossil record.

Here we describe two calcium phosphate-rich, fossil bearing carbonate units from the early Cambrian Ingta and Sekwi formations in Yukon territory, Canada. These units contain abundant phosphatized fossil material as well as phosphatic cements and laminae. Fossils from the Ingta Formation include internal molds of biomineralizing taxa such as Anabarites and phosphatic replacement of originally organic remains such as the tubular Rugatotheca . Additionally, these fossils are associated with microbially laminated phosphatized layers and intraclasts with phosphatic cements. Fossils from the Sekwi Formation include phosphatic internal molds of biomineralizing taxa such as archaeocyathids, phosphatic replacement of biomineralizing taxa such as helcionellids and trilobites, and originally phosphatic biomineralizers such as linguliformean brachiopods. Notably, the originally phosphatic brachiopods show evidence of secondary silicification, which is not observed in other phosphatized fossils from the deposit. This suggests that silicification may have happened before phosphatization of other materials or that the characteristics of the brachiopod shells made them more susceptible to silicification. The Sekwi Formation also bears apatite-cemented intraclasts but lacks microbially laminated phosphatic layers. The variety of materials preserved as apatite minerals including replacement textures, molds, and cements implies multiple phases of early diagenetic phosphatization. This inference is further supported by rare earth element data and uranium/lead ages for these phosphatic materials, which suggest their complex and protracted diagenetic and phosphogenesis history. The comparison of these two units from the same basin reveals how local and regional factors may affect this distinct taphonomic mode from the early Cambrian.

title: Entrepreneurially Minded Learning in Earth Science Education: Curiosity, Connections, and Creating Value in the Classroom
session_title: Learning to be a Geoscientist: Professional Exposure, Agency, and Transferable Skills in Undergraduate Education. (Posters)
authors: Leonard-Pingel, Jill [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Newark, OH, USA
abstract:
Earth Science education is evolving as we seek to prepare students to address complex Earth Science and environmental questions that are interdisciplinary, global in scope, and require collaboration and holistic thinking. In this new, ever-changing landscape, content knowledge alone is no longer sufficient; students must also develop grit, perseverance, and the confidence to embrace uncertainty and tackle difficult problems. While these skills can be challenging to cultivate in traditional classroom settings, Earth Science educators can learn from other disciplines that have long sought to develop these attributes in their students. One promising approach is Entrepreneurially Minded Learning (EML). Originally developed within business and management education to prepare future entrepreneurs and organizational leaders, EML has recently gained traction across STEM disciplines, particularly in engineering programs, as a means of equipping graduates with the mindsets and behaviors that support innovation, adaptability, and effective problem-solving. Central to EML are the three C's of the entrepreneurial mindset: Curiosity, Connections, and Creating Value. Although rooted in entrepreneurial education, these principles are not focused on business acumen or management skills. Rather, they represent broadly applicable competencies that are equally valuable for scientists, researchers, and Earth Science professionals, making them a natural fit for Earth Science education.

Integrating the 3 Cs into our classrooms may require pedagogical adjustments, including a willingness to prioritize skill development alongside content coverage. While this may reduce the amount of material addressed, the tradeoff is often increased student engagement and deeper investment in learning. Fortunately, educators have access to numerous examples of 3 C-focused activities through resources developed by the KEEN Foundation and hosted on the Engineering Unleashed website. In this presentation, I will explore the relevance of the 3 Cs to Earth Science education, discuss potential resources for instructors interested in exploring how to integrate 3 C classroom activities into their teaching, and highlight activities and instructional modifications I have implemented to intentionally nurture these competencies. These examples demonstrate that meaningful development of the 3 Cs can result from small, deliberate changes to classroom practice, yielding lasting impacts on student engagement, learning, and future success.

title: Firmground "Megaburrows" in the Lower Silurian Osgood Formation of Southwestern Ohio: The Spoor of Homalonotid Trilobites?
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Thomka, James [1], Brett, Carlton [2]
affiliations: (1) Center for Earth and Environmental Science, State University of New York at Plattsburgh, Plattsburgh, New York, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA
abstract: The lower Silurian (late Llandovery-early Wenlock; Telychian-Sheinwoodian) Osgood Formation is a mixed carbonate-siliciclastic unit that can be traced widely throughout the greater Cincinnati Arch region. The basal interval of this unit consists of a dolomitic carbonate bed sharply overlain by a variably thick interval of clayshale, the contact between these lithologies representing a major flooding surface, potentially associated with the highest eustatic highstand of the entire Silurian Period. At the former Cemex quarry near Fairborn, southwestern Ohio, the flooding surface contact between the basal Osgood carbonate and the overlying clayshale was exposed as a prominent bench, permitting examination of features present along that bedding plane. Although late-diagenetic dolomitization resulted in loss of most macrofossils, the surface was heavily bioturbated. An ichnofauna dominated by fodinichnia is documented (e.g., Chondrites , Rhizocorallium , Arthrophycus , Treptichnus -like forms), presumably reflecting mining for scarce organic matter distributed among fine sediments deposited during the early phase of significant base-level rise. However, the most prominent ichnofossils are exceptionally large (width of 10+ cm), slightly sinuous burrows with extremely sharp walls that cross-cut the fodinichnial burrows. The infill of these “megaburrows” is thoroughly mined by Chondrites , obscuring any potential bioglyphs or backfill structures that may have once been present, but such forms are consistent with particularly large forms of Cruziana . Both the sharpness of the burrow walls and the preferential mining of burrow-infilling sediment indicate that the “megaburrows” were emplaced in a firmground, probably developed during continued base-level rise. This would require appendages capable of excavating a large open burrow in firm sediments; hence, a large trilobite seems a probable tracemaker. This interpretation is further supported by the discovery of several articulated trilobite thorax segments of appropriate size to produce a “megaburrow”. The size and morphology of these skeletal remains suggest that the homalonotid trilobite Trimerus may have been responsible for generating such remarkable ichnofossils. Unfortunately, the surface at the quarry containing these fossils has subsequently been destroyed, leaving the images, measurements, and samples associated with this study as the only remaining records of these (likely trilobite-generated) burrows, which must be among the largest known from the early-middle Paleozoic. Nevertheless, this study serves to illustrate the extent to which Trimerus and other unusually large trilobites can influence the ichnological and sedimentological record.

title: Paleobotany of the Mingus Shale (Desmoinesian, Pennsylvanian), Palo Pinto County, Texas
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: King, Clifton Astor [1], Rosscoe, Steven J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Kimbell School of Geosciences, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA
(2) Kimbell School of Geosciences, Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX, USA
abstract: During the Middle Pennsylvanian, along the margins of the Eastern shelf of the Permian Basin, deltas prograded from the Ouchita Mountains in the east, into swampy lowland environments. River channels and flood plains crossing these lowlands created a variety of wetland and drier habitats in close proximity to one another. Plant fossils have been collected from two outcrops of the Mingus shale located 15 miles southwest of Mineral Wells, Texas. The western locality, at the base of the Lake Palo Pinto Creek spillway (MSPP), is less than two miles away from the eastern locality, Ward Mountain (WMTN). Floral assemblages of marattialean ferns, filicalean ferns, lycopsids, cordaitaleans, sphenopsids, pteridosperms and coniferophytes have been recovered from these sites. Despite the short distance between the localities, the degree of preservation and floral diversity varies significantly. Fossils collected from WMTN are large, well-articulated and represent a diverse flora. MSPP has produced smaller fragmented plants dominated by marattialean ferns and lacks many of the species found to the east. Large, well-preserved mats of two species of Sphenophyllum are present at WMTN while MSPP specimens are fewer in occurrence and of a single species. Large fern pinna have been recovered at WMTN whereas MSPP fern specimens are only fragments of pinnules. Several species are found only at WMTN including Mixonera sp ., Macroneuropteris sp ., and Neropteris sp. . Restricted to WMTN are specimens of Walchia, Annularia, Cordaitanthus, Calamites, Sigillaria and Stigmaria. Fragment size, diversity, and preservation increase as depositional distance from the paleo-shoreline decreases. The MSPP floral assemblage is interpreted as allochthonous, while the WMTN assemblage is parautochthonous.

title: Change in Ostracod Sexual Dimorphism in Response to the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM)
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Fearon, Julian [1], Clapham, Matthew E. [2], Self-Trail, Jean M. [3], Yasuhara, Moriaki [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, UC Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz, CA, USA

abstract: Ostracods are highly sexually dimorphic microbenthos that are some of the few multicellular fossils common in samples ranging through early Cenozoic hyperthermals, such as the Paleocene Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) (Hunt et al, 2017). The record of the PETM in the Atlantic Coastal Plain has excellent geochemical proxies, but fewer studies on how these environmental changes affected community composition and evolutionary trajectory of organisms. We measured length to height ratio amongst male and female adult ostracods to see if sexual dimorphism decreased with increased stress due to warming and acidification. Since shell dimension is linked to sexual fitness, changes in shell morphology can give us insight into evolutionary trade-offs between sexual selection and metabolic constraints. Shell formation is one of the most energy expensive maintenance processes in ostracods. However, shells provide protection from predators and display male sexual fitness (Fernandes et al. 2018). We found that sexual dimorphism lessened after the carbon isotope excursion (CIE). This may be due to a reduction in reproductive soft tissue structures, or possibly metabolic burden on making large tests. We found that this trend encompassed community change (in that species with less extreme sexual dimorphism made up a larger part of the community post-PETM than pre-PETM) and evolutionary change in single species.

title: Seasonal Variability (And Lack Thereof) of Living Benthic Foraminifera in Aransas Bay, Texas
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Lowery, Christopher Michael [1], Davis, Marcy [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Institute for Geophysics, Austin, TX, USA
(2) University of Texas, Institute for Geophysics, Austin, TX,
abstract:
Benthic foraminifera are important and often-used bioindicators in estuaries, providing important information on ecosystem response to metal pollution, eutrophication, and other anthropogenic disruptions. However, before we use monitoring to track deviations from a baseline, we must first determine what that baseline is. Since 2023 we have been collecting living (Rose Bengal stained) benthic foraminifera from Aransas Bay, TX, during the University of Texas’s Marine Geology and Geophysics Field Course, which takes place every May. Aransas Bay, like many Coastal Bend bays, experiences large variations in salinity throughout the year (from <10 to >40 PSU) and a gnawing concern about the Field Course data is that it only captures the late spring phase of that variability and is thus not representative of annual average change. To alleviate this concern, we carried out a sampling campaign in August, November, and February 2025-2026 at 25 stations across Aransas Bay. Combined with Field Course sampling in May 2026, this provides a full year’s worth of seasons for analysis. We found that, overall, the dominant genera (typically Ammonia or, closer to the inlet, an equal mix of Ammonia and Elphidium ) at each station across the bay are stable on a seasonal basis. There is variability in the minor component of assemblages, with miliolids, agglutinated foraminifera, bolivinids, and Buliminella elegantissima changing their proportions within the 10-20% of the assemblage not comprised of Ammonia and/or Elphidium . Overall living foraminifera abundance varies throughout the year, and peaks in May. Proportions of taxa in dead assemblages at individual stations are stable throughout the year.

Taken together these data indicate that 1) seasonal variability in Aransas Bay is mainly expressed as changes in total foraminifera and in the relative abundance of relatively rare taxa. Predominant genera do not change from season to season. This means that 2) annual sampling is sufficient to track long-term trends in dominant genera and 3) changes in dominant genera that occurred between 2023 and the last sampling in Aransas Bay in August 1951 are real and not an artifact of the month the samples were taken.

title: Rapid formation of beachrock drives landscape change and lithifies archaeological archives on Little Ambergris Cay, Turks and Caicos Islands
session_title: Geoarchaeology of the Land–Sea Interface: Processes, Preservation, and Palaeolandscape Reconstruction
authors: Cantine, Marjorie [1], Hibner, Brianna M. [2], Nash, Kyle [3], Pavia, Frank [4], Trower, Lizzy [5], Gomes, Maya L. [6], Sinelli, Peter [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,

(6) Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD,

abstract:
One of the last places on Earth reached by humans, the Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI) are low-lying carbonate islands that lie between the Caribbean Sea and the Atlantic. Abundant production of carbonate sediment in platformal waters, its rapid transport by wind and waves, and the speedy formation of beachrock create dynamic landscapes across this archipelago. Inhabitation by Lucayan peoples spans seven centuries on the TCI and includes multiple waves of migration, ceramic styles, and a high degree of cultural diffusion.

Our study site, a small TCI island, Little Ambergris Cay, yields rich radiocarbon and sedimentological datasets from both sediment core and outcrop. These datasets allow us to track the island’s evolution in space and time. Our results indicate that the island first nucleated on mid-Holocene antecedent topography, followed by rapid growth and accretion during the late Holocene. Our model for island growth provides quantitative rates for island accretion and growth. Our data demonstrate that the landscape changes rapidly, over human-relevant timescales. These results are further amplified by direct observations of both historical and Lucayan-era artifacts lithified within beachrock. We also present the results of in situ beachrock formation experiments that document beachrock formation over timescales of months. We document this mode of preservation and its extent on LAC. We leverage the results of in situ experiments, and integrate sedimentological observations from outcrop and sediment core, to present a process-based model to predict where and how artifacts preserved in this way may occur.

Holocene chronologies from the TCI—both archaeological and geological—which are currently critically limited by the inherent difficulty of translating radiocarbon measurements into precise, robust ages. We also present our efforts to more precisely date Lucayan sites and constrain a marine radiocarbon reservoir correction for the TCI by using paired terrestrial-marine samples, samples of known collection age, and paired U-Th/radiocarbon dating.

title: Sediment Movement in the Mackinaw River
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Hobson, Raegan [1], Tranel, Lisa [2], Peterson, Eric W. [3], Anders, Alison M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State University, Bloominton, IL, USA
(2) Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(3) Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(4) University of Illinois at Urbana-Champ, Urbana, IL, USA
abstract:
River channels change size and shape in response to their sediment load and streamflow. The rates of erosion and deposition can cause a river to deviate from its equilibrium state, in which it maintains its longitudinal profile and shape over time through processes like bed scour and erosion. Sediment transport and deposition affect many aspects of the ecosystem; excessive sediment can lead to poor water quality, algal blooms, and deposition build-up. Insufficient sediment can lead to channel incision, bank erosion, and changes in the particle-size composition of the channel bed. Understanding erosional and depositional processes throughout medium-gradient rivers is essential for effective sediment management and related habitat management, and for supporting ongoing conservation and understanding impacts on larger rivers. Our research aims to understand erosion and sediment transport in the Mackinaw River system, which flows through glaciated areas of central Illinois. This river is categorized as a medium-gradient river, meaning it has a slope between 0.51 and 2.0% and transports sediments from the Wisconsinan, Illinoian, and Pre-Illinoian glaciations to the Illinois River.

We will track coarse bedload sediment movement through a straight section and a bend in the river. By placing radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags in 100 sediment samples at each location. When we return to the field sites after increased flow events, we will use an antenna to detect the tags and record the identification number and location to track the samples' movements over time. We will measure cross-sections throughout the study to monitor changes in the riverbank and channel bed.

We will investigate the relationship between sediment mass and distance traveled. Masses of samples placed in the river range from 27.89g to 3600g. We expect the mass and distance traveled by the sediment in the Mackinaw River to be independent of each other due to the distribution of sizes across the river channel. We anticipate the cross sections to show little change in the channel bed due to the continuous availability of sediment input from glacial till. Greater change may occur along the riverbanks associated with bank undercutting and collapse or sediment accumulation along bars.

title: Forbidden zircons reveal Laurentia’s liaisons
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Amidon, William Henry [1], Cooper, Evan G.K. [2], Warner, Peter [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Climate Sciences, Middlebury College, Middlebury, Vermont, USA
(2) Earth and Climate Sciences Department, Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT, USA
(3) Earth and Climate Science Department, Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT, USA
abstract: Significant uncertainty remains around the exact timing and geometry of rifting along the eastern margin of Laurentia during the Neoproterozoic breakup of the supercontinent Rodinia. This study addresses these questions using a repository of “forbidden” detrital zircons (~765 to 940 Ma) found in Neoproterozoic and Early Cambrian cover sediments of eastern Laurentia. Numerous zircon age populations are observed, many of which are likely derived from conjugate terranes during the breakup of Rodinia. Comparison of these populations along the Laurentian margin and with potential conjugate sources suggests that the margin from southern Quebec to northern Tennessee accumulated Neoproterozoic sedimentary cover that included contributions from western Baltica. This cover was later eroded and/or recycled prior to and during the Sauk transgression. Zircon populations from Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic meta-sediments from the Oaxaca, Chortis, and Acatlan terranes of Mexico show strong similarities to the eastern United States and Quebec, suggesting they might have served as a sediment bridge between western Baltica and eastern Laurentia. The absence of “forbidden” ages in Cambrian cover sediments in Texas and the upper Midwest suggest the decaying Grenville orogeny acted as a topographic barrier, or that interior watersheds were flowing east or south during much of Neoproterozoic time. Finally, our zircon compilations strongly support origination of the Cuyania terrane of the Andean Precordillera from the Ouachita embayment of eastern Laurentia.

title: A lever to move the world: Late Devonian black shales, CO2 sequestration, and atmospheric O2 buildup
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology
authors: Segessenman, Daniel C. [1], Sahoo, Swapan K [2], Kaufman, Alan Jay [3], Gilleaudeau, Geoff J [4]
affiliations: (1) Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
(2) Shaligram Research Institute, Houston, TX, USA
(3) Geological, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA
(4) Atmospheric, Oceanic, Earth Sciences (AOES), George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
abstract:
The Devonian-Carboniferous transition (DCT) represents a critical transition in which forests expanded across the continents for the first time, vertebrates proliferated in terrestrial ecosystems, atmospheric oxygen levels rose to near modern levels (and above), and the Earth entered a prolonged icehouse period characterized by repeated glacial-interglacial cycles. Widespread organic-rich black shales deposited during the Middle to Late Devonian gave way to more carbonate-rich facies in the Early Mississippian in the shallow epeiric seas that covered much of the North American continent.

Continental-scale burial of organic matter is a well-known driver of both CO 2 sequestration and atmospheric O 2 buildup on geologic timescales based on the relatively simple mass balance of oxygenic photosynthesis. However, the extent to which the widespread deposition of Late Devonian organic-rich black shales across North America contributed to the global buildup of atmospheric O 2 and the sequestration of atmospheric CO 2 remains unknown. Here, we present estimates of rock quantity combined with a dataset of total organic carbon (TOC) from the Bakken Shale of the Williston Basin (present-day North Dakota, Montana, and Saskatchewan) to estimate potential global O 2 accumulation and CO 2 sequestration driven solely by the organic-rich Bakken Formation. We found that an estimated global p O 2 rise of 170 ppm and p CO 2 fall of 235 ppm would result from deposition of only 5 m of shale containing 10 wt.% TOC across the area of the Williston Basin alone.

This preliminary estimate suggests that deposition of organic-rich shales across North America during the Late Devonian may have had a globally significant impact on CO 2 sequestration and O 2 buildup across the DCT. Further analysis using more sophisticated rock quantity estimates from Macrostrat and more spatially abundant TOC values from multiple basins across North America will enable detailed characterization of the extent to which uniquely widespread deposition of organic-rich shale in North American epeiric seas may have contributed to critical climatic and biogeochemical changes across the DCT.

title: Projected Expansion and Subsequent Contraction of Alaska's Wildfire-Susceptible Area by 2100
session_title: High mountain headwaters: Snow, ice and alpine hydrology
authors: Putkonen, Jaakko Kalervo [1], Patterson, Hayden [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Institute Mining & Technology, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Geological Engineering, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, North Dakota, USA
abstract: Forest fires alter the environment in numerous and often significant ways, including the release of nutrients, proliferation of pioneer plants, opening of the canopy, increasing the runoff and erosion, and specifically in the Arctic regions, degradation of permafrost. As the forest fires are largely controlled by the climate and the Global Climate Models are predicting notable changes in the Arctic climate by 2100 there is reasonable expectation that areas affected by forest fires will shift geographically in the future. Currently existing fire models predict fires in the time scale of days and weeks, and no spatially discretized projections out to 2100 exist for Alaska. Therefore, there is ample motivation to determine how the area where the fires are most likely to occur may migrate in the future. We developed a seasonal dryness index based on historical fire and climate data which allows us to delineate the areas where most of the fires occurred and the largest area of forest burned in the past. We tracked the spatial distribution in GCM projected cells that fall below the seasonal dryness threshold. This allows us to predict where the majority of the fires will occur and the largest area will burn in the future. Our research shows that with the GCM projected changes in Alaskan climate, the predicted wildfire occurrence area will grow to be 43% greater than today’s area by 2052, and then decrease and be 39% smaller than today’s area by 2100. Moreover, the centroid of the predicted wildfire occurrence area will shift 431 (+-34) km North by 2100.

title: Impact on a Budget: Making Fossils and Launching a New Geoscience Outreach Program
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation
authors: Kelly, Bridget T. [1]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science, Southwest Minnesota State University, Marshall, Minnesota, USA
abstract:
As educators, we recognize the value of outreach in strengthening educational pathways into the geosciences. Positive outreach experiences, increased self-efficacy, and sustained mentorship contribute to student interest in geoscience programs and careers. These efforts are particularly important given that the geosciences remain one of the least diverse STEM disciplines, with relatively few students from diverse backgrounds entering the geoscience workforce.

For many early-career faculty, however, starting a new outreach program can seem challenging or even daunting, particularly when starting at a new institution or in a new region without an established network of community connections. The good news is that launching a successful outreach program is easier than many people realize. Early-career educators do not need to wait until they are fully established or deeply connected within their communities to begin outreach efforts.

Here, I will share preliminary outcomes and lessons learned from the first two years of launching a geoscience outreach program that has engaged more than 1,300 elementary students. Drawing on these experiences, I will discuss how new educators and anyone interested in starting a new outreach program can begin meaningful outreach with limited resources, including practical ideas for getting started, ways to leverage existing programs, and strategies for building community networks. I will also highlight a simple, low-cost, portable fossil-making activity that leaves a lasting impact on elementary students.

In addition to the benefits for elementary students, outreach programs can provide valuable opportunities for undergraduate and graduate student growth by strengthening résumés and building transferable workforce skills. Geoscience educators, particularly those in their early careers, may also benefit through interdisciplinary collaborations, service and community engagement, and professional development. Even small programs can create momentum that leads to new partnerships and future funding opportunities.

title: Seaway Closure, Oceanographic Restructuring, and Biodiversity Dynamics in the Neogene Tropical Eastern Pacific: A Multi-Proxy Study
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic (Posters)
authors: Fleisher, Noah [1]
affiliations: (1) Arizona Astrobiology Center, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract:
The modern Tropical Eastern Pacific (TEP) hosts extraordinary marine productivity and biodiversity, with strong coastal and equatorial upwelling fueling major fisheries, as well as the famous ecosystems of the Galápagos archipelago. However, prior to the Neogene formation of the Panama Isthmus and the closure of the Central American Seaway, warm Caribbean water would have flowed freely into the Pacific, producing vastly different oceanographic conditions. Here, we present a multi-proxy study linking seaway closure to increased upwelling and restructuring of TEP biodiversity and ecosystem dynamics across deep time.

Using sampling-normalized marine fossil occurrence records from The Paleobiology Database (PBDB), we reconstruct broad patterns in biodiversity across the Cenozoic, showing a significant increase in diversity continuing throughout the Miocene and Pliocene. Marine microfossil occurrence data from the Neptune Sandbox Berlin (NSB) database show stark differences in diatom abundance as compared with calcareous plankton (foraminifera and nannofossils) and radiolarians. While calcareous plankton and radiolarians were abundant in the TEP during the mid-Miocene, peaking around 14–15 Ma, diatoms were virtually absent until 11–12 Ma. Diatom diversity then began increasing as the other plankton groups declined. This shift is mirrored in ocean sediment composition, which exhibits a significant drop in weight percent CaCO 3 alongside an increase in biogenic silica. At the same time, there was a large influx of terrigenous sediment, indicating enhanced continental weathering as the Central American Seaway shoaled. While the other plankton groups recovered in the Pliocene, diatoms continued diversifying through the Pleistocene.

Because diatoms thrive in silica- and nutrient-rich waters, their Neogene proliferation, parallel to macroevolutionary diversification in the PBDB record, provides strong evidence for the establishment of modern, high-productivity TEP upwelling. Finally, stable isotope records contextualize these regional ecosystem dynamics and oceanographic shifts with the broader climatic changes occurring globally throughout the late Cenozoic.

title: Beyond Better Maps: Quantifying Geological Information Recovery Across UAS Remote Sensing Systems

authors: Soldano, Vincent Alexander [1], Hartshorn, Evan [2], Hibbard, Shannon [3], Calvin, Wendy [4], Sion, Brad [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NEVADA, USA; Division of Earth and Ecosystem Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Division of Earth and Ecosystem Sciences, Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV, USA

abstract:
Recent advances in uncrewed aerial system (UAS) imaging sensors have produced platforms with varying spectral capabilities, enabling direct evaluation of how spectral sampling and fidelity influence mineral discrimination in geologic mapping. However, the extent to which these improvements enhance geological interpretation has not been adequately quantified. Previous work has demonstrated that UAS imaging sensors can detect environmental hazards such as acid mine drainage (AMD) and identify diagnostic mineral species. However, complex spectral mixing in these environments complicates mineral discrimination and geologic interpretation. Our objective is to quantify how differences in UAS imaging sensor capabilities influence recoverable geological information. We hypothesize that UAS imaging sensors with greater spectral sampling and fidelity will recover more geological information, enabling more comprehensive site-scale characterization and improved detection of complex geochemical signatures.

We test our hypothesis by comparing three UAS remote sensing datasets from the Jones-Kinkaid Mine at Perry Canyon, Nevada, where seasonal AMD discharge and efflorescent sulfate minerals have been documented following remediation efforts. We compare MicaSense multispectral imagery with Headwall VNIR hyperspectral imagery and HySpex Mjolnir VS-620 hyperspectral imagery. Similar ground sampling distances of approximately 3 – 5 cm isolate spectral sampling and fidelity as the primary variables for comparison. Sensor outputs were compared through mineral classification, mapped alteration patterns, and spatial analyses to evaluate differences among the three datasets.

Comparison of the multispectral and hyperspectral datasets showed that all three sensors identified comparable alteration patterns while differing in the level of mineralogical detail recovered. These differences become increasingly important where broader spectral range, denser spectral sampling, and higher spectral fidelity provide additional diagnostic information for resolving complex mineral systems. These findings demonstrate how differences in spectral capability influence the quantity and quality of recoverable geological information, enabling more informed selection and application of remote sensing tools for geologic investigations.

title: Repeated Global Ocean Acidification Events during the Triassic-Jurassic Transition: Fluid Inclusion Analysis from Deep-Sea Bedded Cherts
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Hudgins, Michael Naylor [1], Olsen, Paul E [2], Schaller, Morgan Naylor [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA; Center for Environmental and Stable Isotope Analysis, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
(2) Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, NY, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA; Center for Environmental and Stable Isotope Analysis, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
abstract: Ocean acidification driven by emplacement of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) is widely invoked as the primary kill mechanism for the marine end-Triassic extinction (ETE; 201.564 Ma), yet direct evidence linking individual eruptive phases to episodes of acidification and biodiversity loss is elusive. We analyzed fluid inclusions preserved in deep-marine bedded cherts from the Inuyama succession, Japan, to reconstruct deep-ocean CO 2 concentrations ([CO 2 ] aq ) and carbonate chemistry through the Triassic-Jurassic transition. Fluid inclusion analyses reveal that deep-ocean [CO 2 ] aq tripled during the ETE, accompanied by pronounced decreases in pH and aragonite saturation state (Ω arag ) coincident with the initial marine faunal turnover. This pattern repeats ~650 kyr after the initial CO2 rise and is associated with another marine extinction. Astrochronologic correlation aligns these acidification events with the first and third CAMP eruptive phases recorded in the Newark Supergroup, establishing a temporal link between volcanically driven carbon release, deep Panthalassa acidification, and pulses of marine extinction. To evaluate the magnitude of carbon release required to generate these perturbations in the Inuyama fluid inclusion record, we used the interactive Long-term Ocean-Atmosphere-Sediment Carbon Cycle Reservoir (iLOSCAR) model. Model simulations indicate that multiple injections of ~50,000 Gt CO 2 reproduce the timing, magnitude, and structure of the reconstructed pH and Ω arag changes, supporting repeated CAMP-derived carbon release as the primary driver of marine extinctions during the Triassic-Jurassic transition. Together, the fluid inclusion record, astrochronology, and carbon cycle modeling provide evidence that pulsed volcanic CO 2 emissions triggered deep-ocean acidification and successive pulses of marine extinction during the ETE.

title: HOLSEA Datahub: An Open-Source Web Portal for Global Relative Sea-Level Data since the Last Glacial Maximum
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Khan, Nicole [1], Gu, Yifei [2], Creel, Roger [3], Mukherjee, Udita [4]

abstract:
Here, we present the HOLSEA Datahub, an integrated web portal designed to facilitate the standardized synthesis of relative sea-level (RSL) reconstructions since the Last Glacial Maximum. This comprehensive database comprises over 15,000 validated index and limiting points spanning all continents, enabling broad spatial comparisons that minimize bias. The database structure clearly distinguishes between primary observations and their interpretations, allowing datasets to be refined as methods and theories advance.

The portal provides dynamic visualization tools and statistical frameworks to explore spatiotemporal patterns of RSL change. Through an interactive interface, users can query and analyze datasets based on geographical location, chronology, and indicator type. This standardized approach enables robust comparisons between diverse sea-level indicators, from sedimentary sequences to biological and archaeological remains. A structured submission protocol, real-time data validation and peer-review process ensures consistent data quality and uncertainty assessment across contributions. The portal's collaborative infrastructure facilitates synthesis of datasets for large-scale analyses of ice-sheet sensitivity, solid Earth deformation, and sea-level projections. Integration with existing RSL databases enhances the temporal and spatial coverage of available records.

The HOLSEA Datahub marks a significant advance in the standardization and accessibility of RSL data, providing essential constraints for understanding Earth system responses to deglaciation. This unified database will support robust statistical analyses of rates and mechanisms of RSL change, ultimately improving our ability to project future sea-level rise.
