session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Wang, Bronwen [1], Labay, Keith [2], Ellefsen, Karl [3], Wood, Nathan J [4]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Alaska Science Center, Anchorage, AK, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Alaska Science Center, Anchorage, Alaska, USA
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, Co, USA
(4) United States Geological Survey, Portland, Or, USA
abstract: Many mineral commodities presently defined as “critical” were not targeted in past mining operations and often are not the primary target for existing or new mines. Instead, most were byproducts or coproducts or were discarded in waste. Deposit model geochemical signatures could help anticipate additional extraction targets or byproducts opportunities but comprehensive geochemical signatures that identify enrichments of target elements, critical minerals, and other non-target elements are lacking. The Critical Minerals in Ore (CMiO) dataset provides the opportunity to develop comprehensive geochemical signatures. Using this dataset and a consistent and reproducible approach, we developed lists of typically anomalous elements in ores of a specific deposit type. Two criteria for anomalous concentrations, five- and ten-times average crustal abundance, were set as thresholds and represent moderately and highly anomalous concentrations, respectively. Each element was evaluated individually. Commonality was established first for each unique deposit and then for the deposit type. If 50 percent or more of the samples from a unique deposit exceeded the thresholds for a given element, the element was flagged as “anomalous” in that deposit. If 50 percent or more of the unique deposits of a specific deposit type were flagged as anomalous for an element, the element was flagged as “anomalous” for the deposit type. Lists of moderately and highly anomalous elements were generated for all 112 deposit types in the CMiO database. Lists of elements with no analysis in any unique deposit of a given deposit type and those with data censored at reporting limits above the thresholds were also captured. This was done to differentiate these elements from those that truly did not meet the thresholds. Ag, Sb, As, Te, and Bi are the critical minerals most frequently included as highly anomalous for the CMiO deposit types. Os, Rh, Ru, and Ir are the critical minerals most frequently lacking any information for a deposit type, reflecting their sparsity of coverage in the dataset. For volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits, comparison of the lists of highly anomalous elements to published geochemical signatures highlight difficulties resulting from differing nomenclature, the expansiveness of the lists, and the ambiguity of approach.

title: An Adaptive Implicit-Explicit Algorithm for Simulating Multi-Decadal Land Subsidence Due to Groundwater Pumping in Southern San Joaquin Valley, California
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Pant, Susmita [1], Smith, Ryan G. [2]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: Over the last century, an alarming rate of groundwater overdraft has resulted in severe land subsidence in the California’s San Joaquin Valley. Modeling is often required to manage and mitigate future subsidence, but subsidence models can be complex and computationally expensive. Most of the available physics based one-dimensional deformation models use finite difference methods, which rely either on implicit or explicit formulation. The fully explicit finite difference method is computationally efficient but can become numerically unstable depending on the spatial and temporal discretization and on hydrogeologic parameter values. Maintaining stability may therefore require extremely small-time steps, greatly increasing the total cost of multi-decadal simulations, or a coarser spatial grid, affecting the accuracy. Fully implicit methods are stable, but require solving a system of equations, which increases computational effort. To balance these tradeoffs, we developed an adaptive finite-difference model that uses the explicit formulation when the stability criterion is satisfied and automatically switches to the implicit formulation when necessary. As a result, the framework enabled us to efficiently simulate long term land subsidence in the Southern San Joaquin Valley from 1971 to 2025 while allowing flexible spatial and temporal discretization. The model is designed to simulate the compaction of clay lenses with the upper and the lower aquifers as well as the deformation of the Corcoran Clay at a daily time step. The application is demonstrated through a case study at a high subsidence location in the southern San Joaquin Valley. Model calibration combined three deformation constraints: Sentinel-1 InSAR displacement observations from June 2015 to December 2023, a cumulative deformation estimate derived from ALOS rates for June 2007 to July 2010, and long-term elevation-change records covering 1949 to 2005. Validation was done using January 2024 to December 2025 Sentinel -1 InSAR observations. At the location, the model estimated 6.1 m of cumulative subsidence from 1971 to 2025 and reproduced observed deformation well during calibration (NSE = 0.987, RMSE = 4.38 cm, NRMSE = 3.3%) and validation (NSE = 0.877, RMSE = 1.84 cm, NRMSE = 9.7%). This light-weight python-based modeling framework does not require a 3D groundwater flow model and can be applied elsewhere for improved stability in characterizing land subsidence due to groundwater withdrawals.

authors: Kinczyk, Mallory J. [1], Beddingfield, Chloe B. [2], Bland, Michael T. [3], Hemingway, Douglas J. [4], Martin, Emily S. [5], Patterson, Gerald W. [6]
affiliations: (1) Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD, USA

(5) Center for Earth and Planetary Studies, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
(6) Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, Laurel, MD, USA
abstract:
Enceladus’ complex surface and the presence of young, heavily tectonized regions, including the South Polar Terrain, make it a compelling target for understanding icy satellite formation and evolution as well as investigating the conditions that influence planetary habitability. The Cassini spacecraft provided deep insight into Enceladus’ current state including present-day thermal conditions (Hemingway & Mittal, 2019). However, Enceladus’s long term thermal evolution remains a mystery. This gap in understanding limits our ability to constrain the longevity of its internal ocean, timescales of endogenic geologic activity, and potential habitability.

In contrast to the tectonized terrains, Enceladus’ ancient, heavily cratered surfaces preserve evidence of early geologic activity and clues regarding Enceladus’ thermal history. Characterizing geologic features within the cratered terrains provides observation-based insight into the long-term evolution of the ice shell and can place constraints on the evolution of tidal stresses and heat flow affecting the surface expression of geologic features. Many craters within Enceladus’ ancient terrains appear to have been viscously relaxed, where their depths are shallower than what is expected for fresh craters and can be attributed to elevated heat flow in the subsurface (Bland et al., 2012). Further, global models of present-day heat flux suggest there are spatial variations in heat flow across the ice shell (Hemingway & Mittal, 2019), although these models are a snapshot in time and do not capture temporal variability. Observational studies of the cratered terrains have found evidence of extreme viscous relaxation in regions where modeled present-day heat flux is relatively low (e.g., Kinczyk et al., 2024).

We present updates on a morphological assessment of crater relaxation on Enceladus and comparisons of relaxation state to models of present-day heat flux. These data feed into a larger effort to use the spatial distribution of relaxed craters and models of crater relaxation to gain insight into the thermal history of the cratered terrains. In comparing the distribution of relaxed craters to models of present-day heat flux, we may determine whether these models are sufficient to explain the observed relaxation states of craters and, in turn, whether there is observational evidence that Enceladus has experienced one or more past episodes of elevated heat flux.

abstract: The demand for critical minerals is increasing as society and technology advance. Among the most critical are rare earth element (REE)-bearing minerals such as monazite (Mnz), which occurs in placer deposits worldwide. The purpose of this study is to determine the extent to which modern fluvial systems within the Broad River watershed draining the southeastern Appalachian orogen captures the range of potential source terranes for Coastal Plain placer monazite deposits in SC. Panned heavy mineral concentrates were collected along the Broad, Pacolet, and Tyger Rivers and from coastal barrier islands. Methods include panning heavy mineral concentrates (HMCs), heavy liquid and magnetic separations, SEM/BSE imaging to characterize mineralogy and Mnz zoning, and LASS-ICP-MS to collect Mnz U-Pb ages and REE concentrations. Results are compared to in situ LASS U-Pb ages for Mnz in potential crystalline source terranes of the southern Blue Ridge and Piedmont, and for detrital Mnz in first order stream heavy mineral concentrates. Monazite-bearing heavy mineral assemblages are dominated by ilmenite, epidote, hornblende, garnet, and kyanite/sillimanite, consistent with a dominantly metamafic/metapelitic source terrane. Detrital monazite (DMnz) ages define three primary age modes: Neo-Acadian (~365-350 Ma) and early Alleghanian (~340-300 Ma), which alternate as the dominant mode, and a minor but persistent Acadian mode (~410-370 Ma). Taconian (~470-440 Ma) and Grenvillian (~1.0-1.4 Ga) grains are rare. The fluvial DMnz age distributions are highly similar to those from HMCs in Coastal Plain clastic units along the Fall Line. Modern beach deposits exhibit the same modes but with the Alleghanian mode dominating. Bedrock ages for monazite-fertile crystalline rocks of the Inner Piedmont and Cat Square terranes - southeast of the Brevard Fault Zone - also exhibit the same DMnz age distributions, consistent with a paleo-Broad fluvial system delivering DMnz to the Coastal Plain. The rarity of Taconian detrital monazite ages, which characterize Blue Ridge terranes northwest of the BFZ, is a key constraint on provenance. REE patterns of Mnz vary mostly in proportion of heavy REE (HREE) as expressed by varying Gd/Lu values. Gd/Lu is highest (i.e., steepest HREE patterns) in prograde garnet-bearing lithologies and lowest in rocks exhibiting retrograde garnet breakdown. This same pattern is observed in DMnz of modern fluvial and Coastal Plain samples, providing a second monazite provenance fingerprint.

abstract: The Bonita Peak Mining District comprises 48 inactive mines in the San Juan Mountains northwest of Silverton, Colorado. Since mining ceased in 1991, acid mine drainage from the district has posed an ongoing water-quality challenge, culminating in the 2015 Gold King Mine spill and the district's subsequent Superfund designation. Many of these sites were surveyed during their operational history, but no comprehensive digital model of the tunnel networks previously existed. Leveraging the archiving efforts of the San Juan Historical Society alongside modern data from the Colorado Division of Reclamation Mining and Safety, we digitized historical maps of the Gold King, Gold Prince, Mogul, and Sunnyside mines into modern GIS formats and compiled them into a comprehensive 3-D model of the collective mine workings. The resulting dataset is aimed to improve public understanding of the mining district and serve as a foundation for future hydrologic, historic, and geologic research in the region.

title: Legacy Mine Tailings as a Source of Critical Minerals: A Case Study from the Stirling Zn-Pb-Cu-Au-Ag Mine, Nova Scotia
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources
authors: Parsons, Michael B. [1], Petts, Duane C. [2], Percival, Jeanne B. [3], Cheng, Terry C. [4], Deriaz, Julie [5]
affiliations: (1) Natural Resources Canada, Geological Survey of Canada, Dartmouth, NS, Canada

abstract: Increasing global demand for critical minerals and lengthening timelines for permitting new mines have led to strong interest in reprocessing legacy mine wastes. There are more than six billion tonnes of tailings at active and abandoned metal mines across Canada; however, many questions remain concerning the economics, technical feasibility, and regulations associated with reprocessing. The goal of this study is to evaluate the critical metal content and mineralogy of tailings at the former Stirling Mine in Nova Scotia, the spatial distribution and recoverability of critical metals, and the potential for reprocessing to reduce environmental risks. The Stirling Mine operated from 1927-1931, 1935-1938, and 1951-1956, extracting Zn, Pb, Cu, Au, and Ag from a volcanogenic massive sulphide deposit and generating 930,000 tonnes of tailings. In 2023 and 2024, we collected tailings from hand-dug pits to investigate the effects of weathering in near-surface tailings. In June 2024, we drilled 33 boreholes through the tailings, recovering samples for geochemical, mineralogical, particle size, and metallurgical testing. Geochemical analyses of the tailings using ICP-ES/MS following 4-acid digestion (and fire assay for Au) show the following median metal concentrations ( n =152): 1.19 wt.% Zn, 0.35 wt.% Pb, 0.18 wt.% Cu, 0.50 g/t Au, and 21 g/t Ag. A subset of tailings was analyzed using ICP-ES/MS following sodium peroxide fusion, revealing the following median concentrations of potential by-product critical elements ( n =51): 6.6 mg/kg Ga, 1.1 mg/kg Ge, and 0.80 mg/kg In. Critical minerals in the tailings are hosted by primary sulphide, sulphosalt, silicate, and carbonate minerals including pyrite, sphalerite, chalcopyrite, galena, tennantite, chlorite, muscovite, talc, and dolomite. Metal-bearing, weathering-related secondary phases are present in the near-surface oxidized tailings, including smithsonite [ZnCO 3 ], cerussite [PbCO 3 ], aurichalcite [(Zn,Cu) 5 (CO 3 ) 2 (OH) 6 ], and Pb-Mn-Zn phases. Preliminary results from mineral processing and metallurgical experiments show that approximately 80% of the sulphur in the tailings could be removed by separating the <75 µm fraction, thereby reducing the risk of acidic drainage and metal leaching. Diagnostic leach tests are ongoing to evaluate the most effective methods for critical metal recovery from both oxidized and unoxidized tailings. Results from this study are being used to assess the viability of reprocessing historical tailings to recover valuable elements and reduce risks to local ecosystems and surrounding communities.

title: Trusting the Change We Measure: Uncertainty in Lidar Topographic Differencing and Machine Learning Fault Trace Mapping
session_title: Imaging, measuring, and characterizing the Earth’s changing surface through remote sensing
authors: Brigham, Cassandra Alison Palm [1], Scott, Chelsea [2], Arrowsmith, Ramon [3]
affiliations: (1) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(2) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
(3) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract:
Repeat lidar and satellite imagery resolve centimeter-scale surface change, and hazard decisions for wildfires, landslides, and earthquakes depend on them. A measured change is only usable if its value exceeds its uncertainty. Errors in differencing maps are spatially correlated at scales from meters (point misclassification, poor scanning geometry) to kilometers (flight-line stripes, metadata errors) and can mimic or hide real change. Maps that anticipate change carry uncertainty as well: fault and rupture traces mapped from topography reflect mapper interpretation, data quality, geomorphic expression, and aleatory variability. For both, we estimate the magnitude and spatial scale of each error source, then test the resulting uncertainties against known answers.

Topochange, an open-source Python package running on demand in OpenTopography (an NSF-funded data facility) and standalone via GitHub, splits differencing error into bias, correlated error at multiple scales, and noise, then computes the uncertainty of mean change over any feature. In synthetic tests, reported 2-sigma intervals capture the known value near the intended 95% rate. We apply our workflow to the 2025 Eaton Fire (CA), where sediment from burnt hillslopes threatens to feed debris flows endangering communities downstream. The method confirms post-fire channel aggradation by dry ravel; apparent hillslope lowering is within uncertainty, so noise is not mistaken for erosion. We extend the method to volume change (landslides, sedimentation, lava flows), informing risk assessment and land use planning.

Surface change due to an earthquake is bracketed by two fault maps: a pre-earthquake fault trace map using landforms from previous ruptures, which guides fault zoning and lifeline siting, and a post-earthquake rupture map, which characterizes earthquakes and informs emergency response. Currently, experts map traces manually, a slow process that is difficult to reproduce. We adapt DINOv3, a vision foundation model, to map San Andreas Fault traces in the Carrizo Plain, CA, from 1 m lidar topography and 3 m PlanetScope imagery. We fine-tune under 3% of the model’s parameters on expert linework. The model predicts the probability that a pixel lies along a fault trace, with estimates of mapping uncertainty (from mapper confidence buffers) and model uncertainty (ensembles), tested with cross-validation and independent data; we recover the primary fault traces with >80% accuracy. The maps can be used as inputs for forecasting surface rupture location to mitigate fault displacement hazard.

authors: Wood, Adam Elendi [1], Wiesenberg, Nicholas [2], Wiles, Greg [3]

abstract: Old growth trees growing in Ohio (>250 years old) have been witness to natural and anthropogenic changes. A little over a 140 years ago, northwest Ohio witnessed the erasure of one of its largest wetlands, the Great Black Swamp. Initially a barrier for early Euro-American settlers, the Black Swamp was profoundly changed and the extant trees were witness to the land-use changes in addition to the changing climate. By analyzing tree ring records in Northwest Ohio, from Goll Woods State Nature Preserve (a remnant of the Black Swamp) Shagbark Hickory, White Oak and Burr Oaks sampled by the Indiana University Tree Ring Lab show a positive relationship to summer precipitation and a negative one with maximum summer temperatures. They also show evidence of witnessing land-use change throughout the mid-late 19 th century. During the 1820s-1880s, as vegetation declined from land clearing, the remaining vegetation faced a profound change in ecology. Growth releases in the trees can be dated using tree-ring analysis. The land clearing in the Maumee Valley region appears non-uniform as the growth releases from the various sites in Goll Woods vary in time. The oaks show early releases with the White Oak and Burr Oak releasing in the 1850s and 1820s, respectively. The Hickory exhibits a sudden release within the early 1870s, with a subtle decline during the 1900s. Sorting out the natural and anthropogenic signals in the trees is a challenge as to some extent the profound changes in land use and hydrology driven by settlement could also feedback on and contribute to changes in climate. This dendrohistorical case study from Northwest Ohio can be applied more broadly across Ohio to include the other nine old-growth sites. We will extract additional climatic and settlement history from the witness trees of these sites on the 250 th anniversary of the nation.

title: LALI-TOF-MS for Geoscience: From Elemental Mapping to Quantitative Geochemical Screening
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Valim Angelo, Tiago [1], Narbey, Melissa [2], Williams, Ellen [3], Williams, Jeff [4]
affiliations: (1) Faculty of Geology, Rio de Janeiro State University, Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil; Automated Mineralogy Incubator, AXT Pty Ltd, Perth, WA, Australia
(2) Automated Mineralogy Incubator, AXT Pty Ltd, Perth, WA, Australia
(3) Exum Instruments, Exum Instruments, Denver, CO, USA
(4) Exum Instruments, Exum Instruments, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Laser Ablation Laser Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (LALI-TOF-MS) provides a rapid approach for direct chemical analysis of geological solids with minimal sample preparation. Because each laser shot produces a full mass spectrum, including isotopic information where peaks are resolved, the method supports point analysis, line scans, raster mapping, and quantitative calibration within a single workflow. This presentation evaluates LALI-TOF-MS as both a spatial mapping tool and a quantitative geochemical screening method for mineral exploration, petrogenesis, geochronology support, and geometallurgy.

Geological examples show how LALI-TOF-MS can link elemental distributions to mineral textures and geological processes. Thin-section analyses reproduce major-element mineralogical patterns observed by electron-beam methods while extending coverage to trace and low-mass elements such as Li, Y, Ba, and Th. Mineral elemental maps of major, minor, trace, and rare earth elements reveal compositional zoning, trace-element variability, and domains suitable for follow-up isotope or geochronological analysis. Examples from zircon, titanite, sulfide-bearing samples, spodumene, and carbonates illustrate applications to trace-element zoning, critical-metal deportment, alteration, and textural controls on element distribution.

A key emphasis is quantification. Trace-element quantification in USGS glass reference material GSE-1G demonstrates the ability to measure major, minor, trace, low-mass elements such as Li and Be, and rare earth elements at ppm levels in the same analytical session. Lithium quantification examples further demonstrate how calibrated raster analyses can be applied to geological materials with different compositions and mineralogies. These examples show that LALI-TOF-MS outputs can move beyond relative elemental maps toward concentration-based datasets when appropriate standards and calibration strategies are used.

Together, these applications position LALI-TOF-MS as a complementary method to TIMA, SEM-EDS, EPMA, LIBS, and LA-ICP-MS. Rapid LALI-TOF-MS screening can identify domains of interest, prioritize targets, evaluate mineral-hosted trace elements, and guide more time-intensive quantitative or high-precision analyses. Areas for further evaluation and development include matrix effects, standard availability, detection limits, and calibration transferability across heterogeneous geological materials. With continued development, LALI-TOF-MS offers a versatile workflow for generating fast, spatially resolved, and increasingly quantitative geochemical information from solid geological samples.

authors: Romero, Matias [1], Marcott, Shaun A. [2], Cuzzone, Joshua K. [3], Mizerit, Ignacio [4], Caffee, Marc W. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA

abstract:
Establishing robust glacial chronologies is essential for constraining the timing of ice fluctuations, evaluating the synchronicity of climate evolution between hemispheres, and understanding the climate forcings that drive changes in the cryosphere. In northern Patagonia, however, the timing and structure of the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and subsequent deglaciation remain poorly constrained, limiting our understanding of Southern Hemisphere climate dynamics during the last glacial cycle.

Here, we present 57 new 10 Be surface exposure ages from samples of moraine boulders and exposed bedrock surfaces collected along a ~300 km north-south transect on the eastern margin of the Patagonian Andes. This chronology indicates ice expansion by ~35 ka, culminating in a regional glacial maximum at ~25 ka. Deglaciation began between 20 and 19 ka across major outlet lobes and Patagonian valleys and continued with sustained retreat until ice readvanced at ~14 ka, coincident with the Antarctic Cold Reversal. We integrate these new geochronological constraints with transient ice-sheet model simulations with the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM) to investigate the relative roles of climate forcing and non-climatic controls, including topography, hypsometry, and basal thermal regime, in pacing the timing and spatial pattern of ice-sheet evolution. Together, these results provide new constraints on the evolution of the Patagonian Ice Sheet and improve our understanding of the mechanisms controlling Southern Hemisphere ice-sheet response during the last deglaciation.

title: Persistence of Chloride in Chicagoland’s Shallow Aquifers Under Sensible Salting Scenarios
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Hadley, Daniel R. [1], Cullen, Cecilia [2], Abrams, Daniel B. [3]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State Water Survey, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL, USA

abstract: Decades of road salt use in the Chicagoland area has led to an accumulation of chloride in the region’s shallow aquifers, affecting both municipal production wells and domestic wells. The increase in chloride has prompted several communities to implement expensive treatment options and adopt sensible salting practices to mitigate against increased corrosivity and associated total dissolved solids (TDS), yet chloride remains elevated in several collar counties with regions exceeding USEPA’s secondary MCL of 250mg/L. We present a chloride modeling study in Kane County, IL using a MODFLOW-NWT/MT3D-USGS model that incorporates transient recharge and variable chloride application rates based on land use. The model is calibrated to decades of chloride data gathered from municipal and private wells open to glacial sands and gravels or the underlying weathered bedrock, and simulates chloride out to 2050 and beyond under various sensible salting scenarios. Scenarios included chloride reductions on major roads only, the entirety of the county road network, and commercial areas that are point sources of chloride. We discuss: 1) the importance of land use and model geology refinement to achieve calibration, 2) the persistence of chloride that remains in the shallow aquifers even under aggressive salt-reduction strategies, and 3) the implications of slow residence time in the shallow aquifers for PFAS contamination and transport. Understanding the movement and transit times of chloride has important implications for other shallow aquifers in northern latitudes as they evaluate risk to their shallow water supplies.

title: Defining the spatial structure in fault roughness
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
authors: Kirkpatrick, James [1], Baumgarte, Julia [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, McGill University, Montreal, QC, USA
abstract: Fault surfaces exhibit a variety of striations, grooves, and mullions at a broad range of length scales that are interpreted to form during slip as opposing sides of the fault interact via wear. When opposing sides of a fault are in contact, this surface roughness and geometry dictate the population of contact asperities that govern the frictional strength and stability of the fault as well as the separation between wall rocks, which contributes to the fluid flow architecture. Roughness is traditionally characterized with the power spectrum of the surface height field, which exhibits a ubiquitous power-law relationship with the spatial frequency for natural fault surfaces. However, this characterization of roughness is insensitive to spatial structure, so it does not capture the organized patterns of roughness that are recognizable as striations, grooves, and mullions, and faults that appear visually very different are indiscernible in the power spectrum characterization. To complement the power spectrum, we apply wavelet analysis to identify coherent structures in fault surfaces captured at various spatial scales. We utilize the 2-D continuous wavelet transform (CWT) using the anisotropic Morlet wavelet function. Our results indicate that discrete features within fault surface geometry can be distinguished at a broad range of spatial scales as continuous bands of high wavelet power, confirming that fault surface roughness is non-random. Using rock friction experiments on samples manufactured to have controlled surface roughness, we show that this non-randomness affects the frictional strength and wear processes of faults. Rougher faults are stronger over the range of low confining pressures tested. Our results imply that modelling fault roughness as a random self-affine height field may inaccurately represent the frictional behavior and structural evolution.

abstract:
Eumorphocystis multiporata Branson and Peck, 1940 is a diplopore-bearing blastozoan echinoderm genus that has been previously described from the Late Ordovician of Oklahoma, Tennessee, and Virginia of the United States. Here, we describe a new occurrence of E. multiporata from the Bobcaygeon Formation (Katian) of Canada near Ottawa that preserves the full suite of diagnostic features of the taxon.

The specimen described herein has an ovate thecal shape, measuring 46 mm in height, that narrows distally into basal plates surrounding a stem. The oral area is well-preserved, with five ambulacra surrounding the mouth. The anus is circular and preserved within the CD interambulacral area. The feeding appendages are proximally recumbent on the theca and become erect more distally. The feeding appendages are composed of three plate types, the ambulacral cover plates, ambulacral floor plates, and modified thecal plates at the base of the appendage. In the middle of the appendage is a coelomic canal, between the thecal plates and the ambulacral floor plates. Diplopore respiratory structures are preserved across thecal plates within shallow, circular pits and do not appear to cross plate boundaries. The stem has a slight curve distally and is composed of individual holomeric plates.

The feeding appendages of E. multiporata have been subject to debate in recent years due to the similarities they share with early crinoids, particularly in the triplate structure pierced with a coelomic canal. While E. multiporata is classified as a diploporan blastozoan, phylogenetic analyses have placed Eumorphocystis as a sister taxa to crinoids, linked through a number of synapomorphic traits such as the feeding appendage structures. This new occurrence data of E. multiporata expands the known biogeographic range of this taxon and can be used in phylogenetically-informed studies to better explore the shared evolutionary history between blastozoans and crinozoans.

abstract: Across Kentucky, the frequency and impacts of flood events have become increasingly more concerning. Understanding patterns of Kentucky’s late Quaternary flood events and how they relate to major hydrological changes is key to developing resilience against these changes. Project 2: Paleoperspectives of CLIMBS (Climate Resilience through Multidisciplinary Big Data Learning, Prediction, and Building Response Systems) is focused on developing reconstructions of these changes through the analysis of palynoflora to create a Holocene-based paleoclimate record for Kentucky. Floracliff Nature Preserve, located on the banks of the Kentucky River in extreme southern Fayette County, Kentucky, contains a succession of overbank and point bar deposits preserved at the base of a limestone cliff. Soil and sediment analysis has identified specific flooding horizons, most notably an erosional surface at 1.16 m. Palynological analysis of similar floodplain sediments in eastern Kentucky have been successfully utilized to reconstruct past changes in rainfall regime associated with significant flooding events. Here we present the results of analysis of samples obtained at every 5 cm from an approximately 3-m deep trench through the deposit. These produced a diverse array of pollen, spores, and non-pollen palynomorphs, including fungi. The pollen and plant spore record was used to reconstruct regional conditions present during deposition using CREST in R. The fungal spore record permits highly localized conditions to be assessed. Preliminary data suggests that shifts in precipitation seasonality noted at other sites, especially rapid transitions from warm, summer-wet to warm, summer-dry occur. Here we present updated palynological results and rainfall regime reconstructions.

title: Sampling Strategies for Microplastics: A Case Study for Mammoth Cave National Park
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science (Posters)
authors: Basnet, Rakesh [1], Locke, Sharon [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Science, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, Illinois, USA
(2) Center for STEM Research, Education, and Outreach, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL, USA
abstract:
Most of the Microplastic (MP) research has been centered in water systems and marine environments, while terrestrial protected areas with karst cave systems remain poorly studied. Mammoth Cave National Park (MACA) in Kentucky, the longest known cave system on Earth, draws more than 600,000 visitors each year. This increasing tourism raises concerns about whether fibers shed from clothing, general littering, and abrasion accumulate in the park's most fragile ecosystems. This study proposes a stratified sampling strategy to capture variability across visitor-use gradients, supporting robust spatial analyses on MP abundance, characterization, and source identification within the cave and adjoining area of the park.

The study area will be divided into strata that reflect four different levels of visitor presence across heavily trafficked tour routes and entrances, moderately used chambers further from the main paths, low-access or restricted sections, and adjoining surface features like trailheads, parking lots, campgrounds, and sinkholes. The ten random sampling locations in each stratum will ensure representative spatial coverage within each stratum. The proximity sampling will be done at distances of 2.5, 5, and 7.5 meters from visitor-use features to capture localized contamination patterns associated with tourism infrastructure and human movement. This hierarchical design combines statistical rigor with operational efficiency, and enables comparisons across visitor-use categories with minimized sampling bias.

Soil samples from the top 10 cm and surface sediments from brushing the top layer will be collected and stored cold using contamination-control protocols, including field blanks. Organic material will be digested with 30% hydrogen peroxide, after which zinc chloride density separation isolates the MPs, which are then filtered onto glass microfiber paper. Particles are sorted visually under a stereomicroscope, using ImageJ software for assisting the counts. Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy will be used to characterize MP particle size and polymer composition.

The proposed sampling design will enable comparisons of microplastic abundance among visitor-use zones, identify spatial hotspots using GIS-based spatial statistics, and evaluate relationships between visitor proximity and microplastic characteristics. This should show whether MP levels genuinely track visitor pressure, whether synthetic fibers dominate near high-traffic areas, and whether contamination is spatially patterned rather than diffuse. The findings will provide park managers with an approach for long-term environmental monitoring and guide future assessments of tourism-related pollution in sensitive karst ecosystems.

title: The PETM Induced Long-Term Declines in Test Secretion for the Planktic Foraminifer Morozovella in the Mid-latitude SE Atlantic

authors: Apel, Emily Virginia [1], Hupp, Brittany N. [2], Bryant, Roger N. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA

abstract: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM; ca. 56 Ma) was a period of intense warming linked to a rapid release of carbon to the ocean-atmosphere system, which drove environmental shifts like ocean acidification and changes in water column structure. Studies of subsequent climatic events in the Eocene, like the Eocene Climatic Optimum (EECO), show that the planktic foraminiferal genus Morozovella suffered declines in response to warming and decreased pH, which also occurred during the PETM. A study from ODP Site 865 in the tropical Pacific and preliminary data from ODP Site 1266 in the SE Atlantic shows that some morozovellids did decrease in abundance during the PETM. Studies from other locations have shown that morozovellids adapted through ecophenotypic responses. For instance, the species Morozovella allisonensis appeared during and was restricted to the peak PETM and has been interpreted as an ecophenotypic response to ocean acidification, as its test is less ornate and more fragile. It is unclear, however, if morozovellids that declined at Site 865 and Site 1266 experienced similar morphological changes due to decreased carbonate saturation during the PETM and what contributed to their decline in the EECO and beyond. To investigate this, we present morphometrics data for morozovellids from ODP Site 1263 in the SE Atlantic. We measured shell wall thickness and length of external protrusions (i.e., muricae) for each final whorl chamber of morozovellid specimens from the M. aequa/subbotinae/gracilis clade. Comparing metrics between chambers allows us to disentangle the effects of diagenesis vs. ontogeny, as dissolution should uniformly reduce these parameters across chambers but not alter inter-chamber differences. Average wall thickness and muricae length decreased during the peak event, did not return to pre-event levels, and further decreased post-event. Inter-chamber differences in these metrics also decreased, indicating that the initial layers secreted to build each new chamber were likely thinner. This suggests that the decrease in carbonate saturation during the event drove tradeoffs in test secretion whereby new chamber addition was prioritized over chamber thickening. The persistence of this phenomenon beyond the peak PETM suggests that decreased carbonate saturation left a lasting imprint on the ability of morozovellids to secrete robust tests, which may have contributed to this genus’ subsequent decline during the EECO and their eventual extinction later in the Eocene.

affiliations: (1) Physics and Geosciences, Angelo State University, San Angelo, TX, USA

abstract: The Upper Triassic Dockum Group of western Texas preserves fluvio-lacustrine deposits with an important vertebrate fossil record, but detailed facies analyses and paleosol studies remain limited. remain limited. This study investigates the depositional system and facies architecture of the Dalby Ranch sandstone within the Trujillo Member of the Cooper Canyon Formation in southern Garza County, Texas. Two study areas were investigated: Study Area 1 was located at the base of the Trujillo Member, consists of a thick sandstone body with interbedded mudstone and conglomerate. The basal contact is erosional, locally conglomeratic, and incises underlying mudstone. Sedimentary structures include horizontal and low-angle planar bedding (Sh, Sl), with subordinate trough cross-bedded, planar cross-bedded, and ripple-laminated sandstone (St, Sp, Sr). Internal scour surfaces and thin fine-grained and conglomeratic intervals are common. These characteristics indicate deposition within a fluvial channel system that experienced repeated fluctuations in flow energy and discharge. The absence of clearly defined accretion surfaces precludes determination of whether lateral or downstream accretion dominated channel growth. Study Area 2, located at a slightly lower stratigraphic level within the Colorado City Member of the Cooper Canyon Formation, contains a thicker succession of predominantly fined-grained deposits. Siltstone and claystone beds contain sediment-filled desiccation cracks, indicating repeated subaerial exposure and deposition within an overbank setting. A laterally extensive coarse-grained unit occurs within the succession and overlies an erosional scour surface; locally conglomeratic basal deposits indicate channel reorganization. The unit consists primarily of medium-grained sandstone, including a lower ripple-laminated interval (Sr) capped by scour surface and overlain by horizontal and low-angle planar-bedded sandstone (Sh and Sl). This succession records changing flow conditions and at least two depositional episodes. The sandstone body is interpreted as a possible crevasse-channel deposit within an overbank succession. These preliminary observations indicate a fluvial system characterized by active channel migration, episodic high-energy discharge events, and associated floodplain deposition, providing a framework for future paleocurrent and facies-architecture analyses within the Dockum Group.

abstract:
Excavations, shallow seismic and geothermal surveys at the granite Unfinished Obelisk site in Aswan revealed an ancient canal used to transport massive stone blocks, such as obelisks and colossal statues, from the quarry to the Nile. From there, they were transported on boats to Luxor or northward toward the Delta. To further trace the route of this canal, an archaeological and geographical survey of the area's topography was conducted, along with a review of old photographs. This was done to understand the area's ancient landscape and determine likely extensions of this canal or other possible means of transporting the massive quarry blocks to the Nile.

Due to the area being largely covered by buildings and the difficulty of excavating, an alternative method was sought to trace the canal's entire remaining route. Satellite radar and Google Earth imagery were used to identify likely residual and alluvial soil accumulations within topographically low areas where archaeological excavation is difficult or not permitted, e.g., the Muslim Fatimid cemetery. Some natural low areas were subject to annual Nile floods and had fewer obstructions requiring excavation, making them more attractive for the seasonal transport of obelisks or other large blocks.

Many topographically low areas are centered along fracture traces and lineaments. These are revealed by narrow, nearly straight, and vertical zones of fracture concentration. These facilitate mechanical and chemical weathering of granite rocks containing dolerite dykes (used as hammerstones), as well as erosion and the alignment of headland drainage segments and larger valleys. All are priority areas to search for the canal's extension to the Nile from its well-defined docking area at the foot of the Unfinished Obelisk.

Radar imagery is well suited to detect and monitor land surface deformation, which may indirectly reflect buried features such as the canal. Preliminary results are provided of our ongoing InSAR time series analysis, applying atmospheric corrections necessary for InSAR measurements in the Aswan region.

authors: McDermott, Robert G. [1], Kreiner, Douglas C. [2], Lease, Richard O. [3], O'Sullivan, Paul B. [4], Metcalf, James R. [5], Flowers, Rebecca M. [6]
affiliations: (1) Alaska Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA

abstract:
The tectonic framework of the Northern Cordillera is defined by accreted terranes and strike-slip fault systems that are often repeatedly reactivated in response to evolving plate boundary configurations. Timing constraints for intracontinental fault systems are thus key to understanding assembly and terrane translation in the region but lacking in southwestern Alaska. We present apatite fission track (AFT) and apatite and zircon (U-Th)/He (AHe, ZHe) data from 34 samples collected in the Kuskokwim Mountains (KMs) and associated Iditarod-Nixon Fork fault (INFF) system that has accommodated ~90 km of dextral offset since ca. 60 Ma.

Samples distributed up to 40 km across and over ~320 km along strike of the INFF corridor include folded siliciclastic strata of the ca. 120–80 Ma Kuskokwim Group (KG) and cross-cutting Late Cretaceous volcano-plutonic complexes. Pooled AFT (n=26) and mean AHe (n=9) dates in all samples range from 47.4 ± 2.6 (1σ) to 26.6 ± 3.8 Ma and 49.9 ± 6.6 to 25.2 ± 3.7, respectively, and young towards the INFF. Mean ZHe dates (n=10) from ~70 Ma plutonic rocks are 70.2 ± 5.6 (1σ std. dev.) to 64.4 ± 6.0. ZHe dates from KG rocks define modes at ~110, 90, and 55 Ma that, in-tandem with likely source ages and effective Uranium content of individual zircon grains, suggest partial date resetting.

Inverse and forward thermal history models reveal a multi-stage thermal history. Models from KG samples imply peak burial temperatures of ~140–180 ℃ at least locally. Plutonic rocks underwent rapid post-emplacement cooling to temperatures ≤150 ℃. Following thermal quiescence, all samples cooled to <50 ℃ at ~60 Ma, 40 Ma, or 30 Ma, which we interpret to record exhumation related to the INFF and subsidiary fault networks. Episodic ~60 and 40 Ma exhumation is coeval with accelerated Kula Plate convergence and demise, respectively, and documented counterclockwise rotation of western Alaska. Exhumation at ~30 Ma may reflect renewed dextral slip along the INFF as a far-field response to contemporaneous initial flat-slab subduction of the Yakutat microplate. We thus suggest Cenozoic exhumation intervals reflect multiple reactivations of the INFF in response to evolving far-field plate boundary configurations. Thermal history models additionally limit total post-70 Ma exhumation to ≤4–5 km, consistent with preservation of epizonal ore deposits across the KMs.

title: Lithologic Control on Asymmetric Damage Along the Crustal-Scale Denali Fault Zone, Southwest Yukon, Canada and Implications for Paleo- and Present-Day Fluid Flow
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Caine, Jonathan Saul [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
The internal structure of very large-displacement, crustal-scale strike-slip fault zones exhumed from the Earth’s brittle crust remains difficult to map and characterize. Such mapping is essential for ground-truthing conceptual, kinematic, mechanical, hydrologic, geothermal, seismogenic, and tectonic models. The eastern Denali fault zone (EDFZ) hosts exceptional bedrock exposures in SW Yukon, allowing for characterization at seven areas spread over ~168 km, spaced ~25 km apart.

Large variations of sedimentary and crystalline rock lithologies are juxtaposed along a highly localized fault core, no more than a few 10s of m wide, that accommodated at least 370 km of dextral separation since ca. 52 Ma. Where observable, the fault core is dominated by foliated to non-foliated carbonaceous, clay-rich cataclasites. Subsidiary damage on either side of the core exhibits heterogeneity and asymmetry in structural intensity, structure types, and mineralogy, all of which are correlated with the host lithology.

Where host lithologies are dominated by clay-rich, clastic sedimentary rocks, kinematically linkable damage is only a few 10s of m wide. Single fracture faults with small displacements, striated and mirrored surfaces as well as high-intensity open fractures are locally pervasive. In metabasaltic greenstones and associated, well-indurated, volcanogenic metasedimentary rocks, semi-sealed hydrothermal calcite ± hematite ± chlorite slip surfaces form a complex and pervasive network of background damage. Distinctive brittle fault zones with their own cataclastic cores and damage zones are nested within the background damage in an ~8 km wide zone from the mapped trace of the master fault zone. Orientation and kinematic analyses show a complex slip partitioned strike‐slip fault system. Despite the complex slip distributions, strain inversion results show end-member, subhorizontal, northeast-directed reverse and north-directed dextral strike-slip that reflect far-field relative plate motions over the last 30 m.y.

The along-strike configuration of mixed lithologic strength and juxtapositions appears to result in a heterogeneous and asymmetric damage zone with order-of-magnitude variations in width and deformation intensity. Further, this complex, multiple conduit-barrier system indicates that lithology is a major, regional-scale control of overall permeability structure and thus both paleo- and present-day fluid flow. Given the geologic evidence for ancient and modern hydrothermal fluid flow, fault-controlled high-relief topography, and recent geophysical modeling indicating an elevated geotherm, segments of the EDFZ have been identified as prospective targets for geothermal resource potential.

title: The Cost of Staying Cool: Assessing the Environmental Impacts and Community Perspectives of Reflective Pavement for Urban Heat Mitigation
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry
authors: Libbing, Sydney [1], Banner, Jay L. [2], Clamann, Andrew [3]
affiliations: (1) Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX,
(3) Watershed Protection Department, City of Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
Rapid urban development in Austin, Texas, has increased impervious surfaces, altering watershed hydrology while exacerbating the urban heat island effect. Reflective pavement sealants containing titanium dioxide (TiO₂) have been proposed to reduce pavement temperatures, but their environmental fate remains poorly understood. This study evaluates the impacts of a TiO₂-containing reflective pavement sealant on water quality in the Onion Creek watershed of Austin, Texas, where the City of Austin conducted a pilot reflective pavement project in June 2024, while also assessing community perspectives regarding its implementation.

Titanium (Ti) concentrations were measured monthly in the baseflow of the receiving waterway upstream and downstream of the reflective pavement neighborhood to evaluate temporal and spatial trends. During storm events, sheetflow and storm-drain outfall were sampled at reflective (test) and conventional (control) pavement plots to quantify Ti transport. Bioavailable Ti was measured in storm-deposited sediments to assess Ti accumulation.

Following installation, baseflow Ti concentrations increase above historical background levels before declining toward pre-installation concentrations over twelve months. Throughout the study, Ti concentrations remain below known toxicological thresholds (<3 ppb). Ti concentrations are significantly higher immediately downstream of the test plot than upstream but indistinguishable at the far downstream site, indicating localized impacts that diminish with downstream dilution. Storm runoff exhibits substantially higher Ti concentrations, with sheetflow at the test plot reaching 857 ppb and storm-drain outfall reaching 128 ppb, demonstrating that storm events are major periods of elevated Ti mobilization.

Mass-balance calculations estimating stormwater mixing with Onion Creek baseflow indicate that runoff from the existing reflective pavement could produce an in-stream Ti concentration of approximately 482 ppb during storm events, periodically exceeding sublethal effect and acute toxicity concentrations for aquatic organisms (60 ppb; 318 ppb). Simulated expansion of reflective pavement (2-100x) increases estimated concentrations to 622-850 ppb. Storm-deposited sediments from the test plot contain elevated bioavailable Ti, consistent with field observations of cracking, raveling, and sealant-coated gravel, indicating that pavement degradation mobilizes Ti-containing particles during storm events.

Survey responses (n=132) indicate limited public awareness of reflective pavement but interest in additional information before broader implementation. Together, these findings demonstrate that reflective pavement can generate substantial Ti mobilization during storm events and highlight the importance of evaluating watershed-specific dilution capacity, ecological risks, and community perspectives before expanding reflective pavement applications.

abstract:
A recent seismic investigation by Porter et al. (2026) resolved two low velocity zones below the intraplate San Francisco volcanic field (SFVF) in north-central Arizona, interpreted to be partially molten mafic and felsic zones in the lower and middle crust, respectively. Geographically widespread Late Pleistocene mafic to felsic magma generation complementary to these zones is permitted, although not required, by previous constraints on eruption ages. New SHRIMP-RG U,Th-disequilibrium dates on Sugarloaf Mountain high-silica rhyolite-hosted zircon and allanite surfaces yielded a maximum eruption age of 79 ± 6 ka (2s; n=31; MSWD =0.86). The impetus for eruption may have been accumulation of volatiles from crystallizing mafic influxes and their differentiates, enhanced by possible contributions from hydrothermally altered assimilants. Similar maximum eruption dates of 72 ± 5 ka (n=21; MSWD = 1.1) and 71 ± 6 ka (n=15; MSWD = 0.51) were also yielded by the surfaces of zircons from vitrophyric plugs at Strawberry and O’Neill Craters, respectively. At these craters, syn-eruptive mixing of basalt with trachyte resulted in eruption of progressively more evolved compositions, with some entrainment of high silica rhyolite zircons. Collectively, these three felsic eruptions, distributed across 140 km 2 , could be the products of an ~75 ka silicic magmatic-volcanic flare-up. Coeval mafic eruptions at the two craters along with ~70 ka surface exposure dates (Fenton and Niedermann, 2014) for mafic eruptions at SP Crater (70 ± 7 ka) and Doney Mountain (67 ± 3 ka) broaden the composition and regional extent of an eastern SFVF magmatic flare-up to mafic-felsic magmatism over ~400 km 2 . Considered in tandem with the seismic results, this previously unrecognized magmatic flare-up warrants renewed consideration of the region’s geothermal potential and volcanic hazards.

abstract: Isla Tortuga (IT) is a basaltic volcanic island located in the Guaymas Basin (GB) within the Gulf of California oblique rift along the Pacific–North American plate boundary. In 2023, an expedition to IT collected samples for petrographic, geochemical, and geochronological analyses. Previous International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 385 drilling recovered several kilometers of sediment from the GB, intersecting sills intruding Quaternary sediments. Petrographic observations indicate that these sills and IT lavas share similar mineral textures and geochemical characteristics. Geochemical data from sills associated with the off-axis Ringvent system at IODP Sites U1547 and U1548 (Ge et al., 2023) show La/Yb (~0.5–1.0) and Nb/La (~2.0– 3.5) values comparable to the earliest eruptions of IT. In contrast, new geochemical data from sills drilled at IODP Sites U1545, U1546, U1547, and U1548 exhibit higher La/Yb (~5.0) and lower Nb/La (~0.2–0.5) values, more closely resembling the youngest IT eruptions. Older IT lavas show a magmatic evolution toward slightly more differentiated compositions, reflected in lower MgO (~7 wt.%) and increasing La/Yb (2–5), while Nb/La remains relatively constant (0.5–1). This pattern suggests that magma evolution was dominated by fractional crystallization. In contrast, the most recent IT eruptions display more primitive compositions (MgO > 7.5 wt.% and La/Yb ~2), suggesting a magma recharge event before the latest eruptive phase. Based on geochemical analyses and petrographic observations, we hypothesize that IT and the sills are part of the same magmatic plumbing system in the GB. This study presents (1) new geochemical data from sills drilled at Sites U1545–U1548, (2) new geochronological constraints for IT, and (3) an integrated petrological and geochronological framework for magmatism in the GB. The integration of geochemical and geochronological data provides petrogenetic and temporality insights into the magmatic evolution that formed IT and the GB sills, and their possible linkage.

title: PFAS Distribution and Hydrologic Controls in Surface Waters in Robeson County, North Carolina
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Posters)
authors: Maharjan, Madan [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geography, University of North Carolina, Pembroke, NC,
abstract:
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent contaminants that enter surface waters through wastewater effluent, industrial and urban runoff, landfill drainage, contaminated groundwater, and other diffuse and point sources. This study evaluated the spatial distribution, chemical composition, and hydrologic controls on PFAS concentrations and mass loads in the Lumber River and its tributaries in Robeson County, North Carolina. Surface-water samples were collected from 22 locations during May 2026, including sites near wastewater-treatment plants, landfills, developed areas, and tributary confluences. Eleven river locations were sampled twice—before and after a rainfall event approximately two weeks apart—resulting in 33 valid analytical samples. Samples were analyzed by a commercial laboratory for 37 PFAS compounds using EPA Method 1633.

Total detected PFAS concentrations ranged from nondetect to 360.4 ng/L and exhibited substantial spatial and temporal variability. The highest concentration occurred at the Boardman site, where total PFAS increased from 156.6 to 360.4 ng/L between sampling events. This sample was dominated by PFOA, PFHxA, PFOSA, PFPeA, PFOS, and PFNA. Elevated concentrations were also measured downstream of the Lumberton wastewater-treatment plant (111.5 ng/L), at Big Swamp (103.7 ng/L), and at Gallberry Swamp (87.4 ng/L). PFOA was a dominant component in the Lumber River, whereas GenX/HFPO-DA was detected primarily in Big Swamp, suggesting that the two stream systems may be influenced by different PFAS sources or transport pathways.

Global Moran’s I demonstrated significant positive spatial autocorrelation indicating that PFAS values were spatially clustered rather than randomly distributed. Streamflow exerted an important control on both concentration and mass loads. Increased rainfall and tributary inflow diluted PFAS concentrations at some locations, but greater discharge increased the transported PFAS mass at others. Little Raft Swamp contained relatively low PFAS levels and appeared to dilute the middle reach of the Lumber River. In contrast, downstream increases associated with Big Swamp and another third-order tributary indicated additional PFAS inputs to the river.

These findings identify localized PFAS hotspots and distinct chemical signatures within the watershed while demonstrating that concentration alone may not adequately characterize downstream PFAS transport. Additional seasonal monitoring paired upstream–downstream sampling, source-specific testing, and hydrologic measurements are needed to distinguish potential sources and quantify PFAS transport through the connected river network.

title: Impact Cratering on Metal-Rich Asteroids: Connecting Experiments, Simulations, and Psyche
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials
authors: Alexander, Amanda M [1], Marchi, Simone [2], Elkins-Tanton, Lindy [3]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, Boulder, CO,
(2) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
(3) Space Sciences Laboratory, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, California, USA
abstract:
Impact cratering is the primary process governing the evolution of small bodies, yet the deformation and fragmentation of metal-rich targets remain poorly constrained. The NASA Psyche mission is currently en route to a metal-rich main belt asteroid. The spacecraft will visit its namesake asteroid in 2029, which is thought to be 30-60 vol% metal. To best interpret craters observed on Psyche, and to understand the evolutionary history via impacts, we have coupled impact experiments into iron meteorites with numerical simulations to benchmark and explore impact cratering scenarios on metal-rich targets. The goal of this work has been to build a database of crater morphologies and extent of deformation of metal-rich materials which may be relevant to the Psyche asteroid.

We observe a diversity of crater morphologies, depth to diameter ratios, and impact-generated porosities which may be informative of how Psyche relates to known iron meteorites. Craters will be mapped by the Psyche spacecraft in detail and depth-diameter will be inferred for craters >1 km in size. Bulk porosity of Psyche will be constrained from gravity data. Such data can then be compared to the findings compiled in this study.

abstract: Projected to disappear in the next few hundred years, Barnes Ice Cap, located on the central Baffin Island plateau, is the last remaining vestige of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. Beneath Holocene-age ice rests ice from the last glacial period which in turn overlies ice with d 18 O values similar to Holocene values. This ice stratigraphy highlights Barnes Ice Cap’s position as an endpoint for an ice-age deglacial sequence and, conversely, a primary inception point for subsequent continental-scale glaciation. Here we present paired in situ cosmogenic 26 Al- 10 Be measurements from bedrock just emerging from beneath Barnes Ice Cap to assess how often this bedrock becomes ice free during Pleistocene interglacial periods. We combine these measurements with a novel approach using paired 26 Al- 10 Be measurements in a 3-meter bedrock core to explore how often the LIS completely disappears through the Pleistocene and into the late Pliocene.

title: Implementing Landslide Hazard Science in Working Forest Landscapes: Lessons from a New Education Program in Oregon
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment
authors: Patton, Annette [1], Kline, Norma [2], Christiansen, Alicia [3], Collette, Camille [4]
affiliations: (1) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(2) Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA
(3) Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
(4) Oregon Department of Forestry,
abstract:
Effective landslide risk reduction depends not only on advances in hazard assessment, but also on the successful transfer of scientific and regulatory information to landowners and natural resource professionals. In Oregon, steep forested terrain is susceptible to landslides that threaten public safety, infrastructure, and ecosystem resources, yet many woodland owners and practitioners have limited training in slope stability, landslide recognition, and relevant forest practice regulations. To address this gap, Oregon State University Extension and the Oregon Department of Forestry developed a workshop series titled Landslides in Forested Landscapes , which combines process-based geomorphic principles, hazard recognition, regulatory guidance, and field-based learning.

The program was piloted in two regions of Oregon and designed for woodland owners, tribal forestry staff, and local government natural resource professionals. Workshop content focused on landslide processes and triggers, field indicators of instability, interpretation of imagery and mapping resources, and application of Oregon Forest Practice Rules to steep-slope management. Field components provided participants with opportunities to evaluate landslide features and discuss site-specific risk factors.

Evaluation results from the pilot workshop indicate gains in participant knowledge and confidence. Following the workshop, all respondents reported improved understanding of landslide risk factors and indicators of slope instability, including improved understanding of landslide risk factors and confidence in using imagery and mapping resources. Qualitative feedback emphasized the value of integrating classroom instruction with field observations of both slow-moving and debris-flow landslides.

This case study demonstrates how programming oriented towards practitioners and land managers can serve as a mechanism for implementing landslide hazard science at the local level and highlights opportunities to improve practitioner understanding of landslide risk, hazard recognition, and risk-informed land management. The approach provides a transferable model for connecting landslide science, regulatory frameworks, and local decision-making.

title: Grain Size From WATSON and SuperCam Suggests Lack of Mudstones in the Neretva Vallis Fan: Implications for Interpreting Depositional Environments in Jezero Crater, Mars
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Rivera-Hernández, Frances [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
abstract: Constraining grain size is essential for interpreting the transport history and depositional environments of sedimentary rocks explored by the Perseverance rover in Jezero crater, Mars. The size of grains provides information about their transport history, specifically the speed of paleo-fluid flows. When placed in stratigraphic context, grain size also provides clues about how past environments may have changed over time. On Mars, grain size can be determined visually from images and estimated using the Gini Index Mean Score (GIMS), a proxy derived from point-to-point chemical variability in Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) data. GIMS estimates grain size where image resolution or coverage is limited and helps distinguish mudstones from sandstones. In this study, the GIMS is applied to Perseverance SuperCam LIBS data from sols 442-907 and calibrated to 22 rocks with known grain size from Wide-Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering (WATSON) and Remote Micro-Imager (RMI) images. The calibration was then applied to 117 additional rock targets to estimate their grain size. Preliminary results suggest that 89% of these rocks have medium- to granule-sized grains and are likely coarse-grained sandstones and pebbly sandstones. About 7% of the rocks have very fine- to medium sand-sized grains and are likely fine- to medium-grained sandstones. The remaining 4% of rocks have grains silt and smaller and are likely mudstones or siltstones; helping confirm the presence of mudstones in the fan. The mudstones are located near each other and restricted to stratigraphic horizons at the fan bottom. Sandstones occur throughout the fan, but fine- to medium-grained sandstones are not abundant at the fan top, which instead consists of 97% coarse-grained sandstones and pebbly sandstones. Conglomerates are also present at the fan top but these were not included in the GIMS analysis. Combined with image-based texture observations, these results suggest that (1) most rocks in the Neretva Vallis fan were transported by high-energy flows and are likely fluvial and (2) the restricted occurrence of mudstones implies that long-lived lacustrine deposition was limited. Together, this is consistent with a transition from subaqueous fan-delta deposition to predominantly subaerial alluvial fan deposition through time. Ongoing work is focused on evaluating sedimentary textures from images and connecting them with GIMS results to help constrain the depositional environment and transport history of the Neretva Vallis fan rocks.

title: In Situ Rb-Sr Geochronology by LA-MC-ICP-MS/MS
session_title: Laser-ablation advances in geochronology and thermochronology: From technique development to innovative applications
authors: Cruz-Uribe, Alicia Marie [1], Melton, Hayward [2], Yap, Teng Ee [3], Tissot, Francois LH [4], Arkula, Cemil [5], Garber, Joshua Michael [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Maine, Orono, ME,

(5) University of Maine, Orono, ME,
(6) University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland,
abstract: The coupling of laser-based sampling to tandem mass spectrometers (ICP-MS/MS) has sparked a renaissance in the application of the Rb-Sr system to terrestrial and planetary geochronology. Multicollector-based MS/MS systems expand the geochronologic toolbox beyond high Rb/Sr mica minerals to include feldspars and other materials with limited Rb/Sr spread on isochron diagrams, and enable high precision analysis of samples that are volume-limited and texturally complex. A number of key considerations still exist that hinder the widespread application of this technique, including laser-induced elemental fractionation, the availability and characterization of appropriate reference materials, and data reduction strategies. Though, with these challenges come new opportunities, including the integration of high speed mapping and high precision isotope analyses. Here we use an ESL NWRfemto laser ablation system coupled to a ThermoFisher Scientific Neoma MC-ICP-MS/MS to evaluate 87 Rb/ 86 Sr and 87 Sr/ 86 Sr of primary and secondary reference materials for Rb-Sr geochronology of micas, feldspars, and glasses. These materials include traditional glasses from NIST, USGS, MPI-DING, and IAG; newly developed phlogopite glasses doped with high Rb/Sr; nanoparticle pressed powder pellets (MicaMg phlogopite, FK-N feldspar, SRM607 feldspar); and natural k-feldspar, muscovite, and biotite materials of known age. A key takeaway from these analyses is that the measurement precision that we achieve with the Neoma MS/MS now exceeds the accuracy to which 87 Rb/ 86 Sr is known in any glass reference material.

title: Summer Water Pollution Trends of an Urban Ohio Stream
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes
authors: Goldbaum, Emerald [1], Welch, Kathleen Ann [2], Warix, Sara [3], Wilson, Aaron [4], Diaz, Melisa [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA; Byrd Polar Climate and Research Center, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(2) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA; Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
(4) Byrd Polar Climate and Research Center, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
(5) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, ; Byrd Polar Climate and Research Center, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA
abstract: Climate change has led to an increase in extreme weather events, characterized in Ohio by increased short-term drought bracketed by extreme precipitation and temperature. Deviations in precipitation and increased occurrence of drought can impact the transport and storage of chemicals in local surface waterways. For example, pollutants (i.e. heavy metals, agricultural runoff, and microplastics), dissolved ions, and nutrients can accumulate on or near the surface during dry periods and may be readily flushed into streams and lakes by rainfall overland flow. However, the variables that control how watersheds, especially with high levels of human influence and management, chemically respond to drought are unclear. To test this, we collected weekly water samples across four points from head to mouth from Adena Brook, an urban stream running through the densely populated Clintonville neighborhood of Columbus, Ohio. The samples were analyzed for pH, dissolved oxygen, water isotopes, anions (F-, Cl-, SO42-, NO3-, PO43-), cations (Li+, K+, Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+), nutrients (NH3, NO2-, NO3-, PO43-), metals (Pb, Cu, As), dissolved and particulate organic carbon, and microplastics over the course of the summer 2026 season (June to September). We will share our comparisons of water quality to flow rate, temperature, humidity, precipitation, and drought indices from the same time period to demonstrate which factors most greatly impact water quality parameters. Water isotope analysis will also inform the timing and source of water movement through the stream. We anticipate that the head samples will have the highest concentrations of pollutants because of decreased flow rates allowing for increased accumulation, and because the head of the stream likely receives more direct pollutant input from highway/road runoff that then accumulates further downstream at the more stagnant mouth. Changes in precipitation will show the most impact on pollutant concentrations, with spikes in runoff bringing more dissolved and particulate matter into the stream from the surrounding watershed. As shifts in precipitation and temperature become more severe in the Midwest, understanding the factors contributing to chemical stability in streams, and how chemistry varies throughout, can aid surrounding communities in addressing surface water quality hazards and contribute to local environmental remediation efforts.

title: Statistical characterization and modeling of damage/process zones in subseismic normal faults: the role of mechanical stratigraphy
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms. (Posters)
authors: Bistacchi, Andrea [1], Casiraghi, Stefano [2], Mittempergher, Silvia [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Milano - Bicocca, Milano, Italy
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Milano - Bicocca, Milano, Italy
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Milano - Bicocca, Milano, Italy
abstract:
Being able to quantify and model fracturing properties in damage or process zones of small-scale subseismic faults is of huge interest in every kind of project involving the storage and/or migration of fluids in the subsurface. Depending on their architecture, these faults can act as conduits, barriers or combined highly anisotropic conduits/barriers, and being small, with offsets at or under the limit of seismic resolution, but quite often very frequent, they remain very elusive, and yet they can dramatically influence the hydraulic behavior of reservoirs and seals.

Here we present a quantitative outcrop analogue study on spectacular coastal cliff outcrops of the islands of Malta and Gozo, where normal faults with offsets up to a few 10s of meters crosscut a sequence of porous calcarenites with variable petrophysical and geomechanical properties.

Statistical distributions of all measurable fracture parameters have been obtained with rigorous procedures developed by our group in the last 10 years, and include, for each set or for the full network, spatial distribution, kinematics and deformation mechanism, orientation, topology, length and height, density, intensity, representative elementary area (Bistacchi et al., 2020, SE; Martinelli et al., 2020, JSG; Casiraghi et al., 2025, SE).

Petrophysical and geomechanical properties have been characterized in the field with semi-quantitative methods and in the lab with porosimetry, microCT, monoaxial, triaxial, and Brazilian tests, and yield a detailed picture of the behavior of the calcarenites under progressive deformation.

The elastoplastic constitutive models include non-linear effects, such as strain weakening, poroelasticity, strength envelopes with a cap (i.e. porosity collapse in compression), and are used to define material behavior in advanced P-FEM large-deformation non-local numerical simulations where faults emerge spontaneously as plastic shear zones with realistic geometry and topology.

Comparing the statistical mapping of fracture parameters with the evolution of material properties in numerical simulations (i) validates the modelling approach and (ii) provides insight into fracturing processes in the nucleation and early propagation (process zone development) vs. mature slip (damage zone) stages of faults in these layered sequences.

In conclusion, combining quantitative observations on outcrop analogues, petrophysical and geomechanical datasets, and advanced numerical simulations, provides important indications on the development of process and damage zones, and hence on hydraulic properties, for faults that are otherwise almost invisible in seismics.
