title: Time-constrained Paleoenvironmental Reconstruction of the Kootenai Formation using stable isotopes, Carbon Isotope Chemostratigraphy and Fossil Microvertebrate Assemblages
session_title: New Voices in Paleontology
authors: Gonzalez, Glen [1], Suarez, Celina A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract:
The Kootenai Formation (KF) in southern Montana was deposited during the Sevier Orogeny and is characterized by a basal conglomerate with interlayered sandstone, siltstone, and limestone. Detrital zircon geochronology estimates the age of the Kootenai Formation to be between 135–110 Ma (Aptian–Albian); however, maximum depositional age (MDA) has been estimated to range up to 145–110 Ma. Despite its significance in North American Cretaceous geology, the unit remains relatively understudied, thus continued chronostratigraphic and lithostratigraphic research is needed to determine the age of the KF and its relationship to other Western Interior Basin (WIB) strata.

This study integrates carbon-isotope ( δ 13 C) chemostratigraphy of bulk organic carbon with existing U-Pb geochronology to refine chronostratigraphic control of the KF by correlating isotopic trends to the global C-isotope record. Furthermore, a microfossil assemblage recovered from the Upper Kootenai provides critical paleoenvironmental context, where oxygen-isotope ( δ 18 O) analysis of these biogenic remains can help constrain lacustrine basin hydrology (open vs. closed system dynamics).

Preliminary analyses indicate that the Upper Kootenai exhibits a negative/positive shift similar to carbon isotope excursions found within Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a (OAE 1a), indicating a potential minimum depositional age of ~120 Ma. The recovered microfossil assemblage contains diverse taxa, including Osteichthyes, Crocodyliformes, Amphibia, and Chondrichthyes. These specimens exhibit strong faunal affinities with microvertebrate assemblages from the Cloverly and Cedar Mountain formations, providing biostratigraphic support for regional correlation in both depositional timing and paleoenvironmental conditions. Together, these proxy data establish a high-resolution chronostratigraphic framework for early foreland basin development of the WIB.

title: Differential erosion and hillslope asymmetry in a southern Appalachian landscape
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Granger, Darryl E. [1], Huang, Xianmei [2]
affiliations: (1) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
(2) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN,
abstract:
The Valley and Ridge landscape in southwestern Virginia is characterized by linear sandstone ridges, with repeating spurs and hollows on the more erodible mountain flanks. Spurs developed in the Devonian Brallier Formation, a turbiditic siltstone, are remarkably regular over a distance spanning >100 km. The spurs trend roughly north-south, often oblique to the ridge, and exhibit persistent asymmetry. West-facing slopes are gentler and wooded with conifers, while east-facing slopes are steeper and wooded with deciduous trees.

Previous work by Hack and Goodlett (1960) in the Little River basin nearby also noted topographic asymmetry, with steeper deciduous-forested slopes facing northeast and gentler conifer-forested slopes facing southwest. They attributed the difference in vegetation to soil moisture, with conifers preferring the drier south-facing slopes subject to higher solar radiation. Solar radiation, however, does not explain the east-west pattern we observe.

We measured bedding and joint orientations in the bedrock in a section of Brushy Mountain. No joints correspond to preferential hillslope angles. However, the intersection of a set of joints with the bedding planes forms a set of V-shaped troughs plunging gently to the east. Although these wedges are below the critical slope for failure, individual chips of saprolite may be more susceptible to wedge-type release on the east-facing slopes, for example by frost-driven processes. The joint-bedding plane intersections also provide a flowpath through the otherwise impermeable siltstone, carrying moisture to the east-facing slopes, consistent with observed vegetation.

If increased moisture and easier saprolite disaggregation facilitate erosion on the east-facing slopes, then differential erosion rates would promote ridge migration and a feedback that would tend to align hillslopes perpendicular to the joint-bedding plane intersection, as observed.

To test this hypothesis, we measured erosion rates using 10 Be in fine-grained quartz on paired samples from steep and gentle slopes in the same valley at four different locations. Erosion rates at two pairs of sites agree closely at ca. 11-13 m/My. However, erosion rates at two other sites differ, with the steep slope eroding twice as fast at 21-25 m/My. Although the results are ambiguous, they provide support to the differential erosion hypothesis, perhaps through stochastic processes such as shallow landsliding.

title: Laramide Structural Influence on the Preservation of Dinosaur Bones, Morrison Formation, Central Colorado
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Petrie, Jemma [1], Simonsen, Adam [2], Sonheim, Ryan Jacob [3], King, Michael Ryan [4], Petrie, Elizabeth S. [5]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geological Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Geology, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(3) Geology, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(4) Geology, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(5) Geology, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
abstract:
Fractured bones of a Haplocanthosaurus were recovered from the Gordon-Bramson-Brothers Quarry in the lower part of the Jurassic Morrison Formation south of Snowmass, Colorado. These fractures were previously postulated to be the result of Pleistocene ice wedging within shallowly exhumed strata. This study tests that hypothesis by comparing fracture orientations measured in quarry-adjacent outcrops with those observed in bone fragments.

Structure-from-Motion photogrammetry was used to collect fracture orientation and spacing data and reorient previously quarried fossils. Fracture planes cutting the bones were mapped using the compass tool in CloudCompare. Fracture data obtained from structural transects at outcrops in the Jurassic Morrison/Curtis Formations and Entrada Sandstone show regularly spaced fractures (Cv = 0.4-0.6) that dominantly strike north with dips ≥50°. Fractures mapped within the bones have parallel to subparallel orientations (±11°) and regular fracture spacing (Cv = 0.4-0.6), consistent with the fracture spacing observed in sandstone and limestone outcrops.

A chevron bone could be reoriented using its position on the published quarry map by applying a 22° clockwise rotation. After restoration, fractures within the chevron strike east (mean strike 85° ± 11°) and dip steeply south (60-85°).

Thin-sections from outcrop and bone fragments show that veins formed in the subsurface. Outcrop samples contain both extensional and shear veins that cut and locally offset ooids and quartz grains, as well as evidence of pressure solution and cataclasis. In the bone fragments, veins crosscut mineralized pore spaces, indicating that at least one phase of mineralization predated fracturing. Calcite veins in both outcrop and bone samples contain mechanical twins, indicating deformation under elevated confining pressures and temperatures in the subsurface. Evidence of Laramide structural influence in the study area includes steeply dipping beds (>60°) and nearby faults that cut the Paleozoic and Mesozoic units. The regular fracture spacing observed in both outcrop and fossil bone suggests a strata-bound fracture system, potentially formed during Laramide uplift and tilting prior to surface exposure. However, nearby faults may have locally influenced fracture orientations.

This study demonstrates a method for restoring fossil orientation for geologic analysis. When adequate quarry documentation exists, fossil fragments can be reconstructed to extract fracture data. Petrographic evidence suggests that the bones were mineralized and fractured in the subsurface and potentially exploited by later Pleistocene freeze-thaw processes.

title: Magmatic Evolution and Metasomatic Controls on Sn–Rare Metal Mineralization in the Mesoproterozoic Massangana Granite Massif, Rondônia Tin Province, SW Amazonian Craton
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics
authors: Debowski, Beatriz Pereira [1], Geraldes, Mauro César [2], Souza, Valmir da Silva [3]
affiliations: (1) Graduate Program in Geosciences (GeoPOS), Faculty of Geology, Rio de Janeiro State University (UERJ), Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil
(2) Department of Geology, State University of Rio de Janeiro, UERJ, Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil
(3) Institute of Geosciences, University of Brasília, Brasília, DF, Brazil
abstract:
The Mesoproterozoic Massangana Granite Massif, one of the principal tin-bearing plutons of the Rondônia Tin Province (SW Amazonian Craton), records the evolution of a highly fractionated A-type granite system overprinted by fluorine-rich metasomatic processes responsible for Sn and rare-metal mineralization. This study integrates detailed petrography and whole-rock geochemistry to reconstruct the magmatic–metasomatic evolution of the massif and its relationship to mineralization.

The granitoids comprise coarse-grained to porphyritic amphibole and biotite alkali-feldspar granites, medium biotite-granites, fine-grained pink leucocratic granite, topaz granite, and late pegmatitic leucogranites. The fine-grained leucocratic facies is enriched in incompatible elements (HREE, Y, Nb, and Ta) and may represent a late magmatic pulse that pre-enriched critical elements before hydrothermal redistribution, although additional mineralogical and geochronological data are required to test this interpretation.

Mineralization is associated with successive metasomatic facies derived from the granitic protoliths. Four principal assemblages were recognized: (1) cassiterite-bearing quartz veins and quartz greisen hosted by fractured biotite alkali-feldspar granite; (2) siderophyllite–topaz greisen and chlorite–phengite greisen developed near granite–amphibolite contacts; (3) lenticular sodic episyenites associated with siderophyllite- and/or zinnwaldite-bearing greisens; and (4) topaz–zinnwaldite greisen and albitized pegmatitic leucogranites associated with topaz granite. Topazite locally represents an advanced stage of fluorine-rich metasomatism, characterized by extensive replacement of feldspars by topaz. Mineralized zones are preferentially concentrated along granite margins, where exogreisens are spatially associated with quartz veins and pegmatoid bodies, whereas endogreisens occur within the pluton and are dominated by Li-bearing mica (zinnwaldite).

Metasomatic evolution involved feldspar recrystallization, albitization, episyenitization, topazization, greisenization, and silicification. Sodic episyenites display the highest ΣREE contents among the analyzed mineralized facies (1,720–2,007 ppm), together with elevated Nb concentrations, suggesting that episyenitization may have locally enhanced the concentration of critical elements.

The Massangana Granite Massif records a continuum highly fractionated magmatic evolution to hydrothermal alteration, where late evolved melts and F-rich fluids promoted progressive chemical transformation. The coexistence of episyenites, topaz-rich rocks, greisens, pegmatitic leucogranites, and cassiterite-bearing quartz veins reflects complex element redistribution. Enrichment in Nb, Ta, Sn, and REE highlights the interplay between magmatic differentiation, fluid–rock interaction, and mineral precipitation in a genetically related Sn–rare metal system.

title: A Decade of Geology for Resilience and Sustainability – A Program Proposal
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Wessel, Gregory R [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology in the Public Interest, Vashon, WA, USA
abstract:
In the 1970s, a group within the GSA envisioned a massive project that would provide a comprehensive look at the geology of North America. Called the Decade of North American Geology , it lasted over two decades and included the participation of thousands.

A project like DNAG may not be as easy today. Our ways of connecting with others and the products of our work are far different now, but the current need for collaboration and cooperation is far more pressing than it was half a century ago.

The problems faced by society today are ones we created. They are also the problems for which we must find expedient solutions. Our challenge is to foster hope, trust, and collaboration to create an infrastructure that promotes broader and more effective applications of science and engineering at the grassroots level . It is imperative that we create such a framework to benefit the global community and the planet.

If you could step into the future and ask your great-grandchildren what our primary responsibility is today, they would say that we should address the causes of climate change and mitigate its impact on society. For that reason, we propose a program like DNAG that will be a joint effort but will be more targeted to enable an exchange of geologic information and geoscientific expertise at the local level . We propose a Decade of Geology for Resilience and Sustainability .

Our mission will be to promote and enable applied grassroots geoscience in a multi-disciplinary environment. Initially, our goals will include:

· Increasing public awareness of the value and utility of the application of geoscience to advancing societal resilience and sustainability at the community level,

· Enabling geoscience to be effectively applied to positively impact community resilience or sustainability,

· Identifying ways to institutionalize changes necessary at the local level to guarantee continued movement toward resilience and sustainability, and

· Working with communities and educators to expand geoscience education at the local level and engage students in the work of enhancing resilience and sustainability in their communities, to prepare the next generation for this work.

If you’d like to be a part of it, contact us at gwessel@publicgeology.org.

title: Variability in Gold Transport and Deposition across the Hog Mountain Orogenic Gold Deposit, Alabama
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part II)
authors: Poole, Joshua D. [1], Bilenker, Laura [2], Gottardi, Raphaël Z [3], Kerschen, Naomi [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA; Senior Staff Geologist, Wellborn Mining, LLC, Ashland, AL, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
abstract:
Hog Mountain is an orogenic gold deposit in the southernmost Appalachians of east-central Alabama. Like several of the Southeast’s major gold deposits, it is hosted within the Eastern Blue Ridge terrane. Although confined to a relatively small tonalite body intruded into metasedimentary rocks of the Wedowee Group, at least two distinct mineralization zones are preserved. Previous research and mining focused on the northern mineralization zone, where large extensional Au-bearing quartz veins contain simple sulfide assemblages and Bi-Te phases. Gold transport and deposition in the northern zone is interpreted to have occurred from a reduced, near-neutral hydrothermal fluid and facilitated by Bi-rich melts [1]. In contrast, the recently explored southern mineralization zone is dominated by texturally distinct, laminated and shear-deformed quartz veins. The goal is to determine whether veins from the southern zone record the same ore fluid and gold deposition mechanisms observed in the north, expressed through different structural pathways, or instead record a spatially evolving hydrothermal system.

This study applies mineralogical and geochemical characterization across the deposit by targeting quartz veins that vary in texture, deformation, sulfide distribution, and alteration style. Observations from geologic mapping and drill core logging are integrated with petrography, reflected-light microscopy, scanning electron microscopy with backscattered electron imaging and energy dispersive spectroscopy, cathodoluminescence imaging, and laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Results from these new southern zone samples are compared with previous results of the northern zone [1]. Quartz veins from the southern zone are commonly laminated, boudinaged, and dynamically recrystallized, with pyrrhotite-dominant sulfide assemblages occurring as planar to anastomosing ribbons. Similar to the northern zone, Bi-Te phases and native gold occur as droplet-like blebs and discrete grains along quartz grain boundaries and discontinuous sulfide trails extending into quartz.

We interpret the differences and similarities between the northern and southern zones to indicate heterogeneous strain accommodation within the tonalite and a broadly similar ore fluid. The resulting vein architecture controlled the physical sites of ore deposition, while related ore fluids produced comparable sulfide assemblages, Bi-Te phases, quartz, and native gold. This contribution refines the genetic model for Hog Mountain by evaluating the variability of gold transport and deposition mechanisms across contrasting structural sinks within an orogenic gold system.

[1] Brueckner et al., 2021, Economic Geology, 116(2).

title: Flora response to climate change through the Miocene Climate Optimum
session_title: New approaches to old fossil collections
authors: Morrison, Kate [1], Love, Renee [2], Reichgelt, Tammo [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, Utah Valley University, Orem, Utah, USA
(3) Department of Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut, USA
abstract: Evidence of ancient climate change provides unique insights into not only past environmental interactions but also in understanding how current climate trends can impact plant physiology and ecosystems functioning. Future climate projections are similar to those of the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO), ~17-14 million years ago. Here we utilize paleobotanical climate proxies—Leaf Margin Analysis (LMA), Leaf Area Analysis (LAA), Climate Leaf Multivariate Program (CLAMP) and Bioclimatic Analysis (BA)— to derive quantitative paleoclimate estimates from eight different fossil sites in northern Idaho syn- and post-MCO. These sites, which are included in or are related to the Clarkia Fossil Beds (sites P35, P41, P42, P47), Oviatt Creek localities (sites P40, P38, P34), and Jungle Point (P36), span between 12.5 to 15.6 Ma. Reconstructed mean annual temperatures for Clarkia sites are between 10.2 °C and 14.3 °C and Oviatt and Jungle point sites are between 11.0 °C and 14.3 °C. Reconstructed mean annual precipitation for Clarkia sites is between 100 and 133 cm/yr while Oviatt and Jungle Point sites is between 104.7 and 166 cm/yr. These estimates indicate that sites younger than 15 Ma (P35, P41, P42, P47) may have sustained higher temperatures similarly occurring in the Miocene Climatic Optimum leading into the Middle Miocene Climatic Transition (MMCT) than originally thought. However, mean annual precipitation measurements show a much drier Miocene after 15 Ma. Investigating floral diversity changes may elucidate the regional response and why these younger, more transitional localities would stay relatively warm post-MMCO.

title: Integrating Field Mapping, Digital Outcrop Models, and LiDAR: A Case-Study from the Brady Mountain Area, AR
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Fleming, Zachariah [1], Read, Michael T. [2], Darko, Emmanuel [3]
affiliations: (1) Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX,
(2) Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX,
(3) RIZZO International, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract: This study presents mapping of Ordovician exposures from the Brady Mountain area, located in the central Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas. Situated within the broader Benton Uplift, the study area contains large scale folding, associated with the Ouachita Orogeny, across the area, which has been mapped at the regional scale. Our work looks to better understand the structural details of the study area by presenting a high-resolution map which was created through traditional boots-on-the-ground mapping, Digital Outcrop Models (DOMs) analysis, and regional LiDAR datasets. Additionally, supplemental conodont biostratigraphy is used to enhance current age control of the map units. The addition of modern toolsets into the field geology workflow is growing, and this case-study represents some of the key advantages of such toolsets. In particular, the study area lies in a highly vegetated region with limited outcrop exposure, limiting the possibilities for extensive boots-on-the-ground mapping. To combat the exposure issue, we utilized two remote sensing techniques; the first was to use slope maps and hillshade relief maps of the study area, derived from statewide LiDAR imagery, to extend map-lines. Additionally, the maps showed subtle topographic ledges which correlated to bedding traces and were used to identify areas of interest and potential structures and discontinuities, which were then assessed in follow-up field work sessions. The second remote sensing technique used in this study was to create multiple DOMs throughout the field area which allowed for detailed analysis post-field, including direct measurement of data from the models. Ultimately, the study area reveals primarily E-W striking thrust faults with associated folds, which are overturned to the south in most cases. N-S trending fault traces apparently crosscut the folds and thrust faults, indicating multiple phases of deformation. This is also supported by cleavage orientations from the area which show two distinct sets: one oriented NE-SW and another N-S. Further work will look to develop 3-dimensional models and place the area in the framework of the Ouachita orogeny at large.

title: Venus Volcanism and Earth's Submarine Eruptions: Environmental Similarities, Modeling Constraints, and Common Characteristic Morphologies
session_title: Venus and Earth: Separated at Birth
authors: Gregg, Tracy K.P. [1], Sakimoto, Susan E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
(2) Space Science Institute, Lakewood, CO, USA
abstract:
Venus’ atmosphere is dominated by CO 2 (>96%). At mean planetary radius (mpr), the atmospheric pressure is 9.3 x 10 6 Pa and the temperature is ~460°C. For comparison, Earth’s atmosphere is mostly N 2 (~78%), with a pressure of 1.0 x 10 5 Pa and average global temperature of ~15°C. At mpr, Venus’ atmosphere is likely to behave as a supercritical fluid. These ambient conditions strongly impact how lava flows will cool, which directly affects lava emplacement dynamics and final flow morphologies. The best terrestrial analog to Venusian surface atmosphere-lava interactions is at the bottom of the ocean: thermal convection of seawater cools basalts at similar rates as the convecting CO 2 -dominated Venusian atmosphere. Furthermore, the pressure at ~900 m below sea level on Earth is similar to the ambient pressure at Venus’ mpr. This combination keeps magmatic gasses dissolved within the lavas and quenches the lava-flow surface within seconds. The quenched glass crust then insulates the underlying lava and drastically slows the cooling rate. This combination of faster crust growth and slower interior cooling has significant impacts on observed flow morphology.

The most abundant lava flow morphology at mid-ocean ridges is “lobate,” characterized by broad (>1 m across), thin (<50 cm) lobes that coalesce to form a smooth, flat-lying surface that would appear flat and featureless at the resolution of Magellan Synthetic Aperture Radar. They are morphologically similar to the Venusian surfaces imaged by the Venera and VEGA landers. Assuming a tholeiitic basalt, lavas with these morphologies on the sea floor might generate channelized a’a’-like flows if they were emplaced on land on Earth. Our initial modeling suggests that model results from terrestrial submarine and Venusian surface conditions are similar to each other, and differ significantly from terrestrial subaerial flow results. However, we note that depth-averaged modeling (1-D) does not capture these differences well, and that they are best observed with a 2-D or 3-D modeling approach where the internal temperature structure of the flow is resolved in the model, and lava properties are temperature-dependent.

We suggest that closer investigation of the emplacement of submarine lava flow emplacement can provide significant insight to the behavior of Venusian volcanoes, and vice versa.

title: Defining Accessible Materials for Students with a Visual Impairment in Physical Geology Courses
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Manning-Berg, Ashley [1], Dizon, Darren [2], Mendez, Guadalupe [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical Sciences, San Diego Mesa College, San Diego, CA, USA
(2) San Diego Mesa College, San Diego, California, USA
(3) San Diego Mesa College, San Diego, California, USA
abstract:
Results of a Google search for the “best general education science courses for visually impaired students” include an AI-generated answer: “environmental science, astronomy, and introductory biology,” arguing that these subjects can be taught with tactile graphics, 3D models, auditory simulations, and hands-on experimentation. Geology is a recommended course because it “utilizes raised-relief maps, physical rock and mineral samples, and tactile models of planetary or crust structures.” Since professors are generally not involved in creating students' schedules, academic advisors and disability services advisors may recommend these classes for students with visual impairments.

The search results also return links to websites with resources teachers can use to make their courses more accessible to this underserved student population. Unfortunately, the suggested environmental resources offer ideas for teaching about plants and do not address the topics taught in geology-based courses, and the reasons for recommending visually impaired students enroll in a geology course are flawed. For faculty teaching Physical Geology, there is little guidance on adapting course materials. Adaptable resources, such as tactile images, are published on the International Association for Geoscience Diversity (IAGD) website, and a few university-specific news stories about others’ experiences in a Physical Geology course are the primary resources available to geology professors.

The idea of teaching a visually impaired student in geology can initially feel overwhelming and even somewhat isolating. Many of us can visualize ways to replicate many of the graphics in our textbooks and labs more tactile, but there is limited insight into best practices for creating these images, and our disability offices may be able to provide only limited support due to budget constraints that limit access to critical tools for printing the images from the Geoscience Tactile Image Repository and a general lack of understanding of how geology is taught, and the topics that are covered in a geology class.

Here we present our collaborative journey to find an accessible way to teach geology to a visually impaired student during the 2025-2026 academic year at a community college. We present the challenges and successes we faced from both the professor's and the student's perspectives, and suggest ways to make geology courses more welcoming for students with visual impairments.

title: Modeling Debris-Flow Runout Following the 2022 Pipeline Fire in Northern Arizona, USA
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society (Posters)
authors: Crowder, Corey [1], McGuire, Luke A. [2], Youberg, Ann M. [3], Liu, Tao [4], Moitra, Pranabendu [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(2) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(3) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
(4) New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission, Santa Fe, NM,
(5) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ,
abstract: Postfire debris flows pose a threat to communities and infrastructure. Runout modeling represents a substantial source of uncertainty in postfire debris-flow hazard assessments. The area inundated by debris flows is influenced by flow mobility parameters in addition to volume, sediment concentration, and local terrain. To better constrain mobility parameters for postfire debris flows, we mapped the area inundated by debris flows that initiated in two small watersheds burned in the June 2022 Pipeline Fire in northern Arizona, USA. The debris flows transported a combined volume of 17,000 m 3 of sediment out of the two source watersheds and inundated an area of 520,500 m 2 . We simulated debris-flow runout using the Herschel-Bulkeley rheological model in HEC-RAS v7.0. Input debris-flow hydrographs at the upstream boundary were determined by scaling clear water hydrographs, which were estimated through rainfall-runoff simulations of the debris-flow triggering storm. Rheological parameter ranges were determined through Bayesian posterior analysis by comparing modeled and observed inundation extent. Laboratory analyses are ongoing to compare model calibrated parameters with those determined through experiments with a rotating ball rheometer. Sediment samples used in rheometer experiments were collected from debris-flow deposits along the runout path. Results of this study identify combinations of rheological parameters that best reproduce observed runout behavior and clarify how uncertainty in these inputs affects predicted inundation. These findings provide constraints for applying a single-phase rheological model to the prediction of debris-flow inundation in a region where fire activity is increasing.

title: Every P Pool Has a Story
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry
authors: Blake, Ruth E. [1], Moller, Spencer R [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sc, Yale University, New Haven, CT,
(2) Ecology, Evolution and Behavior, University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN, ; Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
abstract: The first published study combining sequential chemical extraction of specific phosphorus (P) pools from marine sediments (Ruttenberg,1992) with oxygen isotope analysis (d 18 O P ) of each pool in 2010 (Jaisi and Blake, 2010), presented a new investigative tool and opened new avenues of inquiry and discovery. This coupled analytical approach-- d 18 O P analysis of individually extracted and separate P pools was quickly adopted across distinct environmental matrices, primarily by the soil /agricultural sciences and environmental engineering communities.Their assimilation of sequential extraction ( e.g. , SEDEX, Hedley) coupled to d 18 O P has provided significant new insights into P cycling, transport, and transformations in soils and marine sediments by microbiota, and more recently by plants (Pfahler et al., 2013). Although studies of marine sediments are relatively sparser, they have firmly demonstrated the utility of d 18 O P analysis of separate sediment P pools. Moreover, geochemical modeling of coupled marine sediment P i -d 18 O P and co-existing pore fluid dissolved phosphate d 18 O P data further indicates a direct link between rates of dissolved P i -water O isotope exchange and rates of sedimentary organic carbon respiration. This, for the first time, anchors measured dissolved P i d 18 O P values (which also reflect specific microbial metabolic activities) to rates of microbial metabolism and the amount of biodegradable organic carbon in sediments (Zhao et al., 2021). Here, we detail the story behind each P pool. Both adsorbed P (includes Fe and Al--oxy-hydroxides/oxides) and authigenic P pools reflect formerly dissolved P i which carries signatures of its sources ( e.g., regeneration from organic matter) and P cycling pathways ( e.g., microbial P i uptake, or P i cycling/turnover with resetting to new ambient T and d 18 O-water). Marine water column (paleo)temperature is reflected in d 18 O P values of bioapatite and also of dissolved P i in the water column that becomes adsorbed to/ occluded within non-biogenic hydrothermal iron oxides/oxy-hydroxides. Finally, the detrital P pool reflects sediment P provenance ( e.g, riverine or airborne input), and the residual organic P pool (in the case of SEDEX) derives primarily from surface organic matter.

title: ‘Yes, go ahead and cut that shell’ – Building a Collection Meant to be Used, with an Example from the Pliocene
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part II)
authors: Ivany, Linda C. [1], Moss, David Kelton [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY, USA
(2) Department of Environmental and Geosciences, Sam Houston State University, Huntsville, TX, USA
abstract: There is simply nothing like the experience of being part of an actively growing, cutting-edge, meticulously maintained research collection. When LCI arrived at the Florida Museum of Natural History for a masters degree, Roger Portell had only been in charge of the invertebrate paleontology collection for two years, but it seemed clear even then that he had the goal of making it one of the best-run collections in the country and a vision for how he was going to do it. With the mindset of an accountant, the discipline of a professional, and the passion of an avocational paleontologist, he set about building the collection and its infrastructure into a flagship example of how collections can be run for maximum effectiveness and impact. Central to Roger’s philosophy is that a research collection is there to be used – and he actively advocates for and facilitates this in so many ways. As but one illustration, a conundrum for those of us who study the chemistry and/or internal architecture of fossils is the need for destructive sampling. Through his partnership with then-curator Doug Jones, Roger had an early appreciation for using fossils to study life history and environment, and whenever possible he archived sufficient material to allow such work. These approaches have been central to our own research. In the spirit of this ‘Cenozoic celebration’, we share an example using fossil bivalves from the Pliocene. The ocean quahog, Arctica islandica , is the slowest growing and longest-lived bivalve known today. A North Atlantic cold-water taxon, populations around Iceland regularly produce individuals of 200+ years of age. Bivalves from higher latitudes today generally tend to be longer lived and slower growing than those at lower latitudes. To the degree that temperature plays a role in life history, Arctica living during the warmer Pliocene should exhibit faster growth and shorter lifespans than those today. We collected fossil Arctica from the Pliocene Tjörnes Beds of NE Iceland to compare their life histories and paleotemperatures with shells directly offshore today. Shell chemistry confirms significantly warmer Pliocene temperatures, and growth parameters derived from shell cross sections indeed reveal short lifespans and faster growth in comparison to modern shells. Such work is greatly expedited by collections designed to be used in diverse ways.

title: Quantifying Timescales of Magma Reservoir Dynamics Using Petrochronologic Changepoint Analysis
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers.
authors: Mohr, Michael T. [1], Schaen, Allen Joseph [2], Jicha, Brian R. [3], Schmitz, Mark D. [4]
affiliations: (1) Boise State University, Boise, ID,
(2) Tucson, AZ,
(3) University of Wisconsin-Madison, Middleton, WI,
(4) Boise State University, Boise, ID,
abstract:
High-precision zircon petrochronology has revealed that the large silicic magma reservoirs that generate super-eruptions evolve through protracted periods of accumulation, assembly, and storage followed by comparatively rapid rejuvenation and remobilization prior to eruption. Although stages of magmatic evolution are commonly recognized in time-resolved zircon trace element records, quantifying when and how quickly transitions in magmatic reservoir processes occurred remains challenging. The Miocene Apache Leap tuff (ALT), a large-volume, caldera forming eruptive unit in the Superstition Volcanic Field (central Arizona), is one example of a super-eruption with a well-resolved magmatic history, where the timing of magmatic processes and eruption have been independently established through tandem U-Pb zircon petrochronology and Ar/Ar sanidine incremental heating analyses. The zircon record preserves >200 ka of magmatic input and crystallization characterized by high inter- and intra-grain variance in multiple zircon trace-element proxies of magmatic differentiation. However, a marked shift in the mean and variance of these proxies prior to eruption is interpreted to reflect a reservoir tipping-point toward mush remobilization leading to eruption. Establishing a quantitative estimate of the timing of this transition requires an approach that accounts for analytical uncertainty, multivariate shifts, and intracrystalline geochemical superposition.

Here we explore petrochronologic changepoint analysis as an approach for identifying statistically significant transitions in magma reservoir evolution leading up to a super-eruption. Our approach integrates multiple parametric and nonparametric changepoint detection algorithms within a Monte Carlo resampling algorithm to propagate geochronologic uncertainty and respect intragrain geochemical superposition. When applied to our ALT zircon petrochronology dataset, independent changepoint methods consistently detect a geochemical transition within a similar pre-eruptive time interval, providing confidence in the inferred transition despite the differing underlying algorithms of each detection method. Preliminary results yield a changepoint distribution, that when combined with our independently constrained ALT eruption age, places the petrochronologic transition at 33 +50/-31 ka prior to eruption. This analysis provides quantitative temporal constraints for a transition in magma reservoir characteristics, interpreted to mark the shift from prolonged reservoir assembly to mush remobilization leading up to the ALT super-eruption. We suggest that petrochronologic changepoint analysis provides a statistically robust and objectively reproducible framework for identifying and quantifying transitions in petrochronologic records.

title: Development and Installation of a Modular Corrosion Monitoring Array Within Southeast Florida’s Saltwater-Intrusion-Affected Coastal Urban Environment
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Flores, Juan Pablo [1], Lau, Kingsley [2], Eschenburg, Holly [3], Sukop, Michael C. [4]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Environment, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
(2) Department of civil and environmental engineering, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(3) Institute of Environment, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(4) Institute of Environment, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
abstract:
The Southeast Florida coastal region is characterized by a densely developed urban corridor built on low, flat terrain and underlain by the highly transmissive Biscayne Aquifer. Ongoing saltwater intrusion within this environment places buried physical infrastructure at risk of corrosion. The corrosion impact of salinity fluctuations near the saltwater wedge is still not well understood. There is a lack of continuous, long-term, in situ resistivity and electrochemical measurements collected from electrodes in direct contact with the formation in a vertical profile. The need for data to improve understanding of subsurface corrosion within this complex hydrogeologic environment prompted development of a novel monitoring system. Our modular corrosion monitoring array is designed to measure at multiple depths in direct contact with the formation: local and extended corrosion rates, corrosion activity, and the electrical properties of the surroundings. The modular design consists of seven sensing modules, each containing one silver chloride reference electrode, one counter electrode, and four working electrodes. Extension modules separate the sensing modules, creating seven monitoring depths extending to 100 feet below the ground surface. The electrode geometry allows for configurations that measure localized corrosion rates, adjacent subsurface resistivity approximately 6 inches into the formation, extended subsurface resistivity at approximately 20 inches, and larger through electrical coupling of working electrodes across the full vertical profile.

The modules are constructed in-house with off-the-shelf components and a PVC structure. Each working electrode is spring-loaded, allowing for temporary compression into PVC caps during installation in the well casing. To create this compression, a PVC decentralizer bow system was designed and attached opposite the working electrodes. This system allows them to spring out and force contact with the formation upon casing removal. Backfill materials consist of silica flour around the sensing modules to approximate the permeability of the surrounding rock matrix and uncoated bentonite clay in the extension modules to restrict vertical groundwater flow. Design and pre-assembly of the modules have been completed for installation at three sites on Florida International University’s Biscayne Bay Campus. Future work includes connecting the modules during well installation and linking each array to a relay and data logger. Corrosion measurements will be paired with depth-specific groundwater samples from an adjacent multilevel monitoring well as part of FIU’s Coastal Subsurface Monitoring project.

title: Grain-size Contrasts Stall Escarpment Retreat
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Drobnich, Kate [1], Siar, MK [2], Gallen, Sean F. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: The enigmatic evolution of passive margin Great Escarpments – large abrupt steps in topography found along passive margins globally – remains one of the most contested topics in landscape evolution. Great Escarpments are thought to form post-continental rifting, and current theory and numerical landscape evolution models suggest that their stark topographic asymmetry indicates landscape disequilibrium where escarpments rapidly retreat (> 1 km/Myr) over geologic time. However, cosmogenic radionuclide data from escarpments generally show comparably low erosion rates on upland and escarpment draining rivers indicating slow to no motion with rates typically less than several tens of meters per million years. Numerous studies have attempted to reconcile this discrepancy, yet none satisfactorily explain the slow rates of escarpment retreat required by cosmogenically-derived erosion rates. Here, we show from studies of the Blue Ridge Great Escarpment in the southeastern U.S. and an active-margin escarpment in Puerto Rico that differences in fluvial sediment grain size on opposing sides of escarpment divides can explain comparable erosion rates and sluggish migration rates amidst dramatic topographic asymmetry. Utilizing both published and new 10 Be and 36 Cl catchment averaged erosion rates, both escarpments show similar erosion rates on the upland and escarpment, but pebble counts from 46 basins along the Blue Ridge and 49 basins in Puerto Rico reveal coarse grain size fractions, D 84 , are 2 to 3 times larger on escarpment-draining rivers and median grain size fractions are comparable to 3 times larger. Applying bedrock river incision models that account for hydraulic geometry and sediment grain size, we demonstrate that grain size can effectively explain differences in across-divide fluvial relief while maintaining comparable erosion rates, slowing escarpment retreat. Channels adjust their hydraulic geometry to accommodate transport of the median grain size fraction, allowing the coarse fraction to serve as an armor layer protecting the bedrock channel from erosion during typical flood events. Essentially, coarser grain sizes on steep escarpment-draining rivers decrease erodibility, allowing for comparable erosion rates to finer-grained, gentler upland channels. We use these results to argue that previously unrecognized geomorphic feedbacks in landscape dynamics slow escarpment retreat and preserve escarpment morphology over geologic time scales. If correct, these results have profound implications for the evolution of Great Escarpments globally.

authors: Puthalath, Saranya [1], Kirk, Matthew F. [2], Nippert, Jesse [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environment, Kansas State University, United States of America, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA; Division of Biology, Kansas State University, United States of America, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
(2) Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS,
(3) Division of Biology, Kansas State University, United States of America, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas, USA
abstract:
Stable isotopes in precipitation provide powerful tracers of hydroclimatic processes; however, their interpretation requires unravelling the influences of local atmospheric conditions and regional moisture transport. We present an analysis of more than twenty years of precipitation isotope observations (δ 18 O and d-excess) from the Central Great Plains (Konza Prairie), USA, to identify the controls on seasonal and interannual isotope variability. Warm-season isotope enrichment was largely associated with enhanced convective precipitation and sub-cloud evaporation under high vapor pressure deficit. In contrast, atmospheric back trajectories indicate that the Gulf of Mexico moisture transport through the Great Plains low-level jet strongly modulates isotopic composition despite the predominance of continental moisture sources.

Extreme hydroclimatic years also demonstrate these contrasting controls. The 2012 drought exhibited higher δ 18 O and reduced d-excess, reflecting enhanced evaporative fractionation under dry conditions, while the exceptionally wet year of 2019 showed isotopic enrichment linked to intensified Gulf moisture transport. Together, these findings reveal that precipitation isotope variability in the Great Plains shows the combined effects of local evaporative demand and large-scale moisture transport processes. Given ongoing challenges in representing humidity trends and regional hydroclimate dynamics in climate models, improved characterization of moisture sources and isotope variability will help better evaluate model projections and interpret long-term climate change in semi-arid continental regions.

title: Water Quality and Recharge of Springs in Southwest Kyrgyzstan
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Fryar, Alan E. [1], Orunbaev, Sagynbek [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Environmental Sustainability and Climate Science, American University of Central Asia, Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic
(3) Environmental Sustainability and Climate Science, American University of Central Asia, Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic
abstract:
The Kyrgyz Republic (Kyrgyzstan) is a landlocked, largely mountainous country in Central Asia. Given its location and limited precipitation (annual average < 600 mm/year), its water resources are particularly sensitive to climate change. As part of providing guidance to local stakeholders and resource managers, we are characterizing water quality and delineating recharge zones of selected springs in rural areas of Batken province in southwest Kyrgyzstan. This region lies within the arid Fergana basin and is flanked by the Turkestan and Alay ranges.

During June 2025, we sampled 23 springs for field parameters, metals, anions, nutrients, and stable isotopes. These springs are used for drinking and domestic supply, irrigation, livestock watering, aquaculture, and recreation. TDS ranged from 179 to 2771 mg/L (median 375 mg/L). Solute concentrations were below drinking water guidelines for all but 2 springs (Ba at one and NO 3 - at another). Ca and HCO 3 - were the dominant ions at 17 of 23 springs, consistent with carbonate lithology. The 5 springs with TDS > 750 mg/L had SO 4 2- as the dominant anion. Bivariate plots of major ion concentrations on a charge-equivalent basis (Ca + Mg vs. HCO 3 - + SO 4 2 ; Na + K vs. Cl - ; (Na + K) – Cl - vs. (Ca + Mg) – (HCO 3 - + SO 4 2- )) have strongly linear trends. These indicate that water chemistry is dominated by dissolution of calcite, dolomite, and gypsum, with Na and K contributed by dissolution of evaporites and cation exchange.

Stable isotope values ranged from -83.4 to -54.9‰ (median -72.6‰) for δ 2 H and from -11.94 to -8.96‰ (median -10.82‰) for δ 18 O. Values scatter along a δ 2 H–δ 18 O trend with a slope of 5.72 (r 2 = 0.541), which falls below the local meteoric water line for Central Asia (slope = 7.56) and is consistent with partial evaporation during recharge. Although water temperature decreases with elevation (slope = -0.75°C/100 m, r 2 = 0.581), δ 18 O shows a weak positive correlation with elevation (slope = 0.104‰/100 m, r 2 = 0.201), which is likely to be an artifact of local atmospheric circulation. Analyses of logged water levels and temperatures at 3 monitored springs, in conjunction with meteorological data and mapping of snow cover in inferred recharge areas, should provide additional information on timing and mechanisms of recharge.

title: Impacts of Water Management on National Water Model Errors
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling (Posters)
authors: Hutchins, Christina [1], Marshall, Adrienne [2], Bakar, Sophia [3], Triana, Enrique [4], Landsteiner , Sam [5]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Geology and Geol Eng, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Geology and Geol Eng, Golden, CO, USA
(3) RTI International, USA
(4) RTI International, USA
(5) RTI International, USA
abstract: Reservoirs fundamentally alter streamflow magnitude and timing by changing how, where, and when water flows through a river system. Hydrologic models are valuable tools for understanding streamflow dynamics, but at continental scales they simplify human modifications. The National Water Model (NWM) is a continental-scale hydrologic model, developed by NOAA’s Office of Water Prediction and NCAR, that simulates streamflow over most of the contiguous US. It supplements NWS river forecasts, extends coverage to locations without an official forecast, and includes a reanalysis run spanning 1979–2023. The NWM currently includes approximately 5,000 reservoirs in its framework but simulates them using only a simple fill-and-spill approach that fails to capture operational complexity. While comprehensive testing of the NWM has been conducted, the effect of simplification of reservoir operations on model performance has not yet been evaluated. We evaluate model performance with respect to streamflow observations at 6,388 GAGES-II gauges based on the center of timing (CT), standard deviation of timing (SDoT), and 95th (Q95) and 5th (Q5) streamflow percentiles. Overall, NWM errors indicated that the model does not accurately represent the effects of water management on streamflow. CT and SDoT errors at regulated versus unregulated basins were minimal, with modeled CT slightly too late and SDoT too wide at both. In contrast, model errors with respect to high and low flows varied substantially between regulated and unregulated basins. Median modeled low flows (Q5) were too high in both regulated and unregulated basins, but the error was much greater in regulated basins (84.4% ± 409% IQR) than unregulated (14% ± 167). Median modeled high flows were slightly too low in both basin types, with slightly less bias in regulated basins (-1.7% ± 64%) than unregulated basins (-4.4% ± 35%). This signature-based approach allows us to identify locations where operational representation could be improved by incorporating site specific reservoir operation schemes.

title: Using gprMax to Create Numerical Models of No Casket Burial Scenarios
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Jornacion, Alana Isidro [1], Schneider, Blair Benson [2], Alves Borges, Ayla [3]
affiliations: (1) Allan Hancock College, Santa Maria, California, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
(3) University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas,
abstract:
Human approach to death and subsequent burial is fundamental to who we are, shaping cultures over centuries of practice. That said, there is a large gap in the written documentation of certain burial regimens, including those in 19 th to early 20 th century America. During that time period, there were many cultural and technological shifts occurring, which changed how certain burials were performed. Many different groups of people were passing through Kansas during this time period, leading Kansas to reflect those differing burial practices. A significant portion of burials from this time period are located in potter’s fields, which were areas that were often used to bury unidentified, unclaimed, or destitute individuals.

Due to the ethics around modern day burial preservation, excavation has heavy restrictions in place. Instead, a noninvasive way to learn more about these sites is to use ground penetrating radar (GPR). GPR transmits electromagnetic waves through the subsurface and these waves return reflections when they encounter different materials.

Despite its promise, GPR data is often difficult to interpret due to the noise produced by other (non-burial) naturally occurring objects in the subsurface. There is little research done on how the size of the human (adult, child, or infant sized) and the stage of bone deterioration affects GPR detection of burials. For this research, we used gprMax, a Python software, to simulate different burial conditions in GPR data. In gprMax, several variables can be tested and controlled, including burial depth, body size, stage of bone deterioration, GPR antenna frequency used, and soil type. The results of the models are then comparatively analyzed to actual GPR data from the Alma City Cemetery in Alma, Kansas. The goal of this analysis is to improve data interpretation and allow for more comprehensive trend categorization. Future research can include more complex modeling scenarios to help further improve GPR burial interpretation.

This work was conducted as part of the Geo-Launchpad internship program, supported by the NSF NGF operated by EarthScope Consortium.

title: Carbonate Stable Isotope Blueprint for Interpreting Ancient Wetland Facies
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies (Posters)
authors: McDonald, Abigail Rose [1], Fetrow, Anne C. [2]
affiliations: (1) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA
(2) Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO,
abstract: Wetland (palustrine) environments are climate-sensitive ecosystems that act as carbon sinks and climate change bellwethers, making accurate interpretation of their sedimentary archives essential for paleoclimate reconstruction. Palustrine environments are characterized by frequent water table fluctuations between shallow lacustrine/fluvial conditions and subaerial exposure resulting in alternating phases of carbonate and siliciclastic deposition and pedogenic modification. Although abundant in the geologic record, palustrine deposits remain understudied and are frequently miscategorized as shallow lakes. This oversimplification discounts their depositional complexity and can lead to the misinterpretation of paleoclimate records. Here we aim to establish a modern interpretive framework for palustrine facies and geochemical signatures to provide a blueprint for better using wetland paleoenvironment and paleoclimate records. Las Tablas de Daimiel National Park (LTD) in south-central Spain is a modern terrestrial wetland ecosystem with active carbonate deposition driven by alkaline surface runoff and groundwater discharge. This setting undergoes profound seasonal autumn-winter flooding and summer dry-down, generating overprinted and heterogeneous sedimentological features. LTD has been used as a primary modern analogue for palustrine facies found in the geologic record. We assess sediment cores (40-80cm) across four sub-aerially exposed sites. To identify diagnostic palustrine facies and differentiate phases of inundation and exposure, we use sedimentary description, loss on ignition, X-ray diffraction, and bulk carbonate stable isotope geochemistry (δ13C and δ18O). Carbonate stable isotope data show considerable variation among facies and across depths. Facies-averaged δ13C values range from –7.71‰ to –1.70‰ while δ18O ranges from –4.62‰ to –0.39‰. Carbonate-dominated facies show the most positive δ13C and δ18O values, suggesting carbonate precipitation is more closely tied to dry-down events with significant evaporation. Cores taken near edges of the basin show an increase in δ13C and decrease in δ18O approaching the modern era. These data indicate that the basin has become more persistently flooded with incomplete dry-down allowing for increased exchange with the atmosphere. Cores towards the center of the basin show consistent δ13C and δ18O values, reflecting reduced hydrologic variability. We will integrate these data into the existing Iberian Peninsula paleoclimate records to disentangle changes in regional and global hydroclimate and the influence of human land use. In addition, this modern framework will improve the interpretation of ancient wetlands; enabling further utilization of these valuable sedimentarysystems.

title: Quaternary Deformation of Alluvial Fans Along the South Granite Mountains Fault System, Wyoming
session_title: Earthquake Signatures in the Landscape
authors: Mauch, James [1], Jensen, Collin [2], Stafford, James [3], Rodrigues, Kathleen [4], Schwaderer, Colby [5]
affiliations: (1) Wyoming State Geological Survey, Laramie, WY,
(2) Wyoming State Geological Survey, Laramie, WY,
(3) Wyoming State Geological Survey, Laramie, WY,
(4) Desert Research Institute, Reno, NV,

abstract: The South Granite Mountains fault system (SGMFS) is a 135-km-long, high-angle, north-dipping normal fault that bounds the north flanks of Crooks Mountain, Green Mountain, and the Ferris and Seminoe Mountains in central Wyoming. Normal faulting along the SGMFS accommodated the Neogene gravitational collapse of the Laramide Sweetwater Arch, and discontinuous, linear fault scarps across alluvial fans attest to continued Quaternary deformation. Previous paleoseismic studies have estimated slip rates to be less than 0.1 mm/yr through dating and displacement analysis of latest Pleistocene to Holocene alluvial and colluvial deposits. However, older alluvial fans with larger fault scarps remain undated, providing an opportunity to extend the time span over which slip rates are calculated and assess the temporal variability of these rates. Our work addresses this gap through new mapping, lidar fault scarp topographic profiles, and luminescence dating at Cherry Creek in the northern Ferris Mountains, where three levels of alluvial fans are offset by well-expressed fault scarps. We focus on the oldest and youngest of these fault-displaced alluvial fans, mapped by Geomatrix Consultants in 1988 as Q1c and Q3c, respectively. Fault scarp topographic profiles yield vertical surface offsets of approximately 5 m for Q1c and 2 m for Q3c, suggesting a history of progressive and recurrent Quaternary surface displacement. Four pending luminescence ages, two each from Q1c and Q3c, will allow calculation of fault slip rates across multiple earthquake cycles. This work provides context for the evolution and seismic hazard of the SGMFS and contributes to broader research on active intraplate faults with incomplete or fragmented surface expressions.

title: Investigating the Deglaciation History of Cordilleran Ice Sheet in British Columbia, Canada
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations
authors: Romero, Matias [1], Rubin, Calen [2], Marcott, Shaun A. [3], Shakun, Jeremy D. [4], Darvill, Christopher [5], Gregoire, Lauren J. [6], Reyes, Alberto V. [7], Menounos, Brian [8], Jones, Andrew G. [9], Caffee, Marc W. [10]

abstract:
Modern observational records are too short for evaluating the response of ice sheets to climate change on centennial to millennial timescales. Geological records of ice sheet change, however, offer direct insights into the style of deglaciation over such timescales, including rates of thinning and spatiotemporal patterns of ice margin retreat.

During the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), the Cordilleran Ice Sheet (CIS) in mid-latitude western North America occupied regions with complex topography and steep climate gradients, making it a valuable natural laboratory for studying ice sheet behavior. While numerous studies have reconstructed the position of its ice margins during the last deglaciation (19-11 ka), vertical records documenting the timing and magnitude of volume loss and ice thinning are sparse. Therefore, addressing these data gaps is essential for understanding the final demise of the CIS and its role in past climate and sea level changes during the last deglaciation.

To address this limitation, we sampled erratic boulders and bedrock surfaces for cosmogenic 10 Be exposure dating to constrain the timing of ice retreat and thinning across the former ice sheet interior. More than 100 samples were collected from elevations ranging from ~500 to 2500 m across a 3x10 5 km 2 area between the Coast and Rocky Mountains of British Columbia. We will present initial results from ~40 newly derived surface exposure ages and their implications for the timing, magnitude, and spatial pattern of ice sheet deglaciation.

abstract:
New geologic mapping supported by the FEDMAP component of the USGS National Cooperative Geologic Mapping Program (NCGMP) and in cooperation with the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) provides insights into the geology and critical mineral deposits in the Bessemer City 7.5-minute quadrangle, NC. The map extends from the eastern flank of the Inner Piedmont Cat Square terrane across the central Piedmont suture into the Kings Mountain sequence of the peri-Gondwanan Carolina superterrane. The dextral greenschist facies Kings Mountain shear zone marks the central Piedmont suture within the map area. The Inner Piedmont Cat Square terrane is composed of polydeformed, variably migmatitic muscovite schist, metagraywacke and amphibolite intruded by the Devonian Cherryville Granite (380–355 Ma) and Mississippian(?) pegmatite. The Cambrian to late Neoproterozoic Kings Mountain Sequence consists of schist, phyllite, quartzite, and marble of the Blacksburg Formation, and schist, phyllite, quartzite, metaconglomerate, manganiferous schist, and amphibolite of the Battleground Formation. Map units generally strike north to northeast and dip gently to moderately southeast in the Inner Piedmont, whereas map units dip steeply in the Kings Mountain Sequence. The Blacksburg and Battleground Formations are folded and cut by several dextral shear zones, which expose two elongate bodies of metatrondhjemite and metadacite of the Bessemer City gneiss (~514 Ma). The High Shoals Granite (~319 Ma) intruded the Battleground Formation; the Sunnyside granite stitches the Central Piedmont suture between the Inner Piedmont Cat Square terrane and the Carolina superterrane. Early Jurassic diabase dikes strike north-northwest across the older rocks.

The map area contains industrial, precious, and critical mineral deposits. The central portion of the Carolina tin-spodumene belt lies within the quadrangle, as well as numerous historic prospects and mines for tin and lithium (spodumene) including the Hallman-Beam Mine. Mapped spodumene-bearing and muscovite-bearing pegmatites are discontinuous bodies that are generally parallel to strike; however, the main spodumene ore pegmatite in the Hallman-Beam Mine strikes about N80°W. Other potential critical mineral deposits include cassiterite (tin), rare earth element-enriched regolith, and manganese. Aeromagnetic and radiometric surveys conducted by Earth MRI over the Piedmont will provide additional insight into the framework geology and critical mineral deposits.

title: Mush Rejuvenation Beneath a Stable Mantle Source: The Tenorio Volcanic Complex, Costa Rica
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Hidalgo, Paulo J. [1], Alpizar, Yemerith [2], Alvarado Induni, Guillermo E. [3], Ryan, Peter C. [4], Hames, Willis E. [5], Taylor, Waldo [6], Kirn, Russ [7], Crye , Kiersten [8]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA,
(3) Universidad de Costa Rica,
(4) Middlebury College, Middlebury, VT,
(5) Auburn University, Blacksburg, VA,
abstract:
The Tenorio Volcanic Complex (TVC), at the southeastern terminus of Costa Rica’s Guanacaste Volcanic Range, records ~480 kyr of near-continuous eruptive activity — from Middle Pleistocene foundational volcanism through Late Pleistocene edifice construction to Holocene rejuvenation (<10 ka–~300 BCE). This long record offers a rare opportunity to isolate what changes in a magmatic system over geologic time, and what doesn’t.

Integrating bulk-rock geochemistry, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar and 14 C geochronology, thin-section petrography, and least-squares mass-balance modeling, we show that the mantle wedge source beneath TVC has remained genetically uniform for nearly half a million years: incompatible trace-element systematics (Ba/Th, Zr–Th, Ti–V) and a continuous TiO 2 /Zr–Zr depletion array preserve one coherent slab-fluid signature throughout. Apparent major-element “splits” among TVC lavas are not source effects but products of upper-crustal fractional crystallization; mass-balance inversion (F = 0.37, ΣR 2 = 0.29) shows 63 wt.% crystal extraction (Plag 38.5% + Opx 11.8% + Cpx 7.2% + Mt 5.3%) converts basaltic-andesite parents to evolved dacites, building a plagioclase-dominated cumulate root beneath the massive.

Our key result: this steady-state architecture broke down in the Holocene. Multi-generational plagioclase (calcic An 65-70 mantles), peritectic clinopyroxene coronas on resorbed orthopyroxene, and oxidized hornblende rims record mafic recharge invading and reheating stalled Pleistocene mush. We tie this shift directly to a structural cause: transtensional tearing along the inner boundary of the Guanacaste Arc Sliver, expressed locally as the 8-km-long Tenorio Graben, fractured the mature reservoir and let least-differentiated, high-MgO basaltic-andesite melts bypass the mush entirely, erupting from peripheral parasitic cones before they could differentiate. Sporadic, extreme Nb enrichments (>500 ppm) further suggest these same translithospheric fractures tap localized OIB-like mantle heterogeneities.

TVC thus demonstrates a clean decoupling between mantle-scale and crustal-scale controls on volcanism: a single fault system reorganized magma transport and eruptive behavior without perturbing the underlying mantle melting engine. Despite this evidence of Holocene explosive activity and active faulting, TVC lacks an official hazard map or monitoring network, a gap consistent with regional preservation bias against distal tephra in wet tropical settings. As eco-tourism development expands across the seismically active Tenorio Graben, these findings establish an urgently needed geological baseline for hazard zoning and future monitoring.

title: Barium Isotopes as Tracers of Sediment Recycling in Colombian and Mexican Arc Magmas
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Gutiérrez Aguilar, Fabián [1], Gómez Tuena, Arturo [2], Errázuriz Henao, Carlos [3], Sánchez Gutiérrez, Andrea V. [4], Parolari, Mattia [5], Arrieta García, Gerardo [6], Martínez Serrano, Raymundo G. [7], Solís Pichardo, Gabriela [8]

abstract: Subduction zones transport sediments into the mantle, enabling sediment-derived components and their geochemical signatures to be transferred to arc magmas. However, distinguishing biogenic from terrigenous or hydrothermal contributions remains challenging. The continental arcs of Colombia and Mexico offer an ideal geological setting to address this question because Ba-rich biogenic sediments are subducted with the Nazca plate beneath the Northern Volcanic Province of Colombia (NVPC), whereas terrigenous and hydrothermal sediments are subducted with the Rivera and Cocos plates beneath the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (TMVB). Despite similar calc-alkaline affinities, their volcanic rocks differ markedly in average Ba concentrations. To investigate the origin of this contrast, we present the first high-precision 135 Ba– 137 Ba double-spike-corrected Ba isotope dataset for lavas from the NVPC and TMVB. These measurements, combined with published geochemical data, allow us to test whether contrasting biogenic and terrigenous/hydrothermal sedimentary inputs impart distinguishable Ba isotope signatures to arc magmas. In the NVPC, high-Mg andesites from Nevado de Santa Isabel volcano, where the slab lies at a depth of ~140 km, display isotopically light δ 138 Ba /134 Ba NIST3104a values (-0.10‰ to -0.07‰), whereas lavas from Cerro Machín volcano, where the slab reaches a depth of ~160 km, record the heaviest Ba isotopic compositions of the Colombian suite (-0.04‰ to +0.01‰). The western TMVB exhibits the opposite relationship with slab depth, with lavas from Colima volcano, where the slab lies at ~90 km depth, yielding heavier compositions (-0.04‰ to -0.01‰) than those from the more landward Tequila volcano (-0.09‰ to -0.03‰), where the slab reaches an estimated depth of ~320 km. We suggest that the observed Ba isotope variability in lavas from the NVPC and TMVB reflects contributions from subducted barite reservoirs of contrasting marine origins. Whereas barite destabilization may be limited at shallower slab depths beneath Nevado de Santa Isabel and Colima, deeper breakdown of relatively heavy pelagic barite beneath Colombia and isotopically light hydrothermal barite beneath Mexico could shift Cerro Machín and Tequila lavas toward heavier and lighter Ba isotope compositions, respectively. These results highlight the potential of Ba isotopes to trace the cycling of biogenic and terrigenous/hydrothermal sedimentary components from the seafloor through the mantle wedge and back to the surface via arc volcanism.

title: A 130-Year Sedimentary Charcoal Record of Historical Wildfires from Jackson Lake, Wyoming

abstract:
Despite frequent and severe wildfires in Grand Teton National Park, high-resolution fire reconstructions remain scarce. We reconstruct fire history from Jackson Lake sedimentary charcoal, calibrating charcoal accumulation against documented fires and Landsat-derived burn maps.

We analyzed the 49-cm-long GT7A core, collected in 2019 from the northern end of Jackson Lake near the inflow of the Snake River. ²¹⁰Pb and ¹³⁷Cs dating indicates that this core spans the period 1902-2021, with an average sedimentation rate of 0.42 cm yr⁻¹. Charcoal counts were converted to charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR; pieces cm⁻² yr⁻¹) using the age-depth model, providing the basis for fire-history reconstruction. CHAR peaks exceeding the median threshold (4.58) identified 15 potential fire episodes. Several peaks corresponded with historically documented fires from the Jackson Hole record, including the Bear Paw Bay Fire (2009), located 9.95 miles south of the core site; the Wilcox Fire (2000), located 2.34 miles to the northwest; the Moran Fire (2000), located 3.55 miles to the southwest; the Yellowstone Fires (1988), located 9.39 miles to the north, northeast, and northwest; 4.22 miles to the south; and the Big Burn (1910), located approximately 370 miles to the northwest in Idaho and Montana. Most confirmed fire events were located to the north, northeast, and northwest of the core location, while three events occurred to the southwest and south. The highest CHAR peak corresponded to the lightning-ignited Waterfalls Canyon Fire (1974), located within the parks prescribed natural fire management zone.

This research aims to expand charcoal analyses to additional short sediment cores across Jackson Lake to evaluate spatial variability in charcoal deposition and improve interpretations of CHAR signals relative to historical fire events over the past 130 years.

abstract: The rapid increase in plastic production and inadequate waste management have intensified the release of plastic-associated endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) into tropical riverine environments, posing significant ecological and human health concerns. Open burning of plastic waste, informal e-waste recycling, and indiscriminate disposal of municipal solid waste have emerged as important sources of persistent organic pollutants (POPs), including phthalic acid esters (PAEs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), in Indian riverine catchments. This study synthesizes observations from recent investigations across tropical riverine systems and urban waste hotspots in India, revealing elevated concentrations of plastic waste-derived endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), including phthalic acid esters (PAEs), heavier PBDE congeners, and tetra- and penta-chlorinated PCBs, particularly in regions impacted by open waste burning and informal recycling activities. The COVID-19 pandemic further intensified plastic waste generation through increased consumption of personal protective equipment (PPE), contributing to enhanced environmental loading of these contaminants. Long-term persistence and bioaccumulation of EDCs, including their transfer through aquatic food webs and detection in bovine milk near contaminated dumpsites, highlight their potential risks to ecosystem integrity and human exposure. Tropical climatic conditions, characterized by intense monsoonal runoff, high temperatures, and dynamic hydrological processes, further influence the transport, redistribution, and fate of these contaminants within riverine catchments. Addressing this emerging challenge requires sustainable remediation strategies that complement improved waste management. An integrated Artificial Intelligence (AI) mediated nature-based treatment approach combining constructed wetlands with advanced nanocomposite-based adsorption systems offers a promising solution by simultaneously enhancing contaminant removal, reducing secondary pollution, and restoring ecosystem functions. Such hybrid treatment technologies provide a sustainable pathway for mitigating plastic waste-linked EDCs in tropical riverine environments while supporting long-term water security, ecological resilience, and environmental sustainability.

title: The Crossroads of Productivity: Integrated PFZ Detection in the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna Influence Zone
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Chowdhury, Siraj Uddin Md Babar [1], Chowdhury, Nur Uddin Md Khaled [2]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Space Oceanography Division, Bangladesh Oceanographic Research Institute (BORI), Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Bangladesh

abstract:
The northern Bay of Bengal (nBoB) is a socio-economically vital marine region, yet its fisheries face increasing pressure from environmental variability and climate-driven changes. Traditional identification of Potential Fishing Zones (PFZs) often relies on surface-level satellite data, which fails to capture the subsurface dynamics and vertical nutrient transport critical to fish aggregation. This study addresses this gap by implementing an integrated framework that combines field observations with a high-resolution coupled ocean-biogeochemical model, the Coastal and Regional Ocean Community (CROCO) model coupled with the PISCES ecosystem module.

The model was configured at a 9 km spatial resolution to simulate complex interactions, including nutrient cycling, phytoplankton growth, and wind-driven circulation. Validation against in-situ CTD measurements and satellite datasets showed strong agreement, particularly for sea surface temperature (SST) and chlorophyll-a distribution. Our findings identify thermal fronts (>0.04°C/km) and elevated chlorophyll-a concentrations as primary indicators of PFZs, with the most favorable conditions occurring in January. The results also emphasize the profound influence of freshwater discharge from the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) system, which sustains high coastal productivity even when wind-driven upwelling is weak. By integrating thermal structure, wind stress curl, and biological productivity, this study establishes a process-based approach for fisheries forecasting. This research provides essential insights for ecosystem-based management and the advancement of the Blue Economy in the region.
