abstract: Mesozoic magmatism in the Mojave Desert represents a southern extension of the Sierra Nevada Magmatic arc. The Granite Mountains in the eastern Mojave Desert are composed of Jurassic to Cretaceous intermediate to felsic plutonic rocks. We undertook a geochemical and geochronological study to better understand the petrogenesis of the Granite Mountains plutonic rocks and the source of Mesozoic Mojave Desert magmatism. In this study, fifteen samples from across the Granite Mountains were analyzed for zircon U-Pb, trace-element, and Hf isotopic compositions and whole-rock major- and trace-element concentrations. Zircon U-Pb analyses yielded both Jurassic (162–149 Ma; n = 87) and Cretaceous (80–75 Ma; n = 315) magmatic ages. Rare Proterozoic inherited grains ranged in age from 1780–1550 Ma (n = 4) with ε Hf values of -28.4 to -35.0, corresponding to exposed Proterozoic wall rock surrounding the Granite Mountains. Hf analyses of magmatic zircon yielded a restricted range of ε Hf values from -8.3 to -13.4 across all ages and compositions, consistent with derivation from an enriched lithospheric mantle source, with little impact from crustal assimilation. Whole-rock major- and trace-element data for Cretaceous and Jurassic samples each define single liquid lines of decent reflecting progressive evolution of the magmatic system through partial melting, magma mixing, and/or fractional crystallization. The Hf isotopic composition of the Granite Mountains plutonism is consistent with the upper limit of initial ε Nd and ε Hf values of Mesozoic plutonic rocks across the eastern Mojave and ε Nd of nearby mantle xenoliths, potentially reflecting a wide-spread lithospheric mantle source. Such an enriched source composition would permit a more limited role of crustal recycling in isotopically enriched Mesozoic plutonic rocks and indicate that a larger volume of juvenile crust was generated by Sierran magmatism in this area.

title: Insights into Lunar Basaltic Magmatism and Regolith Composition from Dominion Range (DOM) Meteorite 18262
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials (Posters)
authors: Medema, Emily Grace [1], McLeod, Claire Louise [2], Shaulis, Barry [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Earth Sciences, Miami University, Miami, OH, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Earth Sciences, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA

abstract:
Repeated bombardment, melting, and fragmentation of the lunar surface over billions of years has established a lunar regolith which dominates the Moon’s surface environment. As these regolith materials comprise the ground over which rovers and astronauts will explore, characterization of regolith materials is crucial for supporting future surface exploration missions. One approach to advancing understanding of lunar regolith composition and evolution is through the study of regolith breccias.

Dominion Range (DOM) 18262 is one of eight lunar basaltic regolith breccias returned from the 2018-2019 Antarctic Search for Meteorites (ANSMET) season. Through a detailed textural, mineralogical, and geochemical analysis of DOM 18262, this study aims to investigate the petrogenesis of its regolith components while contributing to the knowledge of the Moon’s geological evolution.

Work to date on a 1.2cm by 1.2cm thin section of DOM 18262 has involved characterization via microscopy: PLM, and SEM-EDS. Meteorite DOM 18262 is a clast-poor (<10%) breccia where a glassy matrix surrounds clasts, mineral fragments, glass spherules, melt pockets, and melt veins. A glassy, variably vesiculated fusion crust surrounds ~90% of the sample with some segments texturally akin to lunar agglutinates. The clast inventory includes basalts, impact melt breccias, microbreccias, and 3-phase symplectites. Basaltic clasts are the most common and are characterized primarily by unzoned plagioclase and variably zoned clinopyroxene with variable proportions of minor fayalitic olivine and ilmenite in addition to accessory troilite, apatite, silica, spinel, and alkali feldspar. These basaltic components also characterize the mineral fragment population found throughout the matrix. Collectively, these petrographic observations are consistent with the samples’ basaltic regolith classification and are similar to those reported for select paired stones (e.g., DOM 18543, 18666).

Electron MicroProbe data will quantify the chemical composition of the meteorite’s components (clasts, fragments, glass) identified via microscopy, guided by spatial context provided via SEM-EDS. Chemical data will evaluate if DOM 18262 shares a similar lunar provenance to that of its paired stones, for which a comparative dataset exists. This includes assessing 1) the potential derivation of basaltic components from an ancient, highly fractionated, Fe-rich and low-Ti magma, and 2) the delivery of anorthositic material to the site of regolith breccia petrogenesis and the development of potential cryptomare.

title: Integrating AI-Driven Analytics with Immersive Geological Field Education
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Wilkinson, Lindsey [1], Hidalgo, Paulo [2]
affiliations: (1) Physical Science, Estrella Mountain Community College, Avondale, Arizona, USA

abstract:
Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), digital outcrop models, and high performance computing are changing the way geologists collect, analyze, and interpret geological data. As computational tools become more common in professional geoscience workflows, field education has an opportunity to prepare students to use these technologies while reinforcing the observational and interpretive skills that remain fundamental to geology. Automated fracture detection and remote predictive mapping can quickly identify structural features from point cloud datasets, but geological complexity, exposure quality, weathering, and field relationships still require direct observation to evaluate and refine computational interpretations.

We present a framework for incorporating AI-assisted digital outcrop analysis into geological field education through field-based exercises that combine computational analyses with traditional geologic mapping. Students use point cloud datasets and digital outcrop analyses to evaluate fracture patterns and structural interpretations before testing these predictions through field observations, structural measurements, and geologic mapping. Comparing computational interpretations with field evidence allows students to validate, refine, or reject predicted structural features while developing a better understanding of both the capabilities and limitations of these emerging tools.

Field observations provide the foundation for geological interpretation, while computational analyses offer an additional source of information that students learn to critically evaluate through mapping and direct observation. By integrating digital technologies into immersive field experiences, students strengthen observational skills, spatial reasoning, and geologic interpretation while gaining experience with computational workflows that are becoming increasingly common in professional practice. This framework provides an approach for preparing future geoscientists to thoughtfully integrate emerging technologies with field-based investigation while reinforcing the value of immersive geological field education.

title: Recurrent Coseismic (?) Landslides along the Ninemile Fault, Missoula Valley, Montana
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment (Posters)
authors: Sears, James W [1], Willingham, Amanda [2], Gavillot, Yann [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Montana, Missoula, Mt, USA
(2) Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Butte, Montana, USA

abstract:
Lidar mapping indicates recurrent landslide activity proximal to the Ninemile Fault. The landslides cut shorelines of Glacial Lake Missoula, and are thus younger than the last emptying of the lake <13,000 years ago. Though landslides occur in the surrounding area, the higher incidence of landslides along the Ninemile Fault corridor indicates that they may be coseismic. Ongoing mapping efforts will determine how many landslide events have occurred along the Ninemile Fault and, if they were coseismic, investigate recurrence of landslide-inducing earthquakes over the past 13,000 years. If possible, magnitudes of landslide-inducing earthquakes will also be estimated.

Older landslides, identified by smoothed geomorphic features, overrode older lake terraces. Younger landslides, identified by sharp feature morphology, often reactivated older landslides. Sag ponds are common within the younger landslides. Some younger landslides overrode Holocene alluvial terraces and floodplains possibly younger than 2,000 years.

One location near Fournier Creek provides particularly valuable cross-cutting relationships for determining relative ages of landslide activity. Here, toes of older landslides initially abutted the Ninemile Fault scarp along a strike-line valley. Landslide deposits were subsequently eroded back from the scarp on the valley bottom, re-establishing a creek run. Later, a younger landslide reactivated within the older landslide, crossed the valley bottom, and again abutted the fault scarp, damming the drainage. The drainage ponded behind the abutment until an overflow gulch cut across the toe of the younger landslide. This study aims to use carbon dating in conjunction with mapping to constrain timing of pond formation here and in other landslide-related ponds along the landslide belt.

abstract:
The Amundsen Sea Embayment (ASE) is an under-explored sector of the West Antarctic continental shelf, where sea-ice cover is typically dense. During recent decades, the glaciers draining one third of the vulnerable West Antarctic Ice Sheet into the ASE were affected by rapid thinning and associated grounding zone and calving front retreat. Simultaneously, sea-ice cover decreased, increasing accessibility to the ice-sheet margin. Within the Southern Ocean, the Amundsen Sea Polynya (ASP) and Pine Island Bay Polynya of the ASE are among the most biologically productive. Multiple international expeditions collected marine sediment cores from the ASE, with recent expeditions by the NSF- and NERC-funded Thwaites Glacier Offshore Research (THOR) team having recovered sediment cores near the ice fronts of major glaciers and ice shelves, including Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers.

As ice extent in polar regions continues to rapidly change, it is imperative to establish baselines for factors that shape the global carbon cycle, including biological productivity in and near polynyas. Here, we examine seafloor surface sediment samples from 62 marine core sites from the ASE (spanning from the inner shelf to the outer shelf and from Cranton Bay in the east to the Getz Ice Shelf in the west) for evidence of biological productivity by determining organic carbon and nitrogen contents, stable carbon isotopes of the bulk sediments, total diatom abundance, and estimating biogenic barium contents from barium to aluminum ratios (Ba/Al). Grain size distributions are measured to characterize glacial and marine depositional environments and identify the presence of meltwater plumites. Cranton Bay, an oceanographically isolated embayment northeast of Pine Island Bay, has the highest observed total organic carbon, followed by the ASP in the southwestern ASE. Ba/Al ratios are highest on the outer shelf, followed by Cranton Bay and the ASP. Comparison of δ 13 C ratios and total organic carbon to total nitrogen ratios of the bulk sediments suggests marine algae as the predominant source of organic matter. These data also indicate that several samples collected proximal to Thwaites Glacier contain organic matter derived from terrestrial C 3 plants, which may have been eroded from Mid-Cretaceous plant-bearing sediments known from the area. We explore these findings in the context of modern environmental conditions and propose explanations for the observed regional differences in productivity proxies.

abstract: Along the coastlines of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, brightly colored microbial aggregates colonize the sediment-water interfaces of ephemeral salt marsh pools. These millimeter-scale pink and green aggregates, informally referred to as “berries,” constitute syntrophic sulfur-cycling communities comprised of purple sulfur bacteria, sulfate-reducing bacteria, cyanobacteria, and diatoms. Recent organic geochemical examinations of carbon cycling in euxinic environments have revealed that lipids, biomolecular components of cellular membranes, signaling pathways, and energy stores, can be subject to rapid sulfurization, enhancing their long-term preservation in sediments. To characterize the carbon cycling mechanisms in the microbial aggregates, free and sulfur-bound lipids were isolated from berries collected at two field sites: the Great Sippewissett Salt Marsh of Falmouth, Massachusetts and the West End Salt Marsh of Provincetown, Massachusetts. Sulfur-bound lipids were subjected to desulfurization prior to instrumental analysis. A variety of acetogenic and isoprenoid lipids were recovered from both marshes, including fatty acids, steroids, hopanoids, and aromatic carotenoids. These lipids were analyzed via gas chromatography mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography mass spectrometry, gas chromatography combustion isotope ratio mass spectrometry, and elemental analyzer isotope ratio mass spectrometry. Findings from these analyses were used to establish an inventory of lipid isotopic offsets for purple sulfur bacteria and environmental cyanobacteria, which both perform Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle carbon fixation. These offsets were additionally compared to characteristic lipid isotopic offsets previously established for cultured cyanobacteria. Altogether, these findings may aid future source-lipid assignment efforts during the biogeochemical analysis of ancient environments.

abstract: Continental arc flare-ups commonly coincide with crustal thickening and shifts toward less radiogenic isotopic compositions in arc magmas. Still, it remains unclear whether these changes are consequences of elevated magmatic flux or reflect lithospheric processes that cause flare-ups. We investigated a Late Cretaceous-Paleocene flare-up in the North Cascades continental arc, Washington, USA, using high-precision CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon geochronology, whole-rock (La/Yb)ₙ ratios as a proxy for crustal thickness, and zircon Hf isotope data from 27 samples from 9 plutons with crystallization ages spanning 79–63 Ma. The geochronologic data show incremental pluton emplacement, and the (La/Yb)ₙ trends indicate that individual plutons have distinct, local crustal thickening histories. We find no evidence for substantial crustal thickening immediately before flare-up initiation. Instead, the crust thickened progressively during pluton emplacement and was driven primarily by mantle-derived magmatic addition, with tectonic shortening playing a secondary role. Zircon ε Hf values range from approximately –1 to +10 across the plutons. Juvenile values of +7.5 to +10 from some of the plutons are indistinguishable from primitive Cascadia arc basalts and indicate derivation from asthenosphere-dominated parental magmas. Less radiogenic values are restricted to some plutons emplaced during peak magmatic flux and are best explained by localized crustal assimilation or mixing with metasediment-derived crustal melts. Mixing models show that <30% crustal melts are required to reproduce the observed variability. The presence of juvenile and crustally modified magmas in coeval, but spatially distinct, plutons indicates that assimilation was spatially heterogeneous and restricted to discrete trans-crustal magma systems. We conclude that the flare-up was initiated and sustained by increased mantle-wedge melt production, whereas crustal thickening, crustal melting, and isotopic pull-downs were secondary responses to elevated magma flux.

authors: Hagood, Gabriela Yalitza [1], Wilson, Emma [2], Visaggi, Christy C. [3]

abstract:
Georgia State University (GSU) is a large, urban minority-serving public institution in Atlanta with a student population of more than 53,000. Students interested in the geosciences and related environmental fields have varied academic, professional, and career planning experiences across campuses. Degree requirements for majors (geosciences, environmental science, data science and GIS), concentrations (geology, environmental geosciences, geography, urban studies), and certificates (GIS, water sciences, sustainability) are outlined in the catalog, yet connections to future careers can be challenging to understand. While department events and career-focused courses promote career exploration and preparation, such opportunities are not experienced by all students, and in particular are disconnected from students at our perimeter campuses. External resources provided more broadly can be helpful, however, it can still be difficult to navigate dispersed information and make connections to coherent pathways for future careers.

Through the Sustainability Fellowship Program at GSU, student-faculty teams have been developing a modular Notion-based website (GSU Geosciences: Student Resources) designed to be used as an educational and advising tool. This resource was created through an iterative process of identifying common student questions; reviewing university, departmental, and course materials; researching external resources; and reorganizing information around the stages of academic and career development. Sections use plain-language summaries to make connections across university resources, programs, transferable skills, research, internships, resumes, networking, professional learning, certifications and licensure, and more. In addition, a goal of this effort is to promote the diversity of individuals who contribute to the geosciences. Students learn about who geoscientists are, how the field is relevant to our lives, and are guided to explore subdiscipline and identity-based communities. Learning about alumni through spotlights is another feature with options to connect to individuals professionally.

Publishing these resources in a publicly accessible format online extends its educational function beyond a single course or period of enrollment. Alumni, prospective students, educators, or other visitors can continue to use the resources outside of formal student coursework. Because the site is adaptable and built largely from existing institutional and professional materials, its structure can be replicated by others. It demonstrates how a low-cost digital platform can supplement teaching and advising, broaden access to professional knowledge, and help all students understand how informed academic and career choices connect to meaningful futures in geosciences.

abstract: Here, we summarize seven months (October – May) of desalinated water flow injections into Ein Ravid Spring together with the main outflow of the Reverse National Water Carrier (RNWC) into Lower Nahal Tzalmon and the Sea of Galilee. In contrast to the three flow experiments that lasted for only two consecutive days in late December 2022 (Bergman et al., 2025), the stable and continuous flow allowed to monitor the hydrology (hydrographs, transmission losses, water temperature and groundwater levels), turbidity and channel bed activity during constant conditions after the initial bores. The desalinated flow releases included 1000 m 3 /hr (0.28 m 3 /sec) from Ein Ravid Spring and 4000 m 3 /hr (1.11 m 3 /sec) from the main release site of the RNWC - a total of 5000 m 3 /hr (1.39 m 3 /sec). Once the flow stabilized downstream, the constant discharge attenuated to 3600 m 3 /hr (1.0 m 3 /sec) when reaching the lake, due to friction and transmission losses estimated at 28% of water volume loss. Air temperature, desalinated water temperature and stream temperature were correlated as the channel course is mostly exposed to solar radiation, riparian vegetation is currently missing and the flow cannot sustain a steady diurnal temperature which a healthy aquatic habitat would favor. Turbidity values were high (up to 9700 mg/l) during the first bores, but the constant flow completely cleared of mineral suspended sediment and was replaced by biological activity (algae) implying exhaustion and limited amounts of fines available on the bed surface and banks at baseflow. Bedload transport of sand up to 50 mm coarse gravel was minimal with transport distances up to 3-9 m according to painted tracers. Load captured by three basket bedload samplers was meager - probably associated with loose material up to coarse gravel but most of it was organic debris. The fine suspended sediment deposited in the alluvium consolidated the bed, the loose particles were transported and probably increased the shear stress needed for incipient bed motion for future flows. However, the bed was not actually disturbed in terms of scour and the channel morphology was not modified as no significant natural flow arrived from upstream during the entire hydrological year.

title: Dune-Field Mixing and Sediment Provenance in the Mojave Desert, CA, USA, Assessed with Detrital Zircons
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands
authors: Preston, Sarah [1], Day, Mackenzie [2], Bell, Elizabeth A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA, USA

abstract: Detrital zircon geochronology assumes sediment transport is confined to a topographic basin or watershed. Although this assumption is valid for fluvial deposits, it may not hold for aeolian-transported sands, which may be carried across topographic divides between basins. Dune fields in the Mojave Desert and Death Valley National Park provide an excellent testing ground in which to evaluate aeolian zircon transport and basin-to-basin mixing, as there are several dune fields separated by considerable distance and topographic barriers. We collected 10 sand samples from four dune fields and performed LA-ICP-MS U-Pb dating. The resulting age distributions showed approximately 13 distinct peaks ranging from 0.760 to 187 Ma. Mesquite Flat Dune Field and Eureka Dune Field are located approximately 60 km apart, but lie in different topographic basins. Age distributions in the Mesquite Flat and Eureka were similar to each other, with large peaks at 168 Ma and smaller peaks at approximately 15.0, 23.3, and 87.2 Ma, representing a large source contribution from nearby middle Jurassic granitic rocks and lesser contributions from proximal lower Miocene and upper Cretaceous plutonic rocks. The Mesquite Flat samples showed an additional minor peak of uncertain provenance at 10.8 Ma that was not present in the Eureka samples. Some 120 km to the south are the Ibex Dune Field and Dumont Dune Field, 12 km apart and separated by the Ibex Hills. Age distributions in the Ibex Dune Field and Dumont Dune Field were also similar to each other, with pronounced peaks at 12.0 Ma and very small peaks at 145 and 184 Ma, likely derived from Miocene volcanic rocks to the north and Jurassic granites or metamorphic rocks to the west and southeast. The age similarity in these paired dune fields, despite their topographic separation, suggests mixing occurs between topographic basins. The age difference between the Mesquite Flat Dune Field and Ibex dune field, despite their lack of topographic separation, suggests that local sources contribute the most sediment to the dunes. We will present on these local sources and their implications for sediment provenance and intra- and inter-basin transport.

title: Modeling Soil Geochemical Variability Across Antarctic Ice-Free Regions Using Machine Learning
session_title: Geoinformatics and Data Science: A Showcase In Undergraduate and Graduate Student Research (Posters)
authors: Eliason, Lily Kate [1], LeMonte, Joshua J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
abstract:
Antarctica's permanently ice-free regions contain some of the most unusual soil chemistry on Earth. These regions' distinct environmental conditions influence soil formation factors, resulting in soil conditions endemic to Antarctica. Machine learning has recently been used to map Antarctic soil chemistry elsewhere on the continent (Siqueira et al., 2024), but in the Transantarctic Mountains, South Victoria Land, North Victoria Land, and North-west Antarctic Peninsula, a prior study applied multiple linear regression with moderate predictive success (Willmore, 2024). Still, general understanding of these regions remains restricted by limited and spatially uneven sampling.

Here we show that machine learning can predict soil geochemistry across all four regions using environmental predictors, extending laboratory measurements to nearly 16,000 unsampled locations. A total of 171 soil samples from 28 sampling locations were analyzed for properties including pH, cation exchange capacity, stable isotopes, elemental composition, and mineralogy, and paired with 22 spatial predictors derived from digital elevation models, climate data, and geologic maps, including elevation, distance to coast, climate variables, geography, and lithology. Random Forest and XGBoost models were evaluated using Leave-One-Location-Out (LOLO) cross-validation, a spatially explicit approach suited to the high variability and limited sample size (Meyer et al., 2018).

XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy across most targets, with Random Forest performing competitively, and predictions remained consistent across five random seeds. Predictability varied considerably across soil properties, with those linked to biological and weathering processes more reliably mapped and many others showing weak environmental control. Predictions were strongest for nitrogen-cycling properties, particularly nitrogen isotopes (δ 15 N) and total nitrogen, along with digest potassium and sodium, and compositional phosphate.

Overall, this approach demonstrates how spatial modeling can address the limitations of sparse data with nonlinear relationships. These results also offer insight into broader questions, including the effects of climate change, the environmental limits of life, and the habitability of soils as analogs for other planetary surfaces. Large-scale geochemical analysis of Antarctic ice-free regions will deepen understanding of soils formed under extreme conditions and help guide future field sampling efforts.

abstract:
Alkaline lakes have some of the highest phosphate concentrations in natural waters, and thus, these carbonate-rich lakes are a plausible setting for the origin of life (Toner and Catling, 2020). To test the extent to which reaction with calcite may reduce dissolved phosphate concentrations, we conducted a flow-through, fluid-rock interaction experiment for 107 days. We used a peristaltic pump to deliver a salty and alkaline solution (pH of 9.9, 0.72 eq alkalinity/kg, 0.93 mol Na/kg, and 0.21 mol P/kg) at a flow rate of 0.02 g/min into a 120 ml Teflon jar reactor, which contained 1.00 g of 60-125 μm Iceland spar. Geochemist’s Workbench calculations of this system suggest that calcite dissolution will lead to the formation of hydroxylapatite. The reactor was well mixed and held at a constant temperature with a sous vide cooker in a water bath on a stirring plate. The experiment used five temperature stages (30, 40, 50, 40, and 30°C). Each stage was run for ~17 days to facilitate steady conditions before five samples were collected downstream of the reactor over the following week. Fluid samples showed minimal change in pH, alkalinity, Na, P, and Ca. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Raman spectroscopy analyses both identified only calcite on pre- and post-experimental minerals samples. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images illustrated μm-scale smaller crystals that covered the larger Iceland spar surfaces, but energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) chemical analyses indicated a similar calcite composition. Thus, calcite dissolved from the larger crystals during the course of the experiments, but ions immediately reprecipitated as smaller crystals of calcite and not apatite. This suggests that calcite-fluid interaction in alkaline lake settings will not reduce elevated phosphate.

Toner, J. D., & Catling, D. C. (2020). A carbonate-rich lake solution to the phosphate problem of the origin of life. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , 117 (2), 883-888.

title: Reconstructing the Largest-Known Ammonoid, Parapuzosia seppenradensis
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Schretter, Jayden [1], Peterman, David [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
abstract: Ammonoids are an eye-catching clade in invertebrate paleontology and are particularly interesting targets to study the life habits and ecology of ancient marine animals. Reconstructions are possible because specific shell morphologies impose distinct constraints on hydromechanics (i.e., buoyancy, mass distribution, stability, maneuverability, and swimming efficiency). The largest and possibly most charismatic ammonoid is Parapuzosia seppenradensis. The largest-known specimen (lectotype, displayed at the LWL Museum of Natural History in Münster) is ~1.8 m in diameter but lacks a substantial portion of the adoral body chamber. Without a complete specimen at this scale, detailed body mass measurements are difficult to obtain, and the hydromechanical properties mentioned above remain elusive. Throughout ontogeny, this species spans the largest range of scales of any ammonoid (millimeters to meters), which presents unique research opportunities because hydrodynamics strongly depend on scale. Furthermore, body mass can be used to explore metabolic scaling and physiological properties. We estimate the volume of the body chamber in P. seppenradensis by using the angular body chamber length of the closely related P. leptophylla. Isometric shell models were constructed in Blender from published line drawings of the coiling geometry and whorl-section shape. Body chamber volume is estimated to be 0.495 m3, and assuming a cuttlefish-like (Sepia officinalis) mantle cavity ratio, P. seppenradensis soft body likely weighed ~390 kg, 80% the mass of the largest captured colossal squid (Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni). We intend to make an allometric version of the model with published ontogenetic data. By reconstructing the missing body chamber until neutral buoyancy is satisfied, we can develop a more accurate estimate of the soft body mass at various developmental stages. Lastly, these reconstructions will support future research into P. seppenradensis hydromechanics, metabolism, and physiology, potentially leading to breakthroughs in our understanding of 1) how ammonoid swimming constraints change with scale, and 2) the trophic dynamics of giant cephalopods through time.

abstract: A finite element numerical model of the Piceance Basin is being developed to better understand the petroleum systems and geothermal potential of this complex basin. Located in northwest Colorado, the Piceance Basin has a complex tectonic and depositional history which includes multiple depositional styles and phases of tectonic uplift, subsidence, and erosion, making it an excellent natural laboratory to study the impact of basin evolution on petroleum systems and geothermal potential. Modeled units were defined structurally by mapping key horizons from outcrop into the subsurface to create a robust structural framework. This framework is populated with lithologies from new paleogeographic maps for each depositional unit created from core, outcrop, well cuttings, and well log data. The geologic history of the basin was modeled and calibrated to new vitrinite reflectance data and over 9,000 corrected bottom hole temperature measurements. The result is a geologically robust three-dimensional model of the Piceance Basin that quantifies maturity of potential source rocks and geothermal potential within the basin. This study offers insights into the evolution of the Piceance Basin and emphasizes the value of large-scale subsurface data integration for resource evaluation.

title: Preliminary investigation of the Miocene Selendi Basin and implications for orogenic collapse in Western Anatolia, Türkiye

abstract: Recent research has linked delayed faunal dispersion into and through western Anatolia in the early Miocene to a topographic barrier in excess of 3.5 km. Today, the region lies much lower (<750 m) due to regional extension. The underlying mechanism of elevation loss during extension has been linked to several models including slab rollback, westward extrusion, and orogenic collapse. Key to this argument are several supradetachment basins in the region that formed in response to regional extension. In particular, the timing and rate of basin formation, and its relationship to paleoelevation, provides a key test of geodynamic models. However, detailed basin analysis and chronostratigraphic control of Oligo-Miocene basins in western Türkiye are currently lacking. We investigated the Selendi Basin using traditional basin analysis methods including lithofacies characterization, paleocurrent analysis, and conglomerate clast counts. We also conduct detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology by laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Preliminary results indicate that the Selendi Basin is a relatively undeformed sedimentary package with a thickness of about 500 m, much thinner than previously expected and thinner than regional basins of likely similar age, some of which being greater than 1 km thick. The stratigraphy is dominated by volcaniclastic sediments, and shows a transition from alluvial fan and fluvial deposition to lacustrine sedimentation. Basin sediments were likely sourced from the footwall of the normal fault-bounded basin, but the detailed sediment routing within and potentially between other basins in the region remains uncertain and requires further field investigation. Preliminary detrital zircon U-Pb age distributions are dominated by Miocene ages with a dominant mode at ~17-14 Ma, as well as a smattering of older ages, with none older than 850 Ma. Maximum depositional age calculations based on the youngest 25 grains place the timing of deposition between 15 and 14 Ma. Preliminary results suggest the timing of basin formation may have been contemporaneous with elevation loss and the opening of this major faunal migration corridor. If true, this supports orogenic collapse as the primary driver of extension in the region.

abstract: As part of a campaign to evaluate the influence of extremes within the late Devonian (late Famennian) climate system in North America, we present new major element geochemistry of Upper Devonian paleosols from fluvial-to-transitional marine paleoenvironments in the Appalachian Basin (north-central Pennsylvania). Paleosols serve as a useful guide to past climate conditions—especially in the deep time terrestrial record where many other proxies have been altered. Sixty-eight well-developed Upper Devonian paleosols were sampled across north-central Pennsylvania (from both core and outcrop) to capture proximal-distal and temporal geochemical trends within the Upper Famennian Lock Haven, Catskill, and Huntley Mountain Formations. These units record deposition on fluvial to tidally influenced environments just before, and during, deposition of ~361–359 Ma hinterland-proximal diamictites that have been interpreted as subtropical Appalachian Mountain glacial strata. While the sedimentology and paleopedology in some places (primarily in the Catskill Formation) have been previously described, we present companion geochemical analyses. Major element geochemistry was analyzed using benchtop Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence. Paleo-weathering proxy values indicate intermediate chemical weathering (e.g., values between 70–80 for the Chemical Index of Alteration; CIA) and show little spatial or temporal variation, including no evidence for a shift from semi-arid to semi-humid conditions (as proposed in previous Famennian studies). Additionally, while we would typically expect periglacial environments to show CIA values that reflect a lower degree of chemical weathering, it is possible that the CIA values may be elevated owing to, for example, known aluminum-rich schist sources in the hinterland. Further work is required to assess the extent to which provenance overwhelms climate signals in this dataset, including our ability to evaluate whether these data are consistent with a proglacial signal.

authors: Hagen, Amy P.I. [1], Schmitz, Mark D. [2], Pruss, Sara B. [3], Gill, Benjamin Charles [4]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, USA; Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA

abstract: Radiometric age control is limited in the Cambrian Period, especially during Series 2 (~521 to ~506.5 Ma). However, recent work on Cambrian strata in the western US has demonstrated that Cambrian-aged detrital zircons are present but rare. Given the number of important evolutionary events that occurred during Cambrian Series 2, such as the extinction of reef-building archaeocyaths, acquiring more age control on the strata recording these events is critical. With this in mind, we used detrital zircon geochronology to constrain the deposition of the upper Harkless Formation (Cambrian Series 2) of Esmeralda County, Nevada. At our study locality near Gold Point, NV, we sampled two sandstone beds: one that directly overlies an archaeocyathan reef that is thought to be the last robust archaeocyathan reef in the western US before the clade’s decline, and one that occurs ~10 m above. Zircons were separated from both samples and analyzed via Laser Ablation Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (LA-ICPMS) to derive preliminary age dates. The ages of five Cambrian grains were further refined using Chemical Abrasion Isotope Dilution Thermal Ionization Mass Spectrometry (CA-ID-TIMS). The resulting maximum depositional age (MDA) of the upper Harkless Formation was found to be 521.3 ± 0.8 Ma, much older than the expected Stage 4 (514–506 Ma). However, LA-ICPMS data suggest that our two samples contain similar distributions of zircons except for one key difference: the presence of a 1.1 Ga population in our lower sample that is greatly diminished in our upper sample. The loss of this 1.1 Ga population is also recorded between 523 and 508 Ma in the Sixtymile and Tapeats formations of the Grand Canyon and appears to be related to the Sauk I-II sea level change across Laurentia. We therefore suggest that our upper Harkless beds are comparable in age to the Sixtymile Formation of the Grand Canyon, and that our two samples may bracket the Sauk I-II regression. This highlights the use of zircon population “fingerprints” to better refine depositional ages using regional correlations when young zircons are not present in a particular locality.

title: Considerations for Input Data Selection, Parameters, and Approaches for Geochemical Modeling of CO2 Injection
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies
authors: Mahmood, Fazilatun [1], Kalkhaa, Chantsalmaa [2], Livers-Douglas, Amanda [3]
affiliations: (1) Energy & Environmental Research Center, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, ND, USA
(2) Energy & Environmental Research Center, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, North Dakota, USA
(3) Energy & Environmental Research Center, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks, North Dakota, USA
abstract:
CO 2 injection into saline formations initiates geochemical reactions that can alter the physical and chemical properties of the storage system. Dissolution of CO 2 is often instantaneous and immediately decreases the initial pH of formation brine. This change can impact wellbore infrastructure, as low-pH environments can corrode wellbore materials (casing and tubing), compromising wellbore integrity. Accurate prediction of CO 2 -induced pH changes in formation brine using geochemical modeling thus plays an important role in selecting wellbore materials for carbon capture and storage projects. Geochemical modeling is a complex and coupled process that requires careful consideration of multiple input datasets, parameters, and approaches that should be selected wisely to ensure real-world and site-specific simulation results. However, given the heterogeneous nature of subsurface geology and geochemistry such as mineralogy and brine water chemistry, and the potential range in operating conditions for CO 2 injection, selection of input data that are representative of the expected reservoir environment over the lifetime of a project is challenging. To address this issue, the Energy & Environmental Research Center conducted a study examined multiple sets of input data, modeling parameters, and methodologies to develop a range of geochemical scenarios for carbonate and clastic storage complexes. The study evaluated how variations in input data and modeling assumptions influence predicted mineral reaction rates and change in pH.

Site-specific baseline data for several prospective storage complexes in the Williston Basin were used to establish geochemical properties of the reservoir prior to CO 2 injection such as in situ brine composition (cations, anions, salinity, pH, alkalinity, and brine density), rock mineral composition, and reservoir pressure and temperature. Multiple simulations were conducted to capture the full range of mineralogic data, address vertical mineralogical heterogeneity, and account for minerals that have a strong pH buffering capacity. Additionally, both equilibrium- and kinetic-based approaches were evaluated to simulate mineral reactions. Results indicated that equilibrium-based simulations tend to overestimate the pH buffering capacity of minerals. This finding highlights the importance of incorporating kinetic approaches in geochemical modeling to capture CO 2 –brine–mineral interactions to better assess their potential impact on storage complexes and wellbore integrity.

title: FAIR Outcrops: Data Stewardship for Digital Geoscience
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data
authors: Burnham, Brian S [1], Hodgetts, David [2]
affiliations: (1) VRGeoscience Limited, Manchester, United Kingdom
(2) VRGeoscience Limited, Manchester, United Kingdom
abstract:
Outcrops are irreplaceable records of Earth history and are fundamental to geoscience research, education, and training. Digital outcrop models (DOMs), typically generated from photogrammetry (e.g., UAV, mobile phone) and/or lidar workflows, are commonplace and have transformed the way geoscientists collect and analyse field data. Sufficient and accessible digital dataset preservation and sharing, however, has not kept pace with this growth. Many DOMs and related metadata sit on individual or institutional hard drives, are behind paywalls or expired file-share links that make them inaccessible and uncitable, despite significant data collection and analysis costs. Moreover, these storage methods are not compliant with FAIR data expectations of contemporary scientific research. Fundamentally, a DOM that cannot be found, accessed, or reused provides little scientific value beyond its original study – a problem that only compounds as DOM numbers increase across the community.

To address this problem directly the cloud-native platform outcrop.io has been developed. Aligned with FAIR data principles, the platform provides a permanent, browser-accessible custodian for 3D digital outcrop data that is designed for interactivity without specialist desktop software. Uploaded models carry structured, standards-compliant metadata that can be assigned a DOI through an integrated digital repository (e.g., Zenodo) that makes it findable, citable, and archive-quality. A versioned interpretation system records annotation layers, labels, and structural measurements with a full audit trail – facilitating re-evaluation of DOMs as geoscientific concepts and techniques advance. Collaboration tools, including peer review workflows, organisation-level reference libraries, and community activity feeds are supported by an AI-powered semantic search layer that facilitates natural-language discovery across outcrop metadata and linked academic literature.

Together, these capabilities position outcrop.io as a case study in what FAIR-driven digital outcrop data infrastructure requires more broadly in the geosciences.

title: Regional screening methodologies for geologic carbon storage: Insights from statewide and stacked 3D modeling of the subsurface in Kansas

authors: Bhattacharjee, Souvik [1], Eltom, Hassan [2], Bream, Brendan R [3], White, Mark [4], Gumble, Jason [5]
affiliations: (1) Subsurface Dynamics Laboratory, Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, Kansas, USA

abstract:
Kansas contains one of the most promising saline aquifer systems for geologic carbon storage in the U.S. Midcontinent; however, regional-scale assessments of storage potential that recognize subsurface uncertainties are nonexistent. To address this gap, two complementary studies were conducted to evaluate CO 2 storage resources from statewide to basin scales and to enhance confidence in regional carbon capture and storage (CCS) screening.

The first study evaluates the Cambro–Ordovician Arbuckle Group across Kansas using a statewide 3D faulted framework geocellular model that integrates well tops, well logs, and structural interpretations. Regional CO 2 storage potential was assessed through spatial chance-of-adequacy (COA) mapping based on four fundamental CCS play elements: reservoir presence, reservoir quality, seal, and CO 2 phase state. Results indicate statewide CO 2 effective storage resource (GCO 2 ) of approximately 24–75 Gt, with a best estimate of ~39 Gt. These findings identify the Arbuckle Group as the primary regional saline reservoir target and the most promising option for large-scale CO 2 storage in Kansas.

Building on the regional-scale assessment, the second study investigated the robustness of the Arbuckle Group as the principal CO 2 storage reservoir under alternative geological modeling assumptions within the stacked saline aquifer system of the Sedgwick Basin. This model includes the Arbuckle Group, Chattanooga interval, Mississippian strata, and Cherokee Group. The analysis evaluated the influence of alternative gross rock volume frameworks, layering schemes, and geological heterogeneity on storage resource estimates. Basin-scale P50 GCO 2 were estimated to range from 10.1 to 10.8 Gt, with an overall uncertainty range of 6.4–21.1 Gt. Across all modeling scenarios, the Arbuckle consistently accounted for the largest proportion of the total storage resource and exhibited less variability in estimated storage capacity. These results indicate that geological uncertainty has a greater impact on the spatial distribution of storage potential than on the overall volume of CO 2 storage resource.

These studies demonstrate that the Arbuckle Group is both the largest regional CO 2 storage reservoir in Kansas and the most resilient to uncertainties arising from alternative geological interpretations. The findings enhance confidence in regional CCS resource assessments while highlighting that geological heterogeneity can significantly influence the spatial distribution of storage potential. As a result, this work serves as a foundational tool for regional CCS screening, investment planning, and Class VI permitting efforts.

title: Advancing multi-isotope ratio analysis of nitrate with a new Orbitrap IRMS workflow
session_title: Urban groundwater and geochemistry (Posters)
authors: Mancuso, Christy J [1], Davidheiser, Brett [2], Tuthorn, Mario [3]
affiliations: (1) Thermo Fisher Scientific, Albany, NY, USA
(2) Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA
(3) Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany
abstract:
Stable isotope analysis of nitrate provides a powerful approach for tracing nitrogen sources, transformation pathways, and biogeochemical processes in environmental systems. Variations in nitrogen and oxygen isotope composition can help distinguish processes such as nitrification and denitrification and constrain natural, agricultural, and anthropogenic nitrogen inputs. However, conventional nitrate isotope analysis may require multiple analytical procedures and substantial sample preparation to obtain complementary isotope information.

We present an integrated Orbitrap-based isotope ratio mass spectrometry workflow for multi-isotope analysis of intact nitrate ions that combines the Thermo Scientific™ Orbitrap™ Isora™ Mass Spectrometer and Isotope Discoverer™ Software. The approach resolves isotopologues containing ¹⁵N, ¹⁷O, and ¹⁸O and determines δ¹⁵N, δ¹⁷O, and δ¹⁸O within a single analytical method. Automated alternating introduction of samples and reference materials supports continuous sample-reference bracketing, correction for instrumental drift, and two-point calibration to international isotope scales.

Analytical performance was evaluated using nitrate reference materials. Average measurement precisions were 0.6‰ for δ¹⁵N, 0.5‰ for δ¹⁸O, and 0.9‰ for δ¹⁷O. High-resolution detection also provides access to low-abundance nitrate isotopologues such as such as ¹⁵N¹⁸O¹⁶O₂⁻, ¹⁴N¹⁷O¹⁸O¹⁶O⁻, and ¹⁴N¹⁸O₂¹⁶O⁻ that may offer additional information on overlapping sources and biogeochemical processes.

This workflow provides comprehensive, molecular-level nitrate isotope information with reduced sample requirements and creates new opportunities to distinguish overlapping nitrogen sources and biogeochemical processes in environmental systems.

authors: Kasanin-Grubin, Milica [1], Antic, Nevena [2], Strbac, Snezana [3], Roncevic, Vukasin [4], Zivanovic, Nikola [5], Stojadinovic, Sanja [6]
affiliations: (1) Institute of Chemistry, Technology and Metallurgy Serbia, University of Belgrade, Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia
(2) Institute of Chemistry, Technology and Metallurgy Serbia, University of Belgrade, Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia
(3) Institute of Chemistry, Technology and Metallurgy Serbia, University of Belgrade, Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia
(4) Institute of Chemistry, Technology and Metallurgy Serbia, University of Belgrade, Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia
(5) Faculty of Forestry, University of Belgrade, Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia
(6) Institute of Chemistry, Technology and Metallurgy Serbia, University of Belgrade, Serbia milica.kasanin@ihtm.bg.ac.rs, Belgrade, Serbia
abstract:
Urban forests are vital socio-ecological systems, yet their soil properties remain poorly understood. Evaluating urban forest functionality requires distinguishing between inherent (persistent) properties—such as soil texture, clay mineralogy, and drainage class inherited from geological parent material—and dynamic (manageable) properties—such as soil organic carbon (TOC), pH, electrical conductivity (EC), and nutrient availability—which respond rapidly to human management and environmental stressors.

As part of the "Urban Forest Soil Indicators as a Tool for Climate-Smart Forestry" (UrbanFoS) project, this study evaluated topsoil and subsoil physico-chemical properties across five contrasting Serbian urban and peri-urban forest complexes: Stepin Lug, the Faculty of Forestry Arboretum, Kamenički Park, Letnjikovačka Šuma, and Park Borići. Soil samples were analyzed for texture, pH, EC, cation exchange capacity (CECA), TOC, macronutrients (N, P, K), and base cations (Ca, Mg, Na, Al, Fe, Mn). Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with Varimax rotation was applied to isolate primary soil drivers.

The results demonstrate biogeochemical gradients driven by the interaction of parent material and anthropogenic land-use legacies. A strong reaction gradient was observed, ranging from acidic-to-neutral, leached soils in the semi-natural forest of Stepin Lug (pH 5.2-7.0) to highly alkaline, calcium-enriched urban soils in the Arboretum and Kamenički Park (pH 7.5-8.6). Coniferous dominated Park Borići, showed the highest carbon density (TOC 5.0-7.7%) and Ca accumulation (>30,000 mg/kg), driven by needle litter decomposition over calcareous substrate. On the contrary, Kamenički Park has silt content 10-50%, directly reflecting its historical land use as an industrial clay-quarry. Vertical stratification was pronounced across all sites, with TOC and Total N declining by 30-50% from topsoil to subsoil.

Multivariate factor analysis resolved three components: Component 1 (EC, total N, pH, available K, Ca, TOC), representing manageable biogeochemical status and urban alkalinization; Component 2 (silt, clay, sand, Fe), reflecting inherent, inherited physical soil texture; and Component 3 (total K, Na, Al), capturing mineralogical composition.

These findings provide crucial baseline indicators for urban soil diagnosis, proving that climate-smart forestry interventions must target manageable chemical parameters (pH, carbon inputs) while accounting for immutable textural constraints.

title: Reconnaissance Mineralogical Study of West Bayan Obo Ore Samples: Are the REE Orebodies a Metamorphosed Minamitorishima-like REY-Mud Deposit?
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Love, Rachel [1], Friehauf, Kurt [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Kutztown University of Pennsylvania, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Geology, Kutztown University of Pennsylvania, Kutztown, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
The Bayan Obo REE Mining District, located in Inner Mongolia, China, is comprised of the Main, East, and West Orebodies. The Main and East Orebodies are relatively massive, while the West Orebodies are more finely stratabound. A prevailing theory proposes that the West Orebodies are intrusive carbonatite sills or extrusive lava flows. Alternatively, others propose that the West Orebodies may be the result of exhalative seafloor hydrothermal deposits (e.g., Chao et al., 1997).

We analyzed samples from the West Orebodies to characterize the mineralogy to see if there are potential similarities between West Orebody geochemistry and modern seafloor metalliferous sediments. In effect, are the West Bayan Obo Orebodies metamorphosed metalliferous seafloor sediments?

Field Emission Electron Microscopic (FE-SEM) and Energy Dispersive Spectrometric (EDS) analysis of samples in this study indicated monazite and bastnaesite are the main REE minerals, set in dolomite gangue. We additionally observed barite, magnetite, biotite, and fluorite.

The marked abundance of monazite ((REE)PO 4 ) as a REE-bearing mineral suggested a potential similarity with phosphate-bearing modern metalliferous seafloor sediment deposits.

Comparisons between the published bulk chemical compositions of the West Bayan Obo deposits, Minamitorishima REY-enriched seafloor muds, and Atlantis II Deep metalliferous muds revealed an enrichment of phosphorus and REEs. Phosphorus correlates strongly with REE concentration in Minamitorishima muds and in Atlantis II deep muds, suggesting REE occurs in REE-bearing apatite or monazite.

However, the relative concentrations of REEs to phosphorus are less in samples from West Bayan Obo than REY-muds or Atlantis II Deep metalliferous sediment due to 2-4 times higher phosphate and lower REE concentrations in the modern sediment. Minamitorishima REY-muds also differ in enrichment of LREEs relative to HREEs, suggesting a difference in mineralization process.

Although West Bayan Obo ores have some geochemical similarities with modern REE-bearing seafloor sediment, the concentrations and relative proportions of phosphate and REE do not suggest West Bayan Obo is a metamorphosed REY-mud deposit.

title: Field observations of landslides from Hurricane Helene in the Blue Ridge of northwestern North Carolina, northeastern Tennessee and southwestern Virginia
session_title: Emerging Research into the Impacts of Hurricane Helene in the Southern Appalachians
authors: Merschat, Arthur James [1], Mirus, Benjamin B. [2], Thigpen, Ryan [3], Johnson, Bradley G. [4], Brown, Summer [5]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Zionville, NC,
(2) USGS, Golden, CO,
(3) University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY,
(4) Davidson College, Davidson, NC,
(5) University of Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA
abstract: Remnants of Hurricane Helene, Sept. 25–27, 2024, triggered numerous landslides and devastating flooding across parts of the Blue Ridge of North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. This landslide mapping and assessment focused on the northernmost area heavily impacted from the storm: parts of Watauga, Avery, and Ashe Counties, NC, Johnson County, TN, and Smyth and Grayson Counties, VA. Initial observational descriptions of the landslides are presented with a comparison to past events. Landslides mapped are separated into several types: hyperconcentrated earth flows or “blowouts,” debris flows, translational or rotational slides, and modified slope failures. Blowouts, the most common type, occurred on steep grassy slopes and consisted of soil with a mixture of vegetated clumps, saprolite, and rock. Blowout tracks were 10–338 m long, and scarp widths of 10–30 m that often cut down 1–2 m to the top of bedrock. Blowouts often occurred in clusters, and some merged down slope. Debris flows had longer tracks, 96–1085 m, and consisted of a mixture of soil, rock, trees, vegetation, and other debris. Head scarps were 10–114 m wide and cut down through 1–3 m of colluvium to bedrock. Bedrock structures controlling the initiation of failure locations included joints, fractures, and foliation. Seven debris flows on Howards Creek initiated on steep slopes with aspect and slope close to the orientation of the foliation in bedrock (330/20–40° NE). Modified slope failures included landslides that initiated on road cuts, road embankments, steep cut slopes, and other slopes modified by construction (e.g., failed drainages or septic fields). Although the slope modification was important to initiate these slides, some localized along preexisting bedrock (saprolite) structures. Limited eyewitness accounts suggest many landslides occurred around 11AM local time on Sept. 27, as the remnants of the inner eyewall of the storm passed over the area. Comparison with past landslide events from 1916, 1940, and 2004 shows close spatial relations and similar controls of slope, but the locus of landslides is shifted due to storm paths. Collectively, the impact of landslides from Hurricane Helene highlights the importance of basic geologic and landslide mapping to build robust datasets to better understand and model the occurrence of landslides, which can help strengthen the planning and rebuilding of mountain communities.

title: New Geologic Map of the Upsal Hogback 7.5-Minute Quadrangle, Churchill County, Nevada
session_title: Geologic Maps and Their Derivatives (Posters)
authors: Andrews, William M. [1], Faulds, James E. [2], Anderson, Kyle [3], Merrell, McKenzie [4], Kratt, Christopher B [5]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Bureau Mines & Geology, Reno, NV, USA
(2) University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA
(3) Dept of Geological Sciences and Engineering (CTEMPS), University of Nevada Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(4) Dept of Geological Science and Engineering (CTEMPS), University of Nevada Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(5) Center for Transformative Environmental Monitoring Programs, University of Nevada Reno, Reno, NV, USA
abstract:
The Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, in partnership with the Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering at the University of Nevada Reno, has completed new geologic mapping of the Upsal Hogback 7.5-minute quadrangle in Churchill County, Nevada. This work was undertaken to assess volcanic and earthquake hazards, as well as potential geothermal resources. It was supported by Statemap program funding through the USGS NCGMP. Detailed field work provided foundation for assessing geoframework relationships between Miocene volcanic strata, Miocene and later faults, Pleistocene alluvial and lacustrine units, late Pleistocene basaltic tuff cones, and Holocene eolian and playa deposits. Near-surface geophysical investigations using seismic refraction, multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW), and electrical resistivity tomography were employed at selected locations. The inverted velocity and resistivity structure aids in making geologic interpretations.

Bedrock outcrops in the northern part of the area expose Miocene volcanic rocks, including basalt flows, a rock avalanche deposit, porphyritic dacite domes and flows, and a capping dacitic tuff of Parran Mesa (7.5 Ma). The Miocene section is exposed in a series of gently west-tilted fault blocks bounded primarily by NNE-striking, E-dipping normal faults. The tuff of Parran Mesa is tilted less than underlying ~9-12 Ma units, suggesting a major episode of late Miocene extension. Multiple Quaternary rock falls (pre-Lahontan and post-Lahontan) are mapped on south end of one of the fault blocks. Hillslopes are dominated by alluvial fans modified by Lake Lahontan shoreline processes. The basin floor is dominated by lacustrine deposits of Pleistocene Lake Lahontan, overlain by extensive eolian sand dunes, sand sheets, and playa deposits.

In the southeastern part of the area a series of Quaternary tuff cones represent multi-phase phreatic eruption of basaltic lavas (approx. 15-18ka) through Lake Lahontan. The tuff cones contain abundant juvenile basaltic clasts, as well as extensive evidence of reworking into basaltic sandstone and conglomerate layers. Common lithics of andesite and rhyolite up to ~2 m long are probably derived from subsurface bedrock units. Field evidence suggests rapid post-eruption degradation of the Upsal Hogback tuff cones with reworked material deposited adjacent to the cones. Numerous linear scarps in lacustrine sediment are interpreted as related to possible late Quaternary faults.

title: Digital Outcrop Reconstruction and Facies Characterization of a Point-Bar Deposit Using Multispectral Drone Imagery, Coal Canyon, Colorado
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Rewold, Kenzie [1], Tellez, Javier [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Point-bar deposits preserve important information about how rivers transport and deposit sediment. They also serve as useful analogs for understanding subsurface reservoir architecture. This study uses multispectral drone imagery to create a three-dimensional digital outcrop model of a point-bar deposit exposed in Coal Canyon, Colorado. The goal is to reconstruct the original geometry of the outcrop and identify the main sedimentary facies preserved within the deposit.

A multispectral drone survey is conducted to collect high-resolution images of the outcrop. These images are processed using Structure-from-Motion photogrammetry to generate a georeferenced three-dimensional digital model that preserves the size, shape, and geometry of the exposed point-bar system. The digital outcrop is then used to map key stratigraphic surfaces, identify sedimentary facies, and document the spatial relationships between depositional elements. Measurements extracted directly from the model, including bed thickness, lateral continuity, channel geometry, and dimensions of major depositional features, provide a quantitative description of the outcrop.

Field observations are integrated with the digital outcrop model to improve facies interpretation and evaluate how different lithologies are distributed throughout the point-bar deposit. Preliminary results show that combining multispectral drone imagery with digital outcrop modeling provides an efficient way to document fluvial architecture while preserving field-scale relationships. The reconstructed outcrop will provide the foundation for future work that will apply machine learning to classify lithologic responses from multispectral data and develop a three-dimensional geological model of the point-bar system.

title: Mid-Pleistocene Transition Foraminiferal Assemblages from the Ross Sea, Antarctica
session_title: Insights from microfossils and their modern analogs: from traditional to emerging approaches
authors: Elkin, Adam Matthew [1], Leckie, R. Mark [2], Kim, Erin [3], Prunella, Catherine [4], Seidenstein, Julia [5], Shevenell, Amelia E. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
(2) Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(4) New York Sea Grant, Bronx, NY, USA
(5) Earth and Environmental Science, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA
(6) College of Marine Sciences, University of South Florida, Saint Petersburg, FL, USA
abstract: Approximately 1.25 to 0.75 Ma, Earth’s climate shifted from 41 kyr to 100 kyr glacial-interglacial cyclicity during the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT). Although this shift in global climatic cycles is well-documented in the geological record, the associated forcings and feedbacks remain an active area of research. Foraminiferal assemblage data are useful for understanding past shifts in climate, ocean dynamics, and marine ecology. Here we present foraminiferal assemblage and stable isotope data across the MPT from the Ross Sea of Antarctica. These data enable the assessment of foraminiferal biodiversity and ocean circulation changes across this major climate transition. We generated benthic and planktic foraminiferal assemblages in early to middle Pleistocene age sediments (~1.6 to 0.7 Ma) recovered from the Ross Sea shelf edge. These samples were obtained from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 374 Hole U1523A (74°9.02’ S, 176°47.70’ W), which was drilled at a water depth of 828 m. This site is influenced by the strength of the Antarctic Slope Current (ASC), which regulates the intrusion of warm Circumpolar Deep Water onto the Ross Sea shelf. Prior to the MPT, most benthic foraminiferal assemblages are dominated by Globocassidulina spp. in conjunction with a lower planktic:benthic foraminiferal ratio. Beginning around 1.24 Ma (MIS 37), during the onset of the MPT, there is a marked increase in Nonionella spp. and Rosalina globularis. Between MIS 35 and 27 (~1.19 Ma and 0.97 Ma), Nonionella spp. and Trifarina earlandi alternate in relative abundance, with Nonionella spp. being more common during interglacials, suggesting a stronger ASC during the glacials of the MPT. We observe a marked reduction in foraminiferal abundances during glacial intervals after MIS 31 (~1.07 Ma), while abundant foraminifera are present and assemblages are dominated by planktic species during interglacials. We also observe an increase in the abundance of benthic species T. earlandi during the MPT. These trends, coupled with lithologic variations and stable oxygen and carbon isotope data from T. earlandi and planktic species Neogloboquadrina pachyderma suggest a strengthening of the ASC during the MPT, with important implications for heat and nutrient delivery to the continental shelf.

title: Tidal control on delta and estuary channel morphology
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Paramita, Valina Rizky [1], Olariu, Cornel [2]
affiliations: (1) Jackson School of Geoscience, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(2) Jackson School of Geoscience, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract: We analyze channel geometry in Holocene deltas and estuaries to identify tidal control on channel widening, defined here as the increase in channel width from the upstream fluvial zone toward the shoreline. Measuring channel width between the shoreline and the upstream fluvial zone allows quantification of width variation along the fluvial-to-marine environment. Shorelines at zero meters elevation were defined using coastal digital elevation model (DEM) data, with shoreline channel width defined as the largest gap between continuous shoreline segments. The channel bars, where present, were excluded from these measurements. Upstream width was measured at point locations within the fluvial zone, identified by high sinuosity. Tidal range data were obtained from global tidal range maps, and topographic gradient was calculated from DEM data between the upstream point and the shoreline. Systems were broadly classified as deltas or estuaries based on morphology and the coastal-plain gradient adjacent to the channels. Deltas are characterized by low gradients, whereas estuaries occupy higher gradients. The result indicated that tidal range has a positive correlation with channel-mouth (shoreline) width. Then, we quantified the relationship between tidal range at the coast and the narrowing coefficient of the channel width. This coefficient indicates how fast the channel narrows landward from the mouth. We found a weak negative trend between the narrowing coefficient and tidal range. It shows that rapid narrowing, forming channels with a wider mouth and short transition, likely happens due to low tidal range. At higher tidal range, rapid narrowing tends to form only very close to the shoreline, but the funnel shape extends landward with a lower narrowing rate. These findings clarify the tidal imprint on channel geometry and provide transferable constraints for reconstructing paleo-geomorphology in ancient delta and estuary systems, interpreting subsurface data, and reconstructing paleo-tidal ranges. Additional data on global-scale distribution for channel depth and sediment grain size analysis across diverse tidal systems are still needed to refine these relationships and generate more representative parameters for ancient reconstructions.

title: Is Cenozoic exhumation of Colorado’s High Plains synchronous or diachronous?
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: Abbott, Lon D [1], Renfrow, Taran D [2], Biscuola, Helena D [3], Flowers, Rebecca M. [4], Metcalf, James D [5], Kainz, Sabrina [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(4) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(5) Earth Science Department, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, USA
(6) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
Colorado’s High Plains rise to over 2000 meters elevation, anomalously high for a region that experienced little Phanerozoic crustal shortening. When and why the area experienced epeirogenic surface uplift remains a first-order question in North American tectonics. Regional paleoaltimetry studies produce different results depending on the technique used; interpretations range from the High Plains and adjacent Rocky Mountains having experienced a spasm of Late Cenozoic surface uplift to zero or negative surface uplift since the Late Cretaceous-Eocene Laramide Orogeny. Examination of the region’s exhumation history, can, if interpreted cautiously, shed light on the region’s surface uplift history.

The need for caution stems from the fact that surface uplift, climate change, and drainage reorganization can all trigger rapid exhumation episodes. The expected spatial exhumation patterns differ between different postulated tectonic and non-tectonic exhumation triggers, so characterization of exhumation patterns and magnitudes can illuminate which potential explanations fit the data and which don’t.

A previously published study used apatite and zircon (U-Th)/He thermochronology to document an episode of Miocene and younger, kilometer-scale exhumation on Colorado’s southeastern High Plains from the Spanish Peaks to the Kansas border. The current study explores whether Colorado’s northeastern High Plains experienced that same exhumation episode or not. We sampled Laramide-age dikes and sills in the Golden, Boulder, and Lyons areas because young intrusive rocks have experienced simple thermal histories compared to those of Precambrian basement or detrital samples whose apatite and zircon grains may have experienced variable degrees of thermal resetting. But no intrusive rocks crop out on the northeastern High Plains east of Boulder, so in hopes of extending the study farther east, we are also conducting (U-Th)/He analysis of Sussex Sandstone cuttings from two horizontal wells drilled by Occidental Petroleum near Wattenberg. Our analysis is ongoing, but preliminary results indicate that this portion of the northeastern Colorado High Plains last experienced kilometer-scale exhumation in the Eocene. This presentation will describe our results and discuss the implications of what appears to be diachronous exhumation across Colorado’s High Plains – Eocene in the northeast and Miocene to recent in the southeast.

title: Developing Workforce Skills and Scientific Thinking through Participation in an Interdisciplinary Undergraduate Research Experience
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Koy, Karen [1], Drake, Dawn [2], Elias, Ashley [3], Ganong, Carissa [4], Grantham, Michael [5], Majewska, Ania [6], Mills, Mark [7], Walton, Kristen [8]
affiliations: (1) Biology, Missouri Western State University, Saint Joseph, MO, USA
(2) Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
(3) Biology, Missouri Western State University, Saint Joseph, MO, USA

abstract:
Participation in research allows undergraduate students to develop both hard and soft workforce skills. In the fall of 2020 we developed an interdisciplinary, place-based research program at a small public primarily undergraduate institution as a way to increase undergraduate participation in research. The Pond Team uses campus ponds as research sites for projects from a variety of biological and environmental disciplines. We recruit students from biology, geosciences, and the humanities. Students can join at any point in their college education. The broad range of disciplines and student experience also functions as a recruitment point for the departments involved as well as the University overall.

Students on the Pond Team are paired with a faculty mentor in one of several areas: ecology, geology, virology, geography/GIS, or organismal biology. They work directly with that faculty member in the research lab and/or the field. The Pond Team holds weekly to biweekly meetings where individual research teams present research updates, and faculty give workshops on topics such as how to use statistical software, read a journal article, create a good conference poster, or do well in a job interview. At the end of the semester, students present their research in a departmental poster symposium.

Between the fall semester of 2020 and the spring semester of 2023, 35 undergraduate students participated in the Pond Team for a total of 68 student-semesters. Twenty students participated in a single semester, while the remaining 15 students participated in 2 – 6 semesters. Students completed pre- and post-surveys during each semester, as well as a validated survey for self-assessment of learning gains (SALG) in specific skills at the end of each semester. Students reported high perceived gains in all categories measured: skills, thinking and working like a scientist, personal gains related to research work, and attitudes and behaviors of a researcher. In addition, students tended to agree that the experience prepared them for a career and/or graduate school. These results suggest that the incorporation of regular team meetings focused on job-related skills in addition to research updates positively impacts the preparation of students for workforce engagement.
