title: From the Colorado Plateau to the Labrador Sea: Connecting the California and Bell Paleo-rivers across the Wyoming Rockies
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: Sears, James W [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Montana, Missoula, Mt, USA
abstract:
Dickinson et al. (2012) proposed that the "California paleo-river" had transported distinctive detrital zircons from bedrock sources in the southern Cordilleran magmatic arc and southern Arizona Mogollon Rim across the Colorado Plateau to deposit them in the Paleogene Colton Formation delta in Lake Uinta of the Green River lake system. Balkwill et al. (1982) mapped the pre-Pleistocene continental-scale "Bell paleo-river" from a large delta in the Labrador Sea to headwaters in the Sevier orogen and foreland basin of Canada and the western USA. Here I propose that these paleo-rivers were connected across the Wyoming Rockies in late Eocene to middle Miocene time, when Lake Gosiute of the Green River lake system spilled into the Bell River basin over a divide in the Granite Mountains. The resulting fluvial system drained from the Colorado Plateau to the Labrador Sea in Oligocene through middle Miocene time. It was coincident with early erosion of the Grand Canyon as dated by Flowers et al. (2008).

The spillover is recorded by stratigraphy and detrital zircon provenance of strata in the Granite Mountains. The Eocene Wagon Bed Formation records a transition to fluvial facies from facies and fossils of Lake Gosiute, including laminated oil shales, stromatolites, fish scales, and freshwater gastropods (Palko, 2023). The Oligocene White River Formation was unconformably deposited on the Wagon Bed Formation on a surface of north-trending fluvial channels and moderately rough topography. One paleo-river channel was 3 km wide with a 30-m tfluvial conglomerate bed at its base (Love, 1970). The overlying Miocene Split Rock Formation is a fluvial-aeolian deposit that defines part of a Miocene paleo-valley traced from northern Colorado to northern Wyoming. Detrital zircons from the White River and Split Rock formations (Rowley and Fan, 2016) are compatible with zircons of the California River delta that indicate provenance from the southern Colorado Plateau and Cordilleran magmatic arc.

The spillover crossed from the Wyoming Rockies onto the Montana Plains where it joined the Yellowstone paleo-river, which joined the Bell River in southern Canada. Although diluted by Canadian Shield Archean sources, detrital zircons from the Bell River delta in the Labrador Sea are compatible with those of the California River delta, implying a 5000-km long fluvial connection of the Bell River delta and the southern Colorado Plateau.

title: Distinguishing Earthquake- and Flood-Triggered Turbidities Through High-Resolution Grain Size Analysis, Lake Lachuá, Guatemala
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Talapureddy, Hemanth Kalyan Kumar Reddy [1], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [2], Nasser, Nawaf [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, Missouri, USA
(2) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(3) Department Of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, Missouri, USA
abstract: Lake turbidites are important sedimentary deposits that can be used to reconstruct past environmental events and their triggers, including those generated by earthquakes and floods. Lake Lachuá in Guatemala sits at an ideal location to study earthquake- and flood-triggered turbidites. This study utilized sediment gravity cores and uses high-resolution subsampling and grain-size analysis of event deposits to discriminate between seismic and flood events. Eight sediment cores were collected throughout Lake Lachuá with 20 events identified throughout the basin. Grain-size analysis from two sediment cores reveals two distinct turbidite signatures: (1) a gradual fining-upward turbidite without a coarse basal sand lamina, and (2) an abrupt, coarse-grained base grading upward into finer silt and clay. We interpret the gradual fining-upward turbidite as flood-triggered and the abrupt coarse-base turbidite as earthquake-triggered. To confirm event origins, grain size signature results were cross validated with an age depth model, comparing event ages with historical hurricane and earthquake records. Preliminary age-depth and turbidite type comparisons show that six events tentatively correspond to four historical hurricanes and two earthquakes. These findings show that grain size is a reliable indicator for recognizing turbidite origins and contribute to our understanding of earthquakes and extreme precipitation events in Guatemala.

title: Widespread marine deoxygenation during Ordovician Stairsian extinction as indicated by marine carbonate carbon and sulfate sulfur isotope records
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)

abstract:
The Early Paleozoic was marked by two major biodiversification episodes that were important to the evolution of marine ecosystems. The Cambrian Explosion (545 to 525 Ma) was a major diversification of skeletonized marine metazoans, followed by the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE; 471 to 458 Ma), when marine biodiversity nearly tripled. Between these two events was a ~40-million-year plateau in marine biodiversity characterized by a series of extinction events. While the mechanisms behind these extinctions are debated, marine deoxygenation is one proposed driver. Here we investigate one of these extinctions, the Ordovician Stairsian extinction (~484 Ma). Sedimentary successions from the Yangtze platform in South China and the northern Laurentian margin in the Western United States show positive excursions in carbonate carbon isotope (δ 13 C carb ) records just after the extinction event. Records from Western US also display a positive carbonate-associated sulfate sulfur (δ 34 S CAS ) isotope excursion. These trends have been interpreted as representing global changes to the carbon and sulfur cycles related to the increased burial of organic carbon and pyrite sulfur in sediments under anoxic marine conditions.

However, the isotopic excursions associated with the Stairsian extinction have only been identified in a handful of successions that were deposited in the Panthalassic and Paleotethys Oceans. We assessed whether these isotopic signals are representative of global changes in carbon and sulfur cycles by investigating a succession deposited in the Iapetus Ocean and located in the present-day Chesapeake and Ohio Canal Historical Park of Maryland, USA. Just after the Stairsian extinction, this section contains a δ 13 C carb excursion of +4‰ and a δ 34 S CAS excursion of +15‰. These transient excursions are consistent with previous studies and support the hypothesis that they represent global changes to the carbon and sulfur cycles. Sulfur and carbon isotope box modeling confirms that transient increases in marine organic carbon and pyrite sulfur burial under anoxic conditions was the most likely scenario to generate these isotopic excursions. Together our new isotopic records and modeling results indicate that changes to ocean redox chemistry across this interval was a key environmental shift that drove this extinction before the GOBE.

title: An Emerald Lining: the Potential of Dead Ash Trees to Supply Large Woody Debris in Riparian Corridors
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part I)
authors: Galster, Josh C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Montclair State University, Montclair, NJ, USA
abstract: Rivers are dynamic, interconnected systems that respond to driving forces inside and outside their watersheds. This study examines the potential effects of an invasive insect species, the emerald ash borer Agrilus planipennis , on river morphology by surveying the composition of dead trees in river corridors in New Jersey. The emerald ash borer is an invasive beetle in North America that is particularly adept at killing the deciduous ash tree. While this destruction of trees can have profound impacts on forest ecosystems and biodiversity, it is hypothesized that it may create a significant future supply of large woody debris if a large proportion of dead and dying ash trees are located near rivers. Large woody debris is an important component of river morphology, and is often lacking in modern streams in Eastern North America due to historic deforestation. Ash trees (including the black, white, and green species) are a common component of northern New Jersey forests, and can often occur in alluvial soils. However, the composition of dead trees in river corridors is unknown, so eight rivers across northern New Jersey were surveyed to determine the frequency and characterization of the dead trees in these areas. Tree height, breast height diameter, location, and genus (especially ash or not) were recorded for over 150 trees. Additionally, river bankfull width was measured to determine the relative height of the tree compared to the stream width. While ash trees only represent 5% or less of the trees in New Jersey, over 50% of the dead trees in or near rivers were ash. A large majority (~80%) of the dead trees were taller than bankfull width, suggesting their ability to become large woody debris once falling. Also, the majority of all dead trees were still standing (as opposed to falling or leaning) and represent a potential future supply of large woody debris to rivers. Future studies include monitoring the status of these trees to determine how many of them become large woody debris.

title: More Than a Workshop: SERC’s Integrated Approach to Designing Transformative Professional Learning Experiences
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Douglas, Brianna [1], Collette, Amy [2], McDaris, John [3]
affiliations: (1) SERC, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
(2) SERC, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
(3) SERC, Carleton College, Northfield, MN, USA
abstract:
Professional development workshops are often used to share teaching resources, disseminate project outcomes, and build communities of practice. However, the impact of a workshop depends not only on the content delivered, but also on how participants engage, collaborate, and apply what they learn. SERC’s workshop philosophy is grounded in research on learning and emphasizes active participation, shared expertise, community building, and opportunities for participants to translate ideas into practice.

SERC workshops are designed as collaborative enterprises rather than traditional expert-led training. Conveners facilitate interactions among participants, creating opportunities to share experiences, develop resources, build professional networks, and advance collective understanding of effective geoscience education. Participants contribute valuable knowledge and leave with resources, strategies, and plans they can immediately apply.

Supporting this philosophy requires more than workshop facilitation. SERC’s unique approach integrates implementation, technical, administrative, and evaluation expertise throughout the workshop lifecycle. The Serckit content management system provides the technical infrastructure for communication, participant engagement, and an enduring record of workshop products. In addition, SERCkit facilitates data collection mechanisms that allow evaluation processes to provide real-time feedback to support continuous improvement. This integrated system allows SERC to partner with projects and organizations to design workshops that are responsive, sustainable, and aligned with educational goals.

This poster highlights the philosophy, practices, and collaborative infrastructure that distinguish SERC’s approach to professional learning and demonstrates how intentional workshop design can create lasting impacts beyond a single event.

abstract: Gravel mining on floodplains to meet demands of urban development represents an aggressive driver of landscape change. Yet, few studies have traced the paths of transformation over decadal timescales from integrated perspectives. Using mixed methods, this contribution tells the story of the evolution of the South Platte River floodplain near Denver, Colorado, under population pressures. GIS documented land-use change from 1937 – 2020; remote sensing detected the transition of mining pits into water reservoirs. A corpus of 1,263 newspaper articles (1990-2024), from Denver Post and Rocky Mountain News , revealed changing themes of social discourses. Results showed how agriculture (56 percent in 1937 to 7 percent in 2020) gave way to increasing human land use, with water reservoirs in the study area dominant by 2016. Of 172 gravel pits examined, 40 percent became permanent reservoirs. Another 12 percent were reservoirs at one time. Social contestation of mining remained limited in newspapers and websites, which often portrayed the floodplain as hybrid infrastructure for water supply and recreation. The example of the South Platte floodplain illustrates how a different trajectory of landscape change is possible, beyond degradation wrought by human activity. It also daylights the gravel extraction underpinning the present landscape and the governance choices that elevated human uses over nonhuman habitats.

title: Geologic Mapping of the Jones Crater Region on Mars: Reconstructing a History of Fluvial, Impact, and Erosional Processes
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars (Posters)
authors: Wilson, Sharon A. [1], Grant, John A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
(2) Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, USA
abstract:
Our United States Geological Survey (USGS) Scientific Investigation Map (SIM) encompasses Jones crater and the medial to distal portions of the Samara-Himera and Paraná-Loire valley systems. The 1:1,000,000 scale map covers four Mars Transverse Mercator (MTM) quadrangles, -20022, -25022, -20017, and -25017 (from 17.5°S to 27.5°S between 335°E and 345°E). The primary objectives of this mapping effort are to constrain the relative timing, duration, and importance of aqueous processes in relation to other geologic processes, and to integrate these four quadrangles with previously published USGS maps to the east, west, and north. The regional framework provides a comprehensive view of the landscape that supports morphologic and morphometric studies of valleys and fluvial/alluvial deposits, while improving constraints on the timing of fluvial activity and its implications for the climate history of Mars.

The map includes a variety of geologic units, including craters, central peaks, crater floors, fan-shaped deposits, valleys, channels, and the widespread terra unit. Mapped linear features include fluvial channels, wrinkle ridges, Ladon basin impact ring structures, crater rims, grabens, scarps, and troughs. Within the map, the Samara-Himera and Paraná-Loire valley systems are generally degraded, except where segments adjacent to the Jones crater ejecta were reactivated by drainage associated with ice that melted following the Late Hesperian impact. The Noachian to Hesperian aged terra unit, mapped broadly in adjacent quadrangles, forms a widespread, variably dissected surface between degraded impact craters and is interpreted to be formed and modified through multiple processes, including impact cratering, ejecta emplacement, prolonged weathering, and erosion primarily by water and wind. In our map area, the terra unit is mantled, exhibits a dark signature in THEMIS daytime infrared data, and has variable albedo in CTX data. Unlike the terra unit in adjacent quadrangles, the surface here commonly exhibits a stippled texture on the plains and is locally stripped over length scales of 500m to 1 km. This stripping is most prevalent within valleys and along the interior walls of craters.

This regional geologic map highlights the timing and interaction of fluvial, impact, and erosional processes, advancing our understanding of the long and complex evolution of the Margaritifer Terra region.

abstract: Global tectonic maps show rifted margins that broke Archean-Paleoproterozoic cratons as well as active rifts that have propagated into cratons, yet there remains a longstanding knowledge gap on how strain is accommodated in such an old cold lithosphere. We explore the data-rich Tanganyika-Rukwa Rift Zone in East Africa, where en-echelon magma-poor rifts have initiated across an Archean craton and an adjacent Proterozoic orogenic belt. We integrate a new machine learning-enhanced earthquake catalog developed from local seismic arrays with geologically constrained models of lithospheric strength profiles. The machine-learning catalog produced a significantly enhanced seismicity density and better constrained seismicity depth distribution. The catalog reveals a ubiquitous seismogenic depth zonation in the craton-hosted rifts that contrasts those of the orogen-hosted rifts. Further, models of representative lithospheric yield strength envelopes elucidate the controls on the contrasting strain localization patterns, demonstrating how the integration of advanced computational techniques enhance our understanding of bulk deformation in the continental lithosphere.

title: From SPICE to MDICE: Thirty Million Years of Cambrian-Ordovician Marine Carbon Cycle Evolution Recorded in Western Maryland, USA
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Posters)
authors: Hagen, Amy P.I. [1], Gadsby, Julia Terese [2], Hermosillo, Natalie Grace [3], Pruss, Sara B. [4], Brezinski, David K. [5], Gill, Benjamin Charles [6]
affiliations: (1) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA, ; Yale University, New Haven, CT,

(4) Smith College, Northampton, MA,
(5) Maryland Geological Survey, Baltimore, MD,

abstract:
The late Cambrian to Middle Ordovician (494–458 Ma) was a pivotal interval in Earth’s history in terms of both the evolution of the biosphere and the carbon cycle. Frequent biotic turnover events in the late Cambrian and earliest Ordovician were often accompanied by excursions in the marine carbon isotope record, such as the end-Marjuman extinction and the SPICE (Steptoean Positive Isotopic Carbon Excursion). The concurrence of these events suggests a link between extinctions and the carbon cycle disruptions represented by isotope excursions. However, while the Early to Middle Ordovician saw continued carbon cycle instability, it also saw an end to these extinction events and a marked increase in biodiversity referred to as the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE). Fundamentally, our ability to understand the complex relationships between the biosphere and the carbon cycle hinges upon identifying which aspects of the marine carbon isotope record reflect global or local changes to the carbon cycle and which are diagenetic artifacts.

Here, we present a new high-resolution Cambrian-Ordovician carbonate carbon isotope (δ 13 C) record from the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park near Clear Spring, Maryland, USA. We measured, logged, and sampled over 2000 meters of strata consisting of shallow carbonate facies at 1- to 3-meter resolution to produce ~1100 δ 13 C and δ 18 O measurements. Using previously collected biostratigraphic data for temporal context, we identified four globally recognized carbon isotope excursions present in our section. The late Cambrian SPICE is preserved ~100 meters above the base of the section as a +5.5‰ δ 13 C shift over ~70 meters. Next, the Ordovician TSICE (Top Skullrockian Isotopic Carbon Excursion) appears as a sharp, asymmetrical +3‰ excursion spanning ~50 meters. In the Floian, our section preserves a +4‰ excursion spanning nearly 500 meters that appears in a few other localities globally but is yet unnamed. The MDICE (Middle Darriwilian Isotopic Carbon Excursion), a +6‰ excursion, is preserved near the top of our studied section. Ultimately, the preservation of these four global excursions, plus local δ 13 C features, in a location with relatively continuous deposition and consistent shallow carbonate facies provides an exciting opportunity to investigate carbon cycle dynamics leading into and during the GOBE.

title: Kinematic and Geophysical Evidence for the Loss of Alpine Permafrost from Rock Glaciers on Mt. Mestas (Colorado)
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers
authors: Gomez, Francisco [1], Smith, Margi [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
(2) University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
abstract: This study focuses on Mt. Mestas, in the Spanish Peaks region of Colorado, where rock glaciers developed at relatively low elevations during the Late Quaternary. In addition to supporting local ecosystems, these rock glaciers serve as important water resources for local communities, owing to the accessibility provided by their low altitudes. Rock glacier kinematics on Mt. Mestas were measured using Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) spanning 2015 through 2025. Vertical and horizontal displacements were differentiated using multiple satellite viewing geometries. Further kinematic constraints were provided by repeated surveys of sparse monument networks using GNSS also spanning 2014 through 2025. Collectively, these observations demonstrate a larger component of downward vertical displacement than would be expected by down-slope movement of the rock mass. This implies significant settlement likely resulting from the loss of volume of ice lenses. The subsurface structure of one rock glacier was further investigated using electrical resistivity tomography (ERT). These results depicted the spatially variable distribution of subsurface ice, as well as suggesting the presence of ice lenses. The results further demonstrate how a larger rock glacier body has likely separated into smaller rock glaciers as the landform has degraded during the Holocene. The present-day rates of surface settlement provide first-order constraints on the rates of ice loss, which has implications for the longevity of the freshwater resource provided by the rock glaciers.

title: “What’s Next?” Promoting Divergent, Critical, and Systems Thinking to Expand Beyond AI-Generated Professional Case Studies in Undergraduate Geoscience Courses.
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Gleasman, Gavin [1], Gleasman, Cory [2], Boyd, Evelyn A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Salem State University, Salem, MA, USA
(2) Department of Curriculum & Instruction, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
(3) Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
abstract:
The Earth is a complex system with dynamic interdependencies. Alterations to a single component (e.g., geosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, etc.) commonly trigger cascading effects across the system. Professional geoscientists are tasked with solving the interconnectedness between these components. Meanwhile, geoscience education should equip future professionals with the diverse skills needed to successfully navigate these interconnected systems on Earth.

The cognitive processes of divergent, critical, and systems thinking have been identified as vital skills for student development, helping them solve multifaceted challenges. Divergent thinking promotes the generation of creative questions. While critical thinking prompts the rigorous evaluation of information. Finally, these analyses culminate in systems thinking, a holistic approach which solves challenges not in isolation but as a connected network.

The educational use of case studies fosters the development of divergent, critical, and systems thinking by presenting students with real-world problems. The pedagogical practices of inquiry-based learning (i.e., engaging students through exploration) and constructivism (i.e., constructing knowledge through experience) not only emphasize the use of case studies to authentically engage students and actively develop cognitive processing skills, but also serve as a powerful career-preparation tool. Students may simulate cognitive and procedural practices that were performed by professionals in the geoscience field in a low-pressure training scenario.

However, case studies are often presented as structured systems with fixed historical data sets and guided solution pathways. Conversely, the Earth system is dynamic and always evolving. We aim to use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enhance case studies, making them adaptive and capable of emulating Earth's dynamic nature; utilizing variable data inputs and multiple solution pathways in evolving scenarios.

We have developed and implemented an active learning and career-preparation activity with scaffolded high-order learning objectives to: (1) apply content knowledge to effectively prompt an AI platform to produce a case study, (2) analyze and evaluate both applied and missing data sets within the case study, and (3) design a solution to help solve or limit the challenge presented. The use of an ill-structured case study developed in real time has successfully enabled students to expand their cognitive processing skills and explore several pathways to address complex simulated challenges on Earth. Furthermore, this approach serves as an accessible adaptive professional development tool for both geoscientists during active enrollment at a university or advanced workforce training.

title: When is a Cigar Just a Cigar? Evaluating Elongate Sandstone Concretions as Paleocurrent Indicators in the Hell Creek and Fort Union Formations
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part II)
authors: Tobin, Thomas S. [1], Caro, David [2], Wilson Mantilla, Gregory [3], Novak, Filip [4], Haywood, Asher [5], Stupakoff, Nissa [6], Mehra, Akshay [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL,

abstract:
Elongate concretions are widely observed within sandstone strata in the Cretaceous Hell Creek and Paleogene Fort Union formations of central and eastern Montana. These concretions form primarily through the carbonate cementation of otherwise less-well-indurated sandstone layers. They are typically 5-10 meters long, and 1-2 meters wide and thick with tapered ends, with a cigar-like shape that confers their informal name. While the cigars preserve original bedforms (most commonly trough and planar crossbedding), their expression is not directly controlled by such sedimentary structures. Evidence for this decoupling comes from examples of bedding passing into and out of concretions and articulated skeletons being preserved only partially within concretion (with the other part being located within surrounding, sandstone). Given these observations, it is likely that concretions formed in a post-depositional diagenetic stage, likely during the flow of paleogroundwater. Researchers have proposed that the orientation of these concretions follows that of the original paleocurrent directions, suggesting that groundwater flow was guided by sedimentological subtleties within a thicker sandstone unit. If true, measurements of concretion trend should provide estimates of fluvial paleocurrents and their variance. Here we test this hypothesis through direct comparison of cigar orientations to primary paleocurrent indicators.

Our preliminary dataset (pre-2026) comprises 591 orientation measurements, including 75 pairs of concretion-paleocurrent measurements. Additional data were collected during the Summer 2026 field season. We calculated the deviation between cross bed dip direction and the nearest orientation of the concretion long axis. The average absolute value of difference was 20° (±17°, 1σ), indicating that cigars do generally approximate paleocurrent direction, but with substantial variation (up to 86°). For single sandstone channels from which five or more concretion orientations were measured (n=9), the average standard deviation was 10°, indicating the orientations of concretions within-channel were consistent. However, variation of within-channel cross-bedding directions (n=27 channels) was much higher (42°). When comparing the average cross-bedding direction to the average cigar orientation, we found similar differences to those found at the individual concretion level (21°). In short, there is more variation indicated by cross-bedding than is captured by concretion orientation. While it is possible that concretion orientation is responding to paleogroundwater flow that is roughly parallel to paleocurrent direction, the exact nature of this relationship remains underconstrained.

title: Palynology and Detrital Zircon Geochronology of the Fossiliferous Beaver Creek Locality

authors: Moore, Kallie L [1], Hendrix , Marc S. [2], Zippi, Pierre A. [3], Crowley, James L. [4], Gardner, James D. [5]
affiliations: (1) UM Paleontology Center, The University of Montana, Missoula, MT, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, The University of Montana, Missoula, Montana, USA

abstract: Since the 1970s, lacustrine strata found at the Beaver Creek Locality (BCL) have yielded a diverse fossil assemblage that includes plants, invertebrates (arthropods and mollusks), and vertebrate (amphibians and fish) skeletons with carbonized soft tissues. The BCL has been referred to as a fossil lagerstätte due to the taxonomic diversity and outstanding preservation. The main BCL outcrop is part of a small roadcut located northwest of Lincoln, in Powell County, Montana. The strata consist of laminated fine-grained paper shale, oil shale, mudstone, silt/claystone, coal, and bentonite beds. From previous mapping in other areas of western Montana, this lithology is equivalent to the Renova Formation, which is estimated to be roughly 53-19 Ma. As such, a wide range of ages have been proposed for the BCL, from late Eocene to early Miocene. To restrict this age range, zircon from four bentonite samples was dated by LA-ICPMS and palynological analysis was undertaken. Three samples have almost entirely 38-40 Ma zircon that is interpreted as being syndepositional. While the seven outcrop samples sent for palynological analysis were weathered, some information was recoverable. In four of the samples, Celtis tschudyi was found, indicating an age restricted to the Eocene. All samples lacked middle Eocene and older thermophilic pollen. Both Malvacipollis tschudyi and Intratriporopollenites cf. stavensis , from one sample, restrict the age to no younger than early Oligocene. The results from the palynology and zircon analyses support a late Eocene age and give a better constraint of this site to the Climbing Arrow Member of the lower Renova Formation.

title: Deep Time, Shared Stories: Exploring Relationships with Mining in the Keweenaw Peninsula
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Vye, Erika C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Great Lakes Research Center, Michigan Technological University, Houghton, MI,
abstract:
The rich geodiversity of the Keweenaw Peninsula provides a platform for people to learn about deep time, Earth's dynamic processes, and the varied relationships people have with our geologic underpinnings. While the billion-year geologic history of the Keweenaw has sculpted shorelines, peninsulas, islands, harbors, and other unique landscape features, the Keweenaw is renowned and celebrated for hosting Earth's largest accessible native copper deposit. For millennia, people have fostered meaningful relationships with the Copper Country, including the Western Hemisphere’s oldest metalworkings, the enduring Anishinaabe relationship with miskwaabik , and the nation’s first major copper mining district. Less interpreted is how geology has shaped, and continues to shape, relationships between mining and current environmental challenges within our community. In what ways does the geology impact land, life, and culture? How have the stories of all beings in the Keweenaw been impacted by this gift of copper from the deep Earth?

The intersection of deep time, industrial history, and cultural heritage has been the foundation for a series of geoheritage initiatives in the Keweenaw that explore the compelling geostories of our place with a focus on: a) connecting Earth system processes and the region's extractive past to modern environmental challenges; b) building community partnerships that bridge diverse local perspectives, knowledges, and values for place-based educational programs; and c) elevating Earth Science literacy by interpreting the wide-ranging impacts of copper mining on our communities today - such as cultural identity, subsistence uses, recreation, and sense of place. Acknowledging and honoring the varied stories, values, and relationships developed over millennia with Keweenaw copper fosters a deepened appreciation for the geologic gifts of the past while inspiring our shared responsibility for the impacts of mining, both present and future.

title: Quantitative Seismic Geomorphology of Deep-Water Depositional Elements in the North Carnarvon Basin, Australia
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Marso, Samuel [1], Tellez, Javier [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The North Carnarvon Basin, offshore Western Australia, contains well-preserved deep-water depositional systems that provide an excellent opportunity to study submarine geomorphology using 3D seismic data. Understanding the geometry and distribution of these depositional elements helps improve interpretations of sediment transport, depositional processes, and reservoir architecture. This study develops a workflow that combines seismic attributes and unsupervised machine learning to identify, characterize, and measure deep-water depositional elements.

Several geometric and amplitude-based seismic attributes are used to enhance features that are difficult to recognize on conventional seismic amplitude data. Unsupervised machine learning techniques, including K-means clustering, Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), are applied to multi-attribute datasets to assist in the interpretation of submarine channels, channel-levee complexes, basin-floor lobes, mass-transport deposits, and other deep-water depositional elements. The different methods are compared to evaluate how well they highlight depositional features and support seismic interpretation.

After interpretation, the identified depositional elements are measured to quantify characteristics such as channel width, thickness, sinuosity, levee dimensions, lobe extent, and spacing between features. These measurements are compiled into a statistical database that will be used to describe the variability of deep-water depositional elements and provide quantitative input for future three-dimensional geomodeling efforts. Preliminary results indicate that integrating seismic attributes with machine learning improves the identification of depositional elements and provides an efficient workflow for quantitative seismic geomorphology. title: More Than Just Mud: New Geochemical Evidence For Waulsortian Mud Mound Development In The Early Carboniferous
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: McCabe, Kayla E [1], Marroquín, Selva Mariana [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
(2) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
abstract:
Waulsortian mud mounds are an unusual style of carbonate buildup that proliferated globally during the Early Carboniferous (~350 Ma) before disappearing by the end of the Mississippian. These deepwater micritic bioherms appear to overlap with one of the largest carbon isotope excursions of the Phanerozoic, the Tournaisian Carbon Isotope Excursion (TICE; +6–7‰). Although these buildups have been studied for decades, their emergence during this interval and disappearance remains unresolved. Numerous hypotheses have been proposed to explain mound development, including basin architecture, local topographic highs, hydrographic flows, and methane fed seeps. These hypotheses largely invoke local environmental or physical controls and have therefore been difficult to reconcile into a unifying framework for mound development. Here, we apply paired carbon isotope geochemistry (carbonate and organic carbon) to Waulsortian mud mound fabric to identify geochemical evidence for the processes responsible for mound development.

To evaluate whether Waulsortian mud mounds preserve a characteristic signature of microbially mediated carbon cycling, we integrate paired carbonate (δ 13 C carb ) and organic carbon (δ 13 C org ) isotope data with petrographic observations from mound and adjacent non-mound facies of the Tournaisian Tin Mountain Formation at Bat Mountain, California. Our results show that δ 13 C carb from mound facies remained isotopically similar to temporally equivalent strata and limited isotopic variability within the mound. This may indicate that mound growth occurred over a relatively brief interval compared to the duration of the carbon isotope excursion. In contrast, δ 13 C org values are variable and offset from adjacent non-mound facies, producing heavy carbonate-organic carbon isotope signatures (15-20‰ average offset). Carbonate-organic carbon isotope values within mound fabric indicate that localized microbially mediated carbon cycling accompanied Waulsortian mud mound development at Bat Mountain. Ongoing high-resolution petrography, scanning electron microscopy, and preliminary biomarker analyses will be used to identify mineralogical and geochemical evidence for biological processes that may have promoted alkalinity and mound growth (e.g. microbial metabolisms). Together, these data establish a geochemical framework for evaluating the biogeochemical processes that accompanied Waulsortian mud mound development and will guide future comparisons among mound-bearing localities.

title: Impacts of iron on lead (Pb) capture in urban stormwater catchment ponds and implications of sediment iron speciation

authors: Zweifel, Christof [1], McBride, Sara [2], Pollack, Lea [3], Janke, Ben [4], Finlay, Jacques [5], Snell-Rood, Emilie [6], Santelli, Cara [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota,

abstract: Many cities contain lead (Pb) in air, soil, and water from ongoing industrial emissions alongside legacy leaded paint and gasoline. Throughout the breakdown and movement of Pb-containing material, iron (Fe) is an important mediator, controlling reactivity and mobility. However, the effects of changing redox conditions on Pb associations with common soil Fe minerals as sediment is buried in stormwater ponds must be investigated to understand the fate of urban Pb pollution. Fe enters pond sediments from soil, infrastructure, vehicle wear, and iron enhanced sand treatments used to adsorb reactive phosphate. Pb flows through stormwater infrastructure via erosion and surface runoff, where Pb is captured in pond sediments as sulfides and adsorbed species. Sediments are elevated for Pb (200-2,000 ppm) in several ponds from the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area MN, USA. This study combines laboratory experiments and synchrotron based techniques to investigate the importance of Fe-Pb interactions for retaining Pb within sediments. Sediments contained 3-5 wt% Fe and a mixture of galena, organic-bound Pb, and Fe(III) oxide-bound Pb. Sediment Fe(III) oxide-bound Pb may be unstable, yet seemed to persist in reduced porewaters that contained an average of 15 ppm dissolved Fe, low sulfate, and high organic matter. Using synchrotron based X-ray fluorescence (XRF) mapping and µ-X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), we investigated the spatial co-occurance of Fe and Pb species. Pb was present in isolated hotspots, far above background levels, while Fe was distributed more uniformly. Fe and Pb spots were mutually exclusive in some sediment sections, but highly correlated in others. Bulk XAS and µXAS spectra will determine the bulk Fe speciation and micro-scale Fe speciation at Pb hotspots. The high spatial heterogeneity shows the need for synchrotron based XRF mapping and µXAS to gather information on the role of Fe within Pb capture. Experimentally, all of the relevant Fe species lowered dissolved Pb from synthetic stormwater. Interactions between synthetic stormwater and local sediments revealed a strong pH dependence for Pb dissolution, the possibility of Pb rich colloids > 0.22 µm, and significant impacts of Fe on Pb dissolution. Better understanding the local speciation of Fe and its sorption capabilities will inform how we understand stormwater Pb pollution, and has implications for Pb capture when Fe is applied for phosphate remediation.

title: Integrating Ground-Penetrating Radar and PlanetScope Imagery to Quantify Late Quaternary Coastal Dune Morphodynamics and Environmental Change at the Rancho Guadalupe Dunes Preserve, California
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Smith, Jacob Parker [1], Kelly , Joshua [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Geology, and Environment, California State University, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) Department of Geography, Geology, and Environment, California State University, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California, USA
abstract: The Rancho Guadalupe Dunes Preserve is a sub-region of the larger Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes complex and represents the largest remaining intact coastal dune ecosystem in California. Driven by late Quaternary sea-level changes and strong northwesterly winds, the dune field transitions from active coastal foredunes to stabilized inland parabolic dunes. To quantify contemporary (2017-2024) through late Quaternary morphodynamics (2017–2024), we combined geomorphic mapping with ground-penetrating radar surveying. Comparison of a 2017 USGS LiDAR digital elevation model with topographically corrected GPR data acquired in 2024 reveals a net loss of surface elevation (mean change of -1.01 m) along the cross-shore survey path, attributable to stoss-slope deflation. Over the same period, the primary transverse dune crest migrated landward by 20.1 m (2.88 m/yr). Subsurface GPR profiling with a GSSI 200 MHz antenna along a 1,327-m cross-shore survey path revealed stratigraphic features such as clinoforms, horizontally conformable reflectors, and erosional truncations, indicative of distinct modes of geomorphic change. Borehole data from the neighboring Guadalupe Oil Field, located to the north of the study area, were cross-referenced with the GPR profiles to contextualize the site's geologic and paleoenvironmental history. Combining GPR stratigraphic patterns with regional sedimentation rates and pollen markers reveals distinct late Holocene climate phases. A 5-m-thick sequence of horizontally conformable reflectors at the dune surface is interpreted as a former swale pond. Known sedimentation rates suggest that aggradation occurred over ~3,000 years, corresponding to the Mid-Holocene warm period from 9.5 to 5.5 ka. Integrating surface and subsurface geomorphic analyses of the Rancho Guadalupe Dunes has revealed substantial morphodynamic variability from the Late Quaternary to the present, likely in response to known climate changes in Central California.

abstract:
Carbonate U-Pb geochronology provides a framework for constraining the timing of both sediment deposition and later fluid-rock interactions. Laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry U-Pb dating of carbonates (LA carb) has advanced rapidly in the last decade, but there currently is no dolomite reference material. Researchers recognize a matrix dependance for U-Pb fractionation, which means the lack of a dolomite reference material has hindered efforts to date dolomite. Dolomite is abundant in the marine carbonate record, often serves as a hydrocarbon reservoir, and is associated with ore-bearing hydrothermal systems. We have identified a natural dolomite sample with well-behaved U-Pb systematics with enough material that it can be shared as a potential dolomite reference material. This sample has a range of U concentrations up to ~ 300 ppm and a range of U/Pb from 100 to 500 with the highest U/Pb ratios plotting on concordia. Pb concentrations range from 0.005 to 0.10 ppm and Th concentrations range from 0.0001 to 0.06 ppm. Isotope dilution dating of this dolomite yields an age of 13.678 ± 0.025 Ma.

The proposed dolomite reference material is from the Turkana Basin, Kenya, where it occurs as massive cement associated with calcite in a conglomerate of the Lothidok Formation. This grain-supported conglomerate occurs with large tree trunks that likely fell in the flooding event that created the deposit. Fragments of wood are permineralized by dolomite and found within the earliest dolomite generations, so we named the sample Turkana Basin Wood (TBW). The botryoidal dolomite occurs as radiating bundles of fibers that evolve into densely packed blades. XRF mapping shows that these bladed crystals have sectoral zoning, suggesting rapid deposition. This is an unusual dolomite with Zr concentrations approaching 1000 ppm and Zr/Hf ratios of more than 250. Synchrotron Zr and U EXAFS analyses show that the Zr and U are in the dolomite structure, and FE SEM and Raman analyses substantiate that these elements are not in nano-inclusions. This dolomite has well behaved U-Pb systematics and is a promising dolomite LA Carb reference material.

title: Determining Maximum Depositional Ages and Testing Stratigraphic Correlations for Paleoproterozoic Diamictites That Record the Rise of Atmospheric Oxygen

authors: Luo, Yang [1], Rudnick, Roberta L. [2], Rioux, Matthew [3], Cottle, John M. [4], Kylander-Clark, Andrew R.C. [5], Seward, Gareth [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science and Earth Research Institute, University of California - Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, California, USA

abstract:
The Duitschland and Rooihoogte Formations of the Transvaal Basin, South Africa, were deposited during the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) and both show evidence for loss of mass-independent fractionation of sulfur isotopes (MIF-S) up section. Due to poor outcrop and limited age constraints, debate has ensued regarding whether they are correlative or whether Duitschland is older than Rooihoogte; the former supports a step-function rise of atmospheric oxygen, while the latter supports an oscillatory rise. To test the stratigraphic relationship between the two formations, we report new detrital zircon U-Pb dates for two drill-cores through diamictites of the Rooihoogte Formation in the southwestern Transvaal basin: DP22 (648–648.5m depth) and EBA1 (1191–1192m depth). The DP22 diamictite has a 207 Pb/ 206 Pb Youngest Statistical Population (YSP) maximum depositional age (MDA) of 2495±25Ma (2σ, MSWD=1.54, n=85), and EBA1 diamictite has a 207 Pb/ 206 Pb YSP MDA of 2421±25Ma (2σ, MSWD=1.01, n=18), compared to 2424±7Ma (recalculated 207 Pb/ 206 Pb YSP MDA, 2σ, MSWD=0.97, n=8) for published detrital zircon data for the upper Duitschland diamictite that crops out in the northeastern Transvaal basin. Kernel density estimates and cumulative distribution functions demonstrate that all three datasets share a major modal peak (~2.5 Ga) and similar Archean age spectra, indicating similar provenance. However, relative to EBA1 and the upper Duitschland diamictite, DP22 diamictite contains a greater proportion of older zircons, and displays a systematically older cumulative age distribution and older MDA, indicating that it may tap a different provenance. In contrast, the EBA1 detrital population is statistically identical to that of the upper Duitschland diamictite in MDA, age spectra and cumulative age distributions, supporting a similar provenance and possible stratigraphic correlation. Nevertheless, geochemical evidence indicates that the matrices of both EBA1 and DP22 are composed of sediment derived from source regions that underwent strong oxidative weathering, as marked by depletion of redox-sensitive elements, and fractionated Mo isotopes (d 98 Mo = – 0.8‰), yet the EBA1 diamictite records a strong MIF-S signal. Thus, while the detrital zircon data for the upper Duitschland and Rooihoogte Formations suggest they are correlative and thus consistent with a step-function rise in atmospheric oxygenation, the previously published geochemical evidence for oxidative weathering prior to the GOE supports an oscillatory rise in atmospheric O₂.

Key words: GOE, Duitschland Formation, detrital zircons, MDA

title: PZero: a user-friendly, open-source 3D geomodelling platform written in Python
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Bistacchi, Andrea [1], Hussain, Waqas [2], Monti, Riccardo [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Milano – Bicocca, Milano, Italy
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Milano – Bicocca, Milano, Italy
(3) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Milano – Bicocca, Milano, Italy
abstract:
Commercial 3D geomodelling software has reached a high level of development but it can be unsuitable for many applications: it is typically specialized for the oil and gas and mineral deposits industries, but licensing costs can be prohibitive for small-scale projects and often out of reach for public agencies.

Over the last decade, several open-source libraries have emerged to test new geomodelling paradigms and provide tools to the community. However, various technical barriers, such as the lack of a GUI, make many of these tools difficult for geologists to adopt.

We developed PZero: a user-friendly system with an intuitive GUI. PZero manages all objects of a geomodelling project: points, lines, and surfaces with a geological modelling role, geological cross-sections and maps, wells and well logs, digital elevation models, geophysical datasets, structured and unstructured volumetric meshes, and fluid or hydrogeological contacts.

PZero projects are centered on a geological legend, designed to be intuitive for geologists, consistent with implicit modelling algorithms. Other properties can be visualized and analyzed in a multi-window system. A recent addition—the Structural Topology Model—defines topological relationships between solid units and their boundaries (tectonic, stratigraphic, or intrusive), easing modelling of complex structures and the creation of watertight solid models.

PZero includes tools for 2D cross-section and map analysis, orientation analysis (e.g. stereoplots), statistics, and general plotting. Implicit interpolation is implemented via the Loop3D library, and dedicated tools support 3D modelling from high-resolution surface data, including efficient visualization of Digital Outcrop Models. First-order uncertainty is handled through transparently traceable alternative scenarios, and the integrated PyMeshIt library supports building watertight solid volumes and tetrahedral meshes, e.g. for FEM simulations.

These tools make PZero especially valuable for applications where commercial software is not straightforward to use, such as 3D models that also integrate surface geological data—of interest to geological survey agencies—and energy transition projects, such as geothermal developments, where integrating geological modelling and meshing, or managing uncertainty with scenarios, can be fundamental.

Since PZero is written in Python and uses Numpy, linking other modelling libraries is straightforward, and PZero can serve as a convenient platform to develop and test new modelling algorithms.

Our aim now is to share this work with colleagues, gather feedback, integrate new algorithms, apply it to real-world case studies, and keep it growing.

title: Modeling Land Subsidence: So Many Choices, So Little Data!
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Smith, Ryan G [1], Pant, Susmita [2]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: Land subsidence due to groundwater withdrawals poses a major risk to infrastructure and aquifer storage capacity in many of the world’s unconsolidated aquifer systems. In most aquifer systems that experience significant consolidation, the surface subsidence is caused by a combination of rapid consolidation of coarse-grained layers or thin fine-grained layers, and delayed, long-term consolidation of thick clay lenses that can take decades to equilibrate to the water level, or head, of the primary aquifer that is measured in monitoring wells. In order to accurately characterize land subsidence, many models have been developed to simulate head and consolidation within clays. One great challenge of developing these models lies in choosing a conceptual model and model forcings that capture the key information needed to simulate subsidence as accurately as possible. Two critical pieces of information, that are often not well known, are the number and thickness of clay layers in the subsurface, and the head in the aquifer, which is treated as a boundary condition to simulate the heads within clay layers. For example, many regions with high subsidence are limited to one measurement of head per year, but confined aquifers in heavily pumped regions often experience 30 m or more of seasonal head change. Pulling from recent modeling work in the western US, this presentation will focus first on the impact of modeling choices relating to clay layers and head in the aquifer. Next, the presentation will explore methods to improve estimates of model forcings, with case studies in Utah and California.

title: Assessing Center-Pivot Irrigation Status and Patterns in the La Plata Basin, South America, Using Remote Sensing and Statistical Methods
session_title: Geoinformatics and Data Science: A Showcase In Undergraduate and Graduate Student Research (Posters)
authors: Ward, Colton [1], Nozari, Soheil [2], Camargo, Aiden [3], Smith, Ryan [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Mathematics, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(2) Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA

abstract: Data on irrigation status and irrigation patterns worldwide are critical for understanding agricultural water use, crop production, and regional water resource management. Existing global irrigation mapping products generally lack the spatial and temporal resolution required for these applications and often exhibit reduced accuracy in tropical and subtropical regions where irrigation is predominantly supplemental. Previous studies have explored machine learning approaches; however, in areas where ground-truth data are sparse, these methods can be difficult to train and validate. These challenges are particularly relevant to the humid and subhumid La Plata Basin, where irrigation is largely supplemental, and ground-truth data are limited. Statistical analyses of satellite remote sensing data offer a potential alternative to supervised classification approaches. In this study, we statistically analyze differences in Landsat-derived Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Land Surface Temperature (LST) between center-pivot fields and surrounding grasslands and pastures to determine the annual irrigation status of center-pivot fields across 10 subregions within the La Plata Basin from 2004 to 2024. Within each subregion, center-pivot fields are grouped into clusters with similar phenological characteristics and peak growing periods based on their monthly NDVI trends. For each peak NDVI time window within each cluster, we compute maximum NDVI and mean LST for the center-pivot interior and its 2500 m grassland-pasture annulus to characterize peak vegetation vigor and surface thermal conditions, respectively. This produces comparative distributions where effect size is quantified using Cohen's d. Preliminary results indicate a strong separation between center-pivot fields and surrounding grasslands and pastures. LST exhibited Cohen's d values around 1.5 (range: 0.6–2.0), while NDVI showed Cohen's d values between 1.0 and 3.0, with occasional outliers exceeding 4.0. These results indicate a strong cooling and greening effect of irrigation, respectively. Observed LST values generally ranged from 25–30 ℃ for center-pivot fields and 30–45 ℃ for the surrounding annuli. NDVI values were typically around 0.5 for center-pivot fields compared to 0.2-0.4 for the surrounding annuli. These preliminary findings demonstrate the proposed statistical framework's potential to distinguish irrigated center-pivot fields from the surrounding non-irrigated landscape. Future work will refine thresholding techniques and statistical classification models to determine the annual irrigation status of individual center-pivot fields and support the development of a comprehensive annual center-pivot irrigation database for the La Plata Basin.

title: Nitrogen Isotope Records from Archaeological Freshwater Mussel Shells to Assess Anthropogenic Impacts Over Time

authors: Andrus, C. Fred T. [1], Smith, Maya [2], Davenport, Christian [3]

abstract:
Nitrogen isotope measurements from the organic fraction of marine mollusk shells have proven useful for detecting changes to nitrogen cycling caused by both natural and anthropogenic processes. Analysis of sub-fossil and archaeological shells permits tracking such changes over time. Validation studies have been published demonstrating that these measurements may be similarly useful in freshwater habitats, but this approach has not yet been applied to archaeological mussel shells. Here we report additional modern validation data and an application of this method to assess potential anthropogenic impacts to the Florida Everglades since prehistoric times. The methods and results of this project will be contextualized with a discussion of complications caused by factors such as site formation processes and diagenesis.

Shells of Elliptio jayensis from the Belle Glade (~950 yrs BP) and Wedgworth middens (age ~ 3800 BP) along the south shore of Lake Okeechobee were analyzed for stable nitrogen isotope ratios (δ 15 N). The resulting data were compared to those measured in modern shells collected nearby, and 5 suites of museum-archived samples collected from the 1940- 2000’s. Validation studies demonstrate that shell δ 15 N values trend heavier with increased agricultural and urban impacts. Our samples reflect this pattern with prehistoric shells having lower δ 15 N values than most post-industrial age samples. The heaviest δ 15 N values were measured in shells from the 1980’s then trend lighter, with the most recent shells resembling prehistoric δ 15 N values. These results will be discussed in context of documented changes to the hydrology and agricultural practices in the area and explore the potential utility and challenges applying this method in other times and places.

title: Building Local Karst Infiltration Models Using Legacy Data and Remote Imagery: Implications for Resource Management
session_title: New Frontiers in Cave and Karst Science
authors: Furtner, Margaret J [1], Sovie, Adia R [2], Tobin, Benjamin W [3]
affiliations: (1) National Cave and Karst Research Institute, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Carlsbad, NM, USA
(2) Tuscon Bird Alliance, Tucson, AZ, USA

abstract: Karst aquifers are highly vulnerable sources of global drinking water, however, their complexity and heterogeneity pose significant challenges for effective research and management. Infiltration studies require technical expertise, time, resources, and access to remote and sensitive caves, limiting investigation. However, cave inventories and cave maps represent already existing, overlooked datasets which can help characterize infiltration dynamics in regional karst landscapes. This study aims to predict infiltration patterns surrounding two caves, one hypogene and one epigene, by combining cave survey speleothem observations and remotely sensed imagery as Random Forest (RF) model inputs. Recorded speleothem presence/absence tied to georeferenced cave stations act as proxies for historic and active infiltration and serve as model targets. Model variables were sourced from remotely sensed USGS 3DEP DEMs and NAIP multispectral images and include elevation, aspect, topographic wetness index, flow distance, distance to sinks, distance to drainage pathways, and visible atmospherically resistant index. Using a 10-fold cross validation, two local RF models were trained and evaluated using their respective legacy targets and surface variables, and prediction maps depicting infiltration probability in the nearby areas were generated. Both models effectively predicted speleothem occurrence on the held-out test datasets, achieving strong AUCs at 0.87 (hypogene) and 0.83 (epigene). The hypogene cave’s model had higher accuracy, precision, and recall than the epigene cave’s model. This discrepancy is possibly linked to the caves’ formation processes; the hypogene cave allows for better decoupling between model predictors and primary formation processes. Frequent flooding at the epigene cave influences its speleothem distribution, causing its model to distinguish areas of diffuse infiltration versus rapid recharge. These models and their resulting prediction maps demonstrate a simple yet robust tool reliant only on available data that can aid in karst resource management decisions.

title: An annually resolved lake sediment carbonate δ18O record from lowland Guatemala reflects Circum-Caribbean atmospheric circulation over the past 220 years
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: McDonald, Sydney [1], Gibson, Derek [2], Konecky, Bronwen [3], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Systems and Sustainability, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, IL, USA
(2) Carbondale, IL, USA

(4) Department of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
abstract: Establishing robust proxy-precipitation relationships is necessary to improve paleoclimate interpretations for Central America, where a scarcity of local-scale and high-resolution paleo-records limits the resolution of current climate models. To address this need, we developed an annually resolved record of oxygen isotope ratios ( 18 O: 16 O; δ 18 O) preserved in the sedimentary archive of Lake Lachuá, Guatemala, spanning the past 220 years and compared it with meteorological reanalysis data spanning the past 100 years. This comparison showed that the Lachuá δ 18 O record was in-phase with annual precipitation totals (i.e., increased precipitation corresponded with higher δ 18 O values and vice versa), opposite to the expected relationship described by the “amount effect”. We propose that the Lachuá sediment δ 18 O reflects changes in moisture transport pathways, driven by expansions and contractions of the North Atlantic Subtropical High (NASH). During NASH expansions, the Caribbean Low-Level Jet (CLLJ) becomes southerly-displaced and more meridional. This lengthens the distance that vapor masses travel before reaching Lachuá, increasing downstream rainout and resulting in reduced precipitation and lower δ¹⁸O values in precipitation delivered to the site. Under a contracted NASH, the opposite occurs: The CLLJ flows zonally and directly to Lachuá, resulting in increased precipitation and higher precipitation δ 18 O. Our data demonstrate that δ 18 O preserved in the Lachuá sediments can be used to track variability in Circum-Caribbean atmospheric circulation through time and provides a framework for deeper-time proxy-climate interpretations at the site.

abstract:
The >1000-km-long sinistral Atacama Fault System (AFS) of northern Chile is a major intra-arc strike-slip fault system that accommodated the trench-parallel component of Mesozoic oblique subduction. The AFS preserves deformation across the brittle–ductile transition, exposing tourmaline-bearing mylonites and cataclasites formed at different crustal depths within Early Cretaceous arc plutons and adjacent metasedimentary rocks. Tourmaline mineralization suggests that deformation and fluid flow were closely coupled. Although elevated geothermal gradients associated with arc magmatism have been proposed to weaken the continental arc crust, the extent to which crustal fluids contribute to strain localization remains poorly constrained. Because tourmaline crystallized during deformation and is highly resistant to later isotopic resetting, it preserves an exceptional record of fluid sources and fluid-rock interaction.

We present preliminary triple oxygen isotope analyses of tourmaline from four tourmaline-rich shear zones spanning ~200 km of the ​​​​AFS. These samples represent different positions along the arc and expose deformation formed at different structural levels within the brittle-plastic transition. Preliminary tourmaline δ¹⁸O (VSMOW) values span more than 11.5‰ across the sampled AFS. Although δ¹⁸O values vary systematically along strike, the dominant control is host lithology (e.g., igneous versus metasedimentary framework), demonstrating that syntectonic tourmaline preserves local fluid-rock interaction and isotopic heterogeneity rather than recording complete isotopic homogenization during fluid flow. The southernmost sample, in the Mantoverde region, yields an exceptionally low δ¹⁸O value (+1.3±0.2‰), which cannot be generated by magmatic or metamorphic fluids alone and instead requires infiltration of isotopically depleted meteoric waters into the Atacama Fault System. These data provide the first isotopic evidence that surface-derived fluids penetrated deeply into this long-lived intra-arc shear zone and were preserved in syntectonic ​tourmaline.

Ongoing work combines hydrogen and triple oxygen isotope systematics with host-rock compositions to determine fluid-rock ratios within each shear zone segment. These estimates will be compared with independently determined peak differential stresses and deformation conditions to evaluate whether increased fluid flux promoted mechanical weakening and strain localization. Together, these results will provide new constraints on fluid circulation through continental magmatic arcs and the role of fluids in facilitating long-lived intra-arc deformation.

title: Tracking the Cretaceous Fox Hills-Hell Creek Aquifer Throughout Eastern Montana: Implications for Sequence Stratigraphy
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Johanson, Alex [1], Gunderson, Jay [2], Rogers, Raymond R. [3]
affiliations: (1) Groundwater Assessment Program, Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Butte, Montana, USA; Structural Geology and Tectonics Lab, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
(2) Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology, Billings, Montana,
(3) Macalester College, Saint Paul, MN,
abstract:
The Fox Hills-Hell Creek aquifer (FHHC) is a principal regional aquifer and critical water resource in eastern Montana. The aquifer is a combination of two distinct sandstone-bearing units. The Upper Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) Fox Hills Formation is a laterally extensive shallow marine sandstone deposited during the final retreat of the Western Interior Seaway. The overlying Hell Creek Formation (also Maastrichtian in age) consists of spatially variable packages of terrestrial sandstones deposited by laterally migrating fluvial channels. These Hell Creek sandstones are packaged between mudstones which accumulated on adjacent floodplains.

Previous hydrologic studies identified the lower portion of the Hell Creek Formation to be significantly sandier than the upper portion, placing it in hydraulic connection with sandstones of the underlying Fox Hills Formation. The finer-grained facies that characterize the upper portion of the Hell Creek Formation act as a regional confining unit. To date, little attention has been focused on the stratigraphic implications of this regional shift in terrestrial facies within the Hell Creek Formation and its potential implications for the accommodation history within the basin.

We mapped both the top of the Fox Hills Formation and the top of the FHHC aquifer using geophysical logs from over 750 wells across eastern Montana. The top of the Fox Hills Formation is marked at the top of the first coarsening-upward sand deflection above the shale baseline of the Bearpaw Formation. The top of the FHHC aquifer is picked where there is an upward decrease in sandstone bodies and mudstone (shale) becomes the dominant lithology. It is commonly picked at the base of the first 40-50 ft thick shale encountered above the top of the Fox Hills.

We produced isopach maps for the Fox Hills Formation and the FHHC aquifer. The Fox Hills Formation is a tabular sand body with a 50-150 ft thickness across the 100,000 km 2 study area. The lower Hell Creek portion of the aquifer shows significant spatial variability in thickness, ranging from >400 ft in Powder River County to <100 ft in Sheridan County. The top of the FHHC aquifer coincides with a change in alluvial architecture throughout the region, and may reflect a change in the accommodation regime across the Powder River and Williston Basins.

title: Brachiopod Body Size Versus Shape: The effects of Competition in the Late Ordovician Richmondian Invasion
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Ess, Madeline P. [1], Banker, Roxanne M.W. [2], Maciech, Samantha [3], Dineen, Ashley A. [4], Roopnarine, Peter D. [5], Tyler, Carrie [6]
affiliations: (1) Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, ; Maimi University, Oxford, OH, USA
(2) Providence College, Providence, RI,
(3) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, North Las Vegas, NV,
(4) University of California, Berkeley, CA,
(5) California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA,
(6) University of Nevada, Las Vegas, NV,
abstract: Rising global sea temperatures today are enabling widespread biotic invasions, particularly in marine environments, as biogeographical barriers break down. The fossil record can be used to assess the impacts of past invasions on ecosystem structure and functioning on evolutionary timescales to better manage invasions today. Here we use brachiopod species from benthic marine communities of the Cincinnati Arch (USA) to compare the body size and shape (length) of invaders versus incumbents across the Late Ordovician (Katian) Richmondian Invasion. The size (volume) and shape (length measured from the hinge to the commissure) of 137 brachiopod species from six third-order order stratigraphic sequences (C2-C7) were measured. In C2 and C3, there were negligible numbers of invaders, however, C4 to C7 encompasses the three known invasion pulses. Invaders in C4 had smaller median body size relative to incumbents, and mean incumbent and invader size differed from C5 to C7 (Wilcox test, p < 0.01 within stages), with median body size becoming increasingly similar. This is consistent with initial invaders having faster growth rates and maturation resulting in smaller body sizes relative to incumbents, allowing them to monopolize space and resources when they first arrive. A late wave of invading cephalopod predators arrived in C7, perhaps also leading to reduced invasive brachiopods sizes in C7 relative to incumbents, as invading predators may have been familiar with them as prey. After establishment, both invader length and body size decreased in C5, possibly due to competition for resources. When considering body length alone, which is the measured from the hinge to the commissure, length differed between incumbents and invaders again from C5-C7 (Wilcox test, p < 0.01 within stages). From C5-C7, incumbents became longer, while invaders became shorter, a shape change that likely affected lophophore shape and efficiency, and resulted in niche partitioning, i.e., character displacement. These results suggest that there were significant differences in brachiopod body size between incumbents and invaders, in part due to changes in shape, and were likely driven by competition.

title: A Multi-step ID-TIMS Approach for Complex Zircons: Resolving Emplacement Ages of the Mt. Marcy Anorthosite Massif
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Karmakar, Sourav [1], Eddy, Michael Patterson [2], Ibanez-Mejia, Mauricio [3], Ickert, Ryan [4]
affiliations: (1) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(2) Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
(3) University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(4) Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA
abstract: The duration and construction of Proterozoic massif-type anorthosites remain difficult to resolve because metamorphic zircon overgrowths commonly obscure primary crystallization ages and complicate high-precision U-Pb analysis. We applied a modified CA-ID-TIMS approach integrating stepwise chemical abrasion, prolonged leaching of split zircon grains, and paired U-Pb-Hf isotope measurements to reconstruct the emplacement history of the approximately 3000 km² Mt. Marcy massif anorthosite in the Adirondack Highlands, USA. Stepwise dissolution demonstrates that standard chemical abrasion does not fully remove younger metamorphic zircon domains, whereas extended leaching preferentially removes altered and metamorphic material and exposes preserved igneous cores. The resulting U-Pb data identify at least two closely spaced intrusive episodes: the Port Kent-Westport unit crystallized at ca. 1160 Ma, followed by emplacement of the St. Regis-Marcy unit at ca. 1158 Ma. These ages indicate that the massif was assembled incrementally within less than 2 Myr. Initial ε Hf values also differ between the units, with the Port Kent-Westport unit yielding lower values (+2.3 to +3.1) than the St. Regis-Marcy unit (+3.0 to +5.6), indicating construction from compositionally distinct magma batches rather than a single well-mixed reservoir. Their juvenile Hf isotope compositions overlap those of associated Adirondack AMCG granitoids, consistent with a broadly related depleted mantle-derived magmatic system. The Mt. Marcy massif was assembled rapidly through the emplacement of exceptionally large, discrete intrusive increments. These results highlight the value of dissolution-resolved U-Pb-Hf analyses for reconstructing complex zircon growth histories, while the scale and closely spaced timing of the intrusive increments indicate exceptionally high magma flux during the formation of these massifs.

title: Understanding Eastern Kentucky Flooding Through Hydroclimatological Data and Geospatial Analysis
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Jack, Asher David [1], Fisk, Kasha [2], Kibria, Md Golam [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Engineering Sciences, Morehead State University, Morehead, KY, USA
(2) Department of Engineering Sciences, Morehead State University, Morehead, KY, USA
(3) Department of Engineering Sciences, Morehead State University, Morehead, KY, KY, USA
abstract: Flooding events in eastern Kentucky are becoming more frequent and severe, raising concerns. Understanding flood patterns and their links to major hydrological shifts is essential for building resilience. Project 2: Paleoperspectives of CLIMBS aims to reconstruct past climate patterns by analyzing hydroclimatic data, thereby establishing a paleoclimate record for Kentucky. This study combines paleoclimate reconstruction, extensive hydroclimate data, groundwater and surface water observations, and geospatial modeling to assess historical and current hydrologic changes in the Kentucky River basin. Historical streamflow trends from U.S. Geological Survey gauges in the Kentucky River basin were analyzed alongside land-cover data from 1985 to 2025 to assess the effects of forest loss, surface mining, and other landscape disturbances within the Kentucky River Watershed. Digital elevation models, lithology, terrain-derived indices, and hydrologic variables were integrated into spatial raster analyses to assess runoff generation and compare watershed conditions before and after an extensive flood event. The analysis shows a significant transformation of forested ridgelines into barren or disturbed areas, where reduced vegetation and altered soil structure can increase runoff potential and worsen downstream flooding. Analyzing shallow groundwater monitoring data helps evaluate how changes in shallow groundwater levels before, during, and after heavy rainfall can increase soil saturation and generate overland flow, even in areas previously not classified as hazard zones. The susceptibility maps and hydrologic data produced will aid the Kentucky Geological Survey and community partners in identifying high-risk zones, guiding monitoring and mitigation efforts, and enhancing resilience against future flood events in eastern Kentucky.
