title: The Legacy of Stone in Jamaica
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: James-Williamson, Sherene Andrea [1], Dolphy, Jorjan Elizabeth [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Geology, The University of the West Indies, Mona Campus, Kingston, Jamaica
(2) Geography and Geology, University of the West Indies, Kingston, Jamaica
abstract: Stone has anchored the landscapes and lifeways of Jamacia across centuries, embodying geoheritage values that span Indigenous, colonial, and contemporary contexts. For the Taíno, stone was integral to cosmology and survival, expressed in petroglyphs, zemis, and tools that inscribed meaning into limestone and riverine settings. Colonial expansion re‑cast stone as fortifications, plantation architecture, and urban monuments, embedding both domination and resistance in the built environment. Maroon communities mobilized stone in defensive settlements and sacred sites, while vernacular builders adapted local materials to sustain everyday resilience. Today, this legacy faces pressures from development, quarrying, construction, and climate impacts. All of which represent resource extraction that challenges the continuity of cultural and ecological values. This paper situates Jamaica’s stone heritage within Caribbean and global geoheritage discourse, emphasizing how domestic narratives, Indigenous perspectives, and international frameworks converge in the stewardship of geodiversity. By tracing this historical continuum and confronting present threats, the paper suggests integrated approaches that recognize stone not only as a resource but as a cultural archive of identity, memory, and resilience in Small Island Developing States.

title: North Atlantic Subtropical High Variability Over the Last Millennium: Extremes, Volcanic Forcing, and Hydroclimatic Patterns
session_title: Volcano-climate interactions
authors: Bregy, Joshua C. [1], Maxwell, Justin T. [2], Robeson, Scott M. [3], Harley, Grant L. [4], Trouet, Valerie [5]
affiliations: (1) Independent/Unaffiliated (Academia), Independent/Unaffiliated, Greenville, SC, USA
(2) Department of Geography, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(3) Department of Geography, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
(4) Department of Earth and Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, ID, USA
(5) Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA; Department of Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract: Summer circulation and moisture patterns in the Southeast United States are controlled by the position of the North Atlantic subtropical high. In a warming climate, the subtropical high is projected to strengthen and expand west, but there remains uncertainty regarding its variability and linkages to natural drivers. Here, we use a tree-ring network across the Southeast United States to reconstruct the relative intensity of the pressure gradient across the subtropical high’s western flank over the past 870 years. Variations in the flank’s position and the pressure gradient have been a major driver of the hydroclimate—including creating a Southeast-Caribbean moisture dipole—since 1140 CE. We document a significant increase in flank positional variability since 1900 CE, with westward migrations becoming more extreme. Likewise, major volcanic eruptions cause a multiyear period of westward positioning. Several mechanisms connect eruptions to extreme shifts in the subtropical high, including cross-equatorial cold-air advection. The resulting thermal gradient intensifies the westward expansion of the subtropical high. Consequently, eruption-induced shifts lead to distinct regional moisture gradients, amplifying regional moisture dipoles. Our record highlights important changes in flank behavior, which has important implications for water resource management in a warming world.

title: Mesoproterozoic Lower Crustal Reworking Recorded by Mafic Xenoliths from the Henry Mountains, Utah
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Wickland, Tyler [1], Mahan, Kevin [2], Wickland, G. Lang [3], Allaz, Julien [4], Newell, Dennis L. [5], Goncalves, Philippe [6], Bell, Aaron [7], Zawaski, Michael [8]
affiliations: (1) Earth Science, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Earth Science, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(3) Earth Science, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(4) Earth and Planetary Science, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland
(5) Water, Earth and Environmental Sciences, Utah State University, Logan, Utah, USA
(6) Chrono-Environment, University of Marie and Louis Pasteur, Besançon, France
(7) Earth Science, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(8) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA; Geosciences, Fort Lewis College, Durango, Co, USA
abstract:
Crustal xenoliths entrained by Oligocene intrusions of the Henry Mountains provide direct samples of the middle to lower crust beneath the northern Colorado Plateau. We integrate petrography, mineral chemistry, thermobarometry, Sr-Nd isotopes, U-Pb zircon and titanite geochronology, and clinopyroxene trace-element modeling to investigate the Proterozoic construction and reworking of this crust. The xenoliths comprise garnet-bearing and garnet-free mafic assemblages in which early garnet and pyroxene are variably replaced by amphibole. Thermobarometry and phase equilibria modeling records a range of amphibolite- to granulite-facies conditions of 0.5-1.3 GPa and 600-900°C, with garnet-bearing samples generally yielding pressures above 0.8 GPa and garnet-free samples below 0.8 GPa. While most of these equilibria were likely achieved during the Proterozoic, one sample appears to have new secondary garnet that grew during early interaction with the host magma, which constrains xenolith entrainment depth for that xenolith to 40-45 km. Zircon U-Pb data from three garnet-bearing xenoliths records distinct Paleoproterozoic and Mesoproterozoic growth. The cathodoluminescent dark cores from the zircons principally yield ca. 1.6-1.7 Ga dates, including a concordant 1640±10 Ma population (2s). Brighter zircon mantles and overgrowths yield dates of 1388±17 Ma, 1396±43 Ma, and 1384±37, including zircon locally included in garnet. Titanite intergrown with amphibole that replaced an earlier clinopyroxene-bearing assemblage yields a date of 1390±9.1 Ma, directly constraining the age of Mesoproterozoic hydrous metamorphism with Zr-in-titanite temperatures of 725-740°C.

Isotopic and trace-element data distinguish juvenile additions from reworked crust. Values of ε Nd (1400 Ma) range from +3 to −5. Most xenoliths approach juvenile compositions, whereas a garnet-rich sample has low ε Nd (1400 Ma) with ¹⁴⁷Sm/¹⁴⁴Nd above chondritic values, consistent with restite produced by partial melting of crust containing an inherited Paleoproterozoic component. Garnet-free pyroxene-bearing xenoliths have mantle-like initial ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr near 0.7025 and clinopyroxene-derived equilibrium melts that are distinct from N-MORB and resemble enriched continental-arc basalts, supporting their interpretation as mafic meta-cumulates. More radiogenic ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr values above 0.705, particularly in apatite, record later fluid modification. These results indicate that the Picuris orogeny involved juvenile mafic magmatism, partial melting of older crust, garnet growth, and hydrous metamorphism at deep-crustal levels of the Colorado Plateau. These events substantially reorganized Paleoproterozoic lower crust and established the heterogeneous architecture later sampled by the younger magmatism.

title: A Closer Examination of Late Holocene Drought Episodes From a Southern Great Basin Lake Core Record
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Theissen, Kevin [1]
affiliations: (1) University of St.Thomas, Saint Paul, MN, USA
abstract:
We combine new high-resolution scanning X-ray fluorescence (5 mm resolution) and clumped isotope derived paleotemperature data with previously reported isotopic (δ 18 O, 87 Sr/ 86 Sr, and 234 U/ 238 U) and total inorganic carbon (TIC) data from Lower Pahranagat Lake (LPAH), a highly alkaline, spring-fed southern Nevada lake to explore three recognized droughts over the past 3.5 ka. The LPAH core record has an excellent radiocarbon age chronology, and we previously established that both carbonate production and δ 18 O measured from carbonates are highly responsive to evaporative conditions.

The Late Holocene Dry Period (LHDP; 3.1-1.8 ka) is an especially interesting climate episode for the LPAH record with the most evaporative conditions for the Late Holocene as indicated by anomalous δ 18 O values (isotopic enrichments of >9‰), high TIC, and Sr and U isotopic compositions that show significant reductions in water supply to the lake from the primary aquifer source. The increased resolution of the scanning XRF data indicates that the LHDP was characterized by three multi-century long droughts separated by two wetter intervals of shorter duration in this southern Great Basin location. Clumped isotope derived water temperatures average 14.5 ± 2.2 °C, indicating the LHDP was in relatively cool conditions.

The Medieval Climate Anomaly (MCA; 1.2 – 0.8 ka) is indicated with a more modest increase in δ 18 O values (about 4‰) in the early MCA but two significant TIC peaks and Sr and U isotopic compositions that show reduced water from the primary aquifer, though not as much as for the LHDP. High-res XRF data allows us to better see multiple phases of the MCA. Though it was less evaporative, clumped isotope water temperatures average 18.6 ± 2.3 °C, indicating the MCA was warmer than the LHDP.

The current drought interval (last ~200 years) is indicated by δ 18 O enrichment of 4‰ and a slight rise in TIC. One clumped isotope derived temperature for this interval of 23.2 ± 2.3 °C indicates this is the warmest drought interval for the last 3.5 ka, undoubtedly influenced by ongoing human-induced warming.

title: Bayesian Reconstruction of Cenozoic Deep-sea Temperature, Ice Volume, and Milankovitch-scale Sea-level Variability: Enhancing Pacific Estimates of Benthic Foraminiferal δ¹⁸O Using Gaussian Process Priors and the Global CENOGRID Database
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Schmelz, William J. [1], Miller, Kenneth G. [2], Kopp, Robert E. [3], Wright, James D. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
(4) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
abstract:
We apply a Bayesian hierarchical model to reconstruct Cenozoic deep sea temperature (DST) and ice-volume changes using global benthic foraminiferal δ 18 O and Mg/Ca data. The model parameterizes how much of the δ 18 O benthic variation reflects temperature change, and a benthic foraminiferal paleotemperature equation is used to estimate δ 18 O sw . Barystatic sea level (BSL) is then derived using ice-sheet model that relates δ 18 O sw and BSL change. Parameter calibration aligns model output BSL and DST variations with independent sea-level estimates and Mg/Ca-derived DST. Our approach is conceptually similar to previous efforts to decompose δ 18 O benthic using Mg/Ca data as a temperature constraint, but differs by explicitly simulating ice-sheet volume changes within a Bayesian inversion framework.

We model global compilations of both the δ 18 O benthic (CENOGRID) and Mg/Ca data (Cramer et al., 2011; supplemented by Miller et al., 2024) are with Gaussian Process priors to isolate estimates of Pacific basin values. This modeling leverages data from 17 sites that are correlated using the standardized chronological framework CENOGRID represents. Integrating data from multiple sites across ocean basins helps enhance the high-frequency representation of Pacific δ 18 O benthic variability by supplementing intervals when Pacific data are sparse and minimizing site-specific variability not shared among the global records.

The results indicate a modestly sized Antarctic ice sheet was present through most of the Paleocene and Eocene. Large Antarctic and modest Northern Hemisphere ice sheets (NHIS) developed after the Eocene-Oligocene transition, though the NHIS melted during most interglacial periods and through the Miocene Climate Optimum. Spectral analyses indicate that climate state influences variations in the amplitude of orbitally forced variability through the Cenozoic. Milankovitch forcing produced 100 kyr BSL variability that increased from ~5 m in the Paleocene-Eocene to 30–40 m through the Oligocene and Early to early Middle Miocene, before diminishing to 20–30 m in the late Middle to Late Miocene. The amplitude rose again to ~40 m in the Early Pliocene and has increased to 80–100 m over 100 kyr cycles during the past Myr. Constructive interference of precession, obliquity, and eccentricity produces large variations in deep-sea paleotemperature and BSL. Although the largest periodic variability in Cenozoic BSL generally corresponds with eccentricity, our analyses indicate this forcing component contributes about half of the largest BSL rise and fall events through the Pleistocene.

title: Crunchy on the Outside, Warm and Gooey on the Inside: Thermal History and Rheological Evolution of Obsidian Dome, Inyo Craters, CA
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Kenderes, Stuart [1], Andrews, Graham [2], Befus, Kenneth [3], Isom, Shelby [4], Whittington, Alan [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environmental Sciences, Indiana University, Indianapolis, Indiana, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Hull, Hull, United Kingdom
(3) Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(4) Leidos, Reston, VA, USA
(5) Heat And Mass Transfer & Experimental Rheology (HAMsTER) lab, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
Silicic lavas commonly exhibit transitions between effusive and explosive behavior. Even the silicic lava domes of the Inyo Craters, CA, type examples of small effusive rhyolite eruptions, began with explosive crater-forming activity. Understanding the rheological behavior of obsidian lavas is vital for hazard assessment, but flow behaviors are controlled by complex and often simultaneous changes in the intrinsic properties of the lava, such as temperature, texture and composition (including dissolved water content), during emplacement. Obsidian Dome is a 600 year-old rhyolite lava in the Inyo Crater chain that has been sampled by scientific drilling proximal to the vent and near the flow margin. We collected spatially constrained samples from the two drill cores, and outcrops from the surface and flow margin. We measured residual water content, porosities, cooling rates, and apparent viscosity as a function of depth through the flow, and across the flow.

Residual water contents preserved in the drill core proximal to the vent are on average higher than predicted from equilibrium solubility, and connected porosities of up to 41% suggests that water loss continued during emplacement. Calorimetrically determined cooling rates show fastest cooling near the top and bottom of the flow, and slowest cooling in the flow interior (0.3°C per year), consistent with 1-dimensional conductive cooling models using temperature dependent thermal properties. We show that prolonged cooling and elevated dissolved water contents (>0.4 wt. %) preserved near the conduit at the base of the flow, and flow thickness of ~50 m on a less than 5° slope, are sufficient to generate a self-heating basal shear zone capable of driving passive transport and extension in the upper flow. Combined with outcrop observations we conclude that Obsidian Dome experienced two distinct emplacement styles, an early exogenous or “tank-tread” style followed by an endogenous or inflationary style once advance of the flow margin stalled.

title: Rock Magnetism & Paleomagnetic Analysis of the Controversial Michigan Basin Jurassic Red Beds
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources (Posters)
authors: Markel, Jennifer Clair [1], Elling, Reece [2], Weber, John [3], Schulte, Alec [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Grand Valley State University, Allendale, MI, USA
(2) Geology, Grand Valley State University, Allendale, MI, USA
(3) Geology, Grand Valley State University, Allendale, MI, USA
(4) Geology, Grand Valley State University, Allendale, MI, USA
abstract: The youngest stratigraphic unit on Michigan’s geologic bedrock maps has been a popular topic of debate in recent years, specifically its “true” age. A Jurassic age for these Michigan “Red Beds" (MRB) has persisted in nearly all geologic literature since the 1960s. There are few known outcrops of these rocks due to the glacial drift that buries the majority of Michigan’s bedrock. The most prominent sub-facies within these outcrops are near Ionia, MI and are a hematite cemented orange-to-red colored cross-bedded quartz arenite sandstone. We sampled three outcrops, collecting a total of 27 paleomagnetic cores. Because of the hematite cement, we were able to conduct rock magnetism and paleomagnetic analysis. If the sandstones were cemented shortly after deposition, the paleomagnetic directions could be compared to the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of North America to identify the time period when they most closely overlap the path. Our hypothesis was that the virtual geomagnetic poles (VPGs) would align with the APWP during an older time period than the accepted age; despite this, the three resulting VGPs suggested overprinting on some outcrops and a Jurassic age with an overlap of ~160-170 Ma. This analysis provides support for the long-held Jurassic age determination of the contested MRB; however, because the hematite cement could have formed long after deposition, additional sampling of cores drilled into the MRB could support for a more accurate age determination of these sandstones and potential changes to the geologic bedrock map of the famous Michigan Basin.

title: Paleoecology of a marginal marine ichnocoenosis: Petrographic and CT scanning insights from the Juniata Formation in Tennessee
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part I)
authors: White, Andrew P. [1], Platt, Brian F [2], Hembree, Daniel I [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, The University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS,
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS,
(3) Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,
abstract:
The Late Ordovician contains one of the most significant ecological turnovers in Earth's history, yet marginal marine ecosystems from this interval remain understudied despite their importance for understanding the transition toward modern terrestrial environments. The Upper Ordovician Juniata Formation preserves abundant trace fossils that provide one of the few records of these ecosystems. In the lower Juniata Formation of eastern Tennessee, two amalgamated trace-fossil-bearing facies preserve an unusual ichnocoenosis preferentially cemented by sparry calcite and surrounded by concentric bands of iron-bearing minerals.

The ichnocoenosis occurs within a single massive bed that transitions upwards from gray calcareous siltstone into a red very fine sandstone. Modern vegetation and erosion obscure much of the lateral continuity and internal architecture of these beds, although laterally continuous strata immediately above and below display wavy erosional bases. Thin sections prepared in multiple orientations through both facies reveal iron-rich bands concentrated along burrow margins, recording a localized redox front that extended downward from the red sandstone. Multiple generations of recrystallized calcite cement, locally replaced by quartz, overprinted primary carbonate fabrics.

Three-dimensional morphologies reconstructed from thick sections, polished slabs, and X-ray computed tomography reveal four distinct trace-fossil morphologies. The most common trace morphology present is long (>20 cm, 0.5-1 cm diameter), dominantly vertical burrows that are consistent with the previously described Skolithos ichnofacies. Alongside them, some similarly long (~10 cm), burrows with an identical diameter possess branches that radiate out at the base of a vertical shaft and are tentatively assigned to Chondrites isp. Other, smaller (<5 cm long, <0.5 cm wide), finely branching trace fossils have been found in a lower tier with an identical radiating pattern at their base, assigned to Chondrites isp. as well. A fourth morphology displays a complexly horizontally branching architecture of unknown affinity The distribution of trace morphologies, together with their diagenetic mineralization and comparison with modern marginal marine infaunal communities, suggests deposition in an estuarine or upper shoreface setting characterized by fluctuating redox conditions. This ichnocoenosis preserves a distinct, multi-tiered Late Ordovician infaunal community, providing new insights into the benthic partitioning, early diagenesis, and environmental conditions within marginal-marine ecosystems during the early stages of the ocean-to-land biotic transition.

title: Outcomes and Impacts of the First Five Years of the GeoSPACE Accessible Field Camp Program
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Marshall, Anita Stone [1], Thatcher, Sean [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL,
(2) Engineering and Environmental Sciences, City University of New York, Staten Island, NY, USA
abstract:
The GeoSPACE Field Program was developed to address the extreme lack of an accredited and accessible geoscience field courses utilizing a unique hybridized field course model and mentoring program. The goals of the project were to 1. develop an accessible hybrid field camp using inclusive strategies and technology, 2. establish a network of peer and professional mentors that extends beyond the field course, 3. create opportunities to help student participants advance from undergraduate to the next level of their career progression (graduate school or professional work), and 4. to encourage systemic change and serve as a catalyst for sustainable solutions to the lack of accessible experiential learning in the geoscience. At the 5-year anniversary of the program, we evaluate the preliminary outcomes and impacts of the project and consider future directions.

The field course takes place in northern Arizona and online through real-time remote engagement in collaborative teams. Designed as a capstone-level field course for undergraduates, students apply traditional field skills, geospatial tools, communication technologies, and collaborative data interpretation to complete field projects in volcanology and planetary geology. Both the in-person and virtual participation modes are designed to be accessible and inclusive for a broad range of participants. From 2022 to 2026, a total of 80 students participated in the program from 22 universities and 3 countries. While the program initially targeted students with disabilities, it attracted students from a wide range of identities and life-circumstances that excluded them from other field programs. After the program, students stay connected to the program through a dedicated social media space in Discord which enables connections with students from other year groups, and the sharing of opportunities, advice and connections.

During the five years of this program, we have utilized a reflective iterative approach to make improvements to the program with input from students and faculty to improve student skill development, career readiness, and identity as geoscientists. Through a qualitative analysis of student feedback and longitudinal progress-tracking of participants following the program, we present a snapshot of our progress to date, the lasting impact on participants, helpful lessons learned from a programmatic perspective, and goals for the future.

title: Shifts in Evolutionary Modularity Over the Late Ordovician Mass Extinction in a Trilobite Family
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Vargas-Parra, Ernesto Ezequiel [1], Hopkins, Melanie Jane [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California Riverside, Riverside, California, USA; Divison of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History, New York, New York, USA
(2) Division of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA
abstract: Animals are organized in packages. These packages, or modules, are composed of traits that have the potential to evolve semi-independently such that change in one module does not necessarily beget change in another. At the macroevolutionary level, this decoupling and relaxation of evolutionary constraints is thought to promote evolvability. Thus, it is thought that modularity facilitates rapid diversification in diverse evolutionary directions as evolutionary rates among modules may vary along phylogenetic branches. The extent to which modularity mediates organismal response to environmental change, especially during biotic crises, is unknown. Trilobites provide an unmatched fossil record, due to their biomineralized exoskeleton, to examine modularity at the macroevolutionary level in deep time, particularly in the context of mass extinction. Specifically, modularity in the trilobite cephalon (head shield) is of interest due to it being a complex structure composed of several fused segments which served multiple functions. The Ordovician trilobite family “Pterygometopidae” well-expresses this segmentation in the glabella, or medial lobe of the cephalon. Previous Bayesian phylogenetic work resolved relationships within this family and related taxa showing that Pterygometopidae is paraphyletic with Phacopidae nested within the subfamily Eomonorachinae, which survives the Late Ordovician mass extinction to radiate post-extinction in the Silurian. Pre-extinction, the best fit model of modularity in the cephalon is one where the eye constitutes a module with the posterior part of the glabella contrasting with modularity patterns observed at the species level. Post-extinction, the structure of modularity (number and arrangement of modules) is relatively unchanged, yet the degree of modularity between partitions shifts such that within-module integration is stronger. Rates of evolution vary by subfamily and, along branches, by module. High-disparity/high-rate subfamilies within Pterygometopidae become extinct by the end of the Ordovician. Interestingly, Eomonorachinae has relatively low disparity and low evolutionary rates leading up to the Late Ordovician mass extinction which its descendant Phacopidae survives. Further, disparity and evolutionary rates remain relatively low in Phacopidae as it radiates in the Silurian. Modularity patterns of surviving lineages may have influenced recovery over a macroevolutionary bottleneck following a mass extinction. Future work will examine the extent to which extinction itself may be a driver of modularity patterns through time, particularly in the context of ongoing biotic crises, and its effects on intrinsic forces governing trait (co)variation.

title: Muscovite and beryl chemistry of the Spruce Pine Pegmatite District, North Carolina: implications for pegmatite petrogenesis and the formation of high-purity quartz
session_title: Granite-related mineral systems: Advances in understanding their genesis, distribution, and exploration implications (Posters)
authors: Curry, Adam C [1], Wise, Michael A [2]
affiliations: (1) North Carolina Geological Survey, Raleigh, NC, USA
(2) Department of Mineral Sciences, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C., USA
abstract: The Spruce Pine Pegmatite District (SPPD) covers an area of ~800 km 2 in the Eastern Blue Ridge of North Carolina and consists of the Neoproterozoic Ashe and Alligator Back Metamorphic Suites intruded by the Paleozoic Spruce Pine Plutonic Suite and numerous pegmatites. Pegmatites in the SPPD were originally mined as early as the 1860s for mica and feldspar, with quartz as a byproduct, but with the increasing need for high-purity quartz (HPQ), defined as having < 50 ppm of trace elements, in solar photovoltaics and semiconductors, the SPPD is now the main global supplier of HPQ. Despite the economic importance of this deposit globally, few studies have focused on the SPPD in recent decades. The SPPD is dominantly REE-rich Group 2 pegmatites, with one Li-rich Group 1 pegmatite (McHone), in addition to the mineralogically-simple pegmatites containing HPQ; this diversity of pegmatite chemistry makes the SPPD an ideal site to understand both the extreme enrichment of critical metals in magmas, as well as the intense exclusion or depletion of metals in other magmas required to make HPQ within the same pegmatite district. The major minerals in pegmatites of the SPPD are plagioclase, quartz, K-feldspar, and muscovite, with accessory phases including biotite, epidote, garnet, tourmaline, beryl, apatite, spodumene, pollucite, fluorite, allanite, samarskite, columbite-tantalite, and uraninite, among many others, reflecting the diverse pegmatite chemistry. This study uses beryl chemistry from six localities and muscovite chemistry from 13 localities to assess petrogenesis and degrees of fractionation, put the SPPD in the context of other pegmatite districts globally, and understand the formation of economic HPQ pegmatite deposits. Muscovite K/Rb ratios indicate primitive to moderate levels of fractionation in SPPD magmas as do the Na/Li ratios and Cs contents of beryl, except for Cs-rich beryl from the Li-rich McHone pegmatite that reflects quite extensive fractionation. Muscovite from a locality that lacks beryl and produces much of the world’s HPQ supply shows K/Rb values in the range of 50 to 170. Other pegmatites in the SPPD with similar K/Rb signatures in muscovite that also lack rare element mineralization may prove to be worthy candidates for the crystallization of HPQ.

authors: McCoy, Hannah L [1], Finnegan, Seth [2], Klompmaker, Adiël [3], Leeson, Morgan [4], Milagros-Thompson, Carmi [5], O'Dea, Aaron [6], Leonard-Pingel, Jill [7]

abstract: The Isthmus of Panama formed through the Miocene to Late Pliocene, severing the connection between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and causing significant disruption to Caribbean marine ecosystems. During the final stages of Isthmus emergence, the Caribbean Sea experienced increases in salinity and carbonate deposition, as well as decreases in nutrient availability and primary productivity due to reduced upwelling. Although these changes to the physical environment are well-documented, and there have been several studies on their impact on the benthic marine communities of the Caribbean, the connection between reduced planktonic productivity and its impacts on specific bivalve communities and trophic groups is still understudied. The abundant equatorial bivalve mollusks belonging to the family Corbulidae would have been directly affected by a decrease in productivity, as they are suspension-feeding bivalves. Corbulidae are very abundant in the Neogene marine record of the Isthmus of Panama, making them an excellent focus for this research. This research focuses on a collection of corbulid bivalves from the southwestern Caribbean that range in age from ~11 Ma to 7 Ka. We examine fossil corbulids that were previously collected by the Panama Paleontology Project (PPP) in the 1990s-2000s. These samples were previously collected as bulk samples, sieved, identified to genus, and counted. In order to generate automated size measurements, each corbulid was photographed with the umbo directed upwards on a flat black surface, with a scale bar, using StackShot to create a stacked image. Digital images of shells were measured using AutoMorph, a morphometric software that uses stack images to quantify 2- and 3-dimensional traits, i.e., height, length, and depth for each shell, providing approximate measurements of shell biomass. Automorph compilations of body size measurements from different time periods will allow testing the hypothesis that decreases in primary productivity in the Caribbean drove a decrease in overall body size and a decrease in abundance of corbulid bivalves in the Caribbean post-isthmian closure. Abundance counts of both the corbulid bivalves, as well as predatory gastropods (e.g., naticids and muricids), will also test the hypothesis that the proportion of Caribbean primary consumers to predators increased after the isthmus formed, resulting in lower incidence of predation in the Caribbean in the later Neogene.

title: Fault Kinematic Analysis of the Noa Dihing Fault System, Easternmost Himalaya
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Chance, Dena MW [1], Betka, Paul M. [2], Howes, Ceci [3], Lang, Karl A [4], Rakshit, Raghupratim [5], Swartz, Jake [6]
affiliations: (1) Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA

abstract: The Himalayan orogen, shaped by the ongoing indenter tectonics of the India-Eurasia collision, forms the highest and largest active mountain range on earth. The collisional orogen terminates along its eastern flank at a triple junction of continental fault systems that separate the India, Burman, and Eurasian plates. The tectonic setting in the region is controlled by clockwise crustal flow of Eurasia around the eastern Himalayan syntaxis, the transition from collision to oblique subduction of the India plate along the Sunda subduction zone, and the India-Eurasia-Burma triple junction. The Noa Dihing fault (NDF) is a major crustal structure at the apex of the triple junction that separates crystalline rocks of the Himalayan wedge from deformed foreland basin strata of the Indo-Burman accretionary prism. Despite its' clear tectonic importance, few studies have examined the kinematic evolution of the NDF. Through analysis of brittle fault-slip data, this study aims to constrain the tectonic evolution of the NDF and characterize deformation within the Himalayan wedge related to the converging Burma terrane (BT). Fault slip data (n=200) measurements reveal two populations of brittle faulting in the NDF fault system. The first population is defined by north- to northwest-striking thrust faults (n=35) that represent the development of the Himalayan wedge. The second population is defined by northwest-striking thrust and right-lateral strike slip faults that cross-cut thrusts of the first population. The younger cross-cutting faults splay from the Noa Dihing fault and northern end of the Sagaing fault. Brittle deformation at the eastern terminus of the Himalaya is attributed to convergence between the Burma terrane and the eastern Himalayan wedge. The Noa Dihing fault system accommodates right-lateral and reverse faulting in a contractional horse-tail splay structure that cross-cuts the Himalayan wedge. These new results are a part of a larger study aimed at characterizing the ongoing evolution of the eastern terminus of the Himalayas and the NDF. Ongoing work in Raman spectroscopy is planned to identify peak metamorphic temperatures of the units of the NDF to identify thermal breaks and constrain uplift across significant brittle fault zones.

affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA

abstract: Our research team initiated the construction of a geological database to assist in evaluating the exploration potential for geological hydrogen in the Sacramento Basin in northern California. This project involved evaluating the results of previous investigations that utilized paper copies of geophysical logs from oil and gas wells drilled in the basin during the mid to late 1900s. Research efforts consisted of identifying well names, operators, and locations of over 600 wells used in historical studies. General Public Land Survey System well location data from these studies was cross-referenced with wells listed in the online California Department of Conservation (CDC) oil and gas well database. In most cases, the general well-location information indicated the presence of multiple wells in an area, and identification required a direct comparison with scanned raster images of the logs available through the CDC. Additional CDC data, including well latitude/longitude, and surface/log datum elevations, were also collected. Raster logs were depth registered and all data incorporated into a digital database that was imported into industry subsurface evaluation software for stratigraphic correlation and mapping purposes. Key formation tops recorded in each by previous investigators were used to establish a stratigraphic framework for the Cenozoic-Mesozoic rocks of the basin. Continued work will focus on identifying reservoir/seal lithologies and structural features that exist in close proximity to potential geological hydrogen source rocks to direct future exploration efforts in the basin.

title: Evaluating GRACE-Derived Groundwater Storage Change Using Well Observations Across New Mexico
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: Tesfamichael, Tewodros [1], Timmons, Stacy S. [2], Guerra, Peter [3]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Tech, New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) NMT, New Mexico Bureau of Mines and Mineral Resources, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
abstract:
Groundwater- monitoring networks provide essential information about aquifer conditions, but irregular records, uneven coverage, and uncertain storage properties complicate regional groundwater-storage assessment. Satellite gravimetry from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On missions provides spatially integrated observations of terrestrial water-storage variability. Estimating the groundwater component requires subtracting non-groundwater storage terms, before comparison with ground-based observations.

Groundwater-storage anomaly was estimated for New Mexico and its major groundwater regions using GRACE mascon terrestrial water-storage anomalies and modeled soil-moisture, and snow-water-equivalent, and canopy-water-storage anomalies. Groundwater-level observations were aggregated temporally and spatially and converted to storage change using assigned aquifer-storage properties. Annual comparisons were emphasized because irregular well records, and seasonal variability, spatial mismatch, and incomplete monitoring limited the reliability of statewide monthly comparisons.

At the statewide scale, GRACE-derived and well-based estimate showed strong temporal correlation (r = 0.86), but agreement in magnitude was more limited: with an RMSE 34.44 mm, mean GRACE-minus-well bias was −10.43 mm, and the difference in estimated trends was −2.53 mm/yr. Annual correlations were also positive in the Central (r = 0.88), High Plains (r = 0.69), Lower Rio Grande (r = 0.81), Northeast (r = 0.83), Pecos (r = 0.87), and Upper Rio Grande (r = 0.67) regions. These correlations indicate similarity in annual temporal behavior, not equivalence of storage magnitude. Substantial bias or trend differences in several regions indicate disagreement between the two estimates, while other regions showed weak or opposing annual behavior. Differences between GRACE-derived and groundwater well-based estimates may reflect differences in monitoring density and distribution, aquifer heterogeneity, scale mismatch, uncertainty in specific yield, and errors in modeled non-groundwater components.

The study presents an integrated framework for comparing satellite gravimetry, land-surface-model components, and well-level observations for estimation groundwater storage anomalies across spatial scales. The results identify regions where independent estimates show broadly consistent behavior over time, and regions with disagreement warrants additional evaluation of aquifer conditions, groundwater use, storage parameters, and monitoring network adequacy before drawing conclusions.

title: The Crux of the Late Cenozoic Plate Margin Extensional System of Southwestern North America, Total Displacement Across Death Valley (California, USA)
session_title: Maps, Metamorphic Cores, and Mentorship; a session honoring the career contributions of Jeff Lee
authors: Andrew, Joseph [1]
affiliations: (1) Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
abstract:
The late Cenozoic tectonic evolution of southwestern North America is a well-studied example of continental margin extensional tectonics. Despite intense study, there is no complete interpretation for the regional tectonic and magmatic evolution and no clear consensus on its geodynamics. The critical missing link in the magmatic and deformation evolution occurs between the Miocene tectono-magmatic evolution of the Colorado River extensional corridor (CREC) in western Arizona, and the Pliocene and younger activity of the Walker Lane belt (WLB) along the Nevada-California border. This key missing segment is the Death Valley extensional region (DVER), a large-magnitude extensional system. The DVER is a classic location for examining extensional processes, it’s a place of fieldtrips and intense geoscientific study but there is no resolved scientific consensus on the amount of extension and thus its place within the regional geodynamic system.

New data support an interpreted reconstruction marker across the DVER. A WSW-migrating trend of shallow rapakivi granite pluton emplacement from 13.1 to 11.6 Ma in the footwall of the WSW-directed Kingston Peak detachment fault. The only other similar shallow level rapakivi granite in the DVER is the Little Chief (LC) granitic porphyry, in the hanging wall to the DVER. The LC pluton has a similar exposure area as the slightly older granitic plutons and was emplaced in two phases at 11.4 and 11.3 Ma. It also contains an older intrusive felsic phase preserved as locally abundant felsic enclaves. The LC pluton could thus be the continuation of the slightly older pluton emplacement trend and has since been displaced away. If this match is correct, then this displacement is ~100 km to the WNW. This is a total displacement, a composite of the different extension directions and associated transform fault displacements and is not the extension on one fault. This ~100 km WNW-displacement can be evaluated using the known deformation history of the DVER from previous studies to estimate the different time components of displacement as the DVER evolved from top-WSW to top-NW extension. The amount, kinematic, and timing data of this large displacement vector help evaluate the missing link in the tectonic evolution of the southwestern USA, linking the CREC to the WLB in one continuous, evolving and migrating system of tectonics and magmatism.

title: The timing and temperature of high-pressure (HP) metamorphism in western Grenville Province: constraints from U-Pb zircon geochronology and Ti-in-zircon thermometry
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Cao, Wentao [1], Slagstad, Trond [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Sciences, State University of New York at Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, ; Buffalo Museum of Science, Buffalo, NY, USA
(2) Geological Survey Norway, PO Box 6315 Sluppen, Trondheim, Norway
abstract: Recent studies of the Mesoproterozoic Grenville Province proposed tectonic models (Gervais et al., 2023) that differ from previous models (e.g., Rivers et al., 2008). One important factor is the timing of Grenville orogenic phases, especially the Ottawan phase (e.g., 1090 Ma vs. 1030 Ma). To address the contrasting differences in tectonic models, we applied U-Pb geochronology, trace element geochemistry and thermometry to zircon in specimens collected from western Grenville Province. Sample 19-05 is a mafic granulite from the Go Home domain of the Algonquin terrane. Zircon from the specimen yielded a Grenville age of 1092.5 ± 4.2 Ma (MSWD = 1.8), with a trace element pattern without Eu anomaly. Ti-in-zircon thermometry of the Grenville-age domains yielded a temperature of 662 ± 22 °C, with activity values of SiO 2 and TiO 2 as 0.75. Zircon U-Pb age of the protolith, which displays a negative Eu anomaly, is constrained to be 1428.0 ± 6.0 Ma with MSWD = 7.8. Sample 18-35 is a partially melted retrogressed eclogite collected from Mattawa area in the Bonfield domain of the Algonquin terrane, immediately above the Allochthonous Boundary Thrust. Zircon in the specimen yielded a U-Pb age of 1102.8 ± 5.6 Ma with MSWD = 3.1, assuming activities of SiO 2 and TiO 2 as 0.75; these zircon grains display a trace element pattern showing predominantly no negative Eu anomaly and a Ti-in-zircon temperature of 605 ± 39 °C. The nearby garnet-bearing gneiss 19-46 from the same Bonfield domain yielded a Grenville age of 1089.1 ± 1.6 Ma (MSWD = 2.9), without an Eu anomaly in its trace element pattern, and a Ti-in-zircon temperature of 670 ± 37 °C with the same activity assumption. Our results constrained the timing of HP metamorphism to be 1089 – 1103 Ma, consistent with the traditional model and previous age determination (e.g., Rivers et al., 2009; Marsh et al., 2014). However, the temperature calculated using Ti-in-zircon thermometry is significantly lower than phase equilibrium estimates of at least 800 °C. These calculated temperatures suggest that the zircon grains recorded the timing of prograde metamorphism during earlier stages of the Grenvillian metamorphism. More data on the timing and location of metamorphism is critical in fully evaluating the different tectonic models.

title: Geoheritage in Education: Sharing the Legacy and Potential of the Geosciences
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Robeck, Edward C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Education & Outreach, American Geosciences Institute, Alexandria, VA, USA
abstract:
By extending knowledge of Earth's systems into realms of social dynamics, geoheritage offers educators opportunities to situate geoscience learning within authentic societal contexts, allowing students to see how geoscience informs complex real-world challenges. Geoheritage case studies are particularly valuable because they demonstrate that, while the social, cultural, economic, and political dimensions of certain activities cannot be understood through geoscience alone, they also cannot be fully understood without it. In this way, geoheritage provides an argument for the importance of geoscience education by illustrating how geoscience contributes essential evidence to interdisciplinary reasoning.

Geoheritage sites illustrate how geoscience processes and materials are connected to values along aesthetic, cultural, economic, and other dimensions that motivate human activity. At many sites, these values overlap and may come into conflict. For example, the histories of some geoheritage sites reveal tensions between cultural and economic priorities that have shaped relationships within and between Indigenous and settler communities. Such case studies provide educators with opportunities to connect geoscience concepts to ideas such as agency, justice, and social power while maintaining geoscience as an essential part of the discussion.

For example, understanding how mineral-forming processes produce an uneven global distribution of critical resources helps explain why extraction is concentrated in particular locations, creating conditions in which competing environmental, cultural, and economic priorities emerge. Likewise, understanding geologic timescales helps students evaluate the consequences of extractive activities and related changes to landscapes that affect communities differently. In ways such as these, geoscience helps define the physical constraints and possibilities within which societal decisions are made.

Geoheritage thus provides educators with a powerful means of demonstrating that geoscience is not simply a body of disciplinary knowledge, but an essential foundation for understanding and engaging with the complex societal decisions that arise where Earth's resources, landscapes, and people intersect.

title: Long-lived axial drainage along the Indus suture zone in southern Tibet supports Oligocene formation of the modern Gangdese Range drainage divide

authors: Sperry, Westley [1], Sundell, Kurt [2], Laskowski, Andrew K. [3], Howlett, Caden James [4], Lin, Ding [5]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA

abstract: The Himalayan-Tibetan orogen is home to Earth’s highest topography and thickest continental crust. Within this unique geologic context, drainage systems develop under the competing influence of tectonic and climatic factors. The Yarlung River drainage between the Gangdese Range to the north and the Himalayas to the south is one such drainage. Several hypotheses have been proposed for the formation of the Gangdese drainage divide, including lithospheric removal and associated surface uplift; oroclinal bending and associated drainage reorganization; and a lithologic contrast between the dominantly igneous rocks of the Gangdese Range and more erodible surrounding sedimentary rocks. Here we consider a fourth, structural hypothesis: Focused rock uplift related to a deep-seated crustal ramp. To test these hypotheses, we characterized sedimentary sections within the suture zone south of the modern drainage divide using traditional basin analysis tools and detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology. We also sampled modern rivers along the suture zone for detrital zircon analysis. Results from a new ~1100 m thick composite stratigraphic section interpreted as Oligocene-Miocene conglomeratic strata are entirely siliciclastic, dominated by sandstones and pebble conglomerates with subordinate mudstones. Repeated fining-upward packages and erosive, clast-supported conglomerates are consistent with a fluvial depositional environment. Detrital zircon U-Pb age distributions from the new stratigraphic section are characterized by Late Cretaceous and Eocene age modes related to Gangdese magmatism. Quantitative comparison reveals that they are most similar to Dazhuka and Xigaze formations and are broadly interpreted to be correlative to the Oligocene-Miocene Kailas Formation. These age distributions are dissimilar to proximal modern rivers and instead are similar to modern rivers tapping lithologies farther east; this supports a west-flowing river during deposition, consistent with previous interpretations of a middle Miocene reversal of the Yarlung River. The lack of igneous clasts in conglomerates supports the interpretation of a distal source. The timing of deposition along a well-established axial system, when placed in the context of recent mapping efforts along the Indus suture zone, is consistent with a structural driver for the formation of the modern drainage divide.

title: Petrologic Investigation of San Andres Formation Carbonates on the Central Basin Platform in the Permian Basin: Considerations for Geologic Carbon Storage Potential
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies (Posters)
authors: Valenzuela, Jose L. [1], Trentham, Robert C. [2], Flowers, Brian [3], Henderson, Miles A. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Chemistry and Geosciences, The University of Texas Permian Basin, Odessa, Texas, USA

abstract:
Evaluations of carbon dioxide enhanced oil recovery (CO 2 -EOR) projects in the Permian Basin have revealed a delayed production response during the Goldsmith San Andres Unit CO 2 pilot in Ector County Texas. Researchers working on the study attributed this behavior to the likely presence of a dual-porosity/permeability system consisting of a primary intergranular pore-network and secondary dissolution-enhanced fusilinid moldic pores. As CO 2 migrated from the interconnected intranular system into the larger fusilinid molds, capillary pressure contrasts and pore-throat restrictions may have promoted temporary sequestration of CO 2 within the moldic network. Storage in the molds would continue until reservoir pressure increased sufficiently to overcome egress pore-throat pressures, allowing CO 2 to re-enter the primary porosity network and improve sweep efficiency.

Thick intervals of fusulinid-rich open-marine ramp carbonates in the San Andres Formation are present across the Central Basin Platform and Northwest Shelf of the Permian Basin. These intervals have been affected by later diagenetic events resulting in a complex petrologic history, including selective dissolution of fusulinid tests, leading to the development of this dual porosity/permeability network. These San Andres reservoirs have been the target of CO 2 sequestration projects across the Permian Basin.

This study characterizes the nature of the porosity and permeability system in San Andres Formation of the North McElroy Field located on the Central Basin Platform. Traditional petrographic analyses using petrographic thin sections and scanning electron microscopy of rock chips are used to evaluate the distribution, geometry, and connectivity of porosity networks in the field. Petrographic data gathered in this study provides key information needed for further computational modeling of CO 2 through the dual porosity-permeability networks of the San Andres Formation. The nature of this dual porosity/permeability system may represent a significant opportunity to increase the effectiveness of long-term carbon storage while minimizing remobilization and leakage if reservoir pressures can be maintained below the threshold required to reconnect flow through the secondary pore network and represents an important step in our understanding of sequestration mechanisms for future carbon storage projects and CO 2 -EOR projects in San Andres Reservoirs.

title: Hydrogeochemistry and Mine Wastes: Conceptualization, Characterization and Modeling
session_title: New approaches and emerging technologies for the prevention, control, and remediation of acidic rock drainage and legacy mine waste
authors: Nordstrom, Darrell Kirk [1]
affiliations: (1) Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Conceptualization is the foundation of successful remediation for any hazardous waste site. Mine site conceptualization begins with one’s background and experience with geology, hydrology, water chemistry, microbiology, mining, and mineral processing. Because these are typically not courses covered by civil engineering curricula, industry and regulatory agencies must either hire this expertise or learn these skills through extensive training. If the conceptualization of a site is inadequate, costly mistakes are inevitable.

Characterization of a site requires a similar skill set as needed for conceptualization. It includes detailed knowledge of best practices for sampling procedures, time and costs needed to do adequate characterization, and how to incorporate data into a site model that addresses fluxes and reservoirs of contaminant substances. Water analyses should be “reasonably” complete with major ions, trace elements, redox species, and a few relevant isotopes. Seasonal trends and storm event trends should be sampled to determine how precipitation events and change of seasons affect aqueous contaminant mobility.

Modeling is often a guessing activity full of assumptions and misconceptions that become clearer and improved through hypothesis testing and further data collection. Model types, their inherent assumptions, their limitations, and the codes used to implement the models should all be transparent to the stakeholders. Sometimes nothing beyond a conceptual model is needed for a site, and sometimes a site can be so complex that different models should be developed, and the experts should discuss dissimilar conclusions and plot a path forward that resolves controversial concerns. A complex model that has never been tested is an experiment that could fail.

The most important skill set is a solid knowledge of natural and man-made water contaminants and their reactions with minerals and waste materials. Equally important, an expert should be humble enough to recognize that these sites are very complex and can perplex even the best experts, requiring a cautious iterative approach to find the most cost-efficient remediation. Because these guidelines have not often been followed, or have been intentionally avoided, treatment and remediation have not achieved the success they should have. Remediation is more of an experiment than a text book case. Hence, research is needed and contingency plans organized accordingly. Scientists and engineers working together have a higher probability of success than when they work separately.

title: Characterizing Local Marine Redox Conditions Through The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event From A Deep Water Facies Of Western Laurentia

authors: Hammen, Natalie S. [1], Adiatma, Yoseph Datu [2], Goldman, Daniel [3], Leslie, Stephen A. [4], Reid, Rachel E B [5], Gill, Benjamin Charles [6], Owens, Jeremy D. [7], Young, Seth A. [8]

abstract:
The Ordovician Period (487–443Ma) marks a significant interval in Earth history that was characterized by great ecological, environmental, and climatic changes. The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE) represents a series of global shifts within marine ecosystems, including significant increases in biodiversity and ecosystem complexity. Coeval changes in the climate and marine ecosystem imply that changing paleo-environmental conditions likely played a role in driving the biodiversification event. An increase in atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels is hypothesized to be one of the main drivers of these changes. Therefore, gaining a better understanding of changing Ordovician marine water column conditions, particularly during the GOBE interval, can potentially provide new insights into how environmental factors may have facilitated this major shift in the marine biosphere.

To further understand the role oxygenation played in the GOBE, detailed studies that characterize marine bottom water conditions at different paleogeographic localities that exhibit various lithologies are needed. Notably, little work has focused on characterizing marine redox conditions in deeper water environments during this interval. In this study, multiple paleoredox proxies are used to investigate local, and potentially global, marine redox conditions in the Early through Late Ordovician (Floain–Sandbian stages) from organic-rich shales of the Phi Kappa Formation at the Little Fall Creek and Trail Creek Road sections in central Idaho, USA. Specifically, we utilize the iron speciation proxy to identify anoxic and euxinic bottom water conditions. Additionally, a suite of trace metal concentrations (Mn, U, V, and Mo) will be used to assess the local redox conditions, particularly early anoxic to sulfidic conditions. These geochemical data will help provide new insights into the marine redox conditions from continental slope/basinal settings of the western Laurentian margin in the Panthalassic ocean during this important interval of Earth history.

abstract: Round Top Laccolith of the Sierra Blanca Peaks in West Texas, is one of the few recognized HREE resource prospects for US critical mineral production. Vapor-phase crystallization, well examined along grain boundaries through the laccolith’s F-rich rhyolite textures, produced disseminated REE-fluoride mineralization. Round Top is just one of a 5-laccolith complex, and although a common magmatic event (~35-36Ma) is attributed to the similarities in rhyolite textures, existing geochemical data indicate that each of the laccolith peaks have their own petrogenetic evolution. Whether vapor-phase crystallization produced the same, a diminished, or fundamentally different REE mineral assemblage among the other laccoliths, however, remains unresolved. Zircon studies have shown mineral overgrowth textures indicative of vapor phase alteration at Triple Hill, confirming hydrothermal alteration is not restricted to Round Top. Sierra Blanca and Triple Hill zircons were found to carry much higher Y contents than Round Top’s, a primary compositional clue that either source magma or early REE enrichment processes differ from peak to peak. Comparisons to the isotopic work tracing Round Top’s magma source to a Precambrian crustal basement rock raises questions regarding the other peaks' petrogenetic history. Petrographic and mineral-chemical (SEM/EPMA) analysis of samples from Little Blanca and Little Round Top identify and compare REE-mineral assemblages, textures, and abundances to Round Top mineral assemblages. A common enrichment process extends Round Top’s economic model across the complex rather than a uniquely anomalous singular deposit in the region - a distinction critical for future exploration.

title: The Postcranial Osteology, Phylogenetic Relationships, and Musculature of Desmatosuchus smalli (Pseudosuchia, Aetosauria) from the Upper Triassic (Norian) Cooper Canyon Formation of western Texas
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns

affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas, USA
abstract: Desmatosuchus smalli is a Late Triassic aetosaur from the Cooper Canyon Formation in the Dockum Group in West Texas. The holotype (TTU-P 9024) for D. smalli is from the Post Quarry located in southern Garza County, Texas. The holotype has been previously described in prior works but the postcrania has not been given a full and thorough description. Additionally, new elements from both the holotype and other collection specimens are described including the atlas, axis, cervical, dorsal, sacral, and caudal vertebrae, chevrons, ribs, interclavicle, radius, tibia, pes, and osteoderms. Although D. smalli is very similar to its sister taxa D. spurensis , there are notable postcranial differences that separate D. smalli from D. spurensis. These include: (1) the possible presence of a ventral keel in the cervical vertebrae, (2) raised cross-hatching ornamentation, (3) the elongate and slender dorsal eminence (spike) on the pectoral lateral plates, (4) a more developed pyramidal dorsal eminence in the anterior dorsal lateral plates, (5) the dorsal eminences of the middle and posterior dorsal lateral plates are ventrally recurved, (6) the dorsal paramedians becoming more sigmoidal posteriorly with the lateral side flexing dorsally, and (7) a more conical, recurved spikey dorsal eminence in the posterior dorsal and caudal lateral plates. Because D. smalli is part of the pseudosuchian (crocodilian) lineage of archosaurs, the musculature of modern crocodilians can be compared to the muscle scars found on the fossils. The musculature structures on the pectoral and forelimb bones align with the characteristics of scratch-digging animals suggesting that D. smalli (and possibly other aetosaurs) was a scratch-digging animal. Lastly, by updating the phylogenetic characters of D. smalli in the most recent aetosaur character matrix, the phylogenetic position of D. smalli and relation to other aetosaurs is solidified.

title: Co‐evolution of early Earth environments and microbial life: Extrapolating lessons learned up and down the time scale and to distant worlds
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)
authors: Lyons, Timothy W. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, CA, USA
abstract: My journey in studies of ancient Earth and distant planets began with a dissertation deep dive into the anoxic modern Black Sea. My first significant step back in time logically landed in the Devonian for many reasons, including the importance of oceanic redox extremes and evolution at that time. Any successes in these efforts are connected by a straight line to a wonderful collaboration with Brad Sageman and our colleague Dave Hollander. This was a special, formative time for me, elevated in many ways by a life-long friendship with Brad. He has taught me much about how to best integrate geochemistry within comprehensive studies of Earth's past and specifically the need for the full geologic context, and this boost led me naturally to complementary questions about the earliest chapters of Earth's coevolving life and environments. Two records of Earth history capture this evolution of life and its co-evolving ecosystems with interpretable fidelity: the geobiological and geochemical traces preserved in rocks and the evolutionary histories captured within genomes. The earliest vestiges of life are recognized mostly in isotopic fingerprints of specific microbial metabolisms, whereas fossils and organic biomarkers become important later. Molecular biology provides lineages that can be overlayed on geologic and geochemical records of evolving life. All these data lie within a framework of biospheric evolution that is primarily characterized by the transition from an oxygen-poor to an oxygen-rich world. In this review presentation, I will explore the history of microbial life on Earth and the degree to which it shaped, and was shaped by, fundamental transitions in the chemical properties of the oceans, continents and atmosphere. I will examine the diversity and evolution of early metabolic processes, their couplings with biogeochemical cycles and their links to the oxygenation of the early biosphere. I will discuss the distinction between the beginnings of metabolisms and their subsequent proliferation and their capacity to shape surface environments on a planetary scale. The evolution of microbial life and its ecological impacts directly mirror the Earth’s chemical and physical evolution through cause-and-effect relationships. And all of this will build from the foundation of those earlier studies with Brad and the vital lessons learned.

title: Leveraging 3D x-ray tomography to explore rock fracture evolution and thermal stress memory in extreme climates, Beacon Valley Antarctica
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution (Posters)
authors: Eppes, Martha Cary [1], Draebing, Daniel [2], Lamp, Jennifer [3], Schröer, Laurenz [4], Winardhi, Chandra [5], Swanger, Kate [6], Dahlquist, Maxwell P. [7], Rinehart, Alex [8], Cnudde, Veerle [9], Ackroyd, Bradley [10]

abstract:
Rock cracking is a key mechanism contributing to Critical Zone architecture. It breaks down rocks at the surface of Earth and other planets, allowing wind and water to ‘move mountains’. Yet we know extraordinarily little about how cracking evolves over the geologic timescales in which a Critical Zone operates. Stress memory in rocks is a well-documented phenomenon whereby fracture damage imparted by previous stress does not progress until stresses exceed prior maximums. However, such memory remains underexplored in the context of low-magnitude, environmental thermal stresses, key drivers of rock breakdown globally. Here, to document the evolution of both overall crack growth, and stress-memory related rock cracking response to environmental stresses under extreme cold conditions, we examined 5 rock samples collected in Beacon Valley Antarctica of the same Ferrar Dolerite, but that were exposed over durations ranging from 80,000 to 1.9 million years (10Be exposure ages).

Prior work revealed fractures in these rocks to be too few and small for normal microscopy – presumably due to the extreme arid cold conditions of Antarctica. So, using the TESCAN CoreTOM scanner, we collected 8 µm resolution 3D x-ray scans of three 7 mm diameter cores from each rock preserving the natural top surface. We collected a 2nd higher resolution (3.5 µm) scan of the sample we identified as the crackiest (highest number and lengths of visible cracks). We then subjected all cores to 10 heat treatment cycles from 10°C to 50°C – replicating maximum temperature range and absolute temperatures presumed in the Antarctic environment – and rescanned. Overall, preliminary analyses suggest that all cores are generally characterized by prominent, ~2-5 mm long surface-parallel cracks within ~2 mm of the natural surface, and by diffuse ~30-300 µm cracks throughout the cores that also appear dominantly surface-parallel. The youngest sample has notably fewer of the near-surface parallel cracks, and appears to have cracked the most during heating, producing more diffuse cracks. The oldest sample has notably more diffuse cracks, with little visible change overall. We infer decreasing cracking rates over time, attributable at least in part to increasing environmental stress memory. These results have implications for understanding the rates and processes of any fracture-related phenomena operating in the Critical Zone.

authors: Nikolic, Mark C. [1], Spicer, Jake [2], Teamey, Paige [3], Payne, Jonathan L. [4]

abstract: Stanford Young Investigators (SYI) is an eight-week long summer internship program that provides an authentic research experience for high schoolers from around the Bay Area in different labs at Stanford University. I lead the ‘History of Life and Biodiversity’ (HOLB) group within SYI, which comprises 16 interns and focuses on paleobiology and Earth history and combines experiential learning with genuine, collaborative research. Prior to this summer’s program, I conducted fieldwork in the House Range of Utah, where I surveyed several sites for fossils visible on the surface and within in situ rocks. Of course, taking 16 high school students to such remote field localities would be extremely resource intensive, carries many safety risks, and is inaccessible for many. So, I also collected bulk disaggregated rock and sediment from trailing piles of previous trilobite excavation efforts from each site and sent them back to the lab. Thus, I brought the field to them. The interns were given the boxes of material and devised projects with it in groups as if they were in the field themselves. They first developed methods for sifting, sorting and working through the sediments to find even the smallest of trilobite fossils (~0.5mm). This got them familiar with different tools and methods for collecting paleontological material in both the field and lab, including sieves, microscopes, etc. In total, they found >1000 trilobite and agnostid fossils from which they collected linear morphometric data both with calipers and digitally. With their dataset and the knowledge they had gained through interactive lessons, they tested different aspects of collection biases on size and their impact on paleobiological interpretations. Within the program period, they obtained a hands-on ‘field’ experience, conducted genuine research, and produced novel, quality, publishable results. This group program demonstrates the strength and further potential of this kind of in-lab, hands-on, ‘simulated fieldwork’ project as both a learning experience and to produce novel and publishable data all while increasing accessibility to the paleo/geosciences.

title: Geoscience Implications of Border Infrastructure Development in the Big Bend Region of Texas
session_title: International Collaborations in the Geosciences: Celebrating Science Without Borders
authors: Urbanczyk, Kevin Mark [1]
affiliations: (1) Sul Ross State University, Meadows Research Institute for West Texas Water, Alpine, Texas, USA
abstract:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), through U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), has initiated a large border infrastructure program in the Big Bend region of Texas. The proposed projects, located within the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector between Fort Quitman and Amistad Reservoir, include a combination of approximately 30-foot steel bollard barriers, low-profile vehicle barriers, and extensive patrol roads integrated with surveillance technology. Multiple multi-billion-dollar federal contracts have been awarded or announced for border infrastructure projects distributed across five segments of the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector.

The program area encompasses some of the most ecologically significant and least-developed landscapes in the United States, including Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River. Proposed construction includes hundreds of miles of new and improved patrol roads through previously roadless terrain, including Mariscal Mountain in Big Bend National Park and the Lower Canyons of the Rio Grande.

The implications of this infrastructure extend well beyond the physical footprint of the barriers. Potential impacts include fragmentation of wildlife movement corridors used by wide-ranging species such as American black bear ( Ursus americanus ) and desert bighorn sheep ( Ovis canadensis nelsoni ), increased erosion and sediment delivery to the Rio Grande, alteration of surface-water and groundwater processes, degradation of habitat for federally listed species including the Texas hornshell ( Popenaias popeii ), consumption of limited groundwater resources, and changes to the wilderness character and recreation-based economy of the Big Bend region. Construction also has the potential to affect internationally significant cultural landscapes, including archaeological sites and prehistoric rock art of the Big Bend and Lower Pecos regions, where extensive cultural resources occur within or adjacent to proposed infrastructure corridors. The long-term resilience of border infrastructure to extreme flood events within the steep, highly dynamic canyons of the Rio Grande also remains an important engineering and environmental question.

Many of these projects are proceeding under statutory authorities that waive compliance with numerous federal environmental laws, limiting the environmental review process. However, the region already supports extensive long-term monitoring of hydrology, ground water, water quality, and ecological resources, providing a unique opportunity to quantify environmental change before, during, and after construction.

abstract: The largest federally recognized Native American Tribe in the United States, the Navajo Nation, has an area of over 27,000 square miles. One of the biggest present-day problems faced by the Navajo people is access to clean and safe water resources. More than 30% of the Navajo homes lack access to safe and drinkable water, and people need to haul water on a regular basis. This study assessed community needs for water usage (drinking/household chores/gardening/livestock management). Survey results showed that although over 88% of the respondents use bottled water for drinking, over 44% of the respondents use water hauled from unregulated sources for livestock management. It was also found that over 58% of the respondents used the same barrels to haul water from both regulated and unregulated sources. Livestock in the Navajo Nation mainly rely on windmill-pumped groundwater in which naturally elevated arsenic, uranium, and other heavy metals pose a serious threat to the animals’ well-being. The possibility of bioaccumulated heavy metals in animal meat and dairy products is an additional risk to human health. This study identified the need to establish community-level water filtration systems to reduce heavy metal exposure risks from crops, animal meat, and dairy products produced and managed by using unregulated groundwater sources. Our research group initiated the Navajo Technical University- New Mexico Tech- Navajo Nation Water Purification Project (N 4 WPP), a comprehensive collaboration focusing on research, education, outreach, and workforce development among university and industry partners, with numerous smaller partnerships on specific aspects of the project. Since its inception, this project started trust-building exercises with local Navajo communities, tribal government, tribal agencies, Navajo chapter houses, and state and federal agencies. This project revolves around a common Navajo philosophy: Tó éí ííná (water is life). The first successful deployment of a 500-gallon-per-day, community-level, water filtration system took place in the Becenti Chapter located in the eastern Navajo agency in northwestern New Mexico. The filtration system uses cross-linked polyvinylidene fluoride (CPVDF) hollow-fiber membranes that can effectively remove salt, nutrients like nitrates and phosphates, metals and other inorganic constituents from the contaminated groundwater. The treated water from this system initially will be available to community members for livestock management, irrigation, and other non-consumptive uses, and eventually developed for drinking purposes.

authors: Price, Madeline [1], Rosscoe, Steven J [2]
