abstract: North-Central Texas was characterized by a westward-prograding delta complex during the Pennsylvanian Period. The East Mountain Shale is a primarily marine shale deposited along the offshore margins of the delta. Geochemical measurements and observations of lithology were used to correlate two outcrops of the East Mountain Shale. The EM180-2 outcrop is approximately six meters thicker than the EM180-1 outcrop despite only being separated by a two-lane highway. To determine if the shortening at EM180-1 was the result of a slower depositional rate or of erosional loss, geochemical profiles were generated throughout the sections. Data was collected at 10-centimeter intervals using a Gamma Surveyor II handheld gamma ray spectrometer and a KT-20 handheld magnetic susceptibility meter. A third section (EM180-3) situated between the primary two sections was later added to the study to develop stronger correlation using both a lower sandstone marker bed and an upper calcareous shale marker bed known as the Bath Bend Bed. At EM180-1 potassium (K), uranium (U), and thorium (Th) concentrations generally increase upward. The lowest readings were from the sandstone marker bed, and the highest readings were from the shale just above the Bath Bend Bed. The Bath Bend Bed stands out due to a sharp decrease in K, U, and Th. These trends are also observed in the other two sections. EM180-1 shows relatively stable magnetic susceptibility with the only notable increase occurring into and above the Bath Bend Bed. The Bath Bend Bed showed similarly high readings at the other two outcrops. The data suggest that all three outcrops experienced similar depositional rates. The sandstone is equally thick between EM180-1 and EM180-2, and the Bath Bend Bed is equally thick between EM180-1 and EM180-3. Geochemical events were also equivalent in size and spacing between outcrops. The thick upper shale at EM180-2 is not preserved in the shorter outcrops, indicating missing material. This supports the interpretation of an erosional event prior to the deposition of the overlying Lake Pinto Sandstone.

abstract:
To unravel the details of Earth’s fascinating history, it is essential to place the array of regional geology and the evolution of the multitudes of different types of life onto a common geologic time scale. For over a decade, our teams have been compiling and standardizing lexicons of the thousands of named geological formations of our planet into online databases ( GeoLex.org ) and migrating the Treatise of Invertebrate Paleontology into online public databases. The GeoLex suite currently includes most of Asia-Africa (nearly 10,000 formations) and is interlinked with the MacroStrat database ( macrostrat.org ) for North America (also over 10,000 geologic formations). The graphic-interfaces for the Lexicon include regional maps and generalized lithostratigraphic columns. Following the lead of Macrostrat's ROCKD app, this project is in partnership with UNESCO's Commission for the Geologic Map of the World and other geological surveys to enable direct linking of online geologic maps to details on the associated geologic formations and their former paleogeographic setting.

The extraction and systematic populating of the Treatise database from the ca. 30,000 pages of its 50 published volumes was only possible by developing specialized AI agents. The completed Treatise database encompasses approximately 35,000 genera with their images of all major invertebrate groups and select vertebrate groups through the Phanerozoic, and is temporarily hosted at Treatise.GeoLex.org before moving to its permanent home at the Paleontological Institute, Univ. Kansas. The user-generated diversity curves can be exported to the online TimeScale Creator visualization system ( tsconline.timescalecreator.org ) to view against other aspects of Earth history. The genera in the "fossil" field of Lexicon entries are auto-linked to their entries and images in the online Treatise .

Each of these projects required standardizing the use of regional stages to the international geologic timescale. The current age model is GTS2020, but the database system enables rapid updating to future age models.

This open-access suite of lithostratigraphic and paleontological databases on a common timescale will enable improved paleogeographic maps of the Earth’s surface, the investigation of diversity curves for different fossil phyla and classes, and is a valuable resource for AI applications.

This project is a contribution to the OneEarth project of the Deep-time Digital Earth and to the IUGS International Commission on Stratigraphy.

title: Mafic Magma Intraplating of Metasediments in Lower Continental Crust
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust
authors: Dumond, Gregory [1], Williams, Michael L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
abstract: Recent attempts to constrain the bulk composition of lower continental crust via seismic receiver function analysis and geochemical modeling support one prevailing view that the deep crust is predominantly mafic. However, several observations from granulite terranes and limited xenolith data support the hypothesis that significant volumes of lower continental crust may involve felsic material originally deposited at the surface. This contradiction is reconciled using field relationships and data from one of Earth’s largest lower crustal granulite terranes combined with phase equilibria modeling to demonstrate that intraplating of mantle-derived mafic magmas into felsic metasedimentary gneisses produces deep crustal seismic observables at cratonic and Cordilleran Moho conditions. Intraplating of mantle-derived magmas and partial melting of supracrustal rocks residing in the deep enhances differentiation of continental crust and produces significant variability in composition, structure, and lower crustal seismic velocity and density. This heterogeneity is largely masked by the low spatial resolution of seismic observations and leads to underestimation of the volume of felsic lower continental crust. The presence of voluminous supracrustal rocks residing in the deep continental crust implies that weathering, erosion, and tectonic stirring of the upper crust into the lower crust are critical processes for redistributing crustal heat production. Mafic magma intraplating of these supracrustal rocks facilitates significant crustal differentiation that can yield an andesitic lower crustal bulk composition.

title: Microbes in Groundwater, Kewaunee County, Wisconsin: An Example of Academic Match-making
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Muldoon, Maureen A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Wisconsin Geological & Natural History Survey, Madison, WI,
abstract:
The fractured Silurian dolomite aquifer is an important, but vulnerable, source of water supply in rural northeastern Wisconsin. In areas where soils are thin, there is a history of long-term water-quality problems with elevated nitrate, bacteria levels, and instances of non-potable "brown water" impacting domestic wells. Sporadic outbreaks of water-borne disease have focused attention on the presence of enteric pathogens in the aquifer. As resource managers tried to address these water-quality problems, there was no consensus as to whether the main source of fecal contamination was human or bovine waste. A resource collaboration between microbiologists and hydrogeologists, facilitated by Randy Hunt, brought together “the best science available” to address this issue. Collaboration with the United States Geological Survey (USGS) also brought state-of-the art monitoring resources to the project.

The Kewaunee County Groundwater project had three main objectives: 1) evaluate the extent of contamination in the county, 2) determine the source of the pathogens, and 3) determine the timing of peak transport for viruses and indicator bacteria. We completed county-wide randomized sampling of over 600 private wells stratified by depth-to-bedrock. One sampling round was conducted during recharge conditions and one during non-recharge conditions. Over 208 wells were positive for total coliform , E. coli , or NO 3 -N over 10 mg/l. We then sampled from the wells with water-quality concerns to determine the source of pathogens. Five rounds of samples, at approximately quarterly intervals, were tested for human-specific microbes, bovine-specific microbes and non-specific pathogens using qPCR. The results were that both human and bovine wastewater were a source of well contamination and that the timing and source of contamination varied with groundwater recharge and dates of manure application.

This research helped elucidate the extent and sources of contamination (human vs. bovine) and highlighted human health concerns ultimately lead to a change in the state code that governs manure applications in areas underlain by the Silurian dolomite aquifer. Those changes, which call for reduced manure applications where the depth to rock is less than 20 feet, highlighted the need for better depth to bedrock maps. A second collaboration between the Wisconsin Geological and Natural History Survey (WGNHS) and the USGS (also facilitated by Randy) received considerable funding to create better depth-to-bedrock maps for the region using airborne electromagnetic mapping data.

title: Re-evaluating the Role of Strike-Slip Versus Normal-Slip Faulting Between the Carolina and Falls Lake Terranes in the Eastern Piedmont of North Carolina
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Sims-Clark, Abaigeal Rena [1], Fishel, Emma Rose [2], Kleman, Jacob William [3], Blake, David E. [4], LaMaskin, Todd A. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
(2) Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
(3) Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
(4) Earth and Ocean Science, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
(5) Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
abstract:
In the North Carolina eastern Piedmont, understanding the kinematics of a major fault zone that separates the suprastructural, greenschist-facies easternmost Carolina terrane from the infrastructural, amphibolite-facies Falls Lake terrane is key to reconstructing the structural evolution of the region. This fault zone was previously considered to be a segment of the ductile dextral Nutbush Creek fault zone, a strand of the Eastern Piedmont fault system formed during late Paleozoic Alleghanian orogenesis. Prior mapping depicts planar fabric orientations compatible with regional strike-slip fault trends. However, linear fabric orientations are orthogonal to strike trends and down-dip plunges are inconsistent with strike-slip faulting.

To re-evaluate fault kinematics, we conducted eight traverses across the fault zone using traditional and digital mapping techniques and collected oriented rock samples and fabric element measurements. The easternmost Carolina terrane contains metamorphosed intermediate to felsic and locally ultramafic arc-related plutonic rocks. The Falls Lake terrane contains layered biotite muscovite ± garnet schist locally meta-ultramafic pods. We created a detailed geologic map and fabric element stereograms across the terrane boundary. The stereograms highlight a dip-slip mineral stretching lineation in west-dipping foliations. We then produced thin sections oriented parallel and perpendicular to lineation to identify mesoscale to microscale structures including planar S-C elements, porphyroclast and porphyroblast rotations, and lithologic and foliation offsets to determine slip sense. Kinematic indicators consistently display ductile normal slip in contrast to dextral slip along the Nutbush Creek fault both north and south of the study area. No evidence for strike-slip kinematics was observed. In addition, occurrences of bull quartz, silicified cataclasite, and epidosite reflect a late brittle overprint.

Based on our lithologic and structural analysis, fault strand slip is consistent with ductile-brittle normal faulting. This is similar to the nearby Jonesboro and Fishing Creek faults that define the eastern margin of the Deep River Triassic rift basin. We propose that the fault zone and terrane boundary in this study, previously considered part of the Nutbush Creek fault, be renamed the Upper Barton Creek normal fault and we suggest that it is associated with Paleozoic-Mesozoic rifting of Pangea as opposed to strike-slip faulting during Alleghanian orogenesis. The Falls Lake terrane may be an uplifted portion of the Carolina terrane in the footwall of the Upper Barton Creek fault due to crustal extension.

title: Teaching Individuals, Not Courses: Connecting Faculty Identity, Student Identity, and Belonging in Geoscience Education
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Part I)
authors: Shepherd, Stephanie L [1], Wahid Cotton, Bradlee [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
(2) Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL, USA
abstract:
Research on evidence-based instructional practices is fundamentally changing our approach to teaching in postsecondary geoscience education. While many of us embrace approaches such as active learning, transparent teaching, and inclusive course design, we often struggle with the successful implementation of new instructional strategies. It requires instructors to develop teaching approaches that are authentic to their own identity while intentionally creating learning environments where students feel seen, valued, and capable of belonging within the geosciences.

Two complementary case studies illustrate how identity and transparency can strengthen the implementation of research-based instructional practices. The first focuses on the Auburn University Summer STEM Institute (AUSSI), a faculty professional development program designed to help STEM instructors implement evidence-based teaching through backward course design, active learning, transparent teaching, and reflective practice. Rather than encouraging faculty to replicate a particular teaching style, AUSSI supports instructors in making intentional instructional decisions that align with the learning sciences, their disciplinary context, and their own teaching philosophy.

The second case study draws on ongoing research examining student identity in geoscience education and explores how students' sense of belonging, prior experiences, and perceptions of themselves as geoscientists influence engagement, persistence, and professional identity development. Together, these examples suggest that transparency—clearly communicating the purpose behind learning activities, assessments, and instructional decisions—helps connect faculty and students in the learning process, allowing evidence-based instructional practices to become more meaningful and effective. These case studies highlight strategies that instructors can adapt within their own courses to create significant learning experiences and prepare the next generation of geoscience professionals.

title: Chemical weathering and biogeochemical cycling in the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias, Yosemite National Park, California
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution (Posters)
authors: Lukens, Claire [1], Lizarraga, Thalia Marisol [2], Ambrose, Anthony [3]
affiliations: (1) Life and Environmental Sciences, UC Merced, Merced, CA, USA
(2) Life and Environmental Sciences, University of California, Merced, Merced, California, USA
(3) Ancient Forest Society, South Lake Tahoe, California, USA
abstract:
Soil geochemistry plays an important role in soil health, integrating rock weathering, biogeochemical cycling, and inputs from dust or anthropogenic sources. Changes in geochemistry with depth reflect the interplay of these processes, and paint a picture of the nutrients available to terrestrial ecosystems. Here we present geochemical data from 11 soil depth profiles in the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoia trees (Sequoiadendron giganteum) in Yosemite National Park. Soils were collected within 10 m of large sequoia trees with a hand auger from depths ranging from 0 cm to 1.5 m. Samples were dried, ground, heat-treated, and analyzed for elemental geochemistry using a Bruker Tracer 5 portable XRF.

Through our analysis, we found that the bulk mass transfer coefficient (“tau”) averages -0.27 ± 0.03 and shows no significant correlation with soil depth, suggesting that the soil profiles are well-mixed to depths >1 m. Elemental tau calculations reveal a more complex story driven by elemental mobility, biological cycling, and atmospheric inputs. For instance, calcium is depleted overall relative to rock (tau = -0.9 to -0.7), but is less depleted at soil depths <50cm. In contrast, P is enriched relative to bedrock and becomes more enriched closer to the surface, likely reflecting more intense biogeochemical cycling in the top 50 cm. Our geochemical data can be used to disentangle the relative inputs of dust, rock weathering, and biological cycling of essential nutrients. We find that dust contributes small amounts of essential nutrients like P, but rapid biological cycling better explains P enrichment in topsoils. Combined with additional geophysical and atmospheric data, our geochemical observations could be used to assess the potential resilience of these giant trees to climate change, including increased drought and changing dust deposition patterns.

title: Bridging the Waterline: Multitemporal Sonar and Mobile Laser Mapping of Channel Change
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Part II)
authors: Alho, Petteri [1], Kasvi, Elina [2], Kankare, Ville [3], Blåfield, Linnea [4], Kaartinen, Harri [5], Kukko, Antero [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Geology, University of Turku, Turku, SW Finland,
(2) Department of Geography and Geology, University of Turku, Turku, SW Finland, Finland
(3) Department of Geography and Geology, University of Turku, Turku, SW Finalnd, Finland; Finnish Geospatial Research Institute, Espoo, Finland
(4) Department of Geography and Geology, University of Turku, Turku, Finland
(5) Finnish Geospatial Research Institute, Espoo, Finland
(6) Finnish Geospatial Research Institute, Espoo, Finland
abstract:
High-resolution change detection in gravel-bed rivers is commonly divided by the waterline: laser scanning captures exposed banks and bars, whereas sonar resolves the submerged channel. We present a multitemporal workflow integrating mobile laser scanning and multibeam sonar to map channel adjustment along a meandering reach of the Oulanka River in northeastern Finland. Repeat surveys were conducted during open-water periods and georeferenced within a common GNSS-based reference framework. Laser point clouds were classified to separate terrain and vegetation, sonar observations were filtered and corrected for vessel motion and water-level variation, and the datasets were merged into seamless topobathymetric surfaces. Surface differencing was then used to identify erosion and deposition across the channel bed, point bars, banks, and the wet–dry boundary.

Preliminary comparisons reveal spatially coherent patterns of bed-level change that cannot be reconstructed from either sensor alone. Sonar resolves pool, riffle, and thalweg adjustments beneath the water surface, while mobile laser scanning captures bank retreat, bar-surface modification, and exposed sediment storage at finer local detail. The combined approach also exposes important uncertainty sources, including variable point density, acoustic shadowing, vegetation, changing water levels, platform trajectory, and cross-sensor registration. These effects must be incorporated into spatially variable levels of detection before sediment budgets are interpreted.

The Oulanka case demonstrates how repeated, complementary close-range surveys can provide continuous wet–dry observations of gravel-bed river morphodynamics. The workflow supports event-scale change detection, sediment-budget analysis, and evaluation of how floods and seasonal flow variability reorganize channel morphology.

title: 3D Geological Modeling for Assessment of Potential Hydrogen Geostorage, Anadarko Basin, Oklahoma, USA

authors: Smith, Cordelia D [1], Milad, Benmadi [2], Hayman, Nick [3], McGlannan, Austin J [4], Huerta, Nicolas [5], Baek, Seunghwan [6], Aldana, Ivan [7], Kwan, May [8], McDonald, Zane [9]

abstract:
The DISSPATCH H2 project assessed the feasibility of using underground depleted oil and gas reservoirs in the Anadarko Basin to store H 2 gas. The Bromide Formation of the Simpson group was identified as a target for H 2 storage based on high porosity and permeability values and historical oil and gas production in the eastern Anadarko Basin. A 3D geologic model was created for the Simpson Group, integrating data from core measurements, well logs, and previous studies.

The Anadarko Basin is structurally complex, requiring a model reflecting the structural variability. The Woodford and Sylvan shales seal the reservoirs in the study area. Formation tops for the Woodford through the Simpson Group were interpreted from well logs and used as the basis for gridded formation surfaces, providing the foundation for the structural model.

Three cores spanning several formations in the Simpson Group were described and sampled. Core plugs from the samples were used to run porosity and permeability measurements and used to calibrate calculated Petrophysical logs for porosity and permeability. Sequential Gaussian Simulation was used to create petrophysical volumes mapping the spatial variability of porosity and permeability.

The model showed that porosity and permeability in the Simpson Group vary substantially across the structurally complex Anadarko Basin and within individual formations. A township-sized section of the model was extracted to conduct multiple simulation scenarios evaluating H 2 gas behavior in the reservoir, which indicated high sensitivity to changes in porosity and permeability with gas migrating along high permeability pathways. Areas of high porosity and permeability within the Bromide Formation of the Simpson group appear to be potential candidates for subsurface hydrogen storage.

title: Modern Analogs for Ancient Provenance: Insights from Quaternary Sierra-to-Sea Sediment Routing and Provenance Signal Propagation
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Malkowski, Matt [1], Sickmann, Zach [2], Choudhry, Rida [3], St.Peter, Jack Daniel [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(2) Marine Science Institute, University of Texas,
(3) Marine Science Institute, University of Texas,
(4) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
abstract: Provenance signatures in Quaternary sediments of California from the foothills of the Sierra Nevada through the Central Valley and into San Francisco Bay and the Pacific outer coast provide important insights into how we interpret the Mesozoic-to-present clastic record of western North America. We present recent and ongoing multi-method provenance analyses to illustrate at least two key points from this setting. First, and most foundational, is the persistent influence of the convergent-margin paleogeography that characterized the California margin for over 100 million years through to the Quaternary S2S system. Spatial patterns in surface geology inherited from this convergent margin phase act to both provide leverage in identifying key trends in sediment production and transport pathways, and to illustrate potential pitfalls in interpreting provenance data from ancient settings. As an example, provenance signals in the Sierra-to-sea system are not transmitted with uniform fidelity. Zircon-poor mafic and ultramafic source terranes are systematically underrepresented downstream relative to their true sediment contribution, meaning detrital zircon populations alone can misrepresent true catchment lithology and areal contribution in both modern and ancient systems. Moreover, batholith sources yield at least an order of magnitude more zircon than non-granitic sources. Second, the Sierra-to-Sea S2S system illustrates the role of glacial-interglacial climate cycles in provenance signal propagation. Climatically driven shifts in the locus of erosion in the Sierra Nevada, between the glacially eroded southern Sierra and precipitation-driven northern Sierra, generate distinct geochemical and detrital zircon age signatures that propagate from the mountains to the marine realm. However, the coupling of these regional climate-induced changes in source region erosion and global marine sea level cycles leads to spatial heterogeneity in where these detrital climate signatures are preserved. We highlight at least one sequence of proximal Sierran foothill fluvial terraces which shows clear alternating glacial-interglacial sediment compositions. Conversely, in the marine realm, highstand flooding of the San Francisco Bay embayment sequesters interglacial sediment in the estuary while glacial period detrital signatures transported to the marine realm during lowstands are more pervasive across outer coast and deep-marine sediments. Continued efforts to better characterize and differentiate between tectonic-, eustatic-, and climate-modulated multivariate provenance signals on timescales typically resolved in the rock record could be further leveraged for more accurate paleogeographic and paleoclimatic reconstructions of western North America.

title: AI for GeoDummies: Enhancing Geoscience Workflows with Accessible Artificial Intelligence(Special Session: Generative Artificial Intelligence)
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: House, Nancy J [1]
affiliations: (1) Littleton, CO, USA
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming geoscience, yet many practitioners struggle to leverage it effectively for daily technical tasks. This presentation demystifies AI by offering a practical guide for non-specialists seeking to harness these tools for skill development, communication enhancement, and research acceleration—without requiring advanced computational expertise.

Focusing on large language models (LLMs), we demonstrate how AI serves as an interactive tutor for complex topics like seismic interpretation, wave propagation, rock physics, and reservoir characterization. Attendees will learn to utilize AI for:

Learning & Synthesis: Explaining equations, summarizing technical papers, translating concepts into visuals (e.g., ray-path animations), and generating Python scripts for data analysis.

Productivity: Editing abstracts, proposals, and presentations (e.g., PowerPoint slides), alongside automating RFP documentation.

Research Support: Streamlining public-data searches, formatting production data, calculating unconventional reservoir type curves, and visualizing seismic attributes.

Practical case studies highlight emerging applications, including computer vision adaptations for seismic-volume interpretation—enabling fault detection, facies mapping, and stratigraphic pattern recognition via image-classification techniques.

Critically, we emphasize that AI is not a replacement for domain expertise. Tools may produce erroneous code, misleading interpretations, or "hallucinated" outputs if unchecked. Success hinges on:

Guarded Implementation: Using bounded questions, curated input data, and iterative prompting.

Expert Oversight: Mandating geoscientist validation for all AI-generated content.

Data Security: Avoiding exposure of proprietary/client data in public AI platforms.

The goal is to empower geoscientists to work faster and learn more efficiently while upholding scientific rigor. By integrating AI as a collaborative assistant—not an oracle—professionals can enhance innovation without compromising accountability for final interpretations. This talk bridges the gap between AI’s potential and its pragmatic, ethical deployment in geoscience.

title: Unraveling Regional Hydrogeology and Lithium Brine Origins Using Dissolved Noble Gases in Adjacent High Elevation Andean Salares
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers
authors: DeShong, Tyler [1], Boutt, David F. [2], Moran, Brendan J. [3], Dar, Tanveer Ali [4], Benson, Thomas R [5], Gibbons, Luis [6], Butler, Kristina [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, Ma, USA; Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, Syracuse University, Syracuse, NY, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, MA,

abstract:
South America’s “Lithium Triangle” contains numerous closed basin brine systems constituting approximately half of global lithium resources, including ~80% of global lithium brine. The adjacent Salares de Pozuelos and Pastos Grandes (Salta, Argentina) host comparable lithium brine concentrations despite their different evolutionary histories. Established lithium brine evolution characteristics cannot account for the Salar de Pozuelos resource magnitude. Physical water budgets, groundwater modeling, and solute mass balances have been used to demonstrate mismatches between a single catchment’s topographic and hydrologic watersheds, including in Pozuelos. Solute cycling from buried lacustrine systems is known to sustain dissolved ion concentrations, including lithium, for near-surface brines throughout the Lithium Triangle; but tracing brine evolution across closed basins, by invoking interbasin flow, has not yet been explicitly demonstrated.

Here we use dissolved noble gas (Ar, Kr, Xe, Ne, 4 He, 3 He) concentrations in the Pozuelos and Pastos Grandes aquifers to proxy recharge origins and groundwater residence times. Across both basins, we compare fresh and brine waters sampled from a range of depths to discern input pathways to the topographically and hydrologically downgradient Pozuelos deposit. Near-surface brines in both basins are relatively depleted in noble gases compared to inflow waters marginal to the salar nuclei, but are proportional to atmospheric concentrations, indicating a near-surface brine genesis. This is supported by ample crustal 4 He production and comparably low R/Ra values in both basins’ brines (< 0.2)—indicating, for Pozuelos brine, groundwater residence times much longer than known geochronologic constraints on salar evolution (~0.5 Ma).

Atmospheric equilibration of both basins’ inflow waters differ in their projected air saturated water envelopes despite having similar brine noble gas fingerprints, which is consistent with geochronologic indicators that Pastos Grandes brine began evolving ~2.5 Myr before Pozuelos brine. Pairing these results with a prior solute mass balance study in Pozuelos, which shows that modern solute fluxes from the topographic catchment cannot support the salar ’s lithium deposit over its known lifespan, this indicates that Pozuelos brine is partially disconnected from the topographic basin’s modern inflows, and is likely dependent on Pastos Grandes for brine evolution. We further use these results to build upon a global repository of dissolved noble gas data from closed basin lithium brines in Salar de Atacama, Chile, and Clayton Valley, Nevada.

title: A Novel Curvature-Based Approach to Assessing Grain Roundness from Low-Resolution Three-Dimensional Image Data
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology
authors: Yuan, Henry D. A. [1], Strauss, Justin V. [2], Pamukcu, Ayla [3], Meisenheimer, Doug [4], Mehra, Akshay [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(3) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
(4) Doerr School of Sustainability, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
(5) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
Grain roundness serves as a record of transport processes. Consequently, geologists have developed a variety of methods for measuring roundness, including both qualitative observations and quantitative metrics. In general, estimates of roundness derived from three-dimensional (3D) data, typically collected with X-ray Computed Tomography (CT), are preferable to observation-based and two-dimensional (2D) methods because the former can be subjective and the latter are subject to substantial measurement errors. However, even 3D roundness metrics become unreliable for small grains imaged at standard resolutions (e.g., grains <200 microns long imaged at 3 microns/voxel), which result in relatively low per-grain resolution (i.e., the average grain is represented by fewer voxels). In such cases, roundness metrics often exhibit significant dependence on grain size, leading to potentially biased measurements that make it difficult to compare roundness values across different grains. Therefore, new 3D roundness metrics are necessary for extracting accurate paleoenvironmental information from the shapes of small grains.

Detrital zircons (DZ) are one kind of sedimentary grain that exemplify this challenge. Researchers often use DZ for geochronometry, and the distribution of their radiometric ages can help determine sediment provenance. In cases where DZ provenance analyses provide evidence for continental-scale transport, grain roundness can encode the mode of transport, as aeolian transport rounds grains much more quickly than fluvial transport. However, accurately measuring the roundness of detrital zircons is challenging because of their microscopic size–usually tens to hundreds of microns long.

Here, we define two new 3D roundness metrics based on a grain's surface curvature. We test our new metrics on synthetic DZ grains and real DZ samples, comparing the performance of our methods to existing metrics. We show that, compared to other approaches, one of our metrics more reliably quantifies roundness for triangular mesh resolutions less than 5,000 vertices, while the other offers a resolution-invariant method of measuring roundness. These metrics will allow us to generate accurate detrital zircon roundness data, which will facilitate efforts to reconstruct past sediment transport networks with these grains. We further anticipate these new metrics will be useful for a variety of applications in the broader Earth sciences and engineering disciplines.

title: A Preliminary Assessment of Diatom Assemblages in a Wetland Soil, East Texas, USA
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science (Posters)
authors: Rectenwald, Sarah Gabrielle [1], Rashall, Jenny Gabrielle [2]
affiliations: (1) Nacogdoches, TX, USA
(2) Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
abstract: Wetland soils support complex biogeochemical processes that collectively influence nutrient cycling and overall ecosystem productivity. Microbial phototrophs such as diatoms contribute substantially to these processes. Despite extensive study of aquatic diatoms and their use as indicators of environmental change, soil-dwelling diatom communities remain comparatively understudied. This study aims to investigate contemporary soil diatom assemblages within a palustrine wetland in East Texas, USA, and to evaluate their relationships with physicochemical soil properties. Thirty sampling locations were established along five transects within a 108-acre palustrine wetland in Angelina County, Texas. Vegetative cover was sampled in fixed-radius plots at each sampling location. Soil samples were collected at each sampling location, and electrical conductivity and pH of each soil sample were measured in-situ prior to collection. Field indicators of wetland soil and hydrology were also recorded at each sampling location. In the laboratory setting, samples were processed using hydrogen peroxide and hydrochloric acid to remove organic and carbonate material, respectively, to isolate diatoms for microscopy. Preliminary analysis of diatom assemblages living in the sampled soils revealed species of the genera Eunotia, Pinnularia, and Ulnaria. Following complete characterization of diatom assemblages, statistical analysis will be used to identify the presence or absence of significant statistical relationships between observed taxa and soil physicochemical characteristics. Findings from this research will advance understanding of an understudied component of the wetland soil microbiome and assess its potential relevance for environmental monitoring.

title: Late Cretaceous (Campanian and Maastrichtian) Hoploscaphites in the Western Interior of North America
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Landman, Neil H. [1], LeMone, Peggy [2], Gilman, Peter [3]
affiliations: (1) American Museum of Natural History, New York, NY, USA
(2) 2048 Balsam Drive, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(3) 2048 Balsam Drive, Boulder, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Approximately 45 species of Hoploscaphites inhabited the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) during the Campanian and Maastrichtian (Landman, 2026). The degree of endemism of Hoploscaphites changed over the course of time from the middle Campanian to the end of the Maastrichtian. Hoploscaphites appeared in the WIS in the lower middle Campanian Baculites obtusus Zone. For most of the Campanian, the species of Hoploscaphites represented a mixture of endemic forms such as H . gilli and more broadly distributed forms such as H . ikorfatensis and H . praequadrispinosus , defining a broad Euroamerican Biogeographic Province. However, in the upper Campanian B . eliasi Zone (corresponding to the late Campanian Event), a new clade of Hoploscaphites appeared in the WIS, characterized by more closely coiled forms with shorter shafts and more abbreviated hooks (e.g., H . plenus ). In the rest of the Campanian and throughout the Maastrichtian, the species of Hoploscaphites in the WIS are endemic, although they closely resemble forms in the Boreal Chalk Facies of Europe. These species show trends toward increased tuberculation and more compressed whorl sections, possibly in response to a change in the environment of the WIS toward more nearshore settings and an increase in the number and kinds of predators.

title: Late Middle Devonian Rise of the Ozark Dome Created Restriction of the Midcontinent Seaway
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Kadel, Jana [1], Paton, Timothy Robert [2], Athanasopoulos, Nina [3], Emsbo, Poul [4], Malone, David H. [5], McLaughlin, Patrick I. [6]
affiliations: (1) Geography Geology and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(2) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL,
(3) Earth Science and Environmental Change, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana-Champaign, Illinois, USA
(4) US Geological Survey, Federal Center MS973, Denver, CO,
(5) Illinois State University, Normal, IL,
(6) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL,
abstract:
Upper Devonian to lower Mississippian black shales of the U.S. midcontinent contain elevated levels of critical minerals. While many metalliferous black shales in the sedimentary record are associated with discrete (<1 m.y.) oceanic anoxic events, the Upper Devonian New Albany-Chattanooga interval in the southern midcontinent spans >20 m.y. The source of this prolonged shallow to deep marine anoxia is debated but may primarily be a result of restricted exchange with the open ocean imposed by uplift of the Ozark Dome from far-field forces of the Acadian orogeny.

To test the “Ozark barrier” hypothesis, a transect of sections were studied in western Tennessee. The Hardin Sandstone and overlying Chattanooga Shale were sampled at 30 cm resolution in three sections from the Alabama to Kentucky borders. In the lab, cleaned and trimmed samples were described and analyzed using portable X-ray fluorescence. Results were plotted in cross sections with existing data. Two samples of the Hardin Sandstone were crushed, panned, and heavy liquid separated. Zircon grains were mounted and polished in epoxy pucks and analyzed with LA-ICP-MS at the Arizona Laserchron Center. Geochronologic results were converted to probability-density plots to evaluate sediment provenance.

The new Tennessee data, together with nearby subsurface data sets, demonstrate that uplift of the Ozark Dome during the Middle Devonian extended across the area of the Reelfoot embayment, closing the long-lived deep-water connection between the midcontinent seaway and the open ocean. Chronostratigraphic correlation and isopach maps of the Hardin Sandstone indicate formation of an incised valley following blockage of the embayment. Although reworked Middle Ordovician sandstones of the Ozark Dome dominate much of the midcontinent, detrital zircon analysis of the Hardin sandstone indicates that the valley fill is sourced from the Appalachian margin. These patterns indicate a shallow marine passage persisted between the uplifted Ozark and Nashville domes providing restricted exchange of open ocean surface water with the midcontinent seaway that contributed to the spread of anoxia, chemical stratification, and accumulation of critical minerals.

title: New Landslide Inventory Mapping in the Southwestern San Juan Mountains, Colorado
session_title: Advances in Landslide Inventory Mapping and Landslide Hazard Assessment (Posters)
authors: Harvey, Jonathan [1]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Fort Lewis College, Durango, CO, USA
abstract:
The San Juan Mountains of southwest Colorado comprise a high-relief landscape underlain by heterogenous lithology and subject to deep glacial and fluvial incision. Slope instabilities are widespread. Recent landslide inventory mapping has documented a diverse assemblage of landslide types and revealed much more extensive landslide coverage than previously recognized. Although several more prominent landslides were identified in earlier 1:24,000 mapping efforts, the availability of high-resolution lidar coverage (2020) has enabled refinement of those deposit locations and recognition of hundreds of previously unmapped features. The first project deliverable of this new mapping effort is a landslide inventory map for La Plata County that will be shared with County officials and eventually integrated into the Colorado Geological survey’s statewide landslide inventory.

In this progress report I share representative case studies that illustrate the strong influence of lithology and geomorphic setting on landslide style and distribution, including rock avalanches sourced from glacially oversteepened limestone cliffs, rotational slumps developed within weak sedimentary units such as the Morrison Formation, translational slides along actively incising tributaries, and large block spreads affecting the hogbacks lining the San Juan uplift. This project highlights the value of lidar-based inventory mapping for providing insights into regional controls on landslide occurrence and associated hazards.

title: Groundwater Contributions to Streamflow in the Colorado River Headwaters as Estimated by Using Tritium
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions
authors: Bern, Carleton R. [1], Jurgens, Bryant C. [2], Ruckhaus, Manya [3]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) US Geological Survey , Water Resources Division, Sacramento, CA,
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract: Groundwater discharge sustains streamflow in many watersheds worldwide, but the resiliency of streamflow to periods of drought and aridification is poorly understood. Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen (half-life is 12.32 years) that can be useful for identifying groundwater contributions to streamflow. Precipitation that falls to the land surface may enter the groundwater system as recharge and can travel long distances at slower velocities before discharging to a stream as base flow. Thus, tritium concentrations in groundwater will be lower compared to precipitation and can contrast sharply with water arriving in streams from shorter distances at faster velocities (quickflow). By sampling during low-flow periods when groundwater discharge dominates streamflow, the age, or mean transit time, of base flow can be estimated. This study monitored tritium in precipitation and streamflow at sites across the headwaters of the Colorado River from 2021 to 2025. Ages of base flow ranged from 7 to 16 years across 11 sites, as estimated by lumped parameter modeling. Older base flow correlated with sites with lower runoff efficiency. Fractions of base flow were modeled using sampling data and extrapolated across the hydrograph to estimate groundwater contributions to streamflow across entire water years. During the 2021 drought year, the median groundwater contribution to streamflow was 82%. In contrast, that value was 58% during the more typical water year of 2023. Total groundwater contribution to streams increased in years with greater precipitation and runoff, reflecting how infiltration of snowmelt and precipitation push groundwater out of the subsurface to become streamflow. These results illustrate how tritium can improve understanding of groundwater contributions to streamflow. The approach could be a useful monitoring tool in other regions experiencing drought and aridification.

title: Conodont Biostratigraphy of Lower-Middle Devonian (Emsian-Middle Givetian) Grand Tower and Lingle Formations, Illinois Basin
session_title: Microfossil Con Queso – Conodont Questions of Importance –North American Pander Society Meeting
authors: Day, Jed [1], Gouwy, Sofie [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography, Geology & Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(2) Natural Resources Canada, Canadian Geological Survey, Calgary, Alberta, USA
abstract:
Lower-Middle Devonian carbonate platform strata in the central and southern Illinois Basin are included in the Bailey, Backbone-Clear Creek (undifferentiated), Grand Tower and Lingle formations, overlain by Middle-Upper Devonian shales of the Blocher Member of the New Albany Shale. This report outlines our results on the conodont biostratigraphy of the Grand Tower and Lingle formations penetrated by one six inch and two four-inch diameter cores housed at the Illinois State Geological Survey (ISGS). These are the ISGS White County, and Story and Brown cores. All were drilled in White County, southeastern Illinois and are housed at the ISGS core library in Champaign, Illinois. The Grand Tower and Lingle formations were sampled continuously in the White County core. Ninety-three samples were taken from the Lingle and Grand Tower sections available in ISGS Brown (54) and Story (39) cores. The Blocher Member of the New Albany was sampled at and above its contact with the Lingle in the Brown and Story Cores. All but one carbonate sample yielded conodonts, and samples from thin sandstones in the basal 1-2 m of Blocher Member (basal New Albany) did not yield conodonts.

The Dutch Creek Member of the Grand Tower spans part of the Emsian Stage (Lower Devonian) with a fauna dominated by Latericriodus ( L. nevadensis, L. alces, L. robustus ). The Lower-Middle Devonian boundary is identified in the upper Dutch Creek by the first appearance (FA) of P. partitus (= partitus Zone). The overlying Haunted House Member (=un-named upper member) of the Grand Tower is entirely Eifelian age. The Eifelian-Givetian boundary (=base hemiansatus Zone) is identified in the lower Lingle by the last appearance (LA) of Icriodus michiganus , immediately followed by the FA of I. arkonensis . The successive FAs of I. brevis and P. varcus identify the bases of the timorensis and varcus zones in the lower Lingle. The LA of I. obliquimarginatus succeeded by the FA of P. ansatus identify the ansatus Zone in the middle of the Lingle. Samples in the Brown and Story cores from the upper Lingle at and just below the contact with the Blocher Member contain abundant conodonts including I. brevis, I difficilis, L. l. latericrescens , and P. l. linguiformis gamma morphotype, P. varcus and P r. rhenanus . These indicate the upper Lingle and overlying Blocher are no older than ansatus Zone.

title: The IAP Global Geological Database, LithQuery, and PaleoMapper: Full Support from Geological Data Querying to Custom Map Generation
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: Havens, Emma [1], Du, Wen [2], Ling, Yingyi [3], Scotese, Christopher R. [4]
affiliations: (1) PALEOMAP Project, Evanston, IL,
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
(3) Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA

abstract:
The International Association of Paleogeographers (IAP) has assembled a standardized Global Geological Database (GGDB) consisting of >2 million geological records spread across >300,000 geographical localities spanning the Phanerozoic and Neoproterozoic. Each database record describes the latitude and longitude, formation name, age, lithology, environment of deposition, reliability, and data source of each geological sample. In order to analyze and visualize these geological records, the IAP has developed a set of software tools written in Python to filter and plot these data on plate tectonic, paleogeographic, and paleoclimatic reconstructions. The programs are designed to be intuitive and user-friendly.

LithQuery allows users to query the GGDB by age, lithology, and environment of deposition. LithQuery creates lithologic and environmental overlays that can be plotted on plate tectonic, paleogeographic and paleoclimatic maps. The software comes with the latest version of the GGDB and can be found at https://github.com/Emma-Havens/LithQuery.

PaleoMapper generates maps and animations of paleogeographic reconstructions. Users can upload overlays from LithQuery and/or their own point data and adjust the age of reconstruction, map projection and extent, and layer colors and opacity. PaleoMapper comes with a global plate model, coastline and country border data, and raster maps, though all basemap files can also be swapped and customized. Data, maps, and animations can be exported to a variety of formats (.shp, .gpml, .pdf, .svg, .mp4). PaleoMapper can be found at https://github.com/Emma-Havens/Paleomapper.

title: Global Distribution and Climatic Viability of Martian Alluvial Fans
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Morgan, Alexander Michael [1], Palucis, Marisa Christina [2], Lutz, Katherine [3]
affiliations: (1) Planetary Science Institute, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
(3) Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA
abstract:
The discovery of widespread sedimentary deposits using MOC and CTX images has revolutionized our understanding of the complexity of Mars’ geologic history. In particular, alluvial fans and putative deltas preserve a record of widespread fluvial sediment transport across the martian highlands. We used CTX imagery to document the global distribution of >1500 fan landforms. Crater counting statistics on fan-hosting craters show that numerous alluvial fans occupy Hesperian and Amazonian impact craters, confirming localized fluvial erosion persisted relatively late into martian history. Both alluvial fans and putative deltas appear at lower elevations than Late Noachian and Early Hesperian valley networks, indicating a shift among climatic zones capable of supporting liquid water.

To constrain the physical conditions required for fan formation, we extracted topography for ~500 alluvial fan catchments using CTX and HRSC stereo-derived digital elevation models. We calculated solar insolation and diurnal shadowing within these catchments across orbital obliquities ranging from 15° to 65°. We then built a thermophysical model to identify the surface pressure and obliquity combinations required to generate enough snowmelt for sediment transport across each fan. The model calculates ice accumulation and runoff in both regional macroclimates and topographically shielded microclimates, isolating both seasonal and inter-obliquity regimes. We then track the stability of water on the fan surface against evaporative and conductive heat losses to determine if the flow can transport sediment to the distal margin before freezing. Model outputs directly quantify the specific atmospheric and orbital thresholds necessary for sediment transport, constraining the physical conditions required for late-stage martian hydrology.

title: Climate vs source material as controls of clay mineralogy for the Miocene in the Turkana Basin, Kenya
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic (Posters)
authors: Ransom, Zachary David [1], Weissman, Zoe [2], Stinchcomb, Gary E. [3], Minya, Aggrey [4], Henkes, Gregory A. [5], Beck, Catherine C. [6]
affiliations: (1) Hamilton College, Poolesville, Maryland, USA
(2) Hamilton College, Clinton, Ny, USA
(3) University of Memphis, Memphis, TN,
(4) University Of Memphis, Memphis, TN,
(5) Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY,
(6) Geoscience, Hamilton College, CLINTON, NY, USA
abstract:
Clay minerals are used as paleoclimate proxies because their formation is partly driven by the pH and soil climate, namely temperature and moisture. For example, kaolinite forms under humid climates with intense leaching, while smectite commonly forms under semi-arid to sub-humid climates with limited leaching. However, the source material (e.g., basalt vs. gneiss) in a depositional setting can also dictate the availability of ions and the resulting clay minerals that form. Thus, understanding if a clay mineral assemblage reflects sediment source, climate conditions, other environmental factors, and/or diagenetic histories is an important component when applying proxies to reconstructing paleoenvironments and paleoclimates.

This study builds upon existing descriptive and geochemical work on fine-grain sediments, especially paleosols, from Miocene outcrops in the Turkana Basin. Data from two Miocene sites, Locherangan (~17.5 Ma) and Sibiloi (~12.9 Ma), were compared as they represent lacustrine and fluvial -dominated depositional environments respectively. Using X-ray diffraction (XRD), this study seeks to constrain the relative influence of climate (e.g. moisture regime) and source material on the mineralogy. Variations in source material are likely related to the tectonic history of the region through changes in drainage basin hydroconnectivity. These factors, climate and tectonics, are critical for understanding the context of early hominoid evolution.

XRD data were collected on a Rigaku Miniflex with a copper source, operated at 40 kV, and 15 mA, and data were analyzed using Profex, an open-source program for analyzing XRD spectra. Spectra were collected from the 2θ range 2.5°- 75°, with a step size of 0.02°, and a speed of 4°/min on unoriented bulk sediment slides. Mineralogically, these slides agreed with separate thin section analysis that identified quartz, feldspar, muscovite, and pyroxene (enstatite). Additionally, cristobalite was present in the samples from Sibiloi which is likely a diagenetic mineral as it has been documented in other studies in paleosol overlain by basalt flows such as at this site. A high-angle XRD reflection at ~62° 2θ occurs in many of the samples suggesting the presence of dioctahedral clay minerals that may include illite, montmorillonite or kaolinite. Forthcoming XRD analysis on the oriented clay fraction will be used to better characterize the clay mineral assemblage in these samples and to distinguish between discrete and interstratified phases.

title: XRF Chemostratigraphy Across the Mississippian-Pennsylvanian Transition in East-Central Pennsylvania

authors: Thornburg, Jesse D. [1], Oest, Christopher [2], Davis, Tim [3], Peterson, Stephen Patrick [4]
affiliations: (1) Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, USA
(2) Pennsylvania Geological Survey, Middletown, PA,
(3) Temple University, Philadelphia, PA,
(4) State of Delaware, Wilmington, DE,
abstract:
A well-preserved, conformable 630 m section of roadcut along Rt. 61 south of Pottsville, Pennsylvania exposes the Upper Mississippian Mauch Chunk Formation and its transition into the Lower to Middle Pennsylvanian Pottsville and Llewellyn Formations. Grayish-red Mauch Chunk sandstones and paleosol-bearing mudstones record predominantly arid and semi-arid conditions. The overlying coarse-grained conglomerates and coal-bearing Pottsville and Llewellyn Formations record a shift to humid, peat-forming environments. The driving mechanism for this shift in depositional style is somewhat contested. The influx of coarse-grained sediment within the Pottsville Formation has been attributed to tectonic uplift in the source terrane. Alternatively, climatic shift at the Mississippian-Pennsylvania boundary has been invoked as a mechanism to raise sediment yield from the source highlands.

We test the relative influence of tectonics and climate geochemically utilizing immobile element ratios (Th/Sc, Al2O3/TiO2, Cr/Th, Zr/Sc). These elements resist diagenetic alteration and therefore track source composition and their relative proportions can elucidate climate and potential unroofing signals. This was accomplished with a transect of 60 samples, focused on the 200 m surrounding the contact between the Pottsville and Mauch Chunk Formations, with ~20 in the Mauch Chunk at ~5 m spacing, ~20 across the boundary at ~1-2 m spacing, and ~20 in the Pottsville and Llewellyn Formations at ~5 m spacing.

The Mississippian - Pennsylvania Boundary approximately corresponds to the contact between the Pottsville and the Mauch Chunk Formations. We place the upper contact of the Mauch Chunk Formation at the highest grayish red mudstone in this gradational sequence. We are additionally testing the gradual transitional nature across this boundary found here but that is regionally absent elsewhere, as well as whether documented paleocurrent changes correspond to genuine changes provenance.

title: Plio-Pleistocene Drainage Reorganization of the Big Lost River in the northeastern Snake River Plain
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools (Posters)
authors: Rasmussen, Andrea [1], Anderson, Caden [2], Sundell, Kurt [3], Nawotniak, Shannon [4]
affiliations: (1) Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho,
(2) Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(3) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,

abstract: Neogene Basin and Range tectonism and the passage of the Yellowstone hotspot produced the modern topographic expression of the eastern Snake River Plain (ESRP). Previous work in the Big Lost Trough (BLT), a basin in the northern ESRP, records evidence for a major drainage reversal between 2 and 3 Ma. Specifically, the BLT is interpreted to have captured the Big Lost River, Little Lost River, and Birch Creek due to the formation the northwest-trending Arco Volcanic Rift Zone and associated topographic highs. A recently published compilation of ESRP volcanism calls the existence of the Arco Volcanic Rift Zone into question, especially at the necessary spatial and temporal scales. To evaluate the drainage reversal hypothesis, we characterized sedimentary units from drill cores throughout the BLT and collected detrital zircon U-Pb ages using laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Drill core characterization shows that in the last 1.2 Ma, sedimentary and igneous units in the BLT are thickest in the west proximal to the Big Lost River. Detrital zircon U-Pb ages from sandstones are dominated by Eocene Challis magmatism, with subordinate Neoproterozoic (710–650 Ma), and lesser Paleoproterozoic and Archean ages. The Neoproterozoic zircon are only present in the Pioneer Core Complex, which is only drained by the Big Lost River, indicating that it is the primary sediment source for the BLT. Volcanic vents currently exposed at the surface in this area are consistently far younger than the necessary timeline, and limited subsurface data from coreholes is inadequate to identify the locations of active vents during the time in question. Further, larger spatiotemporal patterns of volcanism across the ESRP are inconsistent with the rift model. We suggest three alternative models for the drainage reorganization, which are not mutually exclusive, that do not invoke volcanic rift zones including (1) Localized subsidence related to Basin and Range extension; (2) Nonuniform subsidence related to the dense midcrustal sill beneath the ESRP; and (3) Differential uplift and subsidence related to the passage of the Yellowstone hotspot. Given the timing and rate of North American plate movement, and comparison to the modern Yellowstone physiography characterized by doming related to the active caldera and adjacent subsidence to the southwest in the immediate wake of its passage, we prefer the latter hypothesis.

authors: Bombard, Samantha [1], Leckie, R. Mark [2], Harwood, David M. [3], Browne, Imogen [4], Stanchak, Felipe [5], Shevenell, Amelia E. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA; Geosciences, Union College, Schenectady, NY, USA
(2) University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA,
(3) Univ Nebraska - Lincoln, Dept of Earth & Atmospheric Sciences, Lincoln, NE,
(4) Royal Society Te Apārangi, Wellington, New Zealand
(5) University of South Florida, Saint Petersburg, FL,
(6) University of South Florida, Saint Petersburg, FL,
abstract:
With the expiration of the International Ocean Discovery Program, researchers have been encouraged to revisit existing sediment cores to apply new techniques that were not around when the cores were collected. One of the main concerns with reviving decades old cores is that the sediment cannot yield reliable data due to alteration of primary characteristics of the core, such as carbonate preservation. We revisited Antarctic cores from Deep Sea Drilling Project (Leg 28, 1972-1973) Sites 272 (eastern Ross Sea) and 273 (western Ross Sea) reexamined the Early to Middle Miocene records from the Ross Sea continental shelf to investigate how the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO) and Middle Miocene Climate Transition (MMCT) changed water mass behavior and extant changes of the Antarctic Ice Sheet. We use a multiproxy approach utilizing foraminiferal assemblages, benthic foraminiferal stable isotopes, Natural Gamma Radiation, Magnetic Susceptibility, and available shipboard data.

In August 2025, as part of the Ocean Core Teacher-Researcher and Curriculum Experience (Ocean TRACX) program, we collaborated with 5 middle/high school teachers to collect new data from Sites 272 and 273 to complement what has already been done (e.g., sampling for foraminifera). When these cores were collected over 50 years ago, shipboard downhole physical property data collection was not available. The Early to Middle Miocene archive halves of Holes 273 and 273A were scanned at the Gulf Coast Repository for Natural Gamma Radiation (NGR) and Magnetic Susceptibility (MS). The NGR data were collected on the Natural Gamma Radiation Logger (NGRL) at a resolution of 10 cm and the MS data were collected on the Whole-Round Multisensor Logger (WRMSL) at a resolution of 2 cm. We also collected additional samples for foraminiferal assemblages and stable isotope analyses.

Our project found several key findings regarding revisiting old cores, 1) NGR and MS can be collected and produce data that complements the existing foraminiferal data, 2) Collected samples do have foraminifera present, and the samples yielded robust stable isotopic values, 3) It is possible to produce reliable data from cores after 50 years of collection and storage. In regard to the Miocene, these data revealed that the Antarctic Ice Sheet was dynamic and behaved differently across the Ross Sea embayment.

abstract: Central Texas aquifers supply millions of residents and support fragile spring ecosystems. Hydrogeologic research is essential to preserve these water resources amid threats from development and climate variability. Radon-222 (Rn-222) is a radioactive decay product of Uranium-238 which can be used as a groundwater tracer. Rn-222 activity in spring water is a function of the aquifer lithology, residence time, recharge dynamics, and groundwater velocity, providing information about flow paths, permeability, and surface water-groundwater interactions. However, baseline Rn-222 data for springs in Central Texas is limited. We establish initial measurements of Rn-222 activity in Central Texas springs, and compare results across the region. 52 samples were taken from 5 spring complexes, providing the first Rn-222 activity measurements in these springs. 250mL grab samples were collected during baseflow conditions from May-August 2026 and analyzed using the RAD8 (Durridge Co.) following recommended protocols of the manufacturer. We analyzed 38 samples from 4 springs in the karstic Edwards Aquifer Barton Springs complex (Old Mill, Eliza, Barton Main; TWDB: 5842914) that averaged 46 +/- 10 pCi/L and ranged 30-81 pCi/L. Old Mill Spring had the highest average Rn-222 activity (65 pCi/L, n=3), potentially due to influence from the saline portion of the Edwards Aquifer. Eliza and Barton Main had lower Rn-222 activity, inferred to be a result of similar conduit flow paths, consistent with previous studies. We analyzed 4 samples from the Krause Springs complex (TWDB: 5739302) within a coupled Cretaceous clastic and Paleozoic carbonate aquifer, that averaged 72 +/-19 pCi/L and ranged 38-118 pCi/L. A variety of Quaternary alluvial springs within the Colorado River watershed averaged 83 +/-21 pCi/L (n=9) and ranged 52-201 pCi/L. Springs of the Hamilton Pool complex (Middle Trinity Aquifer), a stacked carbonate clastic aquifer, averaged 287 +/-18 pCi/L and ranged 87-685 pCi/L (n=6). Edge Spring (TWDB: 5747318) had the highest Rn-222 activity. Results varied within and across spring complexes, remaining lowest in the karstic Barton Springs complex and higher in porous clastic and mixed aquifers likely due to lithological and permeability differences. This study provides baseline Rn-222 data, laying the groundwork for future hydrogeologic research in Central Texas.

title: Participation, Preparation, and Educational Pathways in the International Earth Science Olympiad
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Gauli, Pareeksha [1], Locke, Sharon M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Sciences,, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, Edwardsville, IL, USA
(2) Department of Environmental Sciences, Southern Illinois University, Edwardsville, IL, USA
abstract:
The International Earth Science Olympiad (IESO) brings together young participants from different countries to engage in theoretical and practical Earth Science activities, field investigations, collaboratives projects, and international exchange. Participants may enter the competition with different levels of prior interest, preparation, support, and expectations for the future. This study investigates why students choose to participate in IESO, how they prepare for the competition, what challenges and meaningful experiences they encounter, and how they perceive IESO in relation to their interest in Earth Science and future educational and career decisions.

A mixed-methods study is being conducted for the 19th IESO in Turin, Italy, in August 2026. Participants representing their countries at IESO will be invited to complete a 10-15 minute online survey. The survey examines their initial interest in Earth Science, motivations for participating, preparation time, access to training resources, teacher and mentor support, preparation challenges, and perceived readiness. It also examines participant's perceptions of whether IESO influenced their understanding of Earth Science, confidence as science learners, ability to connect Earth Science with real-world problems, collaboration with students from other countries, and future educational and career intentions. Participants may also volunteer for a 20-25 minute semi-structured interview exploring their pathways at IESO, preparation experiences, meaningful moments, personal growth, changing perspectives, and future aspirations.

Quantitative survey data will be summarized and compared across relevant participant and preparation characteristics. Open-ended survey responses and interview data will be analyzed thematically to identify shared and contrasting experiences. The study will examine whether participants entered IESO with an established interest in Earth Science, whether their perspectives developed through preparation, and how national preparation systems and individual experiences relate to their developing educational and career pathways. Findings will provide partcipant-centered insight into motivation, preparation, support, challenges, and engagement with Earth Science in an international competition setting.

Keywords: International Earth Science; Earth science education; Student motivation; Preparation experiences; Educational pathways; Science identity.

title: Monitoring Ground Water Flow to the San Solomon Springs In Far West Texas
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes (Posters)
authors: Urbanczyk, Kevin Mark [1]
affiliations: (1) Sul Ross State University, Meadows Research Institute for West Texas Water, Alpine, TX, USA
abstract:
The San Solomon Spring group is located in far west Texas in the vicinity of the town of Balmorhea. The group includes Phantom Springs, San Solomon springs which is the main flow to Balmorhea State Park and other springs in the Balmorhea area. The spring flow is substantial for the region (~25 cfs) but appears to be experiencing a gradual decline. The group is part of a regional ground water system with sources from as far away as Van Horn to ~100 km to the west. The hydrogeology of the flow system includes the West Texas Bolson aquifer, the Capitan Reef Complex Aquifer, the Rustler aquifer, the Edwards-Trinity Plateau aquifer and the Igneous aquifer.

Attempts to understand the regional ground water flow to the springs include the work of Sharp (1989) that interpreted the flow to at originate in the Wild Horse basin with cross formation flow in the Capitan reef in the Apache mountains followed by flow into ETPA and emergence at the Balmorhea area. More recent work by Nicot and others (2022) evaluates influence of local precipitation on the flow.

Monitoring of the flow has been hampered by lack of access to private property in the infererred flow path area. We have recently been able to gain access to 2 wells for monitoring 16 km west of Balmorhea. These are targeted for continuous ground water level monitoring. As part of a coordinated local effort, we are optimistic that more strategically located wells will be made accessible in the suspected flow path as we cultivate relationships with land owners.

(2) Geology, Portland State University -- Geology, Portland, OR,

(4) Department of Geology, Portland State University, Portland, OR, USA

abstract:
Climate change has been causing a major retreat in the Pacific Northwest glaciers and the rivers they feed are therefore a sensitive indicator for their hydrology and sediment transport processes. The White River basin (1414 km 2 ) draining the southern flank of Mount Hood in northcentral Oregon is an 85-km long major tributary of the Deschutes River (27000 km 2 ). It is known for the milky glacial flour produced during the summer-fall snowmelt and ice melt, affecting irrigation in Tygh Valley, recreational sports, and aquatic habitat. The sediment is sourced from a debris fan exiting the White Glacier at its headwaters and extending several km downstream. This is an active, steep, unconsolidated deposit mainly eroding volcanic mudflows and pyroclastic deposits from the Old Maid (1760-1810 AD), Timberline (450-500 AD) and Polallie (30-12 ka) eruptive periods. The grain sizes within the fan range from fine ash to 5 m boulders, mostly of low-silica dacite and andesite, with some older Miocene basalt clasts.

We installed an automatic-continuous optic turbidity sensor on the White River debris fan, below the Oregon Route 35 highway bridge to measure suspended sediment transport dynamics. It was calibrated in situ using local fine sediment (<63 microns), with discharge measured via acoustic doppler velocimeter. Continuous discharge used 50% of the established USGS gauge downstream, corrected for distance. A 4-km long grain size survey of the fan, was performed to estimate its fine component (< 2 mm).

Results show expected suspended sediment events during the winter flood and spring floods. However, during fall, there were small transport events that lasted up to 3 days uncorrelated to discharge. In the winter flood, suspended sediments peaked more frequently than the hydrograph but once the flood recession was over there was no transport of fines. The single-peaked spring flood showed complex behavior of multi-peaks of suspended sediment transport events, including a 3-week hyper-concentration event. During the recession of the freshet, a 2-month multi-peaked suspended sediment event suggested transport of fines with anti-clockwise hysteresis under saturated conditions. In the summer, a period of high turbidity which exceeded sensor measurement capacity lasted for 3.5 weeks. In conclusion, the White River generates numerous suspended sediment events fueled by a near-endless supply of fine sediment from the debris fan, decoupled from typical hydrograph patterns.

title: Temperature and Continental Weathering Across the Mid-Pleistocene Transition From the North Atlantic Ocean
session_title: Revisiting the archives: New discoveries from existing core collections (Posters)
authors: Kalu, Queen A. [1], Nana Yobo, Lucien [2], Peral, Marion [3], Grossman, Ethan L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(3) EPOC (UMR 5805), University of Bordeaux, Pessac, France
(4) Geology & Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
abstract:
The Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT; ~1.2-0.7 Ma) marks the fundamental reorganization of Earth's climate system from predominantly ~41-ka to ~100-ka glacial-interglacial cycles. Although changes in ice-sheet dynamics and ocean circulation have been widely invoked to explain this transition, the roles of ocean temperature change and continental weathering remain incompletely constrained. Here, we investigate these processes using oxygen, carbon, clumped (δ 18 O, δ 13 C, Δ 47 ), and osmium ( 187 Os/ 188 Os) isotope records from IODP Expedition 397 Site U1587 (Iberian Margin, eastern North Atlantic), spanning Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 36-16 (1.2-0.62 Ma).

Paired Δ 47 and benthic foraminiferal δ 18 O measurements reconstruct bottom-water temperature and seawater δ 18 O, allowing the separation of temperature and global ice-volume effects. Benthic δ 13 C records constrain deep-water ventilation, water-mass structure, and carbon storage. Seawater 187 Os/ 188 Os records track changes in the balance between radiogenic continental weathering and unradiogenic mantle-derived sources.

Integration of these records will resolve the timing and phasing of ocean temperature, ice-volume, carbon-cycle, and weathering changes across this transition. This multiproxy framework will test whether continental weathering primarily responded to MPT climate reorganization or participated in feedback that facilitated the emergence of longer, higher-amplitude ~100-kyr glacial cycles.
