title: Preliminary Augite Chemistry of the Qob2 Basaltic Andesite: Implications for the Magmatic System of the Goat Rocks Volcanic Cluster
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Cyr, Emma [1], Brunstad, Keith [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Science, State University of New York at Oneonta, Oneonta, NEW YORK, USA
(2) Earth and Atmospheric Science, State University of New York at Oneonta, Oneonta, New York, USA
abstract: The Goat Rocks volcanic cluster represents an extensively eroded, extinct volcanic system within the south-central Washington Cascade Range. The Basaltic Andesite flow (Qob2) of Bear Creek Mountain erupted from the Goat Rocks ~1.31 ± 0.04 Ma and is associated with the same eruptive phase as the Tieton Andesite lava flows. By studying the Qob2 flow, we aim to better understand the conditions within the magma chamber prior to its eruption and determine whether Qob2 was a precursor to, and potential driver of, the eruption of the second Tieton Andesite flow (Qta2). In this study, we compiled chemical analyses and petrographic descriptions of Qob2 augite (aug) phenocrysts to perform geothermometry and oxybarometry calculations during future studies. Analyses were conducted using a Hitachi 3030 SEM and QuantX 70 Bruker EDX. Preliminary results indicate that the aug compositions are more similar to that in dacitic and rhyolitic systems than from basaltic andesites or andesites, with compositions ranging from ~ 48–56 wt.% SiO₂, 0.5–2 wt.% TiO₂, 0.5–2 wt.% Na₂O, 8.5–13 wt.% MgO, 15–21 wt.% CaO, and 9–18 wt.% total FeO. In general, within evolved silicic magmas, aug may be preserved as phenocrysts, glomerocrysts, or inherited xenocrystic phases. Relative to aug crystallized from mafic magmas, these aug are characterized by higher Fe, Mn, lower Cr, and in some cases, slightly elevated Al and Ti contents resulting from lower crystallization temperatures and changing mineral-melt partitioning behavior. The aug compositions of sample KAB15020 closely resemble those reported from calc-alkaline dacite and rhyolite systems of the Cascade arc, where they record progressive magmatic differentiation, increasing oxidation, decreasing crystallization temperatures, and iron enrichment, including examples from Mt St. Helens and Mt Hood. Aug phenocrysts in Qob2 are compositionally variable and occur predominantly as broken crystals within plg- and Fe oxide bearing glomerocrysts, ranging in habit from euhedral to anhedral. Many phenocrysts exhibit embayed and resorbed margins, and some also contain quenched glass along their margins. The results of this study suggest that Qob2 records interaction with an evolved system and provide critical constraints for testing whether it represents a precursor magma to the Qta2 eruption.

title: Styles, Magnitudes, and History of Collapse in Arabia Terra, Mars: Constraints from CTX DTMs

abstract:
Here we examine the geologic characteristics of topographic depressions across the highland plateau adjacent to the dichotomy boundary and assess the boundary-parallel (quasi-latitudinal) extent of subsidence and collapse and the styles, magnitudes, and distribution of individual collapse sites, including those associated with impact craters. The study area encompasses a ~1500-2000 km wide (~N to S) band above ~10°N latitude in Arabia Terra from Mawrth Vallis (~20°W) through Deuteronilus Mensae (~35°E). We are utilizing a combination of feature mapping and cataloguing using high-resolution images, topographic analyses with CTX digital terrain models (DTMs), and crater counting in order to evaluate: a) the collapse history of the highland plateau along the dichotomy boundary, including magnitudes of collapse at local sites and volume estimates for the material removed, with constraints for void space/volatile content of the plateau; b) processes of plateau degradation, including effects of both regional inter-crater and localized, intra-crater deposition, as well as remobilization of volatiles along crater rim slopes; and c) plateau evolution with specific chronologic constraints developed for collapse events and cratered terrain degradation, including focused studies of individual craters as sites of deposition.

A key part of our geological analysis of the study area includes generation (using the Ames Stereo Pipeline) and analysis of high-resolution CTX DTMs. The study region contains abundant CTX stereo coverage, allowing for widespread characterization of the region at resolutions significantly improved over MOLA. We are creating hillshade rasters, slope and contour maps, color altimetry images, and disparity and good pixel maps, aligned to MOLA for comparison and extrapolation. The final controlled 24 m/pxl CTX DTMs and associated orthoimages have 24 and 6 m/pxl resolutions, respectively. We have currently produced ~200 CTX DTMs spanning the northern half of the study area, covering Eden, Ismenia, and Siloe Paterae, Ismenius Cavus, Mamers Vallis, Dein and Bamberg craters, as well as much of southern Deuteronilus Mensae. We have mosaicked the DTMs to create a single, cohesive product with consistent elevation ranges. Work to be done includes adding remaining DTMs to the mosaic, adjusting the mosaic to remove inconsistent individual DTMs, and production of ~100 more DTMs over regions of interest in the southern part of the study area.

abstract:
The Mars 2020 Perseverance rover houses various imaging and spectroscopic instruments with the express intent of finding and contextualizing biological indicators in and around its landing site, Jezero Crater, at the Martian surface. One widely identified feature of interest is the ‘leopard spots’ first found in mudstones in Neretva Vallis, the inlet channel to Jezero Crater [1, 2]. A terrestrial analog for the ‘leopard spots’ found in Martian rocks are the reduction spheroids seen in ancient (> 0.5 Ga) red bed sediments. This study uses a group of rocks from Stoer, Scotland (~1 Ga), another from Dingwall, Scotland (0.5 Ga), and another from Budleigh Salterton, England (~0.25 Ga) exploring a wide range of observational techniques to gain a fuller picture of the characteristics of reduction spots and better constrain potential biological indicators preserved within. The primary work consists of micro-Raman and -luminescence spectroscopy with laser wavelengths of 532 nm, 785 nm, and 830 nm. The use of multiple lasers will allow us to resolve fluorescence that may overlap the Raman shift and develop a technique to identify and resolve the underlying molecules. This is applicable to the Perseverance rover’s SHERLOC and SuperCam Raman instruments, as some studies suggest the peaks may be cesium-bearing phosphates, rather than organic peaks. By focusing on the readily apparent features in these reduction features, future missions can identify potential biosignatures. The current SuperCam Raman aboard Perseverance and the future Raman Laser Spectrometer (RLS) aboard ExoMars Rosalind Franklin both use a 532 nm laser; this study can therefore report on what may overlap in this specific region in analogs for the Martian sediments. Additionally, the BioFinder, a time-gated fluorescence bio-detector [3], will help to better classify specific areas of interest in a given reduction spot. Finally, a remote time-resolved Raman spectroscopy setup, a bulk Raman spectroscopy method at the University of Hawaii [4], will be used to better characterize these spots and their host rocks at larger scales comparable to flight instruments.

title: Internal Strain Localization in the Papoose Flat Pluton: Evidence from Structure, Petrography, and Geochemistry
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Flint, Miranda [1], Putirka , Keith [2]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Fresno, Fresno, CA, USA
(2) California State University, Fresno, Fresno, Ca, USA
abstract:
Continental arc plutons preserve records of magma assembly and deformation, yet the processes responsible for internal strain localization during emplacement remain debated. The relatively isolated Papoose Flat Pluton (PFP), located in the northern Inyo Mountains of eastern California, provides an opportunity for emplacement-related deformation to be examined with limited overprinting from adjacent plutons. The PFP has traditionally been interpreted as a forcefully emplaced body with deformation concentrated along its margins.

This study addresses whether the PFP was assembled through multiple intrusive pulses and whether repeated magma emplacement contributed to the formation or reactivation of a broad internal high-strain zone. Gradational transitions from protomylonite to orthomylonite and ultramylonite were identified through field mapping. Structural measurements, oriented samples, petrography, paleomagnetism, and a newly generated whole-rock XRF dataset were used to evaluate variations in strain, mineralogy, and composition. This XRF dataset provides new geochemical constraints on the internal architecture of a pluton for which bulk geochemical characterization has previously been limited.

Spatially organized compositional variation and discrete Fe–Mg groups were identified within the pluton interior and across the mylonitic zone. These preliminary results could suggest that the high-strain zone developed during incremental pluton assembly. The observed geochemical differences may represent distinct magma pulses, deformation-related mineral redistribution, or both. Overall, emplacement-related strain is favored over movement along a regionally continuous fault.

title: Iron speciation and trace element geochemistry as biosignatures of biological soil crust communities

authors: Sheldon, Nathan D. [1], Seguin, Catherine [2], Dzombak, Rebecca [3], Howard, Cecilia [4]

abstract: The record of terrestrial biosignatures in the Precambrian is generally sparse relative to the marine record, due to a range of taphonomic and collection bias factors. However, a variety of lines of evidence now suggest that there was life on land in a wide array of settings. While many of those settings are still proximal to water as lake, floodplain, and tidal settings, there is significant potential for a record of life in more aridland settings that is relatively unexplored. Biological soil crusts represent complex consortia of phototrophic and heterotrophic life that in modern settings, are responsible for significant, global-scale contributions to primary productivity and elemental cycling. Herein we examine biological crusts from Utah (USA) both at different developmental stages and relative to uncrusted soil to look for potential biosignatures that could be applicable to the geologic record. In addition to previously recognized biosignatures like enrichments in C and N, we also find species-specific Fe enrichments revealed by sequential Fe extraction as well as evidence for Fe oxidizing bacteria based upon Fe species transformations. In addition, trace metal depletions of metals involved in nitrogen fixation (Mo, V), methanogenesis (Ni), and various cellular functions (Zn) are present in various stages of biological soil crust development relative to uncrusted sand. While none of these potential biosignatures are definitive on their own, this work provides a framework for life detection based upon multiple elemental transformations that could be applied to continental Precambrian settings.

title: The selective signature of local environmental change: a case study from the late Neogene San Joaquin seaway
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Stowe, Kayli Arisa [1], Finnegan, Seth [2], Samuels-Fair, Maya [3]
affiliations: (1) University of California, Oakland, CA,

abstract: The influence of traits on extinction risk is usually evaluated at the global scale, but trait-environment interactions vary locally. Consequently, there is a need for regional studies that evaluate extinction risk in the context of local environmental change. Epicontinental seaways, which are limited today but have been extensive during much of Earth history, provide mesocosms ideal for regional analyses. The San Joaquin Basin in central-southern California was flooded by the Pacific Ocean during the Miocene and Pliocene, creating the San Joaquin seaway. The environmental conditions of the seaway were dynamic and strongly influenced by tectonically and eustatically-driven changes in marine connectivity and variation in freshwater input from rivers draining the nearby Sierran highlands. Connectivity between the seaway and the open ocean was progressively reduced between 2.3 and 2.0 Ma, culminating in a transition to a non-marine basin. The stepwise restriction and ultimate demise of the San Joaquin seaway is recorded by a thick sequence of highly fossiliferous sediments that are well-exposed in the Kettleman Hills, Coalinga Anticline, and Reef Ridge on the western margin of the San Joaquin Valley. Of the ~350 molluscan species with a fossil record in this region, ~65% are now extinct. Previous studies of the Kettleman Hills have identified seven distinct clusters of last occurrences that appear to coincide with eustatic sea level changes and have hypothesized that they represent local extinction pulses driven by changes in salinity, temperature, and productivity. We examine how changing environmental conditions influence extinction rates and relative extinction risk, focusing on traits including body size, feeding mode, trophic level, and salinity tolerance and using capture-mark-recapture (CMR) to control for uneven sampling and preservation. CMR-estimated extinction rates depart substantially from a face-value reading of last occurrence clusters. Salinity fluctuations, particularly full-marine to brackish transitions, increased estimated local extinction rates in the San Joaquin seaway. Extinctions occur preferentially (but not exclusively) among species intolerant of low-salinity conditions. No other traits are significantly associated with extinction risk at any time.

authors: Bowers, Zoe E. [1], Roberts, Eric [2], Suarez, Marina B. [3], Atkinson, Brian [4], Smith, Selena Y. [5]

abstract: The James Ross Basin of the Antarctic Peninsula preserves the only known exposures of Upper Cretaceous sedimentary strata from anywhere in Antarctica. In 2024, a six-week NSF-supported expedition (G-074-E) to James Ross Island, in the Antarctic Peninsula, resulted in the collection of a diverse assemblage of plant and vertebrate macrofossils from the Santonian-Campanian Santa Marta Formation, along with supporting geological samples for age dating. Prior to this expedition, these strata were not known to preserve vertebrate fossils, and the abundance of terrestrial plants was unexpected. The primary aim of this study is to conduct the first radioisotopic dating of these deposits, and several other Upper Cretaceous units on James Ross, Vega, and Snow Hill islands. Additional project goals include investigating aspects of the sedimentology and sedimentary provenance of this Late Cretaceous back-arc basin. To achieve these goals, sixteen volcanic tuff and volcanoclastic sandstone samples were collected from throughout the stratigraphy for U-Pb zircon geochronology via laser ablation inductively coupled mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS) and petrographic and geochemical analysis. In addition, 19 well-preserved invertebrate shells from the Hidden Lake and Santa Marta formations were collected for Sr-isotope stratigraphy. Preliminary results indicate alternating periods of syndepositional magmatic activity in the adjacent volcanic arc, along with periods of magmatic quiescence, and that provenance and sediment routing into the basin are primarily from erosion and transport from the arc itself, west of the basin. Several of the volcanic tuffs are surprisingly zircon poor, limiting their potential for U-Pb dating and suggesting alternating bimodal magmatism in the arc. Current dating results for the upper Santa Marta Formation (Beta Member) at two key localities yield U-Pb detrital zircon maximum depositional ages of ~80–76 Ma, consistent with initial Sr-Isotope stratigraphy results which suggest a depositional age of ~79–77 Ma. This combined data provides significantly improved tie points for testing (and potentially recalibrating) the published magnetostratigraphy. Similarly, a period of terminal Cretaceous syndepositional volcanism in the arc can be deduced based on populations of detrital zircons and tuffs between ~69–65 Ma, permitting significantly improved age control and paleomagnetic calibration of portions of the Lopez de Bertodano Formation across the K/Pg boundary in the basin.

title: Climate Control on Sediment Architecture of Outer Shelf Mudstones - Woodford Shale, Oklahoma, USA
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience
authors: Fishman, Neil S. [1], Egenhoff, Sven Olaf [2]
affiliations: (1) PetroLogic Solutions, LLC, Boulder, CO, USA

abstract:
This contribution explores how long-term versus short-term sea-level changes, most likely triggered by climatic fluctuations, influence sediment architecture of the Woodford Shale on the deep shelf. The Woodford Formation in the Arbuckle Mountains, Oklahoma, consists of alternating shales and radiolarian cherts that are largely structureless, with shales generally being several times thicker than the cherts. The entire succession is thought to represent about 29 million years. In thin section the shales show mm- to sub-mm-scale planar laminations, and so do the cherts. Only visible in thin section are also sub-millimeter accumulations of silt grains lining individual laminations laterally. With few exceptions, the beds are laterally consistent in make-up, thickness, and number on an outcrop scale. A total of over 369 shale-chert couplets make up the Woodford Shale. The unit is subdivided into a lower member with a moderately thick shales and chert beds, a middle member with relatively few chert intercalations, thick shales, and very few carbonates, and an upper member with abundant cherts and overall thin shale units in between.

The succession is interpreted to represent influx of terrigenous shale during lowstands, and accumulation of mostly radiolarians during highstands (cherts). Shales were deposited in pulses with short hiatuses in between during which agglutinated foraminifera, responsible for the clusters of silt grains, accumulated on the ocean floor. Each of the shale-chert couplets represents one fluctuation of relative sea level. Considering that more than 369 fluctuations of sea-level are visible in the succession, these sea-level changes likely reflect variations in obliquity (41k years) rather than eccentricity (100k years) which would lead to more time than what is represented by the entire Woodford. The entire succession shows a moderate highstand at the base, represented by the lower Woodford, a lowstand with minor carbonates in the middle member, and a significant highstand represented by the upper member. These different sea-level positions are interpreted to represent second-order cycles showing that third-order cycles had no visible influence on deposition of the Woodford shale in the Arbuckle Mountains. The Woodford as a prime example of outer shelf deposition, therefore shows that obliquity-induced climate changes even influence the deep shelf that is free of any third-order cycle influence with only second-order cycles having a moderate impact on this distal depositional environment.

title: Geoheritage as a Guide to Understanding Geoscience Intersections with Human Activity—Past, Present, and Future
session_title: The Astro-Geoheritage of the Solar System: Past Explorations and Future Considerations
authors: Robeck, Edward C. [1], Mossa, Lindsay Catherine [2], Brase, Lauren Elizabeth [3], McGee, Sequoyah [4]
affiliations: (1) Education & Outreach, American Geosciences Institute (AGI), Alexandria, VA,
(2) Education & Outreach, American Geosciences Institute (AGI), ANNAPOLIS, MD,
(3) Education & Outreach, American Geosciences Institute (AGI), Alexandria, VA,
(4) Education & Outreach, American Geosciences Institute (AGI), Alexandria, VA,
abstract:
Geoheritage is a framework through which various principles are applied to certain locations leading some of them to be designated as geoheritage sites . This presentation proposes that there are benefits to applying those principles to a wide array of locations, whether they are geoheritage sites or not, in which human activities have taken place in the past—and will in the future.

The GSA position statement on geoheritage includes a rationale that starts out, “ ‘Geoheritage’ is a generic but descriptive term applied to sites or areas of geologic features with significant scientific, educational, cultural, and/or aesthetic value.” There is much to be gained by exploring how these values have interacted with human activity in situations where geologic processes, features, and materials have had a central role—such as migration, mining, infrastructure development, and living with natural hazards. Those explorations deepen the understanding of how geology and other geosciences have shaped human experience. Communicating those understandings is inherent in the idea of geoheritage, as is the idea of conserving the sites so those understandings are available to future generations.

Yet, within the simple elegance of the statement quoted above lies the complexity that can emerge as the concept of geoheritage is operationalized. That complexity stems in large part from the fact that a single site can be imbued with several values simultaneously. For example, an aesthetically rich site can also hold great cultural significance, while also embodying economic value due to the presence of mineral deposits. History shows that actions occurring at sites where values intersect have shaped the relationships among and within interested groups. Analyses of interactions stimulated by those values and relationships has motivated a vibrant body of multidisciplinary international geoheritage scholarship. This scholarship provides insights into many historical events, enhancing how they are understood and communicated, while also providing justifations for conservation efforts at the sites being studied and others.

What is important, too, is that just as geoscience-enabled activities led to recognition of geoheritage sites of today, similar ongoing activities today will produce the new geoheritage sites of the future. Therefore, the deliberate extension of geoheritage principles across ongoing geoscience-connected activities can be expected to provide insights that allow people to anticipate and perhaps mitigate difficulties while enabling the benefits of enhanced understanding.

title: Integrating Hydrochemistry, Hydrostratigraphy, and Airborne Electromagnetic Data to Characterize Brackish Groundwater
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources (Posters)
authors: Tesfamichael, Tewodros [1], Timmons, Stacy S. [2], Guerra, Peter [3]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Tech, New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) New Mexico Tech, New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) New Mexico Tech, New Mexico Bureau of Mines and Mineral Resources, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
abstract:
Brackish groundwater is known to occur in the Estancia Basin of central New Mexico, but irregular sampling, limited vertical control, and incomplete well-construction records hinder delineation of its three-dimensional distribution. We integrated total dissolved solids (TDS) and major-ion chemistry, well-depth information, geology, hydrostratigraphy, and AEM resistivity to characterize brackish-groundwater, evaluate its hydrochemical controls, and identify priority domains for depth-specific verification.

Among available observations from 495 sites, 150 TDS concentrations ≥1,000 mg/L, 44 have concentrations ≥3,000 mg/L, and 5 have concentrations ≥10,000 mg/L; the maximum reported concentration is 42,657 mg/L. Major-ion data indicate that the hydrochemical evolved from fresh Ca-HCO₃ and Na-HCO₃ waters to sulfate- and chloride-rich waters with elevated TDS. These patterns are consistent with process related to mineral and evaporite dissolution, evapoconcentration, and longer residence times, but the available data do not establish a single basin-wide salinity source or unique hydrochemical evolution pathway. The strongest spatial trend between elevated-TDS observations and conductive AEM features occurs in the central and eastern basin, particularly valley-fill and playa-influenced area.

Existing depth information cannot establish transition depth, thickness, continuity of brackish groundwater volume. Depths below approximately 150 m, where current chemistry support is sparse. In 213 depth-aligned chemistry-AEM pairs, TDS and bulk resistivity remain unrelated (R 2 =0.009; Spearman rho=-0.019, p=0.780), suggesting that neither reported well depth nor AEM resistivity shows a statistically significant association. Comparisons are also affected by uncertainty in well locations, construction records, sampling dates, AEM resolution, and correspondence between estimated well-bottom elevations and actual producing intervals. Conductive AEM responses overlap with saline pore water, clay-rich sediments, lithologic variability, saturation, or combinations of these factors. AEM resistivity therefore cannot independently demarcate brackish groundwater or define its depth, thickness, or continuity.

This study presents a framework for integrating hydrochemical, hydrostratigraphic, and AEM evidence to prioritize brackish-groundwater verification targets without inferring resource extent from conductivity alone.

title: Understanding community-level heavy metal exposure pathways from contaminated groundwater sources in the Navajo Nation
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Holland, Angela [1], Carver, Monique [2], RoyChowdhury, Abhishek [3]
affiliations: (1) Natural and Applied Sciences Department, Bentley University, Waltham, MA, USA

abstract: A significant shortage of fresh water is a big challenge throughout the Navajo Nation, the largest federally recognized Native American Tribe in the United States. Currently, more than 30% of the Navajo homes lack access to safe and drinkable water. People need to haul water from far distances to fulfill their household needs. Navajo communities are predominantly dependent on ranching and farming. Livestock in the Navajo Nation mainly rely on windmill-pumped groundwater in which naturally elevated arsenic, uranium, and other heavy metals pose a serious threat to the animals’ well-being. The possibility of residual arsenic and uranium in animal meat and dairy products is an additional risk to humans. Our research group conducted a community survey to understand Navajo people’s water usage behavior and type of water sources used for daily activities. The questions tracked whether households used bottled water, water from regulated or unregulated sources, or rainwater for different purposes including drinking, cooking, bathing, gardening, and livestock use. The survey also asked people about their habits with water hauling practices such as whether they use the same barrels for regulated and unregulated sources, and how often the households cleaned their storage tanks. Survey results showed that although over 88% of the respondents use bottled water for drinking, over 44% of the respondents use water hauled from unregulated sources for livestock management. It was also found that over 58% of the respondents used the same barrels to haul water from both regulated and unregulated sources, while over 40% of the respondents never cleaned their barrels. This survey clearly displayed possible human exposure pathways for arsenic, uranium, lead, selenium, and other commonly found contaminants in groundwater of the Navajo Nation. The results of this survey will be used in future community outreach events such as Chapter House meetings to educate Navajo communities about these dangers and appropriate corrective measures.

title: Hydrostratigraphic Controls on Machine Learning Groundwater Prediction: Evidence from 35 Texas Monitoring Wells
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Omar, Ahmed [1], Chu, Tianxing [2], Murgulet, Dorina [3]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Environmental Sciences Department, Center for Water Supplies Studies, Conrad Blucher Institute for Surveying and Science, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA; Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Suez Canal University, Ismailia, Egypt, Arab Rep.
(2) Department of Computer Science, Conrad Blucher Institute for Surveying and Science, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
(3) Center for Water Supplies Studies, Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
abstract:
Predicting groundwater levels across heterogeneous aquifers is challenging because recharge, storage, hydraulic connectivity, and confinement vary spatially. We evaluated whether antecedent hydroclimatic information and hydrostratigraphic grouping improve XGBoost predictions of monthly depth to water (DTW) across 35 Texas monitoring wells classified as confined (15), semiconfined (5), or unconfined (15). Classification used aquifer designation, outcrop position, formation lithology, evidence of confining units, and available well information. Model inputs included GRACE water-storage anomalies, rainfall, normalized difference vegetation index, maximum and minimum temperature, hydraulic conductivity, slope, and sand percentage.

To prevent temporal leakage, observations were ordered chronologically within each well. The earliest 70% were used for training, the following 15% for validation, and the latest 15% for testing. Models using 2- and 12-month antecedent windows were evaluated on the same 6,320 model-ready observations. For the global model, extending the window from 2 to 12 months reduced test root mean squared error (RMSE) from 11.484 to 11.018 m and mean absolute error (MAE) from 7.135 to 6.974 m, while R² increased from 0.964 to 0.967, indicating a modest benefit from the longer window.

Using the 2-month window, and hydrostratigraphic grouping reduced RMSE from 15.409 to 12.909 m for confined wells, from 7.536 to 6.971 m for semiconfined wells, and from 7.199 to 6.173 m for unconfined wells. Corresponding MAE decreased from 9.957 to 9.605 m, from 6.234 to 5.746 m, and from 4.630 to 3.795 m, while R² increased from 0.957 to 0.970, from 0.966 to 0.971, and from 0.818 to 0.866. Overall, the findings indicate that hydrostratigraphic grouping enhances regional DTW prediction by capturing class-specific groundwater dynamics, although benefits vary across antecedent-window lengths and hydrostratigraphic settings. Incorporating hydrostratigraphic information directly into machine learning workflows may therefore improve the reliability and transferability of regional groundwater predictions.

title: Radiation Damage Annealing in a Natural Zircon: Domain-Dependent Kinetics from a Raman Step-Heating Experiment
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond (Posters)
authors: Wetmore, Allison [1], Rahl, Jeffrey M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
abstract:
Helium diffusion in zircon exerts a fundamental control on the accumulation of radiogenic ⁴He produced by alpha decay of U and Th, and must be well understood to yield robust thermochronologic interpretations. Helium diffusivity is strongly influenced by the accumulation of radiation damage, making the kinetics of damage annealing an important, though incompletely understood, component of (U-Th)/He thermochronology. Here we present results from a step-heating experiment on a zoned zircon from the Blue Ridge of central Virginia, to test whether a laboratory-calibrated annealing model reproduces the recovery behavior of a natural sample.

The grain was heated at 750°C in a muffle furnace for cumulative durations of 5 min, 30 min, 90 min, 180 min, 6 h, 12 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 96 h. In between each heating step, the grain was cooled and mapped by Raman spectroscopy on a 2 micron grid; maps were co-registered across steps using a custom MATLAB image-alignment routine. Because the analyzed domains lie on a crystal face oriented such that the nu3 mode is suppressed, radiation damage was tracked via the nu2 peak's FWHM and position, converted to alpha dose using a known empirical calibration. The grain is compositionally zoned with respect to its Raman properties, allowing us to track four domains spanning nu2-based alpha dose estimates from ~0.9 × 10¹⁸ α/g in the least-damaged domain to ≥1.8 × 10¹⁸ α/g in the most heavily damaged domains (exceeding the calibration's resolvable range prior to annealing).

All four domains show annealing with progressive heating, documented by decreasing FWHM and increasing peak position. However, application of a high-quality annealing model (Ginster et al., 2019) produces misfits in every domain, with the character of the discrepancy dependent on each domain's initial damage level, from a simple rate offset in the least-damaged domain to a significant deceleration in recovery rate in the most heavily damaged domains. All domains evolve continuously through the full experiment; in the studied parameter space, there is no evidence for an abrupt change in annealing rate indicative of a transition in annealing mechanism. These results highlight the challenge of applying laboratory-calibrated annealing models to natural zircon, and suggest that annealing behavior may depend on factors beyond current damage state and temperature alone.

title: What If Anything Replaced Late Cretaceous Ammonites in the Cenozoic Era?
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Veloso, Job Lukas [1]
affiliations: (1) Biology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract: Extinction provides a natural experiment for understanding the paleoecology of ancient species through their removal from communities. Convergent evolution often replaces extinct species with similar morphotypes. But does the same process refill food webs and trophic pyramids devastated by extinction by evolving dissimilar anatomies that nevertheless function in ecologically similar ways? And how often are particular morphologies/and or niches never replaced? In this talk we present new isotopic data from extant as well as extinct cephalopods (and other animals) to explore the questions about the effects of the total extinction of ammonite cephalopods by early in the Paleocene at the latest. We sampled a variety of Cenozoic to recent vertebrates and invertebrates for nitrogen and carbon isotopes, and validate this process by presenting community wide sampling from Late Cretaceous, ammonite and nautiloid bearing communities from the late Cretaceous of Vancouver Island and Baja California, as well as from the Eocene of Washington State and the London Clay, and compare these to community sampling from Mesophotic Zone communities in Fiji and Papua New Guinea. Sepiid cephalopods appear the most similar to many ammonites in terms of comparative isotopic values as well as jaw and radula morphology. The Cenozoic nautiloid Aturia appears to have evolved a goniatitic morphology convergent on ammonoids after the K Pg mass extinction.

title: Andes-like Elevations across the North American Cordillera in the Eocene
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse
authors: Cassel, Elizabeth J. [1], Smith, Michael Elliot [2], Acosta, R. Paul [3], Jicha, Brian R. [4], Breecker, Dan [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, MOSCOW, ID, USA
(2) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(3) Atmospheric, Oceanic & Earth Sciences Department, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA
(4) University of Wisconsin-Madison, Middleton, WI, USA
(5) University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
abstract: Earth's major mountain belts reflect a combination of tectonic plate boundary, internal, and mantle-derived stresses, as well as intraplate crustal thickness and buoyancy differences. Evidence for widespread Cretaceous and Paleogene mountain building extends across western North America, from the Pacific coast to the Rocky Mountains, yet the height and timing of their topographic development are poorly understood, limiting our understanding of the drivers of their evolution. To better understand the elevation history of the range, we reconstruct the magnitude of paleoelevations across the northern U.S. Cordillera from 58-26 million years ago using hydrogen stable isotope ratios from volcanic glasses. These glasses were hydrated by ancient precipitation, the hydrogen isotope ratios of which are directly affected by elevation. Our large, widespread dataset thus documents moisture transport from paleo-coastal locations to the continental interior at high-resolution, allowing for the continental scale comparison required to locate the range crest. Hydrogen stable isotope ratios progressively decrease by over 100‰ from the paleo-Pacific shoreline to western Montana and Wyoming. Isotope-enabled 3D climate modeling requires peak paleoelevations of at least 4.5 km circa 50 million years ago to explain these observations. Modeled Eocene topography includes a 500 km-wide area of high topography exceeding 3 km that stretched from the inactive Sierra Nevada arc to the Sevier thrust belt – the Nevadaplano. The highest paleoelevations, however, occur further east than previously hypothesized based on upper crustal deformation. They also persisted for tens of millions of years, necessitating lower crustal flow of orogenically thickened, thermally primed crust.

title: Can Probabilistic Models Address the Issue of Incomplete Landslide Inventory Dataset?
session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies (Posters)
authors: Pokhrel, Sushank [1], Patton, Annette [2]
affiliations: (1) Water Resources Graduate Program, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA
(2) College of Forestry, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA
abstract:
Accurate landslide early warning has the potential to save lives but requires understanding of the diverse conditions that may trigger landslides across large areas. Heavy precipitation is the primary driver of landslide initiation in Oregon. This study aims to improve landslide prediction models in western Oregon (the Cascades, the Coast Range and the Southwestern Interior) with the objectives to (a) derive landslide-triggering rainfall thresholds and analyze regional differences, (b) determine if soil moisture derived from a leaky-barrel hydrologic model improves the predictive performance of the model, and (c) develop models that can predict the probability of rainfall-triggered landslides with high spatial resolution. Furthermore, we hypothesize that limiting model training to areas with high quantity and quality of landslide reporting will mitigate the influence of reporter bias and incomplete landslide data.

Preliminary modeling uses gridded IMERG Late half-hourly precipitation with 0.1-degree resolution and landslide inventory dataset compiled from multiple sources, including the National Landslide Inventory V3 and records from the Oregon Department of Transportation. The study area was divided into 0.1-degree grid cells, and analysis was performed on “hotspot” cells with at least five recorded landslide events since 2000. To develop binary logistic regression models, the landslide dataset was coupled with three predictor variables (3-hour rainfall, 36-hour rainfall and soil moisture, representing short-duration rainfall, long-duration rainfall and soil saturation, respectively). The study further evaluates multiple combinations of these predictors using metrics such as Youden’s Index and Area Under the Curve (AUC) via a leave-one-out cross-validation approach to identify the best predictive model.

Preliminary analysis identified 113 “hotspot” pixels. A Type-I ANOVA for Generalized Linear Models in these pixels revealed that soil moisture does not improve the predictive performance of the model when 36- and 3-hour rainfall are already included as predictors. Furthermore, the initial threshold analysis suggests a high sensitivity of the models towards low-magnitude precipitation events. This reflects the issue of utilizing an incomplete landslide inventory dataset, where only a fraction (~7%) of the total dataset has complete temporal information. Ongoing work focuses on accounting for gaps in the temporal information of landslide events by implementing simulation techniques to evaluate the completeness of the landslide inventory dataset and refine it. This will help to calibrate the thresholds and further improve the predictive performance of the models.

title: Plagioclase Slip System Analysis of Progressively Developed Fabrics Across a Granulite Facies Shear Zone
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Flores, Deanna [1], Lusk, Alexander Dmitri [2], Tikoff, Basil [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(3) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
abstract:
The Morin anorthosite, Quebec, Canada, is a plagioclase-dominated intrusive complex with a largely undeformed main body and an eastern limb sheared by the granulite facies Morin shear zone (MSZ). Rocks deformed within the MSZ preserve three dominant deformational fabrics: protomylonites, mylonites, and ultramylonites. These are differentiated by foliation and lineation intensity, pyroxene content, dominant recrystallization mechanism, degree of grain size reduction, and deformation temperature. At the micro-scale, these fabrics range from mixed grain size, core-and-mantle relationships with discernible subgrains, to strongly foliated fabrics primarily consisting of relatively small grains with rare ribbon porphyroclasts.

For each fabric type, we performed crystallographic, electron backscattered diffraction-based analysis of dominant slip systems using a combination of inverse pole figures, crystallographic vorticity axes, and a subgrain-based method applied to porphyroclasts. In the subgrain-based method, orientation data across individual low-angle grain boundaries (LAGB) are plotted with the LAGB trace and local misorientation axes; the configuration among these constrains a unique slip plane and direction. Applying this approach, (010)[001] is the dominant slip system in bulge recrystallized mylonites and ultramylonites. Similarly, core porphyroclasts from core-and-mantle fabrics in the protomylonites also tend to favor (010)[001], but also accommodate strain through a broader range of active slip systems, including but not limited to: (100)[010], (010)[100], and (001)[010]. Ongoing weighted Burger’s vector analysis is expected to further resolve active slip systems in these rocks. Sample data, micrographs, and plots were compiled in StraboMicro to support porphyroclast-level comparison and future data accessibility and usability.

affiliations: (1) EarthScope Consortium, Washington, DC, USA

(3) EarthScope Consortium, Washington, DC, USA

abstract:
Becoming a geoscientist requires more than gaining scientific knowledge and technical skills. Students also need opportunities to explore career paths, practice professional communication, build relationships, and understand how their academic experiences can translate to the workplace. EarthScope Consortium, a non-profit which operates the NSF National Geophysical Facility (NGF), leads three summer internship programs supporting professional growth at different points in a student’s academic journey.

Geo-Launchpad introduces community college students, many with no previous research or internship experience, to research, technical skills, and careers through mentored geoscience projects. Research Experiences in Solid Earth Science for Students (RESESS) provides more advanced undergraduates with intensive mentored research experiences in geophysics. The EarthScope Student Career Internship Program serves undergraduates, recent graduates, and graduate students through project-based positions within EarthScope and the NSF NGF. Together, the programs create a progression from early exposure to more advanced research and career preparation.

EarthScope staff provide intentional professional development training to students in all three programs. The training is focused on goal setting, workplace professionalism, collaboration, networking, career exploration, and scientific communication for different audiences. Interns practice these skills through their projects, relationships with their mentors, interactions with geoscience professionals, and poster and oral presentations.

External evaluations of the internship programs conducted in 2024 and 2025 included intern surveys, focus groups, mentor surveys, and an alumni survey. Results show professional growth that reflects the different academic levels and goals of each program. In 2025, Geo-Launchpad interns reported that their understanding of geoscientists' daily work increased from 50% to 100%, while their ability to initiate networking interactions increased from 25% to 75%. Among RESESS interns, their awareness of resources for pursuing a career in science increased from 45% to 92%, and their comfort networking with professional scientists increased from 38% to 77%. Student Career interns reported that their understanding of daily work and career paths within scientific non-profit organizations increased from 25% to 100%. Internship alumni findings also suggest that these benefits last beyond the summer: 86% of Geo-Launchpad alumni reported that the internship helped them secure later educational or professional opportunities. External evaluations of the 2026 programs are underway, with results expected to demonstrate that interns in all three internship programs experience similar positive trends in professional growth.

title: Clumped and triple oxygen isotopes in pedogenic carbonates reveal temperature and seasonality across the late Paleocene–early Eocene in the Bighorn Basin, Wyoming
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Allen, Matthew L. [1], Wisniewski, Anna Lloyd [2], Unruh-Friesen, Evan [3], Newman, Will [4], Weaver, Lucas N. [5], Passey, Benjamin H. [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; University of Michigan Museum of Paleontology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
(5) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; University of Michigan Museum of Paleontology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
(6) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
abstract:
The late Paleocene–early Eocene (LPEE) hothouse interval experienced long-term warming punctuated by rapid hyperthermal events, yet terrestrial climate responses remain less well constrained than those of the oceans. Paleosol successions in the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming preserve an exceptional archive of continental environmental change, but most previous studies have focused on the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) and the early Eocene. Using legacy collections of pedogenic carbonates spanning the middle Tiffanian (~59 Ma) through the middle Wasatchian (~54 Ma) North American Land Mammal Ages (NALMAs), we combine clumped (Δ 47 ) and triple oxygen (Δ′ 17 O) isotope analyses to reconstruct both carbonate formation temperatures and the evaporative history of soil waters in paleosols.

Carbonate samples were screened for diagenetic alteration using isotopic criteria, while petrographic and electron microprobe analyses are ongoing. Preliminary results indicate that most samples preserve interpretable primary signals. Reconstructed carbonate formation temperatures range from approximately 18 to 35°C and, together with previously published datasets, reveal substantial variability throughout the succession. Reconstructed soil-water Δ′ 17 O values indicate substantial evaporative enrichment throughout the interval, which is surprising given previous interpretations of wet conditions before and after the PETM.

The magnitude of Δ 47 variability substantially exceeds changes in mean annual temperature predicted by climate model simulations and inferred from independent terrestrial proxy records. We therefore propose that part of this variability reflects shifts in the seasonality of pedogenic carbonate formation rather than changes in mean annual climate alone. Climate-model simulations suggest that greenhouse and orbital forcing can alter the seasonal distribution of precipitation, permitting either shoulder-season- or summer-weighted precipitation and pedogenic carbonate formation.

These results suggest that paired Δ 47 -Δ′ 17 O analyses may provide not only independent constraints on terrestrial temperature and water availability but also insight into the seasonality of pedogenic carbonate formation and precipitation across ancient greenhouse climates.

title: Calderas, Cauldrons, and Coexistence: Scientific Heritage and Geoheritage Lessons from the San Juan and Mogollon–Datil Volcanic Fields
session_title: Mining Heritage in the United States: Linking Historical Use with Geoconservation Practices
authors: Tormey, Daniel R. [1]
affiliations: (1) Catalyst Environmental Solutions, Catalyst Environmental Solutions, Santa Monica, CA, USA
abstract:
The San Juan volcanic field of Colorado and the Mogollon–Datil volcanic field of New Mexico preserve two of the most important records of the mid-Cenozoic ignimbrite flare-up in western North America. Together they record more than 20,000 km³ of silicic volcanism between about 40 and 18 Ma, including dense caldera clusters, resurgent structures, regionally extensive ignimbrites, and the Fish Canyon Tuff, one of the largest known explosive eruptions on Earth. They are also scientific heritage landscapes: places where field mapping and synthesis by generations of geologists, from Burbank’s recognition of a San Juan “volcanic sink,” through Smith and Bailey’s resurgent-cauldron model, to Lipman’s caldera mapping and Cordilleran synthesis, helped establish the modern understanding of large silicic systems.

That intellectual lineage is part of the geoheritage. The landscapes preserve not only the products of crustal-scale magmatism, but also the field relationships through which fundamental concepts of caldera collapse, resurgence, ignimbrite emplacement, tectono-magmatic evolution, and magmatic–hydrothermal ore formation were recognized and tested.

The same volcanic systems also created the hydrothermal mineralization that supported major mining districts, especially in the San Juan field. This produces a management paradox in protected landscapes: mining may threaten or obscure volcanic features and leave significant environmental legacies, yet mining and industrial heritage are also process-linked consequences of the volcanic system and part of the cultural and scientific story.

Using the San Juan and Mogollon–Datil fields as paired case studies, we present a coexistence framework for managing volcanic geoheritage and mining heritage together. Core functions include joint inventory, risk-based access, integrated interpretation, legacy-mine remediation that preserves representative exposures where feasible, and explicit geoheritage recognition in protected-area planning. The broader lesson is that protection alone does not ensure recognition. These volcanic provinces should be managed as layered landscapes: natural archives of the ignimbrite flare-up, mining and cultural landscapes, protected areas, and scientific heritage terrains shaped by the people who learned how to read them.

abstract: The Fram Strait is a critical study area for evaluating global climate trends and deep-water mass exchanges between the Arctic and North Atlantic Oceans. The International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 403 recovered multiple sediment cores from the Eastern Fram Strait in 2024. This study examines the high-resolution sedimentary and porewater geochemistry from Sites U1624 (Isfjorden Drift) and U1618 (Vestnesa Ridge). Porewater chemistry was determined onboard the JOIDES Resolution. Sequential chemical extractions via sodium acetate (carbonate phase extraction), ascorbic acid (reactive phase extraction), and sodium dithionite (crystalline phase extraction) were carried out on frozen sediment samples. Iron (Fe) and Manganese (Mn) phases were extracted, along with associated trace metals. Fe and Mn were found to covary through depth intervals, which indicates both were responding to similar redox-controlled mobilization and precipitation processes. Cobalt, nickel, copper, and vanadium occurrences broadly followed the Fe-and Mn-oxide phases. This is notable, as these elements are commonly incorporated into Fe- and Mn-oxides during diagenesis. Reactive and crystalline Fe phases show strong downcore variability, especially at Site U1618, suggesting repeated shifts in depositional and/or porewater redox conditions during sediment burial. Compared to Site U1624, Site U1618 preserves stronger redox variability and greater evidence of diagenetic overprinting, highlighting the importance of local depositional and diagenetic controls on geochemical records from the Eastern Fram Strait.

title: Geochemical Records of Environmental Change and Human Activity During the Classic Maya Period at Cenote Xcach
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES
authors: Frederick, Kate M [1], Lane, Parker [2], Arnold, T. Elliott [3], Vachula, Richard S [4], Waters, Matt [5]
affiliations: (1) West Chester University, West Chester, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) West Chester University, West Chester, Pennsylvania, USA

abstract: During the Classic Period (200-950 CE), the ancient Maya civilization underwent substantial environmental stress from deforestation, erosion and drought across the Yucatán region and population growth. Although anthropogenic environmental degradation and socio-political instability have been proposed as drivers of this shift, critical geographic gaps remain between these regions. Here we present organic bulk and biomarker data from a high-resolution sediment core from Cenote Xcach, a previously unstudied lake located in the northern Yucatán lowlands. We employed a multi-proxy geochemical approach to reconstruct human occupation and agricultural activity at Xcach. Stable isotopes of nitrogen (δ¹⁵N) and total organic carbon-to-nitrogen (TOC:TN) ratios were used to determine changes in organic matter source to the lake. These data were coupled with phosphorus (P), mercury (Hg), and fecal stanol abundances, which reflect lake productivity, the cultural use of cinnabar-based vermilion pigment, and human population change, respectively. Phosphorus and Hg concentrations exhibit strong positive relationships with bulk δ¹⁵N values. A pronounced δ¹⁵N enrichment (ca. 4‰) during the Classic Period coincides with elevated P concentrations, consistent with increased nutrient loading associated with human wastewater inputs, agricultural fertilization, and/or slash-and-burn land management. Following this peak, declining δ¹⁵N values during the post-Classic period correspond with a marked increase in TOC ratios (>10), indicating a transition toward greater terrestrial organic matter input and forest regrowth after possible site depopulation. Together, these complementary proxies document a sequence of intensified land use, elevated demographic pressure, and subsequent ecological recovery. Ongoing analysis of charcoal abundances and coprostanol concentrations will further constrain the timing and magnitude of population change, agricultural practices, and fire activity at this minimally studied site, adding to the complexity of environmental pressures on the Classic Maya prior to the Terminal Collapse.

abstract: Fossilized shark tooth enameloid is demonstrated to preserve original isotopic values that reflect an individual’s ecology and habitat preferences even at geologic timescales. The Eocene (56–33.9 Ma) marks a major climate transition from greenhouse to icehouse conditions. During such climate fluctuations, shark teeth can provide important information about the environmental conditions of marine environments and the ecological impacts of climate transitions over time. In this study, we measured the stable phosphate oxygen (δ 18 O p ) and zinc (δ 66 Zn) isotope compositions in enameloid as well as estimated total body lengths (TL) from tooth crown heights of the extinct sand tiger sharks Striatolamia macrota and Carcharias sp. from seven different marginal marine localities in the Gulf of Mexico that span the Eocene. We then compared shark δ 18 O p values to isotope-enabled Eocene iCESM climate model outputs of predicted δ 18 O p * values within the Gulf Coastal Plain to assess possible migration and habitat use over time. The δ 18 O p values suggest that extinct sand tigers were likely ectothermic, recording surrounding seawater temperature, similar to extant sand tiger sharks. These marginal marine environments supported a variety of ontogenetic stages based on the range of TL estimates. Previous studies of tooth size distribution indicate some localities as nursery versus adult habitats, but δ 18 O p values do not suggest ontogenetic habitat partitioning within or across localities. Rather, across ontogeny, extinct sand tiger sharks likely tracked preferred environmental conditions over shallow marine habitats in the Gulf of Mexico and possibly the Western North Atlantic as seasonality increased across the Eocene. Extinct sand tiger shark δ 18 O p values are broadly consistent with regional and global sea temperature cooling trends. Preliminary δ 66 Zn values suggest a relationship between TL and inferred trophic position at some localities. This study is the first to assess the utility of extinct sand tigers as recorders of ambient conditions and impacts of climate change on shark ecology from the Eocene Gulf of Mexico. Our results demonstrate that extinct sand tigers provide robust records of shallow marine conditions while simultaneously capturing aspects of shark ecology.

title: Active Faults as Hydraulic Barriers to Cross-Fault Flow: Compartmentalization and Pumping-Induced Stress on the Earthquake Valley Fault, Southern California, with M6+ Potential
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
authors: Weingarten, Matthew [1], Fisher, Jennasea [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, San Diego State University, San Diego, CA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, San Diego, California, USA
abstract: Active faults can act as barriers to groundwater flow, dividing a basin into compartments that respond independently to pumping. Here, we examine the Earthquake Valley Fault (EVF) in Warner Basin, southern California - a subvertical, dextral strike-slip fault that transfers slip between the Elsinore and San Jacinto faults at about 2 mm/yr and last ruptured at ~M6.3 around 1890. Groundwater has been pumped from Warner Basin since the 1950s at 7.4 to 8.6 million cubic meters per year, and wells on both sides of the fault have long records. Using intervals when one compartment was pumped while adjacent compartments were monitored, we found that the Agua Tibia South strand of the EVF behaves as a strong barrier. Drawdown is large in the pumped compartment and hydraulic conductivity estimates vary by two orders of magnitude across the structure. Finally, we reconstruct the transient pressure and stress history on the fault by computing the pumping-induced poroelastic stress changes. Pressure and stress change are asymmetric across the fault and comparable in magnitude to the tectonic loading rate. Groundwater use in the basin is a measurable part of the stress budget on the Earthquake Valley Fault, which has not ruptured since 1890.

title: Differential Evolution of Body-Size-Space in Paleozoic Marine Invertebrates
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology
authors: Nikolic, Mark [1], Heim, Noel A. [2], Monarrez, Pedro M. [3], Payne, Jonathan L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
(2) Tufts University, Medford, MA,
(3) Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA,
(4) Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
abstract: Body size often gets overlooked in metazoan disparity studies in favour of more complex multidimensional trait spaces. This gap represents a missed opportunity as an animal’s body size is one of its most fundamental and least abstract traits. It is also perhaps the most studied morphological trait, yet it has never been subject to broad-scale analysis of disparity through time. Here, we assessed the evolution of body-size through time in nine classes of marine invertebrates from their first appearances in the Cambrian and Ordovician radiations until the end of the Permian. We analysed the rate of expansion of the body-size-space and characterised its differential filling through time in each group, including across two mass extinction events. To do this, we utilised a dataset of biovolume and stratigraphic age information for >10,000 metazoan genera across the Paleozoic. Moreover, we jointly simulated body-size evolution on trees using parameters extracted from the diversification history for each class under several evolutionary scenarios to allow multiple-hypothesis testing. We find that for most - but not every - class, the rate of body-size-space expansion is highest, and the maximal range occurs, very early in the lineage’s evolutionary history. The evolution of disparity also generally occurs faster than expected under brownian motion given each clades diversification history: indicating an ‘early burst’. However, the filling of the space generally lags behind, and the generating processes differ among clades. In general, mass extinctions tend to have little effect on total body-size disparity within a class, but they differ in the dynamics of replacement and successive diversification of subclades. We provide the first attempt to define, quantify and characterise the body-size-space in one of the most important intervals of time in the history of life. Early bursts of evolution in body-size appear to be common, but their dynamics differ in complex and nuanced ways among higher clades.

title: Evolution of the Atrypida (Brachiopoda) through space and time: a case study of evolution through biodiversification and extinction events
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns
authors: Sproat, Colin David [1], Huang, Bing [2], Baarli, B. Gudveig [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Canada
(2) Key Laboratory of Palaeobiology and Petroleum Stratigraphy, Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing, China

(4) Department of Geosciences, Wachenheim Science Center, Williams College, Williamstown, Massachusetts, USA
abstract: The Atrypida brachiopod order evolved during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event and were among the most common brachiopods in tropical paleoenvironmental settings through the Silurian and Devonian before their extinction during the Frasnian-Famennian event in the Late Devonian. As shown by a recently revised phylogenetic tree, many fundamental characters of the order evolved early in the evolution of the lineage followed by a period of relative stasis where much of the earlier morphological disparity was pruned from the evolutionary tree. These features, such as the orientation of the spiralia and associated structures evolved in different parts of the world in the Late Ordovician. For example, the early clade containing Anazygidae had spiralial orientations varying from apices that were medially to dorsomedially oriented. Despite these differences, taxa within this group such as Zygospira, and Catatzyga had a solid jugum connecting their spiralia, strong dorsal sulcus and ventral fold and became common in the shallow marine platforms and basins of Laurentia in the Late Ordovician. Conversely, the Spirigerinidae evolved separated jugal processes instead of a jugum, strong ventral sulcus and dorsal fold and were common on the plates and terranes that comprise central and eastern Asia today. Both lineages were affected by the Late Ordovician Mass Extinction but following the mass extinction endemism broke down and the surviving lineages shared a increasingly dorsibiconvex shell profile with large, dorsomedially-directed spiralia with jugal processes and increasingly large size. The only significant traits to evolve at this time were a concavoconvex profile and spiralial grooves. Although diversity continued to increase, little evolutionary innovation led to stagnation of the lineage. An initial pulse of extinction in the Pridoli marked the final disappearance of the early atrypide lineages, including the Protatrypinae and Clintonellinae, and the beginning of the decline of the Lissatypidae and Septatrypinae. Part of this decline was reversed by the explosion in diversity of the large convex atrypides with large spiralia within the Variatrypinae, Atrypinellinae, and Spinatrypinae through the Devonian but these relatively evolutionarily conservative lineages were unable to prevent the ultimate demise of the lineage during the Late Devonian. This underscores that lineages with high biodiversity may be vulnerable to extinction if their morphology is so constrained that natural selection cannot adapt the lineage to environmental and ecological changes.

title: The Impact of Inherited Structures on the Subduction Zone Lower Plate Interface: Insights from the Exhumed Attic Cycladic Crystalline Complex, Greece.
session_title: Undergraduate and Graduate Geoscience Student Research Showcase
authors: Stockli, Daniel F. [1], Turek, Sage [2], Soukis, Konstantinos [3], Laskari, Sofia [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(2) University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(3) National and Kapodistrian Univ Athens,, Faculty of Geology and Geoenviron, Athens,
(4) National and Kapodistrian Univ Athens,, Faculty of Geology and Geoenvironment, Athens, Greece
abstract:
Understanding the dynamics of subduction zones is one of the most active areas of geological research because of their fundamental role in controlling natural hazards and resources. The study of high-pressure low-temperature (HP/LT) rocks formed within subduction zones that are in exhumed by metamorphic core complexes provides a unique opportunity to investigate otherwise inaccessible deep crustal processes. Particularly, those rocks that derive from the uppermost portion of the subducting lower plate offer valuable constraints on the mechanisms governing subduction zone evolution. Furthermore, the geometry and structural architecture of the incoming lower plate can significantly influence the development of the subduction interface. Such inherited structures may affect subduction zone evolution and the processes operating within the subduction channel.

The Attic-Cycladic Crystalline Complex (ACCC, Aegean Sea, Greece) comprises rocks exhumed from the Hellenic Subduction Zone, and is one of the leading areas for studying subduction zone evolution, particularly processes related to the subduction channel. The geology on the Cycladic islands of Andros and Tinos is dominated by the Cycladic Blueschist Unit (CBU), which occupies most of the lower plate. The CBU is characterized by a series of structurally stacked underplated slices that formed during subduction and were subsequently exhumed as part of the ACCC, and attenuated during extensional deformation associated with the North Cycladic Detachment System (NCDS).

This study identifies and compares the underplated units of Andros and Tinos to determine the influence of the original stratigraphic sequence on duplex formation and underplating geometry. U-Pb geochronology has provided provenance history and maximum depositional ages (MDAs), which are integrated with field and microstructural analysis. This multidisciplinary approach provides information on the original depositional geometry and elucidates the process leading to coherent underplating versus periods of successive stacking along the subduction channel. Our results reveal that there are significantly more underplated units in Tinos, while the Andros samples share similar detrital provenances and were coherently underplated. We attribute these differences to the original stratigraphy of the downgoing plate, which strongly controls the architecture of the subduction channel and the number of underplated slices.

title: Applying Three Luminescence Dating Methods on Late Quaternary Glacial Moraines in the Beartooth Mountains, Montana, USA
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations
authors: Smith, Cindy Lou Mei-Ying Skipper [1], Brown, Nathan D. [2], Barth, Aaron M. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Texas Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA
(3) Geology, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ, USA
abstract:
Reconstructing the chronology of cirque glaciers’ advance and retreat helps to inform the historical climatic conditions in a region. In this study, we apply three luminescence dating techniques to three different morainal sequences associated with cirque glaciers in the Beartooth Mountains, located in the southern region of Montana and northern Wyoming. These glaciers have previously been constrained with Be-10 surface exposure dating of morainal boulders, revealing a late Holocene readvance. We collected samples from both previously sampled and unsampled boulders, as well as sediment from nearby morainal till. The sediment samples were collected in several transects, as close as possible from the crest of the lateral moraines to the modern ice margin. The three luminescence methods applied are rock surface exposure dating, utilizing boulder samples, sediment burial dating, utilizing morainal till, and portable luminescence reader signals, also from morainal till. Be-10 is more commonly used to date glacial moraines than luminescence, and especially in simple exposure scenarios. Be-10 is very useful on timescales ranging from thousands to millions of years, whereas luminescence is typically best used on timescales ranging from several days to several thousand years.

Our initial results show that there is some agreement between Be-10 and luminescence rock surface exposure ages, however with a high degree of scatter and with no systematic offset between techniques. Luminescence rock ages found in our study range from 100 to 10,000 years, and Be-10 ages from Barth et al. 2022 range from 700 to 2,250 years. In addition to this, sediment burial ages are in the proper stratigraphic order, and the burial ages themselves are comparable with the Be-10 results, ranging from 800 to 13,000 years. There is some systematic relationship observed along the transects in the portable luminescence reader results, however no dates as these results do not themselves yield ages. Here we will discuss possible interpretations for this observed scatter between methods, and provide updated results. There is strong potential for developing luminescence methods for morainal deposition, particularly within the Holocene, helping to quicken sample preparation time and reduce research expenses, compared to Be-10 and other cosmogenic radionuclide techniques.

title: Defining Shallow-Water Redox Conditions Across the SPICE in the Central Appalachian Mountains
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Posters)
authors: Irizarry, Kayla [1], Hagen, Amy [2], Gill, Benjamin [3], Lau, Kimberly [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA
(3) Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA
(4) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
abstract:
The Steptoean Positive Isotopic Carbon Excursion, or SPICE event, was a global +3–6‰ shift in δ 13 C values during the late Cambrian (~493 Ma). It has been hypothesized that this event represents widespread marine deoxygenation prompting biological turnover and increased burial of organic carbon, driving a positive carbon isotope excursion. However, more work is needed to assess the timing and magnitude of redox changes in shallow water tropical environments. Here, we present two proxies for local redox conditions, the cerium anomaly (Ce/Ce*) and iodine to calcium ratios, along with complementary major and trace element concentration data, to constrain redox conditions in two shallow carbonate sections from Clear Spring, Maryland and Lebanon, Virginia, USA that record the SPICE. Both sections are composed of dominantly peritidal with minor subtidal carbonate shoal facies, but the Clear Spring section exhibits greater facies variability compared to the Lebanon section.

At the Lebanon section, Ce/Ce* results record anoxic conditions through the SPICE interval (mean = 1.18) and a shift towards more oxic conditions (mean = 0.87) concurrent with a return to background carbon isotope values. The Clear Spring section records persistently anoxic conditions, with relatively invariant Ce/Ce* values through the Pre-SPICE, SPICE, and Post-SPICE interval (mean = 1.1). In this section, inferred anoxic conditions are supported by I/Ca ratios, which are consistently low (<1 μmol/mol) throughout the section. These preliminary results indicate that the deeper-water Lebanon section records a redox shift, with more anoxic seawater corresponding to the SPICE and a shift towards more oxic conditions in the falling limb and post-SPICE interval. The contrasting persistently anoxic conditions that are recorded in the Clear Spring section suggest a highly heterogenous redox landscape across the shelf in the Appalachian Basin during the SPICE.

title: Tectonic Orogenic Field Theory (TOFT): Vortextural Volumetric Tensor Geometry for Rock Deformation
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics
authors: Bean, Henry Patrick [1]
affiliations: (1) Salem, VA,
abstract:
Tectonic Orogenic Field Theory (TOFT) proposes a conservation-based geotectonic framework in which the finite-strain ellipsoid is reinterpreted as the three-dimensional fundamental volumetric tensor cell of geologic structure rather than solely a descriptive kinematic marker. Using the Cell Method, deforming rock masses are algebraically discretized into self-similar fractal, offset stacked, primary and dual tensor cells complexes governed by the principle of least action and the conservation of mass, energy, matter, momentum, inertia, and force. Finite-strain density is interpreted as a geometric proxy for cumulative tectonic work and force–strain fields through geological spacetime and is further proposed to represent the fossilized macroscopic expression of the four fundamental forces active during rock deformation.

TOFT proposes that rock deformation is homologous by analogy to the deformation of all matter subjected to stress. Structural Homology describes the global conservation-controlled force–strain field that is independent of scale, rheology, and tectonic environment, whereas Structural analogy describes the local material response governed by mineralogy, chemistry, crystallography, fluids, boundary conditions, and deformation history. Structural variability therefore reflects different expressions of a common volumetric tensor topology viewed from local perspective.

The governing relationship, RM⁴O ≥±≤ E²S²TF², expresses dynamic equilibrium between the Rock–Mass–Matter–Mechanics–Matrix of Orogen and the Ellipsoidal–Energy–Stress–Strain–Tectonic–Force–Field. Each ellipsoid manifold preserves finite-strain density, vortextural rotational history, energy distribution, structural memory, and tensor orientation. These tensor cells form a multiscale hierarchy linking crystal lattices, mineral grains, rock fabrics, folds, shear zones, faults, terranes, and mountain belts with lithospheric global deformation through common conservation principles.

TOFT predicts that finite-strain density, vortextural rotational geometry, tensor orientations, and volumetric topology exhibit conservation-governed scale invariance across geological scales and spacetime. This hypothesis is globally repeatable and mappable, by comparing these properties using multiperspective observation, algorithmic analysis and geophysical imaging. Resulting three-dimensional Cell Method models, support TOFT as a unified predictive framework for orogenic evolution, whereas systematic departures would define the theory's limits and guide refinement.
