title: Using seasonal temperature patterns at karst springs to constrain matrix input
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Covington, Matthew D. [1], Dzikowski, Roman [2], Luhmann, Andrew James [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(3) Wheaton College, Earth and Environmental Science, Wheaton, IL, USA
abstract: In a study of thermal patterns at 11 springs in the mantled karst of NW Arkansas, we found that most (9) of these sites had a detectable seasonal variation in temperature with a range of amplitudes and lags behind air temperature. While previous work on seasonal temperature patterns has focused on the production of seasonal variations by either sinking streams (in-phase variation) or temperature conduction to depth in shallow aquifers (out-of-phase variation), we also consider damping and lag relationships produced by flow through a conduit or porous media. Both of these models predict relationships between the amplitude and lag of thermal signals when compared against air temperature. Such relationships allow us to examine a continuum of seasonal thermal behaviors from in-phase to highly lagged. Offset from the theoretical relationship can be produced by introduction of matrix flow, defined as water with no temperature variation. Matrix input reduces signal amplitude but does not influence lag. Therefore, these offsets can potentially be used to estimate matrix contributions to a given spring from analysis of the amplitude and lag of the seasonal signal. At the NW Arkansas sites, we find a strong negative correlation between event scale variability in temperature and estimated matrix fraction, such that sites with greater estimated matrix fractions show less variation in temperature due to storms or other recharge events. Here, we also extend this work using temperature data from a broader set of karst sites outside of Arkansas to further explore the hypothesis that matrix contribution can be estimated using seasonal temperature signals.

title: Deciphering the Tempo and Causes of the K/Pg Mass Extinction: A Case History From Seymour Island, Antarctica
session_title: Data-driven approaches for aligning geologic information in time
authors: Ward, Peter Douglas [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Biology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract: The causes of mass extinctions have been a principal area of paleobiological research since the time of Cuvier and d’Orbigny. This is certainly the case for understanding the events that produced the K/Pg mass extinction, with asteroid impact, Deccan Trap-driven global warming, or some combination of the two being invoked in this century’s literature. Here we present new data on paleontological ranges, sequence stratigraphy, and light stable isotopes from Seymour Island, Antarctica, and we compare these findings to coeval strata in the Bay of Biscay. We present an alternative to the published two-phase extinction model of Tobin (2017) and argue that the pattern of last occurrences is consistent with a single extinction episode at the K/Pg boundary, with one or more earlier pulses of last occurrences that have a sequence-stratigraphic origin. We underscore that last occurrences cannot generally be read as times of extinction; having them reflect times of extinction requires a large (>0.9) and near-constant per-bed probability of occurrence, neither of which is generally true. We also present new data showing the presence of widespread cold seep influences on molluscan shell growth. Last, we present the first trophic-level estimates for mollusks spanning the K/Pg boundary in Antarctica, based on a new method of extracting nitrogen isotopes from aragonitic fossils. These data are combined with new C meta estimates of ammonite activity that were first defined by Tobin and Ward (2015) for Antarctic mollusks, but for which no species-level data identification was available until this talk.

title: Hydrogeologic Controls on Groundwater Recharge across an Elevation Gradient, Northern Colorado Rockies
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers (Posters)
authors: Largo, Randy [1], Rugenstein, Jeremy [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geoscience, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: Groundwater stored in deep aquifers is a critical water resource along Colorado's Front Range, yet recharge sources and hydrologic connectivity between surface and groundwater remain poorly constrained. This study investigates the connectivity between precipitation, surface water, and deep bedrock aquifers in Northern Colorado. We sampled monthly precipitation, stream, and groundwater in the northern Front Range across an elevation gradient and analyzed the oxygen (𝛿 18 O) and hydrogen (𝛿 2 H) values of these samples. To ensure a large spatial sampling network, we enlisted multiple citizen science volunteers to sample their residential wells, which range in depth between 380 and 600 ft depth. We supplement this well data set with three precipitation samplers and a long-term time series of steam samples from the Front Range. Preliminary results show that groundwater 𝛿 18 O and 𝛿 2 H values become progressively more depleted with increasing elevation, consistent with the altitude effect observed in meteoric precipitation. Mean groundwater 𝛿 18 O exhibits a significant negative relationship with elevation, yielding an isotope lapse rate of -5.75 ‰/km (R 2 = 0.43, p =0.0016. This groundwater lapse rate provides a quantitative basis for comparison with precipitation and stream water isotope elevation relationships to evaluate recharge processes across the Colorado Front Range. In contrast, 𝛿 18 O and 𝛿 2 H exhibits no consistent relationship with well depth (125 to 600ft) and most groundwater sites display only limited seasonal variability throughout the year. Groundwater samples plot on or near the global Meteoric Water Line, indicating recharge is primarily derived from meteoric precipitation with minimal evaporative modification prior to recharge. The results will be used to assess the connectivity between local precipitation and stream water and groundwater recharge as well as groundwater contributions to streamflow. Understanding these processes is increasingly important as declining snowpack, earlier snowmelt, and more frequent drought place greater pressure on groundwater resources. By improving characterization of recharge sources and groundwater-surface water interactions, we aim to better inform water resource management for the rural households that rely on bedrock aquifers for water. This study also engages local communities through a volunteer sampling network, increasing spatial coverage while enhancing public awareness of groundwater sustainability in regions reliant on private wells.

title: Structure and Kinematic Evolution of the Naga Fold-Thrust Belt, Northeast India
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Posters)
authors: Swartz, Jackson P. [1], Betka, Paul M. [2], Rakshit, Raghupratim [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA, USA
(2) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA,
(3) Department of Geology, Jagannath Barooah University, Jorhat, Assam, India
abstract: The central Himalayan orogen is uplifted due to progressive indentation of the Eurasian plate by the Indian plate. At the eastern terminus of this collision, the Burma sliver terrane, a microplate, converges obliquely with the trailing edge of the Indian plate. This collision forms a triple junction of fault systems between the Indian, Eurasian, and Burman plates. The southwest arm of the India-Eurasia-Burma triple junction is the Naga fold-thrust belt, a 280 km-long accretionary wedge that has been variously interpreted as representing dextral transpression and thrusting between the Indian and Burma plates. This study investigates the kinematic evolution of the Naga fold-thrust belt in northeast India using field mapping, fault-slip analysis, and the construction of balanced cross-sections along three transects across the frontal thrusts. Results demonstrate that a partitioned transpression model best explains the kinematic evolution of the Naga fold-thrust belt. A series of imbricate NE-striking, SE-dipping thrust faults was observed in the foreland, between the frontal Naga thrust in the NW and the out-of-sequence Disang thrust in the SE. Progressive counterclockwise rotation of bedding orientations southeast of the Disang thrust is consistent with a partitioned component of left-lateral strike-slip shear in the hinterland. Shortening estimates derived from kinematic modeling for the frontal structures along the three transects are 34.3 ± 10 km, 31.9 ± 11 km, and 30.0 ± 9 km from southwest to northeast. A single, shallowly dipping, continuous detachment with a footwall ramp is favored over multiple stratigraphically controlled detachments. Slip over the footwall ramp forms a forelimb that explains the formation of the regional syncline observed in the hanging wall of the Disang thrust. The Disang thrust is interpreted as an out-of-sequence thrust that formed to restore critical taper following subcritical wedge development. The rheological contrast between the weak Disang Group shales and the competent Tipam and Barail sandstones is inferred to control the transition from discrete thrust propagation in the foreland to distributed transpressive deformation in the hinterland. A depth-to-detachment contour map and three-dimensional detachment model provide geometric constraints on the subsurface rupture geometry for future hazard assessment. The frontal thrust system is segmented along strike, which may have important implications for seismic hazard analysis, as not all frontal structures may fully rupture in a large earthquake.

abstract:
Drone imagery has been collected in concert with two separate sampling campaigns and stratigraphic mapping across the Cretaceous Hell Creek (HC) and Paleogene Fort Union (FU) formations in Montana and South Dakota to constrain sample positioning and evaluate stratigraphic continuity in both areas. Each of the sites presented here spans the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K/Pg) boundary: Lahti Butte, SD, including a new boundary locality captured in the same survey, and Iridium Hill, Nirvana, Biscuit Butte, and adjacent exposures north of Jordan, MT.

Imagery was flown at a range of altitudes and processed into rectified orthophotographs and digital surface models with ~0.02-m resolution. Where available, publicly available airborne lidar grids served as the geodetic base, and shifts were applied to align the drone products horizontally and vertically.

For sampling across the K/Pg boundary, stratigraphic boundaries are necessarily resolved by cm- to mm-scale observations and sampling at outcrop, providing the critical link between geochemical and biological markers across the K/Pg boundary. Ongoing work at these sites includes sedimentary mercury and total organic carbon chemostratigraphy, palynostratigraphy, and megafloral and other paleontological collecting, all of which depend on precisely placing a sample or specimen within the stratigraphic record relative to the boundary. The drone products do not replace that fieldwork; rather, precise 3D positioning places each measured section, sample site, and locality within a common spatial framework and allows key surfaces to be traced laterally beyond existing sample sites. We are using these data to reconstruct 3D stratigraphic relationships among sites and to quantify lateral and vertical continuity, both to test whether stratigraphic and geochemical signatures are regionally persistent or reflect local depositional architecture, and to target future sampling.

Each survey is also a snapshot of a rapidly eroding landscape, and with repeated surveys, it converts these perishable outcrops into a time series, documenting the exposure and loss of the boundary interval while permanently archiving localities and sample sites. The combined imagery, models, and video also support virtual field trips into these historically consequential sections.

authors: Hunt, Brian B. [1], Helper, Mark A. [2], Scheirer, Daniel [3], Walter, Callum A. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas at Austin, Bureau of Economic Geology, Austin, TX, USA

abstract: The Trans-Pecos Volcanic Field—the southernmost conterminous US volcanic field—is a Tertiary volcanic-arc and rift system spanning 48–17 Ma. Rocks comprise a diverse magmatic suite with mafic, intermediate, and alkali-rich compositions. In the Davis Mountains, rocks are predominantly felsic (peralkaline rhyolites and quartz trachytes) and include calderas previously identified through geologic mapping and petrographic studies (Parker and Henderson, 2021). These rocks hold high potential for critical minerals, including rare earth elements, therefore geologic maps of these features are important. However, recent compilation geologic mapping for STATEMAP confirms that the topographic and structural margins of the Paradise Mountain (35.8 Ma) and El Muerto (36.6 Ma) calderas in the Davis Mountains remain poorly constrained by field observations and geologic mapping alone. This study utilizes a May 2026 USGS data release of high-resolution airborne magnetic surveys, funded by the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, to map structural boundaries of these caldera systems. Released digital datasets include reduced-to-pole total magnetic intensity (TMI) and first vertical derivative (1VD) rasters (Scheirer and Walter, 2026; https://doi.org/10.5066/P1EOKG6I). We integrated datasets with existing geologic maps and field observations to provide an initial map of the structural boundaries of the Paradise Mountain and El Muerto calderas. The 1VD layer was particularly effective for mapping because it enhances shallow geological features, sharpens anomalies, and suppresses deep regional signals. In the Davis Mountains, the data reveal a large, NW-trending igneous body defining the Davis Igneous Complex, with well-defined arcuate features on the TMI. The 1VD further reveals internal arcuate structures interpreted as structural margins and intra-caldera faults of the Paradise Mountain and El Muerto calderas. In addition, the magnetic data can help identify Basin and Range normal faults and pyroclastic or other volcanic flow deposits. The approach to mapping the calderas in the Davis Mountains was validated in the volcanic Chinati Mountains located 100 km southwest of the Davis Mountains along the US-Mexico border. Geologic mapping by Cepeda and Henry (1983) demonstrate a near 1:1 correlation between structures interpreted on the 1VD magnetic data and previously mapped structural margins of the overlapping Chinati (33.0 Ma) and Infiernito (37.3 Ma) calderas. Ultimately, high-resolution magnetic data prove to be an effective tool for identifying and mapping calderas, faults, and related igneous structures.

title: Following Jay Quade’s Footsteps: Using Triple Oxygen Isotopes to Open More Windows into Ancient Landscapes and Climates
session_title: Unraveling Earth's Stories in Extreme Environments through Field Geology and Isotope Geochemistry: A session in honor of Jay Quade (Posters)
authors: Levin, Naomi E. [1], Gardin, Axelle [2], Lee, Elena Y. [3], Mengesha, Million Alemayehu [4], Waters, Eric R [5], Passey, Benjamin H. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(2) Institut des Sciences de l’Évolution de Montpellier, Université de Montpellier, Montpellier, France
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
(5) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA

abstract:
The oxygen isotopic composition of continental carbonates is a widely used tool for understanding mountain uplift, ancient lakes, climate oscillations, and the habitats of our early ancestors. The versatility of this tool stems both from the abundance of carbonates in terrestrial strata and the sensitivity of their oxygen isotopic composition to climatic, topographic, ecologic, and geologic variables. However, these systems are complicated. It has taken decades of careful study in modern and ancient systems to develop them as robust tools for understanding Earth history. Jay Quade was fundamental to developing these tools, with meticulous, creative, and collaborative work across multiple continents and time periods. Always curious about new approaches, Jay had started to explore triple oxygen isotope geochemistry because of its unique ability to identify the influence of evaporation on oxygen isotope compositions.

Here we present an overview of our recent work on the triple oxygen isotope composition of soil carbonates, palustrine carbonates, travertines, and biominerals with examples from eastern Africa, South America and North America, spanning the Jurassic through Pleistocene. Much of this work was in collaboration with Jay or inspired by him. While we initiated these studies to assess the role of evaporation on δ 18 O records and evaluate paleoaridity, our initial results indicate the importance of landscape-scale and ecologic processes on Δ 17 O variation. Some of the key takeaways from our work include 1) Δ 17 O values can differ significantly between facies, 2) a single paleosol can exhibit a large gradients in soil carbonate Δ 17 O values (> 60 per meg across 0.5 km transect), 3) there is systematic variation in carbonate δ 18 O and Δ 17 O values between nearby coeval sites, and 4) Δ 17 O values of soil carbonates from the Jurassic to Pleistocene fall within similar ranges as those observed for soil carbonates today. Collectively, these initial investigations show that Δ 17 O values of carbonate vary across landscapes, tracking differences in evaporation and source water inputs. Building on these observations, we propose frameworks for using Δ 17 O data to test models for how evaporation fluxes should vary with depositional mode, ecology, and climate. This landscape-scale context is critical for developing Δ 17 O values of continental carbonates as tools for paleoclimate and paleoenvironmental reconstruction.

title: Utilizing Infrared and Ultraviolet Multispectral Imaging to Identify Raw Material Sources for Lithic Refit Analysis in the Southern High Plains
session_title: Mineralogical Insights from Modern Spectroscopic Techniques (Posters)
authors: Howard, Tristan Elizabeth [1]
affiliations: (1) Heritage and Museum Sciences, Museum at Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract: Traditional approaches to lithic refit analysis often rely on the assessment of physical attributes alone rather than on quantifiable archaeometric data, limiting the ability to link flaked stone tools with their parent nodules. Nodules are the objective core from which flakes are struck off and contain identifiable compositional signatures. This project explores how hyperspectral imaging is used to determine the raw geologic sources from which these tools are made, enabling the replicability and accuracy of refits. The study area focuses on the Southern High Plains of Texas, also known as the Llano Estacado. Samples include chert derived from the Edwards, Ogallala, and Tecovas formations, along with flint from the Alibates Dolomite Formation. Using a modified Nikon Z5 Full Spectrum mirrorless camera with an attachable UV bandpass transmission filter and multispectral IR filters, images were produced and processed in the Landmark 3D application. Images of lithic artifacts with the same associational context captured pigments, textures, surface morphologies, organic and chemical residues, including features visible only under UV or IR wavelengths. As a result, multivariate datasets were created and categorized by geochemical composition alongside macroscopic characteristics. By integrating hyperspectral imaging with visual assessment, this project introduces a reproducible, quantitative approach to lithic refit analysis. Improved precision in matching flakes to parent nodules reveals information about prehistoric tool production and mobility behaviors of past hunter-gatherers. The methodology refined in this project could be applied to other artifact classes, cultural objects, or geological materials, expanding the role of non-destructive spectroscopy in geoarchaeological and heritage scholarship.

title: A Test of Spectral Gamma-Ray Response in Lithologic, Depositional Environment, and Provenance Discrimination in the Cutler Group, Eastern Utah
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Gonzales, Kaileigh [1], King, Michael Ryan [2], Burton, Bradford [3], Petrie, Elizabeth S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(2) Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO,
(3) Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(4) Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO,
abstract:
Spectral gamma-ray measurements are increasingly used to characterize sedimentary rocks because variations in potassium (K), uranium (U), and thorium (Th) reflect mineral composition, provenance, and clay content. This study evaluates whether spectral gamma-ray signatures can be useful in distinguishing lithology and clastic facies associations representing eolian, fluvial, shoreline bar-channel system, and shallow marine depositional environments within the Late Pennsylvanian to Permian Cutler Group near Moab, Utah.

One hundred sixty-five measurements were collected with a handheld gamma-ray scintillometer at one-foot intervals through a composite measured stratigraphic section. At each location, detailed sedimentologic observations were recorded.

In analysis of the lithologies, limestone and sandstone produced similar calculated gamma-ray API values; however, sandstone contained higher potassium concentrations, whereas limestone contained higher uranium concentrations. Thorium values were similar between lithologies. Elevated potassium in sandstone likely reflects arkosic sediment derived from the ancestral Uncompahgre highlands, whereas elevated uranium in limestone may reflect post-depositional secondary uranium enrichment.

Sandstone data were further examined by facies association (FA) to evaluate relationships between spectral gamma-ray measurements and depositional environments. Clay-rich sandstones were excluded from analysis to isolate non-clay mineralogical effects. The eolian facies (FA1) are characterized by very fine- to fine-grained trough cross-bedded sandstone with flat contacts and local convolute bedding. Shoreline facies are represented by two subdivisions in FA2. The shallow marine facies (FA2a) consist of intensely bioturbated very fine- to fine-grained sandstone interbedded with silty sandstone and mudstone and contains the highest sandstone uranium concentrations (average 7.8 ppm), potentially related to mud-lined burrows and spreiten. The bar and channel facies (FA2b) consist of fine- to medium-grained sandstones with shell lags, limited bioturbation, and sigmoidal bedding.

The fluvial facies (FA3) consist of medium- to coarse-grained trough cross-bedded sandstone with concave up channel bases and contains the highest potassium concentrations (4.3-6.8%), consistent with less mature, western-driven sediment. FA1 and FA2 (a, b) generally exhibit lower potassium concentrations than FA3. Thorium values overlap in all facies associations.

In conclusion, spectral gamma-ray data clearly distinguish sandstone and limestone lithologies and differentiate fluvial deposits (and related eastern provenance) from other depositional environments through potassium variations, whereas uranium and thorium values overlap amongst most facies and provide limited depositional discrimination with the potential exception of the burrowed shoreface facies.

title: Experimentally Calibrated Ta and Nb in Rutile Geochemistry
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Cao, Liang [1], Trail, Dustin [2], Chen, Hsin-Yu [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Science, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Science, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA
abstract:
Rutile has long been recognized as a mineral that can incorporate Ta 5+ and Nb 5+ in its crystal structure, and it is well documented in hydrothermal ore systems. It can also survive sedimentary transport away from its source which makes it a potential tool for mineral exploration of Ta and Nb.

Rutile was experimentally synthesized under hydrothermal conditions in the presence of Ta 2 O 5 or Nb 2 O 5 under 650-1200 °C and 1 GPa using a piston cylinder device. In most experiments, the oxygen fugacity was buffered at the Ni-NiO equilibrium. Experimental products were characterized by a scanning electron microscope paired with energy-dispersive X-ray (SEM-EDS), and the rutile chemistry was measured by laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS). We find that both the concentration of Ta and Nb in rutile follow a broad linear log([Ta] or [Nb]) vs. 1/T relationship, consistent with thermodynamic predictions.

Our measured Ta and Nb in rutile concentrations are systematically higher than those reported in literature where Ta 2 O 5 and Nb 2 O 5 buffering phases were absent. When comparing our experimental fits that are down temperature extrapolated to natural systems with rutile and a Nb/Ta buffering phase, our results often underestimate the measured Nb/Ta content. This is likely due to charge compensating cations such as Al 3+ or Fe 3+ that results in increased Nb/Ta in rutile in complex natural systems. Even so, our results indicate that rutile can be developed into a geochemical proxy for Ta and Nb-bearing ores, especially combining with other sediment provenance techniques like thermobarometry, Nb/Ta ratios, redox indicators, and geochronology. This strategy can be performed in situ or ex situ to constrain Nb and Ta source regions.

title: A Loxomegaglyptid Clam Shrimp from an Unusual Green Chert Facies of the Jurassic Morrison Formation in Wyoming
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Salisbury, Jacob [1], Hegna, Thomas Arthur [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA
abstract:
In the 1950s Copeland MacClintock identified a peculiar green chert facies thought to represent a lacustrine environment near the top of the Morrison Formation. This unusual lithology was interpreted as a secondarily chertified claystone. Within this two-foot thick bed of green chert (at the south Square Top Butte section in Natrona County) was a fauna of clam shrimp. The fossil clam shrimp stand out from the rock with a slight blue color when compared to the green matrix.

In comparison to Asia, clam shrimp are very poorly known in the Mesozoic of North America. In the Jurassic of the western US, clam shrimp have only been reported from the Moenave Fm., Morrison Fm., and Navajo Sandstone. The clam shrimp from the south Square Top Butte section seem to be distinct from the forms reported from the Morrison Formation in Colorado and Utah. The clam shrimp studied herein are tentatively assigned to the family Loxomegaglyptidae. Future study will clarify the relationship of the Morrison Formation clam shrimp to those elsewhere in the world.

title: Inseparability of Society, Hazards, and Geoscience
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Rubin, Jeff [1]
affiliations: (1) Wilsonville, OR,
abstract:
Hazards are a human concept: potential harm to life, assets, or other things people value. Most hazards have a natural origin, but potential harm is determined largely by human decisions and actions: risk is a function of hazard and associated vulnerability. Events that are not directly caused by a human agent are mostly unpreventable, thus societal options form an overlapping temporal and conceptual spectrum: minimizing impacts (mitigation), improving short-term response (preparedness), and developing long-term response (recovery). More than a third of the US population live in counties with high wildfire risk, more than 40% reside in coastal counties, exposed to some combination of acute and chronic hazards, and almost half of the US population are exposed to seismic hazards. Every locality faces threats from one or more types of extreme weather and many face flood hazards as well. Reducing risk related to natural hazards demands applications at every societal scale and across a broad and deep geoscience range, including tectonics and structural geology, seismology, volcanology, oceanography, meteorology, climatology, hydrology, geohealth, geomorphology, and remote sensing – all facilitated by effective engagement in science communication and science policy development.

Our growing ability, enabled by rapidly emerging technology, to gather and interpret information on natural events and processes, will expand opportunities for geoscientists to contribute to societal hazard response. Evidence-based, realistic hazard and vulnerability assessments (HVAs) identify and characterize hazards in terms of probability of occurrence and severity of impact; they are the foundation of every aspect of hazard reduction before, during, and after impact. Geoscientists can work with state and local emergency management agencies to develop/improve HVAs and the plans they inform by identifying, assessing, and communicating the combination of hazard, impact, and associated uncertainty – including in their own communities. Probabilistic and deterministic modeling is essential for HVAs and developing realistic planning and exercise scenarios. Real-time modeling tied to detectors and sensors can improve warning accuracy and precision, buying time for protective actions. Enhanced remote and near-earth sensing paired with automated image interpretation can provide early damage estimates and help identify recurring and secondary hazards. Incident data collection and multi-system analysis can better define and forecast interconnected and secondary hazards, e.g., earthquake aftershocks, earthquakes and landslides, and climate change, wildfires, and slope stability.

abstract:
I’ve known Rolfe Mandel for a very long time. We first met when I accepted a position at the Museum of Anthropology at the University of Kansas, and the rest is history...of a sort! Although I’m primarily a Near Eastern archaeologist, my KU position focused on CRM in the Plains, and Rolfe was an obvious source of information for me. Thus began a long and productive professional relationship as well as, and perhaps more importantly an enduring friendship. Accordingly, this presentation is more of an odyssey of the broad scope of our research together rather than a technical recitation of Rolfe’s many accomplishments.

While Rolfe is mainly known for his American research, he also has an extensive record in the Near East. Over the years Rolfe and I worked together on projects in Egypt, Jordan, and Cyprus in addition to ones in the Great Plains. But, one of our first projects was in South Dakota with a memorable stop in Oshkosh, Nebraska. Egypt and Jordan followed, both with their research and dietary delights. Subsequently, Cyprus made its mark and without Rolfe’s detailed geoarchaeological assessment of the controversial site of Akrotiri Aetokremnos our conclusion of human involvement in pygmy hippo extinction would have been much less robust. I look forward to sharing some of these memories and stories, even if Rolfe might wish I didn’t.

abstract:
Mt. Vulture is an unusual volcano located on the eastern margin of the Southern Apennines in Italy. Unlike common silica rich volcanic systems, it has experienced long periods of dormancy while erupting silica-poor alkaline and carbonatitic magmas.The physical and chemical processes responsible for these quiescence periods and transport of low-viscosity magmas remain poorly constrained. Quantifying the physics of transport of these magmatic compositions is therefore important to comprehend the eruption dynamics at Mt. Vulture.

This study combines petrography, geochemical, microstructural, thermal analysis, and experimental rheology to characterize the physical behavior of alkalic magmas at Mt Vulture. Using a suite of three different lava rock compositions collected in Melfi and at the Mt. Vulture summit, we present new data on total volatile concentration using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), glass transition temperature using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and the viscosity of melts and multiphase magmas at different temperatures and strain rates using near-glass transition, subliquidus, and superliquidus viscometry. We further characterize the natural rocks and experimental run products through microstructural and mineralogical analyses using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), as well as whole-rock geochemistry (major, minor, and trace elements, together with radiogenic Sr-Nd-Pb isotopes) of representative Mt. Vulture samples using a combination of X-ray fluorescence (XRF), inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), and multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (MC-ICP-MS). The ongoing research will help establish a rheological window in which alkalic-magmas remain sufficiently fluid for transport through the lithosphere and connect it with the eruption frequency at Mt. Vulture.Through constraining how low-viscosity melts evolve during storage and ascent, this study aims to explore how Mt Vulture can show prolonged periods of quiescence despite producing magmas expected to transport through the crust efficiently.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Exploring Geology Through Urban Structures
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Schwartz, Julia [1], Dalton, Jack [2]
affiliations: (1) Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA
(2) Geology, Wichita State University, Wichita, Kansas, USA
abstract:
Kansas is characterized by relatively flat topography, providing few natural rock outcrops that can be easily incorporated into undergraduate geology instruction. Combined with limited laboratory time, this presents a challenge for providing students with authentic field experiences that reinforce classroom concepts. Wichita State University faces an additional obstacle as a predominantly commuter institution with a nontraditional student population. Many students balance coursework with employment, families, and other responsibilities, making extended field trips impractical. Yet meaningful interactions with geologic materials remain essential for developing observational skills, connecting course concepts to the real world, and fostering continued interest in the geosciences.

In order to support student needs, we look to the urban environment around us to see how geology can transform cities into accessible outdoor classrooms by utilizing building material, monuments, and public art installations as field sites. These unconventional exposures allow students to investigate geologic materials within their own community while eliminating many of the logistical barriers associated with traditional field excursions. Historical research is integrated with field observations to illustrate both the geologic origin and societal use of Earth materials.

Three urban field sites were selected based on their proximity to the university, accessibility for students, and the presence of unique geologic features. The sites represent three distinct areas of geologic inquiry. Site 1 is an astronomical-themed public art installation that can serve as an outdoor laboratory for investigating the relationships between objects in our solar system. A downtown historical building serves as Site 2 and provides an accessible location where students apply rock and mineral identification techniques, reinforcing introductory geologic concepts through field-based observation. Fossiliferous limestone blocks along a nature walk at Site 3 allow students to identify fossil assemblages and interpret Paleozoic marine depositional environments represented throughout the region.

These activities demonstrate that meaningful field experiences do not require spectacular natural outcrops. Urban geology allows us to leverage locally available resources. This provides an accessible, low-cost, and scalable model for increasing student engagement, strengthening observational skills, and connecting geologic concepts to the communities in which students live.

title: Tectonic refining of lower continental crust
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Smye, Andrew [1], Klein, Benjamin [2]
affiliations: (1) Penn State, University Park, PA, USA
(2) University of Lausanne, Lausanne,
abstract: Juvenile arc crust extracted from the mantle at volcanic arcs is mafic, yet bulk continental crust is intermediate in composition. The transition between these states can be explained by tectonic refining during orogenesis. Arc-continent and continent-continent collisions entrain felsic, upper-crustal rocks into the lower crust; subsequent crustal extension drives mafic underplating. Anatectic melt extraction preferentially removes felsic material from the lower crust during granulite-facies metamorphism, while foundering of dense, silica-poor residues into the mantle removes (ultra)mafic material during periods of lithospheric thinning. These processes leave lower continental crust as a bimodal mixture of mafic and felsic rocks whose composition records tectonic history. The Ivrea-Verbano lower crustal section provides an exemplar case study for the framework proposed here: metasedimentary rocks were entrained into the lower crust during Variscan contraction, followed by underplating of mantle-derived magmas during post-orogenic extension. Lower crust of the tectonically active Basin and Range province, SW USA, shares salient aspects of this metamorphic, tectonic and magmatic evolution. Exhumed granulite terrains with lower-crustal residence times exceeding the thermal time constant of continental lithosphere (~200 Myr) are also strongly bimodal. Residence times (the dated interval between peak metamorphism and cooling below granulite-facies temperatures) provide a direct test of lower-crustal representativeness that supersedes retrograde P–T path shape, which constrains thermal length scale rather than the duration. Conversely, granulite terrains with shorter residence times—typically small, rapidly exhumed tectonic slivers—preserve snapshots of the refining processes in operation: crustal thickening, felsic entrainment, and syn-extensional mafic magmatism. Simple box model calculations show that juvenile intraoceanic arc crust converges to an intermediate bimodal state within one to two refining cycles (~100–200 Myr), regardless of variations in tectonic history. An intermediate lower crust emerges from selective compositional losses (foundering + anatectic melting) acting on roughly balanced input fluxes from the mantle (magmatic underplating) and the upper crust (sediment production).

title: Giant Hypostomes and the Paleoecology of the Ordovican Trilobite Isotelus
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Post, Sam [1], Hegna, Thomas Arthur [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA
abstract: Trilobites were marine arthropods that lived 250-520 MYA. Under their head, they had a hard plate called the hypostome. It formed the floor of the mouth and is therefore important for understanding their feeding and diet. Despite this importance, its function is not well understood. Examination of some giant Isotelus hypostomes from the Ordovician of North America has allowed us to answer questions about its paleoecology. Isotelus hypostomes are distinctive due to the forked posterior margin. The interior side of these forks had dense terrace lines that were likely used as a grinding surface for food processing. Terrace lines that are less densely packed imply a larger food source. The two giant hypostomes are both about 12 cm across—by using them to estimate the size of the animal that possessed them, they would have rivaled the size of the largest known trilobite. As Isotelus has indeterminate growth, these hypostomes would have come from very old trilobites. The giant hypostomes give us a far end member for studying the change in shape that comes with growth. Notably, Isotelus exhibits non-isometric growth in its hypostome, gaining more width than length as it grows. The terrace lines, however, maintain roughly the same spacing achieved much earlier in ontogeny. This suggests that once the animal hit a certain size, its food source did not change.

title: 3-d deformation band network development during doming of Navajo sandstone, Henry Mountains, Utah
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems (Posters)
authors: Horsman, Eric [1], McDaniel, Matthew [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Environment & Planning, East Carolina Univ., Greenvile, North Carolina, USA
(2) Earth, Environment & Planning, East Carolina Univ., Greenville, NC, USA
abstract:
Deformation bands (DBs) in porous sandstone influence subsurface fluid flow in folded strata, but most studies of these structures are confined to approximately cylindrical folds. We describe deformation band network development in the Navajo sandstone during 3-d doming in the Henry Mountains of southern Utah. We measured DBs in two field areas with different magnitudes of folding: an unfolded control area (0% shortening), and a low-strain dome (~1% shortening) known as Pulpit Arch. Exceptional exposure allows us to characterize curvature throughout both field areas. This spatial variation in curvature provides a framework to interpret observed characteristics of DB network development (e.g. intensity, orientation, length, etc.)

The control area is located immediately east of Pulpit Arch and exposes sub-horizontal strata of the Navajo sandstone, which is approximately 200 m thick in this region. DB intensity at the 4 control area stations was low, averaging 0.03 m -1 . Observed DBs in the area strike NNW-SSE and dip sub-vertically, which agrees with the orientation of fractures recognized by other workers throughout the region. The low-strain Pulpit Arch dome has a diameter of ~2.5 km, an amplitude of ~200 m, and maximum bedding dips of ~12 degrees. DBs measured at 23 stations distributed across the exposure area of the Navajo sandstone in the dome have intensities ranging from 0.0 m -1 to 0.53 m -1 , with a mean of 0.30 +- 0.12 m -1 . A weak correlation exists between dome curvature and DB intensity. DBs dip steeply (mean of 82 degrees) relative to restored bedding. DB strike varies considerably, but the two principal modes are oriented NE-SW and E-W. These orientations align roughly with modest asymmetries in the 3-d geometry of the Pulpit Arch dome. Preliminary evidence suggests the earliest DBs were dominantly tangential, and most radial fractures at a given station developed later. But the entire Pulpit Arch dome represents a very early stage of folding and DB patterns throughout are consistent with a period of diffuse structural development prior to significant organization. In-progress work will extend this analysis by adding data from a more intensely folded dome in the same stratigraphic unit.

abstract: Researchers have recognized the many challenges that students face when they transition from one educational level to another; however, research on how to support students through the transition from undergraduate to graduate-level education and research is more limited. Through a National Science Foundation S-STEM grant, this project is supporting 45 low-income master's level graduate students to complete their degree and transition to the workforce or further graduate education. The setting is a Midwestern public regional university where a high proportion of undergraduates have part-time jobs and, consequently, graduate education is perceived by students as a significant opportunity cost. The program of study combines scholarships with a coordinated set of academic and social supports to facilitate student transitions into graduate school. The science faculty team members have active research programs examining local and regional watersheds using different but complementary disciplinary perspectives. Concurrently, the program’s education research team is examining student success through the theoretical lens of academic integration. Each scholar completes interviews near the start and end of the academic year, and researchers use these data to determine how components of the program influence student success. The interview protocol examines student perceptions of impactful components of the cohort program and explores student career interests and intentions. A team of four coders reviewed transcripts of 33 total student interviews collected during Fall 2024, Spring 2025, or Spring 2026. The "Career" code was one of nine major thematic codes, and it consisted of seven possible sub-codes. The results showed that these students’ career aspirations cross multiple sectors: academia, government, and industry. Several students mentioned a desire to connect their career to helping people and/or society. However, students’ intentions were tempered by concerns about the job market and availability of positions in their desired field. The study results give insight on the ways that students could or could not make connections between their graduate research project and the type of career they would like to pursue. This variability suggests a need for intentional mentoring on the students’ next transition, from graduate education to the workforce or doctorate. The findings also point to the value of professional networking events outside the university to ensure that students hear different perspectives on how to navigate a science career.

title: FFeldspar compositions from spherulites in Rockhound State Park, New Mexico: implications for temperature of formation during lava eruptions
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Salinas, Cassie Dee [1], Dunbar, Nelia W. [2], Iverson, Nels [3], Copeland, Peter C. [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, Texas, USA
(2) Bureau of Geology, New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Bureau of Geology, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
(4) University of Houston, Houston, TX,
abstract:
The rhyolite of Little Florida Mountains (Clemons, 1980) (~24.4 Ma, McLemore and Dunbar, 2000) is exposed in Rockhound State Park in southwest NM. Most of this exposure consists of flow-banded rhyolite including layers of crystalline rhyolite interbedded with obsidian.

Spherules are present with diameters ranging from a few mm to 10’s of cm. The spherulites vary in texture from complex to simple. Some spherulites are dense, with a distinct core (by color and texture) and banded layers of quartz and felspar in the outer edge. Others are expanded and contain deposits of layered agate in the void spaces. The simple texture is composed of quartz and felspar intergrown on a micron scale with little variation in texture though the volume of the spherulite. On some samples, an outer rind (mostly feldspar?) is present.

Six spherulites were examined using a JEOL JXA-iHP200F electron microprobe at New Mexico Bureau of Geology including backscatter electron imaging, chemical maps, and quantitative geochemical analyses. All samples consisted of intergrown quartz, alkali feldspars, minor Fe-Ti oxides and void space. The range of textures and crystal sizes both within and between is highly variable.

Quantitative analyses show some samples appear to contain a single potassic feldspar whereas others contain a wide range of alkali felspar compositions. The very small size and intergrown texture of these felspars make it uncertain as to whether these samples contain only two end-member compositions (which may be combined due to the relatively large 10 µm spot size) or the samples show a solid solution between observed end members. The rinds on the spherulites are composed of end-member K-feldspar, suggesting low- T secondary hydrothermal deposition.

The feldspar compositions and textures of the intergrown quartz and felspar suggest crystallization at magmatic temperatures. The presence of a single potassic feldspar in the cores of some spherulites suggests crystallization at temperatures above the feldspar miscibility gap (> 740°C). For samples with a range of alkali feldspar compositions, we estimate a crystallization temperature of 680±20°C.

Based on the high and restricted temperature range we obtain from these compositions, we conclude growth of these spherulites occurred shortly after the eruption of the rhyolitic lavas in which they are found.

title: Hydrologic Extremes from High River Stage to Drought Drive Surface Water–Groundwater Mixing and Nitrous Oxide Production in a Karst Aquifer
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Yoon, Seonkyoo [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Florida, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
abstract: Karst critical zones, which cover approximately 20% of Earth's ice-free land surface, are characterized by rapid hydraulic connections between surface water (SW) and groundwater (GW) through conduits and fractures. These dynamic flow paths create highly variable redox environments that strongly influence nitrogen cycling, yet the role of hydrologic variability in regulating SW–GW mixing and nitrous oxide (N 2 O) production remains poorly understood. We investigated how hydrologic conditions spanning high river stage to drought regulate SW–GW mixing and microbial N 2 O production in the Santa Fe River Sink–Rise karst system of northern Florida. Hydrograph analysis, dye tracing, and functional gene analyses were integrated across multiple groundwater wells and surface-water windows to directly link hydrologic exchange with microbial nitrogen transformations. Our results demonstrate that both high river-stage and drought conditions promote SW–GW mixing through distinct hydrologic mechanisms. High river stage rapidly transports oxygen-rich surface water into the karst aquifer, whereas prolonged drought lowers groundwater levels and enhances hydraulic exchange between conduits and the surrounding carbonate matrix. Despite these contrasting hydrologic conditions, both generate transient redox environments at SW–GW interfaces. Functional gene analyses indicate that these mixing zones favor incomplete denitrification by suppressing the final step of denitrification (N 2 O reduction to N 2 ), resulting in elevated N 2 O production. Dye-tracing observations independently identify hydrologically active mixing zones that spatially coincide with elevated N 2 O concentrations. Our findings demonstrate that hydrologic variability regulates greenhouse gas production through coupled hydrologic and microbial processes and identify surface water–groundwater mixing as a fundamental control on N 2 O production in karst critical zones.

title: Measured and Modeled Contaminant Mobility in Uranium Mill Tailings with Column Tests
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Williams, Seth Isaiah [1], Clark, Ja'Myiah S [2], Johnson, Raymond H. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA; RSI EnTech, LLC, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(2) Natural Resources and Environmental Design, North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, Greensboro, NC, USA; RSI EnTech, LLC, Grand Junction, CO, USA

abstract:
Cores were collected during the installation of monitoring wells at Rifle Disposal Site in Rifle, Colorado, where wells were implemented to support tailings dewatering efforts. Column studies were conducted on the core samples under oxic and anoxic conditions to quantify and model the mobility of contaminants including uranium and vanadium, within mill tailings. Major cations, anions, and metals were analyzed using Ion Chromatography and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS). Geochemical processes controlling contaminant release, including mineral dissolution, mineral precipitation, and metal sorption-desorption reactions, were modeled using the geochemical modeling software PHREEQC. Measured results indicate sulfate, uranium, and vanadium were the major contaminants released during leaching, with uranium exhibiting greater release under oxic conditions. Geochemical modeling identified gypsum dissolution as the primary control on sulfate concentrations, and uranium and vanadium release was governed by carnotite dissolution coupled with desorption processes. Model predictions were sensitive to differences in thermodynamic data among available geochemical databases, introducing uncertainty into the interpretation of controlling reactions.

These findings provide a basis for improving dewatering system operations and maintenance by limiting oxygen ingress. Geochemical amendments (such as hydroxyapatite) can reduce uranium mobility and are being tested on the same tailings’ materials. These hydroxyapatite experiments will test the long-term stability of uranium sequestration and are applicable to any site with a goal of permanently fixing uranium to the solid phase.

title: Effect of Residual Chlorine on the Stability of Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agent Gadobutrol (Gadavist) and Its Behavior in Simulated Gastric Fluid

authors: Kanaththage, Malsha Indeewari [1], Coyte, Rachel Marylee [2], Rubasinghege, Gayan [3]
affiliations: (1) Chemistry, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, USA

abstract:
Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are increasingly detected in aquatic environments due to their widespread clinical use and persistence during wastewater treatment. Understanding the stability of these compounds under environmentally relevant conditions is essential for assessing their potential transformation and health implications. This study evaluated the stability of the macrocyclic GBCA, Gadobutrol (Gadavist), in the presence of residual chlorine and its subsequent behavior under simulated gastric conditions. Gadavist (10 ppm) was [RC1] incubated with sodium hypochlorite, and residual chlorine was monitored daily to represent residual chlorine (2- 0.5 ppm) in drinking water at 25 °C for seven days under dark and simulated sunlight conditions, along with the control. Following incubation, samples were analyzed using ion chromatography coupled with inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (IC-ICP-MS). Preliminary chromatographic results showed greater changes in gadolinium speciation in chlorine-treated samples than in the untreated control, with sunlight exposure producing more pronounced alterations than dark storage. To evaluate the potential implications of these transformations following ingestion, chlorine-treated samples were exposed to simulated gastric fluid (SGF) and compared with untreated GBCAs. Initial IC-ICP-MS results suggest that residual chlorine may alter the chemical behavior of Gadavist and influence its stability under gastric conditions.

These preliminary findings indicate that residual chlorine, particularly when combined with sunlight exposure, may compromise the environmental stability of Gadavist despite [RC2] its macrocyclic structure. Ongoing work will verify GBCA concentrations and determine the implications of chlorine-induced transformations for human exposure through drinking water.

abstract: Students who identify strongly as geoscientists are more persistent in their studies and are more likely to pursue careers within the geosciences. Like geoscience identity, sense of belonging is also a strong predictor of persistence and success. Sense of belonging can be evaluated by measuring the frequency and type of interactions or collaborations students engage in during a course. Students who collaborate with their peers more often and in more ways are more likely to have a strong sense of belonging within their academic community. This pilot study was designed to evaluate if social network analysis methods could be used in combination with a geoscience identity survey to analyze how the frequency and type of student collaborations in and outside of the classroom impact strength of geoscience identity in undergraduate geoscience students. We surveyed students across four courses: Physical Geology, GIS, Igneous and Metamorphic Petrology, and Sedimentology and Stratigraphy. The survey included three parts. In Part 1, students reported the type and frequency of collaborations they engaged in with other students in class. Collaboration types included: in-class activities, class projects, homework/studying, and “other geology activities.” Part 2 was a 23-item geoscience identity survey, and Part 3 collected demographic information including class standing, major and minor, gender identity, and race/ethnicity. We used social network analysis methods to map geoscience identity scores and demographics onto student collaboration networks. Initial results suggest that strength of geoscience identity is correlated with frequency of collaboration; students who collaborate more frequently with their classmates also identified more strongly as geoscientists.

abstract: The Quaternary geologic history of the Dolores River, an important tributary to the Colorado River, is unestablished. We investigate how recent rapid base level fall at the confluence has migrated upstream along the Dolores River, by carrying out detailed geological mapping of the Quaternary units and dating of associated fluvial terraces using optically stimulating luminescence. The mapping and extent of the terraces were determined by geologic analysis using LiDAR data and confirmed with field based descriptions of the units. Initial work suggests a lengthy terrace record of up to 350 m above river level with a series of inset strath terraces within the canyon up to 90 m above the river. Previous age constraints on two terraces using OSL and a U-series dating on a carbonate rind suggests a rapid incision rate of ~0.4 millimeters per year for the lower 40 m of the canyon. Continuing work using optically stimulating luminescence dating on related terraces will further refine the chronology of the fluvial terraces and better define the incision rate history of the Dolores River.

abstract: Recent investigations have documented a marine K-Pg boundary section in northeastern Mississippi that captures the chaotic record of sedimentary deposits in a shallow water environment following the asteroid impact. We focus on a chalk bed approximately 1 m thick that is interpreted to have been deposited immediately after impact (Foram Zone P0). The deposit contains 1000s, if not 10s of 1,000s, of ammonite jaws. The jaws are isolated rather than in situ (preserved inside the body chamber), and have been interpreted as reflecting a mass kill following the impact, perhaps due to suffocation linked to the catastrophic resuspension of sedimentary material at the time. Most of the jaws are attributed to Discoscaphites iris ., because this is the most common species of Discoscaphites in this time interval. We analyzed the oxygen and carbon isotope composition (δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C‰ VPDB) of four lower jaws through ontogeny. The jaws are all approximately 1 cm in length and are probably from mature individuals (by comparison with in situ jaws in the upper Maastrichtian of New Jersey). We extracted 9 to 10 samples of calcite from each specimen, spanning hatching to maturity. The pattern of δ¹⁸O is nearly the same in all specimens, reflecting a warm period at hatching, a cooler period during most of ontogeny, and another warm period at maturity. If the isotopic/temperature pattern represents an annual signal, it suggests that the ammonites lived for one year. In addition, the surfaces of the jaws exhibit small striae spaced at intervals of 17 – 34 μm. In one specimen in which they were counted (still preliminary), there are ~390 such striae, suggesting that they were deposited daily. The oxygen isotopic/temperature pattern also implies that the asteroid impact occurred in the northern hemisphere spring or summer, possibly coinciding with ammonite spawning. The δ¹³C record shows a consistent increase toward higher values through ontogeny, with a marked increase at the onset of maturity, reflecting a slowing of growth and reduced incorporation of metabolic carbon into the calcite.

abstract: Notostracans are often called “living fossils,” however, the taxonomy of extinct notostracans remains poorly resolved, as highlighted by Geyer et al. (2024). Fossil notostracans are known from two localities in the United States; the Permian-aged Enid Formation in Oklahoma and the Triassic-aged Bull Run Formation in Virginia. Both occurrences were previously assigned to the extant genus Triops , but these identifications were made with a limited critical evaluation of diagnostic morphology. Re-examination of the Permian Oklahoma material shows that it belongs to the genus Olesenocaris , previously only known from the Triassic of France. The Virginia specimens represent a new species of the genus Apudites . These revisions indicate that previous assignments to Triops were insufficiently supported. This reinforces the need for further rigorous systematic revision of fossil notostracans. Although notostracan body plans are morphologically conservative through time, they were not evolutionarily static. Detailed anatomical and systematic studies demonstrate that the extant Triops cancriformis lacks a confirmed fossil record, undermining its long-standing characterization as a “living fossil.”

title: Preliminary Cosmogenic 10Be Constraints on Tributary Catchment Denudation Along the Kali Gandaki Valley, Central Nepal Himalaya
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Mongovin, Daniel D.T. [1], Taylor, Michael H. [2], Bhandari, Basant [3], Murphy, Michael A. [4], Forte, Adam Matthew [5], Grom, Vivian [6], Hidy, Alan J [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA

abstract:
The Indo-Asia collision zone, forming the Himalayan mountain range and Tibetan Plateau, comprises the highest elevations and topographic relief on Earth and provides an exceptional natural laboratory for evaluating the surface expression of crustal-scale deformation. The Kali Gandaki River is a major transverse river system that cuts across the central Nepal Himalaya, intersecting major tectonostratigraphic units, structural boundaries, climate gradients, and high uplift and exhumation rates within the Himalayan thrust wedge. Spatial patterns of erosion and river incision along this system may therefore provide insight into how thrust-wedge geometry and kinematics influence landscape evolution.

We present preliminary terrestrial cosmogenic nuclide data from modern tributary sediment samples collected during 2024 fieldwork along the upper-central Kali Gandaki valley. These samples were collected to estimate basin-averaged denudation rates and evaluate whether spatial variations in erosion correspond to predicted gradients in rock uplift, exhumation, and structural segmentation within the thrust wedge. New 10 Be concentration results provide first-order constraints on the relative distribution of catchment-scale denudation, while exposure and burial-dating samples from stranded gravel deposits are currently being analyzed and will provide future constraints on river incision over 10 3 –10 5 yr timescales. Tributary sediment 10 Be concentrations will be converted to erosion-rate estimates using CRONUS-Earth v3-compatible production scaling, AMS standardization, and DEM-derived catchment parameters.

This contribution presents the project framework, initial 10 Be concentration dataset, and workflow for evaluating whether spatial patterns of erosion across the Kali Gandaki valley correspond to tectonic forcing within the Himalayan thrust wedge. By comparing denudation patterns with catchment morphology, lithology, channel steepness, mapped structural boundaries, and existing geodetic and geologic datasets, this work tests whether surface-process datasets can record spatial gradients in tectonic forcing or are instead dominated by other geomorphic, climatic, and/or sediment-routing processes such as sediment supply, lithology, glacial influence, and mass wasting. These preliminary results provide a foundation for evaluating how crustal-scale deformation is translated into erosion and topographic development across the central Nepal Himalaya.

title: Post-Laramide Contraction in the Rocky Mountain Region: Oligocene Reactivation of the Mosca Creek Thrust, Southern Colorado
session_title: From outcrop to orogen—field-based perspectives on stratigraphy, structural geology, and mineral resources in the Rocky Mountain region—a session in honor of David A. Lindsey
authors: Malavarca, Samantha L. [1], Singleton, John [2], Holm-Denoma, Christopher S. [3], Broeder, Hunter Joseph [4], Rahl, Jeffrey M. [5], Souders, Kate [6], Gilmer, Amy K. [7]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(4) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State Univ, Geosciences, Fort Collins, CO,
(5) Earth and Environmental Geoscience Department, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA,
(6) US Geological Survey, Denver,
(7) U. S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
abstract: Laramide contraction in the southern Rocky Mountains is generally interpreted to have waned by the middle Eocene, and the youngest previously recognized contraction near the Sangre de Cristo Range involves the ~49 Ma Cuchara Formation. Localized extension associated with the Rio Grande Rift was established in the range by ~30 Ma. We present evidence that the W-dipping Mosca Creek Thrust underwent a younger pulse of top-NE directed contractional reactivation at ~33–30 Ma. The thrust places Paleoproterozoic crystalline rocks over the Pennsylvanian Minturn Formation and is exceptionally exposed in erosional windows at Mosca Creek and South Zapata Creek. New 1:10,000-scale geologic mapping, structural analysis, and monazite and zircon U-Pb geochronology document comparable Oligocene deformation at both localities. At Mosca Creek, the thrust core contains mylonitic and brittle-ductile domains with asymmetric fabric recording top-NE shear. Quartz preserves fracturing and evidence for crystal plasticity including localized bulging recrystallization and subgrain development, indicating deformation under transitional brittle-ductile conditions. Monazite grains within this top-NE shear fabric are elongate, boudinaged or sigmoidal, and locally developed in strain shadows around stretched quartz grains. These grains yield a Tera-Wasserburg lower-intercept age of 32.5 ± 0.7 Ma, directly dating monazite growth during contractional shear. Near South Zapata Creek, ~15 km along strike to the south, top-NE shear is recorded by foliated cataclasite containing S-C-C’ fabrics and sigmoidal quartz ribbons. Aplite sills cut cataclasite in the fault core but also locally record top-NE shear, demonstrating late-kinematic emplacement. Zircon U-Pb dating of an undeformed aplite in the footwall yields a crystallization age of 32.4 ± 1.3 Ma, and a deformed sample from the thrust core yields an age of 29.2 ± 0.9 Ma, confirming Oligocene contractional reactivation coeval with that at Mosca Creek. We interpret these relationships to record a discrete pulse of contractional strain localized along inherited thrust architecture during a well-documented magmatic interval along the western flank of the range. Similar brittle-ductile top-NE fabrics are preserved along other range front structures including the Independence Mine Shear Zone and Deadman Creek Thrust, suggesting that contractional deformation under elevated temperatures associated with Oligocene magmatism may have been more widespread. These findings support a transition from contraction to extension that was pulsed, asynchronous, and spatially heterogenous rather than an abrupt regional kinematic reversal.

title: Spinicaudatans: The Puzzle of Arthropod-Style Growth with Molluscan-Style Marginal Accretion
session_title: Paleontology, Phylogenetic/Morphological Patterns (Posters)
authors: Saldanha, João Pedro [1], Hegna, Thomas Arthur [2]
affiliations: (1) Programa de Pós Graduação em Geociências, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
(2) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA
abstract: As a rule, arthropods grow by molting their exoskeleton. Clam shrimp break this rule with their carapace, which grows by marginal accretion at the outer edge of the carapace. Previous hypotheses to explain this postulated that during each molt, they grew an entire new carapace beneath — giving an arthropod flavor to molluscan style marginal accretion. To evaluate this, we examined both histological slides and SEM mounts of clam shrimp carapaces from multiple genera. These examinations revealed a bilayered carapace with an internal cuticular membrane and a thicker external cuticle — both containing the expected endo-, exo-, and epicuticle. In cross-section, the external epicuticle exhibits staggered interruptions and elevations that mark the growth lines, whereas the overlying endocuticle and exocuticle are composed of continuous lamellae. These findings are incompatible with the previous model, which require cuticle superposition. Our model indicates that only the epicuticle is retained throughout ontogeny, while growth is accommodated through progressive remodeling of the external endo- and exocuticle.

title: The Tephra Information Portal (TIP) - Facilitating Access to Tephra Samples, Data, and Metadata and Supporting Data Archiving Using Community-Recommended Practices
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation
authors: Kuehn, Stephen C. [1], Nalesnik, Abigail [2], Lehnert, Kerstin Annette [3], Figueroa-Salazar, Juan David [4], Cao, Sean [5], Celnick, Mollie [6], Wallace, Kristi L. [7], Crass, Scott [8], Harmon, Dain [9], Kurbatov, Andrei [10], Newton, Anthony [11], Novak, Nathan [12]

abstract:
Well-documented tephra data and sample information are foundational to the use of tephra deposits in tephrostratigraphy, geochronology, and volcanology. Because tephra correlation relies on comparing multi-parameter data, the ability to locate and access appropriate datasets is essential. Without that data, correlations cannot be made. Reliable access to comprehensive, high-quality datasets is also essential for research transparency, reproducibility, and robust evaluation of interpretations.

In fall 2024, we launched an NSF-supported project to develop the Tephra Information Portal (TIP), aiming to provide a central point of access to tephra geochemical and sample information, serving researchers who study tephra or rely on tephra datasets. This system is being built as a collaboration between the tephra community and the IEDA2 data facility as a prototype of the Framework for FAIR Data Communities (FFDC). The FFDC concept aims to provide a solution for geoscience data communities to use existing data infrastructure (e.g. repositories, databases, tools, portals) and tailor these to the needs of each specialized community. It also leverages efforts of existing infrastructure to achieve resilience and sustainability of data and services.

The Tephra Information Portal’s design and goals have been shaped by the needs of the tephra research community, building on more than a decade of research community organizing and consensus-building which led to comprehensive recommended practices for tephra data collection and reporting (Wallace et al., 2022; https://zenodo.org/records/6568306). The Tephra Community Page at EarthChem (https://earthchem.org/communities/tephra) provides guidance, resources, and recommendations including suggested sample, method, and geochemistry templates.

The TIP provides a central hub for tephra data, integrating information from multiple, distributed data systems (PetDB, GeoDIVA, TephraBase, SESAR) under a single point of access. The initial user interface allows searching by volcano and by geographic location. PetDB-hosted data can additionally be queried by geochemical concentrations (e.g., SiO2, MgO, etc.) and material type. Because much existing tephra data is not yet in accessible systems, we are also curating multiple large volume legacy datasets (e.g. USGS Tephrochronology Laboratory, Moffett Field, CA) to make these resources broadly available and accessible through the TIP.

authors: Nunes, Daniel C [1], Smrekar, Suzanne [2], Hensley, Scott [3], Whitten, Jennifer [4], Cascioli, Gael [5], Buczkowski, Debra [6], Dyar, Darby [7]
affiliations: (1) Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA

abstract: The Science Team for VERITAS Mission to Venus, which is scheduled for launch in 2032, conducted a field campaign in Iceland in August of 2023 in conjunction with the German Aerospace Center’s Microwaves and Radar Institute. The goal of the campaign is to collect VERITAS- and Magellan-like synthetic aperture radar data (X- and S-band, respectively, with resolution and performance characteristics accounted for) over various analog volcanic sites accompanied by in situ characterization of the surface geology, texture, and dielectric properties to provide ground truth. DLR’s airborne radar imaged three regions of interest (ROIs) totaling over 1000 km^2, and the surface team characterized with permittivity probes, lidars, drone-cameras of 41 5- by 5-meter patches and collected ~100 kg of samples for laboratory analyses. These ROIs correspond to three volcanic sites: Fagradalsfjall, Holuhraun, and Askja. The encompass different morphologies, (pahoehoe, lava ponds, lobate flows, a’a), lithologies (basaltic to rhyolitic), and partial to full sedimentary cover (sand and tephra), thus enabling us to examine the interaction of radar waves of different wavelengths with different possible surface analogs to Venus. The Team has now completed the initial processing of the data, and we here report key findings relevant for the analysis of upcoming VERITAS data. (1) Mapping the VERITAS-like SAR data produced boundaries that are in closer agreement with published geologic maps than maps created with the Magellan-like data. When ambiguities are encountered in mapping SAR, high-resolution topographic data, similar to what will be collected by VERITAS, permit us to address many of these ambiguities. (2) Sub-centimeter digital elevation models (DEMs) show that while we can spectrally tell apart smooth from rough surfaces, there is essentially a continuum of spectral shapes, and that distinguishing different structures through one- or two-dimensional Fourier spectra is not clear cut. However, large roughness concentrated in small-scale features (e.g., cracks or jagged rocks) can spatially bleed out when reducing the posting or resolution of DEM and bias upwards the average roughness of the surface. We are currently using these data to test VERITAS radar processing pipeline and help validate our requirements. We are also planning to expand this study and continue to build a library of surface types that will support our interpretation of the new Venus data in the 2030’s.
