title: Paleomagnetism of the Paleocene Ghost Rocks volcanics, Kodiak Alaska: Implications for Proposed Plate Interactions with the Western Margin of North America
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Housen, Bernard [1], Roeske, Sarah M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
(2) University of California, Davis, CA,
abstract:
One of John Garver’s long-term research activities has been aimed at a better understanding of the paleogeography of terranes and evolution of the western margin of North America. We present updated analyses of paleomagnetic data from volcanic rocks (andesitic-basaltic pillow lavas) from the Paleocene Ghost Rocks, part of the Chugach Terrane, located on the SW portion of Kodiak Island. Mapping of the rocks exposed in Alitak Bay revealed small faults that have divided the area into rotated blocks. Other locations have more coherent structures. The paleomagnetic results have well-defined magnetization directions from 26 sites. With the Alitak sites corrected for differential rotation, the combined data pass the paleomagnetic tilt test (with peak clustering between 80% and 110% untilting) and reversals tests. The tilt-corrected mean is D= 331, I = 52.6, N=26, k = 18, α 95 = 7. Due to the block-rotation for the Alitak sites, and the possibility of original slope, inclination-only means were calculated using untilting values of 100% (I = 53.5, 37 N paleolatitude), and 90% (I = 60.3, 41 N paleolatitude). Using the 55 Ma reference pole for North America from Gallo et al 2023, the expected paleolatitude for Kodiak Island is 64 N, and an estimate of translation for the 90% untilting direction is 2500 +/- 800 km.

The Ghost Rocks paleomagnetic results are inconsistent with tectonic models that do not include translation of the Chugach Terrane, such as the Resurrection Plate model as proposed by Haeussler et al 2003. The preferred “small Resurrection” tomotectonic model of Fuston and Wu 2021 places the southern Kula-NA-Resurrection r-t-r triple junction and the Chugach Terrane at ~ 50 N at 60 Ma- proposing a limit of ~ 1200 km of translation. The Ghost Rocks paleomagnetic data are consistent with the model of Garver and Davidson (2017), who used detrital zircon provenance and other geological evidence to propose a location of the Chugach Terrane outboard of Wrangellia at 70 Ma, and is consistent with hot-spot motion corrected plate models (Dubrovine and Tarduno, 2008) for the location of the Kula-Farallon ridge, which does not require an intervening Resurrection Plate. Reconciling paleomagnetic data with advances being made by tomotectonic models will likely require examination of differences between the mantle frameworks and plate locations constrained by geomagnetic field geometry.

title: Meteorological Conditions Associated with the 2024 Wildfire Minimum in South Korea
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: Na, Yeseong [1], Youngji, Joh [2]
affiliations: (1) Princeton High School, Princeton, NJ, USA
(2) Seasonal-to-Decadal Variability and Predictability Division, NOAA, Princeton, NJ, USA
abstract: Wildfires are a recurring environmental hazard in South Korea, and several of the country's most damaging fire seasons have occurred since the early 2020s. Fire number and burned area in 2022, 2023, and 2025 substantially exceeded those of most years in the preceding decade. Against this backdrop, wildfire statistics published by the Korea Forest Service show that 2024 recorded the lowest number of wildfires and the smallest burned area among the years 2022-2025. However, the weather and atmospheric conditions associated with this difference have not yet been clearly identified. This study investigates the conditions related to the relatively low wildfire activity in South Korea in 2024. We compare national wildfire records, surface weather observations, and atmospheric reanalysis data for 2024 with corresponding data for 2022, 2023, and 2025. Wildfire activity is evaluated using the number of fires, total burned area, seasonal timing, and the occurrence of fires exceeding 5 ha. The physical variables examined include precipitation, wind speed, and relative humidity. Monthly and seasonal anomalies are calculated to determine how conditions in 2024 differed from those in years with greater wildfire activity and whether regional atmospheric circulation affected moisture conditions and fire-spreading winds. Our analysis of Korea Forest Service records shows that wildfire occurrence during the four-year period was concentrated in early spring, and that fires exceeding 5 ha occurred in 2022, 2023, and 2025 during the spring fire season, whereas none were identified in 2024. In this presentation, we will introduce the seasonal and interannual characteristics of recent South Korean wildfires and examine whether wetter conditions, weaker winds, higher humidity, or a combination of these factors limited wildfire growth in 2024. Because ignition in South Korea is predominantly human-caused, understanding which meteorological conditions permit or suppress fire growth is essential for seasonal wildfire outlooks and for allocating suppression resources, and characterizing a low-activity year provides a useful complement to studies focused on extreme fire seasons.

title: Repeated Reactivation Reveals Persistent Weakness in Colorado's Continental Lithosphere
session_title: Proterozoic Tectonics of Western Laurentia: New Perspectives on Crustal Growth, Orogenesis, Mineralization, and Intracontinental Reworking
authors: Lusk, Alexander Dmitri [1], Hillenbrand, Ian [2], Thompson, Jay Michael [3], Frothingham, Michael Geoffrey [4], Lowers, Heather [5], Allen, Joseph L. [6], Swartz, Jackson Perry [7]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(2) Denver, CO,
(3) U.S. Geological Survey -, Denver, CO,
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(5) US Geological Survey, Denver, CO,
(6) Concord University, Athens, WV,
(7) Western Washington University, Madison, AL,
abstract:
Northeast-trending Proterozoic shear zones exposed across Colorado are viewed as classic examples of repeated reactivation and progressive strain localization traditionally linked to the Yavapai (1.72–1.68 Ga), Mazatzal (1.66–1.60 Ga), and Picuris (1.47–1.35 Ga) orogenies. These structures have also been suggested to influence much younger deformation and mineralization associated with the late Mesozoic to Cenozoic Colorado Mineral Belt. Linking specific structures or fabrics to individual deformation episodes remains challenging, particularly for lower temperature (ultra)mylonites. Here, we present new geochronology and structural interpretations that directly date mixed plastic–brittle deformation in these shear zones, demonstrating a longer and more complex reactivation history than previously recognized. In-situ U-Pb monazite, xenotime, and titanite ages, combined with in-situ Rb-Sr mica geochronology, document progressive down temperature reactivation of mylonitic, ultramylonitic, and recrystallized pseudotachylite fabrics in the Grizzly Creek, Homestake, and Moose Mountain shear zones at ca. 1.6, 1.4–1.3, 1.2, and 1.1 Ga. We interpret the ca. 1.2–1.1 Ga ages of ultramylonite and recrystallized pseudotachylite to represent previously unrecognized, widespread reactivation more than 1000 km inboard from the active Laurentian plate boundary during the Grenville orogeny.

Our findings support the interpretation that Proterozoic shear zones in Colorado acted as persistently weak structures over much of the Proterozoic and were repeatedly reactivated under evolving thermomechanical conditions. This long-lived weakness has broad implications for lithospheric rheology, the transmission and accommodation of far-field stress, and the potential for seismicity within inherited structures far from active plate boundaries. Further, our results highlight the importance of detailed petrochronologic characterization that integrates mineral ages, textures, and chemistry with microstructural context, particularly in multiply deformed rocks.

title: Phosphatized Eurypterid Muscles from the Williamsville Formation (Silurian Bertie Group; New York)
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry
authors: Hegna, Thomas Arthur [1], Bicknell, Russell D. C. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Environmental Sciences, SUNY Fredonia, Fredonia, NY, USA
(2) College of Science and Engineering, Flinders University, Bedford Park, South Australia, Australia
abstract:
Phosphatized muscle tissue was first identified in fossil fish in 1888 by Otto Reis. In the nearly 150 years since, phosphatized muscle tissue has been identified in a number of other fossil organisms. Fossil eurypterids, however, have never been observed to have phosphatized muscles—the only examples of fossil eurypterid muscles are preserved in pyrite and clays.

We report here on the first eurypterid with phosphatized muscles from the Williamsville Formation in the Buffalo area of New York State. The specimen, belonging to the species Eurypterus dekayi , displays clear phosphatized muscle fibers in the basal podomeres of limb VI. Structureless phosphatic deposits are also found near the base of limbs II-V, interpreted to represent the location of coxal muscles. EDS analyses not only confirmed the calcium phosphate composition, but also revealed ‘shadows’ in the silicon map that may correspond to the position of limbs II-V. Though the phosphatization pathway is fairly well understood, the cause of the silica shadows is not yet known.

title: International Partnerships for Sustainable Impact: Co-Creating Groundwater Science, Capacity, and Safe-Water Solutions Across the Global South
session_title: International Collaborations in the Geosciences: Celebrating Science Without Borders
authors: Bhattacharya, Prosun [1]
affiliations: (1) KTH-International Groundwater Arsenic Group, Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering,, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
abstract:
Groundwater-quality challenges caused by geogenic and emerging contaminants transcend national boundaries, yet durable responses must be locally anchored, jointly developed, and sustained beyond individual project cycles. This presentation synthesizes lessons from more than three decades of international partnerships linking groundwater research, doctoral education, institutional capacity development, technological innovation, and safe-water implementation across Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

In Bangladesh, collaboration among universities, government institutions, UNICEF, development partners, local drillers, and communities translated arsenic research into practical approaches for identifying and accessing safer aquifers. Hydrostratigraphic interpretation, sediment characterization, and groundwater geochemistry supported development of the field-operable Sediment Color Tool. Subsequent partnerships contributed to integrated groundwater-information systems containing approximately 6.3 million well records from 54 districts, together with dashboards and decision-support processes for groundwater-quality assessment, safe-source selection, and evidence-based planning. These scientific insights, datasets, and institutional relationships provide a foundation for process-informed predictive intelligence and AI-enabled groundwater decision support.

In Tanzania, long-term partnerships integrated fluoride and arsenic mapping, hydrogeochemical research, locally adaptable treatment technologies, doctoral training, laboratory and field capacity development, and community engagement. Co-supervision, shared analytical approaches, and sustained field collaboration helped establish a cohort of locally based scientists and strengthened capacity to address national groundwater-quality priorities. In Bolivia, studies of volcanic–geothermal and salt-flat basins combined field hydrogeology, advanced geochemical analysis, and doctoral education to improve understanding of arsenic, boron, lithium, salinity, and related risks in water-scarce environments. The resulting process-based interpretations create opportunities for predictive mapping and digitally supported water-resource assessment.

Comparison identifies six conditions for sustainable impact: jointly defined priorities; complementary expertise; long-term mentoring and co-supervision; shared field, laboratory, and data practices; engagement with implementing institutions and communities; and mechanisms translating research into operational tools and practice. Digital databases, dashboards, geospatial models, and professional networks support continuity and scaling. Their integration with hydrogeological and geochemical process understanding offers a pathway toward explainable AI, predictive groundwater intelligence, and future digital-twin applications, but cannot replace trust, equitable participation, mutual learning, local ownership, and enduring scientific leadership.

International partnerships are therefore essential scientific, educational, and digital infrastructure. When co-created research is linked to capacity development, field-operable innovation, data systems, policy engagement, and implementation, it can generate new geoscientific knowledge and durable improvements in groundwater and safe-water security.

title: Geology and preliminary Cr-illite 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Seventymile listwanitized ophiolites—contractional and extensional fault-related fluid flow in the Alaska Yukon Tanana upland
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada (Posters)
authors: Caine, Jonathan Saul [1], Mercer, Cameron Mark [2], McDermott, Robert Gregory [3], Todd, Erin [4]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(3) U.S. Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA
(4) U.S. Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK, USA
abstract:
Ophiolitic, greenschist facies klippen of the Seventymile terrane are exposed throughout the Alaska-Yukon Tanana upland. Ophiolite klippen and parauthochthonous amphibolite facies Devonian-Mississippian basement show a dismembered map pattern reflecting a complex structural history involving obduction, imbrication, and extension. We present new field, X-ray diffraction (XRD) mineralogy, and fault rock geochronology data from two areas, Salcha and Healy, to address uncertainties regarding ophiolite evolution, kinematics, and emplacement age.

Basal shear zones (BSZs) exposed at Salcha and Healy are characterized by listwanite and talc-rich rocks in sharp contact with metamorphic sole and basement gneiss, respectively. BSZ kinematics indicate top-N contraction and possibly later S-directed extension. Listwanite also occurs as discrete, tabular fracture zones internal to klippen. Listwanite XRD (n=11) show mineral assemblages containing magnesite, dolomite, quartz, ankerite, Cr- illite, chlorite, and minor talc. Listwanites show textural evidence for episodic Mg silicate transformation to Mg carbonates; microbrecciation of vein and massive domains; and clots, stringers, and disrupted microveins of Cr-illite.

New 40 Ar/ 39 Ar step-heating experiments on Cr-illite-rich whole rock chips (n=8) of listwanite help characterize the timing of ophiolite emplacement and fault/fracture-related fluid flow. 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates comprise two groups based on 40 Ar compositions: radiogenic dominated (RD; 40 Ar* >50%, n=110) and atmospheric dominated (AD; 40 Ar* <50%, n=70). Dates from RD and AD groups range ~266-64 Ma (median ca. 115 Ma) and ~175-42 Ma (median ca. 71 Ma), respectively, and are positively skewed. RD and AD date distributions overlap but show distinct peaks, with scatter to older dates in both populations.

Date distributions, 40 Ar compositions, and listwanite textures are interpreted as reflecting multiple periods of coupled deformation, permeability creation, and hydrothermal fluid flow contemporaneous with evolving tectonic regimes. Subordinate Late Triassic to Early Jurassic RD (±AD) dates may be related to contractional ophiolite emplacement and regional metamorphism. Dominantly Early Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous RD dates may reflect hydrothermal activity during the transition from regional contraction to extension. AD dates (dominantly Late Cretaceous to Eocene) may indicate ongoing hydrothermal activity well into an extensional regime. The older (middle Cretaceous) peak of RD dates may reflect an early regime of thickened crust with limited circulation of meteoric fluids. Conversely, AD dates centered at ~71 Ma may reflect shallower fluid-flow associated with regional extension and exhumation to the Earth’s near-surface.

title: Selecting appropriate zircon for crustal thickness estimates: Implications for delayed faunal migration in western Anatolia
session_title: From mantle to mountains: understanding interactions between deep Earth and surface processes from geologic data and modeling
authors: Sundell, Kurt [1], Saylor, Joel [2], Göğüş, Oğuz [3], Bodur, Ömer [4], Mackaman-Lofland, Chelsea A. [5], Barnes, Grant [6], Zweigart, Macy [7]
affiliations: (1) Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(2) University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC,
(3) Eurasia Institute of Earth Sciences, Istanbul Technical University, İstanbul, Turkey
(4) Eurasia Institute of Earth Sciences, Istanbul Technical University, İstanbul, Turkey
(5) University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN,
(6) Idaho State University, USA
(7) Idaho State University, USA
abstract: Recent paleoaltimetry estimates of early Miocene western Anatolia suggest high (>3.5 km) topography, which has been interpreted to have acted as a significant barrier to faunal migration. Assuming Airy isostatic balance, this elevation predicts thickened (>50 km) crust. Although thermobarometry estimates support the notion of a thickened crust at this time, no quantitative estimates of crustal thickness exist. We conducted laser ablation ICP-MS for U-Pb geochronology and trace element geochemistry on >2500 detrital zircon grains from eight samples collected from measured stratigraphic sections across western Türkiye. We applied these data to a new multivariate classification routine to determine potential rock types of detrital zircon, trained on a global data set of >20,000 published analyses. Measured stratigraphy and detrital zircon maximum depositional ages from the Gördes, Selendi, and Gediz basins are consistent with mixed fluvial-lacustrine deposition between 18 and 14 Ma. Detrital zircon U-Pb age distributions record a broad mix of 600-350 Ma and 250-200 Ma ages related to Gondwanan and Pangean orogenic episodes, and prominent early Miocene age modes interpreted to be related to synextensional magmatism during orogenic collapse. Classified Miocene zircons are consistent with the local geology and potential sediment sources, as they are inferred to be dominantly sourced from granites, felsic volcanic rocks, and lesser intermediate and mafic igneous rocks. Estimates of early Miocene crustal thickness vary based on rock type. Specifically, zircon inferred to be formed in felsic rocks yield median crustal thickness estimates of ~30 km, with corresponding elevation estimates below sea level. On the other hand, zircon inferred to be from intermediate to mafic igneous rocks give crustal thickness estimates >50 km, consistent with paleoaltimetry and thermobarometry, collectively supporting the interpretation that high topography delayed early Miocene faunal migration across western Anatolia. This study demonstrates that proper data filtering and geochemical classification of zircon are critical to obtaining realistic estimates of paleocrustal thickness.

title: Integrated Lab Analog and Numerical Modeling Study of Chilean Torta Domes: Analogs for Venusian Pancake Domes

abstract:
Pancake domes are one of the few Venusian volcanic features suggested to be non-basaltic. However, without spectroscopic data or chemical analyses, their inferred compositions, crystallinities, and emplacement timescales rely on model results. Existing emplacement models are limited by assumptions such as a parabolic upper surface shape and/or an isothermal interior. New thermo-rheological models that allow variable interior temperatures (i.e. crust growth), allow arbitrary surface shapes, and incorporate temperature-dependent lava properties are needed to better understand dome emplacement and cooling. These models require accurate physical property data for various compositions. We sampled three dacitic domes and two mafic flows from the Altiplano-Puna volcanic complex in Chile. The domes were selected for similar steep-sided shapes (Tocorpuri and Chillahuita) or volumes (Chao) to the pancake domes, while the flows (Volcan San Pedro and La Poruña) provide crystal-rich mafic comparisons.

We measured the key properties needed for modeling: major elements by X-Ray Fluorescence, density by helium pycnometry, thermal diffusivity by light flash analysis, heat capacity by differential scanning calorimetry, and viscosity by parallel-plate viscometry. Bulk lava densities are 1950 to 2310 kgm -3 , with dense rock equivalent densities of 2500-2600 kgm -3 (dacite) and 2700-2800 kgm -3 (mafic). Thermal diffusivity measured from 25 to 500˚C is 0.59 to 0.32 mm 2 s -1 (dacite) and 0.70 to 0.47 mm 2 s -1 (mafic). Heat capacities are 900-1100 Jkg -1 K -1 at 50˚C, rising to 1100-1300 Jkg -1 K -1 at 600˚C. Using calorimetry, the glass fraction is estimated as 5 to 20% (dacite) and 0 to 5% (mafic). Viscosities for 850 to 1000˚C are ~10 9 to 10 12 Pa.s. (dacite). These values are much higher than for obsidian at the same temperature, emphasizing the importance of crystals in lava dome rheology. By varying applied stress, we can constrain the maximum yield stress for the Chao dacite to be ~3kPa at 950˚C, which is much lower than predicted from its morphology (aspect ratio). Our results demonstrate the importance of experimental measurements rather than relying on modeled properties. With these data, we will build computational models of the lava rheologies and material parameters for use in modeling under terrestrial then Venusian surface conditions, with the goal of constraining which inputs (composition, crystallinity, and temperature dependent rheology, effusion rate, vesicularity, etc.), can reproduce the circular, steep-sided dome morphology.

title: Assessing the Impacts of the Dragon Bravo Megafire on Karst fed Headwaters Springs to the Colorado River in Grand Canyon National Park
session_title: The State of Headwaters
authors: Houlgate, Liam [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
abstract: Understanding the impacts of wildfires on groundwater in the Southwestern US is crucial for identifying both short- and long-term changes in arid and semi-arid aquifer systems. The Dragon Bravo megafire burned more than 145000 acres of forest on the Kaibab Plateau in Northern Arizona from 4 July 2025 to 28 September 2025. The Kaibab Plateau makes up the north rim of the eastern Grand Canyon and experiences a yearly bimodal precipitation regime that corresponds to bimodal recharge to the complex fractured karst aquifer system below. The unique ecosystems and remote settings of springs and streams on the Kaibab Plateau make direct monitoring efforts difficult. This research leverages remote continuous monitoring of spring water quality parameters, spot sampling, and discharge measurements to describe the hydrogeological and geochemical response of springs on the Kaibab Plateau. In the water year following the wildfire, a karst fed hillslope spring called Robbers Roost and a sandstone rheochrene spring called North Canyon Wash were re-instrumented with multi-parameter sensors and were regularly visited for sample collection. These sites provide important post-fire comparisons of temperature, pressure, and conductance records to pre-fire values, as these parameters were continuously monitored before the fire. New dissolved organic matter and optical turbidity sensors were also installed post-fire to continuously record organic carbon concentrations and turbidity and have captured multiple discharge pulse events at both study sites. The relationship between dissolved organic matter and turbidity can indicate the degree to which burnt forest litter has infiltrated into the subsurface via sinkholes or has mobilized into stream channels by overland runoff. Significant variability in groundwater chemistry has also been observed in the post-fire water year when compared with pre-fire records. Continuously monitored and spot sampled values of nitrate concentrations are higher than pre-fire levels from the previous 5 years. Concentration differences in other major ions related to discharge values measured at the time of sampling demonstrate a difference in seasonal water quality because of the fire. Findings from this research will assist resource managers in post-fire water quality monitoring and recovery efforts in burned landscapes underlain with karst aquifers and further describe the unique hydrogeology and geochemistry of the Kaibab Plateau.

title: Integrating MicroCT Morphometrics with Molecular Phylogeny to Explore the Taxonomic Placement of Cibicidoides wuellerstorfi
session_title: Cushman Foundation Symposium: Timescales, Rates, and Mechanisms of Climate and Ocean Change Over the Last 250 Million Years: Insights from Foraminiferal Evidence
authors: Burkett, Ashley Morgan [1], Thomas, Ellen [2], Katz, Miriam E. [3], Silye, Lóránd [4], Alegret, Laia [5], Disaró, Sibelle Trevisan [6], Rathburn, Anthony E. [7], Bergh, Eugene [8], Borrelli, Chiara [9], Leon-Rodriguez, Lizette [10]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, OK,
(2) Wesleyan University, Middletown, CT,
(3) Schenectady, NY,
(4) Babeş-Bolyai University, Cluj-Napoca, Romania
(5) University of Zaragoza, Zaragoza, -,
(6) Universidade Federal do Paraná, Paraná, Brazil

(8) North-West University, Potchefstroom, South Africa
(9) University of Rochester, Dept. Earth and Environmental Sciences, Rochester, NY,
(10) Ellington Geological Services,
abstract:
The evolutionary relationships among species assigned to Cibicidoides , Lobatula , and related genera remain the subject of ongoing debate as morphologic and molecular evidence have not always resulted in consistent taxonomic interpretations. One of the most widely used deep-sea benthic foraminifera, Cibicidoides wuellerstorfi , is central to this discussion because of its importance in paleoceanographic and geochemical studies.

To provide new morphologic evidence relevant to this long-standing taxonomic question, we combined high-resolution micro-computed tomography (MicroCT) with published molecular data. Over a hundred specimens of C. wuellerstorfi were imaged using a Zeiss Xradia MicroCT system, and three-dimensional image analysis was performed in Dragonfly software to isolate and quantify the proloculus. Measurements of proloculus size and volume reveal a distinct bimodal distribution that may explain morphotypes historically recognized within C. wuellerstorfi .

Published genetic sequences and phylogenetic analyses are also available for species assigned to Cibicidoides , Lobatula , Cibicides , and Planulina , although previous studies have differed in their interpretation of relationships among these taxa. Here, we evaluate MicroCT-derived morphometric data alongside published molecular phylogenies to determine whether quantitative morphologic characters are consistent with the proposed phylogenetic placement of C. wuellerstorfi . Previous molecular studies have suggested a closer relationship between C. wuellerstorfi and taxa assigned to Lobatula than with some species currently placed within Cibicidoides , despite morphologic similarities among these taxa. Rather than resolving broader systematic relationships, our results provide an independent morphologic dataset for evaluating these relationships and identifying areas requiring further investigation. Integrating non-destructive MicroCT morphometrics with molecular evidence provides a framework for reevaluating benthic foraminiferal systematics and identifying morphologic characters that may better reflect evolutionary relationships.

title: Stratigraphy and Petrology of Cryogenian Basalts in Death Valley
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Braun, Rita [1], Nelson, Lyle Lee [2]
affiliations: (1) Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract: Neoproterozoic volcanic and magmatic rocks along the western margin of Laurentia are sparsely preserved but provide critical records of continental rifting during the breakup of the supercontinent Rodinia. We present stratigraphic, petrologic, and geochemical data from volcanic units within the Cryogenian Kingston Peak Formation in the Panamint Range, Death Valley, to evaluate the tectonic and paleoenvironmental settings of local volcanism during this interval. These results document Cryogenian glaciovolcanic facies produced by ice-magma interactions, inform interpretation of previously published geochronologic data from these units, and help to constrain the tectonic evolution of southwestern Laurentia during the Neoproterozoic, as well as the tectonic setting of regional Snowball Earth deposits.

title: Arizona’s project to promote opportunistic recharge enhancement at landscape levels
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Springer, Abraham E. [1], Mroczek, Caelum [2], Gupta, Neha [3]
affiliations: (1) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ,
(2) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ,
(3) University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
abstract: In water stressed regions that rely heavily on groundwater resources, innovative solutions are needed to enhance the recharge and storage of aquifers. A partnership between Arizona’s state water agency, Northern Arizona University, Arizona State University, and the University of Arizona studied the locations and methods for protecting and enhancing groundwater recharge across the state. The study identified areas with significant snow in coniferous forests as one priority for enhancing recharge through improved forest management processes, especially on fractured and karst terrain. Existing and novel geospatial data were fused to develop a statewide suitability mapping analysis method. Although the primary objectives of an existing landscape-level forest restoration partnership, the Four Forests Restoration Initiative, do not consider recharge, our study provides the land and water resource managers with theory to enhance recharge for the benefit of downstream water users while achieving priority management objectives (i.e. forest health and resilience). This study is one of the few examples of evaluating ecohydrogeological processes at landscape levels to evaluate recharge as a co-benefit of management strategies with the use of large data sets. A decision support framework case study for selecting and implementing opportunistic recharge enhancement will be presented.

title: Modern Thermochronology of the Carolina Tin-Spodumene Belt and Associated Spodumene Pegmatites
session_title: Geochronology of Ore Deposits Containing Critical Minerals: Analytical Advances and Applications
authors: Morrison, Dylan Jacob [1], Coleman, Drew [2], Curry, Adam [3], McDonald, Christopher Steven [4], Pye, Alexandra Eleanor [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Marine, and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(2) Department of Earth, Marine, and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA

(3) Division of Energy, Mineral, and Land Resources, North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality, Raleigh, NC, USA; Department of Earth, Marine, and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(4) Arizona State Univ, School of Earth and Space Exploration, Tempe, AZ,
(5) Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ,
abstract:
The timing of emplacement and thermal evolution of lithium-cesium-tantalum (LCT) pegmatites in the Carolina Tin-Spodumene Belt (CTSB), North Carolina, remain poorly understood despite their importance for Appalachian magmatism and critical mineral resources. We integrate incremental-heating and in situ 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology, electron microprobe analysis, petrography, and wall-rock contact-zone transects to evaluate pegmatite emplacement ages and emplacement-related thermal resetting. Step-heating muscovite analyses from pegmatite interiors yield ages ranging from 330 to 315 Ma, whereas 40 Ar/ 39 Ar amphibole and biotite analyses along two pegmatite-wall rock transects display progressively older ages from near the pegmatite (~311–330 Ma) to the host amphibolite (~340–373 Ma). In situ analyses identify Permian (~282–275 Ma) symplectite associated with K-rich spodumene rims, followed by Triassic (~214 Ma) and Jurassic (~155 Ma) hydrothermal veins that record multiple post-crystallization fluid events without resetting primary pegmatite chronometers.

Thermal diffusion modeling predicts cooling through muscovite closure within years to decades of shallow dike intrusion, consistent with rapid conductive heat loss. Preservation of localized thermal aureoles indicates that intrusion-related heating was spatially restricted and dissipated rapidly into comparatively cool wall rocks, demonstrating that muscovite 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages closely approximate crystallization ages rather than prolonged regional cooling histories. The Ar ages are consistent with mapped cross-cutting relationships, including older spodumene-bearing pegmatites (~330 Ma) intruded by younger barren pegmatites (~315 Ma). Although regional exhumation and localized Ar loss may contribute to age variability, the observed muscovite age range supports multiple intrusion events within the CTSB. This integrated thermochronologic approach provides a framework for resolving emplacement histories in rare-element pegmatite systems across collisional orogenic belts.

title: Trilobite Evolutionary History Features Six Major Evolutionary Faunas Mediated by Major Mass Extinctions
session_title: Paleontology, Diversity, Extinction, Origination
authors: Adrain, Jonathan [1], Pérez Peris, Francesc [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(2) Museum of Comparative Zoology and Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract: That significant evolutionary faunas were a key aspect of trilobite evolutionary history was first reported in 1998, and the Ordovician faunas discriminated in that study, the Whiterock and Ibex evolutionary faunas, have become widely cited features of the group's macroecology. The original analysis was carried out using four temporal intervals of the Ordovician, with families as the units of analysis and genus counts per interval serving as the data. Following decades of data synthesis of the primary taxonomic literature and vast recent improvements in our knowledge of paleotectonic elements, intracontinental biostratigraphy, and intercontinental correlation, it is now possible to explore the comprehensive evolutionary history of the group at high taxonomic and temporal resolutions. We divided the Paleozoic into 36 sampling intervals (six Cambrian, seven Ordovician, eight Silurian, seven Devonian, five Carboniferous, and three Permian). In the Early Paleozoic, intervals correspond mostly to stratigraphic stages, but owing to sparse data due to the great decline in diversity of the group Late Paleozoic intervals are longer. Families were again the units of analysis, but all trilobite families (numbering 168) were included. Data were the species diversity of the families by sampling interval. Species level data were compiled (with constant taxonomic synthesis and revision) in a relational taxonomic database from the primary literature. The number of accepted formally named trilobite species is currently 22,254. Hierarchical cluster analysis was carried out, using several space conserving strategies. All found the same groups: all trilobite families belong to one of six major evolutionary faunas. The previously discovered faunas were recovered, and a further four major Cambrian patterns were identified. Most of the shifts in dominance between the faunas are associated with major extinction events.

title: An assemblage of carbonaceous compression macrofossils from the late Mesoproterozoic – early Tonian Changlingzi Formation, Liaonan region, North China
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age
authors: Qiu, Mingyang [1], Li, Guangjin [2], Tang, Qing [3], Pang, Ke [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences at Virginia Tech, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Blacksburg, VA, USA
(2) Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing, China, China
(3) School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China, China
(4) Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing, China, China
abstract: Tonian Period (~1000-720 Ma) fossils, encompassing both body fossils and molecular fossils, have offered essential insights into the rise of crown-group eukaryotic algae and the establishment of the symbiotic relationships. Macroscopic carbonaceous compression fossils, as one of the most common fossil types of the Tonian Period, have garnered significant attention in research areas concerning the origin and evolution of eukaryotic algae. Here we report a well-preserved and moderately diverse assemblage of carbonaceous compression macrofossils from the late Mesoproterozoic – early Tonian Changlingzi Formation (1100 -924 Ma) in southern Liaoning Province, North China. The assemblage is dominated by Chuaria circularis , Tawuia dalensis , and Protoarenicola sp. Through optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), we confirm the micrometer-scale annulation structure of Protoarenicola sp. Energy spectrum analysis, focused ion beam SEM, and Raman spectroscopy have been used to reveal the potential affinity of epibiontic organisms on Chuaria , Tawuia , and Protoarenicola . A compilation of fossil occurrences shows that Protoarenicola, together with Pararenicola and Sinosabellidites , has only been found in the late Mesoproterozoic – Tonian strata, suggesting potential stratigraphic significance. The new fossil assemblage from the Changlingzi Formation provides valuable materials for exploring the origin and evolution of macroscopic eukaryotic organisms as well as symbiosis among early eukaryotes.

title: Uncovering the Microplastic Legacy of the 2017 Durban Nurdle Spill in South African Coastal Sediments
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part II)
authors: Moore, Gavin [1], Smolen, Justin [2], Jaiswal, Kuhu [3], Hillegeist, Evan [4], Rice, Isaac [5], Sundell, Kurt [6], Nielsen, Ryan [7], Perez, Nicholas [8]
affiliations: (1) Chemistry, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
(2) Chemistry, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(3) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA
(4) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(5) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
(6) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID,
(7) Geosciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, USA
(8) Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX,
abstract:
In 2017, approximately 49 metric tons of polyethylene (PE) nurdles, the lentil-sized pellets from which plastic products are molded, spilled from shipping containers into the ocean near Durban, South Africa. Because the timing, location, and plastic type are all known, the spill offers a rare natural experiment: does a single release leave a recognizable signature in sediments nearly a decade later? Polypropylene (PP), a second common and chemically similar plastic, entered the same sediments only through scattered everyday sources, never from the spill. Coastal-river differences in PP therefore record what the coastal environment alone does to plastic, providing a built-in control. Sediments from three coastal and five river sites were processed by density separation, fluorescent staining, and automated imaging, with each particle's polymer identified by infrared microspectroscopy and machine learning. Within every sample, we asked how alike the particles were in three respects: physical size; carbonyl index, an infrared measure of plastic weathering; and whole-spectrum fingerprint, which reflects the manufacturer's resin recipe. Particles sharing one origin and entry time should be unusually alike. Comparisons used two-sided permutation tests at the sample level, clustered by site.

Coastal sediments held roughly five times more PE than river sediments. Particle size did not distinguish the groups: after nearly a decade of fragmentation, the spread of sizes was essentially identical everywhere. Spectroscopic analysis, however, revealed that coastal PE samples had less variable weathering states than river PE samples, as moving from rivers to the coast roughly halved the spread in carbonyl index. Meanwhile, the spread in PP barely changed. This contrast between the polymers, the signature a spill should produce and coastal conditions alone should not, ran in the predicted direction but fell just short of statistical significance. Resin fingerprints agreed: coastal PE clustered tightly, as expected of pellets from a single manufacturer, while coastal PP grew more varied.

The enrichment, shared weathering state, and matching fingerprints of coastal PE are consistent with a shared origin and entry event and were not observed in collected PP microplastics. Weathering chemistry and resin fingerprint, not particle size, preserve evidence of point-source plastic releases on decadal timescales, even when other metrics fade.

title: Fingerprinting Mercer Ice Stream Provenance in West Antarctica: Detrital Zircon U-Pb and Trace and Rare Earth Element Insights into Antarctica’s Subglacial Geology
session_title: From Outcrop to Isotope: Bridging Field Observations and Detrital Analytical Tools
authors: Campbell, Timothy D [1], Orme, Devon A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Bowdoin College, Brunswick, ME, USA; Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
(2) Montana State University, Bozeman, MT,
abstract: Antarctica's geologic history preserves a record of the amalgamation and breakup of past supercontinents, including Rodinia and Gondwana. Yet, Antarctica's subglacial geology remains cryptic because the East and West Antarctic Ice Sheets bury 98% of the continent’s bedrock. Since flowing ice entrains and transports sediment, provenance analysis offers constraints into the ice-covered upstream geology. Sediment in the Ross Embayment integrates material with both East Antarctic and West Antarctic affinities. Previous provenance studies on the Ross region partly relied on low- n (<100) detrital zircon (DZ) U-Pb geochronologic age spectra from ice stream sediment, Transantarctic Mountain (TAM) outlet glaciers, and the continental shelf, which may miss rare but diagnostic age modes. We present a large- n U-Pb, Lu-Hf, and trace-element fingerprint of detrital zircons from beneath Mercer Ice Stream, a key missing ice stream in past reconstructions. We report 558 U-Pb ages and 50 Lu-Hf/trace-element analyses, which are dominated by Ross Orogen-aged grains (~540-510 Ma; 47%) alongside significant Grenville (900-1350 Ma; 22%) and older Proterozoic-Archean age modes. We identify rare, Jurassic-Cretaceous-aged zircons ( n = 3). Th/U and trace element analyses indicate primarily igneous granitoid sources, while εHf results reveal that Ross-aged zircons were derived from multiple crustal reservoirs. Results are consistent with East Antarctic margin sources but cannot be explained solely by juvenile granitoids exposed in the southern TAM near Reedy Glacier, Mercer’s current primary tributary. Rare Jurassic-Cretaceous-aged zircons may suggest minor West Antarctic input. A multidimensional scaling comparison of ice stream detrital zircon U-Pb ages shows that Mercer is most similar to Kamb, followed by Whillans, and most different from Bindschadler. Several low- n continental shelf sediments plot far from the ice stream cluster, possibly reflecting sampling limitations rather than geologic differences. Collectively, we present a high-resolution provenance fingerprint for the Mercer Ice Stream and demonstrate why large-n, multi-proxy DZ datasets are necessary to constrain sediment routing pathways to elucidate Antarctica’s ice-covered geologic history.

title: Geophysical and geochronological evidence for reactivation of the rifted Laurentian margin in the New England Appalachians
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part I)
authors: Bourke, James [1], Webb, Laura E. [2], Karabinos, Paul [3], Long, Maureen [4]
affiliations: (1) Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA
(3) Williams College, Williamstown, MA,
(4) Yale University, New Haven, CT,
abstract: The New England Appalachians provide a unique window into a host of fundamental geologic phenomena which include modification of the crust and mantle lithosphere through Neoproterozoic continental rifting, Paleozoic terrane accretion and Appalachian orogenesis, and Mesozoic rifting. Recent (SEISConn, 2016-2019; GENESIS, 2021-2025) and ongoing (NEST, 2018-Present) temporary broadband seismological experiments have revealed the lithospheric structure in unprecedented detail. However, their station spacing (~10 km) has restricted the analysis to deeper crust and upper mantle imaging, limiting our ability to connect mapped bedrock geology and the well-imaged deeper structures. We present results from recent seismological deployments using hundreds of short-period nodal seismometers with high density spacing (< 500m), tracing geologic structures at the surface into their projections at depth. One of our arrays crosses the transition from Laurentian crust to the rifted Laurentian margin, modified during Neoproterozoic rifting, and over the western boundary of the Gondwanan-derived accreted Moretown terrane in northwestern Massachusetts. We observe two throughgoing crustal features in the receiver function imaging that correlate with the surface region between coherent Laurentian and rifted Laurentian crust, and between rifted Laurentian crust and the accreted Moretown terrane. Between the coherent Laurentian crust and accreted Moretown terrane we observe a Moho-offset between the thicker Laurentian crust (~50 km) and thinner Appalachian crust (~30km). The displacement that produced the Moho offset that is dominantly accommodated by the interface between coherent Laurentia and rifted Laurentian crust. Between these two dipping features is a zone of complex signals within the lower crust of rifted Laurentia, which is interpreted as a heterogenous zone of basal crustal and mantle materials. The rifted Laurentian zone displays signals that form convergent structural patterns within the upper-to-mid rifted crust, implying the rifted Laurentia margin operated as a zone of mechanical weakness, concentrating deformation through Paleozoic accretion and orogenesis. We interpret the interface between coherent Laurentian and rift-modified Laurentian crust as the downward continuation of reactivated Taconic thrusts that can be traced from the near surface to the Moho. We synthesize our seismological results with 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology and (micro)structural analyses that indicate these faults moved multiple times since 420 Ma. These results shed light on how a rifted continental margin can influence terrane accretion and subsequent overprinting.

title: GeoCORK for U-Pb Geochronology Data Management
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data
authors: Metcalf, Kathryn [1], Burges, Jarrod [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, Fullerton, Fullerton, CA,
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, New Jersey, USA
abstract: Geochronology datasets are growing quickly as they become cheaper and faster to produce. There are several sources and formats for U-Pb geochronology data and several analysis tools that require different input formats, so managing collections of data is complex and time-consuming. GeoCORK is a desktop application to create and manage personal databases of U-Pb geochronology data and metadata. The source code and current release for Windows and Mac are freely available on GitHub. Data are stored in a SQLite database with 58 tables that are linked to samples, aliquots, grains (optional), spots, and U-Pb analyses, and user interfaces give researchers flexibility and control managing collections without coding. The import wizard supports Excel files with multiple samples and sheets, and import formats can be saved for reuse. An item can have multiple user-defined tags, and many of them can be nested. GeoCORK stores data in the original units and formats, but it can convert and display data according to the selected values in the settings for easier comparison. For complex filtering of data and metadata across the database, conditions can be nested and joined with combinations of match all, match any, or match none. Filter criteria can be saved for viewing and exporting, and the results automatically update as the database grows and changes. The exporter has predefined export formats for common U-Pb analysis tools and allows custom formatting with support for multiple sheets. GeoCORK was designed to expand to more methods in the future. We are currently working on integrating geochemistry data which is increasingly collected along with U-Pb geochronology. To promote findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) data principles, we are working to integrate importing from and exporting to online databases directly from GeoCORK. We welcome feedback on the current release of GeoCORK as well as community needs and future directions.

title: FROM LIABILITY RELIEF TO GOVERNED REMEDIATION: AN IMPLEMENTATION FRAMEWORK FOR U.S. GOOD SAMARITAN MINE CLEANUP
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Morgan, Molly Catherine [1], Smith, Nicole [2], Holley, Elizabeth A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Colorado School of MinesMining Engineering, Golden, CO,
abstract:
Abandoned hardrock mines release acid mine drainage and metals from unstable wastes, but non-liable organizations have been deterred from cleanup by potential liability under the Clean Water Act and Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA). The Good Samaritan Remediation of Abandoned Hardrock Mines Act of 2024 creates a pilot program that lowers this barrier. It does not determine who controls risk thresholds, how projects advance under uncertainty, or how performance is verified. We ask what governance conditions are needed for pilots to remain legitimate, adaptive, and accountable.

Using a qualitative, abductive framework-building design, we integrated statutory and program review, seven semi-structured stakeholder interviews, participant observation at a 92-person implementation summit, and comparative stress tests of Herculaneum, Missouri; the Dommel River, Belgium-Netherlands; and Iron Mountain Mine, California. Three requirements emerged: (1) co-governance giving affected local and Tribal governments and communities consequential influence over risk, monitoring, and escalation; (2) staged, performance-based permissions with enforceable milestones and off-ramps that preserve remediation primacy; and (3) transparent environmental and financial monitoring tied to public reporting, independent verification, and regulatory consequences.

We translate these findings into a provisional Regenerative Commons Framework spanning baseline design, investigative sampling, limited remediation, full remediation and optional recovery where legally permissible, and closure or long-term stewardship. Resource recovery remains subordinate to cleanup, and financial assurance is treated as a governance condition rather than an administrative afterthought. The framework is not a validated national model but a testable implementation architecture. Pilot success should be evaluated through governance performance as well as environmental outcomes.

title: Response of Headwater Wilderness Springs and Streams in Grand Canyon National Park to Fire and Flooding
session_title: The State of Headwaters
authors: Whitehouse, Jack Duncan [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona Univ, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
abstract: Springfed headwater tributary streams supply up to 5 % of the base flow of the Colorado River through Grand Canyon. These ecosystems support nearly half of the vegetation species in the greater ecoregion. These systems are receiving increasing frequency and threats from human induced fires followed by flooding. A two-decade long study was conducted at Cottonwood Creek Springs ecosystem (CCSE) to analyze ecohydrogeological interactions and resilience within its spring-fed headwater tributary riparian corridor in central Grand Canyon and its relationship between the fire damage and localized flooding in washes. The increased damage of climate change during the two-decade long study has shown the threat to spring ecosystems that intense fires and localized flooding can cause. CCSE experienced significant change in terms of geomorphology and plant life as the post fire and post flood caused the channel to erode and expose bedrock in portions of the stream. However, the response of vegetation growth in the CCSE showed profound resilience and recovery post flood in flooded areas, but still yet to show any growth of cottonwood trees in burned areas. Wet-dry maps from the two-decade long research explains some of the seasonal factors of spring that affected flow rate, the percentage of flow, and where flow stops and starts. Wet-dry maps show the seasonal change through the years and how climate change has drastically diminished the amount of flow through CCSE, ultimately making the recovery of both post fire and post flood for the riparian environment significantly harsher.

title: Improving the Chronology of Late Pleistocene-Holocene Glacial Retreat from Marine Sediment Core Records in the Antarctic Peninsula
session_title: Reconstructing the extent and timing of Late Quaternary glaciations
authors: Totten, Rebecca L. [1], Heberlein, Marianne Gisela [2], Tobin, Thomas S. [3], Anderson, John B. [4], Wellner, Julia S. [5], Fernandez, Rorigo [6]
affiliations: (1) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Tuscaloosa, AL, ; CONSERVE Research Group, Alabama Water Institute, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(2) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(3) University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(4) Rice University, Houston, TX, USA
(5) University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA
(6) Universidad de Chile, Santiago, Chile
abstract:
Twentieth Century glacial retreat was widespread and rapid in the Antarctic Peninsula, and it is unclear if this synchronous event is unique to the period of recent warming, or if precedent exists in the Late Pleistocene-Holocene record. To constrain future glacial contribution to sea-level rise, it is critical to build models with an understanding of controls on glacial stability over centennial to millennial time scales and in response to climatic and oceanographic events. Here we present a database of marine geological records to compare tidewater glacier histories across the Antarctic Peninsula, and we further compare these to deep ocean records and an ice core to investigate controls on glacial stability over the last 15,000 years.

First, to compare the glacial histories of fjords that drain these tidewater glaciers, in addition to deep ocean sites, recalibration of radiocarbon chronologies of published sediment records must be systematically applied. Moreover, radiocarbon reservoir corrections for the Antarctic Peninsula have relied on sparse, offshore sample sets; new, living carbonate-producing organisms can be dated to improve reservoir age corrections. In 2026, the R/V Sikuliaq collected new living bivalve samples from the seafloor in the Firth of Tay, which will be used to improve corrections for the northeastern Antarctic Peninsula, in addition to newly collected living calcareous foraminifera from the southwestern Antarctic Peninsula.

The comparison of 12 sites reveals that glacial retreat was highly asynchronous from the Late Pleistocene to Mid Holocene, with up to over 9,000 yr difference between the onset of initial grounding line retreat from Maxwell Bay and from Beascochea Bay. The Mid Holocene Climatic Optimum differed a little over 4,000 from the onset of its expression in Maxwell Bay to the mid latitude fjords of the peninsula. During the Late Holocene, however, glaciers responded much more synchronously, with less than 2,000 yr and 800 yr difference in the response to the Neoglacial and the Little Ice Age, respectively. Therefore, the synchronicity of glacier behavior dramatically increased during the Holocene. Variable response to earlier Holocene climate events underscores local controls on glacial stability, which contrasts with the last century, when almost all of Antarctic Peninsula tidewater glaciers retreated, resulting in a uniquely synchronous event.

abstract: At California State University, Fresno, located in the Central Valley, the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences (EES), under the College of Science and Mathematics, offers a class called Climate Change Solutions (EES 115S). This class focuses on learning about climate change, promoting climate action, and engaging in service learning in the Fresno area. Initially developed and implemented in 2024 with NSF GEO RISE programmatic support (award #2120051), the course has evolved its service-learning to be: 1) more impactful beyond the community of students, faculty, staff, and Fresno State, and 2) more sequentially and academically (i.e., “vertically integrated”) with first-year through programmatic capstone experiences. Over two years, we have expanded service and course-based research learning beyond Fresno State, building partnerships with community members invested in the success of our students, and which co-curricularly support a range of impactful volunteer opportunities at community gardens located in neighborhoods, at STEM camps for kids teaching them about climate change through activities, and learning and participating in river and wildfire cleanup and management. To bridge this high-impact course with the college’s first-year experience (CSM 10 and CSM 15), our current work focuses on creating collaborative learning experiences that span across classes. In CSM 10 and 15, first-year students build foundational skills in the scientific method, literature review, and research design centered on sustainability. We are expanding this framework so upper-level EES 115s students conduct community-engaged research that directly serves regional environmental needs, while simultaneously serving as peer mentors and role models for the first-year CSM students. This cross-class integration allows introductory students to see real-world applications of their early research concepts, while empowering upper-level students to cultivate leadership skills—building a sustained, multi-tiered pipeline of student-driven climate action and community impact.

title: Assessing the Alteration of Depositional Sedimentary Sulfur Isotopes Under Thermal Alteration Using Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry
session_title: New Advances in Geobiology and Geomicrobiology (Posters)
authors: Marroquín, Selva M [1], Konavaluk, Hanna [2], Blum, Tyler [3], Bonamici, Chloe E. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(2) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI,
(3) The University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(4) University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA
abstract: The sedimentary sulfur record is critical for interpreting how marine environments have evolved throughout Earth’s history as the burial of reduced sulfur species impacts global climate through drawdown of atmospheric CO 2 and buildup of O 2 . Furthermore, depositional conditions, such as ocean chemistry, microbial activity, and redox conditions in deep geologic time are recorded in the pyrite sulfur isotope composition. However, it remains an open area of study whether depositional δ 34 S signals are retained after deep burial and exposure to the geothermal gradient, later stage metamorphism, and hydrothermal fluid flow. In this work, we seek to assess the response of iron sulfide δ 34 S during high temperature diagenesis and hydrothermal fluid flow, using in-situ sulfur isotope analyses of individual sulfide grains. Samples were collected within a single stratigraphic horizon of the Upper Cretaceous Pierre Shale (Maxwell, NM) along a 22 m transect perpendicular to a Cenozoic mafic intrusion (9 m). Here, we present Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) δ 34 S data on individual sulfide grains and additional mineralogical and lithological constraints (e.g. X-ray diffraction, vitrinite reflectance and total organic carbon content). The thermal influence of the mafic dike, as well as fluids evolved from the dike or through heating-induced dehydration reactions, has driven variable amounts of recrystallization of framboidal pyrite to pyrite grains, and the formation of pyrrhotite. Both recrystallization of primary pyrite and reaction to pyrrhotite appear systematically within the transect, along with a decrease in total organic carbon content with proximity to the dike. Sulfur isotopes in samples distal and proximal to the intrusion show different patterns of sample-scale variability. δ 34 S values within pyrite average around -33‰ and become heavier (avg. -25 ‰) with proximity to the dike before returning to the depleted average 2.5 m from the dike. Pyrrhotite δ 34 S is consistently enriched (avg. -24‰) but shows less within-sample spread when compared to pyrite. These data suggest there may have been isotopic exchange with a higher δ 34 S fluid in a given sample as pyrite was being converted to pyrrhotite through hydrothermal alteration. Despite evidence for sample-scale reorganization of sulfur, we find that the average pyrite sedimentary δ 34 S signatures in the studied bed remained broadly preserved across the hydrothermal alteration halo of the intrusion, where temperatures reached up to ~300°C.

title: Kinematics, Geometry, and Timing of Laramide Deformation in the Fenner Hills, Eastern Mojave Desert, CA
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Sabatino, Frances [1], Wells, Michael L. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
(2) Department of Geoscience, University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Las Vegas, NV, USA
abstract:
The Fenner Hills are a N-S trending range in the eastern Mojave Desert, between the Old Woman-Piute Mountains and the New York Mountains. The southern Fenner Hills display a stacked sequence of recumbently folded and imbricated Proterozoic basement gneiss and Cambrian metasedimentary rocks, which are cross-cut by a granodiorite pluton. Although strain is distributed throughout the imbricate stack, it is heterogeneous within the various lithologies, with localized areas of high strain exhibiting strong W-dipping foliations and SW-trending stretching lineations. We refer to these highly strained rocks as the Fenner Hills Shear Zone (FHSZ). Unlike other nearby shear zones, age and kinematics of deformation in the FHSZ were previously poorly understood. We present preliminary field and microstructural observations combined with geochronological data to address its age and tectonic significance.

The kinematics of the FHSZ are most evident in the Proterozoic Fenner Gneiss, a K-feldspar porphyritic orthogneiss. Asymmetric porphyroclasts and shear bands record top-SW shear. Deformation occurred under high temperature (>600°C) conditions as indicated by nearly complete dynamic recrystallization of K-feldspar, and grain-boundary migration and chessboard extinction microstructures in quartz. The SW-dipping foliation together with top-SW kinematics suggests that, unless there was significant horizontal axis rotation, the FHSZ is an extensional shear zone. However, the elevated temperatures and garnet-staurolite-andalusite assemblages in the metamorphosed Cambrian Bright Angel Shale require Mesozoic thrust burial in its history. The presence of east-vergent folds and locally bidirectional micro-scale kinematics suggests the FHSZ initiated as a compressional shear zone and was reactivated as a result of Late Cretaceous extension.

A new LA-ICP-MS zircon U-Pb age of 74.2±1.1 Ma from the cross-cutting but locally weakly deformed biotite granodiorite, possibly correlative to the Goffs Pluton, constrains the age of the FHSZ to predate intrusion at 74 Ma. Regional structural correlations suggest that the FHSZ may be part of a Late Cretaceous extensional fault system that includes top-SW extensional shear zones of Late Cretaceous age recognized in the New York and Old Woman Mountains. We conclude that the FHSZ provides valuable insight into Late Cretaceous extension and shear zone reactivation in the Mojave, occurring towards the end of the Laramide orogeny along the inferred path of the subducted Conjugate Shatsky Rise oceanic plateau.

title: A Test of the Eclogite Delamination Model for the Uplift of the Wallowa Mountains: Insights from Hornblende Trace Element Crustal Thickness Estimates
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Palucho, Kayla Veronica [1], Johnson, Kenneth [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Houston-Downtown, Houston, TX, USA
(2) University of Houston-Downtown, Houston, TX, USA
abstract:
Understanding how continental crust evolves through time requires reliable estimates of crustal thickness in ancient arc systems. Bulk-rock trace element ratios, including Sr/Y and La/Yb, are widely used as indicators of crustal thickness but may be modified by crystal accumulation and magmatic differentiation which obscure primary melt signatures and introduce uncertainty into crustal thickness estimates.

Lower crustal (eclogite) delamination has been proposed as a trigger for uplift of the Wallowa Mountains in northeastern Oregon and the ensuing eruption of Columbia River flood basalts. The Wallowa batholith, which comprises most of the Wallowa Mountains, provides an ideal test of this hypothesis. Previous studies, utilizing whole rock Sr/Y and La/Yb and zircon Eu/Eu*, have suggested substantial crustal thickening beneath the Wallowa batholith during its 18-million-year magmatic history (140-122 Ma); however, the samples used have a significant cumulate component and thus do not represent melt compositions.

Melt compositions in equilibrium with hornblende were determined using hornblende trace element abundances. The chondrite-normalized La/Yb values (ranging from 4.5 and 7.1) were then used to calculate crustal thickness, according to the calibration of Chapman et al., 2015. A best fit trend line through the data (host tonalite/granodiorite and hornblende cumulates) show that the crust underlying the Wallowa batholith experienced thickening from ~32 to 41 km (~10 to 12.5 kbar) from 140 to 125 Ma (the 122 Ma pluton does not contain hornblende). The upper pressure estimate (12.5 kbar) is near the amphibolite/eclogite facies transition; thus, formation of a garnet amphibolite to eclogite root beneath the Wallowa Mountains during Cretaceous time is permissible. Results of this study show the promise of using mineral-derived melt compositions to estimate crustal thickness.

title: Multistage Mineralization of Dinosaur Bones from the Jurassic Brushy Basin Member, Morrison Formation, Western Colorado
session_title: Laws of the Grave: Advances in Taphonomy across the Paleontologic Record (Posters)
authors: Sonheim, Ryan Jacon [1], King, Michael Ryan [2], Petrie, Elizabeth S. [3], Zanno, Lindsay [4]
affiliations: (1) Natural & Environmental Sciences, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, Colorado, USA
(2) Natural & Environmental Sciences, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(3) Natural & Environmental Sciences, Western Colorado University, Gunnison, CO, USA
(4) NC Museum of Natural Sciences, Paleontology, Raleigh, NC,
abstract:
Permineralization and replacement affect the preservation, texture, and color of fossil bones. Post-burial fracturing can reopen mineralized bone to subsurface fluids and produce additional mineralization. This study compares four dinosaur bone samples from different geographic locations within the Late Jurassic Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation in Curecanti National Recreation Area (CURE) near Gunnison, Colorado, with five fracture-mineralized samples from a sauropod within the Morrison Formation at the Gordon-Bramson-Brothers Quarry near Snowmass, Colorado. Two additional specimens from the Cedar Mountain Formation were examined to assess potential host lithology controls. The study evaluates the paragenetic stages within bone pore spaces and tests whether fractures introduced new minerals, reworked earlier minerals, or both. Optical petrography of thin sections was used to identify mineral composition, veins, and establish mineralization sequences from cross-cutting and overgrowth relationships.

The four CURE samples do not preserve a single, common pore mineralization sequence. The first contains early iron oxide along pore walls, followed by microcrystalline quartz, a second iron-rich band, and a later, coarser microcrystalline quartz, recording two episodes of precipitation. Two of the samples are dominated by calcite-filled pores that coarsens toward their centers. One of these preserves iron oxide staining that predates calcite and microcrystalline quartz that postdates calcite in some pore centers. The last CURE sample contains fine-grained red-orange calcite along pore margins, coarser yellow calcite toward centers, and an unidentified green acicular mineral. These differences demonstrate distinct mineralization histories among bones from the same stratigraphic unit. Cedar Mountain Formation specimens show broadly similar mineralization but less extensive iron enrichment, suggesting that host-sediment geochemistry and associated paleoenvironmental conditions may influence bone paragenesis.

The five Snowmass specimens preserve earlier pore fills and later fracture-controlled mineralization. Fractures crosscut mineralized pores and contain fine-grained calcite and quartz. Some fracture assemblages differ from adjacent pore fill, indicating precipitation from later fluids, whereas others contain silica-rich fragments resembling earlier pore-filling minerals, suggesting potential reworking. These textures indicate that fracturing postdated pore mineralization, disrupted earlier fills, and incorporated dominantly cataclasis fragments into later fracture cement. Renewed fluid movement therefore produced both new mineral precipitation and reworking of earlier minerals. Initial pore mineralization varied among individual bones and may have been influenced by local host-sediment conditions, whereas fracturing created a secondary diagenetic stage that increased complexity.

title: Evaluating Subsurface Flowpath Controls on Seasonal Stream Chemistry in a Permafrost Catchment
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Grose, Amelia L [1], McKenzie, Jeffrey M. [2], Celupica-Liu, Corrine [3], Grewal, Arsh [4], Zarnetske, Jay P. [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada
(2) Earth and Planetary Sciences, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada
(3) McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada
(4) University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, SK, Canada
(5) Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI,
abstract:
Stream chemistry reflects dominant water flowpaths, allowing streams to act as integrated sensors of hydrological and landscape processes occurring throughout the catchment. In Arctic catchments underlain by continuous permafrost, subsurface flowpaths are controlled by water and frost table depth, making stream chemistry a potentially useful indicator of active layer dynamics. Although Arctic stream chemistry exhibits pronounced seasonal variability, it remains unclear whether these changes are driven by evolving subsurface flowpaths or by other hydrological and biogeochemical processes. In temperate regions, the shallow and deep hypothesis provides one explanation for this seasonal variability, positing that stream chemistry is a function of water table depth and the average soil water chemistry profile within a catchment. However, this hypothesis has not been directly evaluated in permafrost landscapes, where both water table position and the seasonally deepening frost table control subsurface flowpath depths.

To evaluate if seasonal changes in stream chemistry can be explained by changing flowpath depths, we use a two-dimensional, variably saturated coupled groundwater flow and energy transport model, SUTRA 4.0 (U.S. Geological Survey), to simulate seasonal thaw dynamics and subsurface flowpaths. The study site is a low-gradient hillslope in the Upper Kuparuk River catchment on the North Slope of Alaska, USA. The model uses measured precipitation, SWE, soil hydraulic properties, and ground temperatures in the shallow (<1 m) subsurface to simulate active layer development and the depth of subsurface flowpaths throughout the summer thaw season. We compare simulated seasonal flowpath evolution with the assumptions of the shallow and deep hypothesis to determine whether evolving subsurface flowpaths explain observed seasonal patterns in stream chemistry. These findings will improve our ability to use streams as sensors of landscape processes and active layer dynamics, and strengthen predictions of hydrologic responses to continued Arctic warming.

title: Neither Gone nor Forgotten: Aluminous Schists with Multiple Generations of Sillimanite Preserve Syn- and Post-Tectonic Grenvillian Metamorphic History at Enchanted Rock, Llano Uplift, Texas
session_title: Petrology, Economic Geology, and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Stevens, Liane M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Aviation Sciences, Stephen F Austin State University, Nacogdoches, TX, USA
abstract:
The regional metamorphism of Packsaddle domain schists within the Enchanted Rock contact aureole, exhumed by the Llano uplift of central Texas, was expected to be strongly overprinted by late, fluid-rich metamorphism associated with the post-Grenville intrusion of anorogenic granitoids. Instead, these aluminous schists preserve a complex history of regional metamorphism (M 2 ), partial melting, contact metamorphism/static overprinting (M 3 ), and possible isothermal decompression. This metamorphic history is preserved as a large number of phases (quartz, biotite, garnet, sillimanite, K-feldspar, cordierite, sapphirine, muscovite, chlorite, plus evidence for early andalusite and relict orthopyroxene); multiple generations of sillimanite; and numerous disequilibrium textures (isolated phases, pseudomorphs, symplectites, rims).

Sillimanite is present in four different habits: 1) coarse, squarish grains with diamond-shaped subgrains indicative of sillimanite pseudomorphs after andalusite; 2) coarse, elongate crystals and diamond-shaped basal sections; 3) fibrolite; and 4) fine, acicular prisms. The sillimanite pseudomorphs suggest early growth of andalusite at lower P-T conditions. Both the elongate crystals and fibrolite are parallel to the dominant foliation, which has been associated with regional metamorphism. The fine, acicular prisms are not always parallel to foliation, suggesting syn- to post-tectonic growth. Intergrowths of cordierite and green sapphirine are associated with both the elongate and the acicular sillimanite. The elongate sillimanite may be rimmed by cordierite + sapphirine symplectite, followed by an outer cordierite moat that separates sapphirine from quartz in the matrix. Pods of intergrown cordierite and sapphirine, rimmed by cordierite, may contain fine, acicular sillimanite.

Interpretation of sillimanite habits and microstructures suggests preservation of much of the prograde M 2 P-T path, as well as part of the retrograde path. The peak assemblage (biotite + plagioclase ± fibrolite ± K-feldspar ± sapphirine ± cordierite ± melt) and the cordierite-sapphirine symplectite suggests high- T regional or contact metamorphism to upper amphibolite or lower granulite facies during M 2 , with cordierite-sapphirine symplectite also possibly formed through isothermal decompression at peak T. The Al 2 O 3 - and MgO-rich phases could derive from a protolith that experienced multiple episodes of partial melting. This work to identify phases, phase relationships, and petrologic domains, and interpret metamorphic history was done in preparation for thermodynamic phase modeling and in situ geochronology. Future work could better constrain the conditions and timing of M 2 and improve understanding of the Grenville orogeny in the Llano uplift.
