title: Reconstructing Climate during the Late Paleozoic Ice Age using Sequence Stratigraphy and Conodont Oxygen Isotope Composition from the Midcontinent Basin, USA
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session
authors: Daniel, Jenelle [1], Griffin, Julie McDermott [2], Holterhoff, Peter [3], Montanez, Isabel P. [4]
affiliations: (1) California State University - Sacramento, Citrus Heights, CA, USA
(2) California State University - Sacramento, Carmichael, CA, USA
(3) Perot Museum of Nature and Science, Dallas, TX, USA
(4) University of California, Davis, CA, USA
abstract: Reconstructing Late Paleozoic Ice Age (LPIA) climate changes can help explain modern climate because the LPIA is Earth’s penultimate icehouse. Epicontinental deposits from the LPIA record global glacial cycles via connection with the open ocean but also document regional environmental conditions. Regional hydroclimate changes likely affected eperic seawater chemistry given their proximity to land, shallow water and unique circulation including episodic restriction from the open ocean. Seawater chemistry is recorded in the phosphate oxygen isotope composition (𝛿 18 O PO4 ) of conodonts. Here we use sequence and 𝛿 18 O PO4 stratigraphy to reconstruct glacioeustasy and low-latitude regional hydrology in the eperic Midcontinent Sea. Sequence stratigraphic analysis of Pennsylvanian-age deposits along a North-South transect in eastern KS and OK confirm that eccentricity-driven glacioeustasy created cyclothems. Analysis of the Swope, Mound Valley, and Dennis cyclothems reveals multiple temporal orders of sea level change. Swope deposits record a highstand sequence, and in the south are overlain by lowstand Mound Valley sediments. A subsequent sea level highstand deposited the Dennis across the entire Midcontinent region. Samples from the Swope, Mound Valley, and Dennis were also collected in Kansas City, MO and Nowata Co., OK at the centimeter-scale and analyzed for conodont 𝛿 18 O PO4 . Average 𝛿 18 O PO4 values within the Swope, Mound Valley, and Dennis cyclothems are within error of each other, despite sequence stratigraphic analysis indicating the Mound Valley cycle was deposited during a glacial maximum with higher seawater 𝛿 18 O. Both the Swope and Dennis exhibit high-frequency variability in conodont 𝛿 18 O PO4 attributed to variations in local hydrology, but these fluctuations are not present in the Mound Valley. The lack of high-frequency fluctuations may be due to limited sampling resolution, or because of the glacial deposition of the Mound Valley. Within the Swope and Dennis, 𝛿 18 O PO4 is consistent with lithological interpretations of sea level change. Within the Mound Valley, lithological interpretation of black shale indicates a rise in sea level, with an expected decrease in 𝛿 18 O PO4 . However, 𝛿 18 O PO4 increases within the black shale. We explore multiple reasons for this disagreement, including changes in hydrology or mineralization environment. These high-resolution lithologic and 𝛿 18 O PO4 stratigraphies from the Midcontinent Sea suggest multiple forcing mechanisms driving global and regional climate change during the LPIA. Understanding these forcing mechanisms will improve our knowledge of icehouse climates.

title: PRELIMINARY ABIOTIC GEOCHEMICAL AND HEADSPACE MONITORING IN ENCELADUS-ANALOG BRINE–MINERAL REACTORS
session_title: Planetary Potpourri (Posters)
authors: Claggett, Brad W [1], McKinney, Brett [2], Clough, Lily [3], Theiling, Bethany [4]
affiliations: (1) Math & Science, Northeastern Oklahoma A&M College, Miami, OK, USA
(2) Physics, University of Tulsa, Tulsa, OK, USA
(3) Geology & Physics, University of Tulsa, Tulsa, OK, USA

abstract: Enceladus' plume chemistry indicates ongoing interaction between a carbonate-bearing ocean and rocky core, where abiotic water-rock reactions may generate chemical changes that complicate biosignature interpretation. We developed an accessible, modular reactor platform to establish abiotic baselines for Enceladus-analog brines interacting with planetary-relevant substrates in an undergraduate-centered laboratory. The ocean-composition brine contains 0.20 M NaCl, 0.050 M Na₂CO₃, and 0.020 M NaHCO₃. Liquid-phase screening used 50 mL flasks containing 25.00 mL brine and 2.500 g substrate, with pH, conductivity, and temperature monitoring. Substrates included San Carlos olivine, Ward's serpentinite, carbonaceous asteroid simulant, Jezero crater simulant, and olivine-rich material; brine-only blanks distinguished substrate-mediated changes from changes occurring in brine alone. A complementary headspace module used 250 mL side-arm flasks containing 50.00 mL brine and 5.000 g substrate, monitored for CO₂, pressure, temperature, and room barometric pressure. Liquid-phase measurements remained strongly alkaline (pH 10.48-10.83 across recorded flask measurements), demonstrating measurable but modest treatment-scale variation without loss of the high-pH carbonate-buffered state. We sampled the headspace for 32 hours at 5-minute intervals (n = 385) and obtained two CO₂ sensor time series with means of 2484 ± 204 ppm (range 1825-3223 ppm) and 671 ± 8 ppm (range 655-695 ppm; mean ± SD). After accounting for barometric and temperature effects, pressure changes ranged from -0.036 to +0.011 kPa, providing no evidence of sustained net gas production during the time-series experiment. These results demonstrate both the feasibility and quality-control requirements of low-cost, time-resolved Enceladus analog experiments. Planned work will replicate selected brine-substrate responses, expand headspace and terminal liquid analyses to include CO₂, pressure, alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon, phosphate, and Ca²⁺, and compare abiotic and microbial treatments under validated low-O₂/anaerobic conditions to define false-positive biosignature boundaries.

title: Stable Isotope Paleoecology of Ungulates from the Early Miocene (Early Hemingfordian) Runningwater Formation of Nebraska, USA
session_title: Linking Tectonics, Climate, and Evolution Across the Late Cenozoic (Posters)
authors: Ward, Clark T. [1], Hackenmiller, Evie V. C. [2], Lukens, William E. [3], Fox, David L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota- Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(2) Department of Anthropology, University of Minnesota- Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, USA
(3) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, VA,
(4) Department of Earth and Environmental Science, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN,
abstract: During the early Miocene, the large-bodied herbivorous mammal guild was dominated by ungulates with brachydont (low-crowned) dentition characteristic of browsers, with mesodont taxa (mixed-feeders) increasing in richness over time. Diversity of brachydont ungulates was highest during the Hemingfordian North American Land Mammal Age, higher than and non-analogous to any modern ungulate community. The Runningwater Fm of Nebraska, USA (early Hemingfordian, ca. 19–18 Ma), represents a paleovalley fill at the base of the Miocene Ogallala Group. We used stable carbon (d 13 C) and oxygen (d 18 O) isotope ratios in fossil tooth enamel to investigate the ecology of an ungulate assemblage from the Runningwater Fm and present the oldest Miocene stable isotope dataset from the North American Great Plains, extending the isotope record of diets, habitats, and climate into an important period during the early Miocene. We sampled enamel from seven taxa: Aletomeryx (Dromomerycidae), Menoceras (Rhinocerotidae), Merychyus (Merycoidodontidae), Parahippus (Equidae), Michenia , Oxydactylus , and Protolabis (Camelidae). Previously published paleoecological data, including hypsodonty index, microwear, and mesowear, predict that Parahippus was a grazer, Aletomeryx was a mixed-feeder, and all other taxa were browsers. The d 13 C values ranged from -11.6‰ to -7.7‰ V-PDB, indicating most taxa foraged in open C 3 habitats, with little separation among taxa. We employed a Monte Carlo method to estimate the fraction C 4 grass consumed by each specimen ( f C4 ), drawing from >15,000 published modern plant d 13 C data and correcting for diet-enamel enrichment, atmospheric d 13 C, and pCO 2 . Depending on assumptions, some individuals, particularly of Menoceras and Parahippus , had statistically non-zero f C4 , suggesting up to 35% C 4 consumed. This result contrasts with microwear and mesowear analyses that indicate Menoceras was a browser. We suggest all taxa lived in C 3 -dominated open habitats with a minor C 4 component and had disparate diets. The d 18 O values ranged from 21.1‰ to 32.2‰ V-SMOW. Menoceras d 18 O values are lower than all other taxa but were not significantly different due to disparate sample size among genera. The d 18 O data suggest that Menoceras was dependent on drinking surface water, consistent with large body mass, while the other, smaller taxa possibly extracted sufficient water from their diet. Future work, including 87 Sr/ 86 Sr analyses and investigation into diagenesis, may illuminate further resource partitioning or possible biases in our data due to post-burial alteration.

title: Integrated Seismic Refraction and Electrical Resistivity Imaging of Fractured Limestone at Mineral Wells Fossil Park, Texas
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Emishaw, Luelseged Mengesha [1]
affiliations: (1) Midwestern State University, Wichita Falls, TX,
abstract: Mineral Wells Fossil Park, Texas, is underlain by Pennsylvanian shale and limestone deposited in a deltaic environment. Delineating competent limestone and fracture-controlled groundwater pathways is critical for understanding the site's shallow geologic framework. We integrated seismic refraction tomography and two-dimensional electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) along coincident profiles to characterize subsurface lithology and structure. The seismic refraction inversion defines a laterally continuous velocity structure with weathered sediment and sedimentary rock extending to ~10 ft below ground surface (bgs), unweathered sedimentary rock to ~15 ft bgs, and competent limestone at ~25 ft bgs. The inverted P-wave velocities are consistent with expected values for these lithologies. A 216-ft Wenner-Schlumberger ERT profile images a pronounced dipping low-resistivity anomaly interpreted as a fractured, water-bearing zone within the limestone, where interconnected fractures enhance permeability and groundwater infiltration. Adjacent conductive zones are interpreted as shale, providing additional lithologic constraint. The integrated interpretation demonstrates the complementary strengths of seismic refraction and ERT: seismic refraction constrains the weathering profile and depth to competent limestone, whereas ERT resolves fracture-controlled zones that are not evident from seismic velocities alone. These preliminary results demonstrate the value of combining seismic and electrical methods to characterize lithologic boundaries and fracture networks in shallow sedimentary environments for hydrogeologic and engineering investigations.

abstract:
The Les Huston Field Camp in Colorado lies in a floodplain between two hogback formations, where the surface geology consists of the Morrison Formation and the Dakota Group. Seismic refraction, gravity, and electrical resistivity tomography were carried out along 3 NW-SE and S-N profiles. Refraction data were acquired using a sledgehammer source with 5 m geophone spacing and 15 m offset for profile 1 and 10 m along the entire 115 m spread. Electrical resistivity was acquired at 4 m electrode spacing over a total of 124 m. The resistivity specifications were adopted for the gravity survey along the 3 profiles. We reveal a structural configuration resulting from the down-thrown block and relate it to the NE-SW-trending structural grain observed at the surface. Drone imagery was used to constrain the distribution and orientation of faults and joints at the surface, while geophysical imaging shows their subsurface continuity. This structure is observed as an isolated demarcation within the high-resistivity anomaly, an inflection in the seismic velocity boundary from 2000-2300 ms -2 , while gravity shows a high anomaly from the SE and a sudden drop at this transition.

We interpret the hydrogeological profile based on the combined imaging and link the structure to surface deformation observed and geophysical imaging. We calibrate our results against previous geophysical imaging. Both basin-axis-parallel and oblique structures influence the distribution of aquifers and competent ground that may support large load-bearing requirements.

title: Thermal Structure of Orogenic Lower Crust: Insights from Zircon, Monazite, and Garnet Petrochronology of the Serre Massif, Calabria

authors: Abdale, Lindsey [1], Smye, Andrew [2], Festa, Vincenzo [3], Micheletti, Francesca [4], Fornelli, Annamaria [5], Millonig, Leo J. [6], Gerdes, Axel [7], Schoonover, Erik Jeffery [8]

(2) Penn State University, University Park, PA,
(3) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra e Geoambientali, Università degli Studi di Bari, Bari, BA, Italy
(4) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra e Geoambientali, Università degli Studi di Bari, Bari, BA, Italy
(5) Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra e Geoambientali, Università degli Studi di Bari, Bari, BA, Italy

abstract:
Knowledge of the thermal structure and evolution of orogenic lower crust is key to understanding how partial melting differentiates continental crust and concentrates rare metals. During crustal thickening, energy for melting is supplied by radiogenic decay of U, Th, and K and from the mantle, but the relative importance of these sources remains uncertain.

Here, we present a petrochronological investigation into the thermal evolution of an archetypal lower-crustal section. The Serre Massif, Calabria (Italy), comprises a ~4-km-thick section of peraluminous migmatitic gneisses with amphibolite-to-granulite-facies assemblages (garnet + sillimanite + biotite + plagioclase + quartz ± K-feldspar ± cordierite ± ilmenite ± rutile). Previous investigations imply melting pressures of ~0.9-1.03 GPa (Fornelli et al., 2012). Titanium-in-zircon thermometry from six samples spanning the section yields temperatures of 680 and 750 °C that are invariant with depth, contrasting with the Ivrea-Verbano Zone (Wyatt et al 2022)—a Variscan lower crustal section potentially once contiguous with Serre—where temperatures increase with structural depth.

Zircon, monazite, and garnet trace elements and U-Pb geochronology are broadly consistent with melt production via Bt + Pl + Sill + Qtz = Gt + Kfs + melt ± rutile. Yttrium-, Nb-, and HREE-depleted zircon and monazite domains record melt crystallization during cooling, while garnet preserves HREE-, Y-, Mn-, Ta-, and Eu-rich cores to depleted rims, recording prograde growth during melt production. Six garnet U-Pb ages, mostly from rim domains, cluster at ~310 and ~290–302 Ma, dating diachronous peritectic garnet nucleation and amalgamation during heating and melt drainage at different structural levels. The overlap with zircon-rim (~308-295 Ma) and monazite ages (~325-290 Ma) reflects spatially decoupled melt production, extraction, and crystallization sustained across the section.

These observations indicate that the Serre lower crust (i) remained near the hydrous solidus for >~1 Myr and (ii) preserved a shallow thermal gradient (<~15 °C/km). Calculations test whether this thermal structure reflects buffering by the latent heat of fusion during biotite dehydration. Buffering of large volumes of fertile lower crust offers a mechanism for the short emplacement window of regional late-Variscan granitoids (~306-292 Ma).

title: Experimental Formation of Serpentine Minerals in a Peridotite at Low Temperature-Pressure Conditions.
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Busch, Nancy [1], Goldstein, Arin [2], Martin, Celine Alix [3]
affiliations: (1) Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA; American Museum of Natural History, New York City, New York, USA
(2) Amherst College, Amherst, Massachusetts, USA; American Museum of Natural History, New York City, New York, USA

abstract:
Serpentine group minerals form through the interaction of water with ultramafic minerals at low temperatures (<600°C). Serpentinization alters the density, volume, and composition of a rock, and occurs on a wide-scale primarily in oceanic crust . While serpentinization as a process is broadly understood as ultramafic minerals + water = serpentine + magnetite, there is still little known about the detailed processes. Previous experiments by various authors has often conflicted with accepted conventions and models of serpentinization. In addition, serpentinization at particularly low temperatures and pressures is understudied, despite the prevalence of serpentines formed at either seafloor or surface conditions.

We aim to unravel the very first steps of serpentinization through experiment. We submerged six pieces of peridotite (Olivine + orthopyroxene + clinopyroxene + spinel), all originating from a single xenolith of unknown origin, into seawater for 12 months at 110°C and surface pressure. We removed one piece every 2 months and created thin sections for each sample. Using Raman Spectroscopy, we identified the mineral assemblage for each sample then used Electron Microprobe Analysis for qualitative assessment of the chemical composition of individual mineral grains.

Serpentine formation is not evident, possibly due to reaction time at these conditions for alteration to occur in a 12 month period. However, shifts in chemical composition were consistently observed in all minerals. In particular, Mg# increased after 2 months, attributed primarily to a decrease in Fe across our samples. Progressive fracturing of mineral grains is also observed, with pyroxenes appearing the most deteriorated. This contradicts widely accepted models where olivine alters prior to initiation of pyroxene alteration. Overall, our analysis exposes gaps in the understanding of serpentinization at low pressures and temperature.

title: Mapping and Characterization of Previously Undocumented Igneous Intrusions surrounding the Tinton/Mineral Hill Magmatic Complex, South Dakota-Wyoming
session_title: Using mafic and ultramafic deposits to decipher volcanic and magmatic processes (Posters)
authors: Amalfitano, Thomas W [1], Domagall, Abigail [2], Schilling, Jill [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Atmospheric sciences, SUNY Oneonta, Oneonta, NY, USA; School of Natural Sciences, Black Hills State University, Spearfish, SD, USA

abstract: The Black Hills dome in western South Dakota is the easternmost extent of the Rocky Mountains, formed during the Laramide Orogeny between 70 and 40 Ma. Magmatism occurred throughout the northern Black Hills between 60 and 37 Ma and produced numerous intrusive bodies such as sills and dikes, with some extrusive diatremes. Magmas intruded through the 1.8 -1.7 Ga Precambrian crystalline basement rocks and into the 541-66 Ma overlying sedimentary cap. This 90 km-long belt of Tertiary intrusions trends ~N80W from Bear Butte to the east, west to the Missouri Buttes: intrusions may become progressively younger from east to west. Regional studies also identify a N40W trend of carbonates and kimberlites extending from the Black Hills in the south into Alberta during a similar emplacement window. In the northwestern Black Hills, the Tinton/Mineral Hill complex has been extensively studied due to its role in local mineral resources. Multiple smaller intrusions to the west of the Tinton/Mineral Hill magmatic complex have recently been found during field exploration in Surprise Gulch. Igneous float was followed upslope to four new outcrops of black-dark gray, aphanitic (<5% phenocrysts) igneous rock that were mapped and sampled. Preliminary thin section analysis reveals melanite garnet, leucite, nepheline, calcite, and aegirine-augite. Geochemical results of this same sample indicate an alkaline tephrite to phonolitic tephrite composition, while trace element analysis shows enrichment of barium, strontium, and vanadium. These geochemical data appear related to previously published data from the Tinton area. All Surprise Gulch samples show similar hand sample textures suggesting outcrops may represent separate exposures of one sill or several petrogenetically related intrusions. These newly mapped exposures expand the known area of intrusive activity associated with the Tinton and Mineral Hill complex connecting Surprise Gulch to the larger regional alkaline magmatic system.

title: Integrated Assessment of Saltwater Intrusion in the Chicot Aquifer near the Texas Gulf Coast
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Lamb, Harrison [1], Gebremichael, Esayas [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental & Geological Sciences, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Environmental & Geological Sciences, Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, Texas, USA
abstract: Saltwater intrusion is an increasing threat to coastal aquifers, degrading freshwater resources through the landward migration of saline groundwater driven by both natural processes and human activities. Along the Texas Gulf Coast, continued population growth, extensive groundwater extraction, land subsidence, sea-level rise (SLR), drought, and recurrent storm surge events have increased the potential for saltwater contamination of groundwater resources. This study investigates the occurrence, spatial distribution, and controlling factors of saltwater intrusion within the shallowest sub-aquifer of the Texas Gulf Coast Aquifer System, the Chicot aquifer, within the coastal areas of Orange, Jefferson, Chambers, Harris, Galveston, and Brazoria counties, Texas. Specifically, the study (1) delineates areas affected by saltwater intrusion across the study area, considering surface deformation, SLR, and other key drivers; (2) evaluates the spatial and temporal evolution of groundwater salinity in the impacted areas during the past two decades using key physicochemical water quality indicators; and (3) identifies the primary geologic, hydrologic, and anthropogenic controls that facilitate vertical and lateral saltwater intrusion while recommending potential mitigation strategies. This is achieved through a number of approaches, including applying geostatistical and spatial statistical analyses, such as Kriging and Getis-Ord Gi*, to in-situ groundwater quality datasets. These results are integrated with land subsidence rates derived from Sentinel-1 data over the past decade using Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) techniques, regional geology, stratigraphy, and groundwater-level data to identify susceptible areas. Based on these findings, priority areas are identified for ground-based validation using Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) and Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) surveys. Expected outcomes include regional maps identifying areas affected by groundwater salinization, documentation of spatiotemporal changes in groundwater salinity over the past two decades, and forecasts of areas vulnerable to future saltwater intrusion based on current trends in the combined natural and anthropogenic drivers. These results provide a scientific basis for groundwater resource management and support the development of strategies to reduce future saltwater contamination in Texas coastal aquifers.

title: Rapid Marine Redox Oscillations Linked to the mid-Silurian Mulde/lundgreni Extinction: Evidence from Thallium Isotopes

authors: Maaleki-Moghadam, Mahdi [1], Lindskog, Anders [2], Goodin, John T [3], Noble, Paula J. [4], Kaljo, Dimitri [5], Hints, Olle [6], Owens, Jeremy D. [7], Young, Seth [8]

abstract: The mid-Silurian Mulde/ lundgreni event (MLE) was one of the more severe biotic crises of the early Paleozoic, eliminating roughly 95% of graptolite species and 75% of radiolarian taxa while sparing most shallow-water benthic communities. The event coincides with a double-peaked positive carbon isotope excursion (CIE) and a phase of global cooling, however global ocean redox conditions are largely understudied throughout this interval. Here, we present new thallium isotope (ε²⁰⁵Tl) records from three mid-Homerian to earliest Gorstian sections spanning Laurentia (Abbott River and Twilight Creek, Arctic Canada) and Baltica (Priekule-20 core, Latvia), supported by iron speciation and trace-metal data confirming locally reducing depositional conditions at all three sites. Rather than a single, sustained anoxic event, the records reveal a series of rapid (≲250 k.y.) swings between expanded and diminished global seafloor anoxia. A pronounced expansion of marine anoxia is coincident with the extinction and survival intervals and the first CIE peak, followed by renewed oxygenation during the biotic recovery, and additional redox oscillations through the second CIE peak and into the earliest Gorstian. Rather than persistent, large-scale anoxia, our results indicate that repeated, high-frequency oscillations in global marine oxygenation — paced by sea-level and climate change — were the primary driver of the MLE, offering a mechanistic link between ocean deoxygenation, the double-peaked CIE, and the selective loss of pelagic and hemipelagic taxa.

title: Evaporite Sedimentology of the First Core of the Permo- Triassic Spearfish Formation, North Dakota: Evidence for Lacustrine Deposition
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling
authors: Onah, Comfort E. [1], Benison, Kathleen C. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(2) Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
abstract:
The recently recovered EERC Halite #1 core from McKenzie County, North Dakota represents the first core through the Spearfish Formation, contains the first halite samples from this formation, and provides a unique opportunity for a comprehensive sedimentological investigation. The depositional environment remains unclear, as previous studies have relied largely on well logs and incomplete outcrop exposures that preserve only portions of the formation. Here, we use a combination of detailed core description and thin-section petrography to describe the sedimentary features that provide new insights on the depositional setting of the Spearfish Formation.

The Spearfish Formation is comprised mainly of evaporites and red beds, which appear lithologically similar to the underlying Permian Opeche Shale. Stratigraphically between the Opeche Shale and the Spearfish Formation is the Permian Minnekahta Limestone. Both the Opeche Shale and Minnekahta Limestone have been interpreted as saline lake deposits. The lithologies of the Spearfish Formation in the core, listed from most abundant to least abundant, are red mudstone, bedded halite, displacive halite, bedded gypsum, red sandstone, and pale gray mudstone. The red mudstones contain discontinuous lamina, mudcracks, and dewatering structures. Bedded halite is composed of chevron and cornet crystals, cumulate crystals, and some thin microcrystalline salt efflorescent crusts. Some bedded halite appears to have recrystallized crystals. The displacive halite lithology consists of randomly oriented, clear halite crystals in a matrix of red-brown mudstone. Bedded gypsum units are composed of halite pseudomorphs after bottom-growth, swallow-tail gypsum crystals. Thin lamina of red quartz arenite has bimodal grain size distribution and low-angle cross-bedding. Rare lamina of gray mudstone is massive. We interpret the bedded halite and bedded gypsum to have formed in ephemeral salt lakes, the displacive halite to have formed in saline mudflats, and the siliciclastics to have formed in associated environments, including saline and dry mudflats and eolian sandflats. This new data about the Spearfish Formation adds to our growing knowledge of Pangean environments.

title: Case Study: Incorporating Digital Collections, Hands-on Exercises, and Field Trips into Geoscience Education Workshops
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Morrison, Kate [1], Love, Renee [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Spatial Sciences, University of Idaho, Moscow, Idaho, USA

abstract:
With the growing use of climate proxies and modeling projections for near-future climate change gives rise to a parallel need to promote engagement in climate research and mitigation planning. Increased student interest can be motivated by educational experiences in real-world settings highlighting large-scale issues with high socio-economic impact. To address this, we conducted a five-week educational workshop with university undergraduate students focusing on climate proxies from the Miocene Climatic Optimum (~17-14 million years ago) and development of future climate projections. This study utilized Design-Based Research (DBR) to develop an interactive methodological approach for addressing preconceived notions regarding climate change. Our approach applies Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and Mindfulness practices to enhance the translation, transfer, and impact of the curriculum.

Preliminary results of the surveys showed that a majority of participants saw an importance in learning about climate change. When asked if learning about climate change is important, on a scale of 1-5 (1=not at all; 5=very important), the average score was 4.8. Further, a mean score of 4.9 indicated perceived importance in understanding past climate. However, the surveys revealed that a majority of participants presented feelings of "Climate Anxiety". 72% indicated they felt a negative emotion while 28% described a neutral or indifferent emotion about the topic. Despite this, when asked how the participants felt when thinking about taking direct action toward climate change solutions, 81% of participants indicated a positive emotion. This suggests that learning about actionable solutions could potentially help alleviate "Climate Anxiety" and improve engagement in climate sciences.

title: Jurassic Sedimentary Basins of Western U.S.-Mexico Border Region: Sedimentary and Magmatic Record of a Regional Crustal Breakaway Zone
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Lawton, Timothy F. [1], Leggett, William J. [2], Mauel, David J. [3], Amato, Jeffrey M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
(2) National Park Service, Hans Flat, Utah, USA

abstract:
Jurassic sedimentary basins along the western extent of the U.S.-Mexico border region developed at a boundary between broad regions of fundamentally different tectonic style and magmatic character in the North American Cordillera. In the southwestern United States and northernmost Sonora, voluminous magmatism from ~190–158 Ma took place in a low-standing magmatic arc that left a record of voluminous plutonic activity. The arc was paired with a broad eastward-thinning backarc basin that is best preserved on the Colorado Plateau. In Mexico, magmatism continued southward in two belts that included a western extensional arc near the continental margin recorded by scattered plutons in western and southern Mexico and a broad eastern belt of extended crust termed the Nazas igneous province. Silicic pyroclastic and subordinate intermediate volcanic rocks produced by Nazas magmatism occupy extensional basins within a region-wide array of sinistral transcurrent faults. The basins and their flanking basement blocks are currently regarded as widely dispersed relative to their original positions.

The border basins were generally elongate parallel to the international border from Caborca, Sonora, to Ojinaga, Chihuahua. A nearly complete stratigraphic succession in north-central Sonora includes: (1) The Lower Jurassic Basomari Formation, composed of coarse subaqueous debrites derived from nearby Proterozoic basement, volcanic-lithic fluvial sandstones, thick intervals of red siltstone and uncommon distal ash-fall tuffs; (2) the Middle Jurassic Rancho San Martín Formation, a succession of volcanic-lithic fluvial sandstone, lacustrine strata containing intermediate hyaloclastites and pillow lavas, silicic ignimbrites and feldspathoquartzose eolianites containing detrital zircons of mixed Appalachian and local arc provenance; and (3) the Upper Jurassic Cucurpe Formation, composed of subaqueous basalt flows, marine turbidites and basinal mudrocks. Lower and Middle Jurassic strata of some basins contain significant percentages of detrital zircon ages in the range 262–227 Ma, an age group considered to record anatectic melting of the late Paleozoic collisional orogen. Although the Jurassic sedimentary basins of the SW US-Mexico border region have long been considered to record intra-arc and backarc sedimentation, we interpret them as formed by crustal extension that accompanied collapse of the late Paleozoic orogenic hinterland. The border basins likely formed in a crustal breakaway zone between an intact Jurassic arc-backarc system and allochthonous crustal blocks that experienced significant translation during opening of the Gulf of Mexico.

abstract:
Terra rossa are reddish, clay-rich soils found blanketing limestone and dolomitic bedrock substrates throughout the Mediterranean. These soils vary in thickness from centimeters to meters and infill karst and fractures to several meters, but their provenance and origin remain debated. Previous research attributes terra rossa formation solely to the weathering of insoluble residue left by limestone dissolution, but more recent work posits that insoluble residue alone is insufficient to account for the formation of terra rossa and suggests a polygenetic origin entailing a combination of allochthonous dust influx and chemical weathering. Grain size analysis of these terra rossa can provide insights into their genesis, but the soil’s clay-rich nature presents challenges in obtaining accurate grain-size distributions.

We utilized a laser particle-size analyzer (LPSA) on two terra rossa soil profiles collected in the Radovin and Bosilijevo regions of Croatia. The profile from Radovin is of unknown age and field data suggests increasing clay content with depth and significant sand throughout the profile. The profile at Bosilijevo is of Quaternary age and situated in a karstic fissure of Mesozoic limestone. Field data suggests a silty loam that increases in clay content with depth. Two pretreatment methods were tested prior to LPSA analysis. Method 1 removed carbonates with 1.7M buffered acetic acid and then organics with 30% hydrogen peroxide. Method 2 only applied the hydrogen peroxide treatment. Following pretreatment, dispersant was added and samples were sonicated immediately prior to LPSA analysis. For both methods, particle size distributions measured by the LPSA did not corroborate the increase in clay content observed in the field suggesting incomplete disaggregation of clay minerals during pretreatment. Work is ongoing to determine the most effective methods to facilitate laser particle size analysis so that differences in the soil forming processes and/or nature of allochthonous sediment input to these terra rossa can be assessed.

title: Earthquake Magnitude and Intensity as Expressed in K-12 Trade Books: Design Considerations for Student Sensemaking and Outreach Development
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: Pyle, Eric J [1], Sumy, Danielle F [2], Booker, Kaliyah [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology & Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, Virginia, USA
(2) Directorate for Technology, Innovation, and Partnerships, U.S. National Science Foundation, Alexandria, VA,
(3) Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, Richmond, Virginia, USA
abstract:
While formal K-12 education in the U.S. has traditionally placed an emphasis on learning reading and language arts, one has to ask about the actual content of the reading and whether or not students find these materials interesting or relevant. A frequently used tool in these settings are trade books, which are non-textbook, theme-oriented and broadly-marketed books available from libraries or from online distributors. These books offer smaller bites of content and a greater chance of supporting not only formal science education, but also free-choice reading outside of the school day. Trade books can also express relevant Earth phenomena in a more timely fashion than textbooks. However, with useful descriptions also come misconceptions, and trade books may share limited or obsolete concepts that would hinder learning appropriate concepts.

Solid Earth concepts that involve both relevance and the potential for dated concepts is the textual expression of earthquake magnitude and intensity. In this research, we examined 76 K-12 earthquake-focused trade books published from 1990-2021, found in a large metropolitan library located outside of Washington, DC. These books are also available in the libraries of major West Coast cities. Using NVivo 14 coding software, a recursive analysis was conducted on 826 quotes on earthquake magnitude, intensity, and their relative impact. Primary codes employed were generated through reflection on prior research (Nyarko et al., 2024; Pyle et al, 2023), expanded through further discussions on text, with emergent coding permitted. Early analyses show a greater number of magnitude references over intensity, with spikes in publication frequency in the years immediately following large magnitude, widely reported, earthquake events. Other trends indicate a shift towards more accurate descriptions of earthquake magnitude in more recent publications, with personalization across grade ranges focused on expressions of earthquake intensity. We anticipate that this long-term analysis could inform the development of scientifically accurate representations of earthquake measurement, particularly as earthquake phenomena are more widely known through the media and through digital notifications. With these tools in hand, students will have more relevant science reading material, and science teachers will have an audience primed for discussion supporting sensemaking. In addition, researchers and emergency managers can develop and use, proactively and retroactively, accurate trade book depictions of magnitude and intensity to inform their outreach efforts and public information.

title: How well are we preparing students for the geoscience workforce? Results from a survey of teaching practices
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Egger, Anne E [1], Viskupic, Karen M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, Central Washington University, Ellensburg, WA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
abstract:
Students who graduate with a bachelors degree in geoscience can be qualified for a wide range of jobs across sectors. Geoscience jobs are available in local, state, and federal governments; scientific and technical services (such as consulting) in the private sector; and the energy and extractive industries. Employers across sectors seek to hire entry-level employees with broad geoscience knowledge, general and specific scientific skills, and tendencies such as attention to detail and a desire to learn that we call dispositions. We wondered: to what extent are instructors in geoscience degree programs helping students develop the skills and dispositions they will need to be hired and succeed in the geoscience workforce?

We sought to align a survey of geoscience teaching with new research in (1) the skills and dispositions that geoscience employers seek in bachelors-level employees and (2) the efficacy of inclusive teaching strategies. We modified and expanded questions from the National Geoscience Faculty Survey to ask instructors if students in their courses engage in specific activities to develop the skills most frequently mentioned in advertisements for entry-level geoscience jobs, including communication and field skills. For these questions, content validity was established through expert review and grounding new questions in evidence-based research. In addition, we developed new questions that address the extent to which instructors were explicit about developing dispositions and supporting career preparation in their course. We tested all questions with instructors from two institutions and conducted follow-up interviews to establish construct validity for new questions about dispositions.

The revised, validated survey was widely disseminated during the 2025-26 academic year. Responses come from instructors who teach the full range of courses for undergraduate geoscience majors. Results indicate that a large proportion of respondents incorporate skills that are important in the workforce in their courses, including working as part of a team, using spreadsheets, and documenting field conditions. Most respondents indicate that students are likely to develop dispositions such as attention to detail in their course, though fewer report making use of evidence-based strategies to support disposition development. A smaller proportion report incorporating activities that build students’ awareness of and preparation for entering the workforce. These results highlight areas where instructors would benefit from professional learning and resources to inform teaching approaches that support today’s students.

title: Molecular Geoarchaeological Applications: Analysis of Molecular Biomarkers and their Stable Isotopes from Late Quaternary Sediments from Spirit Eye Cave, Far West Texas
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials
authors: Kidwell, Jasmine [1], Hoggarth, Julie [2], Hockaday, William C. [3], Fulton, James [4], Schroeder, Bryon [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(2) Department of Anthropology, Baylor University, Waco, Texas, USA
(3) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX,
(4) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
abstract: The Chihuahuan Desert of far west Texas remains understudied regarding its cultural, climatic, and environmental history, as existing proxy datasets are sparse and inconsistent in temporal resolution. With the goal of adding to these limited datasets, this study applies molecular geoarchaeological techniques to the sedimentary archives of dry deposits within Spirit Eye Cave in far west Texas. This approach generates new well-resolved molecular records, including hydroclimate and paleoecology, to pair with regional human demographic data reconstructed from radiocarbon summed probability distributions. We focus on recovering sedimentary molecular fossils, or biomarkers (such as leaf waxes, fecal stanols, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons), which preserve environmental records often lost in this now-arid region. Lipids and other biomarkers extracted from Spirit Eye Cave sediments were characterized using Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS). To reconstruct shifting ecologies and hydroclimate, compound-specific stable isotope analysis by Gas Chromatography-Combustion-Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry (GC-C-IRMS) was used to measure the δ 13 C and δD values of plant leaf waxes. Chronological control for these biomarker records was established via radiocarbon dating of selected total free lipid extracts. These molecular data were integrated with complementary datasets, including elemental profiles from portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF), total organic carbon and nitrogen, bulk sediment stable isotopes δ 13 C and δ 15 N, and computerized tomography (CT) sediment density values. Combined, these multi-proxy data holistically reconstruct coupled shifts in plant ecology, fire regimes, human presence, and hydroclimate, with pronounced changes at the end of the Pleistocene, during the onset of the Younger Dryas, and throughout the Mid-Holocene aridity. Ultimately, this framework contextualizes regional human demographic variability from the Late Pleistocene through the Holocene within changing ecological systems, capturing both gradual and abrupt transitions.

title: Subsurface Resource Modeling in Kansas
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Bream, Brendan R [1], Bhattacharjee, Souvik [2], Bunse, Emily G [3], White, Mark [4], Gumble, Jason E [5]
affiliations: (1) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
(4) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
(5) Kansas Geological Survey, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
The Kansas Geological Survey (KGS) is developing several new regional-scale three-dimensional geologic models to evaluate subsurface energy, water, and mineral resources. Recent models represent integrated fit-for-purpose resource estimates for carbon capture and storage (CCS), geologic hydrogen, critical minerals investigations, and Permian evaporite studies. These efforts leverage decades of KGS geologic research and extensive subsurface datasets – including thousands of wells with wireline logs, formation top interpretations, geophysical surveys, core analyses, and subsurface dynamic data such as injection/production data and drill stem tests.

Early adoption of integrated modeling workflows requires experienced subsurface modelers working closely with research experts to accelerate efforts and appropriately define model scope and resolution. The current KGS modeling workflow uses SLB Petrel software and adapts proven methodologies from the oil and gas industry with a central principle of “model early, model often, and model at multiple scales”. The effort is tailored for the geology and data in Kansas but takes inspiration from similar efforts by other public institutions such as the Alberta and Illinois Geological Surveys. We have utlized a faulted framework methodology and workflow to represent structural configurations and stratigraphic juxtapositions across fault systems such as the Nemaha Ridge and Central Kansas Uplift. As new geological, geophysical, and engineering datasets become available, models are iteratively refined to improve their accuracy and usefulness as well as create alternative scenarios that often equally satisfy input datasets.

Kansas is an excellent location to establish this workflow due to its geology, mature hydrocarbon development, comprehensive public datasets and the KGS’ strong collaborative partnerships with private industry and federal agencies (e.g., US DOE and USGS). The KGS commitment to disseminate geologic products in a variety of data formats via accessible digital platforms (e.g.,the KGS ArcGIS Hub and the USGS NGMDB Catalog) fits with a 1923 state statute “…to make as far as possible a complete geological survey of the state of Kansas”. Ultimately, the goal of the current subsurface effort is to reduce geological uncertainty, guide future data acquisition, and define the subsurface resource potential in an objective, consistent, regional framework. This framework is the foundational subsurface element of the “Borders to Basement” initiative that intends to connect subsurface modeling outputs with surficial geology, revenue, and other spatial datasets the KGS stewards.

title: Lithospheric Structure and Evolution of the Neoproterozoic Ad Damm-Fatima Fault System

authors: Abanumay, Faris [1], Emishaw, Luelseged Mengesha [2], Katumwehe, Andrew B. [3], Chernet, Samuel G. [4], Alshehri, Fahad [5], Mickus, Kevin Lee [6]

abstract: This study uses a gravity data analysis and two-dimensional gravity modeling to characterize the lithospheric structure beneath the AFZ and FFZ in the western Neoproterozoic Arabian Shield of Saudi Arabia along the Red Sea. The AFZ separates the Neoproterozoic Asir terrane in the southeast from the Jeddah terrane to the northwest, while the Fatima Fault Zone is exposed within the Jeddah terrane. The AFZ is considered a potential zone of deformation along which a Red Sea transform fault divides the southern Red Sea spreading center segment from the more advanced continental rift segment to the north. The Bouguer gravity anomaly map and gravity models show that the Jeddah terrane within the study area displays a relatively high Bouguer gravity anomaly reaching ~70 mGal, while the Asir terrane exhibits a low gravity anomaly of ~ -15 mGal. Conversely, the Fatima Fault Zone is characterized by a high Bouguer gravity anomaly reaching ~110 mGal. The average thickness of the crust and the subcontinental lithospheric mantle are 30 km and 60 km, respectively. The depth to the gravity Moho shows N-S trending crustal thinning along the eastern Red Sea margin (~20-25 km) and across the Fatima Fault Zone. In some locations, the crust is thicker beneath the AFZ (~40 km). These findings, along with evidence of dextral strike-slip movement along the Ad Damn Fault Zone, suggest that the western part of the Arabian Shield is being reactivated, likely accommodating strain from the eastward shift of the Red Sea rift axis.

title: Dietary Adaptations of Sympatric Large Herbivores across the Mio-Pliocene Boundary at Lothagam (West Turkana, Kenya)
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials (Posters)
authors: Uno, Kevin T [1], Sankau, Linet [2], Campisano, Christopher J. [3], Green, Daniel [4], Su, Denise F [5], Rowan, John J [6]
affiliations: (1) Department of Human Evolutionary Biology, Harvard University, Massachusetts, Boston, USA
(2) Institute of Human Origins, Arizona State Univeristy, Phoenix, AZ, USA
(3) Institute of Human Origins, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA

abstract: The expansion of C 4 -dominated environments during the Late Miocene and early Pliocene marked a profound transformation in the structure of eastern African terrestrial ecosystems. Numerous studies have shown that many families of large eastern African mammalian herbivores adopted C 4 diets during this time, including those from the Lothagam sequence (West Turkana, Kenya), which spans the Late Miocene to the Pliocene (~7.5 to 3.5 Ma). However, our understanding of how ecosystem changes influence herbivore community ecology, including resource competition, adaptation to vegetation changes, and coexistence strategies, remains limited. Here, we investigate the relationship between body size, dietary ecology, and dietary shifts in large herbivores at Lothagam from the Late Miocene to early Pliocene. We combined carbon stable isotopes (δ¹³C) of tooth enamel with reconstructed body mass to test two hypotheses: (1) herbivores partitioned their niches by body mass within grazing, mixed-feeding, and browsing dietary guilds, and (2) herbivore taxa displayed significant shifts towards greater C 4 consumption through time. Our findings indicate significant diet overlap across body masses, with no significant relationship between body size and diet among Lothagam herbivores as predicted by ecological theory (e.g., Jarman-Bell). Several taxa show significant dietary changes at the Mio-Pliocene boundary, but the direction of change varied. The rhino Ceratotherium and suid Nyanzachoerus syrticus increased their reliance on C 4 grasses in the early Pliocene, whereas Bovini consumed more C 3 vegetation in the Pliocene than in the Late Miocene. These shifts in δ¹³C values are interpreted as a complex dietary response reflecting evolutionary strategies among herbivore lineages to minimize competition following significant turnover in vegetation structure that began in the Late Miocene.

title: The Role of Structural Inheritance and Progressive Fault Zone Development in Low-sulfidation Epithermal Deposits of the Manhattan District, Nevada
session_title: Hydrothermal Ore Deposits: From Source to Sink (Part II)
authors: Frieman, Ben M. [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Maxey, Easton [3], Simonson, Seth [4], Pokrandt, Harrison [5]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden,

(4) North Dakota State College of Science, Wahpeton, North Dakota, USA

abstract: Precious metal mineralization in the low-sulfidation epithermal deposits of Nevada may be variably controlled by structural inheritance, while also being influenced by first-order structure that developed coeval with Miocene extensional tectonics. This study aims to define these structural elements in the low-sulfidation gold-silver deposits of the Manhattan district, central Nevada. At Manhattan, mineralization is predominantly hosted by Paleozoic metasedimentary rocks and post-dates widespread Tertiary (~27-25 Ma) volcanism, with existing isotopic dating of adularia suggesting mineralization occurred in the Miocene (~19-17 Ma). Multiple legacy open pits provide abundant exposures, although most are physically inaccessible. Thus, this study combines traditional field observations with orientation data derived from UAV-based, 3D models using Mira Geoscience’s HiveMap software. Traditional mapping provided critical context for digital interpretations and facilitated kinematic analysis of observed fault generations, while the digital mapping was essential for defining decameter-scale structure. Pre-mineral structure includes widespread folding that relates to Mesozoic orogenesis. Where proximal to ore-controlling faults, limestone units form a preferred host rock for later mineralization due to preferential replacement. Sandstone units display more variable ore styles ranging from replacement in more permeable units to the development of conjugate, mm-scale veins arrays in more competent units. Folds in these units are asymmetric, isoclinal, recumbent, and are NW-plunging. Deviations in fold geometries are developed proximal to younger ore-related faults. These syn-mineral faults are predominantly extensional, forming conjugate oblique-slip networks. Major ore zones occur along fault planes and/or form hanging wall replacement or stockwork zones. Bladed calcite and adularia are common within and adjacent to ore zones as well as dense to spaced extensional fractures. The relative timing of these extensional fractures is unclear but are interpreted herein as fracture networks that developed in linkage to step-over zones during progressive development of the normal fault arrays. The latest generation of faults are steeply dipping, predominately sinistral strike-slip faults. Kinematic analysis indicates that the normal fault network formed during NNW-SSE-directed extension, while the strike-slip faults generally cross-cut mineralization. This suggests that mineralization occurred as part of progressive development in a transtensional regime that culminated in strike-slip localization. Mineralization occurs the conjugate normal fault arrays and in more cryptic, locally extensive fracture networks during a transitional period of Miocene Basin and Range development.

title: Development of a High-Resolution DRASTIC-LU Groundwater Vulnerability Map for Edisto, South Carolina
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Swanson, Matthew Paul [1], Levine, Norman S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Masters Environmental and Sustainability Studies, College of Charleston, Charleston, SC, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Geosciences, College of Charleston, CHARLESTON, SC, USA
abstract:
Groundwater resources in the coastal community of Edisto, South Carolina, are highly vulnerable to contamination because of shallow surficial aquifers, low topographic relief, and highly permeable sandy soils. In low-lying estuarine and barrier-island settings, these inherent hydrogeologic vulnerabilities are amplified by groundwater–surface-water interactions, tidal fluctuations, sea-level rise, and episodic coastal flooding. Anthropogenic pressures, particularly widespread reliance on onsite wastewater treatment systems and continued coastal development, create additional localized risks of contaminant loading to freshwater groundwater resources.

This coastal-hazards research was funded through the NSF EPSCoR Research Infrastructure Improvement Program. It applies a modified DRASTIC-LU overlay and index model within a Geographic Information Systems environment to evaluate intrinsic and land-use-related groundwater vulnerability across Edisto Island. The model integrates the seven standard DRASTIC parameters—depth to groundwater, net recharge, aquifer media, soil media, topography, vadose-zone characteristics, and hydraulic conductivity—with land-use patterns to develop a spatial index of groundwater pollution potential. Although standard DRASTIC assessments are commonly completed at approximately 30 m resolution, and detailed coastal-community studies may use 10 m grids, this study develops a 1 m high-resolution DRASTIC vulnerability model for local-scale screening.

The Edisto DRASTIC analysis was calculated on a 1 m raster grid to preserve the spatial detail of LiDAR-derived topography, the groundwater-depth surface, soils, land cover, and parcel-scale datasets. The 1 m grid represents the spatial resolution of the model output; effective model accuracy is controlled by the spatial resolution, sampling density, classification uncertainty, and temporal representativeness of the seven DRASTIC input variables.

The resulting vulnerability map identifies spatial heterogeneity and potential hotspots where shallow groundwater and permeable soils coincide with septic-dominant residential development. Parameter-sensitivity and map-removal analyses are used to quantify the influence of individual variables and evaluate uncertainty associated with seasonal recharge and tidal fluctuations. The model provides a cost-effective screening tool for prioritizing groundwater monitoring, source-water protection, septic-management strategies, and sustainable land-use planning. Future studies could validate vulnerability classes using observed nitrate, chloride, specific conductance, fecal indicators, or documented septic-system impacts. This localized application demonstrates how high-resolution geospatial data can connect hydrogeologic analysis with community-scale coastal planning and groundwater protection.

title: Hydrogeology of Paris France
session_title: Hydrogeology Discipline Session
authors: Bobeck, Patricia [1]
affiliations: (1) Geotechnical Translations, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
The Paris Basin is about 500 km wide and overlies a faulted and folded substrate. The Basin is underlain by Triassic, 250 million years old, at a depth of 3000 m. The surface geology of the Paris basin is Tertiary. Until the Miocene, depositional environments alternated between shallow marine, evaporitic lagoonal, and continental and lacustrine.

Paris groundwater comes primarily from the Oligocene age Fontainebleau sand, present at the top of buttes témoins, overlying marls and gypsum. The buttes témoins and the springs are located primarily north of Paris, in the region of Belleville and Montmartre, which were annexed to Paris in 1860. When water from the sand encounters the underlying marl, it ponds and or flows to the land surface as a spring. As early as the 12th century, Parisians carefully collected this water, constructed stone-lined ditches to convey the water to hubs where the water entered larger aqueducts that conveyed it to the king's residence, to the property of monks, and to public fountains. One aqueduct, the Medicis aqueduct, was built in 1623 and provided water to the Fontaine Medicis in Luxembourg Garden until 1904.

In 1833 François Arago instructed Louis-Georges Mulot to drill an artesian well on the site of an abandoned slaughterhouse in Paris. The Grenelle well, drilled to a depth of 548 meters, produced water that rose 30 meters above the ground surface. The Grenelle well was dismantled in 1903, but three artesian wells drilled in Paris are still producing. All flow from depths of 580 meters and produce Albian age water that has been in the subsurface 25,000 years. One well that had a temperature of 28°C was used to supply a swimming pool. Today the three wells provide free water for citizens who walk to the wells to get their supply of pre-tritium water.

title: Stratigraphy, Depositional Environments, and Geochronology of the Middle Miocene Kalatum Member of the Lothidok Formation within the Southern Lothidok Range, Turkana, Kenya
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record (Posters)
authors: Ropati, Tye N [1], Cote, Susanne [2], Deino, Alan L. [3], Lukens, William E. [4], Muchemi, Francis [5], Munyaka, Venanzio [6], Rossie, James B. [7], Peppe, Daniel J. [8]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(2) Department of Anthropology and Archaeology, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
(3) Berkeley Geochronology Center, USA
(4) Department of Geology and Environmental Science, James Madison University, Harrisonburg, Virginia, USA
(5) National Museums of Kenya, Nairobi, Kenya
(6) Department of Civil Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, Indiana, USA
(7) Department of Anthropology, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York, USA
(8) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, Texas, USA
abstract:
The Early and Middle Miocene Lothidok Formation of the southern Lothidok Range in the Turkana Basin, northern Kenya has been the focus of paleontological studies for nearly a century. The Kalatum Member of the Lothidok Formation documents the Middle Miocene fauna, potentially documenting faunal evolution and change during the Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO) and the Miocene Climatic Transition (MCT). However, the age, depositional environments, and relationships of fossil sites of the Kalatum Member are unresolved.

To better constrain the age, lithologies, and sedimentary sequence of the Kalatum Member, we utilized several field- and lab-based techniques. A preliminary stratigraphic framework for the Kalatum, based on sections from several areas across the southern Lothidok Range, documents a laterally variable fluvial sequence interrupted by both intervals of volcanic input—including tuffs, ignimbrites, and lahars—and periods of landscape stability. The prevalence of laterally equivalent paleosols, channel sands, and channel lag conglomerates, and the regular occurrence of scoured basal contacts and decameter-scale pinch-outs of channel bodies suggest local depositional environments were dominated by intermittent stream systems that experienced variable levels of flows and frequent channel avulsion as they drained toward a larger trunk system. Paleosol characteristics indicate a relatively dry and seasonal paleoenvironment. In addition to stratigraphy, geologic mapping of fossils, strata occurrences, and relevant structural deformation, was competed to ensure the continuity of measured sections and the validity of stratigraphic placements of fossiliferous horizons. Preliminary geochronology, based on a combination of multiple 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates, magnetostratigraphy, and sediment accumulation rates indicates that the Kalatum Member was deposited between ~13 and 15 Ma, meaning that the member documents the end of the Miocene Climatic Optimum into the Miocene Climatic Transition. Future work will focus on expanding the local magnetostratigraphy to complement the 40 Ar/ 39 Ar dates and improve the precision of depositional age in intervals between tephra. Further, correlations between the sections and disparate fossil sites will be determined via sandstone petrography and microprobe analysis of tephra. A more complete stratigraphic framework for the Kalatum Member will make it possible to better understand the age of fossil occurrences within the unit, which includes multiple hominoid taxa, allowing for a greater temporal resolution to study the evolution of Afro-Arabian mammal communities during an interval of major global climate change.

title: A Hydrogeophysical and Hydrochemical Evaluation of Kirsch Spring, Arbuckle-Simpson Aquifer, Oklahoma
session_title: A Showcase of Undergraduate Research in Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Semple, Kelsey [1], Haygood, Lauren [2], Wilson, Glory [3], Igwebuike, Ndubuisi [4], Halihan, Todd [5]
affiliations: (1) Oklahoma State Univ, Owasso, OK,

abstract: The Arbuckle Simpson Aquifer (ASA) is a critical water supply for south-central Oklahoma. The ASA is a fractured karst aquifer composed of limestone, dolomite, and sandstone, defined by complex structural geology such as large fault structures and unique hydrogeologic connectivity. The study area, located within this region, overlays multiple geological formations, including the Vanoss Group and Tishomingo and Troy Granites, which is separated by a fault running perpendicular to the Blue River. The Kirsch Spring is situated on the fault, where it is suspected to be fed by multiple groundwater flow paths, making it an important location to assess how geology influences water sourcing and quality. We installed an ERI line of 840 meters with 15-meter spacing to better understand recharge and fault dynamics within this location. Additionally, we installed a transducerand barometer at Kirsch Spring that collects seasonal information, such as conductivity, temperature, water level, and atmospheric pressure. Previous fieldwork included a topographic survey, and a “dry conditions” ERI image to identify fault structures. Recent fieldwork included running the ERI line in “wet conditions” to identify recharge features. Future work is anticipated to include coring at least one identified fault structure for additional microbiology and water chemistry analyses. This work will contribute to both stakeholder engagement, and our understanding of the discharge of the southern boundary of the karst aquifer system.

title: From Hydrochemical Data to Process-Informed AI: A Critical-Zone Framework for Trace-Element Mobility in Volcanic–Geothermal Systems of the Central Bolivian Altiplano

abstract:
Large hydrochemical datasets reveal spatial and statistical patterns, but data alone do not identify the processes that generate them or ensure transferable artificial-intelligence predictions. This study develops a process-based framework for arsenic (As), boron (B), lithium (Li), and antimony (Sb) mobility in selected volcanic–geothermal systems and connected environments of the Central Bolivian Altiplano. We hypothesize that AI models guided by geological, hydrological, and hydrochemical process information will be more interpretable and transferable than models based mainly on correlations among measured concentrations. The study integrates 257 groundwater and surface-water samples collected during rainy and dry seasons with 35 sediment and geothermal-precipitate samples from selected areas of the Sajama and Turco basins and part of the Desaguadero Basin.

Process hypotheses were evaluated by integrating geological, hydrological, aqueous, and solid-phase evidence. Volcanic units, ignimbrites, hydrothermally altered materials, Quaternary basin-fill deposits, faults, and geothermal manifestations were used to identify candidate source domains. Water-body type and upstream-to-downstream concentration patterns were examined to assess potential groundwater–surface-water connections and transport pathways. Major-ion facies, seasonal changes in pH, electrical conductivity, redox potential, and trace-element concentrations, together with aqueous speciation, mineral-saturation indices, and solid-phase enrichment, were used to test signatures consistent with water–rock interaction, cation exchange, evaporation, mixing, redox-dependent mobilization, and temporary storage.

The sampled waters ranged from Ca–Mg–HCO₃ to Na–HCO₃ and Na–Cl–HCO₃ compositions. Arsenic and B reached maximum concentrations of 1,793 and 28,156 µg/L, respectively, with the highest values near geothermal manifestations. Spatial variability was generally greater than seasonal variability. Because isotopic tracers, quantitative mixing models, and direct mineralogical confirmation were unavailable, source contributions and solid-phase controls are treated as testable hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

These observations contribute to a preliminary, quality-assured and harmonized database for future expansion across the Bolivian Altiplano. In mining-affected sectors, source attribution must distinguish geogenic from anthropogenic inputs. The framework provides process descriptors and constraints for AI models in which statistical learning is guided and evaluated by hydrogeochemical understanding rather than treated as a substitute for it.

title: Deformed Shorelines Constrain Earthquake Recurrence and Fault Geometry in the Seattle Fault Zone (Washington, USA).
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Crider, Juliet G. [1], Davis, Elizabeth J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Dept. of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
abstract:
The Seattle fault zone is an array of blind thrust faults that run beneath the Seattle urban core in Washington State. Prior work documents a M~7.5 earthquake at 923–924 CE, which deformed a coastal wavecut platform into a broad anticline above the fault with as much as ~8 m uplift at the crest of the fold. We show that a submerged shoreline crossing the fault zone also has comparable folding of the same amplitude. The submerged shoreline is mappable for >35 km perpendicular to the fault zone and is attributed to a late-glacial, sea-level lowstand that ended at about 11 ka. Because both surfaces are deformed by equivalent amounts, the 923 CE earthquake must be the only large earthquake on the fault since ~11 ka.

The geometry of the fault is poorly known. The active strand of the Seattle fault does not break the surface, there is limited bedrock exposure, and the subsurface structure is not well imaged in existing seismic reflection data. We investigate whether the fold defined by the deformed shorelines can provide quantitative constraints on fault geometry. Two-dimensional kinematic models relate geometric parameters of a thrust fault to the form of a fold above the fault tip, including the position of the fault at depth, the dip of the fault, and the slip magnitude. We illustrate several approaches to invert profiles of the folded shorelines for fault parameters. To account for measurement uncertainties in the shoreline data, we bootstrap 1000 admissible realizations of each surface and run inversions that test ~10 6 models. Results thus far suggest that inverting kinematic models of these deformed shorelines alone can provide only broad constraints on fault geometry.

title: A Preliminary Analysis of Modern and Historic Diatom Assemblages from Buckeye Lake, Ohio, USA
session_title: Investigating Earth’s Past, Present, and Future with Continental Scientific Drilling
authors: Smith, Chloe G. [1], McLellan, Oliver [2], Leonard-Pingel, Jill [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth Sciences, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA
(2) The Ohio State University School of Earth Sciences, Upper Arlington, OH,
(3) Ohio State University, Newark, OH,
abstract:
Ohio’s lakes are important economic, recreational, and cultural hubs; however, they are subjected to harmful pollutants such as nutrient inputs from agricultural runoff, which have a drastic impact on the water quality and health of lacustrine ecosystems. Buckeye Lake, Ohio’s oldest manmade reservoir, is a prime example of the ways in which nutrient pollution impacts the health of lake ecosystems and communities that depend on them. Over the past few decades, total phosphorus (TP) concentrations have been elevated enough for the lake to experience hypereutrophic conditions. Resultant blooms of microcystin (a harmful algae) have reached dangerous levels during the summer months, shutting down recreational areas. Examining environmental proxies helps inform the local community’s nutrient management strategies. Here, we examine past water quality of Buckeye Lake by assessing changes in diatom assemblages through the retrieval and analysis of a lacustrine sediment core. Many species of diatom prefer highly specific ranges of water quality parameters (e.g., pH and TP); as such, changes in their relative abundance (RA) in death assemblages can reflect past changes in these parameters.

To examine the modern diatom assemblage of Buckeye Lake, sediment samples were collected from the top ~1 cm of the sediment surface using either an Eckman dredge or gravity corer. Additionally, to examine historical diatom assemblages, a sediment core was collected using a Bolivia piston corer. Diatom RAs will be determined through counting and imaging ~500 diatom valves (half-shells) from modern samples, and ~300 subfossil valves from each core sample. Based on previous analyses of modern diatom assemblages from other hypereutrophic manmade reservoirs in the same ecoregion as Buckeye Lake, we expect the modern/core-top assemblage of the lake to be dominated by species in the genera Aulacoseira (e.g., A. ambigua and A. subarctica ) and Discostella (e.g., D. stelligera and D. pseudostelligera ). Throughout the sediment core samples, we expect to see an increase in the RAs of diatoms that prefer eutrophic conditions, such as small species in the genus Stephanodiscus (e.g., S. parvus and S. hantzschii ). The results of this research will be shared with our community partner, Buckeye Lake for Tomorrow, who will integrate information about baseline nutrient states into their environmental management strategy.

title: Mineralogy-Based Geometallurgical Domaining of Bond Work Index at the Cerro Verde Porphyry Cu-Mo Deposit, Peru
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources (Posters)
authors: Ghosh, Suvrajit [1], Tharby, Michael [2], Bruno, Samuel [3]
affiliations: (1) Exploration, Freeport McMoRan, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(2) Exploration, Freeport McMoRan, Tucson, Arizona, USA
(3) Sociedad Contractual de Minera El Abra, El Abra, El Loa, Chile
abstract: Cerro Verde has used automated mineralogical characterization for ore and plant support since 2005, part of a broader shift across geometallurgy toward mineralogy-based rather than purely lithological domain classification, since a single lithology can show highly variable metallurgical response while different lithologies can behave identically. Here we extend that mineralogy-first approach to comminution, testing whether intra-lithologic mineralogical variation better predicts Bond Work Index (BWI) than lithology alone. Three operational and block-model data sources were initially screened for completeness and distributional quality. Two operational data extracts had extensive missing values and remained highly skewed, with 85-99% of records within a narrow range even after imputation, transformation, and outlier removal, and were unusable for analysis; subsequent analysis therefore focused on a more complete block-model dataset. We cleaned the block-model data and used cluster analysis to test whether mineralogical variation could form BWI domains that were not evident when BWI was examined by lithology alone. When plotted against both lithology and alteration type, BWI formed no discernible domains: every rock type and alteration class spanned nearly the full 8-20.5 kWh/t range. We then applied Gaussian mixture model clustering to mineral-proxy combinations including quartz, pyrite, K-feldspar, and sericite-clay within the three most abundant units, Yarabamba Granodiorite and the Cerro Verde and Santa Rosa phases of the Early Dacite-Monzonite Porphyry, which together comprise ~69% of all samples. Several lithology-specific mineral assemblages produced distinguishable BWI populations, whereas others exhibited substantial overlap. Quartz content produced consistent, inversely related BWI domains in two independent units: mean BWI fell from 15.4 to 12.5 kWh/t as quartz rose from 38.0% to 48.8% in the Cerro Verde porphyry, and from 15.6 to 12.8 kWh/t as quartz rose from 37.6% to 45.1% in the granodiorite. The Santa Rosa porphyry did not yield well-defined mineralogical domains despite testing the same proxy set, suggesting either a homogeneous geometallurgical response in that unit or a data-density limitation. Our findings indicate that at Cerro Verde, geometallurgical domains are controlled by mineralogical variation nested within, rather than defined by, broad lithologic units, with quartz content tracking BWI more reliably than rock type or alteration intensity, and that data completeness and validation are essential prerequisites for operational domaining.
