abstract:
The Early Eocene was a time of an overall warm climate punctuated by rapid increases in pCO2 and temperature, known as hyperthermals. Paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental reconstructions are needed to understand the response of terrestrial systems driven by changes in temperature and the hydrologic cycle. Laramide Basins, such as the Wind River Basin (WRB) stretching north to south across the western United States, can be used to capture latitudinal effects from hyperthermal events. The Wind River Formation of central Wyoming is characterized by fluvial sandstones and conglomerates interbedded with floodplain paleosols and mudstones. Here, we present new paleosol-based paleoprecipitation data for two sites: 1) Dubois Badlands (DB) Wilderness Study Area near Dubois, WY, and 2) Hell's Half Acre (HHA), near Casper, WY. Mammalian biostratigraphy, detrital zircon U/Pb dates, and preliminary magnetostratigraphic records constrain the DB site to ~53 to 50 Ma, coinciding with the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum (EECO). Deposits from the HHA site are identified as Eocene and ongoing magnetostratigraphic work will improve this chronology.

Lithostratigraphic sections measured at the DB and HHA sites capture ~170 m and ~ 100 m, respectively. Floodplain paleosols (n = 47 Dubois; n = 35 Hell’s Half Acre) were described using pedogenic features such as color, grain size, texture, and horizonation, and sampled for bulk geochemistry and magnetic mineralogy for paleoprecipitation proxies. Bulk geochemical samples were pulverized via shatterbox and commercially analyzed at ALS Chemex in Reno, NV, through ICP-MS. Rock magnetic samples were measured on a 2G Enterprises 760R-4K Superconducting (SQUID) Rock Magnetometer u-channel system to obtain anhysteric remanent magnetization (ARM) and isothermal remanant magnetization (IRM) for each sample. Preliminary bulk geochemical paleoprecipitation estimates at the DB site range from 338 to 695 with a mean of 412 mm yr-1, and the HHA site range from 675 to 806 with a mean of 747 mm yr-1. Preliminary magnetic mineralogy paleoprecipitation estimates at the DB site range from 255 to 362 with a mean of 301 mm yr-1, and at the HHA site range from 236 to 720 with a mean of 328 mm yr-1. Both proxies indicate that the DB site was consistently drier than the HHA site. Ongoing improvements to the chronology through detrital zircon and magnetostratigraphy will improve our understanding of the pace of terrestrial response to hyperthermal events.

title: From Geological Resources to Geoheritage Values: Assessing and Interpreting Geodiversity and Its Elements to Enhance Public Understanding
session_title: Integrating geoscience history, philosophy, and geoheritage: the past illuminates the future
authors: Štrba, Ľubomír [1], Kršák, Branislav [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geo and Mining Tourism; Faculty of Mining, Ecology, Process Control and Geotechnologies, Technical University of Košice, Košice, Slovak Republic
(2) Department of Geo and Mining Tourism; Faculty of Mining, Ecology, Process Control and Geotechnologies, Technical University of Košice, Košice, Slovak Republic
abstract:
The relationship between society and geological landscapes has changed significantly over time. Rocks, minerals, fossils, and landforms were historically perceived mainly as sources of raw materials, objects of scientific study, or features of curiosity and aesthetic appreciation. In recent decades, however, they have increasingly been recognized as components of natural heritage with scientific, cultural, aesthetic, and societal importance. This transition, reflected in the concepts of geodiversity and geoheritage, represents more than a change in terminology; it reflects a broader philosophical shift from viewing the abiotic environment primarily as a resource toward understanding it as a valuable part of Earth’s history and human identity. This contribution explores how the identification, assessment, and communication of geoheritage values can broaden public understanding and support conservation, sustainable tourism, and regional development.

Geological features recognized as geoheritage preserve evidence of Earth’s evolution, providing insights into past environmental changes and future challenges related to planetary sustainability. Beyond their scientific significance, geological features are closely connected with human history, influencing settlement patterns, mining traditions, architecture, cultural narratives, and regional identities. These links create opportunities to communicate geoscience beyond scientific communities by placing geological processes within broader social and cultural contexts. The aesthetic and recreational values of geological landscapes further strengthen this relationship by inspiring curiosity, emotional connections with nature, and appreciation of geodiversity through geosites, protected areas, and geoparks.

The interpretation and assessment of these interconnected values provide a foundation for sustainable geotourism, particularly through the ABC concept, which integrates abiotic, biotic, and cultural heritage into a unified interpretation of landscapes. By linking geoheritage and geodiversity with biodiversity and local communities, geotourism becomes not only a form of responsible tourism but also a tool for public education, conservation, and regional development. This approach supports geopark management, strengthens local identity, and encourages community participation in heritage protection. By connecting geological evidence with cultural meaning, historical reflection and the philosophy of geosciences provide a framework for understanding geoheritage as both a record of Earth’s evolution and a shared resource for building more sustainable and resilient societies.

title: Paleotopography of the Eocene Sierra Nevada, California, as Recorded by Fossil Leaf-Wax δ²H
session_title: Rock Fishing the Americas: Celebrating the multifaceted career of John Garver from Baja to Alaska and Elsewhere, from Thermochronology-Raman advances, Hydrology, Geoscience-Outreach, Geo-health, to Global Tectonics Processes and Beyond
authors: Brandon, Mark T. [1], Hren, Michael T. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
abstract:
The stable isotopic composition of clay minerals, volcanic glass, and leaf waxes found in paleochannels of the northern Sierra Nevada (California, USA) suggests that the region’s topography during the Paleogene was higher than present. However, this interpretation is still debated due to challenges in reconciling the topography and geomorphology of modern and ancient landscapes. In this study, we present new leaf-wax hydrogen isotope data (δ²HnC29) derived from individual fossil leaves preserved in Eocene-Oligocene alluvial gravels of the northern Sierra Nevada. These data are used to reconstruct past precipitation δ²H. We utilize modern water samples and the OPI model (Orographic Precipitation Isotopes, Brandon, 2022) to estimate the distribution of precipitation isotopes across the western North American Cordillera. We use this modern reference as a basis to interpret isotopic fractionation associated with orographic lifting and rainout over the Eocene Sierra Nevada. For our modeling, we have removed the influence of the Coast Ranges (which had yet to emerge above sea level) and adjusted for a warmer Eocene climate. Our results show that: (1) Eocene δ²HnC29 values decrease from west to east across the Sierra Nevada, consistent with orographic lifting and Rayleigh fractionation along the prevailing Westerly wind path; (2) the δ²HnC29values of bulk sediment and individual leaves are in good agreement, which indicates that the leaves were locally derived and have perserved their original isotopic values; and (3) the northern Eocene Sierra Nevada was approximately 30% higher than it is today. Our 30% estimate is based on our OPI modeling, which indicates that Φ, which is the ratio of past to present isotopic fractionation, changes linearly with the ratio of past to present topography. Our modeling also accounts for the influence of Eocene versus present temperatures on the fractionation processes during orographic precipitation.

Overall, our results closely align with previous estimates and support the interpretation of a high-standing magmatic arc during the mid-Cretaceous, followed by a reduction in topography during the Late Cretaceous and early Cenozoic, and then renewed uplift in the late Cenozoic.

title: Controls on long-runout debris flow occurrence in North Carolina during Hurricane Helene: Insights from detailed UAV surveying integrated with geologic and geomorphic mapping
session_title: Emerging Research into the Impacts of Hurricane Helene in the Southern Appalachians
authors: Thigpen, Ryan [1], Johnson, Sarah [2], Brown, Summer [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA; Kentucky Geological Survey, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY,
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA
abstract: From September 25 th to 27 th , 2024, a predecessor rain event combined with the arrival of the Helene tropical low in North Carolina produced the largest outbreak of long-runout (>0.5 km lateral extent) debris flows and landslides in the recorded history of this region. Many of these debris flows caused catastrophic damage and resulted in loss of life. The largest debris flows, including >20 flows with lengths >1.5 km, occurred along a corridor ~30 km wide from Chimney Rock to Burnsville that includes some of the highest relief in the region along the Blue Ridge escarpment and into the Black Mountains. This corridor is also broadly coincident with the highest recorded storm precipitation totals (>787 mm; >31 in) and hourly precipitation rates (>73.7 mm/hr; 2.9 in/hr), owing to the combined effects of NW-directed moisture flow and intense orographically-enhanced convection. Witness reports and time-stamped media indicate that most flows were triggered from 8-11 AM on September 27th, with flow initiation focused within the southern part of the corridor and then shifting progressively northward with the intense rainfall bands. Bracketing major flow occurrences in this small temporal interval provides an important link between atmospheric conditions and flow initiation in this system. Additionally, integration of post-event UAV surveys with detailed geologic and geomorphic mapping is helping us better characterize and understand fundamental features and processes in these long runout debris flows. Height-to-length (H/L) ratios of these long-runout flows generally range from 0.20-0.30. Notable outliers include the Celo Knob flow (H/L ~0.33), which preserves one of the spatially largest initiation zones (~0.74 km 2 ) in the entire system, and two ultra long-runout flows known colloquially as Big Ivy and Craigtown, that yield the lowest H/L values of ~0.18 and ~0.14, respectfully. At ~5.1 km, the Big Ivy flow has the greatest total length in the system. The Craigtown flow tragically produced 13 fatalities, the highest number for a single complex in eastern U.S. history. Preliminary analyses indicate that these very low H/L flows likely included the greatest entrainment volumes recognized from this storm. Ongoing work focuses on understanding the pre-conditions governing initiation zone and channel morphology, factors that may contribute to production of these relatively high entrainment volumes, and links between precipitation rate and flow initiation.

abstract: Subsurface experiments at the Nevada National Security Site (NNSS) require detailed understanding of fracture-controlled gas migration, crucial for the Low-Yield Nuclear Monitoring (LYNM) program. The goal of the LYNM program is to improve the US’ ability to detect and analyze low-yield underground nuclear explosions, and a major pillar of this research is Physics Experiment-1 (PE-1). PE-1 is a series of underground chemical explosion experiments in NNSS’s P-Tunnel that utilize high explosives with gas tracers to simulate nuclear events. Before detonation, scientists conduct extensive geologic mapping, geophysical borehole logging, and physical sampling. Understanding and predicting the migration of the gas tracers is a key component to post-detonation results. P-Tunnel experiments can produce unique results due to lithology, which is primarily porous volcanic tuff with known fractures in the area. Despite extensive inter-laboratory permeability data, existing pore and fracture characterization methods produce limited prediction results for heterogeneous lithologies such as volcanic tuff. NNSS collaborated with the National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL), who specialize in multiscale geologic characterization through their computed tomography (CT) scanning facility, composed of medical, industrial, and micro-CT scanners, as well as other petrophysical equipment. We adapted NETL’s image processing methods, which utilize the open-source software ImageJ and ilastik to preprocess and segment the CT scans, and applied advanced processing techniques to the volcanic tuff samples. Refined segmentations were generated using the deep learning framework nnU-Net, and postprocessing was performed using various Python packages including PoreSpy, scikit-image, and openCV. We retrieved quantitative outputs from the tuff samples such as total volume of negative space, pore connectivity estimates, and fracture morphology. The data obtained from these new methods were compared to existing permeability data for P-Tunnel lithology to improve transport predictions and strengthen models for NNSS missions.

title: Dominant fabric of the metamorphic core of the south-central Brooks Range records mid-Cretaceous extension and exhumation
session_title: Casting a line into deep time to constrain subduction and crustal evolution of the western North American plate margin: Celebrating the career of Marty Grove
authors: Craig, Jason W [1], Miller, Elizabeth Louise [2], Dumitru, Trevor [3], Toro, Jaime [4], DesOrmeau, Joel William [5], Cruz-Uribe, Alicia Marie [6]
affiliations: (1) EPS, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
(2) EPS, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA

(4) West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
(5) University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV,
(6) University of Maine, Orono, ME,
abstract:
Mesozoic exhumation of high-pressure metamorphic rocks of the south-central Brooks Range, Arctic Alaska, has been attributed either to Jurassic–Early Cretaceous thrusting or to post-contractional, mid-Cretaceous extension. We test these models along the John River transect using geologic mapping, structural and microstructural analysis, in situ LA-ICP-MS white mica and biotite Rb–Sr geochronology, zircon (U-Th-Sm)/He (ZHe) and apatite fission-track (AFT) thermochronology, together with published 40 Ar/ 39 Ar, zircon U-Pb, Raman thermometry, and phengite barometry constraints.

The transect exposes a series of normal-fault-bounded structural domains that preserve two generations of metamorphic fabrics. Older S 1 /S D−1 fabrics and associated high-pressure mineral assemblages record Jurassic–Early Cretaceous convergence and crustal thickening. S D−1 white mica Rb–Sr ages centered near 138 Ma, ca. 140 Ma metamorphic zircon growth, and ca. 170–130 Ma 40 Ar/ 39 Ar spectra broadly constrain this earlier shortening related metamorphism. The younger S 2 /S D fabric is a variably developed crenulation to penetrative cleavage with N–S stretching lineation that defines a broad dome across most of the metamorphic core (including the Central, Schist, and Phyllite belts). Metamorphic zircon overgrowth ages of 114 ± 6 Ma, S D -domain white mica Rb–Sr ages with a weighted mean of 109 ± 4 Ma, and the youngest white mica 40 Ar/ 39 Ar release ages near 110 Ma constrain its development.

S 2 /S D cuts across major normal faults that omit substantial structural and metamorphic section, indicating syn- to post-faulting thermal and deformational overprinting during north–south stretching. Stretching, tectonic thinning, and broad doming unroofed blueschist- to eclogite-facies rocks before cooling recorded by ZHe ages centered near 95 Ma, a 91 ± 4 Ma Rb–Sr age from syn- to post-S D biotite, and AFT ages centered near 58 Ma. These relations indicate that S 2 /S D development, metamorphism, and cooling were tightly coupled from ca. 114–90 Ma during post-contractional, regionally distributed extension rather than continued thrusting. Increasing temperatures during extension are consistent with magmatic addition of heat to the crust, potentially related to High Arctic Large Igneous Province magmatism and a broad belt of syn-extensional plutons south of the Brooks Range. The Brooks Range extensional complex of Arctic Alaska and its continuation into Chukotka record a large, plate-boundary-scale extensional system inferred to have developed during mid- to Late Cretaceous opening of the Amerasia Basin and rollback of a north-dipping paleo-Pacific slab.

title: Quantifying Geothermal Groundwater Discharge and Solute Fluxes to Great Salt Lake Using Environmental Tracers
session_title: Advancing Understanding of Regional Groundwater Flow Systems and Groundwater Sustainability Through Environmental Tracers (Posters)
authors: Petersen, Justin [1], Carling, Greg [2]
affiliations: (1) Brigham Young University, Department of Geological Sciences, Provo, UT, USA
(2) Brigham Young University, Department of Geological Sciences, Provo, UT, USA
abstract:
Groundwater is one of the most poorly constrained components of the Great Salt Lake (GSL) water budget, yet it may have an outsized influence on lake chemistry, salinity, and ecosystem resilience. In particular, geothermally influenced groundwater may contribute modest water volumes while delivering disproportionately large dissolved-solute loads. This project investigates geothermal groundwater inputs to the Bear, Weber/Ogden, and Jordan River systems and evaluates how those inputs shape the chemistry and isotopic composition of water entering GSL. Strontium isotopes ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) provide an effective tracer because they reflect source geology and remain conservative during water–rock interaction, allowing groundwater contributions to be distinguished from riverine inputs.

Preliminary results suggest that major tributaries receive focused inputs of radiogenic groundwater near the Wasatch Front. Along the Bear River, 87 Sr/ 86 Sr values reflect bedrock lithology throughout the upper basin, then rise sharply in the lower basin to ~0.718–0.719. The Weber River shows a similar increase below the Ogden confluence, and available spring data identify highly radiogenic geothermal waters consistent with deep, fault-controlled flow paths. These patterns point to spatially concentrated hydrothermal groundwater discharge regions that may strongly influence tributary solute delivery to GSL.

By combining longitudinal river sampling, hot spring sampling, discharge constraints, and strontium-isotope mass-balance modeling, this study will improve GSL water and solute budgets and provide results directly relevant to salinity change, wetland health, dust risk, and long-term lake management.

authors: Kinsley, Christopher William [1], Carter, Jack Norman [2], Weij, Rieneke [3], Oster, Jessica Leigh [4], Lodge, Bethan Grace [5], Bolden, Isaiah W [6], Niespolo, Elizabeth M [7], Sharp, Warren D. [8]

abstract:
Speleothem archives record proxies of past changes in the terrestrial climate system over the Late Cenozoic. Chronological models for speleothems of Pleistocene–Holocene age are commonly generated by uranium-thorium (U–Th) dating, but accurately correcting for initial Th (i.e., 230 Th that does not result from in-situ decay of uranium) remains one of the most significant obstacles to precise and accurate U–Th dating. Two methods are broadly used to correct for initial Th: (1) direct estimation using isochron techniques; or (2) assuming a constant, model value of the initial 230 Th/ 232 Th ratio. However, isochron approaches are resource-intensive while corrections made using a single, assumed initial Th value with arbitrary uncertainty may fail to characterize significant variations in initial Th, potentially leading to inflated age uncertainties and inaccurate ages. Improved approaches to correct for initial Th would aid efforts to build robust age models in speleothems globally.

IBIS (a Bayesian approach for U–Th dating in speleothems) provides suitable initial Th corrections in diverse stalagmites without relying on isochron analyses or model-dependent assumptions about the source or isotopic composition of initial Th. We apply IBIS to all available U–Th measurements from the SISAL database and together with the relevant proxy information, explore potential mechanistic controls on initial Th, including dust loading, site vegetation coverage, and commonly measured elemental and isotopic ratios in speleothems. We also examine high and variable initial Th at Hato Cave (Curaçao), hosted by a mid-Pleistocene coral reef. There, we have measured initial Th in drip water and farmed calcite and we pair those observations with U–Th data from mid-Holocene stalagmites that provide initial Th estimates via isochrons and IBIS, and with trace element compositions measured on selected stalagmite samples. We find that Hato Cave waters and calcite have initial 230 Th/ 232 Th ratios up to five times higher than average crust that vary significantly over short spatial and temporal scales. An improved understanding of initial Th variability, combined with the IBIS model, may provide more robust initial Th corrections for a wide variety of speleothems.

title: Detrital zircon analysis of sandstones within the great American carbonate bank (Lower Ordovician, U.S. midcontinent)
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Melrose, Avery [1], Malone, David [2], McLaughlin, Pat [3], Malone, Jack [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography, Geology, and Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(2) Department of Geography, Geology, and the Environment, Illinois State University, Normal, Illinois, USA
(3) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, Illinois, USA
(4) Iowa Geological Survey, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
abstract:
Sandstones within the upper Cambrian (Pabian) to Lower Ordovician great American carbonate bank (GACB) have received relatively little study. Their provenance and sedimentary characteristics can provide new insights into paleogeographic and tectonic reconstructions as well as cross-platform fluvial and aeolian transport processes that remain poorly understood.

In the Laurentian midcontinent the GACB succession is dominated by fine-grained carbonate strata that record the maximum transgression of the Sauk megasequence. Several variably thick quartz arenite beds occur locally within the Prairie Du Chien Group. Fourteen samples were collected from this interval in Iowa, Wisconsin, Illinois and Indiana outcrops and cores. Detrital zircons were separated and analyzed by LA-ICPMS at the University of Arizona Laserchron Center (n=241).

The results of the detrital zircon analysis are largely consistent with paleogeographic reconstructions for central Laurentia during formation of the GACB. Twelve of the samples, collected from the shallower facies of the Wisconsin Arch, are statistically indistinguishable and share a dominant 2700 Ma age peak, reflecting sourcing from the Superior province several hundred kilometers upwind to the paleo-east. These results are consistent with the textural and structural evidence for eolian transport. The sample from Denzer Wisconsin, which is less than 5 km from the from the exposed Baraboo Hills, has a population of 1700-1900 Ma zircons, which were likely recycled from the Mesoproterozoic Baraboo Formation. The southern Indiana sample, which was collected from strata near the platform margin, has a distinct provenance signature, with abundant 1000-1300 Ma zircons that were derived from the Grenville terrane more than 500 km to the northeast. A previously published age set from near the platform margin in Missouri shares this Grenville zircon population which may represent lowstand cross-platform fluvial transport and redistribution by storm and longshore currents.

title: The power of periostracum: Using δ13C and δ15N values to establish North American freshwater mussel diets prior to the arrival of the non-native Corbicula fluminea
session_title: Won't you be my Neighbor? Quantifying Realized Niche Transitions Through Time and Space
authors: Balaji, Lilja Elyse [1], Arill, Kirsten [2], Crowley, Brooke Erin [3], Douglass, Sarah Alee [4], Miller, Joshua H. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH,
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Department of Anthropology, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA
(4) Illinois Natural History Survey, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, Illinois, USA
(5) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH,
abstract: It is suspected Corbicula fluminea (Chinese Basket Clam) is contributing to population declines of native freshwater mussels (Unionidae) in North America through dietary competition, but establishing molluscan dietary ecology using observational data is challenging. Stable carbon (δ 13 C) and nitrogen (δ 15 N) isotope values of soft tissues can track dietary resources, though such tissues are generally only available from modern (recently living) individuals. This leaves a knowledge gap regarding historical unionid diets and any dietary shifts following Corbicula 's arrival. Periostracum (the outermost proteinaceous shell layer) is deposited during shell growth and preserved in museum shell collections, potentially solving this problem. However, before using periostracum as a dietary proxy, isotopic differences between periostracum and soft tissues driven by differences in amino acid composition, an individual’s ontogenetic stage (age), and turnover rate (periostracum does not remodel, whereas soft tissues have 120- to 333-day turnover cycles) need to be evaluated. We compared δ 13 C and δ 15 N values of mantle, foot, and periostracum from two unionids ( Lampsilis cardium : n = 14 ; and Ortmanniana ligamentina : n = 13) that were live-collected in 2024 from the Kishwaukee River at the I-90 bridge in Rockford, Illinois, where Corbicula first arrived in 2023. Because obtaining enough periostracum for isotopic analysis often requires sampling multiple years of growth (annuli), which may impact resulting offsets, we thin-sectioned the shells to determine age and annuli sampled to the nearest third of a year. Periostracum δ 13 C values were, on average, 1.1 ± 1.0‰ less than either mantle or foot, but this difference decreased with age – indicating an ontogenetic effect rather than a sampling artifact of annuli count. The δ 15 N values were systematically higher in the periostracum for both species (mean difference = 0.9 ± 0.4‰), with no significant relationship to annuli sampled or the individual’s age. Understanding the structure of periostracum as a historical dietary proxy, we compared these 2024 isotopic results to those from Lampsilis (n=3) and Ortmanniana (n=13) specimens collected prior to the arrival of Corbicula (2015-2019). Accounting for ontogenetic differences among specimens collected prior to and after Corbicula ’s arrival, we found no significant differences in δ 13 C or δ 15 N values over time for either species. Our results suggest adult unionid diets remained relatively stable following the Corbicula invasion, but continued monitoring is recommended.

title: Origin and Geochemical Evolution of the Fry Mountains Segment of the Independence Dike Swarm, Southeast California
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Raines-Hepple, Jackson [1], Moore, Nicole E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Pomona College, Claremont, CA,
(2) Pomona College, Claremont, CA,
abstract:
The Independence Dike Swarm (IDS) is a series of northwest trending dikes formed in the Late Jurassic Period (ca. 148 Ma), cropping out along 600 km of Eastern California. It consists of hundreds of dikes that range from basalt to rhyolite that intruded through an extensional regional fracture system created during the Nevadan Orogeny. The Fry Mountains segment is located in the south central Mojave Block, a transitional portion of the Basin and Range bounded by the San Andreas and Garlock Faults. This segment contains both mafic and felsic compositional endmember dikes.

Nine dike samples were collected from the Fry Mountains segment to determine the mantle source character and crustal differentiation history of the IDS in this region. Three mafic dikes are porphyritic tephrite basanites to trachy-basalts (43.6-45.6 wt.% SiO 2 , 4.5-6.0 wt.% MgO) containing plagioclase phenocrysts within a plagioclase-hornblende matrix with variable biotite, magnetite, and/or orthoclase. Six felsic dikes (63.6-70.82 wt.% SiO 2 , 0-0.3 wt.% MgO) are aphanitic to porphyritic trachytes to rhyolites consisting of quartz and potassium feldspar phenocrysts with variable plagioclase, magnetite, muscovite, and/or biotite.

Sample PI26-5 is the least differentiated and most primitive dike (43.6 wt.% SiO 2 , 6.0 wt.% MgO, Mg# 56.3 , 191 ppm Cr, and 98 ppm Ni). This sample has a relatively flat HREE pattern (normalized to chondrite) which suggests a depleted upper mantle source, whereas relative LREE enrichment combined with a calc-alkaline signature is consistent with subduction zone origin where slab-derived fluids introduced LREE. Batch modal melt modeling of REE confirms this dike can be produced by low partial degrees of melting (<5%) of a depleted upper mantle source fluxed by subduction fluids.

The felsic dikes all have negative Eu anomalies on a chondrite-normalized REE diagram, indicating significant plagioclase fractionation. Geochemical trends in Harker diagrams for all samples suggest the mafic dikes may represent the parent magmas of the felsic dikes, the latter derived through fractional crystallization combined with other differentiation processes including magma mixing and/or crustal assimilation. Fractional crystallization REE calculations, using the most primitive mafic dike sample (PI26-5), confirm the felsic dikes can be the product of variable amounts of fractionation of plagioclase and mafic minerals from a mafic parent similar to the most primitive dike.

title: Methods of Reconstructing Paleoenvironments in 3D for use in Science Communication
session_title: Technology and tools for 3D visualization of field and lab data in teaching and research (Posters)
authors: Berryhill, Konrad [1], Lovelace, David M. [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(2) Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Geoscience, Madison, WI, USA
abstract:
Paleoart, in its many forms, can be used to quickly convey complex paleobiological information to the viewer. Despite being an equally important aspect of an artwork, the paleoenvironment represented is often overlooked in favor of the fauna. Informative paleoenvironmental reconstructions require the incorporation of data derived from multiple disciplines to build an accurate prehistoric setting (i.e., sedimentology, ichnology, paleoclimatology, paleoecology, etc.). A proper depiction of an extinct ecosystem can provide the viewer with a unique opportunity to visually explore a snapshot of a prehistoric time period, highlighting what is different in comparison to modern environments and also what hasn’t changed.

One way to maximize the impact of paleoenvironmental reconstructions is to create the scene digitally in 3D such that the viewer can be shown a set of paleobiological models within the sedimentological and stratigraphic framework of a geologic formation. 3D rendering allows for environments to be displayed from multiple angles in a 3D space and enables easy customization with a collection of uniquely created assets depicting the biology and geography of a formation. This poster will follow the workflow for creating a reconstruction of a floodplain environment from the Triassic Popo Agie formation in Wyoming. The result is a process utilizing different specialized software to create models of the fauna and flora, reconstruct the geography and surface paleosols of the geological unit, and composite and render the models in a scene. The methods used in accomplishing this include digital sculpting and modeling, photogrammetry, procedural particle and material systems, and scene lighting and rendering. The software used in this project includes Blender, ZBrush, Mari, RealityScan, Substance Designer, and Photoshop.

title: Evidence for Neogene Tilting and Uplift of the Central Sierra Nevada, CA: Geospatial Analysis of the Table Mountain Latite Paleochannels
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Shields, Jessie E. [1], Pluhar, Christopher J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, California State University, Fresno, CA, USA
abstract: Controversy surrounds whether the Sierra Nevada, CA experienced tilting and uplift during the Neogene, due to disagreement between older and emerging data typers. We re-examined the Table Mountain Latite from Tulloch Reservoir to Parrot’s Ferry. The Table Mountain lava filled Miocene drainage channels, and subsequent erosion produced extensive inverted topography. Using drillers logs and mapping, we demonstrate what was proposed 100 years ago - one potion near Columbia, CA has not suffered this inversion and thus represents an “instantaneous” snapshot of the Stanislaus River still within its paleochannel. With modern LiDAR-derived DEMs in a GIS environment, we show that the current paleodownstream direction of this portion of the Table Mountain Latite is inconsistent with the slope of its upper and lower surface in some places. Due to its meandering character, some reaches of the Table Mountain Latite flowed eastwards and/or northwards, but the current surface slopes westwards and/or southwards. Either the Sierra Nevada have not tilted since emplacement and lava flowed uphill, or the lava flowed downhill and the slope was modified by subsequent tilt of the region, i.e., this portion of the Sierra Nevada microplate. The unit top surface shows a sinusoidal relationship with the largest slopes pointing southwards and negative slopes pointing north and east. When we backtilt the data for Sierran tilt, the sinusoid disappears yielding a stream gradient that is similar to pre-tilt gradients proposed elsewhere. Post-emplacement erosion has modified the surface somewhat, increasing data dispersion, but the conclusion remains robust.

title: Leveraging Subsidence Data from InSAR to Estimate Groundwater Storage Change in the Western United States
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: Smith, Ryan G [1], Pant, Susmita [2], Al Fatta, Abdullah [3], Li, Jiawei [4]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(3) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(4) Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract: In the face of groundwater depletion, managers need actionable information to develop strategies to mitigate storage loss. However, traditional methods for estimating storage loss routinely provide results that differ significantly, sometimes by an order of magnitude. Basic groundwater balances show that annual groundwater storage loss is a reasonable first-order estimate of pumping reductions needed to sustain future aquifer storage. Thus, extreme uncertainty in storage loss leads to extreme uncertainty in management of this critical resource. Satellite observations from Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provide estimates of land subsidence, which is associated with one component of groundwater storage loss (consolidation), with an accuracy of ~ 5 mm/year. This dataset can be leveraged to improve groundwater budgets, but is generally not useful on its own, as it is completely insensitive to the other components of groundwater storage loss (drainage of pores and expansion of water). Here, we present methods to integrate InSAR data with in-situ records of groundwater withdrawals and water levels, to produce robust estimates of groundwater storage change. We present multiple frameworks for combining these datasets depending on the availability of in-situ data, presenting case studies in California, Utah and Colorado. The framework presented here is flexible and can be implemented to estimate groundwater storage change in other regions that experience significant subsidence.

title: A Stratigraphic Reevaluation of the Mt. Simon Formation at Its Type Locality: Implications for the Elk Mound Group
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Ziemer, Reed Monti [1], LeBarron, Bodie Chase [2], Alemu, Tadesse Berhanu [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin Eau Claire, Eau Claire, WI, USA
(2) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin Eau Claire, Eau Claire, WI, USA
(3) Geology and Environmental Science, University of Wisconsin Eau Claire, Eau Claire, WI, USA
abstract:
We present new, high-resolution stratigraphic columns and facies characterization of the Cambrian Mt. Simon Formation at three localities in west-central Wisconsin, including at its type section in Eau Claire and two nearby outcrops used for correlation. Logged bed by bed from top to bottom, the columns document sand dominated lithologies, grain size trends, bedding, sedimentary structure, and trace fossils supported by field descriptions and systematic digital imagery.

The Mt. Simon Formation is the basal unit of the Elk Mound Group, resting nonconformably on the weathered Mesoproterozoic basement. It is overlain by the Eau Claire Formation and then the Wonewoc Formation, which together underlie the Tunnel City Group. Deposition occurred when a shallow sea flooded the upper Midwest, including central Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Illinois during the Cambrian. The formation is economically important: it is a regional aquifer, and a leading target for carbon-dioxide sequestration in the Illinois basin.

Despite its significance, the type section lacks a modern study that integrates a detailed measured column, advanced analytical characterization, and digital documentation; the most recent published description is more than half a century old. Re-describing the type section is timely because recent work has proposed an open-coast, wave-dominated tidal-flat model for the Elk Mound Group (MacNaughton et al., 2019). In this model, sandy, mud-poor flats preserve co-occurring storm-generated parallel lamination and fair-weather wave ripples alongside indicators of shallow water and repeated subaerial exposure, marking a sharp departure from classic mud-rich tidal interpretations. Our columns provide the physical-stratigraphic framework needed to test this model at the type locality and reevaluate the group. Planned analytical work includes thin-section petrography, SEM-imaging, and bulk XRD of gradational contacts to refine facies and provenance interpretations.

title: Consistent structural controls on karst flow path development revealed by combined aerial and subterranean lidar, Grand Canyon, USA
session_title: Innovations in Geological Mapping
authors: LaSala, Blase [1], Sankey, Temuulen Tsagaan [2], Springer, Abraham E. [3], Nebel, Mark [4], Palmer, James D. [5]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, National Cave and Karst Research Institute, Carlsbad, New Mexico, USA; Northern Arizona University, School of Informatics, Computing and Cyber Systems, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
(2) School of Informatics, Computing and Cyber Systems,, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
(3) School of Earth and Sustainability, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
(4) National Park Service (Emeritus), Grand Canyon National Park (Emeritus), Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
(5) Steve Sanghi College of Engineering, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
abstract:
Defining recharge areas for karst springs is important for identifying sources of contamination and predicting the effects of drought. However, delineation is challenging because flow is concentrated within hidden conduit networks that often bear little relation to surface topography or drainage.

In Grand Canyon National Park, springs discharging from the deep Redwall-Muav aquifer support an array of endemic species and are currently the sole source of drinking water for the park and some adjacent tribes. Recent detections of E. coli , destructive wildfires, and planned infrastructure underscore the urgency of delineating recharge areas for these springs. Qualitative dye tracer studies have established point-to-point connections between sinkholes and springs, but quantitative characterization of flow paths across this rugged terrain remains infeasible. We instead analyzed the geometry of cave passages and overlying structure to quantify regional structural controls on flow path development.

We previously mapped over 10 kilometers of hydrologically active cave passages, including small flooded passages and vertical pits, in three dimensions at centimeter resolution using a mobile laser scanner. Here we integrate subsurface geometry with sub-meter aerial lidar of the overlying terrain and present a fully automated method for extracting bedding plane orientations from both datasets. Bedding orientations derived independently from each dataset agree within combined measurement uncertainty, confirming that surface and subsurface structure can be quantified in a common framework. Within both Muav Limestone caves, fractures and joints aligned with the local dip direction are preferentially enlarged, while being located on opposite sides of the plateau. These consistent surface and subsurface orientations support previous predictions that the basal Bright Angel Shale strongly controls flow path development within the Redwall-Muav aquifer, and suggest that flow path development might be regionally predictable.

By linking three-dimensional cave geometry to bedding exposed along canyon cliffs, our approach offers a scalable path toward understanding recharge in karst systems where tracer methods are impractical.

abstract: The present study aims to monitor the water quality using remote sensing in Maumee Bay, western Lake Erie, where problems associated with suspended sediment, nutrient loading, and harmful algal bloom (HABs) are frequent. The objective of the study was to retrieve and process quarterly data from Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2 (2020-2025) for extracting information about suspended sediment and chlorophyll concentration to examine seasonal patterns, sediment plume dynamics, and tracking algal bloom development. The result suggests that the indicators derived from remote sensing techniques represent an excellent information resource for designing and implementing resource conservation and ecological management strategies and offer an analytical basis for prevention and restoration strategies.

title: Stable Isotope Paleoecology and Paleoclimatology of the late Holocene Rock Springs Cave Fauna (Utah, USA)
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Ramos, Hannah [1], Gehring, Calvin [2], Zanazzi, Alessandro [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, Utah Valley University, Orem, UT, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, Utah Valley University, Orem, UT, USA
(3) Department of Earth Science, Utah Valley University, Orem, UT, USA
abstract:
To investigate late Holocene paleoclimate, paleoenvironment, and mammalian paleoecology in Utah, we analyzed carbon and oxygen stable isotope ratios in fossil tooth enamel from Rock Springs Cave (39.9155° N, 113.7931° W; ~90 km southeast of Wendover). The teeth represent 14 individual mammals from 7 taxa: striped skunks ( Mephitis mephitis) , red foxes ( Vulpes vulpes ), bobcats ( Lynx rufus ), mule deer ( Odocoileus hemionus ), bighorn sheep ( Ovis canadensis ), North American porcupines ( Erethizon dorsatum ), and pronghorns ( Antilocapra americana ). The samples have been radiocarbon dated to 2470 ± 30 14C years BP . Following established enamel preparation procedures, we sequentially subsampled and pretreated the teeth, producing 245 samples for isotope analysis.

Stable carbon isotope ratios (i.e., carbon-13/carbon-12 ratios) provide information on the proportion of C3 versus C4 plants in an animal’s diet based on differences in their photosynthetic pathways and carbon isotope fractionation. In ecosystems dominated by C3 plants, these ratios can serve as proxies for mean annual precipitation and vegetation openness. Oxygen isotope ratios (i.e., oxygen-18/oxygen-16 ratios) in enamel reflect the composition of meteoric water and, at mid-latitudes, correlate with temperature—making them useful for paleotemperature reconstructions. Additionally, sequential sampling within each tooth allows to infer seasonal variation in climate and resource availability.

By analyzing carbon and oxygen stable isotope ratios from a diverse assemblage of mammals, we aim to reconstruct late Holocene vegetation, climate, and seasonality at Rock Springs Cave and evaluate how species with different ecological niches responded to these conditions. Comparisons among taxa provide insight into habitat structure, resource availability, and climatic stress, offering a framework for understanding how western U.S. mammalian communities respond to environmental change and how these responses may inform interpretations of modern climate change.

title: Fractures and Fluid Pathways: Quantitative Characterization of the Reactivated Douglas Fault Damage Zone, Wisconsin
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms. (Posters)
authors: Braunagel, Michael John [1], Duncan, Ethan [2], Daniels, Nathan [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Minnesota Duluth, Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, Duluth, MN, USA
(2) University of Minnesota Duluth, Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, Duluth, MN, USA
(3) University of Minnesota Duluth, Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, Duluth, MN, USA
abstract:
Fault damage zones exert a first order control on subsurface fluid flow by governing fracture connectivity, permeability anisotropy, and the distribution of deformation surrounding fault cores. Consequently, damage zone architecture influences rupture mechanics, fluid flow, and crustal strength during fault evolution and reactivation through multiple tectonic events. Here, we present quantitative structural observations from the Douglas Fault in northwestern Wisconsin, which integrate detailed outcrop mapping and fracture network analysis, to demonstrate how progressive rock failure is recorded in damage-zone architecture during early normal faulting conditions and subsequent inversion of the North American Midcontinent Rift.

At multiple study sites, the steeply dipping Douglas Fault thrusts highly fractured basaltic hanging wall rocks of the Chengwatana volcanics over less damaged Bayfield Group sandstones in the footwall. Mapping and thin-section analyses reveal a strongly asymmetric damage zone, with a >100 m wide zone of pervasive multi-generational fractures in the hanging wall, including opening-mode veins, shear fractures, and microcrack networks. Cumulative fracture-frequency plots display a steep inner-zone intensity gradient that transitions outward to a broad, diffuse outer damage zone with perpendicular distance from the fault core, and fracture orientations define two dominant sets: NE–SW trending, subvertical extension fractures with deformed calcite veins and an overprinting NW–SE striking set of shear to hybrid fractures. The footwall rocks record lower fracture density and compactional microcracking consistent with distributed deformation in semi-consolidated sedimentary deposits. These structural gradients record progressive strain localization while preserving evidence for multiple phases of deformation. The resulting fracture architectures define mechanically distinct domains which are expected to exhibit contrasting permeability anisotropy and fluid-flow behavior during the fault’s history.

By quantitatively linking fracture intensity, orientation, connectivity, and structures across the Douglas Fault damage zone, this study demonstrates how outcrop scale structural observations can inform conceptual and numerical models of fault controlled permeability. For example, the observed fracture architecture further suggests that successful inversion of the steeply dipping Douglas Fault likely required transient fluid overpressure and localized reductions in fault strength, potentially requiring progressive fracture sealing and frictionally weak fault gouge generated during earlier extensional slip.

title: From Forcing to Stratigraphy: A Sediment-State Model for the Middle Jurassic Entrada Sandstone, Utah
session_title: Aeolian environments and drylands (Posters)
authors: Cousins, David [1], Hern, Caroline [2]
affiliations: (1) Subsurface Energy Resources, Illinois State Geological Survey, Urbana, IL, USA
(2) Clastic Reservoir Characterization, Shell Exploration and Production, Houston, TX, USA
abstract:
Sequence-stratigraphic models for the Entrada Sandstone (San Rafael Group, Utah) treat relative sea level as the dominant control on erg accumulation and destruction. In these models, a rise in relative sea level raises the water table and traps eolian sediment in the capillary fringe, while fall or stillstand produces bypass or erosional supersurfaces. Sediment supply is formally independent in this framework, but in practice it is reconstructed backward from the facies it is meant to explain, and inferred to parallel the rate of sea-level rise, since transgression delivers sand to coastal source areas for onward eolian transport. Climate enters only as a consequence of sea level, never as a driver in its own right.

We revisit this framework using a sediment-state approach, in which sediment supply, sediment availability and the transport capacity of the wind are constrained independently of the rock record, and used to predict phases of erg construction, stabilisation and deflation, and the surfaces that separate them. We ask whether an independent climate signal, using orbitally paced insolation as a proxy for precipitation, vegetation cover and erg-interior sediment availability, can explain facies patterns that the sea-level-only models leave unresolved.

Recent 40Ar/39Ar tephrochronology shows that Entrada deposition spans at least the interval from 168.1 to 160.8 Ma, providing the first absolute time control for correlations that were previously only relative. We use these anchors to place existing sea-level and climate records on a common, dated timeline, and to classify the resulting supply and availability configurations through time.

Using the Entrada Sandstone as a test case, this approach offers a route to bring orbital climate forcing into terrestrial eolian sequence stratigraphy, and to ask how much of an erg’s architecture the sea was ever responsible for.

title: Teaching Paleontology using CUREs: Examining Paleoecological Changes in Molluscan Communities across the Plio-Pleistocene of North and Central Florida
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part II)
authors: Visaggi, Christy C. [1], Weinstein, Sofia R. Y. [2], Portell, Roger W. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA; Center for Excellence in Teaching, Learning, and Online Education, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA
(2) Geosciences, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, USA
(3) Florida Museum of Natural History, Gainesville, FL, USA
abstract:
Teaching of paleontology often involves lecture periods focused on disciplinary concepts and lab-based activities that explore common phyla in the fossil record. By integrating course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) into the paleontology classroom, students have a chance to learn about the fossil record by contributing to authentic research questions. Team-based approaches to research have been utilized via a CURE model in the Principles of Paleontology course at Georgia State University (GSU) since 2013. Being able to offer students a chance to engage in research as part of the curriculum has been particularly valuable in expanding access to such opportunities at this large urban minority-serving institution. Through six iterations of the course since the initial launch, undergraduate and graduate students from a variety of disciplines (anthropology, biology, environmental science, geosciences) have learned paleontology by doing paleontology in studying molluscan fossils from Cenozoic deposits of the southeastern U.S.

Marine molluscan communities of the Western Atlantic experienced a series of extinction episodes across the Plio-Pleistocene. Existing research has focused mostly on fossils from the Carolinas and southern Florida leaving a biogeographic gap in knowledge for much of north and central Florida along the boundary between the Carolinian and Gulf provinces. Since 2018, paleontology students at GSU have primarily examined specimens from the understudied Nashua and Anastasia Formations in this region and have contributed new data to our understanding of marine communities from these deposits. Class research experiences include sieving, sorting, collecting, and analyzing data on whole and fragmented shells to study the diversity, abundance, ecological structure, and predation recorded in these assemblages. Students have presented their findings on campus and prepared co-authored abstracts for regional meetings offering the chance for students to share their research directly with the professional community. title: 3D Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) Simulations of Tullimonstrum gregarium
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n)
authors: Potter, Jacob James [1], McCoy, Victoria E. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI,
(2) Geosciences, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI, USA
abstract: Tullimonstrum gregarium , more commonly known as the Tully Monster, remains one of the most charismatic organisms of the famous Middle Pennsylvanian Mazon Creek fossil site in northeastern Illinois, due to its unique morphology. It had a torpedo shaped body ending in a vertical tail fin, a rigid eyebar wider than the width of the body, and an elongate anterior proboscis. Tullimonstrum gregarium is also very common relative to other Mazon Creek fossil organisms, with the Field Museum of Natural History alone housing upwards of 3,000 Tully Monster fossils. As an abundant member of the Kankakee-Essex biota within the Mazon Creek ecosystem, Tullimonstrum was likely ecologically important, yet their unique morphology makes ecological interpretation difficult. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD), however, can illuminate the function of various features of the Tullimonstrum body plan by visualizing and quantifying their effect on hydrodynamics. For example, previous two-dimensional CFD simulations suggested that the proboscis could be a critical control feature used for turning and braking. Two-dimensional simulations cannot, however, account for more complex interactions between features like the eyebar and the tail fin complex. These more complex interactions require visualization in three dimensions. In this study, we generated new three-dimensional CFD simulations of Tullimonstrum in order to better visualize and quantify the hydrodynamics of this strange organism. Specifically, several three-dimensional reconstructions of Tullimonstrum gregarium with different proboscis positions were modeled in three-dimensional CFD simulations to investigate how proboscis position influences hydrodynamics. Additionally, three-dimensional simulations visualized flow around the eyebar, tail fin complex, and other body features, providing insight into body stability in a flow. Collectively, these simulation results help constrain the ecological niche of Tullimonstrum gregarium by providing insight on swimming speed and stability.

title: Morphometric Evidence for Megaflood-Boulder Control on River Morphology in the Eastern Himalaya
session_title: Mountain hydrology, glacial landscapes, and changing flow and sediment dynamics in mountain rivers (Posters)
authors: Santana, Gabriel G. [1], Huntington, Katharine W. [2], Duvall, Alison R. [3], Shobe, Charles M. [4], Montgomery, David R. [5], Lang, Karl A. [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(3) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(4) U.S. Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station, USFS Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fort Collins, CO, USA; Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(5) Earth and Space Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(6) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
abstract: Episodic disturbances over short timescales, including highly variable discharge events and coarse-sediment delivery, are increasingly recognized as capable of driving adjustments in channel steepness and width. Because these adjustments govern how efficiently rivers incise and transport load, such disturbances can shape the form and evolution of mountain landscapes long after the event itself. Prehistoric megafloods represent the extreme end-member of these disturbances. With peak discharges >10⁶ m³/s, they impose an abrupt forcing not only through high water discharge but through the deposition of large, rarely mobile boulder bars that may remain on the landscape for thousands of years. 1D channel evolution modeling, guided by hydraulic simulations and field observations of megaflood deposits, suggests these boulders drive persistent channel disequilibrium in active mountain landscapes: where they accumulate, they armor the bed and slow incision, and the channel steepens locally to offset the loss of erosional efficiency. Yet whether this predicted signature is expressed in real landscapes with a history of megaflood boulder deposition remains unknown. Here we use topographic analysis of the Yarlung–Siang River in the Eastern Himalaya, where some of the most extreme prehistoric glacial-lake-outburst floods on Earth are documented, to test the prediction directly. Across 44 mapped megaflood boulder deposits, we quantify normalized channel steepness and width within a multi-scale framework, comparing boulder-rich reaches against boulder-free reaches of the same trunk channel, and against basins that record no history of megaflooding, while accounting for lithologic and climatic controls. We further assess whether channel width absorbs part of the same signal, narrowing as boulder cover concentrates incision on the exposed bed, or widening as boulders deflect flow against the banks. Unlike the localized, stochastic supply of smaller-caliber material by hillslope processes, megaflood boulders are emplaced synchronously throughout the river corridor, where they persist for millennia, making them the extreme end-member of coarse-sediment delivery to mountain rivers. Characterizing their imprint on channel steepness and width tests how episodic disturbances leave a measurable, persistent signature on bedrock channel form.

title: Following Gadolinium Beyond the MRI: Distribution, Speciation, and Transport in New Mexico Surface Waters
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Ezzaldine, Ahmad [1], Kanaththage, Malsha Indeewari [2], Coyte, Rachel Marylee [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) Chemistry, New Mexico Inst. Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM,
abstract:
Every day, thousands of patients receive gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) to improve magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Although these compounds are designed to pass safely through the human body, they are not effectively removed during conventional wastewater treatment and are increasingly detected in rivers and streams worldwide. In arid regions such as New Mexico, where communities rely heavily on limited water resources and water reuse, understanding the environmental fate of this medical-derived gadolinium is becoming increasingly important.

This study investigates the distribution, chemical speciation, and physical partitioning of anthropogenic gadolinium in surface waters across New Mexico using ICP-MS and IC-ICP-MS. Concentrations vary substantially among sampling locations, with the highest concentrations occurring downstream of urban areas and wastewater discharges, while several sites show little or no detectable anthropogenic signal. Speciation analysis identifies ProHance as the dominant intact GBCA at most locations, demonstrating that this medical imaging agent can persist in aquatic systems decades after its introduction. Comparison of anthropogenic gadolinium measured by ICP-MS with intact GBCAs quantified by IC-ICP-MS shows close agreement at several sites but reveals additional non-intact anthropogenic gadolinium at others, indicating the presence of transformed Gd species or other anthropogenic Gd-bearing forms.

Filtration and acid digestion experiments further evaluate how gadolinium is transported in aquatic systems. Nearly identical concentrations in 0.45 µm and 0.22 µm filtrates indicate no significant Gd retention on coarse colloids/ fine particulates in this size fraction . In contrast, higher concentrations following acid digestion of unfiltered samples at selected sites reveal an additional particulate-associated fraction.

These findings improve our understanding of the environmental fate of medical-derived gadolinium and provide new insight into its transport through arid aquatic systems.

title: Relationship Between Heavy Metal Concentrations in Tap Water and Depression Prevalence Across U.S. Counties
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation (Posters)
authors: Das, Kripa [1], Brock, Ashley Primavera [2], Singh, Andrew Mahendra [3], Khandaker, Nazrul I. [4]
affiliations: (1) Queens High School for the Sciences, York College of the City University of New York, Jamaica, NY, USA; York College Geology Infrastructure Project, Jamaica, NY, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Sciences, Brooklyn College of the City University of New York, Brooklyn, NY, USA; York College Geology Infrastructure Project, Jamaica, NY, USA
(3) Earth and Physical Sciences, York College of the City University of New York, Jamaica, NY, USA; York College Geology Infrastructure Project, Jamaica, NY, USA
(4) York College of the City University of New York, Jamaica, NY, ; York College Geology Infrastructure Project, Jamaica, NY, USA
abstract:
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a prevalent global psychiatric disorder characterized by a persistent feeling of sadness, a loss of interest and/or pleasure, and a withdrawal from normal daily functioning such as work, school, and relationships. An estimated 220 to 332 million people, and around 5.7% of adults, are suffering from depression worldwide, making it a leading cause of disability. Multiple studies have established that depression may arise from both genetic and environmental factors, and heavy metal exposure, including cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), selenium (Se), and manganese (Mn), has been implicated in depression pathogenesis (Li et al., 2025). Building on that link, we hypothesized that counties with higher rates of heavy metal violations in public tap water would show higher crude depression prevalence.

In this study, we compare heavy metal contamination in tap water across urban U.S. counties, including Kings County, CA and Navajo County, AZ, with local depression rates. Utilizing data from the EPA's SDWIS Fed Data Warehouse, we calculated the rate of heavy metal related violations to drinking water regulations on public water systems (PWS) in each county per 100,000 residents, then compared these rates directly to each county's crude depression prevalence among adults 18 and older, as reported by the CDC.

We found only a weak positive association between heavy metal contaminants in tap water and depression prevalence, with an R² value of 0.048, indicating our hypothesis was not strongly supported. Still, these findings support continued investigation into environmental contributors to mental health. The weak association likely reflects the many other factors that shape depression risk, including genetic, psychological, and socioeconomic factors, as well as the fact that PWS violation data measure regulatory exceedances rather than actual individual exposure.

Future studies should incorporate individual exposure data, account for inconsistencies in PWS reporting across states, and use multivariable statistical models to better characterize the relationship between drinking water quality and depression.

title: Planning, Piloting, and Managing Multi-Institutional Geoscience Education Research: Lessons from a Project Across Four Universities
session_title: Current Advances in Geoscience Education Research (Posters)
authors: Czajka, Charles Doug [1], Ryker, Katherine [2], Viskupic, Karen M. [3], Teasdale, Rachel [4], Aird, Hannah M. [5]
affiliations: (1) Utah Valley University, Orem, UT,
(2) University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC,
(3) Boise State University, Boise, ID,
(4) CSU Chico, Chico, CA,
(5) CSU Chico, Chico, CA,
abstract:
Characterizing the broad impact of instructional interventions necessitates collecting student data across multiple institutions. We have been collaborating for over three years to collect data to quantify the relationship between reformed teaching and student learning. We developed four treatment lessons (Critical Minerals, Landslides, Mass Extinctions, Glacial Ice) and one control lesson (Mineral Properties), which are taught each semester at four US institutions in introductory geology courses. Each treatment lesson has been taught at three different categories of instructional reform (student-centered, transitional, teacher-centered) over multiple semesters. Student learning is measured with two paired sets of questions; one compares students' responses on exam questions with those at the start of the semester; the second compares clicker question responses at the start and end of the class period when the lesson was taught. Pre- and post-instruction surveys also ask students to rate their interest in the lesson topic. Post-instruction surveys additionally ask students to report perceptions of their learning.

The project design called for uniformity in course structure across institutions to minimize course and institution level variation and to streamline data collection. All instructors use similar topic schedules, number of exams, survey timings, and grading schemes. Challenges of managing the internal consistency of data collection at all institutions fall into three broad categories: course organization, instructional intervention and assessment, and data management and analysis. Course organization considerations include standardizing important aspects of the courses that might lead to variations in student data, accommodating changes in instructor availability, and accounting for low student attendance. Instructional interventions and assessments need sufficient time to be piloted and modified, as it can often take multiple semesters to finalize lessons and create reliable assessment instruments. Finally, data management quickly becomes challenging when collecting from multiple instructors, institutions, instruments, and learning management systems. Having a clear data management plan that includes strategies to clean, analyze, and accurately interpret data is critical to the project's success. We will share some of the challenges, accomplishments, and lessons learned from planning, collecting, and managing a large, multi-institutional data set using evidence and examples from our project.

title: Lakes, Rain, and Groundwater, Oh My! - Contributing Sources to the Hydrogeology of an Interdunal Wetland
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Dickey, Carter [1], Groenheide, Kate [2], DeVries-Zimmerman, Suzanne Jean [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Hope College, Holland, MI, USA
(2) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Hope College, Holland, MI, USA
(3) Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Hope College, Holland, MI, USA
abstract: We have studied the ecohydrology of a 1.25 ha interdunal wetland in a Lake Michigan coastal dune complex in Allegan County, Michigan, USA for 10 years. The wetland area is bounded by the Kalamazoo River to the north, Oxbow Lagoon, an offshoot of the Kalamazoo River to the east and south, and by Lake Michigan-Huron (MH) on the west. A sand layer ~22m thick underlies the wetlands between Lake MH and the river. The U.S. Drought monitor indicated abnormally dry conditions in spring 2025 transitioning to moderate drought, then returning to abnormally dry conditions until January 2026. Lake MH water levels were below the lakewide historic average from January 2025 until March 2026 when they rose above this average. In April 2025 we installed two Hobo data loggers in monitoring well 2 in the center of the wetlands. In June 2026 we installed two additional dataloggers in wells along a ~185m transect from the wetlands’ center (well 2) to the wetlands’ northeast corner (well 3) over a dune ridge to well 10 ~226 m west of Oxbow. Wells 2 and 3 are in areas dominantly vegetated with Cladium mariscoides while well 10 is vegetated with Ammophila breviligulata . Wells 2 and 3 show peakiness during rain events wherein water levels rise quickly due to temporary ponding during the event, then fall steeply afterwards. On days without rain, a strong diurnal pattern of falling groundwater levels during the day and rising levels during the night, indicating daytime evapotranspiration losses and nightly groundwater replenishment, is noted. Well 2 water levels also show a rise in elevation concurrent with that noted in the Lake MH 2025–2026 lake level curve, demonstrating the hydrologic connection between the aquifer underlying the wetlands and Lake MH. Well 10 water levels do not exhibit this same trend as they remain elevated for several days after the rain event before tapering off, mirroring the Kalamazoo River discharge curve. This suggests a strong river influence to this well’s hydrology as well as a hydrologic divide between wells 3 and 10. River water levels then show a diurnal fluctuation which is also noted in well 10’s water levels. Hence, our work indicates that the wetland’s hydrology is influenced by the interaction of multiple factors.

title: Coring Alpine Ice Patches in the Northern Rocky Mountains: Seven Millennia of Ice Lost in Eleven Years
session_title: Session in Honor of the Career of Rolfe Mandel especially in Geoarchaeology, Soils, and Geomorphology (Part II)
authors: Lee, Craig M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Sociology & Anthropology, Montana State University, Bozeman, MT, USA
abstract:
Perennial alpine ice patches are unique archives that can preserve archaeological and paleoecological materials for millennia, yet their internal stratigraphy and relationship to artifacts released by melting remain unclear. In 2013, we cored two transverse ice patches separated by 525 km, one in Glacier National Park and the other at archaeological site 48PA3147 in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Based on prior observations of melting ice-patch faces at more northern latitudes, we hypothesized that organic “lags”—concentrations of dung, windblown vegetation, insects, and sediment accreted on melt surfaces—would preserve an ordered record of warm intervals and provide a means of assessing archaeological potential in instances where persistent seasonal snow obscures an ice patch and its margins.

The 2013 effort used a sleeved or double-barreled “Prairie Dog” corer and recovered six stratified lags and one isolated organic concentration from the TL2 ice patch at 48PA3147. Macrobotanical analysis identified grasses, sedges, alpine forbs, conifer needles, charcoal, moss, lichen, rodent feces, feathers, and abundant insect chitin. Much of the assemblage represents local vegetation and forage deposited as dung by bighorn sheep and other animals; lower-elevation plants transported upslope through animal digestive tracts and windlofted charcoal from regional fires provide further paleoecological information.

The deepest dated specimen at TL2, a grasshopper or locust fragment recovered ca. 2.5 m below surface, yielded an age of 6130 ± 30 14C yr BP, demonstrating preservation of mid-Holocene biological material deep within the patch. One age inversion suggests that some lags may represent time-averaged melt horizons, but their succession nevertheless preserves a record of repeated warming and ablation.

Most soberingly, by the end of the 2024 field season, TL2—the first ice patch successfully cored in the Greater Yellowstone—had melted out entirely, eliminating an ice-borne stratigraphic archive that had persisted for roughly seven millennia.

Ice-patch coring and archaeology link stratigraphy, paleoecology, climate history, and Indigenous land use while allowing archaeological reconnaissance during high-snow years. In a session honoring Rolfe Mandel, this study highlights integrative geoarchaeology’s value for interpreting and documenting a rapidly changing Quaternary landscape.

title: Mesoproterozoic NW-SE Shortening under Greenschist-Facies to Brittle-Plastic conditions in the Skin Gulch Shear Zone and South Fork Antiform, Northern Colorado Front Range
session_title: Proterozoic Tectonics of Western Laurentia: New Perspectives on Crustal Growth, Orogenesis, Mineralization, and Intracontinental Reworking
authors: Singleton, John [1], Frawley, Dylan Liam [2], Broeder, Hunter Joseph [3], Malavarca, Samantha L. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,
(2) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,
(3) Colorado State Univ, Geosciences, Fort Collins, CO,
(4) Colorado State University, Longmont, CO,
abstract:
Basement rocks in the northern Colorado Front Range record widespread Paleoproterozoic (~1.78–1.65 Ga) metamorphism and penetrative deformation associated with the Yavapai orogeny, but Mesoproterozoic (~1.4 Ga) deformation related to the cryptic Picuris orogeny has been increasingly recognized across the region. We present new structural and thermochronological data that provide evidence for Mesoproterozoic deformation along the NE-trending Skin Gulch shear zone (SGSZ) and South Fork antiform in Poudre Canyon northwest of Fort Collins. Amphibolite-facies mylonitic and gneissic fabrics (~1.7 Ga?) in the SGSZ are locally overprinted by mylonites and brittle-plastic reverse faults that record NW-SE shortening. These structures are characterized by quartz subgrain rotation ± bulging dynamic recrystallization, feldspar fracturing, and/or narrow (<1 mm thick) sheared chlorite+white mica zones, consistent with dominantly greenschist-facies deformation conditions. Two brittle-plastic shear zone samples have well-defined quartz crystallographic preferred orientations with c-axis opening angles corresponding to ~300–400°C dislocation creep temperatures. Mylonitization locally involves the ~1.4 Ga Silver Plume Granite and pegmatites that are likely Mesoproterozoic. A sample of Paleoproterozoic biotite paragneiss from the SGSZ yielded an apatite U-Pb date of 1317 ± 33 Ma (Tera-Wasserburg lower intercept) and a biotite 40 Ar/ 39 Ar date of 1328 ± 5 Ma. These dates collectively record the timing of cooling across greenschist-facies conditions and approximate the age of mylonitization and brittle-plastic strain. The ~1.33–1.32 Ga timing of this NW-SE contraction is notably younger than Mesoproterozoic magmatism and deformation elsewhere in the Rocky Mountain region and suggests that the Picuris orogeny may have at least locally been a more protracted event than previously thought.

The South Fork antiform, ~2–3 km NW of the SGSZ, is a SE-vergent structure associated with a previously unmapped ~10 m-thick, NW-dipping reverse-sense shear zone on the overturned southeastern limb. Microstructures in the shear zone and weakly developed axial planar foliation in the antiform hinge are consistent with greenschist-facies deformation conditions. Gneissic foliation surfaces commonly preserve brittle-plastic flexural shear with lineations that parallel the antiform profile plane. As with the SGSZ, we interpret these structures to record Mesoproterozoic NW-SE shortening superposed on ~1.7 Ga amphibolite-facies fabrics. Mesoproterozoic deformation was likely more widespread across the northern Front Range than previously recognized, and future work will focus on constraining the timing of greenschist-facies and brittle-plastic deformation in the region.
