abstract:
The Upper Triassic Chinle Formation records a time of major biotic turnover in terrestrial ecosystems, including the origins of dinosaurs (Langer et al., 2013). The Chinle Formation outcrops span the southwestern United States, representing a vast fluvial system deposited near the paleo-equator of central Pangaea (Kent & Tauxe, 2005). The Petrified Forest Member in the Chama Basin of northern New Mexico contains multiple rich and diverse fossil localities (e.g. Snyder, Eucoelophysis , Hayden, and Canjilon Quarries), which have influenced early dinosaur evolution.

Paleontologists identified the Snyder Quarry for further study because it yields an abundance of well-preserved fossils, including associated and articulated dinosaur skeletons. The site is interpreted as a mass death assemblage of terrestrial vertebrates from a paleo-wildfire. Biostratigraphy indicates a Norian (Revueltian) age for the Snyder Quarry. Currently, the only published radiometric age in the Chama Basin comes from the Hayden Quarry, where a youngest single zircon grain was dated to be 211.9 ± 0.7 Ma (Irmis et al., 2011). The Hayden Quarry is hypothesized to be stratigraphically lower than the Snyder Quarry, but outcrop discontinuity and lateral facies change complicate both local and regional lithostratigraphic correlations. More precise U-Pb age constraints are required to integrate these paleontological discoveries into the global fossil record.

Our study utilizes U-Pb geochronology on samples from Upper Triassic Petrified Forest Member exposures at the Snyder Quarry. Interbedded sandstones and mudstones from four fossiliferous horizons were sampled for detrital zircon analysis. Initial LA-ICPMS measurements will identify the youngest zircon population to be further analyzed by high precision ID-TIMS. The resulting maximum depositional ages will provide precise constraints for the Upper Triassic strata and fossils, which currently rely on biostratigraphy for temporal and stratigraphic resolution. Correlations can then be drawn within the Chama Basin and across the broader Chinle Formation stratigraphic record.

abstract: While glaciers leave a mark on mountain landscapes, the importance of glacial erosion in mountains at a global scale remains insufficiently constrained despite over a century of research aimed at quantifying the rates and magnitudes of such erosion. Measuring rates of landscape change across the Quaternary in repeatedly glaciated mountain landscapes requires the ability to accurately partition the relative role of glacial versus fluvial processes in forming relief; however, the modification of landforms by surface erosion hinders quantification of process rates over the last few million years. This study presents 32 paired 26 Al and 10 Be cosmogenic nuclide burial ages from allochthonous, quartz-bearing sediment deposited within a paleophreatic karst system in the northern Carpathians. These data quantify Pliocene-to-present timing of valley incision and karst system reactivation, as well as erosion rates over time. Post-burial, muon production-correction yields 24 fully resolved ages, six minimum ages, and two unresolvable ages. Burial ages are interpreted to document the tempo of valley incision via phreatic passage formation and reveal that ~80% of current valley relief (~700 m) had developed by approximately 1.6 Ma. Paleoerosion rates derived from this dataset suggest little change in the processes generating sediment washed into the karst networks since the Pliocene. These results suggest that river incision dominated relief creation in Carpathian valleys that bear the imprint of glaciation. Our findings suggest the importance of investigating other mid-latitude mountainous regions worldwide to determine if they have similar erosion and topographic histories.

title: Influence of the Carnian Pluvial Episode on the Popo Agie Formation.
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part I)
authors: Lovelace, David M [1], Kufner, Aaron M [2]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, UW-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(2) Geoscience, UW-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
abstract:
Late Triassic terrestrial strata from the western USA preserve a relatively continuous record. High-resolution radioisotopic dates have constrained the lowermost Chinle Formation to an age no older than the earliest Norian (ca. 225––227 Ma). Although the Dockum Group does not have radioisotopic age constraints, biostratigraphic correlations have historically demonstrated that the lowermost Dockum Group pre-dates the oldest Chinle Formation strata (e.g., presence of non-leptosuchomorph phytosaurs), and is likely correlative (in part) to the Popo Agie Formation, Chugwater Group. Recent work has presented maximum depositional ages for the top and bottom of the upper Popo Agie (ca. 227 Ma and 229 Ma, respectively). Age-depth models calibrated to upper Popo Agie depositional rates suggest the base of the Popo Agie is around 231–232 Ma. Some models extend as early as 236 Ma, but without a clear hiatus this seems less likely.

The base of the Popo Agie (lower carbonate unit) is a microconglomerate largely composed of recycled soil carbonate nodules; bone clasts are not uncommon. Recent discoveries of vertebrate fossils in the lower Popo Agie suggest that these units are much more fossiliferous than previously supposed. Taken together, the sedimentology and vertebrate fauna of the lower Popo Agie displays a sharp environmental contrast to the underlying Jelm Formation.

There is a notable shift from the paleo-aridisol/inceptisol dominated deposits of the upper Jelm Formation, which also contain small estivating amphibians specialized to deal with seasonal hyperaridity (i.e., Ninumbeehan ), to the much higher energy conglomerate-bearing fluvial deposits containing numerous terrestrial archosaur taxa, and the overlying fluviolacustrine deposits dominated by vertic paleosols and stereospondyl amphibians. The shift from an environment with strong seasonal aridity to a sub-humid environment with enough through flowing water to deposit the highest energy interval in the Chugwater Group suggests a significant increase in annual precipitation/accomodation. Although there is currently a dearth of quantitative evidence, both modeled temporal constraints and depositional environments are consistent with the effects of the Carnian Pluvial Episode (ca. 234–232 Ma), a period with globally increased precipitation and humidity. We hypothesize that the upper Jelm Formation may represent earliest Carnian deposition, while initial Popo Agie Formation deposition corresponds to the CPE, the formation preserves mid to late Carnian deposition at least partially overlapping with the lowest Dockum Group.

title: Tsunami-lain Grainstone Beds in a Shallow, Tranquil, Muddy Epeiric Sea: The Selkirk Member of the Red River Formation (Upper Ordovician), Williston Basin of Southern Manitoba, Canada
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology
authors: Pratt, Brian R. [1], Sproat, Colin D. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, SK, Canada
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, SK, Canada
abstract: Dolomitic limestones of the Selkirk Member of the Red River Formation (Katian, Upper Ordovician) of southern Manitoba were deposited in the shallow, equatorial, epeiric Williston Basin which was contiguous with a vast epicontinental sea that covered a large part of Laurentia. The Selkirk consists of thoroughly bioturbated, fossiliferous and bioclastic wackestone and packstone deposited within the photic zone. Northeast of Winnipeg, the member is 43 m thick and the lower part is quarried for Tyndall Stone because of its striking fabric (‘tapestry’) due to selective dolomitization related to Planolites and Palaeophycus burrows. Macrofossils include a diverse fauna of unusually large receptaculitids, stromatoporoids, gastropods, nautiloids, tabulate corals, solitary and colonial rugose corals, plus rare trilobites and brachiopods. Bioclasts include abundant, variably bioeroded crinoid ossicles, along with calcareous green algae and mollusc and coral fragments. The massive muddy limestone is punctuated by lenticular beds consisting of bioclastic and intraclastic grainstone to rudstone locally exhibiting variably distinct planar and unidirectional cross-lamination and crude normal grading. Dislodged shells and skeletons are commonly incorporated. These beds are ~0.5–5 m wide and up to 10 cm thick, have erosional bases, and are circular, elliptical, or lobate in plan view. Some beds appear concentrated along certain horizons whereas others are not. Paleocurrent direction cannot be determined precisely with the mostly two-dimensional quarry outcrop, but it seems to have been broadly towards the present-day north. Shallow subsurface cores indicate that grainstone beds are present up to about ~50 km to the southwest, west, and northwest, but are absent in the northern outcrops hundreds of kilometers away. They are also absent in cores in the deep subsurface of southern Saskatchewan. Like many comparable, high-energy beds punctuating low-energy facies, they have been reflexively assumed to be tempestites. However, evidence for storm wave-induced oscillatory currents is absent. Instead, the sedimentary attributes may be attributed plausibly to tsunamis triggered by movement on basement faults, those inferred in the central part of the basin as well as cryptic local structures. This interpretation suggests that other high-energy event beds in ostensibly tranquil epeiric sea deposits may not be due only to storms, thereby challenging interpretations of paleoclimate, bathymetry, and syndepositional tectonic activity.

title: Role of Reactive Fracture Processes for Fault Fluid Flow Behavior
session_title: Fault zones and fluid flow, from outcrops to algorithms.
authors: Eichhubl, Peter [1]
affiliations: (1) Bureau of Econonic Geology, Jackson School of Geosciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
The role of faults in governing basin- to crustal-scale fluid flow is primarily controlled by the fault architecture which describes the spatial arrangement of the structural elements of the fault, and by the fluid properties and hydrodynamic boundary conditions. It is generally recognized that the structural and diagenetic properties of the fault damage zone largely control flow along faults. Interactions among chemical water-rock interactions and fracture processes in fault damage zones may thus be essential to understand fault-controlled fluid flow with relevance to the migration of mineralizing brines, noble gases, natural hydrogen, hydrocarbons, and for underground storage of CO 2 , H 2gas , and wastewater.

Building on field and laboratory studies investigating the effects of chemical environment on fracture mechanical properties, we evaluate the interplay between chemical reactions and fracture processes on fault flow properties for a variety of subsurface systems. Fracture growth is controlled by the magnitude of the loading stress and by the propagation velocity under subcritical loading conditions with the latter quantified by the fracture growth index. Critical fracture growth under rapid loading is expected for coseismic fault slip events. Provided coseismic stress changes are quasistatic, they would favor growth of single fractures and thus result in simple fracture geometries whereas dynamic loading tends to result in fragmentation. Subcritical fracture growth can result in complex fracture geometries, expected for stable fault slip or during postseismic slip.

Chemically reactive fluid-rock systems can both impede and enhance fracture growth depending on mineral and fluid composition. Fault-related hostrock alteration can result in both fault strengthening (e.g. silicification) and weakening (argillitization) depending on hostrock lithology and aqueous fluid composition affecting damage zone fracture architecture and width. In two- or multiphase fluid systems, lower water saturation and thus reduced water-rock interaction generally increase fracture toughness and subcritical index indicating higher resistance for fracture growth but also higher subcritical fracture propagation rate. The opposite is observed in halite which we attribute to reduced healing processes under dry gas-saturated conditions. These observations indicate that fracture growth processes and damage zone evolution are generally controlled by a competition between dissolution and associated weakening reactions, and precipitation and associated strengthening reactions. This competition is specific to the rock and fluid composition and stress loading conditions and could vary across the seismic cycle.

title: Neoacadian Regional Metamorphism, Magmatism, and Syncollisional Extension in the Eastern Blue Ridge of Northwestern North Carolina
session_title: From Rodinia to Pangea- Evolution of the Appalachian-Caledonides Orogen (Part II)
authors: Hull, Sarah W. [1], Stewart, Kevin G. [2], Strickland, Anna H. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA; Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA
(2) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(3) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
abstract: The southern Appalachian Blue Ridge records a complex history of deformation associated with three major Paleozoic orogenic events. Yet, the timing and conditions of Neoacadian deformation are not well constrained in this region. Our recent mapping and age estimates north of the Grandfather Mountain window in northwestern North Carolina reveal a significant Neoacadian signature. Here we identified a major extensional shear zone, comprising the Idlewild and Grassy Creek faults, two top-to-the-south, oblique-normal faults. Dynamic recrystallization of quartz and feldspar within the shear zone indicates faulting occurred under amphibolite-facies conditions (~500-600°C). Thermo-geochronology and thermobarometry were used to constrain the timing and conditions of metamorphism in the region surrounding the shear zone. Temperature estimates across the region are consistent at ~600°C. A pressure difference was calculated across the shear zone with GBPQ geobarometry revealing ~1.0 GPa in the footwall and Si-in-muscovite geobarometry revealing ~0.36-0.72 GPa in the garnet-absent hanging wall, consistent with major extensional displacement. Hornblende 40 Ar/ 39 Ar thermochronology from within the shear zone provides a minimum possible age of extension at ~352 Ma. This age corresponds with the hornblende 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages from the footwall, ranging from ~346 Ma to ~359 Ma. Similarly, zircon U-Pb geochronology of a foliated granite within the hanging wall yields a crystallization age of ~352 Ma, providing a maximum possible age of the event responsible for the development of foliation within the granite. The foliation within the granite is subparallel to the well-developed regional foliation, including the foliation within the shear zone. This indicates that shearing may have occurred during the foliation-forming event associated with the deformation of the granite. Given the convergence of geo- and thermochronological data around an age of ~352 Ma, we suggest that this age represents a distinct event in the history of the Eastern Blue Ridge, marked by widespread deformation, syncollisional extension, and magmatism during the Neoacadian orogeny. This extension may have been driven by gravitational collapse following crustal overthickening during late Paleozoic mountain building, providing important structural evidence for the Neoacadian orogeny in the Eastern Blue Ridge.

title: The International Commission on Stratigraphy’s Subcommission for Timescale Calibration and Plans for GTS2030
session_title: ‘GTS2030’ – Toward an Open Science Geologic Time Scale
authors: Schmitz, Mark D. [1], Cramer, Bradley Douglas [2], Da Silva, Anne-Christine [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
(3) Sedimentary Petrology Laboratory, Liège University, Liège, Belgium
abstract:
The Subcommission on Timescale Calibration (STC) is the newest subcommission of the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS), and was founded to foster the growing movement of geoscientists who work at the intersection of time and stratigraphy, and promote their integration with the traditional stratigraphic communities of the ICS. The charge of the STC includes to advise and counsel existing ICS Subcommissions on geochronological issues, to delineate best practices and the role of inter-laboratory calibrations to chronostratigraphic and timescale problems, and to provide a venue for increasing collaboration between chronostratigraphic and geochronologic research. The STC has been tasked with coordinating the next Geologic Time Scale 2030 compilation as an ICS production.

The STC is actively recruiting Corresponding Members and pursuing the formation of Task Groups organized around the four disciplinary components that are melded to create a numerically calibrated Geologic Time Scale: Integrated Stratigraphy, Astrochronology, Radioisotope Geochronology, and Age Modeling. The recent GSA Penrose Conference “Defining the Future of Timescale Calibration” in Iowa City, Iowa hosted 85 scientists from 17 countries to launch this work. This first major in-person meeting of the STC allowed participants to coalesce into proto-Task Groups and collaboratively develop a shared vision of their contributions to GTS2030, reflecting on and responding to a set of prompts including the guiding science, data and metadata deliverables, connections and communications with other ICS Subcommissions, and open science alignment for the GTS. The STC Corresponding Membership and Task Groups will be formalized and connections to the time period-focused Subcommissions sought in the coming months, building upon the momentum generated at the Penrose and STRATI 2026.

The STC has set an aggressive timeline for coproduction of the GTS2030 with the other Subcommissions of the ICS. While the STC will coalesce the talent needed for updating the methodological chapters, the time period-focused Subcommissions will be responsible the content of the period-focused chapters of the GTS2030. The success of GTS2030 will depend upon the mechanisms we develop for inter-Subcommission collaboration and coordination. We invite broad community engagement with the STC Task Groups to establish community data standards for time scale calibration and aggregate new data and algorithms that can build an open science GTS2030 framework.

title: Stratigraphic and Depositional Distribution of Vertebrate Fossils in the Morrison Formation of Southeast Wyoming
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Mautz, Blake Westen [1], Slattery , Josh [2], Southwell, Beth [3], Connely, Melissa [4]
affiliations: (1) Laramie, Wyoming, USA
(2) Cheyanne, Wyoming, USA
(3) Laramie, Wyoming, USA
(4) Laramie, Wyoming, USA
abstract:
The Morrison Formation of southeast Wyoming preserves a diverse vertebrate assemblage that provides important insights into Late Jurassic terrestrial ecosystems. Although this region has yielded abundant vertebrate fossils since the 1870s, the stratigraphic and depositional distribution of Morrison faunas remains poorly synthesized. To address this gap, we quantified the taxonomic composition and stratigraphic distribution of vertebrate ichno- and body fossils within the newly designated Lake Como, Talking Rocks, and Indian Fort members of the Morrison Formation to evaluate whether differences in faunal composition corresponded to stratigraphic position, depositional environment, and preservational conditions.

Preliminary results reveal substantial changes in preservation patterns and vertebrate faunal composition throughout the Morrison Formation succession. Vertebrate ichnofossils, represented primarily by sauropod and theropod tracks, are concentrated within the basal limestone of the Lake Como Member, where shallow lakes and ponds provided stable substrates favorable for track preservation. Vertebrate body fossils occur in both macro- and microbone beds. Macrobone beds are distributed throughout the Morrison Formation, whereas microbone beds are comparatively rare and occur primarily near the top of the Talking Rocks Member and in the overlying Indian Fort Member. Macrobone beds are dominated by large-bodied dinosaurs, whereas microbone beds preserve a more taxonomically diverse assemblage of small-bodied vertebrates, including fish, reptiles, dinosaurs, and mammals. Dinosaur assemblages also changed through time, shifting from large-bodied, sauropod-dominated faunas in the lower Morrison Formation to communities with greater representation of small-bodied ornithischians, particularly Nanosaurus , within the upper Morrison Formation. Theropod taxa, including Allosaurus , megalosaurids, and Ceratosaurus , likewise become more common higher in the section. Together, these stratigraphic changes in bone-bed composition and dinosaur community structure correspond to the transition from well-drained floodplains in the lower Morrison Formation to increasingly wet, fluvial- and wetland-dominated environments in the upper Morrison Formation. Overall, these preliminary results indicate that environmental conditions and taphonomic processes played important roles in shaping the composition and preservation of vertebrate assemblages throughout the Morrison Formation in southeast Wyoming.

title: A New Benchmark in Mars Exploration: 1000 meters of Elevation Gain and Lithostratigraphic Measurement by the Curiosity Rover, Gale Crater, Mars
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Seeger, Christina [1], Edgar, Lauren A. [2], Fedo, Chris [3], Grotzinger, John P. [4], Mondro, Claire A. [5], Vasavada, Ashwin [6]
affiliations: (1) Rice University, Houston, TX,
(2) Johnson Space Center, Houston, TX,
(3) Univ of Tennessee, Knoxville, Knoxville, TN,
(4) California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA,
(5) Planetary Science Institute, Knoxville, TN,
(6) NASA JPL, Pasadena, CA,
abstract: In the brief history of Mars rover exploration, driven distance represents a measure of engineering and, more indirectly, science success. In 2026, the Curiosity rover drove past an elevation 1000m above its landing site, defining a new benchmark in mission success. The engineering component of that milestone was mostly captured as the integrated drive distance, punctuated by elevation-specific challenges related to navigating ridges and ledges. The science value of the traverse is to have measured ~1000m of stratigraphic section (not accounting for dip) that records ~100,000 to 100 million years of Mars’ environmental history between 3.6 – 3.2Ga. A cumulative stratigraphic column was created through analysis of rover image data to define facies based on textures, grain size, rounding, and bed thicknesses, compiled principally for rocks investigated in the rover drive direction. Annually, a small evaluation team does a first pass analysis, which is then reviewed by a larger working group with specialization in sedimentary geology, and then reviewed by the entire science team; this process was used for the past decade to create and update a lithostratigraphic log. The log currently recognizes 3 groups, 7 formations, and 18 members that represent 16 fluvial, deltaic, lacustrine, and eolian depositional facies including variable diagenetic overprints expressed by diverse compositional and textural attributes. A major unconformity between the Mt. Sharp and Siccar Point groups represents a cycle of exhumation, erosion, and subsequent deposition. The ~1km-thick column includes ~36km of lateral traverse which includes a ~N-S change from fluvial to deltaic to lacustrine facies due to erosion of the southern crater wall and northward progradation of clastic wedges into the lacustrine basin; a similar vertical change in facies is recorded across a thickness of 100s of meters, culminating in eolian facies that represents progressive drying of the Gale crater sedimentary basin. Merging compositional data from the rover’s instrument suite to integrate chemostratigraphic trends into the log reveals vertical and lateral variations associated with multiple episodes of diagenesis. These too are expressed vertically as well as laterally; for example, in traversing up and over the Vera Rubin ridge it was discovered that despite consistent lithostratigraphic facies there was a lateral change from hematite-rich/clay-poor/carbonate-absent to hematite-poor/clay-rich/carbonate-present compositions indicating a strong diagenetic overprint.

title: Evaluating Shallow-Water Redox Conditions Across the SPICE at Shingle Pass, Eastern Nevada
session_title: Reading between the layers with Stratigraphic Paleobiology: Innovations in applying stratigraphic principles to the fossil record (Posters)
authors: Savage, Ava [1], Irizarry, Kayla [2], Lau, Kimberly [3], Patzkowsky, Mark [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA
(2) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA
(3) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA
(4) Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA
abstract:
During the Cambrian, repeated trilobite extinction events disproportionately affected shallow-water fauna. One of these events, the End-Marjuman extinction event, roughly coincides with the Steptoean Positive Carbon Isotope Excursion (SPICE), a globally recognized 4-6 ‰ positive carbon isotope excursion near the base of the Paibian Stage. Positive carbon isotope excursions are important because they can record major disturbances to the global carbon cycle, reflecting enhanced burial of isotopically light organic carbon that can also alter the dissolved oxygen levels in the ocean. Global redox proxy records suggest intensified anoxia during SPICE, raising the possibility that oxygen stress contributed to extinction and ecological restructuring in shallow-marine habitats. However, the extent to which redox changes impacted shallow shelf environments remains poorly constrained.

This study evaluates whether cerium anomalies (Ce/Ce*) in carbonate rocks at Shingle Pass, eastern Nevada, record a shift from relatively oxic shallow-water conditions before the SPICE to more anoxic conditions during the event. Carbonate samples were collected at 2 to 4 m stratigraphic intervals through Cambrian strata for geochemical and petrographic analysis. Carbon isotopes were analyzed to identify the SPICE in the measured section. Cerium anomalies (Ce/Ce*) are used as a carbonate-based proxy for local redox conditions. Facies observations help to distinguish true redox shifts from shifts driven purely by changes in depositional environment.

Preliminary Ce/Ce* data at Shingle Pass record a shift to more anoxic conditions concurrently with the SPICE during an interval of local shallowing. This shift in redox conditions may reflect real oceanographic conditions associated with the SPICE, or they may reflect a change in the source of the Ce/Ce* related to an environmental shift or diagenesis. Petrographic characterization of thin sections and major element analysis will be used to constrain the source of the Ce/Ce* signal. These results will help test whether expanded shallow-water anoxia contributed to Cambrian trilobite turnover in the Eastern Nevada region.

title: A Phase Change Material Encapsulated Clay Aggregate Additive for Passive Anti-Icing of Pavement Infrastructure (HELIX)

authors: George, Esther [1], Cho, Evangeline [2], Patel, Devi [3], Kiritharan, Annchja [4], Singh, Andrew [5], Khandaker, Nazrul I. [6], Dhar, Ratan Kumar [7]
affiliations: (1) Irwin Altman Middle School 172, Floral Park, NY, USA
(2) Irwin Altman Middle School 172, Floral Park, NY, USA

(5) Earth and Physical Sciences, York College of the City University of New York, Jamaica, NY, ; York College Geology Infrastructure Project, Jamaica, NY, USA
(6) Earth and Physical Sciences, York College of the City University of New York, Jamaica, NY, ; York College Geology Infrastructure Project, Jamaica, NY, USA

abstract:
Current winter road maintenance relies on chemical salts and heavy snowplows that damage infrastructure and vehicles. A Utah State University study estimates this combined corrosion and vehicle damage at $16 to $19 billion annually in the United States (Shi et al.). This project introduces HELIX (Hybrid Encapsulated Latent-heat Infrastructure X-shell), a concrete and asphalt additive that acts like a solar-powered heater to prevent ice from forming on critical transit surfaces. At its core, the system transforms porous organic expanded clay pebbles by dehydrating them at 350°F and infusing them with a specialized Soy-Phase Change Material (PCM) blended with 5% ultrathin graphite flakes, which conduct heat through the material. To guard against failure, 2% to 5% Calcium Magnesium Acetate (CMA) is suspended within the matrix as a backup deicer in case the outer shell is damaged. Each infused aggregate is protected inside a triple layer shell consisting of a water activated Bentonite clay self healing layer, a Portland cement and Silica Sol mineral armor, and an epoxy resin moisture barrier.

Laboratory tests showed that this bio based thermal battery system can be mixed into standard infrastructure mixtures. During testing, the HELIX pavement kept its surface temperature above freezing, between 45°F and 52°F, even in extreme freezing conditions. This performance is consistent with the built in 1/4 inch chopped carbon fibers, added at 0.5% by weight, helping conduct stored heat toward the surface, though isolating that specific effect would require testing with and without the fibers.

Future manufacturing optimizations will use fast drying coatings and vibration techniques to maximize PCM compaction. Preliminary experimental data suggest this could boost energy storage by roughly 10 to 15%, though this has not yet been confirmed at full scale. By offering an alternative to traditional road salt, HELIX offers a path toward self warming infrastructure. While initially targeted for local municipal roads, this scalable technology is designed for broader application across high volume public highways and commercial airport runways, with the potential to reduce winter transit delays and reduce reliance on chloride based deicing salts.

authors: Malone, John "Jack" Ethan [1], Clark, Ryan J. [2], Walenceus, Rachel S. [3], Kerr, Phillip James [4]
affiliations: (1) Iowa Geological Survey, Iowa City, Iowa, USA; School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA

abstract: The Holy Cross and New Vienna 7.5’ quadrangles are a continuation of a multi-year initiative by the Iowa Geological Survey under the USGS STATEMAP program to update the bedrock geology of Dubuque County, which is situated on the boundary between the East-Central Drift Plain and the Paleozoic Plateau landform regions. Both landform regions are characterized by thin (<50 feet) glacial and eolian deposits draped over bedrock, and thicker (<200 feet) valley units consisting of Holocene age terraces. The bedrock of the Holy Cross and New Vienna quadrangles are dominated by strata of the Silurian and Ordovician System. The 2010 statewide bedrock map (1:500,000 scale) does not differentiate strata of the Silurian succession and lumps the Hopkinton, Blanding, Tete des Morts, and Mosalem formations. Delineation and division of these Silurian units was accomplished by careful study of well chip samples, core, and outcrop. Geologic reconnaissance of outcrops and quarries within the mapping area was conducted during field activities, and additional subsurface information was derived from the analysis of over ~170 borehole records. Each record was checked for locational accuracy using drillers logs, historic plat books, county accessor information, and direct communication with landowners. The depth to the surficial-bedrock contact was determined for each well and assigned an elevation value by subtracting it from the surface digital elevation model (DEM). Additional information was gained from an assessment of the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) County Soil Survey by identifying soil series that indicate shallow bedrock. A bedrock elevation map was created by manual digitization of elevation contours (drawn at a 25-foot contour interval) using Esri ArcGIS Pro 3.4 software, and a bedrock elevation raster was then generated using interpolations of the bedrock surface. A Quaternary thickness map was created by subtracting the bedrock elevation raster values from the surficial DEM raster. The resulting surface was rounded to the nearest integer and contours were generated from this result and then smoothed. A single rock core was drilled to assess local stratigraphic variability not captured in well cuttings, to verify thicknesses of select map units, and establish future subdivisions of mappable units in Dubuque County.

title: Computational Modeling of Biogenic Hydrogen Production in Geological Carbon Storage Sites
session_title: Advances in Understanding and Predicting the Geochemical and Microbiological Conversion and Transport of Hydrogen in Deep Geological Repositories
authors: Vilcaez, Javier [1]
affiliations: (1) Boone Pickens School of Geology, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, USA
abstract: On average, two-thirds of the oil remains in reservoirs after primary and secondary recovery operations, representing a vast resource that could potentially be converted as CH₄ and/or H₂. In an initial modeling and simulation effort, we showed that biogenic conversion of CO₂ to CH₄ using H₂ produced from the degradation of oil hydrocarbons is possible in carbonate reservoirs due to the pH-buffering effect of carbonate mineral dissolution. In a more recent effort, we used CO2Bio, the TOUGHREACT module we developed to simulate geological carbon storage (GCS) in depleted oil reservoirs under biotic conditions, to assess the field-scale feasibility of biogenic H₂ production in a sandstone reservoir (the Morrow B sandstone reservoir in the Farnsworth Field Unit). The formulated model accounts for water-rock interactions, the solubility of oil into formation water, and the mutual solubility of CO₂, CH₄, H₂, H₂S, and brine. The kinetic model in CO2Bio captures the dynamics of microbial growth of H₂-producing (fermenters) and H₂-consuming (methanogens and sulfate-reducing bacteria, SRB) microbial species as a function of the pH that results from CO₂ dissolution into formation water. Kinetic parameters, including the specific growth rate and half-saturation constant for each microbial reaction, were estimated by fitting the model to experimental data obtained from batch reaction experiments conducted under GCS conditions. This presentation addresses key knowledge gaps by incorporating new experimental chemical and microbiological data and extending the modeling framework to account for oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), as well as initial microbial diversity and concentration, thereby improving the predictions of biogenic H₂ production on a case-by-case basis.

title: Characterizing Well Responses in the Karstic and Structurally Complex Upper Trinity Aquifer in South-Central Texas, USA
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Bertetti, F. Paul [1], Mendiondo, Karen [2], Romero, Brennan [3], Nunu, Rebecca [4], Schmidt, Logan [5]
affiliations: (1) Edwards Aquifer Authority, San Antonio, TX, USA
(2) Edwards Aquifer Authority, San Antonio, Texas, USA
(3) Edwards Aquifer Authority, San Antonio, TX, USA
(4) Edwards Aquifer Authority, San Antonio, TX, USA
(5) Edwards Aquifer Authority, San Antonio, TX, USA
abstract:
The hydrogeologic connections between groundwater wells and surface waters are known to be complex and uncertain in karst systems due to the fast flow characteristics and episodic nature of recharge associated with solution enhanced features and conduits. These karst characteristics affect inter-aquifer hydraulic communication, aquifer recharge, and an aquifer’s potential vulnerability to water quality degradation. The Edwards and Upper Trinity aquifers are extremely important water resources in South-Central Texas and supply drinking water needs to more than 2.5 million people. The semi-arid region faces continuous development, and the vulnerability of the aquifers to treated wastewater discharges is a concern for many. The Edwards Aquifer Authority has established a field research site adjacent to Cibolo Creek in the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone to study various components of the water balance of the two aquifers. Five groundwater wells are located on the site, four of which are completed in the Upper Trinity Aquifer.

The region of the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone and its associated contacts with the hydrogeologic units of the Upper Trinity Aquifer is structurally complex with multiple faults of varying offsets creating barriers and paths for flow. Recent rain events have recharged both aquifers, as evidenced by water level increases in all four Upper Trinity wells. Although these wells are completed in the same hydrogeologic unit and are located within a 600-m radius, two of the wells show rapid increases in water levels of more than 20 m within 36 hours during large recharge events, while the other two show more modest increases on the order of 3 to 12 m over much longer periods, 3 to 23 days. Moreover, the largest responses are in wells located farther from the creek. We present comparisons of the well responses along with geochemical evidence that links the water level changes to surface water input. The particular location and type of karst features or outcrops that control the responses are still unknown, but the rapid response and verifiable connection to surface water emphasizes that greater distance from streams and depth of wells are not protections from exposure of wells to contamination in this region.

title: Surveying Lava Tubes with Lidar: Analogs for Lunar Pits
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Garry, William Brent [1]
affiliations: (1) NASA Goddard Spaceflight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA
abstract: The morphology and preserved flow textures in lava tubes provide information about their formation, but the challenge is producing a map that captures the full three-dimensional morphology. While two-dimensional maps provide relevant details about the shape, textures, and dimensions, they are also static and limited by scale. Lidar surveys produce detailed three-dimensional models that show the morphology of the tube at the meter-scale and texture details at the centimeter-scale. Point cloud models of lava tubes created from lidar surveys provide continuous x,y,z coordinates of all areas in the tube to analyze the changes in morphology, the spatial relationship with the surface terrain, and the distribution of flow textures and hazards. We have conducted surveys of lava tubes in multiple volcanic terrains. We will show morphologic maps of several lava tubes including, Lava River Cave (Flagstaff, Arizona), Indian and Arco Tunnel, plus Bear Trap Cave (Craters of the Moon National Monument, Idaho), and Nāhuku lava tube (Hawai'i). Each lava tube provides a unique case study for understanding their formation in different flow fields and as analogs for lunar pits and lava tubes on the Moon. On the Moon, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spacecraft has imaged and characterized mare pits (voids) that could be connected to lava tube caves. It is unclear from orbital imagery what geologic features could be observed, discovered, or encountered inside an accessible tube on the Moon. Therefore, exploration and characterization of terrestrial lava tube caves provide insight into the potential complex morphology, flow textures, and hazards that may be encountered inside lunar lava tubes. This study will showcase the utility of using lidar to map terrestrial lava tubes and how they can serve as analogs for lava tubes and pits on the Moon.

title: Temperature-Driven Changes in Permafrost Thaw and Groundwater Chemistry at Three Alaskan NEON Aquatic Sites
session_title: Cold-Regions Hydrology and Hydrogeology (Posters)
authors: Catolico, Nora [1], Monroe, Josh [2]
affiliations: (1) National Ecological Observatory Network, Battelle, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) National Ecological Observatory Network, Battelle, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
The National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) is a continental-scale observatory that provides long-term, standardized, open-access data for understanding ecosystem change. NEON includes 81 terrestrial and freshwater field sites across 20 ecoclimatic domains, including tundra and taiga sites, where continuous sensor measurements are paired with physical, organismal, and biogeochemical observations.

Arctic and subarctic ecosystems are being disproportionately affected by temperature changes, with warming linked to permafrost degradation, altered hydrology, and changes in carbon and nutrient cycling. Here, we examine relationships between air temperature and seasonal thaw depth at three Alaskan NEON aquatic sites: Toolik Lake, Oksrukuyik Creek, and Caribou Creek. Since 2018, maximum summer air temperature has increased by 2–3 °C at these sites (DP1.00003.001), accompanied by increases in maximum thaw depths of up to 20 cm (DP1.20099.001). Over the same period, groundwater chemistry data (DP1.20092.001) indicates increases in NH 4 -N, TDS, TDN, TOC, and SO 4 , potentially reflecting greater subsurface connectivity, increased groundwater influence, and enhanced mineral weathering. These results highlight the value of NEON observations for investigating the influence of temperature changes on permafrost-influenced hydrologic systems. Additional collocated NEON data products, such as surface water chemistry, continuous discharge, and geomorphology maps, are available for further analysis of hydrologic connections within these systems.

title: Basaltic Detectives: Determining Source Regions and Paleodrainage Across the Southern High Plains, North America by Petrographic Analysis of Ogallala Basalt Cobbles
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Harr, Margaret Claire [1], Eichler, Carla M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Life, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA
(2) Department of Life, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA
abstract:
Petrographic analysis of basaltic samples collected from the Miocene Ogallala Formation at Caprock Canyons, Janes Quarry, and Southeastern Colorado shows data that lead to inferences of these samples’ source regions and transport histories.

Several different populations have been observed via petrographic analysis to be in various conditions of weathering and alteration: hardly any weathering - and fresh olivine glomerocrysts - occur in one population; partial weathering and olivine alteration occur in another population; and, in another population, most to all olivine has completely altered to iddingsite, and/or the population is extremely weathered. Populations are also either vesicular or non-vesicular, with calcite and/or barite forming in and around the vesicles in the vesicular basalts. Other phenocrysts (e.g., feldspar, biotite) in the samples also range from fresh to completely altered. Magma mixing is suspected in some samples due to present rims around phenocrysts, dissolution of phenocrysts, and present xenocrysts. Other populations of note show zoning, indicating they underwent fractional crystallization. There are two possible source regions: a northerly source originating in the lava flows of northern New Mexico/southern Colorado, and a southerly source originating in the Trans-Pecos region. By collecting and comparing data from both formations and possible source regions, the latter can be deduced, and paleodrainage systems can be traced, both of which give a more complete understanding of the southwestern United States’ geology during the Cenozoic.

title: INTO THE TROPICS: MUSEUM COLLECTIONS AS A CRADLE FOR SPECIMEN RESEARCH AND FIELD (MIS)ADVENTURES IN THE TROPICAL AMERICAS
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part I)
authors: Hendy, Austin J.W. [1]
affiliations: (1) Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
It is understood that museum collections are a vital and fundamental basis for much of what we do as paleontologists. They are treasurehouses of opportunity, supporting traditional specimen based taxonomy, datasets for the training of AI tools, or mines from which large-scale problems can be addressed. They are also a springboard from which fieldwork can rediscover lost sites, fill gaps, and push the boundaries of what is known. Roger Portell has exemplified all of this through his stewardship of the extraordinary Florida Museum of Natural History Intertebrate Paleontology collection. This collection and its committed curator have left a rich legacy of educated, inspired, and disciplined museum professionals, academics, and avocational researchers.

It is with these shared sentiments that the Invertebrate Paleontology collection of the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHMLA) has embarked on its present transformation. While built on a backbone of extensive regional coverage, the aggregation of former academic collections, and a legacy of prolific researchers, the collection suffered greatly from lack of investment and advocacy in recent decades. The collection is again growing, ensuring regional faunas are not lost to construction, securing orphaned materials from the dumpster, digitizing critical components, and building a dedicated community of interns, volunteers, and supporters. Critically we are evaluating priorities in light of deteriorating funding, the need to decolonize, and a desire to become a more diverse and inclusive environment.

A passion shared with Roger Portell is our desire to be in the field, and more often than not in parts of the tropical Americas. Florida is on the biogeographic and evolutionary doorstep of the Caribbean. Similarly, California is but a political concept, sharing common geology and biogeographic linkages with Baja California, the Gulf of California, and the paleontological riches of Costa Rica, Panama, and beyond. These are all places that must be explored, sampled, and studied to understand our past and our future, and collections are a cradle for such activities. The Invertebrate Paleontology collection of NHMLA is embracing its historic connection to Baja California and the Gulf of California, and is working intentionally to foster collaborations with Mexican colleagues grounded in research ethics, respect for paleontological heritage, and the capacity building to support future generations of paleontologists and their collections.

title: Geomet and Two-Way Science: Drivers of the Critical Minerals Future
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Olson Hoal, Karin [1], Pearce, Mark A [2]
affiliations: (1) Mineral Country, LLC, Golden, CO, Australia; Department EAS, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, Australia
(2) Mineral Resources Business Unit, CSIRO, Perth, WA, Australia
abstract: The present critical minerals rush refers to the more than half of the periodic table of elements which are now or may in the future be considered strategically and industrially important for energy technologies, data needs, commerce and trade, and military and defense. Decision making with respect to these elements is currently driven by projections, policies, and economic scenarios, largely in the absence of science and society. In the minerals sector, geomet is a tool for transforming how resources can be better extracted by linking geoscience with engineering for improved operations, less uncertainty, and reduced impacts. Similarly, two-way science refers to new approaches that improve the sector through engaging people in the science, bringing in diverse perspectives from indigenous, landowner, rural and urban communities. Two-way science enables knowledge sharing and the building of capability and entrepreneurship. Geomet and two-way science thus link geoscience directly to society to drive a positive future minerals sector. The current critical minerals rush is missing this connective tissue, and key personnel are most needed now but not being trained. Fundamental to future success is the characterization of materials — geology, mineralogy, geochemistry, mineral deportment, metallogeny — for scenario-driven outcomes, together with two-way science — knowledge sharing, capability building, and economic engagement. These two areas have traditionally been viewed by the mining sector as the less important front and back ends of projects which may rather be driven by cash flow economics and static flowsheets. The common linking element lies in language, communicating the simple science and engineering of minerals projects across the diverse internal project personnel as well as to members of society. With more than half of future resources expected to come from under characterized resources beneath indigenous or rural communities, the sector may well fail if it does not realign to a flowsheet driven first by geoscience and society. The new minerals sector is potentially a positive shift for future generations - it does not need to be the mining industry of the past. This work derives from a Fulbright collaboration with the Australian CSIRO.

title: Connecting Geoscience Education and Professional Practice: The ASBOG Faculty Ambassador Program
session_title: Geology and Society - Beyond 250
authors: Patton, Jason [1], HELMKE, MARTIN F. [2], Kath, Randy L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Arkansas Tech University, Lamar, AR,
(2) West Chester University, West Chester, PA,
(3) University of West Georgia, Carrollton, GA,
abstract:
With ~88% of geoscience undergraduates entering the workforce and ~78% of U.S. citizens living in regulated states, offering licensure-qualifying degrees is vital. However, to combat declining enrollments, universities are renaming programs and compressing upper-level courses. Unlike Canada's clear P.Geo. guidance, these U.S. curricular changes create disconnects with state boards and risk diluting core competencies, raising the question: are these academic shifts uplifting or eroding the foundation of today’s geology graduates?

To address these challenges, the Association of State Boards of Geology (ASBOG) is developing a Faculty Ambassador Program to strengthen communication and collaboration between academic geoscience programs, the professional licensing community, and employers who depend on a well-prepared workforce. The program creates a national network of faculty serving as points of connection between ASBOG and their institutions, helping students and colleagues better understand the role of professional licensure in geoscience careers.

During its initial phase, the program provides ambassadors with practical information and resources accessible through a dedicated web platform. Resources include examination schedules, study materials, webinars on the Fundamentals of Geology (FG) exam and test-taking strategies, examination blueprints, task-analysis/occupational survey data, state licensure requirements, and institutional performance metrics via ASBOG’s Curriculum Performance Assessment Tool (CPAT). By making these tools accessible, the program helps faculty connect curriculum, advising, and career preparation with the learning outcomes and competencies expected of practicing geologists.

The program also establishes a direct, consistent channel for ASBOG to gather faculty perspectives on curriculum trends, workforce needs, licensure advocacy, and barriers preventing students from taking the FG exam. Future activities include faculty guidance materials, curriculum-alignment resources, collaborative webinars, and meetings bringing faculty together with practicing geologists and subject-matter experts.

title: Extension and Transtension in the Western Basin and Range: New Insights from the Pah Rah Range, Western Nevada
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse
authors: Goldsby, Ryan [1]
affiliations: (1) Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology, Reno, NV, USA
abstract: The Basin and Range Province varies considerably in the timing, magnitude, and style of extension during the Cenozoic, the boundaries of which have received much interest due in part to relatively high modern strain rates and tectonic implications for the collapse of the Sevier orogenic plateau. Western Nevada represents the boundary of the actively extending Basin and Range against the unextended Sierra Nevada, however, the timing and magnitude of extension in areas of the Basin and Range is not fully understood, particularly where magnitudes and styles of extension transition. The Pah Rah Range south of Pyramid Lake, Nevada, is located at a transition from highly extended crust to the south, and less extended regions of northwest Nevada. Extension is expressed as high-angle ~N-S striking normal faults, and NW-SE striking oblique-slip faults associated with the Walker Lane. Here, geologic mapping, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar sanidine ages of Oligocene ash-flow tuffs and Miocene mafic volcanics, bulk geochemistry, and structural measurements are used to interpret shifting timings and styles of deformation in the area. A significant angular unconformity between mid-Miocene mafic volcanics and late Oligocene ash-flow tuffs record early deformation and tilting in the region, which predates the eruption of the ~13 Ma Pyramid Sequence basaltic andesites and related rocks. Three distinct styles of active and inactive normal and oblique-normal faults are observed, which assert a strong control over deformation, mineralization, and extensional evolution of western Basin and Range.

title: Terminal Classic Maya droughts driven by Pacific-Atlantic coupled forcing
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Ghosh, Suvrajit [1], Obrist-Farner, Jonathan [2]
affiliations: (1) Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
(2) Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, USA
abstract: Terminal Classic Droughts (TCD, ~800–1100 CE) in Mesoamerica were multi-year dry periods characterized by precipitation reductions estimated at ~40–50%, which coincided with abandonment of large Maya urban centers. Although prior explanations for the droughts emphasized solar-forced ITCZ displacement and Pacific-Atlantic SST gradient changes, comparable forcing recurred after the TCD without producing regionally coherent drying of similar magnitude, indicating that neither process alone is sufficient to explain the observations. Here we present a ~2000-year-long sediment record from Lake Atitlán in the Guatemalan Highlands, a statistical synthesis of multi-proxy records from the region, and climate model analysis to identify the oceanographic and atmospheric processes responsible for the TCD. Distinct intervals of elevated authigenic calcite accumulation in the Atitlán sediment core indicate reduced lake levels and increased evaporative concentration. These intervals coincide with previously documented dry episodes from the Maya Lowlands on the Yucatan Peninsula. Statistical analysis that incorporates age-depth model uncertainties across 20 Mesoamerican proxy paleoclimate records reveals a coherent pattern of regional drying from 800 to 1100 CE, with 16 of the 20 sites recording drier-than-median conditions. Unforced control simulations from CESM2 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR reveal Pacific-Atlantic circulation variability that can produce precipitation reductions of >40% across Mesoamerica. The modeled precipitation reduction is driven by El Niño-like Pacific warming that results in atmospheric subsidence over the region, while concurrent intensification of the North Atlantic Subtropical High strengthens Caribbean easterlies, amplifying the regional precipitation deficit. Because ongoing human-mediated warming is projected to intensify El Niño-like Pacific states and strengthen the North Atlantic Subtropical High, combined Pacific-Atlantic circulation changes represents a significant hydroclimate hazard for Mesoamerica, with severe consequences for the tens of millions who depend on subsistence agriculture.

title: Using historic landslide mapping, field, and airborne lidar methods, to better understand >100 years of slope failures in the Chimney Rock, NC, area, after the late September 2024 tropical cyclone Helene and the predecessor rainfall event

authors: Waters-Tormey, Cheryl [1], Hartman, Courtney [2], Kinner, David A. [3], Platt, Sophia [4], Wooten, Richard [5]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences and Natural Resources, Western Carolina University, Cullowhee, NC,
(2) North Carolina Geological Survey, Black Mountain, NC, USA

(4) Geosciences and Natural Resources, Western Carolina University, Cullowhee, NC, USA
(5) NCGS (Ret.), FLETCHER, NC, USA
abstract:
Steep terrain and frequent orographically enhanced extreme precipitation events make the Blue Ridge Escarpment (BRE) prone to slope failures. Many BRE slopes contain colluvium overlying fresh bedrock of variable lithology and structures. A better understanding of bedrock discontinuity networks and differential weathering would assist risk modeling and local landslide hazard reduction efforts.

The study area contains two km-scale WNW-oriented landscape features: the eastern Hickory Nut Gorge trench lineament and the Shumont reentrant. Integrating slope failures documented by the NC Geological Survey with collaborators, geologic mapping, airborne lidar (2017, 2025), and aerial photography (2019, 2025), offer a valuable opportunity to examine relationships between slope features, debris flow initiation zones (IZs), rock slope failures, and bedrock geology. This poster complements a related presentation, seeking discussion of interpretations.

Bedrock is a ~100-m-thick body of mostly amphibolite gneiss between two bodies of granodioritic Henderson Gneiss in transitional contact with felsic gneiss (HG-FG), all exhibiting a gently SE-dipping transposition foliation. One hypothesis for slope failure localization was a structural contact proposed in regional geologic maps above the lower HG-FG, but a strain gradient, metamorphic grade contrast, or offset contacts, are not observed.

Geological and lineament mapping indicate steeply dipping NW-, NE-, and E-striking planar joint sets occur in all lithologies and structural depths. Joints are larger and more widely spaced in HG-FG, where rock slope failure has produced cliffs with narrow fracture-controlled drainage pathways upslope of boulder clast-supported, vegetated, colluvium. Rock slope failures and slides in lower slope colluvium indicate these are active systems. Rare fault zones record minor NNW-SSE to NE-SW extension in the eastern field area but are not associated with recent slope failures.

Ongoing work suggests several patterns: (1) Steep, curved fractures connecting joint sets, or connecting joints in step-over geometries, forming complex 1- to 100-m scale discontinuity surfaces in HG-FG that terminate against other joints and foliation-parallel fractures. Block release generates overhangs (2012 rock fall) and detached slabs (i.e., Rumbling Bald Cave, Chimney Rock Mountain promontories). Curved fracture orientations suggest propagation controlled by pre-existing planar fractures and topography. (2) Runoff within fracture-controlled drainages in HG-FG slopes into HG-FG colluvium generated most Helene IZs, several in the 2016 Party Rock fire footprint. Comparison with earlier debris flows suggest runoff generation is a significant process in the study area.

title: Remediation of Lead Contamination from Former Smelting Sites in the USA, 1980–2025
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Posters)
authors: Alpers, Charles N. [1], Parsons, Michael B. [2]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Sacramento, CA, USA
(2) Geological Survey of Canada, Dartmouth, NS, Canada
abstract:
Smelting is one of the major sources of lead (Pb) to the global environment, both historically and currently. Primary smelting is defined as pyrometallurgical recovery of metals including Pb, zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), nickel, precious metals, and others, from ores or concentrates. Secondary smelting refers to metal recycling, also using pyrometallurgy. In the case of secondary Pb smelting, the main source of Pb scrap is the recycling of lead-acid batteries.

Currently there are no active primary Pb smelters in the USA; the last one to close was in Herculaneum, Missouri in 2013. There are currently 11 active secondary Pb smelters in the USA. Modern smelting facilities are highly regulated to minimize harmful air emissions. Most of the primary and secondary Pb smelting sites that were active in the USA during the 1880s through the 1980s operated with less effective emission controls, resulting in contamination of soils at the smelter sites and in surrounding areas with Pb and other metal(loid)s, including arsenic and cadmium. Metal(loid) concentrations in soils, sediments, and other environmental media in these areas have commonly been found to exceed regulatory criteria, requiring remediation to protect human and ecological health.

Several dozen historical smelters and surrounding areas were remediated in the USA from 1980 to 2025 by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and various state agencies under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (or Superfund) and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Using publicly available records, total remediation costs were compiled for 50 former Pb(-Zn-Cu) smelters (35 primary and 15 secondary) and surrounding regions. Corrected for inflation to 2025 US dollars, the total remediation costs were $6.76 billion ($5.22 billion for primary smelters and $1.54 billion for secondary smelters). As part of these efforts, more than 51,600 residential and commercial properties were remediated (> 42,000 properties associated with primary smelters and >9,600 properties associated with secondary smelters). The magnitude of these efforts provides some perspective on the effects of smelting and its environmental legacy in the USA, which produced approximately 35 to 40% of global Pb supply from 1900 to 2021.

title: Sustained ocean oxygenation in the early Tonian Period? New carbonate uranium isotope records from Siberia and Australia
session_title: Integrated Stratigraphic, Geochemical, and Paleobiologic Perspectives on Earth System Evolution: A Session in Honor of the Contributions of Bradley B. Sageman (Part II)
authors: Gilleaudeau, Geoffrey J [1], Gan, Tian [2], Farkas, Juraj [3], Nagovitsin, Kostya [4], Ivanova, Natalia [5], Bartley, Julie K. [6], Shirley, Ana [7], Breeden, Benjamin T [8], Knoll, Andrew H. [9], Kaufman, Alan Jay [10]
affiliations: (1) George Mason Univ, Atmospheric, Oceanic, Earth Sciences (AOES), Fairfax, VA, USA
(2) George Mason University, Fairfax, VA, USA; Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
(3) Adelaide University, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia

abstract: Although much debate has centered on the relationship between ocean oxygenation and the evolution of complex life during the Cryogenian and Ediacaran periods, comparatively few constraints currently exist on ocean redox conditions during the preceding Tonian Period (1000 to 720 Ma). To fill this gap, here we present new carbonate uranium isotope (δ 238 U) data from two sections that span negative δ 13 C excursions in the early Tonian. The Upper Turukhansk Uplift succession from Siberia contains a discrete negative δ 13 C excursion in the upper Shorikha Formation, whose age is constrained by a newly published volcanic zircon U-Pb age of 963 ± 6 Ma at the base of the formation, ~500 m conformably below the δ 13 C excursion. Thus, the negative δ 13 C excursion in the upper Shorikha Formation is tentatively correlated to the ~940 Ma Majiatun anomaly identified in North China. In our section from Siberia, carbonate δ 238 U values are consistently very low prior to the δ 13 C excursion (approximately –0.8‰), but rise sharply to higher values (~–0.2‰) coincident with the negative δ 13 C shift, and remain elevated for the remaining ~300 m of section. We preliminarily interpret this positive δ 238 U shift as a global ocean oxygenation event, although effects of carbonate saturation state and ferruginous ocean conditions on the δ 238 U signal cannot be ruled out. We also present stable strontium isotope (δ 88 Sr) data from this Siberian section, which show a lack of change across the δ 13 C excursion, potentially arguing against carbonate saturation control on U isotopes, thus supporting an oxygenation event. We also present δ 238 U data from the ~880 Ma BRISA anomaly (formerly the ‘Bitter Springs’ anomaly) in the Amadeus Basin, Northern Territory, Australia. Here, δ 238 U values are uniformly high (~–0.4‰ to –0.1‰) in the pre-excursion Gillen Formation and through the negative δ 13 C excursion in the Loves Creek Formation, suggesting a potential continuation of well-oxygenated oceans through the early Tonian Period. Thus, our preliminary δ 238 U data suggest that the early Tonian Period may represent an overlooked early Neoproterozoic interval of well-oxygenated oceans, which is consistent with the widespread presence of sulfate evaporites in Tonian successions. In addition, carbonate δ 238 U data suggest that the early Tonian oceans may have been better-oxygenated than the later Ediacaran oceans that witnessed the diversification of complex, macroscopic organisms.

session_title: Advances in understanding landslides processes and risks: monitoring, societal impacts, and mitigation strategies (Posters)
authors: Bryan, Ashley [1], Kavalchek, Elise [2], Gnesko, Laura [3], Smithies, Sarah [4], Stahl, Timothy [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Climate Science, Tufts University, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

abstract: Recent high-intensity rainfall events have triggered widespread landsliding at Living Springs, Banks Peninsula, New Zealand, causing damage to infrastructure, reforestation projects, recreation networks, and ecological restoration areas, while detrimentally increasing sediment delivery into Whakaraupō/Lyttelton Harbour. Understanding the controls on slope failure is critical for managing landslide risk and reducing catchment sediment yield along with associated ecological impacts. This study investigates geomorphic, geologic, hydrologic, and vegetation controls on landsliding within loess-mantled slopes underlain by volcanic bedrock. Mapped landslides are concentrated within broad catchments, where gully development promotes sediment transport into the bays downslope. Failure commonly occurs at the interface between loess and underlying volcanic materials, where contrasts in permeability promote the development of perched groundwater and failure surfaces. GIS-based volumetric analysis indicates that landsliding contributes approximately 70% of total hillslope sediment production across the study area. Preliminary geotechnical testing suggests residual shear strength is lowest (28°) within remolded loess, increasing susceptibility to reactivation following initial failure. Landslides are most frequently associated with moderately steep slopes (22-45°) in gulleys, likely due to elevated pore-water pressures during rainfall. Preliminary observations also suggest vegetation type and shallow root depths influence superficial stability, causing loss of newly planted native reforestation efforts due to limited reinforcement of loess soils. These findings identify the primary controls on rainfall-induced landsliding at Living Springs and highlight the importance of catchment hydrology, loess-bedrock stratigraphy, and vegetation management in slope stabilization. The results provide a framework for targeted mitigation strategies, such as prioritizing reforestation in conjunction with engineered slope stabilization methods like retaining walls, aimed at reducing landslide risk, protecting ecological efforts, and limiting sediment delivery to Whakaraupō/Lyttelton Harbour.

abstract:
Previous studies show that modeling tools can effectively guide large-scale wetland restoration initiatives. However, these efforts primarily relied on ecosystem service models, watershed models, lumped or spatial models, which often oversimplify or overlook the physical characteristics and dynamic processes of individual wetlands. As a result, their applicability to inform practical restoration and management decisions remains limited. The objective of our study was to demonstrate how coupling field observations with an advanced, physically-based hydrologic model can accurately simulate complex wetland systems to guide future restoration and management.

Specifically, we developed a 3-D HydroGeoSphere (HGS) model to simulate flow and dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) transport in a 2-ha, newly constructed H2Ohio wetland site located in central Ohio, i.e., Brooks Park (BROP). Simulation results over the simulation period (March - September, 2024) showed that our model was successful in simulating and reproducing the intricate hydrologic processes and dynamics at the BROP, featured with bidirectional flows and nutrient exchanges at both upstream and downstream boundaries (Murphy’s Run and Buckeye Lake, respectively) as well as the more complicated internal transfer/pumping of water and solute mass from the Main Pool to the West Pool (i.e., the “pump-and-dump” process).

The model was further applied to evaluate and identify pumping strategies that would optimize nutrient-reduction efficiency of the BROP while minimizing operational costs, i.e., reducing overall pumping. Comparing the modeling results across five different operational scenarios, we found that increasing the volume of water pumped from the inlet Main Pool to the West Pool led to a greater overall nutrient retention. However, the marginal benefit is limited: DRP retention would increase only from 0.51 kg to 0.62 kg, even though pumping rates increased by as much as fivefold. A more valuable finding is that adaptive pumping strategy (i.e., activating pumps only during periods of high concentration in March 2024) had the potential to substantially reduce operational costs (four times less) without compromising nutrient-reduction efficiency. These findings emphasize the need for continuous water-quality monitoring in restored wetlands and the precise alignment of pumping schedules with fluctuating nutrient levels.

abstract: The Late Cretaceous–Early Paleogene Southwestern US Corridor was underlain by the flat Farallon slab, as evidenced by underplated Orocopia schist. This flat-slab subduction produced the Arizona Highland, yet its pre-extensional crustal geometry remains debated between (1) a wide, symmetric plateau or (2) an asymmetric plateau with a focused, thickened root in the Arizona Transition Zone (ATZ). To evaluate these scenarios, we perform geodynamic modeling of 25–10 Ma gravitational collapse-driven extension. Our results demonstrate that the initial pre-extensional architecture dictates the geodynamic collapse mechanism: a wide, symmetric plateau generates broad, distributed deformation, whereas an asymmetric plateau with an ATZ root creates a sharp lateral potential energy gradient. This gradient drives channelized lower-crustal extrusion, which exerts basal traction that localizes asymmetric, NE-dipping Metamorphic Core Complex (MCC) detachment faults along the SW edge of the ATZ. This root-driven mechanism successfully reproduces the observed distribution of MCCs, the NE-dipping detachment geometry, and the present-day Moho ramp. These findings indicate that a focused crustal root beneath the ATZ—such as that produced by Laramide 'bulldozing'—is mechanically required prior to 25 Ma to govern Miocene extensional style.

title: Coupling Titanium Zoning and Melt Inclusion Compositions in Quartz: Implications for Use of Ti-in-Quartz in Assessing Storage Conditions and Dynamics of Large Silicic Magma Systems
session_title: Mineral-Scale Archives of Magma System Dynamics
authors: Tierney, Casey [1], Reid, Mary [2], Burns, Dale [3]
affiliations: (1) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ,
(2) Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ, USA
(3) Stanford University, Geological Sciences, Stanford, CA, USA
abstract:
The coupling of titanium concentrations and zoning in quartz with experimental solubility models (i.e., TitaniQ) and diffusion coefficients can be a powerful tool in understanding the dynamics and timescales of silicic magma system assembly and storage. However, separating the influence of temperature versus parent melt composition (via titania activity [aTiO 2 ]) on Ti partitioning into quartz is problematic, and can propagate into major uncertainty in modelled results (e.g., temperatures, timescales) and subsequent interpretations.

To test the role of temperature versus melt composition we contrast Ti concentrations in quartz with estimates of entrapment temperature and parental melt composition from spatially paired melt inclusions from the enormous (>5300 km 3 ) and compositionally zoned (68-77 wt.% SiO 2 ) 74 ka Youngest Toba Tuff (YTT). Quartz were separated from five compositionally diverse YTT pumices, and where crystals have been demonstrated to exhibit spatiotemporally affinity to their host melts, with crystallization of most quartz occurring under granite minimum (eutectoid) conditions that buffer bulk composition and temperature.

Overall Ti in YTT quartz crystals (n=76) varies between ~25 and 100 ppm, and exhibit marked systemic variations in Ti concentrations and zoning (e.g., distinct rim and interior domains) that correlate with host pumice type. Quartz crystals in the lowest-silica pumice have higher average Ti contents and greater Ti variations than those in high-silica pumice. In 59 pairings from 30 individual crystals, quartz Ti concentrations exhibit little correlation with Zr in adjacent melt inclusions (R 2 = 0.04), and therefore calculated zircon saturation temperatures (R 2 =<0.03). In contrast, strong correlations are observed between quartz Ti and melt inclusion Ti (R 2 = 0.65), as well as feldspar-sensitive trace elements and ratios in the melt (Sr, Ba, Rb/Sr, Y/Ba; all R 2 >0.55).

Overall, the contrasts between Ti-in-quartz and melt inclusion compositions indicate that melt composition (and Ti in particular, via aTiO 2 ) is the primary factor controlling Ti zoning in YTT quartz, not temperature. Modelling indicates parent melt composition, and therefore Ti variation and zoning, in YTT quartz can be linked to crystallization and resorbtion of YTT phase assemblages responding to open-system processes. More broadly, these findings indicate that use of Ti-in-quartz to assess magmatic conditions (e.g., TitaniQ as thermometer) and dynamics of silicic systems requires caution, and more careful evaluation of often dynamic factors, especially aTiO 2 .

title: Latest Pleistocene and Holocene paleoenvironmental change and extreme events recorded at Walker and Parker Lakes, eastern Sierra Nevada, CA

authors: Miller, Sara [1], Larsen, Darren J. [2], Heynen, Mikatrin [3], Stabinsky, Abigail [4], Grimmett, Peter [5], Jensen, Britta J.L. [6], Raberg, Jonathan [7], Harmon, Lydia J. [8]

abstract: California is extreme. In this study, we analyze postglacial sediment sequences contained in two sub-alpine lakes in the central eastern Sierra Nevada, CA, to determine the timing and pattern of environmental changes and extreme events related to seismicity, volcanism, and wildfire for the past ~14 ka. We target sediments at Walker Lake (37.873°N, -119.168°W, 2422 m asl, ~0.3 km 2 , max depth ~11 m) and Parker Lake (37.834°N, -119.159°W, 2540 m asl, ~0.1 km 2 , max depth ~7 m), two small moraine-impounded lakes positioned at the base of their respective adjacent glacial valleys along the range front. Multiple sets of sediment cores were recovered from both sites in an overlapped manner using a modified Livingston corer and surface-sediment corer operated from a floating platform. All cores were split lengthwise into working and archive halves and imaged using a Geotek linescan camera. A composite sedimentary sequence was constructed for each lake by correlating individual cores using prominent tephra layers and distinct sediment laminations, and age control was established using radiocarbon dating of terrestrial plant material. Cores from Walker Lake terminate on strongly-laminated, clay-rich glacial lacustrine sediments, confirming near complete recovery of the postglacial sequence. Cores from Parker Lake terminate on a basin-wide coarse-grained event deposit, dated to the early Holocene. The lithostratigraphy at both sites contains multiple types of event deposits, including tephra layers, sand horizons, and turbidites. We analyze a suite of sediment physical, biological, and geochemical parameters, including magnetic susceptibility, bulk density, organic matter content, elemental abundance, sediment accumulation rate, sand concentration, and charcoal abundance. Preliminary results suggest that local volcanism, seismicity, and wildfire activity have varied substantially throughout the Holocene, with associated changes in sediment physical and organic matter parameters in response to changing environmental conditions. These results contribute to a better understanding of how alpine and sub-alpine environments in the eastern Sierra have experienced and responded to past extreme events.
