title: Planetary Geoheritage in Practice: Training Crew in Field Geology from Apollo to Artemis
session_title: The Astro-Geoheritage of the Solar System: Past Explorations and Future Considerations
authors: Skinner, James A. [1]
affiliations: (1) U.S. Geological Survey, Astrogeology Science Center, Flagstaff, AZ,
abstract: Planetary geoheritage includes places and artifacts associated with exploration as well as the methods developed to explore another world. Northern Arizona preserves an unusually continuous record of that practice. The USGS Branch of Astrogeology was established in Flagstaff in 1963 in part because Meteor Crater and the young volcanic terrain of the San Francisco Volcanic Field provided accessible settings for planetary geologic research and astronaut training. Apollo crews trained at natural sites selected for different purposes: Meteor Crater exposed an impact structure, disrupted strata, and ejecta, whereas Sunset Crater and surrounding volcanic terrain provided basaltic units and constructional landforms. At Cinder Lake, USGS and NASA went further. Beginning in 1967, hundreds of craters were produced with explosives across a cinder surface using the mapped size and distribution of craters within a portion of Mare Tranquillitatis. A lunar map was effectively translated into terrestrial terrain on which astronauts could practice navigation, observation, communication, equipment use, sampling, and field procedures before encountering comparable problems on the Moon. These exercises linked maps, traverses, observations, and samples into a geologic workflow and required crews to communicate field interpretations to science and operations teams working remotely. That connection remains relevant for Artemis. During the 2024 Joint Extravehicular Activity and Human Surface Mobility Test Team 5 (JETT5) exercise, astronauts worked in the San Francisco Volcanic Field while a Science Evaluation Room operated from Houston. Preparation included geologic maps, prioritized field locations, traverse plans, and other science-operations products, and the exercise tested how scientific decisions changed as communications and imagery available to the remote team changed. Artemis south-polar exploration differs substantially from Apollo, particularly in illumination, terrain, mobility, communications, and the remotely sensed information available before crew arrival. Its methods therefore cannot simply reproduce Apollo practice. The heritage worth retaining is not a fixed set of procedures, but the accumulated capability to move from remote observations to geologic interpretation, from interpretation to field decisions, and from field results back to a revised understanding of the terrain. Current USGS lunar mapping and analog activities continue to test and document these relationships. Northern Arizona matters not only because Apollo astronauts trained there, but because the geologic practice developed there remains in active use and continues to evolve for renewed human exploration of the Moon.

title: How Well Do Tsunami-Deposit Extent and Recurrence Reflect Earthquake Size? Examples from Kamchatka
session_title: Recurrence of what?
authors: Bourgeois, Joanne [1], Pinegina, Tatiana [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Space Science, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
(2) Institute of Volcanology & Seismology, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskiy, Kamchatka, Russia
abstract:
There is a clear and quantifiable (albeit complex) relationship between seismogenic tsunami size (near- and far-field runup, nearfield inundation and along-coast extent) and the generating earthquake rupture size and pattern. Because of excellent tephrochronology on Kamchatka, tsunami recurrence, including size, has been determined at a number of localities, the best being Avachinsky Bay (Pinegina et al. 2018). At this locality, we have quantified tsunami recurrence by the scale of runup and inundation--the latter we think being more reliable as an earthquake size indicator. Also at this locality, we have documented three particularly large earthquakes (out of about 30 total) in the last 4000 years, using evidence of co-seismic subsidence (Pinegina et al. 2020).

Given that Kamchatka has a robust record of historic earthquakes and tsunamis in addition to its prehistoric tsunami deposits, we can contribute to an interrogation of the question, “Recurrence of what?” For prehistoric cases, our ability to map/determine along-coast rupture length remains a significant hurdle. The July 2025 Kamchatka Mw 8.8 earthquake and its tsunami are shedding more light on our ability to quantify paleotsunamis and their generative earthquakes. What can we learn from these historic and prehistoric events, what are the challenges, and how might what we learn be applied to other subduction zones?

title: Cold Seeps as Transient Refugia During Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 in the Western Interior Seaway
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Brophy, Shannon K. [1], Titus, Alan [2], Corsetti, Frank [3], Berelson, Will [4], Bottjer, David J. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(2) Bureau of Land Management, Kanab, Utah, USA
(3) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(4) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
(5) University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
Cold seeps occur along continental margins worldwide where they support productive chemosynthetic-based communities. Seeps provide key ecosystem services through carbon sequestration and provide essential resources for commercially important species. Yet, their ecological functions change through time, and many are threatened by anthropogenic stressors. The fossil record provides a means to examine the resilience of these ecosystems during past biodiversity crises.

Western Interior Seaway (WIS) strata preserve an expanded record of Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2; ~94Ma), a major carbon-cycle perturbation marked by extinctions across the Cenomanian–Turonian boundary. Although OAE2’s impacts on WIS fauna are well studied, seep ecosystems and their potential to buffer organisms from regional stress remain poorly understood. We compared WIS seep assemblages with coeval non-seep faunal datasets (Utah, Arizona) and evaluated how the ecological role of seeps varied through time. Methane-derived authigenic carbonates (MDACs) occur throughout an 11-m section of the Tropic Shale (Utah) and record several hundred thousand years of dynamic seep activity. MDAC morphology, petrography, and isotope geochemistry (δ 13 C carb , δ 18 O carb ) were used to reconstruct changes in methane flux and carbonate formation. Macroinvertebrate abundance and diversity were quantified for comparison.

The lower seep interval records effusive seepage, high rates of methane oxidation, and extensive carbonate precipitation at the sediment-water interface. Large, fossiliferous, micritic MDACs yield δ 13 C values between ~–31 to –38.5‰ and seawater-like δ 18 O signatures, consistent with a methane-derived carbon source. Fossils are commonly preserved in three-dimensions and retain original shell material, indicating rapid cementation. These assemblages are substantially more abundant and average more than twice the generic and functional richness of non-seep assemblages. Early cementation likely enhanced fossil preservation, so this enrichment likely reflects both ecological and taphonomic processes. Up-section, MDACs decrease in size and extent, suggesting waning methane flux and a shift to diffusive seepage. MDACs are less 13 C-depleted, more diagenetically altered, and fossil preservation deteriorates. Assemblages are characterized by fragmentary fossils, impressions, and resistant fish remains as diversity declines.

These patterns suggest that effusive seeps acted as transient refugia during OAE2, maintaining ecologically complex communities during regional environmental stress–though this capacity weakened as methane flux and carbonate formation declined. This deep-time record highlights how changes in seep processes alters their resilience during crises and provides a framework for evaluating modern seeps as they face increasing anthropogenic disturbances.

title: Correlating Ignimbrite Flare-Up Rhyolites in the Organ Mountains, New Mexico: Constraints from Outcrop and Petrographic Observations
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: FitzGerald Taylor, Chloe Lauren [1], Thines, Jennifer [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
Reconstructing genetic relationships among tuffs is often limited by incomplete exposure and post-eruptive burial, faulting, and alteration, all of which obscure field relationships. In older caldera systems, distinguishing between proximal and distal deposits requires careful evaluations of field and petrographic evidence rather than relying on proximity alone.

The Organ Mountains in southern New Mexico are ideal for studying silicic volcanism due to exposure of late Eocene to early Oligocene (33-37 Ma) igneous rocks formed by a series of caldera-forming eruptions and the associated intrusive plumbing system. The Cueva Tuff, Achenback Park Tuff, and Bar Mountain Tuff have long been linked to the Organ Caldera as products of eruptions spanning ~226,000 years. Previous work has largely focused on the geochemistry of the more voluminous and better exposed Cueva and Bar Mountain Tuffs and potential intrusive-extrusive links. Field and petrographic observations of the Achenback Park Tuff, including fine-grained matrix, low crystallinity, and lack of fiamme and lithics, are more consistent with eruption from a distal source. Based on field relationships and petrography, we hypothesize that the Achenback Park Tuff originated from a source external to the Organ Caldera system rather than being co-genetic with the Cueva and Bar Mountain Tuffs.

By reconstructing the eruption sequences of these three tuffs and comparing the petrography, we will determine whether these tuffs share a common magma source or represent distinct systems. Furthermore, we plan to provide a framework for correlating tuffs across the extensive Mogollon-Datil Volcanic Field, where faulting and alteration has similarly made correlations and linking to source calderas difficult. Due to prior work relying largely on geochemistry, this field and petrographic approach offers an alternate means of evaluating eruption processes.

title: Were Theropod Dinosaurs Living along the Western Interior Seaway Opportunistic Piscivores? Making a Case Using Stable Isotope Geochemistry
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part II)
authors: Fricke, Henry C. [1], Rogers, Raymond R. [2], Phillips, India [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO,
(2) Geology, Macalester College, Saint Paul, MN,
(3) Geology, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
abstract:
Theropod dinosaurs were important components of terrestrial ecosystems during the late Cretaceous, typically occupying the highest tropic levels. Dental microwear, bite marks, stomach & coprolites contents along with studies of functional morphology all suggest that larger theropods such as tyrannosaurs were carnivorous, and evolved to feed on co-existing herbivorous dinosaurs (e.g. hadrosaurs & ceratopsians). While most large theropods no doubt relied on such food sources, those living in coastal environments would have had an alternative meat-based food source available to them: fish. In the same way that extant bears are often opportunistic piscivores (e.g. feeding on spawning salmon in coastal settings), it is possible that large theropods living along the coast of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) had similar behaviors.

It is possible to test this hypothesis by measuring carbon isotope ratios (d13C) of dinosaur tooth enamel bioapatite and of fish scale ganoine collected from vertebrate microsites of late Campanian age. Isotopic data from terrestrial herbivores and from co-existing fish indicate that the meat of each type of animal was isotopically distinct, and because carbon in tooth enamel is sourced from diet, the relative proportion of herbivore versus fish meat eaten by a theropod influences the d13C of its enamel. Intriguingly, d13C values of theropods from microsites in better-drained upland environment farther from the coast are consistent with a diet of ‘herbivore meat’, but in fluvial-wetland environments closer to the shoreline the d13C of theropods suggests that fish meat was also being consumed by these animals. In other words, isotopic data suggest that at least some coastal theropods displayed opportunistic piscivory.

If correct, these interpretations raise a host of interesting questions regarding dietary behaviors and habitat preferences of theropod dinosaurs living along the WIS, and how these preferences may have varied among taxa, during ontogeny and over time.

title: Is There an Objective Definition for a Mass Extinction (and Should There be One)?
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Clapham, Matthew E. [1]
affiliations: (1) University of California, Santa Cruz, CA,
abstract: Paleontologists have considered the concept of mass extinction events for more than 70 years, with the topic blossoming into a multidisciplinary research area encompassing paleobiology, sedimentology, geochemistry, and other fields. If asked to define what makes an event a mass extinction, most would note attributes such as the severity of taxonomic loss, disappearances of lineages across the tree of life, a widespread-to-global scope both on land and in the oceans, and a short temporal duration. Indeed, qualitative definitions of the mass extinction concept have consistently included these descriptors since the earliest publications. However, there remains debate about how many events can be called a mass extinction, and whether the modern biodiversity crisis is or will be joining the group. Does this matter, and would it improve mass extinction research to have a more objective definition of a mass extinction, distinguishing it from other types of events and the background? I will review whether and how mass extinctions differ from or are similar to other events in terms of severity, taxonomic and geographic scope, temporal duration, and ecological consequences. Are there objective criteria that distinguish mass extinctions, and what can this tell us about the modern biodiversity crisis?

title: The Stability of Sulfide in Oxidized Silicic Melts and the Sulfur Content at Sulfide Saturation of Hazardous Magmatic Systems
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Coulthard, Daniel A. [1], Sisson, Thomas W. [2], Blatter, Dawnika L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Warner College of Natural Resources, Fort Collins, CO, USA
(2) California Volcano Observatory, U.S. Geological Survey, Volcano Science Center, Moffett Field, CA, USA
(3) California Volcano Observatory, U.S. Geological Survey, Volcano Science Center, Moffett Field, CA, USA
abstract:
At the temperatures of basaltic magmas, sulfide can separate as immiscible liquid that later crystallizes, but at the cooler temperatures of common andesites, dacites, and rhyolites, sulfides can crystallize directly from silicate melt and by reaction of sulfur in melt or vapor with Fe-rich minerals (mainly oxides). Sulfide (S 2- ) concentrations are low in silicate melt or vapor relative to sulfate at the oxidation states of many arc magmas, yet reflected-light petrography routinely reveals traces of sulfide in oxidized, intermediate and evolved arc volcanic rocks, including those from voluminous explosive eruptions (Mount St. Helens, Mount Mazama, Mount Veniaminof, Novarupta/Katmai, Santorini, Toba). Sulfides commonly occur as small ( £ 10 micron) inclusions in FeTi oxide minerals.

Electron-probe microanalysis reveals that most of the sulfide is Cu-bearing pyrrhotite or Fe-Cu monosulfide solid solution (MSS, in some cases also with low concentrations of Ni). FeTi oxide mineral pairs confirm relatively high oxygen fugacities of the examined magmatic systems (ΔFMQ: +0.8–1.9 log units) with the presence of chalcophile elements stabilizing sulfide at oxygen fugacities higher than would be so in those elements’ absence.

To develop a more quantitative understanding of how Cu and Ni expand igneous sulfides’ stability to higher oxidation states, we performed thermochemical modeling using sulfide compositions, published whole rock compositions, temperatures ranging from 790–980 °C, and oxygen fugacities inferred from two-oxide oxybarometry. Forward modeling allowed us to infer the amount of sulfur needed to form sulfide in each magma (assuming the whole rock composition used is representative of the composition of the magma near the time of eruption). Additionally, the forward model allowed us to predict the composition of the sulfide formed, which enables a direct comparison between the predicted and observed compositions. Reverse modeling involved using the observed sulfide compositions and physicochemical data to predict the amount of sulfur in the system.

title: A Brief History of Modeling Time
session_title: ‘GTS2030’ – Toward an Open Science Geologic Time Scale
authors: Trayler, Robin B. [1]
affiliations: (1) Life and Environmental Sciences, University of California, Merced, Merced, CA, USA
abstract:
Developing the underlying age model – going from chronostratigraphy to numerical time – is a critical problem for developing a an authoritative Geologic Time Scale. Over the past c. 40 years the underlying methods have evoloved and must continue to do so for GTS 2030. Understanding the history and nuances of these methods can inform best practices for future GTS development.

Algorithms for age-depth modeling can be placed into two categories, those based on classical frequentist statistics and, more recently, Bayesian methods; Each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Frequentist methods are underlain by mathematics with centuries of history. They can be easily reproduced using a wide variety of free software and are not computational intensive, allowing models to be fit to data in a matter of seconds. However, within the context of stratigraphic age-depth modeling, frequentist statistics have several drawbacks. They can be inflexible and may not accurately capture the complexities of the rock record. Moreover, they often underestimate uncertainties and can violate fundamental geologic principles. More recently, Bayesian methods have been developed to address many of these shortcomings. A critical improvement is the incorporation of prior information into age-depth model construction. Bayesian age-depth models can be made to absolutely respect fundamental geologic principles, such as superposition, using the relative ordering of events to reduce model uncertainties. Furthermore, since most Bayesian models use a sedimentation model to “interpolate” numerical time between geochronological tie-points, they can be conditioned to have sedimentation rates similar to those expected for the lithology of a given stratigraphic section. However, most Bayesian models are computationally intensive and may take minutes to hours to fit a given section.

There are several challenges to translating existing models from single stratigraphic sections to Geologic Time Scales (regional or global). For example, when tens or even hundreds of individual sections are composited into a chronostratigraphic scale, information about sediment characteristics is lost, making it difficult to specify appropriate prior distributions for accumulation “rate”. Likewise, handling the uncertainties that arise from the construction of the chronostratigraphic scaling becomes substantially more important. Despite these challenges, Bayesian methods are clearly the way forward for GTS construction, offering a flexible framework that can grow and change for the next and future iterations of the Geologic Time Scale.

abstract:
Hierakonpolis has a complex living history ~4000 BCE - present. This Temple-Town with mud brick walls and temple structures has been occupied for ~6026 years containing homes, farms, production sites, bread ovens, temple offerings, and Islamic iron foundries.

Possibly an early Capital of the Nation State of Egypt, the Namer Pallet was discovered here linking the ruling of Upper and Lower Egypt for the first time. The first recorded archeological excavation occurred in 1897-1899 by Quibell and Green. Later Archeologists, Walter Fairservis worked this site 1967-1994, followed by Elizabeth Walters, 1999-present.

Six millennia of habitation make groundwater characterization and modeling challenging. Archeological remains, inter-fingering spatial variations of regional Wadi Abu Sufian and Nile sediments, farming, local water use, sewage disposal, site impacts related to the regional Wadi Sa'ayda Land Reclamation project’s irrigation return flows increased hydraulic heads under the Temple Town by 1.0-1.5m, caused pooling within excavations, site and regional salinization problems. Complexities are revealed by topography, vegetation, soil, hydrogeologic, chemical and archeological observations. Seismic surveys have located the water table within 10 cm, defining aquifer limits, artifacts and several sources of recent encroaching groundwater.

As our 27+ years of field data and observations are added to a GIS database obtained from archeological digs, 115 temperature holes, 146 shallow piezometers, 20 10 M - 30 M deep holes and regionally 24 variable depth holes new intricacies are revealed.

We focus on the Temple-Town site, its maze of mud brick hydraulic barriers. Accumulating evaporite salts react with smectite, illitic and kaolinitic limey soils, changing hydraulic properties, destroying stratigraphic sequences, unique artifacts, mud brick homes and cropland farmed for >5,000 years. Temperature, Salinity, pH, Specific Conductance, Conductivity and water level data analyzed through time reveal adjacent piezometers have values with orders of magnitude differences making water table and quality contour mapping challenging.

Under consideration are mud brick structures, pot chard clusters, Nile terraces and alluvium, interfingering wadi deposits, bedrock, local water sources and regional Wadi Sa’ayada land reclamation project, sources of recharge, deep and shallow water sources causing pooling, salinity and chemistry differences. The site’s ~6026 years of history, chemistry, hydrology, geomorphology and soil mechanics create a challenging problem to solve as we try to determine the source, connectivity and chemistry of each adjacent water pool.

authors: Ver Ploeg, Ava Q. [1], Warner-Cowgill, Ethan [2], McDiarmid, Fisher [3], Rogers, Raymond [4]

abstract:
The Cretaceous Almond Formation in the Rock Springs Uplift of Wyoming records a transition from nonmarine to marine depositional environments within the Western Interior foreland basin. This study examines the sedimentology through the lower ~140 m of the Almond Formation and the microstratigraphy of the fossil-bearing Turtle Hill microvertebrate locality, which caps the studied interval. Interpretations are based on field observations and laboratory analyses (petrography, micro-XRF, SEM-EDS, and XRD). Two stratigraphic columns were described to track facies and fossil occurrences through the unit. From a compositional perspective, sandstones in the unit consist of angular to subrounded quartz, with variable grain size and sorting. Sandstones in the basal 15 m are silica-cemented, whereas overlying sandstones are largely calcite-cemented. Petrographic analyses reveal abundant recycled quartz, mm-scale ironstone concretions, and accessory mica and titanite. The uppermost sandstone bed exhibits hummocky and swaley bedding, climbing ripples, and soft-sediment deformation. The shift to marine deposition up-section is consistent with increasing accommodation and regional transgression.

The ~2 m-thick Turtle Hill section capping the studied interval consists of thin interbeds (cm-scale) of gray to reddish-brown claystone, carbonaceous gray shale, and thin fine-grained sandstone beds that yield abundant terrestrial and marine fossils. Microstratigraphic analysis documents systematic changes in grain size, carbonate content, abundance of carbonaceous material, and fossil assemblages. Plant hash layers and coal stringers are abundant in the lower portions of the section but disappear upward as carbonate-rich intervals become more common. Fossils are concentrated within three distinct horizons. The lowermost fossil-rich bed is a microvertebrate concentration that yields a remarkable abundance of fossils, including teeth from chondrichthyans and osteichthyans, as well as terrestrial mammals, plants, and invertebrates. This basal bonebed is overlain by a 5.5 cm thick dark gray mud/shale bonebed that preserves fish and rare turtle fossils. This bed is in turn overlain by the uppermost fossil-rich horizon, which is a 10–20 cm thick shell bed that yields oysters and scattered small bones. Fossils in this interval include both fully terrestrial and fully marine taxa, preserved together in beds that accumulated along the shoreline of the advancing Western Interior Seaway. This relatively thin fossil-rich interval provides an outstanding opportunity to document a diverse, marginal marine ecosystem during the latest Campanian–earliest Maastrichtian.

abstract:
Reservoir sediments preserve information about watershed processes and provide insight into sediment transport and the spatial distribution of sediment-associated elements. However, few studies have compared modern sediment distribution between reservoirs located in contrasting physiographic provinces of the southeastern United States. This study compares Clarks Hill Lake, located in the Piedmont physiographic province, and Blue Ridge Lake, located in the Blue Ridge physiographic province, to evaluate how watershed setting influences sediment grain size and elemental abundance. We hypothesize that sediment grain size is the primary control on the spatial distribution of elemental abundances in both reservoirs. Surface sediment samples were collected using a Ponar grab sampler from 30 locations in Clarks Hill Lake between November 2025 and April 2026 and 43 locations in Blue Ridge Lake during July 2026. Grain-size distributions are being determined by laser diffraction, and elemental abundances are being measured using X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Spatial interpolation will be used to evaluate sediment distribution patterns and their relationship with elemental abundance within each reservoir. Preliminary observations indicate distinct depositional environments characterized by variations in sediment grain size between shallow and deep basin settings. We expect fine-grained depositional areas to exhibit higher concentrations of lithogenic and redox-sensitive elements than coarse-

grained sediments because of their greater mineral surface area and adsorption capacity. Comparing these reservoirs will provide insight into how physiographic setting, watershed lithology, basin morphology, and sediment transport influence modern sediment distribution across Georgia reservoirs. The results will improve understanding of sedimentary processes relevant to reservoir management, watershed change, and future limnogeological investigations.

abstract:
Calculating accurate discharge timeseries data is a critical component of assessing biological and climatic functionality within aquatic ecosystems. NEON produces continuous discharge data at 27 stream and river monitoring sites across the United States. Beginning in the 2025 data release, NEON discharge data are cleaned and gap-filled to produce a timeseries that is, to the greatest extent possible, free of both gaps and erratic periods.

During data cleaning, data are reviewed, and quality flags are applied to gaps and periods that require correction. Constant offsets are applied where data shifts have occurred. Flagged periods are then corrected using gap-filling methods such as linear interpolation (for short gaps) and regression coefficients (for longer gaps) based on relationships between co-located sensors, or co-located monitoring stations (e.g., USGS gauges).

The quality and continuity of the NEON Water Year 2022 – 2024 discharge dataset was evaluated by assessing the strength of the relationship between field discharge measurements (treated as truth) and modelled estimates and by calculating the number of gaps present in the record. The analysis found that NEON discharge data are well-correlated with field measurements during this period and that the record is essentially continuous across sites. These findings support the use of data cleaning and gap-filling methods to improve data quality and continuity and indicate that NEON discharge data are suitable for use in answering critical research questions in freshwater ecology at the continental scale.

title: Amplification of Tectonic Subsidence by Sediment Supply, Compaction, Sea Level Rise, and Sediment Grain Density
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change (Posters)
authors: Wernicke, Brian [1], Macdonald, Francis A. [2], Anttila, Eliel S.C. [3]
affiliations: (1) Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Science, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, California, USA

abstract: Simple forward analytical models that approximate passive margin subsidence were constructed to explore relationships between sediment supply, sediment compaction, sea level rise, sediment grain density and sedimentary accommodation space (AS). The model consists of three layers, L1 to L3, with deposition at sea-level beginning at t0, and ending at times t1, t2 and t3. Tectonic AS (Y) is constant from t0 to t2, and zero from t2 to t3. The two lower layers are sandstone with porosity of 50% above S=1000 m sedimentary depth (wet density 1825 kg/m3), and 0% below 1000 m (2650 kg/m3). The dolostone is modeled at constant porosity of 8% (2702 kg/m3). L1 thickness at t1 (“L11”) is S=1000 m, scaling Y at 633 m at t1. For a case in which sediment supply is limited, L22 is taken as 1000 m. Compaction at t2 creates C=500 m of AS in addition to Y=1267 m, resulting in water depth of 500 m and S=1500 m. A key distinction between tectonic AS and compaction AS is that Y reflects an increase in distance between the base of S and sea level, and C a decrease in thickness of S, which has no effect on Y. For a second case in which sediment supply is limited only by sea level from t0 to t2, Y is still 1267 m, but filling 500 m of AS to sea level on a compacting substrate amplifies L22 from 1000 to 2875 m. Thus S = 3375 m, a factor 2.25 greater than the sediment supply-limited case. From t2 to t3, we add a sea-level rise of 200 m, and a change in sediment density of L33 to 2702 kg/m3. Total AS is 700 m, C=500 m from compaction of the upper 1000 m of L22 (the expelled pore water is removed to the deep ocean). This results is L33=2874 m of dolostone. Thus, half the thickness of S=5749 m at t3 is generated without tectonic subsidence. The net amplification of subsidence, compared to the case with limited supply and no compaction, sea-level rise, or increase in sediment grain density (i.e. S = 2000 m), is a factor 2.9.

title: Trunk Stream or Multiple Sources? Grain-Size-Controlled Petrography of Ogallala Sand and Gravel, Southern High Plains, USA
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: Eichler, Carla M [1], Lehman, Thomas [2]
affiliations: (1) Life, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, West Texas A&M University, AMARILLO, TX, USA
(2) Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract:
Provenance interpretations in siliciclastic systems commonly rely on a single grain-size fraction, yet source-rock signatures can vary systematically with particle size even within sediment derived from a single source. This raises the possibility that source-area interpretations based on one size class alone may be incomplete or misleading. This study uses grain-size-controlled point-count petrography and heavy mineral analysis of fine sand, coarse sand, and granule gravel from the Miocene Ogallala Formation of the Southern High Plains, USA, to test this effect directly and to resolve competing models of Ogallala sediment dispersal. Approximately 40 samples, from drill cuttings obtained at water wells and from outcrops along the escarpments bounding the High Plains, were separated into three size fractions and used to produce roughly 150 thin-sections for point-count analysis, supplemented by heavy mineral separates from seven sites.

Bulk composition is relatively uniform across the Southern High Plains: lithic grains are abundant and predominantly derived from sedimentary rocks, with lesser metamorphic and volcanic contributions, and the non-opaque heavy mineral assemblage is dominated by epidote, garnet, tourmaline, zircon, titanite, and rutile at all sites sampled. Composition nonetheless varies gradually from north to south: metamorphic and volcanic lithic grains and feldspar diminish southward, while sedimentary lithic grains, particularly carbonate rock fragments, increase. The abundance of metamorphic lithic grains, polycrystalline quartz, microcline, epidote, and garnet at northern sample sites points to headwaters in metamorphic rocks exposed in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, with sediment transported southeastward across the Southern High Plains. No consistent stratigraphic trend in composition was found at any of six sites where multiple depositional sequences could be sampled, indicating that source-area contributions remained broadly stable through time at a given locality.

Critically, three major Ogallala paleo-valley systems, though nominally representing separate drainages, show statistically indistinguishable bulk compositions and heavy mineral assemblages. This pattern is more consistent with derivation from a single dominant trunk stream than from several independent source areas, and offers a diagnostic that may extend to other multi-channel Cenozoic basin fills elsewhere. These results also independently corroborate, through a comparatively economical petrographic method, provenance conclusions previously drawn from detrital zircon geochronology in this region, underscoring that size-fraction-controlled point-count petrography remains a valuable tool for provenance assessment in settings where dense geochronological sampling is impractical.

authors: Miller, Elisha J. [1], George, Sarah W.M. [2], Saroni, Justina [3], Lifton, Nathaniel A. [4], Soreghan, Michael [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK,

abstract: In active tectonic settings, the spatial distribution of tectonic knickpoints reflects variations in fault slip, influencing erosion within catchments and sedimentation into adjacent basins. We combine geomorphometric analysis of catchments with cosmogenic nuclide analysis of detrital sediments collected from five of these catchments along the Kigoma normal fault in the Lake Tanganyika rift system to assess the first-order controls between normal fault growth and surficial processes. Our geomorphometric indices show that knickpoint height and normalized channel steepness ( K sn ) in transient river segments decrease towards the fault tips but localized drainage capture impacts these metrics. Erosion rates derived from paired 10 Be and 26 Al concentrations range from 11–29 m/Myr, with the highest rates in central catchments and decreasing toward the fault tip, consistent with our inference from the watershed analysis that fault displacement decreases toward the fault tip. This spatial trend mirrors the distribution of cumulative slip associated with fault propagation growth model inferred from seismic reflection data from the adjacent hanging wall strata. Paired 10 Be and 26 Al results are consistent with steady-state-erosion across sample sites. Erosion rates in Lake Tanganyika’s tropical setting are comparable to other continental rift settings; however, they are 3 times lower than erosion rates seen in collisional systems. However, this may be indicative of vegetation and its potential to buffer erosional processes compared to less vegetated areas. Overall, our results demonstrate how fault geometry is expressed at the surface and impacts the spatial variation in erosion across an actively uplifting fault.

abstract:
The Robert Noyce Teacher Scholarship program addresses the national need for exceptional STEM master teachers in high-need schools, with a focus on teachers with similar demographics as the diverse communities they serve. Over six years (2020-2026), a Noyce STEM project based out of California State University Dominguez Hills, in partnership with the Los Angeles Unified School District and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHMLA), supported 30 master teachers, including secondary biology, chemistry, and mathematics teachers, and elementary school teachers. In addition to achieving credentials and computer science authorizations, National Board certification, and undertaking action research, the teachers participated in a number of geoscience-focused activities.

Week-long workshops on the Geology of Los Angeles, Marine Biology, and Climate Change, explored specific themes with content experts that could be incorporated into lessons addressing Next Generation Science and Common Core mathematics standards. An outcome of that programming was incorporation of teacher feedback into online resources supporting NHMLA’s Los Angeles Underwater exhibit, which focused on the discovery and significance of fossil finds around the Los Angeles area. Teachers also participated in two week-long field trips to Utah, led by professional geologists, where they learned about basic geology principles (geologic time, the rock cycle, stratigraphy and evolution), landscape change, land use issues, and ultimately dinosaurs. Along the way teachers were hosted by content experts (educators, rangers, scientists, and museum professionals) who explained their career journeys, their work, and its connections to STEM standards. Summative evaluations indicated that these field trips were among the most memorable and impactful experiences for teachers during the program, both personally and in the classroom. Two teachers also conducted research projects with NHMLA that sought to combine collection activities with opportunities for teacher professional development or student engagement. One facilitated a national network of museum professionals and local teachers engaged in digitization of marine biological collections, while the other developed classroom resources and unit plans related to locally relevant paleontological discoveries and exciting new museum acquisitions.

In summary, this Noyce STEM project facilitated an exchange of ideas, promoted professional networking, and greatly improved teacher and student content awareness and competency in the geological sciences. Furthermore, the combination of field experiences and personal interaction with content experts facilitated the integration of geoscience into local classrooms.

title: Structural Architecture and Tectonic Assembly of the Northern Guatemala Suture Zone: Constraints From Detailed Field Mapping
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology (Posters)
authors: Hull, Sarah W. [1], Flores, Kennet E. [2], Strickland, Anna H. [3], Requena, Jamie [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA; Earth and Ocean Sciences, University of North Carolina Wilmington, Wilmington, NC, USA

(3) Earth, Marine and Environmental Sciences, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, USA
(4) Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Guatemala
abstract:
Suture zones juxtapose rocks derived from continental, oceanic, mantle, and subduction-interface environments, preserving the record of plate convergence and collisions. However, the structural complexity of these terranes commonly obscures the contact relationships and tectonic processes responsible for their assembly. Detailed field mapping is therefore essential for reconstructing their deformational history.

The Guatemala Suture Zone (GSZ) in central Guatemala records Mesozoic convergent-margin evolution along the boundary between the North American and Caribbean plates. However, the mechanical processes and structural geometries responsible for exhuming high-pressure rocks and shaping its present-day architecture remain debated. Prior models for the GSZ north of the Motagua Fault depict the Chuacús Complex as a coherent unit of high-grade metamorphosed continental basement overthrust by high-pressure, low-temperature (HP-LT) subduction-zone mélange and overriding ophiolitic sequences; however, the contact relationships between these major units are not well constrained.

Detailed outcrop-scale mapping and structural analyses across two complementary transects spanning the principal tectonic contacts north of the Motagua Fault reveal a more complex architecture. The first transect documents E-W striking thrust contacts where low-grade metasedimentary rocks and ophiolitic rocks structurally overlie an assemblage of serpentinite, amphibolite, garnet-albitite, and fault-bounded slices of the Chuacús Complex, recording tectonic juxtaposition between upper plate, subduction-interface, and continental basement. The second transect exposes ophiolitic serpentinite containing mafic dikes that is structurally overthrust by a serpentinite-matrix mélange characterized by block-in-matrix fabrics containing eclogite and other high-pressure blocks. Together, these transects demonstrate that the northern Guatemala Suture Zone consists of fault-bounded tectonic packages representing distinct structural levels, rather than laterally continuous ltihotectonic belts depicted in previous regional models.

Petrographic and kinematic analyses of Chuacús Complex lithologies indicate an episode of amphibolite-facies deformation overprinted by greenschist-facies, top-to-the-NE thrusting, likely associated with the Late Cretaceous, northeast-directed collision of the Northern Ophiolite belt and subsequent ophiolite obduction onto the North American continental margin. A regionally developed E-W striking foliation likely records deformation during or following the juxtaposition of continental, mantle, and oceanic packages, reflecting regional contraction under variable metamorphic conditions ranging from amphibolite to lower-greenschist facies. These observations require a reassessment of existing structural models for the northern Guatemala Suture Zone and provide a structural framework for integrating ongoing geochronologic, petrologic, and geochemical investigations aimed at reconstructing the tectonic assembly of the suture zone.

session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Trout, Laurel Barbara [1], Littleton, Aidan Layne [2], MacKenzie, Kristen A. [3], Toth, Natalie [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, Denver Museum of Nature and Science, Denver, Colorado, USA

abstract: Microvertebrate localities, or microsites, are fossiliferous deposits containing small, often delicate vertebrate remains which preserve taxa typically underrepresented in macrovertebrate assemblages. As such, data sourced from microsites can provide valuable faunal information on sampled paleoecosystems. Here we compare microsite data of select aquatic and semi-aquatic taxa, chondrichthyans and amphibians, between two Upper Cretaceous geologic formations: the Dinosaur Park Fm. (DPF), located in Alberta, Canada, and the Fruitland/Kirtland Fms. (FKF), located in New Mexico, United States. During the Late Campanian, the DPF and FKF shared generally similar depositional environments on the sub-continent of Laramidia as coastal wetlands comprised of rivers, streams, and lakes along the northern and southern coastline of the Western Interior Seaway, respectively. Using microvertebrate data, we aim to establish whether there exists a functional difference in the chondrichthyan and amphibian fauna between the DPF in the north and FKF in the south. FKF microvertebrate material was collected from five microsites over the span of eight years by DMNS field crews, while microvertebrate count data for DPF was sourced from Cullen & Evans (2016). R Studio v.4.4.1 was used to analyze microsite data via the Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity index, an index that quantifies the difference in relative abundance between sites using count data. DPF microsites formed two large clusters of similarity, with FKF microsites either adjacent to DPF clusters or forming a separate cluster entirely. Our results indicate that while Caudata display the greatest difference in relative abundance between the two formations with a Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index of 0.442, relative abundances of selected taxa remain statistically similar. This study demonstrates a successful framework for quantifying relative abundance of selected taxa between geographically disparate sites using microsite count data. Future directions could include applying this framework with increased sampling from the FKM, along with additional sampling from mid-latitude microsites dated to the Late Campanian.

title: Is Coats Land, Antarctica a tectonic tracer from West Texas linking southern Laurentia and Kalahari in Rodinia?
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Kadam, Ira [1], Beattie, Julian [2], Loewy, Staci L. [3], Dalziel, Ian W. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA
(2) University of Texas, Austin, Texas, USA
(3) University of Texas, Austin, TX, USA

abstract:
Coats Land may be a tectonic tracer linking Kalahari and southern Laurentia within the Neoproterozoic supercontinent Rodinia. Coats Land, a small crustal block of East Antarctica, is separated from the adjacent Mawson Craton by a Pan-African (600 Ma) suture and from the Kalahari Craton by Natal-Maud sutures (~1 Ga), indicating an independent Mesoproterozoic history. Loewy et al. (2011, Geology) identified the collinear Pb isotope signatures or igneous rocks from Coats Land and from the Keweenawan Large Igneous Province of Laurentia, and proposed the paleomagnetically reasonable juxtaposition of Coats Land, southern Laurentia, and Kalahari at ~1 Ga.

Two of the three outcrops of Coats Land bedrock contain ~1100 Ma A-Type granophyre and rhyolite (G-R), similar in composition to and contemporaneous with the Red Bluff Granitic Suite (RBGS) and Thunderbird Rhyolite in the Franklin Mountains of West Texas. The RBGS has previously been divided into five magmatic stages based on cross-cutting relationships. This study will present results of whole-rock geochemical analyses of specimens previously collected from Coats Land and new and previously collected samples of all five stages of the RBGS to evaluate whether the G-R and RBGS may be two parts of the same magmatic province to test the proposed connection between Coats Land and West Texas.

Confirmation that Coats Land was part of Southern Laurentia at 1.1 Ga would provide a piercing point for Kalahari Laurentia juxtaposition in Rodinia and have important implications for Neoproterozoic and Early Paleozoic paleogeography.

abstract:
Across southwestern and south-central Colorado, a major swarm of at least 100 NW-trending diabase dikes occurs within an area of abundant Ediacaran to Ordovician intraplate alkalic magmatism. The dike swarm cuts two alkaline plutonic complexes: the ~575 Ma Powderhorn Complex and the ~ 524 Ma McClure Mountain Complex. One diabase dike that intrudes the Powderhorn Complex has yielded a preliminary CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb zircon age of ~537 Ma.

We report geochemical data for 25 representative NW-trending dikes extending from Unaweep Canyon near the Colorado-Utah border to the Wet Mountains in south-central Colorado. We also include 5 samples of NNW-trending diabase dikes in the Front Range, ~80 km north of the Wet Mountains.

The dike samples show typical trace element patterns for tholeiitic to alkaline within-plate or continental basalts, with moderate LREE enrichment. On the Th/Yb versus Nb/Yb diagram, these dikes define a vertical trend extending upward from the E-MORB field, indicating the dikes originated from asthenospheric melts that interacted with continental lithosphere previously modified by subduction. On the TiO 2 /Yb versus Nb/Yb diagram of Pearce (2008), most of the samples define a trend extending upward from the E-MORB field into the tholeiitic OIB field, showing that much of the magma originated from relatively deep partial melting in the mantle where garnet was stable in the source. The five samples of NNW-trending dikes in the Front Range plot together with the main NW-trending dikes on all the diagrams, suggesting that the Front Range dikes are an offshoot from the main swarm. On the Th/Nb versus TiO 2 /Yb LIP-printing diagram of Pearce et al. (2021), the sample distribution suggests derivation from a mantle plume that interacted somewhat with subcontinental mantle lithosphere.

Previous workers have suggested that the Colorado intraplate magmatism is linked to widespread Ediacaran-Cambrian magmatism in the Wichita igneous province in the Southern Oklahoma aulacogen to the southeast. In Oklahoma, intrusion of a large NW-trending diabase dike swarm represents the latest magmatic phase and shows close geochemical similarities to the Colorado dikes. Dike samples from the aulacogen overlap with samples from the Colorado swarm but plot entirely in the mantle plume array in the Pearce et al. (2021) diagram, suggesting an important role for mantle-plume activity in both regions.

abstract:
Earth systems underscore all aspects of life on our planet, yet many are unfamiliar with its content and potential as a career path. At Santa Fe College in Gainesville, FL, the Natural Sciences department offers a two week long immersive Introductory Geology course in southern Utah and northern Arizona that introduces students to the geosciences in a natural geological laboratory. As a primarily two-year college with four satellite campuses in rural areas, Santa Fe College serves a broad community of students. Our field course provides a vital opportunity for these students to explore professional pathways and define career goals in the geosciences whilst in a supportive and encouraging environment.

Over the past three years, this trip has provided hands-on geologic experiences to multiple cohorts of students. As this course has evolved, it has been scaffolded to serve students of varying ability levels. The course content covers regional stratigraphy and geologic history, erosional and depositional environments, rock deformation, mineral and rock identification, and other fundamental concepts of earth science whilst providing students with a physical science credit. Ultimately, we hope to provide a template for similar institutions to adopt a field based course for typically underreached student populations.

session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Kruger, Joseph Michael [1], Owoyombo, Temitope [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Lamar University, Beaumont, TX, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Space Sciences, Lamar University, Beaumont, Texas, USA
abstract:
Land subsidence is a known problem in the Houston, Texas region as well as in the coastal areas of Louisiana. However, few studies have been conducted in southeast Texas between Houston and the Texas-Louisiana border. This study resurveys National Geodetic Survey (NGS) survey benchmarks, that were monumented between 1918 and 2006, using a survey-grade GNSS system.

The first resurveying campaign took place between October 2010 and October 2012. This resurvey was designed to compare the remeasured benchmark orthometric heights (elevations) to the oldest orthometric heights published by the NGS, which were assumed to have been measured when the benchmarks were monumented. Subtracting the new elevations from the old elevations and dividing that elevation difference by the time difference between the oldest and recent measurements yielded a land subsidence rate (-) or uplift rate (+). With this first resurveying campaign, 359 benchmarks were remeasured with vertical rates calculated between -15.5 mm/yr (subsidence) to +5.5 mm/yr (uplift) over a 5 to 92-year period.

The second resurveying campaign took place in two phases, with a total of 312 benchmarks found and measured between June 2023 and May 2025. The same instrumentation and methods were used for the second campaign, as well as the same geoid and datums. This more recent data was compared to the previous resurveying campaign to again determine the subsidence and uplift rates, but with more accuracy because the dates and times of the measurements during both surveys is known, with no assumptions. A maximum subsidence rate of -16.6 mm/yr and a maximum uplift rate of +10.0 mm/yr were determined between the first and second resurveying campaigns which were 11 to 15 years apart.

These more recent rates are similar to the maximum and minimum rates observed between the first resurvey campaign and the original benchmark measurements during monumentation, however the rates do not necessarily correlate spatially between the two time periods. This indicates that the original rates, which were determined by assuming the oldest elevations were measured during monumentation may be in error or that subsidence and uplift rates changed over time. Comparison of vertical rate maps from both surveys indicate where the differences occur, if the rates are relatively consistent or if they change dramatically over time.

title: Indigenizing STEM Education in Hawaiʻi: Professional Development for Learning, Growth, and Responsibility
session_title: Impactful Indigenous Geoscience: STEM, data science, and education
authors: Chinn, Pauline W. U. [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI, USA
abstract: In the College of Education, place-based, culturally sustaining science education aligns with the State of Hawaiʻi's constitutional and policy orientation to sustainability through a Hawaiian cultural lens. The K-12 public school and University of Hawaii systems share a vision of creating a Hawaiian place of learning grounded in values oriented to collaboration and sustainability. In 2015, the Hawaiʻi Department of Education’s Board of Education adopted Nā Hopena Aʻo, a framework for learning outcomes applicable across content areas and grades. Grounded in six Hawaiian proverbs, outcomes of learning are increased senses of belonging, responsibility, excellence, aloha, total well-being, and Hawaiʻi. These educational policies reflect the 1978 constitution and state laws that protect both culture and the environment, beginning in 1974 with the Hawaii Environmental Policy Act. The shortage of Hawaiian language teachers shows how far Hawaiʻi has come since the 1978 constitution established Hawaiian as the state’s second language, mandated Hawaiian Studies, and revitalized the Hawaiian language from its critically endangered status. However, most pre-service and in-service teachers are not Native Hawaiian, and even if raised in Hawaii, lack knowledge of both Hawaiian and their students' cultures, places, and histories. Lack of preparation to situate instruction in students' familiar places and experiences contributes to students asking, "Why are we learning this?" and leads to three strategies to connect educators to the places, communities, and students they teach. The first strategy, community mapping, is a biogeocultural and historical exploration into their students' district (ahupua'a) to identify interdisciplinary resources for curriculum development. Exploration includes interviews with longtime residents, archival and experiential research to create a map of Indigenous and post-contact places, placenames, and geographic resources. The second strategy, curricular mapping, incorporates these resources into curricular activities that are simultaneously place-, culture-, and standards-based. The final strategy is to develop instructional activities that utilize students' cultures, places, and Indigenous knowledge as assets for science learning. Research from an NSF-funded professional development program to develop place-, culture-, and standards-based STEM curriculum oriented to sustainability showed that teachers developed and utilized STEM resources in their community and students were more interested in Hawaiian culture, STEM courses, and careers in conservation when they were engaged in authentic place-based inquiry that led to actionable knowledge for their lives nd communities.

title: Revised Fault Mapping in the Dallas 7.5-Minute Quadrangle near Ridgway State Park, Ouray County, Colorado
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: White, Jonathan L. [1]
affiliations: (1) CSM/Colorado Geological Survey, LITTLETON, CO,
abstract: The Dallas 7.5-minute quadrangle lies approximately 10 km north of the San Juan Mountains in Ouray County, southwestern Colorado. In the northwest quadrant the Ridgway fault trends east-west and has 300-350 m of north-side-up displacement that forms the southern margin of the Uncompahgre Plateau at Log Hill Mesa above the town of Ridgway. The mapped fault system includes several near-vertical normal branch faults that curve northeastward from the main fault, across the Uncompahgre River Valley to the Ridgway Reservoir and Ridgway State Park. Where exposed, the main fault exhibits high-dip drag-fold deformation in both the hanging and footwall. Eastward, the fault and associated deformation become difficult to trace in the folded Mancos Shale and overlying surficial deposits. Previous work suggests the Ridgway fault is a Laramide reactivation of pre-existing basement structures associated with the Pennsylvanian uplift of the Ancestral Uncompahgre Mountains. Laramide movement along these structures uplifted the present-day Uncompahgre Plateau. The Ridgway fault is included in both the Colorado Geological Survey (CGS) Earthquake and Fault Map Server and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Quaternary Fault and Fold Database. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation has conducted seismotectonic studies and a risk assessment of the Ridgway Reservoir dam. New mapping conducted by the CGS under the USGS STATEMAP program includes the identification of previously unrecognized branch faults where offsets have formed a graben. The graben is underlain by Upper Cretaceous Mancos Shale that had down-dropped approximately 170 m relative to the adjacent horst ridgelines composed of resistant Cretaceous Naturita Formation (Dakota Sandstone), Burro Canyon Formation, and Jurassic Morrison Formation. It is unclear if Quaternary deposits are displaced by the newly mapped faults. The weak, easily eroded shale bedrock within the graben is partially buried by Bull Lake glaciofluvial gravel deposits and subsequent landslides. The paleochannel within the graben records an earlier course of the Uncompahgre River before the river was diverted to its present valley.

title: Fire after the Ice: Reconstructing Postglacial Fire History at Middle Mountain Bog, New Hampshire.
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Conley, Bryan [1], Pendleton , Simon [2], Doner, Lisa [3], Neely, John [4], Guiterman, Christopher [5]
affiliations: (1) Environmental Science and Policy Program, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH, USA
(2) Environmental Science and Policy Program, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH, USA
(3) Environmental Science and Policy Program, Plymouth State University, Plymouth, NH, USA
(4) NH Department of Natural and Cultural Resources, Concord, NH, USA
(5) Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado-Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: New Hampshire forest composition and wildfire risk are changing under pressure from climate change and other anthropogenic pressures. To address these changes, updated forest management practices, especially on the use of prescribed fire, are needed. Reconstructions of fire histories in New Hampshire can provide important context in the development of future forest management practices. Lakes and bogs can preserve charcoal generated by fires, recording variations in fire frequency and regime over millennia. Here we present a reconstruction of fire activity from deglaciation to present preserved in the bog sediments from Middle Mountain Bog in Conway, New Hampshire. A 208 cm sediment core was extracted from the bog in 2024, capturing deglacial sediments at the bottom. Selected charcoal fragments and macrofossils were radiocarbon-dated, producing an age-depth model yielding a core basal age of ~17 ka. The cores were subsampled at one-centimeter intervals to produce a high-resolution record of charcoal particle concentrations across 3 grain sizes (125-250, 250-500,> 500 µm). Initial charcoal abundance and size distributions are variable throughout the record, suggesting the bog is capturing both local and farther-afield fire events and/or experiencing fluctuations in fire regime. Charcoal analyses are ongoing to complete the record. We are awaiting additional radiocarbon ages to reduce uncertainty in the initial age model as well. The complete record will provide insights into how fire has evolved on the landscape and what impacts that might have on vegetation changes and forest composition following the ice sheet's retreat. More recent segments of the record may shed light on Indigenous burning practices, European settlement, land clearing, agriculture, or other anthropogenic land uses. In summary, this new long-term record of fire regime will provide valuable information to researchers, conservation organizations, and land management partners.

title: Beyond the Flow-Weighted Mixture: An Axisymmetric MODFLOW-USG Workflow for Simulating Turbulent Wellbore Transport in Long-Screened Wells
session_title: Advances in hydrologic modeling
authors: Valencia, Miguel E. [1], Day-Lewis, Frederick D. [2], Hankins, Abbey S [3], Langevin, Christian [4], Iveson, Rebecka [5], Mackley, Rob D [6]
affiliations: (1) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA, USA
(2) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA, USA
(3) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richalnd, WA, USA
(4) S.S. Papadopulos & Associates, Inc., USA
(5) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA, USA
(6) Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA, USA
abstract:
Conventional groundwater models often simplify well construction details, such as filter packs and turbulent wellbore dynamics (common under high extraction rates or restrictive downhole equipment), typically assuming laminar flow. Consequently, these simplified representations may not fully capture the complex aquifer-well interactions, potentially masking vertical aquifer heterogeneity. These approximations can bias concentration estimates, increasing uncertainty and leading to underestimated aquifer contamination and suboptimal remediation strategies.

To address these limitations, we developed a high-resolution, open-source Python workflow using MODFLOW-USG coupled with the Connected Linear Network (CLN) package to simulate turbulent pipe flow within the well, using Darcy-Weisbach friction formulations. The refined axisymmetric model features over 50,000 nodes, utilizing a logarithmic radial discretization extending 2,000 feet and 500 vertical layers (of uniform 1-ft thickness) to explicitly parameterize casing zones, screens, and permeable filter packs (e.g., sand) which are characteristic of long-screened wells at remediation sites.

Transient simulations demonstrate that extraction induces strong upward vertical gradients below the pump intake. This mechanism acts as a hydraulic sweep, funneling deep contaminant mass upward through the highly conductive wellbore. Simulations also capture post-pumping recovery, revealing the wellbore remains a preferential conduit for ambient mixing after extraction ceases. This internal mixing modifies the resulting breakthrough curves compared to standard, non-turbulent conceptual models, producing samples that represent flow-weighted mixtures rather than depth-specific concentrations.

To bridge the gap between advanced numerical methodologies and applied practice, this workflow integrates an interactive 3D graphical user interface (GUI) for visualizing complex spatial concentration profiles and transient cell-by-cell fluxes. By accurately resolving internal wellbore mixing, this framework helps hydrogeologists interpret sampling data and optimize long-screen well operations. Future work will expand this foundational framework to address bypass flow, discrete packer systems, and automated parameter estimation.

title: A Tale of Two Drifts: Reconstructing Surface Water Variability on Eirik and Gardar Drifts from Planktonic Foraminiferal Species Counts
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Sarkar, Ria [1], Neitzke-Adamo , Lauren [2], Wright , James D. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ, USA; Rutgers Geology Museum, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
(3) Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
abstract:
The North Atlantic plays a critical role in regulating Earth's climate. Geochemical and sedimentological marine proxy records demonstrate that oceanographic conditions during the last glacial interval differed from the modern ocean (Broecker, 1991; Hunter et al., 2007; Channell et al., 2014, and others). Changes in ocean circulation have been documented during abrupt millennial-scale climate events that punctuated the last deglaciation, including Heinrich-1 (H1), the Bølling–Allerød (BA), and the Younger Dryas (YD) (e.g., Hodell et al., 2009, 2015; Muschitiello et al., 2019). Understanding changes in both surface and deep-water circulation in the North Atlantic is essential for identifying the mechanisms that drive abrupt climate variability.

This study integrates paleontological, sedimentological, and geochemical analyses of sediment cores 15JPC (Eirik Drift; 2,240 m water depth) and 13JPC (Gardar Drift; 3,082m water depth). Downcore planktonic foraminiferal species counts were analyzed to reconstruct rapid climate and water-mass changes from the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) to the present. These cores were selected because they contain expanded deglacial sections, exhibit high sedimentation rates, and are located downstream of major North Atlantic deep-water sources, including Denmark Strait Overflow Water (DSOW) and Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water (ISOW). Core 13JPC has recently obtained seven AMS radiocarbon dates, providing improved age control, as well as planktonic δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C records, ice-rafted detritus (IRD) counts, and calculated sedimentation rates. Core 15JPC includes previously generated benthic and planktonic δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C records along with percent coarse fraction data. The primary objective of this study is to develop comparable paleoceanographic records from both cores to evaluate variations in water-mass contributions and deep-water circulation since the LGM.

Preliminary results reveal the expected dominance of the polar planktonic species, Neogloboquadrina pachyderma (sinistral) in core 15JPC, whereas the subpolar species Globigerina bulloides increases during warmer intervals and dominates much of core 13JPC. At 13JPC, elevated percent coarse fraction, increased IRD abundance, and higher sedimentation rates during the YD coincide with increased benthic δ¹³C values measured in Planulina wuellerstorfi from 15JPC. Together, these observations are interpreted to reflect vigorous North Atlantic deep-water formation, consistent with a conveyor circulation operating in an "on" mode during the YD. Records from both cores support this interpretation, but more analyses are needed to better understand these relationships and changes in water masses during the last deglaciation.

title: Revisiting Ninety-Year-Old Structural Data From the Barrovian Sequence of Dutchess County, New York
session_title: More than just wet feldspar: Developments on the Origin, Properties and Evolution of Continental Lower Crust (Posters)
authors: Blatchford, Hannah [1], Bogedain, Brett [2], Koita, Gouro [3], Hamelin, Clementine [4]
affiliations: (1) Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI,
(2) Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI,
(3) Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, MI, USA
(4) William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA, USA
abstract:
Rocks exposed in Dutchess County, New York were metamorphosed during the Taconic orogeny to form a Barrovian sequence that has been widely used as a teaching example in undergraduate petrology courses. Dutchess County is a “classic” example of Barrovian metamorphism in that the field area contains the complete sequence of index minerals from chlorite through sillimanite–K-feldspar; it is also classic in that it was first mapped and described in the 1930s (i.e., Balk, 1936; Barth, 1936), before the area returned to its current state of extensive forest cover. Studies in the intervening ninety years have included somewhat limited thermobarometry, thermochronology, and structural studies, which have yielded P-T-t estimates of peak and retrograde metamorphism, and recognition of an Acadian structural overprint within a study area occupying a portion of Dutchess County. To date, however, there has been no work directed at documenting the extent of the Acadian overprint across the rest of Dutchess County, nor have recognized map-scale shear zones been investigated to characterize the timing and conditions of their activity. This has left the metamorphic geology research and teaching communities with an incomplete picture of the Dutchess County Barrovian sequence.

As an early step in working on this problem, we present a structural analysis of Dutchess County rocks using measurements derived primarily from the mapping work of Balk (1936), and compare their data to measurements and structures derived from comparatively more recent work completed in restricted areas of Dutchess County (i.e., Ratcliffe and Burton, 1990; Proctor et al., 2013). The newly digitized structural dataset of Balk (1936) consists of >2200 measurements of bedding, foliation, fold axes, and lineations, including >700 foliation-lineation pairs. Given the current limited outcrop access due to dense vegetation and land ownership considerations, reevaluation of previously published structural data is an accessible approach to building a detailed structural framework in which to place future targeted petrochronology work.

title: Using digital data systems to support transparent evaluation of field-based models: Uncertainty, Salience, and Critical Outcrops
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Nelson, Ellen M. [1], Shipley, Thomas [2], Tikoff, Basil [3], Trevino, Sarah [4], Wilson, Cristina [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin– Madison, Madison, WI,
(2) Temple University,
(3) University of Wisconsin– Madison,
(4) Southern Methodist University,
(5) Oregon State,
abstract: Over the recent decade, the way we collect and share geologic data has gone through an immense transformation as the community develops new technology and software for recording and sharing information. However, for all these innovations, little consideration has been put forth towards understanding what new types of data that would be worth collecting and sharing. Historically, mappers have used field notebooks to record their progression scientific thinking and model development for a region. The observations made and the data collected during a field campaign was distilled into a static map and an associated report or paper. These mediums limit the amount of information that can be shared with practitioners who did not go to a particular field area and require end users to make inferences about the process of data collection. Digital data systems can be used to share some of the more multifaceted dimensions of field work and model development that until now have been relegated to an individual’s notes. Here we present three associated data types– uncertainty, salience, and critical outcrops– which can be readily evaluated and shared using modern workflows. Uncertainty provides a semi-quantitative evaluation of field observations, salience provides an evaluation of the weight of a particular observation in regard to a conceptual model of a region, and critical outcrops highlights which areas are the most important for model development. The three data types can be incorporated easily into current mapping workflows. The resulting map layers efficiently show the distribution of quality and/or influential outcrops, which could guide data collection during current or future field campaigns. The inclusion of these new types of data aims to bring more information from the field which will enable reviewers, colleagues, students, and future practitioners to make more nuanced evaluations of models. By telling others exactly which data point was used to create a conceptual model, and how certain the underlying observations are, the trust in models increases. Furthermore, a preserved record of the uncertainty and criticality of data could help direct future decision-making, by human scientists or other agents, regarding revaluation of where more research resources should be expended.

title: A novel method for measuring phytolith carbon concentrations reveals the impact of phytoliths on carbon sequestration
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution
authors: Economos, Rita C. [1], Stiles, Elena [2], Stromberg, Caroline A. E. [3], Jacobs, Bonita Fine [4], Nagashima, Kazu [5], Nolan, Travis [6], Freeman, Craig [7]
affiliations: (1) University of Hawai'i at Manoa, Honolulu, HI,
(2) California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(3) University of Washington, Seattle, WA,
(4) Southern Methodist University, Dallas, TX,
(5) University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, Honolulu, HI, USA
(6) Southern Methodist University, Dallas, TX, USA
(7) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
abstract:
Phytoliths, microscopic silica bodies (~10–40 μm), form when living plants take up monosilicic acid through their roots and deposit them in their tissues. They are particularly abundant in Poaceae (grasses) and form a sizable silica pool in grassland soils after grass tissue decays. Phytoliths incorporate carbon in their silica matrix, so-called phytolith-occluded carbon (PhytOC). Whether PhytOC contributes to the significant underground carbon storage in grasslands is debated, but has major implications for global carbon sequestration estimates, as >40% of terrestrial surfaces are currently covered by natural and agricultural grasslands. Bulk grass phytolith carbon content estimates range from 0.1% to >10%, resulting in major differences in modeled sequestration estimates.

We present a novel approach for measuring individual phytolith carbon concentrations that uses secondary ionization mass spectrometry. We sampled four greenhouse-grown grasses and seven wild grasses collected in the Great Plains, USA, together covering a range of ecological settings (open- vs. closed-habitat grasses, C 3 vs. C 4 ). Grass silica short cell phytoliths (GSSCPs) were mounted in indium and analyzed using the CAMECA 1280 Ion Microprobe at University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. A spot size of 3–4 μm allowed for analyses within phytoliths without overlapping grain margins. A calibration curve was generated using a set of homogenized nanopowder mixtures of SiO 2 and C with concentrations from 0.11 to 2.8 wt% C.

Measured carbon concentration in 175 phytoliths ranged from below detection (~0.01 wt% C) to above the calibration curve threshold. Average greenhouse-grown sample concentrations ranged from 0.04–1.3 wt% C, excluding Chusquea culeou (bambusoid), which exceeds measurement thresholds using our analytical setup. Species average concentrations in wild grasses ranged from 0.014–0.69 wt% C. Wild C 3 grasses have low PhytOC (0.014–0.21 wt% C) and low intra-phytolith variability. C 4 species contain higher wt% C (0.24–0.69 wt% C) and display more intra-phytolith variability. Broader taxonomic sampling and analysis of non-GSSCP phytoliths are needed to fully understand carbon concentration patterns within Poaceae. Our preliminary results indicate both a wide range of PhytOC values among grasses in general and the tendency for C 4 species to sequester more carbon than C 3 taxa. If this latter finding holds true with additional sampling, it will have tremendous implications for carbon cycle functioning and thus for climate mitigation strategies.
