title: Evaluating the Influence of Provenance on Paleo-Weathering Proxies in Upper Devonian Paleosols of North-Central Pennsylvania
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Revas, Angelena Rose [1], Wetherspoon, Rachel [2], Trop, Jeffrey M. [3], Roop, Cassidy [4], Barth, Aaron M. [5], Pfeifer, Lily S. [6]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ, USA
(2) Geology, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ, USA
(3) Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, USA
(4) Bucknell University, Lewisburg, PA, USA
(5) Geology, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ, USA
(6) Geology, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ, USA
abstract: Major-element oxide proportions from paleosols have long been used as proxies for chemical weathering, but recent studies identify limitations regarding how provenance may overwhelm paleoclimate signals in such proxy applications. The Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA), a widely applied paleo-weathering proxy, was used to assess chemical weathering as recorded by 68 Upper Devonian paleosols in the Appalachian Basin (north-central Pennsylvania). These paleosols record paleo-weathering conditions on basinal floodplains just before, and during, deposition of ~361–359 Ma hinterland-proximal diamictites (Spechty Kopf Formation) that have been interpreted as subtropical Appalachian Mountain glacial strata. With a relatively tight cluster of CIA values ranging from ~70–80, the paleosol geochemistry, without consideration of provenance, is interpreted to reflect intermediate chemical weathering. A lower chemical weathering signal (lower CIA values) is typically expected for pro-periglacial conditions (dominated by physical weathering). However, CIA values may be elevated owing to, for example, abundant aluminum-rich schist sources in the hinterland (evinced by abundant detrital muscovite in fluvial strata, schist-phyllite clasts in contemporaneous diamictites, and Famennian muscovite ages in fluvial strata and schist sources). To assess the extent to which provenance affects these weathering signatures, we present the major-element geochemistry of Appalachian basement terranes that best-represent the source of Appalachian basin sediment (paleosols) based on previous paleocurrent data, lithofacies trends, detrital ages, and Late Famennian (~360 Ma) bedrock cooling ages. Metamorphic and igneous bedrock units ( N = 10) from Eastern Pennsylvania to Western Connecticut were sampled and analyzed using Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence. In addition, metamorphic and igneous clasts from the coeval Spechty Kopf diamictite were isolated, sorted, and analyzed by clast lithology type ( N = 5). We present A-CNK-FM (Al 2 O 3 - CaO+Na 2 O+ K 2 O - Fe 2 O 3 +MgO) ternary diagrams and assess the distribution (and weathering trends) of source-to-sink CIA values. Preliminary results for CIA show that source terrane geochemistry overlaps with paleosol geochemistry but has a much larger scatter, including low CIAs (pegmatites) and high CIAs (Western CT schist, Spechty Kopf clasts). This study tests and builds upon developing methods to separate the climate signature from provenance.

title: Combining Detrital Zircon U-Pb Ages and Grain Size to Trace Sediment Provenance from Coastal to Deep-Marine Environments, New Zealand
session_title: Geochronology Across Scales: Highlighting New Perspectives from Emerging Researchers. (Posters)
authors: Unger, Abigail Elizabeth [1], Sharman, Glenn R [2], Martin, Gabrielle A [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
(3) University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
abstract:
Sediment routing from source terranes to depositional sinks reflects the interplay of tectonics, climate, and transport processes, but tracing these pathways is challenging in tectonically complex settings. The South Island of New Zealand offers a natural laboratory for this problem: its Eastern and Western Provinces carry distinct detrital zircon age signatures, allowing sediment derived from each province to be traced from source to sink. We combined detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology with grain-size analysis across a set of modern and offshore samples: coastal sites at Wharariki Beach and Farewell Spit and offshore deep-sea cores from the Taranaki Basin. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) was used to compare sample similarity, and mixture modeling was used to estimate how much each potential source terrane contributed. We also paired grain-size data with U-Pb age to test whether zircon size can serve as an additional provenance indicator, distinguishing locally derived from far-traveled sediment.

Contributions from the Eastern and Western Provinces vary between coastal and offshore samples: MDS results separate samples by provenance affinity, and mixture modeling indicates differing proportions of source-terrane contribution across sites rather than a single uniform mixing signal. Grain size adds another layer to this pattern. At Wharariki Beach and Farewell Spit, locally derived Cretaceous and Devonian (plutonic-sourced) zircon are consistently coarser and span a wider grain-size range, while distally sourced Permo-Triassic and older (>500 Ma) zircon are finer-grained and more restricted in size. A similar, though more subdued, relationship is observed in the deep-water Taranaki Basin cores. This grain-size/age relationship is a promising additional tool for distinguishing near- from far-traveled sediment, complementing the U-Pb provenance signal, and providing a clearer picture of how sediment moves from northern South Island source regions into modern coastal and deep-marine sinks.

title: Static U and Th Isotope Measurement using Multi Daly (MD)-Multi-Collector (MC)-ICP-MS for U-Series Dating

abstract:
Incorporation of multiple high-sensitivity Daly detectors on the Nu Plasma 3D MC-ICP-MS facilitates fast static measurement of multiple low-abundance isotopes, such as 229 Th, 230 Th, and 232 Th or 233 U, 234 U, 235 U, and 236 U. The Texas Isotope Geochemistry Research (TIGR) Lab in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at The University of Texas at Austin has one of the first Nu Plasma 3D MC-ICP-MS with 6 Daly and 16 Faraday detectors, designed to facilitate static multi-Daly analysis of Pb, U and Th isotopes.

The newly-created procedure measures all masses of U and Th in Daly detectors except 238 U. Individual measurements, including on-peak zero measurement and washout take ~17 minutes. Standard sample bracketing using spiked in-house standards corrects for analytical mass bias and machine drift. Replicate analyses of 10 ppb solutions yield accurate 234 U/ 238 U ratios with reproducibility of 0.14% (2SD). Analyses of an in-house calcite standard yields ages that are within uncertainty of ages generated by MC-ICP-MS at University of Minnesota and by thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS) in the TIGR lab yet using sample masses approximately half of those needed for peak hopping on ICP-MS and one tenth of that necessary for TIMS. MD-MC-ICP-MS enables high-precision U/Th ages on small samples (ie. 20-30 mg of speleothem with 100 ppb U) broadening sampling capabilities and enabling the use of less spike. The TIGR lab routinely uses these MD-MC-ICP-MS procedures to measure U/Th ages of stalagmites, corals, calcite veins and ostrich eggshells, facilitating research in a broad range of scientific fields.

title: Planetary Heritage: Learning from Existing Practice and Shaping a New Field
session_title: The Astro-Geoheritage of the Solar System: Past Explorations and Future Considerations

abstract: The field of planetary science presents a distinctive combination of interdisciplinary scientific questions, international cooperation, public interest, and emerging policy pressures that make the development of a planetary heritage framework especially timely. Here, planetary heritage refers broadly to places and environments recognized as significant to the scientific study, exploration, or broader human understanding of planetary worlds. Developing such a framework will require a multidisciplinary movement grounded in the planetary sciences, including planetary geology, astrobiology, planetary atmospheric science, planetary oceanography, astrophysics, and related disciplines. A planetary heritage framework should therefore be broad enough to recognize significance across these areas of inquiry and include terrestrial sites that support studies of planetary processes and environments or inform mission planning. The communities of practice that have developed around geoheritage and astronomical heritage offer valuable experience for this emerging field. Planetary heritage will further need a public-facing and internationally cooperative approach that reflects the way planetary science itself is practiced.

title: Cretaceous rotation of the Late Cretaceous Beaverhead Group, Southwest Montana, associated with fold and thrust belt deformation
session_title: Tectonic evolution of orogenic belts and their hinterland plateaus: From formation, growth, to collapse (Posters)
authors: Nelson, Ellen M. [1], Housen, Bernie A. [2], Garcia Lasanta, Cristina [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin– Madison, Madison, WI,
(2) Western Washington University, Bellingham, WA,
(3) Western Washington University,
abstract: Paleomagnetic data from the Beaverhead Group and other Cretaceous sedimentary units of Southwest Montana help to constrain the timing and extent of vertical axis rotation during thrusting and uplift attributed to the Sevier and Laramide orogenies. Samples of interbedded sandstone lenses within the ~88 to 60 Ma Beaverhead group were collected from 43 sites south of Dillon, MT. Removal of overprinting magnetic vectors using alternating field and thermal demagnetization reveal a stable remanent magnetization in at least 20 of the sampled sites. High temperature versus magnetic susceptibility plots suggest that titanomagnetite is the primary magnetic carrier. However, moderate Hcr to Hc and Mrs to Mr ratios indicate the an admixture of single domain and multi-domain size magnetic minerals is present. A distinct Hopkinson’s effect in all measured samples could suggest the presence of some smaller presence of pseudo-single domain grains or a mix of single and multi-domain grains. A positive conglomerate test is used to support the claim that this magnetization is primary, and thus can inform about the origin of this unit. One site preserves reversed polarity which may be used to help constrain the age of deposition. The rest of the sites preserve normal polarity. The sites are influenced by inclination shallowing, with a flattening factor of up to 0.84. Declinations from these sites after tilt correction are variable, and suggest both clockwise and counterclockwise rotations impacted different locations where the Beaverhead Group was sampled. The results from this study, in conjunction with previous paleomagnetic analysis from the area provide details for kinematics of the units effected by folding and thrusting, and will be used to evaluate how the individual, fault-bound, blocks were rotating relative to one another.

affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA; Georgia Space and Rocks (GASPAR) LLC, Loganville, Georgia, USA

abstract:
In addition to the Warm Springs of Georgia, made famous by President Franklin Roosevelt who convalesced in the waters, the central uplift massif of the c. 800 Ma Roosevelt impact structure (RIS) hosts many extensively mineralized hydrothermal breccias. Latent heat from the impact, along with enhanced heat flow above an upwarped mantle, probably contributed to the protracted development of these deposits. But certain large polymict dikes, composed of some meta-sedimentary clasts unknown in the region, more likely were injected during rebound as observed in other large impacts, e.g. Sudbury (Tuchscherer and Spray, Econ. Geol. , 2002).

A special case of those are the ferruginous dikes we previously reported (Harris et al., GSA, 2024) that contain quartzite clasts exhibiting abundant planar deformation features (PDFs) and feather features (FFs). Impact-emplacement of these dikes is supported by the identification of iridium and platinum in the matrix using SEM/EDS at accelerating voltages greater than 30 kV. Analyses of these dikes by LD-ToF-MS demonstrate the presence of lithium, indicative of subsequent alteration by hydrothermal fluids.

The distribution of shock-deformed rocks and impact melt breccias in the RIS interior, together with COCORP seismic data, imply that the rim has a diameter greater than 300 kilometers. Consequently, impact-related rocks might extend to the margins of the exposed Piedmont in northwestern Georgia. Meta-geyserite and additional suevite-like ferruginous breccias occur in positions where we place the outer rim. LD-ToF-MS data show that these breccias contain carbon and fluorine.

Fluorine also may indicate hydrothermal processes, but we are scrutinizing the carbon. LD-ToF-MS data suggest the possibility that it occurs with Si-C. This would be consistent with finding a TiC grain (which are common in primitive meteorites) in the central injection dikes. We previously (Harris et al., LPSC, 2021; Harris et al., GSA, 2025) raised the possibility that the RIS is associated with the c. 800 Ma comet/asteroid shower in the Earth-Moon system (Terada et al., Nature Comm., 2020) and the c. 810 Ma Bitter Springs negative ∂ 13 C anomaly. Bottke et al. ( Planet. Sci. J. , 2026) has proposed that the disruption of a primitive carbonaceous parent body to produce the Eulalia asteroid family could have precipitated those events. Such an event would further strengthen multiple connections with the Roosevelt impact.

title: Dinosaur track and invertebrate trace preservation by early calcite cements at the Maastrichtian Carreras Pampa site in Torotoro National Park, Bolivia
session_title: Deciphering the Sedimentological Mechanisms Governing Preservation of Vertebrate Tracks Across Diverse Depositional Environments
authors: Nick, Kevin E. [1], Zuniga, Saul Marcelo [2], Llempen, Nelson Alem [3], Biaggi, Roberto E. [4]
affiliations: (1) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA
(2) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA, USA
(3) Loma Linda Univ Library, Loma Linda, CA, USA
(4) Loma Linda University, Loma Linda,, CA, USA
abstract:
A bedding plane at the Carreras Pampa site, Torotoro National Park (TTNP), Bolivia, contains over 15,000 theropod foot tracks, tail drag traces, hundreds of bird tracks, more than one hundred dinosaur swim traces, and invertebrate traces. All vertebrate categories include long trackways recording variations in behavior and their abundance increases the likelihood of observing track overprinting. The tracked bed is in the lower middle unit of the Maastrichtian El Molino Formation.

The large abundance of trace fossils allowed establishment of an ichnostratigraphy that begins with deep foot tracks (some with tail traces) that cut wave rippled bedforms, indicating initial preserved tracks followed decreasing lake level. Successive overprinting shows a general decrease in track depth through time controlled by changing substrate rheology, with overlapping of bird tracks on track expulsion rims and surface exposures of invertebrate traces. The final tracks are scratches of swimming theropods that crosscut all other features and indicate lake level rise prior to mudstone deposition. An inverse correlation between the depth of track and the order of formation was generally observed. The time span over which the tracks formed is indicated by the stratigraphy of overprinting and cross-cutting relations as some animals stepped on previously formed tracks and must have been of limited duration since tracks survived coeval degradation.

The tracked surface was buried by a fine mudstone, but details of preservation suggest stabilization occurred before burial and begs the question of how trace stratigraphy was generated and preserved. Three lines of evidence support a model of early calcite cementation to explain track and invertebrate trace appearances. First are the stratigraphic relationships with track depth inversely related to order. Second, the preserved textures of acicular and bladed isopachous calcite crusts on carbonate and quartz grains indicate primary cement textures were preserved. Third, the preservation of intergranular space and oversize pores required early cementation. Abundant carbonate grains of nested ostracods, ooids, and peloids show paleoenvironmental conditions favored carbonate precipitation. Microbial effects on track preservation cannot be excluded, but no direct evidence for them was observed. Our preferred model is that carbonate and quartz grains were stabilized by incipient calcite cements that increasingly stabilized the substrate while tracks and traces accumulated. Records of animal activity were a critical constraint in deciphering early cementation.

title: Along-strike variation in exhumation and topographic evolution in the Eastern Cordillera of Peru and Bolivia
session_title: Pre–Neogene Tectonic evolution of South America
authors: Saylor, Joel [1], Martin, Samuel [2], Shekut, Samuel [3]
affiliations: (1) University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC,
(2) University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
(3) University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
abstract:
The Eastern Cordillera of Bolivia and Peru intercept southward-transported, moisture-bearing air masses, leading to significant orographic rainout and both along- and across-strike variability in aridity. Nevertheless, the exhumation of the Bolivian and Peruvian Eastern Cordillera are typically considered as a two-dimensional problem where the primary variation is across strike. Similarly, topographic evolution is typically compared to the latitudinally adjacent Altiplano and Western Cordillera. Latitudinally homogenous exhumation is most easily envisioned as the result of variation in taper of an internally homogeneous orogenic wedge. However, a growing body of research has highlighted along-strike variation in the timing of exhumation and topographic growth in the Eastern Cordillera, possibly resulting from upper plate heterogeneities or variations in lower plate behaviour. The non-uniform uplift and exhumation of the Eastern Cordillera has first-order implications for history of moisture intrusion into the Altiplano.

In this presentation we synthesize thermochronological, stratigraphic, provenance, and flexural modelling data to test the hypothesis that significant along-strike variability in exhumation and topographic evolution was driven by collision and southward migration of one or more oceanic plateaux. Thermochronology indicates a broadly north-south younging trend in the onset of exhumation. In contrast stratigraphic and provenance data indicate that a north-south trend of Eastern Cordilleran exhumation in southern Peru is mirrored by a south-north trend in southern Bolivia, such that the region most recently impacted by Eastern Cordilleran exhumation appears to be ~18°S. Flexural modelling provides additional support for this scenario; indicating that topographic growth occurred most recently at ~18°S. This topographic gap in the Eastern Cordillera has implications for moisture penetration into the Altiplano. The timing of aridification in the Altiplano at ~18°S postdates that to the north or south, reflecting the lower topography in the Eastern Cordillera.

We conclude that the topographic and exhumational history of the Eastern Cordillera is inconsistent with simple north-south migration of a subducted oceanic plateau or with latitudinally homogenous orogenic wedge behaviour. Instead it suggests that exhumation of the Eastern Cordillera was primarily due to reactivation of Mesozoic rift structures by far-field stresses, resulting in initial exhumation and topographic uplift focused at the latitudes of the northern and southern Altiplano. We speculate that the far field stresses may have been induced by collision of one or more oceanic plateaux.

abstract: When walking through the desert landscapes of New Mexico, it may seem like you have been transported to a different planet. Unsurprisingly, these terrestrial landscapes share many similarities with other planetary bodies such as Mars. In the Quebradas area, just east of Socorro, NM, many units host massive outcrops of Paleozoic sulfate minerals, primarily gypsum. Nearby, younger lacustrine sulfate deposits from the central Rio Grande rift are also present. Sulfate deposits have been found in various locations on Mars, including the Gale and Jezero craters. Similar systems on Earth are important analogs that we can use to investigate the habitability of ancient Martian environments and test analytical methods for biosignature detection. In this work, we assess the Quebradas as a geochemical and depositional analog for sulfate-rich environments on Mars by combining past investigations of the geologic history of each planet with mineralogical, isotopic, and organic preservation data collected from gypsum samples in the Quebradas. Bulk mineralogy was determined by powder X-ray diffraction and thin section petrography. Gypsum was found to be the dominant sulfate mineral in all samples, frequently with minor quartz, clays, or other salts. Mars has a more complex sulfate mineralogy, such as the Mg-sulfates found in the Gale crater, which is not represented in the Quebradas. 𝛿 34 S values of the Quebradas sulfates range from -3.5 to +17.6‰, while the younger sulfates range from +3.8 to +6.5‰ and are consistent with an evaporitic lacustrine system. 𝛿 34 S values in the Quebradas have a smaller range than those reported on Mars, meaning that additional processes beyond the depositional conditions of the Quebradas are necessary to explain the full isotopic range of Martian sulfates. Carbon content was determined using infrared spectrophotometry and evolved gas analysis. Organic carbon was scarce, <0.4 wt. %, and usually associated with other phases, such as clays, indicating that clay-associated sulfates may better preserve organics. While failing to replicate certain Martian environments perfectly, sulfate units in the Quebradas do contain many Mars-like features such as depositional and mineralogical similarities and low organic volume. This makes sulfates in the Quebradas area and central Rio Grande Rift an analog environment well tailored to investigating habitability and biosignature detection in sulfate-bearing units.

title: Characterizing Selenium Distribution and Sources in Surface and Groundwater of the Southern Great Salt Lake Wetlands
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Flexhaug, Megan Nicole [1], Carling, Gregory T. [2], Lopez, Samuel F. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA; Utah Water Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
(2) Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
(3) Utah Water Science Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract:
Great Salt Lake (GSL) is a critical habitat for millions of migratory birds, acting as a crucial migration waypoint in their travels. Recent analyses of a limited number of American avocet and black-necked stilt eggs collected from the south shore of GSL have shown elevated selenium (Se) values, raising concerns about future exceedances of GSL-specific Se water quality standards and potential impacts to food webs. While surface water inputs have been previously monitored for Se, groundwater has remained an undercharacterized Se source, potentially accounting for the missing Se load identified in previous mass-balance studies. The central focus of this study is to quantify water chemistry along the south shore of GSL in order to determine the distribution and sources of Se in groundwater seeps and surface water tributaries. Additional objectives include understanding Se speciation and characterizing other trace metal contaminants such as arsenic (As) and lead (Pb).

Over a one-year period, we conducted biweekly sampling of six routine surface water sites and collected 50 groundwater samples from seeps identified via thermal drone imagery and on the ground reconnaissance. Surface and groundwater samples were analyzed for a suite of geochemical constituents, including trace elements like Se and As. Preliminary results show that groundwater sites have an average Se concentration of 4.00 micrograms per liter (μg/L), with a maximum value of 20.27 μg/L. Surface waters show that Lee Creek has an average Se concentration of 2.40 μg/L across all 3 sites, whereas both the Jordan Valley and Kennecott outfalls have higher Se concentrations, Jordan Valley averaging 11.02 μg/L, with a maximum of 23.14 μg/L and Kennecott averaging 17.63 μg/L with a maximum of 22.09 μg/L. Arsenic is also a contaminant of interest, and approximately 30% of the groundwater samples exceed the EPA saltwater acute criteria maximum concentration of 69 μg/L, with the highest value reaching 1,752.5 μg/L. Further testing is necessary to ascertain if occurrences of higher Se concentrations have more to do with seasonal variations, nearby industry, or spatial location. This study will provide valuable information about Se and trace element dynamics of terminal lakes such as GSL, allowing for more accurate data in order to protect this keystone ecosystem and informing further research and actions.

title: Initial Insights into Paleoenvironmental and Paleofaunal Characteristics of a Recently Exposed Outcrop of the Clayton Formation in Tippah County, Mississippi
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Usachenko, Natalya [1]
affiliations: (1) Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality, Mississippi Office of Geology, Jackson, Mississippi, USA
abstract:
A recently exposed outcrop of the Clayton Formation in Tippah County, Mississippi was measured and is currently being described and sampled for ongoing geologic and paleontologic analyses. The Clayton Formation represents Danian-aged sedimentary deposits that stratigraphically and temporally succeed the Cretaceous-Paleogene event layer exposed in the Mississippi Embayment.

The outcrop was measured to be approximately 9 meters (30ft) thick from the base of exposure to the overlying weathered soil horizon. The individual sedimentary layers are gradational and consist of glauconitic calcareous silts and sands, sandy limestone, and carbonaceous silty clays. The sediments range from highly to sparsely fossiliferous, exhibiting vertebrate and invertebrate macro and microfauna and extensive bioturbation.

The entire measured section is currently broadly divided into seven primary beds: the basal bed consists of dense, fossiliferous calcareous silty sandstone abundant in bryozoans and small ostreids. This transitions into a relatively solid, dense, calcareous sandy limestone with limited bioturbation. The overlying bed is darker, sandier, and heavily bioturbated, with many burrow clasts containing numerous bryozoans. This grades upward into an almost coquina-like shell dense layer exhibiting more extensive aragonitic preservation as well as an abundance of decapod, osteichthyan, selachian, and occasional crocodilian fossil material. Overlying strata consist of an upward fining sequence into fossiliferous, fine-grained quartzose clayey sand. The top of this sequence grades into micaceous carbonaceous fissile silty clay containing oblong phosphatic nodules along the gradational contact as well as a high concentration of plant matter. The final interval is a highly glauconitic, heavily bioturbated sand containing a phosphatic pebble lag, intermittent bivalves, and nautiloid molds near the top.

It is currently hypothesized that this sequence of deposits formed in a relatively shallow marine environment that underwent fluctuating influences from transitionary coastal lagoon or estuarine environments. Bulk sediment samples from each measured layer are being processed for paleofaunal characterization at a finer resolution.

title: Middle and Upper Permian Lithofacies and Strontium Isotopic Study of the FS-337 Drill Core from the Central Basin Platform of the Permian Basin, West Texas
session_title: The data that define the strata: advances in applying geochemistry and geochronology to geologic mapping and stratigraphic correlation (Posters)
authors: Deese, Nathan [1], Uddin, Ashraf [2], King, David T. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Auburn, Alabama, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL,
(3) Department of Geosciences, Auburn University, Auburn, AL,
abstract:
Middle and Upper Permian stratigraphy of the Central Basin Platform within the Permian Basin of West Texas preserves a detailed record of changing depositional environments associated with fluctuating sea levels during the final stages of formation of the Permian Basin. This study investigates the FS-337 drill core, a 1,067-foot section taken from the Central Basin Platform. This well penetrates through parts of six formations from top to bottom: Dewey Lake (27 ft – 70 ft), Rustler (71 ft – 551 ft), Salado (555 ft – 812 ft), Tansill (812 ft – 903 ft), Yates (903 ft – 1039 ft), and Seven Rivers (1,040 ft – 1,067 ft). Each stratigraphic horizon records a distinct stage of evolution in the basin, transitioning from shallow marine carbonate deposition within the lower formations to increasingly restricted evaporitic conditions before fully transitioning to terrestrial sedimentation. The Seven Rivers and Yates formations represent a carbonate shelf environment with some mixed siliciclastic layers, suggesting subtidal conditions. This transitions to the Tansill and Salado formations, that include some evaporitic sequences. This suggests a progressively shallowing tidal flat environment. These sequences of evaporites thicken towards the Rustler and Dewey Lake formations, wherein continental sediments suggest a complete cessation of marine deposition across the Central Basin Platform.

By performing sedimentologic and petrographic analysis of the drill core, this study aims to reconstruct the depositional history of the Central Basin Platform during Middle and Late Permian in relation to sea level change. After establishing the general stratigraphic framework, geochemical analysis via 87Sr/86Sr will be conducted to further establish relative dates and a more precise timeline for facies deposition. Heavy mineral analysis will also be performed on the terrestrial formations to determine provenance and give more insight into how the area evolved post marine recession. These methods together will help to provide a detailed framework of how the Central Basin Platform evolved during Middle and Late Permian and will ultimately help answer the question of how the fluctuating sea levels and eventual total recession affected the deposition within the region.

title: Geodesy and Seismicity of the Apennine Mountains as a Test of Buoyancy-Driven Mountain Building
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Wernicke, Brian [1], Bradley, Kyle [2]
affiliations: (1) Division of Geological and Planetary Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA
abstract: Analog experiments, numerical modeling and field observations (e.g. Chemenda et al., 1995, EPSL 132; Butler et al., 2013, EPSL 377; Price and Wernicke, 2021, JGeol 129, respectively) suggest that the positive buoyancy of partially subducted continental crust may be a significant or even primary source of stress driving the development of thrust and nappe structure, crustal thickening and the topographic rise of orogens. In the case of the Alps, Adria appears to have fully “docked” against the European foreland by 33 Ma (lower marine Molasse overlap in the Inn Valley), prior to the tectonic interposition of the Pennine and Helvetic zones between the Austroalpine allochthon and Europe ca. 30-15 Ma. The basic physics of (1) partial subduction of continental crust, coupled to the downgoing slab during plate convergence, followed by (2) buoyancy forces overwhelming coupling due to thermal weakening, and (3) crustal thickening via up-slab buoyant rise of detached upper continental crust, mainly after convergence, may best account for the timing and kinematics of Alpine nappe structure and mountain building. The model predicts that up-slab motion may occur in the absence of significant plate convergence. An important analog of this type of “endogenous” source of stress may now be occurring along the modern SW flank of Adria, where it is subducting southwestward beneath the Apennines. We compiled the regional GPS velocity field with earthquake hypocenters and focal mechanisms beneath the Italian Peninsula. The GPS data indicate, in a relatively static European reference frame on the SW, NE and N sides of Adria, the east flank of the Peninsula is moving ca. 5 mm/yr northeastward away from the SW coast of Italy (which is relatively static in the European frame), toward the Dalmatian coast. NE-SW seismic cross-sections across the Peninsula image a SW-inclined zone of thrust faults as deep as 70 km beneath the Apennines, overlain by an upper crustal zone of normal faulting, centered on the Apennine crest. The seismicity defines a SW-inclined slab of crust between the normal and thrust faults moving upward along the top of the Adria. The motion of the slab may thus be an active example of the 30-15 Ma northward motion of the Pennine zone between a relatively static Adria above and the European plate below.

title: Geologic Map of Sand Creek and South Colony Lakes, Sangre de Cristo Range, Colorado
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Frawley, Dylan Liam [1], Singleton, John [2], Broeder, Hunter Joseph [3], Brogan, Hari [4], Lobbezoo, Sam [5]
affiliations: (1) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,
(2) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO,
(3) Colorado State Univ, Geosciences, Fort Collins, CO,
(4) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
(5) Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
abstract:
The Sangre de Cristo Range of south-central Colorado records deformation associated with Proterozoic polyphase contraction, Pennsylvanian–Permian Ancestral Rocky Mountain (ARM) contraction, Late Cretaceous–Early Paleogene Laramide contraction, and the onset of Rio Grande Rift magmatism and extension in the Oligocene. A ~100 km 2 geologic map was produced along the crest of the range in and around Sand Creek and South Colony Lakes—as well as the eastern range front—with emphasis on structural data collection associated with ARM and Laramide deformation, and Mesoproterozoic (~1.4 Ga) deformation. Previous investigators have proposed the expression of ARM deformation in the Sangre de Cristo Range based on the presence of growth strata within the Pennsylvanian–Permian Crestone Conglomerate. New mapping has documented an intraformational angular unconformity within the Crestone Conglomerate as associated with the Little Sand Creek fault System and the Sand Creek syncline, as well as a structural framework for the involvement of the Sand Creek and Little Sand Creek fault systems and the Marble Mountain thrust in ARM deformation. In addition to mapping, extensive collection of brittle fault data is used to better characterize the geometries and kinematics of suspected ARM and Laramide related structures. ARM deformation in the area may have initiated as a foreland-style fold and thrust system, followed by a period of oblique-reverse slip along steep, basement-involved structures. Although it is difficult to quantify the reactivation of ARM structures during the Laramide due to ~NE directed shortening associated with both orogenies, we suggest that Laramide age structures in the map area preferentially exploit mechanically weak stratigraphy in the modern eastern range front.

Detailed mapping has also been used to characterize the style and spatial distribution of Mesoproterozoic age solid state deformation of the ~1.4 Ga Music Pass pluton. Fabrics are predominantly symmetric, and the deformation of feldspar megacrysts reflect plane to flattening strain. The presence of grain boundary migration in quartz and syn-kinematic growth of amphibole suggests amphibolite-grade deformation at temperatures >500° C. Apatite U/Pb yields a Tera-Wasserburg lower intercept age of 1338±15 Ma (timing of cooling below ~500–450°C), providing a minimum age constraint for fabric formation. Mesoproterozoic deformation involved the development of a sub-vertical ~NW-SE-striking fabric due to broadly NE-SW directed coaxial shortening, followed by the subtle folding of foliations about a steeply west-plunging axis.

title: Timing and P–T Evolution of the High-Pressure Schist Belt, Brooks Range, Northern Alaska: Constraints from Lu–Hf Garnet Geochronology and Quartz-in-Garnet Barometry
session_title: From Minerals to Mountains: Interdisciplinary Investigations of Orogenic Systems (Part II)
authors: Pham, Minh T.T. [1], Vogl, James [2], Baker, Peter Louis [3], Vervoort, Jeff David [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA
(3) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
(4) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
abstract:
The Brooks Range of northern Alaska preserves an example of ophiolite obduction and continental margin subduction followed by arc–continent collision in the Early Cretaceous. Continental margin subduction and exhumation are recorded by the >600-km-long Schist Belt, which comprises largely greenschist-overprinted blueschist assemblages and two mafic eclogite lenses. The timing of high-pressure metamorphism has remained poorly constrained, relying primarily on Ar/Ar data and a single unpublished U–Pb zircon study. Previous studies have broadly estimated peak pressures at ~9–16 kbar and maximum temperatures at 500–550°C. Consequently, the pressure–temperature–time (P–T–t) evolution of the Schist Belt remains poorly constrained.

Here, we present seven new Lu–Hf garnet ages (2σ) from the Schist Belt. Southern Schist Belt eclogites yielded ages of 136.0 ± 1.0 Ma near the Dalton Highway and 130.5 ± 1.0 Ma in the Cosmos Hills, ~250 km west. The other five ages are from the blueschist/greenschist rocks that host the eclogites. A meta-sandstone near the southern–northern boundary along the Dalton Highway yielded an age of 124.3 ± 1.4 Ma. Two meta-sedimentary samples from the northernmost Schist Belt along the Dalton Highway yielded ages of 115.4 ± 0.6 Ma and 115.3 ± 0.5 Ma. Interlayered blueschist metapelite and greenschist metabasite from the northern Schist Belt farther west along the Wild River yielded ages of 113.9 ± 0.4 Ma and 113.5 ± 0.3 Ma, respectively. These data document ~22 m.y. of spatially variable garnet growth across the Schist Belt and define a broadly northward-younging pattern.

This new age pattern provides an opportunity to evaluate competing models for the timing and mechanism of continental burial and exhumation of the Schist Belt. In one model, garnets in the southern eclogites record peak burial, whereas younger northern garnets formed during decompression and exhumation. Alternatively, the northward-younging ages may record progressive underplating of structurally distinct crustal slices into the subduction channel, with the ~114–115 Ma garnet growth marking later peak burial in the northern Schist Belt. We are evaluating these models by integrating Lu–Hf garnet growth ages with quartz-in-garnet Raman elastic barometry. This work will provide the first integrated P–T–t framework for the Schist Belt and establish constraints on the tectonic evolution of the Brookian subduction system.

title: Technological Advancements in LA-ICPMS Helping Petrologic Research: What Can We See and What are the Limitations on Accuracy
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part II)
authors: Allen, Charlotte M [1], Caulfield, John T [2], DeBruyn, Mitchell [3], Jenkins, Kate [4], Laupland, Elise B [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia; Central Analytical Research Facility, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia

(2) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia; Central Analytical Research Facility, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia
(3) Central Analytical Research Facility, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia
(4) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queenslnd, Australia
(5) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia
abstract:
Over the past 30 years, Laser Ablation ICPMS has afforded the opportunity not only to date accessory minerals using U and Pb isotopes but also to simultaneously collect mineral trace element data that record compositional features of the evolving host magma. Concentrations as low as a few ppm are measurable. With these data from mineral species like zircon, parts of petrologic histories are revealed; these are especially useful for strongly altered rocks and detritus in which zircon survives. While quantification techniques have not changed much, hardware has improved so that laser positioning is dependable at almost the micron scale, and the ICPMS’s detectors, electron multipliers, are ten percent faster (shorter dead time). The coupled technology across both the laser and the ICP permits spot drilling using beams at the 10s of micron scale and with modern fast detectors, collection of data necessary for dating and 20 trace elements with overall mass cycle times of ~0.4 s. Software providers give tools to view images of the analysis before or after while undertaking data reduction for further data refinement.

Although spot drilling at the scale of 20-60 microns is still the norm, mapping through accumulated line scans reveals mineral trace element zonation not evident in cathodoluminescence or SEM backscatter imaging. Because of the hardware improvements above, mapping of up to 10 isotopes is achievable, and grains 100 by 100 microns can be scanned in under an hour. Laser robustness and longevity is necessary for delivery of these great shot numbers.

Our group has focused on some of the factors that limit accuracy for age and trace element composition and the perceived trace element noise in a sampled population. These include the obvious but overlooked: what is sampled (cracks, inclusions, sector zoning) and the technique’s nemesis, matrix matching. Every element in every target ablates somewhat differently and accurate quantification requires a theoretical exactly matched reference material. Through careful imaging of the ablation site under different conditions and the signals produced for different minerals and glass we recommend instrument settings that mitigate this fundamental obstacle.

title: A Chemo-Topographic Transect Across the Coast Range and Cascades, Central Oregon: Modern Insights into Water Chemistries of Hydrologically Open to Balance-Filled Lakes with a Caution about Deep Time Interpretations.
session_title: LAKE SYSTEMS THROUGH SPACE AND TIME—SEDIMENT AND GEOLOGICAL ARCHIVES OF CLIMATE, WATER, ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND ECONOMIC RESOURCES (Posters)
authors: Finkelstein, David B. [1], Curtin, Tara [2]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Hobart & William Smith Colleges, Geneva, NY, USA
(2) Geoscience, Hobart & William Smith Colleges, Geneva, NY, USA
abstract:
To identify environmental and geographic controls on lacustrine water chemistry, we analyzed 22 central Oregon lakes and reservoirs along an elevational (2–1,942m a.s.l.) and longitudinal gradient spanning six geomorphic regions. The transect extends from the Pacific Ocean, up and over the Coast and Cascade Ranges to the High Lava Plains. Coast Range lakes are primarily sand-hosted, whereas inland basins are hosted in volcanic and sedimentary bedrock. Dominated by meteoric recharge, the hydrologically open, overfilled lakes have water residence times spanning months to decades, while the reservoirs reflect balanced-fill conditions.

Lakes and reservoirs were sampled five times over 13 years. Temperature, pH, total dissolved solids (TDS) and alkalinity were measured in the field. Samples were analyzed for major cations and anions and stable isotopes (δD, δ 18 O). Surface water pH (6.6–8.6) exhibited no systematic variation with substrate or elevation. While most systems are dilute (average TDS = 26.8ppm; alkalinity = 21.8mg/L CaCO 3 ), High Lava Plains lakes are concentrated (average TDS = 337ppm; alkalinity = 291.2mg/L CaCO 3 ).

Dominant cations and stable isotopes differentiate geomorphic regions. In the western Coast Range, sodium dominates due to proximity to marine aerosols. Calcium dominates in eastern Coast Range systems and Western and High Cascades due to differing substrate. Isotopic values track distillation and evaporation across the topography. Coast Range waters range from –5.7 to –9.3‰VSMOW for δ 18 O and –37.8 to –63.6‰VSMOW for δD, whereas Cascade waters are depleted (δ 18 O: –9.7 to –12.1‰VSMOW; δD: –71.5 to –86.5‰VSMOW).

Isotopic compositions show no relationship with air or water temperatures but document a Rayleigh distillation signature extending 100km inland and up to 1km in elevation. Above 1km, evaporation dominates. Though waters remain seasonally supersaturated with respect to calcite and dolomite, shallow lacustrine sediments lack discrete carbonate precipitates.

Average annual precipitation and bedrock across this topographic gradient controls the major ions and stable isotopic composition of these lakes. Reconstructing stable isotopic compositions of lake water typically requires an assumption of paleotemperature. Caution should be used when interpreting deep-time water/air temperatures from carbonates from overfilled to balance-filled lakes within the coastal plain of mountainous regions. Hydrologically open to balance-filled lakes preserved in deep time may record paleoprecipitation along topographic gradients independent of lake water temperature.

title: Using Paleomagnetism and Rock Magnetism of Ethiopian Igneous Rocks from the East African Rift System to Understand Subsurface Mantle Evolution
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: McCoy, Deborah [1], Tesfay, Kahsay Nugsse [2], Peppe, Daniel J. [3], Dworkin, Steve I. [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
(2) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, Texas, USA
(3) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX,
(4) School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA
abstract: The Ethiopian flood basalt province and volcanism of the East African Rift System preserve three distinct lava types: low-Ti (LT), high-Ti1 (HT1), and ultra-high-Ti1 (HT2) basalts. The geochemical variations of these lava types reflect mantle source heterogeneity and magma differentiation. To identify lava types and characterize their rock magnetic properties, we integrated whole-rock major-element geochemistry with rock magnetic analyses of Oligocene Maychew flood basalts and younger Selisa rift volcanics. Geochemical data show that the Maychew lavas comprise ultra-high-Ti transitional basalt–picrite compositions (TiO₂ >4 wt%), whereas the Selisa rift volcanics are low-Ti tholeiitic basalts (TiO₂ = <3 wt%), indicating derivation from compositionally distinct mantle sources. The ultra-high-Ti Maychew basalts exhibit substantially higher bulk magnetic susceptibility than the younger rift lavas, reflecting differences in magnetic mineral abundance. Hysteresis and first-order reversal curve (FORC) analyses indicate that both volcanic suites are dominated by pseudo-single-domain magnetic grains with subordinate single-domain contributions, demonstrating favorable magnetic mineral assemblages capable of preserving stable primary remanent magnetization. These preliminary results characterize the geochemical composition of the regional volcanic products and the grain-size distribution of their magnetic minerals. This framework provides a basis for future micro-textural and mineralogical investigations of Fe–Ti oxides using scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy to further resolve the links between magmatic evolution, magnetic mineralogy, and paleomagnetic behavior.

title: Assessing Workforce Skill Development and Research Contributions in the Paul Edwin Potter Internship at the Illinois State Geological Survey
session_title: Developing and Assessing Workforce Skills in Geoscience Courses and Programs
authors: Dendy, Sarah [1], Callahan, Ellise H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Charachterization Center, Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA
(2) Geochemistry, Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA
abstract:
Early-career geoscientists need opportunities to apply academic knowledge, develop professional skills, and understand the impact of applying geoscience research to serve their communities. The Paul Edwin Potter Internship at the Illinois State Geological Survey (ISGS) is a 10-week paid program in which undergraduate and master’s students contribute to active research under one-to-one mentorship from survey scientists.

Since its establishment in 2022, the program has served 45 interns across five cohorts. Intern projects span environmental geology, coastal processes, groundwater resources, Quaternary geology, paleontology, and energy-resource management. Projects are deliberately scoped to give interns ownership of a defined line of inquiry—from initial questions and project planning through data collection, analysis, interpretation, and communication—within broader ISGS research that serves the State of Illinois and its residents. Project work is complemented by curriculum addressing research skills, field and laboratory methods, data management and security, responsible use of artificial intelligence, scientific writing, public communication, professional networking, and career preparation. Interns also participate in technical workshops, field experiences, research discussions, and capstone presentations.

An ongoing program evaluation examines three interconnected outcomes: development of workforce skills and professional identity, contributions to applied research, and progression toward subsequent educational or professional goals. Evidence includes program records, ten 2026 intern exit-survey responses, a developing inventory of research outputs, and alumni follow-up. A mentor exit survey will provide an additional perspective on intern development, research contributions, and the effectiveness of the program’s mentoring structure.

Preliminary evidence indicates that interns value working on authentic projects, experiencing the research process from inception to completion, taking ownership of their learning, receiving guidance while developing independence, and interacting with professionals across disciplines. Documented outputs include technical reports, conference posters, datasets, and analyses used to advance research into subsequent phases. Alumni follow-up will examine how the experience contributed to graduate education, employment, and other geoscience pathways.

This presentation describes the Potter Internship’s structure and assessment approach and considers how state geological surveys and similar organizations can integrate authentic public-service research, mentoring, and intentional workforce preparation within a short-term internship serving students at multiple degree levels.

title: Evaluating Multispectral sUAS Mapping of Kaolinite-Rich Stratigraphy in Western Colorado
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Hanks, Matthew [1], Baker, Gregory S. [2], Hood, William C. [3], Aslan, Andres [4]
affiliations: (1) Physical and Environmental Sciences, Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(2) University Of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
(4) Colorado Mesa University, Grand Junction, CO, USA
abstract: Rapid identification of kaolinite-rich stratigraphic units could reduce the amount of field sampling required during geologic mapping. This study evaluated whether multispectral imagery acquired with a small uncrewed aircraft system (sUAS) could distinguish the Ohio Creek and Wasatch Formations near De Beque, Colorado, by mapping spectral signatures associated with kaolinite abundance. The central hypothesis proposed that sUAS-derived multispectral imagery could identify kaolinite-rich stratigraphy with at least 70% agreement relative to laboratory-supported field measurements while requiring substantially less time and effort than traditional ground sampling. Multispectral imagery was collected over representative exposures at Shale Ridge, where the kaolinite-rich Ohio Creek Formation and kaolinite-poor Wasatch Formation are well exposed. The imagery was processed into a high-resolution 3D model, and mineral-indicator metrics were derived primarily from the near-infrared (NIR) spectral response, where kaolinite-bearing materials exhibit relatively high reflectance. Interpreted kaolinite distributions and stratigraphic contacts were compared with ground-truth data from field samples analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify kaolinite and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) to characterize bulk geochemistry. Agreement between the multispectral classification and laboratory-supported field data was evaluated using a binary classification of inferred kaolinite abundance. Maximum agreement reached 68%, falling slightly below the predefined 70% threshold; therefore, the hypothesis was not supported. Reduced agreement likely reflects the combined effects of topographic relief, terrain shadowing, vegetation cover, cloud variability, and changing illumination and viewing geometry, all of which influence spectral response. Despite these limitations, multispectral sUAS imagery remains a promising reconnaissance tool for rapidly identifying areas that warrant detailed field investigation. The approach can improve the efficiency of mineralogical mapping by reducing unnecessary sampling while directing laboratory analyses toward the most informative locations.

title: Geology of the Half-Mile Shoals 7.5-Minute 1:24,000-Scale Quadrangle in Central Alabama
session_title: Best Student Geologic Map Competition
authors: Priakos, William H. [1], Cemen, Ibrahim [2], Granath, James W. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA
(3) Granath & Associates Consulting, Highlands Ranch, CO, USA
abstract:
During this project, the Half-Mile Shoals 7.5-minute 1:24,000-scale quadrangle in Central Alabama was mapped in detail using funds provided by the USGS EDMAP Program to I. Çemen. The stratigraphy and structures in the quadrangle were reconciled with those of the three adjacent 7.5-minute quadrangles (Woodstock, McCalla, and West Blocton East quadrangles), and a balanced structural cross-section was constructed.

Stratigraphic units present in the quadrangle range from Middle to Late Cambrian to Late Cretaceous. These units are the Middle to Late Cambrian Conasauga Formation, Late Cambrian to Early Ordovician Knox Group, Middle Ordovician Chickamauga Limestone, Silurian Red Mountain Formation, Devonian Chattanooga Shale, Early Mississippian Fort Payne Chert, Late Mississippian Floyd Shale, Late Mississippian to Early Pennsylvanian Parkwood Formation, Pennsylvanian Pottsville Formation, and, unconformably overlying the Paleozoic units, the Late Cretaceous Coker Formation. These units are present in the adjacent quadrangles and extend into the Half-Mile Shoals quadrangle, which encompasses an area in the hanging wall of the Jones Valley thrust sheet in the Appalachian fold-thrust belt. Other major structural features in the area include a northeast-striking thrust fault, with a tight syncline-anticline pair in its hanging wall and a cut-off syncline in its footwall. These structures are parasitic to the northwest limb of the Cahaba synclinorium, which occurs along the trailing edge of the thrust sheet and is truncated by the Montevallo Thrust Fault to the southeast.

Based on our geologic mapping and detailed structural observations, we constructed a balanced structural cross-section to constrain the kinematic development of the structural features in the area. When restored, the cross-section provides the amount and percentage of structural shortening in the area.

title: Detrital Zircon Geochronology of Midcontinent Rift-Fill Strata in Iowa, USA
session_title: Sedimentary Geology Division/SEPM Student Research Poster Competition: Dynamics of Stratigraphy and Sedimentation
authors: Roberts, Matthew Paul [1], Malone, David H. [2], Malone, John E. [3]
affiliations: (1) Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(2) Illinois State University, Normal, IL, USA
(3) Iowa Geological Survey, Iowa City, IA, USA
abstract: Sandstone units penetrated by deep drill cores within the Iowa segment of the ~1100 Ma Midcontinent Rift provide a rare opportunity to investigate sediment provenance and stratigraphic relationships in a poorly characterized portion of the Rift. Although correlative sedimentary rocks exposed in the Lake Superior region have been studied, the origin and depositional history of Iowa Rift-fill strata remain uncertain. Detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology was conducted by laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS) on three core splits: one from the Nonesuch (Eischeid well; (15,101-15,102 ft) and two from the Freda (Eischeid and Lehman wells; 11,383-11,386 ft and 2,953.6-2,954.6 ft). A total of 457 zircons were analyzed. The Nonesuch sample had two principal age peaks: 1640 and 1750 Ma, which are consisted with the ages of local basement rocks. The two Freda samples are statistically indistinguishable from Freda data sets in Michigan and Wisconsin, with most zircons ranging from 1000-1450 Ma in age. The origin of these zircons is less well constrained. The geon 14 subset can be derived from local Quimby Granite, the geon 13 zircons could be derived from the Spencer intrusive complex along the Western Spirit Lake Tectonic zone. Each of these plutons are proximal to the Eischeid well. The small number of geon 11 grains can be derived from Midcontinent Rift volcanic rocks. Alternatively, these zircons can be derived from distal Grenville source areas. We do not favor this possibility because of the paucity of the ubiquitous Archean zircons available. The absence of Midcontinent Rift derived zircons indicates that rift rocks were either zircon infertile or buried by the time these strata were deposited. We favor a model where local source areas from the rift shoulder provided the bulk of the sediment to this depositional system.

abstract: The Miocene China Ranch beds of southeastern Death Valley, California, are exposed throughout the fault-bound transtensional China Ranch basin (CRB) and locally overlie Precambrian basement or Miocene volcaniclastic and/or megabreccia deposits. Numerous studies have characterized deposits in various parts of the CRB, but holistic analysis is lacking. Geologic mapping (EDMAP contracts G21AC10535 and G23AC00202) and geochronological studies applying 40 Ar/ 39 Ar and detrital zircon (U/Pb) dating methods constrain the distribution and age of the deposits. The oldest sedimentary deposits in the western part of the CRB overlie Miocene granite megabreccia and give a maximum depositional age (MDA) of 13.2+/-0.4 Ma. Whereas in the eastern part of the CRB, China Ranch beds disconformably overlie pre-transtensional volcaniclastic deposits interbedded with colluvium and carbonate tufa along the Alexander Hills that yield an MDA of 11.1+/-0.3 Ma. The China Ranch beds include as many as eight 40 Ar/ 39 Ar-dated ash-flow tuff beds ranging in age from 11.12+/-0.03 to 6.79+/-0.03 Ma. The ages of the ash-flow tuff beds generally decrease in age from west to east within two sub-basins, which partially overlap in age. The CRB strata generally dip east with folding focused along faults, decreasing in intensity from west to east. In the northeastern part of the basin post-CRB gravel-rich deposits overlie the China Ranch beds with angular unconformity to disconformity, and yield an MDA of 11.6+/-0.47 Ma, reflecting reworking of older deposits. A second post-CRB gravel-dominated deposit overlies the China Ranch beds with apparent angular unconformity and fills in deep canyon topography, suggesting deposition post-topographic inversion of the CRB. The CRB developed on remnants of an earlier Miocene extensional basin system ranging in age from approximately 13 – 11 Ma that likely included parts of the Ibex Pass and Sperry Hills regions. The CRB is interpreted to reflect deposition in a strike-slip basin undergoing progressive dextral slip along the WNW-ESE bounding faults. Accommodation space created by dextral slip likely diminished in the CRB after approximately 8.5 Ma as the basin was progressively offset by SW-NE and SSW-NNE sinistral-oblique-slip faults. Subsequent slip along the Sheephead-Willow Wash fault system was largely dip slip, down to the south. Post-CRB deformation along mainly sinistral oblique and dip-slip faults accommodated topographic inversion and local basin development.

title: Constraints on repeated polygonal ground formation at Gale crater, Mars
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Turner, Madison [1], Hughes, Emmy B [2], Rapin, William [3], Banham, Steven G [4], Rivera-Hernandez, Frances [5], Caravaca, Gwénaël [6], Cowart, Aster [7], Kite, Edwin S [8]
affiliations: (1) Carl Sagan Center, SETI Institute, Mountain View, California, USA; Department of the Geophysical Sciences, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA
(2) Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(3) Institut de Recherche en Astrophysique et Planétologie, Université Paul Sabatier Toulouse, Toulouse, France
(4) Department of Earth Science and Engineering, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom
(5) School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, USA

(7) Planetary Science Institute, Tuscon, Arizona, USA
(8) Department of the Geophysical Sciences, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA
abstract:
As the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) Curiosity rover traverses through the layered sulfate unit, Curiosity is tasked with characterizing the depositional and diagenetic environments recorded within the strata to better understand Mars’ ancient climate (Milliken et al., 2010). The repeated presence of regularly spaced centimeter-scale polygons at multiple stratigraphic intervals marks it as a key facies in the layered sulfate unit.On Earth, polygons form in a variety of environments in conditions ranging from surface desiccation cracks to cooling basalt columns (Goehring, 2013). Thus, understanding the formation environment for this facies in the layered sulfate unit is essential to understanding past environmental conditions on Mars.

We utilize Curiosity’s Mast Cameras (MastCams), Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), and Navigation Cameras (NavCams) to analyze the stratigraphic setting and morphology of polygon horizons (Grotzinger et al., 2012). The polygons occur consistently throughout layered sulfate stratigraphy, including coarser-grained, cross-bedded sandstones, and finer-grained, thinly layered strata. Additionally, Curiosity’s imaging suite was used to constrain polygon cell sizes to 3.5— 8 cm in diameter, with no distinct trends in polygon cell size with stratigraphy. Measurements of junction angles peak with a normal distribution at 120°, consistent with observations of features consistently being 5—6 sided. We also combine measurements of vertical cracks with the orientation of bedding in the hostrock to quantify any systematic deformation. MAHLI images show various polygonal ridge textures, including open cracks (marked by double ridges), and allow for more comprehensive estimates of grainsize for the polygon-hosting bedrock.

In combining these data with compositional data from ChemCam, we identify the following key characteristics of the polygon facies in the layered sulfate unit: the polygons commonly exhibit a 3D cell-structure, and do not have a bed-parallel top or bottom boundary; polygonal ridges occur as both open cracks, often with a grayish, platy fill material, or closed cracks; and examples of vertical shear and cross-cutting relationships imply post-depositional formation. We combine these data to compare these features to those formed in various scenarios on Earth. Using this approach, we constrain facies formation to three potential mechanisms: groundwater expulsion from overburden pressure, volumetric contraction due to chemical weathering, or seasonal contraction in an arid environment.

title: Investigating Geomorphic Controls on 210Pb and 137Cs-based Chronologies in Subaqueous Nearshore Sediments along the Connecticut Coast
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Gautam, Saranya [1], Ouimet, William B. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA
(2) Earth Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT,
abstract:
Sedimentation rates along the dynamic coastal zone are rarely quantified, despite their extent and their importance in understanding coastal sediment dynamics and sea level rise. ²¹⁰Pb and ¹³⁷Cs chronometers are widely accepted tools for age-depth modeling, but chronologies are mostly developed for lakes and salt marshes. Most age models (CRS, CF:CS, Plum) assume constant or consistent sediment influx, an assumption the coastal nearshore zone frequently violates.

In this study, we investigate ²¹⁰Pb and ¹³⁷Cs-based chronologies from 10 sediment cores spanning coastal Connecticut, with sites including a diverse range of geomorphic settings such as sheltered coves, tidal channels, and high-energy tidal inlets. These chronologies are compared to bulk Pb profiles, whose well-documented regional history serves as a proxy for industrial sediment preservation. Sites with consistent sediment preservation are modeled using the CRS method, which uses excess ²¹⁰Pb inventory to construct age-depth relationships, whereas sites with episodic records require alternative approaches.

Sedimentation rates for continuously accumulating sites range from 0.15 to 0.2 cm yr⁻¹ while higher energy settings preserve episodic records that fall outside standard age model assumptions. Some sites preserve bulk Pb that may predate the 1920 marker, indicating earlier local industrial inputs that complicate its use as a single chronological marker. These chronologies provide a means of distinguishing pre- and post-1920 baselines for sedimentation rates, with implications for sediment budget and sea-level reconstruction studies.

title: Summer Rains and Snow Drought Intensity Affect Seasonal Vegetation and Groundwater Connections
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Bloxham, Hannah [1], Godsey, Sarah [2], Pryor, Amber [3], Sniadach, Anna [4]
affiliations: (1) Geoscience, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(2) Geoscience, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(3) Geoscience, Idaho State University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
(4) Geoscience, Idaho Sate University, Pocatello, Idaho, USA
abstract: In the mountainous western US, snow drought —when winter precipitation falls as rain instead of snow— promotes earlier plant green-up and potentially dire downstream water stress during the following summer, unless groundwater or summer rains ameliorate water stress. During droughts, proximity to a perennial spring has been shown to sustain riparian plant water use in quartzite parent material, but it is unknown whether spring-adjacent plants in limestone parent material exhibit similar drought response patterns. To address this gap, the rate of sapflow of a Serviceberry tree located in limestone parent material in a research watershed in southeastern Idaho was continuously recorded every 15 minutes starting in summer 2026. Soil moisture sensors were installed in a nearby soil pit at depths of 20 and 45 cm. Data collected from groundwater and stilling wells in the same watershed were used to compare water levels and streamflow during three drought years: 2021, 2022, and 2026. Accumulated precipitation and snow water equivalent relative to a 30-year average (1991-2020) were calculated for all three drought years, revealing that 2026 experienced the most intense snow drought of these three years. Nonetheless, sapflow patterns in limestone during 2026 were similar to sapflow patterns in quartzite during the previous droughts in 2021-2022. Because the 2026 drought was more severe compared to the previous 2021 and 2022 drought years, it remains unclear if quartzite would be able to match limestone springs’ ability to mitigate intense drought effects. Data from the full 2026 growing season will allow the evaluation of summer rain effects on the connections between vegetation and groundwater during droughts in the mountainous western US.

title: Lidar-Sourced Fracture Analysis of Volcanic Members of the Igneous Aquifers of Trans-Pecos Texas
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data (Posters)
authors: Kelsch, Jesse Moore [1], Chambers, Carissa L. [2], Piper, Amanda Rose [3]
affiliations: (1) Natural Sciences, Sul Ross State University, Alpine, TX, ; Meadows Research Institute for West Texas Water, Sul Ross State University, Alpine, TX, USA

abstract: The Igneous Aquifers of Trans-Pecos (western) Texas, USA, consist of more than 40 Oligocene to Miocene volcanic and plutonic units in an area of ~13,000 square kilometers. These igneous rocks of the Trans-Pecos Magmatic Province store and conduct groundwater in part within tectonically induced fractures that post-date emplacement and cooling. Here we present structural data describing fracture patterns in a 250 square-kilometer section of the Igneous Aquifers’ extent, where four widespread extrusive rock units and several small laccolith-forming intrusions crop out. We used CloudCompare software to analyze state-provided, free, 1-meter LiDAR data for fracture-plane orientation, length, spacing, and density and assessed these characteristics’ variability by rock unit. All igneous units in the study area were present at the onset of Rio Grande rift extension ~30-28 Ma when crustal extension was oriented northeast-southwest, and therefore also at the ~15-13 Ma rotation of crustal stretch direction to a northwest-southeast orientation. However, at the scale of the LiDAR data one of the rock units exhibits fracture orientations that are only consistent with the later, northwest-southeast strain direction. Other units exhibit fracture orientations consistent either with both crustal stretch directions or with neither stretch direction. Other preliminary results show that fracture density and length also vary by rock unit. Outcrop- and digital-outcrop-model analyses will follow to determine if the same characteristics exist at finer scales. This work introduces the first study in a larger project to conceptualize the fractures within the greater Igneous Aquifers such that a groundwater flow model or models may be built that accurately considers predominant, structurally dictated recharge, storage, and flow paths. These results relating certain fracture characteristics to rock type will be tested in many more locations where rocks of the Igneous Aquifers are exposed.

title: Exploring Disparity Through Theoretical Morphospaces: From Ammonoids to Mollusks and Back Again
session_title: 50th Friends of the Cephalopods: Advances in Evolution, Biogeography, and Ecology
authors: Contreras Figueroa, Gabriela [1], Hendy, Austin J.W. [2]
affiliations: (1) Invertebrate Paleontology, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, California, USA
(2) Invertebrate Paleontology, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
abstract:
Theoretical morphology provides a relevant framework for investigating the developmental and evolutionary constraints of biological form. By constructing theoretical morphospaces, it becomes possible to visualize all geometrically possible morphologies and compare them with those observed among living organisms and in the fossil record. Mollusks are particularly suited for this approach because their shells exhibit remarkable morphological and ecological diversity, in addition well-defined geometric growth patterns.

Several geometric models have been developed to describe molluscan shell morphology. Among them, models based on standardized geometric parameters are especially valuable because they allow direct comparisons among diverse shell morphologies using measurements obtained from real specimens. Here, we employ a geometric model based on the logarithmic spiral equation within a fixed coordinate system, in which the shell aperture is defined using a local moving coordinate system. The resulting parameters generate theoretical morphospaces applicable to planispiral, helicoidal, conical, and bivalved shells. This model has previously been applied successfully to analyses of morphological disparity in bivalves and gastropods, revealing the impact of ecological restructuring following the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. This is particularly noticeable in strategies of locomotion and life habits associated with nutrient-poor environments.

We extend this framework by investigating the ecomorphological disparity of Late Cretaceous (Campanian–Maastrichtian) cephalopods from Western North America. Our approach integrates the proposed geometric model with the shell ecomorphological framework of Westermann, allowing theoretical morphospaces to be interpreted in terms of ecological categories. Preliminary analyses indicate that the disparity observed in cephalopod morphospaces is closely associated with Westermann’s ecological modes, including planktonic, nektonic, demersal, and vertical-migrant lifestyles. This integrated approach provides a quantitative framework for exploring the ecomorphological factors that influenced the ecological distribution, and paleobiogeography of ammonoids during the final stages of their evolutionary history.

Finally, we discuss how theoretical morphospaces provide new opportunities to investigate the paleoecological and evolutionary processes that have shaped the diversification and extinction of molluscan lineages through geological time.

title: Basin and Range-Style, Mesozoic Tectonics of SE China, Its Magmatic Record, and the Slab Dynamics of the Palaeo-Pacific Plate
session_title: Tectonics on Tap: Raising a Glass to the Enthusiastic Contributions of John Wakabayashi to Field and Applied Geology
authors: Dilek, Yildirim [1], Jiang, Xiao-Yan [2], Zhang, Feng-Qi [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Environmental Earth Sciences, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA
(2) State Key Laboratory of Ore Deposit Geochemistry, Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guiyang, Guizhou 550081, China
(3) School of Earth Sciences, Zhejiang University, Zijingang Campus, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China
abstract: Triassic geology of SE Asia was controlled by flat-slab subduction of the Palaeo-Pacific plate beneath SE China. This slab dynamics resulted in strong coupling between the lower & upper plates, causing push-over tectonics and contractional deformation in SE China. Flat subduction-induced edge flow and aesthenospheric uprising led to the production of high-K granites, syenites and mafic rocks. Slab foundering, accelerated subduction rates and subduction hinge retreat in the Early Jurassic caused rapid rollback of the downgoing slab. Strong decoupling of the upper and lower plates resulted in pull-away tectonics , producing extensional deformation in SE China. Decompression melting of the upwelling aesthenosphere produced OIB-type melts, which interacted with the subcontinental lithospheric mantle (SCLM) to form A- and I-type granitoids. Segmentation of the Palaeo-Pacific plate in the Early Cretaceous resulted in steeply dipping slabs & their faster rollback, facilitating lithospheric-scale extension and oceanward migration of calc-alkaline magmatism. This extensional deformation played a significant role in the formation of metamorphic core complexes, widespread crustal melting, and development of Basin and Range-type tectonics and landscape evolution in SE China. Our model suggests various external causes and shows that changes in subducting slab widths, subduction velocities, and the degree of coupling–decoupling between the lower - upper plates played a major role in driving tectonic mode switches during the Mesozoic evolution of SE China. We propose the late Cretaceous–Eocene tectonics of the Western US Cordillera as an analogue for the Mesozoic tectonics of SE China. Widespread Cretaceous granitoids in the Peri–South China Sea region represent the remnants of a once contiguous Late Mesozoic magmatic arc system that bounded the southern margin of continental Southeast Asia. Trench-slab retreat caused the eastward migration of this magmatic arc and created microcontinental blocks that were rifted away from Asia and drifted S with the opening of the South China Sea. With the convergence direction of the subducting plates becoming more oblique with respect to the active margins of E-SE China & the Western US Cordillera through time, oblique subduction and the associated strain partitioning in the upper continental plates resulted in transtensional deformation. Major strike-slip fault systems developed, strongly affecting the crustal architecture of the continental margins in both regions. The geology of Mesozoic E-SE China is a great natural laboratory to investigate the slab-controlled continental dynamics through time.

title: Integrating Airbourne Geophysics, Borehole Records, Geophysical Logs, and Continuous Core to Map the Northeast Mahomet Aquifer, Illinois
