authors: Dendy, Sarah [1], Mwakanyamale-Gilkie, Kisa [2], Thomason, Jason F. [3], Keefer, Donald A. [4], Stumpf, Andrew J. [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth Characterization Center, Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA

(3) Illinois State Geological Survey, Champaign, IL, USA
(4) Illinois State Geological Survey, CHAMPAIGN, IL, USA
(5) University of Illinois, Champaign, IL, USA
abstract:
Helicopter time-domain electromagnetics (HTEM) provides spatially extensive information about variations in the electrical properties of the subsurface. These variations can reflect differences in grain size and lithology, helping distinguish relatively coarse-grained aquifer materials from finer-grained confining deposits. Because HTEM measurements are indirect, borehole records, geophysical logs, and direct observations from core are used to support modeling of geophysical data into geological models.

The Northeast Mahomet Aquifer project integrates HTEM with existing borehole records, borehole geophysical logs, and recently collected continuous core to develop three-dimensional interpretations of the Mahomet Aquifer system and surrounding glacial deposits in east-central Illinois. Three borehole locations were strategically selected either to provide direct geologic control for classifications of the HTEM response or to investigate areas where the subsurface interpretation remained uncertain. Continuous core and natural gamma logs were collected at each location.

VERM-26-01 (API 1218327292-00), in Vermilion County, was continuously cored to a total depth of 292 ft and encountered weathered shale bedrock beneath alternating diamicton and sand-and-gravel intervals. FORD-26-01 (API 1205321566-00) reached a total depth of 195 ft, terminating in calcareous diamicton. Preliminary field observations document alternating diamicton and sand and gravel, together with a densely fossiliferous lacustrine interval from approximately 100 to 110 ft. FORD-26-02 (API 1205321567-00) reached a total depth of 150 ft and terminated in diamicton. Field observations document shallow lacustrine sediment from approximately 7 to 15 ft, followed by a heterogeneous succession that includes diamicton, laminated clay, and very fine sand.

Detailed descriptions of the Vermillion County and Ford County cores, and correlations among core lithology, natural gamma logs, existing borehole records, and HTEM-derived models are underway. The integrated analysis will link subsurface variations in the geophysical response to observed lithology, refine the geometry of aquifer and confining materials, and resolve areas of uncertainty within the three-dimensional interpretation. This approach combines the regional coverage of airborne geophysics with the vertical detail of borehole records, geophysical logs, and continuous core to strengthen groundwater characterization and geologic mapping in Illinois.

abstract:
Various investigations have produced competing proposals for the age, duration, and supposed drivers of Ocean Anoxic Event 1a (OAE1a). The variance amongst these works are in large part driven by the scarcity of in-situ radioisotopic dates for the event, as well as debate concerning the relative age of Ontong Java Plateau (OJP) volcanism. Million-year differences among age models has led to discrepancies in the interpretation of driving mechanisms, although emplacement of the OJP is commonly cited as the most likely causal mechanism. This hypothesis is supported by marked global shifts to unradiogenic osmium and negative carbon isotope values that define OAE1a onset.

In an effort to address the geochronologic disparities associated with OAE1a, we have developed a new astrochronologic model from a core record of OAE1a recovered from the Vocontian Basin, France (Les Sauzeries core or “LS”), where hemipelagic deposits preserve sedimentary oscillations that prior studies have shown to be modulated by astronomically-controlled climate cycles. Numerous detailed astrochronologies for this time period exists, but our methodology leverages the robust radioisotope geochronology developed by Li et al. (2024), which measured 19 U-Pb dates in a series of rhyolitic tuffs intercalated within mudstones of the Soashibetsu-gawa Formation in Hokkaido, Japan.

Here, we (1) summarize the geochronology constructed from Hokkaido which has yielded age assignments for the global d 13 C segment boundary chemostratigraphy developed for OAE1a in prior studies; (2) Utilize both d 13 C and Os records to identify selected tie-points in the coeval LS record and present the new “floating” astrochronology for the LS core (constructed using the Astrochron software package); and (3) Discuss the geospatial variability among d 13 C and Os records during this interval, which preserves a distinct shift when comparing Hokkaido to the various Tethys records. Our age-calibrated chemostratigraphic tie-points allow the floating age model to be anchored in geologic time. This work, which refines the time scale for OAE1a, supports the OJP hypothesis for OAE1a initiation by placing the age of onset at 119.53 +0.05/-0.06 Ma .

title: Organic geochemistry and taphonomy of Mongolian Organic Spore-like Microfossils Across the Taishir Anomaly
session_title: Biological and Environmental Change during Earth's Middle Age (Posters)
authors: Caskey, Talia [1], Cohen, Phoebe A. [2], Bartesaghi, Martina Berrutti [3], Junium, Christopher K. [4]
affiliations: (1) Williams College, Williamstown, MA,
(2) Williams College, Williamstown, MA,

abstract:
In this study we examined the morphology, taphonomy, and organic geochemistry of single red algal microfossils (OSM, organic spore-like microfossils) found in the Cryogenian Taishir and Ediacaran Ol Formations of the Tsagaan-Olom Group, Mongolia. These fossils span the Cryogenian-Ediacaran boundary and persist through the Taishir negative carbon isotope anomaly, one of the most pronounced negative carbon isotope anomalies in Earth’s history. Various potential mechanisms for this excursion have been proposed including global perturbations in seawater δ 13 C, large-scale oxidation of organic carbon reservoirs, and precipitation of isotopically enriched authigenic carbonates. Better understanding the OSM assemblage may lead to new insights into this profound carbon cycle disturbance.

We performed energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to further characterize the elemental composition of the OSMs to assess whether their organic walls contain aluminosilicates, found in similar fossils from Kazakhstan, which allow us to better understand their mode of preservation, and taxonomic affinity. To determine the δ 13 C values of individual microfossils, we utilized a nanoEA -- an elemental analyzer attached to a stable isotope mass spectrometer. We present new isotopic data through the Taishir anomaly from the Ho Daava and Northern Taishir localities. Across 16 Northern Taishir horizons and 7 Ho Daava horizons, we measured the δ 13 C values of 10 OSMs per horizon, the bulk organic matter from the same fossiliferous intervals, and compared these to existing carbonate carbon isotopic values. Average OSM values are on average 0.5-1.5 per mil more enriched than bulk organic matter δ 13 C values at Ho Daava, and do not follow the negative excursion present in bulk carbonate and bulk organic values. At the Northern Taishir locality, OSM values are on average equivalent to or more depleted than bulk organic values and, while variable, more closely track the negative excursion.

These analyses will allow us to better understand how OSMs were preserved, how and why their carbon isotopic compositions vary from bulk values, and provide more nuance into our understanding of how eukaryotic organisms recorded and responded to carbon cycle perturbations in the Neoproterozoic.

title: Sedimentation history of Medusae Fossae Formation
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Turner, Madison [1], Annex, Andrew M [2]
affiliations: (1) Carl Sagan Center, SETI Institute, Mountain View, California, USA; Department of the Geophysical Sciences, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA
(2) Carl Sagan Center, SETI Institute, Mountain View, California, USA
abstract:
The Medusae Fossae Formation (MFF) is the largest sedimentary deposit on Mars (Tanaka et al., 2014). Despite being Mars’ largest depocenter, the depositional history of the MFF is still heavily debated. Many possible depositional scenarios are indistinguishable due to the statistical uncertainty involved in fitting a crater population to a modeled population at a specific isochron, meaning that small crater populations yield large chronology errors (Michael, 2016). For a younger sedimentary deposit like the MFF with few craters on most of the yardang-capped strata, this translates to a poorly constrained chronostratigraphy. We address this uncertainty by mapping embedded and exhumation-era craters and using Poisson cratering statistics. While traditional crater chronology fits crater distributions dependent on crater diameter, Poisson cratering statistics calculates the likelihood of a given distribution to occur at any point in Mars’ history (Michael, 2016).

We use orbital imagery from the Context Camera (CTX) (Dickson et al., 2024; NASA/JPL/MSSS/The Murray Lab) to complete a comprehensive survey of all craters accumulated during deposition (embedded craters) and erosion-era craters over 160 m in diameter. Embedded craters along mapped geologic contacts of the MFF are used to constrain the basal unconformity between underlying Noachian and Hesperian units and the MFF sediments. Embedded craters mapped within the MFF deposit are used to estimate sedimentation rates, because the number of craters accumulated during deposition is inversely proportional to accumulation rates (Hartmann, 1974). Lastly, a survey of all erosion-era craters accumulated post-depositionally on the MFF are used to constrain the most likely exhumation age of the entire deposit. When combined, these data provide a complete picture of the sedimentation history of the MFF, with results showing the most probable chronostratigraphy and providing time integrated probability curves for the crater distributions (Annex and Lewis, 2024).

Initial results from Zephyria Planum, an equatorial sedimentary lobe of the MFF east of Gale crater, suggest early deposition, fast accumulation, and an Early Hesperian (~3 Ga) exhumation age. In comparing these results with those from the other MFF lobes, we can better understand the sedimentation history of the entire deposit, and address questions about its formation and evolution as a single, sedimentary deposit.

abstract: Collocated observations of stream and air temperatures can be used to understand the hydrology of streams. Different water sources, especially groundwater, have been shown to impart distinct patterns on stream temperatures relative to local air temperature that can be used to investigate spatial and temporal variability in groundwater inputs to streams. In this talk, I will present new paired stream - air temperature observations collected in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado, USA throughout 2024, 2025 and 2026 and explore how patterns in stream - air temperature metrics may relate to differences in hydrology from stream to stream and through time. By examining stream – air temperature metrics alongside biweekly stream and groundwater ion chemistry and stable water isotope measurements, this talk will demonstrate how distributed, continuous temperature measurements can supplement more traditional chemistry-based hydrological methods.

authors: Lopez-Murillo, Esteban David [1], Gómez Pérez, Luis Enrique [2], Milián de la Cruz, Ricardo Enrique [3], Martens, Uwe C. [4], Myers, Corinne [5]
affiliations: (1) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA

(2) Museo de Paleontología Eliseo Palacios Aguilera, Tuxtla-Gutiérrez, Chiapas, Mexico; Instituto de Ciencias Biológicas, Universidad de las Ciencias y Artes de Chiapas, Tuxtla-Gutiérrez, Chiapas, Mexico

abstract:
The Chicxulub impact, triggering the end-Cretaceous mass extinction (K-Pg), hit ~ 3000 km from the ancient coasts of North America. However, Late Maastrichtian and Early Danian faunas from proximal sites in the Caribbean-southern Gulf of Mexico region are not well characterized, even though shallow marine sedimentary rocks from the Maya Block (Chiapas, MX, and northern Guatemala) preserve a record of continuous sedimentation from the Campanian through Danian. The molluscan faunas in these environments are the first direct victims, survivors, and newly originating species associated with the K-Pg. Recent fieldwork to resample classic sites, as well as investigate new localities have yielded exciting new insights into this most recent mass extinction event.

Chiapas localities preserve early Late Maastrichtian assemblages including cephalopods with Tethyan affinities ( Desmophyllites larteti , Menuites fresvillensis , Pachydiscus neubergicus , P. armenicus and Hauericeras fayoli ), early extinction of inoceramid bivalve extinction potentially correlatable to the middle Maastrichtian event (MME), and rudist bivalves and nerineid and actonellid gastropods surviving to the K-Pg boundary. Recovery faunas from this area include diverse assemblages of oysters, echinoids, and gastropods 8m above the boundary and the first coral path reefs only 20m above the boundary. Guatemalan sites preserve a similar fauna: Latest Maastrichtian deposits yield the same rudist bivalve species, only carbonate platform deposits were observed. Nerineid, acteonellid and rudist bivalves show record up to the K-Pg boundary deposits. No ammonites were recovered from the Latest Maastrichtian of northern Guatemala; however, some finer and muddier grained float indicate deeper shelf deposits might exist in the Petén region. Earliest Danian deposits from Guatemala show a general deepening of the Maya block, so no molluscan faunas were recovered from the deeper water turbiditic deposits.

Connection of these faunas to the evolution of sedimentary facies also preserved at these sites represents a unique window into the Earth-life transitions occurring across a major extinction event immediately adjacent to the source of environmental perturbation. Given that the K-Pg is a mass extinction with timing similar to the human induced biodiversity crisis of today, these investigations will help inform the pattern and timing of macroevolutionary recovery, and paleoecological and paleobiogeographical patterns of deceased, survivor and newcomer taxa in a wake of disaster.

title: Repurposing Rockview, Another Generational Opportunity or Land Grab?
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Parizek, Richard Rudolph [1], Parizek, Katarin Amelia [2], Parizek, Byron Richard [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences Emeritus, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA

abstract:
After 111 years, Penn State's State Penn neighbor, Rockview, closed Feb. 13, 2026. Trustees acquired skills assigned to its 2845-acre Forestry Camp. To provide food for inmates, state schools, and hospitals, others tended 1800 acres of fruit, garden and vegetable crops, along with livestock. Disposition of the remaining 5819 acres awaits, including forest, prime farmland, and water-resource potential. Area generational decisions are not new. Revolutionary War land grants spawned 19 Centre County regolith-sourced iron furnaces and forges, Penn State's founding, and its subsequent 171-year development, with a current $11.1 billion annual budget and the largest paying alumni. Continued growth is assured by the convergence of I-99, I-80, and U.S. 322, expanded air service, a diversified work force, and vibrant retirement communities, all within an attractive Ridge and Valley setting that includes parks, state forests, game lands, and world-class trout fisheries.

Some consider Rockview ideal for low-cost housing. Others fear oversized procurement and data centers. Preservation of prime farmland, adding to 11,333 acres secured, has support given the 18% farm acreage lost in the county this decade. Holdings could be added to Mount Nittany Conservancy & Lions Paw for recreation, wildlife propagation, and as a recharge source for one of two distinctive Rockview aquifer settings. Mountain flank limestones, some with conduits, support Logan Branch headwater springs and fisheries. The second includes two valley-centered, fracture-flow carbonates with negligible runoff. Together, their recharge could exceed 5,819 ac-ft/yr. Excess 20% and 30% AEP flows at McBride Gap, 269 and 329 ft 3 /s, respectively, could be piped by gravity for engineered recharge and prolonged storage within these valley-centered aquifers, helping sustain inevitable regional growth.

Clear Water Conservancy proposes two 100-ft wide wildlife corridor options connecting Mount Nittany to forested Spring Creek Canyon, its hiking trail, and trout fisheries. We urge mapping of fracture-trace intersection test sites favoring two dolomites within the karst valley-centered corridor, thereafter configuring corridor boundaries to include as many Zone 1 wellhead protection sites as needed and supported by recharge adequate for maximum sustained yields. Also transecting Rockview are gently-dipping, high-quality Valentine Limestone reserves, which are stratigraphic continuations of resources quarried and mined nearby for 100+ years. Providing extraction avoids karstified reserves, portals, allowing unobtrusive subsurface mining, could be located on or adjacent to other properties.

title: Electrical Resistivity Investigations of Subsurface Water in Agricultural Land and Restored Prairie at Glacier Creek Preserve, Nebraska
session_title: Using Geophysics to investigate Near Surface Geological Problems
authors: Oakley, David Owen Smith [1], Mount, Gregory J [2], Dere, Ashlee Laura Denton [3], Deuerling, Kelly M [4]
affiliations: (1) Geography/Geology Department, University of Nebraska Omaha, Omaha, Nebraska, USA
(2) Department of Geosciences, Indiana University of Pennsylvania, Indiana, Pennsylvania, USA

abstract: Glacier Creek Preserve is a nature preserve that encompasses the watershed of a small first-order stream near Omaha, Nebraska. A portion of the preserve has been restored to native tallgrass prairie, while the rest of it remains under agricultural cultivation. To investigate water movement within the subsurface of these contrasting land use regimes, we conducted a series of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) surveys within the preserve. The first ERT surveys were conducted in 2019 and consisted of a long line crossing the watershed, with some additional lines perpendicular to it. Building on the results of that work, a second set of ERT surveys was conducted in summer 2026, consisting of high-resolution surveys over anthropogenic terraces in both the agricultural and restored prairie portions of the preserve as well as two lines crossing the boundary from restored prairie to agriculture at approximately constant elevation and a line along a portion of the restored prairie hillslope. Results of these surveys consistently show lower resistivity in the shallow subsurface of agricultural land than restored prairie, which is consistent with a previously published conceptual model of shallow water infiltration in agricultural land and deeper infiltration with longer flow paths in the restored prairie. Terraces are present in both restored prairie and agricultural land, and ERT results suggest that water is retained upslope of terraces and possibly redirected to flow under them. These results are especially prominent on the restored prairie hillslope, where they show that the terraces preserve an impact of past agricultural land use even as the vegetation has been restored to tallgrass prairie. Finally, resistivity data also reveals the contact between loess and underlying glacial till and suggests that this contact is an important hydrological boundary with influence on the formation of slope wetlands within the catchment. Further geophysical investigations are ongoing to better characterize the subsurface critical zone under both agriculture and native vegetation.

affiliations: (1) National Cave and Karst Research Institute, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) National Cave and Karst Research Institute, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, USA
abstract:
Dissolved organic matter (DOM) in mountain karst aquifers has not been broadly assessed. DOM can be controlled by local vegetation, in-stream biological processes, and regional scale processes that can contribute organic material to the hydrologic system. As water moves through karst systems, direct and diffuse recharge, snowmelt-driven recharge, and aquifer properties may also play a role in what is observable. This study focuses on documenting variability of dissolved organic fluorescence (fDOM) in karst systems of the Kaweah River watershed to assess variability of dissolved organic compounds between karst springs, sinks, and cave drips.

Using parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC), we modeled fDOM in springs, cave drip water, and surface streams from samples collected during high flow conditions in June 2026. fDOM results suggest the presence of three primary organic compounds: a photooxidized petroleum-like substance, terrestrial humic-like substances, and protein-like amino acids. Springs at mid-elevations were dominated by the photooxidized petroleum-like substances, suggesting potential anthropogenic contaminants in these karst sites. These may be derived from atmospherically deposited contaminants accumulating in snowpack, soils and vegetation or fire related compounds, that are then degraded and mobilized by runoff. Drip waters contained very little terrestrial humic-like substances but were dominated by protein-like amino acids signatures, similar to tryptophan and tyrosine, that may be attributed to microbiologic productivity in overlying soils. Surface streams and cave springs associated with sinking streams included substantial amounts of terrestrial-humic like materials, suggesting faster flow and more direct interactions with vegetation. These findings suggest that under high flow conditions, karst systems are discharging a variety of organic compounds associated with both local biology and regional scale processes that were retained in both the surface hydrologic system and karst aquifers.

title: Additional Cranial Anatomy of the Early-Diverging Aetosaurine Stenomyti huangae Reveals Morphological and Biomechanical Variation: Interpretation for Dietary Specialization
session_title: 38th Annual Undergraduate Research Exhibition Sponsored by Sigma Gamma Epsilon
authors: Pierri, Carolina [1], Garcia-Gonzalez, N. Alex [2], Kluesner, Carter W. [3], Kufner, Aaron M. [4], Lovelace, David M. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Wisconsin-Madison, UW-Madison Geology Museum, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(2) University of Wisconsin-Madison, UW-Madison Geology Museum, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(3) University of Wisconsin-Madison, UW-Madison Geology Museum, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(4) University of Wisconsin-Madison, UW-Madison Geology Museum, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
(5) University of Wisconsin-Madison, UW-Madison Geology Museum, Madison, Wisconsin, USA
abstract:
The heavily armored aetosaurs (Pseudosuchia) are well known throughout much of the Late Triassic (237–201.4 Ma) and have been widely used as a biostratigraphic control for strata lacking more quantitative constraints. Though cranial elements are limited for various taxa, skull anatomy provides important insight into ecological diversity, feeding adaptations, and evolution in aetosaurs. The cranial remains recovered of Stenomyti huangae , an early-diverging aetosaurine from Upper Triassic outcrops in Eagle Basin, Colorado (Chinle Formation), allows for further morphological interpretations of early aetosaurs. High-resolution synchrotron computed tomography (CT) was used to digitally segment and reconstruct the cranial elements using non-destructive imaging techniques for ease of description and interpretation. To assess variation in cranial morphology and its possible functional implications, the reconstructed anatomy was compared with previous descriptions of Aetosaurus ferratus, Aetosauroides scagliai, Typothorax coccinarum, Neoaetosauroides engaeus, Desmatosuchus haplocerus, and Paratypothorax andressorum .

New observations from reconstructed cranial elements of Stenomyti huangae reveal unique features differing from many derived aetosaurs, including a narrow, tapered snout, elongated ascending process, and bulbous dentition that comparatively suggest alternate jaw morphology and feeding mechanics influencing dietary specialization. The comparative study between S. huangae and related aetosaurs revealed that these characteristics vary widely from the commonly more robust skull morphology and respective specialized dentitions. The previously suggested heterogeneity in feeding mechanics and food strategy among aetosaur taxa is consistent with these physical distinctions, reinforcing that aetosaurs did not reflect a single generic herbivorous feeding style, but rather occupied a variety of ecological niches through morphological diversification. This study contributes further anatomical information for evolutionary comparisons and advances our knowledge of the functional and ecological variety within Aetosauria by expanding on the known cranial anatomy of Stenomyti huangae .

title: Applying a Framework for STEM Cultural Change to Analyze the Implementation of a Regional Geoscience Learning Ecosystem in California’s Central Valley
session_title: Making Sense of Methodologies and Theoretical Frameworks in Geoscience Education Research
authors: Brady, Mara E. [1], Selvans, Michelle [2], Mine, Aric Howard [3], Weinman, Beth [4], Richaud, Mathieu [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, California State University, Fresno, Fresno, CA, USA
(2) Department of Geology, California State Polytechnic University-Humboldt, Humboldt, CA, USA
(3) Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, California State University, Fresno, Fresno, CA,
(4) Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, California State University, Fresno, Fresno, CA, USA
(5) Department of Earth & Environmental Sciences, California State University, Fresno, Fresno, CA,
abstract:
The geosciences remain among the least racially diverse STEM fields, with limited progress over the past four decades. Decades of research has informed our understanding of evidence-based educational reforms, especially work focused on improving racial diversity in STEM. However, translating these practices and reforms to enact meaningful changes remains elusive. Change research, i.e. understanding how change happens in STEM departments, bridges the gap between theory and practice so that evidence of what works well from discipline-based education research (DBER) approaches can be applied to enact change within STEM departments and programs.

Here, we present a case study of the San Joaquin Valley Geoscience Learning Ecosystem, a regional initiative designed to transform institutional culture and strengthen recruitment, engagement, and persistence for first-generation, low-income, and racially/ethnically diverse students in Geology and Environmental Science undergraduate majors at two public, access-oriented, Hispanic-Serving Institutions in California: Fresno State (regional comprehensive university) and the State Center Community College District (two year colleges). The project established a student cohort program, a faculty professional learning community, and community-based research experiences grounded in culturally-relevant pedagogy, place-based learning, and project-based learning.

Drawing on project implementation and reflective analysis, we apply Reinholz et al. (2019)’s framework for STEM culture change, previous applications of which have focused primarily on research-intensive universities and within other STEM disciplines. Specifically, we analyze our geoscience-specific cultural change using the following four frames: structures and formal roles, language and symbols, people, and power and decision-making. Our analysis shows that sustained professional learning communities, shared disciplinary language, coordinated transfer relationships, and distributed leadership supported cultural change, while cross-institution collaboration helped address and complement structural barriers unique to two- and four-year settings. These findings and related recommendations for geoscience practitioners, in particular, highlight that effective change is discipline- and context-sensitive and can benefit from sustained connections across institutional boundaries within a disciplinary STEM learning ecosystem, offering adaptable strategies for STEM reform.

title: Anomalous Kinematics of Mid-Pennsylvanian Structures in Nevada
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n) (Posters)
authors: Cashman, Patricia H. [1], Sturmer, Daniel M. [2]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences and Engineering, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV, USA
(2) Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA
abstract:
The Upper Paleozoic stratigraphy of Nevada -- stacked sedimentary basins separated by unconformities -- formed during protracted sinistral-oblique convergence along the southwest Laurentian margin. Two of the unconformities are associated with widespread subaerial exposure, indicating significant tectonic uplift. Here, we focus on the second of these uplifts, expressed as a pair of unconformities in Desmoinesian (mid-Pennsylvanian) time. These unconformities are close in age and overlap in geographic extent, so their effects cannot always be distinguished. To study mid-Pennsylvanian tectonism, we examined structures in Atokan rocks that are unconformably overlain by Desmoinesian or Missourian rocks. These structures are preserved in an east-west belt at least 300 km wide across north-central Nevada, with a minimum north-south extent of 150 km.

In east-central Nevada, both unconformities, C5 (early Desmoinesian) and C6 (late Desmoinesian to Missourian) are preserved at Buck Mountain, Spruce Mountain and the southern Pequop Mountains. The Hogan Formation, interpreted to be a relatively deep-water deposit (Schiappa et al., 2017), lies between them. Karst developed on the C5 surface records subaerial exposure prior to deposition of the Hogan. North- and west-verging folds, and local imbricate thrust faults that step up-section to the northwest, pre-date the C5 unconformity. Farther west at Carlin Canyon, deep erosion on the C6 unconformity removed any evidence of C5 or Hogan (if it was present). This records significant tectonic uplift associated with erosion on C6 in north-central Nevada. North-northwest-vergent overturned folds and imbricate thrust faults underlie the C6 unconformity; they are probably coeval with pre-C5 folds elsewhere, but this cannot be determined unequivocally. Still farther west, Pennsylvanian rocks containing unconformities and karst are present at Edna Mountain and the Dry Hills. Folds in these rocks are southwest- to northwest-vergent and lie below the C5 unconformity. Pennsylvanian rocks in southern and eastern Nevada (e.g., Syncline Ridge, Arrow Canyon Range, and Mountain Springs Pass) are outside of the zone of Pennsylvanian structures and erosion. However, although deposition was continuous across the C5 and C6 time intervals in those areas, the rocks record abrupt changes in depositional environment coeval with the unconformities farther north.

In summary, mid-Pennsylvanian (Desmoinesian) structures exposed across north-central Nevada record widespread shortening and top-to-the-northwest kinematics. They represent a distinctive event in the protracted sinistral-oblique convergence along the southwest Laurentian margin.

title: Zircon (U-Th)/He Thermochronology of the Newark Basin during the Rift-to-Drift Transition
session_title: Paleogeography and Tectonics of Deformed Continental Margins
authors: Foster-Baril, Zachary Stephen [1], Stockli, Daniel F. [2], Flansburg, Megan Elysia [3], Kinney, Sean Thomas [4], Olsen, Paul E. [5]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida, USA; Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, NY, USA
(2) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(3) Oberlin College, Oberlin, OH,
(4) Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ,
(5) Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, NY,
abstract: The Eastern North American Margin is a valuable analog for continental rifted margins; however, questions related to the timing and magnitude of its tectono-magmatic-thermal evolution remain. Mesozoic syn-rift strata preserved in predominantly top-ESE half-grabens provide a key record of the rift-to-drift lithospheric evolution leading to the opening of the Atlantic Ocean. While previous zircon and apatite fission-track data from the northern Newark Basin have documented widespread reset and non-reset ages in the footwall and basin due to a topographically driven hydrothermal system, no comprehensive low-temperature thermochronologic inverse model exists. To address this, we present new zircon (U-Th)/He data and time-temperature inverse models from a transect across the southern Newark Basin. Mean apparent zircon (U-Th)/He ages from the crystalline footwall, syn-rift strata, and the crystalline hanging wall range between 222 Ma and 167 Ma. The zircon (U-Th)/He mean ages of the footwall samples generally decrease toward the basin-bounding fault, in contrast to the intra-basin samples, which show a complete thermal reset of the zircon. Weighted mean paths from HeFTy inverse time-temperature models of footwall samples reveal a consistent cooling rate from the Alleghenian Orogeny through the initiation of Triassic-Jurassic rifting, punctuated by a slight increase in cooling rate during initial rifting in the Carnian. A footwall sample most distal from the border fault shows a slight increase in cooling rate in the Norian. This increase in cooling is consistent with the influx of alluvial sedimentation sourced from the footwall during Norian rift flank uplift. All footwall and hanging wall samples show a decrease in cooling rate spanning the Late Triassic to Middle Jurassic, indicating a diachronous transition to slower cooling during the rift-to-drift transition. The Carnian Stockton Formation core samples record complete thermal resetting at ~200 Ma, driven by burial and CAMP magmatism. Subsequently, the samples record rapid post-rift cooling that slowed between the Middle and Late Jurassic during the transition to a passive margin, after which the cooling rate decreased. One basin sample records two inflection points in its time-temperature model suggestive of localized Jurassic hydrothermal activity. These results provide important constraints on the tectono-magmatic-thermal evolution of the Newark Basin rift-to-drift transition and are consistent with vitrinite reflectance and fission-track studies indicating significant post-rift erosion of the proximal domain during the Jurassic.

title: Fishing for Truchas in the uppermost Pecos: Reexamination of the Truchas Peaks metamorphic terrane
session_title: One orogeny is not like the other: changes in orogenic styles through the Proterozoic
authors: Grambling, Tyler [1], Grambling, Nadine [2], Aronoff, Ruth Frances [3], Gevedon, Michelle [4]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Sciences Department, Denison University, Granville, OH, USA
(2) Granville, OH, USA
(3) Earth, Environmental, & Sustainability Sciences, Furman University, Greenville, SC, USA
(4) Geology Department, Colorado College, Colorado Springs, CO, USA
abstract:
Discovery of near-equilibrium Al2SiO5 triple point assemblages in the Pecos-Truchas region of North-Central New Mexico in the late 1970s invigorated interest in Mesoproterozoic deformation and metamorphism along the Laurentian margin. Decades of variable interpretations of ca. 1.4 Ga contractional orogenesis, extensional tectonics, and “anorogenic” magmatism culminated in designation of the ca. 1.5 to 1.3 Ga Picuris Orogeny. Despite widespread acceptance of Picuris-aged contraction, fierce debate over P-T-t trajectories alongside the nature of local and penetrative deformation during this extensive interval of Mesoproterozoic Laurentian history continues.

Here, we turn our attention to the rock of the Vadito, Hondo, and Tramps Groups collected during the seminal 1970s research on the Al 2 SiO 5 triple point in the Truchas Range. While historically essential to Mesoproterozoic Laurentian geology, the Pecos-Truchas region has received limited attention since the late 1980s due, in large part, to remote, technically challenging terrane to reach similar units readily accessible in the nearby Picuris Range, complex mineral assemblages, and interpretations of fluid-driven reaction gradients that confound conventional assessment of metamorphic isograds. We aim to capitalizing on archived samples to reassess kinematic, microfabric, and metamorphic relationships in the Truchas area in the framework of our current understanding of the Picuris Orogeny and previously unpublished mapping of the Truchas and Santa Fe ranges. Detailed microstructural and phase relationships from this classical locality aid in parsing out the individual orogen-defining episodes across the 200-m.y. history of the continental-scale Pinware-Baraboo-Picuris Orogeny that are commonly interpreted from single localities or lumped across the duration of the event.

title: Constraints on Young, KREEP-rich Lunar Magmatism from 207Pb/206Pb SIMS Geochronology of the Lunar Basaltic Meteorite Northwest Africa 16895
session_title: Planetary sample science: Unlocking the history of lunar, Martian, and asteroidal materials (Posters)
authors: Rollin, Soren M. [1], Crow, Carolyn A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
(2) Department of Earth Science, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract:
Recovered in 2023, Northwest Africa (NWA) 16895 is a lunar basaltic meteorite dominantly consisting of compositionally-zoned augite and laths of plagioclase and ilmenite. Initially classified as a martian augite basalt, it was reclassified following updated oxygen isotope analyses, in agreement with the high An# in plagioclase (93.0 ± 1.8) , high Fe/Mn ratios in silicates (95 ± 7 in olivine; 60 ± 5 in clinopyroxene), and lack of magnetite despite abundant ilmenite.

A 0.94-gram subsample of NWA 16895 was first characterized by backscatter electron imaging and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy point analyses using a Tescan Vega-3 XMU variable pressure scanning electron microscope at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to identify minor and accessory phases suitable for geochronology, including baddeleyite (ZrO 2 ), chlorapatite (Ca 5 (PO 4 ) 3 Cl), and Si-Al-K-rich mesostasis.

Pb-isotopic analyses of these phases were then conducted using the Cameca ims-1290 secondary ion mass spectrometer (SIMS) at UCLA. A 207 Pb/ 206 Pb isochron age for NWA 16895 was determined using an inverse isochron to plot 207 Pb/ 206 Pb against 204 Pb/ 206 Pb to constrain the crystallization age and initial Pb-isotopic composition of NWA 16895. The data were reduced to limit terrestrial 204 Pb influence, yielding a 207 Pb/ 206 Pb inverse isochron age of ~1.96 Ga (n = 11; MSWD = 1.3; p(χ 2 ) = 0.21). The inverse isochron demonstrates a low influence of terrestrial 204Pb contamination and an enriched, KREEP-like initial-Pb value.

Shock petrographic estimates suggest that this age represents the primary crystallization age of NWA 16895 from a basaltic melt with a KREEP-rich component. The increasing sample suite of young, ~2 Ga basaltic lunar samples with variable KREEP compositions–including the Chang’e 5 and 6 basalts and the lunar basaltic meteorite NWA 16286–continue to constrain the timing, modes, and mechanisms of late lunar magmatism and the variable incorporation of KREEP-rich components. These developments continue to improve our understanding of the processes and timescales of prolonged lunar magmatism.

title: Engineering Biochar and Bone Char for Selective Immobilization of Heavy Metals Under Controlled Conditions
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Peregrina-Llanes, Mauricio [1], González-Méndez, Blanca [2], Loredo-Portales, René [3], Molina-Freaner, Francisco [4]
affiliations: (1) Posgrado en Ciencias de la Tierra, Instituto de Geología UNAM Estación Regional Noroeste, Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico
(2) Instituto de Geología, Secihti-Instituto de Geología UNAM Estación Regional Noroeste, Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico

(3) Instituto de Geología, UNAM Institutio de Geologia Estacion Regional Noroeste, Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico; UNAM-LANGEM, Laboratorio Nacional de Geoquímica y Mineralogía, Ciudad de México, Mexico, Mexico
(4) Ecología de la Biodiversidad, Instituto de Ecología UNAM, Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico
abstract: Biochar, a carbon-based material derived from organic residues, offers a promising route for remediation of soil and water systems through its capacity to bind heavy metals, an ability that can be further enhanced via activation treatments. This study examined how chemical and biological activation influence the performance of two biochars generated from arid-zone biomass byproducts: pecan-pruning orchard residue and bovine femur bones in improving heavy metals immobilization. Chemical activation involved NaOH impregnation (0.5, 1, and 2 M) for periods of 3 to 24 h, followed by a thermal treatment step. Bone char was subjected to biological activation using vermiwash, a liquid byproduct of vermicomposting, applying both fresh and 10-month-aged extracts at 6- and 24-h impregnation intervals. Adsorption capacity was assessed through batch experiments targeting Pb (single-element solution) and Cd, Cu, Mn, and Zn (multi-element solution), each at 100 mg L⁻¹, comparing treated versus untreated materials. The chemically activated biochar (0.5 M NaOH, 18 h, plus thermal treatment) achieved enhanced immobilization with the largest increases observed for Mn (15%) and Cd (20%); notably, Pb removal was greater in the unmodified material. Biologically activated bone char (aged vermiwash, 24 h) improved immobilization efficiency, driven by gains in surface area, porosity, and surface functional groups, with the strongest effects seen for Cu (29%) and Zn (17%). Together, these findings support the viability of regionally sourced pecan pruning and bovine bone as low-cost remediation materials in arid environments, while underscoring the added complexity of multi-element contamination and the potential benefit of combining both activated biochar and bone char for more robust, sustainable remediation outcomes.

title: U-Pb Pyrochlore Geochronology and Applications to Carbonatites: An Exploration of the Amba Dongar Carbonatite Complex, Deccan Traps Large Igneous Province
session_title: Geochronology of Ore Deposits Containing Critical Minerals: Analytical Advances and Applications (Posters)
authors: Green, Theodore [1], Naik, Anmol [2], Khadri, Syed F.R. [3], Schoene, Blair [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
(2) School of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Goa University, Taleigao, Goa, India
(3) Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh, India
(4) Geosciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA
abstract: Carbonatite complexes are spatially and temporally associated with several large igneous province (LIP) flood basalt eruptions, but their contributions to the total volatile outputs of LIPs have been understudied, in part because their timing has been difficult to constrain. Given the high CO 2 and SO 2 contents of the carbonatite and alkaline magmas that form carbonatite complexes, these eruptions may provide an explanation for noted inconsistencies between the timing and magnitude of flood basalt degassing and climate proxy records during many LIP eruption intervals. In the Deccan Traps LIP, for example, detailed geochronologic and stratigraphic records of basaltic eruptive pulses are not temporally aligned with climate proxies during the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction, contributing to ongoing debates about the relative contributions of the Deccan Traps LIP and the Chicxulub impactor to that extinction. The Amba Dongar carbonatite complex in Gujarat, India is a volatile- and rare earth element-rich component of the Deccan Traps that may represent a significant non-basaltic volatile flux of that LIP. However, the Amba Dongar eruptions are challenging to place into the broader context of Deccan Traps volcanism and degassing because they lack minerals like zircon that are commonly used for high-precision geochronology. To address this, here we present pyrochlore U-Pb TIMS dates for three samples of the Amba Dongar carbonatite complex, along with degassing estimates. The dates show a high degree of scatter across the late Cretaceous, which makes synchronicity with other Deccan Traps eruptions difficult to resolve at present but indicates potential utility for pyrochlore TIMS geochronology for carbonatites with additional method development. Better constraining these eruptions will allow for more detailed Deccan Traps LIP degassing models and comparison to climate proxy records to further explore its contributions to the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. Pyrochlore has only been used infrequently as a U-Pb dating tool, but its abundance in many carbonatite systems and high U content warrant further exploration. As pyrochlore is an important niobium ore, this method development also has implications for understanding the timing and formation of mineral resources at Amba Dongar and in other critical mineral systems.

title: Do Hurricane Helene-Triggered Landslides Follow Historical Patterns of Slope Instability?
session_title: Emerging Research into the Impacts of Hurricane Helene in the Southern Appalachians (Posters)
authors: Das, Raja [1], Wegmann, Karl W. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, Virginia, USA
(2) North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC,
abstract:
Hurricane Helene triggered widespread landsliding across the southern Appalachians, providing an opportunity to evaluate how extreme-event landslide patterns compare with the pre-existing record of slope instability. This study applies spatial point-pattern analysis to 8,512 Helene-triggered landslides and 5,727 pre-Helene landslides, with process-specific comparisons focused on debris flows and debris slides. Ripley’s K and the variance-stabilized L function, evaluated against Monte Carlo envelopes under complete spatial randomness, were used to quantify scale-dependent clustering within the two temporal populations. Spatial correspondence was further evaluated using nearest-neighbor distances between Helene-triggered and pre-Helene failures and same-type proximity for debris flows and debris slides.

Both inventories are significantly clustered across all scales examined (0.1–10 km), with Helene-triggered landslides showing a stronger departure from spatial randomness than the pre-Helene inventory. Helene-triggered landslides occur at a median distance of 4.6 km from the nearest mapped pre-Helene failure, with 14.6% occurring within 1 km and 26.7% within 2 km. Same-type spatial correspondence differs at shorter distances: 11.1% of Helene debris slides occur within 1 km of a pre-Helene debris slide, compared with 6.6% of Helene debris flows occurring within 1 km of a pre-Helene debris flow. At 5 km, approximately 32.5% of both failure types occur near a historical failure of the same type.

These preliminary results indicate stronger regional clustering associated with the Helene-triggered inventory and differences in short-range spatial correspondence among failure processes, providing insights into how historical landslide inventories may inform regional landslide susceptibility assessment across the southern Appalachians.

title: Multiscale Mineralogical Observations of Telluride Minerals from the Perseverance Volcanogenic Massive Sulfide Deposit, Matagami Camp, Quebec, Canada
session_title: Formation, distribution, and preservation of critical mineral resources: Advancing our understanding through petrology, geochemistry, structure, and geodynamics (Posters)
authors: Kasprowicz, Filip [1], Monecke, Thomas [2], Kocher, Simon [3], Pierre, Samuel [4]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Lakewood, CO, USA
(2) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(3) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(4) Lavoisier H2 Geoconsult, Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, France
abstract: The metalloid element tellurium (Te) has been designated a critical mineral in the United States due to its role in advanced manufacturing, semiconductor production, and the development of thin-film solar panel technologies. While the abundance of Te in the upper crust rarely exceeds 3 ppb, tellurium is frequently enriched by a factor of 1,000 to 10,000 in volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) deposits, where concentrations typically range from 20 to 150 ppm and can locally reach highs of 400 ppm. VMS deposits represent a potentially significant source for meeting global tellurium demand, however a major knowledge gap persists regarding the characteristics, abundance, and enrichment mechanisms of telluride minerals in these unique environments. The past producing Te-rich Perseverance VMS deposit in the Matagami camp of the northern Abitibi greenstone belt in Quebec, Canada, yielded 5.1 Mt of ore grading 15.8% Zn, 1.24% Cu, 29.4 g/t Ag, and 0.4 g/t Au. Postdepositional deformation and greenschist-facies metamorphism dramatically altered the structure and mineral fabrics of the deposit, introducing widespread grain coarsening, recrystallization, and ductile deformation textures. This study expands upon previous research by the authors establishing a spatial and textural link between metamorphic textures and the presence of telluride phases by incorporating new samples from the Perseverance Main orebody alongside new analytical results. Tellurides were found to follow similar patterns of filling triple junctions, forming multi-phase inclusions, and occupying fractures in cataclastic pyrite grains. Tellurium endowment in new and previously collected samples was determined through bulk rock geochemistry, and high-resolution field emission scanning electron microscopy analyses identify distinct subgrain development (1 to 5 µm) within coarse pyrite crystals (50 to 500 µm). These pyrite subgrains are encased by rims of submicron-scale Te phases, providing further evidence of a spatial and temporal relationship between discrete telluride mineral formation and metamorphic recrystallization processes.

title: Functional Change and Recovery Across the K–Pg Boundary in the Western Interior Seaway and Gulf Coastal Plain
session_title: Progress in paleoecology: reconstructing life-history, behavior, physiology, and ecological interactions in the fossil record (Part II)
authors: Hopkins, Joseph [1], Myers, Corinne [2], Roopnarine, Peter D. [3], Purcell, Ceara K.Q. [4]
affiliations: (1) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM,
(3) California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, CA,
(4) Albuquerque, NM,
abstract:
The Cretaceous–Paleogene (KPg) mass extinction eliminated a substantial proportion of marine taxa, but the extent to which it disrupted ecological roles, functional redundancy, and assemblage structure across regional and local geographic scales remains unresolved when entire marine assemblages are considered. This study evaluates changes in taxonomic richness, functional richness, trait selectivity, and ecological structure across the KPg boundary in marine assemblages of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) and Gulf Coastal Plain (GCP).

Occurrence-level data from the Paleobiology Database, U.S. Geological Survey datasets, and legacy datasets (Purcell, 2023; Myers, 2013) were standardized into a unified occurrence database, assigned to substage-level time bins, and grouped into 12 analytical units from the middle Campanian through the Thanetian. Functional traits were assigned at the genus and species levels using diet, motility, and tiering following Bambachian megaguild logic (Bambach, 1983). Analyses of standardized taxonomic richness, functional-group richness, redundancy, occupancy, trait survivorship, and functional composition are to be conducted to characterize ecological restructuring across the extinction and recovery interval.

Based on patterns documented by Edie et al. (2025, 2018) as well as Roopnarine et al. (2019), we anticipate taxonomic losses will exceed losses in functional diversity, reflecting selective ecological restructuring while retaining functional redundancy rather than total functional collapse. Comparisons between the Western Interior Seaway and Gulf Coastal Plain will evaluate whether these patterns are consistent across regional settings and show the trajectory of functional recovery through the Paleocene.

title: Luminescence Dating of Maar Eruptions in the Clear Lake Volcanic Field
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems
authors: Cordero, Karissa [1], Brown, Nathan D. [2], Ball, Jessica L. [3], Ruth, Dawn Catherine Sweeney [4]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, Texasa, USA
(2) University of Texas, Arlington, TX,
(3) United States Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA,
(4) United States Geological Survey, Moffett Field, CA,
abstract:
The Clear Lake Volcanic Field in northern California has experienced explosive volcanic activity over the past 2.1 million years, with the most recent eruptions forming maars along the margins of Clear Lake. The timing of these eruptions remains poorly constrained due to a paucity of datable organic carbon and the complex depositional environments associated with maar tephra. While radiocarbon dating suggests that several eruptions occurred between ~8,500 and 13,500 cal yr. BP, it remains unclear whether additional eruptions took place within the last 2,000–3,000 years as suggested by oral histories of local Indigenous communities. Additionally, radiocarbon ages may be affected by the reservoir effect, resulting in erroneously old ages.

In this study, we have refined the maar eruption chronology of the CLVF by applying single-aliquot regenerative post-infrared infrared stimulated luminescence (post-IR IRSL) dating of K-feldspar grains to several maar craters along the edge of Clear Lake. Preliminary luminescence ages from maar craters surrounding the lake range from 5.5 ± 1.3 ka to 35.1 ± 13 ka, consistent with the established geologic framework of the area. These ages were compared with existing radiocarbon ( 14 C) age constraints. Currently, five sampling locations have both luminescence and radiocarbon ages available for comparison. Of these, two agree within 1σ uncertainty, two yield luminescence ages that are older than the corresponding radiocarbon ages, and one yields a younger luminescence age. The older luminescence ages are interpreted to be from contamination of radiocarbon samples by younger carbon, likely introduced through groundwater infiltration or root intrusion. Such contamination would bias the radiocarbon ages younger. In contrast, the younger luminescence age is interpreted to be from contamination of the radiocarbon sample by older carbon associated with a documented carbon seep at the lake bottom, where magmatic CO₂ may have introduced a reservoir effect, producing an artificially old radiocarbon age. These luminescence ages provide additional constraints on the timing of the most recent maar eruptions, informing future volcanic hazard assessments and monitoring strategies in this region.

Keywords: OSL, luminescence dating, maar eruptions, post-IR IRSL

title: Lead concentration and bioaccessibility decline with time after wildland-urban interface (WUI) fires
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part I)
authors: Kim, Christopher S. [1], Gabriel, Mia [2], O'Connell, Christine [3], Vejar, Manny [4]
affiliations: (1) Chapman University, Orange, CA,
(2) Chapman University, Orange, CA, USA
(3) Schmid College of Science and Technology, Chapman University, Orange, CA, USA
(4) Chapman University, Orange, California, USA
abstract:
The increasing frequency and severity of wildfires globally pose an emerging threat to the environment and human health. Wildfires occurring at the wildland-urban interface (WUI) can cause widespread damage to the built environment, mobilizing a wide range of toxic substances including metals such as lead (Pb), which can persist in the form of long-covered layers of lead-based paint in older (pre-1978) homes.

The 2025 Eaton Fire (Altadena, CA) destroyed 9000+ structures including 4300+ single-family homes, where the median timeframe of construction was 1945-1948. The release of Pb from the combustion of these structures resulted in substantial local surface deposition of Pb as ash and debris as well as downwind transport of Pb-enriched materials within the resulting smoke plumes. The distribution and bioaccessibility of Pb in ash-impacted soils immediately after the fires and in the subsequent months post-containment is largely unknown yet has significant importance due to the reconstruction and ongoing rehabitation of homes on these sites.

Soil sampling was conducted at 1, 6, 12, and 18 months post-containment of the 2025 Eaton Fire, sampling from ten burned residential sites located within the fire boundary and ten unburned sites within 3.5 km of the ash plume. Handheld X-ray fluorescence spectrometers were used to collect in situ measurements of a range of metals at multiple (n=40-50) locations at each site, measuring at both the soil surface and subsurface (5 cm depth). Soil samples were then collected from selected locations at each property at soil depths of 0–1 cm, 1–5 cm, and 5–10 cm. Samples were air-dried and sieved to recover potentially ingestible particles (≤250 µm), then underwent in vitro lead bioaccessibility analysis using simulated gastric fluid (SGF) extractions. Sampling was repeated at the same locations at each time point.

Key findings include: 1) [Pb] is initially elevated in surface soils of burned sites relative to unburned sites, with [Pb] progressively declining to background concentrations; 2) Pb bioaccessibility declines over time in soils from burned sites; and 3) soils from unburned lots show relatively constant [Pb] and Pb bioaccessibility as a function of both time and depth. This suggests progressive off-site transport of lead-enriched soils via weather events and remediation efforts.​ These findings provide critical insight into post-WUI fire metal contamination, informing future public health and soil remediation strategies

title: Compaction-driven cycles at a pycnocline: reef to fore-reef transition, Permian Reef, West Texas
session_title: What the facies? Carbonate sedimentology and paleoenvironmental proxies
authors: Jeffery, David L. [1], Slootman, Arnoud [2]
affiliations: (1) Petroleum Engineering and Geology, Marietta College, Marietta, Ohio, USA
(2) Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan
abstract: The initiation of reef growth of the Permian Reef occurs at the basal transition of the reef into fore-reef breccias. Within this interval, thin, meter scale lenses of in situ reef boundstone nucleate on the breccia substrate. Boundstone beds interfinger up-dip into half meter scale beds of coated grain grainstone with up-slope dipping cross bedding. Along the Tejas Trail in Pine Canyon in Guadalupe Mountains National Park, this association forms parasequences. Parasequence sets stack in a retrogradational, aggradational, then progradational pattern. Retrogradation is likely caused by compaction of the underlying debris as the main reef progrades over the fore-reef. As compaction slows relative to sedimentation rate of growth and debris accumulating at the toe of the approaching reef front, parasequences aggrade, then prograde. The Pine Canyon exposure is a transition with either a broad debris platform ahead of the reef front, or within a submarine canyon or embayment. The exposure of this transition at McKittrick Canyon along the Permian Reef Trail is steeper and composed mainly of a wedge of meter scale beds of coated grain grainstone with up-dip directed cross beds. This is interpreted to indicate the reef has prograded to the edge of the debris slope and forms a steep reef front slope continuous with the fore-reef slope. These facies occur at a persistent depth along the reef front on the order of 150-200 meters and have been observed at numerous locations where facies are adequately exposed. This is consistent with the hypothesis that a pycnocline at the base of the well mixed water stratum impinged upon the slope above an oxygen minimum zone. Internal waves and internal tsunamis along the pycnocline helped mix and move water from the deeper, oxygen poor layer upward, providing nutrients for reef growth.

title: Descriptive and Comparative Analysis of Novel Late Cretaceous Cartilaginous Fish Teeth from the Southwestern Limestone Deposits of Puerto Rico.
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Jimenez Ramirez, Jean [1], Santos, Hernan [2]
affiliations: (1) University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez, Cabo Rojo, Puerto Rico, Puerto Rico
(2) University of Puerto Rico Mayagüez, Cabo Rojo, Puerto Rico
abstract: Fossil elasmobranchs, commonly known as sharks and rays, from the Late Cretaceous of the Caribbean have a relatively scarce fossil record. Here, we report a novel collection of previously undescribed elasmobranch remains from the El Rayo Formation and the Parguera Limestone in southwestern Puerto Rico. These formations represent marine depositional environments along the southern edge of Puerto Rico during the Late Cretaceous. Within these units, we recovered isolated elasmobranch teeth that exhibit several diagnostic features indicative of lamniform and myliobatiform affinities, despite their fragmentary condition. These findings indicate the presence of generalist sharks and durophagous rays, suggesting a more complex and dynamic marine ecology than previously reported. Owing to these assemblages, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of Cretaceous Caribbean marine ecosystems and biogeography.

title: The Paleogeographic History of the End-Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway: Persistence and Connection During the Maastrichtian
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Part II)
authors: Slattery, Joshua S [1], Landman, Neil H. [2], Minor, Keith P. [3], Tenney, Zachary [4], Sandness, Ashley L [5]
affiliations: (1) Cheyenne, Wyo, USA
(2) Division of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History, New York, New York, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Texas Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
(4) Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Wyoming, Laramie, Wyoming, USA
(5) Cheyenne, WY, USA
abstract:
The Maastrichtian Western Interior Seaway (WIS) has traditionally been interpreted as a shallow epeiric sea that gradually retreated from the continental interior during the Maastrichtian. More recent paleogeographic reconstructions have suggested that the seaway became completely isolated from the Gulf of Mexico during the early Maastrichtian and persisted only as a restricted arm of the Arctic Ocean or Hudson Seaway into the late Maastrichtian and Paleocene. However, the timing, extent, and connection of the final stages of the WIS remain poorly constrained despite their importance for understanding Late Cretaceous oceanic circulation, climate, and biogeographic patterns.

To address these questions, we compiled published records together with new stratigraphic, sedimentological, and paleontological data to reconstruct paleogeography and depositional environments for successive ammonite biochrons ranging from the early Maastrichtian Baculites baculus biochron to the late Maastrichtian Hoploscaphites nebrascensis biochron. This high-resolution framework allowed us to document changes in the extent of the seaway over time and evaluate marine connection among the WIS, the Gulf of Mexico, the Arctic Ocean, and the Hudson Seaway.

Our results indicate that the retreat of the WIS was more complex than a simple long-term regression. Ammonites, inoceramids, ichnofossils, marine reptiles, and other fossil groups indicate continued faunal exchange among the WIS, the Gulf of Mexico, the Arctic Ocean, and the Hudson Seaway for longer than previously recognized. Our data suggest that northern connections persisted at least through the middle Maastrichtian Baculites grandis Biochron or slightly later, whereas southern connections remained established until at least the late Maastrichtian, although perhaps not into the latest Maastrichtian. Nevertheless, the seaway itself persisted until at least the Cretaceous/Paleogene boundary and into the Paleocene as the Cannonball Sea. These results provide a revised model for the final history of the WIS and improve our understanding of Late Cretaceous paleogeography, faunal migration, oceanic circulation, and environmental change in North America.

title: Investigating Microplastic Incorporation in Modern Agglutinated Foraminiferal Tests from Sabine Lake, Southeast Texas, USA
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Minella-Warner, Darion [1], Rashall, Jenny [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental and Geospatial Sciences, Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, Texas, USA
(2) Department of Environmental and Geospatial Sciences, Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, Texas, USA
abstract: Microplastics have become ubiquitous in both terrestrial and aquatic environments. As an emerging contaminant, the effects of microplastics on aquatic ecosystems are still being investigated. Aquatic organisms may ingest microplastics starting at a low trophic level, passing particles through the food web. Some organisms, such as agglutinated forms of the single-celled foraminifera, have also been found to incorporate microplastics from their surroundings into their tests. The objective of this study is to identify potential microplastic incorporation within the test wall of agglutinated foraminifera, focusing on estuarine agglutinated foraminifera from Sabine Lake, Southeast Texas, USA. To investigate the incorporation of microplastics in agglutinated foraminifera, 10 samples were collected on a roughly north-south transect along the Texas-Louisiana border using an Eckman dredge. The transect crosses the natural salinity gradient of Sabine Lake, passing from the freshwater-influenced, low salinity waters of the northern portion of the lake into the higher salinity, marine-influenced southern waters. After collection, the samples were rinsed through a 63-micron mesh sieve to remove clays and were allowed to dry. Once dried, 300 specimens per sample were picked to assess variability in the assemblages. The southernmost samples are dominated by calcareous benthic foraminifera, whereas the middle and northernmost samples display a predominately agglutinated assemblage. The most abundant agglutinated taxa amongst the samples include species belonging to the genera Ammobaculites , Caronia , Haplophragmoides , and Miliammina . For microplastic analysis, agglutinated foraminiferal tests will soak in a mixture of Nile Red dye and acetone, which will preferentially bind to microplastics rather than mineral grains in the test wall. After drying, the samples will be observed using a stereomicroscope equipped with cyan lighting (490-515 nm wavelength) and an orange filter to fluoresce any microplastics in the test. The data collected in this study will contribute to the growing understanding of agglutinated foraminifera and their response to pervasive microplastics in the environment.

title: Comparison of Sedimentological and Redox Variation Across the Beaufort Hinge of Northern Alaska: Similarities and Differences in Cores from the Colville Foreland Basin and Nascent Arctic Ocean during the Aptian-Albian
session_title: Cretaceous Mudstones of the Western Interior Seaway: New Insights into Sedimentary Inputs and Processes Impacting Geologic Resources Potential
authors: Whidden, Katherine [1], Lease, Richard Oliver [2], Macquaker, Joe [3]
affiliations: (1) United States Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA
(2) United States Geological Survey, Anchorage, AK,
(3) University of Aberdeen, Aberdeen, Scotland, United Kingdom
abstract:
Lower Cretaceous sediments in Arctic Alaska are volumetrically dominated by mudstones. Some are highly enriched in organic carbon and their deposition was associated with local redox variations in bottom waters. Environmental controls responsible for this redox variability were subtle. This work aims to investigate the underlying stratigraphic and structural controls on the effectiveness of local carbon sequestration.

Early Cretaceous collisional tectonics in northern Alaska led to formation of the east-west trending Brooks Range and Colville foreland basin. The Colville foreland basin was bounded to the north by the Beaufort Hinge, which served as the rift shoulder for the Early Cretaceous opening of the western Arctic Ocean and likely acted as the northern margin of a silled basin. To better understand depositional conditions associated with localized organic carbon sequestration, Aptian-Albian fine-grained rocks were characterized in two cores, using thin section petrography, organic and trace element data. A southern core, N. Kalikpik-1, is from the outer part of the Colville forelandbasin and a northern one, Orion-1, is from the rift shoulder adjacent to the Arctic Ocean. Organic carbon isotopes (d 13 C org ) were used to establish a ca. 127-110 Ma chemostratigraphic framework for evaluation of lateral facies variability.

The Early Cretaceous mudstones accumulated slowly at ~3 m/Myr and are relatively thin compared with locations elsewhere in North America. Both cores are dominated by mudstones and are distinctive because they contain out-sized clasts previously interpreted to be dropstones derived from sea-ice. Sediments from the Orion-1 core contain significantly more poorly sorted silt- and sand-size grains (mainly quartz) organized into thinner beds than those from the N. Kalikpik-1 core which are dominated by bioturbated mudstones organized into poorly preserved genetic beds. These data suggest that sedimentation rates in the north were higher and that the northern site was closer to a sediment source, possibly the Beaufort Hinge. Notably, both cores contain diminutive burrows. These burrows are preserved through the OAE1a interval in the N. Kalikpik-1 core, indicating suboxic to oxic conditions during the isotopic excursion. The trace element data illustrate similar redox patterns throughout with a lower, mainly oxic interval that includes OAE1a, and an upper suboxic/anoxic interval. Rapidly changing (on geological scales) redox conditions were likely driven by proximity to sediment and nutrient sources, changing sedimentation rates and particularly extent of ice.

title: Challenges and Successes in Expanding Quaternary Fault Databases for Geothermal Play Fairway Analysis in Southern New Mexico: A Case Study from the East Potrillo Fault Zone
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Prush, Veronica Blythe [1], Kelley, Shari A. [2], Gallant, Kyle Kip [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA
(2) New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Los Alamos, NM,
(3) NMBGMR/NMT, Albuquerque, NM,
abstract:
Recent efforts to identify blind geothermal systems using geothermal play fairways analysis have focused on integrations of geological and geophysical datasets, including crustal heat flow measurements, regional strain rate estimates, gravimetric, and magnetotelluric data (e.g., Faulds et al., 2015). These investigations demonstrate that promising blind geothermal system plays are frequently collocated with surficial Quaternary-active faults, especially within the Great Basin region of western North America. Because of the enhanced local permeability resulting from increased fracture density development within complex fault zones, structural complexities like extensional jogs, fault intersections, and horsetail splays represent the most viable targets for geothermal resource development (Giddens and Faulds, 2025).

New Mexico has received recent attention as a target for geothermal exploration due to its relatively high crustal heat flow attributed to Rio Grande rift-related lithospheric thinning and emplacement of Cenozoic volcanic intrusions (Grimes and Nelson, 2025). Despite this interest, Quaternary fault mapping in target regions for geothermal exploration remains largely incomplete, particularly in southern New Mexico and near the transition zone between the Basin and Range and Rio Grande rift provinces. Here we use high-resolution digital elevation models and derivatives to identify previously unrecognized Quaternary fault scarps and zones of enhanced fault complexity in southern New Mexico. We highlight an example from the East Potrillo fault zone, where a horsetail splay near the southern termination of the fault is collocated with a known region of elevated heat flow. We describe challenges of remotely mapping faults in this low-strain setting and outline successful methodological approaches in identifying previously unrecognized fault scarps within the often cryptic neotectonics landscape of southern New Mexico.

Faulds, J.E. et al., 2015, Integrated Geologic and Geophysical Approach for Establishing Geothermal Play Fairways and Discovering Blind Geothermal Systems in the Great Basin region, Western USA: A Progress Report, in GRC Transactions, v. 39, p. 691-700.

Giddens, M.H., and Faulds, J.E., 2025, Analysis of Step-Overs (or Relay Ramps) in Normal Fault Systems in the Great Basin Region, Western USA: Implications for Geothermal Exploration and Development, in Proceedings of the 50th Workshop on Geothermal Reservoir Engineering, Standford, California, Stanford University, SGP-TR-229, p. 1-15.

Grimes, J., and Nelson, D. (Eds.), 2025, The Future of Geothermal in New Mexico: A Land of Geothermal Enchantment: Project InnerSpace, 237 p.

title: Strategies for using constrained optimization (CONOP) to quantify chronostratigraphic uncertainty
session_title: Data-driven approaches for aligning geologic information in time
authors: Sullivan, Nicholas B. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, Penn State, State College, PA, USA
abstract:
The calibration of Earth history depends on transforming ordinal biostratigraphic successions into high-resolution numerical timescales. While radioisotopic ages provide essential temporal anchors, integrating High-Resolution Event Stratigraphy (HiRES), magnetostratigraphy, and astrochronologic constraints can substantially improve temporal resolution while providing explicit estimates of uncertainty. Here I present a quantitative framework that combines the regional synthesis capabilities of Constrained Optimization (CONOP) with high-frequency temporal constraints derived from cyclostratigraphy.

Two complementary strategies are explored for incorporating astrochronologic constraints into CONOP. In the first, cyclostratigraphic durations and astronomical tuning are incorporated directly into the optimization matrix as interval constraints. In the second, composite CONOP solutions are evaluated against independent astrochronologic models using lines of correlation. The framework is demonstrated using two contrasting datasets: a Cenozoic Southern Ocean synthesis integrating microfossil and magnetostratigraphic data, and a regional composite of Pennsylvanian cyclothems.

Beyond producing optimized composite chronologies, this framework provides a quantitative means of assessing chronostratigraphic uncertainty. Ensembles of near-optimal CONOP solutions are analyzed to characterize the stability of key stratigraphic events, yielding probabilistic estimates of isochroneity, correlation reliability, and temporal uncertainty. Rather than a single best-fit composite, the approach captures the range of chronostratigraphic solutions supported by the available data, providing a more rigorous basis for evaluating the Geologic Time Scale.
