title: Insights into Florida’s Geologic CO2 Storage Potential
session_title: Subsurface Characterization and Advanced Modeling for Carbon Storage, Hydrogen, Geothermal, and Emerging Energy Technologies
authors: Maurrasse, Florentin J. [1], Tejada, Lukas [2], Sanchez-Hernandez, Yosmel [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Environment, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
(2) Earth & Environment, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(3) Fugro, Houston, Texas, USA
abstract:
Extensive oil exploration of the deep carbonate platform of the Florida Peninsula in the twentieth century provided a wealth of information on the lithologic succession and structure of the South Florida area to depths reaching the igneous basement [1;2;3;4]. As recent interests in potential areas for geologic CO 2 storage are actively seeking to identify viable sites for permanent CO 2 sequestration, geologic data archived in collections of unpublished materials provide preliminary insights into the unique storage a potential of South Florida. Applying these available resources, our objective is to present such possibility from the late George Winston’s extensive collection of unpublished data that can provide a foundation to expand the current understanding of the CO 2 storage potential of South Florida. Based on these documents, we review and reconstruct the deep stratigraphy of South Florida and perform a qualitative characterization of its viable CO 2 storage capability.

Stemming from the dislocation of Gondwana, the western Tethys was developing while the Florida Peninsula remained a stable and consistently shallow, slowly subsiding, undisturbed carbonate factory. The apparent best potential sequences are in the South Florida Basin where the oldest unit, the nonabsorbent Basal Transgressive Clastics (Upper Jurassic) are overlain by 1700 ft (518 m) of the Wood River Fm composed of microcrystalline sucrosic dolomite which yield well-connected intercrystalline porosity, interbeds of micritic and oolitic limestones partially dolomitic with vuggy pores. The overlying Bone Island Fm (Uppermost Jurassic – lowermost Berriasian) has an eastern basinward trend and ranges in thickness from 575 - 1630 ft (175-497 m) with up to 23% porosity. Thus, both formations show suitability for fluid intake, therefore with adequate potential for CO 2 storage and confinement.

These successions will provide adequate injection and confining zones with no risk of leakage pathways. We propose that further studies should develop a robust evaluation of the stratigraphic and geochemical characterization of the expected carbon storage sites in the South Florida Basin.

title: Geothermal Control on Deep Lithium Enrichment in Salar Brines: A Geo-Hydrodynamic Study of Laguna Verde, Atacama Region, Chile
session_title: Beyond Ores: Characterization and Extraction of Critical Minerals from Unconventional and Secondary Resources
authors: Alam, Mohammad Ayaz [1], Bhattacharya, Prosun [2]
affiliations: (1) Departamento de Ingeniería Geoespacial y Ambiental, Universidad de Santiago de Chile, Santiago, Región Metropolitana de Santiago, Chile
(2) Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
abstract:
Direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies are increasingly promoted as an environmentally preferable alternative to evaporation-pond mining in salars, since they avoid large-scale water loss to evaporation. However, DLE introduces a different set of hydrogeological risks: continuous brine pumping and reinjection can perturb salar hydrology, induce subsidence, and impact the shallow freshwater aquifers and wetlands on which local ecosystems and communities depend. A more sustainable path forward requires identifying brine horizons that can be selectively extracted with minimal disturbance to these shallow, connected systems.

This study investigates the role of geothermal fluids in concentrating lithium (Li) within deep brine horizons that lie beneath shallow freshwater aquifers in salars, using the Laguna Verde basin (Atacama Region, Chile) as a natural laboratory. Prior work by the author documented a geothermal system beneath Laguna Verde and found Li concentrations in thermal waters up to seven times higher than in non-thermal waters (lagoon, feeder streams, snowmelt). Recent exploratory drilling in the basin reported average Li concentrations of 203 mg/L, reaching up to 409 mg/L at depth, coincident with elevated subsurface temperatures (20–30 °C), suggesting that geothermally driven convective overturn of brine horizons progressively enriches Li with depth, which is analogous to trends reported at the Maricunga salar.

We propose an integrated geo-scientific characterization combining field campaigns, petrographic and bulk-rock geochemical analysis of candidate Li source rocks, physicochemical characterization of meteoric, thermal, and subsurface brine end-members, and compilation of public well-log data (lithological, hydrogeological, geochemical). These datasets will feed a coupled thermo-hydro-geochemical numerical model (groundwater flow, heat transfer, solute transport, and geochemical reactions) to quantify the Li mass balance and predict enrichment trajectories at depth. Results aim to establish whether geothermally driven, depth-selective brine extraction using hydrocarbon-industry-style oriented drilling can substantially reduce the hydrological footprint of lithium mining in fragile salar ecosystems.

title: A Phylogenetic and Biogeographic Analysis of Turritellid Gastropods in the U.S. Coastal Plain across the end-Cretaceous Mass Extinction
session_title: Phylogenetic and Computational Approaches in Paleobiology and Paleoecology (Posters)
authors: Crowley, Kiera D. [1], Anderson, Brendan M. [2], Allmon, Warren D. [3]
affiliations: (1) School of Geosciences, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA; Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Norman, OK, USA
(2) Paleontological Research Institution, Ithaca, NY, USA
(3) Paleontological Research Institution, Ithaca, NY, USA
abstract:
Turritellid gastropods are diverse and abundant constituents of benthic marine assemblages of Late Cretaceous and early Paleocene age worldwide, especially in the U.S. Gulf, Atlantic, and Pacific Coastal Plains. Despite their frequent occurrence in these regions, no formal attempts have been made to test the evolutionary linkages between turritellid species known from the Late Cretaceous and those from the early Paleocene. However, characterizing the phylogenetic structure of turritellids in the U.S. Coastal Plains is of great importance for understanding the effects of the end-Cretaceous mass extinction on the evolutionary history of the clade. Given that only one U.S. species is known to stratigraphically span the K-Pg (in an impact-distal location on the Pacific Coast), it remains unclear without phylogenetic assessment whether the near-total species extinction and subsequent, geologically-rapid rebound of turritellid diversity is the result of regional extirpation followed by recolonization of impact-proximal localities, the rapid appearance of new species, or the persistence of multiple Cretaceous lineages in unsampled refugia.

Here, we conduct a Bayesian tip-dated phylogenetic analysis utilizing the fossilized birth–death process to investigate evolutionary relationships among ~45 species of turritellid gastropods spanning the Late Cretaceous to early Paleocene. We use well-preserved museum specimens and newly collected specimens from fieldwork at K-Pg outcrops in the Coastal Plain, and incorporate larval and juvenile morphological characters that are least susceptible to homoplasy in the clade. Wherever possible, we use a high-resolution biostratigraphic framework to temporally calibrate our model and best constrain divergence times for turritellid species. Preliminary results suggest that at least three different lineages of Coastal Plain turritellids are ancestral to documented Paleocene species, which implies that prior extinction rate estimates for the clade are inflated. Finally, we use our time-calibrated phylogeny as a framework for investigating biogeographic patterns of extinction across the K-Pg. We use a discrete-state Markov model to estimate the most probable geographic origin for ancestral nodes, and assess whether observed extinction patterns are the result of regional extirpation at impact-proximal localities or geographically non-selective extinction. This temporally- and spatially- constrained phylogenetic analysis yields deeper insight into potential biogeographic mechanisms shaping the pattern of widespread taxonomic extinction in turritellids, and provides a more nuanced estimation for the magnitude and timing of the clade’s recovery across the end-Cretaceous mass extinction.

title: Foraminiferal Assemblages of the Maastrichtian Nacatoch Formation, Corsicana, Texas, USA
session_title: New Advances in Mesozoic Paleontology, Stratigraphy, and Paleogeography of the Western Interior of North America (Posters)
authors: Rashall, Jenny [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental and Geospatial Sciences, Stephen F. Austin State University, Nacogdoches, Texas, USA
abstract: The Nacatoch Formation of North Texas is the sandy, middle unit of the Maastrichtian-age Navarro Group, underlain by the Neylandville Marl and overlain by the Corsicana Marl. The Nacatoch Formation, which is primarily composed of sandstone with interbedded mudstone, locally records shelf facies deposited during a period of regression in the early to middle part of the Maastrichtian. The extensive sandier intervals of the Nacatoch Formation yield a sparse foraminiferal assemblage, particularly when compared to the adjacent marl units. Consequently, the foraminifera of the Nacatoch Formation have received significantly less attention than those of other Navarro Group formations. The earliest investigation into the foraminiferal assemblages of the Nacatoch Formation was completed in the mid-1940s as part of a report on Late Cretaceous foraminifera from the Gulf Coast Plain region. Thirty-two taxa were identified from three outcrop localities of the Nacatoch Formation in northeast Texas. Following this initial assessment, the only subsequent detailed study of Nacatoch Formation foraminiferal assemblages is an unpublished thesis from the late 1980s. The study identified 129 taxa across 40 samples of the Nacatoch Formation. Samples used in the thesis were taken from six subsurface cores collected across the northeastern Texas area, providing context for both stratigraphic and geographic variability in diversity. Due to the numerous taxonomic revisions among Cretaceous planktic and benthic foraminiferal groups since this last assessment was completed, reevaluation of Nacatoch Formation foraminiferal assemblages is necessary. The present study utilizes a nearly continuous 200-ft section of subsurface core from Corsicana, Texas, originally collected for use in the aforementioned unpublished master’s thesis on foraminifera of the Nacatoch Formation. The remaining core was resampled at regular 1.5-ft intervals to record discrete assemblage changes across both the sandstone and mudstone lithofacies. Abundance and diversity of taxa vary throughout the core, with the most common species belonging to the genera Anomalinoides and Gaudryina . This study presents a detailed record of foraminiferal species distribution throughout the Nacatoch Formation in a modern taxonomic framework.

title: Wetland Restoration impacts on water fluxes between the surface and shallow subsurface
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions (Posters)
authors: Watts, Lyn [1], Hatch, Christine [2]
affiliations: (1) Binghamton University, Vestal, NY, USA
(2) University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA
abstract: Goals of wetland restoration include slowing down and ponding water, increasing residence time, and utilizing groundwater seeps to thermally and hydrologically buffer the wetland ecosystem. In addition to creating meandering streams that slow the velocity of water through the site, wetland restoration projects in coastal Massachusetts often involve building microtopography that are designed to mimic the ground surface in historic forested wetlands in the region (with hummocks and hollows created by downed trees). We focus on a single wetland site, restored in 2020, to assess how the restoration, including the built microtopography impacts water fluxes at the surface and within the root zone. We combine 8 years of continuous soil moisture monitoring, site wide water table estimates using paired piezometers, and seasonal aerial surveys of water inundation, to assess the impact of restoration on water movement in the vadose zone. Post-restoration data show a steady increase in soil moisture within the root zone, as well as a seasonally elevated water table that intersects the ground surface in some of the larger microtopographic depressions. Inundation at the surface fluctuates seasonally, but remains significantly wetter than the site surface pre-restoration, even during an extreme regional drought. Across all of these findings there is significant heterogeneity across the site as well as within small spatial scales, revealing the impact of microtopography in creating distinct micro-hydrologic conditions. These findings show promising results for wetland restorations in the region and confirm that the site is on a trajectory to develop into a climate resilient wetland over the next decade.

title: Understanding Pre-Eruptive Magmatic Processes at the Socorro Caldera Complex Using Zircon Geochronology and Geochemistry
session_title: Advances in the study of Magmatic and Volcanic Systems (Posters)
authors: Yermakov, Yakov [1], McLean, Noah [2], Krawczynski, Mike [3]
affiliations: (1) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS,
(3) Washington University, Campus Box 1169, Saint Louis, MO,
abstract:
Identifying the mechanisms that drive a stable magmatic system to transition into an active caldera-forming eruption event is a critical question for hazard mitigation. Sequentially erupted ignimbrites at the Socorro Caldera Complex, situated within Mogollon-Datil Volcanic Field (New Mexico), serve as an ideal natural laboratory for tracking chemical and thermal evolution of the magmatic plumbing system and its eruption initiation mechanisms. The compositionally zoned Lemitar Tuff contains less felsic enclaves in the uppermost section and erupted from the Hardy Ridge caldera, which belongs to a major complex of nested and westward younging calderas. We compare it with the underlying crystal-poor Vicks Peak Tuff, erupted from the nearby Nogal Canyon caldera, situated south of the major complex. To quantify magma storage, remobilization timescales and reconstruct chemical and thermal evolution, we employ high-precision zircon U-Pb geochronology coupled with trace and rare earth element geochemistry (TIMS-TREE).

Initial ID-TIMS U-Pb dates indicate the Lemitar Tuff possesses a high (810 ± 118 kyr, 2σ) zircon age dispersion, reflecting a long-term crystal mush state. Conversely, the Vicks Peak Tuff exhibits no resolvable zircon age dispersion, which may record rapid melt assembly without long-term storage conditions. These units, erupted 743 ± 91 (2σ) kyr apart, represent two endmembers in the spectrum of zircon age distributions observed for large felsic eruptions.

Preliminary zircon TREE data support different evolution pathways for parental magmas of these tuffs. Compared to the Lemitar tuff, Vicks Peak zircons are systematically lower in Hf and Eu/Eu*, coupled with higher Th/U and Dy/Yb ratios, which may indicate a compositionally distinct melt source. Time-resolved chemical data for the long-lived Lemitar Tuff show no strong compositional trends through time. Zircons from the less felsic enclaves yield broadly similar compositions to the host Upper Lemitar rhyolites, but have slightly higher Th/U and Dy/Yb ratios. These signatures could potentially record limited crystallization from a less evolved or rejuvenated melt batch. Paired core-rim zircon fragment analyses display normal fractionation trends during crystal growth, with increasing Hf and decreasing Eu/Eu*. However, the youngest zircon core-rim pairs exhibit a reversed pattern, which may be interpreted as evidence for thermal rejuvenation or magma recharge prior to eruption.

title: Back to Mohr Circle Space: Reconstructing Dynamic Stress and Rock Failure Near Salt
session_title: Faults, Fractures, and Geomechanics in Subsurface Energy and Mineral Systems
authors: Reeher, Lauren [1]
affiliations: (1) Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT, ; Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
abstract:
The ability to relate patterns of brittle rock failure to stress conditions permits geologists to better understand the nature of rock deformation in natural geologic settings. This relationship is classically evaluated in Mohr circle space, where empirically derived failure criteria provide context for interpreting paleostress. Near mechanically weak bodies such as salt, the local stress field can deviate from regional tectonic stresses in both orientation and magnitude, creating dynamic stress environments.

In a study of fractured Jurassic Moab Member sandstone bordering the exhumed Salt Valley salt wall in the Paradox Basin, Utah, we documented a system of conjugate shear fractures that records a spatially variable paleostress environment. Utilizing high resolution structural mapping and UAV derived photogrammetry, we demonstrate a systematic transition in stress regimes relative to the underlying salt geometry. Notably, under regional Laramide tectonic compression, the local stress field transitions from an extensional faulting regime directly above the salt wall roof to a strike slip faulting regime as it approaches the vertical salt wall margin. We applied a computationally efficient elastic dislocation modeling approach to simulate the stress response to salt wall amplification under this tectonic compression. Both observed and modeled results demonstrate consistent spatially variable local stress states, validating this approach for interpreting complex stress states adjacent to salt without explicitly modeling salt rheology.

Furthermore, this spatial transition is accompanied by a systematic change in conjugate dihedral angles, reflecting a gradient in critical differential stress magnitude approaching the salt body. When arrayed in Mohr circle space, these field observations provide rare empirical evidence that a non-linear failure criterion is most applicable for assessing brittle failure in this natural geologic environment. Because this non-linear relationship predicts changes in fracture angle based on critical differential stress, we also suggest a pathway to estimate absolute paleostress magnitudes when calibrated with appropriate rock mass scaling parameters.

Ultimately, these two spatial trends, specifically the transition in local stress regimes and the systematic variation in conjugate failure angles, demonstrate how mechanically weak salt bodies profoundly alter regional tectonic stresses. By integrating these field trends with elastic dislocation modeling and non-linear failure criteria, we can reconstruct both the orientation and magnitude of paleostress, providing a robust framework for predicting rock failure near complex subsurface mechanical heterogeneities such as salt.

title: Microfossils Analysis for Provenance of Carbonate Gravels in the Ogallala Formation, Texas

authors: Eichler, Carla M. [1], McKinney, Alexandra Virginia [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Life, Earth, and Environmental Science, West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA
(2) Department of Life, Earth, and Environmental Science, West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA
abstract:
I am researching the Miocene cobbles and gravels of the Ogallala Formation in the southern high plains. The samples contain diagnostic microfossil assemblages that provide important evidence for the provenance of the Paleozoic carbonate source rocks from which they were derived. Brachiopod shell pieces in varying conditions and sizes are present in all samples examined and represent one of the most consistently occurring fossil groups. Diagenesis is evident in both fossil pieces and matrices varying across all samples. The assemblages are dominated by echinoderm fossils, including both transverse and longitudinal skeletal fragments. Lunate fossil pieces interpreted as crinoid arm elements are also common. Crinoids and brachiopods constitute the most abundant microfossil allochems in the samples, indicating derivation from shallow marine carbonate depositional environments. Less abundant fossil groups include bryozoans, foraminifera, and non-crinoid echinoderms, although their relative abundance varies among samples.

The observed microfossil assemblages strongly suggest derivation from Pennsylvanian carbonate formations exposed in eastern New Mexico, particularly the Sandia, Gray Mesa, and Atrasado formations, as well as the Sangre de Cristo and Manzano mountain ranges of the Madera Limestone Group of northern New Mexico. This interpretation is supported by the depositional environments, fossil assemblages, and regional correlations of these formations.

title: Out of Left Field: Using C/N Ratios to Understand how Sheep Impact Soil Health and Chemistry Through Prescribed Grazing Methods
session_title: Critical Zone and Soil Geomorphology: Intersection of Processes Linked to Climate, Ecology, Fire and Landscape Evolution (Posters)
authors: Strunk, Mollie [1], Burns, Lauren [2], Kneeshaw, Tara A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Grand Valley State University, Caledonia, MI, USA
(2) Tending Tilth, Michigan, USA

abstract: This study quantified soil organic matter in the particulate organic matter (POM) and mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) fractions in a field managed by prescribed sheep grazing over one year. Prescribed sheep grazing is a growing land management practice in Michigan, but there is limited quantitative data on its carbon sequestration potential. The field at an old paper mill in Vicksburg, MI was divided into two 2-acre plots: treated (grazed) and unmanaged (control). 18 soil cores were taken to 60 cm depth, with 4 subsamples of 15 cm for each core. Particle size fractionation was used to separate POM and MAOM, then elemental analysis was used to find C/N ratios, which were used as a proxy for carbon stabilization. Bulk density and soil moisture were collected at each site to support findings through soil structure, and ongoing nutrient and XRF analysis are being integrated to better understand factors contributing to organo-mineral association mechanisms. POM and MAOM C/N ratios show a consistent increasing trend over time in the 30-45 cm and 45-60 cm depth intervals in the grazed site that is not present in control samples, with high C/N ratios being caused by low nitrogen levels. %C in the grazed site POM steadily decreased over time at the surface depth, but was increasing by July in the 3 subsurface depths. This may be reflective of the first grazing event that began 7 days after samples were collected in May. In the MAOM grazed fraction, %C decreased in the first two depths, but increased in the second two depths by November. %N in the grazed site MAOM does not show increase over time, while POM %N is low at all depth intervals. These trends indicate the short-term cycling carbon pool is experiencing nitrogen leaching or other denitrifying processes and a carbon accumulation at depth not seen in the control site. As we continue to further explore the influence of prescribed sheep grazing on soil chemistry, we can better understand how these grazing activities impact carbon sequestration and long term stabilization processes.

title: The effects of burial diagenesis on the stable-isotopic composition and clumped-isotope thermometry of authigenic siderite from Pennsylvanian strata in the Appalachian Basin
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n)
authors: He, Ran [1], Currie, Brian [2], Kalmer, Mayme [3], Ingalls, Miquela [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
(2) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(3) Department of Geology & Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Siderite is a common authigenic mineral that is abundant in Pennsylvanian strata in the Appalachian Basin where reducing conditions in soils, wetlands, and marginal-marine/marine environments favored its formation. Pennsylvanian strata in the basin experienced an overall increase in burial-related temperatures due to enhanced flexural subsidence and the flux of fluids from the adjacent Alleghenian orogenic belt to the east. This distal-to-proximal thermal gradient provides a natural laboratory to characterize burial-related diagenetic changes on siderite stable isotope composition, as well as its effect on clumped isotope temperatures (T(Δ 47 )). Samples were collected along distal-proximal transects of the basin from eastern Ohio to northeastern Pennsylvania and from northeastern Kentucky to southeastern West Virginia. Sampled siderites included pedogenic sphaerosiderite and rhizocretions, as well as early authigenic concretions. Samples of marine/nonmarine limestones and pedogenic calcite were also collected to provide comparisons between the different carbonate types. Programmed-pyrolysis and vitrinite-reflectance modeling indicate that samples experienced maximum burial temperatures ranging from ~80 °C in the western-most parts of the basin, to ~210–290 °C in the eastern-most parts. Siderite samples yielded δ 13 C values ranging from –9.2‰ to +13.7‰ VPDB, and δ 18 O values from –12.8‰ to –3.3‰ VPDB. Calcite sample δ 13 C compositions ranged from –8.0‰ to +4.4‰ VPDB, and δ 18 O from –15.0‰ to –4.4‰ VPDB. Both siderite and calcite δ 18 O show a weak west-to-east decrease across the basin, which may suggest more extensive diagenetic alteration, but could alternatively reflect spatial variability in meteoric-water δ 18 O. Siderite clumped isotope measurements on a subset of samples yielded T(Δ 47 ) increases from ~48 °C in the western parts of the basin to ~105 °C in eastern parts, mirroring the west-to-east thermal-maturity gradient. The lower siderite T(Δ 47 ) temperatures relative to the calculated burial temperatures indicate partial solid-state reordering and/or closed-system recrystallization below peak burial temperatures. Together, these patterns indicate that early-diagenetic siderite is progressively destabilized with increasing thermal maturation. In addition, T(Δ 47 ) values recorded in this study are consistent with previously reported clumped-isotope temperatures from marine mollusks in the Appalachian Basin and pedogenic calcite from the adjacent Illinois Basin, suggesting that under comparable time–temperature histories, siderite behaves similar to calcite.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Sustainability: Revolutionizing Climate Action and Pollution Mapping
session_title: AI and Machine Learning in Predictive Groundwater Science: Integrating Hydrogeology, Geochemistry, and Geospatial Modeling
authors: Chakraborty, Paromita [1], Schei, Andreas B [2], Ponnuswamy, Vinoth Kumar [3], R, Annie Uthra [4], Saraswat, Vishal [5], Bhattacharya, Prosun [6]
affiliations: (1) Centre for Research in Environment, Sustainability Advocacy and Climate Change, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Chengalpattu, Tamil Nadu, India
(2) The Royal Norwegian Embassy, New Delhi, New Delhi, India
(3) Department of Medicinal and Applied Chemistry, Kaohsiung Medical University, Kaohsiung city, Kaohsiung, Taiwan
(4) Department of Computational Intelligence, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, Chengalpattu, Tamil Nadu, India
(5) Bosch Global Software Technologies Private Limited, Bosch Cybersecurity University, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

abstract:
The accelerating impacts of climate change, biodiversity loss, resource depletion, and the widespread release of anthropogenic pollutants have intensified the need for innovative and scalable solutions to address complex environmental challenges. Traditional environmental monitoring and management approaches are often constrained by fragmented datasets, delayed assessments, and limited predictive capabilities, hindering effective environmental governance and timely intervention. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly emerging as a transformative technology capable of overcoming these limitations by enabling intelligent analysis of large, diverse, and continuously evolving environmental datasets.

This review explores the expanding role of AI in advancing environmental sustainability through applications in climate modelling, environmental monitoring, pollution assessment, ecosystem management, and sustainable resource utilization. By integrating data from remote sensing platforms, Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks, environmental observations, and numerical models, AI-driven techniques—including machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision—facilitate high-resolution environmental mapping, anomaly detection, predictive analytics, and early warning systems for climate- and pollution-related risks.

Particular emphasis is placed on the emerging role of AI in addressing complex chemical pollution, including plastic-associated chemicals, persistent organic pollutants (POPs), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and other contaminants of emerging concern. AI-assisted frameworks can improve source apportionment, contaminant transport modelling, hotspot identification, ecological and human health risk assessment, and the optimization of remediation and circular economy strategies. The integration of AI with digital twins, autonomous monitoring platforms, and decision-support systems further enhances adaptive environmental management under rapidly changing climatic conditions.

Despite these opportunities, challenges related to data quality, model transparency, computational demands, ethical considerations, and regulatory acceptance remain significant barriers to widespread implementation. Future research should prioritize explainable AI, standardized environmental data frameworks, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the integration of AI with environmental policy to ensure trustworthy and sustainable decision-making. By bridging environmental intelligence with scientific innovation, AI has the potential to reshape pollution management, strengthen climate resilience, and accelerate progress toward achieving global sustainability goals.

abstract: The Chicxulub impact (~66 Ma) is widely accepted as the primary cause of the Cretaceous–Paleogene (K Pg) mass extinction. At Wahalak Creek in northeastern Mississippi (~1500 km from the Chicxulub crater), the uppermost Prairie Bluff Chalk (PBC) records quiet, below-storm-wave-base deposition prior to impact, whereas the overlying basal Clayton Formation preserves a complex impact-generated event deposit. This deposit contains multiple depositional phases, including a high-energy rip-up interval with pebble- to cobble-sized chalk clasts, a spherule-rich ejecta bed, and a later-stage ammonite jaw-rich channel. The ammonite jaw-rich channel extends approximately 1.2 m vertically and contains tens of thousands of ammonite jaws, predominantly attributed to Discoscaphites, along with Eubaculites, fish remains, oysters, and chalk rip-up clasts. Ammonite jaws are exceptionally preserved, retaining delicate chitinous and calcitic layers, with many articulated in folio rather than butterfly position. The absence of comparable jaw accumulations within the underlying Prairie Bluff Chalk Formation, combined with the preservation of fragile structures, argues against significant reworking. The small rip-up clast size within the jaw channel suggests deposition during a late-stage phase of an impact-generated tsunami. Sediment samples collected at 10 cm intervals through the jaw channel show elevated carbonate content (up to 87.6 wt.% CaCO₃) that returns to values comparable to the underlying Prairie Bluff Chalk toward the top of the section. This carbonate enrichment is interpreted to reflect the suspension and settling of carbonate sediment within the water column during event deposition. Preliminary calcareous nannofossil analyses shows a Late Cretaceous assemblage including Micula murus most likely reworked from the underlying PBC as result of events related to the impact (ground shaking and tsunami scouring and subsequent settling). Stable oxygen and carbon isotope analyses of Discoscaphites jaw calcite preserve seasonal environmental signals recorded during ammonite growth, suggesting that the Chicxulub impact occurred during the Northern Hemisphere spring or summer. We interpret the ammonite jaw-rich channel as a late-stage tsunami-generated marine mass mortality deposit, preserving a rare record of catastrophic ecosystem disruption associated with the K-Pg mass extinction.

title: Indications of Storm Energy Recorded by Stratigraphic Deposits Generated During Coastal Erosion Events Preserved within a Progradational Stretch of Barrier Beach
session_title: Recent Advances and New Voices in Marine and Coastal Geoscience (Posters)
authors: Schmelz, William J. [1], Sherman, Deanna [2], Miller, Kenneth G. [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA

abstract:
The rapidly prograding beach at North Beach, Sandy Hook, New Jersey, preserves a ~25 year stratigraphic record of coastal storm impacts that we use to relate storm-driven forcing to the sedimentary characteristics of deposits these storms left behind. Interpreting GPR data collected on site, we identify over 30 storm-generated stratigraphic erosion surfaces preserved within the beach, and highly-accurate GNSS data constrain the timing of their formation between 2009 and 2025 CE. We combined hydrodynamic and statistical modeling to identify the storms most likely to have produced the preserved erosion surfaces. More than 1000 48-h XBeach simulations run using tide-gauge and wave buoy data were used to train a statistical emulation of the XBeach output, which was calibrated to reconstruct the stratigraphic observations. The modeling results suggest storms exceeding a water-level threshold of 1.3 m above MSL and significant wave heights of 3.8 m resulted in significant coastal erosion. Pre-, during-, and post-event observations from a January 10, 2024 nor’easter, which exceeded threshold conditions, validate the model-inferred thresholds.

Three-dimensional 400-MHz GPR data (~5 cm vertical resolution) identify 12 erosional surfaces generated over the past 7 years that can be traced ~60 m alongshore. Extensive sediment sampling of several of these storm surfaces indicates that the facies and sediment composition of storm deposits differ based on their elevation along the beach profile, while also reflecting geomorphological context. At ~1 to 1.5 m NAVD88, visually apparent truncation surfaces correspond with coarse sand overlain by a thin layer of highly concentrated dark minerals. Closer to 2 m NAVD88, the same event is represented by finer, medium sand, only slightly coarser than fair-weather deposits typical of North Beach, but still overlain by a dark mineral layer. At higher elevations, likely landward of the contemporaneous berm crest, trenches expose very coarse, landward-dipping beds that do not coincide with dark mineral deposits. We interpret these to be overwash or high-runup deposition onto the back beach. We integrate grain size measurements from multiple locations along the beach profile for individual storm deposits, across a number of storms, to develop a quantitative model aimed at estimating the relative energy associated with the coastal erosion events that formed the deposits. This approach represents a framework for interpreting relative storm intensity from preserved beach stratigraphy.

title: Petrochronological detrital zircon provenance as a tracer for geochemical anomalies: The example of Cu porphyries in the Peruvian and Chilean Andes
session_title: Trace elements trace processes: Using mineral chemistry to track geologic change in igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary systems (Posters)
authors: Saylor, Joel [1]
affiliations: (1) University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC,
abstract:
Detrital zircon provenance methods rely primarily on zircon ages to determine sediment sources. However, multiple potential sources may have the same age and/or discrete sources may have geochemistry that is unique and would allow greater insight into sediment derivation or the conditions under which those sources evolved. This is demonstrated, par excellence, in the Western Cordillera of Peru and Chile, where subduction, which has been ongoing since at least the Jurassic, has resulted in specific geochemical anomalies associated with Cu porphyries although those intrusions bear the same age as many surrounding intrusive rocks. Cu mineralization is associated with evolved, oxidized, and hydrous magmas: often those which originate in thick crust.

I test whether a newly developed non-negative Tucker-1 (NNT1) decomposition method can identify zircon grains with the specific geochemical characteristics of Cu porphyries from zircon grains derived from surrounding country rock. Samples come from modern river sediments taken at a range of distances from active Cu mines in mine-bearing catchments and also from catchments with no known Cu porphyries. The samples cover known mining districts in southern Peru and northern Chile. In southern Peru samples come from catchments adjacent to the Cuajone, Quellaveco, and Topquepala mines. In northern Chile, they come from catchments adjacent to the Lomas Bayas and El Salvador mines. Zircon grains were analysed via laser-ablation, inductively coupled-plasma mass spectrometry for U and Pb isotopes and trace and rare earth element concentrations. I factorized the combined dataset using the non-negative Tucker-1 decomposition (NNT1), yielding four endmembers. One of the endmembers features multiple geochemical proxies consistent with derivation from Cu-permissive lithologies (i.e., potential Cu porphyries). Moreover, there is a strong inverse relationship between the proportion of zircon grains with a Cu-permissive geochemistry and the area of mine-bearing catchments. I conclude that the NNT1 decomposition method can yield geologically meaningful petrochronological endmembers and that the proportions of those endmembers reflect the zircon yield, and potentially the sediment yield, from the identified sources. I also conclude that detrital zircon petrochronology and analysis via the NNT1 decomposition method represent viable methods for hunting for geochemical anomalies on the modern landscape and may have applications to deep time.

title: Modeling Firn Storage Loss and Meltwater Runoff Across Glacier Systems Using the Community Firn Model
session_title: Using Geophysics to investigate Near Surface Geological Problems
authors: Morgan, Daniel [1], Ramirez, Larissa [2]
affiliations: (1) Vanderbilt University, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA
(2) Vanderbilt, Vanderbilt, Nashville, TN, USA
abstract:
Firn stores meltwater within pore spaces before it either refreezes or contributes to runoff, making it an important control on glacier hydrology and surface mass balance. Although previous studies have examined firn evolution in individual glacier systems, particularly Greenland, fewer studies have compared runoff thresholds across glacier climates.

Glacier systems representing interior Greenland (cold polar), coastal Alaska (transitional), and New Zealand (maritime) were selected using observations from the NASA ITS _ LIVE velocity dataset. Firn evolution was simulated using the Community Firn Model, incorporating temperature- and accumulation-dependent densification to generate 70 m density profiles and calculate porosity, firn air content, and meltwater storage capacity. Sensitivity experiments evaluated the effects of accumulation rate and pulsed versus steady melt forcing.

The Greenland-like system retained 65–75% of its initial pore space and did not exceed the runoff threshold across the modeled temperature range. In contrast, the New Zealand maritime system retained less than 35% of its initial pore space, with runoff-dominated conditions occurring near −4°C. The Alaska-like transitional glacier exhibited the strongest threshold response, with runoff fraction increasing from <20% to >70% over only 2–3°C of warming and exceeding the runoff threshold near −8°C. Increasing accumulation delayed runoff thresholds by approximately 1–2°C, whereas short-duration melt pulses advanced threshold behavior by roughly 1°C relative to equivalent steady-melt scenarios.

These results indicate that glacier response to warming depends strongly on climate regime, with transitional glacier systems exhibiting the sharpest runoff thresholds and the greatest sensitivity to modest climatic change.

title: Body Size and Extinction Threat in Modern Mollusks with Comparisons to Cenozoic Patterns
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part II)
authors: Heim, Noel A. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Climate Sciences, Tufts University, Medford, MA, USA
abstract:
Mollusks are are on of the most species-rich and functionally diverse groups of animals in the modern ocean. However, marine mollusks are severely underrepresented on the The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. The World Register of Marine Species lists more than 61,000 marine mollusk species. However, only 2,098 species of marine mollusks have been added to the Red List, which constitute just over 3% of know species. Coverage of marine mollusks is in stark contrast to other groups such as marine tetrapods and terrestrial/freshwater mollusks, with approximately 100% and 26% of know species listed on the Red List, respectively. Despite the low coverage of marine mollusks on the Red List, the situation has been improved, with 804 species added since 2016 decade and 210 species were added in 2026.

This study takes advantage of a database of extant and extinct marine mollusk body sizes to evaluate potential body size biases in the species that have been added to the Red List and to compare extinction threat in the modern to the Cenozoic extinction selectivity. The data show that the large-bodied bivalves and gastropods are overrepresented on the Red List. Red List Cephalopods appear to be a random sample with respect to body size—primarily because 759 of the 869 know species are on the Red List. Body size selectivity patterns are mixed among classes. Threatened bivalves species do not show body size selectivity while larger cephalopods are more threatened and smaller gastropod species are more threatened. Gastropod selectivity is the strongest among the three classes and persists even though there is a bias in the Red List towards larger species.

The Red List species list was "degraded" to a genus-level dataset to compare with extinction selectivity across the Cenozoic. For Red List species with more than one species per genus, the most threatened species was used for the whole genus. Over the Cenozoic, smaller genes of bivalves and gastropods are more likely to go extinct than larger genera. For both classes, the modern extinction selectivity is outside the range of Cenozoic background, suggesting the ecological impacts of future extinctions could fundamentally reorganize marine ecosystems.

title: Freshwater input drives Plio-Pleistocene productivity on the Florida Platform
session_title: Cenozoic Celebration: Honoring Roger Portell and His Service to Paleontology (Part II)
authors: Grossman, Ethan L. [1], Sun, Zeyang [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Texas A&M University, COLLEGE STATION, TX, USA
(2) Energy Geosciences Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, USA
abstract: The Plio-Pleistocene Pinecrest beds of western Florida are renowned for their spectacular fossil diversity and abundance. However, it remains unclear whether this enhanced productivity was driven by upwelling, runoff, or submarine groundwater discharge (SGD). Here, we conduct carbonate clumped isotope (Δ 47 ) analyses on Conus gastropod shells previously analyzed for with δ 18 O, δ 13 C, and trace elements (Tao and Grossman, 2010, Palaios 25:796-806) to reconstruct seasonal variation in temperature ( T Δ 47 ) and seawater δ 18 O (δ 18 O w ). Four shells from two stratigraphic units, Unit 7 (2.5 to 3.5 Ma) and Unit 4 (2.0 to 2.5 Ma), were serially-sampled at quarterly to bimonthly resolution. Two shells from Unit 7, which contain a typical marine faunal assemblage, show temperatures ranging from 13 to 27 °C. The other two shells from Unit 4, with co-occurrence of marine and freshwater fossils, show weaker seasonality with T Δ 47 between 17°C and 25 °C. Reconstructed δ 18 O w values for Unit 7 vary from -1.8 to 1.4‰ VSMOW and correlate positively with temperatures. The correspondence of low δ 18 O w values with lower temperatures argues against upwelling as a productivity driver, as upwelling would yield high δ 18 O w values associated with cooler, upwelled water. Unit 4 samples show unusually high δ 18 O w values (0.0 to 3.2‰), especially considering the fossil evidence for freshwater input. Comparison of our data with the seasonal patterns of temperature and seawater δ 18 O for the modern Florida Bay indicates that Unit 7 was deposited in an offshore marine environment whereas Unit 4 was deposited in an estuarine environment similar to the modern Everglades. High δ 18 O w values recorded in Unit 4 specimens correlate with summer temperatures and point to the input of evaporative surface water into the Florida Platform through sheet flow during the summer rainy period. Lower δ 18 O w values recorded in Unit 7 specimens during winter intervals are consistent with submarine discharge of 18 O-depleted groundwaters. Both processes would have acted to promote nutrient delivery and enhance productivity. Lastly, preliminary uranium concentration data for one of the Unit 7 shells are supportive of SGD, but further study is needed.

title: Parasitic Infestation of the World's Last Eocrinoid: Pits and Pathologies in Ampheristocystis (Echinodermata: Eocrinoidea) from the Middle Silurian of Indiana
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy (Posters)
authors: Thomka, James [1], Puritz, Connor [2], Brett, Carlton [3], Billups, Drew [4]
affiliations: (1) Center for Earth and Environmental Science, State University of New York at Plattsburgh, Plattsburgh, New York, USA
(2) Department of Engineering Sciences and Applied Mathematics, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois, USA
(3) Department of Geosciences, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA
(4) Center for Earth and Environmental Science, State University of New York at Plattsburgh, Plattsburgh, New York, USA
abstract: The genus Ampheristocystis (Echinodermata, Blastozoa: Eocrinoidea) represents the last known eocrinoid and the only member of this phylum to persist past the Late Ordovician mass extinction event. Known from the middle Silurian (Wenlock: Sheinwoodian) Massie Formation of southeastern Indiana, it occurs alongside an abundant and diverse fauna of crinoids and blastozoans, several of which served as hosts to enigmatic pit-forming parasites. Infestation resulted in development of embedment structures—ichnotaxonomically assigned to the ichnogenus Tremichnus —commonly associated with pathological swelling and skeletal malformations. This study describes the first occurrence of parasitic pits in a Silurian eocrinoid, specifically in the form of a severely infested theca of Ampheristocystis concentricus . The theca is minute but contains at least seven T. paraboloides pits, all of which are ~1mm in diameter. Major swelling by amorphous secondary stereomic material reflects a pathological reaction from the host. There is no consistency with respect to the location of pits; they occur on both lateral surfaces of the theca with no discernable clustering and occur at both plate junctions and toward plate centers. The abundance of pits and the severe reaction of the host is similar to patterns observed in pit-bearing holocystitid diploporites with elongate (rather than globose) thecal morphologies from the Massie Formation, which is interesting because of the similar elongate thecal shape of A. concentricus . The record of Tremichnus in eocrinoids is sparse, with the only previously documented examples coming from distantly related taxa from the Middle Ordovician of Russia. Hence, this occurrence indicates that this host-parasite relationship either independently evolved in Silurian Laurentian ampheristocystids or initially developed in an ancestral eocrinoid lineage and survived the Late Ordovician mass extinction. Regardless, this example of paleoparasitism provides additional information on the paleoecology of a rare and evolutionarily important blastozoan echinoderm and, more broadly, on early-middle Paleozoic symbiosis.

title: Frankenstein Rivers: Quantifying Glacial Legacy in Post-Glacial Channel Geometry, Sangamon River, Illinois
session_title: Riverscapes in transition: Advances in fluvial geomorphology, sediment transport, deposition, river health, and urban rivers (Posters)
authors: Meghani, Nooreen A. [1]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Society, and Environment, University of Illinois, Urbana, IL, USA
abstract:
Rivers in post-glacial landscapes display a wide variety of morphologies reflecting their myriad origins and histories. Some rivers are relict glacial meltwater or sub-glacial channels. Others developed following deglaciation, incising into headlands from existing baselevels, while still others exploited the organization left by glacial flow to rapidly connect initially isolated basins. Meghani and Anders (2025) showed that drainage density in the post-glacial Central Lowlands of the United States likely increased rapidly following deglaciation and hypothesized that this rapid network growth was not achieved purely through headward propagation. Instead, they suggest that post-glacial rivers are akin to Frankenstein's monster: composed of components from multiple histories that together function as a single watershed. To qualitatively assess the relative contributions of different histories to these 'Frankenstein Rivers,' Meghani and Anders (in prep) have produced a geomorphic map of the Sangamon River watershed in central Illinois, USA. This map identifies regions of similar geomorphic texture (likely shared origin), highlights positive and negative relief structures with 'streamlined' orientations, and suggests origins of the modern Sangamon and its tributaries.

A quantitative evaluation is the next step. Channel geometry and discharge are empirically related in fluvial systems, and glacially derived channels, whether glaciofluvial, subglacial, or relict glacial forms, deviate from these relationships. Width-area relationships typically follow a power law in fluvial systems, where width increases downstream as a function of contributing area raised to the power omega, typically 0.1-1.2 (Rhodes, 1978; Turowski et al., 2025). Here I evaluate relationships among valley width, valley slope, modern drainage area, and sinuosity for the Sangamon River and several of its tributaries. Preliminary analysis shows the expected width-area relationship is broadly consistent along the river (omega ~ 0.47), but segments thought to be glaciofluvial in origin deviate substantially (omega < 0.01), consistent with valley forms inherited from glacial rather than fluvial processes. Sinuosity in tributaries may similarly delineate fluvial development from glacial inheritance: high sinuosity occurs in uplands and near tributary junctions with the Sangamon, while low sinuosity may mark candidate knickzones. Together, these metrics move the Frankenstein River concept from qualitative mapping to quantitative measurement, offering a first estimate of how much of the Sangamon's modern form is stitched together from its glacial past versus reworked by fluvial processes.

title: The Evolving Relationship Between Phosphorites and the Microbial World: a Two-Billion-Year Saga of Environmental Change
session_title: Phantastic Phosphorus and Its Historical Biogeochemistry
authors: Hiatt, Eric E. [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, University of Wisconsin Oshkosh, Oshkosh, WI, USA
abstract:
Phosphate mineralization in marine sediments (phosphogenesis) results from microbial processes. These processes include heterotrophic breakdown of organic molecules that releases PO 4 , photoautotrophs that produce O 2 necessary to create redox gradients, and chemosynthetic bacteria that exploit these gradients, concentrate PO 4 , and drive phosphate mineralization. The phosphate-bacterial connection began in the Paleoproterozoic and continues to the modern. However, the location, size, and nature of sedimentary phosphate deposits have changed through time with geosphere and biosphere coevolution and progressive oxygenation of the oceans. This has led to the nature and locus of phosphogenesis shifting, from small granular deposits in shallow Paleoproterozoic peritidal settings, to larger deposits found in shallow shelf settings in the Neoproterozoic, to massive phosphorite giants with diverse grain types in the Paleozoic and Mesozoic mid-shelf settings, and finally to the outer shelf in the Cenozoic.

The oldest granular phosphorite deposits are found in the Paleoproterozoic and occurred in peritidal environments with stromatolites that produced local oxygen oases. Wave action concentrated mm-scale laminae of phosphate peloids that include fossil bacteria. During the Marinoan Snowball Earth (ca. 640 Ma) in the Neoproterozoic, phosphogenesis occurred under sea ice in western Brazil. Chemosynthetic bacterial communities thrived on the protected, siliciclastic-starved seafloor. Authigenic siderite and carbonate fluorapatite (CFA) laminae alternate with iron-oxide and glaciomarine sediments. Phosphogenesis was associated with organic matter burial and redox gradients. The Permian Phosphoria phosphorite giant demonstrates the connection to extreme oceanographic conditions, which led to a wide diversity of environmental conditions and grain types. The extreme conditions were required to create widespread anoxia and dysoxia on the seafloor. Phosphogenesis in outer shelf settings was associated with extreme organic matter burial, elevated trace metals, and a δ 13 C (PO4–CO3) of -10 ‰, while nearshore environments were marked by low organic matter burial, low trace element concentrations, and a δ 13 C (PO4–CO3) of -3 ‰.

Through time, phosphorite geochemistry and textures were controlled by environmental factors, but what has remained consistent is the association with organic matter and minerals that reflect redox gradients (including sulfide minerals), peloidal grains, and evidence of bacteria (body fossils, microbial sedimentary structures). Based on these associations and microtexture observations, it is clear that CFA results from bacterial passive mineralization, and the resulting phosphorite largely reflects the persistence of oceanographic conditions.

title: Quantifying Fault Offset Uncertainty from Displaced Landforms: A Case Study from the San Andreas Fault

affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA

abstract: Slip rate analyses are crucial for assessing seismic hazard along active faults. However, a lack of methodological consistency in calculating offset uncertainty has hindered progress in creating unified models of fault activity rates through time. We present a methodology for calculating three-dimensional fault displacement and uncertainty using a principal component-based approach. We apply our methods to the Wallace Creek site along the strike-slip San Andreas fault in southern California. At this location we determine an offset of 129.6 +/- 6.9 m, within uncertainty of prior displacement estimates at this site. Our methods provide a straightforward assignment of three-dimensional offset and uncertainty based solely on variation of landform morphology that can be readily integrated into seismic hazard assessments.

title: Nitrogen Isotope Values of Land Snail Shell Carbonate-Bound Organic Matrix as a Proxy for Snail Diet
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials (Posters)
authors: King Phillips, Ezekiel [1], Yanes, Yurena [2], Verheyden, Anouk [3], Gillikin, David P. [4], Miller, Joshua H. [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Cincinnati, Department of Geosciences, Cincinnati, OH,
(2) University of Cincinnati, Department of Geosciences, Cincinnati, Ohio,
(3) Union College Geology Department, Schenectady, NY,
(4) Union College, Schenectady, NY,
(5) University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH,
abstract: The carbon stable isotope values of fossilized land snail shells are often used as a proxy for understanding the relative dominance of C3 vs. C4 plants on ancient landscapes, though this relies on the assumption that snails are indiscriminate grazers of, mainly, vascular plants. In contrast, recent isotopic investigations have revealed that many contemporary species living in forested habitats exhibit more complex dietary habits, often including fungi, biofilms, leaf litter, and other foods. This dietary complexity can be more fully evaluated using a two-isotope system (carbon and nitrogen) to better differentiate between food sources that may overlap in isotopic values. Fortunately, technological innovations have opened new opportunities to evaluate nitrogen isotopes (d15N) of the carbonate-bound organic matrix (CBOM) in both modern and fossil snail shells. While studies of aquatic bivalves have shown that CBOM can reliably track diet, similar investigations have not been applied to land snails. Filling the void, we conducted nitrogen isotope analyses of snail shell CBOM to investigate the reliability of this technique for evaluating snail diets. We focused our study on two living species ( Ventridens ligera , Mesodon thyroidus ) from East Fork State Park in Southwestern Ohio. We hypothesized that the d15N values of snail shell CBOM correlate with those of whole-body soft tissues, which in turn, reflect the snail’s consumed foods. Preliminary results indicate that the d15N values of the CBOM of both species are positively and significantly correlated with the values of their body tissues during the growing season (R 2 = 0.62, p = >0.01; and R 2 = 0.81, p = >0.01, for V. ligera and M. thyroidu s, respectively). The results from this study support the use of snail shell CBOM as a dietary proxy, potentially allowing new opportunities to investigate the diets and environments of species without the need for preserved whole-body tissues.

authors: Richard, Emilie Michelle [1], Calhoun, Nancy [2], Amaral, Tristan [3], Siebert, Cora [4], Flournoy, Ariana M [5], Langstroth, Casey [6]
affiliations: (1) Washington State Department of Natural Resources, Washington Geological Survey, Olympia, WA, USA

abstract:
Alluvial fans are hotspots of debris flow risk, especially after wildfire. In Washington state, fans are often areas of residential and agricultural development. Since 2016, the Washington Geological Survey (WGS) has counted more than 230 debris flows on alluvial fans. More than 40% of those damaged infrastructure. However, not all counties include these landforms in their Geologically Hazardous Area code provisions, and not all jurisdictions know where their alluvial fans are.

To better understand where debris flow hazards exist, the Washington Geological Survey has spent the past decade mapping alluvial fans across the state. Our mapping approach builds on the lidar-based protocol developed by the Washington Geological Survey for landslide mapping (Slaughter et al., 2017). Mapping all the alluvial fans in a state is a daunting task, so over the years, we’ve honed our GIS techniques to streamline mapping while maintaining quality.

In this presentation, I will share some of our mapping mantras, useful base data layers, symbology preferences, and new attribute automation workflows. I will also demonstrate how we use this inventory to conduct post-wildfire debris flow assessments and highlight other practical applications of alluvial fan inventories.

As human development on alluvial fans continues to expand and wildfires increase in size and severity, comprehensive alluvial fan maps are simple and effective tools that decision makers can use to protect people and infrastructure from debris flows and related hazards.

title: The endocast of the early-diverging phytosaur Parasuchus bransoni (Archosauriformes) and preliminary incorporation of endocranial characters into phytosaur phylogenetics

authors: Blomberg, Owen H. [1], Kufner, Aaron M. [2], Hartman, Scott A. [3], Lovelace, David M. [4]
affiliations: (1) Biology, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Wellesley Hills, MA, USA
(2) Geoscience, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, USA
(3) Biology, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, USA

abstract:
Phytosaurs are superficially crocodile-like archosauriform reptiles that are relatively common macrofaunal components of the non-marine Upper Triassic. Most phytosaur taxa are described almost exclusively from their highly diagnostic cranial material which, in turn, forms the basis for our understanding of their phylogenetic relationships. Most anatomical studies of phytosaurs have focused on the external features of the cranium, with few instances of internal cranial descriptions. This is clear in character matrices used in phylogenetic inference of the internal relationships of phytosaurs. Advances in computed tomography have facilitated a new wave of investigation into the endocranial anatomy of phytosaurs without the need for destructive sampling techniques. Despite this, most phytosaur species lack an endocranial description, and those descriptions that do exist have not incorporated these new observations into a phylogenetic framework.

Here we present the first description of the cranial endocast of a referred specimen of Parasuchus bransoni , an early diverging phytosaur, from the ochre unit of the Popo Agie Formation in Fremont County, Wyoming (UWGM 1978). The endosseous labyrinth (inner ear) of UWGM 1978 exhibits similar semicircular canal thickness and anteroposterior lobe asymmetry to the more basal phytosaur Wannia scurriensis than to the putative congener Parasuchus angustifrons . In addition, the morphology of a sinus within the roofing bones of the skull, described in other phytosaurs as either the pineal body or dural venous sinus, is clarified. This structure may represent part of the paratympanic sinus system, which is considered plesiomorphic to Archosauria, but its presence in phytosaurs may indicate 1) an earlier appearance of the paratympanic sinus system in Archosauriformes or 2) rather than a sister relationship of Phytosauria+Archosauria, a more derived position of phytosaurs within crown clade archosaurs. Incorporation of novel morphological characters of the endocranium into the phylogenetic study of phytosaurs may help clarify the taxonomy of Parasuchus and further refine our understanding of phytosaur phylogenetics.

title: 3D Kinematic and Geomechanical Evolution of the Thermopolis Anticline: Evaluating Laramide Foreland Deformation through Integrated Numerical Modeling and Field-Based Datasets
session_title: Latest Research Advances in Structural Geology and Tectonics (Posters)
authors: Reeher, Lauren [1], Yonkee, Adolph [2], Weil, Arlo Brandon [3]
affiliations: (1) Utah Geological Survey, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
(2) Weber State University, Ogden, UT, USA
(3) Bryn Mawr College, Bryn Mawr, PA, USA
abstract:
The Thermopolis anticline, located in the Laramide foreland of Wyoming, exhibits a complex structural architecture with curved, segmented domes connected across relay zones with localized vertical-axis rotations. Understanding the structural evolution of such systems is challenging given the blind nature of underlying basement faults. We integrate inverse and forward trishear kinematic modeling with 3D boundary element geomechanical modeling (BEM) to understand fold-fault growth and evolving stress and incremental strain fields. These numerical results are compared against field-based datasets that include minor fault kinematics, anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) fabrics, and paleomagnetism.

Inverse trishear modeling constrained acceptable fault geometries, followed by forward modeling of 16 progressively restored cross sections to develop 3D surface models of fault propagation and associated folding of a Triassic datum. Geomechanical BEM was executed in two phases. First, remote stress loading conditions were applied to evaluate expected general fault slip distributions. Second, slip distributions were prescribed on the 3D fault framework model based on the 2D trishear models for three kinematic stages: fault initiation at depth, main fault-fold propagation, and late-stage fold tightening. Modeled stress and incremental strain fields were visualized using perturbations in maximum shear stress magnitudes and σ 1 /e 3 orientations along the Triassic surface datum, revealing dynamic changes that broadly match field datasets. The model shows distributed WSW-ENE shortening during fault initiation, which matches layer-parallel shortening (LPS) directions estimated from early minor wedge faults and AMS fabrics. During main propagation, shear stress increases along variably striking forelimb segments connected by relay zones, and σ 1 trajectories refract near oblique linkages, consistent with paleostress directions from secondary faults along steep forelimbs.

Our integrated approach suggests that the evolution of the Thermopolis fold-fault system included fault nucleation along basement weaknesses, upward propagation and lateral linkage of faults, and an increasingly heterogeneous local stress/strain field during Laramide shortening, ultimately forming the observed complex 3-D structural fold geometry and associated deformation fabrics

title: Toward Rigorous Intercomparison of InSAR Products: Resolution, Validation, and Uncertainty in Coastal Subsidence Estimates
session_title: Land Surface Subsidence—Processes, Impacts, and Ongoing Challenges
authors: Shirzaei, Manoochehr [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA
abstract: Interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) has become a primary tool for mapping coastal subsidence and vertical land motion (VLM) at fine spatial resolution, informing flood-risk, infrastructure, and sea-level-rise assessments across vulnerable coastlines. As multiple InSAR-derived products now cover overlapping regions, the community increasingly relies on cross-product comparison to assess reliability. However, the methodology used to compare products can itself introduce substantial artifacts, and disagreement between products is often attributed to underlying data quality when it instead reflects choices made in the comparison framework. We examine three such choices using coastal subsidence products for the U.S. Gulf Coast as a case study. First, spatial aggregation prior to comparison can reduce pixel density by orders of magnitude, suppressing genuine fine-scale variability and manufacturing apparent disagreement at coarser scales. Second, GNSS validation networks selected for geophysical stability versus those spanning a product's full application domain answer different questions about accuracy and should not be treated as interchangeable. Third, disagreement thresholds derived from inter-product spread, rather than from independent uncertainty quantification, can be internally inconsistent, in some cases flagging results that are not otherwise in dispute. We further show that differences in observation window between compared products can alone account for a substantial share of reported disagreement, independent of any error in either dataset. Together, these findings argue for a set of shared benchmarking practices: common reference validation networks with transparent processing documentation, standardized reporting of spatial resolution and observation window alongside published products, and uncertainty thresholds grounded in first-principles error propagation rather than inter-product comparison. We propose a coordinated community forum, following models such as ISSI International Teams, to establish these standards and improve the reproducibility of InSAR-derived geodetic products more broadly.

abstract: Mercury remains a global contaminant of concern due to its persistence, long-range atmospheric transport, bioaccumulation, and adverse ecological and human health effects. Kuwait faces unique mercury management challenges associated with its hydrocarbon-based economy, legacy industrial contamination, waste management activities, and marine-dependent food consumption. This review synthesizes current knowledge on mercury sources, environmental distribution, exposure pathways, and governance to evaluate Kuwait's progress toward implementing the Minamata Convention. Environmental monitoring studies indicate mercury concentrations of 0.008–0.8 mg/kg in coastal sediments, 0.56–0.83 mg/kg in landfill soils, and up to 86 ng m⁻³ in the atmosphere, with elevated levels near industrial and urbanized areas. Mercury concentrations in commercially important fish reached 1.65 mg/kg, exceeding international food safety guidelines in several species and highlighting seafood consumption as an important exposure pathway. Although Kuwait has established strong analytical capabilities and is advancing its Minamata Initial Assessment (MIA) and National Implementation Plan (NIP), implementation remains constrained by fragmented regulations, limited long-term biomonitoring, insufficient continuous emission monitoring systems (CEMS), and gaps in mercury speciation and integrated environmental surveillance. This review proposes AI-enabled decision support systems that integrate environmental monitoring, biomonitoring, emission inventories, geospatial information, and regulatory indicators to identify contamination hotspots, prioritize interventions, optimize monitoring networks, and support adaptive policy implementation. Integrating artificial intelligence with Best Available Techniques (BAT), Best Environmental Practices (BEP), and evidence-based governance can strengthen mercury management, improve compliance with the Minamata Convention, and contribute to Kuwait Vision 2035 and the Sustainable Development Goals

title: Geospatial Model of Regolith-Hosted Rare Earth Element Enrichment Potential of the Continental U.S.
session_title: Linking mineral resources and the geologic framework of North America: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) and related activities (Posters)
authors: Li, James [1], DePaolo, Donald J. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Berkeley, Emeryville, CA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Berkeley, Hayward, CA, USA
abstract: Regolith-hosted rare earth element (REE) deposits in southern China form where REE-rich granitic parent rocks undergo prolonged chemical weathering, leaching, vertical redistribution, and retention in clay-rich regolith. Similar deposits could represent a potential domestic REE resource, but their distribution in the United States remains poorly constrained. Using the Chinese deposits as a model, we develop a spatial framework that integrates geologic, geochemical, climatic, and geomorphic information to identify U.S. regions favorable for regolith-hosted REE enrichment and support regional mineral-resource assessment. Granitoid samples from the Global Granite Geochemistry and Outcrop Database are filtered for La concentrations (current model uses La > 120 ppm) and integrated with gridded mean annual temperature, precipitation, regolith thickness, and topographic slope datasets. We derive a steady-state mass-balance model in which enrichment depends on weathering intensity, regolith thickness, erosion rate, REE retention, and the degree of REE depletion or enrichment of the eroding surface layer. Because several physical parameters are not constrained at continental scale, the governing relationship is converted into a dimensionless enrichment-potential index using temperature and precipitation as weathering proxies and slope as an erosion proxy. A residence-time filter removes areas where the timescale for approach to steady state exceeds 10 to 20 Myr. This filter suppresses unrealistically high scores where old, thick soils occur in low-relief regions while preserving areas where weathering or erosion operate to form soil profiles over plausible geologic timescales. High-REE granitoid occurrences are overlaid on the resulting enrichment potential map to identify regions in the continental U.S. where soil-hosted REE deposits like those in China could be expected. Favorable sites are mostly restricted to the Appalachians and mid-continent. The U.S. has many other high-REE granitoids, but they occur in relatively dry or cold regions of the Southwest where enrichment potential is low. Our framework complements regional geologic mapping and geochemical sampling by providing a continental-scale screening tool to prioritize areas for further investigation of regolith-hosted REE resources.

authors: Diop, Rahmatoulaye Thialaw [1], Traore, Maimouna [2], Agbogun, Henry M. D. [3], Atekwana , Eliot A. [4], Ali, Hendratta N. [5], Njilah, Isaac Konfor [6]

abstract: Mangrove sediments are important reservoirs for organic carbon storage, but the amount of carbon preserved depends on the depositional conditions at each site. This study investigates organic matter (OM) content and sediment geochemistry from sediment cores collected at three mangrove sites in the Wouri Estuary, Cameroon: Mungo, located to the west in hydrodynamically restricted waters; KOO, situated in the central estuary within highly constricted water channels; and Dibamba, located to the east in relatively open-water conditions. The objective was to identify the factors controlling spatial differences in carbon storage across the estuary. Organic matter content was measured using loss-on-ignition (550°C), while major and trace element concentrations were analyzed using X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Mean OM content increases from Dibamba (22.1%; range 15.7–30.5%) to Mungo (27.4%; range 11.9–42.6%) and reaches its highest values at KOO (38.4%; range 24.5–49.5%). This increase is accompanied by a decrease in terrigenous element concentrations (Al, Si, Ti, and Zr) and an increase in sulfur content from Dibamba and Mungo to KOO. Lower Al, Si, Ti, and Zr values indicate reduced terrigenous sediment input and less siliciclastic dilution, while higher sulfur concentrations suggest more reducing, anoxic depositional conditions that may be associated with sulfate reduction and limited oxygen availability. The combination of restricted hydrodynamic conditions and highly constricted channels at KOO promotes low-energy sedimentation, minimizes clastic sediment input, and favors the development of anoxic, sulfur-rich sediments, resulting in the greatest preservation of organic matter. In contrast, the relatively open-water setting at Dibamba enhances water exchange and sediment transport, leading to greater siliciclastic input, more oxidizing conditions, and lower organic matter preservation. Mungo, located in restricted waters to the west of the estuary, exhibits intermediate characteristics between these two end members. Overall, the results demonstrate that organic matter accumulation and preservation in the Wouri Estuary are governed by the combined influence of hydrodynamic setting, sediment provenance, sediment chemistry, and redox conditions rather than by hydrodynamics alone. Sites with restricted circulation, low terrigenous sediment influx, and strongly reducing conditions provide the most favorable environments for long-term organic carbon preservation, highlighting the importance of these interacting processes in regulating blue carbon storage in tropical mangrove ecosystems.

title: 400 Million Years of Soils, Teeth and Plants Stable Isotopes: Clues to Earth’s Past Ecosystems
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements
authors: Ekart, Douglas David [1]
