abstract: Thirty five years ago, for a dissertation project, Dr. Thure Cerling tasked me with collecting, analyzing and applying his stable carbon isotope model to paleosols of varying ages for the purpose of reconstructing ancient atmospheric carbon dioxide levels (AJS, 1999). Field work often included travel to vertebrates sites bearing hominoids or dinosaurs or pelycosaurs because teams of researchers understood those localities better and fossil soils are so often associated with and preserved alongside the teeth, bones and organic matter. The result is that in addition to the hundreds of pedogenic carbonates collected, analyzed and reported, thousands of additional analyses of related fossils, both from field work and museum work, went unreported. Many sites have suites of materials such as pedogenic carbonates, occluded organic matter, diverse teeth, eggshells, plants, charcoals and groundwater growths. In several cases diagenetic crosscutting sparites were analyzed to probe burial conditions. Significant numbers of specimens were analyzed by either phosphoric acid dissolution, combustion or laser ablation mass spectrometry according to the phase. The resulting stable isotope dataset represents pedogenic carbonates, teeth and plants scattered across 400 million years of time. Having never given up trying to integrate and report these findings, as well as having gained some relevant skills in industry, there is a lot to share. I will present detailed tables on all specimens, localities and analyses. I have created a software environment that loads these tables for QC, integration, analysis and efficiently illuminates the results across multiple domains. While much remains undone, there are very interesting results emerging, focusing on the Paleozoic at first. There is a strong increasing trend in oxygen isotope values in both teeth and pedogenic carbonates through the available terrestrial Carboniferous and Permian of North America. There appear to be consistent patterns of distributions of both carbon and oxygen isotope between the isotopic compositions of plants, teeth and pedogenic carbonates within suites of samples temporally related. I very much want to share what I am seeing with the community, initiate some feedback and collaboration on how to proceed with this important dataset.

title: Effects of Microplastic Concentration on Clearance Rates in freshwater bivalves

authors: Mocumbi, Bruno Hausse [1], Nagel-Myers, Judith [2], Oldacre, Amanda [3], Angstadt, Kevin [4]
affiliations: (1) St. Lawrence University, Canton, New York, USA
(2) St.Lawrence University, Canton, New York, USA

abstract:
Microplastics are increasingly prevalent in freshwater ecosystems and have been identified as a possible threat to aquatic organisms. Freshwater unionid bivalves are particularly vulnerable because they filter suspended particles from the water column and inadvertently ingest microplastics. This study examined the clearance rates of Elliptio complanata following exposure to different microplastic concentrations to evaluate their response to this exposure and their ability to remove microplastics from the water column.

Microplastic suspensions were prepared in a two step process by grinding high-density polyethylene (HDPE) containers and isolating fragments ≤10 µm through sequential filtration. Mussels collected from a northern New York river were maintained under natural conditions before individual exposure to 100 mL of one of four microplastic concentrations (3.15 × 10², 3.15 × 10⁴, 3.15 × 10⁶, or 3.15 × 10⁸ particles). Water samples were collected hourly for 6 hours, and microplastic concentrations were quantified using a Neubauer hemacytometer. Clearance rates were standardized to body mass.

Preliminary results showed declining microplastic concentrations in all treatments. Standardized clearance rates increased with concentration, reaching 147, 121, and 87.4 mL·g⁻¹·h⁻¹ in the high, medium, and low treatments, respectively. All treatments exhibited a similar temporal pattern, with high clearance during the first hour, reduced filtration during the second hour, increased activity during hours 4–5, and lower clearance by hour 6.

These findings suggest that E. complanata removes microplastics across a broad range of concentrations and that filtration patterns are regulated primarily by normal feeding physiology rather than microplastic concentration alone. The apparent processing of microplastics as natural seston highlights the potential for ingestion and underscores the need to assess the long-term effects of microplastic exposure on unionid mussels and freshwater ecosystems.

abstract: The expansion of microplastics, particles with a diameter below 5mm, into the environment has increased the amount of pollution affecting both people and the ecosystem. This study focuses on the plastic pollutants found along the Trinity River, originating in North Texas. The Trinity acts as a water source for millions of Texans and flows into the Trinity Bay, the site of many commercial fisheries. Sediment samples were collected from the surface layer of point bars at 5 river locations spanning both rural and urban areas. The collected samples were filtered through a newly developed, density based apparatus, to separate the microplastics from the sediment. Analysis was then conducted on the filtered samples using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy and a machine learning model for identification. The findings show some microplastics, such as nylon, are consistently present at every sampled site, while others are uniquely abundant at specific sites. The urban sampling sites contained copious amounts of polycarbonate, which was scarcely present in the rural sampling sites, where we instead found an abundance of polypropylene. These variations in pollution composition across the river suggest the possibility of localized contamination events and can begin to help improve our understanding of the mechanics of the microplastic pollution in rivers.

abstract:
The Upper Ordovician Juniata Formation in central Pennsylvania records a critical environmental transition within a post-Taconic clastic wedge. An exceptionally exposed section is present in roadcut along Rt. 322 in Potters Mills, Pennsylvania. The formation here exhibits repeated packages of fining-upward successions, with evidence of an upward trend moving from shallow marine to fluvial-dominated settings. The depositional environment of the upper units remains heavily debated. Some models interpret these upper units as complex terrestrial coastal plains containing mature paleosols, while others argue that the sedimentary structures reflect a stressed marginal marine or estuarine system. Because this debate has previously relied on visual interpretations of trace fossils, there is a critical need for high-resolution mineralogical data to differentiate true in-situ pedogenesis from subaqueous marine deposition.

We aim here to provide clarity by analyzing vertical mineralogical variations across the purported stacked paleosol sequences using X-Ray Diffraction (XRD). Sampling occurs at tight vertical mudstone intervals to capture the sharp chemical gradients typical of top-down weathering profiles. By analyzing the clay fraction (<2 μm) and utilizing Rietveld refinement we provide a semi-quantitative assessment of the vertical clay-ordering and track shifts in the quartz to phyllosilicate ratios to differentiate paleosols from lower-energy mudstone facies. We have targeted distinct spikes in weathering-product clays, and shifts in the illite/chlorite ratio, which indicate intense chemical weathering and subaerial freshwater leaching rather than a homogeneous mix of marine detrital clays.

title: Elastic Time-Reverse Imaging of Wavemode-Separated Surface-wave Data
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Pels, Madeleine [1], Shragge, Jeffrey [2], Girard, Aaron [3]
affiliations: (1) Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
(2) Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, GOLDEN, CO, USA
(3) Geophysics, Colorado School of Mines, GOLDEN, CO, USA
abstract:
Most near-surface seismic analysis methods treat the often-dominant surface-wave energy as noise to be suppressed before imaging body-wave arrivals. Elastic time-reverse imaging (E-TRI) instead uses backscattered surface-wave energy as signal. Originally developed for microseismic event location, E-TRI has been adapted for near-surface active-source investigations and scatterer detection, with meter-scale subsurface voids a representative target: strong scatterers far smaller than typical near-surface wavelengths. Like elastic reverse time migration (E-RTM), E-TRI is a full-wavefield migration method that correlates two elastic wavefields through an imaging condition to stack coherent energy into an interpretable image. Unlike E-RTM, however, E-TRI derives both wavefields from the recorded data, partitioning them into an outward-propagating transmitted and an inward-propagating backscattered wavefield that are then back-propagated in reverse time. No forward-modeled source wavefield or origin time is required, and the resulting image locates scatterers rather than mapping reflectivity.

A central challenge in surface-wave imaging is the inherently multi-modal nature of dispersive wavefields, which produces non-unique phase-velocity/frequency relationships. Assuming single-mode data causes cross-mode contamination, reduced coherency, imaging artifacts, and lower signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). Many methods isolate the fundamental mode (R0), but this sacrifices usable bandwidth because the data must be bandpassed below the onset frequency of the first higher-order mode (R1). E-TRI instead retains the higher-order modes and migrates them alongside the fundamental. Successive f–k filtering, first on dip magnitude to separate wave modes and then on dip sign to separate transmitted from backscattered energy, yields four data subsets: the transmitted and backscattered fundamental (T 0 , B 0 ) and first higher-order (T 1 , B 1 ) Rayleigh modes. Combining these in reverse-time propagation produces four E-TRI images: I E 00 (T 0 , B 0 ); I E 11 (T 1 , B 1 ); I E 01 (T 0 , B 1 ); and I E 10 (T 1 , B 0 ).

A synthetic test first compares these images for soft- and hard-rock anomalies at ~15 m depth in a layered model representative of the Yuma Proving Ground (YPG), Arizona, and shows that combining transmitted and scattered wavefields raises SNR. A 3D field test then applies E-TRI to vertical, transverse, and radial components acquired on a common grid at YPG. The cross-mode image I E 01 (T 0 , B 1 ) gives the closest depth estimates, locating a void smaller than the ~10 m dominant wavelength to within 1 m laterally and 4 m in depth. The four wave-mode combinations show complementary sensitivity to short-wavelength near-surface anomalies.

title: Governed by Genomes and Bound by Eh-pH: Guiding Microbial Communities for Recovery of Critical Minerals
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: Terra, Rowan R. [1], Gulliver, Djuna [2], Crawford, Caylah [3], Trun, Nancy [4], Bowman, Jessica [5]
affiliations: (1) Duquesne University and the National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL-PGH), Pittsburgh, PA,

(3) Duquesne University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
(4) Duquesne University, Biological sciences, Pittsburgh, PA,
(5) Duquesne University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA
abstract:
Recovering critical minerals and materials from ores and mining byproducts through microbiology requires knowing which organisms are present and the conditions that promote their interactions with metals. We developed a workflow that moved from field-site microbial communities to defined synthetic communities and applied it to relevant critical mineral feedstocks, using two sources: (1) the Mountain Pass Rare Earth Mine in California and (2) the Kentucky Hollow Coal Mine Remediation System in Pennsylvania. We cultured bacteria from each site, sequenced 26 isolates, and produced high-quality draft genomes. Genome-based taxonomy (GTDB-Tk, TYGS, ANI, and dDDH) resolved ten isolates as candidate novel species across eight genera, indicating that much of the culturable diversity was previously undescribed.

The workflow rested on two predictors: genome annotations specifying each strain’s expected metal-handling and catabolic capacity, and an Eh-pH tool that combined Pourbaix metal-stability relations with Baas Becking limits for microbial activity to bound the redox and pH windows in which a target metal is mobile and a community remains active. We used metal-tolerance assays and bioleaching screens to test whether genome-predicted capacity and the Eh-pH windows converged. In a 96-well tolerance screen across eight metals (Al, Mn, Cu, Ni, Co, La, Nd, Gd) at 10 to 100 mg L⁻¹, tolerance matched genomic prediction where the determinants were specific: efflux-rich Cupriavidus and Burkholderia, carrying expanded czc, cop, and mer genomic inventories, tolerated the transition metals at the highest doses (Cupriavidus to 100 mg L⁻¹ copper, Burkholderia to 100 mg L⁻¹ cobalt), whereas the sole methanol-utilizing isolate, a Methylobacterium encoding the lanthanide-dependent methanol dehydrogenase XoxF, tolerated the rare earths and manganese across the full dose range while copper, cobalt, and nickel suppressed it.

The result was a repeatable path for exploring the recovery of critical minerals from primary and unconventional resources. The findings also bear on in-situ recovery and on any non-sterile leaching operation, even at warehouse scale, where the resident microbiota act on the same target metals regardless of intent and should be characterized rather than assumed inert.

abstract: The Independence School Site in the Jackson Purchase region of Kentucky contains a near-complete record of deposition in terrestrial environments from the upper McNairy Formation (Cretaceous) through the lower Clayton Formation (Paleocene). The original palynological investigation of the site in 1970 suggested that this region was coastal, with a mosaic of onshore and near-shore environments. Preliminary re-study of widely spaced samples completed in 2023 supports this, with dinoflagellates and foraminiferal test linings, indicating marine deposition only present in a 10-cm thick bed approximately halfway between a basal lignite and the iridium spike. Plant palynomorphs preserved suggest that the area received moderate to high precipitation, had warm temperate to subtropical temperatures, and uplands likely resembled the mixed mesophytic forests present in the region today. The sediments themselves record first deposition in a topogenous mire, followed by freshwater wetlands that (perhaps) transition to marginal marine environments, then terrestrial near-shore environments. A mixed assemblage of Cretaceous and Danian palynomorphs present at the level of the iridium spike may be suggestive of reworking, or of sample contamination during collection. This re-study left multiple questions, resulting fine-scale re-sampling of the site in spring of 2025. Here we present the results to date of palynological study of these samples, with improved interpretation of variations in paleoecology and paleoclimate recorded across the K-Pg Boundary in Kentucky.

title: Laser-ablation split-stream zircon depth profiling records detrital and metamorphic history of metasomatic rocks, Cemetery Ridge, southwest Arizona

abstract:
Orocopia Schist, a subduction complex underplated and metamorphosed during Laramide flat-slab subduction, is exposed at Cemetery Ridge in southwest Arizona. Included in the quartzofeldspathic schist are rocks that underwent metasomatic alteration. Thermodynamic modeling of non-metasomatic garnet-bearing quartzofeldpathic schist indicates subduction metamorphism was followed by exhumation to ~16 km depth (5.5-5 kbar at ~600 °C) and then heating to >700 °C. Modeling of two samples from a metasomatic quartz-absent biotite-rich lithology yielded conditions of ~4.6 kbar at 720 °C. This study used laser-ablation split-stream ICP-MS depth profiling on unpolished zircons from metasomatic rocks to understand the timing and associated trace element changes accompanying metamorphism during subduction and exhumation.

Ages were determined from depth profiles by selecting portions that appear to represent single-age domains, judged from a plot of calculated 206 Pb/ 238 U ages versus time, where time is a proxy for the depth of laser penetration. Preliminary data analysis yielded 206 Pb/ 238 U zircon ages ranging from 1660-34.3 Ma across samples. 90% of concordant analyses are <180 Ma with peaks at 85 and 45 Ma. Grains that display detrital cores and metamorphic rims yielded cores >60 Ma and rims <60 Ma, while wholly detrital grains yielded ages >60 Ma. Domains >60 Ma have a typical igneous REE pattern of positive Ce and negative Eu anomalies, whereas domains <60 Ma have smaller anomalies or lack them entirely. Metamorphic rims were distinguished from detrital cores by differences in age, Th/U ratio (lower and variable for metamorphic rims) and changes in trace element concentrations and patterns. These patterns suggest a changing reservoir of elements was associated with metamorphic zircon growth during and following subduction. We interpret ages in the 60-35 Ma population to reflect metamorphic zircon growth during transport through the subduction channel and/or subsequent ascent.

A pervasive Miocene (~21 Ma) contact metamorphic (720°C) and metasomatic event crystallized or recrystallized titanite, monazite and rutile and partially reset the oxygen isotope system in feldspars and titanite in all lithologies studied. Depth profiled zircon from this study also document Miocene overgrowth and neoblastic growth but only in the spinel-olivine-tremolite-clinochlore lithology, yielding a 206 Pb/ 238 U age of 22.4±0.8 Ma (n=4). The age is consistent with Miocene granitic rocks that intrude around the Orocopia Schist exposure at Cemetery Ridge.

abstract:
The Dromedary Peak quadrangle encompasses the high-altitude core of the central Wasatch Range, situated approximately 15 miles southeast of Salt Lake City, Utah. This region serves as a critical nexus for the Wasatch Front, providing essential watersheds and high-use recreational areas within Big Cottonwood, Little Cottonwood, and American Fork Canyons. New 1:24,000-scale mapping provides a modernized foundation for understanding the regional geology, hazards, and resources. Notably, this map was a collaborative effort involving all of the Utah Geological Survey (UGS) Mapping Program geologists. The diversity of geology and proximity to the UGS office provided an ideal project to facilitate training of multiple new staff. Utilizing ArcGIS Online on iPads facilitated multi-user simultaneous field and office editing capabilities. This group collaboration facilitated team building, knowledge transfer, communication, and improved workflows for future maps. Challenges included project management, group data structure, uniform target scale, access, and cartography.

The geology of the quadrangle is characterized by a broadly east-dipping succession of Neoproterozoic to Triassic sedimentary rocks. These units record a complex structural legacy, initially deformed by thrusts of the Cretaceous-Eocene Cordilleran orogeny and subsequently modified by low-angle normal faults that have complex spatiotemporal relationships with the Paleogene emplacement of the Wasatch intrusive belt. These structures and rocks are further overprinted by high-angle normal faulting related to Miocene-to-present Basin and Range extension.

Quaternary landscape evolution of the quadrangle is dominated by uplift in the footwall of the Wasatch normal fault that created high topography sculpted by glacial and periglacial processes. This map identifies deposits of glacial cycles corresponding to marine oxygen isotope stages (MIS) 6 and 2. Subsequent deglaciation was punctuated by younger glacial advances, likely during the Younger Dryas, and the development of extensive periglacial features including active rock glaciers, protalus lobes, and protalus ramparts. The quadrangle also preserves a variety of alluvial and mass-wasting deposits from large-scale rock avalanches, rockfalls, debris flows, and landslides, which present ongoing geologic hazards in this steep and high recreational use terrain.

Ongoing efforts initiated by this mapping project involve the geochemical analysis of over 40 igneous dikes, detailed structural analysis of thrust faults, geochronological analysis of post-MIS 2 glacial deposits, and study of the kinematics and water budgets of active rock glaciers.

title: Analysis of Fluid and Melt Inclusions from the Shepherd Mountain and Pilot Knob Iron-Oxide-Apatite (IOA) Deposits in the Southeast Missouri Iron Metallogenic Province

authors: Hunt, William C [1], Sahdarani, Dita [2], Lamadrid, Hector M. [3], Appold, Martin S. [4]
affiliations: (1) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Boonville, MO, USA
(2) Geological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA

abstract:
The Shepherd Mountain and Pilot Knob magnetite deposits are two prominent iron oxide apatite (IOA) deposits in the broader Southeast Missouri Iron Metallogenic Province. The deposits were mined for iron from 1815 to 1861 and from 1968 to 1980, respectively, and are prospective for REE’s. The dominantly silicic composition of the volcanic host rocks suggests that the magmatic iron oxide mineralization likely formed through magma immiscibility arising from a silicic parent magma. Recent studies have suggested that iron oxide melts could form via immiscibility from a silicic magma that assimilated carbonate/sulfate-bearing sedimentary rocks. To find evidence of this, fluid and melt inclusions from the deposits were examined for the presence of carbonate, sulfate, and phosphate aqueous/mineral species.

Petrologic and microthermometric work on the deposits has revealed a complex fluid history with heterogeneous entrapment of two main types of fluid inclusions: (1) liquid-vapor and (2) liquid-vapor-solid(s). Scanning Electron Microscopy-Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) was used to analyze mounds produced from the decrepitation of quartz-hosted fluid inclusions. Carbon and sulfur were both found in these fluid inclusions, though only the concentration of sulfur could be quantified, which ranged from about 1 to 30 weight %. Additionally, Raman spectroscopy of fluid inclusions indicated the presence of carbonate and sulfate aqueous species in some inclusions as well as carbonate/sulfate daughter minerals. Raman spectroscopy also identified carbonate, sulfate, and phosphate phases (calcite, anhydrite, and apatite) in melt inclusions. Other minerals identified include hematite, chlorite, actinolite, pyroxene, K-feldspar, and albite. Laser Ablation-Inductively Coupled Plasma-Mass Spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) performed so far mainly on quartz-hosted fluid inclusions from the Shepherd Mountain deposit indicate them to be rich in calcium and sodium (~3 to 5 weight %) and iron (~0.2 to 1 weight %). The elevated concentrations of calcium and sodium could point the assimilation of carbonate rocks and evaporites by the silicic magmas, and fit with the enrichments of sulfur and phosphate found in fluid and melt inclusions.

title: Building Pathways into Geoscience: Connection, Experience, and Community in Preparing Environmental Geoscientists
session_title: Coordinated Geoscience Outreach Efforts to Broaden Participation
authors: Kneeshaw, Tara [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology Department, Grand Valley State University, Schoolcraft, Michigan, USA
abstract:
Students increasingly enter universities through interdisciplinary environmental programs and may not initially identify themselves as geoscientists. Creating intentional pathways that connect these students with geoscience experiences, mentors, research, peers, and professional communities provides an opportunity to broaden participation while preparing students for environmental careers. Opportunities matter, but connection is what can turn a collection of individual experiences into a pathway toward becoming an environmental geoscientist.

Experiences within the Geology program at Grand Valley State University have informed an evolving model in which students encounter a series of experiential “stepping stones” throughout the curriculum. These progress from introductory experiences to applied coursework, field-based learning, undergraduate research, and capstone experiences, with intentional reflection helping students recognize connections among these experiences and their developing professional identities. Faculty-mentored research provides another important point of connection. Long-term projects allow students to contribute to authentic environmental investigations while developing technical and communication skills, working alongside peers, mentoring newer students, and presenting their work to professional communities.

Lessons from this model are now informing the development of a new interdisciplinary Environmental Science program designed to create multiple entry points into environmental geoscience. The program integrates coursework across environmental disciplines with applied experiences, professional certifications, research opportunities, and career preparation. Rather than treating recruitment, experiential learning, undergraduate research, mentoring, and professional development as separate activities, the goal is to intentionally connect them as components of a pathway into the profession. This approach emphasizes building community alongside skills and experience, helping students make connections with faculty, peers, research projects, field experiences, and the broader geoscience community. In doing so, interdisciplinary environmental programs can provide not only additional routes into geoscience, but also a framework for helping students recognize that they belong within it.

title: Program GtSmNdGrowth, a Discretization and Forward Modeling Sm-Nd Geochronometry Program and Toolbox for Modeling Garnet-bearing Rocks, Optimizing Selection of Analytical Targets, and Evaluating Effects of High-REE Contaminants
session_title: Data in Geochronology: Advances in the Production, Reduction, Integration, and Sharing of Geochronologic Data
authors: Magloughlin, Jerry F. [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geosciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO, USA
abstract:
The Sm-Nd isotope geochronometer is commonly used on garnet-bearing rocks owing to the elevated Sm/Nd of garnet. Several minerals plus garnet (or some portion[s] thereof) are analyzed, with the whole rock or host rock, and an isochron is fit.

Many issues lead to uncertainties including protracted growth of garnet; high-REE dissolvable inclusions (e.g. monazite); and non-dissolvable elevated-REE inclusions such as zircon. Using various analytical and chemical techniques, 17 or more analytical targets are possible. Thus, there is a need for help in choosing the targets leading to the best understanding of the evolution of such a rock.

GtSmNdGrowth uses a discretization and forward modeling approach for complete tracking of Nd and Sm atoms and isotopes in a rock during growth of monazite and garnet, models a second micro-inclusion in garnet, handles partial or complete chemical dissolution of monazite, and performs other functions by tracking garnet growth through 1000 steps using constant volume and constant thickness models. All relevant parameters may be adjusted, resultant isochrons shown, apparent dates calculated, and a York regression carried out. A central goal is to provide guidance on disassembling the rock and garnet, predicting apparent dates for any pair of analyses, and revealing the impact of chemical treatments. Constant or zoned Nd and Sm is modeled, along with the role of non-REE bearing inclusions or ‘dilutants’ in garnet. Seventeen prospective physical targets may be evaluated.

GtSmNdGrowth contains multiple stand-alone ‘toolbox’ functions. One calculates the modal percent of monazite inclusions using SEM observations. Another provides five ways to calculate the area of such grains from thin section or SEM measurements. Other routines calculate monazite and garnet densities, and carry out two-point Rb-Sr and Sm-Nd date calculations. Other routines carry out a York regression, and handle Sm and Nd zoning and non-REE mineral inclusion distributions in garnet. Another routine allows chemical and isotopic predictions based on analysis of an arbitrarily sized circular patch in a garnet slice (e.g., using LA-ICP-MS). It is intended the program will lead to better target (and rock) selection, saving time and expense, and will help anticipate and explain anomalous apparent dates, as well as help choose the combinations best likely to provide accurate dates, considering many analytical pairings are shown to provide large errors and/or erroneous apparent dates.

title: Biogeography of meniscomyine rodents in the late Oligocene: A case study in the interactions between paleoecology and paleogeography
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology
authors: Hopkins, Samantha S.B. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR, ; Museum of Natural and Cultural History, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR, USA
abstract: The Meniscomyinae are a clade of aplodontiid rodents that diversify rapidly in the Late Oligocene primarily in North America (although there are a few species represented in the record of Eurasia at this time as well). From within this group we see the origin of the Aplodontiinae, the clade that includes the single living species of the family, as well as the Mylagaulidae, a strange and enigmatic group of highly specialized burrowing rodents that reached peak diversity in the mid-Miocene and includes the only burrowing rodent ever to evolve horns, Ceratogaulus . While the late Oligocene record of North American rodents is not well preserved in many parts of the continent, the record we have of the late Oligocene members of this clade show high degrees of endemism and ecological diversity that offers clues into how this group shaped the origin of both the low-diversity living aplodontiine lineage and the highly speciose mylagaulid line. New material of a previously undescribed meniscomyine from the Otay Formation in San Diego as well as newly described species from Montana, combined with Rensberger’s published work on Meniscomys and Niglarodon , suggest that these burrowing rodents showed relatively high degrees of habitat specificity that seems to also be reflected in the diversity of their descendents, the Mylagaulidae.

title: Foreland basin architecture on the Kalahari Craton during assembly of Gondwana
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Nelson, Lyle Lee [1], Smith, Emily Frances [2], Swart, Roger [3], Baillie, Iona [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric & Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA
(3) BlackGold Geosciences, Windhoek, Namibia
(4) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA
abstract: The amalgamation of Gondwana included collisions between Kalahari, Congo, and Rio de la Plata cratons. The late Ediacaran-early Cambrian Nama foreland basin formed on the Kalahari Craton as a result of collisions of these cratons which closed the Khomas and Adamastor oceans. The broadly east-west trending Osis Arch has long been recognized as a paleo-topographic high in the Nama Basin and interpreted as a forebulge associated with flexure related to the closure of the Khomas Seaway and the associated Damara Orogen. Here we use stratigraphic fence diagrams across the Nama Basin, accompanied by published geochronological and geophysical data, to demonstrate that the Osis Arch, which separated the Zaris and Witputs subbasins, was restricted to deposition of the oldest part of the Nama, the Kuibis Subgroup. Subsequently, a broadly northwest trending forebulge formed during deposition of the Schwarzrand Subgroup and is responsible for paleogeographic and facies trends during the middle part of Nama deposition, including focusing carbonate deposition along this topographic high. This younger forebulge formed as a result of flexure related to the closure of the Adamastor Seaway and the associated Gariep orogen. This interpretation is consistent with a model in which Damaran subduction infected the southern Adamastor Ocean.

title: Basin-scale Reconstruction of Rivers: An Example From the Cretaceous of Wyoming
session_title: Sediments and Stratigraphy (Posters)
authors: McElroy, Brandon [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Wyoming, Laramie, WY, USA
abstract: Recent advances in paleohydraulic methods provide the ability to quantify the scales of ancient rivers and their basins. In combination with traditional methods for sedimentary provenance, it is possible to apply a mass-conservation approach to understanding the records of fluvial sediment transport. Here, I present analyses based on the hydraulic geometries of ancient channels of the Mesa Verde Group though central Wyoming. These records are marginal marine and exhibit overall regressive sequences. The Cretaceous rivers draining into the Western Interior Seaway through Wyoming during this time have preserved channel forms that qualitatively demonstrate a sedimentary source area. Specifically, the channel bodies are made largely of chert arenites. Quantitatively the channel bodies indicate rivers of a scale that drained from the western ranges (i.e. Fold and Thrust Belt). Combined, it is possible to coherently reconstruct the continental sediment transport systems that drained the western mountains and filled the eastern basins. Finally, it is demonstrable that the Parkman Sandstone, as an example, conserves transported sediment mass in a 2D framework.

title: Vulnerability of Springs in the Pedernales River Basin, Texas Hill Country, to Drought and Development
session_title: Karst Hydrology and Hydrogeology
authors: Yale, Vivian E. [1], Bahamon Pinzon, David [2], Banner, Jay L. [3], Rempe, Daniella M. [4], Hunt, Brian [5]
affiliations: (1) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(2) University of Texas at Austin - Jackson School of Geosciences, Austin, TX,
(3) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
(4) The University of Texas at Austin, Jackson School of Geosciences, Austin, TX,
(5) University of Texas, Austin, TX,
abstract: The Hill Country of central Texas is a rapidly developing area that is prone to drought and flood. Domestic water in northern Hays County in central Texas is primarily withdrawn from the Middle Trinity Aquifer, which also feeds local springs. The increasing demand for water resources due to population growth, limited aquifer recharge from worsening droughts, and karstic nature of the Middle Trinity Aquifer, makes local groundwater resources particularly vulnerable. Geochemical analysis offers insights into residence times, recharge mechanisms, and water sources, which can inform water management strategies. In this study, groundwaters, surface waters and springs were sampled at 29 sites and analyzed for major and trace ions, H, O and Sr isotopes ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr), and bacteria. Results indicate a geochemical groundwater divide mirroring a physical groundwater divide. This divide separates water with a Ca-Mg-HCO₃ composition flowing northwest from water with a Ca-Mg-SO₄ composition flowing southeast. To the northwest, the Middle Trinity Aquifer is exposed at the surface, allowing direct recharge and shorter aquifer residence times. Southeast of the divide, the aquifer is confined by the Upper Trinity Aquifer and contains evaporite deposits, leading to indirect recharge, longer residence times, and high sulfate concentrations. Quantitative models for mineral-solution reactions are used to assess processes of geochemical evolution that can account for trace element (Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca) and 87 Sr/ 86 Sr variations. Model results indicate that ephemeral springs and surface waters show the least geochemical evolution (more similar to soil compositions), while phreatic groundwaters plot with greatest geochemical evolution (more similar to rock compositions), and perennial springs and surface waters have intermediate compositions. Because a water’s geochemical evolution corresponds to its residence time, ephemeral sites likely have the shortest residence times while phreatic groundwaters have the longest. Differences in residence time and chemical composition are interpreted as the result of spatial variations in the presence of confining layers. Residence time inferences are also supported by temporal analyses of ionic and bacterial concentrations at springs, which show fluctuations with rain, primarily following storm events that punctuated droughts. Geochemical analysis of the Middle Trinity Aquifer is important for defining key hydrologic processes and boundaries, which can inform sustainable policies that protect recharge zones and groundwater from the effects of drought and development.

title: Probing the Fluid Histories and Protolith(s) of Chlorite-Rich Hybrid Rocks from the Sivrihisar Massif (Tavşanlı Zone, Northwest Türkiye) using Bulk Rock Geochemistry and Oxygen Isotopes
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Posters)
authors: Beachy, Micah D. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience Department, Ohio University, Athens, OH, USA
abstract:
Metasomatism is the fluid-driven alteration of a rock's bulk chemistry. Hybrid rocks, those that cease to match a common crustal protolith, are an excellent window into fluid movement in subduction zones. Many of these fluids are released by the high pressure, low temperature (HP/LT) breakdown of hydrous minerals such as serpentine, chlorite, and lawsonite, a calcium aluminum silicate rarely preserved because of its limited stability range.

The Sivrihisar Massif is in one of largest and best exposed lawsonite blueschist belts, the Tavşanlı Zone of NW Türkiye. Composed mainly of coherent marble, schist, quartzite and metabasite units, it contains hundreds of meter-scale blueschist and eclogite pods. Lawsonite- and chlorite-rich hybrid rocks occur at pod margins and other lithologic contacts, particularly associated with serpentinite.

Nine Sivrihisar samples, mostly hybrid rocks, were tested for bulk rock major and trace element concentrations. These are combined with pre-existing, mostly unpublished data from twenty other samples – six eclogites, six serpentinites, two metasediments, and a blueschist. Oxygen and hydrogen isotopes were also collected on the serpentinites. Textural and mineralogical analysis is being carried out with a standard petrographic microscope.

Based on lithologic similarity, two rough groups of hybrid rocks are identified. Group 1 rocks consist of chlorite + lawsonite ± epidote ± garnet in varying proportions, while those in Group 2 are dominantly chlorite and may be monomineralic. Some of the latter contain minor magnetite. Both groups may include accessory titanite, rutile (often rimmed by titanite), and apatite. Preliminary bulk-rock geochemical analysis suggests that Group 1 is most similar to the eclogites and Group 2 to the serpentinites. MgO and LOI for both groups are between eclogite (low) and serpentinite (high), with Group 2 > Group 1. CaO, Na 2 O, K 2 O, and P 2 O 5 in Group 2 approximately equal the serpentinites and are generally higher in Group 1. Serpentinites are the most consistent lithology in major element concentrations. Trace elements of Group 1 approximately parallel the eclogites, blueschist, and metasediments, while Group 2 is between these and serpentinite. Both hybrid groups have equal or higher Al 2 O 3 and lower SiO 2 than every other rock type sampled.

abstract: The United States Magnetotelluric Array (USMTArray) data set, collected in the years 2006-2024, consists of more than 1,700 long-period magnetotelluric stations covering the entirety of the contiguous United States on a quasiregular 70km grid. Funding across multiple federal agencies was critical to sustaining this effort to its completion. Important components of the project included active guidance and participation from the MT community, the open and timely availability of all data, and the application of consistent instrumentation and robust data processing. Together with parallel advancement in the development of publicly available three-dimensional (3D) inversion codes, the USMTArray has revitalized the U.S. magnetotelluric community and increased the visibility of magnetotellurics within the Earth-science community. Taken as a whole, these data are visualized as the National Impedance Map, which, together with a 3D synthesis conductivity model of the nation, reveals the electrical architecture of the contiguous U.S. USMTArray data are used by researchers worldwide for fundamental and applied studies, including investigations of continental architecture and evolution, estimation of hazards to critical infrastructure due to geomagnetic storms, and assessment of the nation’s undiscovered geothermal and mineral resources. In a recently published manuscript (Kelbert et al, 2026), we review the history and development of the project, discuss the challenges and successes in its execution, present the National Impedance Map and synthesis conductivity model, and highlight the breadth of research stemming from this rich data set. Here, we summarize this publication and the key scientific outcomes of the USMTArray project for the international electromagnetic induction community.

title: Breaking Ground and Initial Installation of the Coastal Subsurface Monitoring System for Southeast Florida, a Project Update
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas
authors: Eschenburg, Holly J. [1], Lau, Kingsley [2], Flores, Juan Pablo [3], Loyola, Ashley [4], Sukop, Michael C. [5]
affiliations: (1) Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
(2) Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering, Florida International University, Miami, Florida,
(3) Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
(4) Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA
(5) Florida International University, Miami, FL,
abstract:
Southeast Florida is a low-lying coastal area underlain by the exceptionally transmissive Biscayne Aquifer — the region's water supply source. Saltwater intrusion is a major concern, and the toe of the regional saltwater intrusion wedge, which lies several kilometers inland, is well monitored for water supply protection. However, the configuration of the saltwater wedge near the highly developed shoreline is largely unknown. Nearshore groundwater is subject to tidal fluctuation and groundwater inundation is becoming more common, particularly during King tide season. Since the 2021 collapse of the Champlain condominium tower, interest has increased in understanding nearshore groundwater and its possible interactions with infrastructure.

A $10M Coastal Subsurface Monitoring project was funded to address data gaps in nearshore groundwater and subsurface corrosivity. Current plans call for as many as 7 transects each consisting of up to 10 stations within 1 kilometer of the shoreline and on adjacent barrier islands.

The first transect will be located on Florida International University’s North Miami campus. This pilot transect consists of three stations. Each station will consist of 3 boreholes of 30 m depth.

One borehole will be completed as a nested well consisting of 2 conventional monitoring wells, one 30 m deep and one 3 m deep, designed to continuously monitor water table position and salinity with conductivity, depth, and temperature (CTD) loggers. The 30 m monitoring well will also provide access for electromagnetic induction (EMI) logging.

The second borehole will be completed as a sampling well consisting of a single 30 m multichannel tube designed to provide access to 7 isolated zones.

The third borehole will be dedicated to a novel array of corrosion sensing electrodes designed to measure Wenner-array Electrical Resistivity (ER), Linear Polarization Resistance (LPR), and Open-Circuit Potential (OCP).

Physical samples will be collected and logged from each station.

The two CTD loggers and the corrosion sensing array will be connected to a datalogger and cellular telemeter. One station within the transect will also host meteorologic sensors that will report to the datalogger.

Implementation challenges include station design, construction of a novel array of corrosion sensing electrodes, subsurface installation of atypical elements, selection of drilling method, selection of well drilling contractor, procurement of materials, scheduling, and cooperator approvals.

title: Major extinctions and macroevolutionary stress linked to Phanerozoic mega-climate states
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Part I)
authors: Myers, Corinne [1], Sudakow, Ivan [2], Spiridonov, Andrej [3], Stankevič, Robertas [4], Feulner, Georg [5], Livina, Valerie [6]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) Applied Mathematics, The Open University, London, United Kingdom
(3) Geology and Mineralogy, Vilnius University, Vilnius, Lithuania
(4) Vilnius University, Vilnius, Lithuania
(5) Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, Potsdam, Germany; University of Potsdam, Potsdam, Germany
(6) National Physical Laboratory, Teddington, United Kingdom
abstract:
The role of abiotic environmental factors on Phanerozoic diversity and extinction is difficult to disentangle given the complexity of Earth-life systems involved. Yet as we barrel towards increasingly rapid environmental changes today, progress towards understanding these complexities is as imperative ever. Here we derived an index of global macroevolutionary stress to summarize large extinction vulnerability based on generic-level biodiversity records across the Phanerozoic. We link macroevolutionary stress to the environmental context of large time-scale global climate changes via a combination of recurrence-based analyses of empirical data and dynamical systems models. Five recurring and long-lived mega-climate states were identified using joint recurrence analysis of Phanerozoic stable isotope and atmospheric CO 2 records. The fidelity of these states were supported by a climate-carbon cycle dynamical model, which combines an excitable carbon cycle, temperature dependent weathering, and impulsive inputs (such as carbon injection from large igneous province emplacement) with a simple energy-balance model that incorporates ice-albedo feedbacks and logarithmic greenhouse gas forcing.

Results suggest that Phanerozoic biodiversity and its relationship with global climate is, unsurprisingly, hierarchical: we observe an overall positive trend between extinction vulnerability and global temperature records across the Phanerozoic as a whole, however, within individual mega-climate states the relationship is more variable and subject to noise. Notably, macroevolutionary stress appears higher overall near mega-climate transitions than within a given regime. Macroevolutionary stress is also markedly higher during early Paleozoic hothouse conditions versus the Cenozoic icehouse. This evokes a more optimistic view of the potential biospheric response to current and projected future environmental changes linked to extinction vulnerability. In sum, our findings suggest that mega-climate states may be setting a baseline macroevolutionary stress landscape within which short-timescale and event-specific environmental perturbations are more or less likely to result in extreme biospheric vulnerability to extinction.

title: Triple Oxygen Isotopes in Pomacea Shells as a Proxy for Seasonal Hydroclimate and Evaporation.
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part II)
authors: Banerjee, Payal [1], Peshek, Catherine [2], Sharp, Zachary [3], Prufer, Keith [4], Neff, Nadia [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(3) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(4) Department of Anthropology, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
(5) Department of Anthropology, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
Freshwater mollusk shells have the potential to preserve sub-annual records of hydrologic variability, but the influence of evaporation on triple oxygen isotope signals recorded during shell growth remains poorly constrained. Here, we evaluate δ′ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O in Pomacea shell carbonate as a proxy for seasonal changes in surface-water isotope composition, evaporation, and hydroclimate. We combine modern lake-water and shell carbonates from Florida with stream and rain-water measurements and modern to archaeological Pomacea shells from Belize spanning approximately last 10,000 years.

We micro-sampled shell carbonate sequentially along growth increments from multiple modern and archaeological specimens to generate intra-shell δ′ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O profiles. The Belize shells exhibit repeated isotopic variability consistent with seasonal changes in hydrologic conditions. Measured shell carbonate Δ′ 17 O values range from approximately −20 to −130 per meg (VSMOW), while δ′ 18 O values range from ~ −7.5 to −4.5‰ (VPDB). Reconstructed water compositions based on the shell carbonate measurements range from approximately −6 to −3.5‰ in δ′ 18 O (VSMOW) and −25 to 55 per meg (VSMOW) in Δ′ 17 O. Stream and rain-water measurements provide an additional constraint on the modern Belize hydrologic system and allow evaluation of the role of evaporation of meteoric water.

To better constrain the evaporation signal, we analyzed monthly lake waters and a modern Pomacea shell from Florida. Lake-water δ 18 O varies seasonally from 0.03 to 5.36‰ (VSMOW), while measured Δ′ 17 O values range from approximately −43.5 to +8.1 per meg (VSMOW), indicating substantial seasonal evaporative modification of lake water. Preliminary measurements from a modern micro-sampled Florida shell yield δ′ 18 O values of −0.87 to −0.47‰ (VPDB) and Δ′ 17 O values of approximately −149 to −69 per meg (VSMOW). Continued micro-sampling of this shell will test how seasonal changes in lake-water evaporation are transferred into shell carbonate.

Paired water–shell observations from Florida provide a modern framework for interpreting the longer Belize shell record. Our results suggest that combining δ′ 18 O and Δ′ 17 O in Pomacea shells may help distinguish variations associated with meteoric-water input from lake or stream- water evaporation, providing a new sub-annual proxy for reconstructing seasonal hydroclimate and hydrologic balance in tropical and subtropical environments. Applied to archaeological shells from Belize, this approach has the potential to resolve changes in Holocene hydroclimate seasonality that are difficult to capture using conventional lower-resolution archives.

title: A Parking Lot Dinosaur: Mitigation, Excavation, and Preparation of a Sauropod at Dinosaur National Monument, UT
session_title: “All creatures great and small”: Macro to micro approaches and perspectives in stratigraphic paleobiology (Posters)
authors: Hummel, Rudolph Russell [1], Hunt-Foster, ReBecca [2], Sameshima, Andy [3], Simon, Candice Nichole [4]
affiliations: (1) Hermantown, MN,
abstract: Paleontological monitoring was conducted in association with road maintenance at Dinosaur National Monument from June to October of 2025. Fossil resources were sparce across most project areas; however, dinosaur, plant, and bivalve fossils were found in abundance in September beneath the Quarry Exhibit Hall parking lot. Prominent among these were the remains of a Jurassic sauropod dinosaur within the Quarry Sandstone, a three-meter-thick channel deposit within the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation. An initial salvage operation occurred during the fall of 2025 and a second in the spring of 2026, with the goal of removing all possible dinosaur bones from the site before paving the parking lot. The fall dig recovered fifteen caudal vertebrae, four limb elements, and an unknown number of pedal elements. In the spring, a further three caudal vertebrae were collected, along with additional elements belonging to at least two additional sauropods, one theropod, and two ornithischians. The Quarry Sandstone dips to the south at 70°, which made the excavation challenging. Thirteen of the vertebrae collected in the fall were articulated and plunging to the west at the proximal end. The distalmost vertebrae in the series were located immediately below the road base installed during construction of the original parking lot in the 1960s and show signs of damage by construction equipment. The gravel and road base include fragments of neural spines damaged at this time. Preparation of the caudal vertebrae is currently underway and has been complicated by the heavy presence of bivalve shells immediately overlying many bones, which cause poor separation between the matrix and bone. This project represents the first major excavation in fresh exposure of the Quarry Sandstone since 1924, and further preparation is expected to yield fresh insights into the stratigraphy and paleontology of these historic fossil beds.

title: Network Analysis of Mineral Species and Their Modes of Formation Through Deep Time
session_title: Geoinformatics advances scientific discoveries: Machine Learning, Cyberinfrastructure, and Open Data in the digital geological era
authors: Morrison, Shaunna M [1], Prabhu, Anirudh [2], Hazen, Robert M. [3]

abstract:
Mineral diversification is commonly described as the accumulation of new mineral species through time, but Earth’s mineralogy is also a structured system of relationships among minerals, environments, and planetary processes. Here, we apply network analysis to the full known suite of International Mineralogical Association-approved mineral species and their paragenetic modes of formation, using a dataset of 5,656 mineral species, 57 paragenetic modes, and 10,556 mineral-mode pairs. The resulting bipartite networks link each mineral species to the environments in which it is known to form, providing a global-scale representation of mineral formation from pre-solar stellar condensates and solar nebular processes to modern anthropogenic mineralization.

The network reveals that Earth’s mineral diversity is not randomly distributed among formational environments. Instead, it is organized by a small number of major planetary drivers, including water, redox evolution, rare-element concentration, and biological activity. Water-associated paragenetic modes dominate the network: approximately 81% of known mineral species can form through water-related processes, and 56% incorporate essential OH- or H2O in their structures. Biologically mediated modes are also disproportionately important, encompassing approximately half of known mineral species, with about 34% forming exclusively through biotically influenced processes. Rare elements, though representing only a tiny fraction of crustal atoms, are essential constituents of roughly 40% of mineral species and cluster in specialized topological neighborhoods associated with evolved igneous, hydrothermal, and biologically influenced environments.

Network topology also captures differences in mineral versatility. Most mineral species are paragenetically restricted: 59.5% occur in only one mode of formation and 82.2% occur in one or two modes. In contrast, a small number of abundant, geochemically versatile minerals, including pyrite, magnetite, calcite, quartz, hematite, and albite, connect many environments and act as network hubs. Pyrite, known from 22 paragenetic modes, is the most connected mineral species in the dataset.

These results show that mineral networks provide a quantitative framework for identifying the planetary processes that generate mineral diversity. They also suggest that network structure itself may encode planetary-scale signatures of water, redox evolution, rare-element concentration, and life, offering a new approach for comparing Earth’s mineralogical history with those of Mars, the Moon, and other planetary bodies.

title: New Exposures of the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary in Tippah County, Mississippi, USA: Sedimentological Context for the End-Cretaceous Mass Extinction in the Mississippi Embayment
session_title: Mass extinctions and the current biodiversity crisis: Lessons from the past to inform the future (Posters)
authors: Platt, Brian F. [1], Retrum, Julie B. [2], Gifford, Jennifer N. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, The University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
(3) Geology and Geological Engineering, University of Mississippi, Oxford, MS, USA
abstract: The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) mass extinction is characterized by a significant loss of biodiversity and profound ecological turnover. The approximately coeval occurrence of the Chicxulub impact in the southern Gulf of Mexico (GoM) is well established, although whether it is the sole causal extinction mechanism or one of multiple is debated. The strata of the Mississippi Embayment, a continental basin once flooded by a sea connected to the GoM, has provided much insight into the nature of the mass extinction. Sites in Texas, Alabama, Mississippi (MS), Arkansas, and Missouri contain important paleontological records as well as the southernmost sedimentological evidence of the influence of the bolide impact in the continental US. Current highway construction in two counties in northern MS is exposing the lithostratigraphic boundary between the Cretaceous Owl Creek Formation (Fm) and the Paleocene Clayton Fm, yielding a wealth of new data about the mass extinction and its environmental context. We present new data from exposures due to construction at several locations in Ripley, MS that represent some of the thickest continuous stratigraphic sections available in the region. Fieldwork was performed to measure stratigraphic sections and collect sedimentological and paleontological samples. Additionally, thin sections were made from samples collected at the stratigraphically lowest site. Results show that the Owl Creek Fm is a gray mixed carbonate-clastic allochemic mudrock coarsening upward to an allochemic sandstone. Cretaceous ammonoid fossils are common. Above this is a tan clastic sandy siltstone that coarsens upward but is modified by recent soil formation. Fossil preservation varies from abundant original aragonitic material lower in the section to dominantly clastic external molds, internal molds, and internal casts higher in the section. Bioturbation is abundant throughout the section, with mm-scale meniscate burrows visible in thin sections and cm-scale burrows in outcrop associated with crustacean body fossils. The location of the boundary with the overlying Clayton is currently uncertain. Excellent exposure of the Clayton Fm at a nearby site allowed data collection from a section >9 m thick. This section records six fossiliferous beds with evidence of at least two transgressive intervals. Whether the top of the Clayton is present is uncertain, but the abundance of body and trace fossils is unusual compared to other Clayton sites in MS.

title: Possible multiple concentric rims at the Sierra Madera impact structure, Pecos County, Texas: Evidence from elevation, gravity, and magnetic transects
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: Shahriar, Md Upal [1], Stewart, Robert R. [2], Oriyomi, Ojelabi [3], Gungor, Nilay [4], Lama, Pragya [5], Bugti, Muhammad Nawaz [6], Muhammady, Nabeel [7]

(2) Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA

abstract: The Sierra Madera structure in Pecos County, west Texas, is one of the best-exposed complex impact structures (astroblemes) on Earth, with an assigned ~13 km outer diameter and a 6-8 km central uplift in which Permian carbonates were raised roughly 1.2 km. Whether the structure is bounded by a single rim or by a set of nested concentric rings has been difficult to establish from erosion-limited surface exposure alone. Here we re-examine the question with a new 9.4 km gravity and magnetic transect (Line 0; 95 stations at ~100 m spacing) acquired about 2 km west of the central uplift during the 2026 University of Houston Field Camp. After a smooth regional field is removed, the residual Bouguer anomaly is not a single moat-and-rim couplet but a train of at least three concentric gravity highs (+0.3 to +0.5 mGal) separated by two to three well-defined lows (-0.3 to -0.5 mGal), repeating with a wavelength of about 2.5 km. A co-located ground-magnetic transect, acquired along the same line over three days, extends ~11.8 km — about 2 km beyond the gravity coverage — and is magnetically quiet over the weakly magnetic carbonate section apart from short-wavelength cultural spikes along the highway; after despiking it defines a broad, low-amplitude (~6-10 nT) low across the interior of the structure, coincident with the ring-syncline zone. We interpret the alternating highs and lows as structurally raised, denser carbonate ridges (rims) alternating with brecciated, down-folded ring synclines (moats); the outermost high coincides with the mapped 13 km rim. The pattern reproduces the ring-syncline-and-rim architecture mapped by Wilshire et al. (1972) and supports the possibility that Sierra Madera preserves a multi-rim (nested-ring) morphology rather than a single rim. Several shorter seismic lines were also acquired and are currently under analysis to help further resolve the crater’s enigmatic structure.

title: Neoproterozoic diamictites and cap carbonates of the Kyrgyz Tian-Shan
session_title: What's New in the Neoproterozoic: Advancing Geochronology, Geochemistry, Geobiology and Climate Records (Posters)
authors: Nelson, Lyle Lee [1], Polomski, Dana [2], Ozyalcin, Cem [3], Orozbaev, Rustam [4], Kasymbekov, Adil [5], Crockford, Peter W [6]

abstract: Climate is a primary control on planetary habitability: fluctuations between ice ages and non-glacial intervals have characterized Earth history and influenced the evolutionary trajectory of life, including the emergence and radiation of metazoans during the Neoproterozoic. Constraints on Precambrian climate largely hinge on the chronology and paleogeographic extent of glacially influenced deposits. Here, we present geologic mapping, stratigraphy, sedimentology, chemostatigraphy, and geochronology data from Neoproterozoic strata of the Kyrgyz Central Tian-Shan. In the Kichi-Naryn area, we document distinctive cap carbonates and carbon isotope excursions that provide a framework for the age and correlation of regional glaciogenic units, yielding new constraints on Neoproterozoic climate history.

title: Residual Stress Heterogeneity in a Naturally Deformed Quartz Ribbon: A Raman Spectroscopic Study with EBSD-Imaged Microstructure
session_title: Mineralogical Insights from Modern Spectroscopic Techniques (Posters)
authors: Rahl, Jeffrey M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Geoscience, Washington and Lee University, Lexington, VA, USA
abstract:
When quartz is subjected to differential or hydrostatic stress, small elastic distortions develop within its crystal lattice, perturbing Si–O bond lengths and angles and producing measurable shifts in Raman peak position that scale with internal strain. Three principal Raman bands of quartz (near 128, 206, and 464 cm⁻¹) respond systematically to stress: the 206 cm⁻¹ band shifts to higher wavenumber with increasing hydrostatic pressure regardless of orientation, while the 128 and 464 cm⁻¹ bands are additionally sensitive to differential stress. These relationships form the basis of quartz-in-garnet Raman barometry, in which residual stress preserved in quartz inclusions is used to estimate entrapment pressure.

Here, I explore an alternative application of Raman spectroscopy of quartz: mapping spatial stress variation within quartz-rich domains. The study focuses on a deformed quartz ribbon in a mylonitic rock from the Blue Ridge, Virginia, compressed along one segment between two adjacent feldspar porphyroclasts acting as rigid indentors. Raman maps of the ribbon interior reveal a spatially coherent, diagonally oriented zone of lower 206 cm⁻¹ position (~205.0–205.5 cm⁻¹ versus a ~206.5–207.5 cm⁻¹ background), demonstrating variable residual stress within the segment of the ribbon most intensely deformed between the indentors. This feature persists after excluding spectra with poor fit quality (R² > 0.9 for all three peaks) and is independently observed in the 128 and 464 cm⁻¹ bands, indicating it reflects a genuine stress signal rather than a fitting artifact. The diagonal zone's orientation is consistent with the local deformation fabric independently resolved by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) in the same area. The amplitude of the 128 cm⁻¹ peak varies smoothly and continuously with position, independent of the 206/464 amplitude ratio, suggesting a distinct microstructural control on this parameter. Ongoing work is registering the Raman and EBSD datasets at pixel scale to test whether the stress-anomalous zone corresponds to a mapped subgrain or Dauphiné twin domain boundary. These results demonstrate that Raman spectroscopy can resolve coherent residual stress heterogeneity in naturally deformed quartz at the microstructural scale.

title: Studying Sulfide Mineralogy to Understand Critical Minerals in the Steeple Rock Mining District, Grant County, New Mexico
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Hausner, Nicolas Michael [1], McLemore, Virginia T. [2], Iverson, Nels [3], Beauchaine, Samantha [4]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Community College of Denver, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Geology, New Mexico Tech/NM Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, NM, USA
(3) Geology, New Mexico Tech/NM Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
(4) Geology, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM, USA
abstract: Volcanic-epithermal vein deposits characterize the Steeple Rock Mining District of Southwest New Mexico, a historical source of gold and the critical minerals silver, copper, lead, and zinc. Critical minerals are nonfuel mineral commodities essential to economic and national security that the U.S. largely sources from international supply chains, which are vulnerable to disruption. This study evaluates critical mineral potential in the Steeple Rock Mining District through sulfide-mineral geochemistry from the precious- and base-metal veins of the Carlisle-Center fault zone. To assess critical mineral enrichment in epithermal vein deposits, trace-element geochemistry details the five sulfide mineral phases found in study samples - covellite (CuS), chalcopyrite (CuFeS 2 ), pyrite (FeS 2 ), sphalerite (ZnS), and galena (PbS). Sulfide phases are characterized by mineralogy and geochemistry using four methods of analysis: Whole-rock geochemistry; reflected-light petrography; X-Ray diffraction; and electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). Reflected-light petrography and X-Ray diffraction identify sample mineralogy, while whole-rock geochemistry indicates the presence of trace critical minerals. EPMA then measures trace elements within the sulfide minerals. From Steeple Rock’s Center Mine, EPMA measures notable concentrations of (1) silver in covellite and (2) tellurium in galena. Tellurium concentrations reach up to 1,700 ppm within galena, while silver averages 5,100 ppm in rims of covellite surrounding galena. With this, covellite recovery is a worthy prospect as an accessory source of Ag, should mining reopen or expand in the future. This study improves understanding of critical mineral distribution in volcanic-epithermal systems and supports ongoing exploration assessments in the district. Results suggest the Steeple Rock Mining District contains great potential for critical mineral enrichment, particularly of Te and Ag. This work was conducted as part of the Geo-Launchpad internship program, supported by the NSF NGF operated by EarthScope Consortium.

title: Kansas’ Hidden Coffins: Creating gprMax Computer Model Simulations for Interpreting Cemetery Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) Data in Kansas
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Scott, Nikodemos My'Joi D'Andre [1], Schneider, Blair Benson [2], Alves Borges, Ayla [3]
affiliations: (1) Piedmont Virginia Community College, Palmyra, VA, USA
(2) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Kansas Geological Survey, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
abstract:
Throughout the 1800’s, Kansas was a crossroads for Americans in search of new lives. Being located in the center of the country led to numerous cultures, religions, social classes, and races coming together in the same region, which resulted in burial practices combining as communities formed. Thanks to new railroads, westward migration, and evolving societal norms, Native Americans, white Europeans, and African Americans crossed paths in a few key Kansas cities, but diseases and hardships of migration led to a spike in deaths. If the deceased could be buried in a cemetery, the direction of burial, headstone placement and styling, casket use and type, and coffin sizes all varied drastically between these groups. Studying burials can shed light on how societal norms and cultural practices evolved during this time.

Many burials in the US cannot be excavated due to preservation laws. Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) is a tool geologists and archaeologists can use to scan the subsurface to find buried targets. Using electromagnetic waves, the GPR will receive waves reflected back from anything different than the surrounding soil. GPR has been successfully utilized for finding burial sites, but there’s less research on the application of GPR in cemeteries in clayey soils, like those found in Kansas. The reason is poor signal strength in dense soil. As coffins age and the wood rots, they can fall in on themselves, distorting readings. These factors combined create data interpretation challenges. Our goal was to create numerous computer simulation models of expected GPR readings from a casket as it collapses using a program called gprMAX. Model results are then compared to actual GPR readings from Valencia Cemetery in Valencia, Kansas, to investigate if 19th-century burials at this cemetery used caskets and, if so, to interpret their conditions and states of decay.

I used the models to generate the collapsing coffin GPR readings in different scenarios that could impact the data, including burial depth, casket collapse state, and GPR antenna frequencies. My models are based on soil composition data from Valencia Cemetery. With this methodology, we can interpret burial-site GPR scans of archaeological settings accurately using noninvasive methods. This work was conducted as part of the Geo-Launchpad internship program, supported by the NSF NGF operated by EarthScope Consortium.

title: Evaluating the Tectonic Evolution of the Hayes Restraining Bend, Denali Fault, Alaska
session_title: Recent developments on the tectonic evolution of Alaska and northwest Canada (Posters)
authors: Roche, Aidan Franco [1], Waldien, Trevor [2], O'Sullivan, Paul [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(2) Geology and Geological Engineering, South Dakota School Of Mines & Technology, Rapid City, SD, USA
(3) GeoSep Services, Moscow, Idaho, USA
abstract: The Denali Fault is an active, intracontinental dextral strike-slip fault in southern Alaska along which oblique convergence of the Southern Alaska Block with interior Alaska drives transpressional deformation. Bulk transpression is manifested by lateral slip on the master fault, shortening across it, and slip on subsidiary splay thrusts to the south. In the eastern Alaska Range, this deformation is localized within the Hayes restraining bend (HRB). The 2002 M w 7.9 rupture on the Susitna Glacier Thrust Fault evidences ongoing deformation within the HRB, yet Quaternary activity on splay thrusts elsewhere in the range is absent, and 1:250,000-scale maps show no faults west of the southern HRB. The crustal response to translation through the bend, and how subsidiary structures initiate, evolve, and are potentially reactivated within it, remains poorly understood. New 1:24,000-scale mapping west of the southern HRB apex, combined with apatite and zircon fission-track and (U-Th)/He thermochronology, tests whether Quaternary slip on splay thrusts south of the Denali Fault reflects reactivation of structures translated into the bend. Mapping identified two distinct packages separated by ~4 km of cover associated with the Nenana River: isoclinally folded greenschist- to amphibolite-facies rocks with interfoliated meta-intrusive rocks to the east, and unfoliated granitoids, greywacke, and limestone to the west. Minor faults within the eastern package display sinistral and normal slip sense. No throughgoing thrusts were identified, yet the lithologic contrast across the Nenana River suggests that a crustal-scale structure is located within the glacial lineament followed by the Nenana River. New apatite (U-Th)/He thermochronology data reveals a distinct westward decrease in cooling ages from the apex of the HRB. Pending cooling ages from samples collected along a transect parallel to the Denali Fault will further resolve spatio-temporal variations in exhumation and assess whether differential exhumation across the covered area supports the presence of a concealed structure. Integrating cooling ages with palinspastic reconstruction of the Denali Fault will test whether exhumation occurred while these rocks occupied the bend apex, distinguishing bend-controlled deformation from far-field forcing.

title: Diagnosing a Pennsylvanian Critical Mineral Deposit: Volcanic Sourcing and Mineralogical Partitioning of Lithium in Mercer Formation Paleosols
session_title: Happy 323 Millionth Birthday, Pennsylvanian Period: A Celebration of Everything Pennsylvania(n)
authors: Sullivan, Nicholas B. [1], White, Timothy S. [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, Penn State, State College, PA, USA
(2) Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, Penn State, State College, PA, USA
abstract:
High-alumina refractory claystone paleosols of the Middle Pennsylvanian Mercer Formation (Northern Appalachian Basin) exhibit exceptional lithium (Li) enrichment, with horizons exceeding 1500 ppm. This presents a geochemical paradox: the enrichment of a highly mobile cation within paleosols that have been extensively leached of nearly all other alkali metals. To resolve the source, transport, and mineralogical hosts of this anomaly, we integrate regional geochemical datasets with XRD, LA-ICP-MS, and high-resolution SEM-EDS mineral mapping.

Regional trace-element associations, together with fine-grained heavy minerals and amorphous silicates, indicate widespread volcanic ash input. We interpret this ash as derived from Alleghenian magmatism associated with highly evolved LCT (lithium-cesium-tantalum) pegmatites. Ash was deposited across a coastal floodplain on an emergent forebulge characterized by limited accommodation space. Following glass devitrification and pedogenic leaching, Li partitioned into two authigenic mineral endmembers controlled primarily by silica availability. In silica-sufficient facies (Al₂O₃/SiO₂ < 0.88), Li is structurally incorporated into ordered dioctahedral chlorite (cookeite) interstratified with illite. In silica-deficient facies (Al₂O₃/SiO₂ > 0.88), extreme desilication forced Li incorporation into disordered kaolinite crystal sheets surrounding diaspore-boehmite nodules. This model identifies high-alumina paleosols as an important unconventional exploration target for critical minerals and provides a framework for understanding Li enrichment in ancient foreland basins.
