title: A Trail through Time: Retracing the Journey of the Ogallala Formation's Rhyolitic Gravels from Volcano to Sediment in the Southern High Plains of Texas
session_title: Geoscience Research Poster Showcase by 2YC and 4YCU Undergraduate Students
authors: Wright, Madeline Grace [1], Eichler, Carla [2]
affiliations: (1) Life, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA
(2) Life, Earth, and Environmental Sciences, West Texas A&M University, Canyon, TX, USA
abstract:
The Ogallala formation serves as a vital resource, containing one of the world’s largest aquifers used for approximately 40% of irrigation for U.S. agriculture. Despite the aquifer’s heavy usage, much of the formation’s origin and transport pathways remain a mystery.

Several authors suggest Miocene-Pliocene paleodrainage networks responsible for Ogallala sediment in the Southern High Plains, which can be narrowed into four main paleodrainage hypotheses: a unified single source area, a 3-lobe fan configuration, a coalescing bajada (multiple sources), and a North-flowing Pecos river drainage. My research aims to build on this past research, by pinpointing the source(s) of Ogallala rhyolitic gravels in the Southern High Plains to determine where sediment travelled. Determining sediment provenance allows reconstruction of the ancient river systems that distributed material across the region, revealing how drainage patterns, sediment routing, and potentially climate conditions evolved during the Miocene epoch. To do so, I collect samples from within the Ogallala formation and potential sources and, using petrographic analysis, I compare the composition and textural patterns of site and source to see if they match.

I started this research with petrographic analysis of rhyolitic gravels from the Ogallala formation in Texas, New Mexico and Colorado, which I referred to in my abstract and poster presentation at the ‘25 GeoConnects conference. This research noted obvious visual features with diagnostic potential, including flow banding, lithics, xenocrysts, and/or multimineralic glomerocrysts, and evidence of possible magma mixing in the form of skeletal quartz and distinct plagioclase rims around alkali-feldspar. Several samples included trace mafic minerals, including biotite and pyroxene. Through these preliminary observations, I observed five rhyolite populations present in the Ogallala formation. These observations helped guide where to sample for potential sources.

After completing this first stage of my research, I switched from a qualitative approach to quantitative, and completed point counts to determine QAP percentages. Additionally, I sampled rhyolite from potential source volcanoes in Colorado and New Mexico. This poster delves into the quartz, alkali-feldspar, and plagioclase (QAP) percentages mapped, observations from petrographic analysis of the new potential source samples, and which hypotheses my research supports or refutes.

title: Occurrence, Distribution, and Environmental Risks of Pharmaceutically Active Compounds Across Tropical River Basins of South India
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part I)
authors: Karayi, Mithun [1], Sharma, Brij Mohan [2], Polishetti, Somasekhar Rao [3], Bláhová, Lucie [4], Yazhini, Crescentia [5], Přibylová, Petra [6], Neppolian, Bernaurdshaw [7], Snow, Daniel D [8], Chakraborty, Paromita [9]

(2) RECETOX, Faculty of Science, Masaryk University, Kotlarska 2, Kotlarska, Czech Republic

abstract:
Pharmaceutically active compounds (PhACs) are emerging contaminants of increasing environmental concern due to their continuous release into aquatic ecosystems, persistence, and potential to induce ecological toxicity and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The COVID-19 pandemic substantially altered pharmaceutical consumption patterns worldwide, increasing the environmental release of several therapeutic compounds. However, comprehensive regional assessments evaluating the occurrence, sources, and environmental risks of pharmaceuticals across multiple tropical river basins following the pandemic remain scarce. This study synthesizes observations from major South Indian river basins, including the Kaveri, Tamirabharani, Periyar, Anjarakkandy, Musi, Adyar, Cooum, and Krishna basins, to evaluate the occurrence, distribution, sources, and environmental risks of pharmaceuticals in surface water and groundwater. Target compounds representing multiple therapeutic classes, together with the wastewater markers caffeine and carbamazepine, were quantified using solid-phase extraction coupled with liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS).

A distinct urban-to-rural gradient in pharmaceutical contamination was observed, with urban rivers consistently exhibiting substantially higher concentrations than suburban and rural systems. Caffeine was the most ubiquitous wastewater marker, reaching mean concentrations of approximately 5 μg L⁻¹ in highly urbanized rivers and remaining consistently detectable across all investigated basins, indicating pervasive inputs of untreated domestic wastewater. Analgesics and angiotensin receptor blockers dominated the pharmaceutical profiles in urban waters, while erythromycin was the predominant antibiotic. Groundwater generally exhibited considerably lower pharmaceutical concentrations than surface waters, although persistent compounds such as caffeine, carbamazepine, and erythromycin were detected at selected locations, indicating localized wastewater infiltration into shallow aquifers. Source apportionment using multivariate statistics and dissolved organic carbon relationships identified untreated domestic sewage, pharmaceutical manufacturing activities, and urban wastewater as the principal drivers controlling the occurrence, transport, and persistence of PhACs.

Risk assessment identified AMR hotspots in highly urbanized river stretches, particularly for azithromycin, erythromycin, sulfamethoxazole, and trimethoprim, while ecotoxicological assessment indicated potential risks to aquatic organisms, including fish and Daphnia. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that wastewater-derived pharmaceuticals are pervasive across tropical South Indian river basins and emphasize the need for integrated watershed-scale monitoring, improved wastewater treatment infrastructure, and management strategies to mitigate pharmaceutical pollution and safeguard freshwater ecosystems.

title: The importance of open-system magma chamber processes in forming a large and long-lived Half Dome-Cathedral Peak magma chamber in the Tuolumne intrusive complex, California
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Memeti, Vali [1], Durning, Sadie [2], Paterson, Scott [3], Gutierrez, Allison [4], Hernandez, Aaron [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University, Fullerton, CA,
(2) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University Fullerton, Fullerton, CA, USA; Department of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
(4) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University Fullerton, Fullerton, California, USA
(5) Department of Geological Sciences, California State University Fullerton, Fullerton, California, USA
abstract:
Cal Barnes’ pioneering research on crustal-scale magma systems emphasized the importance of open-system magma processes. Cal also showed that bridging the gap between macro-scale field geology and micro-scale geochemical analysis leads to critical insights about the complex growth and evolution of plutons. This contribution celebrating Cal’s remarkable career highlights both aspects in understanding the growth and evolution of the 95-85 Ma, 1,100 km 2 Tuolumne intrusive complex (TIC), Sierra Nevada, California.

The TIC is composed of four asymmetrically nested granodiorite units with contacts representing large gradational zones where the ~700 km 2 porphyritic Half Dome (pHD) and Cathedral Peak (CP) units are exposed in the inner TIC. Geologic mapping of this ~8 km wide pHD-CP zone indicates a consistent ring pattern of the following concentrically arranged gradational compositional variations remarkably identical in succession across the TIC: The pHD-typical <3 cm euhedral hornblende, biotite, and <1 cm titanite gradually decrease in abundance toward the CP and are absent in the CP. K-feldspar phenocrysts <3-4 cm in the pHD first drastically increase their size to <12-15 cm K-feldspar megacrysts, then gradually decrease to 2-4 cm phenocrysts in the CP and even smaller sizes toward leucogranites in the CP interior. The megacrystic zone is also typically marked by widespread megacryst clusters and schlieren-bound tubes and troughs. K-feldspars also gradually change shape from more tabular in pHD to more blocky where megacrystic and back to tabular in the CP with interruptions in this trend indicating magma erosion.

We propose that the pHD-CP transition tracks the solidification front of a fossilized magma body that underwent gradual in-mixing of ascending CP magma into pHD across the 700 km 2 TIC interior, keeping it above the solidus ~90-85 Ma (see Durning and Memeti, this meeting). Replenishing magma interrupted a gradually freezing and fractionating magma chamber until the system shut down while preserving older “bathtub rings” of crystallization. Regardless of the size/number of increments that built the inner TIC, the pHD-CP units crystallized as a single entity that was interconnected across the inner TIC. Additional observations support this model: (1) whole rock U-Pb zircon ages are consistent along strike around each transition unit and young inward; and (2) biotite cooling temperature in host rock were reset during pHD-CP time >5 km away from the CP.

title: Unlocking Cambrian Climate Signals: Paired Clumped Isotope Thermometry of Carbonate Rocks and Phosphatic Fossils
session_title: What is old is new again: Using traditional and novel geochemical proxies to reconstruct past environments and their links to changes in the Phanerozoic biosphere (Part I)
authors: Anstey, Fiona [1], Bergmann, Kristin [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Earth, Atmosph, Planet Sci Dept, Cambridge, MA, USA

(2) Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA; Jackson School of Geosciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
abstract:
The Cambrian Period (~540–485 Mya) was a pivotal moment in Earth’s history marked by a geologically rapid radiation of complex marine organisms. However, seawater temperature estimates are poorly constrained, with the existing record based on low δ 18 O values from marine carbonates suggesting ocean temperatures ≥60°C, significantly higher than the thermal tolerance of most modern marine invertebrates. Because mineral δ 18 O is a function of both precipitation temperature and the δ 18 O composition of the precipitating water, these anomalous values may reflect: (1) preferential diagenetic alteration of Cambrian rocks, linked to their original mineralogy; (2) a lower δ 18 O composition of seawater during the earliest Paleozoic; (3) elevated seawater temperatures; or a combination of these three end-member scenarios. Sparse phosphate δ 18 O measurements of co-occurring apatite microfossils, which are potentially more resistant to diagenesis than carbonate, suggest more moderate temperatures of 20–30°C, but these estimates also depend on assumptions about seawater δ 18 O.

Clumped isotope thermometry offers a means to independently assess the fidelity of the oxygen isotope archive, though the Cambrian remains a critical gap in the global clumped isotope record. To evaluate these uncertainties, we compare existing δ 18 O data to clumped isotope-derived temperatures from carbonate and co-occurring apatite fossils across a range of burial histories from 6 globally distributed localities. Here we use carbonate clumped isotope results to assess diagenetic alteration, the point during burial history at which the target mineral stabilized, and evidence of solid–state reordering of C—O bonds. To evaluate the likelihood of solid state reordering, we independently model anticipated clumped temperature changes from burial history estimates from each sample locality. Results suggest carbonate clumped isotope temperatures agree well with model results of solid–state reordering, and localities with more significant burial exhibit evidence of reordering. Co-occurring apatite is less soluble than calcite or dolomite and clumped measurements of carbonate within the apatite lattice may test end-member scenarios. Preliminary clumped isotope data from Cambrian apatite fossils at Maidiping, China, yield a sea-surface temperature of 30°C (n=5 replicates), 93°C cooler than the average co-occurring carbonate clumped isotope temperature (~123°C) at the same locality. These results suggest apatite may better preserve seawater signals, even in localities with significant burial, highlighting phosphatic fossils as a largely untapped archive for reconstructing paleotemperatures for one of the most significant intervals in Earth’s history..

title: The Shifting Redox Landscape: Connecting Legacy and Emerging Contaminants in a Changing Water Cycle
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes
authors: Kumar, Manish [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Civil and Sustainability Engineering, Tecnológico de Monterrey, Monterrey, Nueva Leon, Mexico; Sustainability Cluster, UPES, Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India
abstract:
Redox conditions are among the most dynamic controls on contaminant behaviour in aquatic environments, yet they are often studied within single contaminant classes rather than across the groundwater–surface water continuum. Drawing on research from contrasting hydrogeochemical settings, this keynote explores how changing redox environments link legacy inorganic contaminants with emerging pollutants. Studies of arsenic and other redox-sensitive elements show that mobility cannot be predicted from concentration alone. Seasonal and spatial shifts in oxidation and reduction alter mineral stability, aqueous speciation and element partitioning. In As–Cr–V–Se systems, pronounced redox decoupling shows that co-occurring elements may respond differently to the same hydrogeochemical transition. Research on mercury further demonstrates how redox state, pH and groundwater evolution combine to create spatially variable contaminant vulnerability.

At groundwater–surface water interfaces, these processes become especially dynamic. Riverbank filtration can attenuate contaminants, but the degree of attenuation depends on residence time, sediment–water interactions, microbial activity and the sequence of biogeochemical conditions encountered along the flow path. In contrast, river–aquifer connectivity can also transport wastewater-derived contaminants and antibiotic-resistant microorganisms from surface water into groundwater. These insights extend to emerging contaminants such as pesticides, pharmaceuticals, PFAS and microplastics, whose fate may be indirectly shaped by redox-driven changes in mineral surfaces, organic matter, microbial processes and contaminant interactions. Their importance grows during floods, droughts, recharge events and other hydrological extremes that rapidly reorganize subsurface redox architecture.

Overall, this work shifts redox potential from a static water-quality parameter to a shifting redox landscape in which hydrology controls redox transitions, redox transitions reorganize biogeochemical processes and these processes govern contaminant mobility, transformation and attenuation. This framework bridges classical hydrogeochemistry with the challenge of multi-contaminant water systems under climate change.

title: From Seawater to Carbonate: Triple Oxygen Isotope Signatures of Extreme Evaporation in the Persian Gulf
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Banerjee, Payal [1], Sharp, Zachary [2], Chafetz, Henry S [3], Bergmann, Kristin [4], Atudorei, Viorel N. [5]
affiliations: (1) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM, USA

(4) Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
(5) Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Univ New Mexico, Earth and Planetary Sciences, Albuquerque, NM, USA
abstract:
The Persian Gulf is one of the world's most evaporative marine environments, providing a natural laboratory for evaluating how extreme evaporation modifies seawater isotope composition and how these signals are transferred to precipitating carbonates. Although elevated δ 18 O values in Persian Gulf carbonates are well documented, the behavior of Δ′ 17 O and its preservation during carbonate precipitation remain poorly constrained. Here, we use paired triple oxygen isotope measurements of Persian Gulf seawater and carbonates from Al Jubayl, Saudi Arabia, to evaluate evaporation and water–carbonate isotope systematics under warm, hypersaline conditions.

Measured Gulf waters from Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain range from approximately +2.09 to +4.55‰ (VSMOW) in δ 18 O and −64 to −24 per meg (VSMOW) in Δ′ 17 O. Their high δ 18 O and low Δ′ 17 O compositions indicate substantial evaporative modification relative to unevaporated ocean water. Carbonates from Al Jubayl also exhibit strongly negative Δ′ 17 O values. Calcites range from -4.10 to +1.66‰ (VPDB) in δ 18 O and −157 to −65 per meg (VSMOW) in Δ′ 17 O, whereas Pleistocene dolomites range from -0.23 to +1.71‰ (VPDB) in δ 18 O and −154 to −54 per meg (VSMOW) in Δ′ 17 O, respectively. The preliminary aragonite measurement yields a δ 18 O value of approximately −0.86‰ (VPDB) and Δ′ 17 O value of approximately −126 per meg.

Comparison of water and carbonate compositions with triple oxygen isotope evaporation and carbonate–water fractionation models provide a framework for quantifying the influence of evaporation on carbonate isotope signatures. The Gulf water data demonstrate strong evaporation-driven departures from ocean-water composition, while the Al Jubayl carbonates indicate that these evaporative conditions can produce distinct triple oxygen isotope signatures during carbonate formation. These results establish the Persian Gulf as a modern calibration system for interpreting Δ′ 17 O in evaporative marine carbonates and provide constraints for reconstructing hydrologic conditions in ancient arid carbonate platforms.

title: Students Know How to Use AI. Do They Know How to Think With It?
session_title: Geoscience Education (Posters)
authors: Ashmore, Richard [1], Avery, Erin [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado Denver, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract:
When I began integrating generative AI into undergraduate geoscience courses, many students already considered themselves experienced AI users. In practice, familiarity often appeared to mean knowing how to ask a chatbot a question and obtain an answer. That raised a more interesting teaching question: what does it mean for a student to actually know how to think with AI?

I have explored that question while teaching a variety of asynchronous, online, introductory geoscience courses. Students work through AI-Guided Scientific Inquiries designed around explanation, follow-up questioning, simulation, verification, uncertainty, and scientific reasoning while remaining responsible for interpretation and conclusions. Pre-, mid-, and post-course surveys and reflections provide de-identified, aggregate evidence that complements my classroom experience. A separate non-AI-integrated course provides a baseline view of entering student attitudes.

Preliminary evaluation has complicated some of my own assumptions. Students generally report becoming more confident using AI for learning, but the more interesting development is how they describe that confidence. Over time, students increasingly report checking claims against course materials, supplying scientific context, asking follow-up questions, identifying unsupported assumptions, correcting errors, recognizing uncertainty, and deciding when an AI response should not be trusted.

At the same time, increased capability does not necessarily produce increased enthusiasm. Some students remain concerned about dependence, employment, environmental impacts, academic integrity, or weakened independent thinking. Skeptical students can nevertheless become quite deliberate about questioning, constraining, and evaluating AI.

Self-reported confidence at the beginning of a course cannot establish actual competence or overconfidence. The longitudinal evidence does suggest, however, that familiarity and well-calibrated confidence are not necessarily the same thing.

My experience suggests that AI acceptance is the wrong educational objective. A more useful goal for geoscience may be critical AI fluency: knowing when AI helps, when it needs to be challenged, when it should be rejected, and why the student must remain intellectually responsible for the science.

title: The Great Unconformity in the Central Virginia Blue Ridge: Insights into Neoproterozoic Paleogeography and Paleoclimate
session_title: From Rodinia to Gondwana: Supercontinent Assembly, Breakup, and Earth System Change
authors: Cox, Mara A. [1], Bailey, Christopher M. [2]
affiliations: (1) The College of William and Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia,
(2) William & Mary, Williamsburg, VA,
abstract:
The Great Unconformity is a globally occurring erosional contact that typically separates Mesoproterozoic basement rocks from overlying Phanerozoic cover sequences. In central Virginia, this contact separates the 1.0–1.2 Ga granitic Grenville Basement Complex from the overlying Neoproterozoic Swift Run and Catoctin formations. The significance of this contact is poorly understood. In this study, we used field observations, mapping, and petrographic analysis to investigate a section of the unconformity in the Sherando 7.5′ Quadrangle within the Blue Ridge geologic province of Virginia. Field mapping at a 1:5000 scale led to revisions to the 1977 geologic map produced by Mervin J. Bartholomew for his publication of Geology of the Greenfield and Sherando Quadrangles, Virginia , published as Virginia Division of Mineral Resources Publication 4. These changes include revising the location and geometry of the Great Unconformity and identifying locations where Catoctin greenstone directly overlies the Grenville Basement Complex. Geologic mapping, cross sections, and sample analysis demonstrated that rifting associated with the breakup of Rodinia in this portion of Laurentia and the deposition of Swift Run sediments were coeval processes. Interfingering of the Swift Run and Catoctin formations was observed petrographically, at the outcrop scale, and through geologic mapping. Field work also resulted in the extension of five previously mapped SE-NW trending faults: the Devils Knob, Pond Hollow, Pauls Creek, Grassy Ridge, and Little Stony Creek faults.

Petrographic analysis was done on samples of granitic gneiss taken from <1 m., 5 m., and 50 m. stratigraphically below the unconformity. This revealed a progressive increase in mineral alteration moving towards the unconformity, with the least altered sample originally located 50 m. below the unconformity and the most altered sample originally located <1 m below the contact. This alteration is characterized by the breakdown of feldspar grains and the development of a fine-grained matrix enriched in sericite, chlorite, and epidote. These observations are consistent with the development of a paleoweathering profile that indicates warm and humid climate conditions may have occurred in this region of Laurentia following exhumation of the Grenville Basement Complex and prior to deposition of the overlying cover sequence. These conditions should be considered when evaluating Ediacaran paleoclimate conditions, including the proposed Gaskiers glacial event.

title: Digital Segmentation and Skeletal Reconstruction of the Basal Aetosaur Stenomyti Using synchrotron computed tomography data

abstract: Aetosaurs are a clade of heavily armored, medium- to large-sized omnivorous or herbivorous pseudosuchian archosaurs that occupied terrestrial ecosystems during the Late Triassic (~231– 201 Ma). Several aetosaur taxa have been described in rigorous detail, while the species Stenomyti huangae remains comparatively understudied. Stenomyti huangae is known from three partial skeletons, the holotype (DMNH 60708) and referred specimens (DMNH 61392 and DMNH 34565), containing cranial and postcranial elements from the ‘red siltstone member’ of the uppermost Late Triassic Chugwater Group in the Eagle Basin of Colorado, United States. Many aspects of its osteology are difficult to examine using traditional preparation techniques due to overlapping elements of the carapace and a dense rock matrix. This study utilizes high-resolution synchrotron computed tomography (CT) data of the holotype specimen DMNH 60708 to digitally segment and reconstruct the skeleton of Stenomyti. The CT datasets were imported into the software Dragonfly, where individual skeletal elements were segmented and isolated from both the rock matrix and adjacent bones. These segmented elements were then used to generate 3D models that allow detailed examination of anatomical features previously inaccessible on the exterior of DMNH 60708. The resulting reconstructions allow visualization and description of previously unknown elements (e.g., cervical vertebrae) along with additional anatomical details of previously described elements that were otherwise obscured by the matrix. The use of CT-based segmentation offers significant advantages over traditional preparation by preserving specimen integrity while allowing repeated, non-destructive examination of internal and external structures. These observations can provide valuable comparisons with aetosaurs and other pseudosuchians that may further clarify the relationships of the clade and their role in Late Triassic ecosystems.

abstract: Natural-abundance nitrogen isotope analyses (δ15N) are widely used in marine ecosystem research, with a Web of Science search identifying >6,000 studies since 1978. These studies collectively represent an extensive yet largely underutilized resource for investigating marine food web dynamics at global scales. Here, we introduce the Metazoan Stable Isotope Database for the Global Ocean (mSIDGO), a curated compilation of previously published, ecologically relevant δ15N and carbon isotope (δ13C) data from the open ocean, continental shelf, and estuary ecosystems. The dataset includes marine organisms spanning a range of trophic levels—from macroalgae, particulate nitrogen, and mesozooplankton to fish, mollusks, and marine mammals. The inclusion of low-trophic-level organisms allows for assessment of regional-scale variability in nutrient cycling (i.e., isotopic baseline), while higher trophic-level data support studies on trophic ecology, niche differentiation, and animal movements. The database (version 1) currently contains >13,000 entries, consisting of measurements of individual organisms and aggregate stable isotope measurements from 281 references, largely between 1981 and 2021 (40 years). Entries span 18 phyla and clades, of which 15 are eukaryotic animals (Annelida, Arthropoda, Brachiopoda, Bryozoa, Chaetognatha, Chordata, Cnidaria, Ctenophora, Echinodermata, Mollusca, Nematoda, Nemertea, Porifera, Priapulida, Rotifera) and three are clades of eukaryotic algae (Chlorophyta, Ochrophyta, and Rhodophyta). The dataset is hosted in an open-access repository and will be expanded through community contributions. We envision that applications of mSIDGO will include comparing food web structure across ecosystems and time periods, interpreting isotopic signals in the context of regional nutrient regimes, and identifying trophic level changes over recent decades. Thus, the mSIDGO database will be a useful resource for addressing large-scale ecological questions, for facilitating assessments of ecosystem health, and for predicting how human impacts affect global patterns in marine food webs.

abstract: The middle Eocene Climatic Optimum (MECO) was a hyperthermal event that took place from approximately 40 to 40.5 Ma and lasted for about 500,000 years. It resulted in a 3° to 4° C increase of oceanic surface and deep-water temperatures, and a rise of about 5° to 9° C of continental temperatures during peak MECO, thus interrupting the Cenozoic cooling trend. The objective of the Uinta Basin Project is to generate a multi-faceted model that will correlate patterns of biotic change bracketing the MECO by examining shifts in mammalian community structure prior to, during, and following the hyperthermal. The fossil-rich middle Eocene strata in the Uinta Basin in Utah provide an ideal laboratory because these rocks temporally encompass the MECO. Paleontologists have long recognized significant faunal turnover seemingly related to environmental changes that took place during deposition of the Uinta and Duchesne River Formations, the stratotypes for the Uintan and Duchesnean NALMAs, respectively. For example, the transition from pond turtles to tortoises, and a significant reduction in diversity of arboreal mammalian taxa including primates. However, a high-resolution framework to investigate these faunal changes and to correlate them to the MECO was lacking. To investigate the MECO, 1,635 m of section were measured and sampled from the base of the Uinta Formation to the base of the Lapoint Member of the Duchesne River Formation and 19 stratigraphic marker beds were mapped. Our analyses included U-Pb zircon dating, paleomagnetostratigraphic sampling, carbon and oxygen isotopes, X-ray fluorescence, and an intensive stratigraphically controlled fossil collection program. Isotopic evidence reveals a gradual increase in d 18 O values upsection in the Uinta Formation followed by an abrupt increase in d 18 O at the boundary between the Uinta and Duchesne River formations. These isotopic values correlate to an approximately 5° C temperature increase. On average, temperatures fall throughout the deposition of the Duchesne River Formation. However, this decrease in temperature is marked by large swings in temperature and episodes of increased precipitation and grain size within the rock. These results are preliminary and the investigation is ongoing. Ultimately, it is anticipated that our deep-time model will provide crucial information for scientists investigating the climate-mediated dispersal and invasion events that are certain to occur if our modern world continues to experience rapid warming.

title: A Microscopic View of Global Events: Iron Sequestration during Silurian Oceanographic Disturbances Revealed by Mineral Mapping
session_title: Joint SGD-SEPM-IAS Session: Advances in Sedimentology (Posters)
authors: Sullivan, Nicholas B. [1]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, Penn State, State College, PA, USA
abstract:
The Silurian Clinton Ironstones of central New York are a distinct, time-specific facies widely interpreted as a proxy for ancient marine anoxia and sea-level variability. However, traditional macroscopic classifications of these deposits as simple hematite-chamosite facies obscure a complex diagenetic landscape, reflecting the localized processes that controlled iron sequestration. To resolve this, we utilized high-resolution Scanning Electron Microscopy-Automated Mineralogy (SEM-AM) to quantify modal mineralogy, micro-textures, and mineral-specific grain size across a proximal-to-distal transect of the Appalachian Foreland Basin.

Analysis of four ironstone horizons from the Clinton Group type area, alongside a laterally equivalent phosphatic lag, reveals a compositional spectrum. Proximal, high-energy shoals (Westmoreland) are hematite-dominated (>59%), recording aggressive physical ravinement and oxic exhumation. Conversely, lower-energy facies (Wolcott Furnace) preserve un-winnowed berthierine matrices (8.5%) driven by localized microbial decay of peloids. Critically, mid-ramp and starved hardground environments sequestered massive portions of the upwelled iron budget into early-burial carbonate sinks, yielding ironstones dominated by carbonates (10–21% in Furnaceville and 46–48% in Basal Dawes, respectively).

Micro-textural mapping captures shifting fluid fronts recorded by concentric laminae of apatite, chamosite, hematite, and other early authigenic minerals. We interpret these zoned grains as the physical record of a fluctuating pycnocline operating during prolonged sequence-boundary sediment starvation. Moving basinward, the transition to a euxinic, pyrite-apatite dominated trough confirms a shared, basin-wide genetic mechanism. These SEM-AM maps demonstrate that ironstones and phosphatic lags are biogeochemically coupled products of an oscillating redox boundary, contextualizing ironstones as a diagenetic continuum rather than a monolithic facies.

title: Investigating the Origin of Coexisting Silica-undersaturated and Silica-oversaturated Rocks in the Red Hill Complex, NH
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Posters)
authors: Pope, Mollie [1], Haemmerli, Johannes [2], Schrader, Christian M. [3], Wells, Kolby C. [4]
affiliations: (1) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
(2) School of the Environment, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, State University of New York - Potsdam, Potsdam, NY, USA
(4) Earth and Environmental Sciences, State University of New York - Potsdam, Potsdam, NY, USA
abstract:
The occurrence of cogenetic silica-undersaturated and silica-oversaturated rocks within a single alkaline-silicate igneous system remains a longstanding petrologic problem. A thermal divide separating feldspathoid-normative and quartz-normative melts in silicate phase space should inhibit the derivation of both compositions from a single parental melt through simple fractional crystallization. Yet, numerous alkaline-silicate complexes show this exact petrologic paradox. Processes including crustal assimilation, volatile addition, magma recharge, and silicate liquid immiscibility have been invoked to explain these diverse compositional occurrences within an intrusive suite, but their relative importance and applicability across alkaline systems remain unclear.

The early Jurassic Red Hill Complex in central New Hampshire is one of the oldest intrusions in the White Mountain Magma Series (WMMS), the second largest igneous province in eastern North America. Red Hill is one of two silica-undersaturated bearing intrusions within the province. The complex consists of silica-saturated to silica-oversaturated syenites, a fine-grained granite, and a single, volumetrically dominant zone of silica-undersaturated nepheline sodalite syenite. Combined new and historic whole rock major element data define compositions ranging from ~54 to 76 wt. % SiO 2 and ~15 to 9 wt. % total alkalis across the six lithologic units of Red Hill. Recent fieldwork sampled each of these lithologies, as well as 1- to 12-cm mafic enclaves that may represent parental melt.

The exceptional preservation of both silica-undersaturated and silica-oversaturated rocks at Red Hill provides a natural laboratory to study the petrologic evolution of alkaline-silicate systems. To test whether this compositional diversity reflects crustal assimilation, distinct magma sources, or differentiation from a common parental melt, each lithology is characterized at both the whole rock and mineral-scales. Whole rock trace element compositions, together with Sm-Nd, Lu-Hf and Rb-Sr isotope tracers, will be used to evaluate genetic relationships among lithologies, identify potential source heterogeneity, and assess the extent of crustal contamination. Mineral-scale chemical and isotopic analyses will further refine the timing and extent of these key processes. Combined with analyses of mafic enclaves, these data will provide new insights on the petrogenesis of the Red Hill Complex and its evolution within the broader context of the WMMS.

title: Characterizing the Morphometry of Elliptical Craters on the Saturnian Satellites
session_title: Friends of Hoth, Rogue Moons: Icy Ocean Worlds
authors: Ferguson, Sierra Nichole [1], Denton, Adeene [2], Rhoden, Alyssa [3], Fuhrman, Bethany E S [4]
affiliations: (1) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO,
(2) Southwest Research Institute, Boulder, CO, USA; NASA Postdoctoral Program, USA

abstract: Elliptical craters have been observed on many of the mid-sized Saturnian satellites (Mimas, Tethys, Dione, and Rhea). These craters are thought to have formed as a result of an oblique impact onto the surface. On terrestrial bodies, this particular morphology has been used as a means to examine the impact angle and direction of the impacting material that created the crater. While elliptical craters have already been mapped on several Saturnian satellites, they have yet to have their detailed morphometry (i.e., crater depth/diameter, d/D) fully characterized. Here we utilized high resolution Cassini ISS NAC imagery within the Ames Stereo Pipeline to generate regional scale DEMs of Mimas, Tethys, Dione, and Rhea across the portions of the surfaces that have documented elliptical craters. We utilize 6 topographic profiles across each elliptical crater (spaced in 60° increments) to measure the crater height, which we define as the maximum rim height in that profile, and the crater depth, defined at the lowest point of the crater floor. We present initial results from this survey of elliptical craters on Dione and Mimas. Our preliminary work on Dione has shown that these craters do have shallower d/D values than the more “classical” crater morphologies such as circular craters. In addition, we have characterized the nearby circular craters d/D values to provide a localized value for craters to compare against. As our dataset expands, we anticipate being able to compare the elliptical crater d/D values against their ellipticities, which may provide additional insights into the energy and momentum transfers that occur during the initial crater formation.

title: The Geologic Oracle: A deck for the geo-curious
session_title: Diversifying Geoscience Education Across the Academic Playing Field: Using Creative Methods to Foster the Current and Next Generations of Geoscience Professionals (Posters)
authors: Richter, Sadie Mae [1]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geography and Geosciences, University of Vermont, Burlington, Vermont, USA
abstract:
The Geologic Oracle Deck embraces UNuniformitarianism: the past is the key to the present. Similar to tarot cards, oracle decks offer opportunities for introspection and self-reflection. Oracle decks often provide uplifting guidance—something the weathered geologist may need in this day and age. Each Geologic Oracle Deck “reading” pairs a geologic process with a familiar life experience, and makes geologic concepts relatable and accessible to audiences unfamiliar with the discipline.

Through an oracle reading with this original deck, the audience can explore a geologic system in a fun, creative way. Each card contains an educational explanation of the geologic occurrence and then relates it to personal experiences. For example, the Normal Fault card light-heartedly indicates tension in one’s life. This builds a memorable connection between the audience and their card, transforming what might otherwise be a structural geology term into relatable, understandable themes. With a little creativity, disciplinary vocabulary can become fun and meaningful, potentially engaging students who have not identified with traditional classroom learning.

The Geologic Oracle is not just for the geo-curious! This deck spans geologic disciplines and has something for every level of geologist seeking their inner equilibrium.

title: What I Learned Teaching Geoscience With AI
session_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Other AI-Assistants in Geosciences - Today and in the Near Future
authors: Ashmore, Richard [1], Avery, Erin [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography and Environmental Sciences, University of Colorado Denver, Denver, Colorado, USA
(2) Denver, Colorado, USA
abstract:
Putting generative AI into a geoscience course is easy. Designing a course in which AI contributes without taking over the intellectual work is considerably harder.

Teaching a variety of asynchronous, online, introductory geoscience courses, I have developed AI-Guided Scientific Inquiries that treat generative AI as a bounded learning and thought partner rather than an answer generator or authority. The experience has changed how I think about AI-supported geoscience education.

Several practical lessons have emerged. Giving students access to AI is not the same as teaching them to use it well. Better prompting is useful, but it is not the educational goal. Students need practice questioning responses, requesting evidence, correcting errors, recognizing unsupported assumptions, working through uncertainty, and deciding when another source should remain authoritative. AI can also be too helpful: immediate, polished explanations can remove productive struggle unless an activity deliberately returns scientific reasoning to the student.

Geoscience provides particularly useful conditions for this approach. Students can use AI to explore interacting variables, compare competing explanations, test scenarios, examine cascading Earth-system effects, and reconsider an initial interpretation while still remaining responsible for evidence and conclusions.

The design has also revealed important friction. AI can become verbose, overconfident, agreeable, or disconnected from assignment context. Students may experience repeated documentation as burdensome even when they value the underlying inquiry. Some resist required AI use for academic, environmental, economic, or philosophical reasons. Those reactions do not necessarily indicate failure. A skeptical student who learns to question, verify, constrain, and reject AI may be demonstrating exactly the kind of judgment the course is intended to develop.

My central lesson is that successful AI integration is not about maximizing AI use. It is about designing the relationship between student, instructor, scientific evidence, and AI so that the technology can participate without becoming the authority. The most important question is not what AI can do for a geoscience student, but what intellectual work the student must continue to do.

abstract:
Marine basins provide regional controls on the expression of global perturbations to the ocean-atmosphere system. While several examples are well established in the literature for Mesozoic oceanic anoxic events, details of similar Paleozoic events are still emerging. In the Upper Ordovician the Guttenberg and Hirnantian events have received the most attention. Between the two, the little-known Elkhorn event is particularly insightful for illuminating the processes controlling formation of critical mineral-enriched phosphorites and ironstones.

A new regional Upper Ordovician chronostratigraphic interpretation is derived from sequence stratigraphic analysis that incorporates extensive bio- and chemostratigraphic data sets and facies mapping. The starting point was revision of the Cincinnati reference area where strata of the Elkhorn event cap the succession. This work required refining the definitions of regional stage boundaries based on biostratigraphic criteria. It included chitinozoan studies that generated new biozonation, complementing previous conodont and graptolite work. Building on this foundation, carbonate carbon isotope chemostratigraphy provided increased chronostratigraphic resolution and spatial coverage. This integrated approach was expanded across the U.S. midcontinent to provide a robust regional time-rock framework within which the temporal and spatial extent of facies, including critical mineral-enriched phosphorites and ironstones, could be examined.

The regional analysis reveals that the Elkhorn biogeochemical event is associated with a carbon cycle record featuring two paired positive and negative excursions. The positive excursions are linked with carbonate deposition and capped by widespread paleokarst surfaces. By contrast the negative excursions are associated with transgressive phosphorites, black shales, and ironstones. Mineralization is most extensive in the second set of excursions, including basin center development of the Graf phosphorite (15 m-thick, phosphate and black shale with TOC 20%) and basin margin ironstones mapped over 700 km. These patterns provide a textbook example of a marine chemocline mineral system driven by perturbations to the Late Ordovician ocean-atmosphere system.

title: Post-2022 Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon Fire Water Quality Response; Amounts, Trends, and Impacts

authors: Lindline, Jennifer [1], Takacs, Kiara [2], Foucher, Marine [3], Chadborn, Daniel [4]
affiliations: (1) Natural Resources Management Department, New Mexico Highlands University, Las Vegas, New Mexico, USA
(2) Water Management Section, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA

(4) Psychology Department, New Mexico Highlands University, Las Vegas, NM,
abstract: Wildfire disturbances can have short- and long-term impacts on the health of a watershed. The loss of vegetation, abundance of charred materials, and destabilization of hillsides can increase stream sedimentation and degrade water quality. The 2022 Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon (HP/CC) Fire, the largest wildfire in New Mexico’s history (>340,000 acres), impacted the Gallinas Watershed – the source water for the City of Las Vegas’s drinking water supply, as well as a designated water resource for high quality cold water aquatic life, irrigation, livestock watering, and wildlife habitat (NMAC 20.6.4.215). This study assessed the HP/CC's bearing on water quality using data from USGS real time surface water gaging station 08380500 (Gallinas Creek at Montezuma). Amounts and trends in daily average values for dissolved oxygen, pH, specific conductance, temperature, and turbidity were assessed relative to discharge from September 01, 2022-August 31, 2026, to understand the fire’s impact on potable supplies and ecosystem services. Dissolved oxygen, pH, and specific conductance remained within the normal ranges for state water quality standards throughout the post-fire period. Daily average temperature values exceeded the NMAC 20°C threshold only 11 of 722 days of record (<2%) from 2022-2025 but have routinely surpassed the 20°C threshold during Summer 2026. Turbidity values ranged from negligible to >3500 NTU. More than 25% of the days of record exceeded 20 NTU, the City of Las Vegas’ current water treatment plant limit and more than 50% exceeded the high quality cold water 10 NTU tolerance (NMAC 20.6.4.900). The average yearly turbidity values decreased from Y1 to Y3 with the yearly averages dropping from 61.80 (SD = 153.85) to 24.84 (SD = 66.45). A one-way ANOVA was performed to examine the differences in average turbidity across the first three post-HP/CC years. Results showed that the average yearly data differences were statistically significant across time, F (2, 710) = 5.941, p =.003. We interpret the decreased turbidity averages and narrowed fluctuations in high and low turbidity values as indicating that the post-fire turbidity and sediment loads are attenuating. Persistent temperature exceedances in Summer 2026 reflected extreme and prolonged heat and drought conditions.

title: A tale of two streams: How fair they have aged
session_title: Novel tectonic geomorphology measures of base level, topography, crustal deformation, erosion, and hazards from subduction zones to decaying orogens
authors: Perry, T W [1]
affiliations: (1) none, Scottsdale, AZ,
abstract: The stream longitudinal profile may be conceptualized as a simple proportional response system where stream-channel erosion processes are propagated upstream. Time-dependent development of the longitudinal profile may be simulated in a finite-difference model. The nodal-profile response can be expressed in a parametric form as q·s = r · (v k -1 -1), with q as dimensionless flow, s as slope, r as dimensionless response, and v k as a rock-unit proportional response coefficient for erosion. Intrinsic factors for each unit, such as rock resilience (or 1 - v k ) resisting erosion, are held universally constant within the model; extrinsic factors such as channel flow, q, or associated regional base-level adjustments, can be synchronistically varied. Two streams in the Upper Colorado basin were examined. 1) A 60 km reach of the Dolores R. above the Colorado was modeled for changes consequent to upstream diversion and channel abandonment of Gunnison R. at about 775 ka. The modeled post-abandonment profile was investigated for aspects of profile recovery, areas of terrace formation along regions of reduced channel slope, and consequent impacts from climatically induced variability on flow and rate of base-level change. Convergence on the present-day profile sufficiently revealed abandonment impacts to character of the profile given a regionally consistent rate of base-level change at the confluence with the Colorado River. 2) An 80 km segment of the San Juan – Animas system was simulated from 1375 ka to examine the consequence of stream erosion through several rock units, each unit having a model-associated intrinsic resilience (or hardness). Results show the surprising response of the Animas cutting through more resilient units into softer units below. This erosion-response interaction is reflected in the present-day aspect of the profile. These models for the Dolores and San Juan – Animas, seem to indicate the erosion history and resulting present-day aspect of the longitudinal profile is strongly determined.

title: Geologic Structure of the Layered Sulfate unit, Gale crater, Mars
session_title: The G. K. Gilbert Award Session Honoring Dr. Ken Edgett: Geological Insights Through Imaging of Our Solar System Worlds
authors: Roberts, Amelie Louise [1], Lewis, Kevin [2], Davis, Joel M [3], Turner, Madison [4], Khan, Sabrina Yasmeen [5]
affiliations: (1) Earth & Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, Maryland, USA
(2) Johns Hopkins University, Earth and Planetary Sciences, Baltimore, MD,
(3) Earth Science & Engineering, Imperial, London, United Kingdom
(4) University of Chicago, Lakewood, CO,
(5) Earth & Planetary Sciences, Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, Maryland, USA
abstract:
Aeolis Mons is a ~5.5 km-tall mound of layered sedimentary rock at the centre of Gale crater. Since August 2022 (sol 3575), the Curiosity rover has been exploring the orbitally defined Layered Sulfate unit (LSu) within Aeolis Mons, which comprises distinct, planar-parallel, dark- and light-toned layers visible from orbit. Here, we describe the bedding geometries of these exposed layers from orbit and along the traverse to characterise the geologic structure of the LSu and provide implications for the depositional history of the mound.

From orbit, we mapped 1,004 layers traceable for >200 m in High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) images covering the rover traverse. We calculated bedding orientations by fitting best-fit planes to layer traces from HiRISE stereo-derived digital terrain models, yielding an average regional azimuth/dip of 356°/2.9°. Stereo images from Curiosity revealed gradational boundaries and irregular, discontinuous contacts that may have complicated orbital layer identification. From rover-derived images, we made 72 measurements of layer contacts traceable for >200 m. The base of the LSu has an average azimuth/dip of 324°/2.2°, whereas higher in the stratigraphy and at the rover's current location, the LSu has an average azimuth/dip of 338°/4.5°. The longest traceable contact was a distinct, sharp, irregular erosional surface that outcrops across ~3 km laterally in the upper LSu (Davis et al., 2026, LPSC), with an azimuth/dip of 349°/3.2°.

The 2–5° northwest dip of the LSu is consistent with underlying Mount Sharp units (e.g. Turner et al., 2023, JGR Planets). As the LSu has so far been interpreted as aeolian (e.g., Roberts et al., 2026, JGR Planets), the apparent increase in dip at the current rover location may represent climbing dunes and interdunes rather than the original depositional surface. The distinct, sharp, irregular erosional surface has been proposed to represent a period of regional deflation (Davis et al., 2026, LPSC) and may therefore represent the dip of the depositional surface of the unit. Accounting for the regional dip has implications for the total stratigraphic thickness traversed by the rover, as the topographic slope and the dip of the layers are closely aligned. Over the ~344 meters of elevation Curiosity has climbed within the layered sulfate unit, we estimate that it has ascended through ~153 meters of stratigraphy.

title: The Mineral within the Protein: Predicting Structural and Functional Properties of Proteins from Mineralogical Scaffolds
session_title: New Advances in Geomicrobiology
authors: Terra, Rowan R. [1], Gulliver, Djuna [2], Trun, Nancy [3]
affiliations: (1) Duquesne University and the National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL-PGH), Pittsburgh, PA,
(2) NETL-DOE, Pittsburgh, PA,
(3) Duquesne University, Biological sciences, Pittsburgh, PA,
abstract:
Metals within protein active sites can be compared, in geometric terms, to how those same metals are coordinated within a mineral. Ligands around the metal in a protein often reproduce the coordination found in a natural mineral phase. Our previous work on microbial recovery of critical minerals, which pairs computational genomics with an Eh-pH framework built on Pourbaix and Baas Becking relations, led us to ask whether that mineral can serve as a template to predict a protein’s binding affinity, selectivity, and function.

Terrahedral extracts a metal’s donor shell, superimposes it on real mineral coordinates by Kabsch alignment, and scores the geometric strain against the closest mineral. So far, we have applied it across ten metals (Ca, V, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Mo, W) and the lanthanides, 50+ metalloprotein superfamilies, and 11,832 metal sites, spanning six main roles: electron transfer, hydrolytic and Lewis-acid chemistry, redox and oxygen catalysis, calcium signaling, lanthanide binding, and structural support. A consistent pattern emerged where (1) rigid, catalytically inert sites match their mineral analogs closely, while (2) catalytic and selective sites deviate from them. Because the size and direction of that deviation can track how the metal is used, the strain itself carries information about a site’s function.

We demonstrate the usefulness of this alignment through three examples. In rare-earth systems, we track binding affinity across natural proteins and synthetic peptides, including lanmodulin, whose sites bind lanthanides at picomolar affinity. In manganese systems, we explore how early research into photosystem II could have anticipated its Mn 4 CaO 5 cluster from a mineral template. In acireductone dioxygenase, one cupin scaffold cleaves a different carbon-carbon bond depending on whether it holds iron or nickel, cobalt, or manganese, and the closest-mineral match shifts with the metal, showing that metal identity, not the fold, establishes the reaction.

Coordination geometry and the Eh-pH framework together give a route to predict which metals a protein binds, how tightly, and under what conditions, treating a protein metal site as a mineral. These predictions can support selective metal recovery and catalysis, under which designing proteins and peptides to match chosen geometric strain or congruence to a mineral may increase metal specificity and reaction efficiency.

abstract: We report progress on an integrative study of the Crevasse Canyon Formation in the Acoma Basin of west-central New Mexico, offering new insights into a critical gap in the North American terrestrial record. During the middle to Late Cretaceous, the diversification of flowering plants (angiosperms) led to changes in habitat structure and boosted terrestrial biodiversity alongside major faunal turnovers. However, key time intervals and geographic regions remain poorly understood; in North America, the Coniacian–Santonian terrestrial record is remarkably sparse. The Crevasse Canyon Formation records terrestrial environments increasingly inland of the prograding shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway, with age constraints based on palynology and U–Pb zircon geochronology in the study area ranging from the Coniacian–early Campanian (~90–80 Ma). The depositional system is characterized by isolated, cross-stratified channel sandstones encased in floodplain strata, alongside laterally extensive sandstone bodies. Plant fossils, including pollen, foliage, permineralized woods, flowers, and fruits/seeds, have been collected from a variety of fluvial facies representing overbank and lacustrine deposition along a meandering river system. Preliminary floral analyses demonstrate the presence of both conifer and angiosperm trees, including Cupressinoxylon , Paraphyllanthoxylon , and other coniferous and hamamelid-type woods. Fossil foliage of woody, herbaceous, and aquatic angiosperms is common, including platanoid and lauralean-type leaves as well as other simple-leaved dicots and monocots. Conifers are less abundant than angiosperms at most sample sites; they include the branches and cones of a redwood, as well as foliage of the morphogenera Geinitzia and Brachyphyllum . Cycads are rare, and while ferns are not commonly recovered as leaf macrofossils, their spores are often prevalent in palynological samples. Although fossil vertebrate material is scarce, fragmentary occurrences provide preliminary insights into the local fauna. Together with refined sedimentological interpretations and age model, this work is providing a new window into ecosystems of the southern Western Interior during a transformative but poorly documented phase of terrestrial evolution.

title: Resolving Conflicting Geologic and Thermochronologic Datasets by Testing Post-Exhumation Thermal Perturbations with Field Data: High-Temperature Fluid Flow and it's Effects in the Fra Cristobal Range of South-Central New Mexico
session_title: Cenozoic History of the Southern Rocky Mountains: Transtended, Intruded and Deeply Incised Laramide Geology, Celebrating 50 years of New Data and Improved Understanding
authors: Gallant, Kyle K. [1], Prush, Veronica B. [2], Kelley, Shari A. [3]
affiliations: (1) Earth and Environmental Science Department, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA; New Mexico Bureau of Geology, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM, USA

abstract:
Overprinting tectonic fabrics with cryptic kinematic histories are common in the Rocky Mountain region. The southern Rocky Mountains, primarily formed by the Laramide orogeny, extend into central New Mexico and are dissected by the through-going Oligo-Miocene-aged Rio Grande rift. Detailed geologic mapping, outcrop observations, and stratigraphic constraints in the Fra Cristobal Range of south-central New Mexico demonstrate Laramide-related subaerial exposure of basement rock at ~40 Ma, in conflict with previously published thermochronologic dates that suggest cooling to surface temperatures between 10-15 Ma (e.g., Gavel et al., 2021). Our ongoing mapping efforts in the Fra Cristobal Range have provided more insight a previously recognized but little studied fossilized geothermal system (e.g., Van Allen et al., 1984) collocated with the easternmost boundary fault separating the Fra Cristobal Range from the adjacent Engle-Palomas basin. By combining structural and stratigraphic constraints with thermochronologic datasets in the context of ‘thermal anomaly-focused’ mapping efforts, we can rectify Laramide-related tectonic fabrics with Rio Grande rift-related thermochronologic dates to improve our understanding of the tectonic and thermal history recorded in this region of south-central New Mexico.

By reinterpreting recent thermochronology with updated mapping efforts, we demonstrate how field studies may be targeted to resolve complex thermal histories that are not directly related to large-scale, exhumation-related tectonic processes. The southern Rocky Mountains in central New Mexico may be an ideal locale to further explore these complex processes.

title: New Structural Analysis of Moscow Landing, Sumter County, Alabama: Integrating Digital Outcrop Models and Vintage Data to Refine the Multi-Phase Faulting caused by the Chicxulub Impact
session_title: Advancing Geologic Analysis with Digital Outcrops and Close-Range Remote Sensing Data
authors: Hawkins, William Brown [1]
affiliations: (1) PIX4D, Denver, CO, USA
abstract:
Moscow Landing, in West Alabama, is an exceptional outcrop for studying regional deformation associated with the K-Pg boundary and the Chicxulub impact. While paleontological and stratigraphic interpretations of the site have changed significantly during the past 125 years, the structural interpretation remains constant, with normal faults and associated low-amplitude folds. The 1.5-km-long outcrop includes K-Pg tsunamite bodies (Clayton Sand) and extensive exposures of the Upper Cretaceous (Prairie Bluff Chalk) and earliest Paleocene stratigraphy (Clayton and Porters Creek Formations).

Drone-based and terrestrial imagery collected between 2017 and 2025 was used to make high-resolution digital outcrop models. Comparisons of the new outcrop models and interpretations with published and archived photographs of the site reveal changes in fault geometry and stratigraphy over the past 100 years of riverbank erosion.

Previous interpretations divided the normal faults into three groups along Moscow Landing: faults that cut the Cretaceous and are truncated by the K-Pg boundary; faults that cut the Cretaceous and terminate within the Clayton Sand; and faults that cut the entire section.

This analysis identifies an inverted graben that formed after the deposition of the Clayton Sand but is truncated by the K-Pg boundary. Drawings and photographs from the late 1800s to the present day clearly show the inverted graben. One bounding fault contains over six meters of smeared Clayton Sand graben fill, which previous studies interpreted as an injectite. The Prairie Bluff Chalk within the graben is sheared and folded by the inversion. Although there is little expectation of encountering reverse faults in the Gulf Coastal Plain, the Livingston Fault Zone, which lies directly to the northeast of Moscow Landing, is a regional reverse fault zone.

Deformation at Moscow Landing now includes the following events:

· Chicxulub Impact causes shelf collapse, forming grabens in the Prairie Bluff Chalk that fill with Clayton Sand.

· Compressional event that caused inversion of some earlier impact-related normal faults.

· The K-Pg boundary truncates all the initial impact-related structures.

· The lower Clayton Formation is folded in the earliest Danian.

· Normal faulting cuts the entire Cretaceous and Paleocene section.

title: Using Paleoatmospheric CO₂ to Constrain the Age and Paleoclimate of Late Pleistocene Amazonian Fossil Flora
session_title: Climate, Ocean and Environmental Changes Through Earth History: From Marine and Terrestrial Proxies to Model Assessments (Posters)
authors: Baxendell, Nivale E. [1], Lamb, Rhea [2], Stiles, Elena [3], Tejada, Julia [4]
affiliations: (1) Geosciences, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA, ; Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(2) La Cañada Highschool, La Cañada Flintridge, CA, USA
(3) Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
(4) Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
abstract:
Little is known about how Amazonian vegetation responded to glacial–interglacial climate cycles. Understanding these responses is critical for predicting the future effects of climate change, as the Amazon is a global carbon sink and important regional climate regulator. However, few paleobotanical records provide direct insight into these changes. Here, we investigate a newly discovered late Pleistocene plant fossil deposit along the Madre de Dios River in the western Peruvian Amazon. Preliminary age estimates place these fossils between 100–150 ka, an interval spanning the transition between glacial and interglacial periods. This age uncertainty makes it difficult to determine the climatic conditions under which the flora was deposited. Because atmospheric CO₂ concentrations differed markedly between glacial and interglacial periods, reconstructing paleoatmospheric CO₂ can provide an independent constraint on the age and climatic setting of fossil assemblages. We therefore use a leaf gas-exchange model that combines fossil leaf carbon isotope data with stomatal morphological traits to estimate atmospheric CO₂ concentrations and evaluate whether the assemblage is more consistent with glacial or interglacial conditions.

We analyzed approximately 200 fossil leaf cuticles from our fossil site. Each cuticle was divided for bulk organic carbon isotope analysis using elemental analyzer–isotope ratio mass spectrometry and for stomatal anatomical measurements using epifluorescence microscopy. Stomatal density, pore length, and guard cell dimensions were combined with carbon isotope data in the mechanistic leaf gas-exchange model of Franks et al. (2014) to reconstruct paleoatmospheric CO₂. Preliminary reconstructions yield atmospheric CO₂ concentrations averaging approximately 480 ppm, substantially higher than the 180–280 ppm expected during the late Pleistocene. This discrepancy suggests that model parameters developed primarily from modern temperate plant taxa may not adequately capture the gas-exchange physiology of tropical rainforest species. Ongoing taxonomic identification of fossil morphotypes will enable assignment of appropriate physiological parameters based on their nearest living relatives,producing more robust paleoatmospheric CO₂ reconstructions. These improved estimates will provide stronger constraints on the age and climatic setting of the fossil assemblage and, ultimately, improve our understanding of how Amazonian vegetation responds to climate change.

abstract:
A vast archive of outcrop photographs exists in pre-digital formats, representing a valuable yet underused resource for geoscientists. While some of these images are digitized and are publicly available, most remain in storage as photographic prints and film negatives. These datasets are challenging to work with due to their analog nature and lack of image metadata. However, as more photographic libraries digitize their collections, these vintage images can now be repurposed for modern analysis.

Digitized 35mm negatives, slides, and larger-format imagery provide opportunities to reconstruct past geologic sites and to integrate these reconstructions with contemporary photogrammetric datasets derived from drone-based imagery. Methods for generating georeferenced and scaled three-dimensional models from historical imagery are presented, including practical steps, the software and tools employed, and common challenges.

The example study area in west-central Alabama, southeastern US, includes

vintage aerial photos, scanned 35mm negatives from 1990, and drone-derived models

collected in 2020 and 2025. Results demonstrate that accurate 3D reconstructions can

be achieved by combining these diverse datasets. Vintage image-based models

enhance geologic interpretations and, in some cases, include geologic features not

visible today. The goal is to help geologists unlock historical datasets and apply them to

modern geoscientific research and education.

title: Effects of Dynamic Compression on Mineralogy of Meteorite Chondrites
session_title: Mineralogy, Geochemistry, Petrology, and Volcanology Student Session (Posters)
authors: Marquez, Maximiliano [1], Dorfman, Susannah [2], Chavarria, Luisa [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Earth Sciences & Resources, University of Texas at El Paso, El Paso, TX, USA
(2) Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA

abstract: How can we disrupt the trajectory of an asteroid that has Earth in its path? Collisions between rocky bodies are how our Earth formed and continue to pose a threat to life on Earth today. The vast majority of asteroids in the solar system have the same composition as chondrite meteorites, which are 88% percent of all meteorites that have landed on Earth. Previous studies of effects of planetary collisions and asteroid deflection and disruption protocols rely on experiments on single minerals. However, chondrites are complex rocks, composed of silicate minerals olivine, ortho/clinopyroxenes, and iron rich grains, which makes their physical properties more challenging to study and model. In addition, energetic enough impacts result in chemical reactions and changes in mineral crystal structure. In this study, we examine recovered samples from laser shock experiments on chondrite meteorites Tamdakht, Allen Hills 85069, and Miller Range 07052 to determine effects of dynamic compression on mineralogy. We identify the minerals in the unshocked meteorites by petrography of thin sections. Minerals inside and outside the shocked regions of samples are also analyzed by Raman spectroscopy. We expect to find olivine, pyroxene, and iron rich grains within the meteorites, but shocked regions may have high pressure forms of these minerals or evidence of melting. Our observations will allow us to relate the energy of the impact event to physical and chemical changes in the meteorite structure. The outcome of the project will help us better understand asteroids, as well as having an impact on society of sending explosives to the asteroids if Earth is on its pathway.

title: Multi-Criteria Screening and Spatial Database Integration for Managed Aquifer Recharge Site Selection in the Lower Rio Grande Basin, New Mexico
session_title: Enhancing Aquifer Recharge Across Scales: From Large Managed Systems to Distributed Solutions
authors: Guerra, Peter [1], McCord, James [2], Carilli, Joe [3], Hur, Nayoung [4], Serrano, Ryan [5], Hernandez, Christina [6]
affiliations: (1) Hydrogeology, New Mexico Bureau of Mines and Mineral Resources, Norma Meeks, New Mexico Tech, Socorro, NM,
(2) IRP Water LLC, Albuquerque, NM,
(4) Lynker Intel, Boulder, Colorado, USA
(5) New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission, Las Cruces, New Mexico,
(6) New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission, Las Cruces, NM,
abstract:
The Lower Rio Grande (LRG) Basin in southern New Mexico faces significant water-supply challenges driven by prolonged drought, declining groundwater levels, and competing agricultural and municipal demands. To enhance regional water security and improve aquifer storage, a Phase I Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR) screening study evaluated potential recharge opportunities throughout the basin. The study compiled more than 30 spatial datasets from federal, state, and local sources into a centralized ArcGIS geodatabase. These datasets included surface hydrology, hydrogeology, soil infiltration capacity, land ownership, environmental constraints, water quality, and existing water infrastructure.

The project evaluated opportunities for integrating MAR into 37 existing flood-control dams and detention structures operated by local flood-control districts and federal agencies. Incorporating MAR operations into existing flood-control infrastructure offers a potentially cost-effective strategy for capturing ephemeral runoff while minimizing the need for new land acquisition and infrastructure. Sites were evaluated using a two-stage screening framework that combined quantitative geospatial analysis with qualitative field and operational considerations.

Primary screening criteria included watershed runoff frequency and yield, proximity to water-conveyance infrastructure, soil hydraulic conductivity, vadose-zone thickness, regional groundwater storage capacity, and legal and regulatory constraints. Watershed runoff frequency and yield served as critical first-pass criteria to identify catchments capable of generating sufficient runoff to justify recharge development. To more rigorously quantify water availability, continuous daily hydrologic modeling was performed for candidate catchments to estimate potential long-term recharge yields under variable climatic conditions. Secondary screening criteria included localized flood risk, sediment-management requirements, and proximity to recharge sites and to potential contamination sources. The screening process reduced the initial inventory of 37 flood-control structures to a prioritized subset of high-potential sites suitable for pilot- or full-scale MAR implementation. The resulting centralized geodatabase, hydrologic modeling framework, and site-ranking methodology provide a repeatable decision-support approach for water managers in arid and semi-arid basins seeking to optimize existing infrastructure for the dual objectives of flood mitigation and groundwater replenishment.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Microbial Source Tracking Markers in Texas Coastal Waters Under Hydrologic and Tidal Influences
session_title: Coastal Hydrogeology in an Age of Rising Seas (Posters)
authors: Watson, Allie Fay-Rose [1], Narimani, Roya [2], Douglas, Audrey [3], Murgulet, Dorina [4]
affiliations: (1) Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
(2) Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
(3) Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
(4) Texas A&M University - Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi, TX, USA
abstract: Coastal barrier-island waters are shaped by exchanges among groundwater, tides, runoff, and nearshore surface water, creating variable conditions for microbial transport and persistence. Groundwater-surface water exchange and tidal pumping can redistribute microbes across the beach-aquifer-nearshore interface, and these pathways may become increasingly important as sea-level rise alters coastal hydraulic gradients. Predicting fecal contamination under these changing conditions remains difficult because microbial inputs are often episodic and unevenly detected. This study evaluates machine-learning models for predicting both the detection status and detected concentrations of microbial source-tracking markers in waters across Texas barrier islands. Observations integrate microbial measurements with hydrogeochemical, hydrologic, and meteorological data. Entero1 (general) and GFD (avian) concentrations were generally higher in surface water than pore water, whereas DG3 (canine) and HF183 (human) were characterized by frequent non-detects and intermittent elevated values. Across models, dominant predictors included salinity, groundwater discharge, tides, rainfall, streamflow, redox conditions, and stable isotopes (δ18O, δ2H, and δ13C), although their importance differed among markers. Interpretation remains preliminary because some test subsets were small or single class. Preliminary concentration results suggest that microbial variability is strongly influenced by episodic hydrologic events and changing source inputs, emphasizing the need for additional observations and expanded predictor datasets. Future work will compare random forests, gradient boosting, support vector machines, and other algorithms using grouped validation and expanded hydrogeochemical, groundwater, land-use, and hydrometeorological predictors. Improving prediction of intermittent contamination will help clarify how groundwater–surface water exchange, tidal forcing, and geochemical conditions regulate microbial transport and exposure risk within barrier-island systems.

title: Acumulación de sedimento moderno en la Bahía Siá Mariana, Pantanal norte, Brasil
session_title: Presentaciones de Geociencias en Español: Continuamos con la experiencia en la GSA 2026/Geoscience Presentations in Spanish: Continuing the Experience at GSA 2026 (Part II)
authors: Lo, Edward Limin [1], Yescas, Giovanni [2], Silva, Aguinaldo [3], Kuerten, Sidney [4]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, Georgia Southern University, Statesboro, Georgia, USA; Institute for Water and Health, Georgia Southern University, Savannah, GA, USA
(2) School of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, Georgia Southern University, Statesboro, GA, USA
(3) Faculty of Engineering, Architecture, Urbanism and Geography, Federal University of Mato Grosso do Sul, Campo Grande, MS, Brazil
(4) Geography, State University of Mato Grosso do Sul, Campo Grande, MS, Brazil
abstract: El Pantanal es uno de los mayores humedales de agua dulce del mundo, y a cada vez entendemos mejor sobre sus archivos geológicos. Sin embargo, el paisaje cuenta con muchos cuerpos de agua aunque sin datos sobre la manera en que los sedimentos acumulan. Este estudio pretende responder a la pregunta, ¿cuáles son las proriedades y la distribución de sedimentos en el presente Bahía Siá Mariana? Los sedimentos fueron recuperados con una draga ponar en mayo 2026 en la laguna, incluyendo sedimento en la entrada y salida principal de flujo del Río Mutum, que descarga en el Río Cuiabá. Los siguientes análises fueron llevados a cabo: distribución de tamaño de grano, carbono orgánico total, y abundancia de elementos químicos. Encontramos una distribución de sedimentos que refleja el control del Río Mutum, o sea una ocurrencia elevada de arena cerca de los canales activos. Mientras tanto, la abundancia de arcilla en ciertas márgenes de la laguna también permite mayor abundancia de elementos químicos. Estos datos nos permiten entender el funcionamiento de la laguna en el presente para que mejoremos las interpretaciones en testigos de sedimento. Como la región tienen importancia para los deportes con pesces, este estudio será importante no solo para mejorar el contexto de mudanzas ambientales sino también para la población local.
