title: Occurrence and Antibiotic Resistance profiles of gram-negative bacteria isolated from diverse aquatic environments across Mexico
session_title: Emerging Contaminants in Water and Earth Systems: Fate and Transport Processes, Decision Support, and Regulatory Implications (Part I)
authors: Dogra, Shiwangi [1], Capote, Marcos De Donato [2], Kumar, Manish [3]
affiliations: (1) Escuela de Ingeniería y Ciencias, Tecnológico de Monterrey, Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, Mexico
(2) Escuela de Ingeniería y Ciencias, Tecnológico de Monterrey, Monterrey, Neuvo Leon, Mexico
(3) Escuela de Ingeniería y Ciencias, Tecnológico de Monterrey, Monterrey, Neuvo Leon, Mexico; Sustainability Cluster, School of Advanced Engineering, UPES, Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India
abstract:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health challenge, with aquatic environments recognised as reservoirs and dissemination pathways for resistant bacteria. Wastewater, rivers, groundwater, and other water bodies receive anthropogenic inputs that may facilitate the persistence and spread of antimicrobial-resistant microorganisms. In Mexico, phenotypic surveillance of environmental bacteria across diverse aquatic ecosystems remains limited, constraining our understanding of AMR patterns and the development of One Health surveillance strategies. This study characterizes the phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility profiles of bacterial isolates recovered from 19 water samples taken from wastewater, rivers, groundwater, lakes/wetlands/lagoon, drinking water/tap water, and irrigation water from Monterrey, Queretaro, Santa Fe and Toluca. Total of 58 bacterial isolates recovered from the aquatic matrices were evaluated using the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method against 12 antibiotics representing five antimicrobial classes. The highest number of isolates (n=18) was recovered from Pesqueria and Lerma rivers, followed by groundwater (n=13) and wastewater (n=9). Statistical analyses were performed to evaluate differences in antibiotic responses among isolates and water matrices. Variation in inhibition-zone diameters was observed across the antibiotics tested, with mean values ranging from 17.3 ± 5.0 mm for gentamicin to 22.3 ± 6.7 mm for levofloxacin. Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole exhibited the greatest variability in inhibition-zone measurements whereas ceftazidime-clavulanate showed the lowest variability. Overall, 13 zero-diameter inhibition observations were recorded, including five for imipenem. Comparable environmental AMR findings have been reported in the Aconcagua River, Chile, where 20.8% and 12.5% of tested isolates were resistant to imipenem and meropenem, respectively, demonstrating the occurrence of carbapenem resistance in another Latin American aquatic environment. Surface-water isolates showed the highest mean inhibition zone (21.04 mm), whereas irrigation-water isolates showed the lowest (16.42 mm). However, no significant differences were detected among water matrices after multiple-testing correction (adjusted p > 0.05). Netilmicin showed the strongest unadjusted matrix-associated variation (H = 10.52, p = 0.062). Additionally, 9/58 isolates (15.5%) exhibited a ≥5 mm increase with clavulanate-containing disks, indicating potential β-lactamase-associated phenotypic responses requiring taxonomic and genomic confirmation. This study establishes a baseline for environmental phenotypic AMR surveillance and provides a framework for future bacterial identification, whole-genome sequencing, and genotype-phenotype integration within One Health monitoring.

Keywords: Antimicrobial-resistance; One Health; Mexico; Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion; Bacteria

title: 3D Geological Modeling in the Michigan Basin
session_title: Applications of 3D Geological and Subsurface Modeling: From Energy to Environment
authors: Esch, John M. [1]
affiliations: (1) Michigan Geological Survey, Michigan Geological Survey, Laingsburg, MI, USA
abstract:
Traditional three-dimensional geological models often serve as static final products—digital assets left unutilized on a shelf like a statue. However, the true value of formation structure surfaces and 3D basin models does not reside in the finalized block diagrams; rather, they are merely the "frosting on the cake." The core utility lies in the foundational formation top structure elevation surfaces, which can be extracted and operationalized across diverse secondary workflows to interpret auxiliary data, execute rapid subsetting, and fuel interactive visualizations. Having formation structure elevation surfaces and 3D models for an area or a state allows one to quickly respond to questions or create subprojects by clipping out specific subareas.

Some workflows will be presented using Python Notebooks in ArcGIS Pro to rapidly iterate and flag erroneous formation-top data and an ArcGIS Toolbox for mosaicking the subsurface structure and subcrop/outcrop portions of a formation.

Using a dataset of 65 Paleozoic formations layers from the Michigan Basin, a number of examples will be presented showing the value of this data, including creating geologic cross sections across the basin or a subarea.

Finally, we highlight how these surfaces transition from active analytical tools to powerful communication assets. Whether deployed as physical 3D prints, dynamic animations, or shared interactively within a 3D web app, these models serve as an essential medium for translating complex or controversial geological concepts to non-scientific audiences, managers, policymakers, and other geologists.

title: Understanding Hydroclimatic Variability, Groundwater-Level Dynamics, and Inferred Aquifer Stress in Coastal Bangladesh Using a Physics-Informed Neural Network
session_title: Secured and Safe Groundwater for a Sustainable Planet
authors: Sharma, Sanjeev Kumar [1], Bhattacharya, Prosun [2], Mukherjee, Abhijit [3], Rahman, Saifur [4]
affiliations: (1) ExcelDots AB, Stockholm, Sweden
(2) KTH International Groundwater Arsenic Research Group, Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering,, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
(3) Department of Geology and Geophysics, Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, Kharagpur, West Bengal, India
(4) Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE), Government of Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract:
Coastal aquifers of southwestern Bangladesh are increasingly influenced by hydroclimatic variability, seasonal recharge, groundwater abstraction, salinity, and regional hydraulic connectivity. Variability in monsoon rainfall can alter aquifer recharge, while expanding groundwater use and changing regional flow conditions may intensify groundwater stress. Sparse monitoring and limited pumping records, however, make it difficult to distinguish climate-related recharge responses from anthropogenic and regional influences. This study evaluates whether a physics-informed neural network (PINN) can identify interpretable groundwater-level dynamics from an approximately 11-month logger record collected in Soladana Union, Paikgacha Upazila, Khulna District, Bangladesh. The dataset contains 5,781 sub-hourly observations of groundwater level, specific conductivity, and temperature acquired between 10 September 2025 and 6 August 2026. Measurements were aggregated to daily means and paired with Bangladesh Meteorological Department monthly-normal rainfall for Khulna as a climatological recharge proxy.

The monitored well was represented as a lumped aquifer-storage cell governed by a transient mass balance. A neural representation of groundwater head was constrained by rainfall recharge, linear exchange with a regional reference head, and a smooth time-varying net-forcing term representing the combined effects of unmetered pumping, unresolved recharge or discharge, and regional aquifer exchange. The groundwater-head and forcing networks were trained jointly with four effective physical parameters using daily observations and 2,000 physics-collocation points.

The PINN reproduced the daily groundwater-level record with R² = 0.89 and RMSE = 1.21 m. The inferred net-forcing term increased from approximately 0.18 to 1.9 mm day⁻¹ equivalent during the monitoring period, with a brief plateau during March–April 2026. This trajectory is compatible with increasing cumulative abstraction and/or reduced regional inflow superimposed on seasonal hydroclimatic forcing, although the available data cannot separate these contributions. Groundwater levels rose during April–June 2026 and declined again during July–August, suggesting that monsoon-season recharge temporarily moderated, but did not eliminate, the broader aquifer-stress signal.

An abrupt shift in groundwater level and conductivity on 8 October 2025 may reflect logger maintenance, reinstallation, or datum adjustment. Conductivity values subsequently approaching zero indicate possible sensor drift or fouling and require verification before detailed hydrogeological interpretation.

The study demonstrates the potential of PINNs to distinguish seasonal hydroclimatic responses from longer-term groundwater-stress signals in data-scarce coastal aquifers. Further development requires event-scale rainfall, abstraction estimates, verified logger metadata, independent salinity measurements, additional monitoring wells, and a spatial groundwater-flow formulation.

title: Groundwater Vulnerability in Hydrocarbon-Bearing Formations: Hydrostratigraphic Controls in WCSB
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications
authors: Ferguson, Grant [1], Espinosa Cortes, Rebeca M [2], McIntosh, Jennifer [3]
affiliations: (1) College of Engineering, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Canada
(2) College of Engineering, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Canada
(3) Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, USA
abstract:
To what extent are groundwater wells vulnerable in regions adjacent to shallow oil wells, and what factors govern this susceptibility? These questions are central to ongoing challenges in detecting subsurface contamination and managing the remediation of spills, leakage, and seepage from petroleum infrastructure. Understanding the hydrogeological and geological controls that influence this vulnerability is essential for developing robust monitoring frameworks and targeted mitigation strategies to protect groundwater resources.

Before enacting Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) (Canada I. A., 2023) legislation in 1973, approximately 63,000 oil wells had been drilled in Alberta.

An environmental assessment conducted in 2018 recommended further investigation into the characterization of nonhydrocarbon fractions—particularly those enriched in complex oil-sand residuals (COSR oils)—due to uncertainties regarding their mobility, persistence, and environmental impact. Addressing these knowledge gaps will require the application of advanced analytical techniques and modeling tools (Fingas, 2014; Lee et al., 2015).

This research contributes to advancing geological and hydrogeological modeling in the basin by developing a dynamic, MODFLOW-based numerical model. The study evaluates vertical separation between oil wells and groundwater sources to assess potential hydraulic connectivity or isolation, offering critical insights into subsurface fluid flow dynamics (Jellicoe, 2020; Perra, 2020). Field investigations complement and refine existing datasets, enabling a more integrated understanding of the complex stratigraphic and structural controls that govern fluid migration in the Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin.

This research addresses fundamental questions—when and how oil extraction activities may begin to influence groundwater resources and their use and supports the development of more effective response protocols, monitoring technologies, and remediation strategies aimed at safeguarding freshwater resources.

title: Linking Climate and Pedogenic Carbonates using Benchtop Micro-XRF Analysis: A Case Study from eastern Africa.
session_title: Soils and Paleosols Techniques for Interdisciplinary Advancements (Posters)
authors: Omuyangu, Aggrey Minya [1], STINCHCOMB, GARY EDWARD [2]
affiliations: (1) Earth Sciences Department, University of Memphis, Memphis, TN, USA
(2) Earth Sciences Department, University of Memphis, MEMPHIS, TN, Kenya
(3) Earth and Environmental Science,, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
(4) Department of Geosciences, and Associate Director Turkana Basin Institute, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York, USA
abstract:
Pedogenic carbonates are widely used in the study of past changes in plant communities, soil development processes, and the climate and ecosystems of human evolution. However, there is limited understanding of the trace element geochemistry of soil carbonates, especially at small (µm) spatial scales. Here we use benchtop µ-XRF analysis to understand the dynamics of soil carbonate geochemistry. We examine pedogenic carbonates collected from (i) a transect across a precipitation gradient from Serengeti National Park, Tanzania, (ii) the Chalbi desert, Kenya, and (iii) the Mpala Research Centre, Kenya. Mean annual precipitation (MAP) ranges from 140 to 848 mm/yr at these sites. X-ray spectra were extracted from zones of maximum CaO concentration (>90 %) within the carbonates, which we assume to reflect pure CaCO 3 with minimal parent material interference. Our preliminary results show a decreasing trend in aridity signals as indicated by Na 2 O/SiO 2 and Na 2 O/Al 2 O 3 ratios which negatively correlate with increasing rainfall at R 2 =0.59 and R 2 =0.69, respectively. Decreasing Na 2 O/Al 2 O 3 may reflect less Na in the soil carbonate with declining soil water salinity as MAP increases. Alternatively, this trend may reflect increased leaching and removal of Na+ from colloids (clay) at sites with higher rainfall.

Although the Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) and Chemical Proxy of Alteration (CPA) are designed for bulk geochemical measurements, they were applied on the pedogenic carbonate chemistry and showed moderate to strong correlation with mean annual rainfall (CIA, R 2 =0.70; CPA, R 2 =0.73). These weathering trends suggest that the trace elements within pedogenic carbonate reflect either solution chemistry during calcite precipitation or colloids occluded within the calcite. Although these competing hypotheses (solution chemistry vs. colloid), may not be resolvable using µ-XRF, the results indicate that the trace elements within pedogenic carbonate are related to MAP. Future work will assess more soil carbonates from a greater range of climates to test the robustness of these trends, and continue to test the potential of µ-XRF of pedogenic carbonates as a proxy for reconstructing past rainfall.

Key words: micro-XRF, pedogenic carbonates, precipitation gradient, mean annual precipitation, paleo-precipitation.

title: The Nature of Jurassic Magmatism in the Sierra Nevada: A Comparison of Adjacent Plutons and Dike Swarms
session_title: Magmatic processes from arc to mineral scales and from field to lab: a session in honor of Calvin G. Barnes, MGPV Distinguished Career Award recipient (Part I)
authors: Bates, Caitlin Anne [1], Memeti, Valbone [2], Paterson, Scott [3]
affiliations: (1) California State University, Fullerton, CA,
(2) California State University, Fullerton, CA,
abstract:
The magmatic and tectonic history of the Jurassic arc, Sierra Nevada batholith (SNB), California, is poorly understood due to overprinting Cretaceous magmatism and deformation. This study presents age and petrologic data from Jurassic plutons and nearby dike swarms to examine timing and petrogenetic relationships and implications for the history of the Jurassic arc. In the eastern SNB, the dioritic-granodioritic King Creek and quartz-monzonitic Fish Creek plutons yielded U-Pb zircon ages of 167.7 ± 1.8 Ma and 158.8 ± 1.8 Ma, respectively. The NW-SE striking King Creek basalt-rhyolite dike swarm intruding the King Creek pluton yielded a U-Pb zircon age of 152.8 ± 2.8 Ma, indicating they all formed at slightly different times. In the Western Metamorphic belt (WMB), U-Pb zircon ages for the gabbroic-dioritic Standard (162.6 ± 2.3 Ma), dioritic-granodioritic Granite Creek (164 ± 2.5 Ma), and gabbroic diorite-monzodioritic Cobb Creek (163.72 ± 2.2 Ma) plutons overlap within uncertainty, indicating that they are coeval and may represent a ca. 700 km 2 magma system. The andesite-basalt, E-W striking Sonora dike swarm intrudes and mingles with a unit of the Standard pluton with an age of 159.44 ± 1.6 Ma and thus is interpreted to overlap in age.

The WMB plutons and dikes show a Sr/Nd array ranging from depleted mantle to slightly more evolved compositions consistent with intrusion through accreted materials. In the King Creek area, the plutons and dikes have whole rock Sr/Nd isotopes indicating depleted mantle compositions consistent with intrusion through marine sediments and underlying oceanic basement. Geochemical data suggest that the rhyolite dikes formed from melts from remelting of the pluton.The plutons in both regions represent crystal cumulates inferred from the presence of plagioclase cumulates and the discrepancy between more mafic whole rock compositions and dacitic-rhyolitic melt compositions calculated from hornblende compositions.

A broader comparison of published data on dikes in the eastern Sierra and White-Inyo Mountains (Independence dike swarm), the Snow Lake pendant, and in the Foothills terrane indicate the following: (1) dike ages vary across the arc, (2) dike chemistries match inferred basement types, (3) rhyolite dikes in swarms may be derived from melts from nearby plutons, and (4) dike swarm orientations vary from arc parallel to arc oblique, to arc perpendicular.

title: Geochemical comparison of ferroactinolite-tremolite from Del Norte Co., CA + Catalina Island, CA
session_title: Mineralogical Insights from Modern Spectroscopic Techniques (Posters)
authors: Egan, Shea Porter [1], Mustoe, George [2]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Whatcom Community College, Bellingham, Washington, USA
(2) Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington, USA
abstract: This work focuses on exploring the mineralogical, context of titanite as an uncommon inclusion within ferroactinolite-tremolite rich material which highlights the chronological context of fluid flow and folds that resulted in the inclusion of titanite during two specific windows of subducted ultramafic rock appearing in Del Norte Co., CA + Catalina Island, CA. By comparing samples we are able to analyze petrographic and chemical consistencies and inconsistencies that allow for broader context within the myriad of metamorphic complexes throughout California in the hopes of gaining a broader understanding of how inclusions move through tectonic forces enacted upon them globally. Another angle that has yet to be explored within this context is the exotic protolith of these inclusions and exactly what caused the inclusions to migrate within their respective units. Analytical work for this project includes field photography/observations, RAMAN data analysis, optical petrography, microscopy, SEM-EDS, and XRD involving both localities and respective samples.

title: Chronic Arsenic Exposure and Community Health in the Middle Gangetic Plain, India: Insights from Two Decades of Grassroots Engagement
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part II)
authors: Singh, Saurabh [1], Bhattacharya, Prosun [2]
affiliations: (1) inner voice foundation, VARANASI, UTTAR PRADESH, India
(2) KTH-International Groundwater Arsenic Group, Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH ROYAL INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, Stockholm, Sweden
abstract:
Saurabh Singh¹ and Prosun Bhattacharya²

¹Inner Voice Foundation, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India

²KTH-International Groundwater Arsenic Research Group, School of Architecture and the Built Environment,Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden

The Gangetic plain of northern India is among the world’s most extensively documented regions affected by geogenic arsenic contamination of groundwater. Chronic exposure occurs primarily through groundwater used for drinking and food preparation and may also arise through consumption of crops irrigated with contaminated water. Prolonged ingestion of inorganic arsenic is associated with skin lesions, cancers, cardiovascular disorders, diabetes, developmental effects, and other systemic health consequences. Despite substantial investments in rural drinking-water infrastructure, exposure persists where contaminated groundwater sources remain in use, water-quality surveillance is incomplete, and affected communities lack sustained access to medical screening, treatment, rehabilitation, and reliable arsenic-safe water.

This contribution synthesizes two decades of grassroots engagement by the Inner Voice Foundation in arsenic-affected communities of the middle Gangetic plain. The assessment draws upon field observations, community interactions, water-testing records, available medical and health documentation, and publicly accessible water-quality and demographic information. It examines the continued use of contaminated water sources, reported health conditions among exposed populations, barriers to diagnosis and treatment, and the wider social and economic consequences of chronic arsenic exposure. The contribution also presents experience from the Community Arsenic Mitigation and Rehabilitation Centre (CAMRO), which promotes an integrated approach combining water testing, risk communication, medical referral, community support, rehabilitation, and appropriate mitigation measures.

The evidence demonstrates that arsenic contamination must be addressed as an interconnected hydrogeological, public-health, socioeconomic, and environmental-justice challenge rather than solely as a drinking-water infrastructure problem. Effective intervention requires systematic testing and periodic retesting of wells and piped-water supplies, transparent communication of water-quality results, reliable provision of arsenic-safe water for drinking and cooking, assessment of food-chain exposure, early clinical screening, and long-term support for affected households. Integrating hydrogeochemical mapping with community health information and participatory monitoring can improve the identification of exposure hotspots and support more targeted interventions. A coordinated framework linking geoscience, public health, governance, and community action is essential for reducing preventable exposure and strengthening the effectiveness and accountability of safe-water programs across the Gangetic region.

title: How Beaver Occupation Influenced Burn Severity, Habitat Resilience, and Landscape Recovery Post 2022 Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon Fire
session_title: From Flame to Flood: Wildfire Effects on Landscapes, Riverscapes, and Society (Posters)
authors: Lee, Colman [1], Lindline, Jennifer [2], Foucher, Marine [3]
affiliations: (1) Natural Resources Management Department, New Mexico Highlands University, Las Vegas, NM, USA
(2) Natural Resources Management Department, New Mexico Highlands University, Las Vegas, New Mexico, USA
(3) Natural Resources Management Department, New Mexico Highlands University, Las Vegas, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
High severity wildfires are becoming increasingly common in western forests. Burned areas are prone to increased soil erosion, stream flooding, and water quality impairment. Proactive management strategies are necessary for watershed protection and recovery from forest fire. The > 341,000-acre 2022 Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon (HP/CC) fire severely affected multiple watersheds in northern New Mexico, including major, critical areas like the Upper Pecos, Gallinas, and Tecolote Watersheds, impacting regional water supplies and ecosystem services. Soil burn severity was high across significant portions, creating hydrophobic soils that directly led to major post-fire flooding and debris flows in the region.

This study reproduced methods used by Fairfax et al. (2024) to examine the influence of beaver occupation on burn severity and post-fire sediment loads in the 2022 HP/CC burn scar. Beaver dams were located via satellite imagery throughout the HP/CC burn scar. Beaver dam capacity results calculated by the Beaver Restoration Assessment Tool (BRAT) were downloaded for the Gallinas, Sapello, and Mora watersheds and segmented into bundles (< 2; 2-5; 5-12; and >12 dams/km). Dam capacity is used as a measure of riparian characteristics that would influence fire severity regardless of beaver occupation. A Difference Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) was calculated throughout the HP/CC burn area then used to analyze the burn intensity in valley bottoms near dams compared to valley bottoms without dams but within the same dam capacity range. Additionally, turbidity was measured above and below two active and two inactive beaver dam sites on the Rio Pueblo near Sipapu downstream of the HP/CC burn area in Spring 2026. Analyses showed that for river reaches with the same dam capacity, those with beavers had a statistically significantly lower dNBR than those without beavers (p < 0.0001). Analyses also showed that many of the beaver-occupied river valleys did not burn at all. At all sites, turbidity values tended to be lower below dams than above them. This study supports beaver reintroduction or beaver dam mimicry as a low-cost, low-technology, and nature-based fire mitigation and post-fire restoration tool.

title: Seasonal Variations in Manganese Concentrations and Mineral Stability in the Hyporheic Zone of a Mountain Stream: Implications for the Fate of Metals from Circumneutral Mine Drainage
session_title: Environmental Geochemistry and Health (Part II)
authors: Johannesen, Morgan [1], Schulmeister, Marcia K. [2], Stotler, Randy L. [3]
affiliations: (1) Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(2) Geology, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS, USA
(3) Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada
abstract: Fourmile Creek in the Cripple Creek mining district of Colorado has received metals in discharge since the 1940s. High-sulfate circumneutral effluent from a legacy dewatering adit poses a threat to the surrounding ecology and is the subject of remedial actions. In an initial evaluation of the geochemical conditions that influence the fate of downstream contaminants, we identified differences between surface water and streambed porewaters during high- and low-streamflow conditions in June and October, respectively, at three locations: the circumneutral effluent-receiving reach, 200 meters upstream, and 300 meters downstream. In this study, differences in porewater geochemistry and mineral saturation were also observed at three to five depths in the hyporheic zone of each location. Upstream porewaters in October exhibited higher pH and dissolved oxygen (DO) concentrations accompanied by lower specific conductance values. Downstream DO and specific conductance values were higher in October with lower pH than in June. These parameters remained relatively constant in the effluent-receiving reach. Surface water and porewater oxidation-reduction potentials were higher in June at each location, though all samples were within a range consistent with manganese (Mn) reduction (0.19-0.27 V) in both months. Upstream and downstream porewater Mn concentrations were substantially lower in October, declining from >1000 ppb to <5 ppb, while Mn concentrations doubled from June to October at the effluent-receiving reach. The Mn oxide mineral birnessite was identified in the fine fraction (<2 µm) of bulk sediments via X-Ray Diffraction alongside muscovite, montmorillonite, kaolinite, feldspars and quartz. Initial equilibrium speciation modeling with PHREEQC revealed differences in mineral saturation at each location: porewaters and surface water were oversaturated with respect to iron oxides and oxyhydroxides, aluminum oxides, and silicate minerals in both June and October. Samples from the adit discharge and downstream locations were additionally saturated with respect to calcite, aragonite, and fluorite. Downstream porewaters were oversaturated with respect to rhodochrosite in June, while all locations remained undersaturated with respect to birnessite in both months. Additional speciation modeling will predict controls on manganese oxide and other mineral precipitation under varying conditions. As a tributary to the Arkansas River, the fate and long-term impact of this stream is an environmental health concern, and this work will aid in understanding the potential mobility and loading of metals in Fourmile Creek.

title: Long-term decline in groundwater redox potential reveals heterogeneous mobilization of redox-sensitive trace elements across Mexico
session_title: Coupled Redox–Organic Interactions in the Critical Zone: From Pore Scale Reactions to Landscape Scale Processes
authors: TRIPATHI, Sachin [1], Torres Martinez, Juan Antonio [2], Datta, Saugata [3], Kumar, Manish [4]
affiliations: (1) Escuela de Ingeniería y Ciencias,, Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Monterey, Monterrey, 64849, Nuevo Leon, Mexico, Monterreu, Nuevo Leon, Mexico
(2) Escuela de Ingeniería y Ciencias, Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Monterey, Monterrey, 64849, Nuevo Leon, Mexico, Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, Mexico

abstract: Groundwater redox conditions are fundamental to the mobility of redox-sensitive trace elements (RSEs), yet their long-term evolution and influence on groundwater chemistry remain poorly understood at regional scales. This study evaluated decadal changes in groundwater redox conditions and hydrochemistry using paired observations from 352 monitoring wells across Mexico sampled in 2014 and 2022. Groundwater exhibited a widespread shift toward less oxidizing conditions, with mean oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) declining from 185.8 to 125.8 mV, while 67.4% of monitoring wells showed decreasing ORP. Concurrently, mean Fe, As, Cr, and NO₃⁻ concentrations increased from 0.152 to 0.159 mg L⁻¹, 0.021 to 0.027 mg L⁻¹, 0.0028 to 0.0060 mgL⁻¹, and 4.24 to 5.95 mgL⁻¹, respectively. At the well scale, NO₃⁻ increased in 71.2% of wells, Fe in 41.6%, and Cr in 40.1%, whereas As exhibited heterogeneous behavior, with 39.5% of wells showing no detectable temporal change. Correlation analysis indicated that relationships between ORP and redox-sensitive variables weakened between 2014 and 2022, suggesting that declining redox potential alone did not uniformly regulate trace-element mobility. Principal component analysis resolved two dominant hydrogeochemical controls: PC1 was dominated by major ions (Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , Na + , K + , and SO₄ 2- ), reflecting groundwater mineralization, whereas PC2 was characterized by carbonate chemistry (HCO₃ - , CO₃ 2- ), electrical conductivity, and total dissolved solids, with secondary contributions from ORP, Fe, and Mn, indicating coupled carbonate–redox evolution. Consistent with these results, R-mode hierarchical cluster analysis revealed a reorganization of hydrochemical associations between 2014 and 2022, with major ions consistently forming a distinct mineralization cluster, while ORP, carbonate species, and redox-sensitive trace elements exhibited changing clustering patterns through time. These findings demonstrate that regional groundwater evolution reflects the interaction of redox processes with groundwater mineralization and localized hydrogeochemical conditions, producing element-specific rather than coordinated responses of redox-sensitive trace elements across Mexico. These results provide a regional framework for understanding long-term redox evolution and groundwater quality in heterogeneous aquifer systems.

title: Stable Isotopes and Hydrogeochemistry Reveal Contrasting Water Sources and Processes in Kenya Rift Lakes
session_title: Innovations in research of groundwater-surface water interactions
authors: Agbogun, Henry M. D. [1], Atekwana, Eliot A. [2]
affiliations: (1) Fort Hays State University, Hays, KS,
(2) University of California, Davis, CA,
abstract:
The Kenya sector of the East African Rift System hosts numerous lakes that exhibit large variations in salinity, hydrochemistry, and water sources as a consequence of differing hydrological and tectonic settings. To investigate the origins/evolution of these waters, stable isotope (δ¹⁸O, δD) and hydrochemical data were evaluated from twelve lakes distributed across the Kenyan Rift.

Five hydrogeochemical groups are recognized. (1) Dilute meteoric-recharge lakes, Olbolossat, Victoria, and Naivasha, have low TDS (119–238 ppm), salinity (0.11–0.23 psu), and relatively low DIC. Their δ¹⁸O values range from −7.94 to +1.25‰, indicating contributions from relatively unevaporated high-elevation precipitation, river inflow, and groundwater recharge. (2) Evaporatively modified meteoric lakes, Baringo and Turkana, are isotopically enriched (δ¹⁸O = +3.21 to +5.31‰; δD = +24 to +29‰) but remain comparatively dilute (TDS = 405–2,143 ppm), indicating substantial evaporation of predominantly meteoric and river-derived waters without extreme solute accumulation. (3) Saline alkaline lakes, including Solai, Nakuru, Elementaita, and Turkana Crater Lake, have TDS of 3,830–9,969 ppm, alkaline pH, and elevated DIC. These characteristics reflect restricted drainage, evaporative concentration, and progressive carbonate-system evolution. Turkana Crater Lake is especially isotope-enriched (δ¹⁸O = +7.71‰; δD = +47‰), indicating intense evaporation within a restricted basin. (4) Hypersaline alkaline lakes, Bogoria and Magadi, contain the highest TDS, salinity, and DIC. Lake Bogoria reaches 24,220 ppm TDS and 31.33 psu, whereas Lake Magadi reaches 69,610 ppm and 70 psu. Magadi is nevertheless relatively isotope-depleted (δ¹⁸O = −1.28‰; δD = −17‰), demonstrating that hypersalinity cannot be explained by evaporation alone and suggesting substantial groundwater/geothermal input, prolonged water–rock interaction, and subsequent evaporative concentration. (5) The Bogoria hotspring forms a distinct geothermal endmember, characterized by 95°C temperature, strongly reducing conditions (ORP = −237 mV), very low dissolved oxygen (0.22 ppm), and comparatively depleted water isotopes (δ¹⁸O = −0.55‰), consistent with deeply circulating meteoric groundwater heated within the rift geothermal system.

We propose that mantle-driven rifting influences surface-water chemistry indirectly through elevated heat flow, magmatism, deep volatile release, and fault-controlled groundwater circulation. Rift faults facilitate downward penetration of meteoric water and upward migration of heated, rock-reacted fluids and potentially deep CO₂, whereas evaporation, degassing, and carbonate reactions processes subsequently modify these signatures within individual lake basins. The lake system therefore records variable coupling between surface hydrology and deep tectono-magmatic processes.

title: A Magmatic Anomaly of the Southwest: The Newly Mapped, Classified and Correlated Basalt Flows of Coyote Hills Shield Volcano in the Springerville Volcanic Field, Arizona.

authors: Olivarez, Atzi Cruz [1], Figueroa, Edwin Sis [2], Mnich, Marissa [3], Emmot, Danny [4], Martinez, Jocelin Ortiz [5], Hsu, Jared [6], Van Hoven, Loet [7], Kaiser, Jackson Maxwell [8]

(2) Sonoma State Geology Department, Sonoma State University, Rohnert Park, CA, USA

abstract:
Being one of the most articulately mapped basaltic volcanic regions in the world, the Springerville volcanic field (SVF) in Eastern Arizona contains unsolved geologic problems in a potentially active system, with eruptions as young as 50ka. Situated along the southern margin of the Colorado Plateau, the SVF could offer insights into the eruptive history and evolution of related magmatic systems in the region. The dominantly monogenetic field contains over 400 cinder cones and two polygenetic shield volcanoes—Blue Ridge Mountain on the western margin and Coyote Hills on the eastern edge. While nearly the entirety of the SVF has been mapped in detail, Coyote Hills, a 60 km2 shield volcano, represents one of the final pieces in mapping out the eruptive events within the 3000 km2 field. Apart from the progress of mapping the field, the magmatic origin of the two polygenetic shield volcanoes within the SVF, the exact age of the volcanoes, and the sequencing of the flows of Coyote Hills have been indeterminate since mapping and study of the SVF began.

A total of six weeks of field time over three consecutive summers was spent mapping and sampling the 47 flows of Coyote Hills. Field observations of lithologies based upon phenocryst types and abundance were used to distinguish between basalt flows. The use of satellite imagery and LiDAR aided mapping work in the field in delineating flows of the rather covered and topographically flat volcano. These tools, in combination with field observations, assisted in distinguishing small-volume flows from more extensive units such as flow Qfg23 that dominates the east side of the volcano. Flow mineralogy assessed in the field has since been supplemented by detailed petrographic studies and geochemical analysis conducted on collected flow samples. Point counting of sample thin sections has classified the basalt flows into quantitative lithologic classes used to name each unit and correlate relationships between flows. Four distinct basalt classes are represented within the basalt flows of Coyote Hills, out of 47 individual flows, there is 1 sparse olivine (d-type lithology) basalt flow, 8 olivine-pyroxene-plagioclase (e-type lithology) basalt flows, 24 olivine plagioclase (g-type) basalt flows, and 14 feldspathic (l-type) basalt flows. Results of geochemical analysis conducted on samples indicate limited variability between the basalt flows of Coyote Hills Shield Volcano.

title: Using Silt to Sand-Sized Meteoritic Fragments Preserved in Rapidly Quenched Melt Breccias to Diagnose Impact and Airburst Events and Investigate Impactor Petrogenesis and Origins
session_title: Impact Cratering: From the Earth into the Solar System (Posters)
authors: Harris, Robert Scott [1], Schultz, Peter H. [2]
affiliations: (1) Department of Geology, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
(2) Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
abstract:
Over twenty-five years we have investigated the occurrences of dozens of melt breccias around the world that superficially might be considered to have formed by a variety of processes, including volcanism, lightning strikes, hypervelocity impact melting, pyrometamorphism, anthropogenic smelting, or ceramic manufacturing. The dozen deposits for which we have concluded, based on multiple lines of evidence, formed by rapid melting and quenching during an impact or low-altitude airburst, have an important commonality. Their glassy matrices contain silt to sand-sized clasts of meteoritic rocks.

Several observations demonstrate the improbability that these fragments are entrained from the target or are formed by reactions during vitrification:

1. They belong to the same meteorite type(s), or to closely related groups that would be expected from sampling a larger representative cross section of a body than any single meteorite provides. This consistency can apply to samples distributed over 100s of square kilometers.

2. They are composed of species that weather rapidly in even the most sterile ambient conditions, implying that the encapsulating glass provides protection.

3. They exhibit textures indicative of melting and/or decomposition and digestion into melts that quenched in less time than is feasible to regrow and reabsorb new phases. In some cases, decomposition produces forms that would physically disintegrate in loose sediments. We emphasize these are rock fragments, not just immiscible phases with exotic chemistry that one might find in any disequilibrium melts.

Because these are discrete, multiphase nuggets, they allow petrologic characterization of the asteroids or comets in a way that geochemical signatures do not. Those can be biased or homogenized by the dynamics of any specific impact. Nuggets potentially provide a random sample of the entire body (although preservation is biased toward refractory materials). Note that the “nuggeting” effects on bulk geochemical analyses of impactor contamination are at a premium where the impactor is represented by these fragments. We are working to characterize the degree to which impactor chemistry then is not miscible in the molten target and the degree to which molten target can dilute the impactor signature in a whole-rock analysis. We also present updates on what these fragments have revealed about objects ranging from the angrite parent body to a primitive carbonaceous body that detonated over the Atacama in the early Holocene.

title: Concavity Analysis and Shared Stream-Power Modeling of Interior Wall Catchments in Candor and Coprates Chasmata, Mars
session_title: Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of Mars
authors: Anannya, Anuva [1], Whipple, Kelin X. [2]
affiliations: (1) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State Univ, School of Earth and Space Exploration, Tempe, AZ,
(2) School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA
abstract:
There remains much debate surrounding the nature and sources of surface water on early Mars, with hypotheses including precipitation-fed runoff, ice melt, and groundwater seepage. Valles Marineris (VM), with drainage networks incised into its interior walls postdating canyon formation, provides a unique testbed for this problem. The concavity index is a quantitative tool for determining the dominant formative process of these channel networks. On Earth, graded rivers follow a power-law relationship between local channel gradient (S) and upstream drainage area (A), S = K s A -θ . Here, a concavity index (θ) between 0.4 and 0.6 reflects fluvial processes, whereas debris-flow networks dominated by point-source events typically yield θ < 0.2.

Using CTX (5 m/pix) digital elevation models, we analyzed interior wall catchments in Candor (6.5°S, 72°W) and Coprates (14°S, 62°W) chasmata. We measured θ only in segments that do not span major knickpoints, using chi-z linearization and two slope-area regressions with different binning schemes with TopoToolbox and Topographic Analysis Kit. We find that in Candor, out of n=25 streams, 76% show a transition from colluvial-like to fluvial-like scaling at 1.5 to 50 km² (median 15 km²). In Coprates, ~49% of 63 streams transition at 1.8 to 60 km² (median 9.5 km²). The lower percentages in Coprates likely occur due to smaller catchments, with 84% of non-transitioning streams having maximum drainage areas within the observed transition range. The observed transition areas broadly overlap terrestrial values but are slightly larger, consistent with comparatively weak fluvial processes.

High concavity alone does not prove the presence of fluvial processes or disprove the dominance of colluvial processes. It can also reflect the transition from erosional to depositional zones. To test this, we use the Shared Stream-Power Model in Landlab, coupled to Transport Length Hillslope Diffusion, to simulate the transient evolution of a VM drainage network. The model domain comprises a plateau, an escarpment, and a depositional fan, with no uplift. The experiments spanning intrinsic concavity of 0.25 to 0.7, with and without hillslope coupling, will be compared against the observed stream profiles.

This comparison will help determine whether the observed downstream increase in concavity requires distributed runoff or can be produced by debris-flow dominated processes, and thus whether precipitation-fed runoff reached the VM interior on early Mars.

title: From Arsenic and Multi-Element Groundwater Signatures to Critical-Metal Recovery Potential in Swedish Mineralized Systems
session_title: Arsenic and Associated Geogenic Contaminants in Groundwater: Hydrogeochemical Processes, Co-mobilization, and Predictive Risk and Resource Management (Part I)
authors: Olsson, Richard T [1], Bhattacharya, Prosun [2], Sharma, Sanjeev [3]
affiliations: (1) Department of Fibre and Polymer Technology, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Stockholm, Sweden
(2) Department of Sustainable Development, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Stockholm, Sweden
(3) ExcelDots AB, Stockholm, Stockholm, Sweden
abstract:
From Arsenic and Multi-Element Groundwater Signatures to Critical-Metal Recovery Potential in Swedish Mineralized Systems

Richard T. Olsson¹, Prosun Bhattacharya 2 , and Sanjeev Sharma 3

1 Department of Fibre and Polymer Technology, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, SE-114 28 Stockholm, Sweden.

2 KTH International Groundwater Arsenic Research Group, Department of Sustainable Development, Environmental Science and Engineering, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, SE-11428 Stockholm, Sweden

¹ExcelDots AB, Bromma, Sweden

Groundwater and mine waters circulating through mineralized rocks record fluid–rock interactions that govern groundwater quality, arsenic occurrence, and the mobility of critical metals. Although extensive hydrogeochemical datasets exist, these waters remain underutilized for understanding mineral-system evolution and evaluating their potential as secondary resources of critical raw materials. This study proposes an interdisciplinary framework integrating hydrogeochemistry, digital groundwater monitoring, mineral-system characterization, and advanced materials science to investigate sulfide-dominated mineralized systems.

Geological interpretation, mineralogical characterization, groundwater chemistry, aqueous speciation, and redox conditions are combined to identify the processes controlling the release, transport, attenuation, and co-occurrence of arsenic, Cu, Bi, Sb, Co, Ni, and, where geologically relevant, Ga. Arsenic is considered primarily as a geochemical pathfinder reflecting sulfide mineralization, fluid–rock interaction, and redox evolution rather than as a recovery target. Hydrochemical observations will be integrated with datasets from the Geological Survey of Sweden (SGU) to distinguish regional groundwater backgrounds from mineralization-related waters and identify the geochemical conditions that promote metal mobilization, retention, and secondary enrichment.

Real-time groundwater observations obtained from IoT-enabled monitoring platforms complement conventional hydrochemical investigations by providing continuous measurements of physicochemical parameters, including pH, oxidation–reduction potential, electrical conductivity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, and groundwater level. Drawing upon operational experience from groundwater monitoring systems in India, continuous sensor data will be incorporated to resolve temporal hydrogeochemical variability, strengthen process-based interpretation, and improve predictive understanding of arsenic dynamics and critical-metal transport in both natural and mining-influenced environments.

The resulting hydrogeochemical framework provides the scientific basis for developing selective sorbents, nanostructured functional materials, and electrochemical separation technologies for the concentration and recovery of critical metals from dilute groundwater and mine-water systems. By linking digital groundwater monitoring with hydrogeochemistry and advanced materials science, this work establishes groundwater as both an environmental archive of mineral-system processes and a potential unconventional resource for critical raw materials, supporting sustainable groundwater management, circular resource utilization, and resilient critical-material supply chains.

title: Extremely rapid salt weathering of boulders along the hyper arid shorelines of the Dead Sea
session_title: Quantifying geomorphic processes and rates of landscape evolution
authors: Boroda, Ronen [1], Lensky, Nadav [3], Amit, Rivka [4]
affiliations: (1) Gological survey of israel, Israel
(2) Geoligical survey of israel, Israel
(3) Geological survey of israel, Israel
(4) Geological survey of israel, Israel
abstract: Rock weathering operates pervasively at Earth’s surface and exerts a fundamental control on landscape evolution rates. In hyper-arid environments, where limited moisture availability minimizes chemical and biological weathering, salt weathering represents one of the most effective destructive mechanisms. Although salt dynamics—specifically expansion during repeated cycles of dissolution and recrystallization—are broadly recognized as the primary drivers of this process, the specific environmental conditions under which salt weathering operates and the moisture sources sustaining it in hyper-arid landscapes remain poorly constrained. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an 18-month field experiment, utilizing continuous acoustic emission (AE) measurements to track the diurnal and seasonal timing of salt-driven cracking within six surface boulders on recently abandoned shorelines of the hyper-saline Dead Sea. In parallel, microclimate parameters (temperature (T) and relative humidity (RH)) were monitored continuously. Our results reveal that AE activity persists year-round, exhibiting a pronounced bimodal daily pattern tightly coupled with diurnal RH extremes. This coupling provides direct field-based evidence that salt-driven crack propagation—dependent on cycles of partial or complete crystallization and deliquescence—is not restricted to episodic wetting events but operates continuously on a daily basis. Mechanistically, cracking is driven by a unique dual process: stress-loading associated with salt crystallization during dry afternoon hours (subflorescence) and structural unloading or chemical weakening following salt dissolution during peak-RH early morning hours (deliquescence). Beyond identifying RH as the primary moisture source, our findings demonstrate that continuous salt weathering in hyper-arid terrains is fundamentally regulated by high-frequency diurnal RH oscillations. This bridges the gap between laboratory experiments and field observations, redefining the environmental boundary conditions that dictate rock disintegration in extreme deserts.

title: Gold Medal Lecture Series: Elemental Cycling and Critical Mineral Formation at Convergent Margins: Insights from Petrology
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part I)
authors: Hernandez Uribe, David [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Illinois, Chicago, IL,
abstract:
Convergent margins are an essential setting on Earth. Here, large-scale, long-term elemental recycling occurs. Dehydration associated with subduction-zone metamorphism is key for transporting elements to the mantle, as well as for promoting arc magmatism. Some of the largest and most economically important ore deposits occur as a consequence of this magmatism. For example, porphyry copper deposits (PCDs) occur solely in convergent margins and are responsible for producing most of the world’s copper, along with significant amounts of other metals such as gold.

In this talk, I will discuss how subduction-related processes affect the Earth and influence our economy. I will show how subduction-zone metamorphism controls the timing and magnitude of deep elemental recycling. I will then discuss the intracrustal processes occurring in the overriding plate that not only form PCDs but can shed light on the formation of Earth’s first continents. Together, these studies show how subduction-related processes have shaped Earth’s crustal growth, ore deposit formation, and elemental cycling through time.

title: Gold Medal Lecture Series: The Rocky Road to Equilibrium
session_title: Crustal Petrology: from subduction zones to orogenic systems (Part II)
authors: Spear, Frank S. [1]
affiliations: (1) Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, USA
abstract: The past 50 years or so have seen enormous advances in the application of rigorous thermodynamic modeling to the understanding of metamorphic petrogenesis and in our ability to extract meaningful P–T-t histories from these studies and apply them to a deeper understanding of tectonic processes. These models rely on the assumption that metamorphic rocks recrystallize very near to equilibrium such that the application of equilibrium principles can provide a reliable interpretation of the P–T–t history. A number of observations, however, suggest that not all metamorphic rocks exist in a sequence of near-equilibrium states. Numerical models have been developed that attempt to follow the path a rock might follow as it attempts to regain equilibrium following the nucleation of a new phase. Reactions are assumed to occur only locally (e.g., on a nano scale) and chemical communication between non-adjacent phases takes place via grain boundary diffusion, which is rate-limiting. These relatively simple models reveal textural details and complexities that are impossible to glean from equilibrium studies, which affords an exciting new direction for metamorphic petrology and application to crustal tectonics.

title: Gold Medal Lecture Series: Crustal thickness, heat flow, and the Martian Paradox
session_title: Shake and Bake: Volcanism and Tectonism across the Solar System
authors: Lee, Cin-Ty [1]
affiliations: (1) Rice University, Houston, TX,
abstract: Mars’s fluvial and sedimentary landforms indicate an early hydrologic cycle, yet that water has since disappeared. This is hard to explain because modern Mars is too cold for stable liquid water, and the young Sun was even dimmer. Sustaining liquid water therefore required enhanced greenhouse warming. Hydrogen–carbon dioxide interactions could provide such warming, but the Martian mantle is not reduced enough to supply sufficient hydrogen. I propose that Mars’s hydrologic cycle was controlled by the evolving thermal state of its crust. Surface heat flux, set by crustal radioactivity and mantle heat flow, governed the near-surface geothermal gradient. In the Southern Highlands, thick crust was hot enough to melt the lower crust, produce felsic magmas, and sustain shallow groundwater. High heat flow would have driven hydrothermal circulation, creating a hydrogen pump where ferrous iron-rich basalt is oxidized and hydrogen gas was produced to warm the atmosphere. As hydrogen escaped to space, the amount of available water decreased and the hydrogen pump waned. Mars’s red surface may be the remaining evidence of this process.

title: Gold Medal Lecture Series: From Worried to Activated: Effective Climate Communication in an Online World
session_title: Effective Science Communication in an Age of Information Overload and Misinformation
authors: Hayhoe, Katharine [1]
affiliations: (1) Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA
abstract: In the scientific community, we typically operate on the assumption that facts change minds and, if needed, drive action. Yet on polarized, ideologically-charged issues, research has shown that greater scientific literacy does not necessarily produce greater agreement with the evidence. And when awareness of the risks rises without a matching sense of what we can do about them, people's sense of efficacy can fall, paradoxically leaving them less motivated to act, not more. Online, the challenge is amplified as people increasingly cluster into ideologically homogeneous spaces whose algorithms feed them more of what they already believe. Those same algorithms tend to prioritize conflict and fear – because they increase engagement – over constructive, efficacy-building messages. This in turn drives people to doom-scroll, or even attack allies, rather than build supportive communities. Does this mean scientists should give up on online communication? I don’t believe so; instead, it means we need to be very clear about what we are doing, who we are doing it for, and how. For example, many science communication efforts initially focus on those who outright deny the science — on origins, vaccines, climate, and more. However, data shows they are a vocal but small minority. On climate, the majority of people in every country, including the U.S., are already worried. What they lack most is efficacy: knowing what to do, and trusting that it will work. That gap, between the worried majority and the far smaller number already activated, is exactly where communication can do the most good. A perspective based on public opinion data and behavioral science can effectively reframe both our purpose and our audience: not to change minds, but to move the curious and the worried from concern to action. I argue, with real-world examples from my own work, that we do this most effectively by starting not with facts or fear but with the values people already hold, offering agency and concrete solutions rather than alarm, and meeting people where they are instead of arguing across divides.

title: Santa Teresa, New Mexico Brackish Groundwater Exploration Project
session_title: Using Geophysics to explore and evaluate mineral, energy and water resources
authors: Esparza, Oscar [1], Hanson, Austin [2]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission, Las Cruces, NM, USA
(2) INTERA, Alburquerque, NM, USA
abstract: Prolonged drought conditions resulting from above-average temperatures and below-average snowmelt runoff are a common occurrence throughout the Southwest United States. In the Lower Rio Grande of New Mexico, a growing population and industrial development have added worry to the already stressed water supply. To provide relief to the area near the community of Santa Teresa, NM, the New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission, in collaboration with multiple government agencies and private contractors, is conducting an exploratory project along the southwestern edge of the Mesilla Basin to augment the water supply by potentially developing brackish groundwater. The Kilbourne-Noria subbasin has been identified as an area of interest (AOI) for further investigation of the availability of brackish groundwater resources. In November 2024, an airborne electromagnetic (AEM) survey was conducted within the AOI to help characterize the subsurface. Analysis of this survey has identified drilling locations to further the understanding of the basin’s structure, delineate changes in lithology, and determine the extent and distribution of low-resistivity signatures that may be associated with brackish groundwater.

authors: Wu, Jonny [1], Wang, Jordan [2], Clennett, Edward [3], McCraine, Will [4], Fuston, Spencer Lamar [5], Wakabayashi, John [6]

abstract:
We raise our glass in honor of John Wakabayshi, whose research insights and welcoming enthusiasm inspires a new generation of geoscientists to investigate the Sierra Nevada, Great Valley, and Franciscan ‘triad’ along California. Here we show a model of California subduction history since the mid-Jurassic using dual, independent constraints of mantle slabs and regional ocean plate stratigraphy. Our slab interpretation is augmented by published and unpublished 3D slab mapping, plate reconstructions, and geodynamic models. We synthesize published and unpublished ocean plate stratigraphy from Baja California, the Franciscan, and Washington-BC.

Analysis of mantle slabs shows three distinct California subduction stages:

Stage 1: In the uppermost mantle under California and surrounding regions, we map and reconstruct the California slab window from recently published P- and S- full-waveform tomography SATONA (Hua et al., 2025). The slab window and associated Cascadia slabs to the north bracket the most recent 25-30 Ma of subduction.

Stage 2: Northeast (i.e. downdip) of the slab window, we map a swath of east-dipping, discontinuous slabs that extend to maximum ~1000 km depths. Based on slab unfolding, we link these slabs to continuous, east-dipping Cascadia-Farallon subduction under California since 85±15 Ma;

Stage 3: Below ~1000 km, the deeper mantle shows a distinct structure that is characterized by multiple, slab-like anomalies. Prior to Stage 2, we infer co-eval subduction of multiple ocean plates along California and regions offshore (i.e. intra-oceanic).

Our ocean plate stratigraphy synthesis indicates subduction of progressively younger oceanic crust between 100 to 30 Ma that matches Farallon plate models. In contrast, subducting ocean plate ages between 180 to 100 Ma do not fit Farallon models. Therefore, we infer that Farallon subduction under California was only established after 100 Ma; other now-vanished plates must have subducted under California before 100 Ma.

Among our diverse views, we consider a model that involves multiple subduction zones (i.e. mantle Stage 3) along California from the mid-Jurassic to mid-Cretaceous. In this scenario, a double subduction zone is formed by east-dipping subduction of a ‘Bridge River ocean’ under California and concurrent, east-dipping subduction of Farallon under the Bridge River along an intra-oceanic subduction zone. By ~100 Ma, the Bridge River ocean was fully consumed and Farallon subduction began along California. We discuss alternative views and key challenges for reconstructing California subduction history.

title: Tracing Land Use and Landscape Change across the Ancient Maya Lowlands Through Stable Carbon Isostope Profiles
session_title: Biogeochemical analysis of organic matter preserved in geoarchaeological and paleontological materials
authors: Smith, Byron [1], Beach, Timothy [2], Luzzadder-Beach, Sheryl [3]
affiliations: (1) Anthropology, Cal Poly Humboldt, Arcata, CA, USA
(2) Geography and the Environment, UT Austin, Austin, TX, USA
(3) Geography and the Environment, UT Astin, Austin, TX, USA
abstract: Reconstructing evidence of past human activity preserved in soils relies on multiple proxies that record geomorphic processes, vegetation dynamics, and anthropogenic disturbance through time. However, poor preservation and post-depositional alteration can degrade or obscure many paleoecological indicators. Stable carbon isotopes have become a valuable complementary approach by tracing the sources and pathways of soil organic carbon. This is especially useful for investigating the development and intensity of ancient agroecosystems. This presentation synthesizes investigations from Guatemala’s northern Petén and northwest Belize’s Three Rivers Region to examine ancient Maya land-use change across variable settings. First, we demonstrate the utility of isotope geochemistry in radiocarbon dated profiles in identifying the establishment, intensification, abandonment, and forest recovery of wetland agricultural systems. We then integrated these isotope records to model the relationships between C3 and C4 dominated vegetation, geomorphic processes, and topographic positions. Together, these applications demonstrate the value of stable carbon isotopes for strengthening paleoenvironmental reconstructions where traditional proxies are limited.

title: Indigenous and Western Cultural Conflicts regarding Environmental Perspectives
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part II)
authors: Maybee, J. RisingBuffalo [1]
affiliations: (1) National Park Service - Grand Canyon National Park, Grand Canyon, AZ,
abstract:
There is a rich history within post-contact dynamics which has involved forced relocation of Native Tribes from sacred homelands that are now modern park sites. Part of the removal of Indigenous people who have been and still are connected to the land for thousands of years, includes the replacement of Traditional Knowledge with Western practices regarding environmental preservation. Although the nuances of these cultural conflicts in modern day America seem to be simplistic at times, they have created broader outcomes that can separate rather than unite our cultures. These differing cultural practices have created environmental problems which might have been prevented if Traditional Cultural practices were included in environmental protection plans.

By taking healthy members of the ecosystem (Tribes), of which centuries of practices have been fine-tuned, it has created a disruption of the environment. Together, both Indigenous and Western cultures can work together to find a solution of modern-day environmental concerns while addressing and honoring the past.

Today, talking about the dynamics of modern Western vs. Indigenous Cultural conflicts creates a greater understanding of how we as human beings can work together to find healthy solutions to protect the land which we are all connected to. Exploring case studies of environmental conflicts along with understanding how our cultural worldviews may differ, along with discussing similarities is one step towards collaborative, environmental resolutions which can benefit the earth while honoring the past and protecting the future.

title: Integrating Geodiversity Indices and Social Values in Jamaica
session_title: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives (Part I)
authors: Dolphy, Jorjan Elizabeth [1], James-Williamson, Sherene Andrea [2]
affiliations: (1) University of the West Indies, Kingston,
(2) The University of the West Indies, Department of Geography and Geology, Kingston, Jamaica,
abstract: In the Jamaican and wider Caribbean context, geodiversity and geoheritage remain largely absent from academic discourse and policy frameworks, even as extractive pressures intensify across landscapes. This absence narrows conservation framings to ecosystems alone, overlooking the foundational role of geodiversity as a resource and heritage worth safeguarding. The exclusion of geodiversity from regulatory regimes exposes sites of geological and cultural significance to threats from urbanisation, quarrying, and climate change. This project investigates eastern and parts of northern Jamaica through an integrated quantitative–qualitative approach that foregrounds both material extraction and cultural valuation. A GIS-derived geodiversity index, spatialise geology, geomorphology, palaeontology, pedology, and mineral occurrences, highlighting zones of extraction alongside heritage potential. Complementing this, a community geosystems approach captured social meanings and values through questionnaires and focus groups. Together, these methodologies inform strategies for balancing extraction with geoconservation, and support conceptualisation and nomination of Jamaican geoheritage. By tracing pre-existing landscape interactions and communal attachments to stone, soil, and mineral resources, the study seeks to identify pathways for community-driven stewardship. Ultimately, the project aims to reposition geodiversity as central to Caribbean debates on heritage, extraction, and resilience.

title: Groundwater Recharge Regimes are in Flux
session_title: Henry Darcy Distinguished Lecture Series
authors: Loheide, Steven [1]
affiliations: (1) Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI, USA
abstract: Groundwater provides drinking water for people, supports agriculture, and sustains healthy ecosystems, but has been depleted in some regions due to overuse. Groundwater is replenished through the process of groundwater recharge. After precipitation infiltrates into the soil, a portion is returned to the atmosphere through evapotranspiration, but some may percolate downward until it reaches the water table and recharges the aquifer. The process of groundwater recharge varies substantially in space and through time due to soil type, weather conditions, and vegetation. Case studies will be used to illustrate how groundwater recharge regimes are altered by changes in climate and shifts in land use. Groundwater level responses to recharge events were used to quantify groundwater recharge rate differences at locations with different land cover. Numerical modeling was used to diagnose the causes of changing recharge rates and predict the consequences of these changes across a range of environmental settings. A process based understanding of the factors that drive changes in groundwater regimes is critical to sustainable management of groundwater resources under environmental change and avoiding or minimizing unintended consequences of human activities.

title: Clay-Rich Parting Surfaces, Trace-Fossil Preservation, and Evidence for Moist Interdune Deposition in the Permian Coconino Sandstone
session_title: Paleontology, Paleoecology/Taphonomy
authors: Bartlett, Rickey [1]
affiliations: (1) Geology, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, Michigan, USA
abstract:
The Lower Permian Coconino Sandstone of northern Arizona is widely interpreted as an extensive eolian erg dominated by migrating dunes. Interdune deposits have been recognized within the formation, but their identification has thus far been based primarily on the occurrence of horizontal bedding. Here, we present a more robust dataset integrating field, petrographic, geochemical, and ichnologic evidence for interdune deposition and episodic substrate moisture. These data indicate that clay was locally deposited within the Coconino erg and may have influenced substrate properties and trace-fossil preservation.

Thin silvery-gray fissile parting surfaces occur at several Coconino localities and contrast markedly with the surrounding quartz arenite. Petrographic examination reveals laterally continuous, fine-grained stringers associated with these parting surfaces and locally occurring within vertebrate and invertebrate trace-fossil infills. SEM–EDS elemental mapping demonstrates that the stringers are enriched in Al and K relative to the surrounding quartz-rich sandstone, with minor Mg and Fe also present. Their bedding-parallel geometry, lateral continuity, elemental composition, and occurrence within trace-fossil infills support an allogenic origin for the clay rather than formation through postdepositional alteration. This interpretation is strengthened by the occurrence of spatially discrete aluminous alteration complexes elsewhere in the same specimens. These features exhibit textures and elemental distributions distinct from the laterally continuous clay stringers and are interpreted as localized authigenic alteration.

Clay-rich parting surfaces are repeatedly associated with vertebrate tracks, arthropod traces, and intensely bioturbated bedding surfaces. This association suggests that the presence of clay may have increased substrate cohesion and contributed to the preservation of delicate traces within otherwise quartz-rich eolian sand. Additional evidence comes from quarry exposures where a laterally persistent bounding surface exhibits increasing concentrations of clay toward a topographic low. At this low point, clay-rich horizons are associated with downward-tapering polygonal cracks infilled by fine-grained sediment, consistent with episodes of substrate wetting and desiccation.

Together, these observations demonstrate that clay was present within the Coconino depositional system and was locally concentrated along surfaces that experienced episodic moisture. The association of clay-rich sediment, desiccation structures, depositional topography, and trace fossils supports interpretation of the quarry exposure as a periodically moist interdune and suggests that such environments may have provided localized substrates favorable for biological activity and trace-fossil preservation within the Coconino erg.

title: Site Specific Influences on Use of Saturated Rock Backfill Technology to Treat Mine-Influenced Water
session_title: New approaches and emerging technologies for the prevention, control, and remediation of acidic rock drainage and legacy mine waste
authors: Spietz, Rachel [1], Kirk, Lisa B. [2]
affiliations: (1) RESPEC, 524 Professional Drive, Bozeman, Montana, USA
(2) RESPEC, 524 Professional Drive, Bozeman, Montana, USA
abstract: Mined waste rock, when exposed to oxygen and water, poses a risk of acid generation with leaching of metals and other solutes. Treatment of mine-impacted water (MIW) ranges from passive to active technology, with varying levels of energy input, oversight, and cost requirements depending on the treatment needs and the system design. Saturated backfilled pit reactors offer a middle ground between energy-intensive active treatment systems and entirely passive systems, which are more prone to upset or failure. Successful design of saturated backfilled pit reactors integrates mine planning, development rock placement, hydrogeology, geochemistry, and microbial ecology to utilize the landscape and native microbial populations to carry out biogeochemical processes that improve the quality of MIW. While saturated backfilled pit reactors have been approved for commercial scale water treatment at British Columbia coal mines , the technology requires site-specific investigations to inform design and implementation. In this talk we will compare two saturated backfilled pit reactor locations, one in BC and another in Montana, to highlight how rock type, climate, hydrogeology, geochemistry, and microbial ecology are important considerations in the transfer and implementation of saturated backfilled pit reactor technology.

title: Investigating The Role Of Mineral Crystal Structure in Soil Organic Carbon Stabillity
session_title: Recent Advances in Soil and Paleosol Science (Posters)
authors: crubaugh, bryson wayne [1]
affiliations: (1) Sustainable Earth System Sciences, University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas, USA
abstract:
Soil Organic Matter (SOM) is the primary terrestrial reservoir for Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), holding more carbon than the atmosphere and all global land based vegetation combined. SOM is the cornerstone of the terrestrial carbon cycle contributing to the exchange of nutrients within soils and CO 2 between soils and the open atmosphere. Roughly sixty five percent of all SOM is Mineral Associated Organic Matter (MAOM) and unlike the rest of the particulate matter that makes up SOM, MAOM is adsorptive to mineral surfaces which allows for persistence of organic matter on a much larger and longer scale. The stability of MAOM is not an inherent property of the organic molecules themselves but rather a result of physicochemiocal interactions at the mineral surface and through this adsorption or mineral entrapment within mineral aggregates, organic matter is shielded from microbial access and enzymatic breakdown which prevents the release of organic carbon out of the rhizosphere and into the atmosphere.

My goal was to investigate two different minerals, Kaolinite and Geothite, in order to determine the ability of these different minerals in trapping organic carbon individually and within a soil simulation based on their difference of being a phyllosilicate and iron oxyhydroxide. Using vanillic acid as a molecular proxy for plant derived lignin we processed it alongside the two respective minerals before balancing the PH to 6.0 and shaking them for forty eight hours to ensure thorough mixing. After a brief centrifuging process obtained 1ml of the fluid and diluted it with 14ml DI water. This was repeated with two different concentrations of 200 mgC/L and 1500 mgC/L across three cultures per mineral in order to obtain a solid standard for TOC retained by the minerals. Following this experiment we created artificial soils combining the two minerals at different percentages in order to simulate native soil concentrations and gain a better understanding of mineral to mineral interaction contributing to organic carbon distribution in soils.

I am currently garnering the last of my data and interpreting it to develop my final conclusions about the research and how the crystal structure along with mineral abundance impact SOC stability in soils with Kaolinite and Geothite.

title: What Can We Learn from Local and Indigenous Communities for the Sustainable Management of Geoheritage: Good Practices on UNESCO Global Geoparks
session_title: Webinar 1: Geoheritage Values in a World of Resource Extraction: Sharing Domestic, International and Indigenous Perspectives
authors: Rosado González, Emmaline Montserrat [1], Calder, John Hugh [2]
affiliations: (1) Geography Institute UNAM & Global Geoparks Network, Mexico city,
(2) Saint Mary's University, Boutiliers Point, NS, ; Cliffs of Fundy UNESCO Global Geopark, Nova Scotia, Canada
abstract:
UNESCO Global Geoparks (UGGps) are territories where geological heritage is understood in close connection with natural, cultural, and social values, and where sustainable development is expected to be achieved through a bottom-up and community-based approach. In this context, local and indigenous communities are not only beneficiaries of geopark initiatives, but also important holders of knowledge, practices, and values associated with the territory. Their long-term relationships with landscapes and natural resources can provide valuable insights for understanding, interpreting, conserving, and managing geoheritage. Nevertheless, the incorporation of local and indigenous knowledge into geoheritage management remains uneven and, in many cases, is still limited to cultural interpretation or community participation in specific activities.

This contribution explores how local and indigenous knowledge can strengthen the sustainable management of geoheritage in UGGps, drawing on experiences from UNESCO Global Geoparks, particularly in Latin America and the Caribbean, and in Canada. Building on previous research on community participation, bottom-up approaches, sustainable development, and local communities in UGGps, the study identifies good practices in which local knowledge has been incorporated into decision-making, geoconservation, geoeducation, interpretation, tourism, and territorial development. Particular attention is given to practices that recognize communities as active knowledge holders and co-creators rather than simply as participants or beneficiaries.

The analysis highlights several dimensions of good practice: the recognition of local perceptions and values of geoheritage; the integration of oral traditions, place names, narratives, and traditional practices into geoheritage interpretation; the participation of communities in the identification and assessment of geosites; the transmission of intergenerational knowledge; and the development of sustainable economic activities based on local resources and cultural identity. These experiences demonstrate that combining scientific knowledge with local and indigenous perspectives can lead to more meaningful and socially grounded approaches to geoconservation.

The results suggest that the sustainable management of geoheritage is not only a matter of protecting geological features, but also of understanding the relationships and cosmovision that communities have developed with their landscapes over generations. Learning from these relationships can help territories to develop more inclusive, culturally appropriate, and resilient management strategies, while strengthening the role of communities as custodians and active partners in the conservation and sustainable use of geoheritage.
