title: The mutual calibration of plate reconstruction and realistic geodynamic models
session_title: Bottoms Up: Perspectives from “bottom-up” and “top-down” approaches to tectonic reconstructions
authors: Liu, Lijun [1], Cao, Zebin [2], Dong, Hao [3]
affiliations: (1) University of IllinoisGeology, Urbana, IL,
(2) University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, IL,
abstract: Plate reconstruction describes past plate motion at Earth surface while geodynamic models describe the underlying deep Earth processes over time. Due to the complex nature of Earth dynamic evolution, traditional models with simplified boundary conditions cannot adequately capture the realistic evolutionary behaviors of Earth. Therefore, models assimilating realistic plate kinematics at the surface are necessary to better reproduce geological records and geophysically imaged present mantle structures. Research indicates that this approach is most suitable for studying Earth's evolutionary history since the Cenozoic. Further back in time, however, because plate reconstructions mainly infer from surface observations, their capability to characterize vanished plates—particularly subduction systems predating the Cenozoic—remains limited, which may lead to erroneous simulation results and tectonic interpretations. For instance, reconstructions of subduction during the Mesozoic and earlier all carry certain degrees of uncertainty. Recent efforts to overcome these problems range from inferring early subduction history by unwrapping subducted slabs from deep mantle imaging to rectifying reconstruction models through more quantitative geodynamic modeling using data assimilation. I will show some examples of the latter approach. This strategy can simultaneously advance pre-Cenozoic plate reconstructions and our understanding of the associated deep processes and tectonic history, and it should become a trend in future geodynamic research.

abstract: How shortening is partitioned during late-stage arc-continent collision remains poorly understood where subduction polarity reverses and brittle deformation overprints exhumed basement. We investigate this problem along the coast north of Hualien, Taiwan, at the active junction of the Philippine Sea and Eurasian plates. We integrate approximately 20 km of airgun reflection and refraction profiles with earthquake relocations to evaluate shallow velocity and reflector geometry and their relationship to deformation in the seismogenic crust. The controlled-source data reveal folded, basement-involved structures with opposing vergence. P-wave velocities at a depth of about 1 km locally exceed 6.5 km/s, consistent with uplift of dense basement to shallow crustal levels. The observed structures reflect shortening in Taiwan's foreland-retrowedge system and we are currently testing the possible influence of the oppositely dipping Ryukyu subduction system, implying that collision-related shortening might be distributed across a broad zone rather than confined to a single plate-boundary structure. Preliminary earthquake relocations delineate a subvertical seismicity zone extending to a depth of at least 6 km. The spatial correspondence between this seismicity and the imaged basement structures suggests that steep brittle fault zones cut or partition exhumed basement and may overprint older ductile fabrics. Together, the observations support a crustal architecture in which basement exhumation, oppositely vergent contraction, and later brittle reactivation are linked, although their detailed spatial relationships remain unresolved. Integrating airgun profiling with relocated seismicity links near-surface structure to active crustal deformation and provides a transferable strategy for imaging other arc-continent collision zones.

title: Multivariate Assessment of the Riparian Ecosystem Response to Water Variability Along the Middle Rio Grande, New Mexico
session_title: Advance Ground Surface Modeling for Hydrological and Environmental Applications (Posters)
authors: Quirino Olvera, Leonardo [1], Cadol, Daniel [2]
affiliations: (1) New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Earth and Environmental Science, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
(2) New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Earth and Envrionmental Science, Socorro, New Mexico, USA
abstract:
This study investigates the hydrologic controls on riparian vegetation health along the San Acacia Reach of the Middle Rio Grande, spanning headwaters and Elephant Butte sub basins. Riparian vegetation health is indexed using NDVI derived from Landsat and examined against precipitation, river flow, and soil moisture across multiple spatial and temporal scales, drawing on long-term climate, along with daily snow water equivalent, temperature, solar radiation, and streamflow data. This regional-scale analysis is designed to capture how hydroclimate variability propagates through the basin and reaches riparian vegetation, and to identify where surface water and precipitation signals diverge across the study area.

These hydrologic, climate and vegetation datasets are used to train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network capable of predicting NDVI from river flow and climate historical data. By learning the temporal dependencies between hydrologic drivers and vegetation response, the model aims to provide a forward-looking tool for anticipating riparian vegetation conditions under forecasted streamflow and climate scenarios, extending the analysis beyond retrospective correlation toward predictive capacity.

Together, these approaches are intended to clarify which water sources most directly sustain riparian productivity along this reach and to support conjunctive water management and instream flow policy under frameworks such as New Mexico's Strategic Water Reserve.

title: Reactive Transport of the Rare Earth Element Neodymium (Nd) Using Surface Complexation Models: Assessing the Fate and Transport of an Emerging 21st Century Environmental Contaminant
session_title: From Deep Earth to Digital Twins: Artificial Intelligence in Earth System Science and Predictive Subsurface Systems
authors: Johannesson, Karen H. [1], Dii Horne, Jaxon [2], Costa, Larissa [3], White, Christopher D. [4]
affiliations: (1) Department of Environmental Sciences and Sustainability, University of Massachusetts, Boston, MA, USA

abstract: We investigate the transport of the rare earth element neodymium (Nd) in a hypothetical, shallow groundwater system via a series of numerical experiments that leverage surface complexation models (SCM) simulating Nd 3+ ion sorption onto goethite (alpha-FeOOH) and hydrous ferric oxide (HFO). Neodymium is a key critical metal necessary for the manufacture of permanent magnets, and thus can make up a substantial proportion of electronic waste. One-dimensional reactive transport models are constructed that simulate advective-dispersive flow, mineral dissolution/precipitation, aqueous complexation, and sorption/desorption of Nd along a modeled flow path. Models assume an imbibition phase where Nd-polluted water (1 umol kg -1 ) infiltrates the aquifer, which initially contains groundwater that is nearly devoid of Nd. Subsequently, the aquifer is flushed with the nearly Nd-free water to evaluate the time required to remediate the aquifer. Simulations produce sharp sorption fronts with long tails typical of strongly sorbed solutes . Models run in the presence or absence of dissolved inorganic carbon reveal that Nd transport is strongly affected by aqueous complexation with carbonate anions [i.e., NdCO 3 + + Nd(CO 3 ) 2 - ], which may inhibit sorption of the aquo ion, Nd 3+ . However, SCMs that also include NdCO 3 + sorption, predict enhanced retardation along the flow path. This knowledge gap regarding the fate and transport of Nd in aquifer systems, namely whether only the aquo ion sorbs or if aqueous complexes also sorb, requires additional investigations.

title: Bayesian Age Modelling Reveal a Basin-Scale Signal of Permo–Triassic Vertebrate turnover in South Africa’s Karoo Basin

abstract: The Permo–Triassic mass extinction (PTME; ca. 251.9 Ma) was the most severe biodiversity crisis in Earth history and fundamentally restructured terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Yet the timing of terrestrial ecosystem collapse and recovery remains uncertain. This is because continental successions rarely preserve abundant dateable horizons, and often represent stratigraphically complex fluvial-lacustrine depositional settings. The Karoo Basin of South Africa preserves one of the most complete terrestrial PTME records, but the placement of the Permo–Triassic boundary (PTB) and the temporal equivalence of vertebrate-bearing lithostratigraphy in the upper Balfour and lower Katberg formations remain debated. Here we integrate six new high-precision U–Pb geochronology age populations with Bayesian age–depth modelling from two geographically separated PTB localities (Nieu Bethesda and Bethulie), spanning the traditional vertebrate turnover interval. Using modifiedBchron, we incorporate all currently available radiometric constraints, including ages previously interpreted to support alternative PTB placements. Independent models from both field areas converge on a PTB position within the Palingkloof Member near the traditional base of the Lystrosaurus declivis Assemblage Zone. The resulting chronology at these two age model localities also places the acme of vertebrate turnover in the upper Palingkloof Member, and indicates that deposition of the overlying Katberg Formation commenced during the Early Triassic. These results demonstrate that Bayesian age–depth modelling provides a powerful framework for evaluating competing chronostratigraphic hypotheses in complex continental fluvial successions, and supports the robustness of the established PTB framework in the Karoo Basin.

title: Ore and Gangue Textures of the Lynnda Vein, Merlin Epithermal System, Nye County, Nevada: Implications for High-Grade Gold Distribution

authors: CARDOZO, Maria Teresa [1], TERRY, Lauren [2], MONECKE, Thomas [3], KOCHER, Simon [4], Burisch, Mathias [5]
affiliations: (1) Center to Advance the Science of Exploration to Reclamation in Mining, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA; Geology and Geological Engineering Department, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado, USA

abstract:
The Merlin deposit, located east of Beatty in Nye County, Nevada, is a recently discovered worldclass epithermal gold deposit owned by AngloGold Ashanti. This study investigates the microtextural relationships between ore and gangue minerals to better understand the controls on bonanza-grade gold mineralization. Optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy were used to characterize high-grade ore samples.

Quartz is the dominant gangue mineral and is characterized primarily by mosaic texture formed through the maturation of a noncrystalline silica precursor. Native gold occurs in two distinct microtextural settings. In the first, gold is present along grain boundaries of recrystallized quartz, where it exhibits rounded grain morphologies and heterogeneous compositions. In the second, gold occurs adjacent to or intergrown with iron and manganese oxides, exhibiting irregular grain boundaries and complex mineral intergrowths. The mineralogical and microtextural relationships suggest that both hypogene and supergene gold occur at Merlin.

The observed recrystallization textures of quartz are similar to those observed in other epithermal deposits. The noncrystalline silica precursor is interpreted to have formed because of rapid silica supersaturation in the hydrothermal fluids, presumably caused by vapor formation. Gold microtextures have been modified during the maturation of the silica matrix. The supergene overprint resulted in further modification of vein textures and likely caused liberation of gold from sulfide phases. The results improve the understanding of the paragenesis of the Merlin deposit and provide important geometallurgical information.

title: Evaluating the Hydrothermal Footprint of Geothermal Energy Development in Complex Rift Settings using MODFLOW 6 GWE
session_title: Hydrogeology of Geothermal Resources: From Shallow Systems to Deep Reservoirs
authors: Rush, Michael J. [1], Birdsell, Daniel [2], Foster, Lauren M [3], Reichenbacher, Renee [4], Rehmus, Parker [5]
affiliations: (1) Neptune and Company, Inc., Lakewood, Colorado, USA
(2) Neptune and Company, Inc, Lakewood, Colorado, USA
(3) Neptune and Company, Inc, Lakewooc, Colorado, USA; Reg Review, Louisville, Colorado, USA
(4) Neptune and Company, Inc, Lakewood, Colorado, USA
(5) Neptune and Company, Inc, Lakewood, Colorado, USA
abstract: As global demand for renewable energy grows, numerical modeling is a key tool for assessing the feasibility of geothermal development. However, the potential for deep geothermal pumping to impact shallow hydrothermal resources and protected surface waters remains under-studied. We present a numerical model of a Rocky Mountain rift valley characterized by a low-enthalpy hydrothermal system. Using the MODFLOW 6 Groundwater Energy (GWE) simulator, we apply the fully coupled groundwater flow and heat transport model to a complex network of steeply dipping normal faults and shear zones. These structures act as pathways for upwelling geothermal fluids, establishing a hydraulic connection between deep production zones and the shallow subsurface. The model was calibrated against hydraulic heads, streamflow observations, well and spring temperatures, and thermal gradients. Predictive simulations of deep geothermal pumping reveal significant hydrologic and thermal impacts on the shallow system. Results show groundwater level fluctuations ranging from -1.2 m to +1.6 m, temperature shifts between -5.6°C and +8.3°C, and spring flow reductions of up to 9.6%. Simulations show tributary groundwater depletion in response to extraction, highlighting the implications for water rights administration. These findings demonstrate that in structurally controlled rift systems, the very features that make geothermal energy viable also facilitate impacts that may conflict with surface water rights. This work highlights the necessity of coupled flow and transport modeling in the permitting and long-term management of energy projects to mitigate conflicts between energy production and existing water users.

title: High-Resolution Elemental Mapping in Critical Mineral Systems: From Core to Thin Section
session_title: Research to Accelerate Recovery of Critical Minerals from Primary and Unconventional Resources
authors: DeVerse, Bryan [1], Ruchte, Ben [2], Williams, Bill [3]
affiliations: (1) IXRF, Inc., Austin, TX, USA
(2) IXRF, Inc., Austin, TX, USA
(3) IXRF, Inc., Austin, TX, USA
abstract:
Critical mineral research increasingly depends on spatially resolved geochemical data to characterize mineral associations, elemental zoning, trace-metal distribution, and recovery potential across heterogeneous geological and metallurgical materials. Conventional bulk geochemical methods provide essential compositional information but often obscure the spatial relationships among mineral phases, alteration features, and trace-element hosts. This presentation evaluates high-resolution micro-scale X-ray fluorescence (microXRF) mapping as a non-destructive workflow for linking elemental distributions to critical mineral characterization from drill core and thin section analysis through process-relevant materials.

MicroXRF spectral imaging generates a full X-ray spectrum at each mapped pixel, allowing elemental maps to be interpreted through quantitative analysis, multivariate spectral methods, and phase-distribution assessment. Case examples include rare earth element-bearing materials, lithium-associated mineral systems, and copper smelter flue dust evaluated for trace-metal recovery and leaching feasibility. These examples demonstrate how spatially resolved elemental data can reveal mineralogical and geochemical heterogeneity that may not be apparent from bulk assays alone.

In the copper flue dust application, microXRF provided broad elemental coverage from Na through U and improved sensitivity to minor and trace metal-bearing phases compared with conventional SEM/EDS-based automated mineral analysis. The resulting elemental and phase-distribution information supported improved assessment of metal deportment, potential recovery pathways, and leaching feasibility.

This work highlights the value of integrating microXRF mapping with complementary techniques such as petrography, SEM-EDS, XRD, and bulk geochemistry. The approach supports critical mineral research by improving interpretation of ore-forming systems, mineral associations, and trace-element behavior while preserving samples for downstream analysis. These workflows are relevant to economic geology, geochemistry, mineralogy, and applied critical mineral studies where both compositional and spatial context are required for interpretation.

title: GeoAI Reveals Dramatic Wetland Loss and Landscape Transformation in the Sangamon River Watershed, Illinois
session_title: Geological mapping: Geologic maps underpin many geological interpretations and add significant value. What might the future hold and who will be the mappers?
authors: Amer, Reda [1], Sadaf, Afsheen [2]
affiliations: (1) UMLS Geospatial Collaborative, University of Missouri-St Louis, Saint Louis, MO, USA
(2) UMSL Geospatial Collaborative, University of Missouri-St Louis, St Louis, MO, USA
abstract: Wetlands are integral to watershed hydrology, biodiversity, flood attenuation, and climate resilience, yet their spatial heterogeneity and seasonal variability complicate long-term mapping. We developed an integrated GeoAI framework to quantify wetland and land-cover change across the 13,915-km² Sangamon River Watershed, Illinois, using benchmark years 2000, 2008, 2017, and 2025. Multi-season Landsat 5 TM, Sentinel-2 surface reflectance, Sentinel-1 SAR, spectral indices, terrain, hydrologic-proximity, and texture variables were processed in Google Earth Engine, Google Colab, and ArcGIS Pro. Random Forest, Gradient Tree Boosting, and Support Vector Machine classifiers were evaluated using pixel- and object-based approaches and compared with DNN, U-Net, Attention U-Net, and transformer-based SegFormer models. NLCD-derived stratified samples supported classification of wetlands, forest, agriculture/grassland/barren land, urban/developed land, and water. Results document substantial landscape transformation. Wetland extent declined by 54.85% (860.68 km²) from 2000 to 2025, while forest and open-water areas decreased by 46.51% (694.88 km²) and 36.80% (66.13 km²), respectively. Agriculture/grassland/barren land increased by 820.62 km², and urban/developed land expanded by 799.52 km² (72.92%). Wetland persistence decreased from 87.90% during 2000–2008 to 59.67% during 2017–2025, indicating substantially greater wetland turnover in the later interval. SegFormer achieved the highest classification performance, with overall accuracies of 94% for Landsat and 96% for Sentinel-based models and wetland F1 scores of 0.98. Object-based ML approaches consistently outperformed pixel-based methods, while slope and elevation were among the most influential Random Forest predictors. These findings demonstrate that integrating multi-sensor Earth observations with advanced GeoAI can improve detection of fragmented wetland change and provide a transferable framework for conservation, restoration prioritization, and climate-resilient management of intensively modified agricultural watersheds.

title: What Becomes a Hydrogeologist?
session_title: Reflecting on the past and looking to the future: The ongoing research legacy of Dr. Randy Hunt
authors: Ferre, Ty [1]
affiliations: (1) Hydrology and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
abstract: One of Randy’s gifts is his ability to see the simple in the complex - to identify it, use it to address questions, and communicate it to a broad audience. How can we prepare entry level hydrogeologists to develop this insight? In this talk, I will share my conclusions based on discussions with Randy and others that have led to an effort to define what we need to teach incoming hydrogeologists if we hope to see our field thrive. Hint: it’s not AI.

title: Artemis II to the Moon and Back: The First Step in a New Era of Crewed Scientific Exploration
session_title: GSA Noontime Lecture: Kelsey Young
authors: Young, Kelsey Evans [1]
affiliations: (1) NASA, Kensington, MD,
abstract: The Artemis II crew were the first people to visit the Moon in over 50 years, captivating the global public as they brought everyone along with them on their journey. The lunar data collected by the crew and by their Orion spacecraft was in service of both addressing fundamental questions about lunar and Solar System science as well as to set future crewed planetary missions up for success as the team developed the processes needed to maximize science in Artemis. This presentation explores the Artemis II mission’s lunar journey, with an emphasis on the lunar science objectives developed by the mission’s Lunar Science Team as well as the structure, processes, and operational concepts developed to prepare the crew, Flight Control Team, and Lunar Science Team to address these objectives. Artemis II was but the first step in returning human explorers to planetary exploration; this presentation will examine the science data collected from Artemis II while looking to the future of Earth to Deep Space human scientific exploration.

title: A Journey from Deep Earth Mineral Physics to Applied Nano-Mineralogy
session_title: MSA 2026 Awardees Lectures and Presidential Address
authors: Irifune, Tetsuo [1]
affiliations: (1) Geodynamics Research Center, Ehime University, Matsuyama, Japan, Japan
abstract:
The multi-anvil apparatus developed by the late Prof. Naoto Kawai of Osaka University is known as the Kawai-type multi-anvil apparatus (KMA). In a KMA, a sample is compressed by eight superhard cubic anvils surrounded by six steel anvils. The 6–8 anvil assembly is driven by a large-volume press capable of applying loads of up to several thousand tons. With tungsten carbide second-stage anvils, KMA can generate stable, quasi-hydrostatic pressures of up to ~30 GPa and temperatures as high as 3000℃ in sample volumes ranging from a few mm³ to ~1 cm³.

Using KMA, I developed techniques for quench experiments and in situ X-ray observations under pressure and temperature conditions corresponding to those of the lower mantle. I also developed techniques for measuring sound velocities of high-pressure minerals by combining in situ X-ray observations with ultrasonic interferometry under such extreme conditions. Based on these techniques, I studied phase transitions and associated changes in density and sound velocity in mantle minerals and subducting slab materials. By comparing these mineral physics data with constraints from seismology, geophysics, petrology, and geochemistry, I contributed to our understanding of the mineralogy of the deep mantle.

Building on the KMA techniques developed through mineral physics studies of the deep Earth, I began exploring the synthesis of novel materials, taking advantage of KMA's ability to generate stable ultrahigh pressures in relatively large sample volumes. One of the first such materials was bulk nano-polycrystalline diamond (NPD), which is highly transparent and exhibits ultrahardness exceeding that of single-crystal diamond. Using a large KMA installed in a 6000-ton press, we have succeeded in producing high-purity NPD rods up to ~1 cm in both diameter and length. NPD has found wide application as ultrahigh- pressure anvils and is also being developed for industrial applications.

Another class of novel materials produced using KMA technology is transparent nanoceramics (TNCs) of high-pressure phases, synthesized from glass starting materials at pressures above 10 GPa and moderate temperatures of 1000–1400℃. Their formation is facilitated by rapid nucleation combined with slow grain growth under these conditions. Depending on the birefringence and grain size of the constituent nanocrystals, some TNCs exhibit excellent optical transparency together with hardness exceeding that of the corresponding single crystals, presumably due to the Hall–Petch effect.

title: Geologists in the Critical Zone...in a Critical Time
session_title: 2026 Michel T. Halbouty Distinguished Lecture
authors: Doss, Paul K. [1]
affiliations: (1) University of Southern Indiana, Evansville, IN, USA
abstract: The critical zone is generally understood to define the area from the base of active groundwater to the top of the vegetative canopy. It is the zone where the biotic is intimately connected with the abiotic. Microbes, invertebrates, plants, and animals interact with and depend upon the bedrock, soil, ground and surface waters, soil gases, precipitation, the atmosphere, and climate. It is ecology. And yet, in critical conversations about ecosystems, the abiotic is often conspicuously absent and neglected. Evidence suggests our critical zone is facing an existential crisis. And essentially every living thing is completely dependent upon a functional “healthy” critical zone. The litany of damage, threats, and pressures facing the critical zone is well established and encompasses essentially all elements of every ecosystem: water resource quality and quantity, soil erosion and associated impacts to aquatic systems, cryosphere change, habitat fragmentation, species extinctions and biodiversity loss, oceanic transformations (global currents, temperature, dead zones, acidity), invasive species, increases in extreme weather events, forest loss, atmospheric chemistry, global climate change, and more. This list clearly shows that humans now dominate many if not most critical zone processes, just as we now significantly alter or dominate the global nitrogen, mercury, carbon, and water cycles. Catastrophes bring a remarkable coalescing of human volunteers to help neighbors and communities recover from hazards like hurricanes, floods, earthquakes, war, famine, and wildfires. While many tragic events are increasing due to climate change and population dynamics, they’re largely ephemeral, lasting days, weeks or months. Threats to our singular critical zone manifest on a scale of years, decades and centuries. The public is not equipped to recognize the “slow creep” of change and the danger it poses. Moreover, Capitol Hill is a very real element of the Global Critical Zone. What happens in DC does not stay in DC...it has real and lasting impacts on the integrity of ecosystem function. Geoscientists are best positioned to understand and communicate the operational time frame and threats that face humanity; to help inform policy. Our geoscience community, ALL of us, must coalesce, “Get Up-Stand Up,” and act now! We’re late.

title: Large-Scale Hydrological Modeling: From Subsurface Architecture to Water Dynamics
session_title: GSA James B. Thompson, Jr. Distinguished International Lectureship | Monica Riva
authors: , Monica Riva [1]
affiliations: (1) Politecnico di Milano (POLIMI; Italy), Italy
abstract: Groundwater is a strategic component of the water cycle. It is key to sustain water supply, agriculture, energy production, and freshwater ecosystems. It remains largely invisible, thus contributing to place its characterization and quantitative assessment among the most demanding challenges. These challenges become particularly acute when moving from local investigations to regional and supra-regional scales, where information on subsurface properties is inevitably incomplete, observations are spatially uneven, and computational demands associated with physically-based models can still become prohibitive. At the same time, tackling increasing climate variability, growing water demand, and environmental pressures require reliable tools capable of anticipating responses of groundwater systems and support informed decision-making in the presence of a variety of sources of uncertainty. Recent advances in numerical simulation have significantly improved our ability to represent the complex interactions among groundwater, surface water, and land-surface processes. However, reliable large-scale hydrological predictions require not only increasingly sophisticated numerical models. They also require appropriate strategies to characterize subsurface heterogeneity, quantify uncertainties associated with model structure/formulation and parameters, and assess the way these uncertainties propagate to predictions of quantities of interest. In this context, increasing model complexity can render conventional approaches to parameter estimation, calibration, and uncertainty quantification difficult or even prohibitive. This lecture explores recent advances and remaining challenges in developing physically-based, integrated hydrological models capable of representing groundwater-surface water interactions across large and complex domains. We examine approaches that combine geological observations, probabilistic concepts, physically-based modeling and machine-learning techniques to develop and calibrate three-dimensional hydrogeological models. A key focus is on strategies designed to reconcile physical complexity with computational feasibility. The lecture highlights synergies among sensitivity analysis, surrogate modeling, and sequential parameter estimation, showing how their integration enables computationally demanding hydrological models to be applied in practice while preserving physical consistency and computational efficiency. These concepts are illustrated through the development of one of the first robustly calibrated, large-scale integrated groundwater- surface water models of the Po River District in northern Italy, covering almost 90,000 km².

title: REACHING OUT TO THE PAST TO OUTREACH THE PRESENT: FROM PURE SCIENCE TO INFORMAL SCIENCE EDUCATION IN THE INDIAN SUBCONTINENT
session_title: GSA James B. Thompson, Jr. Distinguished International Lectureship | Nigel Hughes
authors: Hughes, Nigel C. [1]
affiliations: (1) Dept. of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of California, Riverside, CA, USA
abstract: Our planet has bioengineered itself into a condition in which we have the privilege of living briefly upon it. Paleontology offers delightful and insightful opportunities for exploring how this privilege came to be. On the biological side, the extraordinary record of early animal development offered by some species (trilobites in my case) permits glimpses into how ancient animal development was regulated, and how aspects of such development responded to coeval environmental pressures. We can see beyond pattern alone, framing testable questions about underlying processes of developmental control and their evolutionary role. On the geological side, as both witnesses to time and place fossils can help us not only reconstruct ancient world geographies for the time they were living but also apply such understanding to reconstruct subsequent geological history, long after the organisms themselves had perished. Paleontological research requires travel and with that responsibility to the places that generously host investigations. With regard to my ancient development work, for the Czech Republic I am grateful to serve an editorial role in the Bulletins of Geosciences, and with respect to our Himalayan and southeast Asian geological work, friends and I have published and distributed over a thousand copies of the children’s book মনীযার পাথরের বন (Monisha and the Stone Forest) about a village girl’s adventures to understand petrified wood. Our in-production, 15-minute-long geoscience-themed animated movie আমাদের পাহাড়চূড়ায় সমুদ্র (The Ocean on the Top of Our Mountain) is due to be released on YouTube next year. For it to reach its target audience, the children of rural Bengal, we will need the help of Geological Society of America members, please, in watching and promoting it! GSA has generously supported both of these outreach endeavors, for which I am most grateful. I look forward greatly to serving as the James B. Thompson Jr. International Distinguished Lecturer 2026-2027 and visiting eastern India and Bangladesh shortly before the animation goes live.
